Fulfilment of ante-nuptial promise as valid consideration under Hindu law
Reasonable alienation by widow for daughter's marriage as binding on reversioners
Limited estate of Hindu widow under classical Hindu law

card.dispute: Manak Lal, an advocate, challenged the order removing his name from the roll of legal practitioners after being found guilty of professional misconduct for obtaining a fabricated stay order.
issues_decided: Whether the tribunal constituted to inquire into the professional misconduct was improperly constituted due to bias of its chairman?
Whether the failure to examine a key witness (Shri Loya) warranted an adverse inference against the complainant?
Whether the punishment of removal from the rolls was excessive given the appellant's junior status and past record?
holdings: A tribunal member's prior appearance for a party creates a reasonable apprehension of bias, rendering the tribunal's constitution infirm, though such bias can be waived if the party knew of the facts and failed to object.
No adverse inference can be drawn against a complainant for not examining an accomplice witness, especially when the prosecutor acted bona fide in deciding which witnesses to call.
Removal from the rolls is a justified penalty for serious professional misconduct, particularly when the advocate has a prior record of misconduct and the act undermines judicial integrity.
doctrines: Doctrine of apparent bias
Doctrine of waiver of objection to bias
Principle of adverse inference in quasi-judicial proceedings
Standard of professional misconduct and punishment in legal profession

card.dispute: The Official Receiver sought to annul a usufructuary mortgage executed by insolvents in favor of the appellant's predecessor, alleging it was not made in good faith or for valuable consideration within two years of insolvency adjudication.
issues_decided: Whether the burden of proving good faith and valuable consideration in a challenged transfer during insolvency proceedings lies on the transferee or the Official Receiver.
Whether a finding in insolvency proceedings that a transaction is an act of insolvency operates as res judicata against the transferee in a subsequent suit.
Whether the mortgagee acted in good faith and with due care in entering into the mortgage transaction.
Whether the transaction was supported by valuable consideration.
holdings: The burden of proving that a transfer is not in good faith or for valuable consideration lies on the Official Receiver challenging the transaction, not on the transferee.

A finding in insolvency proceedings that a transaction is an act of insolvency does not operate as res judicata in a civil suit involving the transferee, as the latter is not a party to those proceedings.
The mortgagee acted in good faith, having made reasonable inquiries about the borrowers' reputation and financial standing, and there was no evidence he was aware of their impending insolvency.

The transaction was supported by valuable consideration, as evidenced by withdrawal records and credible testimony, and the mortgagee had no duty to scrutinize the internal financial details of the borrowing family.
provisions: Travancore and Cochin General Clauses Act II of 1072 (1897), Section 6(2)
Indian General Clauses Act X of 1897, Section 2(22)
doctrines: Burden of proof in insolvency avoidance actions
Res judicata in insolvency proceedings
Good faith in creditor transactions
Valuable consideration in mortgage transactions

card.dispute: The dispute was between Kirpal Kaur, claiming ownership through her mother Harnam Kaur's adverse possession and subsequent gift, and the collaterals of the original owner, who challenged the validity of the gift and claimed reversionary rights.
issues_decided: Whether Harnam Kaur, a Hindu Jat widow, acquired absolute ownership of the property by adverse possession after 1920
Whether the unregistered agreement of February 6, 1932, could be admitted under Section 49 of the Indian Registration Act to show that her possession was permissive
Whether Harnam Kaur entered possession as a customary heir, thereby limiting her estate to a life interest
holdings: Harnam Kaur, not being a legal heir and having no arrangement with the collaterals, was in adverse possession from 1920, and acquired absolute title by adverse possession after twelve years.
An unregistered document that should have been registered cannot be admitted to show that possession, already adverse, became permissive, as this would circumvent Section 49 of the Registration Act.
The claim that Harnam Kaur entered as a customary heir was not proved; mere mutation and official opinions do not establish such a custom or her status as heir.
doctrines: Adverse possession by a Hindu widow
Inadmissibility of unregistered documents to alter nature of possession
Requirement of proof for customary inheritance

card.dispute: An advocate debarred by the Madras High Court for professional misconduct challenged the Supreme Court's initiation of proceedings to remove his name from its roll of advocates.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court must automatically follow a High Court's order debarring an advocate from practice?
Whether the Supreme Court must conduct a fresh inquiry before removing an advocate's name from its roll based on a High Court's disciplinary action?
Whether the Supreme Court should remove the appellant's name from its roll of advocates after the Madras High Court found him guilty of professional misconduct?
holdings: The Supreme Court is not bound to automatically follow a High Court's order debaring an advocate, but may independently assess the record and findings.
The Supreme Court need not conduct a fresh inquiry; it is sufficient to examine the record and findings of the High Court and Bar Council Tribunal.

An advocate found guilty of serious professional misconduct by a High Court, involving breach of trust, does not meet the high standard of integrity required for enrolment in the Supreme Court and must be removed from its roll.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, Order IV, Rule 30
Advocates Act, 1961 (as interpreted in light of prior Bar Councils Act framework)
doctrines: Judicial discretion in disciplinary proceedings
Standard of integrity for advocates in higher courts
Procedural fairness in professional disbarment

card.dispute: The appellant, a Patwari, was convicted for making incorrect land records in favor of one party and against another, and the State defended the conviction under Section 218 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant made incorrect entries in the khasra knowingly and with intent to cause loss or injury under Section 218 IPC.
Whether the prosecution proved the necessary criminal intent required for conviction under Section 218 IPC.
Whether the incorrect entry in the year 1358 F could have caused legal loss or injury to the complainant given the timeline of possession and relevant land reform laws.
holdings: To sustain a conviction under Section 218 IPC, it is not enough that an entry is incorrect; it must be made with intent to cause, or knowledge that it is likely to cause, loss or injury to a person.
The prosecution failed to prove the requisite criminal intent, and the circumstantial evidence was insufficient to establish that the appellant intended to cause loss or injury.

An incorrect entry for the year 1358 F could not have caused legal harm because the proceedings under Section 145 CrPC had already concluded in the complainant’s favor, and the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act tied hereditary tenancy to possession in 1356 F, not 1358 F.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 16
doctrines: Requirement of mens rea in criminal offences
Presumption of innocence and burden of proof in criminal cases
Temporal relevance of land records for statutory rights

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the assessee, Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy, disputed whether income from the sale of forest trees was agricultural income exempt from tax.
issues_decided: Whether income from the sale of forest trees constitutes agricultural income under Section 2(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether human labour and skill applied to a spontaneously grown forest can render the income from it agricultural income.
holdings: Income derived from land through agriculture includes products raised by basic operations like tilling, sowing, and planting, and requires cultivation of the land as a sine qua non.
Where trees are planted by the owner in denuded parts of a spontaneously grown forest and human labour is applied to their growth, the income from such planted trees qualifies as agricultural income.
doctrines: Cultivation of land as essential for agricultural income
Distinction between basic and subsequent agricultural operations

card.dispute: The Official Receiver in insolvency challenged the payment of owelty money and deposit of funds to a co-sharer under a partition decree, seeking restitution on the ground that no charge was created over the insolvent's property.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for owelty in a partition suit creates a charge by necessary implication even without an express declaration
Whether the Official Receiver in insolvency is entitled to restitution of amounts paid under a valid decree on the ground that no charge was created
Whether the decree holder has a right to priority in payment over the insolvent estate
Whether Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to allow restitution when a decree remains undisturbed
holdings: A decree for payment of owelty in a partition suit creates a charge by necessary implication on the property allotted to the co-sharer liable to pay, even if not expressly declared.
The Official Receiver cannot claim restitution of amounts paid under a valid decree merely because no charge was created; compliance with a subsisting decree bars recovery.
The co-sharer decree-holder has a right to receive payment under the decree independently of any charge, as the liability is personal to the Official Receiver.
Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply where a decree has not been varied or reversed, and payments were made in satisfaction of a continuing decree.
doctrines: Charge by necessary implication
Res judicata
Priority of claims in insolvency
Finality of decrees

card.dispute: The appellants, who had obtained a compromise decree for pre-emption and taken possession of the land, were challenged by respondents (equal-degree pre-emptors) who filed a separate suit for pre-emption, claiming a right to share the land under the Punjab Pre-emption Act.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents, as pre-emptors of equal degree, could succeed in their suit for pre-emption after the appellants had obtained a decree, deposited the purchase money, and taken possession.

Whether the appellants, upon depositing the purchase money and taking possession under the decree, were substituted in place of the vendee and thus acquired a right not subject to the doctrine of lis pendens.
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens bars a transfer made in recognition of a pre-existing and subsisting right of pre-emption.
holdings: A second pre-emptor of equal degree cannot succeed if the first pre-emptor has already exercised their right by obtaining a decree, depositing the purchase money, and taking possession, thereby being substituted in place of the vendee.

The doctrine of lis pendens does not apply to a transfer made in exercise of a pre-existing and enforceable right of pre-emption; such a pre-emptor acquires an indefeasible right upon compliance with the decree.

A pre-emptor is not substituted in place of the vendee until they fulfill the conditions of the decree, including payment and taking possession; only then does their right become complete and immune to claims by equal-degree pre-emptors.
doctrines: Lis pendens
Substitution of pre-emptor in place of vendee
Pre-existing right exception to lis pendens

card.dispute: The former partners of a dissolved salt manufacturing partnership sued to claim that the renewal of a lease obtained by the other partners after dissolution was an asset belonging to the partnership.
issues_decided: Whether the renewal of a lease obtained after the dissolution of a partnership enures to the benefit of all former partners as a partnership asset
Whether the defendants, who obtained the renewed lease, held it in constructive trust for the plaintiffs under the Indian Trusts Act
Whether the principles of English equity regarding renewal of partnership leases apply in this case
holdings: A lease renewal obtained after the partnership has automatically dissolved does not enure to the benefit of all former partners unless there is evidence that partnership assets or goodwill were used to secure it.

The defendants did not occupy a fiduciary position after the partnership ended and thus were not obligated to hold the renewed lease for the benefit of the plaintiffs under Section 88 of the Indian Trusts Act.

A presumption that lease renewal benefits all partners exists in equity but is rebuttable based on facts; it was rebutted here due to lack of partnership continuity, personal qualifications for the lease, and absence of misuse of partnership resources.
doctrines: Constructive trust
Presumption of equity in favour of partnership benefit from lease renewal
Fiduciary duty of partners
Rebuttable presumption of fact

card.dispute: The lessors sued the lessees for ownership and possession of a building constructed on leased land after the lease expired, while the lessees claimed protection from eviction under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the lease included a demise of the building or only the land
Whether the lessees were protected under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Control Act, 1947 from surrendering possession of the building
Whether the lessors could claim a declaration of entitlement to rents and profits from the building
Whether the suit was maintainable despite non-joinder of a deceased defendant's legal representatives
holdings: The lease conveyed only the land, not the building; ownership of the building remained with the lessees during the lease term, but they were bound to surrender it without compensation upon lease expiry.

The Bombay Rents Act does not prevent enforcement of a contractual obligation to surrender possession of a building after lease expiration, as it only creates statutory tenancy for land, not for structures beyond the lease term.

The lessors are entitled to a declaration of right to rents and profits from the building post-lease expiry, even if collection requires access to the land, as the declaration does not demand physical entry.
The suit was maintainable without joining the legal representatives of a deceased defendant who had no active interest in the property or control over the building.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Statutory tenancy under rent control law does not extend lease term beyond contract
Ownership of structures built on leased land remains with lessee unless contract provides otherwise
Declaratory relief can be granted independently of physical possession if rights are established
Non-joinder of parties not necessary if they have no substantial interest in the subject matter

card.dispute: The appellant property owner challenged the compensation awarded for the compulsory requisitioning of his four-storied building by the State of West Bengal for use by the Controller of Army Factory Accounts.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the arbitrator's 10% additional compensation for the potential value of the requisitioned premises.
Whether the principles for determining compensation under the Defence of India Act, s. 19, are the same as those under s. 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the High Court correctly assessed compensation by averaging rents from comparable buildings.
Whether the compensation awarded for the use and burden on the lift was adequate.
holdings: The High Court erred in rejecting the 10% additional compensation for potential value without assigning reasons, as potential value must be considered in compensation like under the Land Acquisition Act.

The principles for determining compensation under s. 19 of the Defence of India Act are the same as those under s. 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including consideration of potentialities of the property.
The High Court did not commit an error in principle by averaging rents from two comparable premises to determine fair compensation.
The compensation for the lift's use was inadequate; Rs. 125 per month was reasonable given dual government department usage, and total compensation was enhanced to Rs. 3,200 per month.
doctrines: Principle of compensation based on potential value of property
Notional fair rent principle
Arbitrator's discretion in assessing value based on available materials

card.dispute: The appellant, H. Venkatachala Iyengar, sought to uphold a will that bequeathed substantial property to him, while the respondents challenged its validity due to suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
issues_decided: Whether the will was validly executed with the testatrix's full understanding and free will
Whether suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the will required the propounder to discharge a higher burden of proof
Whether the trial court misdirected itself in presuming due execution upon proof of signature
holdings: The propounder of a will must prove testamentary capacity and due execution, and when suspicious circumstances exist, must explain them to the satisfaction of the court.

Suspicious circumstances, such as the propounder's dominant role in drafting and lack of independent legal advice, require rigorous scrutiny and cannot be overcome by interested or inconsistent evidence.
Proof of the testatrix's signature does not conclusively establish knowledge or approval of the will's contents, especially when suspicious circumstances are present and not rebutted.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder of will
Suspicious circumstances doctrine in will execution
Presumption under Section 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act
Testamentary capacity and knowledge and approval

card.dispute: The firm G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. contested the Commissioner of Income-Tax's assessment of profit from land sales as business income, claiming it was not an adventure in the nature of trade.
issues_decided: Whether the profit from the sale of four plots of land constituted income from an adventure in the nature of trade under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922.
Whether the burden of proof was properly discharged in classifying the transaction as trading.
holdings: A transaction can be classified as an adventure in the nature of trade if the assessee acted with the sole intention to purchase and sell for profit, especially when supported by a consistent plan and conduct.

The initial intention to sell for profit is a strong but rebuttable presumption; when corroborated by surrounding circumstances, it suffices to classify a transaction as trading even if the asset is typically used for investment.
The onus lies on the revenue to prove the transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade, but once a strong presumption is established through intention and conduct, the burden is met.
doctrines: Adventure in the nature of trade
Onus of proof in tax assessments
Mixed question of law and fact in characterizing income

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the continuation of a partition suit by the mother of a minor plaintiff after the minor's death, arguing the suit abated and could not be pursued.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for partition filed on behalf of a minor abates upon the minor's death during pendency of the suit.
Whether the court's declaration that a partition suit is beneficial to a minor creates a new right or recognizes an existing one.
Whether a suit for partition by a minor is personal to the minor and abates on death under the maxim 'actio personalis moritur cum persona'.
holdings: A suit for partition filed on behalf of a minor does not abate upon the minor’s death; the legal representative may continue it if the suit was beneficial when instituted.
The court’s finding that a partition suit is beneficial to a minor does not create a new right but recognizes a severance in status that occurred when the suit was filed.
A partition suit relates to property, not personal rights, and thus does not abate on the minor’s death under the maxim 'actio personalis moritur cum persona'.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure (implied by context of abatement and legal representation)
doctrines: Severance of joint family status by declaration through litigation
Parens patriae jurisdiction in protecting minor's interests
Abatement of suits not applicable to property-related actions
Recognition of next friend's authority to act for minor in partition suits

card.dispute: M.P. Davis appealed against the High Court's decision that a document he relied upon did not create a partnership between him and his brother for tax registration purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the document (Exhibit 12) created a legal relationship of partnership between M.P. Davis and his brother.
Whether the sharing of profits and description of the document as a 'partnership deed' is sufficient to establish a partnership under the law.
Whether the conduct of the parties and terms of the agreement indicate a true partnership or a master-servant relationship.
holdings: A partnership is not created merely by describing an agreement as a 'partnership deed' or by sharing profits; the real relationship between the parties must be examined.
The absence of capital contribution, lack of authority to manage, inability to share losses, and subordination in decision-making indicate a servant-master, not a partner-partner, relationship.
Control over business, power to approve expenditures, and retention of estate ownership by one party negate the existence of a partnership despite profit-sharing.
The document did not create a partnership as the brother had no proprietary interest in the estate and was subject to the unilateral control of the appellant.
doctrines: Real relation test for partnership under Section 6 of the Indian Partnership Act
Profit-sharing alone does not establish partnership
Partnership requires mutual agency, joint ownership of capital, and shared risk of losses

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that transactions alienating property inherited by his father from his maternal grandfather did not bind his reversionary rights, as the property was ancestral and alienated without legal necessity.
issues_decided: Whether property inherited by a Hindu male from his maternal grandfather under Punjab customary law is ancestral property qua his sons.
Whether the doctrine of stare decisis prevents overruling earlier Full Bench decisions of the Punjab High Court on this point.
holdings: Property inherited by a Hindu male from his maternal grandfather is not ancestral property in relation to his sons under the customary law of the Punjab.
The doctrine of stare decisis is not inflexible and does not apply where a decision is clearly erroneous and its reversal does not affect titles, contracts, or general dealings.
doctrines: Stare decisis
Ancestral property under Hindu customary law
Rule against perpetuating erroneous legal principles

card.dispute: The reversioner Sheo Shankar Dayal sued to claim the property after the death of Mst. Jotkunwar, arguing that a 1906 document was a gift, not a valid surrender, and thus the property should devolve on him as the nearest reversioner.
issues_decided: Whether the 1906 document executed by Mst. Jotkunwar constituted a valid surrender of the entire estate, thereby accelerating succession.
Whether the partial reservation of cultivating rights by Jotkunwar affected the validity of the surrender.
Whether the defendants were in adverse possession, thus barring the plaintiff's suit by limitation.
holdings: A surrender that is not complete and does not involve total self-effacement of the holder cannot accelerate succession to an estate.
Reservation of substantial cultivating rights (91.5 acres) by Jotkunwar meant the 1906 transaction was not a complete surrender and thus ineffective to accelerate succession.
In the absence of a valid surrender, the estate vested in the reversioner upon Jotkunwar’s death, and the suit was filed within time, so it was not barred by limitation.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of complete self-effacement for valid surrender
Acceleration of succession only upon complete surrender of estate
Adverse possession not applicable where no prior title exists due to invalid surrender

card.dispute: The appellants claimed rights as members of a joint family based on a marriage in 'sarvaswadanam' form, while respondents contested the validity of that marriage and the resulting claims to family property.
issues_decided: Whether the marriage of the appellants was validly performed in the sarvaswadanam form, entitling the wife to remain a member of the joint family.
Whether the appellants were entitled to family property based on the alleged sarvaswadanam marriage.
Whether the deed Exhibit A, executed by the last surviving member, validly conveyed family property to the appellants.
holdings: The marriage was not proved to have been conducted in the sarvaswadanam form, as the evidence, including documentary and oral testimony, was insufficient and unreliable.
The appellants did not acquire any rights in the family property because the foundational claim of sarvaswadanam marriage was not established.
Exhibit A did not create any new interest in favor of the appellants as it merely confirmed pre-existing rights, which were found not to exist.
provisions: Malayalee Brahmins' Act, Act III of 1106
doctrines: Proof of custom requires clear and convincing evidence
Admissions by parties in litigation, especially based on hearsay or inconsistent conduct, are unreliable
A deed purporting to confirm rights is ineffective if the underlying rights are not legally established

card.dispute: The defendants appealed against a suit for possession on redemption of certain mortgages, claiming the suit was barred by limitation and that the plaintiff had no right to redeem the entire mortgaged property.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Judge had jurisdiction under the Sangli State Agriculturists Protection Act to entertain the suit.
Whether the plaintiff, not being a party to the execution sale, could maintain a suit for redemption.
Whether the documents of 1892 were admissible to prove separation in estate among coparceners despite non-registration.
Whether the entire mortgaged property or only a moiety was redeemable by the plaintiff.
holdings: The Special Judge had jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the 1915 date-line in the Act applied only to reopening closed transactions, not to bar other reliefs for pre-1915 transactions.
The plaintiff could maintain the suit for redemption without first setting aside the execution sale, as she was the legal representative of the mortgagor and the sale did not bind her interest.

Unregistered documents from 1892 were admissible to prove severance of joint status (separation in estate) under Mitakshara law, as they did not declare partition by metes and bounds and thus did not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.

The plaintiff could redeem only half the mortgaged property, as the other half belonged to her father’s coparcener who had validly sold his share, and the mortgage covered the entire ancestral property.
provisions: Sangli State Agriculturist Protection Act, 1 of 1936
doctrines: Severance of joint family status under Mitakshara law does not require registration if it does not involve partition by metes and bounds.
A legal representative not made a party to an execution proceeding is not bound by the sale in execution of a mortgage decree.
Unregistered documents may be used for collateral purposes like proving separation in estate if they do not create or declare interests in immovable property valued at Rs. 100 or more.
Redemption of mortgaged ancestral property is limited to the share of the mortgagor where co-sharers have separated and alienated their shares.

card.dispute: Raghunath Das sued his brother Gokal Chand for division of jointly held G.P. Notes after a decree declaring his share, claiming exclusion of time spent in failed execution proceedings from limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was for 'specific moveable property' under Article 49 of the Indian Limitation Act or for division of joint property under Article 120
Whether the period spent in execution proceedings could be excluded under Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act
holdings: A suit by a co-heir for division of moveable property held jointly, even after a decree declaring rights, is not a suit for 'specific moveable property' under Article 49 but is governed by Article 120 of the Limitation Act.

Where execution proceedings fail due to lack of jurisdiction, the time spent in such proceedings with due diligence and in good faith can be excluded under Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act when computing limitation for a subsequent suit on the same cause of action.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 2, Rule 2
doctrines: Same cause of action
Due diligence in prosecution of proceedings
Defect of jurisdiction rendering a decree a nullity
Substance over form in characterizing a suit

card.dispute: The sons of a managing director challenged the sale of joint family property to recover a debt owed by their father due to his negligence in office, arguing the debt was not enforceable against them and the sale did not include their shares.
issues_decided: Whether the father's debt arising from negligence in his official duties is avyavaharika (non-commercial and unenforceable against sons under Hindu law)
Whether the institution of a partition suit before the auction sale severed the sons' status and protected their shares from sale
Whether the phrase 'right, title and interest of the defaulter' in s. 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code includes the entire joint family property or only the father's share
holdings: A father's debt incurred due to negligence in discharging official duties is not avyavaharika, as it is not repugnant to good morals, and thus triggers the sons' pious obligation under Mitakshara law.
The pious obligation of sons to pay the father's legitimate debts continues even after partition, and the sale of joint family property for such debts remains valid against the sons' interests.
The phrase 'right, title and interest of the defaulter' in s. 155 allows for the sale of the entire joint family property if the sale documents indicate the whole estate was intended to be sold.
doctrines: Pious obligation under Mitakshara law
Avyavaharika debt doctrine
Doctrine of severance of status upon partition
Substance over form in execution sales

card.dispute: S. K. G. Sugar Ltd. challenged the jurisdiction of an Industrial Tribunal to adjudicate complaints against it under the Industrial Disputes Act, as it was not the employer at the time the dispute was referred.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a 'party' to the industrial dispute referred to the Tribunal on December 2, 1954, despite taking over the lease of the sugar factory on December 6, 1954.
Whether the appellant, as a new lessee, was an 'employer' within the meaning of Sections 33 and 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, in relation to the workmen's complaints.
Whether the Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain applications under Section 33A against the appellant without notice or amendment of the reference.
holdings: The appellant was not a party to the reference as it did not manage the factory on the date of the reference and was not notified of the proceedings.
An employer must be identical at the time of the reference and the alleged discharge or change in service conditions for Sections 33 and 33A to apply.
The Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to proceed against the appellant under Section 33A as it was not the employer during the reference and no notice was served.
doctrines: Doctrine of proper party in industrial adjudication
Doctrine of identity of employer for applicability of Section 33
Doctrine of jurisdictional limitation in ex parte proceedings
Doctrine of notice and fair hearing under statutory procedure

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be the adopted son of the deceased Lakshminarayan and thus entitled to his estate, while the respondent, the widow, denied the adoption and claimed the property as his legal heir.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of the appellant by Lakshminarayan was proved by sufficient evidence
Whether the respondent was estopped from denying the adoption based on her conduct or admissions
Whether acts such as performance of obsequies, residence, possession, or marriage by the respondent could prove adoption
holdings: The adoption was not proved, as the evidence was insufficient, inconsistent, and failed to meet the high standard required to establish a change in succession.
The doctrine of estoppel does not apply to deny adoption when both parties know the true facts; mere admissions or conduct do not create estoppel in such cases.
Acts like performing obsequies, residing together, or managing property do not, without more, prove adoption, especially when other evidence shows no valid adoption occurred.
doctrines: Estoppel in adoption cases
Burden and standard of proof in adoption disputes
Relevance of conduct and admissions as evidence in establishing adoption

card.dispute: The appellants claimed ownership of a coal mine area through adverse possession after intermittent mining, while the respondents claimed rightful leasehold and sought possession and compensation for encroachment.
issues_decided: Whether intermittent mining operations over several decades could establish adverse possession of a coal mine area
Whether possession of a part of a coal seam through sporadic working could mature into title over the entire seam
holdings: Intermittent mining, with long periods of inactivity, does not constitute continuous, open, and hostile possession required to establish adverse possession.
Working a portion of a coal seam does not, even if continuous, confer title to the entire seam by adverse possession.
doctrines: Adverse possession requires continuous and uninterrupted possession for the statutory period
Presumption of possession reverting to the true owner during periods of non-activity

card.dispute: The Special Land Acquisition Officer appealed against the High Court's enhanced compensation awarded to landowner T. Adinarayan Setty for land acquired for a maternity hospital.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in determining the market value of the acquired land by selectively considering only some of the prior sale transactions.
Whether the High Court wrongly used extraneous factors like the purpose of acquisition and delay in use while assessing compensation.
What is the correct market value per square yard of the land based on bona fide prior sales?
holdings: The High Court committed an error by arbitrarily excluding two of six sale transactions when calculating average market value, which must include all comparable sales around the relevant date.

Considerations such as the purpose of acquisition, expert opinions on land suitability, and delay in project implementation are irrelevant and extraneous to determining market value under the Land Acquisition Act.
The correct market value of the non low-lying land is Rs. 11 per square yard, arrived at by including all six sale transactions and avoiding double-counting of the highest price in averaging.
doctrines: Market value determination based on comparable sales
Exclusion of extraneous considerations in compensation
Proper method of averaging sale prices for valuation

card.dispute: The zamindar sued to eject the appellants from sir lands, claiming they were trespassers despite a Magistrate's provisional possession order under CrPC 145; the appellants claimed hereditary tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Revenue Court had jurisdiction to try the ejectment suit under Section 180 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939
Whether the Magistrate's order under Section 145 of the CrPC conferred a right or title to possession enabling the appellants to resist ejectment
Whether the suits abated under Rule 5 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules as amended in 1952
holdings: The Revenue Court has jurisdiction to try ejectment suits under Section 180 of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, where possession is without consent and not in accordance with law.

An order under Section 145 CrPC is a temporary police measure to prevent breach of peace and does not confer title or a legal right to possession; it cannot be used to resist ejectment under Section 180 of the Tenancy Act.

Rule 5 of the amended U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952 does not apply where suits were restarted under the original Rules and no fresh stay order was made under the amended Rules.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, Rule 4 and Rule 5 (original and amended)
doctrines: Police order doctrine under Section 145 CrPC
Jurisdiction of Revenue Courts in tenancy matters
Doctrine of abatement of suits under statutory rules

card.dispute: The parties, members of a joint Hindu family, disputed the partition of family properties, particularly whether foreign immovable properties in Burma and Pudukottai could be included in an arbitration reference made by the trial court after a preliminary decree and during pendency of appeals.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court had the competence to refer the dispute to arbitration after a preliminary decree in a partition suit and during the pendency of appeals.
Whether the arbitration award could legally include directions regarding foreign immovable properties excluded from the preliminary decree.
Whether the arbitrators had the jurisdiction to award interest on the amounts determined in the award.
holdings: The trial court was competent to refer the matters in dispute to arbitration even after a preliminary decree and during pendency of appeals, as the term 'court' under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 includes the trial court and 'suit' includes proceedings connected therewith.

The reference to arbitration and the resulting award were valid, and the arbitrators could decide on properties, including those in Pudukottai, based on the parties' agreement, despite their exclusion from the preliminary decree.
The question of whether arbitrators can award interest was not decided on merits as it was not properly urged before the High Court, and thus could not be raised for the first time in appeal.
provisions: Indian Succession Act, 1925, Section 582 (referred to in context of earlier Code)
doctrines: Competence of court to refer disputes to arbitration with parties' consent
Liberal construction of 'court' and 'suit' under arbitration law
Doctrine of issue estoppel and procedural default in appellate review

card.dispute: The workmen of Dahingeapar Tea Estate fought against the estate's new management over the termination of their services and denial of continuity of service after the estate was sold as a going concern.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of management of a tea estate as a going concern automatically ends the service of employees.
Whether an agreement between buyer and seller can legally deprive employees of their rights to continuity of service and accrued benefits.
holdings: An industrial tribunal cannot decide abstract legal questions about service termination upon business transfer; it must assess facts and industrial justice in context.

The incoming management’s refusal to recognize continuity of service was unjustified where no valid reasons existed and discriminatory conditions were imposed, especially when manual labourers were retained.
doctrines: Protection against unfair labour practices
Continuity of service in transfer of going concerns
Industrial adjudication based on factual findings, not abstract legal questions

card.dispute: Hereditary worshippers (Guravs) sued temple trustees for declaration of their rights and possession after being ousted, claiming the suits were not barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suits filed by the hereditary worshippers were barred by limitation under Article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the trustees' conduct constituted a continuing wrong under Section 23 of the Limitation Act, thereby renewing the cause of action from day to day
holdings: The cause of action arose when the trustees obtained a decree for possession in 1922, and the suits filed decades later were barred by limitation under Article 120.
Ouster by decree constitutes a complete injury to the right, not a continuing wrong; thus Section 23 does not apply where dispossession results from a single wrongful act.
doctrines: Continuing wrong doctrine under Section 23 of the Limitation Act
Complete cause of action rule in cases of ouster
Distinction between continuing injury and continuing effect of a past injury

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether the cancellation of a quasi-permanent land allotment in favor of the respondents occurred before or after a rule change on July 22, 1952, which restricted such cancellations.
issues_decided: Whether the order cancelling the respondents' allotment was made before July 22, 1952, so as to be valid under the applicable rules.
Whether the High Court could interfere with the Deputy Custodian General's factual finding via writ of certiorari.
holdings: The Deputy Custodian General's finding that the allotment was cancelled on May 6, 1952, was based on relevant evidence from the record and was not without basis, even if the formal order was missing.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with a factual finding by a quasi-judicial authority through certiorari, absent an error of law apparent on the record.
provisions: Punjab Refugees (Administration of Evacuee Property) Rules, 1948
Article 226 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Scope of writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Principle of non-interference with findings of fact by quasi-judicial authorities

card.dispute: The appellants claimed title and possession of benami-acquired ryotwari lands, while the respondents argued the transaction was illegal and fraudulent, disentitling the appellants to relief.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could claim relief despite the alleged illegal and fraudulent benami transaction to defraud the Bettiah Raj?
Whether the maxim 'ex turpi causa non oritur actio' bars the appellants' claim?
Whether the illegality in the transaction was so fundamental that the plaintiffs could not establish their case without relying on it?
holdings: A plaintiff is not barred by the maxim 'ex turpi causa non oritur actio' if the illegality is trivial and the claim can be established without relying on the illegal act.
Where a benamidar holds property in trust and the illegality (such as forged signatures) is not central to proving the benami nature, the plaintiff can still enforce their title.
If a party repents before the illegal purpose is achieved and the fraud is not consummated, the court may grant relief despite initial illegality.
The mere use of benami transactions to avoid resumption of land, without concealment or consummated fraud, does not disentitle a plaintiff to a decree.
doctrines: ex turpi causa non oritur actio
locus poenitentiae
benami transaction
public policy exception to illegality

card.dispute: The respondent claimed that a trust deed creating property for two beneficiaries was sham and that the property belonged to the joint Hindu family, while the appellant defended the deed's validity.
issues_decided: Whether the trust deed dated January 17, 1916, was a sham and whether the property was joint family property
Whether the suit for declaration was barred by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, due to omission of consequential relief
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 120 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
holdings: The trust deed was part of a scheme to retain joint family property and was fictitious; the property remained joint family property.
The plea under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was raised too late and could not be allowed as it would prejudice the respondent.
The right to sue accrued only when the Commissioner attempted partition in 1937; the 1940 suit was within six years and thus not barred by limitation.
provisions: Indian Limitation Act, 1908, Schedule I, Article 120
doctrines: Right to sue accrues upon clear and unequivocal threat to a legal right
Plea of limitation may be allowed if it does not prejudice the opposing party's evidence
Admissions of partition by family members are relevant in determining severance in a joint Hindu family

card.dispute: The appellant, a descendant of the founder of a deity worship, claimed private ownership of the temple, deity, and associated properties, while respondents, other descendants, argued it was a public trust.
issues_decided: Whether the deity 'Shri Vyankatesh Balaji' and its properties constituted a public religious trust
Whether the appellant could obtain a declaration of private ownership without joining the deity as a party
Whether certain properties like the Balaji Mandir and Shree Theatre were private or part of the trust
holdings: The deity and temple are public, not private, as worship was open to the public and supported by public contributions over time.
A declaration of private ownership cannot be granted in a suit under Section 5(3) of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, without joining the deity as a necessary party.
Properties such as the Balaji Mandir and Shree Theatre are part of the trust estate, especially where funds were commingled and no clear private source was proven.
provisions: Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, Section 3
Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, Section 5(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Necessary party doctrine
Doctrine of commingling of trust and private property
Public trust doctrine in religious endowments

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that the temple of Shri Balaji Venkatesh and its properties were privately owned, while the respondents contended they constituted a public charitable and religious trust.
issues_decided: Whether the temple of Shri Balaji Venkatesh and its Sansthan constitute a public charitable and religious trust under the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920
Whether the deity is a necessary party in a suit seeking a declaration of private ownership of temple properties
Whether certain properties claimed by the appellant are private or part of the trust
holdings: The temple and its Sansthan constitute a public charitable and religious trust as the deity is accessible to the Hindu public and worship has been continuous and unrestricted for over 200 years.
The deity is a necessary party in suits affecting its interests, and a declaration adverse to the deity cannot be made in its absence.
The appellant failed to prove private ownership of specific properties due to lack of evidence, failure to separate accounts, and not joining the deity as a party.
provisions: Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, Section 5(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Necessary party doctrine
Presumption against mixing private and trust property
Public character of a religious institution inferred from continuous public worship and admissions in historical documents

card.dispute: The assessee, Saroj Kumar Mazumdar, fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether his profit from a single land transaction was taxable as business income or as capital gains.
issues_decided: Whether the single transaction of sale of land was an adventure in the nature of trade under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the dominant intention of the assessee at the time of entering into the agreement was to make a profit through trading or to hold the land as a capital investment
Whether the findings of the Appellate Tribunal on the nature of the transaction can be interfered with by the Supreme Court on appeal
holdings: A single transaction can be an adventure in the nature of trade only if the dominant intention was to make a profit, which must be established by the Department.
The mere possibility of appreciation in value does not make a land purchase a trading venture; the intention at the time of purchase is key.
The Supreme Court, in a majority decision, held that the Department failed to prove the dominant intention to trade, and thus the profit was not taxable as income under Section 10.
doctrines: Dominant intention test for determining adventure in the nature of trade
Distinction between capital investment and trading activity
Principle of finality of findings of fact by tribunals unless there is a question of law or error apparent on record

card.dispute: Radha Prasad Singh (plaintiff) sued Gajadhar Singh and others for pre-emption rights, claiming he had timely notice of a property sale and performed required ceremonies, which the defendants disputed.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff received timely information about the sale of the property on January 2, 1944, as claimed.
Whether the appellate court was justified in reversing the trial court’s finding on the credibility of witnesses regarding the notice and performance of pre-emption ceremonies.
Whether discrepancies in witness testimony regarding the details of the sale information affect the plaintiff’s claim.
holdings: An appellate court may reverse a trial court’s finding of fact if it fails to consider important evidence affecting witness credibility or the probability of the events.
Where a fact is determined by inference from proved circumstances rather than solely by witness demeanor, the appellate court is free to draw its own conclusions.

The High Court was justified in rejecting Jadunath’s testimony due to material inconsistencies and the plaintiff’s implausible conduct in not inquiring about key sale details, undermining the claim of timely notice.
Failure to prove receipt of proper information about the sale on January 2, 1944, defeats the pre-emption claim, regardless of whether ceremonies were performed.
doctrines: Appellate review of findings of fact
Credibility of witnesses and improbability of conduct
Inference from proved facts
Pre-emption under customary law

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and others challenged the applicability of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 to a trust created by Sm. Charusila Dasi, which included properties outside Bihar, arguing it was ultra vires due to extra-territoriality.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 can apply to a religious trust with properties outside Bihar without being ultra vires the legislature's territorial competence.
Whether the Act's application to the Charusila Trust violates constitutional limitations under Articles 245 and 246 of the Constitution of India.
Whether the principles of territorial nexus prevent the Act from being struck down as extra-territorial.
holdings: A state legislature can apply a law to a trust situated in its territory even if some trust properties lie outside, provided there is sufficient territorial nexus.
The Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 is constitutionally valid as applied to the Charusila Trust because the trust was created in Bihar and its administration is based there.
The principle of territorial nexus, previously applied in tax cases, extends to regulatory legislation like religious trust laws.
provisions: Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Sections 1(2), 2(1), 3
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Item 28
doctrines: Territorial Nexus
Legislative Competence
Extra-territoriality
Doctrine of Pith and Substance

card.dispute: The appellants, decree-holders for possession of a house, obtained delivery of possession in execution proceedings without notice to the tenant-respondent, who challenged the legality of the eviction under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, was repugnant to the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and thus rendered inoperative from April 1, 1951?
Whether the Executing Court had jurisdiction to deliver possession despite restrictions under Sections 9 and 16 of the 1948 Order?
Whether the respondent’s application under Sections 47 and 151, CPC, for setting aside the ex parte delivery of possession was maintainable?
Whether the principles of res judicata, waiver, or estoppel barred the respondent from challenging the execution of the decree?
holdings: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, did not automatically come into force in Mysore on April 1, 1951; it was extended only from October 1, 1951, by notification, so the 1948 Rent Control Order remained valid and operative until then.

Sections 9 and 16 of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, restricted the Executing Court’s power to evict a tenant, and thus the court could not lawfully deliver possession in violation of those provisions.
An application under Section 47, CPC, read with Section 151, is maintainable to challenge execution of a decree that violates rent control laws, even if the decree itself was validly passed.

Res judicata, waiver, and estoppel do not apply to bar a tenant from objecting to execution of a decree when the objection is based on statutory rent control restrictions that affect executability, not the decree’s validity.
provisions: Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, Sections 9 and 16
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Act IV of 1882)
Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951 (Act III of 1951)
doctrines: Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of functus officio
Res judicata
Estoppel against statute
Inherent powers of court under Section 151, CPC

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing it was unconstitutional for not explicitly stating that the acquisition was for a public purpose and violated Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 must expressly state that land is being acquired for a public purpose to be valid.
Whether land acquisition for a company can serve a public purpose within the meaning of the Constitution.
Whether the omission of the phrase 'public purpose' in the Section 4 notification renders the acquisition proceedings unconstitutional under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution.
holdings: A notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not need to explicitly state that the acquisition is for a public purpose; it suffices that the government is later satisfied after inquiry that the purpose qualifies as public under Section 40.

Acquisition of land for a company can constitute a public purpose if it involves providing housing, amenities for workers, or constructing public utility works, as these serve broader societal welfare.

The absence of the words 'public purpose' in a preliminary Section 4 notification does not invalidate the proceedings, as the substantive requirement is satisfied through subsequent investigation and satisfaction under Sections 5A or 40.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Doctrine of substantial compliance
Doctrine of prospective investigation in administrative action
Doctrine of constitutional validity of existing laws under Article 31(5)(a)

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant for sub-letting premises, which was prohibited by statute, despite an agreement allowing sub-letting.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement permitting sub-letting is valid despite a statutory prohibition under the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the landlord and tenant being in equal fault (in pari delicto) bars the landlord's suit for ejectment
Whether the landlord waived the right to eject the tenant by agreeing to sub-letting
holdings: An agreement permitting sub-letting in violation of Section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 is void as it contravenes public policy and cannot be enforced.
Parties cannot by mutual agreement override a statutory prohibition based on public policy, even if both are equally involved in the illegality.
A statutory right created for public benefit cannot be waived by private agreement, and the landlord did not waive the right to eject under Section 13(1)(e) by allowing sub-letting.
provisions: Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(e)
Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15
doctrines: In pari delicto
Waiver of statutory rights
Public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Non-enforcement of illegal agreements

card.dispute: The appellant Bhagwantrao claimed a right to hold 'patelki huq inam' lands as part of a family partition, while the revenue authorities resumed the lands and regranted them to the working patel, Vishwasrao, leading to a dispute over whether such inam lands could be partitioned among family members or were solely tied to the office of patel.
issues_decided: Whether 'patelki huq inam' lands are grants of remuneration tied to the office of patel or heritable and partitionable family property burdened with service
Whether a member of a patel's family who has not held the office can claim a share in the inam lands as a matter of right
Whether the State has the authority to resume 'patelki inam' lands when the holder does not perform the associated service
Whether title by adverse possession can be acquired against the State in respect of such service inam lands
holdings: 'Patelki huq inam' is a grant of land in lieu of wages for the office of patel, not heritable or partitionable family property, and remains subject to resumption if service conditions are unmet.
Only the person actually holding the office of patel is entitled to the emoluments, including the use of inam lands; family members not performing the service have no right to a share.
The State, under the Berar Land Revenue Code and the Patels and Patwaris Law, has the power to resume such inam lands if the purpose of the grant is defeated by non-performance or improper transfer.
Adverse possession cannot confer title over service inam lands against the State, as these lands are held under a public grant for official purposes and are not freely alienable.
doctrines: Service inam doctrine
Resumable grant doctrine
Emoluments tied to office doctrine
Bar on civil court jurisdiction in revenue matters

card.dispute: The petitioner, a former cadet who became the ruler of Vadia State, fought with the State of Saurashtra (later Bombay) over whether a hereditary village grant made to him as a 'Bhayat' could be resumed after he ascended the throne.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of the village to the petitioner as 'Bhayat' was absolute and unconditional, or conditional upon his status as a cadet
Whether the grant lapsed when the petitioner became the ruler of the State of Vadia
Whether the State's resumption of the village violated the petitioner's fundamental right to property under the Constitution
holdings: A grant made 'as Bhayat' is not absolute but conditional on the grantee remaining a cadet in a primogeniture-based succession system.
When the grantee ceases to be a Bhayat by becoming the ruler, the grant lapses and reverts to the State.
The State's resumption of the village did not infringe any fundamental right because the grant inherently contained a defeasance clause upon change in status.
doctrines: Conditional grant doctrine
Doctrine of defeasance by change in status
Principle of interpretation of feudal or customary grants in context of succession rules

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a right to retain 'patel ki huq inam' lands after a partition, while the revenue authorities resumed the lands and regranted them to the working patel, leading to a dispute over entitlement and resumption rights.
issues_decided: Whether a member of the patel's family has a hereditary right to a share in the 'patel ki inam' lands irrespective of holding the office.
Whether the State revenue authorities have the power to resume 'patel ki inam' lands when the holder does not perform the associated service.
Whether the appellant acquired title to the disputed lands by adverse possession or through partition.
holdings: A member of the patel's family does not have an automatic right to share in the emoluments or lands attached to the patel's office; such rights are tied to actual office-holding.
The revenue authorities have the power under the Berar Land Revenue Code to resume service-based inam lands if the holder fails to perform the required service or if the grant's purpose is defeated.
The appellant did not acquire title by adverse possession or partition, as service-based inam lands cannot be claimed independently of office tenure, and government resumption is valid.
doctrines: Service tenures are resumable if conditions are not fulfilled
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in service emolument disputes
No hereditary right in service-based inam lands

card.dispute: The appellant, Champalal, and respondent, Mst. Samarath Bai, disputed over the validity of an arbitration award concerning adoption and succession to the estate of the deceased, including rights to property and executorship under a will.
issues_decided: Whether the court had jurisdiction to extend time for filing the arbitration award under Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the arbitrators committed misconduct by pre-deciding the award
Whether the arbitration award was in excess of the powers conferred by the arbitration agreement or contrary to law
Whether the appellant was entitled to challenge the award given his refusal to be adopted as required under the award
holdings: The court had jurisdiction to extend time for filing the award as it was the proper court under Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and no defect arose from the same court handling both Succession and Arbitration proceedings.

The charge of arbitrator misconduct failed because the evidence showed efforts at settlement, not pre-determination, and the alleged statements were not pleaded initially and were deemed afterthoughts.

The award was within the scope of the arbitration agreement and not contrary to law, as the arbitrators were empowered to decide consequences of adoption or non-adoption, including time limits and resulting rights.
The appellant was not entitled to benefit under the award as he refused to be adopted despite the respondent's readiness, and courts found on evidence that his refusal was unjustified.
doctrines: Arbitrator misconduct must be proven and cannot be inferred from settlement efforts
Arbitration award must be upheld if within the scope of reference and not contrary to law
Conditional bequests in wills are enforceable and succession depends on fulfillment of conditions
Principle of estoppel against a party who refuses to perform a condition precedent to claim benefits

card.dispute: The holder of Kavalappara Sthanam and family members challenged the constitutional validity of a Madras law that altered property rights in sthanam properties, following a Privy Council ruling favoring the Sthanee.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Marumakkathayam (Removal of Doubts) Act, 1955 violates Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the Act is protected under Article 31A
Whether the Act amounts to an unconstitutional exercise of judicial power by the legislature
Whether the petitioners have standing to challenge the Act in light of their claimed property rights
holdings: The Act is saved by Article 31A and thus immune from challenges under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31, even if it affects fundamental rights.
An Act that redistributes janmam rights among multiple persons constitutes a 'modification' under Article 31A, even without altering the incidents of the right.
Legislative power includes the authority to enact retrospective laws and override prior judicial decisions, which does not amount to judicial function.
Petitioners whose claimed rights are not affected by the Act or who derive title from an invalid gift lack standing to challenge it.
provisions: Madras Marumakkathayam (Removal of Doubts) Act, 1955 (Act 32 of 1955), Section 2
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence to enact retrospective laws
Doctrine of protection under Article 31A for laws modifying property rights
Separation of powers: distinction between legislative and judicial functions
Doctrine of standing in constitutional challenges

card.dispute: The sons and wife of a Hindu father challenged a mortgage decree on the ground that the underlying debt was immoral, while the mortgagee claimed protection as a bona fide alienee.
issues_decided: Whether the sons challenging a mortgage for an antecedent debt must prove both the immoral nature of the debt and the mortgagee's knowledge of it.
Whether the principles from Suraj Bunsi Koer apply to mortgages as well as sales.
Whether Hindu law on pious obligation should be reinterpreted solely based on ancient Sanskrit texts.
holdings: Sons must prove both that the father's antecedent debt was immoral and that the alienee had knowledge of its immoral character to invalidate the transaction.
The principles in Suraj Bunsi Koer apply equally to mortgages and sales; no distinction exists in the burden of proof.
The long-standing judicial interpretation of Hindu law, especially from Privy Council decisions, must be respected under stare decisis and cannot be overturned by re-examining ancient texts.
provisions: Hindu Law, as interpreted through case law
doctrines: Stare decisis
Pious obligation of Hindu sons to pay father's antecedent debts
Bona fide alienee protection
Equity, justice and good conscience in Hindu law interpretation

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act, 1955, which imposed a uniform basic tax on all lands, including forested lands, arguing it violated fundamental rights and exceeded legislative competence.
issues_decided: Whether the uniform land tax under the Act violates Article 14 by enabling arbitrary exemptions by the government
Whether the Act infringes Article 19(1)(f) and (g) by unreasonably restricting rights to property and occupation
Whether the Act offends Article 31 by depriving persons of property without compensation
Whether the State Legislature had competence under Entry 49, List II, to impose tax on lands covered by forests
holdings: Section 7, which allowed government to exempt lands without guiding principles, violated Article 14 but was severable; the rest of the Act remained valid.
The tax did not violate Article 19(1)(f) and (g) as the rate was low and any restriction on property rights was reasonable.
The Act did not violate Article 31 as it was a valid tax law, and Article 31(1) does not apply to taxation, which is governed by Article 265.
The State Legislature had power under Entry 49, List II to tax land irrespective of whether forests stood on it; 'land' and 'forests' are distinct subjects.
provisions: Constitution of India, Article 14, Article 19(1)(f), Article 19(1)(g), Article 265, Article 31, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entries 18, 19, 49
doctrines: Severability of unconstitutional provisions
Reasonable restrictions under Article 19
Colourable legislation
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The trustees of a deity sued to recover arrears of income from property claimed to be a specific endowment for Kalyanotsavam, while the appellants argued it was a personal grant with a service obligation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable
Whether the plaint could be amended to include a formal prayer for declaration of a specific endowment
Whether the inam grant was a specific endowment for the deity or a personal grant burdened with service
What portion of the income was required to be spent on the deity's service
holdings: The suit was maintainable as the necessary allegations for a trust claim were present in the plaint.
The amendment to add a formal prayer for declaration was permissible since the substance of the claim was already in issue and parties had led evidence.
The grant was a specific endowment for the deity’s Kalyanotsavam, creating a trust, not a personal grant with a service obligation.
The entire income of the inam property was dedicated to the charity, and any surplus must be applied cy-près due to the original intent to exhaust income on religious services.
doctrines: Cy-près doctrine
Principle of specific versus personal endowments
Amendment of pleadings to reflect true cause of action
Use of inam registers as reliable documentary evidence in determining nature of grant

card.dispute: The Maharaja of Baster challenged the Madhya Pradesh government's resumption of his lands under a land reform Act, claiming he was still a Ruler and not a 'proprietor'.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a 'proprietor' within the meaning of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, despite being recognised as a Ruler under the Constitution.
Whether the villages in question fell within the definition of 'mahal' under the Act.
holdings: A person recognised as a 'Ruler' under Article 366(22) for privy purse purposes is an 'ex-Ruler' for other legal purposes and can be classified as a 'proprietor' under the land reform Act.
The appellant was a 'maufidar' as holder of rent-free land, and the term includes those whose land is exempt from tax, not just grantees from a State or Ruler.
The villages were 'mahals' under the Act as they were assessed to land revenue, and the appellant failed to prove otherwise.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 2(m)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 2(j)
doctrines: Doctrine of recognition under the Constitution is limited to constitutional purposes
Statutory interpretation of 'maufidar' based on functional exemption from tax, not source of grant
Burden of proof on party asserting exemption from statutory operation

card.dispute: The landlord Suraj Bhan sought eviction of tenant Moti Ram for shop reconstruction, but the tenant challenged the applicability of amended rent control provisions and the High Court's revisional jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the amended provision allowing High Court revision under Section 15(5) applies to pending appeals when the amendment came into force after the appeal was filed
Whether the amendment to Section 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, imposing stricter conditions for eviction, applies retrospectively to pending eviction proceedings
Whether the High Court, in revision, could independently assess the legality and propriety of the finding that the landlord's requirement for reconstruction was bona fide
holdings: The amendment conferring revisional jurisdiction on the High Court under Section 15(5) applies to pending cases as it does not affect vested rights and relates to the mode of review.

The amendment to Section 13(3)(a)(iii) imposing stricter conditions for eviction is substantive and not retrospective unless expressly stated; it does not apply to proceedings pending before its enforcement.

The High Court, under Section 15(5), has the power to examine the legality and propriety of findings, including whether the landlord's need for reconstruction was bona fide, even if lower authorities found otherwise.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(iii)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(4) and (5)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1956, Section 2 and 3
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Doctrine of prospective and retrospective operation of statutes
Doctrine of necessary implication in statutory interpretation
Revisional jurisdiction broader than civil revision under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The deity, through its trustee, sued the defendants (appellants) for arrears and future payment of income from inam lands, claiming it was a specific endowment for Kalyanotsavam, while the defendants argued it was a personal grant for performing services to the deity.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable by the deity through its trustee.
Whether the amendment to the plaint seeking a declaration of specific endowment was permissible.
Whether the inam grant was a specific endowment for the deity's Kalyanotsavam or a personal grant with a service obligation.
What portion of the inam income must be expended on the deity's service.
holdings: A deity can maintain a suit through its duly appointed trustee for enforcement of a religious endowment.
Amendment of the plaint to include a prayer for declaration of specific endowment was permissible as the facts were already in issue and no new cause of action was introduced.
The inam grant was a specific endowment for the Kalyanotsavam of the deity, not a personal grant, based on inam register entries and admissions by predecessors.
The entire income of the inam land must be devoted to the deity’s purposes, applying the cy-pres doctrine, especially where original income was fully expended on the service.
provisions: Hindu Religious Endowments Act (if implied, though not explicitly cited)
Civil Procedure Code, Order VI, Rule 17 (amendment of pleadings)
doctrines: Cy-pres doctrine
Specific versus personal religious endowment
Amendment of pleadings to conform to issues tried
Admissibility and evidentiary value of inam registers

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the state's acquisition of their land for a labour colony under a government housing scheme, arguing it was not for a public purpose and violated procedural requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was rendered redundant by Article 31 of the Constitution
Whether acquisition of land for a co-operative housing society for industrial workers serves a public purpose
Whether compliance with Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act is mandatory when public funds partially finance the acquisition for a company
holdings: Article 31 did not render Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, redundant; the Act was saved by Article 31(5)(a) as an existing law.
Acquisition of land for building residential quarters for industrial workers constitutes a public purpose, even without reliance on Section 17(2)(b) as amended.
When public funds bear part of the acquisition cost, the acquisition is for a public purpose, and compliance with Part VII of the Act is not mandatory, even if the land benefits a company or society.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 4, 6, 17(2)(b), 39, 40, 41, Part VII
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Presumption of constitutionality of existing laws under Article 31(5)(a)
Distinction between acquisition for a company simpliciter and for a public purpose

card.dispute: Pingle Industries Ltd. fought the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether periodic payments made under a long-term lease for quarrying rights were allowable as revenue expenditure for tax deduction purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the payments made under the quolnama for quarrying rights were revenue or capital expenditure
Whether the right to extract stones constituted a capital asset or a trading stock
holdings: The periodic payments under the quolnama were not revenue expenditure but a lump sum paid in installments for acquiring a capital asset of enduring benefit.
The right to extract stones from quarries was a capital asset, not stock-in-trade, and thus the expenditure was on capital account and not deductible under the Income Tax Act.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Doctrine of substance over form in tax law
Test of enduring benefit for capital expenditure

card.dispute: The landlord-appellants sought to resist the tenant-respondents' claim for re-possession of premises after delayed vacation, arguing that the tenants' failure to vacate by the stipulated date disqualified them from protection under the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree fell within the ambit of Section 15 of the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
Whether the tenants were entitled to re-possession under Section 15(3) despite delayed vacation
Whether time was of the essence in the compromise regarding vacation of premises
holdings: A decree based on compromise in a suit under Section 13(g) can incorporate terms of Section 15 if it substantially complies with its requirements.
Tenants who fail to deliver possession on or before the date specified in the decree are not entitled to the benefits of Section 15(3) of the Act.
Time for vacation of premises is of the essence when the decree is framed under Section 15, even if the agreement is by compromise.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(g)
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 15
doctrines: Substantial compliance with statutory conditions
Time is of the essence in conditional statutory protections
Estoppel not applicable to defeat statutory conditions

card.dispute: R. P. Kapur challenged the continuation of criminal proceedings based on a first information report against him, seeking quashing of the proceedings by the High Court under its inherent powers.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can quash criminal proceedings under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure based on an appreciation of the reliability of evidence?
Whether the delay in police investigation warrants quashing of proceedings?
Whether the allegations in the first information report constitute a valid offence warranting continuation of proceedings?
holdings: The High Court cannot exercise its inherent power under Section 561-A to quash proceedings merely because the evidence may appear unreliable; it can only do so if there is a legal bar, no prima facie case, or manifest lack of evidence.
Inordinate delay in investigation, while deplorable, does not by itself justify quashing criminal proceedings unless it amounts to abuse of process.
The allegations in the first information report were sufficient to constitute the offences charged, and the case must proceed before the trial court to determine the merits.
doctrines: Inherent powers of the High Court
Principle of abuse of process
Prima facie case for prosecution
Separation of powers in criminal trial stages
