card.dispute: The appellant challenged a decree of pre-emption granted to the respondent, who claimed a right to preempt a property sale based on an unregistered agreement and prior transactions, alleging fraud in non-execution of the sale deed.
issues_decided: Whether a right of pre-emption arose under the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, based on an unregistered agreement for sale and not a completed sale deed.
Whether the appellant committed fraud by delaying the execution of the sale deed to defeat the respondent's right of pre-emption.
holdings: No right of pre-emption accrued because a valid sale under the Berar Land Revenue Code requires a transfer of ownership as per the Transfer of Property Act, which necessitates a registered sale deed; an unregistered agreement does not constitute a pre-emptible transaction.
Delay in executing the sale deed was not fraudulent; parties may lawfully avoid pre-emption by legitimate means, and no equity favours a pre-emptor seeking to disrupt a valid, pending transaction.
doctrines: Pre-emption requires a perfected sale
Statutory law overrides personal or customary law in property transfers
No equity in favour of pre-emptor
Fraud not presumed in lawful avoidance of pre-emption

card.dispute: The appellant, as Receiver of an estate, challenged the respondent's claim for unpaid mining rents and royalties under a 1919 lease, disputing the validity of acknowledgments that affected limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the acknowledgments of debt in letters by a former Receiver were conditional and thus invalid under Section 19 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether an acknowledgment by a Receiver of an estate constitutes an acknowledgment by an agent 'duly authorised' under Explanation II to Section 19 of the Limitation Act
holdings: Acknowledgments in the letters were not conditional; the offer to pay upon acceptance did not make the statement of debt dependent on such acceptance.

It is unnecessary to decide whether a Receiver is inherently a 'duly authorised' agent under Section 19, as the acknowledgments were made personally by prior Receivers under a lease executed in their favour, bringing them within the plain terms of the section.
provisions: Indian Limitation Act, 1908, Explanation II to Section 19
doctrines: Interpretation of dispositive documents: earlier parts prevail over later if irreconcilable
Strict construction against grantor in case of ambiguity
Conditional acknowledgment doctrine under Section 19 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The appellant, Shivji Nathubhai, challenged the Central Government's cancellation of his mining leases without a hearing, after a review application by a rival claimant.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government's power under Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, to review and cancel a State Government's mining lease order is a quasi-judicial function
Whether the principles of natural justice required the Central Government to hear the leaseholder before cancelling the lease
holdings: The Central Government, when acting under Rule 54, performs a quasi-judicial function because it determines rights between opposing parties and is required to act judicially.
The principles of natural justice require that a person whose rights are affected by a quasi-judicial decision must be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard before an adverse order is passed.
doctrines: Quasi-judicial function test from Province of Bombay v. Kushaldas S. Advani
Principles of natural justice: audi alteram partem

card.dispute: The legal representative of a watan holder contested the attachment and sale of a building on watan land in execution of a decree, claiming it was either part of inalienable watan property or protected as a residence of an agriculturist.
issues_decided: Whether a building constructed after the creation of watan on watan land becomes part of inalienable watan property under the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874
Whether the appellant qualifies as an 'agriculturist' under Section 60(1), proviso (c), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and if the building is protected from attachment
holdings: A building constructed subsequent to the creation of watan does not automatically become inalienable watan property merely by being situated on watan land; the inalienable character under the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act applies only to the originally granted property.

An 'agriculturist' under Section 60(1), proviso (c), CPC, is any person engaged in agriculture, regardless of other income sources or scale of operation, and a building used for agricultural purposes and occupied by such a person is protected from attachment and sale.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 60(1), proviso (b) and (c)
doctrines: Accession does not alter legal character of inalienable property
Literal interpretation of 'agriculturist' in exemption clauses
Public policy basis for execution exemptions

card.dispute: The appellant and the plaintiff-respondent fought over the right to hold a maintenance grant (potgi) of village Dindur and survey field No. 302 within a Saranjam estate after the death of the previous holder, with the plaintiff claiming rights through adoption and the appellant claiming by survivorship.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's Resolution of December 17, 1941, continuing the potgi holding in favor of the appellant was valid and effective despite a subsequent adoption by the widow of the deceased holder.
Whether the plaintiff-respondent could rely on a family custom of lineal primogeniture to claim the property, and whether such custom could override Government's discretion under the Saranjam Rules.
Whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit challenging the Government's order regarding Saranjam lands under Section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876.
holdings: The Government's Resolution of December 17, 1941, was a valid resumption and regrant of the potgi holding in favor of the appellant, and it was not rendered ineffective by a subsequent adoption未经 government sanction.

The plaintiff-respondent failed to plead or prove a family custom of lineal primogeniture that would divest the appellant’s rights upon adoption, and no such custom could override the Government's discretionary power under the Saranjam Rules.
The suit was barred by Section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, as it involved a claim against the Government in relation to Saranjam lands, over which Civil Courts lack jurisdiction.
doctrines: Sovereign discretion in political tenures
Bar on civil court jurisdiction over revenue matters
Custom must be proved to override statutory or governmental authority

card.dispute: The plaintiff, V (adopted son of a widow of a junior family member), challenged the Government's order continuing a maintenance grant (Saranjam potgi) to D (undivided brother of the deceased), claiming the lands by custom of lineal primogeniture after adoption.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's order of December 17, 1941, continuing the maintenance grant was ultra vires or void?
Whether the custom of lineal primogeniture applied to devolve the maintenance grant on the adopted son?
Whether the suit was barred by Section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876?
holdings: The Government's order continuing the maintenance grant was a valid resumption and re-grant under the Saranjam Rules and did not become void due to an unauthorized adoption.
The plaintiff failed to prove the existence and extent of a family custom of lineal primogeniture that would override the Saranjam Rules or bind the Government.
The suit was barred under Section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, as it involved a claim against the Government regarding Saranjam lands.
doctrines: Saranjam tenure is at the pleasure of the Government and subject to resumption and re-grant
Custom must be specifically pleaded and proved to override statutory or administrative authority
Civil courts lack jurisdiction over claims challenging government orders on Saranjam lands

card.dispute: The appellant contested the respondents' application for accounts and appointment of a receiver under the Arbitration Act, arguing that a necessary party was not joined and that allegations of fraud barred arbitration.
issues_decided: Whether a dispute can be referred to arbitration when a person with an interest in the subject matter is not a party to the arbitration proceedings.
Whether allegations regarding inaccuracies in accounts and suspicions of misappropriation amount to serious fraud that would prevent referral to arbitration.
holdings: A dispute may be referred to arbitration even if a person with an interest in the subject matter is not a party, provided their share is not in dispute.
Allegations that accounts are incomplete, incorrect, or that there is a risk of future misappropriation do not constitute serious fraud sufficient to deny arbitration.
doctrines: Separability of arbitration agreements
Serious allegations of fraud exception to arbitration
Court's discretion under Section 20 to refer disputes to arbitration unless sufficient cause exists

card.dispute: The dispute was between Muslim family members over whether female descendants were entitled to a share of surplus income from a religious endowment and to perform religious duties, despite a family custom excluding women.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for declaration of rights with consequential relief is maintainable under the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, as amended, overrides a custom excluding females from sharing income of a religious endowment
Whether the right to receive income from the endowment is conditional upon performing religious offices like Peshimam, Khatib, and Mujavar
holdings: A suit for declaration of rights with consequential relief, such as injunction, is not barred by limitation under Article 120 unless there is a denial or threat to the right; limitation runs from the date of infringement or clear threat.

The Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, as amended by the Madras Amendment Act of 1949, supersedes contrary customs in matters of wakfs and succession, entitling female members to share in the income of the endowment.
The right to receive income from the endowment is not conditional upon performing religious duties, especially where duties can be performed through deputies and no such condition is recorded.
provisions: Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 (26 of 1937), Section 2
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application (Madras Amendment) Act, 1949 (Mad. 18 of 1949), Section 2
doctrines: Presumption against retrospectivity of statutes
Rule of decision under Shariat in Muslim personal law matters
Maintainability of declaratory suits with consequential relief
Supersession of customs by statutory personal law

card.dispute: The appellant claimed absolute ownership of properties acquired by his uncle and two nephews, asserting they were joint Hindu family property with rights of survivorship, while the respondent, a widow, claimed a share through inheritance.
issues_decided: Whether the properties jointly acquired by an uncle and his two nephews could be considered joint Hindu family property entitled to the incident of survivorship
Whether members of different branches of a Hindu joint family can form a separate corporate unit to acquire joint family property
Whether the decree passed by the Revenue Court operated as res judicata in the subsequent civil suit
holdings: Properties acquired by members of different branches of a joint Hindu family cannot be treated as joint family property unless there is a reunion or blending with the ancestral estate.
Hindu law does not recognize a joint tenancy with rights of survivorship among members of different branches of a family unless they constitute a coparcenary under Mitakshara law.
The decree of the Revenue Court on proprietary title, once confirmed by the Civil Court, operates as res judicata in a subsequent civil suit on the same issue.
doctrines: Res judicata
Mitakshara coparcenary
Survivorship in Hindu law
Blending of separate property with joint family property
Reunion of divided family

card.dispute: Joint family members of Ramjidas, who built a dharmasala, temple, and shops on government land with permission, were evicted by the state and its officers, and challenged the eviction as a violation of their fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners, as joint family members managing the property, were trespassers on government land.
Whether the state could evict the petitioners by executive action without legal proceedings.
Whether the eviction violated the petitioners' fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.
holdings: The petitioners were not trespassers as they constructed and managed the buildings with government permission and in good faith.
The state cannot evict persons in bona fide possession through executive action alone; dispossession must follow legal procedure.
The executive eviction violated the petitioners' fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31, as it was arbitrary and without legal authority.
doctrines: Rule of law
Protection against arbitrary executive action
Fundamental rights to property and equality
Bona fide possession with permission negates trespass
Rejection of absolute application of 'quicquid plantatur solo, solo cedit'

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a joint Hindu family over whether a mortgagee right belonged to the family or was partitioned as separate property, and whether a suit to enforce the mortgage was maintainable despite non-joinder of a family member.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable despite the non-joinder of the step-mother, a co-sharer in the mortgagee right?
Whether the failure of the plaintiff to describe himself as manager in the plaint barred the suit from being treated as one filed on behalf of the joint family?
Whether the mortgagee right was kept undivided at the time of partition among the family branches?
holdings: Non-joinder of a proper but not necessary party does not render a suit non-maintainable nor triggers Section 22 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
A suit filed by the manager of an undivided Hindu family is valid even if he does not describe himself as manager; the substance of the pleading determines the capacity in which the suit is filed.
The mortgagee right was not partitioned but kept undivided among the family branches, and thus remained joint family property enforceable by the family.
doctrines: Non-joinder of parties (proper vs necessary party distinction)
Maintainability of suits by Hindu joint family managers
Doctrine of relation back in execution sales (implied)
Presumption of joint family property in absence of clear partition

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant, claiming personal need for the premises and that the tenant had acquired a suitable residence, but the tenant used part of the premises for professional work with the landlord's consent.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord can seek ejectment under Section 13(1)(e) when the premises are used for both residence and profession with consent?
Whether a tenant can be evicted under Section 13(1)(h) solely on acquiring a suitable residence if the tenancy is for both residence and professional use?
Whether the premises cease to be 'premises' under Section 2(g) when used for combined residential and professional purposes?
Whether the tenant is estopped from arguing dual use after previously claiming residential tenancy for benefit?
holdings: Premises let for residence but used with landlord's consent for professional purposes cease to be solely residential, so ejectment under Section 13(1)(e) is not permissible.
A tenancy used for both residence and profession cannot be terminated under Section 13(1)(h) merely because the tenant acquired a suitable residence, as professional needs remain unmet.
Premises used for both residential and professional purposes continue to fall under Section 2(g) of the Act as 'premises' under the 'other use' category.
A party cannot raise a new plea of approbation and reprobation for the first time in appeal without adducing evidence, especially when both parties acted inconsistently.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 2(g)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(e)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(h)
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions
User of premises altering statutory rights
Res judicata and estoppel in tenancy disputes

card.dispute: The appellants, who occupied shops owned by the New Delhi Municipal Committee and paid monthly amounts described as rent, sought to have their rent standardized under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, but the Committee contested the maintainability of the applications on the ground that no landlord-tenant relationship existed due to non-compliance with statutory formalities.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties within the meaning of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, in the absence of a validly executed contract under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911
Whether the applications under Section 8 of the Rent Control Act were maintainable without a legally enforceable transfer of interest in the property
Whether the mandatory formalities under Section 47 of the Punjab Municipal Act could be bypassed by estoppel or part performance
holdings: A landlord-tenant relationship under the Rent Control Act requires a valid transfer of interest in immovable property, which must comply with the mandatory formalities of Section 47 of the Punjab Municipal Act.

The mere payment of monthly amounts described as rent does not create a landlord-tenant relationship if the underlying contract is unenforceable due to non-compliance with mandatory statutory requirements.

A statutory body like the Municipal Committee cannot be estopped from asserting that a contract is unenforceable when it was entered into without complying with mandatory procedural requirements under its enabling statute.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Sections 2(c), 2(g), 2(j), 8, 38
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory statutory provisions
Ultra vires acts of statutory bodies
Doctrine of estoppel not applicable against statutory corporations violating mandatory legal formalities
Requirement of valid transfer of interest to create landlord-tenant relationship

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant after the contractual tenancy expired, but the tenant claimed continued tenancy rights due to rent payments accepted by the landlord under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether acceptance of rent by the landlord after expiration of a contractual tenancy creates a new tenancy under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether a tenant continuing in possession under statutory protection acquires rights of a 'tenant holding over'
holdings: Acceptance of rent by a landlord after the expiration of a contractual tenancy does not create a new tenancy if the tenant remains in possession due to statutory rent control protections.
A tenant's continued occupation under rent control laws, without fresh agreement, does not amount to a tenancy holding over under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950, Section 12
doctrines: Tenant holding over under Section 116
Statutory tenancy vs contractual tenancy
Effect of rent control legislation on lease continuation

card.dispute: The appellant Fazal Bhai Dhala challenged the Custodian-General's declaration that properties transferred from his brother, an evacuee, were evacuee properties, claiming they were validly transferred before migration.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of immovable properties and dissolution of partnership between Fazal Bhai and his brother Abdulla Bhai were bona fide under the Evacuee Property Act
Whether the Custodian had jurisdiction to set aside the Assistant Custodian's order confirming the transfer and dissolution without specifically mentioning the business in the show-cause notice
Whether the entire properties in Schedules A and B or only Abdulla Bhai's 8 annas share constituted evacuee property after the amendment to the Act
holdings: A transfer of property by an evacuee is ineffective if not bona fide, even if part of a partnership dissolution, and such transfers are void under s. 40 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950.

The Custodian can exercise revisional jurisdiction over a transaction if the party had reasonable opportunity to be heard, even if the notice did not explicitly mention all aspects, provided the context made the scope clear.

Only the evacuee's share in the property, not the entire property, vests as evacuee property, especially after the amendment to s. 2(f) limiting it to 'property of an evacuee' rather than 'property in which an evacuee has interest'.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(f)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 40
Government of India Ordinance No. XXVII of 1949, Section 7(1)
doctrines: Bona fide test for transfers involving evacuee property
Revisional jurisdiction with principles of natural justice
Constructive notice and opportunity of being heard
Vesting of only the evacuee's interest in custodian, not entire property

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an arbitration award was valid despite being made after the statutory time limit, based on a notice to the arbitrators to act after they had already entered on the reference.
issues_decided: Whether the period for making an arbitration award under Rule 3 of the First Schedule to the Arbitration Act, 1940 begins from the date the arbitrators enter on the reference or from a later notice to act by a party.
Whether a party can extend the time for making an award by serving a notice to act after the arbitrators have already entered on the reference.
Whether the arbitrators retained jurisdiction to make an award after the statutory period had expired, in expectation of court extension under Section 28.
holdings: Rule 3 of the First Schedule to the Arbitration Act, 1940 is mandatory and prescribes a fixed time limit for making an award, computed from the date the arbitrators enter on the reference unless a notice to act is given within that four-month period.
A notice to act given after the expiry of four months from the date the arbitrators entered on the reference does not restart the time period; such a notice is ineffective to extend the limitation.

Arbitrators remain competent to act after the statutory period only if they proceed in expectation of court extension under Section 28, but in this case, no such valid basis existed due to untimely notice.
doctrines: Functus officio
Mandatory time limits in arbitration
Judicial extension of limitation period
Notice to act doctrine

card.dispute: The benamidar (nominee) sued for possession based on a conveyance that was part of a collusive plan to defraud creditors; the real owners resisted, alleging the conveyance was fraudulent and void.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants were estopped from pleading fraud in defence of a suit based on a benami conveyance executed to defraud creditors.
Whether public policy permits a court to enforce a decree based on a fraudulent conveyance where both parties were complicit in the fraud.
Whether Section 84 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, is the exclusive source for invoking equitable principles in cases of illegal or fraudulent transfers.
holdings: There can be no estoppel against a party pleading fraud in defence when both parties are equally guilty of the fraudulent transaction.
Courts must apply public policy to refuse relief to either party in a fraudulent conveyance, leaving the property where it is to avoid endorsing illegality.
Section 84 of the Indian Trusts Act is not exhaustive; courts may invoke general equitable principles and public policy in cases outside its scope.
doctrines: Ex turpi causa non oritur actio
In pari delicto potior est conditio defendentis
Public policy against enforcing illegal or fraudulent transactions
Fraud vitiates all transactions ab initio

card.dispute: The landlord (Jyoti Pershad) fought against the Administrator of Delhi over the refusal to execute eviction decrees due to restrictions imposed under the Slum Areas Act, arguing it violated his constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether Section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 is unconstitutional for violating Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution by imposing unreasonable restrictions on property rights.
Whether the power conferred under Section 19(3) of the Slum Areas Act is unguided and arbitrary, thus rendering it invalid.
Whether the Rent Control Act's non obstante clause in Section 38 excludes the application of the Slum Areas Act, making Section 19 inapplicable.
holdings: Section 19 of the Slum Areas Act imposes reasonable restrictions on property rights under Article 19(1)(f), justified by the pressing social need to protect slum-dwellers during slum clearance, and is not violative of Articles 14 or 19(1)(f).

The discretion under Section 19(3) is not unguided or arbitrary, as the Act's preamble and provisions indicate policy limits, and appellate review ensures against misuse, making the restriction constitutionally valid.

The Slum Areas Act, especially Section 19, applies despite the Rent Control Act’s non obstante clause, as both statutes operate in tandem, with the special law (Slum Areas Act) providing additional safeguards in declared slum areas.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 38
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 39
doctrines: Reasonableness of restriction under Article 19(5)
Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Principle of judicial notice of social conditions

card.dispute: The appellant, a co-owner and lessee of a flour mill, contested the receiver's right to dispossess him after the lease expired, arguing that the receiver ceased to function after the final decree and that dispossession required a civil suit, not a summary process.
issues_decided: Whether the receiver continued in office after the final decree when the preliminary decree ordered continuation until discharge and the final decree was silent on the matter.
Whether the receiver could dispossess the appellant (a party to the suit) by summary procedure under Order 40 of the CPC after the lease term ended, or whether a civil suit was necessary.
holdings: A receiver appointed by a preliminary decree continues in office until formally discharged, even after a final decree, if the decree does not terminate the receivership and the suit’s subject matter remains under court supervision.

The court may authorize a receiver to recover possession summarily from a party to the suit, especially where the party agreed to surrender possession upon lease expiry as part of a court-approved arrangement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 40, Rule 1(1)(b) and (d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 40, Rule 1(2)
doctrines: Continuation of receivership beyond final decree
Summary enforcement of undertakings given to the court
Court's inherent power to manage property through a receiver

card.dispute: Members of a joint Hindu family fought over whether a prior partition of family property by appointed arbitrators (Panchas) was binding, and whether a suit for partition of remaining properties was maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether the partial partition carried out by the Panchas was binding on the parties despite the later revocation of the arbitration reference
Whether the suit for partition of remaining properties was maintainable after partial division by arbitrators
Whether the documents recording the partition by Panchas required compulsory registration under the Registration Act
holdings: A partition effected by agreement and implemented through division by appointed Panchas is binding, and the parties cease to be members of a joint Hindu family upon such division.
A suit for partition is maintainable only for the undivided properties, as the already-divided properties are no longer part of the joint family estate.
Documents recording partition by arbitrators, which do not create or transfer rights in immovable property, do not require compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of binding family partition by arbitration (Panchayat)
Doctrine of severance of joint family status upon effective partition
Doctrine of severability in partition: completed division vs. incomplete division

card.dispute: The assessee company fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether increased salami received from sub-leasing coal-mining rights constituted taxable business profits or non-taxable capital appreciation.
issues_decided: Whether the activity of acquiring and sub-leasing coal-mining leases constituted a business under the company's memorandum of association.
Whether the enhanced salami received from sub-lessees was income from business profits or appreciation of capital.
Whether such income was liable to be included in assessable income under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
holdings: Acquiring head leases and granting sub-leases was a business activity within the company's memorandum of association.
The increased salami from sub-leases represented profits from business, not mere appreciation of capital.
Such profits were taxable as business income under the Income-tax Act, 1922, since the company operated as a trader, not a passive landowner.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Business profit vs. income from property distinction
Intention and nature of dealing as determining factor for tax classification

card.dispute: Kesar Singh and another resisted Balwant Singh's civil suit for possession of a bunga, claiming adverse possession and challenging Balwant Singh's status as a descendant of Maharaja Sher Singh entitled to sue.
issues_decided: Whether the Civil Court could examine Balwant Singh's claim to be a descendant of Maharaja Sher Singh despite the Sikh Gurdwaras Tribunal's earlier decision.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Articles 142 or 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
Whether the suit was barred by Order IX Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to a prior dismissed application under Section 25A of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act.
holdings: Sections 36 and 37 of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925 bar any civil court from questioning the Tribunal's final decision, including the recognition of descendants of Maharaja Sher Singh as managers, thereby precluding a challenge to Balwant Singh's lineage in a subsequent suit.

The suit was not barred by limitation because the appellants were in permissive possession as servitors; no adverse possession was established prior to 1933, and thus the 12-year period under Article 144 had not fully run before the 1943 suit.
The appellant could not raise the bar of Order IX Rule 9 CPC as no issue was framed on it in trial court and no evidence was led; the point was not open for consideration in appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order IX Rule 9
doctrines: Finality of tribunal decisions under special statutes
Permissive possession not amounting to adverse possession
Res judicata and issue estoppel in statutory tribunals
Limitation period starting only upon hostile assertion of title

card.dispute: The petitioner, Burrakur Coal Co., Ltd., challenged the validity of a notification under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, arguing that it did not apply to mines that were previously worked but temporarily closed.
issues_decided: Whether the Act applies only to virgin or unworked land, excluding mines previously worked but currently dormant
Whether the provisions of the Act infringe Article 31(2) of the Constitution by not providing adequate compensation for mineral rights
Whether the challenge to the acquisition law is barred by Article 31A(1)(e) of the Constitution
holdings: The term 'unworked land' in the Act includes mines that were previously worked but are currently not in operation, as long as no active mining is ongoing at the time of notification.
The Act satisfies Article 31(2) because it specifies principles and manner for determining compensation; adequacy of compensation cannot be challenged in court due to the proviso in Article 31(2).
Article 31A(1)(e) bars challenges to the validity of the Act on grounds of infringement of Article 31(2), as the law falls within the scope of laws protecting acquisition of mineral-bearing land.
provisions: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14
doctrines: Doctrine of presumption of constitutionality
Doctrine of severability not invoked as entire Act upheld
Doctrine that adequacy of compensation cannot be questioned if procedural requirements of Article 31(2) are met

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of the Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1961, arguing that it violated equality and compensation rights, particularly by exempting certain plantations from land ceiling and acquisition provisions.
issues_decided: Whether ryotwari lands from the former Madras State qualify as 'estates' under Article 31A(2) of the Constitution, thereby shielding the Act from equality challenges
Whether the classification exempting tea, coffee, rubber, and cardamom plantations from land ceiling and acquisition provisions violates Article 14
Whether certain rules under the Act creating a rehabilitation fund exceed the scope of the enabling provision
holdings: Ryotwari lands do not constitute 'estates' under Article 31A(2) where the existing land tenure law does not include them, thus the Act is subject to scrutiny under Article 14.

The exemption of tea, coffee, rubber, and cardamom plantations from land ceiling and acquisition provisions, without regard to size or economic scale, lacks rational basis and violates Article 14; the classification is arbitrary and not justified.
Rules extending the agriculturist rehabilitation fund to persons not affected by the Act are ultra vires Section 80 of the Act and must be struck down.
provisions: The Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1961, Sections 2(39), 3(viii), 52, 57, 58, 59, 64, 80
doctrines: Equal protection under Article 14
Doctrine of classification
Colourable legislation
Severability of unconstitutional provisions

card.dispute: The creditors of certain debtors challenged the validity of property transfers made by trustees to relatives of the trustees, alleging breach of trust and seeking declaration that the properties remained under trust for equitable distribution.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deeds executed by only two of the three trustees were valid under the trust deed requiring majority or unanimous decision?
Whether the transfers to close relatives of the trustees violated the prohibition under the Indian Trusts Act against trustees or their associates purchasing trust property?
Whether the delegation of trustees' duties to a purchaser for redistribution among creditors was lawful?
Whether the transfers were for grossly inadequate consideration and thus voidable as fraudulent alienations?
holdings: A sale by only two trustees was invalid because the trust deed required decisions by majority or unanimity, and such collective decision-making was not followed.
Transfers to relatives of a trustee were invalid under Section 52 of the Indian Trusts Act, which prohibits trustees or their agents from purchasing trust property directly or indirectly.

Delegation of the trustee’s duty to sell to a purchaser who then redistributed property to creditors was unlawful under Section 47 of the Indian Trusts Act, as no power of delegation was granted in the trust instrument.
Transfers for grossly inadequate consideration, without proper valuation and to related parties, were voidable as they constituted intermeddling with the trust estate and breached fiduciary duties.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 8
doctrines: Res judicata in representative suits
Trustee de son tort
Fiduciary duty of trustees
Prohibition on self-dealing by trustees
Inadequacy of consideration as evidence of fraud

card.dispute: The appellants claimed that certain properties, including those held by a Hindu female in limited ownership and those acquired via a compromise decree, should be treated as part of the joint family property of their husband or managed for the family's benefit.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of blending applies to property held by a Hindu female in limited ownership
Whether properties acquired by a family member through a compromise decree belong to the joint family or are his individual property
Whether a manager of a joint family must prove that litigation expenses were borne from separate funds to claim individual ownership of acquired property
holdings: The doctrine of blending cannot apply to property held by a Hindu female as a limited owner because she cannot extinguish her title to merge it into the joint family property.
Properties acquired through a compromise decree in a suit filed by the family manager with family consent and using joint funds belong to the joint family, not the individual manager.
A manager claiming that property was acquired with separate funds must prove it by clear and satisfactory evidence; otherwise, it is presumed to be acquired with joint family funds.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statute, based on customary and case law)
doctrines: Doctrine of blending
Limited estate under Hindu law
Burden of proof in joint family property disputes
Manager's fiduciary duty in joint Hindu family

card.dispute: The respondent sued the appellant for rent arrears and ejectment based on a rent note; the appellant claimed the suit was barred by res judicata due to a prior dismissed suit involving the same parties and cause of action.
issues_decided: Whether the present suit is barred by res judicata despite the prior suit being dismissed on a preliminary objection of defect of parties?
Whether the word 'suit' in Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure includes a part of a suit or an issue within it?
Whether the earlier court's lack of pecuniary jurisdiction affects the application of res judicata?
Whether appellant 1 was a co-lessor under the rent note, making her joinder necessary?
holdings: The word 'suit' in Section 11 must be construed literally to mean the entire suit, not a part or issue, and thus res judicata does not apply to a subsequent suit not fully within the prior court's jurisdiction.
A court must have concurrent jurisdiction—both pecuniary and subject-matter—over the earlier and subsequent suits for res judicata to apply.
The prior dismissal on grounds of non-joinder did not amount to a decision on merits, and thus did not create res judicata.
The rent note recognized the respondent as the sole owner; inclusion of appellant 1 was ceremonial, not indicative of co-ownership.
doctrines: Res judicata
Literal construction of statutory terms
Principle of concurrent jurisdiction
Estoppel by deed or conduct

card.dispute: The appellant landlord sued for rent arrears in the City Civil Court for buildings constructed on leased open land, while the respondents argued that the Bombay Rent Control Act applied, vesting jurisdiction in special courts, not the City Civil Court.
issues_decided: Whether leasing open land for construction of buildings for residential or business purposes constitutes 'letting for residence or business' under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the City Civil Court had jurisdiction to try suits for rent in respect of such premises
holdings: The phrase 'let for residence, education, business, trade or storage' in Section 6 includes leasing open land intended for construction of buildings for those purposes, regardless of whether structures are built.
Premises let for construction of residential or business buildings fall under Part II of the Bombay Rent Act, and thus only special courts under Section 28 have jurisdiction to entertain rent suits.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 6
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 25
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Part II, Schedule I
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Purpose and object of rent control legislation
Jurisdictional exclusivity of special courts under rent control laws

card.dispute: The petitioner, N. Kasturi, claimed a vested interest in half the testator's property under a will in the absence of adoption, while the respondents argued that the clause on which he relied only operated at the time of the testator's death and did not create a contingent future interest.
issues_decided: Whether clause 12 of the will created a vested interest in the appellant subject to defeasance by subsequent adoption.
Whether clause 12 operated at the time of the testator's death or continued to operate thereafter.
Whether the appellant could claim rights under clause 12 in the absence of adoption by the widow.
holdings: Clause 12 of the will was intended to operate only at the time of the testator's death and not thereafter, and thus did not create a continuing contingent interest.
The appellant's rights under the will are governed solely by clause 11, which requires his adoption by the widow before any interest vests in him.
A construction of clause 12 that would read 'and' as 'or' leads to inconsistencies with other clauses and is not supported by the will's language or intent.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 (by context, though not explicitly cited)
doctrines: Rule against postponement of vesting
Testator's intention as gathered from the will as a whole
Clarity and consistency in construction of wills
Avoidance of intestacy as a principle, but not overriding clear testamentary language

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether a decree passed on an arbitration award, as modified by a compromise, was valid and executable.
issues_decided: Whether a court can modify an arbitration award by incorporating a compromise between the parties
Whether a decree based on a compromised award is a nullity if it departs from the original award
Whether the court has jurisdiction to pass a decree reflecting a post-award compromise under the Arbitration Act and CPC
holdings: A court may uphold a compromise that modifies an arbitration award if the changes are within the scope of the original reference and do not invalidate the award.
Where parties modify an award by compromise but do not discard it entirely, the unaltered parts remain binding and the decree incorporating the modification is valid.

If the compromise terms are severable and within the reference, the court may include accepted terms in the operative part of the decree and others in a schedule, with only the operative part being executable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3
doctrines: Enforceability of compromise agreements in arbitration
Doctrine of severability in decree formulation
Court's duty to uphold valid compromises under CPC

card.dispute: Rabia Bai challenged the Custodian-General's rejection of her application to confirm a property sale from an evacuee who sold it before evacuee laws were extended to Madras.
issues_decided: Whether the sale transaction was entered into in good faith under s. 40(4)(a) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether a transaction completed just before the extension of evacuee law to Madras, with knowledge of its impending application, could be rejected for lacking good faith
holdings: A transaction is not in good faith under s. 40(4)(a) if it was deliberately made to evade the application of evacuee laws, even if no such law was in force at the time.
The expression 'good faith' in s. 40(4)(a) must be interpreted contextually, considering the Act's objective to protect evacuee property, not merely as honest belief under the General Clauses Act.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 40(4)(a)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 40(1)
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Purpose and object of emergency legislation
Retrospective application of law to prevent evasion

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an arbitration award in a partition suit, arguing that the limitation period for filing an objection had not begun due to lack of written notice of the award's filing, and sought appeal against the court's decision to uphold the award.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation for filing an objection to set aside an arbitration award begins only upon written notice of the award's filing
Whether the court's order to file the award and pass a decree amounts to a refusal to set aside the award, making it appealable
holdings: The period of limitation under Article 158 of the Limitation Act begins when the parties or their counsel are orally informed of the award's filing; written notice is not mandatory under Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act.

An order recording an award and decreeing accordingly, in the absence of any filed objection, does not amount to a refusal to set aside the award and is not appealable under Section 39(1)(vi) of the Arbitration Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order III, Rule 5
doctrines: Notice to counsel is notice to party
Constructive service of notice
Strict compliance with limitation for challenging awards
No appeal without a formal refusal to set aside an award

card.dispute: The appellant, P. J. Irani, challenged the validity of a government order exempting his leased cinema premises from rent control laws, which allowed him to evict the tenant, Chettiar, who resisted eviction under the protection of the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government's order under Section 13 of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1949, exempting a building from rent control provisions, was ultra vires or unconstitutional under Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the Government's exercise of power under Section 13 was for an extraneous purpose or amounted to an abuse of power
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the Government's exemption order on the ground that the reasons given were insufficient
holdings: The power under Section 13 of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1949, to exempt buildings from rent control is valid and does not violate Article 14 if exercised for legitimate purposes connected with the object of the Act.

The Government's decision to exempt premises from rent control is not subject to judicial review on merits; courts can only examine whether the power was used for an extraneous or ulterior purpose, which was not shown here.
The High Court erred in substituting its own view for that of the Government; as long as the reasons relate to the object of the Act, the order is valid even if some reasons are weak or irrelevant.
provisions: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1949, Section 13
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers
Principle of judicial review limited to legality, not merits
Doctrine of legitimate expectation and fair conduct in administrative action
Test of 'extraneous purpose' in statutory discretion

card.dispute: National Cement Mines Industries, Ltd. fought the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether a payment received from Associated Cement Ltd. was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the receipt of Rs. 77,820 by the appellants under the deed dated May 7, 1935, was of a revenue or capital nature.
Whether the transaction involving the conveyance of rights with a profit-sharing mechanism constituted a commercial arrangement yielding income.
holdings: The receipt under the deed was not a repayment of capital but a share in the profits of a commercial activity, and therefore constituted taxable income.
A transaction conveying property rights while retaining a share in future profits based on sales or production is substantially commercial and yields revenue receipts, not capital.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Substance over form in characterizing income
Commercial nature of profit-sharing transactions

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the acquisition of his land under the Land Acquisition Act for a private company's textile machinery factory, arguing it did not serve a public purpose and violated statutory safeguards.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land for a private company to set up a textile machinery parts factory serves a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether compliance with Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, particularly Sections 40 and 41, is mandatory when land is acquired for a company
Whether the public's inability to use the work directly negates the public purpose requirement
holdings: Acquisition for a private company's factory that produces essential goods like textile machinery parts serves a public purpose if the government reasonably believes it benefits the public.

The provisions of Part VII, including Sections 40 and 41, are not rendered inoperative merely because the public cannot directly use the work; the government has discretion to determine the extent and terms of public use.

The inability of the public to directly access or use the work does not invalidate the acquisition, as public purpose is not contingent on physical public access but on the utility of the work to the community.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine in land acquisition
Principle of harmonious construction to resolve statutory inconsistency
Presumption of constitutionality and non-justiciability of government satisfaction under statutory acquisition
Beneficial construction of statutes to effect legislative intent

card.dispute: The trustees of a temple sought to resume inam lands granted to the ancestors of the respondents for performing temple service, after the grantees alienated parts of the land and discontinued the service, arguing the alienation was void under the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act.
issues_decided: Whether section 44-B(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927 applies to personal inams burdened with service.
Whether the revenue authorities had jurisdiction to resume personal inam lands for non-performance of service and alienation under the Act.
Whether personal inams burdened with service are resumable in their entirety for failure to perform service.
holdings: Section 44-B(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act applies only to service grants or inams meant wholly for charity, not to personal inams burdened with service.
Revenue authorities cannot resume personal inams burdened with service under section 44-B for alienation or non-performance of service, as such inams fall outside the scope of the provision.
A personal inam burdened with service may only have the portion representing the service value resumed, not the entire grant, unless the grant conditions expressly allow full resumption.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, No. 11 of 1927, Section 44-B(1)
Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, No. 11 of 1927, Section 44-B(2)(a)(i) and (ii)
Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, No. 11 of 1927, Section 44-B(2)(f)(i) and (ii)
doctrines: Distinction between service grants and personal grants burdened with service
Principle of statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and context
Doctrine of partial resumption for conditional grants

card.dispute: Holders of Khor Posh maintenance grants from former princely states challenged the constitutional validity of orders annulling their grants after the states merged with India.
issues_decided: Whether the abrogation of maintenance grants by executive action was valid under the Extra-Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947
Whether continued payment of a grant after merger created a enforceable right
Whether a grant recognized and paid by the new administration could be terminated by a mere executive statement
Whether Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, protected pre-merger rights automatically
holdings: An order under Section 4 of the Extra-Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947, has legislative effect and can validly abrogate a grant, even if previously recognized by custom or local law.
Where a maintenance grant was recognized and continuously paid after merger, the right became enforceable and could not be terminated by a mere executive declaration.
Sections 3 and 4 of the Extra-Provincial Jurisdiction Act must be read harmoniously; Section 3 cannot override the specific powers under Section 4.
Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, does not automatically protect or enforce rights from former princely states unless those rights were recognized by the new sovereign.
provisions: Administration of Orissa States Order, 1948, Para. 4(b)
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Doctrine of recognition of rights post-merger
Legislative character of executive orders under special statutes
No act of state against one's own subjects

card.dispute: The appellants claimed a limited right as permanent lessees by adverse possession over jagir land held by the respondent, whose ancestors had been granted the jagir by the Nizam of Hyderabad.
issues_decided: Whether a permanent leasehold interest can be acquired by adverse possession in a jagir granted for life only?
Whether the period of adverse possession against one jagirdar can be tacked to that against a successor jagirdar for limitation purposes?
Whether jagirs in Hyderabad were hereditary and permanent, allowing for perpetual alienations like leases?
holdings: A limited interest in property can be acquired by adverse possession, but not a permanent lease in a jagir that is inherently life-term unless the grant itself provides for perpetuity.
Adverse possession cannot be tacked across successive jagirdars; limitation under Article 144 of the Indian Limitation Act starts afresh with each grantee’s title.

Jagirs in Hyderabad were not hereditary or permanent; each successor held under a fresh grant, and the State retained the right to resume, so jagirdars could not create alienations binding beyond their lifetime.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Tacking of possession
Life tenure of jagirs
State's residual control over grants

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the fixation of standard rent by Rent Controllers for newly constructed premises, arguing the law was unconstitutional and violated natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether Section 7A and Schedule IV of the Delhi and Ajmer-Marwara Rent Control Act, 1947 violate Article 14 of the Constitution by classifying newly constructed buildings separately.
Whether the procedure under Section 7A and Schedule IV violates the principles of natural justice.
holdings: The classification between premises constructed before and after March 24, 1947 is reasonable and does not violate Article 14.
The procedure for fixing standard rent under Section 7A and Schedule IV does not violate natural justice, as the Rent Controller exercises judicial discretion based on evidence.
provisions: The Delhi and Ajmer-Marwara Rent Control Act, 1947, Section 7A
The Delhi and Ajmer-Marwara Rent Control Act, 1947, Section 7
The Delhi and Ajmer-Marwara Rent Control Act, 1947, Schedule IV
The Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 46
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Principles of natural justice in administrative adjudication
Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Doctrine of saving clause in repeal statutes

card.dispute: The assessee, a tea estate owner, fought with the Income Tax Commissioner over whether compensation received for requisitioned factory buildings during WWII was taxable as revenue receipt or non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation received by the assessee for requisition of factory buildings during 1944–1945 was a revenue receipt liable to tax under section 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether any portion of the compensation could be apportioned as taxable revenue under Rules 23 or 24 of the Income-tax Rules
holdings: Compensation received for compulsory requisition of factory buildings, which resulted in complete stoppage of business, was not income or profit from business and thus not taxable under section 10.
Where no business is carried on, no profits can arise; the compensation was a solatium for non-operation of business and not a revenue receipt, so Rules 23 and 24 do not apply.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Definition of income as profit from continuous business activity
Solatium principle for compensation during business stoppage
Business must be carried on for profits to be taxable under section 10

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an unstamped arbitration award could be remitted to the arbitrator to be re-submitted on stamped paper under the Arbitration Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether want of stamp on an arbitration award constitutes an illegality apparent on the face of the award under Section 16(1)(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the court can remit an unstamped award to the arbitrator to re-submit it on stamped paper under Section 16(1)(c) or Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the arbitrator, after making an award, retains authority to re-copy it on stamped paper
holdings: Want of stamp on an award is a defect external to the award and does not amount to an illegality apparent on its face under Section 16(1)(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
The court cannot remit an award solely for stamping under Section 16(1)(c) because remission requires reconsideration of merits, not a ministerial act like re-stamping.
After making an award, the arbitrator becomes functus officio, and the court cannot use Section 151 of the CPC to direct the arbitrator to re-submit the award on stamped paper.
doctrines: Functus officio
Illegality apparent on the face of the award
Inherent powers of court under Section 151 CPC
Ministerial act vs. judicial reconsideration

card.dispute: The daughter and widow of the testator fought against a distant relative over the validity of a will that disinherited them and left the estate to the relative, who sought letters of administration with the will attached.
issues_decided: Whether the will was duly executed and attested in accordance with the Indian Succession Act, 1925, in the face of suspicious circumstances.
Whether the registration of the will is sufficient by itself to dispel doubts about its genuineness and due execution.
Whether the propounder of the will discharged the burden of proving that the testator knew the nature and contents of the will at the time of execution and registration.
holdings: The due execution and attestation of the will were not proved, as the propounder failed to present credible evidence to dispel the suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
Registration of a will, without more, does not automatically establish its validity; the evidence must show that the testator understood the document as a will and knowingly admitted its execution.

The evidence of the registration officer and identifier did not establish that the testator was aware he was executing a will, and thus the registration failed to cure the defects in execution and attestation.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder in cases of suspicious circumstances
Registration not conclusive proof of a will's validity
Requirement of knowledge and conscious admission in will execution

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and former proprietors disputed over the right to hold melas (fairs) on land after the abolition of proprietary tenures, with the state claiming authority under amended land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, violated Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution by acquiring the right to hold melas without compensation.
Whether the right to hold a mela constitutes a 'right in an estate' under Article 31A of the Constitution.
Whether the amending Act, with retrospective effect, validly acquired rights of ex-proprietors even after they became occupancy raiyats.
holdings: The Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, is a valid law under Article 31A as it provides for acquisition of rights in an 'estate', and thus is protected from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
The right to hold a mela is an interest in land appurtenant to ownership and qualifies as a 'right in an estate' under Article 31A.
The retrospective application of the amending Act means the acquisition is deemed to have occurred when the original Act came into force, and thus pertains to intermediaries' rights, not raiyats'.
provisions: Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, Section 4
Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, Section 7A
Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, Section 7B
Bihar Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1959, Section 7C
doctrines: Doctrine of Retrospective Legislation
Doctrine of Protection under Article 31A
Doctrine of Estate Rights in Land Reform Laws

card.dispute: The petitioners, sisters of a deceased Hyderabad Nawab, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 13(2) of the Hyderabad Atiyat Enquiries Act, 1952, which validated and made final government orders on succession to jagir estates, excluding judicial review and civil court jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether Section 13(2) of the Hyderabad Atiyat Enquiries Act, 1952 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by denying civil court jurisdiction over succession claims to jagir estates?
Whether Section 13(2) infringes Article 19(1)(f) by restricting the right to property?
Whether the Chief Minister's order confirming succession extends to non-Atiyat (private) estates of the deceased Nawab?
holdings: Section 13(2) does not violate Article 14 because jagir estates were not heritable; succession was a matter of re-grant by the State, not a legal right enforceable in civil court.
The provision does not infringe Article 19(1)(f) as the jagir holders had only usufructuary rights, and no fundamental right to property in such estates existed.
The Chief Minister's order confirming succession does not apply to non-Atiyat estates; disputes over such property must be decided by civil courts under personal law.
doctrines: Doctrine of non-justiciability of sovereign grants
Doctrine of finality of administrative orders in succession to jagirs
Distinction between heritable property and usufructuary state grants

card.dispute: The respondent-lessor sued to eject the assignee of the lessee, claiming the lease was a tenancy at will terminable by notice, while the lessee's assignee claimed it was a permanent lease.
issues_decided: Whether the lease created a tenancy at will or a permanent tenancy.
Whether the lessee's right to surrender the lease negated the permanency of the tenancy.
What was the true construction of the lease deed regarding the duration and nature of the tenancy.
holdings: The lease was not a tenancy at will but a permanent tenancy, as the terms showed an intention to create a long-term, heritable, and assignable interest.
The lessee's right to surrender the lease does not negate permanency, as such a stipulation can coexist with a permanent lease for the lessee's benefit.
The nature of a tenancy must be determined by construing the entire lease deed, focusing on the parties' real intention, especially in non-standard lease forms.
doctrines: Doctrine of tenancy by intention
Doctrine of construction of lease deeds as a whole
Presumption of permanency in building leases

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and another appealed against the Patna High Court's decision invalidating a Collector's order annulling a land transfer, challenging the constitutional validity and construction of Section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, as amended.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, as amended, is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution despite not directly providing for acquisition or extinguishment of estate rights.
Whether the second proviso added to Section 4(h) by the 1959 Amendment Act operates retrospectively, requiring confirmation by the State Government for orders made before the amendment.
holdings: Section 4(h) is an integral and ancillary part of the Bihar Land Reforms Act aimed at preventing fraudulent transfers to defeat the Act's objectives, and thus is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution.

The second proviso requiring State Government confirmation for annulment orders applies only prospectively; orders made before the 1959 Amendment required only prior sanction, not subsequent confirmation.
doctrines: Doctrine of Ancillary Powers
Prospective vs Retrospective Operation of Amendments
Doctrine of Harmonious Construction
Protection under Article 31A for laws affecting estate rights

card.dispute: The descendants of Thammiah fought over whether he held occupancy rights in certain lands, with some claiming he was only an annual tenant and others asserting hereditary occupancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether Thammiah was an occupancy ryot entitled to hereditary rights in the land prior to the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908
Whether the term 'jeroyati ryot' in official records indicates possession of occupancy rights
Whether mesne profits could be awarded for a period not claimed in the plaint
holdings: Where a ryot's possession predates permanent settlement and the origin of tenancy is lost in antiquity, the law presumes the ryot holds kudivaram (occupancy rights) and the zamindar holds only melvaram (revenue rights).
The use of the term 'jeroyati ryot' in revenue records does not conclusively establish occupancy rights without contextual or local evidence of its meaning.
Mesne profits cannot be awarded for periods earlier than those specifically claimed in the plaint; the High Court erred in awarding profits from 1935 when only post-1940 claims were made.
provisions: Madras Estates Land Act, 1908 (Mad. 1 of 1908), Section 6
doctrines: Presumption of occupancy rights in favor of long-term ryots
Doctrine of lost grant
Principle of pleadings governing relief in civil suits

card.dispute: The Board of Trustees of Ayurvedic and Unani Tibbia College challenged the constitutional validity of the Tibbia College Act, 1952, which dissolved the Board and transferred its assets and functions to a newly created corporation.
issues_decided: Whether the Delhi State Legislature had the legislative competence to pass the Tibbia College Act, 1952, dissolving a registered society and creating a new corporation.
Whether the Act violated the petitioner's rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 of the Constitution.
Whether the Act was repugnant to the central Societies Registration Act, 1860.
Whether the Act was passed with mala fide intent.
holdings: The Delhi Legislature had competence under Entries 10 and 28 of List III (Concurrent List) to dissolve a charitable trust and transfer its property, as these entries cover trusts and charitable institutions regardless of corporate status.
The pith and substance of the Act was the dissolution of a charitable trust and transfer of its assets, not the incorporation of a new body, and thus fell within state legislative competence.
The Act did not violate the Societies Registration Act, 1860, as it did not abrogate that law but merely extinguished the legal existence of the registered society.
The challenge based on mala fides was rejected due to lack of evidence, and the Act was upheld as constitutionally valid.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I Entry 44
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II Entry 32
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III Entries 10 and 28
Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 22
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of charitable trusts in Concurrent List

card.dispute: The Corporation of Calcutta fought with Sm. Padma Debi over whether it could fix the annual valuation of her property above the standard rent fixed under the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the Corporation can fix the annual rental value of a property higher than the standard rent under the Rent Control Act.
What is the meaning of the phrase 'at the time of assessment' in Section 127(a) of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1923?
holdings: The rental value of a property under the Calcutta Municipal Act cannot be fixed higher than the standard rent determined under the Rent Control Act, as the statutory regime makes higher rents unenforceable and unlawful.
The phrase 'at the time of assessment' refers to the entire period from the initial valuation under Section 131 to the final determination of objections under Section 140 of the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 2(10)(b)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 33(a)
doctrines: Distinction between rating law in England and India
Hypothetical rent doctrine
Statutory interpretation of 'at the time of assessment'
Legislative intent through omission of prohibitory clauses

card.dispute: The appellant charity challenged the reversioner R's suit to set aside property alienations made by a Hindu widow, claiming the transactions were binding due to ratification and legal necessity.
issues_decided: Whether the reversioner R was precluded from challenging the alienation due to ratification by conduct or acceptance of benefits
Whether the alienation by the widow was justified by legal necessity
holdings: Mere acceptance of benefits under a transaction or failure to challenge it during the widow's lifetime does not amount to ratification by a reversioner, especially when the reversioner was a minor and lacked knowledge of his rights.

An alienation by a Hindu widow is not justified by legal necessity if the consideration primarily covers administrative, funeral, or documentation expenses, and lacks clear proof of bona fide debts or pressing needs.
provisions: Hindu Law of Alienation by Widow
Letters of Administration (relevant statutory framework implied)
doctrines: Ratification in Hindu law requires full knowledge and intentional affirmation of rights
Doctrine of legal necessity in alienation by Hindu widows

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and a dealer in conch shells disputed whether lease payments for the right to gather shells from the sea were deductible as revenue expenditure or were non-deductible capital expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the lease money paid by the assessee for gathering conch shells from the sea was a revenue expenditure deductible under Section 10(2)(xy) of the Income Tax Act, 1922
Whether the expenditure was of a capital nature, incurred for acquiring an enduring asset or right
holdings: Expenditure for leasing a coastline to exclusively fish for conch shells is capital in nature as it secures an enduring right, not merely stock-in-trade, and is not deductible as revenue expenditure.
The payment was not for acquiring raw materials but for obtaining a speculative and exclusive right to fish, which constitutes a capital asset, even if the rights are non-transferable.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Enduring benefit test
Acquisition of an asset vs. procurement of stock-in-trade

card.dispute: The Khadims of the Ajmer Durgah, representing the Chishtia Soofie religious denomination, challenged the constitutional validity of the Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act, 1955, which established state control over the management of the Durgah, alleging infringement of their fundamental rights to manage religious affairs, property, and religious practice.
issues_decided: Whether the Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act, 1955, and its provisions violate the fundamental rights of the Chishtia Soofies under Articles 25, 26, 19(1)(f), 14, and 32 of the Constitution
Whether the composition of the Durgah Committee under the Act infringes the denominational rights under Article 26
Whether the regulation of Khadims' duties and the Sajjadanashin's functions under the Act violates the right to freedom of religion under Article 25
Whether the provisions for arbitration and enforcement under the Act contravene constitutional rights
holdings: The Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act, 1955, does not violate the fundamental rights under Articles 25, 26, 19(1)(f), 14, or 32, as it regulates only secular aspects of administration and preserves religious practices.

The composition of the Durgah Committee, though not including members of the Chishtia order, does not infringe Article 26, as the Act mandates adherence to Chishti tenets and Muslim personal law in religious matters.

Sections 11(f) and (h), which empower the Committee to regulate duties of Khadims and functions of the Sajjadanashin, do not violate Article 25(1) as they pertain to administrative regulation, not religious practice.

Section 16, providing arbitration for secular disputes, and Section 18, enforcing committee orders, are constitutionally valid as they exclude religious matters and operate within the framework of existing legal remedies.
provisions: Durgah Khwaja Saheb Act, 1955, Section 11(f) and (h)
doctrines: Essential Religious Practices Doctrine
Regulation vs. Management of Religious Affairs
Secular-Religious Distinction in Constitutional Law
Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Principle of Harmonious Construction

card.dispute: The Amalgamated Coalfields Ltd. and others challenged the legality of a coal tax imposed by the Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara, arguing it was beyond the authority of the local body and violated constitutional and statutory provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the imposition of the coal tax in 1935 violated Section 80A(3) of the Government of India Act, 1915, for lack of prior sanction from the Governor-General.
Whether the coal tax ceased to be legally leviable upon the enactment of the Government of India Act, 1935, and later the Constitution of India.
Whether the increase in the tax rate in 1949 was validly challengeable in the petition.
holdings: The validity of a tax depends on the law at the time of enactment; subsequent introduction of Section 80A(3) did not invalidate prior legislative powers, and Rule 5 of the Scheduled Taxes Rules preserved local authority to levy taxes under existing laws.

Taxes lawfully imposed by local authorities before the Government of India Act, 1935, or the Constitution, continue to be valid under Section 143 and Article 277, even if such taxes later fall under central jurisdiction.
An issue not raised in the petition, such as the 1949 tax increase, cannot be considered for the first time in argument and will not be entertained by the court.
provisions: Central Provinces Local Self-Government Act, 1920, Section 51
Government of India Act, 1915, Section 81(1) and (3)
doctrines: Continuity of validly enacted local taxation under transitional constitutional provisions
Rule against raising new grounds not pleaded in the petition
Presumption of legislative competence at the time of enactment
Interpretation of statutory powers using plain language, rejecting ejusdem generis where excluded by wording

card.dispute: The Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy institution challenged the Commissioner's declaration that its temple was a public temple under the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926.
issues_decided: Whether the temple in question was a public temple within the meaning of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926?
Whether the temple was dedicated to or used as of right by the Hindu community or any section thereof for religious worship?
Whether the presumption of a public temple in the Madras Presidency applies to a temple near the Orissa border with distinct religious practices?
holdings: A temple is public under the Act only if it is a place of public religious worship and is dedicated to or used as of right by the Hindu community or any section thereof.
The mere presence of visitors at a temple does not make it a public temple; there must be a right of access by the public as a matter of entitlement.
The presumption that temples in the Madras Presidency are public is weak where the temple is near a regional boundary and has features consistent with private worship.
The evidence showed that the public did not have a right to access the temple, and the Mahant's permission was required, supporting its status as a private temple.
provisions: Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 (Madras Act 2 of 1927), Section 9, Clause 12
doctrines: Presumption of public nature of temples in Madras Presidency
Rebuttal of statutory presumptions by credible evidence
Right of access as a determinant of public religious worship

card.dispute: The appellants, heads of the Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy institution, challenged the Board's declaration that the Jagannadhaswami temple was a public temple under the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926.
issues_decided: Whether the Jagannadhaswami temple is a public temple used by the Hindu community as a place of religious worship as of right?
Whether the presumption that temples in the Madras Presidency are public applies to this temple located near the Orissa border?
holdings: A temple is public only if members of the Hindu community have a right of access to it for worship; mere visitation or worship does not establish such a right if permission is required.
The presumption that temples in the Madras Presidency are public is weak for temples near the Orissa border with distinct regional practices, and can be rebutted by evidence of private use.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, Section 84(2)
doctrines: Presumption of public nature of temples in Madras Presidency
Rebuttal of statutory presumptions by credible evidence
Right of access as a determinant of public temple status

card.dispute: The State of Bombay fought Fakir Umar Dhanse over whether the Collector could demolish unauthorized structures after evicting an occupant from unalienated agricultural land and whether the State was liable for damages for such demolition.
issues_decided: Whether the power of eviction under Section 66 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code includes the power to remove unauthorized structures.
Whether the occupant retains ownership of unauthorized buildings after eviction.
What is the true meaning of 'eviction' and 'vacation' under the Code.
holdings: The power to evict under Section 66 includes the incidental power to remove unauthorized non-agricultural structures to restore the land to its proper agricultural use.
Eviction under Section 66 terminates the occupant's right of use and occupation, and vacation requires removal of unauthorized constructions.
