doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory conditions precedent in rent control legislation
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory provisions to protect tenant rights
Distinction between possession and occupation in rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant claimed redemption of an otti and possession of property, while the respondent claimed superior title through inheritance under Marumakkathayam law after the property's female owner was allegedly exempted from the Travancore Ezhava Act's succession rules.
issues_decided: Whether Bhagavathi Valli was validly exempted from Part IV of the Travancore Ezhava Act under Section 33, affecting the devolution of her makkathayam property.
Whether the absence of a formal issue and pleading on exemption from the Ezhava Act vitiated the trial due to lack of fair opportunity to contest.
Whether the appellant had a valid title to redeem the otti based on inheritance through Meenakshi and Vasudevan.
holdings: The Supreme Court held that Bhagavathi Valli was validly exempted from Part IV of the Travancore Ezhava Act, so her property devolved by Marumakkathayam law, making her sister and niece the rightful heirs.
The absence of a formal issue on exemption did not vitiate the trial as the plaintiff had full knowledge, led evidence, and did not object to the notification or seek to adduce rebuttal evidence.
The appellant had no right to redeem the otti as he failed to establish title through the lawful heirs of Bhagavathi Valli, who were not Meenakshi and Vasudevan due to the exemption.
provisions: Travancore Ezhava Act, 1100 (Act III of 1100), Section 32
Travancore Ezhava Act, 1100 (Act III of 1100), Section 33
doctrines: Marumakkathayam law of succession
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of fair hearing and opportunity to lead evidence despite lack of formal issue

card.dispute: The appellant sued to enforce an agreement settling partnership accounts after dissolution, while the respondents, as heirs, counter-claimed for a full rendition of accounts, seeking to treat the counter-claim as a plaint in a cross-suit after the limitation period had expired.
issues_decided: Whether a counter-claim can be treated as a plaint in a cross-suit in the absence of a statutory provision allowing such treatment
Whether the High Court was justified in directing the trial court to treat the counter-claim as a plaint in a cross-suit despite the bar of limitation
Whether the date of filing of a counter-claim treated as a plaint should be the date of the original written statement or the date of the court's order
holdings: A counter-claim cannot be treated as a plaint in a cross-suit as of right, since no equitable or legal right exists to convert a written statement into a plaint without statutory authority.

The High Court erred in treating the counter-claim as a plaint in a cross-suit because such an order creates a new plaint on the date of the order, which in this case was after the limitation period had expired.
A court cannot deem a counter-claim to have been filed on the date of the written statement to circumvent the bar of limitation, as no amendment can convert a written statement into a plaint.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8, Rule 6
doctrines: No equitable right to counter-claim in absence of statutory provision
Futility of orders creating suits barred by limitation
Date of institution of suit determined by date of plaint presentation
Judicial discretion in amendment of pleadings

card.dispute: The sons of Nagappa fought the Union of India over whether a partition of joint family property could shield their share from attachment and sale for their father's unpaid income-tax liability.
issues_decided: Whether a civil court can question the validity of an income-tax assessment order in a suit for declaration and injunction.
Whether a partition of joint family property before tax assessment bars the tax authorities from attaching the entire property, including the sons' shares.
Whether the partition deed executed on March 14, 1947, was genuine and operative or a sham transaction.
holdings: Civil courts are barred from questioning the correctness or validity of income-tax assessments under Section 67 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
A partition does not automatically prevent the attachment of joint family property for pre-partition tax liabilities if the partition is found to be sham or not genuinely implemented.

The partition was a sham transaction not intended to be operative, as evidenced by continued management by the father, lack of actual division, and suspicious timing, thus not protecting the sons' shares from attachment.
doctrines: Pious obligation of a Hindu son to pay father's legitimate debts
Sham transaction doctrine
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in tax assessment matters

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of tenants alleging unauthorized subletting; the tenants claimed the landlord had acquiesced in the subletting, and the case centered on which law governed the pending revision after a new Rent Control Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'suit or proceeding' in Section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 includes appeals and revision petitions pending at the time of the Act's commencement
Whether the High Court was bound to apply the provisions of the 1958 Act or the repealed 1952 Act in deciding the merits of a revision petition
Whether the subletting in 1950 barred eviction under the 1958 Act, particularly in light of Section 16(1) and the absence of prescribed notice
holdings: The term 'suit or proceeding' in Section 57(2) of the 1958 Act includes appeals and revision cases pending when the Act came into force.
The High Court must apply the provisions of the 1958 Act to decide the merits of a revision petition pending at the time of the repeal of the 1952 Act.
Subletting that occurred before June 9, 1952, even without consent, does not justify eviction under Section 14 of the 1958 Act, and benefit of Section 16(1) is unavailable without prescribed notice.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 35
doctrines: Continuation of proceedings under repealed law
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of implied repeal

card.dispute: The appellants claimed title and possession over 40 acres of land purchased by their father, challenging the respondent's claim based on a mortgage decree and court sale, which the respondent argued bound the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in a second appeal, can interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the trial and first appellate courts on the ground that the evidence was insufficient.
Whether the absence of a registered sale deed barred the appellants from proving their title through other evidence.
Whether the High Court erred in reappreciating evidence and disbelieving documents without identifying a substantial question of law.
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal merely on the ground that the evidence is insufficient; such sufficiency is a question of fact, not law.
The absence of a registered sale deed does not bar proof of title through other admissible evidence, including possession and oral testimony.
A second appeal under Section 100 CPC is maintainable only if a substantial question of law is involved, not for re-evaluation of evidence or credibility of documents.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact rule
Substantial question of law in second appeal
Equity must yield to express provisions of law

card.dispute: The appellant, Manimala Devi, claimed enforcement of two mortgage deeds against properties mortgaged by Rajkumar Singh, after assignments of mortgage rights, while the respondents raised a limitation defence.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagor's interest in all three properties (A, B, and C) was mortgaged under the deeds
Whether part payment by a mortgagor after assignment of his interest in the mortgaged property extends the limitation period under Section 20 of the Limitation Act
Whether dispossession of the mortgagee due to a court sale of the mortgaged property creates a fresh cause of action for enforcement of the mortgage under Section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act
holdings: The mortgagor's interest in all three properties, including Mauza Bahaldih, was validly mortgaged under both mortgage deeds.

A mortgagor who has transferred his interest in the mortgaged property is not a 'person liable to pay the debt' under Section 20 of the Limitation Act; thus, part payment by him does not extend the limitation period against the transferee.

Dispossession of the mortgagee due to a court-ordered sale of the mortgaged property does not create a fresh cause of action for enforcement of the mortgage; Section 68 of the Transfer of Property Act does not extend the limitation period prescribed under Article 132.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Accrual of cause of action under limitation law
Interpretation of mortgage covenants
Effect of assignment on liability under mortgage

card.dispute: The plaintiff and his family members disputed over whether certain non-impartible properties, including buildings, were incorporated into the impartible Vizianagram Zamindari estate.
issues_decided: Whether the trust deed executed by Chitti Babu incorporated non-impartible properties into the impartible zamindari estate
Whether the Vizianagram Fort is part of the impartible estate
Whether the home farm lands were properly classified under the relevant Act
Whether certain properties were identifiable and could be claimed in the partition suit
holdings: The trust deed did not incorporate non-impartible properties into the impartible estate, as it only intended to confer on the son the same interest he would have received by survivorship.
The question of whether the Vizianagram Fort is part of the impartible estate remains undetermined and must be decided in a separate pending suit.
The issue of which properties qualify as home farm lands was not finally decided and must be determined by the appropriate tribunal under the relevant statutory provisions.
Properties not specifically adjudicated upon remain open for future determination, and parties may raise claims on them in appropriate proceedings.
provisions: Section 12 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act
Section 47 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act
doctrines: Primogeniture
Survivorship in impartible estates
Incorporation of properties into impartible estates

card.dispute: Mortgagees challenged the scaling down of a usufructuary mortgage debt under the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, 1951, after displaced mortgagors sought adjustment based on land allotments in India.
issues_decided: Whether a usufructuary mortgage debt falls within the definition of 'debt' under the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, 1951, even without personal liability to repay
Whether a debtor can invoke the Tribunal's jurisdiction under Section 5 to seek adjustment of a mortgage debt, or is such relief limited to redemption suits
Whether the reduction of the mortgage debt was correctly computed based on standard acres rather than market value of the lands
holdings: A usufructuary mortgage debt is a 'debt' under the Act regardless of personal liability, as Section 16(4) explicitly includes such debts for scaling down.
A debtor may apply under Section 5 for debt adjustment; the Tribunal has jurisdiction independent of a suit for redemption.
The value of lands for scaling down is determined by standard acre equivalents reflecting income yield, not market value, in line with rehabilitation rules.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'debt' to include secured obligations without personal liability
Jurisdiction of debt adjustment tribunal under special statutes
Use of standard acre system as proxy for land value in post-partition rehabilitation

card.dispute: The holder of the Vizianagram impartible estate sued for partition of joint family properties, claiming certain immovable and movable properties as impartible, while the respondents contested the impartibility of subsequently acquired properties and the applicability of incorporation to movables.
issues_decided: Whether immovable properties subsequently acquired and incorporated into an impartible estate remain impartible
Whether the rule of incorporation applies to movable properties in a Hindu joint family with an impartible estate
Whether buildings incorporated into an impartible estate under Section 18(4) of the Madras Estates Abolition Act became partible upon abolition of the estate
Whether a trust deed can operate to incorporate non-impartible properties into an impartible estate
holdings: Immovable properties lawfully incorporated into an ancestral impartible estate governed by primogeniture retain their impartible character as part of the joint family estate.
The rule of incorporation does not extend to movable properties; family custom must specifically support impartibility of movables for such status to apply.
Properties incorporated into an impartible estate, including buildings, do not automatically become partible upon the abolition of the estate under the Madras Estates Abolition Act.
A trust deed that settles properties on a son in the same manner as devolution by survivorship does not incorporate partible properties into the impartible estate.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 18(4)
doctrines: Rule of incorporation in Hindu joint family law
Primogeniture as a custom governing devolution of impartible estates
Survivorship in joint Hindu family property
Customary impartibility of movable properties

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant for non-payment of rent arrears within the stipulated time after a notice, while the tenant argued that the landlord waived the default by accepting rent later.
issues_decided: Whether the notice dated April 11, 1959 was valid under Section 4(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955 and Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the landlord waived the right to eject the tenant by accepting rent after the notice was served
Whether the tenant's failure to pay arrears within one month of the notice entitled the landlord to file for eviction
holdings: The notice was ineffective under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act as it gave only 14 clear days instead of 15, but it was valid under Section 4(a) of the Accommodation Control Act.
Acceptance of rent after the notice did not amount to waiver of the right to eject under Section 4(a) because the tenancy continued and rent was lawfully due.
A landlord can rely on a tenant's default in paying arrears within one month of notice under Section 4(a), even if subsequent rent is accepted, to file for eviction.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 4(a)
doctrines: Waiver of contractual or statutory rights
Notice requirements for termination of periodic tenancy
Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent

card.dispute: The appellants claimed ownership and possession of land after redeeming a mortgage, but the respondents, who were in possession, claimed occupancy rights and adverse possession, leading to a dispute over title, possession, and the applicability of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation due to adverse possession by the respondents
Whether the land was in the 'khas possession' of the appellants on January 1, 1955, under Section 6(1)(c) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the relationship of mortgagor and mortgagee continued after redemption in 1941, allowing the land to be deemed under the appellants' constructive possession
holdings: The respondents' possession became adverse to the appellants upon the redemption of the mortgage in 1941, and as the suit was filed within 12 years, it was not barred by limitation.
The land was not in the 'khas possession' of the appellants on January 1, 1955, because the respondents were in adverse possession and not holding the land on behalf of the appellants.

The mortgagor-mortgagee relationship did not subsist after 1941, and mere continued possession by third parties asserting independent title does not sustain the relationship for the purpose of claiming khas possession under the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Khas possession under land reform statutes
Constructive possession
Doctrine of estoppel by possession
Continuing relationship in mortgage after redemption

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the appellants were licensees or tenants of the shop, which determined whether the City Civil Court or the Small Causes Court had jurisdiction to hear the suit for injunction and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the City Civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit given the alleged landlord-tenant relationship between the parties.

Whether a claim or question arising under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, was involved in the suit, thereby vesting exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of Small Causes.
Whether the defence alleging a tenancy relationship raises a question arising out of the Act, affecting the jurisdiction of the court.
holdings: The City Civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit because the plaint did not assert a landlord-tenant relationship nor claim recovery of possession under the Act.
A question whether the appellants were licensees or tenants does not amount to a claim or question arising out of the Bombay Rents Control Act, as the Act does not govern the creation of tenancy.
Even if the defence asserts a tenancy, no question under the Act arises because the suit does not seek eviction of tenants or adjudicate rights created by the Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 51
Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, Chapter VII
doctrines: Jurisdiction determined by the cause of action in the plaint
Exclusive jurisdiction of Small Causes Court under rent control legislation
Distinction between license and tenancy
Court may not deal with claims arising under rent control law without jurisdiction

card.dispute: The heirs of Shehzad Kunwar (the pujari) fought with Raja Ram Karan Bahadur and others over whether Raja Dharam Karan or Shehzad Kunwar was the Shebait (manager) of the Radha Manoharji temple.
issues_decided: Whether Raja Dharam Karan was the Shebait of the deity Radha Manoharji.
Whether Shehzad Kunwar was the Shebait or merely a pujari acting as agent of the Shebait.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation.
holdings: Raja Dharam Karan was the lawful Shebait of the deity, succeeding Raja Indrajit Bahadur and Raja Sheoraj Bahadur, based on continuous management and control over the temple.
Shehzad Kunwar was not the Shebait but a pujari in the service of the Shebait, with no proprietary or managerial rights over the temple property.
The suit was not barred by limitation as Shehzad Kunwar did not assert a clear claim to Shebaitship until 1938, when her will was executed.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory provisions, as case relies on personal law principles)
Indian Limitation Act, 1908 (implied by discussion on limitation of suit)
doctrines: Shebaitship under Hindu law
Devottar dedication and its legal consequences
Doctrine of possession and management as evidence of Shebaitship
Principle that mere performance of seva or puja does not confer Shebait rights

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and a mining company disputed whether the state could collect fees under a repealed state law after a central law superseded it.
issues_decided: Whether the Orissa Mining Areas Development Fund Act, 1952 was impliedly repealed by the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether liabilities accrued under the Orissa Act before its supersession could be enforced despite its repeal by superior central legislation
Whether Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 applies to implied repeals
holdings: The Mines and Minerals Act, 1957 impliedly repealed the Orissa Mining Areas Development Fund Act, 1952 to the extent of repugnancy due to Parliament's superior legislative power.
Liabilities accrued under the Orissa Act before June 1, 1958, remain enforceable even after its implied repeal, as the Central Act did not expressly or impliedly extinguish them.
Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 applies to implied repeals, as the legislative intent to supersede an earlier law carries the same presumption of saving accrued rights and liabilities.
provisions: Constitution of India, Article 246(1), Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 23
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 54
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 18(1)(2)
Orissa Mining Areas Development Fund Act, 1952, Sections 4, 5
doctrines: Implied repeal
Presumption against obliteration of accrued rights and liabilities
Principle of legislative supremacy in case of repugnancy between Union and State laws

card.dispute: The State of Bhopal took possession of agricultural land owned by Champalal and others to eradicate Kans weeds through deep tractorisation and demanded cost contributions, which the landowners challenged as unconstitutional and illegal.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Land (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954 violates Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31(2) of the Constitution
Whether the procedure under Section 7 of the Act for apportioning costs was mandatory and whether non-compliance invalidated the demand for payment
Whether exemption from land revenue could be treated as compensation under Article 31(2)
Whether the demand could be sustained under the Madhya Pradesh Reclamation of Lands Act or under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act
holdings: Section 4(1) read with Section 6(1)(b) is unconstitutional as it authorises arbitrary acquisition of land without opportunity for hearing and without adequate compensation, violating Article 31(2).
Section 7 prescribes a mandatory procedure; the Reclamation Board must compute expenditure and equitably apportion costs, and failure to do so renders any demand for payment illegal.
Exemption from land revenue during possession does not constitute compensation under Article 31(2), as it merely alleviates loss rather than compensating for deprivation of use.
The demand cannot be validated retrospectively under the Madhya Pradesh Act, and the claim under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act was not properly raised and thus cannot be considered.
provisions: Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Land (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954, Sections 4, 6, 7, 8, 9
Madhya Pradesh Reclamation of Lands (Extension to Bhopal) Act, 1957
doctrines: Doctrine of arbitrary state action under Article 19(1)(f)
Doctrine of mandatory procedural compliance in statutory schemes
Doctrine of just compensation under Article 31(2)
Doctrine of waiver of unpleaded grounds in appellate proceedings

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision that the Nistar Officer lacked jurisdiction to correct revenue records and reopen orders recognizing certain individuals as pattadars under land reform legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the Nistar Officer had jurisdiction under Section 15(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, or under Section 47(1) of the Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1947, to correct entries in annual revenue papers and reopen orders made under Section 40 of the 1950 Act.
Whether the Deputy Commissioner could modify past entries in revenue records relating to cultivation status after the relevant agricultural year.
holdings: The Nistar Officer lacks jurisdiction to correct entries in annual revenue papers to reopen orders made under Section 40 of the 1950 Act, as Section 47(1) of the 1947 Act only permits updating records for current changes, not revising past entries.

Entries in revenue records regarding cultivation during a specific year cannot be modified later under Section 47(1), as that section is meant for recording contemporaneous changes, not correcting historical errors.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3(2), Section 4(2), Section 13(1), Section 15(1), Section 40
Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1947, Section 45(1), Section 45(2), Section 45(4), Section 46, Section 47(1), Section 47(2)
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders under land reform statutes
Limited scope of correction of revenue records under annual updating provisions
Distinction between record updating and substantive title determination

card.dispute: The petitioner, Smt. Kaushalya Devi, sought transfer of a criminal case from the court of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Delhi, after the Magistrate filed an affidavit opposing the transfer on behalf of the Delhi Administration.
issues_decided: Whether it was proper for the Magistrate trying the case to file an affidavit opposing the accused's application for transfer of the case.
Whether the impartiality of the criminal trial was compromised by the Magistrate's participation in opposing the transfer application.
holdings: It is wholly improper for a Magistrate trying a criminal case to file an affidavit opposing the accused's application for transfer, as it undermines judicial impartiality.
The Magistrate's act of entering the adversarial arena by contesting the transfer application created a serious threat to fair trial, warranting transfer of the case in the interests of justice.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 420 read with Section 120B
doctrines: Principle of judicial impartiality
Rule against judges assuming partisan roles
Separation of judiciary from executive

card.dispute: The heirs of Hemendra Nath Sen fought over the partition of his estate, specifically challenging the completeness of an arbitral award concerning a glass factory, accounting, management of the company, and misappropriation of funds.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitral award was incomplete for failing to expressly decide on the claim for accounting of company funds.
Whether the award was incomplete for not providing for the future management of the New Indian Glass Works Ltd.
Whether the award was incomplete for not addressing the claim that certain respondents misappropriated company funds and should restore them to the common pool.
holdings: An arbitral award that professes to decide all disputes referred to it is presumed to dispose of all claims; silence on a claim implies rejection if the award is made de praemissis.
The arbitrator is not required to make specific provisions for company management if existing law adequately governs such matters, and silence does not render the award incomplete.
Where an award declares itself final and comprehensive, the omission to address a claim for restoration of misappropriated funds amounts to a rejection of that claim.
doctrines: Presumption of completeness of arbitral awards (de praemissis)
Judicial reluctance to invalidate awards; preference for upholding them if reasonably possible
Silence of arbitrator on a submitted issue implies rejection when award is final and comprehensive

card.dispute: The defendants challenged the legitimacy of a child born from an inter-caste marriage and his right to claim a share in the joint family property, disputing both the validity of the marriage and the retroactive effect of the Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the marriage between Padmavathi and Sadagopa was valid despite being inter-caste under pre-1949 Hindu law
Whether the Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949 retrospectively validates such marriages and legitimises children born from them
holdings: A marriage between Hindus belonging to different castes, though invalid under pre-1949 Hindu law, is validated retrospectively by the Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949.
Children born from such inter-caste marriages become legitimate coparceners with full rights in joint family property due to the retrospective validation of the marriage under the Act.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes
Legitimacy of children from void marriages validated by statute
Statutory validation of inter-caste Hindu marriages

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment and sought an order under Section 13(5) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, requiring the tenant to deposit rent arrears and future rent; the tenant defaulted in depositing some payments, leading to the striking out of his defence, which he challenged.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below failed to apply the modified provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, particularly Section 15(7), which granted discretion to strike out a tenant's defence?

Whether the failure of the courts to consider the tenant's belated payment of rent under the discretionary framework of the 1958 Act rendered the trial not 'according to law' under Section 35 of the 1952 Act?
holdings: The provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, including Section 15(7), which gives the Controller discretion to strike out a tenant's defence, apply to pending proceedings under the earlier 1952 Act due to Section 57's requirement to consider the new law's modifications.

A trial is not 'according to law' within the meaning of Section 35 of the 1952 Act when a court fails to apply a mandatory statutory provision granting discretion, even if the parties did not raise the issue.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(5)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 35
doctrines: Prospective application of amended law with slight modifications
Duty of courts to apply statutory provisions suo motu
Revisional jurisdiction for trial not according to law

card.dispute: The Tilkayat of the Nathdwara Temple challenged the constitutional validity of the Nathdwara Temple Act, 1959, which imposed state regulation on the temple's management, claiming it violated religious freedoms under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Nathdwara Temple is a public or private religious institution.
Whether provisions of the Nathdwara Temple Act, 1959 infringe upon the rights under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution.
Whether Sections 28(2), 30(2)(a), 36, and 37 of the Act are ultra vires the Constitution.
Whether the state can regulate succession and financial administration of a Hindu religious institution.
holdings: A temple is public if it is open to all members of the religious denomination and receives widespread public devotion and offerings, regardless of private lineage succession.
State regulation of temple administration, including finances and management, is valid if it serves public order, morality, or health, and does not interfere with core religious practices.
The application of surplus trust funds under Section 28(2) and (3) via the cy-pres doctrine is constitutional if original religious purposes are fully met.
Section 37, which bars legal proceedings against the state for actions under the Act, does not infringe on individual rights to sue under Section 31 if the individual has a legitimate interest.
doctrines: Doctrine of secular administration of religious institutions
Doctrine of cy-pres (applied only to surplus after fulfillment of trust objects)
Doctrine of essential religious practices
Principle of severability

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to allow the bank to enforce a mortgage on his share of joint family property for his father's debt, claiming the debt was personal and the partition was bona fide.
issues_decided: Whether the partition of joint family property was bona fide and binding on the creditor.
Whether the father's debt to the bank was an antecedent debt for which the joint family property was liable.
Whether the bank could enforce a mortgage on the son's share in the joint family property.
holdings: A partition is not binding on creditors if it is intended to defeat their claims, especially when the father retains all debts and the son gets a clear share.
A loan used to discharge a prior debt owed to the same creditor qualifies as an antecedent debt, making joint family property liable.
The bank could enforce a mortgage on the son's share because the debt was incurred for family benefit and the partition did not absolve joint family liability.
doctrines: Antecedent debt doctrine in Hindu law
Bona fide partition test
Doctrine of constructive notice

card.dispute: The workmen of Subong Tea Estate challenged the validity of their retrenchment by the outgoing management, claiming it was invalid as it was effectively carried out by the new owner after transfer of the estate.
issues_decided: Whether the retrenchment of workmen by the outgoing management was valid under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
Whether the transferee of the tea estate had become the employer before the retrenchment, thereby making the outgoing management incompetent to retrench
Whether compliance with Section 25FF of the Act was sufficient to validate the retrenchment
holdings: Retrenchment can only be validly carried out by an employer who has the authority to do so; once ownership and management transfer, the outgoing employer cannot retrench.
From July 15, 1959, the vendee became the owner and employer, making it responsible for any retrenchment, which must comply with Sections 25F and 25G.
Section 25FF does not apply to retrenchments effected after transfer by the new employer; such retrenchments must meet the full requirements of Sections 25F and 25G.
doctrines: Conditions precedent to retrenchment
Doctrine of continuity of employment
Employer-employee relationship post-transfer of undertaking

card.dispute: The appellant, a member of a co-operative housing society, defaulted on loan repayments for a plot and construction, leading the society to terminate the agreement and seek possession through arbitration; the appellant claimed protection as a tenant under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship between the co-operative society and the member amounted to a landlord-tenant relationship under the Bombay Rents Control Act
Whether the arbitrators appointed under the Bombay Co-operative Societies Act had jurisdiction to decide the dispute despite the Rent Control Act's exclusive jurisdiction clause
Whether the mere plea of tenancy by the member deprived the arbitrators of jurisdiction to grant possession
holdings: The agreement did not create a landlord-tenant relationship; the member was only a 'proposed tenant' who would become a tenant upon full repayment and execution of a sub-lease.
The arbitrators had jurisdiction under the Bombay Co-operative Societies Act to decide the dispute because the society did not invoke landlord-tenant relationship in its claim.

The mere assertion of tenancy by the defendant does not oust the jurisdiction of arbitrators; exclusive jurisdiction under the Rent Control Act arises only when the claim itself is between landlord and tenant.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 298
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of Rent Control Courts
Arbitrator's jurisdiction under co-operative societies law
Plea of tenancy not sufficient to invoke Rent Control Act jurisdiction

card.dispute: The zamindar (Amba Prasad) challenged the right of occupants (respondents) to regain possession of land under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act based on their entry in the 1356F khasra, claiming the entry was fraudulent and that actual possession needed to be proven.
issues_decided: Whether a person recorded as an 'occupant' in the khasra for 1356F is entitled to adhivasi rights under Section 20 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act without proving actual possession in that year.
Whether an entry in the khasra for 1356F can be challenged after the date of vesting if it was not corrected before that date.
holdings: A person recorded as an 'occupant' in the khasra or khatauni of 1356F is entitled to adhivasi status and right to regain possession under Section 20, even without proof of actual possession in that year, provided the entry was not lawfully corrected before the vesting date.

The corrected entry in revenue records prevails only if the correction was made or ordered by a competent court before the vesting date and had become final; otherwise, the original 1356F entry governs adhivasi rights.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20
U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, Sections 28 and 33
doctrines: Fiction of continued entitlement to possession
Primacy of revenue records for determining adhivasi rights
Finality of entries not corrected before vesting

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the acquisition of his colliery by the Union Government, arguing mala fide action, invalidity of Rule 39 of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Rules, 1954, and discrimination under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications of acquisition were vitiated by mala fides
Whether Rule 39 of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Rules, 1954, is ultra vires Section 17 of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Act, 1952
Whether the petitioner had sufficient interest to challenge the constitutional validity of Rule 39
Whether there was discriminatory treatment violating Article 14 of the Constitution
holdings: The notifications of acquisition were not vitiated by mala fides; mere delay and adverse litigation with a government officer do not prove mala fide or conspiracy.
Rule 39 is valid and authorized under Section 17 of the Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Act, 1952, as it serves the Act's purpose of coal conservation.
The petitioner lacked sufficient interest to challenge Rule 39 as he acquired the lease in violation of Mineral Concession Rules requiring Central Government approval for transfer.
No violation of Article 14 was established, as differing decisions on mine reopening over time do not indicate discrimination when based on changing demand.
provisions: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4
Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Act, 1952, Section 17
Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Rules, 1954, Rule 39
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 5
doctrines: Mala fide must be proven by clear evidence; delay alone is insufficient
Delegated legislation validity test under parent Act's scope
Standing to challenge law requires lawful interest in the subject matter
Equal protection under Article 14 allows differential treatment based on changing circumstances

card.dispute: Trustees of temples sued archakas (priests) and alienees for ejectment from temple properties, while archakas claimed ownership of part of the land and right to remuneration.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of lost grant applies to determine the extent of an inam grant where documentary evidence exists.
Whether the deity's title under the inam grant included both melvaram and kudivaram interests.
Whether the High Court could apportion temple property between archakas and trustees in a suit for ejectment based on title.
Whether archakas are entitled to a portion of temple lands as remuneration in an ejectment suit.
holdings: The doctrine of lost grant cannot be invoked when the terms of the grant are clear from official records such as inam registers and statements.
Both melvaram and kudivaram interests in the suit properties were granted to the deity, as evidenced by recitals in revenue documents and conduct of the archakas.
A court cannot direct apportionment of temple property for archaka remuneration in a suit for ejectment based on title; such relief is only permissible in a scheme proceeding.
Archakas cannot claim possession of temple property as remuneration in an ejectment suit where no pleadings or evidence support such apportionment.
doctrines: Doctrine of Lost Grant
Principle of judicial separation between ejectment suits and scheme proceedings
Admission against interest
Presumption from long-standing conduct and documentary description

card.dispute: The appellants (Daya Ram and others) challenged the decree in favor of Shyam Sundari, who claimed a one-third share in land sold by her father's brothers, arguing that the appeal abated due to incomplete impleadment of her legal representatives after her death.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to failure to bring all legal representatives of the deceased respondent on record within the prescribed time
Whether the appellant was required to implead all legal representatives of the deceased respondent once the omission was brought to the Court's notice
Whether the appellant could claim equitable rights based on improvements made to the property despite notice of the respondent's claim
holdings: An appeal does not abate if the appellant, after diligent and bona fide inquiry, brings some legal representatives on record within the time allowed, as they sufficiently represent the deceased's estate in the absence of fraud or collusion.

Once the court is informed that not all legal representatives have been impleaded, the appellant must complete the record; however, the court may decide the appeal on merits if it is clear the appeal will fail, to avoid unnecessary delay.
A purchaser who constructs on co-owned property with notice of a co-owner’s claim cannot assert equitable rights against that claim, as they stand in the position of a trespasser with notice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4(3)
doctrines: Equity between co-owners
Doctrine of abatement of appeal
Representation of estate by legal representatives
Trespasser with notice

card.dispute: The lessee of a mining lease challenged the validity of demands for land cess imposed under the Madras District Boards Act, arguing it could not include royalty payments in its computation and was not recoverable as arrears of land revenue.
issues_decided: Whether the land cess under Sections 78 and 79 of the Madras District Boards Act, when computed to include royalty from mining leases, is a tax on land or a tax on mineral rights.
Whether the imposition of land cess including royalty violates the legislative competence of the State in light of Central laws on mineral regulation.
Whether the land cess can be recovered as an arrear of land revenue under the Madras Revenue Recovery Act.
holdings: The land cess under Sections 78 and 79 is a tax on land within Entry 49 of the State List, not a tax on mineral rights, and its inclusion of royalty in computing annual rent value does not alter its essential character.
The Madras District Boards Act is not impliedly repealed by the Central Mines and Minerals Acts of 1948 and 1957, as the land cess is unconnected with regulation or development of minerals.
The land cess, being a lawful cess imposed on land, is recoverable as an arrear of land revenue under Section 52 of the Madras Revenue Recovery Act.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 (Act LIII of 1948)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 (Act LXVII of 1957)
Seventh Schedule, State List, Entries 49 and 50
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of implied repeal
Tax not invalidated by incidental effect on other legislative fields

card.dispute: The appellant brother sued for partition of properties acquired in the names of the first respondent's family members, claiming they were joint family property, while the first respondent claimed they were acquired from his personal savings.
issues_decided: Whether properties acquired in the name of a coparcener's family members are presumed to be joint family property if the joint family had sufficient nucleus at the time of acquisition
Whether the karta is liable to account for past transactions in the absence of fraud or misappropriation
Whether the properties in question were acquired from joint family funds or personal savings
holdings: Where a joint family has sufficient nucleus at the time of acquisition, property acquired in the name of a coparcener is presumed to be from joint family funds, but this presumption fails if no such nucleus exists.
The karta is not liable to render an account of past transactions unless there is evidence of fraud or misappropriation, and the court may rely on existing evidence to determine available assets.
Properties acquired during a period when the karta did not manage the joint family and had no surplus from joint funds are not joint family property, even if purchased by him.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family Property
doctrines: Presumption of joint family origin of property
Karta's accountability in absence of fraud
Nucleus theory in Hindu joint family law

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent arrears, while the tenant claimed protection under the rent control law due to an ongoing dispute over standard rent.
issues_decided: Whether clause (a) or clause (b) of Section 12(3) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 applies when there is a dispute over standard rent.
Whether the tenant could be evicted for arrears when the standard rent was under dispute and revisions were pending.
holdings: Clause (a) of Section 12(3) applies only when there is no dispute about the standard rent; if a dispute exists, clause (b) governs the case.
A tenant is protected from eviction under clause (b) if they pay or tender the standard rent as determined by the court and costs, even during ongoing disputes over rent fixation.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a) and (b)
doctrines: Strict construction of eviction provisions in rent control legislation
Doctrine of harmonious construction between clauses (a) and (b) of Section 12(3)

card.dispute: The appellant sued to enforce a mortgage by deposit of title deeds, while the respondent challenged the existence and validity of such a mortgage.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgage by deposit of title deeds was created on May 10, 1947, in the absence of a formal document on that date.
Whether constructive delivery of title deeds can satisfy the requirements of a mortgage under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the intention to create a mortgage can be inferred from a subsequently executed and registered memorandum of agreement dated July 5, 1947.
holdings: A mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) requires delivery of title deeds with intent to create security, which can be satisfied by constructive delivery.
Constructive delivery occurs when a debtor, after title deeds are in creditor’s possession, declares that they are to be held as security, even without physical re-delivery.

A subsequent memorandum acknowledging a prior deposit of title deeds with intent to mortgage can validate the mortgage from the date of such acknowledgment, if all elements including intent are present.
doctrines: Constructive delivery
Mortgage by deposit of title deeds
Substance over form

card.dispute: The petitioner, a son of the former Maharaja of Manipur, challenged the partial refusal of the Central Government's consent to file a suit for partition of alleged private properties against the current minor Maharaja.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government can conditionally or partially grant consent under Section 87B of the Civil Procedure Code?
Whether the Central Government can adjudicate upon the merits of a claim while deciding on consent under Section 87B?
Whether the partial refusal of consent in this case violated constitutional rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) and (g)?
holdings: The Central Government cannot impose conditions or partially grant consent under Section 87B when reliefs are based on a single cause of action; such power would amount to judicial adjudication, which is beyond its scope.
The Government is not entitled to decide the merits of a claim while considering consent under Section 87B; its role is limited to screening frivolous or vexatious suits.
Conditional consent invalidly intrudes into judicial functions and may violate constitutional rights; hence, the impugned order is read down to mean full consent was granted.
doctrines: Separation of powers
Judicial review of administrative discretion
Conditional consent invalidity doctrine
Doctrine of constitutional validity of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The plaintiff, highest bidder at an auction, sued for specific performance of a sale contract after the defendant refused to sell; the defendant claimed no contract existed and that delay barred relief.
issues_decided: Whether mere delay in filing a suit for specific performance disentitles the plaintiff to relief under the Specific Relief Act
Whether the plaintiff's conduct induced the defendant to change position to his prejudice
Whether the High Court was correct in granting specific performance despite the delay
holdings: Mere delay in filing a suit for specific performance, without more, does not disentitle a plaintiff to equitable relief under the Specific Relief Act.

To refuse specific performance on grounds of delay, the defendant must show that the plaintiff's conduct induced a change in position causing prejudice, or that it would be inequitable to grant relief.

The plaintiff's explanation for delay—mental distress due to wife's illness and house demolition—was credible, and no prejudice to the defendant was established, so specific performance was properly granted.
doctrines: Equitable relief in specific performance
Laches and delay in equitable claims
Waiver and abandonment of contractual rights
Prejudice due to change of position

card.dispute: The stall-holders claimed to be lessees of meat stalls in a private market, while the owners contended they were mere licensees, affecting rights regarding rent, eviction, and control.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship between the stall-holders and the market owners was that of landlord and tenant or licensor and licensee.
Whether the right to exclusive possession and payment of 'rent' created a lease.
Whether the requirement of notice to vacate indicated a tenancy rather than a licence.
holdings: The decisive factor in distinguishing a lease from a licence is the intention of the parties, to be gathered from the agreement and surrounding circumstances.
Exclusive possession alone is not conclusive of a lease; it must be coupled with an interest in the property.
A requirement to give notice before vacating is not inconsistent with a licence and does not by itself create a tenancy.
The duty of the owner under statutory regulations to control and supervise the market indicates that possession remained with the owner, supporting a licence, not a lease.
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence
Intention of the parties as determining factor
Exclusive possession not conclusive of tenancy
Statutory obligations affecting possession

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the landlord's recovery of possession of agricultural land, claiming protection under an amendment deeming them owners, after the Collector initially upheld but later set aside the landlord's eviction order.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector could exercise revisional powers under Section 76A of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act without calling for the record of the Mamlatdar's order.
Whether the Collector could legally reopen and reverse his earlier decision upholding the Mamlatdar's order after previously rejecting revision applications.
Whether the amended Section 32 of the Act, which deemed tenants as owners, applied to pending eviction proceedings.
holdings: The Collector can exercise revisional power under Section 76A without calling for or examining the record, based on available materials, and decide not to interfere with the Mamlatdar's order.

The Collector cannot, after finally deciding there is no ground for interference, later reopen the matter and reverse the Mamlatdar's order; such a subsequent order is ultra vires and without jurisdiction.
The amended Section 32 does not automatically invalidate a pending eviction application; the eviction proceedings can continue unaffected by the amendment if initiated before its enforcement.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 76A
doctrines: Principle of finality of quasi-judicial orders
Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of constructive res judicata

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Land Acquisition (Madras Amendment) Act, 1961, which provided for lower compensation for land acquired for housing schemes compared to other public purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition (Madras Amendment) Act, 1961 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification in compensation for land acquisition?
Whether the Amending Act is protected under Article 31-A and thus immune from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31(2)?
Whether the adequacy of compensation under the Amending Act is justiciable after the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution?
holdings: The Amending Act creates an arbitrary classification by providing lower compensation for land acquired for housing schemes compared to other public purposes, without any rational basis, thus violating Article 14.
Article 31-A does not protect the Amending Act because the acquisition was not for an 'estate' or for agrarian reform, and thus the Act remains subject to scrutiny under Articles 14 and 31(2).

The Amending Act cannot be sustained as a reasonable classification because the distinction between housing and other public purposes lacks an intelligible differentia with rational relation to the object of the law.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus
Doctrine of equality before law
Justiciability of compensation after constitutional amendment

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of the Land Acquisition (Bombay Amendment) Act, 1948, which fixed compensation for acquired land based on its value as of January 1, 1948, rather than the date of notification under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition (Bombay Amendment) Act, 1948, violated Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, by not providing just compensation for compulsory land acquisition.
Whether the 1948 Amendment Act was saved from invalidity by Article 31(5)(a), Article 31-A, or Article 31-B of the Constitution of India.
Whether a law void ab initio for violating Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, could be validated retrospectively by constitutional provisions.
holdings: Fixing compensation based on an arbitrary earlier date (January 1, 1948), without relevant justification, violated Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, as it failed to provide 'just equivalent' compensation.
Article 31(5) and Article 31-A do not save a law that was void from inception for violating Section 299(2), as they do not revive dead laws or validate pre-constitutional invalidity.

Article 31-B can protect laws listed in the Ninth Schedule from challenges based on fundamental rights, but only if they were validly enacted; it does not validate laws void ab initio for lack of legislative competence.
The Land Acquisition (Bombay Amendment) Act, 1948, being void from inception, could not be upheld, and compensation must be determined under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
doctrines: Doctrine of just compensation
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of constitutional validation
Doctrine of non-revival of void laws

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay fought with tenants in a clearance area over whether the tenants could challenge the demolition of their buildings through a civil suit after not appealing under the statutory mechanism.
issues_decided: Whether sections 354R and 354RA of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, are ultra vires for failing to provide tenants an opportunity to be heard before clearance orders are issued
Whether tenants qualify as 'persons aggrieved' under Schedule GG, clause (2) of the Act and can therefore file an appeal against a clearance order
Whether a civil suit by tenants is maintainable when an alternative statutory remedy under Schedule GG exists
holdings: Sections 354R and 354RA are constitutionally valid because they provide tenants with an opportunity to object during the clearance process and to appeal as 'persons aggrieved', making the restrictions on property rights reasonable.

The term 'person aggrieved' in Schedule GG, clause (2) includes tenants and occupants affected by a clearance order, as the expression is wide enough to cover anyone whose legal interest is adversely affected.

A civil suit by tenants is not maintainable when the statutory remedy of appeal under Schedule GG, clause (2) is available; the finality of the clearance order bars independent judicial challenges in civil court.
provisions: Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, Schedule GG, Clause (2)
doctrines: Doctrine of alternative remedy
Doctrine of statutory finality
Principle of 'person aggrieved'
Rule of reasonable construction of statutory language

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the enforceability of two documents executed in favor of the Bank, claiming they were void as agreements to stifle criminal prosecution and thus opposed to public policy under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act.
issues_decided: Whether the two documents executed by the appellants were unenforceable as being opposed to public policy under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Whether the agreements amounted to a compromise to stifle criminal proceedings
Whether the plaintiffs discharged the burden of proving that the transactions were illegal
holdings: An agreement to settle a dispute by executing security documents is not void under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act if it arises from a bona fide dispute and is supported by valid consideration.
Mere sequence of events, such as a criminal complaint followed by a settlement, does not prove that an agreement was made to stifle prosecution.
The burden to prove that an agreement is opposed to public policy lies on the party alleging it, and such burden requires clear and satisfactory evidence, which was not discharged in this case.
doctrines: Public policy under contract law
Burden of proof in cases alleging illegal agreements
Distinction between motive and consideration in contracts

card.dispute: The landlords sued for ejectment and mesne profits after the lease expired; the tenant company claimed protection under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, including a right to purchase the land.
issues_decided: Whether a stipulation in a registered lease deed requiring the tenant to demolish buildings and surrender vacant possession at the end of the term excludes the tenant's rights under Section 9 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922
Whether such a stipulation falls within the proviso to Section 12 of the Act, which saves agreements 'as to the erection of buildings'
Whether Section 9 of the Act violates the landlord's fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution
holdings: A stipulation in a registered lease requiring the tenant to demolish buildings and deliver vacant possession at the end of the term is a valid agreement 'as to the erection of buildings' within the proviso to Section 12 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, and overrides statutory rights under Sections 3 and 9.
The proviso to Section 12 applies to any stipulation in a registered deed that bears on the erection or continuation of buildings, and such stipulations govern over the Act’s protections.
The constitutional question under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 need not be decided because the tenant had no statutory right under Section 9 due to the valid lease stipulation.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, Section 3
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, Section 9
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1922, Section 12
doctrines: Statutory rights can be excluded by clear contractual stipulations in registered instruments
Proviso to Section 12 operates to preserve contractual rights over statutory rights when parties have specifically addressed building erection in lease terms
Constitutional questions are not decided if the case can be resolved on statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Relatives of debtors sued to cancel documents executed in favor of a bank, claiming they were executed to stifle a criminal prosecution, while the bank sued to enforce one of the documents.
issues_decided: Whether the documents executed by the debtors and their relatives were unenforceable under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act for being in restraint of prosecution.
Whether the subsequent conduct of the debtors indicated recognition of the validity of the transaction.
Whether the burden of proving that the agreement was opposed to public policy was discharged by the plaintiffs.
holdings: An agreement to execute documents as consideration for withdrawing a criminal complaint is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, but such an agreement must be proved by clear and satisfactory evidence.
The failure of the debtors to testify and their subsequent conduct, including litigating without challenging the validity of related agreements, indicated recognition of the transaction’s validity.
Mere sequence of events does not prove an agreement to stifle prosecution; the party alleging illegality must provide strong evidence, which the plaintiffs failed to do.
doctrines: Public policy under Section 23
Burden of proof in cases alleging illegal consideration
Use of subsequent conduct to infer validity of a transaction

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, members of a Hindu joint family, disputed the extent of the widow's share in joint family property after her husband's death, and whether his will effected a severance or family arrangement.
issues_decided: Whether the will executed by the deceased husband amounted to a severance of the joint family status
Whether the will could be construed as a family arrangement binding on the widow
Whether the widow's interest in the joint family property is determined as of the date of her husband's death or the date of partition
holdings: A will by a coparcener does not amount to a severance of the joint family unless there is an explicit declaration of intent to separate, which was absent here.
A will cannot be construed as a family arrangement unless there is clear evidence of agreement and assent by all parties, including the widow or her representatives, which was not established.

Under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, the widow is entitled to the same share as her husband would have received upon partition, determined as of the date of partition, not the date of his death.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3
doctrines: Statutory succession
Severance in coparcenary
Widow stepping into the shoes of her husband
Survival of husband's persona in widow

card.dispute: The lessees of a plot in Calcutta challenged the state's acquisition of part of their land for the Bharat Sevashram Sangha, arguing it did not serve a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition for the Sangha served a public purpose under Section 40(1)(aa) of the Land Acquisition Act, as amended by Act 31 of 1962.
Whether the acquisition, initiated before the 1962 amendment, could be validated retrospectively under Section 7 of the Amending Act.
Whether the government's satisfaction and consent to the acquisition for a public purpose were adequately established.
holdings: Acquisition for constructing social workers' quarters, students' home, publication department, guest house, and panthasala by the Sangha served a public purpose under Section 40(1)(aa) as the Sangha engaged in charitable and religious activities benefiting the public.

Under Section 7 of the Amending Act 31 of 1962, an acquisition made before July 20, 1962, is deemed valid under Section 40(1)(aa) if the purpose falls within that clause, regardless of the government's initial reliance on an earlier provision.
The government's consent to acquisition under Section 40(1)(aa) can be inferred from the agreement, Section 5-A report, and surrounding circumstances, even if not explicitly stated at the time.
doctrines: Retrospective validation of administrative action
Judicial review of public purpose in land acquisition
Presumption of government satisfaction from documentary evidence

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Land Acquisition Act that permitted land acquisition for companies engaged in industry, even if not for a public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether amended Section 40(1)(aa) of the Land Acquisition Act violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution by permitting acquisition for companies without requiring a public purpose
Whether Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962 violates Article 31(2) by deeming past acquisitions for companies as for public purpose
Whether the impugned provisions violate Article 14 by creating unreasonable discrimination
holdings: Amended Section 40(1)(aa) is unconstitutional as it allows compulsory acquisition for companies without requiring the use of land to serve a public purpose, thus violating Article 31(2).
Section 7 of the Amending Act is invalid because it relies on the unconstitutional clause (aa) and cannot validate past acquisitions made without a public purpose.
The provisions create arbitrary classification and violate Article 14 by treating pre- and post-July 20, 1962 acquisitions differently without rational basis.
doctrines: Presumption of constitutionality
Reading down of statutes
Severability doctrine
Rule against arbitrary state action under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant, a Taluqdar, claimed ownership or permanent leasehold rights over nazul land and challenged the forfeiture of his leasehold interest based on his assertions in legal proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's claim to ownership or permanent heritable and transferable rights in nazul land amounted to a disclaimer of the landlord's title resulting in forfeiture of his leasehold interest.
Whether the acts and statements of the appellant, including filing claims and a suit, constituted a clear and unequivocal denial of the landlord's title.
holdings: A tenant does not forfeit their leasehold interest by claiming enhanced rights such as permanent, heritable, or transferable interests, unless there is a clear and unequivocal disclaimer of the landlord's title.

Assertions in legal documents claiming ownership or superior rights, without denying the obligation to pay rent or the landlord’s reversionary interest, do not amount to forfeiture of tenancy under Indian law.
doctrines: Doctrine of forfeiture by denial of landlord's title
Distinction between claiming superior tenancy rights and disclaiming landlord's title

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's suit for ejectment on the grounds that the landlord did not bona fide require the premises for personal occupation, especially since repairs or alterations were intended.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's requirement of the premises for personal occupation under Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents Act is invalidated by his intention to carry out repairs or alterations.
Whether the case falls under Section 13(1)(g) (own occupation) or Section 13(1)(hh) (demolition and reconstruction for letting).
holdings: A landlord's bona fide need to occupy premises for residence is not defeated by his intention to make alterations or repairs; Section 13(1)(g) applies regardless of such changes.

Section 13(1)(hh) applies only when the landlord intends to demolish and rebuild for letting to tenants, not for personal occupation, and thus does not apply where occupation by the landlord is the true purpose.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(hh)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17B
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 17C
doctrines: Strict construction of tenant protection statutes
Bona fide requirement for personal occupation
Non-application of reconstruction clause to self-occupation cases
Judicial reluctance to read implied restrictions into statutory grounds for eviction

card.dispute: The appellant claimed property under a will allegedly executed by Ramdhan in his favour, which the widow and daughters contested, denying the will's genuineness.
issues_decided: Whether the court can consider surrounding circumstances and probabilities to assess the credibility of witnesses in a will dispute.
Whether the propounder of a will must remove all suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
Whether the will in question was genuinely executed by Ramdhan.
holdings: Courts may consider surrounding circumstances and probabilities, beyond mere demeanour, to evaluate witness credibility in will disputes.
The propounder of a will must remove all natural suspicions arising from the circumstances to establish its genuineness.

The will was not proved to be genuine due to suspicious circumstances, including its execution at the propounder’s house, use of high-flown Urdu by a man who could not write it, and lack of registration or immediate disclosure.
doctrines: Propounder's duty to remove suspicious circumstances
Court's right to consider extrinsic probabilities in assessing testamentary documents
Presumption against unnatural wills

card.dispute: The sub-lessee (Rup Chand Gupta) sued to set aside an ex-parte eviction decree obtained by the original lessor (Raghuvanshi Private Limited) against the lessee (Land and Bricks), alleging collusion between the two companies due to common directors.
issues_decided: Whether the ex-parte decree was obtained by collusion between Raghuvanshi Private Limited and Land and Bricks Limited.
Whether the failure to implead the sub-lessee in the eviction suit renders the decree collusive.
Whether the non-contestation of the suit by Land and Bricks, despite common directors with Raghuvanshi, constitutes an improper act for collusion.
holdings: An agreement between plaintiff and defendant not to contest a suit does not amount to collusion unless it is done for a dishonest or sinister purpose.
A landlord may lawfully obtain a decree for possession against a lessee without impleading the sub-lessee, and such omission does not constitute an improper act or collusion.
The failure of a defendant to contest a suit, even when it shares common directors with the plaintiff, is not collusive if the suit is legitimate and the defendant had no plausible defence.
doctrines: Doctrine of Collusion in Judicial Proceedings
Separate Legal Entity Doctrine
Binding Effect of Decree on Sub-lessee

card.dispute: The appellant sought specific performance of an agreement to sell a house, after the respondent's mother (co-owner) died, arguing he should now be compelled to sell the entire property.
issues_decided: Whether Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 applies when the vendor acquires title after the contract to sell, but before the sale deed is executed.
Whether the expression 'subsequently to the sale or lease' in Section 18(a) refers to the actual sale or to the contract to sell.
holdings: Section 18(a) of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 applies when a vendor later acquires title to property contracted to sell, even if the title is perfected after the agreement but during the contract's subsistence.

The phrase 'subsequently to the sale or lease' in Section 18(a) means 'subsequently to the contract to sell or let', not the actual sale or lease, to avoid overlap with Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of specific performance
Doctrine of interpretation to avoid legislative redundancy
Implied representation of competence to sell

card.dispute: The State of Madras acquired lignite-bearing lands under the Madras Lignite (Acquisition of Land) Act, 1953, and the landowners challenged the compensation provisions as violating their fundamental right to just compensation under Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the fixation of market value of land as of April 28, 1947, for compensation purposes under the Madras Lignite Act, 1953, violated Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it existed before the Fourth Amendment
Whether the exclusion of the value of non-agricultural improvements made after April 28, 1947, from compensation amounted to a violation of Article 31(2)
holdings: Fixing compensation based on the market value of land from a date ten years prior to acquisition, without justification, denies the owner just compensation and infringes Article 31(2) as it then stood.
Excluding the value of non-agricultural improvements made after April 28, 1947, from compensation deprives the owner of the just monetary equivalent of the property taken, violating Article 31(2).
provisions: Madras Lignite (Acquisition of Land) Act, 1953, Sections 2 and 3
Constitution of India, Article 31(2) (prior to the Fourth Amendment)
doctrines: Just compensation under Article 31(2)
Prospective appreciation in land value not attributable to acquisition scheme cannot be denied to owner
Value of improvements must be included in compensation for expropriated land

card.dispute: The dispute was between a maintenance decree-holder (Smt. Laxmi Devi) and an auction-purchaser over whether the sale of property in execution of a money decree should be set aside for failing to disclose her prior charge.
issues_decided: Whether auction sales in execution of a decree are governed by Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the omission to mention a charge in the proclamation of sale renders the auction materially irregular
Whether the charge-holder suffered substantial injury warranting setting aside the auction sale under Order 21 Rule 90 of the CPC
holdings: Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to auction sales in execution of decrees because Section 2(d) saves Chapter IV of the Act, including Section 100, from the restrictive definition of 'transfer' in Section 5.
Failure to mention a charge in the proclamation makes the sale materially irregular and prevents the charge-holder from enforcing the charge against the auction-purchaser.

Substantial injury under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC is a question of fact; mere unenforceability of a charge does not automatically amount to substantial injury if other charged properties suffice to meet the claim.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
doctrines: Doctrine of saving clause prevailing over definitional clause
Material irregularity in execution proceedings
Substantial injury as a factual determination in setting aside auction sales

card.dispute: The true owner of a boarding house, who had placed it in the defendant's name to circumvent service rules and tax laws, sued to recover possession after the defendant refused to return it.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's claim to recover possession of the suit property was barred due to the illegality of the benami transaction aimed at tax evasion.
Whether the plaintiff could enforce his right to possession based on an independent agreement to hold and return possession, despite the benami nature of the ownership.
holdings: A transaction is not rendered unlawful merely because it results in tax benefit if the primary purpose was not to evade the Income-tax Act; thus, the plaintiff was not barred from enforcing his title.
The plaintiff's right to recover possession was based on an independent agreement to return possession, which was untainted by illegality and enforceable despite the benami ownership arrangement.
doctrines: In pari delicto potior est condicio possidentis
Benami transaction doctrine
Doctrine of separation of causes of action
Principle of clean hands in equity

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat challenged the rights of jagirdars to forest resources granted by the former ruler of Sant State before its merger with India, after the grant was declared mala fide and cancelled by the Bombay Government.
issues_decided: Whether the non-recognition of a pre-merger grant by the new sovereign amounts to an act of state that extinguishes enforceable rights under municipal law.
Whether rights granted by a former ruler are protected under Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, or Article 31 of the Constitution if not recognized by the new sovereign.
Whether the Tharao granting forest rights constitutes 'law' saved under the Application of Laws Order, 1949.
holdings: Rights granted by a former sovereign are not enforceable in municipal courts unless recognized by the new sovereign, as such rights do not automatically survive merger.

Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and Article 31 of the Constitution do not protect unrecognised rights; they only preserve existing enforceable rights at the time of citizenship transition.
A Tharao granting forest rights is not 'law' within the meaning of statutory provisions preserving pre-constitutional laws, and thus was not saved by the Application of Laws Order, 1949.
doctrines: Act of State Doctrine
Doctrine of State Succession in Municipal Law
Recognition of Pre-constitutional Rights
Municipal Enforcement of International Law

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal and the Ramakrishna Mission fought with landowners over whether the acquisition of land for staff quarters, hostel buildings, and playgrounds served a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether construction of staff-quarters falls within Clause (b) of Section 40(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as being 'likely to prove useful to the public'
Whether construction of staff-quarters can be justified under Clause (aa) of Section 40(1) as part of a public-purpose 'work' by a company
Whether construction of staff-quarters falls under Clause (a) of Section 40(1) for dwelling houses for workmen employed by a company
holdings: Construction of staff-quarters does not serve a section of the public and thus does not fall under Clause (b) of Section 40(1), as individual employees cannot constitute a 'section of the public'.
