doctrines: Severance in status under Hindu joint family law
Strict construction of jurisdiction-bar clauses like Section 66 CPC
Survival of action for accounts post mortem

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Controller's modification of its mining lease terms, arguing it was not an 'existing mining lease' and that the reduction in lease period without compensation violated constitutional protections.
issues_decided: Whether the mining lease in favor of the appellant was an 'existing mining lease' under Rule 2(c) of the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956
Whether the modification of the lease period from 1939 violated Article 31A(1)(e) of the Constitution by affecting 'winning' of minerals
Whether the 1956 Rules were ultra vires the 1948 Act and thus could not continue under Section 29 of the 1957 Act
Whether the Controller was justified in limiting the lease period to 25 years from 1939
holdings: A lease created by an agreement with immediate possession in 1939, even if formalized later, qualifies as an 'existing mining lease' under the 1956 Rules.
The term 'winning' in Article 31A(1)(e) includes extraction and removal of minerals, so the lease modification falls within constitutional protection against compensation claims.
Rules made under the 1948 Act, even if inconsistent with it, are deemed valid under the 1957 Act if they relate to matters covered by the new Act, per Section 29.
The lease period must be aligned with the 1957 Act prospectively; thus, the 20-year limit runs from the Act’s commencement (June 1, 1958), not from 1939.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 8(1)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 29
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948
doctrines: Deemed continuity of rules under subsequent legislation
Prospective application of statutory limits on lease duration
Constitutional protection for laws affecting mineral rights under Article 31A
Incidental benefit to private parties does not invalidate public interest regulation

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) challenged the validity of a fresh notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, issued after the government cancelled an earlier invalid notification, arguing that the process could not be restarted without a fresh notification under Section 4.
issues_decided: Whether the government could cancel an invalid Section 6 notification and issue a fresh one without withdrawing from acquisition under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act
Whether the government's power to issue a Section 6 notification was exhausted by the earlier invalid notification
Whether the delay in issuing the fresh Section 6 notification rendered it invalid
holdings: An invalid notification under Section 6 can be treated as ineffective, and the government may issue a fresh Section 6 notification without withdrawing from acquisition under Section 48.
The government does not exhaust its power under Section 6 by issuing an invalid notification; it may lawfully issue a fresh, valid notification.
The contention about unreasonable delay in issuing the fresh notification was not raised in the lower court and could not be entertained for the first time in the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Recognition of invalidity of administrative action
Power to reissue valid orders after invalid ones
Principle of exhaustion of statutory power

card.dispute: The appellants, owners of the Jaggampeta estate, contested whether the Vantari Muttah land—granted partly for services and partly for rent—was part of their estate and thus subject to abolition under the Madras Estates Abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Vantari Muttah land was excluded from the zamindari estate under Regulation XXV of 1802 due to being granted for public services.
Whether the land formed part of the estate vested in the Government under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948.
holdings: Lands granted for personal services to the zamindar, even with favorable rent, are not excluded from the estate under Regulation XXV of 1802.
The Vantari Muttah was part of the Jaggampeta estate as it was held subject to personal service and remission by the zamindar, and thus fell within the scope of the 1948 Act.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 3(b)
doctrines: Presumption that lands under personal service grants remain part of the zamindari unless clearly excluded
Interpretation of pre-settlement grants based on nature of services and control over remission

card.dispute: The son (Faqir Chand) challenged the mortgage of joint family property by his father to secure a loan, claiming it was not for legal necessity or antecedent debt and should not bind his interest.
issues_decided: Whether a son can restrain execution of a mortgage decree against his father when the sale has not yet occurred.
Whether a son can impeach a mortgage of joint family property not made for legal necessity or antecedent debt, after a decree has been passed.
Whether the passing of a mortgage decree binds the son's interest in the property.
holdings: A son cannot restrain execution of a mortgage decree or stay sale of joint family property unless he proves the debt is non-existent or incurred for illegal or immoral purposes.
A son retains the right to impeach a mortgage not for legal necessity or antecedent debt, even after a decree has been passed against the father.
A mortgage decree does not enlarge the creditor's security; the son's interest remains unbound unless the mortgage was for legal necessity or antecedent debt.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory source, based on case law)
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (implied by mortgage decree context)
doctrines: Legal necessity doctrine in Hindu joint family law
Doctrine of antecedent debt in Hindu law
Rule that sons are bound by father's debts only if for legal or moral purposes
Principle that a decree does not validate an otherwise invalid alienation

card.dispute: The appellant tenant refused to pay rent to the respondent landlords for a brick kiln, claiming the land had vested in the State under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, while the respondents argued the kiln was a 'building' exempt from vesting.
issues_decided: Whether the brick kiln in question constitutes a 'building' within the meaning of Section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951.
Whether the land containing the brick kiln vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh with effect from July 1, 1952, thereby extinguishing the landlords' right to claim rent.
holdings: A structure qualifies as a 'building' under Section 9 only if it is a permanent construction designed for a useful purpose; a mere pit with bricks on the sides does not meet this criterion.
Since the brick kiln was not a 'building', the land vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh from July 1, 1952, and the landlords lost all rights to claim rent thereafter.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 6(a)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 9
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Vesting of property rights in the State under land reform laws
Contextual and factual determination of what constitutes a 'building'

card.dispute: Co-owners of a house disputed whether one group occupying the property owed compensation to the other and if the suit was maintainable under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was incompetent due to non-joinder of an allegedly adopted co-owner
Whether the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 barred the civil court's jurisdiction
Whether the agreement to pay compensation for occupation between co-owners was enforceable
holdings: The suit was not incompetent for non-joinder; adoption was admitted by failure to deny specifically, and oral evidence of adoption was admissible.
The Rent Control Act did not apply because co-owners in joint possession do not have a landlord-tenant relationship merely by one paying compensation.
Co-owners can validly agree that the occupying party pay compensation, even without ouster; such contracts are enforceable in civil court.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII, Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 18
doctrines: Admission by pleading
Tenancy-in-common
Ouster not a prerequisite for compensation between co-owners
Non-derogation from jurisdiction of civil court unless statute expressly ousts it

card.dispute: Co-sharers in a village's proprietary rights fought over the partition of 'home-farm' land after the State acquired the proprietary interest under land reform legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the vesting of proprietary rights in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act extinguished co-sharers' rights to claim partition of home-farm land.
Whether a suit for partition of home-farm land is infructuous after the State's acquisition of proprietary rights.
Whether the rights of co-sharers to seek declaration and partition are maintainable in civil court post-acquisition.
holdings: The vesting of proprietary interest in the State does not extinguish co-sharers' rights to seek a declaration of their share in pre-existing proprietary rights for claiming compensation and proportionate home-farm land.
A suit for partition of home-farm land is not infructuous merely because proprietary rights have vested in the State, as co-sharers retain individual rights over home-farm land.
Rights to partition home-farm land are unaffected by the Act, especially when the village remains undivided and land is in cultivating possession of co-sharers, lessees, or ordinary tenants.
provisions: The Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Sections 3 and 4
doctrines: Distinction between proprietary and individual ownership rights
Survival of civil remedies post-acquisition
Maintainability of partition suits despite vesting in the State

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings on the ground that the mandatory public notice under Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 was not given, rendering the entire process void.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement of public notice under Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 is mandatory or directory
Whether non-compliance with the public notice requirement invalidates the entire acquisition proceedings
Whether the delay in challenging the acquisition barred the petition under Article 226
holdings: The requirement to give public notice under Section 4(1) is mandatory, as the use of 'shall' indicates a legislative intent to make it a condition precedent.
Non-compliance with the mandatory public notice renders the entry onto land unlawful and invalidates all subsequent acquisition proceedings.
The appellants did not delay unreasonably in filing the writ petition, as they challenged the proceedings once they became aware of the awards and had not acquiesced in the process.
doctrines: Strict construction of statutes authorizing compulsory acquisition of property
Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Condition precedent to statutory authority
Doctrine of timely challenge to illegal administrative action

card.dispute: The lessee firm challenged the State Government's takeover and termination of its mining lease, and the Central Government's rejection of its revision, alleging arbitrariness and lack of hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government's action in taking over the colliery and terminating the lease was arbitrary or justified
Whether the Central Government was obligated to provide reasons and conduct a personal hearing before rejecting the revision application
holdings: The State Government's action in terminating the lease was justified due to the lessee's breach of covenant by allowing voluntary work stoppage and endangering the colliery through neglect.

The Central Government fulfilled its procedural obligations under the Mineral Concession Rules by obtaining the State Government's comments and allowing the firm to respond; a detailed reasoned order was not required in this case.
doctrines: Principle of reasoned orders in quasi-judicial functions
Doctrine of procedural fairness in administrative action
Vindication of administrative action based on clear factual record

card.dispute: The Mahant claimed certain properties were his personal holdings, while the Commissioner asserted they were part of a math and thus subject to the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question were part of a math governed by the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939
Whether the properties were personal holdings of the Mahant or religious endowments
Whether the public's right of access is necessary for an institution to qualify as a math under the Act
Whether properties purchased by a Mahant or his chelas in their personal names can be considered math properties
holdings: An institution is a 'math' under the Act if it promotes the Hindu religion, is presided over by a spiritual head with disciples, and succession is by founder’s direction or usage.
Properties used for offering bhog to Lord Jagannath and distributing prasad are religious endowments, even if managed by the Mahant, and belong to the math, not the individual.
Lack of public access does not exclude an institution from being a math; the nature of religious use and dedication determines its status.
Properties purchased by a Mahant or his chelas, even in personal names, become math properties if used for math purposes and their proceeds are mingled with math funds.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 49
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 12(12)
doctrines: Presumption against private ownership of religiously used properties
Doctrine of dedication to religious use
Mingling of accounts as evidence of trust property
Usage and succession as determinative of math status

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from non-residential premises, claiming need for shifting his business, but the tenant argued the landlord was already 'entitled to possession' of another tenanted property and thus ineligible.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord in occupation of a non-residential building as a tenant is 'entitled to possession' within the meaning of s. 8(3)(a)(ii) of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the appellate court's order in revision under s. 17 of the Act.
holdings: A tenant under the Act does not have a right of 'entitlement to possession'; such entitlement refers only to an owner's right, not a tenant's statutory immunity from eviction.
The High Court rightly exercised revisional jurisdiction to correct a material irregularity by the appellate court in failing to follow binding precedent from the same High Court.
provisions: Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 8(3)(a)(ii)
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 8(2)
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 17
doctrines: Statutory immunity from eviction does not equate to a right of possession
Principle of binding judicial precedent within the same jurisdiction
Revisional jurisdiction to correct material irregularity

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant after the lease term ended, claiming the tenant was a trespasser, while the tenant argued that a six months' notice was required under the lease and that the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act protected his possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, particularly Section 3, overrides a contractual requirement for six months' notice before eviction
Whether the Controller under Section 29 of the Act retained jurisdiction after that section was repealed
Whether a landlord can evict a tenant without giving notice when the lease expires by efflux of time and no renewal is agreed
holdings: Section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act does not override contractual notice requirements but only restricts eviction to specified grounds, preserving the tenant's right to notice under the lease.
The repeal of Section 29 did not affect the Controller’s jurisdiction over pending proceedings, which continued until final disposal.

Even after expiry of a fixed-term lease with an option to renew, the landlord must give notice as per the lease terms before eviction, especially where structures are involved and the tenant has exercised the renewal option.
doctrines: Statutory tenancy arises only after contractual tenancy ends and tenant holds over
Rent control laws are protective, not enabling, and do not confer new eviction rights
Non obstante clause in rent laws restricts landlord's rights but does not nullify contractual obligations
Principle of fair opportunity to remove structures under lease agreements

card.dispute: Maqbool Alam Khan claimed title to land based on an oral gift from Najma, while Mst. Khodaija challenged the gift's validity and asserted her right to possession after being dispossessed following a final decree in a prior suit.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was constructively bound by the final decree in Title Suit No. 127 of 1939 despite the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1944 expunging her name as a defendant.
Whether the oral gift of immovable property by Najma to the appellant was valid under Mohamedan law.
holdings: The compromise decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1944 effectively excluded the respondent from being bound by the decree in Title Suit No. 127 of 1939, either actually or constructively, and restitution under Section 144 CPC was valid.

An oral gift of immovable property under Mohamedan law requires declaration, acceptance, and delivery of possession; where the donor was not in possession and did nothing to enable the donee to obtain possession, the gift is invalid.
doctrines: Lis pendens
Res judicata in execution proceedings
Essential elements of a valid gift under Mohamedan law: declaration, acceptance, and delivery of possession
Constructive possession in gifts of property held by a trespasser

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a joint Hindu family over the validity of a family arrangement (Ex. B-1) that allocated three-fifths of family properties to Narasimha and two-fifths to Venkatramaiah, and whether the arrangement required registration under the Registration Act.
issues_decided: Whether a valid family arrangement existed between the members of the joint Hindu family despite the absence of formal legal claims or disputes.
Whether the family arrangement embodied in Ex. B-1 required compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.
holdings: A family arrangement is valid if made bona fide to maintain harmony, even in the absence of legal disputes, provided it is fair and based on mutual consent and family considerations.

An agreement outlining future division of joint family property does not create an immediate interest in immovable property and therefore does not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.
doctrines: Family arrangement doctrine
Doctrine of partition by consent
Doctrine of immediate v. future interest in immovable property

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of property via a 1953 gift deed from her mother, who allegedly inherited it in 1920; the respondents challenged the gift, asserting the mother could not have inherited it because her father-in-law survived her husband, relying on a 1925 statement by the mother in a mortgage suit.
issues_decided: Whether the deceased donor's 1925 statement in a mortgage suit—asserting her husband predeceased her father-in-law—was admissible under Section 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act
Whether the donor's later statement in the 1953 gift deed could be admitted under Section 158 of the Indian Evidence Act to contradict her earlier statement
Whether the 1925 statement was made with conscious knowledge that it was against her proprietary interest
holdings: A statement by a deceased person against their proprietary interest is admissible under Section 32(3) of the Evidence Act, even if not an admission against the party relying on it, provided it was made consciously and with knowledge of its prejudicial effect.

The 1953 gift deed did not directly contradict the 1925 statement, and even if admissible under Section 158, its value was low as it was made during family disputes and in the context of transferring title.

Knowledge that a statement is against one’s interest can be inferred from circumstances; here, the donor, being aware of Hindu law, must have known the 1925 statement harmed her proprietary claim and was made voluntarily.
doctrines: Admissibility of dying declarations and declarations against interest under Section 32(3)
Use of subsequent statements to contradict earlier ones under Section 158
Inference of conscious knowledge from surrounding circumstances

card.dispute: The appellants, tenants facing eviction, claimed protection under the Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, arguing that pending execution of an ejectment decree entitled them to relief, which the respondents (landlords) opposed.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5(1)(a) of the Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, extends protection against ejectment to tenants when a decree for ejectment has already been obtained and is under execution?
Whether the protection under Section 5(1)(a) applies to pending execution proceedings or only to pending suits and appeals?
holdings: Section 5(1)(a) does not protect tenants from execution of an already obtained ejectment decree, as the provision does not include such decrees within its non obstante clause.
The protection under Section 5(1)(a) applies only to pending suits or proceedings initiated before decree, not to execution proceedings following a final decree.
provisions: Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 5(1)(a)
Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 5(1)(b)
Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 5(3)
Sylhet Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1947, Section 14
Assam Urban Areas Rent Control Act, 1949, Section 6(1)
Assam Urban Areas Rent Control Act, 1946, Section 6(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutes
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and prior enactments

card.dispute: The sub-tenant sued the landlord for a declaration of tenancy rights after the main tenant's interest was terminated before the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 came into force, and the landlord argued the suit was barred by the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the suit by the sub-tenant for declaration of tenancy rights is maintainable in a civil court despite Section 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
Whether the dispute regarding the sub-tenancy falls within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller under Section 17(3) of the Act?
Whether the sub-tenant acquired a vested right under Section 18(2) of the Act or under Section 20 of the earlier Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952?
holdings: Section 50 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 does not bar a civil suit by a sub-tenant whose tenancy continued after the main tenancy was determined before the Act's commencement.
Section 17(3) applies only to disputes during the subsistence of the main tenancy after the Act's commencement and does not cover cases where the tenancy ended before the Act came into force.
A sub-tenant becomes a statutory tenant under Section 18(2) of the 1958 Act if the main tenancy was lawfully determined before the Act, and such a right is enforceable in civil court.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 20
doctrines: Statutory fiction of deemed tenancy
Vested rights doctrine
Jurisdictional bar under rent control legislation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant's widow over unpaid rent arrears; the tenant claimed protection by tendering rent before suit was filed.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can claim protection from eviction under s. 12(1) of the Bombay Rents Act by showing readiness to pay arrears before the suit, when the case falls under s. 12(3)(a).
Whether the special provisions of s. 12(3)(a) override the general protection in s. 12(1) when rent is in arrears for six months and not paid within one month of notice.
holdings: Under s. 12(3)(a), once the conditions are met, the tenant cannot claim protection under s. 12(1) even if ready and willing to pay before the suit.
The right to eviction under s. 12(3)(a) arises when rent is in arrears for six months and not paid within one month of notice; a belated tender does not defeat this right.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
doctrines: Specialia generalibus derogant (special provisions override general ones)
Literal interpretation of statutory language
Mandatory interpretation of 'may' as 'shall' in context of statutory eviction provisions

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the inclusion of their names as parties in a debt adjustment proceeding and claimed title by adverse possession, while the respondents sought debt adjustment under the Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act.
issues_decided: Whether the orders impleading the appellants in the debt adjustment proceeding were without jurisdiction
Whether the appellants acquired title to the land by adverse possession
holdings: The court had jurisdiction to add the appellants as parties even after the prescribed time because pending proceedings under the repealed Act were to be continued under the 1947 Act, which allowed addition of parties under CPC Order 1 Rule 10 regardless of time limits.

The appellants did not acquire title by adverse possession as the period of possession was less than 12 years and they failed to prove the first respondent was in possession as a tenant during the prior period to enable tacking.
provisions: Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1947, Section 46
Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1947, Section 56
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 10
Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1939, Section 17
doctrines: Doctrine of deemed continuation of proceedings under a new statute
Doctrine of tacking in adverse possession
Jurisdiction to add necessary parties despite limitation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the compensation awarded for his grove land acquired by the Uttar Pradesh Government for a school hostel, claiming it was undervalued.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of a prior bona fide offer to purchase the land can be a valid basis for determining compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the District Judge's acceptance of such an offer as evidence of market value
Whether the court has discretion to award interest at less than 6% per annum under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
holdings: A genuine and bona fide offer to purchase land by a willing buyer shortly before acquisition is relevant and valid evidence for determining market value.
The High Court erred in rejecting the District Judge’s appreciation of evidence supporting a prior offer, especially when no challenge was made to its authenticity or bona fides.
Under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, once interest is awarded, it must be at 6% per annum; courts have no discretion to award a lower rate in the absence of a state amendment.
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Principle of willing buyer-willing seller
Statutory interpretation of interest provisions
Appreciation of evidence by lower courts

card.dispute: The zamindar of Pargana Agori challenged the state's acquisition of his land for a limestone quarry, claiming it was not for a public purpose and that the state lacked jurisdiction to apply urgent acquisition procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was the owner of mineral and sub-soil rights in the land acquired.
Whether the State Government had jurisdiction to apply the urgent acquisition provisions under Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the notifications issued under Sections 4(a) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act were valid.
holdings: The zamindar is presumed to own mineral and sub-soil rights in his estate unless there is express evidence of transfer, based on historical grants and long-standing conduct.
The State Government lacked jurisdiction to invoke urgent acquisition powers under Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act where the land included mineral rights belonging to the zamindar.
The notifications under Sections 4(a) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, and all subsequent proceedings including the award and reference to court, are ultra vires and quashed by certiorari.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1963 (U.P. Act No. 1 of 1964)
Mirzapur Stone Mahal Act (U.P. Act V of 1886), Section 5
doctrines: Presumption of ownership of mineral rights by zamindars in the absence of express alienation
Ultra vires doctrine applied to executive action exceeding statutory authority
Certiorari to quash illegal administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the acquisition of his land by the State of Uttar Pradesh for limestone quarrying, arguing it was not for a public purpose, the use of urgency provisions was illegal, and he was entitled to sub-soil mineral rights.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition was for a public purpose despite the sale of cement for profit.
Whether the application of Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act to 'arable and waste land' was lawful.
Whether the appellant had proprietary rights over minerals and sub-soil of the acquired land.
holdings: A declaration under Section 6(1) that land is needed for a public purpose is final unless it is a colourable exercise of power; selling cement for profit does not negate public purpose if the overall use benefits the public.
Sections 17(1) and (17)(4) can only apply to 'arable and waste' land; the State lacked jurisdiction to invoke these provisions if the land did not qualify, rendering the notifications ultra vires.

The appellant, as zamindar, retained ownership of sub-soil minerals and mining rights unless expressly alienated; prior leases and historical documents confirm these rights were never transferred to the State.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1963 (U.P. Act No. 1 of 1964)
Mirzapur Stone Mahal Act, 1886 (U.P. Act V of 1886), Section 5
doctrines: Colourable legislation doctrine
Presumption of ownership of sub-soil rights by zamindars
Finality of public purpose declaration under Section 6(1) subject to abuse of power
Ultra vires action by executive when exceeding statutory limits

card.dispute: Ram Lal Puri (vendee) sued Gokalnagar Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. (vendor) for recovery of Rs.50,000 paid as earnest and advance money for a property sale that failed due to Partition; the vendor contested the claim as time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the claim for recovery of Rs.20,000 as earnest money is governed by Article 97 or the residuary Article 120 of the Limitation Act
Whether the claim for the additional Rs.30,000 paid as advance is governed by Article 97 of the Limitation Act
Whether the period of limitation was extended under Section 36(a) of the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, 1951
holdings: The claim for recovery of earnest money is not covered by Article 97 or any specific article of the Limitation Act and is therefore governed by the residuary Article 120, making it within time.
The Rs.30,000 paid as additional advance was part of the purchase price and not earnest money, hence the claim for it is governed by the three-year limitation under Article 97 and is time-barred.

Section 36(a) of the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act does not save the claim because the contract became void earlier due to West Punjab Ordinance 7 of 1947, which rendered sale of evacuee property unlawful.
doctrines: Residuary provision doctrine (Article 120 applies when no specific article applies)
Forfeiture of earnest money under contract law
Effect of frustration of contract due to supervening illegality
Statutory incorporation of common law liabilities

card.dispute: The appellants (mortgagee's successors) and respondent (execution purchaser of mortgagor's equity) disputed the validity of a final foreclosure decree passed by the trial court after correcting a preliminary decree mistakenly framed for sale.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court had the power to correct a clerical or accidental error in the preliminary decree and pass a final decree for foreclosure instead of sale?
Whether the respondent, as an execution purchaser of the mortgagor's equity pendente lite, could challenge the final foreclosure decree?
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to involuntary transfers like court sales during the pendency of a mortgage suit?
holdings: The trial court had inherent power under Sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure to correct an accidental slip in the preliminary decree that did not reflect its true intention, especially when the suit was clearly for foreclosure.
An execution purchaser of the equity of redemption during the pendency of a mortgage suit is bound by the doctrine of lis pendens and cannot acquire rights immune from the suit's outcome.
The principle of lis pendens applies even to involuntary transfers such as court sales, and such purchasers are bound by the final decree in the suit.
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Inherent power of court to correct clerical errors
Principle of 'slip rule' under CPC
Successor-in-title steps into the shoes of predecessor

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (assignees of one brother) sued the defendants (purchasers from the other brother) to enforce a right of pre-emption created by a partition award between two brothers, raising questions about its enforceability against successors and whether it violated the rule against perpetuities.
issues_decided: Whether the pre-emption clause in the partition award binds the successors-in-interest of the original parties?
Whether the covenant of pre-emption is void under the rule against perpetuities?
holdings: The pre-emption clause, though not expressly binding on successors, must be construed as binding on assignees or successors-in-interest given the context and purpose of the partition award.

A covenant of pre-emption does not create an interest in immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act and therefore does not violate the rule against perpetuities, even if no time limit is specified.
doctrines: Rule against perpetuities
Privity of contract and its extension to successors-in-interest
Enforceability of covenants running with the land
Distinction between personal contracts and obligations annexed to property

card.dispute: The dispute was between coparceners of a joint Hindu family and respondents who had an earlier agreement to purchase family properties, over whether a subsequent sale of the mortgaged properties to the mortgagee's sons extinguished the right of redemption and whether possession by the subsequent purchasers was adverse, barring the suit by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the subsequent sale to the mortgagee's sons, despite an earlier agreement to sell, was void or voidable.
Whether the possession of the subsequent purchasers (K and L) was adverse to the respondents, thereby barring their suit for redemption by limitation.
Whether the decree for specific performance in favor of the respondents affected the nature of possession of the subsequent purchasers.
holdings: A subsequent sale, even with notice of a prior agreement, is not void but voidable at the instance of the prior contracting party; title passes except as affected by equitable obligations under s. 91 of the Trusts Act and s. 40(2) of the Transfer of Property Act.

Possession of a subsequent purchaser with notice of a prior contract is not adverse to the prior claimant due to the fiduciary duty arising under s. 91 of the Trusts Act, so the limitation period for redemption is not triggered.

A decree for specific performance binds both the original vendor and the subsequent purchaser; failure to make the purchaser a conveying party, though erroneous, does not alter the non-adverse nature of their possession.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 40, Paragraph 2
doctrines: Fiduciary duty of purchaser with notice of prior contract
Possession not adverse when subject to equitable obligation
Doctrine of constructive trust under Section 91 of the Trusts Act

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision quashing a second notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing it could issue multiple notifications under Section 6 based on a single notification under Section 4(1), while landowners contended such successive notifications were invalid.
issues_decided: Whether a single notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be followed by multiple notifications under Section 6 for different parts of the same land.
Whether Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act implies that a notification under Section 4(1) remains valid indefinitely unless withdrawn under that section.
Whether Sections 17 or 49 of the Land Acquisition Act permit successive Section 6 notifications based on one Section 4(1) notification.
holdings: A single notification under Section 4(1) contemplates only one corresponding notification under Section 6; successive notifications under Section 6 for different portions of the same notified land are not permitted.
A notification under Section 4(1) does not remain indefinitely in force; the government may rescind it at any time under Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, even without invoking Section 48.

Sections 17 and 49 do not authorize multiple Section 6 notifications; they deal with urgency and compensation in special cases, not with the procedural sequence of notifications under Sections 4 and 6.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of procedural provisions in acquisition law
Integration of Sections 4, 5-A, and 6 as a sequential process
Power to rescind notifications under general statutory powers
Doctrine of legislative intent in administrative continuity

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to declare a settlement deed executed by his father and sister in favor of his nephew as fraudulent and collusive, seeking its cancellation, while the defendants upheld its validity.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in presuming undue influence in the execution of the deed of settlement without a proper pleading or evidence on the issue?
Whether the relationship between the donor and donee, along with the donor's advanced age, is sufficient to raise a legal presumption of undue influence?
Whether the burden of proof regarding the free will of the donor in executing the deed can be shifted to the donee in the absence of a pleaded case of undue influence?
holdings: The High Court erred in presuming undue influence without a pleaded case or supporting evidence, as the law requires clear allegations and proof to invoke Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act.
Mere advanced age of the donor and familial relationship with the donee are insufficient to raise a legal presumption of undue influence; such a presumption lacks basis in law and fact.

The burden of proving undue influence lies on the party alleging it, and cannot be shifted to the donee unless the case is properly pleaded and supported by evidence indicating domination and unfair advantage.
doctrines: Doctrine of Undue Influence
Burden of Proof in Cases of Alleged Undue Influence
Presumption of Influence in Transactions between Dominant and Subordinate Parties

card.dispute: The Roman Catholic Mission challenged the resumption of inam lands by the State of Madras under Section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, claiming the inam was personal and not liable to resumption, and that the provision was ultra vires.
issues_decided: Whether Section 44-B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, was within the legislative competence of the Provincial Legislature under the Government of India Acts, 1915 and 1935?
Whether the resumption of inam lands under Section 44-B violated the Constitution by favoring Hindu religious institutions?
Whether the inam in question was resumable due to alienation, and whether adverse possession barred resumption?
holdings: The Provincial Legislature had the competence to enact Section 44-B, as the subject of inams connected with religious endowments fell within the combined scope of land tenure, land revenue, and charitable endowments under the Government of India Acts, 1915 and 1935.
Section 44-B did not violate the Constitution, as resuming alienated inam lands and regranting them to a Hindu temple restored lost benefits and did not amount to giving denominational preference.

The resumption was valid as the inam was alienated contrary to its terms; adverse possession did not bar the Government’s prerogative to resume such lands, as no limitation period applies to this power.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, Section 44-B
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 35
doctrines: Legislative competence under the Government of India Acts
Resumption of inam as administrative action, not forfeiture
No limitation on Government's prerogative to resume inam lands

card.dispute: Worshippers sued to declare a compromise decree, which classified a temple as public and allowed family control over its properties, as not binding on the deity.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for a declaration that the compromise decree is not binding on the temple is barred by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877
Whether the compromise decree in the original petition was valid in law, particularly regarding representation of the deity and the scope of the relief granted
holdings: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 is not exhaustive; courts can grant declaratory relief independently when the suit seeks to protect the deity's trust properties, as worshippers have a legitimate interest.

A compromise decree affecting a temple's status and properties is invalid if the deity was not properly represented, and the relief granted exceeded the statutory scope of the original petition under Section 84(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, Section 84(2)
Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 20
doctrines: Declaratory relief outside Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act
Representation of deity through next friend
Worshipper's locus standi to protect temple properties
Ultra vires compromise decree

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, former partners in a dissolved firm, disputed over the partition of partnership property and whether the appellant, who retained possession and collected rental income, was liable to pay interest on the other partners' share of the income.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, as a co-owner in possession of joint property, was liable to pay interest on rental income received before the suit was filed under the Trusts Act, 1882
Whether the High Court was justified in awarding the respondents a share of rental income for a period not covered by the Commissioner's report
Whether the appellant, as a constructive trustee, was liable to account for unrealized rent due to vacancies in the property
holdings: A co-owner in possession does not become a trustee merely by collecting rent; liability to pay interest arises only upon a breach of trust under Section 23 of the Trusts Act, which was not established here.

The High Court erred in extending the rental award beyond the Commissioner's report period; however, based on the record, a reasonable estimate of Rs. 2,400 was awarded for the unverified period with interest from the date of the final decree.

The appellant cannot be held liable as a constructive trustee for rent not realized due to vacancies, but the High Court’s finding was upheld due to the appellant’s failure to maintain proper accounts.
doctrines: Constructive trust
Breach of trust under the Trusts Act
Equitable liability to account for profits
Presumption against improper retention of funds by fiduciaries

card.dispute: The shebait of a Hindu idol alienated temple property, and a worshipper, who also assisted in temple duties, sued on behalf of the idol to declare the property as belonging to the idol and to recover possession.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which governs suits relating to religious endowments.
Whether a worshipper can represent the idol in a suit when the shebait is acting adversely to the idol's interests.
holdings: A suit by a worshipper on behalf of an idol for declaration of title and recovery of property is not a suit for reliefs specified under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is therefore not barred by that provision.

When a shebait acts adversely to the idol's interests, a worshipper interested in the idol's welfare can be granted ad hoc power to represent the idol in court to protect its property, as the idol stands in a position similar to a minor.
doctrines: Legal personality of a Hindu idol
Ad hoc representation of a juridical person
Shebait's fiduciary duty
Principle analogous to next friend in minor's litigation

card.dispute: The landlords (Dunlop Rubber & Co. Ltd. and others) sued for possession of flats from tenants, claiming they needed the premises for their own occupation under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, through officers occupying as licensees.
issues_decided: Whether the officers occupying the flats under a standard agreement were tenants or licensees.
Whether the company's requirement of the premises for occupation by its officers as licensees amounts to 'own occupation' under Section 13(1)(f) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
holdings: The agreement between the company and its officers created a license, not a tenancy, as it granted only a personal privilege to occupy, revocable upon employment termination, transfer, or death, and did not create any interest in the land.

The company's requirement of the premises for occupation by its officers as licensees constitutes 'own occupation' under Section 13(1)(f), as the occupation is for the company's purposes through its agents.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(f)
doctrines: Distinction between lease and license
Doctrine of service occupation as a form of license
Substance over form in determining tenancy vs. license

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the hotel company tenant for sub-letting rooms and making unauthorized constructions, violating the lease and rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the occupants of hotel rooms were sub-tenants or licensees
Whether the landlord waived the right to object to sub-letting
Whether unauthorized construction by the tenant without government consent constituted a ground for eviction
Whether a room in a hotel being excluded from the definition of 'premises' bars eviction for sub-letting it
holdings: Where a hotel-keeper gives exclusive possession of rooms without retaining control, the occupants are sub-tenants, not licensees, amounting to sub-letting.
Waiver of breach requires clear knowledge and intentional relinquishment; mere knowledge of occupation does not prove waiver of sub-letting consent.
Unauthorized construction on leased land without government consent, despite notice, is a valid ground for eviction under the Rent Control Act.
Even though a room in a hotel is not 'premises' under the Act, sub-letting it in violation of lease terms is a valid ground for eviction of the main tenant.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1) proviso (b), (c), and (k)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 2(g)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 20
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 44
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver requiring intentional relinquishment of a known right
Test for tenancy vs. license based on control and exclusive possession
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts not lightly interfered with
Interpretation of statutory definitions in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The Board of Revenue and the State challenged the High Court's decision quashing orders that required a proper inquiry into whether certain lands claimed by a jagirdar were khudkhast (personal) lands under the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the Jagir Commissioner has exclusive jurisdiction to determine the character of lands claimed as khudkhast under Section 23(2) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the Board of Revenue's orders directing a fresh inquiry in accordance with the Jagir Rules, 1954
holdings: The Jagir Commissioner has exclusive jurisdiction under Section 23(2) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act to determine the character of lands claimed as khudkhast, as this is distinct from disputes over title under Section 37.

The Board of Revenue was justified in remanding the case for a fresh inquiry because the original inquiry violated Rules 23, 24, and 28 of the Jagir Rules, 1954, which mandate proper notice, a hearing date at least two months in advance, and a suit-like inquiry procedure.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 23
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 37
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 47
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Rules, 1954, Rule 23
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Rules, 1954, Rule 24
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Rules, 1954, Rule 28
doctrines: Specialia generalibus derogant
Procedural fairness in administrative inquiries
Exclusive jurisdiction of statutory authorities

card.dispute: The appellant, Bhagat Raja, contested the Union of India's rejection of his revision application challenging a state government decision to grant a mining lease to respondent No. 3 instead of him.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government is required to give reasons (i.e., pass a 'speaking order') when deciding a revision application under Rule 55 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1957.
Whether the absence of reasons in the Central Government's order prejudices judicial review under Articles 227 or 136 of the Constitution.
holdings: The Central Government, when exercising revision powers under Rule 55, performs a quasi-judicial function and must pass a speaking order with reasons.
A speaking order is essential to enable effective judicial review by courts and to prevent arbitrary or extraneous considerations in administrative decisions.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 30
doctrines: Speaking order doctrine
Quasi-judicial functions
Principles of natural justice
Judicial review of administrative action

card.dispute: The Income-tax Department and Amalgamated Development Ltd disputed whether development expenses for plots sold by a predecessor firm were deductible and whether unpaid, mortgaged sale consideration should be treated as taxable income.
issues_decided: Whether expenditure incurred by the company to complete development work on plots sold by the predecessor firm is deductible under the Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the unpaid portion of the sale price, secured by mortgage, should be treated as constructive receipt of income
holdings: Expenditure on development of plots, including those sold by the predecessor firm, is deductible as it was incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes under an integrated development scheme.
Unpaid sale consideration secured by mortgage does not constitute constructive receipt of income and is not taxable in the year of sale if not actually received.
doctrines: Wholly and exclusively for business purpose
Constructive receipt doctrine
Commercial expediency
Integration of business liabilities in asset acquisition

card.dispute: The Deputy Commissioner and Collector of Kamrup challenged the constitutional validity of the Assam Acquisition of Land for Flood Control and Prevention of Erosion Act, 1955, and its Validation Act, 1960, after Durga Nath Sarma contested the acquisition of his land and the compensation offered.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam Acquisition of Land for Flood Control and Prevention of Erosion Act, 1955, violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution by not providing just compensation.
Whether the same Act violates Article 14 by creating unreasonable classification in compensation between lands acquired for flood control and other public purposes.
Whether the Assam Acquisition of Land for Flood Control and Prevention of Erosion (Validation) Act, 1960, is valid despite the invalidity of the 1955 Act.
holdings: The 1955 Act, by limiting compensation to a multiple of land revenue and excluding full value of buildings, fails to provide a just equivalent for acquired land, violating Article 31(2) as it stood before the Fourth Amendment.

The 1955 Act creates arbitrary and unjust discrimination between landowners based solely on the purpose of acquisition, with no reasonable relation to the State's objective, thus violating Article 14.
The 1960 Validation Act is invalid because it depends entirely on the 1955 Act; a legislature cannot validate acquisitions made under a constitutionally void law.
provisions: The Assam Acquisition of Land for Flood Control and Prevention of Erosion Act, 1955
The Assam Acquisition of Land for Flood Control and Prevention of Erosion (Validation) Act, 1960
doctrines: Doctrine of Just Equivalent under Article 31(2)
Doctrine of Reasonable Classification under Article 14
Doctrine of Invalid Validation of Unconstitutional Laws

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, which placed certain land reform laws in the Ninth Schedule, arguing that it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
issues_decided: Whether the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, is valid despite its impact on fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31?
Whether the doctrine of stare decisis applies to constitutional amendments upheld in earlier decisions like Sankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh?
Whether Parliament can amend fundamental rights under Article 368 using the procedure in the substantive part of the article without special limitations?
holdings: The Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, is valid as it falls within the amending power under Article 368, and its effect on fundamental rights is permissible under the existing interpretation of the Constitution.

The principle of stare decisis applies strongly in constitutional matters where large-scale public reliance exists, and earlier decisions upholding Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights should not be overturned.

Parliament has the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including fundamental rights, under Article 368, provided the procedure is followed, and such amendments do not require a special majority beyond what is specified in the article.
doctrines: Doctrine of Stare Decisis
Parliamentary Sovereignty in Constitutional Amendment
Incidental Effect Doctrine
Prospective Overruling (not decided)

card.dispute: The collateral of a deceased man challenged the widow's claim to his property, arguing her prior divorce and remarriage were invalid due to absence of custom permitting remarriage of divorced women among Jats of Jullundur District.
issues_decided: Whether a valid custom of divorce existed among Hindu Jats in Jullundur District permitting a divorced woman to remarry during the lifetime of her first husband.
Whether the Riwaj-i-Am of Jullundur District is a reliable source to prove the non-existence of such a custom.
Whether oral evidence and customs in surrounding districts can establish the existence of a local custom.
holdings: A valid custom of divorce existed among Hindu Jats in Jullundur District, which permitted a divorced woman to remarry during the lifetime of her first husband.
The Riwaj-i-Am of Jullundur District is unreliable as a sole source to disprove a custom, especially when contradicted by oral and comparative evidence.
Customs prevailing in surrounding districts, combined with oral testimony, can support the existence of a local custom, particularly when tribal customs are widespread across regions.
provisions: Hindu Law (as applicable to Jats in Punjab)
doctrines: Proof of custom through oral evidence and surrounding practices
Rejection of unreliable official records in favor of community practice
Dissolution of marriage by custom permits remarriage unless expressly restricted

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, claiming it violated their fundamental rights by restricting land use and development without adequate safeguards.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, violate Article 14 (equality before law) of the Constitution
Whether the said provisions impose unreasonable restrictions on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f), violating Article 19(5)
Whether Section 13 grants arbitrary and uncontrolled power to the local authority to deny commencement certificates
Whether the combined operation of Sections 4 and 11(3) allows indefinite delay in acquiring land for public purposes, causing unreasonable restriction on property rights
holdings: The provisions of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, including Sections 9 to 13, do not violate Article 14 as they contain sufficient procedural safeguards and serve a public purpose.
The restrictions imposed by the Act on land use are reasonable and justified under Article 19(5) in the interest of the general public and urban development.
Section 13 does not confer arbitrary power as it requires inquiry and decision based on the development plan, and is exercised by high-ranking officials familiar with the planning process.
The time frame under Sections 4 and 11(3) for land acquisition is not unreasonable, as delays may arise from financial and logistical constraints inherent in large-scale urban planning.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5)
Equality before law under Article 14
Principle of non-arbitrariness in administrative action
Balancing individual property rights with public interest in urban planning

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications signed by an Under Secretary, arguing lack of authority and incorrect classification of land as 'arable' and 'urgently needed'.
issues_decided: Whether an Under Secretary could lawfully sign notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the power to form an opinion on urgency of land acquisition could be delegated to a Secretary or Under Secretary
Whether the term 'arable land' includes land capable of cultivation as well as land actually cultivated
holdings: Notifications under the Land Acquisition Act can be signed by an Under Secretary if acting under the authority of the government, as the Rules of Business permit such delegation.
The power to form an opinion on urgency under Section 17 rests with the government and can be exercised through authorized officers like the Secretary, provided formal approval exists.
The term 'arable land' includes both land actually cultivated and land capable of cultivation, as supported by statutory context and legal precedents.
provisions: Rules of Business, Gujarat Government, Rules 7, 10, 13, 15
doctrines: Delegation of executive power
Doctrine of lawful authorization in administrative action
Statutory interpretation based on context and historical usage

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land reform laws and constitutional amendments that placed these laws beyond judicial review, arguing they violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament has the power to amend fundamental rights under Article 368 of the Constitution
Whether constitutional amendments are 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and can be struck down if they abridge fundamental rights
Whether the doctrine of prospective overruling can be applied to constitutional amendments
holdings: Parliament does not have the power to amend fundamental rights under Article 368, as such rights are immutable.
Constitutional amendments are 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and must not abridge fundamental rights.
The doctrine of prospective overruling is applicable to constitutional jurisprudence to prevent disruption of past legislative and administrative actions.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 97
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective overruling
Doctrine of implied limitations on amending power
Stare decisis in constitutional law

card.dispute: Kamla Prasad Singh, a private individual, filed complaints against Hari Nath Singh and others for abetting public servants in creating false land records, leading to a legal dispute over whether private complaints were permissible under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the bar under Section 195 Cr.P.C. applies to private complaints for offences under Section 218 IPC.
Whether the offence committed by public servants in preparing false land records falls under Section 192 or Section 218 IPC.
Whether a private person can initiate prosecution for abetment of fabricating false records not intended for use in judicial proceedings.
holdings: Section 195 Cr.P.C. bars private complaints for offences under Section 192/193 IPC when false evidence is intended for use in judicial proceedings.
Section 218 IPC deals with intentional preparation of false records by public servants to save or injure property, independent of judicial proceedings, and is not covered by Section 195 Cr.P.C.
A private complaint is maintainable for abetment of offences under Section 218 IPC as it does not require the record to be used in a judicial proceeding.
doctrines: Distinction between false evidence for judicial use and false record by public servant
Bar on private prosecution under Section 195 Cr.P.C.
Independent nature of offence under Section 218 IPC

card.dispute: The appellants (sons of the testator's daughters) challenged the validity of a will under which the testator's mother inherited all his property, claiming he was a minor and of unsound mind when executing it, while the respondents upheld its validity.
issues_decided: Whether a statement as to age in a will is admissible under Section 32(5) of the Indian Evidence Act to prove majority of the testator
Whether a written statement by a party asserting the testator's majority, made after a dispute arose, is admissible under Sections 32(5) or 32(6)
Whether the subsequent conduct of the parties can support the validity of a will
Whether a discrepancy between the body of the will and the schedule regarding property description results in partial intestacy
holdings: A statement of age in a will is admissible under Section 32(5) as it relates to the existence of a family relationship and indicates the commencement of such relationship by blood.
A statement made after a dispute has arisen about the testator's age is inadmissible under Sections 32(5) and 32(6) because it lacks the required 'ante litem motam' character.
The long-standing conduct of parties recognizing the will's validity and acting upon it supports the conclusion that the will was validly executed.
A discrepancy between the property description in the body and schedule of a will does not create partial intestacy if the will clearly expresses an intention to dispose of the entire property.
doctrines: Ante litem motam
Admissibility of statements relating to family relationships
Use of subsequent conduct to infer acceptance of a document's validity
Harmonious construction of wills to give effect to testator's intention

card.dispute: The assessee firm contested the tax authorities' classification of its sale of land and buildings as an adventure in the nature of trade, arguing it was a capital investment, not a trading activity.
issues_decided: Whether the purchase and sale of land and buildings constituted an adventure in the nature of trade under s. 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the Appellate Tribunal's statement of case was sufficient for the High Court to decide the reference
holdings: A transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade if, on a consideration of all relevant facts and circumstances, it shows an intention to make profit; the question is mixed in law and fact and is reviewable.
The Appellate Tribunal must clearly state its findings of fact and law in the statement of case; a vague or incomplete statement hampers judicial review and serves no useful purpose.
doctrines: Mixed question of law and fact
Totality of circumstances test for adventure in the nature of trade
Duty of tribunal to frame a proper statement of case

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1955, as amended, arguing that the State Legislature lacked competence to enact it and that it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 by allowing arbitrary land reallocation and imposition of contribution costs.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislature was competent to enact the Bombay Town Planning Act under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
Whether the provisions of the Act violated the fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 by conferring arbitrary powers in land reallotment and cost contribution.
holdings: The State Legislature was competent to enact the Bombay Town Planning Act as town planning falls under Entry 18 of List II and Entry 20 of List III of the Seventh Schedule.
The Act does not violate Articles 14, 19, or 31 as it prescribes reasonable restrictions, detailed procedures, and appeal mechanisms, ensuring that powers are not arbitrary or excessive.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 18
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 20
Bombay Town Planning (Gujarat Amendment and Validating Provisions) Act, 1963, Act 52 of 1963
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5)
Test of reasonableness in procedural and substantive aspects
Principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Doctrine of legislative competence under Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The respondents, Sikhs from the village, sued to remove the appellant Mahant from his position at a Gurdwara maintained for Nirmala Sadhus, claiming they had sufficient interest in the trust as villagers and as Sikh followers.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents had a sufficient interest in the trust as Lambardars and residents of the village to maintain a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
Whether the Nirmala Sadhus are part of the Sikh community such that Sikh followers have a right to institute a suit regarding the management of a Dera dedicated to them.
holdings: Mere status as Lambardars or residents of the village does not confer a legal interest in a public trust sufficient to maintain a suit under Section 92, CPC, especially when they are not donors or successors of donors.

Nirmala Sadhus, though originating from Sikh tradition, have diverged significantly in beliefs and practices, aligning more with Hindu Vedanta and Udasi traditions, and are not part of the orthodox Sikh community; thus, Sikhs as a class do not have a legal interest in trusts dedicated exclusively to Nirmala Sadhus.
doctrines: Standing to sue in public trust matters
Doctrinal divergence and religious identity
Interpretation of 'interest' under Section 92, CPC

card.dispute: Three surviving plaintiffs sought to file a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure after one of the four sanctioned plaintiffs died, raising the question of whether the suit was maintainable without fresh sanction.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable by fewer persons than those to whom the Advocate-General's permission was granted, when one of the sanctioned persons died before institution of the suit.
Whether the death of one of the sanctioned plaintiffs before filing the suit renders the subsequent suit by the remaining plaintiffs invalid.
holdings: An authority to sue granted to multiple persons under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a joint authority requiring all sanctioned persons to act together; a suit by only some of them is not competent.
If one of the persons to whom sanction was granted dies before the suit is filed, the remaining persons cannot proceed without obtaining fresh sanction from the Advocate-General.
doctrines: Joint authority doctrine
Maintainability of representative suits under Section 92
Conformity of suit with sanction

card.dispute: The appellant, the sole surviving male heir, contested whether the respondent, his step-grandmother and widow of his grandfather, was entitled to a share in the joint family property that passed by survivorship.
issues_decided: Whether clause (d) of sub-section (1) of Section 8 of the Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933) entitles the step-grandmother of the sole surviving male coparcener to a share when property passes by survivorship.
Whether a theoretical partition under clause (d) can include female relatives beyond those of the penultimate and sole surviving coparceners.
Whether the definition of 'mother' in sub-section (3) extends to the grandmother of the surviving coparcener.
holdings: Clause (d) of Section 8(1) does not create an independent class of entitled females but requires a theoretical partition between the penultimate and sole surviving coparcener to determine who among the females enumerated in clauses (a), (b), or (c) would have a share.

The step-grandmother, being the widow of the grandfather of the sole surviving coparcener, does not fall within any class entitled to a share under clause (a), as the assumed partition is between father and son, where the widow of the father has no claim.

The term 'mother' in Section 8(3), though extended to step-mother, does not include the grandmother of the surviving coparcener; the mutatis mutandis application of mother's rights applies only to the paternal grandmother of the coparcener in the line of the father, not the son.
provisions: The Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933), Section 8(1)(d)
The Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933), Section 8(2)
The Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933), Section 8(3)
doctrines: Theoretical or notional partition
Literal construction of statutory provisions
Doctrine of ejusdem generis (in interpreting extended definitions)
Principle of statutory interpretation in social legislation requiring conformity with language

card.dispute: The Municipality of Taloda fought with the Charity Commissioner over whether a property it held was subject to a public trust for religious and charitable purposes benefiting sadhus, saints, and visitors to a samadhi, or was solely its private property.
issues_decided: Whether the property conveyed to the Municipality was held subject to a public trust under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950
Whether the beneficiaries (sadhus, saints, religious mendicants, and visitors to the samadhi) constitute a section of the public for the purpose of a charitable trust
Whether the decision of the Survey Officer under the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 bars proceedings under the Bombay Public Trusts Act
Whether the Charity Commissioner has the right to appeal against a decision denying the existence of a public trust
holdings: A trust for the benefit of sadhus, saints, religious mendicants, and visitors to a samadhi constitutes a public charitable trust under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, as they form an uncertain and fluctuating body of persons with a common religious bond.

The beneficiaries of the trust, though belonging to a religious group, constitute a section of the public, and the purpose of providing shelter and maintaining a samadhi qualifies as an object of general public utility under Section 9 of the Act.

Proceedings under Section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act are not barred by a Survey Officer’s declaration of municipal ownership, as the trust inquiry does not seek to set aside that order but addresses a distinct legal question.

The Charity Commissioner, as a statutory authority responsible for administering public trusts, has the right to appeal against an adverse decision even if it involves supporting a prior quasi-judicial finding.
doctrines: Uncertain and fluctuating body of persons doctrine
Section of the public doctrine in charitable trusts
Doctrine of constructive trust
Doctrine of statutory interpretation of public trust definitions
Right of statutory authority to appeal

card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Committee appealed against the quashing of its resolution enhancing the rental value of premises occupied by Indian Bank Ltd. from Rs. 1,650 to Rs. 7,200, and the confirmation of that resolution by the Additional District Magistrate.
issues_decided: Whether the notice issued by the Municipal Committee under Section 67(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, was in accordance with law.
Whether the grounds mentioned in the notice—'mistake or fraud or misrepresentation'—were validly invoked and sufficiently particularized.
Whether the respondent bank came to court with unclean hands by making false statements about the completion date of construction.
holdings: A notice under Section 67(1) must specify the reason—fraud, accident, or mistake—for altering an assessment to enable the assessee to respond; a general allegation without particulars violates natural justice and renders the notice invalid.

The use of 'misrepresentation' in the notice is legally impermissible as it is not a ground under Section 67(1); mechanically including multiple grounds without explanation fails to meet statutory requirements.

The appellate court will not interfere with the discretion of the lower court to dismiss a writ petition on grounds of unclean hands, especially when the factual dispute about construction dates was not decided below.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Strict construction of tax statutes
Judge in one's own cause
Clean hands doctrine

card.dispute: Textile mills challenged the municipal corporation's method of levying property tax at a flat rate per 100 sq. ft. of floor area and inclusion of machinery as part of 'land' for taxation.
issues_decided: Whether the method of assessing property tax based on floor area at a flat rate is valid under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949?
Whether Rules 7(2) and 7(3) of the Act, which allow the Commissioner to specify machinery as part of 'land' for taxation without clear guidelines, suffer from excessive delegation?
Whether the inclusion of plant and machinery in 'land' for rating purposes is within the legislative competence of the State?
holdings: The method of taxing based on floor area at a flat rate is invalid as it violates the statutory requirement to assess rateable value based on annual rental value.

Rule 7(2) is ultra vires the State Legislature because the State lacks competence to tax machinery not part of land, and Rule 7(3) suffers from excessive delegation due to absence of guiding principles.
Plant and machinery cannot be deemed part of 'land' for taxation unless clearly authorized by law, and such inclusion exceeds the scope of permissible interpretation or deeming fiction.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 49
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Rule 7(2) and (3)
Constitution of India, Entry 49, List II, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Excessive delegation of legislative power
Principle of rateable value based on rental worth
Deeming fiction cannot override clear statutory language
Equality in taxation under Article 14

card.dispute: The Calcutta Pinjrapole Society challenged the validity of a land acquisition declaration, arguing it did not properly reflect the government's satisfaction as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act must expressly state the government's satisfaction regarding the need for acquisition for a public purpose.
Whether the use of the phrase 'it appears to the Governor' instead of 'the Governor is satisfied' renders the declaration invalid.
holdings: The declaration under Section 6 does not need to expressly state the government's satisfaction; it only needs to declare that the land is needed for a public purpose.
The use of the words 'it appears to the Governor' instead of 'the Governor is satisfied' does not invalidate the declaration, as no specific form is mandated by law.
doctrines: Condition precedent
Declaratory validity
Presumption of regularity in administrative action

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the inclusion of land transferred to his wife in the calculation of his ceiling area under land reform laws, arguing it violated constitutional rights and involved excessive delegation.
issues_decided: Whether Section 32FF of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, which disregards transfers to certain relatives for ceiling purposes, violates the second proviso to Article 31A of the Constitution
Whether the delegation of power to the State Government to specify such relatives under Rule 23A amounts to excessive delegation
Whether the rules for determining fair rent under Rule 28 are ultra vires the Act due to reliance on outdated yield data from the last settlement
holdings: Section 32FF does not violate Article 31A, second proviso, as it serves the purpose of preventing evasion of land ceiling laws by transfers to family members.
The delegation to the State Government under Rule 23A is not excessive, as the Act provides sufficient guidance and framework for the rule-making power.
