Rule 28, which bases fair rent on the last settlement's yield data, is not ultra vires the Act, as no evidence was presented to show that yields have significantly increased to make the rule unreasonable.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32FF
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32G
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Rule 23A
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Rule 28
doctrines: Excessive delegation
Protection under Article 31A
Presumption of constitutionality
Judicial restraint in absence of factual evidence

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser of a portion of mortgaged property, challenged the validity of the mortgagee's sale of the property for lack of notice to him and claimed compensation for improvements under Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a purchaser of a portion of mortgaged property is entitled to notice under Section 69(2) of the Transfer of Property Act before the mortgagee exercises the power of sale
Whether the appellant, as a transferee, is entitled to compensation for improvements made on the property under Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act
holdings: Notice under Section 69(2) need only be given to the mortgagor or one of several mortgagors; a transferee of a portion of the property is not entitled to separate notice if the mortgagors remain interested and the transferee had knowledge of the mortgage.

Section 51 does not apply where the transferee knew the property was subject to a mortgage and did not believe in good faith that he was absolutely entitled to it; thus, no right to compensation for improvements arises.
doctrines: Notice to mortgagor binds transferees under Section 69
Good faith belief in absolute title required for Section 51 improvement claim

card.dispute: The appellants, tenants inducted by a widow after a decree in favor of the adopted son, fought to retain possession of agricultural land under the Hyderabad Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, claiming to be lawful cultivators.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, inducted by the widow after a decree in favor of the adopted son, could be considered 'asami shikmi' under Section 2(13) of the Hyderabad Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1950
Whether the appellants could claim protection under Section 5 of the Act as lawful cultivators despite being inducted by a trespasser
holdings: Persons inducted onto land by someone who lost title and possession via court decree are not 'asami shikmi' under Section 2(13), as the inducer was a trespasser at the time of induction.
Tenants inducted by a trespasser cannot claim protection under Section 5 of the Act, as they are not lawfully cultivating the land in relation to the true owner.
provisions: Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 2(13)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 5
doctrines: Lawful cultivation requirement for tenancy protection
No tenancy rights can arise from a trespasser's act

card.dispute: The appellant (Kalawati) and the respondent (Bisheshwar) disputed whether a land transfer made after July 7, 1949, was void or merely unrecognizable under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, affecting the appellant's right to maintain a suit for eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a transfer of estate after July 7, 1949, is void ab initio or merely barred from recognition under Section 23(1)(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951
Whether the deletion of Section 23(1)(b) prospectively in 1954 and retrospectively in 1956 conferred bhumidhari rights on the transferee
Whether the withdrawal of the transferor (Kapurthala Estate) from the suit affected the maintainability of the suit by the transferee after the removal of the recognition bar
holdings: A transfer made after July 7, 1949, is not void but valid; Section 23(1)(b) only bars its recognition for any purpose under the Act, not its existence.

The deletion of Section 23(1)(b) prospectively from October 10, 1954, allowed the transferee to enforce bhumidhari rights from that date; retrospective amendment in 1956 applied only to compensation and rehabilitation rights.

After the bar on recognition was removed, the transferee could maintain the suit independently; the transferor’s withdrawal did not invalidate the suit as it occurred after the recognition bar was lifted.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 23(1)(b)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 18
doctrines: Distinction between void transactions and those merely unrecognizable
Prospective and retrospective operation of amendments
Deeming fiction in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The nearest reversioner of a deceased husband challenged the validity of an adoption made by the husband's widow after his death, claiming the adopted son was not legally the son of the deceased husband and could not divest prior property rights.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption was invalid because the mother alone gave the child in adoption while the father was alive, contrary to Section 9(2) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956
Whether an adoption by a widow under the Act results in the child being deemed the son of her deceased husband
holdings: The adoption was valid as the deed showed both parents gave the child in adoption; the mention of the mother's consent was in compliance with Section 9(2), not an indication of sole authority.
An adoption by a married Hindu woman, including a widow, makes the child the adopted son of her deceased husband as well, under Section 12 of the Act, integrating the child into the husband’s family.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 5(1)
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 9(2)
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 13
doctrines: Relation back doctrine abrogated by Section 12
Adoption to a person as distinct from adoption by a person
Severance and replacement of familial ties upon adoption

card.dispute: The appellants (Sonawati & Ors) and respondents (Sri Ram & Anr) fought over ownership and possession of agricultural land, specifically whether Pritam Singh (predecessor of appellants) was a protected cultivator (adhivasi) under land reform laws and whether the High Court could grant a decree for possession in a civil suit.
issues_decided: Whether Pritam Singh was an 'adhivasi' under s. 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, based on being recorded as an 'occupant' in 1356 Fasli
Whether Pritam Singh was in 'cultivatory possession' under s. 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952, in 1359 Fasli
Whether the High Court in second appeal could allow amendment of the plaint to claim possession and grant a decree for possession
Whether a civil court has jurisdiction to pass a decree for possession against a trespasser in respect of agricultural land
holdings: A person recorded as 'occupant' in 1356 Fasli is not automatically an adhivasi under s. 20(b) of U.P. Act 1 of 1951 if the entry is inaccurate or not supported by actual possession.
Cultivatory possession under s. 3 of U.P. Act 31 of 1952 requires lawful and continuous possession for the entire year 1359 Fasli; forcible or trespassory occupation does not qualify.

The High Court in second appeal had jurisdiction to allow amendment of the plaint to claim possession and grant a decree when the defendant had obtained possession during litigation through criminal proceedings.
A civil court has jurisdiction to grant a decree for possession in favor of the rightful owner even against a trespasser, and such relief is not barred in agricultural land disputes.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 20(b)
doctrines: Cultivatory possession requires lawful and continuous occupation
Forcible possession does not confer rights under land reform statutes
High Court may amend plaint in second appeal to grant appropriate relief
Civil court jurisdiction not ousted in possession disputes even for agricultural land

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the constitutional validity of the Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue (Additional Assessment) and Cess Revision Act, 1962, which imposed a flat additional land revenue assessment, while landowners argued it violated the right to equality under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3 and 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue (Additional Assessment) and Cess Revision Act, 1962, violate Article 14 of the Constitution by imposing a flat rate without regard to land productivity or classification.
Whether the Act permits arbitrary discrimination by delegating unguided assessment powers to revenue officers.
holdings: A law that imposes a flat additional land revenue without considering established classifications like soil quality or water supply creates unreasonable discrimination and violates Article 14.
Delegating unguided assessment powers to officers without procedural safeguards or avenues for appeal results in arbitrary and unequal application, offending the principle of equality.
provisions: The Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue (Additional Assessment) and Cess Revision Act, 1962, Sections 3, 4, 6, 8
doctrines: Equality before law under Article 14
Permissible classification test
Prohibition of arbitrariness in state action
Reasonable relation between classification and object of law

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a portion of the house used for residence, where the property was originally let out for both residential and non-residential purposes (running a school).
issues_decided: Whether a court can grant a decree for eviction under Section 13(1)(e) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, limited to the portion of premises used for residential purposes when the tenancy is composite (residential and non-residential)?
Whether the contract of tenancy for composite purposes can be divided by the court to allow partial eviction under the Act?
holdings: Section 13(1)(e) applies only when premises are let solely for residential purposes; it does not apply when the letting is for composite residential and non-residential use.
A composite tenancy contract cannot be split by the court to grant eviction for part of the premises, in the absence of any statutory provision authorizing such division.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(e)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 2(g)
doctrines: Unity of contract in tenancy
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions
Bona fide requirement for personal residence as a ground for eviction

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh contested the court-fee payable in a suit where Ram Krishan Burman sought a declaration that a prior decree in favor of Radhey Lal was void and that he was the rightful owner of certain properties.
issues_decided: Whether the suit fell under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act, requiring court-fee based on the market value of the property?
Whether a decree for declaration of title to property constitutes a 'decree for money or other property' under Section 7(iv-A)?
Whether a decree in invitum can be regarded as an 'instrument securing money or other property' under the same provision?
holdings: A suit for declaration of title to property does not fall under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court-Fees Act if it does not seek recovery of money or property.
The phrase 'decree for money or other property' means a decree for recovery, not one concerning title or ownership.
A decree in invitum is not an 'instrument securing money or other property'; only consent decrees based on contracts may so qualify.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Distinction between decrees for recovery and decrees concerning title
Consent decree as a hybrid of contract and judicial order

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and others contested Subodh Gopal Bose's claim to a customary right to commercially quarry limestone from the Lower Murli Hill as a tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the entries in the Custom-sheets under the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885, established a legally enforceable customary right to quarry limestone for trade purposes.
Whether a claimed customary right to commercially exploit limestone could be considered reasonable and legally enforceable.
Whether the respondent could claim tenancy rights over land acquired for the Dehri-Rohtas Light Railway Company.
holdings: Entries in Custom-sheets prepared under s.102 of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885, do not conclusively establish a customary right, as they lack proof of ancient, continuous, and as-of-right usage.
A customary right allowing commercial quarrying of limestone by tenants would be unreasonable if it risks destruction of the land or leads to public conflict, and thus is unenforceable.
No tenancy rights can be claimed over land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, as the original title is extinguished, and derivative rights cannot be enforced post-acquisition.
doctrines: Custom must be ancient, certain, reasonable, and exercised as of right
Profit a prendre by an indefinite body is unenforceable if it threatens destruction of the subject property
Presumptive value of revenue records does not override legal requirements for proving custom

card.dispute: The mutawalli of a Muslim wakf and the Board of Muslim Endowments sued to recover wakf property in Hyderabad lost in 1937; defendants argued the 1956 suit was time-barred under the Indian Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for recovery of wakf property was governed by the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 or the prior Hyderabad Limitation Act.
Whether the suit was time-barred under Article 142 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
Whether the Board of Muslim Endowments or the mutawalli could be regarded as an agent of the State Government, attracting a longer limitation period under Article 149.
Whether the pendency of earlier summary proceedings under the Hyderabad Endowment Regulation entitled the plaintiffs to exclusion of time under Sections 14 or 15 of the Indian Limitation Act.
holdings: The Indian Limitation Act, 1908 applies to the suit, and the Hyderabad Limitation Act ceased to operate upon its extension to Hyderabad under the Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951.
The suit is barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, as it was filed more than 12 years after the 1937 dispossession.
The Board of Muslim Endowments and the mutawalli are not agents of the State Government; thus, Article 149 does not apply.

The plaintiffs are not entitled to exclusion of time under Sections 14 or 15 of the Indian Limitation Act, as the contention was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court and no injunction stayed the present suit.
doctrines: Doctrine of limitation for suits involving immovable property
Doctrine of statutory succession of limitation laws
Doctrine of agency in governmental functions
Doctrine of exclusion of time under limitation law for pending proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord sued the sub-tenant for possession and mesne profits after the original tenant's tenancy was determined by notice, but continued in occupation and sublet part of the premises.
issues_decided: Whether a notice to quit determining a tenancy can be unilaterally withdrawn by the tenant without the landlord's consent
Whether a statutory tenant has the right to sub-let the premises and confer protection under the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act on the sub-tenant
Whether the expression 'tenant' in Sections 12(1)(c) and 13(2) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act includes a statutory tenant
holdings: A notice to quit under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, once served and effective, cannot be unilaterally withdrawn by the tenant without the landlord's consent.
A statutory tenant, who has no estate or interest in the property, cannot sub-let the premises and confer statutory protection on the sub-lessee.
The term 'tenant' in Sections 12(1)(c) and 13(2) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, refers only to a contractual tenant, not a statutory tenant.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 2(11)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 12
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 13
doctrines: Notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act determines tenancy upon expiry
Statutory tenant has only personal right to protection from eviction, not transferable interest
Statutory interpretation: definition of 'tenant' excludes statutory tenant where context so requires

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against a High Court decision declaring a clause in the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 unconstitutional for violating the right to compensation under Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether clause (b) of sub-section (3) of Section 8 of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution by not providing just equivalent compensation.
Whether the High Court was justified in not dismissing the petition on grounds of delay under Article 226.
holdings: Clause (b) of Section 8(3) is unconstitutional as it caps compensation at twice the value on the date of requisition, which may be far below the market value at acquisition, thus failing to provide a just equivalent as required by Article 31(2).
The High Court rightly exercised its discretion to entertain the petition despite delay, as the violation of a fundamental right was involved and the delay did not bar relief.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8(3)
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 7
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 24
doctrines: Just equivalent compensation under Article 31(2)
Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Judicial discretion in entertaining writ petitions despite delay

card.dispute: The plaintiff, adopted by the son of a Hindu joint family, claimed a share in the property left by his adoptive father, while the defendants argued the property became the father's absolute property due to election under the will.
issues_decided: Whether the son's acceptance of probate of his father's will constituted an election under Section 180 of the Indian Succession Act, converting joint family property into his absolute property.
Whether the plaintiff, as an adopted son, was bound by his adoptive father's alleged election under the will.
holdings: Election under Section 180 of the Indian Succession Act arises only when a legatee gains a benefit under the will that they would not otherwise be entitled to; since the son would have inherited the property by survivorship, no election occurred.
The adopted son acquired an independent interest in the joint family property upon adoption and was not bound by any alleged election by his adoptive father, as he did not claim through him.
doctrines: Doctrine of election
Joint family property under Mitakshara law
Right by birth in ancestral property
Independent interest of coparcener

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent on due dates, despite having accepted the delayed payments, and challenged the refusal of revenue authorities and the High Court to grant eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord is entitled to a decree for eviction under Section 25(2) of the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, when the tenant has paid arrears of rent before the application for eviction and the landlord has accepted such payment.
Whether acceptance of delayed rent by the landlord constitutes a waiver of the termination of tenancy based on default in payment.
holdings: Section 25(2) does not entitle a landlord to eviction if the tenant has paid all arrears before the application and the landlord has accepted them, as the cause of action for eviction ceases to exist.

Acceptance of arrears by the landlord before filing the eviction application constitutes a waiver of the right to terminate the tenancy for those defaults, especially where no arrears remain due at the time of application.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 30
doctrines: Waiver of contractual or statutory rights by conduct
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and avoidance of absurd results
No relief against forfeiture in statutory tenancies unless expressly provided

card.dispute: The petitioners, inamdars whose property rights were abolished under the Mysore Inams Abolition Act, challenged the Act's constitutional validity on grounds of inadequate compensation and lack of public purpose, arguing it exceeded state legislative competence.
issues_decided: Whether the Mysore (Personal and Miscellaneous) Inams Abolition Act, 1955 violates Article 31(2) for not providing adequate compensation
Whether the Act exceeds the legislative competence of the Mysore Legislature under Entry 36 of List II and Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule as they stood before the 7th Amendment
holdings: The word 'acquisition' in legislative entries does not implicitly require payment of compensation or public purpose; these conditions are expressly provided in Article 31(2), so their absence in the Act does not render it ultra vires.

The phrase 'subject to the provisions of Entry 42, List III' in Entry 36, List II does not impose implied restrictions on state legislation but indicates parliamentary supremacy on the subject, not constitutional limitations on state power.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, Entry 36, List II
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, Entry 42, List III
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, Entry 33, List I
doctrines: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Implied limitations on statutory interpretation
Protection under Article 31A for agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The tenants and the landlord's son disputed over the enforcement of a decree based on an arbitration award, which directed the tenants to remove machinery and vacate the premises, with objections raised regarding the award's validity and contravention of rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether an objection to the validity of an arbitration award can be raised after a decree has been passed on it in execution proceedings.
Whether a decree for eviction passed in contravention of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 is a nullity.
Whether the decree for eviction could be enforced by the landlord or his son.
Whether the part of the decree directing removal of machinery was valid and enforceable.
holdings: Once a decree is passed on an arbitration award under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, parties cannot later challenge the award's validity in execution proceedings; the decree conclusively establishes the award's validity between the parties.

A decree for recovery of possession passed in contravention of Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 is a nullity because the court failed to determine the existence of a statutory ground for eviction.
Neither the landlord nor his son can enforce a decree that is a nullity due to contravention of mandatory provisions of the Rent Act.
The portion of the decree directing removal of machinery is severable, valid, and enforceable by the landlord's son who was a party to the arbitration.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13
doctrines: Finality of decree on arbitration award
Nullity of decree violating mandatory statutory provisions
Severability of decree terms
Exclusive jurisdiction for challenging award validity under arbitration scheme

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the denial of 15% solatium and adequacy of compensation in land acquisition under the Madras City Improvement Trust Act.
issues_decided: Whether the omission of 15% solatium under the Madras City Improvement Trust Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether compensation based on market value as of the notification date under Section 47 constitutes a 'just equivalent' under Article 31(2)
Whether landowners are entitled to additional compensation for severance damages
holdings: The exclusion of 15% solatium under the Madras Act does not violate Article 14 as the classification is reasonable and based on public purpose.
Compensation determined by market value on the date of notification under Section 47 is constitutionally valid and constitutes a 'just equivalent' under Article 31(2).
Landowners are entitled to solatium at 15% on market value, and the High Court’s award of Rs. 2,500 for severance is upheld due to lack of contrary evidence.
provisions: Madras City Improvement Trust Act, 1945, Section 73
Madras City Improvement Trust Act, 1950, Section 173(2)
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 23(1), Section 23(2), Section 4(1), Section 6, Section 16
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Just equivalent compensation under Article 31(2)
Judicial restraint in valuation appeals
Principle of solatium in land acquisition

card.dispute: Caltex (India) Ltd. and Bhagwan Devi Marodia fought over whether the lessee's delayed application for lease renewal, made 12 days after the stipulated time, should be excused and the lease renewed.
issues_decided: Whether time was of the essence in the contract for renewal of lease under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 55
Whether equitable relief could be granted for failure to apply for renewal within the stipulated time
Whether the lessee's delay due to oversight amounted to a ground for excusing non-compliance with the time condition
holdings: A stipulation as to time in a contract for renewal of a lease is of the essence of the contract, even if not expressly stated, and must be strictly complied with.
Equitable relief against failure to give timely notice of renewal is only available in cases of unavoidable accident, fraud, surprise, or non-wilful ignorance, not mere neglect.
Delay caused by oversight without unavoidable circumstances cannot excuse non-compliance with a time-bound condition in a lease renewal clause.
doctrines: Time as essence of contract in lease renewals
Equitable relief for non-performance only under exceptional circumstances
Strict compliance required for conditions precedent in lease covenants

card.dispute: The Chief Settlement Commissioner challenged the allotment of land to the heirs of Nanak Chand, arguing that since he died before partition, the land should have been allotted in his name, not his sons'.
issues_decided: Whether Nanak Chand, who died in June 1947 before the partition, qualifies as a 'displaced person' under the East Punjab Evacuees Act and related laws.
Whether land allotment for abandoned property in Pakistan must be made in the name of a deceased pre-partition landowner or his heirs.
Whether administrative instructions in Tarlok Singh's Land Resettlement Manual override statutory definitions of 'displaced person'.
holdings: A person who died before the partition and did not migrate due to civil disturbances cannot be considered a 'displaced person' or 'refugee' under the relevant statutes.
Land allotment must be made to actual displaced persons; heirs of a pre-deceased landholder are eligible only if the deceased qualified as a displaced person at death.
Executive instructions, such as those in Tarlok Singh's Manual, cannot override statutory definitions and must be interpreted within the limits of the law.
provisions: The East Punjab Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 22(2)(f) and (ff)
The East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948, Section 2(d)
The East Punjab Displaced Persons (Land Resettlement) Act, 1949, Section 2(c) and 2(b)
doctrines: Rule of law
Supremacy of statutory law over executive instructions
Strict construction of definitions in welfare legislation based on legislative intent

card.dispute: The appellants (sub-tenants) and respondents (new lessees) disputed who became Sirdars of the land under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Reforms Act, 1950, based on their respective tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants continued as sub-tenants under s. 295A of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939 after the surrender of the chief tenant's rights on 15th January, 1951
Whether the appellants retained rights under s. 47(4) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939 beyond 30th June, 1951
Whether the appellants qualified as Sirdars under s. 19(vii) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Reforms Act, 1950
holdings: The sub-lease of the appellants was extinguished upon the surrender of the chief tenant's interest under s. 47(1), and s. 295A did not preserve their sub-tenancy beyond that date.

The right under s. 47(4) is a statutory, limited right to remain in possession for the remainder of the sub-lease term or five years, whichever is shorter, and does not recur or extend beyond that period.
The appellants did not hold the land in the capacity of sub-tenants on 1st July, 1952, and thus did not qualify as Sirdars under s. 19(vii) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Reforms Act, 1950.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 19(vii)
doctrines: Statutory extinction of tenancy rights upon surrender of superior interest
Limited statutory right of sub-tenants under Section 47(4) as a non-recurring, time-bound entitlement
Doctrine of accrual of rights under land reform statutes based on status as of a fixed date

card.dispute: The Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank and the tenants (Dalichand Jugraj Jain) disputed over whether the bank could initiate arbitration under the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act to eject the tenants, or whether the Rent Act vested exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of Small Causes.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the bank and the tenants could be referred to arbitration under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960
Whether the jurisdiction of the Registrar under the Co-operative Societies Act is ousted by Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the High Court could intervene under Article 226 despite the availability of an alternative remedy under Section 154 of the Co-operative Societies Act
holdings: A dispute between a co-operative society and a tenant does not fall under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act if it arises from landlord-tenant relations and not from the society's internal management.

Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 ousts the jurisdiction of the Registrar and confers exclusive authority on the Court of Small Causes to decide eviction matters, even if the landlord is a co-operative society.

The High Court can exercise jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash an interlocutory order even if a limited alternative remedy under Section 154 of the Co-operative Societies Act exists, as it is not a substantial alternative remedy.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Exclusive jurisdiction of special courts under rent control laws
Alternative remedy doctrine under Article 226

card.dispute: The Delhi Motor Company sued U.A. Basrurkar & Ors for possession of three portions of business premises under alleged sub-leases, which were unregistered, leading to a dispute over whether the documents created enforceable lease rights.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered documents constituted a valid and enforceable sub-lease under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the appellant could rely on Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act to enforce rights under an unregistered lease
Whether the appellant could claim specific performance of an unregistered lease agreement under Section 27A of the Specific Relief Act, 1877
holdings: The documents in question amounted to a lease for more than one year and required registration under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act; being unregistered, they could not be enforced.
Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is not available to a plaintiff seeking to enforce positive rights under an unregistered lease, but only as a defence to protect possession.

Specific performance under Section 27A of the Specific Relief Act is not available unless the entire contract is in writing and the lessee has taken possession of the entire leased property, which was not the case here.
doctrines: Part performance doctrine under Section 53A
Requirement of registration for leases exceeding one year
Specific performance of contracts for lease under part performance

card.dispute: The creditors alleged that a firm and its partners committed acts of insolvency through a gift deed by one partner, leading to insolvency adjudications challenged on procedural and substantive grounds.
issues_decided: Whether the three-month period under Section 9(1)(c) of the Provincial Insolvency Act starts from execution or registration of a deed of gift.
Whether an order of adjudication can be made against a firm in its name under the Provincial Insolvency Act.
Whether a firm can be adjudicated insolvent solely based on an act of insolvency by one partner.
holdings: The three-month period for filing an insolvency petition under Section 9(1)(c) begins from the date of registration of the deed, not execution, as registration is when the transfer becomes legally effective.

An order of adjudication can be made against a firm in its name if the conditions are satisfied, as Section 79(2)(c) contemplates such proceedings and rules provide for their operation against partners.
A firm cannot be adjudicated insolvent solely due to one partner's act of insolvency unless it is a joint act or attributable to the firm; such attribution depends on facts and circumstances.
provisions: Provincial Insolvency Act (5 of 1920), Section 6 Explanation
doctrines: Effective date of property transfer under registration law
Attribution of partner's act to the firm
Statutory interpretation to avoid nullification of legislative intent

card.dispute: The appellant, Gopal Krishnaji Ketkar, claimed ownership of a plot of land, while respondents argued it belonged to a public trust of which he was the manager.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed plot of land belonged to the appellant or to the public trust.
Whether the court can draw an adverse inference against a party who withholds important documentary evidence despite the onus of proof lying elsewhere.
holdings: The disputed plot was held to be property of the public trust based on the lack of documentary evidence showing private ownership and the appellant's fiduciary role.
A court may draw an adverse inference against a party who withholds important documents within their possession, even if the burden of proof lies on the other side.
doctrines: Adverse inference from non-production of evidence
Fiduciary possession not equivalent to ownership
Onus of proof vs. duty to produce relevant documents

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a will that bequeathed the deceased's property to the first defendant, who was the maternal uncle and had taken a prominent role in executing the will.
issues_decided: Whether the will was executed by the testator in a sound disposing state of mind.
Whether the propounder of the will, who took a substantial benefit and played a key role in its execution, discharged the burden of removing suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
holdings: A will executed by a testator who is physically weak and in a delirious mental state is not valid, as it lacks a sound disposing mind.

When the propounder of a will takes a prominent part in its execution and benefits substantially, the court must scrutinize the evidence vigilantly, and the burden lies on the propounder to dispel all suspicious circumstances.
doctrines: Suspicious circumstances doctrine in will execution
Burden of proof on the propounder of a will
Sound disposing mind requirement for testamentary capacity
Judicial caution in cases of undue influence or benefit to propounder

card.dispute: The Kangra Valley Slate Co. Ltd. fought with the State of Punjab over the rejection of its application for renewal of a mining lease on the grounds of being time-barred under Rule 28 of the Mines & Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 28(1) of the Mines & Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 prescribed a mandatory time limit for filing a renewal application for a mining lease
Whether the application made by the appellant was within the time limit prescribed under Rule 28
Whether Rule 28 is ultra vires Section 13(2) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
holdings: Rule 28(1) prescribing a six-month deadline for renewal applications is mandatory, not directory, to ensure timely decision-making and continuity in mineral development.
The application was time-barred as the appellant failed to prove it was sent on September 20, 1961; mere date on the application is insufficient to establish timely filing.
Rule 28 is valid and not ultra vires Section 13(2) of the Act, as the Central Government has general rule-making power under Section 13(1) to regulate grant of mining leases, including time limits.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 13(1) and Section 13(2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 18
Mines & Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, Rule 22, Rule 23, Rule 24
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory rule interpretation
Rule of strict compliance with statutory time limits in administrative processes
Doctrine of vires and ancillary powers in delegated legislation
Presumption against inefficiency in regulatory schemes

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of inam property post-abolition, while the revenue authorities contended it should vest in the tank as a charitable institution.
issues_decided: Whether the inam was granted in favour of the appellant's family or in favour of the tank.
Whether a tank can be considered a 'charitable institution' under the Andhra Inams (Abolition & Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956.
holdings: The inam was granted in favour of the tank, not the appellant's family, and the appellant was merely its manager.
Under Hindu law, a tank dedicated for public use is a charitable institution, and thus the inam property vests in the tank post-abolition, to be managed by its manager.
provisions: Andhra Inams (Abolition & Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, Section 2(E)
doctrines: Charitable institution under Hindu law
Dedication of property for public utility as valid charity
Managerial role distinct from ownership in religious/charitable endowments

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed whether an oral agreement to sell shares in a leased site was binding despite no formal document being executed, and whether the High Court could direct allotment of the site in partition without an application under the Partition Act.
issues_decided: Whether there was a valid oral agreement to sell shares in the leased site on July 6, 1952
Whether the oral agreement was ineffective due to contemplation of a formal document or lack of agreed mode of payment
Whether the appellant was a purchaser without notice of the prior oral agreement
Whether the High Court could direct allotment of a specific site in partition without an application under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893
holdings: An oral agreement for sale of property can be binding even if parties intend to execute a formal document later, provided the intention was not to be bound only upon execution.
The absence of an agreed mode of payment does not invalidate a contract if essential terms like price, area, and time of completion are settled.
A purchaser is not bona fide if they had knowledge of a prior oral agreement, especially when supported by circumstantial evidence and conduct.
The High Court cannot direct allotment of a specific portion in partition under equitable powers without an application under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893.
doctrines: Binding nature of oral contracts despite contemplation of formal agreement
Doctrine of completeness of contract despite omission of mode of payment
Notice to purchaser in equity
Jurisdictional limits of High Court in partition matters without statutory application

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's suit for eviction and arrears of rent, claiming overpayment of rent and entitlement to protection under the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to interfere with the appellate court's decree?
Whether the rent was in arrear despite the tenant's claim of overpayment?
Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under Sections 12(1) and 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947?
holdings: The High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC to revise the appellate court's decree because directing the landlord to render an account of overpayments was beyond the court's powers in a possession suit.
Rent is in arrear if overpaid amounts are not deducted within six months of payment, as the right to deduct is barred by limitation under Section 20 of the Bombay Rents Act.
A tenant cannot claim protection under Sections 12(1) and 12(3)(b) if they fail to pay or deposit standard rent during the pendency of the suit and instead claim no liability.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947, Section 20
doctrines: Limitation bars both recovery by suit and by deduction under rent control laws
Principle of readiness and willingness to pay rent as a condition for protection against eviction

card.dispute: The Nair Service Society Ltd. and Rev. Father K. C. Alexander disputed over possession of land (L(1)(a) and L(1)(b)), following the Society's grant of a Kuthakapattom lease and its alleged unlawful dispossession of the plaintiff.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court should have allowed the appellant to amend its pleadings to include a defense based on a subsequent Kuthakapattom lease granted in 1948.
Whether the 1948 Kuthakapattom lease could be given retroactive effect from the date of the first lease in 1939.
Whether laches and delay barred the amendment of pleadings after 17 years of litigation.
holdings: A court may allow amendment of pleadings to include a defense based on subsequent events if it promotes complete justice and does not cause undue prejudice or surprise.
A Kuthakapattom lease granted in 1948 cannot be read as retroactive to 1939 unless the document explicitly provides for it; a formal grant is prospective unless clearly stated otherwise.
Delay in seeking amendment does not automatically bar it if the opposing party can be compensated by costs and no new trial or prolonged litigation would result.
provisions: Travancore Limitation Regulation (VI of 110 M.E.), Section 32
Travancore Specific Relief Act XIII of 1115, Sections 7 and 8
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings
Prospective vs. retroactive operation of leases
Laches and equitable delay
Complete justice doctrine
Subsequent events in litigation

card.dispute: Mulamchand challenged the validity of a contract with the State of Madhya Pradesh for collecting forest produce, claiming it was void under Article 299 of the Constitution and seeking refund of his deposit under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act.
issues_decided: Whether the right to collect forest produce is a proprietary right that vests in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950
Whether a contract with the State not complying with Article 299 of the Constitution is void
Whether the appellant is entitled to restitution under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act for a void contract
holdings: The right to collect forest produce is a proprietary right and vests in the State under Section 4(1)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950.
A contract with the State not complying with Article 299(1) of the Constitution is void and cannot be ratified or validated by estoppel.
A party to a void contract may claim restitution under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act if conditions are met, but must account for benefits received; lack of evidence on quantum bars relief.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(1)(a)
doctrines: Mandatory nature of constitutional contract formalities
Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Quasi-contractual liability under Section 70

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Board of Revenue's decision granting Adhivasi rights to respondents recorded as sub-tenants in the 1356 F record of rights, despite a prior court finding that the sub-letting was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether persons recorded as sub-tenants in the 1356 F record of rights are entitled to Adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, despite a prior court decision negating their tenancy status.
Whether actual possession in 1356 F is necessary to claim Adhivasi rights under the Act.
Whether the Board of Revenue had jurisdiction to interpret Section 20(b)(i) and whether its orders were final.
Whether an inquiry into the correctness of the 1356 F record entry is permissible if no formal correction was made before vesting.
holdings: A person recorded as an occupant in the 1356 F khasra or khatauni is entitled to Adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i), irrespective of a prior judicial finding that the tenancy was invalid.
Actual possession in 1356 F is not required; the statutory fiction deems recorded occupants as entitled to regain possession, even if dispossessed after June 30, 1948.
The Board of Revenue has jurisdiction to interpret Section 20(b)(i), and its final orders under the Act are not subject to collateral challenge on grounds not raised before it.
The entries in the 1356 F record are conclusive for determining Adhivasi rights unless legally corrected or deemed corrected before the vesting date of July 1, 1952.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 20(b)(i)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 232
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Explanation I, II, and III to Section 20
doctrines: Statutory fiction of possession
Conclusive effect of revenue records
Finality of administrative interpretation
Doctrine of occupied possession under land reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Ningawwa, sued to set aside a gift deed executed in favor of her husband, alleging fraud and undue influence regarding the inclusion of certain lands, and sought possession of all four plots of land.
issues_decided: Whether the suit to set aside the gift deed for fraud was barred by limitation under Article 95 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit to set aside the gift deed for undue influence was barred by limitation under Article 91 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
holdings: A suit to set aside a deed induced by fraud is governed by Article 95 of the Limitation Act, and the three-year period begins only when the fraud becomes known to the aggrieved party; the suit was timely as it was filed shortly after the appellant discovered the fraud.

A suit to set aside a deed on grounds of undue influence is governed by Article 91, and the limitation period starts when the plaintiff knows the facts entitling her to relief, not when she escapes the influence; thus, the claim was barred as knowledge existed at the time of execution.
doctrines: Fraudulent misrepresentation as to contents of a document renders the transaction voidable, not void
Distinction between fraud as to character versus contents of a document
Burden of proof in transactions involving undue influence
Limitation period starts from date of knowledge of fraud or undue influence

card.dispute: The appellant, Ragho Prasad Gupta, the real owner of land held benami through Lakhan Lal, contested execution of a decree in favor of the respondent, Shri Krishna Poddar, based on an arbitration award against Lakhan Lal, claiming he was not bound by the decree as he was not a party.
issues_decided: Whether the real owner (benamidar's principal) is bound by a decree passed against the benamidar in litigation with a third party?
Whether the real owner must be joined as a party to be bound by res judicata?
Whether the High Court could interfere under Section 115 CPC with the Munsif's order refusing execution against the real owner?
holdings: A benamidar is a trustee for the real owner, and proceedings by or against the benamidar bind the real owner under res judicata, even if not formally joined, provided the benamidar represented the real owner's interests.
The real owner is bound by the decree if the benamidar or his legal heirs adequately represented his interest in the proceedings, and no prejudice arose from non-joinder.
The High Court can invoke Section 115 CPC to prevent miscarriage of justice, even if the real owner was not a formal party, where ends of justice require enforcement of a valid decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 35
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 23
doctrines: Res judicata
Benami transaction doctrine
Locus standi
Prevention of miscarriage of justice

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased karta of a joint Hindu family sued for partition, claiming he had separated from the family before his death, while other members contested the separation, arguing it was withdrawn.
issues_decided: Whether a unilateral declaration of intention to separate by the karta, once communicated, results in division of status in a joint Hindu family
Whether such a declaration can be unilaterally withdrawn to restore the joint family status
Whether the plaint for partition was validly executed by the karta before his death
holdings: A communicated unilateral declaration of intention to separate by the karta causes a severance of joint status, irrespective of physical division of property.
Once the declaration of separation has taken legal effect through communication, it cannot be nullified by mere withdrawal; reunion requires a fresh agreement.
The karta, though ill, was conscious and in sound mental condition when executing the plaint, which was validly attested and filed before his death.
provisions: Hindu Law (unwritten personal law governing joint family and partition)
doctrines: Severance of status by unilateral declaration in a joint Hindu family
Irrevocability of separation after communication to coparceners
Requirement of agreement for reunion of a divided Hindu family

card.dispute: Shareholders of a dissolved company sued to set aside a property transaction by the company's secretary, claiming ownership of the assets, while the government claimed the assets by escheat.
issues_decided: Whether shareholders of a dissolved company can maintain a suit to recover its assets
Whether the property of a dissolved company vests in the government by escheat or bona vacantia
Whether a transaction by a company secretary before dissolution can be challenged by shareholders after dissolution
holdings: Shareholders of a dissolved company cannot maintain a suit for recovery of company assets as the company ceases to exist and the assets do not devolve on them.
Upon dissolution, the property of a company vests in the government by escheat or as bona vacantia, not in shareholders or creditors.
No effective relief can be granted in a suit by shareholders for recovery of company assets after dissolution, as the company is not a party and assets cannot be restored.
doctrines: Escheat and bona vacantia
Dissolution of a company
Fiduciary relationship
Abatement of claims after corporate dissolution

card.dispute: The dispute was between heirs of a Talukdari estate over whether a deed of trust executed by an adopted son could validly settle the estate properties, given that the widow held a statutory life interest under the Oudh Estates Act.
issues_decided: Whether the adopted son acquired a vested interest in the estate during the lifetime of the widow, thereby enabling him to settle the estate by a deed of trust
Whether the widow's title under the Oudh Estates Act was extinguished by adverse possession
Whether the doctrine of estoppel under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act applied to validate the deed of trust despite lack of title at the time of transfer
holdings: The adopted son did not acquire a vested interest in the estate during the widow's lifetime; her life interest under Section 22(7) of the Oudh Estates Act barred him from alienating the estate.

The widow's title was not extinguished by adverse possession, as mere management of the estate by the Court of Wards or the adopted son, without exclusion of the widow, did not amount to adverse possession.
Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply where a transfer is not made for consideration; the deed of trust here lacked consideration and thus could not be validated by estoppel.
doctrines: Doctrine of adverse possession
Doctrine of feeding the grant by estoppel
Rule that estoppel under Section 43 requires consideration

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed possession of an office cabin in Bombay, where the appellant claimed he was wrongfully dispossessed by the respondent on June 11, 1966.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate must record reasons for being satisfied under Section 145(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Whether a police report is mandatory before a Magistrate can pass a preliminary order under Section 145(1).
Whether a completed dispossession before the preliminary order means there is no existing dispute likely to cause breach of peace under Section 145(1).
holdings: The Magistrate must record reasons for satisfaction under Section 145(1) to enable judicial review, and failure to do so may vitiate the order.

A police report is not mandatory under Section 145(1); the Magistrate may act on 'other information', including a private application, if satisfied about the existence of a dispute and likelihood of breach of peace.

A completed forcible and wrongful dispossession within two months before the preliminary order does not bar proceedings under Section 145; the dispossessed party is deemed to be in possession, and restoration is permissible under the second proviso to Section 145(4).
doctrines: Deemed possession doctrine
Judicial review of administrative satisfaction
Prohibition of self-help in dispossession

card.dispute: Whether the magistrate had jurisdiction to take cognizance of forgery charges under IPC without the prior sanction of the Registrar of Cooperative Societies under the Maharashtra Act.
issues_decided: Whether a nominee appointed under s. 95 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is a 'court' within the meaning of s. 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Whether prosecution for offences under ss. 465 and 471 IPC requires prior sanction of the Registrar under s. 148(3) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act.
Whether s. 146(p) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is repugnant to or partially repeals s. 465 IPC.
holdings: A nominee appointed under s. 95 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is not a 'court' within the meaning of s. 195 CrPC, as the nominee derives authority from the Registrar and lacks independent judicial status.

Sanction of the Registrar under s. 148(3) of the Maharashtra Act is not required for prosecution under ss. 465 and 471 IPC, as the offences under IPC are independent and not covered by the special provisions of the State Act.

Section 146(p) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act does not repeal or override s. 465 IPC, as the two provisions create distinct offences with different ingredients and apply to different circumstances.
doctrines: Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of independent statutory offences
Test for determining what constitutes a 'court' for purposes of s. 195 CrPC
Principle of harmonious construction

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against a decree for eviction for non-payment of rent arrears, claiming protection under Section 12(1) and Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under Section 12(1) of the Bombay Rents Act despite not applying under Section 11(3) to resolve a dispute over standard rent.
Whether the tenant could claim protection under Section 12(3)(b) by depositing part of the arrears during the pendency of the suit.
holdings: A tenant claiming protection under Section 12(1) must, in case of dispute over standard rent, apply under Section 11(3) and pay the court-determined amount before the one-month notice period expires; mere willingness to pay at the time of decree is insufficient.

A tenant cannot claim protection under Section 12(3)(b) unless he pays all arrears on the first day of hearing and continues to pay ongoing rent and increases in court regularly until the suit is decided.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11(3)
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to pay rent must be demonstrated through timely legal action and payment
Special provisions override general protections in tenancy law

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an arbitration award concerning partition of immovable property worth over Rs. 100 required registration under the Indian Registration Act to be admissible in evidence.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitration award affecting immovable property valued over Rs. 100 is compulsorily registerable under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act
Whether an unregistered award can have legal effect and create rights in immovable property
Whether the conferment of exclusive jurisdiction on courts under the Arbitration Act affects the binding nature of an award
holdings: An arbitration award that purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right, title, or interest in immovable property worth over Rs. 100 is compulsorily registerable under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.
An unregistered award is not a mere waste paper; it has legal effect and can create rights in property, but such rights are unenforceable until the award is made a rule of the court.
The binding nature of an award under the Arbitration Act is not diminished by the requirement of court enforcement; the award is final and binding on the parties even before enforcement.
provisions: Indian Arbitration Act, 1940, First Schedule, Paragraph 7
doctrines: Merger of claims into award
Compulsory registration of instruments affecting immovable property
Binding nature of arbitration awards
Distinction between creation of rights and enforceability of rights

card.dispute: The Government acquired land from grantees who had received it under a condition to surrender it without compensation; the dispute was whether the grantees were entitled to compensation under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Government, after initiating proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, could rely on a prior condition requiring surrender of land without compensation.
Whether the existence of a restrictive condition in favour of the State affects the quantum of compensation payable under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the Land Acquisition Act permits acquisition of partial or restricted interests in land.
holdings: After initiating acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, the Government cannot invoke a prior contractual condition to deny compensation.
Compensation must reflect the market value of the grantees' interest in the land, but the existence of a restrictive condition in favour of the State must be factored into the valuation.

The Land Acquisition Act allows for the acquisition of partial or restricted interests in land, and compensation is payable only for the value of the interest actually held by the claimant, subject to any clogs or restrictions.
doctrines: Compensation based on market value of restricted interest
Estoppel against the State in acquisition proceedings
Adaptation of statutory procedure to partial interests

card.dispute: The appellants, Subhagwati and her son Shiromani, challenged a partition deed (Ex.D-4) executed in 1943, claiming they were entitled to equal shares in the joint family property, while the respondents relied on the unregistered deed and alleged customs and acquiescence to deny them full shares.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered partition deed (Ex.D-4) was admissible in evidence under Section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act
Whether the appellant Subhagwati had acquiesced to the partition by signing the deed and thus relinquished her share
Whether the custom of 'Jethansi', granting a larger share to the eldest son in the Agharia caste, was legally valid and enforceable
Whether oral evidence of a subsequent partition could be admitted under Section 91 of the Indian Evidence Act
holdings: A partition deed that allots specific properties to coparceners must be registered under Section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act to be admissible in evidence; unregistered deeds cannot prove title or partition.
Acquiescence or relinquishment of a share in joint family property cannot be inferred if not pleaded or made an issue in the trial court; absence of pleading bars such a defence.

The custom of 'Jethansi' giving a larger share to the eldest son is obsolete and unenforceable unless strictly proven as ancient, certain, and reasonable; mere oral testimony with inconsistencies fails to establish such a custom.
Oral evidence of a partition subsequent to an unregistered deed cannot be admitted under Section 91 of the Indian Evidence Act when the deed was intended to be the sole record of partition.
doctrines: Strict proof of custom doctrine
Doctrine of estoppel by acquiescence
Rule against oral variation of written documents
Mitakshara principle of equal partition

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and the respondents (landowners) fought over whether the acquisition of land under the Mysore Land Acquisition Act, bypassing the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, was valid and constitutional.
issues_decided: Whether the Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act, 1962, validly removed procedural inconsistencies and retrospective discrimination between two land acquisition laws?
Whether the State Government had legislative competence to validate past acquisitions made under the Mysore Land Acquisition Act for Bangalore's development?
Whether the validation of acquisitions under a general law, despite the existence of a special law (City of Bangalore Improvement Act), violated Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the retrospective validation could cure constitutional defects arising from non-compliance with mandatory procedures under the special law?
holdings: A legislature with competence over land acquisition can retrospectively validate actions and remove discrimination by nullifying the application of one of two concurrent laws through a non-obstante clause.

The Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act, 1962, is constitutionally valid as it operates within the State's legislative competence and does not violate fundamental rights merely by creating classification.
Validation of acquisitions under a general law, even if a special law existed, does not violate Article 14 if the legislature has the power to unify the legal regime retrospectively.

Procedural non-compliance with a special law is cured by retrospective validation, provided the legislature has competence and the action does not infringe fundamental rights beyond what can be validated.
provisions: The Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act, 1962, Section 2
The City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945, Section 52
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of retrospective validation
Doctrine of reasonable classification under Article 14
Doctrine of non obstante clause

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of lands in Orathur Padugai, part of the Tanjore Palace Estate, against defendants who asserted occupancy rights, raising questions about the nature of the estate and the classification of the land.
issues_decided: Whether the lands in Orathur Padugai formed an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908
Whether the lands were 'private lands' under Section 3(10)(b) or 'ryoti lands' under Section 3(16)
Whether the 1862 relinquishment by the Government of India constituted a fresh grant creating an estate
Whether the appellant rebutted the presumption that the lands were not private lands under Section 18 of the Act
holdings: The 1862 relinquishment by the Government of India in favor of the Raja's widows constituted a fresh grant, creating an estate under Section 3(2)(d) of the Act.
Orathur Padugai, though not a whole village, formed part of an estate under the Act, and the land was ryoti land, not private land.
The mere ownership of both warams (rights) in dry lands, described as 'Iruwaram' or 'Padugai', does not make land 'private land' unless it is retained for the landholder's personal cultivation.
The appellant failed to rebut the presumption under Section 18 that the lands were not private, as there was no evidence of direct cultivation or intent to retain as home-farm.
doctrines: Fresh grant doctrine
Presumption against private land
Domain or home-farm test for private land
Occupancy rights under ryoti tenure

card.dispute: The alienees of inam lands granted for temple services fought against the State of Madras's resumption of those lands under the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, claiming the grants were only melwaram, not hereditary kudiwaram, and that adverse possession had extinguished the State's right.
issues_decided: Whether the inam grants included both melwaram and kudiwaram rights or only melwaram
Whether the inams were personal service-based or granted to hereditary office-holders
Whether Section 44-B(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 applies retrospectively to inams alienated before 1934
Whether alienees could acquire prescriptive title by adverse possession against the State
holdings: The inam grants included both melwaram and kudiwaram rights, as they were granted to hereditary office-holders as remuneration for temple services.
The inams were not personal service grants but were attached to hereditary offices, making them resumable under Section 44-B.
Section 44-B(2)(a)(i) applies to alienations made before or after 1934, as the phrase 'has made' covers past and future alienations.
Alienees' possession under lease was not adverse to the inamdar or the State, so no prescriptive title could be acquired to defeat resumption.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, Section 44-B
doctrines: Distinction between service-conditioned grants and office-based remuneration grants
Prospective application of statutory provisions with retroactive requisites
No adverse possession against State in respect of resumable inam rights

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant who had erected permanent structures on a leased backyard site in violation of a lease stipulation, while the tenant claimed protection under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant of a vacant site in the backyard of a residential house is a tenant of land under s. 2(2) of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921
Whether such a tenant is entitled to protection under ss. 3 and 9 of the Act when permanent structures are erected in breach of a stipulation in a registered lease deed
holdings: A tenant who leases only the vacant land separately from the residential building is a tenant of land under s. 2(2) of the Act, not a tenant of a building.

A stipulation in a registered lease deed prohibiting the erection of permanent structures is a stipulation as to the erection of buildings within the proviso to s. 12, and overrides the tenant's rights under ss. 3 and 9; thus, a tenant breaching it is not entitled to compensation or purchase rights.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 2(2)
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 3
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 12
doctrines: Strict construction of statutory exceptions
Proviso carving out exceptions to statutory rights
Interpretation of lease stipulations in relation to statutory protections

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the State's refusal to pay compensation for land already taken, after the State initially conceded entitlement but later argued the acquisition was invalid due to lack of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Government can resile from its concession that the appellant was entitled to compensation based on the market value as of February 1, 1955.
Whether a notification under Section 6(1) alone can be treated as a composite notification under Sections 4(1) and 6(1) with the consent of the landowner.
holdings: The Government cannot take inconsistent positions in litigation; having conceded compensation entitlement, it cannot later deny it to avoid liability.
A notification under Section 6(1) may be treated as a composite declaration under Sections 4(1) and 6(1) if the landowner consents, implying waiver of the procedure under Section 5A.
doctrines: Estoppel by conduct
Waiver of statutory procedure
Prohibition against approbation and reprobation

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of successive notifications under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, following a single notification under Section 4(1), after the government sought to validate such actions via the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, which validates past acquisitions based on an exhausted Section 4(1) notification, is constitutionally valid?
Whether the validation of acquisitions without reviving the lapsed notification under Section 4(1) amounts to an encroachment on judicial power or violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution?
Whether the amendment and validation Act offends Article 14 by arbitrarily treating land acquisitions?
holdings: Section 4 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, is invalid because it attempts to validate acquisitions based on a notification under Section 4(1) that had already been exhausted, without legislatively reviving its efficacy.

Such validation, without resuscitating the foundational notification, effectively fixes compensation based on an outdated market value, violating the requirement under Article 31(2) to provide just equivalent compensation.
The Act cannot cure the legal infirmity of dead notifications by mere validation; retrospective amendment of the enabling provision (Section 4) was necessary, which the Act failed to do.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 2
Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 3
Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of Eclipse
Doctrine of Just Equivalent Compensation
Principle of Judicial Review of Validating Legislation
Rule against Arbitrary State Action under Article 14

card.dispute: Private lessees of minor mineral rights challenged the validity of a Bihar amendment and rule that sought to modify existing mining leases, arguing that only Parliament had legislative competence over such matters.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964, specifically Proviso (2) to Section 10(2), was within the legislative competence of the State Legislature.
Whether the second Sub-rule of Rule 20 of the Bihar Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964, could validly apply to pre-existing leases.
Whether Parliament, through the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, had occupied the field regarding regulation of minor minerals, thereby excluding State legislation.
holdings: The State Legislature lacked competence to enact Proviso (2) to Section 10(2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act because Parliament had occupied the field concerning minor minerals under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals Act, 1957.
The second Sub-rule of Rule 20 could not validly alter pre-existing mining leases because such modification requires legislative authority, not mere rule-making power.

The entire legislative field over minor minerals, including regulation and modification of leases, was occupied by Parliament under Entry 54 of List I, rendering State legislation on the subject invalid.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 14
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 16
Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964 (Bihar Act 4 of 1965), Proviso (2) to Section 10(2)
Bihar Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964, Rule 20(2)
doctrines: Occupied field doctrine
Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Vested rights cannot be taken away by executive rule-making

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of execution proceedings and sale of joint family properties, claiming that Tamil Vannian Christians are not bound by the doctrine of pious obligation under Hindu law and that the endorsee of a promissory note could not sue non-executant coparceners.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of pious obligation applies to Tamil Vannian Christians governed by Mitakshara law in matters of inheritance and succession.
Whether an endorsee of a promissory note can sue non-executant coparceners for recovery of a debt and sale of joint family property.
holdings: The doctrine of pious obligation is not merely religious but a legal principle integral to the Mitakshara school of Hindu law and applies to Tamil Vannian Christians who follow that system, as it is consistent with justice, equity, and conscience and not contrary to Christianity.

An endorsee can sue non-executant coparceners if the endorsement transfers the debt; the wording of the endorsement in this case conveyed such transfer, enabling the endorsee to enforce the debt under Hindu law.
provisions: Promissory Note under Indian Stamp Act (implied)
doctrines: Doctrine of pious obligation
Right by birth in Mitakshara coparcenary
Assignment of debt via endorsement

card.dispute: Filmistan Distributors (India) (P) Ltd. and others fought against Baldevdas Shivlal & Anr over whether a consent decree from an earlier suit operated as res judicata to bar re-litigation of the nature of their agreement as a lease, and whether certain cross-examination questions could be disallowed.
issues_decided: Whether a consent decree operates as res judicata to bar a subsequent challenge to the legal nature of an agreement?
Whether an order allowing a question in cross-examination constitutes a 'case decided' under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
Whether the High Court could, in revision, decide the issue of res judicata when the trial court had not finally adjudicated it?
holdings: A consent decree does not operate as res judicata because it is merely a record of a compromise between parties without judicial adjudication on the merits.
An order permitting a question in cross-examination does not amount to a 'case decided' under Section 115, as no right or obligation has been adjudicated.
The High Court cannot decide an issue like res judicata in revision when the trial court has not finally decided it and evidence is still to be led.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
doctrines: Res judicata
Estoppel by decree
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115
Admissibility of oral evidence under Section 92 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Bihar Land Reforms Act and related rules concerning mining leases for minor minerals, arguing that the state legislature lacked competence to legislate on a subject already occupied by a central law.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Legislature had the power to amend Section 10(2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act by adding a proviso regulating mining leases for minor minerals?
Whether Rule 20(2) of the Bihar Minor Minerals Concession Rules, 1964, which applied to existing leases, was valid in the absence of legislative authority?
Whether the subject of regulation of minor minerals was covered by the Central Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, thereby excluding state legislation?
holdings: Parliament, through Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, fully occupied the field of regulating prospecting licences and mining leases for minor minerals, leaving no room for state legislation.

The second proviso to Section 10(2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act was invalid as it encroached upon a field under exclusive Union control, despite incidental connection with land under Entry 18 of List II.

Rule 20(2), which applied to pre-existing mining leases, was invalid because modifying vested rights requires legislative sanction, and the state lacked competence; mere rule-making power could not alter existing leases.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 54
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 23
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 14
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 16
doctrines: Occupied field doctrine
Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of protection of vested rights

card.dispute: The Assistant Commissioner of Urban Land Tax and others challenged the constitutional validity of the Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966, which reimposed a tax on urban land after a prior similar law was struck down, with retrospective effect.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966 falls within the legislative competence of the State under Entry 49, List II or Entry 86, List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
