Whether the Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution by being arbitrary in its valuation mechanism.
Whether the Act imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f).
Whether the retrospective operation of the tax from 1963 renders the Act unconstitutional.
holdings: The Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966 falls within Entry 49 of List II, as it concerns taxation on land, and does not encroach upon Entry 86 of List I, which deals with taxes on income.

The method of determining market value under the Act, including the use of the contractor’s method for comparable buildings, does not invalidate the Act; challenges to specific valuations may be raised in appeals or under Article 226.
A tax of 0.4% on the market value of urban land is not so excessive as to be confiscatory or an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f).

Retrospective imposition of tax from 1963 is valid, as it cures a defect in the earlier invalid law and does not per se violate reasonableness under Article 19(1)(f), especially in the context of taxation.
provisions: Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966, Section 3
Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966, Section 5
Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966, Section 6
Madras Urban Land Tax Act, 1966, Section 2
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 49, List II
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 86, List I
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of reasonableness in taxation
Doctrine of retrospective validation of statutes
Principle that retrospective taxation is not per se unconstitutional

card.dispute: The landlord (C. Mackertich) fought with the tenant company (Steuart and Co. Ltd.) over whether the lease was terminable by 15 days' notice (monthly tenancy) or required six months' notice (yearly tenancy for manufacturing purposes).
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy was for manufacturing purposes so as to attract the six months' notice requirement under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the dominant purpose of the lease, as opposed to exclusive purpose, determines applicability of the six months' notice rule
holdings: The tenancy was not dominantly for manufacturing purposes; thus, it was a month-to-month tenancy terminable by 15 days' notice.
Even assuming the test under Section 106 is dominant purpose, there was no sufficient evidence that the lease was substantially for manufacturing.
doctrines: Presumption of tenancy type under Section 106 based on dominant purpose
Burden of proof on party claiming special tenancy status

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bonafide and reasonable requirement for hotel use, which the tenant opposed under the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord discharged the burden of proving bonafide and reasonable requirement of the premises under Section 21(h) of the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961.
Whether the burden of proving greater hardship shifts to the tenant once the landlord establishes need.
Whether the court must consider all circumstances, including availability of alternative accommodation for both parties, before granting eviction.
holdings: The burden of proving bonafide and reasonable requirement of the premises lies on the landlord and does not shift entirely to the tenant.
Both landlord and tenant must adduce evidence on hardship; the tenant does not solely bear the burden of proving greater hardship upon eviction.
The court must evaluate all circumstances under Section 21(4), including availability of reasonable accommodation for both parties, before deciding on eviction.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
Rent and Mortgage Interest Restrictions (Amendment) Act, 1933, Section 3(1) and Schedule I, paragraph (h)
doctrines: Burden of proof in eviction cases
Reasonable and bonafide requirement
Greater hardship doctrine
Strict construction of tenant protection statutes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the admissibility of a letter as an unregistered document that purported to create a mortgage by deposit of title deeds, while the respondents claimed a mortgage charge on a property for a loan of Rs. 80,000 backed by hundies.
issues_decided: Whether the letter dated December 17, 1951 (Ex. 2) required compulsory registration under the Registration Act, 1908, as it purported to create a mortgage by deposit of title deeds.
Whether the document was merely evidential of an oral agreement or itself constituted the operative contract creating a mortgage.
holdings: A document that contains all the essential terms of a mortgage and is executed contemporaneously with the deposit of title deeds must be registered to be enforceable, even if the mortgage is by deposit of title deeds.

Where a document records the entire bargain between parties with intent to create a security and includes the principal amount, property, and implied terms of repayment and interest, it is an operative instrument requiring registration under Section 59 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 17 of the Registration Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds
Doctrine of compulsory registration of instruments creating immovable property rights
Doctrine of contemporaneous execution indicating operative character of a document

card.dispute: The appellant sought to enforce an arbitration award, while the respondents challenged its validity on grounds of arbitrator misconduct, undue influence, and non-arbitrability of the dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's objection to the award was barred by limitation under Article 158 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the arbitration agreement authorized the arbitrators to decide the dispute based on their personal knowledge
Whether the arbitrators committed legal misconduct by relying on their personal knowledge without informing the parties
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the High Court's revisional order under Article 136 of the Constitution
holdings: Objection to an award under Article 158 of the Limitation Act, 1908, begins only upon service of notice of filing of the award; absence of such notice means the objection is within time.
The phrase 'in whatever manner' in an arbitration agreement does not empower arbitrators to decide disputes based on their personal knowledge unless expressly authorized.
Arbitrators must act in accordance with natural justice; relying on personal knowledge without disclosing it to the parties constitutes legal misconduct.
The Supreme Court, in exercise of discretion under Article 136, will not interfere if the High Court's decision is just and correct.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Legal misconduct in arbitration
Finality and enforceability of arbitration awards
Scope of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the eviction order based on subletting that allegedly occurred before the new rent control Act came into force, arguing that proceedings under the new Act could not penalize pre-commencement actions.
issues_decided: Whether eviction proceedings under s. 11(4) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965, can be based on subletting that occurred before the Act came into force?
Whether s. 34(1) of the 1965 Act allows continuation of proceedings under corresponding provisions of the repealed 1959 Act?
Whether the District Judge had jurisdiction under s. 20 of the 1965 Act to overturn concurrent factual findings of subletting by lower courts?
holdings: Eviction proceedings under the 1965 Act can be based on subletting that occurred before its commencement if a corresponding provision existed in the 1959 Act and the proceeding could have been maintained under the old law.
Section 34(1) of the 1965 Act saves legal proceedings under corresponding provisions of the repealed 1959 Act, and 'corresponding' means analogous, not identical.

The District Judge has broad revisional powers under s. 20 of the 1965 Act to examine legality, regularity, and propriety of orders, including reappreciating evidence, even if it results in overturning concurrent findings.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1959, Section 11(4)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(1) and Section 11(4)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 34(1)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 20
Kerala Interpretation and General Clauses Act, 1125 (Act VII of 1125), Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of corresponding provisions in repeal and saving clauses
Doctrine of continuity of legal proceedings despite repeal
Broad revisional jurisdiction under special statutes

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued the defendants for possession of land, claiming a share in shamlat land that was allegedly wrongly allotted to the defendants during consolidation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption of correctness under Section 44 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 in favour of later jamabandi entries was rebutted in this case.
Whether the lower appellate court was right in relying on earlier jamabandi entries to displace later ones.
holdings: The presumption of correctness attached to later jamabandi entries under Section 44 can be rebutted by evidence showing that the alteration was made mistakenly or without authority.
Where a later entry is found to have been altered without any mutation or order from revenue authorities, the earlier entry may prevail if the change is shown to be erroneous.
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption of correctness of revenue entries
Principle of contemporaneous official records prevailing in absence of authorised mutation

card.dispute: The appellants, Firm Ishar Das Devi Chand and its partners, fought to obtain a temporary injunction to prevent the respondent from taking possession of demised premises in execution of an eviction order, claiming a landlord-tenant relationship based on rent payments.
issues_decided: Whether an order dismissing an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2, CPC is appealable when the trial court also invoked Section 151, CPC?
Whether the appellants made out a prima facie case for grant of temporary injunction based on alleged landlord-tenant relationship?
holdings: An order dismissing an application under Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2, CPC is appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(r), even if Section 151 CPC is also invoked, because the determination of applicability of Order XXXIX Rule 2 is not an exercise of inherent powers under Section 151.

The appellants failed to make out a prima facie case for temporary injunction as they did not establish a landlord-tenant relationship, and the balance of convenience favoured the respondent, especially given laches and dismissal of their earlier application under the Rent Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rules 1 & 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII Rule 1(r)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 4
doctrines: Prima facie case for temporary injunction
Balance of convenience
Laches and delay in seeking equitable relief
Appealability of interlocutory orders

card.dispute: The appellant, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji, claimed ownership of certain properties associated with a temple, while the respondents argued they belonged to the public temple managed by her.
issues_decided: Whether the temple in question is a public or private temple.
Whether the properties listed in the plaint schedule belong to the temple or to the appellant individually.
holdings: A temple is public if it is built for general worship, maintained by public contributions, and treated as such by devotees and management, regardless of its architectural appearance.
Properties used for temple purposes, managed through temple accounts, and funded by temple income are temple properties, even if originally held in the name of the manager.

The Goswami Maharaj is not merely a manager but holds a sacred position as Maha Prabhu in the Vallabha Sampradaya, with a right to use surplus temple income for personal and family maintenance in a reasonable manner.
doctrines: Public temple doctrine
Presumption of temple ownership from usage and management
Religious officeholder's right to benefit from temple surplus

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of a land sale agreement, while the respondents claimed the agreement was void due to non-payment of the advance and a material alteration in the deed.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents proved that only Rs. 350, not Rs. 2,000, was paid as advance under the agreement
Whether the addition of the words 'clear the debts and execute the sale deed free from encumbrances' constituted a material alteration vitiating the agreement
holdings: The court held that the express recital in the agreement that Rs. 2,000 was paid is binding, and the respondents' claim of non-payment is unproven and likely a pretext to avoid the contract.

Even if the clause about clearing encumbrances was added after execution, it is not a material alteration because it reflects the vendor's existing legal duty and does not change the rights or liabilities under the deed.
doctrines: Material alteration doctrine in deeds
Presumption of payment from recital in a written agreement
Burden of proof in cases of alleged non-payment under written instruments

card.dispute: The dispute was between a landlord and tenants over whether the Ahmedabad Small Causes Court had the power to issue a distress warrant for recovery of municipal taxes during a pending application for fixation of standard rent.
issues_decided: Whether the Ahmedabad Small Causes Court had the power to issue a distress warrant under Section 53 of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, in suits triable under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether the pendency of an application for fixation of standard rent barred the court from issuing a distress warrant for recovery of rent or municipal taxes.
holdings: The Ahmedabad Small Causes Court, being governed by the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, had the power to issue a distress warrant under Section 53 of that Act, even in cases exclusively triable under the Bombay Rents Control Act.

The pendency of an application for fixation of standard rent does not suspend the court's jurisdiction to issue a distress warrant, as rent at the contractual rate remains payable until an interim or final order is made.
provisions: Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, Section 53
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 31
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 49
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction
Continuity of rules post-bifurcation
Statutory interpretation of procedural powers

card.dispute: The petitioner, a senior member of a collateral branch, contested the President's recognition of the adopted son as the Ruler of Dholpur, claiming succession rights under personal law and covenants, and alleged infringement of property rights.
issues_decided: Whether the President's recognition of a Ruler under Article 366(22) of the Constitution includes recognition of rights to private property.
Whether the recognition of a Ruler is justiciable or a political act beyond judicial review.
Whether Article 366(22) confers substantive power on the President to recognise a Ruler.
holdings: Recognition of a Ruler by the President under Article 366(22) does not include or confer rights to private property, which are governed by personal law of succession.
The act of recognising a Ruler is a political function under the President’s executive power and is not subject to judicial review on grounds of inheritance or treaty rights.

Article 366(22) inherently confers power on the President to recognise or withdraw recognition of a Ruler, as the phrase 'for the time being recognised by the President' implies an active constitutional power.
doctrines: Political question doctrine
Separation of personal status from property rights
Non-justiciability of disputes arising from treaties and covenants under Article 363

card.dispute: The tenant, M.M. Chawla, fought against eviction by landlord J.S. Sethi for non-payment of rent, claiming entitlement to fixation of standard rent and protection under Section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller is obligated to fix standard rent in a written statement during an ejectment proceeding when the claim is time-barred under Section 12?
Whether a tenant can claim the benefit of Section 14(2) for a second time after having previously availed it in an earlier proceeding?
holdings: The Rent Controller is not empowered to fix standard rent in an ejectment proceeding if the claim is barred by limitation under Section 12; Sections 4, 5, 6, and 15(3) do not allow such determination in default proceedings when no valid dispute exists under the Act.

A tenant who has previously obtained relief under Section 14(2) by depositing arrears to avoid eviction is not entitled to claim the same benefit again in a subsequent ejectment proceeding for fresh default.
doctrines: Limitation bars substantive rights
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions
Principle of finality in tenant protections
Summary adjudication under rent control law

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant's heirs, claiming they acquired a suitable residence and thus became liable for eviction under rent control law, but the tenants used the premises for both residence and profession.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's heirs could be evicted under s. 14(1)(h) of the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1958 after acquiring a residential property, where the original tenancy was for residence-cum-profession.
Whether the omission of the word 'suitable' in s. 14(1)(h) of the new Act applied to pending cases and altered the eviction grounds.
Whether the premises were let for composite use (residence and profession), affecting applicability of the eviction clause.
holdings: A tenant occupying premises for both residence and profession cannot be evicted merely by acquiring another residence, as the professional need remains unfulfilled.
Section 14(1)(h) applies only where premises are used solely for residential purposes; composite use excludes eviction on acquisition of residence alone.
The modification in s. 14(1)(h) by omitting 'suitable' is a clarification, but does not change the result where tenancy was for combined residential and professional use.
The heirs of a tenant continue the same tenancy rights, including protection from eviction when the original tenancy served a composite purpose.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1)(h)
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(h)
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 57
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 2(g)
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 2(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of composite tenancy
Doctrine of statutory continuity in pending proceedings
Doctrine of harmonious construction of repealed and new laws

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased properties from a liquidated cooperative society, claimed title over two survey numbers against respondents who held possession under a prior purchaser in a money suit, raising issues about the applicability of the doctrine of lis pendens.
issues_decided: Whether the release of mortgaged property by the cooperative society was binding despite non-payment of the promised amount.
Whether the mortgage proceedings pending before the Assistant Registrar attracted the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether a prior attachment and court sale in a money suit could defeat the operation of lis pendens.
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens applies to involuntary transfers such as court auctions.
holdings: The release of the mortgaged property was binding on the Society as it was absolute and unconditional, even though the motivating factor was the promise of payment.
Proceedings for a mortgage award constitute pending litigation under Section 52, and the doctrine of lis pendens applies from the date of the petition, regardless of initial procedural errors.
An earlier attachment before judgment does not prevent the application of lis pendens, as attachment does not confer title and does not override the statutory embargo on transfer during litigation.
The principle of lis pendens applies even to court-ordered sales, as a purchaser pendente lite takes title subject to the outcome of the pending litigation.
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Relation back of judicial correction of orders
Bona fide litigation requirement for lis pendens
Principle that purchaser pendente lite is bound by the decree

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee, Amritsar, and private individuals challenged the Punjab State's monopoly on holding cattle fairs under the Punjab Cattle Fairs (Regulation) Act, arguing it violated fundamental rights and amounted to unauthorized requisition of property.
issues_decided: Whether the Punjab Cattle Fairs (Regulation) Act, as amended, is void for vagueness due to the lack of a clear definition of 'cattle fair'.
Whether the State's declaration of municipal or private land as a 'fair area' without compensation violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the State can compel a municipal body to provide services, infrastructure, and staff for state-run cattle fairs.
Whether private persons or local authorities have a right to continue holding cattle markets or fairs after the State assumed a monopoly.
holdings: The amendment defining 'cattle fair' as a gathering of over 25 persons for cattle sale or purchase removed vagueness, and the Act is not invalid on that ground.
The State cannot declare municipal or private land as a fair area and take possession without providing compensation under Article 31(2); such action is an unconstitutional requisition of property.
The Act does not authorize the State to compel a municipal body to provide water, electricity, sanitation, staff, or infrastructure for cattle fairs; such directions are ultra vires and invalid.

While private individuals and local authorities cannot hold 'cattle fairs' due to the State monopoly, they may continue operating 'cattle markets' on their own land, provided they do not fall within a validly declared fair area.
doctrines: Doctrine of unconstitutional vagueness
Doctrine of State monopoly under police power
Doctrine of compensation under Article 31(2)
Distinction between 'market' and 'fair' in regulatory context
Ultra vires doctrine in administrative action

card.dispute: The landlords (Munni Devi & Anr) fought against the tenant (Gokal Chand & Ors) over whether the shop was vacant and could be allotted to another person after alleged default in rent payment.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide on the tenancy and possession of the shop despite an order by the District Magistrate under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947.
Whether the determination of vacancy by the District Magistrate is a conclusive or jurisdictional fact binding on civil courts.
Whether an order of allotment and ejectment by the District Magistrate can override the continued possession of a tenant.
holdings: The civil court has jurisdiction to determine questions of tenancy and possession even if the District Magistrate has passed an order under the Rent Control Act.
The existence of a vacancy is a jurisdictional fact; the District Magistrate’s finding on it is not final and can be challenged in civil court.
An order by the District Magistrate made without proper jurisdiction—such as based on a non-existent vacancy—cannot bar a civil court from deciding the true status of possession.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7A
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 16
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Finality of administrative orders
Separation of administrative and judicial functions

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a Hindu joint family over the validity of a partition deed, the status of certain properties as joint or self-acquired, and the effect of an adoption on inheritance rights.
issues_decided: Whether the partition deed executed in 1944 was valid or bogus and whether it severed the joint family status
Whether the 12 properties acquired between 1911 and 1940 were joint family properties or self-acquisitions of Goudappa
Whether the sale of survey plots Nos. 43 and 77 to defendant No. 3 was binding on the plaintiff
holdings: A mere declaration of intent to partition is not sufficient to sever joint family status if it is shown to be a sham or pretence; the intention must be genuine and unequivocal.

Where a joint family has a nucleus of joint property, acquisitions made during the period are presumed to be joint family property unless proven otherwise; the burden shifts to the claimant of self-acquisition to prove separate source of funds.
A sale by a guardian to a minor without consideration and without independent benefit is not binding on the coparcener, especially when the minor had no independent property.
doctrines: Severance of joint family status by unequivocal declaration
Presumption of joint family property from nucleus
Bogus partition does not affect rights of adopted son

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether the respondent, having accepted benefits under the testator's will, could also retain property settled in his favor prior to the will.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was required to make an election under Section 180 of the Indian Succession Act due to the testator's attempted disposition of property already settled on him.
Whether the testator intended to dispose of the property settled on the respondent in 1935 through general bequest language in the will.
Whether a failure to specifically mention the disposition of settled property excludes the application of the election principle.
holdings: Under Section 180 of the Indian Succession Act, a legatee must elect between retaining their own property and accepting benefits under a will if the testator attempted to dispose of that property.
The testator's intention to revoke prior settlements and treat all properties as his own can be inferred from recitals in the will and the disposition of properties already settled on others.

Election applies even without specific mention of settled property if the will, read as a whole, shows the testator intended to include such property in the bequest, especially through a residuary clause.
doctrines: Doctrine of Election
Testamentary intention
Presumption against disposition of non-owned property

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a partition deed was sham and whether certain properties were joint family assets or self-acquisitions, affecting rights to partition and maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether the partition deed was a sham transaction intended to defeat the rights of widows in the family
Whether there was a severance of joint family status despite the partition deed being bogus
Whether properties acquired between 1911 and 1940 were joint family properties or self-acquisitions by one brother
Whether the High Court could consider a challenge to a sale deed not specifically mentioned in the plaint but listed in the schedule
holdings: A partition deed is invalid if it is a sham designed to deprive family members of maintenance rights, and continued joint possession shows no real division.
A mere declaration of intent to separate does not sever joint family status if the intention is not genuine or unequivocal.
Where a joint family has an adequate nucleus of property, later acquisitions are presumed to be joint unless proven otherwise with clear evidence of separate funds.
A plaint challenging alienations generally, along with a schedule listing disputed properties, sufficiently includes specific sale deeds even if not explicitly named.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family Property
doctrines: Sham transaction doctrine in partition
Severance of joint family status by unequivocal intention
Presumption of joint family property from adequate nucleus
Pleading by reference to schedules in civil suits

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, representing Muslims of Bhind, sued to declare their title and possession over land adjoining a mosque, which the defendants had been using; the defendants claimed adverse possession, and the case centered on whether the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was within the period of limitation under Article 47 of the Limitation Act, 1908, based on the order passed under Section 145 Cr.P.C. on March 4, 1959?
Whether the suit was barred under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908, due to failure to file within 12 years of dispossession?
holdings: The suit did not fall under Article 47 of the Limitation Act because the order under Section 145 Cr.P.C. was passed against individuals, not the plaintiffs or those bound by it, and thus could not serve as the cause of action for the present suit.

The suit was barred under Article 142 of the Limitation Act as it was a claim for possession based on alleged dispossession, and the plaintiffs failed to prove they were in possession within 12 years before filing the suit.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Cause of action accrual in possession suits
Binding effect of Section 145 Cr.P.C. orders under the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which failed to specify the locality where the land was needed.
issues_decided: Whether a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is invalid if it does not specify the locality where land is needed for a public purpose.
Whether a defect in the Section 4(1) notification can be cured by a subsequent notification under Section 6(1) containing full details.
holdings: A notification under Section 4(1) must specify the locality where land is needed; failure to do so renders the notification invalid as it is a condition precedent to further acquisition proceedings.
A defect in the Section 4(1) notification cannot be cured by a subsequent detailed notification under Section 6(1), as the initial notification is a mandatory step in depriving a person of property.
doctrines: Condition precedent in administrative action
Strict construction of notifications affecting property rights
Doctrine of curability of procedural defects (rejected in this case)

card.dispute: The appellant Nathulal sued for possession of a ginning factory and agricultural land after rescinding a sale agreement, while the respondent Phoolchand claimed protection under the doctrine of part performance despite not paying the full sale price.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent could invoke the doctrine of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act in the absence of a registered sale deed
Whether Section 70(8) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 barred the defence of part performance
Whether the respondent was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract
Whether the obligations under the contract were to be performed in a specific sequence
holdings: A transferee in possession under an unregistered contract of sale can invoke Section 53A if he has performed or is willing to perform his part, even without full payment.
Section 70(8) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 does not bar a defence of part performance, as it applies only to validity of sale, not to equitable defences under Section 53A.
A purchaser is deemed ready and willing to perform if arrangements for payment exist, even if payment is not made due to the other party's prior default.
Where a contract implies a sequence of performance, the party whose obligation comes first must perform before being entitled to demand performance from the other.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 70(4)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 70(8)
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance
Sequence of contractual performance
Implied conditions in contracts involving statutory restrictions
Equitable protection under Section 53A

card.dispute: The appellant Navalkha & Sons challenged the setting aside of its confirmed bid for properties of a company in liquidation, after a dispute arose over inadequate publicity of the sale process and subsequent higher offers.
issues_decided: Whether the Company Judge could confirm the sale to the appellant without ensuring adequate publicity and a fair public auction.
Whether the auction conducted between only two bidders, without wider public notice, amounted to a valid public auction under the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959.
Whether the Court must ensure the sale price is adequate and reflective of market value, even in the absence of fraud or irregularity.
holdings: An offeror in a court-supervised sale does not acquire a vested right upon acceptance by commissioners; confirmation rests on judicial discretion to protect the company and creditors.
A sale confined to two bidders without proper public notice does not constitute a public auction and is not a valid exercise of judicial discretion under Rule 273.
The court must ensure the sale price is adequate relative to market value, and failure to do so—especially due to inadequate publicity—renders confirmation an improper exercise of discretion.
doctrines: Judicial discretion in confirming sales
Adequacy of sale price doctrine
Public auction requirement for fairness
Court as custodian of creditors' interests

card.dispute: The bank, as landowner, challenged the municipal corporation's imposition of primary liability on it to pay property tax on land leased to a tenant who constructed a building, arguing the tenant should be liable.
issues_decided: Whether the primary liability to pay property tax under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 lies with the landlord or the tenant when the tenant constructs a building on leased land.
Whether Section 146(2) of the Act contemplates composite assessment of land and building owned by different persons.
Whether long-standing administrative practice can influence the interpretation of an ambiguous statutory provision.
holdings: The primary liability for property tax rests with the landlord when land is leased and the tenant constructs a building, under Section 146(2)(a) of the Act, unless the case falls under Section 146(3).
Section 146 contemplates a composite assessment of land and building as a single unit, even when owned by different persons, and the lessor is primarily liable.
Where statutory language is ambiguous, long-standing administrative practice (contemporanea expositio) is a valid aid to interpretation and supports upholding the municipality’s consistent practice.
doctrines: Contemporanea expositio est optima legum interpres
Composite assessment of land and building under municipal tax law
Primary liability of landlord for property tax despite tenant ownership of structure
Right of recoupment by landlord from tenant under Section 147

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of a trust claiming that property dedicated to maintain a wrestling ground (Akhara) with idols was not a valid religious or charitable trust under Hindu law.
issues_decided: Whether the dedication of property for the maintenance of a wrestling ground constitutes a valid religious or charitable trust under Hindu law
Whether the presence of idols and a religious image in the Akhara renders the trust religious in nature
Whether a trust for promoting a sport without educational or public welfare objectives qualifies as charitable under Hindu law
holdings: A trust for maintaining a wrestling ground, without imparting instruction or serving broader educational or public welfare goals, does not constitute a valid charitable trust under Hindu law.
The installation of idols and religious symbols in the Akhara was primarily to attract wrestlers and did not change the dominant secular purpose of the trust.
Promotion of a sport simpliciter, without linkage to education or public benefit, is not a recognized charitable purpose in Hindu law.
provisions: Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts
doctrines: Dominant intention test for determining the nature of a trust
Hindu law concept of 'Istha' and 'Purta' as bases for religious and charitable purposes
Charitable trust doctrine under English law as persuasive but not binding in India

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the landlord's suit for eviction on the ground that the lease was illegal under Section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents Act due to a prohibited advance payment, while the landlord sought possession for constructing a new building.
issues_decided: Whether the lease fell within the scope of Part II of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, specifically Section 6(1), which applies to premises let for residence, education, business, trade, or storage.
Whether Section 18(1) of the Act applied to render the lease illegal and void due to an alleged prohibited advance payment.
holdings: Part II of the Act applies only when premises are let for the purposes specified in Section 6(1); the future use chosen by the lessee does not determine applicability.

The lease was for constructing buildings of any description, not specifically for residence, education, business, trade, or storage, and thus did not fall under Section 6(1); hence, Section 18(1) did not apply.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(8)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 6(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(3)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Purpose of lease determines applicability of rent control provisions

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (Raghunath & Ors) sued to redeem a house mortgaged by the defendant's father, while the defendants claimed the transaction was an outright sale, not a mortgage.
issues_decided: Whether the document Ex. 4 was a mortgage deed or a sale deed when read with Ex. 26
Whether unregistered document Ex. 26, being compulsorily registrable under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, is admissible in evidence
Whether the High Court could remand the case for the defendants to render accounts when the plaintiffs did not appeal the trial court decree
holdings: Ex. 4 is a mortgage deed, not a sale, as its terms clearly provide for redemption and payment of interest, indicating a security transaction.

An unregistered document required to be registered under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act is inadmissible under Section 49 of the Registration Act as amended, even if not listed in Section 17.
The High Court cannot grant additional relief to a respondent who did not file an appeal; thus, the direction to render accounts was impermissible.
provisions: Transfer of Property (Amendment) Supplementary Act, 1929, Section 10
doctrines: Doctrine of compulsory registration under Section 49 of the Registration Act
Supplemental application of Transfer of Property Act provisions to the Registration Act
Principle of appellate jurisdiction limiting enhancement of relief without cross-appeal

card.dispute: The appellants claimed partition of certain properties from the Venkatagiri Estate and, alternatively, maintenance under an 1889 agreement, after the estate's impartibility was affected by the abolition of zamindari.
issues_decided: Whether the Venkatagiri Estate was impartible by custom or only by statute and agreement, and whether it became partible after the repeal of the Impartible Estates Act, 1904 by the Abolition Act of 1948.
Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to maintenance under the 1889 agreement, particularly plaintiffs 5 to 7 who were illegitimate descendants.
Whether the golden howdah was partible property or part of the impartible estate.
holdings: The Venkatagiri Estate was an ancient impartible estate by custom, not created by the 1889 agreement or the 1904 Act; its impartibility survived the abolition of the zamindari for properties not vested in the government.

Plaintiffs 5 to 7 were not entitled to maintenance under the 1889 agreement as they were not 'purusha santhathi' and the claim was barred by res judicata; the term 'gnatis' in the agreement did not extend to illegitimate sons.
The golden howdah was not part of the impartible estate as it was made of gold, and thus was divisible; however, it had already been divided in 1910 and no further partition was possible.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
doctrines: Res judicata
Customary impartibility of estates
Interpretation of family settlements and wills
Survival of incidents of estate after abolition of zamindari

card.dispute: The deity, through its manager, sued Ramchand, who was in possession of the temple and its properties, seeking possession and an account of temple income, alleging mismanagement and illegal use of temple premises.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by the deity through its manager was maintainable without the sanction of the Advocate-General under Section 92 of the CPC?
Whether the defendant Ramchand was guilty of mismanagement and misappropriation of temple properties?
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to frame a management scheme for a private religious trust?
holdings: The suit by the deity through its manager is maintainable without sanction under Section 92 CPC as it was not a public religious or charitable trust and the suit was not by relatives or beneficiaries.
Ramchand, having converted temple properties for personal use and failed in his duties, is unfit to remain in management and must be ejected.
The civil court has jurisdiction to frame a scheme for the management of a private temple under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC to ensure proper administration and protection of temple assets.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 33
doctrines: Representative suit by a deity through its manager
Court's power to frame management scheme for private religious endowments
Mismanagement by temple custodian leading to loss of right to possession

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant challenged the validity of an ejectment decree passed in favor of a transferee-landlord, claiming lack of jurisdiction, invalid notice, and ineligibility of the transferee to seek eviction based on rent default.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court had jurisdiction to extend time for depositing arrears of rent under Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the notice of ejectment issued under Section 12(2) of the Act was invalid
Whether a transferee-landlord could obtain a decree for possession based on rent arrears accrued before transfer
holdings: The appellate court did not need to decide its jurisdiction under Section 12(3)(b) because the tenant's conduct, including raising false claims and failing to act promptly, disqualified him from equitable relief.
The ejectment notice issued under Section 12(2) was valid, as upheld by the lower courts and not shown to be legally defective.

A decree for possession can be granted in favor of a transferee-landlord if the suit was validly instituted by the original landlord and the cause of action for ejectment existed at that time, even if arrears are assigned.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
doctrines: Validity of cause of action at the time of suit institution
Equitable discretion in granting relief under rent control laws
Assignment of rent arrears does not automatically convert them into mere debt precluding ejectment

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of repeated rent payment defaults, while the tenant claimed protection under rent control laws due to subsequent rent deposits and waiver by acceptance of rent.
issues_decided: Whether acceptance of rent after a notice to quit revives the tenancy and waives past defaults under the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950
Whether the tenant is entitled to protection under Section 14(3) of the 1950 Act despite multiple defaults within 18 months
Whether Section 24 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 operates retrospectively to waive defaults in pending eviction proceedings
holdings: Acceptance of rent after a notice to quit does not create a new tenancy but continues the old tenancy with prior defaults, allowing the landlord to rely on those defaults for eviction.
A tenant is not entitled to protection under Section 14(3) of the 1950 Act if there are three or more defaults within an 18-month period, even if rent is later deposited.
Section 24 of the 1956 Act is not retrospective and does not apply to pending proceedings; it cannot waive defaults occurring before the Act came into force.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 12(1)(i)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 14(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 24
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 4
doctrines: Waiver of notice under tenancy law
Prospective vs retrospective operation of statutes
Substantive rights vs procedural changes in legislation
Continuation of statutory tenancy upon acceptance of rent

card.dispute: The daughters of a pre-deceased son of a Hindu woman claimed succession to her stridhana, against other relatives.
issues_decided: Whether daughters of a pre-deceased son of a Hindu woman are entitled to succeed to her stridhana?
Whether the order of succession to a woman's stridhana under Mitakshara includes son's daughters in preference to the husband?
Whether the Hindu Woman's Rights to Property Act, 1937 alters the succession to a Hindu female's stridhana?
holdings: The daughters of a pre-deceased son do not collectively constitute 'progeny' and are not entitled to succeed to stridhana in preference to the husband under Mitakshara.
The order of succession to stridhana is fixed by Mitakshara, and propinquity alone does not determine priority; the textual order must be followed.
The Hindu Woman's Rights to Property Act, 1937 applies only to the separate property of a male Hindu and does not affect succession to a female's stridhana.
provisions: Hindu Woman's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Order of succession under Mitakshara for stridhana
Rule against applying masculine gender to include feminine in succession where order is explicit
Statutory interpretation: limited applicability of the Hindu Woman's Rights to Property Act, 1937

card.dispute: Rani Bai, the widow of a predeceased son, fought with Shri Yadunandan Ram, who claimed ownership through a gift deed and compromise with another widow, over possession and rights in her father-in-law's inherited property.
issues_decided: Whether the widow of a predeceased son has a right to maintenance from the estate of her father-in-law under the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937
Whether such a widow in possession of property for maintenance can be dispossessed without securing her maintenance rights
Whether a compromise between the legal heir and a third party can extinguish the maintenance rights of a widow in possession
holdings: The widow of a predeceased son is entitled to receive maintenance from her father-in-law's estate and her right cannot be defeated by a transfer made with intent to defeat that right.
A widow in possession of property for maintenance cannot be dispossessed by a trespasser, and her possessory right entitles her to restoration of possession.
A compromise by another heir does not transfer absolute rights to a third party if it ignores the pre-existing maintenance rights of a widow in possession.
provisions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(2)
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 19
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rules 1 and 3
doctrines: Possessory title
Maintenance as a charge on property
Protection of maintenance rights against transfers
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of fair compromise under CPC

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be the posthumously born sons of Raman Nadar, contested the validity of a joint will that bequeathed properties of Krishnan Nadar to Raman Nadar for life, with remainder to his sons or, if none, to his daughters, while Raman Nadar's daughters claimed entitlement after his death.
issues_decided: Whether a bequest in favor of unborn sons, born after the testator's death, is valid under Hindu law applicable at the time
Whether the joint will was intended to take effect only after the death of both testators, thereby validating the bequest to unborn sons
Whether the daughters of Raman Nadar were entitled to a life interest in the properties upon his death
Whether the appellants were legitimate sons entitled to inherit under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in case of intestacy
holdings: A bequest in favor of persons unborn at the time of the testator's death is void under pure Hindu law as established by Tagore v. Tagore, where no statutory exception applied.

A joint will does not validate a bequest to unborn persons if its provisions clearly intend immediate devolution upon one testator’s death, irrespective of a clause stating it takes effect after both deaths.
The bequest to daughters was contingent on the absence of sons at the time of Raman Nadar’s death; since he died leaving sons, the bequest failed, resulting in intestacy.
In case of intestacy, the appellants may be entitled to share under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, but their legitimacy as sons of Raman Nadar must first be determined by the High Court.
doctrines: Communis error facit jus
Rule against bequests to unborn persons under classical Hindu law
Contingent and defeasible bequests
Doctrine of reading a will as a whole to ascertain true intention

card.dispute: The landowner and his sister sued to eject Rati Ram, who claimed to be a tenant under a 15-year lease from their mother; the dispute centered on whether the civil court had jurisdiction and whether the lease was valid.
issues_decided: Whether there was a concluded agreement of lease between the plaintiffs' mother and the defendant
Whether an unregistered lease agreement could be used to prove the character of possession
Whether the plaintiffs' mother had authority to grant the lease during the plaintiffs' minority
holdings: A concluded lease agreement existed, as evidenced by the handing over of a Jamabandi extract for the land, satisfying the terms of the lease document.
An unregistered lease agreement, though inadmissible to create a long-term tenancy, is admissible to prove the character of possession as a tenant.
The issue of the mother's authority to grant the lease was not raised in lower courts and could not be entertained in appeal due to settled practice.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, Section 111
doctrines: Admissibility of unregistered documents for collateral purposes
Civil court jurisdiction barred in tenancy disputes under land reform laws
Principle of issue estoppel and appellate court's refusal to entertain new factual issues

card.dispute: The landlord (S. Kartar Singh) sued to evict the tenants (Chamanlal and others) from a property allegedly used for both residence and legal practice, claiming the tenants had acquired alternative residential accommodation and that the premises were needed for personal use.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy was solely for residence or for combined residential and professional use

Whether the tenant's acquisition of a suitable residence permits eviction under Section 13(1)(h) of the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, when the premises were used for both residence and profession
Whether the permission to use the premises for professional purposes was personal to the original tenant and ceased on his death
holdings: A tenancy created for both residence and professional use cannot be terminated solely because the tenant has acquired a suitable residence, as Section 13(1)(h) applies only to purely residential tenancies.
The concurrent finding of fact that the premises were let for combined residential and professional use is binding and cannot be overturned in appeal.
Permission for professional use, once granted and acted upon, does not cease automatically on the death of the original tenant where the tenancy continues with the same composite purpose.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(h)
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 2(g)
doctrines: Doctrine of composite tenancy
Principle of binding concurrent findings of fact
Continuity of tenancy rights in heirs for composite use
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions in pending proceedings

card.dispute: The heirs of a Hindu testator fought with other beneficiaries over the devolution of properties bequeathed under a will, where the wife and primary legatee predeceased the testator.
issues_decided: Whether the legacy to the wife of Schedule C property lapsed upon her predeceasing the testator
Whether the residuary legacy to Venkataswamy and Seshagirirao under Schedule E was accelerated upon the wife's death during the testator's lifetime
Whether the failure of one purpose of a dual-purpose bequest caused part of the legacy to fall into the residue
holdings: The wife had no beneficial interest in Schedule C property; it was held in trust for two purposes, and since one purpose failed, half the proceeds fell into the residue.

The residuary legacy to Venkataswamy and Seshagirirao under Schedule E was accelerated upon the wife's death during the testator's lifetime, as the will implied the testator’s intention to prevent lapse.
Where a bequest serves two purposes without allocated shares, and one purpose fails, half the fund is presumed to lapse into the residue while the other half remains valid for the fulfilled purpose.
doctrines: Doctrine of acceleration in wills
Doctrine of lapse under Section 105
Presumption of equal division in unallocated dual-purpose trusts
Repugnancy of bequests

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for possession of immovable property, claiming prior possession from 1930 to 1945, while the defendants claimed adverse possession and challenged the plaintiff's right to sue without proving title.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff can succeed in a suit for possession based on prior possession alone, without establishing title, when the suit is filed beyond six months of dispossession under Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.
Whether the defendants established their plea of adverse possession.
holdings: Prior possession of immovable property constitutes a possessory title, which is sufficient to maintain a suit for possession against a trespasser, even if the suit is filed more than six months after dispossession and without proving absolute title.
The defendants failed to prove their plea of adverse possession due to lack of reliable evidence.
doctrines: Possessory title doctrine
Ejectment against trespasser
Burden of proof in adverse possession

card.dispute: The widow of a coparcener and her adopted son sued to eject the illegitimate son of the last surviving coparcener from joint family properties, claiming entitlement as legal heirs and coparceners.
issues_decided: Whether the adopted son of a widow became a coparcener in the joint Hindu family property
Whether the rights of an ordinary tenant under the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 are heritable
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the dispute
holdings: An adopted son of a widow becomes the son of both the widow and her deceased husband, thereby becoming a coparcener in the joint family property.
The heritability of ordinary tenancies under the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 is governed by personal law in the absence of specific statutory restrictions.
The jurisdiction of the civil court was not barred, and the respondent could not raise the issue for the first time before the Supreme Court after not challenging it in the High Court.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 11
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 14
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 86
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 87
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 89
doctrines: Severance of ties with birth family upon adoption
Replacement of familial ties by adoptive family relationships
Heritability of tenancy rights in absence of statutory prohibition
Doctrine of constructive res judicata on jurisdictional issues

card.dispute: The appellant tenant and respondent landlord disputed whether the appellate court could dismiss an appeal based on a valid compromise agreement requiring withdrawal of litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court had the power to dismiss an appeal based on a compromise between the parties.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the appellate court's dismissal of the appeal on the ground of compromise.
holdings: A valid compromise of a dispute, including an appeal, allows a court to dismiss the appeal in accordance with the terms of the settlement under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC.
The appellate court acted lawfully in dismissing the appeal based on the compromise; the High Court erred in holding that no provision compelled withdrawal of an appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i)
doctrines: Enforcement of compromise agreements
Finality of lawful settlement of disputes

card.dispute: The dispute was between a cotton mill company and a municipal authority over the validity of a tax rate imposed on the capital value of lands and buildings, which the company challenged as ultra vires the governing Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Gujarat Imposition of Taxes by Municipalities (Validation) Act, 1963, validly retrospectively validated taxes imposed on the capital value of lands and buildings under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925?
Whether the term 'rate' in Section 73 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act could legally be interpreted to include a tax based on capital value?
Whether the State Legislature had the constitutional competence to authorise municipalities to levy taxes on the capital value of lands and buildings?
holdings: A legislature can retrospectively validate a tax if it removes the legal defect that rendered the tax invalid and possesses the constitutional power to impose such a tax.

The term 'rate' in the original Act was given a restricted meaning by prior judicial interpretation, but the legislature validly redefined it through the Validation Act to include taxes based on capital value.

The State Legislature has competence under Entry 49, List II of the Seventh Schedule to impose taxes on lands and buildings based on capital value, and such a tax does not encroach upon Parliament's power under Entry 86, List I.
provisions: Gujarat Imposition of Taxes by Municipalities (Validation) Act, 1963, Section 3
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 86
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective validation of taxes
Doctrine of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of judicial interpretation versus legislative override by redefinition

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat challenged the High Court's declaration that the acquisition of land under a town planning scheme, using outdated market value for compensation, violated constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1955, particularly Sections 53 and 67, violate Article 31(2) of the Constitution by fixing compensation based on market value many years before the extinction of ownership rights.

Whether the said provisions infringe Article 14 of the Constitution by creating unequal treatment between landowners acquired under town planning schemes and those under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the delay between the declaration of a town planning scheme and its implementation renders the compensation mechanism unconstitutional.
holdings: Fixing compensation under a town planning scheme based on market value at the time of the scheme's declaration, even if long before vesting, does not violate Article 31(2) if the scheme operates within a reasonable time frame.

Sections 53 and 67 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1955, do not violate Article 14 because the method of acquisition under the Act is distinct and exclusive, with no arbitrary choice between statutes leading to discriminatory outcomes.
The fact that considerable time has elapsed since the declaration of a town planning scheme does not, by itself, render the compensation provisions unconstitutional or ultra vires.
doctrines: Principle of statutory exclusivity in acquisition methods
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Deemed acquisition for public purpose under town planning laws
Constitutional validity of compensation mechanisms tied to earlier valuation dates

card.dispute: The state challenged the High Court's decision to quash a notification exempting a trust's property from rent control laws, alleging the exemption was discriminatory.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 3(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 was discriminatory and void under Article 14
Whether the State Government applied its mind to the relevant policy and purpose of the Act before issuing the exemption
Whether the grounds for exemption were germane to the objectives of the rent control legislation
holdings: The notification was quashed because the State Government failed to demonstrate that the exemption was based on relevant considerations tied to the Act’s policy.
An exemption under Section 3(2) must be grounded in reasons that are germane to the purpose of the Act, not merely based on eligibility criteria.
The absence of any affidavit or material showing that the government considered the fairness or policy implications renders the notification arbitrary and invalid.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of Arbitrariness under Article 14
Principle of Reasoned Decision-Making in Administrative Action
Germanness of Grounds to Statutory Purpose

card.dispute: The dispute was between a prospective tenant who advanced a loan for construction of a building and the builders (and subsequent purchasers) who did not let him any portion of the building, over whether the suit for recovery of the loan fell within the jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes under the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship of landlord and tenant is necessary for the Court of Small Causes to have jurisdiction under Section 28 of the Bombay Rents Act?

Whether a suit for recovery of a loan advanced for construction, secured by a deed of charge under Section 18(3), constitutes a claim 'arising out of' the Act so as to fall within the jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes?
holdings: The relationship of landlord and tenant is not a prerequisite for the Court of Small Causes to have jurisdiction; what matters is whether the claim arises out of the provisions of the Bombay Rents Act.

A claim for recovery of a loan advanced under a deed of charge pursuant to Section 18(3) of the Act, even in the absence of a tenancy, constitutes a claim 'arising out of' the Act and is within the jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes under Section 28(1).
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(3)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28(1)
doctrines: Jurisdictional interpretation of 'arising out of' in statutory context
Statutory purpose and scheme interpretation

card.dispute: The lessor's legal representatives and lessees disputed whether a compromise agreement created a fresh lease with a renewal option or merely extended time for possession before ejectment.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise agreement created a fresh lease or merely extended the time for delivery of possession
Whether the renewal clause from the original lease was incorporated into the compromise agreement
Whether the lessor could unreasonably withhold consent for renewal under the lease clause
holdings: The compromise created a fresh lease, not merely an extension of time, as the parties intended to continue the lessee-landlord relationship with all original terms, including the renewal option.
The renewal clause in the original lease was incorporated into the compromise agreement and remained operative despite the fixed end date.
The lessor's consent to renewal cannot be withheld unreasonably, as the lessee's right to renewal is enforceable subject to reasonable conditions.
doctrines: Contra proferentem
Ejusdem generis
Reasonable construction of contractual terms
Doctrine of non-arbitrary exercise of contractual consent

card.dispute: The dispute was between Tahsil Naidu and others (appellants) and Kulla Naidu and others (respondents) over the validity of an adoption by a Hindu widow without the consent of her husband's grandmother, the nearest female sapinda, but with the consent of two of the three nearest male sapindas.
issues_decided: Whether the consent of the majority of the nearest male sapindas is sufficient to validate an adoption by a Hindu widow in the Dravida country in the absence of her husband's authority.
Whether the consent of a female sapinda, such as the husband's grandmother, is necessary to validate such an adoption.
Whether the adoption must be scrutinized for spiritual motives when the required sapindas have given consent.
holdings: The consent of the majority of the nearest male sapindas is sufficient to validate an adoption by a Hindu widow; it is not necessary to obtain the consent of every sapinda or of female sapindas.

The consent of a female sapinda, even if nearer in degree, is not required to validate an adoption, as the term 'kindred' in this context refers only to male agnates (sapindas) under Dravida Hindu law.
When a widow obtains the consent of the requisite male sapindas, the adoption is presumed to be for spiritual purposes, and the court need not inquire into her motive.
provisions: Hindu Law of Adoption (customary, under Dravida branch of Mitakshara)
doctrines: Adoption by widow with sapindas' consent
Male agnates as necessary consents for adoption
Presumption of spiritual motive upon sapindas' consent

card.dispute: The petitioners, Wire-Netting Stores and a partner, challenged the Delhi Development Authority's eviction from a plot in Delhi without following due procedure, seeking restoration of possession and property.
issues_decided: Whether the Delhi Development Authority followed the procedure under Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958 before eviction
Whether the petitioners were entitled to a hearing before eviction under principles of natural justice
Whether the petitioners are entitled to restoration of possession and property seized during eviction
holdings: The Authority failed to comply with Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, as no valid notice specifying grounds for eviction and calling for a show-cause response was produced.
The eviction violated principles of natural justice as no opportunity was given to the petitioners to show cause against the proposed eviction.
The petitioners are entitled to restoration of the premises and return of all seized machinery and goods, with the Authority liable for missing items and costs.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, Section 4
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, Section 5
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Procedural fairness in administrative action
Burden of proof on authority to demonstrate lawful action

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant for non-payment of rent, and the tenant challenged the courts' refusal to extend time for rent payment and deposit.
issues_decided: Whether the District Court had jurisdiction to extend time for payment of arrears of rent under Section 13(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 after the suit was instituted
Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the District Court's order setting aside the trial court's decree in three of the five suits
Whether the tenant's belated deposit of rent and failure to pay monthly dues entitled him to protection under Section 13(5) against eviction
holdings: Courts have jurisdiction under Section 13(1) to extend time for rent payment if the tenant applies, but such extension must be granted before the deadline and on sufficient cause shown.
The District Court erred in setting aside the trial court’s decree in cases where there was clear default and no valid ground for extension; the High Court rightly reversed this.
A tenant who fails to pay arrears within the statutory period and does not apply for extension in time is not protected under Section 13(5), even if deposit is later made.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(5)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(6)
doctrines: Conditional protection against eviction for non-payment of rent
Judicial discretion to extend time for statutory compliance
Binding effect of findings in revision under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant, alleging he had sublet the premises to a company, which the tenant denied, claiming an agency relationship instead.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had sublet the premises to Usha Sales (P) Ltd. or was merely acting as its agent
Whether the agreement between the appellant and Usha Sales created a genuine agency or camouflaged a sub-tenancy
Whether the second appeal to the High Court involved a substantial question of law under Section 39(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
holdings: The agreement's terms and conduct show Usha Sales exclusively occupied and controlled the premises, indicating subletting, not agency.
The arrangement was a camouflaged sub-tenancy, as the appellant had no real control or remuneration, and Usha Sales operated the business independently.
No substantial question of law arose in the second appeal, so the High Court rightly declined to interfere with the Rent Tribunal’s factual findings.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of factual findings in rent control proceedings
Doctrine of no interference in second appeal without substantial question of law

card.dispute: The Bihar State Board of Religious Trusts claimed that certain properties dedicated to an idol constituted a public religious trust under the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, while the respondents, Palat Lall and another, argued that the endowment was private and not subject to the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the endowment created by the will of the testator was a public or private religious trust.
Whether the properties dedicated to the family idol were subject to the provisions of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950.
holdings: An endowment for a family idol, where only family members perform worship and no provision allows public management or right to worship, constitutes a private trust.
The mere admission of public worshippers or the size of the endowed property does not make a trust public; dedication to the public must be clearly intended in the instrument.
doctrines: Distinction between public and private religious endowments
Presumption against inferring public dedication from mere admission of public worshippers
Importance of the instrument of creation and conduct in determining the nature of a trust

card.dispute: The appellant and his brothers disputed whether certain properties, particularly those covered by Exh. B-6, were joint family property available for partition or the appellant's separate self-acquired property.
issues_decided: Whether the properties covered by Exh. B-6 were joint family properties or the separate property of the appellant
Whether the appellant's statement that his father paid the consideration for Exh. B-6 amounted to an admission that the property was joint family property
holdings: The property covered by Exh. B-6 was the separate self-acquired property of the appellant, as the consideration was paid by the father from the appellant's private funds, particularly his dowry amount, and not from joint family funds.

An isolated statement that the father paid the consideration does not conclusively prove joint family acquisition, especially when read with the appellant's consistent claim and conduct showing the property as his separate asset.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Principle of admission in civil proceedings
Separate property vs. joint family property under Mitakshara law

card.dispute: Bouku and his descendants claimed a half share in joint family property, including Ranu's share, against the sons of Makund and Basudeo who asserted prior partition in 1914 barred the claim.
issues_decided: Whether the 1914 arbitration award and preliminary decree effected a valid partition despite the suit being dismissed for non-payment of fees?
Whether Bouku was bound by the 1914 award even if not formally served in the suit?
Whether the arbitrators acted improperly in awarding Makund a 6 anna share instead of a statutory share?
Whether Bouku acquired Ranu's share through adoption of his son or by adverse possession?
holdings: A preliminary decree based on an arbitration award effects a severance of joint family status, and dismissal of the suit for non-payment of fees does not nullify the partition already acted upon.
A party who accepts benefits under an award and has been in possession pursuant to it cannot later deny its binding effect, even if not formally served.
Where a partition is agreed upon by parties and acted upon for decades, a claim of improper division under Hindu law cannot be raised belatedly.
Ranu's share vested in his widow for life, and on her death was to be divided among the three branches; Bouku acquired no title by adoption or adverse possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII, Rule 1
doctrines: Severance by agreement in a joint Hindu family
Binding effect of arbitration awards under consent
Doctrine of res judicata and constructive res judicata
Principle of approbate and reprobate

card.dispute: The appellant, Debi Prasad, claimed to be the nearest heir to his maternal uncle Gopal Das, while the respondents claimed that Shyam Behari Lal was validly adopted by Gopal Das and thus entitled to the property.
issues_decided: Whether Shyam Behari Lal was validly adopted by Gopal Das under Hindu law?
Whether the burden of proof for establishing adoption was discharged by the respondents?
Whether documentary and conduct evidence can prove adoption in the absence of direct ceremonial proof?
holdings: For a valid adoption under Hindu law, there must be a formal ceremony of giving and taking, though no specific form is prescribed.
The burden of proving adoption lies on the person asserting it, and such proof must include both the factum and validity of adoption.
A long and consistent course of conduct, including documentary admissions by the parties, can constitute satisfactory evidence of adoption even without direct proof of ceremony.
Documentary evidence such as school records, tax assessments, nomination papers, and court depositions showing treatment as father and son over decades supports the fact of adoption.
doctrines: Burden of proof in adoption cases
Factum of adoption
Ceremony of giving and taking
Admissibility of conduct and documentary evidence to prove adoption

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax fought with Indian Mica Supply Co. P. Ltd. over whether a payment of Rs. 42,473 for past rent could be allowed as a revenue expenditure deduction under the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the sum of Rs. 40,132 (part of Rs. 42,473) was a revenue payment allowable as a deduction under Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to direct the Tribunal to refer a question of law
holdings: A payment made to regularize a business's right to continue operations, such as rent for a past period due to a compromised lease renewal, is wholly and exclusively for business purposes and qualifies as revenue expenditure.
The High Court was justified in refusing to order a reference where the Tribunal's finding on revenue expenditure was supported by evidence and the legal issue was not substantial.
doctrines: Revenue vs capital expenditure distinction
Tribunal's factual findings not interfered with if supported by evidence
Principle of business expediency in determining deductibility

card.dispute: The dispute was between the grandsons of G's brother (defendants) and Rajaram (plaintiff, daughter's son and reversioner of G) over ownership of tenancy land previously held by G, following a series of gifts, dispossession, and the application of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the widow (L) acquired full ownership rights under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 after re-entering the property as a trespasser in 1951
Whether the plaintiff’s suit as a reversioner was barred by limitation under Section 104(1) read with Article I of the Second Schedule of the C.P. Tenancy Act, 1920
Whether a trespasser in possession of tenancy land can acquire rights by adverse possession under the C.P. Tenancy Act, 1920
holdings: A Hindu woman does not acquire full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act unless she had a right to possession; mere possession as a trespasser does not qualify.
Article I of the Second Schedule to the C.P. Tenancy Act applies only to suits by dispossessed tenants; it does not bar a reversioner's suit based on title, even after limitation expires.
The C.P. Tenancy Act does not allow a trespasser to acquire tenancy rights by adverse possession against third-party reversioners; such rights cannot be extinguished before they accrue.
provisions: C.P. Tenancy Act, 1920, Section 104(1) read with Article I, Second Schedule
