holdings: An entry in revenue records alone is relevant for determining adhivasi status under Section 20(b), but if the entry was made fraudulently or surreptitiously, it cannot confer adhivasi rights.
The Allahabad High Court's view that fictitious entries must still be recognized under Section 20(b) is no longer good law, following the Supreme Court's decision in Sonavati v. Sri Ram.
The appeal did not abate despite non-joinder of one legal representative, as two were already impleaded, and the third could be added later.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 20(b)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 240(a)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 229(c)
doctrines: Fraud vitiates legal rights
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent
Relation back of amendments to include parties

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a half share in a disputed house based on a 1915 family arrangement, while the respondents denied his title, asserting it was extinguished by adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the 1915 document (Ex. I) constituted a valid family arrangement under Hindu law
Whether the appellant's title was extinguished by adverse possession by the respondents
holdings: A document purporting to settle family disputes over property will be upheld as a family arrangement if it reflects a bona fide effort to preserve harmony, even without equal division or prior title.
Adverse possession requires open, continuous, and hostile possession with clear ouster; mere use of property without assertion of exclusive title does not amount to adverse possession.
provisions: Bihar and Orissa Municipal Survey Act, 1 of 1920
doctrines: Family Arrangement Doctrine
Doctrine of Adverse Possession
Doctrine of Ouster in Property Law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the genuineness of a will that excluded her as a daughter while bequeathing property to others, including non-heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the will executed by the testator on November 25, 1945, is genuine.
Whether suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of the will require stricter scrutiny of the evidence.
holdings: A will cannot be rejected merely because it is unnatural or disinherits a legal heir; the court must assess the evidence with greater care if suspicious circumstances exist.
The propounder of a will must prove its execution and attestation; if suspicious circumstances arise, the burden is to explain them to the satisfaction of a prudent mind.
The testimony of independent and respectable attesting witnesses, along with evidence of prior intent, can establish the genuineness of a will even if some witnesses were not invited to attest.
Mere association between a witness and a beneficiary, without direct interest, does not discredit the witness’s testimony in support of a will.
doctrines: Burden of proof in will disputes
Prudent mind standard in proving wills
Suspicious circumstances doctrine
Naturalness of bequests

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and the respondent company disputed whether royalty on coal under pre-1949 mining leases could be raised above 5% via a notification under Section 30A of the Mines & Minerals Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether a notification under the second part of Section 30A of the Mines & Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 can have the effect of raising the royalty rate on coal under pre-1949 leases above the 5% rate specified in Section 9(1) read with the Second Schedule?
Whether the Central Government's 1961 notification modified the royalty rate to allow collection at lease-agreed rates higher than 5%?
holdings: A notification under Section 30A cannot authorize royalty collection at a rate higher than 5% for pre-1949 leases, as it only permits phased application of the statutory rate, not an increase beyond it.

The 1961 notification modified the 5% statutory rate downward, allowing payment at lease rates or 2.5%, whichever higher, but not above 5%; any construction permitting higher rates would exceed statutory power.
provisions: The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 9(1)
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 9(3)
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 16(1)
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 30A
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Second Schedule
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of validity presumption
Doctrine of statutory interpretation to avoid excess of power

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and Swamy Satyanand Saraswati disputed whether the latter had rights to sub-soil minerals (granite) on land granted by a jagirdar, entitling him to compensation upon state acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the grant to the respondent's predecessor included rights to sub-soil minerals by express or implied terms
Whether granite qualifies as a 'mineral' for the purpose of property rights under the grant
What is the proper test to determine if mineral rights are included in a land grant lacking express mention
holdings: The burden lies on the claimant to prove that mineral rights were granted; absence of express or implied grant means such rights remain with the grantor.
Granite is a mineral under the vernacular and commercial understanding at the time of the grant, not merely by scientific definition.
When a land grant contemplates only surface use like cultivation or grazing, and excludes even trees, sub-soil rights are not impliedly transferred.
doctrines: Doctrine of implied reservation of mineral rights
Doctrine of ejusdem generis in interpreting 'minerals'
Burden of proof in establishing proprietary mineral rights

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought the Howrah Municipality over whether delay in filing appeals against a land acquisition compensation award could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether the State of West Bengal had sufficient cause for the delay in filing appeals under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Whether the State acted diligently after discovering on March 4, 1965, that no appeals had been filed.
Whether reliance on incorrect legal advice constitutes negligence that disentitles a party to relief under Section 5.
holdings: Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 must be liberally construed to advance substantial justice, provided there is no negligence, inaction, or lack of bona fides on the party's part.
The State did not delay unreasonably before March 4, 1965, as it only then learned that no appeals had been filed, and thus no negligence can be imputed for that period.
Acting on wrong legal advice does not amount to negligence; a party may still show 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 if it acted diligently upon that advice.
The State took diligent steps after March 4, 1965, including seeking legal advice and filing writ petitions under Article 227, warranting condonation of delay in filing appeals.
doctrines: Liberal construction of limitation laws to serve substantial justice
Sufficient cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
No disentitlement for acting on wrong legal advice
Diligence in pursuing remedies after discovery of error

card.dispute: The State Bank of Travancore (mortgagee) versus members of an Ezhava Marumakkathayam Tharwad over possession of property allegedly recovered by the Tharwad after a junior member's agent took possession, leading to questions about title, agency, and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Tharwad was undivided and whether the first plaintiff was its Karanavan at the time of the suit.
Whether Krishnan Krishnan acquired absolute title to the property or held it only as an agent with a lien.
Whether Krishnan Krishnan or his successors acquired title by adverse possession.
holdings: A Hindu joint family is presumed to be undivided unless proven otherwise; the plaintiffs' evidence that the Tharwad was undivided and that the first plaintiff was Karanavan was unrebutted and sufficient.

Krishnan Krishnan, who deposited money and took possession of the property on behalf of the Tharwad, held only a lien for the amount advanced and not absolute title; thus, his successors could not acquire better title.

Possession by Krishnan Krishnan and subsequent holders was permissive, not adverse, and could not mature into title by adverse possession without proof of hostile assertion known to the true owners for over twelve years.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 53 (mortgage and charge)
Limitation Act, Article 144 (adverse possession of immovable property)
doctrines: Presumption of joint family status in Hindu law
Lien of a person advancing money for redemption of property
Permissive possession cannot ripen into adverse possession without hostile assertion

card.dispute: The heirs of Shah Abdul Rahim disputed the validity of an arbitration award and decree that treated certain properties as Dargah and Khankah properties, claiming they were actually Matrooka (personal) property and that the minor heir was improperly represented.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award and decree were void due to lack of legal guardianship of a minor party
Whether the limitation period for filing a suit for partition was extended due to fraud or concealment
Whether possession of the property by one co-owner amounted to adverse possession against other co-owners
holdings: An arbitration award and decree are void if a minor is represented by a non-guardian without court appointment, rendering the compromise invalid.
Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908, limitation for filing a suit is extended when a party is kept in ignorance of their rights due to fraud or active concealment.
Possession by one co-owner is not adverse unless there is open denial of co-owners' title and unequivocal exclusion; mere possession does not extinguish others' rights.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates proceedings and tolls limitation under Section 18
No adverse possession by co-owner without hostile assertion and ouster
Award void ab initio if minor not represented by lawful guardian

card.dispute: Property owners challenged the constitutional validity of a tax imposed by the Bombay Building Repairs and Reconstruction Board Act, 1969, arguing it violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of buildings for levy of tax under Section 27 of the Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the exemptions granted under Section 28 of the Act are arbitrary and violative of equal protection
Whether the tax imposed is a colourable legislation or lacks a rational nexus with the object of the Act
Whether the levy infringes the right to property under Article 19(1)(f)
holdings: The classification of buildings based on age and construction type is founded on intelligible differentia and bears a rational relation to the Act's objective of preventing building collapses.

The exemptions under Section 28 are valid as the excluded categories—such as owner-occupied, non-residential, and cooperative society buildings—form distinct classes with different legal and economic considerations.
The tax is not based on quid pro quo but on public interest, and unequal individual benefit does not invalidate it under Article 14.
The levy does not violate Article 19(1)(f) as the right to property is subject to reasonable restrictions for public welfare.
provisions: Bombay Building Repairs and Reconstruction Board Act, 1969, Section 27
Bombay Building Repairs and Reconstruction Board Act, 1969, Section 28
doctrines: Intelligible differentia
Rational nexus
Classification test under Article 14
Public purpose in taxation
Reasonable restriction on property rights

card.dispute: The appellant, Veeramachineni Gangadhara Rao, challenged the enforcement of a mortgage claim by Andhra Bank Ltd. over property title deeds he deposited, arguing they secured only his personal loan, not the debts of a company managed by his brother.
issues_decided: Whether the document recording the deposit of title deeds (Exh. A-6) required registration under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908
Whether the deposit of title deeds created a mortgage by implication or was governed by the terms of the written document
Whether the unregistered document could be used to extend the security to debts beyond those of the depositor
holdings: A document recording the deposit of title deeds requires registration only if it embodies the express contract between the parties; otherwise, it is merely evidential and does not need registration.
When parties intend a written document to be the sole record of their agreement regarding the deposit, it must be registered and governs the scope of the security.

If the document is merely a memorandum of an already existing oral agreement, the mortgage arises by operation of law from the deposit, and the unregistered document does not bar oral evidence under Sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act.
doctrines: Implied mortgage by deposit of title deeds
Integration of written agreements as sole evidence of contract
Exclusion of oral evidence when parties reduce bargain to writing

card.dispute: Allenburry Engineers Private Ltd. contested the validity of a notice terminating its tenancy, claiming it was for manufacturing purposes and thus required a longer notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy was for 'manufacturing purposes' within the meaning of Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the one-month notice issued to terminate the tenancy was valid.
holdings: The term 'manufacturing purposes' under Section 106 means making or fabricating articles by skill or mechanical power into a new product with a distinct name, character, or use.
The appellant failed to prove that the dominant purpose of the tenancy was manufacturing; repair and reconditioning of vehicles was incidental to storage and resale, not manufacture.
doctrines: Dominant purpose doctrine
Literal meaning of 'manufacture' in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant, Badrilal, contested eviction by the Municipal Corporation of Indore after his lease expired, claiming a new lease was granted through subsequent payments and correspondence.
issues_decided: Whether a binding contract for a new lease arose between the parties based on the appellant's payments and the Commissioner's acceptance
Whether the appellant became a tenant holding over or a tenant by sufferance after the lease expired
Whether notice was required before eviction of the appellant
holdings: No contract was formed because the Municipal Commissioner lacked authority under Section 80 of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act to enter into a lease without the Corporation's sanction, and the offer lapsed upon filing of the eviction suit.
The appellant was not a tenant holding over because the acceptance of rent at the old rate did not constitute clear recognition of tenancy rights; he remained a tenant by sufferance.
A tenant by sufferance can be evicted without notice since no tenancy rights exist, and the landlord's mere inaction does not create a new tenancy.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, Section 80
doctrines: Doctrine of holding over under Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of tenant by sufferance
Doctrine of competent authority in municipal contracts
Doctrine of revocation of offer by filing of suit

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed ownership and adhivasi sardari rights over certain agricultural plots, based on whether an entry in the revenue record in favour of the respondents' father was fictitious or valid.
issues_decided: Whether an entry in the khasra or khatauni made out of ill-will or hostility by a Patwari can confer adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether a fictitious or malafide entry in revenue records, even if made in discharge of official duties, can be the basis for claiming adhivasi rights
Whether the Deputy Director of Consolidation had jurisdiction to hold that an entry in revenue records was fictitious
holdings: An entry in revenue records made due to hostility or ill-will, though made by a Patwari in official capacity, is fictitious and cannot confer adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.

A fictitious or surreptitious entry in the khasra or khatauni, even if formally recorded, does not entitle a person to adhivasi rights if it lacks authenticity and was made contrary to rules and in bad faith.
The Deputy Director of Consolidation has jurisdiction to determine whether an entry in revenue records is fictitious, especially when supported by findings of civil and revenue courts.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 8, Section 12, Section 20
doctrines: Fictitious entry doctrine
Illegality of malafide administrative actions
Jurisdiction of revenue authorities to examine authenticity of entries

card.dispute: Balmadies Plantations Ltd. challenged the constitutional validity of the Gudalur Janmam Estates Act, 1969, which abolished Janmam estates and transferred lands, including forests, to the State of Tamil Nadu.
issues_decided: Whether the Resettlement of 1926 converted Janmam lands into ryotwari lands, making the 1969 Act inapplicable
Whether forests in Janmam lands constitute an 'estate' under Article 31A of the Constitution
Whether the acquisition of forests in Janmam lands qualifies as agrarian reform under Article 31A
Whether the provisions allowing termination of plantation lessees' rights violate constitutional rights
holdings: The Resettlement of 1926 did not abolish Janmam estates or convert them into ryotwari lands; it only changed nomenclature, retaining the Janmam system.
Janmam lands, including forests within them, fall under 'estate' as defined in Article 31A(2)(a)(i), so the requirement of clause (iii) need not be satisfied.
The acquisition of forests in Janmam lands is not protected by Article 31A because it is not shown to be for agrarian reform; mere transfer of ownership or resource augmentation does not suffice.
The challenge to section 17 regarding termination of lessees' rights is premature as no action has been taken under it; courts will examine such issues if and when they arise.
provisions: Gudalur Janmam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1969 (Act 24 of 1969), Sections 3, 11, 16, 17
doctrines: Agrarian reform requirement for Article 31A protection
Severability of unconstitutional provisions
Doctrine of ripeness in constitutional challenges

card.dispute: The appellant, Devi Singh, fought the Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad over ownership and possession of a property called 'Jumerate Bazaarat', seeking to restrain the Corporation from obstructing his possession and collecting unauthorized amounts from it.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under Section 447 of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation Act was necessary before instituting the suit against the Corporation.
Whether the Firman (Ex.D-17) issued by the Sarfe-Khas authorities had the force of law or was merely an executive act.
Whether the proceedings and orders of the Sarfe-Khas Department regarding the property's title and possession were legally valid and binding.
holdings: No notice under Section 447 of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation Act was required because the suit concerned disputes over title and possession, not acts done under the Corporation's statutory functions.
The Firman (Ex.D-17) was not a legislative enactment but an executive order, and its legal effect must be determined based on its nature as such, not as binding law.

The proceedings before the Sarfe-Khas, including the admission of the plaintiff's title and delivery of possession, cannot be ignored and must be considered in determining the rights of the parties, especially in the absence of any finding of collusion or lack of jurisdiction.
doctrines: Notice requirement for suits against municipal corporations
Distinction between executive and legislative acts
Relevance and evidentiary value of executive orders in title disputes
Principle of remand for proper adjudication of title and possession

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether certain lands (Survey Nos. 16 to 18) were communal lands or had been validly converted into ryotwari lands in favor of the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector's order under Section 20A of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, validly diverted communal lands for other use.
Whether the Assistant Settlement Officer had authority under Section 11 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, to grant a ryotwari patta over communal lands.
Whether the decision of the Settlement Officer under Section 56 of the 1948 Act is final and bars civil court jurisdiction.
Whether civil courts had jurisdiction to decide the dispute despite Section 189(1) of the 1908 Act.
holdings: Under Section 20A of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, the Collector must make a written order specifying a new communal use before diverting communal land; mere declaration that land is no longer needed is insufficient.
The Assistant Settlement Officer lacked jurisdiction under Section 11 of the 1948 Abolition Act to grant a ryotwari patta over communal lands not already classified as ryoti or lanka lands.

Section 56 of the 1948 Act makes only specific disputes (regarding arrears of rent or identity of lawful ryot) final; it does not make patta grants over communal lands conclusive or immune from judicial review.

Section 189(1) of the 1908 Act bars civil court jurisdiction only for matters listed in the Schedule; since no valid Collector’s order under Section 20A was made, the civil court retained jurisdiction under Section 9 of the CPC.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 11
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 56
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of administrative decisions limited to statutory scope
Doctrine of jurisdictional limits of revenue officers
Presumption of continuity of communal rights unless expressly extinguished
Civil court jurisdiction not barred without clear statutory ouster

card.dispute: The appellant, Deo Narain, was convicted by the High Court for causing death under Section 304 IPC after using a spear in a land dispute, while claiming the right of private defence; the State prosecuted him, arguing he exceeded that right.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had the right of private defence of the body under Section 102 IPC when he used force against an unlawful and imminent threat.
Whether the appellant exceeded the right of private defence by using a spear causing fatal injury, despite receiving only a minor injury.
Whether the nature of the weapon used (spear vs. lathi) determines the reasonableness of force in self-defence.
holdings: The right of private defence of the body arises as soon as there is a reasonable apprehension of imminent danger from an unlawful threat, even if no actual serious injury has yet been inflicted.
Using a spear resulting in death does not automatically exceed the right of private defence if the attacker reasonably feared grievous harm or death from a lathi blow to the head.
The reasonableness of force must be judged contextually; one cannot expect a person under sudden aggression to precisely calibrate the force used in self-defence.
doctrines: Right of private defence of the body
Reasonable apprehension of imminent harm
Proportionality in self-defence
Self-defence as preventive, not punitive

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell a property, against defendants who later purchased the same property, claiming they were bona fide purchasers without notice of the prior agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had notice of the prior agreement to sell dated March 1, 1960.
What was the nature and extent of the onus of proof on the appellants to establish that they were bona fide purchasers without notice?
Whether the circumstances surrounding the purchase raised suspicion warranting inquiry into the prior agreement.
holdings: A purchaser of immovable property who fails to make inquiries in circumstances where such inquiries would naturally be expected cannot claim to be a bona fide purchaser without notice.
The onus on a subsequent purchaser to prove they were unaware of a prior agreement is not discharged merely by a bare denial; suspicious circumstances require active inquiry.
Unusual haste in completing a sale, close proximity of parties, and failure to verify property details may indicate constructive notice of a prior agreement.
The appellants had express and constructive notice of the prior agreement, and thus could not claim protection as bona fide purchasers.
doctrines: Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Constructive notice
Onus of proof in cases of competing equitable claims

card.dispute: The appellants (buyers) sued for specific performance of a contract to purchase immovable property after the property was requisitioned by the government, and the respondents (sellers) refused to execute the sale deed despite repeated demands.
issues_decided: Whether the requisitioning of the property by the government discharged the seller's obligation to sell or terminated the contract
Whether the clause providing for refund of earnest money on requisition was for the exclusive benefit of the buyer and could be waived by them
Whether the delay of over two years in filing the suit for specific performance barred the relief
holdings: The non-requisitioning of the property was not a condition precedent to the seller's obligation to sell; the contract did not automatically terminate upon requisitioning.
The clause allowing refund of earnest money on requisition was for the exclusive benefit of the buyers, who could therefore waive it and enforce specific performance.
The delay in filing the suit was not inordinate or prejudicial to the seller, especially since the buyers had consistently pressed for performance and the seller did not allege prejudice.
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver of conditions for exclusive benefit of one party
Doctrine of laches in equity
Condition precedent in contracts for sale of immovable property

card.dispute: Gauri Shanker, the owner of a property, fought with Hindustan Trust (Pvt.) Ltd., the tenant, over non-payment of rent and eviction after a partition decree awarded him ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the notice served by the landlord was valid to terminate the contractual tenancy under the Rent Act
Whether the tenant could raise the issue of invalid notice for the first time in appeal after abandoning it before the Rent Control Tribunal
Whether the amendment to raise the plea of invalid notice after eight years should have been permitted
holdings: A notice demanding arrears of rent under Clause (a) of the proviso to Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act does not amount to a notice terminating the tenancy.

A party cannot be permitted to raise a technical plea of invalid notice for the first time in appeal after having abandoned it before the lower tribunal, especially after a delay of eight years causing prejudice.
The amendment to introduce the plea of invalid notice was rightly disallowed due to laches and the failure to appeal the order allowing amendment does not cure the abuse of process.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, Section III, Clause (g)
doctrines: Doctrine of abandonment of pleadings
Doctrine of laches and acquiescence
Judicial discretion in allowing new points in appeal

card.dispute: The Hitkarini Sabha and the Jabalpur Municipal Corporation disputed over the apportionment of compensation and the quantum of compensation for land acquired by the state for a Home Science College.
issues_decided: Whether the renewal clause in the lease deed dated August 31, 1940, was valid and enforceable for the purpose of apportioning compensation.
Whether the High Court erred in upholding the compensation of Rs. 10 per square foot as reasonable.
holdings: The renewal clause in the lease deed was unenforceable due to uncertainty and the lease itself was invalid because the Municipal Committee lacked authority when it was executed; thus, the clause could not be considered for apportionment.

The compensation of Rs. 10 per square foot was reasonable as the courts considered all relevant factors including development costs and comparable sales, and did not overlook the land's potential value.
doctrines: Doctrine of unenforceability of uncertain contracts
Apportionment of compensation based on valid leasehold interest
Principle of market valuation considering development potential and comparable sales

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant's heirs on grounds of personal need, after the statutory tenant died during appeal, raising questions about whether heirs could claim protection under the rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court should have remanded the case to determine if the contractual tenancy was terminated
Whether the protection under Section 13 of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 is personal to the statutory tenant
Whether the heirs of a deceased statutory tenant qualify as 'tenants' under Section 3(vii) of the Act
holdings: The High Court rightly decided that the contractual tenancy was duly terminated by notice; no remand was necessary as the issue was conclusively decided.
The protection under Section 13 of the Act is personal to the statutory tenant and does not survive his death; heirs cannot claim the same protection.
The heirs of a deceased statutory tenant are not 'tenants' under Section 3(vii) of the Act, as the right to possession is personal and not inheritable.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 3(vii)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22, Rule 11
doctrines: Personal nature of statutory tenancy
Survival of right to sue under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC
Non-inheritability of statutory tenant's rights

card.dispute: The landlord's successors sued to eject the tenant, who claimed protection under rent control laws and estoppel due to constructions on the land.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy fell within the definition of 'accommodation' under Section 2(a) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, requiring prior permission of the District Magistrate for eviction
Whether the landlord was estopped from filing the ejectment suit due to inaction regarding constructions made by the tenant
holdings: The tenancy of bare land without transfer of any constructed accommodation does not fall within 'accommodation' under the Act; hence, Section 3 permission was not required for the ejectment suit.
Mere knowledge or inaction by the landlord regarding unauthorized constructions does not create estoppel preventing the filing of an ejectment suit under the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 2(a)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel
Doctrine of fixtures under lease law
Interpretation of 'accommodation' in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The appellant purchaser challenged the application of the doctrine of lis pendens to two sales of land during a pending partition suit, one being a private sale and the other a revenue sale under the Land Improvement Loans Act.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 28 of Order IV of the Madras High Court Rules, requiring an oral and immediate application for a Letters Patent appeal certificate, is ultra vires?
Whether the sales under Exhibits B-7 and B-51 are affected by the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act?
holdings: Rule 28 of Order IV of the Madras High Court Rules is not ultra vires; it merely regulates the manner of applying for a certificate and does not extinguish the right to appeal.

The sale under Exhibit B-7 is subject to lis pendens as it is a voluntary transfer during pending litigation; however, the revenue sale under Exhibit B-51 is not automatically void under lis pendens if it pertains to land for which improvement loans were taken, due to the pre-existing statutory charge under the Land Improvement Loans Act.
provisions: Indian Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 52
doctrines: Lis Pendens
Pre-existing charge under statute
Involuntary alienation in revenue sales

card.dispute: The appellant tenant sought fixation of standard rent under the Bombay Rent Act, while the respondent landlord claimed the dispute fell under the jurisdiction of the Co-operative Societies Act, not civil courts.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the appellant and respondent falls within the scope of Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the rent fixation application under Section 11 of the Bombay Rent Act
holdings: A dispute involving a lease by a person who later became a member of a co-operative society does not fall under Section 91(1)(b) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act if the lease predated membership and was not entered into as a member.
The civil court has jurisdiction to decide rent fixation proceedings when the dispute does not touch upon the management or business of a co-operative society under Section 91.
doctrines: Jurisdictional exclusivity of co-operative tribunals under Section 91
Ratio decidendi of earlier precedent binding (Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Dalichand Jugraj Jain)

card.dispute: The Kannan Devan Hills Produce Company Ltd challenged the constitutional validity of the Kerala Act resuming its vast land holdings, arguing it was not an 'estate' under Article 31A and the Act did not qualify as agrarian reform.
issues_decided: Whether the land held by the petitioner constitutes an 'estate' within the meaning of Article 31A(2)(a) of the Constitution
Whether the Kannan Devan Hills (Resumption of Lands) Act, 1971 qualifies as a law for agrarian reforms under Article 31A
holdings: An 'estate' under Article 31A means a holding where the holder is the proprietor of the soil and stands in direct revenue relationship with the State, regardless of the presence of intermediaries.

The Act qualifies as agrarian reform as its purposes—promoting agriculture, welfare of agricultural population, and resettling landless cultivators—fall within the broad concept of agrarian reforms upheld in previous decisions.
provisions: Kannan Devan Hills (Resumption of Lands) Act, 1971 (Kerala Act 5 of 1971), Sections 4, 5, and 9
doctrines: Doctrine of agrarian reforms under Article 31A
Doctrine of estate as proprietary landholding in direct relationship with the State

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, particularly provisions affecting rent arrears, ceiling limits, and rights of tenants (kudikidappukars), arguing violations of fundamental rights and lack of protection under Article 31-A.
issues_decided: Whether arrears of rent constitute an 'interest in land' within the meaning of 'estate' under Article 31-A of the Constitution, so as to protect Section 73 of the Act
Whether Section 45-A and the Explanation to Section 85(1) of the Act are valid if Section 73 is upheld
Whether the transfer of agricultural land to kudikidappukars under the Act constitutes agrarian reform protected by Article 31-A
Whether rights of landlords, such as quarrying rights, are affected by vesting under Section 72 of the Act
holdings: Arrears of rent, being a charge on the tenant's interest in land, constitute an interest in land within the meaning of 'estate' under Article 31-A, and thus Section 73 is protected by Article 31-A despite infringing Article 19(1)(f).
Section 45-A and the Explanation to Section 85(1) are valid as they form part of the agrarian reform scheme and are supported by the protection of Article 31-A if Section 73 is upheld.

The transfer of agricultural land to kudikidappukars is part of agrarian reform aimed at land redistribution and is protected under Article 31-A when applied to agricultural land and beneficiaries connected with agriculture.

Section 72, which vests landlord's rights vis-à-vis tenants in the government, falls within the scope of agrarian reform under Article 31-A; however, the Court did not decide on non-agricultural rights like quarrying as they were not raised in the petitions.
provisions: Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964), Section 73
Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, Section 85(1) Explanation
doctrines: Agrarian reform doctrine under Article 31-A
Doctrine of severability
Reading down of statutes to uphold constitutionality
Purpose-based determination of agricultural land

card.dispute: The lessee claimed the right to remain in possession of a cinema house after the lease expired until the market value of the superstructure was ascertained and 50% payment made, while the lessors sought eviction under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act.
issues_decided: Whether the lessee was entitled to retain possession after the lease expired until the market value of the superstructure was determined and 50% payment made.
Whether the Rent Controller could order eviction despite a dispute over the valuation of the superstructure under the lease agreement.
Whether a condition to pay 50% of the market value of the superstructure delayed the lessor's right to take possession upon lease expiry.
holdings: The lessee was not entitled to retain possession after the lease expired; the lessor's right to possession vested immediately upon expiry, subject only to the liability to pay 50% of the market value.
The Rent Controller had jurisdiction to proceed with eviction under Section 13(2) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, as the lease did not expressly postpone possession pending valuation.
A condition to pay 50% of the market value created a financial liability but did not delay the transfer of possession; such valuation was a separable matter for arbitration.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of lease terms
Burden of proving 'contract to the contrary' under Section 108(q) of the Transfer of Property Act
Separability of valuation disputes from possession rights

card.dispute: The plaintiff and defendant fought over ownership and possession of a building site, with the plaintiff seeking declaration of title and permanent injunction against the defendant's interference.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff established a satisfactory title to the suit property.
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a permanent injunction based on possession, despite weak title.
holdings: The plaintiff failed to satisfactorily prove his title to the suit property based on the record, and thus was not entitled to a declaration of ownership.
The plaintiff's long and continuous possession since 1947 entitled him to protection against interference by someone without a better title, warranting a permanent injunction.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 8
doctrines: Possession as a basis for injunction
Res judicata
Title not conclusively established

card.dispute: Two public servants entrusted with carrying out land improvement schemes were prosecuted for preparing false documents and misappropriating funds, and challenged their conviction on grounds of procedural illegality and statutory time bar.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants committed criminal misappropriation and breach of trust by preparing false documents and showing disbursement of funds not actually paid?
Whether investigation conducted without prior permission under Section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act vitiated the trial?
Whether prosecution was barred by limitation under Section 23 of the Bombay Land Improvement Schemes Act, 1942?
holdings: Preparation of false documents showing work done and payment made when neither occurred constitutes criminal breach of trust and dishonest misappropriation, even if the work and payment were later completed.
A defect in investigation under Section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act does not invalidate conviction unless it caused prejudice or miscarriage of justice.
Section 23 of the Bombay Land Improvement Schemes Act does not bar prosecution for acts done in bad faith or not 'under' the Act, such as fabrication of records and misappropriation of funds.
provisions: Bombay Land Improvement Schemes Act, 1942, Section 23(1) and (2)
Bombay General Clauses Act, Definition of 'good faith'
doctrines: Dishonest misappropriation even for a time amounts to offence under IPC
Illegality in investigation does not vitiate trial without prejudice
Good faith requirement for statutory protection under immunity clauses
Acts not done 'under' a statute are not protected by its procedural bars

card.dispute: Private plantation owners challenged the validity of amendments to the Kerala Land Reforms Act, arguing that the state could not acquire their lands used for rubber, pepper, areca, and other plantations, and that such acquisition violated constitutional protections.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Kerala Land Reforms Act, particularly the reduction of land ceiling and reservation of land for public purpose under Section 96(1A), is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution
Whether the exclusion of pepper and areca plantations from exemption while exempting other plantations violates Article 14
Whether lands used for rubber plantations, forests, dairy farms, or trees like teak and eucalyptus are exempt from acquisition under the Act
Whether the Union's control over the rubber industry under the Rubber Act bars state regulation of land used for rubber cultivation
holdings: The amendment allowing reservation of land for public purpose under Section 96(1A) is protected by Article 31A when read as connected to agrarian reform, and the reduction of ceiling limits without full compensation does not violate constitutional safeguards.

The Act does not violate Article 14 by excluding pepper and areca plantations from exemption, provided the lands qualify as 'estates' under Article 31A(2)(a); differential treatment is justified by agrarian reform objectives.
Lands under rubber, teak, or eucalyptus plantations are agricultural and not exempt; forests and jungles are exempt only if not part of an estate; dairy farms within estates are subject to the Act.

The Union's regulatory control over rubber manufacturing under the Rubber Act does not extend to land use or cultivation, so state acquisition of land for agrarian reform does not infringe on Union legislative competence.
provisions: Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964 (as amended in 1969 and 1971), Section 3, Section 86, Section 87, Section 96(1A)
Constitution of India, Article 31-A, Article 31-B, Article 14
Rubber (Production and Marketing) Act, 1947, Section 8, Section 17
doctrines: Agrarian reform as a public purpose under Article 31A
Doctrine of reading down statutory provisions to uphold constitutionality
Legislative competence: distinction between industrial regulation and agricultural land reform
Principle of non-discrimination under Article 14 in the context of land reform classifications

card.dispute: Hindustan Steel Limited challenged the Patna High Court's cancellation of its mining lease, which was granted by the Bihar Government, against the claims of Kalyani Banerjee and others, heirs of prior lessees, who asserted superior title to the mineral rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Controller of Mining Leases had the authority to terminate the original mining lease granted in 1919 under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1952
Whether a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is maintainable when it involves a disputed question of title to property
Whether the Patna High Court could restore possession to the petitioners by cancelling the appellant's lease in a writ proceeding
holdings: Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1952 did not extinguish the original lessees' rights but made them lessees of the State; the Controller had no power to unilaterally terminate the lease before its term.

A writ petition under Article 226 is not maintainable if it requires determination of a disputed title, especially where possession is already with another party and adjudication would amount to a declaration of title.

Where a serious dispute over title and possession exists, the proper remedy is a civil suit; the High Court cannot dispossess a party in possession via writ without conclusive proof of the petitioners' title.
provisions: Mining Lease (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, Rule 6
doctrines: Maintainability of writ under Article 226 in cases involving title disputes
Doctrine of separation of remedies: writ vs. civil suit for title determination
Principle of possession as a factor in equitable relief under writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: Laxmi & Co. appealed against Dr. Anant R. Deshpande and others regarding the validity of an ex-parte decree and execution of a warrant of possession, and whether a preliminary issue under Section 42A of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act should have been framed in the absence of the defendant.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'appears' in Section 42A of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act 1882 requires personal or represented appearance of the defendant on the date of hearing for framing a preliminary issue on tenancy protection under the Bombay Rent Act
Whether the Small Cause Court is obligated to frame a preliminary issue on tenancy under Section 42A even if the defendant does not appear on the hearing date
holdings: The word 'appears' in Section 42A means appearance in person or through a representative at the appointed time; without such appearance, the court cannot frame a preliminary issue on tenancy protection under the Bombay Rent Act.
The Small Cause Court is not required to frame a preliminary issue under Section 42A if the occupant does not appear at the time appointed, as the statutory condition precedent is not satisfied.
provisions: Presidency Small Causes Courts Act 1882, Section 42A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses, Rates Control Act 1947
Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order 21 Rule 100
Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order 21 Rule 103
doctrines: Condition precedent to jurisdiction
Statutory interpretation of 'appearance'
Court's power to notice subsequent events to prevent injustice

card.dispute: The appellant claimed compensation for lands allegedly taken by the government in 1954 under the Indian Forest Act and later under the Land Acquisition Act, but from which it was excluded after partial withdrawal of acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the government took possession of the lands in 1953–1954 under the Indian Forest Act, leading to vesting of ownership.

Whether the government took possession under Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, resulting in automatic vesting of land in the government upon expiry of 15 days from the notice under Section 9(1).
Whether the expression 'whenever the appropriate Government so directs' in Section 17(1) refers to declaration of urgency or to the actual taking of possession.
holdings: There was no satisfactory evidence that the government took possession of the lands in 1953–1954 under the Indian Forest Act; hence, the High Court rightly declined to decide the issue under Article 226.
The government becomes owner only upon actual taking of possession under Section 16 or Section 17(1); there was no material showing such possession was taken under Section 17(1).

The phrase 'whenever the appropriate Government so directs' in Section 17(1) refers to the direction to take possession, not merely to the declaration of urgency; thus, possession does not vest automatically upon expiry of 15 days under Section 9(1) without such direction.
doctrines: Vesting of property in government only upon formal possession under Land Acquisition Act
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between notification and actual possession

card.dispute: The defendants appealed against the enforcement of an arbitration award that declared their personal liability to repay excess family funds and created a charge on their immovable property, challenging its admissibility due to non-registration and insufficient stamping.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award, which created a personal liability and a charge on immovable property, was compulsorily registrable under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act
Whether the unregistered award could be admitted in evidence to the extent it created a severable personal liability
Whether non-payment of proper stamp duty rendered the award inadmissible under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act
holdings: An arbitration award that creates a personal liability to repay money and separately imposes a charge on immovable property consists of two severable transactions; the personal liability part does not require registration and is enforceable independently.

An unregistered document can be admitted in evidence for a collateral purpose, such as proving a personal liability, even if it cannot affect immovable property or serve as evidence of a transaction affecting such property under Section 49 of the Registration Act.

An award not originally on stamp paper is admissible in evidence if a true copy is duly stamped and the requisite stamp duty and penalty are paid, satisfying the requirements of Section 35 of the Stamp Act.
doctrines: Severability of transactions in a single document
Collateral use exception under Section 49 of the Registration Act
Doctrine of substantial compliance with stamping requirements

card.dispute: The Nagpur Improvement Trust challenged the High Court's decision invalidating compensation awarded under the Nagpur Improvement Trust Act, 1936, on grounds of violation of Article 14 due to differential compensation compared to the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the Nagpur Improvement Trust Act, 1936, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by providing lower compensation than the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for similar land acquisitions.
Whether the classification of land acquisition under different statutes based on purpose justifies differential compensation.
holdings: A law that allows the State to acquire land under different statutes with significantly lower compensation for the same type of land violates Article 14 if no reasonable classification exists.
Differential compensation based solely on the acquiring statute or public purpose, without benefiting the affected landowners, constitutes impermissible discrimination under Article 14.
provisions: Nagpur Improvement Trust Act, 1936, Section 59 and Section 61
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Doctrine of reasonable classification
Prohibition of arbitrary state action in property acquisition

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, claiming they were denied an opportunity to object due to the vagueness of the public purpose stated in the notification.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, stating only 'planned development of the area' as the public purpose was sufficiently specific to enable affected persons to file objections under Section 5A.
Whether the absence of a definite scheme or master plan at the time of notification rendered the acquisition proceedings invalid.
holdings: A notification under Section 4 must specify the public purpose with sufficient clarity to enable landowners to effectively exercise their right to file objections under Section 5A.

The phrase 'planned development of the area' is too vague and indefinite to satisfy the requirements of Section 4, especially when no master plan was available or communicated to the landowners at the time.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Effective implementation of statutory rights
Void for vagueness

card.dispute: The widow and daughter of Chhangur Sahu challenged the probate of a will that excluded them, in favor of a relative appointed as executor.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were bound by the advocate's admission that the will was validly executed without their instructions.
Whether the High Court could grant probate solely based on signature comparison and without proper proof of due execution under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act.
holdings: An advocate's admission binding the parties is not valid unless it is made on clear instructions from the clients, especially when they are illiterate and the admission contradicts their initial stance.
Granting probate based solely on signature comparison, without examining attestation as required under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, amounts to a gross miscarriage of justice.
doctrines: Principle of binding effect of advocate's statements
Due execution of wills
Judicial duty to ensure fair trial in probate proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) challenged the inclusion of their land in a development scheme by the Improvement Trust, Amritsar, claiming exemption based on a supposed policy decision to exclude orchard land and alleging discrimination under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Improvement Trust could alter a sanctioned development scheme under Section 43 of the Punjab Towns Improvement Act, 1922 to exempt the appellants' land based on a subsequent policy decision by the State Government.
Whether the appellants had a right to claim exemption from land acquisition under the scheme independently of statutory provisions like Section 43 or Section 56.
Whether the exclusion of similarly situated orchard lands of others and inclusion of the appellants' land violated Article 14 of the Constitution.
holdings: Section 43 of the Punjab Towns Improvement Act, 1922 allows the Trust to alter a scheme between sanction and execution, but does not confer a right on landowners to demand such alteration based on a subsequent policy decision.

No statutory provision permits the modification of a sanctioned scheme through a later policy decision; all objections and exclusions must be addressed before final sanction under Chapter IV of the Act.

The appellants failed to make out a case of discrimination under Article 14, especially since the point was not properly raised in the High Court and no factual comparison was sufficiently established.
doctrines: Finality of statutory development schemes after sanction
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions (Section 43 and Section 56)
No enforceable right to alteration of scheme under Section 43 for private benefit
Non-justiciability of policy decisions post-sanction in absence of statutory authority
Doctrine of opportunity to object during scheme formulation

card.dispute: The appellants, acquitted by the trial court in a murder case, challenged the High Court's reversal of their acquittal and conviction, arguing that the prosecution case was tainted and the High Court erred in reassessing the evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reversing the trial court's acquittal and convicting the appellants despite the presumption of innocence and the trial court's reasonable judgment.
Whether delays in sending the occurrence report under Section 157 Cr.P.C. and alleged tampering with the inquest report and site plan vitiated the prosecution case.
holdings: An appellate court has full statutory power to reappreciate all evidence in an appeal against acquittal, even if the trial court's judgment appears reasonable, provided it considers the presumption of innocence and gives cogent reasons for reversing acquittal.

Minor procedural delays in sending the occurrence report under Section 157 Cr.P.C. or minor discrepancies in documents do not render the entire investigation tainted if the prosecution case remains trustworthy and the accused are not prejudiced.
doctrines: Reappreciation of evidence in appeals against acquittal
Presumption of innocence in appellate review
Principle of trustworthiness of prosecution evidence despite minor irregularities
Limited impact of procedural delay under Section 157 Cr.P.C. on fair trial

card.dispute: The plaintiff in a partition suit sought to withdraw the case after the defendant agreed to buy the plaintiff's share in a cinema property at court-ordered valuation; the dispute was whether the plaintiff could withdraw and file a fresh suit without defeating the defendant's statutory right to purchase.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff can withdraw a partition suit under Order 23 Rule 1 of the CPC after the defendant has invoked the right to purchase under Section 3 of the Partition Act.
Whether the defendant acquired a vested right or privilege under Section 3 of the Partition Act upon applying to buy the plaintiff's share at valuation.
Whether a formal application under Section 3 of the Partition Act is required or if a statement in the written statement suffices.
holdings: A plaintiff cannot withdraw a partition suit under Order 23 Rule 1 CPC once the defendant has exercised the statutory privilege under Section 3 of the Partition Act, as such withdrawal would defeat the defendant's legal advantage.

The defendant acquires a statutory privilege under Section 3 of the Partition Act upon applying to purchase the plaintiff's share at valuation, which the court is bound to honor, restricting the plaintiff's right to withdraw.
A formal application under Section 3 is not required; a clear expression in the written statement indicating willingness to buy at court-ordered valuation suffices to invoke the provision.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 23, Rule 1
doctrines: Dominus litis not absolute in partition suits
Statutory privilege under Section 3 of the Partition Act
Prevention of abuse of process by withdrawal to defeat statutory rights

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, being children of pre-deceased brothers of Shantiraja Kadamba, sued for possession of his immovable properties, challenging the validity of a Will allegedly executed by him in favor of the defendants, particularly his mistress and her son.
issues_decided: Whether the alleged Will dated 10-3-1958 was validly executed by Shantiraja Kadamba.
Whether the Will was forged or executed after the testator's death with the collusion of the defendants, scribe, and attesting witnesses.
Whether the dispositions in the Will were unnatural or unjust, raising suspicion about its validity.
Whether the evidence of handwriting experts could be relied upon to prove or disprove the genuineness of the signature on the Will.
holdings: A Will executed in private with secrecy and attested by disinterested witnesses can still be valid if the circumstances of execution are credible and supported by reliable evidence.
Suspicious circumstances surrounding a Will must be dispelled by satisfactory evidence, but the burden is not insurmountable if the attesting witnesses are credible and independent.
Dispositions in a Will favoring a long-time mistress and her son are not per se unnatural or unjust, especially when the testator had no legal heirs and had already provided for his daughters.

Handwriting expert evidence may be rejected if based on unproven specimens or if the expert lacks familiarity with the script; courts may rely on their own scrutiny when expert opinions are inconclusive.
doctrines: Presumption against forgery of Will if properly attested and supported by credible testimony
Principle of naturalness in testamentary dispositions
Requirement of proof of suspicious circumstances in Will cases
Judicial discretion in evaluating expert evidence on handwriting

card.dispute: The assessee firm disputed with the Income Tax Commissioner whether payments for a mining lease and prospecting licence were revenue or capital expenditures deductible for income tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the 1/20th portion of the lease payment for a previously worked mica mine constitutes revenue expenditure
Whether the fee paid for a prospecting licence is allowable as revenue expenditure
holdings: Expenditure to acquire a mining lease for extracting minerals still embedded in the land is capital in nature, as it secures an enduring right over land, even if prior work reduced extraction effort.
A prospecting licence fee is capital expenditure because it initiates a business and secures the right to explore and extract minerals, not to acquire stock-in-trade.
doctrines: Enduring benefit test for capital vs revenue expenditure
Distinction between acquisition of stock-in-trade and rights over land
Capital nature of expenditure for business initiation

card.dispute: The appellants, former residents of ancestral property sold to the State of Punjab, challenged the state's notice of eviction under the Punjab Public Premises and Land Act, claiming they were not in unauthorized occupation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were in unauthorized occupation of public premises under Section 3 of the Punjab Public Premises and Land Act, 1959
Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to issue an eviction notice under Section 4(1) of the Act
holdings: A person is in unauthorized occupation under Section 3(a) only if they entered possession of premises after they became public; prior possession of private ancestral property does not constitute unauthorized occupation.
The Collector lacked jurisdiction under Section 4(1) to issue an eviction notice because the appellants were not in unauthorized occupation of public premises under Section 3.
provisions: Punjab Public Premises and Land (Eviction and Rent Recovery) Act, 1959, Section 2(d)
Punjab Public Premises and Land (Eviction and Rent Recovery) Act, 1959, Section 3
Punjab Public Premises and Land (Eviction and Rent Recovery) Act, 1959, Section 4(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of unauthorized occupation requiring possession of public premises as a condition precedent
Jurisdictional limitation on administrative action based on statutory prerequisites

card.dispute: Reversioners challenged alienations of property by Hindu widows, including properties allegedly dedicated to charity, claiming entitlement as 'huqdars.
issues_decided: Whether reversioners are precluded from challenging alienations made by a Hindu widow with their assent or as part of a family arrangement
Whether the dedication of properties for charity under Ex. A-2 was complete or partial
Whether the plaintiffs could claim the properties as trustees or reversioners after prior transactions
holdings: A reversioner who assented to or benefited from a widow's alienation cannot later repudiate it and sue for possession; estoppel and election apply upon attaining majority.
A family arrangement, even without formal conflict, is valid if made bona fide to preserve family harmony and the terms are fair.
A dedication for charity is only complete if substantially all income is used for charity; if surplus is left for family use, it creates a charge, not a trust, and the property remains private.
provisions: Hindu Widows' Estates under customary Hindu law
doctrines: Doctrine of election
Doctrine of estoppel against reversioners
Family arrangement
Complete vs partial dedication to charity

card.dispute: The State of Jammu and Kashmir sought to demolish structures occupied by Haji Wali Mohammed and others, who challenged the legality of the notices and demolition process.
issues_decided: Whether the notices under Section 129 of the Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Act were validly served in compliance with Section 239 of the Act.
Whether the 24-hour time given to demolish the structures amounted to a reasonable time under Section 238 of the Act.
Whether the demolition action was illegal due to non-compliance with statutory procedural requirements.
holdings: Service of notice by mere affixation without proof of attempted personal service or affidavit by the process server does not comply with Section 239, rendering the notice invalid.
A 24-hour period to dismantle structures, especially where business was being carried on and no time was given for repairs, is unreasonably short and violates Section 238 requiring reasonable time.
Non-compliance with Sections 238 and 239 renders the entire demolition action illegal and contrary to law, invalidating the municipality's actions.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Act, Samvat 2008, Section 129
Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Act, Samvat 2008, Section 238
Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Act, Samvat 2008, Section 239
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 5, Rule 9
doctrines: Procedural fairness in administrative action
Reasonable opportunity to comply with statutory notices
Strict compliance with statutory service requirements

card.dispute: The State of Assam challenged the High Court's decision to quash the deemed refusal of a mining lease renewal applied for by Om Prakash Mohta and others, claiming the relevant rules were ultra vires and unreasonable.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 24(3) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, which deems an application for renewal of a mining lease to have been refused if not disposed of within 90 days, is ultra vires Section 8 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether the explanation to Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, which deems non-disposal of an application as a refusal for revision purposes, is unreasonable and contrary to the parent Act
Whether the deemed refusal under the Rules violates principles of natural justice or constitutional rights
holdings: Rule 24(3) is valid and intra vires Section 8 of the Act as it falls within the rule-making powers conferred on the government and does not infringe any statutory or constitutional rights.
The explanation to Rule 54 is reasonable and serves the dual purpose of fixing a deemed date of refusal and enabling timely revision petitions; it is not ultra vires the Act.
The deemed refusal does not violate natural justice because the Rules provide a corrective mechanism through revision before the Central Government, which can grant relief if warranted.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 8
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 13(g)
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, Rule 54 with Explanation
doctrines: Deemed refusal doctrine
Rule of statutory interpretation (reasonableness of delegated legislation)
Principle of legislative policy in administrative delay
Quasi-judicial power of revision

card.dispute: The Special Land Acquisition Officer challenged the award of compensation to respondents for government-granted lands acquired for a public project, despite a no-compensation clause in the original grant.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents were entitled to compensation for the acquired lands despite a condition in the grant exempting them from receiving compensation.
Whether the Land Acquisition Officer properly valued the rights of the respondents in the acquired lands.
holdings: Respondents are entitled to compensation for their rights in the acquired lands despite the no-compensation clause, as per precedent set in Seshagiri Rao's case.
The Land Acquisition Officer's valuation of the respondents' rights stands, and the appellant is bound by it, even if no formal award was made.
doctrines: Binding effect of valuation by Land Acquisition Officer
Precedent doctrine (stare decisis) based on Seshagiri Rao's case

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and others fought with Rajasaheb Chandanmull Indrakumar (P) over possession of the virgin area of the Ib River Colliery, which the State had taken over in 1970, while the petitioner claimed rightful possession under an old lease and its renewal.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner company had a legal right to claim possession of the virgin area of the colliery after the original lease expired in 1947.
Whether the High Court could grant relief under Article 226 without determining the existence of a legal right in the petitioner.
Whether the statutory regime under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Acts of 1948 and 1957 barred unauthorized mining operations post-1947.
Whether acceptance of rent by government officers conferred legitimacy on the petitioner's continued possession.
holdings: The High Court erred in granting possession without first determining whether the petitioner had a legal right to the virgin area, especially after the 1917 lease expired in 1947.
Relief under Article 226 requires the petitioner to demonstrate a legal right; mere possession does not entitle one to continue acts forbidden by law.
Mining operations after 1947 required compliance with the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 and 1957; no valid lease existed post-1947.
Acceptance of rent by subordinate officers did not validate possession or create a lease where none existed under statute.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 4, Section 13, Rule 26, Rule 27, Rule 28-A
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4, Section 10
doctrines: Doctrine of legal right in writ jurisdiction
Statutory bar on unauthorized mining leases
Principle of possession not equating to legal title
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct not applicable in absence of legal lease

card.dispute: The dispute was between T.D. Gopalan and the Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments over whether a temple (mandapam) constructed by Gopalan's family was a private or public temple under the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act.
issues_decided: Whether the mandapam was a public temple within the meaning of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927.
Whether user by the public and receipt of public contributions are sufficient to convert a privately established temple into a public temple.
holdings: A temple is public only if it is dedicated or used as of right by the Hindu community or a section thereof; mere permission for public worship does not make a temple public.

The origin, management, and funding of a temple are crucial in determining its character; absence of endowed property and continuous family control indicate a private temple despite public worship or offerings.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, Section 9(12)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 6(20)
doctrines: Presumption against dedication to public
Totality of circumstances test for determining temple character
Public user not equivalent to dedication as of right

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming it was undervalued by the authorities.
issues_decided: What is the proper method for determining the market value of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether potential value of the land can be added separately to the market value as a distinct component?
Whether compensation for severance must be granted when part of a holding is acquired, despite the remaining portion having an entrance?
holdings: Market value must be determined by objective standards, considering comparable sales, expert opinion, and rental capitalization, with due regard to the land’s potential value at the time of notification under Section 4.
Potential value is inherently part of market value and cannot be awarded as a separate additional component like a 10% uplift.
Severance compensation is justified when acquisition diminishes the utility or value of the remaining land, and a mere entrance does not negate this entitlement.
doctrines: Objective standard for market value
Inclusion of potential value in market value
Principle of severance compensation

card.dispute: The Union of India contested whether interest under Section 4(3) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, was payable only on the market value of acquired land or also on the additional 15% solatium awarded under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether interest under Section 4(3) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, is payable on the market value of the land alone or also on the 15% solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the term 'market value' in Section 4(3) of the 1967 Act includes the 15% solatium amount.
holdings: Interest under Section 4(3) of the 1967 Act is payable only on the market value of the land as determined under Section 23(1) of the 1894 Act, not on the additional 15% solatium.
The terms 'market value' and 'compensation' are distinct; 'market value' does not include the 15% solatium, which is a separate component of compensation for compulsory acquisition.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between market value and compensation in land acquisition law

card.dispute: The defendants, who were tenants, entered into an agreement to purchase the property from the plaintiff but failed to pay the instalments; the plaintiff sued for possession after the agreement was cancelled due to default.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement for sale was obtained by undue influence or coercion
Whether the agreement stood automatically cancelled upon default without notice
Whether the defendants reverted to their status as tenants entitled to protection under tenancy law after cancellation of the agreement
holdings: The agreement was not obtained by undue influence or coercion; the courts found no evidence to support such a claim.
The agreement stood automatically cancelled upon default of the first instalment; no notice was required for cancellation as none of the instalments were paid.
The landlord-tenant relationship ended upon the agreement; the defendants did not revert to tenancy status and could not claim protection under tenancy laws after the agreement's cancellation.
doctrines: Automatic cancellation of agreement upon default
Doctrine of forfeiture of payments and possession upon breach
Principle that a party cannot benefit from their own wrong

card.dispute: The landlord, Bai Hiragauri, sued to evict tenants Abdul Kadar Mamadji and Abdul Rahim Musaji for non-payment of rent; the tenants were upheld by the High Court, leading to appeals by the landlord.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain revision applications under Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rent Act as amended in 1965, when the original suits were filed before the amendment.
Whether the concurrent findings of the lower courts that the tenancy fell under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rent Act could be disturbed in revision under Section 115 CPC.
holdings: The High Court could not apply the amended Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rent Act to revision applications arising from suits filed before the amendment, as the appellate decrees had become final under the unamended law.

An erroneous interpretation of a statutory provision by a court does not amount to illegal exercise of jurisdiction or material irregularity, and thus cannot be grounds for interference under Section 115 CPC.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of appellate decrees
Doctrine of no interference in revision without jurisdictional error

card.dispute: Brij Gopal and others sought to enforce an arbitration award for possession of a property against Kishan Gopal, who resisted on grounds of limitation and finality after prior proceedings had dismissed similar claims.
issues_decided: Whether an application by arbitrators under Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 is barred by limitation
Whether the High Court could exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to interfere with the trial court's dismissal of the application
Whether the arbitrators retained jurisdiction to file the award afresh after 14 years
holdings: No period of limitation is prescribed under Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 for filing an award by arbitrators, and Article 181 of the Limitation Act does not apply to such applications.
The High Court, in revision, may refuse relief on grounds of finality and equitable considerations, especially where a prior application to make the award a rule of court was already dismissed.
Arbitrators become functus officio upon delivery of the award and cannot reassert jurisdiction to file the award afresh after a long delay, absent statutory authority.
doctrines: Functus officio
Finality of proceedings
Discretionary nature of revisional jurisdiction
Substantial failure of justice as a threshold for revision

card.dispute: The owner of a shop sought ejectment of the tenant and his sons, claiming the tenant had sub-let part of the shop to them, violating the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had sub-let or parted with possession of part of the shop to his sons.
Whether the sons were in permissive possession as a family arrangement, despite no such plea being raised earlier.
Whether a new factual plea could be allowed for the first time in a special leave petition.
holdings: A tenant who allows family members exclusive possession and control of part of a rented premises is deemed to have parted with possession under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
A plea of permissive occupation by family members not raised in the written statement cannot be considered for the first time in a special leave petition.
Courts will not allow new factual pleas at a late stage if they prejudice the other party and were not part of earlier proceedings.
doctrines: Plea estoppel
Exclusive possession implying transfer of tenancy
Procedural fairness and prejudice in raising new pleas

card.dispute: Datar Singh appealed his conviction for murdering his father and illegal possession of a firearm, challenging the reliability of evidence and claiming a miscarriage of justice.
issues_decided: Whether concurrent findings of fact by lower courts can be overturned in the absence of exceptional circumstances indicating a serious miscarriage of justice.
Whether the prosecution's case based on two eyewitnesses and circumstantial evidence was reliable and sufficient to sustain a conviction for murder.
Whether the non-production of certain witnesses and the appellant's delay in surrendering could be used to infer guilt.
Whether the defense alibi and discrepancies in forensic and testimonial evidence warranted giving the appellant the benefit of doubt.
