provisions: Section 100(1)(c) of the Civil Procedure Code
doctrines: Adverse possession
Amendment of pleadings in changed circumstances
Reversionary rights upon termination of a widow's estate
Complete justice doctrine

card.dispute: The adopted son of a deceased coparcener claimed a share in the joint family property, challenging an earlier partition and gift, while the other coparceners resisted on the ground that the partition and transfer had already extinguished his rights.
issues_decided: Whether a later adoption by a widow can invalidate an earlier partition of joint family property under Mitakshara law?
Whether a gift or alienation made before adoption binds the adopted son?
What share, if any, is the adopted son entitled to when a partition has already taken place?
holdings: An adopted son can claim a share in the undivided coparcenary property as if he were born at the time of his adoptive father’s death, even after a prior partition.
A valid partition and lawful alienation (by gift, sale, or will) made before adoption are binding and cannot be challenged by the adopted son.

The adopted son is entitled to a fair and equitable share from the property available at the time of adoption, but not from already alienated portions; justice requires balancing equities in re-opening partition.
provisions: Hindu Law (prior to Hindu Succession Act, 1956)
doctrines: Doctrine of relation back in adoption
Equitable re-opening of partition
Lawful alienation binding on adopted son
Limited power of widow to alienate property

card.dispute: The children of the testator challenged the validity of a will that bequeathed the entire property to his second wife, alleging undue influence and suspicious circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether a presumption of undue influence arises from the relationship between the testator and his second wife who was the sole beneficiary of the will.
Whether the will was executed under suspicious circumstances, including alteration of date and delayed attestation.
Whether the burden of proof for proving undue influence lies on the propounder of the will or the contestants.
holdings: No presumption of undue influence can be drawn solely from the relationship between a testator and his spouse; such a plea must be specifically proven as a fact.

The alteration of the will's date from 7th to 8th February, if any, was made by the testator himself and does not invalidate the will, especially since it was executed after marriage and supported by credible witness testimony.
The burden of proving undue influence lies on the party alleging it, and mere suspicion or strained family relations are insufficient to invalidate a will that meets all legal formalities.
doctrines: Presumption of undue influence
Burden of proof in will disputes
Sound disposing mind in testamentary capacity

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, descendants of Laxman Govind Mungi, claimed that the suit property was ancestral property belonging to Laxman and that its alienation by Krishnaji and Dattatraya was invalid; the defendant Usman Gani contested this, asserting the property belonged to Jankibai and was validly sold.
issues_decided: Whether the suit property was ancestral property of Laxman Govind Mungi or self-acquired property of Jankibai.
Whether the alienation of the property by Krishnaji and Dattatraya was binding on the plaintiffs.
Whether the first defendant had notice that the property was ancestral in the hands of Krishnaji and Dattatraya from their father.
holdings: The suit property was not ancestral property of Laxman Govind Mungi but belonged to Jankibai, as the sale deed was in her name and mutation records supported her ownership.
The alienation by Krishnaji and Dattatraya was valid as they were absolute owners, and the plaintiffs had no enforceable interest in the property.

The statement in an unregistered receipt referring to 'ancestral ownership' did not prove paternal ancestry, and no adverse inference could be drawn against the defendant who understood it as maternal ancestral property.
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Doctrine of adverse inference
Principle of reasonable probabilities in absence of direct evidence

card.dispute: The respondents sued to set aside a gift deed (Hiba-bil-Ewaz) executed by their predecessor, alleging it was obtained by fraud, misrepresentation, and undue influence; the appellants challenged the High Court's interference in the second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship between the donor and donee was such that the latter was in a position to dominate the will of the former under Section 16 of the Contract Act
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact in second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Whether the burden of proof shifted to the donee to disprove undue influence once an intimate relationship was alleged
holdings: A mere intimate or fiduciary relationship, such as that of father and son, does not by itself establish that one party was in a position to dominate the will of the other; more must be shown to prove 'undue influence'.
The High Court cannot interfere in second appeal unless there is a substantial question of law; erroneous findings of fact, without legal error, are not grounds for reversal under Section 100 CPC.

The burden of proving absence of undue influence shifts to the dominant party only if the transaction is unconscionable and the relationship enables domination; where domination is not proved, the burden does not shift.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rules 2 and 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Sections 100, 101, and 103
doctrines: Undue influence under Section 16 of the Contract Act
Concurrent finding of fact rule in second appeal
Order of inquiry in undue influence cases: relationship, domination, unconscionability, burden of proof

card.dispute: The appellant tenant claimed continued possession of acquired land after the government allegedly took symbolic possession, while the respondents argued the acquisition was complete and valid.
issues_decided: Whether taking of possession under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires actual physical possession on the spot or if symbolic possession suffices.
Whether an occupant can resume possession after the government has taken possession under the Act.
Whether the government can withdraw from acquisition under Section 48(1) after possession has been taken.
holdings: Taking possession under the Land Acquisition Act requires actual physical possession on the spot; symbolic or paper possession is not sufficient.
Once the government validly takes possession, the land vests absolutely in it, and any resumption of possession by the occupant does not nullify the vesting.
The government cannot withdraw from acquisition under Section 48(1) in respect of land already taken into possession.
doctrines: Vesting of property upon possession
Actual possession vs. symbolic possession
Irreversibility of acquisition after possession

card.dispute: Anant Mills Co. Ltd. challenged the constitutional validity of property tax and conservancy tax provisions, and its liability to pay tax for underground electric supply lines laid on municipal land.
issues_decided: Whether the company occupying underground strata for electric supply lines is liable to property tax as an 'actual occupier' under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act
Whether the proviso to Section 129(b) of the Act involves excessive delegation of legislative power
Whether the requirement of depositing disputed tax as a condition for appeal violates Article 14 or nullifies the right of appeal
Whether 'land' under Entry 49, List II, Schedule VII of the Constitution includes underground strata
holdings: A company laying electric supply lines underground is an 'actual occupier' of the subsurface and liable to property tax, irrespective of ownership or formal agreement with the municipality.
The proviso to Section 129(b) does not suffer from excessive delegation as it provides sufficient guidance for rate fixation by the Corporation.
The deposit requirement under Section 406(2)(e) and Rule 42 does not nullify the right of appeal, as appellate authorities can relieve against undue hardship.
The term 'land' in Entry 49, List II includes underground strata, making such areas subject to municipal taxation when occupied.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Entry 49, List II, Schedule VII
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 129
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 137
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 139(1)(a)
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 406(2)(e)
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Rule 42, Schedule A
doctrines: Test of rateability based on de facto occupation, not legal title
Doctrine of permissible classification under Article 14
Doctrine against excessive delegation of legislative power
Presumption in favor of constitutionality of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The developer (D.L.F. Housing) fought with the Delhi Municipal Corporation over whether it was obligated to transfer land set aside for public utility services (like schools and hospitals) in its colonies free of cost or on a 'no-profit no-loss' basis.
issues_decided: Whether the land set aside for public utility services under the development sanctions vested automatically and free of cost in the Municipal Corporation
Whether the agreements forming part of the sanction orders created a fiduciary or trust relationship over the land
Whether the writ petition was maintainable given the absence of key documentary evidence
holdings: The writ court could not conclusively determine the nature of the parties' rights due to lack of essential documents and disputed facts.
The High Court erred in deciding complex factual and legal issues without a proper evidentiary basis, especially regarding the existence of a trust or automatic vesting.
The proper remedy for the parties lies in a regular civil suit, not a writ petition, due to the disputed nature of facts and documents.
provisions: Delhi (Control of Building Operations) Act, 1955, Section 19
Delhi (Control of Building Operations) Regulations, Regulation 5(3)
doctrines: Proper forum doctrine (writ vs. suit)
Doctrine of equitable estoppel
Trust doctrine (requirement of settlor, trustee, and beneficiary)

card.dispute: The Dollar Company, Madras, challenged the compensation awarded for its land acquired by the State, seeking higher compensation than the High Court's award of Rs. 1800 per ground.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in determining the market value of the acquired land at Rs. 1800 per ground.
Whether the price paid by the appellant for the same land 10 months prior is relevant to determining market value.
Whether the High Court wrongly relied on sales of distant or dissimilar properties in assessing compensation.
holdings: An appellate court interferes with a High Court’s valuation only if there is an error in principle or a failure to consider material evidence, not merely because a different conclusion might be reached.
The price paid by the owner for the same property shortly before acquisition is strong evidence of market value, unless special circumstances affecting the sale are proven.
Sales of nearby comparable lands are more relevant than those of distant or dissimilar properties, and the High Court’s reliance on local conditions and industrial potential supports its valuation.
doctrines: Market value determination in compulsory acquisition
Principle of judicial restraint in appellate review of factual findings
Relevance of recent sale price as evidence of market value

card.dispute: Gurucharan Singh (plaintiff) fought Kamla Singh and others over ownership and possession of certain lands after the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, vested estate interests in the State, with conflicting claims based on prior gifts, partition, and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff had 'khas possession' under Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, so as to retain his interest after vesting under Section 4?
Whether the possession of a trespasser can be treated as 'khas possession' of the owner?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to mesne profits and possession despite loss of title under the Act?
holdings: A person does not retain an interest under Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act unless they were in actual or constructive 'khas possession' at the time of vesting; mere title without possession is insufficient.
The possession of a trespasser, even if claimed adversely, cannot be equated with 'khas possession' of the owner, and does not protect the owner’s interest under Section 6.

The plaintiff is entitled to mesne profits up to the date of vesting and a decree for possession of certain plots not possessed by the defendants, but such relief does not override the State’s superior title post-vesting.
doctrines: Khas possession under land reform laws requires actual or constructive exclusive possession
Adverse possession by a trespasser does not benefit the true owner under land reform vesting
State's vesting of land extinguishes private title unless protected by statutory exception

card.dispute: The owner of a cinema theatre sued for eviction of the lessee, claiming the lease was not protected under rent control law as it was not merely for 'accommodation'.
issues_decided: Whether the composite lease of a cinema theatre with building, fittings, and equipment falls within the definition of 'accommodation' under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947
Whether the splitting of rent into components for building, furniture, and equipment is legally valid for determining applicability of rent control
holdings: A lease of a cinema theatre with equipment and fittings does not constitute 'accommodation' under the Act if the dominant purpose is running a business, not merely using the building.
Splitting rent into notional components for building, furniture, and equipment is artificial and cannot bring a composite business lease within rent control protection.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Dominant purpose test
Literal interpretation of statutory definitions
Artificial bifurcation of lease terms

card.dispute: Gorelal Dubey and another applicant contested over the grant of a lease for limestone mining, with one seeking a quarry lease as a minor mineral and the other a mining lease as a major mineral.
issues_decided: Whether the application by Gorelal Dubey was for a minor mineral (limestone for burning for building material) or a major mineral
Whether the State Government could lawfully grant a quarry lease for limestone as a minor mineral without considering a competing application for a mining lease as a major mineral
Whether the quality of limestone in the area should determine the type of lease granted
holdings: An application for a quarry lease for 'limestone for burning purposes' with intent for minor minerals is to be treated as an application for a minor mineral, based on the totality of facts including the description in the application.
The State Government must consider both competing applications for minor and major mineral leases together and cannot ignore one in favor of the other without assessing the limestone quality.
The classification of limestone as a minor or major mineral depends on its quality and intended use; the grant of lease must align with the predominant quality of limestone in the area.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(a) and 3(e)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
doctrines: Totality of facts doctrine in interpreting mineral lease applications
Doctrine of proper classification of minerals based on quality and end-use
Principle of fair consideration of competing mineral lease applications

card.dispute: The Government of Andhra Pradesh and a Gram Panchayat fought with Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd over the legality of a house tax and a permission fee levied on factory and other buildings constructed without prior approval.
issues_decided: Whether the buildings constructed by the respondent fall within the definition of 'house' for the purpose of house tax under the Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964
Whether the Gram Panchayat has legislative competence to levy house tax on factory buildings
Whether the 'permission fee' imposed by the Gram Panchayat is a valid fee or an illegal tax
Whether the legislature's retrospective amendment of the definition of 'house' to include 'factory' encroaches upon judicial functions
holdings: The State legislature has the competence under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to levy house tax on buildings occupied by a factory, even if the factory includes machinery and furniture, as the tax is on the building and not the industrial unit as a whole.
The definition of 'house' can validly include 'factory' through retrospective amendment, and such legislative action does not violate separation of powers or judicial functions.
A fee must have a quid pro quo; the permission fee lacks correlation between the amount charged and services rendered, and hence cannot be sustained as a valid fee.

The permission fee, though labeled a fee, is not a tax on buildings because it is levied at the time of application for permission regardless of whether construction occurs, and thus fails both as a fee and a tax.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 36
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 69
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 125(1)
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 131(2)
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 217(2)(xvi)
doctrines: Quid pro quo for fees
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Distinction between tax and fee
Broad and liberal construction of legislative entries

card.dispute: Godavari Sugar Mills and others challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961, particularly concerning the retention of acquired agricultural land by the State Farming Corporation instead of distributing it to landless peasants.
issues_decided: Whether the amendments to the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961, including insertion of Section 28-IAA, are protected under Article 31A of the Constitution
Whether the provision retaining surplus land with the State Farming Corporation constitutes a measure of agrarian reform
Whether the impugned provisions violate the principle of equality under Article 14
Whether the petitioners had locus standi to challenge the acquisition after vesting of land in the State
holdings: Amendments to the 1961 Act, including Section 28-IAA, are protected under Article 31A as part of a general scheme of agrarian reform aimed at preventing concentration of land and ensuring efficient agricultural use.

Retention of surplus land with the State Farming Corporation for continued cultivation is a valid component of agrarian reform, especially to prevent fragmentation and ensure steady raw material supply to industries.
The impugned provisions do not violate Article 14 as they form part of a reasonable classification within a comprehensive agrarian reform policy.
It is not necessary to decide on locus standi since the constitutional challenge fails on merits due to protection under Article 31A.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961
doctrines: Agrarian reform doctrine
Doctrine of reasonable classification
Doctrine of severability
Doctrine of constitutional protection under Article 31A
Doctrine of implied repeal and amendment

card.dispute: The landlords challenged the tenant's status as a thika tenant under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, seeking eviction on grounds that structures were erected without permission and the land was used for a workshop beyond the permitted garage use.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant qualifies as a thika tenant under Section 2(5) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, despite erecting structures without the landlord's permission?
Whether the use of the premises for a workshop for lorry maintenance violates the tenancy condition restricting use to garage purposes?
Whether the Transfer of Property Act, particularly Section 108(o), overrides the provisions of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act in restricting structural alterations or use?
holdings: A tenant who erects a structure for business purposes on leased land qualifies as a thika tenant under Section 2(5) even without the landlord's prior permission, as the Act does not require such consent.
Using the premises for a workshop to maintain lorries does not violate the lease condition of 'garage use', as garage inherently includes activities related to housing and tending motor vehicles.

Beneficial legislation like the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act must be interpreted liberally in favor of tenants, and restrictions not expressly stated cannot be judicially implied from the Transfer of Property Act.
doctrines: Principle of beneficial interpretation of tenant-protective legislation
Statutory interpretation: no implied conditions in absence of express language
Harmonization of special and general laws: special statute (Thika Tenancy Act) prevails over general law (Transfer of Property Act)

card.dispute: Udasi sect members challenged the inclusion of their places of worship in the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, arguing it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 26.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(4) of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, which makes notifications declaring a place as a Sikh Gurdwara conclusive, violates Article 19(1)(f) and Article 26 of the Constitution?
Whether the appellants had locus standi to challenge the notifications under Article 226?
Whether the provisions of Sections 5, 7, and 8 of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, are unconstitutional when applied to properties not in Schedule I?
holdings: Section 3(4) does not violate Articles 19(1)(f) and 26 if interpreted to allow claims over physical properties without using the term 'Gurdwara', preserving the right to contest ownership before the Tribunal.
The appellants had locus standi to file writ petitions as they were in possession of the disputed properties and had pending claims before the Tribunal.

The challenged provisions are not unconstitutional as applied to properties notified under Section 7, where no inclusion in Schedule I occurred and no rights under Articles 19(1)(f) or 26 were infringed.
doctrines: Presumption of constitutionality
Stare decisis
Locus standi in writ petitions
Harmonious construction to preserve constitutional validity

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, arguing it was not for a public purpose and that the process violated their rights.
issues_decided: Whether the execution of the Interim General Plan for Greater Delhi constitutes a public purpose under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act
Whether the notification under Section 4 was invalid due to a collateral purpose of 'freezing' land
Whether the appellants were denied a fair opportunity of being heard under Section 5A of the Act
holdings: The execution of the Interim General Plan for Greater Delhi is a public purpose as it aims to prevent haphazard development and ensure planned urban growth.
The incidental effect of 'freezing' land values due to a Section 4 notification does not invalidate the acquisition, as this is an inherent consequence of the statutory process.
The appellants were not denied a hearing under Section 5A, as the Collector considered objections and there is no evidence that a representative appeared on their behalf.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Principle of audi alteram partem

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued former tenants for rent and possession, lost on tenancy grounds, then filed a second suit claiming title and possession, which defendants argued was barred by res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the second suit was barred by res judicata due to the decision in the first suit.
Whether the finding of adverse possession by the trial court in the first suit created finality for res judicata purposes.
Whether the dismissal of the appeal against minors on limitation affected the finality of the adverse possession finding.
holdings: A second suit is not barred by res judicata if the matter in issue was not finally decided in the earlier suit.
A finding by a trial court is not final for res judicata if the appellate court dismisses the appeal on other grounds without affirming the finding.
The final decision in the first suit was limited to the absence of landlord-tenant relationship, leaving title and adverse possession open for determination in a subsequent suit.
doctrines: Res judicata
Finality of decision
Constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of a Parliamentary Validation Act that sought to retrospectively validate state legislation and rules relating to mineral leases, which had been previously struck down for lack of legislative competence and ultra vires delegation.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament could retrospectively validate state laws and delegated rules that were declared unconstitutional for want of legislative competence and excessive delegation?

Whether Section 2 of the Validation Act effectively conferred power to validate Rule 20(2) of the Bihar Minor Minerals Concession Rules, 1964, and the second proviso to Section 10(2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950?
Whether retrospective validation of void administrative actions and legislation is permissible under the Constitution?
holdings: Parliament has the power to retrospectively validate laws and actions that were void due to lack of legislative competence or defective delegation, provided the validation does not violate any constitutional limitation.

Section 2 of the Validation Act, along with its Schedule, effectively validated the impugned state legislation and rules by treating them as if enacted by Parliament, despite their earlier invalidity.
Retrospective validation of actions taken under invalid laws is constitutionally permissible, and infirmities in drafting do not defeat the clear legislative intent to validate such actions.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Item 54
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Item 23
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
Bihar Minor Minerals Concession Rules, 1964, Rule 20(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of Retrospective Validation
Doctrine of Delegated Legislation
Legislation by Incorporation
Doctrine of Parliamentary Competence

card.dispute: An advocate was accused by a client of taking money to file a civil suit but failing to do so and instead providing a fictitious suit number, leading to disciplinary action and disbarment.
issues_decided: Whether the advocate committed gross professional misconduct by accepting money but not filing the suit and giving a false suit number.
Whether the evidence presented by the complainant was sufficient to justify disbarment of the advocate.
Whether the disciplinary committee was biased due to the advocate's past complaints and misconducts.
holdings: The court held that while the advocate's conduct was questionable, the complainant's evidence was not entirely truthful or reliable, and thus did not conclusively prove professional misconduct.
The court held that in cases involving disbarment, the evidence must leave no reasonable doubt about guilt, and here, the standard was not met.
The court held that the disciplinary committee was likely influenced by the advocate’s past disciplinary issues, leading to prejudice and denial of the benefit of doubt.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in professional misconduct cases
Standard of proof in disciplinary proceedings against advocates
Judicial review of Bar Council disciplinary decisions

card.dispute: The plaintiff Suraj Bhan claimed sole ownership of certain shops and houses against his uncle and cousins, who contested the validity and terms of prior partitions.
issues_decided: Whether the document Ex. 'Y' dated February 15, 1950, being an unregistered partition deed, is inadmissible in evidence and whether it effected the partition of the shops.
Whether the partition under Ex. 'Y' is binding on defendant 1 (Munna Lal) despite his non-signature.
Whether the shops were purchased from partnership funds and thus entitled each of four partners to a one-fourth share, despite not being pleaded in the written statement.
holdings: A document recording a partition effected by a Punch (arbitrator by mutual consent) is admissible as a memorandum of a past event even if unregistered, as no formal arbitration proceedings were intended.
A partition effected by a Punch is binding on all parties even if one party did not sign the memorandum, especially where subsequent conduct shows acceptance and separate enjoyment of property.

A contention that property was purchased from partnership funds and should be shared equally cannot be raised for the first time in appeal if not pleaded in the written statement or raised as an issue in the trial court.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Sections 107 and 145
Indian Registration Act, 1908 (implied by challenge to admissibility of unregistered document)
doctrines: Memorandum of partition as admissible evidence
Binding effect of partition by Punch or family arbitrator
Principle of constructive res judicata and issue estoppel
Pleadings estoppel: new case not allowed in appeal

card.dispute: The tenant of Plot No. 428 challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification that dispensed with inquiry under Section 5A for multiple plots, including Plot No. 436 which had a pucca construction and allegedly did not qualify for urgent acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, a tenant of one plot, could challenge the entire acquisition notification on grounds that another plot (No. 436) did not qualify for urgent acquisition under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act
Who is entitled to object under Section 5A when land is notified under Section 4(1)—any person in the locality or only those interested in the specific land proposed for acquisition?
Whether a notification under Section 17(4) dispensing with inquiry under Section 5A is invalid if part of the notified land does not qualify as arable or waste land under Section 17(1)
holdings: The appellant, being interested only in Plot No. 428 (which was arable and waste land), could not challenge the notification based on irregularities concerning Plot No. 436, especially since its owner did not object and accepted compensation.

When specific survey numbers are mentioned in a notification under Section 4(1), only persons interested in those specific lands can object under Section 5A; the phrase 'any land in the locality' applies only when an entire locality is notified.

Section 17(4) allowing dispensation of inquiry under Section 5A applies where any part of the land qualifies as arable or waste under Section 17(1); the entire notification is not vitiated if another part may not qualify, especially when the affected party does not object.
doctrines: Standing to challenge administrative action
Doctrine of severability in administrative notifications
Interpretation of statutory language in context (Section 5A in light of Section 4(1))

card.dispute: The appellants and the complainant's party fought over possession of land, with the appellants claiming lawful possession after redeeming a mortgage, while the complainant attempted to forcibly take over the land and destroy the wheat crop.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were in 'settled possession' of the land entitling them to exercise private defence under Sections 99 to 102 IPC
Whether the force used by the appellants exceeded the limits permitted under the right of private defence
Whether the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on the appellants' side affects the reliability of its case
holdings: Possession by a trespasser can mature into settled possession if it is effective, undisturbed, and open, even without formal title; such possession entitles the holder to claim private defence.

The right of private defence allows for use of force proportionate to the threat, judged not by detached standards but by the immediacy of danger; force need not be weighed 'in golden scales' during an attack.
Where the prosecution fails to explain injuries on the accused, the court may either infer the accused acted in self-defence or find the prosecution case unproven beyond reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property and person
Settled possession as a basis for private defence
Proportionality in self-defence assessed contextually, not with detached objectivity
Benefit of doubt when prosecution fails to explain material facts

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession and rent arrears; the tenant challenged the court's order striking off defences for non-payment of rent deposits under the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the court had jurisdiction to strike off the tenant's defences for failing to deposit rent as ordered under Section 11(4) of the Bombay Rents Act.
Whether the use of the phrase 'defences to be struck off' instead of the statutory wording rendered the order illegal.
Whether the suit could be dismissed under Section 12(3)(h) of the Act after the tenant deposited the arrears.
holdings: The court has the power under Section 11(4) to effectively bar a tenant from defending a suit if they fail to deposit rent as ordered, even if the order uses the phrase 'defence struck off'.
The substance of the order matters more than the form; using 'defence struck off' does not invalidate the order if it aligns with the intent of Section 11(4).
Section 12(3)(h) does not apply where the tenant fails to deposit rent during the pendency of the suit; Section 11(4) governs such cases.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11(4)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(h)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XI, Rule 21
doctrines: Substance over form
Statutory interpretation
Jurisdiction of civil courts under rent control legislation

card.dispute: The heirs of Ram Saran Lal and Babu Ram fought with Narendra Nath Sharma over the partition of ancestral and jointly acquired properties, claiming the family remained joint, while the defendant asserted a prior partition and separate status.
issues_decided: Whether the family of Pandit Raman Lal remained joint after his death in 1900
Whether the properties in question were joint family or separate properties
Whether the plaintiffs' suit for partition was maintainable given the alleged long-standing separation
holdings: The family did not remain joint after Raman Lal's death; separation occurred before 1921, as evidenced by consistent separate financial dealings and admissions.
The properties were not joint family assets; the documentary evidence showed individual acquisitions and separate management by Bhagwati Prasad.
The suit for partition was not maintainable as the plaintiffs suppressed the fact of prior separation and failed to explain a decades-long delay in seeking partition.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory provisions, customary personal law)
Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution of India (jurisdictional basis for appeal)
doctrines: Admission against interest
Burden of proof in partition suits
Separation in status under Hindu joint family law
Relevance of long delay and suppression of material facts in equitable claims

card.dispute: The appellant, a landowner, claimed that income from his mango grove was agricultural and thus exempt from income tax, and sought refund of taxes paid over several years after a High Court ruling in his favour for one year, but faced rejection due to delay and finality of assessment orders.
issues_decided: Whether the assessment orders imposing tax on agricultural income were void ab initio due to lack of jurisdiction?
Whether the High Court's refusal to entertain a writ petition under Article 226 on grounds of delay and statutory finality was justified?
Whether the appellant could seek refund of taxes through writ jurisdiction despite non-exercise of statutory appeals?
Whether the court could grant relief based on 'justice' when the law was against the appellant?
holdings: Tax assessments on agricultural income, which falls outside Parliament's legislative competence, may be ultra vires and jurisdictionally invalid, but such orders are not automatically nullities if not challenged in time.
The High Court did not abuse its discretion in refusing the writ petition under Article 226 due to unexplained and inordinate delay by the appellant.
The appellant could not invoke writ jurisdiction for refund where statutory remedies existed and were not pursued, and no statutory duty was owed by the Central Board to order a refund.
Courts cannot override statutory finality and limitation to grant relief based on equitable justice; legality prevails over morality in clear statutory contexts.
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of assessment orders
Laches and delay in invoking writ jurisdiction
Ultra vires taxation and jurisdictional error
Limits of judicial activism in tax matters

card.dispute: The dispute was between coparceners of a Mitakshara joint family over whether a son's deed of release of his father's self-acquired property in 1944 severed his status, and whether he retained a share in the property after it was converted into joint family property in 1946.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of release executed by Arumugam in 1944 caused a severance of his joint family status?
Whether Arumugam remained a member of the joint family in 1946 when the father's self-acquired property was converted into joint family property?
Whether the widow of Arumugam was entitled to a 1/6th share in the joint family property after his death?
holdings: A deed of release by a son relinquishing claims to his father's self-acquired property does not sever joint family status if no joint family property existed at the time and the right to future joint property was not in contemplation.
A coparcener remains a member of the joint family despite temporary separation due to family discord, and does not lose his interest in subsequently created joint family property.
When a coparcener dies, his interest in joint family property devolves on his heirs, including his widow, who can claim partition.
doctrines: Severance of joint family status under Mitakshara law
Doctrine of coparcenary interest by birth
Conversion of self-acquired property into joint family property by act of father
Rule of interpretation of deeds of release restricting operation to rights in contemplation of parties

card.dispute: The minor coparceners and their brothers sued to reopen a 1940 partition of family property, alleging it was unjust and unfair, particularly regarding movable properties, to the detriment of the minors.
issues_decided: Whether a partition involving minor coparceners can be reopened if it is unjust and unfair to them
Whether the partition of movable and immovable properties can be treated separately if one is unjust
Whether the onus of proving fairness of a partition involving minors lies on the party supporting it
Whether monetary compensation can be awarded instead of re-partitioning properties
holdings: A partition involving minors is binding only if done in good faith and in their best interests; if proven unjust or unfair, it can be reopened regardless of time elapsed.
When movable and immovable property partitions are distinct, a court may uphold the fair transaction and reopen only the unfair one.
The burden of proving that a partition was just and fair lies on the party defending it when minors are adversely affected.
Where the share of minors is quantifiable and justice so requires, a court may award monetary compensation with interest instead of ordering a fresh partition.
doctrines: Protection of minors' interests in partition
Bona fide partition binding unless fraudulent or unfair
Separability of partition transactions
Equitable relief in lieu of partition

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of unauthorised subletting and acquisition of alternative accommodation, without serving a written notice to quit, leading to a dispute over whether such notice was mandatory under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a written notice under Section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act is necessary to determine a lease for breach of condition when the Act was made applicable to Delhi only in 1962
Whether the institution of eviction proceedings alone can constitute sufficient intimation of the landlord's intention to forfeit the lease
Whether the principles of justice, equity and good conscience require adherence to the formal requirement of written notice for forfeiture
holdings: A written notice under Section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act is not a requirement of justice, equity and good conscience, and thus not mandatory where the lease predates the Act's application to Delhi.

The institution of legal proceedings for eviction constitutes sufficient indication of the landlord’s intention to determine the lease, satisfying the requirement of forfeiture for breach of covenant.
Formalities like written notice are procedural and statutory, not equitable; the essence of equity lies in the clear communication of intention to forfeit, which can be achieved without writing.
doctrines: Justice, equity and good conscience
Forfeiture for breach of lease covenant
Statutory notice as procedural formality
Prospective application of law

card.dispute: Ramlal & Sons challenged the State of Rajasthan's order to vacate a mining area and sought refund of an allegedly illegal premium paid for a mining lease.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to a writ for grant or renewal of a mining lease after the purported lease period had expired and no formal lease was executed.
Whether the State Government could legally demand a premium for a mining lease without prior approval from the Central Government under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949.
holdings: No writ for grant or renewal of lease can be issued as the purported lease period had expired and no valid lease was ever executed.

The State Government could not lawfully collect a premium without prior Central Government approval under Rule 41(3) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, and must refund the illegally collected amount, deducting compensation already paid.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 5
doctrines: Rule of law and statutory compliance by administrative authorities
Illegality of imposing conditions not authorized by statutory rules
Principle of refund of money collected without legal authority

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the orders of land authorities that excluded certain land from the surplus pool and allotted it to Jagga and Meet Singh as tenants, claiming they were not tenants on the crucial date of 15.4.1953.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the factual findings of the Special Collector, Commissioner, and Financial Commissioner in writ proceedings under Article 226?

Whether the Special Collector committed an error of law or jurisdiction in recording the finding that Rattan Singh s/o Isher Singh was the tenant in 1952-53 despite a clerical error in the Girdwari entry?
Whether the evidence was improperly admitted or recorded without the appellants' knowledge, warranting issuance of a writ of certiorari?
holdings: The High Court cannot act as an appellate authority in writ proceedings; it can only correct jurisdictional or legal errors, not re-evaluate evidence or factual findings.

A finding based on appreciation of evidence, even if arguably erroneous, cannot be disturbed in certiorari unless it is unsupported by evidence or based on inadmissible evidence; here, the finding of tenancy was supported by record.
The admission of evidence, including the Patwari's examination, was not vitiated as it occurred in the presence of parties and with cross-examination, causing no prejudice to the appellants.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Rules, 1856, Rule 20
Article 226 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Limits of writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Supervisory jurisdiction vs. appellate jurisdiction
Error of law apparent on record doctrine
Concurrent findings of fact in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The decree-holder sought to attach and sell a flat owned by a cooperative housing society but occupied by the judgment-debtor; the judgment-debtor challenged the attachment and sale, claiming the right to occupy was not attachable.
issues_decided: Whether the right to occupy a flat in a cooperative housing society is a species of property liable to attachment and sale in execution of a decree?
Whether Sections 29, 31, 47, and 146(a) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, or the society's bye-laws, prohibit such attachment and sale?
Whether Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, permits the attachment of such a right to occupation?
holdings: The right to occupy a flat in a cooperative housing society is a species of property that is both attachable and saleable in execution of a decree.
Sections 29, 31, 47, and 146(a) of the Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, do not contain an express prohibition against attachment or sale of the right to occupation.
Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not limit attachment to specified properties and includes any saleable movable or immovable property, including the right to occupy a flat.
provisions: Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960, Sections 29, 31, 47, and 146(a)
Bye-Laws 9 and 71-D of the Paresh Cooperative Housing Society Limited
doctrines: Property attachable in execution includes all saleable rights, even if not explicitly listed in Section 60 CPC
Statutory interpretation requiring express legislative prohibition to bar attachment of property
Transferability of rights in cooperative housing flats under regulatory framework

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of land acquisition for the planned development of Delhi, arguing that compensation based on the section 4 notification date was unfair and that the public purpose was too vague.
issues_decided: Whether compensation linked to the date of notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act is constitutionally valid
Whether 'planned development of Delhi' constitutes a sufficiently definite public purpose for land acquisition
holdings: Linking compensation to the market value on the date of Section 4 notification is valid, especially where the Constitution presumes reasonableness for public purpose acquisitions and statutory safeguards like interest after three years and recognition of sanctioned improvements exist.

The 'planned development of Delhi' is a valid and sufficiently specific public purpose when acquiring large tracts of land, as it is impractical to specify individual uses for each plot in such a large-scale acquisition.
provisions: Land Acquisition Amendment and Validation Act, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Presumption of reasonableness in public purpose acquisitions
Doctrine of procedural reasonableness under Article 19(5)
Doctrine against dilatory litigation in land acquisition challenges

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a shop for personal use, but a tenant challenged the eviction, claiming prior allotment rights under rent control law, after a void compromise decree was concealed in the eviction application.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree, based on an agreement contrary to public policy, was void.
Whether the tenant's failure to disclose the compromise decree in his eviction application vitiated the allotment order.
Whether the District Magistrate could lawfully issue an eviction order under Section 7A despite the prior compromise decree.
holdings: A compromise decree based on an agreement that violates public policy or law is void, even if passed by consent, and cannot be enforced.
A party seeking discretionary relief must disclose all material facts, including a prior compromise decree, regardless of its validity; non-disclosure vitiates the order.
The District Magistrate has discretion under Section 7A not to enforce an allotment order, but such discretion must be exercised with full knowledge of material facts.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7A
Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, Rule 3
Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, Rule 4
Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, Rule 5
Control of Rent and Eviction Rules, 1949, Rule 6
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Voidness of agreements contrary to public policy
Judicial finality of consent decrees
Duty of full disclosure in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, Surjit Lal Chhabda, declared his separate property as part of his Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and sought assessment of its income in the HUF's status, but the tax authorities assessed it in his individual capacity.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu Undivided Family can exist for tax assessment purposes with only one male coparcener and no ancestral property.
Whether income from a property voluntarily thrown into family hotchpotch by an individual can be assessed as HUF income when the family lacks coparceners other than the male head.
Whether the character of property changes to joint family property upon declaration, in the absence of a pre-existing HUF or male coparcener.
holdings: A Hindu Undivided Family cannot be assessed as a separate taxable entity merely because a male member declares his separate property as HUF property if there is no pre-existing joint family property or coparcener other than himself.

Where property is first introduced into the family hotchpotch by a sole male member with no son, and the family consists only of wife and daughter, the income remains assessable in his individual capacity.

The mere existence of a wife and daughter does not convert separate property into joint family property for tax purposes; the personal law must recognize the property as belonging to the family, not just the individual.
doctrines: Gowli Buddanna's case rule
Kalyanji's case rule
Distinction between ancestral and separate property in HUF taxation
Test of coparcenary and family composition for HUF status

card.dispute: Private applicants challenged the rejection of their mining lease applications by the State Government, which had reserved the areas for public sector exploitation.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government has the power to reserve mineral areas for public sector exploitation under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
Whether the State Government can reject private mining lease applications on the ground that the area is reserved for public use.
Whether Rule 59 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, authorizes the State Government to reserve mineral areas for any purpose.
holdings: The State Government, as owner of minerals within its territory, has the inherent right to reserve mineral areas for public sector exploitation.
The State Government can reject private applications for mining leases if the area is reserved, and such rejection under Rule 60 is valid as the application is premature.
Rule 59 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, validly allows the State Government to reserve areas for any purpose, making them unavailable for private leasing until de-reserved.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 2
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 10
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 17(2) and (4)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 13
doctrines: State ownership of minerals
Inherent power of State to manage its natural resources
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (ejusdem generis not applied to limit reservation power)
Doctrine of legislative competence under Entry 23, List II, Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The Assam Railways & Trading Co. Ltd. fought the Collector of Lakhimpur over the compensation amount for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming a higher market value based on prior negotiations and sale evidence.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement between the parties on land price binds the Collector in determining compensation under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the Collector and courts below correctly determined the market value of the land based on reliable comparable sales.
Whether the market value of the land could be determined by capitalizing its rental value for twenty years.
holdings: An agreement between the parties on land price does not bind the Collector, who must independently determine market value under the Land Acquisition Act.
The Collector and High Court erred in relying solely on unverified sale transactions without considering their comparability or addressing price disparities.
The market value may be determined by capitalizing the rental value for twenty years, provided reliable lease terms are established through affidavits.
doctrines: Independent valuation by Collector
Reliance on comparable sales
Capitalization of rental value

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murdering Vincent Fernandes based on circumstantial evidence and witness testimony, which they challenged in appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's evidence, including witness testimony and identification, was reliable enough to sustain the conviction.
Whether the circumstantial evidence, including recovery of a weapon and other items, was sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
Whether contradictions in official records (Panchanama) and witness accounts affected the credibility of the prosecution's case.
holdings: The testimony of police constables and the witness Antonio was unreliable due to unnatural conduct and lack of inquiry, and thus could not form the basis of conviction.
The test identification parade had no probative value because the identifying witness did not confirm it, and such evidence can only be corroborative, not substantive.

The circumstantial evidence, including the recovery of a cloth, cord, thread, and weapon, lacked probative value due to contradictions in records and commonality of items, and could not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(1)(a)
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Corroboration requirement for identification parades
Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus (unreliable parts affecting overall credibility)

card.dispute: Baljit Singh and others appealed their conviction for murder and related charges arising from a land dispute that led to the death of Sher Singh, claiming the prosecution's version was false and that they acted in self-defence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants committed murder under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether the appellants acted in private defence and, if so, whether they exceeded the right of private defence?
Whether the conviction under Section 147 and 323/149 IPC is sustainable?
What is the appropriate offence to convict the appellants if not murder?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove a premeditated attack by the appellants; the evidence showed the deceased's party initiated the violence to forcibly dispossess the appellants.
The appellants were in lawful possession and entitled to private defence but grossly exceeded it by inflicting 72 injuries, including fatal ones, thus falling under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC.
The common object under Section 149 IPC was not established due to lack of prior conspiracy; hence, convictions under Sections 147 and 323/149 IPC are set aside.

The appellants are guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC with common intention under Section 34 IPC due to a spontaneous joint assault likely to cause death.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2A
doctrines: Right of private defence under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC
Doctrine of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Principle of proportionality in self-defence
Mutual combat ('Marpeet') negating unilateral aggression

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sued for eviction of tenants on grounds of rent arrears and bona fide requirement for business; the tenants died during appeal, raising questions about continuation of the suit and validity of rent payment by cheque.
issues_decided: Whether the legal representatives of deceased tenants could continue the appeal as having a heritable interest in the tenancy
Whether tender of rent by cheque, without prior agreement, constitutes valid payment under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction in second appeal to overturn the lower appellate court's finding on the landlord's bona fide requirement of the premises
holdings: A statutory tenant under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 has a heritable interest in the premises, enabling legal representatives to continue the tenancy and appeal after the tenant's death.
Tender of rent by cheque constitutes valid payment if consistent with implied agreement between parties, especially when cheques have been previously accepted and not dishonoured.
The High Court can interfere with a finding of fact in second appeal if the lower appellate court has ignored material evidence, rendering the finding legally unsustainable.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 2(i)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 14
doctrines: Heritable interest in statutory tenancy
Validity of payment by cheque as legal tender
Jurisdiction of High Court in second appeal on findings based on ignored material evidence

card.dispute: The appellants, including Dalbir Kaur and others, challenged their convictions for the murder of Ajaib Singh and Amir Singh, arguing insufficiency of evidence and errors in witness identification.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt, particularly in the absence of corroboration for key witnesses?
Whether failure to conduct a test identification parade for a crucial witness affects the reliability of identification?
Whether inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts render the prosecution case unreliable?
Whether the benefit of doubt should extend to all accused if granted to one based on the same evidence?
holdings: The prosecution proved the guilt of Dalbir Singh, Dalbir Kaur, and Puran Singh beyond reasonable doubt based on credible eyewitness testimony and circumstantial evidence.

It is unsafe to rely solely on the identification of an accused by a witness who did not participate in a test identification parade, especially when the accused was not well-known to the witness, warranting acquittal of Ajit Singh.
Minor discrepancies in eyewitness accounts do not undermine reliability if the core details of the crime are consistent and the witnesses observed the incident under clear conditions.
Acquittal of one accused on grounds of reasonable doubt does not automatically require acquittal of others if the evidence against them remains credible and conclusive.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Test identification parade and its evidentiary value
Concurrent findings of fact and appellate interference
Reliability of eyewitness testimony under Section 302 IPC

card.dispute: The appellants (owners) fought with the respondent (occupant) over whether he was a licensee or a tenant, and whether he was entitled to protection under the amended Bombay Rent Act after the original licence expired.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was a licensee under a subsisting agreement on 1 February 1973, entitling him to protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act as amended.
Whether the filing of an eviction application under Section 41 of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act impliedly revived or continued the licence.
Whether the conduct of the appellants after the expiry of the licence amounted to granting a fresh or implied licence.
holdings: A licensee whose licence has expired or been revoked does not automatically become a tenant or retain licensee status; to claim protection under Section 15A, there must be a subsisting licence agreement on 1 February 1973.
Filing an eviction application under Section 41 does not imply continuation or revival of a licence; it cannot be construed as granting a right to remain in occupation.
Mere tolerance of continued possession after revocation of licence does not amount to a fresh or implied licence; such occupant is a trespasser unless a new agreement is established.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(4A)
Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, Section 47
doctrines: Revocation of licence by efflux of time
Interpretation of statutes in favour of tenant protection but not beyond clear language
No implied licence without clear conduct or agreement
Principle that judicial findings of fact are not lightly interfered with in revision

card.dispute: The Revenue authorities contested whether a Hindu man married to a Christian woman under the Special Marriage Act could be assessed as part of a Hindu Undivided Family with their son, who was claimed to be a Hindu.
issues_decided: Whether the son of a Hindu father and a Christian mother, born out of a marriage under the Special Marriage Act, can be considered a Hindu governed by Hindu law.
Whether such a son can be a member of a Hindu Undivided Family for tax assessment purposes.
Whether Section 21 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 bars the application of Hindu law to the family or succession in such cases.
holdings: A legitimate child, one of whose parents is a Hindu and who is brought up as a Hindu, is a Hindu under the extended definition in the codifying Hindu law Acts, regardless of the religion of the other parent.
The son in this case was brought up as a Hindu and thus could validly be a member of the Hindu Undivided Family headed by his father.

Section 21 of the Special Marriage Act does not destroy the joint family structure or prevent a Hindu from treating his property as joint family property; it only governs succession under the Indian Succession Act in case of intestacy.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 2(1)(b)
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 3(1)(ii)
doctrines: Extended definition of 'Hindu' under codified personal law
Presumption of child's religion following the father in India
Autonomy of Hindu assessee to constitute joint family property
Non-obstante clause interpretation in Section 21 of the Special Marriage Act

card.dispute: The appellant, Dharam Chand Jain, sought enforcement of a Central Government order directing the State of Bihar to grant him a mining lease, which the State refused to implement.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government was legally bound to implement the Central Government's order dated November 21, 1964, granting the mining lease.
Whether the Central Government could reject the appellant's subsequent revision application based on grounds known at the time of its earlier order.
holdings: The State Government, as a subordinate authority, was legally bound to implement the Central Government's order and could not refuse to do so without seeking revision from the Central Government.
The Central Government erred in law by rejecting the revision application on grounds that were neither new nor justified revisiting its prior unvaried order.
doctrines: Principle of judicial discipline
Superior tribunal's binding authority over subordinate authorities
Doctrine of finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: The owner of a temple contested the Charity Commissioner's determination that the temple was a public trust under the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan at Amalner is a public or private religious endowment.
Whether the evidence established dedication of the temple for public use.
Whether the management and usage patterns indicate a public character of the trust.
holdings: A religious endowment is public if the beneficiaries are an indeterminate section of the public and the founder intended open access for worship.
Continuous public use, acceptance of public donations, and management of property as a public institution indicate a public trust.
The fact that only disciples perform puja does not make a temple private if the public has unrestricted darshan and participates in rituals.
A century-long holding out of the institution as public, along with royal and public grants, confirms its public character.
doctrines: Test for public vs private trust
Dedication by user as of right
Importance of founder's intention
Consciousness of managers and devotees regarding public character

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the tenant's claim that an application for special leave to the Supreme Court qualifies as an 'appeal' under Section 13A of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, thereby entitling the tenant to protection from eviction upon deposit of arrears.
issues_decided: Whether an application for special leave or an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court constitutes an 'appeal' within the meaning of Section 13A of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, as amended by the 1975 Ordinance.
Whether the protection under Section 13A extends to proceedings before the Supreme Court, particularly appeals by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution.
holdings: An application for special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution is not an 'appeal' within the meaning of Section 13A of the Rajasthan Act, as the term is confined to appeals and revisions under the state statute's hierarchy.

The benefit of Section 13A does not extend to proceedings in the Supreme Court, as the legislature intended protection only for suits, appeals, and revisions under the Act, not constitutional remedies beyond the state's judicial framework.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13A
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 22
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLI Rule 1(2)
Supreme Court Rules, 1966, Order XVI Rules 4 and 11
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Distinction between statutory appeals and constitutional remedies
Presumption of legislative awareness of procedural rules

card.dispute: The Hindu Religious Endowments challenged the appointment of non-hereditary trustees to a Shiva temple by the Endowment Commissioner, which the respondents (alleged hereditary trustees) claimed violated their property rights due to lack of prior determination of the temple's public status and their hereditary rights.
issues_decided: Whether non-hereditary trustees can be appointed under Section 27 of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951 without a prior determination under Section 41 regarding the public nature of the institution and existence of hereditary trustees.
Whether the Endowment Commissioner can initiate an inquiry suo moto under Section 41 of the Act.
holdings: Appointment of non-hereditary trustees under Section 27 requires a prior determination under Section 41 that the religious institution is public and has no hereditary trustees; otherwise, the appointment is without jurisdiction and illegal.

The Endowment Commissioner has the power to initiate an inquiry suo moto under Section 41 of the Act even though private parties must file a formal application with court fee, as there is no statutory bar to such action.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Section 27
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Section 40
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Section 41
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Section 44
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Section 74
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951, Rule 43
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 63
General Rules of the Court of the Orissa High Court (G.R.C.O.)
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional error
Doctrine of res judicata
Summary vs. judicial inquiry distinction
Suo moto power of administrative authorities
Principle of statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of a land acquisition order by the Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad for housing the poorer classes, arguing that they were denied a personal hearing as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applies to land acquisition proceedings under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 (as applied in Gujarat).
Whether the procedural safeguards of personal hearing under Section 5A are mandatory and cannot be bypassed even for beneficial welfare schemes.
Whether the appellate remedy provided under Schedule B of the Bombay Act is a sufficient substitute for a prior personal hearing under Section 5A.
holdings: Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act applies to acquisitions under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, and its requirements are mandatory.
Non-compliance with Section 5A’s personal hearing requirement renders the acquisition order invalid from inception, even if confirmed by the State Government.
The appeal mechanism under Schedule B does not replace the necessity of a prior personal hearing, which must be conducted by the Commissioner as per statutory duty.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 (as applied in Gujarat), Section 284N
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 (as applied in Gujarat), Schedule B, Clause 2 and 3
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 (as applied in Gujarat), Schedule C, Clause 2, 3, and 4
doctrines: Rule of natural justice (right to personal hearing)
Mandatory compliance with statutory procedures
Non-derogation from statutory safeguards in welfare legislation
Invalidity of administrative orders lacking foundational legality

card.dispute: The respondents sued to eject the appellants from the suit property, claiming ownership by inheritance, while the appellants claimed ownership by adverse possession under the Portuguese Civil Code.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants acquired title to the suit property by prescription under the Portuguese Civil Code
Whether the appellants' possession was permissive, thereby disentitling them from claiming adverse possession
Whether Article 510 of the Portuguese Civil Code applied to negate prescription due to lack of 'inversion of title'
holdings: Long, continuous, open, and peaceful possession of immovable property for over 30 years, without permissive use, ripens into ownership by prescription under Article 529 of the Portuguese Civil Code.
Possession is not permissive if there is a clear repudiation of the true owner’s title and no recognition of their authority, even if the possessor claims under a third party with no valid title.
Article 510 does not apply where possession was never in the name of the plaintiff; assertion of title under an unauthorized third party suffices to negate possession 'in another's name'.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Prescription under civil law
Inversion of title
Permissive possession

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether an oral family arrangement regarding property distribution was valid and enforceable despite not being registered under the Registration Act.
issues_decided: Whether an oral family arrangement requires compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act
Whether a memorandum filed after a family arrangement creates or transfers rights in immovable property and thus requires registration
Whether the doctrine of estoppel applies to prevent a party from resiling from a family arrangement after accepting its benefits
holdings: An oral family arrangement does not require compulsory registration; only written documents that create, declare, or assign rights in immovable property must be registered.

A memorandum prepared merely for record or to inform revenue authorities about an already completed family arrangement does not create or extinguish rights and is not compulsorily registrable under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.
Parties to a valid family arrangement who have enjoyed benefits under it are estopped from later challenging its validity, even if unregistered, based on equitable principles and judicial precedents.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of estoppel
Equitable principles in property settlement

card.dispute: The heirs of S. Gobinder Singh fought over whether a 1945 will, allegedly bequeathing most of his estate to his grandson Surjit, was genuine or invalid due to suspicious circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the will was executed free of suspicious circumstances
Whether the burden of proof was discharged by the propounder of the will
Whether the attesting witnesses were credible and the attestation valid
Whether the non-examination of the executors raised suspicion about the will's authenticity
holdings: A will surrounded by suspicious circumstances must be proved with strict scrutiny, and the burden lies heavily on the propounder to dispel such suspicions.
The propounder failed to explain suspicious circumstances including the use of unknown attesting witnesses and non-disclosure of the will to family and executors.
The evidence of the attesting witnesses was inconsistent and improbable, rendering their attestation unreliable.
The non-examination of the named executors, one of whom was the defendant’s father-in-law, raised grave doubts about the will’s authenticity.
doctrines: Burden of proof in testamentary cases
Suspicious circumstances doctrine
Requirement of credible attestation under Section 63
Presumption against unnatural and unfair wills

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer and the City Improvement Trust Board challenged the Karnataka High Court's decision on the determination of market value for compensation and the admission of a prior judgment as additional evidence in land acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of land acquired under the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945 should be determined with reference to the date of notification under Section 16 or Section 18 of the Act.
Whether a judgment from a related land valuation case, not filed during trial and pending appeal, could be admitted as additional evidence under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
holdings: The market value for compensation must be determined with reference to the date of notification under Section 16 of the Bangalore Act, as Section 27 read with Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act makes that date the relevant point for valuation.

A judgment not filed during trial and pending appeal cannot be admitted as additional evidence at the appellate stage unless the court records reasons for its necessity under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC and affords the other party an opportunity to rebut it.
provisions: City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945, Sections 16, 18, and 27
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Equity follows the law
Res judicata
Admissibility of judgments in personam
Principle of statutory interpretation: 'what is not excluded must be applied'

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued the defendants for recovery of money owed for cloth sold and goods sent on consignment, while the defendants counterclaimed for a sum they had paid.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff proved his claim for the sale proceeds of 21 bales of cloth sold by the defendants without payment.
Whether the plaintiff established his claim for the price of goods sent to the defendants for retail sale but not paid for.
Whether the plaintiff's claim for cash borrowings by the defendants was substantiated.
Whether the defendants' payment of Rs. 10,000 should be adjusted against the plaintiff's decree.
holdings: The plaintiff proved his claim for the sale proceeds of 21 bales of cloth based on the defendant's admission and corroborative documentary evidence.
The plaintiff failed to prove his claim for goods sent on consignment due to lack of reliable evidence and pleading deficiencies.
The claim for cash borrowings was not proved as no serious evidence was presented in support.
The Rs. 10,000 paid by the defendants must be credited against the plaintiff's decree, and interest shall be awarded at 6% per annum.
doctrines: Admission against interest
Corroboration of documentary evidence
Pleading and proof nexus
Adjustment of admitted payments in decree

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of a long-term tenant claiming bona fide need under a statutory presumption, which the tenant challenged on grounds of interpretation and subsequent statutory omission.
issues_decided: Whether Explanation (iv) to Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972 applies when the tenanted and landlord-occupied portions form part of a single unit of accommodation?
Whether the omission of Explanation (iv) by U.P. Act No. 28 of 1976 has retrospective effect, thereby depriving the landlord of the benefit of the provision?
holdings: Explanation (iv) applies only when the tenanted and landlord-occupied portions together constitute a single unit of accommodation; it does not apply to separate, independent tenements.
The question of whether the omission of Explanation (iv) is prospective or retrospective, and whether the landlord retains a vested right, should be decided by the District Court on remand.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1) with Explanation (iv)
doctrines: Strict construction of landlord-favouring provisions in tenant-protective legislation
Presumption against retrospective operation of amending statutes
