card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Committee sought to recover arrears of licence fees from Kalu Ram under Section 7 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, after the limitation period for a suit had expired.
issues_decided: Whether Section 7 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958 creates a new right to recover time-barred rent or merely provides a special procedure for recovery.
Whether the word 'payable' in Section 7 includes amounts barred by limitation.
holdings: Section 7 does not create a new right to recover rent but only provides a special procedure for recovering rent that is legally recoverable.
The term 'payable' in Section 7 means 'legally recoverable', and thus time-barred arrears cannot be recovered under this provision.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, Section 7
doctrines: Statute of limitations bars remedy but not the underlying right, unless the statute extinguishes the right.
Special statutory procedures do not create new rights if the parent statute only provides enforcement mechanisms.

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a shop from the partners of a reconstituted firm, claiming they were sub-tenants after the original tenant retired.
issues_decided: Whether the original tenant took the shop in his personal capacity or as an agent for the partnership firm
Whether the reconstituted firm could be considered a tenant after the original tenant's retirement
holdings: The rent note clearly named the individual as tenant, and oral evidence could not override this without a valid subsequent agreement under Section 92(4) of the Evidence Act.
The reconstituted firm could not automatically inherit tenancy rights absent notice to the landlord or a new agreement.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Parol evidence rule
Agency in tenancy
Privity of contract

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, arguing that the state failed to justify the urgency required to bypass inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 were validly issued.
Whether the State discharged the burden of proving urgency under Section 17(4) to justify dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A.
On whom lies the burden of proving urgency when the State invokes Section 17(4) of the Act.
holdings: The notifications under Section 4(1) were valid as they served the public purpose of developing residential and industrial areas.
The State failed to prove that urgency was of such a nature as to justify bypassing the inquiry under Section 5A; the mere recital of urgency without specific facts is insufficient.

The burden lies on the State to prove the existence of exceptional circumstances justifying urgency under Section 17(4), especially when facts are within its exclusive knowledge, under Section 106 of the Evidence Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of burden of proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act
Doctrine of application of mind by administrative authorities
Doctrine of limited scope of challenge to public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellants and the first respondent fought over whether the first respondent was entitled to a ryotwari patta for cultivable land based on continuous cultivation since July 1, 1945, under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the first respondent satisfied the requirement of Section 13(b)(iii) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, by proving cultivation from July 1, 1945.
Whether a mere intention to cultivate land is sufficient to meet the requirement of 'has cultivated' under Section 13(b)(iii) of the Act.
holdings: The landholder must prove actual cultivation by himself, his servants, or hired labour from July 1, 1945, to be entitled to a ryotwari patta under Section 13(b)(iii).
The phrase 'has cultivated' requires proof of actual cultivation, not merely an intention to cultivate; thus, the High Court erred in remanding the case on that basis.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 13(b)(iii)
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 15(1)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Requirement of actual cultivation for entitlement to ryotwari patta

card.dispute: The appellant auction-purchaser challenged the right of the mortgagor society to redeem the mortgaged property after the society paid off the mortgage debt, despite the property having been sold at auction by the mortgagee.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagor's right of redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act is extinguished by a mere contract of sale by the mortgagee without registration of conveyance.
Whether a power of sale without court intervention under Section 69 of the Transfer of Property Act extinguishes the equity of redemption upon auction or only upon registered conveyance.
Whether the right of redemption can be lost without a registered instrument under the Indian Registration Act, 1908.
holdings: A mortgagor's right to redeem under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act survives unless the sale is completed by a registered conveyance transferring ownership.
A mere contract of sale or auction by a mortgagee exercising power under Section 69 does not extinguish the equity of redemption in the absence of a registered deed.
The combined effect of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act requires registration to extinguish the right of redemption for immovable property.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Distinction between contract of sale and transfer of title
No distinction between legal and equitable estates in Indian property law

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the State of Punjab, arguing it should be higher and uniformly based on potential building area value.
issues_decided: Whether the entire land, forming one block, should be treated as potential building area for compensation
Whether compensation could be based on earlier acquisition rates or private sale transactions
Whether the High Court could award compensation exceeding the claimants' pleaded rate
holdings: The Supreme Court will not interfere with compensation unless there is a wrong application of principle or a vital valuation factor is overlooked.
Land within a single block may be classified differently for compensation if parts have distinct advantages like road access or proximity to developed areas.
A court cannot award compensation exceeding the rate claimed by the landowner in their appeal, even if market value justifies more.
Market value for compensation must reflect willing buyer-willing seller price, with due regard to timing, size, and comparability of transactions.
doctrines: Principle of belting in land valuation
Appellate court restraint in factual findings
Market value determination based on comparable sales
Compensation limited to claimed relief

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be a tenant or a purchaser in part performance of a contract of sale, while the respondent sought recovery of unpaid amounts and possession of her lands.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant acquired tenancy rights or possession under part performance of a contract of sale under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the power of attorney was a sham or colourable document
Whether the appellant could claim irrevocable licence under Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act due to permanent improvements
Whether the appellant was liable to pay Rs. 4,390 to the respondent and whether he could retain improvements on the land
holdings: The appellant failed to prove a concluded contract of sale or possession in part performance; thus, Section 53A does not apply.
The power of attorney was not a sham; it was acted upon and created a valid arrangement for management and possession.
The appellant cannot claim irrevocable licence under Section 60(b) as improvements were not made 'acting on the licence' but in belief of tenancy or future purchase.
The appellant is liable to pay Rs. 4,390 as per the agreed annual payment, and has no right to retain possession or claim value of improvements.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A
Sham or colourable transaction
Irrevocable licence for permanent improvements
Agent's lien under Section 221

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Beni Chand contested the validity of a will executed by his mother Jaggo Bai, which excluded him and his third wife's children from inheriting her Stridhana property, in favor of her second wife and other descendants.
issues_decided: Whether the propounder of the will discharged the burden of proving its due execution amidst suspicious circumstances
Whether the attesting witnesses satisfied the requirements under the Indian Succession Act
Whether an alienee pendente lite is entitled to be cited in probate proceedings
holdings: The propounder of a will must remove all suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution by satisfactory evidence, and must satisfy the court that the testator was of sound mind and executed the will freely.
A mere description of a signatory as an attesting witness is insufficient; there must be evidence that the witness saw the execution or received personal acknowledgment from the testator.

An alienee pendente lite cannot be cited in initial probate proceedings since their interest arises only during litigation, but may be heard to prevent future objections to bindingness of the judgment.
doctrines: Due execution of will
Burden of proof on propounder in testamentary cases
Principle of onus probandi in cases with suspicious circumstances
Doctrine of attesting witness under Indian law

card.dispute: The appellant company stopped paying additional royalty to the respondent (assignee of head lessee) under a sub-lease, leading to a suit by the respondent for arrears of royalty after the estate was vested in the State under land reforms legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, as assignee of the head lessee, retained an enforceable interest in the lease after vesting of the estate under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the appellant was liable to pay enhanced royalty to the State and could claim reimbursement from the respondent
holdings: The interests of a head lessee in a mining lease are not extinguished by vesting under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, if they are not expressly divested and are saved under Section 10, which creates a statutory lease from the State.

The appellant, having paid royalty directly to the State under the terms of the sub-lease and Controller’s order, remained liable for such payments and could not claim reimbursement from the respondent.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 9
Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(c)
doctrines: Statutory lease doctrine under land reform laws
Parliamentary exposition as an aid to interpretation
Non-obstante clause overriding general provisions
Use of subsequent amendment to interpret earlier statutory ambiguity

card.dispute: The heirs of a landlord who died during eviction proceedings fought to continue the suit against a tenant, claiming the premises were needed for a partnership firm in which the landlord was a partner.
issues_decided: Whether the right to sue for eviction on grounds of personal requirement survives the death of the landlord
Whether the requirement of a partnership firm in which the landlord is a partner amounts to the landlord's personal requirement under the Rent Act
Whether a decree passed in favour of the landlord before his death can be upheld by heirs despite his demise
holdings: The right to sue for eviction based on personal requirement does not automatically survive to all heirs; it depends on whether the requirement benefits surviving family members or heirs.
The requirement of a partnership firm in which the landlord was a partner is not necessarily equivalent to the landlord’s personal requirement for occupation under the Rent Act.
A preliminary decree in favour of the landlord does not become immutable upon death; it can be reconsidered if the heirs cannot establish the same bona fide need.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
doctrines: Survival of cause of action in eviction suits
Personal requirement doctrine
Doctrine of substitution of parties in pending litigation

card.dispute: A co-owner landlord sued for eviction of a tenant on the ground of personal requirement; the tenant contested the suit, arguing that a co-owner cannot be considered the 'owner' under the tenancy law and that all co-owners must be impleaded.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner can be considered 'the owner' under Section 13(1)(f) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 for filing an eviction suit.
Whether all co-owners must be impleaded in a suit for eviction filed by one co-owner.
Whether a tenant can deny the landlord's title under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 when the landlord is a co-owner.
holdings: A co-owner who is acknowledged as the landlord is 'the owner' within the meaning of Section 13(1)(f) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 and can file an eviction suit for personal occupation.
It is not necessary to implead all co-owners in an eviction suit if the defendant has acknowledged the plaintiff as the landlord and the suit is based on reasonable personal requirement.
A tenant cannot deny the landlord's title under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 when the tenancy has been admitted and the landlord's position has been consistently acknowledged.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(f)
doctrines: Co-ownership confers ownership of the whole undivided property, not just a share.
Estoppel against tenant denying landlord's title under Section 116 of the Evidence Act.
Reasonable requirement for personal occupation under tenancy law may include family or dependents of the co-owner.

card.dispute: The State of Madras fought with landholders (Melavaramdars) over whether they were entitled to compensation under the Land Acquisition Act after the estate was notified under the Madras Estates Abolition Act, and if so, the quantum of compensation and the date from which interest should accrue.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents were entitled to compensation under the Land Acquisition Act despite the vesting of the estate under the Madras Estates Abolition Act, 1948
Whether the quantum of compensation awarded to the Melavaramdars was excessive
From what date interest on the compensation should accrue
holdings: The State could not deny the respondents' interest in the land under the Land Acquisition Act after proceeding with acquisition proceedings, especially when it had made them parties; the Abolition Act claim was not pursued due to stayed proceedings.
The quantum of compensation awarded to Melavaramdars at half the rate given to Kudiwaramdars was in line with established judicial formula and did not warrant interference.
Interest on compensation should run from the date of the award by the Land Acquisition Officer, as there was no material showing earlier possession.
doctrines: Estoppel against the government in land acquisition proceedings
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with in appeal
Interest accrues from date of award in absence of earlier possession

card.dispute: The State of Haryana and private parties disputed over whether the Haryana Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973, was valid and whether it could vest ownership of minor minerals in the state, overriding prior lessee rights under central legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the Haryana Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973, is repugnant to the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
Whether existing lessee or licensee rights under the Central Act were affected by the Haryana Act.
Whether the petitioners had locus standi to challenge the notifications without first seeking enforcement of their rights from the authorities.
holdings: The Haryana Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973, is valid and not repugnant to the Central Act, as Parliament did not occupy the field of mineral ownership under the 1957 Act.
Lessee or licensee rights governed by the Central Act continue, but only if they are shown to exist and conform to the Central Act; no such rights were proven in this case.
A petitioner seeking mandamus must first call upon the authority to perform its legal obligation before approaching the court, which was not done here.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 16(1)(b)
Haryana Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973, Section 3(2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 9 (as amended by Act 56 of 1972)
doctrines: Repugnancy under Article 254 of the Constitution
Doctrine of prior resort to administrative remedy for mandamus
Presumption against implied repeal

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat sought to acquire land for a cooperative housing society, issuing successive notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894; landowners challenged the validity of a second Section 6 notification issued after cancellation of the first, arguing it amounted to withdrawal from acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether cancellation of a Section 6 notification amounts to withdrawal from acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether a fresh notification under Section 6 can be issued without reissuing a Section 4 notification, if the earlier Section 6 notification is cancelled as invalid
Whether land acquisition for a cooperative housing society serves a public purpose
holdings: Cancelling an invalid Section 6 notification does not amount to withdrawal from acquisition but is a recognition of its legal invalidity.

The government may issue a fresh Section 6 notification if the earlier one is invalid, without requiring a new Section 4 notification, as the power under Section 6 is not exhausted by an invalid exercise.
Acquisition of land for a cooperative housing society can serve a public purpose, as the need of a section of the public may constitute a public purpose.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Validity of administrative notifications
Doctrine of ineffective exercise of power
Continuity of acquisition proceedings after invalid notification

card.dispute: The dispute was between the descendants of a Muslim saint's family and the local Muslim community over ownership and management of a mosque, its adjuncts, and a graveyard, including the right to officiate as Imam and allegations of mismanagement.
issues_decided: Whether the mosque, its adjuncts, and the graveyard constituted a public wakf by dedication or long usage
Whether the suit was barred by res judicata due to earlier judgments
Whether the suit was barred under Section 55(2) of the Muslim Wakfs Act, 1954 for lack of Board consent
Whether Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applied given the defendants' status as de facto trustees
holdings: The mosque, its adjuncts, and the graveyard were dedicated to public use and had acquired the status of a valid public wakf through long and continuous usage.
The earlier judgments did not decide the public character of the wakf and thus did not operate as res judicata on that issue.
Section 55(2) of the Muslim Wakfs Act, 1954 did not bar the suit as no Wakf Board had been constituted at the time of filing.
The defendants, though asserting personal title, were de facto trustees managing wakf properties, making Section 92 of the CPC applicable for framing a scheme due to mismanagement.
doctrines: Res judicata
Public wakf by dedication and continuous usage
De facto trusteeship under trust law
Judicial discretion in framing schemes for mismanaged religious trusts

card.dispute: The Union of India, as a creditor, sued to declare that a property sale by the son (2nd defendant) to a company (1st defendant) was benami and void against creditors, asserting that the real owner and debtor (3rd defendant) had transferred the property to evade tax recovery.
issues_decided: Whether the house was purchased benami by the 2nd defendant for the 3rd defendant
Whether the sale of the house to the company was a sham transaction to defeat creditors
holdings: A property purchased in another's name with the purchaser's own funds and income shown as one's own establishes a benami transaction; the real owner remains the beneficial owner.
A sale made to a company controlled by the debtor’s family shortly after tax attachment, without real payment, constitutes a sham transaction to defraud creditors.
doctrines: Admissions as substantive evidence under the Evidence Act
Benami transaction doctrine
Sham transaction to defeat creditors

card.dispute: The Union of India fought Moksh Builders and Financiers Ltd. and others over whether a house was benami property of a tax defaulter and whether its sale to a company was a sham transaction to evade tax recovery.
issues_decided: Whether the house at Keeling Road was purchased benami by the father (defendant No. 3) in the name of his son (defendant No. 2)?
Whether the sale of the house to Moksh Builders and Financiers Ltd. was a sham transaction to defeat creditors?
holdings: The house was purchased benami by defendant No. 3 in the name of his son, who was a mere benamidar, as proved by admissions in tax returns and financial capacity.
The sale of the house to the company was a sham transaction intended to defeat tax recovery, given the timing, lack of payment, and domination of the company by the family.
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Sham transaction doctrine
Admissions as substantive evidence under the Evidence Act

card.dispute: Timber Kashmir Pvt. Ltd. challenged the validity of arbitration clauses in forest lease agreements, arguing they were not executed in compliance with Section 122(1) of the Jammu & Kashmir Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the forest lease agreements were validly executed under Section 122(1) of the Jammu & Kashmir Constitution.
Whether the delegation of power to Conservators of Forests to execute leases was lawful.
Whether prior government orders and notifications validated the execution of the leases.
holdings: A contract executed by an officer duly authorized under a valid delegation of power binds the government, even if no separate sanction order exists.
The notification dated 23rd February 1957 expressly authorized Conservators of Forests to execute forest lease agreements, satisfying Section 122(1) requirements.
Once a lease is validly executed by an authorized officer, the document itself serves as evidence of governmental sanction.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel against denying validity of contracts after accepting benefits
Doctrine of delegated authority in government contracts
Validity of ratification of past actions by government orders

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra prosecuted Barjure Kaikhosroo Maarfatia, an honorary accountant of a housing society, for forgery, criminal breach of trust, and falsification of accounts; he was acquitted by the trial court but convicted by the High Court, which he appealed.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved forgery under Section 471 read with Section 467 IPC beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the appellant committed criminal breach of trust under Section 408 IPC by misappropriating cheque proceeds
Whether the appellant falsified the society's accounts under Section 477A IPC
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting the appellant
holdings: The prosecution proved forgery beyond reasonable doubt as the receipt and voucher were forged, and the appellant's explanation about a missing Gujarati voucher was implausible.
The appellant misappropriated the cheque proceeds; his claim of prior cash payment to Sagar was false given the society’s insufficient cash balance and lack of corroborating entries.
The appellant falsified accounts by making false debit entries in the cash book without corresponding credit entries, indicating intentional manipulation.
The High Court rightly reversed the acquittal as the trial court erred in relying on improbable defense explanations unsupported by evidence.
doctrines: Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases
Principle of falsification of accounts through inconsistent or missing entries
High Court's power to reverse acquittal when trial court overlooks material evidence
Presumption against accused when explanation is inherently improbable

card.dispute: The landlords sued the tenant for possession of rented premises on the ground of bona fide personal need, while the tenant resisted on grounds of hardship.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the concurrent findings of the lower courts on the landlord's bona fide need and comparative hardship?
Whether the appellate court should have considered the tenant's offer to surrender part of the premises?
holdings: The High Court erred in setting aside the concurrent findings of fact by the Trial and Appellate Courts on the landlord's bona fide need and comparative hardship without sufficient reason.
The appellate court must consider whether the suit premises can be conveniently split and whether the tenant's offer to surrender part of the premises adequately meets the landlord's need.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts deserve deference
Principle of comparative hardship in eviction suits
Power of appellate court to remand on specific issues

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Lallubhai (respondents) sued for partition and a half share in a house, claiming succession to the widow Bai Kashi's interest, while the heirs of Nanabhai (appellants) contested the claim, arguing no legal necessity for Bai Kashi's sale and no pleaded case for succession.
issues_decided: Whether the three brothers had separated and the suit house was divided, though not by metes and bounds
Whether the sale deed executed by Bai Kashi was for legal necessity
Whether the respondents became entitled to a half share in the suit house after Bai Kashi's death through succession
holdings: The family had separated in status before the deaths of Nathubhai and Lallubhai, and the suit house was divided, though not by metes and bounds, entitling each branch to separate possession.
The sale deed executed by Bai Kashi was not proved to be for legal necessity and thus did not validly transfer her interest to the appellants.
The courts below erred in decreeing a half share to respondents based on succession without proper pleadings; the issue of succession to Bai Kashi’s limited estate must be remitted for determination.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937
doctrines: Limited interest of a Hindu widow under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937
Doctrine of legal necessity in alienation by a Hindu widow
Principle of proper pleading and adjudication only on issues raised by parties

card.dispute: Tenants sought to purchase tenanted land, while landlords (a widow and a minor) claimed protection under the proviso to section 32F(1)(a) of the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, based on a partition limited to agricultural land.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to section 32F(1)(a) applies when only agricultural land is partitioned and not the entire joint family property?
What is the meaning of 'disabled person's share in the joint family has been separated by metes and bounds' in the proviso?
holdings: The proviso to section 32F(1)(a) applies only when the disabled person's share in the entire joint family property, not just agricultural land, is separated by metes and bounds.
Separation 'by metes and bounds' requires an actual, concrete demarcation of the disabled person's share in all joint family assets, not merely a notional or partial partition confined to land.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32F(1)(a) proviso
doctrines: Teleological interpretation
Grammatical and purposive construction
Judicial non-interference with legislative policy in agrarian reform

card.dispute: The Bihar Eastern Gangetic Fishermen Co-operative Society challenged the validity of fishery rights granted to Sipahi Singh over the Gangapath Islampur Jalkar, claiming the settlement was invalid and seeking rights for itself.
issues_decided: Whether the settlement of fishery rights in favor of Sipahi Singh was valid without a registered instrument under the Transfer of Property Act and Registration Act
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel could be invoked against the government in this case
Whether a writ of mandamus under Article 226 was maintainable for enforcement of a contractual obligation
What relief, if any, should be granted to the appellant society for the unexpired period of the fishery term
holdings: A 'profit a prendre' such as fishing rights is immovable property; its transfer must be by registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, failing which no title passes.
Promissory estoppel cannot be invoked against the government when exercising sovereign functions, and no estoppel arises where no formal agreement or deposit was made.
A writ of mandamus under Article 226 lies only to enforce statutory duties, not contractual obligations, and cannot be issued for breach of an unenforceable contract.

The appeal was allowed for the year 1977–78, permitting the government to settle the fishery with the appellant society under its policy, with a direction to refund proportionate jamma to Sipahi Singh if such settlement occurs.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order XLI Rules 4 and 33
doctrines: Profit a prendre as immovable property
No estoppel against the government in sovereign functions
Mandamus for statutory duty only
Requirement of registered instrument for transfer of certain interests in immovable property

card.dispute: The landlord, P.T. Menghani, sought to evict the tenant company, Busching Schmitz Private Ltd, from commercial premises after being ordered to vacate government accommodation, invoking a new statutory right under the amended Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, as amended, applies to premises let out for commercial purposes
Whether a landlord can invoke Section 14A without intending to personally occupy the premises
Whether the court can prevent misuse of the eviction process under Section 14A
holdings: Section 14A does not apply to premises let out for commercial purposes; it is limited to residential tenancies.
The right to eviction under Section 14A is conditional upon the landlord’s genuine need to occupy the premises after being ordered to vacate government accommodation.
Courts have inherent power to prevent abuse of process, including cancellation of eviction orders if the landlord re-lets or fails to occupy the premises, to prevent mockery of the judicial process.
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes to avoid absurdity
Inherent power of court to prevent abuse of process
Principle of unconscionability in enforcement of legal rights
Harmonious construction of amendments as part of a legislative scheme

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the government, claiming it had higher building potential value.
issues_decided: Whether the District Judge erred in awarding compensation exceeding the amount claimed under Section 9 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the High Court was correct in reducing the compensation to Rs. 450 per acre without considering the land's potential for building use.
What was the proper compensation amount based on the land's potential value as building sites?
holdings: A court cannot award compensation exceeding the amount claimed under Section 9 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as per Section 25(1).
The High Court erred in ignoring evidence of the land’s building potential, including payment of diversion charges and proximity to developed areas.
The land had substantial potential value as building sites; compensation is fixed at Rs. 1,250 per acre with 6% interest and 15% solatium.
doctrines: Building potentiality doctrine
Willing buyer-willing seller principle
Objective assessment of market value based on factual circumstances

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of a contract to purchase immovable property, claiming readiness to perform, while the respondents argued time was of the essence and the appellant had defaulted.
issues_decided: Whether the stipulation of time in a contract for sale of immovable property makes time the essence of the contract.
Whether the question of time being of the essence can be raised for the first time in the High Court on appeal in the absence of pleadings or issues in the trial court.
Whether the appellant was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
holdings: Fixing a time period for performance in a contract for sale of immovable property does not automatically make time the essence; there must be strong evidence of such intention to displace the normal presumption.
The issue of whether time is of the essence cannot be raised for the first time in appeal if it was not pleaded or framed as an issue in the trial court.
The appellant proved he was ready and willing to perform his obligations, including having sufficient funds, and the respondents failed to cooperate, justifying the grant of specific performance.
doctrines: Presumption against time being of the essence in immovable property contracts
Requirement of pleadings and issues for raising legal questions in appeal
Burden of proof in specific performance cases regarding readiness and willingness

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent and unauthorized subletting, while the tenant challenged the striking out of his defence and the order for recovery of possession.
issues_decided: Whether failure to comply with a section 15(1) order automatically entitles the landlord to an order for possession without a hearing
Whether the Rent Controller has discretion to extend the time for payment under section 15(1)
Whether the High Court erred in not examining the validity of the order striking out the tenant's defence under section 15(7)
holdings: Non-compliance with a section 15(1) order does not automatically entitle the landlord to possession; the application must still be heard, and the landlord must prove its case.
The Rent Controller has no discretion to extend the one-month time limit prescribed under section 15(1) for payment of arrears.
If the order striking out the tenant’s defence under section 15(7) is found to be erroneous, the tenant must be given an opportunity to defend the eviction application.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Procedural fairness
No estoppel against statute

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of property bequeathed by a widow, Kutumbamma, while respondents argued she only had a life interest and could not transfer absolute title.
issues_decided: Whether the maintenance deed granting Kutumbamma a life interest in the property became an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the deed fell under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, which excludes enlargement of a limited estate
holdings: A widow given a life interest in joint family property for maintenance acquires an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if the property was in her possession when the Act came into force.
The maintenance deed did not fall within Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, as it was not a testamentary disposition or a settlement in contemplation of death.
doctrines: Enlargement of limited estate under Section 14(1)
Distinction between testamentary dispositions and maintenance arrangements under Section 14(2)

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of tenants on the ground that the tenant no longer needed the premises after constructing a new house, leading to a dispute over the applicability of the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's construction of a new house justified eviction under Section 13(1)(i) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the joint family's status as beneficiary of the tenancy affected the right to continued occupation
Whether the High Court was justified in ordering eviction based on equitable considerations despite factual findings against it
holdings: Eviction under Section 13(1)(i) requires a clear right of the tenant or family to occupy alternative accommodation; mere construction of a house by the tenant does not automatically justify eviction.
The tenancy was for the benefit of the joint family, and the new house being self-acquired property of the tenant did not confer occupancy rights on other family members.
In the interest of justice and fairness, the Court modified the eviction order by directing partition of the premises, allowing partial continued occupation by the tenant under specified conditions.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(i)
doctrines: Equitable jurisdiction under Article 136
Humanist approach to justice
Partition as a judicial remedy in landlord-tenant disputes

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for acquiring his land, claiming lack of proper hearing, unreasonable delay, and vagueness in the public purpose stated.
issues_decided: Whether failure to provide a copy of the Collector's report under Section 5A vitiates the inquiry?
Whether there was unreasonable delay between the Section 4 and Section 6 notifications?
Whether the notification under Section 4 was vague for not clearly stating 'fire station' as the public purpose?
holdings: Failure to provide a copy of the report under Section 5A does not invalidate the inquiry if the hearing was otherwise fair and no mala fide is alleged.
A delay of about two and a half years between Section 4 and Section 6 notifications is not unreasonable, given the need to hear multiple objections in a large acquisition.

The description 'station, workshop and parking purpose' in the Section 4 notification sufficiently disclosed the public purpose, especially since the appellant himself acknowledged the fire station purpose in his objections.
doctrines: Principle of fair hearing under statutory inquiry
Reasonable opportunity of being heard
Presumption of regularity in administrative action

card.dispute: A government officer sought to evict two tenants from separate dwelling units in a co-owned property under Section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, after being directed by the government to vacate official accommodation, leading to a dispute over whether he could evict both tenants using the same provision.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can use Section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 to evict more than one tenant when he owns multiple dwelling units.
Whether a co-owner of a property can file an eviction petition under Section 14A.
Whether a person claiming under a will, without probate, can be considered a landlord under the Act.
Whether the right to evict under Section 14A is exhausted after recovering possession of one dwelling unit.
holdings: The right under Section 14A is exhausted once a landlord recovers possession of one dwelling house; it cannot be used repeatedly to evict tenants from multiple units.
A co-owner is a rightful landlord and can initiate eviction proceedings, especially with implied consent of other co-owners.
A person in possession under a will, even without probate, can be treated as a landlord if collecting rent and recognized as such by the tenant.
The proviso to Section 14A(1) limits recovery to one dwelling house, making further evictions on the same ground impermissible.
doctrines: Exhaustion of statutory remedy
Functional test for landlord-tenant relationship
Co-ownership confers standing to sue
Substance over form in landlord identity

card.dispute: The tenant (Khadi Gram Udyog Trust) fought the landlord (Shri Ram Chandraji Virajman Mandir) over whether depositing only the time-barred rent arrears was sufficient to avoid eviction under the U.P. Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether the phrase 'entire amount of rent due' under Section 20(4) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act includes time-barred rent.
Whether a tenant can claim protection from eviction under Section 20(4) without depositing time-barred rent arrears.
holdings: The words 'entire amount of rent due' in Section 20(4) include time-barred rent, as limitation bars remedy but not the existence of the debt.
A tenant cannot claim relief under Section 20(4) unless the full rent due, including time-barred amounts, is deposited at the first hearing.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
doctrines: Remedy barred but right subsists
Statute-barred debt remains due
Appropriation of payments under Section 60 of the Contract Act

card.dispute: The appellants (son, wife, and granddaughter of Purohit Mani Ram) challenged the validity of a will by which the respondent (Smt. Ishroo Devi) claimed ownership of certain properties, arguing that some were joint family properties and could not be entirely disposed of by will.
issues_decided: Whether item 1(a) of the property was self-acquired or joint family property
Whether income from a hereditary priest's profession constitutes joint family property
Whether the testator could dispose of his interest in joint family property by will under Section 27 of the Jammu & Kashmir Hindu Succession Act, 1956
What share of the joint family property the testator was entitled to bequeath, particularly in light of the wife's rights upon partition
holdings: Item 1(a) was self-acquired property of Purohit Mani Ram, as he had sufficient independent income and there was no evidence of ancestral funds being used to acquire it.
Income earned from a hereditary profession, being personal earnings from learning or service, does not become joint family property under Mitakshara law.
Under Section 27 of the Jammu & Kashmir Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a male Hindu can dispose of his undivided interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will.

The wife is entitled to a share equal to that of a son upon partition between father and son, but since the extent of the testator’s interest was not determined, the question of his disposable share in items 1(b) and 2 is remitted to the High Court.
provisions: Jammu & Kashmir Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 27
Jammu & Kashmir Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Explanation to Section 27
doctrines: Mitakshara coparcenary law
Doctrine of self-acquired property
Rule of testamentary disposition of coparcenary interest
Wife's right to equal share upon partition

card.dispute: The descendants of a common ancestor fought over whether conveyances of family property to a company in 1932 disrupted the joint family status and were valid under Hindu law.
issues_decided: Whether the joint family was divided in status before or in 1932 due to the conveyances of property to the company.
Whether the conveyances to the company were valid if made for the benefit of the family, even without formal partition.
Whether certain subsequent documents and affidavits proved continued joint family status after 1932.
Whether certain respondents had standing to challenge the transactions, particularly after delay or lack of objection by other family branches.
holdings: The joint family was divided in status by 1932, as evidenced by the conveyances where each son acted as karta of his own separate joint family.
Even if the family remained undivided, the conveyances were valid because they were made for the family's benefit, aimed at preserving and protecting the property from dissipation.
Subsequent division of movables in 1935 and affidavits claiming continued joint status do not outweigh the documentary evidence of earlier division in 1932.
A coparcener may challenge alienations even if others do not, and delay in challenging does not bar relief where the transaction affects family property.
doctrines: Division in status in a Hindu joint family
Alienation of joint family property for family benefit
Presumption against dissipation of joint family property
Family arrangement and its distinction from alienation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant due to arrears in rent, house tax, and electricity charges, while the tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Rents Act by depositing arrears during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act despite prolonged arrears and non-prosecution of the standard rent fixation application?
Whether the High Court had the power to condone the tenant's defaults in rent payment on compassionate grounds?
Whether the tenant's willingness to pay rent could be presumed despite failure to comply with statutory deposit requirements?
holdings: A tenant is not entitled to protection under Section 12(3)(b) if they fail to deposit rent and arrears as required by the statute, especially when there was no genuine dispute over standard rent.
Courts cannot condone statutory violations under the Bombay Rents Act on compassionate grounds or by making incorrect factual assumptions about rent fixation.
Readiness and willingness to pay rent under the Act requires actual compliance with deposit conditions; inability to pay due to financial hardship does not invoke statutory protection.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(10)
doctrines: Statutory compliance as a condition for protection against eviction
No judicial discretion to condone statutory defaults in rent control laws
Doctrine of readiness and willingness must be evidenced by actual performance under the statute

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, and after a consent decree allowing partial occupation for five years, the tenant resisted execution, claiming the decree was a nullity and created an unregistered lease.
issues_decided: Whether the consent decree for eviction was a nullity for non-compliance with the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955
Whether the compromise decree created a new lease requiring registration under the Registration Act
Whether the executing court can examine pleadings and evidence to validate a consent decree challenged as invalid
holdings: A consent decree for eviction is valid if the pleadings and record show a statutory ground for eviction under the M.P. Act, and the court applied its mind to such compliance.
The compromise did not create a new lease; the dominant intention was eviction with time to vacate, so no registration was required under the Registration Act.
An executing court may examine the pleadings and materials on record to determine if a consent decree is valid and based on a statutory ground for eviction.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 3(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955, Section 4(d) and 4(h)
doctrines: Dominant intention rule in construction of documents
Consent decree must satisfy statutory grounds for eviction
Judicial scrutiny of compromise decrees in execution

card.dispute: Natthu Singh and his sons appealed against their conviction and death sentence for the premeditated murder of four persons, claiming alibi and procedural errors.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC was legally sustainable based on the evidence?
Whether the recovery of incriminating articles like the cap, gun parts, and cartridges was lawful and credible?
Whether the plea of alibi raised by some appellants should have been accepted?
Whether the death sentence was justified given the delay in trial and circumstances of the case?
holdings: The conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is sustainable as the prosecution proved common intention and participation beyond reasonable doubt.
The recovery of the cap, broken gun part, and cartridges was lawful; delay in seizure was explained and does not vitiate the evidence.
The plea of alibi was rightly rejected as it was not raised before the committing magistrate and was inconsistent with proximity to the crime scene.
The death sentence is justified due to premeditation, use of lethal weapons, and absence of mitigating circumstances despite delay caused by the appellants' absconding.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Principle of alibi and its burden of proof
Appreciation of delayed recovery of evidence
Proportionality in sentencing and justification for death penalty

card.dispute: The landlord, Nihal Chand, sought eviction of tenant Kalyan Chand Jain under Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, which the tenant challenged on the ground that the provision did not apply to retired government servants.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act is applicable to a government servant who retired before the provision came into force?
Whether the cause of action under Section 14A(1) accrues upon service of the order requiring vacation of government accommodation?
holdings: Section 14A(1) applies to a government servant who was in service when the order to vacate was served, even if retirement occurred later.
The cause of action under Section 14A(1) accrues on the date the order requiring vacation or payment of penal licence fee is served, not on retirement.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Ordinance 1975, Section 25A to 25C
doctrines: Accrual of cause of action
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Purpose and object of remedial legislation

card.dispute: The appellants (Raj Rani and son) challenged the respondent's (Kailash Chand) suit for partition and possession of 2/3 share in a property, claiming the suit was barred by limitation due to admitted dispossession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff, having admitted dispossession, must prove possession within twelve years under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit was barred by limitation due to failure to establish actual or constructive possession within twelve years
holdings: A plaintiff who admits dispossession in a suit based on title must prove actual or constructive possession within twelve years to succeed under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
Where a co-sharer alleges dispossession, the burden lies on the plaintiff to show that the ouster occurred within twelve years; mere joint ownership does not presume continued possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 96
doctrines: Burden of proof in possessory suits
Constructive possession of co-sharers
Distinction between adverse possession and dispossession

card.dispute: The dispute was between industrial workers and the Competent Authority over whether the Housing Board could enhance rent and demand arrears from workers whose income exceeded the prescribed wage limit under a subsidized housing scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had the power to direct the Housing Board to enhance rent and demand past dues from tenants who crossed the income limit.
Whether the Housing Board could charge enhanced or economic rent retrospectively from the date the tenant's income exceeded the prescribed limit.
Whether the terms of the allotment agreement and regulations permitted modification of rent based on changes in the tenant's income after allotment.
holdings: The State Government has the authority under Section 73A of the Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948, to issue binding directions to the Housing Board for implementing the purposes of the Act, including rent enhancement.

The Housing Board can lawfully charge enhanced or economic rent from industrial workers who exceed the prescribed income limit, even retrospectively from the date of crossing the limit, subject to a three-month concession period.

The original allotment at subsidized rent was provisional, and tenants had no vested right to continue at that rate if their income rose beyond the prescribed limit, as per government policy and the scheme’s intent.
provisions: Regulations 3, 4, 6, and 7 of the Bombay Housing Board
doctrines: Doctrine of Prospective Overruling
Principle of Reasonable Classification
Doctrine of Governmental Power to Issue Binding Directions to Statutory Bodies

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent default, claiming non-payment of furniture rent constituted default under the Bihar Rent Act, while the tenant argued that only non-payment of the Rent Controller-fixed premises rent could be a ground for eviction.
issues_decided: Whether non-payment of rent for furniture, let out under a separate agreement, constitutes a ground for eviction under Section 11(1)(d) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947
Whether failure to deposit arrears within the time specified under Section 11A of the Act warrants striking out the tenant's defence in appeal
holdings: Non-payment of rent for furniture supplied under a separate and independent contract does not constitute a default in payment of rent of the premises, and therefore cannot be a ground for eviction under Section 11(1)(d) of the Act.

A tenant's defence cannot be struck out under Section 11A if the deposit was made within the statutory period through the Nazir, even if delayed, without proper inquiry into the reasons for the mode of deposit.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11A
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 5
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 7
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 4
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory grounds for eviction
Separate tenancy and contract principles
Procedural fairness in enforcement of deposit requirements

card.dispute: The widows of two step-brothers fought over whether the first widow, Nallammal, acquired absolute ownership of 40 acres of family property given to her in lieu of maintenance, or only a limited interest for life.
issues_decided: Whether the property given to Nallammal in 1949 in lieu of maintenance became her absolute property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 14(2) of the Act applied to exclude her from acquiring an absolute interest
Whether she had surrendered possession of the property before the 1956 Act came into force
holdings: Property given to a Hindu female in settlement of maintenance claim constitutes 'stridhan' and becomes her absolute property under Section 14(1) if she is in possession when the 1956 Act came into force.
Section 14(2) does not apply where the property is not received under a will or deed that restricts alienation, but through a family arrangement recognizing no pre-existing right.
The claim that the plaintiff surrendered possession for a maintenance allowance was not proved and did not negate her continued possession at the time the 1956 Act took effect.
provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Explanation to Section 14
doctrines: Doctrine of Stridhan
Doctrine of Family Arrangement
Doctrine of Continuity of Possession under Section 14

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the legal effect of an unregistered lease agreement, claiming entitlement to possession of municipal land based on a resolution and an unregistered kabuliyat, while the respondents sought eviction after a partnership dissolution.
issues_decided: Whether a year-to-year lease or one reserving yearly rent requires compulsory registration under the Registration Act
Whether the resolution of the Municipal Board and the kabuliyat together constitute a lease requiring registration
Whether the appellants could derive any legal right to possession in the absence of a registered lease
holdings: A lease of immovable property from year to year or reserving yearly rent must be registered to be legally enforceable under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act and Section 17 of the Registration Act.
The resolution of the Municipal Board and the kabuliyat do not together constitute a lease requiring registration, as no formal lease was executed.
In the absence of a registered lease, no legal right or title in favour of the appellants arose, and thus they could not claim protection against eviction.
doctrines: Compulsory registration of leases
Doctrine of legal recognition of documents creating or transferring rights in immovable property

card.dispute: The appellant mining lessee challenged the cancellation of his lease and forfeiture of security deposit by the State Government for breach of lease conditions, arguing waiver, violation of natural justice, and improper consideration of extraneous materials.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government waived its right to cancel the lease by issuing a second notice after cancellation.
Whether the lessee was denied a reasonable opportunity of being heard, violating principles of natural justice.
Whether the Central Government's rejection of revision was vitiated by considering breaches from a subsequent notice not part of the challenged order.
holdings: No waiver occurred as the second notice was issued without knowledge of the prior cancellation and there was no intentional relinquishment of rights by the State.
The principles of natural justice were satisfied as the lessee was given an opportunity to respond and the explanation offered was non-exculpatory, amounting to a plea for condonation.
The Central Government did not commit an error by referring to the second notice, as the appellant himself raised it in submissions and no prejudice was caused.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 13
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver
Doctrine of estoppel against the State
Principles of natural justice
Non-application of mind and extraneous considerations in administrative action

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (family of Shivanna Devadiga) sued the defendant (Shivanna's nephew) for possession of Purshottam Restaurant, claiming it was owned by Shivanna and managed by the defendant as a caretaker, while the defendant claimed he was the sole owner.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could decide the case on a 'benami transaction' theory not pleaded by the plaintiffs?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on ownership and possession of the restaurant?
holdings: A court cannot base its decision on a 'benami' plea if it was not raised in the plaint or made part of the issues; deciding on unpleaded grounds violates principles of fair trial.
The High Court erred in law by setting aside the trial court's findings based on a new theory not canvassed in the pleadings, and thus its judgment was set aside.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 3
doctrines: Pleadings bind the court
No decision on unpleaded issues
Benami transaction doctrine

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation challenged the validity of the Karnataka Contract Carriages (Acquisition) Act, 1976, which nationalised private contract carriage operators, who contested the acquisition as violative of constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of private contract carriages for a public purpose under Article 31(2) of the Constitution is valid
Whether the acquisition serves the public purpose as required under Article 31(2)
Whether the principles of compensation under the Act conform to constitutional mandates
Whether the Act violates the rights under Articles 39(b) and (c) by not ensuring equitable distribution of resources
holdings: Acquisition of private transport undertakings for a public purpose, such as improving road transport services, falls within the scope of Article 31(2) and is constitutionally valid.
The concept of 'public purpose' includes state-led nationalisation schemes aimed at social and economic welfare, especially in line with Directive Principles under Part IV of the Constitution.
The method of determining compensation under the Act, including the role of arbitrators and the 'acquisition cost' formula, satisfies the constitutional requirement of fairness under Article 31(2).

Article 39(b) and (c) do not prohibit acquisition of private property for state-run corporations; such measures are within legislative competence and serve the goal of equitable distribution of resources.
provisions: Constitution of India, Schedule VII, List I, Entry 42
doctrines: Progressive interpretation of the Constitution
Public purpose in property acquisition
Harmonisation of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
Flexible interpretation of constitutional provisions in light of social change

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and a cooperative society fought against landowner Sankalchand Khodidas Patel over whether the land acquisition for housing backward class people was valid, particularly regarding public purpose and alleged abandonment of government subsidy.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could decide the appeal on the ground of abandonment of government's intention to pay part of compensation when no such plea was raised in trial court or framed as an issue
Whether the State Government had abandoned its intention to pay part of the compensation from public funds, thereby invalidating the public purpose under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act
holdings: The High Court erred in law by deciding the appeal on the issue of abandonment of government's intention to pay compensation when it was not pleaded, issue was not framed, and not part of the contentions before it.

The State Government did not abandon its intention to pay part of the compensation from public funds; the non-payment was due to protracted litigation, and the government's continued adherence to the acquisition shows ongoing commitment.
doctrines: Principle of constructive res judicata
Requirement of pleading and issue for appellate jurisdiction
Doctrine of public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant (Sunder Dass) sought to evict the respondent (Ram Prakash) from a shop in a government-owned building he purchased at auction, but the eviction decree was challenged on the ground that the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 applied due to a retrospective amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the introduction of a proviso to Section 3 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 with retrospective effect rendered a prior final decree for eviction a nullity
Whether an executing court can examine the nullity of a decree based on lack of inherent jurisdiction due to retrospective statutory amendments
Whether the legal fiction created by retrospective operation of a proviso must be carried to its logical conclusion even if it affects final decrees
holdings: A decree becomes a nullity if the civil court lacked inherent jurisdiction due to a retrospective amendment that ousts jurisdiction, even if the decree was valid when passed.
An executing court may examine whether a decree is a nullity for lack of jurisdiction, as it does not amount to questioning the decree’s correctness but its very existence.
A legal fiction created by retrospective operation of a proviso must be fully applied, including its consequences on prior final decrees, unless expressly restricted by the legislature.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 3 (as amended with proviso)
doctrines: Legal fiction
Retrospective operation of statutes
Nullity of decree for lack of jurisdiction
Finality of decree vs. jurisdictional bar

card.dispute: The appellants (potential reversioners) fought with the respondent (adopted son) over possession of property gifted by Mula, claiming the gift was invalid under custom, while the respondent claimed entitlement after the gift was declared non-binding in a prior suit.
issues_decided: Whether the Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973 barred the respondent from challenging the validity of the gift-deed in question.

Whether the declaratory decree obtained by the appellants in 1966, declaring the gift non-binding on reversioners, benefited the respondent as an heir entitled to a share in the property at the time of Mula's death.
holdings: The Amendment Act of 1973 did not bar the respondent from claiming possession because he did not challenge the validity of the gift; the prior decree had already rendered the gift ineffective at the time of Mula's death.

A declaratory decree that an alienation is not binding on reversioners enures for the benefit of all persons entitled to a share in the property at the moment of the alienor’s death, including subsequently adopted heirs.
provisions: Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, Section 7
Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973, Section 3
doctrines: Declaratory decree benefiting all heirs at the time of death
Non-retroactivity of amendment barring challenges to alienations based on custom

card.dispute: Technicians Studio Private Ltd fought Lila Ghosh and another over whether monthly rent payments after an unregistered 16-year lease created a continuing monthly tenancy protected under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered compromise petition creating a 16-year lease could confer any interest in immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 53A
Whether payment and acceptance of monthly rent under an invalid lease created a de facto monthly tenancy
Whether the appellant was entitled to protection under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 after expiry of the lease period
holdings: An unregistered compromise petition seeking to create a 16-year lease cannot create any interest in immovable property but may allow protection of possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act as part performance.
Mere payment and acceptance of rent under an unregistered lease does not automatically create a monthly tenancy; such a relationship depends on the parties' intention, not implication by law.

Section 53A provides only a defensive right to retain possession, not an active tenancy or title, and does not entitle the possessor to protection under rent control legislation after the lease period ends.
doctrines: Doctrine of Part Performance
Statutory bar under Section 53A as a limited defence, not a source of title
Intention of parties as determinant of landlord-tenant relationship

card.dispute: The heirs of a deceased man contested the right of his widow to sell properties she had received under a compromise for maintenance, claiming she held only a life interest.
issues_decided: Whether the widow acquired an absolute interest in the property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 14(2) of the Act applied to bar the widow's absolute ownership due to restrictions in the compromise
Whether a compromise in lieu of maintenance merely recognizes a pre-existing right and thus falls outside Section 14(2)
holdings: A female Hindu acquires absolute ownership of any property she possesses at the time the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, including property received in lieu of maintenance.

Section 14(2) does not apply to instruments that merely recognize or confirm a pre-existing right, such as a right to maintenance, and thus restrictions in such instruments do not prevent absolute ownership under Section 14(1).
The term 'possessed by' in Section 14(1) includes legal possession under a claim or title, not mere physical possession, and such possession triggers full ownership under the Act.
doctrines: Liberal construction of statutes in favor of women's rights
Recognition of pre-existing rights in property law
Proviso not to override main statutory protection
Transformation of limited interest into absolute interest under Section 14(1)

card.dispute: Velji Lakshmi & Co. (tenant) fought Benett Coleman & Co. (landlord) over whether the tenant could be evicted for demolition of premises under a town planning scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Commissioner had statutory authority to order demolition of temporary structures under the town planning scheme.
Whether the notice for demolition amounted to a valid 'order' under clause (hhh) of Section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947.
Whether the suspension or proposed variation of the town planning scheme rendered the demolition order ineffective.
Whether the landlord or the local authority had the power to evict the tenant on grounds of compulsory demolition.
holdings: The Municipal Commissioner had statutory power under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 to order demolition of structures violating a town planning scheme.
A notice from the Commissioner for demolition under statutory authority qualifies as an 'order' under clause (hhh) of Section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947.
Partial suspension or proposed variation of a town planning scheme does not nullify an existing demolition order if relevant regulations remain in force.

The landlord may seek eviction under clause (hhh) of Section 13(1) of the Bombay Rents Control Act when demolition is mandated by a competent authority, and the local authority's order suffices for this purpose.
provisions: City of Bombay (Building, Works and Reconstruction) Act, 1944, Section 3 and Section 8
Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, Section 55 and Rule 38
Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(hhh), Section 17A, Section 17B, Section 17C
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of temporary legislation and survival of rights
Finality of administrative decisions under town planning laws
Distinction between voluntary and compulsory demolition under rent control law
Legal irrelevance of proposed legislative or policy changes not yet enacted

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the pre-emption decree granted to the respondents under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, claiming the sale was fictitious and collusive to evade land ceiling laws.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the ancestral property by Kabul Singh was a real sale or fictitious and void.
Whether the plaintiffs-respondents were entitled to exercise their right of pre-emption under Section 4 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913.
Whether the collusive decree between vendor and vendees could affect the pre-emption rights of the plaintiffs.
holdings: The sale was a real transaction despite being motivated to evade land ceiling laws, and the pleadings and findings support its validity.
The plaintiffs were entitled to pre-emption under Section 4 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, as the sale was valid and triggered pre-emptive rights.
A collusive consent decree between vendor and vendee cannot bind or defeat the statutory pre-emption rights of others.
doctrines: Doctrine of unclean hands
Statutory right of pre-emption
Collusive suit and binding effect

card.dispute: Co-owners fought over the partition of a small property, with the plaintiffs seeking partition or sale, and the defendant seeking to buy the plaintiffs' share at a lower valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint contained a request under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893 for public sale of the property
Whether Sections 2 and 3 of the Partition Act, 1893 apply when no such request for sale is made
What equitable remedy the court can provide when physical partition is not feasible and the Partition Act does not apply
holdings: The plaint did not contain a request for public sale under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893, as required to invoke Section 3.
Sections 2 and 3 of the Partition Act, 1893 are inapplicable where no co-sharer has requested a public sale.

When partition in specie is impracticable and the Partition Act does not apply, the court may use its equitable jurisdiction to allow one co-owner to retain the property by paying just compensation based on current market value.
doctrines: Equitable jurisdiction of courts in partition suits
Owelty as a mode of partition
Concurrent finding of fact not interfered with

card.dispute: The plaintiffs-respondents sued to establish that the land in question was part of a public religious endowment for a temple, while the defendant-appellant claimed personal rights over the property as the successor Mahant.
issues_decided: Whether the land in village Bahawalpura was dedicated as a public religious endowment for the Temple of Shri Thakurji Maharaj.
Whether the defendant-appellant held the property as a custodian of the deity or as its personal owner.
Whether the defendant could raise a new plea regarding acquisition of Bhumidhari rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, at the appellate stage.
holdings: The entire land in dispute was dedicated as a public religious endowment for the Temple of Shri Thakurji Maharaj, with the Mahant acting only as a custodian.
The defendant-appellant, by his own admissions and conduct, affirmed that the property belonged absolutely to the deity as a juristic person and could not later claim it as personal property.

A new legal plea regarding acquisition of Bhumidhari rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, cannot be entertained at the appellate stage if not raised in pleadings or before lower courts.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 6
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 18
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 209
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 210
doctrines: Juristic personality of a deity
Estoppel by admission
Constructive dedication of property to religious endowment
Pleas must be raised at the earliest opportunity

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their land by the Gujarat government for an Employees' State Insurance Scheme dispensary and staff quarters, claiming procedural defects and lack of public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition was for a public purpose, including construction of staff quarters under the Employees' State Insurance Scheme
Whether failure to mention superstructures in the Section 4 notification invalidated the acquisition
Whether the inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act was legally conducted and by a competent authority
Whether acquisition of land allegedly used as a burial ground for a public trust violated legal or constitutional principles
holdings: Construction of staff quarters for employees of the Employees' State Insurance Scheme serves a public purpose and is valid under the law.
The notification under Section 4 need not specify superstructures separately, as 'land' includes structures under Section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act.

The inquiry under Section 5A was validly conducted by the City Survey Officer appointed as Collector; subsequent appointment of a Special Land Acquisition Officer with retrospective effect did not vitiate the process.
The land was not being used as a functional burial ground, and its acquisition did not violate any legal or public trust protections.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Colourable legislation
Principles of natural justice in administrative inquiry
Conclusive declaration of public purpose under Section 6

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sued to evict tenants (respondents) from a property leased for 10 years, now occupied for over 30 years, claiming personal need to run a hotel due to insufficient income.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords have a 'reasonable requirement' under Section 11(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 to evict the tenants for own occupation and use.
Whether the balance of convenience favors eviction when tenants have run a hotel for decades but the lease was originally for a fixed term.
Whether the courts below erred in law by not properly weighing the hardship to the tenant against the advantage to the landlord.
holdings: A landlord's need to occupy property for generating essential income constitutes a 'reasonable requirement' under Section 11(h), especially when existing income is inadequate for subsistence.
The balance of convenience must weigh relative hardship to tenant against benefit to landlord; it cannot confer absolute immunity from eviction.
Courts must assess all relevant evidence; failure to do so amounts to a patent error of law justifying Supreme Court intervention under Article 136.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, Section 11(h)
doctrines: Balance of convenience in eviction cases
Reasonable requirement for personal occupation
Patent error of law doctrine
Concurrent findings exception under Article 136

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the constitutional validity and recovery of a sugarcane cess imposed by the State of Madhya Pradesh, arguing it was invalidly assessed and collected without a formal assessment order.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1958, particularly Section 23, was constitutionally valid in imposing a cess based on 'an area' linked to factory premises.
Whether the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961, validly retroactively validated the imposition and collection of the cess despite a prior High Court order quashing the notification.
Whether a formal assessment order was required under the State Act and Rules before recovering the cess.
holdings: The term 'an area' in Section 23 of the MP Act is not synonymous with 'local area' in Entry 52, List II, and thus does not exceed the State's legislative competence.

Section 3 of the Sugarcane Cess (Validation) Act, 1961, validly retroactively validated the imposition, assessment, and collection of the cess, rendering ineffective any prior court order quashing it.

No formal assessment order is required under the MP Rules; the Collector's duty to check returns and issue a recovery notice suffices as assessment when the amount is admitted or determinable from records.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1958, Section 23
Madhya Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Rules, 1959, Rule 60, Rule 61, Rule 62, Rule 63
Constitution of India, Entry 52, List II, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Doctrine of Validation by Subsequent Legislation
Doctrine of Presumption of Constitutionality
Doctrine of Deemed Assessment in Taxing Statutes
