card.dispute: The defendants appealed against a partition decree, contesting that two properties—a house and bakasht lands—were self-acquired, not joint family property by blending.
issues_decided: Whether the house at Sadisopore became a joint family property by blending despite being originally self-acquired
Whether the bakasht lands were rightly held to be joint family property despite being intermediary kasht under the Bihar Land Reforms Act
Whether the plaintiffs' pleadings were sufficient to support a finding of blending in the absence of specific averments
holdings: A property originally self-acquired can become joint family property by blending, and courts may examine evidence of blending if the pleadings broadly allege joint family status.
The house at Sadisopore became a joint family property due to blending, supported by ample evidence, even if the land beneath it was excluded.
Concurrent findings of lower courts on bakasht lands becoming joint property are not disturbed, especially when no cross-objection was filed in the High Court.
doctrines: Doctrine of blending of self-acquired property into joint family property
Principle of constructive res judicata and sufficiency of pleadings
Rule against appellate review of findings without cross-objection

card.dispute: The Board of Muslim Wakfs, Rajasthan claimed certain property as wakf property and included it in the wakf list, while the respondents, who were non-Muslim mortgagee-purchasers in possession, challenged the binding nature of this inclusion.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner of Wakfs had jurisdiction to inquire into whether a property was wakf property when challenged by strangers.
Whether the list of wakf properties published under Section 5(2) of the Wakfs Act, 1954 is final and conclusive against non-Muslim strangers in possession.
Whether the special limitation period under Section 6(1) of the Wakfs Act applies to strangers who are not interested in the wakf.
holdings: The Commissioner of Wakfs has jurisdiction to conduct inquiries into the nature of property as wakf, even if challenged by strangers, as part of the statutory survey and reporting function.

The list of wakf properties published under Section 5(2) is final and conclusive only between the Wakf Board, mutawalli, and persons interested in the wakf; it does not bind strangers, especially non-Muslims in lawful possession.
The one-year limitation under Section 6(1) to challenge the wakf list does not apply to strangers; they may file a suit for declaration of title even after one year.
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of statutory lists only as between specified parties
Doctrine of exclusion of strangers from special limitation periods in religious property laws
Principle of statutory interpretation to avoid infringement of rights of non-minority communities

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a property including a kothi (mansion), while the respondent, a mutawalli of a Shia waqf, claimed it was waqf property acquired with waqf funds and the appellant was merely a benamidar.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed property was the personal property of the appellant or a waqf property acquired through benami transaction on behalf of the waqf
Whether the burden of proof in establishing a benami transaction was properly discharged by the respondent
Whether the findings of the lower courts that the property was acquired with waqf funds could be interfered with in appeal
holdings: Property acquired by a mutawalli using waqf funds is presumed to be waqf property regardless of whose name it is in, and the mutawalli cannot misuse power to benefit one beneficiary unjustly.
The burden of proving a benami transaction lies on the party asserting it, and the source of purchase money is the most important test; here, it was conclusively established as waqf funds.
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts based on evidence, especially regarding benami transactions, are not lightly interfered with by the Supreme Court.
provisions: Waqf Act, 1954 (though not explicitly cited, principles of waqf law under Shia personal law are central)
Evidence Act, Section 106 (burden of proof in benami transactions)
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Presumption of waqf property when purchased with waqf funds
Concurrent finding rule in appellate review

card.dispute: The Collector, Raigarh, appealed against the High Court's enhancement of compensation for agricultural land acquired for railway doubling, arguing that the land should not be valued as a potential building site.
issues_decided: Whether agricultural land can be valued for compensation based on its potential as a building site without evidence of actual building activity or development pressure in the vicinity.
Whether fictitious or collusive sale transactions after knowledge of acquisition can be relied upon to determine market value under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
What method should be used to determine compensation when comparable sales are not reliable and there is no evidence of building potential.
holdings: Land cannot be valued as having building potential unless there is concrete evidence of development pressure, proximity to urban amenities, and actual building activity near the acquired land at the time of notification.

Sale deeds executed by claimants shortly after acquisition notice, especially to associates, are fictitious and inadmissible for determining market value if they lack bona fide intent and real consideration.

In absence of reliable comparable sales or proven building potential, compensation for agricultural land must reflect its actual use, and capitalization method cannot be applied without proof of agricultural income.
doctrines: Principle of willing buyer-willing seller for market value determination
Exclusion of speculative or collusive transactions in valuation
Requirement of factual basis for building potentiality in land compensation
Capitalization of rent method subject to proof of agricultural earnings

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a Hindu widow's adoption of a son and the alienation of properties, claiming the adoption was invalid due to lack of sapinda consent and that the adopted son could not inherit under the will.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption by the Hindu widow was valid without the consent of the husband's sapindas.
Whether the adopted son could inherit under the will's bequest to 'putra pouthra santhathies'.
Whether the life estate of the widow under the will ripened into an absolute estate under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
holdings: A Hindu widow's power to adopt does not require the consent of sapindas if the adoption is for spiritual benefit and not to disinherit them.
The term 'putra pouthra santhathies' in a will includes adopted sons and their descendants, as Hindu law recognises adoption as conferring full filial status.
A life estate created by will does not ripen into an absolute estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if it was not a limited interest created under customary or statutory law.
doctrines: Validity of adoption by Hindu widow
Inclusion of adopted children in testamentary terms
Construction of wills in Hindu law
Doctrine of ripening of estate under Section 14(2)

card.dispute: The appellant sought probate of a will bequeathing him the testatrix's property, while the respondent, her adopted son, opposed it, alleging revocation and lack of testamentary capacity.
issues_decided: Whether a presumption of revocation arises when a will is not found after the testator's death
On whom lies the burden of proving revocation of a will under the Indian Succession Act, 1925
Whether the presumption of revocation can be rebutted by evidence in a given case
holdings: No presumption of revocation arises merely because a will is not found; such a presumption, if any, is weak and rebuttable.
The burden of proving revocation of a will lies on the person opposing probate, under Section 70 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
The presumption of revocation is rebutted where there is evidence of the testator’s consistent intention, no motive to revoke, and access to the will by interested parties.
doctrines: Presumption of revocation of will
Burden of proof in testamentary proceedings
Rebuttable presumption based on circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: The dispute was between a landlord and a tenant firm over whether the landlord could initiate an ejectment action without serving a notice to quit under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act after the lease expired and the tenant became a statutory tenant under the Rent Restriction Act.
issues_decided: Whether a statutory tenant is entitled to a notice to quit under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act before an ejectment action under the Rent Restriction Act can be initiated.
Whether the decree for eviction on grounds of the building being dilapidated and unfit for human habitation was justified.
holdings: A statutory tenant who continues in possession after the lease has determined by efflux of time is not entitled to a fresh notice to quit under Section 106, as the contract of tenancy ends with the determination of the lease under Section 111.

The decree for eviction on the ground that the building was dilapidated and unfit for human habitation was upheld, as findings by lower courts were supported by evidence and not interfered with in special leave appeal.
provisions: East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
doctrines: Statutory tenancy
Determination of lease by efflux of time
Notice to quit not required after lease termination
Principle of finality of factual findings in special leave appeals

card.dispute: Ghansham Dass was convicted of murder for killing Kashmiri Lal during a property dispute over a shop; he claimed self-defence, while the prosecution argued unlawful use of force.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant acted in private defence of property when he caused the death of Kashmiri Lal.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant committed murder under Section 302 IPC.
Whether the plea of self-defence was credible given the nature of injuries and evidence on record.
holdings: A person may use force to protect property against trespass, but not if the trespasser poses no threat of grievous harm or death.
Using a deadly weapon like a chhura to cause fatal injuries exceeds the right of private defence of property when there is no imminent danger of death or serious injury.
The conviction under Section 302 IPC is unsustainable where the accused acted in excessive self-defence; liability falls under Section 304 Part I IPC instead.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Excess in private defence
Burden of proof in self-defence claims

card.dispute: The auction-purchaser challenged the setting aside of a court auction sale, arguing that an application by one judgment debtor under Order 21 Rule 90 barred other judgment debtors from applying under Rule 89.
issues_decided: Whether an application by one judgment debtor under Order 21 Rule 90 bars other judgment debtors from filing an application under Order 21 Rule 89.
Whether an application for depositing money under Order 21 Rule 89 without an explicit prayer to set aside the sale is valid.
Whether the pending Rule 90 application by one judgment debtor invalidates a Rule 89 application by others who made the required deposit.
holdings: An application under Order 21 Rule 90 by one judgment debtor does not bar other judgment debtors from filing a valid application under Order 21 Rule 89.
An application under Order 21 Rule 89 is valid if the purpose is to set aside the sale, even if the prayer does not explicitly state it, provided the required deposit is made.
A proper deposit under Rule 89 benefits all judgment debtors, and the pendency of a Rule 90 application by one does not invalidate the Rule 89 application of others.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 93
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction of procedural rules
Doctrine of substantial compliance with procedural requirements

card.dispute: The widow Hirabai claimed a 7/24th share in joint family property, while her son Gurupad contested this, arguing she was entitled only to a 1/24th share after her husband's death.
issues_decided: Whether the widow's share in coparcenary property should be calculated solely based on her inheritance from her deceased husband's interest, or also include the share she would have received if a partition had occurred during his lifetime.
How Explanation I to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 should be interpreted in determining the share of heirs in Mitakshara coparcenary property.
holdings: The widow is entitled to both the share she would have received if a partition had taken place during her husband's lifetime (1/4th) and her share in his interest upon his death (1/24th), totaling 7/24th.

Explanation I to Section 6 mandates a fictional partition immediately before the coparcener's death, and the legal consequences of that fiction must be fully recognized throughout the calculation of shares.
provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 6 Explanation I
Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3
doctrines: Fiction of partition under Mitakshara law
Statutory fiction and its inevitable consequences
Liberal interpretation to advance legislative intent for gender equality in property rights

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a trustee contested a compromise decree in a prior suit, alleging it was obtained by fraud and collusion, thereby affecting the status of a religious endowment.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree in the earlier suit was obtained by fraud or collusion.
Whether the property dedicated constituted an absolute debuttar or a partial dedication.
Whether Panchanan Biswas was a necessary party to the compromise proceedings.
holdings: The compromise decree was not obtained by fraud, as the circumstances alleged did not firmly establish collusion or deception.
The deed of trust could reasonably be construed as creating a partial dedication, given the settlor's intention to benefit family members.
Panchanan Biswas was not a necessary party to the compromise, as his rights were limited to a fixed annuity unaffected by the decree.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of partial dedication in religious endowments
Fraud must be clearly established to set aside a decree

card.dispute: The appellant Lila Gupta, claiming to be the widow of Rajendra Kumar, fought with his relatives over succession to Bhumidari rights, with the respondents challenging the validity of her marriage on the ground that it was contracted in violation of the proviso to Section 15 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether a marriage contracted in contravention of the proviso to Section 15 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is void or merely irregular and valid for all legal purposes.
Whether the proviso to Section 15 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is mandatory or directory in nature.
holdings: A marriage contracted in violation of the proviso to Section 15 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is not void; the proviso is directory, not mandatory, and does not invalidate the marriage.
The temporary bar on remarriage under the proviso to Section 15 is intended to prevent hasty remarriage and confusion in parentage, but its violation does not render the marriage null and void.
doctrines: Directory vs. Mandatory provision
Validity of marriage under statutory restrictions
Principle analogous to Iddat in Muslim law

card.dispute: The appellant Jai Dutt claimed hereditary tenancy rights over state-owned barren land after 12 years of possession, while the State of U.P. treated him as an unauthorized occupier and sought eviction.
issues_decided: Whether prolonged possession of state land without title or authorization can confer hereditary tenancy rights under Section 180(2) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939
Whether payment of rent by the occupier, without documentary evidence, can convert unauthorized possession into lawful tenancy
Whether the Public Authority was obligated to refer the land status dispute to a Civil Judge under Section 7(1) of the U.P. Land (Eviction and Recovery of Rent & Damages) Act, 1959
holdings: Mere continuous possession of state land without lawful title or grant does not create hereditary tenancy rights under Section 180(2) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, especially when the land is used for public purposes and Section 30 restricts such accrual of rights.
Unauthorized possession remains trespass even after long occupation if no lawful entry or rent payment with proof is shown; revenue records indicating 'bila tasfia' confirm lack of legal title.

The Public Authority is not bound to refer a dispute to a Civil Judge under Section 7(1) unless the objection to eviction is prima facie substantial; a finding of unauthorized occupation based on revenue records suffices to reject referral.
provisions: U.P. Land (Eviction and Recovery of Rent & Damages) Act, 1959, Section 3(1)
U.P. Land (Eviction and Recovery of Rent & Damages) Act, 1959, Section 7(1)
U.P. Land (Eviction and Recovery of Rent & Damages) Act, 1959, Section 2(e), 2(h)
doctrines: Doctrine of adverse possession not applicable to state land used for public purposes
Presumption of lawful state ownership over banjar (barren) land
Harmonious construction of tenancy and eviction statutes to prevent unauthorized occupants from acquiring rights
Principle of omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta (all things are presumed to have been properly done) in favor of public authorities

card.dispute: Family members disputed over the validity of a trust settlement dedicating properties to two charities, including whether properties could be validly dedicated for worship at a samadhi (tomb) under Hindu law.
issues_decided: Whether the dedication of properties for the worship of a samadhi (tomb) of an ordinary ancestor constitutes a valid religious or charitable purpose under Hindu law.
Whether the performance of puja at a family ancestor's samadhi, without proof of community-wide religious practice, can sustain a valid trust.
Whether the doctrine of cy-près can be applied to redirect trust income when the original purpose becomes impracticable.
holdings: A dedication of property for puja at the samadhi of an ordinary deceased ancestor is not a valid religious or charitable purpose under Hindu law unless it is shown to be a recognized religious practice of a substantial section of the community.
The burden lies on the person claiming that worship at a samadhi is a religious practice to prove its widespread acceptance; mere family tradition is insufficient.

Where the original charitable purpose becomes impracticable, the doctrine of cy-près applies to redirect income to purposes as nearly as possible to the settlor’s intention, such as feeding poor schoolchildren.
provisions: Hindu Law, general principles of religious and charitable trusts
doctrines: Doctrine of cy-près
Burden of proof in establishing religious practices
Invalidity of private religious endowments lacking public benefit

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants 2 to 7) challenged the decree of specific performance in favor of the respondents (plaintiffs 1 to 3) who had an agreement to purchase land from the fourth respondent, claiming they were bona fide purchasers without notice despite the plaintiffs' prior possession and agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants 2 to 7 were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the prior agreement and possession?
Whether the plaintiffs' possession and registered usufructuary mortgage amounted to constructive notice to the defendants?
holdings: A purchaser must make due inquiry when the property is in possession of someone other than the seller; failure to do so negates bona fide purchase.
A registered usufructuary mortgage in favor of the plaintiffs put the defendants on constructive notice, and their claim of ignorance was invalid given their false plea of non-possession.
doctrines: Constructive notice
Bona fide purchaser for value
Doctrine of lis pendens

card.dispute: The Oriental Gas Company challenged the validity of the method used by the State of West Bengal to calculate compensation for the acquisition of its gas supply undertaking, particularly the use of capitalisation of net income.
issues_decided: Whether the method of capitalisation of net income for determining compensation under Section 8(1)(b) of the Oriental Gas Company Act, 1970 is valid and relevant?
Whether the choice of the five-year period immediately preceding the takeover for calculating average annual income was arbitrary?
Whether Section 9(2), providing for payment of compensation in bonds with 3% interest over 20 years, violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution?
holdings: Capitalisation of net income is a relevant and sound method for valuing a public utility undertaking, as it reflects the profit-yielding capacity and market value of the business as a whole.
The selection of the five years preceding the takeover to compute average income is not arbitrary, especially since the legislature could have chosen a more disadvantageous period for the company.
The mode of compensation through interest-bearing bonds payable in installments does not violate Article 31(2), as the method and timing of payment are within legislative discretion.
doctrines: Just compensation in acquisition cases must reflect market value
Capitalisation of earnings as a valuation method for public utilities
Legislative discretion in determining compensation structure

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant-cobbler on grounds that the leased shop was being used for residential purposes contrary to its commercial lease, while the tenant argued that incidental residential use was necessary and did not violate the lease.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant used the leased premises for a purpose other than that for which it was let out under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, as applied to Himachal Pradesh.
Whether incidental residential use of a shop by a tenant for cooking and sleeping amounts to a change of purpose justifying eviction.
holdings: The use of a portion of a leased shop for cooking and sleeping by a low-income tenant does not constitute a change of purpose under Section 13(2)(ii)(b), especially when the lease does not specify an exclusive commercial purpose.
Welfare legislation like rent control laws must be interpreted in light of social realities, particularly the living conditions of economically weaker sections in India.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(b)
doctrines: Interpretation of welfare legislation in a Third World perspective
Gandhian talisman as a tool for judicial interpretation in cases of doubt
Social context and life realities shaping legal interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant Sandhya Rani Sarkar sought specific performance of a contract for the sale of immovable property, but the respondents contested on grounds of her lack of readiness and willingness to perform her part of the contract, particularly her failure to deposit the balance of consideration in time.
issues_decided: Whether the decree passed by the trial court was a preliminary decree within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Civil Procedure Code.
Whether the delay in depositing the balance consideration could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Whether the appellant was ready and willing to perform her part of the contract, a necessary condition for granting specific performance.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's decree for specific performance.
holdings: A decree in a suit for specific performance requiring the purchaser to deposit the balance of consideration within a stipulated time, with dismissal in case of default, is not a preliminary decree under Section 2(2) of the Civil Procedure Code.
An order extending time to deposit balance consideration does not amount to an amendment of the decree and does not require condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
The appellant failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform her part of the contract, particularly by not showing she had the means to pay the balance consideration at the relevant time.
The High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court’s decree as the appellant had delayed unreasonably and lacked financial readiness, making specific performance unjust.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Discretionary nature of specific performance relief
Condonation of delay under Limitation Act
Interpretation of preliminary decree under CPC

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Boota Singh and others in a case involving murder, conspiracy, and cheating related to the theft and sale of a taxi.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the accused by rejecting the confessional statement of Boota Singh.
Whether the evidence of identification was properly evaluated by the High Court.
Whether the prosecution proved the offences beyond reasonable doubt, including murder, conspiracy, and forgery.
Whether the High Court erred in reversing the Sessions Court's conviction without displacing its key findings.
holdings: A confessional statement can be relied upon if substantially corroborated by independent evidence, and rejection based on speculation without examining corroboration is erroneous.
Identification evidence, though requiring scrutiny, should not be discarded outright if supported by consistent testimony and procedural fairness.
The prosecution established the offences of murder, conspiracy, cheating, and forgery through reliable and corroborated evidence, including documentary and forensic proof.
The High Court must not reverse a conviction based on conjecture; it must critically assess and displace the trial court's factual findings supported by evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration of confessional statements
Benefit of doubt in identification cases
Standard of proof in appeals against acquittal
Interference with acquittal when High Court misreads evidence

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant based on a compromise decree, which the tenant challenged as a nullity for lack of statutory grounds for eviction under the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a decree based on compromise for eviction of a tenant is a nullity if the court does not record satisfaction about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction
Whether the compromise itself must contain an express or implied admission by the tenant that the landlord is entitled to eviction under the Bombay Rent Act
Whether a compromise decree in an eviction suit can be executed if there is material on record indicating statutory grounds for eviction
holdings: A decree for eviction based on compromise is valid if there is material on record from which the court could be prima facie satisfied about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction, even if no explicit satisfaction is recorded.
The compromise decree is not a nullity if the terms of the compromise, read with other materials, show the tenant's implied admission of liability to eviction under the Rent Act.
Courts may presume that the trial court was satisfied about the lawfulness of the compromise unless the contrary is shown, and need not expressly record satisfaction under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Order 23 Rule 3
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses (Rate Control) Act, 1947 - Section 12(3)(b)
doctrines: Implied admission in compromise
Presumption of judicial satisfaction
Validity of compromise decrees in statutory eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The tenant, Udai Chand, fought against eviction by the landlord's legal representatives, claiming he did not admit ownership of the shop by Bhurdas in the rent note, after having previously contested the landlord's title in lower courts.
issues_decided: Whether the special leave petition should be revoked due to misrepresentation of facts in the grounds presented to the Court.
Whether the petitioner is estopped from challenging the landlord's title after having admitted it in the rent note.
holdings: Special leave granted by this Court can be revoked if obtained by misrepresentation of a material fact, especially when the misstatement concerns a decisive issue in the case.
A party invoking the discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 must come with clean hands; false or misleading statements warrant refusal or revocation of special leave.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Misrepresentation leading to revocation of special leave
Estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellant sued 56 respondents to recover possession of land, mesne profits, and accounts, alleging fraud in the execution and misuse of a Power of Attorney, while respondents claimed the appellant was a benamidar and lacked standing.
issues_decided: Whether the Power of Attorney granted by the appellant was void due to fraud and misrepresentation?
Whether the High Court erred in admitting additional evidence (registered sale deeds) under Order 41, Rule 27, CPC?
Whether the appellant, as a nominal pattadar, was a benamidar and thus barred from claiming ownership?
Whether the appellant's compromise with some defendants rendered the appeal against others infructuous?
holdings: The appellant's conduct, including inviting defendant No. 1 to purchase other lands after allegedly discovering fraud, belied his claim of fraud and invalidated his allegations of lack of authority.
The High Court rightly admitted registered sale deeds under Order 41, Rule 27, CPC, as essential for pronouncing judgment, and their admission justified reversal of the trial court’s decree.

The appellant was not a benamidar because no consideration flowed from his father to support a benami transaction, and the land grant by the Nizam did not satisfy the legal requirements for a benami holding.
A compromise with some defendants on grounds of fraud does not render the appeal against others infructuous, especially when the suit also involved questions of authority and title.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct
Principle of additional evidence in appeal under CPC

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to recover possession of lands, alleging that defendants fraudulently transferred his properties using a power of attorney, while defendants claimed the transactions were valid and the plaintiff was a benamidar.
issues_decided: Whether three co-owners can jointly grant a valid power of attorney under the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882
Whether the appellate court could admit additional evidence under Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC
Whether the plaintiff was a benamidar and thus not entitled to claim ownership
Whether the plaintiff's compromise with some defendants rendered the appeal against others infructuous
holdings: Co-principals may jointly appoint an agent through a power of attorney, and such appointment is valid under Section 2 of the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882.
Order 41 Rule 27 CPC does not give a party a right to produce additional evidence, but the appellate court has discretion to admit it if necessary for justice, especially registered documents.
A benami transaction requires consideration from one person for transfer to another; absence of such consideration means the transferee is not a benamidar.
A compromise with some defendants does not render an appeal against others infructuous if the suit is based on broader grounds like scope of authority and title acquisition.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Principle of joint agency
Appellate discretion in admitting additional evidence
Doctrine of compromise not affecting independent claims

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be hereditary trustees of a deity, sued to set aside sales of trust properties from 1905 and 1947, arguing the transactions were void and not binding on the trust, while respondents claimed the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether Section 52A of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, which removes the limitation bar for suits to recover public trust property, revives an already extinguished right due to adverse possession under the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit was barred by limitation in respect of property 1E, sold in 1947 by the plaintiff who claimed to be the trustee
Whether the right to trust properties 1A to 1H was extinguished prior to the enactment of Section 52A in 1955
holdings: Section 52A of the Bombay Public Trusts Act does not revive a right already extinguished by adverse possession under Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908; it only applies if the right existed when the provision came into force.
A right extinguished by adverse possession before 1955 could not be revived by Section 52A, even if the suit was filed after the provision's enactment.
The plaintiff’s sale of property 1E in 1947 conveyed a good title as he had acquired it by adverse possession long before; thus, the claim could not be revived under Section 52A.
The suit was barred by limitation for all properties, including 1E, as the rights had been extinguished well before 1955.
provisions: Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, Section 52A (as amended by Bombay Act 23 of 1955)
Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, Sections 50 and 51
Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, Sections 79 and 80
doctrines: Extinguishment of right by adverse possession under Section 28 of the Limitation Act
Procedural vs. substantive law in limitation statutes
Non-retroactivity of remedial legislation to revive extinguished rights
Finality of decisions by Charity Commissioner under Sections 79-80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, arguing that the simultaneous issuance of notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the invocation of urgency under Section 17 were illegal.
issues_decided: Whether the simultaneous issuance of notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is valid when the urgency clause under Section 17(4) is invoked and inquiry under Section 5-A is dispensed with.
Whether a difference in the wording of the public purpose stated in the notifications under Sections 4 and 6 invalidates the acquisition.
Whether the delay of nearly six years in filing the writ petition, and the non-takeover of possession within that time, renders the acquisition invalid.
holdings: When the government invokes urgency under Section 17(4) and dispenses with the Section 5-A inquiry, it is lawful to issue notifications under Sections 4 and 6 on the same day, as the public purpose would have been considered at the initial stage.

Minor variations in the description of public purpose between Section 4 and Section 6 notifications do not invalidate the acquisition if the core purpose—soil conservation in the Sukhna Lake catchment—remains the same.

Delay of six years in challenging acquisition after completion of the process, coupled with no objection at the time, renders the challenge inadmissible due to laches, regardless of possession being taken later.
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Colorable Exercise of Power
Strict Compliance with Land Acquisition Procedure

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Bai Vajia, who obtained possession of land in lieu of maintenance under a 1909 decree, fought against Thakorbhai Chelabhai and others over whether she became a full owner of the land under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, after taking possession, thereby enabling her to sell it.
issues_decided: Whether property acquired by a Hindu female in lieu of maintenance falls under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, granting her full ownership?
Whether Section 14(2) of the Act excludes such property from becoming full ownership when acquired under a decree for maintenance?
Whether Bai Vajia, as a widow in possession of land for life with restricted powers, qualified as a 'limited owner' under Section 14(1)?
holdings: Property acquired by a Hindu female in lieu of maintenance is included in Section 14(1) and converts her limited ownership into full ownership, regardless of when it was acquired.
Section 14(2) does not exclude property obtained in lieu of maintenance from Section 14(1), especially when such property is explicitly covered under the Explanation to Section 14(1).

A widow in possession of property for life, with exclusive enjoyment and control but no power to alienate, qualifies as a 'limited owner' under Section 14(1), making her eligible for full ownership under the provision.
provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Explanation to Section 14(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act
Liberal interpretation of statutes to advance gender equality
Legislative intent to abolish artificial limitations on women's property rights

card.dispute: The dispute was between Biswabani (P.) Ltd. and Santosh Kumar Dutta & Ors. over whether the company retained its status as a statutory tenant after an unregistered lease agreement expired, and whether it could be forcibly evicted.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant company continued to be a statutory tenant after the expiry of the original lease and an unregistered subsequent lease agreement.
Whether the failure to register a lease agreement for over one year converts a tenant into a mere licensee or trespasser upon expiry.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act when the appellant did not invoke it.
Whether a defective certificate under Article 133(1) warrants dismissal of an appeal involving a substantial question of law.
holdings: A tenant who remains in possession after the expiry of a lease continues as a statutory tenant under rent control law and cannot be forcibly evicted.
An unregistered lease agreement for more than one year does not destroy the tenant's statutory status; such an invalid lease has no effect on existing tenancy rights.
Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply where the tenant was already in possession and the agreement was not registered; the tenant’s status remains unchanged.
A defective certificate under Article 133(1) does not require dismissal of an appeal if a substantial question of law of public importance is involved; dismissal would be a travesty of justice.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950
doctrines: Statutory tenancy
Part performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act)
Irremovability of tenants under rent control laws
Substantial question of law of general public importance (Article 133)

card.dispute: The Revenue (C.I.T., Madras) challenged the assessment of K. S. Rathnaswamy as a non-resident for certain assessment years, arguing he maintained a dwelling place in India.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was a resident in India under Section 4A(a)(ii) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, based on having a dwelling place maintained for him in India.
Whether mere ownership of a share in a joint family house, with a right to occupy it, constitutes 'maintaining a dwelling place' under the section.
Whether a dwelling place maintained by a family manager for other members can be deemed maintained for the assessee.
holdings: To be a resident under Section 4A(a)(ii), it is not enough to have a legal right to occupy a dwelling; the dwelling must be maintained at the assessee's instance or for his benefit.
Mere coparcenary ownership in a joint family house, without more, does not amount to having a dwelling place maintained for the assessee.
The family house was maintained by the karta for the resident family members, not for the assessee, who stayed there as a guest; thus, it did not satisfy the residency condition.
An assessee’s occasional stays in a family house, treated as hospitality, do not make it his dwelling place under the Act.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Requirement of intention and benefit in maintaining a dwelling place
Distinction between legal right to occupy and actual maintenance of a dwelling

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (father and son) sued the defendant (father's brother) claiming ownership of a house based on a patta, while the defendant claimed it was a benami transaction and the property was jointly acquired by him and his deceased brother.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction under which the patta was granted was a benami transaction
Whether the defendant acquired any proprietary interest in the property by making repairs or contributions
Whether subsequent conduct and declarations of the deceased brother could be used to determine his intention regarding ownership
holdings: A benami transaction occurs when property is bought in another's name without intent to benefit that person; here, the deceased intended to confer absolute ownership on the plaintiff's son, so it was not benami.
Expenditure on repairs by the defendant, without lawful claim or consent, does not create a proprietary interest in the property.
Subsequent conduct and declarations against the interest of the deceased are admissible as evidence to prove intention and can be used against his legal representatives.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20, Rule 12
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Presumption of advancement
Admissibility of admissions against interest

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the dismissal of his eviction application, claiming the tenant failed to pay rent, while the tenant argued he had validly deposited the arrears in court under the Relief Act.
issues_decided: Whether deposit of rent in court under Section 31 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act constitutes a valid tender under the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether the tenant's deposit of rent in the same court where the eviction petition was filed amounted to substantial compliance with the requirement of tender on the first hearing.
holdings: A deposit of rent in the court of the Rent Controller, where the eviction petition is filed, constitutes a valid tender under the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the Rent Act if the amount is available to the landlord at the first hearing.

The tenant's deposit of arrears, interest, and costs in the Rent Controller's court, coupled with notice to the landlord, amounts to substantial compliance with the proviso, even if not physically tendered, thus defeating the ground for eviction.
provisions: East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i) and its proviso
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, Section 31
doctrines: Substantial compliance
Custodia legis
Constructive tender

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, sisters of Dr. Arulmani, challenged the validity of a deed of settlement in favor of her niece, alleging it was obtained by undue influence and misrepresentation.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of settlement dated 20th January 1953 was vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation
Whether the circumstances surrounding the execution of the deed were sufficient to set it aside in the absence of direct evidence
holdings: The deed of settlement was not vitiated by undue influence or misrepresentation, as the evidence showed Dr. Arulmani was a strong-willed person acting out of genuine gratitude.
Mere affection, financial help, and frequent visits by the niece did not, without more, constitute undue influence in law.
doctrines: Undue influence under Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act
Presumption of undue influence in fiduciary relationships
Burden of proof in cases of alleged undue influence

card.dispute: The Gujarat State Transport Corporation challenged the High Court's invalidation of a second Section 6 notification for land acquisition, issued after a long delay following a prior invalidated notification, arguing it was valid under amended law.
issues_decided: Whether the second notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, issued after a 14-year gap from the Section 4 notification, was invalid due to unreasonable delay

Whether the Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, retrospectively validated and governed the time limit for issuing Section 6 notifications in cases where Section 4 notifications predated the amendment
Whether the High Court erred in implying a requirement of reasonable time for issuing Section 6 notifications despite statutory time limits introduced by the 1967 Amendment Act
holdings: A statutory power must be exercised within the time prescribed by law, and if exercised within that period, cannot be invalidated solely on grounds of unreasonable delay.

The Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, set a two-year deadline for issuing Section 6 notifications for lands notified under Section 4 before January 20, 1967, and the October 10, 1967 notification was within this period.
Courts cannot imply a reasonableness requirement regarding timing when the legislature has expressly defined the time frame for exercising statutory power.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4(2)
Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Proviso to Section 6(1)
doctrines: Reasonable exercise of statutory power
Legislative validation of procedural irregularities
Prescription of time limit excludes implication of reasonableness in delay

card.dispute: The landlords sued to evict the tenant and recover possession of a non-residential building, but the suit was affected by amendments to rent control law that withdrew exemption for high-rent buildings and caused pending eviction suits to abate.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, by the 1964 Amending Act, caused the pending eviction suit to abate automatically?
Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to treat the abated suit as a fresh suit against the legal representatives of the original tenant after his death?
Whether parties by consent or conduct can confer jurisdiction on a court when a statute has divested it of jurisdiction?
holdings: The suit abated automatically on June 10, 1964, when the Amending Act came into force, as it expressly provided that eviction proceedings in civil courts for non-residential buildings would abate.
The trial court lacked jurisdiction to treat the abated suit as a fresh proceeding against new parties after 1964; amendment of the plaint and addition of parties could not revive a dead suit.
Parties cannot by consent or acquiescence confer jurisdiction on a court when a statute has withdrawn it; jurisdiction cannot be created by waiver or conduct.
provisions: The Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 30(iii)
The Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(2)
The Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(8)
The Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order IX, Rule 9
doctrines: Abatement of suit by operation of law
Jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent
Statutory tenancy and protection under rent control laws
Doctrine of functus officio

card.dispute: The claimants and the State Government appealed against each other regarding the compensation for acquired land, and the dispute arose over whether the State's appeal abated due to non-impleadment of the deceased claimant's legal representatives in the cross-appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's cross-appeal abated for failure to bring the legal representatives of the deceased claimant on record within the limitation period.
Whether substitution of legal representatives in one of two cross-appeals benefits the other cross-appeal.
holdings: The failure to implead legal representatives of a deceased party in a cross-appeal does not cause abatement if they were already before the court in the other appeal arising from the same decree.

Legal representatives appearing in one cross-appeal are deemed to have had a full opportunity to present their case on both sides, satisfying the object of Order XXII Rule 4 CPC, and thus the appeal does not abate.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 4
doctrines: Substance over form
Continuity of suit in appeal
Principle of opportunity to be heard

card.dispute: The tenant (Kewal Singh) challenged the landlord's (Lajwanti) application for eviction on grounds of bonafide necessity and government quarter allotment, including the validity of the summary procedure under Section 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the deletion of a cause of action from the plaint and later seeking to re-include it violates the principle of constructive res judicata under Order II Rule 2 CPC
Whether Section 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification and providing a summary procedure for eviction
Whether Section 25B amounts to excessive delegation of legislative power
holdings: Withdrawal and subsequent re-filing of a cause of action does not attract constructive res judicata if the application was not pressed and no adjudication occurred on merits.

Section 25B does not violate Article 14 as it creates a reasonable classification based on the special need for speedy eviction in cases of bonafide requirement and includes sufficient procedural safeguards for tenants.
Section 25B does not suffer from excessive delegation because it provides clear guidelines and procedural checks, including revision by the High Court and review by the Rent Controller.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, Section 14(1)(e) and (f)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Doctrine of separation of powers
Summary procedure in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: Traders challenged the validity of increased market fees under the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, arguing that the fees were being used for purposes beyond those permitted by law.
issues_decided: Whether the market fee levied under the Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961 was validly utilized for purposes such as construction of link roads, gober gas plants, and loans to electricity boards.
Whether the increase in market fee from Rs. 2 to Rs. 3 per hundred rupees was justified under the Act.
What principles must govern the valid levy and utilization of market fees under the Act?
holdings: Expenditure from market fees must be directly connected to marketing operations; spending on general development like link roads or animal husbandry is not a valid use of market fee collections.

The increase in market fee to Rs. 3 per hundred rupees is invalid as it was based on an erroneous belief that fees could fund broad agricultural development; only up to Rs. 2 is justified based on actual marketing-related expenses.
Future increases in market fees must be supported by proper budgets, balance sheets, and estimates showing a nexus between the fee and services related to agricultural produce marketing.
provisions: Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, Section 23
Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, Section 26
Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, Section 28
doctrines: Fee must have a direct nexus with services rendered
Principle of permissible public purpose under regulatory statutes
Limits on statutory spending to objects within legislative competence

card.dispute: The plaintiff, P. Mariappa Gounder, sued for specific performance of an agreement to purchase a tile factory, and later sought mesne profits and interest during delayed possession, while the defendants contested the quantum of profits and interest claimed in execution.
issues_decided: Whether mesne profits should be awarded at Rs. 25,000 per annum instead of Rs. 15,000 per annum as determined by the High Court?
Whether interest on mesne profits should be awarded at 6% per annum as awarded by the Trial Court or reduced to 4% as held by the High Court?
Whether interest at 6% per annum should be allowed on Rs. 30,000 withdrawn by the defendant from court deposit and later redeposited after reversal of decree?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to costs in the inquiry into mesne profits and in appeal?
holdings: Mesne profits were correctly fixed at Rs. 15,000 per annum based on the lease rent granted by the Receiver, as no reliable evidence showed higher actual profits.
Interest on mesne profits should be awarded at 6% per annum, as the plaintiff endured prolonged litigation and was entitled to full restitution.
Interest at 6% per annum is payable on Rs. 30,000 from withdrawal to redeposit under Section 144 CPC, as part of restitution for wrongful benefit.
The courts below did not err in denying costs to the plaintiff, considering equitable factors including the death of defendant 3.
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution
Mesne profits assessment based on reliable market evidence
Equitable discretion in awarding costs

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's eviction application on the grounds that the building was not in a dilapidated condition requiring immediate demolition and reconstruction.
issues_decided: Whether the condition of the building is a relevant factor in determining the landlord's bona fide requirement under Section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether a landlord can seek eviction solely based on intention to demolish and reconstruct for business improvement without proving the building's dilapidated state
holdings: The condition of the building is a vital factor, though not a sine qua non, in assessing the landlord's bona fide requirement under Section 14(1)(b); it must be considered along with all circumstances.

The mere intention and financial capacity to reconstruct are insufficient for eviction; the existing condition of the building must be evaluated, especially where the Act does not provide for reinduction of the tenant into the new building.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(2)(b)
Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 15
Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 16
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Statutory interpretation based on scheme of enactment
Relevance of surrounding circumstances in eviction cases

card.dispute: Pramod Kumari Bhatia and others contested Om Prakash Bhatia's claim to a sum of money under a will, arguing over its proper construction and entitlement after the death of the testator and his widow.
issues_decided: Whether the will unambiguously intended Om Prakash to inherit the estate after the life interest of Lakshmi Devi ended
Whether the court can supply missing words in a will to give effect to the testator's clear intention
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to admit additional evidence at a belated stage
holdings: The testator clearly intended that his son Om Prakash should be the sole ultimate owner of the estate after the death of Lakshmi Devi, despite the absence of express words to that effect.
Courts have jurisdiction to supply words in a will when the testator's intention is so clear and certain that no other interpretation is reasonably possible.
The High Court did not abuse its discretion in rejecting a belated application to adduce additional evidence, and the Supreme Court will not interfere in such discretionary orders.
provisions: Indian Succession Act, 1925, Section 63 (though not explicitly cited, governs will construction)
General principles of construction of wills under common law as applied in India
doctrines: Curial draughtsmanship to supply words in a will
Strong probability of intention justifying judicial supplementation of will terms
Deference to discretionary powers of High Court in admitting additional evidence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, but the challenge was dismissed due to undue delay in filing the writ petition.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the writ petition was sufficient ground to dismiss it?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the petition without considering the merits due to unexplained delay?
holdings: Unexplained delay in filing a writ petition challenging land acquisition renders the petition liable to be dismissed, especially when the delay exceeds a reasonable period after knowledge of the acquisition.

The High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition on the ground of delay without examining the merits, as the appellants failed to explain the delay of over 17 months from the date of the award.
doctrines: Undue delay and laches in filing writ petitions
Dismissal of writ petitions on grounds of inordinate and unexplained delay

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (trustees) sued to eject the defendant (a descendant) from rooms in a family house dedicated to a deity, claiming exclusive management rights, while the defendant asserted shebaiti rights as a descendant.
issues_decided: Whether shebaiti rights in a family deity vested in the trustees appointed under the will or in the descendants of the testator.
Whether the trustees could maintain a suit for possession of the debutter property without impleading all co-shebaits.
Whether the will effectively disposed of the shebaiti rights or left them to devolve by operation of Hindu law.
holdings: Shebaiti rights in a family deity are heritable under Hindu law and devolve on the descendants of the founder unless expressly disposed of by the will.
The trustees, though entrusted with management, were not constituted as shebaits; the will did not vest ministrant rights in them, leaving shebaitship with the testator's heirs.
A suit concerning debutter property must include all co-shebaits as parties; trustees alone cannot maintain such a suit when legal title vests in the deity.
provisions: Hindu Law of Inheritance and Religious Endowments
doctrines: Shebaitship as heritable property under Hindu law
Devolution of religious office by operation of law in absence of express testamentary disposition
Necessity of joinder of all co-shebaits in suits affecting debutter property

card.dispute: The dispute was between rival claimants over who was entitled to a ryotwari patta for certain lands in Chittoor district following the abolition of estates under the Madras Estates Act.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide a dispute over entitlement to a ryotwari patta under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
Whether the decision of the Settlement Officer under Section 56 of the Madras Act was final and not subject to judicial review by a civil court
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to entertain disputes regarding who the lawful ryot is for a holding, as such disputes are exclusively adjudicated under Section 56 of the Madras Estates Act.
The decision of the Settlement Officer or Tribunal under Section 56(1) and (2) of the Madras Act is final and cannot be questioned in any court of law, barring civil court intervention.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 56
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Finality of administrative tribunal decisions

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of a contract to buy a plot, but the vendors sold it to the first and second respondents during litigation over title; the dispute was whether the appellant was entitled to specific performance despite the subsequent sale.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deed dated December 6, 1957, in favour of the first and second respondents amounted to an amicable settlement within the meaning of the document dated November 18, 1957, thereby disentitling the appellant to specific performance.
Whether the relief of specific performance should be denied on equitable grounds, including alleged construction on the land or the existence of a damages clause in the contract.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation or the land insufficiently identified to grant specific performance.
holdings: The sale deed dated December 6, 1957, was not an amicable settlement contemplated by the November 18, 1957, document; the vendors breached their contract with the appellant by selling to others before the decree confirming their title.

Specific performance should not be denied; the appellant acted fairly, no hardship to respondents was shown, temporary structures do not bar relief, and the damages clause was for securing performance, not offering an alternative remedy.
The objections regarding limitation and identification of the land were not properly raised in pleadings and lack merit; the parties clearly knew the property in dispute.
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable relief in specific performance
Doctrine of contractual breach despite third-party settlement claims
Doctrine of waiver of technical objections not raised in pleadings

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (Neelavathi and others) sued for partition and separate possession of joint family property, paying court fee under Section 37(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees Act, while the defendants contested the adequacy of the court fee, arguing it should be paid under Section 37(i) based on market value.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were in joint possession of the property so as to attract court fee under Section 37(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act
Whether a mere failure to receive income from joint property amounts to exclusion from possession for the purpose of court fee under Section 37(i)
holdings: The question of court fee must be determined by the allegations in the plaint as a whole, not by isolated statements or the final decision on merits.

A plaintiff remains in joint possession in law unless there is a clear and specific averment of exclusion; non-receipt of income or inability to remain in joint possession does not amount to legal exclusion.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, Section 37(1)
Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, Section 37(2)
doctrines: Legal possession of co-owners: possession of one co-owner is deemed possession of all unless exclusion is proved
Court fee determination based on plaint allegations as a whole

card.dispute: The appellants (Orient Distributors) fought with the Bank of India and others over whether they had a right to continue using a passage on the ground floor opening into Errabalu Chetty Street as part of their lease for the first floor premises.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed passage formed part of the lease (demise) granted to the appellants?
Whether the use of the passage constituted an essential element of the tenancy agreement?
Whether the appellants had an easement of necessity or right of way over the disputed passage?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the lower appellate court's finding on a question of fact?
holdings: The disputed passage did not form part of the lease, as there was no documentary evidence or legal basis to conclude that it was included in the oral tenancy agreement.
The passage was not an essential element of the tenancy, as alternative access was available and the tenancy could function without it.
The appellants had no easement of necessity or right of way, since the property was not landlocked and reasonable alternative access had been provided.
The High Court was justified in interfering with the lower appellate court’s finding because the issue involved a legal conclusion from facts, not pure fact.
provisions: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
doctrines: Easement of necessity
Bare licence vs. easement
Interference by High Court in findings of fact when legal inference is involved

card.dispute: The petitioners, allottees of MIG flats, challenged the Delhi Development Authority's levy of a surcharge on the cost price of flats, alleging discrimination and violation of the 'no profit no loss' principle.
issues_decided: Whether the levy of surcharge on MIG flats by the Delhi Development Authority was discriminatory and arbitrary?
Whether the Authority could legally impose a surcharge contrary to its 'no profit no loss' mandate?
Whether the Vice-Chairman had the authority to fix disposal prices including surcharge?
Whether the surcharge resulted in unlawful profit by the Authority?
holdings: The surcharge was not discriminatory as it was used to subsidize housing for lower-income groups, and differential treatment based on time and location was justified.

The levy of surcharge did not violate the 'no profit no loss' principle because the overall operations of the Authority were deficit-ridden, and the surplus from MIG flats was redirected to subsidize LIG, Janata, and CPS schemes.
The Vice-Chairman had valid authority to fix disposal prices, including surcharge, under delegated powers from the Authority via Resolution No. 20 and Regulation 59.
The claim that the Authority made huge profits due to surcharge was factually incorrect, as evidenced by the Authority’s overall financial deficit.
doctrines: Principle of non-discrimination under Article 14
Delegation of statutory powers
Doctrine of 'no profit no loss' in public housing schemes
Judicial review of administrative pricing decisions

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of premises under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, after a sanctioned temporary lease, while the tenant challenged the validity of the sanction, alleging fraud and collusion.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can challenge the validity of a sanction granted under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, even after taking possession under it.
Whether the executing court can examine if the conditions for sanction under Section 21 were fraudulently or collusively fulfilled.
holdings: A tenant can challenge the validity of a sanction under Section 21, as estoppel does not apply against statutory mandates, especially where fraud or collusion undermines public policy.

The executing court has the jurisdiction to examine whether the twin conditions of Section 21—non-requirment for a particular period and residential use—were genuinely met, and may invalidate a sanction obtained fraudulently.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates legal proceedings
Estoppel does not apply against statutory compliance
Public policy limits private agreements
In pari delicto potior est conditio defendantis (left open)

card.dispute: Two Indian Oil Corporation officers were prosecuted for allegedly abusing their positions to fraudulently award a contract to a contractor and inflate work measurements, leading to criminal convictions under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and IPC, which they appealed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants abused their official position under Section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by facilitating the award of contract to A-4.
Whether the prosecution established a corrupt or dishonest motive based on circumstantial evidence.
Whether the removal and substitution of original documents with fabricated ones was proven beyond reasonable doubt.
Whether the convictions based on measurement certificates and bill sanctions could stand in absence of key witnesses.
holdings: The circumstantial evidence did not establish unerringly that the appellants acted with dishonest or corrupt motive or abused their position.
Abuse of position under Section 5(1)(d) requires clear proof of corrupt intent, which was lacking in this case.
The alleged fabrication of documents prior to August 19, 1965 was contradicted by evidence showing such documents were created only in September 1965, undermining the prosecution's timeline.
Non-production of material witnesses like K. S. Joshi, Ramrao, and others created unbridgeable gaps in the prosecution's case, making conviction unsafe.
doctrines: Test of unerring certainty in circumstantial evidence
Presumption of innocence and benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Requirement of corroborative evidence when key witnesses are not examined
Non-attribution of criminal intent based on routine administrative approvals

card.dispute: The appellants, as intermediary landlords, fought to evict respondents, who were tenants-at-will, from land after the estate had vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord-intermediary was in 'khas possession' of the land within the meaning of Section 6(1)(b) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, at the time of vesting.
Whether a bare right to take possession equates to 'khas possession' under the Act.
Whether a contention not raised before the High Court can be agitated for the first time before the Supreme Court.
holdings: Khas possession under Section 6(1)(b) requires actual, physical control of the land, not merely a legal right to take possession.
A landlord's right to evict a tenant-at-will does not amount to khas possession when the tenant remains in actual, lawful possession.
A contention available but not pressed before the High Court cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, as it is deemed abandoned.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Khas possession requires factual control, not just a legal right
Constructive possession not equivalent to actual possession under land reform laws
Principle of abandonment of grounds not raised in lower courts

card.dispute: The landlord sought to eject the tenant for non-payment of rent arrears, while the tenant claimed protection under the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, having deposited the arrears before the first hearing.
issues_decided: Whether depositing arrears of rent before the first date of hearing, but with knowledge available to the landlord on that date, satisfies the requirement of the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the Act?
Whether a deposit made in the court of the Rent Controller prior to the first hearing qualifies as a valid tender under the proviso even if not made on the exact date of hearing?
Whether the decision in Vidya Prachar Trust v. Basant Ram applies to facts where deposit was made in the correct court and was accessible to the landlord?
holdings: A deposit of arrears of rent made before the first hearing before the Rent Controller is valid if it remains available to the landlord on the date of hearing and the landlord is informed of it.
The proviso to Section 13(2)(i) is satisfied when the tenant deposits the full arrears, interest, and costs in court before the first hearing, as the deposit continues to exist on the hearing date.

The decision in Vidya Prachar Trust is distinguishable and does not apply where the deposit is made in the Rent Controller’s court, is accessible to the landlord, and complies with the statutory conditions.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Proviso to Section 13(2)(i)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 19 read with Section 6
doctrines: Substantial compliance with procedural requirements
Beneficial interpretation of social legislation in favor of tenants
Custodia legis (deposit under legal custody of court)

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat fought with former Taluqdars and Inamdars over whether hilly grasslands incapable of cultivation vested in the government under agrarian reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether hilly grasslands with spontaneous grass growth are 'waste lands' under Section 6 of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949 and Section 7 of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952
Whether such grasslands are 'uncultivated lands' within the meaning of the same provisions
Whether the Explanation to Section 6 and Section 7 applies to lands inherently unfit for cultivation
holdings: The term 'waste lands' refers to desolate, barren, or unused land without vegetation; lands with natural grass growth are not 'waste lands'.
The term 'uncultivated lands' means cultivable land left fallow, not land inherently incapable of cultivation; thus, non-cultivable hilly grasslands do not fall under this category.
The Explanation defining 'uncultivated land' as not cultivated for three years applies only to cultivable land and does not extend to land unfit for cultivation.
provisions: Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, Section 6
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, Section 7
Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, Section 14
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, Section 17
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Principle of ejusdem generis
Rule against anomalous or unjust consequences in interpretation

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat fought with landowners and a cooperative housing society over the validity of a land acquisition notification issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after an earlier invalid notification was cancelled and a fresh one issued.
issues_decided: Whether the second notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was valid after the first notification was cancelled due to invalidity.
Whether the government could issue a fresh notification under Section 6 without reissuing a notification under Section 4 when the earlier notification under Section 6 was invalid.
Whether unreasonable delay invalidated the second notification under Section 6.
holdings: A second notification under Section 6 is valid if the first was invalid and treated as ineffective, as the government retains its power to proceed with acquisition for a public purpose.

The government need not reissue a notification under Section 4 if the earlier Section 6 notification was invalid, because the Section 4 notification remains operative until fulfilled by a valid Section 6 declaration.

Delay between cancellation of an invalid notification and issuance of a fresh one does not invalidate the process, especially when the delay stems from legal challenges and the government continues to pursue the acquisition in good faith.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Validity of administrative notifications
Doctrine of ineffective administrative acts

card.dispute: The grandsons and great-grandsons of Narayanarao sued Krishnabai, daughter of Ramachandrarao, to recover possession of certain lands, claiming they were impartible Watan lands governed by primogeniture, while Krishnabai claimed the lands were her father's separate property following a prior partition.
issues_decided: Whether a partition of the joint family property had taken place prior to the 1902 deed (Ex. 39).
Whether the 1902 deed created a restricted estate in favor of Ramachandrarao and his male descendants or an absolute transfer of property.
holdings: A partition of the joint family status occurred prior to the 1902 deed due to Ramachandrarao's clear intimation to sever, making the joint family status defunct before the deed was executed.
The 1902 deed amounted to an absolute transfer of land to Ramachandrarao, not a restricted estate for maintenance, as there was no reservation of reversionary rights or condition of re-entry.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory provisions, based on traditional principles)
doctrines: Partition by unilateral intention under Hindu Law
Evidence de hors the document to prove true nature of a transaction
Irreversibility of severance of joint family status
Rejection of illusory or colorable devices in property transfers

card.dispute: The State of Punjab sought to acquire land from respondents 1 to 21 for a grain market, which was challenged as being motivated by mala fides to benefit a politically influential individual, Respondent No. 22.
issues_decided: Whether the second land acquisition was vitiated by mala fides and misuse of statutory power.
Whether the invocation of emergency powers under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act to bypass inquiry was justified.
Whether the High Court was right in quashing the acquisition declaration based on uncontradicted allegations of political vendetta.
holdings: The acquisition was invalid due to mala fides, as the uncontradicted evidence showed it was driven by political vendetta and personal motives of an influential individual.
The use of emergency powers under Section 17 to dispense with inquiry was unjustified, as there was no real urgency, and it violated principles of natural justice and Articles 14 and 19.
The High Court rightly struck down the acquisition, as the state failed to rebut serious allegations of misuse of power, especially when the implicated individual did not deny the charges.
doctrines: Mala fide exercise of statutory power
Fraud on power
Principle of natural justice
Judicial review of administrative action
Presumption against denial of hearing in land acquisition

card.dispute: The plaintiffs claimed co-ownership of property purchased by the defendant in a court-ordered auction sale conducted by a Receiver, challenging the defendant's title.
issues_decided: Whether a pure question of law, not raised in lower courts, can be considered for the first time in the Supreme Court.

Whether Section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code bars a suit against a purchaser on the ground that the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff, when the sale was conducted by a Receiver under Order 40 Rule 1 CPC.
holdings: A pure question of law, which does not require factual investigation and goes to the root of the case, may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.

Section 66 CPC does not apply to sales conducted by a Receiver appointed under Order 40 Rule 1, as it requires a purchase certified by the court under Order 21 Rule 94, which is not issued in Receiver's sales.
doctrines: Pure question of law doctrine
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of finality of court-certified sales under CPC

card.dispute: The appellant idol, through its shebait, claimed to retain possession of land under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, after granting a sand-extraction arrangement to the respondents, arguing it was a licence and not a lease, while the respondents claimed a leasehold right.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction dated April 27, 1950 (Ex. I) was a licence or a lease for the purpose of extracting sand from immovable property
Whether the appellant could be deemed to be in 'khas possession' of the land under Section 6(1)(i) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953
Whether the appellant was entitled to retain the land under Section 28 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, if not directly working the mine
holdings: The transaction, though labelled a licence, conferred exclusive possession and a right to extract sand for a fixed term for periodic payment, thus satisfying all essential elements of a lease under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act.
