The appellant cannot be deemed to be in 'khas possession' under Section 6(1)(i) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, as possession was effectively with the lessee, not the intermediary.

The appellant is not entitled to retain the land under Section 28 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, as it did not directly work the mine immediately before the vesting date, which is a mandatory condition.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(c) and (d)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6(1)(i)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 27
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 28
doctrines: Substance over form in interpreting documents
Lease vs licence distinction based on exclusive possession and rights granted
Doctrine of partial consumption of subject-matter in mining leases
Exclusive possession and right to enjoy mineral resources constitute a lease even without formalities

card.dispute: The plaintiffs claimed a 3/4th share in the suit property purchased in a court auction, alleging co-ownership, while the defendant claimed sole ownership as the purchaser in the auction.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs could rely on an unregistered agreement to claim title to the property despite the defendant's confirmed court sale and registered conveyance.
Whether the suit was barred under Section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code, which restricts challenges to court-certified purchases.
holdings: An unregistered agreement cannot create an interest in immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act, but the plaintiffs' claim as co-owners is not solely based on the unregistered agreement and thus the suit is maintainable.

Section 66 of the Civil Procedure Code does not apply to sales conducted by a Receiver appointed by the court, as such sales do not involve a court-issued certificate under Order 21, Rule 94, and thus the suit is not barred.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order 21, Rules 64 to 108
doctrines: Equity cannot override statutory requirements for creation of interest in immovable property
Doctrine of lis pendens
Applicability of Section 66 CPC to court sales

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, Bhim Singh and Himmat Singh, sued Kan Singh for possession of a house in Bikaner and damages, claiming ownership under a 1940 patta, while the defendant contested the title and asserted rights based on alleged contributions and family inheritance.
issues_decided: Whether the suit house was acquired by Bharat Singh in a benami transaction in favour of plaintiff No. 2 (Himmat Singh)?
Whether the presumption of advancement could be rebutted by subsequent conduct or declarations of Bharat Singh?
Whether the defendant acquired any proprietary interest in the suit house by making repairs or reconstructions?
Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to mesne profits for the period the defendant remained in possession?
holdings: The transaction was not benami; Bharat Singh intended to confer absolute ownership of the suit house on Himmat Singh, and the patta evidenced a genuine transfer.
Subsequent conduct or declarations of a party against their own interest are admissible to prove the nature of a transaction and can support the presumption of advancement.
Expenditure on repairs or reconstruction by a person without title does not confer proprietary interest in the property, especially without proof of ownership or consent.
The defendant must pay mesne profits at Rs. 50 per month from September 20, 1956, until possession is delivered, with future profits to be determined by the trial court.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 12
doctrines: Presumption of advancement
Benami transaction doctrine
Admissibility of admissions against proprietary interest
Mesne profits under CPC

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the eviction of a tenant, challenging whether a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was necessary before seeking eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is a prerequisite for seeking eviction under a State Rent Control Act.
Whether a lease must be determined under the Transfer of Property Act before a tenant can be evicted under a Rent Control Act.
holdings: A notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is not necessary to initiate eviction proceedings under a Rent Control Act if the statutory grounds for eviction are satisfied.
Determination of a lease under the Transfer of Property Act is not a condition precedent to eviction; the Rent Control Act provides an independent and sufficient basis for eviction.
doctrines: Statutory override of common law remedies
Interpretation of rent control legislation as providing independent grounds for eviction
Harmonious construction of special statutes with general laws

card.dispute: The deity of a temple and the archakas (priests) fought over whether certain property was granted to the temple or to the archakas' ancestors as a hereditary grant burdened with temple service.
issues_decided: Whether the property in dispute was granted to the temple or to the archakas personally
What is the legal effect of entries in the Inam Fair Register and the inam title deed regarding the nature of the grant
holdings: The grant was not made to the deity but to the archakas personally, as a hereditary inam, burdened with the condition of rendering service to the temple.

Entries in the Inam Fair Register and the inam title deed, including designation as 'Devadayam', hereditary nature, and naming of grantees, indicate a personal grant to service holders, not to the temple.
provisions: Inam Commission Act (if implied by context, though not explicitly cited)
General principles of construction of religious endowments and inam grants
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive trust for religious service grants
Doctrine of interpretation of inam documents based on entries and recitals
Principle that hereditary grants support personal ownership even for religious purposes

card.dispute: The appellant, Yogendra Morarji, was convicted of culpable homicide not amounting to murder for shooting dead Kana during a dispute over unpaid dues, and challenged the conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the accused had a right of private defence of the body under Section 102, IPC
Whether the right of private defence extended to causing death under Section 100, IPC
Whether the act amounted to murder under Section 300, IPC
holdings: The accused had a right of private defence of the body as the circumstances showed a reasonable apprehension of physical harm when five men attempted to intercept his vehicle with a common object to extort money by fear of injury.

The right of private defence did not extend to causing death because there was no immediate apprehension of death or grievous hurt, especially since the assailants were unarmed and the vehicle was enclosed.

The act did not constitute murder under Section 300 IPC but fell under Section 304 Part II IPC as it was not done with intention to cause death or knowledge that death was likely in the absence of such apprehension.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Right of private defence of the body
Proportionality in self-defence
Apprehension of grievous hurt for invoking right to cause death in self-defence

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, and sought to halt ceiling proceedings during ongoing consolidation of land holdings.
issues_decided: Whether the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, is constitutionally valid in light of Article 31A and the doctrine of stare decisis.
Whether ceiling proceedings must be stayed during consolidation proceedings under the Consolidation of Holdings Act.
Whether the enforcement of different provisions of the Act on different dates violates Article 14 on grounds of arbitrariness.
holdings: The constitutional validity of Article 31A, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, is binding under Article 141 and stare decisis, and thus the ceiling law is protected from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

Ceiling proceedings can continue during consolidation because the Explanation to Section 5(2) of the Consolidation Act creates a legal fiction that such proceedings are not declarations of title, and no prejudice occurs due to equivalent land substitution.

The State has reasonable latitude in specifying commencement dates for legislative provisions, and the staggered enforcement of the Act does not violate Article 14, especially given the policy context and practical considerations.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, Section 5(2) with Explanation
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, Section 19(1)(b)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Sections 134-137
doctrines: Stare decisis
Basic structure doctrine
Legal fiction
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Judicial review limitations in socio-economic legislation

card.dispute: The appellant Bai Dosabai and respondents (lessee's successors) disputed the enforceability of a lease-cum-purchase agreement over two plots of land, particularly in light of subsequent land reform legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the lease-cum-purchase agreement became void due to the applicability of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act?
Whether the Gujarat Vacant Lands in Urban Areas (Prohibition of Alienations) Act, 1972, rendered the contract unenforceable?
Whether the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, made performance of the contract impossible and invalidated the decree?
Whether a party who claimed rights under beneficial social legislation could still enforce contractual rights upon being found ineligible for such statutory benefits?
holdings: The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act did not render the contract void or incapable of revival once the Act ceased to apply to the land.
The Gujarat Vacant Lands Act, 1972, though it temporarily prohibited alienation, did not invalidate a prior contract that could be performed after the Act's expiration.

The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, did not automatically nullify the decree; the decree could be modified to comply with the Act by appointing a Receiver to seek exemption under Section 21 and develop the land for housing the weaker sections.
A party seeking benefits under social welfare legislation cannot be denied enforcement of contractual rights merely because they claimed statutory protections that were ultimately inapplicable.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Sections 15 and 21
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act
doctrines: Doctrine of conversion (English law, held inapplicable to Indian property law in this context)
Principle of decree modification to conform with subsequent legislation
Futility avoidance doctrine in appellate adjudication
Preservation of contractual rights despite invocation of statutory benefits

card.dispute: The lessors (appellants) fought with the State of U.P. over entitlement to compensation for buildings and structures on leased land acquired by the government after the lease was terminated.
issues_decided: Whether the termination of the lease resulted in the vesting of buildings and structures in the lessors despite the lessee remaining in possession.
Whether acceptance of rent after the notice of termination amounted to waiver of the notice.
Whether compliance with Section 114A of the Transfer of Property Act was necessary for forfeiture of the lessee's rights in the structures.
holdings: Despite the lessee remaining in possession, the buildings and structures became the property of the lessors upon termination of the lease due to an express contractual clause, entitling them to compensation upon acquisition.
Acceptance of rent after the notice of termination did not constitute waiver because the payments were for use and occupation, and the lessee was treated as a trespasser.
Section 114A does not bar the operation of a contractual forfeiture clause; its non-compliance only affects the right to file an ejectment suit, not the transfer of title under the lease agreement.
doctrines: Contractual stipulations override statutory default rules under Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act
Waiver of lease termination requires clear evidence of intent to continue the tenancy
Distinction between forfeiture of tenancy and vesting of property rights under lease terms

card.dispute: The tenant, Devi Dass, challenged the eviction order granted to landlord Mohan Lal, alleging that the sale of the property to Mohan Lal was a sham transaction aimed at evicting the tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could challenge the validity of the sale deed between the original owners and Mohan Lal despite not being a party to it.
Whether the sale of the property to Mohan Lal was a bona fide transaction or a sham to enable eviction.
holdings: A tenant can challenge the validity of a sale deed if it is alleged to be a sham transaction with no real transfer of ownership, even if the tenant was not a party to the deed.
The appellate courts erred in not allowing the tenant to present evidence on the bona fides of the sale; the trial court must determine whether the sale was genuine based on the evidence.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 (by implication, as applicable)
doctrines: Sham transaction doctrine
Bona fide sale doctrine
Principle of judicial review of factual findings

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, as displaced persons, contested the validity of an auction of disputed property following the retrospective amendment of Rule 30 under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 30 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules could be amended retrospectively to validate auction proceedings?
Whether the auction of the disputed property was valid after the retrospective deletion of Rule 30?
holdings: A statute or rule cannot be given retrospective effect to impair vested substantive rights unless the language of the enactment is plain and unmistakable in showing such intent.
The retrospective deletion of Rule 30 invalidated the auction proceedings, which stood annulled, and the parties were restored to the status quo ante.
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective interpretation of statutes
Doctrine of vested rights
Rule against retrospective operation affecting substantive rights

card.dispute: The landowner appealed against the low compensation awarded for his land acquired for a housing cooperative in Muzaffarnagar.
issues_decided: What was the market value of the acquired land as of the notification date under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether the courts below erred in relying on a prior nominal sale by the appellant for college land to determine market value?
Whether the High Court properly evaluated comparable sale transactions in fixing compensation?
holdings: The market value of the land as of November 25, 1948, was Rs. 2/6/- per sq. yard, considering comparable sales and development potential.
A prior sale of the appellant’s land at a nominal rate for a college was not indicative of market value due to the benevolent intent behind it.
Sale transactions like Plot No. 220 at Rs. 7/- per sq. yard are reliable indicators of market value despite differences in size or features.
doctrines: Market value determination based on comparable sales
Rejection of nominal transactions as benchmarks for compensation
Consideration of development potential and location in valuation

card.dispute: Private mine workers challenged the constitutional validity of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act 1976, claiming discrimination under Article 14 for denying them benefits available to workers in nationalised mines.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Amendment) Act 1976 violates Article 14 by discriminating between workmen in prohibited versus nationalised mines
Whether private mine managements can be deemed custodians under Section 5 of the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act 1973
Whether workmen have a fundamental right to work in mines illegally operated in violation of statutory prohibition
holdings: Section 3(3) of the 1976 Act is mandatory and constitutional, serving public interest in conserving national resources; no violation of Article 14 occurs as the classification is reasonable and based on valid state policy.
Private managements cannot be deemed custodians under Section 5 of the 1973 Act without a formal notification; absence of such notification negates any claim to lawful operation of mines.
No fundamental right to work exists in illegally operating mines; the prohibition on mining except by specified agencies under the 1976 Act overrides any claimed rights of workmen.
doctrines: Doctrine of Classification under Article 14
Doctrine of Deemed Custodianship
Public Interest Litigation and Judicial Restraint

card.dispute: The plaintiff, Gapadibai, fought the State of Madhya Pradesh over the attachment of her house for her husband's government dues, claiming it was her personal property and not liable to attachment.
issues_decided: Whether the house in question was the personal property of the plaintiff or her husband.
Whether the State could attach the property for dues owed by the husband when the property was registered in the wife's name.
Whether the burden of proof lay on the plaintiff to prove ownership or on the State to prove a benami transaction.
holdings: A registered sale deed in the name of the plaintiff creates a presumption of ownership, which the State failed to rebut.
The State cannot attach property registered in the wife's name for the husband's debts unless it proves the transaction was benami.
The burden of proving a benami transaction lies on the party alleging it, and the State failed to discharge this burden with evidence.
doctrines: Presumption of ownership from registered documents
Burden of proof in benami transactions
Error of law in reversal of findings based on no evidence

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the High Court's quashing of land acquisition proceedings, arguing that the acquisition for its benefit should be validated under the amended Land Acquisition Act, while the landowners contended the acquisition was invalid as it was for a private company and possession had not vested in the government.
issues_decided: Whether land acquisition for a private company before July 20, 1962, could be validated under Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962
Whether the acquisition was complete if possession had not fully vested in the government
Whether Section 7 could cure invalidity when the land did not vest in the government
holdings: Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962, can only validate acquisitions made for a company before July 20, 1962, if the land has already vested in the government under Section 16 or 17(1) of the Act.
An acquisition is not complete unless full possession of the land is taken by the government, resulting in vesting of title in the government.
Section 7 cannot validate an acquisition that was not complete at the time of amendment, especially where possession and title remained with the original owners.
doctrines: Vesting of title as a condition for completion of acquisition
Doctrine of validation by curative legislation subject to conditions
Doctrine of completeness of acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: Industrial Supplies Pvt. Ltd. (a raising contractor) fought the Union of India over whether it was an 'owner' under the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, and thus entitled to remove its fixed assets and receive a subsidy payment after nationalisation.
issues_decided: Whether a raising contractor is an 'owner' within the meaning of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, such that its assets vest in the Central Government upon nationalisation.

Whether the subsidy receivable by the contractor from the erstwhile Coal Board for stowing and safety operations was impressed with a trust and thus not available to the Central Government under Section 22 of the Act.
holdings: A raising contractor is deemed an 'owner' under the Act due to the legal fiction in Section 3(n), and thus their fixed assets vest in the Central Government upon nationalisation, even if not actual owners.

The subsidy claimed was a reimbursement for past expenses, not trust-bound 'assistance', and therefore formed part of the mine's assets that vested in the Central Government under Section 22(3) and could be used to meet mine liabilities.
provisions: Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, Section 22(3) and (4)
Coal Mines (Conservation, Safety and Development) Act, 1952, Section 4
doctrines: Legal fiction
Resulting trust
Doctrine of inevitable consequences in statutory fiction

card.dispute: The dispute was between plot purchasers in Mandi Fateh and the State of Haryana over whether the municipal committee was estopped from levying octroi duty despite earlier promises of permanent exemption.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Committee had the legal authority to permanently exempt octroi duty under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel could prevent the State or Municipality from levying octroi duty after making a promise of exemption
Whether an act ultra vires the statutory powers of a municipality can be enforced on the basis of promissory estoppel
holdings: The power to impose or exempt octroi duty lies with the State Government under Section 62A of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, and a municipality cannot make a binding promise to permanently exempt such tax.
The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked against a public authority when the promise is ultra vires its statutory powers and would fetter its public duties.
An act that is ultra vires and void ab initio cannot be enforced through estoppel, even if purchasers relied on the promise to their detriment.
doctrines: Promissory Estoppel
Ultra Vires Doctrine
Doctrine of Non-Fettering of Statutory Discretion

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers of land) fought with the respondent (claiming to be a tenant) over whether the respondent had the right to pre-empt the sale of the land based on his tenancy status.
issues_decided: Whether the entries in revenue records (Jamabandi and Khasra Girdawari) showing the respondent as a tenant are presumptively true?
Whether the burden of proving that the landlord-tenant relationship had ceased lay on the appellants?
Whether the respondent was in continuous possession as a tenant up to the date of the suit?
holdings: Entries in the Jamabandi and Khasra Girdawari are presumptively true under Section 44 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, and this presumption stands unrebutted in the absence of evidence showing falsity.

Under Section 109 of the Indian Evidence Act, once a landlord-tenant relationship is established, the burden lies on the party asserting its termination to prove it; the appellants failed to discharge this burden.
The respondent is presumed to have remained in possession as a tenant until the suit was filed, given the unrebutted presumption from official records and continuous entries.
doctrines: Presumption of truth in official revenue records
Burden of proof in termination of landlord-tenant relationship

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a Hindu widow contested whether a family settlement created coparcenaries among branches of a joint family defined by wives, affecting her right to a share in ancestral property.
issues_decided: Whether a coparcenary can be created between artificial family units based on a father's wives under Mitakshara law in the absence of customary law
Whether the use of the term 'tavazhi' in a will or settlement document indicates an intention to create coparcenary rights rather than tenancy in common
holdings: A coparcenary, being a creation of Hindu law, cannot be formed by agreement between selected members of a joint family; only the entire family or a recognized branch can constitute a coparcenary.

Specifying individual shares in a settlement document results in a division of estate, converting joint ownership into tenancy in common, irrespective of subsequent conduct suggesting joint enjoyment.
The term 'tavazhi' used in a document does not, without more, establish an intention to create coparcenary rights with survivorship; it cannot override the legal effect of defined shares.
provisions: Article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Coparcenary as a creature of law, not agreement
Disruption of joint family status by division of rights and property
Tenancy in common arising from defined shares in a settlement
Irrelevance of subsequent conduct to alter legal effect of partition

card.dispute: A widow claimed joint possession of land against her husband's cousins, who had excluded her from revenue records during consolidation proceedings, alleging fraud and breach of assurance.
issues_decided: Whether non-participation by a co-sharer in rents and profits amounts to ouster and enables another co-sharer to acquire title by adverse possession
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the District Judge’s finding of fraud in the consolidation proceedings
Whether a suit for joint possession is barred by Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
holdings: Mere non-participation in rent and profits by a co-sharer does not constitute ouster; possession of one co-sharer is deemed to be possession of all unless clear ouster is proved.

The District Judge’s finding of fraud in the consolidation process, based on the deletion of the plaintiff’s name without legal authority, is a factual finding binding on the High Court in second appeal.
Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 does not bar a civil suit to establish title unless there is an express statutory bar.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 9
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 49
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
doctrines: Constructive trust by co-sharers
Adverse possession requires clear ouster
Presumption of joint possession among co-sharers
Bar of jurisdiction by statute not presumed

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a shop in Ambala Cantonment on grounds of unauthorized sub-letting, while the tenant claimed no sub-letting occurred as the joint Hindu family was the tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had sub-let the premises in violation of Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Whether the 1949 Act could be retrospectively applied to the Ambala Cantonment via a 1974 notification under the amended Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957
Whether the power to extend rent control laws under the 1957 Act was exhausted by the 1969 notification, precluding a fresh extension in 1974
Whether the phrase 'commencement of this Act' in Section 3(2)(c) refers to the 1957 Act or the 1972 Amendment Act
holdings: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) applies only to sub-letting done after the Act's commencement in the relevant area, and the sub-lease must have been created after that date.
The 1974 notification validly extended the 1949 Act to the cantonment with retrospective effect from 26 January 1950 due to the 1972 amendment empowering retrospective application.
The power under the amended 1957 Act to extend rent laws retrospectively is distinct from the earlier prospective-only power, so the 1974 notification was valid despite the 1969 notification.
The phrase 'commencement of this Act' in Section 3(2)(c) refers to the principal 1957 Act, which was deemed to have commenced on 26 January 1950, not the 1972 amendment.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(a)
Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 3
Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 3(2)
Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 1(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (temporal operation of 'has sub-let')
Doctrine of continuing statutory power

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession of leased land after the tenant defaulted on rent and failed to remove structures post-lease expiry; the tenant challenged the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court to grant possession including demolition of superstructures.
issues_decided: Whether the Small Causes Court had jurisdiction under Section 28 of the Bombay Rents Act to entertain a suit for possession of land with a claim for removal of superstructures.
Whether a composite prayer for possession under both contract and statute takes the suit out of the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court.
Whether the landlord is entitled to vacant possession of the land free of structures after lease termination.
holdings: The Small Causes Court has jurisdiction under Section 28 of the Bombay Rents Act to grant possession of land and incidental relief, including removal of superstructures to make the decree effective.
A composite prayer combining reliefs under contract and statute does not oust the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court if the primary relief falls within its statutory competence.
Upon lease termination, the tenant must deliver vacant possession; failure to remove structures results in loss of rights over them, and the landlord may obtain possession free of superstructures.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
doctrines: Incidental and ancillary powers doctrine
Vacant possession upon lease termination
Forfeiture of lease for rent arrears

card.dispute: Private parties challenged the constitutional validity and interpretation of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, arguing that its mining ban did not apply to coking coal mines.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'coal mining operations' in Section 3(3) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976 includes mining of coking coal.
Whether the legislative history of separate laws for coal and coking coal mines indicates that the 1976 Amendment did not intend to nationalise coking coal mines.
holdings: The term 'coal mining operations' in Section 3(3) of the 1976 Act applies to all forms of coal, including coking coal, as coking coal is a species of coal and coking coal mines are included within the definition of 'coal mine'.

Legislative history may assist interpretation but cannot override the clear, sweeping language of the statute; the 1976 Act represents the culmination of a phased nationalisation policy and must be interpreted to include coking coal mines.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Heydon's rule (mischief rule)
Statutory interpretation: history may illumine but not imprison

card.dispute: The petitioner, a landowner, challenged the constitutional validity of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, arguing that certain provisions violated fundamental rights including the right to property and freedom of trade.
issues_decided: Whether the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, furthers the Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c) of the Constitution.
Whether Section 23(1), (2), and (3) of the Act are constitutionally valid, particularly regarding the disposal of excess land.
Whether Section 27(1) imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to transfer property under Article 19(1)(f).
Whether the compensation mechanism under Section 11(6) renders the acquisition process illusory or confiscatory.
holdings: The Act as a whole is designed to implement Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c) by preventing concentration of urban land and ensuring its equitable use for common good.

Section 23(1), (2), and (3) are ultra vires and invalid because they allow preferential disposal of excess land to private entities, undermining public purpose; however, Section 23(4) is valid as it mandates disposal to subserve the common good.

Section 27(1) is unconstitutional to the extent it restricts transfer of property within ceiling limits, as it imposes an arbitrary and unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f).
The ceiling on compensation under Section 11(6) is not illusory or confiscatory, and the adequacy of amount is non-justiciable due to the 25th Amendment and protection under Article 31-A.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(f)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 11(6)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 23
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27(1)
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Unreasonableness of restrictions under Article 19(1)(f)
Non-justiciability of compensation amount post-25th Amendment
Protection of agrarian and urban reform laws under Article 31-A and 31-C

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the acquisition of their land, arguing that the stated public purpose was a sham to benefit a private company.
issues_decided: Whether a declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive and immune from challenge
Whether the failure of the State to produce documentary evidence about the public purpose allows an inference against it
Whether the burden of proving mala fides or colourable exercise of power lies on the landowners or the State
holdings: A declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is conclusive evidence of public purpose and can only be challenged on grounds of mala fides or colourable exercise of power.
The burden of proving mala fides or colourable exercise of power lies on the landowner; absence of State-produced evidence does not shift this burden or justify invalidating the acquisition.

The court cannot infer mala fides merely from the State's failure to produce evidence when the landowners have not affirmatively proven improper purpose or unsuitability of land for public industrial use.
doctrines: Conclusive presumption of public purpose under Section 6
Colourable legislation doctrine
Burden of proof in challenges to administrative action

card.dispute: The landlords sued to evict the tenants for default in rent, despite the tenants depositing arrears, future rent, interest, and costs before the first hearing; the dispute centered on whether such deposit constituted a valid tender under the Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether deposit of rent under Section 31 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934 constitutes a valid tender under the proviso to Section 13(2) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949
Whether future rent can be validly deposited in court for the purposes of compliance with the proviso to Section 13(2) of the Rent Act
Whether the deposit made before the first hearing, but prior to the filing of the suit, satisfies the requirement of payment or tender 'on the first hearing'
holdings: A deposit of rent under Section 31 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934 is a valid tender under the proviso to Section 13(2) of the Rent Act, as it makes the amount available to the landlord without hindrance.
Future rent can be deposited in court, and such deposit does not violate Section 6 or Section 19 of the Rent Act, especially where fair rent has not been fixed by the Controller.

The proviso to Section 13(2) is satisfied if rent, interest, and costs are deposited on or before the first hearing; a deposit made earlier remains valid and constitutes compliance, as it ensures availability of funds on the hearing date.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 13(2)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 6
East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 19
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, Section 31
doctrines: Valid tender doctrine in rent payment
Social legislation interpretation
Bona fide deposit as compliance
Non-technical construction of tenant protection clauses

card.dispute: The appellants (former owners of coal mines and an engineering workshop) fought with the Union of India over the recovery of dues and compensation related to the nationalisation of coal mines and the takeover of associated properties.
issues_decided: Whether the amounts due to the coal mine owners before the appointed day under the Nationalisation Act vested in the Central Government
Whether the Central Government could use realisations from mine dues after nationalisation to discharge pre-nationalisation liabilities
Whether the Engineering Workshop and residential buildings were part of the coal mine for compensation purposes
Whether the High Court could direct immediate payment of disputed amounts without reference to a Commissioner of Payments
holdings: Dues arising before May 1, 1973 (the appointed day) did not vest in the Central Government due to the 1978 Amendment excluding such current assets from vesting.
The Central Government had authority under Section 19(3) and (4) to collect dues and discharge liabilities of the coal mines until June 30, 1975, as a necessary incident of vesting.
The Engineering Workshop and residential buildings were not part of the coal mine under the Act and thus not entitled to compensation under the nationalisation scheme.
Disputes over dues and liabilities must be adjudicated by a Commissioner of Payments under Section 17, not directly decided by the High Court in mandamus proceedings.
provisions: Coal Mines (Taking over of Management) Act, 1973, Section 3(1)
Coal Mines (Conservation and Safety) Act, 1952, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights under nationalisation laws
Doctrine of necessary implication in statutory interpretation
Doctrine of separation between management takeover and full nationalisation
Principle of pari materia in interpreting similar statutory provisions

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's decision to allow a tenant's application under Section 25 of the Delhi Rent Control Act to recall a warrant of possession, after the tenant's earlier suit was dismissed for non-prosecution.
issues_decided: Whether the application under Section 25 of the Delhi Rent Control Act was barred by the dismissal of the earlier suit for default under Order IX Rule 9 of the CPC
Whether the transfer of tenancy rights by the Official Liquidator to the respondent was voluntary and thus fell within the mischief of Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act
holdings: The dismissal of a prior suit for default under Order IX Rule 9 CPC creates a bar not only for the plaintiff but also for those claiming under him, rendering subsequent applications on the same cause of action impermissible.

A transfer of tenancy rights by an Official Liquidator, even if court-confirmed, is a voluntary act falling within Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act if it results in parting with possession without the landlord’s written consent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order IX Rule 9
doctrines: Res judicata
Order IX Rule 9 CPC bar
Voluntary vs involuntary transfer under rent control law

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent, while the tenant claimed protection under both the Rent Control Act and Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can claim relief under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act when the Rent Control Act provides exclusive grounds for eviction.
Whether the terms of the lease deed or general contract law can override the provisions of the Rent Control Act.
Whether the requirement of notice under the Transfer of Property Act applies when eviction is sought under a Rent Control statute.
holdings: Once the conditions for eviction under the Rent Control Act are met, the tenant cannot claim additional protection under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act.
The provisions of the Rent Control Act override the lease terms and general property law, making them inapplicable to the extent they conflict with statutory safeguards.
Eviction under the Rent Act does not require prior determination of lease under Section 106 or forfeiture under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of double protection
Statutory override of contractual and common law rights
Exclusive jurisdiction of rent control legislation

card.dispute: The tenant, Santosh Mehta, challenged the striking out of her defence in an eviction proceeding on grounds of non-payment of rent, which she had paid to her advocate who failed to deposit it.
issues_decided: Whether the power under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 to strike out a tenant's defence is mandatory or discretionary
Whether the order striking out the defence is appealable despite Section 25B of the Act
holdings: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 confers a discretionary, not mandatory, power on the Rent Controller to strike out a tenant's defence, to be exercised only in cases of willful default or gross neglect.
An order striking out a defence under Section 15(7) is appealable under Section 38, and the bar under Section 25B(8) does not apply when the order is not made under Section 25B.
doctrines: Discretionary power doctrine
Directory vs mandatory provision
Appealability of interlocutory orders
Judicial discretion with social context

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his second appeal, challenging the eviction order passed under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, claiming the landlord’s need for the premises was not bona fide.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal summarily without finding a substantial question of law?
Whether the Rent Control Tribunal's decision to allow eviction on the ground of the landlord's changed circumstances was legally sustainable?
Whether the availability of the ground floor of the landlord's own house affected her bona fide need for the tenanted premises?
holdings: The High Court should have examined whether the appeal involved a substantial question of law concerning the interpretation of Section 14(1)(e) and the standard of proof for bona fide need.

The Tribunal’s reliance on the landlord’s 'natural desire' and 'right to choose' her residence is not a valid ground under Section 14(1)(e) unless supported by evidence of changed circumstances affecting bona fide need.
The question of whether the landlord had alternative accommodation available in her own building must be determined based on clear evidence and proper findings.
doctrines: Bona fide need
Substantial question of law in second appeal
Remand for evidence on specific issues

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of ceiling provisions in the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, arguing they violated property rights and failed to provide compensation for homesteads.
issues_decided: Whether Chapter IIB of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, as amended, violates the second proviso to Article 31A(1) of the Constitution by not providing compensation for homesteads taken under land ceiling laws.
Whether the provisions for determining compensation under Section 14V are illusory or arbitrary.
Whether Section 14M(5), which deems land held by private trusts as held by beneficiaries, violates Article 26 of the Constitution.
holdings: The provisions of Chapter IIB do not violate Article 31A(1) because raiyats are generally allowed to retain homesteads within ceiling limits, and compensation is payable if homesteads are acquired and classified as agricultural land.
Compensation under Section 14V, based on a multiple of net annual income up to twenty times, is not illusory but reflects capitalised value and satisfies constitutional requirements.

Section 14M(5) does not violate Article 26 as private trusts remain subject to state's power of eminent domain, and safeguards in Section 14O(3) allow increased ceiling for religious/charitable purposes when necessary.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, Chapter IIB
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Sections 4, 6, 16, 17
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Rules, 1954, Rule 15
doctrines: Eminent domain
Agrarian reform as a public purpose
Property rights subject to constitutional limitations
Presumption of constitutionality for land reform laws

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and others fought against Vaghela Dayabhai Chaturbhai and others over the validity of a government resolution granting leasehold rights over 'bhatha lands' to harijans, adivasis, backward classes, and cooperative societies without public auction, challenging it as violating equality under Article 14 and the provisions of the Bombay Land Revenue Code.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned Government Resolution deviating from public auction for disposal of bhatha lands violates the Bombay Land Revenue Code and its rules?
Whether the classification in the Resolution favoring certain disadvantaged groups and cooperative societies violates the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution?
holdings: The Bombay Land Revenue Code does not mandate public auction as the sole method for disposing of unoccupied lands; thus, the State's resolution to allocate bhatha lands through a preferential selection process does not violate the Code or its spirit.

The classification in the Resolution based on social and economic disadvantage and membership in cooperative societies has a rational nexus with the object of equitable land distribution and social justice, and therefore does not violate Article 14.
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Classification test for equality
Directive Principles of State Policy
Social and economic justice
Equitable distribution of resources

card.dispute: The descendants of Raja Jugal Kishore Singh claimed inheritance to the Bettiah Raj estate through the doctrine of 'putrika-putra' (appointed daughter's son), while the State of Bihar claimed the estate by escheat after the last holder died issueless.
issues_decided: Whether the family of Raja Dhrub Singh was governed by the Benaras or Mithila School of Hindu law
Whether the practice of 'putrika-putra' adoption was valid and in vogue during the time of Raja Dhrub Singh
Whether Raja Jugal Kishore Singh could be considered a 'putrika-putra' of Raja Dhrub Singh
Whether the appellants' claim based on 'putrika-putra' adoption was legally sustainable
holdings: The family of Raja Dhrub Singh was governed by the Benaras School of Hindu law, not the Mithila School, and thus principles of the latter are inapplicable.
The practice of 'putrika-putra' had become obsolete long before the 18th century and was not part of prevailing Hindu law during Raja Dhrub Singh's time.
No valid appointment of a daughter as 'putrika' to beget a 'putrika-putra' was proven, and the claim rests on inconsistent and imaginative pleadings.
The appellants' claim to the estate through 'putrika-putra' adoption fails, and the estate devolves by escheat to the State.
provisions: Ancient Smritis and Commentaries on Hindu Law
doctrines: Rule of escheat
Doctrine of desuetude (obsolescence of legal practices)
Schools of Hindu law (Benaras and Mithila)
Putrika-putra adoption

card.dispute: The appellant, a quarry leaseholder, challenged the recovery of royalty arrears by the state, seeking to quash the assessment order and restrain recovery through a writ petition, which was dismissed by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether Clause 15 of the lease deed constitutes an arbitration agreement.
Whether the decision of the lessor (State) under Clause 15 is an arbitral award and thus not amenable to challenge under Article 226 of the Constitution.
holdings: Clause 15 of the lease deed, which provides for disputes regarding the lease to be decided by the lessor (Governor) with such decision being final, constitutes an arbitration agreement under the Arbitration Act, 1940.

An arbitral award passed under a contractual arbitration clause between the state and a lessee cannot be challenged in a writ petition under Article 226, as the Arbitration Act, 1940 provides a complete and exclusive remedy.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Minor Mineral Rules, 1961, Rule 24
doctrines: Exhaustive remedy under arbitration law
Finality of arbitral awards
Non-availability of writ jurisdiction to circumvent contractual remedies
Doctrine of exclusion of writ jurisdiction when alternative remedy exists

card.dispute: The State of Jammu & Kashmir challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated in 1955 for land allegedly taken over in 1897, arguing that the land had already vested in the State and no compensation was due.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings under the Jammu and Kashmir State Land Acquisition Act, 1934, were valid when the land had already been resumed by the State in 1897 and recorded as State (Khalsa) land.
Whether the State could be compelled to pay compensation for land it already owned, both in title and possession.
Whether the prior decisions in appeal and review created res judicata or estoppel against the State challenging the acquisition proceedings.
holdings: The land acquisition proceedings were a nullity because the State already held full title and possession of the land since 1897; there was no valid subject matter for acquisition.
The State cannot acquire its own land under the Land Acquisition Act, as it is a contradiction in terms to compulsorily acquire property already vested in the Government.
The findings in earlier appeals did not create res judicata or estoppel, as the question of jurisdiction was not within the scope of the limited appeal under the Land Acquisition Act.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir State Land Acquisition Act, 1934, Section 4
doctrines: Nullity of ultra vires administrative action
Res judicata does not apply to jurisdictional errors
Estoppel does not apply where no change of position results from government action
Principle that government cannot acquire its own land

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh fought Ata Mohd over possession of a plot of land adjoining a public street, claiming ownership and right to evict, while the respondent claimed lawful possession under a lease from the Municipal Board.
issues_decided: Whether the property in dispute vested in the Municipal Board under Section 116(g) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act upon the creation of a public street.
Whether the State of Uttar Pradesh retained ownership of the land despite the vesting of the street in the Municipality.
Whether the State could maintain a suit for eviction and possession of the land after the Municipality had granted a lease.
holdings: The vesting of a public street under Section 116(g) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act is limited to the street qua street and does not transfer absolute ownership of the underlying soil to the Municipality.
The State remains the owner of the land underlying the public street and retains the right to take action if the street is used for non-street purposes or if unauthorized constructions exist.
The State is entitled to maintain a suit for eviction and recovery of possession when the Municipality acts beyond its powers in leasing land it does not fully own.
doctrines: Vesting of property in municipal bodies limited to purpose of use
Ownership of land underlying public streets remains with original owner unless expressly transferred
Municipal authority has only statutory control over streets, not absolute ownership

card.dispute: Coal mine lessees challenged the constitutional validity of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, claiming it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31 by terminating their leases without compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the termination of mining leases under the 1976 Amendment Act amounted to 'acquisition' of property by the State within the meaning of Article 31(2)
Whether the Amendment Act violated the petitioners' rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the Act fell within the protective scope of Article 31A(1)(e), which shields laws providing for the extinguishment of rights in property
holdings: The termination of leases under the Amendment Act did not constitute 'acquisition' of property by the State, as the rights were extinguished without vesting in the State or a state-controlled entity.
The Amendment Act did not violate Articles 14, 19, or 31 because it merely extinguished tenuous post-nationalisation interests and did not acquire property requiring compensation.
The Act is protected under Article 31A(1)(e) as it provides for the extinguishment of rights in property for the purpose of state control over coal mines, not acquisition by the State.
provisions: Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, Section 3(3)(b) and (4)
doctrines: Doctrine of Extinguishment vs. Acquisition
Substance over Form
Protection under Article 31A

card.dispute: The Tulsipur Sugar Co. Ltd. challenged the validity of notifications extending municipal jurisdiction over its factory area and imposing octroi tax, claiming procedural defects.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 3 of the U.P. Town Area Act, 1914 extending the town area to include the sugar factory was valid without affording an opportunity of hearing.
Whether the notification dated December 15, 1959 imposing octroi was invalid due to the omission of the second schedule specifying octroi limits.
Whether the defect in the 1959 notification could be cured by the subsequent notification dated April 14, 1960.
holdings: A notification under Section 3 of the U.P. Town Area Act, 1914 declaring an area to be part of a town area is conditional legislation and not subordinate legislation, so audi alteram partem is not required.
The omission of the second schedule specifying octroi limits in the 1959 notification was not fatal as the intended area was clear from the context and prior notifications.
The defect in the 1959 notification was curable by the 1960 notification incorporating the missing schedule, as the authority's intention was unambiguous and the error was inconsequential.
doctrines: Conditional legislation
Subordinate legislation
Audi alteram partem
Curative defect in statutory notification

card.dispute: Coal mine lessees challenged the constitutional validity of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, which terminated their leases, claiming it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament had legislative competence to enact the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976 under Entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule
Whether the Amendment Act violated the petitioners' fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31 by terminating their mining leases
Whether the termination of mining leases constituted 'acquisition of property' by the State under Article 31, requiring compensation
Whether the Amendment Act could be applied to composite leases involving both coal and fireclay mining
holdings: Parliament had valid legislative competence under Entry 54, List I, to regulate coal mines and mineral development in the public interest, even if such regulation affected state subjects under List II.

The Amendment Act did not violate Articles 14, 19, or 31 because it merely extinguished lessees' rights without transferring ownership to the State, thus falling under the protection of Article 31A(1)(e).
Termination of leases did not amount to 'acquisition' of property by the State, as no rights were vested in the State directly; hence, no compensation was required under Article 31(2).
Lessees with composite coal and fireclay mining leases could continue fireclay mining operations during the unexpired lease term, provided they did not engage in coal mining.
provisions: Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Act, 1976, Section 3(3)(b) and (4)
doctrines: Doctrine of pith and substance
Doctrine of extinguishment vs. acquisition of property
Doctrine of legislative competence under Union and State Lists
Principle of protection under Article 31A(1)(e) for laws affecting property rights

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from part of the residential premises, but the Rent Controller rejected the application on the ground that partial eviction was not legally permissible; the High Court reversed this in revision, leading to a challenge on the maintainability of revision against a non-eviction order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court has revisional jurisdiction under Section 25B(8) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1970, to review an order of the Controller refusing to grant possession to the landlord?
Whether an order refusing eviction qualifies as an 'order for the recovery of possession' under Section 25B(8), thereby attracting the bar on appeal and enabling revision?
Whether the High Court's revisional order was invalid for not explicitly incorporating the six-month stay on execution under Section 14(7) of the Act?
holdings: The phrase 'order for the recovery of possession' in Section 25B(8) includes orders both granting and refusing eviction, as excluding refusal orders would create discriminatory appeal rights and violate constitutional principles.
Section 25B(8) provides an exhaustive remedy by way of revision before the High Court for all orders passed under Chapter IIIA, replacing ordinary appeal rights under Sections 38 and 39 of the Act.

An order of the High Court in revision need not explicitly state the six-month stay under Section 14(7); the statutory prohibition operates automatically, rendering the order unenforceable during that period regardless of express mention.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional avoidance
Doctrine of statutory interpretation to avoid discrimination
Exhaustive statutory remedy doctrine
Automatic operation of statutory bars to execution

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, arguing they violated fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31, and questioned the validity of constitutional amendments protecting such laws via Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, as amended, violates Articles 14, 19, or 31 of the Constitution
Whether constitutional amendments placing laws in the Ninth Schedule are immune from judicial review if they damage the basic structure of the Constitution
Whether the doctrine of stare decisis applies to uphold the validity of Articles 31A and 31B
Whether Article 31C, as originally enacted, is constitutionally valid without violating the basic structure
holdings: The Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, as amended, does not violate Articles 14, 19, or 31 and is valid in law.
Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule via constitutional amendments made on or after April 24, 1973, are not immune from challenge if the amendment damages the basic structure of the Constitution.
The doctrine of stare decisis applies to uphold the validity of Article 31A, as affirmed by a 13-Judge Bench in Kesavananda Bharati and reaffirmed in Ambika Prasad Mishra.
Article 31C, in its unamended form prior to the 42nd Amendment, is valid and does not destroy or damage the basic structure of the Constitution.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961
House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Doctrine of stare decisis
Prospective overruling
Judicial review of constitutional amendments

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of a tenant for rent default and applied for allotment of the vacant property under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, but a third party claimed tenancy rights and challenged the allotment.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 16(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act can be made before actual vacation of the premises
Whether the Eviction Officer was required to hear the third party before allotting the vacant premises
holdings: An application under Section 16(1)(a) is maintainable even if the premises are about to fall vacant and not yet actually vacated, as the statute contemplates anticipated vacancies.
The Eviction Officer was not obligated to hear a third party with no legal right or possession over the premises after lawful possession had been delivered to the landlord.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 16(1)(a)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'about to fall vacant'
Principle of futility of hearing a party without legal standing

card.dispute: The dispute was between two members of a Hindu joint family over whether the Nagaruntari estate was impartible under customary primogeniture and whether a maintenance grant (khorposh) gave the defendant rightful possession of certain lands.
issues_decided: Whether the Nagaruntari estate was an impartible estate governed by the rule of primogeniture
Whether the defendant's possession under an unregistered khorposh deed was lawful or that of a trespasser
Whether the plaintiff could maintain a suit for possession and mesne profits without seeking partition
holdings: The Nagaruntari estate was an impartible estate governed by customary primogeniture, and the right of succession followed lineal primogeniture, with junior members entitled only to maintenance.
A member of the joint family in possession under a khorposh grant, even if unregistered, is not a trespasser, and his possession cannot be disturbed by a suit for possession and mesne profits.
The proper remedy for the plaintiff, if disputing the extent of a maintenance grant, was to file a suit for partition, not a claim for possession of specific plots and mesne profits.
provisions: Chota Nagpur Encumbered Estates Act, 1876, Section 12A
doctrines: Rule of primogeniture in impartible estates
Right of maintenance as an incident of joint family membership
Right of survivorship in impartible estates
Incorporation of self-acquired property into an impartible estate
Alienability of impartible estates by gift or will in absence of contrary custom
Use of unregistered documents for collateral purposes

card.dispute: The appellants, including the widow and minor children of a deceased tenant, challenged their eviction based on an ex parte decree, claiming they were not properly served and that their tenancy rights had been transmitted by law.
issues_decided: Whether the ex parte decree against the minor children and widow of the deceased tenant should be set aside due to improper service and inadequate representation of minors.
Whether the tenancy rights of the deceased tenant were transmitted to his widow and minor children under the Rent Act.
holdings: The ex parte decree was set aside because the minors were inadequately represented by a court-appointed guardian with no real interest in the case, and service was ineffective despite being formal.

Tenancy rights under the Bombay Rents Act are transmitted by operation of law to family members residing with the tenant at death, including minor children, who thus have a legitimate stake in the tenancy.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel & Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(c)(i)
Bombay Rents, Hotel & Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel & Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
doctrines: Transmission of tenancy by operation of law
Court's duty as parens patriae to protect minors' interests in litigation
Inefficiency of formal service and nominal guardianship in cases involving minors

card.dispute: The dispute was between tenants and an auction-purchaser over whether the purchaser was entitled to physical or symbolic possession of property bought in a court sale.
issues_decided: Whether an auction-purchaser is entitled to physical possession under Order XXI Rule 95 of the CPC when the property is occupied by tenants who are not judgment-debtors or their representatives.
Whether the provisions of Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act apply to leases created during the pendency of a mortgage suit when the auction-purchaser is not a party to the original suit.
Whether an auction-purchaser can claim physical possession against tenants whose tenancy was created after a compromise decree but before the sale.
holdings: An auction-purchaser is not entitled to physical possession under Order XXI Rule 95 if the property is occupied by tenants not claiming under the judgment-debtor after attachment; symbolic possession under Rule 96 is sufficient.
Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act does not automatically void leases created during pendency of a suit when the auction-purchaser is an outsider not bound by the suit’s outcome.

Tenants in lawful occupation at the time of sale are entitled to retain possession until their tenancy is lawfully determined; the auction-purchaser cannot claim immediate physical possession from them.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order XXI Rules 95 and 96
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act)
Rule of symbolic vs. actual possession in court sales
Principle of privity of contract and constructive notice in mortgage enforcement

card.dispute: Mahboob Saheb and others contested whether the High Court could interfere in a second appeal on factual findings regarding property partition and benami transactions.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reappreciate evidence and reverse a finding of fact regarding partition in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Whether the High Court could pass an order adverse to a party not impleaded in the second appeal
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or reverse a concurrent finding of fact in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved; no such question existed here.
The High Court acted illegally by affecting the rights of the 7th defendant who was not impleaded in the second appeal and thus not a party to the proceedings.
doctrines: Limitation on second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Principle of no adjudication against non-parties

card.dispute: The dispute was between cultivating tenants and landlords over whether the tenants could be evicted for arrears of rent, and whether the Revenue Divisional Officer (RDO) had the power to pass a composite order allowing time for payment before eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the Revenue Divisional Officer can pass a composite order directing payment of arrears within a time frame and ordering eviction in default under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955
Whether the RDO is obligated to grant time to a defaulting tenant to deposit arrears of rent before eviction
Whether the assignment of rent arrears by the previous landlord validly entitled the new landlord to seek eviction
holdings: The RDO has discretion under Section 4(b) of the Act to allow time for deposit of arrears, but is not obligated to do so; the use of 'may' makes it discretionary, not mandatory.

A composite order that allows time for payment and threatens eviction in default is not valid unless the RDO first decides to allow the eviction application; the order must be sequential, not combined.
The assignee of rent arrears is entitled to enforce payment and initiate eviction proceedings for unpaid assigned rent under the Act.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 4(a) and (b)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation (difference between 'may' and 'shall')
Discretionary power of administrative authorities
Assignment of rent and its enforceability by assignee

card.dispute: The dispute was between a co-operative housing society and landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the state government for the society's benefit.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 is mandatory and must be complied with before issuing a notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 when land is acquired for a company or society.
Whether the failure to comply with Rule 4 resulted in a violation of natural justice and rendered the acquisition proceedings invalid.
Whether the respondent was a 'person interested' entitled to object to the acquisition under Section 5A of the Act.
holdings: Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 is mandatory, and its non-compliance invalidates the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The Collector must conduct an inquiry under Rule 4 and consider whether the company made reasonable efforts to acquire the land by negotiation, and failure to do so results in failure of justice.
The respondent, as a purchaser of lessee rights and in possession of the land, is a 'person interested' under Section 3(b) of the Act and entitled to raise objections.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Mandatory compliance with procedural safeguards in land acquisition
Doctrine of failure of justice due to non-compliance with statutory requirements

card.dispute: The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, led by Gulam Abbas, fought the State of U.P. and others over their right to perform religious rites during Moharram on certain wakf properties without interference from Sunni Muslims or restrictive orders under Section 144 Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners' right to perform religious rites on wakf properties is enforceable under Article 32 of the Constitution despite prior litigation.
Whether an order under Section 144 Cr.P.C. can lawfully restrict customary religious practices protected under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution.
Whether the present petition is barred by res judicata or principles analogous to it due to earlier judicial decisions.
holdings: The Shia community has established customary rights to perform religious rites on specified wakf properties, which are protected under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution and enforceable through a petition under Article 32.

Orders under Section 144 Cr.P.C. must be exercised with caution and in a manner that protects, rather than suppresses, fundamental religious rights; such orders should only prohibit religious practices as a last resort when public order cannot be maintained otherwise.

The petition is not barred by res judicata because the parties in the current case are different and fresh evidence, not available earlier, has been presented, making the earlier decisions inapplicable to bar the present relief.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Muslim Wakf Act, 1960, Section 29
doctrines: Res judicata
Fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26
Customary religious rights as part of fundamental rights
Principle of finality of litigation
Guidelines for executive use of Section 144 Cr.P.C. in religious contexts

card.dispute: The landlords sued for ejectment of the tenant based on alleged wilful default in rent payment after sending a notice by registered post that was refused by the tenant; the dispute centered on whether refusal of a registered notice imputes knowledge of its contents.
issues_decided: Whether refusal of a registered notice demanding rent and termination of tenancy imputes knowledge of its contents to the tenant.
Whether failure to serve a valid notice under the U.P. Cantt. (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1952 vitiates eviction proceedings for default in rent payment.
Whether the rent was payable monthly, thereby attracting the provisions of Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Act.
holdings: Refusal of a registered post notice does not, by itself, raise a legal presumption that the tenant had knowledge of its contents, especially in rural or illiterate settings.
Service of notice under Section 20(2)(a) is a condition precedent for eviction on grounds of rent default; non-service invalidates the eviction decree.
Where rent is payable annually, not monthly, Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Cantt. Act does not apply to justify eviction for default.
provisions: U.P. Cantt. (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1952, Section 20(2)(a)
doctrines: Condition precedent to jurisdiction
Presumption of knowledge under Section 114 of the Evidence Act
Proper service of notice

card.dispute: The heirs of Irshad Ali Khan challenged the determination of ownership and cultivating possession of land under the Uttar Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, arguing that Mumtaz Ali did not continue in cultivatory possession until the Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Mumtaz Ali continued to be in cultivatory possession of the land until his death or until the coming into force of the Ceiling Act in 1961?

Whether the prescribed authority and District Judge properly considered the claim that Mumtaz Ali had transferred land to his grandsons or that there was a partition between Mumtaz Ali and Irshad Ali?
holdings: The appeal is allowed and the case remanded because neither the District Judge nor the prescribed authority made a clear finding on whether Mumtaz Ali remained in cultivatory possession of the land up to 1961, which is central to determining ceiling limits.

The prescribed authority must re-examine the appellants' contention that Mumtaz Ali had partitioned the land with Irshad Ali and that his grandsons had purchased portions of the land as early as 1957.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10(2)
doctrines: Remand for proper adjudication of factual issues
Necessity of independent judicial determination of cultivatory possession under land reform laws

card.dispute: The heirs of Jitendra Chandra Bose contested the probate of a will executed by Ranendra Bose, claiming lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence by the propounder Manindra Chandra Bose.
issues_decided: Whether the testator had the requisite testamentary capacity to execute the will on November 8, 1952
Whether the will was executed under undue influence or suspicious circumstances
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's refusal to grant probate
holdings: A testator is presumed to have testamentary capacity unless proven otherwise, and medical conditions alone do not disprove such capacity if there is no evidence of impaired mental faculties.

Mere suspicious circumstances are insufficient to invalidate a will; the court must assess whether they affect the genuineness of execution, and normal choices of scribes and witnesses do not raise suspicion.
An appellate court may reverse a trial court’s finding if the latter relied on speculative inferences rather than direct evidence, especially when the evidence overall supports the will's validity.
doctrines: Presumption of testamentary capacity
Reasonable skepticism in cases of alleged suspicious circumstances
Appellate review of findings based on documentary inference

card.dispute: The landlord, Bharat Sahay, sought eviction of tenant Jain Malleables under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, on grounds of personal requirement due to an obligation to vacate government accommodation, which the tenant challenged based on a later government notification allowing continued occupation under certain conditions.
issues_decided: Whether the second government notification dated 14-7-1977 nullified the landlord's obligation to vacate government accommodation, thereby disentitling him from seeking eviction under section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the landlord remained entitled to seek eviction under section 14A despite having the option to continue occupying government accommodation under modified rent conditions.
holdings: The second notification dated 14-7-1977 did not cancel but only modified the earlier obligation to vacate government accommodation by introducing a graded rent structure, and thus did not negate the landlord's right to seek eviction under section 14A.

A landlord who owns a house and is subject to an obligation to vacate government accommodation—either under general notification or special order—remains entitled to seek eviction under section 14A, even if given an option to continue occupancy by paying penal rent.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation: harmonious construction of notifications and statutory provisions
Doctrine of option versus obligation: mere availability of an option to continue in government accommodation does not extinguish prior obligation to vacate
Doctrine of accrued right: right to eviction under section 14A depends on existence of obligation, not on exercise of option

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide requirement and reconstruction, while the tenant argued the landlord already had suitable alternative accommodation and thus could not claim eviction under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's acquisition of possession from another tenant in the same building amounts to having 'reasonably suitable non-residential accommodation of his own' under Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing leave to amend the written statement under Order VI Rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code
Whether the landlord's requirement for personal use must exist at the time of final disposal of the eviction proceeding
holdings: For eviction under Section 12(1)(f), the landlord’s bona fide requirement must exist at the time of final disposal of the appeal or revision, not merely at the time of filing the suit.
The High Court erred in refusing the amendment to the written statement, as the availability of alternative accommodation is a material fact that must be considered if it arises during litigation.
The question of whether the accommodation obtained by the landlord is reasonably suitable for his claimed purpose must be determined by the trial court based on evidence, and cannot be assumed.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(h)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 18
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Continuing requirement doctrine in eviction cases
Liberal amendment of pleadings to serve justice
Concurrent findings of fact binding on higher courts unless perverse

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the validity of eviction proceedings based on a notice sent by registered post that he refused to accept, arguing that refusal cannot impute knowledge of the notice's contents.
