issues_decided: Whether refusal of a registered postal notice by a tenant amounts to service and imputes knowledge of its contents under the U.P. Cantonment Act and Evidence Act.
Whether willful default in rent payment can be established solely on the basis of non-acceptance of a registered notice.
Whether service of notice under Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Cantonment Act is a condition precedent for eviction on grounds of rent default.
holdings: Refusal of a registered postal notice does not automatically impute knowledge of its contents, especially in Indian socio-cultural context where many refuse such letters due to fear or illiteracy.
A tenant cannot be deemed a willful defaulter merely on the basis of refusing a registered notice without proof of actual knowledge of its contents.
Service of notice as required under Section 20(2)(a) is a condition precedent to eviction for rent default; non-compliance renders the eviction proceedings invalid.
provisions: U.P. Cantonment (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952, Section 14(1)
U.P. Cantonment (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1952, Section 20(2)(a)
doctrines: Condition precedent to jurisdiction
Presumption of knowledge under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act
Service of notice by registered post and its legal effect
Rejection of Western legal presumptions in favor of Indian social realities

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Sheo Dularey Misra's widow challenged the sale of joint Hindu family property by her son Parmeshwar Din Misra, claiming it was not for legal necessity, while the purchaser (K.C. Kapoor) defended the sale's validity.
issues_decided: Whether the property in Lucknow was acquired with joint Hindu family funds and thus formed part of the joint family estate
Whether the sale of the Rae Bareli property by the karta was for legal necessity and justified under Hindu law
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the trial and first appellate courts
holdings: A property acquired by a coparcener using joint family funds, even if not directly traceable, can be presumed to be joint family property when there is a sufficient nucleus of joint family assets and no evidence of separate income.

A sale of joint Hindu family property by the karta is valid if it constitutes an act of prudent management and is for the family's benefit, even without urgent financial distress, satisfying the doctrine of 'kutumbarthe'.
The High Court cannot interfere in second appeal with concurrent findings of fact based on good evidence unless a substantial question of law is involved under Section 100 CPC.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family and Alienation by Karta
doctrines: Legal necessity in alienation of joint Hindu family property
Kutumbarthe (for the benefit of the family)
Presumption of joint family character of property from common nucleus
Estoppel by conduct in pleadings and evidence

card.dispute: The tenant (M.M. Quasim) fought against eviction by landlords (Manohar Lal Sharma & others) who claimed personal requirement and rent default, but a partition had allotted the property to a non-party.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords could continue eviction proceedings after the suit property was allotted exclusively to a non-party in a partition decree.
Whether the landlords had a bona fide personal requirement for the shop given they owned other premises.
holdings: A landlord cannot maintain an eviction suit after losing title to the property through partition, unless the transferee is impleaded or rights are reserved; this must be examined on remand.

A landlord’s claim of personal requirement must be scrutinized in light of available vacant properties; courts must consider the social purpose of rent control laws and not allow evasion through arbitrary choice of premises.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 2(d)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(c)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(d)
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes with regard to legislative object and social context
Fettering of landlord's unfettered right of re-entry under rent control laws
Doctrine of remand when title and maintainability of suit are in doubt

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be a tenant entitled to protection under the Rent Act, while the respondent sought to terminate the 'leave and licence' agreement and recover possession, invoking an arbitration clause.
issues_decided: Whether the Court of Small Causes has exclusive jurisdiction to decide disputes between landlord and tenant under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether an arbitration clause can oust the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court in matters covered by the Rent Act.
Whether the dispute between the parties falls within the ambit of the Rent Act, thereby rendering arbitration inoperative.
holdings: The Court of Small Causes has exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes concerning tenancy and possession under the Bombay Rents Act, and such matters cannot be referred to arbitration.
An arbitration clause in a 'leave and licence' agreement is inoperative if the dispute pertains to tenancy rights created under Section 5A of the Bombay Rents Act.
The social objective of tenant protection under the Rent Act overrides private agreements to arbitrate, as arbitration would deprive tenants of statutory safeguards.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of statutory tribunals
Public policy against ousting tenant protections
Inoperability of arbitration clauses in tenancy disputes under rent control laws

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent arrears, while the tenant claimed waiver due to standing surety for the landlord's sales tax dues and later claimed relief under a statutory provision for depositing money at first hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord waived the right to seek eviction by inducing the tenant to stand surety for sales tax arrears?
Whether the tenant was entitled to relief from eviction under Section 20(4) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act by depositing Rs. 1,980 at the first hearing?
holdings: No waiver occurred because the landlord did not accept any payment from the tenant nor agreed to adjust sales tax liability against rent, and the tenant had not pleaded waiver in his written statement.

The tenant failed to comply with Section 20(4) as the deposit was not unconditional, was not proven to be made at the first hearing, and did not include the full amount of rent, damages, interest, and costs as required.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
doctrines: Waiver by conduct
Strict compliance with statutory conditions for relief from eviction

card.dispute: The sons of the Karta and his brother challenged the sale of joint family property by the Karta and his brother to discharge debts incurred in a new personal business.
issues_decided: Whether the alienation of joint Hindu family property by the Karta and his brother to discharge debts from a new personal business was valid.
Whether the debt incurred by the Karta was an antecedent debt binding on his sons under the doctrine of pious obligation.
Whether the sale could be upheld despite inadequate consideration.
Whether the brother of the Karta could validly alienate his sons' shares in the joint family property for the Karta's personal debts.
holdings: An alienation of joint family property to discharge a debt is valid if the debt is antecedent in fact and time and not for an immoral purpose, especially when incurred by the father, whose sons are bound by pious obligation.
The doctrine of pious obligation applies regardless of whether the father is the Karta, as it arises from the father-son relationship and not managerial status.
Even if legal necessity or pious obligation exists, alienation of joint family property for inadequate consideration cannot be upheld as it is imprudent and not for the benefit of the coparceners.
A brother of the Karta cannot alienate his sons' shares to discharge the Karta's personal debts, as he lacks the privilege to bind his sons for another’s antecedent debt.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory provisions, based on customary and case law)
Constitution of India 1950, Article 136 (implied by Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction)
doctrines: Pious obligation of sons to pay father's antecedent debts
Antecedent debt must be independent of and prior to the alienation
Legal necessity and prudent management in alienation of joint family property
Inadequate consideration vitiates alienation even for legal necessity

card.dispute: The mortgagor and a subsequent purchaser sued the mortgagee for a decree of redemption, while the mortgagee claimed protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act due to part performance of an unregistered sale agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee was entitled to protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act despite non-registration of the sale deed
Whether continued possession by a mortgagee under a mortgage with possession can amount to part performance of a subsequent sale agreement
Whether acts like stamp purchase and draft preparation before execution of agreement constitute acts in furtherance of the contract under Section 53A
Whether a decree-holder purchasing property in a court auction during appeal is entitled to protection if the decree is later set aside
holdings: Section 53A protection is not available to a mortgagee in possession under a mortgage when that possession is not referable to a sale agreement but to the mortgage itself.
Acts done before the formation of a contract, such as buying stamps or drafting a sale deed, cannot be considered acts in furtherance of the contract under Section 53A.
Possession under a mortgage with possession does not transform into possession in part performance of a sale agreement merely by an oral agreement to sell.

A decree-holder who purchases property at a court auction during appeal cannot claim equitable protection if the decree is later set aside, especially when no stay was obtained and the sale was for a nominal value.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIII Rule 11A
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A
Equity of redemption
Voidness of transfers during attachment before judgment
Protection of bona fide purchasers in execution sales

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, which imposed residency and occupation conditions for personal cultivation of land, alleging violations of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(e), and 19(1)(g).
issues_decided: Whether the proviso and explanation added to Section 2(8) of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955 by the 1977 Amendment violate the right to reside and settle under Article 19(1)(e) and the right to carry on any occupation under Article 19(1)(g)?
Whether the said proviso and explanation are arbitrary and discriminatory under Article 14?
Whether sub-sections (3), (4), and (5) of Section 20B inserted by the 1972 Amendment are constitutionally valid?
holdings: The restriction requiring a tenant to reside in the locality for the greater part of the year and derive principal income from agriculture is a reasonable restriction under Articles 19(4) and 19(5), as it serves the public interest of promoting agrarian reform and maximizing agricultural production.

The provision does not violate Article 14 as it applies uniformly to all tenants and has a rational nexus with the goal of ensuring that land is cultivated by actual tillers, without arbitrariness or discrimination.

The sub-sections (3), (4), and (5) of Section 20B of the 1955 Act, inserted by the 1972 Amendment, were upheld as valid, though the Court observed their harshness and recommended a review by the state government.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, Section 2(8) Proviso and Explanation
West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, Section 20B(3), (4), (5)
Constitution of India, Ninth Schedule, Entry Nos. 60 and 81
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(4) and (5)
Test of reasonableness from State of Madras v. V.G. Row
Harmonization of Fundamental Rights with Directive Principles
Equality under Article 14 and absence of arbitrariness

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and rival bidders fought over whether a lease for sand and mineral excavation should be granted through auction or by application.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of a lease for mineral extraction should be made through public auction or by application.
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the lease granted without an auction.
holdings: Public auction is the just and legal method for granting mineral extraction leases to ensure transparency and maximize public benefit.
The State must conduct an auction between rival claimants with a reserved minimum bid to safeguard public interest, even if prior grants were made otherwise.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Rule under relevant notification
doctrines: Public trust doctrine
Principle of transparency in disposal of public resources
Doctrine of fair competition in government licensing

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the quashing of land acquisition proceedings initiated for constructing food grain storage godowns for the Food Corporation of India, arguing whether the Corporation qualifies as a 'Company' under the Land Acquisition Act and whether the acquisition was lawful.
issues_decided: Whether the Food Corporation of India is a 'Company' within the meaning of section 3(e) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the land acquisition for the Food Corporation of India was in accordance with law.
holdings: The Food Corporation of India is a 'Company' under section 3(e) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as it is incorporated by an Indian law and possesses corporate attributes like perpetual succession, power to hold property, contract, and sue or be sued.

The acquisition of land for the Food Corporation of India is invalid as it did not comply with the mandatory provisions of Chapter VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which apply when land is acquired for a company.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'company' based on incorporation by Indian law
Distinction between government departments and autonomous statutory corporations
Requirement of compliance with procedural safeguards in land acquisition for companies

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu banned private leasing of black granite quarries through Rule 8-C, leading private applicants to challenge the rule's validity and its retroactive application to pending lease and renewal applications.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 8-C of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, is ultra vires the rule-making power under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether Rule 8-C violates Articles 301 and 303 of the Constitution by restricting trade and commerce
Whether Rule 8-C applies to applications for renewal of leases
Whether pending applications made before Rule 8-C came into force must be decided under pre-existing rules
holdings: Rule 8-C is valid as it falls within the rule-making power conferred by Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals Act, which allows regulation including prohibition in the public interest.
Rule 8-C does not violate Articles 301 and 303 because it is a law made under parliamentary authority and justified under Article 302 for public interest in mineral conservation.
Rule 8-C applies to renewal applications because a renewal is effectively a fresh grant and must comply with current rules.
Applicants have no vested right to have applications decided under old rules; disposal must follow the law in force at the time of decision, even with delays.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, Rule 8-C
doctrines: Regulation includes prohibition when necessary for public interest
Subordinate legislation is part of the statute if not excluded by express provision
No vested right in grant or renewal of government leases
Prospective application of rules to pending administrative decisions

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over whether mining rights based on a Portuguese-era 'Title of Manifest' could be enforced against the Indian government after Goa's acquisition, and whether the respondent was entitled to a mining lease over the same area granted to the appellant.
issues_decided: Whether rights accrued under Portuguese mining laws survived the acquisition of Goa by India and could be enforced against the Indian government.
Whether the continuation of old laws under the Goa, Daman and Diu Administration Act and Regulation implied recognition of pre-existing mining rights.
Whether the Indian government was obligated to recognize or act upon pending mining applications made under the Portuguese regime.
holdings: Rights accrued under Portuguese law did not automatically survive after Goa’s annexation; they required explicit recognition by the Indian government, which did not occur.
The mere continuation of pre-existing laws under the Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962 does not amount to recognition of rights accrued prior to December 20, 1961.
Applications for mining concessions based on Portuguese-era titles were deemed lapsed, and the Indian government was not bound to consider them under the Mines and Minerals Act and Rules.
provisions: Goa, Daman and Diu Administration Act, 1962, Section 5(i)
Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962, Section 2(a), 3(1), 4(2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 21
doctrines: Doctrine of continuity of laws post-conquest
Doctrine of recognition of rights by successor states
Doctrine of deemed rejection of administrative applications

card.dispute: The landlord sought ejectment of the tenant's family members from a tenanted property, claiming the tenant had ceased to reside there after moving to Canada, and that his family members could not be considered 'members of the family' under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the mother, brother, and sister of a tenant who migrated abroad could be considered 'members of the family' residing in the tenanted premises under Section 14(1)(d) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the landlord had fulfilled the conditions for ejectment under Section 14(1)(d) when family members continued to reside in the premises after the tenant's departure.
holdings: The term 'family' under Section 14(1)(d) includes blood relatives such as parents, siblings, and children, even if the tenant has left the household, provided they reside in the premises.
The landlord cannot obtain ejectment under Section 14(1)(d) if members of the tenant’s family continue to reside in the premises, as the premises are not deemed vacated.
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of beneficial legislation
Wider meaning of 'family' in rent control laws
Presumption against eviction when family members continue residence

card.dispute: Western Coalfields Ltd. challenged the Special Area Development Authority's power to levy property tax on leased lands used for coal mining, arguing it was beyond the State's legislative competence due to central laws on mineral regulation.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Area Development Authority has the power to levy property tax under the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973,
Whether the State's power to impose property tax on lands used for coal mining conflicts with the central legislation on regulation and development of mines,
Whether the property tax imposed is a tax on land or a tax on mineral rights,
Whether the Authority waived its power to tax through an agreement with the company.
holdings: The Special Area Development Authority has the power to levy property tax as it exercises municipal functions under state law.

The State's power to impose property tax under Entry 49, List II, does not conflict with Parliament's power over mines under Entry 54, List I, as taxation is outside the occupied field of mine regulation.
Property tax is a tax on land, not on mineral rights, and is valid even on land used for mining if it is based on annual letting value.
The Authority did not waive its taxing power, as the agreement only referred to octroi tax, and the Chairman lacked authority to waive all taxes.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, Section 69(d)
Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, Sections 127A, 147 Explanation
Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Sections 135, 136, 141
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 2
doctrines: Pith and substance
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of occupied field
Doctrine of waiver by estoppel

card.dispute: Babu Lal challenged the High Court's order granting possession to Hazari Lal and others in execution of a decree for specific performance of a sale agreement, arguing that possession could not be granted without amending the plaint.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could grant possession in execution of a decree for specific performance without a separate prayer for possession in the plaint?
Whether amendment of the plaint is necessary before granting possession in execution proceedings under Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act?
Whether Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act allows for delivery of possession in the same suit without a separate suit?
holdings: The High Court can grant possession in execution of a decree for specific performance even if the plaint did not originally include a prayer for possession, to prevent multiplicity of proceedings.
Amendment of the plaint is not a mandatory precondition for granting possession in execution; courts have jurisdiction to allow such amendments at any stage, including during execution.
Section 28(3)(b) of the Specific Relief Act permits the court to award possession in the same suit upon payment of consideration, and Section 28(4) bars a separate suit for such relief.
doctrines: Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings
Amendment of pleadings to meet ends of justice
Continuing jurisdiction of court over specific performance decrees

card.dispute: The tenant, C.D. Korpal, fought against the eviction suit filed by the landlords, Capt. A.K. Madan and others, who claimed eviction on grounds of bona fide personal requirement.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Rent Controller erred in refusing leave to the appellant to defend the eviction suit?
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the revision application challenging the refusal of leave to defend?
holdings: The court held that where eviction is sought on the ground of bona fide personal requirement and the tenant disputes that ground, leave to defend should generally be granted to allow a full hearing on the merits.
The refusal to grant leave to defend in such circumstances is unjust, and the appellate court must intervene to ensure fair opportunity to the tenant to contest the claim.
doctrines: Principle of fair hearing
Judicial discretion in granting leave to defend

card.dispute: A landlord filed criminal complaints against a tenant and others after losing rent control proceedings over the allotment of a vacated premises.
issues_decided: Whether the criminal court could take cognizance of an offence under Section 201, IPC, based on the complaint?
Whether the allegations in the complaint amounted to an offence under Section 199, IPC?
Whether the invocation of criminal proceedings was an abuse of the process of law?
holdings: No cognizance could be taken under Section 201, IPC, as the complaint lacked any specific allegation about destruction of evidence of a known offence.
Mere rejection of a statement in civil proceedings does not make it false for prosecution under Section 199, IPC; specific falsity supported by contradictory evidence must be shown.
The criminal proceedings were an abuse of the judicial process, especially after the complainant lost in civil and rent control forums and used criminal law to harass the opponents.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 15
doctrines: Abuse of process of law
Requirement of specific averments for perjury under Section 199, IPC
Cognizance requires prima facie material, not just section numbers

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of the tenants on the ground of bona fide personal requirement, while the tenants claimed the premises were let for both residential and commercial purposes, barring eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants were entitled to leave to defend the eviction petition based on the dual purpose of letting (residential and commercial)?
Whether the landlords' claim for eviction on grounds of personal requirement required a full trial considering the tenants' defence?
holdings: Leave to defend should have been granted because the tenants raised a triable issue that the premises were let out for both residential and commercial purposes, which could bar eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.

The Rent Controller must decide whether the landlords' requirement is bona fide and whether the letting was primarily commercial, after affording the tenants an opportunity to file a written statement.
doctrines: Leave to defend in eviction proceedings
Bona fide requirement of landlord
Dual purpose of letting (residential and commercial)

card.dispute: The appellant claimed he was adopted by Jagannathdas and Premwati and thus entitled to half the estate, while the respondents contested the adoption and validity of his claim.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was validly adopted by Jagannathdas and Premwati.
Whether the appellate court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on the fact of adoption based on oral evidence.
Whether a declaration in a trust deed amounts to a valid partition of joint family property without notice to the co-sharer.
holdings: The fact of adoption must be proved like any other fact, and the physical act of giving and taking in adoption is essential; the trial court's finding based on credible oral evidence must be respected.
An appellate court should not re-appreciate oral evidence and overturn trial court findings unless there is a clear error or special circumstance affecting witness credibility.
A mere declaration in a trust deed by one coparcener expressing intention to separate does not effect partition without communication of that intention to the co-sharer.
doctrines: Re-appreciation of oral evidence by appellate courts
Requirement of communication for severance in a Joint Hindu Family
Proof of adoption as a fact requiring credible evidence

card.dispute: The landlady sought to evict the tenant on grounds of unauthorized subletting under the East Punjab Urban Land Restriction Act, 1949, after the contractual tenancy ended, while the tenant claimed subletting was done with written consent during the tenancy and was lawful.
issues_decided: Whether subletting a portion of the premises with the landlord's written consent during the contractual tenancy becomes unlawful upon the tenancy's expiry and grounds for eviction under Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the Act
Whether the mere continuance of a sub-tenant in possession after the tenant becomes a statutory tenant amounts to fresh subletting without consent
Whether tape-recorded conversation can be relied upon as evidence in eviction proceedings
holdings: Subletting done with the landlord's written consent during the contractual tenancy does not become unlawful upon the tenancy's determination and does not constitute a ground for eviction under Section 13(2)(ii)(a).
The continued possession of a lawfully inducted sub-tenant after the tenant becomes a statutory tenant does not amount to fresh subletting, and thus cannot be a basis for eviction.
Tape-recorded conversations, without corroboration or proof of authenticity, are not reliable evidence and cannot form the basis of an eviction decree.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Land (Restriction on Letting) Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(a)
doctrines: Statutory tenancy protection
Lawful sub-tenancy with consent
Corroborative nature of electronic evidence

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be the adopted son of Jagannathdas and Premwati and challenged the validity of a trust created by Jagannathdas, seeking partition and possession of half the estate, while the respondents contested the adoption and the claim.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was validly adopted by Jagannathdas and Premwati on September 24, 1951
Whether the trust created by Jagannathdas was valid and whether it effected a partition of his property from the appellant's share
Whether the appellant's suit was barred by limitation
holdings: The adoption of the appellant by Jagannathdas and Premwati was validly proved and must be recognized, as the trial court correctly found.
A mere declaration in a trust deed without communication to the co-sharer does not amount to a valid partition under Hindu law.
The suit was not barred by limitation as the cause of action arose only when the appellant's rights were infringed by the trust's creation and denial of status.
doctrines: Doctrine of separation in a joint Hindu family requiring communicated intention
Presumption of validity of adoption when supported by evidence and circumstances
Relation back of adoption to the date of ceremony or execution of adoption deed

card.dispute: The Housing Cooperative Society and a member sought to eject the appellant, a licensee and nominal member, from a flat after termination of a leave and licence agreement, raising questions about jurisdiction under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act and the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a dispute over ejectment of a licensee by a housing cooperative society and its member falls under 'dispute touching the business of the society' under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960
Whether Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 ousts the jurisdiction of the Registrar under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960
Whether the decision in Sabharwal Brothers v. Guna Amrit Thandani is applicable to the present facts
holdings: A claim by a tenant co-partnership housing society and its member for ejectment of a licensee who ceased to have lawful possession touches the business of the society under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960.
Section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act does not bar proceedings under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act when the parties do not stand in a landlord-tenant relationship.

The decision in Sabharwal Brothers is distinguishable where the society had let the flat to the member under Form-A regulations, as such letting affects the society's business, unlike in cases of outright sale.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(4A)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Res judicata
Obiter dicta
Non obstante clause reconciliation

card.dispute: The landlord (HUF) sought possession of premises under Clause (e) of the proviso to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, alleging bona fide need, while the tenant contested the application, claiming the landlord was not entitled to eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller must consider the landlord's rebuttal to the tenant's affidavit when deciding on leave to contest under Section 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
Whether the grant or refusal of leave to contest under Section 25B(5) requires a hearing in accordance with principles of natural justice?
Whether the test under Order XXXVII Rule 3(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to applications under Section 25B(5)?
holdings: The Rent Controller must consider the landlord's rebuttal and afford both parties a hearing before deciding on leave to contest under Section 25B(5), as principles of natural justice require a fair opportunity to respond.

The grant or refusal of leave under Section 25B(5) is a crucial stage requiring application of judicial mind and compliance with natural justice, including hearing both parties and examining all material.

The test of 'triable issues' under Order XXXVII Rule 3(5) of the CPC does not apply to Section 25B(5), as the statutory language and purpose differ, focusing only on whether the tenant's facts would disentitle the landlord to possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXVII Rule 3(5)
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Summary procedure in rent control legislation
Literal vs. purposive interpretation of statutes
Burden and standard of proof in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent, but the tenant argued the notice demanding 'damages for use and occupation' instead of 'rent' was invalid under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the notice demanding 'damages for use and occupation' satisfies the requirement of a notice demanding 'rent' under proviso (a) to section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
Whether the High Court erred in holding the notice invalid on a technical ground.
holdings: A notice demanding 'damages for use and occupation' at a rate equivalent to agreed rent, issued after termination of tenancy, amounts to a valid demand for rent under section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
The High Court took an unduly technical view; the substance of the notice, not its label, determines its validity when it effectively demands payment equivalent to rent from a statutory tenant.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, Section 14(1) proviso (a)
Delhi Rent Control Act, Section 14(2) proviso
doctrines: substance over form
statutory tenant liability
hypertechnical interpretation disfavored

card.dispute: The judgment-debtor's successors contested the maintainability of an execution petition for possession, claiming that a compromise in execution proceedings created a fresh lease, thereby extinguishing the original eviction decree.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise in execution proceedings extinguished the original eviction decree and created a fresh lease in favour of the judgment-debtor.
Whether the decree-holder could maintain an execution petition for possession after the judgment-debtor's failure to pay monthly damages as per the compromise.
holdings: The compromise did not create a fresh lease but provided a mode for discharging the original eviction decree, as the intention of the parties was to allow the judgment-debtor time to vacate without ruining his business.
The use of the term 'damages' instead of 'rent' and the decree-holder’s right to execute the decree upon default confirm that the decree remained enforceable and was not replaced by a new tenancy.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 10
doctrines: Intention of the parties governs the effect of a compromise in execution proceedings.
A compromise does not extinguish a decree unless it clearly creates a new contractual relationship such as a lease.

card.dispute: The Archaka (priest) of a temple challenged the validity of a government order granting land patta to the temple, claiming hereditary ownership of the land under an inam title deed burdened with temple service.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant Archaka was entitled to challenge the Deputy Tehsildar's order despite not appearing in the suo motu enquiry?
Whether the prior judicial determination regarding the nature of the inam as granted to the appellant's ancestors was binding on the revenue authorities?
holdings: Failure to appear in a suo motu enquiry does not bar a person from later challenging the order if substantial justice demands reconsideration.
Where prior judicial findings establish the inam was granted to the ancestors of the appellant and not the deity, the revenue authority must reconsider the matter in light of such evidence.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Inams Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1956, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Principle of constructive res judicata
Interest of justice overriding technical dismissal
Binding nature of civil court findings on revenue authorities in respect of title

card.dispute: The widow of Appanna (Jr) sued for partition and possession of a half share in family properties, which the defendants resisted by claiming a prior partition and later a family settlement.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of Appanna (Jr) by Appanna (Sr) was valid?
Whether a prior partition in 1914 barred the plaintiff's claim?
Whether the compromise decree of 1931 affected the joint family status between Jogulu and Appanna (Jr)?
Whether properties acquired by Jogulu were joint family properties?
holdings: The adoption of Appanna (Jr) by Appanna (Sr) was valid, making him a coparcener in the joint family.
The 1914 partition did not finally sever the joint status as subsequent conduct showed continued unity.
The 1931 compromise decree treated Jogulu and Appanna (Jr) as jointly entitled, implying continuation of joint family interests.
Properties acquired by Jogulu were presumed to be from joint family income and thus joint family property.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of coparcenary by birth
Presumption of joint family property in case of acquisitions by a member

card.dispute: The Gujarat State Financial Corporation refused to disburse a sanctioned loan to Lotus Hotels Pvt. Ltd., which had acted on the promise of the loan to set up a hotel, leading to a dispute over whether the corporation could be compelled to perform the agreement via a writ of mandamus.
issues_decided: Whether the sanction of a loan by the Corporation was conditional upon re-financing by IDBI
Whether a writ of mandamus lies to enforce specific performance of a contractual obligation by a state financial corporation
holdings: The loan sanction was not conditional upon IDBI re-financing; the obligation to disburse was independent and binding regardless of re-financing, with only interest and commitment charges affected by IDBI's decision.

A statutory corporation like the Gujarat State Financial Corporation, being an 'other authority' under Article 12, cannot arbitrarily renege on a solemn promise; promissory estoppel applies, and mandamus can enforce performance of statutory duties arising from such promises.
doctrines: Promissory Estoppel
Arbitrariness in State Action
Mandamus for Performance of Statutory Duty

card.dispute: The tenant of a commercial premises in Madras fought against eviction sought by the landlord-waqf on grounds of material alteration and residential use of non-residential premises.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of an additional room on the first floor materially altered the building and impaired its value and utility.
Whether the tenant's use of the premises for occasional stay by himself and his servants constituted a change of user from non-residential to residential purpose.
holdings: The construction of an additional room did not materially impair the value or utility of the building, and thus did not justify eviction.
Occasional use of space by the tenant and servants for resting or guarding valuables does not amount to residential use, and hence does not constitute a breach of a non-residential tenancy agreement.
The court set aside the eviction order and allowed continuation of tenancy upon agreed rent enhancement and payment of arrears.
provisions: Rent Control Act applicable in Madras at the time
doctrines: Doctrine of change of user in tenancy law
Doctrine of material alteration under rent control legislation

card.dispute: The heirs of Haji Umar Kasam sued the Union of India to recover possession of properties in Junagadh that were taken over as evacuee property after 1947, claiming they were wrongfully deprived of their ancestral property.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question were validly declared as evacuee properties under the Junagadh Act and later under the central Evacuee Property Act.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to adjudicate on the status of evacuee property and the validity of orders passed by the Custodian.
Whether the vesting of the properties in the Custodian was valid despite any prior procedural irregularities or lack of proper declaration.
Whether the subsequent notification under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extinguished the appellants' rights in the properties.
holdings: Properties taken over under the Junagadh State Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 1948 and later deemed vested under the central Act were validly evacuee properties, and such vesting could not be challenged in civil court.
Civil courts lack jurisdiction to question the status of evacuee property or the legality of Custodian orders due to statutory bars under Sections 28 and 46 of the Evacuee Property Act.
Section 8(2A) of the Evacuee Property Act validates all prior vesting actions, even if defective, by deeming them valid and retrospective, preventing re-litigation.

Publication of a notification under Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extinguishes all private rights in the property, which then vest absolutely in the Central Government.
provisions: Junagadh State Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 1948, Section 16
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8(2), Section 8(2A), Section 16, Section 27, Section 28, Section 46
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
doctrines: Deeming fiction
Retrospective validation
Jurisdictional bar on civil courts
Doctrine of extinguishment of title by statutory notification

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction for criminal conspiracy and fraud in deceiving an illiterate woman into signing a sale deed by misrepresenting it as a police complaint, thereby depriving her of her agricultural land.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that a criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC was hatched to defraud Smt. Ghogari by obtaining her thumb impression on a sale deed through misrepresentation.
Whether the conviction of the appellants could be sustained based on the evidence of the approver (P.W. 5) and the principal witness (P.W. 27, Smt. Ghogari).
Whether the prosecution's failure to provide the defence with the earlier statements of the approver resulted in a denial of fair trial rights.
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the charge of criminal conspiracy and fraud beyond reasonable doubt due to material contradictions and omissions in the testimony of the principal witness.
The evidence of the approver, who turned hostile 20 months after the incident and whose earlier statements were withheld, cannot be relied upon to sustain a conviction.
The prosecution's non-disclosure of the approver’s earlier statements deprived the defence of a valuable right and warranted an adverse inference, undermining the reliability of the prosecution case.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Adverse inference from non-disclosure of evidence
Distrust of approver's testimony
Corroboration requirement for interested witnesses

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 32(b) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, which exempted buildings constructed on or after August 26, 1957, from rent control, alleging it violated Article 14 by creating an arbitrary classification.
issues_decided: Whether Section 32(b) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification among landlords based on the date of construction.
Whether the invalidity of Section 32(b) renders the entire Act unconstitutional or whether the provision is severable.
holdings: Section 32(b) violates Article 14 as it creates a privileged class of landlords without rational basis, since the incentive to construct new buildings no longer justifies continued exemption after a long lapse of time.

The invalid portion, Section 32(b), is severable from the rest of the Act, which remains valid and operative as it forms a complete and independent code capable of enforcement without the struck-down provision.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 32(b)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 26
doctrines: Doctrine of Reasonable Classification
Doctrine of Severability

card.dispute: The dispute was between a retired armed forces member and a tenant over whether the former could evict the latter under Section 13A1 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, after acquiring the property post-retirement.
issues_decided: Whether a retired member of the armed forces who acquired property after retirement is entitled to seek eviction under Section 13A1 of the Bombay Rents Act?
Whether the plaintiff had a bona fide need for the premises under Section 13(1)(g) of the Act?
holdings: Section 13A1 applies only to members of the armed forces who were landlords of the premises while in service, not to those who acquired title after retirement.
The plaintiff failed to prove a bona fide need for the premises, and the High Court's finding on this was upheld.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13A1
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
doctrines: Liberal construction of statutes to avoid arbitrariness under Article 14
Interpretation of rent control provisions in light of their Statement of Objects and Reasons

card.dispute: The appellant advocate challenged the Bar Council of India's order suspending him for professional misconduct based on allegations of improper legal advice and client solicitation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant and another advocate were guilty of professional misconduct as found by the Bar Council of India's Disciplinary Committee.
Whether the evidence adduced by the complainants was sufficient to prove the charge of professional misconduct.
Whether the complainants themselves were guilty of professional misconduct by employing touts to solicit work.
holdings: The Disciplinary Committee erred in holding the appellant guilty of professional misconduct as the evidence did not meet the required standard of proof.
While suspicion existed about the appellant's conduct, it did not amount to proven professional misconduct under the Advocates Act, 1961.
The practice of touting by the complainants, including through organized bar associations, constitutes professional misconduct and undermines ethical standards in the legal profession.
doctrines: Standard of proof in professional misconduct proceedings
Judicial scrutiny of disciplinary actions against advocates
Prohibition of touting and solicitation in the legal profession
Duty of Bar Councils to uphold professional ethics and support junior advocates

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and others contested whether Radha Krishna Singh and others were the rightful reversioners entitled to inherit the properties of Maharaja Harindra Kishore Singh after his death.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs proved their genealogical link to Bansidhar Singh, the ancestor of the deceased Maharaja.
Whether Ex. J, an entry in a public register by a public officer, is admissible and sufficient to prove pedigree.
Whether recitals in earlier judgments not inter partes can be relied upon to establish genealogy.
Whether the State can claim escheat without filing a formal claim and issuing public notice.
holdings: The plaintiffs failed to prove the essential genealogical links connecting them to Bansidhar Singh and thus did not establish their status as rightful reversioners.
An entry in a public record by a public officer is admissible under Section 35 of the Evidence Act but may not be sufficient to prove title without corroborative evidence.
Recitals in judgments that are not inter partes, including genealogical statements, are inadmissible and cannot be used as proof of pedigree.
The State cannot claim escheat by merely opposing private claims; a formal suit with public notice is required to establish the absence of heirs.
doctrines: Doctrine of post litem motam
Rule against hearsay evidence
Principle of escheat and the burden of proof on the State
Requirement of public notice for escheat claims
Inter partes nature of judicial recitals for evidentiary use

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and others challenged the High Court's decision quashing the non-agricultural (N.A.) land revenue assessment, arguing that the rules allowing such assessment were valid.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 71 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Rules and Rule 81 of the Bombay Land Revenue Rules confer unguided and excessive discretionary power, violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
Whether the rules amount to excessive delegation of legislative power to the executive.
Whether the absence of a mandatory notice before levying N.A. assessment renders the rules invalid for violating principles of natural justice.
holdings: The rules do not confer arbitrary or uncontrolled power as the assessing authority's discretion is limited by floor and ceiling rates, purpose of land use, profitability, and local land values, providing sufficient guidelines to satisfy constitutional requirements.

The delegation of rule-making power under the Acts is not excessive, as the legislature laid down clear policy and purpose, and the executive's role is confined to carrying out the statutory scheme within defined limits.

The absence of a mandatory pre-assessment notice does not invalidate the rules, as the affected party can challenge the demand and seek remedy through appeal, ensuring compliance with principles of natural justice.
provisions: Hyderabad Land Revenue Act, 1317 F, Section 172
Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) Land Revenue Rules, 1951, Rule 71
doctrines: Doctrine of permissible delegation
Guidelines test for non-delegation doctrine
Principles of natural justice in administrative action
Presumption of constitutionality of taxing statutes

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad sought to remove unauthorized construction (walls/railings) on property owned by Ben Hiraben Manilal, who had not constructed them but purchased the property after the construction was done; she obtained an injunction against the removal, leading to a legal dispute over the Corporation's authority under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under section 260(1)(a) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949 can be issued to a property owner who did not construct the unauthorized structure?
Whether the failure to cite section 478 in the show-cause notice invalidates the Corporation's action?
holdings: Section 260(1)(a) read with section 478 empowers the Municipal Corporation to issue a notice for removal of unauthorized construction to the current owner, even if they did not construct it.
A notice under section 260 is not invalidated merely because section 478 was not cited, provided the action is legally sustainable under the Act as a whole.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 260
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 478
doctrines: Beneficial construction of statutes
Harmonious construction
Doctrine that a wrong reference to a legal provision does not vitiate action if justified under another valid provision

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the High Court's interpretation allowing a landholder to exclude additional open land from ceiling limits under the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976, when part of the plot was built upon.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in excluding 1000 sq. metres of open land from the ceiling area for beneficial enjoyment of a building under Section 4(9) of the Act?
Whether a separate parcel of vacant land is required to attract the application of Section 4(9)?
How should ceiling area be computed when land is partly built and partly open?
Whether the landholder can claim exemption for appurtenant land while still including it in total holding for ceiling calculation?
holdings: Section 4(9) does not require a landholder to possess a separate vacant plot; it applies to any open portion within the same plot as the building.
The expression 'land appurtenant thereto' in Section 4(9) refers to land within the same plot, not a distinct parcel, and must be read with Section 2(g)(ii) and (iii).
Ceiling area must be calculated by aggregating all urban land held, including partly built and partly open plots, and allowing only statutorily permitted deductions.
A landholder cannot both claim exemption for appurtenant land and retain it as part of the total area, thus evading ceiling limits.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(9)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(g)(ii) and (iii)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(1)(a) to (d)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 6
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent in social welfare legislation
Prohibition against judicial addition to statutory text
Doctrine of absurdity in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The Union of India and State Government challenged the compensation awarded for land acquired in 1962–63, arguing that the multiplier used to calculate compensation was excessive.
issues_decided: What is the appropriate multiplier (years' purchase) to be adopted in determining compensation for agricultural land acquired in 1962–63 under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the principle of capitalisation of net annual income based on prevailing rates of return on safe investments was correctly applied?
holdings: The High Court and District Court erred in applying a 20 years' purchase multiplier; the correct multiplier for land acquired in 1962–63 was 15 years' purchase, based on expected net returns of at least 8% from agricultural land at that time.

The compensation must reflect the capitalised value of net annual income using a multiplier consistent with prevailing investment returns, considering available safe investment avenues and expected yields by a willing buyer.
doctrines: Capitalisation of net annual income
Principle of years' purchase
Market value determination on date of notification under Section 4(1)

card.dispute: An employee challenged his removal from service by a public sector corporation, alleging violation of principles of natural justice, lack of misconduct under applicable rules, and arbitrariness under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Project and Equipment Corporation of India Ltd. is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Whether the order of removal violated principles of natural justice due to lack of reasoned orders at inquiry, disciplinary, and appellate stages
Whether the alleged misconduct constituted punishable misconduct under the 1975 Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules
Whether the employee was entitled to full back wages after illegal termination, despite taking alternative employment
holdings: Public sector undertakings functioning as state instrumentalities are amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226, especially when they discharge public functions.

An order of penalty in a disciplinary proceeding must be supported by reasons; a mere affirmation of findings without reasoning constitutes non-application of mind and violates principles of natural justice.

Violation of service rules does not amount to misconduct unless specifically categorized as such; Rule 4 of the 1975 Rules does not specify misconduct, and Rule 5 does not make its breach a disciplinary offense.
An employee who secures alternative employment during litigation is not entitled to full back wages, but may receive a reduced amount (e.g., 50%) as equitable relief considering conduct and justice.
provisions: Project and Equipment Corporation of India Ltd. Employees (Conduct, Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1975, Rules 4, 5, 25, 27(19), 35
Project and Equipment Corporation of India House Building Advance (Grant and Recovery) Rules, Rule 10(1)(ii)
Project and Equipment Corporation of India Conveyance Advance (Grant and Recovery) Rules, Rules 8 and 10(1)
doctrines: Principles of natural justice (reasoned orders, non-arbitrariness)
Doctrine of double jeopardy in departmental proceedings
Amenability of public corporations to writ jurisdiction
Equitable relief in service matters (partial back wages)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the selective release of land from acquisition proceedings, alleging violation of equality rights, and sought higher compensation due to delay in possession.
issues_decided: Whether the release of a portion of land from acquisition under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 violated Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the entire acquisition notification became void due to the unconstitutional release of a small portion
Whether compensation should be based on the market value at the time of possession due to significant delay
holdings: The release of land in favor of influential families was arbitrary and violated Article 14, rendering the release order null and void.
The invalidity of the partial release does not vitiate the entire acquisition notification; the original notification remains valid, and the released land is deemed part of the acquisition.
While delay in possession does not legally entitle landowners to enhanced compensation, the Court, as a court of equity, awarded interest at 7.5% per annum for two years as equitable compensation.
doctrines: Doctrine of equality before law (Article 14)
Doctrine of severability
Equitable compensation by courts of equity

card.dispute: The legal heirs of the grandson of an inamdar (Anant Kibe & Ors) sued for partition and separate possession of half the joint family property, including inam lands, against the sole surviving male-line descendant and karta (Purushottam Rao & Ors), who claimed exclusive ownership due to impartibility and devolution by primogeniture.
issues_decided: Whether the inam lands, after abolition under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, became part of the joint Hindu family property eligible for partition
Whether the conferral of bhumiswami rights under Section 158(1)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, extinguished the joint family character of the inam lands
Whether the rule of lineal primogeniture and impartibility continued to apply to the inam lands after the statutory abolition of inam rights
holdings: The extinction of inam rights and conferral of bhumiswami rights under Section 158(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, ended the impartible nature of the estate and restored the joint family character of the property.
The rights of coparceners in a joint Hindu family to seek partition are not extinguished by prior impartibility if the statute abolishes the inam and converts the tenure into bhumiswami rights.
The rule of lineal primogeniture, being an incident of the inam, was abrogated by the Code, and the property devolved as normal joint family property subject to partition.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 158(1)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, Section 39
doctrines: Abrogation of incidents of inam by statute
Survival of joint family rights despite impartibility
Statutory transformation of tenure does not extinguish coparcenary rights

card.dispute: Property owners challenged the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's assessment of property taxes on four categories of properties, arguing that rateable value was incorrectly determined without regard to standard rent principles under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the rateable value of a property for municipal taxation must be based on standard rent principles under Section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, even if the owner fails to produce documentary evidence of construction cost or land price.

Whether assessing authorities can resort to Section 9(4) of the Delhi Rent Control Act to fix standard rent when owners fail to produce satisfactory evidence, instead of estimating the cost and land price themselves.
How the rateable value should be determined for properties constructed in stages, including cases of self-occupied, tenanted, and separately occupied additions.
holdings: The rateable value for property tax must be determined with reference to the standard rent under Section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, and the assessing authority must estimate construction cost and land price if the owner fails to produce satisfactory evidence.

Assessing authorities cannot bypass Section 6 principles and invoke Section 9(4) merely because the owner’s evidence is inadequate; estimation by the authority is required, not avoidance of the statutory formula.

For properties built in stages, the rateable value must be assessed as a whole, with the standard rent formula applied to the entire premises; land cost cannot be double-counted, and additions forming separate units require apportionment of standard rent.
doctrines: Principle of reasonable expected rent as basis for rateable value
Statutory interpretation of standard rent determination
Estimation duty of assessing authorities in absence of owner's evidence
Prohibition of double counting of land cost in staged constructions

card.dispute: A tenant challenged his eviction decree passed under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, claiming the landlord's need for personal use was not bona fide and that procedural requirements for eviction were not met.
issues_decided: Whether the finding of bona fide requirement of the premises by the landlord for her sons' business can be overturned in appeal.
Whether the eviction decree passed under Section 12(1)(f) is invalid due to non-compliance with the requirements of Section 12(1)(h) of the Act.
holdings: The concurrent finding by the trial, appellate, and High Courts that the landlord bona fide requires the premises for her sons' business is not perverse and cannot be disturbed in special leave appeal.

Non-compliance with Section 12(1)(h) does not invalidate an eviction under Section 12(1)(f), especially when the tenant did not raise the plea earlier and the court found that even those requirements were satisfied.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(h)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(7)
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact by lower courts
Perverse finding doctrine
Tenancy protection and bona fide requirement

card.dispute: The appellants, landowners in Kheragarh and Nagala Udaiya villages, challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State of U.P. for constructing a market yard, claiming lack of knowledge, absence of urgency, and inapplicability of Section 17(4) due to a house on the land.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petition challenging the acquisition notifications after two and a half years could be dismissed on grounds of delay and laches.
Whether the order under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, exempting Section 5A, was invalid due to lack of urgency or because a house existed on part of the land.
Whether the court should interfere under Article 226 when factual claims about possession and ownership are disputed.
holdings: A writ petition challenging acquisition proceedings after a delay of two and a half years, without explanation for non-knowledge despite publication, is liable to be dismissed on grounds of laches.
The order under Section 17(4) exempting Section 5A is valid even with administrative delay in project execution, provided urgency existed at the time of notification.
Courts should not interfere under Article 226 when the petitioners' claims involve disputed questions of fact that require evidence and trial.
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Presumption of regularity in official acts
Judicial non-interference in factual disputes under writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: The landlord filed multiple ejectment applications against the tenant for non-payment of rent and bona fide requirement, and the dispute centered on whether the tenant could claim protection under Section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 for a second time after complying with a deposit order in a prior, withdrawn proceeding.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant obtained a 'benefit' under Section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 in the first ejectment proceeding which was withdrawn by the landlord?
Whether the proviso to Section 14(2) bars a tenant from claiming the benefit of that section more than once, even if the prior proceeding was withdrawn and not finally decided on merits?
holdings: A tenant does not obtain the 'benefit' under Section 14(2) if the eviction petition is withdrawn by the landlord, as no order rejecting possession on grounds of compliance with Section 15 was passed.

The proviso to Section 14(2) applies only when the tenant has actually obtained the benefit of immunity from eviction under that sub-section in a prior proceeding; mere compliance with a Section 15 order does not amount to such a benefit if the proceeding ends in withdrawal.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(2) with its proviso
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisos
Distinction between procedural compliance and substantive benefit
Finality of proceedings for accrual of statutory benefits

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant alleging sub-letting to a trading company, based on a photograph showing the company proprietor's son in the shop; the tenant denied sub-tenancy and claimed the presence was innocuous.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court erred in presuming sub-tenancy merely from the presence of a non-family member in the shop.
Whether the Additional District Judge exceeded his revisional jurisdiction by re-appraising evidence.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering under Article 227 with the revisional order.
holdings: Mere presence of a person not belonging to the tenant’s family in the shop does not raise a presumption of sub-letting; the landlord must prove sub-tenancy by positive evidence.

The Additional District Judge did not exceed jurisdiction by correcting a legal error in the trial court’s approach, as revisional courts may intervene when findings are based on a wrong legal premise.
The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 by acting as a court of appeal and re-evaluating findings of fact, which is impermissible in certiorari.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(1)(b)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 25
Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, Section 25
doctrines: Presumption of sub-tenancy not permissible from mere presence of outsider
Error of law apparent on record justifies revisional interference
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 cannot be used to correct errors of fact
Distinction between appellate and revisional jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser of joint Hindu family property from one member, sought partition of the property against the family members, leading to a dispute over the remedy available to such a purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether a purchaser of joint Hindu family property from one coparcener can maintain a suit for partition against the other coparceners.
Whether the remedy of partition is available when the purchased property is the only joint family property and no adjustment of family equities is required.
holdings: A purchaser from a coparcener may have the right to sue for partition of joint family property, but this depends on the existence of other properties requiring equitable adjustment among coparceners.

Where the purchased property is the only joint family property and no family equities need adjustment, the concurrent findings of lower courts upholding partition may be accepted, and the appeal is dismissed.
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Doctrine of equitable partition
Doctrine of coparcenary interest in joint family property

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against a High Court decision that set aside a trial court's eviction decree in favor of the tenant, claiming protection under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, which was extended during the pendency of the first appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court is bound to consider the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, when it was extended during the pendency of an appeal against a trial court's eviction decree?
Whether the term 'decree' in Section 13(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act refers to the final decree disposing of the suit, including an appellate decree?
Whether a statutory protection against eviction applies to pending suits and appeals when the law is amended during pendency?
holdings: The appellate court must apply the law prevailing at the time of its decision, including statutory protections like those under Section 13(1) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, if enacted during the appeal.
The word 'decree' in Section 13(1) refers to the final decree determining the suit, which may be the appellate decree, as the trial decree merges into it upon appeal.

Statutory tenant protections apply to pending suits and appeals if the language of the law so intends, as an appeal is a continuation of the suit and governed by the law in force at the time of appellate decision.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(6)
doctrines: Appellate decree merges trial decree
Change of law during pendency of appeal governs appellate decision
Prospective application of statutes in pending proceedings
Continuation of suit principle in appeals

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to establish title over certain properties based on a chain of gifts and an exchange deed, which the defendant challenged by disputing the validity of the initial gift and subsequent transactions.
issues_decided: Whether the gift deed executed by Thimma Reddy in favor of his wife Naramma was valid and created an absolute interest in her favor
Whether the properties in question were joint family properties or self-acquired properties of Thimma Reddy
Whether Naramma had the capacity to gift the properties to her granddaughter Venkata Lakshmamma
Whether the exchange deed between Venkata Lakshmamma and her husband Yella Reddy validated her title and enabled her to sell the property to the plaintiff
holdings: A gift deed executed by a husband in favor of his wife, expressed to be absolute, creates a valid and complete title in her favor, even if motivated by family circumstances.
In the absence of pleadings, issues, or evidence, properties cannot be presumed to be joint family property merely because of the existence of a Hindu joint family.
A wife who receives an absolute gift from her husband becomes the full owner and is competent to dispose of the property by gift to a third person, including a relative.
Where parties act upon an exchange deed by taking possession, and it is not challenged, such conduct confirms the title of the transferee and validates the transaction.
doctrines: Doctrine of Unfettered Gift in Hindu Law
Doctrine of Estoppel by Conduct
Presumption against Joint Family Property without Evidence

card.dispute: The landlord, V. R. M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina, sought eviction of seven tenants, including M/S. Variety Emporium, on grounds of bona fide personal requirement, which the tenant challenged as unjust and no longer valid due to changed circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide personal requirement for eviction must exist at the time of final disposal of the case, including in revision?
Whether subsequent events, such as partial success in evicting other tenants, should be considered in determining ongoing need?
Whether the appellate and revisional courts erred in failing to consider changed factual circumstances?
holdings: A landlord must prove bona fide personal requirement not only at the time of filing suit but also at the time of final disposal of the case in appeal or revision.
Subsequent events, including partial fulfillment of the landlord's need through eviction of other tenants, must be considered in assessing continued necessity.
Courts must evaluate whether the relief sought remains just and equitable in light of changed circumstances, even if lower courts have decreed eviction.
A tenant can challenge the continued existence of the landlord's need in higher courts until the eviction decree becomes final.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(i) and (iii)
doctrines: Bona fide personal requirement doctrine
Principle of equitable relief in rent control cases
Doctrine of subsequent events in appellate review

card.dispute: The landlord, a government servant, sought eviction of his tenant under Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act after vacating government accommodation and moving into his own residential property; the tenant challenged the maintainability of the eviction petition.
issues_decided: Whether a government servant must be in occupation of allotted government accommodation on the date of filing an eviction petition under Section 14A(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act?
Whether a landlord who owns another residential property available for his use can maintain an eviction petition under Section 14A(1)?
Whether unsuitability of owned residential property allows a landlord to proceed under Section 14A(1) or requires proceeding under Section 14(1)(e)?
holdings: A landlord governed by Section 14A(1) need not be in occupation of government-allotted accommodation at the time of filing an eviction petition; vacating it due to a general order does not bar the right to seek possession.
If a landlord owns another residential property available for personal use, either in his name or that of his wife or dependent child, the eviction petition under Section 14A(1) is not maintainable.

Even if the owned residential property is not reasonably suitable, the landlord must proceed under Section 14(1)(e), not Section 14A(1), as the latter is unavailable when alternative owned accommodation exists.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to prevent profiteering
Purpose and object of rent control legislation
Conditional applicability of special eviction provisions

card.dispute: The tenant and the landlord (and later his transferees) disputed over the fixation of standard rent and the validity of interim orders in a tenancy proceeding that dragged on for decades.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's petition for fixation of standard rent was barred by limitation under Section 11(b) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
Whether the interpolated order dated October 6, 1956, directing payment of interim rent, was legally valid
Whether the delay in filing the appeal against the interim order and the application for condonation of delay should be condoned
Whether the abatement of appeal due to the death of the original landlord required substitution of legal heirs with condonation of delay
holdings: The petition for fixation of standard rent was not barred by limitation as the tenancy commenced in May 1955 and the petition was filed in October 1955 within the prescribed period.
The order dated October 6, 1956, was an interpolated and unauthorized addition to the record, legally non-existent, and thus could not form the basis for striking off the tenant's defence.

The delay in filing the appeal against the interim order was occasioned by the non-communication of the order to the tenant and the subsequent dismissal of the suit; justice required condonation of delay to prevent miscarriage of justice.

The delay in seeking substitution of the deceased landlord’s legal representatives was sufficiently explained and warranted condonation, especially since the transferees had been active parties since 1959 and the duty under Order 22 Rule 10A was belatedly fulfilled.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 8
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 11(b)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10A
doctrines: Miscarriage of justice
Interpolated order as a nullity
Condonation of delay in the interest of justice
Substitution of parties upon death

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to acquit one accused and reduce the conviction of the other from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder based on a private settlement involving a land gift to the victim's widow.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting one accused and reducing the conviction of the other based on a private arrangement involving compensation to the victim's family.
Whether a compromise between parties in a murder case can be a valid ground for acquittal or sentence reduction.
holdings: A private compromise or gift of property to the victim's family cannot justify acquittal or reduction of conviction in a case involving charges under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
Courts must dispense justice according to law, not based on idiosyncratic or palm-tree justice influenced by extraneous factors like family settlements.
doctrines: Rule of law
Judicial impartiality
No private settlement in serious criminal offenses

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for default in rent payment, claiming the tenant failed to comply with a rent deposit order under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has the power to extend time for deposit of future rent under Section 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether a tenant who defaults in monthly rent deposits after a court order is automatically deprived of protection under Section 14(2) of the Act.
