Interpretation of 'transfer' to include testamentary disposition
Legislative intent to restrict tenancy succession to family members in business

card.dispute: The Banwasi Sewa Ashram challenged the Uttar Pradesh government's declaration of jungle lands as reserved forests, affecting Adivasis' possession and cultivation rights, while balancing forest conservation and development projects.
issues_decided: Whether Adivasis in notified forest areas are entitled to file claims despite missing statutory deadlines under the Indian Forest Act, 1927
Whether legal aid must be provided to Adivasis to assert their rights in forest land claims
Whether land acquisition for a thermal power project can proceed amid pending forest settlement proceedings
holdings: Claims under Section 6(c) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 may be entertained even if filed late, provided the process is fair and accessible to Adivasis in notified areas.
Legal aid must be proactively provided to Adivasi claimants without strict adherence to procedural formalities to ensure access to justice.

Land needed for national development projects like the Rihand Super Thermal Power Project may be acquired, but only after compliance with the Land Acquisition Act and proper documentation of dispossession.
doctrines: Public interest litigation
Access to justice
Legal aid as a fundamental right under Article 21
Sustainable development and ecological balance

card.dispute: The petitioner, Bira Kishore Naik, and 700 workmen claimed that their coal mine had vested in the Central Government under the nationalisation laws and sought reinstatement and wages, while the respondents denied the mine's existence on the appointed day.
issues_decided: Whether Natundihi Pahariabera Colliery was a coal mine under Section 2(b) of the Coal Mines (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1973 on the appointed day (January 31, 1973)?
Whether the Central Government had a legal duty to issue a notification taking over the mine under Section 3(2) proviso of the Management Act upon acquiring knowledge of its existence?
Whether the petitioner and workmen were entitled to protection under Section 14 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973?
Whether a writ of mandamus could be issued directing the Central Government to take over the mine and employ the workmen?
holdings: A coal mine under the Management Act requires actual mining operations; mere intention or preparation is insufficient.
The Central Government’s duty to notify a mine arises only if it existed on the appointed day; knowledge alone does not trigger this duty.
Section 14 protection applies only if the mine vested in the Central Government; no such vesting occurred here.
Mandamus cannot be issued to compel the government to operate a mine or employ workers, especially where no legal obligation exists.
provisions: Coal Mines (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1973, Section 2(b)
Coal Mines (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1973, Section 3(2) proviso
Coal Mines (Taking Over of Management) Act, 1973, Section 3(5)
doctrines: Burden of proof in factual disputes
Literal interpretation of statutory conditions
No mandamus without legal right
Presumption against unrecorded mining operations

card.dispute: The legal heir of a deceased tenant fought against eviction, claiming he was a trespasser and not a tenant, thus challenging the Rent Controller's jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the legal heir of a deceased tenant can be treated as a tenant under the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, especially in relation to non-residential premises.
Whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to proceed against the legal heir of a deceased tenant when the heir claimed to be a trespasser.
Whether a legal representative can raise a new plea of independent title or trespasser status in an eviction petition after being brought on record under Order XXII Rule 4 of the CPC.
holdings: The possession of a legal heir succeeding a tenant does not become that of a trespasser merely because the heir is not recognized as a tenant under the Act, as the original possession was permissive.
The Rent Controller retains jurisdiction to proceed with an eviction petition when a legal representative is brought on record, and cannot be ousted by a plea of trespasser status.

A legal representative brought on record under Order XXII Rule 4 CPC cannot raise a defence of being a trespasser or claim independent title if it would oust the Rent Controller’s jurisdiction, especially when the original tenant was a lawful occupant.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 2(h)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(2)(ii)(a)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 4
doctrines: Permissive possession passes to legal heirs
Jurisdiction of Rent Controller in eviction proceedings
Scope of defence by legal representatives under CPC

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the acquisition of their land, claiming it was not for the public purpose of resettling immigrants as stated in the notification, but for building a hospital for crippled children.
issues_decided: Whether the use of the term 're-settlement' in the notification differs from 'settlement' under Section 2(d)(i) of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948
Whether the actual purpose of constructing a hospital for crippled children falls within the public purpose of refugee rehabilitation
Whether internal government correspondence revealing a different purpose invalidates the acquisition notification
holdings: The terms 'settlement' and 're-settlement' are interchangeable in context, as both aim to provide habitation and amenities to displaced persons from East Pakistan.
Constructing a hospital for crippled children is a valid part of refugee rehabilitation, as medical care is an essential amenity for displaced persons.
Internal administrative correspondence indicating subsequent development plans cannot invalidate a valid public purpose notification issued under the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 2(d)(i)
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 4
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 6
doctrines: Colourable exercise of power
Doctrine of public purpose in land acquisition
Principle against going behind acquisition notifications based on internal correspondence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a government order permitting the private sale of math lands, arguing it violated statutory requirements and failed to protect the institution's interests.
issues_decided: Whether the government order permitting sale by private negotiation complied with the proviso to Section 74(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious and Endowments Act, 1966
Whether the competent authority applied its mind to the statutory pre-conditions before permitting the sale
Whether the sale could be directed to be conducted through public auction in the interest of justice
holdings: The government order permitting private sale was invalid due to non-application of mind and failure to record reasons as required by the proviso to Section 74(1)(c).
The mere reference to departmental reports does not constitute compliance with the statutory duty to form an independent opinion on the public interest and institutional benefit.
The lands must be sold by public auction with specified conditions to safeguard the math’s interests and ensure transparency and maximum value.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 74(1)(c)
Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 79(1)
doctrines: Non-application of mind to statutory conditions
Public interest in protection of religious endowment property
Principle of transparency in disposal of charitable property

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assesses disputed whether income received by beneficiaries under two trust deeds should be assessed in their individual capacity or as members of their respective Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs).
issues_decided: Whether the income derived by the beneficiaries under the trust deeds belonged to them individually or to their respective HUFs.
Whether subsequent declarations by the assesses that the income belonged to their HUFs could alter the character of the income.
holdings: The nature of the income is determined by the terms of the trust deeds, not by subsequent declarations; the deeds clearly indicate that the beneficiaries were to receive the property in their individual capacity.

The trust deeds' provisions—such as discretionary powers of trustees over a deceased beneficiary's share and partial distribution to widows—contradict the notion of the beneficiaries holding as Kartas of HUFs.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive receipt
Doctrine of family settlement
Doctrine of intention of the settlor in trust deeds

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the status of a licensee who claimed tenancy rights under the Bombay Rents Act after the original tenant's interest ended, arguing that the licensee could not validly be deemed a tenant.
issues_decided: Whether a licensee in occupation on 1 February 1973 could be deemed a tenant under Section 15A of the Bombay Rents Act regardless of the original tenancy agreement's terms.
Whether a statutory tenant (original tenant) had the right to create a valid licence before 1 February 1973.
Whether the High Court could interfere with factual findings of the appellate bench of the Small Causes Court.
holdings: All licensees in actual occupation of premises (not less than a room) on 1 February 1973 became deemed tenants under Section 15A, irrespective of whether the original tenancy permitted sub-licensing.

The right to create a licence by a tenant was valid before 1 February 1973, and such licences were protected under the Act, as Section 15A's non-obstante clause overrides contrary contractual or statutory provisions.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by interfering with factual findings of the Small Causes Court appellate bench, which were not perverse or legally untenable.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 14(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Mischief rule of statutory interpretation
Non-obstante clause giving overriding effect
Distinction between 'notwithstanding' and 'subject to'
Limits of High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227

card.dispute: Lessees of minor mineral quarries challenged the validity of Gujarat government notifications and circulars enhancing royalty and dead rent rates, and the constitutional power of the state to make such rules under the Mines and Minerals Act.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government has the power under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 to fix and enhance royalty and dead rent rates for minor minerals?
Whether the notifications dated November 29, 1974, October 29, 1975, March 26, 1979, and June 18, 1981, and the circular dated February 12, 1981, are valid and constitutional?
Whether the State can classify building stones into varieties and levy differential royalty rates?
Whether the impugned rules and orders violate the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution?
holdings: The State Government has valid rule-making power under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals Act, 1957 to fix royalty and dead rent, and such power includes the ability to enhance rates.
The 1974 notification enhancing rates was valid and operative until superseded by the 1979 notification; the 1975 notification was invalid, and the 1981 amendment rule was valid and constitutional.
The State can classify minor minerals like building stones into varieties and impose different royalty rates for each category.
The rules and notifications do not violate Article 19(1)(g) as they are reasonable restrictions in public interest and do not unreasonably impair the right to carry on trade.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15(1)
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g)
Delegated legislation and rule-making power under statutory authority
Prospective overruling of precedent
Principle of non-arbitrariness in administrative action

card.dispute: The petitioners, including Dr. Upendra Baxi, challenged the Uttar Pradesh government's decision to shift a Protective Home for girls to inadequate premises, thereby violating the inmates' right to live with dignity.
issues_decided: Whether the relocation of the Protective Home to Adarsh Nagar Rajwara violated the inmates' fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution?
Whether the State failed to comply with court orders regarding living conditions, staff facilities, and rehabilitation of inmates?
Whether the State must constitute a Board of Visitors as mandated by the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women & Girls Act Rules?
Whether the continued detention of women and girls in the Home must be lawful and subject to judicial oversight?
holdings: The State's relocation of the Protective Home to unsuitable premises without court permission violated the inmates' right to live with dignity under Article 21.
The State is obligated to ensure safe, healthy, and humane living conditions in protective institutions, including proper ventilation, sanitation, electricity, and medical and legal aid.
The State must constitute a Board of Visitors within two weeks, including social activists and judicial nominees, to monitor the Home as per statutory rules.
No woman or girl may be detained in the Home without lawful authority, and the District Judge must verify legality of detention during monthly inspections.
provisions: The Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, Rule 40
doctrines: Right to live with dignity as part of Article 21
Judicial monitoring of custodial institutions
Public interest litigation for protection of vulnerable groups
State accountability in rehabilitation and welfare of marginalized women

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax and Chander Sen disputed whether property inherited by a son from his father who died intestate devolved in the son's individual capacity or as karta of his HUF, and whether it should be included in the HUF's wealth or income.
issues_decided: Whether property inherited by a son from his father under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, becomes part of the son's HUF property
Whether the credit balance in the father's firm account, inherited by the son, is assessable as individual property or HUF property under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957
Whether income from inherited assets is assessable in the hands of the son as an individual or as the HUF under the Income Tax Act
holdings: Property inherited by a son from his father under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, devolves in his individual capacity and does not automatically become HUF property.
The sum inherited by Chander Sen from his father's estate, including the credit balance in the firm, belonged to him individually and was not part of his HUF's wealth.
Income from property inherited by a son from his father is assessable in his individual capacity, not as income of his HUF, where no blending with HUF property has occurred.
doctrines: Codification of Hindu law under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Devolution of property as tenants-in-common under Section 19
Rejection of pre-Act Hindu law concepts where statute provides otherwise
No right by birth in inherited property under the 1956 Act

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the eviction order on the grounds that the landlord failed to plead essential facts required under the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for eviction on the basis of bona fide requirement for business.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord must plead all facts required under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 to seek eviction for bona fide business requirement.
Whether the courts below could pass an eviction order when the pleading did not contain all statutory ingredients under Section 10(3)(a)(iii).
holdings: Facts required under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) must be pleaded and proved for eviction; non-pleading generally renders proof irrelevant.
Despite defective pleading, the eviction order was upheld as the issue was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court and all material was already on record.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 21
doctrines: Pleading requirements in eviction cases
Futility of remand when evidence is complete
Principle of waiver of objection due to non-raising in lower courts

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant company and its successor after a corporate amalgamation, alleging unauthorized transfer of tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether a corporate amalgamation under Sections 391 and 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 amounts to a 'transfer of tenancy rights' under Section 10(ii)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Whether the amalgamation violated the lease agreement's prohibition on subletting without landlord’s consent
holdings: A corporate amalgamation that results in the transfer of tenancy rights to the transferee company constitutes a 'transfer' under Section 10(ii)(a) of the AP Act, even if sanctioned by court.
The transfer of tenancy interest without landlord’s consent violates both the AP Act and the lease agreement, making the transferee liable to eviction.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(ii)(a)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 2(ix)
doctrines: Transfer of tenancy by operation of law
Prohibition of unauthorized assignment under rent control legislation
Sanctioned corporate amalgamation not immune from tenancy law restrictions

card.dispute: The widow of a descendant of the founder of the Pushti Margi Sampradaya contested the classification of the Pushti Margiya Moti Haveli and its properties as a public trust under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the Pushti Margiya Moti Haveli at Junagadh and its properties constitute a public trust under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
Whether succession to the trusteeship of the Haveli by inheritance without state sanction is valid.
Whether offerings such as Guruseva Bhet and Charanseva Bhet made to the Guru are part of the public trust or personal gifts to the Guru.
holdings: The Haveli and thirty-eight listed properties constitute a public trust based on public use, contributions, state support, and religious practices indicating a public character.
Succession to the office of trustee by hereditary right without prior state sanction is valid under the religious tradition of the Pushti Margi Sampradaya.
Offerings made directly to the Guru (Guruseva Bhet and Charanseva Bhet) are personal gifts to the Guru and not part of the public trust, as they are not offerings to the deity.
doctrines: Tests for determining public vs private religious trusts in Hindu law
Doctrine of Brahma-Sambandha (rejected as overextended in this context)
Principle of hereditary succession in religious offices

card.dispute: The appellant, Hari Bhanu Maharaj, fought against the Charity Commissioner's declaration that the Laxman Maharaj Math (Ramji Mandir) is a public trust, claiming it as his family's private property.
issues_decided: Whether the Laxman Maharaj Math is a public trust within the meaning of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
Whether the documents relied upon by the Charity Commissioner and the High Court establish the public character of the Math.
Whether the ownership entries in revenue records and state grants indicate a public trust.
holdings: The Math is not a public trust but the private property of the appellant’s family, as there is no evidence of public dedication or continuous public use.
Mere receipt of state grants or occasional public visits during festivals does not convert a private religious institution into a public trust.
Entries in revenue records describing the property as belonging to a deity or temple do not conclusively establish a public trust if ownership by succession is recorded.
A Sanad from 1912 explicitly declaring the land as private property and confirming hereditary rights is determinative of the private character of the Math.
doctrines: Doctrine of dedication for public trust
Presumption of private ownership in absence of clear dedication
Relevance of hereditary succession in determining private religious endowments

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of land allegedly encroached upon by the respondent, who asserted ownership through adverse possession and prior continuous use of a disputed wall and khaprail.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent had encroached on the appellant's land by constructing a mud wall and extending a khaprail in 1961.
Whether the respondent had acquired title by adverse possession under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Whether the appellant proved his case of trespass and entitlement to possession.
holdings: The respondent did not commit encroachment as the disputed wall and khaprail existed for over 28 years prior to the suit and were not recent constructions.
The respondent’s long and continuous possession of the structure, acknowledged by the appellant’s vendor, supports a claim of adverse possession under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The appellant failed to prove his claim of trespass or rightful possession, particularly in absence of pleading or proof that his vendor was in possession post-partition.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Burden of proof in encroachment suits
Requirement of pleading and proof of prior possession in partition disputes

card.dispute: The petitioners, sons and nephews of joint landowners, claimed a right to pre-empt the sale of joint family land by other co-sharers to strangers, challenging the High Court's dismissal of their suit after key pre-emption clauses were declared unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners could claim pre-emption under clause 'Fourthly' of Section 15(1)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, as non-alienating co-sharers of joint family land?
Whether the expression 'other co-sharers' in clause 'Fourthly' includes those who fall within earlier clauses like 'First' or 'Secondly' of the same section?
holdings: The term 'other co-sharers' in clause 'Fourthly' of Section 15(1)(b) refers only to co-sharers not covered by clauses 'First', 'Secondly', or 'Thirdly'.
Petitioners who fall within clause 'First' or 'Secondly' of Section 15(1)(b) cannot claim pre-emption under clause 'Fourthly', even if they are non-alienating co-sharers of joint family property.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Hierarchy of pre-emption rights under personal and property law

card.dispute: The Nizam of Hyderabad and the Wealth Tax Commissioner disputed whether certain properties sold without registered sale deeds still belonged to the Nizam for wealth tax purposes, and whether an annual payment of Rs. 25 lakhs received in lieu of former income was an exempt 'annuity'.
issues_decided: Whether immovable properties sold without registered sale deeds, but with full payment and possession transferred, still 'belonged to' the assessee for inclusion in net wealth under Section 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.

Whether the annual payment of Rs. 25 lakhs made by the Government to the Nizam in lieu of his previous income from Sarf-e-khas constituted an 'annuity' exempt under Section 2(e)(iv) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether the right to receive such annual payment was precluded from commutation into a lump sum, either by express terms or by necessary inference.
holdings: Properties sold without registered sale deeds but with full consideration paid and possession delivered do not 'belong to' the assessee if the transaction is valid under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, and thus are not includible in net wealth.

The annual payment of Rs. 25 lakhs made to the Nizam in lieu of his former income from Sarf-e-khas qualifies as an 'annuity' under Section 2(e)(iv) of the Wealth Tax Act, as it was a fixed sum payable yearly out of government property.

Even in the absence of an express clause, the terms and circumstances of the agreement impliedly precluded commutation of the annuity, satisfying the condition for exemption under Section 2(e)(iv) of the Act.
doctrines: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act (part performance)
Literal and legal meaning of 'annuity' in tax exemption provisions
Implied terms in statutory and contractual interpretation
No equity in taxation; strict construction of tax laws

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant firm, Madras-Bangalore Transport Company (West), alleging it had unlawfully sublet the premises to a newly formed company, Caravan Goods Carrier Private Limited, without consent.
issues_decided: Whether the formation and operation of a private limited company from the same premises by partners of the tenant firm constitutes subletting, assignment, or parting with possession under the Delhi Rent Control Act.

Whether two distinct legal entities — a partnership firm and a private limited company — can be treated as one for the purpose of tenancy if they share the same partners/directors and substantial identity.
holdings: The mere fact that a private limited company operates from the same premises as the tenant firm does not amount to subletting if the firm continues to occupy and control the premises.

A private limited company formed by partners of a tenant firm, functioning as its 'alter ego' or 'corporate reflection', does not constitute a third party for the purpose of subletting under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act when there is substantial identity between the entities.
doctrines: Alter ego doctrine
Substantial identity doctrine
Legal personality vs. practical control in tenancy

card.dispute: Minerva Mills Ltd. challenged the Union of India's takeover of its management and the nationalisation of its sick textile undertaking, including the possession of vacant land not used for operations.
issues_decided: Whether the non-supply of the Investigation Committee's report under Section 15 of the Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, violated principles of natural justice
Whether the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974, is constitutionally valid under Articles 14, 19, 31A, and 31C of the Constitution
Whether vacant land within the mill compound, not currently utilised, forms part of the 'sick textile undertaking' and thus vests in the Central Government under the Nationalisation Act
holdings: Failure to supply the Investigation Committee report does not vitiate the takeover order under Section 18A, as the principles of natural justice were not breached in this administrative action.

The Nationalisation Act is protected under Article 31C and therefore does not violate Articles 14 and 19, as it is supported by a law giving effect to Directive Principles under Article 39(b) and (c).

All land within the mill compound, including vacant and unused portions, forms part of the undertaking under Section 4(1) of the Nationalisation Act and vests with the government, regardless of current utilisation.
provisions: Industrial (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, Sections 15 and 18A
doctrines: Doctrine of Basic Structure
Principles of Natural Justice
Prospective Overruling
Doctrine of Severability

card.dispute: National Textile Corporation Ltd. and others fought with Sitaram Mills Ltd. and others over whether surplus lands appurtenant to a textile mill, used for real estate activities, were part of the 'assets in relation to the textile undertaking' taken over by the government under the Textile Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1983.
issues_decided: Whether the surplus lands appurtenant to the textile mill, used for real estate purposes, fall within the definition of 'assets in relation to the textile undertaking' under section 3(2) of the Textile Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1983.
Whether the real estate activities of the mill constituted a separate business, thereby excluding the surplus lands from the assets taken over under the Act.
holdings: The phrase 'assets in relation to the textile undertaking' in section 3(2) of the Act has a wide connotation and includes all assets, including surplus lands appurtenant to the mill, regardless of their use for real estate purposes.

The surplus lands remained part of the textile undertaking's assets even if used for raising funds, as they were originally acquired and held in connection with the textile business and did not constitute a separate business.
provisions: Textile Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1983, Section 2(d)
Textile Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1983, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Wide statutory interpretation of 'assets in relation to the undertaking'
Subsequent use of assets for non-core purposes does not remove them from the scope of nationalization if originally part of the undertaking

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the validity of leases created in violation of the Rent Control Order, claiming they were void, while the tenants argued the leases were valid between the parties.
issues_decided: Whether a lease created in contravention of clause 22 of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 is void or merely voidable as between the parties
Whether the Notification dated October 24, 1961 exempting certain non-residential premises from Chapter III of the Rent Control Order operates retrospectively
Whether a vacancy arose in the premises in November 1961, triggering the application of clause 22
holdings: A lease in violation of clause 22 of the Rent Control Order is not void but valid between the parties; it can only be challenged by the Deputy Commissioner, not by the landlord in a private dispute.
The Notification dated October 24, 1961 is prospective only and does not retrospectively exempt tenancies created after its issuance based on prior construction dates.
The finding that a vacancy occurred in November 1961 is a concurrent factual determination by lower courts and not interfered with under Article 136.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, clauses 22, 23, 24, 28, 30
doctrines: Doctrine of void vs. voidable transactions
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of notifications
Principle of non-interference with concurrent findings of fact under Article 136

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide personal need, which the tenant resisted, alleging it was a pretext to raise rent.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant landlady had a bona fide requirement for personal occupation of the rented premises.
Whether the delay in filing the eviction petition after the husband's death undermined the claim of bona fide need.
Whether the re-letting of the ground floor of the property negated the claim of personal need.
Whether the rejection of additional evidence regarding pressure to vacate the appellant's Delhi residence was justified.
holdings: A landlady's desire to return to her only owned house to spend her later years constitutes a bona fide need for personal occupation.
Efforts made to secure vacant possession before filing the petition negate any inference of lack of bona fides due to delay.
Re-letting of another part of the building before the eviction petition does not disprove bona fide need for the tenanted portion.
Exclusion of evidence showing eviction proceedings against the appellant in Delhi was erroneous, as it had probative value on her need.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(i)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for personal occupation
Appreciation of evidence and burden of proof in eviction cases
Error in factual assumption vitiating appellate findings

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of arrears in rent, while the tenant claimed he had attempted to pay but the landlord refused to accept payment and that rent was being deposited in treasury.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was in willful arrears of rent despite claiming to have tendered payment and deposited rent in treasury.
Whether the absence of a fixed time for rent payment in the contract allowed the tenant to delay payment without consequence.
Whether deposit of rent in treasury was a valid substitute for payment to the landlord after amendment of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947.
holdings: A tenant remains in arrears if rent is not paid regularly, even if deposited in treasury, particularly when alternate modes of valid payment are available.
Absence of a specified rent payment date in the tenancy agreement does not absolve the tenant from the obligation to pay rent monthly.
After amendment of the Act, depositing rent in treasury is not a valid mode of payment; remittance by postal money order upon landlord’s refusal is the proper remedy.
provisions: Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(d)
Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Willful default in rent payment
Statutory interpretation of rent control legislation
Validity of alternate rent payment methods under rent control law

card.dispute: A government servant and landlord sought to evict a tenant from the first floor of a shared house under urgent provisions of the U.P. Rent Act, claiming need for personal residence, while the tenant argued the landlord already had residential accommodation.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord was entitled to invoke summary eviction provisions under Sections 24B and 24C of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, despite owning another residential unit.
Whether two portions of a single building constitute one or more than one 'dwelling house' within the meaning of the Act.
holdings: A landlord cannot invoke urgent eviction provisions under Sections 24A–24C if they already have a residential unit available for their use, even if it is part of the same building.
Two parts of a building may constitute separate dwelling houses if they are capable of separate occupation and enjoyment, considering factors like entrance, layout, and independent use over time.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Sections 24A, 24B, 24C
Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 3
doctrines: Pragmatic interpretation of statutory terms based on purpose and context
Cumulative test for determining 'dwelling house' based on structural and functional independence

card.dispute: The petitioners, who were setting up an abattoir and meat processing plant, challenged the state government's cancellation of their land use permission, while the state appealed the direction to pay compensation for project costs incurred.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government has the power under Section 257 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966 to suo motu revise an order granting non-agricultural land use permission passed by the Collector.
Whether the exercise of revisional power by the Government after a considerable delay was valid and within the statutory framework.
Whether the cancellation of permission violated the petitioners' right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Whether the State is liable to pay compensation for costs incurred by the petitioners before the show-cause notice was issued.
holdings: The State Government possesses plenary revisional powers under Section 257 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966, including the authority to initiate revision suo motu.
The revisional power under Section 257 can be exercised beyond 90 days if the government acts in public interest and on the basis of material, even if there was delay or lack of diligence.
The cancellation of permission did not violate Article 19(1)(g) as it was justified by public interest, including environmental and communal harmony concerns.
The State must compensate the petitioners for bona fide expenditures incurred up to the date of the show-cause notice, as a measure of fairness despite lawful cancellation.
provisions: Maharashtra Prevention of Water Pollution Act, 1969, Section 18
Maharashtra Prevention of Water Pollution Act, 1969, Section 28
doctrines: Suo motu revisional jurisdiction
Public interest doctrine
Principle of fair compensation
Balancing of fundamental rights with public order and morality

card.dispute: Inamdars challenged the constitutional validity of the Tamil Nadu Inam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Amendment Act, 1969, which brought their lands under a more restrictive land reform law, arguing it violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the 1969 Amendment Act is protected by Article 31A of the Constitution despite violating Articles 14, 19, and 31
Whether the inclusion of certain lands in Schedule 1A of the 1963 Act via the 1969 Amendment amounts to an impermissible legislative encroachment on judicial functions
Whether the subject matter of the legislation (lands with only a right to patta) qualifies as an 'estate' under Article 31A
holdings: Laws providing for the acquisition or modification of rights in an 'estate' are protected by Article 31A and cannot be struck down for violating Articles 14, 19, or 31.
The legislature has the power to declare the nature of land tenure for agrarian reform, even retrospectively, without infringing judicial authority.
The term 'estate' under Article 31A includes ryotwari lands and rights to obtain a patta for agricultural land, making such lands subject to protective land reform laws.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Inam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Amendment Act, 1969 (Act 23 of 1969)
Tamil Nadu Inam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 (Act 26 of 1963)
doctrines: Doctrine of Protection under Article 31A
Doctrine of Agrarian Reform
Doctrine of Parliamentary Sovereignty in Land Reform

card.dispute: The landlord (Smt. Dhanwanti) fought to regain possession of her property from the tenant (D.D. Gupta), who claimed the landlord obtained rental permissions fraudulently under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether successive letting of premises to the same tenant with fresh permissions under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act constitutes fraud
Whether the landlord misrepresented her need for the premises when obtaining permission in 1980
Whether the statutory authorities erred in holding that the landlord practised fraud on the Rent Controller
holdings: Successive letting of premises for limited periods with fresh permissions does not, by itself, prove an intention to let indefinitely or constitute fraud.
A landlord's change in circumstances justifying repeated short-term lettings does not invalidate permission obtained under Section 21 if facts were not concealed.
The statutory authorities committed a grave error by drawing unreasonable inferences from immaterial inconsistencies, resulting in a miscarriage of justice.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates administrative permissions
Supreme Court's discretion under Article 136 to interfere with factual findings in cases of grave injustice
Prohibition against drawing adverse inferences from trivial inconsistencies

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision to partially strike down its policy of privatizing liquor distilleries and granting D-1 and D-2 licenses to existing contractors, which petitioners alleged was mala fide and caused financial loss to the state.
issues_decided: Whether the policy decision to privatize distilleries and grant licenses to existing contractors was mala fide or arbitrary under Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the High Court could bifurcate and invalidate part of a composite policy decision
Whether laches barred the petitioners from challenging the policy after implementation and reliance by licensees
Whether the State was obligated to follow a specific method (tender, auction, fixed fee) for granting licenses under the Excise Rules
holdings: The policy decision to privatize distilleries was made after careful consideration and was bona fide, with no evidence of mala fides or arbitrariness under Article 14.
A policy decision taken as a composite exercise of executive wisdom cannot be bifurcated by courts; it must be accepted or rejected as a whole.

The petitioners delayed unreasonably in challenging the policy after its implementation, and several licensees had already acted upon it, altering their position substantially, warranting dismissal on grounds of laches.
The State is not bound to follow a rigid method like tender or auction for granting liquor licenses; it may adopt a method consistent with public interest and policy objectives.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915, Sections 13, 14, and 62(2)(h)
Rule XXII of the Madhya Pradesh Excise Rules
Rules III to V of the Distillery Warehouse Rules
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Principle of judicial restraint in reviewing policy decisions
Bona fides in executive policy-making
Non-arbitrariness under Article 14

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged the High Court's decision that invalidated provisions of the Maharashtra Housing and Development Act, 1976, relating to land acquisition for housing, which the respondents (heirs of a landowner) opposed as unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 44 of the Maharashtra Housing and Development Act, 1976 violate Articles 14, 19, 21, and 300A of the Constitution
Whether the Act is protected under Article 31C by virtue of seeking to implement Article 39(b)
Whether the acquisition process under the Act satisfies the principle of fairness under Article 300A
Whether Article 21 can be invoked to challenge land acquisition for public housing
holdings: The provisions of Section 44(3) and (4) do not violate fundamental rights as they are protected by Article 31C, which shields laws aimed at implementing Article 39(b).

The Maharashtra Housing and Development Act qualifies as legislation to secure the directive principle in Article 39(b), enabling equitable distribution of resources, and thus attracts Article 31C protection.
Even assuming Article 300A requires fair and reasonable procedure, the Act fulfills all requirements of fair acquisition, including public purpose and opportunity to be heard.
Article 21 cannot be invoked to challenge property acquisition for public housing, as it protects personal liberty, not property rights, absent deprivation of livelihood.
provisions: Maharashtra Housing and Development Act, 1976, Section 44(3) and (4)
doctrines: Doctrine of Harmonious Construction
Doctrine of Eclipse
Principle of Eminent Domain
Transformative Constitutionalism
Expansive Interpretation of Directive Principles

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the High Court's decision invalidating the acquisition of arable land for urban housing, arguing that the delay in issuing the declaration under Section 6 and the presence of some structures on the land did not vitiate the acquisition process.
issues_decided: Whether post-notification delay of nearly one year in issuing the declaration under Section 6 vitiates the acquisition under Section 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether land with some superstructures can be acquired under Section 17(1) when the land is otherwise arable and meant for planned development
Whether the omission to cite Section 17(1A) in the notification renders the acquisition invalid
holdings: A delay of nearly one year between the notification under Section 4 and the declaration under Section 6 does not invalidate the acquisition if the urgency was genuine at the time of notification and there is no mala fide.

Land with scattered superstructures can still be considered arable and suitable for acquisition for planned urban development under Section 17(1), especially when the overall character of the land is agricultural.

The omission to expressly refer to Section 17(1A) in the notification does not invalidate the acquisition, as the power to acquire non-waste, non-arable land for planned development is automatically available when urgency is invoked for such purposes.
doctrines: Doctrine of post-notification delay not invalidating urgency if initial urgency was genuine
Doctrine of substantial compliance in land acquisition notifications
Principle of equitable relief for displaced persons in urban development projects

card.dispute: The State Bank of India challenged the High Court's stay on its suit to recover secured debts from Saksaria Sugar Mills Ltd. and its guarantors, citing a central government notification under the Sugar Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1978.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 7(1)(b) of the Sugar Undertakings Act automatically suspends all contractual obligations of a notified sugar undertaking
Whether secured liabilities to banks and financial institutions are covered by the suspension under the notification
Whether remedies against guarantors are suspended when the principal debtor's obligations are suspended under the Act
holdings: The suspension of contractual obligations under Section 7(1)(b) applies only to those contracts specifically mentioned in the notification, not automatically to all contracts.
Secured liabilities to banks and financial institutions are explicitly excluded from the suspension under the notification and remain enforceable.
The liability of a surety under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act is co-extensive with the principal debtor, and remedies against guarantors are not suspended by the notification.
provisions: The Sugar Undertakings (Taking over of Management) Act, 1978, Section 7(1)(b) and Section 7(4)
doctrines: Co-extensiveness of surety's liability with principal debtor
Specificity of statutory notification for suspension of rights
Revival of suspended rights upon cessation of notification

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged the High Court's order directing the release of seized tin plates from Calcutta Hardware Stores during ongoing prosecution and confiscation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exercised its powers under Article 226 properly in granting an ad interim order releasing seized goods in a criminal and confiscation proceeding.
Whether the impugned order prejudged the merits of the case and undermined public interest and administrative authority.
holdings: The High Court must exercise its wide powers under Article 226 with restraint, especially in matters involving seized goods during ongoing prosecution, to avoid prejudicing public interest and administrative action.

An ad interim order releasing seized goods without adequate security, especially when serious criminal charges and confiscation proceedings are pending, is illegal and amounts to premature adjudication of the merits.
provisions: Essential Commodities Act, 1955, Section 3(1), Section 6A, Section 7, Section 8
doctrines: Judicial restraint in interim orders under Article 226
Balance of convenience and public interest in granting interim relief
Prohibition against prejudging issues pending before trial courts

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal sought to evict Saral Kumar Sen Gupta from a government flat, alleging he violated the tenancy agreement by ceasing to reside there, while his brother and sisters continued to occupy it.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant violated clause (7) of the tenancy agreement by not personally residing in the government flat while family members continued to occupy it.
Whether the tenancy stood automatically terminated under Section 3(2) of the West Bengal Government Premises (Tenancy Regulation) Act, 1976.
holdings: The tenant violated clause (7) of the tenancy agreement by ceasing to personally occupy the premises, as the agreement required his own residence along with family members, not residence by family members alone.
The tenancy stood automatically terminated under Section 3(2) of the Act due to breach of lease terms, entitling the government to recover possession.
provisions: West Bengal Government Premises (Tenancy Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of contractual terms
Automatic termination of tenancy for breach of lease conditions

card.dispute: The appellant, a licensee of a shop, challenged the Municipal Corporation's order to demolish the shop, and the District Judge's refusal to record evidence in his appeal against that order.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure of a civil suit under the Code of Civil Procedure must be strictly followed in an appeal under Section 269(2) of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act, 1976.
Whether the phrase 'as far as it can be made applicable' in Section 384 of the Act mandates technical compliance with CPC procedures in appeals before the District Judge.
holdings: Section 384 of the Punjab Municipal Corporation Act does not require strict or technical adherence to civil suit procedures under the CPC in appeals, applications, or references before the District Judge.

The District Judge may allow recording of evidence under Order 41, Rule 27 of the CPC if deemed necessary, as procedural provisions of the CPC apply only by way of guidance and not as a binding requirement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Doctrine of substantial compliance
Guideline-based application of civil procedure

card.dispute: The tenant, Yudhishter, challenged the landlord Ashok Kumar's eviction petition on grounds of bona fide personal requirement under the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, after the landlord sold another property he had purchased earlier.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate authority had jurisdiction to admit additional evidence in an appeal against the Rent Controller's order?
Whether the landlord's requirement of the premises was bona fide under Section 13(3)(a)(i) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973?
Whether the sale of another residential property by the landlord before filing the eviction petition disqualified him from claiming eviction on grounds of personal need?
Whether the sale of the property was a benami transaction to circumvent the provisions of the Rent Act?
holdings: The appellate authority has express jurisdiction under Section 15(4) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 to admit additional evidence and conduct further inquiry if necessary.
The landlord's need for the premises was bona fide, as he did not have any other residential accommodation in his possession at the time of filing the eviction petition.

The sale of another property by the landlord does not disentitle him from seeking eviction on grounds of personal need, in the absence of evidence showing mala fide intent to defeat the tenant's rights.

The sale was not a benami transaction; the landlord sold the earlier purchased house because it was not in vacant possession, and this was supported by evidence including income-tax records and oral testimony.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(3)(a)(i)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 15(4)
doctrines: Beneficial legislation should be interpreted reasonably and justly to avoid unconstitutional consequences
Presumption of constitutionality in statutory interpretation
Evidence can explain documentary recitals regarding possession

card.dispute: The landlord sought to evict the tenant (husband) under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, on the ground that his wife had been allotted a government quarter, which the landlord claimed disqualified the tenant from retaining the tenanted premises.
issues_decided: Whether allotment of a government quarter to the tenant's wife, not forming part of the matrimonial home, disentitles the husband to retain tenancy under Section 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the husband can be deemed to have acquired alternative accommodation merely because his wife was allotted a residence in her capacity as a government employee.
holdings: Allotment of a residence to the tenant's wife in her official capacity, which is not the matrimonial home and over which the husband has no legal right or dominion, does not disentitle the husband from retaining tenancy under Section 14(1)(h).

Mere allotment of accommodation to the spouse does not amount to acquisition by the tenant unless the tenant has actual or legal access to or control over the new residence; otherwise, it cannot trigger eviction under Section 14(1)(h).
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tenant disentitlement
Doctrine of effective enjoyment and dominion over alternative accommodation

card.dispute: The landlord (B.P. Khemka Pvt. Ltd.) sued the tenant (Birendra Kumar Bhowmick) for eviction due to alleged default in rent payment, while the tenant sought relief under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, including installment payment and protection from eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to the benefit of Section 17(2A)(b) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, despite filing the application for installment payment after the one-month deadline prescribed by Section 17(1), in light of the 1967 Ordinance?

Whether the tenant's delayed payment of rent for two months within a 13-month period amounted to a second default under the proviso to Section 17(4), warranting striking out of the defence and eviction?
Whether the word 'shall' in Section 17(3) of the Act is mandatory or directory, and whether the court has discretion to condone delay and refuse to strike out the defence?
holdings: The one-month limitation under Section 17(1) was rendered inoperative by Section 5 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, VI of 1967, which allowed all tenants with pending suits at the time of promulgation to file applications under Section 17(2A) within one month, with retrospective effect.
A second default under the proviso to Section 17(4) requires non-payment of rent for four months within twelve months; a shorter default does not disentitle the tenant to protection from eviction.

The word 'shall' in Section 17(3) is directory, not mandatory, and must be read as 'may'; courts have discretion to refuse to strike out a tenant’s defence and may condone delays in payment based on the facts and interests of justice.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(2)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(2A)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(4)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967, Section 2
West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967, Section 5
doctrines: Remedial statutes should be interpreted liberally to advance their beneficial purpose.
The distinction between mandatory and directory use of 'shall' depends on legislative intent, context, and consequences of interpretation.
Courts may imply discretion to condone delay where a provision allows refusal to strike out a defence for rent default.

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Outline Development Plan and Regulations for Bangalore on grounds of defective publication in the Official Gazette.
issues_decided: Whether the publication of the Outline Development Plan and Regulations was sufficient under Section 13(4) and Rule 33 of the Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, despite not being bodily incorporated in the Gazette.
Whether the omission to mention the Regulations in the Gazette notice amounted to non-publication.
Whether a procedural defect in publication could be cured by Section 76J of the Act.
Whether the Plan and the Regulations are distinct or form an integrated whole.
holdings: Publication in the Gazette by notifying the public about the availability of the Plan and Regulations for inspection satisfies statutory requirements, even if the full text is not printed in the Gazette.
The failure to explicitly mention the Regulations in the notice does not amount to non-publication, as the Plan and Regulations were treated as a unified document available for inspection.
A procedural defect in publication that does not cause substantial prejudice is curable under Section 76J, especially when the public had effective notice and the defect did not affect the merits.
The Outline Development Plan and the Regulations are not distinct; the Regulations are integral to the Plan and necessary for its implementation.
provisions: Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, Section 13
Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, Section 76J
Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, Section 81A(a)
Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, Section 12
doctrines: Curative provision doctrine (Section 76J as an 'omnibus curative clause')
Distinction between mandatory and directory statutory requirements
Doctrine of substantial compliance
Integration of subordinate legislation with parent plan

card.dispute: The landlord (Bhairab Chandra Nandan) sued for eviction of the tenant (Ranadhir Chandra Dutta) on grounds of unauthorized subletting and bona fide need for family accommodation, which the High Court dismissed, reversing the lower courts' decrees.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of the Trial and Appellate Courts on unauthorized subletting by the tenant?
Whether the appellant landlord had a bona fide need for additional accommodation for his family?

Whether the existence of another property owned by the landlord, occupied by tenants and located over three miles away, bars eviction under Section 13(ff) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1956?
holdings: The tenant's transfer of possession to his brother without the landlord's consent constituted unauthorized subletting, not mere licensing, warranting eviction.
The landlord's need for additional accommodation was bona fide, given the cramped living conditions and family size, despite the High Court's contrary view.

The requirement under Section 13(ff) that the landlord lack reasonably suitable accommodation is not strictly applicable where the landlord seeks only additional space within the same premises and already resides there.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1956, Section 13(ff)
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are not to be disturbed unless perverse
Subletting distinguished from license based on transfer of possession and intent
Bona fide requirement for family occupation assessed contextually with living conditions

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, heirs of their father, disputed whether an arbitration award concerning rights in immovable property required registration under the Registration Act, 1908, and whether it could be made a rule of court.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award, which made rights in immovable property contingent on payment of money, required compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether an unregistered arbitration award could be made a rule of court under the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the maintenance and settlement amounts awarded were adequate in light of inflation
holdings: An arbitration award that does not by itself create, declare, assign, limit, or extinguish any right in immovable property, but only provides for such change upon future payment, does not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.
An unregistered arbitration award, if not required to be registered, can be made a rule of court under the Arbitration Act, 1940, especially when the legality of the award is not challenged.

The Court may modify the terms of an arbitration award in the interest of justice, including increasing maintenance and settlement amounts, to account for inflation and protect the interests of all parties.
doctrines: Doctrine of contingent rights in immovable property
Doctrine of severability in arbitration awards
Principle of justice, equity and good conscience

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against an eviction order based on rent arrears, disputing the amount of rent and the enforceability of the lease terms due to non-registration.
issues_decided: Whether the rent note for one year at Rs. 5,000/- per annum could be treated as a lease from year to year requiring registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act and Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the tenant was in arrears of rent such that the landlord was entitled to eviction under Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act.
holdings: A lease for one year, even if it provides for yearly rent in advance, is not a lease from year to year and does not require registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act or Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act.

The tenant was in arrears of rent for at least two months at the time of the first hearing, and since he failed to pay the full arrears then, the landlord was entitled to eviction under Section 13 of the East Punjab Rent Restriction Act.
provisions: East Punjab Rent Restriction Act, Section 13
doctrines: Requirement of registration for leases exceeding one year
Doctrine of holding over
Condition precedent for rent payment to avoid eviction

card.dispute: The landlord sued the tenant for sub-letting part of the premises without written consent, which the tenant denied, claiming the occupant was given shelter in exchange for services, not rent.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant sub-let part of the premises without the landlord's written consent under Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Act, 1956
Whether rendering services in lieu of occupation amounts to payment of rent sufficient to create a sub-tenancy
Whether the concurrent findings of fact by lower courts can be interfered with by the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution
holdings: To establish sub-tenancy, there must be exclusive possession and payment of rent; neither was conclusively proven here.
Services rendered in lieu of occupation do not constitute rent under the West Bengal Premises Act, as the Act contemplates only monetary consideration.
The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 when essential ingredients for a finding of fact are not established by lower courts, to prevent manifest injustice.
provisions: West Bengal Premises (Rent Control) Act, 1956: Section 13(1)(a), Section 4, Section 5(b), Section 8, Section 9, Section 17(1), Section 17(2), Section 17B, Section 2(d), Section 2(h), Section 13(i), Section 13(j)
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact not binding when essential legal ingredients are not satisfied
Doctrine of exclusive possession for tenancy
Monetary consideration as essential for rent under rent control legislation
Supreme Court's discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 to prevent injustice

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax and Vikram Cotton Mills Ltd disputed whether income from leasing out the company's assets during a temporary suspension of business should be taxed as 'profits and gains of business' or 'income from other sources'.
issues_decided: Whether the income from letting out business assets during a temporary suspension of operations constitutes 'profits and gains of business' under Section 10 of the Income Tax Act.
Whether the activity of leasing out assets in this case amounted to carrying on a business for tax purposes.
holdings: Income from leasing out business assets during a temporary suspension of manufacturing operations can be taxed as 'profits and gains of business' if the intention is to exploit the asset as part of the business and not to abandon it.

The determination of whether leasing constitutes business depends on the assessee's intention, which must be inferred from facts, and a temporary lease with reversion does not terminate business activity.
doctrines: Intention-based test for business continuity
Facts-and-circumstances test for characterisation of income

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Kerala Financial Corporation's decision to sell a tea estate through private negotiation to a partnership firm instead of accepting his higher tender, alleging arbitrariness and violation of fair procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the State instrumentality must always sell public property through public auction or tenders
Whether private negotiation for sale of public property violates Article 14 if the highest bidder defaults
Whether the Corporation's action in selling to the next highest bidder's firm was arbitrary or unfair
holdings: Public property owned by the State or its instrumentalities should generally be sold through public auction or tenders to ensure fairness and transparency.
Departure from public sale is permissible in compelling circumstances, provided the action is fair, reasonable, and free from bias or arbitrariness.
When the highest bidder fails to pay despite extensions, offering the property to the next highest bidder through private negotiation is justified and does not violate Article 14.
The appearance of justice is vital; State actions must not create an impression of favouritism, nepotism, or discrimination.
doctrines: Principle of fairness in administrative action
Doctrine of reasonableness and non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Presumption of constitutionality of State action
Public interest as a guiding principle in disposal of State property

card.dispute: The landlords (Ganpat Ram Sharma & Ors) sought to evict tenant Smt. Gayatri Devi under Section 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, claiming she had alternative accommodation, but the tenant contested the validity and timing of the eviction claim.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant must possess an alternative residence on the date of the eviction application for Section 14(1)(h) to apply
Whether knowledge of the tenant's alternative accommodation by the landlord triggers the limitation period
Whether the landlord must plead and prove the grounds under Section 14(1)(h) strictly
holdings: For Section 14(1)(h) to apply, the tenant must have built, acquired vacant possession of, or been allotted a residence and actually possess the right to reside there on the date of the eviction application.
The cause of action for eviction under Section 14(1)(h) accrues when the landlord knows the tenant has alternative accommodation, and delay in filing may bar the suit if not explained.

The landlord must specifically plead and prove one of the three conditions in Section 14(1)(h); once done, the burden shifts to the tenant to show the accommodation is unsuitable or not available to them.
doctrines: Present possession rule
Accrual of cause of action
Burden of proof in eviction cases
Beneficial legislation interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of premises after a limited tenancy granted under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, while the tenant resisted eviction, challenging the validity of the tenancy creation.
issues_decided: Whether the permission granted under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, without stating reasons for non-requirement of premises, is valid
Whether a written and registered lease agreement is required after obtaining permission under Section 21
Whether the order permitting limited tenancy was 'mindless' and without application of judicial mind
holdings: Permission under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act is valid even if the landlord does not explicitly state reasons for not requiring the premises, provided facts indicate a genuine non-requirement.
Section 21 is a complete code; no separate written or registered lease is required after the Rent Controller's order permitting limited tenancy.
The Rent Controller's order was not mindless but involved application of judicial mind based on the facts and statutory requirements under Section 21.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation respecting consistent judicial practice
Section as a complete code (lex specialis)
Non-requirement of registration for agreements under statutory permission

card.dispute: The tenant challenged his eviction order on grounds of non-bona fide claim of permanent tenancy and the landlord's alleged ineligibility to claim possession for business use under the Andhra Pradesh rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can be evicted under Section 10(2)(vi) for claiming permanent tenancy without bona fides, even without denying the landlord's title?
Whether a landlord can seek eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) for family business purposes, even if not personally running the business?
Whether ownership of other non-residential properties disentitles a landlord from seeking eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) if those properties are not used for business?
holdings: A tenant can be evicted under Section 10(2)(vi) solely for making a non-bona fide claim of permanent tenancy, even without denying the landlord's title, as the grounds are disjunctive.
A landlord may seek eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) for a family business, which includes a son’s business, as it is considered the landlord’s own business when run jointly.
Ownership of non-residential buildings does not bar eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) if those buildings are not used for business and are located in non-commercial areas.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(vi)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
doctrines: Disjunctive interpretation of statutory grounds for eviction
Bona fide requirement for family business as personal requirement
Factual findings by lower authorities entitled to deference on appeal

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a leased property after a limited-term tenancy granted under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, but the tenant resisted, alleging fraud and non-compliance with statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the permission granted under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, was invalid due to alleged fraud or abuse of the statute by the landlord
Whether the tenancy was invalid because the lease agreement was not reduced to writing as required under Section 21
holdings: Permission granted under Section 21 is valid unless fraud is proven; mere repetition of limited-term leases does not imply fraud, and objections must be raised during the tenancy, not after its expiry.
Section 21 is a complete code; a written lease agreement is not necessary for validity, and long-standing judicial interpretation by the Delhi High Court must be respected.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of local laws should follow settled judicial precedent
Doctrine of fraud in obtaining statutory permission
Doctrine of waiver by delay in raising legal objections

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed whether their agreement was a lease or a licence, affecting the appellant's right to remain in occupation of the premises.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties created a relationship of landlord and tenant or licensor and licensee
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the trial court's finding that the appellant was a licensee and not a tenant
Whether the payment under the agreement was rent or compensation
holdings: The nature of the agreement depends on the intention of the parties, not merely on the form or description used in the document.
An agreement granting exclusive possession may still be a licence if the circumstances and restrictions indicate no intention to create a tenancy.
The right of the licensor to inspect the premises and restrictions on use, such as limited hours, support the conclusion that the agreement was a licence, not a lease.
The High Court should not interfere under Article 227 if the trial court's view is plausible, even if another interpretation is possible.
provisions: Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, Section 41
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence
Intention of the parties as the real test
Exclusive possession as a prima facie indicator of tenancy
Principle of non-interference by High Court under Article 227 when trial court's view is plausible

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay fought with the Dr. Hakimwadi Tenants Association and others over whether land reserved for a recreation ground under a development plan had lapsed due to failure to initiate acquisition within the statutory period.
issues_decided: Whether the reservation of land under the development plan lapsed under Section 127 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 due to non-initiation of acquisition proceedings within six months of the notice by the landowners
Whether the trustees waived their right to challenge the acquisition by indicating willingness to sell the land
Whether the delay in filing the writ petition barred the relief under Article 226 of the Constitution
holdings: The reservation of land lapsed under Section 127 of the Act because no acquisition steps were taken within six months of the notice, and the ten-year statutory period had expired.
There was no waiver of rights by the trustees, as their offer to sell was made without admitting the Corporation's authority and was not accepted, and no estoppel arose.
Inordinate delay or laches did not bar the writ petition because the reservation had already lapsed, making the acquisition invalid regardless of delay.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 127
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126
doctrines: Lapse of statutory reservation due to non-compliance with time limits
Waiver requires voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a right and cannot be inferred without estoppel
Laches does not defeat a valid legal claim when the underlying right has been extinguished by operation of law

card.dispute: The widow of Maharaja Pillai claimed absolute ownership over certain properties allotted to her for maintenance, while his son claimed a 1/3rd share, arguing her interest was limited.
issues_decided: Whether the widow acquired an absolute right under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, or a restricted right under Section 14(2).
Whether property given to a widow for maintenance, without an explicit restriction, falls under Section 14(1).
holdings: A Hindu widow put in exclusive possession of property with the right to use its income for maintenance acquires full ownership under Section 14(1), even if the property was not explicitly given in lieu of maintenance.

The right to maintenance is a pre-existing legal right; possession of property for that purpose is sufficient to trigger full ownership under Section 14(1), unless the instrument explicitly imposes restrictions under Section 14(2).
doctrines: Liberal construction of statutes in favour of women's property rights
Presumption that possession in lieu of maintenance ripens into full ownership under Section 14(1)
Section 14(2) as an exception requiring explicit restriction

card.dispute: The appellant, M.S. Jagadambal, claimed possession of land purchased by her husband, alleging encroachment by the respondent trust, while the respondents denied her title and possession and asserted their own title through adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant or her husband was in possession of the suit property within 12 years prior to the suit.
Whether the appellate court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on possession based on conflicting oral evidence.
Whether adverse possession could be claimed over low-lying, seasonally submerged land incapable of use and enjoyment.
holdings: Possession continues with the title holder unless displaced by adverse possession; seasonal submersion of land does not amount to loss of possession.
An appellate court should not reverse a trial court's finding on factual credibility without strong reasons, especially when the trial judge observed the witnesses.
Adverse possession cannot continue over land that is submerged and incapable of use and enjoyment, as de facto possession is a prerequisite.
doctrines: Constructive possession
Appellate review of findings of fact
Adverse possession
Presumption of possession in favor of title holder

card.dispute: The appellants, tenants of a godown in Ghaziabad, challenged their eviction by respondent No. 1, who claimed to be the landlord, under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, after a dispute arose over ownership following the dissolution of a partnership firm.
issues_decided: Whether respondent No. 1 had the legal right to claim rent and file an eviction suit under Section 20(2)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972
Whether the appellants were in arrears of rent for not less than four months as required under Section 20(2)(a)
Whether a valid notice of demand for rent was served upon the appellants within the meaning of Section 20(2)(a)
holdings: A landlord must have a valid title to file an eviction suit; respondent No. 1 could not maintain the suit as the dissolution deed and his own admission showed the premises belonged to Smt. Prakash Kaur.
The appellants were not in arrears of rent as they had consistently paid rent and even deposited over Rs. 35,000 in court, exceeding the amount due.

A notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act does not satisfy the specific notice requirement under Section 20(2)(a); a clear demand notice under the Act is mandatory for eviction on rent default grounds.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30(2)
doctrines: Estoppel against landlord under Section 116 of the Evidence Act does not bar a tenant from challenging the landlord's title if it has ceased
Strict compliance with statutory conditions precedent for eviction under rent control laws
Doctrine of bona fide dispute in title permitting deposit of rent in court under Section 30(2)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the reduced compensation awarded by the High Court for their land acquired for an Aviation Research Centre, arguing it should match the higher rate given for adjacent plots.
issues_decided: Whether the concessional rate at which the government offered land to industrialists reflects the market value for compensation purposes.
Whether the purchase price of the land in 1956 is relevant to determining its market value at the time of acquisition.
Whether the appellants are entitled to the same compensation rate as awarded for adjacent lands acquired under the same notification.
