card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sought eviction of the tenant (respondent) for alleged unauthorized sub-letting of part of commercial premises to a tailor and an ice-cream vendor.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had sub-let part of the premises, thereby parting with exclusive possession?
Whether the sub-letting, if any, was for monetary consideration as required under the Rent Act?
Whether the appointment of a Court Commissioner without prior notice to the parties vitiated the proceedings?
Whether the finding of sub-letting could be upheld in the absence of specific pleading on monetary consideration?
holdings: Exclusive possession was parted with by the tenant, as evidenced by the ice-cream vendor's independent occupation, satisfying the requirement for sub-letting.
An inference of monetary consideration can be drawn from the circumstances when the tenant's explanation is found unsatisfactory, even without direct evidence.
Appointment of a Commissioner without prior notice is permissible if notice would defeat the purpose, under Order 39 Rule 7 CPC.
Pleadings alleging 'sub-letting' are sufficient to encompass consideration; liberal construction is warranted when parties understood the case and led evidence.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, 1908: Order 26 Rule 9, Order 39 Rule 7, Section 115
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949: Sections 13 and 15(5)
doctrines: Substance over form in pleadings
Inference of consideration in clandestine sub-letting
Exclusive possession as determinative of lease vs. licence
Limited scope of revisional court in reappreciating concurrent findings

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over ownership of a plot of land in Sen Colony, Jaipur, with the respondents claiming title through purchase and the appellants asserting ownership through adverse possession and denying tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were tenants of K.K. Sen and thus of the respondents after the sale of the plot.
Whether the appellants could claim protection under the Rajasthan Rent Control Act.
Whether the appellants acquired title by adverse possession.
holdings: The appellants were tenants of K.K. Sen and continued as such after the respondents purchased the land, so their possession did not ripen into adverse possession.
The appellants were not entitled to protection under the Rent Act as they denied the landlord-tenant relationship and never raised the plea in lower courts.
A claim of adverse possession cannot succeed when the possession is under a landlord-tenant relationship and the encroachment is part of the same holding.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Constructive recognition of tenancy under Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act
Plea of statutory protection must be raised at the earliest opportunity

card.dispute: The sons of the Karta of a Joint Hindu Family sued to restrain him from selling coparcenary property, claiming no legal necessity for the sale, while the Karta had entered an agreement to sell the property.
issues_decided: Whether a coparcener can maintain a suit for permanent injunction under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to prevent the Karta from alienating joint Hindu family property?
Whether the remedy of a coparcener lies in challenging an alienation after it is made, rather than preventing it in advance?
holdings: A coparcener has no right to seek a permanent injunction to restrain the Karta from alienating joint family property, as such interference would undermine the Karta's managerial authority.
The coparcener's remedy is limited to challenging an alienation after it occurs, provided it is not for legal necessity or benefit of the estate; he cannot preemptively block the sale.
doctrines: Managerial powers of Karta under Mitakshara law
Fiduciary nature of Karta's role
Remedy of challenging alienation post-facto
No right to injunctive relief against proposed alienation by coparcener

card.dispute: The dispute was between Achal Reddi and Ramakrishna Reddiar over whether possession of land obtained under an oral agreement of sale could be considered adverse for claiming title by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether possession under an executory contract of sale can be adverse to the vendor
Whether the period of possession by a purchaser under an unregistered sale agreement can be added to claim title by limitation
Whether the possession of a predecessor-in-title under an agreement of sale enures to the benefit of the plaintiff for adverse possession
holdings: Possession obtained under an executory contract of sale is permissive and not adverse, as it acknowledges the vendor's title.
A purchaser in possession pursuant to an unexecuted sale agreement cannot claim such possession as adverse against the vendor.
Where possession is referable to a lawful title, it cannot be deemed adverse, even if the agreement is later unenforced.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Estoppel against transferee under executory contract
Derivative possession

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their agricultural land acquired for a police headquarters, arguing that the High Court undervalued the land and incorrectly reduced compensation for 'present value'.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the market value of the land by applying Miram's Tables to compute 'present value' based on a 12-year development lag.
Whether the landowners are entitled to enhanced solatium and interest under the Central Amending Act (Act 68 of 1984) as their appeals were pending on April 30, 1982.
holdings: The High Court correctly determined the market value at Rs. 7,000 per acre and allowed a 25% deduction for roads and open spaces, but erred in further reducing compensation using Miram's Tables to account for delayed development.

The appellants will benefit from the Central Amending Act (Act 68 of 1984) only if the Constitution Bench upholds the Bhag Singh view and overrules Kamalajammanniavaru; the issue is left open pending that decision.
doctrines: Principle of full and fair compensation in land acquisition
Prohibition against discounting future value of land based on speculative development timelines
Retrospective application of amending laws depending on judicial interpretation

card.dispute: Cooperative societies challenged the state's acquisition of land within the Umaid Bhavan Palace premises, claiming it was private property exempt from acquisition under the Rajasthan Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the land within the Umaid Bhavan Palace falls under the definition of 'estate' under Section 2(b) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Owners Estate Act, 1963
Whether the land in question qualifies as 'land' under Section 2(f) of the same Act, given its classification as non-agricultural or 'abadi' land
Whether a transfer of land after August 16, 1971, is void under Section 3(2) of the Rajasthan Urban Property (Restriction of Transfers) Act, 1973
holdings: Land within the Umaid Bhavan Palace, being part of the ruler's private property under Category 'C' in the Covenant, does not fall within the statutory definition of 'estate' and thus cannot vest in the state under Section 7 of the Rajasthan Land Reforms Act.
The land in dispute is 'abadi land' (non-agricultural, built-up area) and falls under the exception to the definition of 'land' in Section 2(f), so it is not subject to acquisition under the Act.

A transfer of land effected after August 16, 1971, is not void under Section 3(2) of the Rajasthan Urban Property (Restriction of Transfers) Act, 1973, as the prohibition does not render such transfers legally invalid.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Owners Estate Act, 1963, Section 2(b)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Owners Estate Act, 1963, Section 2(d)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Owners Estate Act, 1963, Section 2(f)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Owners Estate Act, 1963, Section 7
Rajasthan Urban Property (Restriction of Transfers) Act, 1973, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'estate' and 'land' in land reform legislation
Doctrine of admission by conduct and estoppel in light of state's prior affidavits
Presumption against retrospective invalidation of property transfers

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the sale of his entire 10-acre land in execution of a decree for about Rs. 2,400, arguing that only a portion should have been sold.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court must consider selling only a portion of attached property sufficient to satisfy the decree under Order XXI Rule 64 CPC.
Whether the sale of the entire 10-acre land was illegal for failing to consider partial sale.
holdings: The executing court must determine whether the entire property or only a portion needs to be sold to satisfy the decree; it is a legal obligation, not mere discretion.
Selling the entire property without considering whether a smaller portion could satisfy the decree is illegal and without jurisdiction if the property is divisible.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 64
doctrines: Rule of proportionality in execution sales
Jurisdictional limitation on sale of property in execution

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of tenants on grounds including rent arrears and illegal sub-letting; tenants and a person in possession of a garage disputed the sub-letting claim, asserting he was a trespasser.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants were liable for eviction due to illegal sub-letting of a garage to defendant No. 6
Whether the High Court could interfere with a finding of fact in a writ petition
Whether defendant No. 6 was in lawful possession of the garage on the relevant date
holdings: The tenants did not illegally sub-let the garage to defendant No. 6, as no evidence or plea supported such a finding and Daulat, who made the agreement, had no legal interest in the property.
The High Court could interfere with a finding of fact in a writ petition when the finding was legally unsustainable or based on no evidence.
Defendant No. 6 was a trespasser and not in lawful possession, and thus could not benefit from statutory protections for tenants or sub-tenants.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15(2)
doctrines: Proviso to Section 58 of the Evidence Act requiring independent proof when admission alone is insufficient
Judicial review of findings of fact in writ petitions when findings are arbitrary or legally unsustainable

card.dispute: The company's former employee refused to vacate a company-leased flat after resignation, leading to criminal prosecution under Section 630 of the Companies Act, which the employee challenged on grounds of a bona fide dispute and lack of complainant's competence.
issues_decided: Whether a criminal complaint under Section 630 of the Companies Act is maintainable when the ex-employee raises a dispute over possession of company-leased property.
Whether the dispute raised by the ex-employee was a bona fide dispute requiring civil adjudication.
Whether the complainant, Mr. Atul Mathur, was competent to file the criminal complaint on behalf of the company.
holdings: A complaint under Section 630 of the Companies Act is maintainable if there is no bona fide dispute over the company's right to possession.
The dispute raised by the ex-employee, based on self-serving letters, was not bona fide and did not bar criminal proceedings.
The complainant, as Divisional Sales Manager and attorney of the company, was competent to file the criminal complaint, especially under a general power of attorney.
doctrines: Bona fide dispute doctrine in criminal proceedings under Section 630
Competence of company officers to file criminal complaints
General vs. special power of attorney interpretation

card.dispute: Bhavnagar Municipality claimed ownership and possession of certain lands (including parade ground and Lancers' Quarters) against the Union of India, which was in possession and claimed ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the Resolutions dated 19.1.1948 and 29.2.1948 vested title to the suit lands in the Bhavnagar Municipality
Whether the Municipality was entitled to possession of the suit property based on title
Whether the principle of 'possession follows title' could be invoked by the Municipality in the absence of proven title
holdings: The Resolutions conferred only the authority to sell or lease government lands within municipal limits, not ownership or title, which remained with the State.
The Municipality did not prove title or possession, and thus could not claim possession based on title.
The principle that 'possession follows title' cannot be invoked when title is not legally established and physical possession is with another.
provisions: Government of India Act, 1935 (implied by context of accession and integration)
Rules regarding municipal administration and land revenue (as per conditions in 1965 Government letter)
doctrines: Possession follows title
Vesting of title vs. delegation of authority
Burden of proof in suits for possession based on title

card.dispute: Bajaj Auto Limited, the tenant, fought against eviction by landlord Behari Lal Kohli over alleged unauthorised sub-letting of premises to M/s United Automobiles.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered lease deed's clause permitting sub-letting to 'associate concerns' is admissible in evidence despite non-registration under the Registration Act
Whether M/s United Automobiles qualifies as an 'associate concern' of Bajaj Auto Limited
Whether general permission in the lease deed suffices as written consent for sub-letting under Section 14(1) Proviso (b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
holdings: A term in an unregistered lease deed cannot be admitted in evidence even for collateral purposes if it forms part of the lease transaction, such as granting sub-letting rights.
The appellant created a sub-lease in favour of M/s United Automobiles, which is a separate legal entity and not a licensee, thereby parting with possession under Section 14(1) Proviso (b).

General consent in a lease deed to sub-let to 'associate concerns' without naming the sub-lessee does not satisfy the requirement of specific written consent for a particular sub-letting under Section 14(1) Proviso (b).
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1) Proviso (b)
doctrines: Specific consent required for sub-letting under rent control laws
Inadmissibility of unregistered documents for proving terms of lease
No collateral use exception for lease terms affecting substantive rights

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, alleging sub-letting, material alteration of the premises, and rent default due to the tenant putting up an advertisement hoarding on the shop roof.
issues_decided: Whether fixing an advertisement hoarding on the roof constituted parting with possession of the premises under Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950
Whether the installation of the hoarding amounted to material alteration of the premises justifying eviction
Whether the tenant could be evicted for default in rent when it was the first default and no decree was sustained on that ground
holdings: Mere permission to use part of the premises for an advertisement hoarding does not amount to parting with legal possession if the tenant retains control and exclusive possession.
Fixing a hoarding with iron angles on the roof does not constitute material alteration of the premises justifying eviction under the Rent Control Act.
A tenant cannot be evicted solely on grounds of rent default if it is the first default and no finding supports eviction on that ground.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(e)
doctrines: Parting with legal possession requires transfer of exclusive possession and right to exclude others
Distinction between licence and tenancy based on control and intention
Sub-letting requires transfer of legal possession, not mere permissive use

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of subletting or parting with possession of the shop without written consent, while the tenant denied any such transfer of possession.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had sub-let or otherwise parted with possession of the rented shop without the landlord's written consent under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the landlord's knowledge of the business operation in the premises over the years amounted to implied consent or waiver of the right to seek eviction.
Whether mere acquiescence or permission by the landlord, in absence of written consent, could validate the sub-letting or parting with possession.
holdings: Under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenant must obtain the landlord’s written consent to avoid eviction for sub-letting or parting with possession; oral or implied consent is insufficient.
Mere knowledge or acquiescence by the landlord of a third party’s presence or business in the premises does not constitute waiver of the right to eviction if there is no written consent.
The requirement of written consent under the Act is for public purpose—to prevent disputes—and cannot be waived by implied conduct or delay in action.
doctrines: Written consent requirement for sub-letting
No implied waiver of statutory rights in public interest legislation
Doctrine of waiver requiring intentional relinquishment of a known right

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased landlord fought the Andhra Bank, the tenant, over eviction from leased premises under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, claiming bona fide need for the property.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord could seek eviction for a substantial portion of the leased premises under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) and 10(3)(c) of the Act, despite not needing the entire area?
Whether Section 10(3)(c) permits recovery of non-residential premises for residential use by the landlord?
Whether the death of the landlord during litigation extinguished the family's bona fide need for the premises?
holdings: Where a landlord establishes bona fide need for a substantial portion of leased premises, eviction of the entire premises may be granted if the statute does not permit partial eviction and the unneeded portion is insubstantial.

Section 10(3)(c) allows a landlord occupying part of a building to seek eviction of a non-residential tenant for residential use if the need is bona fide and the hardship to the landlord outweighs that to the tenant.
The death of the landlord does not eliminate the family's bona fide need where the eviction was sought for family accommodation and the family size has increased during litigation.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(c)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Comparative hardship
Substantial portion doctrine in eviction cases

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for allegedly changing the use of leased premises from a cycle and rickshaw repair shop to also selling televisions.
issues_decided: Whether the temporary sale of televisions in premises leased for a cycle and rickshaw repair shop constitutes a change of user under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether a change of user under the Act requires prejudice to the landlord's interest.
holdings: Temporary sale of televisions alongside a repair business does not amount to a change of user under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) where the core use of the premises remains unchanged.
A minor change in the use of commercial premises does not justify eviction unless it prejudices the landlord's interest or causes structural or material harm.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(b)
doctrines: Change of user
Lessee's obligation not to alter the purpose of lease
Interpretation of rent control statutes in light of tenant protection and practical necessities

card.dispute: Hindustan Oil Mills Ltd. and Sampatlal disputed the compensation amount and the relevant date for determining market value of their land acquired by the Andhra Pradesh Government for a Dairy Plant.
issues_decided: Whether the notification dated 28.2.1963, and not the earlier one of 11.5.1961, is the effective notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act for determining the market value of the land.
What is the correct market value per square yard of the land belonging to the company and Sampatlal as of the relevant date?
Whether the extent of land treated as building site (and thus eligible for higher compensation) should include the entire 10 acres owned by the company or only a portion thereof?
Whether the High Court correctly valued the godown structure based on its rental income and a multiplier of 25?
holdings: The notification dated 28.2.1963 is the effective notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, as it superseded prior notifications and correctly identified the ownership and classification of the land.
The market value of the land should be Rs. 9 per square yard for the company’s land and Rs. 8 per square yard for Sampatlal’s land, reflecting the rise in land prices up to February 28, 1963.
Out of the 10 acres owned by the company, only 1 acre, including the godown and appurtenant access, should be treated as building site; the remaining 9 acres should be compensated as ordinary land.
The High Court correctly valued the godown at 25 times the net annual rent of Rs. 10,000, considering the lessee’s obligation to maintain repairs.
doctrines: Supersession of notifications in land acquisition
Market value determination as of the date of effective notification
Use of comparable sales and awards in assessing compensation
Capitalization of rent method for valuing structures

card.dispute: India Cement Ltd challenged the Tamil Nadu government's levy of a local cess on royalty payments made for mining limestone, arguing it was beyond the state legislature's constitutional authority.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu legislature had the constitutional power to levy a cess on royalty from mining leases under the Madras Panchayats Act, 1958
Whether 'royalty' falls within the definition of 'land revenue' for the purpose of taxation under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
Whether the inclusion of royalty within 'land revenue' via an explanation to Section 115 of the Madras Panchayats Act is ultra vires the state legislature
holdings: A cess levied on royalty from mining operations is not a tax on land or land revenue and therefore does not fall under Entry 49 of List II, which authorizes states to tax land revenue.
Royalty is a charge based on extracted minerals and reflects the value of mineral, labor, and capital, not merely land, and thus cannot be treated as land revenue for taxation purposes.

By including royalty within the definition of 'land revenue' through an explanation, the state legislature exceeded its legislative competence, making the levy ultra vires under Entry 50 of List II, which reserves taxation on mineral rights to Parliament.

The levy of cess under Section 115, as extended to royalty, is unconstitutional and void to the extent it applies to mining leases, though it remains valid for other lands where only land revenue is charged.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950: Seventh Schedule, List II, Entries 23, 49, 50
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
doctrines: Principle of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of pith and substance
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged whether land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, could continue under the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (as amended in 1984) without fresh notification after the Central Act became applicable to Kerala.
issues_decided: Whether the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, stood repealed by operation of Article 254 of the Constitution when the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (as amended by Act 68 of 1984), became applicable to Kerala.
Whether pending acquisition proceedings under the Kerala Act could be continued under the Central Act without fresh procedural steps under Section 4(1) of the Central Act.
holdings: The Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, stood repealed by operation of Article 254 of the Constitution due to repugnancy with the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended, which became applicable to Kerala.

Pending acquisition proceedings initiated under the Kerala Act up to the stage of Section 6 declaration could be continued under the Central Act without fresh notification, as valid steps taken under the repealed law are preserved under Section 6(b) of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
doctrines: Doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254
Implied repeal
Doctrine of continuity of proceedings under repealed law

card.dispute: The heirs of Mehta Ravindrarai Ajitrai fought with the State of Gujarat over the compensation amount for land acquired for an industrial estate, claiming higher market value based on post-acquisition sale evidence.
issues_decided: Whether a post-acquisition sale transaction can be considered as evidence of market value under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the sale instance of adjoining land sold at Rs.3 per sq. yard.
What is the proper method to determine the market value of acquired land when comparable sales are available?
holdings: A post-acquisition sale transaction can be considered as evidence of market value if it is proximate in time and there is no evidence of speculative price rise due to the acquisition.

The High Court erred in wholly rejecting the sale instance (Ex. 152) merely because it was post-acquisition; it should have been considered with appropriate deductions for acquisition-induced price rise and adjacency benefit.

The market value must reflect what a willing buyer would pay to a willing seller at arms' length, using comparable sales at or near the date of the Section 4 notification, with adjustments for special factors.
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Admissibility of comparable sale instances
Adjustment for distress and post-acquisition sales

card.dispute: The plaintiff, Mrs. Shobha Venkat Rao, sued defendant No. 3, Krishna Ram Mahale, for wrongful dispossession from a restaurant business she was conducting under a licence agreement, seeking restoration of possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was lawfully dispossessed by the defendant without due process of law
Whether the defendant could retain possession after the alleged expiry of the licence period by taking the plea of unlawful possession of the plaintiff
Whether the appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution warranted interference with the High Court's judgment
holdings: A person in settled possession of property, even as a licensee, cannot be dispossessed otherwise than by due process of law, and any forcible dispossession amounts to trespass.
The defendant had no right to dispossess the plaintiff behind her back, especially through collusion, and could not take advantage of the licence period expiry to justify illegal repossession.
The appeal under Article 136 was dismissed as the defendant’s conduct was oppressive and fraudulent, and the courts below had correctly upheld the plaintiff’s right to possession.
doctrines: Doctrine of lawful possession
Prohibition against self-help in dispossession
Equitable principles against unjust enrichment and fraudulent conduct

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for alleged arrears of rent, while the tenant argued that a large advance payment held by the landlord should be adjusted against rent, making the eviction claim invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the advance rent exceeding one month's rent is refundable or adjustable under Section 7 of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Whether the tenant could be evicted during the subsistence of a 30-year lease in the absence of a forfeiture clause
holdings: Any advance payment exceeding one month's rent is void under Section 7(3) of the Act, and such amount held by the landlord must be treated as immediately adjustable against rent, preventing the tenant from being considered in default.
A contractual tenant with a fixed-term lease of 30 years cannot be evicted during the lease period in the absence of a forfeiture clause, as the tenancy continues under the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 7
doctrines: Nullity of stipulations violating rent control laws
Inapplicability of pari-delicto doctrine against tenants in rent control cases
Protection of contractual tenancy during fixed term without forfeiture clause

card.dispute: Pal Singh (tenant) challenged the maintainability of an eviction petition filed by Sunder Singh, one of the co-owners of the property, seeking eviction on grounds of bona fide need under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether one co-owner of a jointly owned property can maintain an eviction petition under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 in the absence of other co-owners?
Whether the tenant can deny the landlord's title when rent has been paid to one co-owner?
Whether the landlord's need for the premises was bona fide and whether the High Court was justified in not interfering with the appellate court's finding on this issue?
holdings: A co-owner of a property is entitled to file an eviction petition under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 even in the absence of other co-owners, provided the other co-owners do not object to the eviction.

A tenant is estopped under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 from denying the title of a co-owner landlord when rent has been paid to that co-owner, as such conduct implies recognition of landlord-tenant relationship.

The High Court was justified in upholding the appellate court's finding on bona fide need, especially after appointing a commissioner whose report corroborated the landlord's case, and no error was found in not reopening the issue in second appeal.
doctrines: Estoppel against tenant denying landlord's title (Section 116, Evidence Act)
Maintainability of eviction by one co-owner with consent or non-objection of others
Bona fide need as a ground for eviction under rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant society, which was allotted a plot of land with a temporary structure, fought against the respondent's suit for eviction and possession, claiming protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the property allotted to the society constituted 'premises' under Section 2(i) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, thereby attracting rent control protections.
Whether the suit for eviction and possession filed by the respondent in the civil court was maintainable.
holdings: The property allotted was only a plot of land with a temporary structure, which does not qualify as 'premises' under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
A suit for eviction and possession is maintainable in a civil court when the dominant nature of the tenancy is for land, not a building, even if a minor structure exists.
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are not interfered with by the Supreme Court unless perverse.
The dominant purpose test to determine whether a property is let as 'premises' under rent control law.

card.dispute: The landlords (plaintiffs) sought to evict the tenant (defendant No. 1) from a vacant site in Cumbum, while the tenant claimed protection under the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, including a right to purchase the land under Section 9.
issues_decided: Whether defendant No. 1 was a 'tenant' within the meaning of Section 2(4)(i) or Sub-clauses (a) or (b) of Section 2(4)(ii) of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921
Whether the notice terminating tenancy dated 27th April 1979 complied with Section 11 of the said Act
Whether the defendant was entitled to relief under Section 9 of the Act to compel the landlord to sell the land
holdings: The Court did not finally decide whether defendant No. 1 was a tenant under Section 2(4)(i) but left open the possibility that he may fall under Sub-clause (a) or (b) of Section 2(4)(ii) if found to have retained effective control of the premises after subletting.
The validity of the termination notice under Section 11 was not finally decided, as it depended on the determination of tenancy status.

The claim under Section 9 was not finally adjudicated; the Court held that if the defendant is found to be a protected tenant who erected a superstructure, he may be entitled to apply for purchase of the land.
provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 2(4)
Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 3
Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 11
doctrines: Effective possession doctrine
Statutory interpretation of tenant protection laws

card.dispute: Rajatha Enterprises fought against S.K. Sharma and others over the legality of a building constructed in excess of permissible floor area ratio and whether it should be demolished.
issues_decided: Whether the construction violated statutory provisions under the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act and Town and Country Planning Act.
Whether the deviation from permissible Floor Area Ratio (FAR) was compoundable.
Whether demolition of part of the building was justified in public interest.
Whether the petitioner had locus standi to challenge the construction in public interest litigation.
holdings: The construction did not violate statutory provisions substantially, especially since part of the building was for a government school exempt under Section 342 of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act.
The excess constructed area available for compounding was only 742 sq. ft. beyond the 5% permissible limit, which is minor and does not warrant demolition.
Demolition of the 6th floor was unjustified as there was no threat to public safety, no fraud, and the public interest was not prejudiced.
A person not residing in the neighborhood and not personally affected lacks locus standi to maintain a public interest litigation where no public harm is demonstrated.
provisions: Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, Section 14
doctrines: Locus standi in public interest litigation
Principle of proportionality in enforcement of building regulations
Doctrine of compounding minor deviations in building bylaws
Public interest not prejudiced in absence of harm to safety or rights

card.dispute: Miners challenged the validity of a Gujarat government notification increasing royalty rates on minor minerals and providing concessional rates for certain classes of quarry operators.
issues_decided: Whether the royalty levied on minor minerals can be used for general state purposes or must be limited to mineral development
Whether the increased royalty rate violated Article 304(c) of the Constitution by restricting inter-state trade
Whether the differential royalty rates under Rule 21 violated Article 14 by being discriminatory
holdings: A royalty levied under mineral development legislation need not be spent solely on mineral development; its use for general state purposes does not invalidate the levy.
The royalty increase does not infringe Article 301 or 304 as quarrying activity itself does not involve inter-state movement of goods, and thus the levy does not restrict trade.

The concessional royalty rate for Parwana holders and village potters is constitutionally valid as it constitutes reasonable classification under Article 14, based on intelligible differentia and nexus with social welfare objectives.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Incidental levy doctrine in regulatory schemes
Presumption against arbitrariness in delegated legislation

card.dispute: A women's rights group sought compensation from the Delhi Police and Administration for the death of a nine-year-old boy caused by police brutality during a forced eviction allegedly carried out in collusion with a landlord.
issues_decided: Whether the State is liable to pay compensation for the death of a child caused by the tortious acts of police officers acting in the course of their employment.
Whether the State can be held vicariously liable for the actions of its employees, including police officials, in cases of assault and battery resulting in death.
holdings: The State is vicariously liable for tortious acts committed by its employees, including police officers, while acting in the course of their employment, and must compensate victims of such acts.
The mother of a child who died due to injuries sustained in a police-led assault is entitled to compensation from the State, irrespective of any criminal proceedings against the individual officers.
provisions: Indian Penal Code: Section 304/34, Section 308/34, Section 120B
doctrines: Vicarious liability of the State for tortious acts of public servants
Constitutional tort
State liability under Article 32 for enforcement of fundamental rights

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a joint family over whether a chawl property in Ahmedabad was part of the joint family estate liable to partition or had been validly gifted to a daughter-in-law and thus excluded from partition.
issues_decided: Whether the Naroda chawl was joint family property liable to partition
Whether the appellant acquired prescriptive title to the chawl through adverse possession
Whether possession by a landlord through tenants and rent collection can constitute adverse possession
holdings: The chawl was originally joint family property acquired with ancestral funds and belonged to the joint family.
The appellant acquired a prescriptive title by adverse possession for over 12 years from 1946, as her agent collected rent with animus possidendi, and tenants attorned to her as owner.

A landlord can be in effective possession of leased property through tenants' attornment and rent payment, even without physical possession, satisfying the requirements for adverse possession under the Limitation Act.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Possession of agent is possession of principal
Attornment as evidence of possession
Symbolic possession in landlord-tenant context

card.dispute: The dispute was between family members over whether a property (Naroda Chawl) was part of the joint family estate liable to partition or had been gifted exclusively to one member (Defendant No. 6) and thus outside the scope of partition.
issues_decided: Whether Defendant No. 6 acquired exclusive title to the property by adverse possession after an alleged oral gift in 1946
Whether the plaintiff and other family members were in joint possession of the property, thereby negating adverse possession
Whether entries in revenue records and attornment of tenants by paying rent to Defendant No. 6 were sufficient to establish her possession
Whether the management of the property by Defendant No. 1 as agent affected the character of possession
holdings: A person can acquire prescriptive title through adverse possession even if tenants are in physical possession, provided rent is collected and attornment by tenants indicates recognition of ownership.
The possession of an agent is the possession of the principal; an agent collecting rent cannot claim joint or adverse possession against the principal.
Actual physical possession by the owner is not necessary for adverse possession when the property is leased; exclusive control through rent collection and attornment suffices.
A period of over 12 years of exclusive possession, even through agents or family members, can mature into a valid title under the Limitation Act.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Possession through agent
Attornment as evidence of possession
Prescriptive title in leased properties

card.dispute: The landlord (Shiv Chander Kapoor) sued to recover possession of a property from the tenant (Amar Bose) after a fixed-term tenancy ended, but the tenant resisted, claiming the tenancy permission was invalid due to alleged fraud and misrepresentation.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could challenge the validity of the Rent Controller's permission under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act at the stage of execution of possession
Whether the landlord's need for the premises for his son's marriage, with the son being under 21 at the time, rendered the limited tenancy permission invalid
Whether the Controller was required to issue notice to the tenant before granting a warrant of possession upon expiry of a limited tenancy
holdings: The tenant must proactively challenge the validity of the Controller's permission in a proper legal proceeding; otherwise, the permission remains valid and enforceable.
An estimate of a future event like marriage, even if the exact date is uncertain, is sufficient to justify a limited tenancy if it is reasonable and not shown to be a pretence.

No notice is required to be issued to the tenant at the stage of granting a warrant of possession upon expiry of a limited tenancy, as the tenant is already aware of the tenancy period and its expiry.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Presumption of validity of administrative orders
Burden of proving invalidity lies on the party challenging the order
Limited tenancy based on foreseeable future events
Prohibition of frivolous and after-thought pleas in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant (Smt. Annapoorani Ammal) and respondent (G. Thangapalam) disputed whether a 'yadast' document entitled the respondent to specific performance of a contract to convey property, despite the appellant being the registered purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure without a substantial question of law
Whether a 'yadast' document, unregistered and unattested, could form the basis for specific performance of a contract by someone not a party to the original sale
Whether the mother of the appellant, not being the owner or party to the sale deed, could bind the appellant to reconvey the property
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved; mere reappreciation of evidence does not justify interference.
Specific performance cannot be decreed against a person who is not a party to the contract and who has no right to dispose of the property.
A person not owning the property and not a party to the sale deed cannot create an obligation to reconvey it, and such a claim cannot be enforced against a transferee under a registered sale deed.
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Principle of finality of findings of fact by the first appellate court
Enforceability of contracts under specific performance only against parties with title or authority to dispose

card.dispute: Nine co-operative housing societies that were allotted nazul land appealed against the High Court's quashing of the allotment orders, while three non-allotted societies sought directions for fresh allotments based on preferential eligibility.
issues_decided: Whether the allotment of nazul land to nine co-operative societies was arbitrary and discriminatory
Whether the High Court erred in quashing the allotment orders without providing access to government files
Whether the non-allotted societies were entitled to a direction for fresh allotment of land
Whether compensation with interest was due to the societies for cancellation of allotment due to government arbitrariness
holdings: The allotment was arbitrary due to non-disclosure of criteria, deviation from 'first come first served', and preferential treatment to select societies, justifying quashing of orders.
The High Court could rely on internal file notings to assess arbitrariness without breaching principles of natural justice, as it did not base its decision solely on undisclosed material.
Courts cannot direct specific land allotments without comparative evaluation of all applicants; eligibility must be reassessed by the government if it chooses to proceed.
The government must refund amounts deposited by societies with 12% annual interest from deposit date to refund date if allotment is cancelled due to its own arbitrariness.
doctrines: Principle of arbitrariness in administrative action
Rule of 'first come first served' in public allotments
Principles of natural justice
Duty of state to compensate for loss due to arbitrary executive action

card.dispute: The Lucknow Development Authority revoked permission granted to the lessees to construct a multistoreyed building, and the lessees challenged the revocation in writ proceedings, alleging lack of authority and violation of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the Vice-Chairman of the Development Authority had the power to cancel development permission based on alleged fraud and violation of conditions?
Whether the cancellation of permission was vitiated by the Vice-Chairman acting under governmental dictation, thereby surrendering his discretion?
Whether the lessees were denied a reasonable opportunity of being heard in violation of principles of natural justice?
Whether judicial review under Article 226 can extend to examining the merits of the grounds for cancellation?
holdings: The Vice-Chairman had the authority to initiate proceedings to revoke development permission on grounds of misrepresentation, fraud, or breach of conditions under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973.
The cancellation was not vitiated by surrender of discretion, as there was no material showing that the Vice-Chairman acted under compulsion or binding directions from the State Government.

The show cause notice and cancellation order were invalid due to denial of natural justice, as the notice was vague and failed to afford the lessees a meaningful opportunity to respond, including a personal hearing where necessary.

Judicial review under Article 226 is confined to the legality and fairness of the decision-making process, not the merits of the decision; courts cannot substitute their view for that of the authority on factual grounds.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, Section 14
Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, Section 15
Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, Section 37
Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973, Section 41
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers and non-delegation of discretionary authority
Principle of natural justice: audi alteram partem
Scope of judicial review under Article 226
Doctrine of legality in administrative action: relevance of considerations and prohibition of arbitrariness

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired by the Town Improvement Trust, claiming it was undervalued and that potential and special value was not considered.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for the acquired land was legally determined by considering its special and potential value.
Whether the High Court erred in valuing the land on a block rate instead of plot-wise basis.
Whether agreements to sell and development plans could be considered to assess market value.
Whether the Tribunal and High Court overlooked relevant evidence in determining compensation.
holdings: Market value of acquired land must account for its special features and potential for development, especially when located within municipal limits and abutting major roads.
Land with development potential should be valued on a plot-wise basis if evidence shows the owner intended to develop and sell in plots.
Agreements to sell, coupled with applications for layout plans, are relevant to determine market value even if sale deeds were not executed.
Compensation should be enhanced when potential value is inadequately considered, and courts may adjust rates to reflect just value.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Town Improvement Trust Act, Section 68
doctrines: Principle of market value including special and potential value
Plot-wise versus block rate valuation
Use of unexecuted sale agreements as evidence of market value
Judicial review under special leave jurisdiction on error of principle

card.dispute: Residents and municipal bodies challenged the government's draft notification proposing to merge several municipal areas into the Kalyan Corporation, arguing they were not given a hearing before the decision was made.
issues_decided: Whether the government is required to provide a hearing to affected parties before issuing a draft notification under Section 3 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949.
Whether the rules of natural justice apply to the legislative function of the government in forming a municipal corporation.
holdings: The government's power to form a municipal corporation under Section 3 of the Act is legislative in nature, and compliance with the statutory procedure is sufficient; no hearing is required unless expressly mandated by law.
The rules of natural justice, including the right to a hearing, do not apply to legislative or subordinate legislative actions unless the statute specifically requires it.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 3
doctrines: Legislative action exception to natural justice
Separation of powers in administrative law
Delegated legislation and audi alteram partem

card.dispute: The tenant (appellant) challenged the validity of an ex parte eviction decree passed by a civil court, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction because the Haryana Urban Rent Control Act, 1973 vested exclusive authority in the Rent Controller to decide eviction matters.
issues_decided: Whether a civil court decree for eviction is a nullity if passed without jurisdiction under the Haryana Urban Rent Control Act, 1973
Whether such a decree operates as res judicata despite the court's lack of inherent jurisdiction
Whether the tenant can challenge the decree at the stage of execution on the ground of lack of jurisdiction
holdings: A civil court lacks inherent jurisdiction to pass an eviction decree for premises covered by the Haryana Urban Rent Control Act, 1973, as the Controller has exclusive authority; hence, any such decree is a nullity.
A decree passed by a court lacking inherent jurisdiction is void ab initio and does not operate as res judicata, even if confirmed in appeal or revision.
The tenant can challenge the jurisdictional defect at the execution stage, as lack of subject-matter jurisdiction can be raised at any point, even collaterally.
provisions: Haryana Urban Rent Control Act, 1973, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9, Rule 13
doctrines: Inherent lack of jurisdiction renders a decree a nullity (coram non judice)
Res judicata does not apply to jurisdictional defects going to the root of the court's authority
Waiver or consent cannot confer jurisdiction on a court inherently lacking it
Doctrine of restitution under Section 144 CPC remains available against execution of a null decree

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and others fought against landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated simultaneously under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the publication of the notification under Section 4(1) in the locality is mandatory and its non-compliance fatal to acquisition proceedings
Whether the acquisition was vitiated by legal mala fides
Whether the use of the phrase 'after the date of the publication of the notification' in Section 17(4) implies that a Section 6 declaration must come after the Section 4 notification
holdings: The requirement to publish the substance of the Section 4(1) notification in the locality is mandatory, and failure to do so vitiates the entire acquisition process.
The acquisition proceedings were vitiated by legal mala fides as the real purpose was to prevent the construction of a cinema theatre rather than for a genuine public purpose.

The phrase 'after the date of the publication of the notification' in Section 17(4) means that a declaration under Section 6 must be made subsequent to the publication of the Section 4 notification; simultaneous issuance is not permissible.
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with statutory notice requirements
Legal mala fides in administrative action
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction of statutes

card.dispute: The tenant's son challenged the ownership of the new landlords, claiming the original landlord had no title when she sold the property, while the landlords sought eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can deny the title of the original landlord at the time of creation of tenancy under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act
Whether a tenant can challenge the derivative title of a subsequent landlord who acquired the property after the tenancy was created
holdings: A tenant is estopped from denying the title of the original landlord at the time the tenancy was created, even if the lease itself discloses a defect in title.
A tenant may challenge the derivative title of a subsequent landlord, but not the title of the original landlord from whom the tenancy originated.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel under Section 116
Attornment and its estoppel effect
Distinction between original and derivative title in landlord-tenant law

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant for default in rent; the tenant claimed protection under Section 13-A of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, inserted during the pendency of the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could invoke the benefit of Section 13-A despite not applying within one month of the suit's commencement, given the amendment came into force later?
Whether the tenant was disqualified from Section 13-A's protection due to a prior default and subsequent court-determined arrears in a previous suit?
holdings: Tenants can avail the benefit of Section 13-A if they apply within thirty days of the ordinance's commencement, even if the suit predates the amendment, provided the suit was pending and eviction had not occurred.

A tenant who regularly deposits rent and promptly pays court-determined arrears upon application under Section 13-A is not guilty of wilful default and remains eligible for protection under the section.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13-A
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(3)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(4)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(6) proviso
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(7)
doctrines: Retrospective application of remedial statutes
Legislative intent in interpreting rent control laws
Benefit of doubt to tenants in rent control proceedings
Overriding effect of newly inserted provisions in pending suits

card.dispute: Private resin companies challenged the constitutional validity of the Jammu & Kashmir Extraction of Resin Act, 1986, which banned private resin extraction and transferred control to the State, arguing it violated their property rights without compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the right to extract and process resin constitutes 'property' under Article 31(2) of the Constitution
Whether the Jammu & Kashmir Extraction of Resin Act, 1986, violates Article 31(2) by depriving individuals of property without compensation
Whether the Act falls under the exception in Article 31(2A) since the property rights are not formally transferred to the State or a State-owned corporation
holdings: The right to extract, transport, and deal with resin constitutes a valuable property right protected under Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
The Act effectively acquires private property rights for the State without providing compensation, violating Article 31(2).
Article 31(2A) does not apply because the extinguishment of private rights directly results in their vesting in the State, making it a case of compulsory acquisition.
provisions: Jammu & Kashmir Extraction of Resin Act, 1986, Sections 3 and 4
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of compulsory acquisition of property
Doctrine of estoppel against the State (in administrative action)

card.dispute: The tenants (Ashoka Marketing Ltd. and others) challenged the eviction proceedings initiated by nationalised banks (Punjab National Bank and others) under the Public Premises Act, 1971, after their tenancy ended, claiming protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether premises belonging to nationalised banks qualify as 'public premises' under the Public Premises Act, 1971
Whether tenants in such premises can claim protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 after termination of tenancy
Whether the Public Premises Act overrides the Rent Control Act in case of repugnancy
Whether the tenants are estopped from challenging eviction under the Public Premises Act after successfully opposing eviction under the Rent Control Act
holdings: Premises owned by nationalised banks fall within the definition of 'public premises' under Section 2(e) of the Public Premises Act, 1971.
Tenants in unauthorised occupation of public premises cannot invoke the protection of rent control laws after tenancy expires or is terminated.
The Public Premises Act overrides the Delhi Rent Control Act to the extent of repugnancy, especially for premises owned by statutory bodies and nationalised entities.
Tenants who successfully argued that eviction must be under the Public Premises Act cannot later challenge such proceedings and claim protection under the Rent Control Act.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Sections 2(e), 4(1), 7(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of repugnancy between special and general statutes
Principle of estoppel by conduct
Public interest standard in actions by public authorities

card.dispute: The dispute was between Assam Sillimanite Ltd. and the Union of India over the premature termination of mining leases without granting a hearing, violating principles of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the termination of mining leases under Section 4A of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, without affording a hearing, violated principles of natural justice
Whether the petitioner was entitled to compensation for the wrongful termination of the leases
holdings: The premature termination of mining leases under Section 4A without giving the lessee an opportunity of being heard violates the principles of natural justice and renders the order null and void.

The petitioner is entitled to compensation for wrongful termination, and the matter should be referred to arbitration to determine quantum, limited to five years or the unexpired lease period, whichever is less.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4A
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Prospective overruling implied by statutory amendment
Judicial precedent (binding effect of State of Haryana v. Ram Kishan & Ors.)

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (Brij Mohan and others) sued for specific performance of an oral agreement to purchase a building from the defendant (Smt. Mahboobunnisa Begum), which the defendant denied, claiming no concluded contract existed.
issues_decided: Whether an oral agreement for the sale of immovable property was conclusively proved and enforceable for specific performance.
Whether the parties had reached consensus ad idem on all essential terms, including responsibility for obtaining Urban Land Ceiling clearance.
Whether Section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act applies in the absence of a concluded contract due to failure in negotiating a key term.
holdings: Specific performance of an oral agreement for sale of immovable property requires clear and convincing proof of consensus ad idem on all essential terms, which the plaintiffs failed to establish.
A concluded contract cannot be inferred when parties failed to agree on a crucial term—here, who would obtain Urban Land Ceiling clearance—despite negotiations.

Section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply where parties consciously negotiated but failed to finalize terms, as the statutory default rule only operates in the absence of a contrary agreement.
doctrines: Consensus ad idem
Specific performance of oral contracts
Default application of Section 55 of the Transfer of Property Act
Distinction between incomplete negotiations and binding agreement

card.dispute: The landlord, Dev Brat Sharma, sought eviction of tenant Dr. Jagjit Mehta from a residential house in Jalandhar, claiming need for use as a chamber after retirement, while the tenant had been running a clinic from part of the premises.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord was entitled to eviction under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act on the ground of personal need despite the tenant using part of the premises for a clinic.
Whether there was a change of user of the residential premises to non-residential, affecting the tenant's right to continue.
holdings: The landlord was not entitled to eviction because the tenancy was originally created for the purpose of running a clinic, and thus the use of the premises for medical practice did not constitute a change of user.
The absence of a sanctioned urban development scheme in Jalandhar meant that precedents based on such schemes in Chandigarh were not applicable to this case.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, Section 13A
doctrines: Change of user doctrine
Personal necessity for eviction

card.dispute: Dharam Singh (appellant) fought with Aso and another over the validity of a will allegedly leaving him a residential house and agricultural land, disinheriting the testator's two daughters.
issues_decided: Whether the will was duly proved in accordance with law, particularly regarding the role of the registering authority as an attesting witness.
Whether the appellant was entitled to claim a share in the residential house, considering the daughter's marital status and claim.
holdings: A registering authority cannot be considered a statutory attesting witness under the Indian Succession Act, and thus the will was not validly proved due to lack of proper attestation.
The appeal concerning the residential house is allowed on compromise, with the plaintiff agreeing to放弃 her claim, leading to dismissal of the suit regarding the house.
doctrines: Requirement of proper attestation of wills
Doctrine of compromise in appellate proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant contested the sale of an undivided half-share in a family dwelling house to a stranger, seeking an interim mandatory injunction to prevent the transferee from taking possession, arguing that the property belonged to an undivided family and the transferee had no right to joint possession under Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the suit dwelling house belonged to an undivided family within the meaning of Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the transfer of an undivided share in the dwelling house to a stranger transferee is subject to the restrictions under Section 44
Whether the appellant is entitled to an interim mandatory injunction to restore possession pending trial
holdings: A dwelling house held in undivided shares by members of a joint family, without partition by metes and bounds, qualifies as belonging to an undivided family under Section 44, even if members live separately in different portions.

A transferee of an undivided share in a dwelling house of an undivided family has no right to joint possession, and other co-owners can resist such possession under the second paragraph of Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.

An interim mandatory injunction should be granted to restore status quo if the transferee takes possession clandestinely, with knowledge of the co-owner’s rights, causing irreparable injury and where balance of convenience favors the co-owner.
doctrines: Prima facie case in injunction suits
Balance of convenience and irreparable injury in interim relief
Restriction on right of transferee to joint possession in family dwelling houses

card.dispute: The appellants claimed co-tenancy and sirdari rights over land recorded in the names of respondents 5 and 6, leading to a dispute over possession during land consolidation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had valid sirdari rights over the disputed land based on possession?
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the concurrent findings of the consolidation authorities on the nature of possession?
holdings: The appellants were entitled to sirdari rights over a 1/3rd share in the disputed plots based on recorded possession, as upheld by the consolidation authorities.
The High Court erred in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact by the consolidation authorities, which were based on proper appreciation of evidence and records.
doctrines: Principle of concurrent findings of fact
Doctrine of judicial review under Article 226 limited in factual matters

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's reversal of lower court decisions in a suit for permanent injunction, where the respondent claimed adhivasi rights over land based on his father's sub-tenancy and possession recorded in revenue records.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reappreciate evidence and overturn concurrent findings of fact under Section 100 CPC.
Whether the respondent's father was a recorded occupant and sub-tenant entitled to adhivasi rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the second appeal abated due to the death of some proforma defendants.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit for injunction despite incidental title questions.
holdings: The High Court can reappreciate evidence and arrive at an independent conclusion if the lower appellate court committed a procedural error by ignoring admissible evidence or placing the burden of proof incorrectly.

An entry in the Khasra of 1356 Fasli recording a person as sub-tenant is sufficient to confer adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, and the burden lies on the challenging party to prove the entry was made fraudulently or maliciously.
A second appeal does not abate due to the death of proforma parties when the main controversy can be decided between the surviving parties.
A civil court has jurisdiction to decide a suit for permanent injunction even if title is incidentally in question, especially when the suit is not one for declaration of title.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20(b)(i)
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of revenue records
Reappreciation of evidence in second appeal under substantial error in procedure
Doctrine of necessary parties in appeal
Incidental determination of title in civil suits

card.dispute: Private and public sector companies fought over the allocation of mining leases for chrome ore in Orissa, challenging the State Government's reservation of mining rights in favor of public sector undertakings.
issues_decided: Whether the reservation of chrome ore mining rights in favor of public sector undertakings is obligatory and excludes private players entirely
Whether the claims of two public sector companies (OCL and ORIND) for mining leases were validly rejected without proper consideration
Whether the State Government must consider equitable distribution of chromite ore to all industries, including private ones, despite reservation policies
Whether the Secretary, Government of India, was the appropriate authority to adjudicate competing claims for mining leases
holdings: The reservation of mining rights for public sector undertakings is not absolute; the State Government may relax it in exceptional cases based on relevant factors.
The rejection of OCL and ORIND's claims was too cryptic and unsustainable; their applications must be reconsidered afresh by the State Government.
The State Government has a duty to consider equitable distribution of chromite ore to meet legitimate industrial needs, even while maintaining reservation policies.
The Secretary, Ministry of Mines, acted as a recommendatory authority; final decision on mining leases rests with the State and Central Governments under the statutory framework.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 3(f)
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 5A
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 10
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 11
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 17A
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, First Schedule
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Second Schedule
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable distribution of natural resources
Doctrine of reasoned decision-making
Doctrine of proportionality in administrative discretion
Principle of fair opportunity in grant of mining leases

card.dispute: The tenant, Hiraji Tolaji Bagwan, challenged the eviction proceedings initiated by the alleged landlady, Shakuntala, who claimed ownership through a partition deed of ancestral land.
issues_decided: Whether the partition of ancestral property in favor of a wife and minor daughters is valid under Hindu Law
Whether a transferee of land by partition after August 1, 1953, can terminate the tenancy of a protected lessee under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958
holdings: A partition of ancestral joint Hindu family property in favor of a wife or daughter is invalid under Hindu Law, as females do not have pre-existing rights in ancestral property; thus, no valid title could pass to the respondent.

Under Section 38(7) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, a transferee who acquires land by partition after August 1, 1953, cannot terminate the tenancy of a protected lessee whose rights existed before such transfer.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 38(7)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 46
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) (Amendment) Act, 1963
doctrines: Hindu Law on partition of ancestral property
Statutory protection of tenancy rights
Retrospective operation of amendments

card.dispute: The appellants, who ran a plant nursery on acquired land, fought with the State of Haryana over entitlement to compensation for nursery plants and mother trees.
issues_decided: Whether compensation is payable for nursery plants that can be removed and sold after land acquisition.
Whether the valuation of mother trees as timber (wood) is valid when land is acquired for urban development.
holdings: Nursery plants that are grown for sale and can be removed from the land without perishing are not entitled to separate compensation upon acquisition.
Mother trees on acquired land, when the land is valued for its urban potential, may be valued only as timber if they are not integral to a continuing business or irreplaceable.
doctrines: Principle of compensation for severable improvements
Valuation based on intended use of acquired land

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the authority of a court-appointed Receiver to create new tenancies for parts of a disputed property, specifically opposing leases granted to Grindlays Bank and Tata Finlay Ltd.
issues_decided: Whether a court-appointed Receiver has the power to lease immovable property for a term exceeding three years without violating court orders
Whether partial surrender of a tenancy by a tenant results in the termination of the entire tenancy
Whether a new tenancy created by a Receiver in violation of an injunction order can confer rights under tenancy protection laws
holdings: A Receiver does not have inherent power to create new tenancies, especially where restrained by court order; any such act is ultra vires and cannot confer statutory tenancy rights.
Partial surrender of a tenanted property does not amount to surrender of the entire tenancy; the original tenancy continues in respect of the retained portion.

A lease created by a Receiver in breach of a court injunction is invalid and cannot be protected under tenancy statutes, as the Receiver acts as an officer of the court and cannot bind it contrary to its orders.
provisions: Calcutta High Court Original Side Rules, Chapter 21 Rule 5(a)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 11
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 13(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 88
doctrines: Receiver as officer of the court
Injunction violation nullifies third-party rights
Partial surrender does not imply total surrender
Statutory tenancy protection not available when tenancy created in breach of court order

card.dispute: The Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) and tenants disputed whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to fix fair rent when the ownership of the leased properties was in question.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has jurisdiction to decide questions of title under the Tamil Nadu Buildings Lease and Rent Control Act.
Whether the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship is a jurisdictional fact that can be finally decided by the Rent Controller.
Whether the civil court's jurisdiction is ousted in cases where title to the property is disputed between the parties.
holdings: The Rent Controller lacks jurisdiction to finally decide questions of title; such issues fall outside the scope of the Rent Control Act.
The determination of a landlord-tenant relationship by the Rent Controller is not conclusive and does not bind the parties in a civil court.
The civil court retains jurisdiction to adjudicate title disputes even if a Rent Controller has fixed fair rent, as the Act does not expressly oust civil court jurisdiction.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, Sections 4, 10(1), 10(2)(vii), and 19
doctrines: Jurisdictional facts doctrine
Ouster of civil court jurisdiction requires clear statutory language
Res judicata does not apply to decisions on jurisdictional issues by quasi-judicial authorities

card.dispute: The sons of a Hindu joint family challenged the alienation of ancestral property by their father, claiming it was for his personal debts without legal necessity and not binding on them.
issues_decided: Whether the father's alienation of joint family property to satisfy personal debts is binding on the sons under Hindu law
Whether the doctrine of pious obligation applies to debts that are vyavaharik but not for legal necessity
Whether subsequent purchasers of the property are protected by estoppel
holdings: Alienation of joint family property by a father to discharge his personal debts is binding on the sons if the debt is antecedent, not tainted with illegality or immorality, and is vyavaharik.
The doctrine of pious obligation requires that the father's debt must be vyavaharik; sons are liable to pay such debts even if incurred for personal benefit, provided they are not illegal or immoral.
Purchasers who reconstruct property with knowledge of the plaintiffs and without objection are protected by estoppel from title challenges.
doctrines: Doctrine of Pious Obligation
Alienation for Antecedent Debt
Estoppel against challenging title

card.dispute: The appellant (a member of a cooperative society) and respondent No. 1 (a non-member) entered into an agreement for the sale of office premises in a building owned by the society; when the society refused approval, respondent No. 1 filed a claim in the Cooperative Court for specific performance and a direction to the society to approve the transfer. The dispute was whether the Cooperative Court had jurisdiction under Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the parties 'touches the management or business of a society' within the meaning of Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960.
Whether a non-member's claim for specific performance of an agreement with a member, subject to society approval, constitutes a claim against the society 'through a member' under Section 91(1)(b).
Whether the Cooperative Court had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute.
holdings: A dispute over the sale of a member's premises in a society-owned building to a non-member, requiring society approval, does not inherently touch the management or business of the society.
A non-member's claim for specific performance of an agreement with a member is not a claim against the society through a member within the meaning of Section 91(1)(b).
The Cooperative Court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes between a non-member and a member over a private contract, even if society approval is sought as an ancillary relief.
doctrines: Jurisdictional limits of cooperative courts
Literal interpretation of statutory jurisdiction
Distinction between member-society disputes and private contractual disputes

card.dispute: The heirs of Ramchandra Pandurang Sonar (plaintiff) fought with Murlidhar Ramchandra Sonar and others (defendants) over whether certain properties were ancestral or self-acquired, and thus whether the plaintiff had a share in them.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with findings of fact in a second appeal without a substantial question of law being framed.
Whether Survey No. 71 was ancestral property and whether properties purchased from its income were joint family properties.
Whether the goldsmithery business was ancestral, affecting the character of properties purchased from its income.
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with factual findings in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved and properly formulated under Section 100 of the CPC.
Merely because a property came to a coparcener in partition does not make it ancestral; it must have been inherited from a paternal ancestor up to three generations.
Properties purchased from income of a self-acquired property or individual effort remain self-acquired unless blended with joint family property or purchased from ancestral sources.
doctrines: Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Ancestral property must be inherited from paternal ancestors up to three generations
