Self-acquired property does not become joint family property merely by use of its income for purchases

card.dispute: The disinherited daughter challenged the validity of her father's will, executed one day before his death in favor of her sister's sons, alleging suspicious circumstances and lack of testamentary capacity.
issues_decided: Whether the execution of the will was valid despite suspicious circumstances surrounding its creation?
Whether the propounder taking active part in the execution of the will raises suspicion affecting its authenticity?
Whether the courts below erred in failing to scrutinize the will's contents and the testator's mental state despite absence of reason for disinheritance?
Whether this Court can interfere with findings of fact under Article 136 when there is an erroneous application of law leading to miscarriage of justice?
holdings: Mere proof of execution through scribe or attesting witnesses is insufficient to uphold a will if suspicious circumstances exist; the propounder must dispel such suspicions with clear and satisfactory evidence.
Taking active interest by a beneficiary in the execution of a will raises strong suspicion about its authenticity and requires rigorous judicial scrutiny.

Absence of reason for disinheriting a natural heir, especially when heirs are of equal degree, shrouds the will in suspicion and demands judicial satisfaction on voluntariness and testamentary capacity.
This Court may interfere under Article 136 when findings of fact are based on erroneous application of law and result in miscarriage of justice, even if such findings are factual in nature.
doctrines: Presumption of due execution of will rebutted by suspicious circumstances
Requirement of clear and satisfactory evidence to dispel suspicion in will disputes
Judicial scrutiny of testamentary capacity and voluntariness in cases of disinheritance
Interference under Article 136 for miscarriage of justice due to legal error

card.dispute: Tenants and landholders disputed over entitlement to ryotwari pattas for agricultural lands after abolition of inam estates under the Andhra Pradesh Estates Abolition Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the lands in question were private lands of the landholders entitled to ryotwari pattas under Section 3(10)(b)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Land Act, 1908
Whether the landholders had established personal cultivation or intention to resume cultivation as required under Section 15 of the Estates Abolition Act
Whether the tenants were entitled to occupancy rights and thus to ryotwari pattas after abolition of the estate
holdings: Private lands under Section 3(10)(b)(i) must be proven by clear evidence of personal cultivation or lawful reservation; mere claim is insufficient.
The burden of proving private land lies on the landholder, and absence of proof of personal cultivation results in the land being treated as tenanted.
Tenants in possession are entitled to ryotwari pattas if landholders fail to prove the land was under personal cultivation or reserved for it.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 3(10)(b)(i)
Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 15
Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 185(3)
doctrines: Presumption against private land
Burden of proof in land classification disputes
Continuity of occupancy rights post-estate abolition

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the compensation awarded by the state for the compulsory acquisition of its land, seeking higher market value, severance damages, and interest on solatium.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of the acquired land should be enhanced based on prior sale deeds and concessions by the government pleader.
Whether the appellant is entitled to compensation for severance and injurious effects on the remaining land.
Whether interest is payable on solatium as part of compensation under the Kerala Land Acquisition Regulation, 1089.
holdings: The market value of the land is fixed at Rs. 18 per cent for non-wet lands, and Rs. 30 per cent for wet lands; a government pleader’s oral concession cannot bind the state unless made with authority.
The appellant failed to prove any expenditure or damage due to severance; hence, no compensation is payable for severance or injurious effects.
Interest at 6% is payable on solatium as it forms part of compensation, and the term 'compensation' in Section 25(3) includes solatium to recompense loss of land use.
doctrines: Compensation in land acquisition includes market value and solatium as distinct components.
Oral concessions by government counsel do not bind the state unless authorized in writing.
Interest on solatium is allowable if the statutory provision uses 'compensation' broadly to include all elements of recompense.

card.dispute: The appellant sought to evict respondents Nos. 2 and 3 based on a prior appellate finding that they were in possession on behalf of respondent No. 1, claiming res judicata, while respondents contested this, arguing the finding was not binding.
issues_decided: Whether a finding in an appeal, not challenged by or against certain parties, can operate as res judicata against them in a subsequent suit.
Whether an observation made by an appellate court in a prior appeal, in the absence of pleadings or evidence, can bind parties in a later suit.
holdings: A finding in an appeal does not operate as res judicata against parties who were not aggrieved by the appellate decision and had no right to challenge it.
An observation made by an appellate court in the absence of pleadings or evidence between the parties cannot constitute a binding finding for res judicata.
doctrines: Res judicata
Binding nature of judicial findings
Necessity of adversarial contest for res judicata

card.dispute: Sita Ram (appellant) challenged the Deputy Director of Consolidation's order recognizing Chhota Bhondey and others' claims to land shares, arguing the civil court had jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging an order of the consolidation authority regarding rights in land covered by consolidation proceedings.
Whether the dispute over title and shares in land fell within the adjudicatory function of consolidation authorities under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to entertain suits concerning rights or interests in land where consolidation proceedings are ongoing, as such matters are exclusively adjudicated by consolidation authorities under the Act.

Disputes over title, inheritance, and representative ownership of land within notified consolidation areas must be resolved by consolidation authorities, not civil courts, under Sections 5(2) and 49 of the Act.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 4(2)
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 5(2)
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 49
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in matters falling under special statutory tribunals
Doctrine of ouster of jurisdiction in favor of specialized administrative authorities

card.dispute: The licensee of a flat in a cooperative housing society fought the society's attempt to evict him under the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, claiming statutory protection under the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a licensee in occupation of a flat in a tenant co-partnership cooperative society is entitled to protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rents, Hotels & Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether eviction proceedings under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 are maintainable against a protected licensee
Whether the jurisdiction of the Cooperative Court under Section 91(1) prevails over the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes under Section 28 of the Rent Act
holdings: A licensee in actual possession of a flat on 1 February 1973 under a subsisting license is entitled to statutory protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947, and becomes a deemed tenant.

Proceedings under Section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act cannot be used to evict a licensee protected under the Rent Act, as such protection cannot be circumvented by invoking general provisions of the Societies Act.

Where competing jurisdictions exist, the special law (Rent Act) prevails over the general law (Societies Act), and eviction of protected occupants must be governed by the Rent Act and adjudicated by the Court of Small Causes.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(4A)
Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(bb)
doctrines: Generalia specialibus non derogant
Lex posterior derogat priori
Harmonious construction of statutes
Statutory tenancy by operation of law

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenants on grounds including rent arrears, and the tenants challenged the rejection of their rent tender on the first hearing, claiming protection under the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'tenant' in the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 includes a person claiming to be a tenant?
Whether the benefit of the proviso is available even in the absence of an admitted landlord-tenant relationship?
holdings: The word 'tenant' in the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) includes a person claiming to be a tenant, not merely one with an admitted tenancy.
The benefit of the proviso is available regardless of whether the landlord-tenant relationship is disputed, as long as rent is tendered on the first date of hearing to prevent eviction for arrears.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 2(h)(i)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i) proviso
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of rent control statutes in favor of tenants
Statutory interpretation considering context, purpose, and legislative intent
Relief against forfeiture for non-payment of rent

card.dispute: Star Enterprises challenged the City and Industrial Development Corporation's rejection of their highest tenders for lease of plots without assigning reasons, alleging arbitrariness and unconstitutionality.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent Corporation is a 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution.
Whether the rejection of the highest tender without assigning reasons violates Article 14 and the rule of law.
Whether a public authority is duty-bound to record and communicate reasons for rejecting the highest tender in a commercial transaction.
holdings: The Corporation is a 'State' under Article 12 and must act within the rule of law in its dealings with citizens.
A public authority engaged in commercial activity is not arbitrary merely by seeking the best deal, provided it acts bona fide.

Public authorities should record and normally communicate reasons for rejecting highest tenders to ensure transparency, accountability, and credibility, though this principle was not applied retroactively in the case.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 113(3A)
Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 159
doctrines: Rule of law
Principle of judicial review
Doctrine of state action under Article 12
Doctrine of reasonableness under Article 14
Public accountability in administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant lessee challenged the applicability of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act to a lease involving vacant land, a well, and a 'kaichalai', arguing that the 'kaichalai' was not a 'building' under the Act and that the lease was primarily of land.
issues_decided: Whether the 'kaichalai' constitutes a 'building' within the meaning of Section 2(2) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether the joint letting of land and a building falls within the scope of the Rent Control Act even if the land is substantial and the building small
Whether the word 'appurtenant' in Section 2(2) restricts the Act's applicability only to land necessary for the enjoyment of the building
holdings: A 'kaichalai' can be a 'building' under Section 2(2) if it is a material structure intended to be let out and capable of residential or non-residential use.
A composite lease of land and building is governed by the Rent Control Act if the parties intended them to be let together, regardless of size or dominant purpose.
The term 'appurtenant land' should be construed as land the parties intended to let with the building, not merely land strictly necessary for its enjoyment.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(2)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(vii)
doctrines: Composite lease doctrine
Intention of the parties in determining inseparable letting
Liberal interpretation of 'building' and 'appurtenant land' in rent control statutes

card.dispute: The Union of India and others disputed with Dev Raj Gupta and others over the date from which conversion charges should be calculated for changing the land use from residential to commercial and whether such conversion was automatic under the Master Plan.
issues_decided: Whether the letter dated February 15, 1978, amounted to a valid application for conversion of land use from residential to commercial
What is the correct date for determining the conversion charges for change of land use
Whether the Master Plan's classification of land as commercial results in automatic statutory conversion of land use
holdings: A letter inquiring about conversion charges and terms does not constitute a formal application for change of land use; a valid application must clearly express willingness to abide by conditions and be signed by all co-lessees.
The date of the valid application for conversion—February 27, 1981—should be used to determine conversion charges, not a later date assumed due to administrative delay.
Inclusion of land in a commercial zone under a Master Plan does not result in automatic or statutory conversion of land use; permission from the landlord is still required for any change in user.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 20(1)
doctrines: Statutory construction of application requirements
Enabling nature of town planning regulations
Principle of contractual use of leased land

card.dispute: The landlord sought to eject the heirs of a deceased tenant from a commercial shop, claiming they had no right to continue possession after the tenant's death.
issues_decided: Whether tenancy rights in commercial premises under the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 are heritable upon the death of the tenant
Whether the heirs of a deceased statutory tenant are entitled to protection under the Act
Whether the amendment to the definition of 'tenant' under the Act applies retrospectively to divest inherited tenancy rights
holdings: Tenancy rights in commercial premises are heritable under the ordinary law of succession, and heirs succeed not only to the business but also to the tenancy rights protected by the Rent Act.
The heirs of a deceased statutory tenant step into the shoes of the tenant and are entitled to continue in possession until evicted in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
The amendment to the Act does not apply retrospectively; it cannot divest vested heritable rights that arose before the amendment came into force.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 3(vii)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Amendment Act, 14 of 1976, Section 3(ii)
doctrines: Heritability of tenancy rights
Statutory tenancy continuation
Vested rights doctrine
Prospective operation of amendments

card.dispute: The heirs of Tek Chand fought the Union of India over the quantum of compensation for land acquired in Nehru Place, Delhi, arguing that they should receive compensation comparable to that awarded to DLF Co. for similar land.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation for acquired land should be based on the potential for development by the owner.
Whether the compensation awarded to DLF Co. for similar land could serve as a valid benchmark for determining compensation for the appellants' land.
holdings: Compensation in land acquisition must be determined on the basis of a hypothetical sale between a willing seller and willing buyer at the time of notification, without regard to the specific ability of the owner to develop the land.

The enhanced compensation awarded to DLF Co. due to its capacity to develop land and sell developed plots cannot be a basis to deny similar treatment to other landowners; such capacity is not a relevant factor in assessment.
doctrines: Willing buyer-willing seller rule
Hypothetical market value principle
Uniformity and non-discrimination in compensation

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the maintainability of an ejectment suit filed by the Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay after a quit notice was issued by its Assistant Estate Manager.
issues_decided: Whether the ejectment suit filed by the Port Trust was maintainable under Section 41 of the Bombay Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, after termination of tenancy under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
Whether the Assistant Estate Manager had authority to bind the Port Trust by a promise to re-allot premises after reconstruction, making promissory estoppel applicable?
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel can be invoked against a statutory public authority like the Port Trust?
holdings: An ejectment suit by the Port Trust is maintainable under Section 41 of the Bombay Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, where tenancy is lawfully terminated under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
The Assistant Estate Manager lacked actual or ostensible authority to make binding promises on behalf of the Port Trust; thus, any such promise is ultra vires and unenforceable.
The doctrine of promissory estoppel does not apply to prevent a public authority from denying a promise made by a subordinate officer without legal authority, as it would legitimize ultra vires acts.
provisions: Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, Section 41
Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, Section 29(1)(a) & (b) read with Section 133(2A)
General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 6 and Section 17
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Ultra vires acts of public officers
Ostensible authority
Executive necessity

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh sued to reclaim a property gifted by the Maharaja of Chhatarpur to his father-in-law, arguing it was state property, while the appellant claimed it was validly gifted as private property.
issues_decided: Whether the property in dispute was private property of the Ruler of Chhatarpur or state property?
Whether the Ruler retained sovereign authority to designate property as private after May 1, 1948, following integration into the United State of Vindhya Pradesh?
Whether the gift of the property on August 25, 1948, was valid despite the integration?
Whether a subsequent letter and list from a government official could divest the donee of title to the property?
holdings: The property was validly set aside as private property by the Ruler in July 1948, prior to the gift, and remained his to dispose of.
The Ruler did not lose all sovereign powers after May 1, 1948; he retained the authority to designate private property despite integration.
The gift made on August 25, 1948, was valid as it was made in exercise of the Ruler’s sovereign and individual rights over his private property.
A later letter and list from a government official could not divest the donee of title, especially without evidence of acceptance or legal basis for such divestiture.
provisions: Covenant of Rulers of Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand (1948)
doctrines: Sovereignty retention by rulers post-accession
Doctrine of integration without total surrender of sovereignty
Principle of valid private property designation by rulers
Non-retroactive divestiture of property without legal authority

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by the respondent, who purchased property from a former minor, to set aside a prior sale of the property by the minor's guardian.
issues_decided: Whether a suit to set aside a transfer of a minor's immovable property by a natural guardian without court permission or legal necessity is maintainable by a transferee from the ex-minor within three years of majority?
Whether the right to challenge such a transfer is a personal right only or an assignable interest in property?
Whether such a transfer by the ex-minor falls under the prohibition of Section 6(e) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
holdings: A suit to set aside a voidable transfer of a minor's immovable property can be maintained by a person claiming under the ex-minor, including a transferee by sale.
The right of a minor to avoid a transfer by a guardian is not a mere personal right to sue but an assignable interest in the property.

Section 8(3) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 allows enforcement by any person claiming under the minor, which includes a purchaser, and overrides any conflicting interpretation under Section 6(e) of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 5(b)
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8(3)
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Legislative intent in favor of minor's protection
Assignability of contingent property rights
Voidable transfer under guardianship law

card.dispute: The Bangalore Medical Trust fought against residents of the locality who challenged the allotment of a public park site to the Trust for constructing a hospital, alleging violation of town planning laws and statutory procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government or the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) had the power to alter a development scheme and divert a site reserved for a public park to a private entity.
Whether the BDA could delegate or abdicate its statutory decision-making function to the State Government or the Chief Minister.
Whether the residents had locus standi to challenge the diversion of public park land in a public interest litigation.
Whether the exercise of power under Section 65 or Section 15(3) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 could validate an otherwise ultra vires alteration of a development scheme.
holdings: The power to alter a development scheme under Section 19(4) of the BDA Act vests exclusively in the BDA as a corporate body, not in the State Government or the Chief Minister.
The BDA cannot abdicate its statutory duty by acting on directions from the State Government; such action amounts to a complete abdication of power and is ultra vires.
Residents of the locality have locus standi to challenge the diversion of public park land in public interest litigation to protect environmental and recreational rights.
General powers under Section 65 or Section 15(3) cannot override specific statutory procedures and cannot validate an illegal alteration of a development scheme.
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation: specific provisions override general powers
Doctrine of separation of powers and delegated legislation
Principle of participatory decision-making in statutory authorities
Public interest litigation and locus standi for protecting public goods
Administrative action must be rational, objective, and not arbitrary

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the reduction in compensation for their acquired land, arguing that a one-third deduction based on the size of the tract was unjustified given the land's developed nature and location.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of deducting one-third of the market value for large-scale land acquisition applies when the land is already developed and situated in a developed area.
Whether the High Court erred in reducing compensation by applying a deduction without considering the actual development and location advantages of the acquired land.
holdings: A deduction in market value for large tracts is not automatic; it must consider whether the land is already developed and suitable for building without further infrastructure.
When acquired land is adjacent to developed areas with existing amenities like roads and electricity, a deduction from comparable small plot sales is not justified.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination in land acquisition
Deduction for development costs in large tract acquisitions
Use of comparable sales with adjustments for development needs

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a temporary injunction should be granted to prevent the appellants from taking possession of a residential property, based on the respondent's claim that the sale was obtained by fraud.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an ad interim injunction against the appellants in a suit challenging the validity of a court-executed sale deed?
Whether the conditions for granting a temporary injunction under Order 39 Rule 1 CPC were satisfied in this case?
Whether the balance of convenience and irreparable injury favoured the grant of injunction?
holdings: The High Court erred in granting ad interim injunction without proper application of judicial discretion and without finding a prima facie case, irreparable injury, or balance of convenience in favour of the respondent.

A party seeking temporary injunction must establish a prima facie case, likelihood of irreparable injury, and that balance of convenience favours injunction; mere invocation of legal phrases is insufficient.
Where a sale deed has been executed by court and previous courts have denied injunction, and where damages can adequately compensate the respondent, injunction should not be granted lightly.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39, Rule 1(c)
Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
doctrines: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury in injunction jurisprudence
Doctrine of lis pendens
Judicial discretion in granting temporary injunctions

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether certain properties, including a jagir estate and accretions thereto, were impartible separate properties governed by primogeniture or partible coparcenary joint family properties subject to partition.
issues_decided: Whether the Chandurpura Jagir and its accretions constituted an impartible estate governed by the rule of primogeniture or a coparcenary joint family property?
Whether the income and accretions from the jagir, including immovable and movable properties, were partible among coparceners?
Whether the properties covered under Schedule 1 were joint family properties liable to partition despite the impartible nature of the jagir?
Whether the compensation received for resumed jagir lands retained the character of impartible property?
holdings: An impartible estate granted in perpetuity and governed by primogeniture is not a coparcenary property; junior members have no right by birth except to maintenance, and the holder has absolute rights over the estate and its income.

Accretions made from the income of an impartible estate are also impartible if they are immovable and impressed as part of the estate; movable properties do not become part of the estate and remain separate.

Properties not covered by the jagir grant but used as ancestral joint family residences, where improvements were made from jagir income and no separation was proved, remain partible joint family properties.
Compensation received for resumed jagir lands retains the impartible character of the original estate and devolves by primogeniture, not by coparcenary rights.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, Section 158(1)(b)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, Section 164
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 54(7)
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 69
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 82
doctrines: Rule of primogeniture in impartible estates
Doctrine of survivorship in Hindu law
Blending of accretions with joint family property
Extinction of impartibility upon resumption of jagir under land reform laws
Retention of character of property despite change in form (e.g., land to compensation)

card.dispute: East India Hotels Ltd. and Syndicate Bank disputed whether the bank could retain possession of hotel premises after the expiry of a leave and licence agreement, despite the company's refusal to renew it.
issues_decided: Whether a licensee is entitled to protection under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 after the expiry of the licence period if dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law
Whether a suit under Section 6 is maintainable by a licensee whose licence has expired but who remains in settled possession
Whether the nature of possession (lawful or unlawful) affects the right to seek relief under Section 6
holdings: A licensee in settled possession is entitled to protection under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 even after the expiry of the licence if dispossession occurs otherwise than in due course of law.
The maintainability of a suit under Section 6 depends on actual settled possession and unlawful dispossession, not on the continuation of lawful title or agreement.
Law respects possession regardless of title; no one may take the law into their own hands to dispossess another without due process, even after licence expiry.
doctrines: Self-help doctrine
Possession as prima facie title
Due course of law
Settled possession

card.dispute: The appellants, senior members of a cooperative society, challenged the retrospective application of an amended bye-law that regularized the membership of 26 junior members, and the validity of a later notification rescinding the amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the Lt. Governor had the power to issue a retrospective notification under Section 88 of the Delhi Cooperative Societies Act, 1972 to regularize memberships?

Whether the subsequent notification dated 29th August, 1990 rescinding the earlier notification was ultra vires for violating the principle that a quasi-judicial order cannot be reviewed without statutory power?
Whether the rescission of the notification violated principles of natural justice by extinguishing vested rights?
holdings: The Lt. Governor validly issued the 27th October 1987 notification under Section 88 to give retrospective effect to the regularization of memberships approved in a prior quasi-judicial order.

A quasi-judicial order under Section 76 of the Act cannot be reviewed or nullified by a later administrative notification unless the statute confers such power; the 29th August 1990 notification was ultra vires for effectively reviewing such an order.

Where a substantive right is created by a quasi-judicial order and upheld in litigation, it cannot be taken away by a subsequent notification relying solely on general rescission powers under the General Clauses Act, 1897.
doctrines: Doctrine of functus officio
Principle of finality of quasi-judicial orders
Vested rights doctrine
Doctrine of substantive legitimate expectation

card.dispute: The landlord (Gulabbai) sued for eviction of tenants (Nalin Narsi Vohra and others) on grounds of arrears of rent and bona fide need for her husband's tax consultancy office, while tenants contested the claim of genuine need.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide need for personal occupation must exist at the time of final disposal of the eviction proceeding, not just at the time of filing the suit?
Whether additional evidence regarding subsequent events affecting the landlord's need can be admitted during appellate proceedings?
Whether the landlord proved a reasonable and bona fide requirement for the suit premises for her husband's professional use?
holdings: A landlord's bona fide need for personal occupation must continue to exist at the time of final disposal of the eviction proceeding, not merely at the time of filing the suit.
Courts may consider subsequent events and admit additional evidence on bona fide need if relevant, provided principles of fairness are followed.
The landlord failed to prove reasonable and bona fide need, especially after acquiring alternative accommodation, making eviction unjustified.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(2) read with Section 12(3)(a) and Section 13(1)(a)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Bona fide need for personal occupation must persist until final adjudication
Subsequent events affecting relief are admissible and must be considered in eviction cases
Reasonable requirement implies genuine need, not mere desire

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for lands acquired by the State of Haryana at different dates between 1975 and 1978, seeking enhanced compensation based on market value changes after a 1974 benchmark.
issues_decided: What adjustment in compensation is warranted for lands acquired between 1975 and 1978 compared to the 1974 acquisition value?
Whether appellants can be permitted to amend their claim for higher compensation without formal application and despite court-fee deficiency?
Whether substitution of legal representatives after the death of appellants should be allowed despite delay?
holdings: Compensation for land acquired between 1975 and 1978 should be increased proportionally over the 1974 benchmark of Rs. 17.50 per sq. yard, based on fair market appreciation.
Appellants are permitted to amend claims orally to claim enhanced compensation upon payment of requisite court-fee, despite procedural lapses, due to long delay in disposal.
Applications for substitution of legal representatives are allowed with condonation of delay, subject to resolution of any disputes by Land Acquisition Authorities.
doctrines: Principle of comparative market value in land acquisition compensation
Liberal approach to procedural amendments for ends of justice
Condonation of delay in substitution of parties

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the High Court's reversal of a higher compensation award for land and trees acquired under the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, seeking enhanced solatium and remand to adduce additional evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies to proceedings under the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961 for enhanced solatium under Section 23(2)
Whether pendency of an appeal attracts application of Section 30(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for enhanced solatium
Whether the claimant was entitled to remand under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC to adduce additional evidence
Whether the method of valuing both land and fruit-bearing trees separately was legally valid
holdings: The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies to Kerala due to Article 254, but enhanced solatium under Section 23(2) is not available if the award was made before April 30, 1982.
Section 30(2) does not apply to pending appeals; it only benefits awards made by the Collector or Civil Court between April 30, 1982 and September 24, 1984.
Remand under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC is not warranted if the appellant had opportunity to lead evidence but failed to do so.
Valuing both land and trees by capitalization method is illegal; either land with potential use is valued with trees as timber, or tree income is capitalized, not both.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Doctrine of pendent appeal not attracting transitional benefits
Rule against double compensation for same asset
Principle of legislative intendment in transitional provisions
Doctrine of judicial economy in remand for evidence

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the denial of enhanced interest under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, in proceedings where the Collector's award predated the amendment but the Civil Court's decision came after its commencement.
issues_decided: Whether Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, applies retrospectively to acquisition cases where the Collector passed the award before the amendment but the Civil Court decided the reference after its commencement?
Whether the transitional provisions in Section 30 of the Amendment Act limit the applicability of Section 23(1-A) to cases falling under its specified clauses?

Whether the extension of the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to Kerala from 24-9-1984 bars retrospective application of its amended provisions to ongoing proceedings under the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961?
holdings: The language of Section 23(1-A) does not, by itself, warrant a retrospective effect beyond what is permitted under Section 30(1) of the Amendment Act, which sets specific conditions for applicability.

The benefit under Section 23(1-A) is not available unless one of the conditions in Section 30(1)(a) or (b) is satisfied, and the distinction between 'award by Collector' and 'award by Court' in Section 30 shows Parliament's intent to limit retroactivity.
The extension of the Central Act to Kerala from 24-9-1984 does not prevent the retrospective operation of its amended provisions where such retroactivity is authorized by the Amendment Act itself.
provisions: Land Acquisition Amendment Act, 68 of 1984, Section 15
doctrines: Doctrine of Retrospectivity in Substantive Law
Principle of Strict Construction of Retrospective Statutes
Doctrine of Parliamentary Intention in Transitional Provisions
Doctrine of Repeal by Inconsistency under Article 254

card.dispute: The petitioner and his two sons disputed over the inheritance of the adoptive mother's property, with conflicting claims based on wills and a subsequent compromise agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise between the parties was genuine and enforceable despite one party's later denial of receiving payment.
Whether alienations of the suit property by one of the sons during litigation and after the compromise were valid.
Whether the court was bound to record the compromise once its genuineness was established.
What relief should be granted to the alienees who had taken possession under the disputed sale deeds.
holdings: Once a court is satisfied that a compromise is genuine and lawful, it must be recorded and given effect to, leaving no discretion to the court to refuse it.
A party to a compromise cannot later deny its terms, including receipt of payment, especially when the compromise document explicitly states otherwise.
Sale of property pendente lite by a party who has relinquished interest through a valid compromise is invalid, and the alienees acquire no legal title.
Alienees in possession under invalid sale deeds must deliver vacant possession, though mesne profits may be waived to account for alleged improvements and payments.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 - Order 23, Rule 3
doctrines: Pendente Lite Alienation Doctrine
Enforceability of Compromise under CPC
Binding Nature of Signed Compromise
Court's Duty to Record Lawful Compromise

card.dispute: The judgment-debtors (appellants) challenged the auction sale of their property in favor of the auction-purchaser (respondent No. 3), seeking to set it aside after depositing the decretal amount.
issues_decided: Whether the application under Section 47 of the CPC was wrongly treated as an application under Order 21, Rule 90 of the CPC.
Whether the application under Order 21, Rule 89 of the CPC was barred due to the pendency of the Section 47 objection.
holdings: An application under Section 47 of the CPC cannot be automatically treated as an application under Order 21, Rule 90 if the grounds raised are not covered by that Rule.
The bar under Order 21, Rule 89(2) does not apply merely because a Section 47 objection is pending; the Rule 89 application is maintainable if not duplicative of Rule 90 grounds.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
doctrines: Doctrine of maintainability of execution objections
Equitable relief in setting aside auction sales

card.dispute: The owners of a property in Bombay fought with the licensees (respondents Nos. 5 and 6) and the heirs of the original tenant over whether the licensees could claim protection as deemed tenants under the Bombay Rent Act and resist eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the licence in favour of respondents Nos. 5 and 6 was subsisting on February 1, 1973, the date Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act came into force
Whether respondents Nos. 5 and 6 are entitled to protection as deemed tenants under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act
Whether the eviction order passed under the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act against the heirs of the tenant was valid
holdings: The licence in favour of respondents Nos. 5 and 6 was subsisting on February 1, 1973, based on documentary evidence including letters and a declaratory decree.
Respondents Nos. 5 and 6 became deemed tenants under Section 15A of the Bombay Rent Act and can only be evicted in accordance with that Act.
The eviction order against the heirs (respondents Nos. 1 to 4) was valid as they did not contest their tenancy claim and accepted the ejectment decree.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, Section 41
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Deemed tenancy under rent control legislation
Effect of ex parte decree in declaratory suit

card.dispute: The Maharashtra State Financial Corporation sued Jaycee Drugs and its directors (as personal sureties) to recover a loan, seeking a money decree against them jointly and severally under Sections 31 and 32 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether a petition under Sections 31 and 32 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, can be used to obtain a money decree against a personal surety who provided no security.
Whether the amendment by Act 43 of 1985 altered the nature of proceedings under Sections 31 and 32 to allow enforcement of a surety's personal liability through a money decree.
holdings: Proceedings under Sections 31 and 32 of the Act are not executable as money decrees against personal sureties; they are limited to attachment and sale of property, akin to execution proceedings.

The amendment by Act 43 of 1985 did not fundamentally alter the law to allow money decrees against sureties; the liability of a surety can only be enforced through property attachment and sale, not personal judgment.
doctrines: Principle of irresistible clearness in statutory interpretation
Surety treated on par with principal debtor in enforcement, but not subject to personal money decrees under special statutes

card.dispute: The Pratibha Co-Operative Housing Society challenged the demolition order on eight upper floors of its 36-storey building imposed by the Bombay Municipal Corporation for violating Floor Space Index (F.S.I.) norms.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation was justified in ordering demolition of eight upper floors for F.S.I. violation?
Whether the alternative proposal of vertical demolition should have been accepted instead of full floor demolition?
Whether the High Court and Municipal Corporation acted within their jurisdiction in rejecting the Society's proposals?
holdings: The Municipal Corporation was justified in ordering demolition due to clear and flagrant F.S.I. violation exceeding 24,000 sq. ft., and the order had attained finality.
The alternative proposal of vertical demolition was properly examined and rejected on technical grounds, and the Court found no illegality in the Municipal Commissioner's decision.
The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction under Article 226, as the Corporation's decision was not mala fide or arbitrary, and fell within permissible administrative discretion.
provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Judicial restraint in administrative decisions under Article 226
Public interest in enforcing building regulations

card.dispute: Orissa Cement Ltd and others challenged the constitutional validity of cess levied by the States of Orissa, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh based on royalty from mining lands, and sought refund of amounts collected.
issues_decided: Whether the levy of cess based on mining royalty by state legislatures is constitutionally valid when the subject is covered by a central law (Mines and Minerals Act, 1957)?
Whether a declaration of unconstitutionality of a tax or cess automatically entitles the payer to a refund?
Whether the doctrine of unjust enrichment or laches can be grounds to deny refund of unconstitutionally collected cess?
Whether undertakings given during interim orders for refund bind the court’s final decision?
holdings: The levy of cess by the states was unconstitutional as it encroached upon a field occupied by the central Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
A declaration of unconstitutionality does not automatically entitle the assessee to refund; the grant of refund is discretionary and not inevitable.
Courts may refuse refund on grounds of laches, delay, or risk of unjust enrichment, and the State's vital interests are a relevant factor in withholding refund.

Undertakings given during interim orders for refund must be honoured only to the extent consistent with the final decision, and refund shall be made with interest from the date of the relevant high court judgment.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Bengal Cess Act, 1880 (as applicable to Bihar), Sections 4, 5, 6, 9
Madhya Pradesh Upkar Adhiniyam, 1981, Part IV, Section 11
Madhya Pradesh Karadhan Adhiniyam, 1982, Part IV, Section 9
Constitution of India, Article 142, Article 246, Article 265, Article 277
Seventh Schedule, List I Entries 52 and 54, List II Entries 5, 18, 23, 45, 49, 50, 66
doctrines: Doctrine of occupied field
Doctrine of prospective overruling
Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Discretionary power of court in granting relief under Article 142
Laches and delay in enforcement of rights

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, arguing that his consent was withdrawn before acceptance and that the acquisition notification was not published within the mandatory 40-day period.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's consent to land acquisition, subject to lump-sum compensation, was irrevocable after being expressed before the Land Acquisition Officer.
Whether non-publication of the substance of the section 4(1) notification within 40 days in the locality invalidates the acquisition proceedings.
holdings: The appellant's conditional willingness to accept acquisition constituted an offer under the Contract Act, which remained unaccepted and could be withdrawn at any time before acceptance.
Failure to publish the substance of the section 4(1) notification within 40 days in the locality, as mandated by the amended Land Acquisition Act, renders the acquisition void and invalid in law.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 4(1) (as amended by Andhra Pradesh (Amendment) Act, 1983)
doctrines: Offer and acceptance under the Indian Contract Act, 1872
Mandatory compliance with statutory time limits in administrative actions
Voidness of acquisition for non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements

card.dispute: The appellant, Puran Singh Sahni, contested his eviction from a flat in a tenant co-partnership cooperative housing society, claiming protection as a deemed tenant under the Rent Act, while the respondents sought his removal as a trespasser after termination of a leave and licence agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rents Act as a deemed tenant after the termination of his leave and licence agreement
Whether the Cooperative Court had jurisdiction under Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act to decide the dispute
Whether Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution to the extent it applies to non-members
holdings: A licensee whose agreement has been terminated before February 1, 1973, is not entitled to protection under Section 15A of the Bombay Rents Act and remains a trespasser.

A dispute over eviction of a nominal member by a tenant co-partner, touching the business of a cooperative society, falls within the jurisdiction of the Cooperative Court under Section 91, not barred by Section 28 of the Rent Act.
Section 91 of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act is not ultra vires Article 14 when applied to a nominal member involved in a dispute concerning the society’s business.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 5(4A)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(bb)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 15A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 28(1)
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence
Doctrine of deemed tenancy under Section 15A of the Bombay Rents Act
Harmonious construction of special statutes
Pith and substance doctrine in constitutional interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent arrears, while the tenant argued he was protected by amendments to the Bombay Rent Act and that education cess payments made the rent not payable monthly.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's obligation to pay education cess annually takes the case out of the scope of section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rent Act, making rent not payable by the month
Whether parties can by agreement convert a yearly statutory tax liability (like education cess) into a monthly rent payment under the Act
Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under the amended section 12(3) of the Act by depositing arrears before decree
holdings: Education cess is a 'permitted increase' under section 5(7) of the Act and forms part of rent, but if payable annually, it may take the case out of section 12(3)(a).

Parties may by agreement convert a yearly tax liability into a fixed monthly payment, provided it does not exceed the landlord’s actual tax liability, making rent payable by the month under section 12(3)(a).
The tenant failed to pay arrears within one month of notice, and thus did not meet the conditions for protection under section 12(3)(a), justifying eviction.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(7)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 7
doctrines: Permitted increase under rent control law
Statutory right to recover taxes as rent
Contractual modification of statutory payment terms
Interpretation of 'rent payable by the month'

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a share in the properties of the Travancore Royal Family as a member of an undivided marumakkathayam tarwad, while the respondent, the former Ruler, asserted that the properties were his personal assets.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question were joint family properties under Marumakkathayam law or the personal properties of the former Ruler
Whether the covenant entered at the time of integration allowed the Ruler to validly designate properties as his private property
Whether the appellant had a legal right to claim a share in the personal properties of the Ruler
holdings: The properties in suit were not joint family properties but the personal properties of the former Ruler of Travancore, who had the sovereign authority to designate them as such.
The covenant permitted the Ruler to list and retain private properties, and the Government's acceptance of the list did not create new rights but recognized existing claims.
The appellant failed to prove he was a legal heir to the Ruler's personal properties, and no law converted such personal properties into joint family property.
provisions: Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975
doctrines: Sovereign right of rulers to designate private property during state integration
Finality of government-recognized property inventories under covenants
No automatic revival of partition rights in personal property upon abolition of joint family system

card.dispute: The appellant claimed title to 3.06 acres of land based on a sale deed, while the defendants contested the legitimacy of the appellant's predecessor-in-title, Ramaswamy, as the son of Chinnathambi, and the validity of the property transfer.
issues_decided: Whether Ramaswamy was the legitimate son of Chinnathambi born to Pavayee No. 2, who cohabited with Chinnathambi without a formal marriage.
Whether the presumption of marriage arising from long-term cohabitation between Chinnathambi and Pavayee No. 2 was rebutted by the circumstances in the case.
holdings: A man and woman living together for a long time are presumed to be married, and their children are presumed legitimate unless proven otherwise.
The absence of mention of Pavayee No. 2 or her children in a will or compromise deed does not rebut the presumption of marriage arising from cohabitation.
doctrines: Presumption of marriage from cohabitation
Legitimacy of children under Section 112 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: Two brothers, Ramasamy and Muthiah, fought over possession of leasehold properties previously held by their father, with Ramasamy claiming possession and Muthiah claiming entitlement under a will.
issues_decided: Whether Ramasamy was in sole possession of the leasehold properties?
Whether the will and allotment claimed by Muthiah were valid?
Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC?
holdings: Ramasamy was in sole possession of the leasehold properties, as found by the trial and first appellate courts.
Muthiah failed to prove the will or any allotment in his favour, and the plea was rejected.
The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact without jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC, as no substantial question of law was framed.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Possession as a basis for injunction

card.dispute: The Special Tehsildar challenged the compensation awarded for land acquired in 1963 for a housing scheme, arguing that the market value was overstated and that a deduction should be made for development costs.
issues_decided: What is the correct market value of the acquired land as of the date of the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether a deduction should be made from the market value for development expenses like roads and amenities in a housing scheme?
holdings: The market value of land under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act must be based on genuine sale transactions of the same or comparable land around the time of the notification; reliance on awards for other lands is erroneous when actual sale data exists.

When land is acquired for a housing scheme in an undeveloped area, a deduction of one-third from the market value is justified to account for development costs such as roads, drainage, and parks, depending on the land's situation and need for infrastructure.
doctrines: Principle of willing buyer-willing seller for determining market value
Deduction for development charges in housing scheme acquisitions

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of tenants on grounds of bona fide requirement, but the High Court set aside the order on the ground that the married daughters of the original tenant were not impleaded as necessary parties.
issues_decided: Whether married daughters of the original tenant are necessary parties in eviction proceedings under the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of letting, rent and eviction) Act, 1972
Whether non-joinder of married daughters vitiates the eviction proceedings and disentitles the landlord from obtaining ejectment
holdings: Married daughters of a deceased tenant are heirs and thus tenants under Section 3(a)(2) of the Act, entitled to inherit leasehold rights including continuation of business until lawfully ejected.

Non-joinder of married daughters does not vitiate eviction proceedings if they have, by necessary implication, surrendered their tenancy rights by not asserting any interest in the property or business after the tenant's death.
provisions: U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(a)(2)
U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
doctrines: Doctrine of necessary parties
Doctrine of deemed surrender by conduct

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu challenged the quashing of a land acquisition notification by the High Court, which had ruled that the acquisition for a housing scheme was premature because the scheme under the Madras State Housing Board Act had not been framed.
issues_decided: Whether a land acquisition proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be initiated before framing a scheme under the Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961.
Whether the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act was premature and invalid in the absence of a finalized housing scheme.
holdings: A land acquisition proceeding for a housing scheme can only commence after the scheme is framed under the Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, as land acquisition is an integral part of the scheme.

The notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act was premature and invalid because it was issued without a finalized scheme, depriving landowners of the ability to effectively object under Section 5A.
provisions: Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 3
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Chapter VII (Sections 35 to 69)
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 39
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 49
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 53
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 56
Madras State Housing Board Act, 1961, Section 147
doctrines: Doctrine of Pre-Maturity
Principle of Fair Hearing (Audi Alteram Partem)
Statutory Interpretation of Conditional Precedents in Administrative Action

card.dispute: The dispute was between a foster son and the widow of his foster father over whether the widow acquired an absolute or life estate in property bequeathed under a will, and whether she could dispose of it by her own will.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow's life estate under a will becomes an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 14(1) applies retrospectively to wills made before the Act came into force
Whether restrictive covenants in a will prevent a Hindu female from acquiring full ownership under Section 14(1)
holdings: A Hindu widow who held property for life under a will, with a pre-existing right to maintenance, acquires an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as of June 17, 1956.

Section 14(1) is not retrospective but applies to the status of the property as it existed on the date the Act came into force, thereby converting limited estates into absolute ownership if pre-existing rights are present.
Restrictive covenants in a will do not bar Section 14(1) if the female had a pre-existing right to the property; such restrictions are extinguished by the operation of the Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of pre-existing right under Section 14(1)
Distinction between Section 14(1) and Section 14(2) based on nature of acquisition
Legislative intent to abolish discriminatory limitations on Hindu women's property rights

card.dispute: The Ujjain Development Authority fought with landowners over the validity of a 1985 land acquisition notification for town development, after a prior 1980 notification was quashed.
issues_decided: Whether the statutory requirements for the Scheme No. 23 under the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973 were complied with.
Whether the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 could be sustained despite procedural defects.
What relief should be granted where acquisition was invalid but substantial development had already occurred.
holdings: The statutory pre-conditions for the scheme were not strictly complied with, but no mala fides were found, and the defect was curable.
The acquisition notification is upheld by deeming the 1985 notification to have taken effect on 1.1.1988 to account for delayed compliance.
Landowners are entitled to market value as of 1.1.1988, but only 25% of the value increase due to improvements by the authority will be awarded to them.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, Section 50(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of substantial compliance
Equitable adjustment of compensation due to public development
Curative approach to procedural defects in administrative action

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the continuation of land acquisition proceedings, claiming they lapsed due to the failure to make an award within two years of the Section 6 notification.
issues_decided: Whether the two-year period for making an award under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 includes the time during which any action or proceeding pursuant to the Section 6 declaration was stayed by court order
Whether the Explanation to Section 11-A applies only to stays on proceedings up to the making of the award or extends to stays on taking possession as well
holdings: The period during which any action or proceeding pursuant to a Section 6 declaration is stayed by a competent court must be excluded when computing the two-year period for making an award under Section 11-A.
The Explanation to Section 11-A is broadly worded and covers all proceedings under the acquisition process, including stays on taking possession, not just those preceding the award.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Exclusion of stayed periods in limitation calculations

card.dispute: The Amrit Banaspati Company claimed a refund of sales tax from the State of Punjab based on government assurances of incentives for setting up an industry, which the State refused, arguing the promise was against public policy.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of promissory estoppel applies to a government promise to refund sales tax as an industrial incentive
Whether a promise to refund sales tax, not based on any legal provision, is enforceable in law
Whether such a refund scheme is contrary to public policy and void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
holdings: Promissory estoppel cannot be enforced against the State when the promise violates statutory provisions or public policy, even if the promise induced reliance.
A promise by the government to refund sales tax not authorized by law is unenforceable, as taxation and refund powers are strictly governed by statute.

A scheme promising refund of legally collected sales tax to private manufacturers is contrary to public policy and void under Section 23 of the Contract Act, as it diverts public revenue for private benefit.
provisions: Punjab Sales Tax Act, Sections 12 and 30
doctrines: Promissory Estoppel
Public Policy
Sovereign Power of Taxation

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against the eviction order passed in favor of the landlord who sought possession of business premises for use in a partnership business where he was a financing partner.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord proved a bona fide requirement of the premises for his existing partnership business under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960?
Whether a financing partner who is not actively managing the business can be considered as conducting the partnership business and thus entitled to seek possession for its use?
Whether a new legal argument about the landlord being a 'sleeping partner' can be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if the factual basis exists on record?
holdings: The landlord sufficiently proved bona fide requirement of the premises for the partnership business, which included allied activities like cutting, printing, and binding through job work, falling within the scope of the paper and stationery business.

A partner designated as a 'financing partner' is not automatically a 'sleeping partner' if the partnership deed requires active interest in the business's success, and thus may be entitled to seek possession for partnership use.

A legal argument not raised in lower courts cannot be entertained in the Supreme Court even if some facts are on record, unless the factual foundation was properly contested and evidence adduced for it.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for eviction
Doctrine of judicial estoppel and waiver of arguments not raised below
Principle of fair notice and opportunity to contest in pleadings

card.dispute: Chand Rani sued Kamal Rani for specific performance of a property sale agreement, which the High Court reversed, and the Supreme Court upheld the reversal.
issues_decided: Whether time was the essence of the contract in the sale of immovable property despite a general presumption to the contrary?
Whether the plaintiff (Chand Rani) was ready and willing to perform her part of the contract?
Whether the failure to pay Rs. 98,000 within 10 days of the agreement amounted to a breach allowing forfeiture of earnest money?
holdings: Even in immovable property sales, parties may make time the essence of the contract through clear stipulations, as evidenced by the use of 'only' to qualify both amount and time in the agreement.
The plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform her obligations, as she refused to pay Rs. 98,000 unless prior conditions were met that were not contractually required at that stage.
The failure to pay Rs. 98,000 within 10 days constituted a breach, triggering the forfeiture clause and rendering the agreement void.
doctrines: Time is not presumed to be the essence in contracts for sale of immovable property
Doctrine of readiness and willingness in specific performance
Interpretation of contractual terms to determine if time is made the essence

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of Chapter XX-C of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which allowed the Central Government to compulsorily purchase immovable property in certain sale transactions, alleging violation of Article 14 and procedural unfairness.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Chapter XX-C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 violate Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the compulsory purchase order under Section 269UD(1) without a show-cause notice and without recording reasons is valid?
Whether lessees or encumbrance holders are entitled to compensation when the property is acquired under Chapter XX-C?
What relief should be granted given the invalidity of the impugned order?
holdings: The provisions of Chapter XX-C do not violate Article 14 if read down to exclude bona fide lessees or encumbrance holders in possession, and are constitutionally valid when interpreted to serve the legitimate aim of curbing tax evasion.
An order under Section 269UD(1) without a show-cause notice, opportunity to be heard, or recorded reasons is bad in law and must be set aside.

Holders of leasehold rights or encumbrances that are extinguished by acquisition are entitled to claim compensation from the sale proceeds paid to the transferor, as they are 'persons interested' under Section 269UA(2)(e).

The impugned order is set aside, but the statement in Form 37-I is treated as filed on the date of judgment, allowing the authorities to initiate fresh proceedings with due process, and if purchase occurs, the seller shall receive the apparent consideration plus 9% interest from the date of the original invalid order.
doctrines: Doctrine of reading down
Principle of audi alteram partem
Doctrine of severability
Limited retrospective effect to balance legality and public interest

card.dispute: The Food Corporation of India and landowners contested the compensation awarded for the acquisition of over 50 acres of land in village Danewala, with the F.C.I. challenging the enhanced compensation while landowners sought higher payment.
issues_decided: Whether the Food Corporation of India could maintain an appeal against the enhanced compensation under Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the reference court and High Court correctly determined the market value of the acquired land based on comparable sale instances
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the compensation awarded by lower courts
holdings: The Food Corporation of India, as a statutory authority acquiring land for public purpose, is barred from filing a reference under Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act to challenge compensation, but can appeal against enhancement.

The market value of acquired land must be determined by comparing reasonably similar sales, considering time, location, size, and accessibility, and not equating small frontage plots with large interior tracts.

The Supreme Court may interfere with compensation awards only if there is a wrong application of principle or overlooking of material factors affecting valuation, which was found here due to reliance on inapposite sale instances.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in land valuation
Doctrine of interference by Supreme Court under Article 136 on questions of fact
Rule against equating frontage and interior land for valuation purposes

card.dispute: Jammi Raja Rao claimed that the Anjaneyaswami Temple was a private temple and that he was its hereditary trustee, while the temple authorities contended it was a public temple and Rao had no exclusive rights over it.
issues_decided: Whether the Anjaneyaswami Temple is a public or private temple.
Whether the appellant acquired title to the temple properties by adverse possession.
Whether the dedication of the temple property was complete or partial.
holdings: A temple is public if there is proof of public use for worship as of right, and in regions like the former Madras Presidency, there is a presumption that temples are public unless conclusively rebutted.

Title to property of a religious institution cannot be acquired by adverse possession after September 30, 1951, under Section 103 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, and possession after 1946 did not vest title before that date.

Complete dedication of property to a deity is established by entries in official records like the Inam Register, and a claim of partial dedication for family benefit fails if the evidence shows full religious dedication.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 77
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 103
Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Hindu Religious and Endowments Act, 1951, Section 94
doctrines: Presumption of public nature of temples in the former Madras Presidency
Doctrine of adverse possession in relation to religious endowments
Doctrine of complete vs. partial dedication to religious trusts
Principle of concurrent findings of fact not interfered with by Supreme Court unless error of law is shown

card.dispute: Family members of a dissolved partnership firm fought over the division of assets and liabilities, including claims for interest and valuation of property.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitrator can award interest for the pre-reference period when the dissolution deed only envisages interest from the date of valuation.
Whether an arbitrator can rely on valuation reports without examining the valuers as witnesses.
Whether the arbitrator committed misconduct by shifting the venue and denying a witness the opportunity to testify.
What is the scope of court interference with an arbitrator's findings on questions of fact?
holdings: An arbitrator cannot award interest for the pre-reference period if the agreement only allows interest from the date of valuation, especially when the reference predates the Interest Act, 1978.
An arbitrator is entitled to accept a government-recognized valuer's report without examining the valuer as a witness, provided it is reliable and considered properly.
Shifting the venue of arbitration does not amount to misconduct if parties are given adequate opportunity; denial of witness testimony must be assessed on facts to determine fairness.
Courts cannot reappreciate evidence or interfere with an arbitrator's factual findings unless there is patent illegality or procedural misconduct.
doctrines: Pendente lite interest as compensatory and within arbitrator's discretion when agreement is silent
Arbitrator's power co-extensive with court in pending suit references
Principle of finality in arbitration awards on questions of fact
Doctrine of implied terms in arbitration agreements regarding interest

card.dispute: The landlord (K.A. Anthappai) sought eviction of the tenant (C. Ahammed) for bona fide personal residence, which the tenant opposed, claiming the building was unsuitable and he depended on it for livelihood.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the Appellate Authority's finding on the landlord's bona fide need after reassessing evidence in revisional jurisdiction.
Whether the landlord's claim for eviction on grounds of bona fide need can be denied solely because the building requires repairs or alterations.
Whether the Appellate Authority failed to consider the tenant's entitlement to protection under the second proviso to Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965.
holdings: The High Court erred in exercising revisional jurisdiction by reassessing evidence on bona fide need, as the Appellate Authority's concurrent finding was supported by evidence and could not be overturned.
A landlord's bona fide need for eviction cannot be denied merely because the building requires repairs or alterations, as he is entitled to make changes to render it habitable.

The Appellate Authority must consider whether the tenant is entitled to protection under the second proviso to Section 11(3), which bars eviction if the tenant depends on the premises for livelihood and no suitable alternative is available.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(3)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 20
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Bona fide requirement in landlord-tenant law
Protection of tenants engaged in livelihood-based business under rent control statutes

card.dispute: The appellants, Lekh Ram and Brij Lal, were convicted by the Punjab and Haryana High Court for the murder of Sukhcharanjit Kaur under Sections 302/34 IPC; they appealed the conviction, challenging the reliability of the prosecution's evidence and the burden of proof.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants murdered the deceased with common intention under Section 34 IPC?
Whether the High Court erred in placing the burden of proof on the accused to disprove guilt?
Whether the FIR and witness testimonies were reliable and sufficient to sustain the conviction?
Whether there was credible evidence of dowry demand and torture leading to murder?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the charge of murder under Section 302/34 IPC as there was no reliable evidence of common intention or participation in the alleged murder.
The High Court wrongly shifted the burden of proof to the accused, which is impermissible in criminal law where the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The FIR was recorded belatedly and with deliberation, and the testimonies of key witnesses were inconsistent and uncorroborated, rendering them unreliable.
There was no credible or corroborated evidence of dowry demand, torture, or ill-treatment of the deceased, and the defense of natural death due to illness could not be ruled out.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Burden of proof on prosecution
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Requirement of corroboration for prosecution witnesses

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of a lessee cultivating maufi land attached to a temple, fought the temple's pujari (respondent) over their right to continue possession and whether they acquired bhumiswami rights under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code.
issues_decided: Whether the patta granted by the pujari to the lessee created valid sub-tenancy rights under the Code
Whether the lessee or his successors acquired bhumiswami rights under Sections 185, 189, and 190 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code
Whether the possession of the appellants was unauthorized under Section 248(1) of the Code
Whether the application for eviction under Section 248(1) was maintainable, especially after the death of the original lessee during litigation
holdings: The patta granted by the pujari did not confer valid tenancy rights because the pujari held the land as a manager of government property and lacked authority to create enforceable lease rights.
The lessee did not become an occupancy tenant under Section 185, and thus could not acquire bhumiswami rights under Section 190, as no valid tenancy existed on the Code’s commencement.
The possession of the appellants became unauthorized after the death of the original lessee, even if a life-term patta existed, as no rights passed to the legal heirs without permission.
The eviction application under Section 248(1) was maintainable as the land was unoccupied and set apart for a special purpose, and the appellants’ continued possession lacked authorization.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 2
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 13
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 185
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 189
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 190
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 237
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 248(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of supervening events in appellate review
Doctrine of limited managerial authority of temple pujari over government-controlled maufi land
Doctrine of unauthorized possession under revenue codes
Doctrine of non-hereditary nature of life-tenancy in absence of statutory succession
