card.dispute: The trust sued to eject a tenant and recover arrears of rent, with the dispute centering on whether a 15-day notice to quit was valid or if a 6-month notice was required under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the lease was for a term exceeding one year and thus required registration under Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the deeming provision of six months' notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act applied to a manufacturing lease that was not from year to year
holdings: A lease not exceeding one year does not require registration under Section 107, and its terms can be proved even if the document is unregistered.

A manufacturing lease that is not from year to year or deemed to be from year to year does not require six months' notice; fifteen days' notice suffices under Section 106 if no contract specifies otherwise.
doctrines: Deeming provision under Section 106
Requirement of registered instrument for leases exceeding one year under Section 107

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their 20 acres of land acquired for housing, claiming higher market value based on nearby sale deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court committed an error of law by not considering nearby sale deeds (Exs. 38 and 44) for determining market value.
Whether the Reference Court's use of per sq. ft. valuation was legally valid for large land parcels.
Whether the prior purchase price of the acquired land by the owner could form the basis for determining compensation.
holdings: When evidence of the value of the acquired land itself exists, such as the owner’s prior purchase price, there is no need to rely on comparable sales of adjacent lands.
Valuing large land parcels on a per sq. ft. basis is legally unsound, as no prudent buyer would purchase extensive land that way in an open market.
The High Court correctly relied on the owner’s own admission of a tenfold increase in land value from 1957 to 1965, aligning with the Collector’s award.
doctrines: Armchair principle (willing buyer-willing seller test)
Use of prior transaction value in determining market value
Manifest error in application of valuation method

card.dispute: The appellant, a subsequent purchaser of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, claimed entitlement to developed plots under a government land policy, which the state denied on the ground that only original owners at the time of notification were eligible.
issues_decided: Whether a person who purchased land after the publication of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is entitled to benefits under a government land policy providing developed plots in lieu of compensation.
Whether the Government Order dated June 2, 1972 (G.O. No.1802) extends the benefit of the land policy to subsequent purchasers who acquired land after the Section 4(1) notification.
Whether denial of benefits to the appellant amounts to invidious discrimination under Article 14 of the Constitution.
holdings: A person purchasing land after the publication of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does so at their own risk and is not entitled to benefits under a land policy that confers rights only on owners at the time of notification.

The Government Order dated June 2, 1972 does not create a general entitlement but applies narrowly to specific cases where applications, orders, and agreements were made prior to discovery of post-notification purchase; the appellant did not meet these conditions.

No invidious discrimination under Article 14 arises from denying benefits to the appellant, as the policy distinction is based on ownership status at the time of notification, and isolated exceptions do not create enforceable rights.
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights in land acquisition
Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Principle that subsequent purchasers are bound by acquisition proceedings initiated before their purchase

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's quashing of Rent Controller's orders declaring a vacancy in a shop due to alleged sub-letting by inducting a son-in-law as a partner in the tenant's business.
issues_decided: Whether the heirs of a deceased tenant become joint tenants or tenants in common under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972
Whether admitting a son-in-law as a partner in a family-run business amounts to sub-letting or deemed vacancy under the Act
Whether the definition of 'family' under Section 3(g) of the Act includes sons-in-law for the purpose of tenancy continuation
holdings: Upon the death of a tenant, his heirs succeed jointly to the tenancy as joint tenants, not as tenants in common, and continue as a single tenancy unit under the Act.

Admitting a son-in-law as a partner in the business operating from the tenanted premises constitutes sub-letting under Section 25 Explanation (i), leading to deemed vacancy under Section 12(2) and (4).
The definition of 'family' under Section 3(g) is restrictive and does not include sons-in-law; thus, a wider interpretation cannot be given in the context of tenancy protection under the Act.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(g)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(4)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 25
doctrines: Doctrine of joint tenancy in succession of tenancy rights
Deemed vacancy doctrine under rent control legislation
Strict construction of statutory definitions in rent control laws
Rule against absurdity in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu and others challenged the Madras High Court's decision to quash land acquisition notifications issued for housing schemes, arguing they were valid despite delays and procedural lapses.
issues_decided: Whether the public purpose stated in the notifications was vague and invalid due to absence of a final housing scheme at the time of notification.
Whether undue delay in passing awards after the Section 6 declaration vitiated the acquisition proceedings.
Whether non-compliance with Rule 3(b) and (c) of the Tamil Nadu Land Acquisition Rules invalidated the Section 5-A enquiry and subsequent declarations.
holdings: A vague public purpose does not invalidate acquisition if, at the time of notification, there was a genuine intention to implement a housing scheme, even if the final scheme was not yet approved.

Delay in passing awards does not invalidate acquisition where statutory provisions like Section 23(1-A) and Section 48-A of the Land Acquisition Act provide compensation for delay, and the landowners have delayed in challenging the process.

Non-compliance with procedural rules in Section 5-A enquiry does not vitiate proceedings when the challenge is raised after inordinate delay, and the objectors failed to raise the issue at the appropriate time.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Acquisition Rules, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Doctrine of Procedural Fairness
Doctrine of Substantial Compliance
Principle of Beneficial Interpretation of Compensation Provisions

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu challenged the High Court's decision striking down certain rules regulating granite quarrying and sale, while respondents sought to uphold the invalidation of those rules.
issues_decided: Whether the first proviso to Rule 19-A of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, which gives preference to state government companies in granting quarrying leases, is ultra vires the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, or the Constitution

Whether Rules 8D and 19B, which empower the state or a state-owned corporation to regulate the sale and fix minimum prices for quarried granite, are within the rule-making power of the state under Section 15 of the Act
Whether the Government Orders introducing and implementing Rules 8D and 19B are valid
holdings: The first proviso to Rule 19-A, giving preference to state government companies in lease grants, does not violate the Act or the Constitution, as it only establishes a preference and does not exclude private parties entirely.
Rules 8D and 19B are ultra vires Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals Act, as the state lacks rule-making power to regulate the sale or pricing of already quarried minor minerals.
Government Orders No. 214 (in part) and No. 216, made under the invalid Rules 8D and 19B, are also struck down as they derive their authority from invalid rules.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 15(1)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 15(1A)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 18
Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, Section 17(2)
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Principle of delegated legislation
Rule of constitutional validity

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan sought to evict Padmavati Devi, who was in possession of land claimed as government property, under a summary procedure, while she asserted ownership and tenancy rights based on historical grants and tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether summary proceedings under Section 91 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956 can be used against a person raising a bona fide claim to possession of government land?
Whether the Revenue authorities were justified in ordering eviction without adjudicating complex questions of title and tenancy rights?
holdings: Summary eviction under Section 91 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956 cannot be invoked if the occupant raises a bona fide claim to title or possession, as such proceedings are unsuited for adjudicating complex legal and factual questions.
When a bona fide dispute over title or tenancy exists, the proper forum for resolution is a civil court through regular proceedings, not summary revenue proceedings.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1945, Section 6
Jaipur State Grants Land Tenures Act, 1947, Section 8(1)
doctrines: Summary proceedings doctrine
Due process of law
Bona fide dispute doctrine
Adjudication of title in civil courts

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu and others fought against landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated in 1978, challenged on grounds of delay, procedural irregularities, and constitutional violations.
issues_decided: Whether the delay between the notification under Section 4(1) and declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, invalidated the acquisition
Whether exclusion of certain lands from acquisition while including others amounted to arbitrariness under Article 14
Whether failure to conduct a fresh Section 5A enquiry after an errata notification vitiated the acquisition
Whether procedural defects in service of notices under Sections 9 and 10 and delay in award rendered the award invalid
holdings: Delay between Section 4(1) notification and Section 6 declaration does not invalidate acquisition if public purpose is established by the declaration.
Selective exclusion of lands does not amount to arbitrariness or discrimination if based on legitimate planning considerations and not mala fide.
An errata correcting survey numbers relates back to the original notification; a fresh Section 5A enquiry is not required if objections were already considered.
Procedural irregularities in service of notices are curable; delay in award is compensated by interest under Section 28 and additional compensation under Section 23(1A).
doctrines: Relation back of errata in notifications
Curability of procedural irregularities in land acquisition
Conclusiveness of public purpose under Section 6
Compensation as remedy for delay in award
Non-vesting of title in illegal possessors after possession under Section 16

card.dispute: SIPCOT, a state financial corporation, sold mortgaged assets of Contromix Pvt. Ltd. after loan default, and Contromix challenged the sale process as unfair and not in compliance with judicial guidelines.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of mortgaged assets by SIPCOT through tender and negotiation, instead of public auction, violated the principles laid down in Mahesh Chandra v. State of Rajasthan?
Whether the sale price of Rs. 38 lakhs was unreasonably low and failed to secure the best possible value for the property?
Whether SIPCOT was required to notify Contromix before accepting the final offer of Rs. 38 lakhs, and whether its failure to do so invalidated the sale?
holdings: Sale by tender and negotiation is valid if public auction is impractical, provided wide publicity is given to secure the best price; such method is not invalid per se under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1950.
The sale price of Rs. 38 lakhs was not low, as it exceeded the official valuation of Rs. 36.44 lakhs, and the borrower failed to secure a higher offer despite ample opportunity.
Failure to notify the borrower before accepting the final offer was inconsequential where the borrower had sufficient chance to present a better offer during litigation but failed to do so.
doctrines: Principle of fair sale of public property
Doctrine of adequate publicity in asset sales
Judicial guidance from Mahesh Chandra v. State of Rajasthan (AIR 1993 SC 935)

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the Delhi High Court's decision to deny an alternative site to Shivkumar Bhargava, who purchased land after the acquisition notification but claimed entitlement as the final owner.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, who purchased the land after the publication of the s.4(1) notification, is entitled to an alternative site.
Whether ownership for the purpose of entitlement to an alternative site is determined as of the date of the s.4(1) notification.
holdings: A person who acquires land after the publication of a s.4(1) notification is not entitled to an alternative site, even if they become the owner before final acquisition.
Entitlement to an alternative site depends on ownership as of the date of the s.4(1) notification, not at the time of final acquisition.
doctrines: Date of notification rule for determining ownership in land acquisition
Principle of statutory interpretation based on government policy and legislative intent

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's order directing payment of 18% annual interest from 1963 to 1984 on compensation for land taken without formal acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners are entitled to interest at 18% per annum from March 15, 1963, when possession was taken, until November 16, 1984, when the s.4(1) notification was issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether courts can award interest exceeding the rates and periods prescribed under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for possession taken prior to the issuance of a s.4(1) notification.
holdings: Landowners are not entitled to interest for the period prior to the publication of the s.4(1) notification, as the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, governs all aspects of interest payment and does not permit such pre-notification interest.
Courts cannot award interest at rates or for periods beyond those specified in the Act, as it is a complete code on the subject, and common law principles cannot override its provisions.
doctrines: Statutory exclusivity doctrine
Legality of possession under statutory authority
Self-contained code doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the land acquisition proceedings on grounds of delay, invidious discrimination, and a discrepancy in survey numbers, seeking to quash the acquisition of his land.
issues_decided: Whether unexplained delay between the preliminary notification under Section 4(1) and the declaration under Section 6 invalidates the acquisition proceedings.
Whether non-exemption of the appellant's land, while exempting another similarly situated property (Anand Nursery), constitutes invidious discrimination under Article 14.
Whether a discrepancy between the survey number in the Section 4(1) notification (265) and the Section 9 notice (265/1) invalidates the acquisition.
holdings: Delay between Section 4(1) notification and Section 6 declaration does not invalidate acquisition if the process was ongoing and the landowner acquired title after the notification, making the purchase ineffective against the State.
Grant of exemption to another property does not entitle the appellant to the same benefit; erroneous exemptions do not create a constitutional right to equal treatment under Article 14.
A minor discrepancy in survey number (main number vs. sub-division) does not vitiate the acquisition if the main survey number was correctly mentioned in the Section 4(1) notification.
doctrines: Doctrine of unexplained delay in acquisition
Doctrine of invidious discrimination under Article 14
Doctrine of curative interpretation of procedural discrepancies in land acquisition

card.dispute: The Allahabad Development Authority challenged the High Court's order declaring the land acquisition lapsed and directing re-possession by the original owners.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act due to delay in making the award?
Whether the High Court's direction to deliver possession back to the original owners was legally valid after vesting of land in the State?
Whether the principle of res judicata or estoppel applies to a judgment that is erroneous in law and contrary to statutory provisions?
holdings: Section 11-A does not apply to acquisitions where possession was taken under Section 17(1-A) and land had already vested in the State under Section 16; thus, the acquisition does not lapse for delay in award.
Once land vests in the State free from encumbrances, it cannot be divested and re-vested in former owners; the High Court’s direction to return possession was invalid.
A prior judicial order that is erroneous in law and contrary to statutory mandate does not operate as res judicata or create an estoppel against the State.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon possession under Section 16
Non-application of Section 11-A to completed acquisitions
No res judicata effect to judgments contrary to statutory provisions
Statutory mandate prevails over equitable doctrines like estoppel

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a property based on a will bequeathing it to her, while the respondents, as heirs of the original plaintiff, challenged the will's validity and claimed ownership as legal heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated 25.7.1963 was validly executed and proved by the appellant
Whether suspicious circumstances surrounding the will's execution required the propounder to offer additional explanation
Whether the High Court was justified in re-appreciating evidence in second appeal and overturning the first appellate court's finding on the will's genuineness
holdings: A will is proved like any other document; the propounder must establish testamentary capacity, signature, and attestation, especially when no suspicious circumstances exist.
Suspicious circumstances such as undue influence or improper execution must be clear and cogent to outweigh consistent testimony of attesting witnesses.
In second appeal, the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence on factual findings unless there is a substantial error of law or procedure.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
doctrines: Propounder of will must prove execution, especially when suspicious circumstances are present
Re-appreciation of evidence in second appeal is impermissible unless jurisdictional error is shown
Improbability must approach impossibility to reject credible attesting witness testimony in will cases

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification for the planned development of Delhi, arguing it lacked specificity and proper publication in the locality.
issues_decided: Whether the land was needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the mandatory requirement of publishing the substance of the notification under Section 4(1) in the locality was complied with.
Whether a purchaser of land after the Section 6 declaration could challenge the validity of the Section 4(1) notification.
holdings: The specification of 'Planned Development of Delhi' as a public purpose is valid, and the lack of detailed planning does not invalidate the Governor's satisfaction under Section 4(1).
The substance of the notification under Section 4(1) was properly published in the locality, as evidenced by official endorsements and the presumption under Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act.

A purchaser after the Section 6 declaration has no right to challenge the validity of the Section 4(1) notification, but the appeal was not dismissed on this ground since other appellants were original owners.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity of official acts
Public purpose in land acquisition
Mandatory compliance with publication requirements in land acquisition

card.dispute: The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation sought to remove pavement-dwellers from unauthorized encroachments on a public road, while the dwellers claimed a right to continued occupation until alternative accommodation was provided.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the Municipal Corporation not to remove encroachments without providing alternative accommodation
Whether encroachers have a right to judicial protection and what procedural safeguards apply
Whether transfers of encroached land among encroachers are legally valid
Whether the State has a constitutional and statutory duty to provide housing to urban poor
holdings: The High Court's direction to provide alternative accommodation before eviction is valid only in exceptional cases; no universal rule mandates it, but each case must be decided on its facts.
Encroachers are entitled to judicial review and procedural fairness, including a hearing before eviction, especially if long-standing possession is established.
Transfers of encroached public land, including by sale or assignment, are void ab initio as against public policy and constitutional objectives.
The State and municipal bodies have a constitutional and statutory duty to formulate housing schemes for the urban poor, using budgetary allocations under laws like the Urban Land Ceiling Act.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Judicial review as part of basic structure
Public trust doctrine
Void ab initio for transactions contrary to public policy

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the reduction of compensation by the High Court in a land acquisition case for a hydel channel project.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reducing the compensation from Rs.30,000 to Rs.16,000 per acre based on unreliable sale deeds?
Whether the market value determined by the Land Acquisition Collector was legally sustainable?
Whether previous compensation awards in a neighboring village could be relied upon to fix market value?
holdings: The sale deeds cited to prove higher market value were inadmissible due to lack of proof of consideration, non-examination of parties, and suspicion of being inflated for acquisition purposes.
The High Court was justified in relying on final compensation awards from a neighboring village to determine market value in the absence of reliable evidence.
The Collector's valuation was upheld with minor modifications, fixing uniform rates for similar land types based on judicial and state precedents.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Principle of inadmissibility of suspicious and uncorroborated sale deeds in land valuation
Doctrine of judicial notice of previous compensation awards in comparable cases

card.dispute: Delhi Development Authority (D.D.A.) and Skipper Construction Company disputed over the cancellation of Skipper's bid for a plot of land due to non-payment of the balance consideration despite multiple extensions.
issues_decided: Whether the court was justified in granting repeated stay orders against the cancellation of Skipper's bid despite failure to pay the balance amount?
Whether the corporate veil should be lifted to reveal Tejwant Singh as the real beneficiary of sham property transactions?
Whether properties belonging to Tejwant Singh and his family should be attached to compensate defrauded purchasers?
holdings: Courts should not mechanically grant stay orders in property disputes without considering the merits, especially when a party has repeatedly failed to meet payment obligations.
The corporate veil can be lifted when corporate structures are used as mere devices to conceal ownership and defraud creditors, making the individual the true owner of the property.
Properties held through sham transactions may be attached and sold to ensure complete justice to victims of fraud, especially under Article 142 of the Constitution.
doctrines: Lifting of the corporate veil
Complete justice under Article 142
Fraud vitiates legal proceedings
Judicial restraint in granting interim relief

card.dispute: A co-owner sought to invoke Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 during execution of a partition decree against a stranger transferee of another co-owner's share in a family dwelling house.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 applies during execution proceedings of a final partition decree?
Whether a co-owner can invoke Section 4 of the Partition Act against a stranger transferee of a share in a family dwelling house before actual possession is delivered?
holdings: Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 remains applicable from the institution of a partition suit until the final execution of the decree, including during execution proceedings, so long as co-owners are not put in actual possession.
Once a final decree is fully executed and possession is delivered, Section 4 ceases to apply as the dwelling house no longer belongs to an undivided family.
doctrines: Functus officio
Undivided family dwelling house doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the sale of trust property by the trustees to certain purchasers, alleging that the trustees committed fraud on the court by suppressing the appellants' earlier offer while seeking court permission for the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the trustees suppressed a genuine offer from the appellants while seeking court permission to sell the property?
Whether the suppression of the appellants' offer constituted fraud on the court?
Whether the purchasers' subsequent acquisition of the property in good faith could validate the sale despite the fraud?
holdings: The trustees suppressed the appellants' bona fide offer and falsely represented to the court that no higher offer existed, which amounts to fraud on the court.
A decree obtained by fraud on the court is a nullity and cannot be upheld, regardless of the good faith of subsequent purchasers.
The sale permission granted by the court was vitiated by fraud and must be set aside, requiring fresh sale proceedings with updated offers.
doctrines: Fraud upon the court
Nullity of judgment obtained by fraud
Bona fide purchaser doctrine (rejected in case of fraud on court)

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) fought to evict tenants (respondents) for making unauthorized structural alterations to the rented shops and land, alleging material impairment of value or utility under the Punjab Rent Restriction Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's structural alterations to the demised premises materially impaired the value or utility of the building or land within the meaning of Section 13(2)(iii) of the Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1950?
Whether the findings of the lower courts that the alterations did not amount to material impairment were legally sustainable?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the revision petition in limine without examining the legal question involved?
holdings: Structural alterations such as removing partition walls, doors, original roofs, merging shops with verandahs, and constructing new roofs and access points constitute acts likely to materially impair the value or utility of the demised premises under Section 13(2)(iii) of the Punjab Rent Restriction Act, 1950.
The question of whether alterations materially impair value or utility is a mixed question of law and fact requiring application of correct legal principles, which the lower courts failed to do.
The High Court erred in dismissing the revision petition in limine without addressing the substantial legal issue concerning material impairment under Section 13(2)(iii).
doctrines: Material impairment of value or utility from the landlord's perspective
Mixed question of law and fact in eviction cases
Error in dismissing revision petitions in limine without legal examination

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing for a higher market value based on comparable sales and potential for development.
issues_decided: Whether untested sale deeds can be relied upon to determine market value for compensation?
Whether the land possessed potential value as a building site at the time of notification under Section 4(1) of the Act?
Whether the High Court erred in not remitting the case for fresh determination of compensation?
holdings: Untested sale deeds, where neither vendor nor vendee is examined, cannot form the basis for determining compensation as they lack evidentiary value.
Potential value for construction must be established as existing on the date of notification; mere possibility of future development does not justify higher compensation.
The High Court correctly upheld compensation based on comparable settled awards and did not err in refusing remand where evidence was insufficient.
doctrines: Willing buyer-willing seller test for market value
Requirement of proof for comparable sale deeds
Determination of potential value based on facts existing at the time of notification

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Special Land Acquisition Officer for an industrial development project, arguing it was inadequate.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of acquired lands into different categories for compensation was justified
What is the just and adequate market value of the land as of the date of the Section 4(1) notification under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether future potential use of the land can be considered in determining compensation
holdings: The entire acquired land should be valued uniformly as the State did not contest that all lands were of equal value.
The market value of the land is Rs. 35,000 per acre, determined by applying the 'prudent purchaser' test and rejecting reliance on unverified sale deeds and future potential.
Future use of the land for industrial development cannot be considered in fixing compensation under Section 24 fifthly of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
doctrines: Prudent purchaser rule
Prohibition on considering future potential use in compensation
Burden of proof on claimants to establish market value

card.dispute: The dispute was between ITC Bhadrachalam Paperboards and the Mandal Revenue Officer over whether a government order exempting the company from non-agricultural land assessment was valid despite non-compliance with statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether a government order issued under Section 11 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, without complying with mandatory procedural requirements, can be considered valid.
Whether the principle of promissory or equitable estoppel can be invoked against the government to validate an otherwise invalid statutory exemption.
holdings: An exemption order under Section 11 of the Act must comply with mandatory procedural requirements, including publication in the Gazette and laying before the Legislative Assembly; non-compliance renders the order invalid and ineffective.

The doctrine of promissory or equitable estoppel cannot be invoked to validate an act that violates mandatory statutory provisions, as such estoppel cannot override clear legislative mandates or legalize actions outside statutory authority.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 7
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 11
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 13
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Equitable estoppel
Mandatory statutory compliance
Rule of law and constitutional supremacy

card.dispute: M.C. Mehta, a public interest litigant, challenged the leasing of ecologically fragile forest and riverbed land along the Beas River to Span Motels Pvt. Ltd., allegedly linked to Union Minister Kamal Nath, for commercial resort development.
issues_decided: Whether the State, as trustee of natural resources, can lease ecologically fragile forest and riverbed land to a private entity for commercial use under the public trust doctrine.
Whether altering the course of a river and constructing on riverbanks without environmental safeguards violates environmental principles like the precautionary and polluter pays principles.
Whether the government's regularisation and leasing of encroached forest and riverbed land is legally valid in the absence of legislative sanction.
holdings: The State is a trustee of all natural resources and cannot lease ecologically fragile or public trust lands for private commercial use, as this constitutes a breach of public trust.

The precautionary principle and polluter pays principle are integral to Indian environmental law, requiring preventive action against environmental harm and imposing liability on those causing ecological damage.

Leases granted over riverbed and forest land in ecologically sensitive areas are void if they violate the public trust doctrine, especially when granted without legislative authority and for private benefit.
provisions: Indian Constitution, Article 48A (Directive Principle on Environmental Protection)
Indian Constitution, Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty to Protect Environment)
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Precautionary Principle
Polluter Pays Principle
Sustainable Development

card.dispute: The daughter and legatee of Mrs. Primrose Mary Vas fought with her siblings over the validity of a holograph will, seeking letters of administration while others contested undue influence and suspicious circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the holograph will dated 19.6.1964 was validly executed and attested.
Whether there were suspicious circumstances surrounding the will's execution warranting rejection.
Whether the propounder of the will exercised undue influence over the testatrix.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court’s finding on the will’s validity.
holdings: A holograph will, entirely in the testatrix's handwriting and properly attested, is presumed valid and the burden lies on the contestants to prove irregularity.
Suspicious circumstances must be grounded in evidence; mere conjecture or improbability does not invalidate a will supported by credible attestation.
The propounder of a will is not required to dispel every remote suspicion if the evidence affirmatively supports due execution and sound mind.
The High Court erred in re-appreciating evidence de novo and ignoring the trial court’s factual findings supported by evidence and legal presumption.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in due execution of wills
Principle of sound mind and testamentary capacity
Requirement of proof for undue influence
Appellate court's limited scope of review in findings of fact

card.dispute: The appellant (seller) challenged the High Court's decree for specific performance granted to the respondent (buyer), who failed to pay the agreed amount within the stipulated and reasonable time.
issues_decided: Whether the buyer was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract for specific performance?
Whether time was of the essence in the agreement for payment of Rs. 4 lakhs?
Whether the High Court was justified in granting specific performance despite the buyer's default in payment?
Whether the High Court could extend time for payment after passing a conditional decree that made default result in dismissal of the suit?
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must be ready and willing to perform his obligations at all material times; failure to pay a stipulated amount within the agreed or reasonable time shows lack of readiness.
Where a contract expressly states that time is of the essence, or circumstances so indicate, non-payment within the stipulated time constitutes a material breach barring specific performance.
Specific performance cannot be granted if enforcing it would be inequitable, especially where the buyer’s delay prejudices the seller’s ability to secure alternative accommodation.
A conditional decree stating that the suit stands dismissed upon default renders further extension of time unnecessary, and the issue becomes academic if the decree is set aside.
doctrines: Time is not ordinarily of the essence in immovable property contracts, but may be inferred from express terms, nature of property, or surrounding circumstances.
Doctrine of readiness and willingness in specific performance.
Equity and good conscience in granting specific performance.
Conditional decrees and functus officio doctrine in relation to court's power to extend time.

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their land by the Union of India for the planned development of Delhi under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, seeking quashing of the acquisition and release of land already developed or used for recreational purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings could be quashed based on an alleged invalid order under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for release of land from acquisition
Whether the presence of structures and developments on the acquired land rendered the acquisition unjustified
Whether land marked in green in the master plan for recreational use could be acquired for planned development
holdings: An order releasing land from acquisition under Section 48 is invalid without a formal notification; absence of such notification means the acquisition remains valid.
The existence of structures on acquired land does not invalidate acquisition for planned development, especially when the land is part of a large-scale urban development project.
Land designated in green in the master plan for recreational purposes is a legitimate part of planned development and can be acquired for public purpose.
doctrines: Doctrine of formal validity of denotification under Section 48
Doctrine of planned development as a public purpose
Doctrine of unauthorized constructions being at the owner's risk

card.dispute: Female tribal petitioners challenged the exclusion of women from inheriting property under customary law and the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act, seeking equal rights in intestate succession as male tribals.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 7, 8, and 76 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, which exclude tribal women from inheritance, violate Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution
Whether tribal women are entitled to equal rights with men in intestate succession to agricultural and tenancy rights
Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, or Indian Succession Act, 1925, apply to Scheduled Tribes by principle, despite statutory exclusion
holdings: The exclusion of tribal women from inheritance under customary law and the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act is discriminatory and violates Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution.

Tribal women are entitled to equal inheritance rights by intestate succession as male heirs, based on the principles of justice, equity, and good conscience underlying the Hindu and Indian Succession Acts.

While the Hindu and Indian Succession Acts do not directly apply to Scheduled Tribes, their general principles apply to ensure gender equality in inheritance, subject to restrictions on alienation to non-tribals.
doctrines: Principle of gender equality under Articles 14 and 15
Doctrine of justice, equity, and good conscience
Customary law subject to fundamental rights
Non-derogation from constitutional rights despite statutory exceptions

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for default in rent payment and sub-letting, specifically over a 15-day delay in depositing February 1972 rent, leading to a dispute over whether the Rent Controller could condone the delay and whether the High Court could strike out the tenant's defence.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has the discretion to condone a tenant's delay in depositing rent under Section 15(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the High Court could lawfully strike out the tenant's defence under Section 15(7) when the Rent Controller and Tribunal had already exercised discretion not to do so.
Whether the tenant's explanation for the delay in rent payment was sufficient to justify non-striking out of the defence.
holdings: The Rent Controller has discretionary power under Section 15(7) to condone delay in rent deposit and extend time; the provision is not mandatory and must be applied with due regard to facts.
The High Court erred in substituting its discretion for that of the Rent Controller and Tribunal, who had rightly found the default non-wilful and exercised discretion not to strike out the defence.
Despite the legal error, the appeal was dismissed as the tenant's explanation for delay—illness of attorney and partner's preoccupation—was deemed negligent, and remand would not serve justice.
doctrines: Judicial discretion in eviction proceedings
Non-mandatory application of procedural provisions in rent control law
Principle against mechanical application of statutory provisions without considering facts

card.dispute: Star Wire (India) Ltd. challenged the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State of Haryana, claiming it had no knowledge of them, while the State argued the challenge was barred by laches and the petitioner had no valid title.
issues_decided: Whether a purchaser of land after the publication of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can challenge the acquisition proceedings?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition on the grounds of laches?
holdings: A purchaser who acquires land after the publication of a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not acquire a valid title and cannot challenge the legality of the acquisition proceedings.

Unreasonable delay in filing a writ petition challenging acquisition proceedings amounts to laches, which bars the petitioner from obtaining extraordinary relief, even if the petition is filed within the limitation period.
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Vesting of title in the State free from encumbrances
Void title doctrine in post-notification land transfers

card.dispute: The owner of a flat and garage sought eviction of licensees on the ground of bona fide personal requirement, but the High Court and Appellate Bench dismissed her suit, holding she had alternative accommodation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had a bona fide and reasonable need for the suit premises for her own occupation.
Whether the appellant's omission to disclose certain facts about alternative accommodation in her plaint amounted to unclean hands.
Whether the temporary and precarious possession of alternative accommodation could negate a claim for eviction on grounds of personal need.
holdings: A landlord's requirement for personal occupation must be bona fide and reasonable, but not absolute; temporary or insecure alternative accommodation does not disentitle her from eviction relief.
Omission to mention facts about alternative accommodation in the plaint, without fraud or misrepresentation, does not constitute unclean hands or mala fide intention.
Possession of premises on a leave and licence basis is precarious and cannot be treated as suitable alternative accommodation when assessing bona fide need.
provisions: Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, Proviso (f) to Section 11(1)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for personal occupation
Doctrine of unclean hands
Precariousness of leave and licence possession

card.dispute: The appellant (sister) and respondents (brother and others) fought over ownership of property allegedly gifted by their uncle Motilal Gopalji, who later cancelled the gift and made a will in favor of the appellant and another brother.
issues_decided: Whether the gift deed dated May 15, 1965, was a complete and irrevocable transfer of property under the Transfer of Property Act?
Whether the donor had the right to cancel the gift deed during his lifetime?
Whether the subsequent will executed by the donor was valid and effective after the alleged gift?
holdings: A gift is incomplete if it is conditional, possession is not delivered, and acceptance is not proved; such a gift can be lawfully cancelled by the donor during his lifetime.
Where a donor reserves the right to enjoy the property and collect rents for life and does not deliver possession, the gift amounts to a limited and conditional transfer, not an absolute one.
A duly executed cancellation of an incomplete gift renders it ineffective, allowing the donor to dispose of the property by will.
doctrines: Doctrine of incomplete gift
Doctrine of conditional gift
Requirement of delivery of possession and acceptance for a valid gift

card.dispute: The appellant (only son) challenged the partition of a tenanted dwelling house among himself and his three sisters, claiming impartibility under Section 23 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether a tenanted house qualifies as a 'dwelling house' under Section 23 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 23 applies when there is only one male heir and multiple female heirs
holdings: A house that is tenanted and not actually inhabited by family members does not qualify as a 'dwelling house' under Section 23, and thus loses protection from partition.
Section 23 applies even when there is a single male heir; he may prevent female heirs from claiming partition until he chooses to separate his share.
doctrines: Literal interpretation with purposive approach
Right of residence vs. right to partition
Impartibility of dwelling house under Hindu law
Principle of corresponding duty with right

card.dispute: The appellant (Navaneethammal) sued the respondent (Arjuna Chetty) for declaration of title and recovery of possession of land, which the respondent had occupied since 1935 under a lease but claimed to hold in his own right after the lease ended.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's continued possession after the expiry of the lease amounted to a valid surrender and re-entry in his own right
Whether the appellant's suit for possession was barred by limitation under Article 139 of the Limitation Act
Whether the respondent acquired title by adverse possession
holdings: The respondent's possession after the lease expired remained permissive due to implied assent by the landlord, and did not amount to adverse possession.
The suit was not barred by limitation because the tenancy was not determined until the respondent set up a hostile title, which triggered the limitation period under Article 139.
The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the trial and appellate courts that were supported by evidence.
doctrines: Implied assent to continuation of tenancy
Determination of tenancy by surrender
Principle of concurrent findings in civil appeals

card.dispute: Hereditary trustees of Hindu religious and charitable institutions challenged the constitutional validity of certain provisions of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, which abolished their hereditary rights in management and remuneration.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 15 and 16 of the Act, which abolish hereditary trusteeship, violate Article 25(1) of the Constitution?
Whether Sections 17 and 29(5), which provide for a board of trustees with the founder or family member as chairperson, are constitutionally valid?
Whether Section 144, which abolishes emoluments to hereditary trustees, is unconstitutional?
holdings: Abolition of hereditary trusteeship is a permissible secular regulation under Article 25(2) and does not violate Article 25(1), as administration of religious institutions is not an essential religious practice.

Sections 17 and 29(5) are valid, but must be read down to ensure that the founder or a family member presides over the board of trustees to preserve the founder’s role in effective and faithful management.
Section 144 abolishing emoluments is constitutionally valid as it aims to prevent misuse of trust funds and falls within legislative competence, subject to future determination in related cases.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Sections 15, 16, 17, 29(5), 144
doctrines: Essential religious practices doctrine
Secular administration of religious institutions
Reading down of statutory provisions to uphold constitutionality
Legislative primacy in social reform under Article 25(2)

card.dispute: The displaced persons from the Pong Dam project in Himachal Pradesh fought against the Union of India and the State of Rajasthan over the unfair allotment and cancellation of land in Rajasthan meant for them, alleging favouritism towards local Rajasthanis.
issues_decided: Whether the 1992 amendment to the Rajasthan Colonisation Rules, including the introduction of Rule 6-A, violated the rights of Pong Dam oustees?
Whether the cancellation of land allotments to oustees without proper review and notice breached principles of natural justice?
Whether the State of Rajasthan acted unfairly in regularising possession of land by Rajasthanis over rightful oustee allottees?
What remedial measures should be adopted to ensure justice to the oustees whose allotments were cancelled after 1992?
holdings: The 1992 notification amending the Rajasthan Colonisation Rules, particularly the insertion of Rule 6-A and the extension of the period in Rule 6(3), is quashed for being arbitrary and violative of fair procedure.
Cancellations of allotments without affording oustees a meaningful opportunity for review, especially when they were outside Rajasthan, violate natural justice and are invalid.
The State of Rajasthan discriminated against Pong Dam oustees in favour of local residents, undermining inter-State agreements and equitable settlement principles.
A judicial review by a District Judge and a central committee must be constituted to restore lands or provide equivalent alternatives to oustees, with full procedural safeguards and binding outcomes.
provisions: Rajasthan Colonisation (Allotment and Sale of Government Land to Pong Dam Oustees and their Transferees in the Indira Gandhi Canal Colony Area) Rules, 1972, Rule 6(3), Rule 6-A, Rule 8-AAA
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Doctrine of arbitrariness in administrative action
Enforcement of inter-governmental agreements
Remedial judicial supervision in public interest litigation

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the acquisition of their land by the Rajasthan government under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, arguing procedural defects and lack of a sanctioned development scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land under Section 52 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 is valid in the absence of a notified development scheme
Whether failure to make an award within the stipulated time under Section 11-A leads to lapse of acquisition proceedings
Whether non-compliance with part payment of compensation before taking possession invalidates the acquisition
holdings: The State Government can acquire land under Section 52 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for urban improvement or any other public purpose without framing a scheme; such a scheme is mandatory only when the Urban Improvement Trust undertakes the work.
Once possession is taken and land vests in the government under Section 17(1), acquisition does not lapse due to delay or failure in making an award under Section 11-A.
Non-compliance with part payment of compensation under Section 17(3-A) does not render possession illegal or allow the government to withdraw from acquisition.
doctrines: Vesting of property upon publication of notification
Acquisition does not lapse after vesting despite procedural delays
Distinction between government department action and Urban Improvement Trust action under statutory scheme

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for land and building acquired by the Kerala State Electricity Board.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was legally justified in reducing the market value of the acquired land from Rs. 3,000 per cent to Rs. 2,000 per cent?
Whether the High Court erred in not accepting the higher valuation of the building, including a 15% appreciation, awarded by the Reference Court?
holdings: When large extents of land are acquired, compensation must be determined on an acreage basis, not per cent or square foot, and comparable sales of small plots in developed areas do not provide a reliable basis for valuation.

The High Court's valuation of the building, based on the Engineer's assessment and absence of reliable evidence for 15% appreciation, was a valid exercise of appreciation of evidence and not liable to interference.
doctrines: Principle of acreage-based valuation for large land acquisitions
Reliance on comparable sales only when they are of similar extent and location
Appreciation of evidence by appellate courts not to be disturbed without error of law

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the acquisition of their land by the State of Rajasthan under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, arguing procedural defects and lack of a sanctioned scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land under Section 52 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, is invalid in the absence of a notified improvement scheme.
Whether non-compliance with time limits for making an award under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, causes acquisition proceedings to lapse after vesting.
Whether the decision of the Rajasthan High Court in Narain's case applies and affects the validity of the present acquisition.
holdings: The State Government can acquire land under Section 52 of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, for public purposes without a formal scheme if the acquisition is for urban improvement or other purposes under the Act.
Once land has vested in the government under a valid notification, non-compliance with the time limit for passing an award under Section 11-A does not cause the acquisition to lapse.
The Division Bench decision in Narain's case was not binding as it was not approved by a Full Bench and was based on an incorrect interpretation of Supreme Court precedent.
doctrines: Vesting of property upon publication of notification
Non-lapsing of acquisition after vesting despite delay in award
Doctrine of binding precedent and hierarchy of judicial decisions
Statutory interpretation of special enactment for urban improvement

card.dispute: The plaintiff claimed title and possession of a property based on a sale deed dated 5.6.1967, while the first defendant claimed a prior valid sale deed dated 5.5.1967, leading to a dispute over which transaction was genuine and valid.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the trial and first appellate courts in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC.
Whether the adequacy or sufficiency of evidence supporting a finding of fact is a question of law open for review in second appeal.
Whether the High Court erred in reappreciating evidence and holding the plaintiff's sale deed valid despite lower courts' findings of collusion and invalidity.
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved.
The sufficiency or adequacy of evidence to support a finding of fact is not a question of law and cannot be examined in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC.
Reappreciation of evidence and reassessment of probabilities by the High Court in second appeal exceeds its jurisdiction and amounts to a jurisdictional error.
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact doctrine
Substantial question of law requirement in second appeal
Limitation on reappreciation of evidence in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the land acquisition of C.T.S. No. 211 on the grounds that the award excluded C.T.S. No. 218 due to a private settlement, arguing this invalidated the entire acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Officer could lawfully exclude C.T.S. No. 218 from the award based on a private settlement without denotification under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the acquisition of C.T.S. No. 211 could be quashed due to non-acquisition of C.T.S. No. 218.
Whether the acquisition was vitiated by malafides or lack of public purpose.
Whether the delay and conduct of the appellant affected the maintainability of the challenge.
holdings: Once a notification under Section 4 and declaration under Section 6 are issued, the Land Acquisition Officer must pass an award for all notified land unless it is formally denotified under Section 48.
The failure to acquire C.T.S. No. 218 does not invalidate the acquisition of C.T.S. No. 211 if the public purpose remains genuine and unaffected.
Mere irregularity or procedural lapse does not justify quashing acquisition where public interest is served and no malafides are proven.
Courts should balance public interest against private grievances in land acquisition cases and avoid quashing proceedings solely on technical grounds when larger public interest is involved.
doctrines: Doctrine of Proportionality and Public Interest
Doctrine of Continuing Validity of Acquisition
Discretionary Power of Courts in Granting Injunctive Relief
Principle of Balancing Competing Interests in Writ Jurisdiction

card.dispute: The petitioner, representing a public interest group, fought against the Union of India and others over the environmental damage caused by unregulated shrimp farming in ecologically sensitive coastal areas.
issues_decided: Whether intensive and semi-intensive shrimp farming in ecologically fragile coastal zones violates environmental protection laws?
Whether the Coastal Zone Regulation Notification, 1991 applies to shrimp culture activities?
Whether traditional versus modern shrimp farming should be differentiated in regulatory approach?
What remedial measures, including demolition and compensation, are warranted for illegal and harmful shrimp farming?
holdings: Intensive and semi-intensive shrimp farming in coastal regulation zones is prohibited under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the CRZ Notification, 1991, as it causes irreversible environmental harm.
All shrimp culture ponds within the coastal regulation zone must be demolished, and authorities are directed to enforce closure by a fixed deadline.

Traditional and improved traditional shrimp farming may continue with prior approval, but industrial shrimp farming outside CRZ and 1000 meters from Chilka and Pulicat lakes requires authorization and compliance with environmental principles.
The 'Polluter Pays' and 'Precautionary' principles apply; polluters must compensate affected individuals and fund ecological restoration through an Environment Protection Fund.
doctrines: Precautionary Principle
Polluter Pays Principle
Sustainable Development
Public Trust Doctrine

card.dispute: The Jaipur Development Authority challenged the High Court's order directing it to allot land to Daulat Mal Jain and others, despite earlier illegal allotments made under corrupt influence.
issues_decided: Whether the refusal to deliver possession to the respondents, while others had obtained it through illegal allotments, violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether illegal allotments made under corrupt influence can be regularized on the ground of equality or hardship?
holdings: Article 14 cannot be invoked to legitimize illegal or ultra vires actions; equality cannot be claimed based on wrongful benefits obtained by others through illegality.

Though the High Court erred in directing allotment of land based on illegal orders, the Supreme Court in exceptional circumstances upheld the order to prevent hardship, but modified it to allot 250 sq. yds. in another scheme at the original rate.
provisions: Rajasthan Lokayukta and Up-Lokayukta Act, 1973, Section 10
doctrines: Doctrine of Equality under Article 14
Non-legitimization of illegal acts
Equitable modification in exceptional cases

card.dispute: Hereditary priests (archakas) challenged the constitutional validity of provisions in the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act that abolished their hereditary rights to temple appointments.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 34, 35, 37, 39, and 144 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, which abolish hereditary rights of archakas and other temple office-holders, violate Article 25 and 26 of the Constitution?
Whether the abolition of hereditary rights affects the religious rights of Hindus under the Constitution?
What safeguards must be provided to hereditary archakas after the abolition of their hereditary rights to ensure their livelihood and welfare?
holdings: The State can regulate the appointment of archakas in Hindu religious institutions without violating Article 25 or 26, as such regulation falls within its secular power to administer religious endowments.
Abolition of hereditary rights to temple offices does not infringe upon the freedom of religion, as the State may ensure merit-based appointments while preserving religious practices.

The State must ensure the welfare of displaced archakas by creating a corpus fund of Rs.75 crores, rationalizing pay scales, and providing social security measures including housing, education, medical care, and insurance.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, Sections 34, 35, 37, 39, 144
doctrines: State's secular power to regulate religious institutions
Balancing religious freedom with social reform
Welfare state obligation to protect displaced traditional office-holders

card.dispute: Sarvinder Singh fought against Dalip Singh and others over whether respondents, who purchased property during a pending suit, should be impleaded as necessary parties in a title declaration suit.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents are necessary or proper parties to the suit under Order 1, Rule 10 of the CPC?
Whether the transfer of property during the pendency of a suit is valid under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act?
holdings: The respondents are neither necessary nor proper parties to the suit because they cannot challenge the validity of the registered will on which the title claim is based and their rights are not essential for adjudicating the dispute.

The sale deeds executed during the pendency of the suit are hit by the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and are invalid as the transferors lacked authority to alienate the property without court permission.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39, Rule 11
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Necessary and proper parties under CPC

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the acquisition and use of their land under the MRTP Act and sought restitution of surplus land allegedly promised to be returned to erstwhile owners.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the first writ petition could be condoned.
Whether the second writ petition was barred by res judicata.
Whether the petitioners were entitled to restitution of surplus land based on a government resolution.
holdings: The delay in filing the first writ petition was unjustifiable and condonation of delay was not warranted.
The second writ petition was barred by constructive res judicata due to the dismissal of the earlier petition on merits.
Restitution of acquired land is not permissible once possession is taken and compensation paid, even if surplus land is used for other public purposes.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, Section 126(4)
doctrines: res judicata
constructive res judicata
public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: Whether a co-sharer in acquired land can claim enhanced compensation when another co-sharer alone filed a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, without the first co-sharer filing a separate application.
issues_decided: Whether a co-sharer who did not file a Section 18 application can benefit from enhanced compensation awarded in a reference filed by another co-sharer.
Whether Order 1 Rule 10 CPC mandates impleadment of all co-sharers so as to entitle a non-applicant co-sharer to enhanced compensation.
Whether the procedure under the Land Acquisition Act is inconsistent with the CPC in matters of claiming compensation.
holdings: A co-sharer who does not file a valid application under Section 18(1) within the prescribed time is not entitled to enhanced compensation awarded in a reference initiated by another co-sharer.

Order 1 Rule 10 CPC does not apply to override the mandatory requirement of a separate application under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, as the Act prescribes an inconsistent and self-contained procedure.
Jurisdiction of the civil court to determine enhanced compensation arises only upon a valid reference under Section 18; no such jurisdiction extends to co-sharers who did not file a reference.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10
doctrines: Conditions precedent to jurisdiction
Inconsistency between special and general statutes
Self-contained statutory scheme

card.dispute: The plaintiff, Smt. Sawarni, fought against Smt. Inder Kaur and others over ownership and possession of land allegedly inherited from Gurbax Singh, disputing Inder Kaur's claim to be his daughter and challenging the validity of a sale deed she executed.
issues_decided: Whether Roori, not Inder Kaur, was the daughter of Gurbax Singh and thus entitled to inherit his property
Whether mutation entries in revenue records confer title to immovable property
Whether the Will executed by Gurdip Kaur and the succession certificate in favor of Sawarni and Roori establish legal title
Whether the lower appellate court and High Court erred in reversing the trial court’s findings without proper reasoning
holdings: Roori, not Inder Kaur, was the legitimate daughter of Gurbax Singh, and the trial court’s finding to that effect could not be overturned without cogent reasoning.
Mutation in revenue records does not confer title or create any presumptive right over property; it only enables payment of land revenue.
A Will and a succession certificate issued under the Indian Succession Act are legally relevant and cannot be ignored in determining title, especially when not challenged for cancellation.
The lower appellate court’s reversal of the trial court’s decree without addressing material evidence and legal documents was unsustainable in law.
provisions: Revenue Records and Mutation Rules (Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, by implication)
doctrines: Mutation does not confer title
Presumption of correctness of succession certificate
Binding effect of concurrent findings of fact unless per incuriam or perverse
Will as testamentary instrument affecting devolution of property

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his suit to evict the tenant from a shop, claiming personal need and wilful default in rent, after a partition of jointly owned property.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner can maintain an eviction petition against a tenant for his share of a jointly let property after partition.
Whether partition of a tenanted property among co-owners allows individual co-owners to evict the tenant from their respective shares.
Whether the tenant's subsequent purchase of the remaining portion of the property affects the maintainability of the eviction suit.
holdings: A co-owner can initiate eviction proceedings for their share only if the tenanted property has been partitioned by metes and bounds, resulting in definite and identifiable shares.
Partition among co-owners severs the joint tenancy, allowing each owner to act independently as a lessor regarding their share, including terminating tenancy.
When a tenant purchases the remaining portion of the property, their tenancy in that part merges with ownership, making the eviction suit maintainable for the disputed portion.
provisions: Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Lease Control) Act, 1954, Section 15
doctrines: Partition by agreement results in severance of interest even without physical division.
Intention as the true test of partition.
Merger of tenancy into ownership when tenant acquires the property.

card.dispute: The State Bank of Patiala challenged the High Court's decision upholding the quashing of disciplinary action against its employee, S.K. Sharma, for alleged misappropriation and misconduct.
issues_decided: Whether the disciplinary enquiry against S.K. Sharma was vitiated by non-compliance with procedural rules, specifically the non-furnishing of witness statements?
Whether violation of procedural provisions in a departmental enquiry automatically invalidates the punishment order?
What is the appropriate test to determine if a procedural irregularity in a disciplinary enquiry warrants setting aside the order of punishment?
holdings: Non-compliance with procedural rules in a disciplinary enquiry does not automatically invalidate the punishment; the court must assess whether the violation caused prejudice to the employee's defence.
Procedural provisions are generally for the benefit of the employee, and their violation requires examination of whether it resulted in actual prejudice affecting fair hearing.

Where an employee had effective opportunity to review witness statements and cross-examine, and no specific prejudice is shown, the punishment order stands despite technical non-compliance with procedure.
provisions: State Bank of Patiala (Officers') Service Regulations 1979, Regulation 50(4)
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Test of prejudice in procedural violations
Substantial compliance with procedural rules
Distinction between mandatory and directory procedural provisions

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh fought with private respondents over ownership and possession of 30 bighas and 18 biswas of land in Chak Dakana, where the respondents claimed ownership based on a correction in revenue records, while the State claimed ownership since 1950.
issues_decided: Whether an order by the Assistant Settlement Officer directing correction in revenue records can serve as a basis to declare title in favor of the plaintiffs?
Whether the courts below were justified in declaring the plaintiffs as owners based solely on the correction entry in revenue records?
holdings: An entry in revenue or settlement records, even if corrected pursuant to an official order, does not create or extinguish title and cannot by itself serve as a basis for declaring ownership.
Courts cannot declare title in favor of a party based solely on an unproven or absent order of a revenue authority without independent documentary or legal evidence of ownership.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Section 37
doctrines: Revenue entries have only presumptive value and do not confer title
Principle of finality of judicial findings not applied due to error apparent on record

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu fought with Arooran Sugars Ltd over the acquisition of surplus agricultural land under land reform laws and the entitlement to compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 18(1) of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Act, 1961, was valid despite prior amendments affecting compensation provisions.
Whether Sections 4, 5, and 6 of Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978 validly revived the acquisition process and vested surplus land in the state.
Whether the High Court’s directions in earlier writ petitions created a binding obligation to pay compensation, despite subsequent legislative changes.
holdings: The notification issued on 4.4.1973 under Section 18(1) of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Act, 1961, is valid and effective for vesting surplus land in the state, due to the retrospective operation of Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978.

Sections 4, 5, and 6 of Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978 are constitutionally valid and nullify the effect of earlier amendments, thereby restoring the state's right to vest surplus land without compensation under the original scheme.
The High Court’s 1978 direction to determine compensation was an execution order dependent on an earlier judgment; once that judgment is set aside, the direction ceases to have effect.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 18
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 50(3)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of Deemed Acquisition
Doctrine of Retrospective Legislation
Doctrine of Finality of Judicial Orders
Agrarian Reform under Directive Principles of State Policy

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (sons) challenged the validity of a 1959 sale deed executed by their father, claiming he had no right to sell ancestral property, while the defendants (purchasers) argued the sale was valid due to family necessity.
issues_decided: Whether the father, as karta, had the authority to alienate ancestral property without the consent of coparceners?
Whether the sale was made for legal necessity or benefit of the family?
Whether the purchasers made sufficient inquiry into the necessity and title before purchase?
Whether the suit was collusive and filed with ulterior motive?
holdings: A Hindu father as karta can alienate coparcenary property for legal necessity or benefit of the family, including the interests of minor sons.
The sale was valid as it was proven to be for family necessity, supported by recitals in the deed and surrounding circumstances.
The purchasers made reasonable inquiries and acted in good faith, which is sufficient under the law.
The suit was collusive, filed after undue delay, and intended to extract money, not to enforce a genuine legal claim.
provisions: Hindu Law (as per Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law, 16th Edition)
doctrines: Doctrine of family necessity in Hindu law
Doctrine of adverse possession
Good faith purchase for value
Collusive litigation

card.dispute: The Tamil Nadu Housing Board and the legal heirs of A. Viswam disputed over ownership and possession of 1.32 acres of land in Ashok Nagar, Chennai, where the heirs claimed title and sought perpetual injunction against the Board’s use of the land for a public park.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Officer effectively took possession of the disputed land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the respondent could maintain a suit for perpetual injunction over land already acquired for public purpose
Whether the Housing Board, as a transferee of acquired land, could be restrained by injunction despite non-mutation in revenue records
holdings: Taking of possession under the Land Acquisition Act does not require physical entry alone; a pragmatic approach includes symbolic or constructive possession through official acts like recording a Panchnama, especially when large tracts are involved.

Once land is acquired for public purpose and possession is lawfully taken, the original owner cannot maintain a suit for perpetual injunction, even if in factual possession later, as title vests absolutely in the acquiring authority.

Non-mutation of the acquirer’s name in revenue records does not affect vesting of title under the Land Acquisition Act, as Section 12(3) exempts registration, and public purpose projects need not await such formalities.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon acquisition and possession under the Land Acquisition Act
Constructive possession in land acquisition
Inadmissibility of injunction against the government or its agencies in respect of acquired public land
Irrelevance of revenue mutation where statutory vesting occurs

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu fought with Arooran Sugars Ltd over the acquisition of surplus agricultural land under land reform laws and the entitlement to compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 18(1) of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Act, 1961, was valid despite prior amendments affecting the acquisition process.
Whether Sections 4, 5, and 6 of the Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978 constitutionally validated the vesting of surplus land in the government.
Whether the High Court’s earlier directions for compensation determination became functus officio upon the enactment of validating legislation.
Whether the respondent was entitled to compensation at the rate of 2 times the net annual income under the amended law.
holdings: The notification issued on 4.4.1973 under Section 18(1) of the principal Act was validated retrospectively by Section 4 of Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978, making the vesting of surplus land effective from that date.
Sections 4, 5, and 6 of Tamil Nadu Act 25 of 1978 are constitutionally valid and override prior invalidating amendments, thereby confirming the government's vesting of the land.
The High Court’s 1978 direction to determine compensation was an execution order dependent on the earlier judgment, which was set aside; thus, it lost legal force.
The respondent is entitled to compensation at twice the net annual income as per the Tamil Nadu Act 39 of 1972, which reduced the multiplier from 9 to 2, effective 21.12.1972.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 18
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 50(3)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of Deemed Acquisition
Doctrine of Validation by Subsequent Legislation
Doctrine of Retrospective Operation of Laws
Principle of Compensation under Agrarian Reform Laws

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to uphold the restoration of alienated land based on an alleged oral agreement for reconveyance, which the appellate authority had previously rejected.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with a finding of fact on the existence of an oral agreement for reconveyance in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution
Whether the evidence adduced was sufficient to prove the existence of an oral agreement for reconveyance under Section 60 of the Indian Evidence Act
