card.dispute: The State of West Bengal and its authorities evicted tenants from the Great Eastern Hotel premises after acquisition, and the tenants challenged the legality of the forcible eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship of landlord and tenant continued after the acquisition of the hotel undertaking by the State Government under the Act of 1980
Whether the State Government could lawfully evict the tenants by force without following due legal process
Whether Section 6A of the West Bengal Premises Control Act, 1976 could be invoked against tenants who were not unauthorized occupants
Whether the acquisition was for public purpose justifying summary eviction
holdings: The landlord-tenant relationship continued post-acquisition, and the State Government stepped into the shoes of the original landlord.
The State cannot evict occupants by force without following due process of law, even under statutory powers; possession must be recovered through legal proceedings.
Section 6A of the West Bengal Premises Control Act, 1976 does not apply to lawful tenants, only to unauthorized occupants without written permission.
The acquisition of the hotel for better public facilities does not constitute a public purpose justifying extra-legal eviction, as it remains a commercial venture.
provisions: Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1980, Section 4(1), (2), (7), (8)
West Bengal Premises Control Act, 1976, Section 6A
doctrines: Rule of law
Due process of law
Statutory deeming provisions do not override tenancy rights unless explicitly stated
Principle of lawful possession and eviction only through legal authority

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for constructing a permanent structure without written consent, while the tenant claimed such consent had been given and recorded with the Municipal Corporation.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant obtained written consent from the landlord for erecting a permanent structure on the tenanted premises as required under Section 13(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947.
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the tenant’s belated application to summon records from the Municipal Corporation to prove such consent.
holdings: A tenant seeking to defend against eviction under Section 13(1)(b) must specifically plead and prove written consent from the landlord for any permanent construction; mere assertion of municipal sanction is insufficient.

The High Court did not err in refusing to summon municipal records at a belated stage when no such request was made during trial or appeal, especially when the pleadings lacked specific averments about written consent.
provisions: The Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(b)
doctrines: Burden of proof on tenant to establish written consent for permanent construction
Pleading specificity required for affirmative defenses in eviction proceedings
Judicial discretion against entertaining belated applications for production of evidence

card.dispute: The Special Land Acquisition Officer and the State of Karnataka fought with landowners, including Mohd. Hanif Sahib Bawa Sahib, over the compensation amount for land acquired for the Bagalkot new township and a link road.
issues_decided: Whether the reference court erred in calculating the market value of the land at Rs. 6.85 per sq. ft. for the 1985 acquisition?
Whether a deduction of 20% for development charges was justified on top of the base price already accounting for such charges?
Whether the market value fixed for land acquired in 1991 for a link road was reasonable?
holdings: The reference court made a mathematical error in valuing the land at Rs. 6.85 per sq. ft.; the correct value after 10% annual appreciation on Rs. 3 per sq. ft. over seven years is Rs. 5.10 per sq. ft.
No deduction for development charges is permissible where the base price is already derived from a prior determination that accounted for such charges.
The market value of Rs. 7 per sq. ft. for land acquired in 1991, based on appreciation from the corrected 1985 value, is reasonable and upheld.
doctrines: Principle of appreciation in land value due to development
Prohibition against double deduction in compensation calculation

card.dispute: The decree holder obtained an ex parte decree for specific performance of a sale agreement against the original owner, while the objectors (third-party purchasers) claimed prior title and possession of the same land; the dispute centered on whether the objectors could challenge the execution of the decree under Order 21 Rule 99 despite not being physically present on the vacant land.
issues_decided: Whether a third-party purchaser in possession of vacant land can file an application under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC upon dispossession during execution of a decree for specific performance?
Whether 'dispossession' under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC requires actual physical ouster or includes loss of legal control over the property?
Whether the executing court can adjudicate title disputes between decree-holder and third parties under Order 21 Rules 97 and 99 CPC?
holdings: A third-party purchaser claiming possession of vacant land can maintain an application under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC if they lose control over the property due to execution proceedings, even without physical presence.
The term 'dispossession' under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC includes loss of legal control over property, especially in cases involving vacant land, and is not limited to actual physical ouster.

The executing court has jurisdiction to adjudicate competing claims to title and possession between decree-holders and third parties under Order 21 Rules 97 and 99 CPC to prevent multiplicity of proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 97
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 99
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of execution provisions to prevent multiplicity of suits
Possession as control over property, especially in case of vacant land
Adjudication of title in execution proceedings under Order 21 Rules 97 and 99

card.dispute: The Ashok Paper Kamgar Union sought to initiate contempt proceedings against government and private officials for allegedly violating Supreme Court orders related to the revival of a sick paper mill.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed civil contempt by failing to implement the revival scheme for Ashok Paper Mills as per court orders?
Whether the exclusion of the petitioner union from the tripartite agreement amounted to disobedience of court directions?
Whether non-payment of consideration by NCFL and lack of power supply constituted wilful disobedience of court orders?
holdings: The respondents did not commit civil contempt as the failure to implement the scheme was due to multiple factors beyond their sole control and not due to wilful disobedience.
The exclusion of the petitioner union from the agreement was justified due to its non-cooperation, and the alternative agreement with the recognized union did not violate court orders.
Non-payment by NCFL and lack of power supply were not proven as deliberate acts of disobedience, and the material on record did not establish contempt.
doctrines: Wilful disobedience in civil contempt requires deliberate intent to defy court orders
Contempt cannot be founded if compliance depends on third-party actions or external circumstances
Non-compliance due to plausible administrative or operational difficulties does not automatically amount to contempt

card.dispute: The builders and the State of Karnataka challenged the constitutional validity of the Bangalore City Planning Area Zonal Regulations (Amendment & Validation) Act, 1996, which retrospectively allowed higher building heights, after the Karnataka High Court had struck it down for violating planning regulations.
issues_decided: Whether the Bangalore City Planning Area Zonal Regulations (Amendment & Validation) Act, 1996 is constitutionally valid despite retrospectively altering building height norms?
Whether the impugned Act amounts to an unconstitutional usurpation of judicial power by nullifying a court decision?
Whether the legislature can validate executive actions by retrospectively amending the legal basis for judicial invalidation?
holdings: A retrospective amendment that removes the legal basis of a judicial decision and validates prior executive action is constitutionally valid.
Legislation that alters the substantive law, rather than merely nullifying a court's judgment, does not violate the doctrine of separation of powers.
The validity of a statute depends on its legal effect, not the legislature's subjective intent, which is not subject to judicial review.
provisions: Karnataka Town & Country Planning Act, 1965, Section 13
Bangalore City Planning Area Zonal Regulations (Amendment & Validation) Act, 1996, Section 3(1), Section 3(3), Section 4
doctrines: Separation of powers
Retrospective validation of executive action
Doctrine of judicial review limited to legal basis, not legislative intent

card.dispute: Landlords, tenants, and sub-tenants challenged the validity and interpretation of property tax provisions under the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, arguing unfair burden and procedural defects.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned tax provisions of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 are constitutionally valid and properly interpreted?
Whether tenants, sub-tenants, and occupiers are entitled to notice and opportunity in tax assessment proceedings?
Whether the tax structure disproportionately and discriminatorily burdens tenants compared to landlords?
Whether tenants liable to pay a portion of property tax have a right to appeal and access information under the Act?
holdings: The provisions of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 imposing tax liability on tenants, sub-tenants, and occupiers are valid and do not violate constitutional principles.
Tenants, sub-tenants, and occupiers are entitled to written notices and opportunity to participate in assessment, revision, or amendment of consolidated tax rates.
The tax structure placing higher burden on commercial occupants is justified and does not create illegal discrimination between tenants under and above rent thresholds.
Tenants liable to pay a portion of tax have a right to appeal upon pre-deposit and to obtain relevant tax information under Section 178 of the Act.
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Doctrine of proportionality
Principles of natural justice
Fiction of law (tax treated as rent)

card.dispute: The appellants (Bondar Singh & Ors.) challenged the High Court's decree in favor of the respondents (Nihal Singh & Ors.) who claimed ownership of the suit land by adverse possession and sought injunction against interference.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession?
Whether the appellants had taken possession of the suit land in 1957–58, thereby breaking the continuity of the respondents' possession?
Whether the respondents were in possession as sub-tenants (shikmi) of the appellants' mother, negating a claim of adverse possession?
Whether the appointment of a receiver under Section 145 CrPC benefited the appellants' claim to possession?
holdings: The respondents acquired title by adverse possession as they were in continuous, open, and hostile possession of the land since 1931, with clear evidence supporting their claim.
The appellants' claim of taking possession in 1957–58 was false and unsupported, especially since they continued to seek possession before revenue authorities until 1962.
The plea of shikmi tenancy was not properly pleaded and lacked evidentiary support; non-examination of key witnesses like the mother and eldest brother weakened the appellants' case.
The receiver's possession under Section 145 CrPC did not benefit the appellants as the respondents were already recognized as bhoomiswami (owners) prior to the receiver's appointment.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Section 58
doctrines: Adverse possession
Plea must be specifically raised in pleadings
Hostile possession with assertion of title
Burden of proof in possession disputes

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and others fought with Joginder S. Monga and others over the recovery of unearned increase in land value and the rate of interest on disputed payments for Nazul land in Vasant Vihar.
issues_decided: Whether the DDA could lawfully demand Rs. 3,62,44,420 as unearned increase based on an assumed sale consideration of Rs. 7.5 crore?
Whether the respondents were entitled to benefit from the 1999 circular reducing the recovery of unearned increase?
What rate of interest should be applied to the disputed amount pending final determination?
holdings: The DDA cannot base its demand on a hypothetical sale consideration; the unearned increase must be calculated based on actual transaction value or official circulars.
The respondents cannot claim benefit of the 1999 circular as it was issued after their transaction and they had already complied with the High Court's interim order.
Interest pendente lite should be reduced from 18% to 9% to meet the ends of justice, but if payment is not made within six weeks, interest will revert to 18%.
provisions: Delhi Development Authority (Disposal of Developed Nazul Land) Rules, 1981
doctrines: Principle of restitution
Equitable jurisdiction to award interest
Doctrine of fair and reasonable action by state authorities
Prospective application of government policy circulars

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, who claimed protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act based on an unregistered agreement to purchase the property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, against eviction
Whether the appellant's continued possession as a tenant could be treated as part performance of a contract to purchase
Whether a dismissed suit for specific performance bars the plea of part performance under Section 53A
Whether the respondent, as a subsequent transferee, had notice of the prior agreement to sell
holdings: To claim protection under Section 53A, the transferee must have performed or be willing to perform their part of the contract; a judicial dismissal of a specific performance suit negates willingness.
Mere continuation of possession as a tenant does not amount to part performance unless there is a clear change in the nature of possession consistent with the contract.
A person whose suit for specific performance has been dismissed on merits cannot later claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.
A subsequent transferee for value without notice of a prior agreement is not bound by it and may enforce possession rights against a tenant claiming under an unregistered sale agreement.
provisions: Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, Section 21(1)(a) and (h)
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance under Section 53A
Change in character of possession
Equitable protection against subsequent transferees with notice
Bar of defence by adverse judicial finding

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Indian Council of World Affairs Ordinance, 2001, and the subsequent Act of 2001, which took over the management of the Indian Council of World Affairs, alleging violations of Articles 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(c), and 300A of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001, violates the doctrine of separation of powers by overriding a prior judicial decision.
Whether the Act is constitutionally valid under the legislative competence of Parliament as per Entries 62 and 63 of List I of the Seventh Schedule.
Whether the Act infringes fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(c), and 300A of the Constitution.
holdings: The Act does not violate the doctrine of separation of powers merely because it re-enacts provisions of a prior ordinance struck down by a High Court, especially since the earlier judgment was erroneous and not binding.

The Act is validly enacted under Entries 62 and 63 of List I of the Seventh Schedule as the institution was declared one of national importance, empowering Parliament to legislate on its administration.

The Act does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(a), 19(1)(c), or 300A, as the right to property is no longer a fundamental right and the restrictions imposed are reasonable and within legislative competence.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entries 62 and 63
doctrines: Separation of Powers
Legislative Competence
Liberal Interpretation of Constitutional Entries
Fundamental Rights and Reasonable Restrictions

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) challenged the High Court's decision that prevented it from charging 50% of the unearned increase in land value from Mrs. Vijaya C. Gurshaney, who claimed ownership of a plot through a will, despite not being a blood relative of the original allottee.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of Letters of Administration conclusively establishes title in favour of the legatee, preventing DDA from inquiring into the nature of the transaction?
Whether DDA can enforce its policy requiring payment of 50% of unearned increase in land value when property is transferred via will to a non-family member?
Whether the respondent was obligated to comply with the lease deed conditions regarding notice and consent for transfer of interest upon devolution of title by will?
holdings: The grant of Letters of Administration does not confer title to property or bar DDA from examining whether a will is a genuine testamentary instrument or a disguised sale.
DDA, as a statutory authority, can enforce its policy requiring 50% payment of unearned increase in land value when transferring property to non-family members via will.
The lessee’s successor must comply with lease conditions, including giving notice and obtaining consent; failure to do so allows DDA to invoke its rights under the lease agreement.
doctrines: Statutory authority powers
Notice and consent in lease agreements
Unearned increase in land value recovery
Limitations of probate and letters of administration

card.dispute: Ganga Retreat & Towers Ltd. challenged the State of Rajasthan's auction of a property with reduced FAR and non-ceiling-free status, claiming misrepresentation and breach of contract after proceeding with construction.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could avoid the contract on grounds of misrepresentation or fraud after continuing with construction despite knowledge of the true facts
Whether the State Government could be compelled to direct JDA to maintain FAR at 2.0 under Section 90 of the Jaipur Development Authority Act, 1982
Whether the State Government's power under Section 298 of the Rajasthan Municipalities Act, 1959 could be used to modify bye-laws for the benefit of the appellants
holdings: A party cannot avoid a concluded contract on grounds of misrepresentation if, with full knowledge of the facts, it affirms the contract by conduct such as executing the sale deed and constructing on the property.
Section 90 of the JDA Act does not empower the State Government to issue individualized directions to increase FAR for a specific plot; it applies only to general policy and guidelines.
Section 298 of the Rajasthan Municipalities Act grants supervisory power to the State to modify bye-laws in public interest, not to benefit individual parties in private transactions.
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Waiver by conduct
Voidable contract due to fraud
Doctrine of election

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff contested the validity of a settlement in a second appeal, claiming it was not properly recorded under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise in an appeal must strictly comply with Order 23 Rule 3 CPC to be valid
Whether counsel can enter into a binding compromise on behalf of parties without express written authorization
Whether the High Court's decision based on consensus between counsel amounts to a valid decree
holdings: A compromise in an appeal must generally be in writing and signed by the parties under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC to be enforceable.
Counsel with implied or express authority can enter into a valid compromise on behalf of clients, especially when immediate settlement is necessary and personal signing is impractical.
A judgment based on consensus or admission before the court, even if not formally recorded as a compromise, can be valid and binding if there is no impropriety or lack of authority.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 3 Rule 1
doctrines: Doctrine of implied authority of counsel
Doctrine of admission in judicial proceedings
Principle of finality of consent decrees

card.dispute: The Howrah Municipal Corporation challenged the High Court's direction to grant sanction for constructing three additional floors to Ganges Rope Co. Ltd.'s building, which conflicted with amended building rules restricting building height on G.T. Road.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could direct grant of building sanction despite amendment in building rules prohibiting multi-storeyed construction after the application was filed?
Whether a 'vested right' or 'settled expectation' arises in favour of an applicant who obtains court orders for timely decision on building sanction?
Whether the amended Howrah Municipal Corporation Building Rules apply to pending applications for construction sanction?
holdings: Amended building rules apply to pending applications; the law prevailing at the time of decision on sanction governs, not the law at the time of application.
No vested right arises from court orders merely directing consideration of an application within a time frame; such orders do not create an enforceable right to sanction.
Public interest in regulating building heights overrides any settled expectation of the applicant, especially when rule amendments are made by the State.
provisions: Howrah Municipal Corporation Building Rules, 1991, Rule 13
Howrah Municipal Corporation Building Rules, 1991, Rule 3
doctrines: No deemed sanction in absence of express statutory provision
Vested rights doctrine does not apply to administrative expectations
Primacy of public interest over private expectations in regulatory regimes

card.dispute: The appellants, who were personal guarantors for a sick industrial company's loans, challenged the creditor's recovery action against them, claiming protection under Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'suit' in Section 22(1) of SICA includes recovery proceedings against personal guarantors of a sick industrial company.
Whether the 1994 amendment to Section 22(1) of SICA extends protection to guarantors from enforcement of guarantees without the BIFR's consent.
Whether the word 'proceeding' in the first part of Section 22(1) covers executive recovery actions under the U.P. Financial Corporations Act.
holdings: The word 'suit' in Section 22(1) of SICA refers only to judicial proceedings in court and does not include executive recovery actions against guarantors.
The 1994 amendment to Section 22(1) does not bar recovery proceedings against personal guarantors, as its protection is limited to suits against the industrial company itself.
Proceedings under the U.P. Act for recovery of dues are 'proceedings' under Section 22(1) of SICA but do not amount to a 'suit' requiring BIFR's consent when directed against guarantors.
provisions: Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22(1)
U.P. Financial Corporations (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1981
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between 'suit' and 'proceeding'
Legislative intent and context-based interpretation

card.dispute: Kanpur Development Authority challenged the High Court's decision to prevent it from charging significantly escalated costs to allottees of Middle Income Group houses who had applied in 1978 but received no allotment for over 18 years.
issues_decided: Whether the Kanpur Development Authority could lawfully increase the cost of houses by nearly four and a half times the initially estimated cost after an 18-year delay for which the allottees were not responsible?
Whether the escalation in cost must be justified by the authority and kept within limits promised in the original brochure and application form?
Whether the delay in allotment and possession, caused by the authority, affects the enforceability of the original cost terms?
holdings: A development authority cannot arbitrarily escalate the cost of housing beyond the limits indicated in the original brochure, especially when applicants acted in reliance on those terms.
Where the delay in allotment and possession is attributable to the authority, the allottees cannot be burdened with excessive cost escalations or interest on unpaid installments.

An escalation of cost nearly four and a half times the initial estimate—despite a stated cap of 10%—is arbitrary and violates the principle of fair dealing with middle and lower-income group applicants.
The authority must provide material justification for any cost escalation and act reasonably, particularly when applicants have adjusted their finances based on the original terms.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973
Article 226 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel
Principle of Fair Dealing in Administrative Action
Reasonableness in Administrative Decisions (Article 14)
Relief against Arbitrary State Action

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a redeeming co-mortgagor and non-redeeming co-mortgagors disputed over partition of mortgaged property and the limitation period for the suit, which also sought redemption.
issues_decided: Whether the suit, primarily for partition, was governed by the limitation period for partition or for redemption.
Whether a redeeming co-mortgagor acquires the status of a mortgagee under Section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the order of remand by the High Court attained finality and barred re-litigation of the nature of the suit.
holdings: A suit primarily for partition, even if it includes a prayer for redemption on remand, is governed by Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and limitation starts when the right to partition is denied.

A co-mortgagor who redeems the mortgage is not converted into a mortgagee but is entitled to equitable rights of subrogation, including remedies akin to foreclosure or sale under Section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act.
An order of remand can be challenged in the Supreme Court under Article 136, as Section 105(2) of the CPC does not bar such review by a superior court exercising special leave jurisdiction.
doctrines: Doctrine of subrogation by operation of law
Equity of reimbursement
He who seeks equity must do equity
Limitation period based on the true nature of the suit

card.dispute: AWHO and Sumangal Services disputed over land title and damages arising from a turn-key housing project agreement, with AWHO challenging an arbitral award on legal grounds.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitral award regarding title to 14.17 acres of land suffers from legal infirmity under Sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the measure of damages awarded in Claim No. 2 is legally sustainable
holdings: The transfer of title in 14.17 acres of land to AWHO was valid under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, as sale deeds were executed and stamp duty paid, and no legal error was committed by the arbitrator.

The award on Claim No. 2 regarding damages was set aside as the arbitrator failed to apply correct legal principles in assessing damages, particularly in relation to cost of completion and mitigation.
doctrines: Unjust enrichment
Mitigation of damages
Cost of completion as measure of damages
Arbitral award review on question of law

card.dispute: DLF and associated parties challenged the State of Haryana's restriction on transferring community sites in a housing colony, arguing they had the right to lease such land despite executive instructions imposing a cutoff date.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(3)(a)(iv) of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975 restricts the right to transfer community sites after a specified date.
Whether clause (t) of the licence agreement impliedly restricts the colonizer's right to transfer community land.
Whether third-party lessees of community sites are protected if they acquired rights in good faith.
holdings: The court held that Section 3(3)(a)(iv) does not outrightly prohibit transfer of community sites; the State cannot impose arbitrary cutoff dates without statutory backing.
Clause (t) of the licence, which caps profits, does not impliedly restrict the colonizer’s right to transfer land; such a restriction cannot be read into the clause.
Bona fide third-party transferees for value are protected from executive instructions, especially in absence of fraud or illegality, and their rights cannot be jeopardized.
provisions: Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975, Section 3(3)(a)(iv)
Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975, Section 9
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation with exception for absurdity
Liberal interpretation to fulfill the object of the statute
Protection of bona fide third-party transferees

card.dispute: The appellants (private owners) fought the Advocate General and others over whether a Dharamsala used by the public for 125 years constituted a public trust under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether mere long-term public use of a Dharamsala creates a presumption of a public trust under Hindu law
Whether the facts established a complete dedication of the property to a public charitable purpose
Whether the Advocate General could maintain a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the absence of a public trust
holdings: Mere long-term public use of a property as a Dharamsala does not, by itself, prove dedication to a public trust under Hindu law.
A public trust requires clear evidence of complete dedication, including cessation of ownership and vesting in a religious or charitable object, which was absent here.
The Advocate General cannot maintain a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure unless a public trust is established, which was not done in this case.
doctrines: Doctrine of public trust under Hindu law
Doctrine of complete dedication for charitable purposes
Presumption of dedication based on user and conduct

card.dispute: Relatives of Dasu Charan Kul fought over the validity of a 1970 settlement deed, with Pratima Maity claiming it was forged and Krishna Mohan Kul asserting its legitimacy.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of settlement executed by Dasu Charan Kul was valid or void due to alleged fraud and lack of due execution.
Whether the burden of proof regarding the validity of the deed was correctly placed on the defendant who benefited from it.
Whether the concurrent findings of the lower courts could be interfered with under Section 100 CPC.
holdings: A deed executed by an old, illiterate, and physically and mentally infirm person raises a presumption of undue influence, requiring the beneficiary to prove the transaction was fair and freely executed.
The burden of proving due execution and fairness of a deed lies on the person in a position of active confidence or fiduciary relationship who benefits from the transaction.
High Court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact under Section 100 CPC if there is a misreading of evidence, misplacement of burden of proof, or legal infirmity affecting the case.
doctrines: Presumption of undue influence in fiduciary relationships
Burden of proof in transactions involving vulnerable parties
Equity principle requiring fairness in dealings with persons under disability

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, including a tenant and advocate, sought specific performance of an agreement to purchase property from the executor of a deceased owner's will, which was contested by the executor's legal heirs.
issues_decided: Whether a concluded contract arose from the sale agreement subject to ratification by co-heirs.
Whether the executor had the authority to independently enter into a binding sale agreement.
Whether the agreement of sale was enforceable under the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
holdings: An agreement 'subject to ratification' by non-parties is not a concluded contract until ratification occurs and is communicated.
The executor did not act solely in that capacity but also as a legatee, and the agreement was not binding without co-heir approval.
The agreement could not be specifically enforced due to lack of a concluded contract and the court declined to exercise discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act.
doctrines: Condition precedent in contract formation
Doctrine of ratification in agency law
Discretionary enforcement of specific performance

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Md. Mohammad Ali fought with Sri Jagadish Kalita and others over ownership and possession of suit premises, claiming title through purchase, while respondents claimed adverse possession and ouster.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents acquired title by adverse possession against the appellant or his predecessors in interest?
Whether mutation in revenue records by one co-sharer amounts to ouster of other co-sharers?
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the second appeal without framing substantial questions of law under Section 100 of the CPC?
Whether non-payment of rent and taxes alone can establish adverse possession?
holdings: Mere possession by one co-sharer, without a clear denial of the title of others, does not amount to ouster or adverse possession.
Mutation of property in the name of one co-sharer does not by itself constitute ouster; there must be a clear declaration denying the title of other co-sharers.
The High Court failed to frame substantial questions of law under Section 100 CPC, warranting remand for fresh consideration.
Non-payment of rent and taxes is insufficient alone to prove adverse possession; open, continuous, and hostile possession with hostile animus is required.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Ouster of co-sharer
Constructive possession of co-sharers
Res judicata in limited issues

card.dispute: The appellant, Narbada Devi Gupta, challenged the High Court's decision setting aside a trial court decree in her favor, which had ordered the respondent tenant to vacate the suit premises, claiming the tenant had wrongfully fabricated rent receipts to establish tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the rent receipts produced by the tenant were admissible and sufficient to prove tenancy despite lack of direct evidence of execution by the landlady.
Whether the trial court could infer fraud in the creation of rent receipts without a specific plea of fraud in the plaint.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on the credibility of documentary evidence.
holdings: When signatures on documents are admitted and the documents are marked as exhibits without objection, their contents are admissible in evidence, and no further proof of execution is required.
A finding of fraud cannot be based on surmise or presumption if the plea of fraud was not specifically pleaded in the plaint.
The High Court, as a first appellate court, has the authority to re-appreciate evidence and draw different conclusions from the trial court.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVIII Rule 16
doctrines: Plea of fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved
First appellate court's power to re-appreciate evidence
Admissibility of documents upon admission of signatures

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the safety, environmental compliance, and rehabilitation measures related to the Tehri Dam project, seeking judicial intervention to halt the project until these concerns were addressed.
issues_decided: Whether further safety tests are required before impounding the reservoir of the Tehri Dam.
Whether the conditions attached to the environmental clearance dated July 19, 1990 have been complied with.
Whether the resettlement and rehabilitation of project-affected persons has been completed as required.
holdings: The closure of diversion tunnels for reservoir impoundment must not proceed until 3-D non-linear and dam break analyses are completed and reviewed by an expert committee.
Environmental clearance conditions must be fulfilled pari passu with project implementation, and a committee must monitor compliance every three months.
Resettlement and rehabilitation must be fully completed before any impoundment of the reservoir; an independent grievance redressal cell must be established to address oustees' concerns.
provisions: Schedule III of the Notification dated 27th January, 1994 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
doctrines: Pari passu doctrine in environmental clearances
Precautionary principle
Sustainable development
Duty of the State to protect vulnerable sections under Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property, but the defendant had already sold the property to the appellant; the dispute centered on whether the plaintiff was entitled to equitable relief despite not pleading readiness and willingness to perform.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to specific performance of the agreement of sale without pleading readiness and willingness to perform under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the discretionary findings of the lower courts
Whether time was of the essence in the agreement of sale and whether the plaintiff performed within a reasonable time
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform; failure to do so disentitles the plaintiff to equitable relief.
An appellate court should not interfere with the discretionary judgment of lower courts unless it is shown that the discretion was exercised on a wrong legal principle or was arbitrary or capricious.

In contracts for sale of immovable property, time is not presumed to be of the essence, but performance must occur within a reasonable time determined by the terms, nature of property, and surrounding circumstances.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Reasonable time doctrine in contract performance
Appellate court restraint in reviewing discretionary orders

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of 73.3 hectares of dry land for a diamond park, alleging vagueness in public purpose, ecological and security concerns, and excessive land acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the public purpose mentioned in the acquisition notification was unconstitutionally vague
Whether the land acquisition caused ecological and security risks due to proximity to sensitive installations
Whether the extent of land acquired was excessive and beyond reasonable requirements
holdings: A public purpose description in a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is sufficient if it enables affected persons to file objections; mere vagueness without demonstrated prejudice does not invalidate the acquisition.
The establishment of a diamond cutting and polishing park does not pose significant ecological or security threats if no pollution is generated and concerned authorities have raised no objections.

The assessment of land requirement for industrial development primarily rests with the State Government; courts may suggest a fresh review but will not strike down acquisition based on bald allegations of excess.
doctrines: Doctrine of Prejudice in Administrative Action
Doctrine of Wednesbury Reasonableness (non-arbitrariness)
Balancing of Economic and Environmental Interests

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, seeking enhancement and higher solatium.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in denying enhanced compensation based on comparable land sales.
Whether the appellants are entitled to 30% solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, despite the Collector's award being prior to the amendment.
holdings: The High Court correctly refused to enhance compensation as the relied-upon sale of adjacent land was not proven to be comparable in nature and potentiality.
Appellants are entitled to 30% solatium under Section 23(2) as the reference proceeding was pending during the period of retrospective application of the 1984 amendment.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Retrospective application of amending statutes in pending proceedings
Mandatory nature of solatium under the Land Acquisition Act

card.dispute: The plaintiff's heirs claimed ownership of a property under a will bequeathing the entire estate to her, while the defendants, other daughters and grandchildren of the testator's wife, contested the will's validity and the extent of the property devolving under it.
issues_decided: Whether the registered will in favor of the plaintiff was genuine and free from suspicious circumstances
Whether the testatrix, Smt. Yamunabai, was the absolute owner of the entire property at the time of making the will
holdings: A will that disinherits natural heirs is not inherently suspicious; exclusion of daughters in favor of a widowed daughter who cared for the testatrix is natural and does not invalidate the will.
The testatrix Smt. Yamunabai acquired her share in the property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and thus only her 1/8th share passed via the will, not the entire property.
doctrines: Propounder of a will must dispel real and valid suspicious circumstances, not mere conjectures
A will can lawfully alter normal succession; unnatural disposition alone does not render it invalid

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a shop property and sought recovery of possession and arrears of rent, while the temple and its tenant disputed his title, claiming the property belonged to the temple.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant proved his title to the suit property sufficiently to succeed in a civil suit for possession?
Whether the High Court erred in interfering with concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts under Section 100 CPC?
Whether the tenant's attornment to the temple as landlord was valid under Section 116 of the Evidence Act?
holdings: In a civil suit for possession based on title, the plaintiff must prove a high degree of probability to shift the onus to the defendant; if the defendant fails to rebut it, the plaintiff's burden is discharged.
The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC unless a substantial question of law is involved; mere disagreement with factual findings is not sufficient.

A tenant inducted by the plaintiff cannot attorn to another person as landlord during the continuance of the original tenancy, especially when such act is induced by a party in a position of control, violating the rule of estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act.
doctrines: Preponderance of probability
Burden and onus of proof
Estoppel by tenant (Section 116)
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the acquittal of the Chief Minister and others in a criminal case alleging illegal purchase of public sector properties without proper approval and conflict of interest.
issues_decided: Whether the accused had dominion over the properties of TANSI such that the offence under Section 409 IPC could be attracted
Whether there was entrustment of property to the accused as required under Section 409 IPC
Whether the prosecution proved dishonest conversion or disposal of property for personal use
Whether the court should interfere with the High Court's order of acquittal in a proceeding under Article 136 of the Constitution
holdings: Section 409 IPC does not apply where a public servant has only supervisory control and no dominion over company property.
Entrustment under Section 409 IPC requires dominion over property, which was absent here as the Chief Minister did not own or control TANSI assets.
The prosecution failed to prove dishonest misappropriation or conversion of property for personal gain.
The Supreme Court will not re-appreciate evidence in appeals under Article 136 unless there is a manifest error, which was not found here.
doctrines: Doctrine of entrustment under Section 409 IPC
Principle of dominion in criminal breach of trust
Standard of proof in criminal cases requiring clear evidence of dishonest intent
Limited scope of review in special leave petitions under Article 136

card.dispute: The heirs of Rame Gowda and M. Varadappa Naidu disputed over possession of a piece of land, with the defendant's heirs challenging the plaintiff's possession and construction activities.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to injunction despite not proving title to the suit property
Whether the plaintiff's possession was settled and entitled to legal protection against the defendant, even if the defendant were the true owner
Whether a suit for injunction without claiming declaration of title is maintainable
holdings: A plaintiff can obtain an injunction by proving settled possession, even without establishing title, provided the possession is peaceful and undisturbed.
Settled possession, even by a trespasser, entitles the possessor to protection against forcible dispossession by the true owner, who must resort to due process of law.
A suit for injunction is maintainable without a claim for declaration of title, especially when the plaintiff is in lawful, undisturbed possession.
doctrines: Doctrine of settled possession
Possession as prima facie evidence of title
Injunction based on possession, not title

card.dispute: Renu Devi (donee) fought with Mahendra Singh and others (family members) over whether a gift of property made on 22.3.1979 was valid despite the partition decree being formally engrossed only on 24.5.1979.
issues_decided: Whether the gift of property made on 22.3.1979 was valid when the partition decree was not yet engrossed on stamp paper?
Whether the decree dated 13.2.1978 became effective only upon engrossment on 24.5.1979, or had binding effect from its original date?
Whether the doctrine of 'feeding the grant by estoppel' applies to validate a gift made before complete title was acquired?
holdings: A partition decree by metes and bounds becomes effective from its date of passing (13.2.1978), even if engrossed later; the delay in stamping does not invalidate prior acts.
The gift dated 22.3.1979 was valid as the donors had a pre-existing interest and later acquired full title, which related back to the original decree date.
The doctrine of feeding the grant by estoppel applies in India and ensures that subsequent acquisition of title benefits the earlier donee, especially when the transferor cannot deny their own title.
doctrines: Feeding the grant by estoppel
Estoppel by deed
Relation back of decree

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over the ownership and management rights of Shri Madan Mohan Mandir and its shops in Harda, with one side claiming it was a public trust and the other asserting private family ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution after a statutory appeal had already been decided on the same matter?
Whether the order passed by the First Additional District Judge under Section 26(2) of the M.P. Public Trusts Act, 1951, being a deemed decree, attained finality after the dismissal of the appeal?
holdings: The High Court committed a manifest error of law in entertaining the writ petition because the statutory remedy under the M.P. Public Trusts Act had already been invoked and exhausted, making the writ petition not maintainable.
When a statutory appeal lies to the High Court and has been decided, the same order cannot be challenged again through a writ petition, as it leads to conflicting decisions and undermines finality.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 26(2)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 27(3)
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 8
doctrines: Exhaustion of statutory remedies
Finality of judicial decisions
Conflict of decisions
Maintainability of writ petitions

card.dispute: Sharda Devi fought the State of Bihar over whether the land acquisition proceedings were valid, given the State's claim of pre-existing ownership of the land.
issues_decided: Whether the State can initiate land acquisition proceedings over land it already owns.
Whether a dispute regarding the State's pre-existing title to land can be adjudicated in proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain a reference under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act when the State claimed ownership.
holdings: The State cannot acquire land already vested in it; acquisition proceedings are invalid if the land is government-owned.
A dispute over the State's pre-existing ownership interest in land cannot be decided in proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act.
A reference under Section 30 is without jurisdiction if it involves a claim of prior government ownership, rendering the entire proceeding a nullity.
provisions: Bihar Public Land Encroachment Act, 1956, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of inherent jurisdiction
Doctrine of pre-existing government ownership
Doctrine of finality of Collector's award
Waiver of jurisdictional defects not permitted

card.dispute: The appellants (tenants) challenged the eviction order passed against them, arguing that the transferee-landlord could not claim arrears of rent accrued before the transfer of the property.
issues_decided: Whether a transferee of leased property can recover arrears of rent that accrued prior to the transfer in his favour?
Whether the failure to pay such arrears to the transferee-landlord constitutes a ground for eviction under rent control laws?
holdings: A transferee of leased property is not entitled to recover arrears of rent accrued before the transfer unless there is an express assignment of the right to such arrears.

If the right to recover arrears is assigned, the transferee can maintain eviction proceedings on the ground of default in payment of those arrears, provided the total arrears amount to more than six months' rent.
doctrines: Assignment of rights under lease
Successor landlord's liability and rights
Character of arrears of rent as distinct from actionable claim

card.dispute: The appellant (Roop Kumar) and respondent (Mohan Thedani) disputed whether their agreement was a licence or a lease, and whether the appellant could be held liable for commission and possession of the shop premises in New Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement dated 15.5.1975 between the parties was one of licence or lease
Whether oral evidence could be admitted to show that a written agreement was a sham and not intended to operate
Whether sub-tenancy could be created without the landlord's consent under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing damages from Rs.500 to Rs.1200 per month
holdings: An agreement granting possession without transfer of interest in the property, and where the owner retains control, creates a licence, not a lease.
Oral evidence is admissible to prove a document was a sham, but only if it is supported by credible conduct; here, consistent performance under the agreement negated the sham claim.
A tenant cannot create a sub-tenancy without the landlord’s consent under Section 16(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and such an agreement would be illegal.
The High Court rightly enhanced damages based on ground realities and rental increases, especially when the appellant had paid commissions reflecting higher value.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rules 30, 32, 33
doctrines: Best evidence rule
Sham document exception to the exclusion of oral evidence
Doctrine of privity in lease and licence
Illegality of agreements contrary to statutory prohibitions

card.dispute: The plaintiff (Smt. V. Rajeshwari) sued the defendant (T.C. Saravanabava) for declaration of title and possession of a property, which the defendant had been occupying, leading to disputes over res judicata and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plea of res judicata arising from a prior suit could bar the present suit
Whether the defendant had acquired title by adverse possession
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for possession and mesne profits
holdings: A plea of res judicata must be raised in pleadings and supported by proof of previous pleadings, issues, and judgment; it cannot be speculated upon or raised for the first time in higher courts without proper foundation.
The defendant failed to plead and prove a clear, continuous, and hostile possession necessary to establish adverse possession, especially since he previously claimed co-ownership.

The plaintiff is entitled to a decree for possession of the suit property (excluding the 240 sq ft already decreed in a prior suit) and to mesne profits from the date of suit till delivery of possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 12(1)(c)
doctrines: Res judicata
Adverse possession
Pleading and proof of legal pleas

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the arbitration award should be set aside due to alleged lack of reasonable notice and violation of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator provided reasonable notice to the parties
Whether the principles of natural justice were violated in the arbitration proceedings
Whether a party could resile from a prior withdrawal of objections to the arbitration award
holdings: An arbitrator must provide reasonable notice, the adequacy of which depends on the subject-matter and circumstances of the case.
A party alleging violation of natural justice must demonstrate actual prejudice and a real inability to present its case, not merely a technical breach.
A party that unequivocally withdraws objections to an arbitration award cannot later resile from that position without sufficient cause.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of prejudice in procedural fairness
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. and other coal companies challenged the State of Madhya Pradesh's recovery of enhanced coal royalty and the passing on of this cost to consumers, while the State appealed the rate of interest awarded on delayed payments.
issues_decided: Whether the enhanced royalty on coal under Section 9(3) of the Mines and Minerals Act is constitutional and validly recoverable by the State
Whether the principle of restitution applies to interim orders that are later reversed or set aside
Whether the High Court's reduction of interest from 24% to 12% per annum in restitution was justified
holdings: The enhancement of royalty under Section 9(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 is valid, and the State can recover it from lessees who may pass on the cost to consumers.
The doctrine of restitution applies to interim orders; when such orders are reversed, the court must restore parties to the position they would have been in had the interim order not been passed.
The High Court’s reduction of interest from 24% to 12% per annum was reasonable and in the interest of justice, considering commercial rates and the long pendency of litigation.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 9(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution
Inherent jurisdiction of court to do complete justice
Principle of placing parties in status quo ante

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision that declared respondents were not 'land grabbers' under the Andhra Pradesh Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, after the Special Court had ruled against them.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 by re-appreciating evidence and reversing the Special Court's finding that the respondents were land grabbers.
Whether the Special Court committed an error of law by overlooking vital documentary evidence of title and revenue records while declaring the respondents as land grabbers.
holdings: The High Court did not exceed its writ jurisdiction in reversing the Special Court’s decision, as it acted to correct a manifest error of law arising from the disregard of crucial evidence supporting the respondents’ title.

Where a tribunal ignores legally admissible and vital evidence, such as documents of title and unchallenged revenue entries, its decision suffers from an error of law justifying interference under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction over tribunals
Ouster of civil court jurisdiction by special statutes

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged the High Court's direction to pay interest on rental compensation for land acquired through private negotiations, arguing no statutory obligation existed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in directing payment of interest on rental compensation not mandated by the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether rental compensation, being a creation of executive policy, entitles landowners to interest for delayed payment
Whether principles from Sections 17(3-A), 23(1-A), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act can be analogously applied to rental compensation
holdings: The High Court erred in relying on statutory provisions like Sections 17(3-A), 23(1-A), and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act to grant interest on rental compensation, as such compensation is not statutory but based on executive policy.
Despite no statutory obligation, equity demands that delayed payment of rental compensation attract interest at 6% from 1 April 2000, where payment was not already made by that date.
The State must pay rental compensation expeditiously based on the Land Acquisition Officer’s valuation, subject to future adjustment if the final award differs.
doctrines: Equity, justice and good conscience
Doctrine of analogous application of statutory provisions
Principle of fair compensation for deprivation of property

card.dispute: Sukanya Holdings Pvt. Ltd. fought with Jayesh H. Pandya and others over whether disputes arising from the dissolution of a partnership should be referred to arbitration, despite third parties and non-arbitrable claims being involved in the suit.
issues_decided: Whether a court must refer a dispute to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, when the suit involves both matters covered by an arbitration agreement and matters or parties outside it.
Whether a court can partially refer a dispute to arbitration while retaining jurisdiction over other parts involving non-signatory parties or non-arbitrable issues.
Whether Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure mandates arbitration referral even when Section 8 of the Arbitration Act does not apply.
holdings: Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 requires the entire subject matter of the suit to fall within the arbitration agreement for referral; if some claims or parties are outside it, the court need not refer the matter to arbitration.

The Act does not permit bifurcation of a suit into arbitrable and non-arbitrable parts or between parties bound and not bound by an arbitration agreement, as such a procedure is not contemplated by the statutory framework.
Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not override Section 8 of the Arbitration Act and cannot be used to refer disputes to arbitration when the conditions under Section 8 are not met.
doctrines: Kompetenz-Kompetenz (implied in judicial non-intervention under Section 5)
Party autonomy in arbitration
Fusion of jurisdiction doctrine (rejected in favor of strict statutory interpretation)
Doctrine of severability (implicitly considered but not applied due to lack of statutory basis for bifurcation)

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer appealed against the High Court's enhancement of compensation from Rs. 10/sq. yard to Rs. 55/sq. yard for 11.33 acres of agricultural land acquired for housing sites, arguing the rate was excessive.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in relying on small plot sale deeds to determine the market value of large agricultural land acquired for development.
Whether the compensation awarded by the High Court at Rs. 55 per square yard was justified without proper deduction for development costs.
holdings: Sale transactions of small plots can be considered for determining market value only if they are comparable in time, location, and nature, and necessary deductions are made for development when land is to be used for housing sites.

A deduction of 53% from the sale price of a comparable small plot (Ex.B/4 at Rs. 82/sq. yard) is appropriate for development costs, resulting in a fair market value of Rs. 40 per square yard as of the notification date.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales for market value determination
Duty to avoid speculation in assessing potential land value
Rule of 53% deduction for development costs in urban land acquisition
Willing buyer-willing seller test for compensation

card.dispute: Teri Oat Estates (P) Ltd. challenged the U.T. Chandigarh's resumption of leased land for delayed payment of instalments, arguing that the penalty and forfeiture were disproportionate.
issues_decided: Whether the power of resumption under the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952 and Chandigarh Lease Hold Rules, 1973 was validly exercised?
Whether the imposition of penalty and forfeiture of lease was proportionate to the default?
Whether judicial review under Article 14 includes the doctrine of proportionality in administrative actions affecting fundamental rights?
holdings: The power of resumption under Section 8(1) of the Act can be exercised only when the lessee's default is willful or mala fide; mere delay does not justify forfeiture.
Administrative actions that affect fundamental rights must satisfy the doctrine of proportionality, balancing the restriction with the individual's rights.
The doctrine of proportionality is part of judicial review under Article 14 and applies to executive actions, especially where penalties disproportionately affect property rights.
provisions: Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952
Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Buildings Rules, 1973
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorized Occupants) Act, 1971
doctrines: Doctrine of Proportionality
Wednesbury Unreasonableness
Primary and Secondary Review
Judicial Review under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellants, who demolished a leased building and constructed anew, challenged a decree for eviction in favor of the respondent co-owner who claimed landlord-tenant rights.
issues_decided: Whether the demolition of a leased building by the tenant extinguishes the lease and tenancy rights?
Whether a co-owner can maintain a landlord-tenant eviction suit against another co-owner or their transferees?
Whether the doctrine of frustration applies to a lease when the leased building is demolished by the tenant?
holdings: Destruction of a leased building does not terminate the lease if the land remains, especially when the tenant causes the demolition; the lease continues as it includes both land and structure.
A co-owner in possession, with consent of other co-owners, can enforce landlord-tenant rights and maintain an eviction suit against unauthorized occupants or transferees of other co-owners.
The doctrine of frustration does not apply to leases destroyed by the tenant’s own act; it is inapplicable where privity of estate exists under a lease as defined under the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(b)(iii)
doctrines: Doctrine of frustration
Privity of estate in lease
Estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act
Co-ownership and exclusive possession

card.dispute: The appellants and the respondent disputed possession of an ancestral property in Calicut, with the respondent claiming under a will that the appellants alleged was forged.
issues_decided: Whether the District Court had jurisdiction to conclusively adjudicate the validity of a will in a summary proceeding under Sections 192–195 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to interfere with the District Court's order under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
holdings: A summary proceeding under Sections 192–195 of the Indian Succession Act is not the appropriate forum for a detailed or conclusive determination of the validity of a will; such a proceeding is limited to deciding possession, not title.
The High Court erred in treating its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC as discretionary and failed to correct a legal error amounting to a miscarriage of justice.
doctrines: Summary proceedings do not determine title
Judicial discretion must be exercised according to law and not arbitrarily
Principle of finality of possession in succession proceedings

card.dispute: The Welfare Association of Allottees of Requisitioned Premises, Maharashtra, challenged the eviction of occupants from requisitioned premises after the Bombay High Court struck down the 1996 Amendment Act that sought to protect them, leading to a constitutional challenge over the validity of the Amendment Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control, Bombay Land Requisition and Bombay Government Premises (Eviction) (Amendment) Act, 1996 is constitutionally valid?
Whether the Amendment Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating arbitrary classification?
Whether the State Legislature had the competence to enact the impugned Amendment Act?
holdings: The Amendment Act is constitutionally valid as it was enacted to protect a well-defined class of occupants facing eviction due to prior judicial invalidation of continued requisitioning.
The classification made by the Amendment Act satisfies Article 14 as it is based on an intelligible differentia with rational nexus to the object of protecting vulnerable occupants from homelessness.
The State Legislature had the competence to enact the Amendment Act to address local housing emergencies and protect public interest in urban areas like Bombay.
provisions: The Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 (Act No. XXXIII of 1948)
The Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control, Bombay Land Requisition and Bombay Government Premises (Eviction) (Amendment) Act, 1996 (Act No. XVI of 1997)
doctrines: Permissible classification under Article 14
Reasonable restrictions on property rights in public interest
Judicial review of legislative competence and arbitrariness
Reading down statutes to preserve constitutionality

card.dispute: Videocon Properties Ltd sued Dr. Bhalchandra Laboratories and partners for refund of Rs. 38 lakhs paid as earnest money, claiming it was part of the purchase price and entitled to interest and statutory charge under the Transfer of Property Act after the sale failed due to the sellers' default.
issues_decided: Whether the sum of Rs. 38 lakhs paid as 'deposit or earnest money' constitutes part of the purchase price or mere security for performance
Whether the buyer is entitled to interest on the amount under Clause 2.3 of the agreement and statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) survives and can be enforced against the property even in the hands of third parties
holdings: The Rs. 38 lakhs, though termed as deposit or earnest money, was intended by the parties to be part of the purchase price based on the payment structure and contractual terms, and not merely security.

The buyer is entitled to refund of the amount with interest at 21% per annum as per Clause 2.3, and the statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act applies to the amount and interest.

The statutory charge under Section 55(6)(b) attaches to the seller's interest in the property and is enforceable against third parties, surviving until conveyance and possession are delivered, unless the buyer defaults.
doctrines: Statutory charge in favour of buyer under Section 55(6)(b)
Principle of justice, equity and good conscience
Character of earnest money determined by intention of parties and surrounding circumstances

card.dispute: The appellant (Anumati) and her husband jointly held a fixed deposit with an 'either or survivor' clause; the bank pledged the deposit and adjusted it against the husband's debt without the appellant's consent, leading to a dispute over the bank's right to do so.
issues_decided: Whether a joint fixed deposit with an 'either or survivor' clause can be unilaterally pledged by one account holder without the other's consent.
Whether the bank can adjust the amount of a joint fixed deposit against a debt owed by one of the account holders without the other's knowledge or authority.
Whether the bank's action in refusing to pay the appellant her share of the matured fixed deposit was legally justified.
holdings: A joint fixed deposit with an 'either or survivor' clause cannot be unilaterally pledged by one account holder without the consent of the other, as the tripartite contract between the bank and both holders requires joint authority for such a transaction.
The bank cannot set off or adjust a joint fixed deposit against the individual debt of one account holder without the consent of the other, as the debt belongs jointly and not solely to the debtor.
The bank's refusal to pay the appellant her share of the matured fixed deposit was contrary to banking norms and illegal, entitling her to relief under consumer protection law.
doctrines: General lien of banks
Tripartite contract in joint accounts
Set-off of debts in banking law
Principle of joint and several liability

card.dispute: The landlord sued for mandatory injunction to recover possession of a shop from the licensee, but the licensee claimed to be a tenant with protection under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship between the parties was that of landlord and tenant or mere licensor and licensee?
Whether the document styled as a licence deed created a tenancy despite its form?
Whether the appellant was entitled to continue in possession despite the expiry of the licence?
holdings: The real intention of the parties and the substance of the agreement, not the label of 'licence', determine the nature of the relationship.
Exclusive possession, long-term occupation, and conduct of the parties indicate a tenancy, not a mere licence.
Despite the deed being called a licence and its expiry, the continued possession and use as a shop established a tenancy protected by law.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of exclusive possession
Doctrine of intention of parties in creating tenancy

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Endowments and others challenged the High Court's order upholding the hereditary Mutawalli's (Vittal Rao's) rights over a temple, after prior litigation had determined the nature of the temple land's ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the findings in earlier litigation regarding the nature of the gift deed could operate as res judicata despite no formal issue being framed on that point
Whether the doctrine of res judicata applies to a finding that was necessary and essential for the decision in a prior proceeding, even if not formally framed as an issue
Whether the appeal before the High Court was maintainable given that the earlier order was based on consent
holdings: A finding in prior litigation operates as res judicata if it was necessary and essential to the decision, even if no formal issue was framed on it.
The doctrine of res judicata applies to questions directly and substantially in issue, determined by the court as material to the judgment, regardless of technical framing.
An appeal against a consent order is not maintainable when the parties have acquiesced in the earlier decision.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Areas) Wakf Rules, Rule 156
doctrines: res judicata
constructive res judicata
necessity of issue determination for res judicata
consent decree and maintainability of appeal

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Balai Chand Ghosh fought over the partition of property, challenging the validity of a sale by Arindam (a legatee and executor under a will) to Crystal Developers and subsequent purchasers.
issues_decided: Whether the sale by Arindam to Crystal Developers was collusive or invalid due to lack of probate at the time of sale
Whether the probate was obtained fraudulently by not serving all legal heirs
Whether Crystal Developers and subsequent purchasers were bona fide purchasers for value under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the courts below erred in dismissing the defence of good faith purchase based on assumptions without evidence of fraud or collusion
holdings: An executor can validly alienate property under a will even before obtaining probate, and the subsequent grant of probate validates the transaction.
The absence of service on some heirs during probate proceedings does not render the probate fraudulent where there is no evidence of intentional suppression or collusion.

A transferee can claim protection under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act if the true owners' conduct allowed the ostensible owner to appear as the rightful owner, and the transferee acted in good faith after reasonable inquiry.
Concurrent findings of lower courts based on inference without direct evidence of fraud or collusion can be overturned by the Supreme Court when such inferences are unsupported by material evidence.
doctrines: Doctrine of ostensible ownership
Protection of bona fide purchasers for value without notice
Principle against interference with concurrent findings unless based on no evidence or perverse inference

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether the second will of Prati, in favor of his daughter Sodha, was validly executed or forged, and which will—dated 1977 or 1983—should govern succession to his property.
issues_decided: Whether the second will dated 08.05.1983 in favor of Respondent No. 1 was validly executed and free from suspicious circumstances?
Whether the appellants discharged the burden of proving that the second will was forged or executed under undue influence?
Whether the earlier will dated 11.01.1977 was validly revoked by the subsequent will?
holdings: A will must be proved by primary evidence, and if attested, must comply with Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the propounder must prove the testator’s sound mind, free will, and proper attestation.
Suspicious circumstances require the propounder to remove them, but mere thumb impression instead of signature does not invalidate a will if supported by credible witness testimony.
The second will validly revoked the first will, and the appellants failed to prove forgery or undue influence, thus the later will governs the succession.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder in case of suspicious circumstances
Revocation of prior will by subsequent will
Presumption of validity of will if attested and supported by credible evidence

card.dispute: Shareholders of Dale and Carrington Investment Pvt. Ltd. fought over control of the company, specifically challenging the validity of share allotments made by one shareholder to himself.
issues_decided: Whether the allotment of additional shares to Ramanujam was an act of oppression under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act
Whether Prathapan and his family had locus standi to file a petition under Sections 397 and 398 despite alleged FERA violations
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 10F of the Companies Act by re-evaluating findings of fact
What relief is appropriate in cases of oppressive share allotments
holdings: Allotment of additional shares to a shareholder without offering them to others constitutes oppression if done to retain control and defeats minority rights.
Locus standi under Sections 397 and 398 depends on shareholder status at the time of filing; subsequent or prior FERA violations do not bar the petition if shares are validly held and registered.
A High Court may set aside perverse or unsupported findings of fact in an appeal under Section 10F, as perversity raises a question of law.
Relief must undo the wrong; allowing an oppressor to buy out the oppressed at an unfair price rewards misconduct and is improper.
doctrines: Oppression and mismanagement under company law
Locus standi based on status at time of filing
Perversity of findings as a question of law
Ex-post-facto validation of foreign investment compliance

card.dispute: The dispute was between a son (K. Balakrishnan) and his sister (K. Kamalam) over whether a 1945 gift of property from their mother to both of them, when the son was a minor, was validly accepted and thus irrevocable.
issues_decided: Whether a minor can be deemed to have legally accepted a gift of property made by a parent without express acceptance.
Whether the gift-deed executed in 1945 was irrevocable under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, despite lack of formal possession or mutation.
holdings: A gift made by a parent to a minor child is presumed to be accepted, either by the minor or by the parent as guardian, and no express acceptance is required.

A gift of immovable property is complete and irrevocable under Section 126 of the Transfer of Property Act if accepted, even if possession is retained by the donor and the donee does not take active steps to assert ownership.
doctrines: Presumption of acceptance in gifts from parent to child
Implied acceptance of gift by silence or non-repudiation
Irrevocability of completed gifts under Section 126

card.dispute: Escorts Farms Ltd. and transferees challenged the imposition of ceiling on land holdings, arguing that transfers of land were valid, while the State contended the transfers were invalid and aimed at defeating the Ceiling Act.
issues_decided: Whether the land held under a government grant was transferable without permission of the State
Whether the transfers of land after the cut-off date under the Ceiling Act were valid or liable to be ignored
Whether the High Court was justified in imposing heavy costs of ten lakh rupees as damages for unauthorized occupation
Whether the transferees were entitled to a separate hearing before the Appellate Authority
