The Central Government shall examine, in consultation with the National Board for Wildlife, whether sandalwood should be included in Schedule VI within six months.

The Central Government must formulate a conservation policy for sandalwood, including financial reserves, scientific research, and regulations under the Environment Protection Act, 1986, to control illegal trade and mislabeling.
doctrines: Doctrine of Ecocentricism
Doctrine of Incorporation of International Treaties
Principle of Sustainable Use of Biological Diversity
Precautionary Principle

card.dispute: The appellants, owners of land in Thane district, fought for compensation after the state took their land in 1964 without following legal acquisition procedures, and later challenged the high court's dismissal of their claim due to delay and lack of records.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the appellants' claim for compensation on grounds of delay and laches despite persistent efforts by the appellants to pursue their claim.

Whether the state's acquisition of land without following due process under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and without compensation, violated the appellants' fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution.
Whether the appellants are entitled to compensation and fresh acquisition proceedings despite the lapse of several decades.
holdings: The High Court erred in dismissing the claim on grounds of delay, as the appellants had persistently pursued their rights and the state itself had initiated acquisition proceedings in 1981, which lapsed due to its own inaction.

Depriving landowners of their property without legal procedure and compensation violates Article 21, and a welfare state must ensure both compensation and rehabilitation to prevent uprooting and destitution.

The state must initiate fresh acquisition proceedings under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, with compensation based on current market value, and the appellants retain the right to seek enhancement through statutory remedies.
doctrines: Doctrine of Substantial Justice over Technical Laches
Right to Fair Compensation and Rehabilitation
Equality in Treatment of Similarly Situated Persons in Land Acquisition
Welfare State Obligation under Article 21

card.dispute: Vidur Impex & Traders and other companies fought with Tosh Apartments over whether they could be impleaded in a suit for specific performance and whether a receiver appointed by the Delhi High Court should be allowed to retain possession of the property despite a rival receiver appointed by the Calcutta High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants (Vidur Impex & Traders and others) were entitled to be impleaded as parties in the suit for specific performance pending before the Delhi High Court.
Whether the Delhi High Court was justified in appointing its own receiver and directing possession of the suit property, despite a prior receiver appointed by the Calcutta High Court.
holdings: The appellants were not entitled to be impleaded in the suit because they acquired no valid interest in the property due to clandestine transactions in violation of an injunction order, and their application for impleadment was inexcusably delayed.

The Delhi High Court was justified in appointing a receiver as it had prior jurisdiction over the suit; the Calcutta High Court’s appointment was based on suppression of material facts, and comity of courts does not protect such tainted orders.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10, Order 40
doctrines: Doctrine of comity of courts
Principle of prior jurisdiction
Bona fide purchaser doctrine
Contempt of court for suppression of facts

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land allegedly already acquired by the state, fought to claim ownership and seek reconveyance of the land after construction on it, while the state contested the validity of the sale and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants acquired valid title to the land despite prior acquisition proceedings and vesting of the land in the state
Whether the sale deeds executed in 2004–2005 in favor of the appellants were valid despite the land having vested in the state in 1983 and 1986
Whether the appellants were entitled to equitable relief despite using forged documents and misleading the court
Whether the state was obligated to reconvey the land to the original tenure holders or their transferees
holdings: Land acquisition under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, followed by award and payment of compensation, results in vesting of title in the state free from encumbrances, rendering subsequent transfers void.
Sale deeds executed after vesting of land in the state are unenforceable, as the original vendors had no title to transfer, and subsequent purchasers cannot acquire better title.
A party approaching the court must do so with clean hands; use of forged documents and false affidavits disentitles a party from equitable relief.
Reconveyance of vested land is a discretionary executive act, but once land has vested in the state, it cannot be divested unless lawfully de-recognized or returned through proper procedure.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Amendment to the Land Acquisition Act, Section 16-A
doctrines: Doctrine of clean hands
Vesting of title upon acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act
Nullity of transactions violating statutory prohibitions
Non-justiciability of executive discretion in reconveyance unless arbitrary

card.dispute: An NRI appellant challenged the High Court's quashing of criminal proceedings against respondents for allegedly cheating him in a property deal in Greater Noida.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the criminal proceedings under Sections 406 and 420 IPC based on the FIR and protest petition?
Whether the allegations in the FIR, if taken as true, disclose cognizable offences despite the civil nature of the dispute?
Whether the High Court erred in relying on defence documents while exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the criminal proceedings as the FIR and protest petition, if taken as true, disclose a prima facie case of cheating and criminal breach of trust.
Allegations showing inducement to part with money with guilty intention cannot be dismissed merely because the dispute has a civil aspect; criminal proceedings may proceed.
The High Court should not rely on defence documents or conduct a detailed analysis of evidence when considering quashing under Section 482 CrPC; it must primarily examine the FIR on its face.
doctrines: Prima facie case doctrine in criminal proceedings
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Separate civil and criminal jurisdictions doctrine
Mens rea and actus reus in cheating offences
Judicial restraint in quashing criminal proceedings

card.dispute: The Board of Trustees of Port of Kandla terminated a lease for non-payment of rent, and the lessee and her transferee challenged the termination by filing a suit in 1996, which the lower courts upheld, leading to an appeal by the Port Trust.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed in 1996 was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether a party can ignore an order of lease termination and continue to claim possession without challenging the order in court
Whether the termination of lease by the Port Trust was legally effective despite being allegedly invalid
holdings: The suit filed in 1996 was barred by limitation as the cause of action arose in 1978, and the three-year period under Article 58 of the Limitation Act had long expired.
An order of termination, even if allegedly invalid, cannot be unilaterally ignored; the aggrieved party must approach a court within the prescribed limitation period to have it declared invalid.
A termination order produces legal consequences and remains effective until set aside by a competent court, regardless of its alleged invalidity.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II, Rule 2
doctrines: An order remains effective until judicially set aside
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of limitation for declaratory suits

card.dispute: The General Manager of SNP Ventures Pvt. Ltd. challenged the Madras High Court's decision to quash an FIR alleging forgery and fraud by legal advisers of GWL in connection with a property dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR under Section 482 Cr.P.C. at the investigation stage
Whether the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. applies to the alleged forgery of documents prior to their production in court
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR at the investigation stage as the complaint disclosed cognizable offences under Sections 468 and 471 IPC, and the merits of the case should be determined after investigation.
Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. does not apply where forgery of a document occurred before it was produced in court; thus, prior sanction is not required for prosecution.
doctrines: Principle against premature quashing of criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
Doctrine of custodia legis in relation to Section 195 Cr.P.C.
Standard for quashing FIRs laid down in Bhajan Lal's case

card.dispute: Chandran Ratnaswami and K.C. Palanisamy fought over whether criminal proceedings arising from a breach of a Joint Venture Agreement, already settled by the Company Law Board and High Court, should be quashed as an abuse of process.
issues_decided: Whether criminal proceedings based on a civil dispute already finally adjudicated can continue?
Whether the repeated initiation of criminal cases on the same matter constitutes abuse of legal process?
Whether the police have unlimited power to direct reinvestigation in a closed criminal case?
holdings: Criminal proceedings arising from a civil dispute that has been finally decided by a competent forum cannot continue and must be quashed to prevent abuse of process.
Repeated filing of criminal complaints on a matter already dismissed by a magistrate amounts to misuse of legal process and harassment.
Police investigation powers are not unlimited and must be exercised within the framework of the CrPC, without infringing personal liberty.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Finality of judicial decisions
Separation of civil and criminal liability

card.dispute: The bank challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the auction sale of mortgaged property under SARFAESI Act, arguing the borrower should have first exhausted statutory remedies.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in entertaining a writ petition under Article 226 without the borrower first exhausting the alternative remedy under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act?
Whether the sale of the secured property under the SARFAESI Act violated the borrower's rights due to non-compliance with Rule 9 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002?
Whether the borrower was entitled to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court despite prolonged delay and conduct indicating acquiescence?
holdings: Where a statute provides an efficacious and adequate remedy, the High Court should not entertain a writ petition under Article 226 unless exceptional circumstances exist.
Non-compliance with Rule 9 of the 2002 Rules does not automatically invalidate a sale if the borrower has acquiesced and no prejudice is demonstrated.
The borrower’s delay of over four years in challenging the sale, along with conduct such as consenting to the sale, disentitles him from equitable relief under Article 226.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedy
Doctrine of acquiescence
Self-imposed judicial restraint in exercise of writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants) and respondent No.1 (plaintiff) fought over whether the plaintiff was entitled to specific performance of an agreement to sell property after allegedly failing to pay the balance sale consideration and the agreement having been terminated.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract under the Agreement of Sale.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's findings on the plaintiff's readiness and willingness and the termination of the agreement.
Whether the plaintiff could seek specific performance after the agreement was terminated and without seeking a declaration that the termination was invalid.
Whether the fifth defendant was a bona fide purchaser of the suit property.
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove readiness and willingness to perform his obligations throughout; failure to pay the balance consideration and secure required permissions within the stipulated time bars relief.

The High Court erred in reversing the trial court's factual findings on readiness and willingness, which were based on pleadings and evidence, and such findings cannot be overturned without valid legal basis.
Where an agreement of sale is validly terminated and the plaintiff does not seek a declaration that the termination is invalid, the suit for specific performance is not maintainable.

The fifth defendant is a bona fide purchaser as the earlier agreement with the plaintiff had been validly terminated, and thus no subsisting right in the plaintiff existed to defeat the subsequent sale.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform under a contract
Finality of findings of fact by trial court
Maintainability of suit for specific performance after termination of contract
Bona fide purchase under subsequent sale

card.dispute: The Gurudwara Sahib claimed ownership of disputed land through adverse possession against the Gram Panchayat, which claimed ownership and had auctioned part of the land.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was in adverse possession of the suit land since 13.4.1952?
Whether a declaration of ownership based on adverse possession can be granted in a plaintiff's suit?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree of permanent injunction?
Whether the suit was maintainable in its present form?
holdings: The plaintiff was in adverse possession of the suit property since 13.4.1952, as established by documentary evidence.
A declaration of title based on adverse possession cannot be granted to a plaintiff; the plea is available only as a defence, not as a basis for a claim.
The plaintiff is entitled to permanent injunction based on long, uninterrupted possession, which cannot be disturbed except by due process of law.
The suit was maintainable in its present form as no evidence was shown to prove otherwise.
doctrines: Adverse possession as a shield, not a sword
Res judicata
Injunction based on factual possession

card.dispute: The auction purchaser (appellant) challenged the maintainability of a civil suit filed by respondents seeking declaration of title and injunction against the auction of land under the Securitisation Act, claiming exclusive jurisdiction lay with the Debts Recovery Tribunal.
issues_decided: Whether a civil suit is maintainable by co-owners challenging the auction of secured property under the Securitisation Act when no rights were crystallized prior to creation of security interest?
Whether the jurisdiction of civil courts is barred in matters where the Debts Recovery Tribunal is empowered to decide under the Securitisation Act?
Whether aggrieved persons other than the borrower can invoke the remedy under Section 17 of the Securitisation Act?
holdings: Civil court jurisdiction is completely barred in matters concerning measures taken under Section 13(4) of the Securitisation Act, as such matters fall exclusively within the purview of the Debts Recovery Tribunal.
The expression 'any person' under Section 17 includes those who claim an interest in the secured asset and can challenge actions taken under Section 13(4) before the Debts Recovery Tribunal.
Section 34 of the Securitisation Act ousts civil court jurisdiction even for actions 'to be taken' under the Act, not just those already taken, ensuring exclusive adjudicatory role for the Tribunal.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 34
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 35
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
doctrines: Doctrine of ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Doctrine of exclusive statutory adjudicatory mechanism
Doctrine of effective remedy under special statutes

card.dispute: The appellant woman sought protection and maintenance from the respondent man after their long-term live-in relationship ended, but the respondent argued the relationship was adulterous and not in the nature of marriage.
issues_decided: Whether a live-in relationship amounts to a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' under Section 2(f) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
Whether failure to maintain a woman after ending a live-in relationship constitutes 'domestic violence' under Section 3 of the DV Act
Whether the appellant's relationship with a married man qualifies for legal protection under the DV Act
holdings: A live-in relationship qualifies as 'in the nature of marriage' only if it has essential characteristics of marriage, such as mutual companionship, social recognition, and intention to present as a married couple.
Mere cohabitation without marital characteristics does not entitle a woman to protection or maintenance under the DV Act.
A relationship knowingly entered into with a married person, opposed by the legal family, and lacking marital trappings is not a 'domestic relationship' under the DV Act.
provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 2(f)
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 3
doctrines: Relationship in the nature of marriage
Domestic violence under DV Act
Alienation of affection as an intentional tort

card.dispute: The original plaintiffs (intending flat purchasers) sued for specific performance of an agreement to buy flats from a developer, but subsequent buyers challenged their rights, claiming they were bona fide purchasers.
issues_decided: Whether the letter of intent between the plaintiffs and the developer created an enforceable right to specific performance
Whether the absence of registration of the agreement affected the plaintiffs' rights under the law
Whether the subsequent buyers were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of prior claims
Whether the plaintiffs' failure to pay installments entitled the developer to cancel the allotment
holdings: A letter of intent subject to conditions does not create an enforceable right to specific performance unless all conditions, including full payment, are fulfilled.
Under Section 4(1) of the Maharashtra Ownership Flats Act, 1963, an unregistered agreement does not confer any legal right on the purchaser and cannot bind subsequent buyers.
In the absence of a pleaded allegation that subsequent buyers were not bona fide, and without a registered document to impute notice, they are deemed bona fide purchasers for value.
The plaintiffs’ failure to pay revised installments as demanded by the developer amounted to breach, allowing the developer to cancel the allotment.
provisions: Maharashtra Ownership Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963, Section 4(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice through registration
Doctrine of pleadings and proof in civil litigation
Doctrine of specific performance requiring a valid, enforceable contract
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, siblings, disputed the validity of an agreement to exchange properties settled by their father, with the appellant claiming a mutual rectification and the respondent alleging undue influence.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered Agreement Deed (Ex.A-3) dated 1.6.1982 for exchange/rectification of settled properties was valid and enforceable
Whether the appellant discharged the burden of proving the voluntary execution of the agreement
Whether the agreement was vitiated by undue influence or was unconscionable
Whether the parties could rectify the settlement deeds between themselves under Section 26 of the Specific Relief Act
holdings: An agreement to rectify a settlement deed must be initiated by the settlor; the parties cannot unilaterally rectify the deed after registration.
The appellant failed to prove the execution and contents of the unregistered agreement by not examining attesting witnesses or the scribe, leading to its rejection.
The agreement was unconscionable and suspicious due to the disparity in property value and the respondent's dependent position, supporting a finding of undue influence.
A document drafted by an expert, lacking details of scribe or preparation, and executed under familial pressure, cannot be enforced without strict proof of free consent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVIII Rule 16
doctrines: Doctrine of Undue Influence
Burden of Proof in Cases of Alleged Undue Influence
Rectification of Instruments under Statute
Unconscionable Contract

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the compulsory acquisition of their land in Rajasthan, arguing that the acquisition process was time-barred and the state's invocation of urgency provisions was unjustified.
issues_decided: Whether the preliminary notification under Section 4 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 lapsed due to delay in issuing the declaration under Section 6 beyond the time limit set by the 1981 Amendment Act.
Whether the invocation of urgency and dispensation of inquiry under Section 5-A after seven years was legally sustainable.
holdings: The preliminary notification under Section 4 issued before the 1981 Amendment Act lapsed because the declaration under Section 6 was made after the mandatory two-year period from the commencement of the 1981 Amendment Act, as required by Section 5(2) of that Act.

The invocation of urgency under Section 17(1) and (4) of the 1953 Act to dispense with inquiry under Section 5-A after seven years is not legally sustainable, especially for a project like a bus stand that can tolerate delay.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 17(1) and (4)
Rajasthan Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1981, Section 5(1)(b) and Section 5(2)
doctrines: Mandatory time limits in acquisition laws must be strictly followed.
Power to dispense with inquiry under urgency provisions is exceptional and must be justified by immediate need.

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed the validity and due execution of a will dated 24.10.1943 made by Smt. Nagammanni, and whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of lower courts in a second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the will of Smt. Nagammanni was validly executed and duly proved under the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of the Trial and First Appellate Courts in the second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
holdings: A will must be proved in accordance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, but courts must act as a 'Court of Conscience' and consider the totality of circumstances to determine if the will reflects the true intention of the testator, even if there are technical deficiencies.
The High Court can interfere in a second appeal if the concurrent findings of lower courts are perverse, against the weight of evidence, or based on an erroneous appreciation of law or facts.
doctrines: Court of Conscience doctrine in will disputes
Perversity in findings as ground for interference in second appeal

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of a landowner and the State of Karnataka over whether the petitioners, who purchased land after acquisition proceedings had begun, could challenge the revival of those proceedings after the de-notification was quashed.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners who purchased land during the pendency of litigation challenging de-notification are bound by the final order reviving acquisition proceedings?
Whether a purchaser of land after a Section 4 notification under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can challenge the acquisition?
Whether de-notification of land from acquisition is permissible after possession has been taken by the State?
holdings: A person who purchases immovable property during the pendency of litigation involving acquisition proceedings is bound by the final decree, even if not a party to the suit, under the doctrine of lis pendens.
A purchaser of land after a Section 4 notification is issued cannot challenge the acquisition proceedings and has no title; at most, they may claim compensation based on the previous owner's rights.
Once possession of land is taken under Section 16 or 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the land vests in the State free from encumbrances and cannot be de-notified from acquisition.
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Revival of acquisition proceedings by operation of law
Vesting of title in the State upon possession

card.dispute: Omprakash (appellant) sued Laxminarayan and others (respondents) for specific performance of a contract, possession, and permanent injunction based on an agreement to sell land, which the defendants denied executing or acting upon.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to sell, which recites transfer of possession, is a 'conveyance' under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, requiring higher stamp duty?
Whether the agreement to sell is admissible in evidence despite being insufficiently stamped?
Whether the recitals in a document or the pleadings of parties determine its admissibility under the Stamp Act?
holdings: An agreement to sell that transfers possession of immovable property is deemed a 'conveyance' under the Explanation to Article 23 of Schedule 1-A of the Indian Stamp Act, as amended by the Madhya Pradesh Act, and must be stamped accordingly.
An instrument chargeable with stamp duty but insufficiently stamped is inadmissible in evidence unless the deficit duty and penalty are paid under Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act.

The admissibility of a document under the Stamp Act is determined by its recitals, not by the parties' pleadings or denials; if it contains terms of transfer, it must be treated as a conveyance for stamping purposes.
provisions: Indian Stamp (Madhya Pradesh Second Amendment) Act, 1990, Article 23 of Schedule 1-A with Explanation
doctrines: Legal fiction doctrine (deeming an agreement to sell as a conveyance when possession is transferred)
Doctrine of admissibility based on recitals in stamp law
Impounding of insufficiently stamped instruments

card.dispute: RIICO and the State challenged the High Court's decision to quash the cancellation of land allotment to Diamond and Gem Development Corporation Ltd. and to direct provision of an access road.
issues_decided: Whether RIICO had the authority to cancel the allotment of land to the respondent-company under the applicable rules?
Whether the High Court was justified in directing RIICO to provide an access road despite the lease deed placing infrastructure development obligations on the lessee?
Whether the amended Rule 11-A of the Rajasthan Industrial Area Development Rules, 1959, divested RIICO of its title and control over the land?
Whether the respondent-company was entitled to maintain a writ petition without exhausting alternative statutory remedies?
holdings: RIICO retained the authority to cancel land allotments under Rule 24 of the 1979 Rules, and the High Court erred in holding that only the State could cancel the allotment after the 1991 amendment.
The lease deed clearly placed the burden of infrastructure, including access roads, on the lessee; RIICO had no legal or constructive obligation to provide an access road.
Amended Rule 11-A of the 1959 Rules created a legal fiction only to enable sub-leasing by the respondent-company and did not transfer title or divest RIICO of its rights.
The respondent-company failed to exhaust alternative remedies like review, appeal, or arbitration under the lease deed, making the writ petition not maintainable.
provisions: Rajasthan Industrial Area Development Rules, 1959, Rule 11-A
Rajasthan Industrial Area Development Rules, 1979, Rule 24
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedies
Literal interpretation of lease deeds and statutory rules
Legal fiction under statutory deeming provisions
Autonomy of statutory corporations

card.dispute: The Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation (RIICO) fought with a cooperative housing society over whether land acquired for industrial development could be released in favor of the society for residential use after an agreement to sell was made post-acquisition notification.
issues_decided: Whether the housing society could claim rights over land acquired for industrial purposes after a Section 4 notification was issued under the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953.

Whether the High Court was justified in directing the release of acquired land in favor of the housing society despite no formal application for release and the pendency of regularization applications for residential use.
Whether the agreement to sell executed after the Section 4 notification could confer any legal title on the society.
Whether the High Court's findings on non-payment of compensation and discriminatory release of land were supported by evidence.
holdings: An agreement to sell executed after a Section 4 acquisition notification does not create any legal title in favor of the purchaser, especially when the buyer is aware of the acquisition proceedings.
The High Court erred in directing the release of acquired land without comparing the society's case with others and without evidence of discrimination or bona fide application for release.
Acquisition proceedings challenged after long delay and laches were rightly dismissed, and such challenge cannot be revived by third parties like the housing society.
Findings of non-payment of compensation and administrative irregularities in releasing land to other societies were not supported by evidence and were legally perverse.
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Colorable Legislation Doctrine
Eminent Domain
Fraud upon Statute

card.dispute: Rohit Chauhan challenged the sale and gift of land by his father Gulab Singh, claiming it was ancestral coparcenary property in which he had a birthright as a son born after the partition.
issues_decided: Whether the property received by Gulab Singh in partition was ancestral/coparcenary or self-acquired.
Whether the birth of a son revives coparcenary status in property held by a sole coparcener as separate property.
Whether alienations made by a father after the birth of a son in such property are valid without legal necessity.
holdings: Property received by a coparcener through partition, will, or consent decree loses its coparcenary character and becomes self-acquired in his hands.
When a sole surviving coparcener holds ancestral property, it remains his separate property until a son is born, at which point the coparcenary revives and the son acquires an interest.
A father cannot alienate revived coparcenary property after the birth of a son except for legal necessity; alienations without such necessity are void.
doctrines: Revival of coparcenary by birth
Distinction between ancestral and self-acquired property
Alienation of coparcenary property by karta for legal necessity

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed over the apportionment of compensation for acquired land and whether the respondents could intervene in the reference proceedings despite not being parties initially.
issues_decided: Whether a non-party can file an application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC to set aside an ex parte decree?
Whether the court can exercise inherent powers under Section 151 CPC to rectify fraud committed upon a party?
Whether a person who did not apply under Section 18 or Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be impleaded before the Reference Court for apportionment of compensation?
holdings: An application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC can only be filed by a party to the proceedings; a non-party cannot invoke it to set aside a decree.
Inherent powers under Section 151 CPC cannot be used to remedy fraud committed upon a party; such grievances must be addressed through independent legal proceedings.
A person not appearing before the Land Acquisition Collector under Section 18 or 30 of the Act, 1894 cannot directly approach the Reference Court for impleadment or apportionment of compensation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Fraud upon the court vs. fraud upon a party
Jurisdiction of Reference Court under a complete code
Doctrine of res judicata and constructive res judicata
Limitation of inherent powers under CPC

card.dispute: The appellant claimed specific performance of an agreement to sell land, while the respondents denied breach and asserted the appellant's lack of readiness and willingness to perform.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement to sell.
Whether the power of attorney holder could validly depose on behalf of the principal regarding personal knowledge.
Whether the subsequent purchasers had notice of the prior agreement.
holdings: The appellant was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, as supported by witness testimony, and the High Court's contrary finding was perverse.
A power of attorney holder cannot depose on behalf of the principal on matters requiring personal knowledge of the principal.
Subsequent purchasers, except respondent no. 6, had notice of the prior agreement; respondent no. 6 had no notice and retained possession.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order III, Rules 1 and 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII, Rule 9
doctrines: Specific performance of contract
Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Limited capacity of power of attorney holder to testify

card.dispute: The bank challenged the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal's (DRAT) order granting liberty to an auction purchaser to file legal action against it, despite the bank not being a party to the compromise between the borrower and the auction purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether the DRAT had jurisdiction to grant liberty to the auction purchaser to initiate legal action against the bank?
Whether the DRAT can exercise powers beyond those conferred by the SARFAESI Act and the RDB Act?
holdings: The DRAT lacks jurisdiction to grant liberty to any party to initiate legal action against a bank, especially when the bank was not a party to the compromise, as such powers are not conferred by the SARFAESI Act or the RDB Act.

Tribunals like DRAT are creatures of statute and can only exercise powers explicitly or implicitly granted by law; they do not possess inherent powers to pass directions outside their statutory domain.
provisions: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 19(25)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 34
doctrines: Doctrine of limited tribunal jurisdiction
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (special statutes confer specific powers)
Doctrine of separation between courts and tribunals

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh and others fought against M/s. Star Bone Mill & Fertiliser Co. over ownership and title to 3.525 acres of land allegedly leased by the Forest Department to a third party who later sold it to the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the revenue records showing possession can confer title over the suit land?
Whether the sale deed dated 11.11.1959 executed by a lessee who had no title could pass valid title to the respondent?
Whether the courts below erred in relying on Section 90 of the Evidence Act to presume the lease deed's validity from 1943?
holdings: Revenue records do not confer title but only raise a rebuttable presumption of possession; they cannot override the State's proven ownership.
A lessee cannot transfer title better than what it holds; thus, the sale deed executed by a lessee without title is invalid and cannot vest ownership in the purchaser.

Section 90 of the Evidence Act applies to ancient documents and presumes genuineness, but the period must be reckoned from the date of production, not the date of appellate decision; its misapplication here was erroneous.
doctrines: Nemo dat quid non habet
Presumption of possession under Section 110 of the Evidence Act
Rebuttable presumption of title from possession
Estoppel against the statute

card.dispute: The municipal council challenged the lapsing of land reservations in development plans, arguing that acquisition delays under the Land Acquisition Act should not affect reservations under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act.
issues_decided: Whether reservation of land under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 lapses if acquisition is not completed within a specified period under Section 127 of the Act
Whether Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applies to acquisition proceedings under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 by incorporation
Whether the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act apply mutatis mutandis to the MRTP Act in absence of specific reference
holdings: Reservation of land under Section 127 of the MRTP Act lapses if no steps for acquisition are taken within 12 months of notice after 10 years from the plan's enforcement.
Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act does not apply to MRTP Act proceedings as the state law provides its own timeframes and consequences, excluding central law by implication.
The MRTP Act contains a complete code for acquisition; only those provisions of the Land Acquisition Act that are specifically referenced apply, not by general incorporation.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 127
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 128
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 129
doctrines: Legislation by incorporation
Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Statutory interpretation of special enactment

card.dispute: Thomson Press (India) Ltd. sought to be impleaded as a defendant in a pending suit for specific performance of a contract concerning property it had purchased from the original defendants, who were the owners.
issues_decided: Whether a transferee pendente lite can be added as a party defendant in a suit for specific performance under Order I Rule 10 CPC?
Whether the transfer of property during the pendency of a suit affects the rights of the plaintiff in a specific performance suit?
Whether a transferee pendente lite has a substantial interest entitling them to be impleaded under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC?
holdings: A transferee pendente lite is not a necessary party under Order I Rule 10 CPC but may be added if they have a substantial interest in the suit property.
A transfer pendente lite is valid and conveys title, but such title remains subject to the rights of the plaintiff and any decree passed in the pending suit.

Where a transferee acquires the entire interest in the suit property, they are entitled to be added as a party defendant under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC to protect their interest, provided they raise only defenses available to the original defendant.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Transferee pendente lite as representative-in-interest
Substantial interest test for impleadment

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the dismissal of their suit seeking declaration of title to a property, arguing it was maintainable even without claiming possession, while respondents contended the suit was not maintainable due to failure to seek consequential relief of possession.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow holding only a life estate can be considered an absolute owner competent to transfer property under French Hindu Law in Pondicherry.
Whether a suit for declaration of title is maintainable without claiming consequential relief of possession when the defendants are in possession of the property.
holdings: A Hindu widow with only a life estate cannot be deemed an absolute owner and lacks competence to transfer the property; the High Court erred in treating Thayanayagy Ammalle as an absolute owner.

A suit for declaration of title is not maintainable without claiming consequential relief of possession when the defendants are in possession, as failure to seek such relief bars the court from granting a declaratory decree under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Doctrine of maintainability of declaratory suits
Doctrine of life estate under Hindu law
Doctrine against multiplicity of proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant-landlord sought eviction of the respondent-tenant from the suit property, while the respondent claimed ownership through adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could evict the respondent when the relationship of landlord and tenant was not established?
Whether the respondent had perfected title by adverse possession?
Whether the filing of a suit for eviction arrests the running of time for adverse possession?
holdings: The appellant failed to prove the landlord-tenant relationship necessary to sustain an eviction suit.
A person claiming adverse possession must clearly plead and prove open, continuous, and hostile possession known to the true owner.
The institution of a suit for possession arrests the running of time for adverse possession, preventing its completion during pendency of the suit.
provisions: M.P. Rent Control Act (implied by context)
doctrines: Adverse possession
Relation back of decree for possession
Doctrine of laches and repose in limitation

card.dispute: The landlords (Anil Bajaj & Anr) challenged the High Court's order granting the tenant (Vinod Ahuja) leave to defend eviction proceedings under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which the Rent Controller had initially denied.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant raised a triable issue warranting leave to defend against eviction on grounds of the landlord's bona fide requirement?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Rent Controller's order refusing leave to defend?
holdings: A tenant is entitled to leave to defend if a triable issue is raised, but mere allegations without a prima facie case do not suffice; the landlord's bona fide need must be considered even if they own other properties.

The High Court erred in granting leave to defend where the tenant failed to raise a genuine triable issue, as the landlord's intention to use the premises for business cannot be negated by owning other properties or running other businesses.
doctrines: Prima facie case for leave to defend
Triable issue doctrine
Principles of natural justice in summary eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, being members of the same family, fought over the rights to flats constructed on jointly inherited tenanted property in Mumbai, specifically whether five flats should be allotted to the respondents based on their share and subsequent developments during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could mould relief by allotting five flats to the respondents despite the original suit seeking different relief, in light of subsequent events during litigation?
Whether the appellants could be denied relief due to changed circumstances, including construction during pendency of suit and acquisition of part of the property by BMC?
Whether the respondents' claim to 6/15th share in the property was correctly upheld by the High Court?
holdings: Courts may mould relief in light of subsequent events during litigation if the original relief has become inappropriate, justice requires it, and the opposite party is not taken by surprise.

Where property is acquired by a third party like BMC during litigation and construction has already taken place under court orders, equitable relief must reflect current realities to do complete justice.
The respondents' 6/15th share in the suit property was correctly upheld as a question of fact, given their representation of two branches of the family as opposed to the appellants' single branch.
provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Moulding of relief doctrine
Equitable discretion to consider subsequent events
Crystallisation of rights at institution of suit with equitable exceptions

card.dispute: The landlords sought to strike out the tenants' defence for non-payment of future rent as ordered by the Rent Controller, which the tenants challenged as unjustified.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below rightly exercised discretion under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 to strike out the tenant's defence for non-payment of future rent?
Whether delayed or subsequent payments by the tenant can cure the default under Section 15(7)?
Whether the tenant offered a reasonable explanation for non-compliance with the Rent Controller’s order?
holdings: The power under Section 15(7) is discretionary and should be used only for deliberate, negligent, or contumacious failure to pay rent; such failure must be clearly established.
Subsequent payments made after the landlord's application under Section 15(7) are irrelevant to the question of compliance at the time of application.
A tenant's failure to pay even nominal rent on time, without valid explanation, shows contumacious disregard of court orders, justifying striking out of defence.
An offer to pay excessive future rent cannot compensate for past deliberate non-compliance with judicial directions under the Rent Act.
doctrines: Judicial discretion
Contumacious conduct
Strict compliance with court orders
Legislative intent to prevent abuse of legal process by tenants

card.dispute: The Podhu Dikshitars (trustees of the Sabhanayagar Temple) fought the State of Tamil Nadu over the legality of appointing an Executive Officer to administer the temple, claiming violation of their rights under Article 26 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the State could appoint an Executive Officer under Section 45 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 without prescribing conditions for such appointment?
Whether the indefinite duration of the Executive Officer's appointment violates the fundamental rights of the temple trustees under Article 26?
Whether the State's action amounts to an impermissible supersession of the trustees' administrative rights under the guise of regulation?
holdings: The power to appoint an Executive Officer under Section 45 of the 1959 Act cannot be exercised in the absence of prescribed conditions, as 'prescribed' means rules framed under law.
An order taking over temple management must specify a limited duration co-terminus with the remedying of maladministration; indefinite takeover violates fundamental rights under Article 26.
The State cannot achieve indirectly what it cannot do directly; supersession of trustees' rights under the guise of regulation is unconstitutional.
provisions: The Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 45
doctrines: Principle of legality (what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly)
Strict construction of state power infringing fundamental rights
Rule of law in statutory interpretation ('prescribed' requires formal rule-making)

card.dispute: Godrej & Boyce Mfg. Co. Ltd. challenged the acquisition of its private forest land by the State of Maharashtra under the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the repealed Forest Act were applicable to lands restored under Section 22A of the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act, 1977 after their repeal.
Whether the State Government could validly impose restrictions under Section 35 of the Forest Act on private forest owners without complying with procedural safeguards.
holdings: Sections 34A to 37 of the Forest Act, though repealed, were deemed to have been reenacted and remained applicable to lands restored under Section 22A of the Maharashtra Private Forests (Acquisition) Act, 1977.

The State Government must follow the procedural safeguards under Section 35(3) of the Forest Act, including issuing a show-cause notice and considering objections, before imposing restrictions on private forest lands.
doctrines: Doctrine of Deemed Reenactment
Principle of Procedural Fairness
Doctrine of Continuity of Laws

card.dispute: The trustees of Gangai Vinayagar Temple and tenants of a leased property fought over whether the tenants were barred by res judicata from challenging the temple's ownership of the property, after they failed to appeal in two of three related suits.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res judicata applies to findings on ownership in O.S.5/78 when the tenants only appealed in O.S.6/78 and not in the other suits.
Whether Order II Rule 2 CPC, which prevents splitting of claims, bars the tenants from later challenging ownership after failing to appeal in all relevant suits.
Whether a finding on ownership, though not essential to the decree in a suit for injunction simpliciter, can still operate as res judicata if directly and substantially in issue.
Whether filing an appeal in one of multiple related suits amounts to an appeal in all such suits for the purpose of avoiding res judicata.
holdings: A finding on ownership directly and substantially in issue in a suit, even if not essential to the decree, operates as res judicata if not appealed and attains finality.
Order II Rule 2 CPC bars parties from splitting claims and defenses; failure to appeal a decree in a suit where ownership was contested results in res judicata on that issue.
Where a party raises ownership as a defense in multiple suits and litigates it fully, they cannot evade res judicata by appealing only in one suit.
An appeal filed in only one of several related suits does not suffice to challenge findings in others; each decree must be separately appealed to avoid res judicata.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
Puducherry Hindu Religious Institutions Act, 1972, Section 26
doctrines: res judicata
constructive res judicata
rule against splitting of causes of action
direct and substantial issue

card.dispute: Environmental activists challenged the sale of agricultural land in Kutch from one industrial buyer to another, alleging violation of land use laws meant to protect farmland.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of agricultural land from Indigold to Alumina for industrial use violated Section 89A of the Gujarat Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958
Whether the State Government's direction permitting the sale was arbitrary and contrary to law
Whether the Collector failed to conduct a mandatory enquiry under Section 89A(5) when the original purchaser abandoned industrial plans
Whether subsequent sale to a third party for industrial use is permissible under the Act
holdings: Section 89A does not permit resale of agricultural land by an industrial purchaser to a third party; such transfer is invalid.
The State Government's order permitting the sale was arbitrary and violated the statutory scheme of the Tenancy Act.
When a purchaser abandons industrial use, the land must vest in the State with compensation, following procedures under Section 89A(5).
Vesting of land in the State is mandatory upon abandonment of industrial purpose, but equitable disposal to a new investor may occur if public interest and fair compensation are ensured.
provisions: Gujarat Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Areas) Act, 1958, Section 89
Gujarat Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Areas) Act, 1958, Section 89A
doctrines: Doctrine of arbitrariness in administrative action
Principle of statutory interpretation to prevent misuse of agricultural land
Public trust doctrine in land use and environmental protection
Equitable relief in public interest litigation

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers) challenged the High Court's decision to set aside their purchase of a property under the SARFAESI Act, which was sold by a bank to recover dues from the borrowers (respondents).
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the secured asset under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 was valid and in compliance with Section 13 and Rules 8 and 9 of the SARFAESI Rules, 2002.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the sale despite the appellants having acted in good faith and paid the consideration promptly.
Whether the bank's dues were required to be secured again upon setting aside the sale, given that the borrowers had already settled the dues with the bank as per the High Court's earlier order.
holdings: A sale under the SARFAESI Act is void if it violates Section 13 and Rules 8 and 9 of the SARFAESI Rules, 2002, particularly when conducted without proper notice and transparency, leading to undervaluation.
Even bona fide purchasers cannot retain possession if the sale is null and void; however, they are entitled to full refund of sale consideration with reasonable interest and costs.

Once the borrower has discharged the bank's dues as per a court order and the bank accepts it without appeal, the bank has no further claim, and the property must be restored to the borrower upon refund to the purchaser.
provisions: Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Rules, 2002, Rule 8
Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Rules, 2002, Rule 9
doctrines: Principle of fair and transparent sale under SARFAESI
Voidness of sale for non-compliance with statutory procedure
Good faith purchaser not protected against jurisdictional illegality

card.dispute: The Haryana State Agricultural Marketing Board appealed against the order upholding the allottees' refusal to pay instalments due to the Board's failure to provide basic amenities for the plots allotted for grain trading.
issues_decided: Whether the statutory Board is amenable to the jurisdiction of consumer forums for deficiency of service in not providing basic amenities for allotted plots.
Whether the allottees can withhold payment of instalments due to non-provision of amenities despite such provision not being a condition precedent in the allotment letter.
Whether the levy of penal interest and charges on defaulting allottees is justified when the Board failed to develop the market area for over a decade.
holdings: Statutory boards allotting plots with promises of development are subject to consumer forum jurisdiction for deficiency of service under the Consumer Protection Act.

Allottees cannot unilaterally refuse to pay instalments despite non-provision of amenities, as payment is a contractual obligation, but they are entitled to proportionate relief in penalty and interest.
Penal interest and charges may be waived or reduced proportionately where the Board's long-term failure to provide basic facilities renders such levies grossly unfair.
provisions: Punjab Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1961, Section 7
Consumer Protection Act, 1986, Section 2(1)(o) and Section 2(1)(d)
doctrines: Deficiency in service by statutory authorities
Proportionate relief in consumer disputes
Fairness in contractual obligations and penalties

card.dispute: Jal Mahal Resorts challenged the High Court's cancellation of its 99-year lease for a tourism development project near Jal Mahal in Jaipur, which was contested by PIL petitioners over environmental and legal concerns.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in cancelling the entire lease and project due to procedural and environmental violations
Whether the 99-year lease period granted by the State Government was legally valid
Whether the leased area fell under wetland or lakebed, thereby attracting the Wetland Rules, 2010
Whether the project was in conflict with the preservation of the Jal Mahal monument and the surrounding environment
holdings: The High Court's cancellation of the entire project was unjustified; only the lease period and certain land areas required correction.
A 99-year lease is invalid as it amounts to a perpetual lease; the lease period is reduced to 30 years, commencing from the date of this judgment.
The Wetland Rules, 2010 do not apply retroactively to the lease area, as environmental clearance was obtained under prior regulations and the land was not recorded as wetland.
The project does not conflict with environmental or heritage conservation, and the lessee may restart work, subject to designated construction-free zones for public use.
doctrines: Principle of proportionality in judicial review
Non-retroactivity of administrative rules
Public trust doctrine (implied in protection of lake and public access)
Doctrine of legitimate expectation (in continuation of project after legal adjustments)

card.dispute: A group of members of a cooperative housing society and the society itself challenged the auction sale of society land, alleging mala fide and under-valuation, while the state and authorities defended the sale as valid and properly conducted.
issues_decided: Whether the auction sale of land by the cooperative society's General Body was valid and free from mala fide?
Whether the writ jurisdiction was an appropriate forum to challenge the sale based on factual disputes and allegations of undervaluation?
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the auction sale despite allegations of procedural irregularities and lack of transparency?
holdings: A resolution passed by the General Body of a cooperative society with majority support cannot be invalidated on mere allegations of mala fide without strict proof, especially in writ proceedings.
Writ jurisdiction is not an appropriate remedy to adjudicate factual disputes involving allegations of fraud, undervaluation, or procedural impropriety in a cooperative society's decision-making.

The High Court rightly upheld the auction sale as it was conducted under the supervision of the Registrar-appointed Board of Administrators and supported by sufficient material, with no perversity in the findings.
doctrines: Principle of majority rule in cooperative societies
Limited scope of writ jurisdiction in factual disputes
Mala fide is difficult to prove and cannot be inferred from speculation or assumption

card.dispute: The appellant trust sought to declare Galta Peeth as public property and challenge the state's failure to appoint a fresh management committee under the Rajasthan Public Trusts Act, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether Galta Peeth and its properties are public or private trusts?
Whether the High Court erred in upholding the validity of the notification under Section 53 of the Rajasthan Public Trusts Act, 1959?
Whether the state is obligated to appoint a new committee under Section 53 after the previous one's term expired?
Whether public interest litigation is maintainable in disputes concerning religious institutions and trust management?
holdings: The court did not decide the status of Galta Peeth as public or private, as the challenge to the High Court's finding was not substantiated.
The High Court's validation of the committee constituted under Section 53 of the Rajasthan Public Trusts Act, 1959, was upheld as lawful.
The state is not mandatorily required to reconstitute a management committee under Section 53; it is a discretionary power, especially after the amendment substituting 'may' for 'shall'.

Public interest litigation is not maintainable in religious trust disputes when statutory forums exist, and courts should avoid intervening in such matters to prevent misuse and protect fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26.
doctrines: Judicial restraint in religious matters
Doctrine of separation of powers
Limits of public interest litigation
Primacy of statutory adjudication forums

card.dispute: The plaintiff (Inbasegaran) sued for specific performance of a sale agreement over a property allotted to the defendant (S. Natarajan) by the Tamil Nadu Housing Board, while the defendant contested the suit's maintainability under Order 2 Rule 2 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by Order 2 Rule 2 of the CPC due to prior omission to claim the relief in an earlier suit for injunction?
Whether the High Court erred in not deciding all the points it had formulated?
holdings: The suit for specific performance is not barred by Order 2 Rule 2 CPC because the cause of action in the earlier injunction suit was different and did not involve an attempt by the defendant to alienate the property to frustrate the agreement.
The High Court failed to decide all the points it had formulated; hence, the matter is remanded for adjudication on the remaining issues.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2 Rule 2
doctrines: Res judicata and cause of action estoppel under Order 2 Rule 2 CPC
Principle of judicial precedent and contextual application of ratio decidendi

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell property, which the High Court reversed; the dispute centered on whether the plaintiff was entitled to specific performance despite delays and a significant rise in property value.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff demonstrated continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract for specific performance.
Whether the appellate court could interfere with the trial court's discretion in granting specific performance.
Whether a significant rise in property value during litigation justifies refusal of specific performance.
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform from the date of contract to the date of hearing.
An appellate court should not interfere with the trial court's discretionary decision unless it is perverse, arbitrary, or against judicial principles.
A substantial increase in property value during litigation does not, by itself, justify denying specific performance, but courts may impose conditions like additional payment to balance equities.
doctrines: Discretionary nature of specific performance
Equitable discretion guided by law and justice
Balancing of equities in specific performance

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Delhi Development Authority for the Vasant Kunj development scheme, seeking higher compensation, interest, and full recovery of court fees and costs.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court correctly determined the market value of the acquired land and awarded compensation at Rs.14,974 per sq. yard.
Whether the appellants were entitled to higher interest on compensation under Sections 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the High Court erred in awarding only proportionate costs instead of full costs including the entire court fees of Rs.48 lakhs.
holdings: The High Court correctly assessed the market value of the land by averaging comparable sale deeds and applying a 40% reduction for plot size, resulting in fair compensation at Rs.14,974 per sq. yard.
The appellants were already entitled to statutory interest under Sections 34 and 28 of the Act, and the High Court's interest award was in accordance with law, leaving no ground for enhancement.

The High Court properly exercised its discretion under Section 27 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, in awarding proportionate costs; claimants are not entitled to full costs or reimbursement of entire court fees merely due to partial success.
doctrines: Principle of proportionate costs in partial success cases
Appropriation of interest at different stages of compensation enhancement
Use of comparable sale deeds adjusted for relevant factors in determining market value

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a 1982 will that favored the first respondent, contesting its legality due to suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution and registration.
issues_decided: Whether the 1982 will was executed voluntarily and free from suspicious circumstances.
Whether the first respondent's participation in the execution and registration of the will vitiated its validity.
Whether the loss of the original will and reliance on a certified copy affected the will's authenticity.
Whether the testator's lack of knowledge of English undermined the will's validity.
holdings: A will surrounded by unusual circumstances must be scrutinized cumulatively, not based on any single suspicious factor.
Active participation by a beneficiary in the execution and registration of a will does not automatically invalidate it if other safeguards are met.
Reliance on a certified copy of a will is permissible when the loss of the original is reasonably explained and custody is accounted for.
A testator's lack of knowledge of English does not invalidate a will if there is evidence that the contents were explained or confirmed by the registering authority.
doctrines: Cumulative effect doctrine in will disputes
Judicial conscience in probate validation
Presumption of due execution of registered wills
Limited scope of factual review under special leave jurisdiction

card.dispute: KSL & Industries Ltd. appealed against the Delhi High Court's decision to set aside DRAT's order, challenging whether recovery proceedings under the RDDB Act could proceed against Arihant Threads Ltd., a company declared sick under SICA.
issues_decided: Whether Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 (SICA) bars recovery proceedings under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 (RDDB Act).
Whether the later enactment of the RDDB Act with a non-obstante clause overrides the earlier SICA provisions.
holdings: Section 22 of SICA bars all proceedings, including those under the RDDB Act, against a sick company to protect its assets during revival proceedings.
Despite being a later law, the RDDB Act does not override SICA because Section 34(2) explicitly states its provisions are in addition to, and not in derogation of, other laws including SICA.
provisions: Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 34
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Legislative intent
Non-obstante clause interpretation
Special law vs. general law

card.dispute: The landlady, Keshar Bai, sued for eviction of tenant Chhunulal on grounds including denial of her title; the tenant contested, leading to a dispute over whether denial of title alone justified eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's denial of the landlord's title constitutes a valid ground for eviction under Section 12(1)(c) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the concurrent findings of the lower courts on the tenant's denial of title.
Whether the question of title can be finally adjudicated in an eviction proceeding.
holdings: Denial of a landlord's title by a tenant, even after being presented with documentary evidence, is a valid ground for eviction under Section 12(1)(c) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
The High Court erred in disturbing the concurrent factual finding that the tenant denied the landlord's title, which was supported by pleadings and evidence.
In eviction proceedings, the court may incidentally examine title but cannot finally decide it; such proceedings do not amount to a final adjudication on ownership.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(c)
doctrines: Estoppel between landlord and tenant
Incidental jurisdiction over title in eviction proceedings
Res judicata limited to exceptional cases in eviction suits

card.dispute: The appellant, a landowner, challenged the acquisition of its land by the NCT of Delhi, claiming the acquisition proceedings had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Land Acquisition Act due to non-fulfillment of conditions for taking possession.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings in respect of the appellant's land had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
Whether the possession taken by the authorities was valid in law, particularly whether it was actual and in compliance with procedural requirements
Whether the transfer of land by the appellant was invalid under the Delhi Land (Restriction on Transfer) Act, 1972
holdings: Acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act because the government failed to take physical possession of the land within the stipulated time and in accordance with legal requirements.
Possession taken without the presence of independent witnesses and merely on paper does not constitute valid possession; actual physical possession in accordance with law is mandatory.

The transfer of land by the appellant was valid as the competent authority had granted necessary permission, and the 1972 Act does not apply since the land was acquired by NCT, not on behalf of the Central Government.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
Delhi Land (Restriction on Transfer) Act, 1972, Sections 3, 4, and 9
doctrines: Actual possession doctrine under land acquisition law
Lapse of acquisition proceedings under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act
Validity of symbolic vs. physical possession in land acquisition

card.dispute: Maya Devi, claiming to be the absolute owner of a property, objected to its attachment in execution of a money decree in favor of Lalta Prasad against her predecessor-in-title, Prem Chand Verma.
issues_decided: Whether a third party can raise a claim of ownership against a property sought to be attached in execution of a money decree under Order 21 Rule 58 CPC?
Whether a General Power of Attorney and related documents can establish valid title for the purpose of resisting execution?
Whether the executing court must independently examine title claims raised by third-party objectors even if the decree is ex parte?
Whether the decision in Suraj Lamp and Industries Private Limited v. State of Haryana applies retrospectively to transactions prior to its pronouncement?
holdings: A third party claiming ownership of property attached in execution of a money decree is entitled to raise objections under Order 21 Rule 58 CPC, and the executing court must adjudicate such claims on merits.

Where a third party has acquired property for valuable consideration and is not colluding with the judgment debtor, their title must be considered even if based on documents like General Power of Attorney.
Executing courts must carefully examine all objections to execution, especially where the decree was passed ex parte, to prevent miscarriage of justice.
The Suraj Lamp decision, which holds that GPA sales do not convey title, has prospective operation and does not invalidate transactions completed before its pronouncement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 58
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rules 97 to 104
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8 Rule 10
doctrines: Prospective overruling
Third-party rights in execution proceedings
Duty of court in ex parte decrees
Prevention of miscarriage of justice in execution

card.dispute: The appellant, Mosiruddin Munshi, challenged the High Court's quashing of an FIR alleging cheating and criminal conspiracy against Md. Siraj and another in a land sale dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR under Section 482 Cr.P.C. at the preliminary stage?
Whether the allegations in the complaint disclose a cognizable offence under Section 420/120B IPC?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR as the allegations, if taken as true, prima facie disclosed commission of cognizable offences under Section 420 and 120B IPC.
At the investigation stage, the court should not adopt a hyper-technical approach or delve into the merits; criminal proceedings cannot be quashed merely because the dispute has civil overtones.
doctrines: Principle of privity of contract
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
Prima facie case doctrine
Separation of civil and criminal liability

card.dispute: Pratima Chowdhury fought with Kalpana Mukherjee and another over the ownership and possession of a flat allegedly transferred without consideration under suspicious circumstances involving a fiduciary relationship.
issues_decided: Whether the burden of proof lay on Kalpana Mukherjee to prove the fairness and genuineness of the transfer of the flat from Pratima Chowdhury?
Whether the transfer of the flat by Pratima Chowdhury to Kalpana Mukherjee was genuine and voluntary or vitiated by undue influence?
Whether the High Court and Cooperative Tribunal erred in shifting the burden of proof to Pratima Chowdhury?
holdings: The burden of proving the fairness and validity of a transaction lies on the party who benefits from it when it occurs between persons in a fiduciary or confidential relationship.
A transfer made without consideration by a person in a vulnerable position to someone connected with a dominant confidant is presumed to be influenced and invalid unless proven otherwise.
Courts must not shift the burden of proof to the donor in cases involving fiduciary relationships; the beneficiary must prove the transaction's equity and due execution.
doctrines: Doctrine of undue influence
Fiduciary relationship
Presumption of influence in confidential relationships
Burden of proof in equitable transactions

card.dispute: The Pune Municipal Corporation challenged the lapsing of land acquisition proceedings under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, after having awarded but neither paid nor deposited compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'paid' in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act includes deposit of compensation in court under Section 31(2) of the 1894 Act?
Whether depositing compensation in the government treasury satisfies the requirement of payment under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act?
Whether land acquisition proceedings lapse under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act if award was made more than five years before its commencement and compensation was neither paid nor deposited in court?
holdings: For Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, 'paid' includes deposit of compensation in court under Section 31(2) of the 1894 Act when contingencies prevent direct payment to landowners.
Deposit of compensation in a government treasury does not constitute payment under Section 24(2); only deposit in court as per Section 31(2) is valid.
Acquisition proceedings lapse under Section 24(2) if, five years or more before the 2013 Act, an award was made and compensation was neither paid nor deposited in court.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 114
doctrines: Legal fiction
Strict compliance with expropriatory legislation
Doctrine of 'must do in the prescribed manner' (Nazir Ahmad principle)

card.dispute: The appellant HUF challenged the land acquisition of its property in Bamnauli, Delhi, arguing that the proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act because possession was not taken and compensation not paid within five years of the award.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, despite the pendency of court orders maintaining 'status quo'?
Whether the period of court-ordered stay can be excluded when determining the five-year period under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act?
holdings: Acquisition proceedings are deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act if an award was made more than five years before the Act's commencement and neither possession was taken nor compensation paid, regardless of court-ordered stays.
The five-year period under Section 24(2) is absolute; delays due to court injunctions or 'status quo' orders do not extend it, as the legislature intended to protect landowners in long-pending cases.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 114
doctrines: Literal rule of interpretation
Legal fiction
Deemed lapse of acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sought to evict tenants (respondents) from a shop premises, but the tenants invoked an arbitration clause in the tenancy agreement, leading to a dispute over whether the eviction suit could be referred to arbitration.
issues_decided: Whether a dispute between landlord and tenant regarding eviction can be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 when a statutory tenancy law provides exclusive jurisdiction to a civil court?
Whether an arbitration agreement in a tenancy contract overrides the exclusive jurisdiction conferred by Section 6 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997?
holdings: A suit for eviction of a tenant is a dispute relating to recovery of possession governed by a special tenancy law, which confers exclusive jurisdiction on the Civil Judge, and cannot be referred to arbitration.
Arbitration agreements between landlords and tenants are unenforceable when they conflict with statutory provisions like Section 6 of the Tenancy Act that vest exclusive jurisdiction in civil courts.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997, Section 6
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction under special statutes
Public policy against ousting statutory forums for tenant protection
