Repeated litigation by respondent No. 4 constitutes abuse of process, especially when possession was taken in 1986, sites were allotted, and development has occurred over decades.
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in land acquisition matters
Abuse of process of law
Finality of litigation
Settled law on maintainability of suits challenging acquisition

card.dispute: The landlord filed an eviction petition against the tenant for bona fide need, and after possession was delivered, the tenant filed multiple applications challenging the eviction, which the High Court entertained under Article 227; the landlord appealed to the Supreme Court against this interference.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising jurisdiction under Article 227 to entertain the tenant's writ petition against orders passed by the Trial Court in an eviction matter after the decree was executed?
Whether the Trial Court was justified in passing the eviction order ex parte after the tenant failed to appear despite notice?
Whether the High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by directing the Trial Court to allow the tenant's applications?
holdings: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition under Article 227 after the eviction decree was fully executed and possession delivered, as no live lis remained.
The Trial Court was justified in passing the eviction order ex parte as the tenant, despite being aware of the proceedings and having initiated the remand, failed to appear without sufficient cause.
The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by directing the Trial Court to allow specific applications, thereby infringing on the Trial Court's judicial discretion.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(2)(b)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 35
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Principle of finality of executed decrees
Limits on supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Judicial discretion in adjudicating applications
Abuse of process of court

card.dispute: The legal representatives of defendants 2 and 4 challenged the High Court's decree for specific performance of a contract, arguing it was passed after the death of the parties and without substitution of legal representatives, rendering it a nullity.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to decide the second appeal after the death of the appellant and two respondents without substitution of their legal representatives?
Whether the decree passed by the High Court in favour of and against dead persons is a nullity?
holdings: A decree passed by a court in favour of or against a deceased person, without substitution of legal representatives, is a nullity as the court lacks jurisdiction once the appeal abates due to non-compliance with Order 22 Rules 3 and 4 of the CPC.

An appeal abates automatically after 90 days of a party's death if no application for substitution is filed; the court cannot proceed with the appeal unless the abatement is set aside with sufficient cause and delay condoned.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 9
doctrines: Jurisdictional nullity
Abatement of appeal
Suo moto abatement under CPC
Incurable jurisdictional defect

card.dispute: The Kutchi Lal Rameshwar Ashram Trust challenged the Collector's order declaring government ownership of disputed property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, after the death of Mohan Lal, claiming rightful management as a public trust.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to determine the devolution of property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the property stood vested in the State Government under Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 due to absence of legal heirs
Whether the Collector could take possession of the property under Section 167(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
holdings: The Collector lacked adjudicatory jurisdiction to determine succession or heirlessness; such matters fall exclusively under the domain of civil courts or the High Court under the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
The mere absence of a known heir does not automatically vest property in the state under Section 29 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 without a competent judicial determination.

Section 167(2) of the UP Zamindari Abolition Act is applicable only when a transfer is void under Section 166; since no such void transfer was established, the Collector had no power to take possession.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 166
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 167
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers
Doctrine of ejusdem generis
Principle of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of vested rights

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of expiry of tenancy and need for own use, specifically to enable her unemployed son to start a business in the premises.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement of the landlord for 'own use' under the rent control law includes use by a family member, such as a son.
Whether non-examination of the family member (son) for whose benefit the premises is required invalidates the landlord's claim.
holdings: The expression 'for his own use' includes occupation by a family member when there is a genuine need and close economic or familial dependence, and the use benefits the landlord directly.
Non-examination of the family member for whose use the premises is required does not defeat the landlord's claim if the need is otherwise proved and genuine.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(ii)
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of 'own use'
Genuineness of requirement test
Practical approach to landlord's need guided by social realities

card.dispute: The brother and sister disputed over ownership of a residential house after their father's will granted the sister a life interest in the property while giving absolute ownership to the brother and sister jointly.
issues_decided: Whether the widow's life interest in the suit property under the will amounted to a restricted estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the life interest granted to the widow under the will could ripen into an absolute interest under Section 14(1) of the Act
Whether the testator had the legal right to dispose of his self-acquired property by creating a limited estate for his wife
holdings: A life interest created in favor of a Hindu female under a will, with restrictions on transfer and with reversion to others after her death, constitutes a restricted estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Where a female acquires property for the first time under a will that creates a restricted estate, Section 14(1) does not apply, and her interest remains limited as per the will's terms.

A male Hindu has the right under Section 30 of the Act to dispose of his self-acquired property by will, including creating a life interest in favor of his widow, which is valid and not invalidated by Section 14(1).
doctrines: Restricted estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Testamentary disposition under Section 30 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Distinction between acquisition by pre-existing right and by grant under will

card.dispute: The appellants (Hema Khattar and Ashwani Khattar) challenged the High Court's dismissal of their suit for declaration and damages against Shiv Khera, who had initiated arbitration under an agreement to reconstruct a building, over issues of misjoinder of parties and the maintainability of the suit despite a pending arbitration application.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by the appellants was bad for misjoinder of parties or causes of action.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit after an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was filed seeking reference to arbitration.
Whether the arbitration clause in the original written agreement applied to a subsequent oral agreement between the parties.
holdings: The suit was not bad for misjoinder of parties or causes of action, as both appellants had a common interest arising from the same transaction and could jointly file the suit.

The civil court lacked jurisdiction to proceed with the suit once a valid application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was made, as the existence of a valid arbitration agreement required mandatory referral to arbitration.

The arbitration clause in the original written agreement applied to the subsequent oral agreement, as it was a continuation of the same contractual relationship and the arbitration clause survived the termination of the original agreement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 8
doctrines: Mandatory referral to arbitration under Section 8 when an arbitration agreement exists
Survival of arbitration clause post-termination of contract
Test for necessary and proper parties under Order I Rule 8 CPC

card.dispute: Two brothers fought over whether an agreement to sell land by the younger brother (Parminder Singh) to the elder brother (Gurpreet Singh) should be specifically enforced.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement dated 02.07.1995 for sale of land was genuine and enforceable?
Whether the respondent was ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement?
Whether the concurrent findings of the three lower courts can be disturbed in appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution?
holdings: The agreement to sell was genuine, duly signed, and enforceable; the defense of forgery and blank paper was rejected.
The respondent proved readiness and willingness to perform and had partly performed his obligation by paying Rs. 4 lakhs.
Concurrent findings of fact by three courts based on evidence cannot be overturned by this Court unless perverse or against law, which was not the case.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Discretion in granting specific performance
Limited scope of appeal under Article 136

card.dispute: Co-owners of a tenanted property sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of rent default and sub-letting, but the High Court dismissed the suit holding the co-owners lacked standing.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner can maintain an eviction suit without joining other co-owners as parties?
Whether the tenant could be evicted for default in rent and unauthorized sub-letting under the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972?
Whether the tenant was estopped from denying the landlord status of the co-owners?
holdings: A co-owner of a joint property can independently file an eviction suit without impleading other co-owners if they do not object, as each co-owner has full ownership interest in the entire property.

The tenant was liable for eviction due to default in rent payment after notice and for unauthorized sub-letting, especially since he constructed another residence, disentitling him from protection under Section 20(4) of the Act.
The tenant is estopped under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 from denying the landlord status of the co-owners after having recognized and paid rent to them.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel (Section 116, Indian Evidence Act)
Right of co-owner to sue independently for eviction
Statutory grounds for eviction under rent control law

card.dispute: The appellants (New Okhla Industrial Development Authority) challenged the High Court's decision to entertain writ petitions seeking release of acquired land, after prior rejections of such claims in earlier litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in entertaining writ petitions challenging the award under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 after a long delay and without sufficient cause?
Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed due to non-passing of the award within the prescribed period under Section 11A of the Act?
Whether the High Court could interfere with the State Government's rejection of a representation under Section 48(1) of the Act?
holdings: The writ petitions challenging the award were barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC, laches, and delay, as the respondents had earlier opportunities to raise the objection but failed to do so.
Acquisition proceedings did not lapse under Section 11A because possession was taken under Section 17(1), which excludes the applicability of Section 11A.
The High Court exceeded its judicial review jurisdiction by interfering with the competent authority’s decision under Section 48(1), which was based on proper consideration and evidence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Doctrine of laches and delay
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Scope of judicial review in administrative decisions
Finality of acquisition proceedings under urgency provisions

card.dispute: Orissa Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation (IDCO) fought with M/s Mesco Kalinga Steel Ltd. over whether IDCO was legally bound to lease 825.68 acres of land despite Mesco's failure to perform obligations under the allotment terms.
issues_decided: Whether Mesco acquired enforceable rights over the land without executing a lease deed and fulfilling payment obligations
Whether the principle of promissory estoppel could compel IDCO, a statutory body, to execute a lease agreement
Whether the High Court was justified in directing IDCO to lease the land despite Mesco's defaults
Whether the agreement stood automatically terminated due to non-payment of instalments
holdings: No enforceable right arose in favour of Mesco merely on allotment or possession without execution of lease deed and performance of conditions.
Promissory estoppel does not bind a statutory body like IDCO to execute a contract contrary to statutory procedure and prescribed form.
The High Court erred in directing specific performance when Mesco failed to perform its obligations and the agreement stood void for breach.
The agreement automatically terminated upon Mesco's failure to pay instalments within the stipulated time, entitling IDCO to resume the land.
provisions: Airports Authority of India Act, 1944, Section 3
doctrines: Strict performance of conditions precedent
Promissory estoppel not overriding statutory obligations
Automatic termination of agreement on breach of condition
Equity cannot relieve against breach in absence of fraud, accident or surprise

card.dispute: The appellants sought to quash an FIR alleging forgery, forgery of valuable security, cheating, criminal conspiracy, and extortion in a land transaction, after settling with the complainant, but the High Court refused.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court should have quashed the FIR under Section 482 CrPC based on a private settlement between the parties.
Whether the nature of the offences alleged—economic and serious in character—justifies continuation of prosecution despite settlement.
Whether the accused's criminal antecedents and absconding conduct affect the exercise of inherent powers to quash proceedings.
holdings: The High Court can exercise inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash proceedings even in non-compoundable offences, but must consider the nature and gravity of the offence and public interest.
Serious economic offences affecting societal interests, such as forgery and fraud in property transactions, should not be quashed merely due to private settlement.
The accused’s absconding behaviour and criminal antecedents justify refusal to quash the FIR, as continuation serves the ends of justice and prevents abuse of process.
doctrines: Inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Public interest exception to quashing of criminal proceedings
Gravity of offence as a factor in quashing petitions
Settlement in economic offences not a ground for quashing if societal harm is involved

card.dispute: Neera Yadav, a former high-ranking official of NOIDA, fought against her conviction and sentence for corruption in the allocation of plots and altering site plans for personal and others' benefit.
issues_decided: Whether the sentences in two separate corruption cases should run concurrently or consecutively under Section 427 Cr.P.C.
Whether the sentence of imprisonment should be reduced considering the appellant's conduct and surrender of property.
holdings: Sentences for convictions arising from distinct transactions in separate cases can be directed to run consecutively; concurrency is not automatic and depends on the facts and nature of the offences.

The sentence of three years' rigorous imprisonment was reduced to two years due to the appellant's surrender of the contested plot and building, and withdrawal of legal claims, though the conviction was upheld.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(d) and Section 13(2)
doctrines: Single transaction rule for concurrent sentences
Judicial discretion in sentencing under special circumstances

card.dispute: The landlord, Ram Murti Devi, fought to evict the tenant, Pushpa Devi, over alleged arrears of rent and subletting of the shop to another person, Mohd. Ezaj Khan.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Trial Court's finding of subletting in revision?
Whether the tenant's failure to register Mohd. Ezaj Khan as an employee under the UP Shops & Commercial Establishments Act, 1962, supports an adverse inference of subletting?
Whether findings of fact based on appreciation of evidence can be disturbed in revision under Section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act?
holdings: The High Court erred in overturning the Trial Court's finding of subletting, as no illegality or perversity was demonstrated in the factual finding.
The tenant's failure to produce statutory records showing Mohd. Ezaj Khan as an employee permits an adverse inference that he was not an employee but a sub-tenant.

While revisional courts generally do not reappreciate evidence, they may interfere with factual findings if those findings are based on irrelevant considerations or ignore material statutory obligations.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Shops and Commercial Establishments Act, 1962, Section 4-B
Uttar Pradesh Shops and Commercial Establishments Rules, 1963, Rule 2A
Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, Section 25
doctrines: Adverse inference from non-production of statutory records
Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction in factual findings
Mixed question of law and fact in statutory compliance

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, as legal representatives of deceased members of a joint Hindu family, disputed the rightful shares in ancestral property following the deaths of family members and the application of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether a notional partition under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, applies upon the death of a male coparcener for determining shares in joint family property.
How the share of a deceased coparcener devolves under the proviso to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in the absence of a will.
What are the respective shares of the legal heirs of Mithu Sao and Puniya Devi in the joint family property after successive devolutions?
holdings: Upon the death of a male coparcener, a notional partition is deemed to occur immediately before death under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, entitling each coparcener and the widow to an equal share in the joint family property.
The share of a deceased coparcener under Section 6 proviso devolves by intestate succession among his heirs, including the widow, mother, and children, each receiving an equal portion of his share.
The widow of a coparcener is entitled to an equal share as a son in the notional partition and subsequent devolution, affirming the enhanced rights of Hindu women in property under the Act.
doctrines: Notional partition under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Intestate succession in coparcenary property
Equal rights of female heirs in Hindu joint family property

card.dispute: The landlord fought to evict the tenant on grounds of sub-letting and rent arrears, claiming the tenant had illegally parted with possession to a sub-tenant who was running an independent business.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant sub-let the premises to a third party without the landlord's consent
Whether the tenant was in arrears of rent from January 2002 onwards
Whether the burden of proof was properly discharged by the landlord on the issue of sub-letting
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the orders of the lower rent authorities
holdings: Sub-letting is established when the landlord shows the sub-tenant is in exclusive possession, shifting the burden to the tenant to disprove it.
The tenant failed to rebut the presumption of sub-letting despite evidence of independent business by the occupant.
Exclusive possession by a third party, coupled with use of the premises for independent business, supports inference of sub-letting even without direct proof of rent payment.
The High Court correctly set aside the lower courts' orders as the findings on sub-letting were supported by evidence and legal principles.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1)(a) and (b)
doctrines: Burden of proof in sub-letting cases
Preponderance of probability
Inference of sub-letting from exclusive possession
Shifting burden of proof after prima facie case

card.dispute: The tenant's representatives sought to implead the landlords and a bailiff as accused in a criminal case alleging property damage and theft during an eviction, but the landlords and bailiff challenged the summoning order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in summoning the landlords and bailiff as accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. despite their absence from the chargesheet?
Whether statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C. can independently form the basis for summoning accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C.?
Whether there was 'strong and cogent evidence' against the proposed accused to justify their summoning during trial?
holdings: The High Court erred in summoning the landlords and bailiff as accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. because no 'strong and cogent evidence' emerged during trial implicating them.
Statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. cannot independently constitute 'evidence' under Section 319 Cr.P.C.; they may only be used for corroboration.
The mere mention of names in the FIR or in police statements is insufficient to invoke Section 319 Cr.P.C. without supporting evidence led in court during trial.
doctrines: Strong and cogent evidence standard for invoking Section 319 Cr.P.C.
Distinction between evidence led in court and material collected during investigation

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka sought to reclaim the 'Beaulieu' estate property under Section 67 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, alleging the original 1900 conveyance was fraudulent, while private parties claimed lawful ownership based on historical transactions and possession.
issues_decided: Whether Section 67 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 can be used to challenge title to land held by private individuals for over a century?
Whether the State can invoke Section 67 to evict long-standing possessors based on an alleged fraud in a 1900 conveyance deed?
Whether the Deputy Commissioner had jurisdiction to pass an eviction order under Section 67(2) without providing a one-year period for filing a civil suit as per Section 67(3)?
holdings: Section 67 does not empower the State to dispute title of individuals holding property for over 100 years; it applies only to lands not already owned by private parties.
The State cannot invoke Section 67 to challenge a century-old conveyance based on unproven allegations of fraud, especially after having acquired portions of the same land without objection.
The Deputy Commissioner lacked jurisdiction to pass an eviction order within 21 days, as Section 67(3) allows one year for aggrieved persons to file a civil suit, making the order ultra vires.
doctrines: Fraud must be pleaded and proved, not presumed
Long and uninterrupted possession with State acquiescence negates State reclamation claims
Jurisdictional limits of revenue authorities under Section 67
Principle of estoppel against the State in property matters

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a borrower and a subsequent purchaser of mortgaged land disputed whether a 1969 document was a mortgage by conditional sale and if the suit to redeem the property was within limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the document dated 28.07.1969 (Ex.P-1) is a mortgage by conditional sale under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act?
Whether the suit for redemption was filed within the period of limitation under the Limitation Act?
What is the proper form of decree where a subsequent transferee holds title to property that must be retransferred to the original owner upon redemption?
holdings: A document that appears as a sale but is intended to secure a loan is a mortgage by conditional sale under Section 58(c) if the right to repurchase exists upon repayment.
A suit for redemption of mortgaged property is governed by Article 61(a) of the Limitation Act, allowing 30 years from the date the right to redeem accrues.

When a subsequent purchaser holds title to property that must be conveyed to the original owner, the court may direct the purchaser to join in the conveyance and ensure restitution of sale consideration to prevent injustice.
doctrines: Mortgage by conditional sale
Restitution of unjust enrichment
Complete justice under Article 142
Specific performance with joinder of subsequent transferee

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and others challenged the High Court's acquittal of J. Jayalalitha and others in a corruption case involving disproportionate assets and the setting aside of property confiscation orders.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the respondents of charges under Sections 120B and 109 IPC read with Sections 13(1)(e) and 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988?
Whether the conviction and sentence of accused A2 to A4 should be restored based on the evidence on record?
Whether the properties of the accused firms should be confiscated as proceeds of corruption?
holdings: The Supreme Court upheld the prosecution's appeal, holding that the High Court's acquittal was erroneous and that the charges of criminal conspiracy and abetment under IPC and corruption under the Prevention of Corruption Act were substantiated by evidence.
The conviction and sentence of accused A2 to A4 were restored as the evidence proved their involvement in amassing disproportionate assets through shell entities.
The Trial Court was directed to enforce the confiscation of properties and ensure the accused serve their remaining sentences in compliance with the law.
doctrines: Purposive interpretation of anti-corruption laws
Doctrine of constructive possession in asset confiscation
Principle of proportionality in sentencing for corruption
Doctrine of abatement of appeal upon death of accused

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over the validity of a final decree in a partition suit concerning 68 acres 10 guntas of land, specifically whether transferees from a co-sharer could claim rights over the property without the consent of other co-sharers and whether the appellants were barred by delay, waiver, or pattedar rights.
issues_decided: Whether a co-sharer can validly sell the entire joint property under Mohammedan Law without the consent of other co-sharers?
Whether the doctrine of approbate and reprobate applies to the heirs of Late Nawab Jung based on their conduct in earlier proceedings?
Whether the appellants are guilty of inordinate delay or laches in asserting their rights in the final decree proceedings?
What is the effect of the Urban Land Ceiling Act proceedings on the ownership rights in the disputed property?
holdings: Under Mohammedan Law, a co-sharer cannot validly sell the entire joint property without the consent of other co-sharers, and such a sale does not bind non-consenting co-sharers.
The appellants did not take inconsistent legal stands, and thus the doctrine of approbate and reprobate does not apply; their actions were protected by the doctrine of lis pendens.
The appellants did not suffer from inordinate delay or laches, as the preliminary decree had attained finality and final decree proceedings were initiated within limitation.
The Urban Land Ceiling Act proceedings were not properly placed on record and lapsed; the respondents cannot claim better title than their vendor, and the State may examine ceiling issues separately.
provisions: Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1350 Fasli, Section 25
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Doctrine of approbate and reprobate
Principle of constructive res judicata
Rule against unauthorized alienation by co-sharer under Mohammedan Law

card.dispute: The Greater Bombay Co-operative Bank challenged the Bombay High Court's decision setting aside an attachment order and directing the admission of Mr. Nagaraj Ganeshmal Jain as a member of a housing cooperative society, based on an alleged prior sale of the flat.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered agreement to sell can confer any right, title, or interest in immovable property?
Whether the respondent could claim ownership and membership in the society based on an unregistered agreement to sell?
Whether the attachment of the flat by the bank was valid despite the alleged prior sale?
holdings: An unregistered agreement to sell does not transfer any right, title, or interest in immovable property; only a registered deed of conveyance can effect such a transfer under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act provides only a limited defence and cannot be used to assert title or claim membership in a cooperative society.

The respondent had no valid claim to the flat as the alleged agreement to sell was unregistered, unsupported by original documents, and raised suspicions of fabrication; thus, the attachment order in favor of the bank remains valid.
doctrines: Doctrine of Registration under the Transfer of Property Act
Section 53A as a shield, not a sword
Fraud vitiates all transactions

card.dispute: The appellant Vasanthi sued to declare her title and recover possession of a property from Venugopal (deceased), who was in possession under an earlier agreement for sale; the dispute centered on whether Venugopal’s heirs could claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents (heirs of Venugopal) could claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act despite not filing a suit for specific performance.
Whether the appellant had notice of the prior agreement for sale or part performance thereof.
Whether the courts below erred in denying the appellant's claim based on Section 53A.
holdings: To claim protection under Section 53A, the party must prove they were always ready and willing to perform the contract, which the respondents failed to establish.
A transferee for value without notice of a prior agreement or part performance is not barred by Section 53A, and the appellant here acted in good faith.
Mere possession and lapse of limitation for specific performance do not automatically entitle a party to protection under Section 53A without fulfilling all conditions.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A
Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Notice to transferee

card.dispute: The tenant-appellants challenged the eviction order passed in favor of the respondent-landlord, who claimed ownership based on an adoption deed, over a shop in Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant made out a prima facie case to contest the eviction application under Section 25B(4) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
Whether the Rent Controller and High Court erred in rejecting the tenant's application for leave to contest?
holdings: A tenant is entitled to leave to contest an eviction proceeding if the grounds raised disclose a prima facie defence that could defeat the landlord's claim.
The rejection of the tenant's application for leave to contest was erroneous as the grounds relating to ownership, landlord-tenant relationship, and bona fide need raised triable issues.
doctrines: Prima facie defence in eviction proceedings
Liberal approach to grant leave to contest under rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellants, Anand Kumar Mohatta and another, challenged the quashing of an FIR and charge sheet filed against them by the State, arising from a 1993 development agreement where a ₹1 crore interest-free deposit was not returned, leading to criminal prosecution for alleged misappropriation.
issues_decided: Whether the non-refund of a deposit under a development agreement constitutes a criminal offence under the IPC
Whether the FIR and charge sheet should be quashed under Section 482 Cr.P.C. as the dispute is essentially civil in nature
Whether the criminal proceedings were mala fide and constituted an abuse of process
holdings: Non-refund of a deposit under a contractual agreement, without more, does not amount to criminal misappropriation or cheating if there is a bona fide dispute about performance of the contract.
A criminal proceeding arising from a purely civil dispute should be quashed if it is used as a tool of harassment and not for genuine prosecution.
The failure to seek recovery of money through civil remedies, combined with the lack of demand for refund, indicates mala fide intent in initiating criminal proceedings.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 403 (Dishonest misappropriation of property)
Indian Penal Code, Section 409 (Criminal breach of trust)
doctrines: Quashing of criminal proceedings for abuse of process
Distinction between civil and criminal liability in commercial disputes
Mala fide prosecution as grounds for invoking inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: Apollo Zipper India Limited (landlord) sued W. Newman and Co. Ltd. (tenant) for eviction and rent recovery, and the tenant sought leave to defend the summary suit, which the High Court allowed but the Supreme Court reversed.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant raised a substantial defense to warrant leave to defend a summary eviction suit.
Whether the landlord's title over the premises was properly established for the purpose of eviction.
Whether the suit was maintainable under the Transfer of Property Act instead of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act.
holdings: The tenant failed to raise any substantial or arguable defense, and the grounds for defense were frivolous and lacked legal or factual basis, so leave to defend the summary suit should not have been granted.

The landlord's title was prima facie established through the tenant's conduct, including failure to challenge a quit notice, willingness to pay rent, and admissions in pleadings, which barred the tenant from later disputing ownership.
The suit was maintainable under the Transfer of Property Act because the monthly rent exceeded Rs. 10,000, placing the premises outside the protection of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 3(f)
The Rules applicable to the Original Side Jurisdiction of the High Court at Calcutta, Rule 1(B), Rule 6, Rule 9
doctrines: Waiver of objection to notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act if not raised promptly
Attornment by conduct
Summary procedure not to be defeated by raising frivolous defenses

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of a contract to sell immovable property, and the respondents challenged the admissibility of the unregistered sale agreement.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered sale agreement dated 9th July 2003 is admissible in evidence for a suit of specific performance despite mandatory registration requirements under Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act, 1908.
Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the document solely on non-registration without considering its admissibility under the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908.
holdings: An unregistered document containing a contract to transfer immovable property for consideration is inadmissible to confer title or affect property under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, but may be admitted as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance under the proviso to that section.

Such an unregistered document cannot be used to claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, but its genuineness and binding nature can be adjudicated during trial based on oral and documentary evidence.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Admissibility of unregistered documents in specific performance suits
Prospective operation of Section 17(1A) of the Registration Act, 1908

card.dispute: The appellants sought referral to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which the High Court denied, holding that the agreements were not interconnected with the principal lease agreement, while the respondents alleged fraud and non-payment of lease rentals.
issues_decided: Whether the agreements between the parties are interconnected such that the disputes fall within the scope of the arbitration clause in the principal agreement?
Whether allegations of fraud in the transaction are sufficient to deny referral to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
holdings: The four agreements are integral to the common commercial objective of commissioning a solar power plant and are interconnected, warranting referral of all parties to arbitration under the arbitration clause in the principal lease agreement.
Mere allegations of fraud, especially those not involving serious or complex criminal wrongdoing, do not bar referral to arbitration; such issues can be examined by the arbitrator.
doctrines: Separability of arbitration clause
Kompetenz-Kompetenz
Business efficacy of commercial agreements
Seriousness of fraud doctrine

card.dispute: The State Bank of Travancore challenged a High Court interim order that stayed enforcement proceedings under the SARFAESI Act on deposit of a partial amount, despite the availability of an alternative statutory remedy.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a writ petition under Article 226 to stay SARFAESI proceedings without requiring exhaustion of the statutory remedy under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act?
Whether an interim order staying enforcement under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, passed without considering the availability of alternative remedies, is sustainable in law?
Whether the High Court erred in granting interim relief without affording the bank an opportunity to contest the maintainability of the writ petition?
holdings: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition under Article 226 when an efficacious alternative remedy was available under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act.
Interim orders staying SARFAESI proceedings without considering statutory remedies and public interest implications are unsustainable and contrary to settled law.
Courts must exercise caution in granting interim relief in financial recovery matters, especially where public money and national economic health are at stake.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(3A)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedies
Efficacious alternative remedy doctrine
Judicial discipline under Article 141
Public interest in recovery of public money
Circumspection in granting interim relief under Article 226

card.dispute: The State Bank of India (appellant) sought to enforce a mortgage on a flat mortgaged by directors of Allwyn Alloys Pvt. Ltd., while respondents 5 and 6 claimed ownership via a prior sale and possession, challenging the bank's auction of the property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could permit respondents 5 and 6 to approach another forum for adjudicating their title despite the DRT and DRAT having already decided the issue.
Whether the High Court could grant interim relief, including a direction to deposit Rs. 25 lakhs, in a matter governed by the SARFAESI Act.
holdings: The High Court erred in allowing respondents 5 and 6 to approach another forum, as the SARFAESI Act bars civil courts from entertaining disputes over secured assets, which are exclusively within the jurisdiction of DRT/DRAT.

The High Court's direction to deposit Rs. 25 lakhs in an interest-bearing account was unjustified and beyond its powers under the SARFAESI Act, which prohibits injunctions against enforcement actions.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 34
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of DRT under SARFAESI Act
Bar on civil court jurisdiction in secured asset matters

card.dispute: Two daughters claimed equal coparcenary rights in their father's joint family property against their nephew, who filed a partition suit excluding them on the ground that they were born before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and had married prior to the 2005 amendment.
issues_decided: Whether daughters born before the enactment of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 are entitled to coparcenary rights under the amended Section 6 of the Act if the coparcener was alive on 9th September 2005?
Whether the 2005 amendment to Section 6 applies retrospectively to partition suits pending as of that date?
Whether a preliminary decree in a partition suit bars the application of the amended Section 6?
holdings: The 2005 amendment to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act grants coparcenary rights by birth to daughters regardless of when they were born, provided the coparcener was alive on 9th September 2005.
The rights under the amended Section 6 apply to pending partition suits, as the final partition occurs upon the final decree, allowing for amendment of the preliminary decree to include daughters.
A preliminary decree in a partition suit does not extinguish the right of a daughter to claim coparcenary status under the amended law, which crystallizes upon the commencement of the 2005 amendment.
provisions: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, Section 6(1), Section 6(3), Section 6(5)
doctrines: Prospective and retroactive application of amendments
Notional partition and crystallization of rights
Principle of equality and removal of gender discrimination in inheritance
Finality of transactions prior to 20-12-2004 under Explanation to Section 6

card.dispute: Home buyers of Jaypee Infratech Limited projects fought with financial creditors and the Union of India over the distribution of deposited funds and the insolvency resolution process under the IBC.
issues_decided: Whether the court can direct a pro-rata disbursement of Rs 750 crores to home buyers seeking refunds during the pendency of CIRP
Whether JIL, JAL, or their promoters can participate in the CIRP
Whether RBI can be permitted to initiate CIRP against JAL under the IBC
holdings: The court cannot direct preferential payment to home buyers seeking refunds during CIRP as it violates the IBC's equal treatment of creditors and undermines the resolution process.
JIL, JAL, and their promoters are ineligible to participate in the CIRP due to disqualifications under Section 29A of the IBC.
RBI is permitted to initiate CIRP against JAL under the IBC, in line with its regulatory role and the statutory framework introduced by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2017.
doctrines: Parity among financial creditors during CIRP
Strict compliance with eligibility criteria under Section 29A
Judicial non-interference in preferential disbursement during insolvency
Primacy of expert regulatory bodies in financial matters

card.dispute: Dalip Singh (appellant) and Bhupinder Kaur (respondent) fought over whether an agreement to sell property for Rs.1,50,000 was valid and specifically enforceable, with the plaintiff claiming Rs.92,000 was paid as earnest money.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside concurrent findings of fact by the trial and lower appellate courts regarding the validity of the agreement to sell and payment of earnest money.
Whether the pleadings in the plaint and written statement alone could conclusively establish execution of the agreement and readiness and willingness for specific performance.
holdings: The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact without analyzing evidence, as such findings can only be disturbed if perverse or against the weight of evidence.
Mere pleadings in the plaint and their denial in the written statement cannot by themselves constitute proof of execution of an agreement or readiness and willingness for specific performance.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are binding unless perverse
Pleadings are not evidence and cannot substitute for proof

card.dispute: The Himachal Pradesh Cricket Association and others challenged the refusal to quash two FIRs alleging financial misconduct and property damage, claiming the cases were politically motivated civil disputes.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash the FIRs under Section 482 Cr.P.C. despite absence of prima facie criminality
Whether the chargesheets were maintainable after the State indicated it would not prosecute
Whether the proceedings amounted to abuse of process due to mala fides or political vendetta
holdings: The High Court should have quashed the FIRs as no prima facie case of cheating, fraud, or criminal breach of trust was made out.
The continuation of prosecution proceedings was unjustified given the State's decision not to pursue the case.
The investigation appeared biased, and allowing the trial to proceed would amount to abuse of process and injustice.
provisions: Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, 1984, Section 3
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Inherent powers to secure ends of justice
Principle of quashing proceedings in absence of prima facie case
Judicial caution in exercising powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The Indore Development Authority and other appellants challenged whether land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 due to non-deposit of compensation in court, when possession was taken and payment was tendered but refused.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'paid' in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act requires deposit of compensation in court under Section 31(2) of the 1894 Act
What constitutes valid physical possession under land acquisition laws
Whether Section 24 revives time-barred or stale claims
Whether the period of court litigation is excluded from the five-year period under Section 24(2)
Whether the principle of actus curiae neminem gravabit applies to exclude time during which authorities were restrained by court orders
holdings: The term 'paid' in Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act means tender of payment as in Section 31(1) of the 1894 Act; deposit in court under Section 31(2) is not required, and non-deposit does not cause lapse of acquisition.
Physical possession is validly taken by drawing a Panchnama, as per established practice in land acquisition cases.
Section 24 does not revive time-barred or stale claims; such claims cannot be entertained.
The period during which acquisition authorities are prevented from acting due to court orders must be excluded from the five-year period under Section 24(2).
The principle of actus curiae neminem gravabit applies; courts should not penalize authorities for delays caused by judicial orders, and such periods are excluded from Section 24(2) computation.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24
doctrines: Per incuriam
Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria
Tender of payment as discharge of obligation

card.dispute: ITC Limited, the auction purchaser, fought against Blue Coast Hotels Ltd. and others over the validity of a property sale conducted under SARFAESI Act, which the High Court had set aside due to alleged fraud and collusion.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the mortgaged property under Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act was valid despite non-compliance with Section 13(3A)?
Whether the auction purchaser acquired all rights of the secured creditor, including the right to possession and rents?
Whether there was fraud or collusion between the secured creditor and the auction purchaser invalidating the sale?
Whether the High Court was justified in granting equitable relief under Articles 226 and 136 of the Constitution to the debtor?
holdings: Non-compliance with Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act does not invalidate the sale if the debtor's conduct was dilatory and aimed only at delaying repayment.
The auction purchaser did not acquire full rights, including possession and rents, because the secured creditor retained constructive possession and did not transfer all interests.
The finding of fraud and collusion by the High Court was not sustainable, as mere awareness of pending disputes and procedural irregularities do not prove collusion.
The debtor is not entitled to equitable relief under Articles 226 and 136 due to unclean hands and blameworthy conduct in failing to repay the loan despite multiple opportunities.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(3A)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(6)
doctrines: Doctrine of clean hands
Constructive possession under SARFAESI Act
Transfer of rights by secured creditor under Section 13(6)
Equitable jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226

card.dispute: The Jharkhand State Housing Board challenged the maintainability of a suit for permanent injunction filed by private respondents who claimed possession of land allegedly acquired by the Board in 1965.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for permanent injunction is maintainable without seeking a declaration of title when the defendant raises a serious challenge to the plaintiff's title?
Whether the courts below erred in treating the suit as one for declaration of title when the plaint primarily sought only injunction?
Whether the plaintiff can succeed in a bare injunction suit when the defendant claims lawful possession based on land acquisition proceedings?
holdings: A suit for bare injunction is not maintainable if the defendant raises a serious challenge to the plaintiff's title; the plaintiff must seek a declaration of title in such cases.
Courts cannot treat a suit as one for declaration of title if the plaint does not pray for such relief, even if findings on title are made.
When a statutory authority claims possession under land acquisition, and the plaintiff does not seek declaratory relief, the suit for injunction alone cannot be sustained.
provisions: Bihar State Housing Board Act, Section 62
Bihar State Housing Board Act, Section 92
doctrines: Maintainability of suit for injunction
Pleadings must conform to relief sought
Requirement of declaration when title is disputed

card.dispute: The appellants (Kalawati and others) challenged the High Court's decree in favor of Rakesh Kumar for specific performance of an agreement to sell land dated 1986, claiming he was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
issues_decided: Whether Rakesh Kumar was ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement to sell from its execution till the decree?
Whether the vendors (appellants) failed to perform their obligations under the agreement, particularly in obtaining a 'no objection certificate'?
Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the Trial Court's dismissal of the suit for specific performance?
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his obligations, judged by conduct and circumstances throughout the period from agreement to decree.
Mere assertion of financial capacity is insufficient; there must be credible evidence of actual or arranged funds to pay the balance consideration.
A vague contractual obligation, such as obtaining an undefined 'no objection certificate' from unspecified authorities, cannot be enforced and does not justify specific performance.

The High Court erred in granting specific performance when the plaintiff failed to demonstrate readiness and willingness; the Trial Court’s finding was legally sound and should not have been overturned.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness doctrine in specific performance
Burden of proof in specific performance suits
Doctrine of vagueness in contractual terms

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Shami Mohd. and Jamila Begum disputed the validity of a mortgage and sale deed, and whether the mortgage could be redeemed.
issues_decided: Whether the oral gift and will in favor of Shami Mohd. were valid?
Whether the suit for declaration and cancellation of the mortgage and sale deeds was barred by limitation?
Whether the High Court was justified in decreeing redemption of the mortgage without following CPC procedures?
Whether the first appellate court exceeded its jurisdiction by recording findings not based on pleadings or evidence?
holdings: The court did not decide on the validity of the oral gift or will, as the suit was dismissed on other grounds.
The suit was barred by limitation under Articles 58 and 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963, as it was filed beyond the three-year period from the date of knowledge of the deeds.
The High Court erred in decreeing redemption of the mortgage without following the mandatory procedure under Order 34 Rules 7 and 8 of the CPC, and thus the decree could not be sustained.

The first appellate court wrongly recorded findings on inadequacy of consideration and lack of necessity for the mortgage and sale, despite absence of pleadings or evidence on these points, which was impermissible.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34 Rule 7
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34 Rule 8
doctrines: Right of redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act
Mandatory procedural compliance under Order 34 Rules 7 and 8 of CPC
Principle of conscious application of mind by appellate courts
Limitation bar for suits seeking declaration or cancellation of instruments

card.dispute: Emaar MGF Land Limited and Aftab Singh disputed whether a consumer complaint regarding a real estate transaction could be referred to arbitration, given the existence of an arbitration clause and the special jurisdiction of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
issues_decided: Whether consumer disputes fall within the category of non-arbitrable disputes despite an arbitration agreement between the parties.
Whether the amendment to Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, overrides the special jurisdiction of consumer fora under the Consumer Protection Act.
Whether the legislative intent behind Section 8(1) of the Arbitration Act was to override settled law on non-arbitrability of disputes governed by special statutes.
holdings: Consumer disputes are non-arbitrable because the Consumer Protection Act provides a special and exclusive remedy that cannot be bypassed by an arbitration agreement.
The amendment to Section 8(1) of the Arbitration Act does not override special statutes or render arbitrable disputes that are inherently non-arbitrable under public law regimes.

The phrase 'notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order' in Section 8(1) applies only to judicial precedents concerning the scope of judicial inquiry into arbitration agreements, not to override rulings on non-arbitrability under special statutes.
doctrines: Non-arbitrability of disputes under special statutes
Doctrine of implied exclusion of arbitration when special remedies exist
Principle of statutory interpretation: specific remedy excludes others
Public policy exceptions to arbitration

card.dispute: The borrower challenged whether an application under Section 17(1) of the SARFAESI Act is maintainable before physical possession of secured assets is taken by banks, i.e., at the stage of symbolic or constructive possession.
issues_decided: Whether a borrower can file an application under Section 17(1) of the SARFAESI Act before physical possession is taken by the secured creditor?
Whether symbolic or constructive possession under Rule 8 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 amounts to 'possession' under the SARFAESI Act?
Whether the Full Bench judgment of the Allahabad High Court restricting Section 17(1) remedies to post-physical-possession stage is correct?
holdings: A borrower can approach the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 17(1) of the SARFAESI Act at the stage of symbolic or constructive possession, i.e., even before physical possession is taken.
Rule 8 of the 2002 Rules recognises two distinct modes of possession—constructive (under sub-rules (1) and (2)) and physical (under sub-rule (3))—both valid under the SARFAESI Act.
The Full Bench judgment of the Allahabad High Court restricting Section 17(1) remedies to after physical possession is erroneous and is set aside.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(6)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17(1)
doctrines: Constructive possession
Statutory fiction
Maintainability of remedy at pre-possession stage

card.dispute: The appellant consortium challenged the High Court's decision that the Letter of Award created a binding contract, seeking enforcement of an arbitration clause allegedly operative at the bidding stage.
issues_decided: Whether a binding contract arose between the parties upon issuance of the Letter of Award during the bidding process.
Whether the arbitration clause in the draft Concession Agreement or bid documents applied to disputes at the pre-contract bidding stage.
Whether the High Court erred in holding that the Letter of Award created enforceable contractual obligations.
holdings: No binding contract emerged upon the Letter of Award; a contract would only arise upon placement of a purchase order or formal agreement.
An arbitration clause in bid documents governing future contracts does not apply to bidding-stage disputes unless expressly made binding at that stage.

Disputes arising during the tender process are to be adjudicated by civil courts, not arbitration, where the documents specify different dispute resolution mechanisms for pre- and post-contract stages.
doctrines: Doctrine of binding nature of tender documents
Doctrine of separability of arbitration clause
Doctrine of intention to create legal relations
Distinction between concluded contract and agreement to agree

card.dispute: The daughters of a deceased coparcener sued for partition of ancestral property, but the brother contested their right to claim partition, arguing they were not coparceners under the Tamil Nadu amendment due to their pre-amendment marriages.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, as daughters married before 1989, were entitled to claim partition in ancestral property under the Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act, 1989
Whether the daughters could claim a share in the property through succession after the death of their father and mother
holdings: Daughters married before the 1989 amendment are not coparceners and cannot claim partition in ancestral property under Section 29-A of the Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act, 1989.
Daughters are entitled to inherit their father’s and mother’s separate property through succession under Sections 8, 9, 10, 15, and 16 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, even if not coparceners.
provisions: Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act, 1989, Section 29-A
doctrines: Doctrine of coparcenary by birth
Doctrine of succession to separate property under the Hindu Succession Act
Prospective application of statutory amendments affecting inheritance rights

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed over the enforcement of an agreement for sale of a property with a marriage hall, where the respondent sought specific performance while the appellant claimed wrongful possession and sought recovery of the property.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was entitled to specific performance of the agreement for sale?
Whether the respondent proved continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract?
Whether the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the suit property?
holdings: The respondent failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his obligations under the contract, which is a condition precedent for specific performance under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Mere assertions in the plaint about readiness and willingness, without supporting actions or evidence, are insufficient to grant relief of specific performance.
The appellant is entitled to recovery of possession of the suit property as the respondent’s claim for specific performance fails, and the respondent’s continued possession is wrongful.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness doctrine in specific performance
Burden of proof on plaintiff in suits for specific performance

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's order directing him to hand over 8 flats and 16 parking spaces to respondent No.1 under a settlement agreement to which he was not a party.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could grant a mandatory interlocutory injunction against the appellant based on a settlement between respondents to which he was not a party?
Whether the principle of moulding of relief can be applied at the interlocutory stage to impose new obligations on a non-consenting party?
Whether the appellant could be bound by a consent arrangement between the respondents that altered his rights?
holdings: A mandatory interlocutory injunction should only be granted to restore the status quo ante and not to create new rights, especially when the party is not privy to the agreement forming the basis of the injunction.
The power to mould relief is exercisable at the final disposal stage, not at the interlocutory stage, and cannot be used to bind a party not involved in the consent terms.

A party cannot be compelled to perform obligations under an agreement to which they are not a signatory, and courts must not allow one party to benefit from its own failure to perform contractual duties.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX
doctrines: Status quo ante
Mandatory interlocutory injunction
Privity of contract
Moulding of relief

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the state's acquisition proceedings, alleging mala fide intent and fraud, where land was allegedly acquired for public purpose but diverted to private builders at throwaway prices.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act were vitiated by mala fide and fraud
Whether the withdrawal of acquisition after land transfers to private parties was illegal
Whether Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act applies to disentitle the state from acquiring the land
What relief is available to landholders, builders, and subsequent purchasers in light of the fraudulent acquisition
holdings: The decisions to initiate and withdraw acquisition were exercises of fraud on power and are set aside.
An award is deemed to have been passed on 26.08.2007 for lands covered under Section 6 and transferred between 27.08.2004 and 29.01.2010.
The period of invalid acquisition (24.08.2007 to judgment date) is excluded for computing inaction under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act.
Land vests in HUDA/HSIDC free of encumbrances; builders cannot recover sale consideration from landholders but may claim reimbursement of development costs.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
doctrines: Fraud on power
Mala fide exercise of statutory authority
Deemed award doctrine
Relief adjustment in public interest

card.dispute: The appellant, a widow, challenged the respondent nephew's claim to property under a purported gift deed, which she argued was invalid due to consideration and conditional enforcement after her death.
issues_decided: Whether a document styled as a gift deed but executed for consideration can be treated as a valid gift under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

Whether a gift deed that takes effect only after the death of the donor and reserves possession and enjoyment with the donor during her lifetime constitutes a valid gift or should be treated as a will.
holdings: A gift must be voluntary and without consideration; a transfer made for consideration cannot be a valid gift under Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

A gift that takes effect only after the death of the donor and reserves possession and enjoyment with the donor during her lifetime is not a valid gift but is in the nature of a will, and does not effect a completed transfer during the donor’s lifetime.
doctrines: Essential elements of a valid gift: transfer without consideration, acceptance during donor's lifetime, and compliance with formalities.
Doctrine of incomplete gift: where possession and enjoyment are retained by the donor and the gift is conditional, it remains incomplete and revocable.
Distinction between gift and will: a transfer taking effect after death is testamentary in nature and governed by the law of succession, not the Transfer of Property Act.

card.dispute: The brothers disputed whether a 1994 memorandum of settlement, intended to implement their father's oral property division, was valid and enforceable despite being unregistered and unstamped.
issues_decided: Whether the memorandum of settlement dated 09.09.1994 was compulsorily registrable under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether an unregistered and unstamped document can be admitted in evidence for any purpose in a partition suit
Whether such a document can be used for collateral purposes if made admissible by payment of stamp duty and penalty
holdings: A written memorandum recording a family arrangement that effects transfer of rights in immovable property is compulsorily registrable under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.
An unregistered and unstamped document cannot be admitted in evidence for the primary purpose of proving partition or division of property by metes and bounds.
Such a document may be admitted for collateral purposes like proving severancy of title or nature of possession, provided it is impounded after payment of stamp duty and penalty.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XII Rule 3
doctrines: Family arrangement doctrine
Doctrine of severancy in partition
Rule against admissibility of unregistered documents for creating rights in immovable property
Collateral use doctrine for unregistered instruments

card.dispute: The appellant contested the validity of an unregistered exchange deed involving ancestral property, while the respondents sought to declare it invalid and assert their coparcenary rights.
issues_decided: Whether the property received by a coparcener in a partition retains the character of coparcenary property after the birth of his sons?
Whether an unregistered exchange deed involving immovable property valued over Rs. 100 is admissible in evidence?
Whether the appellant can claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act without pleading part performance?
holdings: Property received by a coparcener in partition remains coparcenary property upon the birth of his sons, in which they acquire a right by birth.
An unregistered exchange deed involving immovable property valued at Rs. 100 or more is inadmissible in evidence under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908.
A party cannot claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act without pleading part performance in the written statement.
doctrines: Coparcenary property revives upon birth of son
Inadmissibility of unregistered documents affecting immovable property
Plea of part performance must be specifically pleaded

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants on bona fide need grounds, and the dispute centered on whether an eviction petition against one joint tenant is binding on all legal heirs inheriting tenancy after the original tenant's death.
issues_decided: Whether the legal heirs of a deceased tenant inherit the tenancy as joint tenants or as tenants-in-common under the Delhi Rent (Control) Act, 1958
Whether an eviction petition filed against one of the joint tenants is sufficient to bind all legal heirs of the deceased tenant
Whether the High Court was correct in allowing the objections under Section 47 read with Order XXI Rule 26(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure during execution proceedings
holdings: Legal heirs of a deceased tenant inherit the tenancy as joint tenants, and the tenancy continues as a single unit; occupation by one is deemed occupation by all.
An eviction petition against one joint tenant is sufficient and binding on all joint tenants, as joint tenancy constitutes one tenancy under the law.
The High Court erred in allowing belated objections during execution; the Rent Controller’s order stands as the legal heirs were already bound by the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 26(1)
doctrines: Joint tenancy in tenancy rights
Notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act binds all joint tenants
Principle of res judicata in execution proceedings
Codification of succession law under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956

card.dispute: The builder (appellant) sued the property owners (respondents) for specific performance of a development agreement, which the courts below dismissed due to vagueness in the contract terms.
issues_decided: Whether the development agreement was sufficiently certain to be specifically enforceable under Section 14(3)(c)(i) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963?
Whether the builder had a substantial interest such that monetary compensation would be inadequate, as required under Section 14(3)(c)(ii) of the Act?
Whether a suit for specific performance by a builder against property owners is maintainable under the Specific Relief Act?
holdings: A contract must clearly define the obligations of the parties to be specifically enforceable; vague terms regarding materials, flat sizes, and remuneration render the agreement unenforceable under Section 14(3)(c)(i).
The builder's interest was pecuniary and quantifiable; since monetary compensation could adequately cover the losses, specific performance was not warranted under Section 14(3)(c)(ii).

A suit for specific performance by a builder against landowners is not maintainable when the contract lacks certainty and the relief sought is not equitable, especially where damages are a sufficient remedy.
doctrines: Doctrine of certainty of terms in contracts for specific performance
Doctrine of adequacy of monetary compensation as an alternative remedy
Doctrine of non-enforceability of contracts requiring continuous court supervision

card.dispute: Susme Builders and another developer contested for the right to redevelop a slum rehabilitation project in Mumbai, while the Slum Rehabilitation Authority sought to cancel Susme's letter of intent due to delays and lack of required consent.
issues_decided: Whether the Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA) had jurisdiction to cancel Susme Builders' letter of intent under Section 13(2) or Section 3A(3)(c) and (d) of the Slum Act;
Whether the SRA's order rejecting Susme for lack of 70% slum dweller consent was valid when not specified in the initial notice;
Whether Susme Builders fulfilled the requirement of obtaining 70% consent from slum dwellers;
Whether J.G. Developers' agreements with slum dwellers were enforceable despite being based on false promises.
holdings: The SRA had the authority to cancel Susme's letter of intent under Section 13(2) of the Slum Act, or alternatively under Section 3A(3)(c) and (d), given the unique circumstances where slum dwellers were also landowners.
The SRA's rejection of Susme on grounds of lack of 70% consent was beyond the scope of the notice issued, which only cited delay, and thus that part of the High Court's judgment was set aside.
Susme failed to prove it had obtained 70% consent from slum dwellers even at the time of the Supreme Court hearing and was therefore not entitled to relief.
Agreements by J.G. Developers were legally unconscionable and unenforceable due to false promises of larger flats, disentitling them from continuing the project.
provisions: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 13(2)
Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 3A(3)(c) and (d)
doctrines: Doctrine of fair notice
Doctrine of unconscionability
Equitable jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat appealed against the High Court's acquittal of two public servants accused of accepting a bribe in a corruption case under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the demand and acceptance of illegal gratification under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's conviction based on lack of recovery from one of the accused
Whether the presumption under Section 20 of the Act was rightly applied in the absence of any explanation from the accused
holdings: Demand and acceptance of bribe by public servants can be established through credible witness testimony and corroborative scientific evidence like anthracene powder testing.
The High Court erred in acquitting the accused merely because no money was recovered from one of them, as the evidence showed joint participation in the act.
The presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act is rebuttable, but when the accused fail to offer any explanation, the court may presume acceptance of bribe.
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption under Section 20
Demand as sine qua non for offence under Section 7
Corroboration through scientific evidence in corruption cases

card.dispute: The states of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and the Union Territory of Puducherry fought over the equitable distribution of Cauvery river water.
issues_decided: Whether the Cauvery water agreements of 1892 and 1924 remained valid after Indian independence and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956
Whether the dispute fell under the bar of Article 363 of the Constitution
Whether the 1924 agreement had expired by its own terms
What constitutes an equitable apportionment of inter-state river waters and whether the Tribunal's allocation was just
holdings: The doctrine of paramountcy ceased after the 1947 Independence Act, but the 1892 and 1924 agreements remained valid as they concerned public interest and not sovereignty.
Article 363 does not bar the dispute as it does not involve sovereignty or integrity of India, and concerns a justiciable water-sharing issue.
The 1924 agreement was time-bound for 50 years and expired in 1974; thus, it cannot be enforced beyond that period.
Equitable apportionment of inter-state river waters must consider all relevant factors, including population, geography, and basic human needs, with drinking water as a priority.
doctrines: Doctrine of Equitable Apportionment
Helsinki Rules on the Uses of the Waters of International Rivers
National asset theory of inter-state river waters
Primacy of drinking water in water distribution

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a partition deed dated March 15, 1971, executed by Oubegaranadin, claiming that his sons (respondents 3 to 5) had no right to the suit property during his lifetime under customary law.
issues_decided: Whether the partition deed dated March 15, 1971, executed by Oubegaranadin in favor of his sons, is valid under the applicable personal law?
Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, applies to the parties, who are Christians, in the Union Territory of Puducherry?
Whether the French Civil Code governs the transaction, and if so, whether the formalities under that Code were complied with?
holdings: A partition deed executed by a father in favor of his sons during his lifetime is not valid unless it complies with the formalities of a gift or family settlement under the applicable personal law.
The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, does not apply to Christians in Puducherry, and customary law, influenced by the French Civil Code, governs their property transactions.
The partition deed must satisfy the formal requirements of donation inter vivos under Articles 931, 1075, 1076, and 1077 of the French Civil Code; absence of such compliance renders it void.
doctrines: Customary Hindu Law as applicable to Christians in Puducherry
Doctrine of donation inter vivos
Family settlement as an exception to formal partition
Non-applicability of Hindu Succession Act to non-Hindus

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the validity of a circular issued by the Delhi government requiring hospitals, including Moolchand Khairati Ram Trust, to provide free treatment to economically weaker sections, based on a prior High Court judgment.
issues_decided: Whether the circular dated 2.2.2012 issued by the GNCTD imposing conditions of free treatment on hospitals was valid and legally enforceable.
Whether the conditions for free treatment could be imposed without the hospitals being parties to the original writ petition in Social Jurists v. GNCTD.
