Whether the imposition of free treatment obligations amounted to a unilateral novation of contract violating principles of fair procedure.
holdings: The circular dated 2.2.2012 is valid as it was based on a policy for charitable use of land allotted at concessional rates and supported by findings of a committee inquiry.
Hospitals need not be formal parties to a writ petition if a public interest judgment applies to institutions benefiting from public resources under specific conditions.
The obligation to provide free treatment is not a new contractual term but a fulfillment of original charitable conditions, so no unilateral novation occurs.
provisions: Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991
doctrines: Doctrine of Public Trust
Principle of Charitable Purpose Fulfillment
Doctrine of Prospective Overruling
Principle of Non-Unilateral Novation of Contract

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed whether the respondent was entitled to specific performance of an agreement to sell a shop, as the appellants refused to execute the sale deed despite receipt of earnest money.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-plaintiff proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract for specific performance?
Whether the First Appellate Court and High Court were justified in reversing the Trial Court's dismissal of the suit for specific performance?
holdings: To claim specific performance, a plaintiff must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform, including capacity to pay the balance consideration, supported by evidence; mere assertion is insufficient.

The First Appellate Court and High Court erred in granting specific performance without proper appreciation of evidence on readiness and willingness; the Trial Court's finding was correct and restoration of earnest money with interest was appropriate.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Discretionary nature of specific performance relief

card.dispute: Ambalal Sarabhai Enterprises Ltd. fought with K.S. Infraspace LLP over whether a property dispute concerning an agreement to sell land could be classified as a commercial dispute under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute falls within the definition of a 'commercial dispute' under Section 2(1)(c) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, specifically sub-clause (vii) relating to immovable property used exclusively in trade or commerce.
Whether the Commercial Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit based on the nature of the property's use at the time of the agreement.
holdings: A dispute concerning immovable property is only a commercial dispute under the Act if the property was actually used exclusively in trade or commerce at the relevant time, not merely likely or ready to be used.
The Commercial Court lacked jurisdiction because there was no evidence that the property was actually used for trade or commerce in 2012 when the agreement to sell was executed.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order VII Rule 10
Civil Procedure Code, Order XVA (Case Management Hearing)
Civil Procedure Code, Order XX Rule 1
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Strict construction of jurisdictional provisions
Fast-track adjudication of commercial disputes

card.dispute: The tenant (appellant) challenged the bank's possession of a mortgaged residential flat under SARFAESI Act, claiming tenancy rights, while the bank argued the tenancy was fabricated to obstruct debt recovery.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant-tenant had a valid and bona fide tenancy entitled to protection against enforcement under the SARFAESI Act
Whether the tenancy, if any, could survive after the issuance of a Section 13(2) notice under the SARFAESI Act
Whether the appellant was entitled to interim protection from eviction during SARFAESI proceedings
holdings: A tenant claiming protection under rent laws must prove a valid and bona fide tenancy with credible evidence; mere photocopies of rent receipts are insufficient.

A tenancy created after or continuing beyond the issuance of a Section 13(2) notice is barred under Section 13(13) of the SARFAESI Act and such occupant becomes a tenant-at-sufferance with no legal rights.
A tenant-at-sufferance, akin to a trespasser, cannot resist possession proceedings under SARFAESI Act and is not entitled to protection under rent control laws.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(13)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 35
doctrines: Tenant-at-sufferance doctrine
Bona fide tenancy requirement under SARFAESI Act
Priority of SARFAESI Act over rent control laws
Self-executory nature of SARFAESI proceedings

card.dispute: Arshnoor Singh (appellant) challenged the validity of sale deeds executed by his father Dharam Singh in favor of Harpal Kaur and others, claiming the property was coparcenary and could not be sold without legal necessity.
issues_decided: Whether the suit property remained coparcenary property in the hands of Dharam Singh qua his son Arshnoor Singh
Whether the sale deeds executed by Dharam Singh in favor of Harpal Kaur were valid without legal necessity or benefit to the estate
Whether the subsequent sale deed by Harpal Kaur to respondents 2 and 3 was valid in light of lis pendens
holdings: The share of property allotted to Dharam Singh upon partition remained coparcenary property as regards his male descendant, Arshnoor Singh, who became a coparcener by birth.
Sale of coparcenary property by a father without legal necessity or benefit to the estate is invalid; burden to prove such necessity lies on the alienee, who failed here.
A transfer of property during pending litigation (lis pendens) does not confer title if the transferor had no valid title, rendering the subsequent sale deed void.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 52 (doctrine of lis pendens)
doctrines: Coparcenary property retains its character post-partition for male lineal descendants
Doctrine of legal necessity in alienation of coparcenary property
Doctrine of lis pendens

card.dispute: The appellant, Ajit Kaur, claimed full ownership of disputed land under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, based on prior possession, while the respondents contested her claim, asserting she was a trespasser without a pre-existing right.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant acquired full ownership of the property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, based on her possession of the land.
Whether Section 14(1) applies to a Hindu female who was in possession of property without a pre-existing title or right at the commencement of the Act.
Whether the gift of property to the appellant’s mother for maintenance created a pre-existing right that could mature into full ownership under Section 14(1).
holdings: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, converts a limited estate into full ownership only if the female had a pre-existing right, title, or claim to the property at the time the Act came into force.
Mere possession of property without a vestige of title or lawful claim does not attract Section 14(1); the provision does not confer title on a trespasser.

Where a transfer recognizes a pre-existing right such as maintenance or partition share, Section 14(1) applies and overrides any restrictions, but such rights must be established under the specified modes in the Explanation to Section 14(1).
provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Explanation to Section 14(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of pre-existing right under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Liberal construction of beneficial legislation in favor of Hindu women
Distinction between limited estate and full ownership under Hindu law

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the grant of permanent injunction to a tenant who claimed possession of the premises, which the landlord alleged was vacated in 1991 and where rent had not been paid for over fifteen years.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant proved actual and continuous possession of the suit premises on the date of filing the suit?
Whether the tenant's possession was lawful in the absence of rent payments and requisite licences for business operations?
Whether the appellate courts erred in relying on a prior suit and Purshis Ex.-41 to infer continued possession?
Whether the tenant was entitled to the equitable relief of permanent injunction under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act?
holdings: To obtain a permanent injunction under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, a plaintiff must prove actual possession on the date of filing the suit, which the tenant failed to establish.
Lawful possession requires payment of rent and compliance with legal conditions; non-payment of rent for over fifteen years and lack of business licences negated lawful possession.
The First Appellate Court and High Court erred in inferring possession based on a prior suit and Purshis Ex.-41 without sufficient evidence, overturning concurrent findings unsupported by proof.
A party seeking equitable relief must come with clean hands; suppression of non-payment of rent and exaggerated tenancy claims disentitled the tenant to injunction.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Actual possession as a prerequisite for injunction
Lawful possession requiring payment of rent
Proper appreciation of evidence in appellate review

card.dispute: The appellant (seller) and respondent (buyer) fought over whether the seller breached an agreement to sell agricultural land, entitling the buyer to specific performance despite delays and land ceiling issues.
issues_decided: Whether the seller failed to perform her part of the agreement by not providing necessary title and land ceiling documents?
Whether the buyer's delay in depositing the balance sale consideration and source of funds affected his readiness and willingness to perform?
Whether the seller could raise the plea of hardship in resisting specific performance for the first time in appeal?
holdings: The seller failed to perform her contractual obligation by not providing the original sale deed and land ceiling clearance, justifying the buyer's refusal to pay the balance consideration.
The buyer demonstrated readiness and willingness by depositing the balance amount when directed by the court, and the source of funds did not negate his bonafides.
The plea of hardship cannot be raised for the first time in appeal if not pleaded in the written statement or framed as an issue in the trial court.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Specific performance of contract
Readiness and willingness of the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance
Plea of hardship in specific performance
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts

card.dispute: Homebuyers and petitioners fought against the Union of India and others over the non-completion of Amrapali Group's real estate projects and the misuse of funds, seeking protection of their interests and project completion.
issues_decided: Whether the registration of Amrapali Group under RERA should be cancelled due to violations
Whether the lease deeds granted by Noida and Greater Noida Authorities to Amrapali Group could be cancelled for non-compliance and fraud
Whether dues of authorities and banks could be recovered from project assets or from other properties
Whether homebuyers could be denied possession due to defaults by the builder and authorities
holdings: The registration of Amrapali Group under RERA was cancelled due to gross violations and fraud against homebuyers.
The lease deeds were cancelled and rights vested in a Court Receiver due to breach of terms and collusion with authorities.
Dues of Noida, Greater Noida, and banks must be recovered from attached properties, not from ongoing projects or homebuyers.
Homebuyers are entitled to possession and completion certificates regardless of builder defaults, as their funds were misused by the builder and authorities.
provisions: Lease Deeds executed by Noida Authority and Greater Noida Authority
doctrines: Doctrine of Public Trust
Fraud vitiates all transactions
Parens patriae jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
Principle of equitable protection of homebuyers

card.dispute: Brig. Sukhjeet Singh (Retd.) challenged the rejection of his application to lead additional evidence in appeal to prove a Trust Deed and Resolution permitting sale of trust land, after being convicted for cheating in a land sale case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to allow additional evidence under Section 391 Cr.P.C. to prove the Trust Deed and Resolution dated 18.10.1989?
Whether the rejection of the application for additional evidence was justified on grounds of delay or malafide intent?
Whether the Appellate Court failed to exercise its discretion under Section 391 Cr.P.C. in a case where the trial court did not consider key documents due to non-proof?
holdings: The Appellate Court must consider allowing additional evidence under Section 391 Cr.P.C. when such evidence is necessary for justice, regardless of delay, especially where the trial court did not examine crucial documents.

An application for additional evidence cannot be rejected merely on grounds of belated filing or alleged malafide if the accused has a legitimate need to prove foundational documents affecting criminal liability.
Where a certified copy of a document exists and omission in a typed version is inadvertent, the court should not deny justice on technical grounds or suspicion of misleading the court.
doctrines: Judicial discretion under Section 391 Cr.P.C. to take additional evidence in appeal
Principle of fair opportunity to prove foundational documents affecting guilt
Rule against technical rejection of evidence where justice demands consideration

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority and others contested whether the proviso to Section 24 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 applies to Section 24(1)(b) or Section 24(2), affecting the lapse of land acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 24 of the 2013 Act is a proviso to Section 24(1)(b) or Section 24(2).
Whether land acquisition proceedings lapse under Section 24(2) if five years have passed since the award and physical possession or compensation has not been made.
holdings: The proviso to Section 24 is a proviso to Section 24(1)(b), not Section 24(2), as the language and context of the proviso relate to compensation deposit, not lapsing of acquisition.
Section 24(2) operates independently; if an award is over five years old and physical possession has not been taken or compensation paid, acquisition proceedings lapse regardless of the proviso.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(1)(b)
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
doctrines: Beneficial legislation interpretation
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Proviso as an exception to the main provision
Rule against arbitrary classification under Article 14

card.dispute: DLF Homes Panchkula (P) Ltd. fought with flat buyers over the refund of amounts deposited, including interest, and entitlement to compensation due to delayed possession or cancellation of flat allotments.
issues_decided: Whether flat buyers are entitled to interest on amounts deposited in case of refund or delayed possession, and at what rate and from which date?
How to compute compensation in refund and possession cases involving transfers between original and subsequent allottees?
How to handle refund claims where the original allottee has died and multiple legal heirs are claiming the amount?
Whether additional compensation beyond agreed interest is payable to flat buyers in consumer disputes settled by mutual understanding?
holdings: Flat buyers in refund cases are entitled to interest at 9% from the date of deposit until refund; in possession cases, interest accrues after the agreed three-year period from the date of agreement.
In transfer cases, interest on deposits by original allottees is calculated from the date of transfer; for subsequent deposits by transferees, interest runs from the date of such deposits.

Where an original allottee dies, the refund amount should be distributed between legal heirs (widow and children as one share, mother as the other) with indemnity bonds to protect against future claims.
No additional compensation beyond the agreed interest is payable when disputes are resolved by mutual understanding and in line with prior judicial directions.
doctrines: Principle of compensation in consumer disputes
Doctrine of agreed settlement in appellate proceedings
Indemnity to secure against conflicting claims by legal heirs

card.dispute: DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. fought with homebuyers over delayed possession of flats and the quantum of compensation, including interest and damages, due to such delay.
issues_decided: Whether consumer forums can award multiple heads of compensation for a single default of delayed possession?
Whether the rate of interest and compensation awarded by consumer forums was justified and in line with agreed terms?
Whether transferees of original allottees are entitled to interest from the date of transfer or expiry of assured possession period?
holdings: Consumer forums cannot award multiple heads of compensation like interest, lumpsum damages, and litigation costs for a single default of delayed possession when parties have agreed on a specific rate of compensation.
Interest awarded must be reasonable and not arbitrary; a uniform rate of 9% per annum on deposited amounts is appropriate, replacing higher or rule-of-thumb rates.
Transferees of flats are entitled to interest at 9% per annum from the later of the expiry of three years from the agreement or the date of transfer.
doctrines: Principle of compensation for deprivation of use of money
Rule against double recovery for same cause of action
Judicial restraint in awarding punitive damages

card.dispute: The appellant, Dr. Lakshman, challenged the High Court's quashing of criminal complaints he filed against developers and individuals for cheating, fraud, and criminal conspiracy in a land deal involving Rs.9 crores.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. based on factual disputes and alleged novation of contract?
Whether allegations of cheating and fraud in a civil contract can sustain criminal prosecution despite parallel civil remedies?
Whether the existence of a civil suit or complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act bars criminal proceedings for cheating and conspiracy?
holdings: The High Court erred in entering factual findings on novation, schedule authenticity, and mens rea at the Section 482 stage; such issues require full trial.
A civil dispute may give rise to criminal liability if there are allegations of fraudulent intent, cheating, or criminal breach of trust at the inception of the agreement.
Filing a civil suit or a complaint under Section 138 NI Act does not bar prosecution for offences like cheating and conspiracy where fraud is prima facie alleged.
doctrines: Novation of contract
Mens rea in cheating and criminal breach of trust
Separate remedies for civil and criminal liability
Scope of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The appellants (sons of the donor) challenged the validity of a gift deed executed by their father in favor of the respondent, alleging it was forged and that the property was ancestral, while the respondent claimed the gift was valid and properly executed.
issues_decided: Whether the gift deed was specifically denied in the pleadings so as to require the donee to examine an attesting witness under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Whether the suit property was ancestral in nature and beyond the donor's power to gift
Whether the appellants proved forgery or fabrication of the gift deed
Whether the non-filing of a replication amounts to admission of facts in the written statement
holdings: A specific denial of execution is required to trigger the proviso to Section 68 of the Evidence Act; mere allegations of forgery without denying execution does not suffice.
The suit property was not ancestral but self-acquired, as it was purchased by the donor's father and bequeathed by will, enabling the donor to validly gift it.
Allegations of forgery and fabrication must be specifically pleaded and proved; failure to do so results in the document being presumed valid.
Non-filing of a replication does not amount to admission of facts in the written statement; specific denial in affidavits can preserve the issue for trial.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8 Rule 3
doctrines: Specific denial under Section 68 of the Evidence Act
Burden of proof in cases of alleged forgery
Pleading requirements for fraud and misrepresentation
Admission by pleading or lack thereof

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants in a suit) challenged the High Court's decision to decree a suit for specific performance of a sale agreement based on alleged admissions, which the Supreme Court reviewed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could decree the suit solely on the basis of alleged admissions under Order XII Rule 6 of the CPC without a full trial.
Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to the equitable relief of specific performance without pleading and proving readiness and willingness from the beginning.
Whether categorical admissions were established through statements in a bail application and company balance sheets to justify a decree under Order XII Rule 6 of CPC.
holdings: A decree under Order XII Rule 6 of CPC cannot be granted merely on alleged admissions if there are serious factual disputes and the trial has already commenced; the suit must proceed on merits.
Readiness and willingness to perform the contract, required for specific performance, must be pleaded and proved from the outset and cannot be inferred from post-order conduct.

Statements in a bail application or entries in company balance sheets do not automatically constitute categorical admissions justifying a decree under Order XII Rule 6 without proper pleading and context.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XII Rule 6
Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c) read with Explanation (ii)
doctrines: Judgment on admission under Order XII Rule 6 CPC
Equitable discretion in granting specific performance
Pleading and proof of readiness and willingness in specific performance suits

card.dispute: Duncans Industries Ltd. (corporate debtor) challenged the maintainability of insolvency proceedings initiated by A.J. Agrochem (operational creditor) under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, arguing that prior consent of the Central Government under Section 16G(1)(c) of the Tea Act, 1953 was required.
issues_decided: Whether insolvency proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC are maintainable without prior consent of the Central Government under Section 16G(1)(c) of the Tea Act, 1953 when management of a tea company has been taken over by the Central Government?
Whether the provisions of the IBC override those of the Tea Act, 1953 in case of conflict?
holdings: Proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC are not equivalent to winding up or appointment of a receiver and thus do not require prior consent under Section 16G(1)(c) of the Tea Act, 1953.
The IBC, being a later and special legislation, has overriding effect over the Tea Act, 1953 under Section 238, and its provisions prevail to ensure timely resolution of insolvency.
doctrines: Doctrine of Special Legislation
Doctrine of Lex Posterior Derogat Priori
Doctrine of Overriding Effect under General and Special Laws

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over ownership and possession of certain agricultural lands, each claiming title through patta (land grant) and revenue records.
issues_decided: Whether the patta granted in favour of Gaya Din (appellants' ancestor) was validly issued and by whom.
Whether the respondents-plaintiffs proved their title to the suit properties in a suit for declaration.
Whether the first appellate court and High Court erred in setting aside the trial court's findings on the appellants' possession and title.
holdings: A patta granted in 1929 (Samvat 1986) by an illaqedar was valid, as the system of pawai had not been abolished then, and the subsequent grant under Section 28 of the Vindhya Pradesh Act, 1952 validated occupancy rights.

In a suit for declaration of title, plaintiffs must succeed on the strength of their own title, not on the weakness of the defendant's case; failure to produce title documents results in failure of proof.

The first appellate court and High Court erred in disregarding documentary evidence (Ex.D-20, revenue records, and official orders) showing valid patta and continuous possession by the appellants' family.
provisions: Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 5
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 6
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 22
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 28
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 7(c)
doctrines: Title must be proved on the strength of one's own case in declaratory suits
Revenue entries are not conclusive proof of title
Deemed pattedar status under land reform statutes

card.dispute: The dispute involved whether the High Court could interfere with an NCLT order under Article 226/227 of the Constitution despite the availability of an appeal to NCLAT, and whether allegations of fraud in the initiation of CIRP could be examined by the NCLT/NCLAT.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can interfere under Article 226/227 with an NCLT order when a statutory appeal to NCLAT is available.
Whether NCLT/NCLAT has jurisdiction to inquire into allegations of fraud in the initiation of CIRP.
holdings: The High Court can intervene under Article 226/227 if the NCLT acts without jurisdiction, particularly in matters involving administrative or statutory rights under laws like the MMDR Act, 1957, which fall outside the NCLT's adjudicatory scope.

NCLT and NCLAT have jurisdiction to examine allegations of fraud in the initiation of CIRP under Section 65 of the IBC, and such allegations do not justify bypassing the statutory appeal mechanism under Section 61.
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation of NCLT
Doctrine of alternative remedy
Judicial review under Article 226/227
Fraud vitiates proceedings

card.dispute: The Karnataka Housing Board challenged the maintainability of a revision petition before the National Commission against an order passed by the State Commission in execution proceedings arising from a consumer dispute.
issues_decided: Whether a revision petition under Section 21(b) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is maintainable before the National Commission against an order passed by the State Commission in execution proceedings?
Whether execution proceedings are a continuation of the original consumer dispute for the purpose of invoking revisional jurisdiction?
holdings: A revision petition under Section 21(b) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is not maintainable before the National Commission against an order passed in execution proceedings, as such proceedings are independent and not part of the original consumer dispute.

Execution proceedings are separate and independent from the original suit or consumer dispute and do not constitute a continuation of it, hence cannot be subject to revisional jurisdiction under Section 21(b).
doctrines: Distinction between appellate and revisional jurisdiction
Execution proceedings as independent proceedings
Jurisdictional limits of revisional powers

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's decree granting specific performance of an agreement for the sale of agricultural land, which was originally denied by the Trial Court and affirmed by the First Appellate Court.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to specific performance of the agreement for sale of agricultural land after a long delay and change in circumstances?
Whether the High Court was justified in granting specific performance with enhanced consideration despite long possession by subsequent purchasers?
Whether an alternative relief of compensation would meet the ends of justice in place of specific performance?
holdings: Specific performance of the agreement for sale cannot be granted where there has been long delay, change in land value, and prolonged possession by subsequent purchasers, making enforcement unjust.

The High Court erred in granting specific performance with enhanced consideration without considering the provisions of Sections 21 and 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and the practical realities of the case.

Compensation in lieu of specific performance is appropriate when justice so requires, especially where the plaintiff has also claimed alternative relief and circumstances render specific performance inequitable.
doctrines: Doctrine of specific performance as discretionary equitable relief
Doctrine of compensation in lieu of specific performance
Ends of justice as a guiding principle in granting equitable relief

card.dispute: Hindu and Muslim parties fought over the ownership and possession of the Ayodhya site, specifically the area where the Babri Masjid stood, with Hindus claiming it as the birthplace of Lord Ram and Muslims asserting it as a mosque.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed site is the birthplace of Lord Ram and whether Hindus have continuous worship and belief at the site
Whether the structure at the site was a mosque or a temple and whether it was built after demolishing a temple
Whether the plaintiffs (Hindu parties) have legal standing to sue through their next friends or as juristic persons
Whether the suit is barred by the Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991
holdings: The disputed site is the birthplace of Lord Ram according to the faith and belief of Hindus, supported by oral and documentary evidence, and worship has been continuous at the site.
The three-dome structure (Babri Masjid) was constructed on the site believed to be Lord Ram's birthplace, and there is evidence suggesting a prior temple structure was demolished.
Idols can have juristic personality under Hindu law, and the deity 'Ram Lalla' can be a legal person capable of holding title and being a plaintiff through a next friend.
The Places of Worship Act, 1991 does not apply to this dispute as the suit was already pending and the Act excludes the Ram Janmabhoomi-Babri Masjid site from its operation.
provisions: Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, Section 4
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Juristic personality of deities in Hindu law
Doctrine of adverse possession
Presumption of correctness of government publications (Gazetteers)
Doctrine of waiver of right to worship

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff appealed against the dismissal of a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell a property, claiming the defendant failed to execute the sale deed after receiving part payment.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff sufficiently averred and proved continuous readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract for specific performance?
Whether the trial court's assumptive finding on readiness and willingness could sustain the decree for specific performance?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to amend the plaint at the appellate stage to include averments of readiness and willingness?
Whether the second appeal involved a substantial question of law warranting interference under Section 100 CPC?
holdings: Readiness and willingness to perform must be expressly averred and proved; mere silence in pleadings and lack of testimony on this point renders the suit for specific performance indefensible.
An assumptive observation by the trial court on readiness and willingness cannot substitute for actual pleading and proof required under the Specific Relief Act.
Amendment of plaint to introduce readiness and willingness at the appellate stage is impermissible when it seeks to fill a foundational lacuna in the case.
No substantial question of law arose in the second appeal, and the High Court rightly refused to entertain new grounds not formulated under Section 100 CPC.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27
doctrines: Readiness and willingness as a condition precedent for specific performance
Substantial question of law in second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Amendment of pleadings at appellate stage
Proviso to Section 100(5) CPC as an exceptional power

card.dispute: The appellant (seller) and respondent (buyer) disputed whether the buyer was entitled to specific performance of an agreement for sale of property after the seller cancelled the agreement for non-payment of balance consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for specific performance was maintainable without challenging the cancellation of the agreement for sale.
Whether the respondent proved readiness and willingness to perform his obligations under the agreement.
Whether proper intimation of redemption of mortgage was given by the appellant to the respondent.
holdings: A suit for specific performance is not maintainable if the agreement has been validly cancelled and no declaratory relief is sought to set aside the cancellation.
The respondent failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract, especially by not appearing as a witness or providing evidence of financial capacity.
Proper intimation of redemption was given by the appellant via registered post with a copy of the release deed, fulfilling the contractual obligation.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Adverse presumption against non-examination of a party as witness
Maintainability of suit post-cancellation of agreement

card.dispute: Real estate developers challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code that deemed home buyers as financial creditors.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code infringes fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(g), and 300-A of the Constitution
Whether the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act (RERA) and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code operate in harmony or conflict
Whether home buyers/allottees are covered under Section 5(8)(f) of the Code as financial creditors even before the 2018 amendment
holdings: The amendment to the Code does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(g), or 300-A as it is a reasonable classification and serves a legitimate state interest.
RERA and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code provide concurrent remedies; in case of conflict, the Code prevails.
Allottees of flats were always financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the Code, and the 2018 amendment with its deeming fiction is merely clarificatory.
doctrines: Deeming fiction in statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction of statutes
Beneficial interpretation of remedial legislation

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) challenged the approval of a resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, arguing that it affected its public property rights without its statutory consent.
issues_decided: Whether the NCLT and NCLAT had jurisdiction to approve a resolution plan that created interests over MCGM's public lands without its approval under the MMC Act?
Whether Section 238 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code overrides the statutory rights of a third-party public authority like MCGM over its properties?
Whether a statement by MCGM's counsel in proceedings could bind the corporation in the absence of statutory authority?
holdings: The NCLT and NCLAT lacked jurisdiction to approve a resolution plan that created charges on MCGM's public properties without statutory approval under Sections 92 and 92A of the MMC Act.

Section 238 of the IBC does not override the statutory rights of a third-party public authority like MCGM to control and regulate its properties; such rights remain intact during insolvency proceedings.
A counsel's statement in court cannot bind MCGM unless there is clear authority to do so; estoppel cannot be applied against statutory provisions.
provisions: Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, Sections 92 and 92A
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation (harmonious construction)
Rule in Taylor v. Taylor (statutory method as exclusive)
No estoppel against statutory provisions

card.dispute: The builder (Pioneer Urban Land) fought against flat purchasers (Raghavan and Verma) over the enforceability of one-sided contractual terms and liability to refund payments with interest due to delayed possession.
issues_decided: Whether the contractual terms in the Apartment Buyer’s Agreement were unfair and unenforceable under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Whether the National Commission was justified in awarding interest at 10.7% per annum on the amounts paid by the flat purchasers
Whether the builder failed to fulfill its obligation to deliver possession within the stipulated time or a reasonable period thereafter
holdings: Contractual terms that are one-sided, unfair, and oppressive, especially where there is inequality in bargaining power, constitute an unfair trade practice under Section 2(r) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and are unenforceable.

A flat purchaser is entitled to a refund of all payments made with reasonable interest from the date of each payment until refund, excluding only periods of court-ordered stay at the purchaser’s request.

Failure to obtain an occupancy certificate and deliver possession within the agreed time or a reasonable period renders the builder liable to refund the amount paid with interest, especially when the delay causes financial hardship to the purchaser.
provisions: Haryana Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Rules, 2017, Rule 15
doctrines: Unfair trade practice
Inequality of bargaining power
Unconscionable contract terms
Equitable restitution with interest

card.dispute: The appellant (Poona Ram) and respondents fought over ownership and possession of a plot of land, with the plaintiff claiming possessory title despite lacking documentary proof, while the defendant relied on sale deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff could establish possessory title based on long and peaceful possession without documentary evidence of title.
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the First Appellate Court’s finding that the defendant had proved title and possession.
Whether mere stray or casual acts of possession, such as a vehicle body lying on the property, amount to settled possession.
holdings: A plaintiff claiming possessory title must prove settled, continuous, and peaceful possession for a sufficiently long period; mere casual or intermittent possession does not confer possessory title.

In the absence of documentary title, possession alone can support a claim only if it is established as settled and superior to others; the plaintiff cannot succeed merely because of weaknesses in the defendant's evidence.
The High Court erred in interfering with the First Appellate Court’s factual findings, which were based on proper evaluation of evidence and not perverse or against the record.
doctrines: Possessory title
Settled possession
Presumption of title from possession
Principle of non-interference by High Court in concurrent findings of fact

card.dispute: The dispute was between Raj Kumari and her siblings, including Surinder Pal Sharma, over the ownership and partition of a tenement allotted to their mother Suhagwanti, with Surinder claiming sole ownership via a Will, while others sought partition as legal heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the Will dated 02.01.1992 executed by Suhagwanti in favor of Surinder Pal Sharma was validly executed and proved.
Whether the tenement allotted to Suhagwanti devolved through succession or by testamentary disposition.
Whether the appellant was entitled to a share in the property and a decree for partition.
holdings: A registered Will must still be proved to have been executed freely and with testamentary intent, especially when the testator is illiterate and circumstances raise suspicion.
The propounder of a Will must remove all suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution; failure to do so renders the Will unproven under Section 71 of the Evidence Act.
The Will in question was not proved due to suspicious circumstances, non-disclosure to family, and lack of knowledge by attesting witnesses, leading to its rejection.
doctrines: Doctrine of suspicious circumstances
Requirement of proof of testamentary capacity and free will in case of registered wills
Rule that attesting witnesses must understand the nature of the document in case of illiterate testators

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether a person who has acquired title by adverse possession can file a suit for declaration and recovery of possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, or if such a plea can only be used defensively.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff can use adverse possession as a basis to file a suit for declaration and possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether adverse possession can only be used as a shield and not as a sword in litigation
Whether a person whose title has been extinguished by adverse possession can still evict the adverse possessor
holdings: A person who has perfected title by adverse possession can maintain a suit under Article 65 of the Limitation Act for declaration and recovery of possession.
Adverse possession can be used both as a shield and a sword; the plaintiff may enforce rights based on such title.
Once 12 years of adverse possession is complete, the original owner’s right to eject is extinguished, and the possessor acquires full title to the property.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Tacking of possession
Extinction of title by limitation

card.dispute: The appellant (Ravi Setia) sued for specific performance of an agreement for sale of land, which the High Court set aside on second appeal; the dispute centered on whether the plaintiff remained ready and willing to perform his obligations under the agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff demonstrated readiness and willingness to perform his obligations under the agreement for sale throughout the proceedings.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact in the second appeal.
Whether the plaintiff's failure to deposit the balance consideration within the court-granted time, without sufficient explanation, negated his claim for specific performance.
holdings: The plaintiff failed to demonstrate readiness and willingness to perform his obligations, as evidenced by his unexplained delay in depositing the balance consideration and frivolous grounds for seeking extension of time.
The High Court was justified in interfering in the second appeal because the concurrent findings were based on a misappreciation of evidence and ignored relevant conduct indicating lack of readiness.
Mere extension of time for deposit does not absolve the plaintiff from proving readiness and willingness; pendency of appeal does not justify non-deposit when no stay order was in place.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness as a mandatory requirement for specific performance
Equitable discretion in granting specific performance
Substantial question of law in second appeal based on misappreciation of evidence

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over whether certain properties were self-acquired or had blended into joint family property, and whether the High Court could interfere in a second appeal on factual findings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in re-appreciating evidence and reversing factual findings in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC?
Whether the suit properties were self-acquired or had blended into joint family property?
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or reverse factual findings in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved, such as error in law, inadmissible evidence, or perversity.
Mere residence together or joint use of self-acquired property does not amount to blending; clear intention to abandon separate rights must be proven, which was not established here.
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Blending of self-acquired property into joint family property
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Surinder Kaur challenged the decree of specific performance granted to the legal heirs of Bahadur Singh, who had failed to pay agreed rent for possession of agricultural land held since 1964.
issues_decided: Whether the promise to pay rent was a reciprocal and essential term of the agreement to sell
Whether a vendee who failed to perform an essential term of the contract could still claim specific performance
Whether the courts below erred in granting discretionary relief of specific performance despite the vendee's non-performance
holdings: The obligation to pay customary rent was a reciprocal and essential term of the agreement, as possession was granted on that condition.
A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove performance or readiness to perform all essential terms; failure to do so disentitles them to equitable relief.
The relief of specific performance is discretionary, and courts may refuse it where the plaintiff’s conduct is inequitable or causes hardship to the defendant.
doctrines: Reciprocal promises in contracts
Equitable discretion in specific performance
Readiness and willingness to perform under Section 16(c)
Hardship and inequity under Section 20

card.dispute: The appellant bank challenged whether a Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) is competent to assist a secured creditor in taking possession of a secured asset under Section 14 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002.
issues_decided: Whether the Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) is competent to act under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, in place of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM)?
Whether substitution of CJM for CMM in non-judicial executive functions under the SARFAESI Act is permissible under the law?
holdings: The CJM is equally competent to assist the secured creditor in taking possession of a secured asset under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, as the CMM.
Substitution of CJM for CMM in administrative and executive functions under the SARFAESI Act is consistent with Section 14 and furthers the legislative intent through purposive interpretation.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Contextual construction of statutes
Principle of substitution of functionaries in executive functions

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Police appealed against the High Court's direction to register an FIR and take action against police officers for not registering a criminal case in a property dispute involving alleged cheating under Section 420/34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in directing the registration of an FIR and action against police officers after a preliminary inquiry found the matter to be a civil dispute?
Whether the criminal proceedings initiated by the complainant amounted to an abuse of the process of law?
Whether the dispute between the parties was essentially civil in nature despite allegations of cheating?
holdings: The High Court should not have directed the registration of an FIR or action against police officers when the dispute was civil and no cognizable offence under Section 420/34 IPC was made out.
Filing criminal proceedings after choosing to resolve the dispute by paying off the mortgage and executing a sale deed constitutes an abuse of the process of law.
A dispute concerning property transaction, where the complainant became aware of encumbrances but proceeded with the transaction, remains civil even if allegations of non-disclosure are made.
doctrines: Abuse of the process of law
Distinction between civil and criminal disputes
Finality of magisterial decisions in preliminary inquiries

card.dispute: The landlord and tenant disputed whether their tenancy dispute, governed by a lease agreement with an arbitration clause, could be referred to arbitration given the tenancy laws applicable to the property.
issues_decided: Whether disputes arising from a tenancy agreement governed by special tenancy laws are arbitrable under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether the existence of a special statute providing exclusive remedies bars reference to arbitration by necessary implication
holdings: Disputes arising out of tenancy agreements governed by special statutes that create specific rights and liabilities and provide exclusive remedies are not arbitrable if the statute implies exclusion of civil court jurisdiction.

Where a statute creates a liability not existing at common law and provides a special remedy through designated courts, arbitration is excluded by necessary implication, even in the presence of an arbitration clause.
doctrines: Exclusion of arbitration by necessary implication
Doctrine of sufficiency of statutory remedy
Three categories from Wolverhampton New Waterworks Co. v. Hawkesford

card.dispute: The appellants (original defendants) challenged the High Court's decision to allow the respondent's (original plaintiff's) second appeal and decree his suit for declaration of ownership and permanent injunction based on a sale deed, reversing the lower courts' dismissal of the suit.
issues_decided: Whether a defendant, being a stranger to a sale deed, can challenge its validity in a suit for declaration of title without first initiating independent proceedings to set aside the deed?
Whether an unregistered partition deed (Palupatti) or family arrangement, though not registered, can be considered as evidence or as creating estoppel?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts regarding the sham nature of the sale deed?
holdings: A defendant who is a stranger to a sale deed can raise a plea that the deed is void, fictitious, collusive, or not intended to be acted upon in a suit for declaration, without first challenging it in separate proceedings.

An unregistered document recording a family arrangement or partition (Palupatti) may operate as estoppel and can be used as corroborative evidence of the arrangement and conduct of the parties, even if not admissible as proof of title.

The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts that the sale deed was sham, especially when there were material contradictions in the stated consideration, and such findings were based on credible evidence.
doctrines: Estoppel by family arrangement
Collusive or sham transaction
Concurrent findings of fact
Admissibility of unregistered family settlement

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's decision on whether a Magistrate can order further investigation after cognizance, in a case involving allegations of land grabbing, forgery, and extortion over agricultural land near Surat.
issues_decided: Whether a Magistrate retains the power to order further investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC even after taking cognizance of an offence.
Whether the facts in the application for further investigation were relevant to the FIR and warranted reopening of investigation.
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the Magistrate's order for further investigation.
holdings: A Magistrate retains the power under Section 156(3) CrPC to order further investigation even after cognizance, as the purpose of investigation is to discover the truth and ensure justice.

The facts in the application for further investigation pertain to a separate alleged scam involving forged documents and false claims by the complainants, which do not bear on the original FIR and thus do not justify further investigation in that case.

The High Court was correct in setting aside the Magistrate’s order for further investigation in the original FIR, but erred in holding that Magistrates lose power under Section 156(3) post-cognizance, which is overruled.
doctrines: Inherent truth-seeking function of criminal investigation
Distinction between further investigation and re-investigation
Power of Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC post-cognizance

card.dispute: Interim Resolution Professional of Jaypee Infratech Limited challenged transactions where lenders of Jaypee Assets Limited received mortgage security, claiming they were preferential and void under IBC; the lenders contested their status as financial creditors.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned mortgage transactions constitute preferential transactions under Section 43 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
Whether the lenders of Jaypee Assets Limited qualify as financial creditors of Jaypee Infratech Limited under Section 5(8) of the Code
holdings: Transactions where lenders of a related party (JAL) were granted mortgages over assets of the corporate debtor (JIL) without any disbursement or financial benefit to JIL are preferential and avoidable under Section 43 of the IBC.

Mere creation of mortgage security, without actual disbursement of funds or financial debt owed by the corporate debtor, does not make the secured party a 'financial creditor' under Section 5(8) of the IBC.
doctrines: Preferential transaction under IBC
Definition of financial debt and financial creditor
Look-back period for related party transactions
Forbearance as consideration (rejected in IBC context)

card.dispute: The vendor, B. Santoshamma, sold part of a 300 sq. yard land to one buyer (Pratap Reddy) and later agreed to sell the entire plot to another buyer (D. Sarala), leading to competing claims over the land.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for specific performance of the agreement in favor of D. Sarala could be maintained despite non-joinder of Pratap Reddy, who had a registered interest in part of the land.
Whether the suit to declare the conveyance in favor of Pratap Reddy null and void was maintainable without impleading the vendor as a defendant.
Whether the Trial Court could decree specific performance of the contract for only the remaining 200 sq. yards of land not already conveyed.
Whether the plea of bar under Order II Rule 2 CPC should be raised at the earliest opportunity or can be decided suo moto by the court.
holdings: A transferee with an interest in part of the property is a necessary party in a suit for specific performance; failure to implead such party bars relief against them when the suit is time-barred.
A suit to declare a deed null and void cannot proceed without impleading the executant of the deed as a defendant.

Under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, courts may decree specific performance of the enforceable portion of a contract, even if part of the property has been alienated, to prevent unjust enrichment.
The bar under Order II Rule 2 CPC is a technical plea that must be specifically pleaded and cannot be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court or decided suo moto by the court.
provisions: Limitation Act, 1963, Section 21 and Item 54 of Part II of the Schedule
Code of Civil Procedure, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Necessary party doctrine
Doctrine of lis pendens
Purposive interpretation of specific performance
Principle of fair play in limitation and joinder

card.dispute: The petitioner, Atma Ram, sought specific performance of an agreement to purchase property from the respondent, Charanjit Singh, after his suit was initially decreed by the Trial Court but later overturned by the Appellate Court and High Court on grounds of limitation and maintainability.
issues_decided: Whether the suit, originally filed as one for mandatory injunction with a nominal court fee, could be treated as a suit for specific performance by payment of deficit court fee under Section 149 of the CPC?
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under the Specific Relief Act, particularly in view of Section 16(c) requiring continuous readiness and willingness of the plaintiff?
Whether the Trial Court’s decision to treat the suit as one for specific performance was legally sustainable?
holdings: A suit originally filed as one for mandatory injunction with a nominal court fee cannot be converted into a suit for specific performance merely by paying deficit court fee under Section 149 CPC when the plaintiff deliberately avoided valuing the suit on the sale consideration.

The plaintiff failed to establish continuous readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, especially given the unexplained delay of over three years between the cause of action and filing the suit.
The Trial Court’s decision to treat the suit as one for specific performance was legally flawed, and the appellate courts were correct in reversing the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17
doctrines: Relation back of amendments
Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Discretionary nature of specific performance
Proper valuation and court fee for suits

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether the 30-day time limit (extendable to 60 days) for the District Magistrate to deliver possession of a secured asset under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act is mandatory or directory.
issues_decided: Whether the time limit prescribed under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act for the District Magistrate to deliver possession is mandatory or directory.
Whether failure to deliver possession within the stipulated time under Section 14 renders the District Magistrate functus officio.
holdings: The time limit under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act is directory, not mandatory, as the statute does not specify consequences for non-compliance and the purpose is to ensure expeditious, not automatic, action.
The District Magistrate does not become functus officio after the 60-day period; the duty to facilitate possession continues to serve the Act’s objective of speedy recovery of dues.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17(4A)
doctrines: Directory vs mandatory provision
Functus officio
Statutory interpretation based on object and purpose of legislation

card.dispute: The appellant and state challenged the High Court's acquittal of eight accused persons in a murder and criminal conspiracy case, arguing that the prosecution had established guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt based on circumstantial evidence?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's conviction and acquitting the accused?
Whether the evidence of a handwriting expert and hotel records was sufficient to establish a criminal conspiracy?
Whether the presumption of innocence and standard of proof in criminal cases were properly applied?
holdings: The prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of circumstantial evidence unerringly pointing to the guilt of the accused, and the possibility of an accidental death could not be ruled out.
The High Court's acquittal was not perverse, as it correctly applied the principle that suspicion, however strong, cannot replace proof beyond reasonable doubt.
The handwriting evidence only showed that one accused checked into a hotel six months before the incident, which was insufficient to prove conspiracy or motive.
In appeals against acquittal, the court must not interfere unless the acquittal is based on a perverse appreciation of evidence, which was not the case here.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Standard for conviction based on circumstantial evidence
Perversity test in appeals against acquittal

card.dispute: Canara Bank challenged the maintainability of suits filed by the legal representatives of a guarantor seeking declaration of title over mortgaged property, after the bank obtained a decree from the Debt Recovery Tribunal.
issues_decided: Whether the suits challenging a DRT decree are maintainable without exhausting the alternate remedy of appeal under Section 20 of the RDDBFI Act?
Whether the allegations of fraud in the plaint were sufficient to warrant rejection of the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC?
Whether the delay in filing the suits and vague pleadings regarding limitation warranted rejection of the plaints?
holdings: Suits challenging a decree of the Debt Recovery Tribunal are not maintainable without first exhausting the statutory appeal remedy under Section 20 of the RDDBFI Act, and such suits are liable to be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC.

Allegations of fraud must be specific and supported by material; vague or illusory claims of fraud, especially when not relating to the guarantee or mortgage, render the suit frivolous and an abuse of process.

Pleadings that are vague on limitation, particularly where no specific facts are given for delayed knowledge, cannot overcome the bar of limitation and justify rejection of the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d).
provisions: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 20
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11(d)
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternate remedy
Abuse of process of law
Frivolous and vexatious litigation
Specificity in pleading fraud

card.dispute: The appellant (Dahiben) and other plaintiffs challenged the rejection of their suit seeking cancellation of a registered sale deed on grounds of non-payment of consideration and fraud, which the respondents argued was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for cancellation of a registered sale deed was barred by limitation under Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
Whether the plaint disclosed a cause of action sufficient to resist rejection under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the CPC?

Whether the plaintiffs could claim relief of cancellation of the sale deed on the ground that the purchaser did not pay the full sale consideration by cheque as required by the Collector's permission?
holdings: A suit for cancellation of a registered sale deed must be filed within three years from the date of execution of the deed under Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963; delay beyond this period renders the suit time-barred.

Non-payment of consideration, without allegation of fraud vitiating the deed itself, does not entitle a plaintiff to cancellation of a registered sale deed; the remedy lies in a suit for recovery, not cancellation.

Mere non-compliance with conditions in the Collector’s permission for sale of tenanted agricultural land does not invalidate the sale deed or entitle the seller to cancellation, especially when no action was taken for years and the suit appears vexatious.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d)
doctrines: Illusory cause of action
Abuse of process of court
Doctrine of delayed laches
Distinction between cancellation and recovery of consideration

card.dispute: Deccan Paper Mills challenged whether a suit under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act for cancellation of an instrument is an in rem proceeding binding on all persons, or merely in personam binding only on parties and their privies.
issues_decided: Whether a proceeding under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 for cancellation of an instrument is in rem or in personam?
Whether a judgment under Section 31 binds all persons claiming an interest in the property, even if not parties to the suit?
holdings: A suit under Section 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is an action in personam and not in rem; it binds only the parties and their privies, not the world at large.
Cancellation of an instrument under Section 31 does not affect rights of strangers to the litigation; the relief is limited to the parties and those claiming through them.
doctrines: Action in rem vs. action in personam
Res judicata in declaratory and cancellation suits
Binding effect of declaratory decrees under Section 35 of the Specific Relief Act

card.dispute: Ferrodous Estates (Pvt) Ltd. sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property, which the defendants resisted, leading to a dispute over whether time was of the essence and whether the plaintiff was entitled to equitable relief after long delays.
issues_decided: Whether time is of the essence in a contract for the sale of immovable property when the agreement prescribes specific timelines for performance.
Whether a plaintiff who has significantly delayed in filing a suit for specific performance can still be considered 'ready and willing' to perform their part of the contract.
Whether the courts can deny specific performance on grounds of hardship to the defendant and escalation in property value over time.
holdings: When parties to a sale agreement for immovable property stipulate timeframes for performance, those periods must be given significance, and time can be treated as of the essence depending on the terms and conduct.

A plaintiff seeking specific performance must demonstrate continuous readiness and willingness to perform; prolonged delays and repeated extensions indicate lack of readiness, affecting the court's discretion to grant relief.

Specific performance may be denied where enforcing the contract would cause great hardship to the defendant, especially if the property's value has greatly increased and the defendant has made significant improvements or personal use of the property.
doctrines: Time is not of the essence in contracts for immovable property (qualified by conduct and terms)
Equity and good conscience in granting specific performance
Hardship and change in circumstances as grounds for refusing discretionary relief

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to set aside concurrent findings and decree a suit based on a will, claiming the will was invalid due to suspicious circumstances and non-compliance with legal requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated 30.4.1980 was surrounded by suspicious circumstances and its execution was not proved under Section 63 of the Succession Act.
Whether the courts below misread and misinterpreted the evidence, particularly regarding the attestation of the will.
holdings: A will excluding natural heirs is not inherently suspicious, as the purpose of a will is to alter normal succession; exclusion alone does not invalidate it.

The will was properly attested where two witnesses signed before the Sub-Registrar, and one attesting witness confirmed the presence and signature of the other, satisfying Section 63 of the Succession Act.
The High Court erred in interfering with concurrent findings of fact without sufficient legal basis, especially when the will’s language was clear and attestation complete.
doctrines: Due execution of will
Attestation by two witnesses
Concurrent finding rule
Suspicious circumstances doctrine

card.dispute: The Indore Development Authority and landowners disputed whether land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, due to delays in payment or possession.
issues_decided: Whether land acquisition lapses under Section 24(2) if possession was taken but compensation was not paid or deposited in court
Whether the word 'or' in Section 24(2) should be read as 'and/nor'
Whether Section 24 revives stale or concluded claims
Whether non-deposit of compensation in court leads to lapse of acquisition
holdings: Acquisition does not lapse under Section 24(2) if possession has been taken, even if compensation has not been paid.
The word 'or' in Section 24(2) must be read as 'nor' or 'and', meaning both possession not taken and compensation not paid are required for lapse.
Section 24 does not revive time-barred or concluded claims; it applies only to pending proceedings as of 1.1.2014.
Non-deposit of compensation in court does not cause lapse; it triggers the proviso for fresh compensation under the 2013 Act if majority holdings are affected.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 101
doctrines: Deemed lapse of acquisition proceedings
Interpretation of statutory language (conjunctive vs disjunctive)
Non-retroactivity of procedural rights
Finality of concluded litigation

card.dispute: The Idol of Sri Renganathaswamy and a trust fought over whether the trust could sell part of a property dedicated to religious charity without approval under the Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit regarding the sale of property by a religious trust.
Whether the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 apply to the first respondent trust.
Whether the proposed sale of immovable property by the trust required prior sanction under Section 31 of the Act.
holdings: Civil courts lack jurisdiction to decide matters concerning the administration or management of religious institutions if they are governed by the 1959 Act, due to Section 108's bar on such suits.
The provisions of the 1959 Act apply to any 'specific endowment' for religious charity, regardless of whether the government issued a notification under Section 3 for mismanagement.
A sale of immovable property belonging to a religious institution is null and void unless sanctioned by the Commissioner under Section 31, even if no mismanagement is alleged.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 3
Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 6(19)
Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 31
Tamil Nadu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 108
doctrines: Bar of civil court jurisdiction
Statutory exclusivity in religious endowment administration
Requirement of prior state sanction for alienation of religious trust property

card.dispute: The builder, Imperia Structures Ltd., challenged the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's decision allowing homebuyers to pursue remedies under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 despite the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) being in force.
issues_decided: Whether the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 proceedings are barred by the enactment of RERA.
Whether the registration of a real estate project under RERA ousts the jurisdiction of consumer commissions.
Whether the remedies under RERA and the Consumer Protection Act are mutually exclusive.
holdings: Section 79 of RERA does not bar consumer forums from entertaining complaints; remedies under RERA and the Consumer Protection Act are concurrent.
Registration of a project under RERA does not defer or extinguish allottees’ rights under prior agreements or under the Consumer Protection Act.
Section 18 of RERA, which provides for remedies for delay, operates without prejudice to other available remedies, including those under the Consumer Protection Act.
provisions: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, Section 2(1)(d), Section 12(4), Section 23
Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Section 18, Section 71(1) proviso, Section 79, Section 88
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Concurrent remedies
Savings clause doctrine
Doctrine of legislative intent

card.dispute: The appellant, Kavita Kanwar, sought probate of a two-page Will allegedly executed by her mother, excluding other family members; the respondents contested its validity, alleging suspicious circumstances and a contradictory third page.
issues_decided: Whether the Trial Court and High Court were justified in rejecting the grant of probate to the appellant based on suspicious circumstances surrounding the Will?
Whether the appellant’s inconsistent conduct regarding a purported third page of the Will undermined the authenticity of the document?
Whether the residuary clause in the two-page Will was consistent with the alleged separate distribution directions in the unproduced third page?
holdings: The Will was not proven to have been executed by the testatrix with full understanding of its contents due to unexplained suspicious circumstances.
The appellant’s contradictory stance on the existence and implementation of a third page of the Will severely damaged her credibility and the Will’s authenticity.
A valid Will cannot coexist with unattested, extraneous directions that contradict its residuary clause, especially when such directions are not formally executed.
doctrines: Suspicious circumstances doctrine in grant of probate
Testamentary capacity and due execution
Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus

card.dispute: L&T Housing Finance Limited (secured creditor) vs Trishul Developers (borrower) over the validity of SARFAESI proceedings initiated to recover a defaulted term loan of Rs. 20 crores.
issues_decided: Whether the demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act was invalid due to the use of L&T Finance Ltd.'s seal instead of L&T Housing Finance Ltd.'s seal?
Whether a technical defect in the notice under the SARFAESI Act can invalidate enforcement proceedings in the absence of substantial prejudice?
holdings: A demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act is not invalid merely because of a clerical or technical error in using the wrong company seal, if the identity of the secured creditor is clear and there is no confusion.
Procedural lapses in SARFAESI notices that are trivial and do not cause substantial prejudice cannot be grounds to quash enforcement proceedings.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(3A)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 2(zd)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
No prejudice from technical defect
Judicial review under SARFAESI limited to substantive irregularities

card.dispute: Radha Exports (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLAT's decision allowing K.P. Jayaram to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC, claiming the debt was time-barred and not a financial debt.
issues_decided: Whether the application under Section 7 of the IBC was barred by limitation
Whether the alleged amount constituted a 'financial debt' under the IBC
Whether the NCLAT erred in reversing the NCLT's rejection of the insolvency application
holdings: The application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as the cause of action arose in 2004 and no acknowledgment of debt was made after 2011 to extend limitation.
A personal loan to a company promoter, even if acknowledged, does not constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC if it lacks commercial effect of borrowing and is interest-free.
The NCLAT erred in law by admitting the application; the NCLT rightly rejected it due to absence of enforceable financial debt and limitation bar.
doctrines: Limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963 applied to IBC proceedings
Strict interpretation of 'financial debt' under IBC based on commercial effect of borrowing
No insolvency initiation without a legally enforceable debt

card.dispute: M/S Ultratech Cement Ltd. challenged the State of Rajasthan's order reducing its capital investment subsidy from 75% to 50% and demanding recovery of excess subsidy with 18% interest.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to 75% capital investment subsidy under RIPS-2003 or only 50%.
Whether the State could recover excess subsidy with interest at 18% per annum under Clause 10 of RIPS-2003.
holdings: The appellant was entitled only to 50% of the payable and deposited tax as capital investment subsidy under RIPS-2003; the grant of 75% was erroneous and unauthorized.

The State could recover excess subsidy with interest, but only at 12% per annum as per the appellant's undertaking in Form 2, not at 18% under Clause 10, since no breach or misrepresentation was committed by the appellant.
doctrines: Contemporanea Expositio
Promissory Estoppel
Unjust Enrichment

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Nand Ram (plaintiffs) sued the legal heirs of Jagdish Prasad (defendant) for possession of leased land after the lease expired, while the defendant claimed adverse possession and ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for possession by the lessor after expiry of lease was barred by limitation under Article 66 or governed by Article 67 of the Limitation Act
Whether the defendant's continued possession after lease expiry amounted to a tenancy at sufferance or adverse possession
Whether the defendant could claim title by adverse possession against the plaintiff-lessor without surrendering possession and repudiating tenancy
holdings: A suit by a lessor for possession after determination of tenancy by efflux of time is governed by Article 67 of the Limitation Act, not Article 66, and is within time if filed within 12 years of lease expiry.

A lessee who continues in possession after lease expiry without landlord’s assent becomes a tenant at sufferance; possession remains permissive and not adverse unless there is clear renunciation of tenancy and assertion of hostile title.

A former tenant cannot claim adverse possession without first surrendering possession and openly repudiating the landlord’s title; mere non-payment of rent or continued possession does not convert tenancy into adverse possession.
doctrines: Tenancy at sufferance
Tenant estoppel
Adverse possession
Limitation for suits by lessors
