card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over ownership and possession of a property in Tamil Nadu, with the respondent claiming title and recovery of possession.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's suit for recovery of possession was within the period of limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the High Court erred in allowing the second appeal without framing a substantial question of law as required under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure
holdings: A suit for recovery of possession based on title is barred if filed after twelve years from when the defendant's possession became adverse, and no such relief can be granted if limitation is not pleaded or established.

The High Court cannot allow a second appeal without framing and deciding a substantial question of law; failure to do so vitiates the judgment, and concurrent findings of fact cannot be disturbed on mere equitable grounds.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Substantial question of law in second appeal
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over ownership and possession of a property in Bangalore, with the appellants claiming title or adverse possession through the wife of the original defendant.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could simultaneously plead title and adverse possession over the same property from the same date.
Whether the plea of adverse possession was properly pleaded and proved in accordance with legal requirements.
Whether the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court on document authenticity and possession could be overturned.
holdings: A plea of title and adverse possession cannot be maintained simultaneously from the same date, as they are mutually inconsistent legal claims.
Adverse possession must be specifically pleaded and proved with clarity on when permissive possession became hostile, open, and continuous.
The courts below correctly rejected the appellants' documents and plea of adverse possession; their findings are not disturbed for lack of cogent evidence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 1
doctrines: Adverse possession (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario)
Mutual inconsistency of title and adverse possession pleas
Pleading and proof requirements for adverse possession

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Joginder Kaur (plaintiff) sued to set aside sale deeds executed by her step-sister-in-law, alleging fraud and forgery in a 1990 GPA, while the defendants claimed the suits were barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suits were barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the plaintiff could invoke Section 17 of the Limitation Act due to fraud or concealment
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of the lower courts
holdings: The suits are barred by limitation as the plaintiff failed to prove fraud, and thus the benefit under Section 17 of the Limitation Act is not available.
Section 17 applies only when fraud is pleaded and proved; mere suspicion or discrepancies in documents are insufficient without tangible evidence.
The High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of the trial and appellate courts based on conjectures, especially when the evidence supported the defendants' case.
doctrines: Preponderance of probabilities
Concurrent findings rule
Effect of fraud on limitation

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested over whether criminal proceedings should continue for alleged forgery of receipts and dishonoured cheques related to a land transaction.
issues_decided: Whether the FIR for forgery and cheating based solely on a handwriting expert's opinion should continue when a civil suit on the same issue is pending.
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act when the accused admitted issuing cheques.
holdings: An FIR based solely on a handwriting expert's opinion should not proceed when the issue of forgery is pending in a civil suit, as it may prejudice the parties and amount to abuse of process.

A criminal complaint under Section 138 of the N.I. Act should not be quashed merely due to a dispute between parties; the statutory presumption of liability upon issuance of a cheque continues until rebutted by evidence.
doctrines: Presumption of legality and enforceability of debt under Section 139 of the N.I. Act
Abuse of process of law
Rebuttable presumption in criminal cases
Opinion of handwriting expert not conclusive under Section 45 of the Indian Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellant, Sardar Ali Khan, claimed ownership of a plot based on a 1993 sale deed, while the respondent, an heir of the original owner, challenged the deed's validity and filed criminal charges alleging fraud and forgery, leading to a dispute over whether criminal proceedings could proceed alongside pending civil suits on the same issue.
issues_decided: Whether criminal proceedings under Sections 418, 419, 420, 467, 468, and 471 IPC can proceed when a civil suit challenging the validity of a sale deed is already pending?
Whether the delay in filing the criminal complaint and the nature of allegations amount to an abuse of legal process?
Whether the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the criminal proceedings?
holdings: Criminal proceedings cannot proceed when the core issue—validity of a sale deed—depends on factual disputes already before a civil court.
Filing criminal charges years after the sale deed and even after initiating a civil suit, without new evidence of forgery or impersonation, constitutes abuse of process.
The High Court should have quashed the criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to prevent misuse of legal process in the face of parallel civil litigation.
doctrines: Abuse of process of law
Primacy of civil proceedings in title disputes
Inherent powers of High Court to prevent injustice

card.dispute: The appellant, Satish Chander Ahuja, challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a civil decree granting him an injunction, after the respondent, Sneha Ahuja, had obtained relief under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, concerning residence rights in a shared household.
issues_decided: Whether a civil suit for injunction is maintainable despite pending or concluded proceedings under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005?
Whether an order passed under Section 19 of the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, operates as res judicata or binding precedent in a civil court?
What is the evidentiary value of orders passed under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, in civil proceedings?
Whether findings in criminal or special statute proceedings bind a civil court in determining rights to property or possession?
holdings: Pendency or existence of an order under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, does not bar a civil court from entertaining a suit involving property or possession rights.
An order under Section 19 of the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, is relevant and admissible in civil proceedings but is not binding; it has limited evidentiary value.
Civil courts must decide issues based on preponderance of probabilities and evidence adduced before them, independent of findings in criminal or domestic violence proceedings.
Proceedings under special statutes like the DV Act do not have res judicata effect in civil suits; civil courts retain jurisdiction to determine rights based on evidence.
provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 19
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 26
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XII Rule 6
doctrines: Preponderance of probabilities
Res judicata
Non-binding nature of criminal findings in civil proceedings
Limited evidentiary value of orders under special statutes

card.dispute: The appellant sought to enforce compliance with court undertakings by detaining the respondent's passport, which the High Court set aside; the dispute was over whether the passport could be retained to ensure the respondent's presence in ongoing litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the Single Judge was justified in directing the respondent to deposit his passport for non-compliance with court undertakings?
Whether the Division Bench was correct in setting aside the Single Judge's order directing deposit of the passport?
holdings: The Single Judge had the inherent power to direct deposit of the passport to ensure the party's presence and compliance with court orders, especially after repeated undertakings were breached.
The Division Bench erred in setting aside the Single Judge's order; the direction to deposit the passport was valid and necessary for the progress of the trial and potential contempt enforcement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rule 2A
doctrines: Inherent powers of the court to ensure compliance with orders
Judicial discretion in granting interim measures to secure presence of parties

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's reversal of the Trial Court's decree that declared them owners of certain properties under a Will and invalidated a trust created by the respondents.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Trial Court's finding that the Will dated 20.05.1991 was genuine and valid?
Whether the High Court ought to have remanded the case to the Trial Court instead of deciding it finally?
holdings: The High Court correctly rejected the Will as genuine due to suspicious circumstances and sound appreciation of evidence, justifying its interference with the Trial Court's decision.

Remand under Order XLI Rules 23 or 23A CPC is not warranted when parties have fully led evidence and the appellate court can decide based on record; re-trial is not needed to fill lacunae in a party's case.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 23A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 24
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 25
doctrines: Appellate jurisdiction to remand for re-trial under Order XLI Rules 23 and 23A
Final disposal of appeal under Order XLI Rule 24 when evidence is sufficient
Principle that remand is not a substitute for correcting a party's evidentiary lapse

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether landlord-tenant disputes governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are arbitrable and whether the court or arbitral tribunal should decide arbitrability at the referral stage under Sections 8 or 11 of the Arbitration Act.
issues_decided: Whether landlord-tenant disputes under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are non-arbitrable on grounds of public policy
Whether the court or the arbitral tribunal decides the issue of non-arbitrability at the stage of referral under Sections 8 or 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
What is the scope of judicial review by courts when examining the existence and validity of an arbitration agreement at the referral stage
holdings: Landlord-tenant disputes are generally arbitrable unless they involve tenancy rights in immovable property governed by special statutes that protect tenant interests, in which case they may be non-arbitrable due to public policy.
The court has the initial power under Sections 8 and 11 to decide non-arbitrability, but only in clear cases; otherwise, the matter must be referred to arbitration.

Courts must refer disputes to arbitration unless a party establishes a prima facie case of non-existence of a valid arbitration agreement, based only on writing, communication, and core contractual validity; complex issues must be left to the tribunal.

The standard for judicial intervention is minimal: 'when in doubt, refer'—courts should not delve into merits or subject-matter arbitrability unless it is a clear case of non-arbitrability ('deadwood').
doctrines: Doctrine of non-arbitrability
Prima facie standard in referral proceedings
Separability of arbitration agreement
Minimal judicial intervention in arbitration

card.dispute: The legal heirs of R. Krishnammal (legatees under a will) and the descendants of Lakshmiah Naidu disputed ownership and possession of certain properties, primarily over whether Krishnammal acquired absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether R. Krishnammal became the absolute owner of the suit properties under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the appellants (legatees under the will) had any valid title to the properties based on partition or sale deeds
Whether the compromise decree in O.S. No. 71 of 1958 barred the respondents from challenging the will or partition
holdings: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies if a female Hindu is possessed of property when the question of her title arises, not necessarily at the Act's commencement; possession includes legal or constructive possession.
A female Hindu must have some antecedent title to the property for Section 14(1) to convert her limited interest into absolute ownership; mere possession without title does not suffice.

The appellants failed to prove any valid title through partition or sale deeds, as the first defendant had no rights to transfer, and the compromise decree extinguished Krishnammal’s rights in favor of the respondents.
provisions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(1) and Section 3(2)
doctrines: Conversion of limited estate into absolute ownership under Section 14(1)
Requirement of antecedent title for application of Section 14(1)
Constructive or legal possession suffices under Section 14(1) if ownership rights exist

card.dispute: The appellant daughter claimed coparcenary rights in ancestral property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended in 2005, against her brother and other relatives who contested her rights based on alleged prior oral partition and the father's death before 2005.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, gives coparcenary rights to daughters irrespective of whether the father was alive on the date of amendment (9 September 2005)?
Whether an oral partition or unregistered partition deed is sufficient to deny a daughter's rights under the amended Section 6?
Whether the rights under the amended Section 6 have retrospective effect?
What evidentiary standard must be met to prove a partition that excludes a daughter from coparcenary rights?
holdings: Daughters have coparcenary rights by birth in Mitakshara coparcenary property, whether born before or after the 2005 amendment, with equal rights and liabilities as sons.
A daughter's right accrues from birth, and it is not necessary for the father to be alive on 9 September 2005 for her to claim rights under the amended Section 6.
The amended Section 6 has retroactive effect, but transactions like partition, alienation, or testamentary dispositions before 20 December 2004 are saved from its operation.

Oral partition or unregistered partition deeds are not sufficient to deny a daughter's rights; only partitions by registered instrument or court decree, with strong contemporaneous documentary evidence, may be recognized.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of beneficial legislation
Gender justice and substantive equality
Statutory fiction of partition
Burden of proof in cases involving oral partition

card.dispute: Flat buyers challenged the developer's delay in handing over possession and its recovery of additional charges for electricity and parking, claiming deficiency of service.
issues_decided: Whether the developer was entitled to recover additional charges for setting up a dedicated sub-station under the Apartment Buyers Agreement (ABA)?
Whether the recovery of separate parking charges amounted to a deficiency of service given that common areas were already paid for?
Whether the flat buyers were entitled to compensation for delayed possession and unfulfilled amenities despite contractual stipulations?
holdings: The developer could recover additional electricity infrastructure costs under clause 23(b) of the ABA as the requirement for a dedicated sub-station arose due to regulatory norms and was consistent with the contract.
Separate parking charges were validly recovered as the ABA explicitly excluded parking from the super area pricing and disclosed it separately, negating any deficiency of service.

Flat buyers were entitled to compensation at 6% simple interest for delayed possession and unfulfilled promised amenities, as the developer failed to meet representations made in the brochure and delayed performance beyond contractual timelines.
provisions: KERC (Conditions of Supply of Electricity by the Distribution Licensee) Regulations, 2004, Regulation 3.02(e)
KERC (Recovery of Expenditure for Supply of Electricity) Regulations, 2004, Regulation 3.2.4
Apartment Buyers Agreement, Clauses 1.6, 1.14, 1.15, 23(b), and JDC
doctrines: Doctrine of deficiency of service under consumer protection law
Doctrine of contractual interpretation
Perversity in findings of consumer commissions

card.dispute: An operational creditor (A. Navinchandra Steels) challenged the initiation of insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC by a secured creditor (SREI Equipment Finance) against a company already in winding up, arguing that the winding up petition should take precedence.
issues_decided: Whether a Section 7 insolvency petition under the IBC can proceed when a company is already subject to a pending winding up petition under the Companies Act, 2013?
Whether suppression of a pending winding up proceeding in a Section 7 application renders the petition invalid?
Whether the NCLT's jurisdiction under the IBC is subordinate to the High Court's winding up jurisdiction under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013?
holdings: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 takes precedence over winding up proceedings under the Companies Act, 2013 when the corporate debtor is not irretrievably insolvent, as the primary objective of the IBC is corporate revival.

A Section 7 petition is an independent proceeding and does not become invalid merely because the applicant did not disclose a pending winding up petition; non-disclosure does not automatically vitiate the petition if IBC requirements are met.

The discretionary power of the High Court under Section 434(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot override the mandatory jurisdiction of the NCLT under the IBC once the conditions under Section 7 are satisfied.
doctrines: Primacy of IBC over other laws
Corporate insolvency resolution over liquidation
Secured creditor's right to realize security outside winding up

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Arakeri Abbaiah (plaintiffs) fought against the legal heirs of Muniyappa (defendants) over ownership and possession of 10.54 guntas of land in Bangalore, seeking declaration of title and injunction against interference.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaration of ownership and injunction is maintainable under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 when the plaintiff fails to prove possession?
Whether a declaratory decree can be denied solely because the plaintiff did not claim or prove entitlement to consequential relief like recovery of possession?
Whether the principle of Order II Rule 2 CPC bars a second suit filed after a prior unsuccessful suit involving the same property?
holdings: A suit claiming both declaration and consequential injunction is maintainable under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 even if the plaintiff fails to prove possession; the proviso barring standalone declaration applies only when no consequential relief is claimed.

A declaratory decree of ownership cannot be denied merely because the plaintiff failed to establish possession or claim recovery of possession, provided ownership is proved and the suit is not barred by law.
Order II Rule 2 CPC does not bar a subsequent suit if new grounds of interference with possession arose after the first suit, forming a fresh cause of action.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Maintainability of declaratory suits with consequential relief
Rule against splitting of causes of action (Order II Rule 2 CPC)
Declaratory relief as independent remedy

card.dispute: Arce Polymers Pvt. Ltd. and Andhra Bank challenged the High Court's decision to quash the auction sale of mortgaged property under SARFAESI Act, which had been initiated by the Bank against Alpine Pharmaceuticals for loan recovery.
issues_decided: Whether the Bank was obligated to respond to the borrower's representation under Section 13(3A) of the SARFAESI Act
Whether the borrower's challenge to enforcement proceedings was barred by limitation
Whether the machinery should have been separately valued and auctioned from the immovable property
Whether the valuation report dated 19th February 2018 was valid for the subsequent auction
holdings: The borrower waived its right to challenge non-compliance with Section 13(3A) due to its disingenuous conduct and prolonged negotiations, amounting to estoppel.
The court did not decide this issue as it was rendered unnecessary by the finding of waiver and estoppel on the first issue.
The bank could auction machinery together with land and building; separate valuation or sale of machinery is not mandatory under SARFAESI Act if no prejudice is shown.
The valuation report dated 19th February 2018 remained valid for the auction held later, especially since the final bid exceeded both the reserve and fair market value.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(3A)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Rules, 2002
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver
Doctrine of estoppel
Discretionary relief in judicial review
Principle of equitable discretion based on post-litigation events

card.dispute: Electrosteel Castings Limited (guarantor) sued to declare an assignment of debt fraudulent and avoid recovery proceedings, while UV Asset Reconstruction Company (assignee) claimed enforceability of the debt under SARFAESI.
issues_decided: Whether the suit alleging fraud in the assignment deed is maintainable despite the bar under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002.
Whether general allegations of 'fraud' without specific particulars are sufficient to circumvent the exclusivity of SARFAESI remedies.
holdings: A suit alleging fraud in a debt assignment is not maintainable if it is merely a procedural attempt to bypass the exclusive remedy under Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act.

Allegations of fraud must be supported by specific particulars; mere use of the word 'fraud' without details does not constitute a valid pleading and cannot render a SARFAESI-barred suit maintainable.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 34
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Exclusivity of remedy under SARFAESI Act
Pleading fraud with particularity
Prohibition of clever drafting to circumvent statutory bars

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Hamid Ali Khan challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, for a residential-cum-commercial scheme, alleging lack of urgency and absence of material justifying bypassing the mandatory inquiry under Section 5A.
issues_decided: Whether there was relevant material before the government to invoke Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to dispense with the inquiry under Section 5A?
Whether the competent authority applied its mind to the facts and circumstances while invoking the urgency clause under Section 17(4)?
Whether the delay in issuing the Section 6 declaration and taking possession undermines the claim of urgency?
holdings: The invocation of Section 17(4) to dispense with the Section 5A inquiry was unjustified due to lack of material demonstrating urgency and public purpose.
The authority did not apply its mind to the necessity of urgency, as the Section 6 declaration was issued merely to avoid lapse of acquisition proceedings after one year.
The significant delay in taking possession and issuing the declaration, coupled with contradictory official communications, negated the claim of urgency required under Section 17(4).
doctrines: Application of mind doctrine
Doctrine of urgency in land acquisition
Principle of fair hearing under Section 5A

card.dispute: The appellant, a tenant, challenged the bank's action to take possession of a mortgaged property under SARFAESI Act, claiming protected tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant-tenant was entitled to protection under the SARFAESI Act despite lack of a registered tenancy agreement?
Whether a tenant in possession for more than one year without a registered instrument can resist possession by a secured creditor?
Whether the Maharashtra Rent Control Act protects a tenant-in-sufferance against enforcement under SARFAESI Act?
holdings: A tenant claiming possession for over one year must have a registered instrument; unregistered or oral agreements do not confer long-term possession rights under SARFAESI proceedings.
A valid tenancy existing prior to mortgage cannot be disturbed by the secured creditor, but post-mortgage tenancies must comply with Section 65-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
A tenant-in-sufferance has no protection under rent control laws against enforcement of security interest under SARFAESI Act due to Section 13(13) and the self-executory nature of the Act.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(2)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(13)
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Priority of secured creditor's rights over unregistered tenancies
Requirement of registration for leases exceeding one year (Section 107, TP Act)
SARFAESI Act as a self-executory mechanism overriding rent control protections for tenants-in-sufferance

card.dispute: Convicted individuals challenged their death sentences for murder, while the informant challenged the acquittal of another accused in a family massacre case.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of accused Nos. 1, 3, and 4 beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the recovery of incriminating material under Section 27 of the Evidence Act was legally valid?
Whether the concurrent presence of multiple assailants can be inferred based on the nature of injuries?
Whether the acquittal of accused No. 2 (Nazra) was justified due to unreliable arrest and lack of evidence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of accused Nos. 1, 3, and 4 beyond reasonable doubt, warranting their acquittal and release.
Recovery of clothes based solely on disclosure by an accused without independent corroboration violates Section 27 of the Evidence Act and cannot sustain conviction.
The inference that multiple assailants must have committed the crime based on the number and nature of injuries is speculative and not a substitute for reliable evidence.
The acquittal of Nazra (accused No. 2) was justified due to contradictions in arrest testimony and absence of independent witnesses, and the same doubts apply to the arrests of the other accused.
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Corroboration of recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act
Prosecution must stand on its own evidence

card.dispute: The Jamia Masjid and the legal representatives of K.V. Rudrappa fought over ownership, possession, and title to a property claimed as a Wakf property, previously managed by a Khazi service holder.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by res judicata due to a prior representative suit under Section 92 of the CPC?
Whether a compromise decree in a prior suit barred a subsequent suit on the issue of title?
Whether the third prior suit for injunction simpliciter created res judicata on the issue of title?
Whether a change in circumstances (notification of property as Wakf) affected the applicability of res judicata?
holdings: A representative suit under Section 92 CPC may bind interested parties via res judicata, but only on issues actually and substantially adjudicated; mere prima facie findings on title do not constitute conclusive determination.

A compromise decree does not operate as res judicata on title unless the compromise explicitly resolves the question of title; a compromise limited to possession does not bar a subsequent suit on title.
A suit for injunction simpliciter without adjudication on title or claim for declaration does not create res judicata on the issue of ownership.
A change in legal status of property (e.g., notification as Wakf) after a prior decision constitutes a new fact, negating res judicata if the prior decision did not address the current legal reality.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3A
doctrines: Res judicata
Representative suit
Estoppel by conduct
Prima facie determination vs. conclusive adjudication

card.dispute: Kiran Devi challenged the High Court's order dispossessing her from tenanted premises, which held that the tenancy was held by a joint Hindu family and that the Karta's surrender of tenancy rights to the Wakf Board was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the hotel business operated in the tenanted premises was a joint Hindu family business
Whether the Karta of the joint Hindu family had the authority to surrender the tenancy rights for the benefit of the family
Whether the surrender of tenancy by the Karta was valid and binding on the family members
holdings: Mere payment of rent by ancestors does not raise a presumption that the business was a joint Hindu family business; such a business remains separate unless joint funds were used or earnings blended with joint property.

The Karta of a joint Hindu family has the authority to alienate or surrender tenancy rights if it is for the benefit of the family, even without consent of adult coparceners, provided it meets the criteria of benefit to the estate.

The surrender of tenancy was valid as it ceased an ongoing financial liability due to non-operation of the hotel, thus being for the family's benefit, and the document was properly accepted by the Wakf Board.
doctrines: Doctrine of legal necessity and benefit to estate under Hindu Law
Doctrine of blending of separate property into joint family property
Presumption regarding joint family ownership of immovable property vs. business

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent, brothers who had previously partitioned joint family property, disputed the admissibility of an unregistered and unstamped family settlement deed (Khararunama) and a receipt, which the appellants sought to rely upon to challenge the respondent's title and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered and unstamped Khararunama and receipt are admissible in evidence despite non-compliance with the Registration Act and Stamp Act?
Whether the Khararunama amounts to a document requiring compulsory registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act?
Whether an unregistered document recording a past family arrangement can be admitted as evidence of a collateral transaction?
holdings: A document that merely records a past partition or family arrangement, without creating or declaring new rights, does not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act.
An unregistered document that is only a memorandum of an already completed family arrangement may be admitted in evidence as a record of fact, even if unregistered and unstamped.

Under the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act, an unregistered document may be used to prove a collateral transaction not required to be registered, such as the existence of a prior agreement or arrangement.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of collateral transaction under Section 49 of the Registration Act
Doctrine of admissibility of unregistered documents as proof of past facts

card.dispute: The dispute was between family branches over whether a residential property acquired in 1979 was joint family property entitled to partition, or separate property, following conflicting claims about a prior partition in 1981.
issues_decided: Whether the family remained joint Hindu family after 1960 despite filing separate tax returns
Whether an unproven oral agreement of partition dated 08.03.1981 could legally sever the joint family status
Whether the Tatabad residential property acquired in 1979 was joint family property
holdings: Filing of separate income and wealth tax returns by members does not conclusively prove severance of joint family status under Hindu law.
A claim of partition in 1981, even if unproven, implies the family was joint until that date, contradicting the plea of earlier separation in 1960.
Property acquired in the name of one member using funds from a family-owned company is joint family property if the family was still joint at the time of purchase.
doctrines: Joint Hindu Family and coparcenary
Burden of proof in partition suits
Funding source as determinant of property character

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision allowing a suit by the first respondent to set aside an auction of land conducted by the Moradabad Development Authority, which the respondent claimed was invalid due to lack of actual possession and valid title.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit which in essence arose from proceedings under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976?
Whether the transfer of the suit land from Zahid Hussain to the first respondent was valid under Section 5(3) of the ULCRA?
Whether the High Court erred in affirming the title and possession of the first respondent over the suit land despite the bar under ULCRA?
Whether the auction of the land by MDA was valid in law?
holdings: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to try the suit because the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 impliedly excludes civil court jurisdiction on matters arising from ceiling proceedings.
The transfer of the suit land by Zahid Hussain to the first respondent was null and void as it violated Section 5(3) of the ULCRA, which required prior declaration and notification not fulfilled.
The High Court erred in recognizing the first respondent’s title; the suit failed because the plaintiff had no valid cause of action once the transfer was invalid under ULCRA.
The auction conducted by MDA was valid as it followed lawful procedures under the ULCRA framework, and the suit challenging it was not maintainable.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5(3)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 6
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 8(4)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(1)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 30(5)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 33
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 40
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 42
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 22
doctrines: Implied exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
Complete code doctrine
Finality of statutory tribunal orders
Artful drafting to circumvent jurisdictional bars
Plenary jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136 and Article 142

card.dispute: The appellants (guarantors) challenged the enforcement of a security interest and sale of mortgaged properties under SARFAESI Act, seeking to set aside the auction in favour of the respondent auction purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of mortgaged properties under SARFAESI Act was valid despite prior litigation challenging the sale notice?
Whether the mortgagors' right to redemption survived after registration of the sale in favour of the auction purchaser?
Whether the direction to pay surplus sale proceeds to one of the guarantors (respondent No. 3) was justified?
holdings: The sale conducted under SARFAESI Act was valid and could not be set aside merely because of earlier litigation, as the right to redemption stood extinguished upon registration of sale.
The right of redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act is extinguished upon registration of the sale in favour of the auction purchaser under SARFAESI Act.
The direction to pay surplus proceeds to respondent No. 3 was valid as the sale of her property occurred separately and equity favoured her as an outsider among guarantors.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
doctrines: Extinguishment of right of redemption upon sale under SARFAESI Act
Finality of auction sales once confirmed and registered
Equitable distribution of surplus sale proceeds
Invocation of Article 142 for complete justice

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor, arguing that the financial creditor's claim was time-barred and that proceedings under SARFAESI Act should have been considered under limitation law.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings under the SARFAESI Act before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate qualify as civil proceedings in a court for the purpose of Section 14 of the Limitation Act
Whether the pendency of SARFAESI proceedings can be invoked to condone delay in filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC
Whether the NCLAT was justified in not staying the NCLT proceedings
holdings: Proceedings under the SARFAESI Act before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate are deemed civil proceedings in a court, and thus fall within the ambit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act.
The pendency of SARFAESI proceedings can be considered as 'proceedings in a court' for the purpose of Section 14, allowing exclusion of that period when computing limitation for IBC applications.
The NCLAT was justified in refusing to stay the NCLT proceedings as the delay in filing was attributable to the appellants and no sufficient cause was shown.
provisions: Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 18
doctrines: Doctrine of sufficient cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Doctrine of exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act
Doctrine of purposive interpretation of statutes

card.dispute: Sughar Singh (appellant) sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, after the vendor sold it to others despite receiving part payment; the dispute was over whether the decree for specific performance should be granted.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the decree for specific performance based on alleged non-compliance with Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act and lack of averments regarding readiness and willingness?
Whether the plaintiff proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract?
Whether the discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act can be exercised to deny specific performance when the agreement is proved and the plaintiff is ready and willing?
Whether the subsequent purchasers (defendants 2 to 5) can resist specific performance on grounds of long possession?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the decree for specific performance solely on technical non-compliance with pleading requirements; readiness and willingness can be inferred from conduct and circumstances.

The plaintiff was found to be ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, as evidenced by payment of Rs.40,000 and conduct before and after filing the suit; no requirement to plead demand for registration.

Discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act must be exercised judiciously and not to reward dishonest conduct; specific performance should generally be granted if the agreement is proved and plaintiff is ready and willing.
Subsequent purchasers who bought with knowledge of prior agreement and for doubtful consideration cannot claim protection based on long possession; balance of convenience favours the original vendee.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Judicious exercise of discretion in granting specific performance
Protection of equitable rights under prior agreement
Constructive notice to subsequent transferees

card.dispute: Supertech Limited fought with the Emerald Court Owner Resident Welfare Association over illegal construction of two high-rise buildings that violated building and fire safety regulations and encroached upon green spaces and setbacks.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of Apex and Ceyane towers violated the National Building Code and Uttar Pradesh building regulations regarding minimum distance between buildings?
Whether the consent of the Resident Welfare Association was required under the UP Apartment Ownership Act, 2010 for the revised building plan?
Whether the impugned construction could be permitted despite being in violation of statutory norms and without due approval?
Whether the illegal structures should be demolished and compensation awarded to homebuyers?
holdings: The construction of the two towers violated mandatory distance requirements under the National Building Regulations and National Building Code, which are essential for safety, ventilation, and fire access.
The consent of the Resident Welfare Association was necessary under the UP Apartment Ownership Act, 2010 for any amendment affecting common areas, and its absence rendered the revised plan invalid.
No construction can be regularized if it flouts statutory building regulations and is carried out without proper approvals, especially when it affects public safety and rights of existing residents.
The illegal buildings must be demolished, and the developer must refund homebuyers with 12% interest due to the impossibility of lawful possession.
doctrines: Principle of sustainable development
Precautionary principle
Public trust doctrine
Doctrine of proportionality in environmental and urban planning law

card.dispute: The appellant (Executive Engineer) challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a land acquisition award, arguing that the acquisition proceedings had not lapsed despite delays in publishing the award.
issues_decided: Whether Section 25 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 applies to awards under Section 24(1)(a) of the same Act, replacing the time limit under Section 11A of the repealed Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the land acquisition proceedings lapsed due to delay in making or publishing the award
Whether the award dated 30th October 2014 was backdated and whether such backdating invalidates the acquisition
holdings: Section 25 of the 2013 Act governs the time limit for making awards under Section 24(1)(a), replacing the earlier provision under the 1894 Act.
The limitation period under Section 25 begins from 1st January 2014, and periods of court-ordered stays must be excluded when computing this period.
Even if the award was backdated, it was made within the extended valid period (by 20th March 2015) after excluding the 79-day stay, so the acquisition did not lapse.
The validity of the award is unaffected by belated service of notice or procedural discrepancies, though an inquiry into alleged manipulation may be conducted separately.
provisions: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(1)(a)
The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 25
The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 37
doctrines: Doctrine of repeal and substitution
Doctrine of exclusion of time during court stays
Doctrine of validity of administrative acts despite procedural delays if within extended statutory period
Doctrine of severability of procedural irregularities from substantive validity

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by the first respondent to set aside a sale deed executed in favor of the appellant's predecessor-in-interest after an auction by KSFC, on grounds including res judicata and suppression of facts.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint in the subsequent suit was liable to be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC on the ground that it was barred by res judicata or by any other law?
Whether the trial court could consider the written statement and prior pleadings while deciding an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC?
holdings: A plaint cannot be rejected under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC on the ground of res judicata unless the earlier suit has been finally decided and all conditions for res judicata are clearly disclosed on the face of the plaint.
While deciding an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC, the court must confine itself to the averments in the plaint; the written statement and external records cannot be considered.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11(d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIV
doctrines: Res judicata
Four corners of the plaint
Maintainability of suit

card.dispute: The appellant claimed partition of her step-mother's property, while contesting defendants claimed the property was sold via an agreement and willed to others.
issues_decided: Whether the alleged agreement for sale (Ex. B-10) dated 05.11.1976 was genuine and enforceable
Whether the Will (Ex. B-9) dated 15.06.1978 in favor of defendants 13 and 14 was valid
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the Trial Court's findings on the disputed documents
holdings: The agreement for sale (Ex. B-10) was fabricated, as the defendants failed to prove consideration, payment, or registration, and explanations for non-registration were implausible.
The Will (Ex. B-9) was not proven to be genuine, given suspicious circumstances, lack of corroboration, and the overall dishonesty in defendants' case.
The Trial Court’s findings were based on sound reasoning and should not have been overturned; the High Court erred in interfering with concurrent findings of fact.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact
Suspicious circumstances doctrine in will and document execution
Requirement of readiness and willingness in specific performance

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to set aside a sale deed executed by a second defendant holding a power of attorney, claiming the power of attorney had been cancelled before the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the power of attorney was effectively cancelled before the sale deed was executed.
Whether the sale deed executed by the second defendant was valid despite being for a lower consideration than agreed.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of the lower courts in a second appeal.
holdings: A registered power of attorney cannot be deemed cancelled merely by physical surrender; cancellation must be communicated to the third party and, preferably, registered.
A breach of an oral or unregistered instruction not to sell below a certain price does not invalidate a sale deed executed under a valid power of attorney.
The High Court erred in disturbing concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal, especially when documentary evidence supported the lower courts’ conclusions.
doctrines: Constructive notice under the Registration Act
Doctrine of cancellation of power of attorney
Principle of finality of concurrent findings in second appeal

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction and recovery of rent arrears, and the dispute centered on whether the tenant's defence should have been struck off for non-payment of rent during the pendency of the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the Trial Court's order striking off the defendant's defence under Order XV Rule 5 of the CPC for non-deposit of rent?
Whether the tenant's belated deposit of rent pursuant to the High Court's order absolves the earlier default?
Whether the Trial Court's findings on the tenant's volitional non-performance and lack of bonafide payment could be overturned?
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the Trial Court's order striking off the defence; where a tenant fails to deposit rent without lawful or bonafide justification, Order XV Rule 5 CPC mandates striking off the defence.

Deposits made only after and pursuant to an unsustainable order of the High Court do not cure the prior default; the revival of the Trial Court's order renders such deposits ineffective for protecting the defence.

The tenant's conduct showed deliberate defiance and elective non-performance; absence of bonafide payment or deposit justifies strict application of Order XV Rule 5 CPC, leaving no room for indulgence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XV Rule 5
doctrines: Order XV Rule 5 CPC mandates deposit of rent in landlord-tenant suits as a condition for contesting the suit.
Principle of volitional non-performance justifies strict enforcement of procedural requirements.
Judicial discretion under procedural law must be exercised with circumspection but not at the cost of rendering statutory provisions nugatory.

card.dispute: The appellant, B.R. Patil, challenged the partial decree in a partition suit filed by his sister and sister-in-law, seeking partition of family properties and accounting of rents, while contesting claims of adverse possession and inclusion of certain properties in the joint family estate.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim adverse possession or ouster against his co-owners in respect of the suit properties
Whether properties held in the name of the second defendant (another brother) were part of the joint family property or his separate assets
Whether the exclusion of certain properties from the partition claim was legally sustainable
Whether the impugned judgment was inequitable, particularly considering the appellant's age and circumstances
holdings: A co-owner cannot claim adverse possession unless there is a clear hostile animus and assertion of title inconsistent with co-ownership; mere exclusive possession is insufficient.
Properties acquired by a coparcener using his own resources, especially when not jointly financed, can remain his separate property even within a joint family setup.
Concurrent findings of fact by the Trial Court and High Court on ownership and possession are not interfered with in a special leave petition unless manifestly perverse.
Equitable considerations regarding personal hardship are matters for final decree proceedings and do not justify interference with a preliminary decree.
provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Adverse possession requiring hostile animus
Principle of concurrent findings of fact
Separate property of a coparcener in a Hindu Undivided Family
Limited scope of interference under Article 136

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a plaintiff who sued for specific performance of a 1982 agreement to purchase a site allotted by the Bangalore Development Authority fought against the defendants, including the vendor's successors and a subsequent purchaser, over whether the sale should be enforced.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to sell dated 17.11.1982 was enforceable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872
Whether the second defendant was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Whether the High Court was correct in decreeing specific performance in favour of the plaintiff
What relief, if any, should be granted to the plaintiff in light of the unenforceability of the agreement
holdings: The agreement to sell dated 17.11.1982 is unenforceable as it violates Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, being opposed to public policy by circumventing BDA regulations meant to ensure housing for the homeless.

The finding that the second defendant was not a bona fide purchaser need not be overturned, but even if so, it does not entitle the plaintiff to specific performance due to the illegality of the original agreement.
The suit for specific performance is not maintainable because enforcing the agreement would frustrate statutory objectives and promote illegal profiteering of public land.

While the suit for specific performance is dismissed, justice requires the appellants to pay Rs. 20 lakhs to the plaintiff as compensation, considering the plaintiff's payment of Rs. 50,000 decades ago and the current value of the property.
doctrines: Public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
In pari delicto, though not explicitly stated, the principle is applied in refusing relief to a party equally at fault
Equitable relief under Article 142 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The plaintiff claimed a share in joint family property based on a will and challenged the maintainability of a prior partition, while the defendants argued the suit was barred by res judicata due to a previous finding of partition in 1964.
issues_decided: Whether the award (Exhibit B-13) required registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908?
Whether the finding of partition in 1964 in a prior proceeding operated as res judicata, barring the plaintiff's fresh suit for partition?
holdings: A document that does not itself create a right in immovable property but merely provides for future division does not require registration under Section 17(1)(b) and is admissible in evidence.

A finding of fact on partition, once finally decided by a competent court and not challenged in appeal, operates as res judicata and bars a subsequent suit between the same parties on the same cause of action.
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Test for registration of documents creating rights in immovable property

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed whether Ram Devi, under a 1968 will, acquired a limited life interest or an absolute interest in property, and whether subsequent transfers to the respondents were valid.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, converted Ram Devi's limited life interest under the will into an absolute interest
Whether the will created a new title or merely recognized a pre-existing right, thus determining the applicability of Section 14(2)
Whether the respondents were bona fide purchasers for value despite prior litigation establishing Ram Devi's limited interest
holdings: Section 14(1) does not apply where a will creates a new, limited estate in favor of a female; it only converts limited interests arising by operation of law, not testamentary dispositions.
A will that grants a female a restricted estate for the first time falls under Section 14(2) and remains enforceable, preserving the testator’s intent to limit alienation.
Respondents cannot acquire a better title than Ram Devi; subsequent sales were invalid as they occurred during pending litigation and were not in good faith.
doctrines: Testamentary freedom under Hindu law
Doctrine of restricted estate under Section 14(2)
Bona fide purchaser doctrine
Principle of constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The appellant and her sister inherited property; the appellant challenged the validity of sales made by her sister via a Power of Attorney, leading to a dispute over partition and title when the property was sold to the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the Power of Attorney executed by the appellant conferred authority to sell the property
Whether the respondent could claim protection under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the appellant had constructive notice of the sale under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the failure to challenge prior alienations barred the appellant's claim for partition
holdings: A Power of Attorney must expressly authorize sale; absence of such clause means agent cannot validly sell the property.
Transferee cannot claim protection under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act without proving reasonable care and good faith in verifying authority.
Constructive notice under Section 3 cannot be attributed to the principal for unauthorized acts of the agent under a Power of Attorney.
Failure to challenge prior alienations does not bar a co-owner's right to seek partition and separate possession.
doctrines: Nemo dat quod non habet
Constructive notice
Strict construction of Power of Attorney
Ostensible owner doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant (seller) and respondent (buyer) fought over whether the court should grant specific performance of an agreement to sell land from 1989, or only refund the advance amount with interest.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent proved readiness and willingness to perform the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Whether the High Court was justified in granting specific performance despite delay and non-deposit of balance consideration.
Whether the court could modify the sale consideration due to steep rise in property prices since 1989.
holdings: Readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) must be in spirit and substance, not mere form; specific pleading and reliable evidence suffice without tendering or depositing balance amount.
The High Court rightly exercised discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act to grant specific performance based on conduct of parties and compliance with contractual obligations.
Due to steep rise in property values since 1989 and equitable considerations, the respondent must pay an additional Rs. 1 crore as modified sale consideration to secure the decree.
doctrines: Doctrine of readiness and willingness in specific performance
Judicial discretion in granting specific performance
Equitable modification of contract due to changed circumstances

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal heirs of Padhiyar Prahladji Chenaji (defendant) and Maniben Jagmalbhai (plaintiff) over whether the plaintiff was entitled to a permanent injunction to restrain the defendant from disturbing her possession of agricultural land sold via a registered sale deed in 1975.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a permanent injunction despite failing to obtain a declaratory decree or cancellation of the sale deed?
Whether the relief of permanent injunction can be granted as a substantive relief independent of title?
Whether the plaintiff’s possession of the suit property was lawful, entitling her to protection under the principle of 'due process of law'?
holdings: A permanent injunction is a consequential relief dependent on the success of a substantive claim like declaration or cancellation of deed; it cannot be granted if the plaintiff fails to establish title.

The plaintiff’s possession cannot be considered lawful when the defendant is the absolute owner under a registered sale deed with full consideration paid; thus, no injunction lies against the true owner.

Once a court adjudicates the rights of the parties and determines ownership, due process of law is satisfied, and a person in unlawful possession cannot claim protection from dispossession merely by invoking settled possession.
doctrines: Consequential relief doctrine
Lawful possession requirement for injunction
Due process of law in property dispossession

card.dispute: The appellant, Prabha Tyagi, challenged the dismissal of her application under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005, seeking reliefs against her mother-in-law and others, after the lower courts held that a Domestic Incident Report was mandatory and that she could not claim relief without residing with the respondents at the time of filing.
issues_decided: Whether consideration of a Domestic Incident Report is mandatory before initiating proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 to invoke Sections 18 to 20 and 22?
Whether the aggrieved person must reside with the respondents at the time of commission of domestic violence to claim relief?
Whether a subsisting domestic relationship is required between the aggrieved person and the respondent at the time of filing the application?
holdings: Section 12 of the Domestic Violence Act does not make it mandatory for a Magistrate to consider a Domestic Incident Report before passing orders; such report is only relevant when the application is filed by a Protection Officer or service provider.

It is not necessary for the aggrieved person to reside with the respondents at the time of the violence; a woman entitled to reside in a shared household can seek relief under the Act even if not currently residing there.

A subsisting domestic relationship at the time of filing is not required; an aggrieved person who had a domestic relationship in the past and suffered violence due to that relationship can file an application under Section 12.
provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 12
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 17
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Sections 18-22
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation
Proviso interpretation doctrine
Contextual reading of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellants (sellers) fought the respondent (buyer) over whether the court should grant specific performance of a 1990 agreement to sell 12.60 acres of land, despite a three-decade delay.
issues_decided: Whether the long delay in seeking specific performance renders the enforcement of the agreement inequitable?
Whether escalation in property prices over time, coupled with the plaintiff's inaction, bars the relief of specific performance?
Whether the courts can refuse specific performance despite fulfillment of legal conditions, based on equitable considerations?
holdings: A long delay in seeking specific performance, especially when coupled with inaction by the plaintiff, can render the decree inequitable even if the suit is within limitation.
Escalation in property value over decades, combined with the plaintiff’s failure to act promptly, may justify refusal of specific performance to prevent unjust enrichment.
Courts may refuse specific performance on equitable grounds even if the contract is enforceable, particularly where one party’s conduct causes hardship to the other.
doctrines: Specific performance is discretionary, not a matter of right
Time is not of the essence in immovable property sale agreements unless expressly stated
Equitable discretion to refuse relief due to delay and change in circumstances

card.dispute: The petitioner claimed a 10% plot allotment under a sale deed and NOIDA resolution after a 10-year delay, which the High Court rejected on grounds of delay, laches, and non-maintainability of a writ for specific performance of contract.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition under Article 226 is maintainable for specific performance of a contractual obligation?
Whether the petitioner's claim was barred by delay and laches?
Whether the rejection of a belated representation can give rise to a fresh cause of action?
holdings: A writ petition under Article 226 is not maintainable for specific performance of a contract; such relief must be sought through a civil suit.
The petition was barred by delay and laches as it was filed after 10–16 years, well beyond the limitation period for contractual claims.
Directing authorities to decide belated representations does not create a fresh cause of action; courts must dismiss such petitions at the threshold if barred by delay.
provisions: U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Specific performance of contract not enforceable via writ
No fresh cause of action from rejection of time-barred claims

card.dispute: The Association of Vasanth Apartments Owners challenged the requirement to execute a gift deed for open space reservation (OSR) in favor of the local authority, arguing it violated constitutional rights, while the respondents supported the rule as valid and mandatory.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 19(b) of the Development Control Rules (DCR) requiring a gift deed for open spaces violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the impugned rule is ultra vires the parent Act
Whether the compulsory gift deed amounts to a violation of Article 300A (right to property)
Whether open space reserved under the rule can be used for purposes other than communal and recreational use
holdings: Rule 19(b) does not violate Article 14 as it serves a legitimate public purpose and applies uniformly to developers with layouts over 10,000 sq.m.
The rule is statutory and intra vires the parent Act, forming part of development conditions imposed on builders.
The compulsory gift deed does not violate Article 300A as the owner retains no exclusive possession and holds the land in trust for public benefit.
OSR areas must be used solely for communal and recreational purposes and cannot be diverted for dumping or other unauthorized uses.
provisions: Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority (CMDA) Rules, Rule 61(7) and Rule 61(14)
doctrines: Doctrine of Compelled Dedication
Trust Doctrine in Land Use
Principle of Reasonable Classification under Article 14
Doctrine against Unconstitutional Conditions

card.dispute: The appellant's legal heir challenged the registration of a sale deed, alleging it was executed fraudulently, while the respondents sought its registration despite objections.
issues_decided: Whether the Registrar had jurisdiction under Section 74 of the Registration Act to decide on allegations of fraud and undue influence in the execution of a sale deed?
Whether the mere signing and fingerprinting of a document is sufficient for its registration, or whether 'execution' requires a broader legal validity?
Whether the High Court was correct in upholding the registration of the sale deed based solely on physical execution without examining substantive disputes?
holdings: The Registrar under the Registration Act lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate on serious disputes involving fraud or undue influence, which must be decided by a civil court.

Mere signing and affixing of fingerprints on a document does not constitute 'due execution' if there are substantial allegations of fraud, variance in area, boundaries, undervaluation, or non-receipt of consideration.
The High Court erred in equating physical signing with legal execution; registration cannot override triable civil disputes about the validity of a deed.
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers between registrars and civil courts in title disputes
Doctrine of limited jurisdiction of registrars under the Registration Act
Doctrine of equitable discretion in writ jurisdiction under Article 226

card.dispute: The appellant (Ghanshyam) fought against eviction from property by the respondent (Yogendra Rathi), who claimed possessory rights based on an agreement to sell, while the appellant alleged document manipulation.
issues_decided: Whether the documents relied upon by the respondent, including the agreement to sell, power of attorney, will, and possession memo, confer any enforceable right or title to seek eviction and mesne profits
Whether the appellant could challenge the legal effect of the documents for the first time in the High Court
Whether the respondent had a valid possessory title entitling him to evict the appellant after the licence period ended
holdings: An agreement to sell, coupled with full payment and delivery of possession, creates a possessory title under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, which protects the transferee against the transferor.
A licencee who remains in possession after the licence is lawfully terminated has no right to continue and can be evicted by the person in lawful possession.
Power of attorney and unprobated will do not transfer title; only registered sale deeds under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act can transfer immovable property worth over Rs.100.
The Delhi High Court's recognition of GPA and will as transfer instruments is contrary to statutory law and not binding.
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Licence and revocation of licence
No transfer of title by power of attorney or unprobated will
Statutory requirement of registration for transfer of immovable property

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the requirement for auction-purchasers to clear prior electricity dues as a condition for obtaining a new electricity connection, arguing that the agreement with the previous consumer was deemed terminated due to prolonged disconnection.
issues_decided: Whether the deemed termination of a consumer agreement under Regulation 4.6.1 applies when electricity supply has been disconnected for over 180 days.
Whether an auction-purchaser can be considered a 'consumer' under Regulation 4.6.4 without entering into a new agreement with the distribution licensee.
Whether conditions requiring new owners to pay arrears of previous consumers are valid and enforceable under the Electricity Act, 2003.
Whether the High Court's upholding of the distribution licensee's recovery conditions was legally sound.
holdings: Deemed termination of a consumer agreement under Regulation 4.6.1 occurs if electricity supply remains disconnected for more than 180 days, but this does not absolve subsequent purchasers from statutory conditions for reconnection.
An auction-purchaser is not a 'consumer' under Regulation 4.6.4 unless a new agreement is entered into with the distribution licensee; mere purchase of premises does not confer consumer status.

Conditions requiring new owners to clear outstanding electricity dues of previous consumers are valid under Section 50 of the Electricity Act, 2003, and have statutory force if framed under regulatory powers.
The distribution licensee may lawfully require payment of arrears as a precondition for service, and the High Court’s decision upholding this requirement is correct.
provisions: Electricity (Supply) Code or State Regulatory Commission Regulations (including Regulation 4.6.1 and 4.6.4)
doctrines: Deemed termination of contract
Statutory charge
Regulatory supremacy under Section 50
Public interest and equitable relief under Article 142
Conditional duty to supply electricity

card.dispute: Trinity Infraventures Ltd. and other appellants challenged a High Court judgment that declared a preliminary decree void due to fraud, affecting land rights in Survey No.172 of Hydernagar, while third parties sought protection for their rights in adjacent land (Survey No.163).
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's finding of fraud in the preliminary decree extends to land in Survey No.163 of Hydernagar?
Whether third-party societies not party to the original litigation can be impleaded in appeals to seek clarification of the High Court's judgment?
Whether the High Court's declaration of fraud in the preliminary decree binds the State and other third parties who acquired rights under it?
holdings: The finding of fraud in the preliminary decree pertains only to land in Survey No.172 and does not extend to Survey No.163, as clarified by a subsequent High Court judgment.
This Court cannot clarify or modify a High Court judgment through an application for impleadment or direction, especially when the applicant was not a party to the original proceedings.

Third parties who purchased land from the cooperative society are protected despite dismissal of impleadment, due to the use of 'third parties' in the High Court's judgment and the voidness of the decree.
doctrines: Doctrine of res judicata
Doctrine of impleadment
Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Prafulla Sahoo challenged the validity of a compromise between him and his sister Santilata regarding partition of ancestral and self-acquired properties of their father Kumar Sahoo, while the plaintiff Charulata Sahu sought her rightful share in the properties.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise between the defendants (Prafulla Sahoo and Santilata) in the partition suit was valid and binding?
Whether the daughters of Kumar Sahoo are entitled to a share in both ancestral and self-acquired properties?
Whether the trial court’s preliminary decree of partition requires modification in light of the Hindu Succession Act?
holdings: A compromise between parties in a suit is not binding unless the advocate had express authority to enter into it; the compromise between Prafulla Sahoo and Santilata was invalid due to lack of such authority.
Daughters are entitled to an equal 1/3rd share in both ancestral and self-acquired properties of the father, in accordance with the principles of equity and the spirit of the Hindu Succession Act.

The preliminary decree of partition must be modified to reflect equal shares for all three children, and the appellants are not entitled to the share of the deceased defendant no. 2 due to the invalid compromise.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3
doctrines: Implied authority of counsel
Client autonomy in litigation decisions
Equal inheritance rights of daughters in Hindu law

card.dispute: The State of Uttarakhand and others fought with the legal heirs of Ravi Kumar over ownership of 28.56 acres of land in Village Haripur, claiming the land belonged to the state, while the respondents claimed ownership through inheritance and tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the predecessor of the respondents acquired valid occupancy tenant status under the Oudh Rent Act, 1886 or the United Provinces Tenancy Act, 1939?
Whether the status of 'Sirdar' or 'Bhumidhar' was validly conferred upon the predecessor of the respondents under the Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950?
Whether the 1924 lease deed granted to John Vaughn extended beyond its initial term and whether it could be transferred to the respondents' predecessor?
Whether the High Court's findings on tenancy and ownership were based on sufficient and authentic records?
holdings: The court did not decide the tenancy status definitively due to lack of authentic records and remanded the issue for fresh adjudication.
The conferment of 'Sirdar' or 'Bhumidhar' status could not be upheld without proper documentation and legal validation, which were missing.
The 1924 lease could not be presumed to have been extended or transferred without evidence, and no valid transfer of occupancy rights was established.
The High Court's findings were based on conjecture and insufficient records, and thus the appeals were remanded for a proper factual and legal determination.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(26)
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of heritable but non-transferable tenancy rights
Principle of remand for proper adjudication on insufficient records

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers) challenged the High Court's decision restoring the trial court's dismissal of their suit, seeking declaration of ownership over land sold to them in 1985, against the original vendor and a subsequent purchaser who bought the same land in 2010.
issues_decided: Whether the 1985 sale deed was void ab initio due to the minority of one of the purchasers
Whether the 1985 sale deed was invalid due to non-registration and deficiency in stamp duty
Whether the subsequent purchaser in 2010 could claim protection as a bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Whether the original vendor could reclaim ownership due to pendency of registration of the 1985 sale deed
holdings: The minority of one purchaser did not invalidate the sale deed as the mother, acting as natural guardian for both minor sons, could represent both in the transaction.
A sale deed remains valid and transfers title upon execution and delivery of possession, even if registration is pending due to stamp duty deficiency; the vendor cannot reclaim ownership.
A subsequent purchaser cannot be a bona fide purchaser if the vendor had already transferred all rights in a prior sale; the doctrine does not protect purchasers when the vendor lacks legal title.
The pendency of registration does not benefit the vendor who has already received consideration and delivered possession; the purchaser's rights are protected despite procedural delays.
doctrines: Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Doctrine of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Principle of equitable protection of possession and performance
Void ab initio versus voidable transactions

card.dispute: M/s Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (petitioner) and Katta Sujatha Reddy & Ors. (respondents) fought over the specific performance of a sale agreement and the applicability of lis pendens during review proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the judgment of the Supreme Court dated 25 August 2022 suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record warranting review under Article 137 of the Constitution?
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act applies during the pendency of a review petition?
Whether the High Court was justified in decreeing specific performance to the extent of 90% of the consideration paid under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act?
holdings: The Supreme Court recalled its earlier judgment due to errors apparent on the face of the record concerning limitation and specific performance, thereby restoring the High Court's judgment.
The doctrine of lis pendens applies from the date of institution of a review petition, and any transfer of property after that date is subject to the outcome of the litigation.

It is not a fit case to grant partial specific performance under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act where the purchaser has breached an essential condition of the contract and the suit is barred by delay, laches, and limitation.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules 2013, Order XLVII Rule 1
doctrines: Lis pendens
Error apparent on the face of the record
Delay and laches
Specific performance of contracts

card.dispute: The Mukund Bhavan Trust challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by Shrimant Chhatrapati Udayan Raje seeking declaration of ownership, possession, and cancellation of compromise decrees concerning certain suit lands, on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation.
