issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by the respondent was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the compromise decrees in earlier suits could be set aside by a stranger to those proceedings
Whether the plaint could be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(d) of CPC based on ex facie limitation
holdings: A suit to set aside a transaction based on fraudulent misrepresentation as to contents, not character, is governed by a three-year limitation from the date of knowledge of fraud under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, and is not void ab initio.
A third party not impleaded in earlier suits cannot challenge compromise decrees under Order XXIII Rule 3A of CPC, and such a challenge is barred both substantively and by limitation.
Where a plaint is manifestly barred by limitation on its face, it may be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(d) of CPC to prevent abuse of process and unnecessary litigation.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(d)
Civil Procedure Code, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3A
doctrines: Distinction between void and voidable transactions based on nature of fraud
Bar of maintainability of suit by a stranger to compromise decree
Threshold rejection of plaint for being barred by limitation

card.dispute: Neelam Gupta and others fought against Rajendra Kumar Gupta over possession of 7.60 acres of land, with the defendants claiming adverse possession and the plaintiff asserting title and rightful possession.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants established adverse possession to defeat the plaintiff's claim to the suit property?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of the lower courts?
Whether the period of limitation for adverse possession commenced from the date of the plaintiff's ownership or from the date the possession became adverse?
Whether the appellants violated the status quo order by creating third-party rights during pendency of the appeal?
holdings: Once a plaintiff proves title, the burden shifts to the defendant to prove adverse possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The defendants failed to establish the necessary animus possidendi and continuous, open, and hostile possession required for adverse possession.
The limitation period for adverse possession begins only when possession becomes adverse, not from the date of the plaintiff's acquisition of title.
The contempt petition is rendered infructuous as the decree has become final and is executable, allowing the plaintiff to seek execution instead.
doctrines: Adverse possession requiring nec vi, nec clam, nec precario
Burden of proof shifting upon establishment of title
Perversity in concurrent findings justifying appellate interference
Status quo orders during pendency of appeal

card.dispute: The sellers appealed against a High Court judgment directing specific performance of an agreement for sale of land and building, which the Trial Court had originally dismissed.
issues_decided: Whether the buyer was ready and willing to perform her part of the agreement for sale?
Whether the High Court was justified in granting specific performance despite the buyer's conduct indicating lack of genuine intent to purchase?
Whether a higher court can examine the existence of a jurisdictional fact for maintainability of a suit even if no issue was framed by the trial court?
holdings: A buyer seeking specific performance must demonstrate continuous readiness and willingness to perform; delay in returning a cancelled demand draft undermines such claim.
Conduct of the buyer, including retaining a demand draft until its expiry, casts doubt on her bona fides, justifying denial of discretionary relief of specific performance.
A higher court may examine the existence of a jurisdictional fact essential for granting relief, even if not specifically raised or framed by the trial court, provided no new evidence is needed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(d)
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Doctrine of readiness and willingness in specific performance
Maintainability of suit based on existence of enforceable agreement

card.dispute: The defendant appealed against the decree of specific performance granted to the plaintiffs (Sasikala and K. Satyanarayana) for the sale of a property, claiming the plaintiffs were not ready and willing to perform their part of the contract.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were ready and willing to perform their part of the agreement to sell?
Whether the restriction imposed by the State Government on registration of sale deeds excused the plaintiffs from showing readiness and willingness?
Whether the trial and high courts erred in decreeing specific performance despite lack of evidence of readiness, willingness, and financial capacity?
holdings: A plaintiff seeking specific performance must prove both readiness and willingness through conduct and circumstances, not merely by pleading; absence of draft sale deed or tender of balance amount undermines such claim.

Mere governmental restrictions on registration do not absolve a plaintiff from demonstrating readiness and willingness; especially when others managed to complete transactions under similar conditions.
Courts must assess financial capacity and conduct over time; prolonged silence and inaction after notice of forfeiture negate claims of readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness in specific performance
Time is of the essence in contracts
Equitable compensation in lieu of specific performance

card.dispute: The appellant (Rajesh Kumar) sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, but the defendants (Anand Kumar and others) sold the land to third parties; the dispute centered on whether the appellant was entitled to specific performance despite delays and failure to prove readiness and willingness.
issues_decided: Whether a Power of Attorney holder can depose on behalf of the plaintiff regarding readiness and willingness to perform a contract in a suit for specific performance?
Whether the plaintiff's delay in filing the suit for specific performance, despite awareness of the breach, affects the grant of discretionary relief?
Whether the plaintiff fulfilled the requirements under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, particularly regarding readiness and willingness to perform the contract?
holdings: A Power of Attorney holder cannot testify on behalf of the plaintiff regarding the plaintiff's state of mind, such as readiness and willingness to perform the contract; only the plaintiff can depose on such personal matters and be cross-examined.

Filing a suit for specific performance at the fag end of the limitation period, without explanation for the delay, especially after taking steps like sending a legal notice, negates the claim of readiness and willingness and justifies denial of discretionary relief.

The plaintiff failed to prove readiness and willingness under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as he did not appear as a witness, and the suit was filed after inordinate delay, undermining the claim for specific performance.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness as essential conditions for specific performance
Discretionary nature of relief under specific performance
Personal knowledge requirement for testimony on state of mind
Effect of delay in filing suit for specific performance

card.dispute: The appellants (plaintiffs) sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell 23.98 acres of land originally owned by Sushila Devi, which the High Court dismissed, leading to appeals before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs proved the existence and enforceability of the Agreement to Sell dated 30.08.1990?
Whether the non-appearance of the plaintiffs in the witness box rendered their suits for specific performance unsustainable?
Whether the subsequent sale deeds executed during the pendency of the suit could defeat the plaintiffs' claim for specific performance?
Whether the Agreement to Sell was void for vagueness due to lack of specific boundary details?
holdings: The Agreement to Sell dated 30.08.1990 was valid and enforceable as it sufficiently identified the property through khasra numbers, area, and location, enabling clear identification.
The plaintiffs' failure to personally appear as witnesses did not weaken their case, as competent Power of Attorney holders with personal knowledge of the transaction testified effectively.
Subsequent transfers during litigation are not void ab initio but are subject to lis pendens and cannot prejudice prior rights under a valid agreement for specific performance.
The absence of explicit boundary details in the agreement does not render it unenforceable if the property can be identified with certainty from other descriptions provided.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 52 (Doctrine of Lis Pendens)
doctrines: Doctrine of Lis Pendens
Burden of Proof in Cases of Alleged Fraud
Competence of Power of Attorney Holder to Testify
Enforceability of Contracts with Sufficiently Identifiable Property

card.dispute: The Urban Improvement Trust challenged the High Court's decision quashing land acquisition proceedings initiated by it, which the respondents (landowners) had contested on grounds of delayed compensation and procedural irregularities.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the writ petitions by the respondents was justified.
Whether the notification issued under Section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 was valid.
Whether the compensation was determined and paid lawfully and within the time mandated by law.
holdings: The High Court did not commit any error in condoning the delay in filing the writ petitions, as the respondents had sufficient cause for the delay due to ongoing proceedings and lack of payment of compensation.
The notification under Section 52(1) of the RUI Act was invalid because the compensation was not deposited within six months from August 1, 1987, as required by Section 60A(4) of the same Act.

The acquisition process was unlawful due to non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of timely payment of compensation, violating Article 300A of the Constitution and the principles of fairness in a welfare state.
doctrines: Time is of the essence in payment of compensation under eminent domain.
Strict construction of laws depriving property rights under Article 300A.
Principle of fairness and constitutional obligation in land acquisition by a welfare state.

card.dispute: The grandsons of B and M, daughters of two brothers, fought over whether M inherited an absolute estate through an 1884 arbitration award or only a limited estate, triggering reversionary rights upon her death.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award granted M an absolute estate in the property allotted to her.
Whether the plaintiffs were estopped from challenging the validity of the award despite claiming as reversioners.
holdings: The words 'Malik Mustaqil' in the award clearly conveyed an absolute and unqualified estate to M, as they were strong, clear, and unambiguous, and not limited by other terms in the document.

The plaintiffs were estopped from challenging the award because their predecessors had accepted and acted upon it for over forty years, benefiting from it and inducing M to act on her absolute ownership.
provisions: Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Section 115 (Doctrine of Estoppel)
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act
Estoppel by conduct in property disputes involving reversioners
Acceptance and benefit from an award bars later challenge to its validity

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax, U.P. fought with Gappumal Kanhaiya Lal over whether municipal house-tax and water-tax could be deducted from the annual value of a property for income tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the amount of house-tax imposed under the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 is an annual charge deductible from the annual value of the property under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the amount of water-tax imposed under the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 is similarly deductible as an annual charge under the same provision.
holdings: House-tax levied by a municipal board under the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, and paid by the owner as lessor, is an annual charge not being a capital charge and is deductible from the annual value of the property under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.

Water-tax imposed under the same Act and paid by the owner as lessor is also an annual charge not being a capital charge and is deductible from the annual value of the property under the same provision.
doctrines: Interpretation of 'annual charges not being capital charges'
First charge on property under municipal taxation laws

card.dispute: The plaintiffs appealed against two decrees from the same judgment in a suit for possession of land, where one appeal was filed in time and the other after limitation; the respondents argued the delayed appeal barred the timely one by res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res judicata applies to a timely appeal when another appeal from a separate decree in the same case is filed out of time.
Whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908, for condonation of delay where there is a conflict of judicial decisions on the issue.
holdings: When a single suit results in one judgment and multiple decrees, a timely appeal from one decree remains maintainable even if another appeal from a co-decree is time-barred; res judicata does not apply between appeals arising from the same judgment.
The appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 5 of the Limitation Act where there is a conflict of decisions on the legal question, justifying condonation of delay in filing the second appeal.
doctrines: Res judicata
Condonation of delay
Single cause of action
Conflict of judicial decisions

card.dispute: The decree-holder (Bhawanipore Banking Corporation) fought to execute a mortgage decree against the judgment-debtor's legal representatives, who argued the execution application was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act constitutes a 'review' under Article 182, Clause 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908, so as to extend the limitation period for execution.

Whether an appeal from the dismissal of an application under Order IX, Rule 9, CPC, in connection with proceedings under the Bengal Money-lenders Act, amounts to 'an appeal' under Article 182, Clause 2, thus restarting limitation for execution.
holdings: An application dismissed for default under Section 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act does not amount to a 'review' under Article 182, Clause 3, because the court did not apply its mind to re-open the decree.

An appeal from an order dismissing an application under Order IX, Rule 9, CPC, which is collateral to the decree, does not restart limitation under Article 182, Clause 2, as it is not an appeal 'for the execution of a decree'.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order IX, Rules 9 and 13
doctrines: Doctrine of limitation for execution of decrees
Doctrine of review under the Limitation Act
Principle of effective judicial consideration in review proceedings

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued to recover possession of land based on prior claims as shikmedars and purchasers, which the defendants opposed by pleading res judicata from an earlier suit.
issues_decided: Whether the Munsif who decided the earlier suit had jurisdiction to try the subsequent suit for the purpose of applying res judicata.
Whether the subsequent suit was barred by res judicata despite an increase in the land revenue assessment between the two suits.
holdings: For res judicata to apply, the competence of the court in the prior suit is determined by its jurisdiction at the time of that suit, not at the time of the later suit.
A subsequent increase in the valuation of the property does not negate res judicata if the earlier court could have tried the suit when it was first decided.
doctrines: res judicata
pecuniary jurisdiction
jurisdiction of court at the time of prior decision

card.dispute: The dispute was between a decree-holder seeking execution of a money decree and a widow who claimed priority in possession of the deceased husband's property for unpaid dower over unsecured creditors.
issues_decided: Whether a Muslim widow in possession of her husband's estate is entitled to priority over other unsecured creditors in the payment of her dower debt.
Whether the widow's claim for dower creates a lien on the husband's estate giving her a secured creditor status.
holdings: A Muslim widow's claim for dower is in the nature of an unsecured debt and does not entitle her to priority over other unsecured creditors, even if she is in possession of the husband's estate.

The widow's possession of the estate does not create a legal lien or charge; her right to retain possession is not superior to that of other creditors, and dower ranks pari passu with other unsecured debts.
provisions: Muhammadan Law (unspecified provisions regarding dower and debt priority)
doctrines: Pari passu distribution of unsecured debts in Muslim personal law
No inherent priority of dower over unsecured creditors under Hanafi law
Creditor's lien in possession without legal charge

card.dispute: The plaintiffs and defendants contested over who were the rightful reversioners to the estate of Rai Bahadur Govind Ballab Ray, based on whether Binodini was his natural daughter.
issues_decided: Whether Binodini was the natural daughter of Govind Ballab Ray or merely adopted into the family
Whether the account papers (Exh. 32 series) and almanac entries proved that Binodini was not Govind Ballab's daughter
Whether the appeal by the defendants was maintainable despite initial non-payment of ad valorem court-fee
holdings: The oral evidence, particularly of Khirodemani Dassi, supported that Binodini was the natural daughter of Govind Ballab Ray, and the trial court erred in disbelieving it.
The account papers and almanac entries relied upon by the plaintiffs lacked probative value and were not sufficiently proved to be authentic or contemporaneous.
The High Court had the discretion under Section 149, CPC to allow amendment of the appeal memorandum and accept belated court-fee payment without violating limitation or causing injustice.
doctrines: Probative value of documentary evidence
Discretion of court to allow amendments under CPC
Principle of limitation not a bar when court exercises discretion under Section 149 CPC

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the admissibility of a compromise decree for non-registration, arguing it created a registrable lease, while the respondent claimed it was exempt from registration.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree created a 'lease' within the meaning of Section 17(1)(d) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, requiring compulsory registration.
Whether the compromise decree, though creating an agreement relating to immovable property, fell under the exception to registration under Section 17(2)(vi) as a court decree.
holdings: An agreement for a lease must create a present and immediate interest in land to be registrable; a contingent agreement that depends on future conditions does not constitute a 'lease' under Section 17(1)(d).

A compromise decree that does not immediately create a lease but is conditional on future performance is not compulsorily registrable and falls under the exception in Section 17(2)(vi) for court decrees.
doctrines: Doctrine of immediate and present interest in land for lease agreements
Conditional agreements not amounting to a demise until conditions are fulfilled
Exemption of court decrees from registration under Section 17(2)(vi)

card.dispute: The New Piecegoods Bazar Co. fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether municipal property tax and urban immoveable property tax could be deducted while computing income from property under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether municipal property tax under the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888 is an 'annual charge not being a capital charge' under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether urban immoveable property tax under the Bombay Finance Act, 1932 is similarly deductible under the same provision.
What is the meaning of 'annual charge' and 'capital charge' in section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act?
holdings: A charge for municipal property tax under section 212 of the City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888 is an 'annual charge not being a capital charge' and is deductible under section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act.
Urban immoveable property tax under the Bombay Finance Act, 1932 is of the same character and also deductible under section 9(1)(iv).

The term 'capital charge' refers to a charge securing a liability of a capital nature, while 'annual charge' means a charge securing an annual liability, regardless of whether payments are made in instalments.
provisions: City of Bombay Municipal Act, 1888, Section 212
doctrines: Statutory interpretation: literal meaning of 'annual charge' and 'capital charge'
Principle of legislative intent in tax law
Rejection of analogical reasoning from other sections (e.g., Section 10) in interpreting deductions

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of an agreement to assign a leasehold interest, which the defendant refused to complete on the ground that the lessor had withheld consent.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to assign the leasehold interest was conditional upon obtaining the lessor's consent.
Whether the covenant in the lease deed allowing assignment if consent is not unreasonably withheld creates a separate obligation on the lessor.
Whether the plaintiff could rely on the lessor's unreasonable withholding of consent to claim specific performance despite not joining the lessor in the suit.
Whether the defendant could be compelled to perform the agreement despite the risk of liability for breach of covenant with the lessor.
holdings: The agreement was not conditional on obtaining the lessor's consent; the obligation to obtain consent was a term of the agreement to be fulfilled by the defendant.
The clause stating consent should not be unreasonably withheld does not create an independent covenant by the lessor but only qualifies the lessee's covenant against assignment without consent.
The court could determine whether the lessor unreasonably withheld consent for the purpose of granting specific performance between the parties, even without the lessor being a party to the suit.

The defendant could not avoid specific performance by pleading risk of liability to the lessor, especially since the plaintiff was a respectable and responsible person and the defendant had unconditionally agreed to obtain consent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 27
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonable withholding of consent in lease assignments
Doctrine of beneficial terms in contracts
Doctrine of specific performance despite third-party consent requirements

card.dispute: The plaintiff, who obtained a decree for pre-emption, failed to deposit the sale price within the time fixed by the decree, leading to a dispute over whether his suit stood dismissed for default.
issues_decided: Whether the filing of an appeal suspends the obligation to deposit the pre-emption price within the time fixed by the trial court's decree.
Whether the omission to include a dismissal warning in the decree affects the operation of Order 20, Rule 14 of the Civil Procedure Code.
holdings: Filing an appeal does not automatically suspend the decree; the preemptor must comply with the decree's terms unless stayed by the appellate court.
The mandatory dismissal under Order 20, Rule 14, Civil Procedure Code, applies regardless of whether the decree explicitly states that failure to deposit will result in dismissal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 14
doctrines: Mandatory nature of decree compliance
Automatic dismissal for non-compliance with decree conditions

card.dispute: The State of Tripura sued the Province of East Bengal to declare the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1944 ultra vires and to restrain assessment, after partition separated the estate from the taxing authority.
issues_decided: Whether the court in West Bengal had jurisdiction to try the suit against the Province of East Bengal after partition
Whether the cause of action amounted to a tort, making it actionable under the Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947
Whether section 65 of the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act barred the suit
Whether the suit was infructuous due to a subsequent Pakistani Ordinance
holdings: A court in West Bengal could exercise jurisdiction over the Province of East Bengal if the cause of action was connected with rights or liabilities under the Indian Independence Orders.
The issuance of a tax notice under an allegedly ultra vires law constitutes an actionable wrong, though not a tort, and is remediable by injunction.
Section 65 of the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act does not bar a suit challenging the constitutional validity of the Act or seeking injunctive relief.
The effect of a Pakistani Ordinance invalidating Indian court decrees was not decided, as it was not raised before the High Court and required further examination.
provisions: Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947, Articles 10(2), 12(2)
doctrines: Actionable wrong distinct from tort
Liberal interpretation of post-partition legal orders
State liability for injunctive relief despite sovereign immunity in tort
Maintainability of declaratory and injunctive suits against government

card.dispute: The appellant Kapildeo Singh was convicted for being part of an unlawful assembly and rioting, and the appeal challenged the validity of that conviction due to the failure to determine possession of disputed land, a key issue in assessing self-defence and aggression.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to determine possession of the disputed land vitiated the conviction under s. 147 IPC?
Whether the High Court's assumption that possession was immaterial amounted to a serious miscarriage of justice?
Whether this Court should interfere with the criminal conviction in exercise of its special leave jurisdiction?
holdings: The question of possession was vital to determining who was the aggressor and whether the right of private defence applied, and its omission amounted to a serious and substantial injustice.
The High Court erred in treating possession as immaterial merely because both sides resorted to force, as this misapplied the law and failed to address the core issue in the charge.
This Court may interfere in criminal appeals only when there is a serious and substantial miscarriage of justice, which was present here due to the failure to decide a pivotal factual issue.
doctrines: Principle of private defence of property
Doctrine of unlawful assembly under common object
Miscarriage of justice in criminal appeals
Limits of appellate interference in criminal cases

card.dispute: The appellant contested whether a memorandum of deposit of title deeds was compulsorily registrable under the Indian Registration Act, 1908, thereby affecting the enforceability of an alleged equitable mortgage.
issues_decided: Whether the memorandum of deposit of title deeds dated 23rd October, 1936, was compulsorily registrable under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908
Whether the document created an interest in immovable property by express agreement or was merely evidential of an already completed transaction
holdings: A memorandum of deposit of title deeds requires registration only if the parties intended it to embody the express contract creating the mortgage; otherwise, if it merely records an already concluded transaction, it is not registrable.

The document in question was not intended to create the mortgage but to record a deposit already made with the requisite intent, and thus did not require registration under Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act.
doctrines: Equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds
Distinction between operative instrument and evidential document
Implication of contract from conduct under Section 58(f)

card.dispute: The plaintiff-appellant claimed enforcement of a mortgage deed, while the defendant-contestant denied its validity on grounds of non-attestation, leading to a dispute over whether the document was properly attested in accordance with law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court was justified in reversing the trial court's finding on the attestation of the mortgage deed based on oral evidence?
Whether the trial court's reliance on witness credibility without explicit reference to demeanour is legally valid?
Whether the circumstances surrounding the execution of the mortgage deed were inherently improbable as held by the High Court?
holdings: An appellate court should not reverse a trial court's finding on witness credibility unless there is a demonstrable error or inherent improbability in the evidence, even if the trial judge does not expressly refer to witness demeanour.
The mere absence of express reference to witness demeanour by the trial judge does not diminish the weight of its factual findings based on oral testimony.

The High Court erred in rejecting the plaintiff's version of attestation based on assumed social customs and speculative improbability, where the evidence taken as a whole reasonably supported the trial court's conclusion.
doctrines: Principle of appellate deference to trial court findings on witness credibility
Rule against interference with concurrent findings of fact unless perverse or unsupported
Doctrine of proper attestation under Indian evidentiary law

card.dispute: The dispute was between the sister's sons and the paternal uncle's son of a deceased Hindu maiden over who had superior rights to inherit her stridhan property.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 applies to determine succession to the stridhan property of a Hindu female who died as a maiden.
Who is the nearer heir to the stridhan property of a Hindu maiden under Mitakshara and Mayukha schools of Hindu law when both sister's sons and paternal uncle's son are claimants.
holdings: The Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 applies only to the separate property of a Hindu male dying intestate and does not govern succession to the property of a Hindu female, including her stridhan.

Under Mitakshara and Mayukha law, the paternal uncle's son is a nearer heir than the sister's sons to the property of a Hindu female who dies as a maiden, after the failure of her uterine brothers, mother, and father.
provisions: Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, Section 1(2)
doctrines: Order of succession under Mitakshara law
Order of succession under Mayukha law
Rule of propinquity in determining sapindas
Statutory interpretation of Hindu succession laws

card.dispute: The karta of a Hindu undivided family residing in Ceylon contested the tax authorities' assessment, claiming the family's control and management was wholly outside British India and thus not liable to tax as a resident entity.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu undivided family was a resident under section 4A(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, based on the seat of control and management of its affairs.
Whether the karta’s visits to India and activities there established a second seat of control and management.
Whether the onus of proving non-residence under section 4A(b) lay on the assessee and was discharged.
holdings: A Hindu undivided family is presumed resident in British India unless the assessee proves that the control and management of its affairs is wholly situated outside.
Occasional visits and business activities in India, without evidence of permanent direction from within, do not shift the seat of control and management.
The onus of proving that control and management is wholly outside British India lies on the assessee and was not discharged in this case.
The family may have more than one residence if control is genuinely exercised in multiple places, but dual control must be affirmatively proven.
doctrines: Residence based on seat of control and management
Presumption of residence unless exception is proved
Onus of proof on the assessee to establish non-residence
Analogy of corporate residence applied to Hindu undivided family

card.dispute: The Province of Bombay requisitioned land under the Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance, and the landowners challenged the order, seeking a writ of certiorari on the ground that the government lacked a public purpose for the requisition.
issues_decided: Whether the order of land requisition under the Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance was a judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative act
Whether a writ of certiorari could lie against an administrative act of the Provincial Government
Whether the existence of a public purpose was a condition precedent to the power of requisition, and if its erroneous determination could be corrected by certiorari
holdings: The act of requisitioning land under the Ordinance was administrative, not judicial or quasi-judicial, as it depended on the subjective opinion of the government regarding necessity or expediency.
A writ of certiorari does not lie to challenge administrative acts, even if there is an error in determining a collateral fact like public purpose, absent bad faith.

The determination of public purpose, even if required under the statute, was part of the administrative process and not a separate judicial function; thus, its erroneous determination could not be corrected by certiorari.
provisions: Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance (V of 1947), Section 3
Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance (V of 1947), Section 4
Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance (V of 1947), Section 10
Bombay Land Requisition Ordinance (V of 1947), Section 12
doctrines: Distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial acts
Scope and applicability of the writ of certiorari
Collateral fact doctrine in administrative law
Doctrine of subjective satisfaction in executive action

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a will alienating non-ancestral property on customary grounds, while respondents argued such challenges are barred by statute.
issues_decided: Whether the District Judge improperly admitted additional evidence in appeal under Order XLI, Rule 27 of the Civil Procedure Code
Whether a finding based on inadmissible additional evidence can be sustained in second appeal
Whether a suit contesting alienation of non-ancestral property on the ground of custom is maintainable under Section 7 of the Punjab Custom Act, 1920
holdings: The admission of additional evidence in appeal is a judicial discretion limited to cases where inherent lacunae in the record prevent judgment; it cannot be used to introduce fresh external evidence.
A finding of fact based solely on improperly admitted additional evidence, especially when the evidence has palpable defects not considered, cannot be binding in second appeal.
No person can challenge the alienation of non-ancestral immovable property on the ground that it violates custom, as expressly barred by Section 7 of the Punjab Custom Act, 1920.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 27
doctrines: Judicial discretion in admitting additional evidence
Finality of findings of fact in second appeal subject to legal error
Statutory bar on customary challenges to alienation of non-ancestral property

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers in a certificate sale) claimed that the mokarrari tenancy interest of one Bisheshwar Dayal Singh merged into his lakhraj proprietary interest, thereby extinguishing part of the lease; the respondents (co-tenants) contested this, asserting their right to recover rent over a larger share.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of merger applied when one of several joint mokarraridars acquired a portion of the lakhraj interest held jointly with others?
Whether an inter se partition among mokarraridars affects the integrity of the tenancy in relation to the lessor?
Whether the certificate sale transferred the mokarrari interest due to alleged merger?
holdings: Merger does not occur when one of several joint lessees acquires only a portion of the lessor's interest; there must be complete coalescence of leasehold and reversion in the same person for merger to apply.
An inter se partition among co-lessees does not destroy the unity of the tenancy; they remain collectively liable for the entire rent as a single tenant in law.
The mokarrari interest did not merge and thus was not transferred by the certificate sale; it remained with the co-tenants who were entitled to recover rent over their share.
doctrines: Doctrine of merger in landlord-tenant law
Unity of tenancy among joint lessees
Privity of estate in leasehold law

card.dispute: The appellant, Bijjoy Chand Potra, challenged his conviction under Section 326 IPC for causing grievous hurt, despite being charged only under Section 307 IPC for attempt to murder, and raised procedural objections including inadequate examination under Section 342 CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether a conviction under Section 326 IPC is legal when the accused was charged only under Section 307 IPC and no alternative charge was framed.
Whether failure to fully examine the accused under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code vitiates the trial.
holdings: A conviction under Section 326 IPC is valid even without a formal charge if the facts support it and the accused could have been alternatively charged under Section 237 CrPC, which permits conviction for an uncharged offence that is covered by the evidence and would have been chargeable.
Non-compliance with Section 342 CrPC does not invalidate a conviction unless the accused demonstrates that the inadequate examination caused material prejudice to his defence.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive charge under Section 237 CrPC
Principle of procedural fairness requiring demonstration of prejudice for reversal

card.dispute: The plaintiff claimed specific performance of a contract to buy a bungalow, alleging that the defendant's cable stating a minimum price of Rs. 10,000 was a counter-offer which he accepted, while the defendant sold the property to another buyer for Rs. 11,000.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant's cable stating he would not accept less than Rs. 10,000 constituted a counter-offer capable of acceptance
Whether a concluded contract arose on the plaintiff's letter of 14th August confirming his oral offer
Whether the conduct of the agent (Youngman) indicated acceptance of the plaintiff's offer
holdings: A statement of the lowest price at which a seller is willing to sell is not a counter-offer but an invitation to treat, and does not create a binding contract upon acceptance.
An offer to buy at the stated price is a fresh offer requiring acceptance by the seller; without such acceptance, no contract is formed.
The conduct of the seller and his agent, including seeking permission to sell and entertaining higher offers, shows that no binding offer was made at Rs. 10,000.
Mere communication of an offer by an agent without express authority to conclude a sale does not amount to acceptance unless the principal assents.
doctrines: Invitation to treat
Offer and acceptance
Counter-offer distinction
Harvey v. Facey doctrine

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Police refused to reinstate a permission granted to Gordhandas Bhanji to construct a cinema, after the Government had directed its cancellation, leading to a petition for mandamus under the Specific Relief Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could issue an order under Section 45 of the Specific Relief Act directing the Commissioner to withdraw the cancellation of the cinema construction permission.
Whether the respondent had an adequate alternative legal remedy, such as filing a suit for injunction.
Whether the requirements of Section 46 of the Specific Relief Act (demand and denial) were satisfied.
holdings: The High Court could issue relief under Section 45 of the Specific Relief Act because the Commissioner had a duty to exercise his statutory discretion and could not abdicate it to the Government; the order of cancellation was not his own decision but made under Government instructions.

The respondent had no other specific and adequate legal remedy, as ignoring the cancellation order would have been imprudent and a civil suit for injunction would cause inordinate delay prejudicial to a commercial project.

The requirements of Section 46 were satisfied in substance, as the correspondence between the parties constituted a clear demand for justice and an unequivocal denial, even though not formally addressed to the Commissioner.
provisions: City of Bombay Police Act (1 of 1902), Section 22(1)
Rules for Licensing and Controlling Theaters and Other Places of Public Amusement in Bombay City, 1914, Rules 8, 238–257, 263–283, Rule 250
doctrines: Duty to exercise statutory discretion
Proper use of mandamus under specific relief
Substantial compliance with demand and denial
Adequacy of alternative remedies

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the State of Bombay's refusal to re-assess agricultural land converted to non-agricultural use and pay them the resulting revenue.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's confirmation of the Collector's refusal to re-assess converted land amounts to a valid direction under Rule 92 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code Rules.
Whether the Collector is under a mandatory duty to alter assessment when agricultural land is used for non-agricultural purposes.
Whether the Government can exercise discretion to refrain from altering assessment in such cases.
holdings: The Government's mere confirmation of the Collector's order refusing re-assessment does not constitute a valid direction under Rule 92; such a direction must be explicit and formally notified.

Rule 92 imposes a mandatory duty on the Collector to alter assessment when agricultural land is used for non-agricultural purposes, provided no valid contrary direction has been issued by the Government.

The Government cannot defeat the statutory liability to re-assess by exercising discretion through informal or implicit actions; the power to override Rule 92 must be exercised clearly and unambiguously.
provisions: Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, Rules 81 to 87
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of administrative rules affecting civil rights
Requirement of clear and unambiguous exercise of governmental power that affects private rights
Non-delegation of statutory duty without explicit authority

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed whether the maximum allowable interest under the Bihar Money-lenders Act should be calculated based on the original 1893 loan amount or the 1931 renewed mortgage document.
issues_decided: Whether constructive res judicata barred the decree-holder from arguing a particular interpretation of Section 7 of the Bihar Money-lenders Act.

What constitutes 'the amount of loan mentioned in, or evidenced by, such document' under Section 7 of the Bihar Money-lenders (Regulation of Transactions) Act, 1939, when a later document is executed for a pre-existing loan?
holdings: Constructive res judicata does not apply where the earlier decision did not determine the correct interpretation of a statutory provision.

For the purpose of Section 7, the 'amount of loan' is the amount stated in the later document renewing the loan, not the original loan amount, and interest can be decreed up to that amount if not already exceeded by payments.
provisions: Bihar Money-lenders (Regulation of Transactions) Act, 1939, Section 7
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Statutory interpretation
Legislative acquiescence

card.dispute: The complainant appealed an acquittal order in a criminal case, leading to a retrial order by the High Court, which the appellants challenged on grounds of exceeding revisional jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its revisional powers under Section 439 of the CrPC by overturning an acquittal based on re-appreciation of evidence?
Whether a private party can file a revision petition under Section 439 of the CrPC against an order of acquittal?
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence and reverse factual findings in a revision petition filed by a private party, even if it considers the trial court's judgment perverse, as it lacks power to convert acquittal into conviction.
Section 439 CrPC does not bar a private party from filing a revision petition, but the High Court must not exceed its revisional jurisdiction by effectively undermining the acquittal.
doctrines: Principle of finality of acquittal
Limitation on revisional jurisdiction in criminal cases
Separation of fact-finding and appellate review

card.dispute: The complainant, Polailal Biswas, challenged the acquittal of the appellants (Logendranath Jha and others) in a criminal case involving alleged violence during a land dispute, seeking a retrial through a revision petition under Section 439 of the CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether a private party can file a revision petition under Section 439 of the CrPC against an order of acquittal?
Whether the High Court can re-appreciate evidence and reverse findings of fact in a revision petition against acquittal, without committing an error of law?
holdings: It is unnecessary to decide whether a private party can file a revision petition under Section 439 of the CrPC against an acquittal, as the second ground of appeal was sufficient to decide the case.

The High Court cannot, in revision against an acquittal, re-appreciate evidence and reverse findings of fact merely because it considers them 'perverse', especially in the absence of any error of law; doing so exceeds its powers under Section 439(4) of the CrPC.
doctrines: Limitation on High Court's revisional powers
Finality of findings of fact in acquittal cases
Prohibition on indirect conversion of acquittal into conviction

card.dispute: The appellant Sukhdev Singh contested the respondent Maharaja Bahadur of Gidhaur's claim to ownership of a ghatwali tenure and sub-soil rights, arguing it was a Government ghatwali rather than a zemindary-dependent tenure.
issues_decided: Whether the ghatwali tenure in question was a Government ghatwali or a zemindary (private) ghatwali dependent on the Gidhaur estate
Whether the plaintiff had established possession within 12 years to overcome limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act
Whether the zemindar had ownership rights over sub-soil minerals in the ghatwali tenure
holdings: Where a ghatwali tenure is included within a zemindary and covered by its Permanent Settlement jama, and no clear evidence shows otherwise, it is presumed to be dependent on the zemindary.
A zemindar is presumed to own sub-soil rights in tenancies created by him unless there is evidence he has parted with those rights.
A statement in a District Gazetteer is not conclusive but carries evidentiary weight as an official document compiled from reliable records.
doctrines: Presumption of zemindary ownership of sub-soil rights
Evidentiary value of official records and gazetteers
Burden of proof in establishing independent government tenures

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of the First Amendment Act, 1951, which inserted Articles 31A and 31B to protect land reform laws from judicial review on grounds of violating fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the First Amendment Act, 1951, which curtailed fundamental rights under Part III, is ultra vires the Constitution
Whether Parliament, including the Provisional Parliament, has the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368
Whether the insertion of Articles 31A and 31B required ratification by State legislatures under Article 368
Whether Parliament could validate laws relating to land, a subject in the State List, through constitutional amendment
holdings: Article 13(2) does not apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368, as 'law' in Article 13 refers to ordinary legislation, not constituent power.
Parliament, including the Provisional Parliament, has the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, as it possesses all powers conferred by the Constitution.
The insertion of Articles 31A and 31B does not alter the powers of the High Courts or Supreme Court under Articles 226, 132, or 136, and thus does not require ratification.
Parliament can validate laws, even on subjects in the State List, through constitutional amendment as part of its constituent power under Article 368.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List II, Item 18
doctrines: Constituent power vs. legislative power
Harmonious construction of constitutional provisions
Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of implied limitations (rejected in this case)

card.dispute: The adopted son of Ganga Raju appealed against the High Court's enhancement of maintenance to Rs. 200 per month for each of Ganga Raju's illegitimate sons, while the illegitimate sons cross-appealed for higher maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether an illegitimate son among the regenerate classes is entitled to maintenance as a matter of right under Mitakshara law
What is the appropriate quantum of maintenance payable to the illegitimate sons
holdings: An illegitimate son is entitled to maintenance as long as he lives under Mitakshara law, based on his status as a family member, despite being excluded from inheritance.
The proper maintenance amount for each illegitimate son is Rs. 125 per month, considering the father's estate income, business losses, and the sons' earning capacity.
doctrines: Mitakshara law on maintenance
Right to maintenance based on family status despite illegitimacy

card.dispute: The parties disputed over ownership of land detached from one village and attached to another due to a sudden change in the river's course, and whether the custom of dhar dhura applied.
issues_decided: Whether the custom of dhar dhura applies to sudden changes in the course of a river
Whether the custom of dhar dhura applies when the river flows entirely outside the villages it previously divided
holdings: The custom of dhar dhura can apply to sudden changes in a river's course if supported by cogent evidence, as it is a valid and reasonable custom aimed at preventing boundary disputes.

The custom of dhar dhura does not apply when the river no longer flows within the boundaries of the villages it once divided; in such cases, rights are governed by the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (XI of 1825).
provisions: Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (XI of 1825), Section 2
Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (XI of 1825), Section 4(2)
doctrines: Customary law
Riparian rights
Revival of custom upon changed circumstances

card.dispute: The zemindar (landlord) sued to declare his right to fish in a river within his estate, challenging the claimed fishing rights of villagers who had fished there for years with prior permission.
issues_decided: Whether the villagers' long-standing use of the fishery created a right by prescription, adverse possession, or presumed lost grant
Whether an order under Section 145, Cr.P.C., in earlier proceedings conferred a binding, enforceable right on the fishermen
Whether the benefit of the Section 145 order extended to all villagers or only the parties involved
Whether an exclusive right to fish for a particular species during a specific season could be recognized
holdings: A body of villagers cannot acquire a right to fish by prescription or lost grant unless they form a corporate body or trust, as such rights require ascertainable grantees capable of succession.
An order under Section 145, Cr.P.C., becomes final if not challenged within the limitation period, and can vest possessory rights in the recognized possessors.
The benefit of a Section 145 order is limited to the actual parties or their successors in interest, and does not extend to an entire village or future residents.
An exclusive right to fish in a particular area may be limited to a species or season and still be legally valid, as exclusivity means no co-extensive right exists for others.
doctrines: Doctrine of lost grant
Prescription and adverse possession
Finality of orders under Section 145 Cr.P.C.
Exclusive possession limited by time and species

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to enforce a mortgage bond, and the defendant contested the suit on grounds of limitation and improper attestation of the bond.
issues_decided: Whether payment of interest before limitation, coupled with a later written acknowledgment, revives the period of limitation under Section 20 of the Indian Limitation Act
Whether an acknowledgment made after the institution of a suit can save a time-barred claim
Whether the mortgage bond was properly attested in accordance with law
holdings: A written acknowledgment of payment of interest under Section 20 of the Limitation Act must exist before the suit is filed; one made after institution of the suit does not extend the limitation period.
A suit based on a time-barred debt cannot be saved by an acknowledgment made after the suit has been instituted.
The mortgage bond was not properly attested because the attesting witnesses signed before the executants, and there is no evidence that attestation occurred at the place and time of execution.
doctrines: Acknowledgment under Section 20 must be in writing and made before suit
Doctrine of proper attestation requiring witnesses to attest at the time and place of execution

card.dispute: The State of Seraikella and other princely states sued the Union of India and the State of Bihar to challenge the validity of orders merging them into Bihar and Orissa, claiming those orders were ultra vires and violated their rights under the Instruments of Accession.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit under Article 363(1) of the Constitution?
Whether the plaintiff states had legal capacity to maintain the suit after the commencement of the Constitution?
Whether the validity of the merger orders under section 290-A of the Government of India Act, 1935, could be challenged in court?
Whether the suits abated due to the dissolution of the plaintiff states as legal entities under the new Constitution?
holdings: The Supreme Court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes arising from treaties or agreements with former rulers of Indian States under Article 363(1).
The plaintiff states ceased to exist as legal entities under the Constitution after 26th January 1950 and therefore lacked the legal capacity to maintain the suits.
The Constitution recognizes the territorial integration of the princely states into existing provinces regardless of the legality of the merger orders, making such challenges non-justiciable.
The suits abated upon the commencement of the Constitution because the plaintiff states were no longer recognized as juristic persons capable of suing.
doctrines: Doctrine of abatement of suits upon dissolution of legal personality
Doctrine of constitutional recognition as basis for legal existence
Doctrine of non-justiciability of political agreements under Article 363(1)
Doctrine of implied repeal and constitutional continuity

card.dispute: The appellants, acquitted by the Sessions Judge in a criminal case involving charges of murder and related offences, challenged the High Court's reversal of their acquittal and conviction on appeal by the State.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of the appellants based on the evidence on record.
Whether the prosecution's evidence, particularly regarding the injury to Deva Sukh, was reliable and sufficient to overturn the trial court's findings.
Whether the trial court's assessment of witness credibility and the exercise of private defence by the appellants was reasonable.
holdings: The High Court can review evidence in an appeal against acquittal, but must have very substantial and compelling reasons to overturn the trial court's findings, which benefit from observing witnesses firsthand.

The prosecution's case was based on fabricated or unreliable evidence, particularly regarding Deva Sukh's injury, which was not mentioned in the FIR or dying declarations and lacked corroboration, casting doubt on the entire prosecution story.

The Sessions Judge reasonably concluded that the appellants acted in private defence after being attacked first, and the High Court erred in disregarding the trial court's credibility assessments and the opinion of the assessors.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Sections 325 and 326 read with Section 149
doctrines: Presumption of innocence strengthened by acquittal
High Court's limited power to interfere with trial court's factual findings
Right of private defence under exceptional circumstances
Importance of trial court's assessment of witness demeanor

card.dispute: The dispute was between mortgage decree-holders and judgment debtors, including both agriculturist and non-agriculturist co-debtors, over whether a non-agriculturist debtor could benefit from the scaling down of the decree granted to agriculturist co-debtors under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938.
issues_decided: Whether a non-agriculturist co-debtor is entitled to the benefit of scaling down of a mortgage decree granted to agriculturist co-debtors under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938.
Whether the principle of indivisibility of a mortgage decree applies to prevent partial scaling down of a decree in favour of some co-debtors only.
Whether a decree can legally be split to impose a reduced liability on agriculturist debtors while maintaining full liability on non-agriculturist co-debtors.
holdings: A non-agriculturist co-debtor is not entitled to benefit from the scaling down of a mortgage decree granted solely to agriculturist co-debtors under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1938.

The principle of indivisibility of a mortgage decree does not override the special provisions of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, which permits selective scaling down of debts in favour of agriculturist debtors only.
The Act allows a decree to be split so that agriculturist debtors may have their liability reduced while non-agriculturist co-debtors remain liable for the full amount.
doctrines: Indivisibility of mortgage decree
Statutory exception to general legal principles
Selective application of debt relief based on debtor classification

card.dispute: The appellant, holder of Taluk Kakwara, contested the respondents' attempt to execute a money decree by attaching and selling the taluk, claiming it was held on inalienable Ghatwali tenure.
issues_decided: Whether Taluk Kakwara was a Zemindari Ghatwali tenure or a Government Ghatwali tenure
Whether lands held on Zemindari Ghatwali tenure were alienable
Whether the appellant could object to the sale of Taluk Kakwara in execution of a money decree
holdings: Taluk Kakwara was a Zemindari Ghatwali tenure, forming part of the Kharakpur Zemindari and subject to the Zemindar's control over appointment and dismissal of Ghatwals.
Zemindari Ghatwali tenures are alienable with the consent of the Zemindar, based on the custom of Kharakpur judicially recognized.
The appellant could not claim absolute inalienability, as the tenure was alienable with consent, and prior acts like mortgage showed recognition of this limitation.
provisions: Bengal Regulation I of 1793, Section 8, Clause (4)
doctrines: Doctrine of tenurial status based on historical and customary rights
Doctrine of judicial recognition of local customs affecting property rights
Doctrine of locus standi in suits involving Ghatwali tenures

card.dispute: The District Board, Tanjore and the lessee, M.K. Noor Mohamed Rowther, fought over whether the leased land constituted an 'estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, entitling the lessee to permanent occupancy rights after the lease expired.
issues_decided: Whether the suit land constituted an 'estate' within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908.
Whether the respondent lessee acquired permanent occupancy rights under Section 6 of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908.
holdings: The suit land did not constitute an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) because the original grant was not of a whole inam village, as parts were granted to different persons under separate personal grants prior to or at the time of the main grant.
The respondent was not entitled to permanent occupancy rights under Section 6(2) of the Act, as such rights arise only in relation to lands that qualify as an 'estate' under the Act.
provisions: Madras Estates Land (3rd Amendment) Act, 18 of 1936
doctrines: Definition of 'estate' under statutory interpretation
Burden of proof in establishing statutory entitlements
Use of inam register entries as evidence in absence of original grant documents

card.dispute: The State of Orissa challenged the High Court's order granting interim relief to Madan Gopal Rungta and others pending the filing of a civil suit, without adjudicating their legal rights.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can grant interim relief under Article 226 of the Constitution without deciding the rights of the parties and solely to circumvent the 60-day notice requirement under Section 80 of the Civil Procedure Code.
Whether interim relief can be the sole and final relief granted in a petition under Article 226 when no final determination of rights is made.
holdings: The High Court cannot grant interim relief under Article 226 as the only relief without adjudicating the petitioner's legal rights, especially to bypass procedural requirements like Section 80 of the CPC.
Interim relief under Article 226 must be ancillary to a main relief and cannot be granted independently when the court declines to decide the merits of the case.
doctrines: Ancillary relief doctrine
Judicial restraint in writ jurisdiction
Procedural circumvention not permitted under constitutional writs

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a deceased Hyderabad nobleman fought over succession to his estate, with two groups of claimants—Mahboob Begum and Kadiran Begum and their children—being excluded by a special law that dismissed their claims and barred judicial recourse.
issues_decided: Whether the Waliuddowla Succession Act, 1950 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by arbitrarily discriminating against specific individuals in a private succession dispute.
Whether a legislative act that singles out individuals and denies them access to courts to assert inheritance rights under personal law is constitutionally valid.
holdings: A law that targets specific individuals in a private succession dispute and denies them judicial remedies without a rational basis violates the equal protection guarantee under Article 14.

The mere existence of a prolonged dispute and an adverse administrative report does not justify classifying certain claimants as a separate class and depriving them of legal rights available to others in similar positions.
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Prohibition of arbitrary classification in legislation
Presumption of constitutionality overcome by palpable unreasonableness

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against the acquittal of Ajmer Singh, who was accused of murdering Bagher Singh during a quarrel.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's order of acquittal based on the prosecution evidence.
Whether the defective examination of the accused under Section 342, Criminal Procedure Code, vitiated the trial.
holdings: After an acquittal, the presumption of innocence is strengthened, and reversal is permissible only for very substantial and compelling reasons based on a proper review of the evidence.

A defective examination under Section 342 CrPC does not automatically vitiate a trial; the irregularity is curable if no prejudice is caused to the accused, especially when the facts are simple and the accused was aware of the case against him.
doctrines: Curable irregularity doctrine
Presumption of innocence reinforced by acquittal
Test of prejudice in procedural violations

card.dispute: The petitioners, who had contracts with estate proprietors to collect tendu leaves, lac, and timber, fought against the State of Madhya Pradesh which sought to extinguish these rights after abolishing proprietary rights in land.
issues_decided: Whether the rights granted under the contracts for collecting tendu leaves, lac, and timber vested in the State free from encumbrances under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950
Whether the contracts created proprietary interests or mere licenses
Whether the petitioners' rights amounted to encumbrances on proprietary rights within the meaning of the Act
Whether the Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930, applied to treat the subject matter of the contracts as future goods
holdings: The contracts granted by proprietors were licenses to collect produce and did not confer proprietary rights; thus, the petitioners were not proprietors or holders of proprietary interests under the Act.
The rights of the petitioners were not 'encumbrances' within the meaning of the Act, which referred only to debts, mortgages, or charges, not contractual licenses.
The State could not claim the rights were extinguished as the Act did not provide for the automatic transfer of such contractual rights to the State.

The goods (e.g., tendu leaves, lac) had 'potential existence' and could be the subject of a present sale; thus, they were not 'future goods' under the Indian Sale of Goods Act, making the contracts valid and enforceable.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3(1)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(1)(a)
Indian Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of potential existence of goods
Distinction between proprietary rights and contractual licenses
Interpretation of 'encumbrances' in land reform legislation

card.dispute: The petitioner landlord challenged the allotment of his vacant house to another person under the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, after the Constitution came into force, claiming violation of his fundamental rights under Articles 31(2) and 19(1)(f).
issues_decided: Whether the order of allotment made before the Constitution came into force could be challenged under Articles 31(2) and 19(1)(f) after its commencement?
Whether the taking of possession after the Constitution's commencement amounted to acquisition of property under Article 31(2)?
Whether the power under Rule 81(2)(bb) of the Defence of India Rules allowed allotment of a house for private individual occupation?
Whether the amendment allowing allotment for private individuals was valid under the enabling rule?
holdings: An order made before the Constitution's commencement under a valid pre-constitutional law cannot be challenged for violating fundamental rights under Articles 31(2) or 19(1)(f), as those rights did not then exist.
No acquisition under Article 31(2) occurs when possession is taken after allotment, as the landlord's right to possession ended with the pre-constitutional allotment order.
The power under Rule 81(2)(bb) includes regulating letting to specified persons, including private individuals, and is not limited to cases where property is available for letting.

The amendment allowing allotment for private individuals is valid as the Control Order was issued under broader enabling powers, including the Supplies, Services and Miscellaneous Provisions (Temporary Powers) Act, 1947.
provisions: Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948
Supplies, Services and Miscellaneous Provisions (Temporary Powers) Act, 1947
doctrines: Non-retrospectivity of fundamental rights
Doctrine of vested rights under pre-constitutional laws
Police power vs. eminent domain
Interpretation of regulatory powers in emergency legislation

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Custodian General's decision to allow an appeal by Tekchand Dolwani, an informant, against an order declaring that Ebrahim Aboobakar was not an evacuee, arguing that the order was not appealable and Dolwani was not a 'person aggrieved'.
issues_decided: Whether the order refusing to declare a person an evacuee is an appealable order under Section 24 of the Bombay Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949
Whether Tekchand Dolwani, as the first informant, was a 'person aggrieved' by the Additional Custodian's order and thus entitled to file an appeal
Whether the appeal was properly filed against the order dated 8th February 1950, despite being described as against the order of 9th February
holdings: An order refusing to declare a person an evacuee is an order made under Section 7 of the Ordinance and is appealable under Section 24, as the power to grant relief includes the power to refuse it.
A person who is entitled to be heard in proceedings and whose claim or contention is rejected is a 'person aggrieved' and has locus standi to appeal under Section 24.

An appeal described as being against a consequential order (9th February) but in substance challenging the earlier substantive order (8th February) is valid, and a mere error in description does not vitiate the appeal.
provisions: Bombay Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 7
Bombay Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 24
Bombay Evacuees (Administration of Property) Act, 1949, Section 43
doctrines: Person aggrieved doctrine
Principle of jurisdictional error for certiorari
Substance over form in appellate procedure

card.dispute: The decree-holder sought restoration of an execution case after it was dismissed without being heard, while the judgment-debtor challenged the restoration order in revision.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere in revision against an order restoring an execution case under inherent powers under Section 151 of the CPC.
Whether the Subordinate Judge’s order dismissing the execution case without hearing the decree-holder’s pleader was legally valid.
Whether the High Court acted within its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC in setting aside the restoration order.
holdings: A court may set aside its own order dismissing an execution case if it results in denial of justice due to procedural irregularity, under its inherent powers under Section 151 CPC.

The High Court cannot exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC to correct mere errors of law or fact, unless there is lack of jurisdiction, failure to exercise jurisdiction, or illegal or materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction.

The High Court acted without jurisdiction in setting aside the restoration order because the Subordinate Judge’s correction of his own error did not amount to illegal or materially irregular exercise of power.
doctrines: Inherent powers under Section 151 CPC
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Principle of material irregularity
Doctrine of finality of non-appealable orders

card.dispute: The landlord sued the tenant and sub-tenant for possession of a flat and compensation for unauthorized subletting; the sub-tenant challenged the Small Causes Court's jurisdiction over the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was one between a landlord and tenant under Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, so as to confer jurisdiction on the Small Causes Court.
Whether the claim for compensation against the sub-tenant amounted to a claim for rent within the meaning of the Act.
Whether the joinder of the sub-tenant as a party altered the nature of the suit and deprived the Small Causes Court of jurisdiction.
holdings: The suit was primarily for possession between landlord and tenant; the claim for compensation was incidental and did not change the nature of the suit.
Section 28 empowers the Small Causes Court to deal with any claim or question arising out of the Act, including disputes involving sub-tenants, even if not directly between landlord and tenant.
The sub-tenant, though not a necessary party, is a proper party; their inclusion does not transform the suit into one outside the jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court under Section 28.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)
doctrines: Jurisdiction based on cause of action and nature of suit
Incidental claims doctrine
Proper party versus necessary party doctrine
Doctrine against multiplicity of proceedings

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to recover money based on two mortgages, while the defendant claimed the mortgages were satisfied by an unregistered agreement that modified their terms.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered agreement varied or extinguished an interest in immovable property and thus required registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Indian Registration Act
Whether the agreement fell under the exception to registration under Section 17(2)(v) of the Act
Whether the unregistered agreement could be used in evidence under the proviso to Section 49 of the Registration Act
Whether the equitable doctrine of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act applied
holdings: An agreement that by its own terms limits or extinguishes a mortgagee's interest in immovable property must be registered under Section 17(1)(b), even if it only modifies interest rates or payment terms.
A document is not exempt under Section 17(2)(v) if it itself limits or extinguishes an interest in property, even if it also grants a right to obtain a future registered document.
The proviso to Section 49 does not allow use of an unregistered document to prove an agreement that directly alters mortgage terms, especially when the suit is not for specific performance.
Section 53A does not apply where there is no transfer of property or possession taken in part performance of a contract.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance (Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act)
Requirement of registration for documents affecting interests in immovable property
Distinction between documents evidencing payment and those effecting legal change by their own force

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be tenants under a mortgagee, fought over whether they acquired occupancy rights in khudkasht land after continued possession for over 30 years, despite the mortgagee's limited interest.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgagee can create a lease that enables a tenant to acquire permanent occupancy rights under the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1937
Whether the lessee under a zuripeshgi ijara became a 'settled raiyat' entitled to protection under Sections 20 and 21 of the Bihar Tenancy Act
Whether the mortgagee had the power to settle tenants on the mortgaged land given the terms of the lease
Whether the appellants could raise a new argument about an oral ijara for a portion of the land for the first time in the Supreme Court
holdings: A mortgagee cannot create a lease that allows a tenant to acquire permanent occupancy rights, as it would defeat the mortgagor's right to khas possession and violate the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 76(a) and (e).

The appellants were not 'settled raiyats' under the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1937, because they held land under a mortgagee, not a proprietor or tenure-holder, and thus could not claim occupancy rights under Sections 20 and 21.
The terms of the zuripeshgi ijara deed, which emphasized security for a loan rather than tenancy, restricted the mortgagee from settling tenants, making any such settlement non-bona fide and invalid.
A new argument regarding an oral ijara for a portion of the land could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court when it was not pleaded or argued in the lower courts.
doctrines: Doctrine of limited powers of a mortgagee in possession
Doctrine of bona fide settlement in prudent management
Doctrine of creation of statutory tenancy rights by possession
Rule against raising new arguments for the first time in appeal

card.dispute: Mortgagees appealed against the High Court's decision to grant debt relief under the U.P. Debt Redemption Act, 1940, to mortgagors who were alleged not to be agriculturists at the time of the advance.
issues_decided: Whether the suit fell under the U.P. Debt Redemption Act, 1940, i.e., whether it was a 'suit to which the Act applies' based on a 'loan' as defined in the Act.
Whether the mortgagor Sita Ram was an agriculturist at the time of the advance on July 28, 1931, for the purposes of the Act.
holdings: A suit relates to a 'loan' under the U.P. Debt Redemption Act, 1940, if the advance is recoverable from an agriculturist, and the crucial time for determining agriculturist status is when the advance becomes due, not necessarily when it was made.

Sita Ram remained an agriculturist at the time of the advance because he was not assessed to income-tax on July 28, 1931, as the taxable minimum had not yet been reduced and no assessment had occurred.
doctrines: Interpretation of 'loan' and 'agriculturist' under beneficial debt relief legislation
Timing of assessment for determining status under social welfare legislation

card.dispute: The mortgagor granted a permanent lease of mortgaged property in 1925, and the lessees resisted the auction purchaser's (mortgagee's transferee) claim to possession after a mortgage execution sale.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgagor in possession had the power to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged property before the amendment of the Transfer of Property Act by Act XX of 1929.
Whether such a lease, even if not impairing the mortgage security, binds the mortgagee or an auction purchaser.
Whether the lessee can resist the mortgagee's claim based on the lease created by the mortgagor.
holdings: A mortgagor in possession may only lease mortgaged property in the usual course of management and according to local usage, such as year-to-year for agricultural land or month-to-month for houses.
A permanent lease granted by a mortgagor is not binding on the mortgagee or an auction purchaser if it is not made in the usual course of management, even if it does not impair the security.
The lessee bears the burden of proving that the lease was granted in the usual course of management; failure to do so leaves no defence against the mortgagee’s claim.
doctrines: Usual course of management doctrine
Mortgagor as agent or bailiff of mortgagee
Burden of proof on lessee to establish validity against mortgagee

card.dispute: The widow of a deceased man challenged an arbitration award on the grounds that the arbitrator committed legal misconduct by hearing one party in the absence of the other.
