issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator committed legal misconduct by taking statements from one party in the absence of the other
Whether such misconduct vitiated the award even in the absence of proven prejudice
Whether the plaintiff waived her right to challenge the award on grounds of misconduct
holdings: An arbitrator commits legal misconduct by hearing one party privately and considering evidence not shared with or challengeable by the other party.
Legal misconduct by an arbitrator invalidates the award regardless of whether actual prejudice is proven, as it violates principles of natural justice.
There was no valid waiver of the right to challenge the award on grounds of legal misconduct, especially when not pleaded by the respondent.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Legal misconduct in arbitration
Rule against bias and fair hearing
No party may influence the decision-maker by undisclosed means

card.dispute: The petitioner claimed possession of taluqdari properties bequeathed under a will, while the respondent, the widow of the legatee, resisted the claim asserting her right under the same will.
issues_decided: Whether Dhuj Singh acquired an absolute estate or a life estate under the will of Raja Bisheshwar.
Whether a valid subsequent interest was created in favour of the widow of Dhuj Singh after his death.
holdings: Dhuj Singh did not acquire an absolute estate; the will granted him only a life interest, as the testator's intention was to create successive life estates, and the restraint on alienation was consistent with this purpose.

The will validly created a successive life estate in favour of Dhuj Singh’s widow, who was in existence at the time of the testator’s death, and thus she was entitled to possession during her lifetime.
doctrines: Rule against perpetuities
Doctrine of repugnancy between absolute ownership and restraint on alienation
Construction of wills: intention gathered from the whole document
Validity of gifts to a class with some unborn members

card.dispute: A patnidar sued a zemindar for possession of land and mesne profits; the zemindar sought to set off post-possession rent, revenue, and cesses against the mesne profits awarded.
issues_decided: Whether the zemindar could claim equitable set-off of rent, revenue, and cesses accruing after delivery of possession against mesne profits awarded for prior wrongful possession.
Whether interest should be allowed on mesne profits, and if so, at what rate.
Whether rent (munafa) should be calculated based on annual assets or on a fair and equitable basis.
holdings: Equitable set-off is not maintainable when cross-demands arise from different transactions; mesne profits stem from trespass, while post-possession rent arises from landlord-tenant relationship.
Interest on mesne profits should be allowed at 4% per annum, not 6%, given the plaintiff's delay in seeking computation and the denial of equitable set-off.
The contention that rent should be calculated on a fair share of profits, rather than on annual assets, is not entertained as it was not raised in earlier appeals and lacks evidentiary support.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 17 (principles of equitable set-off)
doctrines: Equitable set-off
Separate causes of action
Principles of restitution and unjust enrichment

card.dispute: The dispute was between Sunderabai, the widow of Devarao, and Devaji, who was adopted by Gangabai (widow of Devarao's predeceased son), over the validity of Devaji's adoption and his right to family property.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of Devaji by Gangabai was valid under Hindu law.
Whether the plaintiff was estopped from challenging the declaration in the compromise award that Gangabai had lost her right to adopt from the beginning.
Whether the consent decree based on arbitration barred the plaintiff's claim by estoppel.
holdings: The court held that the adoption was not valid because Gangabai had lost her right to adopt from the beginning, as declared in the compromise award.
The plaintiff was estopped from denying the declaration in the award that Gangabai had no right to adopt, having accepted Rs. 8,000 as consideration for that declaration.
A party who benefits from a compromise cannot later assert a contrary legal position that would undermine the agreement, to prevent fraud or circuity of action.
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel (constructive and promissory)
Doctrine of Consensual Estoppel under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act
Principle against Circuity of Action and Fraud in Equity

card.dispute: The bus-stand owner challenged the Regional Transport Authority's order shifting the starting place and terminus of buses from his stand, arguing the rule enabling such a shift was ultra vires and violated his fundamental right to carry on business.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 268 of the Madras Motor Vehicles Rules, as amended in 1950, was ultra vires the Madras Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, particularly Section 68(2)(r)
Whether the amendment to Rule 268 violated Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution by unreasonably restricting the right to carry on business
Whether the Transport Authority complied with the procedural requirement of consultation under Rule 268
Whether the order was vitiated by mala fides or bias due to the District Collector's involvement
holdings: The power to alter bus-stand locations is within the rule-making authority under Section 68(1) and (2)(r) of the Motor Vehicles Act, as regulating passenger pick-up and drop-off points inherently includes control over bus-stand locations.

The restriction on using the stand for outward journeys is a reasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(g), as it serves public convenience and does not completely prohibit the business of operating a bus-stand.
Rule 268's consultation requirement is discretionary, not mandatory, and the Transport Authority fulfilled it by consulting the Municipality, which was a valid authority despite its interest.
There was no mala fide or bias; the District Collector acted in an executive capacity, and mere prior involvement in opening a municipal stand does not invalidate the order.
provisions: Madras Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, Section 68(1), Section 68(2)(r)
doctrines: Reasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(g)
Ultra vires doctrine
Delegated legislation and rule-making power
Presumption of constitutionality of statutory rules
Doctrine of non-justiciability of administrative convenience

card.dispute: The tenant, Baburao Shantaram More, challenged the constitutional validity of provisions exempting the Bombay Housing Board from the Bombay Rent Act, arguing that it violated the right to equality under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, which exempts government and local authority premises from rent control, violates Article 14 of the Constitution.
Whether Section 3-A, inserted in the Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948, by the 1951 Amendment, which extends such exemption to the Bombay Housing Board, is ultra vires Article 14.
holdings: Section 4 of the Bombay Rent Act does not violate Article 14 as the classification between tenants of government/local authorities and private landlords is based on an intelligible differentia with rational relation to the Act's object.

Section 3-A of the Bombay Housing Board Act is constitutional because the Board, as a government-sponsored, non-profit body, is distinguishable from private landlords and cooperative housing societies, and thus its exclusion from rent control does not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 14.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 4
Bombay Housing Board Act, 1948 (Act LXIX of 1948), Section 3-A (as inserted by Bombay Housing Board (Amendment) Act, 1951 (Act XI of 1951))
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Classification test for equality
Doctrine of intelligible differentia

card.dispute: The State of Bombay challenged the High Court's decision to release Purushottam Jog Naik on the grounds that his detention order was invalid due to non-compliance with constitutional formalities.
issues_decided: Whether the detention order was validly expressed to be in the name of the Governor under Article 166(1) of the Constitution
Whether a defective detention order can be validated by extrinsic evidence
Whether the affidavit of the Home Secretary was sufficient to prove the Government's satisfaction under the Preventive Detention Act
holdings: An order stating 'By order of the Governor of Bombay' is sufficiently expressed in the Governor's name under Article 166(1), even without the words 'and in his name', as the substance of the requirement is met.
If a detention order does not self-validate, the State may prove its validity through extrinsic evidence, and there is no fixed rule about the type or quantum of such evidence.
The Home Secretary's affidavit can be sufficient proof of the Government's satisfaction if based on personal knowledge or reliable sources, though the Minister's affidavit is not indispensable.
doctrines: Substance over form
Proof of satisfaction in preventive detention
Executive authority and attribution in name of Governor

card.dispute: The zamindar of Ahiri estate challenged the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1951, which vested his estate and 80 malguzari villages in the state, arguing it violated his fundamental right to property under Article 31(1).
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1951, violated Article 31(1) by depriving the petitioner of property without authority of law.
Whether the Act required prior assent of the Governor before being reserved for the President’s consideration under Article 31(3).
Whether the Act could be challenged on grounds of legislative incompetence, fraud on the Constitution, or excessive delegation of power.
Whether the 80 malguzari villages were covered under Article 31-A and whether the Act was protected by Article 31-B.
holdings: The Act was valid under Article 31(1) as it was a law supported by the authority of the state and did not infringe fundamental rights due to compliance with constitutional safeguards.
Article 31(3) does not require the Governor’s assent before a bill is reserved for the President’s assent; a law becomes valid upon receiving Presidential assent.
The Act did not suffer from legislative incompetence, fraud on the Constitution, or impermissible delegation, as the legislature acted in good faith and compensation provisions were adequate.
Even if the malguzari villages were not 'estates' under Article 31-A, the Act was fully protected by Article 31-B, which shields laws in the Ninth Schedule from fundamental rights challenges.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1951
Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, II of 1917, Section 2(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of Presidential assent under Article 31(3)
Fraud on the Constitution doctrine
Non-delegation of essential legislative functions
Protection under Article 31-B (Ninth Schedule immunity)
Interpretation of 'law' in relation to fundamental rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the appealability of an order transferring a suit under clause 13 of the Letters Patent of the Calcutta High Court, claiming it to be a 'judgment' appealable under clause 15.
issues_decided: Whether an order for transfer of a suit under clause 13 of the Letters Patent of the Calcutta High Court constitutes a 'judgment' within the meaning of clause 15?
Whether such a transfer order is appealable as a matter of right under the Letters Patent?
holdings: An order transferring a suit under clause 13 of the Letters Patent is not a 'judgment' within clause 15 because it does not determine the merits of the suit or terminate the proceedings.
Such a transfer order is not appealable under the Letters Patent as it is not a final adjudication that disposes of the suit or affects the rights of the parties conclusively.
provisions: Letters Patent of the Calcutta High Court, Clause 13
Letters Patent of the Calcutta High Court, Clause 15
doctrines: Finality test for 'judgment'
Doctrine of appealability of interlocutory orders

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant, who claimed a permanent and heritable tenancy, leading to a dispute over the nature of the tenancy and whether prior proceedings barred the claim under res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the decision in a previous suit for rent enhancement operated as res judicata on the question of permanency of tenancy in a subsequent ejectment suit.
Whether the cumulative facts established the existence of a permanent and heritable tenancy.
holdings: A prior decision on rent enhancement does not bar a later determination of tenancy permanency, as the issue of permanency was neither directly nor substantially in issue earlier.
Long possession, intergenerational transfers, construction of permanent structures, and absence of rent increases since 1860 collectively prove a permanent and heritable tenancy.
provisions: Bengal Regulation III of 1819 (referred to in context of rent assessment)
doctrines: Res judicata
Inference from cumulative facts
Permanent tenancy in landlord-tenant law

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the validity of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietory Rights Act, 1951, which abolished their estates and provided compensation, arguing it violated constitutional rights and procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the court can examine the adequacy of compensation under the Act in light of Articles 31, 31-A, and 31-B of the Constitution
Whether the Act involved improper delegation of legislative power to the executive
Whether the legislative process, including the Governor's assent and Speaker's certificate, was constitutionally valid
Whether the Act violated covenants of merger under Article 362 by acquiring property designated as personal property of rulers
holdings: The court lacks jurisdiction to question the adequacy of compensation due to the protective shield of Articles 31-A and 31-B of the Constitution.
The delegation of rule-making power regarding compensation installments under Section 9 and 91 is not excessive and does not violate constitutional principles.
The Speaker's certificate that the Bill was passed is conclusive; procedural irregularities in recording the vote do not invalidate the law.
Article 362 does not protect personal property from acquisition, and disputes under covenants are barred from judicial review by Article 363.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietory Rights (Estates, Mahals, Ahenated Lands) Act, 1951
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional immunity from judicial review under Article 31-B
Doctrine of conclusiveness of legislative certification
Doctrine of separation of essential legislative functions
Doctrine of public purpose in land reform legislation

card.dispute: The heirs of Aboobaker Abdul Rehman challenged the Custodian General's posthumous declaration of their deceased father as an evacuee and his property as evacuee property.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian General had jurisdiction to declare a deceased person as an evacuee under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950?
Whether proceedings under the Act can continue after the death of the person against whom they are initiated?
Whether evacuee status and evacuee property are permanent legal conditions independent of the owner's status?
holdings: The Custodian General lacked jurisdiction to declare a deceased person an evacuee, as the statutory scheme requires the person to be alive during proceedings.
The Administration of Evacuee Property Act does not provide for continuation of proceedings after the death of the person, unlike insolvency laws, so such proceedings abate upon death.
Evacuee status is not permanent; it depends on the owner's living status and circumstances, and property ceases to be evacuee property if the owner's disability ends.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 9
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 15
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 16
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 43
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 52
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Abatement of proceedings
Personality of legal status
Legislative intent

card.dispute: Displaced persons from Pakistan challenged the cancellation of their allotment of evacuee land by the Deputy Custodian, claiming violation of their fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f).
issues_decided: Whether the Deputy Custodian had jurisdiction to cancel the allotment of evacuee property under the relevant state and central laws.
Whether the cancellation of allotment without issuing a formal notice violated principles of natural justice.
Whether a subsequent policy directive from the Ministry of Rehabilitation prohibiting cancellation of certain allotments invalidated the Deputy Custodian's order.
holdings: The Deputy Custodian had valid jurisdiction under both the East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, and the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, to cancel allotments of evacuee property.
Although no formal notice for cancellation of allotment was required under the rules, the petitioners were given a reasonable opportunity to be heard, satisfying principles of natural justice.
Interim policy instructions from the Central Government did not have statutory force and could not override validly passed cancellation orders that predated them.
provisions: East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 9(A), Section 22(2)(ff)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(a), Section 12(1), Section 56(2)(h)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Rule 14(2), Rule 14(3), Rule 14(4), Rule 14(6)
doctrines: Principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (distinction between rules and policy directives)
Doctrine of jurisdictional validity of administrative orders

card.dispute: The heirs of Aboobaker Abdul Rehman challenged the Custodian's declaration that he was an evacuee and his properties evacuee properties after his death.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act continue against the successors of a deceased person?
Whether a deceased person can be declared an evacuee posthumously?
Whether property of a deceased person who died before declaration can be declared evacuee property?
holdings: Proceedings under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act abate upon the death of the person during pendency; they cannot be continued against heirs in absence of statutory provision.
A person cannot be declared an evacuee posthumously as the status of evacuee is personal and ceases with death.
Property of a deceased person who was not declared an evacuee during lifetime cannot be declared evacuee property, as vesting must occur during the person's lifetime.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(d)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(f)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 43
doctrines: Abatement of proceedings upon death
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent
Personal nature of evacuee status
Vesting of property during lifetime as a condition precedent

card.dispute: The Deputy Commissioner challenged whether an appeal under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act was invalid for not impleading all creditors as parties, when only some creditors actively participated in the proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether creditors who did not take an active part in proceedings under section 11(2) of the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act are necessary parties to an appeal against an order rejecting a claim?
Whether technical rules of the Civil Procedure Code on impleading parties apply to proceedings under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act?
holdings: Creditors who did not actively participate in section 11(2) proceedings are not necessary parties to an appeal from an order rejecting a claim, as they have no direct right to relief and an effective decree can be passed without them.

Technical rules of the Civil Procedure Code on impleading parties do not strictly apply to administrative proceedings under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act; a liberal approach is appropriate, especially in the absence of collusion between debtor and claimant.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rules 1 and 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 63
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 41, Rule 20
doctrines: Necessary party doctrine under CPC
Liberal interpretation of administrative proceedings
Distinction between necessary and proper parties
Non-application of technical CPC rules to special statutes

card.dispute: Reversioners sued to recover shebaiti rights alienated by a Hindu widow; the alienee claimed the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for recovery of shebaiti rights is governed by Article 124 or Article 141 of the Limitation Act (IX of 1908)
When the period of limitation begins to run against reversioners in a suit for recovery of shebaiti rights after alienation by a widow
Whether possession adverse to a widow shebait is also adverse to reversioners claiming under the last male holder
holdings: A suit for recovery of shebaiti rights from an alienee of a Hindu widow is governed by Article 124, not Article 141, because shebaiti right is a hereditary office, not ordinary immovable property.
The period of limitation under Article 124 begins only when the defendant takes possession adversely to the plaintiff or someone through whom the plaintiff derives title.
Possession adverse to a widow shebait does not commence limitation against reversioners, as they do not claim through her but through the last male holder.
doctrines: Nature of shebaiti as a hereditary office combining elements of property and office
Widow's estate in Hindu law: limited interest with restricted alienation and reversion to male-line heirs
Adverse possession not running against reversioners during widow's tenure

card.dispute: The judgment-debtor sought restitution of properties sold in execution after the Privy Council restored an amended decree, claiming the sale was based on a reversed decree.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the judgment-debtor's property in 1939 was valid despite the amended decree having been temporarily set aside by the Chief Court and later restored by the Privy Council.
Whether the judgment-debtor was entitled to restitution of the sold properties with mesne profits after the restoration of the amended decree.
Whether the failure to pay instalments under the amended decree, even during its pendency in appeal, rendered the entire decretal amount due and justified the sale.
holdings: The sale was valid because the judgment-debtor remained bound by the terms of the amended decree during appeal, as no stay order was obtained, and default in three instalments triggered full liability.
The judgment-debtor was not entitled to restitution because the sale would have been inevitable even if the amended decree had remained in force, and no injustice was caused by the court's execution.

Restitution cannot be granted where the decree-holder has not gained an unfair advantage and the judgment-debtor failed to comply with the decree’s conditions, thereby losing the benefit of instalment payments.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code (Act V of 1908), Section 144
U.P. Encumbered Estates Act (1934 as amended in 1939), Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of Restitution
Principle of inevitable consequence in execution sales
Binding effect of decrees during appeal in absence of stay

card.dispute: The appellants, who were granted land by the Court of Wards, challenged the Sathi Lands (Restoration) Act, 1950, which voided their settlement, while similar settlements with others were left untouched.
issues_decided: Whether the Sathi Lands (Restoration) Act, 1950, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by discriminating against the appellants?
Whether the Act infringes the fundamental right to equal protection of laws by singling out individuals without reasonable classification?
Whether the appellants' right to judicial adjudication of their civil rights was unlawfully denied by the impugned legislation?
holdings: The Act violates Article 14 as it arbitrarily targets the appellants without any reasonable basis or classification, while leaving others in similar positions unaffected.
Legislation that singles out individuals for adverse treatment without differentiating attributes is unconstitutional, even if there is a presumption of legislative validity.
The right of every citizen to access a court for adjudication of civil rights cannot be taken away by a law that nullifies their legal interests without judicial scrutiny.
provisions: Court of Wards Act (relevant provisions governing management of estates)
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Presumption of constitutionality of statutes
Rule against arbitrary and discriminatory legislation
Right to judicial remedy for enforcement of civil rights

card.dispute: The appellant, Purnendu Nath Tagore, challenged the Administrator-General of West Bengal's right to possess 'Tagore Villa' for 15 years under the will of Raja Prafulla Nath Tagore.
issues_decided: Whether Clause 82 of the will conferred an absolute and immediate interest in 'Tagore Villa' on the appellant
Whether the 15-year management period by executors-trustees, delaying possession, was valid under the will and law
Whether the provisions of Section 138 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, invalidated the postponement of possession
holdings: Clause 82 did not confer immediate and absolute possession; the property remained under executor control for 15 years as part of the estate.
The will's scheme vested all properties, including 'Tagore Villa', in executors for 15 years to manage income and fulfill trusts before distribution.
Section 138 does not apply where the will does not confer absolute interest immediately, and postponement for trust administration is valid.
doctrines: Rule in Saunders v. Vautier
Doctrine of repugnancy in wills
Construction of testamentary trusts under Hindu law (Dayabhaga School)

card.dispute: The Motipur Zamindari Company Ltd. and another company challenged the applicability of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 to corporate entities, arguing they could not be classified as 'proprietors' or 'tenure-holders'.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'person' in the definitions of 'proprietor' and 'tenure-holder' under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 includes incorporated companies.
Whether applying the Act to companies would create conflicts with the Companies Act, particularly in winding-up proceedings.
Whether Section 41 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, which provides for penalties, is inapplicable to companies and thus shows legislative intent to exclude them.
holdings: The term 'person' in the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 includes companies, as there is no repugnancy in the Act’s subject or context, and such inclusion is necessary to achieve the Act’s reformative purpose.
The application of the Act to companies does not conflict with the Companies Act, as the company’s right to compensation vests upon acquisition, and liquidators can pursue remedies under the Act.
Section 41 penalties apply to officers or agents of a company who fail to comply with orders, so the section does not render the Act inapplicable to companies.
doctrines: Literal and purposive interpretation of statutes
Inclusion of juristic persons in statutory definitions unless repugnant to context
Principle that penal provisions may apply to corporate agents even if not directly to the corporation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether an order for recovery of possession under the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, qualified for relief under Section 18(1) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'decree for recovery of possession' in Section 18(1) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950, includes an order passed under Section 43 of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882?
Whether courts can interpret a statute to correct perceived legislative mistakes or omissions?
holdings: The expression 'decree for recovery of possession' in Section 18(1) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950, does not include an order made under Section 43 of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882.
Courts cannot assume legislative mistakes or supply omissions in statutes; they must apply the law as written, even if the result appears inequitable.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 18(1)
Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, Section 43
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 12(1)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 16
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of legislative intent
Casus omissus non est demonstrandum

card.dispute: The daughters of Kanakasabapathi Pillai fought over whether a perpetual dedication of property for worshipping his tomb (samadhi) was valid under Hindu law.
issues_decided: Whether a perpetual dedication of property for the worship at a private individual's tomb (samadhi) constitutes a valid religious purpose under Hindu law.
Whether such a dedication, lacking public benefit, can be upheld solely on the basis of claimed religious merit.
holdings: A perpetual dedication of property for worshipping a private individual's tomb (samadhi) is not a valid religious purpose under Hindu law.
For a religious purpose to justify perpetual dedication without public benefit, it must have a Shastraic basis or be widely accepted by a substantial class of Hindus.
doctrines: Shastraic basis requirement for religious endowments
Public policy limitation on expansion of religious merit-based dedications

card.dispute: Two district magistrates were accused of committing contempt of court by forwarding applications containing allegations against a subordinate magistrate handling a pending case, which the High Court held interfered with the administration of justice.
issues_decided: Whether transmitting applications with allegations against a trying magistrate to that magistrate for report amounts to contempt of court
Whether superior judicial officers must censor or redact such applications before forwarding them
Whether mere transmission of potentially prejudicial material, without intent to influence, constitutes substantial interference with justice
holdings: Forwarding applications to the concerned magistrate for report in the normal course of official duty does not constitute contempt of court, as it does not substantially interfere with the administration of justice.
A superior magistrate is not required to redact or censor an application before sending it for report; transmitting the full document is lawful and proper in discharge of supervisory duties.
Contempt jurisdiction should not be invoked merely on grounds of impropriety; there must be real and substantial prejudice to the due course of justice, which was absent here.
doctrines: Substantial interference with justice test
Contempt by prejudice
Judicial propriety vs. real prejudice distinction

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought with the lessor, Shaikh Serajuddin, over whether it was liable to pay rent accrued before 15 August 1947 under a lease entered into by the undivided Province of Bengal.
issues_decided: Whether the liability to pay rent under a lease falls within the term 'financial obligations' in Article 9 of the Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947
Whether Article 8(2)(a) of the Order makes the Province of West Bengal liable for rent accrued before the appointed day
holdings: The liability to pay rent under a lease does not constitute a 'financial obligation' under Article 9 of the Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947.
The State of West Bengal is liable for rent accrued before 15 August 1947 under Article 8(2)(a) of the Order, as the lease was for purposes exclusively of West Bengal after partition.
provisions: Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947, Article 8(2)
Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947, Article 9
doctrines: Ejusdem generis
Interpretation of statutory provisions in context

card.dispute: The dispute was between the shebait of an idol and the heirs of the testator over whether properties were absolutely dedicated to the idol or held by the heirs subject to a charge for the idol's upkeep.
issues_decided: Whether the properties were absolutely dedicated to the idol or subject to a charge in favor of the heirs
Whether the shebait's possession of the property could be adverse to the idol
holdings: The dedication of the property to the idol was absolute, as the will clearly vested ownership in the idol and restricted any interest by heirs or assigns.
A shebait cannot acquire adverse possession against the idol, as his possession is on behalf of the idol and any adverse claim would reward breach of fiduciary duty.
provisions: Will under general principles of testamentary construction
doctrines: Conspectus rule in construction of wills
Fiduciary nature of shebait's possession
No adverse possession by shebait against idol

card.dispute: The mortgagor-tenants sued the mortgagee to redeem the property after he obtained possession under the Orissa Tenancy Act and later purchased it at a court auction; the dispute was whether the mortgagee could retain the property or was bound to allow redemption.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant, as a mortgagee in possession under Section 225 of the Orissa Tenancy Act, could extinguish the plaintiffs' right to redeem by purchasing the property at a court sale.
Whether the defendant held the property as a trustee for the plaintiffs after purchasing it at auction.
Whether the plaintiffs' right to redemption was extinguished by merger or by operation of the Orissa Tenancy Act.
holdings: A mortgagee in possession remains a mortgagee regardless of obtaining title through auction; the right to redemption persists unless extinguished by contract, merger, or statute.
The defendant’s purchase at auction did not extinguish the right to redeem because he stood in the mortgagor’s shoes and reacquired the same mortgagee-in-possession status under Section 225(1).
Merger did not occur because the defendant acquired only the tenant’s estate, not the superior landlord’s interest.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, Section 90 (referred as Trusts Act, though likely a reference to equitable principles under TP Act)
Transfer of Property Act, Section 60 (implied, regarding right to redemption)
doctrines: Once a mortgage always a mortgage
Right to redemption
Merger of estates
Equitable subrogation (implied in mortgagee stepping into mortgagor’s shoes)

card.dispute: The petitioner, a landlord, challenged the takeover of his estate by the Court of Wards under colonial-era regulations as violating his fundamental right to property.
issues_decided: Whether Section 112 of the Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, read with the Ajmer Government Wards Regulation, 1888, infringes the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution?
Whether the infringement of the right to property is saved by Article 19(5) as a reasonable restriction?
Whether the law is protected under Article 31-A of the Constitution as a law modifying property rights?
holdings: The combined effect of Section 112 and the 1888 Regulation abridges the fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f) by allowing indefinite suspension of management and possession based on subjective executive determination.
Such a law cannot be a reasonable restriction under Article 19(5) because it imposes a penalty based on executive discretion without judicial review, negating the right entirely.
Article 31-A does not save the law because it applies only to laws involving acquisition, extinguishment, or modification of proprietary rights, not temporary suspension of management rights.
provisions: Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950, Section 112
doctrines: Subjective executive determination without judicial review violates fundamental rights
Penalty disguised as regulation cannot be a reasonable restriction under Article 19(5)
Doctrine of 'modification of rights' under Article 31-A limited to substantive changes in proprietary rights

card.dispute: A creditor sought to enforce a decree against a joint Hindu family member's interest in coparcenary property, claiming rights to a share of profits and possession, while the family contested the extent of the purchaser's rights and the liability of the sons.
issues_decided: Whether the sons of a judgment-debtor member of a joint Hindu family are liable for the father's debt and whether their undivided interest can be sold in execution even if they are not parties to the suit or execution proceedings.
Whether a purchaser of a coparcener's interest in a joint Hindu family property is entitled to immediate possession or a share of profits from the date of purchase.
holdings: The sons of a joint Hindu family member are bound by a pious obligation to pay the father's legal and moral debts, and their undivided interest in coparcenary property can be sold in execution even if they are not made parties to the suit or execution, provided the debt is not immoral or illegal.

A purchaser of a coparcener's undivided interest in joint family property is not entitled to immediate possession or a share of profits from the date of purchase; such rights can only be enforced through a suit for partition, with possession dating from the actual allotment.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statute, based on personal law principles)
doctrines: Pious obligation of Hindu sons to pay father's debts
Rule in Nanomi Babuasin's case
Doctrine of representation in execution proceedings by a father even if not karta

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought with landowners, led by Mrs. Bela Banerjee, over the constitutional validity of provisions in the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, that declared the public purpose of land acquisition as conclusive and capped compensation at the land's 1946 market value.
issues_decided: Whether the provision making the government's declaration of public purpose conclusive is constitutional under Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the limitation of compensation to the market value of land as of December 31, 1946, violates the requirement of just compensation under Article 31(2).
holdings: A declaration of public purpose by the government cannot be conclusive; the existence of a public purpose must be objectively established as a fact to satisfy Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Fixing compensation for acquired land at its 1946 market value, regardless of the date of acquisition, is arbitrary and fails to provide full indemnity, thus violating Article 31(2).
provisions: The West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 8
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Principle of just compensation
Objective existence of public purpose
Severability of unconstitutional provisions
Legislative discretion subject to constitutional limits

card.dispute: The Assam Bengal Cement Co. Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether annual and periodic payments made to lessors for exclusive limestone rights were deductible as revenue expenditure under the Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the annual payment of Rs. 5,000 under clause 4 of the lease deed was a revenue or capital expenditure.
Whether the lump sum payment of Rs. 35,000 spread over five years under clause 5 constituted revenue or capital expenditure.
Whether these expenditures were allowable deductions under section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
holdings: An expenditure is capital if it brings an enduring benefit to the business as a whole, even if payments are recurring or spread over time.
Payments made to secure exclusive rights that protect and enhance the business’s capital asset are capital in nature, not revenue.
The character of expenditure depends on the nature of the benefit acquired, not on whether payment is made in lump sum or instalments.
Expenditure that appreciates the value of the business or shields it from competition is not deductible as revenue expenditure under section 10(2)(xv).
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Enduring benefit test
Once and for all test
Business purpose vs. capital appreciation

card.dispute: The zemindar challenged the Madras government's acquisition of his estate and under-tenure without adequate compensation under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation provisions of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 constitute a colourable exercise of legislative power under the Government of India Act, 1935
Whether the appellant is entitled to compensation guaranteed under Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935 despite the commencement of the Constitution
holdings: The appellant cannot challenge the compensation provisions as colourable legislation because no corresponding entry in the Government of India Act, 1935's legislative lists invalidates the post-constitutional law.
Article 31(6) of the Constitution bars the application of Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and thus the appellant has no enforceable right to compensation.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 (Act 26 of 1948)
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of constitutional bar under Article 31(6)

card.dispute: Bihari Singh appealed his murder conviction, challenging the reliability of his wife's testimony and the procedural fairness of his trial.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to properly examine the accused under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code prejudiced the accused's right to a fair trial.
Whether the uncorroborated testimony of the accused's wife, given under suspicious circumstances, is sufficient to sustain a conviction for murder.
Whether the trial and appellate courts adequately scrutinized the prosecution's evidence and inconsistencies in witness statements.
holdings: The court must explicitly inform the accused of the specific circumstances of the case against them and allow a meaningful opportunity to respond; failure to do so violates fair trial principles.
A conviction for murder cannot be based solely on the uncorroborated and inconsistent testimony of a witness with a questionable motive and credibility.
Serious lapses in trial procedure and evaluation of evidence justify appellate intervention, even in the absence of formal procedural objections.
doctrines: Right to fair trial
Uncorroborated testimony
Judicial scrutiny of evidence in capital cases

card.dispute: Captain Ganpati Singhji challenged the refusal of a permit to hold a fair on his land by the District Magistrate, arguing that the rules enabling such refusal were ultra vires and violated his fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the rules framed by the Chief Commissioner under the Ajmer Laws Regulation of 1877, delegating rule-making and permit-revocation powers to the District Magistrate, are ultra vires the Regulation
Whether the refusal of a permit based on a policy of issuing permits only to local bodies, not private individuals, is legally valid
Whether the impugned rules infringe the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
holdings: The Chief Commissioner cannot delegate his rule-making power under the Regulation to the District Magistrate; such delegation renders the rules ultra vires.
The fourth sub-rule allowing the District Magistrate to revoke a permit without reason or notice is ultra vires as it creates an arbitrary and uncontrolled power.

The rules do not constitute a proper system of conservancy and sanitation as required by Section 40 of the Regulation, but instead establish an ad hoc control mechanism beyond the scope of the enabling provision.
doctrines: Doctrine of non-delegation of legislative power
Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of reasonable restrictions under Article 19

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the validity of the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, claiming it violated property rights under the Government of India Act, 1935, and the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, could be challenged for violating fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution despite being in the Ninth Schedule.
Whether the Act could still be challenged on the ground of violating section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, even after the insertion of Article 31-B.
holdings: The validity of a law listed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be questioned on the ground that it abridges fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution due to the protection granted by Article 31-B.

Article 31-B bars challenges based on the alleged violation of section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935, where such violation pertains to the same property rights now protected under Part III of the Constitution.
provisions: Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949 (Bombay Act LXII of 1949)
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional immunity under the Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of fundamental rights encompassing pre-constitutional rights
Doctrine of implied bar on judicial review for laws in the Ninth Schedule

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the validity of an ex parte ejectment decree obtained by the liquidator of a banking company through a summary application under the Banking Companies Act.
issues_decided: Whether a claim for ejectment by a liquidator under section 45-B of the Banking Companies Act must be pursued by suit or can be decided through a summary application
Whether a decree passed in a summary proceeding under section 45-B is null and void if the court adopts an incorrect mode of proceeding
holdings: Section 45-B of the Banking Companies Act contemplates summary proceedings by application unless the court or rules require a suit, to ensure speedy resolution in liquidation matters.
A decree passed under section 45-B in a summary application is not a nullity merely because a suit might have been expected; it is valid if the court had jurisdiction over the subject matter.
doctrines: Summary proceeding doctrine
Jurisdictional validity vs. procedural irregularity
Statutory interpretation in light of legislative purpose

card.dispute: The dispute was between collaterals and the sons of a daughter over inheritance of non-ancestral property after the daughter gifted it to her sons.
issues_decided: Whether the property in question was ancestral or non-ancestral
Whether, under Jat custom, daughter's sons inherit non-ancestral property to the exclusion of collaterals
Whether a gift by a daughter of non-ancestral property to her sons amounts to acceleration of succession
Whether exclusion of a small portion of property (a house) from the gift invalidates the surrender and acceleration
holdings: The property was non-ancestral, as established by res judicata and conceded by the plaintiffs' counsel across three courts.
Among agricultural Jats of the village, daughter's sons inherit non-ancestral property to the exclusion of collaterals, based on customary law.
A gift by a daughter to her sons of non-ancestral property amounts to acceleration of succession, vesting the property in the sons immediately.
The omission to include a small portion of the property in the gift due to oversight does not invalidate the surrender if the intention to efface oneself was genuine.
provisions: Customary Law among Agricultural Jats of Village Ralla, District Barnala, State of Pepsu
doctrines: Acceleration of succession
Surrender under customary law
Res judicata
Limited heirship versus full succession under custom

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, after losing a suit and appealing to a higher court, challenged the jurisdiction of the appellate court due to under-valuation of the appeal, claiming it affected the merits of the case.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed by a court of inferior jurisdiction due to under-valuation is a nullity
Whether mere error in the decision on the merits constitutes 'prejudice' under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act
Whether a party who invokes a court's jurisdiction based on their own valuation can later complain of prejudice due to under-valuation
holdings: A decree passed by a court of inferior jurisdiction due to under-valuation is not a nullity if the case was heard on the merits and no real prejudice resulted.
Mere error in the decision on the merits or change of forum does not amount to 'prejudice' under Section 11; prejudice must be directly caused by over- or under-valuation.
A party who chooses a forum based on their own valuation cannot later claim prejudice from that valuation to challenge the jurisdiction.
doctrines: Equitable jurisdiction under Section 11 of the Suits Valuation Act
Doctrine of prejudice in appellate jurisdiction
Principle of estoppel against a party challenging jurisdiction they invoked

card.dispute: The official liquidator of Gaya Sugar Mills Ltd. sought recovery of Rs. 14,77,000 from two respondents who held sale proceeds of company assets, claiming they were agents or trustees of the company, while the respondents resisted on grounds they were not liable under Section 185 of the Companies Act.
issues_decided: Whether the two respondents were liable to return the sale proceeds to the company under Section 185 of the Indian Companies Act
Whether the respondents were trustees or agents of the company in relation to the sale proceeds
Whether the agreement of 1-1-1950 created enforceable rights before court sanction
holdings: Until a scheme under Section 153 is sanctioned, no rights vest in preference shareholders or proposed trustees; the company retains ownership of assets and sale proceeds.
The respondents were agents of the company, not trustees, as the agreement was inchoate and unenforceable, and no trust could arise without completed formalities.
Section 185 applies where a person holds money 'prima facie' belonging to the company, and the official liquidator can recover it summarily from agents in possession.
doctrines: Inchoate agreement
Implied agency
Prima facie entitlement under summary recovery
Trust not created without completed formalities

card.dispute: The appellants, Hem Singh and another, challenged the validity of Harnam Singh's adoption of a collateral in the 8th degree, claiming it violated customary law restricting adoption to 'near collaterals only'.
issues_decided: Whether the custom requiring adoption of 'near collaterals only' among Gill Jats of village Gillanwali is mandatory or directory.
Whether an adoption of a collateral in the 8th degree is valid under the customary law of Gurdaspur District, Punjab.
Whether rules regarding ceremonies and preferences in selection under Punjab customary adoption law are mandatory.
holdings: The phrase 'near collaterals only' in the customary law is not mandatory but directory, allowing discretion to the adopter in selecting a collateral regardless of degree.
An adoption of a collateral in the 8th degree is valid under the customary law of the Gill Jats of Gillanwali village, as the custom does not impose a strict degree-based restriction.
Under Punjab customary law, adoption is secular and intended to appoint an heir; thus, rules on ceremonies and preference in selection are directory, not mandatory.
provisions: Riwaj-i-am (Digest of Customary Law in the Punjab)
doctrines: Directory vs Mandatory Rule
Factum Valet Doctrine
Secular Nature of Customary Adoption in Punjab

card.dispute: The dispute was between a widow, Kamalabai, and other family members over the validity of an adoption she made after the death of her grandson and the son's widow, with Gurunath alias Bhimaji challenging the adoption on the grounds that her power to adopt had already terminated.
issues_decided: Whether a widow's power to adopt revives upon the death of a grandson or the son's widow who was competent to adopt?
Whether the power of a widow to adopt depends on the devolution or vesting of property?
Whether ceremonial competence of a son extinguishes the mother's power to adopt?
holdings: A widow's power to adopt terminates upon the interposition of a grandson or the son's widow competent to continue the line and does not revive upon their subsequent death.
The power of a widow to adopt is independent of questions relating to the vesting or devesting of property and is based on spiritual duties.
The mere attainment of ceremonial competence by a son does not extinguish the mother's authority to adopt.
provisions: Hindu Law of Adoption (unspecified statutory provision, as case predates codified Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956)
doctrines: Doctrine of spiritual necessity in Hindu adoption
Doctrine of irrevocable termination of adoption power upon interposition
Principles of justice, equity and good conscience in absence of Shastric text

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of three appellants in a criminal case involving murder and assault, while the appellants challenged their enhanced conviction and sentence, leading to a dispute over common intention and individual liability under the Indian Penal Code.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of the three appellants under Section 302 IPC and convicting them of murder;
Whether all three appellants shared a common intention to murder Jiraj under Section 34 IPC;
What offence each appellant was individually liable for based on the nature and sequence of their acts.
holdings: The High Court erred in holding all three appellants guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC with common intention under Section 34 IPC, as there was no evidence of a shared intent to kill.
Only Bhopal caused the fatal injury with the intention to kill, thus solely liable for murder under Section 302 IPC; the others lacked the requisite intent.
Kripal and Sheoraj were guilty of voluntarily causing grievous hurt under Section 326 IPC due to use of weapons likely to cause serious injury, but not murder.
The convictions under Section 323 IPC for assaulting the labourers were upheld for all three, but separate fine for Bhopal under this section was set aside.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Development of common intention on the spot
Principle of individual liability in absence of common intention to kill
Distinction between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction and death sentence for the murder of an elderly woman, arguing insufficient evidence and alternative suspects.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant murdered Musammat Sobha?
Whether the possibility of the crime being committed by the deceased’s son-in-law or grandson was reasonably eliminated?
Whether the appellant’s conduct after the death indicated consciousness of guilt?
holdings: The prosecution established beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant caused the death of the deceased by suffocation, as the only reasonable hypothesis consistent with the evidence.
The possibility of the son-in-law or grandson committing the murder was ruled out due to lack of motive and opportunity compared to the appellant.
The appellant’s conduct—failing to inform the family, insisting on immediate cremation—demonstrated consciousness of guilt and an attempt to suppress evidence of unnatural death.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of the doubt in circumstantial evidence cases
Conduct indicating consciousness of guilt
Last seen doctrine (inference from proximity and opportunity)

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the attachment and sale of his properties for tax recovery, claiming violation of fundamental rights under Articles 31(1) and 19(1)(f) due to allegedly illegal assessment proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the enforcement of tax recovery proceedings violates the right to property under Article 31(1) when such deprivation results from tax collection.
Whether the right under Article 265 can be enforced through Article 32 of the Constitution.
Whether the petition under Article 32 is maintainable against finalized tax assessments and recovery actions.
holdings: Article 31(1) applies to deprivation of property otherwise than by tax imposition or collection, not to tax-related seizures.
The right under Article 265 that no tax shall be levied without legal authority is not a fundamental right under Part III and thus not enforceable under Article 32.
A petition under Article 32 is not maintainable to challenge completed tax assessment and recovery proceedings, especially when alternative remedies exist.
provisions: Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, Section 5(1)
Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, Section 8(2)
doctrines: Special provision doctrine
Fundamental rights enforceability under Article 32
Finality of administrative and tax proceedings

card.dispute: The dispute was between two factions of the Malankara Church over ecclesiastical authority, specifically whether the defendants had voluntarily separated from the Church by recognizing the Catholicos, and whether the plaintiffs' denial of the Catholicos's authority constituted a departure from canonical law.
issues_decided: Whether the lower courts committed an error apparent on the face of the record by misconceiving a concession made by the defendants' advocate regarding ecclesiastical authority.
Whether the courts erred in deciding matters outside the agreed-upon issues, particularly on the general powers of the Patriarch which had been excluded by agreement.
Whether the failure to consider whether the plaintiffs' stance amounted to a voluntary separation from the Church, if such was imputed to the defendants, vitiated the judgment.
holdings: A misconception by the court of a concession made by a party's advocate, especially on a point of law, constitutes a sufficient reason for review under the Code of Civil Procedure.
Deciding a case on issues not framed or agreed upon, particularly after parties have limited the scope of trial, amounts to an error apparent on the face of the record.

If the court finds that one party has voluntarily separated from the Church based on certain acts, it must equally consider whether the opposing party’s denial of those acts also constitutes a departure from canonical law.
provisions: Travancore Code of Civil Procedure (VIII of 1100), Section 87
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47, Rule 1
United State of Travancore Cochin High Court Act V of 1125, Section 25
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Review on grounds of sufficient reason analogous to procedural errors
Principle of judicial fairness in ecclesiastical disputes
Binding nature of issues framed and agreed upon in trial

card.dispute: The appellants and the prosecution disputed over the right to cultivate certain lands, leading to a criminal case over whether an unlawful assembly existed when the appellants allegedly attacked a complainant during a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the assembly of the appellants was unlawful under Section 141, IPC, even if it started as lawful.
Whether the conviction under Section 147, IPC, could stand despite acquittal on the dacoity charge.
Whether the common object of the assembly could include assault even if theft was not proven.
holdings: An assembly that is lawful at inception can become unlawful if members subsequently develop a common object to use force, even without prior concert.
The conviction under Section 147, IPC, is valid if the assembly turned unlawful due to an assault, even if the theft charge failed.
The common object of an unlawful assembly can be inferred from conduct, and separate illegal objectives in a charge need not be pleaded in distinct paragraphs if no prejudice results.
doctrines: Transformation of lawful assembly into unlawful assembly
Common object under Section 141 as distinct from common intention under Section 34
Curability of defects in charge under CrPC if no prejudice shown

card.dispute: The taxpayer challenged the constitutional validity of Section 12-B of the Indian Income-tax Act, which imposed tax on capital gains, arguing it was ultra vires the legislative powers of Parliament under the Government of India Act, 1935.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'income' in Entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935 includes 'capital gains'.
Whether judicial interpretations of 'income' in tax statutes have restricted its meaning so as to exclude capital gains.
Whether Section 12-B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, as amended, is intra vires the legislative competence of the Central Legislature.
holdings: The word 'income' in Entry 54 of List I includes capital gains, as it must be given its widest natural and ordinary meaning in a constitutional context.
Judicial interpretations of 'income' in tax statutes do not rigidly restrict its meaning in the Constitution, which must be construed liberally.
Section 12-B imposing tax on capital gains is intra vires the Central Legislature's powers under Entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule.
provisions: Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 54
doctrines: Liberal construction of constitutional entries conferring legislative power
Cardinal rule of literal interpretation in constitutional context
Rejection of rigid legislative practice limiting constitutional terms

card.dispute: The assessee firm, Narain Swadeshi Weaving Mills, fought with the Commissioner of Excess Profits Tax over whether leasing out its plant and machinery after ceasing manufacturing operations constituted 'business' under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, making it liable to tax under Section 10-A.
issues_decided: Whether the letting out of plant, machinery, and other assets by the assessee firm amounted to carrying on 'business' within the meaning of Section 2(5) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940.
Whether Section 10-A of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, could be applied to the assessee firm in the absence of an ongoing business.
Whether the income from leasing out assets could be amalgamated with the incomes of other firms under Section 10-A.
holdings: Leasing out plant and machinery after complete cessation of manufacturing operations does not constitute 'business' under Section 2(5) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, as it lacks continuity and commercial purpose.
Section 10-A is inapplicable where the assessee is not carrying on any business during the chargeable accounting period.
The amalgamation of incomes of other firms with the assessee’s income under Section 10-A is invalid when the assessee itself is not engaged in business.
doctrines: Ordinary conception of business
Continuity and systematic activity as essential elements of business
Distinction between isolated transactions and business operations
Commercial asset test in cessation of business

card.dispute: The Mahant of a Hindu math challenged the constitutional validity of certain provisions of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939 as amended in 1952, which imposed administrative control and financial contributions on religious institutions.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 38, 39, and the proviso to Section 46 of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939 (as amended) violate Articles 19(1)(f), 25, and 26 of the Constitution
Whether Section 49 of the Act, requiring an annual contribution from religious institutions, constitutes a tax or a fee and whether it violates Article 27
Whether the impugned provisions unjustly restrict the rights of religious heads over property and administration of religious endowments
holdings: Sections 38 and 39, which empower an executive officer to frame schemes for religious institutions without judicial oversight, impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property and religious freedom, and are therefore unconstitutional.
The proviso to Section 46, which allows the Commissioner to direct the use of surplus income of a math, unreasonably curtails the trustee’s discretion and violates Article 26, and is thus invalid.

Section 49 imposes a fee, not a tax, as the contribution is specifically used for administrative services benefiting the institutions, and hence falls within legislative competence and does not violate Article 27.
Article 27 is not violated because the contribution under Section 49 serves secular administrative purposes, not the promotion or maintenance of any religion.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 38
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 39
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 46 (proviso)
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, Section 49
doctrines: Doctrine of unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights
Doctrine of secular administration of religious institutions
Quid pro quo test for distinguishing fee from tax
Doctrine of legislative competence under federal structure

card.dispute: Zamindars challenged the validity of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act on the ground that it was passed by a legislature not validly constituted under the covenant of the State of Madhya Bharat.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act (XXVIII of 1951) was void due to being passed by a legislature not validly constituted under the covenant of Madhya Bharat.
Whether defects in the formation of the Madhya Bharat Interim Legislative Assembly affect the validity of laws passed by it after the commencement of the Constitution.
holdings: The validity of laws passed by the Madhya Bharat Interim Legislative Assembly cannot be questioned under Article 385 of the Constitution, as it was a body functioning immediately before the Constitution's commencement and thus recognized by the Constitution.
Article 385 invests functioning legislatures of Part B States with constitutional authority, irrespective of defects in their original formation under prior covenants or agreements.
doctrines: Doctrine of recognition of de facto bodies
Doctrine of constitutional continuity during transition
Doctrine of validation by constitutional provision

card.dispute: Sital Das, claiming to be the duly appointed Mahant of a Ram Kabir sect religious institution, sued to recover possession of land leased by the previous Mahant, arguing the lease was invalid due to lack of legal necessity and improper alienation.
issues_decided: Whether Sital Das was validly appointed as Mahant of the Thakardwara by the Bhek and Sewaks after the death of the previous Mahant.
Whether the lease of 645 Kanals of land granted by the previous Mahant four days before his death was valid and supported by legal necessity.
holdings: Sital Das was validly appointed as Mahant by the Bhek and Sewaks of the Thakardwara on 23rd July 1945, and the appointment was legitimate despite the presiding Mahant belonging to an allied sect and absence of formal notices.

The lease granted by the previous Mahant was invalid as it lacked legal necessity, involved inadequate rent, and was unsupported by evidence of consideration, thus not binding on the religious institution.
doctrines: Legal necessity doctrine in religious endowment management
Doctrine of proper appointment to religious office by recognized spiritual body
Burden of proof on lessee to justify alienation of endowed property

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Calcutta High Court's jurisdiction to hear an appeal on a decree for re-restoration of properties, most of which were located in East Pakistan after Partition, and contested whether a default had occurred under the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta High Court had jurisdiction to hear an appeal filed after 15th August 1947 regarding proceedings pending before a court whose territory was partly transferred to East Pakistan.
Whether an order on an application for re-restoration of properties under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940, is appealable.
holdings: The Calcutta High Court retained appellate jurisdiction under para. 4(2) of the Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947, because the original proceedings were pending before the Subordinate Judge, Alipore, on 15th August 1947, and were to be treated as if they could have been instituted there after Partition.

An application for re-restoration of properties due to default under a decree passed under the Bengal Money Lenders Act is in substance an application for execution, and orders thereon are appealable as decrees under the Civil Procedure Code.
provisions: Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947, para. 4(1) and (2)
doctrines: Continuity of jurisdiction under transitional legal provisions post-Partition
Substance over form in characterizing legal proceedings
Appellate jurisdiction preserved for pending proceedings despite territorial changes

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming as reversioners and purchasers, sued for possession of property against the defendants, who contested the reversionary claim and asserted rights over certain properties dedicated to family deities by a widow.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs proved their status as the legitimate reversioners of Naubat Lal Jha.
Whether the properties in Schedule III, purchased by the widow with savings from the estate's income, formed part of the husband's estate and were therefore liable to be claimed by reversioners.
holdings: The plaintiffs established their status as reversioners through admissible pedigree evidence in the form of Panji entries, which were properly maintained and corroborated their claim, making the concurrent finding of fact binding.

The Schedule III properties did not form part of the husband's estate as the widow, having absolute right over the income, intended to keep them separate; her dedication of the properties to family deities confirmed her intention to treat them as her own.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact not interfered with in appeal unless based on inadmissible evidence
Pedigree evidence admissible under exceptions to hearsay rule
Hindu widow's absolute right to income and discretion to treat accumulations as her own

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a right of pre-emption over a property in Banaras sold by non-domiciles, challenging the lower courts' denial of such right on grounds of the vendor's non-domicile status.
issues_decided: Whether a local custom of pre-emption in Banaras applies only to persons who are natives or domiciled in the area
Whether the right of pre-emption based on custom binds all landowners in the locality regardless of domicile, religion, or nationality
holdings: A local custom of pre-emption exists in Banaras and attaches to house properties irrespective of the owner's domicile or native status.
When pre-emption is based on custom, it becomes part of the local law (lex loci) and binds all lands in the area, unless specific limitations are proved as part of the custom itself.
provisions: Muhammadan Law (as applied through equity, justice, and good conscience)
doctrines: Lex loci
Pre-emption as an incident of property
Custom overriding personal law in territorial application

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to establish the right to assess fair rent from defendants who claimed ancient rent-free possession (Niskar) over land within a permanently settled zamindari, while the defendants asserted a lost grant of Lakheraj status.
issues_decided: Whether a presumption of a lost grant of Niskar could arise in favour of the defendants based on their possession and the 1931 record of rights entry
Whether the defendants could rely on a lost grant from the Maharaja or Mahant after denying their title
Whether the Mahant had legal authority to make a perpetual rent-free grant (Niskar) without consideration
Whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation
holdings: A presumption of a lost grant does not arise when the land was included in the permanently assessed (Mal) lands of a zamindari, as such inclusion negates prior Lakheraj status under Regulation VIII of 1793.
A party who denies the title of the grantor cannot later rely on a presumption of a lost grant from that same grantor.

No presumption of a lost grant can be made if the grant would have been ultra vires the grantor’s powers, such as a Mahant making an unauthorised perpetual rent-free grant without benefit to the institution.

The suit was within limitation under Article 131 of the Limitation Act, as the cause of action accrued only when the defendants clearly asserted a hostile title in 1931 through the record of rights entry.
doctrines: Presumption of lost grant
Ultra vires acts of religious managers
Adverse possession and acknowledgment in records
Estoppel by denial of title

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against the High Court's decision to quash a prosecution for filing a false land claim under a repealed ordinance after the enactment of a new law.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the General Clauses Act, 1897, particularly Section 6(c), (d), and (e), apply when a law is repealed and simultaneously replaced by a new enactment.

Whether a prosecution for filing a false claim under the East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Ordinance, 1948, could proceed after the Ordinance was repealed and replaced by the corresponding Act of 1948.
Whether the saving clause in Section 11 of the 1948 Act preserved penal liability for offences committed under the Ordinance.
holdings: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act applies even when a repeal is accompanied by a new enactment, unless the new law shows a contrary intention to extinguish prior rights or liabilities.

The absence of an express saving clause in the new law does not automatically extinguish liabilities under the old law; the key question is whether the new law manifests an intention to destroy such liabilities.

Section 11 of the East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948, read with the proviso to Section 4, shows that claims filed under the Ordinance were to be treated as filed under the Act, making penal consequences under Sections 7 and 8 applicable.
Prosecution for a false claim filed under the Ordinance is valid under the Act, as the legislative intent was not to extinguish such liabilities upon repeal.
provisions: East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Ordinance, 1948, Section 7
East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948 (Punjab Act XLI of 1948), Section 4 (proviso), Section 8, Section 11
doctrines: Doctrine of survival of rights and liabilities post-repeal
Presumption against extinction of liabilities in absence of contrary legislative intent
Interpretation of saving clauses in repealing statutes
Continuity of penal liability under re-enacted legislation

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of a District Board's bye-law prohibiting him from holding a cattle market, alleging it violated his fundamental right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) and exceeded the Board's statutory powers.
issues_decided: Whether bye-law No. 2 made by the District Board is ultra vires its powers under Section 174(2)(1) of the United Provinces District Board Act, 1922
Whether the bye-law infringes the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
holdings: The District Board's power under Section 174(2)(1) is limited to regulating markets, not prohibiting individuals from holding them; thus, the bye-law is ultra vires.

A complete prohibition on holding a cattle market without providing for licensing or reasonable regulation violates the fundamental right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) and is unconstitutional.
provisions: United Provinces District Board Act, 1922, Section 174(1) and Section 174(2)(1)
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g)
Violation of fundamental rights by excessive delegation or arbitrary regulation

card.dispute: The Dominion of India and another appellant challenged the Bombay High Court's decision that a requisition order on immovable property expired in 1946, arguing it continued under a 1946 Ordinance.
issues_decided: Whether clause 3 of the Requisitioned Land (Continuance of Powers) Ordinance, 1946, continued requisition orders on immovable property beyond September 30, 1946, regardless of their original duration.
Whether the non obstante clause in the Ordinance limited the operation of clause 3 only to requisition orders that would have ended due to the expiry of the Defence of India Act, 1939.
holdings: Clause 3 of the Requisitioned Land (Continuance of Powers) Ordinance, 1946, continued all requisitioned immovable properties under requisition until the Ordinance expired, if they were subject to requisition on September 30, 1946, irrespective of whether the original order was for a limited or indefinite period.

A non obstante clause does not necessarily restrict the scope of an enactment; if the language is clear, the clause serves as clarification, not limitation, and courts must give effect to the plain meaning of the law.
provisions: Requisitioned Land (Continuance of Powers) Ordinance, 1946, Clause 2(3)
Requisitioned Land (Continuance of Powers) Ordinance, 1946, Clause 3
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Non obstante clause interpretation
Strict construction of laws affecting property rights

card.dispute: The Rajahmundry Electric Supply Corporation Ltd. challenged the validity of the Madras Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1949, which declared its electrical undertaking to vest in the Government, on grounds of legislative incompetence.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Legislature had the competence to enact a law for the compulsory acquisition of a commercial or industrial undertaking under the Government of India Act, 1935.
Whether the power to acquire property by a legislature includes, by implication, the power to acquire commercial or industrial undertakings.
holdings: The Madras Legislature lacked legislative competence to enact the impugned acquisition law, as there was no entry in any of the three Legislative Lists of the Seventh Schedule to the Government of India Act, 1935, authorizing compulsory acquisition of commercial or industrial undertakings.
