The power to make laws on matters incidental to a legislative entry does not extend to authorizing compulsory acquisition of industrial undertakings, where the Constitution specifically limits such power to land and requires express authorization for other property.
provisions: Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 9
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of ancillary or incidental powers
Legislative competence
Doctrine of ejusdem generis (implied limitation on legislative power)

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax, Madras, and Mysore Chromite Limited disputed whether the profits from the sale of chrome ore arose or were received in British India for income-tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the profits from the sale of goods arose in British India based on the place where the property in the goods passed.
Whether the profits were received in British India when the assessee received payment through a bank in Madras.
holdings: The property in the goods passed only when the bill of lading was delivered against acceptance of the bill of exchange, which occurred in London; thus, the sale and profits arose outside British India.

Receipt of advance payment in Madras by the assessee’s bank was not receipt of price or profits in British India, as the payment was an advance secured by documents, not a discharge of the buyer’s obligation.
doctrines: Place of accrual of profits based on transfer of property in goods
Receipt of income requires actual or constructive receipt by the payer on behalf of the buyer
Distinction between payment of price and bank advance against security

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether the decree-holders under a money decree were benamidars for another person, seeking relief under the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, 1940, while the respondent claimed rights as the recorded decree-holder.
issues_decided: Whether a court can inquire into whether a decree-holder on record is a benamidar in proceedings under Section 36 of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, 1940
Whether properties purchased at execution sale by a decree-holder or a third party are subject to restoration under Section 36(2)
holdings: In a proceeding under Section 36 of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, 1940, the court cannot go behind the decree to inquire whether the decree-holder on record is a benamidar for another person; only the recorded decree-holder is recognised for relief purposes.

Properties purchased by the decree-holder at execution sale must be restored to the judgment-debtor under Section 36(2)(c), but properties purchased by a third party not acting as the decree-holder’s benamidar are not subject to restoration.
doctrines: Benamidar doctrine
Statutory interpretation of remedial legislation
Limited scope of reopening decrees under special statutes

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for receiving a premium under an executory agreement to lease premises, and they challenged whether such receipt is punishable under Section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the receipt of money under an executory contract for a lease falls within the scope of Section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947?
Whether the phrase 'in respect of the grant, renewal or continuance of a lease' includes agreements where no lease has yet come into existence?
holdings: The phrase 'in respect of the grant, renewal or continuance of a lease' in Section 18(1) requires that a lease must actually exist or be contemporaneously created when the payment is made; it does not cover executory agreements to grant a lease.
Receipt of money under an executory contract, where no lease has come into existence and no landlord-tenant relationship has been established, is not punishable under Section 18(1) of the Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(3)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 6
doctrines: Strict construction of penal statutes
Plain meaning rule
Noscitur a sociis
Rule against extending penal liability based on legislative intent inferred from language

card.dispute: The landlords (Waryam Singh and another) fought against the tenants (Amarnath and another) over the refusal of lower courts to order ejectment despite admitted non-payment of rent under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the Court of the Judicial Commissioner of Himachal Pradesh has power of judicial superintendence under Article 227 of the Constitution over tribunals like the Rent Controller and District Judge functioning under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949?
Whether the lower courts acted arbitrarily in refusing ejectment despite the tenants' admitted failure to pay rent as required under Section 13(2)(i) proviso of the Act?
holdings: Article 227(1) read with Article 241 confers power of judicial superintendence on the Court of the Judicial Commissioner over tribunals, including the Rent Controller and District Judge, functioning within Himachal Pradesh.

The lower courts acted arbitrarily by refusing ejectment despite the tenants' failure to pay rent as mandated by law, warranting interference under Article 227 to keep subordinate tribunals within their legal bounds.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i) proviso
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 14
doctrines: Power of judicial superintendence under Article 227
Arbitrary exercise of discretion by subordinate courts
Continuity of supervisory jurisdiction from Government of India Act, 1915 to Constitution

card.dispute: The appellants, Umrao Singh and another, challenged the adoption and succession of minor Bhagwati Singh to the jagir of Indergarh, claiming themselves as rightful successors, while the respondents asserted that the succession was exclusively within the sovereign authority of the Rajpramukh of Rajasthan.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decide the question of succession to the jagir of Indergarh?
Whether the right to recognize succession to a jagir is a political function vested exclusively in the Rajpramukh under the Covenant of the Rulers of Rajasthan?
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate on succession to a jagir where such succession is determined by sovereign or political authority, as the matter is impliedly barred from civil cognizance.

The power to recognize succession to a jagir, being an incident of sovereignty and political in nature, is exclusively vested in the Rajpramukh under Article 7(3) of the Covenant of the Rulers of Rajasthan, and cannot be reviewed by a civil court.
provisions: Covenant of the Rulers of Rajasthan, Article 7(3)
doctrines: Implied ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Sovereign and political character of jagir succession
Doctrine of non-justiciability of political questions

card.dispute: Zamindars of Madras challenged the validity of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, arguing that certain provisions amounted to a colourable exercise of legislative power and violated constitutional safeguards on compensation for compulsory acquisition of property.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, could be challenged for contravening Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, after the commencement of the Constitution?
Whether the provisions of Section 27(i) and Section 30 of the impugned Act were void as colourable legislation violating constitutional principles of compensation?
holdings: The Madras Act of 1948, enacted before the Constitution and certified by the President under Article 31(6), cannot be questioned in court for contravening Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935.

The doctrine of 'colourable legislation' as applied in the Bihar Land Reforms case does not apply here because the Act is protected by Article 31(6) of the Constitution, which bars judicial review on grounds of inadequate or unjust compensation.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Sections 27(i) and 30
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Protection under Article 31(6) of the Constitution
Immunity from judicial review for pre-constitutional laws certified under Article 31(6)

card.dispute: Wazir Chand challenged the illegal seizure of his goods by the Chamba police at the instance of the Jammu and Kashmir police, claiming violation of his fundamental rights under the Indian Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the seizure of goods by the Chamba police without legal authority violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the petitioner was entitled to a writ under Article 226 despite having filed an application under Section 523 of the CrPC
Whether the Chamba police had jurisdiction to assist Jammu and Kashmir police in seizing property in light of Article 370
holdings: Any seizure of property not authorized by law infringes the fundamental rights of a citizen under Articles 19 and 31, regardless of the ownership dispute.
An application under Section 523 of the CrPC, if dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, does not bar a remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution.

The Chamba police had no legal authority to assist the Jammu and Kashmir police in seizure of goods, especially in absence of magistrate’s order or applicability of Sections 51, 96, 98, or 165 of the CrPC, and given the jurisdictional limitations under Article 370.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), Section 51
Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), Section 96
Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), Section 98
Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), Section 165
Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), Section 523
doctrines: Fundamental rights protection against unlawful seizure
Remedy under Article 226 not barred by ineffective alternative remedy
Jurisdictional limits of police under federal structure and Article 370

card.dispute: The petitioners, holders of jagirs and muafis granted by rulers of erstwhile princely states, challenged the State of Uttar Pradesh's attempt to confiscate these lands, claiming the action was an invalid 'act of State' after the Constitution came into force.
issues_decided: Whether the Government of India or a State Government can invoke the doctrine of 'act of State' to invalidate grants made by rulers of former princely states after the Constitution came into force
Whether the rulers of princely states retained sovereign powers after accession, enabling their acts to be treated as 'acts of State'
Whether the petitioners' rights under Articles 19(f) and 31(1) of the Constitution were violated by the impugned action
holdings: The doctrine of 'act of State' cannot be invoked by the Indian State against its own citizens, especially after the commencement of the Constitution, which established a sovereign democratic republic based on the will of the people.
With the adoption of the Constitution, all vestiges of princely sovereignty ceased, and no ruler or successor government could claim sovereign authority to perform acts immune from judicial review.

The impugned confiscation of jagir and muafi lands violated the petitioners' rights under Articles 19(f) and 31(1), and could not be justified as an act of State; thus, the State was restrained from enforcing the orders.
doctrines: Act of State doctrine
Sovereignty of the people
Fundamental rights under the Constitution
Judicial review of executive action

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan fought with Rao Manohar Singhji, a jagirdar, over the validity of Section 8-A of a Rajasthan Ordinance that stripped certain jagirdars of their right to collect rent, allegedly violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8-A of the Rajasthan Ordinance, as amended, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification among jagirdars?
Whether the State's differentiation based on geographical considerations is a valid ground for classification under Article 14?
Whether the impugned Ordinance lacks a rational basis and thereby denies equal protection of laws?
holdings: Section 8-A of the Rajasthan Ordinance, as amended, violates Article 14 because it creates an arbitrary classification among jagirdars without a rational basis.
Geographical differentiation alone cannot justify unequal treatment under Article 14 unless supported by real and substantial distinctions and evidence, which was lacking here.
A law that deprives certain jagirdars of rent-collecting rights while leaving others unaffected, without reasonable justification, contravenes the principle of equal protection under Article 14.
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Reasonable classification doctrine
Arbitrariness in state action
Geographical basis for classification

card.dispute: The State of Bombay requisitioned premises from private individuals and a trust under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948; the owners/tenants challenged the orders as ultra vires the Constitution, arguing lack of public purpose and violation of property rights.
issues_decided: Whether sections 5(1) and 6(4)(a) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 are ultra vires Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) of the Constitution due to absence of public purpose and reasonable restrictions on property rights.
Whether the allotment of requisitioned premises to 'first informers' of suppressed vacancies violates the principle of equitable distribution and lacks public purpose.
Whether the burden of proof lies on the State or the petitioners to show that the requisitioned premises were 'let' or 'intended to be let' under section 4(3) of the Act.
Whether a writ of mandamus lies to challenge the allotment orders in light of the State's assurance not to disturb possession.
holdings: Requisitioning under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 for the purpose of providing accommodation to the houseless, including first informers, serves a valid public purpose under Article 31(2) and does not violate Article 19(1)(f).

The policy of allotting discovered 'suppressed vacancies' to genuine first informers is a reasonable and equitable method to deter suppression of vacancies and promote public welfare, even if not all houseless persons benefit.
The burden of proving illegality of a requisition order lies on the petitioners, especially when they have superior knowledge about whether premises were 'let' or 'intended to be let' under the Act.
Where the State gives an assurance not to disturb possession, the question of issuing mandamus becomes academic, and the appeal may be dismissed without costs.
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine under Article 31(2)
Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(f)
Burden of proof in challenges to administrative action
Equitable distribution as a facet of public welfare

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a power-of-attorney and subsequent registration of a mortgage deed, arguing improper presentation and lack of bodily infirmity for off-site authentication.
issues_decided: Whether the executant of a power-of-attorney was residing at Cuttack at the time of execution for purposes of authentication under the Indian Registration Act
Whether a power-of-attorney mistakenly presented for registration by an unauthorized person is invalid when later authenticated under section 33
Whether a Registrar's decision on bodily infirmity under section 33(1), proviso (i), can be challenged in court if erroneous
holdings: The term 'resides' in section 33 includes temporary residence; physical presence, eating, and sleeping at a place suffice, regardless of ownership or permanence.
A mistaken endorsement that a power-of-attorney was 'presented for registration' does not invalidate its authentication under section 33, which is an independent and complete act.
A Registrar's finding of bodily infirmity under section 33(1), proviso (i), is within his exclusive jurisdiction; even if erroneous, it does not affect the validity of authentication or registration.
doctrines: Jurisdictional vs. procedural error distinction
Deemed presentation doctrine
Exclusive administrative discretion in registration matters

card.dispute: The petitioners claimed that the State of Orissa violated their fundamental rights by refusing to recognize oral licenses they had purchased from the former estate owner for future fishery rights in Chilka Lake.
issues_decided: Whether the oral licenses for future fishery rights conferred a transferable interest in immovable property protected under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(1) of the Constitution
Whether the right to catch and carry away fish constitutes a 'profit a prendre' and is immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the State's refusal to recognize the licenses amounts to an infringement of fundamental rights
holdings: The right to catch and carry away fish is a profit a prendre, which is immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act and requires a registered instrument for valid transfer when valued over Rs. 100.
Since the oral transactions were not registered under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, no title or interest passed to the petitioners, and thus no fundamental right in property arose.
The State’s refusal to recognize the contract does not infringe fundamental rights as it neither acquired, confiscated, nor took possession of the contract or its benefits.
provisions: Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951 (Orissa Act I of 1952)
doctrines: Profit a prendre as immovable property
Requirement of registration under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act
Non-infringement of fundamental rights where State refuses to recognize private contract

card.dispute: Conviction and sentencing of multiple accused in a mass violence case involving murder, destruction of evidence, and unlawful assembly in a village in Uttar Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with a common object under Section 149 IPC
Whether the convictions under Sections 302/149, 201/149, 148, and 452 IPC were legally justified
Whether the sentence of death confirmed by the High Court was warranted
Whether the leave granted by the High Court was regular and legal
holdings: Mere presence in an unlawful assembly is sufficient for liability under Section 149 IPC if the individual shares the common object, even without committing a specific overt act.
Convictions under Sections 148, 302/149, 201/149, and 452 IPC were upheld for those actively involved in the attack or destruction of evidence.
Death sentences were confirmed for active participants, but reduced to life imprisonment where evidence was not fully corroborated by police records.
The court did not strike down the leave granted by the High Court, implying its acceptance despite procedural concerns.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Common object of unlawful assembly
Benefit of doubt in absence of specific allegations or evidence
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony with police records

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the election of the returned candidate, alleging he was disqualified under the Representation of the People Act for having an interest in a government contract through his father, who allegedly entered the contract on behalf of the joint family.
issues_decided: Whether Kuppuswami Karayalar was a benamidar for Krishnaswami Karayalar (the father of the returned candidate)?
Whether the Tribunal erred in presuming as a matter of law that a business started by a father is a joint family business under Hindu law?
Whether the finding that the contract was entered into on behalf of the joint family was based on a misapplication of law and insufficient factual analysis?
holdings: A finding of benami is a question of fact and will not be disturbed in special appeal if supported by evidence; the Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's finding that Kuppuswami was a benamidar for Krishnaswami.

There is no legal presumption under Hindu law that a business started by a father automatically becomes a joint family business, even though sons may be liable for the father's debts due to pious obligation.

The Tribunal erred in law by presuming the business was joint without evaluating evidence on whether the father acted on behalf of the family; the matter must be remitted for a proper factual determination based on evidence.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 7(d)
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 9(2)
doctrines: Pious obligation doctrine in Hindu law
Benami transaction as a question of fact
No presumption of joint family business under Hindu law for businesses started by a father

card.dispute: Two acquitted accused challenged the High Court's decision to set aside their acquittal in a criminal revision filed by a private complainant.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court applied the correct legal principles in setting aside an order of acquittal in revision at the instance of a private party.
Whether the High Court properly considered the settled limitations on revisional jurisdiction to interfere with acquittals.
holdings: A High Court must exercise extreme caution in setting aside an acquittal in revision, especially when the revision is initiated by a private party, and must show application of judicial mind to established legal principles.
Interference with an acquittal in revision is impermissible unless there is a clear failure of justice or the decision is perverse; mere difference of opinion with the trial court is insufficient.
doctrines: Limited revisional jurisdiction
No appeal against acquittal by private party
Judicial discretion must be exercised judiciously in revision

card.dispute: The appellant, Indira Sohanlal, challenged the Custodian-General's revision of an order confirming her exchange of property with an evacuee, arguing that the confirmation was final and not subject to revision.
issues_decided: Whether the order confirming the property exchange passed in 1952 was subject to revision under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether the Custodian-General had the power to revise an order when no appeal was filed by any aggrieved party
Whether the revisional order setting aside the confirmation was valid in substance and proper in exercise of discretion
holdings: An application for confirmation of a property transaction pending when the 1950 Act came into force must be decided under the new Act, making the order subject to revision under Section 27.
The revisional power under Section 27 is wide and not limited by the availability or non-filing of an appeal; it can be exercised suo motu to examine legality or propriety of any order.
The revisional order was flawed due to lack of clarity in reasoning and remand instructions, warranting its setting aside and remittal for fresh consideration.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 58(3)
East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 5-A
East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 5-B
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Doctrine of continuity of legal proceedings under transitional provisions
Principles of statutory interpretation regarding repeal and re-enactment
Scope and limits of revisional jurisdiction

card.dispute: The parties disputed over possession of certain Sangam lands, with the plaintiff claiming they were given conditionally for maintenance, while the defendants claimed they were transferred absolutely by a deed of 1867.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal to the Supreme Court was competent under Article 133 or Article 135 of the Constitution
Whether the deed of 1867 created a conditional or absolute transfer of the Sangam lands to Krishna Rao's branch
holdings: Article 133 did not apply because it only covers appeals from High Courts in the territory of India, but the right to appeal vested under existing law before the Constitution's commencement.
The appeal was competent under Article 135 as the Federal Court had jurisdiction over such matters immediately before the Constitution came into force, and that right continued.
doctrines: Vested right to appeal
Continuity of jurisdiction under Article 135
Literal interpretation of deeds

card.dispute: The appellant, Machander, challenged his conviction for murder on the grounds of insufficient evidence and failure by the trial court to examine him under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction could be sustained based on circumstantial evidence in the absence of a legally admissible confession.
Whether the failure to examine the accused under Section 342 CrPC rendered the trial unfair and affected the accused's rights.
Whether the case should be remanded for retrial despite the procedural lapse.
holdings: The circumstantial evidence against the appellant was insufficient to conclusively prove guilt, as it equally implicated other family members and did not exclude reasonable hypotheses pointing to another perpetrator.

The failure to examine the accused under Section 342 CrPC was not a mere technical error but a substantial violation of fair trial rights, especially given the reliance on a confession obtained after an eight-day delay.
It would be unjust to remand the case for retrial after over four and a half years of prolonged proceedings, as the accused had already suffered undue harassment and delay.
doctrines: Fair trial rights
Presumption of innocence
Balance of justice between prosecution and accused
Procedural fairness in criminal trials

card.dispute: Maharaj Umeg Singh and others challenged the validity of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, claiming it violated guarantees given to rulers of merged princely states and infringed their fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Act abolishing jagirs was ultra vires the State Legislature due to conflict with the Letters of Guarantee under Clause 5.
Whether the Act violated fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the Court had jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes arising from the Letters of Guarantee.
Whether the petitioner's estate in Moti Moree qualified as a 'jagir' under the impugned Act.
holdings: The State Legislature had plenary power under Article 246 to enact the law; Clause 5 of the Letters of Guarantee did not restrict legislative competence except by prohibiting discriminatory laws.
The Act could not be challenged on grounds of fundamental rights because Article 31-A(2)(a) immunized laws abolishing estates like jagirs from such challenges.
Article 363 barred judicial review of disputes arising from the Letters of Guarantee or merger agreements.
The question of whether Moti Moree was a jagir required detailed factual adjudication; the petitioner must first establish this in a civil suit before relief could be granted.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 (Bombay Act XXXIX of 1954)
doctrines: Legislative competence under Article 246
Bar of jurisdiction under Article 363
Protection of agrarian reform laws under Article 31-A
Non-justiciability of merger agreement disputes

card.dispute: The appellant Prabhu was convicted of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC based on alleged common intention with his co-accused, all of whom were acquitted, leading to a challenge on whether the conviction could stand without evidence of shared intention.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be convicted under Section 34 IPC for murder when all co-accused were acquitted and no prior concert was proven?
Whether the evidence established the appellant's participation in a common intention to commit murder?
Whether the presence of blood on the appellant's clothing was sufficient corroboration to sustain a conviction under Section 34 IPC?
holdings: A conviction under Section 34 IPC requires proof of active participation in a common intention with the actual perpetrator; mere presence at the scene is insufficient.
When all co-accused are acquitted and no prior concert is established, a conviction under Section 34 IPC cannot be sustained even if the accused was present after the crime.
The discovery of blood on the appellant's clothing, without more, does not prove participation in a common intention and cannot substitute for evidence of prior concert under Section 34 IPC.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Requirement of corroboration in unreliable testimony
Presumption of innocence in absence of conclusive evidence

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction and death sentence for murdering Ayyappan during a property dispute, arguing the killing occurred in a sudden fight and that medical negligence caused death.
issues_decided: Whether the injury inflicted by the appellant was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature
Whether the appellant could claim the exception to murder under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC due to sudden fight
Whether the death sentence was appropriate in the circumstances
holdings: An injury that causes diaphragm rupture and organ herniation is sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, even if not immediately fatal.
The exception under Section 300 IPC is not available when the accused stabs an unarmed person who is not involved in the fight and only attempts to pacify the situation.
The death sentence is not warranted where there was no premeditation and the act occurred in the heat of the moment after provocation, though it does not amount to a valid defense.
doctrines: Causation in criminal law: death due to natural consequences of injury, not medical negligence
Sudden fight exception under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC
Proportionality in sentencing: death penalty not mandatory in absence of premeditation

card.dispute: The sisters of the deceased Sheik Ataullah sued their brothers for partition of their shares in his estate, claiming that a waqf deed executed by the brothers in 1933 denied their inheritance rights.
issues_decided: Whether a family custom excluding female heirs from inheritance was established
Whether the plaintiffs' claim was barred by limitation due to adverse possession
holdings: A custom excluding female heirs must be proved by clear and cogent evidence; self-serving statements by interested parties, especially without documentary or independent evidence, are insufficient to establish such a custom.

Possession by one co-sharer is not adverse to other co-sharers unless there is a clear denial of their title and continued exclusion; enjoyment of income from the estate negates any claim of ouster or adverse possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 12
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive possession among co-sharers
Requirement of proof for customs derogating from general law

card.dispute: A collateral male relative (Mahant Salig Ram) challenged the daughter's (Musammat Maya Devi) right to inherit her father's self-acquired property under a claimed local custom excluding daughters.
issues_decided: Whether a special local custom excluding daughters from inheriting self-acquired property of a father existed among Saraswat Brahmins of Pathankot in Gurdaspur district?
Whether the Riwaj-i-am of 1913 is a reliable and trustworthy record of custom sufficient to displace the general custom favouring daughters?
Whether the burden of proof shifted to the daughter to rebut the presumption arising from the Riwaj-i-am?
holdings: The general custom in Punjab favours a daughter's right to inherit her father's self-acquired property, and collaterals must prove a special local custom to displace it.

Entries in Riwaj-i-am are entitled to a presumption of correctness, but the strength of that presumption depends on whether the recorded custom aligns with general practice and whether it adversely affects female rights.

A Riwaj-i-am that contains internal contradictions, is discredited by judicial decisions, and reflects what people wished the custom to be rather than what it was, cannot be reliable evidence to shift the burden of proof.
Where the Riwaj-i-am is unreliable, the general custom prevails, and the daughter is not required to produce instances to rebut a weakened presumption.
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of Riwaj-i-am entries
Burden of proof in custom-based succession disputes
Judicial scrutiny of reliability of customary records
General custom versus special local custom in inheritance

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of provisions allowing his arrest and detention for non-payment of income tax arrears, arguing they violated fundamental rights under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 46(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 offends Articles 13(1), 14, and 21 of the Constitution by enabling recovery through arrest and detention.
Whether Section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, as originally enacted, violated Article 14 due to discriminatory treatment between defaulters in Bombay City and those outside it.
Whether the amended Section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, after October 8, 1954, removes the constitutional infirmity, and if so, whether it applies retrospectively to pending cases.
holdings: Section 46(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 does not violate Articles 14 or 21 when read with Article 13(1), as the law remains valid unless explicitly struck down and can be amended to conform to constitutional requirements.

The original Section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 created unequal treatment violating Article 14 by allowing longer detention for Bombay defaulters compared to others, but this defect was cured by the 1954 amendment.

The amended Section 13 applies to pending recovery proceedings where arrest occurs after the amendment, as the coercive action arises only when prior remedies fail, and the law at the time of arrest governs.
provisions: Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, Section 13
doctrines: Doctrine of Severability and Partial Invalidity under Article 13(1)
Doctrine of Prospective Operation of Constitutional Invalidity
Principle of Reasonable Classification under Article 14
Doctrine of Subsequent Legislation Curing Unconstitutional Provisions

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be the Mahant of the Temple of Bhaironji and entitled to its properties and income, while the respondents contested his right based on the rules of succession among the spiritual lineage.
issues_decided: Whether the rule of succession among the Mahants of the temple was that a Mahant is succeeded by his Chela, Gurbhai, or the Chela of such Gurbhai, and in absence of such successors, the line becomes extinct and succession devolves upon representatives of other surviving lines.
Whether the extinction of a spiritual line occurs only when the last Mahant dies without leaving a Chela or Gurbhai, regardless of other Chelas existing in the broader lineage.
Whether the custom of succession as pleaded by the appellant was sufficiently established despite the absence of prior instances of line extinction.
holdings: A Mahant is succeeded by his Chela, Gurbhai, or the Chela of such Gurbhai; if none exist, the line becomes extinct and succession passes to representatives of other surviving lines.
Extinction of a spiritual line depends solely on the absence of a Chela or Gurbhai of the last Mahant, not on the existence of other Chelas in the wider lineage.
A custom of succession can be established even without multiple historical instances if the circumstances and conduct of the parties confirm its existence and application.
doctrines: Customary succession in religious offices
Doctrine of extinction of spiritual lineage
Legal recognition of unwritten religious customs

card.dispute: The appellants (lessees) challenged the Custodian's notice to cancel their lease of evacuee property, arguing he lacked power under the Act to cancel a lease he himself granted.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian has the power under Section 12(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 to cancel a lease he himself granted.
Whether the non-obstante clause in Section 12(1) limits the Custodian's power to override only statutory bars, not contractual obligations.
holdings: The Custodian has the power under Section 12(1) to cancel a lease he himself granted, as the amendment to the Act deems this power to have always existed.
The power to cancel or amend leases under Section 12(1) is unqualified and absolute; the non-obstante clause does not restrict the Custodian from overriding contractual terms.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 12(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1954, Section 5
doctrines: Doctrine of ex abundanti cautela
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Non-obstante clause interpretation

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the vesting of buildings in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, arguing that the buildings did not form part of the estate and that Section 4(h) was unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether buildings standing on land comprised in a notified estate vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether Section 4(h) of the Act is ultra vires the Constitution for violating the right to realize rent
Whether the use of a building as office or cutchery for rent collection must be determined at the time of notification under Section 3
holdings: Buildings used primarily as office or cutchery for rent collection vested in the State under Section 4(a), even if not used as such at the time of notification, provided they were so used before a post-1946 transfer.
Section 4(h) is not ultra vires the Constitution as it forms part of a valid acquisition law and is protected under Article 31-A, despite restricting transfer rights.
The word 'used' in Section 4(a) must be read with Section 4(h), meaning the relevant time for determining use is before a transfer after January 1, 1946, not at the date of notification.
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Doctrine of reading provisions together (Section 4(a) and 4(h))
Protection of agrarian reform laws under Article 31-A
Test of vires of a law affecting fundamental rights in context of acquisition

card.dispute: Jagirdars of Marwar challenged the constitutional validity of provisions in the Marwar Land Revenue Act that fixed fair and equitable rents, claiming infringement of their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31(2) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the application of the Act only to Marwar jagirdars violates the right to equality under Article 14?
Whether the fixation of rent based on decennial average with exclusion of abnormal years infringes the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f)?
Whether retrospective enforcement of rent rates under Section 86 amounts to acquisition of property without compensation under Article 31(2)?
Whether the power given to the Settlement Officer under Section 86 is arbitrary and uncontrolled, thus violating Article 19(1)(f)?
holdings: A law applying to a part of the state for administrative convenience does not violate Article 14 if the classification is reasonable and based on practical considerations.
Legislation fixing fair and reasonable rent, even retrospectively, does not infringe the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f) as the right includes only the right to recover reasonable rent.
Regulating landlord-tenant relations and fixing rent, even with retrospective effect, is not acquisition of property under Article 31(2) and does not require compensation.
Power conferred on the Settlement Officer to apply rent rates retrospectively is not arbitrary if exercised for recorded reasons and subject to revision by the Board of Revenue.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Regulatory laws saved under Article 19(5)
Distinction between regulation of property rights and acquisition under Article 31
Non-arbitrariness of administrative discretion when guided by reason and subject to review

card.dispute: The State of Bombay fought Mulji Jetha & Co. over whether the company needed fresh permission to alter buildings on land previously approved for non-agricultural use, claiming prior conditions limited construction to approved plans.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector's permission to divert agricultural land to non-agricultural use could be subject to conditions under Section 67 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879
Whether any such conditions could be validly imposed by the Collector alone without an agreement with the Government
Whether the correspondence between the Collector and the occupant could create binding conditions on land use
holdings: Permission to divert land to non-agricultural use under Section 67 could be subject to conditions, but only if agreed upon between the Government and the registered occupant.
The Collector, being distinct from the Government, could not unilaterally impose binding conditions under Section 67 without express authority from the Government.
Conditions alleged based on correspondence between the Collector and the occupant were invalid as there was no agreement with the Government as required by law.
doctrines: Doctrine of Delegated Authority
Doctrine of Strict Interpretation of Governmental Powers
Principle of Privity of Contract in Revenue Grants

card.dispute: Sadhu Ram challenged the refusal of confirmation of his purchase of evacuee agricultural land by the Custodian-General, claiming it violated his fundamental rights under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the retrospective operation of Section 5-A of the East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act amounts to deprivation of property under Article 31 of the Constitution.
Whether the requirement of confirmation of transactions in evacuee property constitutes a reasonable restriction under Article 19.
Whether the refusal of confirmation by the Custodian based on a policy circular raises a question of violation of fundamental rights justifying relief under Article 32.
holdings: Section 5-A, though retrospective, does not amount to deprivation of property but imposes a restriction, and is valid under the Constitution.

The requirement of confirmation for transfers of evacuee property is a reasonable restriction in the interest of public order and state policy, falling under Article 19, not a deprivation under Article 31.

The refusal of confirmation by the Custodian, even if based on irrelevant material or policy, does not violate fundamental rights and cannot be challenged under Article 32 unless the law itself is unconstitutional.
provisions: East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, Section 5-A
doctrines: Reasonable restriction under Article 19
Distinction between deprivation and regulation of property under Article 31
Non-justiciability of quasi-judicial administrative decisions under Article 32 unless fundamental rights are directly infringed

card.dispute: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee sued for possession of a gurdwara property, but the respondents argued the suit was barred by limitation under the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was filed within the one-year limitation period under Section 25-A of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, from the date of the decision or the date of constitution of the Committee, whichever was later.
Whether the date of notification under Section 17 of the Act could be deemed as the date of constitution of the Committee for the purposes of limitation under Section 25-A.
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation because it was filed more than one year after the High Court's decision on June 16, 1936, and the Committee was already constituted before 1930.

The date of notification under Section 17 of the Act cannot be treated as the date of constitution of the Committee; for Committees under Section 85, the date of publication of notification under Section 88(2) is the deemed date of constitution.
doctrines: Deeming provision
Statutory interpretation
Limitation of suit

card.dispute: The Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee appealed against a High Court order that allowed a suit by Raja Shiv Rattan Dev Singh seeking declaration of ownership over a house and shops in Amritsar, claiming they were his private property and not a Sikh Gurdwara.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's order remanding the suit amounted to a final order under Article 133 of the Constitution, making it appealable to the Supreme Court.
Whether the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was barred by Sections 29, 30, or 31 of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, in a suit over property claimed as a private residence and not a Gurdwara.
Whether the High Court erred in making conclusive findings on the merits while remanding the case, thereby prejudging the suit.
holdings: An order remanding a case can be a final order under Article 133 if it finally decides the rights of the parties, even if a formal decree follows later.

The Civil Court retains jurisdiction over suits involving property claimed as private, where no valid claim under the Sikh Gurdwaras Act arises and the Tribunal cannot decide the status of the institution.
A High Court should not make conclusive findings on the merits when remanding a case, as this preempts the trial court’s role; such findings are vacated if they effectively decide the suit.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Sections 109 and 110, Order 45, Rule 2
Sikh Gurdwaras Act, 1925, Section 3(2), Section 7(1), Section 10, Section 16, Section 29(2), Section 30, Section 31(2), Section 37
doctrines: Finality of orders for appealability under Article 133
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction only by clear statutory language
Limited stay versus ouster of jurisdiction
Principle against premature adjudication of merits on remand

card.dispute: The Collector of Bombay sought to levy land revenue assessments on former 'Foras' lands, while the respondents claimed the lands were revenue-free after acquisition and sale by the government.
issues_decided: Whether the occupants of Foras lands acquired a right to hold them subject only to a fixed assessment under the Foras Land Act of 1851.
Whether the Government's right to levy assessment was extinguished when it acquired the lands under the Land Acquisition Act of 1857.
Whether an absolute sale by the Crown necessarily conveys the land free of revenue liability.
Whether the Foras tenure and its incidents revived in favor of the purchasers after the government sold the acquired lands.
holdings: Under the Foras Land Act of 1851, occupants acquired a right to hold the land subject only to the payment of a fixed assessment then payable.
The Government's right to levy assessment was not extinguished by land acquisition; only the occupants' rights were terminated, and the land vested absolutely in the Government.
An absolute sale by the Crown does not automatically convey the land revenue-free; the terms of the deed determine the rights conveyed.
The Foras tenure and its incidents were extinguished upon acquisition and could not revive upon subsequent sale; the purchasers took the land as freehold, not under Foras tenure.
provisions: Foras Land Act (Bombay Act VI of 1851), Section 2
Land Acquisition Act (Act VI of 1857), Section 8
Bombay City Land Revenue Act (Bombay Act II of 1876)
doctrines: Extinguishment of tenure by acquisition
Construction of Crown grants based on documentary intention
No revival of extinguished tenures post-acquisition
Incidents of tenure do not survive statutory repeal and acquisition

card.dispute: The State of Madras and a respondent inamdar disputed whether a post-settlement darmila minor inam, constituting a part of a village within a zamindari, vested in the State under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, and whether the inamdar was entitled to compensation.
issues_decided: Whether a part of a village held under a post-settlement darmila minor inam constitutes an 'estate' under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, and vests in the State under Section 3(b) when the estate is notified under Section 1(4)
Whether a holder of a darmila minor inam is entitled to compensation under the Act
Whether a post-settlement minor inam falls within the protection of Section 20 of the Act, which preserves certain rights in land created by landholders
holdings: A part of a village held under a post-settlement darmila minor inam retains its character as part of the estate and vests in the State under Section 3(b) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, when the estate is notified under Section 1(4).

The holder of a darmila minor inam is entitled to claim a share in the compensation awarded for the estate under Section 44 of the Act, as their interest is transferred to the Government under Section 3(b).

Section 20 of the Act does not protect darmila minor inams because they confer ownership of a part of the estate, which falls under Section 3(b), not under Section 3(c) which governs non-ownership rights like leases.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 1(3), Section 1(4), Section 3(b), Section 3(c), Section 20, Section 25, Section 27, Section 37, Section 44, Section 45
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to effectuate legislative purpose
Mutual exclusivity of ownership and non-ownership rights under land reform statutes
Presumption against statutory interpretation frustrating legislative intent

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the citizenship of Kumar Rani, who migrated to Pakistan in 1948, and the validity of declaring a wakf estate as evacuee property under Bihar and central laws.
issues_decided: Whether Kumar Rani, having migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, could be considered a citizen of India under Article 5 of the Constitution despite her husband remaining in India
Whether the proviso to Article 7 applies where a permit for return to India was issued but later cancelled as unauthorized
Whether the interest of an evacuee in property held as trustee or beneficiary, including wakf property, falls within the definition of 'evacuee property' under the relevant ordinances and acts
holdings: Article 7 of the Constitution overrides Article 5; a person who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 is not a citizen unless they returned under a valid permit for resettlement.
The proviso to Article 7 does not apply when the return permit was issued without required state consent and was properly cancelled, rendering it invalid ab initio.

The definition of 'evacuee property' in the Bihar Ordinance, Central Ordinance, and Central Act includes property held by an evacuee as trustee or beneficiary, and applies to wakf property and interests therein.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 (XXVII of 1949), Section 8(2)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (Act XXXI of 1950), Section 8(2)
Bihar Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, Section 5
Permit System Rules, 1949, Rule 10 and Rule 29
doctrines: Lex specialis derogat legi generali (specific law overrides general law)
Deemed vesting of property under successor legislation
Strict interpretation of constitutional citizenship provisions in post-partition context

card.dispute: The State of Bombay requisitioned premises to house a foreign consulate staff member; the owner challenged it, claiming it was not a 'public purpose' under state powers.
issues_decided: Whether the requisition of property for housing a foreign consulate staff member constitutes a 'public purpose' under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948.
Whether the State of Bombay had legislative competence to make such a requisition for a Union purpose.
Whether the phrase 'any other public purpose' in Section 6(4)(a) should be read ejusdem generis with 'purpose of the State'.
holdings: The requisition for housing a foreign consulate staff member was for a 'public purpose' within the meaning of the Act.
The State of Bombay has the power to requisition property for purposes other than Union purposes under Item 36 of the State List, including general public purposes.
The phrase 'any other public purpose' is not restricted to 'State purpose' and must be given independent meaning to avoid rendering it surplusage.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Item 33
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Item 36
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List III, Item 42
doctrines: Ejusdem generis
Avoidance of surplusage in statutory interpretation
Legislative competence under federal structure
Multiple facets of public purpose

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether certain lands originally held as Watan lands retained their Watan character after the government dispensed with the associated services and levied full assessment, later describing the lands as Japti Sanadi Inam lands.
issues_decided: Whether lands originally held as Watan lands retained their Watan character after the government dispensed with the services and levied full assessment.
Whether the description of lands as 'Japti Sanadi Inam' implies a change in tenure from Watan to ryotwari.
Whether the government has the power to lawfully resume Watan lands and extinguish their Watan character.
holdings: Lands that were originally Watan lose their Watan character when the services are dispensed with, full assessment is levied, and the lands are described as Japti Sanadi Inam, becoming ryotwari holdings.
The term 'Japti Sanadi Inam' signifies that the land was once granted by sanad, was resumed by government, and is now held as a ryotwari occupancy.
The government has the power to resume Watan lands and extinguish their Watan character, especially when the hereditary office and its duties no longer exist.
doctrines: Doctrine of resumption of Watan lands
Doctrine of change in land tenure upon commutation of service
Principle of governmental power to revoke grants tied to abolished offices

card.dispute: Dharman appealed his conviction for murder, arguing that the killing occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation and thus should not attract a murder charge.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's act fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, reducing the offence from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder
Whether the defence of Exception 4 can be considered when not specifically raised in the lower courts
Which part of Section 304 IPC applies based on the appellant's intention
holdings: The killing occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation and in the heat of passion, falling within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, thereby reducing the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Even if Exception 4 was not raised in the lower courts, the Supreme Court can consider it when determining the true nature of the offence based on the proved facts and findings.
The appellant intended to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, so the offence falls under Part I of Section 304 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Exception 4 to Section 300
doctrines: Sudden fight exception under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC
Court's power to determine the true nature of the offence as a question of law

card.dispute: The company challenged whether agarias (salt producers) were workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act or independent contractors.
issues_decided: Whether the agarias fall within the definition of 'workman' under Section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Whether the supervision and control exercised by the company indicates an employer-employee relationship.
Whether payment by piece-work and the right to hire assistants make the agarias independent contractors.
holdings: A person remains a workman even if paid by the job rather than by time, provided the employer exercises control over the work.
Engaging assistants and paying them does not make a worker an independent contractor if they personally perform the work.
The degree of supervision and control by the company over the method and quality of salt production supports the conclusion that agarias are workmen.
The nature of seasonal work and operational difficulties do not override the legal test for determining workman status.
doctrines: Control test for determining employer-employee relationship
Distinction between workman and independent contractor
Personal service as the key criterion for workman status

card.dispute: The Government of Bihar and Nagendra Narain Singh fought Ram Bharosa Singh over the legality of extending a ferry lease without a public auction under the Bengal Ferries Act, 1885.
issues_decided: Whether the District Magistrate had the power to extend the term of an existing lease without holding a public auction.
Whether the withdrawal of tolls from public auction and extension of lease was lawful under the Bengal Ferries Act, 1885 and its rules.
holdings: The District Magistrate has no power, express or implied, to extend the term of a lease beyond its original period; such an extension must be preceded by a fresh public auction.
The requirement of public auction under Section 9 and Rule 2 of the Bengal Ferries Act is a statutory safeguard against arbitrary executive action and cannot be bypassed.
doctrines: Rule of law
Statutory interpretation
Prevention of arbitrary executive action

card.dispute: The Raja of Gouripur and another landowner challenged the constitutional validity of the Assam State Acquisition of Zamindaries Act, 1951 (as amended), which acquired their estates without what they claimed was adequate compensation, alleging violations of fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam State Acquisition of Zamindaries Act, 1951, as amended, is protected under Article 31-A of the Constitution and thus immune from challenges based on fundamental rights under Part III, including Article 14
Whether the Act constitutes colourable legislation or suffers from vagueness in specifying compensation
Whether the Act discriminates between zamindars in violation of Article 14
holdings: The Act is a law for the acquisition of estates under Article 31-A, and therefore its constitutional validity cannot be challenged on grounds of contravention of fundamental rights in Part III, including Article 14.
The doctrine of colourable legislation does not apply as there is no legislative incompetence, and any challenge to quantum of compensation is barred by Article 31-A.
The classification of estates, including differential treatment of Lakheraj estates and compensation scales, has a rational basis and does not violate Article 14.
provisions: Assam State Acquisition of Zamindaries Act, 1951 (Assam Act XVIII of 1951)
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886 (Reg. 1 of 1886)
doctrines: Protection under Article 31-A against fundamental rights challenges
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Principle of reasonable classification under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant, Raja Rajinder Chand, claimed ownership of chil (pine) trees on lands within his Jagir but belonging to private landlords (adna-maliks), who contested that they retained rights over trees on their proprietary lands.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim ownership of chil trees as a successor to the sovereign rights of the pre-conquest Kangra rulers
Whether the 1848 Sanad granted by the British conferred ownership of chil trees on the Jagirdar
Whether entries in the Wajib-ul-arz created or evidenced a valid grant of tree rights in favor of the Jagirdar
Whether the statutory presumption under Section 44 of the Punjab Land-Revenue Act, 1887, was sufficient to establish the appellant's claim
holdings: The sovereign right to chil trees held by the independent Kangra rulers passed to the Sikh and then British conquerors; the Jagirdar, as a mere revenue assignee, did not inherit such sovereign rights.
The 1848 Sanad did not expressly or impliedly transfer ownership of chil trees to the Jagirdar and must be construed narrowly as a revenue grant, not a conveyance of proprietary rights.
Entries in the Wajib-ul-arz do not create title and cannot, without clear evidence, be construed as evidencing a surrender of sovereign rights in favor of the Jagirdar.

The statutory presumption under Section 44 of the Punjab Land-Revenue Act is rebuttable and was displaced by the lack of unambiguous documentary or historical evidence supporting the appellant’s claim.
doctrines: Doctrine of conquest and transfer of sovereign rights
Principle of strict construction of grants by the Crown
Presumption under revenue records and its limitations
Wajib-ul-arz as evidence of custom, not title

card.dispute: The appellant, Rajes Kanta Roy, challenged the execution of a decree against his interest in properties held under a trust deed, arguing that his interest was contingent and not attachable.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's interest in the trust properties was vested or contingent
Whether the interest in property No. 44/2, Lansdowne Road was subject to an additional contingency requiring purchase of alternative accommodation
Whether the compromise decree created an executable charge allowing attachment of the interest
holdings: The appellant had a vested interest in the trust properties, though enjoyment was restricted until the settlor's debts were discharged and obligations fulfilled.
The interest in property No. 44/2, Lansdowne Road was also vested, with only enjoyment restricted by the right of residence of the brother and his heirs until alternative accommodation was provided.
A compromise decree creating a charge on a vested interest, even with restricted enjoyment, allows execution and attachment of that interest.
doctrines: Vested interest vs contingent interest
Restriction on enjoyment does not negate vesting
Principle of representation under Dayabhaga school of Hindu Law

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted based on a jury's majority verdict, but the trial judge disagreed; the dispute was whether the High Court could uphold the conviction without reviewing the entire evidence as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can uphold a jury's majority verdict without considering the entire evidence in a reference under Section 307(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure?
Whether the High Court must independently evaluate the evidence and give due weight to both the jury's verdict and the trial judge's opinion?
Whether the Supreme Court should itself review the evidence when the High Court has failed to do so under Section 307(3)?
holdings: The High Court must consider the entire evidence and the charge before acquitting or convicting an accused in a reference under Section 307(3); it cannot rely solely on limited arguments.
The High Court must give due weight to the opinions of both the jury and the trial judge, and determine whether the verdict could reasonably be supported by the evidence.
The Supreme Court should not itself evaluate the evidence in place of the High Court but must remand the case for proper application of Section 307(3).
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898), as amended by Act XXVI of 1955, Section 307
doctrines: Duty of High Court to consider entire evidence in jury references
Principle of due weight to jury and trial judge opinions
Remand instead of appellate fact-finding by Supreme Court

card.dispute: The petitioners, heads of Hindu religious mathas, challenged the constitutional validity of provisions in the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952 as amended in 1954, which revived earlier schemes for managing mathas that had been invalidated in prior litigation.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 42(1)(b), 42(7), and 44(2) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952 as amended in 1954 impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
Whether Section 79-A of the 1952 Act, which deems previously invalidated schemes as validly framed under the new Act, is constitutionally valid
Whether the impugned provisions infringe the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32
holdings: Sections 42(1)(b), 42(7), and 44(2) do not impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) as they provide sufficient procedural safeguards, including judicial oversight and appeal to the High Court.

Section 79-A is valid as it does not override judicial decisions but deems past schemes to be framed under the new Act, reopening them to challenge under current law and avoiding public inconvenience.

The provisions do not infringe Article 32 jurisdiction, as the right to move the Supreme Court remains intact; any nullification of prior orders results from valid legislative action removing unconstitutionality, not from curtailment of judicial power.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952 (Orissa Act II of 1952), Sections 42(1)(b), 42(7), 44(2), and 79-A
Orissa Act XVIII of 1954 (amending the 1952 Act)
doctrines: Doctrine of Deeming Fiction
Unreasonable Restriction under Article 19(1)(f)
Legislative Competence to Validate Past Actions
Separation of Powers and Judicial Review

card.dispute: The adopted son of a deceased man sued to recover property, claiming a trust was created over funds meant for him and that the second adoption was invalid, while the estate's beneficiaries resisted both claims.
issues_decided: Whether a trust was created over Rs. 75,000 payable to the minor under the Rajinama and whether the deceased was a co-trustee
Whether the second adoption was valid, entitling the second adopted son to inherit under the will
holdings: No trust was created in favor of the minor that made the deceased a co-trustee, as there was no clear and conclusive evidence of transfer of ownership or acceptance of trustee obligations.
The second adoption was valid under the special custom of the Nattukottai Chetti community, and the will duly passed the residue of the estate to the second adopted son.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 11
doctrines: Clear and conclusive evidence required to establish a trust
Recognition of special customs in Hindu adoption
Co-trustee liability requires knowledge or negligence in breach by co-trustee

card.dispute: Displaced persons challenged the cancellation of their quasi-permanent allotment of evacuee agricultural land, claiming violation of their fundamental right to property.
issues_decided: Whether a quasi-permanent allotment of evacuee land constitutes 'property' under Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1), and 31(2) of the Constitution?
Whether the cancellation of such allotment without notice violates the petitioners' fundamental rights?
Whether the interest of a quasi-permanent allottee is protected under Article 31(1) as 'property'?
holdings: The interest of a quasi-permanent allottee in evacuee land is not 'property' within the meaning of Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) because it lacks transferability and is subject to statutory cancellation.
The cancellation of a quasi-permanent allotment under statutory authority does not amount to deprivation without law under Article 31(1), even if the interest were considered property.
Rights of quasi-permanent allottees, though important for rehabilitation, are statutory and provisional, not fundamental, and do not attract constitutional protection as property.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (Central Act XXXI of 1950), Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 28
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 46
Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 (Punjab Act XVII of 1887)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 (East Punjab Act L of 1948)
doctrines: Bundle of rights theory of property
Provisional nature of statutory rights
Doctrine of fundamental rights not extending to statutory interests
Principle of resumption as an incident of statutory tenure

card.dispute: The Uttar Pradesh Government and the landowner H.S. Gupta disputed the compensation amount for the compulsory acquisition of the Dilkusha Estate, particularly the valuation method and entitlement to interest.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in reducing the land compensation from Rs. 1-2-0 to 0-14-0 per square foot by applying the block-rate principle instead of the plot-rate principle.
Whether the claimant was entitled to interest on the excess compensation amount from 8th July 1948 to 12th May 1949 when payment was withheld due to government-initiated proceedings.
holdings: When land is capable of being developed and sold in smaller plots as per an approved layout, compensation must be based on the plot rate, not the lower block rate, especially where there is demand for such plots.

A claimant is entitled to interest at 6% per annum under the Land Acquisition Act on the excess compensation amount withheld due to government-initiated stay, from the date the amount became payable until it was released.
doctrines: Principle of plot-wise valuation in land acquisition
Compensation based on highest potential use and marketability
Entitlement to interest for delayed payment due to government action

card.dispute: The State of Bombay requisitioned premises for housing an officer of the State Road Transport Corporation, and the owner challenged it, claiming it was not for a public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the requisition of premises for housing an officer of the State Road Transport Corporation served a public purpose under Section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948.
Whether providing living accommodation to employees of a public utility corporation constitutes a public purpose.
Whether the government's determination of public purpose is final or subject to judicial review.
holdings: A requisition for housing an officer of a public utility corporation serves a public purpose if it supports the efficient functioning of the corporation, which the public relies upon.
Providing living accommodation to employees of a State Road Transport Corporation is a statutory activity essential to its public function and thus a public purpose.
While the government is prima facie the best judge of public purpose, courts have the authority to review whether a requisition genuinely serves a public purpose.
provisions: Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950, Section 19(2)(a) and (b)
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine
Judicial review of administrative action
Prima facie validity of government determination on public purpose

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction for murder and rioting, arguing that the unlawful assembly and common object were not properly established and that they were prejudiced by the absence of specific charges.
issues_decided: Whether an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC can be formed without prior concert if a common unlawful object develops during the incident
Whether the appellants could be convicted under Section 302/149 IPC when the common object was beating, not killing
Whether the courts below erred in relying on part of a witness's testimony while rejecting other parts
Whether the appellants suffered prejudice due to the absence of a specific charge regarding liability under Section 149 IPC
holdings: An unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC can form spontaneously when five or more persons develop a common unlawful object, even if they initially assembled for a lawful purpose.
Persons can be held liable for murder under Section 302/149 IPC if death is a likely consequence of the common object (beating) and each member knew such a result was probable.
Courts of fact are entitled to accept part of a witness’s testimony and reject the rest; this Court will not re-evaluate such findings in special leave petitions.
No prejudice was shown from the absence of a specific charge under Section 149 IPC, especially since the objection was raised late and not pleaded as a ground earlier.
doctrines: Common object vs. common intention
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Concurrent findings of fact
Presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The appellants (mortgagors' representatives) sued the respondents (alleged tenants) for possession of land, claiming they were trespassers, while the respondents claimed hereditary tenancy rights under the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939.
issues_decided: Whether the lease created by the mortgagee via the Kabuliat of May 26, 1936, was binding on the mortgagors under Section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the respondents could claim hereditary tenancy rights under Section 29(a) of the U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939, despite the invalidity of the lease
holdings: A lease created by a mortgagee binds the mortgagor only if it is prudent and in the ordinary course of management; the lease here was neither prudent nor bona fide and thus not binding.

A person cannot acquire hereditary tenancy under Section 29(a) of the U.P. Tenancy Act unless lawfully admitted as a tenant by someone with authority; since the mortgagee lacked such authority, the respondents acquired no such rights.
doctrines: Prudent owner test for mortgagee's leasing power
Requirement of lawful admission by a person with authority for tenancy recognition
Non-accrual of hereditary rights in mortgaged sir lands under statutory exceptions

card.dispute: The appellants, displaced persons leasing evacuee salt pans, challenged their eviction after the property was auctioned, claiming protection under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, arguing that no valid transfer had occurred to bar their continued possession.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration of the highest bidder at a public auction amounts to a transfer of property under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954
Whether the appellants were entitled to protection from eviction under Section 29 of the Act in the absence of a completed transfer
holdings: A declaration of the highest bidder at an auction does not amount to a transfer of property; transfer occurs only upon full payment and issuance of a sale certificate by the Managing Officer.

The appellants cannot claim protection under Section 29 of the Act because no transfer of the property had taken place, and thus they were not tenants of the new purchaser entitled to two years' protection from eviction.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 29
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Rule 90
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Rule 121
doctrines: Doctrine of conditional sale in auction
Doctrine of statutory protection against eviction

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction by a Gram Cutcherry under the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, arguing that the Act's provisions on concurrent jurisdiction were discriminatory under Article 14 and that two appellants lacked evidence for conviction.
issues_decided: Whether Section 62 of the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, which grants concurrent criminal jurisdiction to Gram Cutcherry and ordinary criminal courts, is discriminatory under Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the conviction of two appellants, Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh, was legally sustainable in the absence of evidence
holdings: The provisions of the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, including Section 62, are not discriminatory under Article 14, as the scheme of the Act mandates trial by Gram Cutcherry unless jurisdiction is lawfully transferred, ensuring no arbitrary choice of forum.
The conviction of Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh was invalid due to absence of any evidence linking them to the offence, and must be set aside as manifestly erroneous.
doctrines: Equality before law under Article 14
Doctrine of judicial review and superintendence under Article 227
Principle of legality in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of Rule 12 of the Assam Fishery Rules, arguing it was ultra vires and repugnant to Section 16 of the Assam Land Revenue Regulation, 1886, insofar as it allowed the State Government to settle fishery rights otherwise than by sale.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 12 of the Assam Fishery Rules is ultra vires or repugnant to Section 16 of the Assam Land Revenue Regulation, 1886.
Whether the State Government has the power under the Fishery Rules to settle fishery rights otherwise than by sale, including through individual settlements.
holdings: Rule 12 is not ultra vires and does not conflict with Section 16 of the Assam Land Revenue Regulation, 1886, as Section 16 does not prescribe any specific policy or principle for acquiring fishery rights, leaving the matter to the State Government's discretion.

Rule 12 expressly empowers the State Government to settle fishery rights otherwise than by sale, including through individual settlements, as the rule carves out an exception to the general prohibition on non-sale settlements.
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of delegated legislation
Doctrine of repugnancy

card.dispute: The appellant, a mutawalli, challenged his conviction and sentence for failing to prepare and submit a budget for the waqf estate as required by the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether Section 58 of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1947 violates Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution by imposing unreasonable restrictions on the mutawalli's occupation
Whether the sentence of imprisonment in default of payment of fine is legal under the Act
holdings: Section 58 of the Bihar Waqfs Act imposes reasonable restrictions on the mutawalli's duties, as the Majlis's power to alter or modify the budget is subject to the waqif's wishes and the Act's provisions, and does not violate Article 19(1)(g).
Imprisonment in default of fine is valid under Section 33 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with Sections 40 and 67 of the Indian Penal Code, even if the Act does not explicitly provide for it.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g)
Doctrine of severability
Supervision of religious institutions' administration

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction by a Gram Cutcherry for crop theft, arguing the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act was discriminatory and their convictions lacked evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 is discriminatory and violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the conviction of Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh was legally sustainable based on the evidence
holdings: The provisions of the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 are not discriminatory as the jurisdiction of Gram Cutcherries is not arbitrary but subject to judicial control by Sub-Divisional Magistrates or Munsifs.
