The conviction of Ramdeo Singh and Sheodhar Singh was invalid due to absence of any evidence against them, and their sentences were set aside.
doctrines: Rule of law and non-discrimination under Article 14
Principle of judicial review under Article 227
Requirement of legal evidence for conviction

card.dispute: The appellant Inayat Ullah challenged the Custodian's notice declaring his deceased brother's property as evacuee property and the refusal to provide copies of materials used to issue the notice.
issues_decided: Whether the notice issued under Section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 was illegal
Whether the Custodian must have sufficient material to justify issuing a notice under Section 7
Whether the High Court should have examined the Custodian's record to assess the bona fides of the notice
Whether the appellant was entitled to copies of materials used by the Custodian prior to issuing the notice
holdings: The notice issued under Section 7 was valid as it complied with the prescribed form and stated grounds for treating the property as evacuee property.
The Custodian is entitled to form an opinion based on information in his possession; courts cannot assess the adequacy of such information at the notice stage.
The High Court was not required to examine the Custodian’s record to verify bona fides, as no evidence of malafide was presented.
The appellant was not entitled to copies of materials prior to the notice, as proceedings under Section 7 commence only after the notice is issued.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 45
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 49
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 56
Code of Criminal Procedure, Sections 480 and 482
doctrines: Separation of administrative and judicial stages in quasi-judicial proceedings
Presumption of validity of administrative action in absence of malafide
Entitlement to documents only after commencement of formal proceedings

card.dispute: Tenants evicted by the Raja of Khandapara challenged the eviction under tenancy protection laws, while the Raja claimed immunity based on merger agreement guarantees and constitutional jurisdictional bars.
issues_decided: Whether the application of the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948 to the Raja's private properties violated the guarantee of full ownership under the Merger Agreement
Whether Article 363 of the Constitution barred judicial inquiry into disputes arising from the Merger Agreement
Whether the Raja was a 'landlord' and the evictees were 'tenants' within the meaning of the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948 as extended by the Orissa Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950
Whether the revenue courts had jurisdiction to decide tenant restoration proceedings in the merged state of Khandapara
holdings: The extension of tenancy protection laws to the Raja's private properties does not violate the guarantee of full ownership, use, and enjoyment under the Merger Agreement, as the guarantee preserves property status but does not exempt it from generally applicable laws.
Article 363 does not bar judicial review when the dispute involves the application of ordinary laws to private property, rather than enforcement of rights under the Merger Agreement itself.

The statutory definitions of 'landlord' and 'tenant' under Section 7(a) of the Orissa Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950 apply, making the Raja a landlord and the cultivators tenants, regardless of prior definitions or customs.

Revenue courts have jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes in merged areas when both the 1948 and 1950 Acts are read together, as the latter supplements the former without creating a lacuna in procedure or authority.
provisions: Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948, Sections 2(a) and (g)
Orissa Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950, Sections 7(a) and (h)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation: harmonious reading of related statutes
Doctrine of merger of princely states and continuation of private property rights
Judicial review under Article 363: distinction between treaty-based disputes and ordinary legal claims
Statutory extension of legal definitions to ensure social welfare legislation applies uniformly

card.dispute: The appellant thika tenant resisted execution of a decree for ejectment, claiming the civil court lacked jurisdiction under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether section 5(1) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 bars civil courts from entertaining execution applications for ejectment decrees against thika tenants
Whether the deletion of section 28 of the Act affected the jurisdiction of civil courts in execution proceedings
holdings: Section 5(1) applies only to original ejectment applications before the Controller, not to execution of decrees; civil courts retain jurisdiction to execute such decrees.
The deletion of section 28 and amendments by the 1953 Act indicate legislative intent to limit protection for judgment-debtor tenants, not to transfer execution jurisdiction to the Controller.
provisions: Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 (West Bengal Act II of 1949), Section 5(1)
Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953 (West Bengal Act VI of 1953), Section 9
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Beneficent construction of welfare legislation
Heydon's rule (mischief rule)

card.dispute: The petitioner, Lilavati Bai, challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Land Requisition Act and the enforceability of a requisition order made by the Government, claiming she was in possession as the widow of the tenant, while the Government claimed the premises had become vacant before the tenant's death.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, as amended, is constitutionally valid under Articles 31(2) and 31(3) of the Constitution.
Whether the Government's declaration of vacancy under Sections 5 and 6 of the Act is binding and not subject to judicial review.
Whether the words 'or otherwise' in Explanation (a) to Section 6 should be interpreted ejusdem generis with preceding terms.
Whether the requisition order was unenforceable as it was issued after the death of the named tenant.
holdings: The Act does not violate Article 31(2) and remains valid; the amending Acts do not require Presidential assent under Article 31(3) as they do not amend the acquisition law itself.
The Government's finding of vacancy under Sections 5 and 6 is conclusive and cannot be reopened by courts, though the court retains jurisdiction to examine procedural compliance.
The words 'or otherwise' in Explanation (a) to Section 6 are expansive, not restrictive, and are not limited by ejusdem generis to the preceding terms.
An order under Section 6(4)(a) remains enforceable even if one of the named persons is dead; service by affixing the order to the premises is valid when actual notice is received.
provisions: Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 (Act XXXIII of 1948), Sections 5, 6, 6 Explanation (a), 13
doctrines: Conclusive proof by legislative declaration
ejusdem generis rule of statutory interpretation
jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226 and Supreme Court under Article 32
enforceability of administrative orders despite procedural irregularities

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for failing to remove a compound wall encroaching on municipal land, arguing that the notice was issued under the wrong section of the Municipal Act.
issues_decided: Whether a conviction can be altered from one section to another when the notice was issued under a wrong section
Whether a requisition is 'lawfully made' under s. 488(1)(c) if the notice cites an incorrect section
Whether the appellant suffered substantial prejudice due to the mislabeling of the notice
holdings: A conviction can be altered to a more appropriate section if the facts and substance of the accusation remain unchanged, even without a formal charge under that section.

A requisition is 'lawfully made' under s. 488(1)(c) if the substance of the notice clearly communicates the requirement to remove an encroachment, regardless of the incorrect section cited in the heading.
No substantial prejudice occurs if the accused understood the nature of the accusation and was not deprived of a fair opportunity to defend, even if the notice cited the wrong section.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, Sections 236 and 237
doctrines: Substance over form
Conviction for an offence not formally charged if established by evidence
No prejudice from technical irregularities in absence of trial unfairness

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of his conviction and death sentence on the ground that the police and magistrate failed to provide him with copies of documents as required under Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether the omission by the police officer to furnish copies of documents to the accused under Section 173(4) of the CrPC renders the trial void?
Whether the failure of the inquiring magistrate to ensure compliance with Section 207A(3) of the CrPC invalidates the commitment and trial?
Whether the word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the CrPC is mandatory or directory?
holdings: The word 'shall' in Sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the CrPC is directory, not mandatory, and non-compliance does not automatically invalidate proceedings.
An omission to provide documents under these sections is a curable irregularity under Section 537 of the CrPC if it does not prejudice the accused's defence.
Magistrates must ensure accused persons are not handicapped in their defence, but failure to do so is not fatal unless actual prejudice is shown.
Where no prejudice is demonstrated, such procedural lapses do not vitiate the commitment or trial.
doctrines: Directory vs Mandatory interpretation
Curability of procedural irregularities
Prejudice test for procedural violations
Substantial compliance doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a suit for possession under Order XXI, Rule 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the plaintiff's application to amend the plaint to include further particulars of title was barred by limitation and caused prejudice.
issues_decided: Whether the application to amend the plaint should be allowed despite the expiry of the limitation period for a fresh suit on the amended claim.
Whether the amendment introduced a new cause of action or altered the nature of the relief sought.
Whether the defendant would suffer injustice that could not be compensated by costs if the amendment was allowed.
holdings: Courts have discretion to allow amendments even when a fresh suit would be barred by limitation, provided it serves the interests of justice.
An amendment that supplies missing particulars without changing the nature of the relief sought does not constitute a new cause of action.
Amendments should be refused only if they cause irreparable prejudice to the defendant that cannot be compensated by costs.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 97, 99, 103
doctrines: Discretionary power to amend pleadings
Interest of justice over technical limitation
No amendment if it causes irremediable prejudice

card.dispute: The appellants, refugees from Rawalpindi, challenged the cancellation of their land allotment in Ratauli village, arguing it was done contrary to departmental rules and principles of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the Deputy Custodian General's order cancelling the appellants' land allotment contained an error apparent on the face of the record justifying certiorari.
Whether the cancellation order violated principles of natural justice or was based on a misinterpretation of departmental rules.
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to issue a writ of certiorari against the allotment decision affecting the appellants' rights.
holdings: A writ of certiorari lies only for an error of law apparent on the face of the record, not for mere errors of fact or law that require argument to establish.
Departmental manuals do not have the force of law, and deviations from them do not amount to a legal error justifying certiorari if the authority had discretionary power.
The order cancelling the allotment did not show a manifest legal error or disregard of law, and the exercise of discretion by rehabilitation authorities is not subject to interference via certiorari.
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Principles of natural justice
Supervisory jurisdiction in certiorari
Distinction between jurisdictional error and mere error of law

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the validity of the Rajasthan (Protection of Tenants) Ordinance, 1949, which imposed restrictions on ejecting tenants and allowed extensions of its operation by the Rajpramukh.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the Ordinance constituted unconstitutional delegated legislation by empowering the Rajpramukh to extend its duration.
Whether the notification extending the Ordinance in 1953 was invalid after the state legislature was constituted in 1952.
Whether the Ordinance violated Article 14 by creating arbitrary classifications and granting unguided exemption powers under Section 15.
Whether the Ordinance violated Article 19(1)(f) by infringing the right to property by obliging landlords to retain tenants.
holdings: Empowering an authority to extend the operation of a complete law based on continuing circumstances is conditional legislation, not unconstitutional delegation.
A notification under Section 3 is not independent legislation but an exercise of statutory power, which survives the cessation of the Rajpramukh's legislative authority.
Section 15 is not void under Article 14 as the preamble provides sufficient policy guidance, and if invalid, it is severable from the rest of the Ordinance.
The Ordinance does not violate Article 19(1)(f) as it is a reasonable, temporary, emergency measure to protect tenants and ensure agricultural stability.
doctrines: Conditional legislation
Delegated legislation
Severability
Reasonableness of restrictions on fundamental rights
Presumption of constitutionality

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Madras High Court's order requiring him to pay court fees based on a valuation of Rs. 15,00,000 for jurisdiction, instead of allowing him to value his claim at Rs. 50,000 for court fee purposes in a suit for partition of joint family property.
issues_decided: Whether the valuation stated in the plaint for jurisdiction determines the valuation for court fees in suits under Section 7(IV)(b) of the Court-Fees Act
Whether the plaintiff must be allowed to specify the value of his claim for court fee purposes if it was omitted initially
Whether the Division Bench was correct in using the jurisdictional valuation for computing court fees
holdings: In suits under Section 7(IV)(b) of the Court-Fees Act, the plaintiff's valuation for court fees determines the value for jurisdiction, not the other way around.
If a plaintiff omits to specify the value of the claim for court fees, the court should ordinarily allow amendment to include such valuation.
The Madras High Court erred in treating the jurisdictional valuation as binding for court fee computation; the appellant was entitled to value his claim at Rs. 50,000 for court fees.
provisions: Madras High Court Fees Rules, 1933, Order 11, Rule 1
doctrines: Primacy of plaintiff's valuation in ad valorem suits under Section 7(IV)(b)
Harmonious construction of Court-Fees Act and Suits Valuation Act
Liberty to amend plaint to specify court fee valuation

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be borrowers, sought relief under the Bengal Money Lenders Act, arguing they were being made to pay more than twice the principal amount in respect of a loan, while the respondents contended the obligation was unpaid purchase money, not a loan.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants qualify as 'borrowers' under the Bengal Money Lenders Act (Bengal Act 10 of 1940).
Whether the unpaid purchase money under a compromise decree amounts to a 'loan' within the meaning of the Act.
holdings: The appellants are not 'borrowers' under the Bengal Money Lenders Act because the obligation arises from unpaid purchase money, not a loan.

An agreement to pay outstanding purchase money in instalments with interest does not, by itself, convert the transaction into a loan; the substance must show an intention to create a lending arrangement.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Unpaid vendor's charge under transfer law

card.dispute: The appellant, a debtor, challenged the constitutional validity of a provision excluding debts owed to scheduled banks from debt relief under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Debt Reduction Act, 1953, arguing it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the question of constitutional validity of a statutory provision falls within the proviso to Section 113 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 228 of the Constitution.
Whether it was necessary to decide the constitutional validity of the impugned provision before addressing severability.
Whether the courts below erred in refusing to refer the constitutional question for determination.
holdings: A question challenging the constitutional validity of a statutory provision is both a question of law under the proviso to Section 113 CPC and a substantial question of constitutional interpretation under Article 228.
The question of severability arises only after a finding that the provision is constitutionally invalid; thus, validity must be decided first.
It is necessary to decide the constitutional validity of a provision to dispose of a case, even if the relief sought may ultimately be unavailable due to non-severability.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Debt Reduction Act, 1953, Section 2(d) (definition of 'debt')
doctrines: Severability doctrine
Principle of constitutional interpretation
Substantial question of law under Article 228

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted based on a jury verdict for offences under Sections 435 and 436 IPC, but the Assistant Sessions Judge disagreed and referred the case to the High Court, which accepted the verdict without reviewing the entire evidence, leading to a challenge on procedural grounds.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court acted in violation of Section 307(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure by failing to consider the entire evidence before accepting the jury's verdict.
Whether the High Court's conviction of the appellants without independently evaluating the evidence was legally sustainable.
holdings: The High Court must consider the entire evidence and give due weight to the opinions of both the Sessions Judge and the jury before accepting or rejecting a jury verdict in a reference under Section 307(3) CrPC.
If the High Court does not evaluate the full evidence, its acceptance of a jury verdict violates Section 307(3) CrPC and cannot stand, even if the verdict appears plausible.
doctrines: Proper appellate review in jury trial references
Due weight to findings of fact by jury and trial judge
Ends of justice standard in setting aside jury verdicts

card.dispute: Sohanlal and the Union of India contested with Jagan Nath over the possession of a rehabilitated refugee house in West Patel Nagar, Delhi, after Jagan Nath was evicted and Sohanlal was allotted the property.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition under Article 226 is maintainable for declaring title to immovable property and directing restoration of possession.
Whether a writ of mandamus can be issued against a private individual (Sohanlal) who is in possession of property allegedly illegally allotted after another person's eviction.
Whether Jagan Nath had acquired a legal right to the property entitling him to restoration of possession through a writ.
holdings: A writ petition under Article 226 is not an appropriate remedy where the decision requires determination of title and would effectively amount to a civil decree.
A writ of mandamus cannot be issued against a private individual not colluding with the state, especially when they are in lawful possession under a government allotment.
Illegal eviction does not automatically entitle a person to restoration of possession via writ if the property is now held by a third party without collusion and the title is disputed.
doctrines: Separation of remedies: writ jurisdiction vs. civil suit for title disputes
Mandamus against private individuals
Bona fide possession under government allotment

card.dispute: The trustees of a Hindu temple fought with the State of Mysore over whether a denominational temple could restrict public entry during certain religious ceremonies under the Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act.
issues_decided: Whether Article 26(b) of the Constitution, protecting a religious denomination's right to manage its religious affairs, is subject to Article 25(2)(b), which allows public access to Hindu temples for worship.
Whether the right to exclude the general public during specific religious ceremonies in a denominational temple is protected under Article 26(b).
Whether the modifications in the High Court decree reserving certain ceremonies exclusively for members of the Gowda Saraswath Brahmin community are constitutionally valid.
holdings: Article 26(b) must be read subject to Article 25(2)(b); the right of the public to enter Hindu temples for worship prevails over denominational rights to total exclusion.
Denominational rights under Article 26(b) are protected when limited to specific religious ceremonies, provided the public’s right to worship remains substantial.
The High Court’s decree allowing exclusion during certain ceremonies strikes a fair balance between public access and denominational rights and is constitutionally valid.
provisions: Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act (V of 1947), Section 2(2)
Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act (V of 1947), Section 3
doctrines: Rule of harmonious construction
Denominational rights under Article 26(b)
Public right to temple entry under Article 25(2)(b)

card.dispute: Sohan Lal (Jagan Nath) and the Union of India disputed the allotment and possession of a government house, with Sohan Lal claiming illegal eviction and the Union arguing ineligibility, while Sohan Lal sought restoration of possession via a writ petition against both the Union and a private allottee, S.
issues_decided: Whether a writ of mandamus under Article 226 is maintainable when there is a serious dispute of fact and title to property?
Whether a writ of mandamus can be issued against a private individual who has taken possession of property without collusion or knowledge of illegal eviction?
Whether the High Court could declare title and order restoration of possession in a writ petition where a civil suit would be a more appropriate remedy?
holdings: A writ of mandamus under Article 226 is not appropriate when the decision requires resolving disputed questions of fact or determining title to property; such matters must be decided in a civil suit.
A writ of mandamus does not normally lie against a private individual, especially one who has taken possession bona fide and without collusion with the state in an illegal eviction.
Where restoration of possession depends on declaring title, the remedy must be through a civil court, not through a writ, as the latter would amount to passing a decree.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction) Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVII of 1950), Section 3
doctrines: Separation of remedies: writ jurisdiction vs. civil suit for title disputes
Mandamus as a public law remedy not available against private individuals absent collusion
Illegality of eviction without compliance with mandatory procedural requirements

card.dispute: The Board of Agricultural Income Tax, Assam, fought with zamindar assessees, including Smt. Sindhurani Chaudhurani, over whether salami payments received for granting agricultural leases were taxable as agricultural income.
issues_decided: Whether salami payments made prior to the creation of tenancy constitute agricultural income under the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1939
Whether salami is a capital receipt or a revenue receipt
Whether salami falls within the definition of 'rent or revenue' derived from land under Section 2(a)(1) of the Act
holdings: Salami, being a single, non-recurring payment made before the creation of tenancy as consideration for granting possession, is not rent or revenue but a capital receipt.
Payments described as salami, made prior to leasing and not recurring, do not constitute agricultural income and are not taxable under the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act.
The true indicia of salami are its non-recurring nature and timing before tenancy; such payments do not arise from the ongoing use of land and thus are not revenue.
doctrines: Capital vs. revenue receipt distinction
Literal interpretation of 'agricultural income'
Doctrine of precedent (distinguishing earlier cases on factual grounds)

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming under a registered will, sued to recover money on a mortgage without first obtaining probate; the respondents challenged their locus standi, and the High Court dismissed the suit due to lack of attestation of the will, which was later granted probate during the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court can admit additional evidence, such as a probate granted after the High Court decision, in an appeal?
Whether the appellants had locus standi to sue without prior probate of the will?
Whether the probate, being a judgment in rem, binds the respondents even though they were not parties to the probate proceedings?
holdings: The Supreme Court has inherent power under Order 45, Rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules to admit additional evidence necessary for justice, including facts arising after the impugned judgment.
The grant of probate after the High Court's decision removes the infirmity in the appellants' locus standi due to lack of attestation under Section 63(1)(c) of the Indian Succession Act.
A probate is a judgment in rem and binds all persons, including non-parties; thus, the respondents are bound by the probate even if they were not heard in those proceedings.
doctrines: Judgment in rem
Inherent powers of the Supreme Court
Locus standi in probate matters
Appellate review considering supervening events

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming to be legatees under a will, sued to enforce a mortgage, but the defendants challenged their locus standi due to lack of proper attestation of the will and absence of probate at the time of suit.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs had locus standi to maintain the suit as successors-in-interest of the testator without probate of the will?
Whether additional evidence (grant of probate) could be admitted at the appellate stage in the Supreme Court?
holdings: Locus standi to sue as successors under a will requires valid execution of the will, including proper attestation under Section 63(1)(c) of the Indian Succession Act, which was initially lacking.
The Supreme Court can admit additional evidence, including a probate granted after the High Court decision, as it is a judgment in rem and justice requires considering supervening facts.
doctrines: Judgment in rem
Supervening events in appellate review
Inherent powers of the Supreme Court to admit additional evidence

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, as amended, alleging discriminatory procedures, arbitrary powers, and inadequate compensation for land taken for public purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act for correction of revenue records violates Article 14 by being discriminatory compared to the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901
Whether Chapters II and III of the Act confer arbitrary powers on consolidation authorities and deny judicial protection, violating Article 14
Whether Section 29-B provides inadequate compensation for land acquired, violating Article 31(2) of the Constitution as it stood before the Fourth Amendment
holdings: The procedure under the impugned Act, though different from the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, is not arbitrary and satisfies the principles of natural justice, thus not violating Article 14.

The classification created by the Act for consolidation areas has a rational nexus with the object of efficient land consolidation, and the exclusion of regular court jurisdiction in favor of an arbitrator under Section 22 is necessary and valid under Article 14.

The compensation under Section 29-B, consisting of cash and indirect benefits from common facilities created by consolidated land, is adequate even if Article 31(2) applies pre-Fourth Amendment, given the minimal land taken and direct benefits to tenure-holders.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954 (U.P. Act V of 1954), Sections 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 29-B, 49
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Principles of natural justice
Rational classification
Adequacy of compensation under pre-Fourth Amendment Article 31(2)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Punjab Security of Land Tenure Act, 1953 (as amended in 1955), which limited land holdings for self-cultivation and granted tenants rights to purchase land at below-market prices.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislature had competence under Entry 18, List II of the Seventh Schedule to enact laws modifying land tenure and ownership rights.
Whether the impugned Act violated fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 of the Constitution.
Whether the Act amounted to extinguishment or modification of rights in an estate within the meaning of Article 31A.
holdings: Entry 18 of List II empowers the State Legislature to enact laws regulating land tenure, including limiting landholdings and modifying rights of landowners, as 'rights in or over land' are within its scope.
The impugned Act does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(f), or 31 because it is protected by Article 31A, which saves laws providing for the acquisition or modification of rights in estates.

The Act modifies landowners' proprietary rights in their holdings by restricting self-cultivation, transfer rights, and sale terms, thus falling within the ambit of 'modification of rights in an estate' under Article 31A.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 18, List II, Seventh Schedule
Punjab Security of Land Tenure Act, 1953 (Punj. X of 1953), Section 18
Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 (Punj. XVII of 1887), Sections 3(1), 3(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of pith and substance
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Agrarian reform under Article 31A

card.dispute: The Official Assignee challenged a deed of gift made by an insolvent, claiming it was void under insolvency law, while the donees (the insolvent's family) argued it was actually a transfer for valuable consideration and sought to prove this with oral evidence.
issues_decided: Whether Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act bars the appellants from leading oral evidence to prove that the deed of gift was in reality a transfer for valuable consideration.

Whether the Official Assignee, in proceedings under Section 55 of the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, is a representative in interest of the insolvent such that Section 92 of the Evidence Act applies.
holdings: Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act does not apply when the dispute is between a party to an instrument (or their representative) and a stranger to it; thus, the appellants can lead oral evidence to prove the transaction was for consideration.

The Official Assignee, when acting under Section 55 of the Presidency-towns Insolvency Act, is not a representative in interest of the insolvent but acts for the benefit of creditors, making Section 92 inapplicable.
doctrines: Doctrine of mutuality in evidence law
Rule against varying written documents by oral agreement (with exception for disputes involving strangers)
Representative-in-interest doctrine under insolvency law

card.dispute: The trustees of a trust estate contested the method of assessment of agricultural income-tax, arguing they should be assessed under Section 11(1) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, as common managers on behalf of annuitants, rather than as owners liable for the full tax.
issues_decided: Whether the trustees held the land from which agricultural income was derived 'on behalf of' the annuitants within the meaning of Section 11(1) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948.
Whether the annuitants were 'jointly interested' in the agricultural income so as to attract the application of Section 11(1) of the Act.
holdings: Trustees, as legal owners of trust property, do not hold land 'on behalf of' beneficiaries or annuitants in the sense of agency; they hold it in their own right, though for the benefit of others, and thus do not fall under Section 11(1) of the Act.

Annuitants under a trust deed, each entitled to a separate and individual annuity, are not 'jointly interested' in the agricultural income, as their interests are not undivided; hence, Section 11(1) does not apply.
provisions: U. P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, Section 2(11)
U. P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, Section 3
U. P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948, Section 11(1)
doctrines: Distinction between 'holding for the benefit of' and 'holding on behalf of'
Legal ownership of trustees under trust law
Requirement of joint interest for application of deeming provisions in tax statutes

card.dispute: The tenants and sub-tenants sued for a declaration of their protected tenancy status under the Bombay Rents Act, which the landlord contested after having already obtained an eviction decree in the Small Causes Court.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay City Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit seeking declaration of tenancy and sub-tenancy rights under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether a claim for tenancy protection arising under the Act can be decided by a court not specified under Section 28 of the Act
Whether Section 29A of the Act allows a civil court to determine questions of title that arise under the provisions of the Act
holdings: The City Civil Court lacked jurisdiction because Section 28 of the Bombay Rents Act exclusively vests adjudication of claims arising under the Act in specified courts, and the City Civil Court is not one of them.
A suit seeking protection from eviction under the Act, even if framed as a declaration, must be decided by a court designated under Section 28 since the claim arises out of the Act.
Section 29A permits adjudication of title in a civil court only if the title does not arise out of the Act; claims of tenancy created by the Act must be determined under Section 28.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29A
Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882, Section 49
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction under special statutes
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Incidental determination of title vs. title arising out of statute

card.dispute: The se-pataidar resisted the durpatnidars' suit for recovery of arrears of rent, claiming it was barred because the durpatnidars failed to give notice of succession or get their names mutated in the landlord's rent-roll within six months as required by the Bengal Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether the six-month time limit under Section 15 of the Bengal Tenancy Act for giving notice of succession or getting mutation in the rent-roll is mandatory or directory
Whether failure to comply with the time limit under Section 15 bars a successor's right to recover arrears of rent by suit indefinitely
Whether mutation in the landlord's rent-roll can be proved by secondary evidence in the absence of the original rent-roll
holdings: The six-month time limit under Section 15 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is directory, not mandatory, and non-compliance does not extinguish the right to recover rent.
Section 16 only postpones the remedy to sue for arrears of rent until the duties under Section 15 are performed; it does not create a permanent bar.
Mutation in the rent-roll can be proved not only by the original or certified copy of the rent-roll but also by secondary evidence when the original is unavailable.
provisions: Bengal Tenancy Act (Act VIII of 1885), Section 15
Bengal Tenancy Act (Act VIII of 1885), Section 16
Bengal Act IV of 1928 (amending the Bengal Tenancy Act)
doctrines: Directory vs mandatory statutory provisions
Strict construction of penal provisions
Secondary evidence in proof of mutation

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sought enhancement of rent from the tenant (respondent), claiming the accommodation was newly constructed after June 30, 1946, making it eligible for rent revision under the U.P. Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the landlord's suit for enhancement of rent under Section 5(4) of the U.P. Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the civil court's order under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to an erroneous finding on a jurisdictional fact?
holdings: A civil court can only entertain a landlord's suit for rent enhancement under Section 5(4) if the accommodation was newly constructed after June 30, 1946, and the reasonable annual rent is inadequate; otherwise, the court lacks jurisdiction.

If a subordinate court erroneously finds a jurisdictional fact (like date of construction) and thereby assumes jurisdiction it does not possess, the High Court can interfere under Section 115, CPC, to correct such illegality.
provisions: U.P. Temporary Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 2(a), Section 2(f), Section 3A, Section 5(4), Section 6
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Illegality in exercise of jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Doctrine of limited revisional powers of High Court

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Bhurangya Coal Co. disputed whether profits from the sale of movable fixtures were assessable under section 12B of the Income-tax Act, 1922, based on when title passed in a composite sale of colliery assets.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of movable properties, including fixtures, on 30th March 1946, was assessable under section 12B of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the sale deed of 17th May 1946 conveyed fixtures mentioned in part 2 of the schedule, thereby bringing them under capital gains taxation.
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to remand the case for further evidence on the nature of the properties sold.
holdings: Title to movable properties, including fixtures, passed on delivery on 30th March 1946, before section 12B came into force, so gains from their sale are not taxable under that section.
The sale deed of 17th May 1946 conveyed only immovable properties listed in part 1 of the schedule; fixtures in part 2 were intended to be sold as movables and were not transferred under the deed.
The High Court correctly refused to remand the case, as the appellant did not seek additional evidence before the Tribunal and could not raise the issue for the first time before the High Court.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice of contract terms
Doctrine of interpretation of conveyancing documents based on expressed intention
Principle that title to movables passes upon delivery unless otherwise agreed

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the assessee, Rai Bahadur Jairam Valji, disputed whether compensation received for the premature termination of a limestone supply contract was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation of Rs. 2,50,000 received for terminating the May 9, 1940 contract was a revenue or capital receipt
Whether the termination of a major trading contract amounts to destruction of the profit-making apparatus, making compensation a capital receipt
Whether the principles from Van Den Berghs Ltd. v. Clark and Glenboig Union Fireclay Co. apply to compensation under trading contracts
holdings: Compensation received for terminating a trading contract is a revenue receipt if it arises from rights under the contract and not from injury to a capital asset.
The termination of a contract for carrying on business does not make the compensation capital unless it affects the entirety of the profit-making structure.
The receipt is taxable as income when it adjusts profits expected under a trading agreement, not when it compensates for loss of a capital asset.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Profit-making apparatus doctrine
Compensation for termination of trading contracts as revenue receipt

card.dispute: The appellant and the Union of India appealed to the Federal Court against a High Court decision on compensation for requisitioned property, but the maintainability of the appeals was challenged.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal under section 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, before the High Court is a judicial proceeding or an arbitration proceeding
Whether the decision of the High Court in such an appeal constitutes a 'judgment, decree or order' under sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure
holdings: An appeal under section 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, retains the character of arbitration proceedings, and the High Court acts as an arbitration tribunal, not a court in the ordinary sense.

The decision of the High Court in an appeal under section 19(1)(f) is an 'award' and not a 'judgment, decree or order', and thus does not satisfy the requirements for appeal to the Federal Court under sections 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
provisions: Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, Section 3(a)(ii)
Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, Section 2(b)
doctrines: Distinction between reference to a court as a court versus as an arbitrator
Continuity of arbitration character in appellate proceedings
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on nature of tribunal and proceedings

card.dispute: The reversioner challenged the validity of an adoption made by the widow of the deceased, but the key issue was whether the widow became the absolute owner of the property under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, despite not being in physical possession at the time the Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies if a Hindu widow is not in actual physical possession of the property at the time the Act came into force?
Whether constructive possession by a widow through a permissive occupant qualifies as 'possession' under Section 14 of the Act?
Whether a reversioner can challenge an adoption after the widow has acquired absolute ownership under Section 14?
holdings: The word 'possession' in Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is used in the widest sense and includes constructive or legal possession, not merely physical control.
A Hindu widow is deemed to be in possession of her husband's property under Section 14 if the occupant holds it permissively, even if not physically present.
Once a widow becomes the absolute owner under Section 14, a reversioner loses all rights to challenge alienations or adoptions, as no spes successionis remains.
doctrines: Constructive possession
Transformation of limited estate into absolute ownership
Spes successionis extinguished by statutory vesting of absolute interest

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an appeal could be filed in the Supreme Court against a High Court's decision in an appeal under the Defence of India Act, 1939, where the High Court had modified an arbitrator's award on compensation for requisitioned premises.
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the High Court in an appeal under s. 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939 is a 'judgment, decree or order' within the meaning of ss. 109 and 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Whether the Supreme Court could grant special leave to appeal under Art. 135 when the High Court's decision was not a judgment, decree or order but an award
holdings: An appeal under s. 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act is part of an arbitration proceeding, and the High Court's decision therein is an award, not a judgment, decree or order under the Code of Civil Procedure.

Since the High Court's decision is an award and not a judgment, decree or order, no appeal lies to the Supreme Court under ss. 109 or 110 of the CPC or under special leave jurisdiction under Art. 135 read with s. 3(a)(ii) of the Federal Court Act.
provisions: Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1948, Section 3(a)(ii)
doctrines: Distinction between court acting as a court and court acting as an arbitrator
Continuity of arbitration character in appellate proceedings
Finality of awards in statutory arbitration

card.dispute: Gallu Sah challenged his conviction for abetting arson, arguing that the principal offender was acquitted and there was no proof the fire was set in consequence of his order.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be convicted under Section 436 IPC read with Section 109 IPC for abetting arson when the principal offender was acquitted.
Whether the act of arson was committed in consequence of the appellant's abetment, as required by law.
holdings: A person can be convicted for abetment even if the principal offender is acquitted, provided the offence was committed in consequence of the abetment.

The appellant was rightly convicted under Section 436 IPC read with Section 109 IPC because the person who set fire to the hut did so in consequence of his instigation, and was a member of the unlawful assembly.
doctrines: Abetment in consequence of instigation
Conviction for abetment independent of principal offender's conviction

card.dispute: The landlord was prosecuted for withholding municipal water supply to a tenant; the tenant claimed the landlord failed to restore the connection, while the landlord argued he was not liable for his predecessor's default and the tenant never enjoyed the supply after the Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's omission to restore water supply, cut off due to predecessor's default, amounts to 'withholding an essential supply' under Section 24(1) of the Bombay Rents Act.
Whether the tenant must have enjoyed the essential supply after the Act came into force to invoke Section 24.
holdings: An omission by the landlord to restore an essential supply, which he could have done by paying a prescribed fee, is attributable to him under Explanation II of Section 24, even if the initial cutoff was due to a predecessor's default.

For Section 24 to apply, the tenant must have enjoyed the essential supply after the Act came into force; enjoyment before the Act does not suffice, as applying the law otherwise would amount to ex post facto legislation contrary to Article 20(1) of the Constitution.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 24
doctrines: Strict construction of penal provisions
Prohibition against ex post facto laws
Legislative intent interpretation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the auction-purchaser and the court-appointed Receiver over whether a revenue sale of property in the Receiver's possession was illegal due to lack of court leave and notice, and whether the civil court could entertain a suit to set it aside.
issues_decided: Whether the revenue sale was illegal for want of leave of court and notice to the Receiver?
Whether the suit to set aside the sale was barred by Sections 157 and 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928?
holdings: A revenue sale of property in the possession of a court-appointed Receiver is illegal if conducted without the court's leave and without notice to the Receiver.

A suit challenging such a sale is not barred by Sections 157(1) or 192 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, as the grounds for challenge fall outside the specific statutory remedies and involve a declaration of rights in rem.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 40, Rule 1
doctrines: Audi alteram partem
Jurisdictional limitation of civil courts under special statutes
Distinction between void and voidable acts in revenue sales
Territorial and hierarchical limits of statutory remedies

card.dispute: The successors of a mortgagor sued to redeem the mortgaged property, seek accounts, and recover surplus profits, while the mortgagee's successor claimed the transaction was a lease or, alternatively, that no account was due under Section 77 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction was a mortgage or a lease
Whether the mortgagee was liable to render accounts under Section 76 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether Section 77 of the Transfer of Property Act applied to absolve the mortgagee from rendering accounts
Whether the express terms of the mortgage deed prevented a claim for surplus profits
holdings: The transaction was a mortgage because it involved a debt secured by property, regardless of the name given to it.
A mortgagee in possession is generally bound to keep and render accounts under Section 76, but this duty can be excluded by contract.

Section 77 applies where the parties contract that receipts from the property are to be taken in lieu of interest, even if the mortgagee pays a fixed sum to the mortgagor, so long as the receipts are appropriated entirely towards interest.
The express terms of the deed, including the mortgagor’s waiver of any claim to increased produce, meant the mortgagee had no duty to account for surplus receipts.
doctrines: Intention of the parties governs characterization of a transaction as mortgage or lease
Doctrine of anomalous mortgage under Section 98
Contractual exclusion of mortgagee's duty to account under Section 77

card.dispute: The erstwhile Taluqdars challenged the State of Bombay's demand for full land revenue after the expiry of a 30-year jama fixation period, claiming protection under a saving clause in the land revenue code.
issues_decided: Whether the jama fixed under the Gujarat Taluqdars Act, 1888 constitutes a 'settlement of land revenue' under Section 117R of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, and thus continues in force until a revision settlement is made.
Whether the appellants remained liable to pay only the declared jama after its 30-year term expired, or became liable to pay the full land revenue assessment thereafter.
holdings: The jama fixed under Section 22 of the Gujarat Taluqdars Act, 1888 is distinct from land revenue assessment and does not qualify as a 'settlement of land revenue' under Section 117R of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879.

The declaration of jama for a fixed term of thirty years ceased to operate upon expiry of that period, and the appellants became liable to pay the full land revenue assessment as per the settlement register from 1955–56 onward.
provisions: Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, Section 5(2)
doctrines: Distinction between jama and land revenue assessment
Statutory interpretation of 'settlement of land revenue'
Operation of saving clauses in revenue legislation

card.dispute: The third surviving testator claimed sole ownership of all properties under a joint will by survivorship, while the legatees claimed entitlement under the will.
issues_decided: Whether the jointly executed document operated as a transfer inter vivos creating joint tenancy with right of survivorship
Whether the document was a valid joint will operating as separate testamentary dispositions
Whether subsequent conduct of parties could alter the construction of the will
holdings: The document was a testamentary disposition, not a transfer inter vivos, and did not create joint tenancy with right of survivorship.
A joint will, even if made by multiple testators, operates as separate wills for each testator and disposes of individual properties upon death.
Subsequent conduct of parties cannot alter the clear and unambiguous terms of a will.
doctrines: Construction of joint wills
Tenancy-in-common vs joint tenancy
Rule against using subsequent conduct to alter unambiguous will terms
Testamentary disposition versus inter vivos transfer

card.dispute: The appellants, members of an unlawful assembly, challenged their conviction for murder under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC for killing Rameshwar during a forcible land takeover.
issues_decided: Whether the murder was committed in prosecution of the common object of the unlawful assembly to take forcible possession of land
Whether the other members of the unlawful assembly knew that murder was likely to be committed in furtherance of the common object
Whether the sentence of death for Mizaji and life imprisonment for others was justified
holdings: The murder was immediately connected to the common object of taking forcible possession, as the assembly was prepared to use lethal force to achieve it.
The members of the unlawful assembly knew or must have known that murder was likely to be committed, given the weapons carried and their threatening conduct.
The death sentence for Mizaji and life imprisonment for others were justified as all were equally liable under Section 149 IPC for the murder committed in prosecution of the common object.
doctrines: Common object of unlawful assembly
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Knowledge of likelihood of commission of offence in furtherance of common object

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to recover possession and mesne profits of certain lands resumed by the Miraj State in 1910, but the defendants contested the suit as barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's suit was within the period of limitation under the Limitation Act
Whether the plaintiff could invoke Section 14 of the Limitation Act to exclude the time spent prosecuting a previous suit in a court lacking jurisdiction
Whether the plaintiff discharged the burden of proving due diligence and good faith in prosecuting the earlier suit
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation because the plaintiff failed to show that the prior suit was prosecuted with due diligence and good faith under Section 14 of the Limitation Act.
To claim benefit under Section 14, the plaintiff must affirmatively prove due diligence, good faith, same cause of action, and lack of jurisdiction in the prior court.

The omission to include the value of the property in the plaint for over ten years, despite knowledge of the high value, showed lack of due care and attention required for 'good faith' under Section 2(7) of the Limitation Act.
The burden of proving compliance with Section 14 lies on the plaintiff and does not shift to the defendant to prove mala fides or lack of diligence.
provisions: General Clauses Act, definition of 'good faith'
doctrines: Burden of proof in limitation pleas
Good faith under the Limitation Act requiring due care and attention
Exclusion of time under Section 14 only upon fulfillment of all statutory conditions

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's interference with orders of the Appellate Authority under the Excise Act, which had upheld the grant of country spirit shops, arguing that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can issue a writ of certiorari under Article 226 to correct an error of fact apparent on the face of the record.
Whether the High Court can interfere under Article 227 on grounds of erroneous application of executive instructions lacking statutory force.
Whether the High Court's exercise of supervisory jurisdiction was justified in setting aside the Appellate Authority's order.
holdings: The High Court cannot issue a writ under Article 226 to correct an error of fact, even if apparent on the face of the record; such power extends only to errors of law apparent on the record.
Non-compliance with executive instructions, which lack statutory force, does not invalidate an order passed by a quasi-judicial authority acting within its statutory jurisdiction.

The High Court exceeded its supervisory powers under Articles 226 and 227 by scrutinizing the merits of the Appellate Authority’s decision rather than confining itself to jurisdictional or legal error.
provisions: Eastern Bengal and Assam Excise Act, 1910 (as amended by Assam Act 23 of 1955), Section 9
Eastern Bengal and Assam Excise Act, 1910, Rule 343
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Limits of writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Scope of supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Distinction between statutory powers and executive instructions

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction on the grounds that the trial was vitiated by the prosecution's failure to examine Raghbir, a material witness who claimed constitutional protection against self-incrimination.
issues_decided: Whether the trial was vitiated by the prosecution's failure to examine Raghbir as a witness.
Whether Section 167 of the Indian Evidence Act applied to the non-examination of Raghbir.
Whether Raghbir was a material witness essential to the prosecution's case.
Whether the sentence imposed on appellant Narain was justified.
holdings: The trial was not vitiated by the failure to examine Raghbir, as the prosecution did not formally tender him as a witness and there was no rejection of evidence under Section 167.
Section 167 of the Indian Evidence Act does not apply where the prosecution abandons a witness without formally offering him, and no evidence is 'rejected' within the meaning of the section.
Raghbir was not a material witness essential to the prosecution's case, as he arrived after the alleged offences and could not testify about the core events of assault and abduction.
The higher sentence on Narain was justified because he directed the attack on Mani Ram, even though no specific grievous injury was directly attributed to him.
doctrines: Test for materiality of a witness based on necessity to the prosecution narrative
Principle that prosecution is not bound to call witnesses who may support the defence
Doctrine of adverse inference not applicable where no deliberate suppression of material witness by prosecution

card.dispute: The mortgagor, Seth Ganga Dhar, sued to redeem a mortgage before 85 years had passed, but the mortgage deed barred redemption for that period and allowed redemption only within a six-month window thereafter, failing which the deed would be deemed a sale in favour of the mortgagee.
issues_decided: Whether the 85-year bar on redemption constituted a clog on the equity of redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the court could invalidate the long redemption period on grounds of unconscionability or oppression
Whether the suit for redemption, filed before expiry of the 85-year period, was maintainable
holdings: A term restricting redemption for a long period is not automatically a clog on the equity of redemption; the court must assess whether the bargain was unconscionable or oppressive based on the facts.
The 85-year restriction was not unconscionable, as the parties dealt on equal footing, the interest was fair, and no evidence showed the mortgagor was under financial pressure.
The suit for redemption was premature because it was filed before the agreed 85-year period expired, and the court upheld the enforceability of the term.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Clog on equity of redemption
Unconscionable bargain
Relief against penalty

card.dispute: Jagirdars and contractors fought over whether they acquired legal property rights in forest trees and produce after government restrictions and abolition of jagirs in Madhya Bharat.
issues_decided: Whether property in forest trees passed to the petitioners under contracts or licenses granted by jagirdars or forest officers after the imposition of restrictions under the Jagir Forests (Prevention of Indiscriminate Cutting) Act, 1950
Whether ratification by the State Government of acts of forest officers could confer property rights on the petitioners
Whether Sections 26(2)(a) and 34 of the Madhya Bharat Forest Act, 1960, enabled the petitioners to claim property in the trees they cut
Whether the petitioners had a fundamental right under Article 32 to challenge the State's refusal to allow removal of forest produce
holdings: Property in forest trees did not pass to the petitioners as the contracts expired and no valid sale or transfer occurred after the restrictions under the Cutting Act and abolition of jagirs.
Acts of forest officers done without authority were not ratified by the government, and thus could not confer legal property rights on the petitioners.
Sections 26(2)(a) and 34 of the Forest Act only exempt from penalties and do not confer property rights; they do not enable transfer of ownership of forest produce.
No fundamental right under Article 32 was infringed because the petitioners never acquired legal property rights in the trees or produce, so no deprivation occurred.
provisions: The Jagir Forests (Prevention of Indiscriminate Cutting) Act, No. 55 of 1950, Section 3
The Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, No. 28 of 1951
The Madhya Bharat Forest Act, No. LXXIII of 1960, Sections 4, 26(2)(a), 29, 34
doctrines: Doctrine of ratification of unauthorized acts
Distinction between license and transfer of property
Requirement of valid legal basis for property rights under fundamental rights enforcement

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of Chaukidari Chakaran lands after purchasing them from the Zamindar, while the respondents, prior holders under a Patni settlement, resisted on the ground that the sale of a portion of the Patni was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of Chaukidari Chakaran lands in 1899 created a distinct Patni separate from the existing Patni of village Ahiyapur
Whether the sale of the Chaukidari Chakaran lands for arrears of rent was valid despite being part of a larger Patni estate
holdings: The grant of Chaukidari Chakaran lands under Exhibit B created a separate and distinct Patni, independent of the original Patni of Ahiyapur, as evidenced by clauses allowing independent transfer and sale.
The sale of the Chaukidari Chakaran lands for arrears under the Bengal Patni Taluks Regulation, 1819 was valid because they formed a distinct Patni and could be sold separately.
doctrines: Rule of construction: earlier clauses in a deed prevail over later repugnant clauses
Principle of valid partition and separate alienation of tenures under agreement between parties
Doctrine of merger not applied where deed evinces intention to create independent tenure

card.dispute: Landowners in Himachal Pradesh challenged the constitutional validity of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, on grounds that it was passed by an improperly constituted legislature and violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, was passed by a duly constituted legislative assembly after the formation of the new State of Himachal Pradesh.
Whether the impugned Act could be validly enacted without a properly constituted legislature, despite pending legislation from the old assembly.
holdings: The Legislative Assembly that passed the impugned Act was not the duly constituted assembly of the new Himachal Pradesh, as no notification under Section 74 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, had been issued to bring it into existence.

The session convened by the Lieutenant Governor on August 16, 1954, was improperly treated as the 'second session' of the old assembly, which had ceased to exist, and thus lacked constitutional authority to pass legislation for the new state.
provisions: Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 9
Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954, Section 15(1)
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 74
Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 14
Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 25
Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 35
doctrines: Doctrine of proper legislative competence
Doctrine of deeming provisions not overriding constitutional requirements
Doctrine of continuity of legislative sessions

card.dispute: Former landholders in Rampur challenged the Uttar Pradesh government's abolition of their jagirs, zamindaris, muafis, thekedari, and pattedari rights under two land reform Acts.
issues_decided: Whether the merger agreement between Rampur State and the Dominion of India protected the petitioners' land rights from abolition under state legislation.
Whether the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, and its application to Rampur via notification, was constitutionally valid.
Whether thekedars and pattedars were mere managers of state land and thus outside the scope of the Thekedari and Pattedari Abolition Act, 1954.
holdings: The merger agreement did not protect land rights because clause (iii) allowed successor governments to override prior agreements inconsistent with general policy, and abolition was such a policy.

The application of the Abolition Act to Rampur was valid, especially after the 1958 amendment retrospectively validated the definition of 'estate', removing any delegation or substantive change objections.

Thekedars and pattedars were not mere managers but lessees with heritable interests, and thus fell within the scope of the Thekedari Act, which was validly enacted and compliant with constitutional requirements.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, No. I of 1951, Section 2(1) and Section 3(8)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, No. XIV of 1958
Rampur Thekedari and Pattedari Abolition Act, No. X of 1954, Section 2(6)
Constitution of India, Article 31(2), Article 363, Entry 18 of List II, Seventh Schedule
States Merger (United Provinces) Order, 1949, Articles 7 and 8
doctrines: Doctrine of successor government policy overriding prior agreements
Doctrine of retrospective validation of legislative amendments
Doctrine of permissible delegation of legislative power to executive for geographical application
Doctrine of classification of land tenure based on substance over form

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the respondent, Sri Ramakrishna Deo, fought over whether income from the sale of forest trees was agricultural income exempt from tax.
issues_decided: Whether the income from the sale of forest trees constituted agricultural income under Section 2(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the burden of proving agricultural income lay with the assessee or the tax authorities
Whether the finding of the Appellate Tribunal on the mode of growth of trees was binding on the High Court
holdings: Income from the sale of forest trees is not agricultural income unless the trees were planted by human effort and agricultural operations were performed.
The burden of proving that income is agricultural and thus exempt lies on the assessee claiming the exemption, not on the tax authorities.
The Appellate Tribunal's finding that the trees were of spontaneous growth and not planted is a finding of fact binding on the High Court in a reference under Section 66(1).
doctrines: Burden of proof in tax exemption claims
Finality of findings of fact by tribunals in tax references
Definition of agricultural income under the Indian Income-tax Act

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser of mortgaged properties, sought to be added as a party in an appeal against a mortgagee's execution proceedings, claiming her rights were at risk due to a pending appeal filed by the transferor.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be added as a party under Order 22, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
Whether the appellant, as a transferee, could be brought on record under Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure to continue an appeal filed by her transferor.
Whether the appellant had a sufficient interest to be heard in execution proceedings affecting her purchased property.
holdings: Order 22, Rule 10 does not apply where the transfer occurred before the appeal was filed and no application was made in the court where the suit was pending.
Section 146 allows a person claiming under a party to continue an appeal filed by that party, as an appeal is a proceeding within the meaning of the section.
A purchaser pendente lite with a direct interest in the subject-matter of litigation is entitled to be brought on record to protect their rights, even if not originally a party.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10
doctrines: Pendente lite transfer
Substitution of parties
Liberal construction of procedural provisions to advance justice
Rights of assignee under Section 146

card.dispute: Shrimati Shantabai claimed a fundamental right to cut and appropriate wood from forest land based on an unregistered document, which the State restricted after vesting proprietary rights in itself under a subsequent abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered document conferred a valid right to cut and appropriate wood from forest land under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
Whether the right claimed amounted to a property right protected under Article 19(1)(f)
Whether the document required registration under the Transfer of Property Act and the Registration Act
holdings: The order restricting the petitioner from cutting wood did not infringe her fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) because she had no valid property right enforceable against the State.
A right to cut trees is a benefit arising out of land and, unless it involves only standing timber, constitutes an interest in immovable property requiring registration.
The unregistered document failed to transfer any legal interest in immovable property, and thus could not form the basis of a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(f).
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 (No. 1 of 1951), Section 3
doctrines: Fundamental rights depend on existence of a legal right
Distinction between standing timber (movable) and trees as immovable property
Benefit arising out of land as an interest in immovable property
Registration requirement for transfer of immovable property

card.dispute: The managing committee of Parsa High English School challenged the Bihar government's order to displace them and take control of the school, claiming violation of their rights as trustees of the school property.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Article 182 of the Bihar Education Code has the force of law under Article 13 of the Constitution to divest the managing committee of control over the school property.
Whether the government's actions in displacing the managing committee and threatening to take possession of the school were legally justified.
holdings: Amended Article 182 of the Bihar Education Code does not have the force of law as it lacks statutory authority and is merely an administrative order, thus cannot deprive the petitioners of their rights as trustees.
The government cannot interfere with the managing committee's control over the school or its property without lawful authority, and any such action is unconstitutional.
doctrines: Doctrine of State action under Article 12
Principle of lawful deprivation of property under Article 31
Administrative order vs. statutory law distinction

card.dispute: The appellants, former managing committee members of a Darga Sharif, challenged the Sunni Central Board of Waqf's authority to take over the Darga's properties, claiming they were not a valid waqf, while the Board raised preliminary objections of limitation and non-compliance with notice requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Section 5(2) of the United Provinces Muslims Waqf Act, 1936?
Whether the period of injunction during earlier litigation could be excluded under Section 15 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908?
Whether the suit was incompetent for non-compliance with the notice requirement under Section 53 of the Waqf Act?
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation as it was not filed within one year of the Board's notification under Section 5(1), as required by Section 5(2) of the Waqf Act.
The order removing the appellants from office did not amount to an injunction staying the suit under Section 15 of the Limitation Act, and thus no suspension of limitation was warranted.
The suit was not maintainable as the appellants failed to serve the mandatory two-month notice under Section 53 of the Waqf Act before instituting the suit.
provisions: United Provinces Muslims Waqf Act, 1936, Section 5
United Provinces Muslims Waqf Act, 1936, Section 53
doctrines: Strict construction of limitation statutes
Notice requirement as a condition precedent to suit
No equitable extension of limitation periods

card.dispute: Landlords and jagirdars challenged the validity of the Ajmer Abolition of Intermediaries and Land Reforms Act, 1955, which vested their estates in the state, arguing it was beyond legislative competence and violated property rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Ajmer legislature had the competence to pass the Act, given that the acquired property vested in the President (Union), raising a federal legislative competence issue under the Seventh Schedule.
Whether Section 8 of the Act, which cancelled leases retrospectively, violated the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
Whether Section 38, which fixed maximum rent, imposed an unreasonable restriction on property rights.
Whether a jagirdar, defined as an assignee of land revenue, could be considered an 'intermediary' whose entire estate (including proprietary land) was liable to be resumed under the Act.
holdings: The competence of a legislature to acquire property depends on the purpose of acquisition, not on where the title vests post-acquisition; since the Act served state purposes, the Ajmer legislature was competent under Entry 36, List II.
Section 8's retrospective cancellation of leases was valid as part of a land reform measure and did not unreasonably infringe on property rights under Article 19(1)(f).
Section 38's rent control was a reasonable restriction under the State's police power to regulate tenancy and implement land reforms.
A jagirdar is not merely an assignee of revenue but a holder of an estate; thus, the entire proprietary interest, including uncultivated land, is liable to resumption under the Act.
provisions: Ajmer Abolition of Intermediaries and Land Reforms Act, 1955, Sections 4, 8, 38
Ajmer Tenancy and Land Records Act, 1950
Government of Part C States Act, Section 21
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 33; List II, Entry 36; List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Legislative competence based on purpose of law, not incidental effects
Doctrine of severability not invoked as entire Act found valid
Property rights subject to reasonable state regulation for public purpose
Historical and textual interpretation of land tenure systems

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1956, which mandated compulsory purchase of surplus agricultural land by tenants.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the impugned Act violate the fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.
Whether Section 7 of the Act involves excessive delegation of legislative power to the executive.
Whether the criteria for varying ceiling areas and economic holdings under Section 7 are constitutionally valid.
Whether the Act offends the principle of non-discrimination under Article 14 due to potential for arbitrary executive action.
holdings: The Act is valid as it falls within the ambit of Article 31A and does not violate Articles 14, 19, or 31, as it serves the public purpose of equitable land distribution.
Section 7 does not entail excessive delegation because the legislature laid down sufficient policy and guiding standards for the executive to vary ceiling areas.
The criteria in Section 7—situation of land, productivity, backward area status, and prescribed factors—are adequate and must be interpreted ejusdem generis, preventing arbitrary use.
Presumption of constitutionality applies; mere possibility of executive abuse does not invalidate legislation, as courts can strike down only the abuse, not the provision itself.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 18, List II, Seventh Schedule
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1956, Sections 32 to 32R
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1956, Section 7
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Presumption of constitutionality
Ejusdem generis rule of statutory interpretation
Separation of powers
Public interest test in executive action

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Calcutta National Bank Limited disputed whether rental income from a building owned by the bank was liable to excess profits tax under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether rental income received by a banking company from letting out part of its building constitutes 'business' income under the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940
Whether Rule 4(4) of Schedule I to the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 applies to a company whose main business is banking, not property holding
holdings: Rental income from property owned and constructed by a banking company forms part of its business income if the property was held as an investment to earn profit, even if banking is the primary business.

Rule 4(4) of Schedule I to the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940 applies independently to include rental income in business profits, even if the company’s functions are not wholly or mainly the holding of property.
provisions: Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, Schedule I, Rule 4(4)
doctrines: Rule of liberal interpretation of fiscal statutes to carry out legislative intent
Schedule can expand statutory definition if language is clear, despite heading or primary purpose
Business includes activities beyond core operations if conducted for profit

card.dispute: The appellant agnate challenged the respondents' claim to succeed to a Hindu estate, disputing their pedigree that traced them as sons of half-sisters of the last male owner.
issues_decided: Whether a joint statement in a 1917 petition (Ex. 1) was admissible under Section 32(5) of the Indian Evidence Act when only one of the three declarants was dead and the statement was made during litigation.
Whether the oral testimony of P.W. 2 and P.W. 4 regarding family relationships was admissible under Section 50 of the Indian Evidence Act.
Whether the declarant in Ex. 1 had special means of knowledge about the pedigree to satisfy Section 32(5).
