holdings: A statement in a petition filed during litigation can be admissible under Section 32(5) if it was made before the specific dispute in the current case arose, even if one declarant is alive.
Oral evidence of relationship by persons related to the family is admissible under Section 50 as opinion based on reputation and conduct.
The declarant in Ex. 1 had special means of knowledge about the pedigree because he was the grandson of the common ancestor through one of the alleged daughters.
doctrines: Ante litem motam
Special means of knowledge
Opinion as to relationship under Section 50

card.dispute: The Jogta Coal Co. Ltd. and the Commissioner of Income-Tax disputed whether the Appellate Tribunal could disregard the purchase price allocation in a sale deed and include goodwill in the cost of assets for claiming depreciation under the Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Appellate Tribunal had the jurisdiction to go behind the sale deed and revalue the consideration paid for assets, including attributing part of it to goodwill not mentioned in the deed?
Whether the Income-tax Officer could disregard the conveyance and fix his own valuation for depreciation purposes under section 10(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act?
holdings: The Tribunal cannot conjecture or revalue the cost of assets unless there is evidence that the transaction was not at arm's length or was artificial; the original cost to the assessee as per the sale deed must generally be accepted.

The question whether the Income-tax Officer could go behind the conveyance to determine the true allocation of purchase price, especially in absence of goodwill mention, required reference to the High Court under section 66(1).
doctrines: Original cost to the assessee doctrine
Doctrine of non-interference with commercial valuation in arm's length transactions
Doctrine of reference of questions of law to High Court under section 66

card.dispute: The Mahant of Salouna asthal challenged the applicability of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 to his institution, claiming it was a private trust and not subject to state regulation requiring submission of financial returns.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 applies to private religious trusts.
Whether the Salouna asthal constitutes a public religious trust within the meaning of the Act.
Whether the provisions of the Act, if applied to private trusts, would violate Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
holdings: The Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950 does not apply to private religious trusts, as the definition of 'religious trust' in Section 2(1), read with Section 4(5), excludes private trusts.
The Salouna asthal is not proven to be a public trust, and in absence of contrary evidence, the prior declaration that it is a private trust stands.
It is unnecessary to decide on the constitutional validity of the Act's application to private trusts, as the Act does not apply to them.
provisions: Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Section 2(1)
Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Section 4(5)
Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Section 43
Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Section 48
doctrines: Distinction between public and private religious trusts in Hindu law
Rule of construction based on legislative history and context
Doctrine of severability and constitutional avoidance
Visitorial power in English law distinguished from Hindu law

card.dispute: Mahants of religious institutions challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, arguing it violated their fundamental rights and improperly classified trusts.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act violates Article 14 by unequal treatment between Hindu, Sikh, and Jain religious trusts
Whether the Act infringes Article 19(1)(f) by unduly restricting the management rights of trustees
Whether the Act contravenes Articles 25 and 26 by interfering with the practice and management of religion
Whether Section 70 of the Act imposes an unconstitutional tax
holdings: The classification between Hindu, Sikh, and Jain trusts is valid as the legislature may distinguish based on administrative needs and religious distinctions.
The restrictions on trustees under the Act do not violate Article 19(1)(f) as they are reasonable and aimed at preventing mismanagement of trust property.
The Act does not infringe Articles 25 and 26 because it regulates secular administration of trusts without interfering with religious practices.
Section 70 levies a fee for administrative expenses, not a tax, and therefore does not violate constitutional provisions including Article 27.
provisions: Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, Sections 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 28, 29, 32, 55(2), 60, 70
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Distinction between tax and fee under constitutional law
Secular administration vs. religious practice under Articles 25 and 26
Regulatory restrictions as reasonable under Article 19(1)(f)

card.dispute: The petitioners, who had agreements with former proprietors for rights to collect tendu leaves and other forest produce, challenged the State's abolition of these rights under a land reform Act, claiming violation of their fundamental rights under Article 32.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners had an 'interest in proprietary right' under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950
Whether the rights granted under the agreements amounted to proprietary rights or were merely contractual or licensing rights
Whether the State's vesting of such rights in itself under the Act violated the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 31 (right to property)
holdings: Rights to forest produce, including tendu leaves, trees, and land use, granted by proprietors were part of proprietary rights and thus vested in the State free of encumbrances under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act.
The petitioners' rights, even if arising from contract or license, did not constitute proprietary interests protected under the Act, and hence were not immune from vesting.

The State's action under the Act did not infringe any fundamental right of the petitioners because it did not take over their contracts or licenses, and no property right in them was recognized under the law.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Sections 2(6), 3, 4
Central Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1917, Sections 2(13), 47(3), 202
doctrines: Vesting of proprietary rights in the State free of encumbrances
Definition of 'proprietary right' based on statutory context and subject-matter
Distinction between proprietary rights and contractual or license rights

card.dispute: The Calcutta Company Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether an estimated future development expense could be deducted as a business expense under the mercantile system of accounting.
issues_decided: Whether an accrued liability for future development expenses, though not yet incurred, is an allowable deduction in computing business profits under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the mercantile system of accounting permits deduction of estimated expenses where liability has accrued, even if payment has not been made.
holdings: An accrued liability for future expenses, arising from a contractual obligation under the mercantile system of accounting, is deductible in the year the liability arises, even if the expense is not yet paid.

Deductions not specifically listed in Section 10(2) may still be allowed if they arise from accepted commercial practices and are incidental to the business, provided there is no express or implied prohibition in the Act.
doctrines: Accrued liability doctrine
Mercantile system of accounting
Principle of true and correct profit computation

card.dispute: Mineral Development Ltd. challenged the cancellation of its mica mining licence by the Bihar government, alleging violation of fundamental rights and lack of reasonable opportunity to be heard.
issues_decided: Whether the cancellation of the mining licence under Section 25(1)(c) of the Bihar Mica Act, 1947, violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution?
Whether the requirement of 'repeated failure' under Section 25(1)(c) was satisfied in this case?
Whether the petitioner was afforded a reasonable opportunity to show cause before cancellation of the licence, as required by the second proviso to Section 25(1)?
holdings: The cancellation of the licence under Section 25(1)(c) without proof of 'repeated failure' to comply with the Act was invalid and violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g).
The condition of 'repeated failure' under Section 25(1)(c) was not met, as the alleged violations stemmed from a single inspection and were not substantiated as recurring defaults.

The petitioner was not given a reasonable opportunity to show cause, especially since no further hearing was held after submission of explanation, and seized records were not returned, violating principles of fair procedure.
doctrines: Principle of reasonable opportunity in administrative action
Test of reasonableness in restrictions on fundamental rights
Doctrine of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The Maharajadhiraj challenged the State of Bihar's reassessment of income from leasehold properties, claiming it was a capital receipt from a loan, not taxable agricultural income, and that the tax officer lacked power to revise his own exemption order.
issues_decided: Whether the Agricultural Income-tax Officer had jurisdiction under Section 26 of the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1938, to revise his own order of exemption and assess income that had been disclosed in the return but initially treated as non-taxable.
Whether the income received from the zarpeshgi leasehold properties constituted agricultural income assessable to tax, or was a capital receipt in repayment of a loan.
holdings: The Agricultural Income-tax Officer has the power under Section 26 to revise his own order and assess income that escaped taxation, even if it was disclosed in the return and initially treated as exempt, provided it was an error in assessment.

The amount paid under the zarpeshgi lease was a premium, not a loan, and the income derived from the leasehold agricultural land was agricultural income, assessable under the Act, regardless of the recipient's characterization of it as capital receipt.
doctrines: Power of tax officer to revise own order for escaped assessment
Substance over form in characterizing receipts for tax purposes
Tests for distinguishing lease with premium from mortgage under transfer law

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of land from the tenant for non-payment of rent for three consecutive years under a Mulegeni deed, but the tenant argued that the tenancy could not be terminated without prior notice.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy was validly terminated without the landlord giving prior notice of termination as required under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as applied by the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the Bombay Revenue Tribunal’s decision requiring prior notice for termination was an error apparent on the face of the record, justifying a writ of certiorari by the High Court.
holdings: Under Section 3 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, the provisions of Chapter V of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, apply to tenancies covered by the Act, and Section 111(g) requires written notice of termination for forfeiture due to breach of condition, even if the lease allows re-entry on default.
An error that requires detailed legal argument and is not self-evident cannot be considered an error apparent on the face of the record, and thus cannot be corrected by a writ of certiorari.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 3
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25
doctrines: Interpretation of beneficial legislation in favour of tenants
Error apparent on the face of the record
Notice requirement for forfeiture under lease agreements
Application of general property law to tenancy statutes

card.dispute: Whether the conviction of certain accused for causing grievous hurt under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC was valid when no accused was found guilty of the substantive offence of grievous hurt, and murder was committed instead.
issues_decided: Whether members of an unlawful assembly can be convicted under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC when the principal offence committed was murder under Section 302 IPC.
Whether a conviction under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC is invalid in the absence of a proven substantive act of grievous hurt by any specific member.
holdings: Members of an unlawful assembly can be convicted under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC even if the principal offence committed was murder, provided grievous hurt was in furtherance of the common object or was a likely consequence.

Section 149 IPC allows vicarious liability for offences members knew were likely to be committed; thus, conviction for grievous hurt is valid even if no member is separately convicted for it, and murder was actually committed.
doctrines: Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC
Common object of unlawful assembly
Constructive liability in group offences

card.dispute: The appellant, a former ward of the Court of Wards, challenged the validity of compromise decrees in appeals concerning property disputes, arguing that the Court of Wards failed to appoint statutory representatives as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to appoint a representative under Section 56 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, renders proceedings invalid
Whether the word 'shall' in Section 56 is mandatory or directory
Whether non-compliance with Section 56 affects the validity of a compromise decree
holdings: Section 56 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, mandates the appointment of a representative for a ward, and the word 'shall' in the provision is imperative, not discretionary.
Proceedings conducted without the statutory representative of a ward, as required by Section 56, are null and void, including any compromise decree passed therein.
The compromise decrees in the appeals were invalid because the Court of Wards failed to appoint separate representatives, resulting in the same officer acting for both parties.
provisions: U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, Section 56
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXII
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Nullity of proceedings for non-compliance with mandatory statutory requirements
Legislative intent as the key to statutory construction

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether a deed described as a sale was actually a mortgage by conditional sale, entitling the transferors to redeem the property.
issues_decided: Whether the deed dated September 10, 1931, was a sale or a mortgage by conditional sale.
Whether the unregistered agreement to pay interest at 9% is admissible in evidence.
Whether the consideration in the deed was adequate to support a sale.
Whether the surrounding circumstances and conduct of the parties indicate a mortgage.
holdings: A deed described as a sale is a mortgage by conditional sale if the dominant intention is to secure a debt and there is a provision for reconveyance on repayment.
An unregistered agreement containing a personal covenant to pay interest is admissible in evidence even if it relates to immovable property, as it does not create or transfer an interest in land.
Inadequacy of consideration, when substantial, supports the inference that the transaction is a mortgage rather than a sale.
Contemporaneous conduct and surrounding circumstances, including the right to reconvey within a fixed period and the obligation to pay interest, indicate a mortgage rather than an absolute sale.
doctrines: Mortgage by conditional sale
Dominant intention doctrine
Admissibility of personal covenants without registration
Inadequacy of consideration as indicium of mortgage

card.dispute: The respondents sued to declare a deed of trust in favor of a deity (Pares Nath Thakur) as sham and fictitious, seeking to have the properties sold in execution of their decree, while the deity resisted the claim.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of trust executed in favor of the deity was a fictitious document?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal?
On whom lay the burden of proof in a suit challenging the validity of a registered deed of trust and an order upholding a third-party claim in execution?
holdings: A question of whether a trust deed is fictitious is essentially a question of fact, and cannot be re-examined in second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved.

The High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact by misplacing the burden of proof, which properly lay on the plaintiffs to prove the deed was fictitious and the execution court's order erroneous.
The burden is especially heavy on a plaintiff seeking to set aside a court order upholding a third-party claim under Order 21, Rule 60 of the CPC based on a registered deed of trust.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 60
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 63
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact rule
Burden of proof in challenging registered documents
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The appellant, Prem Nath Kaul, challenged the validity of the Jammu and Kashmir Big Landed Estate Abolition Act, XVII of 2007, enacted by Yuvaraj Karan Singh, claiming it was ultra vires and that he was entitled to retain possession of his land.
issues_decided: Whether Yuvaraj Karan Singh had the legislative competence to enact the Big Landed Estate Abolition Act in 1950.
Whether the application of certain provisions of the Indian Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir, including Article 370, had stripped the Yuvaraj of plenary legislative powers.
Whether the Act was invalid for not providing compensation to landowners.
Whether the Act was invalid due to repugnancy with earlier central laws under Article 254 of the Indian Constitution.
holdings: Yuvaraj Karan Singh was vested with full legislative powers by Maharaja Hari Singh’s 1949 proclamation and was competent to enact the Big Landed Estate Abolition Act in 1950.
The application of Articles like 245, 254, 255, and 385 to Jammu and Kashmir was notional and did not alter the plenary powers of the State’s ruler at the time.
The absence of immediate compensation under the Act did not invalidate it, as the State’s law at the time did not require it, and later constitutional changes preserved the Act under Article 31(5).
Article 254 of the Indian Constitution was inapplicable because the Concurrent List and related constitutional framework had not been extended to Jammu and Kashmir at the time.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Constitution Act, 14 of 1996 (1930), Section 5
doctrines: Plenary legislative power
Notional application of constitutional provisions
Doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254
Rule of construction from Maxwell's Interpretation of Statutes
Doctrine of constitutional competence

card.dispute: The State of Saurashtra appealed against a decree in favor of Memon Haji Ismail Haji, who had sued for a declaration that an Administrator's order resuming his immovable property was illegal.
issues_decided: Whether the resumption of property by the Administrator of Junagadh before formal annexation by India was an act of State.
Whether such an act of State is justiciable in municipal courts.
holdings: The assumption of administration of Junagadh by the Dominion of India was an act of State, and any resumption of property by the Administrator during that period was part of that sovereign act.
An act of State performed by the sovereign power against aliens outside the State is not justiciable in municipal courts, even if arbitrary, unless the sovereign purported to act under domestic law.
doctrines: Act of State doctrine
Non-justiciability of sovereign acts in municipal courts
Status of former princely states post-paramountcy lapse

card.dispute: The appellant collateral challenged the respondent sister's claim to inherit her brother's self-acquired property under a claimed customary law of the Punjab.
issues_decided: Whether a sister can inherit her brother's self-acquired property in preference to collaterals under a special custom of the Jat agriculturists of the Punjab.
Whether a general custom excluding sisters from inheritance to non-ancestral property, as recorded in Rattigan's Digest, is entitled to judicial notice.
Whether the respondent could rely on Hindu law as a fallback after failing to prove the custom.
holdings: A sister can inherit her brother's self-acquired property in preference to collaterals if a valid local custom is proved, as such customs are not negated by general statements in Rattigan's Digest without specific application to self-acquired property.

No general custom excluding sisters from inheriting self-acquired property can be presumed; all customs must be specifically proved and are not entitled to judicial notice under Section 57(1) of the Evidence Act unless consistently recognized by courts.

Even if the custom were not proved, the respondent could rely on Hindu law as the personal law under Section 5 of the Punjab Laws Act, since the appellant failed to prove any contrary custom, and the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929, gives sisters preferential heir status over collaterals.
doctrines: Judicial notice of custom
Burden of proof in establishing customary law
Primacy of personal law in absence of proved custom
Hierarchy of rules of succession under the Punjab Laws Act

card.dispute: The petitioners, co-sharers in a composite property, challenged the Deputy Custodian's sale of the entire property after the evacuee co-sharer's interest was vested in the Custodian, claiming violations of fundamental rights and invalid vesting.
issues_decided: Whether the vesting of the evacuee's property in the Custodian under an invalid ordinance was validated by subsequent legislation, particularly the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1960
Whether the property in question was composite property under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951
Whether the sale of the entire composite property under s. 10 of the 1951 Act violated Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution
holdings: The retrospective validation under s. 8(2A) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, inserted by Act 1 of 1960, cured any initial invalidity in the vesting of evacuee property, deeming it validly vested even if originally defective.
Property in which an evacuee held a share and which could not be physically partitioned qualifies as composite property under the 1951 Act, justifying separation of interests through sale.

The sale of composite property under s. 10(1)(a)(iii) does not violate Articles 19(1)(f) or 31, as it is a lawful measure for separating evacuee interests when partition is impracticable and alternatives are unavailing.
provisions: U.P. Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, Sections 2(c) and 5
Administration of Evacuee Property (Chief Commissioner's Provinces) Ordinance, 1949, Section 5
Administration of Evacuee Property (Chief Commissioner's Provinces) Amendment Ordinance, 1949, Section 8
Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949 (Ordinance XXVII of 1949), Sections 7 and 8
Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Ordinance, 1950, Section 4
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (Act XXXI of 1950), Sections 7 and 8
Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1960 (Act 1 of 1960), Section 2 (inserting s. 8(2A))
Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 (Act LXIV of 1951), Section 10
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective validation
Doctrine of deeming provisions
Doctrine of legislative competence and continuity of vesting
Doctrine of proportionality in property rights under fundamental rights

card.dispute: The heirs of Ramasami Pillai fought with the Sri Subramaniaswami Devasthanam over whether Ramasami Pillai, who was insane when succession opened, could inherit property and whether a family arrangement entitled him to a share.
issues_decided: Whether insanity must be congenital to disqualify a Hindu from inheritance under customary law
Whether a family arrangement entitled Ramasami Pillai to a share in the property despite his disqualification
Whether the Devasthanam's suit for possession of certain properties was barred by delay in execution of a prior decree
holdings: Under Hindu law, insanity (unmatha) need not be congenital to exclude a person from inheritance; it is sufficient if it exists when succession opens.
The alleged family arrangement was not proved, as the affidavit relied upon did not establish a completed compromise and key parties were not examined.
The Devasthanam was entitled to possession of the properties in Schedule 4-A, as there was evidence that M. Picha Pillai had obtained possession otherwise than through decree execution.
provisions: Hindu Inheritance (Removal of Disabilities) Act, 1928, Section 1
doctrines: Mimamsa rules of interpretation
Doctrine of precedent in Hindu law
Requirement of proof for family arrangements

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax and Calvary Mount Estates (Private) Ltd. fought over whether expenses for maintaining immature, non-bearing rubber trees could be deducted from agricultural income under the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether expenditure on the upkeep and maintenance of immature non-bearing rubber trees qualifies as a deductible expense under section 5(e) of the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955
Whether the decision under the Travancore Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act on similar facts applies to the present case
holdings: Expenditure incurred on the maintenance of immature rubber trees is deductible under section 5(e) if it is wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation and not of a capital or personal nature.

The decision in Civil Appeals Nos. 290–292 of 1959 under the Travancore Cochin Act applies by analogy, as the provisions are substantially similar and the purpose of the expenditure aligns with the statutory language.
provisions: Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955, Section 5(e)
Travancore Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, Section 5(j)
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation based on similar provisions
Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)

card.dispute: The landlord (Deshraj) sued for fixation of fair rent after prior notice under an ordinance; the tenant (Akhtar Hussain) contested, claiming a fresh notice under the subsequent Act was mandatory.
issues_decided: Whether a fresh notice under Section 7(2) of the United State of Gwalior, Indore and Malwa (Madhya Bharat) Accommodation Control Act, Samvat 2006 (M.B. 15 of 1950) was necessary to institute a suit after the ordinance was replaced by the Act?
Whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to decide the claim when the plaint was returned by the civil court due to the enactment of the Act?
Whether the Rent Controller's order operated retrospectively, exceeding his authority?
holdings: Section 7(2) requires a notice for rent fixation but does not mandate that the notice be given after the Act came into force or in a specific form; a prior notice under the ordinance suffices.
The jurisdiction to fix rent vested in the Rent Controller upon the Act's enforcement; the civil court rightly returned the plaint, and the subsequent suit before the Rent Controller was valid.
The Rent Controller’s order was prospective, not retrospective, and thus within his statutory authority.
provisions: United State of Gwalior, Indore and Malwa (Madhya Bharat) Accommodation Control Act, Samvat 2006 (M.B. 15 of 1950), Section 7(2)
doctrines: Jurisdictional competence of statutory tribunals
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of orders
Notice as a condition precedent in rent control proceedings

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax sought to assess three widows as an 'association of persons' for income tax purposes on income from jointly held assets, which the widows contested.
issues_decided: Whether the three widows constituted an 'association of persons' under Section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether joint receipt of income without joint management or enterprise is sufficient to constitute an association of persons.
holdings: An association of persons under Section 3 requires a combination of individuals joining in a common purpose or action with the object of producing income, profits, or gains.
Mere joint ownership or receipt of income, without any joint activity to produce income, does not constitute an association of persons.
The widows, despite receiving income jointly and not exercising separate enjoyment, did not perform any act contributing to income production and thus did not form an association of persons.
doctrines: ejusdem generis
common purpose test for association of persons
construction of undefined statutory terms in context

card.dispute: The management of Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. and its workmen disputed over the encashment of privilege leave and equal leave entitlements between subordinate and clerical staff.
issues_decided: Whether a long-standing practice of encashing privilege leave became a binding condition of service
Whether subordinate staff are entitled to the same leave benefits as clerical staff
holdings: A consistent practice of encashing privilege leave since 1948 for specified purposes ripened into a condition of service, and its withdrawal in 1957 was unjustified.

Subordinate staff are entitled to 30 days of privilege leave like clerical staff, but cannot be granted more than 12 days combined sick and casual leave as it exceeds the statutory cap under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954.
provisions: Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954, Section 22
doctrines: Service condition by conduct or practice
Statutory limits on judicial or quasi-judicial modification of leave benefits

card.dispute: The company contested whether its income from shops and stalls in a market it developed should be taxed as business income under section 10 or as property income under section 9 of the Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether income from letting out shops and stalls by a company formed to develop markets is taxable as 'profits or gains of business' under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the nature of the company's objects or activities changes the character of rental income from property
holdings: Income from letting out shops and stalls is income from property under section 9, not business income under section 10, even if derived by a company formed to develop markets.
The character of income as arising from property is not altered by the fact that the owner is a company with business objects related to property development or management.
doctrines: Mutually exclusive heads of income
Character of income determined by source, not taxpayer's status or objects

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of personal inams in Bombay, challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, which abolished their rights to pay reduced land revenue and retain the difference, arguing it violated their property rights without compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the rights extinguished by the Act relate to an 'estate' within the meaning of Article 31-A of the Constitution
Whether the Act violates Article 31 for non-provision of compensation
holdings: The right of an inamdar to appropriate the difference between full land assessment and quit-rent is a right in an estate under Article 31-A(2)(b) because it is a privilege in respect of land revenue and inams are explicitly included in the definition of 'estate'.

The absence of compensation for the loss of the inamdar's benefit under Sections 4 and 5 does not invalidate the Act, as Article 31-A protects such laws from challenges under Article 31, which is the sole constitutional source of compensation.
provisions: Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, Sections 4, 5, 7, 17
doctrines: Doctrine of protection under Article 31-A
Definition of 'estate' and 'rights in an estate' under constitutional law

card.dispute: The dispute was between the widow and daughters of a Hindu Jat man and his collaterals over succession to his self-acquired property and the validity of a gift made by the widow to the daughters.
issues_decided: Whether under the customary law of Grewal Jats in Ludhiana, daughters are preferred over collaterals in succession to self-acquired property.
Whether a gift by a Hindu widow of her husband's self-acquired property to her daughters amounts to a valid surrender that accelerates their succession rights.
Whether the doctrine of partial surrender or partial self-effacement is recognized in Hindu law.
holdings: Under the customary law of the Grewal Jats of Ludhiana, daughters are preferential heirs to self-acquired property over collaterals, as established by Rattigan's Digest and not contradicted by Riwaj-i-am, which applies only to ancestral property.
A gift by a Hindu widow of self-acquired property to her daughters does not constitute a valid legal surrender because it is not a complete self-effacement of her interest in the entire property.

The doctrine of surrender in Hindu law requires total effacement of the widow’s interest; partial surrender, whether by retaining property or gifting only part to reversioners, is not legally recognized.
doctrines: Doctrine of surrender in Hindu law
Customary law of succession among Hindu Jats
Theory of complete self-effacement

card.dispute: The Maharani of Morvi State fought with the Income Tax Commissioner over whether her cash annuity of Rs. 35,807, received in lieu of a village grant, qualified as a maintenance allowance exempt from tax under a 1950 taxation order.
issues_decided: Whether the cash annuity of Rs. 35,807 paid to the appellant was a maintenance allowance within the meaning of paragraph 15(1)(i) of the Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the Tribunal's finding that the annuity was maintenance
holdings: A cash annuity paid in lieu of a village granted for maintaining the status and dignity of a ruler's widow qualifies as a maintenance allowance under paragraph 15(1)(i) if the original grant was for maintenance.
The High Court erred in re-evaluating factual findings of the Tribunal; it could not substitute its own view when there was material to support the Tribunal's conclusion.
provisions: Part B States (Taxation Concessions) Order, 1950, paragraph 15(1)(i)
doctrines: Principle of judicial deference to quasi-judicial findings of fact
Substance over form in determining nature of income

card.dispute: The Indian and Pakistani governments disputed the implementation mechanism for the cession of part of Berubari Union and exchange of enclaves, specifically whether parliamentary action under Article 3 or constitutional amendment under Article 368 was required.
issues_decided: Whether the implementation of the Indo-Pakistan Agreement regarding the cession of part of Berubari Union requires legislative action under Article 3 of the Constitution.
Whether such implementation requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
Whether both Article 3 and Article 368 are necessary for implementing the agreement.
holdings: Parliament cannot implement the cession of Indian territory to a foreign state by a law under Article 3, as it applies only to internal territorial adjustments within India.
Cession of Indian territory to a foreign state requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368, as it entails alteration of Article 1 and the First Schedule.
A law under Article 368 alone is sufficient; however, if Parliament first amends Article 3 to include cession powers, then a subsequent law under the amended Article 3 may also be used.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional amendment under Article 368
Doctrine of territorial integrity of the Union of India
Doctrine of implied limitations on Article 3

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the appointment of respondent 4 as Village Munsif of PP based on hereditary descent under the Madras Hereditary Village-Offices Act, 1895, alleging violation of equality rights under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the office of Village Munsif is an 'office under the State' within the meaning of Article 16 of the Constitution
Whether Section 6(1) of the Madras Hereditary Village-Offices Act, 1895, which provides for selection of new office-holders from families of last holders, violates Article 16(2) of the Constitution
Whether the petitioner, having applied under the impugned Act, can challenge its constitutional validity
holdings: The office of Village Munsif is an office under the State and thus subject to the equality provisions of Article 16(1) and (2) of the Constitution.

Section 6(1) of the Madras Hereditary Village-Offices Act, 1895, insofar as it mandates selection from families of last holders, constitutes discrimination on the ground of descent and violates Article 16(2).
A citizen can challenge the constitutional validity of a statute even if they applied under it, especially when fundamental rights are infringed.
doctrines: Equality of opportunity in public employment
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of descent
Enforceability of fundamental rights despite prior invocation of statutory benefits
Voidness of statutory provisions inconsistent with fundamental rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an appeal filed without a certified copy of the decree, arguing it was incompetent and time-barred, while the respondents contended they were entitled to file the appeal once the decree was eventually prepared and copied.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal filed without a certified copy of the decree is incompetent under Order 41, Rule 1 of the CPC when the decree had not been drawn up by the trial court despite an application for a certified copy being made.
Whether the delay in filing the appeal should be condoned when the defect was due to the trial court's failure to draw up the decree and the appellate court's oversight in admitting the appeal.
Whether the High Court had the discretion to allow the filing of a certified copy of the decree after the appeal was admitted and to proceed with the appeal on merits.
holdings: An appeal is not automatically incompetent under Order 41, Rule 1 of the CPC if the decree had not been drawn up by the trial court despite the appellant's application for a certified copy; the defect may be cured by subsequent filing.

The failure to file a certified copy due to the trial court's default does not render the appeal time-barred if the copy is filed as soon as the decree is prepared, and the appellant acted without delay.

The High Court has the discretion to allow an adjournment to cure a procedural defect in filing an appeal when the defect arose from circumstances beyond the appellant's control, and it is just to do so.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 11
doctrines: Procedural law should not defeat justice
Appellate discretion to cure technical defects
Judicial fairness in cases of administrative delay

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of a parliamentary Act that validated the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates Act, which had been struck down due to a defect in the legislature's constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament had the competence to enact a law validating the proceedings of a legislature that was not duly constituted?
Whether the Abolition Act violated the fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution?
Whether the Abolition Act was protected under Article 31A from challenges based on fundamental rights?
holdings: Parliament had the legislative competence under Article 240, read with Entries 248 and 97 of List I, to validate the constitution and proceedings of the Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly despite the defect in its formation.
The provisions of the Abolition Act did not infringe fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31, as the Act provided for compensation and served a public purpose.
The Abolition Act fell within the protection of Article 31A, and thus could not be challenged for violating Articles 14, 19, or 31, especially since it received presidential assent.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 (Himachal 15 of 1954), Sections 11, 15
Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly (Constitution and Proceedings) Validation Act, 1958 (Act No. 56 of 1958), Sections 3, 4
doctrines: Doctrine of validation of legislative proceedings
Doctrine of parliamentary competence under residuary powers
Protection under Article 31A for agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The appellants, two brothers, challenged the Board of Revenue's refusal to allow them to change their method of computing agricultural income for tax purposes, claiming a right to switch methods annually without permission.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 6 of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act restricts an assessee's right to change the method of computation only within a single assessment year or indefinitely without Board permission.
Whether the Board of Revenue applied its mind in refusing permission to change the method of computation.
Whether the proviso to section 6(1) violates Article 14 of the Constitution by conferring unfettered and potentially discriminatory discretion on the Board.
holdings: The proviso to section 6(1) bars an assessee from changing the method of computation once chosen, unless with the Board’s permission; the restriction is not limited to one assessment year.
The Board of Revenue did apply its mind to the appellants’ request, as evidenced by the reasoned note and endorsements leading to the decision.
The discretion conferred by the proviso is not arbitrary or violative of Article 14, as it is exercised by a high authority and guided by the scheme of the Act.
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation based on language and scheme
Non-arbitrariness of discretionary power when exercised by high authority
No violation of equal protection where differential treatment is based on reasonable classification or administrative necessity

card.dispute: The karta of a Hindu undivided family and the Income Tax authorities disputed whether his salary as a bank treasurer, secured by family property, was individual income or joint family income.
issues_decided: Whether the relationship between the treasurer and the bank was that of an employer and independent contractor or master and servant
Whether the emoluments received by the treasurer constituted individual income or income of the Hindu undivided family
holdings: The treasurer was a servant of the bank, not an independent contractor, because the bank exercised sufficient control over his duties and appointment.
The salary received by the treasurer was his individual income, not part of the joint family income, as there was no outlay or detriment to family property in securing the post.
doctrines: Master-servant relationship test based on control and supervision
Principle of partible family income based on detriment to or use of joint family property

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of Section 39 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866, after his application for an eating house license was refused by the Commissioner of Police without a hearing.
issues_decided: Whether Section 39 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866, violates the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution by conferring arbitrary and unguided discretion on the Commissioner to grant or refuse licenses?
Whether the absence of procedural safeguards in Section 39 renders it an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(6)?
Whether a writ of mandamus should issue to restrain criminal proceedings based on the invalid license provision?
holdings: Section 39 of the Calcutta Police Act, 1866, infringes Article 19(1)(g) as it grants unguided and arbitrary discretion to the Commissioner without objective criteria to regulate the grant or refusal of licenses.
The lack of procedural fairness, such as a right to hearing, reasoned order, or appeal, makes the restriction unreasonable under Article 19(6), rendering the section constitutionally invalid.
A writ of mandamus issues to prohibit further criminal proceedings against the petitioner for operating without a license under the now-invalid Section 39.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6)
Procedural fairness in administrative discretion
Severability and constitutional validity of pre-constitutional statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a thika tenant, fought against the Administrator-General of West Bengal over whether he was entitled to relief under Section 28 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, despite the section's retrospective omission by the 1953 Amendment Act while his application was pending.
issues_decided: Whether a pending application for relief under Section 28 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, could be decided in favour of the tenant after the section was omitted retrospectively by the 1953 Amendment Act.
Whether Section 1(2) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953, operates to deny relief under the omitted Section 28 in pending cases.
Whether the amendment should be interpreted in a manner favourable to tenants due to its beneficent nature.
holdings: Section 1(2) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953, clearly and retrospectively removed the applicability of Section 28, even to pending applications, and no relief could be granted under it.
The amended Act, in its new form, must be deemed to have always applied to pending proceedings, including those under Section 28, thereby extinguishing the court’s power to grant relief.
Courts must apply the plain grammatical meaning of statutory language even in beneficent legislation, and cannot create ambiguity to favour a particular outcome when none exists.
doctrines: Principle of retrospective operation of statutes
Plain meaning rule in statutory interpretation
Rule of beneficial construction in ambiguous beneficent legislation
Doctrine of judicial propriety in overruling precedent

card.dispute: The Maharajadhiraja claimed that his trustee remuneration, calculated as 15% of agricultural income from trust lands, was exempt from income tax as agricultural income, while the Commissioner of Income-Tax contended it was taxable as it was remuneration for services, not agricultural rent or revenue.
issues_decided: Whether remuneration received by a trustee from agricultural income of trust property qualifies as 'agricultural income' under Section 2(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether such remuneration is exempt from taxation under Section 4(3)(viii) of the Act
holdings: The source of the trustee's remuneration is the covenant in the trust deed for services rendered, not the right to receive rent or revenue from agricultural land, so it does not qualify as agricultural income under Section 2(1)(a).

The character of income changes when appropriated as remuneration; even if computed as a percentage of agricultural income, it loses its agricultural character and is not exempt under Section 4(3)(viii).
doctrines: Character and source doctrine in determining agricultural income
Principle that income does not inherit the character of its source when received under a contractual obligation for services

card.dispute: The Maharaja and the Income Tax Commissioner disputed whether payments received by the Maharaja from granting bauxite prospecting licences were capital or revenue receipts for tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the amounts received by the appellant from granting prospecting licences constituted capital or revenue receipts under the Income Tax Act.
Whether the right granted under the prospecting licence amounted to a transfer of a portion of capital asset or merely a right to use the capital asset.
holdings: The payments received by the appellant for granting prospecting licences were capital receipts because they represented a transfer of a right to a portion of the capital asset (bauxite), not merely its use.
A grant allowing the licensee to enter, dig, and take away bauxite samples up to 100 tons constituted a realisation of the capital asset, not a revenue-generating use of it.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Nature of salami as a capital receipt
Realisation of capital asset versus user of capital asset

card.dispute: Displaced persons from West Pakistan challenged the validity of rules limiting compensation for rural houses on grounds of violation of Article 14, claiming denial of equal protection of laws.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 5 of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954, and Rule 65 of the Rules under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation Act), 1954, violate Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the classification between rural and urban evacuee properties, and between substantial and non-substantial rural buildings, is arbitrary and discriminatory?
Whether the valuation thresholds (Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 20,000) for rural houses constitute an unreasonable classification?
holdings: The classification under the impugned rules is not arbitrary but has a reasonable nexus with the object of equitable rehabilitation of displaced persons.
Distinction between rural and urban properties, and between types of rural buildings, is based on intelligible differentia and valid under Article 14.
The valuation thresholds for compensation are justified by Inter-Dominion Agreements and practical administrative needs, and do not violate equality.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954 (Act 12 of 1954), Rule 5
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation Act), 1954 (Act 44 of 1954), Rule 65
East Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948 (East Punjab Act 12 of 1948)
doctrines: Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Reasonable nexus test
Principle of equitable rehabilitation in post-partition context

card.dispute: Displaced persons from West Pakistan challenged the validity of rules that denied them compensation for rural buildings unless their claims exceeded Rs. 10,000 or Rs. 20,000, alleging discrimination under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 5 of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954, and Rule 65 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, violate Article 14 by creating arbitrary classifications?
Whether the classification based on the value of rural buildings and size of land allotted has a rational nexus with the object of rehabilitation?
Whether the rules denying compensation for rural buildings below specified values are discriminatory and unconstitutional?
holdings: The classification under the rules is not arbitrary and satisfies the test of Article 14 as it is based on intelligible differentia linked to rehabilitation policy.
There is a reasonable nexus between the classification (landholding size and building value) and the object of equitable rehabilitation of displaced persons.
The rules do not violate Article 14 because they operate within a comprehensive scheme that provides alternative compensation through housing allotments or rehabilitation grants.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Rule 65
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonable classification under Article 14
Principle of equal protection of laws
Rational nexus test

card.dispute: The appellants, municipal rate-payers, challenged the validity of sales of municipal land by a continuing committee of the old elected members, arguing they were functus officio after the new Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether the members of the municipal committee continued under the repealing Act were functus officio after three years from the commencement of the new Act due to inapplicability of term provisions?
Whether the new Act provided for holding the first general election to constitute a new committee?
Whether the continuing committee had the power to sell municipal land?
holdings: The members of the old committee were not functus officio merely because three years had passed, as their term continued until the first meeting of the newly elected committee under the new Act.

Section 16(1) of the Hyderabad District Municipalities Act, 1956 must be read as authorizing the first general election, with the time requirement inapplicable to it, to give effect to legislative intent.
The continuing municipal committee, duly sanctioned by the government, had the power to sell municipal land.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation with modification to avoid absurdity
Mischief rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of functus officio
Principle of reading down a statute to give effect to legislative intent

card.dispute: The managing agent of a company challenged the validity of investigation notices issued under the Companies Act, arguing they violated constitutional protections against self-incrimination and equality.
issues_decided: Whether the investigation proceedings under Section 240 of the Companies Act, 1956 violate Article 20(3) of the Constitution by compelling self-incrimination
Whether the provisions enabling investigation under Sections 239 and 240 of the Companies Act, 1956 violate Article 14 by creating an unreasonable classification
holdings: Investigation under Section 240 is not a criminal proceeding, and the requirement to produce documents or give evidence does not amount to being 'accused of an offence', so Article 20(3) is not violated.

The classification of company managers as a distinct class subject to investigative powers is based on intelligible differentia and bears a rational relation to the object of the Companies Act, so Article 14 is not violated.
doctrines: Testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3)
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Prospective application of statutory investigation powers

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's confirmation of a decree allowing the respondent to exercise a right of pre-emption based on alleged co-occupancy, arguing that no valid sale had occurred at the time the suit was filed.
issues_decided: Whether a right of pre-emption under the Berar Land Revenue Code can arise before a valid and registered sale is completed under the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether a contract for sale, without registration, can trigger the right of pre-emption.
Whether the appellant's delay in executing the sale deed constituted fraud to defeat the pre-emptor's right.
holdings: A right of pre-emption arises only after a valid and registered sale under the Transfer of Property Act; until ownership is transferred, no pre-emptible transaction exists.
A mere contract for sale does not transfer any interest in immovable property and cannot be the basis for enforcing pre-emption rights.
Parties may lawfully avoid the accrual of pre-emption rights by delaying registration, and such conduct does not amount to fraud if no completed sale exists when the suit is filed.
provisions: Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, Chapter XIV
doctrines: Condition precedent of valid sale for pre-emption
Inapplicability of personal law where statutory transfer law applies
Pre-emption as a weak statutory right not favoured by courts

card.dispute: The appellant contested the respondents' application under the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, arguing that a mortgage debt on property in India was not a 'debt' under the Act and thus not recoverable.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgage debt constitutes a 'pecuniary liability' under Section 2(6) of the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, 1951
Whether the Act applies to mortgage debts secured on immovable property situated in India
Whether the rights of prior or subsequent mortgagees are prejudicially affected by a decree under Section 13 of the Act
holdings: A mortgage debt creates a pecuniary liability and falls within the definition of 'debt' under Section 2(6) of the Act.
The Act applies to mortgage debts secured on property in India, as there is no restriction in the Act limiting its scope to properties in West Pakistan.
A decree under Section 13 of the Act does not affect the rights of prior or subsequent mortgagees, whose interests remain protected.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXXIV, Rule 1
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Overriding effect of special statutes
Protection of third-party interests in mortgage enforcement

card.dispute: The appellant, a holder of a personal inam, challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, and the Collector's order imposing non-agricultural land assessment on his inam land in Surat.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, is constitutionally valid under Article 31-A of the Constitution?
Whether the Sanad granted to the inamdar makes the terms immutable and prevents the State from abolishing the inam?
Whether the Collector was correct in assessing the inam land under Section 52 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, as non-agricultural land?
Whether Section 52 of the Code applies when an assessment is deemed to exist under Chapter VIII-A by virtue of Section 117-R?
holdings: The Act is constitutionally valid as it falls within the protection of Article 31-A, which permits abolition of personal inams without payment of compensation.
The grant of a Sanad does not make the inam terms immutable; the State can abolish inams by law, as upheld in prior decisions.
Section 7 of the Act does not exempt non-agricultural inam lands from full assessment under Sections 4 and 5; it only prevents vesting of such lands in the State.
Section 52 applies because no actual assessment was made under Chapter VIII-A; the deeming provision in Section 117-R does not constitute a real assessment under that Chapter.
provisions: Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952, Sections 4, 5, 7
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional protection for agrarian reform laws under Article 31-A
Doctrine of statutory interpretation: deeming provisions do not override actual legislative intent
Doctrine that rights under Sanads are not immune from legislative abolition

card.dispute: The appellants, members of a Rajput group, challenged the High Court's conviction and sentence in a rioting case where they were found guilty of culpable homicide following a temple dispute with cultivators.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Judge's acquittal of the appellants.
Whether the High Court's findings on the existence of an unlawful assembly and common object were legally sound.
Whether the prosecution's evidence, particularly of key witnesses, was reliable enough to sustain conviction.
Whether the appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution warranted interference with the High Court's factual findings.
holdings: The High Court correctly reversed the acquittal as the Sessions Judge erred in rejecting credible and consistent prosecution evidence without valid reason.
The appellants were members of an unlawful assembly with a common object to beat the cultivators, justifying conviction under Section 149 IPC.
The evidence of prosecution witnesses Goga, Chandra, and Doongar Singh was natural, consistent, and corroborated, and thus reliable for conviction.
No substantial or grave injustice was done, and the High Court's findings did not shock the judicial conscience, so interference under Article 136 was unwarranted.
doctrines: Principle of substantial and compelling reason for interference in appeals against acquittal
Doctrine of unlawful assembly and common object under Section 149 IPC
Principle of natural and consistent testimony outweighing minor discrepancies
Doctrine of limited appellate review of factual findings in criminal cases

card.dispute: The natural guardian of two minor children, who had migrated to West Pakistan, fought against the State of Madhya Bharat and another guardian over the custody and management of the minors' property, claiming misappropriation and violation of personal law rights.
issues_decided: Whether a right to guardianship under personal law can be enforced through a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution
Whether the decision of a competent court appointing a guardian bars a constitutional remedy under Article 32
Whether misappropriation of minors' property by a court-appointed guardian can be challenged via a writ petition under Article 32
holdings: A right to guardianship under personal law is not a fundamental right enforceable under Article 32 of the Constitution.
The decision of a competent court appointing a guardian cannot be circumvented by a petition under Article 32; judicial orders must be challenged through appeals, not constitutional writs.
Claims of property misappropriation by a guardian must be pursued through civil suits or proceedings under the Guardian and Wards Act, not through Article 32.
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedies
Enforceability of fundamental rights only under Part III
Non-justiciability of civil rights via constitutional writs when alternate remedies exist

card.dispute: The former Ruler of Sonepur challenged the State of Orissa's assessment of agricultural income tax on his private property, claiming immunity under a merger agreement and exclusion from the definition of 'person' under the tax law.
issues_decided: Whether the merger agreement guaranteed immunity from agricultural income tax on the ex-Ruler's private property.
Whether the amendment to the definition of 'person' in the Orissa Agricultural Income-tax Act excluded ex-Rulers from tax liability.
Whether the guarantee under Articles 4 and 5 of the merger agreement is enforceable in court despite Article 363 of the Constitution.
holdings: The personal rights and privileges guaranteed under the merger agreement do not extend to immunity from taxation of private property.
The deletion of 'Ruler of an Indian State' from the definition of 'person' was a formal amendment due to political changes and did not intend to exempt ex-Rulers from tax liability.
Article 362 of the Constitution requires due regard to merger agreements but does not create justiciable rights; such guarantees cannot be enforced in court if legislation is inconsistent with them.
doctrines: Non-justiciability of political assurances under Article 363
Distinction between personal privileges and property rights
Prospective operation of constitutional and legislative changes

card.dispute: The appellants, deriving agricultural income from land acquired by the Calcutta Municipal authorities, fought the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether such income was exempt from tax as agricultural income under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the land, after acquisition and lump-sum redemption of land revenue, remained assessed to land revenue within the meaning of the Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether agricultural income from the land qualified as 'agricultural income' exempt from taxation under s. 2(1)(a) of the Act
holdings: The land ceased to be assessed to land revenue after the Government accepted a lump-sum payment equivalent to 20 years' purchase, which extinguished all future liability to land revenue.

As the land was permanently discharged from land revenue, income derived from it did not qualify as 'agricultural income' under s. 2(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and thus was not exempt from taxation.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1857 (Act VI of 1857), Section XXVI
doctrines: Redemption of land revenue by capitalised lump-sum payment
Extinguishment of assessment through conveyance discharging all revenue liability
Interpretation of deeds: use of recitals to resolve ambiguity in operative terms

card.dispute: Jagirdars challenged the constitutional validity of regulations abolishing and commuting jagirs, claiming they were a colourable exercise of legislative power and violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Military Governor was conferred legislative authority by the Nizam's Farman of September 19, 1948
Whether the legislative authority of the Military Governor was subject to limitations or reservations
Whether the Abolition and Commutation Regulations were a colourable exercise of legislative power
Whether the Regulations violated the fundamental rights of the jagirdars under the Constitution
holdings: The Military Governor was vested with full administrative authority, including legislative power, by the Nizam's Farman, as the phrase 'all authority for the administration of the State' encompassed legislative, executive, and judicial powers.

The legislative authority delegated to the Military Governor was not circumscribed by implied limitations; the Nizam retained sovereignty but did not impose restrictions on extinguishing jagirdars' rights.
The doctrine of colourable legislation does not apply to a delegate of sovereign power whose authority is not constitutionally limited; thus, the Regulations cannot be invalidated on that ground.

The Regulations extinguished jagirdars' rights before the Constitution came into force, and the Constitution does not have retrospective effect to revive extinguished rights or invalidate pre-constitutional laws.
provisions: Hyderabad (Abolition of Jagirs) Regulation, 1358 Fasli, s. 6(4)
Hyderabad Jagir (Commutation) Regulation, XXV of 1359 Fasli, s. 4(1)(c), 4(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of delegation of sovereign authority
Non-retrospectivity of the Constitution
Immunity of laws in the Ninth Schedule under Art. 31(B)

card.dispute: The assessee and the Commissioner of Income-Tax disputed whether a partition of a Hindu undivided family in 1944 was genuine and entitled to tax benefits under the Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether there was legal evidence to support the Tribunal's finding that the partition was not genuine and not meant to be acted upon in the first appeal?
Whether there was legal evidence to support the finding that the partition dated December 30, 1944, was genuine and effective in the second appeal?
holdings: The Tribunal's finding that the October 16, 1944 partition was not genuine was based on sufficient material, and the High Court rightly upheld it.
The December 30, 1944 partition was supported by additional evidence, including sworn statements of the sons, and the Tribunal was justified in treating it as genuine and effective.
doctrines: Genuineness of partition depends on factual evidence and intent to divide
Findings of fact by tribunals can be upheld if supported by legal evidence

card.dispute: The appellant-landlords challenged the rescission of their ejectment decree in favour of respondent-tenants who claimed protection under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, after amendments had omitted the relevant provision.
issues_decided: Whether an order of remand by the High Court, not appealed against, can be challenged in an appeal from the final order?
Whether Section 28 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, remained applicable to pending proceedings after it was omitted by the 1953 Amendment Act?
holdings: An order of remand is interlocutory and does not terminate proceedings; its correctness can be challenged in an appeal from the final order if no appeal was available or was not taken.
Section 28 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act ceased to be applicable to pending proceedings upon its omission by the 1953 Amendment Act, and could not be invoked thereafter.
provisions: The Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, Section 28
The Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953, Section 1(2)
doctrines: Res judicata
Interlocutory order
Prospective and retrospective operation of statutes
Jurisdiction of court to rescind decree

card.dispute: The mortgagor applied for relief under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act, 1934, seeking reduction of interest to the amount of unpaid principal on the date of application, while the mortgagee resisted, arguing the earlier decree should stand.
issues_decided: Whether the finding of a civil court decree can be accepted if it results in interest exceeding the unpaid principal on the date of application under s. 14(4)(a) of the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act, 1934?
Whether the date of the suit or the date of the application determines the applicability of the interest cap under s. 14(4)(a)?
Whether a prior decree bars the Special Judge from modifying the amount due under the Act?
holdings: The Special Judge must ensure that the interest held due on the date of application does not exceed the unpaid principal on that date, regardless of the earlier decree.
The words 'on the date of the application' in s. 14(4)(a) are mandatory and must be applied to benefit the applicant, even if the decree was passed before the application.
A prior decree is not binding if its effect is inconsistent with s. 14(4)(a), and the Special Judge must modify the finding to comply with the statutory cap on interest.
doctrines: Beneficial construction of remedial legislation
Inconsistency doctrine in statutory interpretation
Legislative intent to protect encumbered landowners

card.dispute: The decree-holders sought further execution for eviction after having previously accepted symbolic possession and allowed the judgment-debtor to remain on the premises, which the respondents resisted on the ground that the decree had already been fully executed.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for khas possession can be partially executed with a view to later seek full physical eviction.
Whether a fresh execution proceeding is permissible after the decree-holder has acknowledged full delivery of possession.
Whether a purchaser from the respondent before the appeal could be added as a party to the appeal.
holdings: A decree-holder who accepts symbolic possession and acknowledges full delivery cannot later seek further execution for physical eviction, as the decree is deemed fully executed.
Once a decree is fully executed and the execution case is dismissed on that basis, no further execution proceeding is permissible.
A purchaser from the respondent under a conveyance made prior to the appeal can be added as a party to the appeal, following the principle in Saila Bala Dassi v. Nirmala Sundari Dassi.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 35
doctrines: Full execution bars further execution
Principle of approbate and reprobate
Representation of transferee pendente lite

card.dispute: The appellants (adopted son and his guardian) challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by the respondents seeking a declaration that the adoption was factually and legally invalid, after the adoption had been confirmed by the Central Government under the Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877.
issues_decided: Whether the confirmation of an adoption by the Central Government under the third proviso to Section 23 of the Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877, bars a civil suit challenging the factum and validity of the adoption?
Whether Section 119 of the Regulation, read with Section 23, ousts the jurisdiction of civil courts to examine the legality and factum of an adoption once confirmed by the Central Government?
holdings: The confirmation of an adoption by the Central Government under the third proviso to Section 23 involves a determination of both the widow's power to adopt and the factum of adoption, and thus such matters cannot be re-agitated in a civil court.

Section 119 of the Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877, bars civil courts from entertaining suits that challenge decisions made under the Regulation, including the confirmation of adoption under Section 23, as such decisions are deemed legally and rightly done.
provisions: Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877, Section 23
Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877, Section 24
Ajmer Land and Revenue Regulation, 1877, Section 119
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction by statutory provision
Deemed validity of administrative decisions
Finality of executive confirmation in succession matters

card.dispute: The Associated Hotels of India Ltd. and its managing director fought with R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthalia over the execution in India of a decree passed by the Federal Court of Pakistan, and whether Pakistani evacuee laws invalidated their right to recover the decretal amount.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed by the Federal Court of Pakistan could be executed in India under the Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947
Whether the decree was rendered ineffective by Pakistan's evacuee property laws
Whether the situs of a foreign judgment debt determines its enforceability in India
Whether a transfer certificate was required to execute the decree in India
holdings: Decrees of courts in territories that became Pakistan, if part of proceedings pending before Partition, are deemed decrees of competent courts in India and are executable without being treated as foreign judgments.
The evacuee laws of Pakistan do not affect the validity or enforceability of a decree in India, especially where the Custodian did not treat the decree as evacuee property before January 1, 1957.

The situs of a judgment debt for enforcement purposes is not confined to where it was recorded; it may also be enforceable where the judgment-debtor resides, particularly in the context of post-Partition realities.

No transfer certificate is required to execute a decree passed by a Pakistani court in India if the decree is deemed effective under Article 4 of the Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947.
provisions: Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947, Article 4, Clauses 1, 2, 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 45, Rule 15
Pakistan Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, Section 11, Section 13, Section 6
Pakistan (Administration of Evacuee Property) Act, 1957, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Legal fiction of continuity of jurisdiction post-Partition
Situs of judgment debts in conflict of laws
Deeming provisions in statutory interpretation
Effect of foreign evacuee or enemy property laws on Indian enforcement

card.dispute: The State of Kerala and tax authorities versus C. M. Francis & Co over whether sales tax arrears could be recovered under Section 13 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act after a prosecution and warrant for recovery under Section 19 of the Act and Section 386 CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether the remedy under Section 19 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act excludes the remedy under Section 13 of the same Act for recovery of tax arrears.
Whether the authorities can simultaneously or alternatively proceed under both Section 13 and Section 19 for recovering unpaid sales tax.
holdings: The remedies under Sections 13 and 19 of the Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act are not mutually destructive; both are available unless the statute expressly or by necessary implication provides exclusivity.
The tax authorities may choose to proceed under either Section 13 or Section 19, or both, for recovery of arrears, as the provisions do not oust each other.
provisions: Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act, Section 13
Travancore Cochin General Sales Tax Act, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of multiple remedies
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of no implied exclusion of remedies

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of government ghatwali tenures, challenged the applicability of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, arguing their tenures could not be acquired by the State due to special status, legislative competence, and non-repeal of Bengal Regulation XXIX of 1814.
issues_decided: Whether government ghatwali tenures are excluded from the operation of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 under Sections 23(1)(f) and 32(4)?
Whether the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, falls outside the legislative competence of the State Legislature as it pertains to Entries 1 and 2 of List I (Defence and Armed Forces)?
Whether the Act overrides Bengal Regulation XXIX of 1814, a special law governing ghatwali tenures?
holdings: All ghatwali tenures, including government ghatwalis, fall within the definition of the Act; inapplicability of specific provisions like Sections 23(1)(f) or 32(4) does not exclude such tenures from the Act’s operation.

The pith and substance of the Bihar Land Reforms Act is acquisition of property, which falls under Entry 36, List II, and has no substantial connection to Entries 1 and 2 of List I (Defence and Armed Forces).
The Act, being a valid exercise of legislative power, applies to ghatwali tenures despite Bengal Regulation XXIX of 1814; a prior special law does not bar subsequent general land reform legislation.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I (Entries 1, 2), List II (Entry 36)
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of implied repeal
General law prevails over special law in case of inconsistency, unless constitutionally protected

card.dispute: A jagirdar (landlord) sought recovery of rent as arrears of land revenue under a now-rescinded government notification, while tenants challenged the validity of the proceedings and the notification itself.
issues_decided: Whether the Rajasthan Revenue Courts Act, 1951, repealed Section 85 of the Marwar Tenancy Act, 1949, thereby invalidating the procedure for rent recovery?
Whether the rescission of a notification under Section 85 of the Tenancy Act bars further proceedings on an application made before rescission?
Whether tenants could raise for the first time in the Supreme Court the contention that the notification was invalid due to lack of 'general refusal' to pay rent?
holdings: Section 85 of the Marwar Tenancy Act was not repealed by the Rajasthan Revenue Courts Act, 1951, and continued to operate, requiring its own ex parte procedure for rent recovery applications.

The power of the Revenue Officer to act on an application under Section 85 arises upon a valid application being made while the notification is in force, and such power is not lost upon subsequent rescission of the notification.
The tenants could not raise the validity of the notification for the first time in the Supreme Court, as it was a factual and legal issue not raised before the High Court.
provisions: Rajasthan Revenue Courts (Procedure and Jurisdiction) Act, 1951, Section 2
Rajasthan Revenue Courts (Procedure and Jurisdiction) Act, 1951, Rule 114
doctrines: Continuation of statutory provisions despite enactment of subsequent law
Doctrine of vested power: once jurisdiction is triggered, it is not lost by subsequent withdrawal of enabling condition
