Principle of issue estoppel and waiver: new grounds not raised in lower courts generally not entertained in higher courts

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax challenged the deduction claimed by Calvary Mount Estates (Private) Ltd. for expenses on maintaining immature, non-bearing rubber trees.
issues_decided: Whether expenses incurred on the maintenance and upkeep of immature non-bearing rubber trees are deductible under the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955?
Whether the decision in Travancore Rubber & Tea Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax, Kerala is applicable to this case?
holdings: Expenditure on immature non-bearing rubber trees is deductible under s. 5(e) of the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955, if incurred wholly and exclusively for the plantation.
The judgment in Travancore Rubber & Tea Co. Ltd. applies here, as the provisions of the Madras Act are substantially similar and more favourable to the assessee.
provisions: Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955, Section 5(e)
Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950, Section 5(1)
doctrines: Principle of judicial precedent (stare decisis)
Liberal interpretation of tax deductions for agricultural purposes

card.dispute: The Mineral Development Ltd. challenged whether a mining sub-lease is subject to the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, and rules made under it.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'mining lease' under Section 3(d) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 includes a sub-lease.
Whether the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 made under Sections 5 and 6 of the Act apply to a sub-lease granted after the Act and Rules came into force, even if the original lease predated the Act.
holdings: The term 'mining lease' in Section 3(d) includes a sub-lease, as the nature of the transfer remains a lease regardless of whether the lessor is the owner or a lessee.
Rules made under Sections 5 and 6 apply to sub-leases granted after the Act and Rules came into force, as such sub-leases are 'mining leases' within the Act's definition.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 3(d)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 5
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 6
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Section 7
doctrines: Plain meaning rule
Statutory interpretation in light of legislative purpose
Inclusion of derivative leases within the term 'lease'

card.dispute: The State of Bihar fought Rani Sonabati Kumari over whether the State could be held in contempt for issuing a notification under the Bihar Land Reforms Act after a temporary injunction was granted against it.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Bihar can be proceeded against for contempt under Order 39, Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure for disobeying a temporary injunction?
Whether the publication of a notification under Section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, while an injunction was in force, constitutes disobedience by the State?
Whether the act of issuing the notification can be attributed to the State Government under Article 154(1) of the Constitution?
holdings: The State of Bihar can be held liable for contempt under Order 39, Rule 2(3), CPC, as the provision applies to the State when it is bound by an injunction, by necessary implication.
Issuing a notification under Section 3(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act in defiance of a court injunction constitutes disobedience, enforceable through contempt proceedings.
The act of issuing the notification is attributable to the State Government, as the Governor is responsible for actions of subordinates taken in his name under Article 154(1) of the Constitution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39, Rule 2(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39, Rule 4
doctrines: Contempt of court for disobedience of injunction
Necessary implication in statutory interpretation
Executive responsibility under constitutional governance
Rule of law and judicial authority

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the High Court's quashing of an agricultural income-tax assessment by an Additional Collector, arguing he had valid authority under a retrospectively amended law.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Collector had jurisdiction to assess agricultural income-tax across districts under the original 1949 Act
Whether the 1956 Amending Act retrospectively validated assessments made by Additional Collectors lacking jurisdiction under the original law
Whether a review application under Section 11 of the Amending Act is the exclusive remedy to challenge an order quashed on jurisdictional grounds
holdings: The Additional Collector was not competent to assess tax under the original 1949 Act due to lack of extra-territorial jurisdiction.
The 1956 Amending Act retrospectively validated all prior assessments by Additional Collectors, deeming them lawful as if the amendment existed at the time.
A review under Section 11 of the Amending Act is not the exclusive remedy; an appellate court may uphold an assessment based on the amended law even if a review was rejected.
provisions: United Provinces Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1949 (U.P. Act III of 1949), Section 14
United Provinces Land Revenue Act, 1901 (U.P. Act III of 1901), Section 14(A)
U.P. Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1956 (U.P. Act XIV of 1956), Section 4-a, Section 10, Section 11
doctrines: Retrospective validation of administrative acts
Deemed jurisdiction by statutory amendment
Appellate court's duty to apply amended law

card.dispute: The State of Vindhya Pradesh challenged the judicial commissioner's declaration that certain provisions of the Abolition of Jagirs Act were unconstitutional, while jagirdars contested the Act's overall validity.
issues_decided: Whether Section 22(1) of the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs Act is void as colourable legislation or discriminatory?
Whether Section 37 of the Act, ousting civil court jurisdiction, is repugnant to Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
Whether Clause (4)(e) of the Schedule, dealing with compensation calculation, violates constitutional protection against deprivation of property without compensation?
holdings: Section 22(1) is not colourable legislation as the legislature had competence under Entry 18, List II, and the provision applies to a distinct class of jagirdars, thus not violating equality principles.
Section 37 does not conflict with Section 9 of the CPC, as a valid legislative bar under a competent law excludes civil court jurisdiction, which Section 9 itself contemplates.

Clause (4)(e) of the Schedule is constitutional because the jagirdar retains land and is compensated by relief from land revenue, even if required to pay rent, so no deprivation without compensation occurs.
provisions: Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 22(1)
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 37
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Schedule Clause (4)(e)
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 18, List II
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Classification and equality under constitutional law
Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Protection of property rights under Article 31A

card.dispute: The Superintendent of Central Prison, Fatehgarh, appealed against the release of Ram Manohar Lohia, who was detained for delivering speeches instigating cultivators not to pay enhanced irrigation rates, challenging the constitutional validity of Section 3 of the U.P. Special Powers Act, 1932.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the U.P. Special Powers Act, 1932 imposes a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) in the interest of public order under Article 19(2)
Whether the impugned section can be saved by applying the doctrine of severability
holdings: A restriction on free speech in the interest of public order must have a proximate and reasonable nexus to public order; mere possibility of disturbance is insufficient.

Section 3 is void in its entirety as it lacks a proximate connection between speech and public order and cannot be severed to save a constitutional portion due to inextricable mixing of valid and invalid applications.
doctrines: Proximate connection test for restrictions on free speech
Doctrine of severability in the context of fundamental rights
Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and others fought against Maharaja Brijendra Singh over the constitutional validity of provisions in the U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, particularly two provisos to Section 11 that limited compensation for acquired land.
issues_decided: Whether the two provisos to Section 11(1) of the U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, were unconstitutional for contravening Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935
Whether the inclusion of the impugned Act in the Ninth Schedule via the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, retrospectively protected it from challenges based on pre-constitutional laws
holdings: The two provisos to Section 11(1) could not be challenged on the ground of contravening Section 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935, as Article 31-B read with the Ninth Schedule rendered such challenges invalid.
The inclusion of the Act in the Ninth Schedule protected it from being deemed void or ever having been void, even if it previously contravened rights under the Government of India Act, 1935.
provisions: U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, Section 11
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional validation through the Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of implied incorporation of pre-constitutional rights into fundamental rights
Doctrine of retrospective protection under Article 31-B

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal acquired land from Naba Kumar Seal for settling immigrants without a development scheme; the dispute was whether this acquisition violated fundamental rights and required a development scheme under the law.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, particularly Section 7, violates Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31(2) of the Constitution
Whether a development scheme under Section 5 of the Act is mandatory before or after land acquisition under Section 7 in cases of urgency
holdings: Section 7 of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(f), or 31(2) as it permits reasonable classification and is protected by Article 31B through inclusion in the Ninth Schedule.

The framing of a development scheme under Section 5 is not mandatory in urgent cases under Section 7; such a requirement would render Section 7 ineffective and defeat the legislative purpose of expediting land acquisition for public purposes like immigrant resettlement.
provisions: West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 7
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 5
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 6
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of severability
Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Immunity from fundamental rights challenge under Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule

card.dispute: The Travancore Rubber and Tea Co., Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax, Kerala over whether expenses for maintaining immature rubber trees could be deducted from agricultural income under the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether expenses incurred on the upkeep and maintenance of immature rubber trees constitute a permissible deduction under s. 5(j) of the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950.
Whether the phrase 'the agricultural income' in s. 5(j) limits deductions only to expenses that yield income in the same accounting year.
holdings: Expenditure on the maintenance of immature rubber trees is allowable as a deduction if it is wholly and exclusively for deriving agricultural income, even if the trees do not yield income in the same year.
The use of the definite article 'the' before 'agricultural income' does not restrict deductions to expenses that produce income in the same assessment year; future income from such trees is relevant.
doctrines: Revenue expenditure vs capital expenditure distinction
Principle of deductibility of expenses laid out wholly and exclusively for deriving agricultural income
Interpretation of fiscal statutes in light of business reality and commercial common sense

card.dispute: The Upper Ganges Sugar Mills Ltd. claimed adhivasi rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, 1950, based on its recording as a thekedar in 1356 F, while landlords contested that such possession was not in its own right.
issues_decided: Whether the company, recorded as a thekedar in the 1356 F revenue records, qualified as an 'occupant' under Section 20(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether possession under court-ordered stay or as a thekedar disqualifies a person from being considered an occupant in their own right
holdings: A person recorded as an occupant in the 1356 F Khasra or Khatauni is entitled to adhivasi rights under Section 20(b), regardless of whether the entry describes them as a thekedar, provided the possession was in their own right.
The nature of possession must be determined by evidence beyond the revenue entry; continued recording as thekedar after theka expiry does not negate possession in one’s own right.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20(b)
U.P. Land Revenue Act, Sections 28 and 33
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of occupancy rights based on revenue records

card.dispute: The appellant company claimed ownership of mineral rights on land and challenged the refusal of a quarrying permit, seeking a declaration and mandamus to compel the Collector to grant the permit.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had established ownership of mineral rights in the land based on statutory presumptions or possession.
Whether the Collector's refusal to grant a quarrying permit was legally valid and subject to judicial review.
Whether the repeal of the Delhi (Control of Buildings) Act, 1955 entitled the appellant to a mandamus for issuance of a new permit.
holdings: The presumption under Section 42(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, that minerals belong to the landowner, applies only if a record of rights is produced; absence of such a record prevents invocation of the presumption.
An applicant's prior conduct of seeking permits constitutes an admission against ownership, and mere possession under permit does not raise a presumption of ownership under the Indian Evidence Act.
The repeal of the statute under which the permit was refused does not entitle the applicant to mandamus if no fresh application is pending before the authority at the time of judgment.
doctrines: Presumption of ownership under statutory record of rights
Admission by conduct
Mandamus requires a pending application or legal right enforceable at the time of judgment
Non-justiciability of government discretion in resource management absent statutory rights

card.dispute: The appellant, a Sub-Divisional Magistrate, was convicted of contempt by the Orissa High Court for allegedly disobeying its interim stay order; he challenged the conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the Chief Justice and Judges of a High Court should be made parties in appeals against contempt convictions by that court
Whether a subordinate court commits contempt by acting without knowledge of a superior court's order
Whether the appellant intentionally disobeyed the High Court's stay order
holdings: It is neither necessary nor appropriate to make the Chief Justice and Judges parties in contempt appeals unless relief is claimed against them; the proper style should be 'in re' the alleged contemnor.
Contempt for disobedience of a superior court's order requires intentional disobedience; mere ignorance of the order negates intent and cannot constitute contempt.
The appellant did not commit contempt as he had no authentic knowledge of the High Court's stay order and acted in good faith; the conviction and fine are set aside.
doctrines: Contempt by disobedience requires mens rea
Authentic knowledge of court orders is essential for contempt liability
Good faith action by judicial officers without intent to disobey does not amount to contempt

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the validity of a government notification that fixed a lower maximum rent under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, arguing it involved excessive delegation of legislative power.
issues_decided: Whether Section 6(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, constitutes excessive delegation of legislative power by empowering the government to fix a lower maximum rent without sufficient guidelines.
Whether the absence of standards or policy in Section 6(2) renders it unconstitutional under Article 226 of the Constitution.
holdings: Section 6(2) of the Act is void because it delegates legislative power without laying down any policy, standard, or guiding principles, resulting in uncontrolled and arbitrary executive authority.

The power conferred on the Provincial Government to fix a lower rate of maximum rent on 'any other suitable basis' is so vague and unrestricted that it amounts to an abdication of essential legislative function.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 6(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Rule of law
Separation of powers

card.dispute: A Sub-Divisional Magistrate was convicted of contempt by the High Court for ordering restitution of possession despite an alleged interim stay; he appealed, challenging both the conviction and the practice of naming High Court judges as respondents.
issues_decided: Whether the Sub-Divisional Magistrate was guilty of contempt for passing an order while an interim stay was allegedly in force.
Whether the Chief Justice and Judges of the High Court should be named as respondents in an appeal against a contempt conviction.
holdings: A subordinate court cannot be guilty of contempt unless it had authentic knowledge of a superior court's order and intentionally disobeyed it; mere receipt of unverified information does not constitute knowledge.
The Chief Justice and Judges of the High Court should not be made parties in contempt appeals; such proceedings should instead be titled 'In re' the alleged contemner to uphold judicial propriety.
provisions: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (principles applicable by precedent)
doctrines: Intentional disobedience doctrine in contempt
Doctrine of authentic communication of judicial orders
Judicial propriety in naming judges as parties

card.dispute: The surviving non-evacuee heirs of Abdul Hai challenged the vesting of entire properties in the Custodian under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, claiming it violated their property rights as they never became evacuees.
issues_decided: Whether the order under Section 11 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, vesting the entire property in the Custodian was valid when only a 4/7th share was declared evacuee property under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950.
Whether the failure to file claims by non-evacuee claimants justified vesting of the entire composite property in the Custodian under Section 11 of the 1951 Act.
holdings: Section 11 of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, cannot vest the entire property in the Custodian when only a portion was declared evacuee property under the 1950 Act; it applies only where the whole property was declared evacuee property.

The vesting of entire property under Section 11 is impermissible if the evacuee interest was already determined and limited; the section does not allow extinguishing non-evacuee shares without lawful separation.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on context and prior provisions
Presumption against deprivation of property without authority of law
Binding effect of prior declarations under special statutes

card.dispute: The petitioner sought cancellation of a decree for partition of Watan lands, claiming they were inalienable hereditary remuneration attached to the office of Patil and not liable to civil court process.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court could entertain a petition for cancellation of a decree originally passed by the Privy Council after the abolition of its jurisdiction.
Whether a certificate under Section 10 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, addressed to the Supreme Court instead of the Privy Council, is valid.
holdings: The Supreme Court, by operation of statutory and constitutional fictions, is to be treated as the court that passed the decree formerly issued by the Privy Council and can therefore entertain the petition.

A certificate under Section 10 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, is valid if addressed to the Supreme Court as the successor to the Privy Council’s jurisdiction, despite the original decree being passed by the latter.
provisions: Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, Sections 5 and 8
doctrines: Succession of jurisdiction
Statutory fiction
Res judicata not applicable to jurisdictional changes

card.dispute: The heirs of Pyare Mohan Bannerji contested whether a direction in his will to pay half the income of his property to a charity created a trust or merely a charge.
issues_decided: Whether the will created a trust or a charge in favor of the Uttarpara Hitakari Sabha.
Whether the legal heirs were under a fiduciary obligation to pay half the net income to the charity.
holdings: The direction in the will created a trust, not merely a charge, because the testator intended the charity to receive regular, perpetual payments.
The legal heirs took the property subject to a fiduciary obligation to pay half the net income to the charity, ensuring the permanence and fulfillment of the charitable purpose.
doctrines: Intention to create a trust
Distinction between trust and charge in will construction
Perpetuity of charitable trusts

card.dispute: The appellant contested his conviction for operating a salt works without a factory licence, arguing it did not qualify as a 'factory' under the Factories Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the salt works constituted a 'factory' within the meaning of Section 2(m) of the Factories Act, 1948.
Whether the term 'premises' in the definition of 'factory' includes open land without permanent buildings.
Whether the process of converting sea water into salt amounts to a 'manufacturing process' under Section 2(k) of the Act.
holdings: A salt works spread over open land with temporary structures qualifies as a 'factory' if used for a manufacturing process.
The term 'premises' includes open land, land with buildings, or buildings alone, and is not limited to enclosed or permanent structures.
Converting sea water into salt through human-guided evaporation and collection is a 'manufacturing process' as it transforms a non-commercial substance into a marketable product.
doctrines: Manufacturing process involves transformation into a different, marketable article
Statutory interpretation of 'premises' based on functional use rather than structural permanence

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an arbitration award in a partition suit, claiming the court failed to specify the time for the award and that he received less than his rightful share.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration reference was invalid due to non-compliance with Section 23(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 for not specifying the time for making the award in the order of reference
Whether the award was invalid for being filed after the prescribed time
Whether the award could be set aside because the appellant received less than half the share in the property
holdings: The requirement to fix a time for the award under Section 23(1) is mandatory, but the reference is not invalid if the time is specified elsewhere in the proceedings, such as in court diary entries.
An award filed after the initial deadline is not invalid if the court has extended the time through subsequent orders, even if informally recorded.

An award cannot be set aside merely because the arbitrator allotted less area to a party; it must be shown that the arbitrator acted dishonestly or the award is otherwise invalid, which was not proven here.
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Limited judicial interference in arbitration awards
Doctrine of honest judicial discretion of arbitrators

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the declaration of her husband's property as evacuee property, claiming infringement of her fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31, and sought restoration of the property.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition under Article 32 is maintainable to challenge a final order of competent authority declaring property as evacuee property?
Whether the petitioner could claim infringement of fundamental rights when the underlying right was negatived by a final administrative decision?
Whether non-compliance with procedural rules in issuing a notice under Section 7 of the Act affected the jurisdiction of the authorities?
holdings: A petition under Article 32 is not maintainable where a competent authority has finally decided that the alleged fundamental right does not exist, unless that decision is a nullity.
Infringement of a fundamental right cannot be claimed if the right itself has been conclusively negatived by a final order of a competent authority.
Procedural irregularities in issuing a notice under Section 7 do not amount to lack of jurisdiction, especially when the party participated in proceedings without raising the objection.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(d)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 16(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 28
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Maintainability of Article 32 petitions
Jurisdictional defect vs. erroneous decision
Doctrine of res judicata in writ petitions

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutionality of provisions of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, after his application to confirm a land purchase from an intending evacuee was rejected by the Custodian.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 2(d) and 40(4)(a) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 violate Article 31(2) of the Constitution by enabling property deprivation without authority of law?
Whether Section 40(4)(a) confers arbitrary power on the Custodian by using the standard of 'good faith'?
Whether the petitioner was discriminated against in the confirmation of his property transaction?
holdings: Sections 2(d) and 40(4)(a) are not subject to Article 31(2) due to the exception in Article 31(5)(b)(iii), which permits laws concerning evacuee property declared by law.

Section 40(4)(a) does not confer arbitrary power; the term 'good faith' has established legal meaning, and the Custodian's power is judicial in nature, so absence of detailed standards does not invalidate it.
The petitioner was not discriminated against; the Custodian’s decision is judicial, and disparate outcomes in similar cases do not amount to unconstitutional discrimination.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(d)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 40(4)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional exceptions under Article 31(5)(b)(iii)
Judicial character of administrative powers
Non-arbitrariness in statutory discretion with established legal standards

card.dispute: The appellants (Dafedar Niranjan Singh and another) challenged the Custodian-General's revision of an earlier order releasing two houses to them, arguing that the revision power could not apply to orders that had already become final under prior evacuee property laws.
issues_decided: Whether the deeming provision in Section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, applies to orders that had already attained finality under earlier ordinances
Whether Section 27 of the Act allows the Custodian-General to revise final orders made under repealed ordinances
Whether the chain of deeming provisions in successive evacuee property laws preserved the validity of actions taken under earlier laws
holdings: Section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, does not apply retrospectively to affect the finality of orders made under prior ordinances before the Act came into force.

The Custodian-General cannot exercise revisionary powers under Section 27 to set aside an order that had become final under a previous ordinance, as such retrospective operation is not permitted by law.
The deeming fiction in Section 58(3) applies only to pending actions at the time of the Act’s commencement, not to orders already final under earlier laws.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 58(3)
Patiala Evacuees (Administration of Property) Ordinance, Samvat 2004 (No. IX of 2004)
Patiala and East Punjab States Union Ordinance No. XIII of Samvat 2006
Patiala and East Punjab States Union Ordinance No. XVII of 2006
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of administrative orders
Doctrine against retrospective operation of statutes affecting vested rights
Doctrine of deeming fiction in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Petitioners challenged the dismissal of their writ petitions by various High Courts and sought similar reliefs in the Supreme Court under Article 32, raising the issue of whether such petitions were barred by res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether a dismissal of a writ petition by a High Court on the merits under Article 226 bars a subsequent petition under Article 32 on the same facts and for the same relief?
Whether a dismissal in limine or for procedural reasons like laches or alternative remedy constitutes a bar of res judicata under Article 32?
Whether a withdrawal of a writ petition before the High Court creates a bar to a subsequent Article 32 petition?
holdings: If a writ petition under Article 226 is dismissed on the merits after full argument, the decision operates as res judicata and bars a subsequent petition under Article 32 on the same grounds.

A dismissal of a writ petition on grounds of laches, alternative remedy, or in limine without a speaking order does not constitute a bar of res judicata unless the order conclusively determines the merits.
A writ petition withdrawn by the petitioner without decision on merits does not create a bar of res judicata against a later petition under Article 32.
doctrines: Res judicata
Merits of writ petition
Alternative remedy doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant sought to introduce a statement made by the respondent before an Income-tax Officer in a civil suit for recovery of money, but the Commissioner refused to produce it, citing confidentiality under Section 54 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether Section 54 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 prohibits the production of a statement made by a person before an Income-tax Officer in civil court proceedings
Whether the prohibition under Section 54 is absolute or can be waived by the assessee
holdings: Section 54 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 imposes an absolute prohibition on courts requiring production of any record, document, or evidence from income-tax proceedings, regardless of relevance to the case.
The confidentiality mandate under Section 54 cannot be waived by the assessee; the prohibition remains operative even if the assessee consents to disclosure.
doctrines: Absolute statutory confidentiality
Non-waiver of statutory privilege

card.dispute: The appellant challenged a decree for pre-emption after withdrawing the pre-emption amount deposited by the respondent, raising the question of whether he could maintain the appeal despite having accepted the benefit of the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, by withdrawing the pre-emption price from court, became precluded from challenging the decree in appeal.
Whether the doctrine of approbation and reprobation bars a party from appealing after accepting a benefit under the decree.
holdings: Withdrawing the pre-emption amount does not amount to adoption of the decree, and without a statutory provision or established equitable principle, the appellant cannot be deprived of his statutory right to appeal.
A party is not automatically barred from appeal by accepting a benefit under a decree if the relief sought on appeal is not inconsistent with that acceptance.
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Equitable principle of election
Estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the Wakf Manager disputed whether the wakf should be assessed as an individual or as an association of persons at the maximum tax rate due to indeterminate shares of beneficiaries.
issues_decided: Whether the individual shares of the beneficiaries under the wakf deed were indeterminate or unknown within the meaning of the first proviso to Section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the mutawalli receives income on behalf of 'any person' under Section 41(1), given that wakf property vests in the Almighty under Muslim law.
holdings: The individual shares of the beneficiaries were indeterminate because the wakf deed did not specify or imply fixed shares, leaving distribution to the mutawalli's discretion for maintenance and charitable purposes.
The mutawalli receives income on behalf of the beneficiaries, not the Almighty, and thus Section 41(1) applies; the wakf is liable to tax at the maximum rate when shares are indeterminate.
provisions: Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, Section 41(1), First Proviso
doctrines: Vicarious assessment of trustees under tax law
Indeterminate shares doctrine in trust taxation
Statutory fiction of mutawalli as trustee despite religious doctrine of divine ownership

card.dispute: The appellants, who had exchanged properties with evacuees and occupied evacuee properties in India, fought against the Custodian General's order requiring them to account for rents and profits from those properties after the confirmation of the exchange was set aside.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian of Evacuee Property has the power to direct a person in unauthorized possession of evacuee property to render accounts of rents and profits in a summary manner.
Whether the provisions of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, or the rules made thereunder authorize the Custodian to recover rents and profits without resorting to a civil suit.
holdings: The Custodian of Evacuee Property does not have the power under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, or the rules made thereunder to compel a person in unauthorized possession to render accounts of rents and profits in a summary manner.

The recovery of rents and profits from unauthorized occupants must be pursued through the ordinary legal remedy of a civil suit, as no provision in the Act or rules authorizes such recovery by summary order.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 10
doctrines: Doctrine of strict interpretation of statutory powers
No summary recovery without express statutory authority

card.dispute: The appellant (foster son) and respondents (testator's daughters) disputed whether the daughters or the testator's brother had the right to select the specific plots of land bequeathed under the will.
issues_decided: Whether the gift under the will was void for uncertainty under Section 89 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925
Whether the right to select the specific plots of nanja and punja land in vattam No. 149 belonged to the legatees (daughters) or to the testator's brother (Seetharama)
Whether the English rule of benevolent construction, allowing legatees to make selection in cases of non-specific bequests, applies in India
holdings: A will is not void for uncertainty under Section 89 if it expresses a definite intention that can be made certain through construction or application of equitable principles.

Where a testator has not expressly or impliedly reserved the right of selection to himself or a third party, the right to select specific properties from a described class of properties belongs to the legatees.

The English rule of benevolent construction, which allows legatees to select in cases of non-specific bequests, is applicable in India as a rule of common sense and should be applied where the will does not show a contrary intention.
The use of the phrase 'he shall give' in the will did not confer a power of selection on the brother; the testator intended the daughters themselves to have the right to select their allotted land.
doctrines: Rule of benevolent construction
Doctrine of selection by legatees
Principle of avoiding invalidity for uncertainty through reasonable interpretation

card.dispute: Dr. Mohammad Saheb Mahboob Medico challenged the declaration of his property as evacuee property on grounds of constitutional validity and timing of asset transfer.
issues_decided: Whether Section 22(b) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by treating two groups of asset-transferors differently.
Whether the transfer of a substantial portion of assets before being declared an intending evacuee can be considered under Section 22(b) for declaring property as evacuee property.
holdings: The classification between persons transferring assets before and after October 18, 1949, is valid as they are not similarly situated, and thus does not violate Article 14.

The circumstance of transferring a substantial portion of assets is relevant under Section 22(b) regardless of whether the transfer occurred before or after the declaration of being an intending evacuee.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 22(b)
Administration of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, Section 2(d)(iii)
doctrines: Equal Protection of Laws under Article 14
Reasonable Classification Doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioners, heirs of Khadim Ali, challenged the Custodian's declaration that two houses were evacuee property, arguing they were deprived of their shares without notice or opportunity to be heard.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian could declare the entire property as evacuee property without serving notice on all interested parties under Section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether the male petitioner lost his rights by filing a time-barred appeal before the Custodian-General
Whether the notification under Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, extinguished the petitioners' rights in the property
holdings: No interest in property can vest in the Custodian under Section 8 without prior notice under Section 7 to the concerned person; since petitioners were not served notice, their shares did not become evacuee property.
Filing a time-barred appeal by a non-party does not create estoppel or bar a constitutional remedy under Article 32, especially when the appeal was dismissed without adjudicating rights.
Section 12 of the Displaced Persons Act only extinguishes rights of evacuees; since petitioners were never declared evacuees, their rights remain unaffected by the notification.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of notice as a prerequisite to deprivation of property rights
Principle of jurisdictional limitation in administrative action
No estoppel against fundamental rights under Article 32

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of the adoption of the respondent's sister's husband under the Goda Dattak custom, claiming it violated customary and Hindu law restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether under the Goda Dattak custom, a widow can validly adopt her sister's husband as a son to her deceased husband.
Whether the adoptee in a Goda Dattak adoption must belong to the adoptive father's family if members are available.
Whether the consent of the husband's sapindas is required for a valid adoption under the Madras School of Mitakshara when the husband had given prior authority for adoption.
holdings: The rule in Dattaka Mimansa against adopting a person related through a prohibited relationship (Viruddha Sambandha) is recommendatory, not mandatory, and the wife's sister's husband does not fall within this prohibition.

There is no established custom in Goda Dattak adoption requiring the adoptee to be from the adoptive father's family if possible; such a restriction was not proved by authoritative texts or consistent practice.
When the husband has given prior authority for adoption, the consent of his sapindas is not required, even under the Madras School of Mitakshara.
doctrines: Goda Dattak custom
Dattaka Mimansa rule on Viruddha Sambandha
Prior spousal authority overriding sapinda consent

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued to declare a will ineffective and claimed possession of land, arguing it was ancestral property which the testator could not bequeath, while the defendants claimed the testator had validly bequeathed it.
issues_decided: Whether the land in dispute, received in consolidation proceedings, was ancestral property of the joint family
Whether ancestral character of property is lost when ancestral and self-acquired lands are consolidated
Whether the absence of revenue records showing possession by the immediate common ancestor negates ancestral character
holdings: Land received in consolidation retains its ancestral character to the extent it corresponds to ancestral land previously held.
The ancestral nature of property is not lost due to consolidation, and the proportion corresponding to ancestral land remains ancestral.
If a remote ancestor's possession is recorded and there is no evidence of non-ancestral acquisition, the land is ancestral even if the immediate common ancestor’s possession is not recorded.
doctrines: Ancestral property in Hindu law
Rule of apportionment in consolidation of ancestral and self-acquired land
Presumption of ancestral origin from inheritance in absence of proof of separate acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of notifications declaring a forest as protected under Bihar's Private Forests Acts, arguing that the omission of lessees' names and the effect on his lease rights violated constitutional provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the omission of the names of the lessee-manjhis in the notification under the Bihar Private Forests Act rendered the notification invalid
Whether the restriction on management and control of forest land amounted to 'acquisition of property' under s. 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935
Whether the enforcement of the impugned Acts violated the appellant's fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) of the Constitution
holdings: The omission of the lessees' names in the notification did not invalidate it, as the statutory procedure was otherwise complied with and the lessees were served.
The imposition of governmental control over forest management without affecting legal title does not constitute 'acquisition of property' under s. 299(2) of the Government of India Act, 1935.

The extinguishment of the appellant's lease rights prior to the Constitution's commencement in 1950 barred him from invoking fundamental rights under Part III, as no continuing deprivation arose post-January 26, 1950.
doctrines: Acquisition of property requires transfer of ownership or title, not mere regulatory control
Fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution cannot be invoked for rights extinguished before its commencement
Statutory validation of procedural irregularities in notifications

card.dispute: The appellant resisted execution of a decree for possession in favour of the respondent, claiming that the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, had extinguished the respondent's proprietary rights and vested them in the State, making the decree inexecutable.
issues_decided: Whether the coming into force of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, during the pendency of an appeal, rendered a decree for possession in favour of a proprietor inexecutable?
Whether the executing court could refuse execution of a decree on the ground that the decree-holder had lost his subsisting right to possession due to statutory vesting of rights in the State?
Whether the appellant, having been declared a malik makbuza under Section 41 of the Act, could object to the execution of the decree despite not challenging its validity?
holdings: A decree for possession based on proprietary rights becomes inexecutable if those rights are extinguished and vested in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, after the decree but before execution.
The executing court can refuse execution where a change in law has divested the decree-holder of the subsisting right to possession, even if the decree itself is not challenged as invalid.

A person declared as malik makbuza under Section 41 of the Act acquires a right to possession that can be set up as a bar to execution of a decree in favour of a former proprietor whose rights have been extinguished.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Sections 2(g), 2(k), 3, 4, 7, 41, 46
doctrines: Doctrine of supervening impossibility or change of law rendering a decree inexecutable
Doctrine of statutory vesting extinguishing private rights
Execution bar based on subsequent acquisition of rights by judgment debtor

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, and after concurrent findings by lower courts in favor of eviction, the tenant challenged the order in revision before the High Court, which reversed the factual finding; the landlord appealed to the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in exercise of revisional powers under Section 35(1) of the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, can re-assess the value of evidence and substitute its own findings of fact for those of the courts below.
Whether a revisional court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact in the absence of a statutory right to second appeal.
holdings: The High Court cannot re-assess evidence or substitute its own factual conclusions in revision unless there is a miscarriage of justice or the decision is not 'according to law'.
Revisional powers under Section 35(1) do not permit interference with concurrent findings of fact merely because the High Court might have reached a different conclusion.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 34
Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 35(1)
doctrines: Distinction between appeal and revision
Revisional jurisdiction limited to preventing miscarriage of justice
Concurrent findings of fact not lightly disturbed in revision

card.dispute: The appellants, accused of murdering Harphool during a criminal trespass, claimed self-defence, while the State argued they were part of an unlawful assembly with a common object to commit trespass using deadly force.
issues_decided: Whether the right of private defence of property ceases when trespassers express regret and seek permission to continue trespassing.
Whether an unlawful assembly continues to exist after partial completion of its common object.
Whether the accused could claim self-defence when attacked by the aggrieved landowner during ongoing criminal trespass.
Whether the death caused was in prosecution of the common object of the unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC.
holdings: The right of private defence of property does not cease merely because trespassers express regret or plead to continue; the aggrieved party may lawfully prevent further trespass.
Criminal trespass continues until the trespasser fully exits the property; expressing intent to stop does not end liability.
A trespasser cannot claim self-defence against the property owner's resistance during ongoing criminal trespass, especially when armed and part of an unlawful assembly.
When members of an unlawful assembly are armed and agree to use force, it can be inferred they knew their actions could cause death, making them liable under Section 149 IPC for murder.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Unlawful assembly and common object
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Continuity of criminal trespass

card.dispute: The appellants, who were allotted rural evacuee land after the cancellation of earlier allotments to respondents 4 to 9, challenged the Custodian General's power to cancel their allotment in revision proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian General had the power to cancel a quasi-permanent allotment of rural evacuee property made after July 22, 1952, in a revision application under Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950?
Whether Rule 14(6) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Rules, as amended, restricted the Custodian General's powers under Section 27?
Whether the inherent or statutory power to rectify a wrong allotment allows cancellation outside the exceptions in Rule 14(6)?
holdings: The Custodian General cannot cancel a quasi-permanent allotment of rural evacuee property made after July 22, 1952, unless the case falls within the exceptions specified in Rule 14(6) of the Rules.
The power of the Custodian General under Section 27 is limited by the Rules; he cannot do what the subordinate authority was prohibited from doing under Rule 14(6).
The amended Rule 14(6) abrogated any inherent power of the Custodian to cancel an allotment for restitution, as such power is now confined to the enumerated exceptions.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 26
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Rules, Rule 14(6)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory limitation of administrative power
Doctrine of inherent powers being subject to statutory restrictions
Principle of legality in administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant (International Contractors Ltd) sold property to the respondent (Prasanta Kumar Sur) and later agreed to reconvey it; the dispute arose when the appellant repudiated the reconveyance agreement and the respondent sued for specific performance without formally tendering the purchase money.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent could seek specific performance of the reconveyance agreement without making a formal tender of the purchase money after the appellant's repudiation of the contract.
Whether the appellant's denial of the existence of a valid agreement constituted a total repudiation of the contract.
holdings: Where a party to a contract for sale totally repudiates the agreement before performance is due, the other party need not make a formal tender of the purchase money to seek specific performance.

A clear and unequivocal denial of the existence of a contract amounts to repudiation, entitling the aggrieved party to sue for specific performance without tendering money, as such tender would be a useless formality.
doctrines: Doctrine of anticipatory repudiation
Useless formality doctrine in tender of performance
Agency of solicitor in contractual communications

card.dispute: Inder Singh claimed he was validly adopted by Nathu, a Jat of Ludhiana, and thus entitled to inherit his property, but Gurdial Singh contested the validity of the adoption.
issues_decided: Whether a valid customary adoption among Jats of Ludhiana requires both a declaration and general treatment of the adoptee as a son.
Whether the adoption of Inder Singh by Nathu was valid despite Nathu's subsequent repudiation and cancellation of the adoption deed.
holdings: For a valid customary adoption among Jats of Ludhiana, both a declaration of adoption and general treatment of the appointee as a son are essential.
A mere declaration or execution of an adoption deed, without actual treatment as a son, is insufficient to prove adoption, especially when the adopter later repudiates the act.
doctrines: Customary adoption requires clear intention and manifestation through conduct
Adoption under customary law is irrevocable once validly completed, but validity depends on fulfillment of customary formalities

card.dispute: The landlord fought with the protected tenant over whether the amended provisions restricting termination of tenancy applied to a notice given before the amendment but expiring after it came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Section 34(2A) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, as amended in 1952, applies to tenancy termination notices issued before the amendment but expiring after its commencement?
Whether the landlord acquired a vested right to possession upon serving notice under Section 34(1), thereby exempting him from the new restrictions in Section 34(2A)?
holdings: Section 34(2A) applies if the tenancy terminated after the amendment came into force, regardless of when the notice was served, because the right to possession matures only upon termination of the tenancy.

A notice under Section 34(1) does not create a vested right; the landlord’s right to possession arises only after the notice period expires, so the amended restrictions apply if the tenancy ends post-amendment.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 34(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 34(2A)
doctrines: Vested rights doctrine
Prospective operation of amendments
Beneficial interpretation of tenant protection laws

card.dispute: The appellant money-lender challenged the maintainability of the respondent borrower's second suit under the Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940, seeking to reopen earlier mortgage decrees after a prior suit had already reopened only the personal decree.
issues_decided: Whether a second suit by a borrower under s. 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940, for reopening decrees not challenged in a prior suit is maintainable despite the earlier omission to claim full relief.

Whether the principle of res judicata or Order 2 Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a subsequent suit under s. 36 of the Act when the court failed to grant full relief in the first proceeding.
Whether the duty of the court under s. 36 of the Act to grant full relief is mandatory, irrespective of the borrower's limited prayer in the first application.
holdings: Section 36 of the Bengal Money-lenders Act, 1940, contemplates one suit for complete relief; if a borrower omits to seek full relief and abandons part of it, he is barred from filing a second suit for the remaining relief.
The principles of res judicata and constructive res judicata under s. 11 and Order 2 Rule 2 CPC apply to suits under s. 36 of the Act unless overridden by statutory mandate.

The court has a mandatory duty under s. 36 to reopen all affected decrees once moved, regardless of the borrower's limited prayer; failure to do so does not permit a fresh suit if the first suit was a proper proceeding under the Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2, Rule 2
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Mandatory judicial duty under statute
Waiver and estoppel in statutory remedies

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a notification under which the State took over parts of their zamindari estates, arguing that the State could not take over an estate in parts rather than as a whole unit.
issues_decided: Whether a portion of an estate within the territorial operation of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, can be taken over by the State even if other parts of the same estate fall outside the Act's operation.
Whether the issuance of separate notifications for different parts of the same estate violates the principle that an estate must be taken over as a unit.
Whether the Madras Scheduled Areas Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Regulation, 1951, validly extended the operation of the 1948 Act to the excluded areas of the estate.
holdings: A portion of an estate falling within the territorial jurisdiction of the Abolition Act constitutes an 'estate' under the Act and can be validly taken over, even if other parts lie outside its operation.

The issuance of multiple notifications to vest different parts of an estate does not invalidate the acquisition, provided the State's intent was to take over the entire estate within its legislative competence.

The 1951 Regulation validly extended the 1948 Act to Scheduled Areas, enabling the State to take over the remaining part of the estate, thereby fulfilling the legislative purpose of abolishing intermediaries.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Sections 1(4), 2(3), 3, 24, 25
Madras Scheduled Areas Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Regulation, 1951, Section 2, Para 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution
doctrines: Territorial competence of legislation
Principle of harmonious construction
Purpose and policy of land reform legislation
Doctrine of severability in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Villagers contested the levy of special canal charges after being found responsible for a canal cut, arguing it violated constitutional protections against penalties for past acts.
issues_decided: Whether the use of canal water without authorization constitutes an 'offence' under Article 20(1) of the Constitution
Whether the imposition of enhanced water charges amounts to a 'penalty' within the meaning of Article 20(1)
Whether Sections 3 and 4 of the Pepsu Sirhind Canal and Western Jumna Canal Rules (Enforcement and Validation) Act, 1954, violate Article 20(1) by applying rules retrospectively
holdings: The unauthorized use of canal water is not an 'offence' under Article 20(1) because no law prohibits such use; it only prescribes charges for it.
The imposition of special water rates under canal rules is a charge for service, not a penalty, and thus does not trigger Article 20(1) protection.
Sections 3 and 4 of the 1954 Act do not violate Article 20(1) because they do not impose criminal punishment or penalties for past offences.
provisions: Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 31
Pepsu Sirhind Canal and Western Jumna Canal Rules (Enforcement and Validation) Act, 1954, Sections 3 and 4
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Principle of no penalty without law (nullum crimen sine lege)
Distinction between civil liability and criminal penalty

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that certain brahmottar lands granted to temple officials were inalienable and that their transfer to strangers was void, while the respondents defended the validity of the transfers.
issues_decided: Whether the brahmottar lands in question were heritable and transferable under the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886
Whether the appellant had successfully proved that the lands could be alienated only to a specified class of persons (Bardeuries)
Whether the burden of proof lay on the appellant to establish restrictions on the transferability of the lands
holdings: Under the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, lands held by Bardeuries and recorded as brahmottar are deemed heritable and transferable as the holders fall under Section 8(1)(a) and become land holders with rights under Section 9.
The statutory recognition of heritable and transferable rights under the Regulation overrides any alleged traditional or religious restriction on alienation to strangers.
The burden of proving a restriction on transferability of land lies on the party asserting it, and failure to discharge this burden renders the claim legally unsustainable.
provisions: Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 3(g)
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 8(1)(a)
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 9
doctrines: Burden of proof in property disputes
Statutory recognition of heritable and transferable rights
Effect of colonial land reforms on pre-existing grants

card.dispute: Two brothers disputed over the appointment as Mutawalli of a wakf, leading the Commissioner to appoint a third brother temporarily, which the eldest brother challenged as illegal.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner had the authority to appoint a temporary Mutawalli under Section 40 of the Bengal Wakf Act after delegation of power under Section 29.
Whether the Rules framed by the Government restricted the Commissioner from making the appointment and required only a report and recommendation to the Board.
Whether the existence of a dispute between claimants constituted an 'impediment' under Section 40 justifying a temporary appointment.
holdings: The Commissioner can appoint a temporary Mutawalli if the Board has delegated its powers under Section 29 of the Bengal Wakf Act, as delegation includes both powers and duties when they are inseparable.
The Rules requiring the Commissioner to report and recommend do not apply when the Board has validly delegated its powers, as statutory delegation overrides inconsistent rules.
A dispute between rival claimants constitutes an 'impediment' under Section 40, justifying the appointment of a temporary Mutawalli until the dispute is resolved.
doctrines: Delegation of powers includes duties when they are interwoven
Harmonious construction of statutes and rules
Statutory delegation overrides inconsistent administrative rules

card.dispute: The reversioners challenged the validity of a sale of property by a widow to discharge a mortgage debt, claiming it was not binding on them.
issues_decided: Whether a sale of property by a Hindu widow to discharge a usufructuary mortgage is binding on reversioners.
What is the proper course for a Division Bench when faced with conflicting decisions of earlier Benches of the same High Court?
holdings: A Hindu widow may sell property subject to a usufructuary mortgage if the sale is justified as a prudent act to discharge debt and secure estate income, and such sale binds reversioners.
When a Division Bench encounters conflicting decisions of coordinate benches, it should refer the matter to a Full Bench rather than choosing between them or departing without reference.
provisions: Hindu Law (customary and case law principles on widow's powers)
doctrines: Prudent owner doctrine
Doctrine of binding precedent among coordinate benches
Per incuriam
Full Bench reference for conflicting decisions

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, owners of adjoining collieries, disputed whether the appellants had encroached on the respondents' coal mines and removed coal, and whether the suit for damages was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 48 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, based on the date the respondents acquired knowledge of the encroachment.
Whether the burden of proof regarding knowledge of encroachment lay on the plaintiff or the defendant.
Whether the coal left in the encroached area was irretrievably lost to the respondents due to statutory mining barriers.
holdings: The suit was not barred by limitation because the respondents acquired knowledge of the encroachment only in 1941, within three years of filing the suit.
The initial burden of proving the date of knowledge of encroachment lies on the plaintiff; once discharged, the burden shifts to the defendant to prove earlier knowledge.
The coal remaining in the encroached area was rendered unworkable due to statutory barrier requirements and was effectively lost to the respondents.
doctrines: Burden of proof in limitation cases under Article 48
Shifting of evidentiary burden under Section 101 of the Evidence Act
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts given deference in appeal

card.dispute: Brick kiln owners challenged the continued validity of a royalty levy imposed by the erstwhile Patiala State after the extension of central excise law to Part B States in 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the royalty on bricks imposed by the Patiala State's 1919 order was a law corresponding to the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944
Whether such royalty law was repealed by Section 13(2) of the Finance Act, 1950 upon the extension of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 to Part B States
holdings: The Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 does not contain a negative provision saving other goods from local excise laws; it only applies to goods specified in its First Schedule.
The royalty order on bricks by the Patiala State was not a law corresponding to the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, and therefore was not repealed by Section 13(2) of the Finance Act, 1950.
provisions: Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, Section 2(d)
Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of repeal by implication
Doctrine of correspondence in statutory repeal
Principle of negative implication in tax legislation

card.dispute: The auction purchaser challenged whether a letter from the mortgagor to the mortgagee amounted to an acknowledgment of liability, thereby saving the limitation period for the mortgagee's suit.
issues_decided: Whether the letter dated March 5, 1932, constituted an acknowledgment of the mortgagee's right under Section 19 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908.
Whether an acknowledgment under Section 19 can be implied from the language and surrounding circumstances of a document.
holdings: A letter referring to the mortgagee's interest and urging him to 'take up the whole' to stop a sale acknowledged the subsisting jural relationship of mortgage and amounted to an acknowledgment under Section 19.
An acknowledgment under Section 19 need not be express but can be implied from the context and circumstances, provided it recognizes the existence of a jural relationship.
doctrines: Doctrine of implied acknowledgment
Doctrine of subsisting jural relationship

card.dispute: Kartar Singh and two others challenged their conviction for murder and attempted murder in a premeditated free fight, arguing that the unlawful assembly was not proven and that liability should be individual in such fights.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 149 IPC is sustainable when ten out of thirteen accused were acquitted and only three were convicted.
Whether in a premeditated free fight, each participant is liable only for their individual acts or can be held constructively liable under Section 149 IPC.
holdings: A conviction under Section 149 IPC is valid if the evidence shows the presence of more than five persons in the unlawful assembly, even if only some are convicted, provided the named accused were not all proved to be absent.

In a premeditated free fight where both parties arm themselves and intend to fight, there is no right of private defence and a common object to cause injuries exists, making Section 149 IPC applicable for constructive liability.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Common object of unlawful assembly
No right of private defence in premeditated free fights
Common intention under Section 34 IPC as an alternative basis for liability

card.dispute: The appellants and the respondent fought over whether the respondent, adopted after 63 years of his adoptive father's death, could divest the appellants of properties inherited from a collateral ancestor.
issues_decided: Whether an adoption can divest the heirs of a collateral who inherited property from a sole surviving coparcener?
Whether the title of a person inheriting from a collateral is absolute or subject to defeasance upon subsequent adoption in the family?
Whether the doctrine of relation back of adoption allows the adopted son to claim property that passed through collaterals before the adoption?
holdings: When a person inherits property as a collateral succeeding to a sole surviving coparcener, the inheritance is absolute but subject to defeasance by a valid adoption in the family.
The title of one who inherits from such a collateral is not absolute freehold but remains subject to defeasance so long as there is a possibility of adoption by a widow of the family.
An adopted son, by virtue of the theory of relation back, can divest mesne transferees who claim under a collateral, because their title is defeasible and extinguished upon valid adoption.
doctrines: Doctrine of Relation Back of Adoption
Defeasible Title in Coparcenary Succession
Heir of Collateral Inheriting Subject to Defeasance

card.dispute: The appellants, who were minors during a partition suit, challenged the validity of a preliminary decree passed by consent without court permission for their guardian, seeking to set it aside in an appeal against the final decree.
issues_decided: Whether a preliminary decree passed without compliance with Order 32, Rule 7(1) of the CPC is a nullity or merely voidable.
Whether such a decree can be challenged in an appeal against the final decree in the absence of an appeal against the preliminary decree.
Whether Section 97 of the CPC bars a challenge to the legal validity of a preliminary decree in an appeal from the final decree.
holdings: A decree passed in contravention of Order 32, Rule 7(1) is not a nullity but is voidable only at the instance of the minor.
The minor must challenge such a preliminary decree by a direct appeal against it, not in an appeal against the final decree.
Section 97 of the CPC bars any challenge—whether to factual correctness or legal validity—of a preliminary decree if no appeal was filed against it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 32, Rule 7
doctrines: Voidable decree doctrine
Bar of constructive res judicata under Section 97
Protection of minors in litigation

card.dispute: The appellant sued to restrain the respondents from entering his land, while the respondents claimed to be tenants cultivating the land, raising the issue of whether the civil court or the Collector had jurisdiction to decide the landlord-tenant relationship.
issues_decided: Whether a dispute regarding the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship falls under the jurisdiction of the Collector under Section 7(1) of the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit involving a dispute over the status of tenant.
holdings: Section 7(1) of the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948 does not empower the Collector to decide disputes about the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship; it only covers five specified categories of disputes between established landlords and tenants.
Disputes concerning the very existence of a landlord-tenant relationship must be decided by the civil court, which retains jurisdiction over such issues.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Jurisdictional exclusivity of civil courts in absence of clear ouster
Presumption against ouster of civil court jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellant, Mahanth Ram Das, sought an extension of time to pay deficit court fees after a peremptory High Court order stating that failure to pay within three months would result in the appeal being dismissed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the power to extend time for payment of court fee after a peremptory order that non-payment would result in dismissal of the appeal.
Whether the High Court could exercise its inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure or review the matter under Order 47, Rule 1 despite the appeal having 'stood dismissed'.
holdings: Peremptory procedural orders, though strict in form, are in essence in terrorem and do not completely bar a court from considering timely applications for extension of time based on sufficient cause.

The High Court had the power under Sections 148 and 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure to extend time even after the deadline, and could have exercised its inherent powers under Section 151 to prevent injustice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47, Rule 1
doctrines: in terrorem
inherent powers of the court
liberal interpretation of procedural law to prevent injustice

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of pre-settlement minor inams, challenged the constitutional validity of the Orissa Estates Abolition (Amendment) Act, 1954, which brought minor inams within the definition of 'estate', arguing that the amendment was not a law for compulsory acquisition for public purpose and that minor inams were outside the scope of the abolition law.
issues_decided: Whether the Orissa Estates Abolition (Amendment) Act, 1954, which expanded the definition of 'estate' to include minor inams, was protected under Article 31A of the Constitution despite not being a standalone law for acquisition.
Whether minor inams, not comprising whole villages and including both melwaram and kudiwaram rights, fall within the constitutional and statutory definition of 'estate'.
Whether the rule of ejusdem generis applies to limit the meaning of 'inam' in the definition of 'estate' under Article 31A(2)(a).
holdings: An amending Act that extends the scope of an existing law on compulsory acquisition of property for public purpose is protected under Article 31A if it receives the President's assent, as the assent validates the extension to new categories of property.

Minor inams, even if not covering entire villages and combining both occupancy and proprietary rights, are included in the term 'estate' as the Constitution expressly defines 'estate' to include 'any inam'.

The rule of ejusdem generis does not apply to the specific term 'inam' in Article 31A(2)(a); it may only apply to the general phrase 'other similar grants', which must be read in light of 'jagir, inam or muafi'.
provisions: Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1951 (Orissa 1 of 1951), Section 2(g)
Orissa Estates Abolition (Amendment) Act, 1954 (Orissa XVII of 1954)
doctrines: Presidential assent as a condition for protection under Article 31A
Rule of ejusdem generis
Doctrine of inclusion by express mention ('any inam') overriding general definitions

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a mortgagee appealed against a High Court decision allowing the mortgagor's heirs to maintain a suit for redemption after the mortgagee purchased the property in a rent sale due to his own failure to pay arrears.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee's purchase of the mortgaged property in a rent sale extinguished the mortgagor's right to redeem
Whether the suit for redemption was maintainable without first setting aside the sale
Whether the mortgagee's default in paying rent triggered the application of Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act
holdings: The principle of 'once a mortgage, always a mortgage' applies until termination by agreement, merger, or court order.
If a mortgagee purchases the equity of redemption due to his own default, the mortgage is not extinguished and the purchase is held in trust for the mortgagor.
A mortgagor can maintain a suit for redemption without setting aside a sale when the sale resulted from the mortgagee's breach of duty.
Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act applies where a mortgagee gains an advantage by breaching his obligations, requiring him to hold the benefit for the mortgagor.
doctrines: Once a mortgage, always a mortgage
No one should profit from their own wrong
Fiduciary duty of mortgagee under Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act
Constructive trust arising from breach of duty by mortgagee

card.dispute: The Assistant Custodian, Headquarters, Patna, appealed an order by the Assistant Custodian, Giridih, declaring certain properties not to be evacuee property; the dispute was whether the appeal was maintainable under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Assistant Custodian, Headquarters, is a 'person aggrieved' under Section 24(1)(a) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, entitled to file an appeal against an order releasing property from evacuee status.
Whether an appeal under Section 24(1)(a) can be filed by one Custodian against the order of another Custodian.
holdings: The Assistant Custodian, Headquarters, is not a 'person aggrieved' within the meaning of Section 24 of the Act, as the term refers only to private parties affected by a declaration of evacuee property, not to government officers.

No Custodian or Assistant Custodian can file an appeal against the order of another Custodian under Section 24, as the Act contemplates a hierarchical administrative and revisional mechanism, not inter-office appeals.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 24(1)(a)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 26
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 6
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'person aggrieved'
Hierarchy of administrative authorities under a statute
Distinction between appeal and revision in administrative law

card.dispute: Tenure-holders challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to land tenure abolition laws that deemed certain non-permanent tenants as permanent, reducing the purchase price they could claim from tenants.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3, 4, and 6 of the Bombay Land Tenure Abolition Laws (Amendment) Act, 1958, violate the fundamental rights of tenure-holders under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the impugned provisions amount to colourable legislation by creating a new class of permanent tenants under the guise of amending evidence rules
Whether the amendment is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution
holdings: The provisions of the impugned Act, by deeming certain tenants as permanent, effectively created a new class of tenants and altered substantive rights, not merely evidentiary rules.
Such creation of permanent tenants reduced the purchase price payable by tenants to former tenure-holders, thereby infringing their right to property without adequate compensation.
The Act, in substance, amounted to confiscation of property rights and was not saved by Article 31A as it did not fall within the scope of laws providing for acquisition of estates.
provisions: Bombay Land Tenure Abolition Laws (Amendment) Act, 1958, Sections 3, 4, 6
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32H
Bombay Taluqdari Tenure Abolition Act, 1949, Section 5A
Constitution of India, Article 14, Article 19(1)(f), Article 31, Article 31A
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Doctrine of separation of powers
Right to property under Article 31
Principle of constitutional validity under Article 14
