card.dispute: Displaced persons challenged the Custodian's cancellation of their quasi-permanent land allotment and reallocation to others, seeking restoration or compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian General retained power to cancel or revise allotments after the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 came into force.
Whether the appellants were entitled to protection under Section 10 of the 1954 Act despite losing possession before the critical notification date.
Whether Rule 74 of the 1955 Rules barred transfer of disputed property during pendency of proceedings.
holdings: After the 1954 Act, the Custodian General lost authority to cancel or revise allotments because evacuee property vested in the Central Government, ending the Custodian's control.
The appellants were not entitled to protection under Section 10 of the 1954 Act as they did not hold or possess the land on the date of the notification, which is a necessary condition.
Rule 74 does not apply to quasi-permanent allotments or proceedings under the earlier Evacuee Property Act, and thus did not bar the transfer in question.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Sections 10, 27
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Sections 12, 19
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rules 74, 102
doctrines: Functus officio
Specific provision prevails over general provision
Vesting of property extinguishes prior administrative authority

card.dispute: The Mahant of the Asthal Estate fought with the State of Bihar over whether he was liable to be assessed for agricultural income-tax for the year when the estate was under a Court Receiver.
issues_decided: Whether the owner of an estate is liable to agricultural income-tax when the estate is under the management of a Court Receiver.
Whether the appointment of a Receiver under the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act makes the Receiver the sole assessee liable for tax.
holdings: The income collected by a Court Receiver remains the income of the owner, and the owner remains liable to agricultural income-tax despite the Receiver's possession.
Section 13 of the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act allows the Receiver to be treated as an assessee for recovery purposes but does not exempt the owner from tax liability.
doctrines: Charging provision vs. machinery provision distinction
Liability of owner despite possession by a receiver

card.dispute: The appellant tenant sought fixation of standard rent for a plot of land under the Bombay Rents Act, but the landlord contended the land was agricultural and thus outside the Act's scope.
issues_decided: Whether the plot of land was 'premises' within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 at the time of letting.
Whether the application for fixation of standard rent under Section 11 of the Act was maintainable.
holdings: The material date to determine if land qualifies as 'premises' is the date of letting, not the date of application for standard rent fixation.
Land assessed for agricultural purposes at the time of letting does not qualify as 'premises' under Section 5(8)(a) of the Act, and thus Part II of the Act does not apply.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(8)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 6(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11
doctrines: Temporal applicability of statutory definitions
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on context and subject matter

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1960, arguing that the Bill lapsed upon dissolution of the State Assembly before presidential assent, and that certain lands (Pandaravaka Verumpattom) were not 'estates' under Article 31A.
issues_decided: Whether a Bill reserved for the President's assent lapses upon dissolution of the State Legislative Assembly.
Whether the Kerala Agrarian Relations Bill could be reconsidered and passed by a newly elected Assembly after dissolution.
Whether Pandaravaka Verumpattom and Puravaka lands qualify as 'estates' under Article 31A(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the rights of 'raiyat' and 'under-raiyat' in 'estates' under Article 31A(2)(b) include holdings not derived from intermediaries.
holdings: A Bill reserved for the President's assent does not lapse upon dissolution of the State Legislative Assembly and may be reconsidered by a newly elected Assembly.
The President can validly return a pending Bill for reconsideration to a newly constituted Assembly, and subsequent assent is constitutionally valid.
Puravaka lands, being Jenmi lands, fall within the definition of 'estate' under Article 31A(2) as amended by the Fourth Amendment, but Pandaravaka Verumpattom lands do not.

The terms 'raiyat' and 'under-raiyat' in Article 31A(2)(b) are to be understood in their ordinary sense and include cultivators holding under proprietors, and the phrase 'or other intermediary' does not limit their scope.
provisions: Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1960 (Kerala Act 4 of 1961)
doctrines: Doctrine of lapse of Bills upon dissolution
Doctrine of constitutional continuity of legislation
Doctrinal interpretation of 'estate' under Article 31A
Strict construction of provisions abrogating fundamental rights

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, both displaced persons from West Pakistan, disputed the validity of a re-allotment of evacuee land, with the respondent challenging the cancellation of his original allotment and the appellant contesting the timeliness and legality of the revision application before the Custodian General.
issues_decided: Whether the revision application filed before the Custodian General was barred by limitation
Whether the Custodian General had the power to cancel an allotment made on or before July 22, 1952
holdings: The revision application was not barred by time; Rule 31(5) of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 is directory, not mandatory, and the Custodian General may entertain revision beyond sixty days if he exercises discretion reasonably.

The Custodian General had the power to cancel the allotment made on December 2, 1949, as the proviso to Rule 14(6) lifts the restriction on cancellation for revisions filed under Section 27 within the prescribed time, which includes discretionary extension beyond sixty days.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 56
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 14
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 31(5)
doctrines: Directory vs. Mandatory Rule
Reasonable Exercise of Discretionary Power
Presumption of Regularity in Administrative Proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, a brother-in-law of the insolvent, challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the sale of the insolvent's properties to him, which the respondent creditor claimed was for an inadequate price.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of the insolvent's properties by the official receiver could be set aside on the ground of inadequate consideration alone.
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 75 of the Provincial Insolvency Act to interfere with the District Judge's order in revision.
holdings: A sale in insolvency proceedings can only be set aside on grounds such as fraud, collusion, irregularity affecting price, or unconscionably low price; mere inadequacy of price without proper valuation and encumbrance assessment is insufficient.

The High Court has no jurisdiction to interfere in revision under the proviso to Section 75 unless it finds the lower court's order was not according to law; failure to apply this standard vitiates its interference.
doctrines: Judicial review of administrative discretion in insolvency sales
Principle of adequacy of consideration in insolvency auctions
Hierarchy of interests in insolvency: creditors first, then insolvent, then purchaser

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the dismissal of his application for reference to court on the ground that it was time-barred under the Land Acquisition Act, as he received no notice of the award within the prescribed period.
issues_decided: Whether the application under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act was time-barred when the landowner did not receive notice of the award under Section 12(2)
Whether the 'date of the award' for limitation purposes under the proviso to Section 18 should be construed as the date of communication of the award, not merely its making or filing
holdings: An award under the Land Acquisition Act is not effective until it is communicated to the landowner, either actually or constructively; mere making or filing does not complete the award.

The phrase 'date of the award' in the proviso to Section 18 must be read in light of Section 12(2)'s mandatory notice requirement, so limitation runs from the date of communication, not the date of making.
doctrines: Communication is essential for the legal effectiveness of an administrative award
Limitation periods affecting substantive rights must be construed to ensure aggrieved parties have knowledge before time begins to run
Literal interpretation of statutory limitation clauses rejected when it leads to injustice
Constructive notice principle in administrative law

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the mortgagees' claim to proprietary rights in sir land and accession of other lands to the mortgage, arguing that sir was not included and later-acquired lands could not be part of the mortgage.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgage included the proprietary rights in the sir land of the mortgagor despite no mention in the plaint and no application under Section 50 of the Central Provinces Tenancy Act
Whether lands that came into the mortgagor's possession after the mortgage, including those previously in the name of the mortgagor's mother, became accession to the mortgaged property
Whether the mortgagees could claim a share in lands that were formerly under ex-proprietary tenancy but later extinguished and came into possession of the mortgagor
holdings: A mortgage of all proprietary rights in a share includes the proprietary right in sir land even if not explicitly mentioned, provided the deed covers all appurtenant rights, and no application under Section 50 is needed if possession is not transferred.

When ex-proprietary tenancy is extinguished and sir land comes into the possession of the mortgagor, it becomes an accession to the mortgaged property under Section 70 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Lands not originally part of the mortgaged property but later coming into the mortgagor’s possession as part of the proprietary estate are subject to the mortgage and may be sold in execution, even if not specified in the plaint, in a suit for sale.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 11, Rule 2
doctrines: Accession to mortgaged property under Section 70
Inclusion of appurtenant rights in a mortgage by implication
No requirement of Section 50 sanction for simple mortgage without possession

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of land acquisition by the government for a private company's textile machinery parts factory, arguing it did not serve a public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land for a company's factory qualifies as a 'work likely to prove useful to the public' under Section 40(1)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the agreement under Section 41(5) mandating public access to the work is a condition precedent for acquisition when the public cannot physically use the facility.
Whether the notification under Section 6 of the Act was invalid due to non-compliance with Section 41(5).
holdings: Acquisition for a company is valid if the Government is satisfied that the work will be useful to the public, even if the public does not directly use the facility.
Section 41(5)'s requirement of public access applies only where the nature of the work permits such use; it does not invalidate acquisitions for specialized industrial facilities.
The Government's satisfaction regarding public utility is final and not subject to judicial review on merits, provided it is not arbitrary or mala fide.
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Presumption of constitutionality and governmental satisfaction
Rule of beneficial interpretation

card.dispute: The jagirdar Raja J. Rameshwar Rao challenged the inclusion of Rs. 75,820 from the sale of developed land plots as business income, claiming it was not business but a public welfare activity.
issues_decided: Whether the sum of Rs. 75,820 could be regarded as income from business based on the evidence?
Whether the expenditure on acquiring and developing land could be claimed as revenue expenditure under section 14(5)(a) of the Hyderabad Income-tax Act?
holdings: A single venture of acquiring land, developing it into plots, and selling them in parcels constitutes a business activity, and the profit is taxable as business income.

The expenditure on land acquisition and development cannot be claimed as revenue expenditure under section 14(5)(a) when the activity is held to be a business, as that provision applies only to 'other sources' and public welfare works.
doctrines: Business includes a single speculative or developmental venture if carried out with profit motive
Revenue expenditure under public welfare exceptions does not apply when income is assessed under 'business'

card.dispute: The landlord (Pandit Kishan Lal) sought eviction of the tenant (Singer Sewing Machine Company) and its assignee (Ganpat Ram Khosla) after the company transferred possession of the shop to Khosla without consent.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy of the company came to an end upon its unilateral notice and transfer of possession to Khosla.
Whether Khosla, as an assignee without landlord's consent, could be proceeded against under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether the High Court was correct in quashing the Controller’s eviction order on the ground of lack of jurisdiction.
holdings: A tenancy does not terminate by unilateral assignment; the tenant remains liable unless possession is delivered to the landlord after due notice.
An assignee of a tenant who takes possession without landlord's consent is not a trespasser but holds under the original tenancy and is liable to eviction proceedings.
Proceedings under s. 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act are maintainable against both the original tenant and the assignee if tenancy continues.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
doctrines: Distinction between assignment and surrender of tenancy
Continuation of tenancy in absence of valid surrender or notice
Maintainability of eviction proceedings under rent control legislation

card.dispute: Landlords sought ejectment of tenants for non-payment of rent for three years, but authorities refused possession on equitable grounds or based on prior relief granted under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Mamlatdar has power under s. 29(3) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 to grant relief against forfeiture on equitable grounds when rent is unpaid for three years?
Whether a tenant who received relief under s. 25(1) for default in one year can have that year's default excluded from the computation of three years of default under s. 25(2)?
Whether tenants are entitled to relief against forfeiture under s. 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 in light of the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948?
holdings: The Mamlatdar has no power under s. 29(3) to grant relief against forfeiture on equitable grounds where a tenant has defaulted in rent for three years; relief is only available under statutory conditions in s. 25(1).
A default in rent for a year for which relief was granted under s. 25(1) still counts toward the three-year default under s. 25(2); the default is not merged or erased by the grant of relief.

Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply to tenancies governed by the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 as it is inconsistent with the latter statute’s exclusive scheme for relief.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 3
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29
doctrines: Statutory rights override equitable relief
Inconsistency between general and special laws
Merger of default into relief order rejected

card.dispute: The appellant landowner sued the respondents for constructing a bund and trenches that blocked floodwater from flowing naturally from his higher land to their lower land, causing crop damage.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had a right of drainage over the respondents' land based on immemorial user
Whether the respondents were entitled to obstruct the natural flow of floodwater by constructing bunds and trenches in the name of self-protection
Whether the flooding was an unusual or usual occurrence, and its relevance to the right of drainage
Whether the 'common enemy' doctrine applies to surface water in the context of natural drainage rights
holdings: A right of drainage exists if the flow of water over another's land has occurred from time immemorial, even if the exact date of origin is unknown.
A lower landowner cannot obstruct the natural flow of water along its established course, even for flood protection, unless the flood is extraordinary.
Usual or periodic flooding qualifies as a natural phenomenon, entitling the higher landowner to drain such water onto lower lands.
The 'common enemy' doctrine does not override natural drainage rights under Indian law, especially where water follows a customary or natural course.
doctrines: Natural right of drainage
Immemorial user
Riparian rights
Common enemy doctrine (distinguished and limited)

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutionality of the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, after the state requisitioned part of his tea estate, arguing it was beyond the state's legislative power and violated the right to compensation under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 is ultra vires the State Legislature as it pertains to tea estates, a subject under Parliament's exclusive jurisdiction?
Whether the Act violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution for failing to provide for compensation or specify principles for determining compensation for requisitioned land?
holdings: The Assam Act is intra vires the State Legislature as it deals with land requisition for public purpose, not regulation of the tea industry, which remains under Parliament's control.

The Act satisfies Article 31(2) because it provides for compensation through agreed amounts or court reference, where principles from the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 are applied mutatis mutandis to determine compensation for requisition.
provisions: Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Sections 3, 6, 7, 8
Constitution of India, Article 31(2), Article 372, Schedule VII, List I, Entry 52
doctrines: Principle of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of mutatis mutandis
Doctrine of implied continuity of pre-constitutional laws under Article 372
Test of pith and substance for determining legislative competence

card.dispute: The mortgagor's legal representative sued the mortgagee's successor for redemption of mortgaged tenures and account of excess rent realisations, after the tenures were vested in the State free from encumbrances under land reform legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the decree for redemption became infructuous after the mortgage tenures were vested in the State free from encumbrances under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the civil court could direct accounts to be taken despite final determination of mortgage claims by the Claims Officer under the Act
Whether the Claims Officer had jurisdiction to consider excess realisations by the mortgagee from the mortgaged properties
holdings: The redemption decree became infructuous once the mortgaged tenures vested in the State free from encumbrances under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, as the mortgage security no longer existed.

The civil court could not direct accounts to be taken under the redemption decree, as the Claims Officer had already determined the mortgage accounts under the Act, and such determination was final under Section 18(3).
The Claims Officer had jurisdiction under Section 16(2)(b) to examine the extent of realisations by the mortgagee, including whether excess amounts were recovered from the mortgaged properties.
doctrines: Doctrine of Infructuousness of Decrees
Doctrine of Finality of Administrative Determination
Doctrine of Jurisdictional Exclusivity of Statutory Tribunals

card.dispute: The trustee of a temple and hereditary pujaris disputed over the management and control of the temple, including the pujaris' rights to offerings and disciplinary control by the trustee.
issues_decided: Whether a scheme framed under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be modified by an application if the scheme itself reserves power to amend it.
Whether the District Judge had jurisdiction to revise the scheme without a fresh suit under Section 92.
Whether the revised scheme clauses affected the private rights of the pujaris, particularly regarding their share in offerings and power of punishment by the trustee.
holdings: A scheme framed under Section 92 CPC may include a provision for future modification by application, as long as it pertains to administration and not private rights.
Modifications to a scheme for administrative purposes can be made by application without a fresh suit under Section 92 CPC, provided the scheme authorizes such changes.
Clauses affecting the pujaris' rights to offerings and disciplinary powers must not infringe on their private rights and must include safeguards against abuse of power.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Sections 15, 16, 18
doctrines: Scheme modification for administrative purposes
Protection of private rights in religious endowments
Judicial safeguard against abuse of managerial power

card.dispute: The landlords sued to evict the tenants, who claimed protection as 'protected tenants' under a repealed tenancy law, leading to a dispute over whether their rights survived the repeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had acquired a 'right accrued' as protected tenants under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939 before its repeal.
Whether Section 88 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 expressly removed the rights of protected tenants in areas within two miles of Poona City.
Whether Section 89(2)(b) of the 1948 Act preserved rights accrued under the repealed 1939 Act despite the exclusion under Section 88.
holdings: A right as a protected tenant under the 1939 Act accrued automatically upon fulfillment of conditions, without need for formal enforcement action, and was preserved under the 1948 Act.
Section 88(1) of the 1948 Act excludes the application of its provisions to certain areas but does not expressly extinguish rights already accrued under the earlier law.

Section 89(2)(b) of the 1948 Act saves rights accrued under the repealed Act, and the omission of the word 'instituted' before 'continued and disposed of' does not limit the preservation of such rights.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 31
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights under repealing statutes
Presumption against abrogation of rights by implication
Continuation of accrued rights despite exclusion of statutory application in certain areas

card.dispute: The holders of a Cis-Sutlej jagir, their son, and the jagirdar's wife fought over the apportionment of compensation and entitlement to interest after the State compulsorily acquired jagir lands.
issues_decided: Whether the acquired jagir lands were inalienable and the jagirdar had only a life interest
How the compensation should be apportioned among the jagirdar, his son, and his wife
Whether interest is payable on compensation from the date of possession to the date of payment
holdings: The jagir lands were inalienable, and the jagirdar held only a life interest, not absolute ownership.

Compensation for three villages is divided equally between the jagirdar and his son; for the fourth village, the principal is invested and the wife receives maintenance from the interest during her lifetime.
Interest at 4% per annum is payable on compensation from the date of possession to the date of payment, as a matter of equitable right, unless statute clearly excludes it.
provisions: East Punjab Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property (Temporary Powers) Act, 1948, Section 5
doctrines: Equitable right to interest upon compulsory acquisition of land
Presumption against statutory deprivation of property without full compensation
Life interest in inalienable jagir property

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the constitutionality of a provision allowing the Controller to select a tenant for a vacant house, arguing it violated his fundamental right to property and equality.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(3)(a) of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951 imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
Whether Section 3(3)(a) violates Article 14 of the Constitution by conferring unguided discretionary power on the Controller to select a tenant.
holdings: The selection of a private individual as a tenant by the Controller does not impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property, as it serves a public purpose and applies only when the owner does not need the house.
Section 3(3)(a) does not violate Article 14 because it provides sufficient guidance for tenant selection, including suitability, consideration of landlord's views, and judicial review mechanisms.
provisions: Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 3(3)(a)
doctrines: Reasonable restriction on fundamental rights
Public purpose doctrine
Guidelines against arbitrariness under Article 14
Judicial review as a safeguard against administrative discretion

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the execution of a mortgage decree against his bhumidari rights after the abolition of his zamindari rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether bhumidari rights created under Section 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 can be sold in execution of a pre-existing mortgage decree on proprietary zamindari rights.
Whether the mortgagee can enforce its security against property that has vested in the State under the Act.
holdings: The bhumidari rights conferred under Section 18 are new rights created by statute and distinct from the original proprietary rights, which had already vested in the State under Section 6; hence, they are not subject to pre-existing mortgage decrees.

Where proprietary rights are compulsorily acquired under the Act, the mortgagee's sole remedy is to claim compensation under Section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act, not execution against resettled bhumidari rights.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(a)(i)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(h)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18
doctrines: Vesting of property in the State extinguishes prior proprietary interests
Statutory creation of new rights distinct from extinguished rights
Mortgagee's remedy limited to compensation when property is compulsorily acquired

card.dispute: The appellants, who had a right of preemption, challenged a sale deed executed on January 31, 1946, claiming their preemption right was triggered upon execution, while the respondents argued the sale was complete only upon registration on February 9, 1946.
issues_decided: Whether a sale by a registered deed is complete on the date of execution or on the date of registration.
Whether the right of preemption under Muslim law arises when the sale deed is executed or only after registration is complete.
The interpretation and interplay between Section 47 and Section 61 of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, regarding the effective date of a registered sale deed.
holdings: A sale requiring registration is not complete until the registration process is finalized under Section 61 of the Indian Registration Act, even if the deed is executed earlier.
Section 47 of the Registration Act allows a registered document to operate from the date it would have, had registration not been required, but does not determine when the sale is legally complete.
The right of preemption must be exercised after the sale is complete; a premature talab made before registration is invalid if the sale is deemed complete only upon registration.
The intention of the parties as expressed in the deed governs when the sale takes effect, and if the deed shows intent for immediate transfer, the sale may be treated as effective from execution.
doctrines: Doctrine of relation back under Section 47 of the Indian Registration Act
Doctrine of completion of sale by registration
Intention of parties as determining the effective date of transfer
Law of preemption under Muslim personal law and its interaction with statutory transfer

card.dispute: The sons of Jawala Prasad sought to execute a partition decree for possession of a house, but the application was challenged as time-barred due to delay by their father, the karta, in executing the decree.
issues_decided: Whether Section 7 of the Indian Limitation Act applies to a decree for joint possession in a partition suit.
Whether the father, as karta of the joint Hindu family, could give a valid discharge of the liability under the decree, thereby starting the limitation period for the minor sons.
holdings: Section 7 of the Indian Limitation Act applies to non-monetary decrees, including decrees for possession in partition suits, as 'discharge' encompasses satisfaction of any legal liability, not just payment of debt.

The karta of a Hindu joint family can accept possession under a partition decree on behalf of minor sons, thereby discharging the liability and triggering the limitation period under Section 7, unless restricted by Order 32, Rules 6 or 7 of the CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 32, Rules 6 and 7
doctrines: Doctrine of discharge under Section 7 of the Limitation Act
Karta's authority to bind minor family members in property matters
Limited restriction on guardian's power under Order 32, Rules 6 and 7 of CPC

card.dispute: Salig Ram challenged Munshi Ram's claim to inherit a half share in the property of their natural grandfather, Nanak Chand, after Munshi Ram had been adopted into another family.
issues_decided: Whether an adopted son can inherit from his natural grandfather under Hindu law or customary law in Amritsar district among Brahmins and Khatris.
Whether the principle of representation allows an adopted son to step into the shoes of his predeceased father for inheritance purposes.
Which custom governs succession in this case: the general Punjab custom or the local Amritsar district riwaj-i-am?
holdings: Under Hindu law and the applicable customary law in Amritsar district among Brahmins and Khatris, an adopted son cannot inherit from his natural grandfather if the grandfather is survived by another son.
The principle of representation does not permit an adopted son to inherit from his natural grandfather when doing so would contradict the conditions of the applicable custom.

Customary law in Amritsar district among Brahmins and Khatris allows an adopted son to inherit from his natural father only if the father left no other son; this right does not extend to inheritance from the grandfather.
doctrines: Burden of proving custom
Principle of representation in inheritance
Primacy of local custom over general custom when proven
Conflict between statutory law, general custom, and local riwaj

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession after the tenant's lease expired, but the tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Rents Control Act, 1947, which restricted landlords' rights to recover possession.
issues_decided: Whether Section 12(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 applies to pending suits when Part II of the Act comes into force in a particular area
Whether Section 12(1) has retrospective operation despite earlier judicial observations that Section 12 is prospective
holdings: Section 12(1) applies to suits pending when Part II of the Act is extended to an area, as it governs the right to decree, not merely the filing of suits.
The language of Section 12(1) is such that it operates when a decree for possession is to be passed, and thus applies retrospectively to pending proceedings.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 6
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1)
doctrines: Prospective and retrospective operation of statutes
Principle that a section may be prospective in one part and retrospective in another
Rule of construction of provisos and saving clauses

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a sale certificate and final decree in a mortgage suit, claiming that a property was wrongly described and that subrogation rights of second mortgagees affected the purchasers' title.
issues_decided: Whether a mistake in the plot number in the final decree and sale certificate, where the property is otherwise fully described, amounts to a mere misdescription or invalidates the sale.
Whether the second mortgagees could claim subrogation to the first mortgagee's rights in the absence of an agreement or earmarked funds for redemption.
holdings: A mistake in the plot number in the decree and sale certificate does not invalidate the sale if the property's identity is clearly established by boundaries, area, and khata number.
Subrogation cannot be claimed in the absence of an agreement or earmarked funds in the mortgage deed for redeeming the prior mortgage.
doctrines: Misdescription vs. misidentification in property sales
Doctrine of subrogation in mortgage law

card.dispute: Displaced non-fauji allottees challenged the cancellation of their land allotments in favour of fauji families in a village declared as a 'fauji village'.
issues_decided: Whether the order dated October 9, 1951, by the Director of Relief and Rehabilitation amounted to a final order cancelling the allotments.
Whether the cancellation order could be implemented after June 15, 1952, in view of Rule 49 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950.
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Article 226 to review its own order by impleading affected parties who were not originally before it.
holdings: The order dated October 9, 1951, was a final decision to oust non-fauji allottees, not merely a proposal, as it directed steps for their removal and resettlement.
The non-implementation of an order before June 15, 1952, did not bar its implementation thereafter, especially after the second proviso of Rule 49 was deleted on August 4, 1952.
The High Court has inherent power under Article 226 to review its order to prevent miscarriage of justice, particularly when affected persons were not initially heard.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 14(6)
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 49
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Inherent power of review in courts of plenary jurisdiction
Doctrine of finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958, arguing it did not fall under Article 31A protection as their lands were not 'estates' under existing tenurial law.
issues_decided: Whether the lands held by the petitioners in Vidarbha region qualify as 'estate' or its local equivalent under Article 31A(2)(a) of the Constitution.
Whether the impugned Act is protected by Article 31A despite the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, not using the term 'estate'.
holdings: The term 'estate' under Article 31A(2)(a) includes local equivalents defined in regional land revenue laws, even if the word 'estate' is not used.
Lands held under the State and subject to land revenue, such as those held by Bhumiswamis under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, fall within the class of 'estate' or its local equivalent.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Sections 2(7), 2(20), 145, 146
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Sections 2(17), 2(18)
doctrines: Doctrine of local equivalents under Article 31A
Doctrine of constitutional protection for agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Padmini Kunwar Ju Sahiba, challenged the state's resumption of her rights under a Lambardari lease, claiming she was not a jagirdar under the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a 'jagirdar' within the meaning of Section 2(1)(c) of the Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952
Whether a Lambardari lease constitutes an 'Ijara' or mere lease of land revenue under the Act
Whether the state had the authority to resume the appellant's rights under the challenged notification
holdings: A person is not a 'jagirdar' under Section 2(1)(c) merely because they hold a lease; the term 'Ijaredar' in the Act refers only to those holding leases of land revenue or proprietary rights, not rights in land itself.
A Lambardari lease that confers actual rights in land, including rights to cultivate, improve, mortgage, and sell, is more than a mere 'Ijara' and does not fall under the definition of 'jagirdar'.
The state cannot resume rights under the Abolition Act where the lessee does not fall within the statutory definition of 'jagirdar' or 'Ijaredar' as understood in context and ordinary meaning.
provisions: Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 2(1)(c)
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 2(1)(d)
Vindhya Pradesh Abolition of Jagirs and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 5
doctrines: Literal and contextual interpretation of statutory definitions
Principle that undefined terms in statutes should be given their ordinary meaning
Doctrine of ejusdem generis applied to inclusive definitions in land reform legislation

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and Lt. Col. K. S. R. Swami disputed whether the Collector's permission to reclaim and cultivate forest land prevailed over the Forest Officer's prohibition, and whether the respondent's rights in the land had been extinguished under the Bihar Private Forest Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector's permission under Rule 8 of the Bihar Protected Forest Rules to clear land for cultivation prevails over the Forest Officer's prohibition under Rule 4.

Whether the respondent's rights in the forest land were extinguished under Section 19 of the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1948, prior to the final notification constituting the land as a protected forest.
holdings: The Collector's permission under Rule 8 to clear land for cultivation is valid and binding; Rules 1 to 4, which regulate tree removal, do not apply when land is to be cleared for cultivation, which falls exclusively under Rule 8.
Rights under the Bihar Private Forests Act, 1948 are extinguished only after the final notification under Section 30; until then, pending claims and inquiries, the respondent's rights remain intact.
provisions: Bihar Protected Forest Rules, Rules 1 to 4 and Rule 8
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutory rules
Doctrine of implied repeal and precedence of specific provisions
Procedural fairness in extinction of rights
Pregnant negative in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Kalimata Thakurani of Kalighat and certain shebaits, over the management scheme of the temple and its properties, including representation of shebaits, their remuneration, and procedural safeguards.
issues_decided: Whether the managing committee under the scheme over-represents the shebaits and requires restructuring
Whether the shebaits are entitled to a share in the offerings or should be treated merely as pujaris
Whether the scheme must include a provision allowing parties to apply to the District Judge for directions on unresolved matters
holdings: The shebaits should not form the majority in the managing committee; their representation should be reduced to five, with six non-shebait members appointed by specified public and religious bodies, ensuring majority external oversight.

Shebaits are not mere pujaris but hold a property right in the office and are entitled to reimbursement and remuneration, including a share in offerings, for services and expenses rendered in temple worship.
The scheme must allow parties to apply to the District Judge for directions on implementation issues; a new clause (56-A) should be added to permit modification of the scheme by court application.
doctrines: Shebaitship as a property right
Principle of equitable temple management with external oversight
Judicial restraint in religious disputes involving title
Power of court to modify schemes for religious endowments

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, arguing it violated the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether a law providing for the acquisition or requisition of property by the State under Article 31(2) is subject to the restrictions of Article 19(1)(f).
Whether the decision in Babu Barkya Thakur's case is inconsistent with Kochuni's case after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955.
holdings: A law authorizing the State to acquire or requisition property under Article 31(2) is not subject to the protection or reasonableness test under Article 19(1)(f) and cannot be challenged on that ground.

Kochuni's case did not overrule Bhanji Munji's case for laws under Article 31(2); the two decisions are not in conflict, as Kochuni's case dealt with deprivation other than by acquisition or requisition.
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)
Doctrine of implied limitation on fundamental rights

card.dispute: The defendant challenged the valuation of properties and adequacy of court fees paid by the plaintiff in a suit for possession of family properties and religious endowments.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant could raise the issue of inadequate court fee and valuation of suit properties as a matter in dispute between the parties.
Whether the defendant could invoke the High Court's revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order determining court fees.
holdings: The Court Fees Act is intended to collect revenue, not to provide defendants with a technical means to obstruct the trial; the defendant cannot treat valuation as a disputed issue between the parties.
A defendant has no right to file a revision petition in the High Court under Section 115 of the CPC challenging a court fee order unless there is a jurisdictional error or illegality.
provisions: Madras Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, Section 12(2)
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction limited to jurisdictional errors
Court fee as a revenue measure, not a procedural weapon

card.dispute: The appellant contested the Union Government's modification of a mining licence, which restricted his prospecting area and allowed a rival claimant to obtain a lease over part of the disputed land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could quash the Union Government's order modifying the mining licence grant.
Whether the High Court could direct the State Government to grant the mining lease to the appellant despite the Union Government's directions to the contrary.
Whether the Union Government had jurisdiction to pass an order under Rule 57 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949, when no review application was pending.
holdings: The High Court cannot quash an order passed by the Union Government as it lacks territorial jurisdiction over the Union Government.
Directions to the State Government to grant a mining lease cannot be issued unless the Union Government's conflicting order is first set aside.
The Union Government's review proceedings were not finally disposed of by September 1952, so it had jurisdiction to pass the April 1954 order under Rule 57.
doctrines: Territorial jurisdiction of High Courts
Doctrine of finality of administrative orders
Principle of subordinate decision-making in federal administrative structure

card.dispute: The appellants sought to extend the time for depositing security for costs in an appeal to the Supreme Court, but the Calcutta High Court rejected the application, claiming it lacked jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court has jurisdiction to extend time for furnishing security for costs under Order 45, Rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, after the amendment of 1920.
Whether Order XII, Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, confers jurisdiction on the High Court to extend time for furnishing security in a proper case.
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction to extend time for furnishing security under Order 45, Rule 7, when read with other provisions of the Code and the context of appellate procedure.
Order XII, Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950, expressly empowers the High Court to grant further time or make other orders as justice requires, even if security is not filed in time.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 45, Rules 7, 10, 11
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XII, Rule 3
doctrines: Concurrent interpretation of statutory provisions
Rule of liberal construction of procedural rules to serve justice
Doctrine of judicial precedent and overruling erroneous decisions

card.dispute: The State of Saurashtra fought against grantees of the Nawab of Junagadh over whether the Administrator's cancellation of property grants between 1947 and 1949 was justiciable and whether the grantees could enforce their rights in Indian courts.
issues_decided: Whether the cancellation of grants by the Administrator of Junagadh was an act of state and thus non-justiciable in municipal courts.
Whether the respondents' property rights under the Nawab were enforceable against the Indian Dominion after the change of sovereignty.
Whether Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, protected the respondents' property rights upon the assumption of administration by India on November 9, 1947.
holdings: The cancellation of grants by the Administrator was an act of state and not justiciable in municipal courts, as it involved the new sovereign’s refusal to recognize pre-existing rights.

Individuals in annexed territories can only enforce rights in municipal courts that are recognized by the new sovereign; prior rights under the former ruler are unenforceable without such recognition.

Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, does not create new property rights but only protects existing ones; since the respondents’ rights were not recognized by the Indian Dominion, the provision did not apply.
doctrines: Act of State doctrine
Doctrine of recognition of rights under a new sovereign
Non-justiciability of political questions involving sovereignty

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and its officers challenged a High Court order quashing their decision to allow Melas on land claimed by Shanti Devi as a raiyat, disputing her right to hold Melas after the vesting of estates in the State.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in issuing a writ of certiorari quashing the Revenue authorities' decision to allow Melas on the disputed land?
Whether Shanti Devi had acquired a genuine raiyati right over the land prior to the vesting of the estate in the State?
holdings: Even if the land was bakasht property of the proprietor, prior to the 1959 amendment, the State had no right to hold Melas on such land to the exclusion of the raiyat in possession.
On the principle that apparent state of facts is presumed true unless disproved, Shanti Devi is deemed to have acquired genuine raiyati status before vesting, entitling her to hold Melas.
provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in transactions
Doctrine of vested rights
Judicial review under Article 226

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a land consolidation scheme that reduced the land allotment to evacuee allottees without compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents had a sufficient legal interest in the allotted evacuee land to maintain a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
Whether the consolidation scheme, which substituted lands of lesser value without compensation, was valid under the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948.
holdings: An evacuee allotted land on a quasi-permanent basis has a valuable legal right entitled to judicial protection under Article 226, even if not a fundamental right to property.
A consolidation scheme that reduces an allottee's land without providing equal value or compensation violates the East Punjab Holdings Act and is illegal, even if directed by the government.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 14
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 15
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 10
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 14(6)
doctrines: Judicial protection of statutory rights
Ultra vires doctrine
Principle of正当 procedure in administrative action

card.dispute: The Sonapur Tea Company challenged the constitutional validity of the Assam Fixation of Ceiling on Land Holding Act, 1957, which extinguished its rights over excess land claimed by tenants under agrarian reform measures.
issues_decided: Whether the rights extinguished by the Assam Fixation of Ceiling on Land Holding Act, 1957, fall within the expression 'rights in relation to an estate' under Article 31A(2)(b) of the Constitution?
Whether the impugned Act is a colourable legislation, enacted with the ulterior motive of profiting from land acquisition rather than genuine agrarian reform?
holdings: The rights extinguished by the Act, including those of landholders under the Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, qualify as 'rights in relation to an estate' under Article 31A(2)(b) and are thus protected from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
The Act is not colourable legislation; its pith and substance is agrarian reform aimed at abolishing intermediaries and transferring land to cultivators, not profiting from land disposal.
provisions: Assam Fixation of Ceiling on Land Holding Act, 1957, Sections 4, 5, 16, 18
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Sections 3(g), 9
doctrines: Doctrine of colourable legislation
Liberal interpretation of 'rights in relation to an estate'
Protection of agrarian reform laws under Article 31A

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh stopped paying a pension and revenue remission to Kunwar Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, a descendant of a former jagirdar, after enacting the Zamindari Abolition Act; the dispute was whether these payments were 'interests in land' that were extinguished by the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the annual pension of Rs. 30,612-13-0 granted in 1838 for relinquishing rights over 166 mahals was an interest in land extinguished by the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, 1950
Whether the remission of land revenue on 12 mahals constituted an interest in land that was extinguished under the Act
holdings: A pension fixed as a percentage of land revenue but granted as compensation for settling a civil claim is not an interest in land and survives the vesting of estates under the Zamindari Abolition Act.
A remission of land revenue on specific mahals constitutes an interest in land revenue and is extinguished by the operation of the Zamindari Abolition Act.
provisions: U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, Section 32, clauses (a) to (d)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (U.P. Act 1 of 1951), Section 3(8), Section 4, Section 6(b)
doctrines: Extinguishment of rights under land reform legislation
Distinction between interest in land and compensation for relinquished rights
Statutory interpretation based on legislative scheme and absence of compensation mechanism

card.dispute: The petitioner, Thakur Bahadur Singh, challenged the state's demand for payment of hukamnama, arguing it was a 'tribute' whose liability was extinguished under the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the liability to pay hukamnama falls within the definition of 'tribute' under Section 4(a) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952
Whether the inclusive definition of 'tribute' in Section 2(r) of the Act extends to ad hoc payments like hukamnama
holdings: The term 'tribute' in Section 4(a) refers only to recurring payments attributable to specific years, not ad hoc payments like hukamnama.
Despite the inclusive definition in Section 2(r), the context and purpose of the Act show that 'tribute' must be construed narrowly to exclude one-time or irregular charges.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 2(r)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 4(a)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 8
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Use of legislative purpose to construe ambiguous definitions
Presumption against interpretations causing unintended hardship

card.dispute: The Andhra Bank sued R. Srinivasan and others for recovery of money; after one defendant died, his legal representatives were brought into the suit, and the dispute centered on whether the Hyderabad Court retained jurisdiction and whether the legatees under the will were legal representatives.
issues_decided: Whether the Hyderabad Court retained jurisdiction over the suit after the death of a defendant when his legal representatives were non-residents.
Whether persons who are legatees of only a part of a deceased's estate qualify as 'legal representatives' under Section 2(11) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
holdings: A court retains jurisdiction over a suit even after the defendant's death if the suit was initially filed in a competent court; the procedural addition of non-resident legal representatives does not affect the court's jurisdiction.

A person who inherits only a part of a deceased’s estate under a will qualifies as a 'legal representative' under Section 2(11) of the CPC if they represent the estate in law, and the term is not limited to universal legatees or heirs.
doctrines: Continuity of jurisdiction in personal actions upon death of defendant
Broad interpretation of 'legal representative' under CPC
Rule of private international law not applicable where original court had jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Central Talkies Ltd. challenged the validity of permission granted by an Additional District Magistrate for a tenant's eviction, arguing only the District Magistrate or his specifically authorised officer could grant such permission under the U.P. Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional District Magistrate was competent to grant permission for an eviction suit under Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947.
Whether the District Magistrate under the Act is a persona designata, making his office non-delegable.

Whether the notification under Section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, empowering an Additional District Magistrate, overrides the definition of 'District Magistrate' in the Rent Control Act.
holdings: The Additional District Magistrate was competent to grant permission under Section 3 of the U.P. Rent Control Act, as the government notification conferred all powers of the District Magistrate under any law, including the Rent Act.
The District Magistrate under the Act is not a persona designata; the office is defined functionally and allows delegation to officers authorised under the Act or by law.

Section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, enables the Provincial Government to confer powers of the District Magistrate under any law, which includes the Rent Control Act, and such power is not restricted by the Act’s definition of 'District Magistrate'.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 2(d)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Persona designata
Delegation of statutory powers
Interpretation of 'includes' in statutory definitions
Prevailing effect of general statutory notifications over specific office designations

card.dispute: The Custodian of Evacuee Property challenged the High Court's decision to allow an appeal against an order declaring property as evacuee property, where subsequent legislation had changed the appellate forum from the High Court to the Custodian-General.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings initiated under the first Mysore Act (1949) continued to be governed by its appeal provisions after it was repealed and replaced by subsequent legislation providing different appellate mechanisms.
Whether the right of appeal to the High Court under the first Mysore Act was saved after its repeal, or whether it was replaced by appeal to the Custodian-General by necessary intendment.

Whether the High Court could entertain an appeal or exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to review an order passed by the Custodian after subsequent laws had transferred appellate authority to the Custodian-General.
holdings: Proceedings commenced under Section 8 of the first Mysore Act are in substance equivalent to proceedings under Section 5 of the second Mysore Act or Section 7 of the Central Act, and must be deemed to continue under the latter due to deeming provisions in Section 53(2) and Section 58(3).

The legislature, by necessary intendment, intended to replace the right of appeal to the High Court with an appeal to the Custodian-General, even though there was no express repeal of the appeal right, as long as an alternative remedy was provided.

The High Court could not act as an appellate authority but could only exercise supervisory jurisdiction under Article 226; however, it could not interfere unless there was a jurisdictional error or a patent legal error, which was not present here.
provisions: Mysore Administration of Evacuee Property (Emergency) Act, 1949, Section 5, 6, 8, 30
Mysore Administration of Evacuee Property (Second) (Emergency) Act, 1949, Section 22, 23, 25, 53(2)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
doctrines: Doctrine of necessary intendment
Doctrine of deeming fiction in statutory interpretation
Supervisory vs. appellate jurisdiction in writ proceedings
Principles of natural justice in quasi-judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The Dooars Tea Co. Ltd. challenged the Commissioner's inclusion of the market value of unsold agricultural produce (bamboos, thatching grass, fuel timber) used in its tea business as taxable agricultural income.
issues_decided: Whether agricultural produce used for the assessee's own business but not sold constitutes agricultural income under the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1944
Whether Rule 4(2) of the Rules under the Act permits computation of income from agricultural produce not sold in the market
holdings: Agricultural produce utilized by the assessee for its own business constitutes agricultural income under Section 2(1)(b)(i) of the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, even if not sold or converted into money.
Rule 4(2) applies to cases where agricultural produce is not sold at all, and allows computation of market value based on cultivation expenses, rent, and a reasonable profit margin.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Contextual interpretation of statutory clauses
Residuary rule construction

card.dispute: The Darcah Committee, Ajmer fought the State of Rajasthan over whether a Magistrate acting under Section 234 of the Ajmer-Merwara Municipalities Regulation, 1925, is an 'inferior criminal court' under the Code of Criminal Procedure, making criminal revision permissible, and whether recovery proceedings were valid without prescribed rules.
issues_decided: Whether a Magistrate entertaining an application under Section 234 of the Ajmer-Merwara Municipalities Regulation, 1925, is an 'inferior criminal court' under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Whether an application under Section 234 is invalid if rules under the Regulation have not been framed and no form for demand under Section 222 has been prescribed.
holdings: The Magistrate acting under Section 234 does not function as an inferior criminal court under the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the proceedings are recovery-oriented and civil in nature, and the Magistrate acts as a 'persona designata' under statutory designation.

The absence of framed rules or prescribed forms for demand under Section 222 does not invalidate the claim for recovery under Section 234, as the statutory power to recover costs remains enforceable despite procedural gaps.
doctrines: Persona designata
Ministerial vs. judicial enquiry
Finality of claims after statutory appeal period

card.dispute: The Lokmanya Mills challenged the Barsi Borough Municipality's method of computing house tax on mills and factories based solely on floor area, arguing it violated the statutory basis for annual letting value under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipality could lawfully compute annual letting value for house tax solely on the basis of floor area of mills and associated buildings under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925.
Whether Rule 2C, which fixed annual letting value based on floor area, was intra vires Section 58 of the Act.
holdings: A rate under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925 must be based on capital value or annual letting value, which means the rent a hypothetical tenant would reasonably pay; it cannot be based solely on floor area.

Rule 2C is ultra vires because it arbitrarily fixes annual letting value without regard to actual rental value, thereby violating the statutory method and depriving taxpayers of their right to challenge valuation.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'annual letting value'
Ultra vires doctrine
Principle of reasonable valuation for taxation

card.dispute: The Rajah of Vizianagaram challenged whether foreign creditors could prove their claims in the winding up of an unregistered English company in India.
issues_decided: Whether foreign creditors are entitled to prove their claims in the winding up proceedings of an unregistered company in India.
Whether the winding up of an unregistered company in India benefits only Indian creditors or all creditors globally.
holdings: Foreign creditors can prove their claims in the winding up of an unregistered company in India as the proceedings benefit all creditors, not just Indian ones.
The distribution of assets in winding up must be rateable among all creditors, and there is no legal basis to exclude foreign creditors from such proceedings.
doctrines: Principle of rateable distribution of assets among all creditors in winding up
Ancillary winding-up doctrine: foreign liquidation proceedings are complementary to the principal winding up in the country of incorporation
Deemed continuation of dissolved foreign companies for the purpose of winding up in India

card.dispute: The State of Vindhya Pradesh fought with lessees over whether the suit for damages and injunction should have been filed against the State of Vindhya Pradesh or the Union of India.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Vindhya Pradesh, a Part C State, was a proper defendant in a suit for breach of contract over a tendu leaf lease.
Whether, under the Code of Civil Procedure and the General Clauses Act, a suit against a Part C State should name the Union of India or the State as defendant.
holdings: The State of Vindhya Pradesh was a distinct legal entity capable of being sued, and the suit was properly filed against it.
Under Section 79(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with the General Clauses Act, the proper defendant in a suit against a Part C State is the State itself, not the Union of India.
provisions: Government of Part C States Act, 1951, Section 38(2)
doctrines: Legal personality of Part C States
Doctrine of proper party in suits against government
Interpretation of statutory definitions in context of federal structure

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against a joint arbitration award in favor of two brothers, Labhu Ram and Nathu Ram, for land acquisition compensation; after Labhu Ram's death, the appeal continued only against Nathu Ram, raising the question of whether the appeal abated entirely due to failure to bring Labhu Ram's legal representative on record.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal abates as a whole when one of the joint decree-holders dies and their legal representative is not brought on record?
Whether the appellate court can proceed with an appeal against a surviving co-decree-holder where the decree is joint and indivisible?
Whether specification of shares in revenue records allows an appeal to proceed against one co-decree-holder after the death of the other?
holdings: An appeal does not automatically abate in its entirety upon the death of one joint decree-holder, but may abate as to the entire appeal if the decree is joint and indivisible and the rights of the deceased remain intertwined with those of the surviving respondent.

Where a decree is joint and indivisible, the appellate court cannot proceed with the appeal against the surviving respondent alone, as it cannot modify the decree even indirectly without affecting the rights of the deceased respondent’s legal representatives.

Mere mention of separate shares in revenue records does not make the decree divisible; the nature of the claim and decree determines divisibility, and a joint claim based on joint ownership results in an indivisible decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 4
Punjab Land Acquisition (Defence of India) Rules, 1943, Rule 3, Rule 6, Rule 10, Rule 18
doctrines: Abatement of appeal due to non-impleadment of legal representative
Indivisibility of joint decrees
Principle of effective adjudication and execution of decrees
Doctrine of necessary parties in appeals

card.dispute: The Union of India contested the de-requisition of a building requisitioned during the emergency, which was later used for a private dance and music school, against the owner's claim for its return.
issues_decided: Whether the Letters Patent appeal was maintainable within 30 days under High Court Rules despite the 20-day limitation under the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the continued use of a requisitioned property for a purpose other than that for which it was originally requisitioned obligates the government to de-requisition it
Whether a fiction under s.24(2) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 validates continued possession if the original purpose no longer exists
holdings: Rule 4 of the Punjab High Court Rules allowing 30 days to file a Letters Patent appeal is a special law under s.29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1908, and overrides the 20-day period in Article 151.
The government must release requisitioned property when the purpose for which it was requisitioned ceases to exist, even if used for another public purpose.
The deeming fiction in s.24(2) of the 1952 Act does not validate continued possession if the original requisition purpose no longer exists under the Defence of India Rules, r.75-A.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 3
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 24(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of deeming fiction
Doctrine of limitation and special law override
Doctrine of purpose-specific requisition

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's refusal to grant a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1), arguing that the appellate decree, though partly in his favour, varied the trial court's decision and thus was not merely confirmatory.
issues_decided: Whether an appellate decree that varies the trial court's decision in favour of a party can be considered an affirmance under Article 133(1) of the Constitution.
Whether a party benefiting from a partial variation by the High Court can claim a right to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1).
holdings: An appellate decree that varies the trial court's decision on a matter in controversy cannot be regarded as an affirmance, even if the variation favours the appellant.

A variation in the decree on a substantive issue, such as property rights or interest, constitutes a change in the decision on merits and entitles the party to seek a certificate under Article 133(1).
doctrines: Doctrine of substantial variation
Literal and purposive interpretation of constitutional provisions
Adjudication on merits as basis for appeal

card.dispute: The builder claimed unpaid dues for additional construction work not covered by the contract, while the owner sought compensation for defective work and challenged the builder's claim.
issues_decided: Whether the builder was entitled to compensation for additional work despite failure to prove an oral agreement on rates?
Whether the court could award compensation under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in the absence of an express or proven oral contract?
Whether the owner could claim set-off for defective work in the builder's suits after his own suit for damages was dismissed?
holdings: A party who performs work under a contract without intending it to be gratuitous is entitled to compensation for the value of the benefit conferred, even if no express or oral agreement is proven.
Where additional work is done and benefit received, compensation may be awarded under Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, even if quantum meruit was not specifically pleaded.
A party cannot reagitate a claim for damages for defective work as an equitable set-off in another suit after the original suit for such damages has been dismissed and no appeal filed.
doctrines: Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Principle of quantum meruit
Equitable set-off

card.dispute: The landlord (Trimbak Damodhar Raipurkar) sought to eject the tenant (Assaram Hiraman Patil) after a lease expiry, but the tenant claimed continued tenancy under amended tenancy laws requiring specific notice for termination.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1952 apply retrospectively to tenancies existing before its commencement
Whether the landlord's right to eject the tenant accrued before the amendment came into force
Whether a valid notice under the amended law is mandatory for termination of tenancy
holdings: The amending Act of 1952 is not retrospective but applies to existing tenancies, as it regulates future rights and does not alter past obligations.
A landlord's right to eject accrues only upon actual termination of the tenancy, not upon giving notice; thus, the right had not vested before the amendment took effect.
The statutory requirement of a valid notice under the 1952 Amendment Act must be complied with to terminate a tenancy, even if notice was given before the amendment.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Sections 5, 14(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1952, Section 2
doctrines: Distinction between vested rights and existing rights
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutes
Statutory extension of tenancy overriding prior contractual terms

card.dispute: The appellant sought to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133(1) of the Constitution, but the High Court refused a certificate, holding its decree was one of affirmance and did not involve a substantial question of law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate decree passed by the High Court was one of affirmance within the meaning of Article 133(1) of the Constitution?
What is the correct test to determine if a decree is one of affirmance or variation for the purpose of appeal under Article 133(1)?
Whether a variation in costs or interest affects the character of an appellate decree as one of affirmance?
holdings: A decree is not one of affirmance if it varies the trial court's decision in any respect on the merits; the extent of variation is immaterial.
The correct test is to compare the appellate decree as a whole with the trial court's decision as a whole; any variation makes it a decree of variation.
A variation in costs does not change the character of a decree as one of affirmance, but a variation in interest on the merits does, as it forms part of the dispute.
doctrines: Literal construction of constitutional provisions
Substance over form in appellate decrees
Adjudication on merits as basis for determining affirmance

card.dispute: Multiple plaintiffs filed twelve suits against different sets of defendants over land rights, which were decided by a common judgment; after some appeals were dismissed for default and others on merits, the remaining defendants challenged the res judicata bar and whether consolidation proceedings rendered their appeals infructuous.
issues_decided: Whether the appeals before the Supreme Court became infructuous due to consolidation operations under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
Whether the second appeals before the Board of Revenue were barred by res judicata
holdings: The appeals were not rendered infructuous by consolidation operations because the relevant amendments to the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act were prospective and did not apply to cases where consolidation was already completed.

The bar of res judicata did not apply because the prior final judgments were against different parties and involved different plots, and a common judgment in multiple suits does not create a single binding decision for all purposes.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 5
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 11
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 49
doctrines: Res judicata
Prospective operation of amendments
Infructuous appeals

card.dispute: The client prosecuted his lawyer for criminal breach of trust alleging misappropriation of Rs. 5000, leading to a dispute over whether a retrial could be ordered after acquittal due to lack of handwriting expert evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could direct a retrial after the accused was acquitted by the trial Magistrate?
Whether the fiduciary relationship between lawyer and client justified a retrial despite failure of prosecution to call a handwriting expert?
Whether an accused can be subjected to a second trial for the same offence due to the prosecution's failure to adduce all available evidence?
holdings: The High Court cannot order a retrial after acquittal merely because the prosecution failed to produce all evidence, including expert testimony.
The fiduciary relationship between a lawyer and client does not justify departing from established rules of criminal jurisprudence in criminal trials.
An accused cannot be tried twice for the same offence solely because the prosecution did not avail itself of the opportunity to prove its case fully.
doctrines: Double jeopardy
Fiduciary relationship
Standard of proof in criminal cases
Appellate review in criminal appeals

card.dispute: Basant Ram and others challenged the reduction of their land allotment after the Central Government declared their villages as sub-urban, arguing that the land had already become part of the compensation pool under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and could no longer be dealt with under earlier evacuee property rules.
issues_decided: Whether evacuee property notified under Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, ceases to be evacuee property and becomes part of the compensation pool.
Whether the Central Government retains power under Rule 14(6)(iii)(d) of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, to vary allotments after such notification.
Whether any action to cancel or vary allotments after the notification must be taken under Section 19 of the 1954 Act.
holdings: Upon notification under Section 12(1) of the 1954 Act, evacuee property vests absolutely in the Central Government, extinguishing all prior rights, and becomes part of the compensation pool.

Once property is included in the compensation pool under Section 12, it can no longer be administered under the 1950 Act or its rules, and the Central Government loses power to act under Rule 14(6)(iii)(d) of the 1950 Rules.
Any variation or cancellation of allotments of such property after notification must be done under Section 19 of the 1954 Act, and no action based on the 1950 Rules is valid thereafter.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, Rule 14(6)(iii)(d)
The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 14
The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 16
The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of extinguishment of rights upon statutory vesting
Doctrine of implied repeal and legislative competence
Functus officio doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondents' right to pre-empt the sale of agricultural land, with the dispute centering on whether amendments to the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 could retrospectively affect pending pre-emption appeals.
issues_decided: Whether Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended in 1960, has retrospective effect on pending appeals?
Whether the amendment creating a new class of preemptors (tenants) can be applied retrospectively to a suit where the right did not exist at the time of filing?
Whether a decree in a pending pre-emption appeal must conform to the amended provisions even if the right to pre-empt was based on the unamended law?
