provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 5(a)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(1)(a)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of concession in appellate proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, who purchased property from the Tanjore Palace Estate, disputed the respondent's claim to occupancy rights under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, arguing the property was not part of an 'estate' and that the Government's restoration of the property to the Rajah's widows was not a fresh grant.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's restoration of the private properties of the late Rajah of Tanjore in 1862 constituted a fresh grant or a revival of pre-existing rights
Whether the property in question formed part of an 'estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, thereby entitling the respondent to occupancy rights
holdings: The seizure of all properties of the late Rajah by the British Government was an act of State, extinguishing all pre-existing rights; the subsequent restoration was a fresh grant by Government bounty, not a revival of prior title.

The property, comprising three non-contiguous blocks known as Pattiswaram Padugai, constituted a mokhasa village under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, and thus formed part of an 'estate', entitling the respondent to occupancy rights.
provisions: Madras Estates Land Act, 1908 (Madras Act 1 of 1908), Section 55
Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, as amended by Madras Act 18 of 1936
doctrines: Act of State doctrine
Doctrine of extinguishment of title by sovereign act
Doctrine of fresh grant by Government bounty

card.dispute: The Cantonment Board, Ambala challenged whether a portion of a bungalow occupied by a military officer was exempt from house tax as being in the occupation of the Central Government.
issues_decided: Whether occupation of a property by a military officer amounts to user for public purposes under the Cantonments Act, 1924
Whether such occupation amounts to occupation by the Central Government within the meaning of Section 99(2)(f) of the Cantonments Act, 1924
Whether the authentication of the assessment list was valid under Section 96 of the Cantonments Act, 1924
holdings: Occupation of a property by a military officer for residence constitutes use for public purposes under the Cantonments Act, 1924.

A building leased to the Central Government and occupied by a military officer under its permission is in the occupation of the Central Government, entitling it to tax exemption under Section 99(2)(f).
The authentication of the assessment list by three members initially and the fourth later does not satisfy the statutory requirement under Section 96 of the Cantonments Act, 1924.
doctrines: Constructive occupation
Statutory interpretation of 'occupation' in tax exemption clauses
Deemed government occupation through licensees

card.dispute: The inamdars of certain villages challenged the State of Orissa's notifications under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952, claiming their inams were not estates recognized by the British Government and thus not liable to abolition.
issues_decided: Whether mere inaction by the British Government amounts to recognition of inam grants under s. 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908
Whether the Government's decision to discontinue inquiry into pre-settlement inams constituted recognition of the inamdars' titles
Whether procedural rules for inam confirmation can amount to recognition of title
holdings: Mere inaction by the Government, without more, does not constitute recognition of a title; there must be an express acknowledgment or an unequivocal act leading inevitably to that conclusion.

The Government's decision to discontinue proceedings on pre-settlement inams after considering conflicting claims amounted to recognition of the inamdars' title as under-tenure holders under the zamindar.

The mere existence of Inam Rules providing for inquiry and confirmation of titles does not, by itself, amount to recognition of any specific inamdar's title in the absence of actual application of those rules.
doctrines: Recognition by overt act
Acquiescence as recognition under compelling circumstances
Procedural rules do not confer substantive rights

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction under the Indian Penal Code for offences committed in 1948 in the princely state of Jhabua, which was not then part of the Dominion of India, arguing that the IPC was not applicable at the time.
issues_decided: Whether the Indian Penal Code was applicable in the princely state of Jhabua in 1948 when the offences were committed.
Whether the appellant could be tried in 1955 under the Indian Penal Code for offences committed in 1948 in a former princely state.
holdings: The Indian Penal Code was made applicable in Jhabua State by the Raja's notification before 1948, and thus was the law in force at the time the offences were committed.

The continuation of the Indian Penal Code was secured by Madhya Bharat Ordinance No. 1 of 1948 and preserved under Section 6 of the Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951, allowing punishment for offences committed in 1948 under the IPC even after merger.
doctrines: Doctrine of continuity of laws post-merger
Savings clause under repealing legislation

card.dispute: The appellants, who were lessees of land, fought to eject the respondent tenant, claiming to be landowners entitled to possession for personal cultivation under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether a lessee of land can be considered a 'landowner' within the meaning of Section 2(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
Whether a lessee can eject a tenant-at-will under Section 14A(1) of the Act.
holdings: A lessee who holds land under another and is liable to pay rent is a 'tenant' under Section 4(5) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, and cannot be a 'landowner' under Section 3(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887.
A person who is a tenant cannot be a landowner under Section 2(1) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, and thus has no right to eject a tenant-at-will under Section 14A(1) of the Act.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(1)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A(1)
East Punjab Displaced Persons (Land Resettlement) Act, 1949, Section 2
doctrines: Definition of 'landowner' must be interpreted in context of statutory definitions in related land laws.
A lessee in possession who pays rent is a tenant, not a landowner, and cannot claim rights reserved for landowners.

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, challenged the High Court's finding that all four accused, including an acquitted co-accused, acted with common intention, and contested the sufficiency of evidence against one of them, Gurmukh Singh.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could examine the correctness of the acquittal of a co-accused when no appeal was filed against that acquittal.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Gurmukh Singh shared the common intention to commit murder as alleged under Section 34 IPC.
Whether the circumstance of Lal Singh retrieving his licensed gun from police custody could be used to infer a pre-concerted plan.
Whether Mohinder Singh was an independent witness whose testimony could reliably support the prosecution's theory of common intention.
holdings: The High Court has the authority to consider the evidence relating to an acquitted co-accused when adjudicating an appeal by convicted accused, especially when the trial court’s acquittal is relied upon to challenge the prosecution’s case.
The prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Gurmukh Singh was present at the scene or participated in the attack, and thus he was entitled to the benefit of doubt and acquitted.

The mere fact that Lal Singh retrieved his licensed gun from police custody, without being questioned about it during trial, cannot be fairly used as an incriminating circumstance to infer a pre-concerted plan.
Mohinder Singh could not be regarded as an independent witness, as his evasive answers and association with Malook Singh’s group indicated partisanship, undermining the reliability of his testimony.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Testimony of partisan witnesses
Use of unexplained conduct as incriminating evidence

card.dispute: The Collector of Monghyr carried out repairs to private irrigation works under Section 5A of the Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922 without recording reasons, and later demanded cost-sharing from landlords, who challenged the legality of the demands.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement to record reasons under Section 5A(1) of the Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922 is mandatory
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to quash the cost recovery demands
Whether the respondents were estopped from challenging the orders due to acquiescence or benefit received
holdings: The requirement under Section 5A(1) to record reasons for bypassing notice under Section 3 is mandatory, and failure to do so renders the Collector's order null and void.
The High Court had jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash the demands for cost recovery, as they were based on void orders lacking legal foundation.
Benefit from the repair work and failure to object immediately does not constitute acquiescence or estoppel, especially since Section 5A does not require prior notice to the landlord.
provisions: Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 3
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 4
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 5
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 5A
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 5B
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 11
Bihar Private Irrigation Works Act, 1922, Section 12
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with statutory conditions precedent
Orders without jurisdiction are void ab initio
No estoppel against the State in exercise of statutory power
Availability of writ jurisdiction when alternative remedies are insufficient

card.dispute: The Board of Revenue and others appealed against the High Court's decision that the respondents were entitled to a hearing before the Board decided on stamp duty liability under Section 56(2) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Revenue acts in a quasi-judicial capacity when dealing with a reference under Section 56(2) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
Whether the principles of natural justice require that a party be given a hearing before the Board of Revenue decides on stamp duty liability under Section 56(2).
holdings: The Board of Revenue acts in a quasi-judicial capacity when deciding matters referred under Section 56(2) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, as it involves the construction of instruments and application of law.

The principles of natural justice require that the executant of an instrument be given a hearing before the Board of Revenue imposes stamp duty or penalty under Section 56(2), due to the significant financial consequences involved.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial function
Rule of audi alteram partem

card.dispute: The plaintiff-respondents sued to recover possession of land from the appellants, who had remained in possession after the mortgage was redeemed, but the appellants claimed the plaintiffs lost their right to possession when the estate vested in the State under land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for recovery of possession was barred by limitation
Whether the plaintiff-respondents had a subsisting title to recover possession after the vesting of the estate in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether 'khas possession' under Section 6 of the Act includes subsisting title to possession even without physical cultivation
holdings: The suit was filed within twelve years of the mortgage redemption and was not barred by limitation.

After vesting under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, all proprietary rights, including the right to recover possession, vested in the State, and the plaintiffs ceased to have any subsisting title to sue for possession.
The expression 'khas possession' in Section 6 of the Act requires actual cultivation or horticultural operations by the proprietor; it does not include mere subsisting title to possession.
doctrines: Vesting of proprietary rights in the State extinguishes private rights to possession
Literal interpretation of 'khas possession' based on statutory definition
No private right to recover possession survives after abolition of intermediary interests

card.dispute: The Trust Mai Lachmi Sialkoti Bradri challenged the Amritsar Improvement Trust's scheme to acquire its property, arguing the area was not a 'damaged area' under the Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951, and thus the acquisition was ultra vires.
issues_decided: Whether the area in question was a 'damaged area' within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951.

Whether a notification under the Punjab Damaged Areas Act, 1947 could be deemed to be a notification under the Punjab Damaged Areas Act, 1949 by virtue of Section 22 of the Punjab General Clauses Act.
Whether the scheme framed under the Act was immune from challenge due to the conclusiveness clause in Section 5(4) of the Act.
holdings: The area was not a 'damaged area' under the 1951 Act, as it was neither notified under that Act nor under the 1949 Act, and thus the Improvement Trust lacked jurisdiction to frame the scheme.
The notification under the 1947 Act could not be deemed to be under the 1949 Act because the 1947 Act was not repealed, and the 1949 Act did not come into full force before the 1947 Act lapsed.

Section 5(4) of the Act does not bar challenges to a scheme that is wholly outside the authority's jurisdiction, as conclusiveness applies only to procedural compliance, not to jurisdictional defects.
provisions: Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 2(d)
Punjab Development and Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 5(4)
doctrines: Lack of jurisdiction vitiates administrative action
Doctrine of implied repeal
Conclusiveness of statutory notifications
Continuation of laws under transitional provisions

card.dispute: The petitioners, rubber plantation companies, challenged the validity of an amendment to the Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950, which disallowed deductions for expenses on immature rubber plants, claiming it was ultra vires and discriminatory under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Explanation 2 to Section 5 of the Agricultural Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, which disallows deductions for expenses on immature plants, is constitutionally valid?
Whether the denial of deductions for expenses on immature rubber plants, while not applying to tea plantations, results in discriminatory treatment under Article 14?
holdings: The State Legislature has the competence to define what deductions are allowable in computing agricultural income, and Explanation 2 to Section 5 is a valid exercise of that power.

The exclusion of tea plantations from the scope of Explanation 2 does not violate Article 14, as the difference in treatment is based on a rational distinction due to the mixed agricultural and commercial nature of tea income.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 46, List II, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Principle of legislative competence in taxation matters
Doctrine of reasonable classification under Article 14
Literal and wide interpretation of the term 'income' in fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The Regional Settlement Commissioner denied Sunderdas Bhasin compensation for multiple rural buildings in West Pakistan each valued under Rs. 10,000, and he challenged the denial claiming the total value should be considered.
issues_decided: Whether the value of multiple rural buildings each valued under Rs. 10,000 can be aggregated to exceed the threshold for separate compensation under Rule 65(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules
Whether Rule 57 provides alternative compensation for displaced persons whose individual rural buildings are valued below the threshold in Rule 65(2)
holdings: Rule 65(2) refers to the assessed value of each individual rural building, not the aggregate value of multiple buildings; compensation is not payable if each building is below the specified value.

Displaced persons with rural buildings each valued under Rs. 10,000 are compensated through allotment of a house or site with a building grant under Rule 57, not through separate monetary compensation.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, Rule 57
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, Rule 65
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Contextual interpretation in light of inter-Dominion agreements
Presumption against aggregation unless context permits

card.dispute: The Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. challenged the validity of an amendment to the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act that disallowed deductions for expenses on maintaining immature tea plants, arguing it was beyond the state legislature's power and inconsistent with constitutional definitions of agricultural income.
issues_decided: Whether Explanation 2 to Section 5 of the Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961, which disallows deductions for expenditure on immature tea plants, applies to agricultural income from tea plantations
Whether the state legislature can deviate from the method of computing agricultural income for tea as defined under the Indian Income-tax Act and Rules
Whether the expenditure on upkeep of immature tea plants is of a revenue or capital nature
holdings: Explanation 2 to Section 5 does not apply to tea plantations because it would make agricultural income under the State Act inconsistent with the definition in the Income-tax Act, which controls under the Constitution.

The computation of agricultural income from tea must follow the method prescribed under the Indian Income-tax Act and Rule 24, as 'agricultural income' in the Constitution refers to the definition in the central enactments and rules.
Expenditure on the upkeep and maintenance of immature tea plants is revenue expenditure, not capital, and thus potentially deductible under the relevant provisions.
provisions: Constitution of India, Article 366(1), Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 46
Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, Section 5, Clause (j), Explanation to Section 2(a)(2)
Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1961 (Ker. IX of 1961), Section 2
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Doctrine of incorporation by reference
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of repugnancy between central and state laws on matters of definition

card.dispute: The appellant, Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia, challenged the cancellation of his liquor shop license before the High Court via a writ petition, but did not include rival claimants Phudan Manjhi and Bhagwan Rajak as parties, who had successfully opposed his license before the revenue authorities.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition seeking certiorari against an administrative order is maintainable without impleading parties in whose favour the order was made?
Whether parties directly affected by a writ of certiorari are necessary parties to the petition?
holdings: A writ of certiorari to quash an order affecting the rights of a successful party before a tribunal cannot be maintained without making that party a respondent, as they are necessary parties whose rights would be adversely affected.
The omission to include necessary parties whose rights are directly impacted renders the writ petition incompetent, and the High Court cannot pass an effective order in their absence.
doctrines: Necessary and proper parties in writ proceedings
Principle of natural justice: no one should be adversely affected without being heard
Doctrine of effective judicial remedy

card.dispute: Vijay Pratap Singh and his father R sought permission to sue as paupers for declaration of title to a taluqdari estate, against Dukh Haran Nath Singh who claimed the estate as an adopted son, but their applications were rejected by lower courts.
issues_decided: Whether a petition to sue in forma pauperis can be rejected on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action after a full trial-like scrutiny of the merits?
Whether an application to sue in forma pauperis is a personal remedy and bars transposition of another party as co-applicant?
holdings: A court deciding a pauper suit application must only determine if the allegations, if true, disclose a cause of action; it cannot conduct a detailed inquiry into the merits or possible defences.
An application to sue in forma pauperis is not personal; Order 1, Rule 10 of the CPC applies, allowing joinder of parties if they also qualify as paupers and seek to join legitimately.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIII, Rule 5(d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 10
U.P. Act III of 1910, Section 8 and Section 21
doctrines: Cause of action in pauper suits
Limited scope of inquiry under Order XXXIII
Joinder of parties in civil suits

card.dispute: Babu Lal challenged the legality of a complaint filed against him for using a forged document in a civil suit, arguing that the court should have used a different procedural route under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure under Section 479A of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to an offence under Section 471 of the Indian Penal Code for using a forged document.
Whether the court could proceed under Section 476 CrPC to initiate prosecution for using a forged document when it did not invoke Section 479A.
holdings: Section 479A CrPC applies only to offences involving intentional giving of false evidence or fabrication of false evidence under Sections 193–195 IPC, and does not cover the offence under Section 471 IPC.
Courts retain the power to proceed under Section 476 CrPC for prosecuting someone for fraudulently using a forged document, as such an offence is not excluded by Section 479A(6) CrPC.
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction under special statutory provisions
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between fabrication of false evidence and use of forged documents

card.dispute: The appellant, Afzal Ullah, was prosecuted for running a market without a licence under municipal bye-laws, and challenged the validity of the bye-laws and his conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned bye-law requiring a licence for running a market is ultra vires the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916
Whether the word 'market' in the bye-law applies to a grain market operated through four or more shops on private land
Whether the bye-law is invalid due to mala fide intention or procedural defects such as lack of publication or improper enactment
holdings: The bye-law requiring a licence for operating a market is valid as it falls within the powers conferred by Section 298(1) and clauses (d) and (dd) of Section 298(2)-F of the Act.
Four or more shops selling grains on a single plot constitute a 'market' in the ordinary sense, justifying regulation under the municipal bye-laws.
Allegations of mala fides, non-publication under Section 94(3), and failure to pass by special resolution cannot be raised for the first time in appeal and do not invalidate the bye-laws.
provisions: United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, Section 298(2)-F(d) and (dd)
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Doctrine of ancillary powers
Principle against raising new pleas at appellate stage

card.dispute: The appellant contested the sale of his cultivating rights in sir and khudkasht lands in execution of a money decree, claiming protection under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the cultivating rights in sir and khudkasht lands are protected from attachment or sale in execution of a decree under Section 43 of the Abolition Act.
Whether a prior attachment of proprietary rights extends to the cultivating rights in sir lands after the vesting of proprietary rights in the State.
holdings: Section 43 of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950 bars attachment or sale of cultivating rights in sir and khudkasht lands unless the debt was secured by mortgage or charge on those rights.
The sale of cultivating rights in sir lands after the Abolition Act came into force is without jurisdiction if no mortgage or charge existed, even if attachment preceded the Act.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 43
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 38
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(2)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 2(g)(i)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21 Rule 90
doctrines: Protection of tenancy rights post-abolition of proprietary rights
Doctrine of statutory protection against execution of unsecured debts

card.dispute: The sons of an insolvent father challenged the validity of the Official Receiver's sale of their share in joint family property, claiming the sale was invalid because only the father's share vested in the receiver.
issues_decided: Whether a preliminary decree in a partition suit constitutes a 'final decision' by a competent court within the meaning of the first proviso to Section 28A of the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, as amended in 1948.
Whether the sale of the sons' share by the Official Receiver was protected under the proviso excluding transfers subject to a prior final court decision.
holdings: A preliminary decree in a partition suit, once confirmed by a higher court and not appealed, amounts to a final decision on the rights adjudicated, even though a final decree is later required for execution.

The preliminary decree determining that the Official Receiver had no power to sell the sons' share constituted a final decision, thereby protecting the sons under the proviso to Section 28A, rendering the sale ineffective.
doctrines: Finality of preliminary decrees
Doctrine of res judicata as applied to preliminary decrees
Interpretation of 'final decision' in statutory context

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (descendants of Ghuda Singh) claimed inheritance to Harnam Singh's estate, arguing that customary adoption did not sever Ghuda Singh's ties with his natural family, while the defendants contended that formal adoption excluded him and his descendants from inheriting in the natural family.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of Ghuda Singh was a formal adoption under Hindu law or a customary appointment of an heir under local custom (Riwaj-i-am)?
Whether, under the custom of the Jats of Tehsil Zira, an adopted son and his descendants lose their right to inherit property from collaterals in the natural family?
Whether the instances cited by the defendants establish a custom contrary to the one recorded in Rattigan's Digest?
holdings: The adoption of Ghuda Singh was not proven to be a formal adoption under Hindu law; it was a customary appointment of an heir, which does not completely sever the adopted son’s connection with his natural family.
Under the custom of the Jats of Tehsil Zira, an adopted son does not lose the right to inherit from collaterals in his natural family, except in the presence of natural brothers.

Isolated instances of property devolution do not establish a contrary custom unless they are consistent, certain, and uncontested; the cited instances were insufficient to displace the established custom in Rattigan's Digest.
provisions: Customary Law - Jats of Tehsil Zira, Ferozepore District
Riwaj-i-am (Customary Law Digest of Ferozepore District)
Rattigan's Digest of Customary Law, Article 48
doctrines: Customary adoption vs. formal adoption under Hindu law
Test of validity and proof of custom: consistency, certainty, and long usage
Presumption in favor of established customary law in absence of contrary evidence

card.dispute: Residents of village Gudur sued to restrain the Andhra Pradesh government from altering the Chennur anicut, claiming it would affect their water supply, while the government argued the suit was barred by law.
issues_decided: Whether the proposed alterations to the Chennur anicut fall within the scope of 'improving efficiency' under Section 3 of the Madras Irrigation Tanks (Improvement) Act, 1949
Whether the suit, though seeking only a declaration, is effectively a suit for injunction barred by Section 4 of the Act
Whether the government's failure to issue a notice under Rule 5 of the 1950 Rules invalidates its proposed action under Section 3
Whether the validity of Section 3(1) of the Act could be challenged for the first time in appeal
holdings: Measures that increase the water supply to a tank by modifying upstream structures like anicuts are covered under Section 3 if they have a direct and proximate relation to the tank's efficiency.
A suit seeking a declaration that would effectively compel the government to refrain from exercising powers under Section 3 is barred by Section 4, even if no formal injunction is sought.

The failure to publish a notice under Rule 5 does not invalidate the government's proposed action under Section 3, especially when the action has not yet been taken and the procedural step can still be completed.
The validity of a statutory provision like Section 3(1) cannot be challenged for the first time in an appeal by special leave if it was not raised in the lower courts.
doctrines: Direct and proximate relation test for statutory interpretation
Doctrine of effective remedy and futility of declarations
Procedural requirements as directory versus mandatory
Rule against raising new grounds in special leave appeals

card.dispute: The appellant, Arjun Singh, sought to set aside an ex parte decree passed against him in a civil suit, after earlier applications for relief were rejected on grounds including res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res judicata applies to bar a subsequent application under Order IX, Rule 13 of the CPC after a prior application under Order IX, Rule 7 was rejected?
Whether there is a material difference between 'good cause' under Order IX, Rule 3 and 'sufficient cause' under Order IX, Rule 13 of the CPC?
Whether an order passed in one of multiple consolidated suits can operate as res judicata in another suit?
Whether the decree in suit 134 of 1956 was an ex parte decree or a decree on merits?
holdings: The principle of res judicata is not limited to Section 11 CPC and can apply to different stages of the same suit or interlocutory orders if the matter was directly and substantially in issue.
There is no material difference between 'good cause' under Order IX, Rule 3 and 'sufficient cause' under Rule 13; the standards are substantially similar.
Consolidation of suits for hearing does not make an order in one suit res judicata in another; each application must be decided independently based on the specific suit and rule invoked.
The decree in suit 134 of 1956 was ex parte, not on merits, as the court proceeded in the absence of the defendant and explicitly recorded it as such.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 7
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVII, Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XVII, Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 1
doctrines: Res judicata
Inherent powers of the court under Section 151 CPC
Ex parte decree vs decree on merits
Consolidation of suits and its legal effect

card.dispute: The appellant, a trustee of a charitable trust, was convicted for receiving a donation from a tenant as a condition for granting a lease, which was challenged as violating rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the payment of Rs. 3,251/- as 'donation' to a charitable trust for granting a lease constitutes 'premium or other like sum' or 'consideration other than standard rent' under Section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether the appellant, as a trustee receiving rent on behalf of the trust, falls within the definition of 'landlord' under the Act.
Whether premises owned by a charitable trust are exempt from the provisions of the Act.
holdings: A payment labeled as 'donation' is still 'premium' or 'consideration' under Section 18(1) if it is made as a condition for granting a lease, regardless of the label used.
A trustee who receives rent on behalf of a charitable trust is included in the definition of 'landlord' under Section 5(3) of the Act.
Charitable trusts are not automatically exempt from the Act; exemption requires a government order, and the rent here was neither nominal nor concessional.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 18(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(3)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 4(2)(ii)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Substance over form in determining illegal premiums or consideration
Deeming provisions in rent control laws

card.dispute: The Watandar and tenant disputed over the right to enhanced rent and apportionment of compensation for compulsorily acquired watan lands.
issues_decided: Whether the Watandar was entitled to enhance rent after the 1911 government order fixing rent at Rs. 1245/4/-
Whether the Collector or Government could validly declare the 1863 lease null and void under Section 9 of the Watan Act
Whether the Watandar was entitled to more than the capitalised value of rent in compensation for acquired lands
holdings: The Watandar was not entitled to unilaterally enhance rent as the 1911 government order only modified the rent under a continuing perpetual lease, not created a new tenancy.
No valid declaration under Section 9 of the Watan Act was made to nullify the 1863 lease; hence, the lease remained in force with revised rent.
The Watandar's share in compensation is limited to the capitalised value of the rent (25 times the annual rent), not a larger portion based on enhanced tenancy rights.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation of administrative orders
Capitalisation of rent for compensation purposes
Requirement of explicit declaration to nullify alienation under Section 9

card.dispute: The appellants, as decree-holders, sought to enforce payment under a composition deed, but the respondents argued the claim was time-barred and no valid acknowledgment of liability extended the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Limitation Act can be applied by analogy to proceedings not specifically covered by its schedule or provisions
Whether a letter written by the second defendant’s vakil to the trustees amounted to an acknowledgment of liability under Section 19 of the Limitation Act
holdings: The provisions of the Limitation Act, including those on suspension of limitation, apply only to cases expressly or by necessary implication covered by the Act and cannot be extended by analogy to other proceedings.

A letter referring to the liability of trustees under a composition deed does not constitute an acknowledgment of personal liability by the defendant, and thus does not satisfy Section 19 of the Limitation Act to extend the limitation period.
doctrines: Strict construction of limitation law
Acknowledgment of liability under Section 19 requires admission of personal subsisting liability
No extension of limitation by analogy
Distinction between personal liability and trustee liability

card.dispute: The Board of Commissioners sought to modify a court-approved scheme for temple management, specifically challenging the remuneration and duties of the Karnam (a hereditary temple official), leading to a dispute over whether the High Court could abolish his customary share in temple collections.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could modify the scheme to deprive the hereditary Karnam of his customary share in dibbi collections even when performing duties personally.
Whether the High Court could effectively abolish a hereditary office without a specific prayer or pleading to that effect.
holdings: The High Court erred in modifying the scheme to deny the Karnam his customary remuneration for personal service, as no such relief was sought in the pleadings and the office was hereditary.
A hereditary office cannot be virtually abolished by judicial modification of a scheme where the dispute was limited to regulating remuneration when a deputy is employed.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, Section 57(9)
doctrines: Doctrine of pleadings: Courts cannot grant relief not claimed or pleaded.
Principle of hereditary office: Hereditary rights in religious offices cannot be judicially abolished without specific grounds and prayer.
Doctrine of limited judicial modification: Courts modifying schemes must stay within the scope of the dispute raised.

card.dispute: Co-sharers disputed whether the respondent could exercise a right of pre-emption over a house built on leasehold land sold by the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the right of pre-emption under Muhammadan law infringes the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
Whether a right of pre-emption can be exercised in respect of a house standing on leasehold land
holdings: The law of pre-emption among co-sharers does not infringe the fundamental right to carry on trade or business under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

A right of pre-emption cannot be exercised in respect of a house standing on leasehold land because pre-emption requires full ownership of the property and applies only to freehold, not subordinate tenures.
The right of pre-emption must encompass the entire bargain and cannot be applied to a superstructure separate from the land, especially when the land is leasehold and not pre-emptible.

A pre-emptor cannot claim pre-emption of a property if the vendor lacks proprietary rights over the land, as the superstructure disassociated from the land becomes movable property, which is not subject to pre-emption.
doctrines: Right of pre-emption under Muhammadan law
Entire bargain doctrine
Reciprocity in pre-emption
Distinction between freehold and leasehold interests in pre-emption

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax challenged the High Court's decision that income from a property held by two wives was not taxable as the husbands' income under Section 16(3)(a)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the income from property held by wives arose from assets indirectly transferred by their husbands under Section 16(3)(a)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether indirect transfers through family members (son to mother, father-in-law to daughter-in-law) can attract inclusion of income in the husband's total income.
holdings: Income arising to a wife from assets transferred indirectly by her husband, even through third parties within the family, must be included in the husband's total income if the transaction is a device to circumvent tax liability.

A chain of interconnected gifts among family members, matching in amount and timing with property purchase, constitutes indirect transfer under Section 16(3)(a)(iii), even without direct transfer from husband to wife.
doctrines: Substance over form
Indirect transfer doctrine
Tax avoidance through familial transfers

card.dispute: The Deputy Director of Consolidation challenged the High Court's decision directing the Settlement Officer to grant permission for land exchange under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, during ongoing consolidation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether Section 16A(2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 is mandatory and requires the Settlement Officer to grant permission for land transfer unless it defeats the scheme of consolidation
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by directing the Settlement Officer to grant permission for land exchange
Whether a conflict between the proposed land exchange and final consolidation principles or proposals must exist for rejection of the application under Section 16A(2)
holdings: Section 16A(2) is mandatory: the Settlement Officer must grant permission for land transfer unless the proposed transfer is likely to defeat the scheme of consolidation.

The Settlement Officer may reject a transfer only if it conflicts with final principles under Section 18 or confirmed proposals under Section 23; otherwise, permission must be granted if statutory conditions are met.

The High Court erred in directing the Settlement Officer to grant permission, as the officer must independently assess whether the transfer conflicts with consolidation principles or proposals and pass a reasoned order.

An admission in pleadings about land contiguity cannot be strictly held against a party where facts were overlooked due to focus on legal issues, and the Settlement Officer must reassess factual positions in light of the law.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 13
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 14
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 15
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 16A
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 18
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 19
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 20
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 23
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of statutory provisions
Principle of speaking orders in administrative decisions
Doctrine of judicial restraint in supervising quasi-judicial officers
Factual admissions and estoppel in judicial proceedings

card.dispute: Mine owners challenged the government's canalization of manganese ore exports through the State Trading Corporation, which excluded new entrants and allegedly violated their fundamental right to carry on trade.
issues_decided: Whether the notification canalizing exports of manganese ore through the State Trading Corporation amounted to an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Whether a virtual monopoly created by administrative action without a specific law violates Article 19(1)(g) read with Article 19(6).
Whether the exclusion of mine owners without prior export performance from exporting manganese ore was constitutionally valid.
holdings: Canalizing exports through a state agency that results in virtual monopoly and cripples private trade constitutes an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) unless accompanied by definite rules ensuring fair treatment.

Article 19(6), as amended, does not permit the State to create a monopoly by mere administrative action; such action must be supported by a valid law to be protected from challenge under Article 19(1)(g).

The government's policy of granting export quotas only to established exporters and the State Trading Corporation, while excluding others, infringed the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) as it lacked equitable and transparent principles.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(6)
State monopoly and Article 19(1)(g) infringement
Requirement of rule-making for fair administrative action

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for theft of fish from a tank possessed by the respondent; they claimed a bona fide right to catch fish as recorded tenants, while the respondent claimed lawful possession under a lease.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had a bona fide claim of right to catch fish in the tank, negating the dishonest intention required for theft under Section 379 IPC
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal by the Additional Sessions Judge based on lack of dishonesty
holdings: A bona fide claim of right, even if ultimately unfounded, can negate the dishonest intention necessary for theft, especially when the accused acted openly and under a reasonable belief of entitlement.

The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal; the circumstances, including disputed possession and prior recognition of the appellants' tenancy, supported a genuine belief in their right to catch fish, precluding conviction for theft.
doctrines: Animus furandi
Bona fide claim of right as a defence to theft
Ferae naturae (fish as wild animals subject to possession)

card.dispute: The appellant company, successor to Banajee, challenged the state's imposition of land revenue on seven villages granted free from such liability in 1847, arguing the Salsette Estates Act could not validly abolish this exemption.
issues_decided: Whether the 1847 grant of villages was a lease or farm within the meaning of the Salsette Estates Act
Whether the appellant held the villages under an agreement with the State within the meaning of Section 2(d) of the Act
Whether the exemption from land revenue under the 1847 grant was protected from abolition under Section 3(3) of the Act
holdings: The 1847 grant was not a lease or farm but an absolute grant of land and revenue rights, subject to certain covenants, and thus not in the nature of a farm under the Act.

The grantee held the villages under an agreement with the State because the exemption from land revenue was granted subject to enforceable covenants, creating contractual obligations under Section 2(d).

Section 3(1) of the Act imposes land revenue liability despite prior exemptions, and Section 3(3) does not save the estate-holder’s exemption; only rights of persons other than the estate-holder are protected.
provisions: Salsette Estates (Land Revenue Exemption Abolition) Act, 1951, Section 2(b)
Salsette Estates (Land Revenue Exemption Abolition) Act, 1951, Section 2(d)
Salsette Estates (Land Revenue Exemption Abolition) Act, 1951, Section 3
Salsette Estates (Land Revenue Exemption Abolition) Act, 1951, Section 4
Salsette Estates (Land Revenue Exemption Abolition) Act, 1951, Section 5
doctrines: Sovereign prerogative to collect land revenue is distinct from ownership
Conditional grants create contractual agreements even if property is held absolutely
Statutory abolition of revenue exemptions applies to estate-holders unless expressly protected
Doctrine of ejusdem generis in interpreting 'agreement' in land revenue statutes

card.dispute: The Champaran Cane Concern, claiming to be a co-ownership entity, disputed its assessment as a partnership firm for agricultural income-tax purposes under the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was a partnership firm or a co-ownership concern for the purpose of assessment under the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948.
Whether the common manager of a co-ownership concern is assessable under Section 13 of the Act.
holdings: The assessee was a co-ownership concern, not a partnership firm, as there was no agreement to form a partnership and no agency relationship between the co-owners.
Where a co-ownership concern carries on joint cultivation, the common manager is liable to be assessed under Section 13 of the Bihar Agricultural Income-tax Act.
doctrines: Distinction between co-ownership and partnership
Mixed question of law and fact
Principle of agency in partnership

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of mortgagees, challenged the redemption of a 19th-century usufructuary mortgage and the award of mesne profits to the mortgagors.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of election barred the appellants from challenging the validity of the mortgage terms after having accepted benefits under them
Whether mesne profits could be awarded against the mortgagees before full payment of the redemption amount including compensation for improvements
holdings: A party who accepts benefits under a transaction must abide by all its terms; successors of a mortgagee who enjoyed benefits under revised mortgage terms are estopped from reasserting the original indefinite mortgage.
Mesne profits cannot be awarded against mortgagees until full redemption amount including compensation for improvements is paid; they must instead pay interest on amounts deposited.
doctrines: Doctrine of Election
Approbation and Reprobation
Equitable estoppel

card.dispute: Hazara Singh Gill sought transfer of two criminal cases from Punjab to outside the state, alleging bias and executive influence due to his political opposition to the Chief Minister and powerful local figures.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner has made out a sufficient case for transfer of criminal proceedings on grounds of apprehension of bias and lack of fair trial.
Whether the court can rely on the petitioner's uncontroverted affidavit in the absence of a specific reply by the state.
holdings: Where a petitioner makes serious allegations of executive interference and bias in a criminal case, and the state fails to specifically deny them, the court may infer a reasonable apprehension of unfair trial.
In transfer petitions under Section 527 CrPC, the court may act on uncontroverted affidavits, and the absence of a reply affidavit renders the petitioner's allegations effectively uncontested.
doctrines: Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done
Doctrine of apprehension of bias in administration of justice

card.dispute: The petitioner, a property owner in Bareilly's Civil Lines, challenged the validity of special taxes (house tax, latrine tax, and scavenging tax) imposed only on that area by the Municipality.
issues_decided: Whether Section 128(1) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, authorizing differential taxation within a municipality, violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the imposition of taxes only on the Civil Lines area is constitutionally valid under the doctrine of reasonable classification
Whether the procedure under Sections 131–136 of the Act was followed in imposing the taxes
Whether the mention of an incorrect clause (128(1)(xii)) in the notification invalidates the scavenging tax imposed under the correct power (128(1)(xi))
holdings: Section 128(1) does not violate Article 14 as it provides a reasonable basis for classification and taxation based on benefits received.
The classification of taxing only the Civil Lines area is valid because the area received special amenities and services funded by these taxes.
The procedural requirements under Sections 131–136 were presumed to have been followed, and no evidence was presented to prove non-compliance.
Mentioning the wrong clause (xii) in the notification is a mere clerical error and does not invalidate the tax if the authority had power under another valid clause (xi).
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1916, Sections 131 to 136
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Presumption of regularity in statutory proceedings
Doctrine of de minimis non curat lex
Doctrine of effective substance over technical form

card.dispute: The appellant, Jang Singh, sought pre-emption of land and deposited an amount one rupee short due to a court clerk's error; the respondent moved to dismiss the suit for non-compliance with the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's deposit, short by one rupee due to a court-issued challan error, amounted to non-compliance warranting dismissal of the pre-emption suit.
Whether the court's mistake in directing an incorrect deposit amount could excuse the litigant's failure to comply strictly with the decree terms.
Whether the District Judge was justified in setting aside the Subordinate Judge's order dismissing the suit.
holdings: A litigant who acts in good faith on a court-issued direction, such as a challan, is not solely responsible for an error in the amount to be deposited.
When a court and its officers contribute to a litigant's failure to comply with a decree, the court must rectify its own mistake before dismissing the suit.
The decree was not fully complied with, but the appellant must be given an opportunity to cure the deficiency caused by the court's error by depositing the remaining one rupee.
provisions: Specific Relief Act, Section 16 (implied, regarding decree compliance)
Civil Procedure Code, Order XXI (execution of decrees, implied)
doctrines: Actus curiae neminem gravabit (the act of the court shall injure no one)
Substantial justice over technical compliance
Court's duty to rectify its own errors in execution

card.dispute: The sons of Umed Singh challenged the sale of ancestral agricultural land by their father, claiming it was void against them as reversionary heirs.
issues_decided: Whether a Jat holder of ancestral agricultural land in Jhajjar Tehsil, Rohtak District, has an unrestricted customary right to transfer such land for consideration.
Whether the existence of sons affects the holder's power to alienate ancestral property under local custom.
Whether prior judicial decisions recognizing unrestricted alienation power in Jat holders are binding despite doubts expressed in colonial-era customary law manuals.
holdings: A Jat holding ancestral agricultural land in Jhajjar Tehsil, Rohtak District, has an unrestricted customary power to transfer it for consideration, and such transfer cannot be set aside by sons or reversionary heirs unless made for immoral purposes.
The existence of a son does not limit the alienation power of a Jat holder of ancestral land in this region, as the custom applies equally regardless of whether the holder has sons.

Courts must follow consistent judicial precedent recognizing unrestricted alienation rights, even if older manuals express doubt, especially when those doubts have been overridden by long-standing practice and decisions.
doctrines: Customary law overriding textual doubt
Stare decisis in customary property law
Agnatic theory in inheritance and alienation restrictions

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings, arguing that the President's notification under Article 258(1) ceased to be effective after the formation of Gujarat as a new state without its government's consent.
issues_decided: Whether the President's notification under Article 258(1) of the Constitution, entrusting Central functions to State officers, continued to be valid after the reorganisation of Bombay State and the creation of Gujarat without fresh consent from Gujarat's government.
Whether a notification issued under Article 258(1) has the force of law and can survive under Section 87 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.
Whether the Commissioner of Baroda could validly issue notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after May 1, 1960, based on the prior notification under Article 258(1).
holdings: Article 258(1) only authorises the entrustment of executive functions and does not amend or create law; thus, a notification under it is an executive act without legislative force.
A notification under Article 258(1) does not have the force of law and cannot be considered a 'law in force' under Section 2(d) and Section 87 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.

After the formation of Gujarat, the continuation of the 1959 notification required the consent of Gujarat’s government, which was not obtained; hence, the Commissioner lacked authority to act under it after May 1, 1960.
Notifications issued under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, by the Commissioner under the invalid delegation were themselves invalid and were struck down.
doctrines: Executive vs legislative functions distinction
Doctrine of survival of laws under reorganisation statutes
Principle that delegation of executive power does not amount to amendment of law
Doctrine of implied repeal and continuation of laws under Section 87 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act

card.dispute: A widow and her minor son sued for partition of joint family property and a share in property devised by will; after the minor's death, the question was whether the suit could continue and whether the will property had become joint family property.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for partition of joint family property by a minor abates upon the minor's death during the pendency of the suit
Whether property devised under a will to certain coparceners becomes part of the joint family estate by blending
holdings: A suit for partition by a minor does not abate upon the minor's death; the right to partition is a property right that devolves on the legal representative and the suit can be continued if it was for the minor's benefit.

Property remains separate unless there is clear evidence of the owner's intention to abandon separate ownership and blend it with the joint family; mere use by family members or commingling of benefits is not sufficient.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family and Partition (unspecified statutory source, based on customary and case law)
doctrines: Survival of property rights after death of minor
Doctrine of blending of separate property into joint family property
Protection of minor's interest in partition suits

card.dispute: The mortgage decree-holders appealed against the High Court's decision allowing the judgment-debtor, who had not previously claimed relief, to seek debt relief under an amended statute after an appellate decree.
issues_decided: Whether the decree in question was passed before or after the commencement of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, for the purpose of applying the amended Section 19(2)
Whether a judgment-debtor could claim relief under the amended Madras Agriculturists Relief Act after prior rejection of relief claims, given the amendment created a new right
Whether the principle of res judicata barred a fresh application for relief under the amended Act
holdings: The operative decree is the appellate decree; thus, a decree passed by the High Court in 1942 is deemed to be passed after the commencement of the principal Act for purposes of the amended Section 19(2).
Section 19(2) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, as amended in 1948, creates a new right for agriculturist debtors to claim relief even if prior applications were rejected.
The principle of res judicata does not bar a claim under the amended Act where the amendment confers a new right not previously available.
doctrines: Merger of decrees
Res judicata
Prospective operation of amendments creating new rights

card.dispute: Kirpal Singh challenged his conviction and death sentence for murder, arguing in part that the committal proceedings were flawed due to the Magistrate's failure to record evidence of witnesses to the offence.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate committed an error by committing the accused for trial without recording the evidence of witnesses to the actual commission of the murder.
Whether the conviction based on the testimony of a single witness who identified the accused by voice and gait, without seeing his face, was legally sustainable.
holdings: A Magistrate conducting committal proceedings for a serious offence like murder has a duty to consider, in the interests of justice, whether it is necessary to record the evidence of witnesses not produced by the prosecution, especially those to the actual commission of the offence.

Identification of the accused by a witness through voice and gait, coupled with prior familiarity and circumstantial consistency, can be sufficient to sustain a conviction even without visual identification of the face during the assault.
doctrines: Judicial duty of Magistrate in committal proceedings
Discretion in witness examination under amended CrPC
Reliability of identification by voice and gait

card.dispute: The husband (appellant) challenged the wife's (respondent) right to execute a maintenance decree against his remaining properties after she had already purchased some charged properties in a prior execution.
issues_decided: Whether a maintenance decree creating a charge on properties is fully satisfied when the decree-holder purchases part of the charged properties in execution.
Whether the decree-holder must first exhaust remedies against properties acquired by her before proceeding against properties still held by the judgment-debtor.
holdings: An executory charge-decree for maintenance remains enforceable as future amounts become due, and the charge continues over all originally charged properties jointly and severally, regardless of partial execution.

The executing court cannot compel the decree-holder to proceed against properties she acquired; she may choose to enforce the charge against any of the charged properties, and the judgment-debtor cannot insist on priority of execution against the decree-holder's properties.
doctrines: Charge vs. mortgage distinction (jus ad rem vs. jus in rem)
Principle of joint and several liability of charged properties in maintenance decrees
No marshalling of assets in favor of judgment-debtor in charge decrees

card.dispute: The appellant corporation sought to substitute legal representatives and set aside the abatement of a suit after the death of the original defendant, but applied beyond the prescribed time; the respondents opposed this, leading to a dispute over whether the delay was justified.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the Subordinate Court's finding of 'sufficient cause' for delay in applying to set aside abatement and for substitution of legal representatives.
Whether the Subordinate Court had jurisdiction to decide questions of fact regarding sufficient cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Whether an error in determining 'sufficient cause' amounts to a jurisdictional error justifying revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
holdings: The High Court cannot overturn findings of fact on 'sufficient cause' made by a subordinate court in revision unless there is a jurisdictional error.
The Subordinate Court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine factual questions about whether sufficient cause existed for delay in making applications under Order XXII, Rules 4 and 9 of the CPC.
An erroneous interpretation or application of the Limitation Act may justify revision, but mere disagreement with a finding of fact does not.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rules 4, 9(2), 9(3)
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC limited to jurisdictional errors
Principle of sufficiency of cause under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Doctrine of factual autonomy of subordinate courts in limitation matters

card.dispute: The appellant (Mrs. Madden) and respondents (Dr. Katiai & others) fought over whether a contract for the sale of a house property required specific performance, despite the vendor's withdrawal of an application for required government sanction.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement for sale was a completed contract despite the condition requiring sanction from the Chief Commissioner.
Whether the trial court was correct in refusing specific performance on the ground that the agreement was inchoate.
Whether the appellant could raise new pleas in the Supreme Court that were not raised in the High Court.
holdings: A contract requiring the vendor to obtain government sanction is a completed contract, and the obligation to apply for such sanction is implied in the agreement.
The failure to obtain sanction does not render the contract inchoate; the court can decree specific performance subject to the sanction being granted.
New pleas not raised in the High Court or in pleadings cannot be allowed for the first time in the Supreme Court.
provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10 (though not explicitly cited, the principles of specific performance are governed by this Act)
doctrines: Doctrine of specific performance of contracts
Implied terms in contracts
Principle of pleadings and estoppel against raising new grounds in higher courts

card.dispute: Noor Khan challenged his conviction for murder after the High Court overturned his acquittal, arguing that the trial was vitiated by the failure to supply him with police-recorded witness statements under Section 161 CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to supply the accused with statements recorded by police under Section 161 CrPC vitiates the trial
Whether the destruction of police notes and preparation of substitute statements affected the fairness of the trial
Whether the accused suffered prejudice due to non-supply of original jottings or notes used to prepare witness statements
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal despite alleged procedural irregularities
holdings: Failure to supply statements under Section 161 CrPC does not automatically vitiate a trial; the court must assess whether actual prejudice resulted to the accused.
The trial is not rendered illegal solely because original police notes were destroyed and statements were prepared from memory, if the court finds no resulting prejudice.
Prejudice cannot be presumed where the accused did not raise a specific plea of prejudice in the High Court or support it with substantial argument.
The High Court’s reversal of acquittal is sustainable if supported by reliable evidence, even amid procedural defects, provided no real prejudice is shown.
doctrines: Prejudice test in criminal procedure
Procedural irregularity not fatal without demonstrated prejudice
Judicial review of High Court's reversal of acquittal
Safeguard of statutory rights under CrPC

card.dispute: The New Central Jute Mills Co. Ltd. challenged the Uttar Pradesh Board of Revenue's order holding that its mortgage deed, executed in Uttar Pradesh but relating to property in West Bengal, was not duly stamped because it used West Bengal stamps instead of Uttar Pradesh stamps.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgage deed executed in Uttar Pradesh but relating to property in West Bengal is 'duly stamped' if it bears stamps purchased in West Bengal under its stamp law?
Whether stamp duty liability arises under the law of the state where the instrument is executed, or where the property is situated?
Whether Section 19A of the Stamp Act applies to resolve conflicts between stamp duties of different states?
holdings: An instrument executed in a state is liable to stamp duty under that state’s law, and must bear stamps of that state to be considered 'duly stamped' at the time of execution.

Where an instrument is executed in one state and relates to property in another, liability arises first in the state of execution; further stamping is required in the second state only if its duty rate is higher.
Section 19A ensures that when an instrument becomes chargeable in a second state at a higher rate, only the excess duty must be paid in that state, avoiding double burden.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Rule 3 (Uttar Pradesh Rules)
doctrines: Duty arises at execution
State-specific application of stamp law post-amendment
Principle of avoiding double stamp duty
Harmonious construction of state stamp laws

card.dispute: The clients of an advocate filed a complaint alleging professional misconduct after he failed to return money he had received on their behalf from court-ordered sale proceeds, and the advocate challenged the High Court's order suspending him for five years.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to proceed with professional misconduct proceedings against the advocate without awaiting a criminal trial.
Whether there was procedural irregularity in allowing the complainants to lead additional evidence after the advocate had examined himself.
Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the testimony of a witness who claimed the money was paid to the clients.
Whether the five-year suspension of the advocate was excessive.
holdings: Professional misconduct proceedings can proceed independently when the misconduct is directly linked to an advocate's duty to a client, without requiring a prior criminal conviction.
No procedural unfairness occurred in the sequence of evidence, as the advocate did not raise prejudice before the District Judge or High Court and none is evident on record.
The High Court was justified in rejecting the witness's testimony as false and unworthy of belief, even if he were the real client, due to contradictions and lack of credibility.
The five-year suspension was appropriate given the gravity of misappropriating client funds and fabricating a defence, and the punishment was not excessive.
doctrines: Distinction between professional misconduct connected to client duties and other misconduct requiring criminal conviction
Court's discretion in regulating professional conduct of advocates
Principle of judicial deference to findings of fact and witness credibility by superior courts

card.dispute: Landlords attempted to execute expired possession decrees, leading to violent resistance by tenants; the dispute was whether the tenants' resistance constituted criminal trespass and unlawful assembly.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords' entry onto the land after the expiry of execution warrants amounted to criminal trespass
Whether the tenants' resistance constituted an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Whether the appellants participated in the unlawful assembly and committed offences under Sections 304 Part II, 326, 324, 323 IPC read with Section 149 IPC
Whether the sentences imposed were appropriate, especially for women and elderly accused
holdings: Entry on property under expired execution warrants does not amount to criminal trespass if the entrants acted in good faith and without intention to annoy, intimidate, or insult.
An assembly formed with the common object of using violence to prevent lawful possession is unlawful, even if the landlords' possession attempt was technically invalid.
Mere presence in an unlawful assembly with knowledge of its common object is sufficient for liability under Section 149 IPC, even without individual acts of violence.
Sentences for women and elderly accused were reduced to time already served, considering their limited roles and age, though convictions were upheld.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 24 and 25
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Good faith execution of court processes
Intention to annoy in criminal trespass

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the state for industrial tenements and urban development, arguing that the government bypassed mandatory objection procedures under Section 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether a notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act could be issued without complying with Section 5-A when land is acquired for planned development under Section 17(1-A)?
Whether Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, which dispenses with Section 5-A, applies to non-waste, non-arable land acquired under Section 17(1-A)?
Whether the government could lawfully direct that Section 5-A would not apply in the acquisition process?
holdings: Section 17(1-A) allows early possession of non-waste, non-arable land for planned development but does not dispense with Section 5-A procedures.
Section 17(4), which permits bypassing Section 5-A, applies only to waste or arable land and was not extended to Section 17(1-A) by amendment.
The government cannot lawfully omit Section 5-A compliance in cases under Section 17(1-A); such an action is ultra vires and invalidates the Section 6 notification.
provisions: Kanpur Urban Area Development Act, 1945, Section 71
Kanpur Urban Area Development Act, 1945, Section 114
Land Acquisition (U.P. Amendment) Act, No. XXII of 1954, Section 6
doctrines: Substantial compliance with procedural safeguards in property acquisition
Strict interpretation of statutory exceptions to procedural rights
Legislative intent through amendment structure
Independence of sub-sections within a statutory provision

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the municipal corporation's imposition of a tax on vacant land based on its capital value, arguing it was ultra vires the enabling Act and beyond the legislature's competence.
issues_decided: Whether the municipal rate on vacant land based on capital value is authorized under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925
Whether a tax on land assessed on capital value falls under provincial legislative competence under the Government of India Act, 1935
holdings: The Explanation to Section 75 and Rule 350-A, read with Section 73, validly permit the imposition of a municipal rate on the capital value of land, as the charging provision is on land and not on capital assets.

A tax on land measured by its capital value falls under 'taxes on lands and buildings' (List II, Item 42) and not 'taxes on capital value of assets' (List I, Item 55), thus within provincial legislative competence.
provisions: Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List I, Item 55
Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List II, Item 42
doctrines: Distinction between subject matter of tax and method of assessment
Legislative competence based on pith and substance of the tax
Ultra vires doctrine applied to delegated legislation

card.dispute: The dispute was between multiple claimants, including the respondent and the appellant, over who was the rightful sole heir to an intestate's impartible estate, with the respondent seeking security from the appellant in possession under Section IV of the Bengal Wills and Intestacy Regulation V of 1799.
issues_decided: Whether Section IV of the Bengal Wills and Intestacy Regulation V of 1799 applies when the deceased left only one heir.
Whether the District Judge had the power to require security from a person in possession claiming as a single heir under that section.
holdings: Section IV of Regulation V of 1799 applies only when there are multiple heirs, not when a single heir claims succession under Section III.
The second part of Section IV does not authorize courts to require security from a person in possession claiming as the sole heir to an intestate's estate.
provisions: Bengal Wills and Intestacy Regulation V of 1799, Section 3
Bengal Wills and Intestacy Regulation V of 1799, Section 4
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction of statutes
Plain meaning rule

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction under Section 149 IPC, arguing that they could not be held vicariously liable for acts of acquitted co-accused in the absence of a valid finding of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons.
issues_decided: Whether a conviction under Section 149 IPC is sustainable when fewer than five accused are convicted and others are acquitted without appeal against their acquittal.
Whether the High Court could rely on Section 149 IPC to hold the appellants liable for acts committed by acquitted persons.
Whether the prosecution established the existence of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons, including unidentified members, as required under Section 149 IPC.
holdings: A court may convict fewer than five persons under Section 149 IPC if the charge or evidence shows the involvement of additional identified or unidentified members in the unlawful assembly.

The High Court erred in applying Section 149 IPC to hold appellants liable for acts of acquitted persons without a reasoned finding that the unlawful assembly included others beyond the named accused.

For vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC, there must be evidence supporting the existence of an unlawful assembly of five or more persons, and the conviction cannot rest solely on the acts of acquitted co-accused.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Vicarious liability in unlawful assembly
Common object doctrine under Section 149 IPC
Principle of constructive liability
Requirement of reasoned judicial findings on essential ingredients of an offence

card.dispute: The appellant, a Hindu reversioner, sued to recover properties alienated by two widows who claimed absolute ownership under their husband's will; the respondents resisted, arguing the appellant was an undischarged insolvent and the widows had absolute estates.
issues_decided: Whether an undischarged insolvent, after absolute discharge, can maintain a suit for possession of property devolving on him by succession
Whether the will conferred life estates or absolute estates on the two widows
Whether the appeal abates due to non-substitution of a deceased respondent's legal heirs
holdings: An insolvent who obtains absolute discharge can sue for property devolving on him; any undisposed property vests in him as surplus, subject to provable debts and costs under the Insolvency Act.

The will granted only life estates to the widows, as the language used—'during her lifetime' and 'shall remain with'—indicates limitation, unlike clauses granting absolute estates which used terms like 'fully entitled' and omitted life contingencies.
An appeal does not abate in its entirety due to failure to substitute a deceased party; abatement is limited to the property in which the deceased had an interest, if co-owners are still parties.
doctrines: Devolution of property on an insolvent after discharge
Rule of testamentary construction: words indicating limitation vs. absolute bequest
Partial abatement of appeal due to death of party

card.dispute: The heirs of Severina Sobina disputed whether she received a life interest or an absolute interest in movable property under her mother's will, and whether her male children were entitled to the property after her death.
issues_decided: Whether clause 3(c) of the will conferred an absolute interest or a life interest on Severina Sobina
Whether the words 'after her lifetime' created a remainder interest in favour of Severina's male children
Whether the testatrix intended to make a direct gift to the male children or merely define the nature of Severina's interest
holdings: The use of the phrase 'after her lifetime' indicates that Severina was granted only a life interest, not an absolute interest.
The remainder in absolute interest was conferred on Severina's male children, as the clause created successive interests, not joint ownership.
Words referring to the male children are words of purchase, not limitation, establishing them as direct beneficiaries after Severina's death.
doctrines: Cardinal rule of will construction: effect must be given to every testamentary disposition if legally possible
Principle of avoiding repugnancy in will clauses
Distinction between words of limitation and words of purchase in testamentary gifts

card.dispute: The appellant sub-tenant challenged the validity of an eviction notice, claiming his tenancy under the landlord began from the date of the original tenant's ejectment, while the landlord argued the tenancy continued on the original monthly terms.
