issues_decided: Whether the sub-tenant's tenancy with the landlord commenced from the date of ejectment of the original tenant (June 16, 1955), thereby altering the tenancy period.
Whether the notice of ejectment requiring possession by the end of April 1957 was valid under the law.
holdings: The sub-tenant becomes a tenant of the landlord upon lawful determination of the original tenancy, but the terms and conditions, including the start and end of the tenancy period, remain unchanged from the original sub-tenancy.
The notice of ejectment was valid because the monthly tenancy continued to run from the first to the last day of the calendar month, unaffected by the date of ejectment of the original tenant.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Continuity of tenancy terms upon statutory succession
Statutory creation of direct landlord-tenant relationship upon ejectment of intermediate tenant

card.dispute: The decree-holders appealed against the High Court's decision allowing judgment-debtors, who were agriculturists, to seek scaling down of a compromise decree under the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise decree is subject to scaling down under the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, if it was not fully executed before the Act's commencement
Whether the compromise decree operates as res judicata or creates an estoppel preventing the judgment-debtors from seeking relief under the Amending Act
Whether the High Court erred in revising the finding on the status of the judgment-debtors as agriculturists under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code
holdings: A compromise decree that has not been fully executed before the commencement of the Amending Act is subject to scaling down under Section 16(iii) and Section 19(2) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, as it is not a final decree in the sense of being fully satisfied.

A compromise decree does not operate as res judicata or create estoppel by judgment because it is not a judicial determination of rights but an agreement accepted by the court; thus, the agriculturist-debtors can invoke new statutory rights under the Amending Act.

The High Court did not err in revising the finding on agriculturist status under Section 115 CPC, as it called for evidence and drew its own inference, which is permissible when correcting a legal error apparent on the record.
doctrines: Res judicata
Estoppel by judgment
Statutory interpretation of remedial legislation
Finality of compromise decrees

card.dispute: Surviving appellants sought to continue a second appeal after one co-appellant died and his legal representatives were not brought on record, raising the question of whether the appeal could proceed.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal could be maintained by surviving appellants after the death of a co-appellant and abatement of the appeal as to him?
Whether Order 41 Rule 4 of the CPC allows surviving appellants to continue an appeal against the entire decree after abatement as to a deceased co-appellant?
Whether Order 41 Rule 33 of the CPC empowers an appellate court to pass a decree in favor of a deceased appellant whose appeal has abated?
holdings: An appeal filed jointly by all plaintiffs abates as to a deceased appellant if his legal representatives are not brought on record, and the surviving appellants cannot continue the appeal where there is a joint and indivisible interest.

Order 41 Rule 4 CPC does not apply where all plaintiffs jointly file an appeal; it only allows one or some to appeal against the whole decree, not to continue after abatement due to a co-appellant’s death.

Order 41 Rule 33 CPC does not empower an appellate court to pass a decree in favor of a deceased appellant after abatement; it cannot override the mandatory consequences of abatement under Order 22 Rule 9.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rules 2, 3, 9, 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rules 4, 33
doctrines: Abatement of appeal
Joint and indivisible interest
Finality of decree upon abatement

card.dispute: The landlord fought the tenant over whether the tenant was in arrears of rent, based on a withdrawn deposit, and whether special leave to appeal should be revoked due to misrepresentation.
issues_decided: Whether the special leave to appeal was obtained by the tenant through suppression of material facts regarding the withdrawal of a deposit of Rs. 400/-
Whether the Supreme Court should revoke special leave granted based on a misleading petition
holdings: Special leave to appeal must be vacated when obtained by suppressing material facts and creating a false impression about the status of a deposit in court.
A party seeking special leave under Article 136 has a duty of full candour; failure to disclose adverse facts forfeits the right to discretionary relief.
doctrines: Doctrine of full and frank disclosure in special leave petitions
Revocation of special leave for suppression of material facts

card.dispute: The Raja Rameswara Rao challenged the taxability of interim maintenance allowances received under the Hyderabad (Abolition of Jagirs) Regulation, claiming they were not income but capital receipts.
issues_decided: Whether interim maintenance allowances paid under the Hyderabad (Abolition of Jagirs) Regulation, 1358F, are taxable as income or are non-taxable capital receipts.
Whether such allowances form part of the commutation sum and thus have a capital nature.
Whether payments made after April 1, 1950, were in the nature of income or capital.
holdings: Interim maintenance allowances paid under the Regulation for the period before April 1, 1950, are revenue receipts and taxable as income.
These allowances are distinct from the commutation sum, which is a capital receipt, and do not form part of it.
Payments made after April 1, 1950, require determination of their nature—whether as part of the commutation sum (capital) or as interim income (revenue).
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Statutory source as the origin of income
Nature of compensation payments as income when recurring and regular

card.dispute: The surviving appellants sought to continue an appeal for ejectment and rent after one co-appellant's appeal abated due to failure to substitute his legal representatives within time.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal could proceed under Order XLI, Rule 4 of the CPC when one co-appellant's appeal had abated due to non-substitution of legal representatives?
Whether Order XLI, Rule 33 empowers an appellate court to pass a decree in favor of a deceased appellant whose appeal has abated?
Whether the abatement of one co-appellant's appeal affects the maintainability of the appeal by the surviving appellants where there is a common right?
holdings: The appeal could not proceed on behalf of the surviving appellants once the appeal by a co-appellant with a joint interest abated, as the decree would affect rights already finalised against the deceased's legal representatives.
Order XLI, Rule 33 does not empower an appellate court to pass a decree in favour of a deceased appellant whose appeal has abated, as the appeal must be competent and pending.

Where co-appellants have a common right, the abatement of one appeal bars the continuation of the appeal by others, to prevent conflicting decrees and protect the finality of the decree against the deceased.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXII, Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXII, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLI, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLI, Rule 33
doctrines: Abatement of appeal
Finality of decree
Common right and interest in joint appeals
Non-derogation from procedural finality

card.dispute: The appellant, a co-sharer in an Inam village, claimed compensation from the Union of India for unauthorized use of river water by military authorities, asserting ownership over the flowing water of the river Valdevi.
issues_decided: Whether the sanad granting the Inam village included a grant of the flowing water of the river Valdevi.
Whether the appellant had riparian rights entitling him to claim damages for diversion of river water.
Whether the diversion of river water by the military authorities caused legally compensable injury to the appellant.
holdings: The word 'water' (jal) in the sanad refers only to stationary water in tanks or wells, not to flowing river water; thus, no title to the flowing water was granted.
Title to the riverbed does not automatically confer title to the flowing water; such a grant must be explicit, which it was not in this case.
The appellant cannot claim riparian rights as a basis for compensation because the plaint did not plead such a cause of action and there is no evidence of damage to riparian rights.
doctrines: Necessary implication in construction of grants
Riparian rights doctrine
Rule against extending property rights to flowing water without explicit grant

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership over the running water of the river Valdevi flowing through his Inam village Vadner, against the Union of India and the State of Bombay, seeking compensation for military use of the water.
issues_decided: Whether the Sanad granted to the ancestors of the appellant conveyed title to the flowing water of the river Valdevi.
Whether the grant of the soil of the village, including the riverbed, necessarily includes the right to the flowing water of the river.
Whether the appellant could claim relief based on riparian rights, even if no title to the flowing water was established.
holdings: The term 'water (jal)' in the Sanad refers only to stationary water in tanks or wells, not to flowing river water, which would require an explicit grant using the word 'nadi'.
Title to the riverbed does not automatically confer title to the flowing water, as the right to flowing water is not an incident of land ownership and can only be acquired by severance.

The appellant cannot raise a claim based on riparian rights for the first time in appeal, especially when the plaint and evidence were founded solely on a claim of ownership and no damage to riparian rights was pleaded or proved.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Necessary implication in construction of grants
Riparian rights as natural rights subject to reasonable use
Rule against raising new grounds in appeal not raised in pleadings

card.dispute: The appellants (Shankarlal Aggarwal and others) challenged the Division Bench's decision to set aside the Company Judge's confirmation of a property sale in winding-up proceedings, seeking to enforce their purchase of the company's assets for Rs. 2,25,000.
issues_decided: Whether the order of the Company Judge confirming the sale was an administrative or judicial order and thus appealable under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of Calcutta High Court.
Whether the liquidators had the power to proceed with a resumed auction without fresh advertisement after granting an interval to the original highest bidder to pay the deposit.
Whether the Company Judge's confirmation of the sale could be interfered with on appeal due to non-consideration of material facts affecting the fairness of the auction.
Whether the Division Bench was justified in directing a resale instead of confirming the sale to the appellants at their earlier bid of Rs. 3,35,000/-.
holdings: The order confirming the sale was a judicial order, not merely administrative, and therefore appealable under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent.

The liquidators exceeded their powers under Condition 5 of the sale by proceeding with a resumed auction after a significant interval, as the failure to deposit immediately triggered the right to re-auction, but only if done without delay.

The Company Judge failed to consider material facts, such as the departure of bidders due to the delay, which prejudiced the fairness of the auction; thus, the appellate court was justified in setting aside the confirmation.

The appellants had no legal right to purchase the property at Rs. 3,35,000/- based on an undertaking given during a stay application, and the Division Bench was within its powers to order a fresh sale instead.
provisions: Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of Calcutta High Court
doctrines: Distinction between administrative and judicial orders
Appellate interference with discretionary orders
Doctrine of material consideration in exercise of judicial discretion
Principle of fair auction and prejudice to bidders

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for three murders based on a witness's prior statement before a committing court; they challenged the conviction after the witness retracted her testimony in sessions court.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of a witness recorded under Section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, and later retracted in trial court, constitutes substantive evidence requiring corroboration?
Whether the court can rely solely on a retracted statement to convict the accused without extrinsic corroboration?
holdings: Evidence recorded under Section 288 CrPC is substantive and does not legally require corroboration.
However, when a witness gives two contradictory statements on oath, it is unsafe to rely on either without extrinsic corroboration, especially to confirm the accused's participation in the crime.
A court may rely on the prior statement without corroboration only if it is satisfied of its truth based on intrinsic and surrounding circumstances.
In this case, the prior statement was uncorroborated and contained material inconsistencies, making it unsafe to base a conviction upon.
doctrines: Substantive value of prior testimony under Section 288 CrPC
Judicial caution in relying on contradictory sworn statements
Need for corroboration in cases involving retracted testimony

card.dispute: The State of Orissa appealed against the High Court's writ preventing it from dispossessing two former Zamindars of Maliah lands without their consent or due process.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could issue a writ under Article 226 to protect the respondents' possession of Maliah lands without determining their legal right or title.
Whether mere long possession of granted land creates a legal right enforceable against the State under Article 226 after resumption of the grant.
Whether the High Court's interim writ restraining executive action was valid in the absence of a final determination of rights.
holdings: A writ under Article 226 can only be issued if the petitioner has a legal right that is infringed or threatened; mere possession under a resumable grant does not constitute such a right.
The High Court cannot grant interim relief under Article 226 without a foundation of legal right, especially when title disputes require adjudication in a regular suit.

Possession derived from a state grant that is resumable does not entitle the grantee to protection via writ against the State once the grant is resumed, absent a determination that the resumption was invalid.
doctrines: Separation of powers between writ and civil jurisdiction
No writ relief without a legal right
Interim relief under Article 226 must be ancillary to a substantive claim

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by one person, after a notice under Section 80 CPC was served by two persons, seeking to represent multiple inamdars against the application of rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether a suit is maintainable when notice under Section 80 CPC is served by two persons but only one of them files the suit with court permission to sue as a representative plaintiff?
Whether a representative suit requires prior authorization from all persons represented, and must their details be included in the notice under Section 80 CPC?
Whether court permission is required before serving a notice under Section 80 CPC in a representative suit?
holdings: A suit is maintainable under Order 1 Rule 8 CPC even if notice under Section 80 CPC was served by two persons but only one files the suit, provided the court grants permission to sue as a representative plaintiff.

Section 80 CPC does not require the names or details of persons represented to be included in the notice; only the plaintiff’s particulars are required, and no prior authorization from represented persons is necessary.

Court permission under Order 1 Rule 8 CPC is required for instituting a representative suit, not for serving the notice under Section 80 CPC, as the Code does not provide for prior permission to serve notice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 8
doctrines: Representative suit doctrine
Strict compliance with statutory notice
Doctrine of court permission in representative actions

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the High Court's decision to allow a reference to a civil court for reassessment of compensation, arguing the application was time-barred under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the application for reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act was within the period of limitation
Whether the civil court can examine the question of limitation when a reference is made under Section 18
holdings: The application for reference was within time because the six-month limitation period under Section 18 began only when the respondents actually knew the essential contents of the award, which was on July 22, 1955, and the application was made within six months of that date.
It is unnecessary to decide whether a civil court can examine the question of limitation on a Section 18 reference, as the issue is academic in this case given the finding on the date of knowledge.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive knowledge in limitation
Principle of natural justice in statutory interpretation
Essential contents of award as basis for limitation period

card.dispute: The state acquired part of a property including an outhouse and portion of open space for an electric wire, and the landowners contested the adequacy of compensation and sought acquisition of the entire house.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents could raise, for the first time in appeal before the High Court, the contention that the entire house should be acquired under Section 49 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, after the award was made under Section 11

Whether the claim under Section 49(1) for acquisition of the whole house must be made before the award under Section 11, and whether such a claim can be raised during reference proceedings under Section 18
holdings: A claim under Section 49(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, that the entire house should be acquired must be made before the award under Section 11; it cannot be raised for the first time in appeal after the reference under Section 18.

The procedures under Section 18 (compensation reference) and Section 49 (objection to partial acquisition of house) are distinct; a claim under Section 49 cannot be mixed with or raised during proceedings under Section 18 after the award.
doctrines: Procedural distinction between compensation claims and objections to partial acquisition
Mandatory timing of objections under Section 49(1) before award under Section 11
Separation of remedies under Section 23 and Section 49

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the exemption from property tax claimed by British India Corporation Ltd. and another company for buildings used by factory workers, arguing whether such use qualified as 'for the purpose of a factory' under the Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether buildings used for employee welfare facilities (games rooms, clubs, residential quarters) are 'used for the purpose of a factory' and thus exempt from property tax under Section 4 of the Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1940?

What is the meaning of the term 'rent' in Rule 18(4)(ii) of the Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Rules, 1941 — whether in the wider sense (including license fees) or narrower sense (only tenant-landlord payments)?
holdings: Buildings used for employee welfare facilities such as games rooms, clubs, and residential quarters are 'used for the purpose of a factory' if they are necessary for the welfare and efficiency of workers, and thus qualify for tax exemption under Section 4 of the Act.

The term 'rent' in Rule 18(4)(ii) means payment by a tenant to a landlord for demised property in the narrower legal sense, and does not include payments made by licensees; hence, no tax is leviable where employees occupy premises on license.
provisions: Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1940, Section 3
Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1940, Section 4
Punjab Urban Immovable Property Tax Rules, 1941, Rule 18
doctrines: Purpose-based interpretation of statutory exemptions
Noscitur a sociis
Contemporanea expositio
Principle of equal treatment in statutory interpretation (parity between machine and worker efficiency)

card.dispute: The temple trustee sued the respondent for damages for use and occupation of land, claiming the transaction letting the respondent into possession was invalid; the respondent claimed he was a rightful ryot with permanent occupancy rights and that the civil court lacked jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, admitted to uncultivated waste land for cultivation, became a 'ryot' under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908
Whether the letting of ryoti land to the respondent amounted to a lease for more than five years requiring sanction under Section 76 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit for recovery of damages for use and occupation of ryoti land
holdings: A person admitted to possession of ryoti land for cultivation becomes a 'ryot' under Section 3(15) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, even if the land was initially waste, provided it is brought under cultivation.

The admission of a ryot to ryoti land does not amount to a lease for more than five years under Section 76 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, even if permanent occupancy rights arise under Section 6 of the Estates Land Act, and thus does not require prior sanction of the Endowments Board.

A suit by a landholder against a ryot for recovery of rent or for ejectment is triable only by a Revenue Court under Section 189 of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, and is not cognizable by a civil court.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, Section 76
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory occupancy rights
Doctrine of exclusive jurisdiction of revenue courts
Doctrine of validity of temple land transactions without board sanction for leases not exceeding five years

card.dispute: The sons of Umed Singh sued to declare void the sale of ancestral lands by their father, challenging whether Jats in Jhajjar Tehsil had a customary right to freely sell ancestral property despite having sons.
issues_decided: Whether a custom existed among Jats of Jhajjar Tehsil in Rohtak District granting unrestricted power to alienate ancestral agricultural land for consideration.
Whether the existence of sons limited the customary power of a male holder to transfer ancestral property.
Whether the earlier decision in Budal v. Kirpa Ram, denying such customary power, should be followed.
holdings: Jats holding ancestral agricultural land in Jhajjar Tehsil, Rohtak District, have an unrestricted customary right to transfer such land for consideration, provided the transaction is not for immoral purposes.
The customary power to alienate ancestral land for consideration applies equally to holders with or without sons; the presence of sons does not restrict this power.
The decision in Budal v. Kirpa Ram (1914) is not binding and has been consistently disapproved by later authorities; it should not be followed.
doctrines: Customary law
Unrestricted alienation of ancestral property
Stare decisis
Agnatic theory of inheritance

card.dispute: The appellant, a revenue sale purchaser, sued to eject the respondents; the dispute centered on whether the suit abated due to a subsequent amendment protecting tenure-holders, despite possession being delivered during appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the suit abated under the Bengal Land Revenue Sales (West Bengal Amendment) Act, 1950, due to its pendency during the amendment's commencement
Whether delivery of possession during appeal prevented abatement under the Amending Act
Whether Section 4 of the Amending Act had retrospective effect
holdings: The suit abated under Section 7(1)(a) of the Amending Act because it was pending in appeal when the Act came into force and could not have been validly instituted under the amended law.
Delivery of possession during appeal did not prevent abatement, as the suit had already abated upon the Act's commencement; Section 7(2)'s protection for executed decrees did not apply.
Section 4 of the Amending Act, though prima facie prospective, had retrospective effect to the extent made applicable to pending litigation by Section 7 of the same Act.
provisions: Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859, Section 37
Bengal Land Revenue Sales (West Bengal Amendment) Act, 1950, Section 4
Bengal Land Revenue Sales (West Bengal Amendment) Act, 1950, Section 7
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes
Abatement of pending litigation due to supervening law
Appeal as continuation of the original suit

card.dispute: The Bihari Mills appealed to the Board of Appeal against an Arbitrator's order under the repealed Bombay Town Planning Act, 1915, and the question was whether that appeal was valid under the new 1954 Act.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies from an order of an Arbitrator appointed under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1915 to the Board of Appeal constituted under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 after the repeal of the 1915 Act.
Whether the saving clause in Section 90 of the 1954 Act preserves the jurisdiction of the Tribunal of Arbitration for deciding appeals against the Arbitrator’s proposals.
holdings: No appeal lies to the Board of Appeal under the 1954 Act against an order of an Arbitrator appointed under the 1915 Act, as the Arbitrator did not become a Town Planning Officer under the new Act.

The saving clause in Section 90 of the 1954 Act continued the Arbitrator's appointment and pending proceedings but did not revive or continue the Tribunal of Arbitration, so no valid appellate authority existed for the 1915 Arbitrator's decisions.
provisions: Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954 (Bom. 27 of 1955), Section 90
Bombay Town Planning (Amendment and Proceedings Validation) Act, 1960 (Maharashtra Act XXIV of 1960), Section 2(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of continuity of proceedings under saving clauses
Doctrine of strict interpretation of appellate jurisdiction
Doctrine of non-continuance of repealed tribunals in absence of express provision

card.dispute: The Collector of South Satara versus Laxman Mahadev Deshpande over whether the respondent was entitled to compensation under Section 9 of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, for the abolition of his watan rights in land and remuneration.
issues_decided: Whether the rights of a watandar in watan land were abolished, extinguished, or modified by the provisions of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950
Whether compensation for such abolition, extinction, or modification was already provided under the Act, thereby excluding the application of Section 9(1)
holdings: The provisions of Section 3 of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, automatically abolish the watan, extinguish the office, and modify the tenure of the land, irrespective of executive resumption.

Section 4 of the Act, which grants occupancy rights in lieu of watan land, constitutes sufficient compensation, thereby excluding the right to additional compensation under Section 9(1) where no other provision exists.
provisions: Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 3
Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 4
Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 6
Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 9
doctrines: Statutory abolition vs. executive resumption
Compensation by regrant of occupancy rights as valid substitute for monetary compensation
Interpretation of legislative intent in abolition statutes

card.dispute: The State of Madras vs. Karumuthu Thiagarajan Chettiar over whether the State could issue notifications under Act 30 of 1947 regarding Inam lands in Siruvengai-Peruvengai village, which the respondent claimed was not an 'estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908.
issues_decided: Whether Siruvengai-Peruvengai village constituted an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, based on whether the entire village was granted and confirmed as Inam.
Whether confirmation of only half the village by the Inam Commissioner was sufficient to constitute the village as an 'estate' under the Act.
holdings: An Inam village qualifies as an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) only if the entirety of the original grant was confirmed or recognized by the Government, not merely a part.
The issuance of title deeds for only a portion of the originally granted village does not amount to confirmation of the whole grant, and thus the village does not qualify as an estate under the Act.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1947 (Act 30 of 1947)
doctrines: Doctrine of complete confirmation: For an Inam village to be an estate, the entire original grant must be confirmed by the Government.
Sovereign discretion of the Inam Commissioner: The confirming authority may choose to recognize only part of an original grant, and such partial recognition does not confirm the whole.

card.dispute: The State of Punjab sought to adjudicate S. Rattan Singh as an insolvent based on his alleged liability as a surety for a debt, while Rattan Singh denied being a surety and challenged the jurisdiction of the insolvency court.
issues_decided: Whether the Head of the Department under the Patiala Recovery of State Dues Act has the power to determine if a person is a defaulter under Section 4 of the Act.
Whether a Civil Court has jurisdiction to decide the question of default when the Act provides an alternative remedy.
Whether an Insolvency Court can go behind a decree to examine the genuineness of the debt in insolvency proceedings.
holdings: The Head of the Department has the authority under Section 4 of the Patiala Recovery of State Dues Act to determine both the amount due and whether the person is a defaulter.
Civil Courts lack jurisdiction to entertain disputes regarding default when the Act vests exclusive power in the departmental authority under Section 11.
An Insolvency Court can examine the validity and genuineness of a debt, even if it is based on a decree, to ensure only bona fide creditors initiate insolvency proceedings.
provisions: The Patiala Recovery of State Dues Act (Act IV of 2002 BK), Section 4
The Patiala Recovery of State Dues Act (Act IV of 2002 BK), Section 11
doctrines: Insolvency Court's power to go behind a decree
Exclusivity of departmental adjudication under special statutes
Estoppel not binding on Insolvency Court in creditor verification

card.dispute: The tenant challenged her eviction on the grounds that she had paid arrears before the appellate decree, arguing that the amended law should not apply retrospectively to defeat her right to pay arrears during appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act applies to suits instituted after its commencement, even if the arrears arose earlier
Whether the tenant had a vested right to pay arrears at the hearing of the appeal under the unamended law
Whether the notice served before the amendment satisfied the requirements of Section 12(2) post-amendment
holdings: The amended Section 12(3)(a) applies to all suits filed after its commencement, regardless of when the arrears arose, as it governs the procedure for eviction.
The right to pay arrears at the hearing of the suit was not a vested right; the amendment does not retrospectively impair any substantive right.
A notice served before the amendment complies with Section 12(2) if it meets the statutory requirements, even if it did not warn of the consequences of non-payment.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(1), (2), (3)(a)
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Statutory interpretation of mandatory provisions
No vested right in procedural benefits

card.dispute: The coparceners of a joint Hindu family contested the legitimacy of a minor's claim to a share in the family property, challenging the validity of his parents' intercaste marriage.
issues_decided: Whether the intercaste marriage between Padmavathi and Sadagopa was valid under Hindu law despite being between a Brahmin and a Shudra before the Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949 came into force.
Whether the Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949 retrospectively legitimizes children born from such intercaste marriages that were invalid under pre-existing Hindu law.
holdings: The Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949 retrospectively validates marriages between Hindus of different castes, sub-castes, or sects, even if performed before the Act came into force.
The validation of the marriage under the Act confers legitimacy on the children born from such marriages, entitling them to coparcenary rights in the joint family property.
provisions: The Hindu Marriages Validity Act, 1949, Section 3
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes
Legitimation of children through validation of marriage
Statutory validation of intercaste marriages under Hindu law

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant for non-payment of rent, while the tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Rents Act by depositing interim rent and seeking fixation of standard rent.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to protection against eviction under s. 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act based on readiness and willingness to pay standard rent
Whether the District Court's decision on the tenant's protection under s. 12 was subject to revision by the High Court under s. 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to interfere with the appellate order of the District Court in revision when no further appeal was permitted under the Act
holdings: A tenant is protected from eviction under s. 12(3)(b) if standard rent is determined and the tenant has paid or tendered it; mere irregularity in payment does not bar protection if willingness to pay is otherwise established.
The High Court cannot exercise revisional jurisdiction under s. 115 CPC merely on grounds of error in law or fact if the subordinate court had jurisdiction and decided the matter within its powers.

Where a statute bars further appeal after a specified appellate stage, the High Court’s revisional power under s. 115 CPC is limited to cases of lack of jurisdiction, illegal exercise of jurisdiction, or material irregularity—not mere erroneous conclusions.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction under s. 115 CPC is not a substitute for appeal
Error of law or fact does not amount to illegal exercise of jurisdiction unless it affects jurisdiction itself
Statutory bar on appeal restricts High Court's revisional powers to jurisdictional defects

card.dispute: The appellant landholder contested whether his inam-granted lands constituted an 'estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, to avoid rent reductions imposed under the Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the lands held under inam grants constituted an 'estate' within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908.
On which party lies the burden of proof to show that certain lands form or do not form an 'estate' under the Act.
holdings: Lands granted by name as a village under inam can constitute an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d), even if minor inams exist, provided the excluded portions were granted before the major inam.

The burden of proving that lands do not constitute an 'estate' lies on the party asserting it, as there is no statutory presumption either way, and the general principles of the Indian Evidence Act apply.
provisions: Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 1
doctrines: Burden of proof under the Indian Evidence Act
Presumption in land tenure cases
Statutory interpretation of 'estate' in agrarian laws

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State of Bombay for constructing a bus depot and office buildings for the State Transport Corporation, arguing the acquisition was not legally valid.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was invalid due to vagueness of purpose
Whether the acquisition proceedings were collusive and mala fide
Whether the State Transport Corporation qualifies as a 'local authority' under the Land Acquisition Act
holdings: The Court did not find the notification under Section 4 invalid for vagueness, as the purpose was sufficiently clear to constitute a public purpose.
The acquisition was not found to be mala fide or collusive, but the challenge succeeded on other legal grounds.

The State Transport Corporation is not a 'local authority' under the Land Acquisition Act, and since compensation was not paid from public revenue and Part VII of the Act was not followed, the acquisition is invalid.
provisions: Bombay State Road Transport Act, 1950, Section 29
doctrines: Deemed validity of prior corporate actions
Definition of 'local authority' under general statutory interpretation
Requirement of public expense in acquisitions for non-governmental entities
Non-applicability of state law definitions to central acts without repugnancy

card.dispute: The Union of India sought to recover arrears of income-tax from the assets of Sen Brothers and Co. in the hands of a receiver who was not assessed, leading to a dispute over whether tax could be recovered from a successor receiver or only from the originally assessed receivers.
issues_decided: Whether the Union of India could proceed against the assets of Sen Brothers and Co. in the hands of a receiver (M. K. Sen) who was not assessed under the Income-tax Act?
Whether sub-section (2) of section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act allows recovery of tax from a successor receiver or only from the person directly assessed?
holdings: The High Court correctly held that tax recovery proceedings cannot be initiated against a receiver who was not assessed and who succeeded an assessed receiver, in the absence of a direct assessment on the firm or its owners.

Since Bibhuti Bhusan Sen, an originally assessed receiver, was reappointed, the question of substituting a non-assessed receiver became moot, and the Union of India could proceed against him personally as the assessee.
provisions: Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, Section 43
doctrines: Principle of direct assessment and recovery under fiscal law
No recovery without assessment doctrine

card.dispute: The heirs of a deceased man challenged the validity of a gift he made to his minor wife, arguing it was invalid because her mother, not a legal guardian, accepted it on her behalf.
issues_decided: Whether a gift by a husband to his minor wife is valid if accepted by her mother in the absence of a legal guardian of her property.
Whether the gift of immovable property under Muhammadan law was complete without delivery of possession to a法定 guardian.
holdings: A gift by a husband to his minor wife is valid under Muhammadan law if accepted by her mother when no legal guardian of her property is available, provided there is clear intention and divestment of ownership.
The gift of immovable property is complete if the donor manifests a clear intention to transfer and performs an overt act such as handing over a registered deed to a person in charge of the minor.
doctrines: Completion of gift (Hiba) under Muhammadan law
Relaxation of possession rule in absence of legal guardian
Intention and delivery as essential elements of gift
Benefit to minor as overriding consideration in absence of guardian

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the Madras Land Reforms Act, 1961, arguing it violated their fundamental rights by imposing discriminatory land ceiling and compensation provisions.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5(1) of the Madras Land Reforms Act, 1961, violates Article 14 by creating unequal treatment in land ceiling limits based on an artificial definition of 'family'.
Whether Section 50 read with Schedule III violates Article 14 by providing discriminatory compensation based on slabs of net annual income.
Whether the invalidity of Sections 5 and 50 results in the entire Act being struck down as unconstitutional.
holdings: Section 5(1) creates a double standard and uses an artificial definition of 'family', leading to discrimination among equally situated individuals within natural families, thus violating Article 14.

Section 50 read with Schedule III imposes a progressively reduced rate of compensation for higher income slabs, resulting in discriminatory treatment akin to a 'cut' in compensation, violating Article 14.
Sections 5 and 50 are foundational to the Act; their unconstitutionality renders the entire Madras Land Reforms Act, 1961, void.
provisions: Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 5(1)
Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 50
Madras Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Schedule III
doctrines: Equality under Article 14
Test of reasonable classification
Doctrine of severability (implied rejection)
Substantive due process in compensation

card.dispute: The Administrator-General of West Bengal and the Commissioner of Income-Tax disputed whether the income from an estate during administration should be assessed under Section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, on behalf of the testator's sons or as income of the administrator.
issues_decided: Whether the Administrator-General received the estate's income on behalf of the testator's sons within the meaning of Section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether Section 41 applies when the administration of the estate is incomplete and the sons' shares in the income are not determinate.
holdings: Section 41 does not apply unless the income is received by the administrator on behalf of the beneficiaries with definite and determinate shares.
During incomplete administration, the Administrator-General receives income as executor, not on behalf of residuary beneficiaries, and thus the income is not attributable to them under Section 41.
doctrines: Principle of beneficial ownership during estate administration
Rule that residuary beneficiaries have no determinate interest in estate income until administration is complete
Executor's discretion in applying estate income for administration negates receipt on behalf of beneficiaries

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, both claiming succession as Mahant of a Dera of Sanyasi Sadhus in Punjab, disputed who had the rightful title based on custom, appointment, or status as Gurbhai or Chela of the deceased Mahant.
issues_decided: Whether a Gurbhai automatically succeeds to the office of Mahant in the absence of a Chela without appointment by the Bhekh or fraternity under general law in Punjab
Whether the appellant established a special custom entitling a Gurbhai to succeed without such appointment
holdings: There is no general law in Punjab entitling a Gurbhai to succeed to the Mahantship without appointment by the Bhekh or fraternity; succession is governed by the specific custom of each religious institution.

The appellant failed to prove the existence of a custom in this Dera allowing succession of a Gurbhai without appointment by the Bhekh or confirmation by the fraternity, as required under customary law.
doctrines: Customary law governs religious institutions in the absence of general statutory law
Office of Mahant is usually elective and requires confirmation by the fraternity
Burden of proving special custom lies on the party asserting it; mere status as disciple or Gurbhai is insufficient without proof of usage

card.dispute: The appellant sought specific performance of a contract to purchase joint Hindu family property from the karta, opposed by adult coparceners who denied legal necessity or family benefit.
issues_decided: Whether a karta can alienate joint family property for alleged benefit of the family without consent of adult coparceners
Whether the transaction was for the benefit of the family within the meaning of Hindu law
Whether specific performance of the contract should be granted in the absence of allegations and evidence of family benefit
holdings: A transaction for the benefit of a joint Hindu family must be one that actually or reasonably confers benefit at the time of execution, and is not limited to defensive acts.
A karta cannot alienate joint family property on the ground of family benefit when adult coparceners oppose the transaction and were not consulted.
Specific performance will not be granted where the plaintiff fails to allege or prove that the sale was for family benefit and adult members resist the transaction.
doctrines: Manager's power of alienation under Hindu law
Doctrine of necessity and benefit in joint family transactions
Discretionary grant of specific performance

card.dispute: The Builders Supply Corporation and the Union of India disputed over priority in recovering debts from a common debtor's security deposit, specifically whether tax arrears owed to the government had priority over a private decree-holder's claim.
issues_decided: Whether the common law doctrine of priority of Crown debts applies to income tax arrears in India.
Whether Section 46 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, or the Public Demands Recovery Act displaces the doctrine of priority of government debts.
Whether the Union of India is entitled to priority in recovering tax arrears over a private decree-holder from the same debtor's assets.
holdings: The doctrine of priority of Crown debts, as part of common law, continued in force in India under Article 372(1) of the Constitution and applies to income tax arrears.

Section 46 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, does not displace the doctrine of priority; it merely provides for recovery of tax arrears as if they were land revenue without altering substantive rights.
The Public Demands Recovery Act is procedural and does not contain any provision that abrogates or modifies the doctrine of priority of government claims over private creditors.
provisions: Public Demands Recovery Act (Bengal Act XIII of 1913), Sections 3, 4-10, 26, 38, and Schedule I
doctrines: Doctrine of priority of Crown debts
Doctrine of survival of common law in India post-constitutional commencement
Principle of procedural vs. substantive law distinction

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of land allotted to him as a refugee, but the allotment was cancelled on the ground that the land was in an urban area and thus ineligible for allotment under the Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant acquired an indefeasible title to the land upon issuance of the sanad, immune from cancellation even if the allotment order was set aside.
Whether Rule 2(h) of the Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an arbitrary distinction based on the timing of allotments.
holdings: The issuance of a sanad does not confer an indefeasible title; if the underlying allotment order is set aside, the title based on it also ceases to exist.
Rule 2(h) does not violate Article 14 merely because it operates prospectively and distinguishes between allotments made before and after the rule's commencement.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 40
Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955, Rule 2(h)
doctrines: Prospective operation of rules does not violate equality under Article 14
Title derived from administrative order falls with the order if invalidated

card.dispute: The Board of Revenue, Uttar Pradesh, contested whether stamp duty was payable only on Rs. 100,000 or also on Rs. 3,89,000 paid to clear a mortgage before the conveyance of property.
issues_decided: Whether the Explanation to Section 24 of the Indian Stamp Act requires unpaid mortgage money to be included in the consideration for stamp duty when the mortgage has been paid off before conveyance.
Whether the phrase 'sale of property subject to a mortgage' refers to the property or the nature of the sale.
Whether Rs. 3,89,000 paid before conveyance and Rs. 11,000 remaining mortgage liability should be included in the stamp duty valuation.
holdings: The Explanation to Section 24 applies only to unpaid mortgage money; if the mortgage is paid before conveyance, that amount is not added to the consideration for stamp duty.
The phrase 'subject to a mortgage' qualifies the sale, not the property, meaning the explanation applies only if the sale is made subject to the mortgage.

Rs. 3,89,000 paid to the mortgagee before conveyance was not part of the consideration for the immovable property and thus not liable to stamp duty under the Explanation; Rs. 11,000, though unpaid, was not the vendees' liability and the property was sold free of charge, so it also does not attract duty under the Explanation.
doctrines: Strict construction of taxing statutes
Deemed consideration under Explanation to Section 24
Principle that stamp duty follows actual consideration unless statute deems otherwise

card.dispute: The mortgagor's legal representative sued to redeem mortgaged land sold in execution of a rent decree, claiming the mortgagees' purchase through benamidars did not extinguish the right of redemption.
issues_decided: Whether the right of redemption survives when mortgaged property is sold in execution of a rent decree due to default by both mortgagor and mortgagee.
Whether Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act applies to prevent mortgagees from benefiting from a sale caused by their own default in paying rent.
Whether the mortgagees gained an advantage by availing themselves of their position as mortgagees by purchasing the property at the court sale.
holdings: The right of redemption is not extinguished when mortgagees purchase the property at a court sale brought about by their own default in paying rent, even if the mortgagor also defaulted.

Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act applies where a mortgagee, by failing to pay rent as required, contributes to a sale and then purchases the property, thereby gaining an advantage by virtue of their position.
A mortgagee who defaults in paying their portion of rent and then buys the property at execution sale must hold the property for the benefit of all interested parties, including the mortgagor.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Section 90 of the Trusts Act (duty to hold advantage for benefit of all interested parties)
Benami transaction doctrine (implied)

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over the terms of a fresh preliminary decree in a mortgage suit, particularly regarding interest entitlement and accountability for rents and profits from the mortgaged property.
issues_decided: Whether the fresh preliminary decree was in conformity with the directions of the Supreme Court and High Court.
Whether the appellants were liable to account for rents and profits from the mortgaged property from the date of filing the suit.
holdings: A fresh preliminary decree passed after compliance with appellate directions is final if not appealed, and cannot be amended unless it departs from the court's judgment.

The direction to account for rents and profits from the date of filing the suit was incorrect; it must be limited to the period from the original preliminary decree, as the High Court's earlier direction on this point was legally wrong.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 6
doctrines: Conformity of decree with judgment
Finality of decree in absence of appeal
Usual course in mortgage redemption

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the respondent's election to the state Legislative Assembly on the ground that the respondent was disqualified under Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, due to a mining lease containing a pre-emption clause in favor of the government.
issues_decided: Whether a mining lease with a government pre-emption clause constitutes a 'contract' under Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Whether such a contract, if any, is in the course of the candidate's trade or business
Whether the contract is for the supply of goods to the government within the meaning of Section 7(d)
holdings: A mining lease with a government right of pre-emption does not amount to a subsisting contract for the supply of goods, as there is no obligation on either party until the government exercises the right by notice.
A contract entered into in the course of trade or business includes a contract that initiates the business; prior transactions are not required.

The mere reservation of a right to purchase minerals does not constitute a contract for the supply of goods under Section 7(d), as no offer or acceptance exists until the government issues a notice specifying quantity and time.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 7(d)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory disqualification
Requirement of a subsisting contract for disqualification
Distinction between a right of pre-emption and a contract for sale

card.dispute: The Champaran Cane Concern challenged its assessment as a partnership firm under the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, claiming it was a co-ownership concern assessable only under Section 13.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was a partnership firm within the meaning of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, or merely a co-ownership concern.
Whether the assessment under Section 3 of the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act was valid or whether Section 13 applied instead.
Whether the High Court erred in treating the filing of returns as a 'firm' as conclusive evidence of partnership.
holdings: The existence of a partnership is a mixed question of law and fact, and a finding based on a wrong legal principle is not binding.
Mere joint ownership, appointment of a common manager, and profit-sharing in proportion to shares do not establish a partnership without an agreement to carry on business as partners.
The absence of agency between co-owners and lack of agreement to form a partnership means the assessee is a co-ownership concern, assessable under Section 13 of the Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act.
Labeling the concern as a 'firm' in tax returns does not constitute an admission of partnership where the form lacked a 'co-ownership' option and the term 'firm' may be used colloquially.
provisions: Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 2
Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 3
Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 13
Bihar Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 28(3)
doctrines: Partnership requires agreement to carry on business with mutual agency
Distinction between co-ownership and partnership
Mixed question of law and fact
Presumption against implied partnership from profit-sharing alone

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the final decree for mesne profits, arguing that the period for accounting should not exceed three years from the preliminary decree as per CPC Order XX Rule 12, and contested the enhancement of profits by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could raise for the first time in appeal the legal objection that mesne profits could only be awarded for three years from the date of the preliminary decree under Order XX Rule 12, CPC
Whether the direction in the preliminary decree to account for mesne profits up to the date of delivery of possession was valid despite the limitation in Order XX Rule 12(1)(c), CPC
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the amount of mesne profits without sufficient reasoning
holdings: A party cannot challenge the correctness of a preliminary decree in an appeal against the final decree if they did not appeal against the preliminary decree, due to the bar under Section 97 CPC and the principle of res judicata.
Even if a direction in a preliminary decree is legally erroneous, it remains binding and enforceable unless corrected in appeal, as long as it is clear and complete on its face.
The High Court erred in enhancing the amount of mesne profits without providing adequate reasons or basing the enhancement on evidence, and such enhancement must be set aside.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 12
doctrines: Res judicata
Finality of preliminary decrees
Enforceability of decrees despite legal error

card.dispute: The Collector of Sultanpur and another appealed against the High Court's direction to adjust the respondent's agricultural income-tax liability against compensation bonds due under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 8-A of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules mandates the Collector to adjust agricultural income-tax dues against compensation payable to an intermediary.
Whether agricultural income-tax assessed after vesting but for a period prior to vesting falls within the scope of Section 6(d) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act.
holdings: Rule 8-A is mandatory and obliges the Collector to realize agricultural income-tax dues by adjusting them against compensation; the phrase 'without prejudice to the right of the State Government' does not make the adjustment optional.

Agricultural income-tax assessed for the previous year ending June 30, 1952, pertains to income earned before vesting and thus falls within Section 6(d), making the respondent eligible for adjustment under Rule 8-A.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 6(d)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 26
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, Rule 8-A
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of statutory rules
Substance over form in tax liability characterization
Recovery of dues by set-off under land reform legislation

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax assessed Raja Ratan Gopal on the total income of four co-sharers as an 'association of persons,' while he claimed assessment only on his individual 1/4 share of the estate's income.
issues_decided: Whether the four co-sharers of a jagir estate constitute an 'association of persons' under the Hyderabad Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, liable to be assessed as a unit
Whether the assessee is entitled to deduct expenses incurred for the maintenance of palace and other estate buildings under the applicable tax law
holdings: Co-heirs who inherit equal shares in an estate without forming a joint enterprise for earning income do not constitute an 'association of persons' and must be assessed individually on their respective shares.

Expenditure incurred for the maintenance of estate buildings is deductible under section 6(e) of the Hyderabad Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, or corresponding provisions, as it is not private or personal but related to estate administration.
doctrines: Association of persons test: requires a joint enterprise with common purpose of producing income
Principle of deductibility of revenue expenditure for estate administration

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax contested whether the income from a trust created by Rani Bhuwaneshwari Kuer could be included in her taxable income for 1947–48.
issues_decided: Whether the trust created by the assessee was revocable within six years under Section 16(1)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the third proviso to Section 16(1)(c) exempted the trust income from being included in the settlor's income
Whether the settlor's receipt of a share of trust income disqualified the entire trust from the protection of the third proviso
holdings: The trust was not revocable within six years because the right of revocation was suspended until the termination of certain long-term leases, which extended beyond six years from the date of the trust.

The third proviso to Section 16(1)(c) excludes from the settlor's income only that portion of the trust income which is not revocable for six years and from which the settlor derives no direct or indirect benefit.

The fact that the settlor reserved a share of the income does not deprive the rest of the trust income from the protection of the third proviso; the proviso applies to income allocated to other beneficiaries who meet the conditions.
doctrines: Substance over form in tax law
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Conditional exclusion of trust income from settlor's taxable income

card.dispute: The Revenue challenged the validity of a partition deed executed by the assessee with his minor children, arguing it was a transfer of self-acquired property to minors under Section 16(3)(a)(iv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, rather than a genuine partition justifying separate assessments under Section 25A.
issues_decided: Whether the partition deed dated December 19, 1952, effected a valid partition of joint family property entitling the parties to separate assessments under Section 25A of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the blending of self-acquired property with joint family property, evidenced only by a recital in the partition deed, was sufficient to establish antecedent blending prior to partition.
Whether the transaction amounted to a direct or indirect transfer of assets to minor children within the meaning of Section 16(3)(a)(iv) of the Act.
holdings: A valid partition occurred on December 19, 1952, making separate assessments under Section 25A justified, as the deed reflected a genuine intention to partition joint family property.

A recital in the partition deed stating continuous blending of self-acquired property with ancestral property until the date of partition is sufficient to establish antecedent blending, even without prior documentary evidence.
The transaction did not constitute a transfer under Section 16(3)(a)(iv), whether direct or indirect, because the property had already been treated as joint family property before partition.
doctrines: Doctrine of blending (corpus theory in Hindu law)
Doctrine of partition in Hindu Undivided Family law
Fiction of indirect transfer under fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax appealed against the High Court's decision that surplus from the sale of assets after business closure could not be taxed under the proviso to Section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the surplus from the sale of assets after the business had ceased could be taxed as profits under the second proviso to Section 10(2)(vii) of the Income Tax Act, 1922
Whether the Appellate Tribunal had validly estimated the sale value of the buildings in the absence of material
Whether the legal fiction in the proviso could be extended to deem business as ongoing in the previous year for taxation purposes
holdings: The proviso to Section 10(2)(vii) applies only if there was actual business during the previous year; a legal fiction cannot create deemed business after closure.
The Appellate Tribunal’s estimate of sale value without evidence or material basis is invalid and cannot stand.
Legal fictions in tax law must be confined to their intended purpose and cannot be extended beyond the legislative intent.
provisions: Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, Section 10(2)(vii), second proviso
doctrines: Legal fiction limited to legislative purpose
Proviso as an exception to the main provision
Principle of harmonious construction

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Kumbakonam Mutual Benefit Fund Ltd disputed whether the Fund, a company engaged in banking among shareholders, was exempt from income tax as a mutual benefit society under the principle of mutuality.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of mutuality applies to an incorporated company where profits are distributed to shareholders regardless of their contribution to or participation in the fund's activities.
Whether the income of the assessee company is exempt under Section 10(2)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, on the ground that it is a mutual concern between contributors and participators.
holdings: The principle of mutuality does not apply when profits are distributed to shareholders merely by virtue of their shareholding, even if they have not contributed to or utilized the fund’s services.

An incorporated company cannot claim exemption under the mutuality doctrine if its structure and profit distribution resemble that of a commercial banking company, despite limiting transactions to shareholders.
doctrines: Principle of mutuality
Corporate entity vs. unincorporated association distinction in tax exemption
Identity of contributors and participators as essential for mutuality

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax challenged the Andhra Chamber of Commerce's claim for tax exemption on rental income, arguing the company's objectives were not charitable under the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the promotion of trade, commerce, and industry constitutes a charitable purpose under s. 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the power to urge or oppose legislation affecting trade renders the company's purpose political and non-charitable
Whether the benefit must be to the whole public or can extend to a section of the public for a purpose to be considered charitable
holdings: Promotion of trade, commerce, and industry is an object of general public utility and qualifies as a charitable purpose under s. 4(3)(i), even if the benefit is limited to a section of the public.
An object to urge or oppose legislation is ancillary if not dominant, and does not disqualify an institution from charitable status when the primary purpose remains beneficial to public utility.
A charitable purpose need not benefit all of humanity; it is sufficient if it benefits a substantial section of the public as opposed to specific individuals.
doctrines: Doctrine of dominant purpose
Charitable purpose including objects of general public utility
Ancillary political activity not disqualifying charitable status

card.dispute: The Collector of Kamrup and the State of Assam fought with landowners over the validity of an acquisition of land that was initially requisitioned under Defence of India Rules, not under the Assam Land Act.
issues_decided: Whether land acquired under Section 4 of the Assam Land Act must first be requisitioned under Section 3 of the same Act.
Whether an acquisition order made before a requisition order under Section 3 is valid if a retroactive requisition is later issued.
Whether Section 11 of the Assam Land Act bars judicial review of an acquisition that lacks a valid requisition under Section 3.
holdings: Section 4 of the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 allows acquisition only if land is requisitioned under Section 3; absence of such requisition invalidates acquisition.
A requisition order issued after acquisition, even with retroactive effect, cannot validate an acquisition that lacked a prior valid requisition under Section 3.
Section 11 does not protect an acquisition from judicial scrutiny if it was not made in exercise of power conferred by the Act due to lack of compliance with Section 3.
provisions: Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 3
Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 4
Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 11
doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory conditions precedent
Non-retroactivity of validating acts without express authority
Limitation on ouster clauses in administrative action

card.dispute: The landlord sought to eject the tenant for removing crops from the threshing floor and not depositing rent in court, while the tenant claimed compliance with rent payment by sending money order after the landlord refused to accept her legal share.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's removal of crops from the threshing floor violated Section 7 of the Madras Cultivating Tenants (Payment of Fair Rent) Act, 1950
Whether the tenant's failure to deposit rent in court under Section 3(3) of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 disqualified him from protection against eviction
Whether the Revenue Divisional Officer properly exercised discretion under Section 3(4)(b) of the Protection Act
Whether the High Court was justified in exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 6-B of the Protection Act and Section 115 of the CPC
holdings: Removal of crops does not violate Section 7 of the Fair Rent Act if done to prevent spoilage and not to avoid due division, especially after measurement by revenue authorities.
A tenant's failure to deposit rent in court under Section 3(3) does not automatically disentitle him to protection if he acted in good faith and attempted alternative payment.
The Revenue Divisional Officer must exercise discretion under Section 3(4)(b) based on facts; refusing to do so merely because rent was not deposited is a failure to exercise jurisdiction.
The High Court can interfere under Section 115 CPC when a quasi-judicial authority fails to exercise discretion, and such interference is sustainable under Article 136 of the Constitution.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3
Madras Cultivating Tenants (Payment of Fair Rent) Act, 1950, Section 7
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 6-B
doctrines: Doctrine of judicial discretion
Doctrine of failure to exercise jurisdiction
Principle of fair rent and due division of produce
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 136

card.dispute: The decree-holder sought execution of a mortgage decree by selling properties, while the judgment-debtor sought to set aside the sale for non-compliance with Section 35 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether non-compliance with Section 35 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940 renders a court sale a nullity or merely an irregularity
Whether the judgment-debtor could waive the benefit of Section 35 of the Act
Whether the sale could be set aside under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure despite no substantial injury
holdings: Non-compliance with Section 35 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act does not render a sale a nullity but at most an irregularity, as the provision is for the benefit of the judgment-debtor and not jurisdictional.
A judgment-debtor may waive the protection of Section 35 of the Act, as it is a personal benefit and not a rule of public policy affecting jurisdiction.
A sale cannot be set aside under Order XXI, Rule 90 of the CPC in absence of substantial injury and where the judgment-debtor failed to object or participate despite notice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 64, 66, and 90
doctrines: Distinction between nullity and irregularity in legal proceedings
Doctrine of waiver of statutory benefits for personal protection
Test of public policy versus private benefit in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant sued to recover money from respondents, claiming that a sub-lease granted to one partner bound the entire partnership firm, making all partners liable.
issues_decided: Whether the sub-lease granted by one partner bound the partnership firm under Section 22 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Whether the other partners of the firm could be held liable for the obligations under the sub-lease
holdings: A partner's act binds the firm only if the instrument is executed in the firm's name or with an intention to bind the firm; the sub-lease here was not so executed.
The firm is not liable where the parties did not intend to bind it, and the transaction was found to be in the individual capacity of the partner.
doctrines: Doctrine of binding firm by partner's act under Section 22
Requirement of intention to bind the firm in contractual transactions

card.dispute: The appellant landowner contested the taxability of interest received under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, claiming it as a non-taxable capital receipt, while the tax authorities treated it as a taxable revenue receipt.
issues_decided: Whether interest awarded under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, on compensation for acquired land, constitutes a capital receipt or a revenue receipt.
Whether such interest is taxable under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
holdings: Statutory interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act is not compensation for loss of possession but compensation for the delayed use of money, and thus is not a capital receipt.
Such interest is a revenue receipt and is taxable under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, as it arises from the State's withholding of compensation amounts.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Statutory interest as compensation for delayed payment
Principle from Westminster Bank Ltd. v. Riches on the taxability of interest

card.dispute: The appellant, Gulabchand Chhotalal Parikh, fought with the State of Bombay over whether his liability as a surety was discharged, after the High Court had previously rejected this claim in a writ petition and later in a civil suit held to be barred by res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether a decision on merits in a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution operates as res judicata in a subsequent civil suit between the same parties on the same matter.
Whether Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code is exhaustive in determining res judicata, or whether general principles can apply when the proceeding was not a 'suit'.
holdings: A decision by the High Court on merits in a writ petition under Article 226, after full contest, operates as res judicata in a subsequent civil suit between the same parties on the same matter, even if the earlier proceeding was not a 'suit' under the CPC.

Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code is not exhaustive; res judicata can apply based on general principles when a competent court has decided a matter after affording a fair opportunity to contest, regardless of the nature of the proceeding.
doctrines: Res judicata
General principle of finality of judicial decisions
Constructive res judicata (not applied)

card.dispute: The illegitimate son and daughter of a female vendor fought to pre-empt her sale of agricultural land, claiming they were entitled under the Punjab Pre-emption Act as amended.
issues_decided: Whether the terms 'son or daughter' in Section 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended, include illegitimate children of a female vendor.
holdings: The terms 'son or daughter' in Section 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act refer only to legitimate children, as there is no express provision or contextual indication to include illegitimate children.
doctrines: Normal rule of statutory construction
Contextual interpretation of statutory language

card.dispute: The Deputy Custodian of Evacuee Property and others fought with the Official Receiver of the estate of Daulat Ram Surana over whether the latter's property could be declared evacuee property after it had vested in the Official Receiver due to insolvency proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether property that vested in the Official Receiver under the Provincial Insolvency Act could still be declared evacuee property under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act
Whether the High Court erred in relying on the decision in Ebrahim Aboobaker's case to bar the declaration of evacuee property
What is the correct construction of Section 7(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act in light of the Act's object and other provisions
holdings: The vesting of property in the Official Receiver under insolvency law does not prevent it from being declared evacuee property under Section 7(1) if it met the criteria under Section 2(f) at the time of declaration.
The decision in Ebrahim Aboobaker’s case, which dealt with the death of an alleged evacuee, is not applicable to cases involving insolvency and vesting of property in the Official Receiver.

Section 7(1) must be interpreted liberally, considering the Act’s purpose, to allow declaration of evacuee property even if transferred or vested prior to declaration, so long as the enquiry was validly conducted.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(f)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7(1A)
doctrines: Liberal construction of statutes in light of their object
Vesting of property does not automatically exclude it from being evacuee property
Distinction between personal and property-based proceedings under evacuation laws

card.dispute: The creditors (Gamini Krishnayya and others) sued to recover a debt from agriculturist debtors (Curza Seshachalam and others) who claimed relief under the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act, arguing the debt should be scaled down under Section 9(1), while creditors claimed only Section 13 applied as the promissory note was executed after the Act's commencement.
issues_decided: Whether a debt incurred after the commencement of the Madras Agriculturists' Relief Act but arising from an original liability before the Act is governed by Section 9(1) or Section 13
Whether the renewal of a pre-commencement debt through a post-commencement transaction excludes the application of Section 9(1)
Whether Section 13 limits relief only to interest calculation or allows tracing back to the original debt
holdings: A debt renewed after the Act's commencement remains subject to Section 9(1) if the original indebtedness arose before the Act but after October 1, 1932.
Execution of a new promissory note after the Act does not convert a pre-commencement liability into a post-commencement debt for the purpose of applying Sections 8 or 9.
Courts must examine the origin of the indebtedness; Section 13 does not bar application of Section 9 where the original debt predates the Act.
doctrines: Look-back doctrine in debt relief legislation
Substance over form in determining applicability of relief statutes
Statutory discharge of excess liability under agrarian relief laws

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a suit for recovery of possession and mesne profits on the ground that it was barred by a previous suit for mesne profits concerning the same property.
