issues_decided: Whether a plea under Order 2 Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code can be entertained without production of pleadings from the previous suit
Whether the cause of action in the present suit was the same as in the earlier suit for mesne profits
holdings: A plea of bar under Order 2 Rule 2 CPC requires proof of identity of cause of action, which can only be established by producing the pleadings from the previous suit; mere reference to the prior suit is insufficient.
The court cannot infer the cause of action in a previous suit based on conjecture or deduction; without the plaint being on record, the technical bar under Order 2 Rule 2 cannot be invoked.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2 Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Identity of cause of action
Technical bar under res judicata principles
Proof requirement for pleading-based defences

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murder for killing three men who were harvesting crops on a disputed plot, claiming the right of private defence, while the prosecution argued it was a premeditated attack.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were guilty of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC;
Whether the appellants had the right of private defence extending to causing death under Section 103 IPC;
Whether the act amounted to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC;
Whether the appellants' possession of licensed firearms affected their liability.
holdings: The appellants, acting with common intention, attacked and killed the deceased from close range while they were peacefully harvesting under police protection, constituting murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
The right of private defence of property extending to causing death was not available as the deceased posed no threat of instant death or harm and the appellants had time to seek police protection.
The exception under Section 300 IPC, Exception 2, does not apply because the appellants acted with premeditation and caused more harm than necessary in self-defence.
Mere use of licensed firearms by unlicensed persons does not absolve them of liability under the Arms Act or affect the criminal liability for murder.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Right of private defence under Section 99 and 103 IPC
Exception to murder for exceeding self-defence in good faith
Proportionality and necessity in self-defence

card.dispute: The appellant sought to restrain the respondent-decree holder from transferring the disputed property and to compel them to furnish security after already obtaining possession following decree execution, during the pendency of an appeal in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court can exercise inherent powers under Order XLV, Rule 5 of the Supreme Court Rules to put the decree-holder on terms after execution of the decree?
Whether the Supreme Court can restrain the decree-holder from transferring the suit property or direct them to furnish security pending appeal?
holdings: The Supreme Court cannot exercise inherent powers to impose conditions like furnishing security or restraining transfer of property after the decree-holder has lawfully obtained possession, as this would interfere with the finality of execution and is not in the interests of justice.

Once a decree is unconditionally executed, the decree-holder may deal with the property as per law, and subsequent orders restricting such rights cannot be made even under inherent powers, absent special statutory authority.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XLV, Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLV, Rule 13
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XX, Rule 1
doctrines: Inherent powers of the Supreme Court
Doctrine of lis pendens
Unconditional execution of decree

card.dispute: Mortgagors sought to compel the mortgagee to account for profits from the mortgaged property before and after the preliminary decree, which the mortgagee resisted.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee is liable to account for profits from the mortgaged property after the preliminary decree when the decree does not explicitly require it.
Whether the mortgagee is estopped from denying liability to account for profits realized between the date of the plaint and the preliminary decree.
holdings: A mortgagee in possession must account for net receipts from the mortgaged property after the preliminary decree, and the court may credit such receipts to the mortgagor when determining the final amount due.

The doctrine of estoppel does not apply where the mortgagor's payment of a reduced amount under the decree does not constitute detriment, even if the mortgagee previously admitted liability to account for profits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rules 2 and 4
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel under Section 115, Evidence Act
Mortgagee's duty to account for profits post-preliminary decree

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their prosecution under sections 193, 199, and 211 of the Indian Penal Code for filing a false contempt of court application against certain respondents.
issues_decided: Whether a proceeding for contempt of court constitutes a criminal proceeding for the purpose of section 211 IPC
Whether falsely charging someone with an offence under a special law (like the Contempt of Court) attracts liability under section 211 IPC
Whether the term 'offence' in section 211 IPC includes offences under special laws
Whether the prosecution under sections 193, 199, and 211 IPC was maintainable based on a partly false complaint
holdings: A proceeding for contempt of court need not be classified as a criminal proceeding for section 211 IPC to apply; the section penalizes false charges of offences, not just criminal proceedings.
Falsely charging a person with an offence under a special law, such as the Contempt of Court, constitutes an offence under section 211 IPC.
The term 'offence' in section 211 IPC includes acts punishable under any special or local law, as defined in sections 40 and 41 IPC.
A prima facie case existed for prosecution under sections 211, 193, and 199 IPC where the core allegation in the contempt application was found false by the High Court.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of inclusive definition under IPC
Distinction between institution of criminal proceedings and making a false charge

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenant-lessees from agricultural land within two miles of Surat Borough Municipality, while the tenants claimed protection under tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 applied to land within two miles of the Surat Borough Municipality after the 1952 amendment
Whether the appellants' tenancy rights under the 1939 Act were saved and enforceable under the 1948 Act
Whether the landlord could evict the tenants except in the manner prescribed by the 1948 Act
holdings: The 1952 amendment extended the 1948 Act to areas within two miles of the Surat Borough Municipality, making its protections applicable to existing tenancies.
The appellants' tenancy rights, preserved under Section 89(2) of the 1948 Act, continued and were governed by the Act after the 1952 amendment.
After the 1952 amendment, the respondent could not evict the appellants except in the manner prescribed under Section 14 of the 1948 Act.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1952
doctrines: Savings clause doctrine
Prospective operation of exemption provisions
Statutory continuation of tenancy rights despite repeal

card.dispute: The Idol of Thakurji Shri Govind Deoji contested the Board of Revenue's demand for Matmi dues following a change in Shebait, arguing it was not liable as the grant was in favor of the idol, not the Shebait.
issues_decided: Whether a grant made in favor of an idol is liable to Matmi dues under Rule 5 of the Jaipur Matmi Rules, 1945 upon the death of a Shebait.
Whether the idol, as a juridical person, can be considered to have 'died' so as to trigger succession and Matmi liability.
Whether the writ petition filed by the idol was maintainable despite the order being nominally against the Shebait.
holdings: A grant made to an idol does not attract Matmi dues under Rule 5 because the idol, as a juridical person, does not die and thus has no successor.
Since the grant is in favor of the idol and not the Shebait, the Shebait’s change does not trigger liability for Matmi dues from the idol's property.
The writ petition by the idol is maintainable because the enforcement of Matmi dues would affect the idol's properties, even if the order was nominally against the Shebait.
doctrines: Juridical personhood of idols in Hindu law
Distinction between grants to idols and grants to Shebaits
Maintainability of writ petitions by religious idols
Principle that succession-based dues do not apply to perpetual juridical entities

card.dispute: The appellant Isher Singh, claiming ownership under an oral will, contested whether the respondents' heirship to the deceased Jati was res judicata in a subsequent suit for possession.
issues_decided: Whether the finding on the respondents' collateral relationship to the deceased in a prior suit was res judicata in the present suit.
Whether the appellate court had jurisdiction to decide the issue of heirship when the trial court had dismissed the suit on other grounds.
Whether the parties were litigating under the same title for the purpose of res judicata.
holdings: A finding on heirship was res judicata because it was directly and substantially in issue, pleaded, framed as an issue, and decided on evidence in the prior suit.
The appellate court had jurisdiction to decide the heirship issue even if the trial court dismissed the suit on another ground, as the issue was necessary for complete relief.
The parties litigated under the same title because the appellant's claim included both title under the oral will and possessory rights, making res judicata applicable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 22
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Jurisdiction of appellate court to decide issues not affecting decree
Same title doctrine in res judicata

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the quantum of compensation awarded for land acquired by the State, seeking court determination despite no formal reference by the Land Acquisition Officer on that issue.
issues_decided: Whether the court had jurisdiction to determine the quantum of compensation in the absence of a reference by the Collector under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the State's failure to object before the Subordinate Judge amounted to a waiver of the jurisdictional defect
holdings: The court has no jurisdiction to decide the quantum of compensation unless a reference is made by the Collector under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The absence of jurisdiction due to non-reference is a fundamental defect that cannot be waived by the State's failure to object at the lower court level.
doctrines: Jurisdictional competence under statute
Non-waiver of lack of inherent jurisdiction
Finality of award under the Land Acquisition Act

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for irregular payment of rent without sufficient cause, while the tenant argued past conduct before the amendment could not be considered and that payment of arrears barred eviction.
issues_decided: Whether s. 9(1)(ii) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 applies only prospectively, excluding conduct prior to the enactment of s. 14A in 1955
Whether a tenant can be evicted under s. 14A(1) after paying arrears of rent as directed under s. 14A(ii)
holdings: The conduct of a tenant prior to the amendment introducing s. 14A can be considered to determine if rent was not paid regularly without sufficient cause under s. 9(1)(ii); a statute is not retrospective merely because it considers past conduct.

A tenant’s payment of arrears under s. 14A(ii) does not bar eviction under s. 14A(1), as the two clauses address different grounds: one for non-compliance with recovery orders, the other for habitual irregularity in rent payment without sufficient cause.
provisions: The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)(ii)
The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A(1)
The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A(ii)
doctrines: Prospective application of statutes
Non-retrospective application with consideration of past conduct
Distinction between punitive eviction for non-compliance and eviction for habitual default

card.dispute: The widow and daughters of Pappachari fought over ancestral property with the wife and daughter of his congenitally deaf-mute son, Puttuswami, over whether a disqualified heir by birth defect could become sole surviving coparcener.
issues_decided: Whether a congenitally disqualified heir (deaf-mute) becomes a coparcener by birth under Mitakshara law
Whether such a disqualified heir can acquire ancestral property by survivorship in the absence of other male issue
Whether the Madras High Court Full Bench decision recognizing the distinction between 'share-taker' and 'share-enjoyer' should be upheld
holdings: A congenitally disqualified heir is a coparcener by birth with a vestigial or incipient interest in ancestral property, though unable to actively participate.
Upon the death of the father without other male issue, the disqualified heir's vestigial interest matures into full ownership by survivorship.
The distinction between 'share-taker' and 'share-enjoyer' is valid and consistent with Hindu law, and the Full Bench decision in AIR 1946 Mad 287 is binding and should not be overruled.
doctrines: Coparcenary by birth under Mitakshara
Right of survivorship
Vestigial interest in property
Doctrine of judicial precedent
Distinction between share-taker and share-enjoyer

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a right to canal water based on a prior agreement between the government and a landowner, which the state refused to recognize after the right was transferred.
issues_decided: Whether there was a valid concluded agreement between the Government and Karale for the supply of irrigation water
Whether the agreement, if any, complied with the requirements of s. 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935
Whether the appellant could succeed to the rights under the agreement through transfer
holdings: The correspondence and conduct between the Government and Karale amounted to a concluded agreement in substance, though no formal document was executed.

An agreement made in the exercise of provincial executive authority must be expressed to be made by the Governor and executed by authorized persons; failure to meet these conditions renders the contract void.
The agreement in question was not expressed to be made by the Governor nor executed by an authorized person, and thus was void under s. 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935.
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with formalities in government contracts under s. 175(3)
Doctrine of executive authority in contract formation by government
Voidness of contracts not adhering to statutory formalities

card.dispute: The dispute was between rival claimants to the estate of a deceased person over whether an administrator could be appointed under Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827 when one claimant had taken possession after the commencement of proceedings but not before.
issues_decided: Whether the relevant date to determine possession under Rule 9 of Bombay Regulation VIII of 1827 is the date of the order appointing an administrator or the date of commencement of proceedings.
Whether possession obtained by a claimant after the commencement of proceedings bars the appointment of an administrator under Rule 9.
holdings: The relevant date to assess possession under Rule 9 is the date of commencement of proceedings, not the date of the order appointing the administrator.
Possession acquired by a claimant after the commencement of proceedings does not prevent the appointment of an administrator under Rule 9.
doctrines: Summary administrative determination does not bar civil court jurisdiction
Lis pendens considerations do not apply to possession acquired during proceedings under Rule 9

card.dispute: The appellant, who had obtained possession of properties under a trial court decree later set aside on appeal, contested applications by the respondents for restitution of properties and recovery of costs, claiming both applications were barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restitution is an application for execution of a decree and thus governed by Article 182 of the Limitation Act
Whether the amendment of the appellate decree on August 24, 1950, was substantial enough to reset the limitation period under Article 182(4) of the Limitation Act
holdings: An application under Section 144 CPC for restitution is an application for execution of a decree and is governed by Article 182 of the Limitation Act, not Article 181.

An amendment to a decree that alters the rights of the parties, such as striking out a decree-holder, constitutes a substantial amendment under Article 182(4), resetting the limitation period from the date of amendment.
doctrines: Substantial amendment doctrine under limitation law
Execution of decree including restitution under Section 144 CPC
Harmonious construction to avoid anomalies in procedural law

card.dispute: The Mahant of Sri Hathiramjee Mutt and the Board of Trustees of the Tirumalai Tirupathi Devasthanam disputed over mesne profits from temple properties previously managed by the Mahant.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the rate of interest on mesne profits from 6% to 4% and 3%.
Whether the allowance of 1/3rd of mesne profits for improvements made by the Mahant was correct.
Whether the calculation of mesne profits for certain items was accurate.
Whether the deduction of 10% collection charges for house property was consistent with the High Court's judgment.
holdings: A removed trustee who continues in wrongful possession is not entitled to equitable reduction in interest rate; normal rate of 6% applies.
A 1/3rd reduction in mesne profits for improvements left behind by the Mahant was justified under the law.
The High Court correctly calculated mesne profits based on proven income sources; no error in quantum.
The decree allowing 10% collection charges stands as it was based on a joint memo filed by consent of parties.
doctrines: Equitable reduction in interest not available to wrongful possessor even if former trustee
Right of a possessor to compensation for permanent improvements under adverse possession principles

card.dispute: Collateral relatives of Pohla (the deceased) fought with his sister and her son over inheritance of ancestral and non-ancestral properties, claiming exclusion based on custom.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed properties were ancestral or non-ancestral
Whether the nature of the property (ancestral or not) is material in determining inheritance rights
Whether there existed a family custom excluding sisters and their sons from inheriting non-ancestral property
Whether the respondents (sister and her son) were preferential heirs over collaterals under personal law
holdings: Where ancestral and non-ancestral lands are mixed and cannot be separated, the entire property is treated as non-ancestral unless specific portions are proven to be ancestral.
Land ceases to be ancestral if acquired otherwise than by descent, and mixed holdings are presumed non-ancestral in absence of clear demarcation.
The courts below correctly applied personal law as no valid custom was proven to exclude sisters and their sons from non-ancestral property among Jhalli Jats of Ludhiana.
Paragraph 24 of Rattingan's Digest, which excludes sisters from inheriting non-ancestral property, is too broadly stated and not binding where personal law or contrary custom applies.
provisions: Riwaj-i-am (Customary Law) of Jhalli Jats of Ludhiana Tehsil
doctrines: Presumption of non-ancestral property in mixed holdings
Custom must be specifically proven to override personal law in inheritance
Doctrine of descent in determining ancestral property
Judicial rejection of overly broad legal digests in favor of contextual personal law

card.dispute: Ten convicted persons challenged their death sentences for murders committed by a village faction acting as an unlawful assembly, arguing that the sentences were imposed mechanically based on possession of firearms.
issues_decided: Whether a person can be sentenced to death under Section 302/149 IPC without personally committing the murder, merely for being a member of an unlawful assembly where murder was committed in pursuit of a common object
Whether the High Court applied a mechanical test in confirming death sentences for those carrying firearms
Whether every prosecution witness must be examined for the evidence to be valid
holdings: A person convicted under Section 302/149 IPC for murder by an unlawful assembly can be sentenced to death even if they did not personally commit the act, provided the circumstances justify it as a matter of judicial discretion.

The High Court did not apply a mechanical test in confirming death sentences; the use of firearms and the brutal nature of the crime justified the sentence for most, though not for three younger accused who acted under familial pressure.
It is not mandatory for the prosecution to examine every witness it cites; the validity of evidence depends on the overall reliability and not on the mere number of witnesses examined.
doctrines: Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC
Judicial discretion in sentencing to death
Principle of common object in unlawful assembly
Appellate review of death sentences

card.dispute: The appellant company refused to complete a land sale contract after war-time requisitioning delayed development work, claiming frustration; the respondent buyer sued for specific performance.
issues_decided: Whether the contract was discharged by frustration under Section 56 of the Contract Act due to government requisitioning of the land.
Whether the suit for specific performance was premature since development work was not completed at the time of filing.
holdings: A contract is not frustrated under Section 56 when performance becomes temporarily unlawful due to government requisitioning, especially if the delay was foreseeable and time was not of the essence.
A suit for specific performance is not premature if the condition precedent (development work) is completed before the final decision, allowing courts to grant relief based on subsequent events.
doctrines: Doctrine of Frustration of Contract
Supervening Impossibility
Performance within Reasonable Time
Court's Power to Consider Subsequent Events

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Mukund Deo appealed against a decree in favor of Mahadu and others, who claimed possession of land sold by Rukhma Bai, arguing the sale was invalid due to lack of legal necessity and that they were rightful reversioners.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to interfere with findings of fact in a second appeal under the applicable civil procedure law.
Whether the sale of the property by Rukhma Bai was supported by legal necessity.
Whether Vitha Bai predeceased Rukhma Bai, affecting the plaintiffs' right to claim as reversioners.
holdings: The High Court had jurisdiction to decide questions of fact in second appeal because the suit was governed by the Hyderabad Civil Procedure Code, which allowed factual review, and the change to the CPC, 1908 did not retrospectively bar such jurisdiction.
The appellants failed to prove that the sale by Rukhma Bai was for legal necessity, and the High Court rightly held the alienation invalid on that ground.

The High Court correctly upheld the trial court's finding that Vitha Bai predeceased Rukhma Bai, based on revenue records and witness testimony, and this factual determination was not disturbed in appeal.
provisions: Hyderabad Civil Procedure Code (Act 31 of 1323 Fasli), Section 602
doctrines: Substantive right to appeal is governed by law at the time of suit institution and survives procedural changes unless expressly or necessarily abrogated.
Principle of factual findings in second appeal preserved when original jurisdiction allows it, even if later procedural law restricts such review.
Revenue records may be used as evidence to determine succession and timing of death in property disputes.

card.dispute: The petitioners, members of a joint Hindu family, sought to sue the former Maharaja of Tripura and the Union of India for maintenance, but the Central Government refused consent required under Section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure, leading to a constitutional challenge.
issues_decided: Whether Section 87B of the Code of Civil Procedure violates Article 14 of the Constitution by granting special protection to former rulers.
Whether Section 87B imposes an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f).
holdings: Section 87B does not violate Article 14 as the classification of former rulers as a separate class is based on historical and legislative context and is not arbitrary.
The restriction under Section 87B on suing former rulers without central consent is reasonable and in the public interest, considering the need to honor post-independence integration agreements.
doctrines: Equality before law
Reasonable classification
Protection of fundamental rights
Doctrine of precedent

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant to reconstruct the property, claiming bona fide need, while the tenant argued the eviction was mala fide and that the landlord's real intent was to deny future accommodation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the District Court's order in revision on grounds of alleged mala fide intention of the landlord under Section 17 of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951.
Whether an erroneous finding on the landlord's bona fides amounts to a jurisdictional error under the proviso to Section 17(1) of the Act.
holdings: The High Court's revisional jurisdiction under Section 17 of the Act is limited to jurisdictional errors and does not extend to correcting errors of fact or law when an appeal lies to the District Court.

A finding on the landlord's bona fides, even if erroneous, does not amount to a jurisdictional error; the court retains jurisdiction if it applies the correct legal test, regardless of the conclusion reached.
provisions: Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 8(2)(ix)
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 17
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction limited to jurisdictional errors
Bona fide requirement as a jurisdictional condition, but findings thereon not jurisdictional if legal test is correctly applied

card.dispute: The Municipal Board, Manglaur and Sri Mahadeoji Maharaj fought over whether the Municipality could build structures on unmetalled strips of land adjacent to a public road on the respondent's property.
issues_decided: Whether the unmetalled strips of land between the metalled road and drains constituted part of the public pathway by dedication.
Whether the Municipality had the right to construct structures like a statue, piyo, and library on the said strips.
Whether the landowner could reclaim possession of the dedicated pathway.
holdings: A public pathway includes not only the metalled portion but also adjacent unmetalled strips if they are necessary for maintenance and have been under public use or control.
The Municipality, though vested with control over the public pathway, cannot erect structures that are not necessary for the maintenance or use of the road as a highway.
The owner of the soil retains possessory rights in theory but cannot reclaim possession of land dedicated to public use, as it vests in the Municipality for public purposes.
doctrines: Dedication by public user
Vesting of public streets in municipal authorities
Exclusive municipal control over public pathways for maintenance purposes
Landowner's residual rights subject to public use

card.dispute: The decree-holders sought to continue execution proceedings after the original petition was marked 'closed', while the judgment debtors argued the new application was time-barred as a fresh petition under Section 48 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether an execution petition marked 'closed' for statistical purposes is finally disposed of or remains pending.
Whether the subsequent application (E.P. No. 58/53) constitutes a fresh application within the meaning of Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
holdings: An order marking an execution petition as 'closed' for statistical purposes does not amount to dismissal; the petition remains pending if the court intended to keep it alive.

A subsequent application is not a fresh one under Section 48 if it substantially seeks execution against the same parties and properties as the original, even with minor omissions or procedural changes.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 23(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 57
doctrines: Substance over form in judicial orders
Continuity of execution proceedings
Finality of dismissal versus administrative closure

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to declare her ownership of land and regain possession, while defendants admitted her title but claimed they had been cultivating the land as tenants for over 25 years and acquired occupancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether Article 142 or Article 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 applies when the defendant admits the plaintiff's title and claims possession as a tenant.
Whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation.
holdings: When a defendant admits the plaintiff's title and claims possession derived from the plaintiff as a tenant, the case falls under Article 144, not Article 142, because there is no allegation of dispossession or discontinuation of possession.
The suit was not barred by limitation as Article 144 applies, placing the burden on the defendant to prove long possession and occupancy rights.
doctrines: Burden of proof in ejectment suits when tenancy is admitted
Presumption of continued possession in absence of allegation of dispossession

card.dispute: The appellant resisted the respondent's suit for redemption of a mortgage, arguing the transaction became an absolute sale after 15 years due to a stipulation in the deed, while the respondent claimed it remained a mortgage redeemable despite the time lapse.
issues_decided: Whether the stipulation in the mortgage deed, making the property an absolute transfer after 15 years, amounts to a clog on the equity of redemption.
Whether courts can apply the principles of justice, equity, and good conscience to invalidate such stipulations in the absence of the Transfer of Property Act.
holdings: A stipulation that a mortgage becomes an absolute sale upon non-payment within a fixed time constitutes a clog on the equity of redemption and is unenforceable.
Courts may apply the principles of justice, equity, and good conscience to invalidate oppressive mortgage stipulations, even where the Transfer of Property Act does not apply.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Clog on equity of redemption
Principles of justice, equity and good conscience
Judicial duty to enforce equitable principles in absence of specific law

card.dispute: The heir of a mortgagor sued to redeem a property mortgaged in 1919, despite a stipulation that failure to repay within 15 years would transfer ownership to the mortgagee; the mortgagee's heir resisted, claiming the property had already vested in him.
issues_decided: Whether a stipulation in a mortgage deed that ownership vests in the mortgagee if the debt is not repaid within a fixed period creates a clog on the equity of redemption and is unenforceable?
Whether courts can apply principles of justice, equity and good conscience to invalidate such stipulations even in the absence of the Transfer of Property Act being formally in force?
Whether the mortgagor's right to redeem survives beyond the stipulated repayment period despite non-payment?
holdings: A stipulation that ownership automatically vests in the mortgagee upon expiry of a repayment period unreasonably restrains the equity of redemption and is unenforceable.
Courts are bound to apply principles of justice, equity and good conscience in mortgage disputes, even where statutory law like the Transfer of Property Act is not formally applicable.
The mortgagor's right to redeem remains enforceable beyond the stipulated time, subject only to the law of limitation, and cannot be extinguished by a clog on redemption.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Clog on equity of redemption
Justice, equity and good conscience
Principles of Hindu law on mortgage (Adhi)

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a masonry structure could be erected on a disputed site claimed as part of a public street, with the respondents seeking injunctions and the appellants asserting ownership.
issues_decided: Whether special leave to appeal should be revoked because the appellants did not first seek leave under the Letters Patent of the Madras High Court.
Whether the judgment of the Single Judge in the second appeal was legally sustainable given its failure to address legal issues under Section 100, CPC.
holdings: The failure to seek leave under the Letters Patent does not automatically bar special leave under Article 136, and this Court may still exercise discretion based on the facts and interests of justice.

A judgment in a second appeal must comply with the requirements of Section 100, CPC, and cannot merely state a decree without reasoned analysis; the impugned judgment was set aside for lacking legal reasoning.
doctrines: Discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100, CPC
Principle of reasoned judicial decisions

card.dispute: The appellant contested the Custodian's demand to recover Rs. 85,000 deposited by his sister before she migrated to Pakistan, claiming it was a loan barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Section 48 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 allows recovery of a sum payable in respect of evacuee property as an actionable claim?
Whether the right to recover the deposited amount was barred by limitation at the time the property vested in the Custodian?
Whether the appellant could raise for the first time in the Supreme Court the plea that recovery was barred by limitation even if the amount was a deposit?
holdings: The amended Section 48 allows recovery of sums payable in respect of evacuee property, including incorporeal property like an actionable claim, and applies to the Custodian's recovery action.
The right to recover the deposit had not been barred by limitation when the sister migrated, as limitation began only upon demand, which occurred after vesting.
The appellant could not raise the limitation bar for the first time in the Supreme Court, as he had not pleaded it before the authorities and had instead claimed the amount was a loan.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 48 (as amended by Act No. 91 of 1956)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 9
doctrines: Retrospective application of procedural law
Vesting of actionable claims as evacuee property
Res judicata and estoppel against raising new pleas in higher courts

card.dispute: The Municipal Council, Khurai challenged the High Court's decision quashing a revised tax assessment list, arguing it had validly amended the list under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, after reverting to old tax rates and delegating revision powers to a sub-committee.
issues_decided: Whether the assessment list, revised after reverting from a slab system to old tax rates without fresh notice and objections, was validly finalized under the Act.
Whether the power to hear and decide objections to the assessment list could be delegated to a sub-committee under Section 78 of the Act.
Whether the authentication of the assessment list under Section 140 made it final, enabling amendment under Section 141.
holdings: The assessment list was not prepared according to law because assessees were not given an opportunity to object to the revised tax liabilities after reverting to old rates, violating Section 137 and Article 265 of the Constitution.
The power to hear and decide objections could not be delegated to a sub-committee under Section 78, as delegation is limited to specified individuals, not committees.
Since the assessment list was not lawfully prepared, it did not attain finality under Section 140, and thus could not be amended under Section 141.
doctrines: Doctrine of strict compliance with tax procedure under Article 265
Doctrine of lawful opportunity to be heard in tax assessment
Doctrine of limited delegation of statutory powers

card.dispute: The assessee challenged the Income Tax Officer's method of computing profit from the sale of properties in Malaya, arguing that the loss claimed should be accepted instead of the profit determined using a currency conversion schedule.
issues_decided: Whether the Income-tax Officer was justified in using the conversion rates from the Debtor and Creditor (Occupation Period) Ordinance, 1948, to compute the cost price of properties purchased in Japanese currency and sold in Malayan currency.
Whether the Department could depart from a previous method of computation to adopt a more accurate method for ascertaining profit or loss in a subsequent assessment year.
holdings: When a property is purchased in one currency and sold in another, profit or loss can only be determined by converting both values into a common currency standard using a reasonable conversion rate.

The Income-tax Officer was justified in adopting the Schedule of the Ordinance as it provided the only reliable conversion rates available, despite the Ordinance's primary purpose being debt adjustment.
The Department is not precluded from adopting a correct method of computation in a later year even if a different method was used previously, to ensure accurate assessment of income.
provisions: Debtor and Creditor (Occupation Period) Ordinance, 1948 (Federated Malaya States)
doctrines: Principle of fair and accurate computation of capital gains
Use of administrative discretion in adopting reliable valuation methods
Non est factum doctrine not applicable to prevent correction of prior erroneous assessments

card.dispute: Descendants of a former ruling chief challenged the state government's rejection of their pension application without reasons under the C.P. and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the power under Section 5(3) of the Act to grant a pension is discretionary or obligatory when conditions are satisfied.
Whether the government must record reasons while rejecting an application for pension under Section 5(3).
holdings: The word 'may' in Section 5(3) is mandatory when the applicant fulfills the conditions, such as being a descendant of a former ruling chief; the government is then obligated to grant a pension or money grant.
The government must act in a quasi-judicial manner and record reasons for rejecting a claim under Section 5(3), as the decision affects rights and no alternative remedy is available.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948, Section 5(2)
C.P. and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948, Section 5(3)
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of 'may' in statutory provisions benefiting public or protected classes
Principle of quasi-judicial fairness requiring reasoned orders in administrative decisions affecting rights

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant for failing to deliver possession after the lease expired, but the tenant claimed protection under the Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, which came into force during the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, applies retrospectively to pending proceedings.
Whether Section 5(1)(a) of the Act protects a tenant from ejectment when a permanent structure was built within five years of the lease, even if the suit was filed before the Act came into force.
holdings: A statutory provision is retroactive if it explicitly states so or if the intention to make it retroactive clearly arises from its language and context.

Section 5(1)(a) of the Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, applies to pending appeals because its language and scheme show legislative intent to protect tenants who built structures within five years of their lease, regardless of when the suit was filed.
provisions: Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 2
Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 5
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes
Protection of vested rights
Statutory interpretation of tenancy laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Raja Birakishore, challenged the constitutional validity of the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1954, which transferred management of the temple from his family to a state-appointed committee.
issues_decided: Whether the Shri Jagannath Temple Act, 1954 violates Article 14 by singling out one temple for special regulation
Whether the Act infringes the appellant's rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) by depriving him of property and management rights
Whether Section 15(1) and other provisions of the Act interfere with the religious affairs of the temple, violating Article 26(d)
Whether the Act violates secular character of temple administration and fundamental rights under Articles 27 and 28
holdings: The Act does not violate Article 14 as the Jagannath Temple holds a unique position of national importance and may be treated as a separate class.
The transfer of management does not amount to acquisition under Article 31(2) nor does it violate Article 19(1)(f), as the appellant remains Chairman and retains ceremonial roles.
Section 15(1) does not infringe religious rights under Article 26(d) as it only regulates the secular aspects of temple rituals, not their religious performance.
The provisions on administration, supervision, and discipline relate to secular management and do not violate religious freedom under Articles 26, 27, or 28.
doctrines: Classification under Article 14
Distinction between secular and religious activities in temples
Property rights vs. religious management rights
Pleading requirements for invoking fundamental rights

card.dispute: The appellant, a former royal family member, challenged the Orissa government's discontinuation of his cash maintenance allowance after the merger of Dhenkanal State into India.
issues_decided: Whether the sanad granting a cash allowance and land was a legislative act (law) or an executive act.
Whether the sanad continued in force under Articles 366(10) and 372 of the Constitution after the merger.
Whether the government could discontinue the cash allowance by executive action.
holdings: A grant by an absolute monarch must be examined for its nature, scope, and context to determine if it is legislative or executive; no automatic rule treats all such acts as law.
The sanad was a personal, hereditary grant made under family custom and was purely an executive act, not law, and thus did not survive under Article 372.
The government, as successor to the Ruler, could modify or discontinue the cash allowance by executive action, as quantum of maintenance is an executive function under continuing customary law.
provisions: Order 31 of 1948, clause 4(b), issued by Government of Orissa under Extra-territorial Jurisdiction Act, 1947, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Distinction between legislative and executive acts applies even to absolute monarchs
Continuation of laws under Article 372 depends on the act being legislative in nature
Executive discretion in determining quantum of maintenance under customary obligations

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their lands without compensation during consolidation proceedings, arguing violations of Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of proprietors' rights in shamlat deh and abadi deh without compensation violated Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act as amended and the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act fell within the protection of Article 31-A
Whether the reasoning in K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras should be applied to invalidate the impugned land reforms
holdings: The acquisition of rights in village common lands (shamlat deh) and settled village areas (abadi deh) without compensation is protected under Article 31-A as part of agrarian reform.
Legislative measures assigning land to village panchayats or artisans serve rural development and fall within the scope of 'modification of rights in an estate' under Article 31-A.
The Kochuni case is limited to its facts and does not bar a liberal interpretation of Article 31-A where the law forms part of a comprehensive agrarian reform scheme.
Provisions enabling redistribution and planning of rural lands, including for community use, are constitutionally valid under Article 31-A even if they extinguish or modify proprietary rights.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948 (Act 50 of 1948) as amended by Punjab Act 27 of 1960
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1954 (Act 1 of 1954)
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of 'estate' and 'rights in an estate' under Article 31-A
Agrarian reform as a valid basis for extinguishment or modification of property rights
Ancillary measures in furtherance of rural development are protected under Article 31-A
Doctrine of precedent limited to factual context, as seen in the distinction of K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras

card.dispute: The appellant, who had a right to cut trees granted by a zamindar, challenged the state's acquisition of that right under an amendment to the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment under Section 5(aa) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act vests in the State the right to cut trees held by a third person, not the intermediary, as of the vesting date.
Whether the absence of a compensation mechanism for such third-party rights renders the amendment unconstitutional.
holdings: Section 5(aa) clearly vests in the State all rights to trees or forest produce, regardless of whether they are held by the intermediary or a third person, as the phrase 'held by an intermediary or any other person' includes such third-party rights.

The lack of compensation does not invalidate the amendment because, after the 17th Constitutional Amendment and inclusion of the Act in the Ninth Schedule, such laws are immune from constitutional challenge on grounds of compensation.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 (West Bengal Act 1 of 1954), Section 5(aa)
Constitution of India, Article 31(2), Ninth Schedule, 17th Amendment
doctrines: Doctrine of plain meaning
Doctrine of legislative competence to amend laws retrospectively
Doctrine of constitutional immunity under Ninth Schedule

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondent's right to pre-empt a property sale based on a local custom of vicinage, arguing that such a custom violates fundamental rights under the Indian Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether a customary law of pre-emption based on vicinage is void under Article 19(1)(f) read with Article 13 of the Constitution
Whether 'custom or usage having the force of law' is included in the expression 'laws in force' under Article 13(1) of the Constitution
holdings: A law of pre-emption based on vicinage, whether statutory or customary, imposes unreasonable restrictions on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) and is void to the extent of inconsistency with Part III of the Constitution.

Custom or usage having the force of law in India is included in the term 'laws in force' under Article 13(1), and thus subject to constitutional scrutiny and invalidity if inconsistent with fundamental rights.
doctrines: Voidness of laws inconsistent with fundamental rights
Incorporation of custom into 'law in force' under constitutional interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants seized cattle from a field they claimed as theirs, purporting to act under the Cattle Trespass Act, 1871; the cattle owners used force to rescue them, leading to injuries and a death, and the appellants were convicted for murder and grievous hurt.
issues_decided: Whether illegal seizure of cattle, purporting to be under s. 10 of the Cattle Trespass Act, 1871, amounts to theft under s. 378 IPC
Whether the owner of seized cattle has a right to use force to rescue them
Whether the appellants had the right of private defence of person when confronted by the cattle owners
holdings: A person who seizes cattle believing they are trespassing on his land and causing damage, and who intends to take them to the pound, does not commit theft even if mistaken about ownership of the land.
The owner of illegally seized cattle has no right to use force to rescue them; the proper remedy is a civil action under s. 20 of the Cattle Trespass Act.
The appellants had the right of private defence of person as they could reasonably apprehend use of force by the cattle owners, who approached armed and aggressively.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Right of private defence of person
Dishonest intention under theft
Wrongful loss in theft

card.dispute: The Ruler of Dhenkenal challenged the Orissa Private Lands of Rulers (Assessment of Rent) Act, 1958, which imposed rent on her previously exempt private lands, claiming it violated constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether Section 6 of the Orissa Act violates Article 14 by creating arbitrary classification in assessing rent on private lands of Rulers?
Whether the definition of 'Ruler' in the Act is inconsistent with Article 366(22) of the Constitution, rendering the Act invalid?
Whether the Act violates Article 31 by depriving Rulers of property without authority of law?
holdings: Section 6 does not violate Article 14 as it prescribes fair, equitable, and rational criteria for rent assessment, with a reasonable nexus to the Act's objective, and the classification is valid under the doctrine of permissible class legislation.

The broader definition of 'Ruler' in the Act, including relatives and dependants, does not conflict with Article 366(22) because constitutional definitions apply only to the Constitution unless context requires otherwise, and the definition here serves to identify taxable lands.

The Act does not violate Article 31 as it merely imposes a tax or assessment on land, not amounting to acquisition or deprivation of property, and falls under the exception in Article 31(5)(b)(i) for tax laws.
provisions: Orissa Private Lands of Rulers (Assessment of Rent) Act, 1958, Section 2(h)
Orissa Private Lands of Rulers (Assessment of Rent) Act, 1958, Section 5
Orissa Private Lands of Rulers (Assessment of Rent) Act, 1958, Section 6
doctrines: Presumption of constitutionality
Permissible classification under Article 14
Doctrine of reasonable nexus
Statutory interpretation of definitions in context

card.dispute: Landowners affected by agrarian reform laws challenged the constitutional validity of the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, which added 44 state laws to the Ninth Schedule, seeking to protect them from judicial review.
issues_decided: Whether the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, is valid under Article 368 without ratification by half the States, given that it affects fundamental rights and judicial powers under Article 226.
Whether Parliament has the power to amend fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution, including through the insertion of laws in the Ninth Schedule.
Whether Parliament can validate state laws relating to land reform that it itself could not have enacted.
holdings: The Seventeenth Amendment does not require ratification by half the States under the proviso to Article 368, as it does not amend the federal structure or the powers of High Courts under Article 226 in a way that triggers the special procedure.
Parliament has the power to amend Part III of the Constitution, including by enacting Articles 31A and 31B and adding laws to the Ninth Schedule, subject to reconsideration in a future case.

The petitioners failed to make out a case for striking down the Seventeenth Amendment on the arguments presented, though doubts were expressed about the extent of Parliament's amending power, particularly regarding basic features of the Constitution.
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine (inchoate form, with doubts raised)
Doctrine of implied limitations on amending power
Doctrine of constitutional permanency of basic features
Doctrine of harmonization between oath to uphold the Constitution and amending power

card.dispute: The appellant claimed title to property purchased benami in 1914 by his father through another, but the respondent, a transferee from the nominal purchaser, resisted the claim, leading to a suit for declaration and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's suit based on a benami transaction is barred by Section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Whether a suit for possession based on adverse possession is maintainable when the benami claim is barred
holdings: Section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars any suit against a person claiming title under a court-certified purchase on the ground that the purchase was benami in favour of the plaintiff or someone through whom the plaintiff claims.

A plaintiff may maintain a suit based on adverse possession if the real owner's possession ripens into title under the Limitation Act, but such a plea must be clearly pleaded and proved, including when possession became adverse.
doctrines: Bar on benami claims under Section 66 CPC
Adverse possession as an independent basis of title

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's suit for ejectment, arguing that the use of Order 37 of the CPC under the Bombay Rents Act was invalid and that the court should have exercised inherent powers under Section 151 to set aside the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the court could exercise inherent powers under Section 151 of the CPC to set aside a decree passed under Order 37 when Rule 4 of Order 37 provides an express remedy.
Whether Rule 8 of the rules under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, which applies Order 37 of the CPC, is ultra vires the Act.
holdings: Inherent powers under Section 151 of the CPC cannot be used to set aside a decree passed under Order 37 when Rule 4 of that Order provides an express procedure for such relief; those powers are only for exceptional cases where no other remedy exists.

Rule 8, which applies Order 37 of the CPC to suits under the Bombay Rents Act, is not ultra vires, as procedural rules requiring tenants to comply with conditions to be heard do not conflict with the discretionary powers of courts under the Rent Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 49
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 37, Rule 2 and Rule 4
doctrines: Inherent powers under Section 151 CPC are residual and applicable only in absence of express remedies.
Procedural rules do not override substantive rights if they merely regulate the manner of exercising discretion.

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, both displaced persons, fought over the possession of 60 acres of evacuee agricultural land in Hyderabad, where the appellants were allotted the land and issued sanads, but the allotment was later set aside in favor of the original lessees (respondents).
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government's order under Section 33 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, setting aside the allotment to the appellants, was valid and within jurisdiction.
Whether the sanads issued to the appellants could survive after the order of allotment on which they were based was set aside.
Whether the Deputy Secretary had sufficient material to justify setting aside the allotment order.
holdings: The Central Government's order under Section 33 was valid as it dealt with rectifying an error in a 'thing done' regarding a rehabilitation grant, and its power extended to setting aside the allotment and directing dispossession.
A sanad issued on the basis of a valid allotment cannot survive if the underlying allotment order is set aside, as the grant derives its validity from the continuing existence of that order.
The Deputy Secretary had sufficient material to conclude that the original leaseholders (respondents) were entitled to restoration, thereby justifying the reversal of the allotment.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 33
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
doctrines: Validity of administrative action under statutory revision powers
Conditional survival of property grants upon underlying administrative orders
Principle that a grant cannot subsist if its foundational order is invalidated

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and the respondent, Sirajuddin Khan, fought over whether super-tax could be deducted while calculating net income for compensation under a land abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'income-tax' in Rule 2(2)(c) of Schedule I to the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act includes super-tax.
Whether super-tax paid on total income can be attributed to income from a specific source, such as big forest, for deduction purposes.
holdings: The term 'income-tax' in the Act does not include super-tax, as they are distinct taxes and the legislature used 'income-tax' specifically, excluding super-tax by omission.
Super-tax cannot be attributed to income from a particular source like big forest because it is levied on total income, making its allocation to specific sources legally impermissible.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Schedule I, Rule 2(2)(c)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between income-tax and super-tax as separate fiscal levies
Rule against using speculative allocation in statutory computation

card.dispute: The State of Bombay sought to resume management of agricultural lands owned by the respondents for remaining fallow, leading to a legal challenge over the validity of delegated authority to conduct the enquiry and pass the order.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government can delegate not only powers but also incidental duties under Section 65(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Laws Act, 1948, read with Section 83
Whether the Deputy Collector, as a delegate, could authorise subordinate officers to collect evidence and inspect land without violating the principle of 'delegatus non potest delegare'
holdings: Section 83 permits delegation of both powers and duties incidental to those powers, as they are interwoven and cannot be separated; a power coupled with a duty may be delegated to the same person.

The Deputy Collector need not personally conduct the on-site enquiry; he may collect evidence through subordinates, as long as he himself evaluates the material and makes the final decision, which does not amount to impermissible further delegation.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Laws Act, 1948, Section 65
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Laws Act, 1948, Section 83
doctrines: Delegated legislation
Delegatus non potest delegare
Power coupled with duty

card.dispute: The proprietor of an inam estate challenged the state's 1956 notice proposing a second reduction of rent, arguing that the Rent Reduction Act did not permit revisiting rent already fixed in 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had the power under the Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, to initiate proceedings in 1956 for a second reduction of rent after final fixation in 1949.
Whether the amending Act of 1960 (Andhra Pradesh Amendment Act, IX of 1960) could validate proceedings initiated prior to its enactment.
Whether the notice issued in 1956 could be treated as valid under Section 3-B of the amended Act, which allowed correction of errors in earlier rent orders.
holdings: The State Government had no power under the original 1947 Act to revise or reduce rent already fixed under Section 3(2) after the initial determination.
The 1960 Amending Act, including Section 3-B allowing correction of errors, operated prospectively and could not validate actions taken before its commencement.
The 1956 notice could not be retroactively validated under Section 5 of the Amending Act because it was not issued under the error-correcting framework of Section 3-B.
provisions: The Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 2
The Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 3(2)
The Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 8
The Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1960, Section 3-B
The Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1960, Section 5
doctrines: Prospective operation of amending statutes
Doctrine of validation by subsequent legislation
Principle of finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: The State of Madras contested C. J. Coelho's claim for full deduction of interest paid on borrowed money used to purchase a plantation under the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the interest paid on borrowed funds for purchasing a plantation constitutes capital expenditure and is thus non-deductible under Section 5(e) of the Act.
Whether the interest payment was a personal expense and therefore not deductible.
Whether the interest was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation, qualifying it for deduction under Section 5(e).
holdings: Interest paid on borrowed money used to acquire a plantation is revenue expenditure, not capital expenditure, as it does not create a new asset or confer an enduring benefit.
Interest payments to service a loan for a plantation are not personal expenses, as they are incurred in the capacity of a business owner, not for personal needs.
Expenditure on interest for funds borrowed to purchase a plantation is wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation when viewed as part of an integrated business transaction.
provisions: Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955, Section 5(e)
Madras Plantations Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955, Section 5(k)
doctrines: Revenue vs. capital expenditure distinction
Wholly and exclusively for business purpose doctrine
Integrated transaction doctrine in business expenditure

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications on the grounds that the land was being acquired for a company, not a public purpose, and that the notifications failed to comply with statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, declaring acquisition for a public purpose were valid when the entire compensation was to be paid by a private company.
Whether the notifications could be read as substantially declaring acquisition for a company despite not explicitly stating so.
holdings: Where the entire compensation is to be paid by a company, a notification under Section 6 must explicitly declare that the land is needed for a company; a declaration of public purpose is invalid if no public funds are used.

A notification stating land is required for a 'public purpose' such as a factory does not implicitly mean acquisition for a company, as a factory may be owned by government, a local body, or an individual.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 17(1) read with Section 17(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of strict compliance with statutory prerequisites for land acquisition
Doctrine of substance over form in statutory interpretation (applied and rejected in this context)

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and Modern Cultivators, Ladwa fought over whether the State was liable for damages due to flooding of the plaintiff's land caused by a canal bank breach.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res ipsa loquitur applies to the breach in the canal bank.
Whether an adverse inference of negligence can be drawn against the State for non-production of official documents.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 2 of the Limitation Act.
holdings: The rule of res ipsa loquitur applies where a canal bank breaches, as it would not occur without lack of proper care, making the breach prima facie evidence of negligence.

An adverse inference of negligence can be drawn against a party that deliberately fails to produce documents ordered by the court, especially when those documents likely would have been unfavorable to its case.
Article 2 of the Limitation Act does not apply because the damage did not arise from a statutory act done or purportedly done under the Canal Act, and the suit was therefore within time.
provisions: Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 6
Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 15
doctrines: Res ipsa loquitur
Adverse inference from non-production of evidence
Statutory immunity and limitation for statutory acts
Negligence in tort under common law
Rylands v. Fletcher rule and its exceptions

card.dispute: The Matadhipati of a Mutt challenged the validity of a scheme framed in 1939 under the Madras Act of 1927, which transferred administration of the Mutt to an Executive Officer, arguing that its enforcement in 1952 violated his fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether a scheme framed under a pre-Constitution law and not enforced before 1950 can be challenged as violating fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f) when enforced after the Constitution came into force.
Whether Section 103(d) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 requires pre-existing schemes to be tested for consistency with the 1951 Act or the Constitution.
holdings: A scheme validly framed under pre-Constitution law, even if enforced after 1950, does not violate Article 19(1)(f) merely due to post-Constitution enforcement; fundamental rights are not retrospective.
Section 103(d) deems pre-existing schemes valid and operative under the 1951 Act without requiring fresh examination of their consistency with the Act or the Constitution.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 103(d)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 62(3)(a)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927 (Mad. XI of 1927), Section 63
doctrines: Non-retrospectivity of fundamental rights
Deeming provisions in statutes
Continuity of pre-Constitution schemes under post-Constitution legislation

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's decision that it lacked revisional jurisdiction to set aside an order by a Municipal President regarding unauthorized constructions made by Leela Jain.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had revisional jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan City Municipal Appeals (Regulation) Act, 1950, to interfere with a final order passed by a municipal authority when no appeal lay against such order under municipal law.
Whether the proviso to Section 4(1) of the Act should be interpreted as limited only to appealable orders or whether it extends to non-appealable, final orders of municipal authorities.
holdings: The proviso to Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan City Municipal Appeals (Regulation) Act, 1950, empowers the State Government to call for records and exercise revisional jurisdiction over final, non-appealable orders passed by municipal authorities.

The words 'order passed by a Municipal authority' in the proviso are not restricted to appealable orders and must be given full effect, even if this allows broader state interference in municipal matters, as the statutory language is clear.
provisions: Rajasthan City Municipal Appeals (Regulation) Act, 1950, Section 4(1) (with proviso)
Rajasthan City Municipal Appeals (Regulation) Act, 1950, Section 3
doctrines: Statutory construction of provisos
Revisional jurisdiction of State Government
Finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan challenged the validity of certain provisions of the Rajasthan Jagirdars' Debt Reduction Act, 1937, which affected the execution of a mortgage decree in favor of Mukanchand against a former jagirdar.
issues_decided: Whether the exclusion of certain debts from the purview of the Rajasthan Jagirdars' Debt Reduction Act under the impugned part of Section 2(e) violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether Section 7(2) of the Act, which restricts recovery of reduced debt to only the compensation and rehabilitation grant, is constitutionally valid
holdings: The impugned part of Section 2(e) violates Article 14 as it lacks a rational basis for classifying certain creditors differently, with no intelligible differentia linked to the Act's objective of relieving jagirdars' debt burden.

Section 7(2) is valid as it imposes reasonable restrictions in the public interest by protecting resumed jagirdars from total financial ruin, allowing rehabilitation by limiting recovery to compensation and rehabilitation grants.
provisions: Rajasthan Jagirdars' Debt Reduction Act, 1937, Section 2(e)
Rajasthan Jagirdars' Debt Reduction Act, 1937, Section 7(2)
doctrines: Permissible classification under Article 14
Reasonable restrictions in public interest

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the validity of a criminal trial conducted by a First Class Magistrate for an offence under the Uttar Pradesh Private Forests Act, 1949, which prescribed trial only by Second or Third Class Magistrates.
issues_decided: Whether a First Class Magistrate has jurisdiction to try an offence under Section 15(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Private Forests Act, 1949, when the Act specifies that such offences are triable only by Magistrates of the Second or Third Class.
Whether the trial conducted by a Magistrate who was later conferred First Class powers is void for lack of jurisdiction.
holdings: The trial of offences under Section 15(1) of the Uttar Pradesh Private Forests Act must be conducted only by a Magistrate of the Second or Third Class, as expressly provided in Section 15(2), and no other Magistrate has jurisdiction.

A trial conducted by a First Class Magistrate, where the statute restricts trial to lower-class Magistrates, is void under Section 530(p) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, even if the Magistrate had previously recorded evidence.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Private Forests Act, 1949, Section 15
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Second Schedule
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Third Schedule
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional exclusivity
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (plain meaning rule)
Doctrine of implied exclusion of higher courts when lower courts are specifically designated

card.dispute: The heirs of Azam Ali, through their purchasers, challenged the validity of a mortgage and sale of a tea estate by Ismail, the eldest son, to the Azamabad Tea Company, claiming they had superior title.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by res judicata or order IX rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to a prior dismissed suit (Suit 58 of 1931).
Whether Ismail had full ownership or ostensible ownership of the tea estate, enabling him to validly mortgage the property.
Whether the plaintiffs could claim a 2 annas 13 gundas share based on a sale by Ashfaq to Pir Baksh and subsequent purchase by the plaintiffs.
holdings: The suit was substantially barred by Order IX Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure because the cause of action was identical to the earlier Suit 58 of 1931, despite new allegations of possession.

Ismail was not the full owner, but his co-heirs had allowed him to appear as the ostensible owner, making them estopped from challenging the mortgage and sale under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act.

The claim to Ashfaq’s 2 annas 13 gundas share was not rejected outright, but the matter was remitted to the trial court to determine the reality of the sale, as suspicious circumstances required further scrutiny.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 9
doctrines: Res judicata and constructive res judicata
Ostensible ownership and estoppel under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of constructive res judicata under Order IX Rule 9

card.dispute: The appellant, a mutawalli of waqf properties, challenged his removal by the Sadr of the Bihar Subai Sunni Majlis-E-Awqaf over allegations of mismanagement and disobedience of orders.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in not considering all arguments raised by the appellant.
Whether the amendment to Section 27(2)(h) of the Bihar Waqfs Act, 1948, allowing the Majlis to remove a mutawalli, applies retrospectively to orders disobeyed before the amendment.
Whether the Sadr had the authority to remove the mutawalli under Sections 37 and 38 of the Act.
holdings: The Supreme Court will not entertain claims that the High Court failed to consider specific arguments unless the omission is admitted or proven; High Courts, as Courts of Record, are presumed to have considered material points.

The amendment to Section 27(2)(h) allowing the Majlis to remove a mutawalli applies to disobedience of orders issued before the amendment, as the law intended to address past misconduct and no vested right exists to remain in office after proven misconduct.

The Sadr had the authority to act under Section 37 in an emergency when a meeting of the Majlis was not feasible, and the subsequent approval by the Majlis validated the action; delegation under Section 38 was not necessary in such circumstances.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in judicial proceedings
Prospective application of amending statutes with retroactive factual basis
Doctrine of necessity in administrative action
Delegation of powers in emergency situations

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the acquittal of respondents charged with forest offences in Tripura, arguing they violated the Indian Forest Act, 1927 in reserved forests.
issues_decided: Whether the forests in question were 'reserved forests' under Chapter II of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, making the accused liable under Section 26(1)
Whether the notifications issued under the Tripura Forest Act corresponded to 'reserved forest' notifications under Section 20 of the Indian Forest Act
Whether the prosecution could sustain charges under Section 26(1)(a), (d), and (h) in the absence of a valid notification under Section 4 of the Indian Forest Act
holdings: The forests were not 'reserved forests' under Chapter II of the Indian Forest Act, as the Tripura notifications did not correspond to Section 20, but instead aligned with protected forests under Chapter IV.
The provision corresponding to the Tripura Forest Act is found in Chapter IV, not Chapter II, hence the accused could not be prosecuted under Section 26(1) which applies to reserved forests.
Without a notification under Section 4 of the Indian Forest Act, conviction under Section 26(1)(a) for making fresh clearings is not sustainable.
doctrines: Doctrine of Corresponding Provision
Strict Construction of Penal Statutes
Requirement of Valid Notification for Criminal Liability

card.dispute: The Union of India prosecuted individuals for forest offences under the Indian Forest Act, but the respondents argued the areas were not 'reserved forests' as required, leading to a dispute over whether notifications under a prior Tripura Forest Act could be deemed valid under the Indian Forest Act.
issues_decided: Whether forest areas notified under the Tripura Forest Act became 'reserved forests' under the Indian Forest Act after the merger of Tripura with India.
Whether the provisions of the Tripura Forest Act correspond to Chapter II (reserved forests) or Chapter IV (protected forests) of the Indian Forest Act.
Whether prosecutions under Section 26(1) of the Indian Forest Act were valid in the absence of a valid notification constituting the area as a 'reserved forest'.
holdings: Notifications issued under the Tripura Forest Act do not constitute 'reserved forests' under Chapter II of the Indian Forest Act, as the Tripura Act corresponds instead to Chapter IV dealing with 'protected forests'.
The object and purpose of the Tripura Forest Act align with Chapter IV of the Indian Forest Act, which protects specific trees and regulates use, rather than fully reserving forests under Chapter II.
In the absence of a valid notification under a provision corresponding to Chapter II, prosecutions under Section 26(1) for offences in 'reserved forests' cannot be sustained.
provisions: Tripura Forest Act, 1257 T.E. (Act 2 of 1257 T.E.), Section 5
doctrines: Doctrine of corresponding provisions
Doctrine of statutory interpretation by object and purpose
Doctrine of deeming provisions and their limits

card.dispute: The landlord and tenant disputed whether the landlord's failure to pay compensation within three months of the decree, despite the decree not specifying the time for payment, led to automatic dismissal of the eviction suit under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921.
issues_decided: Whether the mandatory three-month payment period under Section 4(4) of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921 applies even if the decree under Section 4(1) does not specify the time for payment
Whether a landlord can avoid dismissal of the eviction suit under Section 4(4) due to a defective decree that omits the three-month payment condition
holdings: The three-month payment requirement under Section 4(4) is mandatory and applies regardless of whether the decree under Section 4(1) specifies the time for payment.

A decree's failure to include the three-month payment condition does not exempt the landlord from compliance with Section 4(4); non-payment within three months results in automatic dismissal of the suit.
provisions: The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 4(1)
The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 4(4)
The Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 10
doctrines: Mandatory statutory interpretation
Protection of tenant rights as legislative intent
Substantive compliance over procedural defects
