card.dispute: The mining company challenged the Central Government's rejection of its review application against the State Government's refusal to renew its certificate of approval, arguing it was denied a fair hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government acts in a quasi-judicial capacity when reviewing a State Government's refusal to renew a certificate of approval under Rule 57 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949.

Whether the Central Government violated the principles of natural justice by relying on a report from the State Government without disclosing it to the appellants or giving them an opportunity to respond.
holdings: The Central Government exercises quasi-judicial power when reviewing a refusal to renew a certificate of approval under Rule 57(2) read with Rule 59 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949.
A decision based on undisclosed material from the State Government, without affording the applicant a chance to respond, violates the principles of natural justice and is void.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Rules, 1949, Rule 57
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Rules, 1949, Rule 59
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial function
Right to fair hearing

card.dispute: The appellants claimed title to disputed lands as accretions under the Bengal Alluvion and Deluvion Regulation, XI of 1825, while the respondents contested this claim.
issues_decided: Whether the court could infer that the appellants' ancestors held frontier plots during 1845–1863 based on possession records from 1892–1909?
Whether the presumption of continuity under Section 114 of the Evidence Act applies retrospectively over a long time gap?
Whether the appellants established title to the accreted lands under Section 4(1) of Regulation XI of 1825?
holdings: An inference of continuity of possession may be drawn under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, but not over a long time gap without supporting evidence.
It is unsafe to presume that possession during 1892–1909 implies possession during 1845–1863 due to the significant time interval and changing land conditions.
The appellants failed to prove that the disputed lands were accretions to plots held by them or their ancestors, thus failing to establish title under Regulation XI of 1825.
provisions: Bengal Alluvion and Deluvion Regulation XI of 1825, Section 4(1)
doctrines: Presumption of continuity of state of things
Burden of proof in claims based on accretion
Proper apportionment of accreted land based on original river frontage

card.dispute: The widow and sons of Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladin challenged the declaration that his daughter Zarina, who migrated to Pakistan, had a 7/48th share in his property, which the Custodian sought to declare as evacuee property.
issues_decided: Whether the notice issued under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 was sufficiently specific to identify the properties in which Zarina held a share.
Whether certain properties claimed to belong to Khan Bahadur were rightfully his or belonged to others, including benami holdings or charitable dedications.
Whether Khan Bahadur, as a Khoja Muslim in Hyderabad State, could validly make a will under Hindu customary law or was governed by Muslim law under the Shariat Act, 1937.
Whether the share of Zarina in the assets of the firm 'Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladdin & Co.' could vest in the Custodian.
holdings: The notice was sufficient to identify most properties, including the firm's assets and immovable properties listed in the will, but the reference to 'any other property left by him' was too vague to support inclusion.

Properties like Noor Bagh and Market Street were held to be Khan Bahadur’s, as benami holdings; Paterghatti land was not proved to be dedicated as wakf; Rockland and firm assets were his based on will and partnership deed.

Khojas in Hyderabad State were governed by Muslim law, not Hindu customary law, and could not rely on a custom contrary to Mohamedan law; thus, Khan Bahadur could not make a valid will, and his estate devolved intestate.
No part of the assets of 'Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladdin & Co.' vested in the Custodian as it was not mentioned in the notification or the will, and the claim over it failed.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8(4)
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Doctrine of repugnancy to Muslim law: custom cannot override Mohamedan law unless permitted by statute
Intestate succession under Muslim law
Requirement of specificity in statutory notices under administrative law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his murder conviction based on a confessional first information report (FIR) given to a police officer, arguing it was inadmissible under Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act.
issues_decided: Whether a confessional FIR made to a police officer is wholly inadmissible under Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act, or only the part admitting the commission of the offence is barred.
Whether parts of a confessional statement disclosing motive, preparation, or subsequent conduct can be admitted as independent relevant facts.
Whether Section 27 of the Evidence Act permits the admission of any portion of a confessional FIR leading to discovery of facts.
holdings: A confessional statement to a police officer is entirely inadmissible under Section 25 of the Evidence Act, including parts about motive, preparation, or conduct, as the taint of confession attaches to the whole statement.
Sections 24, 25, and 26 bar proof of all incriminating admissions in a confessional statement, not just the admission of the offence, to preserve the sections' efficacy.
Only portions of a confessional FIR that lead to discovery of facts under Section 27, or those identifying the maker, are admissible; the rest is excluded.
doctrines: Exclusion of confessional statements to police
Taint of confession doctrine
Partial admission under Section 27
Constructive custody under Section 27

card.dispute: The assessee and the Income Tax Commissioner disputed whether capital gains from the sale of factory assets were assessable in the year 1948-49, depending on when the sale or transfer occurred.
issues_decided: Whether a sale or transfer of capital assets took place before April 1, 1948, within the meaning of s. 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether delivery of possession of immovable property constitutes a transfer under s. 12B in the absence of a registered conveyance.
Whether capital gains arose in respect of movable assets like furniture and goodwill based on the timing and nature of transfer.
holdings: No sale or transfer of immovable property occurred before April 1, 1948, because title could only pass upon execution and registration of a conveyance.
Delivery of possession alone does not amount to transfer under s. 12B; effective conveyance is required for capital gains to arise.
Title to movable property like furniture can pass by delivery with intent, so capital gains on furniture were assessable; goodwill, being intangible, did not pass separately before April 1, 1948.
doctrines: Doctrine of passing of title in immovable property
Doctrine of constructive transfer versus actual conveyance
Doctrine of accrual of capital gains upon effective transfer

card.dispute: Members of a Malabar tavazhi sued the manager and others for maintenance, claiming that the Chalakkode property belonged to the tavazhi and its income should be considered for maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether the 1st and 4th defendants were managers of the tavazhi properties
Whether there is a presumption under Marumakkathayam law that property acquired in the name of a manager belongs to the tavazhi
Whether the presumption applies to a de facto manager
Whether the appellants proved that the Chalakkode property was self-acquired
holdings: The 1st defendant was the karnavati and the 4th defendant was the de facto manager of the tavazhi properties, thus standing in a fiduciary relationship with its members.

Under Marumakkathayam law, there is a strong presumption that property acquired in the name of a karnavati or karnavan is tarwad or tavazhi property, which stands unrebutted unless disproved by clear evidence.
The presumption extends to a de facto manager who controls the property and its accounts, especially when they fail to produce accounts or prove personal funding.
The appellants failed to rebut the presumption, as no credible evidence showed the Chalakkode property was purchased from private funds; the burden shifted to them and was not discharged.
provisions: Marumakkathayam Law (customary law, no specific statute)
doctrines: Presumption of joint family property in matriarchal systems
Fiduciary duty of tarwad/tavazhi managers
Burden of proof shifting in property disputes under customary law
De facto management triggering legal presumptions

card.dispute: The landholder Ajoy Kumar Mukherjee challenged the Local Board of Barpeta's imposition of a licence fee for holding a market on his land, arguing the tax was beyond the state's legislative power and violated equality under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam Legislature had the competence to impose a tax on markets under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
Whether the tax imposed on the appellant's market violated Article 14 of the Constitution due to discriminatory treatment compared to neighbouring markets.
holdings: The tax under Section 62 of the Assam Local Self Government Act, 1953 is a tax on land used for a market, not on the market or transactions therein, and thus falls within Entry 49 of List II, making it within the state legislature's competence.

The appellant failed to provide sufficient factual evidence to prove discriminatory tax treatment; therefore, the tax rate fixed for his market did not violate Article 14, as the burden of proving discrimination was not discharged.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
Assam Local Self Government Act, 1953, Section 62
Assam Local Self Government Act, 1953, Section 63(3)
doctrines: Legislative competence based on entries in the Seventh Schedule
Burden of proof in alleging violation of Article 14
Tax characterization doctrine: substance over form in determining the nature of a tax

card.dispute: The appellant, who stood as surety for the purchase of cut timber at an auction, challenged his liability to pay the remaining instalments after the timber was destroyed by fire before full payment or formal contract ratification.
issues_decided: Whether the property in the timber passed to the buyer at the time of the auction on 24th December 1956, despite the formal contract being ratified later by the Chief Conservator of Forests.
Whether the reservation of the right to stop removal of timber under Forest Contract Rules implied a reservation of property in the goods until full payment.
Whether the contract could be validly ratified after the subject matter (timber) was destroyed by fire.
holdings: Under Section 20 of the Sale of Goods Act, property in specific goods in a deliverable state passes to the buyer when the contract is made, even if delivery or payment is postponed.

The right of the State to stop removal of timber under Rule 8 does not amount to reservation of property; it is a statutory lien under Section 83 of the Indian Forest Act, not a contractual reservation.

A contract for the sale of goods may be ratified after destruction of the goods if the risk of such loss was inherent in the provisional agreement, especially where the contract contemplates such risks under the rules.
doctrines: Passing of property in unconditional contracts for specific goods
Ratification of acts after loss of subject matter in commercial contracts
Statutory lien under forest laws not equivalent to reservation of ownership

card.dispute: The dispute was between Bhagwan Das, a displaced person and landowner, and the State of Punjab over whether he qualified as a 'small landowner' entitled to evict a tenant under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, despite an increase in the income and value of his land due to improvements after allotment.
issues_decided: Whether a landowner who was a small landholder at the commencement of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, ceases to be one if the value or income of his land increases subsequently due to improvements.
Whether the land can be re-evaluated at the time of a tenant eviction application under Section 14-A based on its current income or yield.
Whether Section 19-F(b) of the Act permits re-evaluation of land for determining status as a small landowner when no new land has been acquired.
holdings: A landowner who was a small landowner at the commencement of the Act remains so unless he acquires additional land; subsequent increase in land value or income does not alter his status.
For determining eligibility under Section 14-A, the land must be evaluated as it stood at the commencement of the Act, not at the time of the eviction application.
Section 19-F(b) allows re-evaluation only for land acquired after commencement of the Act by inheritance, bequest, or gift, not for land whose value increased due to improvements.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)(i)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14-A(1)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19-F(b)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 10-A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19-B
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of land tenure laws in favor of tenant protection
Once a small landowner, always a small landowner unless additional land is acquired
Temporal fixation of land status at the commencement of the Act

card.dispute: The owner of a house sued his occupant for ejectment, arrears of rent, and future mesne profits, while the occupant claimed he was not a tenant but had constructed the house and was to stay until reimbursed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could sustain a decree for ejectment on the ground of licence when the plaintiff had originally claimed ejectment on the basis of tenancy
Whether the appellant occupant was liable to pay future mesne profits after the decree for ejectment
holdings: A decree for ejectment can be upheld on the ground of licence if the evidence shows permissive possession, even if the plaintiff primarily pleaded tenancy, provided the defendant had a fair opportunity to contest the issue.
A defendant who remains in possession after a decree for ejectment is granted must pay future mesne profits or damages for use and occupation at a reasonable rate.
doctrines: Relief on alternate grounds in pleadings
Mesne profits following ejectment decree
Substantial justice over technical pleading requirements

card.dispute: The appellant sought restitution of property sold in execution of an ex-parte decree after that decree was set aside, even though a fresh decree was later passed against him.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to restitution under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure after the ex-parte decree was set aside, despite a subsequent decree being passed against him.
Whether the sale of the appellant's property in execution of the set-aside decree could be upheld when the decree-holder himself was the purchaser.
holdings: A party is entitled to restitution under Section 144 when a decree is set aside, regardless of a subsequent decree being passed against them, as the obligation to restore arises the moment the original decree is reversed.

When a decree-holder purchases property in execution of their own decree and that decree is later set aside, the sale becomes invalid and the decree-holder must restore the property, as they cannot benefit from an erroneous decree.
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution
Principle of equitable restoration upon reversal of decree
Distinction between decree-holder purchaser and bona fide third-party purchaser

card.dispute: The appellants, representing the Udasi sect, challenged the validity of a sale deed of a dharamshala property, claiming it was a wakf and non-transferable, while respondents argued the sale was necessary to prevent total loss of the property.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgage deed of June 1, 1933 was supported by legal necessity and binding on the trust
Whether the sale deed of June 14, 1945 was valid and supported by legal necessity
Whether the decision in an earlier suit (No. 3 of 1943) operated as res judicata
holdings: The mortgage deed of June 1, 1933 was supported by legal necessity as it was incurred to meet pressing financial needs of the trust and recognized over time.
The sale deed of June 14, 1945 was valid and supported by legal necessity because it prevented the total loss of the dharamshala and benefited the trust by saving a portion of the property.
The decision in Suit No. 3 of 1943 did not operate as res judicata because it did not directly adjudicate the same issues or parties in the present suit.
doctrines: Legal necessity in alienation of religious endowment
Manager's power analogous to that of a guardian of an infant heir
Res judicata in suits involving religious institutions

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased property previously declared evacuee property, challenged the Custodian-General's revisional jurisdiction to entertain the State of Uttar Pradesh's application contesting the ownership of the property.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian-General had jurisdiction to entertain a revision application under Section 27 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, regarding an order made under the repealed Ordinance 12 of 1949?
Whether the procedure followed by the Custodian-General in the revision proceedings violated the principles of natural justice?
holdings: The Custodian-General had the power to entertain the revision application because the deeming provisions in Section 58(3) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, deemed actions under the earlier repealed ordinances as if done under the 1950 Act, preserving appellate and revisional jurisdiction.

The revision proceedings were vitiated by a breach of natural justice as the appellants were not given an opportunity to inspect documents or rebut evidence relied upon by the State, and the Custodian-General failed to formally admit additional evidence or allow rejoinder.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 58(3)
Administration of Evacuee Property Central Rules, 1950, Rule 31(9)
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
doctrines: Deeming fiction under statutory continuity provisions
Principles of natural justice in administrative proceedings
Preservation of appellate and revisional jurisdiction despite repeal

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax fought with Kailas Rubber & Co. Ltd. over whether the sale proceeds of old, unproductive rubber trees used for latex production constituted taxable agricultural income or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the sale proceeds of old and unyielding rubber trees grown for latex are capital receipts
Whether the sale proceeds of rubber trees originally purchased as yielding trees but later sold after becoming unproductive are capital receipts
holdings: Sale proceeds of rubber trees that were cultivated for latex and later sold after ceasing to yield are not agricultural income but capital receipts.
The sale of such trees, originally acquired as productive assets but later felled when unproductive, represents realization of capital assets, not revenue.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Definition of agricultural income under tax law

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for possession of agricultural land on redemption of a mortgage, while the defendants claimed they were protected tenants under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the nature of the transaction (mortgage or lease) when the defendant claimed to be a protected tenant under the Act.
Whether the civil court could decide the issue of tenancy without referring it to the Mamlatdar under Section 70(b) of the Act.
Whether the first appellate court could make findings on the mortgage debt after holding that it lacked jurisdiction to determine tenancy status.
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to determine if a defendant is a protected tenant under the Bombay Tenancy Act; such issues must be referred to the Mamlatdar under Section 70(b).
If a defendant raises a tenancy plea in a possession suit, the civil court must stay the suit and refer the issue to the Mamlatdar, not dismiss the suit outright.
A civil court cannot make inconsistent findings by asserting jurisdiction over a mortgage claim while denying jurisdiction over the tenancy issue arising from the same transaction.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70(b)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85A
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of revenue authorities over tenancy disputes
Reference of preliminary issues to administrative authorities
Consistency in jurisdictional findings by civil courts

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of deceased mortgagees, challenged the declaration of mortgaged land as evacuee property on grounds of lack of notice and violation of their mortgagee rights.
issues_decided: Whether notice under Section 7(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, to deceased mortgagees was valid and sufficient
Whether the declaration of the property as evacuee property affected the mortgagee rights of the appellants
Whether the Custodian could take action against the appellants or their tenants in the absence of separation of interests under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951
holdings: Notice issued to deceased persons under Section 7(1) was ineffective, but the Custodian acted within the scope of available information and complied with procedural requirements.

The declaration of property as evacuee property did not affect the mortgagee rights of the appellants, as it only vested the evacuees' equity of redemption in the Custodian, subject to existing mortgagee interests.

The Custodian cannot take action against the appellants or their tenants until the interests are separated under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951, as the property remains encumbered by mortgage rights.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice
Doctrine of separation of interests in composite property
Principle of vested rights subject to encumbrances

card.dispute: The landlord and tenant disputed the standard rent of a cinematograph theatre under the Saurashtra Rent Control Act, including issues about valuation of land and building, rate of return, and possession of parts of the premises.
issues_decided: Whether a second appeal under s. 28 of the Saurashtra Rent Control Act is governed by s. 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the courts below erred in including the full purchase price of land and buildings in cost computation
Whether the courts below correctly applied a 7% return on investment to determine standard rent
Whether deductions should be made from standard rent due to non-delivery of possession of cellar and restaurant space
holdings: A second appeal under s. 28 of the Saurashtra Rent Control Act is subject to the limitations of s. 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the High Court can dismiss it under Order 41, Rule 11 without reappreciating evidence.

The purchaser of land with existing structures intended for demolition may be regarded as having paid for the land and debris value; thus, the entire purchase price may be considered in cost computation, less credit for sale of debris.
The rate of return for standard rent depends on local conditions and multiple factors; a 7% gross return on investment was not an error in principle for a cinema theatre in Bhavnagar.

Non-delivery of possession of leased parts affects tenant's remedies but is not relevant to fixing standard rent; however, if the cellar was not part of the tenancy, Rs. 100 should be deducted from the standard rent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 11
doctrines: Second appeal limited to substantial questions of law
Standard rent determination based on composite factors including location and use
Valuation of property for rent control purposes includes land and debris where old structures are demolished
Possession issues affect tenancy rights but not standard rent fixation under rent control law

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and The Panbari Tea Co. Ltd fought over whether annual instalments of premium received under a lease were taxable as revenue receipt or capital gains.
issues_decided: Whether the annual instalments paid as premium under a lease constitute revenue receipt or capital gain
Whether the form of payment (in instalments) affects the character of premium as capital receipt
Whether the substance or nomenclature of the transaction determines the nature of payment under a lease
holdings: Periodical payments for continuous enjoyment of lease benefits are rent (revenue receipt), while price paid for transfer of right to enjoy property is premium (capital gain).
Premium, even when paid in instalments, remains a capital receipt if it is consideration for transfer of a right to enjoy property.
The substance of the transaction, not the label used, determines whether payment is premium or rent; nomenclature is relevant but not conclusive.
Where parties are knowledgeable and use terms 'premium' and 'rent' deliberately, and economic conditions do not suggest camouflage, payments should be treated as per their designated nature.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Intention of parties in contractual interpretation

card.dispute: The Bombay Municipal Corporation challenged the validity of delegating its commissioner's quasi-judicial powers to evict tenants under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, arguing that such delegation was proper despite being subject to the commissioner's control and revision.
issues_decided: Whether the delegation of quasi-judicial powers under Sections 105B to 105E of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act by the Commissioner is valid when such delegation is made subject to his control and revision.
Whether the phrase 'under the Commissioner's control and subject to his revision' in Section 68 invalidates the delegation of judicial or quasi-judicial functions.
holdings: The amendment to Section 68, including the delegation of powers under Sections 105B to 105E, shows a legislative intent to allow delegation of quasi-judicial powers, and such delegation is valid when permitted by law.

The phrases 'under the Commissioner's control' and 'subject to his revision' in Section 68 refer to administrative oversight, not interference with the delegate's decision-making, and thus do not invalidate the delegation of quasi-judicial powers.
provisions: Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, Sections 105B to 105E
doctrines: Delegation of quasi-judicial powers
Reasonable construction of statutory language
Administrative control vs. judicial independence in delegation

card.dispute: The mortgagors challenged the mortgage debt's non-scaling under the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, arguing the mortgagee's interest was transferred to a family charity without valuable consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of a usufructuary mortgagee's interest to a family charity was for valuable consideration within the meaning of s. 9-A(10)(ii)(b) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act
Whether a transfer in discharge of a pre-existing obligation constitutes valuable consideration
holdings: A transfer of mortgage interest to a family charity in discharge of a prior obligation to pay a sum to the charity constitutes valuable consideration under s. 9-A(10)(ii)(b).
Forbearance by the charity from enforcing the family’s obligation to pay a dedicated sum is sufficient detriment to constitute valuable consideration under the law.
provisions: Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938 (as amended by Act XV of 1943 and Act XXXII of 1943), Section 9-A(10)(ii)(b)
doctrines: Valuable consideration
Forbearance as consideration
Transfer in discharge of obligation

card.dispute: Landlords sued tenants for ejectment over unauthorized structures; tenants removed structures during litigation, raising whether ejectment could still be granted.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant remains liable for ejectment under the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, after removing unauthorized structures during the pendency of the suit.
Whether the repeal of the 1952 Act by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the introduction of Section 14(11), constituted a radical departure requiring application of the new law to pending cases.
holdings: A tenant who removes unauthorized structures during the pendency of an ejectment suit may be granted relief if reasonable time to remedy the breach was not given, analogous to relief against forfeiture under Section 114-A of the Transfer of Property Act.
The introduction of Section 14(11) in the 1958 Act was not a radical departure but a clarificatory and slightly modificatory provision, so pending cases continued to be governed by the 1952 Act.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1) proviso (k)
Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 57(2) and Section 14(1) proviso (k) and Section 14(11)
doctrines: Relief against forfeiture
Continuation of proceedings under repealed law
Interpretation of transitional provisions
Clarificatory vs. radical statutory amendment

card.dispute: One of two joint managers of a religious endowment (muth) sought court directions to sell cattle and cultivation rights, which the other manager opposed, leading to a dispute over whether the court had jurisdiction under the scheme or was barred by Section 92(1)(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the District Judge had jurisdiction under the scheme to direct the sale of trust property without a fresh suit under Section 92 of the CPC.
Whether Section 92(1)(f) of the CPC bars court directions for the sale of trust property when such power is conferred by a scheme settled under Section 92.
holdings: A scheme settled under Section 92 of the CPC may include a provision allowing managers to seek court directions for the administration of the trust, and such applications do not require a fresh suit under Section 92.

Section 92(1)(f) does not restrict the ordinary administrative powers of trustees or managers to sell or dispose of trust property; it only governs cases where court authorization is otherwise needed due to restrictions in the trust deed or exceptional circumstances.
doctrines: Ordinary administration of trust doctrine
Scheme modification under court supervision
Public trust protection from frivolous litigation

card.dispute: Landlords and tenants contested whether unauthorized structures erected by tenants warranted ejectment under rent control laws, specifically interpreting the first proviso to section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, in light of prior legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the first proviso to section 57(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 applies to pending proceedings initiated under the earlier 1952 Act.
Whether the addition of section 14(11) in the 1958 Act constitutes a radical departure or a clarification/modification of the 1952 Act regarding tenant ejectment for unauthorized constructions.
holdings: The first proviso to section 57(2) applies only if the 1958 Act merely clarifies or modifies the 1952 Act; otherwise, the old law governs pending cases.

The introduction of section 14(11) in the 1958 Act is a clarificatory and slight modification of the prior law, allowing relief to tenants who remove unauthorized structures within reasonable time, consistent with principles analogous to section 114A of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1) and (11)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(k)
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Pending proceedings governed by old law unless new law is clarificatory
Relief against forfeiture for remediable breaches under lease law

card.dispute: The appellants sued to declare their title to a property and that certain deeds were void, but did not seek possession, which was under attachment under Section 145 of the CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for declaration of title is barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act when possession is not claimed and the property is under attachment under Section 145 of the CrPC.
Whether the proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act requires a claim for possession when the defendant is not in possession and cannot deliver it.
holdings: A suit for declaration of title is competent without claiming possession when the property is under attachment under Section 145 CrPC, as the defendant is not in possession and cannot deliver it.
The further relief contemplated by the proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act must be against the defendant; it does not apply when possession is with a magistrate not party to the suit.
It is not necessary to claim possession in a declaratory suit when the property is in custodia legis, such as under Section 145 CrPC attachment.
doctrines: Custodia legis
Competence of declaratory suits
Proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax contested the taxability of the goodwill amount received by Mugneeram Bangur & Co upon the sale of its land development business as a going concern to a company promoted by its partners.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was engaged in the business of purely buying and selling land, making the profit from sale of land taxable as income.
Whether any part of the slump price in a going concern sale is attributable to stock-in-trade (land) and thus taxable as business profit.
holdings: The assessee was not merely buying and selling land but was engaged in land development, which distinguishes it from a trading business focused solely on land sales.

In a slump sale of a going concern, no part of the sale price is taxable as income if no portion is attributable to stock-in-trade, especially when no independent valuation of assets was made at the time of sale.
provisions: Income-tax Act, 1922, Section 2(1)(bb) (as relevant to definition of income and profits of business)
doctrines: Slump sale doctrine
Corporate veil in tax transactions
Distinction between capital appreciation and trading profit
Realisation sale vs ordinary trading sale

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Straw Products Ltd. disputed whether depreciation 'actually allowed' under the Bhopal Income-tax Act included depreciation that would have been allowed had the company not been exempted from tax under an agreement with the Ruler.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'depreciation actually allowed' in the Taxation Laws (Merged States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1949, includes depreciation that was not actually granted due to tax exemption?
Whether the 1962 Amendment Order retrospectively clarifies the meaning of 'depreciation actually allowed'?
Whether the High Court could consider the 1962 Amendment Order when deciding a reference arising from earlier assessment years?
Whether the assessee qualified as a person 'exempted from tax' under the Explanation added by the 1962 Order?
holdings: The term 'depreciation actually allowed' does not include depreciation that was never allowed; however, the 1962 Amendment Order retrospectively deems it to include such depreciation if exemption was due to an agreement with a Ruler.
The 1962 Amendment Order has retrospective effect and applies to assessments from 1949 onward, including the years 1952-53 and 1953-54.
A court or tribunal may apply a law amended with retrospective effect when deciding a reference, provided the question is framed broadly enough and no new facts need to be investigated.
A company exempted from taxation under an agreement with a Ruler qualifies as 'exempted from tax' under the Explanation, even if it was not formally assessed under the prior State law.
provisions: Taxation Laws (Merged States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1949, Paragraph 2
Taxation Laws (Merged States) (Removal of Difficulties) (Amendment) Order, 1962, Explanation to Paragraph 2
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutory amendments
Deeming provisions in tax law
Principle of legislative intent in interpretation of tax statutes
Amendment of law during pendency of appeal

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax challenged the assessment of surplus income of a Muslim wakf, arguing it should not be taxed in the hands of trustees under Section 41 of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether Section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 applies to the surplus income received by the managing trustees of a Muslim wakf.
Whether the Nattamaigars received the income in their own right or on behalf of the beneficiaries (kasupangudars).
Whether the properties of the wakf vested in the Nattamaigars or only the management and administration did.
holdings: Section 41 applies where income is received by managers or trustees on behalf of others, regardless of whether legal vesting occurs.
The Nattamaigars were not beneficial owners but managers receiving income on behalf of the kasupangudars for distribution in definite shares.
The scheme did not vest property in the Nattamaigars; it only vested management and administration, consistent with Muslim law where property vests in God.
doctrines: Managerial vs. beneficial interest
Non-applicability of English trust doctrine to Muslim wakf
Doctrine of vesting not determinative under Section 41

card.dispute: The appellant Dr. G.H. Grant and the State of Bihar disputed over who was entitled to receive compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, after the land vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had the authority to make a reference under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act after making an award under Section 11.
Whether the State, having acquired title to the land after the award, could be considered a 'person interested' entitled to claim compensation.
Whether a dispute over entitlement to compensation arising after the award can be referred to court under Section 30.
holdings: The Collector has the power under Section 30 to refer disputes about entitlement to compensation even after making an award under Section 11, as the powers under Sections 18 and 30 are distinct.
The State became entitled to compensation upon vesting of land under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, despite not being interested at the time of the award.
A dispute over who is entitled to compensation, arising due to statutory transfer of title after the award, is referable to court under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act.
doctrines: Statutory vesting of title
Reference of disputes on entitlement to compensation
Distinction between apportionment and final adjudication of compensation rights

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and P.K.N. Co. Ltd. fought over whether profits from the sale of immovable properties by the company were taxable as business income under the Indian Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the company was carrying on a business in real estate so as to make profits from property sales taxable as revenue income
Whether the nature of transactions in immovable property depends on the company's memorandum of association or its actual conduct
Whether incidental sales of properties indicate an intention to carry on trade in real estate
holdings: Profits from the sale of immovable properties are not taxable as business income if the primary object of the company was not real estate trading but plantation and rubber production.
The mere presence of powers to deal with property in a company's memorandum does not determine the nature of income; the substance of transactions and intention are what matter.
Occasional and incidental sales of properties due to necessity or management difficulties do not transform investment into a business of dealing in real estate.
doctrines: Substance over form
Incidental vs. dominant purpose
Nature of transaction based on factual circumstances

card.dispute: The appellant, Dwarka Nath, challenged the decree of the High Court that declared his adoption invalid, while the respondents contested the validity of the adoption on grounds of lack of prior authority from the deceased husband and absence of valid consent under the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912.
issues_decided: Whether the consent of the Court of Wards under Section 37 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, renders an adoption immune from challenge in a civil court on grounds of lack of authority under personal law?
Whether the findings of the Court of Wards regarding the husband's authority to adopt are binding on a civil court?
Whether oral statements made 27 years after the alleged event could be admitted under Sections 32(7) and 157 of the Indian Evidence Act to corroborate the authority to adopt?
Whether the suit was barred by delay or acquiescence?
holdings: The consent of the Court of Wards under Section 37 does not cure defects in adoption arising from lack of authority under personal law; civil courts retain jurisdiction to examine such questions independently.
The conclusion of the Court of Wards on the question of authority to adopt is not binding on a civil court, which may independently determine the issue according to personal law.

Statements made 27 years after the alleged event before the Court of Wards are inadmissible under Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act, as they were not made at or about the time of the fact and the Court of Wards is not an authority legally competent to investigate such facts for the purpose of Section 157.
The suit was not barred by delay or acquiescence, as the respondent had consistently challenged prior adoptions and had not accepted the validity of the adoption in question.
provisions: U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, Section 37
U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, Section 53
doctrines: Civil court jurisdiction not ousted by administrative consent
Primacy of personal law in adoption matters
Limited scope of Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act
Rule against collateral estoppel in administrative findings

card.dispute: The Regional Settlement Commissioner appealed against the High Court's decision that Rule 19 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, applies to agricultural property held by a joint Hindu family in West Pakistan.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 19 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, applies to claims for compensation in respect of agricultural land owned by a joint Hindu family?
Whether Chapter IV of the Rules, including Rule 19, is inapplicable to agricultural land because Chapter VIII specifically deals with such claims?
holdings: Rule 19 applies to agricultural land claims by joint Hindu families, as its language is general and not restricted to non-agricultural property.

Chapter IV rules, including Rule 19, are not overridden by Chapter VIII; they serve different purposes—Chapter IV determines the unit of assessment, while Chapter VIII governs compensation calculation for that unit.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 19
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 20
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Chapter IV
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Chapter VIII
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 5
doctrines: Principle of harmonious construction
General words in statutory rules are to be given their full meaning unless restricted by context
Special provisions for joint families in compensation schemes

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant for default in rent, and the sub-tenant claimed protection under the Rent Control Act as a deemed tenant after the original tenancy ended.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-lessee can acquire tenant rights under Section 13(2) of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950 without the landlord's consent to sub-letting when the sub-letting is by a tenant of the first degree
Whether the clause 'and the sub-lease is binding on the landlord' in Section 13(2) applies to both classes of sub-tenants defined in Section 13(1)
Whether sub-letting in violation of the lease agreement bars the sub-lessee from acquiring rights under Section 13(2)
holdings: A sub-lessee from a tenant of the first degree acquires tenant rights under Section 13(2) even without the landlord's consent to sub-letting, as such consent is not a condition precedent for the first class of sub-tenancies.

The requirement that 'the sub-lease is binding on the landlord' in Section 13(2) applies only to sub-tenancies created by a tenant inferior to the tenant of the first degree, not to those created by a tenant of the first degree.

Section 13(2) protects sub-lessees even if the sub-letting violates the lease agreement, as the statute confers rights independently of contractual validity, provided the tenancy was lawfully determined.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 12(1)(c)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 13(2)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1948, Section 11(3)
doctrines: Statutory protection of sub-tenants
Deemed tenancy
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Distinction between classes of sub-tenancies

card.dispute: Harbhajan Singh challenged the allotment of land under the East Punjab Consolidation Act, leading to a dispute over whether the Director could review his own earlier order dismissing the revision application.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government or the Director had the power to review an order passed under Section 42 of the East Punjab (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1951.
Whether the Director could legally pass an order on August 29, 1958, allowing the revision application after having already dismissed it on April 3, 1958.
holdings: The Director had no statutory power to review his own order dated April 3, 1958, dismissing the revision application under Section 42, as the Act did not confer express review powers.
The order dated August 29, 1958, allowing the application, was ultra vires and without jurisdiction, as it amounted to an unauthorized review of a final order.
provisions: East Punjab (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1951, Section 42
doctrines: Principle of finality of quasi-judicial orders
Statutory power required for review
Ultra vires doctrine
No inherent power to review in absence of statutory authority

card.dispute: The dispute was between the petitioner, representing a village (Dharmajigudem), and the Government of Andhra Pradesh over the location of a primary health centre, which the government ultimately directed to be located in another village (Lingapalem) based on a Panchayat Samithi resolution.
issues_decided: Whether the government's order of March 7, 1962, cancelling the Panchayat Samithi's resolution was made under Section 62 of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, and whether it was validly passed.
Whether the government had the power under Section 72 of the Act to review its earlier order dated March 7, 1962.
Whether the government's order of April 18, 1963, was vitiated by failure to give notice to the affected village representatives.
holdings: The order of March 7, 1962, was made under Section 62 of the Act and was invalid because it was passed without giving the Panchayat Samithi an opportunity for explanation as required by Section 62(2).
The government had no power under Section 72 of the Act to review an order made under Section 62, as Section 72 does not confer review jurisdiction over quasi-judicial orders passed under Section 62.

The order of April 18, 1963, was invalid because it was made without giving notice to the representatives of Dharmajigudem village, who were prejudicially affected, in violation of the proviso to Section 72(1) of the Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, Section 62
Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, Section 72
Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, Rule 6
Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959, Rule 7
doctrines: Functus officio
Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Rule of statutory interpretation (distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial powers)
Doctrine of vires and jurisdictional error

card.dispute: The appellant stepmother claimed full ownership of her deceased husband's properties under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, challenging the execution of a decree in favor of respondents who claimed to be nearer heirs.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 has retrospective operation to apply to a male Hindu who died before the Act came into force.
Whether Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 confers full ownership on a female Hindu who was in possession of the property without any legal title.
holdings: Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not operate retrospectively; it applies only when succession opens after the Act's commencement.

Section 14(1) does not confer title on a female Hindu who had no vestige of title or lawful possession; it only converts a limited estate into full ownership, not validating possession by a trespasser.
doctrines: Non-retrospectivity of statutory succession laws
Conversion of limited estate to absolute ownership under Section 14
No title by mere possession without lawful acquisition

card.dispute: The defendants challenged the validity and fact of Muddappa's adoption by Eramma (Sr.) to her deceased husband Channe Gowda (Sr.), and whether she had authority to make such an adoption under Mysore law.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of Muddappa by Eramma (Sr.) was factually proved;
Whether Eramma (Sr.) had the legal authority to adopt a son to her deceased husband under the Hindu Law (Women's Rights) Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933).
holdings: The adoption was factually proved by credible evidence, including the testimony of the adoptive mother and independent witnesses, and the contemporaneous adoption deed.

A widow is presumed to have authority to adopt unless the husband expressly prohibited it in writing; the presumption under Section 9(1) of the Mysore Hindu Law (Women's Rights) Act, 1933 is rebuttable only by proof of such express prohibition, which was not established here.
provisions: Hindu Law (Women's Rights) Act, 1933 (Mysore Act 10 of 1933), Section 9(1)
doctrines: Presumption of authority to adopt under statutory law
Rebuttable presumption in adoption cases
Giving and taking as essential to adoption

card.dispute: The respondents, interested in a public temple, sued the appellant, who managed the temple's affairs, seeking his removal, an account of trust funds, and a scheme; the dispute centered on whether the appellant was liable to pay simple or compound interest on uninvested trust funds.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was liable to pay compound interest on trust funds used in his business
Whether the rule of damdupat limits interest payable by a trustee on uninvested trust funds
holdings: The appellant was not liable to pay compound interest because it was not proven that he used trust funds in his personal business.

A trustee who retains trust funds uninvested for a long period is liable to pay simple interest at an equitable rate (4% per annum), and the rule of damdupat does not apply to such equitable interest.
provisions: Hindu Law as interpreted in Colebrooke's Digest
General principles of equity regarding trustee liability
doctrines: Rule of damdupat
Equitable liability of trustees for interest on uninvested trust funds
Distinction between debtor-creditor relationship and trustee-cestui que trust relationship

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment of the tenant, who claimed protection under tenancy laws and argued that civil courts lacked jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 43C of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, as amended in 1956, protects tenants in suits filed before the amendment but not finally decided?
Whether civil courts have jurisdiction to decide questions regarding tenancy status under the Act, or must refer such issues to the Revenue Court?
holdings: The proviso to Section 43C restores protection to tenants who were protected under the original 1948 Act, even if that protection was removed by the 1952 Amendment, provided the suit was pending when the 1956 Amendment came into force.
Civil courts lack jurisdiction to decide questions about tenancy or protected tenancy under the Act; such issues must be referred to the Mamlatdar as Revenue Court under Sections 70 and 85.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 43C (proviso)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1956 (Act 13 of 1956)
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of Revenue Court
Proviso as an exception to substantive provisions
Referential jurisdiction in civil suits involving tenancy issues

card.dispute: The Income-Tax Officer sought to treat a distribution of Rs. 850,000 by a company in liquidation as taxable dividend, while the liquidators argued it included non-taxable capital gains from agricultural land and that 'current year' profits were not 'dividends'.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in issuing a writ of prohibition when an alternative remedy was available under the Income-tax Act.

Whether profits earned by a company in the period between the end of the previous year and the commencement of liquidation ('current profits') are 'accumulated profits' and thus deemed 'dividend' under s. 2(6-A)(c).
Whether capital gains from the sale of agricultural land, which are not chargeable to tax in the hands of the company, can be treated as 'dividend' when distributed during liquidation.
holdings: The High Court has discretion under Article 226 to issue a writ even if an alternative remedy exists, and its exercise will not be interfered with unless arbitrary.
Profits earned by a company after the end of the previous year but before liquidation are included in 'accumulated profits' and are deemed 'dividend' under s. 2(6-A)(c) as amended, and thus taxable.

Capital gains from the sale of agricultural land, which are excluded from 'capital assets' under s. 2(4A) and not chargeable as capital gains, do not form part of 'accumulated profits' and hence their distribution is not taxable as 'dividend' under s. 12-B.
doctrines: Deemed dividend doctrine under s. 2(6-A)(c)
Principle of legislative override of judicial precedent
Distinction between capital appreciation and revenue profits
Doctrine of ejusdem generis in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant, a managing trustee, contested whether agricultural income-tax assessments for 1954-55 and 1955-56 should have been made under Section 12 or Section 13 of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1939.
issues_decided: Whether the assessment of agricultural income-tax should have been made under Section 12 or Section 13 of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1939.
Whether the managing trustee holding trust property partly for himself and partly for beneficiaries falls under Section 13 of the Act.
holdings: Section 12 applies when a person holds agricultural land partly for their own benefit and partly for beneficiaries, and the trustee in this case fell under this provision.
Section 13 applies only to common managers, receivers, or administrators acting on behalf of jointly interested persons, not to trustees under a private trust deed.
The trust deed vested property in trustees, and the managing trustee did not qualify as a 'common manager' or 'receiver' under Section 13.
doctrines: Literal and contextual interpretation of statutory provisions
Principle of excluding one provision when another specifically applies (expressio unius est exclusio alterius)
Intention of the settlor in trust creation determines nature of property holding

card.dispute: The assessee, a dealer in iron scrap and hardware, was taxed on profit from selling a jute press he had purchased; he challenged whether this profit arose from a trading venture and was thus taxable.
issues_decided: Whether the profit from the sale of a jute press by the assessee constituted income from an adventure in the nature of trade under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether an isolated transaction of purchasing and selling property, with a profit motive, can be presumed to be a trading venture.
holdings: A profit motive alone does not make an asset's sale taxable as income; an accretion to capital is not income merely because it was expected to yield profit.
An isolated transaction unconnected to the assessee's regular business, without evidence of trading intent or commercial conduct, does not constitute an adventure in the nature of trade.
doctrines: Adventure in the nature of trade
Profit motive not decisive for taxability
Isolated transaction doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant, a former occupant of requisitioned premises, challenged the Collector's order directing him to vacate the premises after de-requisitioning, claiming tenancy rights against the landlord.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector, as the requisitioning authority, could lawfully direct the allottee to vacate the premises upon de-requisitioning.
Whether the appellant became a tenant of the landlord upon de-requisitioning due to prior conduct or statutory provisions.
Whether the requisitioning of 'premises' was valid under the Act, given the definition of 'land'.
holdings: The Collector had the statutory authority under Section 9(7) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 to direct the allottee to vacate and deliver possession upon de-requisitioning.
The appellant did not acquire tenancy rights against the landlord merely by occupation during requisition; such private arrangements do not bind the Collector or affect de-requisitioning.
The term 'land' in the Act includes 'premises', and the requisition was valid; the argument was not raised in time and was disallowed.
provisions: Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948, Section 2(2), Section 2(3), Section 4, Section 5, Section 6, Section 8, Section 8AA, Section 9, Section 11, Section 15
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 4
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of de-requisitioning powers
Non-creation of tenancy rights by operation of requisition laws
Finality of administrative action in de-requisitioning

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the respondent's election to the State Legislative Assembly, claiming the respondent was not an Indian citizen under Article 173 of the Constitution as he was a Nepali citizen.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was a citizen of India under Article 5(c) of the Constitution at the time of the election.
Whether the respondent had acquired a domicile of choice in India by the end of 1949.
Whether ownership of property in Nepal and use of a royal title affected the claim to Indian domicile.
holdings: A person can acquire Indian citizenship under Article 5(c) by establishing a domicile of choice in India before 1950, through residence and a genuine intention to permanently reside.
The intention to permanently reside in India (animus manendi) can be inferred from a person's conduct, including property acquisition, family settlement, and social and political activities in India.
Owning property in Nepal and using a royal title do not negate a claim of Indian domicile if the person's actual conduct shows a settled intention to reside permanently in India.
Conduct and circumstances before and after a material date are relevant to determine domicile at that time.
doctrines: Domicile of choice
Animus manendi
Relevance of post-facto conduct in determining intention

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the state government's notification declaring a fort wall within his property as a protected monument under a Travancore-era regulation, arguing it infringed his fundamental right to property and that the regulation was impliedly repealed by later central laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Travancore Ancient Monuments Preservation Regulation (1 of 1112/M.E.) was impliedly repealed by the extension of the Central Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 to Travancore-Cochin.
Whether the Central Acts of 1951 (LXXI of 1951) and 1958 (XXIV of 1958) impliedly repealed the State Regulation in respect of the monument in question.
Whether the fort wall qualifies as an 'ancient monument' under the State Regulation or falls under 'archaeological sites or remains' in the Concurrent List.
holdings: The Central Act of 1904 did not declare any monument to be of national importance, so it could not occupy the field under Entry 67 of List I; thus, the State Regulation under Entry 12 of List II remained valid and was not impliedly repealed.

Central Acts LXXI of 1951 and XXIV of 1958 applied only to monuments specified in their Schedules or declared of national importance; since the fort wall was not so declared, these Acts did not displace the State Regulation.

The fort wall is an 'ancient monument' as it is a surviving structure from a former period, not an archaeological site for study; thus, it falls under Entry 12 of List II, and the State had authority to notify it under its Regulation.
provisions: Travancore Ancient Monuments Preservation Regulation (1 of 1112/M.E.-1936-37)
Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 (Central Act VII of 1904)
Ancient and Historical Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Declaration of National Importance) Act, 1951 (Central Act LXXI of 1951)
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 (Central Act XXIV of 1958)
Part B States (Laws) Act, 1951 (Act III of 1951), Section 3
Constitution of India, Entry 67 (List I), Entry 12 (List II), Entry 40 (List III), Article 363
doctrines: Implied repeal doctrine
Doctrine of occupied field
Principle of constitutional demarcation between legislative lists
Distinction between 'ancient monument' and 'archaeological site or remains'

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the rejection of his application for a court reference to claim higher compensation for land acquired under the West Bengal Land Act, arguing it was filed within a reasonable time despite being beyond the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8(2) of the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, read with Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, prescribes a limitation period for filing an application for reference to court for enhanced compensation.
Whether the phrase 'in respect of any reference made to the Court' in Section 8(2) applies only after a reference is made or also to applications seeking such a reference.
holdings: Section 8(2) of the West Bengal Act, read with Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applies to applications for reference and prescribes a limitation period; thus, the appellant's application filed beyond six months from the award date was time-barred.

The phrase 'in respect of any reference made to the Court' in Section 8(2) includes applications seeking a reference, not just proceedings after a reference is made, thereby incorporating the limitation under Section 18(2) of the Central Act.
provisions: West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 8(2)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation (mutatis mutandis application of central law provisions)
Limitation period implied by statutory incorporation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a mortgage deed and the right of the lender to sue, where the deed was executed in the name of a benamidar and the lender attested the deed.
issues_decided: Whether a lender of money, who is not a party to the mortgage deed, can validly attest the deed.
Whether the actual lender of money, as the beneficial owner, can maintain a suit on a mortgage executed in the name of a benamidar.
holdings: A person who is not a party to a mortgage deed but has lent the money can validly attest the deed, as attestation requires only witnesses who are not parties to the deed, even if they are part of the transaction.

The actual lender of money, being the beneficial owner, is entitled to sue on a mortgage deed executed in the name of a benamidar, as the right to sue vests in the person who provided the consideration.
doctrines: Attestation by non-party to deed
Benami transaction and right to sue
Beneficial ownership entitles enforcement of rights

card.dispute: Landlords sued tenants for ejectment after obtaining permission from the Commissioner in revision, but the High Court held the permission invalid; landlords appealed.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3(4) and 16 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 bar civil court jurisdiction over challenges to permission orders granted under Section 3(3)
Whether the Commissioner's permission under Section 3(3) was invalid due to lack of jurisdiction
holdings: Sections 3(4) and 16 bar civil courts from entertaining challenges to the correctness or propriety of permission orders, unless the order is wholly invalid or a nullity due to violation of mandatory provisions or natural justice.

The Commissioner’s revisional power under Section 3(3) is not limited to jurisdictional errors; it includes correcting illegality, material irregularity, or wrongful refusal to act, and thus the permission granted was valid.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(3)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(4)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 16
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction requires clear statutory language and adequate alternative remedy
Orders violating mandatory statutory conditions or principles of natural justice are nullities and challengeable in civil courts
Revisional jurisdiction not confined to jurisdictional defects but extends to illegality and material irregularity

card.dispute: The appellant, appointed as manager of evacuee shops, challenged his removal and claimed ownership, while the Deputy Custodian sought to cancel his appointment and reallocate the shops.
issues_decided: Whether the Deputy Custodian had the power to cancel the appellant's appointment as manager under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether the order of removal was invalid due to being issued under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954
Whether the appellant had a legal right to allotment and sale of the evacuee shops based on prior communications
holdings: The power to appoint a manager under Section 10(2)(b) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 includes the implied power to remove or suspend, especially when read with Section 16 of the General Clauses Act.
An order by a public authority is valid if made within its competence under any law, even if incorrectly cited; substance prevails over form.
Mere communication indicating in-principle allotment does not create a legal right to ownership or possession in absence of finalized terms or contract.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(2)(b)
doctrines: Implied power doctrine
Substance over form
No mandamus for contractual obligations

card.dispute: The alienee of undivided shares in a Hindu joint family property sued for partition and possession, but the defendants argued the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for partition and possession by an alienee of undivided joint family property is governed by Article 144 of the Limitation Act
From when the period of limitation begins to run in such a suit
Whether symbolic delivery of possession by court in execution proceedings breaks adverse possession
Whether the alienee was entitled to a 4/5th share or only a 2/3rd share in the joint family property
holdings: A suit by an alienee for partition and possession of a coparcener's share falls under Article 144 of the Limitation Act, as the primary relief is for possession of the alienated share.
Limitation begins to run from the date the alienee becomes entitled to sue, which is when possession of co-parceners becomes adverse—here, from the date of purchase of the undivided share.
Symbolic delivery of possession by court to the alienee, even if irregular, is legally effective to break continuity of adverse possession by co-parceners.
The alienee is not entitled to a share belonging to a coparcener not included in the sale; thus, the alienee could not claim the share of a son born before sale but not made a party to execution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rules 33(2) and 96
doctrines: Adverse possession of an undivided interest in joint family property
Alienee does not become a coparcener but has an equity to enforce partition
Symbolic possession can interrupt adverse possession if lawfully granted
Rule of accrual of cause of action in partition suits by alienees

card.dispute: Martin Burn Ltd. challenged the Corporation of Calcutta's valuation of its premises for municipal rates, arguing the wrong method was used and the valuation was excessive.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the power to remand the case for valuation by the Court of Small Causes after the time limit under s. 131(2)(b) had expired
Whether the case amounted to a cancellation of valuation under s. 131(2)(b) or a revision under s. 147
Whether the High Court’s remand order was beyond the scope of the appellant’s objection under s. 139
holdings: The High Court could lawfully remand the case to the Court of Small Causes for valuation when the Executive Officer could no longer act due to the expiry of the time limit.
The case falls under revision under s. 147, not cancellation under s. 131(2)(b), so the revised valuation will take effect retrospectively for the full period.
The remand was within the scope of the appeal as the objection challenged the valuation itself, not merely the method, and the court could reassess the quantum.
provisions: Indian Limitation Act, 1908, Parts II and III
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of administrative valuation subject to statutory appeal
Doctrine of retroactive effect of revised valuation under municipal law
Principle of effective remedy when statutory authority cannot act due to time bar

card.dispute: The appellants, acquitted by a Magistrate of certain offences, challenged the High Court's order setting aside the acquittal and directing a retrial for a more serious offence under Section 467 IPC which required trial by the Court of Session.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate acted within jurisdiction by trying the appellants for lesser offences while ignoring a prima facie serious offence under Section 467 IPC over which he had no jurisdiction?
Whether the High Court had the power under the Code of Criminal Procedure to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when a serious charge triable exclusively by the Court of Session was omitted?
Whether the High Court could direct framing of a charge under Section 467 IPC even though it was not mentioned in the complaint?
holdings: A Magistrate must not selectively try only those charges within his jurisdiction while ignoring a main, serious offence over which he lacks jurisdiction; he must frame a charge under Section 467 IPC and commit the case to the Court of Session if the evidence so discloses.

The High Court has jurisdiction under Section 423 CrPC to set aside an acquittal and order a retrial when a Magistrate improperly omits a serious charge triable exclusively by the Court of Session, even if the trial on other charges was with jurisdiction.
The High Court can direct the framing of a charge under Section 467 IPC even if not mentioned in the complaint, provided the evidence on record prima facie supports such an offence.
doctrines: Proper judicial jurisdiction based on nature of offence
High Court's supervisory and appellate jurisdiction over acquittals
Duty of Magistrate to commit cases to Sessions when serious offences are disclosed
Prima facie case determining jurisdictional obligations

card.dispute: The petitioner firm claimed a fundamental right to pluck and trade tendu leaves under a pre-existing agreement, challenging the Madhya Pradesh State's monopoly over tendu leaf trade established by a new law.
issues_decided: Whether the earlier Supreme Court decision in favor of the petitioner operated as res judicata against the State under Article 32 of the Constitution.
Whether the right to pluck tendu leaves constituted a 'right to property' protected under the Constitution.
Whether the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, extinguished the petitioner’s rights under its agreement with the former estate proprietor.
holdings: The earlier decision does not operate as res judicata because the cause of action under the new statute is distinct and involves different legal circumstances.
A right to pluck tendu leaves does not amount to a 'right to property' before the leaves are severed from the tree; it is merely a contractual licence, not a proprietary right.

The Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, grants the State a monopoly over purchase and transport of tendu leaves, thereby extinguishing prior contractual rights not expressly saved by the law.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964 (M.P. Act 29 of 1964), Section 5
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act
doctrines: Res judicata
State monopoly under regulatory legislation
Distinction between licence and property right
Doctrine of implied repeal and legislative override

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Commissioner's declaration that a temple was a public excepted temple, arguing it was a private family temple, and sought to set aside the order without impleading the public as parties.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Section 64(2) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act requires the public to be impleaded as parties under Order I Rule 8 of the Civil Procedure Code.
Whether the Commissioner's decision declaring a temple a 'public excepted temple' can be challenged in court without joining members of the public as defendants.
holdings: A suit under Section 64(2) of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act does not require the public to be impleaded as parties, as it is not a suit of the nature contemplated by Order I Rule 8 of the Civil Procedure Code.
The Commissioner represents the public interest in religious endowments, and individual members of the public have no locus standi; thus, they need not be joined as parties in such suits.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952, Section 6(5)
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952, Section 6(13)
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952, Section 54
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1952, Section 64
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 8
doctrines: Locus standi
Representative litigation
Statutory interpretation
Public interest in religious endowments

card.dispute: The mortgagee's successors challenged the validity of a redemption proceeding under the U.P. Agriculturists' Relief Act after the land was vested in the state under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the pendency of a proceeding under the U.P. Agriculturists' Relief Act was affected by its repeal via the 1953 Amending Act, deemed effective from 1 July 1952.
Whether the jurisdiction of the Munsif's Court to decide the redemption application was ousted by the Zamindari Abolition Act or its amendments.
holdings: Pending legal proceedings under the U.P. Agriculturists' Relief Act were not invalidated by its retrospective repeal, as Section 6 of the U.P. General Clauses Act preserves rights and proceedings commenced before repeal.

The jurisdiction of the Munsif's Court continued despite the Abolition Act, especially because Section 23 of the 1956 Amending Act explicitly saved pending proceedings from being affected by legislative changes.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1956, Section 23
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1953, Section 1(2) and Section 67
doctrines: Doctrine of saving of pending proceedings
Doctrine of retrospectivity and its limits
Preservation of jurisdiction under general clauses acts
Legislative intent to continue proceedings despite repeal

card.dispute: Defendants appealed against the High Court's decision to allow the plaintiff to amend his plaint in a partition suit, which had initially appeared to seek severance of joint family status.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was for severance of joint family status or merely for partition by metes and bounds.
Whether the High Court was justified in allowing amendment of the plaint to delete the words 'and have' and 'and are'.
holdings: The suit was not for severance of joint family status but for partition by metes and bounds, as the plaint as a whole indicated a prior severance and sought only physical division of properties.
The amendment to delete 'and have' and 'and are' was properly allowed, as the words were inserted by mistake and the amendment did not alter the character of the suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rule 17
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of pleadings to determine true nature of a suit
Amendment of pleadings to prevent multiplicity of suits and secure justice

card.dispute: The plaintiff, as assignee of M's sons, sued to redeem property sold by M to the defendant, arguing the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale; the defendant claimed it was an outright sale with a repurchase clause and the right to redeem had lapsed.
issues_decided: Whether the document Ex. B-1 constituted a mortgage by conditional sale under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or a sale with a condition for retransfer.
Whether the plaintiff, as assignee of the equity of redemption, was entitled to redeem the property despite the time stipulation in the deed.
