holdings: A transaction ostensibly a sale is a mortgage by conditional sale if the condition for reconveyance is in the same document and the parties intended a security arrangement, evidenced by factors like inadequate consideration and retention of possession.

The relationship of debtor and creditor, along with the property serving as security for a debt, distinguishes a mortgage by conditional sale from a sale with a repurchase clause, regardless of the deed's form.
The plaintiff, as assignee of the equity of redemption, is entitled to enforce redemption if the transaction is a mortgage, even if the original mortgagor failed to act within the stipulated time.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rule 7
doctrines: Intention of the parties determines the nature of a transaction despite its form.
Equity of redemption is assignable.
Inadequate consideration and non-transfer of patta are indicia of a mortgage rather than a sale.

card.dispute: Sub-tenants claimed direct tenancy under the landlord after the tenant was evicted, but the landlord contested the lawfulness of the sub-tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide a dispute over the lawfulness of a sub-tenancy under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1951
Whether the sub-tenants could claim direct tenancy under Section 16(2) without a determination of lawful sub-letting by the Rent Controlling Authority
Whether the exception in Section 45(2) allowing civil court jurisdiction over 'title to accommodation' applied to the sub-tenants' claim
holdings: The lawfulness of a sub-tenancy is a matter exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Rent Controlling Authority under Section 15(3), and civil courts are barred from deciding it under Section 45(1).
Section 16(2) only benefits sub-tenants if the sub-letting was lawful; such a determination must first be made by the Rent Controlling Authority, not a civil court.
The phrase 'title to accommodation' in Section 45(2) refers to rights independent of the Act, not statutory rights like deemed tenancy under Section 16(2); thus, civil courts lack jurisdiction.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 15(3)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 16(2)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 45(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1951, Section 45(2)
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of rent control authorities
Statutory ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Literal and purposive interpretation of rent control statutes

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Jabalpur fought with landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings for an improvement scheme, which the High Court quashed on grounds of lack of statutory authority.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned improvement scheme was validly framed under Section 277(1)(B)(i) of the City of Jabalpur Corporation Act, 1948 for forming new or altering existing streets to provide building sites for city expansion.
Whether the scheme could be justified under Section 277(1)(A)(c) as being for the construction of buildings for the accommodation of the poorer and working classes.
holdings: The scheme was not authorized under Section 277(1)(B)(i) because it did not involve forming new or altering existing streets for city expansion, but was instead for developing and selling plots to the public.

The scheme did not serve the purpose of providing accommodation for the 'poorer and working classes' within the meaning of Section 277(1)(A)(c), as it targeted middle-class buyers capable of purchasing houses worth Rs. 7,500.
provisions: City of Jabalpur Corporation Act, 1948, Section 277(1)
City of Jabalpur Corporation Act, 1948, Section 281(1)
City of Jabalpur Corporation Act, 1948, Section 285(1)(a) and (b)
City of Jabalpur Corporation Act, 1948, Section 291
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory powers in land acquisition
Doctrine of colourable legislation (ultra vires if beyond conferred powers)
Principle that public purpose must conform strictly to statutory objects

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether the respondent's right to redeem a mortgage was extinguished after failing to pay the decretal amount within the stipulated time, and whether the High Court could interfere under revisional jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to overturn the District Court's interpretation of a decree extinguishing the right of redemption.
Whether the construction of a decree regarding the extinction of the equity of redemption relates to the jurisdiction of the subordinate court so as to invoke Section 115.
holdings: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by interfering with the District Court's interpretation of the decree, as the error pertained to a question of law not connected to the court's jurisdiction.
The construction of a decree, like that of a document of title, is a question of law, but unless it affects the jurisdiction of the court, it cannot be corrected in revision under Section 115.
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction limited to jurisdictional errors
Distinction between errors of law affecting jurisdiction and those that do not

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the hearing of his appeal by a single judge of the Kerala High Court after the law changed from requiring a Division Bench, claiming a vested right to appeal before a larger bench under the earlier law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had a vested right to have his appeal heard by a Division Bench under the Travancore-Cochin High Court Act, 1949, despite the subsequent amendment by the Kerala High Court Act, 1958.

Whether the change in the composition of the bench hearing the appeal retrospectively affected the appellant’s substantive rights, including the right to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 133.
holdings: No party has a vested right to be heard by a specified number of judges; the composition of the bench is a procedural matter that can be altered by legislative changes.

The right to appeal is substantive, but the mode of hearing (single judge or Division Bench) is procedural and does not create a vested right; thus, the amendment did not infringe any legal right of the appellant.
provisions: Travancore-Cochin High Court Act, 1949, Sections 20 and 21
doctrines: Vested rights doctrine
Procedural vs. substantive law distinction
Doctrine of implied repeal
Intrinsic unity of legal proceedings

card.dispute: A reversioner sued to declare a widow's alienation of her husband's estate void, and the alienees challenged the maintainability of the suit after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force and after the widow's death.
issues_decided: Whether a declaratory suit by reversioners against alienees for setting aside a widow's alienation is maintainable after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
Whether the heirs of a deceased widow are necessary parties in an appeal against a decree dismissing a declaratory suit challenging her alienation.
Whether an appeal is defectively constituted if the widow, impleaded as a respondent, dies during its pendency and her heirs are not brought on record.
holdings: A reversioner can maintain a declaratory suit challenging a widow's alienation made before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, even after the Act came into force, as reversionary rights are not extinguished retroactively.

The heirs of a widow are not necessary parties in a declaratory suit or appeal against alienees where no relief is claimed against the widow personally and the suit targets the validity of alienation.
An appeal is not defectively constituted due to the non-joinder of a deceased widow’s heirs, as the cause of action survives against the alienees and no inconsistent decree can result.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XVI, Rule 12(a)
doctrines: Survival of cause of action
Necessary and proper parties
Declaratory suit under Hindu law

card.dispute: Ram Charan Das challenged the validity of a family settlement (Ex. Y-13) that resolved disputes over property managed by the Court of Wards, after having benefited from it.
issues_decided: Whether the document Ex. Y-13 constitutes a valid family settlement.
Whether a party who has accepted benefits under a family settlement can later challenge its validity.
Whether the family settlement amounts to a transfer or creation of interest in property under s. 37(a) of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912.
holdings: A family settlement entered into bona fide to resolve disputes among family members is valid even if not all parties have a legal claim to the property.
A party who accepts benefits under a family settlement is estopped from challenging its validity.
A family settlement does not amount to a transfer or creation of interest in property within the meaning of s. 37(a) of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912.
provisions: U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, Section 37(a)
doctrines: Family settlement as a means to resolve disputes
Doctrine of estoppel
Bona fide compromise not amounting to alienation

card.dispute: The mortgagors sued to redeem mortgaged land after the mortgagee purchased it in rent and certificate sales; the dispute was whether the mortgagee's purchases enured for the mortgagors' benefit under Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee gained an advantage by availing himself of his position as such, triggering Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act
Whether the mortgagee's default in paying a small portion of rent contributed to the sale of the property
Whether the mortgagors were entitled to redeem the entire or part of the mortgaged property
holdings: Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act does not apply where the mortgagee's default in rent payment is trifling and not a real cause of the sale.
The mortgagee did not gain an advantage by his position or default, so the purchase did not enure for the mortgagors' benefit.
The equity of redemption was extinguished by the sales; however, a small unsold portion could still be redeemed as no cross-appeal challenged the partial decree.
doctrines: Section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act: advantage gained by a qualified owner in derogation of others' rights must be held for their benefit
Equity of redemption extinguished by valid sale of mortgaged property

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the son-in-law's right to deposit rent arrears on behalf of the deceased tenant's heirs under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, claiming the heirs were not personally cultivating the land.
issues_decided: Whether the heirs of a cultivating tenant can be considered as carrying on personal cultivation if the son-in-law, as a family member, performs physical labour on the land.
Whether the son-in-law can be regarded as a member of the family for the purpose of 'personal cultivation' under the Act.
Whether the respondent was putting in physical labour in the cultivation of the land, warranting protection under the Act.
holdings: A son-in-law can be considered a member of the family under the Act, and if he performs physical labour, the heirs may qualify as cultivating tenants.
Supervision of cultivation does not amount to physical labour; actual contribution of physical effort is required for personal cultivation.
No finding was made on whether the respondent performed physical labour, so the matter must be remitted for a proper factual determination.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 2(a)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 2(ee)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3(3)(a)
doctrines: Definition of personal cultivation requiring physical labour by tenant or family members
Inclusion of heirs as cultivating tenants if family members contribute physical labour
Remittal for factual determination in absence of findings on record

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the legality of the transfer of Berubari Union No. 12 and Chilahati village to Pakistan under the Constitution (Ninth Amendment) Act, 1960, claiming these areas were part of India's territory.
issues_decided: Whether the portion of Chilahati village was part of West Bengal within the meaning of the First Schedule of the Constitution due to administration 'as if' it were part of the province.
Whether the continued administration of Chilahati by West Bengal resulted in its constitutional inclusion in India through adverse possession.
holdings: The phrase 'administered as if they formed part of that Province' in the First Schedule refers only to territories merged via formal agreements, not areas temporarily administered due to oversight; thus, Chilahati was not constitutionally part of West Bengal.

Adverse possession cannot be claimed by private parties against the Union of India’s clear acknowledgment of foreign title; the plea was not raised in the writ petition and is not maintainable under international law in this context.
provisions: Constitution of India, First Schedule, Entry 13
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional interpretation based on historical context
Doctrine of merger of territories
Non-applicability of adverse possession in international territorial disputes

card.dispute: The appellant, a decree-holder against an evacuee, sought payment from the evacuee's property vested with the Custodian, which was refused on grounds of lack of jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the Custodian has power under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 to entertain a claim for satisfaction of a debt due by an evacuee.
Whether the deletion of clause (m) of Section 10(2) and Rule 22 of the Act impliedly removed the Custodian's power to pay debts due by the evacuee.
Whether a civil court decree is binding on the Custodian when considering claims against evacuee property.
holdings: The Custodian has the power under Section 10(2)(n) to pay any sum to a person entitled thereto, including creditors, from the evacuee’s funds, as part of administration duties.
The deletion of Section 10(2)(m)'s reference to debt payment and Rule 22 did not remove the Custodian’s power under Section 10(2)(n) or general powers under Section 10(1).
A decree is not binding on the Custodian; he must independently determine the genuineness of a claim, acting judicially and not arbitrarily.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(2)(m)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(2)(n)
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of administrative discretion with judicial fairness
Doctrine of continuity of statutory powers unless expressly repealed

card.dispute: The petitioner sought to bring on record the legal representatives of a deceased respondent in appeal proceedings, contending that their earlier inclusion in final decree proceedings should benefit the appeal, which had abated due to delay.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in bringing the legal representatives of a deceased respondent on record in an appeal can be condoned on the ground that they were already brought on record in final decree proceedings?
Whether an order bringing legal representatives on record in final decree proceedings enures for the benefit of an appeal filed against a preliminary decree?
holdings: There were no sufficient grounds to condone the delay in bringing the legal representatives of the deceased respondent on record in the appeal.

An order bringing legal representatives on record in final decree proceedings does not enure for the benefit of an appeal against a preliminary decree, as an appeal is a continuation of the suit but a suit stage cannot retroactively validate an appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rules 3, 4 and 11
doctrines: Doctrine of abatement of suit or appeal on death of a party
Principle that an appeal is a continuation of the suit
Rule that introduction of legal representatives at one stage of the suit enures for subsequent stages, but not retroactively to prior stages

card.dispute: The landlord, Ramchandra, sought to eject tenant Tukaram over land in the Vidarbha region, claiming a right to personal cultivation under pre-existing tenancy law, amid a transition from the Berar Act to the Bombay Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Section 38 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958 apply to pending proceedings initiated under the Berar Act, 1951 before the 1958 Act came into force
Whether the conditions and restrictions in sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 38 apply to enforcement of rights acquired under the Berar Act
Whether the Tahsildar must follow the procedure under the 1958 Act or the earlier Berar Act in disposing of pending ejectment applications
holdings: Section 38 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1958 does not apply to proceedings pending under the Berar Act, 1951, as it is prospective and does not affect rights already acquired.

Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 38 do not apply to applications enforcing rights under the Berar Act, as those provisions are tied to new tenancy terminations under Section 38(1), not pre-existing rights.
Pending proceedings under the Berar Act must be continued and disposed of as if the 1958 Act had not been passed, subject to procedural transfer to the corresponding authority under the new Act.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 38
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 132(2) and (3)
Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of saving of pending proceedings
Doctrine of prospective operation of statutes
Doctrine of continuity of rights under repealed laws

card.dispute: The landlords sought permission to sue for eviction of tenants, and the dispute centered on whether the State Government's revisional power under the U.P. Act was quasi-judicial and required adherence to natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the revisional power of the State Government under Section 7-F of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 is quasi-judicial in nature.
Whether principles of natural justice must be followed by the State Government while exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 7-F.
Whether the earlier decisions of the Allahabad High Court holding the power under Sections 3(2) and 3(3) as administrative were correct.
holdings: The revisional power under Section 7-F is quasi-judicial because it affects statutory rights of tenants and must be exercised in accordance with principles of natural justice.
Authorities under Sections 3(2), 3(3), and 7-F must follow principles of natural justice as they adjudicate rights of landlords and tenants in a quasi-judicial manner.
The proceedings before the District Magistrate and Commissioner are quasi-judicial, given the requirement to assess legality, propriety, and regularity of orders, and to serve justice.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(2)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(3)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 14
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 15
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial function doctrine
Judicial propriety and hierarchy in overruling precedent

card.dispute: The appellant, claiming ownership of immovable properties attached by the Union of India in execution proceedings, filed a suit under Order 21, Rule 63 of the CPC to challenge the attachment, but the suit was dismissed as time-barred because the lower courts held that the mandatory notice under Section 80 CPC did not apply, and thus the period of notice could not be excluded from limitation.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Order 21, Rule 63 of the Code of Civil Procedure is subject to the mandatory notice requirement under Section 80 of the CPC?
Whether the period of notice under Section 80 can be excluded from the period of limitation for a suit under Order 21, Rule 63?
holdings: A suit under Order 21, Rule 63 of the CPC is a suit against the Government and falls within the plain, unambiguous language of Section 80, which is mandatory and applies to all suits against the Government regardless of their nature.

The period of notice under Section 80 CPC must be excluded from the limitation period for a suit under Order 21, Rule 63, as the notice requirement applies, and failure to give such notice renders the suit premature, not barred by limitation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 63
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 58
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Mandatory nature of statutory notice under Section 80 CPC
Cause of action in a possessory and title dispute arising from execution proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, after the respondent municipality sought to evict him, arguing his status as a protected tenant under the earlier 1939 Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant of land held on lease from a local authority could retain protected tenant status under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, despite having acquired such status under the 1939 Act before the 1948 Act came into force.
Whether Section 89(2)(b) of the 1948 Act saved the rights of protected tenants of local authority lands acquired under the 1939 Act.
Whether Section 88(1)(a) of the 1948 Act expressly excluded the application of protection provisions to leases from local authorities, thereby overriding prior rights.
holdings: Section 88(1)(a) of the 1948 Act expressly excludes the application of the Act’s protection provisions, including Section 31, to lands leased from local authorities, thereby negating protected tenant status under the 1948 Act.
The saving clause in Section 89(2)(b) does not preserve protected tenant rights under the 1939 Act where an express provision like Section 88(1)(a) removes such protection.
Section 88(1)(a) applies retrospectively to extinguish protected tenant status for leases from local authorities, as its language is broad and not limited to future leases.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 31
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89(2)
doctrines: Express exclusion prevails over saving clauses
Retrospective application of statutory exclusions
Statutory interpretation of tenancy protection laws

card.dispute: The dispute was between former jagirdars and the State over whether the jagirdars, after becoming occupants of forest lands under the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, had the right to cut and remove trees from those lands.
issues_decided: Whether the abolition of jagirs under the 1953 Act extinguished the jagirdars' rights to trees on forest lands.
Whether jagirdars, upon becoming occupants under Section 5 of the Act, acquired rights to trees under Section 40 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code.
Whether Section 9 of the Abolition Act impliedly saved the jagirdars' rights to trees not explicitly reserved to the State.
holdings: The abolition of jagirs under Section 3 of the 1953 Act extinguished all rights of jagirdars, except those expressly preserved by the Act.
Becoming an 'occupant' under Section 5(1)(b) did not confer rights to trees on forest land unless a survey and settlement had been completed, which had not occurred here.

Section 9 of the Abolition Act did not implyly preserve jagirdars' rights to trees; the absence of an express saving, unlike in the case of mineral rights under Section 10, meant no such rights survived abolition.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, Sections 3, 5, 9, and 10
Bombay Land Revenue Code, Sections 40, 65, and 68
doctrines: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Doctrine of implied repeal and statutory construction
Doctrine of reservation of state rights in natural resources

card.dispute: Thika tenants challenged the landlord's suit for their ejectment, claiming protection under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, while the landlord argued the land was exempt due to its inclusion in an improvement scheme under the Calcutta Improvement Trust Act, 1911.
issues_decided: Whether Section 30(c) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, applies to land liable for betterment fee under the Calcutta Improvement Trust Act, 1911, thereby exempting it from the Act's protections.
Whether the mere liability to pay betterment fee means the land is 'required' for carrying out the provisions of the Improvement Trust Act.
holdings: Section 30(c) does not apply merely because land is liable to pay betterment fee; the land must be directly required for carrying out a specific provision of the Improvement Trust Act.

The indirect financial benefit to the Improvement Trust from betterment fees does not equate to the land being 'required' for the Act’s provisions, so tenants retain protection under the Thika Tenancy Act.
doctrines: Beneficial legislation interpretation
Literal and contextual interpretation of statutes
Avoidance of redundancy in statutory interpretation
Distinction between purpose and provision in statutory construction

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the maintainability of a Letters Patent appeal before a Division Bench after a Single Judge of the High Court dismissed its second appeal under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether a Letters Patent appeal lies from a judgment of a Single Judge deciding a second appeal under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the legislature, by enacting Section 43 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, has taken away the right to a Letters Patent appeal
Whether the expression 'appeal to the High Court' in Section 39 includes a Letters Patent appeal as part of the same appellate process
holdings: An appeal under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent lies from a judgment of a Single Judge unless the statute expressly or by necessary implication takes away that right.
Section 43 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, by declaring orders under the Act as final, excludes further appeals including Letters Patent appeals.
An appeal under Section 39 of the Act and a Letters Patent appeal are distinct; the former is statutory and the latter is a separate remedy, not part of the same appellate process.
The expression 'appeal to the High Court' does not include a Letters Patent appeal, which is a fresh appeal against the order of a Single Judge and not a continuation of the original appeal.
provisions: Letters Patent for the High Court of Lahore, Clause 10
Letters Patent for the High Court of Lahore, Clause 11
doctrines: Finality of orders under special statutes
Statutory exclusion of appeals by necessary implication
Distinction between statutory appeals and Letters Patent appeals
Principle of 'final order' excluding further judicial review unless otherwise provided

card.dispute: The plaintiffs claimed possession of suit properties from defendants who asserted tenancy rights under kanom deeds, leading to a dispute over whether the defendants were protected from eviction under agrarian reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the deed dated February 5, 1929 (Ex. A-3) constituted a kanom within the meaning of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963
Whether the deed dated February 27, 1941 (Ex. B-2) operated as a valid assignment of kanom rights from Baithan to defendants 1 to 5
Whether defendants 1 to 5 became kanomdars and thus tenants entitled to protection from eviction under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963
holdings: The deed dated February 5, 1929 (Ex. A-3) is a kanom within the meaning of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, as the definition is substantially identical to that in the earlier Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, and the plaintiffs had so admitted in the High Court.

The deed dated February 27, 1941 (Ex. B-2), though styled a release and using the word 'surrender', operated as a valid assignment of kanom rights because it was for valuable consideration, registered, and showed a clear intention to transfer all rights.
Defendants 1 to 5 became kanomdars and therefore tenants under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, and are entitled to fixity of tenure and protection from eviction under Section 13 of the Act.
provisions: Malabar Tenancy Act, 1929 (Madras Act XIV of 1929), Section 21
Malabar Tenancy Act, 1929, Section 23, second proviso, Clause (iii)
doctrines: Admission binds party in later proceedings
Construction of deed based on substance over form
Intention to transfer determines nature of deed
Fixity of tenure under agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The State of U.P. and others contested whether Zamindari Abolition Compensation Bonds could be compulsorily accepted in payment of agricultural income-tax dues by an intermediary, Sri Narain.
issues_decided: Whether compensation bonds issued under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950 can be accepted in payment of agricultural income-tax dues.
Whether the compensation remains payable after delivery of bonds to the intermediary.
Whether Rule 8-A of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Rules mandates acceptance of bonds for tax payment.
holdings: Neither Section 6(d) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950 nor Rule 8-A authorizes or requires the acceptance of compensation bonds in lieu of agricultural income-tax payment.
Compensation ceases to be payable once it is discharged by delivery of bonds or cash; the bonds themselves are not legal tender and need not be accepted by the government for tax dues.
The negotiability of the bonds allows transfer to willing purchasers but does not impose an obligation on the State to accept them in discharge of public dues.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(d)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 68
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Rules, Rule 8-A
doctrines: Legal tender doctrine
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of compensation discharge

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and a licensing authority vs. Hari Krishan Sharma over whether the State Government could lawfully require all cinema licence applications to be forwarded to it for disposal, bypassing the licensing authority.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government, under s. 5(2) of the Punjab Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952, can assume original jurisdiction to decide licence applications that are statutorily assigned to the licensing authority.
Whether executive instructions by the State Government can override the statutory scheme allocating initial decision-making power to the licensing authority.
holdings: The State Government cannot, under the guise of control under s. 5(2), usurp the licensing authority's statutory power to decide licence applications in the first instance.

The statutory scheme mandates that the licensing authority must process applications initially; the Government can only act as an appellate or revisional authority, not as the original decision-maker.
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers within administrative authorities
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on legislative scheme
Doctrine of limited executive control over delegated powers

card.dispute: The Sub-Divisional Officer, Mirzapur, challenged the High Court's issuance of a writ of prohibition preventing the State Government from reopening compensation proceedings, after it was not notified of the hearing on the respondent's objection to the compensation assessment.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government, as a necessary party under Section 343 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, must be served with specific notice of the hearing date in objection proceedings.
Whether the Compensation Officer has the inherent jurisdiction to reopen proceedings where a necessary party was not notified.
Whether the High Court was justified in issuing a writ of prohibition against the reopening of the objection proceedings.
holdings: The State Government is a necessary party to compensation proceedings under Section 343, and without specific notice of the hearing, the proceedings are not binding on it.

The Compensation Officer has inherent power under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to reopen proceedings where a necessary party was not served with notice, even after final rolls are signed.
The High Court erred in issuing a writ of prohibition, as the Compensation Officer had jurisdiction to decide whether to reopen the proceedings, which must be determined first.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 343
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 52
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1952, Section 61
doctrines: Necessary party doctrine
Inherent powers of a tribunal
Doctrine of nullity for non-service of notice
Principle of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh fought Raja Yadvendra Dutt Dube over whether a fresh assessment for agricultural income tax could be made after the statutory time limit had expired, based on a return filed before a jurisdictionally incompetent authority.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Revision could lawfully direct the Collector to make a fresh assessment after the limitation period under s. 25 had expired
Whether a notice issued by a Sub-Divisional Officer under s. 15(3) was valid when the assessee's gross agricultural income exceeded Rs. 1 lakh
Whether the Collector could proceed with assessment based on a return filed pursuant to an invalid notice without issuing a fresh notice under s. 15(3)
holdings: The Board of Revision could not direct a fresh assessment after the limitation period under s. 25 had expired, as such a direction would violate statutory time limits.
A Sub-Divisional Officer lacks jurisdiction to issue a notice under s. 15(3) or assess income when the assessee's gross agricultural income exceeds Rs. 1 lakh, making the notice and assessment void.
The Collector cannot rely on a return filed in response to an invalid notice; a fresh notice under s. 15(3) is required, which cannot be issued after the expiry of the assessment year.
doctrines: Jurisdictional limits of assessing authorities
Validity of proceedings based on ultra vires actions
Statutory limitation and finality of assessment proceedings

card.dispute: The State of Orissa challenged the assessment of a joint Hindu family's agricultural income, disputing whether the family qualified for concessional tax rates and whether milk income was agricultural income.
issues_decided: Whether a joint Hindu family consisting of the sons of two deceased brothers qualifies as a family 'consisting of brothers only' under Clause B of the Schedule to the Orissa Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1947.
Whether income from milk derived from cows and buffaloes maintained on agricultural land constitutes agricultural income under the Act.
holdings: For the purpose of the Orissa Agricultural Income-tax Act, an undivided Hindu family consisting of the sons of deceased brothers is regarded as a family 'consisting of brothers only' due to the inclusive definition in the Explanation to the Schedule.
Income from milk derived from cows and buffaloes maintained on agricultural land is agricultural income, as settled by precedent in Commissioner of Income-tax v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy.
provisions: Orissa Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1947, Schedule, Clause B
doctrines: Inclusive definition interpretation
Precedent bindingness (stare decisis)

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and an ex-Zamindar disputed whether Zamindari Abolition Compensation Bonds could be accepted in lieu of payment of agricultural income-tax dues.
issues_decided: Whether Zamindari Abolition Compensation Bonds are legally acceptable in payment of agricultural income-tax dues.
Whether section 6(d) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rule 8-A of its rules mandate or permit the acceptance of bonds for tax payment.
Whether compensation remains payable after the issuance of bonds, allowing tax recovery from future encashment.
holdings: The delivery of compensation bonds under the Act discharges the State's liability, and the bonds do not remain as payable compensation after issuance.

Neither section 6(d) of the Act nor rule 8-A authorizes the acceptance of bonds in payment of agricultural income-tax; they only permit deduction of tax arrears from compensation before its disbursement.
The negotiability of bonds does not make them legal tender, and the government is not obligated to accept them for tax payments.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(d)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 68
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Rule 8-A
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Rules 62, 63, 64, 65
doctrines: Legal tender doctrine
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of discharge of liability by performance

card.dispute: The State of Madras notified a village held under a permanent under-tenure as a zamin estate under the Abolition Act, and the respondent, who possessed it, challenged the legality of the notification.
issues_decided: Whether the village in question was a zamin estate within the meaning of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
Whether a village held under a permanent under-tenure and included in a zamindari can be classified as a zamin estate
Whether the Government's notification declaring the village as a zamin estate was valid
holdings: A village held under a permanent under-tenure, even if included in a zamindari, does not become a zamin estate under the Act.
Permanent under-tenure villages are specifically excluded from the definition of 'zamin estate' and fall under 'under-tenure estate'.
The Government's notification declaring such a village as a zamin estate is void if it misclassifies an under-tenure estate as a zamin estate.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 2(15)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'zamin estate' and 'under-tenure'
Doctrine of legal classification based on tenure, not popular usage

card.dispute: The Cantonment Board, Ambala sought to recover arrears of rent from Pyarelal through a Magistrate under the Cantonments Act, but Pyarelal challenged the Board's power to do so, leading to a dispute over the interpretation of s. 259 of the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate had jurisdiction under s. 259 of the Cantonments Act, 1924 to recover arrears of rent claimed by the Cantonment Board based on a lease agreement.
Whether rent owed under a lease between the Cantonment Board and a tenant is 'recoverable under the Act or the Rules' within the meaning of s. 259(1).
Whether the repeal of Rule 42 of the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937 affected the Board's power to recover rent via Magistrate.
holdings: Rent claimed solely under a lease agreement with the Cantonment Board is not 'recoverable under the Act or the Rules' and thus does not fall within the scope of s. 259(1) of the Cantonments Act.
Section 259 applies only when the liability to pay rent arises from powers or duties conferred by the Act or Rules, not from private contractual leases.

The word 'rent' in s. 259 must be understood in its ordinary sense as payment from tenant to landlord, and does not include sums recovered by the Board under s. 257, where it stands in the place of an owner for recovery of expenses.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of ejusdem generis
Principle that statutory powers of recovery must be strictly construed

card.dispute: The bank sued to enforce an equitable mortgage based on deposit of title deeds, while the defendants argued the documents required registration and were unenforceable.
issues_decided: Whether the letter at exhibit 7(a) constituted a registrable instrument creating an equitable mortgage under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether exhibits 7(b) and 12 were integral to the mortgage transaction and required registration
Whether an unregistered document can still allow enforcement of an equitable mortgage based on oral agreement and deposit of title deeds
holdings: A document does not require registration if it is merely evidential and not intended by the parties as the sole agreement creating the mortgage.
Exhibits 7(a), 7(b), and 12 did not constitute a written bargain intended to be the exclusive record of the mortgage and thus did not require registration.
Deposit of title deeds with intent to create security, supported by oral agreement, can create an enforceable equitable mortgage even without a registered document.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 34, Rule 4
doctrines: Equitable mortgage by deposit of title deeds
Integration of written documents into a mortgage transaction
Rule against oral evidence substituting written contracts when parties adopt a document as their sole agreement

card.dispute: The landlord filed an application for possession under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act after terminating the tenancy; the tenant argued the application was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: From which date does the limitation period begin to run for an application under Section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948?
Whether the right to obtain possession is deemed to accrue to the landlord at the date of default in rent or at the date of termination of tenancy?
holdings: The limitation period for an application under Section 29(2) begins from the date of termination of the tenancy, not from the earlier date of default in rent.
The right to obtain possession is deemed to accrue to the landlord on the date the tenancy is terminated by notice under Section 14(1)(b), even though actual possession requires a Mamlatdar's order.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14(1)(b)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29(2)
Mamlatdars' Courts Act, 1906 (Bombay Act No. 2 of 1906), Section 5(3) and Section 5(4)
doctrines: Legal fiction of deemed accrual of right
Accrual of cause of action
Interpretation of limitation periods in tenancy laws

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a mortgagee's claim under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 was barred by limitation and whether the Claims Officer could rely on a foreign decree to determine the amount due.
issues_decided: Whether the claim filed under Section 14(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 was barred by limitation
Whether the claim could be based on a decree of the Pakistan High Court, treated as a foreign judgment
Whether the parties challenged the correctness of the amount determined by the Claims Officer
holdings: A claim under Section 14(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act must be made within six months of vesting, but the underlying claim to recover must not be time-barred; if a decree exists, its limitation is assessed separately under the Limitation Act.
A claim before the Claims Officer can be based on a foreign decree if the pleadings and conduct show it was intended, even if not formally filed, and the parties understood it as such.

The appellants did not challenge the amount found due by the Claims Officer because their arguments focused only on limitation, leading to a remand for fresh determination of the amount without pre-judgment on the decree's binding effect.
doctrines: Foreign judgment recognition
Substantive vs. procedural limitation
Pleading estoppel
Remand for factual determination

card.dispute: The mortgagees challenged the Appellate Officer's order that reopened their mortgage account to treat interest payments above five percent per annum as reducing the principal, claiming it violated the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether Section 9(1) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 authorizes reopening of mortgage accounts from the date of mortgage to recalculate interest liability?
Whether payments made at a rate higher than five percent per annum simple interest but within the contractual rate can be treated as reducing the principal amount?
holdings: Section 9(1) of the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 applies only to liability still due and does not empower the Competent Officer to reopen accounts from the beginning or reallocate past interest payments towards principal.

Payments made at a rate above five percent per annum simple interest but within the contractual rate cannot be treated as reducing the principal; only future interest liability is capped at five percent per annum simple.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statute
Non-obstante clause interpretation
Principle of accrued rights under contract

card.dispute: The appellants' father, a ryotwari sub-lessee, was sued for ejectment by the respondent landlord after the Court of Wards released the estate; the dispute was whether the sub-lessee became an occupancy tenant under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, despite the landlord being a minor when the lease was granted.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant became an occupancy tenant under s. 185(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954,
Whether the exception in s. 185(3) applies where the landlord was a minor at the time of lease but not at the commencement of the Code
holdings: A ryotwari sub-lessee becomes an occupancy tenant under s. 185(1) if the land is of the prescribed nature and no exception applies.
The exception in s. 185(3) applies only if the landlord was a disabled person under s. 168(2) at the commencement of the Code, not at the time of lease.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 185(1)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 185(3)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 168(2)
doctrines: Prospective operation of statutory provisions
Statutory acquisition of tenancy rights
Interpretation of disability clauses in land revenue laws

card.dispute: The tenant (Babu Lal) challenged the validity of orders directing him to vacate the premises and allow allotment to another person under the U.P. Rent Control Act, after the landlord-tenant relationship continued post-allotment order.
issues_decided: Whether the District Magistrate could pass an allotment order under Section 7(2) when the accommodation was 'about to fall vacant' rather than actually vacant
Whether the allotment order under Section 7(2) took immediate effect despite the tenant still being in occupation
Whether proceedings under Section 7A were maintainable when the tenant continued occupation after an allotment order
holdings: The District Magistrate has power under Section 7(2) to pass an allotment order if the accommodation is about to fall vacant, not only when it is already vacant.
An order under Section 7(2) takes immediate legal effect upon issuance and does not await actual vacation of the premises.
Continuing tenancy after an allotment order, especially through a new agreement, constitutes occupation in contravention of the order, justifying action under Section 7A.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7(2)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7A(1)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7A(2)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7A(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective vacancy
Immediate effect of administrative allotment orders
Contravention of statutory orders through continuation of tenancy

card.dispute: Narayanan and Viswanathan contested the income tax assessment on their share of a jointly devised estate, arguing that two younger grandsons born posthumously should also inherit, thereby altering tax liability.
issues_decided: Whether the will of Chockalingam Chettiar bequeathed property to a class of grandsons including those born after his death.
Whether possession of the legacy was deferred beyond the testator's death, thus allowing posthumously born grandsons to inherit.
Whether the assessment of income tax on only two grandsons alive at the testator's death was valid.
holdings: A bequest to a class of persons takes effect at the testator's death under Section 111 of the Indian Succession Act, unless possession is expressly deferred.
The will did not defer possession beyond the testator's death; thus, only grandsons alive at that time were entitled to the legacy.
The income tax assessment on Narayanan and Viswanathan, as the only eligible legatees at the time of the testator's death, was valid.
doctrines: Rule of class gifts under Section 111 of the Indian Succession Act
Vesting of legacy at the date of the testator's death
Principle of contemporaneity in construction of wills

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the Mysore Village Offices Abolition Act, 1961, which abolished hereditary village offices, arguing it was colourable legislation and violated fundamental rights under Articles 16 and 311.
issues_decided: Whether the Mysore Village Offices Abolition Act, 1961 is constitutionally valid or amounts to colourable legislation?
Whether the abolition of hereditary village offices violates the fundamental right to equality under Article 16 of the Constitution?
Whether the posts in South Kanara were governed by the Madras Hereditary Village Offices Act or its principles, thereby attracting protection under Article 311?
holdings: The Act is not colourable legislation as the State legislature had competence to abolish hereditary offices and convert them into stipendiary posts, and the change in nature of posts was substantial.

Article 16 applies to hereditary offices because there was no pre-existing property right in the office independent of the office itself; thus, a law favoring hereditary succession violates Article 16.

The hereditary principle in South Kanara was recognized through Standing Orders of the Madras Board of Revenue, but the impugned Act validly abolished such practice, and the abolition does not amount to 'removal' under Article 311.
provisions: Mysore Village Offices Abolition Act, 1961 (Act 14 of 1961), Section 6(1)
Madras Hereditary Village Offices Act, 1895 (Act 3 of 1895)
doctrines: Colourable legislation
Fundamental right to equality in public employment (Article 16)
Doctrine of hereditary office as property
Principle of abolition versus removal of public office

card.dispute: Landowners challenged a consolidation scheme that reserved land for the Panchayat's income, arguing it violated constitutional protections against uncompensated acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether reservation of land for Panchayat income constitutes 'acquisition' under the second proviso to Article 31A(1) of the Constitution
Whether such acquisition was complete before the Seventeenth Amendment introduced the proviso
Whether compensation at market value is required when a landholder's holding falls below the statutory ceiling due to such reservation
holdings: Reservation of land for Panchayat income amounts to acquisition by the State under Article 31A, as Panchayat falls within the definition of 'State' under Article 12, and thus triggers the second proviso requiring compensation.

Acquisition is not complete until possession is transferred under Section 24 of the East Punjab Holdings Act; therefore, the scheme was subject to the second proviso introduced by the Seventeenth Amendment.
When a cultivating tenant's land is reduced below the statutory ceiling due to acquisition, compensation at not less than market value must be paid, regardless of how the acquired land is used.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 18
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 19(1)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 20(3)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 21
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 23A
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 24
doctrines: Acquisition by the State doctrine under Article 31A
Definition of 'State' under Article 12
Principle of compensation at market value for acquisition reducing holdings below ceiling

card.dispute: The appellant, Abdul Waheed Khan, sought to eject the respondents, Bhawani and others, as shikmi tenants, but the respondents counterclaimed in civil court for possession based on their title as khatedars.
issues_decided: Whether a civil court can entertain a suit based on title despite a prior revenue officer's decision under the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932
Whether the presumption of correctness of entries in the Record of Rights under Section 95 bars a civil suit on title
Whether the suit was barred by limitation
holdings: Section 200(1) of the Bhopal State Land Revenue Act does not bar a civil court from adjudicating a suit based on title, as questions of title fall outside the exclusive domain of revenue officers.

An entry in the Record of Rights under Section 89(2), decided under Section 93, creates only a rebuttable presumption of title under Section 95 and does not preclude a civil court from determining the true title.

The suit was filed within the limitation period under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, 1908, as the claim for possession was added after dispossession and the overall cause of action remained within time.
provisions: Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, Section 71
Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, Section 89
Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, Section 93
Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, Section 95
Bhopal State Land Revenue Act, 1932, Section 200(1)
doctrines: Presumption of correctness in revenue records is rebuttable in civil suits on title
Revenue officer's jurisdiction does not exclude civil court jurisdiction over title disputes
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are not re-examinable in appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the termination of its mining lease and sub-leases by the Controller of Mining Leases, arguing that the leases should only be modified, not terminated, under applicable mining laws.
issues_decided: Whether the mining lease in question was an 'existing mining lease' subject to modification under the Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956
Whether the Controller had the authority to terminate the lease for non-compliance with the 20-year limit under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether the termination of sub-leases was valid despite lack of notice in separate proceedings
holdings: Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 continues subsisting mining leases with the State as the deemed lessor, preserving the lease as an existing lease subject to modification under central law.

An existing mining lease for minerals other than coal, iron ore, or bauxite must conform to the 20-year limit from its original commencement date, and failure to do so warrants termination under the 1957 Act and 1949 Rules.
Termination of a head lease automatically terminates all sub-leases, rendering procedural irregularities in separate sub-lease proceedings immaterial to the outcome.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948, Sections 4, 5, 7
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 8, Section 16
Mining Leases (Modification of Terms) Rules, 1956, Rule 2(c), Rule 4, Rule 6, Rule 7
doctrines: Doctrine of Deemed Continuation of Leases
Doctrine of Legislative Intention in Statutory Interpretation
Doctrine of Automatic Termination of Sub-Leases upon Termination of Head Lease

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the grant of an excise licence to the respondent, arguing that the respondent's prior payment of compensation for a forest offence made him unsuitable, a decision upheld by the Board of Revenue but overturned by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether compounding of a forest offence under Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation 1891 has the same legal effect as an acquittal under Section 345(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898
Whether the Board of Revenue could consider the respondent's conduct in paying compensation for a forest offence when determining suitability for an excise licence
Whether the High Court was justified in issuing a writ of certiorari to quash the Board of Revenue's decision
holdings: Section 62 of the Assam Forest Regulation 1891 does not equate to an acquittal; payment of compensation amounts to acceptance of the charge and does not clear the character of the person.
The Board of Revenue was legally entitled to consider the respondent's conduct in paying compensation as relevant to his suitability for an excise licence.
The High Court erred in issuing a writ of certiorari as the Board did not exceed its jurisdiction or commit an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act 5 of 1898), Section 345(6)
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Scope of writ of certiorari
Effect of compounding an offence

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant of land who had constructed buildings and let them out; the tenant claimed protection from eviction under a tenancy law.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant who constructs permanent structures for residential or business purposes on leased land is entitled to protection from eviction under Section 5(1)(a) of the Non-agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, Assam Act 12 of 1955, even if the structures are let out to others.
Whether the phrase 'for residential or business purposes' in Section 5(1)(a) requires the tenant to use the structures personally for such purposes.
holdings: The protection under Section 5(1)(a) applies if the structure is adapted for residential or business purposes, regardless of whether the tenant uses it personally or lets it out.
The statutory protection is available to the tenant of the land, and letting out the constructed buildings does not cause the tenant to lose such protection.
provisions: The Non-agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, Assam Act 12 of 1955, Section 5(1)(a)
The Non-agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, Assam Act 12 of 1955, Section 3(g)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation: courts must not read additional conditions into a provision not expressly stated.
Retrospective operation of statute: Section 5 of the Act has retrospective effect.

card.dispute: The Central Bank of India (tenant) appealed against the Rent Controller's refusal to issue a commission to inspect the landlord's residence, arguing it was necessary to challenge the landlord's claim of bona fide need for eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies under Section 38(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 against an interlocutory order of the Controller refusing to issue a commission for inspection of premises?
Whether the refusal to issue a commission affects a party's right or liability, thereby making it appealable?
holdings: Section 38(1) does not allow appeals against interlocutory or procedural orders that do not affect the substantive rights or liabilities of the parties.

The Controller's refusal to issue a commission for inspection is a procedural order and not appealable under Section 38(1), though such an order may be challenged in an appeal against the final order.
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of orders
Doctrine of limited construction of appeal provisions
Distinction between interlocutory and final orders

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the dismissal of their writ petition for certiorari on the grounds of delay, as it was filed six days beyond the 90-day practice period due to unexpected court closure during Diwali.
issues_decided: Whether the 90-day period for filing a writ petition under Article 226 is a binding rule of limitation or merely a rule of practice
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the petition without considering laches or special circumstances
holdings: A 90-day period for filing a writ petition under Article 226 is a rule of practice, not a binding rule of limitation, and does not automatically bar relief.
The High Court must consider whether there was laches or undue delay in light of the circumstances, and cannot reject a petition solely for non-compliance with a practice rule without such inquiry.
doctrines: Rule of practice vs. rule of limitation
Laches and equitable discretion in writ petitions
Judicial review of administrative delay

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax appealed against the High Court's ruling that harvested crops purchased by the respondent company were not its agricultural income under the Coorg Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether the value of harvested crops purchased by the assessee constituted agricultural income under the Coorg Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1951.
Whether income from the sale of harvested crops bought from a previous owner could be treated as agricultural income of the purchaser.
holdings: Income from the sale of crops already harvested at the time of purchase does not constitute agricultural income of the purchaser, as no agricultural operations were performed by them.
Agricultural income arises only when the assessee raises the produce or performs processes inherent to cultivation; mere purchase and sale of harvested crops does not qualify.
doctrines: Doctrine of agricultural income
Principle of derivation of income from agricultural operations

card.dispute: The Cochin Devaswom Board sought to recover michavaram and renewal fees from Kanam tenants, who challenged the demand, arguing that the Travancore-Cochin Kanam Tenancy Act, 1955, granted them proprietary rights and abolished such dues.
issues_decided: Whether the Travancore-Cochin Kanam Tenancy Act, 1955 applies to lands held from Devaswoms in the Cochin area.
Whether the Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution by applying only to the Cochin area and not the entire Kerala State.
holdings: The Travancore-Cochin Kanam Tenancy Act, 1955 applies to Kanam tenants holding land from Devaswoms in the Cochin area, as the kychit (undertaking) constituted a tenancy contract under the Act.
The Act does not violate Article 14, as the Kanam tenure systems in Cochin, Travancore, and Malabar were historically and legally distinct, justifying differential treatment.
provisions: The Travancore-Cochin Kanam Tenancy Act, 1955 (Act 24 of 1955), Sections 2(4), 2(6), 2(11)
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Partial statutory supersession without express repeal

card.dispute: The forest authorities sought to impose compensation and penalty on contractor Rattan Singh for alleged illegal tree felling, but he argued that disputes over breach of contract must be decided by the Chief Conservator as arbitrator under the contract, not by the Divisional Forest Officer.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 15(1) of the Central Provinces and Berar Forest Contract Rules empowers the Divisional Forest Officer to determine if a contractor breached the contract by causing damage in a reserved forest.

Whether a dispute over breach of contract must be referred to the Chief Conservator of Forests under Clause 9 of the contract, even if rules authorize the Divisional Forest Officer to assess compensation.
Whether the penalty imposed under Rule 30(1) is valid without a prior determination of breach by the designated arbitrator.
holdings: Rule 15(1) does not authorize the Divisional Forest Officer to decide whether the contractor, his servants, or agents caused damage or breached the contract; it only empowers assessment of compensation after liability is established.

Where a dispute arises over performance or breach of contract, Clause 9 requires reference to the Chief Conservator of Forests as arbitrator, and this procedure must be followed regardless of the Forest Rules.
A penalty under Rule 30(1) cannot be imposed without first determining breach of contract through the arbitration mechanism in Clause 9, which was not done here.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Forest Contract Rules, Rule 15(1)
Central Provinces and Berar Forest Contract Rules, Rule 30(1)
Central Provinces and Berar Forest Contract Rules, Clause 9 of the contract
doctrines: Doctrine of contractual arbitration
Doctrine of statutory interpretation: specific provision prevails over general
Separation of liability determination and compensation assessment

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the bank's claim that they owed Rs. 10,000 advanced after a mortgage, and whether the suit for recovery was within limitation.
issues_decided: Whether a certified copy of an entry in the bank's books under Section 4 of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, without more, can prove a loan of Rs. 10,000?
Whether the suit was within the period of limitation for enforcing personal liability?
holdings: A certified copy of a bank's account entry is only prima facie evidence and cannot, by itself, establish a borrower's liability; independent evidence is required when the borrower disputes the entry.
The suit was time-barred for personal liability as it was filed beyond six years from the mortgage date and no valid acknowledgment extended the limitation period.
doctrines: Prima facie evidence
Burden of proof in banking transactions
Acknowledgment of liability under limitation law
Admissibility of documentary evidence

card.dispute: The appellants claimed redemption of land alleging the transactions were usufructuary mortgages, while the respondents claimed they were kanam-kuzhikanam holders entitled to tenure rights.
issues_decided: Whether the transactions under Exs. A-1 and B-1 were kanam-kuzhikanam or usufructuary mortgages.
Whether the transactions fell within the definition of 'kanam-kuzhikanam' under Section 2(23) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964.
holdings: The transactions were kanam-kuzhikanam, not usufructuary mortgages, as they were transfers of a right to enjoy the property, not security for a debt.
The documents satisfied the conditions of Section 2(23) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, and the absence of any mortgage recital supported their classification as kanam-kuzhikanam.
provisions: Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964), Section 2(23)
Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (Act 1 of 1964), Section 13
doctrines: Distinction between lease and mortgage
Substance over form in characterizing transactions
Relevance of parties' description of a transaction in determining its nature

card.dispute: The appellant Chhi Ram challenged his murder conviction based on the reliability and corroboration of an approver's evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below correctly applied the two-pronged test for evaluating the evidence of an approver as laid down in Sarwan Singh's case.
Whether the approver's evidence was reliable and sufficiently corroborated to sustain the conviction.
holdings: The first test for an approver's evidence is that it must show the witness is reliable, meaning no inherent improbability or finding of falsehood.
The second test requires sufficient corroboration on material particulars, which is essential for an approver but not always for other witnesses.
The High Court properly applied both tests by finding the approver's main story reliable and corroborated, even though part of his evidence was rejected for lack of corroboration.
doctrines: Sarwan Singh test for approver's evidence
Principle of corroboration of approver's testimony
Judicial caution in accepting uncorroborated parts of an approver's statement

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether an order modifying an arbitrator's award in consolidation proceedings under the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act was appealable under Section 39 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether Section 39 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 applies to arbitrations conducted under Section 37 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954.
Whether the decision of the Civil Judge modifying the arbitrator's award is appealable.
Whether Section 12(6) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, which declares the arbitrator’s decision final, bars appeals under the Arbitration Act.
holdings: Section 37 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, read with Sections 46 and 47 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, makes the provisions of the Arbitration Act, including Section 39, applicable to arbitration proceedings under the Act.
The decision of the Civil Judge modifying an arbitrator's award is appealable under Section 39 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
The finality clause in Section 12(6) of the U.P. Act refers to the award as confirmed or modified through proceedings under the Arbitration Act, and does not bar statutory appeals under Section 39.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, Section 12
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, Section 37
doctrines: Statutory arbitration
Finality of arbitral awards subject to statutory remedies
Harmonious construction of statutes

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compulsory acquisition of their land under a supplementary industrial development scheme framed by the Delhi Improvement Trust, alleging it was invalid and meant to benefit a private company.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land under the supplementary scheme was for the purposes of the U.P. Town Improvement Act (1908)
Whether the Trust had the power to compulsorily acquire land for the supplementary scheme
Whether the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Part VII procedure was mandatory when land was to be allotted to a company after development
holdings: The original and supplementary schemes together formed a composite town expansion scheme under the Act, aimed at industrial development and decongesting Delhi, thus serving public purpose.
The Trust had power to compulsorily acquire land under Section 23(a) and Section 56 of the Act, even without an express provision in Section 32, as the power was implied for executing the scheme.

Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was not required because the land was acquired for a public scheme, not directly for a private company, and subsequent allotment did not alter the public purpose.
provisions: United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, Section 23(a)
United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, Section 24(h)
United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, Section 32
United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, Section 56
doctrines: Composite scheme doctrine
Public purpose in town planning
Implied powers of statutory authorities
Non-application of Land Acquisition Act when acquisition is under alternative statutory framework

card.dispute: The insurer cancelled the fire and flood insurance cover before issuing the policy, after floods began; the insured sued to enforce the cover.
issues_decided: Whether Condition (10) of the fire policy, allowing cancellation by either party, applied to the interim cover before policy issuance
Whether the cancellation was valid after risk had commenced due to rising floods
Whether the condition allowing unilateral cancellation was reasonable
holdings: A binding insurance contract arises upon acceptance and cover note issuance, and its terms include standard policy conditions, including cancellation rights.
The insurer can validly cancel coverage under a mutual cancellation clause before loss becomes inevitable, even after risk commencement, if cancellation occurs before certainty of loss.
A clause allowing either party to cancel insurance at will is reasonable and enforceable, as it reflects mutual contractual freedom and commercial practice.
doctrines: Contract formation by acceptance and cover note
Freedom of contract in insurance terms
Enforceability of mutual cancellation clauses
No judicial rewriting of commercial contracts

card.dispute: The heirs of Chinnayal (appellants) and the heirs of Neelayadakshi (respondents) fought over ownership of properties inherited and bequeathed under wills and gifts, and whether future mesne profits could be awarded despite no specific prayer in the plaint.
issues_decided: Whether the will executed by Chinnayal in September 1940 was validly proved and attested
Whether the respondents were the rightful reversionary heirs of Neelayadakshi
Whether the court could decree future mesne profits in the absence of a specific prayer in the plaint
holdings: The will was not proved because the attesting witness's signature was not properly established, and the appellants failed to prove due execution.
The respondents were entitled as next reversioners of Neelayadakshi, and the appellants could not raise a contrary plea at a late stage as no issue was framed on it earlier.
Where a suit is for possession and mesne profits, the court may decree future mesne profits under Order 20 Rule 12 CPC even without a specific prayer, as the rule allows discretionary relief.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 12
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rules 1, 2 and 7
doctrines: Rule of attestation under Indian Succession law
Doctrine of reversionary rights under Hindu law
Discretionary power of court to award future mesne profits under Order 20 Rule 12 CPC

card.dispute: The appellants' heirs were substituted after one appellant's death, but some heirs were later found to have been left out; the respondents claimed the appeal abated due to incomplete representation.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to failure to bring all legal heirs of a deceased appellant on record
Whether the heirs brought on record can represent the entire estate including those not impleaded
holdings: An appeal does not abate if not all heirs of a deceased appellant are brought on record, provided there is no fraud, collusion, or circumstances affecting fair trial.
The heirs who are brought on record fully represent the estate and bind absent heirs, unless there was a special defence that could not be raised in their absence.
The failure to include all heirs due to oversight or doubt about heirship is not fatal if the representation is bona fide and the trial was fair.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of representative capacity in abatement of suits or appeals
Doctrine of binding effect of decree on absent legal heirs
Principle of substantial justice over technical omissions

card.dispute: The appellant firm claimed a refund of customs duty, arguing that the State of Rajasthan was contractually bound to honor a tax concession granted by the former State of Bharatpur.
issues_decided: Whether the contractual liability of the former State of Bharatpur to grant a customs duty concession was binding on the successor State of Rajasthan.
Whether the Rajasthan (Regulation of Customs Duties) Ordinance No. 16 of 1949 superseded the alleged contractual obligation.
Whether Article 306 of the Constitution preserved the appellant's right to the concession.
holdings: A contractual liability of a former Indian State is not automatically binding on a successor State; it must be expressly or impliedly recognized by the successor, which Rajasthan did not do.
Even if there was implied recognition, the contractual liability was superseded by the Rajasthan (Regulation of Customs Duties) Ordinance No. 16 of 1949, which did not preserve the alleged rights.
Article 306 does not apply to contractual concessions but only to continuing taxation powers under agreements between the Union and Part B States; it does not protect private contractual claims.
provisions: Government of India Act, 1935, Seventh Schedule, List II, Item 21
Rajasthan (Regulation of Customs Duties) Ordinance No. 16 of 1949
doctrines: Successor state doctrine in Indian constitutional law
Legislative competence to alter contractual obligations of predecessor states
Doctrine of implied repeal
Principle that constitutional provisions must be expressly restrictive to limit legislative power

card.dispute: The mortgagor (Gyasi Ram) and mortgagee (Brij Bhushan Das) disputed whether a final decree for redemption should be granted when the mortgagor deposited the full amount due under the preliminary decree but fell short on an additional interest amount required during a stay of proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the additional interest paid during the stay of appeal, as per the appellant's undertaking, forms part of the 'amount adjudged due' under Order XXXIV, Rule 7(1)(c)(i) and (ii) of the CPC for the purpose of final decree in a mortgage redemption suit.
Whether a final decree for foreclosure should be passed when the shortfall in deposit was only in respect of interest arising from a stay order, not included in the preliminary decree.
holdings: The additional interest payable during the stay, based on the appellant’s undertaking, does not constitute 'subsequent costs, charges, expenses and interests' adjudged under Order XXXIV, Rule 7(1)(c)(i) and (ii) of the CPC, as it was not part of the preliminary decree and was not judicially adjudged.

The mortgagor is entitled to a final decree for redemption if he deposits the amount due under the preliminary decree and any adjudged subsequent interest, even if there is a shortfall in payment of interest arising solely from a stay order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure (Act 5 of 1908), Order XXXIV, Rule 7(1)(c)(i) and (ii)
Code of Civil Procedure (Act 5 of 1908), Order XXXIV, Rule 8(1)
doctrines: Adjudged amount doctrine
Final decree in mortgage redemption suits

card.dispute: The tenant, Gurbax Singh, fought for the right to purchase land from his landlord under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, after the landlord 'selected' the land under Section 5-B instead of 'reserving' it under Section 5(1).
issues_decided: Whether the Financial Commissioner erred in law by holding that no valid reservation was made under Section 5(1) of the Act.
Whether an area 'selected' under Section 5-B of the Act can be equated with a 'reserved area' under Section 5(1), thereby denying the tenant the right to purchase under Section 18.
holdings: A valid reservation under Section 5(1) requires verification of the landlord's application by the Patwari; absence of such verification means no valid reservation was made.
An area selected under Section 5-B is equivalent to a reserved area under the Act, and thus tenants have no right to purchase such land under Section 18.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 5(1)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 5-B
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
