Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Rules 3, 5, and 6
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to effectuate legislative purpose
Doctrine of equivalence in statutory processes (reservation vs. selection)
Presumption against defeating the purpose of a statute

card.dispute: The appellant contested the inclusion of a gifted house in his father's estate for estate duty, arguing the father was entirely excluded from possession after the gift.
issues_decided: Whether the donor was entirely excluded from possession and enjoyment of the property after the gift under Section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953
Whether the phrase 'by contract or otherwise' in Section 10 requires a legally enforceable arrangement for the donor's continued residence
Whether the 1965 amendment to Section 10 reflects the prior legislative intent regarding residence based on filial affection
Whether the entire property, held jointly with the wife, could be included in the deceased's estate
holdings: For Section 10 to apply, the donee must have assumed and retained possession to the entire exclusion of the donor, both conditions being cumulative.
The donor's continued residence, even without a legal right and based solely on filial affection, means he was not entirely excluded from possession and enjoyment.
The 1965 amendment to Section 10 is not retrospective and cannot be used to interpret the earlier version of the law.
Where property is jointly held but funded entirely by the deceased and income assessed in his name, the entire property may be included in his estate for duty purposes.
doctrines: Entire exclusion doctrine
Non-retrospectivity of amendments
Substance over form in property ownership

card.dispute: The company disputed whether a court-appointed Receiver could file a winding-up petition over a tax-related debt directed to be paid to the government, and whether the company had neglected to pay a debt under the Companies Act.
issues_decided: Whether a court can authorize a Receiver to file a winding-up petition under Order XL Rule 1(d) of the Civil Procedure Code
Whether a Receiver is a 'creditor' under Section 439(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1956
Whether the Receiver’s direction to pay the debt to the Additional Collector violated Section 434 of the Companies Act
Whether the company 'neglected to pay its debt' within the meaning of Section 434
holdings: A court can authorize a Receiver to file a winding-up petition under Order XL Rule 1(d) of the CPC if the Receiver acts in the interest of the estate and within judicial control.
A Receiver appointed by court, enforcing a claim on behalf of a creditor, can act as a 'creditor' under Section 439(1) of the Companies Act for winding-up purposes.
Directing payment to the Additional Collector under Section 46 of the Income-tax Act does not violate Section 434 of the Companies Act, as such payment fully discharges the company's liability.
Failure to pay the amount as directed, despite a valid statutory notice and no bona fide dispute, constitutes 'neglect to pay debt' under Section 434.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XL Rule 1(d)
doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory notice under Section 434 of the Companies Act
Doctrine of discharge of debt through statutory direction under tax law
Bona fide dispute as a bar to winding-up petitions
Judicial control over Receivers acting beyond their authority

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Assistant Charity Commissioner's authority to conduct a fresh inquiry into whether his trust was a public trust, after a prior finding under the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act had declared it not to be a public trust, but no entry of that finding was made in the register.
issues_decided: Whether the Registrar was legally bound to make an entry in the register of public trusts even if his finding was that the trust was not a public trust under the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, s. 7
Whether a right to file a suit under s. 8 of the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act arises from the finding itself or only from the entry in the register
Whether the prior inquiry under the Madhya Pradesh Act was 'anything duly done' and remained pending, thus being saved under s. 86(3)(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act after repeal
holdings: The Registrar is obligated to make an entry in the register of public trusts in accordance with his finding, whether positive or negative, under s. 7 of the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act.
The right to file a suit under s. 8 arises from the finding of the Registrar, not the entry; the entry is merely consequential, and failure to make it does not bar the right to challenge the finding.

The inquiry under the Madhya Pradesh Act was 'anything duly done' and remained pending due to the unfulfilled duty to enter the finding; thus, it was saved under s. 86(3)(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, and a fresh inquiry under the Bombay Act was not competent.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 5
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 6
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 7
Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of saving clauses
Doctrine of continuity of legal proceedings after repeal
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Finality of administrative findings

card.dispute: The Indian Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. sought to evict Biswanath Sonar, a monthly tenant, without giving six months' notice expiring with the end of a year of tenancy, while Sonar claimed protection under Section 9(1)(iii) of the Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 9(1)(iii) of the Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act applies to a tenant holding on a month-to-month basis who has occupied the land for more than one year
Whether the phrase 'end of a year of the tenancy' in Section 9(1)(iii) requires the notice to expire on the anniversary of the tenancy's commencement
holdings: Section 9(1)(iii) applies to tenants who have occupied land for more than one year, even if the tenancy is from month to month, and not only when there is a fixed term exceeding one year.
The phrase 'end of a year of the tenancy' means the anniversary of the commencement of the tenancy, and a valid notice must expire on that date after six months' notice, even for monthly tenancies.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on context
Protection of long-term tenants
Notice requirements for termination of periodic tenancies

card.dispute: The Jammu & Kashmir Bank reversed credit entries in a borrower's account after the State Government mistakenly made double payments; the borrower's successors challenged the bank's right to do so without consent.
issues_decided: Whether the bank could unilaterally reverse credit entries in a constituent's account at the instance of the State Government due to mistaken double payments.
Whether Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act applies to allow a bank to reverse payments made by mistake into a third party's account.
Whether the Government, as agent, could direct the bank to return money mistakenly credited to a constituent's account.
holdings: A bank cannot reverse credit entries in a constituent's account without the constituent's consent, even if the payment was made by mistake by the payer.
Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act does not apply when money is paid to a bank for credit to a third party's account; the money becomes the constituent's property upon credit.
The Government, as agent for payment, cannot compel the bank to return mistakenly paid funds by reversing entries without the constituent's authority.
doctrines: Section 72 mistake principle
Bank-customer relationship
Agency in payment contexts

card.dispute: The appellant investment trust claimed repayment of a mortgage debt from the respondent, whose land had vested with the State under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act; the respondent argued the debt was extinguished under the Orissa Money Lenders Act for having paid more than double the principal as interest.
issues_decided: Whether the Claims Officer under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act can consider the provisions of the Orissa Money Lenders Act while determining a claim.
Whether a debt is 'legally and justly due' under the Abolition Act if the interest received exceeds twice the principal, as prohibited by the Money Lenders Act.
holdings: The Claims Officer must determine if a claim is 'legally and justly due' and may consider whether it is barred by other laws, including the Orissa Money Lenders Act.
A claim for which more than double the principal has been paid as interest is extinguished under the Money Lenders Act and cannot be recognized as 'legally and justly due' under the Abolition Act.
doctrines: Exhaustive interpretation of statutory claims process
Integration of ameliorative legislation in statutory interpretation
Principle that a claim must be legally enforceable to be 'justly due'

card.dispute: The dispute was between a joint Hindu family and the Income Tax Commissioner over whether the family could be reassessed as a unit after a partition had been officially recorded under Section 25A of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu undivided family can be reassessed as a unit under Section 34 after an order under Section 25A(1) has recognized a partition.
Whether the Income-tax Officer can ignore a prior order under Section 25A(1) in a subsequent assessment year.
Whether the family continued to exist as a Hindu undivided family after the decree of partition.
holdings: Once an order under Section 25A(1) records a partition, the family ceases to be assessable as a Hindu undivided family unless that order is set aside by a competent authority.
An Income-tax Officer cannot reassess the family as undivided in a later year by ignoring a valid Section 25A(1) order, even if each assessment year is otherwise self-contained.
The existence of a Hindu undivided family for tax purposes ends upon a valid partition order, and mere co-ownership after partition does not revive joint family status.
doctrines: Finality of Section 25A(1) order
Assessment year as a self-contained unit
Doctrine of res judicata in tax proceedings (limited application)

card.dispute: Jamuna Singh challenged his conviction for abetting the burning of a hut under IPC s. 436 when the person he allegedly abetted (Jodha Singh) was acquitted of the offence.
issues_decided: Whether a person can be convicted of abetment under IPC s. 109 when the alleged principal offender has been acquitted of the substantive offence.
Whether the conviction for abetment under s. 436 read with s. 109 IPC can be sustained in the absence of the offence being committed in consequence of the abetment.
Whether the appellant's act of instigation alone, without the offence being committed by the person instigated, can constitute abetment under a different section of the IPC.
holdings: A person can be convicted of abetment even if the person alleged to have committed the offence is acquitted, provided the abetment was by instigation or conspiracy.

When the abetted offence is not committed in consequence of the abetment, the abettor cannot be convicted under s. 109 IPC but may be liable under s. 115 IPC if the offence is punishable with life imprisonment or death.
Instigation to commit an offence punishable with life imprisonment constitutes abetment under s. 115 IPC even if the offence is not actually committed by the person instigated.
Conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 IPC was legally unsustainable; it was altered to conviction under s. 436 read with s. 115 IPC with reduced sentence.
doctrines: Abetment as a distinct offence
Liability for abetment without commission of the substantive offence
Distinction between abetment by instigation/conspiracy and abetment by intentional aid
Legal effect of acquittal of principal offender on abettor's liability

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the State's recovery of a deficiency amount from a re-auctioned forest contract, claiming no enforceable contract existed under Article 299(1) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Article 299(1) of the Constitution bars the existence of an implied contract with the Government.
Whether the deficiency amount could be recovered as arrears of land revenue under Section 155(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code.
holdings: Article 299(1) of the Constitution prohibits implied contracts with the Government; any contract must strictly comply with its requirements to be enforceable.
Section 155(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code does not permit recovery of amounts based on an implied contract, as no valid contract existed under Article 299(1).
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, Section 155(b)
doctrines: Strict compliance with constitutional contract formalities
No implied contracts with the Government doctrine
Public interest in preventing unauthorized government liability

card.dispute: The appellant, an auction-purchaser, challenged the refusal to confirm a sale of immovable property executed under an ex parte money decree that was later set aside.
issues_decided: Whether a sale in execution of an ex parte money decree can be confirmed if the decree is subsequently set aside.
Whether the auction-purchaser, a stranger to the suit, is entitled to confirmation of the sale despite the decree being nullified.
holdings: A sale validly conducted in execution of a decree must be confirmed if no application to set it aside is made under Order XXI, Rules 89–91, even if the decree is later set aside.
The confirmation of a sale protects bona fide third-party purchasers; the reversal of a decree does not invalidate a completed execution sale to a stranger.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 89 to 92
doctrines: Protection of bona fide purchaser for value
Finality of execution sales
Statutory remedy under Order XXI, Rules 89–91 as exclusive

card.dispute: Collaterals of S in the 8th degree (appellants) fought with descendants of K (respondents) over possession of land left by S, where K claimed to be the formally adopted son of M, a collateral of S, and thus entitled to preferential inheritance under Jat custom in Amritsar District.
issues_decided: Whether the adoption of K was a formal adoption or a mere customary appointment of an heir under the Jat custom of Amritsar District.
Whether an adopted son, by way of customary appointment, can succeed to the property of collateral relatives of the adoptive father.
Whether the Riwaj-i-am records and judicial precedents support the right of an adopted son to inherit collaterally in the adoptive family.
holdings: Under the customary law of Jats in Amritsar District, a formal adoption that results in complete transplantation of the adopted son into the adoptive family entitles him to succeed to the collateral relatives of the adoptive father.
If the adoption is merely a customary appointment of an heir without severance of ties with the natural family, the adopted son has no right to succeed to the collaterals of the adoptive father.
The Riwaj-i-am and judicial decisions support the distinction between formal adoption and appointment of an heir, with only the former conferring collateral succession rights in the adoptive family.
The burden lies on the party claiming formal adoption to prove a clear intention to sever ties with the natural family and establish full integration into the adoptive family.
doctrines: Customary law recognition
Formal vs. informal adoption under custom
Complete transplantation doctrine in adoption
Presumption of correctness of Riwaj-i-am

card.dispute: The appellant claimed protection from eviction and fixity of tenure under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, asserting he was a kuzhikanamdar or kudiyiruppu holder, while the respondent sought redemption of the property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a kuzhikanamdar within the meaning of s. 2(28) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963
Whether the appellant was the holder of a kudiyiruppu under s. 2(26) of the Act
holdings: A transfer of land without the fruit-bearing trees standing on it and without the right to enjoy those trees does not constitute a kuzhikanam under s. 2(28), even if the transferee has the right to plant new trees.
The appellant is not a holder of kudiyiruppu as there was no evidence that the building was residential or that the land was necessary for its convenient enjoyment.
doctrines: Statutory definition interpretation
Exhaustive definition under statute

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a perpetual lease of ghatwali estate lands granted in 1873, claiming it was void for lack of sanction by the Board of Revenue and improper execution by the Deputy Commissioner.
issues_decided: Whether the Bengal Ghatwali Lands Act, 1859 overrides the Court of Wards Act, 1870 in respect of leases of ghatwali lands
Whether the lease was validly executed by the Deputy Commissioner on behalf of the Court of Wards
Whether the lease required sanction by the Board of Revenue under the Court of Wards Act, 1870
holdings: The Bengal Ghatwali Lands Act, 1859, being a special statute, prevails over the general provisions of the Court of Wards Act, 1870 regarding leases of ghatwali lands.

The lease was validly executed by the Deputy Commissioner on behalf of the Court of Wards, and the presumption under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act applies due to long unchallenged possession.
Even under the Court of Wards Act, 1870, the sanction of the Board of Revenue is presumed in light of official conduct and prolonged undisturbed possession.
provisions: Bengal Ghatwali Lands Act, 1859, Sections 1 and 2
The Court of Wards Act, 1870, Sections 8, 9, 13
doctrines: Generalia specialibus non derogant
Presumption of regularity in official acts

card.dispute: The appellants, including Lakhan Mahto, challenged their conviction and sentence by the High Court, which had altered Lakhan's conviction from constructive liability under Section 302/149 IPC to a substantive offence under Section 326 IPC despite his acquittal on the main charge under Section 302 IPC, and the State had not appealed that acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to alter Lakhan Mahto’s acquittal on the charge under Section 302 IPC and convict him under Section 326 IPC in an appeal filed only by the convicted person against his conviction under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether Section 149 IPC creates a substantive offence or merely enables vicarious liability?
Whether a conviction under Section 302/149 IPC can be altered to a conviction for a substantive offence like Section 326 IPC when the accused was acquitted of direct liability for that offence?
holdings: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to convert an acquittal into a conviction when the State did not appeal the acquittal, as appellate powers under Section 423(1)(b) CrPC are limited to the scope of the appeal and cannot override an unchallenged acquittal.
Section 149 IPC creates a distinct and substantive offence based on membership in an unlawful assembly with a common criminal object, not merely a rule of evidence or vicarious liability.

An appellate court cannot alter a conviction under Section 302/149 IPC to one under Section 326 IPC for a substantive offence when the accused was acquitted of the specific act constituting that offence, as it amounts to convicting for an uncharged and unproven act.
doctrines: Limited scope of appellate jurisdiction in criminal appeals
Substantive nature of offence under Section 149 IPC
Principle of double jeopardy and protection against conviction in absence of appeal by prosecution
Distinction between direct and constructive liability in criminal law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a registered release deed executed in favor of the respondents, claiming it was induced by misrepresentation and could not operate as a conveyance of title.
issues_decided: Whether the release deed was vitiated by misrepresentation, fraud, or undue influence
Whether a registered release deed without consideration can effectively transfer title to immovable property
Whether a release deed can transfer title to a person who has no prior interest in the property
holdings: The appellant failed to prove that the release deed was executed under misrepresentation, as he had legal advice, presented the deed for registration, and his plea was an afterthought.
A registered release deed without consideration can operate as a valid gift under Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, if it shows clear intention to transfer title and is properly attested.
A deed styled as a release can transfer title to a person having no prior interest in the property, provided the language evidences an intention to convey ownership.
doctrines: Doctrine of intention to transfer in conveyancing
Gift as a mode of transfer without consideration
Rule of attestation and proof of execution under the Evidence Act

card.dispute: Lachhi Ram appealed his conviction for murder by poisoning, arguing that the trial and high courts wrongly relied on the uncorroborated testimony of an approver.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below correctly applied the legal principles for appreciating the evidence of an approver.
Whether the approver's testimony was sufficiently corroborated to base a conviction upon.
holdings: The evidence of an approver must be reliable and inherently probable, and must be corroborated in material particulars to be the basis of a conviction.
The approver's testimony was reliable and sufficiently corroborated by independent evidence on key aspects of the prosecution's case, justifying the conviction.
doctrines: Corroboration of approver's evidence
Reliability of approver as a witness
Principle of cautious appreciation of accomplice testimony

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of shares in inam villages, claimed compensation under the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, after their inams were abolished, arguing they were entitled to compensation for loss of rights over land and assessment collection, while the Revenue Tribunal and Government denied liability under statutory bars.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' inams were grants of land revenue (second category under s. 2(1)(e)(ii)) or grants of villages with partial exemption from land revenue (first category under s. 2(1)(e)(i))
Whether the appellants were entitled to compensation under s. 17(1) of the Act for loss of right to recover assessment from inferior holders
Whether the appellants suffered compensable loss due to extinction of rights of reversion and forfeiture
holdings: The inams were grants of villages with partial exemption from land revenue, not grants of land revenue, and thus fell under the first category in s. 2(1)(e)(i), attracting the bar of s. 17(5).

The loss from abolition of the right to recover assessment from inferior holders is not compensable under s. 17(1) because it stems from making exempt land liable to full assessment, which is barred by s. 17(5).
The appellants failed to prove any actual loss from extinction of rights of reversion and forfeiture, and such ephemeral rights do not entitle them to compensation under the Act.
provisions: Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, Section 2(1)(e)
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, Section 5
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, Section 10
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, Section 17(1)
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1953, Section 17(5)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of compensation bars
Distinction between grant of land and grant of land revenue
Requirement of demonstrable loss for compensation claims

card.dispute: The appellant claimed possession of land from respondents who were tenants inducted by a usufructuary mortgagee, after the mortgage was redeemed, but the respondents resisted eviction citing protection under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether tenants inducted by a usufructuary mortgagee can continue in possession after redemption of the mortgage?
Whether the respondents acquired the status of Khatedars under Section 15 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, and thus gained statutory protection against eviction?
Whether the appellant could eject the respondents on the ground that they were trespassers after redemption?
holdings: Tenants inducted by a mortgagee do not automatically lose possession upon redemption if statutory rights have accrued during the mortgage period.
Section 15 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, conferred Khatedar status on the respondents, entitling them to statutory protection under Section 161 of the Act.
The respondents were not trespassers within the meaning of the Act, as they were lawfully inducted tenants whose rights were preserved by statute.
doctrines: Statutory vesting of rights
Protection against arbitrary eviction
Limitation of mortgagee's power to create perpetual interests

card.dispute: The mortgagee sought to withdraw a claim filed under the Bihar Land Reforms Act after part of the mortgaged property vested in the State and part did not, leading to a dispute over whether he could pursue remedies under ordinary law for non-vested properties.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgagee who filed a claim under Section 14 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act for vested property is barred from pursuing remedies under ordinary law for non-vested portions of the mortgaged property.
Whether filing a claim under Section 14 constitutes an irrevocable election of remedies, preventing withdrawal of the claim.
Whether the doctrine of election applies when a mortgaged property consists of both vested and non-vested properties.
holdings: The Bihar Land Reforms Act only bars civil court remedies for properties that have vested in the State; it does not take away the mortgagee’s right to pursue remedies under ordinary law for non-vested properties.
Filing a claim under Section 14 does not amount to an irrevocable election of remedies; the mortgagee may withdraw the claim and pursue alternative remedies for non-vested properties.
The doctrine of election does not apply in this context because the Act does not confer jurisdiction over non-vested properties or prohibit parallel remedies for them.
doctrines: Doctrine of Election
Principle of Marshalling

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of land purchased from a person later declared an evacuee, and sued for declaration of title, which the Custodian resisted on the ground that the suit was barred by the Evacuee Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaration of ownership by a transferee of an evacuee is barred by Section 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950.
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decide title when the property has been declared evacuee property under the Act.
holdings: A suit by a transferee claiming ownership of property from an evacuee is barred under Section 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act if the property admittedly belonged to the evacuee and the claimant failed to appear before the Evacuee Property authorities after notice.
The civil court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate on the status of evacuee property where the Act provides an alternative remedy through appeal and revision under Sections 24 and 27.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 46
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 24
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
Exhaustion of statutory remedies
Doctrine of constructive notice under Section 53A

card.dispute: The appellant contested the inclusion of interest received from Ceylon's Estate Duty Authorities in his taxable income for 1958-59, claiming it was a capital or casual receipt exempt from tax.
issues_decided: Whether the interest received under a foreign court decree on refunded estate duty is taxable as income under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the interest receipt is exempt under Section 4(3)(vii) as a casual and non-recurring receipt
Whether the interest received is a capital receipt as part of a deceased's estate
holdings: Interest paid under a Ceylon Supreme Court decree on refunded estate duty is taxable income under the Indian Income-tax Act, as it represents compensation for delayed use of money and has the quality of income, not capital.
The interest receipt is not casual or non-recurring merely because it is a lump sum; it accrued de die in diem and was foreseeable, thus falling outside the exemption in Section 4(3)(vii).
The appellant cannot claim the receipt as a capital sum from a deceased estate at this stage, as the issue was not raised before the Appellate Tribunal or referred to the High Court.
doctrines: Interest as revenue receipt
Casual and non-recurring receipt doctrine
Limits of High Court's jurisdiction under tax reference

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's refusal of a certificate of fitness to appeal against its order dismissing a petition under Articles 226 and 227, which had upheld the Commissioner's jurisdiction to set aside a debt discharge in land reform proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution constitutes a 'civil proceeding' for the purpose of appeal under Article 133(1)
Whether an order dismissing a petition under Article 226 is a 'final order' within the meaning of Article 133(1)
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing a certificate of fitness under Article 133(1)
holdings: Proceedings under Article 226 are 'civil proceedings' when they involve the determination of civil rights, even though they are in the High Court's extraordinary original jurisdiction.

An order dismissing a petition under Article 226 is a final order if it conclusively decides the controversy before the High Court, particularly on the issue of jurisdiction, irrespective of whether it affects the underlying dispute.
The High Court erred in refusing the certificate of fitness because the order was a final order in a civil proceeding involving a substantial question as to the jurisdiction of a tribunal.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 19(1)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 22
doctrines: Finality of orders in writ proceedings
Civil proceeding under Article 133
Extraordinary original jurisdiction under Article 226
Appealability of interlocutory orders affecting jurisdiction

card.dispute: The landlord (S. Rama Iyer) and tenant (Sundarasa Ponnapoondar) disputed whether a cultivating tenancy relationship existed, affecting the Revenue Court's jurisdiction to decide on rent deposit.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had revisional jurisdiction under Section 6B of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act read with Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to review the Revenue Court's finding on the existence of a tenancy relationship.
Whether the Revenue Court's determination that no cultivating tenancy existed was a final finding immune from revision.
holdings: The High Court can revise a Revenue Court's decision if it erroneously refuses to exercise jurisdiction based on a preliminary fact like the existence of a tenancy.

The existence of a landlord-tenant relationship is a preliminary question for jurisdiction; an erroneous finding on it is revisable under Section 115(b) of the CPC when the court fails to exercise jurisdiction it legally possesses.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 6B
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction of High Court
Preliminary fact doctrine
Jurisdictional error doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a mortgage foreclosure suit filed by the adopted son of the mortgagee, which was later amended to include additional plaintiffs and defendants after the limitation period had expired.
issues_decided: Whether the addition of new parties under Order 1, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure affects the period of limitation under Section 22 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit for foreclosure was barred by limitation when deemed to be instituted as regards the added parties
Whether Article 147 of the Indian Limitation Act applies to a suit for foreclosure under an anomalous mortgage
holdings: Section 22 of the Indian Limitation Act applies to the addition of any new plaintiff or defendant, and the suit is deemed to be instituted as to them on the date they are added.
A suit added under Order 1, Rule 10 is barred by limitation if the cause of action was already time-barred on the date of addition, and no benefit of earlier institution date can be claimed.
Article 147 of the Indian Limitation Act applies only to English mortgages; a suit for foreclosure under an anomalous mortgage is governed by Article 132.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10(1) and (2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
Part-B States (Laws) Act, 1951, Section 6 and Section 30
doctrines: Deemed institution of suit for new parties under Section 22 of the Limitation Act
No extension of limitation period for added parties without statutory saving
Distinction between English and anomalous mortgages in limitation law

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming title to garden land, sued to recover possession from the third defendant who held a lease granted by the executrix of the testator's will; the dispute centered on whether the executrix had power to lease the property despite specific testamentary provisions.
issues_decided: Whether clause 4 of the will, authorizing the executrix to sell property for marriage expenses, restricted her power to lease the property under the Probate and Administration Act, 1881
Whether the executrix's power to deal with immovable property was limited by the express terms of the will
holdings: The specific authorization in clause 4 of the will to sell property for marriage expenses did not restrict the executrix's general power to lease property in the course of administration.

Under Section 90(1) of the Probate and Administration Act, 1881, the executrix retains full power to deal with property unless the will contains clear language restricting such power, which was absent here.
doctrines: Expressum facit cessare tacitum does not apply to restrict powers of an executrix without clear language
Presumption against implied restriction on testamentary powers under Section 90(1)

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the District Judge's jurisdiction to transfer a reference from a Magistrate under Section 146(1) Cr.P.C. to another Civil Court, arguing the reference was to a persona designata and that civil procedure did not apply.
issues_decided: Whether the reference under Section 146(1) Cr.P.C. is to a persona designata or to a constituted civil court.
Whether the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code, particularly Section 24, apply to a proceeding arising from a Magistrate's reference under Section 146(1) Cr.P.C.
holdings: The reference under Section 146(1) Cr.P.C. is to a civil court as a judicial body, not to a persona designata, because the statute refers to the court, not the individual judge.

Section 24 C.P.C. applies to transfer proceedings arising from a Section 146(1) Cr.P.C. reference, as the term 'proceeding' includes all judicial adjudications before a subordinate court, not merely civil suits.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure (Act 5 of 1898), Section 146(1)
Code of Civil Procedure (Act 5 of 1908), Section 24
Code of Civil Procedure (Act 5 of 1908), Section 141
doctrines: Persona designata doctrine
General applicability of civil procedure to proceedings before civil courts unless expressly excluded
Broad interpretation of 'proceeding' in statutory context

card.dispute: A Hindu widow claimed partition and separate possession of her husband's share in a coparcenary property, leading to a dispute over whether her interest became heritable and extinguished the coparceners' right of survivorship.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow, under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, acquires a defined and heritable interest in coparcenary property upon claiming partition, even without physical division or exclusive possession.
Whether the right of survivorship of other coparceners in the husband's share is extinguished upon the widow's claim for partition.
Whether the interest acquired by a widow under Section 3(2) of the Act devolves on her husband's heirs upon her death, even if partition is not completed by metes and bounds.
holdings: A Hindu widow acquires the same interest as her husband in coparcenary property upon his death under Section 3(2) of the 1937 Act, and this interest becomes defined and vested upon her claim for partition.
The right of coparceners to claim the deceased coparcener’s interest by survivorship is extinguished once the widow makes an unequivocal claim for partition.
The widow’s interest, once defined by a partition claim, devolves upon the heirs of her husband upon her death, even without physical division or exclusive possession.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(2)
Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(3)
doctrines: Right of survivorship under Mitakshara coparcenary
Statutory right to partition for Hindu widows
Vesting of interest upon demand for partition

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an auction sale of its factory, claiming it was a nullity due to non-compliance with payment rules, and contested the appealability of the order setting aside the sale.
issues_decided: Whether an order setting aside an auction sale as a nullity is a final decree appealable under the Civil Procedure Code
Whether such an order falls within the scope of 'execution proceedings' under Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code
holdings: An order setting aside an auction sale as a nullity is a final determination of the rights between the judgment-debtor and the auction-purchaser, and thus constitutes a decree appealable under Section 96 of the Civil Procedure Code.
Such an order relates to the execution, discharge, or satisfaction of a decree and falls within Section 47, making it appealable even if a resale is ordered.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 84
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
doctrines: Finality of decree
Rights of auction-purchaser
Execution proceedings under Section 47

card.dispute: The appellant, a cardamom plantation owner, challenged the inclusion of stock sold in the assessment year in his taxable agricultural income, arguing it was already taxed when produced in prior years.
issues_decided: Whether agricultural produce itself constitutes income when received, or only upon sale, use, or consumption.
Whether income from sale of agricultural produce accumulated from previous years is taxable in the year of sale.
holdings: Agricultural produce does not become income merely upon receipt; income arises when the produce is sold, consumed, or used in the assessee's business.
Income from the sale of agricultural produce, even if grown in prior years, is taxable in the year of sale and is not exempt on the ground that it may have been taxed earlier.
provisions: Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955, Section 3
Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955, Section 4
Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955, Section 65
doctrines: Definition of income as monetary return from disposal or use
Taxability based on realization, not production

card.dispute: The landlord (Rao Nihalkaran) sought to eject the tenant (Ramgopal) after terminating his tenancy for personal cultivation, but the tenant claimed occupancy rights under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, despite prior termination of tenancy and pending ejectment proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether a person whose tenancy was terminated before the commencement of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code could be considered a 'tenant' under Section 185(1)(ii)(a) and acquire occupancy rights
Whether Sections 261 and 262(2) of the Code exclude the application of Section 185 in pending ejectment proceedings
holdings: A person whose tenancy was lawfully terminated before the Code's commencement can still be considered a 'tenant' under Section 185(1)(ii)(a) if they were in possession as a tenant and continued to hold the land until the Code came into force.

Sections 261 and 262(2) do not preserve pre-commencement ejectment rights; pending civil suits must respect the statutory grant of occupancy rights under Section 185, and procedural continuity does not override substantive rights created by the Code.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 185(1)(ii)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 261
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 262(2)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'tenant' to include those with terminated tenancies for the purpose of conferring occupancy rights
Preservation of accrued rights under repealed laws does not apply when the right was not created under the repealed statute
Procedural saving clauses do not nullify substantive rights conferred by new legislation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the dismissal of his appeals on the ground of res judicata after two of the respondent's appeals were dismissed on preliminary grounds, leading to a finality of the trial court's decision on title.
issues_decided: Whether the dismissal of appeals on preliminary grounds like limitation or failure to print records results in res judicata for common issues decided on merits in connected suits?
Whether a decision in one of multiple connected suits becomes res judicata in appeals from other suits between the same parties involving the same issues?
Whether the High Court's dismissal of two appeals confirmed the trial court’s decision on title, thereby barring re-litigation in the remaining appeals?
holdings: Where two appeals arise from suits with common issues and one appeal is dismissed on a preliminary ground, the dismissal confirms the trial court’s decision on merits and operates as res judicata.
The doctrine of res judicata applies when the effect of an appellate dismissal is to leave the trial court’s decision on a common issue unaltered and final.
Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars re-hearing of issues already finally decided, even if the finality arises from dismissal of an appeal on procedural grounds.
doctrines: res judicata
substance over form
finality of judgment

card.dispute: The appellants (decree-holders) challenged the High Court's reduction of interest in a mortgage suit, arguing that the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act did not apply because the suit was no longer pending when only an appeal was ongoing.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'suit' in Section 6 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act includes an appeal pending after a preliminary decree?
Whether the amended Section 3 of the Usurious Loans Act, as extended by the Punjab Act, applies to reduce interest in an appeal stage?
holdings: The word 'suit' includes an appeal because an appeal is a continuation of the original cause and does not create a new one; a preliminary decree does not terminate the suit.

Section 6 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act applies retrospectively to pending appeals, so courts must apply the amended Section 3 of the Usurious Loans Act to limit interest to 7.5% even at the appellate stage.
provisions: Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, Section 5
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, Section 6
doctrines: Retrospective application of statutes
Continuation of suit doctrine
Distinction between procedural and substantive laws

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a municipal tax enhancement and rejection of her review petition by an officer appointed after the municipality's supersession.
issues_decided: Whether the officer had jurisdiction to reject the review petition under Section 117(1) of the Bihar and Orissa Municipal Act, 1922 after the municipality was superseded.
Whether the enhancement of assessment under Section 107(1)(c) was valid in the absence of proof that the original assessment was incorrect due to fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.
holdings: The officer lacked jurisdiction to decide the review petition because the Committee under Section 117(1) could not be replaced by a single officer; only the Commissioners' roles could be substituted under Section 386(1)(b), not the statutory Committee itself.

The enhancement of the assessment under Section 107(1)(c) was invalid because the municipal authorities failed to prove the original assessment was incorrect due to fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake, as required by law.
provisions: Bihar and Orissa Municipal Act, 1922, Section 107(1)(c)
Bihar and Orissa Municipal Act, 1922, Section 117(1)
Bihar and Orissa Municipal Act, 1922, Section 386(1)(b)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation to avoid rendering a provision unworkable
Rule that jurisdiction must strictly conform to statutory authority
Burden of proof on the authority seeking to amend an assessment under Section 107(1)(c)

card.dispute: The current trustees of a temple sued former trustees for rendition of accounts, and the dispute centered on whether such a suit was maintainable under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether ex-trustees are liable to render accounts of their management to subsequent trustees regardless of allegations of negligence or willful default.
Whether Section 93 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 bars a civil suit for rendition of accounts against ex-trustees.
Whether Chapter VII of the Act provides an exclusive mechanism for resolving disputes over accounts, thereby excluding civil court jurisdiction.
holdings: Every trustee, including an ex-trustee, is legally bound to render accounts of their management irrespective of any allegation of negligence or willful default, as accountability is inherent in the fiduciary role.

Section 93 does not bar a suit for rendition of accounts in civil court if the matter is not covered by specific provisions of the Act, as it only restricts suits on matters for which the Act provides a remedy.
Chapter VII of the Act does not provide an exhaustive or exclusive mechanism for disputes over rendition of accounts by ex-trustees and does not oust the jurisdiction of civil courts in such matters.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 93
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 74
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Chapter VI
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Chapter VII
doctrines: Fiduciary accountability of trustees
Exhaustive vs. supplementary statutory machinery
Interpretation of ouster clauses in administrative statutes
Savings of common law remedies unless expressly excluded

card.dispute: The State of Assam challenged whether a Mauzadar, a revenue official in the Assam Valley, held a civil post under the State and was thus entitled to protection under Article 311(2) of the Constitution against dismissal without inquiry.
issues_decided: Whether a Mauzadar in the Assam Valley holds a civil post under the State within the meaning of Article 311(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the absence of a fixed salary or full-time employment disqualifies a position from being a 'civil post' under Article 311.
holdings: A Mauzadar in the Assam Valley is a holder of a civil post under the State and entitled to protection under Article 311(2) due to the master-servant relationship with the State, including rights of appointment, control, and dismissal.
A civil post need not carry a definite rate of pay or require full-time service; part-time or commission-based roles can still constitute a civil post if they involve state duties and control.
provisions: Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 69
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 124
Assam Land and Revenue Regulation, 1886, Section 53(A)
doctrines: Master-servant relationship test for determining civil post
Functional test for existence of a civil post under the Constitution
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on context and function

card.dispute: The appellants, mortgagees of Dhanakoti Ammal's property, challenged the High Court's reduction of the interest rate from 15% to 10% compound interest and further to 6% from the date of suit, seeking enforcement of their mortgage claims against the property now held by the respondent purchaser.
issues_decided: What rate of interest is reasonable under Section 3 of the Usurious Loans (Madras Amendment) Act, 1937, considering the circumstances of the loan transaction?
Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the rate of interest to 10% compound with yearly rests?
Whether the High Court could lawfully reduce the interest rate to 6% from the date of filing the suit?
holdings: Under Section 3 of the Usurious Loans (Madras Amendment) Act, 1937, courts must assess a reasonable interest rate by considering the security, debtor's financial condition, repayment risks, and compounding terms at the time of the original transaction.

The High Court correctly reduced the interest to 10% compound with yearly rests, as the security was not inadequate and the risk from a potential title challenge was not serious given prior judicial rejection of such claims.
The High Court had discretion to reduce interest pendente lite to 6%, even without stating reasons, especially given the long delay in filing suit and the substantial interest already accrued.
doctrines: Reasonable interest rate determination based on transactional circumstances
Judicial discretion in awarding interest pendente lite
Balancing creditor risk and borrower protection in usurious loan cases

card.dispute: The State of Bihar prosecuted S. K. Roy for failing to pay provident fund contributions, alleging he was an employer as the owner of a coal mine, which Roy denied.
issues_decided: Whether S. K. Roy was the owner of a coal mine within the meaning of Section 2(b) of the Mines Act, 1952.
Whether the coke plant owned by Roy fell within the definition of a coal mine under the Coal Mines Provident Fund and Bonus Schemes Act, 1948.
holdings: The respondent was not the owner of a coal mine under Section 2(b) of the Mines Act, 1952, as his coke plant, though adjacent to a coal mine, was not used for coal extraction and did not belong to the mine.
For machinery, works, or sidings to be part of a coal mine, they must belong to and be under the same ownership as the mine; mere physical adjacency is insufficient.
provisions: Coal Mines Provident Fund and Bonus Schemes Act, 1948, Section 2(c)
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation requiring harmonious construction
Use of subsequent legislation to interpret ambiguous prior law
Doctrine of 'appurtenance' in defining what belongs to a statutory entity

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh sought to acquire the Pargana Agori under land reform laws, while the Raja claimed it was not an 'estate' liable to acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether Pargana Agori constituted an 'estate' within the meaning of Art. 31A(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution
Whether the acquisition was for agrarian reform purposes under Art. 31A
holdings: A grant of land by the British for services rendered, in the nature of a jagir or inam, constitutes an 'estate' under Art. 31A(2)(a)(i), even if based on restoration of prior rights.
The acquisition of such jagir or inam lands is a necessary step in agrarian reforms and is protected under Art. 31A of the Constitution.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 3(8)
doctrines: Doctrine of classification under Article 31A
Principle of retrospective validation of land reform laws
Broad interpretation of 'jagir' and 'estate' in agrarian reform context

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh sued Kaluram, the surety for a forest contractor who defaulted on payments, to recover dues; Kaluram claimed he was discharged because the State allowed the contractor to remove forest produce before payment, thereby losing the security.
issues_decided: Whether the surety was discharged under Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act due to the creditor parting with the security without consent
Whether the State had a security interest in the forest produce before full payment by the contractor
Whether inaction by forest authorities in preventing removal of goods constitutes parting with security
holdings: A surety is entitled to the benefit of all securities the creditor holds at the time of the suretyship contract, and is discharged to the extent the creditor loses or parts with such security without the surety’s consent.

The State had a valid security interest in the forest produce through a statutory charge under Section 83 of the Madhya Pradesh Forest Act and the right to prevent removal until payment, which constituted real and substantial security.

Allowing the contractor to remove forest produce without payment amounted to parting with security, even without formal documentation, because the State lost practical control and enforcement power over the collateral.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Forest Contract Rules, Rule 29(2), Rule 33(2), Rule 16
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable subrogation
Surety discharged on loss of security
Creditor's duty to preserve collateral

card.dispute: The appellants sold certain lands in Punjab, and the respondents claimed a right of pre-emption; the dispute centered on whether that right extended to different lands allotted to the appellants in consolidation proceedings in lieu of the sold lands.
issues_decided: Whether the right of pre-emption can be exercised over land allotted in consolidation proceedings in lieu of the originally sold land
Whether Section 24 of the Patiala and East Punjab States Union Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act preserves pre-emption rights over consolidated land
Whether Section 25 of the Act excludes other rights, such as pre-emption, from attaching to consolidated land
holdings: Section 24 preserves all rights and obligations, including disabilities like pre-emption, attaching to original holdings, so pre-emption rights extend to land allotted in consolidation.
The right of pre-emption, being an incident of property, runs with the land and applies to consolidated land allotted in lieu of the original holding.
Section 25, dealing specifically with leases and encumbrances, does not negate the continuation of pre-emption rights under Section 24, as pre-emption is an inherent incident of ownership.
provisions: Patiala and East Punjab States Union Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, Section 24
Patiala and East Punjab States Union Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, Section 25
doctrines: Pre-emption as an incident of property
Burden and benefit of pre-emption running with the land
Statutory interpretation of rights and obligations under consolidation laws

card.dispute: The appellants, members of a joint Hindu family, contested whether they qualified as 'displaced debtors' under the Displaced Persons (Debts Adjustment) Act, 1951, to adjust debts owed to the State Bank of India after migrating from Harunabad (now in Pakistan).
issues_decided: Whether a person must have had an exclusive place of residence in Pakistan to qualify as a displaced debtor under the Act
Whether 'place of residence' requires permanent or exclusive dwelling
Whether displacement of a business equates to displacement of a person under the Act
Whether members of a joint family can be deemed displaced based on the residence of some family members
holdings: A person can be a displaced debtor even if they had residences in both India and Pakistan, provided they were displaced from a residence in Pakistan due to partition or civil disturbances.
‘Place of residence’ means a dwelling house, not necessarily permanent or exclusive; a person may have multiple places of residence.
The Act contemplates displacement of a person, not merely the closure or displacement of a business; personal displacement is required.
Mere membership in a joint family carrying on business in Pakistan does not automatically make all members displaced debtors without proof of individual residence in Pakistan.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'place of residence'
Doctrine of personal displacement vs. business displacement
Burden of proof in establishing status as a displaced debtor

card.dispute: The landlord sued for full rent despite delivering only two of three bedrooms; the tenant refused to pay any rent, claiming a right to suspend payment entirely.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to suspend payment of the entire rent due to partial non-delivery of premises
Whether the tenant should instead be liable to pay a proportionate part of the rent
Whether the court should allow apportionment of rent in the absence of a specific plea
holdings: A tenant is not automatically entitled to suspend the entire rent when given partial possession; the right to suspend depends on the facts of each case.
Where a tenant enjoys a substantial portion of the leased premises without much inconvenience, equity requires payment of a proportionate rent.
Courts may allow apportionment of rent even without a specific plea if it is necessary to prevent inequity, especially when the landlord failed to deliver full possession.
provisions: Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, Section 38
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable apportionment of rent
Suspension of rent as a discretionary remedy
Principle of justice, equity and good conscience

card.dispute: The Union of India enacted a law to acquire the undertaking of The Metal Corporation of India Ltd., and the dispute was whether the method of determining compensation under the law violated the constitutional requirement of just compensation under Article 31(2).
issues_decided: Whether the Metal Corporation of India (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1965 provides for compensation as required by Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the principles laid down in the Act for determining compensation are relevant to the value of the property at the time of acquisition.
Whether the compensation principles in the Act are so arbitrary or illusory as to render the law unconstitutional.
holdings: A law acquiring property must provide for compensation that represents a 'just equivalent' of the property taken, either by fixing the amount or specifying valid principles for its determination.
Principles of compensation that are unrelated to the market value of the property at or around the time of acquisition are invalid under Article 31(2), even if they are mechanically applied.

The use of cost price for unused machinery and written-down value under tax law for used machinery are irrelevant to actual market value and thus fail to meet constitutional standards of compensation.
When a key component of compensation (like machinery) is assessed by invalid principles, and the undertaking is acquired as a whole, the entire compensation scheme fails, rendering the Act void.
doctrines: Just equivalent doctrine
Fraud on power doctrine
Non-severability of invalid compensation clauses in acquisition laws

card.dispute: The Thirunagar Panchayat sued the Madurai Co-operative House Construction Society to restrain it from obstructing the Panchayat's statutory duties over roads and public amenities in a housing colony, claiming these vested in the Panchayat under the Madras Village Panchayats Act.
issues_decided: Whether parks, playgrounds, schools, libraries, and other amenities created by the Society in the colony vest in the Panchayat under Section 58 of the Madras Village Panchayats Act, 1950
Whether dedication of such amenities to public use brings them within the scope of Section 58
holdings: Section 58 of the Madras Village Panchayats Act, 1950 only vests property in the Panchayat if it belongs to or has been customarily administered for villagers; it does not apply to amenities created by a private society.
Dedication of amenities to public use does not trigger vesting under Section 58; customary title or customary administration is required.
doctrines: Customary vesting of communal property
Statutory interpretation based on grammatical structure and context

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision that declared the Metal Corporation of India (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1965, unconstitutional for violating Article 31 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Metal Corporation of India (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1965, provides for 'compensation' within the meaning of Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the principles for determining compensation under the Act are relevant and non-arbitrary as required by Article 31(2).
Whether the invalidity of compensation principles for machinery renders the entire Act unconstitutional.
holdings: A law acquiring property must provide for 'compensation' as a just equivalent of the property taken, either by fixing the amount or specifying relevant principles leading to such a result.
Principles that fix compensation based on cost price or written-down value under tax law, without reference to market value at acquisition, are irrelevant and arbitrary under Article 31(2).

When a major part of an undertaking (like machinery) is compensated under invalid principles, and the undertaking is acquired as a unit, the entire acquisition law fails for lack of constitutional compensation.
provisions: The Metal Corporation of India (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1965
doctrines: Just equivalent doctrine
Doctrine of severability
Judicial scrutiny of compensation principles

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that certain premises in Madurai were private family property, while the respondent contended it was a public temple under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether the subject matter of the dispute—whether the property was private or a public temple—was capable of valuation for the purpose of appeal under Article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution
Whether the High Court was correct in refusing a certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court on the ground that the property had no market value
holdings: The subject matter of the dispute must be valued based on the plaintiff's claim in the plaint, and since the appellant claimed the property as private and alienable, it was capable of valuation.

The High Court erred in holding the property incapable of valuation merely because it was alleged to be a temple, as the claim of private ownership rendered it potentially alienable and thus assessable in monetary terms.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 1
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927, Section 84(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 45, Rule 1
doctrines: Valuation of subject matter for appellate jurisdiction
Principle of determining jurisdiction based on the plaintiff's claim
Doctrine of alienability of private religious property

card.dispute: The appellants, former jagirdars, challenged the dismissal of their appeals for non-prosecution and the rejection of their restoration applications as time-barred by the Revenue Tribunal under the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the Revenue Tribunal had the power to dismiss appeals for non-prosecution under the Jagirs Abolition Act, or was bound to decide them on merits even in case of default.
Whether the applications for restoration of dismissed appeals were filed within the prescribed limitation period under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958.
holdings: The Tribunal had no power to dismiss appeals for non-prosecution; it was obligated by s. 17(1) read with s. 20 of the Jagirs Abolition Act to decide every appeal on merits and record its decision, even if the appellant defaulted.

The applications for restoration were filed within thirty days of receiving the dismissal order, as required by Regulation 21, and were therefore within time; the Tribunal erred in treating them as time-barred.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, Section 13
Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, Section 17(1)
Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, Section 20
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Mandatory interpretation of statutory duties
Finality of tribunal decisions
Limitation period calculation from date of receipt of order

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax contested whether the income of the Kasturbai Walchand Trust became exempt from tax after the beneficiary surrendered her interest, arguing the trust was not yet wholly charitable.
issues_decided: Whether the surrender of the beneficiary's interest in the trust income made the trust wholly charitable from that date, exempting its income from tax under s. 4(3)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922.
Whether the exemption under s. 4(3)(i) depends on the immediate application of income for charitable purposes or includes accumulation for such purposes.
holdings: The surrender of the beneficiary’s interest extinguished her rights, causing the trust to be held wholly for charitable purposes from that date, making the income exempt under s. 4(3)(i).
Exemption under s. 4(3)(i) applies even if income is accumulated for future charitable use, not only when immediately applied.
doctrines: Doctrine of accumulation for charitable purposes
Doctrine of valid surrender of beneficial interest by a competent beneficiary

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued the second defendant for damages under an indemnity bond after the sale of a minor's share in land was set aside, claiming loss despite retaining possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs sustained a loss entitling them to damages under the indemnity bond when they retained possession of the property?
Whether the purchase of the disputed share in a court auction by the plaintiffs' brother-in-law affected their claim for damages?
What is the proper measure of damages for breach of warranty of title under an indemnity bond when possession is not lost?
holdings: No cause of action for damages arises under an indemnity bond or warranty of title unless the vendee is dispossessed or suffers actual loss.
Retention of possession, even after the sale is set aside, means no failure of consideration and thus no right to recover the purchase price.
The plaintiffs are entitled only to actual pecuniary losses incurred, such as expenses in defending title and amounts paid in court auctions, not hypothetical or full consideration losses.
provisions: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 124 (Contract of Indemnity)
Limitation Act, Article 97 (Suit for compensation for breach of contract)
doctrines: Failure of consideration
Actual loss rule in indemnity claims
Possession as fulfillment of contractual obligation in sale of property

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a tenant challenged the landlord's execution of an eviction decree without obtaining fresh permission under the amended Section 19 of the Slum Areas Act, after the original execution application was filed pre-amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 19 of the Slum Areas Act applies retrospectively to pending execution proceedings.
Whether a fresh permission under the amended Section 19 is required to continue an execution application filed before the amendment.
holdings: The amendment to Section 19 does not apply to pending execution proceedings unless expressly or by necessary implication intended to do so.
An execution application filed before the amendment, with prior permission under the old law, remains valid and does not require fresh permission under the amended Section 19.
provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Amendment Act, 1964, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective operation of amendments
Doctrine of vested rights in pending proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants sought to redeem their 3/4th share in mortgaged land, but the respondents claimed the suit was barred by limitation due to lack of acknowledgment extending the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the statements relied upon by the appellants constituted acknowledgments of subsisting mortgage liability under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the suit for redemption was barred by limitation
holdings: An acknowledgment under Section 19 must relate to a subsisting liability and be made with the intention of admitting that jural relationship; mere reference to a mortgage does not amount to acknowledgment.
The documents relied upon were not made with the intention of admitting a subsisting mortgage liability and thus did not extend the limitation period; the suit was barred by limitation.
doctrines: Doctrine of acknowledgment under Section 19 of the Limitation Act
Intention to admit jural relationship must be clear or reasonably inferable from the statement and surrounding circumstances

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed a decree but the plaintiff, Daulat Ram, died during proceedings and his legal representatives were not brought on record, raising the question of whether the appeal could continue against the other respondents.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abates due to the death of the plaintiff and non-impleadment of his legal representatives.
Whether the appeal can proceed against the surviving respondents despite the abatement as against the deceased.
holdings: An appeal abates in its entirety if it cannot proceed without conflicting with a decree that has become final due to the death of a party.
If a decision in favor of the appellant against surviving respondents would contradict the binding decree affecting the deceased party, the appeal must abate totally.
doctrines: Abatement of appeal
Consistency of judicial decrees

card.dispute: The appellant widow challenged the High Court's decision allowing the respondent to claim property as a persona designata under the testator's will, despite no valid adoption.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was entitled to the property as a persona designata under the will of L.
Whether the will evinced an unconditional gift to the respondent or made the gift contingent upon adoption.
holdings: The will did not contain direct words of disposition in favor of the respondent; thus, no gift was made to him as a persona designata.
The gift of property was conditional upon the respondent being adopted by the widow, and since adoption did not occur, the claim under the will fails.
doctrines: Construction of wills
Gift to persona designata
Condition precedent in testamentary gifts

card.dispute: The appellants sought to file an arbitration agreement and refer a dispute to arbitration, but the State argued the application was time-barred under the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applies to an application under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
Whether Section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 makes the Limitation Act applicable to applications for filing arbitration agreements.
holdings: Article 181 of the Limitation Act applies only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure, not to applications under the Arbitration Act, 1940.
Section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act does not govern applications under Section 20; it only applies to proceedings before an arbitrator, not to court applications for filing agreements.
doctrines: Implied exclusion of non-Code applications from Article 181
Separation of court proceedings and arbitration proceedings under limitation law

card.dispute: The appellants sought to enforce an arbitration agreement with the State of Himachal Pradesh for disputes over herb collection rights, but the State resisted, claiming the application was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 to file an arbitration agreement is governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the Limitation Act applies to applications for referring disputes to arbitration under the Arbitration Act, 1940
holdings: Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908 does not govern applications under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, as such applications are not under the Code of Civil Procedure.

Section 37(1) of the Arbitration Act, 1940 does not make the Limitation Act applicable to applications for filing arbitration agreements; limitation is for the arbitrator to decide, not the court at the referral stage.
doctrines: Separability of arbitration agreements
Kompetenz-kompetenz (arbitrator's authority to rule on own jurisdiction including limitation)
Judicial non-interference in arbitration at pre-reference stage

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing that the procedures followed, including the appointment of the inquiry officer and opportunities for hearing, were flawed.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Land Acquisition Officer was 'specially appointed' under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules and thus competent to conduct the inquiry and report.
Whether the inquiry under Rule 4 must be conducted after the Section 4 notification, not before.
Whether the appellants were entitled to a second opportunity to be heard before the issuance of the Section 6 notification after having participated in the Section 5A inquiry.
Whether the State Government acted mala fide or without applying its mind in issuing the acquisition notifications.
holdings: A Special Land Acquisition Officer authorized by general notification to perform the functions of a Collector is competent to conduct an inquiry and submit a report under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules.
The inquiry under Rule 4 can validly precede the Section 4 notification, as it aids the government in forming a tentative conclusion about the need for land for public purpose.

No second opportunity to be heard is required before issuing a Section 6 notification if the landowners have already been heard during the Section 5A inquiry, as the Act does not mandate duplication of hearings.

Mere repetition of acquisition attempts does not prove mala fide; the government applied its mind independently, especially evidenced by prior cancellation of a notification based on unsuitability of land.
doctrines: Doctrine of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (reading provisions in context)
Doctrine of finality of administrative satisfaction
Presumption of constitutionality and regularity of administrative action

card.dispute: The petitioners, textile mill owners in Ahmedabad, challenged the Gujarat Education Cess Act, 1962, alleging discriminatory tax treatment under Article 14 due to differing cess burdens across three city zones.
issues_decided: Whether the Gujarat Education Cess Act, 1962, violates Article 14 by imposing a double tax burden on properties in the middle zone compared to single taxes in the inner and outer zones.
Whether Section 12 of the Cess Act becomes invalid because the assessment book it relies on was struck down by the Supreme Court for using a flat rate and including plant and machinery in valuation.
Whether the Cess Act violates principles of natural justice by not providing independent procedures for objections or appeals against the cess assessment.
holdings: The differential tax treatment across zones does not violate Article 14 because the classification is based on legitimate distinctions in land use and existing tax regimes, and the rates may be equitably adjusted.
Section 12 of the Gujarat Education Cess Act remains valid even if the underlying assessment book is invalid, as the section can operate with a future, constitutionally compliant assessment.
The Cess Act does not violate natural justice since it is an arithmetical addition to taxes already assessed under procedures that allow objections and appeals.
doctrines: Equality before law (Article 14)
Doctrine of severability
Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of incorporation by reference in taxation statutes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a notification and declaration under the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, arguing that they were issued without proper authority and without the State Government applying its mind.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4 and declaration under Section 6 of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, required the personal satisfaction of the Governor or the Minister-in-charge.
Whether the proceedings under Section 4 of the Act were covered by Item 18 of the Standing Order, requiring the matter to be dealt with by the Minister-in-charge.
Whether the Assistant or Deputy Secretary had the authority to issue the notification and declaration under the Act.
holdings: The satisfaction required under Sections 4 and 6 of the Act is that of the State Government, not necessarily the personal satisfaction of the Governor or Minister, and can be formed by officers authorized under the Rules of Business.
Item 18 of the Standing Order does not apply to the issuance of a notification under Section 4 of the Act, as the Land Planning Committee has no statutory role at that stage.

The notification under Section 4 and declaration under Section 6 were validly issued by the Assistant and Deputy Secretaries, as the Minister had authorized such delegation under Standing Order No. 5.
provisions: West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, Section 4, Section 6, Section 3, Section 5
West Bengal Land Development and Planning Rules, Standing Order No. 2, Item 18, Standing Order No. 5
doctrines: Delegation of executive power under statutory rules
Doctrine of satisfaction in administrative action
Rule of lawful authorization under governmental standing orders

card.dispute: The children of foster children of a childless Hindu testatrix fought over whether they would inherit the property per capita or per stirpes after the death of the foster children.
issues_decided: Whether the foster children inherited the property as joint tenants or as tenants in common under the will.
Whether the children of the foster children would inherit the property per capita or per stirpes.
holdings: Under Hindu law, joint tenancy is unknown except in coparcenary; the will did not create a joint tenancy, so the foster children held as tenants in common.
Where a will gives a life estate to foster children with a vested remainder to their children, the remainder passes per stirpes, not per capita.
doctrines: Joint tenancy not recognized in Hindu law outside coparcenary
Rule of stirpital distribution in wills
Vested remainder under wills
Construction of wills based on testator's intention and legal principles
