card.dispute: The assessee, Sarbaranjan Bysack, claimed that four properties were dedicated to family deities and thus not taxable, while the Income-tax Department argued they remained part of his taxable estate.
issues_decided: Whether the four properties were absolutely vested in the family deities as 'debutter' properties or remained with the heirs subject to a charge for worship expenses.
Whether the income from the four properties was taxable in the hands of the assessee.
holdings: The properties were not dedicated to the deities; title did not pass to them. The phrase 'set apart' meant only that income should be used for worship, not that ownership changed.
The four properties formed part of the residuary estate and were subject to a charge for worship expenses; thus, their income was taxable in the hands of the assessee.
doctrines: Doctrine of dedication to deity
Principle of construction of wills and decrees
Taxability of income from properties subject to religious charges

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the inclusion of income from settled lands in his assessable agricultural income, arguing the settlement was not revocable and thus not taxable under the Madras Agricultural Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the settlement deed created a revocable transfer within the meaning of section 9(1) of the Madras Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1955
Whether the third proviso to section 9(1) exempted the income from taxation
Whether section 9(1) of the Act was ultra vires or violated Article 14 of the Constitution
holdings: A settlement is revocable under section 9(1) if it allows the settlor to reassume control over the assets; the reservation of power to cancel or alter the deed makes it revocable.
The third proviso does not apply where the settlor retains a power to revoke at any time, as the settlor continues to derive indirect benefit and control.
The constitutional challenge to section 9(1) cannot be raised in revision proceedings before tax authorities or courts; it must be pursued in an appropriate proceeding.
doctrines: Revocable transfer doctrine in tax law
Doctrine of incidental power reservation making a transfer revocable
Rule against raising constitutional challenges in tax revision proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant mortgagee challenged the order of priority in which receipts from the mortgaged property were applied, arguing that interest on the principal should rank before expenses for repairs and maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether the priorities under Section 76(h) of the Transfer of Property Act are subject to those in Section 76(d)
Whether Section 76(d) establishes a priority order inconsistent with Section 76(h)
Whether expenses for repairs beyond the surplus after paying taxes and interest can be added to the principal under Sections 63A(2) or 72(b)
holdings: Section 76(d) does not establish a priority order but limits the mortgagee's obligation to make repairs to the extent of surplus after paying taxes and interest on principal.

Section 76(h) governs the order of application of receipts: first management expenses and those under clauses (c) and (d), then interest on such expenses, then interest on principal, then principal itself.
There is no conflict between Sections 76(d) and 76(h); the former concerns the scope of repair liability, the latter the priority of payments from receipts.
Expenses incurred without proof of necessity or compliance with Sections 63A(2) or 72(b) cannot be added to the principal.
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Priority of payments in mortgage accounting
Necessity and limitation of mortgagee's right to recover repair costs

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority's refusal to state a case for the High Court's opinion under Section 57(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, after it had imposed stamp duty on a deed of trust.
issues_decided: Whether the Authority is legally bound to state a case under Section 57(1) of the Indian Stamp Act when a substantial question of law is raised, even if no case is pending before it.
Whether the High Court has jurisdiction to direct the Authority to state a case under Section 57(1) despite the finality of the assessment and initiation of recovery proceedings.
holdings: The Authority is under a statutory duty to state a case under Section 57(1) if a substantial question of law is involved, regardless of whether the case is pending before it.
The remedy under Section 57(1) is not defeated by the completion of assessment or initiation of recovery; the High Court can compel the Authority to state the case via mandamus.
doctrines: Mandatory interpretation of 'may' in statutory context when duty is imposed on public officers
Availability of mandamus to enforce statutory duty under revenue law
Substantial question of law as a precondition for reference under Section 57
Continuing jurisdiction for legal remedy despite finality of administrative action

card.dispute: The tenant (Bant Singh Gill) fought against the landlords (Shanti Devi & Ors) over whether a pending ejectment suit abated due to the applicability of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and whether an appeal lay against the trial court's rejection of his abatement application.
issues_decided: Whether the right of appeal against the trial court's order was governed by the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 or the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the order rejecting the application for abatement of the suit was appealable under Section 34 of the 1952 Act
holdings: The right of appeal against an order in a suit pending under the 1952 Act continues to be governed by that Act, even after its partial repeal by the 1958 Act, due to the saving clause in Section 57(2) of the 1958 Act.

An order rejecting an application for abatement of a suit on a preliminary issue is not a final order under Section 34 of the 1952 Act and is not appealable; the proper remedy is to challenge it in an appeal against the final decree.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 34
doctrines: Doctrine of saving clause under transitional provisions
Doctrine of finality of appealable orders
Doctrine of interlocutory orders not being appealable

card.dispute: The Collector of Akola requisitioned land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act for resettling flood victims, and the landowners challenged the order, claiming it was invalid because the purpose was permanent, not temporary.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Land Requisition Act authorizes requisitioning for a permanent public purpose
Whether the power to requisition under the Act is limited to temporary purposes only
Whether there is an antithesis between requisitioning under the Bombay Land Requisition Act and acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act
holdings: The power to requisition under Section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act is not restricted to temporary purposes; it extends to any public purpose, whether temporary or permanent.
The temporary nature of the Act does not imply that the purposes for which land may be requisitioned must also be temporary.
There is no conflict between the power to requisition under the Bombay Land Requisition Act and the power to acquire under the Land Acquisition Act; both can coexist and be used independently.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
No implied limitation on statutory powers
Coexistence of requisition and acquisition powers

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the Manager of the Court of Wards disputed whether income tax could be assessed on the estate of Bettiah during pending litigation over its ownership and a claim of escheat to the State of Bihar.
issues_decided: Whether an assessment could be made on the Manager of the Court of Wards in respect of the income from the Bettiah Estate while title litigation was pending.
Whether the income, if assessable, was chargeable at the maximum rate under Section 41(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
holdings: An assessment should not be finalized while litigation over title and escheat is pending; proceedings must await the outcome of the suit to determine liability.
The question of tax rate under Section 41(1) is academic if the assessment itself is premature due to unresolved ownership.
provisions: Bengal Court of Wards Act, 1879, Section 13
doctrines: Doctrine of premature assessment
Doctrine of ripeness in tax proceedings
Principle of deferral of tax liability pending resolution of title disputes

card.dispute: The Collector of Aurangabad and the government claimed priority in recovering sales-tax arrears from sale proceeds held by a court, over a decree-holder (Central Bank of India) in an execution proceeding.
issues_decided: Whether Section 119 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act authorizes distraint of movable property in the custody and possession of a court.
Whether taxes other than land revenue under the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act enjoy priority over private debts under Section 104.
Whether the common law doctrine of 'priority of Crown debts' was applicable in the erstwhile Hyderabad State before the Constitution came into force.
holdings: Section 119 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act empowers the Collector to distrain movable property regardless of whether it is in the judgment-debtor's possession or in court custody, as the provision is not restricted by such conditions.
The priority under Section 104 of the Hyderabad Land Revenue Act applies only to land revenue, not to other taxes; hence, sales-tax arrears do not have statutory priority over private debts.
The English common law doctrine of priority of Crown debts is not applicable in former Hyderabad State as there is no evidence it was judicially recognized there before 1950.
doctrines: Priority of Crown debts
Substantive law vs. procedural law distinction
Doctrine of judicial recognition of common law in pre-constitutional states

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax fought the Managing Trustee of Jalakhabai Trust over whether certain portions of the trust's income were exempt from taxation under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether a question of law arose from the Tribunal's order regarding the exemption of 1/8th of the income from Schedule B and C properties under section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922?
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to direct the Tribunal to submit a statement of case on the 1/8th share of income?
holdings: A question of law did arise from the Tribunal's order concerning the interpretation of clause 13(b) of the trust deed and its impact on tax exemption under section 4(3)(i).
The High Court erred in not directing the Tribunal to submit a statement of case on the 1/8th share of income, as such a legal question warranted reference.
doctrines: Question of law arising from tribunal orders
Judicial review of tribunal referrals under tax law

card.dispute: The Collector of Varanasi appealed against a High Court decision enhancing compensation awarded for land acquired under the Defence of India Act, 1939, challenging both the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear the appeal and the method used to calculate compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court had jurisdiction under Article 136 to hear an appeal against the High Court's decision under Section 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939
Whether the High Court, while acting under Section 19(1)(f), functions as a 'court' or as a persona designata
Whether the High Court erred in law in determining compensation based on a non-contemporaneous sale deed
holdings: The Supreme Court has jurisdiction under Article 136 to hear appeals against decisions of the High Court under Section 19(1)(f) of the Defence of India Act, 1939, as such decisions are judicial determinations by a court.
The High Court, when exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 19(1)(f), functions as a 'court' and not merely as a persona designata.

The High Court erred in relying on a sale deed from 1951 to determine compensation for land acquired in 1946, as it was not a contemporaneous transaction and the land size was not comparable; the decision was set aside and remitted for fresh determination.
doctrines: Persona designata doctrine
Contemporaneity principle in land valuation
Special leave jurisdiction under Article 136

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax and Motor and General Stores (P.) Ltd fought over whether the transfer of a cinema house and assets in exchange for shares constituted a 'sale' or an 'exchange' for tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction involving the transfer of assets for shares was a sale or an exchange under s. 10(2)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the substance of the transaction, rather than its form, should determine taxability in the absence of mala fides.
holdings: The transaction was an exchange, not a sale, as the consideration was the transfer of shares and not money, so s. 10(2)(vii) did not apply.
In the absence of mala fides or fraud, tax liability must be determined by the legal form of the transaction as embodied in the document, not by its alleged substance.
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine limited by legal form in absence of fraud
Strict construction of taxing statutes based on legal rights of parties

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and National Storage Pvt. Ltd. disputed whether the company's income from hiring out film storage vaults should be assessed under 'income from property' (Section 9) or 'profits and gains of business' (Section 10) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was carrying on a business or merely letting out property for rental income.
Whether the income derived by the assessee fell under Section 9 (income from property) or Section 10 (profits and gains of business) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the letting of specially constructed vaults with added services constituted an adventure in the nature of trade.
Whether the assessee could be assessed under both Section 9 and Section 10 for different components of the same income.
holdings: The assessee was carrying on an adventure or concern in the nature of trade by providing specially designed vaults along with significant services, thus constituting a business activity.
Income derived from such activity is assessable under Section 10, not Section 9, because the property was occupied for business purposes and the income arose from a complex service, not mere rent.
The subject matter hired out was not just property but a composite service including fire alarms, staffing, and railway booking facilities, making it a concern in the nature of trade.
The Act does not allow splitting of income from the same source into rental (under Section 9) and business income (under Section 10) when the assessee is in occupation for business purposes.
doctrines: Mutually exclusive heads of income
Adventure or concern in the nature of trade
Composite transaction doctrine
Common notions of practical men test

card.dispute: The Divisional Forest Officer refused to issue orders for felling and removing trees from land owned by respondents who had acquired proprietary rights as tenants under the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates & Land Reforms Act, 1953, leading to a dispute over whether trees were included in the transferred rights.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'right, title and interest of the land-owner in the land' under Section 11 of the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates & Land Reforms Act, 1953 includes trees standing on the land.
Whether the Compensation Officer was competent to transfer proprietary rights in trees to the tenant under Section 11 of the Act.
holdings: The expression 'right, title and interest of the land-owner in the land' under Section 11(6) of the Act includes trees standing on the land, as the word 'owner' is comprehensive and transfers all rights from the landowner to the tenant.
The transfer of land under Section 11 of the Act includes trees unless a contrary intention is shown, and the Compensation Officer had the authority to effect such transfer.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates & Land Reforms Act, 1953, Section 2(5)
Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates & Land Reforms Act, 1953, Section 11
Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates & Land Reforms Act, 1953, Section 84
doctrines: Doctrine of inclusion of appurtenances in transfer of property
Estoppel by conduct
Principle of statutory interpretation in land reform laws

card.dispute: The widow and sons of a Hindu joint family's karta challenged the validity of property transfers made to his concubine, claiming they were void gifts, while she claimed they were valid transfers for past services.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of joint family property to a concubine in consideration of past cohabitation is valid under Hindu law and the Indian Contract Act, 1872
Whether such a transfer is hit by Section 6(h) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether disruption of the joint family validates an earlier invalid gift by the karta
holdings: Past cohabitation constitutes motive, not valid consideration under Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, so the transfer was an unenforceable gift.
Gifts to a concubine for past cohabitation are not void under Section 6(h) of the Transfer of Property Act, but are invalid under Hindu law if made from coparcenary property.
An invalid gift by a karta of coparcenary property is not validated by subsequent disruption of the joint family.
doctrines: Past consideration is not valid consideration under contract law
Karta's limited power to alienate coparcenary property
Motive vs. consideration in property transfers

card.dispute: The Custodian of Evacuee Property declared a house evacuee property after the owner migrated to Pakistan; the owner's wife, claiming ownership under a will, sued in civil court to challenge the declaration and sought injunction against eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a civil court can entertain a suit challenging a declaration of evacuee property under Section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, on grounds of title.
Whether the jurisdiction of civil courts to decide questions of title in evacuee property is barred by Section 46 of the Act, even if the issue involves complicated questions of law.
holdings: The determination of whether property is evacuee property under Section 7 includes questions of title, and the Custodian has jurisdiction to decide such issues, whether of fact or law.

Section 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, completely bars civil and revenue courts from entertaining any suit or adjudicating on whether property is evacuee property, regardless of the complexity of legal questions involved.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 4
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 24
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 28
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 46
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Doctrine of exclusion of jurisdiction by statute
Principle of statutory finality overriding civil court jurisdiction

card.dispute: The assessee challenged the Appellate Tribunal's addition of Rs. 50,000 as income from undisclosed sources, arguing that the decision was arbitrary and based solely on counsel's concession without proper evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the Tribunal had any material basis to reduce the addition of Rs. 1,37,000 to Rs. 50,000 as income from undisclosed sources.
Whether the Tribunal was justified in law in reducing the addition based on counsel's statement that the assessee was willing to be assessed on Rs. 50,000.
holdings: The Tribunal must decide based on evidence and reasoning; an estimate of undisclosed income without supporting reasons or materials cannot be sustained.
A judicial or quasi-judicial authority cannot base its decision on counsel's concession alone; it must evaluate the evidence and ensure a fair trial on merits.
doctrines: Rule of natural justice
Duty to base decisions on evidence
Prohibition of arbitrary or speculative findings

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment of tenants before the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 came into force; the dispute centered on whether the amended Act could apply to this pre-Act suit and whether the civil court retained jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant could claim protection under Section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 in a suit filed before the Act came into force.
Whether the omission of Sections 28 and 29 by the 1953 Amendment deprived civil courts of jurisdiction over pre-Act ejectment suits.
holdings: Section 3 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 applies retrospectively to pending suits, requiring landlords to prove one of the specified grounds for ejectment even in pre-Act suits.

The omission of Sections 28 and 29 did not render ejectment suits infructuous; civil courts retained jurisdiction to decide such suits under the amended Act, but could not enforce compliance with the prospective requirements of Sections 4 and 5.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes by express or necessary implication
Prospective vs. retrospective application of rent control laws
Jurisdiction of civil courts in light of statutory ouster

card.dispute: The members of one artificial branch of a joint family governed by Aliyasanthana law sued the sole surviving member of the other branch for partition, claiming the 1900 deed only effected a division for convenience, not an outright partition.
issues_decided: Whether the 1900 registered deed effected an outright partition of the joint family properties under Aliyasanthana law.
Whether the deed could be deemed a partition under Section 36(6) of the Madras Aliyasanthana Act, 1949.
holdings: The 1900 deed did not effect an outright partition as it created artificial branches, not natural kavarus, and retained community features like mutual succession and restrictions on alienation.
The deed cannot be deemed a partition under Section 36(6) of the Madras Aliyasanthana Act because the distribution was not among all kavarus as defined by the Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement for convenient enjoyment without disruption of joint family status
Doctrine of deemed partition under statutory fiction
Survivorship in joint families governed by Aliyasanthana law

card.dispute: The dispute was between former Mahants and their successors over whether properties held by the Mahants of Uttar Giri Math were personal or religious endowment properties.
issues_decided: Whether properties acquired and transferred by successive Mahants were personal or math (religious endowment) properties
Whether alienations of property by a Mahant are valid if the property is held to be personal
Whether succession from Guru to Chela necessarily renders property religious in character
holdings: Properties held by Mahants are presumed to be personal unless proven to be dedicated to the math; mere succession from one Mahant to another does not make property religious.
A Mahant may validly transfer personal property, and such transfers are binding even if made to disciples, provided no trust or religious purpose is established.
The fact that a Mahant is a religious figure does not legally disqualify him from owning personal property; secular character of property is not lost merely due to religious status.
provisions: Hindu Law of Religious Endowments (customary law)
General principles of property and trust under Hindu Law
doctrines: Presumption of personal property in absence of clear dedication
Blending doctrine not applicable without clear intent to dedicate
Religious profession does not negate capacity to hold private property

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant and sub-tenant; the dispute centered on whether the appellate court had jurisdiction to evict the sub-tenant when the tenancy was not fully determined and no arrears of rent were due.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court had jurisdiction under s. 28 of the Bombay Rents Act to evict a sub-tenant when the tenant-in-chief was not evicted.
Whether a sub-tenant becomes a tenant-in-chief under s. 14 of the Act merely upon the expiry of a notice terminating the tenancy.
holdings: The appellate court lacked jurisdiction to evict a sub-tenant in a suit under s. 28 of the Bombay Rents Act when the tenant-in-chief was not ordered to be evicted, as the Act only allows eviction of a sub-tenant along with the tenant.

Section 14 of the Bombay Rents Act does not deem a sub-tenant to become a tenant-in-chief merely upon the expiry of a termination notice; the tenant’s interest must fully end, including loss of statutory protection under s. 12, before s. 14 applies.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 14
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 28
doctrines: Jurisdictional limits of special courts
Statutory interpretation of tenancy determination
Doctrine of deemed tenancy under rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant (auction purchaser) and respondents (mortgagors) disputed whether the executing court could extend time for depositing dues after a consent-based deadline expired, or was bound to confirm the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court had power to extend time for depositing the amount after the agreed-upon date had passed, in the absence of fresh consent from the decree-holder and auction-purchaser.
Whether Order XXI Rule 92 of the CPC mandates confirmation of sale once conditions are met and no deposit is made before confirmation.
Whether Order XXXIV Rule 5 allows the court to grant time extensions or merely permits deposit before confirmation of sale.
holdings: The court must confirm a sale under Order XXI Rule 92 when an application to set it aside is dismissed and no deposit is made before confirmation, unless a valid agreement extends time by consent.
Order XXXIV Rule 5 does not empower the court to grant time extensions but allows a judgment-debtor to deposit dues at any time before confirmation of sale.
Once time granted by consent expires, the court cannot extend it further without fresh consent, as Section 148 CPC does not apply to such agreed periods.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 92
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV, Rule 5
doctrines: Harmonious construction of procedural provisions
Consent decree binds parties and court
Mandatory nature of confirmation of sale under CPC

card.dispute: Hans Raj challenged the receiver's possession of certain properties claimed as his own, not belonging to the insolvent, after the insolvency of his brother.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's application was under Section 4 or Section 68 of the Provincial Insolvency Act (Punjab Act 5 of 1920)
Whether the application was barred by limitation under Section 68
holdings: An application challenging the act of a receiver in taking possession of property must be made under Section 68, not Section 4, of the Provincial Insolvency Act.
An application under Section 68 is time-barred if filed beyond 21 days from the date of the impugned act of the receiver.
provisions: Provincial Insolvency Act (Punjab Act 5 of 1920), Section 4
Provincial Insolvency Act (Punjab Act 5 of 1920), Section 68
doctrines: Limitation bar under Section 68
Jurisdictional scope of Section 4 as defining court powers, not procedure

card.dispute: The appellants, a Hindu undivided family, challenged the validity of Section 32-KK of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, which treated the family as a single unit for landholding limits, thereby preventing individual coparceners from claiming separate entitlements to the permissible area of land.
issues_decided: Whether Section 32-KK of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955 infringes Article 19(1)(f) and is protected by Article 31-A of the Constitution
Whether Section 32-KK creates discrimination against members of a Hindu undivided family in violation of Article 14
Whether Section 32-KK amounts to legislation for agrarian reform within the meaning of Article 31-A
Whether Section 32-KK discriminates on the ground of religion under Article 15 by applying only to Hindu undivided families
holdings: Section 32-KK is protected by Article 31-A and does not violate Article 19(1)(f) as it merely equates a Hindu undivided family with an individual for land ceiling purposes without altering other property rights.
The provision does not violate Article 14 as it does not discriminate unreasonably; it uniformly applies to all Hindu undivided families to prevent circumvention of land ceiling laws.
Section 32-KK constitutes agrarian reform legislation aimed at equitable distribution of surplus land and falls within the scope of Article 31-A.
The challenge under Article 15 was not examined in depth as it was not raised in the writ petition and insufficient evidence was provided to establish discriminatory impact on non-Hindus.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-KK
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-FF
doctrines: Agrarian reform under Article 31-A
Protection of laws relating to estates from fundamental rights challenges
Presumption of constitutionality for land reform legislation
Non-justiciability of policy choices in land reform in absence of manifest arbitrariness

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Director of Consolidation of Holdings' order that took his gher land for village abadi extension, arguing it violated statutory procedure and equitable sharing requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government's power under Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings Act can override a confirmed scheme without following the procedure under Section 36
Whether the Director's order violated Section 18(c) and Rule 16(ii) by taking land from a single proprietor without rateable contribution
holdings: The power under Section 42 is independent of Section 36; the State Government may revise a scheme without following the publication and objection procedure required for initial confirmation.

Section 18(c) must be interpreted to require that land taken for common purposes, including abadi extension, be contributed rateably by all proprietors, in line with Rule 16(ii), to avoid unconstitutional acquisition by the State.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 18
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 36
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 42
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Rule 16(ii)
doctrines: Principle of constitutional avoidance
Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
Rateable contribution for common purposes in land consolidation

card.dispute: The collaterals of the 5th degree and the daughter of a deceased Sidhu Jat landowner fought over succession to his non-ancestral property.
issues_decided: Whether collaterals in the 5th degree take precedence over a daughter in succession to non-ancestral property under the customary law of Sidhu Jats in Muktsar Tahsil, Ferozepore District, Punjab.
Whether a special custom, as recorded in Riwaj-i-am, can displace the general custom in Rattigan's Digest regarding succession to non-ancestral property.
Whether the presumption of correctness attached to entries in Riwaj-i-am can be rebutted, especially when they affect the rights of female heirs.
holdings: The customary law among Sidhu Jats of Muktsar Tahsil, Punjab, regarding non-ancestral property is the same as the general custom in Rattigan's Digest: a daughter takes precedence over collaterals.
Entries in Riwaj-i-am referring to succession do not apply to non-ancestral property and thus cannot establish a special custom displacing the general rule favoring daughters.

The presumption of correctness of Riwaj-i-am entries is weakened when they adversely affect female succession rights, and such presumption can be rebutted by evidence showing contrary practice in neighboring areas or judicial decisions.
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of revenue records (Riwaj-i-am) is rebuttable, especially when affecting rights of females.
Special custom must be clearly proven to displace a general custom.
Courts must carefully protect the inheritance rights of female heirs against claims based on potentially biased male-dominated records.

card.dispute: The Khambalia Municipality challenged the state government's notification converting its area into a nagar panchayat, arguing the law enabling such conversion allowed excessive delegation of power and was applied arbitrarily.
issues_decided: Whether the power to conduct inquiry under Section 9(1) of the Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1961 could be delegated to the Development Commissioner
Whether Section 9 of the Act applies to municipal districts
Whether the notification converting the municipality into a nagar was issued mala fide
Whether Section 9 of the Act suffers from excessive delegation of legislative power
holdings: The power to make a declaration under Section 9(1) necessarily includes the power to conduct the preceding inquiry, and the Development Commissioner was duly authorized to do so.
A municipal district is an administrative unit under Section 9(1), and a local area co-extensive with it can be declared a nagar, leading to the dissolution of the municipality.
The notification was not proven to be mala fide; the court did not find sufficient evidence of improper motive.

Section 9 of the Gujarat Panchayats Act, 1961 is unconstitutional due to excessive delegation, as it provides no guiding principles for declaring or altering local areas, leaving unchecked discretion with the government.
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Doctrine of implied powers (inquiry incidental to declaration)

card.dispute: L.M. Chhabda And Sons fought the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether Rs. 92,240 paid as mesne profits for a closed cinema theatre could be deducted as a business expense for the assessment year 1955-56.
issues_decided: Whether the amount of Rs. 92,240 was allowable as a deduction in determining the business income of the assessee for the assessment year 1955-56?
Whether the business of Prakash Talkies was part of an integrated business of exhibiting films carried on by the appellants during the relevant year?
holdings: An outgoing attributable to a closed business cannot be allowed as a deduction under section 10(1) if the business was not carried on in the relevant previous year.
Separate maintenance of books and independent operation of theatres indicate distinct businesses; mere common ownership or head office accounting does not prove an integrated business.
doctrines: Unity of business doctrine
Integration and interdependence test for single business

card.dispute: The petitioners, a partnership firm, challenged the jurisdiction of the Allahabad High Court to issue a writ against an Appellate Officer located in Delhi, whose order affected their property declared as evacuee property under central and state evacuation laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Allahabad High Court has jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue a writ against an Appellate Officer whose office is located in Delhi but who was appointed by the Uttar Pradesh State Government and conducted proceedings within Uttar Pradesh.
Whether the order of the Competent Officer in Uttar Pradesh merged with that of the Appellate Officer outside the territorial jurisdiction, thereby ousting the High Court's writ jurisdiction.
holdings: The Allahabad High Court has jurisdiction under Article 226 to issue a writ against the Appellate Officer because the officer was appointed by the State Government and functionally operated within Uttar Pradesh, despite the office being located in Delhi for administrative convenience.

The doctrine of merger does not bar writ jurisdiction when the appellate authority, though physically located outside the state, exercises powers under a state statute and conducts proceedings within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
doctrines: Territorial jurisdiction under Article 226
Doctrine of merger of orders
Functional test for determining location of authority for writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Karta of a Hindu undivided family and others challenged the assessment of income in the name of an association of persons (including a minor and a firm) and the treatment of an individual as its principal officer, questioning the constitutional validity of the procedure and the application of res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by granting unguided power to assess income in the name of an association of persons or its members
Whether the finding that an association of persons existed from 1952-53 to 1956-57 is sustainable based on the evidence
Whether the doctrine of res judicata applies to assessment findings in one year for subsequent years
Whether a prior declaration is required to treat a person as the principal officer of an association of persons before assessment proceedings
holdings: Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, does not violate Article 14 as the quasi-judicial functions of the Income-tax Officer and the duty to prevent tax evasion provide sufficient guidance.
The Tribunal's finding that an association of persons existed from 1952-53 onwards is a factual determination supported by evidence and cannot be overturned by the High Court in a reference.
The doctrine of res judicata does not apply to assessment proceedings for different years, especially when the composition of the association changes.

No prior declaration is needed to treat a person as the principal officer; service of notice under Section 63(2) and assessment order recording the status is sufficient, and the issue can be challenged during appeal.
doctrines: Rule of law and non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Finality of findings of fact by quasi-judicial bodies
Res judicata not applicable to fiscal proceedings across assessment years
Principle of sufficient compliance with statutory procedure in tax assessment

card.dispute: Tenants of ryotwari land in Gwalior challenged their forcible eviction by landlords who claimed the tenants' rights were extinguished due to arrears in land revenue payment.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can forcibly eject a tenant for non-payment of land revenue without following legal process
Whether the proviso to s. 137 of the Qanoon Ryotwari renders summary dispossession unlawful
Whether a proceeding under s. 163 of Qanoon Ryotwari requires inquiry into the legality of possession, not just de facto possession
holdings: A landlord cannot forcibly eject a tenant for arrears of land revenue; dispossession must follow due process of law.

The proviso to s. 137 Qanoon Ryotwari, allowing arrears to be accepted under certain conditions, implies that extinguishment of tenancy is not automatic and requires administrative or judicial action.
A suit under s. 163 Qanoon Ryotwari must examine whether dispossession was wrongful, i.e., not in due course of law, not merely who was in possession.
doctrines: No self-help doctrine: prohibition on taking law into one's own hands
Summary possession remedy preserves possession regardless of title
Forcible dispossession not justified even if tenancy has ended

card.dispute: The petitioner, a partnership firm of displaced persons, challenged the rejection of its revision petition as time-barred, arguing that rule 104 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1954, which imposed a thirty-day limitation, was ultra vires section 24 of the Act.
issues_decided: Whether rule 104 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1954, which prescribes a thirty-day period for filing a revision petition, is ultra vires section 24 of the Act.
Whether the rule-making authority under the Act could lawfully impose a time limit for invoking the revisional jurisdiction of the Chief Settlement Commissioner.
holdings: Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, grants the Chief Settlement Commissioner revisional power exercisable 'at any time', and rule 104 cannot impose a thirty-day limitation as it indirectly restricts this statutory power.

The rule-making authority under section 40 of the Act lacks competence to prescribe a time limit for revision petitions, as the enabling provision does not include 'time within which' for revision, unlike other clauses, and such a rule conflicts with the parent statute.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 40
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 23
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1954, Rule 104
doctrines: Doctrine of ultra vires
Principle of statutory interpretation (ejusdem generis and negative implication)
Rule of law that delegated legislation cannot override or curtail statutory powers

card.dispute: The mahant of a trust administered in Madhya Pradesh claimed exemption from land transfer provisions under the Bombay Tenancy Act, arguing that the trust was deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act due to amendments, but the tenant contested this, saying the trust remained outside Maharashtra's jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether a trust administered in Madhya Pradesh, with only a small portion of its property in Maharashtra, can be deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 as amended in 1960?
Whether such a trust qualifies for exemption under Section 88B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948?
holdings: A trust administered entirely in Madhya Pradesh, even if holding some property in Maharashtra, cannot be deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, as the amendment was meant only for trusts brought within Maharashtra’s territory due to state reorganization.

For exemption under Section 88B, the trust must be or be deemed registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act; since this trust is not, it does not qualify for the exemption from deemed purchase by tenants.
provisions: Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, Section 28 and Schedule AA
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88B
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and territorial application
Deemed registration limited by jurisdictional and administrative realities
Avoidance of dual regulatory control over a single trust

card.dispute: The appellant, Mahendra Pratap Singh, was acquitted of murder charges by the Sessions Court; the private respondent filed a revision in the High Court, which set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial, prompting an appeal to the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in revision under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can set aside an acquittal and order a retrial based on a reappreciation of evidence?
What are the limits of the High Court's revisional powers when reviewing an order of acquittal?
Whether a manifest illegality or gross miscarriage of justice existed in the Sessions Court's acquittal to justify interference in revision?
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with an acquittal in revision merely because it takes a different view of the evidence; interference is only justified if there is a manifest illegality or gross miscarriage of justice.
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 439 CrPC does not allow the High Court to reweigh evidence or draw fresh inferences as in an appeal; such action undermines the finality of acquittals.

An order of acquittal can be set aside in revision only if there is a glaring procedural defect, such as lack of jurisdiction, exclusion of material admissible evidence, or consideration of inadmissible evidence.
doctrines: Manifest illegality doctrine
Gross miscarriage of justice
Limits of revisional jurisdiction
Finality of acquittal in criminal cases

card.dispute: The respondents sued the appellants for recovery of Rs. 18,000 and interest due to loss suffered when the appellants failed to pay off a prior mortgage as covenanted in a sale deed.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was governed by Article 83 or Article 116 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908
When the cause of action arose for a suit based on an implied contract of indemnity in a sale of encumbered property
holdings: A covenant by a purchaser in a sale deed to pay off an encumbrance creates an implied contract of indemnity, making Article 83 of the Limitation Act applicable.
The cause of action for a suit on an implied contract of indemnity arises when the vendor is actually damnified, not when a decree is passed against them.
doctrines: Implied contract of indemnity
Actual damnification as trigger for limitation
Covenant to pay encumbrance as indemnity

card.dispute: The appellant sought to evict the respondent from a house under a compromise decree, while the respondent claimed protection as a tenant under the Orissa House-Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree created a lease or a licence
Whether the respondent was entitled to protection as a tenant under the Orissa House-Rent Control Act, 1958
holdings: The compromise decree did not create a lease because the intention of the parties, evidenced by the decree holder's prior suit for eviction and the right to evict without court intervention, was not to establish a landlord-tenant relationship.
The use of the word 'rent' and a five-year period of possession are not conclusive; the right to immediate eviction upon default shows the arrangement was a licence, not a tenancy.
doctrines: Intention of the parties is the decisive test to distinguish between lease and licence
Exclusive possession and payment of rent are not conclusive indicators of a lease
Substance of the agreement prevails over its form in determining legal relationship

card.dispute: The assessee, M. A. Jabbar, fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether the lease payment for sand extraction was a deductible revenue expenditure or a non-deductible capital expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the lease money paid for removing sand from a riverbed constitutes revenue or capital expenditure under the Income-tax Act.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the factual findings of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal.
holdings: The lease payment was revenue expenditure because it was made solely to obtain stock-in-trade (sand) and did not result in acquiring a capital asset or enduring benefit.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by overturning binding factual findings affirmed by the Tribunal, which were not challenged as being without evidence.
doctrines: Doctrine of revenue vs capital expenditure
Principle of bindingness of factual findings by lower tribunals
Commercial expediency test for revenue expenditure

card.dispute: Lessees of mortgaged property challenged the mortgagee's right to recover possession after purchasing the property in execution of a mortgage decree, claiming their leases were binding.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee was precluded by res judicata from challenging the validity of the leases due to earlier claim proceedings under Order 21, Rule 58, CPC.
Whether the leases granted by the mortgagor after the mortgage decree was passed were binding on the mortgagee.
Whether an auction-purchaser at a sale in execution of a mortgage decree takes the property free of leases not binding on the mortgagee.
holdings: The adverse orders in the claim proceedings under Order 21, Rule 58 CPC operated as res judicata only regarding attachment in execution of the money decree, not the mortgage decree; thus, the mortgagee could still assert rights under the latter.

Leases granted by a mortgagor out of the ordinary course of management, especially after the property was advertised for sale, are not binding on the mortgagee, particularly when created in bad faith to harm the mortgagee’s interest.

An auction-purchaser at a sale in execution of a mortgage decree acquires the mortgagee’s rights and is not bound by leases that do not bind the mortgagee, even if valid between the mortgagor and lessee.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 58 and 63
doctrines: Res judicata in execution proceedings
Mortgagor as agent or bailiff of mortgagee
Doctrine of lis pendens (Section 52, Transfer of Property Act)
Rights of auction-purchaser in mortgage execution sales

card.dispute: The heirs of a Hindu widow contested the right of her daughter to inherit property after the widow was dispossessed by the husband's collaterals, arguing the daughter could not claim full ownership under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as the widow was not in possession when the Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether a dispossessed Hindu widow is deemed to 'possess' property within the meaning of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the daughter of the widow could succeed to the property as full owner under Section 14(1)
holdings: A Hindu widow remains 'possessed' of property under Section 14(1) even if dispossessed by trespassers, as long as she retains her legal right or title to it.
Section 14(1) applies to convert a widow's limited ownership into full ownership if she had a legal interest at the time of the Act's commencement, enabling her heirs to inherit the property.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive possession in property law
Doctrine of statutory conversion of limited estate into absolute estate

card.dispute: The tenant (Mulraj) challenged the landlord's (Murti Raghonathji Maharaj) suit for ejectment on the ground that the permission to sue was granted after a stay order was issued, rendering it a nullity.
issues_decided: Whether a stay order passed by a superior court automatically nullifies proceedings in a lower court even if the lower court has no knowledge of the stay order.
Whether the Magistrate retained jurisdiction to grant permission to sue after a stay order was passed but not communicated to him.
Whether proceedings conducted without knowledge of a stay order are a nullity.
holdings: A stay order does not automatically deprive a court of jurisdiction; it only prohibits further action once the court has knowledge of the order.
Proceedings carried out by a court unaware of a stay order are not a nullity and remain valid.

A court may set aside interim proceedings under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure if a stay order is later brought to its notice and justice so requires, but such power must be invoked promptly.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 5
doctrines: Jurisdiction is not automatically ousted by a stay order without notice
Principle of legality of proceedings in ignorance of a stay order
Inherent powers of court under Section 151 to prevent abuse of process

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay and the Royal Western India Turf Club disputed over the correct rateable value of the Club's leased property for municipal taxation purposes, specifically which expenses could be deducted under the profits basis method.
issues_decided: Whether a 10% statutory deduction under s. 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act excludes additional deductions for repairs and maintenance of the race course
Whether expenses for upkeep of the totalisator, track, and related operations are deductible in determining net rateable value
Whether the licence fee paid by the Club for conducting race meetings can be fully deducted, and if it should be apportioned between landlord and tenant
Whether the net rateable value can legally be lower than the actual rent paid by the tenant
holdings: The 10% statutory deduction under s. 154(1) does not preclude additional deductions for actual and necessary repair expenses, as the statutory allowance is standard and not compensatory for specific outgoings.

Expenses for maintaining the totalisator, track, and related operations are legitimate business outgoings that contribute to earning receipts and must be allowed in full when determining net rateable value.

The entire licence fee paid by the Club for conducting race meetings is deductible as a business expense, as the licence is for operational purposes and not a dual-purpose charge shared with the landlord.

The net rateable value may lawfully be less than the actual rent paid, as rateable value is based on hypothetical rental value considering the property’s use, restrictions, and income potential, not actual lease terms.
doctrines: Profits basis method of rateable value assessment
Hypothetical tenant principle in municipal valuation
Deduction of legitimate business outgoings in rate assessment
Exclusive possession and use restrictions affecting valuation

card.dispute: The appellants, relatives of a long-time tenant, used force to repel the complainant's party from taking possession of land purchased at auction; the dispute was whether the appellants had a right to private defence.
issues_decided: Whether the complainant had lawful possession of the land after the warrant of delivery issued on June 22, 1962.
Whether the appellants had a right of private defence under Section 97 IPC when they used force to resist the complainant's party on July 1, 1962.
Whether the complainant's party constituted an unlawful assembly committing criminal trespass.
Whether the appellants exceeded the permissible force allowed under the right of private defence.
holdings: The complainant did not acquire lawful possession merely through a warrant issued without proper authority; formalities alone do not transfer possession if the act is unauthorized.
The appellants had a valid right of private defence as they were protecting the continued possession of their relative, who was in settled possession and unaware of the alleged delivery.
The complainant's party, entering the land with a weapon and intent to intimidate, committed criminal trespass and formed an unlawful assembly.
The force used by the appellants was proportionate to defend possession and did not exceed the limits permitted under Section 99 IPC.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Acquisition and Disposal of Evacuee Property) Act, 1954, Section 19(3)
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Settled possession vs. casual trespass
Proportionality of force in self-defence
Unlawful assembly under common object

card.dispute: The dispute was between building owners and the Bombay Municipal Corporation over whether income from an advertisement displayed on the building's roof could be included in the property's rateable value for municipal taxation.
issues_decided: Whether income from a licence agreement for displaying advertisements on a building's roof can be included in the rateable value of the property under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888.
Whether the nature of income as 'licence fee' rather than 'rent' excludes it from consideration in determining annual letting value.
Whether rent control restrictions under the Rent Act bar the inclusion of additional income from non-rent sources in rateable value.
holdings: Income derived from a licence to display advertisements on a building can be included in the rateable value because a hypothetical tenant would consider such additional income when determining the rent they are willing to pay.
The distinction between 'rent' and 'licence fee' is irrelevant for rating purposes; what matters is the beneficial value the property yields, regardless of the legal character of the income.
Rent control laws limiting rent do not prevent the inclusion of other income from the property in rateable value, as such income arises from additional privileges, not tenancy.
doctrines: Hypothetical tenant doctrine
Beneficial use doctrine
Rateable value determination based on market potential

card.dispute: The appellant, a decree-holder against two evacuees, challenged the validity of Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and the acquisition of the judgment-debtors' property by the Central Government, claiming it violated his fundamental rights and impaired his ability to recover dues.
issues_decided: Whether Section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution by extinguishing a decree-holder's right to execute against evacuee property?
Whether Section 12 of the 1954 Act violates Article 14 by discriminating between creditors of evacuees and non-evacuees?
Whether the amendment to Section 10(2)(m) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, is ultra vires?
Whether the appellant can still claim relief from moneys held by the Custodian prior to vesting of property in the Central Government?
holdings: Section 12 of the 1954 Act does not violate Article 19(1)(f) as it does not affect the decree-holder's right to hold or dispose of the decree; the appellant had no proprietary interest in the evacuee property.
Section 12 does not violate Article 14 as there is a reasonable classification between evacuee and non-evacuee property, with a rational nexus to the object of rehabilitating displaced persons.
The amendment to Section 10(2)(m) of the 1950 Act is not challenged on its merits, and the Court does not find it ultra vires in this context.

The appellant may seek payment from moneys held by the Custodian before vesting under Section 10(2)(n) read with Section 10(1) of the 1950 Act, if he proves the release deeds were fraudulent and the property belonged to his judgment-debtors.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(1)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(2)(m)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 10(2)(n)
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
No fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f) in respect of third-party property
Doctrine of severability and prospective operation not applied
Fraud upon creditors as a ground to challenge transfer of property

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Indore levied house tax on gross annual letting value, while property owners challenged the levy, arguing it should be on net value after a 10% statutory deduction as required by the new Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the house tax could be levied on gross annual letting value under the repealed Indore City Municipal Act after the enactment of the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1954
Whether the assessment list prepared under the old Act could be adopted under Section 79(1) without complying with Sections 75 and 76 of the new Act
Whether Section 2(c) of the 1954 Act saved the levy of tax on gross annual letting value inconsistent with Section 73(2)
holdings: Tax cannot be levied on gross annual letting value after the 1954 Act came into force, as it mandates assessment on net annual value after deducting 10% for repairs.
An adopted assessment list under Section 79 must comply with Sections 75 and 76, including publication, opportunity to object, and authentication, to be conclusive.
Section 2(c) saves only those rules and levies consistent with the 1954 Act; thus, a tax based on gross value is not saved as it contradicts Section 73(2).
doctrines: Doctrine of Consistency in Deemed Legislation
Doctrine of Statutory Construction (reading 'if' as 'as if')
Principle of Prospective Operation of Repeal and Savings

card.dispute: The dispute was between Munni Lal (appellant) and Bishwanath Prasad (respondent) over whether leasehold (parjoti) land in Benaras could be subject to pre-emption under a local custom co-extensive with Muslim law.
issues_decided: Whether the lower courts had correctly found that the custom of pre-emption in Benaras applied to leasehold (parjoti) land.
Whether leasehold (parjoti) land can be the subject of pre-emption under a custom co-extensive with Muslim law.
holdings: The lower courts did not find that the custom of pre-emption in Benaras applied to leasehold (parjoti) land; they only found that the custom was co-extensive with Muslim law.
Pre-emption under Muslim law requires full proprietary ownership; it does not apply to leasehold interests, and thus parjoti land cannot be pre-empted under a custom co-extensive with Muslim law.
doctrines: Pre-emption under Muslim law requires full ownership in both the pre-emptor and the property sold.
Reciprocity is a foundational principle of pre-emption in Muslim law.

card.dispute: The appellant company refused to vacate state-leased premises after the lease expired, and challenged the Punjab Public Premises and Land (Eviction and Rent Recovery) Act, 1959 as violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Act violates Article 14 by discriminating between occupants of public and private premises
Whether the Act violates Article 14 by allowing the State to choose between eviction under the Act or by civil suit
holdings: The classification between occupants of public and private premises is valid and bears a reasonable relation to the Act's objective of expeditious recovery of state property.

The State's option to proceed under the Act or by civil suit does not violate Article 14, as equal protection does not require identical remedies and the choice of procedure is constitutionally permissible.
provisions: Punjab Public Premises and Land (Eviction and Rent Recovery) Act, 1959, Section 5
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Equality before law does not prohibit differential remedies for the State
Option of remedies does not violate equal protection

card.dispute: The appellant buyer challenged the respondent's right to pre-empt the sale of a house based on a common outer entrance under J&K's Right of Prior Purchase Act.
issues_decided: Whether a right of pre-emption under Section 15(fourthly) of the Right of Prior Purchase Act (J&K) requires joint ownership of the common outer entrance.
Whether Section 15(fourthly) of the Act violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution by imposing an unreasonable restriction on the right to property.
holdings: The right of pre-emption under Section 15(fourthly) arises from the existence of a common outer entrance, irrespective of joint ownership of that entrance.
The restriction imposed by Section 15(fourthly) is reasonable as owners of properties with a common entrance resemble co-sharers, justifying pre-emption under Article 19(1)(f).
provisions: The Right of Prior Purchase Act (J. & K. Act 11 of 1993), Section 15(fourthly)
doctrines: Right of pre-emption as a right of substitution
Reasonable restriction on property rights
Analogous co-ownership doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant sought to reduce the decretal amount under the U.P. Zamindar's Debt Reduction Act, claiming the decree related to a secured debt, while the respondents opposed, arguing the debt was unsecured when the suit was filed.
issues_decided: Whether a decree that creates a charge on immovable property can be considered as 'relating to a secured debt' under Section 4 of the U.P. Zamindar's Debt Reduction Act, 1953, if the debt was unsecured at the time the suit was filed?
Whether the date for determining if a debt is secured under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act is the date of filing the suit or the date of the decree or application?
holdings: A decree does not relate to a secured debt under Section 4 of the Act merely because it creates a charge; the debt must have been secured at the time the suit was filed.
The determination of whether a debt is secured under Sections 3 and 4 must be made as of the date the suit was filed, not at the time of the decree or application.
provisions: U.P. Zamindar's Debt Reduction Act, 1953, Section 2(m)
U.P. Zamindar's Debt Reduction Act, 1953, Section 3
U.P. Zamindar's Debt Reduction Act, 1953, Section 4
doctrines: Temporal application of statutory conditions
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of consistent interpretation across related statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, members of an Agarwala Jain family, fought over the distribution of ancestral property following the death of their parents, specifically contesting the validity of a will and a sale deed involving the parents' shares in a partition suit.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal is maintainable without a copy of the preliminary decree when the trial court refuses to prepare a fresh decree after redistribution of shares due to the death of parties.
Whether a second preliminary decree can be passed in a partition suit to amend shares after the death of a party and before the final decree.
Whether a Jain widow has an absolute or limited interest in her share of ancestral property allotted in a preliminary decree, and can therefore validly alienate it.
Whether a will executed by a father in favour of one son, excluding others, is genuine and valid, particularly when it disposes of a share in ancestral property after severance of status.
holdings: An appeal is maintainable without a copy of the decree if the defect is not due to the appellant's fault and the trial court unreasonably refuses to frame a formal decree.
A court may pass a second preliminary decree in a partition suit to amend shares upon the death of a party, provided the final decree has not yet been passed, and such a decision is appealable.
A Jain widow, in the absence of a contrary custom, holds only a limited interest (widow's estate) in ancestral property and cannot validly alienate her share; thus, a sale deed by her is invalid.

A Hindu coparcener can validly bequeath by will his defined share in ancestral property after severance of status and a preliminary decree, and the will is valid if duly executed and supported by natural circumstances.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 1
doctrines: Severance of joint family status upon filing of partition suit
Limited interest of Hindu widow in ancestral property
Validity of wills based on naturalness and due execution
Amendability of preliminary decree before final decree in partition suits

card.dispute: The appellant's father purchased a house in execution of a decree against Ram Lal, a lunatic, without appointment of a guardian-ad-litem; after Ram Lal died heirless, the Maharaja of Jaipur took possession, leading to a suit by the appellant for possession, contested on the ground that the decree and sale were void.
issues_decided: Whether a decree passed against a lunatic without appointment of a guardian-ad-litem is a nullity
Whether a sale in execution of such a void decree is valid
Whether the property of a person who dies without heirs passes by escheat to the sovereign under Hindu law
holdings: A decree passed against a lunatic without appointment of a guardian-ad-litem is a nullity, void ab initio, and without jurisdiction, akin to a decree against a minor.
A sale in execution of a decree that is a nullity is void ab initio and cannot convey any title to the purchaser.
When a person dies without leaving any heir, his property passes by escheat to the sovereign, a principle recognised in Hindu law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 32, Rule 15
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 89, 90, 92
doctrines: Decree against a person of unsound mind without guardian-ad-litem is a nullity
Sale in execution of a void decree is void ab initio
Principle of escheat in Hindu law

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over whether a pending appeal in a suit for possession of land abated due to amendments in the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for recovery of possession of land falls within the scope of the amended Section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, and thus abates upon notification of consolidation operations.
Whether the amended Section 5 of the Act, passed by the State Legislature, is ultra vires for encroaching upon the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
holdings: The amended Section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, applies to suits for possession because such suits necessarily involve determination of rights or interests in land, which the section covers.
The amendment does not violate the Constitution or affect the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction; it merely renders the appeal abated due to a change in law by the State Legislature within its competence.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 (U.P. Act 5 of 1954), Section 5 (as amended by U.P. Act 21 of 1966)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 209
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Sections 3, 4, 8, 8A, 9, 11, 11A, 24, 28, 40, 48, 49
doctrines: Doctrine of Eclipse
Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Doctrine of Legislative Competence under the Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The assessee, a joint Hindu family, claimed two debts as bad debts for tax deduction purposes, but the tax department and courts disputed whether these debts became bad during the relevant accounting year.
issues_decided: Whether there was material for the Tribunal to find that the debts of Rs. 3,25,000 and Rs. 16,005 were not bad debts arising during the money-lending business of the assessee.
What was the true nature of the transactions and whether the debts could be claimed as bad debts for computing assessable income.
Whether there was material for the Tribunal to conclude that the debts had become bad prior to the year of account in question.
holdings: The Tribunal had sufficient material to conclude that the debt of Rs. 3,25,000 was not a bad debt arising during the relevant accounting year, as no interest was charged and no recovery steps were taken for nearly a decade.
The debt of Rs. 16,005 could not be claimed as a bad debt in the relevant year because, despite a decree, no execution efforts were made, indicating it had become bad earlier.
For a bad debt deduction, the assessee must show the debt was good at the start of the year and became bad during that year; failure to do so bars the claim.
doctrines: Bad debt deduction requires proof that the debt was recoverable at the beginning of the year and became irrecoverable during the year.
Findings of the Tribunal will not be overturned if there is sufficient material to support them, even if the evidence is self-serving or vague.

card.dispute: The appellant, a money-lending Hindu undivided family, contested the tax assessment on interest income allegedly received via U.P. Encumbered Estates Bonds issued in satisfaction of a debtor's liability.
issues_decided: Whether receipt of U.P. Encumbered Estates Bonds in satisfaction of a debtor's liability constitutes receipt of income on the date of receipt by an assessee maintaining accounts on cash basis.
Whether the entire face value of the bonds, or only the difference between the principal due and the market value of the bonds at the time of receipt, is taxable as income.
Whether the same income was subject to double taxation in consecutive assessment years.
holdings: Receipt of commercial assets like bonds in satisfaction of a debt constitutes receipt of income for a cash basis assessee, as income is deemed received when the asset with embedded value is obtained.
Only the difference between the principal amount due and the market value of the bonds at the time of receipt is taxable, not the full face value of the bonds.
The Department must ensure no double taxation; if the same income was taxed in the assessment year 1949–50, adjustments must be made to avoid duplication.
doctrines: Cash basis of accounting
Accrual vs. receipt of income
Substance over form in taxability of non-cash receipts
Prohibition of double taxation

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to recover lease money paid to both the landlord and the State, after the State claimed the money following a disputed vesting of the estate under the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 3 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, was validly published as required by law?
Whether the estate of the landlord was effectively vested in the State on the date of the Gazette notification?
Whether the landlord or the State had the right to collect lease money for the year 1952?
holdings: Publication of a notification in the Official Gazette alone does not satisfy the mandatory requirement of Section 3(2) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, which also requires publication in at least two issues of two newspapers.
Due to non-compliance with Section 3(2), the vesting of the estate under Section 4(a) did not take effect on the date of the Gazette notification.
The landlord remained the proprietor until actual dispossession and had the right to collect lease money for 1952; the State had no right to collect it for that period.
doctrines: Strict compliance with mandatory statutory procedures for land vesting
Burden of proof in establishing publication of statutory notifications
Doctrine of factual admission in pleadings and its legal consequences

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the right of a registered society (Prabartak Sangha) to claim transfer of land under Section 24 of the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, after under-tenants transferred their interest to him.
issues_decided: Whether the conditions under Section 24 of the West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, were satisfied in this case
Whether Section 24 of the Act is ultra vires the Constitution for creating an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f)
Whether the respondent society was an 'intermediary' under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, and thus divested of its rights
holdings: The society, as immediate landlord of the under-tenants, satisfied all conditions under Section 24: the disputed land was contiguous to its land and was bona fide required for expanding its educational institution under clauses (b) and (c) of Section 4.

Section 24 does not impose an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f) because contiguity is not the sole basis; the provision aims at adjusting landlord-tenant rights and preserving institutional or community interests, making it constitutionally valid.

The society was not an 'intermediary' under Section 2(1)(i) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, because it was itself a non-agricultural tenant, and thus its rights did not vest in the State.
provisions: West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, Section 24
West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, Section 3
West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, Section 4
West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, Section 23
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 2(1)(i)
doctrines: Unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f)
Contiguity as a factor in statutory pre-emption
Definition and vesting of intermediary interests under land reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant jagirdar claimed that mango trees he planted along a roadside constituted a 'grove' under the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, and thus should remain his property after abolition of jagirs.
issues_decided: Whether trees planted along both sides of a road can constitute a 'grove' within the meaning of Section 5(b)(iv) of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951.
What is the legal meaning of the term 'grove' in the context of property rights retained by a jagirdar after abolition of jagirs.
holdings: A 'grove' under Section 5(b)(iv) means a cluster of trees sufficiently numerous and closely grouped to prevent the land from being primarily used for any other purpose, such as cultivation, and must form a substantially homogeneous unit.

Trees arranged in a line along a roadside primarily intended to provide shade do not automatically qualify as a 'grove', but if at any point they are dense and numerous enough to meet the test, such area may constitute a grove requiring further inquiry.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 5(b)(iv)
Madhya Bharat Revenue Administration and Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007
doctrines: Literal and contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Presumption that undefined words in statutes carry their ordinary dictionary meaning
Principle of fair opportunity to prove factual claims in administrative and judicial proceedings

card.dispute: Street vendors challenged the New Delhi Municipal Committee's ban on selling cooked food on public streets, claiming it violated their fundamental right to carry on trade and exceeded the Committee's statutory powers.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Committee had the power under s. 173 of the Punjab Municipal Act to ban the sale of cooked food on public streets in the absence of bye-laws under s. 188
Whether the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and its rules ousted the municipality's power to regulate or prohibit such sales
Whether the ban violated the petitioners' fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution to carry on trade
holdings: Section 173 of the Punjab Municipal Act empowers the Committee to prohibit sale of cooked food on public streets to prevent insanitary conditions, even without specific bye-laws under s. 188.
The Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and its rules do not override s. 173 of the Punjab Municipal Act, as they address food purity, not public hygiene from street vending.
The right to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g) is subject to reasonable restrictions; the ban was valid as it served public health and did not constitute an unreasonable or arbitrary restriction.
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights
Doctrine of repugnancy
Statutory interpretation of municipal powers
Public health as a valid ground for regulatory action

card.dispute: The Sub-Divisional Magistrate issued orders under Section 18 of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, against premises occupied by the respondents, who challenged the validity of the proceedings and the constitutional validity of Section 18.
issues_decided: Whether Section 18 of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification?
Whether a Magistrate can proceed under Section 18 when a cognizable offence under Section 3 or Section 7 of the Act is disclosed in the police report?
holdings: Section 18 creates two distinct and reasonable classes of cases—one where offences under Sections 3 or 7 are also made out, and another where only preventive action under Section 18 is warranted—and thus does not violate Article 14.
