When a police report discloses a cognizable offence under Section 3 or 7, the Magistrate must first proceed under Section 190(1)(b) CrPC after a valid investigation, and cannot bypass trial and appeal by resorting solely to Section 18.
provisions: Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, Section 18
Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, Section 3
Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, Section 7
Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, Section 13
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Harmonious construction of statutes
Mandatory nature of cognizance in cognizable offences
Separation between preventive and punitive measures

card.dispute: The Secretary, Home (Endowments), Andhra Pradesh, and Digyadarsam Rajindra Ram Dasjee fought over whether the latter validly succeeded as Mahant of a Math and whether the government had jurisdiction to suspend him and assume management under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether a vacancy occurred in the office of the Mahant on March 18, 1962, triggering the Commissioner's power under Section 53 of the Act.
Whether the government had jurisdiction to suspend the respondent and assume control of the Math under Section 53 when he claimed succession by private agreement.
holdings: A vacancy under Section 53(1) of the Act must be an unfilled office; if a successor assumes office by a recognized legal right, no vacancy exists to justify state intervention.
The government cannot suspend a trustee who succeeds by private agreement and recognized authority; such suspension amounts to removal, which is only permissible under Section 52 of the Act.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 53
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959, Section 52
doctrines: Doctrine of vacancy requiring actual absence of a legally recognized officeholder
Doctrine of limited administrative intervention in religious office succession

card.dispute: The receiver of a trust property sought to set aside a court auction sale in execution of a decree, without depositing the decretal amount, on the ground that the decree-holder had agreed to postpone recovery pending a scheme suit under Section 92 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a deposit under Order XXI, Rule 89(b) CPC can be dispensed with when the decree-holder agrees to postpone recovery but the decree remains unsatisfied?
Whether an executory agreement to make future provision for a decretal debt amounts to satisfaction or adjustment of the decree under Order XXI, Rule 89 CPC?
holdings: If a decree has been satisfied or adjusted under Order XXI, Rule 2 CPC, no deposit is required under Rule 89(b); however, mere postponement of recovery does not satisfy or adjust the decree.
A promise to make future provision for a decretal debt, even if accepted by the decree-holder, does not extinguish the decree or obviate the need for deposit under Rule 89(b).
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 89(b)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 2
doctrines: Satisfaction or adjustment of decree
Executory agreement vs. performance
Doctrine of waiver by agreement

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the execution of a final decree for sale of mortgaged property, arguing that the preliminary decree had been varied in appeal and thus the final decree could no longer be executed after three years from the appellate order.
issues_decided: Whether a final decree for sale remains executable when the preliminary decree is varied in appeal without a fresh final decree being passed.
Whether the executing court must recognize variations in the preliminary decree even if no fresh final decree is passed.
Whether a fresh final decree must be passed within three years of the appellate order when the preliminary decree is modified.
holdings: A final decree based on a preliminary decree that has been varied in appeal does not automatically become inexecutable; the executing court must give effect to the modified preliminary decree.
The executing court must recognize and enforce the changes made by the appellate court in the preliminary decree, even if no formal amendment to the final decree is made.

No fresh final decree is required unless the appellate court specifically directs preparation of one; the original final decree stands varied by operation of law in line with the modified preliminary decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV
doctrines: Final decree dependent on preliminary decree
Execution in accordance with appellate modification
No automatic extension of redemption period on confirmation of preliminary decree

card.dispute: Shah & Co. challenged the state's requisition of their business premises, arguing the transfer of tenancy was valid and the requisition violated their fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the assignment of tenancy rights under the Rent Control Act permitted under a government notification prevents the premises from being deemed vacant under the Requisition Act
Whether the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 infringes the petitioners' fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
holdings: An assignment of tenancy rights permitted under the Rent Control Act does not prevent the premises from being deemed vacant under the Requisition Act, as the two laws operate in different fields and the Requisition Act creates an independent fiction of vacancy.

The Requisition Act deals with property, not trade or business, so Article 19(1)(g) does not apply; and the petitioners had no valid tenancy rights due to the colourable nature of the assignment, so they could not claim infringement of Article 19(1)(f).
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15(1)
doctrines: Colourable device doctrine
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of judicial review exclusion
Doctrine of law being in pari materia

card.dispute: The appellant and his lessee disputed the apportionment of compensation for acquired land, while the respondent, a decree-holder against the lessee, claimed an interest in the lessee's share and sought to be impleaded as a party in the reference proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, as a decree-holder attaching the lessee's share of compensation, is a 'person interested' under Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and thus entitled to be impleaded in the reference proceedings.
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to entertain revision petitions against the Civil Judge's order rejecting the impleadment application.
holdings: A person claiming an interest in compensation, such as an attaching decree-holder, is a 'person interested' under Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, even without an interest in the land, and is entitled to be heard in proceedings affecting that interest.

The High Court had revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC because the Civil Judge's order amounted to a refusal to exercise jurisdiction and involved material irregularity, and the order was not an 'award' under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act.
doctrines: Person interested under Land Acquisition Act includes those with a claim to compensation, not just land
Principle of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings
Revisional jurisdiction for material irregularity or refusal of jurisdiction

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra prosecuted Jamnabhai Purshottam Assar for failing to obtain factory licences after the government notified his premises as a factory under the Factories Act, claiming he was the occupier despite having leased the premises and machinery to independent partnership firms of ex-workers.
issues_decided: Whether the owner of factory premises who leases them to independent partnership firms of ex-workers is an 'occupier' under Section 2(n) of the Factories Act, 1948
Whether Section 85(1)(ii) of the Factories Act applies to a situation where workers operate a manufacturing process under a leave and licence agreement without the owner's control
Whether the notification under Section 85(1)(ii) validly deems the owner as occupier when there is no ongoing control or employment relationship
holdings: An 'occupier' under Section 2(n) must have ultimate control over the affairs of the factory; mere ownership or receipt of rent does not make one an occupier.
Section 85(1)(ii) applies only when workers operate with the owner's permission or under an agreement implying control, not where independent firms run the business under lease or licence.
A notification under Section 85(1)(ii) cannot deem an owner as occupier if the owner has no control and the workers are not working under an agreement giving the owner supervisory authority.
doctrines: Ultimate control test for determining occupier
Deeming provisions subject to factual control and operational independence
Statutory interpretation of 'permission' and 'agreement' in regulatory context

card.dispute: The appellants (coparceners) challenged the validity of a sale of joint family property by the widow of a deceased coparcener, arguing she lacked power to alienate without their consent.
issues_decided: Whether a widow, after acquiring full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, can alienate her share in coparcenary property without the consent of male coparceners.
Whether the restrictions on alienation applicable to male coparceners under the Benares School of Mitakshara law apply to a widow's interest in joint family property.
holdings: A widow who acquires an interest in joint family property becomes a full owner under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and can alienate her share without the consent of coparceners.
The restrictions on alienation under the Benares School of Mitakshara law do not apply to a widow's interest; Parliament did not intend to impose such limitations on her full ownership rights.
provisions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Mitakshara coparcenary law (Benares School) on alienation by male coparceners

card.dispute: The assessee property owners challenged the taxability of interest awarded on compensation for property acquired by the state, claiming it was not income but compensation for deprivation.
issues_decided: Whether interest awarded on compensation for requisitioned and acquired property is taxable as income under the Income-tax Act, 1922
Whether the right to interest arose from statute or was created solely by arbitral award
Whether clauses (a) to (g) of Section 19(1) of the Defence of India Act, 1939 exclude the application of substantive law on interest
holdings: Interest received on compensation for compulsory acquisition of property is taxable as income if the right arises from statute or agreement.
The right to interest in this case arose from Sections 28 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and was merely enforced by the arbitrator and court.
Section 19(1)(g) of the Defence of India Act does not exclude substantive laws on interest; it only excludes procedural laws not covered by the arbitration code.
provisions: East Punjab Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property (Temporary Powers) Act, 1948, Section 5
doctrines: Taxability of interest as income when obligation arises from statute or agreement
Implied agreement to pay interest upon compulsory acquisition of property
Distinction between procedural arbitration law and substantive rights to interest

card.dispute: The dispute was between a mortgagee and trustees of a public trust over whether a court-ordered sale of trust property in execution of a mortgage decree was valid without the Charity Commissioner's sanction.
issues_decided: Whether a court sale in execution of a mortgage decree constitutes a 'sale' under s. 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act requiring prior sanction of the Charity Commissioner
Whether failure to deposit the amount specified in the proclamation of sale under O. 21, r. 89 of the CPC bars setting aside the sale
Whether a Single Judge of a High Court is bound by decisions of coordinate or larger benches of the same court
Whether a Full Bench judgment arising from a reference has legal validity
holdings: A court-ordered sale in execution of a decree does not fall within the scope of 'sale' under s. 36(a) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, which applies only to voluntary transactions by trustees.
Non-deposit of the amount specified in the proclamation of sale under O. 21, r. 89 CPC does not automatically bar setting aside the sale if substantial compliance or other equitable grounds exist.
A Single Judge of a High Court is bound by decisions of coordinate benches, Division Benches, and Full Benches of the same court and cannot disregard them merely based on personal judicial opinion.
A Full Bench judgment rendered on a reference has full legal authority and cannot be dismissed as 'non-existent in law'; such references are constitutionally valid and procedurally proper.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 89
doctrines: Binding nature of judicial precedent
Doctrine of stare decisis
Principle of judicial decorum and propriety
Voluntary vs. compulsory transaction distinction in trust law

card.dispute: The Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. challenged the validity of municipal notifications, house tax rules, and assessment of tax on factory buildings including open lands by the District Municipality of Ulhasnagar.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications setting up the municipality were invalid for violating Sections 4 and 7 of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901
Whether the House Tax Rules were valid and conforming to Sections 59–63 of the Act
Whether factory buildings could be assessed at a flat rate on carpet area
Whether open lands could be included in the assessment of factory buildings under the House Tax Rules
holdings: The Court did not decide the validity of the notifications as it found the issue more appropriately addressed in pending appeals before the appellate tribunal.
The Court did not rule on the conformity of the House Tax Rules with Sections 59–63, deferring the matter to the appellate tribunal.
The Court did not decide on the flat-rate assessment method, leaving it for determination in the pending appeals.

The inclusion of open lands in the assessment of factory buildings was ultra vires the House Tax Rules, as the Rules only applied to buildings with roofs and expressly excluded open lands from taxation.
provisions: House Tax Rules under Section 46, Rules 1, 3(7), 3(9), and Schedule 1
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Statutory interpretation
Deference to appellate tribunals on pending factual and legal issues

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the application of a tenant to acquire proprietary rights in land owned by the Union under the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, claiming the Act did not apply to State-owned lands.
issues_decided: Whether the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 applies to lands owned by the Union or State Government.
Whether the State can be exempted from the operation of a land reform law by implication.
holdings: The Act applies equally to lands owned by private individuals and those owned by the State, as there is no express or implied exclusion of State-owned lands.
The State cannot claim exemption from a law unless it is expressly stated or necessarily implied, and no such implication exists here.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, Sections 3, 4, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15-24, 27, 48, 54(1)(g)
doctrines: Principle of equal application of social welfare legislation to State and private entities
No implied exemption of the State from legislation absent express or necessary implication

card.dispute: The Union of India (as landlord) contested whether the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954 applied to lands owned by the State, thereby allowing occupancy tenants like Jubbi and Dunia to acquire proprietary rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954 applies to lands owned by the Union or State Government.
Whether the Act implicitly exempts the State from its operation when it abolishes proprietary rights of landowners and vests them in tenants.
holdings: The Act applies equally to lands owned by the State and private citizens, as there is no express or necessary implication of exemption for the State.
The legislature's object of social and economic justice requires abolishing landlordism uniformly, so excluding State-owned lands would create an unjust anomaly and cannot be presumed.
provisions: The Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954, Sections 3, 4, 11, 15, 27
The Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954, Sections 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 48, 54(1)(g)
doctrines: Principle of equal application of social welfare legislation to State and private entities
Presumption against implied exemption of the State from beneficial land reform laws

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's declaration that Section 8(3)(b) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, was unconstitutional for violating Article 31(2) of the Constitution, which guarantees just compensation for acquired property.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8(3)(b) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution by prescribing an arbitrary method for determining compensation.
Whether the High Court erred in not dismissing the petition on grounds of delay under Article 226.
holdings: Section 8(3)(b), which limits compensation to twice the market value at the time of requisition regardless of later market increases, fails to provide a just equivalent and is arbitrary, thus violating Article 31(2) of the Constitution.

The High Court did not err in exercising its discretion to entertain the petition despite delay, as fundamental rights violations are not easily barred by delay, and the court properly considered the importance of the constitutional issue.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8(3)(b)
doctrines: Just equivalent doctrine under Article 31(2)
Arbitrariness in compensation determination
Judicial discretion in writ petitions involving delay

card.dispute: Vidya Vati, a landowner restored to possession of her land after a court decree, challenged the state's imposition of land ceiling limits under the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, arguing she should be allowed to retain excess land either because the ceiling applies only at the Act's commencement or because she should be exempted for planting an orchard.
issues_decided: Whether the land ceiling under Section 32-A(1) applies only at the time of the Act's commencement or continues to apply in the future if landholding exceeds the limit.
Whether a landowner not in possession on the Act's commencement but later restored can claim exemption under Section 32-K for planting an orchard.
holdings: The ceiling under Section 32-A(1) is not limited to the date of the Act's commencement but applies whenever a person owns or holds land exceeding the permissible limit during the Act's operation.

A landowner who was not in possession on the Act's commencement cannot claim orchard exemption under Section 32-K(1)(vi) by giving a belated undertaking, as the statutory period to plant an orchard begins from the Act's commencement and cannot be extended by judicial interpretation.
provisions: The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-A(1)
The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-K
The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-L
The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-M
The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-B
The Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-E
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent inferred from statutory scheme
Courts cannot create exceptions to fill legislative lacunae

card.dispute: The tea companies challenged the Commissioner's assessment of their agricultural income and the imposition of a surcharge, arguing that the central income-tax authority's computation of tea income should be binding.
issues_decided: Whether the Agricultural Income-tax Officer is bound to accept the central income-tax authority's computation of tea income for assessing agricultural income under the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act.
Whether a surcharge on agricultural income-tax could be levied for the assessment year 1957-58 under the Kerala Surcharge on Taxes Act, 1957.
holdings: The Agricultural Income-tax Officer must accept the central income-tax authority's computation of tea income and assess only 60% of that income as agricultural income, as the Kerala Act does not empower the state officer to make an independent computation.
No surcharge on agricultural income-tax could be levied for the assessment year 1957-58 under the Kerala Surcharge on Taxes Act, 1957, as held in Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. v. State of Kerala.
provisions: Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, Sections 2 and 5
doctrines: Doctrine of binding effect of central tax assessment on state agricultural income computation
Principle of legislative competence in taxation between central and state governments
Rule against implying powers in taxing statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a Pramukh of a Kshettra Samiti, challenged the Uttar Pradesh government's notifications abolishing his Khand and terminating his Samiti, leading to loss of office.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications under Sections 3 and 8 of the U.P. Kshettra Samities and Zila Parishads Adhiniyam, 1961, are ultra vires and repugnant to the scheme of the Act
Whether Sections 3 and 8 involve excessive delegation of legislative power to the Executive
Whether Sections 3 and 8 violate Article 14 by enabling indirect removal of elected members
holdings: The power to abolish Khands and reconstitute Samitis is an express legislative grant to the Executive and consistent with the Act's scheme.
Sections 3 and 8 do not entail excessive delegation as the Act lays down clear policy and guiding principles for the Executive to follow.
The termination of a Samiti due to abolition of a Khand does not violate Article 14, as it is a consequence of administrative reorganization, not a tool for arbitrary removal.
provisions: U.P. Kshettra Samities and Zila Parishads Adhiniyam, 1961, Sections 3, 4, 8, 8A
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Principle of separation of powers
Rule against arbitrariness under Article 14
Doctrine of implied powers in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants, members of a Hindu undivided family, challenged the state's inclusion of their post-partition lands in surplus land calculations, arguing that the partition predated the relevant legislation and that Section 32-KK could not be applied retrospectively.
issues_decided: Whether Section 32-KK of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, introduced by the 1962 Amendment Act, applied retrospectively to partitions occurring before its enactment.
Whether the expression 'this Act' in Section 32-KK refers to the principal Act or the 1962 Amendment Act for the purpose of determining the commencement of the provision.
Whether the Collector could disregard a partition deed executed in 1956 when determining surplus land under the Act.
holdings: Section 32-KK must be deemed to have come into force on October 30, 1956, as per Section 1(2) of the 1962 Amendment Act, and applies to partitions after that date.
The phrase 'this Act' in Section 32-KK refers to the 1962 Amendment Act, not the principal Act, due to the specific commencement clause in Section 1(2).

The partition effected by the appellants in September 1956 could not be disregarded under Section 32-KK, as the provision was not in force at that time and could not be applied retrospectively beyond legislative intent.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-FF
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1962, Section 1(2)
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1962, Section 7
doctrines: Principle of retrospective legislation requiring express or necessary legislative intent
Harmonious construction of statutes
Rule against ignoring specific commencement clauses in amendment acts

card.dispute: The workmen of Brahmputra Tea Estate challenged the termination of their services and sought relief from the incoming management, which had purchased part of the company's assets, claiming liability for their reinstatement or compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the incoming management (first respondent) was liable for the claims of the workmen after purchasing part of the tea estate.
Whether the Labour Court erred in dismissing the reference as infructuous without issuing notice to the Receiver or Official Liquidator.
holdings: The incoming management was not liable for the workmen's claims as it was not a successor-in-interest and did not assume liabilities of the previous management under the sale deed.
The Labour Court should not have dismissed the reference as infructuous but was duty-bound to issue notice to the Receiver or Official Liquidator and adjudicate the workmen's claims against them.
doctrines: Successor-in-interest liability
Duty of Labour Court to implead proper parties
Adjudication of retrenchment claims under Section 25F
Application of Section 25FF in case of transfer of undertaking

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the land acquisition by Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation for street widening, arguing procedural defects and lack of genuine public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the municipality could initiate land acquisition without first attempting to purchase the land by private treaty
Whether tenants of temporary structures erected after the s. 4 notification could challenge the acquisition
Whether the delay in determining compensation invalidated the acquisition proceedings
Whether the acquisition was bona fide for a public purpose
holdings: The municipality can request compulsory acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act without first attempting to purchase the land by private treaty; no such precondition exists in law.
Tenants who occupied structures built after the s. 4 notice, with an undertaking not to claim compensation, had no enforceable interest in the land and could not challenge the acquisition.
Delay in compensation determination does not invalidate acquisition if the proceedings are eventually pursued; unreasonableness must be proven, which was not here.
The notification under s. 6 is conclusive evidence of public purpose; the appellants failed to show mala fide intent or that the acquisition was merely to peg down land prices.
doctrines: Conclusive presumption of public purpose under Section 6
No requirement of prior private treaty attempt for compulsory acquisition
Lessees' lack of standing to challenge acquisition without proprietary interest
Bona fides of acquisition not rebutted by mere delay

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of tax assessments by the Antarim Zila Parishad, arguing lack of authority and violation of constitutional rights, while the respondent claimed alternative remedies were available.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition solely on the ground of alternative remedy under s. 128 of the U.P. District Boards Act, 1922
Whether the taxing provisions were ultra vires the Constitution
Whether the assessment order violated principles of natural justice
holdings: The High Court must consider whether statutory remedies are adequate when natural justice is violated or a law is ultra vires, even if an alternative remedy exists.
A writ of certiorari can be issued under Article 226 despite alternative remedies if the impugned action is based on an ultra vires provision.
Violation of natural justice by a tribunal entitles a party to directly approach the High Court under Article 226 without exhausting statutory appeals.
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedies is a discretionary rule, not mandatory
Ultra vires legislation permits direct judicial intervention
Violation of natural justice overrides requirement to exhaust statutory remedies

card.dispute: The appellant claimed specific performance of a contract to cut teak trees in a jagir, after the State acquired proprietary rights over the forest under a land reform law.
issues_decided: Whether the forests and trees in the jagir vested in the State under the Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1951
Whether the standing timber sold under the contract had become 'ascertained goods' so as to pass property to the appellant before vesting
Whether a new contract was concluded between the appellant and the State in February 1955
holdings: Forests and trees were proprietary rights under the Act and vested in the State upon notification, extinguishing prior private rights.
Property in trees does not pass under a sale contract until they are felled and identified; unascertained standing trees remain part of the estate and vest in the State.
A new contract was not formed because the appellant’s response to the State’s proposal was a conditional acceptance, not an unqualified one.
provisions: Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1951, Sections 3, 4, 5
doctrines: Doctrine of ascertained goods under the Sale of Goods Act
Distinction between licence and proprietary interest
Doctrine of conditional acceptance in contract law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for offering a bribe, arguing that the tape-recorded conversation with a police decoy was inadmissible as evidence and violated his constitutional right against self-incrimination.
issues_decided: Whether a tape-recorded conversation between the accused and a police decoy, recorded without the accused's knowledge, is admissible in evidence under the Indian Evidence Act
Whether the tape recording amounts to a 'statement to police' barred by Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Whether the use of the tape recording violates the accused's protection against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) of the Constitution
holdings: A contemporaneous tape recording of a relevant conversation is a relevant fact under Section 7 of the Indian Evidence Act and is admissible if the time, place, accuracy, and voices are proved.
A conversation between the accused and a police decoy, not knowing police are recording, is not a 'statement to police' under Section 162 CrPC and is not barred.

Merely recording a conversation without the accused's knowledge does not amount to compulsion under Article 20(3); the accused's voluntary statements do not attract constitutional protection against self-incrimination.
doctrines: Res gestae
Admissibility of electronic evidence
Protection against self-incrimination
Voluntariness of statements in entrapment scenarios

card.dispute: The landlord obtained a decree for eviction after the Commissioner granted permission to sue, but the State Government later revoked that permission under s. 7(F); the tenant challenged the enforceability of the decree.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for eviction becomes unenforceable if the State Government revokes the permission to sue under s. 7(F) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 after the decree is passed.
Whether the power of the State Government under s. 7(F) can render a suit invalid if exercised after the suit has been instituted with valid permission under s. 3(1).
holdings: A decree for eviction obtained in a suit validly instituted with permission under s. 3(1), which became final upon confirmation by the Commissioner under s. 3(3), does not become unenforceable due to a subsequent revocation of permission by the State Government under s. 7(F).

The power of the State Government under s. 7(F) is supervisory and cannot nullify a suit or decree once the suit has been validly instituted with the required permission; such power must be exercised before the institution of the suit to be effective.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(1)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(3)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(4)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7(F)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 14
doctrines: Finality of judicial decrees
Supervisory power of executive authority
Statutory interpretation based on grammatical construction
Doctrine of maintainability of suits under rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant company claimed specific performance of a lease renewal covenant after the estate's vesting in the State, which the State resisted on grounds of statutory extinguishment of rights.
issues_decided: Whether the covenant for renewal of a mining lease created an enforceable interest in land binding on the State after vesting of the estate under the Bihar Land Reforms Act?
Whether Rule 40 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 applies to statutory leases created under Section 10 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act?
holdings: A covenant for future renewal of a lease is an encumbrance, not an interest in land, and was extinguished upon vesting of the estate under Section 4 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act; hence, the State was not bound by it.

Rule 40 of the Mineral Concession Rules applies only to leases granted by the Government and not to statutory leases under Section 10; even if applicable, the renewal period would be limited to the remaining term post-vesting, which had already expired.
doctrines: Extinguishment of encumbrances upon vesting of estate
Statutory lease as distinct from contractual lease
Covenant running with the land not creating proprietary interest

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation for their acquired orchard land and disallowance of a statutory 15% allowance under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could rely on documents not part of the record without giving the appellants an opportunity to rebut them
Whether the value of trees in an acquired orchard forms part of the market value of the land for the purpose of the 15% allowance under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act
Whether the High Court was justified in disallowing the statutory 15% allowance on the value of trees
Whether the appellants were entitled to costs in light of the enhancement of compensation
holdings: The High Court erred in considering documents not part of the record without affording the appellants an opportunity to rebut, violating principles of natural justice.
Trees standing on acquired land are 'things attached to the earth' and form part of the land; their value must be included in the market value for determining compensation.
The 15% statutory allowance under Section 23(2) applies to the market value of the land, including the value of trees, and must be allowed.
Courts have discretion in awarding costs; no interference is warranted when the claim was exaggerated and evidence largely rejected.
doctrines: Principles of Natural Justice
Market Value Determination in Land Acquisition
Inclusion of Attached Things in Definition of Land
Judicial Discretion in Award of Costs

card.dispute: The appellant, a displaced person, challenged the Bank of India's claim for recovery of debts, seeking refund of amounts from insurance policies, apportionment of joint liability, and contesting interest awarded under the Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951.
issues_decided: Whether interest could be awarded under Section 29 of the Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951 from August 15, 1947, considering the debtor's paying capacity
Whether the debt was a joint liability requiring apportionment under Section 22 of the Act
Whether insurance policies fell within the scope of Section 17 of the Act, disentitling the appellant to a refund of realized amounts
Whether the term 'renewal' in Section 2(6) of the Act applied to the acknowledgment or confirmation of existing debt with further advances
holdings: Section 29(1)(b) allows interest up to 4% per annum from August 15, 1947, if the debtor's paying capacity exceeds liabilities; such was the case here, justifying the award of interest.
The liability was solely that of the appellant, as admitted in his petition; thus, no apportionment under Section 22 was required.
Insurance policies are movable property; their assignment to the bank brings them under Section 17, and no refund is due unless realization exceeds the debt.
The term 'renewal' in Section 2(6) does not cover acknowledgments involving further advances; the debts in question were validly recognized as original debts under the Act.
provisions: The Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951, Section 2(6)
The Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951, Section 17
The Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951, Section 22
The Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951, Section 29
The Displaced Persons (Debt Adjustment) Act, 1951, Section 32
The General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 3(clauses 26 and 36)
doctrines: Paying capacity test for award of interest under special debt adjustment laws
Sole liability established by admission in pleadings
Assignment of movable property under security agreements
Statutory interpretation of 'renewal' in debt definition

card.dispute: The dispute was between the waqf authority and lessees over whether certain properties were waqf properties dedicated by a deed of waqf, and whether a copy of the deed could be admitted as evidence to prove this.
issues_decided: Whether the copy of the waqf deed was admissible in evidence under the Evidence Act when the original was not produced.
Whether clause (f) of Section 65 of the Evidence Act requires a certified copy to be produced when the case also falls under clause (a).
holdings: Secondary evidence in the form of a plain copy of a document is admissible under Section 65(a) of the Evidence Act when the original is in the possession of the opposing party and not produced despite notice.
Clause (a) of Section 65 is not controlled by clause (f); if a case falls under clause (a), any secondary evidence is admissible even if a certified copy could have been produced under clause (f).
doctrines: Secondary evidence doctrine
Admissibility of documentary evidence
Rule of harmonious construction in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants and the respondent contested over who should be the rightful trustees of a private charitable trust after the death of the last trustee, Rangayya II.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent is the sister of Rangayya II and thus entitled to claim trusteeship.
Whether the succession to the hereditary trusteeship is governed by the ordinary rules of Hindu law in the absence of a contrary provision in the will.
Whether the appellants, as nephews of Rangayya II, are entitled to succeed as 'Vamsathar' under the will of Rangayya I.
holdings: The respondent is the sister of Rangayya II, as conclusively established by judicial admission and supporting evidence, and this fact is binding on the appellants.
In the absence of a special custom or continuing direction in the will, succession to hereditary trusteeship of a private charity follows the ordinary rules of Hindu law of inheritance.

The will of Rangayya I only prescribed succession up to the 'Vamsathar' of Dharmalinga Sethurayar; once Rangayya II became trustee, he became a new stock of descent, and further succession is governed by Hindu law, not the will.
provisions: Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 (Act II of 1929)
Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Hereditary trusteeship in private charities passes to natural heirs in absence of contrary provision
Judicial admission binds the party making it, especially among family members
Succession to offices like shebaitship or trusteeship follows general rules of inheritance under Hindu law

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth-Tax and Smt. Muthukrishna Ammal disputed whether her leasehold interest in salt pans, terminable annually by either party, constituted an 'asset' under the Wealth-tax Act, 1957, and thus liable to be included in her net wealth.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's leasehold interest in salt pans was an 'asset' under Section 2(e)(v) of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957, given that the lease could be terminated annually by either party.
Whether an interest in property revocable at any time within six years from the valuation date falls within the exclusion from 'assets' under Section 2(e)(v).
Whether the fact that the lease had remained unrevoked for over six years before the valuation date made it an 'asset' despite its revocability.
holdings: An interest in property available to an assessee for a period not exceeding six years from the valuation date is not an 'asset' under Section 2(e)(v) of the Wealth-tax Act, 1957, and thus not includible in net wealth.
The precarious and revocable nature of the lease, terminable annually by either party, meant the interest was not available for a period exceeding six years, even if it had already lasted longer.

The phrase 'is available to an assessee for a period not exceeding six years' refers to future availability from the valuation date, not past enjoyment, and does not require continuous possession for six prior years.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Temporal interpretation of 'available' in tax law
Exclusion of revocable interests from taxable assets

card.dispute: The appellant mortgagee challenged whether the respondents, who were jointly liable for a mortgage debt exceeding Rs. 25,000, could be considered 'debtors' entitled to debt relief under the Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether a Single Judge of a High Court is bound by decisions of coordinate benches and larger benches of the same court.

Whether each of several joint mortgagors, collectively liable for a debt exceeding Rs. 25,000, can be treated as individually liable for a share below the threshold and thus qualify as a 'debtor' under the Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954.
Whether the provisions of the Saurashtra Act justify treating a joint mortgage debt as divisible for the purpose of determining debtor status.
holdings: A Single Judge of a High Court is ordinarily bound to follow judgments of coordinate benches, Division Benches, and Full Benches of the same High Court.
Under the Transfer of Property Act, each joint mortgagor is liable for the entire debt, and the Saurashtra Act does not provide for splitting the joint liability into individual shares.

The Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act does not alter the principle of joint and several liability; thus, if the total debt exceeds Rs. 25,000, none of the co-debtors can be treated as a 'debtor' under the Act, even if their individual shares would be below the limit.

The decision in V. Ramaswami Ayyangar v. T. N. V. Kailasa Thavar is distinguishable as it involved a different statute with specific provisions for debt separation, which are absent in the Saurashtra Act.
provisions: Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 2(6)(i)
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 7(1)
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 16
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 19
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 20
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 21
Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors' Relief Act, 1954, Section 29
doctrines: Joint and several liability
Principle of stare decisis within a High Court
Statutory interpretation to avoid absurd results
Indivisibility of joint debt in absence of statutory provision for apportionment

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the assessee, Abdul Hai Azim Ullah, fought over whether rental income from certain shops should be taxed as income from other sources or whether the transactions were usufructuary mortgages, exempt from such taxation.
issues_decided: Whether the agreements regarding the shops constituted leases or usufructuary mortgages under the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the income derived by the assessee from the shops was taxable as income from other sources.
holdings: The agreements in question were usufructuary mortgages because they involved possession of property to liquidate a debt through appropriation of rents and profits, not a lease.
Since the transactions were usufructuary mortgages, the rental receipts were not taxable as income from other sources, but applied toward mortgage debt repayment.
doctrines: Usufructuary mortgage doctrine
Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of intention of parties in characterising transactions

card.dispute: The appellant tenant claimed protected tenancy status under the Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, as amended in 1953, while the respondent landlord sought eviction, raising the issue of whether the amended Act ousted civil court jurisdiction in pending appellate proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the amendments introduced by the Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases (Amendment) Act, 1953, particularly Sections 16A and 16B, apply to pending appellate proceedings.
Whether the civil court's jurisdiction was ousted in favor of revenue courts for determining tenancy status in an appeal already pending when the 1953 Act came into force.
Whether a Letters Patent Bench can re-examine an interlocutory order passed by a Single Judge referring a tenancy issue to revenue authorities.
holdings: The 1953 amendments do not apply to pending appellate proceedings as there is no express or implied legislative intent to make them retroactive to such cases.
Sections 16A and 16B of the 1953 Act do not bar civil courts from deciding tenancy issues in appeals already pending, as the language used does not extend to appellate proceedings.

A Letters Patent Bench has the jurisdiction to review an interlocutory order of a Single Judge, even if it involved a referral to revenue authorities, as such orders do not bar subsequent appellate scrutiny.
provisions: Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, Section 16
Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases (Amendment) Act, 1953, Section 16A
Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases (Amendment) Act, 1953, Section 16B
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction requires express statutory language or necessary implication
Principle of retroactivity: statutes affecting substantive rights are not presumed to apply retrospectively
Interlocutory orders not finally disposing of a case can be reviewed in appeal against the final decree

card.dispute: The appellant, a decree-holder in a pre-emption suit, deposited purchase money after the court-fixed deadline; the respondents sought restitution of property, claiming automatic dismissal of the suit due to default.
issues_decided: Whether the stay order by the High Court in the second appeal stayed only delivery of possession or also the obligation to deposit purchase money.
Whether the appellant's delayed deposit of purchase money amounted to a default, disentitling him to possession.
Whether the High Court’s confirmation of the decree implied a fresh period for depositing the purchase money.
holdings: A stay order in a pre-emption decree under Order 20 Rule 14 CPC operates on reciprocal obligations; staying possession also stays the requirement to deposit purchase money.
Default in depositing purchase money within the original time does not bar enforcement if the stay order prevented performance and the deposit was made during the stay.
When a High Court confirms a pre-emption decree in a second appeal, it implies a fresh starting point for depositing the purchase money from the date of its decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 14
doctrines: Reciprocal obligations in conditional decrees
Implied extension of time in appellate decrees
Doctrine of restitution

card.dispute: The appellant claimed co-ownership in a business allegedly converted into joint family property, while respondents asserted it remained a separate business.
issues_decided: Whether the business of Ambika Stores became a joint family property by being thrown into the common stock.
Whether the appellant became a co-owner of the business by contributing his labour.
holdings: A self-acquired business becomes joint family property only if there is a clear intention by the coparcener to waive separate rights; mere recitals in documents or conduct for external purposes do not suffice.
Contribution of labour alone does not make a person a co-owner; without evidence of mutual agreement or recognition of ownership, the relationship remains that of employer and employee.
doctrines: Doctrine of blending or waiving separate property in Hindu law
Doctrine of intention in conversion of self-acquired property to joint family property

card.dispute: The appellants (mortgagees) claimed possession of 'sir' land from the respondent (widow of a mortgagor), who had been dispossessed after the mortgagee acquired proprietary rights in insolvency and arbitration proceedings, while she claimed restoration of occupancy rights under tenancy law.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagors retained cultivatory rights in 'sir' land after executing usufructuary mortgages in 1895
Whether the mortgagors acquired occupancy or ex-proprietary occupancy rights under the Central Provinces Tenancy Act
Whether the mortgagee could acquire cultivatory rights through execution of decree or insolvency proceedings in violation of statutory protections
holdings: The mortgagors retained cultivatory rights after the 1895 mortgages since the mortgage did not expressly include such rights and they continued cultivation.
By 1920, the mortgagors became occupancy tenants under Section 10 of the Central Provinces Tenancy Act, as they were neither sub-tenants nor absolute occupancy tenants.

The mortgagee could not acquire cultivatory rights through execution or insolvency proceedings as such transfers were barred by Sections 12 and 49 of the Act and lacked required revenue authority permission.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Tenancy Act, 1883
doctrines: Statutory protection of occupancy tenants against transfer of cultivatory rights in execution or insolvency
Retention of tenancy rights despite transfer of proprietary rights
Requirement of revenue authority permission for valid transfer of ex-proprietary occupancy rights

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of pre-emption decrees in favor of the legal representatives of Neki, arguing that the statutory right to pre-emption was not heritable and that a subsequent amendment barred the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the statutory right of pre-emption under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 is a heritable right that survives the death of the pre-emptor.
Whether Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended in 1960, retrospectively bars the legal representatives of a deceased pre-emptor from obtaining a decree.
holdings: The statutory right of pre-emption under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 is a heritable right that passes to the legal heirs of the pre-emptor and can be enforced by them in suit.

Section 31 of the amended Punjab Pre-emption Act does not bar a decree in favor of legal representatives where the suits were filed and sales occurred after the amendment, and the right to pre-empt was validly exercised before death.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rules 1 and 11
doctrines: Right to sue survives to legal representatives
Retrospective operation of statutes
Heritability of statutory rights

card.dispute: The Gram Sabha, Besahani, and the respondents, Ram Raj Singh & Ors, fought over possession of five plots of land, with the respondents claiming Sirdari and Bhumidari rights and challenging an ejectment order.
issues_decided: Whether the Sub-Divisional Officer's ejectment order under s. 212A(6) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, was valid in the absence of a direction to pay compensation
Whether the respondents' suit was time-barred under s. 212A(7) and Rule 338 of the U.P. Rules, 1952
Whether the High Court was correct in decreeing the suit without remanding for trial on unresolved issues regarding Bhumidari rights
holdings: An order under s. 212A(6) must include a direction to pay compensation to be valid; absence of such direction renders the ejectment order invalid and not binding under s. 212A(7).
Since the ejectment order was invalid, the respondents' rights were not extinguished, and their suit under s. 209 was maintainable within six years of dispossession.
The High Court erred in decreeing the suit; it should have remanded the case for trial on the issue of acquisition of Bhumidari rights and other undecided issues.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 212A(6)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 212A(7)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 209
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 189(c)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 338
doctrines: Condition precedent in statutory interpretation
Validity of administrative orders under statutory conditions
Remand for trial when findings are incomplete

card.dispute: The appellant, a co-sharer, claimed a right to reconveyance of land sold to the first respondent, challenging the validity of the Collector's jurisdiction to entertain his application under the Bihar Land Reforms Act due to non-attachment of a registered sale deed at the time of filing.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to entertain the application under Section 16(3) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act when the sale deed was not yet registered on the date of filing the application.
Whether the requirement under Rule 19 of the Bihar Land Reforms Rules to attach a copy of the registered sale deed is mandatory or directory.
holdings: The Collector had jurisdiction to entertain the application even if the sale deed was not registered on the date of filing, as long as the transfer was completed before the Collector passed the order.

The requirement under Rule 19 to attach a copy of the registered sale deed is directory, not mandatory; substantial compliance by attaching a certified copy of the unregistered deed, along with proof of deposit and other necessary information, is sufficient for the application to be validly entertained.
provisions: Bihar Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling Area and Acquisition of Surplus Land) Act, 1962, Section 16
Bihar Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling Area and Acquisition of Surplus Land) Rules, 1963, Rule 19
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory distinction in statutory interpretation
Substantial compliance doctrine
Jurisdiction based on substance rather than technical non-compliance

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an order by an Additional District Magistrate requisitioning a shop under the Defence of India Act, arguing that only a District Magistrate had the authority to make such an order.
issues_decided: Whether an Additional District Magistrate can exercise powers delegated to a District Magistrate under Section 29 of the Defence of India Act, 1962, solely by virtue of a notification under Section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Whether the expression 'District Magistrate' in the notification under Section 40(1) of the Defence of India Act includes an Additional District Magistrate.
holdings: An Additional District Magistrate cannot exercise powers under Section 29 of the Defence of India Act merely by virtue of being invested with powers of a District Magistrate under Section 10(2) of the CrPC, as the delegation was specifically to officers of the status of District Magistrate.

The words 'District Magistrate' in the notification must be given their ordinary meaning and cannot be read to include 'Additional District Magistrate' unless the context requires, which it does not in this case.
doctrines: Strict interpretation of delegation of statutory powers
Presumption against extension of drastic powers to subordinate authorities
Doctrine of persona designata (distinguished)

card.dispute: The Godhra Borough Municipality and Godhra Electricity Co. Ltd disputed over the method of determining the capital value of non-residential buildings for levying a rate under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'rate' under Section 73 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925 refers to a tax on capital value or annual value of buildings.
Whether the capital value for rate assessment should be based on the original cost of construction minus depreciation or on a contractor's method of valuation.
Whether the balance sheet data of a company constitutes 'reliable data' under Rule 5 for determining capital value.
holdings: The term 'rate' in Section 73, though not defined, should be interpreted with reference to English rating law, and it generally refers to a tax on annual or rateable value, not capital value, unless the statute specifies otherwise.

The capital value for rate assessment must be determined using the contractor's method, which includes estimating current construction cost, allowing for depreciation, land value, and market investment rates, rather than relying solely on historical cost.

Balance sheet figures prepared under the Companies Act are not 'reliable data' for rate assessment as they reflect accounting entries, not market or structural valuation relevant to property taxation.
provisions: The Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, Section 73
The Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, Section 75
The Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, Rule 4
The Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, Rule 5
doctrines: Use of English statutory interpretation for Indian statutes with similar origin and purpose
Contractor's method of valuation for determining effective capital value
Distinction between accounting value and taxable value in property assessment

card.dispute: The managing trustee of a public charitable trust sought possession of trust land for personal cultivation, but the tenant and revenue authorities contested whether a trustee could be considered a 'landlord' entitled to cultivate personally under the tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether a managing trustee of a public charitable trust can be considered a 'landlord' under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958
Whether a managing trustee can 'cultivate personally' within the meaning of Section 2(12) of the Act
holdings: A managing trustee in whom trust property is vested is a 'landlord' under the Act and entitled to apply for possession of land for personal cultivation.
Cultivation by a managing trustee is 'on one's own account' within Section 2(12) if done by his own labour or under his personal supervision, even though the property belongs to the trust.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 2(12)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 36(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 38(1)
doctrines: Definition of landlord based on vesting of property
Personal cultivation includes cultivation under personal supervision by hired labour
Distinction between trustee and manager of idol or juristic person

card.dispute: The karta of a Hindu undivided family challenged his arrest and detention for non-payment of income tax assessed on the family, arguing he was not personally liable as the assessee.
issues_decided: Whether the karta of a Hindu undivided family can be treated as an assessee in default for the family's tax liability under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Whether the Tax Recovery Officer can initiate detention proceedings against the karta when the assessment and recovery certificate are issued against the Hindu undivided family.
Whether the manager of a Hindu undivided family can be deemed personally liable for arrest and detention under Section 222 of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
holdings: A Hindu undivided family is a distinct taxable entity under the Income-tax Act, 1961, and the karta cannot be deemed the assessee merely by virtue of his managerial status.
Proceedings for arrest and detention under Section 222 can only be initiated against the assessee, which in this case is the Hindu undivided family, not its karta.
No provision in the Income-tax Act deems the karta personally liable for the family's tax default, and thus his detention was unauthorized.
doctrines: Distinct legal entity doctrine for Hindu undivided family under tax law
Principle of lawful initiation of recovery proceedings only against the assessee
No personal liability of karta for HUF's tax arrears absent statutory provision

card.dispute: The appellant refused to execute a conveyance of 41 acres of jirayat land to the respondent, claiming that enforcement of the sale agreement would cause the respondent's landholding to exceed the statutory ceiling under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether a contract for sale of agricultural land is void if its performance may result in the purchaser holding land in excess of the statutory ceiling.
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decree specific performance of such a contract despite provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
holdings: A contract for the sale of agricultural land is not void merely because its performance may result in the purchaser holding land in excess of the statutory ceiling; the seller cannot resist enforcement on that ground.

The civil court has jurisdiction to grant a decree for specific performance of a sale agreement; the statutory scheme does not exclude such jurisdiction, even though the Mamlatdar alone can later determine if the acquisition exceeds the ceiling and vest excess land in the government.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 5
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 34
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 35
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70(mb)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84C
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85
doctrines: Statutory forfeiture does not invalidate a transfer between parties
Civil court jurisdiction is not ousted unless expressly excluded by statute
A contract is not void under Section 23 of the Contract Act unless its object or consideration is to defeat the law

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Khanmull appealed against a High Court decree that modified the trial court's award of interest in a mortgage recovery suit, challenging the calculation of principal and interest under the Mysore Money Lenders Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in re-determining the principal amount of the original loans by examining prior transactions instead of relying on the mortgage deed amounts.

Whether the arrears of interest under Section 17 of the Mysore Money Lenders Act should be calculated up to the date of the trial court decree, the date of the High Court decree, or the date fixed for redemption.
holdings: The term 'principal of the original loan' in Section 17 of the Mysore Money Lenders Act requires courts to determine the actual cash advanced, disregarding any interest added later, justifying the High Court's inquiry into prior transactions.
Arrears of interest under Section 17 are limited to the amount accrued up to the date of the trial court decree, as appellate decrees relate back to the original decree date for this purpose.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rule 11
Usurious Loans Act (Mysore Act IX of 1923)
doctrines: Relation back of appellate decree
Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Separation between pre-decree and post-decree interest

card.dispute: Sub-tenants claimed the right to purchase agricultural land from the landowner under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, which the authorities and courts denied.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-tenant is entitled to apply for purchase of land under Section 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
Whether the definition of 'tenant' under the Act includes a sub-tenant for the purpose of purchasing land from a landowner
holdings: A sub-tenant is not a tenant of the landowner and therefore not entitled to purchase land under Section 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
The legislative scheme and definitions in the Act show that only tenants directly holding from landowners can exercise the right to purchase, not sub-tenants.
The proviso disabling tenants who sublet from applying does not confer rights on sub-tenants, as the Act does not resolve potential conflicts between tenant and sub-tenant claims.
The language and structure of Section 18 indicate the legislature did not intend to extend purchase rights to sub-tenants, even if they have long possession.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent
Hierarchy of tenurial rights

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the applicability of the Usurious Loans Act, 1918 to a 1933 mortgage deed executed in Bangalore Civil and Military Station, arguing that the Act had not commenced in that area at the time of the mortgage.
issues_decided: Whether the Usurious Loans Act, 1918 became applicable to the Bangalore Civil and Military Station upon its original enactment in 1918 or only when it was formally extended to that area in 1937.
Whether a mortgage deed executed in 1933 could be considered an agreement or security made after the commencement of the Usurious Loans Act for the purposes of claiming relief under it.

Whether a suit for redemption and accounting under a usufructuary mortgage is barred by the provisions of the Usurious Loans Act if the agreement predates the Act's commencement in the relevant territory.
holdings: The 'commencement' of an Act refers to when it comes into force in a particular territory, not merely when it is passed or comes into operation elsewhere.
The Usurious Loans Act, 1918 commenced in the Bangalore Civil and Military Station only on 1 April 1937, not in 1918, because the area was not part of British India at the time.
Since the mortgage deed was executed in 1933, before the Act commenced in that area, the Act does not apply, and the suit for redemption and surplus cannot be governed by its provisions.
doctrines: Territorial commencement of legislation
Distinction between 'commencement' and 'coming into operation' of an Act
Substance over form in characterizing suits under fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The appellants (mortgagees) challenged the High Court's decree determining the principal amount and interest payable under two mortgage deeds, arguing that the court wrongly recalculated the original loan amounts and misinterpreted the period for allowable arrears of interest under the Mysore Money Lenders Act, 1939.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in going behind the mortgage deeds to determine the 'principal amount of the original loan' under s. 17 of the Mysore Money Lenders Act, 1939
Whether arrears of interest under s. 17 include interest up to the date of the decree, the date of institution of suit, or the date fixed for redemption
holdings: The term 'principal amount of the original loan' in s. 17 means the actual cash advanced, not the amount stated in the mortgage deed; courts must examine prior transactions to determine the true principal.

Arrears of interest under s. 17 are limited to interest accrued up to the date of the trial court's decree, not the date of appeal or redemption, as the appellate decree relates back to the original decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rule 11
Mysore Usurious Loans Act, 1923 (Mys. Act 19 of 1923)
doctrines: Relation back of appellate decree
Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Separation between pre-decree and post-decree interest

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a final appellate order in a rent control case, arguing that the amended law giving the High Court wider revisional powers could not be applied retrospectively.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, as amended by Gujarat Act 18 of 1965, could be applied to a case where the appellate decision had already attained finality before the amendment came into force.

Whether the High Court could exercise wider revisional jurisdiction under the amended Section 29(2) in place of the limited jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure when the revision petition was filed under the latter.
holdings: An appellate order that had become final under the original law cannot be reopened by retrospective application of an amending act that confers wider revisional powers on the High Court, in the absence of an express or implied retrospective provision.

The amendment to Section 29(2) was not procedural but substantive, as it conferred new jurisdiction on the High Court to review final orders, and thus could not be applied to pending petitions unless made retrospective.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29(1) and (2)
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of judgments
Doctrine of prospective and retrospective operation of statutes
Distinction between procedural and substantive amendments

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of the tenant based on a compromise decree, which the tenant later challenged as invalid for violating rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise decree for eviction is valid if it does not record the existence of statutory grounds under Section 13 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
Whether a decree passed in contravention of Section 13(1) of the Act is a nullity
holdings: A compromise decree for eviction must reflect that one or more statutory grounds under Section 13(1) exist; otherwise, it violates the mandatory provisions of the Act.
A decree passed without ensuring compliance with Section 13(1) is a nullity and cannot be executed, even if based on a compromise.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Nullity of decree for non-compliance with mandatory statutory conditions
Court's duty to satisfy itself of statutory grounds for eviction even in compromise cases

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent on the grounds that the respondent was disqualified from contesting due to his interest in subsisting government contracts at the time of nomination.
issues_decided: Whether the contracts between the respondent's firm and the State Government were 'subsisting' under Section 9A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, at the time of filing nomination.
Whether a partner in a firm having government contracts is disqualified under Section 9A even if the contract is in the firm's name.
Whether dissolution of the partnership before nomination without notice to the government removes the disqualification under Section 9A.
holdings: A contract remains subsisting under Section 9A if any part of the work, including repairs or rectification of defects, is yet to be performed, even if the main work is substantially complete.
A partner in a firm has sufficient interest in government contracts entered into by the firm to attract disqualification under Section 9A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Dissolution of a partnership without notice to the government does not absolve a partner from liability under government contracts, and thus does not remove disqualification under Section 9A.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 9A
Article 299 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Substantial performance doctrine
Doctrine of continuing contractual liability
Strict interpretation of electoral disqualifications

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be joint founders of a religious trust, sued for the removal of the managing trustee and for a scheme of management due to alleged mismanagement, while the respondents contended that the trust was solely founded by one person who had the exclusive right to manage it.
issues_decided: Whether the contributors to the trust at its inception were joint founders entitled to rotational management in proportion to their contributions
Whether a contributor to a private trust, who is not a founder, can file a suit for removal of a trustee or for framing a scheme of management
Whether the allegations of mismanagement and breach of trust against the managing trustee were substantiated
holdings: Not every contributor to a trust at its foundation becomes a joint founder; only those who collectively establish the trust with a shared intention of control are founders.

A person interested in the proper administration of a private trust, including a contributor, has the right to file a suit for removal of a trustee or for framing a scheme if there is mismanagement or breach of trust.
The allegations of mismanagement, including non-performance of pujas and fabrication of accounts, were not proven, and the concurrent findings of the lower courts must be respected.
provisions: Charities Act or relevant statutory framework (by reference to English and Indian authorities)
doctrines: Doctrine of joint foundation in trusts
Principle of standing to sue for breach of trust
Concurrent finding rule in factual determinations by lower courts

card.dispute: Traders challenged the validity of notifications establishing a regulated agricultural produce market in Gaya and Barh, and the levy of licence and market fees under the Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, claiming unreasonableness, lack of infrastructure, and violation of Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the market area declared under Section 4(1) was unreasonably wide
Whether a market must have a well-defined site with equipment and facilities to be validly established
Whether the licence and market fees levied were in the nature of taxes and therefore illegal
Whether selective implementation of the Act in Gaya and Barh violated Article 14
holdings: The State Government's power under Section 4(1) to declare a market area is subject to reasonableness, but the declared area in Gaya was not so wide as to be unreasonable or unworkable.
A market is validly established by declaring the market proper and market yards under Section 5(2) based on the committee's recommendation; physical infrastructure is not a precondition.
The fees levied are regulatory fees, not taxes, as they are commensurate with services provided like dispute resolution, grading, weighment, and market regulation.
The State is not obligated to implement the Act uniformly across Bihar; phased implementation does not violate Article 14.
provisions: Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, Section 2(h)
Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, Section 4(1)
Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, Section 5(2)
Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1960, Section 18(ii)
Bihar Agricultural Market Produce Rules, 1962, Rule 59
doctrines: Reasonableness in exercise of statutory power
Test of 'fee' versus 'tax' based on quid pro quo
Gradual implementation of legislation does not violate equality under Article 14

card.dispute: The landlord (Lajwanti) sought execution of a decree for possession of factory premises against the tenant (Lal Chand and others), who resisted on the ground that removing machinery required prior permission under the East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether section 3 of the East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948 bars execution of a decree for possession of factory premises.
Whether the earlier proceedings created res judicata against re-attempting execution.
Whether the consent decree allowing possession was void due to contravention of the 1948 Act.
holdings: Section 3 of the East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948 does not prohibit execution of a decree for possession, as delivery of possession does not amount to dismantling a factory.
The prior orders did not finally decide the inexecutability of the decree; hence, res judicata did not apply to bar a fresh execution application.
The consent decree was not void merely because it involved vacating factory premises, as the Act does not override court-ordered possession.
provisions: East Punjab Factories (Control of Dismantling) Act, 1948, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Res judicata
Sanctity of consent decrees
Statutory interpretation (no implied bar on court execution)

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee Jalalabad and displaced persons (including Lachhman Dass) disputed over ownership of shops wrongly declared as evacuee property and transferred under the Compensation Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 is ultra vires the Constitution under Article 31(2)
Whether the section provides for a public purpose and adequate compensation
Whether the impugned section can be saved by Article 31(2A) or severability
holdings: Section 20B does not serve a public purpose because it allows the Central Government to deny restoration of property based on convenience rather than public interest.
Section 20B fails to prescribe principles for determining compensation, including the time for valuation, and thus violates Article 31(2).
The section is not severable and cannot be saved by Article 31(2A); it is void in its entirety.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20B
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine under Article 31(2)
Principles of compensation in acquisition laws
Doctrine of severability

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant, who claimed occupancy rights under the Madras Estates Land Act and later claimed protection as a 'cultivating tenant' under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant acquired occupancy rights under Section 6(1) of the Madras Estates Land Act after the expiry of the 12-year period in Section 8(5).
Whether the agreements under Section 8(5) automatically confer occupancy rights after 12 years.
