Whether the tenant qualifies as a 'cultivating tenant' under the amended definition in the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955.
holdings: Section 8(5) of the Madras Estates Land Act does not automatically confer occupancy rights under Section 6(1) upon expiry of the 12-year period; the contractual relationship continues unless altered by law.
The language of Section 8(5) is plain and does not imply that tenancy agreements under it terminate or convert into occupancy tenancies after 12 years.
A 'cultivating tenant' must personally contribute physical labour or that of family members; supervision or managerial roles do not qualify under the amended definition.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 2(1)(d)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Strict construction of exceptions to general statutory rights
Requirement of physical labour for 'personal cultivation' under tenancy protection laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Loonkaran Sethiya, challenged the State Bank of Jaipur's right to execute a decree in his favour through a power of attorney after he sought to revoke it.
issues_decided: Whether the power of attorney given by the debtor to the bank was irrevocable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 202
Whether the power of attorney amounted to an equitable assignment of the decree proceeds to the bank
Whether an equitable assignee can execute a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure without formal assignment under Order XXI, Rule 16
Whether the bank could continue execution proceedings in the decree-holder's name despite asserting its own right
holdings: A power of attorney given by a debtor to a creditor bank to execute a decree is irrevocable when it is coupled with the bank's interest in securing repayment.
Where a debtor earmarks decree proceeds for repaying a debt, it constitutes an equitable assignment of those proceeds to the creditor, even without formal transfer.
An equitable assignee of a decree may execute it under Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure, even if not recognized under Order XXI, Rule 16.
Execution proceedings initiated in the decree-holder's name may continue despite the bank's independent right, to serve justice and avoid technical dismissal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 16
doctrines: Power coupled with interest
Equitable assignment
Irrevocability of agency when agent has an interest
Substance over form in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee, Jalalabad, claimed ownership of property wrongly declared as evacuee property and challenged the constitutional validity of Section 20B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, which allowed the government to deny restoration of such property and instead provide compensation in kind or cash.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution?
Whether the provision of compensation under Section 20B satisfies the requirement of 'public purpose' under Article 31(2)?
Whether Section 20B prescribes adequate principles for determining compensation as required by Article 31(2)?
holdings: Section 20B violates Article 31(2) because it permits deprivation of property without ensuring that the non-restoration serves a public purpose, allowing executive discretion based on convenience rather than public interest.

Providing alternative property or cash solely because a displaced person occupies the property does not constitute a public purpose if it prioritizes administrative convenience over justice to the rightful owner.

Section 20B fails to lay down clear principles for determining compensation, as it does not specify the time at which value is to be assessed or guarantee equivalent compensation, violating the constitutional mandate under Article 31(2).
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20B
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 27
doctrines: Public purpose doctrine under Article 31(2)
Principles of just compensation
Doctrine of severability
Rule of law and constitutional limitations on executive power

card.dispute: The appellant Girasdar sought to evict tenants and obtain land allotment for personal cultivation, but tenants resisted, invoking conditions in a 1949 government letter prohibiting eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, bound by conditions in a 1949 government letter prohibiting eviction of tenants, could seek allotment of land under Section 19 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951.
Whether the rights of tenants under the 1949 letter constitute 'rights or privileges' under Section 18 of the Act that cannot be abridged by Chapter IV allotment proceedings.
holdings: The appellant, having accepted the grant subject to the 1949 conditions, could not seek eviction of tenants through a Section 19 application, as it would violate those binding conditions.
Under Section 18 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951, tenants' rights arising from the 1949 government letter are protected and cannot be abridged by an allotment order under Chapter IV.
doctrines: Doctrine of binding conditions on land grants by government
Statutory protection of pre-existing tenant rights under Section 18
Non-derogation from statutory rights by subsequent administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant Girasdar sought to obtain land for self-cultivation under the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951, despite a prior condition imposed by the Government of India that he could not evict tenants from the granted land, which the tenants and authorities opposed.
issues_decided: Whether the condition imposed by the Government of India that the grantee could not evict tenants constitutes a right or privilege of the tenant under Section 18 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951
Whether a Girasdar bound by such a condition can file an application under Section 19 of the Act for allotment of land for self-cultivation by evicting tenants
holdings: The condition that the grantee cannot evict tenants is a right or privilege of the tenant arising out of the grant within the meaning of Section 18 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951, and cannot be abridged by any provision of the Act.

A Girasdar who has accepted a grant subject to a condition against eviction cannot file a valid application under Section 19 for land allotment if it results in eviction, as such action would violate the tenant’s protected rights under Section 18.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel by acceptance of benefit with conditions
Primacy of statutory protection of tenant rights over landlord's claims
Non-derogation from statutory rights of tenants under Section 18
Act of State doctrine in recognition of grants by Government

card.dispute: Mahesh Bhagat (plaintiff) sued to recover possession of land plots from tenants inducted by a prior leaseholder, claiming the lease was a mortgage and that the tenants could not acquire occupancy rights after the lease expired.
issues_decided: Whether the thika patta was a lease or a usufructory mortgage
Whether the tenants inducted by the leaseholder acquired raiyat status and occupancy rights under the Bihar Tenancy Act
holdings: The thika patta was a lease, not a usufructory mortgage, as it created a tenancy for 40 years without a right of redemption and was not intended as security for a debt.

The tenants, being settled raiyats under a tenure-holder and lawfully inducted, acquired occupancy rights under Section 21(1) of the Bihar Tenancy Act, which are conferred by law and not dependent on the lessor's title.
doctrines: No one can give a better title than they have
Statutory conferral of occupancy rights to settled raiyats

card.dispute: The appellant sought to enforce a compromise in execution proceedings that allowed interest at 1% per month, higher than the original decree rate, which the respondent challenged as unenforceable.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise in execution proceedings, where the judgment-debtor agrees to pay interest at a rate higher than the decree rate, is enforceable in execution.
Whether the executing court has the power to record and enforce such a compromise under the Code of Civil Procedure.
holdings: Parties can lawfully compromise their rights under a decree, and such a compromise, if recorded under Order 21 Rule 2 CPC, is enforceable in execution proceedings even if it includes higher interest than decreed.

The executing court has exclusive jurisdiction under Section 47 CPC to determine questions relating to the execution of a decree, including enforcement of a compromise involving postponed execution with enhanced interest.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of compromise in execution proceedings
Exclusive jurisdiction of executing court under Section 47 CPC
Enforceability of post-decree agreements as adjustments, not amendments

card.dispute: The appellants (sub-lessees of a homestead) fought the respondents (purchasers of the main lease) over whether the suit for possession of the homestead was maintainable under the Bihar Tenancy Act or the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the sub-lease of a homestead, originally part of an agricultural lease, is governed by the Bihar Tenancy Act or the Transfer of Property Act.
Whether the High Court was justified in departing from a long-standing judicial interpretation that treated such sub-leases as agricultural leases.
holdings: A sub-lease of a homestead forming part of an agricultural lease is governed by the Bihar Tenancy Act if the main lease is agricultural, as consistent judicial interpretation over 55 years established this rule.

A long-standing judicial interpretation affecting property rights should not be overturned merely because a later court deems it legally incorrect, especially when titles and transactions have been based on it.
doctrines: Stare decisis
Rule of settled interpretation affecting property
Expressio unius est exclusio alterius

card.dispute: The appellant landowner sued to recover possession of land from respondents who claimed to be statutory owners under the Bombay Tenancy Act, asserting tenancy during Court of Wards' management.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents became statutory owners of the suit land on 'tillers' day' (1 April 1957) under Section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948

Whether the respondents were subsisting tenants on 11 May 1958, the date of cessation of Court of Wards' management, so as to acquire statutory ownership under the first proviso to Section 88 of the Act
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the question of past tenancy, or whether it was barred by Sections 70 and 85 of the Act
holdings: Tenants did not become statutory owners on 'tillers' day' because the Act was inapplicable during Court of Wards' management from August 1956 to May 1958.
Respondents were not subsisting tenants on May 11, 1958, as their tenancy under the 1956 kabuliyat ended on May 31, 1957, so they did not acquire statutory ownership under Section 88.
The civil court had jurisdiction to decide questions of past tenancy for determining statutory ownership, as Sections 70 and 85 do not bar such inquiries when the main issue is title.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85A
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction must be expressly stated or necessarily implied
Statutory ownership under 'tillers' day' depends on subsistence of tenancy on the relevant date
Revenue court jurisdiction under Section 70 is not exclusive for determining past tenancy when title is in question

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Indore sought to acquire part of Shri K.N. Palshikar's land for a road widening scheme, leading to a dispute over compensation, solatium, and the Corporation's right to withdraw from acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation could withdraw from acquisition proceedings under the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956
Whether the respondent was entitled to solatium in addition to compensation
Whether the High Court could consider the sufficiency of compensation in revision under Section 392 of the Act
holdings: The Act does not permit the Corporation to withdraw from acquisition proceedings; vesting of land in the Corporation occurs automatically under Section 305 upon fulfillment of conditions.
The respondent is entitled to a 15% solatium because the procedure under Section 387(3), which incorporates the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, includes solatium as part of the compensation framework.
The High Court, in revision under Section 392, cannot re-examine the sufficiency of compensation or factual determinations made by the District Court.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 305
Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 387
Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 392
doctrines: Incorporation by reference of procedural provisions from one statute into another
Automatic vesting of property upon fulfillment of statutory conditions
Limitation of revisional jurisdiction to questions of law and jurisdiction, not factual reassessment

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi refused to sanction building repairs by Kishan Das, claiming the land would be covered by a future road under the Master Plan; the respondents challenged this refusal in court.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner could refuse sanction under s. 336(2)(a) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act on the ground that the proposed use violated the Master Plan under the Delhi Development Act.
Whether the Master Plan alone, without a Zonal Development Plan, could prohibit the use of land under s. 14 of the Delhi Development Act.
Whether the proposed construction contravened any law within the meaning of s. 336(2)(a) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act.
holdings: The Commissioner cannot refuse sanction under s. 336(2)(a) unless the proposed use violates a specific legal provision; a broad proposal in the Master Plan without precise land allocation does not constitute such a violation.

Section 14 of the Delhi Development Act applies only when a specific and definite use of land is indicated in the Master Plan or a Zonal Development Plan; in the absence of such indication, the section does not prohibit existing or proposed use.

The Master Plan’s general recommendation for road width does not amount to a prohibition on land use; without a Zonal Development Plan specifying land reservation for roads, there is no contravention of law under s. 336(2)(a).
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory powers to refuse building sanction
Requirement of definite land use designation for enforcement under development plans
Distinction between broad planning objectives and enforceable land use restrictions

card.dispute: The Official Trustee of West Bengal and others versus Sachindra Nath Chatterjee over the validity of a court order permitting changes to a trust deed and the trustee's liability for accounting.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta High Court had jurisdiction under Chapter XIII of its Original Side Rules to permit the settlor to alter the terms of a trust deed by a deed inter vivos.
Whether the High Court's order allowing such alteration was valid or void for lack of jurisdiction.
Whether the Official Trustee could be held liable as a trustee de son tort for disbursing trust income pursuant to the impugned order.
From what date accounting by the Official Trustee should commence.
holdings: The Calcutta High Court lacked jurisdiction under Chapter XIII to authorize alterations to the beneficial terms of a trust; its powers were limited to administrative and interpretive matters.
The order permitting the settlor to alter the trust deed by deed inter vivos was beyond the court's jurisdiction and therefore void, not merely illegal.
The Official Trustee, having acted in good faith under a court order, is not liable as a trustee de son tort and should be held to the same liability as a lawful trustee.
Accounting by the Official Trustee need only commence from the date of the suit's institution, not from when he took charge of the trust estate.
provisions: Trustees and Mortgagees Powers Act, 1866, Section 43
Calcutta High Court Original Side Rules, Chapter XIII
doctrines: Inherent jurisdiction of equity courts is limited to administrative and emergency management of trusts, not modification of beneficial interests.
Orders beyond jurisdiction are void, not merely voidable.
Trustee acting under a court order is not a trustee de son tort.
Equity will not permit re-opening of transactions conducted in good faith under a court order.

card.dispute: The Oriental Investment Co. (P) Ltd fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether it was an investor or a dealer in shares and properties, and whether its gains from such sales could be taxed as business profits.
issues_decided: Whether the question of being a dealer versus an investor is a mixed question of law and fact?
Whether the High Court had the jurisdiction to examine the application of legal principles to facts in such cases?
Whether the questions framed by the Supreme Court earlier were appropriate to the real controversy?
Whether the Tribunal should be directed to frame fresh questions for the High Court under s. 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922?
holdings: The question of whether an entity is a dealer or an investor is a mixed question of law and fact, and thus subject to judicial review on the application of legal principles.
The High Court has the jurisdiction to examine whether the Tribunal correctly applied legal principles to the facts, even if the primary facts are accepted.
The previously framed questions were inappropriate because they treated a mixed question as purely factual by focusing only on the existence of material.
The appeals are allowed, the High Court's judgment is set aside, and the Tribunal is directed to frame fresh questions reflecting the true legal controversy.
doctrines: Mixed question of law and fact
Jurisdiction of High Court under reference provisions
Finality of findings of fact unless unsupported by evidence or perverse
Proper framing of legal questions in tax references

card.dispute: The appellant, highest bidder for liquor retail rights, challenged the cancellation of his bid and denial of licences, while the state had granted licences to the next highest bidder.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's failure to comply with Rule 19(1) and (3) justified cancellation of his bid
Whether the Divisional Commissioner could cancel the sale after confirming the appellant's bid under Rule 17(1)
Whether the next highest bidder could be awarded the licence under Rule 17(4) after the original sale was cancelled
Whether the appellant was a benamidar, making his bid invalid under Rule 12
holdings: The appellant substantially complied with Rule 19 by making required deposits; non-compliance with immovable property statement and surety requirements did not justify cancellation.
Once the highest bid is confirmed under Rule 17(1), the Divisional Commissioner cannot unilaterally cancel it; such cancellation is invalid without a valid revision power.
Rule 17(4) applies only if the highest bid is rejected at the time of sale, not after confirmation and subsequent cancellation; thus, awarding the licence to the next bidder was impermissible.
Mere financial backing by others does not make a bidder a benamidar; the state failed to prove the bid was benami, and acceptance of the bid barred later challenge on that ground.
provisions: Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967, Rule 12
Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967, Rule 17(1), (2), (4)
Mysore Excise (Disposal of Privileges of Retail Vend of Liquors) Rules, 1967, Rule 19(1), (3), (4)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Doctrine of estoppel against administrative authorities
Principle of lawful delegation and ultra vires acts
Presumption of validity of administrative confirmation unless lawfully revised

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over whether an agreement to sell shares was vitiated by fraud due to non-disclosure of substantial dividends, and whether the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to sell shares was voidable due to fraud and concealment of material facts
Whether the plaintiff had the means to discover the fraud with ordinary diligence
Whether the suit was barred by limitation, particularly regarding the exclusion of time when the defendant was abroad
Whether the valuation of shares by the High Court was correct
holdings: An agreement is voidable if one party conceals material facts, especially under a fiduciary duty, and the other party would not have consented had they known the truth.
The defendant’s contention that the plaintiff could have discovered the fraud with ordinary diligence fails when both lower courts found fraud and no such plea was raised earlier.
Section 13 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applies even if the cause of action arose abroad or the defendant was abroad when it accrued; the time of absence must be excluded.
The value of shares must be assessed based on market evidence around the date of transaction, not later valuations during a price boom.
doctrines: Fraudulent concealment under fiduciary duty
Relation back of fraud discovery for limitation
Exclusion of time under Section 13 of the Limitation Act
Objective valuation of property based on contemporaneous market data

card.dispute: The reversioners of a widow challenged the validity of an exchange of raiyati land she had made during her lifetime, which the High Court upheld as valid, leading to an appeal before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could disallow a plea under Section 27 of the Sonthal Parganas Settlement Regulation, 1872, raised for the first time before it
Whether the transferee could claim adverse possession under Article 141 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, against reversioners
Whether an exchange of land constitutes a 'transfer' within the meaning of Section 27(1) of the Regulation
Whether the suit was barred by Section 11 of the Regulation due to prior settlement proceedings
holdings: The High Court erred in rejecting the plea under Section 27 merely because it was raised late; courts must notice such pleas due to the section's mandatory nature if the land is raiyati and no exception applies.

A transferee from a widow with a life estate cannot acquire title by adverse possession against reversioners; the reversioners have 12 years from the widow’s death to recover possession under Article 141.
Exchange amounts to transfer under Section 27 as it involves mutual transfer of ownership, and the prohibition in Section 27 applies regardless of the form of transfer.
Section 11 does not bar the suit because the validity of the exchange was not decided by any settlement officer and thus cannot have decree-like finality.
provisions: Sonthal Parganas Settlement Regulation 3 of 1872, Section 27
Sonthal Parganas Settlement Regulation 3 of 1872, Section 11
doctrines: Mandatory statutory prohibition on alienation of raiyati land to protect tribal community interests
Rule against adverse possession by transferees from life tenants under Hindu law and Article 141
Substance over form in determining 'transfer' under statutory prohibitions
Finality of settlement officer's decisions only on matters actually decided by them

card.dispute: The dispute was between a private complainant and a Deputy Superintendent of Police, over whether the officer acted in official duty while allegedly threatening the complainant and enabling hawkers to take possession of disputed land, triggering a criminal complaint requiring sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant police officer was acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty when the alleged offences were committed.
Whether prior sanction under Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was required to prosecute the appellant.
holdings: The acts attributed to the appellant—threatening arrest and physical assault, and directing hawkers to occupy disputed land—did not bear a reasonable connection to his official duties.
Since the appellant’s alleged actions could not be reasonably claimed as part of official duty, sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. was not required for prosecution.
doctrines: Reasonable connection test for official duty under Section 197 Cr.P.C.
Purported discharge of official duty doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant sued to set aside a contract on grounds of undue influence and, in the alternative, sought specific performance of certain terms; the respondent challenged the maintainability of the alternative relief.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff can simultaneously seek rescission of a contract and, in the alternative, specific performance of the same contract.
Whether the absence of an averment of readiness and willingness to perform the contract vitiates a claim for specific performance.
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure to interfere with the trial court's decision on the maintainability of alternative reliefs.
holdings: A plaintiff cannot sue for rescission of a contract and in the alternative for specific performance, as the Specific Relief Act, 1877 permits only the reverse alternative, and such a claim is inconsistent and not maintainable.
A suit for specific performance requires an averment of continuous readiness and willingness to perform; its absence means no cause of action for specific performance exists.
The High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure to correct the trial court’s error of law that affected its jurisdiction to grant relief.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 7
doctrines: Inconsistency of alternative reliefs in pleadings
Election of remedies doctrine
Doctrine of readiness and willingness in specific performance
Revisional jurisdiction for errors affecting jurisdiction

card.dispute: The lessors sued the lessees and transferees for unpaid rent and interest for Fasli years 1356 to 1360, leading to disputes over joint liability, limitation, and applicable interest rate.
issues_decided: Whether the lessees were jointly and severally liable for the rent
Whether the suit was barred by limitation for the years 1356 and 1357 Fasli
Whether the contractual rate of interest at 1% per annum applied or was overridden by statute
holdings: Lessees and their transferees were jointly and severally liable for the rent under Section 43 of the Indian Contract Act, as the lease imposed a joint obligation.
The suit for rent arrears for 1356 and 1357 Fasli was barred by limitation under Article 2(b)(1) of Schedule III of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885, despite no written plea.
The statutory interest rate of 6¼% per annum under Section 67(1) of the Bihar Tenancy Act applied, overriding the contractual 1% rate.
doctrines: Joint and several liability under contract law
Statutory limitation overriding contractual claims
Statutory interest rate prevailing over contractual stipulation

card.dispute: Purtabpore Co. Ltd fought the Cane Commissioner of Bihar and others over the validity of an order reallocating sugarcane supply areas, which took away part of its reserved area in favor of another sugar mill.
issues_decided: Whether the Cane Commissioner's order modifying the reservation of sugarcane supply areas was quasi-judicial and required compliance with natural justice
Whether the order passed by the Cane Commissioner under the Sugar Cane (Control) Order, 1955 was valid when made under directions from the Chief Minister
Whether the appellant was an aggrieved party entitled to challenge the order
holdings: An order under clause 6(1) of the Sugar Cane (Control) Order, 1955 that modifies a reservation of supply area is quasi-judicial and must comply with principles of natural justice.
An order passed by the Cane Commissioner under directive from the Chief Minister is invalid as it compromises independence and fairness in quasi-judicial proceedings.
The appellant was an aggrieved party because its proprietary interest in the sugarcane supply was adversely affected by the reallocation, regardless of subsequent orders.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial character of administrative action
Doctrine of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the maintainability of a suit for eviction on the grounds that the landlord's permission to file the suit was revoked and later reinstated with a delayed effective date.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for eviction was maintainable after the Commissioner revoked the initial permission under Section 3(3), and the State Government subsequently set aside that revocation under Section 7F with a future effective date.
Whether the permission to institute the suit was valid on the date the decree was passed.
holdings: When the State Government sets aside the Commissioner's revocation of permission under Section 7F, the original permission under Section 3(1) is revived, making the suit validly instituted.

A direction by the State Government that the suit be filed after four months means the permission becomes effective on that future date, and as long as the suit is pending and the permission is valid when the decree is passed, the suit is maintainable.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(1)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(3)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(4)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7F
doctrines: Revival of permission upon setting aside of revocation
Maintainability of suit based on validity of permission at the time of decree

card.dispute: The appellant, Raja Dhruv Dev Chand, sought a refund of rent paid for leased agricultural land in undivided Punjab, claiming frustration of contract due to partition and communal riots making cultivation impossible, while the respondents, as successors-in-interest, opposed the refund.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies to leases of agricultural land after a completed transfer of property.
Whether the lessee can avoid liability to pay rent when unable to use the leased land due to external events like riots and partition.
Whether the rights and obligations under a lease are governed by contract law or by the Transfer of Property Act after the lease is executed.
holdings: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act does not apply to completed transfers of property under a lease; frustration of contract does not void the lessee's obligation to pay rent.
A lessee cannot avoid a lease or claim rent refund merely because of inability to use the land, unless the property is destroyed or permanently unfit for its intended use.
The relationship under a lease is one of property transfer, not executory contract, and thus governed by the Transfer of Property Act, not the doctrine of frustration in contract law.
doctrines: Doctrine of frustration of contract
Distinction between executory contract and completed conveyance
Transfer of right to enjoy under lease

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the state's takeover of management of their agricultural land under the amended Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, arguing it violated constitutional protections.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 65 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 is ultra vires for conferring arbitrary power
Whether the amendment is protected from challenge by Article 31-A(1)(b) or Article 31-B of the Constitution
Whether the takeover of land management for an indefinite period falls within the scope of 'limited period' as required by Article 31-A(1)(b)
Whether the law permits deprivation of property based on subjective satisfaction of an officer without objective standards
holdings: The amendment to Section 65 is not protected by Article 31-A(1)(b) because the law does not prescribe a definite limit for the period of management, making the takeover effectively indefinite.
Article 31-A(1)(b) only protects takeovers of management that are for a limited and ascertainable period; indefinite management amounts to deprivation without compensation.
The absence of objective criteria for determining 'inefficient use' of land and the reliance on subjective satisfaction of an officer render the law unreasonable and arbitrary.
The state cannot claim protection under Article 31-A(1)(b) when the law allows continued management without a real time limit, even if termination is theoretically possible.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 65
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 61
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 82
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonable classification
Doctrine of arbitrariness under Article 14
Doctrine of protection from deprivation of property under Article 31
Doctrine of limited period of management under Article 31-A(1)(b)

card.dispute: The reversioners of a deceased male bhumidhar challenged a gift of bhumidhari land made by his widow, claiming she held only a life estate and could not transfer ownership beyond her lifetime.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow who became a bhumidhar under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, holds the property as an absolute owner or only for life
Whether the use of the terms 'interest' and 'holding' in Sections 171, 172, and 172A indicates a limited estate in female bhumidhars
Whether the absence of testamentary power in female bhumidhars implies a restriction on their power to transfer property inter vivos
holdings: A female bhumidhar who inherits under Sections 171, 172, or 172A of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act becomes the absolute owner of the holding during her lifetime, with no residuary interest vested elsewhere.
The use of the terms 'interest' and 'holding' in the Act does not indicate a limited or life estate for female bhumidhars; the terms are used interchangeably and do not imply a lesser estate.
The restriction on making a will does not imply an inability to transfer property during life; a female bhumidhar can gift or sell her holding despite lacking testamentary power.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 152
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 171
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 172
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 172A
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 169
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 340
U.P. Agricultural Tenants (Acquisition of Privileges) Act, 1949, Section 7(c)
doctrines: Rule against perpetuities and abeyance of estates
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Presumption against implied repeal or restriction

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming as tenants of a deity, fought with neighboring landlords over ownership of land allegedly transferred by river-induced accretion from their village to the deity's land.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to dismissal against the deity who was not a necessary party
Whether the trial court's decision operated as res judicata between co-defendants (the deity and contesting defendants)
Whether the appeal became incompetent due to inconsistent potential decrees
holdings: The appeal did not abate as no party died; abatement does not apply to dismissal for procedural default against a non-necessary party.
Res judicata does not apply between co-defendants where the appellate court has not finally decided the issue in their presence.
An appeal remains competent against other respondents even if dismissed against a non-necessary party like the deity.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 146 (Res judicata)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI (Appellate Procedure)
doctrines: Res judicata between co-defendants
Necessary and proper parties in appeal
Finality of decree and res sub judice upon filing of appeal

card.dispute: The first mortgagee sued on a mortgage, making the puisne mortgagee a party; after the mortgagor paid off the first mortgagee without sale, the puisne mortgagee filed a separate suit for a mortgage decree, raising questions of maintainability and interest entitlement.
issues_decided: Whether a puisne mortgagee can maintain a separate suit for enforcement of his mortgage after the first mortgagee's suit ended without sale due to payment by the mortgagor.
Whether the puisne mortgagee is entitled to contractual interest at the agreed rate after the date of suit.
holdings: A puisne mortgagee is not entitled to the benefit of the first mortgagee's decree and must file a separate suit to enforce his mortgage, which is maintainable even if the prior mortgage was satisfied without sale.

Interest on the mortgage debt is payable at the contractual rate up to the date of suit, but thereafter only at a reasonable rate—here, 6% per annum simple interest—from the date of suit to realization.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rule 11
doctrines: Puisne mortgagee's right to independent suit
Distinction between contractual and judicial interest
Priority of special provisions over general ones in CPC

card.dispute: Shakuntala Devi Jain appealed against the dismissal of her objections to the execution of a partition decree, challenging the High Court's rejection of her appeal for non-filing of a certified copy of the order under Section 47 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal from the order deciding objections under Section 47 CPC was incompetent due to non-filing of a certified copy of the order?
Whether the delay in filing the certified copy of the order could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act?
holdings: An appeal from an order under Section 47 CPC is incompetent unless the memorandum of appeal is accompanied by a certified copy of the order, as such an order is deemed a decree under Section 2(2) CPC.

The delay in filing the certified copy can be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act if sufficient cause is shown, especially where the delay was due to the appellant's repeated attempts and the negligence of the court's copying department.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 1
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Deeming fiction of 'decree' under Section 2(2) CPC for Section 47 orders
Judicial discretion in condoning delay to advance substantial justice

card.dispute: The decree-holder contested the State Bank of Jaipur's right to execute a decree in its own right based on a power-of-attorney, claiming the bank was only an agent and not an equitable assignee.
issues_decided: Whether the power-of-attorney granted to the bank was irrevocable and coupled with an interest.
Whether the power-of-attorney amounted to a legal or equitable assignment of the decree to the bank.
Whether the bank, as an equitable assignee, could execute the decree without formal transfer under Order XXI, Rule 16 of the CPC.
holdings: A power-of-attorney is irrevocable if it is coupled with an interest, as provided under Section 202 of the Indian Contract Act, especially when it secures the agent’s financial interest.
The power-of-attorney, though not a legal assignment, created an equitable assignment by earmarking the decree amount for debt repayment, constituting a special fund for the bank’s benefit.

An equitable assignee of a decree can execute it under Section 146 of the CPC, even without formal transfer under Order XXI, Rule 16, relying on the principle established in Jugalkishore Saraf v. Raw Cotton Co. Ltd.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 16
doctrines: Power coupled with interest
Equitable assignment
Irrevocability of agency when tied to agent's interest

card.dispute: The State of Bihar stopped paying a permanent malikana allowance to Maharaja Pratap Singh after his estates were vested in the state; he challenged this, claiming the allowance was not an interest in the estate and thus not affected by the vesting.
issues_decided: Whether the permanent malikana allowance constituted a proprietary or intermediary interest that vested in the State under Section 3 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the respondent was entitled to compensation under Section 24A of the Act for the cessation of malikana
holdings: The permanent malikana is a monetary grant in lieu of proprietary rights, not an interest in the estate, and therefore did not vest in the State upon notification under Section 3.
The right to malikana is not an intermediary interest in any estate; hence, the respondent is not entitled to compensation under Section 24A of the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
doctrines: Vesting of estates free from encumbrances
Distinction between proprietary interest and pensionary allowance

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat contested compensation claims by taluqdars for land, irrigation structures, and riverbeds under the Bombay Taluqdari Abolition Act, 1949, including entitlement to solatium and the method of valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the right to pay jama at a concessional rate (60% of full assessment) was a compensable right under Section 14 of the Bombay Taluqdari Abolition Act, 1949
Whether taluqdars were entitled to 15% solatium in addition to compensation under Section 7 of the Act
What method should be used to determine compensation for irrigation bunds, tanks, and wells
Whether compensation was payable for river beds and bhathas (cultivable riverbed areas)
holdings: The right to pay jama at a concessional rate was a temporary concession, not a legal right, and therefore not compensable under Section 14 of the Act.
Taluqdars are entitled to 15% solatium under Section 7 of the Act, as the Revenue Tribunal misinterpreted the law in denying it.
Compensation for irrigation bunds, tanks, and wells must be based on annual income yield, not reinstatement cost, unless reinstitution is genuinely intended.
No compensation is due for submerged river beds, but claims for bhathas and cultivable portions of river beds may be investigated further.
doctrines: Market value as basis for compensation in land acquisition
Solatium as statutory compensation enhancement
Supervisory jurisdiction of High Court under Article 227
Yield-based valuation for irrigation structures

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat appealed against the High Court's decision directing compensation to be paid to Jetawat Lalsingh Amarsingh, a non-jagirdar, for the abolition of his rights to Gharkhed lands and a cash allowance from the jagir under the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the right to own and possess Gharkhed lands free from assessment constitutes a right to or interest in property under Section 14(1) of the Act.
Whether the right to receive an annual cash allowance from the jagir constitutes a right to or interest in property under Section 14(1) of the Act.
Whether a non-jagirdar is entitled to compensation under Section 14(1) if such rights are extinguished or modified by the Act.
holdings: A right to enjoy land without liability to pay assessment is a valuable interest in property; its modification due to the abolition of the jagir entitles the holder to compensation under Section 14(1).
A right to receive a cash allowance chargeable on the jagir constitutes an interest in property and is compensable under Section 14(1) when abolished.
Section 14(1) applies to non-jagirdars whose rights or interests in property are abolished or modified by the Act, provided compensation is not already provided for.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 14(1)
Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 3
Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 2
Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 4
doctrines: Interest in property doctrine
Compensation for extinguishment of rights
Statutory interpretation of abolition laws

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat contested whether Jetawat Lal Singh Amar Singh was entitled to compensation for loss of rights in Gharkhed lands and a cash allowance after the abolition of a jagir under the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the right to own and possess Gharkhed lands free from assessment constitutes an interest in property under Section 14(1) of the Act.
Whether the right to receive a cash allowance from the jagir constitutes an interest in property entitled to compensation under Section 14(1) of the Act.
holdings: The right to enjoy Gharkhed lands without liability to pay assessment was an interest in property; its modification by imposition of assessment under the Act entitled the holder to claim compensation.
The right to receive a cash allowance from the jagir was a charge on the property and thus an interest in property; its extinguishment upon abolition of the jagir entitled the holder to compensation.
provisions: The Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 14(1)
The Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 3
The Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagir Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 4
doctrines: Interest in property doctrine
Modification of property rights requiring compensation

card.dispute: The State of Kerala challenged the High Court's decision invalidating a building tax imposed solely on floor area under the Kerala Buildings Tax Act, 1961, on grounds of violating the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Kerala Buildings Tax Act, 1961, which levies tax solely on the basis of floor area, violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the legislature's failure to make rational classification in a taxing statute results in denial of equal protection of laws?
Whether a tax law based exclusively on floor area, without regard to building use, construction cost, or location, is constitutionally valid?
holdings: A taxing statute must not only be within legislative competence but also comply with constitutional provisions, including Article 14 guaranteeing equal protection of laws.
The legislature has wide discretion in fiscal matters, but must adhere to rational classification; failure to do so may result in unconstitutional discrimination.

Levying tax solely on floor area without considering building use, construction nature, location, or economic value violates Article 14 due to lack of rational basis and results in arbitrary discrimination.
The impugned tax is invalid as it treats dissimilar buildings alike without reasonable basis, thereby denying equal protection under the law.
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Rational classification doctrine
Unconstitutional arbitrariness in taxation
Legislative competence subject to fundamental rights

card.dispute: The tenant Surja sought to purchase land from landlord Hardeva under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, but Hardeva claimed the land was part of his reserved or selected area, making it ineligible for purchase.
issues_decided: Whether the question of whether the land was part of the reserved or selected area is a jurisdictional fact affecting the Assistant Collector's authority under Section 18 of the Act.
Whether the Financial Commissioner had the power to examine the jurisdictional issue in revision even if it was not raised before the Assistant Collector or Collector.
Whether the Financial Commissioner properly exercised his revisional powers under Section 24 of the Act read with Section 84 of the Tenancy Act.
holdings: The question of whether the land is part of the reserved or selected area is a jurisdictional fact; if the land falls within such area, the tenant has no right to purchase and the Assistant Collector lacks jurisdiction.

The Financial Commissioner, exercising powers akin to the High Court under Section 24 read with Section 84, can examine whether a subordinate authority wrongly assumed jurisdiction, even if the issue was not raised earlier.
The Financial Commissioner failed to properly assess the merits of the Commissioner’s report and should have determined whether the selection was valid and timely before dismissing the revision.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 24
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Revisional jurisdiction to correct lack of jurisdiction
Finality of orders when jurisdiction is improperly assumed

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and others fought against landowners, including the Godavari Sugar Mills, over the validity of amendments to the Maharashtra State Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, particularly Section 28, which regulated sugarcane supply from surplus lands vested in the state.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Amendment Act of 1962 is protected under Article 31B of the Constitution despite not being explicitly listed in the Ninth Schedule
Whether the State Legislature had the competence to enact Section 28 of the impugned Act under Entry 35, List II of the Seventh Schedule
Whether Section 28 of the Act is rendered ineffective due to repugnancy with orders issued under the Defence of India Rules
holdings: Article 31B protects not only an Act listed in the Ninth Schedule but also its amendments made up to the date of inclusion, even if the amending Act is not separately listed.
Section 28 falls within the legislative competence of the State under Entry 35, List II, as it pertains to lands vested in the State and their efficient management and use.
Valid central orders under the Defence of India Rules override inconsistent state laws, but no repugnancy exists here as Section 28 and the 1963 order can operate concurrently.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 35, List II
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 18, List II
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 42, List III
doctrines: Doctrine of inclusion of amendments under Article 31B
Doctrine of repugnancy under Article 251
Ancillary and incidental legislation
Prospective overruling (mentioned but not applied)

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and others contested Sardar D.K. Jadav's claim that certain tanks on 'occupied land' were exempt from vesting in the State under the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute regarding exemption of tanks under s. 5(c) of the Abolition Act is to be decided by the Jagir Commissioner under s. 17
Whether the High Court can independently decide the jurisdictional fact of whether the tanks were situated on 'occupied land'
holdings: Section 17 of the Abolition Act applies only to disputes over jagirdari title or rights for compensation purposes and does not cover disputes about whether property falls under s. 5(c) exemption.

The High Court has the authority in writ proceedings to independently determine jurisdictional facts, such as whether tanks were on 'occupied land', where the administrative authority's jurisdiction depends on such a finding.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act Samvat 2008 (Act 28 of 1951), Section 2(i)(ix)
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act Samvat 2008 (Act 28 of 1951), Section 3
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act Samvat 2008 (Act 28 of 1951), Section 4
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act Samvat 2008 (Act 28 of 1951), Section 5(c)
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act Samvat 2008 (Act 28 of 1951), Section 17
Madhya Pradesh Revenue Code 1959 (Act 20 of 1959), Section 251
doctrines: Jurisdictional fact doctrine
High Court's power of judicial review under Article 226
Limited scope of administrative tribunal jurisdiction

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and revenue authorities versus tenants and Bhai Ardaman Singh over whether the Collector could order restoration of land possession under the Pepsu Tenancy Act for dispossession that occurred before the Act came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Section 43(1)(b) of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953 has retrospective operation
Whether the Collector can act on subjective satisfaction or must make a judicial determination of facts
Whether the condition precedent under Section 43(1)(b) was satisfied to invoke the Collector's jurisdiction
Whether an order passed without jurisdiction can be sustained on grounds of substantial justice
holdings: Section 43(1)(b) does not have retrospective operation; it cannot apply to dispossession occurring before the Act came into force.
The Collector must make a judicial determination of facts to establish jurisdiction, not act on subjective satisfaction.
Jurisdiction under Section 43(1)(b) requires showing the person in possession is not entitled to it under the Act; absence of such entitlement is a condition precedent.
An order passed without jurisdiction cannot be upheld merely because it achieves substantial justice or another authority might have had power to grant relief.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953, Section 43(1)(b)
doctrines: Condition precedent to jurisdiction
Judicial character of quasi-judicial proceedings
No implied retrospectivity
Nullity of acts without jurisdiction

card.dispute: Sugra Bibi, the widow of a deceased joint mutwalli, sued for the removal of the surviving mutwalli, Hazi Kummu Mia, and the appointment of her son as the new mutwalli, while the respondent argued the suit was not maintainable without the Advocate-General's consent under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code.
issues_decided: Whether the wakf in question falls within the ambit of Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code as being created substantially for public charitable or religious purposes
Whether the suit, seeking removal of a mutwalli and appointment of a new one, requires the written consent of the Advocate-General under Section 92(1) CPC
Whether the suit was brought in a representative capacity for the benefit of all beneficiaries or merely to enforce a private individual right
holdings: A wakf falls under Section 92 CPC if it is created substantially for public charitable or religious purposes, even if some benefits accrue to the settlor's family.
The suit sought reliefs under clauses (a) and (b) of Section 92(1) CPC and was representative in nature, thus requiring the written consent of the Advocate-General for maintainability.

A suit for removal of a mutwalli and appointment of another, concerning a public wakf, is not maintainable without the Advocate-General’s consent, as it affects public rights, not just private interests.
doctrines: Representative suit doctrine
Public trust doctrine
Doctrine of maintainability of suits affecting public charitable trusts

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh fought with grant recipients over the constitutional validity of a law abolishing cash grants and retaining part of the arrears, challenging whether it violated property rights under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Cash Grants Act, 1963 violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
Whether the acquisition of money and choses in action under the Act is permissible under Article 31(2)
Whether the compensation provided under the Act satisfies the requirement of 'just equivalent' under Article 31(2)
Whether the Act can be sustained as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(5)
holdings: The Act violates Article 19(1)(f) as it imposes an unreasonable restriction not justified under Article 19(5) for want of a public purpose.
Money and choses in action cannot be acquired under Article 31(2) unless for a genuine public purpose and with full compensation.
Compensation amounting to only fifty percent of arrears is not the 'just equivalent' of property taken and thus violates Article 31(2).
An Act that allows the State to enrich its coffers by extinguishing liabilities without full compensation is not a valid exercise of police power or eminent domain.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Cash Grants Act, 1963
doctrines: Harmonious construction of fundamental rights
Public purpose requirement in property acquisition
Just equivalent compensation doctrine
Colourable legislation doctrine
Police power vs. power of eminent domain

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat prosecuted a trustee, Acharya Shri Devendraprasadji, for failing to comply with a notice from the Charity Commissioner seeking details about unauthorized constructions; the prosecution was challenged on whether the notice was valid under the Bombay Public Trusts Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Charity Commissioner has the authority under Section 37 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act to call for information beyond 'statement' or 'report' as defined by the Act and rules?
Whether the items requested in the Commissioner's notice amount to a 'statement' or 'report' within the meaning of Section 37(1)(c)?
holdings: The term 'statement' or 'report' under Section 37(1)(c) refers only to formal documents required under the Act or rules, not general information.
The Charity Commissioner cannot compel a trustee to provide wide-ranging information not falling within the defined terms of 'statement' or 'report'.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Distinction between 'statement/report' and 'information' in administrative law

card.dispute: The State of Kerala challenged the quantum of compensation awarded to P. P. Hassan Koya, a kanamdar, for land and buildings acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, arguing that the method of valuation was incorrect.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, as a kanamdar, was entitled to apportionment of compensation for both land and buildings despite the jenmi not objecting to the award.
Whether the method of determining compensation by separately valuing land and buildings at 'break-up value' was legally valid.
holdings: A kanamdar has a legally recognized interest in the land and is entitled to apportionment of compensation for both land and buildings, irrespective of the jenmi's acceptance of the award.
Compensation for land with buildings must be determined as a composite unit based on market value, not by separately assessing land value and the break-up value of structures.
doctrines: Composite valuation of land and buildings
Market value determination through capitalization of rent
Extinction of all private interests upon acquisition

card.dispute: Thakore Sobhag Singh challenged Thakur Jai Singh's claim to succeed to a jagir on the basis of adoption, arguing that the adoption was invalid without prior sanction of the Jaipur Ruler and that the Board of Revenue lacked jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Revenue had jurisdiction to decide disputes regarding adoption and succession to jagirs in Jaipur State.
Whether the Jaipur Matmi Rules, 1945, required prior sanction of the Ruler for adoptions made before the Rules were promulgated.
Whether the High Court's decision on the validity of adoption under personal law and the non-applicability of the Matmi Rules was binding as res judicata.
holdings: The Board of Revenue had jurisdiction under the Rajasthan Jagir Decisions and Proceedings (Validation) Act, 1955, to decide disputes relating to succession to jagirs, including questions of adoption.
The requirement of prior government sanction for adoption under Rule 14(2) of the Jaipur Matmi Rules, 1945, is prospective and does not apply to adoptions made before the Rules were promulgated.

The High Court’s decision that the adoption was valid under personal law and that the Matmi Rules did not invalidate it was binding as res judicata between the parties, even though the Board was directed to decide the case accordingly.
provisions: Rajasthan Jagir Decisions and Proceedings (Validation) Act, 1955
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 2(d)
doctrines: Res judicata
Prospective operation of rules
Validation of laws by retrospective legislation
Jurisdiction of revenue courts over succession disputes

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision quashing its notification under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, which sought to prospect for coal on land leased to M/s. Khas Karanapura Colliery Ltd.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4(1) violated Section 4(4) of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957 by including land with premises for processes ancillary to coal mining?
Whether the High Court could consider the violation of the second limb of Section 4(4) even if not specifically pleaded in the writ petition?
Whether the lessee was aggrieved by the notification under Section 4(1) so as to have standing to file a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution?
Whether the delay in filing the writ petition amounted to laches, warranting denial of relief?
holdings: The notification was invalid as it included land with premises for processes ancillary to coal mining, which are protected under the second limb of Section 4(4) of the Act.
The court could examine the issue under the second limb of Section 4(4) despite lack of specific pleading, as all facts were before the court and the issue was fully argued.
The lessee was aggrieved by the notification because Section 5 of the Act suspended mining operations in the notified area, directly affecting its business.
A delay of about five and a half months in filing the writ petition did not constitute laches, as it was within a reasonable time from the notification.
provisions: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4(1)
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4(4)
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 5
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 7
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Doctrine of standing (locus standi)
Principle of statutory interpretation (purposive interpretation)
Principle of judicial review under Article 226

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the Patna High Court's decision quashing a notification for acquiring land from Khas Karanapura Colliery Ltd., arguing whether the notification violated Section 4(4) of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 4(1) of the Act violated the exemption in Section 4(4) by including land where coal mining operations were actually carried on or where ancillary processes to coal extraction were conducted.
Whether the High Court could consider the second limb of Section 4(4) despite lack of specific pleading in the writ petition.
Whether the writ petition was premature or barred by laches.
holdings: The notification was invalid as it included land with structures like railway sidings, boiler houses, and fan houses where processes ancillary to coal extraction were carried on, falling under the second limb of Section 4(4).
The High Court could examine the second limb of Section 4(4) even without specific pleading, as all facts were before the court and the issue was argued before the lower court.

The writ petition was not premature or barred by laches, as the notification under Section 4(1) immediately rendered the mining lease ineffective under Section 5, causing real and immediate harm to the respondent.
provisions: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4(1)
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4(4)
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 5
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 7
doctrines: Doctrine of ancillary structures in mining operations
Doctrine against premature judicial challenge
Principle of effective judicial remedy under Article 226
Rule against laches in constitutional remedies

card.dispute: The Karta of a Hindu joint family gave a notice under Section 80 CPC before partition; after partition, the divided members joined as plaintiffs in the suit, and the dispute was whether a fresh notice was required by the divided members.
issues_decided: Whether the notice given by the Karta of a Hindu joint family before partition is sufficient for the suit filed after partition by the divided coparceners?
Whether the plaintiffs established their title as 'Raiyat Sarkar' over the nazul plots based on long possession?
holdings: The notice given by the Karta before partition was valid and sufficient for the suit filed after partition, as there was substantial identity between the person giving notice and the plaintiffs, and the notice enured to the benefit of all coparceners.

The plaintiffs failed to prove continuous and long possession of the nazul plots for the statutory period; the land remained recorded as Government property (Milkiat Sarkar), and no title as Raiyat Sarkar was established.
doctrines: Substantial identity doctrine in notice under Section 80 CPC
Principle of long possession not applicable where land is recorded as Government property

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed possession of a building site in village Nagli Abdulla, where the respondents claimed rights under Section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Reforms Act, 1950, after being dispossessed during 1947 communal disturbances and returning in 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'held' in Section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Reforms Act, 1950 means mere physical possession or lawful possession on the date of vesting?
Whether a trespasser in physical possession of a building on the vesting date can claim deemed settlement under Section 9?
holdings: The word 'held' in Section 9 means 'lawfully held' and requires possession based on legal title, not mere physical possession by a trespasser.
The deemed settlement under Section 9 benefits only those who lawfully held the building on the vesting date, not those who obtained possession wrongfully.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Reforms Act, 1950, Section 9
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Contextual and purposive interpretation
Presumption of legislative intent to uphold justice and equity

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that the respondent widow held the property as a limited owner under a widow's estate, while the respondent argued she became a full owner under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent widow became a full owner of the property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, despite the award specifying a 'widow's estate'.
Whether Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, applies to bar full ownership when property is allotted by an arbitration award prescribing a restricted estate.
holdings: A female Hindu who inherits property under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, and receives her share via partition before the 1956 Act's commencement is 'possessed' and 'acquired' the property, becoming a full owner under Section 14(1).
Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1) and applies only when there is no pre-existing right; it does not apply where the female had an inherited interest before the award or decree.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of widening of ownership under Section 14(1)
Proviso-like operation of Section 14(2)
Constructive possession and pre-existing rights

card.dispute: The dispute was between the purchaser of evacuee property and the lessee and sub-lessee of a cinema hall, over whether the lease created by the mortgagee survived the sale of the property and whether the tenants were protected under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy created by a mortgagee in possession survives the termination of the mortgage interest and binds the purchaser of the property
Whether the lessee and sub-lessee were entitled to protection under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to possession before the expiry of the lease term
What amount of mesne profits was payable
holdings: A tenancy created by a mortgagee in possession does not survive the termination of the mortgage interest unless adopted by the mortgagor or a successor; the lessee cannot claim rights beyond the mortgagee’s interest.
The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 does not apply where the tenancy ceases to exist due to the extinction of the mortgagee's interest.
The purchaser, having acquired full title after the mortgage was satisfied, was entitled to immediate possession despite the unexpired lease term.
Mesne profits are limited to the actual rent paid under the lease, here Rs. 250 per month, even if below market rate.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
doctrines: Derivative title doctrine
Coterminous interest of mortgagee and lessee
Survival of tenancy only with consent of mortgagor or successor
Mesne profits based on actual rent paid

card.dispute: Ayesha Bibi challenged the validity of a wakf and sought a share in the property, while the Commissioner of Wakfs opposed the compromise decree on grounds of lack of notice under the Bengal Wakfs Act, 1934.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner of Wakfs was entitled to special notice of a compromise petition under Section 70(1) of the Bengal Wakfs Act, 1934 when he was already a party to the suit and had appeared in it.

Whether a decree passed on compromise in a suit relating to wakf property is void if the Commissioner was not given separate notice of the compromise, despite having been served and appearing in the suit.
holdings: The Commissioner of Wakfs, having been made a party to the suit, served with summons, and having appeared and filed a written statement, was deemed to have received sufficient notice under Section 70(1) of the Bengal Wakfs Act, 1934.

No separate or special notice of a compromise petition is required under the Act when the Commissioner has full knowledge of the suit and participated in it; thus, the decree on compromise is not void for lack of such notice.
doctrines: Notice under statutory provisions must be construed in light of actual participation and knowledge.
A party’s active appearance and contestation in a suit satisfies statutory notice requirements even in the absence of formal notice for subsequent stages.

card.dispute: The beneficiaries of a wakf-alal-aulad challenged the inclusion of their right to receive a share of income from the wakf property as an asset assessable to wealth tax.
issues_decided: Whether the right to receive a specified share of income from a wakf-alal-aulad constitutes an 'asset' under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether such a right is capable of valuation for wealth tax purposes under Section 7(1) of the Act.
Whether the right to income from the wakf, if meant solely for maintenance and support, falls outside the scope of 'assets' under the Act.
holdings: The right to receive a share of income from wakf property is an 'asset' under Section 2(e) of the Wealth Tax Act, as the term 'asset' includes every kind of property or interest in property, unless specifically exempted.
Even if the income right is for maintenance and support, it remains an asset because the statutory definition is comprehensive and not restricted by personal or non-transferable characteristics.
The value of such a right can be determined hypothetically as per Section 7(1), assuming a sale in an open market, regardless of whether actual sale or commutation is possible.
doctrines: Comprehensive statutory interpretation of 'asset'
Hypothetical market valuation under tax law
Judicial recognition of non-possessory income rights as property

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) and respondents (tenants) fought over whether the tenants were entitled to a newly constructed building on their ancestral village site after returning from fleeing communal riots, under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: What is the meaning of the word 'held' in Section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950?
Whether a person in mere physical possession of a building on the vesting date, without legal title, is entitled to deemed settlement under Section 9?
Whether the respondents, who returned after riots, were entitled to the benefit of Section 9 despite the original buildings being demolished and replaced by the appellants.
holdings: The word 'held' in Section 9 means 'lawfully held' and implies possession based on legal title, not mere physical possession.
A trespasser or unauthorized occupant cannot acquire rights under Section 9 solely by being in physical possession on the vesting date.
The respondents, as lawful holders of the site, were entitled to the protection of Section 9, and the appellants’ construction on the site did not confer rights under the Act.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 9
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Sections 2(1)(c), 13, 17, 18, 21, 144, 204, 240A, 298, 304, 314
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes to align with justice and reason
Contextual and purposive interpretation
Presumption against harsh or absurd legislative intent
Deemed settlement based on lawful possession

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondent's right to pre-empt land sold by her stepmother, arguing she was not entitled under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 as amended.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, being the daughter of the deceased husband of the vendor (a widow), had a right of pre-emption under s. 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913.
Whether the 1964 amendment to s. 15(2)(b) of the Act, which clarified the class of pre-emptors, has retrospective operation.
holdings: The right of pre-emption under s. 15(2)(b) includes the son or daughter of the husband of a female vendor, even if not her own child, to keep the property within the male lineal descent of the last holder.
The 1964 amendment was clarificatory in nature and thus applies retrospectively, validating the respondent’s pre-emption right in pending cases.
doctrines: Retrospective operation of clarificatory or declaratory statutes
Principle of consanguinity in pre-emption rights
Rule against extending statutory language beyond its plain meaning

card.dispute: The appellants, who constructed public buildings in the princely state of Surguja, claimed payment from the State of Madhya Pradesh after its merger, based on a promissory note executed by the Maharaja; the State refused to pay, raising the defence of 'act of State'.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Madhya Pradesh, as the successor state, was liable to honour the contractual liability of the erstwhile princely state of Surguja?
Whether the request by the State for details of the claim amounted to an implied acceptance of liability?
Whether the defence of 'act of State' was available to the successor state to reject claims arising from the former princely state?
holdings: The successor state is not automatically bound to honour the liabilities of the merged princely state unless it has expressly or impliedly accepted such liability.
Mere request for details of a claim does not constitute implied acceptance of liability or waiver of the defence of 'act of State'.
An 'act of State'—the exercise of sovereign power over newly acquired territory—bars enforcement of pre-existing rights or claims in municipal courts unless the new sovereign has recognized them.
doctrines: Act of State
Succession of states in municipal law
Implied waiver of legal defence

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the assessee, V. Jagan Mohan Rao, disputed whether a Privy Council decision constituted 'definite information' justifying reassessment under s. 34, and whether a payment of Rs. 1,15,000 to the vendor's sons to release their claims was allowable as revenue expenditure under s. 10(2)(xv).
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the Privy Council constituted 'definite information' within the meaning of s. 34(1)(b) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, justifying reassessment?
Whether the sum of Rs. 1,15,000 paid by the assessee to the vendor's sons for releasing their claims was allowable as a business expenditure under s. 10(2)(xv)?
holdings: The decision of the Privy Council is 'definite information' under s. 34(1)(b), enabling the Income-tax Officer to reopen assessment even if part of the income was previously assessed.
A lump sum payment made to perfect title to a capital asset is capital expenditure, not revenue, and is not allowable as a business expense under s. 10(2)(xv), even if partly related to profits.
doctrines: Doctrine of 'definite information' under s. 34
Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Enduring benefit test for capital expenditure

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and a shareholder, Shaila Behari Lal Singha, disputed whether amounts distributed from capital gains (from land acquisition compensation and salamis) were taxable as dividend or as income from other sources.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could condition its answers to referred tax questions on the outcome of pending appeals in this Court.
Whether the High Court must independently decide, based on facts, if salami receipts constitute capital gains.
Whether the High Court must determine, factually, if land acquisition compensation is capital gain.
Whether the question of taxability of capital gains as income from 'other sources' (not dividend) was before the Court.
holdings: Even with party consent, the High Court must record final answers and reasons; it cannot make its answers subject to decisions in other pending cases.
The High Court must decide on a case-by-case basis whether salami receipts constitute capital gains based on the facts.
The High Court must assess factually whether part of land acquisition compensation is capital gain, as statutory interest on such compensation is income, not capital gain.
The question of whether receipt from capital gains is taxable as income from 'other sources' under s. 12 was properly referred and not decided in prior appeals.
doctrines: Finality of High Court's answers to tax references
Factual determination of capital vs. revenue receipt
Doctrine of precedent and binding effect of Supreme Court decisions
