card.dispute: The appellant company and respondents disputed over the release of compensation money for acquired land, pending an appeal in a specific performance suit.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC to interfere with the Additional District Judge's order staying proceedings under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether the High Court could pass an ex parte order on May 8, 1969, clarifying its earlier order without notice to the appellant?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC as there was no jurisdictional error, illegality, or material irregularity in the Additional District Judge's order.
The ex parte order of May 8, 1969, passed without notice and effectively reversing a judicial order, was unsustainable under Sections 151 and 141 CPC.
doctrines: Limits of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Prohibition against treating revision as an appeal
Principle of audi alteram partem in ex parte orders

card.dispute: The sons, widow, and daughters of Jwala fought over whether they could collectively claim possession of ancestral land sold by Jwala, and whether the widow and daughters could benefit from a prior declaratory decree despite customary law barring female heirs from contesting alienations.
issues_decided: Whether the widow and daughters of Jwala could inherit a share in the ancestral property alienated by him, despite being barred under Punjab customary law from contesting the alienation.

Whether the declaratory decree in Suit No. 75 of 1920, obtained by a son, enured to the benefit of all legal heirs including the widow and daughters after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
Whether the appellate court could grant relief to the widow and daughters even though they did not file an appeal or cross-objections against the decree that dismissed their claim.
holdings: A declaratory decree against alienation of ancestral property benefits all legal heirs entitled to the estate upon succession, including those who could not originally challenge the alienation under custom.

The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to devolution of the estate upon death, and heirs like the widow and daughters, though barred by custom from contesting alienation, can inherit the re-vested property.
An appellate court can grant relief to respondents or parties not appealing under Order 41, Rule 33, CPC, if the decree 'ought' to have been passed in their favour in law, to prevent injustice.
provisions: Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1 of 1920, Section 6
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 12
doctrines: Doctrine of reversionary rights in ancestral property
Prospective application of statutory inheritance rights over customary law
Appellate court's power to grant relief ex debito justitiae under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC

card.dispute: The male and female heirs of Jwala fought over whether female heirs could claim possession of ancestral property alienated in 1916 based on a declaratory decree obtained by a male reversioner, despite a Punjab custom and statute restricting such rights to male-line descendants.
issues_decided: Whether female heirs could benefit from a declaratory decree obtained by a male reversioner to challenge alienation of ancestral property, despite the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, which restricted such rights to male-line descendants.
Whether the appellate court could grant relief to the female heirs who did not file appeals or cross-objections in the High Court.
holdings: Female heirs are entitled to inherit the property that reverted to the estate upon the father's death, even if they could not originally challenge the alienation, because the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, grants them equal inheritance rights when succession opens after its enactment.

An appellate court can grant relief to parties who did not appeal or file cross-objections under Order 41, Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, if justice so requires and the decree ought to have been in their favour.
provisions: Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, Section 8
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 41, Rule 33
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20, Rule 12
doctrines: Retrospective application of inheritance rights under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Appellate court's power to grant relief to non-appealing parties under Order 41, Rule 33

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be tenants, sought a temporary injunction to prevent the respondents from taking possession of premises in execution of an eviction order, which the trial court dismissed.
issues_decided: Whether the order dismissing the application for temporary injunction was appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1 of the CPC?
Whether the appellants were entitled to a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 or Section 151 of the CPC?
holdings: An order dismissing an application for temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 2 CPC is appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1 CPC, even if the court holds that the application does not meet the requirements of that rule.

The appellants were not entitled to a temporary injunction as they failed to establish a prima facie case of tenancy or that the threatened eviction constituted an 'injury' under Order XXXIX Rule 2 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII Rule 1
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 4
doctrines: Prima facie case for temporary injunction
Balance of convenience
Laches and delay in seeking equitable relief
Appellate jurisdiction over interlocutory orders

card.dispute: The Deputy Commissioner of Agricultural and Sales Tax argued that Palampadam Plantations Ltd., which sold spontaneously grown trees from its private forest, was a 'dealer' liable to sales tax under the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether a person owning and maintaining a private forest, selling trees of spontaneous growth, qualifies as a 'dealer' under Section 2(viii) of the Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963.
Whether such a person is liable to sales tax on the sale of timber from spontaneously grown trees under the Act.
holdings: A person who merely owns and maintains a private forest but does not engage in any activity to produce or uproot trees does not sell goods 'produced' by them and thus is not a 'dealer' under Section 2(viii).

The word 'produced' in the Act requires an element of volition, effort, and a process such as manufacture, agriculture, or horticulture; spontaneous growth without human intervention does not constitute production.
provisions: Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963, Section 2(viii)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Requirement of human effort for 'production' in tax law

card.dispute: Estates Development Ltd fought the Union of India and others over the cancellation of its land allotment granted as rehabilitation for property lost in Pakistan after Partition.
issues_decided: Whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner had jurisdiction to cancel the land allotment under Section 24(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 without a finding of fraud, false representation, or concealment of material fact.
Whether the reliance on jamabandi records from 1951 was valid to determine ownership status as of August 15, 1947.
holdings: The Chief Settlement Commissioner lacked jurisdiction to cancel the allotment under Section 24(2) because no finding of fraud, false representation, or concealment of material fact was made, which is a mandatory condition precedent.
A finding that the allotment was 'undeserved' or that title was unproven does not equate to a finding of fraud or misrepresentation required by Section 24(2) of the Act.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24(2)
doctrines: Condition precedent
Jurisdictional error
Mandatory statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, as representatives of a mosque and madrasa, sued to declare a house as wakf property and recover possession from defendants who claimed ownership through sale deeds from the original donor, challenging the validity of the 1914 wakf.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of wakf dated June 21, 1914 was valid and had been acted upon.
Whether the wakf was void for uncertainty due to non-specification of the mosque benefited.
Whether the plaintiffs' suit was barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act.
Whether the High Court could grant a decree for possession and mesne profits when those prayers were not explicitly decided by the trial court.
holdings: A wakf inter vivos is complete upon declaration by the owner; physical transfer of possession or mutation in records is not required, and the donor may serve as mutawalli.
A wakf is not void for uncertainty if the beneficiary mosque is identifiable from the donor’s subsequent conduct or declarations, even if not specified clearly in the deed.
The suit was not barred by limitation as it was filed within six years of the donor’s death, and Article 142 of the Limitation Act did not apply to wakf enforcement actions in these circumstances.

The High Court’s decree for possession and mesne profits requires remand for proper determination, as the trial court did not adjudicate those specific prayers and eviction under the Bihar Buildings Act required consideration by the appropriate authority.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 18
doctrines: Wakf inter vivos
Presumption of validity of wakf
Burden of proof to show wakf is illusory
Doctrine of uncertainty in charitable trusts

card.dispute: The Mathadhipathi of a Hindu math challenged the constitutional validity of Sections 46 and 47 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, which suspended him pending inquiry and authorized state administration of the math's affairs.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 46 and 47 violate Article 14 (equality before law),
Whether they infringe Article 19(1)(f) (right to property),
Whether they contravene Articles 25(1) (freedom to practice religion) and 26(b) and (d) (rights of religious denominations),
Whether the temporary state administration of a math during suspension of its head amounts to an unconstitutional interference with religious autonomy.
holdings: Sections 46 and 47 do not violate Article 14 as they prescribe reasonable and justiciable conditions for inquiry and suspension based on specific grounds like mismanagement or immoral conduct.
The provisions do not unreasonably restrict the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) as they are regulatory and aimed at protecting trust assets during inquiry.

The temporary administrative intervention under Section 47 does not breach Articles 25(1) or 26(b) and (d) because it does not interfere with religious practices or permanently displace religious authority.
Section 47 is constitutionally valid as it only allows temporary state administration during suspension or succession disputes, preserving the denomination’s ultimate right to manage its affairs.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 46
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 47
doctrines: Essential religious practices doctrine
State regulation of secular aspects of religion
Balancing fundamental rights with administrative necessity
Temporary administrative takeover as a reasonable restriction

card.dispute: The assessee, Durga Das Khanna, fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether a lump sum payment of Rs. 55,200 received from lessees for constructing a cinema house was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the sum of Rs. 55,200 received by the assessee was an advance payment of rent and thus a revenue receipt taxable under the Income-tax Act
Whether the lump sum payment constituted a premium (salami) and, if so, whether it was a capital or revenue receipt
Whether the nature of the receipt could be determined solely as a question of law or depended on the facts and circumstances of the case
holdings: The Rs. 55,200 was not advance rent, as the lease contained no stipulation for treating it as such or for adjusting it against rent, and thus could not be taxed as a revenue receipt.

A lump sum payment like salami or premium is prima facie a capital receipt, especially when non-recurring and not linked to periodic rent, and the burden lies on tax authorities to prove it as revenue.
The character of a premium as capital or revenue depends on the facts of each case, not as a pure question of law, and here the facts supported it being a capital receipt.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Prima facie capital nature of salami or premium
Facts-based determination of taxability of lease premiums

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant from six shops, alleging unauthorized sub-letting and a consolidated tenancy; the tenant denied sub-letting and claimed only a rent increase, not a new tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy of all six shops constituted one integrated tenancy after a consolidated rent was agreed upon in 1953
Whether two of the shops were sub-let without the landlord's permission
Whether sub-letting before the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950 came into force could be a ground for ejectment under Section 13(1)(e)
holdings: A mere increase in rent does not create a new or integrated tenancy; the original tenancies continued with altered rent, so no surrender and re-grant occurred.
Sub-letting of two shops was established, and since no permission was pleaded or proven, it was unauthorized, justifying ejectment from those two shops.

Section 13(1)(e) applies to sub-letting that occurred before the Act came into force if the sub-letting continues at the time of the suit, as the provision uses present perfect tense and contemplates ongoing violations.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(e)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 26
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 27(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of tenancy by estoppel
Doctrine of continuing wrong
Principle of statutory interpretation based on tense and context

card.dispute: An unsuccessful election candidate alleged that the winning candidate committed corrupt practices during a parliamentary election.
issues_decided: Whether granting land revenue exemption via government ordinance before elections amounts to a corrupt practice under Section 123(1)(A) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
Whether announcing increased dearness allowance to government employees before elections constitutes a corrupt practice under Section 123(1)(A).
Whether distributing dummy ballot papers omitting the opponent's election symbol conveys withdrawal of candidacy and amounts to a corrupt practice under Section 123(4).
Whether active canvassing by a police officer with the candidate's consent amounts to a corrupt practice under Section 123(7).
holdings: Government action granting land revenue exemption does not amount to a gift or promise of gratification under Section 123(1)(A) when done in public interest and not by the candidate personally.
Announcement of dearness allowance to government employees to avert strike does not constitute a corrupt practice under Section 123(1)(A) as it was not a personal benefit offered by the candidate.

Distributing dummy ballot papers without an opponent's symbol does not necessarily convey withdrawal of candidacy; no corrupt practice under Section 123(4) is established without clear evidence of such intent.
Mere allegations of police canvassing are insufficient to prove corrupt practice under Section 123(7); credible evidence and proof of consent are required.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 123(1)(A)
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 123(4)
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 123(7)
doctrines: Corrupt practice under Representation of the People Act requires proof of agency and intent
Government policy decisions made in public interest do not automatically become electoral malpractices

card.dispute: The appellant claimed preemption rights over land purchased by the respondent, who argued he waived such rights by acting as a broker in the sale.
issues_decided: Whether waiver of a preemptive right under s. 26(f) of the Bengal Tenancy Act requires a contract or agreement with consideration
Whether the appellant's conduct amounted to a valid waiver of his right of preemption
holdings: Under Indian law, waiver does not require a contract or consideration; it is sufficient if there is an intention not to insist on the right.
In preemption cases, positive acts showing acquiescence or relinquishment of the right lead to forfeiture, consistent with principles derived from Mohammedan Jurisprudence.
doctrines: Waiver without consideration
Forfeiture by acquiescence in preemption law
Distinction between waiver and estoppel

card.dispute: The appellant bank challenged the dismissal of its application to set aside a property sale in execution proceedings, claiming it was an interested party and that the amended procedural requirements did not apply retroactively.
issues_decided: Whether Clause (b) of the proviso to Order 21, Rule 90, CPC, inserted on June 1, 1957, applies to an application filed before that date?
Whether the executing court must be given discretion to allow compliance with the deposit or security requirement under Clause (b) even after the application has been heard on merits?
holdings: Clause (b) of the proviso applies to applications pending when it came into force, as 'entertain' means to adjudicate upon, and this Court is bound by prior precedent interpreting it thus.

The High Court erred in refusing to remand the case; the executing court must be allowed to exercise its discretionary power under Clause (b), especially where parties proceeded on the assumption that the clause did not apply.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90, proviso (as amended)
doctrines: Prospective application of procedural law
Judicial discretion in procedural compliance
Binding precedent doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants (successors of landlords) challenged the execution of a decree under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act against their bhumidhari rights and trees after the abolition of zamindari.
issues_decided: Whether bhumidhari rights granted under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act can be proceeded against in execution of a decree under the U.P. Encumbered Estates Act
Whether trees constituting a grove, belonging to the debtor, can be attached and sold in execution of such a decree
holdings: Bhumidhari rights are new rights created under the Abolition Act and are not proprietary rights in land; hence they can be proceeded against under Section 24 of the Encumbered Estates Act for decree execution.

Trees constituting a grove did not vest in the State under the Abolition Act and remain the debtor's property, liable to attachment and sale in execution under Section 24 of the Encumbered Estates Act.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18
doctrines: Doctrine of extinguishment of proprietary rights upon vesting under land reform laws
Doctrine of substitution of mortgagee's rights by a money decree under special statutes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, arguing that state tenancy laws did not apply in cantonment areas due to Parliament's exclusive legislative power over house accommodation there.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act applies to cantonment areas given Parliament's exclusive power under Entry 3, List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution
Whether the regulation of house accommodation in cantonment areas includes landlord-tenant relationships
holdings: Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on landlord-tenant relationships concerning house accommodation in cantonment areas under Entry 3, List I, overriding state laws.
The expression 'regulation of house accommodation in cantonment areas' includes control of rents and tenancy laws, thereby excluding state legislatures' competence in this field.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 3, List I
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 18, List II
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entries 6 and 7, List III
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence and repugnancy under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of exclusivity of Union power in matters enumerated in List I
Doctrine of subject-to clauses in constitutional entries

card.dispute: The association of rubber chappal manufacturers challenged the levy of duty under the Rubber Act, 1947 as amended, arguing it was unconstitutional and arbitrarily imposed on users rather than producers.
issues_decided: Whether the duty levied under Section 12 of the Rubber Act, as amended, falls within Parliament's legislative competence under Entry 84 of List I of the Seventh Schedule or alternatively under Entry 97 read with Article 248 of the Constitution
Whether Section 12(2) of the Rubber Act confers unguided and arbitrary power violating Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the rules framed under the Act, particularly Rules 33, 33A, and 33D, provide sufficient clarity on whom the duty is levied
holdings: The duty remains an excise duty within Entry 84 of List I even if collected from users, as the method of collection does not alter its essential nature.

Parliament has legislative competence under Entry 97 of List I read with Article 248 to authorize collection from users, even if not excise, and the delegation of power is guided by policy and purpose, satisfying Article 14.
The rules, especially Rule 33D, clearly indicate that the duty is to be collected from manufacturers, providing sufficient clarity and avoiding arbitrary application.
provisions: The Rubber (Production and Marketing) Act, 1947, Section 12
The Rubber (Production and Marketing) Act, 1947, Section 25
The Rubber (Production and Marketing) Act, 1947, Rules 33, 33A, 33B, 33D
Constitution of India, Entry 84 of List I, Seventh Schedule
Constitution of India, Entry 97 of List I, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Essence of tax doctrine: the nature of a tax is determined by its substance, not the machinery of collection
Legislative competence under residuary power (Entry 97 and Article 248)
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Delegated legislation with policy guidance satisfies constitutional requirements

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the Controller's method of calculating fair rent under the Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, arguing that 'cost of construction' meant original construction cost, not market value at enactment.
issues_decided: Whether 'cost of construction' in Section 4(3)(b)(i) of the Act refers to original construction cost or market value at the time of enactment.
Whether the rules prescribing rates for cost of construction are valid if they equate 'cost of construction' with market value.
holdings: The expression 'cost of construction' in Section 4(3)(b)(i) means the original cost of construction, not the market value at the time of enactment, especially when contrasted with 'market value' in Section 4(3)(b)(ii).

Rules that equate 'cost of construction' with market value at enactment go beyond the statutory framework and are invalid, as they result in impermissible delegation and double counting of allowances.
provisions: Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 4(3)(b)(i), (ii), (iii)
Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Rules, Rule 12
Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Schedule II, Note (2)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine against excessive delegation of legislative power
Rule against double counting in statutory valuation

card.dispute: The Kalanka Devi Sansthan, a private religious trust, fought to recover possession of agricultural land from a tenant for 'personal cultivation' under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, which the Revenue Tribunal and High Court denied.
issues_decided: Whether a private religious trust or idol, as a juristic person, can claim to 'cultivate personally' under Section 2(12) of the Act through its servants or hired laborers.
Whether Explanation I to Section 2(12), which deems certain disabled persons to cultivate personally, applies to a juristic person like a Sansthan or idol.
Whether the exclusion of juristic persons from claiming personal cultivation violates constitutional rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f).
holdings: The expression 'to cultivate personally' requires a direct nexus between the cultivator and agricultural operations, which must be under the personal supervision of a natural person, not a legal person like a trust or idol.

Explanation I to Section 2(12) applies only to natural persons with physical or mental disabilities, not to juristic persons like idols or trusts, and thus does not extend personal cultivation rights to them.
The exclusion of juristic persons from claiming personal cultivation does not violate Articles 14 or 19(1)(f) as the Act is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 2(12)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 2(22)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 36
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 38
doctrines: Doctrine of personal cultivation requiring direct supervision by a natural person
Distinction between natural and juristic persons in tenancy law
Constitutional immunity under Article 31A for agrarian reform laws

card.dispute: The State and convicted persons appealed against a trial court judgment in a criminal case arising from a violent clash over a right of way, leading to death and injuries on both sides.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the charges of murder and assault beyond reasonable doubt based on unreliable witness testimony
Whether the accused could be convicted under Section 304/34 IPC without proof of common intention to cause injury
Whether the High Court correctly relied on a discredited witness to establish the role of the accused
Whether the distinction between common intention (Section 34 IPC) and unlawful assembly (Section 149 IPC) was properly applied
holdings: The prosecution case fails if the sole relied-upon witness is found to be untrustworthy and no corroborative reliable evidence exists.
A conviction under Section 304/34 IPC requires proof of active participation and common intention to commit the offence, which cannot be inferred merely from possession of weapons.
A court cannot selectively rely on parts of a witness's testimony that align with other evidence if the witness is found to have deliberately suppressed material facts.
An intention to enforce a right of way, even by force, does not amount to a criminal common intention under Section 34 IPC unless there is an intention to commit a crime.
doctrines: Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
Separation of truth from falsehood in witness testimony
Requirement of proof of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Distinction between civil dispute and criminal liability

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents contested over the right to ratable distribution of sale proceeds from properties charged under a security bond, where the respondents sought equal distribution as decree-holders while the appellant claimed priority based on the charge.
issues_decided: Whether the security bond creating a charge under Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act required attestation by two witnesses under Section 59
Whether the decree declaring the charge enured for the benefit of the decree-holder despite no formal amendment to the plaint
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to pass a decree for sale of properties outside its territorial jurisdiction
Whether the respondents were entitled to ratable distribution of the sale proceeds
holdings: A charge under Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act does not require attestation by two witnesses; registration under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act is sufficient.
The decree validly declared a charge in favor of the decree-holder even without amending the plaint, as the oral prayer sufficed and the omission was merely an irregularity.
The respondents cannot challenge the High Court's territorial jurisdiction in execution proceedings when they seek benefit from the sale conducted under that decree.
Proceeds from sale of properties charged under Section 100 must first satisfy the charge-holder; ratable distribution to other decree-holders is only from any surplus.
doctrines: Doctrine of notice
Principle of ratable distribution
Constructive jurisdiction in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The State Bank of Travancore sought to enforce a charge on properties allotted to M.C. Chacko under a family settlement deed to recover debts from letters of guarantee executed by his father, which Chacko contested.
issues_decided: Whether a charge was created on the properties in favor of the bank under the family settlement deed.
Whether the bank, not being a party to the deed, could enforce any such charge.
holdings: The recitals in the deed did not show an intention to create a charge in favor of the bank; they only established a family arrangement for indemnity among family members.
A person not party to a contract cannot enforce its terms unless they are a beneficiary under a trust or part of a family arrangement, which the bank was not.
doctrines: Doctrine of privity of contract
Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of charge under transfer of property

card.dispute: The appellant filed an appeal in the wrong court due to a valuation error, leading to a delay; the respondent contested the condonation of delay under the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to condone the delay in filing the appeal under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908, on the ground of mistake by counsel.
Whether the valuation of the original suit or the amount decreed determines the forum for appeal when the decree is for a lesser amount than the original valuation.
holdings: Mistake of counsel can be a valid ground for condoning delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act if it is bona fide and not used to conceal laches or ulterior motives.

When a suit is valued above the jurisdictional limit of the District Court, the appeal must go to the High Court regardless of the reduced valuation in appeal, as the original valuation determines the forum.
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Bona fide mistake of counsel
Jurisdiction determined by original valuation in suit

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that a 1949 deed effected a partition of joint family property for tax assessment purposes, while the State contended it was merely a maintenance arrangement.
issues_decided: Whether the deed dated December 30, 1949, amounted to a genuine partition of joint family property.
Whether the deed was invalid or ineffective under Section 24(1) of the Rewa State Land Revenue and Tenancy Code, 1935.
Whether the partition, if any, constituted a transfer hit by Section 24(1) of the Rewa Code.
Whether the appellant was liable to be assessed on the entire property despite the deed.
holdings: The deed did not effect a partition of joint family shares but was only a provision for family maintenance.
Since no transfer of property or interest occurred, the deed did not violate Section 24(1) of the Rewa Code.
A partition that amounts to transfer would be invalid under Section 24(1) of the Rewa Code, but this deed did not amount to such a transfer.
The appellant remained liable to assessment on the entire property as the deed did not legally partition the joint family property.
provisions: United Provinces Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 24(1)
Rewa State Land Revenue and Tenancy Code, 1935, Section 24(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of partition in Hindu law
Doctrine of maintenance versus partition
Principle of construction of partition deeds

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State for setting up a memorial to Mahatma Gandhi on their land, arguing procedural and legislative defects.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958 is ultra vires the legislature.
Whether the Commissioner of Baroda Division could issue a notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act without a fresh notification under Section 4.
Whether the notifications under Sections 4 and 6 were invalid due to non-compliance with Sections 77 and 78 of the Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949.
Whether the purpose of setting up a memorial to Mahatma Gandhi constitutes a 'public purpose' under the Land Acquisition Act.
holdings: The Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1958 is valid and does not exceed legislative competence.
A fresh notification under Section 4 is not required before issuing a notification under Section 6 by a successor authority after state reorganisation.
Compliance with Sections 77 and 78 of the Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 is not a precondition for initiating land acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act.

Acquisition of land for a memorial to Mahatma Gandhi at a place associated with him is a 'public purpose' within the meaning of Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, independent of municipal purposes.
provisions: Commissioners of Divisions Act, Bombay Act 8 of 1958, Sections 3(3), 3(4)
doctrines: Public purpose in land acquisition
Validity of delegated legislation
Doctrine of conclusive evidence under Section 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act
Doctrine of statutory interpretation regarding alternative procedures

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased mortgagor sought relief under debt relief statutes to limit the amount payable to redeem mortgaged property, against the mortgagee's claim for a higher amount based on a prior decree.
issues_decided: Whether the legal representatives of a deceased mortgagor can claim relief under Section 30 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934
Whether the suit for redemption falls within the scope of the Usurious Loans Act, 1918
Whether an anomalous mortgage creates a 'debt' under the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934
What constitutes the 'amount actually advanced' under Section 30 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934
holdings: A suit for redemption of an anomalous mortgage is a suit in respect of a debt, and the liability survives the mortgagor's death, enforceable against his estate.
Legal representatives of a debtor can claim relief under Section 30 of the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, as the statute does not restrict relief to the original debtor.
The Usurious Loans Act, 1918 does not apply to a suit for redemption of a mortgage where the security was created before the Act's commencement.
The 'amount actually advanced' under Section 30 means the principal lent, not the amount declared due in a prior decree, and interest in excess of statutory limits must be deducted.
provisions: Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, Section 7
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, Section 30
doctrines: Anomalous mortgage
Survival of debt obligation after death
Statutory interpretation of 'debt' and 'suit in respect of a debt'
Limitation on decree amount under debt relief legislation

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a half share in certain properties and challenged the validity of a 1927 partition, while the respondent claimed sole ownership of one property and sought eviction of the appellant.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to a share in the properties claimed on the basis of joint family or joint business funds
Whether the 1927 partition was valid and binding on the appellant
Whether the appellant had an irrevocable license to remain in possession of property item No. 6 under Section 60 of the Indian Easement Act
Whether the appellant could raise a new legal argument for the first time in the Supreme Court based on admitted facts
holdings: Properties purchased in the name of one brother are presumed to be his absolute property unless there is cogent evidence that they were acquired from joint family or joint business funds.
A partition in which a person was represented as a minor is binding if courts find he was indeed a minor at the time, and concurrent findings of fact are not lightly disturbed.
A plea of irrevocable license under Section 60 of the Indian Easement Act cannot be entertained if not raised in pleadings, no issue framed, and no evidence led.
A new legal argument not pleaded or developed in lower courts cannot be raised in the Supreme Court even if based on admitted facts, especially when it requires factual determination.
doctrines: Benami transaction doctrine
Concurrent finding of fact rule
Pleading and issue estoppel
Presumption of ownership from title

card.dispute: Zamindars and an occupancy tenant's descendant fought over possession of land and rights under land reform laws after the tenant's death.
issues_decided: Whether the suit and appeal abated under the Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules after the death of a party.
Whether Lalai, as a trespasser, could acquire Sirdari or Adivasi rights based on possession in 1356 F.
Whether the Zamindars could be deemed to hold the land as khudkast under Section 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act despite a trespasser's possession.
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the petition on locus standi without considering the final decree under Section 180 of the U.P. Tenancy Act.
holdings: The suit and appeal did not abate solely due to the death of a party; substitution of heirs is required under procedural law.
Mere possession without official recording as an occupant in 1356 F does not entitle a person to Adivasi or Sirdari rights under the Act.
The expression 'deemed to be held as khudkast' may include constructive possession by the owner even if dispossessed by a trespasser close to the vesting date.
The High Court erred in dismissing the petition on locus standi without fully examining the effect of the final decree in favor of the Zamindars.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 18(1)(a)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, Rule 4 and Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22, Rule 4
doctrines: Constructive possession
Abatement of suit
Deemed ownership under land reform laws
Res judicata
Locus standi in writ petitions

card.dispute: Citizens of India challenged the implementation of an international tribunal's award demarcating the boundary between India and Pakistan in the Rann of Kutch, claiming it amounted to ceding Indian territory without a constitutional amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the implementation of the tribunal's award in the Rann of Kutch dispute required a constitutional amendment under Article 3 of the Constitution
Whether the disputed sectors were part of the territory of the State of Kutch and therefore Indian territory prior to the award
Whether the award operated as a cession of Indian territory
holdings: Implementation of an arbitral award settling a boundary dispute does not require a constitutional amendment under Article 3 if it merely defines an indefinite boundary and does not cede territory.

Territory becomes part of India through sovereign control; mere claims or administrative assertions without evidence of de facto sovereign authority do not establish that disputed areas were Indian territory.

An award that demarcates a previously undefined boundary based on equitable considerations does not amount to cession of territory, especially where sovereign authority over the area was never effectively exercised.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entries 10 and 14
doctrines: Doctrine of effective occupation for establishing territorial sovereignty
Doctrine that boundary settlements by arbitration do not require constitutional amendment if not involving cession
Principle of non-cession of territory without clear constitutional authority

card.dispute: The appellant Jagirdar challenged the dismissal of his appeal as time-barred for claiming compensation under the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, arguing that the time taken to obtain a copy of the order should be excluded from the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the time taken to obtain a copy of the Jagir Commissioner's decision can be excluded when computing the 90-day appeal period under Section 29 of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act?
Whether the provisions of the Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, particularly Sections 34 and 149(2), allow for the application of general limitation principles, including condonation of delay?
Whether the Board of Revenue acted judicially in dismissing the appeal without considering condonation of delay?
holdings: The time spent in obtaining a copy of the judgment forming the basis of the decision must be excluded when computing the 90-day appeal period under Section 29 of the Jagirs Act.
Sections 34 and 149(2) of the Ryotwari Act incorporate the general principles of the Limitation Act, 1908, including the power to condone delay under Section 5, unless expressly excluded.
The Board of Revenue failed to act judicially by dismissing the appeal on limitation grounds without considering whether the appellant had sufficient cause for delay.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 29
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 30
Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samwat 2007, Section 34
Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samwat 2007, Section 149(2)
doctrines: Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Principle of exclusion of time taken to obtain copies for limitation computation
Judicial duty to consider sufficient cause before dismissing on limitation grounds
Interpretation of special statutes by reference to general principles of limitation

card.dispute: The petitioning creditor challenged the validity of two mortgages executed by the insolvent in favor of the appellants, claiming they were not supported by consideration and were intended to defraud creditors.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, under the first proviso to Section 75(1) of the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, could reappreciate findings of fact made by the District Court in appeal.
Whether the mortgages in question were supported by valid consideration and thus could be upheld under Section 53 of the Provincial Insolvency Act.
holdings: The High Court has no power under the first proviso to Section 75(1) to reappreciate evidence or disturb findings of fact by the District Court; its role is limited to ensuring the decision is according to law, not revising factual conclusions.

The mortgage for Rs. 10,000 is valid to the extent of Rs. 10,500 (including interest) based on documentary entries and admissions in the insolvent’s books; however, the Rs. 4,500 cash payment claimed was not satisfactorily proved due to lack of corroborative evidence.
provisions: Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, Section 75(1), first proviso
doctrines: Limited scope of High Court's revisional jurisdiction
Burden of proof in insolvency proceedings regarding consideration
Admissibility and evidentiary value of entries in account books as admissions

card.dispute: Rival pre-emptors contested the amount of pre-emption money fixed by the High Court, with the appellants challenging the reduction of the deposit amount despite losing their statutory right to pre-emption due to a retrospective amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had a right to appeal against the High Court's decree reducing the pre-emption amount when their own right to pre-emption was extinguished by a retrospective amendment.
Whether the trial court's decree in favour of the appellants became final and binding despite the consolidation of suits and the subsequent amendment.
holdings: The appellants had no right to appeal because the retrospective amendment to the Punjab Pre-emption Act removed their entitlement to a pre-emption decree, and the High Court’s decision did not adversely affect their extinguished rights.

The trial court’s decree in favour of the appellants was not final or independent, as the consolidated suit meant both pre-emptors’ rights were determined together, and the appellants could not benefit without the superior pre-emptors first failing.
provisions: Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1931, Section 31 (as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20, Rule 14
Punjab High Court Rules and Orders, Chapter 1-M(c), para 3
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes extinguishing rights
Finality of decrees in consolidated suits
Hierarchy of pre-emptive rights under pre-emption law
Locus standi to appeal based on legal aggrievement

card.dispute: The appellant, a leaseholder, challenged the State of Assam's notice of resumption of leasehold land, arguing the State lacked authority under the lease and constitutional law.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can entertain a petition under Article 226 when the dispute involves alleged executive overreach in resuming leasehold property.
Whether the dispute involved a mere question of title or raised substantial questions of public law.
Whether the State of Assam could lawfully resume the property under the lease and through executive action without judicial process.
holdings: The High Court has supervisory jurisdiction under Article 226 to ensure public authorities act within legal limits, even when private rights are involved, if public law issues are raised.
A petition under Article 226 is maintainable if it challenges the legality of executive action affecting property, and does not solely involve disputed title.
The appellant was not merely enforcing a contractual right; the case raised constitutional questions about the State's power to resume property by executive action.
doctrines: Prerogative writs in public law
Supervisory jurisdiction of High Courts
Distinction between private rights and public law remedies

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee, Amritsar, challenged the constitutional validity of the Punjab Local Authorities (Aided Schools) Act, 1959, and the State's takeover of its schools and property, including forced contributions, without compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the retrospective operation of the notification under Section 5 of the Act is valid
Whether the amendments to Sections 52(1)(g) and 59 of the Punjab Municipal Act under Section 6 of the 1959 Act violate Article 31(2) of the Constitution
Whether Sections 3(2) and 6 of the 1959 Act, which transfer proprietary rights and trigger acquisition of property and funds, are protected under Article 31A(1)(b)
Whether the State legislature had competence to enact the impugned provisions
holdings: The notification under the proviso to Section 5 cannot have retrospective effect in absence of express or implied language; takeover of management is effective only from the date of notification.
The amendment inserting clause (g) in Section 52(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act is void as it amounts to compulsory acquisition of property without compensation, violating Article 31(2).

Sections 3(2) and 6 of the 1959 Act are unconstitutional to the extent they result in acquisition of property and funds without compliance with Article 31(2), even if protected by Article 31A(1)(b) for management takeover.

It is unnecessary to decide legislative competence since the provisions violate Article 31(2); however, the State lacks power under List II to enact compulsory contribution provisions affecting municipal property.
provisions: Punjab Local Authorities (Aided Schools) Act, 1959, Section 3(2)
Punjab Local Authorities (Aided Schools) Act, 1959, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective operation of statutes
Doctrine of constitutional protection under Article 31A
Doctrine of compulsory acquisition of property without compensation violating Article 31(2)
Doctrine of severability

card.dispute: The mortgagors contested the decree absolute for sale, arguing that deposits made towards principal discharged the debt, that interest should not exceed the principal, and that the Custodian of Evacuee Property had no right to claim the decree.
issues_decided: Whether deposits made by the mortgagors in court should be appropriated to principal instead of interest
Whether the High Court's clarification order restored the interest rate to 3% after November 10, 1946
Whether interest awarded can exceed the principal amount under the Madhya Pradesh Money Lenders Act, 1934
Whether the Custodian of Evacuee Property could be impleaded and claim a decree absolute for sale
holdings: Payments unappropriated by the creditor are to be applied first to interest and then to principal; the mortgagors failed to prove any agreement for appropriation to principal.
The High Court did not reduce the post-November 10, 1946 interest rate to 3%; the 4% rate continued as per the appellate decree.

Section 9 of the Madhya Pradesh Money Lenders Act, 1934 prohibits decreeing interest exceeding the principal, but the awarded interest (Rs. 746-30) was less than the principal (Rs. 33,866-51), so the cap was not breached.
The Custodian of Evacuee Property could be impleaded and represented the mortgagee’s interest; the internal rights between mortgagees need not be decided for a decree absolute for sale.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 9
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21, Rule 1
doctrines: Appropriation of payments to interest before principal
Finality of appellate decrees and interpretation of court orders
Statutory limitation on interest under money lending laws
Representation of mortgagee interest in decree for sale

card.dispute: The landlord (Nanney Lal) obtained permission to file an eviction suit against the tenant (Mohammad Ismail), who challenged the permission before the Commissioner and later the State Government, which revoked the permission; the dispute was whether the eviction suit remained maintainable after the revocation.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for eviction becomes incompetent if the State Government subsequently revokes the permission granted by the District Magistrate under Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent & Eviction Act, 1947?
Whether the revisional power of the State Government under Section 7-F affects the maintainability of a suit already filed with prior permission?
holdings: A suit validly instituted with the required permission under Section 3 does not become non-maintainable merely because the State Government later revokes that permission under Section 7-F.
The power of the State Government under Section 7-F is exercisable only before the institution of a suit and cannot invalidate proceedings already commenced.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent & Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent & Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent & Eviction Act, 1947, Section 16
doctrines: Finality of judicial proceedings
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and language
Principles of natural justice in quasi-judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The Municipal Board, Sitapur fought with Prayag Narain Saigal & Firm over the validity of the water tax imposed by the Board due to alleged procedural non-compliance.
issues_decided: Whether non-publication of the preliminary proposal under Section 131(3) read with Section 94 invalidates the tax imposition
Whether failure to publish the modified proposal under Section 132(2) renders the tax invalid
Whether non-publication of the special resolution under Section 94 invalidates the tax
holdings: Substantial compliance with Section 131(3) suffices; omission to publish the proposal separately is a curable irregularity if inhabitants had notice and opportunity to object.
Non-publication of a modified proposal reducing tax rate or increasing exemption limit does not cause prejudice and is cured by Section 135(3).
Non-publication of the special resolution under Section 94 is a procedural irregularity that does not invalidate the tax where the official notification under Section 135(2) has been issued.
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Curative effect of conclusive proof provisions
No invalidation for procedural irregularities without substantial prejudice

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the validity of action taken under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961, after the Golaknath judgment, on the ground that it violated fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961, incorporated in the Ninth Schedule by the Seventeenth Amendment, can be challenged for violating fundamental rights under Part III of the Constitution.
Whether actions taken under a Ninth Schedule Act after the date of the Golaknath judgment (February 27, 1967) are void if they infringe fundamental rights.
Whether the doctrine of prospective overruling, as applied in Golaknath’s case, invalidates post-1967 actions under Ninth Schedule laws.
holdings: Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule by the Seventeenth Amendment are protected from challenge on grounds of infringement of fundamental rights under Article 31B, regardless of when action is taken under them.
The doctrine of prospective overruling in Golaknath’s case did not invalidate prior constitutional amendments or actions taken under Ninth Schedule laws after February 27, 1967.
Parliament’s power to insulate laws from judicial review via the Ninth Schedule remains effective for actions taken even after the Golaknath judgment.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceilings on Holdings) Act, 1961 (Act 27 of 1961)
doctrines: Doctrine of Prospective Overruling
Parliamentary power to exclude laws from judicial review via Ninth Schedule
Protection of laws under Article 31B from fundamental rights challenges

card.dispute: The appellant, N. V. Narendranath, contested whether his family—consisting of himself, his wife, and two minor daughters—could be assessed as a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) for wealth tax purposes after receiving ancestral property on partition, or whether he should be taxed as an individual.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu Undivided Family can consist of a sole surviving coparcener, his wife, and daughters for assessment under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether property received by a coparcener on partition with his father and brothers retains the character of joint family property when he has no male issue at the time of partition.
holdings: A Hindu Undivided Family under the Wealth Tax Act can consist of a single male coparcener, his wife, and daughters; the absence of a second male coparcener does not negate HUF status.

Property received by a coparcener on partition remains joint family property in his hands if it retains ancestral character and is capable of devolving on future male issue, and thus belongs to the HUF consisting of himself, wife, and daughters.
doctrines: Continuity of joint family property after partition
Ancestral property retains HUF character in hands of sole coparcener
Hindu law concept of coparcenary and joint family

card.dispute: The appellant claimed increased maintenance from trust income, while respondents argued the trust's primary purpose was charity, not family maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether the dominant purpose of the trust was family maintenance or charity.
Whether the cy-pres doctrine could justify increased maintenance payments to the appellant.
holdings: The dominant intention of the settlor was to benefit charities, as shown by the trust deed's structure, priority of charitable expenses, and discretionary nature of family maintenance.
The cy-pres doctrine does not apply to non-charitable purposes like family maintenance, so increased maintenance could not be justified under it.
doctrines: Cy-pres doctrine
Construction of trust deeds to ascertain settlor's dominant intention

card.dispute: The dispute was between Nathu Prasad, the recorded tenant, and Ranchhod Prasad & Ors, sub-lessees, over whether the latter acquired occupancy rights despite the sub-lease being in violation of statutory restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether sub-lessees inducted in contravention of s. 73 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, could acquire occupancy rights under s. 185(1)(ii)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959
Whether such sub-lessees were protected under the Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-lessee Protection Act, 1955
holdings: A person inducted as a sub-lessee in violation of s. 73 read with s. 78 of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, is deemed a trespasser and does not acquire occupancy tenant status under s. 185(1)(ii)(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959.

The Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-lessee Protection Act, 1955, does not protect sub-lessees deemed trespassers under s. 78 of Act 66 of 1950, and thus such persons cannot claim rights as ryotwari sub-lessees under the 1959 Code.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 185(1)(ii)(b)
Revenue Administration and Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act 66 of 1950), Sections 73, 75, 76, 78
Madhya Bharat Ryotwari Sub-lessee Protection Act, 1955 (Act 29 of 1955), Sections 2(b), 3
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tenant protection laws
Exclusion of trespassers from statutory benefits
Doctrine of occupancy rights by operation of law

card.dispute: The National & Grindlays Bank Ltd. (landlord) challenged the Bombay Municipal Corporation's composite property tax assessment on leased land and a separately constructed building, arguing that the tenant, not the landlord, should bear primary liability.
issues_decided: Whether Section 146(2) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 contemplates a composite assessment of land and building when owned by different persons.
Whether the primary liability for property tax under Section 146(2)(a) falls on the landlord of the land, even if the tenant constructed the building.
Whether the landlord can be considered the 'lessor of the premises' under Section 146(2)(a) when only the land, not the building, was leased.
holdings: Section 146(2) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 mandates a composite assessment of land and building when a tenant constructs on leased land.
The primary liability for property tax in such composite assessments lies with the landlord of the land under Section 146(2)(a), unless the case falls under Section 146(3).
The term 'lessor of the premises' in Section 146(2)(a) includes the lessor of land on which a tenant has built, even if the building is not leased by the landlord.
doctrines: Contemporanea expositio
Primary liability in tax assessment
Composite assessment of property

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of an oral agreement to re-convey property sold to the defendant, while the defendant later offered in writing to sell part of the property but the plaintiff did not accept that offer.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff proved the existence of an oral agreement for re-conveyance of property sold.
Whether the High Court could decree specific performance based on the defendant's unilateral offer in the written statement.
Whether the plaintiff's suit for specific performance was maintainable in the absence of pleading readiness and willingness to perform.
holdings: The plaintiff failed to prove the oral agreement for re-conveyance due to lack of credible and disinterested evidence, and the burden of proof was not discharged.
A decree for specific performance cannot be based on a defendant's offer in a written statement when the plaintiff has not accepted it or pleaded performance of that agreement.
A suit for specific performance requires the plaintiff to plead readiness and willingness to perform; its absence renders the suit non-maintainable.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order 7, Forms 47 and 48
doctrines: Burden of proof in cases involving oral agreements for specific performance
Requirement of pleading readiness and willingness in suits for specific performance
Court cannot grant decree based on unilateral offer not accepted by plaintiff

card.dispute: The sugar company challenged the attachment and sale of its immovable and movable properties by the Land Reforms Commissioner to recover arrears of income-tax, sugar cess, and cane supply dues, arguing procedural irregularities and restrictions under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the restrictions in Section 279 and Section 286(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act apply to the recovery of dues under other statutes like the Income-tax Act, Co-operative Societies Act, and U.P. Sugar Factories Control Act when such dues are recoverable as arrears of land revenue
Whether the Collector must first exhaust remedies under Section 279 clauses (a) to (e) before attaching and selling immovable property under Section 286
Whether the sale of movable property after immovable property had already realized more than the dues was illegal or unnecessary

Whether the failure to stay the sale upon intimation from the Income-tax Officer or the appointment of the purchaser as Authorised Controller invalidated the sale or prevented the company from setting it aside under Rule 285-H
holdings: The provisions of Section 286(2) allow recovery of miscellaneous dues as arrears of land revenue from any immovable property without being bound by the sequence of recovery processes in Section 279 or the restrictions in Section 286(1).
The Collector is not required to first resort to movable property or personal arrest before attaching immovable property; the recovery processes under Section 279 can be invoked in any order.

Although selling movable property after sufficient recovery from immovable property was unnecessary, the failure to raise this issue before lower authorities barred the court from invalidating the sale on that ground.

The sale was not vitiated by the Collector ignoring the Income-tax Officer's stay request or by the purchaser becoming Authorised Controller, especially since the company did not attempt to deposit amounts under Rule 285-H to set aside the sale.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 279
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 286
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Rule 285-H
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 30(e)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation (harmonious reading of sub-sections)
Doctrine of waiver by failure to raise issues before lower authorities
Doctrine of separation of recovery processes in revenue law
Doctrine of legality of simultaneous execution against person and property

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict tenants for non-payment of rent for two years and sought forfeiture of tenancy; tenants claimed relief against forfeiture under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court can grant relief under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act if the tenant failed to comply with conditions in the trial court.
Whether the jurisdiction to grant relief against forfeiture lies exclusively with the court of first instance.
Whether the appellate court properly exercised its discretion in granting relief against forfeiture.
holdings: The appellate court has jurisdiction to grant relief under Section 114 even if the tenant failed to comply with payment conditions in the trial court, as an appeal amounts to a rehearing.
Relief against forfeiture under Section 114 can be granted by an appellate court if the tenant pays or tenders the arrears, interest, and costs at the hearing of the appeal.
The discretion to grant relief is not barred by prior failure to pay, but must be exercised equitably, considering the tenant's conduct and the equities of the case.
doctrines: Relief against forfeiture
Equitable discretion in lease enforcement
Clean hands doctrine
Appellate court's power to rehear and grant equitable relief

card.dispute: The assessee challenged the inclusion of the estimated value of a retained plot as profit from a land transaction, arguing it was not a trade and that profits could only be determined after full disposal.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction constituted an adventure in the nature of trade
Whether the profit could be assessed before the sale of the entire land, including the retained plot
holdings: A transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade if, on a totality of circumstances, it shows a profit-making scheme involving organisation and planning, even if it is a single transaction.

For income tax purposes, profits from a trading adventure must be computed annually, and stock-in-trade (including unsold plots) must be valued at the end of the year using commercial accounting principles.
doctrines: Adventure in the nature of trade
Annual assessment principle
Stock-in-trade valuation under commercial accounting

card.dispute: The appellant lessor refused to renew a lease after ten years, and the respondent lessee sued for specific performance of the renewal clause, leading to a dispute over whether the renewal covenant violated the rule against perpetuity under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the option to renew a lease every ten years constitutes a transfer of property under Section 14 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the renewal clause in the lease offends the rule against perpetuity
Whether a covenant for perpetual renewal creates an interest in property that falls within the ambit of Section 14
holdings: Section 14 applies only to transfers of property, and the renewal clause does not amount to a transfer of property or any interest therein.
The option to renew the lease does not create an interest in property that would violate the rule against perpetuity under Section 14.
A covenant for renewal, even if it runs with the land, does not create an interest in property under Indian law and thus is not subject to the rule against perpetuity.
doctrines: Rule against perpetuity
Covenant running with the land
Transfer of property as defined under the Transfer of Property Act
Distinction between personal covenant and interest in property

card.dispute: The appellants, transferees of leasehold rights in an abolished impartible estate, challenged the Board of Revenue's calculation of compensation and denial of interest on rents collected by the government.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to rents assessed under ryotwari settlement or only to rents reduced under the Madras Rent Reduction Act
Whether Rule 1(ii) under the Abolition Act was valid and consistent with Section 20(2) in computing compensation
Whether cesses paid by lessees could be deducted in determining net annual income for compensation
Whether the appellants were entitled to interest on rents collected by the government but not paid to them
holdings: Appellants were entitled only to rents collected under the Madras Rent Reduction Act, not to higher ryotwari land revenue, which was a separate liability between the government and tenants.
Rule 1(ii) is valid and not repugnant to Section 20(2) of the Abolition Act, as it permissibly limits compensation to 20 times net annual income or the unexpired lease period, whichever is less.
Cesses payable by lessees must be deducted from gross rent to determine net annual income, as 'rent' under the lease and relevant statutes includes such cesses.
Appellants are entitled to 6% interest on unpaid rents collected by the government, based on equitable principles and Section 55 of the Abolition Act, despite no express statutory provision.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 20(2), Section 22, Section 23, Section 55
Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Repugnancy between statutory rules and parent Act
Equitable entitlement to interest in absence of statutory provision
Interpretation of 'rent' to include cesses and local taxes
Compensation based on net annual income and unexpired lease period

card.dispute: The Raja Bahadur Kamakhya Narain Singh fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether profits from sales of gold and shares were taxable as revenue receipts or non-taxable capital receipts.
issues_decided: Whether the profit from the sale of gold purchased in 1940 was a revenue receipt taxable as business income or a capital receipt exempt from tax
Whether the sale of shares, including Karanpura Development Co. Ltd., resulted in taxable revenue or non-taxable capital gains
Whether the High Court could interfere with the Tribunal's findings on the nature of transactions when those findings involved mixed questions of fact and law
holdings: Profit from the sale of gold held for nearly four years and sold only after war conditions improved was a capital receipt, not taxable as business income, because the conduct showed investment, not trading.

Profits from share sales, particularly those aimed at gaining control of a company, are capital receipts if the intention was not to trade but to restructure investments, and thus not taxable as revenue.
The High Court erred in treating mixed questions of fact and law as pure questions of fact; it has the jurisdiction to review and interfere with such findings in reference proceedings.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Mixed question of fact and law doctrine
Intention of the assessee in determining nature of receipt
High Court's jurisdiction in reference under Section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act

card.dispute: The appellant buyer sued the State and the Jagirdar for compensation after being prevented from cutting and removing timber under a sale contract, following the vesting of the Jagirdar's estate in the State.
issues_decided: Whether the property in the timber passed to the buyer before the trees were cut and severed from the land under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930
Whether the buyer could claim compensation for logs not cut due to the vesting of the estate in the State
Whether the contract created an enforceable right against the State after vesting under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Property Rights Act, 1950
holdings: Under Section 18 of the Sale of Goods Act, property in unsevered standing trees does not pass to the buyer until they are cut and appropriated to the contract; since severance had not occurred before vesting, no property passed.
The buyer had no right to cut the timber after the estate vested in the State, as the contract was for future goods not in a deliverable state, and no proprietary interest had transferred.
The State was not liable for breach of contract as the agreement created only a personal obligation on the Jagirdar, which did not bind the State upon vesting of the estate.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Property Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Property Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Property Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 6(2)
doctrines: Rule of property passage in goods attached to land
Distinction between proprietary rights and personal contractual rights
Non-enforceability of unregistered contracts affecting immovable property
Doctrine of state immunity in respect of pre-vesting private contracts

card.dispute: The appellant claimed that the respondents unlawfully trespassed on land he had recently obtained possession of, while the respondents argued they could not be convicted under IPC Sections 441/447 because the appellant was not present at the time of trespass.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was in actual possession of the land at the time of the respondents' trespass
Whether the respondents intended to annoy the appellant within the meaning of Section 441 IPC
Whether the complainant must be physically present at the time of trespass to constitute the offence under Sections 441/447 IPC
holdings: The appellant was in actual possession of the land even though it was vacant, as he had lawfully obtained physical possession through court execution.
The respondents' act of trespassing and starting construction two weeks after eviction demonstrated a clear intention to annoy the appellant, with no other dominant motive evident.
The law does not require the person intended to be annoyed to be physically present at the time of trespass for the offence under Sections 441/447 IPC to be made out.
doctrines: Intention to annoy under Section 441 IPC must be the dominant aim, not merely a likely consequence
Actual possession suffices for trespass; physical presence at the time of entry is not required

card.dispute: The dispute was between the brothers and sister of a deceased Hindu man over whether the brothers inherited his property in preference to the sister when it passed through his widow.
issues_decided: Whether, under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, brothers take precedence over sisters in Class II, Entry II of the Schedule when inheriting a Hindu male's property.
Whether the use of Arabic numerals (3) and (4) before 'brother' and 'sister' in Class II, Entry II indicates a hierarchy of succession.
holdings: The court held that heirs within the same entry of Class II, including brother and sister, inherit simultaneously and equally, with no preference based on Arabic numerals.

The use of Arabic numerals in the Schedule does not create separate entries or indicate order of succession; such an interpretation would contradict the equal treatment of male and female heirs under the Act.
doctrines: Equal treatment of male and female heirs in inheritance
Statutory interpretation based on scheme and context, not mere numbering

card.dispute: The appellant, Seth Badri Prasad, challenged whether Srimati Kanso Devi, as a widow, held the disputed property as a full owner or only as a limited owner under a widow's estate, seeking to restrain her from alienating it.
issues_decided: Whether Smt. Kanso Devi became a full owner of the property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, despite the award specifying a widow's estate.
Whether the exception in Section 14(2) applies to property received by a widow through partition under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937.
holdings: A female Hindu who possessed property at the time of the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, becomes a full owner under Section 14(1), regardless of prior limited interest.
Section 14(2) does not apply where the female had a pre-existing right to the property; it only excludes cases where the property is acquired afresh under a restrictive instrument, will, or decree.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (Act XVIII of 1937), Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act
Exception for restricted estates under Section 14(2)
Preservation of pre-existing rights in partitioned property

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's decision to entertain a writ petition under Articles 226 & 227 after a revision petition under Section 115 CPC had already been dismissed, challenging the same appellate order in a tenancy dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can entertain a petition under Articles 226 and 227 after a revision petition under Section 115 CPC has been dismissed against the same order.
Whether the order of the appellate court merges into the revisional order of the High Court when a revision petition is dismissed.
holdings: The High Court cannot entertain a writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 when a revision petition under Section 115 CPC against the same order has already been dismissed, as it leads to conflicting decisions and abuse of process.

The order of a subordinate court merges into the order of the High Court when the High Court exercises its revisional jurisdiction, and even if no merger occurs, the High Court should not allow parallel proceedings on the same order after one remedy is exhausted.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Merger of judicial orders
Finality of revisional orders
Abuse of process
Superior court's appellate jurisdiction encompassing revisional powers

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land originally allotted to a displaced person, challenged the High Court's decision restoring that allotment after it was cancelled by the Chief Settlement Commissioner on grounds of alleged fraud in submitting land records.
issues_decided: Whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner had valid grounds to cancel the allotment of land on the basis of alleged fraud in the submission of Khasra-Girdwari entries.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of the Chief Settlement Commissioner under Article 226 of the Constitution.

Whether the satisfaction of the Chief Settlement Commissioner under Section 24(2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, that fraud was committed, could be reviewed by the High Court.
holdings: The Chief Settlement Commissioner can cancel an allotment only if satisfied that it was obtained by fraud, false representation, or concealment of material facts, and this satisfaction must be based on credible evidence.
The High Court has the power under Article 226 to review whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner’s satisfaction was based on proper material and not arbitrarily arrived at.

The order of the Chief Settlement Commissioner was invalid because it was based on no evidence, as the original Khasra-Girdwari records were not available and no reliable proof of forgery was presented.
doctrines: Judicial review of quasi-judicial orders
Requirement of evidence for jurisdictional facts
Principle of non-arbitrariness in administrative action

card.dispute: The sons of Meda (appellants) challenged the maintainability of a suit for redemption of a mortgage by the plaintiffs, claiming it was barred by limitation after their earlier application under the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act was rejected.
