issues_decided: Whether the order of the Assistant Collector rejecting the petition under Section 4 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act 2 of 1913 was final and conclusive under Section 12 of the Act.
Whether the suit for redemption was barred by Article 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908, due to failure to file within one year of the rejection of the petition.
holdings: An order by the Assistant Collector rejecting a petition for redemption on the ground that the matter involves complicated questions of fact and law, and directing the parties to approach the civil court, does not constitute a final order under Section 12 of the Act and does not bar a subsequent suit for redemption.

Article 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908, applies only to suits seeking to set aside an order of a government officer; it does not apply where the order merely refers the parties to civil court without deciding any substantive right, and thus the suit for redemption was not time-barred.
provisions: Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act 2 of 1913, Section 4
Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act 2 of 1913, Section 9
Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act 2 of 1913, Section 12
doctrines: Substance over form
Finality of administrative orders
Maintainability of civil suits after administrative rejection

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land and constructed buildings after a land acquisition notification, challenged the validity of the acquisition proceedings on grounds of inadequate notice and denial of opportunity to be heard, which the High Court dismissed in limine.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition in limine on the ground that it involved disputed questions of fact?
Whether the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act was valid and provided sufficient notice to landowners?
Whether purchasers of land after a Section 4 notification could challenge the validity of the acquisition proceedings?
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction under Article 226 to decide both questions of law and fact; dismissal in limine is only justified if the petition is frivolous or unmaintainable, which was not the case here.

A notification under Section 4 must provide sufficient information to landowners; failure to publish plans or clearly indicate the land intended for acquisition renders the proceedings potentially invalid.

Purchasers of land after a Section 4 notification can challenge the validity of acquisition if the notification was vague or did not clearly include their land, especially when they have made substantial investments.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Judicial review of administrative action
Validity of statutory notice in acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants (Sitabai and her adopted son) fought with the respondent (Ram Chandra, the illegitimate son of Sitabai and the deceased coparcener) over possession and rights in joint family property after the death of the last male coparcener.
issues_decided: Whether joint family property loses its character when only one coparcener survives but a widow of a deceased coparcener is still alive.
Whether a child adopted by a widow becomes a coparcener in her deceased husband’s joint family.
Whether the tenancy rights of an ordinary tenant under the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950 are heritable in the absence of express statutory provision.
holdings: Joint family property retains its character in the hands of the surviving coparcener if the widow of a deceased coparcener is alive and entitled to maintenance from the estate.
A child adopted by a widow becomes the adopted child of both the widow and her deceased husband, thereby becoming a coparcener in the joint family.
In the absence of a statutory bar, the heritability of an ordinary tenant’s rights is governed by personal law, and such rights can be inherited under Hindu law.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Sections 11, 12, 14
Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950, Sections 86, 87, 89
doctrines: Continuation of joint family property despite sole surviving coparcener
Legal fiction of adoption creating ties with deceased husband
Heritability of tenancy rights under personal law in absence of statutory prohibition

card.dispute: The State of Bihar appealed against the acquittal of Mathu Pandey and others, who were accused of murdering two men while preventing them from collecting mahua fruits from disputed land.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents were part of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC while preventing theft of mahua fruits from land they possessed
Whether the respondents could be held constructively liable for murder under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC
Whether the respondents had the right to private defence of property under Section 103 IPC, including causing death
Whether the respondents could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC for common intention to commit murder
holdings: An assembly asserting a right of private defence within legal limits cannot be deemed unlawful under Section 141 IPC, even if force is used to protect property.
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC does not arise if the murder was not in prosecution of the common object or was beyond what was contemplated by the assembly.
The right of private defence of property extends to causing death under Section 103 IPC if theft is accompanied by circumstances reasonably causing apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
Conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 requires proof of common intention to murder, which was not established in this case.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Constructive liability under unlawful assembly
Common intention
Limits of self-help in criminal law

card.dispute: The mortgagees sought to execute a mortgage decree against Bakasht land after the entire mortgaged estate had vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, and the mortgagors resisted execution, claiming it was barred by law.
issues_decided: Whether the objection to execution was barred by res judicata due to earlier dismissal of similar objections for default.
Whether execution of a mortgage decree is permissible against land that has vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the remedy of the mortgagee is confined to claiming compensation under Chapter IV of the Bihar Land Reforms Act.
holdings: An objection is not barred by res judicata if it was not heard and decided on merits; mere dismissal for default does not constitute a decision on the issue.
When an entire mortgaged estate vests in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, execution of a mortgage decree against such estate is barred under Section 4(d) of the Act.

The mortgagee’s sole remedy is to claim compensation under Section 14 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, and no civil court or execution proceeding can lie for recovery of money secured by a mortgage on vested estate.
doctrines: Res judicata
Statutory bar to civil jurisdiction
Exhaustion of statutory remedy
Vesting of property free of encumbrances

card.dispute: The plaintiffs (mortgagors) fought the mortgagee's sons over whether a civil suit for redemption of a mortgage was time-barred after an earlier application under the Punjab Redemption of Mortgages Act was rejected by the Assistant Collector.
issues_decided: Whether the Assistant Collector's rejection of the redemption application under s. 4 of the Punjab Act amounted to a final order under s. 9 requiring a suit to be filed within one year under Art. 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the subsequent civil suit for redemption was barred by limitation
holdings: An order by the Assistant Collector rejecting a redemption application on the ground that it involves complicated questions of fact and law does not constitute a final adjudication under s. 9 of the Punjab Act and thus does not trigger the one-year limitation under Art. 14 of the Limitation Act.

A civil suit for redemption is not barred by limitation when the earlier application was not decided on merits but was dismissed merely because the matter required a full trial, as such an order does not affect the mortgagor’s right to sue in a civil court.
provisions: Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab Act 2 of 1913), Section 4
Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab Act 2 of 1913), Section 9
Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab Act 2 of 1913), Section 12
doctrines: Substance over form in judicial orders
Finality of administrative orders under special statutes
Maintainability of civil suits after summary proceedings
Limitation bar for setting aside government orders

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondent's right to pre-empt land sold by her mother, arguing she had no such right under the Punjab Pre-emption Act as it stood before the 1964 amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 15(2)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act by the 1964 Amendment Act has retrospective operation
Whether the respondent, as the daughter of a female vendor who inherited property from her husband, had a right of pre-emption even before the 1964 amendment
holdings: The 1964 amendment to the Punjab Pre-emption Act is clarificatory and declaratory, and therefore must be given retrospective effect to pending proceedings.

The right of pre-emption under Section 15(2)(b) of the Act vests in the son or daughter of the husband of the female vendor, including her children from that husband, and this was the intended meaning even before the 1964 amendment.
provisions: Punjab Pre-emption Amendment Act, 1960, Section 4 and Section 31
doctrines: Retrospective operation of clarificatory or declaratory statutes
Principle of consanguinity in pre-emption rights
Interpretation of statutes to reflect legislative intent and scheme

card.dispute: The landlord (Shri Vidya Prachar Trust) sought eviction of the tenant (Pandit Basant Ram) for non-payment of rent, while the tenant claimed that depositing rent in court under the Relief of Indebtedness Act constituted valid tender.
issues_decided: Whether a deposit made by a tenant under Section 31 of the East Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934 amounts to a valid tender of rent under Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether such a deposit can save a tenant from eviction for default in rent payment.
holdings: A deposit under Section 31 of the Relief of Indebtedness Act does not constitute a valid tender of rent under the Urban Rent Restriction Act, as the former is meant for debtor-creditor relationships involving interest, not landlord-tenant relations.

The tenant remains in default for eviction purposes unless rent is paid or tendered directly in accordance with the procedure under Section 13 of the Rent Restriction Act, including before the Rent Controller on first hearing.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 19 read with Section 6
East Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, Section 31
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory provisions for rent payment and eviction
Contextual interpretation of 'any person who owes money' based on the overall scheme of the Act
Deposit in court as a mechanism to stop interest applies only in debtor-creditor contexts with interest obligations

card.dispute: The State of Assam challenged the High Court's decision quashing best judgment assessments made under the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act for failure to file returns, where no individual notices under Section 19(2) or proceedings under Section 30 were issued.
issues_decided: Whether assessment proceedings can commence solely with a general notice under Section 19(1) of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act without individual notice under Section 19(2)?
Whether a best judgment assessment under Section 20(4) can be made beyond three years of the financial year without initiating proceedings under Section 30?
Whether issuance of notice under Section 30 is mandatory when no return is filed and no assessment was initiated during the relevant year?
holdings: Assessment proceedings under the Act do not commence merely with a general notice under Section 19(1); they require either an individual notice under Section 19(2) or initiation under Section 30.
A best judgment assessment under Section 20(4) cannot be made after the expiry of three years from the financial year unless valid proceedings under Section 30 are initiated.

Where no return is filed and no assessment occurs during the relevant year, income is considered 'escaped assessment' under Section 30, and proceedings under that section are necessary for valid reassessment.
doctrines: Escaped assessment doctrine
Principle of statutory notice in tax assessment
Best judgment assessment limitations

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the state government's notification reducing rent rates for ryoti land in Kalipatnam village, arguing that the classification of land as 'delta dry' was based solely on an irrelevant settlement register entry from another village.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of land under the Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act could be based solely on a settlement register entry from a different village without factual inquiry
Whether the Special Officer fulfilled the statutory obligation under Section 2 of the Act to determine rent based on relevant material
Whether the exclusion of civil court jurisdiction under Section 8(1) applies when the order is made without any evidentiary basis
holdings: Classification of land must be based on relevant and factual material specific to the village; reliance on a settlement register from another village is legally insufficient.
A determination made without relevant evidence violates fundamental principles of judicial procedure and is void.
Section 8(1), which bars civil court jurisdiction, does not apply when the government order is ultra vires and based on no evidence.
provisions: Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 2
Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 3(2)
Madras Estates Land (Reduction of Rent) Act, 1947, Section 8(1)
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Principle of judicial review
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction not automatic when statutory conditions are not met

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a sale of Patel-ki-Watan inam land to the respondent's father and whether the suit for possession was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the alienation of Patel-ki-Watan inam land in favor of the respondent's father was void under the applicable Wat Hukums and the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act (III of 1874)
Whether the suit for recovery of possession was barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act
holdings: Alienation of Patel-ki-Watan inam land was void as specific Wat Hukums of the Kolhapur State prohibited such transfers, and the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act did not override these binding local laws.
The suit was not barred by limitation because Article 142 does not apply when the defendant did not dispossess the plaintiff but is merely in wrongful possession.
provisions: Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874 (Act III of 1874), Section 5
doctrines: Primogeniture in succession to impartible inams
Specific local laws (Wat Hukums) prevail over general statutory provisions applied 'in spirit'
Doctrine of non-applicability of Article 142 where there is no dispossession by the defendant

card.dispute: The appellant, claiming to be the adopted son of Lakshmibai, fought with the respondent, who claimed to be the sister's son of Veerbaswantji Rao Deshmukh, over possession of certain properties previously decreed to Lakshmibai and later transferred via execution and compromise.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff's subsequent suit for possession based on title was barred by Order 2, Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to a prior suit for impleadment in execution proceedings.
Whether the cause of action in the earlier suit for declaration of right to be impleaded was the same as in the later suit for possession based on title.
holdings: Order 2, Rule 2, CPC bars a plaintiff from splitting a cause of action, but only when the same cause of action underlies both suits; here, the prior suit was based on execution rights, while the later suit was based on title, so no bar applies.

A cause of action is the foundation of the suit; since the earlier suit did not enable the plaintiff to claim possession based on title, the later suit is not barred for non-joinder of claims under Order 2, Rule 2, CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2, Rule 2
doctrines: Cause of action estoppel
Rule against splitting of causes of action
Maintainability of successive suits on different causes of action

card.dispute: The State of Haryana and the Rohtak Improvement Trust reconstituted by it fought against rate-payers who challenged the legality of the Trust's reconstitution after the municipal committee was reconstituted.
issues_decided: Whether the Rohtak Improvement Trust could be initially set up in 1958 when the Municipal Committee was superseded?
Whether the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, ceased to apply upon reconstitution of the Municipal Committee, requiring re-notification?
Whether the Government had the power to reconstitute the Improvement Trust after its dissolution under Section 103 of the Act?
holdings: The Trust could be validly created in 1958 despite the Municipal Committee being superseded, as Section 4A allowed the Government to appoint trustees during supersession, and the Administrator had the power to oppose the Act's application.
Once the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, was applied to a municipality, it continues to apply even after reconstitution of the Municipal Committee; no fresh notification is required.
The Government has the power under Sections 3 and 4 of the Act, read with Section 12 of the General Clauses (Punjab) Act, 1898, to reconstitute a dissolved Improvement Trust when necessary.
doctrines: Doctrine of Continued Operation of Statute
Doctrine of Necessary Implication
Doctrine of Plenary Power under Enabling Statutes

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat challenged the Commissioner's order setting aside the Collector's permission granted to Patel Raghav Natha to convert agricultural land into a non-agricultural building site.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner could exercise revisional powers under Section 211 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code after more than a year from the Collector's order granting permission under Section 65.
Whether the Commissioner was required to record reasons while setting aside the Collector's order.
Whether the Commissioner could decide questions of title to land in exercise of revisional powers under Section 211.
holdings: The Commissioner must exercise revisional powers under Section 211 within a reasonable time, which in cases involving building permissions should be within a few months of the Collector's order; a delay of over a year was unreasonable.
The Commissioner is required to record at least brief reasons when setting aside an order under Section 211 to enable effective judicial review and to inform the aggrieved party.
The Commissioner should not decide disputed questions of title in revision; such issues must be referred to a civil court.
doctrines: Principle of reasonable time for administrative action
Doctrine of reasoned decisions in administrative law
Rule against administrative determination of title disputes

card.dispute: The State of U.P. contested whether a Gujaranama deed executed by the Raja of an impartible estate in favor of his brother constituted a gift or sale under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, thereby affecting the brother's entitlement to a rehabilitation grant.
issues_decided: Whether the Gujaranama deed amounted to a transfer by way of gift or sale within the meaning of Section 23(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the respondent was entitled to a rehabilitation grant under Section 79 of the Act
Whether procedural irregularities before the Rehabilitation Grants Officer warranted remanding the case
holdings: A transfer from an impartible estate to a younger brother in lieu of his customary right to maintenance is not a gift or sale under Section 23(1) of the Act and thus remains valid for rehabilitation grant purposes.
The respondent, as a member of the joint family entitled to maintenance from the impartible estate, was eligible for a rehabilitation grant under Section 79 of the Act.
No remand is required for procedural irregularities where no disputed questions of fact were raised and the challenge was purely on a question of law.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 23(1)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 79
doctrines: Joint family property doctrine in relation to impartible estates
Right of maintenance as a joint family right in impartible estates
Doctrine of survivorship in Hindu joint family law
Principle of spes successionis distinguished from enforceable rights

card.dispute: The State of U.P. contested the adequacy of court fees paid in a suit seeking a declaration of ownership over property, claiming it fell under a higher fee category involving cancellation of a decree.
issues_decided: Whether the suit fell within the scope of Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as amended by the U.P. Legislature, requiring court fee based on the value of the property?
Whether a decree for a mere declaration of title constitutes a 'decree for money or other property' under Section 7(iv-A)?
Whether a decree can be considered an 'instrument securing money or other property' within the meaning of Section 7(iv-A)?
holdings: A suit for a mere declaration of title to property does not fall under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as it does not seek recovery of money or property.
The phrase 'decree for money or other property' means a decree for recovery, not one merely concerning or declaring title to property.
A decree, including a consent decree, is not an 'instrument securing money or other property' unless it records a contract with that effect; a mere decree does not secure property by itself.
provisions: Court Fees Act, 1870, Schedule II, Clause 17(iii)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Substance over form in determining the nature of a suit
Judicial concern against frivolous procedural delays

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh fought with Mahant Kamal Puri over the right to manage the Basaiya Mata shrine and its properties, originally taken over by the Gwalior State in 1932 and 1939.
issues_decided: Whether the orders of 1932 and 1939 by the Gwalior State extinguished the Mahant's title to manage the shrine
Whether the State could retain management of the shrine after the Constitution came into force without statutory authority
Whether the suit for restoration of management was barred by adverse possession
holdings: The orders of 1932 and 1939 were administrative and temporary, not intended to extinguish the Mahant’s title as shebait.
After the Constitution, the State cannot retain management of religious property without lawful statutory authority, especially when the Mahant's title remains intact.
Possession by the State was not adverse to the Mahant’s rights, so the suit was not barred by limitation or adverse possession.
provisions: Gwalior State Places of Worship and Religious Endowments Aid and Administration Act, 1930, Section 30
doctrines: Doctrine of temporary administrative takeover
Preservation of private religious management rights post-constitutionalism
No adverse possession by government in custodial management

card.dispute: The appellants (Sukhram Singh and another) challenged the respondent's (Smt. Harbheji) right to lease land based on her husband's physical infirmity, and whether a prior order declaring them Adhivasis was final.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 157(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, introduced by Act 20 of 1954, applies retrospectively despite lack of express retrospective language
Whether the order passed by the Compensation Officer on October 25, 1956, finally determined the appellants' status as Adhivasis, thereby barring re-litigation
holdings: Section 157(1)(a), though not expressly made retrospective, must be read as having retrospective effect because the amendment to Section 21(h) was made retrospective and both amendments were part of a cohesive legislative scheme.

The order of the Compensation Officer on October 25, 1956, lacked finality because he failed to frame an issue and refer it to the competent court as required by Section 240H, and thus could not conclusively determine the appellants' status.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 21
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 157
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 240(F)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 240(G)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 240(H)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 229B
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 234A
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutes implied from context and legislative intent
Presumption against retrospectivity rebutted by cohesive legislative scheme
Finality of administrative orders dependent on compliance with statutory procedure

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh fought with lessee Satya Narain Prasad over whether a notice to terminate his ferry lease, issued by an Executive Engineer, was valid under the Northern India Ferries Act, 1878.
issues_decided: Whether the notice dated July 22, 1953, issued by the Executive Engineer, complied with Section 10 of the Northern India Ferries Act, 1878.
Whether the respondent was required to plead all legal grounds challenging the notice's validity in the plaint.
holdings: A notice under Section 10 must clearly convey the State Government’s intention to cancel the lease and must be issued by the Government or an officer duly authorised; a notice by a mere officer without proof of authority is invalid.
It is not necessary for a plaintiff to state every legal ground for challenging a notice’s validity in the plaint; a general challenge suffices.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory notice
Doctrine of governmental authority and delegation

card.dispute: The State of Punjab fought with Sardar Sewa Singh Gill and others over possession of land granted for a ghee factory after the company was wound up.
issues_decided: Whether the land granted to the company reverted to the State upon winding up of the company
Whether the notice given by the Director of Industries on August 14, 1952, was valid under the fourth proviso to clause 6(a) of the Agreement
Whether the company could retain possession of the land after its winding up without a valid notice for removal of machinery
holdings: The land granted to the company reverted to the State upon the winding-up order, as per the third proviso to clause 6(a) of the Agreement.
The notice dated August 14, 1952, given to the provisional liquidators was valid and satisfied the requirements of the fourth proviso to clause 6(a).
The company had no right to retain possession after reversion of title to the State; possession must be handed over within six months from the date of this judgment.
provisions: Agreement between Patiala State and Promoters, clause 6(a) with third and fourth provisos
doctrines: Doctrine of reversion of property upon termination of conditional grant
Doctrine of valid notice under contractual terms

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Sub-Divisional Officer, Mandla and Pirma Gond over whether a tank had vested in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950 or under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, and whether the subsequent lease of the tank by revenue authorities was valid.
issues_decided: Whether the tank in question had already vested in the State under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, thereby excluding its vesting under Section 251(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959.
Whether the proprietor was afforded a proper opportunity of hearing under Section 251(1) of the Revenue Code before the vesting order was passed.
holdings: The tank vested in the State under the Abolition Act, 1950, and could not vest again under Section 251(1) of the Revenue Code, as that section applies only to tanks not already vested in the State.
The failure to provide a proper opportunity of hearing under Section 251(1) of the Revenue Code invalidated the vesting proceedings, and the High Court's factual finding on this point was binding.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 5(g)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 251(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Principle of harmonious construction
Rule of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment of the tenant on grounds of arrears of rent and personal necessity, but the tenant argued the first notice was waived by the landlord's subsequent conduct.
issues_decided: Whether the first notice terminating tenancy for arrears of rent was waived by the landlord's issuance of a second notice and other conduct
Whether the court was bound to decree eviction under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act due to non-payment of arrears after the first notice
Whether the second notice could be treated as ineffective or non-est so as to revive reliance on the first notice
holdings: A notice terminating tenancy is waived if the landlord performs an act showing intention to treat the lease as subsisting, with the tenant's express or implied consent.
Serving a second notice to quit, describing the tenant as a monthly tenant and claiming rent up to a later date, constitutes implied waiver of the first notice.
The landlord cannot selectively rely on the first notice after affirming the tenancy's continuation through subsequent acts and a second notice.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
doctrines: Waiver of notice under Section 113 of the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of implied consent and conduct negating termination of tenancy

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and landholders disputed whether Chapter IV of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960, which set ceiling limits on landholdings, was 'in force' when determining compensation for compulsory acquisition under Article 31-A of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Chapter IV of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960, though not brought into force by notification, constituted a 'law in force' under Article 31-A, proviso 2 of the Constitution.

Whether the amendment to the Act in 1965, which provided for compensation at less than market value, violated the proviso to Article 31-A due to compulsory acquisition of land within the ceiling limit.
holdings: A law is not 'in force' merely by enactment if it requires notification for operation and such notification has not been issued; operational status depends on actual enforcement, not constitutional existence.

The proviso to Article 31-A, which guarantees market value compensation, does not apply where no ceiling limit was in force at the time of acquisition, as the repealed Chapter IV was never operational.
doctrines: Doctrine of 'law in force'
Doctrine of prospective operation of statutes
Principle of constitutional validity of compensation in land acquisition

card.dispute: Landowners in Parbhani District challenged the constitutional validity of a state law that transferred ownership of their land to tenants under tenancy reform legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Act of 1961, which re-enacted and validated earlier tenancy laws with retrospective effect, is protected from constitutional challenge under Articles 19 and 31?
Whether the original Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, as amended, was invalid for lack of presidential assent under Article 31(3)?
holdings: The Maharashtra Act of 1961, being included in the Ninth Schedule via the Seventeenth Amendment, is immune from challenges based on violation of fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31.

The failure to obtain prior presidential assent for the parent Hyderabad Act does not invalidate it, especially since subsequent amending acts received presidential assent, implying approval of the parent regime.
provisions: Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950 (Act XXI of 1950)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1954 (Act III of 1954)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Re-enactment, Validation and further Amendment) Act, 1961
doctrines: Doctrine of curative legislation
Doctrine of implied validation
Doctrine of protection under Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of presumed presidential assent

card.dispute: The assessee (a Hindu undivided family) contested the validity of reassessment proceedings and the classification of a payment of Rs. 1,15,000 as capital rather than revenue expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the Income-tax Officer could validly initiate reassessment under Section 34(1)(b) of the Income-tax Act based on a subsequent judicial decision clarifying the correct legal position?
Whether the payment of Rs. 1,15,000 to the vendor's sons to release their claim to the spinning mill was a capital or revenue expenditure?
holdings: A judicial decision clarifying the true state of law constitutes 'information' under Section 34(1)(b), enabling valid reassessment even if prior assessment was made in good faith but on incorrect legal understanding.

A lump sum payment made to remove a cloud on title to a capital asset is capital expenditure, even if part of the claim relates to profits, and no apportionment between capital and revenue is permissible.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice of law
Capital vs revenue expenditure distinction
Enduring benefit test for capital expenditure

card.dispute: The tenant (appellant) sought summary eviction of the landlord (respondent) under s. 84 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act after voluntarily surrendering possession, but without compliance with statutory procedures.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can invoke s. 84 for summary eviction when an alternative remedy under s. 29(1) is available?
Whether s. 84 applies where possession was handed over to the landlord through an invalid surrender?
Whether the Collector has jurisdiction under s. 84 to entertain a tenant's application when the dispute arises from tenancy rights under the Act?
holdings: A tenant cannot invoke s. 84 for restoration of possession if the claim is based on tenancy rights under the Act; the remedy lies under s. 29(1).
Where a surrender is invalid due to non-compliance with s. 15, tenancy continues and the landlord’s possession is not lawful, but the proper remedy remains under s. 29(1), not s. 84.
Section 84 applies only when the tenant claims possession on his own title as a tenant against a wrongful occupant, not when asserting rights under the Act, which would render s. 74 superfluous.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 15
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70(clause n)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 74
doctrines: Doctrine of alternative remedies
Doctrine of statutory interpretation to avoid redundancy
Doctrine of continued tenancy despite voluntary surrender without legal formalities

card.dispute: The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family governed by Marumakkattayam law, challenged the constitutional validity of the Expenditure-tax Act, 1957, arguing that its application to Hindu families but not to Mappilla families under the same customary law violated Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3(1) of the Expenditure-tax Act, 1957, which treats Hindu undivided families as a taxable unit, violates Article 14 by excluding Mappilla families governed by the Marumakkattayam law from similar treatment?
Whether the classification between Hindu and Mappilla families for taxation purposes is arbitrary and discriminatory?
holdings: The classification under the Expenditure-tax Act is valid as it is based on reasonable differentia and does not violate Article 14, since the legislature has wide discretion in designing tax systems.

The exclusion of Mappilla families from the definition of 'Hindu undivided family' for taxation is not arbitrary, given their small numbers, regional concentration, and distinct social characteristics, and thus does not amount to impermissible discrimination.
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonable classification
Legislative discretion in taxation
Equality before law under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Settlement Commissioner's reduction of his verified claim for property lost in West Pakistan, arguing that the revisional authority lacked jurisdiction and acted on errors of law.
issues_decided: Whether the Settlement Commissioner had jurisdiction to revise an order passed by the Claims Commissioner under the 1950 Act while exercising powers under the 1954 Supplementary Act
Whether the revisional power under Section 5(1)(b) of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954 extends to valuation of claims

Whether Rule 18 of the Displaced Persons (Verification of Claims) Supplementary Rules, 1954 must be construed ejusdem generis, thereby limiting the scope of 'any other sufficient reason' in clause (iv)
Whether the order of the Settlement Commissioner was vitiated by errors of law apparent on the face of the record
holdings: The Settlement Commissioner, acting under the 1954 Supplementary Act, had the jurisdiction to revise orders passed under the 1950 Act, including those made in revision by the Claims Commissioner.
The revisional power under Section 5(1)(b) includes both verification and valuation of claims, as 'verified claim' in the 1954 Act encompasses the final determination including valuation.

Clause (iv) of Rule 18, 'any other sufficient reason,' is not restricted by ejusdem generis to the first three clauses, as the listed grounds do not form a coherent class; even if they did, the grounds used were analogous to clause (iii).
The Settlement Commissioner’s order was based on conjectures and surmises unsupported by evidence, constituting errors of law apparent on the record, warranting its setting aside.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Verification of Claims) Supplementary Rules, 1954, Rule 18
doctrines: Errors of law apparent on the face of the record
Revisional jurisdiction
Ejusdem generis rule of statutory interpretation
Principle of giving effect to all statutory words

card.dispute: The appellant, Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., challenged the validity of the town planning scheme and the valuation decisions made under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, particularly contesting the lack of reasoned order and denial of effective appeal rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Town Planning Officer's decision dated February 24, 1962, was invalid for being a non-speaking order violating principles of natural justice?
Whether the appellant was denied a meaningful right of appeal under Section 34 of the 1954 Act due to non-communication of reasons?
holdings: A decision under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, is not ultra vires merely for being non-speaking if the reasons are available in the final scheme accessible for public inspection.
The right of appeal under Section 34 is not illusory if the party has an opportunity to inspect the final scheme containing the reasons, even if not sent directly.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Doctrine of effective remedy
Doctrine of constructive notice

card.dispute: The Union of India sought to recover the deficiency in price from the respondent, M/s. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram, after the resale of a liquor license, claiming the respondent defaulted on payment after winning the auction.
issues_decided: Whether a binding contract arose upon the respondent's highest bid at the auction, despite non-payment of one-sixth of the annual fee within seven days.
Whether the Chief Commissioner's confirmation under Clause 33 was a condition precedent to a completed sale.
Whether the respondent was liable to pay the deficiency arising from the resale of the license.
holdings: A binding contract is not formed merely by the highest bid; it requires confirmation by the Chief Commissioner as per the conditions of sale.
Clause 33 makes the bid subject to confirmation, rendering the acceptance conditional and not absolute until such confirmation.
The respondent is not liable for the deficiency in resale price because the sale was not confirmed and thus no enforceable obligation arose.
provisions: Delhi Liquor Licence Rules, Rule 5.34, Clauses 21, 22, 16, 18, 31, 33
doctrines: Conditional acceptance in contract law
Requirement of confirmation as a condition precedent
No liability for damages in absence of completed contract

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of a contract to assign a mining lease, claiming acceptance of an offer through a plaint filed in another suit, while the defendant argued no concluded contract existed due to lack of valid acceptance before revocation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint in a prior suit constituted a valid acceptance of the defendant's offer to assign the mining lease.
Whether service of a copy of the plaint amounted to communication of acceptance under the Contract Act.
Whether a concluded contract existed before the offer was revoked.
holdings: A plaint in a suit not for specific performance does not constitute acceptance of an offer to assign a lease.
Service of a plaint through court process is not a valid mode of communicating acceptance under the Contract Act.
No concluded contract arises unless acceptance is communicated before revocation; mere mental assent is insufficient.
doctrines: Communication of acceptance is essential for a binding contract
Acceptance must be communicated in a usual and reasonable manner
Revocation of offer effective before acceptance terminates the power to accept

card.dispute: The tenant (appellant) challenged the landlord's possession of land after an invalid surrender, seeking eviction under Section 84 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, while the landlord claimed the tenant's remedy lay under Section 29(1).
issues_decided: Whether a surrender of tenancy not complying with Section 15 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act is valid and effective to terminate tenancy?
Whether a tenant can invoke Section 84 of the Act to seek summary eviction of a landlord who is in possession after an invalid surrender?
Whether Section 84 and Section 29(1) of the Act provide alternative remedies or are mutually exclusive?
holdings: A surrender of tenancy not made in writing or verified under Section 15 of the Act is invalid and does not terminate the tenancy.
A landlord who takes possession after an invalid surrender is not in 'unauthorised occupation' for the purposes of Section 84 if the possession stems from a statutory process, even if flawed.
Section 84 applies only where there is no other remedy under the Act; if a tenant's right arises under the Act, Section 29(1) is the exclusive remedy, not Section 84.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 15
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 74
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 64
doctrines: Exhaustion of statutory remedies
Statutory interpretation of mutually exclusive remedies
Invalidity of non-compliant statutory surrender

card.dispute: The appellants, bidi manufacturers, challenged the validity of transport restrictions under the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Leaves Trade Regulation Act, arguing that requiring permits for movement of tendu leaves to workers violated their fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the transport restrictions under Section 5(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Leaves Act and Rule 9 violate Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution?
Whether the permit requirement for distribution of tendu leaves to mazdoors (workers) is reasonable?
Whether the impugned restrictions are protected under Article 304(b)?
holdings: The State's monopoly and associated transport restrictions for tendu leaves are valid and reasonable to prevent exploitation of growers and ensure effective implementation of the Act.

A permit system for movement of leaves from purchase point to warehouse, branches, and sattedars is reasonable, but requiring permits for distribution to mazdoors by sattedars is not intended by the law and would be unreasonable.
The restrictions, as read down, are justified under Article 304(b) as they serve public interest and do not discriminate against inter-State trade.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Tendu, Pattu (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 5(2)
Madhya Pradesh Tendu, Pattu (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Rule 9
doctrines: Principle of constitutional construction favoring validity of legislation
Doctrine of reading down statutes to avoid constitutional invalidity
Reasonableness test under Article 19(1)(g)
Balancing of public interest and fundamental rights

card.dispute: The Patna Electric Supply Co. Ltd. fought the Patna Municipal Corporation over whether it had to pay ground rent for electric poles erected on municipal land and whether the dispute had to be resolved under the Indian Telegraph Act.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the electricity licensee and the municipal corporation falls under Section 15 of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885.
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the writ petition on the ground that the remedy under the Indian Telegraph Act was exclusive.
holdings: Section 15 of the Indian Telegraph Act applies only to disputes between a telegraph authority and a local authority, not to an electricity licensee under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910.

The High Court erred in holding that the dispute must be referred to arbitration under Section 15 of the Indian Telegraph Act, as the provisions of that Act are not incorporated by reference into the Indian Electricity Act.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Exclusion of implied incorporation of statutes
Jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226

card.dispute: The shebait of two Hindu deities challenged the validity of income tax assessments imposed on the deities' properties, arguing that a deity cannot be taxed as an 'individual' under the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu deity can be assessed to income tax as an 'individual' under Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether a Hindu deity, being a juristic person, can be taxed through its shebait.
Whether the word 'individual' in Section 3 of the 1922 Act includes artificial juridical persons like a deity.
holdings: A Hindu deity is a juristic entity capable of holding property and can be taxed through its shebait, who manages the deity's estate.
The term 'individual' in Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 includes artificial juridical persons, and thus encompasses a Hindu deity.
The later definition of 'person' in the Income-tax Act, 1961 clarifies that 'individual' includes juridical persons, supporting the interpretation of the earlier Act.
doctrines: Juristic personhood of religious idols
Principle of statutory interpretation using subsequent legislation to resolve ambiguity
Shebait as manager of deity's property for legal and tax purposes

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, claiming ownership of a plot called 'Badi Takia', sued for damages after defendants placed a Tazia on part of the plot; defendants claimed the land was wakf property, giving them the right to use it.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs have title to the Badi Takia plot.
Whether any part of Badi Takia, particularly where the Tazia was placed, is wakf property.
holdings: The plaintiffs and their ancestors have been long-time possessors and managers of Badi Takia, and no evidence established a formal wakf by declaration or will; thus, ownership remains with the plaintiffs.

Mere long user of the mosque within Badi Takia by Muslims does not prove the entire plot or the specific portion where the Tazia was placed is wakf; defendants failed to prove wakf status of that plot.
doctrines: Presumption of wakf by immemorial user
Burden of proof in establishing wakf

card.dispute: The appellants, who were occupants of land leased since 1895, fought against the respondents' attempt to recover possession after consent decrees, claiming protection under rent control laws and challenging the validity of multiple decrees.
issues_decided: Whether the leased land fell within the definition of 'premises' under s. 4(2)(b) of the Bombay Rent Restriction Act, 1939, thereby attracting rent control protections
Whether the consent decree created a new tenancy protected under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the court was legally competent to pass two separate decrees in the same suit
holdings: The lease of land for constructing houses did not make it 'premises' under s. 4(2)(b) of the Bombay Rent Restriction Act, 1939, as the principal purpose was not business or trade.
The consent decree did not create a new tenancy; it merely allowed continued possession for five years with high mesne profits, without establishing landlord-tenant relationship.
The court could pass more than one decree in a suit, especially on compromise or at different stages, under Orders XXIII r. 3 and XII r. 6 of the CPC.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 12, Rule 6
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3
doctrines: Interpretation of 'premises' in rent control statutes
Creation of tenancy by consent decree
Multiple decrees in a single suit

card.dispute: The assessee fought the tax authorities over whether proceeds from selling teak trees—uprooted to make way for rubber plantations—constituted taxable agricultural income or non-taxable capital receipts.
issues_decided: Whether the sale proceeds from teak trees removed with their roots constitute capital receipts or agricultural income.
Whether expenses incurred in earlier years for growing the teak trees are deductible if the sale is treated as income.
holdings: Sale of teak trees removed entirely with their roots, ending any possibility of regeneration, affects the capital structure and results in a capital receipt, not revenue.
The profit motive in planting trees does not convert a capital accretion into taxable income; the nature of the receipt depends on whether the source continues to produce income.
doctrines: Capital vs. revenue receipt distinction
Source theory of income
Profit motive not determinative of revenue receipt

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of an execution proceeding for ejectment against a company in liquidation, arguing that leave under Section 171 of the Companies Act, 1913 was required but not obtained before initiating execution.
issues_decided: Whether leave under Section 171 of the Companies Act, 1913 is a condition precedent to the institution of execution proceedings against a company in liquidation.
Whether the High Court was obligated to certify the appeal under Article 133(1)(b) or (c) of the Constitution given the legal controversy over Section 171.
holdings: Leave under Section 171 is not a condition precedent that renders execution proceedings void ab initio; such proceedings are merely ineffective until leave is granted, and are deemed instituted on the date leave is obtained.
The Supreme Court will not certify an appeal under Article 133(1)(b) or (c) if it agrees with the High Court’s decision on the merits, as certification in such cases would be futile.
doctrines: Condition precedent vs. procedural irregularity
Futility of appeal doctrine
Continuation of suit doctrine (execution as part of original proceeding)

card.dispute: Antu and others were accused of murdering Bakshish Singh and injuring Labh Singh during a land dispute, and the appeal challenged whether the accused were rightly held as aggressors and guilty of murder.
issues_decided: Whether the death of Bakshish Singh and injuries to Labh Singh were caused by members of the appellant's party.
Whether the appellant's party was the aggressor in the incident.
Whether the appellant Antu was guilty of murder beyond reasonable doubt.
holdings: The injuries and death occurred during an incident on 17th July 1967, and were caused by members of the appellant’s group.
The prosecution failed to prove that the appellant’s party was the aggressor, as possession of the land was disputed and the accused had been in prior possession.
The appellant Antu was not proved guilty of murder beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies in the prosecution’s version and disproportionate injuries on the accused side.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt
Aggressor test in self-defence
Evaluation of possession in land disputes
Corroboration of oral testimony with material evidence

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Bhagwan Das (appellants) fought against Chet Ram (respondent) over whether a tenant evicted before filing a pre-emption suit could still claim the right to pre-empt the sale of land.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant who was dispossessed and whose tenancy was terminated before filing a suit for pre-emption could maintain the suit under Section 15(1)(a) Fourthly of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913.
Whether the right to pre-emption under the said provision requires the tenant to remain in tenancy up to the date of the decree.
holdings: A tenant must maintain his tenancy status up to the date of the decree in a pre-emption suit; if his tenancy is terminated before or during the suit, he loses the right to pre-empt.
The statutory right of pre-emption under Section 15(1)(a) Fourthly is attached to the land and not merely personal, so the tenant must hold the land as a tenant continuously until the decree.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A(i) read with Section 9(1)
doctrines: Continuity of qualification doctrine in pre-emption
Pre-emptor must maintain superior right until decree
Statutory right attaching to land, not personal right

card.dispute: The appellants, a father and son, challenged the deemed purchase of their land by tenants under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, claiming protection under Section 32F(1)(a) due to the son's minority at the time of partition.
issues_decided: Whether a partial partition of joint family property qualifies for the benefit of Section 32F(1)(a) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948?
Whether the second appellant was entitled to the protection under Section 32F(1)(a) given the share he received in the partition?
holdings: Section 32F(1)(a) requires a complete partition of joint family property; a partial partition does not qualify for its protection.

The second appellant was not entitled to the benefit of Section 32F(1)(a) because he received a 1/5th share despite being entitled only to a 1/6th share, and the mother's rightful share was not accounted for.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 31
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32F(1)(a)
doctrines: Finality of findings by tribunal as the ultimate fact-finding authority
Strict compliance with statutory conditions for claiming protection under tenancy laws

card.dispute: The Bombay Municipal Corporation and the Life Insurance Corporation of India disputed whether the educational cess recovered by a landlord from tenants under the Rent Act could be included in the annual rent for determining the rateable value of a building under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act.
issues_decided: Whether the permitted increase in rent under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947 (due to educational cess) forms part of the annual rent for fixation of rateable value under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888
Whether such increase, though not deemed an increase in rent under Section 7 of the Rent Act, can still be considered in computing the annual rent reasonably expected to be received
holdings: The permitted increase in rent under Sections 10, 10A, and 10AA of the Rent Act is part of the rent the landlord is entitled to receive and must be included in the annual rent for determining rateable value under Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888.
Section 7 of the Rent Act prohibits charging rent above standard rent but does not bar inclusion of statutorily permitted increases in the actual or expected rent for municipal valuation purposes.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 5(7)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 5(10)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 7
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 10
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 10A
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Act, 1947, Section 10AA
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of rent under municipal and rent control laws
Inclusion of permitted increases in rent for rateable value determination
Distinction between rent control restrictions and municipal valuation criteria

card.dispute: The dispute was between Century Spinning & Manufacturing Company and the Ulhasnagar Municipal Council over whether the municipality could lawfully levy octroi duty on the company after having allegedly given an assurance not to do so for seven years.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition in limine without considering its merits.
Whether a public body can be held to an undertaking or representation made to a citizen on which the citizen has relied to their detriment.
Whether the representation by the municipality not to levy octroi could create an enforceable obligation despite the absence of a formal contract.
holdings: The High Court must not dismiss a writ petition under Article 226 in limine without valid reason, especially when the petition raises a prima facie case of unjust or arbitrary action by a public authority.
A public body is bound by representations or promises made to citizens if those citizens have altered their position in reliance on them, even if no formal contract exists.

Where a statute requires a specific form for a contract with a public body, the obligation arising from a representation may still be enforced in equity if a citizen has suffered prejudice by acting upon it.
doctrines: Promissory estoppel against public authorities
Equitable enforcement of representations by public bodies
Judicial discretion in writ jurisdiction under Article 226

card.dispute: The appellant Jagirdar contested whether interest received on delayed payment of compensation for abolition of his jagir was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the interest payable under Section 8(2) of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act, 1951 forms part of the compensation and constitutes a capital receipt
Whether such interest is taxable as a revenue receipt under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
holdings: Interest under Section 8(2) is distinct from compensation and does not form part of it, as the legislature clearly distinguished between the two.
The interest is a revenue receipt, payable for delay in payment, and is therefore taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1922.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act, 1951, Section 8
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act, 1951, Schedule I
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagir Act, 1951, Sections 13, 14, 15
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Marginal notes do not override clear statutory language
Statutory interest for delayed payment is a revenue receipt

card.dispute: The landlord (Bhajan Lal) fought against the tenant (Shadi) over whether the tenant could exercise his right to purchase the land under Section 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, despite a pending ejectment proceeding for non-payment of rent.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can exercise the right to purchase land under Section 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 while an ejectment proceeding under Section 14A is pending.
Whether the initiation of an ejectment proceeding extinguishes the tenant's right to purchase the land.
holdings: A tenant remains a tenant until an ejectment order is actually passed; therefore, the right to purchase under Section 18 remains intact if exercised before the ejectment order.
The pendency of an ejectment proceeding does not bar a tenant from exercising the statutory right to purchase land, as the tenancy continues until formally terminated by order.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
doctrines: Statutory tenancy continues until formal termination
Non obstante clause does not retroactively extinguish rights
Priority of statutory rights over pending proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, whose house was burnt, challenged the High Court's dismissal of his petition for special leave to appeal against the acquittal of a third accused whom he had separately complained against, after the police had prosecuted the first two accused.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had locus standi to file a petition for special leave to appeal under Section 417(3) of the Cr.P.C. against the acquittal in a case instituted on his complaint.
Whether the case instituted on the appellant's complaint merged with the police case, thereby depriving him of the right to appeal.
holdings: The appellant was entitled to file a petition for special leave to appeal under Section 417(3) Cr.P.C. because a distinct case was instituted on his complaint, in which an acquittal was recorded.
There was no merger of the two cases—one based on police report and the other on private complaint—as their separate identities were maintained throughout the proceedings up to the Sessions Court.
doctrines: Locus standi in criminal appeals by private parties
Distinction between cases instituted on police report and private complaint
Doctrine of separate legal identity of criminal cases

card.dispute: The occupancy ryot (respondent) sued his cultivating tenants (appellants) for possession of land; the tenants claimed protection under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, but the courts found they had wilfully denied the landlord's title.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try a suit for possession when the defendant claimed to be a cultivating tenant protected under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955.
Whether a tenant who wilfully denies the landlord's title is entitled to the benefits of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955.
holdings: The civil court has jurisdiction to try a suit for possession if the defendant fails to prove both that he is a cultivating tenant and entitled to the benefits of the Act; the court must transfer the suit to the Revenue Divisional Officer only if both conditions are satisfied.

A cultivating tenant who wilfully denies the landlord's title is disentitled to the protection of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, under Section 3(2)(d), and thus the civil court may proceed with the suit.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3(2)(d)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 6A
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 6
doctrines: Jurisdictional bar doctrine: Civil courts are ousted from jurisdiction when a statute confers exclusive authority on a special tribunal, but only if the conditions for such ouster are fully met.
Conditional applicability of statutory protection: Statutory tenant protections are forfeited upon wilful denial of landlord's title.

card.dispute: The dispute was between former tenants and a subsequent lessee over whether the tenants could regain possession of agricultural land after voluntarily surrendering it to the landlord without complying with statutory formalities.
issues_decided: Whether a surrender of tenancy not in writing and not verified before the Tehsildar is valid under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958
Whether a landlord can lawfully take possession of tenanted land without an order from the Tahsildar, even with the tenant's consent
Whether a tenant evicted in violation of Section 36(2) can claim restoration of possession under Section 36(1)
holdings: A surrender of tenancy is invalid unless it is in writing and verified before the Tehsildar as required by Section 20 of the Act.
A landlord cannot lawfully obtain possession of tenanted land without an order from the Tahsildar, even if the tenant voluntarily delivers possession.
A tenant who has been evicted in contravention of Section 36(2) is entitled to apply for and obtain restoration of possession under Section 36(1), regardless of voluntary surrender.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 20
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 36
doctrines: Statutory compliance as condition precedent for surrender of tenancy
Non-derogation from statutory protection of tenancy without due process

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Ch. Surat Singh fought with Manohar Lal and others over the maintainability of two appeals due to non-joinder of Lt. Col. G.S. Yadav, a necessary party.
issues_decided: Whether Civil Appeal No. 610 of 1966 is maintainable without impleading Lt. Col. G.S. Yadav as a party?
Whether Civil Appeal No. 611 of 1966 is maintainable in the absence of Lt. Col. G.S. Yadav despite his earlier impleadment in the first appeal?
holdings: An appeal is not maintainable if a necessary party, such as a legal representative impleaded in the lower appellate court, is not included, and failure to implead is fatal to the appeal.
Non-impleadment of a party known to have been involved in earlier proceedings, despite belated attempts to add them, renders the appeal liable to be dismissed for lack of due diligence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4
doctrines: Necessary and proper parties doctrine
Principle of due diligence in procedural matters

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the election of the respondent from a Scheduled Tribes constituency, claiming the respondent was not a member of the Munda tribe as required, since 'Patar' was not listed in the Scheduled Tribes Order.
issues_decided: Whether evidence can be admitted to show that 'Munda' in the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 includes sub-tribes like Patar not specifically listed
Whether a person's admission that they are not a member of a Scheduled Tribe is conclusive in an election petition
Whether non-inclusion of a sub-tribe in the Presidential Order implies its exclusion from the general tribal entry
holdings: Evidence is admissible to determine the intended scope of an entry like 'Munda' in the Scheduled Tribes Order, but cannot be used to add new communities not contemplated by the Order.
An admission by a person that they are not a member of a Scheduled Tribe is relevant but not conclusive evidence in an election petition; the legal status remains a question of law.
The mere absence of a sub-tribe's name in the Order does not mean it is excluded from a broader tribal category like Munda if it is socially and culturally part of that tribe.
doctrines: Presidential Order interpretation doctrine
Election petition standard of proof
Tribal identity based on social and cultural criteria

card.dispute: The assessees challenged the validity of recovery certificates issued by the Revenue, arguing that the recovery proceedings were barred by limitation under the Income Tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the recovery proceedings initiated under Section 46 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 were barred by limitation when commenced more than one year after the first default but before the last instalment was due?
Whether the date for computing the limitation period under Section 46(7) should be the date when the last instalment was due under the instalment plan, or the date of the initial demand?
Whether an agreement allowing payment by instalments, with a clause making the entire amount exigible on default, affects the commencement of the limitation period for recovery?
holdings: Where an assessment provides for payment by instalments, the one-year limitation period for recovery under Section 46(7) begins from the date the last instalment is due, not from the date of the initial demand.
The language of clause (iv) of the proviso to Section 46(7), though poorly drafted, clearly intends to extend the limitation period until the last instalment becomes due when instalments are granted.

The assessment order incorporating the instalment agreement brings the case within the proviso, allowing the Revenue to wait until the last instalment date to initiate recovery, even if earlier instalments are defaulted.
doctrines: Limitation period for tax recovery
Interpretation of statutory provisos
Incorporation of agreements into assessment orders
Waiver of default clauses in tax recovery

card.dispute: Chaju Ram, an illiterate detenu, challenged the legality of his preventive detention by the State of Jammu & Kashmir, claiming he was not explained the grounds in a language he understood and that the grounds were vague.
issues_decided: Whether the grounds of detention were properly communicated to the illiterate detenu in a language he understood.
Whether the grounds of detention were sufficiently specific to enable the detenu to make a meaningful representation.
holdings: When a detenu is illiterate or does not understand the language of the detention order, the grounds must be explained in a language he understands; merely obtaining a thumb impression on an English document does not satisfy this requirement.
The grounds of detention were vague and insufficient as they lacked specific details about the alleged conspiracy, making it impossible for the detenu to make an effective representation.
provisions: Jammu & Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964, Section 3(2) read with Section 5
doctrines: Rule of law in preventive detention
Right to effective representation
Procedural fairness in administrative detention

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Rajasthan Mines Ltd. disputed whether arrears of rent and royalty received by the company were taxable as income and whether the profit from the sale of mining properties was taxable as business income.
issues_decided: Whether the arrears of rent and royalty received by the assessee were taxable as revenue receipts.
Whether the profit from the sale of the mining properties was taxable as income from a business or trading adventure.
holdings: The right to collect arrears of rent and royalty, acquired by purchase, does not constitute income; the receipt is capital in nature and not taxable as revenue.

The sale of properties by the assessee was not part of a trading adventure; the transaction was isolated and not carried out in the course of business, hence the profit is not taxable as business income.
doctrines: Nature of receipt: distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Adventure in the nature of trade
Appellate review of findings based on inference from primary facts

card.dispute: The Corporation of Calcutta fought with the Life Insurance Corporation of India over whether the annual value of a rented building for municipal tax assessment should be based on the rent received by the tenant from sub-tenants or the standard rent payable to the landlord.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 168(1) of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1951, limits the annual value to standard rent only when an order fixing standard rent has been made under Section 9 of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950.
Whether the rent received by a tenant from sub-tenants can be considered in determining the annual value of the building for assessment of the consolidated rate.
holdings: The proviso to Section 168(1) does not alter the principle that statutory rent control limits the hypothetical rent; even without a formal order, the standard rent as defined by law is the maximum that can be considered.

The annual value for municipal assessment must be based on the rent the owner could reasonably expect to receive, not the rent a tenant receives from sub-tenants; sub-letting income is irrelevant to the assessment.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 2(10)(b)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 9
doctrines: Statutory rent control as a market circumscription
Hypothetical willing lessor-willing lessee test
Irrelevance of sub-tenant rent in municipal valuation

card.dispute: The appellants (D. N. Roy and S. K. Bannerjee) challenged the Central Government's order setting aside a mining lease granted to them, which was initiated through a revision application by a third party (5th respondent).
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government's order of September 30, 1964, disposed of the entire application filed by the 5th respondent under Rule 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960.
Whether the Central Government could validly exercise suo moto powers under Section 30 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, without notice to the lessee.
Whether the impugned order dated November 5, 1964, passed without affording an opportunity to the appellants, was vitiated by procedural unfairness.
holdings: The two prayers in the 5th respondent’s application—cancellation of the appellants’ lease and grant of lease to himself—were interdependent, and rejection of one on time-bar grounds implied rejection of the entire application.
The Central Government cannot validly exercise suo moto powers without clearly invoking them and providing notice and an opportunity to be heard to the affected party.

An order purportedly based on a third party’s revision application cannot be sustained on the basis of unannounced suo moto powers, especially when no opportunity was given to the lessee to contest the action.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 30
doctrines: Principle of interdependence of reliefs in connected claims
Rule of fair procedure in administrative action
Doctrine of opportunity to be heard in exercise of quasi-judicial powers
Limitation on undisclosed exercise of statutory powers

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a contingent right to property under a will and codicil, while the respondents argued that the earlier suit's decision barred the claim under res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the decision in the 1935 suit operated as res judicata in the 1957 suit
Whether the findings on the merits in the 1935 suit were binding despite the plaintiff's lack of right to sue
Whether the nature of the estate inherited by Lochanappa under the will was an absolute estate
holdings: A decision operates as res judicata if it finally disposes of a matter on multiple independent grounds, each sufficient to support the judgment.
Findings on the merits made by a court after full trial bind the parties in subsequent litigation, even if one ground could have disposed of the case.
The court's determination that Lochanappa acquired an absolute estate under the will was a binding adjudication on that issue.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 11
doctrines: Res judicata
Obiter dicta vs. binding findings
Multiple grounds for decision in res judicata

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted for murder and related charges in connection with a land dispute over a casuarina tope, challenged their convictions and sentences, particularly the enhancement of sentence to death by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the irregularities in the investigation vitiated the prosecution case?
Whether the evidence was sufficient to prove the presence and participation of accused No. 4 in the offence?
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentences of accused Nos. 1 and 3 to death while not doing so for accused Nos. 2 and 4?
holdings: Mere irregularities in investigation do not vitiate the trial unless there is proof of dishonesty or abuse of power by the police; no prejudice was shown here.
The concurrent findings of the trial and appellate courts that accused No. 4 was present and armed with a gun are reliable and supported by eyewitness testimony and circumstantial evidence.

The High Court’s reasoning for enhancing the sentence to death for accused Nos. 1 and 3 but not for 2 and 4 was arbitrary and unsound; the enhancement was set aside and the original life sentences restored.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact by lower courts
Principle of prejudice in investigation irregularities
Doctrine of proportionality in sentencing
Limited role of drunkenness as a mitigating factor

card.dispute: The Guntur Municipal Council revised rental values for property tax purposes, and the Rate Payers' Association challenged the revision as illegal for exceeding fair rent limits under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the municipality must assess annual rental value in accordance with the Rent Control Act in force during the assessment period.
Whether a distinction can be made between properties with and without a formally fixed fair rent under the Rent Control Act for assessment purposes.
holdings: The annual rental value for municipal taxation must reflect the fair or standard rent lawfully payable under the Rent Control Act in force during the assessment year.
No distinction is permissible between properties where fair rent is fixed and where it is not; municipal authorities must determine fair rent using principles from Section 4 of the Rent Control Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 4
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 7
doctrines: Fair rent determination under rent control legislation
Ultra vires assessment
Hypothetical tenant test for annual rental value
