card.dispute: The appellant, Goli Eswariah, challenged the imposition of gift tax on his act of throwing self-acquired property into the joint family stock, arguing it did not constitute a 'transfer' or 'gift' under the Gift Tax Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the act of a Hindu coparcener throwing self-acquired property into the joint family stock constitutes a 'transfer of property' under Section 2(xxiv)(d) of the Gift Tax Act, 1958.
Whether such an act amounts to a 'gift' within the meaning of Sections 2(xii) and 4(a) of the Gift Tax Act, 1958.
holdings: The act of throwing self-acquired property into the joint family stock is a unilateral act and does not constitute a 'transaction' under Section 2(xxiv)(d) of the Gift Tax Act, as it requires an agreement between two or more parties.
Such an act does not amount to a 'transfer of property' or 'gift' under the Gift Tax Act, since there is no donor-donee relationship, no acceptance required, and no bilateral disposition.
doctrines: Doctrine of throwing into the common stock under Mitakshara law
Unilateral act vs. bilateral transaction
Literal and contextual interpretation of 'disposition' and 'transaction'
Principle of no transfer in absence of donor-donee relationship

card.dispute: Whether an isolated money-lending transaction in a district where the lender is unregistered invalidates a suit for recovery under the C.P. Money Lenders Act, 1934.
issues_decided: Whether an isolated loan transaction in a district without registration falls under the prohibition of s. 11F of the C.P. Money Lenders Act, 1934
Whether the decision in Cornelius v. Philips applies to the interpretation of the C.P. Money Lenders Act
Whether long-standing judicial interpretation of the Act should be overturned affecting settled rights
holdings: Section 11F only prohibits carrying on the business of moneylending without registration, not isolated transactions; such transactions are not void.
The English case Cornelius v. Philips is inapplicable because the statutory scheme of the C.P. Act differs from the English Act.
A long-standing judicial interpretation creating settled rights should not be overturned unless clearly erroneous, especially where property and contracts rely on it.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 2(v)
Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 11C
Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 11D
Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 11F
Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 11G
Central Provinces and Berar Money Lenders Act, 1934, Section 11H
doctrines: Stare decisis
Statutory interpretation
Presumption against disturbing settled legal rights
Legislative acquiescence in judicial interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant landlord sought to execute a decree for eviction against respondents, but the respondents challenged the decree as a nullity due to non-compliance with statutory protections against eviction under the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree for eviction is a nullity for failing to comply with Section 13(1) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
Whether a court can pass a decree for possession without independently satisfying itself about the existence of grounds for eviction under the Rent Control Act
holdings: A decree for recovery of possession passed without the court independently satisfying itself that a ground for eviction under Section 13(1) exists is beyond the court's jurisdiction and is a nullity.
A compromise decree that bypasses statutory safeguards under Section 13(1) of the Rent Control Act cannot confer jurisdiction on the court and is unenforceable.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(b)(i)
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation of courts under rent control statutes
Nullity of decrees passed without jurisdiction
Non-derogability of statutory tenant protections by compromise

card.dispute: The dispute was between the daughter's son and the paternal uncle of a deceased Hindu male over who had a preferential right to inherit his separate property after a series of female life-estate holders.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 applies to a Hindu male who died intestate before the Act came into force but was succeeded by a female heir who died after the Act's commencement.
When does succession to the estate of a last male Hindu owner open if a female heir held a life-estate?
holdings: The Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 applies not only to males dying after February 21, 1929, but also to those dying before if succeeded by a female life-estate holder who died after that date.
Succession to the estate of the last male owner opens upon the termination of the female life-estate, not at the death of the male owner.
provisions: Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 (Act 2 of 1929), Section 1(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of postponement of reversionary rights until termination of life-estate
Doctrine of spes successionis
Prospective application of succession laws based on the time succession opens

card.dispute: Hatti and Sunder Singh disputed over the declaration of bhumidari rights and possession of agricultural land, with Sunder Singh filing a suit in civil court challenging the declaration in favor of Hatti.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit for declaration of bhumidari right and possession under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954
Whether the provisions of the Act bar civil court jurisdiction in matters concerning bhumidari rights and possession
Whether a question of title arising in revenue proceedings can be directly adjudicated by the civil court
holdings: The civil court lacked jurisdiction because the reliefs claimed fall under the exclusive domain of the Revenue Assistant under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954.
Sections 84, 185, and item 4 of the First Schedule bar civil court jurisdiction; remedies must be pursued before the Revenue Assistant.
A civil court can only decide title issues referred by the Revenue Court under section 186 and cannot entertain direct suits on title.
provisions: Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, First Schedule, Item 4
Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, First Schedule, Item 19
Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, First Schedule, Item 28
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
Statutory bar on civil jurisdiction
Revenue court primacy in land reform matters
Reference of title issues under section 186

card.dispute: Hirday Narain challenged the assessment of his income as that of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and the inclusion of his minor sons' income under Section 16(3)(a)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, after the family property was partitioned.
issues_decided: Whether Section 16(3)(a)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 applies to assess the income of minor sons in the hands of an HUF after partition.
Whether the Income-tax Officer has discretionary power under Section 35 to refuse rectification of a mistake apparent from the record.
holdings: Section 16(3)(a)(ii) does not apply to include the income of minor sons in the assessment of an HUF; it applies only when the income is assessed in the hands of an individual.

The power under Section 35 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 to rectify a mistake apparent from the record is not discretionary; the officer must exercise it when a valid claim is made and conditions are satisfied.
doctrines: Rectification of mistakes apparent from record
Enforcement of statutory rights through mandatory interpretation of enabling provisions
Status of Hindu Undivided Family as a taxable entity

card.dispute: India Electric Works Ltd fought James Mantosh and another over whether the time spent litigating a prior suit could be excluded under Section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act to save a subsequent claim for future mesne profits from being time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff could claim benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act by excluding the time during which the earlier suit was pending.
Whether the court's inability to entertain a claim for future mesne profits in a pure money suit amounted to 'defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature' under Section 14.
holdings: The plaintiff was entitled to deduct the time during which the earlier suit was pending under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, as the claim was not decided on merits due to a defect analogous to lack of jurisdiction.

A decree for future mesne profits in a pure money suit was not maintainable, and the appellate court’s setting aside of such a decree created a new cause of action, allowing the plaintiff to file a fresh suit within time.
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'other cause of a like nature' in Section 14
New cause of action arising when a decree is set aside on appeal
Deduction of time during pendency of a bona fide earlier suit

card.dispute: The income-tax authorities issued notices under Section 34 to one of the daughters of a deceased assessee for reassessment; she challenged the validity of the notices, claiming she was not a legal representative.
issues_decided: Whether the notices issued under Section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 to the daughters of the deceased assessee are valid in law
Who qualifies as a legal representative of a deceased assessee for the purpose of assessment under Section 24B of the Act
Whether the Income-tax Officer made a bona fide enquiry before issuing the notices to only some of the legal representatives
holdings: Notices relating to assessment year 1949-50 are invalid as they pertain to a period after the assessee's death.
Where a deceased has multiple legal representatives, the Income-tax Officer must assess the estate against all legal representatives or those who jointly represent the estate.
The Income-tax Officer must make a bona fide enquiry and base notices on a clear determination of who the legal representatives are, whether under a will, Hindu law, or a compromise decree.
doctrines: Doctrine of bona fide enquiry
Doctrine of sufficient representation of estate by legal representatives
Principle of non-abatement of proceedings if legal representatives are correctly impleaded

card.dispute: The landlady sought to terminate a tenant's lease for personal cultivation, but the tenant contested the validity of the termination, raising issues about the applicability of tenancy laws and the authority of the mother to lease the property when the father was alive.
issues_decided: Whether the mother, despite the father being alive, could be considered the natural guardian of the minor daughter and thus competent to lease the property on her behalf.
Whether the tenancy was created 'not earlier than April 1, 1957', making the application under Section 39 of the Bombay Tenancy Act maintainable.
Whether the application filed by the appellant after attaining majority was barred by limitation under Section 39.
holdings: When parents live separately and the father takes no interest in the minor's affairs, the mother may be treated as the natural guardian for managing the minor's property.
A tenancy created prior to April 1, 1957, even if continued after that date, does not attract Section 39 of the Bombay Tenancy Act.
Section 39 does not allow a minor to file an application within one year of attaining majority; the limitation period is fixed from the date the Act came into force.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 6
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Sections 38, 39
doctrines: Natural guardianship under Hindu law
De facto guardianship in cases of parental separation
Strict interpretation of statutory limitation and eligibility for relief under tenancy laws

card.dispute: The sons of a displaced joint Hindu family sought compensation as separate co-sharers under Rule 19(2) of the Displaced Persons Rules, but the authorities and later the Supreme Court held they must be treated as a single unit under Rule 19(3)(b).
issues_decided: Whether Rule 19(3)(b) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules excludes sons from being counted as separate members entitled to claim partition when the joint family consists only of a father and his sons.
Whether the High Court was correct in holding that Rule 19(3)(b) does not apply to a joint family consisting solely of a father and his sons.
holdings: Rule 19(3)(b) excludes lineal descendants in the main line of another living member entitled to claim partition, including sons of a father in a joint family, even when no other family member exists.
A joint Hindu family of only a father and his sons must be treated as one unit for compensation; Rule 19(3)(b) applies, and Rule 19(2) does not, as the sons are excluded from separate apportionment.
provisions: The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, Rule 19(2) and (3)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Unitary treatment of joint Hindu families for compensation purposes

card.dispute: Kanpur Sugar Works Ltd fought the State of Bihar over whether the outer enclosure of its factory premises was liable to pay ground rent under Section 7(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act or exempt as homestead land under Section 5(1).
issues_decided: Whether the outer enclosure used for residential quarters, offices, and ancillary facilities qualifies as homestead land under Section 5(1) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the buildings and land in the outer enclosure are 'used as' factories or mills under Section 7(1) and thus liable to ground rent.
holdings: Land used for residential quarters, clubs, dispensaries, garages, and other facilities for factory staff, though beneficial to the factory, are not 'used as' factory or mill buildings and thus fall under homestead land protection of Section 5(1).
The expression 'used as' in Section 7(1) requires direct use as a factory or mill; ancillary use for employee welfare does not bring land within Section 7(1) liability for ground rent.
The definition of 'factory' under the Factories Act, 1948, cannot be imported into the Bihar Land Reforms Act due to differing statutory objects and schemes.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on plain meaning of 'used as' versus 'used for'
Contextual and purposive interpretation of statutes with differing objects
Exclusion of ancillary or indirect uses from statutory liability under land reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant (judgment debtor) challenged the execution of a compromise decree, arguing it was unenforceable because it included unregistered immovable property.
issues_decided: Whether the decree creating a charge on machinery and deposit of title deeds for an equitable mortgage required registration under the Registration Act
Whether the properties charged under the decree were immovable by nature
holdings: A decree creating a charge only on movable machinery does not require registration under the Registration Act.
Machinery listed in the decree, unless permanently embedded in the earth, remains movable property and does not attract the requirement of registration.
doctrines: Doctrine of Registration of Deeds
Test of movability of property based on degree of annexation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Khajamian Wakf Estates and others, and the State of Madras, over the constitutional validity of laws abolishing inam estates and leaseholds as part of agrarian reform.
issues_decided: Whether the Madras Inam and Leasehold Abolition Acts were protected under Article 31A of the Constitution
Whether the Acts violated Articles 14, 19, 26, or 31 by acquiring property without adequate compensation
Whether the reduction of tenants' arrears of rent was within the State's legislative competence
Whether religious institutions' rights under Article 26 were infringed by the acquisition
holdings: The Acts fall within Article 31A as they abolish intermediaries and establish direct government-occupant relationship in agrarian reform, thus immune from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
Acquisition under the Acts does not violate Article 31(2) as compensation is provided for the estate as a whole, even if not itemized for each interest.
The State legislature had competence under List II, Entries 18 or 30, to reduce tenants' arrears of rent or debts, which are matters related to land or agriculturists.
Article 26 does not prevent the State from acquiring property of religious denominations; such acquisition ends their right to administer it, which is constitutionally permissible.
provisions: Madras Inam Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 (Act 26 of 1963), Section 18
Madras Leaseholds (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 (Act 27 of 1963)
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 (Act 30 of 1963)
Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 18 and Entry 30
doctrines: Agrarian reform doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of protective classification under Article 31A
Doctrine of compensation as a whole

card.dispute: The mortgagees (appellants) challenged the redemption of a mortgage by the son of the original mortgagor, claiming the sale transaction was invalid due to defective power of attorney, while the respondents (vendees) asserted valid title and right to redeem.
issues_decided: Whether the first power of attorney was valid under the Indian Registration Act, 1908
Whether the second power of attorney could ratify the earlier invalid transaction and relate back in time
Whether the suit for declaration without prayers for cancellation or injunction was maintainable under the Specific Relief Act
Whether the suit was properly framed without impleading the son of the mortgagor (Vernon Seth Chotia)
holdings: A power of attorney executed abroad by an Indian must be authenticated by a Notary Public under s. 33 of the Indian Registration Act; absence of such authentication renders it invalid.

A subsequent valid power of attorney that expressly ratifies a prior defective one relates back to the date of the original act and validates the earlier transaction, provided the principal is disclosed.
A suit for declaration alone, without seeking cancellation of an order or injunction under s. 42 of the Specific Relief Act, is not maintainable when such reliefs are necessary.
A suit involving property rights and transactions by an agent must include the principal as at least a proper party; failure to do so renders the suit improperly framed.
doctrines: Relation back of ratification
Presumption of regularity of official acts
Maintainability of declaratory suits under Specific Relief Act
Necessity of proper parties in suits involving property transactions

card.dispute: The Janapada Sabha challenged the validity of a state law that retrospectively validated coal cess levies previously declared illegal by the Supreme Court, while coal producers contested the law's effectiveness and constitutionality.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Koyala Upkar (Manyatakaran) Adhinayam, 1964, could retrospectively validate cess levies that were declared illegal for lack of prior government sanction
Whether a legislature can enact a law to nullify the effect of a binding judicial decision under the Indian constitutional framework
Whether the validating statute was sufficiently clear in amending the earlier enactment to cure the legal defect
holdings: A statute cannot retrospectively validate administrative actions that were declared illegal by a final judicial decision if it does not clearly amend the law to cure the defect.
The legislature cannot override or nullify a binding judicial declaration of law under Article 141 of the Constitution, even by retrospective amendment.
A validating law must clearly specify the nature and text of the amendment to the original enactment; a mere deeming fiction without specifying amendments is insufficient and invalid.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Koyala Upkar (Manyatakaran) Adhinayam, 1964, Section 2(a), Section 2(b), Section 3(1)
Central Provinces Local Self Government Act, 1920, Section 51(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Doctrine of separation of powers
Rule of strict construction in taxing statutes
Binding nature of Supreme Court decisions under Article 141

card.dispute: The Lt. Governor of Himachal Pradesh challenged the quashing of a notification cancelling land acquisition proceedings, after possession had been taken, over land belonging to Avinash Sharma.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government can cancel acquisition notifications under Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 after possession has been taken under Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether land vests in the Government free from encumbrances upon compliance with Section 17(1), even if initial possession was taken illegally.
Whether the power under Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act allows withdrawal from acquisition after vesting of land.
holdings: Once possession is taken under Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the land vests in the Government free from all encumbrances, regardless of prior illegal possession.
The power to cancel notifications under Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 cannot be exercised after the land has statutorily vested in the Government under Section 17(1).
Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act does not permit withdrawal from acquisition after vesting; cancellation of notifications at that stage would circumvent statutory safeguards.
doctrines: Statutory vesting of property
Doctrine of implied limitation on general powers
Non-revival of rights after statutory vesting

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the tenant's contention that the building was let out for dual use (trade and residence), challenging the High Court's interference with lower courts' findings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 of the C.P.C. to interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts on the nature of the tenancy?
Whether an error of law by a court with jurisdiction amounts to a jurisdictional error justifying interference under Section 115 of the C.P.C.?
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere under Section 115 of the C.P.C. unless there is a procedural or jurisdictional error, not merely a legal error, by courts having jurisdiction.
An error in deciding a matter within jurisdiction does not constitute a jurisdictional defect; hence, concurrent findings of fact by lower courts cannot be overturned on such grounds.
doctrines: No interference under Section 115 CPC for mere errors of law when no jurisdictional defect exists
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are binding in absence of jurisdictional error

card.dispute: The landowner contested the tenant's statutory ownership of leased land, claiming the tenant lost rights by not exercising purchase options under amended law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could raise a contention under s. 42(c) of the Act for the first time before the High Court
Whether the insertion of s. 43(14A) by Act 2 of 1962 affected the operation of s. 46(1) retrospectively
holdings: The appellant could not raise a contention based on s. 42(c) for the first time before the High Court without having pleaded it earlier or laid any factual foundation.
The operation of s. 46(1), which transferred ownership to tenants as of April 1, 1961, was not affected by the subsequent insertion of s. 43(14A) as it lacked retrospective effect.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 41
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 42
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 43
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 46
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Land (Vidharbha and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 49A
doctrines: Prospective vs. retrospective operation of amendments
Res judicata and pleading estoppel
Statutory vesting of property rights

card.dispute: The landowners appealed against the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, challenging the valuation principles used.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Tribunal's valuation of the land for acquisition purposes.
Whether the Tribunal erred in relying on Ext. 42 (a consent-based Collector's award) as evidence of market value.
Whether the Tribunal's method of valuing front and rear belts of land separately and applying a 12.5% reduction was legally sound.
holdings: The High Court erred in interfering with the Tribunal’s valuation as there was no error of principle or procedural defect warranting such interference.

A consent-based Collector's award, though administrative, can constitute good evidence of market value if it reflects a formal agreement between the parties at the time of declaration under Section 6.
The Tribunal’s approach of valuing frontage land separately and applying a 12.5% reduction for bulk acquisition was valid and not open to legal challenge.
provisions: Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911, Rule 9 of the Schedule
doctrines: Principle of non-interference by appellate courts in expert valuation unless there is an error of law or procedure
Use of comparable sales and consent awards as evidence of market value in land acquisition
Valuation adjustment for bulk acquisition and locational benefits

card.dispute: The appellants, owners of a rice mill, shifted their mill to a new site after land acquisition, and the respondents, owners of a nearby mill, objected to the post-facto permission granted under the Rice Milling Industry (Regulation) Act, 1958, claiming it would harm their business.
issues_decided: Whether shifting a rice mill without prior permission under Section 8(3)(c) of the Act renders the shift illegal and actionable by a competitor.
Whether the authority granting permission under Section 8(3)(c) must consider the same factors as under Section 5(4) of the Act, including impact on existing competitors.
holdings: Section 8(3)(c) is regulatory, not prohibitive; non-compliance may attract penalty but does not invalidate the shift or give competitors a right to object under Article 19(1)(g).

The factors in Section 5(4) apply only to permits for new or defunct mills, not to relocation of existing mills under Section 8(3)(c); thus, no obligation to consider local competition or resources arises.
doctrines: Regulatory vs. prohibitive statutory provisions
Locus standi in administrative challenges
Fundamental right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g)
Statutory interpretation based on classification of mills

card.dispute: The appellant, Nagarmal Tekriwal, was prosecuted for storing foodgrains without a license under the Bihar Foodgrains Dealer's Licensing Order, 1966, and claimed exemption as an agriculturist.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption under clause 3(2) of the Bihar Foodgrains Dealer's Licensing Order, 1966, that stored foodgrains are meant for sale applies to agriculturists.
Whether unregistered lease deeds can be considered in a criminal case for a collateral purpose.
Whether oral evidence from next-door neighbours can be rejected solely on the ground of proximity or interest.
holdings: The presumption under clause 3(2) does not apply to agriculturists, as they are expressly excluded; thus, storage alone cannot imply intent to sell if the person is engaged in agriculture.
Unregistered lease deeds are admissible in criminal cases for collateral purposes, such as proving possession of land for cultivation, even if not admissible for title.
Oral evidence from next-door neighbours cannot be rejected merely due to proximity or assumed interest; it must be evaluated on intrinsic credibility.
provisions: Bihar Foodgrains Dealer's Licensing Order, 1966, Paragraph 3(2)
doctrines: Presumption against accused in regulatory offences is rebuttable, especially with statutory exemptions.
Collateral use doctrine: unregistered documents may be used for purposes other than establishing title.
Rule against automatic rejection of interested witnesses' testimony in criminal cases.

card.dispute: The appellant (Mohan Lal) and respondent (Mohun Ram) fought over whether the respondent tenant could acquire proprietary rights in land previously owned by the appellant, a minor, under the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent remained a tenant entitled to apply under Section 11(1) after the lease expired.
Whether the appellant-minor had no other means of livelihood except the land in question, thus qualifying for protection under Section 11(2).
Whether the statutory right of maintenance under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act can be considered a 'means of livelihood' under Section 11(2).
holdings: A tenant does not cease to be a tenant upon lease expiry if possession continues and no decree of eviction or abandonment occurs; thus, the respondent could apply under Section 11(1).

The appellant-minor was not entitled to protection under Section 11(2) because he had other means of livelihood, including an interest in ancestral property and two houses on the land not sought to be acquired.

The statutory right of maintenance under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act is not automatically a 'means of livelihood' under Section 11(2), but may be considered depending on facts; here, it was not necessary to rely on it due to other assets.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954, Section 11(1)
Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1954, Section 11(2)
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 20
doctrines: Doctrine of continued tenancy after lease expiry
Fact-specific determination of 'means of livelihood'
Protection of minors in land reform statutes

card.dispute: The appellants, lessees of open land, fought with the respondent landlord over whether a prior court decision rejecting their claim for standard rent determination under the Bombay Rents Act was res judicata, after a later judicial interpretation had changed the legal position on the Act's applicability.
issues_decided: Whether a decision on the jurisdiction of a court based on an erroneous interpretation of law operates as res judicata?
Whether a question of law, particularly regarding the applicability of a statute, can be binding as res judicata in subsequent proceedings between the same parties?
Whether the earlier rejection of the application for standard rent determination barred a fresh application under the doctrine of res judicata?
holdings: A decision on the jurisdiction of a court based on an erroneous interpretation of law does not operate as res judicata, even between the same parties.
A question of law, especially concerning court jurisdiction, cannot be binding as res judicata if it was wrongly decided, as it would create a rule contrary to statutory law.

The earlier decision rejecting the application for standard rent was not final on the merits because it was based on a misinterpretation of the Bombay Rents Act and thus did not bar a fresh application.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Res judicata
Jurisdiction of court
Erroneous interpretation of statute
Rule against creating binding illegal precedents

card.dispute: The appellant claimed exclusive ownership of a pharmacy gifted by his father, while the respondent sought partition of family properties, including that pharmacy, as joint assets.
issues_decided: Whether the pharmacy known as Hindi C.C. Works (formerly Darul Adviya) was joint family property liable to partition?
Whether the appellant should be permitted to amend his written statement to claim that the other two pharmacies were also joint properties?
Whether the suit was bad for partial partition due to defective framing of issues?
holdings: The High Court's finding that the pharmacies were not gifted but only placed under the management of sons does not bind the parties due to lack of proper pleadings and issues.
The High Court erred in taking a technical view by rejecting the amendment application; justice required allowing the amendment to plead that the other two pharmacies were joint properties.
The trial court’s decision on properties already declared joint (Lists A-1, A-2, B, C-1, C-2, D-1, F) is final and not subject to re-opening on remand.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17 (Amendment of Pleadings)
doctrines: Liberal approach to amendment of pleadings in the interest of justice
Technicalities should not defeat substantial justice
Findings without proper issues do not bind parties

card.dispute: Madhu Limaye and another challenged their detention and the requirement to furnish an interim bond under Section 117(3) of the CrPC without a prior inquiry into the truth of the information alleging breach of peace.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate can require an interim bond under Section 117(3) CrPC without commencing an inquiry into the truth of the information?
Whether the detention of the petitioners was legal in the absence of a proper inquiry under Chapter VIII of the CrPC?
Whether Sections 91 or 344 CrPC can be used as alternatives to Section 117(3) for securing an interim bond in cases under Chapter VIII?
holdings: The expression 'pending completion of the inquiry' in Section 117(3) CrPC requires the Magistrate to have commenced the inquiry, meaning the trial under summons procedure, before asking for an interim bond.
Without commencing an inquiry or examining the truth of the information, a Magistrate cannot lawfully require an accused to furnish an interim bond or remand them to custody.
Sections 91 and 344 CrPC do not apply to proceedings under Chapter VIII of the CrPC, which has its own detailed procedure for cases involving security for keeping the peace.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Chapter VIII
doctrines: Commencement of inquiry doctrine
Statutory interpretation of 'pending completion of inquiry'
Specificity of Chapter VIII procedure over general provisions

card.dispute: The landholder and tenants disputed whether the tenants' application for possession of leased land, based on breach of a compromise agreement, was maintainable under the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, and whether it was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants' application under Section 32 of the Act was barred by limitation
Whether the application could be treated as one under Section 46 of the Act despite being filed under Section 32
Whether the landholder had terminated the tenancy under Section 44 of the Act, enabling relief under Section 45 and Section 46
holdings: An application filed under Section 32 is barred by limitation if made more than two years after the cause of action arose.
An application cannot be treated as one under Section 46 unless the tenancy was lawfully terminated under Section 44 and the facts show non-compliance with Section 45.

The mere inclusion of a personal cultivation clause in a compromise does not imply termination under Section 44; the nature of the original application must be examined to determine applicability of Section 46.
provisions: Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 32
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 44
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 45
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 46
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory provisions in tenancy law
Limitation bars applications filed beyond prescribed period
Application of relief provisions only when statutory preconditions are satisfied

card.dispute: Mannan Lal and Mst. Chhotaka Bibi disputed whether a special appeal with initially deficient court fees, later made up, was pending before the Allahabad High Court on November 12, 1962, and thus saved from abolition under the U.P. High Court (Abolition of Letters Patent Appeals) Act, 1962.
issues_decided: Whether a special appeal with deficient court fees, later cured, was pending on the date immediately preceding the enforcement of the U.P. High Court (Abolition of Letters Patent Appeals) Act, 1962.
Whether Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure validates a memorandum of appeal with deficient court fees from the original date of filing once the deficiency is cured.
Whether Section 4 of the Court Fees Act renders a memorandum of appeal ineffective until fees are made up, thereby preventing it from being 'pending' during the interim period.
holdings: An appeal is pending from the date of presentation of the memorandum, even if court fees are initially deficient, provided the deficiency is later cured in accordance with court directions.

Section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure operates to give retrospective effect to the filing of a memorandum of appeal once deficient court fees are made up, as if the fees had been paid originally.
Section 4 of the Court Fees Act does not nullify the pendency of an appeal when read harmoniously with Section 149 of the Code, which allows curing of fee defects with retroactive validation.
provisions: The U.P. High Court (Abolition of Letters Patent Appeals) Act, 1962, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of retrospective validation under Section 149, CPC
Doctrine of pendency of legal proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant (Nain Singh) fought to reclaim possession of suit properties after the High Court dismissed his suit, holding that the abolition of jagirs extinguished his rights, despite a prior appellate court remand.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could review the correctness of a remand order under Section 105(2), Civil Procedure Code, when no appeal was filed against it.
Whether the plaintiff retained a right to claim compensation under the Jagir Abolition Act, 1951, and thus had a continuing interest in establishing ownership.
holdings: A remand order under Order 41, Rule 23, CPC, when not appealed, cannot be challenged later; Section 105(2) bars re-litigation of its correctness, and inherent powers under Section 151 cannot override this bar.

The plaintiff retained a legal interest in proving ownership as of the date of the Jagir Abolition Act's enforcement, entitling him to compensation, and justice required impleadment of the State to finally determine all rights.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23
doctrines: Inherent powers doctrine (Section 151 CPC)
Res judicata and preclusion under Section 105(2) CPC
Doctrine of impleadment for complete relief

card.dispute: The Jagirdar (Nainsingh) sued distant relatives of his deceased tenant for possession of properties; the dispute centered on whether the civil court had jurisdiction and the effect of the Jagir Abolition Act, 1951 on his rights.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could review the correctness of a remand order not appealed against under the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the Jagirdar lost all rights to the suit properties upon the abolition of jagirs under the Jagir Abolition Act, 1951
holdings: The High Court could not review the correctness of a remand order once the time to appeal it had lapsed, as Section 105(2) of the CPC bars such challenges after failure to appeal.

The Jagirdar did not lose all rights to the suit properties upon vesting in the State; he retained a right to claim compensation under the Jagir Abolition Act, 1951 if he proved ownership as of the vesting date.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23
doctrines: Preclusion of challenge to remand order under Section 105(2) CPC
Inherent powers under Section 151 CPC cannot override specific provisions or be used as appellate powers
Survival of right to compensation despite vesting of property under abolition statutes

card.dispute: The fourth accused challenged his conviction for murder under common intention, conspiracy, and abetment, arguing that the evidence did not support the findings of the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence supported the conviction of the fourth accused under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC (common intention)?
Whether the evidence was sufficient to sustain the conviction of the fourth accused under Section 120-B IPC (criminal conspiracy)?
Whether the fourth accused could be held guilty under Section 302 read with Section 109 IPC (abetment of murder)?
holdings: The evidence did not conclusively prove the fourth accused's presence at the scene during the murder, so his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC was set aside due to benefit of doubt.
The cumulative circumstantial evidence, including prior threats and conduct, sufficiently established a criminal conspiracy under Section 120-B IPC, which was upheld.
The fourth accused's active instigation and animus towards the deceased supported his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 109 IPC for abetting the murder.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 requires active participation or presence at the scene of crime.
Criminal conspiracy can be inferred from circumstantial evidence due to its secretive nature.
Abetment by instigation can be established through overt acts and expressions of animus.
Benefit of doubt is granted when evidence does not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

card.dispute: The appellant and the first respondent fought over whether mining lease applications deemed refused under the Mineral Concession Rules should be granted, and whether the Central Government could review the State Government's belated grant of a lease.
issues_decided: Whether the failure of the State Government to dispose of mining lease applications within the prescribed time under Rule 28(1-A) results in a deemed refusal under Rule 57(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949.
Whether the State Government retains jurisdiction to grant a mining lease after the deemed refusal period has expired.
Whether the Central Government can review and set aside a lease granted by the State Government after the deemed refusal.
holdings: Failure to decide on a mining lease application within the time mandated by Rule 28(1-A) results in a deemed refusal under Rule 57(2) for all purposes under the Mineral Concession Rules.
The State Government loses jurisdiction to grant a mining lease once the period for disposal has expired and a deemed refusal has occurred.

The Central Government, as a statutory revisional authority, can review and set aside a lease granted by the State Government after a deemed refusal, even if done in compliance with a High Court writ.
doctrines: Deemed refusal doctrine
Statutory estoppel
Jurisdictional limitation after statutory time limits
Quasi-judicial authority of revisional bodies

card.dispute: The adopted son of a Hindu widow challenged the validity of a property settlement she made in favor of her daughter, claiming the adoption related back to the husband's death, rendering the widow incompetent to alienate the property.
issues_decided: Whether the full ownership conferred on a Hindu female under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is defeasible by an adoption made after the Act came into force.
Whether the fiction of relation back of adoption under Hindu law applies to defeat the absolute ownership rights conferred by Section 14(1).
holdings: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 grants absolute ownership to a Hindu female over property she possesses, and this right cannot be defeated by any rule or fiction of Hindu law, including the relation back of adoption.

The fiction of relation back in adoption is abrogated under Section 4 of the Act where it conflicts with the rights conferred by Section 14(1), as the Act supersedes prior Hindu law texts and interpretations.
doctrines: Doctrine of relation back of adoption
Abrogation of customary and textual Hindu law by statutory provision
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Presumption against continuity of law when statute is unambiguous

card.dispute: The appellants (tenants) fought with the respondent girasdars over whether the girasdar family was divided or undivided at the time of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, which determined entitlement to separate gharkhed land allotments.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner, as a delegate of the State Government, had the power to review and set aside an earlier order passed by the Saurashtra Government under Section 63(2) of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act?
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the Commissioner's order and directing the Revenue Tribunal to decide the matter afresh?
holdings: A reviewing power is not inherent and must be expressly or by necessary implication conferred by law; since no such power was granted to the Government under the Act, its delegate could not lawfully review and set aside the Government's earlier order.
The High Court was correct in setting aside the Commissioner's order because it lacked legal authority, and the Revenue Tribunal must now decide the case in accordance with law.
doctrines: Doctrine of inherent powers
Doctrine of delegation of powers
Principle of finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: The company claimed deductions for management and miscellaneous expenses related to agricultural operations, which the tax authorities disputed.
issues_decided: Whether expenses on management, staff, and infrastructure were allowable as deductions under s. 6(2)(b)(iv) of the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948.
Whether modern agricultural practices justify broader interpretation of 'expenses of cultivation'.
holdings: Expenses for management, supervision, technical assistance, and allied activities are deductible if incurred for raising crops, marketing, and transportation.
Section 6(2)(b)(iv) must be interpreted broadly to include modern organizational needs of large-scale farming, not limited to basic cultivation activities.
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of tax deductions in agriculture
Economic reality doctrine
Doctrine of purposive construction

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent and costs, while the tenant claimed protection under the Bombay Rent Act by having paid arrears of rent.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act despite not paying the costs of the suit.
Whether the High Court could exercise discretion in favour of the tenant when the payment of costs was not brought to its notice during revision.
holdings: A tenant is entitled to protection from eviction under Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act only if they pay or tender both the arrears of rent and the costs of the suit; failure to pay costs disentitles the tenant to such protection.
This Court will not interfere with the High Court's exercise of discretion when the alleged payment of costs was not presented before it during the revision or review proceedings.
doctrines: Conditional protection against eviction
Judicial discretion in revision petitions
Procedural estoppel by omission

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a displaced person contested the cancellation of an excess land allotment made under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, claiming permanent rights over the full allotted area.
issues_decided: Whether the Section Officer-cum-Managing Officer and the Chief Settlement Commissioner had jurisdiction to revise and cancel part of an earlier allotment order?
Whether the reliance on Fard Taqsim and Khasra Girdawari records from Pakistan was valid for determining the nature of land abandoned and thus the entitlement to allotment?
Whether the cancellation of allotment of 15-17 1/2 standard acres for being in excess of entitlement was justified?
holdings: The Section Officer-cum-Managing Officer and the Chief Settlement Commissioner had jurisdiction under Sections 19 and 24(1) of the Act to review and cancel allotments found to be in excess of entitlement.
Fard Taqsim and Khasra Girdawari are authentic and important revenue records that can be relied upon to determine the classification and irrigation status of land abandoned in Pakistan.

The allotment was rightly reduced by 15-17 1/2 standard acres as the evidence showed the original land was not entirely canal-irrigated, and the excess was not justified under the rehabilitation scheme.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 19
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24(1)
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 33
Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, Sections 31 to 40
doctrines: Principle of jurisdictional validity of administrative authorities to review their own orders
Reliance on official revenue records for factual determination in rehabilitation claims
Doctrine of excess allotment correction based on accurate entitlement assessment

card.dispute: The plaintiffs and defendants fought over whether the defendants were entitled to restitution of possession and mesne profits after the plaintiffs recovered possession in a title suit, following the vesting of the suit lands in the State of Bihar under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants are entitled to restitution under Section 144 of the CPC after the suit estate vested in the State of Bihar.
Whether the State of Bihar, as the vested owner, should have been impleaded before granting restitution.
Whether the defendants can claim mesne profits for a period after the estate had vested in the State.
holdings: Once an estate vests in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, the right to possession and to recover possession also vests in the State, and private parties cannot claim restitution against each other.
The State is entitled as of right to be impleaded under Section 4(ee) of the Act, and failure to implead it before deciding restitution renders the order legally flawed.
Defendants cannot claim mesne profits for any period after the estate vested in the State, as the State becomes the lawful possessor entitled to such profits.
doctrines: Vesting of property in the State extinguishes private rights of possession
Deemed possession under statutory fiction
Necessity of impleading the State in proceedings affecting vested property

card.dispute: R.K. Garg challenged his arrest under Section 107/117 CrPC and the validity of a Section 144 CrPC order prohibiting land-grabbing activities in Saharanpur district.
issues_decided: Whether Section 144 CrPC is constitutionally valid and can be used in a general preventive manner.
Whether the District Magistrate had sufficient material to issue the Section 144 order.
Whether the broad application of the Section 144 order across the entire district was excessive or justified.
holdings: Section 144 CrPC is constitutionally valid and permits preventive orders in emergencies to maintain public order.
A District Magistrate may issue a general order under Section 144 CrPC based on credible information of an impending threat to public peace, even without individualized notice.
The wide territorial application of the order was justified given the organized, large-scale nature of the land-grabbing movement and the need for immediate preventive action.
doctrines: Preventive detention and executive action in maintenance of public order
Judicial deference to executive discretion in emergency measures
Proportionality in the use of preventive orders under Section 144 CrPC

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the auction sale of his property share, claiming it was vitiated by a material irregularity due to the omission of the auction time in the notice, and sought to set it aside.
issues_decided: Whether an order under Order XXI, Rule 90 CPC is a 'judgment' under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent of the Allahabad High Court, making it appealable?
Whether the omission of the hour of auction in the sale proclamation constituted a material irregularity that caused substantial injury and warranted setting aside the auction sale?
holdings: An order deciding an application under Order XXI, Rule 90 CPC is a 'judgment' within the meaning of Clause 10 of the Letters Patent because it determines valuable rights of the parties, such as the purchaser's right to confirmation of sale.

A material irregularity under Order XXI, Rule 69 CPC does not automatically vitiate a sale; the applicant must prove that the irregularity caused substantial injury, particularly that it led to inadequacy in the sale price, which was not established here.
provisions: Letters Patent of the Allahabad High Court, Clause 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 69 and 90
doctrines: Material irregularity in auction sales must be linked to actual prejudice
Test for 'judgment' under Letters Patent based on determination of valuable rights

card.dispute: The appellant mortgagor sought vacant possession of his mortgaged property from the Custodian after paying off the mortgage debt, but the Competent Officer had ordered the property's sale instead.
issues_decided: Whether the Competent Officer could direct the Custodian to deliver vacant possession of the mortgaged property upon payment of the mortgage debt in the absence of an agreement with the Custodian.
Whether the order for sale of the mortgaged property could stand after the mortgage debt was fully paid and accepted.
holdings: The Competent Officer cannot order the Custodian to deliver vacant possession of the mortgaged property unless there is an agreement between the Custodian and the mortgagor, as such an order would conflict with the Custodian's powers under the Administration of Evacuee Property Rules.

Once the mortgage debt is fully paid and accepted, the order for sale of the property cannot stand, as there is no outstanding debt to satisfy; however, only symbolic possession can be granted to the mortgagor in the absence of an agreement with the Custodian.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 12
Administration of Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950, Rule 14
doctrines: Overriding effect of special statutes
Conditional exercise of statutory discretion
Symbolic possession in lieu of vacant possession

card.dispute: The National Coal Development Corporation challenged the High Court's decision invalidating the acquisition of Manmohan Mathur's land for coal prospecting due to non-issuance of a mandatory notification under Section 7 of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land under Section 9 of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, without a prior notification under Section 7, was invalid?
Whether the retrospective amendment by the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Amendment Act, 1969, validating such acquisitions, could cure the procedural defect?
Whether Parliament had the competence to create legal fictions to validate otherwise invalid acquisitions?
holdings: An acquisition under Section 9 of the 1957 Act without a prior Section 7 notification is invalid if assessed under the original law.

The retrospective amendment by the 1969 Act deems a Section 7 notification to have been issued where no objection was filed under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, thereby validating the acquisition.

Parliament has the constitutional competence to create legal fictions through retrospective legislation, even if such fictions override judicial decisions, and courts cannot invalidate such laws on grounds of propriety alone.
provisions: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 7
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Section 28
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Amendment Act, 1969, Section 3
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Amendment Act, 1969, Section 3A
doctrines: Doctrine of Retrospective Legislation
Doctrine of Legal Fiction
Parliamentary Sovereignty
Validation of Invalid Administrative Actions

card.dispute: Nine appellants convicted of murder, grievous hurt, and destruction of evidence in a land dispute-related violence challenged their convictions and sentences.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the murder of Raj Ballabh Dubey by the appellants beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the right of private defence was available to the accused
Whether the delay in holding test identification parades prejudiced the accused
Whether the concurrent findings of the lower courts on guilt and circumstances of the offence could be interfered with
holdings: The appellants Raj Kishore Singh, Bindheyachal Singh, and Ram Bachan Bhar were guilty of murder under Section 302/34 IPC based on reliable eyewitness testimony and circumstantial evidence.
The right of private defence was not available as the prosecution party was not the aggressor and had fled, making any subsequent assault by the accused unjustified.
Delay in test identification parades did not prejudice the accused, especially since the witnesses were known to them and the parades would have only corroborative value.
The concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and High Court, being based on credible evidence, should not be disturbed by the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are entitled to great weight
Right of private defence is not available against fleeing persons
Test identification parade is not substantive evidence but only corroborative

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of an execution application filed in 1956, arguing it was barred by limitation and that the decree holder lacked good faith in pursuing execution.
issues_decided: Whether the 1956 execution application was barred by limitation under Section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 15 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the decree holder acted in good faith and with due diligence in pursuing execution proceedings
Whether the principle of res judicata barred the appellant from challenging the revival of execution proceedings in 1950
holdings: The execution application was not barred by limitation as the period of stay ordered by the Allahabad High Court was excluded under Section 15 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
The decree holder acted in good faith and with due diligence, and was entitled to protection under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
The appellant was barred by res judicata from challenging the 1950 revival of execution proceedings as no such objection was raised before the executing court.
doctrines: Exclusion of time during stay of execution under Section 15, Limitation Act
Res judicata in execution proceedings
Good faith and due diligence in execution under Section 14, Limitation Act

card.dispute: The landlord sought to evict the tenant after obtaining permission under the U.P. Rent Control Act, but the tenant challenged the validity of that permission in the eviction suit on the ground that the Rent Control Officer did not consider the tenant's need for accommodation.
issues_decided: Whether the permission granted by the Rent Control and Eviction Officer under Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, can be challenged in a suit for eviction.
Whether failure to consider the tenant's need for accommodation renders the permission invalid and liable to be questioned in a collateral proceeding.
holdings: The decision of the Rent Control and Eviction Officer under Section 3 is quasi-judicial and final unless challenged under Section 7-F of the Act or by writ under Article 226; it cannot be questioned in a collateral eviction suit.

Even if the Officer committed an error in not considering the tenant's needs, such error does not nullify jurisdiction and cannot be raised as a defence in an eviction suit if no remedy under the Act was pursued.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 16
doctrines: Finality of quasi-judicial orders
No collateral attack on administrative orders
Rules of natural justice not violated by erroneous decision within jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision requiring ad valorem court-fee on his cross-objections against an arbitrator's award in a land acquisition case, instead of a fixed fee under the Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether the award of an arbitrator under Section 8 of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, constitutes an 'order' for the purpose of appeal under the Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959
Whether Section 7(1) of the Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959, requires ad valorem court-fee on appeals against such awards
Whether cross-objections filed by a respondent in an appeal are covered under Article 3 of Schedule I of the Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959
holdings: An arbitrator's award under Section 8 of the 1952 Act is a binding decision and qualifies as an 'order' even if not executable or having the force of a decree.
Section 7(1) of the Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959, mandates ad valorem court-fee on appeals against compensation orders in land acquisition cases, regardless of whether the order is a decree.
Cross-objections seeking modification of an award are analogous to a memorandum of appeal and fall under Article 3 of Schedule I, requiring ad valorem court-fee.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 11
Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959, Article 3, Schedule I
Bombay Court-Fee Act, 1959, Article 13, Schedule II
doctrines: Ad valorem court-fee principle
Substance over form in legal pleadings
Interpretation of 'order' in fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of the bank's suit on a mortgage, arguing it was barred by Section 67A of the Transfer of Property Act and that the interest rate was penal.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by Section 67A of the Transfer of Property Act due to prior mortgages involving the appellant and his wife?
Whether the stipulated interest rate of 12% was penal and contrary to the Usurious Loans Act, 1918?
holdings: Section 67A does not apply where prior mortgages involved co-mortgagors (appellant and his wife), as they are not the same mortgagor; thus, the bank could enforce the mortgage separately.
The interest rate of 12% was unfair and penal; it was reduced to 10.5% until the preliminary decree and 6% thereafter.
doctrines: Doctrine of cumulative mortgage enforcement under Section 67A
Penal interest doctrine under Usurious Loans Act

card.dispute: S.A. Dange, a Communist Party leader, challenged his preventive detention under CrPC sections 107/117 and the constitutional validity of CrPC sections 144, 107, 114, and 117, seeking release via habeas corpus.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner's arrest and detention under Sections 114 and 107/117 CrPC were lawful and justified by a reasonable apprehension of breach of peace
Whether Sections 144, 107, 114, and 117 of the CrPC are constitutionally valid
Whether the petitioner’s detention was invalid due to jurisdictional or procedural irregularities
holdings: A magistrate may lawfully order preventive arrest under Section 114 CrPC and require a bond under Section 107/117 if there is a reasonable apprehension of breach of peace, even before an overt act occurs.
Sections 144, 107, 114, and 117 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as interpreted and applied, are constitutionally valid and do not violate fundamental rights.
The petitioner’s arrest was justified based on his admissions and supporting material showing a real threat to public order, despite the absence of a completed illegal act.
doctrines: Preventive detention for maintaining public order
Reasonable apprehension of breach of peace
Judicial review of constitutional validity of statutory provisions
Principle of infructuousness in writ petitions

card.dispute: Tenants claimed the right to purchase land from landowners under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, and the dispute centered on whether they needed to have been in continuous occupation for six years before the Act came into force on April 15, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant must have completed six years of continuous occupation of land by April 15, 1953, to claim the right to purchase under Section 18(1)(i) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
Whether a tenant must have been in tenancy on the date the Act came into force to claim the right to purchase.
holdings: A tenant is entitled to claim the right to purchase under Section 18(1)(i) if they complete six years of continuous occupation by the date of application, not necessarily by April 15, 1953.
It is not necessary for a tenant to have been in tenancy on April 15, 1953; the right to purchase depends on fulfilling conditions at the time of application, not at the commencement of the Act.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18(1)(i)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18(1)(ii)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18(1)(iii)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9-A
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Legislative intent inferred from statutory scheme and structure
Distinction between categories of tenants based on possession and timing of ejectment

card.dispute: The zamindar's successors sued the State of West Bengal for recovery of revenue collected after resumption of ferries and for a declaration that the revenue liability was abated; the State contested on grounds of limitation, jurisdiction, and adequacy of compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit for abatement of revenue following the resumption of ferries by the government.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation.
Whether the compensation paid for the resumption of ferries included the capitalized value of future revenue abatement.
holdings: The civil court had jurisdiction to decide claims for abatement of revenue despite administrative rules, as no statutory provision expressly or impliedly barred such suits.
The suit was not barred by limitation as it related to continuing wrongful collection of revenue.
The compensation paid for the ferries did not include the capitalized value of revenue abatement, as there was no evidence to support such an inclusion in the agreement or correspondence.
doctrines: Jurisdiction of civil courts cannot be excluded by implication; exclusion must be clear and express.
Doctrine of continuing cause of action applies to wrongful revenue collection.
Compensation for resumption does not automatically include abatement of future revenue unless clearly stated.

card.dispute: The appellant challenged recovery proceedings for agricultural income-tax arrears, claiming they were time-barred under the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, while the revenue authorities argued the proceedings commenced in time.
issues_decided: Whether recovery proceedings under the U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act commence when the assessing authority directs the Collector to recover the arrears or only when coercive steps like attachment are taken.
Whether the proceedings for recovery of tax and penalty for assessment years 1360F to 1363F were barred by limitation under Section 32(2) of the Act.
holdings: Recovery proceedings commence when the assessing authority makes a motion to the Collector to recover the amount as arrears of land revenue, not when coercive measures are taken.
Proceedings for years 1360F to 1362F were within time as orders were made within one year of the last instalment due; for 1363F, the order was beyond one year and thus barred.
doctrines: In pari materia
Commencement of recovery proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's refusal to interfere with the Sessions Judge's order setting aside their discharge in a criminal case under Section 436 IPC, arising from a property dispute and alleged arson.
issues_decided: Whether the committing Magistrate exceeded his jurisdiction by evaluating the credibility of witnesses and effectively deciding the case instead of merely determining if there was a prima facie case.
Whether the Sessions Judge was justified in setting aside the Magistrate's order of discharge.
Whether the High Court was correct in refusing to interfere with the Sessions Judge's order.
holdings: A Magistrate conducting a committal inquiry under Section 209 CrPC must determine only whether there is sufficient credible evidence to establish a prima facie case, not whether the accused is guilty.
If there is some evidence that could reasonably sustain a conviction, the Magistrate must commit the case to the Sessions Court, even if the evidence is contested or has inconsistencies.

The Magistrate exceeded his jurisdiction by disbelieving prosecution witnesses and preferring defense evidence, thereby trying the case instead of committing it, warranting the Sessions Judge's intervention.
The Sessions Judge and High Court were correct in holding that the Magistrate's discharge order was invalid due to jurisdictional overreach.
doctrines: Prima facie case standard in committal proceedings
Limited scope of Magistrate's inquiry under Chapter XVIII CrPC
Prohibition against Magistrate acting as a trial court in committal proceedings

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the transfer of land by the landlord after taking possession for personal cultivation, claiming a right to restoration under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958, as the landlord ceased cultivation within 12 years.
issues_decided: Whether Section 52 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958 applies to cases where possession was taken under the Berar Act before the 1958 Act came into force?

Whether a landlord who took possession under the Berar Act but had not completed two years of personal cultivation by December 30, 1958, is subject to the 12-year cultivation requirement under Section 52?
holdings: Section 52 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958 applies to cases where possession was taken under the Berar Act if the two-year personal cultivation period required under the Berar Act was not completed by December 30, 1958.

The extension of the cultivation period from two to twelve years under Section 52 applies to landlords who had not fulfilled their pre-existing obligation under the Berar Act by the commencement date of the 1958 Act.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 52
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Section 132(2)(i)
Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, Section 9(6)
Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, Rule 9
doctrines: Non-retrospective application of statutes
Savings clause under Section 132(2)(i)
Continuity of accrued rights under repealed legislation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Gift Tax Officer and D. H. Nazareth over whether Parliament had the constitutional competence to enact the Gift Tax Act, 1958, particularly with respect to gifts of agricultural land and buildings, or whether such power lay exclusively with State Legislatures under Entries 18 and 49 of the State List.
issues_decided: Whether the Gift Tax Act, 1958, falls within the legislative competence of Parliament under the residuary powers in Entry 97 of the Union List and Article 248 of the Constitution?
Whether the power to impose a gift tax is covered by Entries 18 or 49 of the State List, thereby excluding Parliament's power to legislate on the subject?
holdings: Parliament has the exclusive power to enact laws on matters not enumerated in the State or Concurrent Lists, including the power to impose taxes not mentioned in those Lists, under Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List.

The pith and substance of the Gift Tax Act is a tax on the act of gifting property, not on lands and buildings as such; hence, it does not fall within Entries 18 or 49 of the State List and is validly enacted under Parliament’s residuary powers.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, Union List, Entry 97
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, State List, Entry 18
Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, State List, Entry 49
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Residuary powers of legislation
Doctrine of enumerated powers

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and the Licensing Authority refused a 'no objection certificate' to Krishna Cinema for an annexe built before formal approval, leading to a legal challenge over procedural fairness and jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether construction of a cinema annexe before grant of a no objection certificate under Rule 89 is a bar to obtaining the certificate later
Whether the State Government can exercise the licensing power directly despite the Licensing Authority being the designated officer under the Act
Whether the State Government's refusal to grant a no objection certificate without applying its mind and giving reasons is legally valid
Whether the expression 'absolute discretion' in Rule 5(2) confers arbitrary power on the State Government
holdings: Completion of a cinema building before the grant of a no objection certificate does not automatically bar its conversion if the structure complies with rules.
The State Government cannot assume the licensing function of the District Magistrate; it can only exercise control, not supplant the Licensing Authority.
An appellate order under Section 8A must record reasons; failure to do so and not applying mind to facts renders the order invalid.
The phrase 'absolute discretion' does not confer arbitrary power; the discretion must be exercised judicially within statutory limits.
doctrines: Principle of reasoned decision-making in quasi-judicial proceedings
Doctrine of non-delegation of statutory powers
Rule against arbitrary exercise of discretion
Requirement of application of mind in administrative decisions

card.dispute: The landowner (Smt. Jatan Golcha) challenged the sale of leasehold rights of a company in liquidation (Golcha Properties Ltd.) in her land, done without her notice or hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, not being a party before the Company Judge, could file an appeal against the order for sale of leasehold rights affecting her property.
Whether the failure to issue notice to the landowner before selling leasehold rights violated principles of natural justice.
Whether the remedy of the appellant was limited to filing a suit with prior leave under Section 446 of the Companies Act.
holdings: An appeal under Section 483 of the Companies Act lies against any order in winding up proceedings, and the appellant could maintain it despite not being a formal party.
The rules of natural justice required the Official Liquidator and Company Judge to issue notice to the landowner before selling leasehold rights affecting her property.
The appellant could not be deprived of her right to appeal due to procedural default by the authorities; a suit was not her only remedy.
doctrines: Rule of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Right to appeal as an exception to party status
Prejudicial effect as basis for allowing appeals by non-parties

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the annulment of a land settlement made in their predecessors' favor, claiming it was done without a hearing and in violation of due process under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Collector's order annulling the settlement on May 24, 1961, was void for lack of a hearing under Section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the Deputy Collector's report constituted the final order under Section 4(h), thereby rendering the Additional Collector's hearing unnecessary.
Whether the State Government's confirmation of the annulment was premature, having been issued before the appeal to the Collector was heard.
holdings: An order annulling a settlement under Section 4(h) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, is void if passed without affording the affected party an opportunity of being heard.
The Deputy Collector’s report was recommendatory, not final; the Additional Collector passed the final order and thus was required to provide a hearing.
The Government’s confirmation of the annulment was premature, but the main ground for relief was the lack of hearing before the Additional Collector.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem (right to a hearing)
Doctrine of finality of administrative orders
Doctrine of jurisdictional error in administrative action

card.dispute: The temple and the archaka's family disputed whether certain properties were temple assets or hereditary service inam granted to the archaka's family.
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the Madras Religious Endowments Board under s. 57(1) operates as res judicata in a subsequent suit.
Whether the proceeding before the Board under s. 57(1) is a summary proceeding.
Whether the question of title to the properties was directly and substantially in issue in the Board's proceeding.
holdings: A decision by the Board under s. 57(1) of the Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927, if not challenged under s. 57(3), becomes final and binding and operates as res judicata.
Proceedings under s. 57(1) are not summary; they involve an exhaustive inquiry and contemplate judicial review via suit, making the decision capable of creating res judicata.
The question of property ownership was directly and substantially in issue in the scheme-framing process, as determining temple assets is essential to proper administration.
provisions: Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927, Section 57(1)
Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927, Section 57(3)
doctrines: Res judicata
Exhaustive administrative inquiry
Finality of administrative decisions when not challenged judicially

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction for assaulting and causing the death of Sheonandan Singh, arguing that the prosecution's version of events was inconsistent with the physical evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the concurrent findings of the trial and High Court could be overturned based on discrepancies in the prosecution's story and physical evidence.
Whether the location and pattern of bloodstains contradicted the prosecution's claim that the initial assault occurred near the well.
Whether the presence of weapons and bone fragments in the dalan supported the defence's claim of a counter-attack.
Whether the appellants' conduct after the incident, including Shital Singh's visit to the police station and hospital, indicated innocence.
holdings: Concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and High Court are not to be disturbed unless there is a clear error, and the defence failed to show such an error.
