The presence of significant blood near the well supports the prosecution's version that the initial assault occurred there, and the absence of a return blood trail does not discredit the prosecution.
The discovery of weapons and bone fragments in the dalan does not prove a fight occurred there, especially without evidence linking them to the victims or proving human origin.
Shital Singh’s visit to the police station and hospital does not establish innocence, particularly in light of the injuries sustained by the victims and lack of credible explanation for them.
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Benefit of doubt in criminal appeals
Evaluation of oral and circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: The State of Assam and Assam Tea Co. Ltd fought over whether the state's 1964 notifications incorporating part of the company's tea estate into the Nazira Town Committee were valid after the repeal of the 1923 Municipal Act and enactment of the 1957 Act.
issues_decided: Whether the 1951 notification extending sections 4 and 5 of the Assam Municipal Act, 1923 to the Nazira Town Committee continued in force after the 1923 Act was repealed and replaced by the 1957 Act.

Whether the State Government had the competence under the 1957 Act to issue notifications in 1964 revising the boundaries of the Nazira Town Committee without extending sections 4 and 5 of the 1957 Act afresh.
holdings: Under Section 26 of the Assam General Clauses Act, 1915, a notification issued under a repealed enactment continues in force if not inconsistent with the re-enacted law and no express provision supersedes it.
The 1951 notification under the 1923 Act remained valid and was deemed to have been issued under the 1957 Act, empowering the State Government to include contiguous areas into the Town Committee.
doctrines: Doctrine of continuation of statutory instruments after repeal and re-enactment
Doctrine of deeming provisions in statutes
Principle of consistency in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The mortgagors' representatives filed suits to redeem mortgages over 60 years old, and the mortgagees contested the suits as barred by limitation, with disputes over whether acknowledgments or statutory applications extended the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether certified copies of statements in mutation proceedings could prove acknowledgments of mortgage debts in the absence of original documents or witness testimony.
Whether presumptions under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, Section 44 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, or Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act could validate such acknowledgments.
Whether Section 12 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913, extends the limitation period for filing a suit for redemption after dismissal of an application under Section 4 of the Act.
holdings: Certified copies of mutation statements cannot prove acknowledgments without original documents or evidence verifying the signatories' identities or authority.

No presumption under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, Section 44 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, or Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act applies to prove genuineness of signatures in mutation records without proof of official duty to verify signatories.

Section 12 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913, does not extend the limitation period for redemption suits; it only makes summary orders final unless a suit is filed within one year of the order.
doctrines: Proof of signature and execution requires direct or presumptive evidence
Presumption of regularity of official acts does not extend to authentication of private signatures
Limitation periods cannot be extended by statutory appeal mechanisms unless expressly provided

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and the respondent, Champalal Kishanlal Mohta, fought over whether the sale of standing timber agreed to be severed under a contract constitutes a 'sale of goods' liable to sales tax under the Bombay Sales Tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of standing trees agreed to be severed under a contract amounts to a 'sale of goods' under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959.
Whether the retrospective amendment to the definition of 'goods' by Maharashtra Act 15 of 1967 is valid and applicable.
holdings: Standing timber agreed to be severed under a contract of sale qualifies as 'goods' under Section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, and thus constitutes a sale of goods for taxation purposes.

The expression 'sale of goods' in Entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution has the same meaning as in the Sale of Goods Act, and a State Legislature may validly include such goods via an inclusive definition, even retrospectively.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 54, List II, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record (review doctrine)
Inclusive definition under statutory interpretation
Doctrine of legislative competence regarding taxation of sale of goods
Retrospective operation of amendments

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat fought with the Jagirdar, Kumar Shri Ranjit Singhji Bhavan Singhji, over whether he was entitled to compensation for teak trees in his abolished jagir.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent had ownership rights over teak trees in the jagir villages.
Whether the teak trees were reserved or protected forests under the Indian Forest Act, thus excluding compensation.
Whether the restriction on alienation in the Sanad affected ownership of trees.
holdings: A jagirdar granted absolute rights over villages is also owner of trees growing on the land unless those rights were lawfully restricted.
No compensation can be denied for trees unless there is clear evidence that they were declared reserved or protected forests under law.
A restriction on alienation in a sanad does not negate ownership of natural growth like trees on the land.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1954, Section 11
doctrines: Principle of absolute grant
Presumption of ownership of natural accretions
Requirement of clear statutory restriction to extinguish rights

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over whether a reduction in royalty rates for coke despatches, as per an unregistered agreement, was valid under a registered lease.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered document effecting a reduction in royalty rates under a registered lease is admissible and enforceable?
Whether the appellant proved that the reduced royalty rates were implemented from July 1952 as claimed?
holdings: A document that varies essential terms of a registered lease, such as rent or royalty, must be registered to be valid; an unregistered agreement reducing royalty is not enforceable.
The appellant failed to prove that the reduced royalty rates were effectively implemented from July 1952, as required by the terms of the lease.
doctrines: Essential terms of a registered lease, like rent, cannot be altered by an unregistered document
Principle of enforceability of lease variations only through registered instruments

card.dispute: The All India Tea And Trading Co. Ltd. and the Collector of Darrang fought over the compensation amount for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: What was the appropriate compensation rate for the acquired market land?
Whether the High Court erred in determining compensation without considering the rising land prices and development in the locality?
holdings: The compensation for the acquired land should be assessed based on its market value in a developing locality with comparable sales and infrastructure growth.
The rate of Rs. 15,000 per Bigha, consistent with similar land in connected appeals, is appropriate, along with 15% additional compensation for compulsory acquisition.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Consideration of development and appreciation in land value for fair compensation

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the acquittal of Kartar Singh, while Kartar Singh's son appealed against his conviction for seven murders, involving conflicting witness statements and admissibility of prior statements made before the Committal Court.
issues_decided: Whether the statements of witnesses Kartar Kaur and Ranjeet Singh made before the Committal Court could be relied upon despite being disowned in trial as made under 'police pressure'.
Whether the High Court erred in disbelieving the testimony of witness Samandar Singh.
Whether the prosecution failed to prove the participation of Kartar Singh in the murders under Section 34 IPC.
Whether the procedure under Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act was complied with when the entire prior statement was read to the witness without specifically pointing out contradictions.
holdings: Prior statements made before the Committal Court are admissible and can be relied upon if the witness admits making them, even if later disowned as being under pressure, especially when such pressure is implausible given the sequence of judicial recordings.

The High Court erred in rejecting Samandar Singh’s testimony solely because others did not hear the pistol shot; discrepancies in perception due to wakefulness or position are natural and do not discredit credible testimony.

Kartar Singh was guilty under Section 302/34 IPC as his presence, armed with a pistol, active firing, and shared intent with his son established common purpose in the murders, despite not physically committing each act.

Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act does not require each contradictory passage to be put to the witness when the entire statement is read and the witness admits it as theirs; substantial compliance suffices when the witness has an opportunity to explain.
doctrines: Common purpose under Section 34 IPC
Admissibility of prior consistent statements
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Substantial compliance with procedural requirements

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Tarlok Singh, who had been convicted of murdering Ishar Kaur under Section 302 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the prosecution witnesses Harnam Kaur and Kartar Singh and acquitting Tarlok Singh despite the trial court's conviction.
Whether the delay in sending the First Information Report to the Magistrate casts doubt on the prosecution's version of events.
Whether the prosecution version of the incident was probable and consistent with human conduct.
holdings: The High Court was justified in disbelieving the prosecution witnesses due to material contradictions and improbabilities in their testimony, even if they were partially reliable.
The unexplained delay in transmitting the First Information Report created suspicion about the authenticity of the prosecution's timeline and case version.
The prosecution's account of the incident was improbable, particularly regarding the conduct of the accused and the witnesses, undermining the reliability of the evidence.
doctrines: Appreciation of witness credibility by appellate courts
Principle of partial reliability of witnesses
Presumption of innocence and benefit of doubt in criminal appeals

card.dispute: The Collector of Darrang and Assam Industries (P) Ltd. contested the compensation amount for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, specifically differing on valuation of land used as a market (hat) and the remaining agricultural land.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for the hat land at Rs. 15,000 per bigha was justified based on prior sales and rental value?
Whether the compensation for the non-hat land should be increased from Rs. 300 to a higher rate based on lease evidence?
holdings: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s valuation of the hat land at Rs. 15,000 per bigha, finding it reasonable based on a prior sale and rental income, even if post-notification sales were disregarded.

The Court held that the non-hat land deserved higher compensation at Rs. 1,000 per bigha, rejecting claims of collusion in leases and recognizing their evidentiary value for market rate determination.
doctrines: Relevant date for compensation is the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Compensation may consider prior sales and rental value, but not speculative or post-notification transactions
Lease evidence may be used to determine market value unless proven collusive

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Gift-Tax, Kerala fought with Dr. George Kuruvilla over whether a gift of a hospital building and land to his son was exempt from gift tax under Section 5(1)(xiv) of the Gift Tax Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the gift of a hospital building and land by a medical practitioner to his son was made 'in the course of carrying on a profession' within the meaning of Section 5(1)(xiv) of the Gift Tax Act, 1958.
Whether the gift was made bona fide for the purpose of the donor's profession, entitling the assessee to exemption from gift tax.
holdings: A gift is exempt under Section 5(1)(xiv) only if it is made in the course of carrying on a business, profession, or vocation and is proven to be bona fide for that purpose.

The mere fact that the donee later joined the donor's profession and the property was used for the same purpose does not, without more, prove the gift was made in the course of or for the purpose of the profession.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of tax exemption clauses
Burden of proof in claiming tax exemptions

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the High Court's decision that a notification exempting a land sale from pre-emption rights was issued mala fide, after the plaintiffs had already obtained a decree for pre-emption.
issues_decided: Whether the notification issued under Section 8(2) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, excluding a specific land sale from pre-emption rights, was issued mala fide.
Whether a party challenging state action on grounds of mala fides must specifically name the officer(s) responsible for the alleged misconduct.
holdings: A notification issued under Section 8(2) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, that excludes a land sale from pre-emption rights during pendency of a pre-emption suit may be held mala fide if material facts are suppressed and proper procedures ignored.
A party alleging mala fide action by the state is not required to name the specific officer(s) responsible; imposing such a burden would be intolerable and contrary to law.
doctrines: Mala fide administrative action
Burden of proof in challenging state action
Suppression of material facts vitiating official orders

card.dispute: The appellant Subedar challenged his conviction in a dacoity and murder case based on circumstantial evidence, claiming a miscarriage of justice.
issues_decided: Whether the circumstantial evidence against the appellant was sufficient to sustain his conviction under Section 396 IPC read with Section 109 IPC.
Whether the courts below erred in failing to properly scrutinize the reliability of witness testimony and in ignoring material evidence.
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with concurrent findings of guilt by the trial and high courts in a criminal appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
holdings: Circumstantial evidence must conclusively point to the guilt of the accused and exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence; the evidence here failed this test.
The testimony of prosecution witnesses was infirm and contradictory, and could not safely be relied upon to establish the appellant's presence at the scene or abetment of the crime.
The Supreme Court can interfere under Article 136 when there is a grave miscarriage of justice due to misapprehension of evidence or ignoring material facts, even if two courts have convicted.
doctrines: Principle of circumstantial evidence requiring a complete chain excluding innocence
Doctrine of reappreciation of evidence in cases of grave injustice under Article 136
Requirement of fair opportunity to accused under Section 342 CrPC

card.dispute: The Forest Department cancelled timber tally rights granted to Ram Sanehi Singh, who challenged the cancellation as violating natural justice and sought relief through a writ petition.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petition under Article 226 was maintainable despite the dispute arising from a contractual agreement with a public authority.
Whether the order of the Divisional Forest Officer cancelling the tally was void for violating the principles of natural justice.
holdings: A writ petition under Article 226 is maintainable even if the right claimed arises from a contract, when the impugned action is by a public authority exercising statutory power.
An administrative order affecting a person's property rights must comply with natural justice; denial of a hearing renders the order illegal and void, regardless of its administrative nature.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Maintainability of writ petitions against public authorities in contractual disputes
Rule against bias and right to hearing in administrative actions

card.dispute: The Union of India, as owner of the Central Railway, sued the Lonavla Municipality for refund of taxes paid on railway properties, claiming the consolidated tax was not covered by the notification making railways liable to pay house-tax.
issues_decided: Whether the consolidated tax imposed by the Lonavla Municipality under the Bombay District Municipal Acts of 1901 and 1925 was a 'tax on buildings and lands' within the meaning of the Central Government's 1917 notification under Section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890.
Whether the Union of India was liable to pay the consolidated tax that included a water rate component despite not availing municipal water services.
holdings: A consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands is legally a 'tax on buildings and lands' and falls within the scope of the 1917 notification making railway properties liable to such tax.

The inclusion of a water rate component in the consolidated tax does not change its character as a general tax on buildings and lands, especially when it is levied on a sliding scale irrespective of actual water consumption.
provisions: Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, Section 59(1) and second proviso, Clause (c)
Bombay District Municipal Act, 1925, Section 73 and Section 110
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Historical context in interpretation of notifications
Substance over form in tax classification

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the Lonavla Municipality's imposition of a consolidated tax on railway lands and buildings, arguing it exceeded the scope of central government notifications under the Indian Railways Act.
issues_decided: Whether the consolidated tax imposed by the municipality under clause (c) of the second proviso to Section 59 of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, falls within the scope of 'tax on lands and buildings' as notified under Section 135 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890.
Whether the change from separate house tax and water rate to a consolidated tax altered the legal nature of the liability of the railway administration.
holdings: A consolidated tax assessed as a rate on buildings and lands under clause (c) of the second proviso to Section 59 is legally a 'tax on lands and buildings' and thus covered by the 1917 notification under Section 135 of the Indian Railways Act.
The historical context and purpose of the 1917 notification confirm that the Central Government intended to include the consolidated tax, not merely a house tax, within the railway's liability.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Use of historical and contextual background in statutory interpretation
Substance over form in tax characterization

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of the respondent's second suit on the grounds that the condition to pay defendants' costs from the first suit had not been fulfilled.
issues_decided: Whether the second suit was maintainable despite non-compliance with the condition of paying costs from the first suit
Whether the subject-matter of the second suit was the same as that of the first suit under Order 23 Rule 1, CPC
holdings: A court may permit withdrawal of a suit with liberty to file a fresh suit on the same subject-matter, subject to conditions, but such conditions only apply if the subject-matter is identical.
The subject-matter of a suit refers to the cause of action and relief claimed; mere identity of issues or property does not make the subject-matter the same.

The second suit was maintainable because its cause of action and relief sought—possession based on title from inheritance—differed from the first suit’s claim for partition and declaration of adoption.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 1
doctrines: Identity of subject-matter under Order 23 Rule 1 CPC
Cause of action and relief determine the subject-matter of a suit
Non-compliance with a condition precedent does not bar a suit if the subject-matter differs

card.dispute: The Revenue challenged the genuineness of a property transfer by a Muslim husband to his wife in satisfaction of an enhanced meher (dower debt) of Rs. 1 lakh, seeking to assess the property's income in the husband's hands under Section 16(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to reframe questions in a reference under Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922?
Whether the question referred by the Tribunal—regarding taxability of income from property transferred in satisfaction of enhanced meher—was a valid question of law?
holdings: The High Court has no jurisdiction to reframe or introduce new questions in a reference under Section 66(1); it can only answer the question of law referred by the Tribunal.
The High Court erred in reframing the reference; the proper course was to either answer the question as framed or call for a supplementary statement of case if clarification was needed.
doctrines: Limited scope of High Court's advisory jurisdiction in tax references
Principle of jurisdictional restraint in references under Section 66(1)

card.dispute: The appellant, Zora Singh, a military personnel, fought to retain an allotment of land in India granted in lieu of land he claimed to have been awarded in Pakistan for gallantry or meritorious service, which the authorities cancelled on grounds of forged documents and lack of entitlement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had previously concluded the genuineness of the documents relied upon by the appellant, thereby binding the Commissioner on that finding.
Whether the Commissioner's finding that the documents were forged was vitiated by reliance on extraneous or invalid reasons.
Whether the appellant was entitled to the land allotment based on a gallantry or meritorious service award, as supported by additional evidence.
holdings: The High Court did not previously conclude the genuineness of the documents; it only remanded the matter for reconsideration, so the Commissioner was free to assess authenticity.
A finding based on objective evidence is not vitiated by some extraneous reasons, as long as sufficient legal evidence supports the conclusion, unlike in cases of subjective satisfaction.
The appellant failed to prove he received a gallantry or meritorious service award; no official record or gazette notification existed, and he did not meet the service requirements for such an award.
doctrines: Supervisory jurisdiction in certiorari
Objective vs. subjective satisfaction in administrative decisions
Principle of sufficiency of evidence in judicial review

card.dispute: The Union of India and the respondents (trustees of R.K. Modi) fought over whether the government could set off excess rent payments made under a mistaken belief about the correct standard rent against the landlord's claim for arrears.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant (Union of India) paid rent in excess of the standard rent by mistake between April 1950 and May 1960.
Whether the appellant was entitled to set off or adjust the alleged excess rent payments against the respondents' claim for arrears of rent.
holdings: The appellant could not claim adjustment of excess rent payments because it failed to apply to the Rent Controller within six months of each payment as required by Section 7 of the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950.

The appellant was not entitled to equitable set-off under general law or under Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as the statutory remedy under the Rent Control Act was exclusive and the plea of mistake was not substantiated.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 7
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 11
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 17
doctrines: Statutory exclusivity of remedy
Non-applicability of equitable set-off where a specific statutory remedy exists
Mistake under Section 72 requires proof of involuntary payment due to error

card.dispute: The landlord filed a suit for ejectment and rent recovery; the tenant later challenged the jurisdiction of the court that passed the decree during execution proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court can entertain a jurisdictional challenge to a decree if the objection does not appear on the face of the record?
Whether a decree can be treated as a nullity in execution if the lack of jurisdiction requires factual investigation?
holdings: An objection to the jurisdiction of the court that passed a decree can be raised in execution only if it appears on the face of the record; otherwise, the executing court cannot go behind the decree.
A decree is not a nullity in execution merely due to alleged lack of inherent jurisdiction if determining that lack requires examining facts or interpreting lease terms not apparent on the record.
provisions: Bombay Rents Hotel & Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 5(8)
Bombay Rents Hotel & Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 6
doctrines: Decree binding until set aside
Jurisdictional challenge in execution limited to face of record
Nullity exception for lack of inherent jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Amritsar Improvement Trust sought to implement a development-cum-housing scheme including areas outside municipal limits, which respondents challenged as ultra vires the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the Amritsar Improvement Trust could include areas outside municipal limits in a 'development scheme' under Section 24(1) of the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922.

Whether a scheme purporting to be a 'development scheme' but including areas outside municipal limits could be validated as an 'expansion scheme' under Section 24(2) even without forming the required opinion.
Whether the government's sanction under Section 41 could validate a scheme that was inherently ultra vires.
Whether the impugned scheme could be partially upheld if part of it was invalid.
holdings: A 'development scheme' under Section 24(1) cannot include areas outside municipal limits; only an 'expansion scheme' under Section 24(2) may do so, subject to the Trust forming the requisite opinion.
The Trust cannot be deemed to have framed an 'expansion scheme' without expressly forming the opinion required by Section 24(2); the mislabeling of a scheme cannot be cured by later justification.
Government sanction under Section 41 cannot validate a scheme that is ultra vires the Act, as the power to frame schemes is limited and conditional.
The scheme is one and indivisible; it cannot be partially valid and must fall as a whole if any part is ultra vires.
doctrines: Condition precedent to exercise of power
Doctrine of strict interpretation of statutory powers
Doctrine of indivisibility of schemes
Non-justiciability of government sanction when ultra vires

card.dispute: The appellants (Asnew Drums Private Ltd.) challenged the Bombay High Court's dismissal of their appeal against the District Judge's order for the sale of mortgaged property to recover dues owed to the Maharashtra State Finance Corporation.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies to the High Court against an order of sale of mortgaged property passed by the District Judge under Section 32(8) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, read with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Whether the High Court was justified in summarily dismissing the appeal
holdings: An appeal lies to the High Court against an order of sale under Section 32(8) of the State Financial Corporations Act, as the phrase 'in the manner provided in the Code of Civil Procedure' includes the procedural right to appeal under Order XLIII, Rule 1(j) of the CPC.
The High Court was not justified in summarily dismissing the appeal, especially when this Court had granted special leave, indicating a prima facie case on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII, Rule 1(j)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Inclusion of appellate remedies in procedural 'manner' under statutes
Rejection of persona designata theory in this context

card.dispute: The appellants (Bachan Singh & Ors.) challenged the validity of a suit for possession filed by the respondents (Gauri Shankar Agarwal & Ors.), claiming a valid lease and that the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the lease in favour of the appellants was valid under the U.P. Tenancy Act
Whether the suit filed by the respondents was barred by limitation
holdings: A lease granted by an agent without the required written consent of the landlord or his manager is invalid, and subsequent ratification cannot be considered if not raised before the appellate authority.

A finding of fact by a revenue authority that possession began in 1950 is binding, and a suit based on that timeline is within limitation; challenges to evidentiary basis must be raised before the appellate authority to be considered.
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Principle of ratification in contract law
Binding nature of findings of fact in revenue proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted under Section 302/149 IPC and other sections for the murder of Bhullan and Rameshwar and injuring Ram Chandra, challenged their conviction, arguing that the prosecution failed to explain injuries on the appellant Bankey Lal and that the evidence was unreliable.
issues_decided: Whether the failure of the prosecution to explain injuries on the accused necessitates discarding the entire prosecution case
Whether the First Information Report (FIR) and dying declaration must fully disclose multiple attack sites for the prosecution version to be accepted
Whether the fact that the accused party first reported the incident undermines the prosecution's case
holdings: The failure of prosecution witnesses to explain injuries on the accused does not automatically discredit their testimony if other evidence corroborates the core events.
An FIR and dying declaration need not contain exhaustive details, especially when given under exigent circumstances, and omissions do not necessarily weaken reliable evidence.
The fact that the accused reported the incident first does not discredit the prosecution, particularly when the injured party was too incapacitated to report it.
doctrines: falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
corroboration of testimony
appreciation of evidence in criminal appeals

card.dispute: Co-sharers fought over whether a partition suit could proceed for bakasht land after the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 came into force, which vested such land in the State and created tenancy rights for those in khas possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' possession of bakasht land triggered the operation of Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, thereby preventing the passing of a final decree in a partition suit.
Whether a co-sharer in constructive possession retains rights under the Act despite not being in physical possession.
Whether the deeming provision of Section 6 benefits all co-sharers when one is in khas possession.
holdings: The operation of Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act does not exclude co-sharers from its benefits merely because they are not in physical possession.
A co-sharer is in constructive possession through another co-sharer, and such possession is legally recognized under the Act.
The deeming provision of Section 6 enures to the benefit of all co-sharers who are in legal possession, entitling them to be recognized as raiyats.
provisions: Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, Chapter IV
doctrines: Constructive possession of co-sharers
Deemed tenancy under land reform statutes
Benefit of deeming provisions to all entitled persons in law

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed whether the respondent's deposit of the sale amount on January 2, 1960, after the stipulated deadline of January 1, 1960 (a holiday), amounted to a valid performance under a compromise decree.
issues_decided: Whether a party's failure to perform an act by a stipulated date in a compromise decree, due to the date being a holiday, constitutes a breach when performance occurs on the next working day.
Whether an executing court can construe a compromise decree in light of applicable law without varying its terms.
Whether a compromise decree is to be treated purely as a contract, binding absolutely, or as a judicial order with different legal implications.
holdings: A party required to perform an act by a specified date in a decree may perform it on the next working day if the last date falls on a court holiday, as the law recognizes such practical impossibility.
An executing court may interpret a decree in accordance with law without altering its terms; construing compliance in light of holidays does not amount to modification.

A compromise decree, though based on agreement, is more than a private contract—it is a judicial order and must be enforced as such, subject to legal principles governing court orders, not strict contractual rules.
doctrines: Substantial compliance with decree
Judicial construction of consent decrees
Distinction between contract and court decree
Performance on next practicable day doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, arguing it violated their fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31(2) of the Constitution in relation to the acquisition of property in Amritsar’s walled city.
issues_decided: Whether the Act violates Article 14 due to arbitrary power to declare areas as 'damaged' and alleged discretion to acquire under more favorable laws.
Whether the restrictions imposed by the Act are unreasonable and violate the rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g).
Whether the acquisition and compensation provisions of the Act violate Article 31(2).
holdings: The power to declare an area as 'damaged' under the Act is not arbitrary or unguided, as it is based on the clear purpose of rehabilitating areas affected by serious communal riots.
The Act does not violate Article 19(1)(f) and (g) as the restrictions are reasonable and imposed for a public purpose, with adequate procedural safeguards.

The compensation mechanism under the Act complies with Article 31(2), as it is based on principles similar to the Land Acquisition Act and includes provision for alternative accommodation and fair market value.
provisions: Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 2(d)
Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 3
Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 12
Punjab Development of Damaged Areas Act, 1951, Section 20
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Balancing of fundamental rights with public interest
Principle of fair compensation under Article 31(2)
Incorporation by reference of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Maharashtra Sugar Mills Ltd. disputed whether a portion of managing agent commission, attributable to tax-exempt agricultural income, could be deducted from the company's gross profits.
issues_decided: Whether expenditure on managing agent commission is deductible under s. 10(2)(xv) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, even if part of the business income is agricultural and not taxable.
Whether Rule 23 of the Income-tax Rules permits apportionment of managing agent commission between agricultural and non-agricultural income.
holdings: Expenditure is deductible under s. 10(2)(xv) if incurred wholly and exclusively for the business, regardless of whether all income from the business is taxable.
Rule 23 does not authorize disallowance of managing agent commission; it only bars deduction of cultivation-related expenses, not managerial remuneration.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Deduction allowed if expenditure is wholly and exclusively for business purpose
No apportionment of expenditure required based on taxability of income streams

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the validity of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1965, particularly its amendments affecting land rights and acquisition, claiming violation of constitutional protections.
issues_decided: Whether Chapter III of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1965, which modifies landlords' rights, is protected under Article 31-A(1) of the Constitution
Whether the second proviso to Article 31-A(1) requires payment of market value compensation when land under personal cultivation is acquired
Whether Chapter IV of the Act, dealing with ceiling limits, could be invalidated when its provisions were not brought into force
holdings: Chapter III modifies landlords' substantive rights in their estates and thus falls within the protection of Article 31-A(1), saving it from challenges under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

The second proviso to Article 31-A(1) does not apply because no ceiling limit was in force without a notification under Section 1(3), and Bhagchar cultivation does not constitute 'personal cultivation' by the landlord.
The High Court should not have examined the constitutional validity of Chapter IV since it was not in force, and courts cannot rule on the vires of unenforced provisions.
provisions: Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1965, Chapter III and IV
doctrines: Doctrine of severability
Doctrine of prospective overruling
Principle that unenforced statutory provisions cannot be challenged for constitutional invalidity

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Gift Tax challenged whether a coparcener who took a lesser share in a Hindu Undivided Family partition, thereby allotting a greater share to others, made a 'gift' liable to gift tax.
issues_decided: Whether a partition in a Hindu Undivided Family amounts to a 'transfer of property' under the Gift Tax Act, 1958
Whether a coparcener's acceptance of a lesser share in partition constitutes a 'gift' under Section 2(xii) of the Act
Whether the transaction falls within the extended definition of 'transfer of property' under Section 2(xxiv), including clause (d), of the Act
holdings: Partition of joint Hindu family property is not a transfer of property under general law, as it merely converts joint enjoyment into several ownership without conveying new title.
A coparcener has no definite share in joint family property before partition; hence, taking a lesser share does not amount to a voluntary transfer or 'gift' under Section 2(xii).

The act of accepting a smaller share in partition does not constitute a 'transaction' under Section 2(xxiv)(d) aimed at diminishing one's property to increase another's, as no individual property interest exists prior to partition.
doctrines: No transfer of property in partition of HUF
Indeterminate share of coparcener before partition
Literal interpretation of tax statutes

card.dispute: Five appellants challenged their convictions for murder, rioting, and related offences, claiming alibi and lack of overt acts to sustain liability under joint liability provisions.
issues_decided: Whether Chandrika Prasad Singh successfully established an alibi to disprove his presence at the scene of the crime.
Whether the other four appellants could be convicted under Section 326/149 IPC without proof of individual overt acts, based on their membership in an unlawful assembly with a common object.
holdings: The plea of alibi raised by Chandrika Prasad Singh failed because the evidence did not conclusively prove his absence from the scene at the time of the incident, and the onus of proving alibi was not discharged.

Members of an unlawful assembly who were present at the scene and shared the common object could be convicted under Section 326/149 IPC even without proof of individual overt acts, if others in the assembly committed assaults in furtherance of the common object.
doctrines: Doctrine of alibi
Doctrine of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Common object of unlawful assembly

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assessee fought over whether a secretly received sum of Rs. 1.50 lakhs by the assessee, not disclosed in his accounts, was taxable as income or should be presumed to be an adjustment of principal.
issues_decided: Whether the undisclosed receipt of Rs. 1.50 lakhs by the assessee was taxable as income in the year of receipt
Whether, in the absence of specific appropriation, a payment received by a creditor should be presumed to be applied first to interest or to principal for tax purposes
Whether the system of accounting followed by the assessee (Chetty system) is relevant in determining the nature of the receipt
holdings: An undisclosed receipt not accounted for is taxable as income when it is advantageous for the assessee to treat it as interest to evade tax.
The presumption that a payment is first applied to outstanding interest applies unless the circumstances show the creditor intended otherwise.
The system of accounting is irrelevant when the receipt itself is not entered into the books, indicating an intent to conceal income.
doctrines: Presumption in favour of interest appropriation
Taxpayer's right to choose most favourable appropriation in dispute with revenue
Materiality of concealment in determining taxability

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the compensation awarded for three plots of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, seeking higher compensation based on comparable sales and nearby land values.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for plot 67/1A-1 should be enhanced based on comparable land values in the vicinity.
Whether the compensation for the hilly, non-road-facing plot 67/1A-2 and 67/2 should be increased despite topographical disadvantages.
Whether plot 67/1A-4, abutting the main K.K. Road, should be compensated at the same rate as lands near Civil Lines due to locational advantage.
holdings: The court held that plot 67/1A-1, though not as advantageously located as lands in Ex. P-7, warranted enhanced compensation at Rs. 500 per cent due to proximity to developed areas and road access.
The court upheld the lower compensation for the 255-cent hilly plot without road frontage, holding that its difficult terrain justified no enhancement.
The court enhanced compensation for plot 67/1A-4 by Rs. 250 per cent, holding it deserved parity with Civil Lines-area lands due to road frontage and level terrain.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Rejection of mechanical reliance on comparable sales without locational and physical comparison
Consideration of physical features like road frontage, topography, and usability in determining compensation

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax and the respondent, Kirpashankar Dayashankar Worah, disputed whether a trustee administering a family trust is liable to be assessed to wealth tax under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether a trustee holding property under a private trust is assessable to wealth tax under Section 21(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether the shares of the beneficiaries in the trust were determinate or indeterminate, affecting the rate of tax under Section 21(4).
holdings: A trustee is assessable to wealth tax under Section 21(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, as the Act treats the trustee as holding property on behalf of beneficiaries, regardless of the general law of trusts.

Where the shares of beneficiaries in a trust are indeterminate due to the settlor and other beneficiaries being alive and entitled to benefits, the trustee must be assessed at the maximum marginal rate under Section 21(4).
doctrines: Strict construction of taxing statutes with benefit to the assessee
Avoidance of rendering statutory provisions otiose
Statutory fiction of holding property 'on behalf of' beneficiaries as equivalent to 'for the benefit of'
Use of precedent from analogous provisions in the Income-tax Act

card.dispute: The assessee company, Dalmia Jain & Co. Ltd., fought the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether litigation expenses incurred in defending a suit were deductible as revenue expenditure or were non-deductible capital expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the litigation expenses incurred by the assessee were of a capital or revenue nature.
Whether the expenditure was incurred for acquiring a new asset or for protecting the existing business.
holdings: Expenditure incurred to protect the trade or business of the assessee is revenue expenditure, even if the assessee is defending a claim.
Litigation expenses are deductible as revenue expenditure if incurred wholly and exclusively for business protection, regardless of the outcome of the litigation.
doctrines: Capital vs. revenue expenditure distinction
Deduction based on purpose of expenditure
Revenue expenditure for business protection

card.dispute: The original members of the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan society challenged the constitutional validity of the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan Act, 1962, which reconstituted their society into a statutory body and transferred its property, arguing it violated their fundamental rights to freedom of association and to hold property.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan Act, 1962 violates the right to freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c) by altering the composition of the society without consent of its original members.
Whether the Act is protected under the reasonable restrictions clause of Article 19(4).
Whether Parliament had legislative competence to enact the Act creating a new statutory body not declared as an institution of national importance.
Whether the transfer of all properties of the society to the new Sammelan violates the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f).
holdings: The Act violates Article 19(1)(c) as it alters the composition of the association, infringing the members' right to determine who forms part of their association.
The restriction imposed by the Act is not saved under Article 19(4) as it does not serve sovereignty, integrity, public order, or morality.
Parliament lacked legislative competence to create a new body (Sammelan) not declared as an institution of national importance, even if the original society was so declared.
The transfer of all property to a new legal entity without dissolving the original society constitutes an unreasonable restriction under Article 19(1)(f), violating the right to hold property.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 63, List I, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Freedom of association includes the right to control the composition of an association.
Reasonable restrictions under Article 19 must fall within the specified grounds and be proportionate.
Legislative competence must align with the subject matter and declaration made in the Constitution.
Total deprivation of property without dissolution of the original body is not a reasonable restriction in public interest.

card.dispute: The appellant property owner challenged the validity of property tax demands on the grounds of excessive delegation under the Act and the failure to maintain ward-wise assessment books as allegedly required.
issues_decided: Whether Section 129 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949 suffers from excessive delegation due to absence of a maximum tax rate
Whether Rule 10 of the Taxation Rules mandates the maintenance of ward-wise assessment books or is merely directory
Whether the tax levy is invalid for being based on a single city-wide assessment book instead of ward-wise books
holdings: Section 129 does not involve excessive delegation because the Act and rules provide sufficient framework and ultimate control lies with elected councillors subject to state oversight.
Rule 10 is permissive, not mandatory, and grants the Commissioner discretion to maintain either one city-wide assessment book or separate ward-wise books.

The use of a single assessment book does not invalidate the tax levy, and rules referring to 'ward assessment books' must be read as applying to any assessment book, regardless of territorial division, to avoid absurdity and ensure legislative intent.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 129
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 454
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 455
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 456
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 457
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 406
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 10
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 13
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 15
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 19
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 9
Taxation Rules under the Act, Rule 30
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of purposive interpretation
Presumption against rendering statutory provisions ineffective

card.dispute: The appellant, Gurdip Singh, challenged his conviction and death sentence for murdering his father, arguing that the circumstances warranted a lesser sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence supported conviction under Section 302 IPC for murder
Whether the death sentence was justified in the circumstances of the case
holdings: The appellant was rightly convicted under Section 302 IPC as the evidence, including eyewitness testimony and forensic proof, established that he intentionally fired the fatal shots.
The death sentence was set aside and commuted to life imprisonment due to the possibility of provocation by the deceased, making it not the 'rarest of rare' cases warranting capital punishment.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Principle of proportionality in sentencing
Credibility of prosecution witnesses and use of extra-judicial confession

card.dispute: The State of Kerala appealed the acquittal of Dominic Varkey, who was accused of murdering his elder brother George, leading to a dispute over whether the killing was in self-defence.
issues_decided: Whether Dominic Varkey acted in private defence of his body against a real and imminent threat from his brother George
Whether Dominic exceeded the right of private defence by using disproportionate force
Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the Sessions Court's acquittal
holdings: A person exercising the right of private defence is entitled to defend themselves if there is a reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt or danger to life, judged objectively from the circumstances at the time.
The right of private defence does not require the defender to endure risk; the force used must be proportionate to the threat, but need not be minimal if the danger is real and immediate.
The High Court erred in convicting the appellant as the evidence supported that George was the aggressor and Dominic acted within the bounds of self-defence.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Right of private defence
Reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt
Proportionality in self-defence

card.dispute: The Mishra family members appealed their convictions for assaulting Shyamdutt Tiwari over possession of garden land, challenging the High Court's reversal of their acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's order of acquittal based on unreliable evidence
Whether the convictions under Sections 307, 326, 324, and 109 IPC were legally sustainable based on the nature of injuries and roles of the accused
Whether the trial suffered from misjoinder of charges due to joint trial of accused involved in two related incidents
holdings: The High Court was justified in sifting credible evidence, including the victim's testimony and a recorded statement (Ext. 7), to overturn the acquittal.
Convictions under Section 307 IPC were reduced to Section 326 or 324 IPC where injuries, though grievous, did not conclusively show intent to murder.
Joint trial was valid as both incidents formed part of a single transaction with common accused and a shared unlawful objective.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in cases of insufficient proof of intention to kill
Common object of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Corroboration through dying declaration (later treated as corroborative statement)
Principle of joint trial in cases forming part of a single transaction

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Dewan Bahadur Brij Mohan Zutshi claimed title to certain lands allegedly granted by the Maharaja of Ratlam, which the State of Madhya Pradesh disputed.
issues_decided: Whether the alleged grant of land to Dewan Bahadur Brij Mohan Zutshi was valid and enforceable.
Whether the order of the Maharaja dated May 10, 1948, could confer title despite the prior merger of the state and the subsequent withholding of approval by the Regional Commissioner.
holdings: An alleged grant by a ruler after the merger of a princely state into the Indian Union is unenforceable unless accepted by the successor government.
An order by a ruler pending approval under a post-merger review mechanism does not create a legal right if approval is not granted.
doctrines: Doctrine of merger of princely states
Principle of successor government's acceptance for post-merger grants

card.dispute: Juwar Singh appealed his conviction for murder and unlawful assembly, claiming he was wrongly identified and had injuries supporting his alibi.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant Juwar Singh was rightly convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC and Section 148 IPC based on eyewitness testimony?
Whether the medical evidence of the appellant's injury supports his defence of having been assaulted while trying to pacify the fight?
Whether discrepancies in eyewitness accounts undermine their reliability?
holdings: The conviction based on consistent eyewitness testimony is valid even if there are minor discrepancies, as the core version of events remains credible.
The medical evidence of a lacerated wound on the appellant does not support his defence, as it was caused by a blunt object like a lathi, not a sickle, and timing was unestablished.
The concurrent findings of the trial and high court are reliable and should not be overturned in the absence of material contradictions affecting credibility.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts
Reliability of eyewitness testimony

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether secondary evidence of an insufficiently stamped written agreement to grant a lease could be admitted in court.
issues_decided: Whether sections 35 and 36 of the Stamp Act bar the admission of secondary evidence of an insufficiently stamped instrument
Whether a copy of a document can be considered an 'instrument' under the Stamp Act
Whether admission of execution of an unstamped document cures the defect of insufficient stamping
holdings: Sections 35 and 36 of the Stamp Act bar secondary evidence of an instrument that is insufficiently stamped; only the original, if duly stamped or validated under the proviso, is admissible.
A copy of a document does not qualify as an 'instrument' under sections 35 or 36 of the Stamp Act and cannot be admitted in lieu of the original.

Admission of execution of an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document does not cure the statutory bar to its admissibility; only payment of stamp duty and penalty on the original lifts the bar under section 35.
doctrines: Strict compliance with stamping requirements
Bar on secondary evidence of insufficiently stamped instruments
Doctrine of curative admission under Section 36 limited to original documents

card.dispute: The reversioners of a deceased Hindu male challenged the validity of alienations made by his widow, who had acquired property through a compromise in a prior suit.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise between the widow and the reversioners in 1941 was illegal and therefore inadmissible in evidence
Whether the reversioners are estopped from challenging the alienations by the widow of property recognized as absolutely hers under the compromise
Whether the compromise amounted to a family arrangement
Whether the plea of estoppel can be considered when not specifically pleaded in the written statement
holdings: A compromise between a Hindu widow and the presumptive reversioners, giving her absolute ownership of part of the property in return for relinquishing her life estate in the rest, is not illegal even if it enlarges her estate.

Parties to a compromise are estopped from later challenging alienations of property recognized as absolutely owned by the widow under that compromise, based on representation, reliance, and detriment.

A settlement between near relatives over ancestral property, aimed at resolving disputes and preserving family harmony, qualifies as a family arrangement even if not all parties are in direct line of succession.

A plea of estoppel can be considered even if not specifically pleaded, provided the pleadings and issues framed are broad enough to encompass it and the opposite party had a fair opportunity to contest it.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statutory source, principles of life estate and reversionary rights)
Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Section 115 (Doctrine of Estoppel)
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel (constructive and promissory estoppel in property disputes)
Family Arrangement Doctrine (recognition of settlements among relatives to resolve disputes)
Doctrine of Representation in Compromise (binding effect of mutual concessions in family disputes)
Principle of Judicial Estoppel (preclusion from resiling from a prior position accepted in compromise)

card.dispute: The assessee, a firm owning a hotel in Lahore (now in Pakistan), claimed tax deductions for interest paid on loans related to the property after it was declared evacuee property and vested in the Custodian under Pakistani law; the Revenue denied the claim, arguing the firm ceased to be the 'owner' for tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee remained the 'owner' of the evacuee property in Pakistan for the purposes of Section 9(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 after it was vested in the Custodian under the Pakistan (Administration of Evacuee Property) Ordinance, 1949.
Whether the assessee could claim deductions for interest paid on loans used to acquire the property, in the absence of any right to receive income from it.
holdings: The assessee ceased to be the 'owner' of the property within the meaning of Section 9(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 during the relevant assessment years because it had no right to receive income from the property after vesting in the Custodian.
For tax liability, ownership must include the right to receive income; mere residual or ultimate ownership is insufficient to claim deductions under Section 9(1).
doctrines: Test of entitlement to income for tax liability
Constructive ownership not sufficient for tax deductions
Distinction between legal ownership and beneficial ownership for tax purposes

card.dispute: The company and the tax department disputed whether income from services like electricity, water, and lifts provided to tenants was taxable as business income under Section 10 or as income from other sources under Section 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the income from services rendered to tenants constituted a separate business activity taxable under Section 10 of the Income Tax Act, 1922
Whether the High Court could re-evaluate the facts found by the Appellate Tribunal when answering a reference
holdings: Income from providing services like electricity, water, lifts, and maintenance to tenants constitutes a distinct business activity and is taxable under Section 10 as business income if such services are substantial and independently organized.
The High Court cannot go behind the facts recorded by the Appellate Tribunal when answering a reference; it must decide the legal question based on the facts as found by the Tribunal.
doctrines: Finality of findings of fact by the Appellate Tribunal
Distinction between income from property and income from business
Rule against re-appreciation of evidence by High Court in tax references

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 6(xvii) of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, and Rule 4(4) of the Rules made thereunder, alleging violations of Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g), and 31(1) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 6(xvii) and Rule 4(4) are protected from challenge under Articles 14, 19, and 31 by virtue of Articles 31A and 31B of the Constitution.
Whether Rule 4(4) falls within the powers conferred by Section 6(xvii) read with Section 44 of the Act.
Whether the impugned provisions are part of a land reform scheme eligible for protection under Article 31A.
holdings: Section 6(xvii) and Rule 4(4) are protected under Articles 31A and 31B as they form part of a land reform scheme in Uttar Pradesh.
A rule made under a statute included in the Ninth Schedule and within the powers of the parent Act cannot be challenged under Articles 14, 19, or 31.
Rule 4(4) does not exceed the authority conferred by Section 6(xvii) read with Section 44 of the Act and is therefore valid.
provisions: U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 6(xvii)
U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 44
U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1961, Rule 4(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of protection under Article 31B via inclusion in the Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of vires of delegated legislation
Doctrine of land reform under Article 31A

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the Bombay High Court for the murder of Shankar Timji Rawool, challenged their conviction after being acquitted by the trial court, raising questions about the reliability of prosecution evidence and medical testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of the appellants based on its reappraisal of evidence and rejection of medical testimony?
Whether the prosecution version of the incident was reliable and supported by medical evidence?
Whether the High Court erred in discrediting the medical evidence without properly questioning the doctor?
holdings: The High Court erred in discrediting the medical testimony without giving the doctor an opportunity to explain, and its reliance on textbook passages to reject evidence was improper.
The prosecution witnesses' account of a brutal assault by multiple accused was consistent and supported by the nature of injuries, which could have been caused by sticks and a Palkovata.

The High Court failed to appreciate that longstanding enmity could lead to exaggeration or false implicating, and its approach to evidence evaluation was flawed, warranting interference by the Supreme Court.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 34
doctrines: Reappraisal of evidence in appeals against acquittal
Judicial caution in cases involving enmity and hostile witnesses
Proper evaluation of medical evidence in criminal trials

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether a kanam transaction was a lease (creating tenancy rights) or a mortgage (giving a right of redemption), affecting the appellants' protection against eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the document Ex. B-6 created a tenancy or a mortgage.
Whether the payment of land revenue by the transferee amounted to rent or michavaram, indicating a landlord-tenant relationship.
Whether the nature of the transaction could be determined solely by the description of the deed as 'kanam'.
holdings: The nature of a kanam transaction depends on its terms, surrounding circumstances, and intention of the parties, not merely on its label as 'kanam'.
Payment of land revenue by the transferee does not constitute rent or michavaram payable to the grantor and does not establish a tenancy.
The absence of renewal terms, customary dues, and proportion of advance to property value indicate a mortgage, not a lease.
A transaction is a mortgage if the enjoyment of property is in lieu of interest on an advance and includes a right to repayment and return of documents.
doctrines: Substance over form in characterizing transactions
Intention of parties as key to determining nature of property transfer
Dominant purpose test: enjoyment vs. security for debt

card.dispute: Mahabir Prasad, one of three joint decree-holders, appealed an order dismissing execution of the decree, but the High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground it abated due to non-impleadment of his deceased co-decree-holder's legal representatives.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abates entirely when one of the jointly interested decree-holders dies and their legal representatives are not brought on record within the limitation period, where only one decree-holder filed the appeal and others were impleaded as respondents.
Whether Order 41 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows an appellate court to decide the appeal in favour of all decree-holders even if not all are parties to the appeal.
holdings: The appellate court can exercise power under Order 41 Rule 4 CPC to reverse or vary a decree in favour of all decree-holders if the decree is based on a common ground, even if one of the jointly interested parties was impleaded as a respondent and their legal representatives were not brought on record after death.

An appeal does not abate if a deceased party’s legal representative is already on record in another capacity; it suffices to formally describe them as the heir and legal representative, even if others are not impleaded within the limitation period.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of abatement of appeal
Doctrine of legal representation in pending proceedings
Principle of consistent decrees in joint claims

card.dispute: The Union of India prosecuted Major Som Nath, a Garrison Engineer, for dishonestly allowing crops on acquired land to be removed without accounting for them, leading to his conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
issues_decided: Whether there were standing crops on the acquired land at the time possession was taken by the appellant on 13-2-63
Whether the appellant dishonestly delayed handing over possession of the land to the contractor to allow the crops to be removed
Whether the prosecution failed to place circumstances against the accused as required under Section 342 CrPC
Whether non-examination of certain witnesses and non-production of the usufruct register vitiated the trial
holdings: There were bumper crops of sarson, gram, and lusan on the land when possession was taken on 13-2-63, as established by credible documentary and oral evidence.

The appellant dishonestly delayed handing over possession to the contractor until after the crops were cut and removed, showing fraudulent intent under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
The trial court properly put all incriminating circumstances to the accused under Section 342 CrPC, including the existence of crops and delayed possession.
The non-examination of certain witnesses and non-production of the usufruct register did not prejudice the accused, as evidence on record was sufficient and corroborated.
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by trial and appellate courts are entitled to great weight
Previous statements can only be used for contradiction under Section 145 of the Evidence Act, not as substantive evidence
Non-examination of witnesses not fatal if evidence on record is sufficient and consistent

card.dispute: The appellant, as receiver of a sthanam estate, challenged the levy of estate duty on the entire property after the death of the sthanamdar, arguing only his 1/114th share was liable under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 affect the levy of estate duty under the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
What is the true effect of Section 7(3) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 on the devolution of sthanam property?
Whether estate duty is leviable on the entire sthanam property or only on the deceased sthanamdar's notional share?
holdings: The provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 are relevant to determine the interest in property that passes on death for estate duty purposes.
Section 7(3) of the Hindu Succession Act creates a legal fiction only for distribution, not for altering the extent of the sthanamdar's interest during his lifetime.
The entire sthanam property is liable to estate duty because the sthanamdar held the full interest, which ceased on death, and devolution of the whole property triggers the duty.
doctrines: Legal fiction
Devolution of property
Constitutional avoidance
Cesser of interest on death

card.dispute: The assessee company fought with the State of Kerala over whether it could claim certain expenses as revenue deductions for agricultural income-tax despite having capitalized them in its accounts.
issues_decided: Whether the capitalisation of Rs. 79,680 in the company's accounts as expenditure on immature rubber plants precluded its claim as a revenue expense for agricultural income-tax purposes.
Whether the Tribunal was justified in disallowing the expenditure without allowing the assessee to prove that the account treatment did not reflect the true nature of the expenses.
holdings: The mere fact that an assessee capitalised an expense in its accounts does not conclusively bar it from claiming the expense as a revenue deduction for tax purposes.
The Tribunal must allow the assessee an opportunity to prove that the accounting treatment does not reflect the true nature of the expenditure before disallowing the claim.
provisions: Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950, Explanation (2) to Section 5
doctrines: Admission in accounts is not conclusive in tax matters
Principle of opportunity to be heard (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the determination of surplus agricultural land under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, claiming partition and inclusion of family members born after the appointed day and land purchased in one member's name.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had effected a valid partition of the joint family property before the appointed day under the Act.
Whether the ceiling area of a family can be recalculated due to an increase in family members after the appointed day.
Whether a family member who purchased land in his own name prior to the appointed day can be included as a family member for the purpose of additional ceiling area under Section 6 proviso.
holdings: The concurrent finding by the Deputy Collector and Revenue Tribunal that no valid partition occurred was not interfered with, as the evidence did not establish severance of status or division of property.

The ceiling area under the Act is fixed with reference to the family composition and land holdings as on the appointed day (January 26, 1962), and is not subject to revision due to subsequent changes in family size.

A family member who holds land separately is not to be counted for additional ceiling area unless the land is treated as family property, in which case both the land and the member are included in the family holding.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 3
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 4
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 5
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 6
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 8
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 9
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 12
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact by lower authorities not lightly disturbed
Fixation of ceiling area on appointed day doctrine
Separate holding affecting family membership for ceiling purposes

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence in a case involving rioting, criminal trespass, and murder during a land dispute over crop possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants Parichhat, Sunnu, and Sitaram could be convicted under Section 326 read with Section 34 IPC based on common intention
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the acquittal of the appellants by the Sessions Court
Whether Gangu had the right of private defence when he caused the death of Kashiram
Whether Gangu was entitled to the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958
holdings: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires a pre-arranged plan and participation in the offence; mere presence is insufficient for vicarious liability.
The High Court erred in overturning the acquittal of Parichhat, Sunnu, and Sitaram as there was no evidence of a prior meeting of minds or active participation.
Gangu had a right of private defence but exceeded it; his act amounted to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC.
Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 does not apply to offences punishable with life imprisonment, so Gangu was not eligible for probation.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires prior meeting of minds and pre-arranged plan
Right of private defence must be proportionate and based on reasonable apprehension of harm
Principle of double jeopardy and finality of acquittal unless there is grave error
Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC not attracted without active participation or shared object

card.dispute: Raghubir Singh challenged his conviction for murder and the death sentence imposed on him, arguing that the evidence was insufficient and that the acquittal of his co-accused warranted his own acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's conviction for murder was sustainable based on the evidence, particularly in light of the acquittal of his co-accused?
Whether the sentence of death was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case?
holdings: The appellant's conviction was upheld because the eyewitness and medical evidence, along with the first information report, established his guilt beyond reasonable doubt, despite the acquittal of his co-accused due to benefit of doubt.

The death sentence was set aside and commuted to life imprisonment, as the facts of the case did not warrant the extreme penalty, and the court must exercise discretion under Section 367(5) Cr.P.C. with care.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony by medical and circumstantial evidence
Judicial discretion in sentencing under the amended Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: Rai Singh challenged his conviction and death sentence for the double murder of Mohan Lal and Bindraban, arguing insufficient and tainted evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Rai Singh committed the murders of Mohan Lal and Bindraban
Whether the testimony of witnesses disbelieved in part could still support conviction of the appellant
Whether the medical evidence on tattooing of gunshot wounds was correctly interpreted by the High Court
Whether the appellant's conviction under the Indian Arms Act could stand independently
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove Rai Singh's guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to lacunae in evidence and unreliable medical testimony.
A witness disbelieved on some aspects may still be relied upon for parts of their testimony, but only after careful scrutiny.
The High Court erred in rejecting the doctor's finding on tattooing without giving him an opportunity to explain, causing prejudice to the accused.
The conviction under the Indian Arms Act cannot stand once the main conviction for murder is set aside.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Sifting of witness testimony
Presumption of innocence
Judicial scrutiny of forensic evidence

card.dispute: The appellant (decree-holder) challenged the High Court's decision to allow the judgment debtors to apply for debt reduction under the amended U.P. Zamindars' Debt Reduction Act, 1952, after the original rejection of their application.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the U.P. Zamindars' Debt Reduction Act, 1952, as amended in 1962, could be invoked by the judgment debtor to seek reduction of a secured debt even if the mortgaged property was not charged under the decree.
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a review application after the amendment of the Act, despite the original rejection of the application and dismissal of the appeal.
holdings: The amendment to the U.P. Zamindars' Debt Reduction Act, 1952, by Act 20 of 1962, operated retrospectively from 25 May 1953, and deemed the words 'charged under the decree' to have been deleted, thereby allowing debt reduction applications for secured debts on estates acquired under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.

The High Court could entertain the application as a valid proceeding under the special jurisdiction conferred by the 1952 Act, despite procedural labels like 'review', because the amendment corrected an error apparent on the face of the record and the Act overrides the CPC.
provisions: U.P. Zamindars' Debt Reduction Act, 1952, Section 4
U.P. Zamindars' Debt Reduction (Amendment) Act, 1962, Section 2
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
doctrines: Retrospective operation of statutory amendments
Deeming fiction in statutes
Substance over form in legal proceedings
Error apparent on the face of the record as a ground for review

card.dispute: Six accused were charged with murder and rioting during an unlawful assembly to demolish a thatch; two were acquitted, and the remaining four challenged their conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 149 IPC can be sustained when only four out of six accused were convicted and two were acquitted.
Whether the appellants can be convicted under Section 34 IPC for common intention in the absence of a valid conviction under Section 149 IPC.
