holdings: Conviction under Section 149 IPC requires certainty that at least five persons were part of the unlawful assembly; if the charge names only six and two are acquitted, the remaining cannot be convicted under Section 149 unless the common object is proven among five.
Where a preconcerted plan and common intention are established through conduct and circumstances, conviction under Section 34 IPC is valid even without a conviction under Section 149 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Constructive criminal liability under Section 149 IPC
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Requirement of prior concert for common intention

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of occupancy land under 'old grants' in a cantonment area, sought a writ of mandamus to compel the Government to execute a lease under Rule 27 of the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937, which the Government refused, asserting discretion in the matter.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 27 of the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937, confers a mandatory or discretionary power on the Military Estates Officer to grant a lease for regularisation of old grants.
Whether the appellants had a legal right to claim a lease under Rule 27 and Schedule VII of the Rules.
holdings: Rule 27 uses the word 'may', which ordinarily indicates discretion, not a mandatory obligation, and thus the Military Estates Officer has the discretion to grant or refuse a lease in cases of old grants.
The requirement of Central Government or delegated authority's approval under Rule 27 further confirms the discretionary nature of the power, and refusal is permissible if sufficient reasons exist.
doctrines: Discretionary vs. mandatory interpretation of statutory language
Doctrine of 'may' implying discretion unless context demands otherwise
Principle of reconsideration in accordance with law when discretion is involved

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, arguing it violated the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) by imposing unreasonable restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 is ultra vires the Constitution under Article 19(1)(f) read with Article 19(5)?
Whether the absence of a provision for notice, representation, or appeal against a requisition order renders the Act unreasonable?
Whether the bar on civil court jurisdiction under Section 11 of the Act makes the restrictions imposed unreasonable?
holdings: The restrictions imposed by the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 are reasonable and saved under Article 19(5) as they serve public purposes and include fair compensation.
The lack of a formal notice or appeal mechanism does not invalidate the Act, as representations against requisition orders can still be made and considered by the government.
Section 11, which bars civil court challenges, does not make the Act unconstitutional, since orders that are mala fide or for collateral purposes remain judicially reviewable.
provisions: West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 3
West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 7(3) and (4)
West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 8
West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 8A
West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 11
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5)
Judicial review of administrative action
Principle of fair compensation in property requisition

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the legality of land requisition orders issued by the Collector of Hooghly in Chandernagore, arguing that the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 did not apply to the former French territory and that the Collector lacked jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 extended to Chandernagore after its merger with West Bengal.
Whether the Collector of Hooghly had jurisdiction to requisition land in Chandernagore under the 1948 notification.
holdings: The West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948 applied to Chandernagore as it was extended under Section 17 of the Chandernagore (Merger) Act, 1954 and Section 3 of the Chandernagore (Assimilation of Laws) Act, 1955, as it related to matters in List II of the Seventh Schedule.

The Collector of Hooghly had authority to requisition land in Chandernagore under the 1948 notification, which must be construed according to the territorial limits of the district as they existed at the time of exercise of power.
provisions: Chandernagore (Assimilation of Laws) Act, 1955, Section 2(c), Section 3, Section 4
West Bengal Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 3(1)
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II Entry 36, List III Entry 42
doctrines: Territorial extension of state laws post-merger
Repeal of pre-existing laws upon assimilation
Construction of administrative jurisdiction in light of territorial changes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the annulment of a 1946 land settlement, claiming it was wrongly invalidated by revenue authorities for allegedly defrauding the State of Bihar under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the revenue authorities had sufficient material to conclude that the 1946 settlement was made with the object of causing loss to the State.
Whether the annulment of the settlement under Section 4(b) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 was justified based on conjecture about rental rates.
holdings: The annulment of the settlement was invalid because the revenue authorities relied on the low rental rate as evidence of fraud without any comparative data on prevailing rates at the time.
A finding of fraudulent intent under Section 4(b) must be based on evidence, not conjecture or assumptions about land value or rental rates.
doctrines: Principle of reasoned decision-making
Requirement of evidentiary basis for administrative action
Prohibition of arbitrary state action under Article 14

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued to recover money under a mortgage bond, while the defendants claimed credit for a Rs. 19,000 payment allegedly made in 1953 and endorsed on the bond.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants made a payment of Rs. 19,000 on 31 December 1953 and were entitled to credit for it under the mortgage bond
Whether the endorsement on the mortgage bond for Rs. 2,600 was altered to read Rs. 26,000 and whether the document was tampered with
Whether letters and pleadings from a different firm could be used to prove the amount due under the mortgage
holdings: The defendants proved the genuine endorsement of a payment of Rs. 19,000 on 31 December 1953 and were entitled to credit for it in the mortgage decree.
In the absence of a pleaded case, issue, or evidence of tampering, the court cannot infer that the figures on the mortgage bond were altered by the defendants.
Documents from a different firm not shown to the defendants in cross-examination cannot be used to prove the truth of the amount due under the mortgage.
doctrines: Burden of proof in cases of document tampering
Relevance and admissibility of inter-party documents
Principle that a party must plead and prove allegations of forgery or alteration

card.dispute: The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, contested whether interim payments received under the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 were capital or revenue receipts for income-tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether interim payments under s. 50(2) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 constitute capital or revenue receipts.
Whether the decision in Raja Rameshwar Rao v. CIT applies to payments under s. 50(2) of the Madras Act.
holdings: Interim payments under s. 50(2) of the Madras Estates Act are capital receipts as they form part of compensation for the acquisition of the estate, not revenue from income.
The decision in Raja Rameshwar Rao v. CIT is distinguishable because it dealt with maintenance allowances under a different statutory scheme and does not apply here.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 50(2)
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 3
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 39
doctrines: Character of receipt depends on the nature of the payment and its underlying purpose, not merely its label.
Distinction between capital receipt (for loss of capital asset) and revenue receipt (for loss of income) in tax law.

card.dispute: The appellant tenant claimed that payments under a compromise should adjust a decree for eviction and damages, while the respondent landlord contested the validity and timing of those payments.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was precluded from challenging the limitation and mode of payments after not appealing against the remand order in the first appeal.
Whether the High Court erred in interfering with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in a second appeal.
holdings: A party who does not appeal against a remand order under Order 43 Rule 1(u) CPC is precluded from disputing its correctness in subsequent proceedings, including in a second appeal.
The High Court cannot overturn concurrent findings of fact by two lower courts in a second appeal unless there is a substantial question of law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43, Rule 1(u)
doctrines: Preclusion under Section 105(2) CPC
Concurrent findings of fact in second appeal
Remand in execution proceedings

card.dispute: Som Nath, a Major in the Military Engineering Service, was prosecuted for allowing crops on acquired land to be removed without accounting for them, leading to a conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, which he challenged on grounds of invalid sanction and procedural defects.
issues_decided: Whether the government's sanction for prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act was valid and covered the charges under Section 5(1)(c).
Whether the prosecution failed to examine necessary witnesses, thereby prejudicing the accused.
holdings: For a sanction to be valid, it must clearly relate to the facts constituting the offence; if not evident on record, the prosecution must prove those facts were before the sanctioning authority and that it applied its mind to them.

The prosecution is not required to examine all possible witnesses if the essential facts are sufficiently established through other credible evidence; non-examination of certain witnesses does not vitiate the trial if no prejudice is shown.
doctrines: Principle of valid sanction for prosecution
Duty of prosecution to establish essential facts without mandatory requirement to examine all witnesses
Use of prior statements to contradict witnesses under Section 145 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to eject the defendant from a loft, claiming the defendant was a licensee whose license had been terminated, while the defendant claimed to be a protected tenant under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties created a lease or a licence
Whether the defendant was entitled to protection under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the High Court's certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court was validly granted
holdings: The nature of the agreement depends on whether it creates an interest in the property, not merely on the label used; exclusive possession is a significant but not decisive factor.
An agreement granting exclusive possession, coupled with commercial use and absence of control by the owner, creates a lease, not a licence, even if termed otherwise.
A High Court must give reasons for granting a certificate under Article 133(1)(c), but the defect does not require vacating the certificate if the appeal lacks merit.
doctrines: Lease vs licence distinction
Intention of parties test
Exclusive possession as indicia of tenancy
Doctrine of substance over form

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged amendments to the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, arguing they violated his right to property under Articles 19 and 31 by indefinitely postponing recovery of purchase price from tenant-purchasers.
issues_decided: Whether the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1964 is protected under Article 31A of the Constitution?
Whether the amendments unreasonably infringe the petitioner's right to property under Article 19(1)(f)?
holdings: The impugned amendments fall within the protection of Article 31A as they are part of agrarian reform legislation aimed at securing equitable land distribution.

The amendments do not unreasonably restrict property rights under Article 19(1)(f) as they preserve the landlord's right to recover purchase price through tribunals and maintain the scheme of agrarian reform.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1964 (Maharashtra Act 31 of 1965)
doctrines: Agrarian reform doctrine
Doctrine of constitutional protection under Article 31A
Doctrine of reasonable restrictions on property rights

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh sought to restrict the transport of tendu leaves imported from outside the state, while a bidi manufacturer challenged such restrictions as violative of constitutional provisions on free trade.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5 of the Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964 prohibits the transport of tendu leaves imported from outside the state.
Whether the restrictions on transport of imported tendu leaves violate Articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution.
Whether the state's monopoly over tendu leaves extends to imported leaves.
holdings: Section 5 does not apply to tendu leaves imported from outside Madhya Pradesh, as the Act's purpose is limited to establishing a monopoly over locally grown leaves.
Restrictions on movement of imported tendu leaves within the state are not integral to the state monopoly and would violate Articles 301 and 304 if imposed.
The state monopoly under the Act is confined to tendu leaves produced within the state and does not extend to imported leaves.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 5
Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 11
Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 12
Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 15
Madhya Pradesh Tendu Patta (Vyapar Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1964, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional avoidance
Doctrine of essential features of state monopoly
Principle of purposive interpretation

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and the respondent Jagirdar, Sardar D.K. Jadhav, disputed whether certain tanks on jagir land were saved from vesting in the State under Section 5(c) of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court properly considered the claim under Section 5(c) of the Abolition Act after remand by the Supreme Court.
Whether the tanks in question were situated on 'occupied land' as defined under Section 2(1)(ix) of the Act, thereby qualifying for protection under Section 5(c).
Whether partial occupation of the tanks by tenants affects the applicability of the saving clause in Section 5(c).
holdings: The High Court complied with the Supreme Court’s remand order by properly adjudicating the claim under Section 5(c) and was not barred from considering additional contentions raised by the State.

For a tank to be protected under Section 5(c), it need not be entirely within khud-kasht or homestead land; it suffices if the entire tank area is spread across occupied land, including tenanted land or land held as khud-kasht or homestead.

Partial occupation of a tank by tenants does not negate the protection under Section 5(c), as long as the entire tank lies within 'occupied land' belonging to or held by the Jagirdar or any other person as defined in Section 2(1)(ix).
provisions: Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 2(1)(ix)
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 4
Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, 1951, Section 5(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of occupied land interpretation
Doctrine of partial vesting and saving of property rights
Doctrine of purposive interpretation of abolition statutes

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan, as successor to the District Board, Sikar, sued the Thikanedar of Sikar to recover cess and contributions for certain years, which the respondent refused to pay in full, leading to a dispute over the maintainability of the suit and limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by the District Board, Sikar, was maintainable under the Jaipur District Boards Act, 1947?
Whether the plea of non-maintainability was properly raised by the respondent despite not being explicitly framed as an issue?
holdings: The suit was not maintainable because the District Board had no statutory right to recover cess or contribution directly from the Thikanedar; the liability was to the Government, not the Board.

The plea of non-maintainability was properly raised in the written statement by denying the Board's right to levy cess and contribution, and thus could be considered even if not precisely framed as an issue.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Maintainability of suit based on statutory authority
Plea of non-maintainability can be considered if inherent in the pleadings

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra fought with Laxman Abaji and others over who was entitled to occupancy rights in land after the abolition of inams, specifically whether the crucial date for determining entitlement was the 1955 vesting date or July 1, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord-tenant relationship continued between July 20, 1955, and July 1, 1960, after inams were abolished and land vested in the State.
What is the relevant date for determining entitlement to occupancy rights under the Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954?
holdings: The relationship of landlord and tenant continued until July 1, 1960, as the rights and obligations under the tenancy law were preserved by Section 33 of the Act and relevant provisions came into force only on that date.

The crucial date for determining occupancy rights is July 1, 1960; if the inamdar was lawfully in possession on that date after a valid surrender by the tenant, the inamdar is entitled to occupancy rights.
provisions: Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954, Section 3(1)
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954, Section 3(2)
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954, Section 33
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954, Section 1(3)(b)
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams (Amendment) Act, 1956, Section 4
doctrines: Continuation of tenancy relations post-vesting until statutory provisions take effect
Statutory construction of transitional provisions in land reform laws

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and the assessee, Shyama Charan Shukla, disputed whether the state had jurisdiction to assess and recover sales tax for transactions in areas transferred to Maharashtra after November 1, 1956, under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'arrears' in Section 78 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 requires quantification of tax liability before it can be considered due.
Whether the State of Madhya Pradesh had jurisdiction to assess tax on sales from areas transferred to Maharashtra after November 1, 1956.
holdings: The word 'arrears' in Section 78 refers to tax that has become due by operation of law upon the occurrence of a taxable event, and does not depend on formal assessment or quantification.
The right to recover such arrears is determined by the location of the place of assessment, but the existence of arrears is not contingent on completed assessment proceedings.
doctrines: Literal meaning of 'arrears' as unpaid dues due by law
Apportionment of tax liabilities between successor states

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of a lawyer, Ram Niranjan Singh, who was charged with murder under Section 302 IPC for shooting two men, Murder and Sri Ram.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in acquitting the respondent of the murder of Murder (one of the victims) on the grounds of private defence
Whether the Sessions Judge erred in treating the shooting of Murder and Sri Ram as separate incidents
Whether the respondent had the right of private defence when he shot Murder
holdings: The High Court rightly acquitted the respondent because the evidence supported that the attack by Murder and the mob was continuous and posed a grave threat to life.
The incident involving the deaths of Murder and Sri Ram was an integrated event and could not be artificially split to deny the accused the right of private defence.
The respondent had the right of private defence under Exception 3 to Section 100 IPC, as the circumstances showed an imminent threat to life from a mob attack.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Exception 3 to Section 100
doctrines: Right of private defence of body and property
Continuity of unlawful aggression
Integrated incident doctrine in private defence

card.dispute: The Collector of Lakhimpur appealed against the High Court's enhancement of compensation awarded to landowner Bhuban Chandra Dutta for acquired land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in determining the market value of acquired land based on small-sized comparable sale deeds?
Whether the compensation awarded at Rs. 15,000 per bigha was justified given the size and nature of the land and comparable sales?
holdings: Market value for larger plots cannot be equated with prices fetched by small adjoining plots, as larger tracts typically sell at lower rates per unit area.
Compensation should reflect realistic market conditions; Rs. 10,000 per bigha was just and sufficient, aligning with the original claim and adjusted for plot size differences.
provisions: Assam Land Requisition and Acquisition Act, 1948
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Rule against overvaluation based on non-comparable small plot sales

card.dispute: The appellants, brothers Tara Chand and Siri Ram, were convicted of murder under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC for the killing of Major Subhash Chander, and they appealed against their conviction and death sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC or a lesser offence under Section 304 Part I IPC.
Whether the appellants acted in private defence of person or property under Sections 96 to 106 IPC.
Whether Khasra No. 174/2 was in the actual possession of appellant Tara Chand at the time of the incident.
holdings: The appellants were not guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC with common intention under Section 34 IPC, but were guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Part I of Section 304 IPC due to excessive use of force beyond the right of private defence.

The appellants had a right of private defence of property under Section 97 IPC, but the injuries inflicted were disproportionate and excessive, thus exceeding the limits permitted under Section 99 IPC.

Khasra No. 174/2, though officially transferred to the village Panchayat, remained in the actual physical possession of Tara Chand, supported by tractor marks and surrounding circumstances, entitling him to defend it.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act 1948, Section 23
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Excess in private defence
Standard of proof in criminal appeals
Appreciation of evidence in cases involving conflicting versions

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought the shebaits of a deity over whether a tank fishery was under lease to third parties, affecting ownership after state acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the tank fishery was held under a valid lease immediately before the date of vesting under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954
Whether the proviso to Section 6(2) of the Act applied, thereby making the alleged lessees direct tenants of the State
holdings: An arrangement allowing another party to fish in a tank for a yearly payment and obligation to clean it, without transfer of interest in the sub-soil or embankments, does not constitute a lease but a licence.
In the absence of a registered deed, a long-term lease of non-agricultural land cannot be legally enforced under the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 4
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 5(1)(a) and (c)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 6(1)(c) and (e)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 6(2) and proviso
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 44(2a)
doctrines: Doctrine of khas possession
Lease vs licence distinction
Requirement of registration for valid lease of immovable property

card.dispute: The State of Bihar appealed against the Patna High Court's decision to reduce the respondent's conviction from murder under Section 302 to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I, IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in altering the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I, IPC based on the occurrence of a sudden fight and absence of premeditation
Whether the prosecution established the complete genesis and manner of the occurrence to rule out a sudden quarrel or heat of passion
holdings: The High Court's finding of a sudden clash between the parties near the time and place of occurrence is supported by material, including injuries on the accused, and justifies conviction under Section 304 Part I, IPC.
The prosecution failed to fully explain the origin of the incident, and in case of doubt about premeditation or sudden quarrel, the benefit of the doubt must go to the accused.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Sudden fight and heat of passion as mitigating factors for culpable homicide
Requirement of prosecution to prove entire genesis of occurrence

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the High Court's acquittal of eight accused and rejection of a reference on the death sentence of Ram Gopal in a murder case involving Chhatrapal.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the nine respondents committed murder under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether the eyewitness accounts, particularly of Sukkhi, were reliable and consistent?
Whether the nature and distribution of injuries on the victim supported the prosecution's version of a violent attack by nine armed men?
Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the accused based on contradictions and improbabilities in the evidence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies and improbabilities in eyewitness testimony.
The testimony of Sukkhi, the alleged eyewitness and servant of the deceased, was unreliable due to material contradictions between his statements to police and in court.
The limited number of injuries on the lower body contradicted the claim that nine armed men, including those with spears, fully participated in the attack.
The High Court was justified in acquitting all accused as the prosecution case was undermined by false implication of some accused and lack of corroborative evidence.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration of evidence in murder cases
Improvidence of prosecution story based on injury pattern

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a property owner contested a claim by lessees for refund of deposit and damages, arguing that the agreement to lease was frustrated due to partition and communal violence making performance impossible.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies to leases or only to agreements to lease
Whether the agreement in question had become impossible to perform due to supervening events
Whether the lessor was obligated to deliver physical possession of the leased property
holdings: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies only to executory contracts, such as an agreement to lease, and not to completed leases which are conveyances.

An agreement to lease becomes void under Section 56 when supervening events make performance impracticable or useless, even if not physically impossible, provided the foundation of the contract is destroyed.

The lessor was not required to deliver physical possession under the contract; the lessee was responsible for obtaining possession after registration, which became impossible due to partition and violence.
doctrines: Doctrine of frustration
Distinction between agreement to lease and lease as a completed conveyance
Supervening impossibility rendering contract void

card.dispute: The petitioners, who were unsuccessful bidders for Kendu leaves trade rights, challenged the constitutional validity of provisions in the Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Act, 1961, as amended in 1969, alleging violations of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g) due to arbitrary, discriminatory, and mala fide appointments of purchasers and agents.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3(2)(a), 8(1), and Rules 5-B(6)-(16), 6(3), and 7(1) of the Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Act, 1961, as amended, violate fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Whether the revised policy under the 1969 Amendment Act and rules framed thereunder is arbitrary, discriminatory, and mala fide.
Whether the appointment of purchasers and agents, including additional agents and purchasers, without selecting the highest tenderers, amounts to maladministration or breach of State monopoly.
holdings: The impugned provisions of the Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Act and rules do not violate Articles 14, 15, or 19(1)(g) as they are reasonably related to the State's monopoly and public purpose.
The revised policy under the 1969 Amendment is valid and not arbitrary or mala fide, as it enables effective control over the Kendu leaves trade.
Government may prefer lower tenderers over higher ones based on overall suitability, past performance, or reliability, and such discretion does not violate equality or fairness under Article 14.
provisions: Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Act, 1961, Section 3(2)(a)
Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Act, 1961, Section 8(1)
Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Rules, Rule 5-B(6), (7), (8), (9), (16)
Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Rules, Rule 6(3)
Orissa Kendu Leaves (Control of Trade) Rules, Rule 7(1)
doctrines: State monopoly doctrine
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness in State action
Presumption of constitutionality of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant Sukra Mahto was prosecuted for defaming the respondents by calling them illegitimate sons born of a concubine during a land dispute proceeding, and the case centered on whether this statement was protected under the Ninth Exception to Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's statement accusing the respondents of being illegitimate sons born of a concubine was made in good faith under the Ninth Exception to Section 499 IPC
Whether the impugned statement was made for the protection of the appellant's interests or for public good, as required by the Ninth Exception to Section 499 IPC
holdings: To claim protection under the Ninth Exception to Section 499 IPC, the accused must prove they acted in good faith by making a reasonable inquiry with due care and attention, not merely holding a subjective belief.
The mere pendency of a legal proceeding does not justify defamatory statements; the statement must be necessary for protecting a legitimate interest, which was not established here.
doctrines: Good faith under the Ninth Exception to Section 499 IPC
Requirement of due care and attention in making defamatory imputations
Protection of legitimate interest as a condition for exception to defamation

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the Punjab & Haryana High Court's decision that Parliament lacked the power to amend the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, via the Finance Act, 1969, to include agricultural land in net wealth for taxation.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament had legislative competence under Entry 86 of List I to amend the Wealth Tax Act to include the capital value of agricultural land in net wealth.
Whether the tax on net wealth, including agricultural land, fell within the State's power under Entry 49 of List II.
Whether the subject matter of wealth tax, as defined in the Wealth Tax Act, was covered by Entry 86 of List I or Entry 97 of List I read with Article 248.
holdings: The tax on net wealth under the Wealth Tax Act is not covered by Entry 86 of List I, as it involves aggregation of assets and deduction of all debts, differing fundamentally from a tax on capital value of assets.
Entry 49 of List II does not cover wealth tax because it contemplates tax on lands and buildings as discrete units, not as part of aggregated net wealth.
The subject matter of wealth tax, including agricultural land, falls under Entry 97 of List I (residuary powers) read with Article 248, as it is not covered by any entry in List II or List III.
Parliament has the constitutional authority to levy wealth tax on agricultural land through residuary powers, and the amendment via Finance Act, 1969, is intra vires.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 86
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 97
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
doctrines: Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Doctrine of Residuary Powers under Article 248
Doctrine of Separation of Fields between Union and State Taxation

card.dispute: The sons of the vendors filed a suit for pre-emption of land sold by their fathers; the vendees challenged the suit on grounds of collusion and limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs' suit was collusive due to financial and residential support from their vendor-fathers.
Whether the suit for pre-emption was barred by limitation under Article 10 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
holdings: Mere assistance by vendor-fathers in supporting their sons' pre-emption suit financially or otherwise does not amount to collusion, as the right of pre-emption is personal to the sons and they are not acting as benamidars.

When a part of the sold property remains in possession of tenants, the vendees cannot be said to have taken 'physical possession' of the whole property, so the limitation period starts from the date of registration of the sale deed under Article 10 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
doctrines: Doctrine of physical possession in pre-emption suits
Doctrine of collusion in judicial proceedings requiring a secret, deceitful arrangement

card.dispute: Religious landholders challenged the Mysore Land Revenue (Surcharge) Acts of 1961 and 1962, arguing the state lacked competence to enact them and that the surcharge was discriminatory under Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Mysore Legislature had the competence to enact the Land Revenue (Surcharge) Act, 1961 and its amendment.
Whether the surcharge imposed under the Acts violated Article 14 of the Constitution due to differential tax treatment between regions.
holdings: The surcharge is an enhancement of land revenue, not a separate tax, and falls within Entry 45 of the State List; thus, the Mysore Legislature was competent to enact the law.

The temporary imposition of surcharge during ongoing land resettlement and survey does not violate Article 14, even if it results in unequal taxation, as it is based on intelligible differentia with rational relation to the state's objective.
doctrines: Classification test under Article 14
Temporary measures doctrine in fiscal legislation
Doctrine of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The assessee company fought with the tax authorities over whether a loss from selling a colliery and dividend income from trading shares could be set off against other income under the Income Tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the loss of Rs. 11,257 on the sale of colliery assets, on which depreciation was claimed earlier, is allowable under Section 10(2)(vii) when the business was carried on for part of the year?
Whether dividend income from shares forming part of stock-in-trade can be set off against carried-forward business losses under Section 24(2)?
holdings: A business loss on the sale of assets is allowable under Section 10(2)(vii) even if the business was carried on for only part of the year, provided the loss is written off in the books and the assets were used for business.
Dividend income from shares held as stock-in-trade forms part of business income and can be set off against carried-forward business losses under Section 24(2).
doctrines: Business loss set-off
Integration of business income and dividends from trading shares
Finality of Tribunal's findings of fact

card.dispute: The Kamavan of a Hindu undivided family contested whether income from family properties allotted to members under a family settlement remained taxable as family income under the Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the income from properties allotted to members under a family settlement continues to be the income of the Hindu undivided family for tax purposes
Whether such income is liable to be included in the family's assessable income when used to discharge family obligations
holdings: Income from family properties remains the income of the Hindu undivided family if the settlement does not create an overriding charge or absolute rights, and the family's joint status continues.
Where income is applied to discharge a family obligation after receipt, it is assessable as family income; only income diverted before reaching the assessee escapes taxation.
doctrines: Distinction between diversion of income by overriding charge and application of income
Receipt in law, not physical receipt, determines income attribution to an assessee

card.dispute: The state appealed the acquittal of seven accused who were alleged to have assaulted four men with weapons during a land dispute, leading to a conviction by the High Court which the accused are now challenging in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution witnesses' testimony could be disbelieved solely on the ground of their familial relationship?
Whether material discrepancies in the prosecution evidence warranted rejection of the entire case?
Whether the injuries on the accused-appellants were sufficient to support a plea of private defence?
Whether the conviction under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC was legally sustainable based on the evidence?
holdings: Familial relationship among prosecution witnesses does not automatically discredit their testimony if it is otherwise consistent and credible.
Minor discrepancies in the prosecution evidence, such as the timing of police intimation, do not undermine the overall reliability of the case.
The minimal injuries on the accused compared to 56 injuries on the victims make the defence version of a counter-attack implausible and unworthy of belief.
Conviction under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC is valid when injuries were inflicted in furtherance of a common object by members of an unlawful assembly.
doctrines: Common object of unlawful assembly
Credibility of related witnesses
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Principle of consistency in prosecution evidence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the execution of a decree for possession of mortgaged properties, arguing that certain lands and houses were not covered by the decree due to prior orders and occupancy rights under land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the decree under execution included the properties mentioned in items 3, 4, 5, 6, and 10 of the Darkhast
Whether the decree-holder could claim possession of lands in respect of which occupancy certificates had been issued under the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951
holdings: The decree did not entitle the respondents to possession of the properties in dispute, as those items were not part of the appellate order and had been excluded due to occupancy rights; the execution court erred in not construing the decree in light of the pleadings and prior proceedings.
The Board's decision not to direct possession of lands with occupancy certificates became final as it was not appealed, and thus the parties were bound by it, regardless of its legal correctness.
provisions: Saurashtra Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1954, Section 4
doctrines: Binding effect of unchallenged findings in decree proceedings
Duty of execution court to construe decree in context of pleadings and prior orders
Finality of orders on issues not appealed against

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their convictions for murder and attempted murder, with the prosecution alleging a violent assault resulting in three deaths, while the defense claimed self-defense against an unlawful intrusion.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Asa Singh, Sewa Singh, Darshan Singh, and Kehar Singh committed murder under Section 302 IPC?
Whether Iqbal Singh was rightly convicted for his role in the murders based on the evidence presented?
Whether the injuries sustained by the accused support their claim of self-defense?
Whether the recovery of blood-stained weapons from the accused corroborates the prosecution's case?
holdings: The prosecution's evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical and forensic corroboration, conclusively established the guilt of Asa Singh, Sewa Singh, Darshan Singh, and Kehar Singh under Section 302 IPC.
The conviction of Iqbal Singh was set aside due to reasonable doubt, as the nature of the injuries did not match the use of a spear and no blood-stained weapon was recovered from him.
The minor and superficial injuries on Asa Singh and Darshan Singh were inconsistent with their claim of being attacked by three armed men, weakening their self-defense plea.
The recovery of blood-stained spears and kirpans from the accused, in compliance with disclosure statements, strengthened the prosecution's case against them.
doctrines: Benefit of reasonable doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony by forensic evidence
Evaluation of self-defense claims based on injury patterns
Reliance on disclosure statements under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act

card.dispute: Co-owners of a housing scheme subdivided land and sold plots; purchasers claimed one plot was reserved for a Dharmshala and sued to prevent its sale and use, while the defendant claimed valid ownership through purchase.
issues_decided: Whether plot No. 19 was legally reserved for use as a Dharmshala to the exclusion of the co-owners' right to sell it.
Whether a representation via loudspeaker or map description created a binding obligation or interest in the plot.
Whether the co-owners were estopped from denying the reservation of the plot for a Dharmshala.
holdings: Mere description of a plot as 'Dharmshala' in maps not annexed to sale deeds does not create a legal reservation or divest co-owners of their title.
Announcements over loudspeakers during property promotion are puffery and do not constitute binding representations capable of creating legal rights.
Estoppel does not create an interest in immovable property unless supported by clear evidence and legal provisions such as Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel
Doctrine of Puffery in Property Representation
Incorporation by Reference in Contracts

card.dispute: The dispute was between the former Commissioner of Endowments and a respondent over whether the Commissioner committed contempt of court by refusing to follow a binding High Court precedent while disposing of a revision petition under the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, as a quasi-judicial authority, committed contempt by not following a binding decision of the Orissa High Court?
Whether the appellant's conduct in distinguishing the High Court's decision was bona fide or mala fide?
Whether a wrong statement in an order regarding pending proceedings in the Supreme Court amounts to scandalising or undermining the authority of the High Court?
holdings: A quasi-judicial authority subject to the superintendence of the High Court under Article 227 must follow its binding decisions, and deliberate refusal to do so amounts to contempt.
Deliberate avoidance of a binding precedent by giving factually incorrect or illegitimate reasons constitutes mala fide conduct and is contumacious.
A public statement falsely suggesting that a matter is sub judice before the Supreme Court, when no such appeal is pending, undermines the authority of the High Court and amounts to contempt.
provisions: Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, Section 27
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, Section 41
Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, Section 9
doctrines: Binding nature of superior court precedents on subordinate tribunals
Contempt of court for willful disobedience or undermining judicial authority
Mala fide conduct in judicial or quasi-judicial functions
Principle of judicial decorum and detachment

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of the appellants in a murder case, leading to their conviction by the High Court, which the appellants challenged in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Court's acquittal and convicting the appellants based on the prosecution's evidence.
Whether the prosecution witnesses were credible and their testimonies reliable enough to sustain a conviction.
Whether the High Court properly applied the principles governing appellate review in cases of acquittal.
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal as it failed to give due weight to the trial court's assessment of witness credibility and the presumption of innocence.
The prosecution witnesses were not credible due to contradictions, interest in the outcome, and lack of corroboration, making their evidence insufficient for conviction.
An appellate court must exercise caution in appeals against acquittal and should not disturb findings of fact unless there is a clear error, which was absent here.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Benefit of doubt
Appellate review in criminal cases
Credibility of prosecution witnesses
Principle of caution in appeals against acquittal

card.dispute: The legal representatives of two deceased brothers fought over whether their family was divided in status in 1349 B.S. or 1351 B.S., and whether properties acquired before the division were joint family property liable to partition.
issues_decided: Whether the family was divided in status in Magh 1349 B.S. or in 1351 B.S.
Whether properties acquired by the brothers before the division of status were joint family properties liable to partition.
holdings: The family was not divided in status in 1349 B.S.; the division occurred in 1351 B.S., as established by documentary evidence including family letters and joint property purchases.

Acquisitions made by the three brothers before 1351 B.S. were joint family properties where the joint family had sufficient nucleus and the brothers participated in management, especially in absence of individual account books.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified statute, based on joint family and partition principles)
doctrines: Presumption of joint family property from common nucleus
Rejection of oral evidence in favor of documentary evidence
Joint management as indicator of continued joint family status

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased applicant for a mining lease challenged the grant of the lease to another applicant, alleging defects in the latter's application and seeking to continue the appeal after the applicant's death.
issues_decided: Whether defects in an application for a mining lease, such as lack of a map or incomplete area details, render the application invalid under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949
Whether the legal representatives of a deceased applicant can continue an appeal for a mining lease
Whether a delayed application for mining lease is deemed rejected under Rule 28(1-A) if not disposed of within nine months
holdings: Defects in an application regarding map or area details are directory, not mandatory, and do not invalidate the application if the lease can be properly executed with correct details later.

The right to apply for a mining lease is personal and tied to qualifications; it does not survive the applicant's death, and legal representatives cannot continue the application or appeal without a fresh application.

The new legal ground regarding deemed rejection under Rule 28(1-A) could not be entertained as it was not raised in the lower court and the appeal was not maintainable due to lack of continuation rights by heirs.
doctrines: Directory vs Mandatory Rule Distinction
Survival of Right to Sue
Deemed Rejection Doctrine
Equity in Administrative Action

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and M/s. Manna Ramji & Co disputed whether compensation received by the firm for loss of earnings due to government requisition of its business premises was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation received by the assessee for loss of earnings during requisition of business premises constitutes a revenue receipt taxable under the Income Tax Act?
Whether the method of calculating compensation affects its character as a capital or revenue receipt?
Whether the case of Sonairam Doongermall or The Glenboig Union Fireclay Co. is applicable to the facts of this case?
holdings: Compensation paid for loss of profits during the requisition period, where the business continues in the same manner, is a revenue receipt as it represents lost profits and not destruction of a capital asset.
The method of computing compensation, such as a lump sum based on years of profit, does not alter the essential character of the receipt, which depends on the nature of the payment, not its measure.
The decision in Sonairam Doongermall is distinguishable because the assessee there ceased business entirely, whereas here the business continued, making the compensation akin to profit.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Revenue receipt character based on continuity of business and nature of loss
Finality of Tribunal's findings of fact in tax references

card.dispute: The Controller of Court of Wards, Kolhapur, appealed against the High Court's order directing it to hand over possession of certain survey numbers, previously assigned to family deities by the jagirdar's father, to respondent G.N. Ghorpade, the successor jagirdar.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in proceeding ex parte and refusing to admit the appellants' delayed counter-affidavit in the special civil applications?
Whether the respondent had established a prima facie right to possession of the disputed survey numbers in the absence of any denial by the appellants?
holdings: The High Court did not commit an error in refusing to admit the appellants' counter-affidavit due to inordinate delay, especially after multiple adjournments were granted and the appellants failed to file the affidavit despite having sufficient time.

In the absence of any rebuttal affidavit, the statements made by the respondent in his affidavits constituted prima facie evidence of his right to possession, which the High Court was entitled to accept.
doctrines: Principle of ex parte proceedings in writ petitions
Prima facie case in absence of rebuttal
Judicial discretion in adjournment and admission of evidence

card.dispute: The petitioner, Daud Ahmed, challenged the District Magistrate's order requisitioning his personally occupied premises without inquiry into alternative accommodation.
issues_decided: Whether the second proviso to Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 applies when a landlord is in actual occupation of the premises after a tenant's vacation.
Whether the District Magistrate must conduct an inquiry before forming an opinion that alternative accommodation exists for the person in occupation.
Whether the failure to provide an opportunity to the occupier to present facts about alternative accommodation violates principles of natural justice.
holdings: The second proviso to Section 3 applies when the premises are in actual occupation, including by the landlord, and the District Magistrate must form an opinion on the existence of suitable alternative accommodation.
The opinion that alternative accommodation exists must be based on factual inquiry and cannot be formed without examining relevant facts or giving the occupier a chance to be heard.

The principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem, require that the occupier be given an opportunity to present their case before requisitioning if their right to property is affected.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3 (second proviso)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7
doctrines: Audi alteram partem
Rule of natural justice in administrative action
Factual basis for statutory opinion

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for abetment of forgery in the registration of a lease, arguing that the private complaint was invalid without prior permission under Section 83(1) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908.
issues_decided: Whether Section 83(1) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 requires prior permission for a private person to file a complaint for an offence under the Act?
Whether Section 83(1) is mandatory or permissive in nature?
holdings: Section 83(1) applies only when an offence under the Act comes to the knowledge of a registering officer in his official capacity and does not bar a private person from filing a complaint.
The language of Section 83(1) is permissive, not prohibitive, and does not require private complainants to obtain prior permission to initiate prosecution.
doctrines: Permissive vs. mandatory statutory interpretation
Principle of legality in criminal procedure
Private right to prosecute in absence of explicit statutory bar

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) fought with the State of U.P. over the determination of compensation for forests vested under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, particularly regarding the method of calculating average annual forest income and inclusion of income from wood processing and poola grass.
issues_decided: Whether the average annual forest income under Section 39(1)(e) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 can be computed by arithmetically adding income over 25 years and appraised annual yield on the vesting date.
Whether income derived from processing wood constitutes forest income under the Act.
Whether income from licensing poola grass collection is 'sayar income' and should be considered separately in compensation.
holdings: The average annual forest income under Section 39(1)(e) must be computed by considering both past income and appraised yield, but not by arithmetically adding the two figures.
Forest income refers only to the price of standing timber; income from processing wood is trade income and not includable as forest income.
Income from licensing poola grass collection is 'sayar income' under Section 39(1)(c) and must be considered separately from forest income.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 39(1)(e)(i) and (ii)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 39(1)(c)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(26)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of compensation provisions
Distinction between forest income and trade income
Use of multiple valuation methods without arithmetical addition

card.dispute: Fonseca Private Ltd. challenged an eviction order issued by a government official under the Defence of India Rules, claiming the official lacked authority to issue such an order.
issues_decided: Whether the Deputy Secretary had the authority to issue an eviction order under Rule 155 of the Defence of India Rules on behalf of the Central Government.
Whether the impugned order under Rule 155 was valid despite being issued by an unauthorised officer.
holdings: Only the Central Government or an officer specifically authorised under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules can issue an order under Rule 155 of the Defence of India Rules.
An order issued under Rule 155 by an officer without legal authority is illegal, ineffective, and void, and must be quashed.
provisions: Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, Rule 3 and Rule 11
doctrines: Doctrine of ultra vires
Principle of authorised delegation of power

card.dispute: The appellants, unauthorized occupants of public premises, challenged the constitutional validity of eviction orders passed under the 1958 Act and validated retrospectively by the 1971 Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, which validates actions taken under the repealed 1958 Act, is constitutionally valid?
Whether the retrospective validation of eviction proceedings under the 1958 Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether a deeming provision can validate actions that were previously held unenforceable due to constitutional infirmities arising from procedural options under general law?
holdings: Section 20 of the 1971 Act retrospectively validating actions under the 1958 Act is valid, as it amounts to a re-enactment removing prior grounds of unenforceability.
The validation does not violate Article 14, as the 1971 Act eliminates discriminatory potential by removing alternative eviction procedures.
A deeming provision can cure prior unenforceability caused by extraneous legal contexts, provided the procedure itself did not ab initio violate constitutional rights.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1958, Section 5(1)
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 15
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 20
doctrines: Doctrine of Deeming Provisions
Doctrine of Retrospective Validation
Doctrine of Equal Protection under Article 14
Doctrine of Re-enactment to Cure Procedural Infirmity

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their convictions and death sentences for murder, arguing that the medical evidence contradicted eyewitness accounts and that the sentence was excessively harsh.
issues_decided: Whether the medical evidence contradicts the eyewitness testimony regarding the deceased's ability to run and speak after sustaining the first injury
Whether discrepancies in the timing of the deceased's last meal undermine the credibility of the eyewitness account
Whether the failure to seize the vessel used to bring water to the deceased indicates fabrication of evidence
Whether the death sentence is justified given the brutality of the murder and the clarity of evidence on fatal injuries
holdings: The medical evidence does not rule out the possibility that the deceased could run a short distance and speak after the first injury, so the eyewitness accounts are credible and not contradicted by medical opinion.
Minor discrepancies in the timing of the last meal do not discredit the eyewitness testimony, as such evidence is based on general impression and not precise timekeeping.
The investigating officer was not required to seize the water vessel or irrigation tools, as they had no direct connection to the offence, and their absence does not indicate evidence fabrication.
The death sentence is justified for those who inflicted the fatal injuries, as the murder was brutal and callous, and the evidence clearly identifies the perpetrators of the fatal blows.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Principle of corroboration of eyewitness testimony by medical evidence
Judicial discretion in evaluating sentence severity in capital punishment cases

card.dispute: The landlord filed an eviction suit within five years of the building's completion but obtained the decree after five years; the tenant contested whether the decree was exempt from rent control restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether exemption under the Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, notification of 1965 requires both the suit and decree for eviction to be completed within five years of the building's completion.
Whether a decree passed after the five-year exemption period is still exempt from Section 13 if the suit was filed within that period.
holdings: The exemption from Section 13 applies if the eviction suit was filed within five years of the building's completion; the timing of the decree is not restricted by the exemption period.
The notification only requires the suit to be instituted during the exemption period; the decree may be passed thereafter and still remain exempt from Section 13.
provisions: Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 3
Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Presumption against rendering legislative provisions ineffective

card.dispute: The appellant, Haridwar Singh, challenged the government's decision to award a bamboo coup lease to the sixth respondent via private treaty after his own higher bid in an auction was not confirmed due to lack of government approval.
issues_decided: Whether a concluded contract arose between the appellant and the government upon provisional acceptance of his auction bid, subject to government confirmation?
Whether the government's settlement of the forest coup lease in favor of the sixth respondent by private treaty violated Rule 10(1) of the Rules of Executive Business of the Bihar Government?
Whether Rule 10(1), insofar as it requires prior consultation with the Finance Department, is mandatory or directory?
holdings: No concluded contract existed because the acceptance of the bid was subject to government confirmation, which was not communicated to the appellant, and the offer was later revoked.
Rule 10(1) as relaxed does not prohibit leasing forest coups by private treaty, but requires compliance with specified conditions when leases are made through auction.
The requirement of prior consultation with the Finance Department under Rule 10(1) is mandatory, not directory, and failure to consult invalidates the lease settlement.
provisions: Rules of Executive Business of the Bihar Government, Rule 10(1) and (2)
doctrines: Acceptance subject to confirmation does not create a binding contract until confirmation is communicated.
Distinction between mandatory and directory provisions in administrative rules based on language, subject matter, and consequences of non-compliance.

card.dispute: The appellant and his brothers saved their father's estate from debt; two other brothers executed deeds relinquishing future inheritance rights for consideration, but later sued for partition of the same properties after their father's death.
issues_decided: Whether a renunciation of future inheritance rights under Muslim Law is void and unenforceable during the lifetime of the ancestor
Whether the doctrine of estoppel under Section 115 of the Evidence Act can apply to bar a claim to inheritance after such a renunciation
Whether the deeds in question could be treated as part of a family arrangement or settlement
holdings: A mere expectancy of inheritance does not constitute a vested right, so its renunciation during the ancestor's lifetime is not a valid transfer but not inherently prohibited under Muslim Law.

The principle of equitable estoppel under Section 115 of the Evidence Act applies to prevent a person from denying a prior conduct or representation, even under Muslim Law, when it affects rights that later vest.

The deeds, supported by consideration and forming part of a course of conduct, created an estoppel against the executors, barring them from claiming inheritance rights after their father's death, regardless of whether they amounted to a formal family settlement.
doctrines: Equitable estoppel
Family arrangement
Spes successionis
Doctrine of estoppel in Muslim Law

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the Revenue's impounding of a deed of assignment and its assessment of stamp duty based on an alleged hidden consideration from prior agreements.
issues_decided: Whether the deed of assignment incorporated the terms of prior agreements with flat occupants, thereby affecting stamp duty valuation
Whether the Revenue could independently inquire into the value of consideration beyond what was stated in the deed
holdings: Mere reference in a deed to prior transactions does not incorporate their terms; there must be clear intent to incorporate, which was absent here.
The stamp duty under Article 23 must be based on the consideration 'as set forth in' the instrument; the Revenue cannot conduct an independent valuation inquiry.
doctrines: Incorporation by reference
Literal interpretation of stamp duty provisions
Stare decisis in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants second party) appealed against a decree for specific performance of a sale contract, but the appeal was challenged for abatement due to the death of respondent No. 3 (vendor) and non-impleadment of his legal representatives.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abates as a whole when one of the respondents dies and their legal representatives are not impleaded in time?
Whether Order 41 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure allows the appellate court to proceed with the appeal in such a situation?
Whether the vendor is a necessary party in a suit for specific performance where a subsequent transferee is also involved?
holdings: The appeal abates as a whole when a necessary party dies and their legal representatives are not brought on record, as the court cannot pass a consistent decree without them.
Order 41 Rule 4 CPC does not save the appeal if the absence of a deceased party’s legal representatives leads to inconsistent or incomplete reliefs.

The vendor is a necessary party in a specific performance suit because the sale deed must be executed by them, especially to incorporate special covenants, and any alternative relief for refund requires their presence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 5
doctrines: Abatement of appeal due to non-joinder of legal representatives
Necessary party doctrine in specific performance suits
Rule against inconsistent decrees in appellate proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the forfeiture of money paid and resumption of a site by the State under Section 9 of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, arguing it violated constitutional rights under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f).
issues_decided: Whether Section 9 of the Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, which allows resumption of a site and forfeiture of instalments paid, violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the power under Section 9 imposes an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold property under Article 19(1)(f)
holdings: Section 9 of the 1952 Act violates Article 14 as it allows arbitrary and unguided discrimination in choosing between remedies, with no criteria for when resumption or recovery as arrears of land revenue will be used.

The provisions of Section 9 impose an unreasonable restriction on the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) by allowing forfeiture and resumption despite the existence of a statutory charge, and without relief against forfeiture, making it disproportionate and unconstitutional.
provisions: Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, Section 3
Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, Section 8
Capital of Punjab (Development and Regulation) Act, 1952, Section 9
doctrines: Right to equality under Article 14
Unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights
Doctrine of arbitrariness in state action
Relief against forfeiture in property law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the death sentence under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code on grounds of violation of fundamental rights under Articles 19, 14, and 21 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence under Section 302 IPC violates the freedoms under Article 19(1) of the Constitution
Whether the unguided judicial discretion in imposing the death penalty violates Article 14
Whether the absence of a separate sentencing procedure violates Article 21's requirement of 'procedure established by law'
holdings: The death penalty does not violate Article 19 as it does not render the law unreasonable or contrary to public interest.
Judicial discretion in sentencing, though broad, does not violate Article 14 as it is based on individualized assessment of facts and is subject to appellate review.

The procedure established by law under Article 21 includes the trial and post-conviction sentencing considerations, and the absence of a separate formal sentencing procedure does not invalidate the death penalty.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 306(2) and Section 309(2)
Constitution of India, Article 14, Article 19(1), Article 21, Article 72(1)(c), Article 134, List III (Seventh Schedule) Entry 1 and 2
doctrines: Procedure established by law (Article 21)
Equal protection of laws (Article 14)
Judicial discretion in sentencing

card.dispute: Displaced persons challenged the cancellation of their land allotments, arguing that the government lacked power to retrospectively amend rules defining 'agricultural land'.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government had the power to give retrospective effect to an Explanation added to Rule 49 under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
Whether a rule framed without retrospective authority but laid before Parliament can be validated by such laying.
holdings: The Central Government lacked power to make a retrospective rule under Section 40 of the Act, as the section did not expressly or by necessary implication authorize retroactive rule-making.
The requirement to lay rules before Parliament does not validate a rule that is ultra vires the parent statute; courts can still strike it down if beyond delegated authority.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 40
doctrines: Subordinate legislation cannot be retrospective unless the parent statute authorizes it expressly or by necessary implication.
Parliamentary scrutiny (laying rules before legislature) does not cure substantive invalidity of ultra vires rules.

card.dispute: The appellant, Janak Singh, challenged his conviction and death sentence for the murder of his mother-in-law, Phoolmati, over a land dispute and alleged motive to marry her daughter.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's eyewitness accounts of the murder were reliable despite discrepancies in distance estimates and the defense claim that the shooting occurred inside the house.
Whether the medical evidence contradicted the eyewitness testimony by suggesting multiple shots were fired, thereby undermining the prosecution's case.
Whether the recovery of evidence from the well site after a delay rendered the investigation suspicious and inadmissible.
holdings: Eyewitness testimony identifying the appellant as the shooter at the well was credible and consistent with the victim's posture and injuries, and minor variations in estimated distance did not undermine reliability.

The medical evidence showing eleven pellet injuries did not necessarily indicate multiple shots, as a single discharge could have caused all injuries given the victim’s crouched position and alignment of body parts.
The delay in police recovery of physical evidence from the well did not vitiate the investigation, as officers were occupied with urgent tasks and no evidence suggested the shooting occurred indoors.
doctrines: Principle of reliability of eyewitness testimony in absence of material contradictions
Harmony between medical and eyewitness evidence in homicide cases
Judicial caution against speculative challenges to forensic investigation timelines

card.dispute: The owner of premises challenged the protection claimed by a private company, which had taken over the business and possession from a sub-lessee, under the Bombay Rent Act, arguing it was not entitled to protection from eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the private company was protected under Section 15(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act for being a sub-lessee or assignee in possession before the 1959 Ordinance came into force
Whether Section 15(2) of the Act validates subsequent assignments or transfers made by sub-lessees or assignees, as opposed to those made directly by tenants
holdings: Section 15(2) of the Bombay Rent Act validates only sub-leases, assignments, or transfers made by tenants, not those made by sub-lessees or assignees.

To be protected under Section 15(2), the person must have been a sub-lessee of the tenant and in continuous possession since before the 1959 Ordinance; mere possession by a subsequent assignee is insufficient.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, Section 15(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, Section 15(1) with proviso and explanation
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, Section 5(ii) and 5(ii)(aa)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXI, Rule 100
doctrines: Validation of otherwise prohibited sub-letting by retrospective legislation
Literal interpretation of statutory terms like 'tenant' to exclude sub-lessees
Requirement of continuous possession at the time of ordinance commencement for protection

card.dispute: An advocate, Hiralal Jain, challenged his commitment to trial for criminal conspiracy and cheating in connection with fraudulent land compensation claims.
issues_decided: Whether there was prima facie evidence to commit the appellant for trial on charges under Sections 120B, 419, 420, 467, 471, and 511 IPC
Whether the acts of the advocate in filing applications and identifying claimants, along with receiving a fee, constituted sufficient grounds for inferring criminal conspiracy
Whether circumstantial evidence, such as the fee received and role in identification, could support a charge of conspiracy
holdings: There must be prima facie evidence of criminal conspiracy or other charges to justify commitment of an accused to the Court of Session.
Mere filing of applications and verification by an advocate, without evidence of prior knowledge or agreement, does not establish conspiracy under Section 120B IPC.
Acts such as accepting a fee, verifying identities, and undertaking responsibility for refund do not, by themselves, constitute incriminating circumstances supporting conspiracy.
doctrines: Prima facie evidence requirement for commitment
Doctrine of criminal conspiracy requiring prior agreement
Use of circumstantial evidence in commitment proceedings

card.dispute: The landlords (Kani Ram and others) fought against the tenants (Smt. Kazani and others) over the validity of a decree of ejectment passed by compromise under the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, and whether the objection to its validity was barred by constructive res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the decision in prior execution proceedings on the validity of the ejectment decree operated as constructive res judicata in subsequent execution proceedings.
Whether the decree of ejectment passed by compromise under the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, was a nullity.
holdings: The decision in the earlier execution proceedings on the validity of the decree involved a mixed question of law and fact, and therefore, the principle of constructive res judicata applied, barring re-litigation of the issue.
The decree of ejectment passed on compromise was valid if the court had satisfied itself that grounds under Section 13 existed, and its validity could not be re-agitated in later proceedings.
provisions: Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 16
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Mixed question of law and fact
Validity of compromise decrees under rent control legislation

card.dispute: The appellant, a person below 21 years of age, sought to claim the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act after being convicted under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC, which is punishable with life imprisonment.
issues_decided: Whether a person below 21 years of age convicted of an offence punishable with life imprisonment can claim the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958?
Whether the possibility of awarding a lesser sentence excludes an offence from the category of offences punishable with life imprisonment for the purpose of invoking probation?
holdings: A person convicted of an offence punishable with life imprisonment, even if below 21 years of age, cannot claim the benefit of Section 6 of the Probation of Offenders Act, as the provision explicitly excludes offences punishable with life imprisonment.

The fact that a lesser term of imprisonment may also be awarded does not remove the offence from the category of those punishable with life imprisonment; the mere possibility of life sentence is sufficient to bar probation under Section 6.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Exclusion of serious offences from probation benefits
Judicial recognition of penological reform for youthful offenders

card.dispute: The appellant, a Naib Tehsildar, was convicted of accepting a bribe of Rs. 100 from a complainant for facilitating land possession, and challenged the conviction and sentence before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, read with Section 161 IPC, can be sustained based on the testimony of the complainant and corroborating police evidence?
Whether non-examination of independent witnesses, including the attesting witness to the seizure memo, vitiated the prosecution case?
Whether the evidence of prosecution witnesses, particularly PW 1 and police officers, was reliable and sufficient to uphold the conviction?
Whether the authority who granted sanction to prosecute was competent under the law?
