Whether the installation of a live wire mechanism on top of jail walls constitutes a violation of Article 21 by imposing a disproportionate penalty for escape attempts
holdings: The presence of armed police outside the jail, even in appurtenant structures, does not infringe upon the fundamental rights of prisoners as it does not interfere with their personal liberty under Article 21.

The live wire mechanism atop jail walls does not violate Article 21 because prisoners have no fundamental right to escape lawful custody, and the device is a preventive measure that does not constitute 'procedure established by law' violating personal liberty unless triggered by an escape attempt.
doctrines: Procedure established by law under Article 21
Fundamental rights of prisoners
Reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights
Non-retrogression of fundamental rights
Interpretation of personal liberty expansively

card.dispute: The respondents sued Charan Singh, a trustee of a religious trust, for breaching his duties by interfering with religious recitals and congregations at a Gurudwara, seeking enforcement of trust obligations without obtaining the required consent under Section 92 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code for want of the Advocate General's consent
Whether the reliefs claimed in the plaint fell within the scope of Section 92(1)(a) to (h)
Whether the suit was maintainable as a representative action for enforcement of public trust duties
holdings: A suit is governed by Section 92 CPC only if it alleges a breach of a public religious or charitable trust and seeks one of the specified reliefs under the section.
The maintainability of a suit under Section 92 depends on the allegations in the plaint, not on the written statement or the defendant's conduct.
Relief under Section 92 must be of the same nature as those listed in clauses (a) to (g); clause (h) does not cover reliefs that are fundamentally different in kind.
A suit seeking enforcement of a trustee's duties in relation to a public religious trust, but not seeking any of the specific reliefs under Section 92, is not maintainable under that provision.
doctrines: Maintainability based on plaint allegations
Strict construction of Section 92 CPC
Public trust enforcement doctrine
Relief must conform to statutory categories

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder and sentenced to death by the High Court, challenged the severity of their sentence, seeking commutation to life imprisonment.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence imposed on the appellants for murder was justified under Section 302 of the Penal Code.
Whether mitigating circumstances warranted commutation of the death sentence to life imprisonment.
What role the appellants played in the commission of the murders compared to other accused.
holdings: The death sentence should be commuted to life imprisonment as the appellants did not play a dominant role in the murders and the circumstances showed provocation by the deceased.
The appellants, being immature youths acting under the instigation of an elder, and having undergone prolonged mental torture due to the death sentence, warranted leniency.
The court has discretion under Section 302 IPC to impose life imprisonment instead of death, especially where the murder lacks marked brutality.
Disparity in sentencing among co-accused, with others receiving life imprisonment despite causing more fatal injuries, supported commutation.
doctrines: Doctrine of proportionality in sentencing
Mitigating circumstances in capital punishment cases
Discretionary sentencing under Section 302 IPC
Principle of comparative gravity among co-accused

card.dispute: The reversioners of W challenged the validity of a gift made by his widow to her daughter, arguing that under customary Punjab law, they had a superior claim to the property upon the widow's death.
issues_decided: Whether succession to the estate of a Hindu male opens at the death of the last full owner or at the death of a female limited owner who inherited the property.
Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to determine succession upon the death of a limited female owner who died after the Act came into force.
Whether customary law of Punjab, which restricted daughters' rights in ancestral property, governs the succession in this case.
holdings: Succession opens upon the death of a female limited owner, not at the death of the last male holder, and is governed by the law in force at the time of her death.
Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to determine succession upon the death of a limited owner, even if the last male holder died before the Act came into force.
The customary law of Punjab does not apply because the reversioners' rights were not vested and the Act governs succession as it stood in 1963, when the widow died.
provisions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937
doctrines: Succession opens on death of limited owner
Prospective application of statutory law
Spes successionis does not constitute a vested right
Legal fiction of deemed death of last male owner on death of limited female owner

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's determination of compensation for land acquired for the Malaprabha Project, arguing that it relied on a precedent from a different village and ignored evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in fixing compensation based on its earlier decision in respect of lands in a different village without considering local evidence.
Whether the claimants were entitled to higher compensation despite not filing claims before the Land Acquisition Officer under Section 9.
holdings: The High Court's compensation determination, though not fully reasoned, was not unsupportable, even if it relied on a precedent from another village.
Claimants who did not file claims under Section 9 were not entitled to compensation higher than what the Land Acquisition Officer awarded.
doctrines: Principle of reasoned judicial decision-making
Requirement of evidence in compensation determination
Consequence of non-appearance before Land Acquisition Officer

card.dispute: Gojer Bros. Pvt. Ltd. and Ratan Lal Singh fought over whether a decree for possession could be set aside under Section 17D of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1968, after the High Court had affirmed it post-amendment.
issues_decided: Whether Section 17D of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1968 applies to a decree confirmed by the High Court after the Act came into force.
Whether the trial court's decree merged into the High Court's appellate decree.
holdings: Section 17D does not apply to decrees confirmed by the High Court after the commencement of the 1968 Act, as the appellate decree is the operative decree for execution.
The decree of the trial court merges into the decree of the High Court when the appeal is decided on merits and the appellate decree becomes the sole enforceable decree.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1968, Section 17D
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 12(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of merger of decrees
Prospective application of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The dispute was between a mortgagee (Ganga Bai) and the mortgagor and his sons over the validity of a partition and the maintainability of an appeal challenging a preliminary mortgage decree after a long delay.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in allowing an amendment to the memorandum of appeal after a delay of over 7½ years without any explanation or application for condonation of delay.
Whether an appeal lies against a mere finding of fact in a decree, where the finding does not affect the rights adjudicated in the decree.
Whether the finding that the partition was colourable would operate as res judicata and thus be appealable.
holdings: The High Court erred in allowing an amendment to the appeal after 7½ years without any explanation for the delay or application for condonation, as such unexplained delay defeats the interest of justice and affects accrued rights.
An appeal is not maintainable against a mere finding of fact in a judgment if the decree does not adversely affect the appellant's legal rights or obligations.
A finding that does not directly and substantially affect the rights in issue and would not operate as res judicata cannot be the basis of an appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 89
doctrines: Res judicata
Inordinate delay in seeking amendment
Maintainability of appeal against a finding of fact

card.dispute: Landowners in Jammu and Kashmir challenged the constitutional validity of the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1972, claiming it rendered them landless and violated fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1972 is protected under Article 31A of the Indian Constitution.
Whether the exclusion of 'orchards' from the definition of 'land' amounts to discriminatory treatment violating Article 14.
Whether the Act violates the right to property and other fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31.
holdings: The Act constitutes a valid agrarian reform legislation aimed at equitable distribution of land to tillers and is protected under Article 31A.
The differential treatment of orchards is reasonable and justified by the Act's scheme, given their agricultural specificity and local conditions, and does not violate Article 14.
The Act does not violate Articles 19 or 31 as it falls within the exception provided by Article 31A, which shields agrarian reform laws from such challenges.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1972
doctrines: Agrarian reform as a valid basis for property restriction
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Protection of laws under Article 31A from fundamental rights challenges

card.dispute: The appellants (reversioners) and respondent (legatee of a Hindu widow) fought over whether properties acquired from the income of the husband's estate were accretions to the estate or belonged absolutely to the widow.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in limiting its hearing to specific findings instead of the entire appeal
Whether 5 acres lost due to the widow's failure to pay land revenue should be debited against her share
Whether costs incurred by the reversioner in litigation should be accounted for in property allocation
Whether the widow treated the acquired properties as accretions to her husband's estate
holdings: When an appellate court calls for findings on specific issues, the appeal is not disposed of, and parties retain the right to argue the entire appeal upon receipt of those findings.
A Hindu widow is not liable for negligence in managing the estate unless guilty of willful waste; reversioners cannot claim compensation from her separate properties for losses during her lifetime.
Costs incurred by a reversioner in litigation are accounted for in settled decrees and cannot be separately added to the principal when allocating estate properties.

Mere management of acquired properties alongside inherited ones, or failure to challenge sales of her life interest, does not prove a widow intended to treat such properties as accretions to her husband's estate.
provisions: Hindu Law (unspecified sections, as case interprets principles of limited estate)
doctrines: Limited estate of a Hindu widow
Presumption of absolute control over income and its investments by a widow
No liability for negligence without willful waste
Estoppel not presumed from conduct inconsistent with full ownership

card.dispute: The Government of Mysore and others challenged the validity of notifications issued under the Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, which declared certain areas as slum and clearance areas, arguing that the affected persons were not given a hearing, violating principles of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Sections 3, 9, and 12 of the Mysore Slum Areas Act, 1958 violate the principles of natural justice by not providing a hearing to affected persons before declaring an area as a slum or clearance area
Whether Section 12(1)(b), which allows acquisition of land other than slum areas for rehabilitation, is constitutionally valid
Whether Section 15, dealing with compensation for land acquired under the Act, is valid in law
holdings: Sections 3, 9, and 12(1)(a) and (b) of the Act are valid, but the notifications issued under them are void because affected persons were not given an opportunity to be heard, which is essential for fair administrative action.
Section 12(1)(b) is constitutionally valid as it serves the purpose of slum clearance and rehabilitation and includes a provision for showing cause, satisfying the requirements of natural justice.
It is not necessary to decide on the validity of Section 15 as the State informed the Court that a subsequent amendment aligned compensation under Section 12 with the Land Acquisition Act.
provisions: Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, Section 3
Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, Section 9
Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, Section 12
Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, Section 15
Mysore Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1958, Section 16
doctrines: Principles of Natural Justice
Right to Hearing in Administrative Action
Subjective Satisfaction of Administrative Authority
Procedural Fairness in Statutory Notifications

card.dispute: The cooperative society challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications issued in 1960 and 1961 nearly a decade later, after the acquisition process had substantially progressed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' challenge to the land acquisition notifications was barred by inordinate delay
Whether the delay in filing writ petitions affected the maintainability of the challenge to acquisition proceedings
holdings: A challenge to notifications under sections 4 and 6 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act must be made within a reasonable time; a delay of nine years renders the challenge inadmissible.
Allowing challenges after long delays that permit the government to complete acquisition proceedings encourages dilatory tactics and undermines administrative finality.
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Dilatory tactics in land acquisition challenges
Reasonable time for challenging administrative notifications

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Collector's order that reopened a prior determination of surplus land, arguing it was invalid and violated natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to review his 1961 order declaring no surplus land after the 1962 amendment introduced Section 32-DD(b) with retrospective effect.
Whether the Collector’s 1963 order, which ignored a civil court judgment based on Section 32-DD(b), violated the principles of natural justice.
Whether a civil court judgment declaring that a mutation was not a real transfer falls within the scope of Section 32-DD(b) as diminishing the landholding of a person.
holdings: The Collector’s 1961 order was valid when passed and could not be nullified retroactively by a later-amended provision not in force at the time.
The Collector violated natural justice by failing to give appellants 2 and 3 an opportunity to be heard before reopening the case in 1963.
A judgment that declares a mutation was not a real transfer does not 'diminish' a person’s holding under Section 32-DD(b) because the land never legally belonged to that person.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-DD(b)
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Retrospective operation of statutes
Declaratory nature of judgments
Interpretation of statutory language in light of legal reality

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of tenants on grounds of subletting, after the Saurashtra Rent Control Act was repealed and replaced by the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under the Transfer of Property Act was necessary to terminate the tenancy on grounds of subletting.
Whether the right to recover possession for subletting under the Saurashtra Rent Control Act survived its repeal under the saving clause of the Bombay Rent Act.
Whether the landlord had an accrued right or privilege to evict the tenant for subletting done during the operation of the Saurashtra Act.
holdings: No notice under the Transfer of Property Act was required to terminate tenancy for subletting, as mere subletting is not a ground for forfeiture unless the lease agreement prohibits it.
The right to recover possession under the Saurashtra Rent Control Act for subletting accrued when the subletting occurred and survived the Act’s repeal under the saving clause of the Bombay Rent Act.
The landlord had a legal privilege to terminate the tenancy and an accrued right to sue for possession under the Saurashtra Act, which continued after repeal as it arose during the Act’s operation.
doctrines: Accrued rights doctrine under saving clauses
Distinction between right and privilege in jurisprudence
Survival of privileges and rights post-repeal
Forfeiture of lease for breach of condition under Transfer of Property Act

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested whether the judgment in a prior suit operated as res judicata on the issue of title to certain properties between them, affecting the validity of an arbitration award determining their status as co-bhumidars.
issues_decided: Whether the prior judgment between co-plaintiffs could operate as res judicata on the issue of title to the properties?
Whether the second arbitration award, which held the prior judgment did not operate as res judicata, suffered from an error of law apparent on the face of the record?
Whether the appellants could challenge the order remitting the first award for fresh arbitration despite no appeal lying under Section 39 of the Arbitration Act?
holdings: A judgment can operate as res judicata between co-plaintiffs if there was a conflict of interest, necessity to decide it for granting relief, and actual judicial determination of the issue.

The second arbitration award was vitiated by an error of law apparent on the face of the record because it incorrectly treated the prior High Court judgment as not constituting res judicata when it did.
The appellants were not precluded from challenging the correctness of the order remitting the first award, as no appeal lay under Section 39, and they could raise it in a subsequent appeal.
doctrines: Res judicata between co-plaintiffs
Error of law apparent on the face of the award
Finality of judicial decisions

card.dispute: The son and wife of Gurbachan Singh were convicted for his murder and destruction of evidence; they appealed, challenging the reliability of prosecution witnesses and the sufficiency of evidence, especially against the wife.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of Uma Paul and Surjit Kaur is reliable enough to sustain the conviction of both appellants?
Whether the conviction of Bachni under Section 302/34 and Section 201 IPC is proved beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the death sentence awarded to Jagdip Singh should be commuted to life imprisonment?
holdings: The testimony of Uma Paul and Surjit Kaur is reliable regarding Jagdip Singh firing the fatal shot, as corroborated by the investigation and accepted by lower courts.

The conviction of Bachni is not proved beyond reasonable doubt, as the first information report omits her alleged role, and later embellishments in witness accounts undermine their credibility against her.
The death sentence for Jagdip Singh is justified given the gravity of the offence and absence of mitigating circumstances warranting judicial interference.
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration and consistency in first information report
Selective application of common intention under Section 34 IPC

card.dispute: The appellant's legal representatives challenged the cancellation of a 1953 property transfer, which the State deemed non-bona fide under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, arguing it was made to increase retained land or compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the 1953 transaction involving dedication of property to a deity constituted a 'transfer' under Section 5A of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953
Whether the transfer was non-bona fide under Section 5A(7) for the purpose of increasing retained land or compensation
holdings: A transaction dedicating property to a deity for religious and charitable purposes constitutes a 'gift' and hence a 'transfer' under Section 5A of the Act.

The authorities below failed to properly apply Section 5A(7) by not examining whether the transfer was made to increase retained land or compensation; mere suspicion or repetition of statutory language is insufficient to cancel a transfer.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 5A
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 5A(7)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6(1)(i)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 16(1)(b)(vi)
doctrines: Substance over form in determining nature of transfer
Requirement of reasoned decision-making in administrative cancellation of transfers
Bona fides of transfer must be assessed with reference to statutory criteria under Section 5A(7)

card.dispute: The appellant, a former Income-tax Officer, challenged his dismissal from service, claiming violations of principles of natural justice during the departmental enquiry.
issues_decided: Whether the departmental enquiry violated the principles of natural justice by denying the appellant a fair opportunity to defend himself.
Whether the show-cause notice dated 5-5-1955 was vague and failed to disclose the grounds for proposed punishment.
Whether the appellant was prejudiced by not being informed of the Enquiry Officer’s punishment recommendation.
Whether the addition of charges during the course of the enquiry rendered it oppressive.
holdings: The enquiry did not violate natural justice as the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to explain his conduct at every stage, including personal hearing and review of evidence.
The show-cause notice was valid even without a detailed summary of evidence, as the appellant had already received the Enquiry Officer’s report and was asked to comment on it.
The appellant was not prejudiced by non-disclosure of punishment recommendation, as the Enquiry Officer’s report did not contain any such recommendation.
The issuance of a third charge-sheet during the enquiry was not oppressive, as it was an amplification of earlier charges and the appellant was given adequate time to respond.
provisions: Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Reasonable opportunity of hearing
Departmental enquiry fairness
Punishing authority not bound by enquiry officer's findings

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the adoption of Kartar Singh was valid under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, specifically whether there was an intention to transfer him from his birth family to the adoptive family.
issues_decided: Whether there was an intention to transfer the adopted child from his birth family to the adoptive family within the meaning of Section 11(vi) of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956.
Whether an adoption ceremony conducted with 'giving and taking' but claimed to be under custom can be valid after the 1956 Act abolished customary adoptions.
holdings: The ceremony of giving and taking in an adoption is inherently symbolic of transferring the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family, and satisfies the intent requirement under Section 11(vi) of the Act.

After the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 came into force, customary adoptions ceased to operate; thus, any valid adoption must comply with the Act, and the reference to 'custom' in the deed does not negate the legal intent to adopt under the statute.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 4
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 11(vi)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory adoption under the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956
Doctrine of abolition of customary law by statute
Doctrine of intention in adoption ceremonies

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence for the murder of Paras Nath, claiming errors in the appreciation of evidence and absence of common intention.
issues_decided: Whether the concurrent findings of the trial and appellate courts on the reliability of eyewitness testimony can be overturned.
Whether the delay in lodging the First Information Report (FIR) undermines the prosecution's case.
Whether Ram Ajore shared a common intention with Lalai to commit murder under Section 34 IPC despite not directly participating in the assault.
holdings: The credibility of eyewitnesses, including Radhey Shyam, was properly assessed by the lower courts, and there is no reason to interfere with their concurrent findings.
The delay in filing the FIR is explainable by the circumstances of fear, darkness, and distance, and does not vitiate the prosecution's case.
Ram Ajore, though not physically assaulting the victim, actively supported the commission of murder by armed presence, demonstrating common intention under Section 34 IPC.
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Appreciation of eyewitness testimony

card.dispute: The petitioner company challenged the constitutional validity of the special eviction procedure under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 and the Bombay Government Premises (Eviction) Act, 1955, alleging it violated Article 14 by being discriminatory compared to civil suit procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the special eviction procedure under Chapter VA of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 is discriminatory and violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the procedure before an administrative tribunal is inherently more prejudicial than a civil court suit to attract Article 14 scrutiny?
holdings: The special eviction procedure under Chapter VA does not violate Article 14 as it is not substantially or qualitatively more drastic or prejudicial than a civil suit.

An administrative procedure cannot be presumed discriminatory merely because it differs from a civil court process; the comparison must be objective, considering fairness, appeal mechanisms, and access to justice.
provisions: Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, Chapter VA (Sections 105A–105H)
doctrines: Equality before law (Article 14)
Test of substantial discrimination in procedural laws
Objective comparison of administrative vs. judicial procedures
Presumption against invalidity of legislative procedure without real and substantial disparity

card.dispute: The landowners appealed the quantum of compensation awarded for their land and buildings acquired by the State Government for public offices, arguing that the valuation methods used were flawed.
issues_decided: Whether the potential value of the land was properly considered by the lower courts.
Whether the land and buildings should have been valued together as a composite unit instead of being separated and the land subdivided by the 'belting' method.
Whether the multiple of 27 used for capitalising rental value of buildings was adequate or should have been increased to 33-1/3.
holdings: The potential value of the land was considered by the High Court, but the appellant failed to provide evidence of unique features justifying a higher valuation.
The 'belting' method of valuing a 50-foot strip adjoining the road at a higher rate was justified, especially since the appellant himself had advocated for it, and it operated to his benefit.
The multiple of 27 for capitalising rental income was reasonable, particularly given the age of the buildings and the interest rates on government securities at the time.
provisions: Hyderabad Land Acquisition Act (IX of 1309 Fasli)
doctrines: Principle of belting in land valuation
Capitalisation of rental income for compensation
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with in absence of legal error

card.dispute: The plaintiff-respondents sued to eject the defendant-appellant from school premises and recover arrears of rent, while the defendant claimed a right to occupy the premises without rent under a trust deed.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal is maintainable under Article 133(1)(b) of the Constitution of India
Whether the defendant-appellant is liable to pay rent for occupation of the school premises
holdings: An appeal falls under Article 133(1)(b) if the judgment involves, directly or indirectly, a claim or question respecting property valued at not less than twenty thousand rupees, distinct from the subject matter of the dispute.
The defendant-appellant is liable to pay rent as the school received government grants based on rent payments, and the managing committee acknowledged the rent liability in official records.
doctrines: Distinction between subject matter of dispute and property in respect of which a claim arises under Article 133(1)
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct or representation

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant claimed protection against eviction under Section 4B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, after his lease expired and protection as a protected tenant was withdrawn.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 4B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 after the expiry of his tenancy and withdrawal of protected tenant status.
Whether the appellant, as a tenant by sufferance, was entitled to notice during the Collector's inquiry under Section 88B(2) of the Act.
holdings: Section 4B does not apply where a tenant remains in possession without the landlord's consent after the lease and protected status end; such a person is a trespasser, not a tenant holding over.
A tenant by sufferance has no right to notice during a Collector's inquiry under Section 88B(2), which is confined to the Trust and the Collector for issuing a certificate.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4B
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88B(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4A
doctrines: Tenancy by sufferance
Privity of contract in tenancy
Conclusive evidence clause
Holding over requires landlord's consent

card.dispute: The appellant Maruti Bala Raut claimed to be a protected tenant under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, in two proceedings concerning different parts of the same land, while the respondents contested his tenancy status as of 11 August 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal exceeded its powers under Section 76 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, in interfering with findings of fact made by the Special Deputy Collector?
Whether the High Court, in exercise of its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution, could reappreciate evidence and substitute its own findings on questions of fact?
holdings: The Revenue Tribunal exceeded its revisional powers under Section 76 by reappreciating evidence and setting aside the Special Deputy Collector's factual findings, which it could not do as it was not an appellate authority.
The High Court, while entitled to supervise under Article 227, cannot reappreciate evidence or substitute its own view on factual questions; doing so exceeds the scope of its jurisdiction.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 76
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 does not include reappreciation of evidence

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of assault under Sections 326 and 325 IPC; they challenged the conviction based on unreliable prosecution evidence and improper reliance on evidence from a cross-case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could rely on evidence from a cross-case to confirm the appellants' conviction.
Whether the prosecution witnesses' testimony was reliable enough to sustain the conviction.
Whether the injuries on the accused supported a plea of private defence.
Whether the conviction could be upheld based solely on the evidence recorded in the present case.
holdings: A criminal conviction cannot be based on evidence from another case, especially without the accused's consent; the High Court erred in relying on a cross-case.
The prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt as the key witnesses gave inconsistent and improbable testimony.
The disproportionate injuries on the accused, including stab wounds, make it probable that they acted in private defence.
In the absence of reliable evidence, the conviction cannot be sustained and the appellants must be acquitted.
doctrines: Principle of fair trial
Right to private defence
Prohibition against using evidence from one case in another without consent
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay and Polychem Ltd disputed whether land on which a building was under construction was rateable for municipal taxation purposes.
issues_decided: Whether land in the process of being built upon is rateable under the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888
Whether the doctrine of sterility applies to render such land non-rateable
Whether Indian law on rateable value is governed by beneficial occupation or ownership value
holdings: Land on which a building is under construction remains rateable under the Act and does not become non-rateable merely because construction has begun.
The doctrine of sterility, based on English law of beneficial occupation, does not apply in India where rateable value is determined by the value of property to the owner, not the occupier.
Land under construction should be rated no lower than vacant land unless part of it is fit for occupation; no statutory exemption exists for such land.
doctrines: Doctrine of sterility
Hypothetical tenant test for rateable value
Principle of rateable value based on ownership

card.dispute: The Municipality of Bhiwandi and Nizampur appealed against a High Court decree holding it liable for damages caused by flooding due to its allegedly negligent construction work near a nallah.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipality's actions were done in good faith under Section 167 of the Bombay District Municipal Act
Whether negligence alone amounts to mala fides for the purpose of losing statutory protection
Whether the Municipality's conduct amounted to reckless disregard of consequences despite the statutory definition of 'done in good faith'
holdings: An authority does not act in good faith if it suspects something is wrong but fails to make further inquiries.
Being aware of potential harm and proceeding without action constitutes reckless disregard, which is legally equivalent to mala fides.
Negligence alone is not mala fides, but reckless disregard—where consequences are foreseen and ignored—removes protection under Section 167.
Section 167 does not protect a municipality when its actions show conscious indifference to likely harm, even if the act was not malicious.
doctrines: Good faith
Mala fides
Reckless disregard
Statutory immunity

card.dispute: The Municipal Council, Tirupathi, contested whether the Tirumalai Tirupathi Devasthanam's New Choultry building was exempt from property tax under the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920.
issues_decided: Whether the New Choultry building qualifies as a 'choultry' under Section 83(1)(b) of the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, and is thus exempt from property tax.
Whether the ancillary shops, offices, and service facilities within the choultry premises are part of the choultry and covered by the tax exemption.
Whether the minimal service charges or rental income from certain facilities disqualify the entire building from exemption under Section 83(1)(b).
holdings: A 'choultry' is a shelter or resting place for travellers and pilgrims, and its meaning must evolve with changing needs and standards of comfort.
Ancillary facilities like shops and offices that serve pilgrims are integral to the choultry's function and fall within the tax exemption if they support charitable purposes.
Minimal service charges or insignificant rental income do not constitute 'rent' that would negate exemption, especially when the income is used exclusively for the choultry's maintenance.
The entire complex qualifies for exemption under Section 83(1)(b) as the evidence shows no profit motive and the income is insufficient to cover maintenance costs.
provisions: Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, Explanation to Section 83
doctrines: Strict construction of taxing statutes
Benefit of doubt in case of ambiguity goes to the taxpayer
Exemption must be strictly proved but interpreted in light of purpose and context
Incidental commercial activity does not negate charitable purpose if it supports the main objective

card.dispute: The appellants (new owners of premises) fought with the respondent tenant over whether the tenant could waive the protection of Section 3 of the U.P. Rent Act to allow eviction despite no valid allotment order.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could waive the benefit of Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, which bars courts from entertaining certain eviction suits.
Whether Section 3 of the Act is based on public policy and thus non-waivable by a tenant.
holdings: Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 is based on public policy as it protects a weaker class (tenants) from exploitation and ensures equality of bargaining power.
The benefit of Section 3 cannot be waived by a tenant, as it is not merely a private right but a protection rooted in public policy, and courts are barred from entertaining suits contrary to it.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-A
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
doctrines: Public policy doctrine
Non-waivability of statutory protections based on public policy
Judicial interpretation of public policy based on community welfare

card.dispute: The petitioners, unauthorized occupants of government land in Tamil Nadu, challenged the constitutional validity of eviction proceedings under the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, alleging violation of Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, violates Article 14 by providing a special eviction procedure alongside ordinary civil remedies.
Whether the existence of dual procedures—one special and expedited, the other ordinary and slower—leads to arbitrariness and discrimination under Article 14.
Whether the procedural safeguards in the Act are sufficient to protect the rights of the affected persons.
holdings: A special procedure for eviction of unauthorized occupants from government land does not violate Article 14 merely because an alternative civil remedy exists, provided the special law serves a clear public purpose.
The mere possibility of discriminatory application of two parallel procedures does not invalidate the special procedure; there must be a real risk of discrimination, not a fanciful one.
The procedural safeguards in the Act—such as notice, opportunity to respond, appeal, and writ jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227—are sufficient to prevent arbitrariness and ensure fairness.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 2
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 3
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 5
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 6
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 7
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 14
doctrines: Doctrine of arbitrariness under Article 14
Principle of equal protection of laws
Test of real risk of discrimination vs. fanciful possibility
Sufficiency of procedural safeguards in administrative action

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the constitutional validity of the proviso to Section 11 of the Mysore Land Acquisition Act, 1961, which required prior government approval for compensation awards made by the Deputy Commissioner.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 11 of the Mysore Land Acquisition Act, 1961 violates Article 31(2) of the Constitution.
Whether the absence of explicit guidelines for the State Government's approval under the proviso renders it unconstitutional.
holdings: The award under Section 11 is an administrative offer of compensation made by the Deputy Commissioner as an agent of the State Government, and final approval resting with the government does not violate Article 31(2).

The State Government must act in accordance with the provisions of the Act when approving awards, and adequate safeguards exist through statutory remedies, so the lack of explicit guidelines does not invalidate the proviso.
doctrines: Doctrine of Agency in administrative law
Principle of constitutional validity of delegated authority with statutory safeguards
Doctrine of adequate procedural safeguards in property acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant sought to enforce a decree for a promissory note by executing a sale of family agricultural land, which the respondents (sons born after the sale) challenged as void under the Mysore Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1928.
issues_decided: Whether the attachment and sale of agricultural land in execution of a decree for a non-mortgaged debt violated Section 14(1) of the Mysore Agriculturists' Relief Act, 1928
Whether the respondents, born after the sale, could challenge the validity of the execution sale
Whether the suit was barred by res judicata due to earlier proceedings to which the respondents were not parties
holdings: An attachment before judgment of agricultural land for a debt not secured by a specific mortgage is invalid under Section 14(1), rendering the subsequent sale void ab initio.
Persons born after a void sale can challenge it because a void sale transfers no title, and they acquire rights by birth in joint family property.
A suit is not barred by res judicata if the parties were not involved in prior litigation and the earlier courts lacked jurisdiction.
doctrines: Void ab initio
Right by birth in joint family property
Constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant and sub-tenants on grounds of unauthorized sub-letting, while the tenant claimed protection under the pre-amendment version of the Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960 apply to a sub-letting that occurred in 1957, after the relevant cut-off date but before the Act came into force?
Whether the tenant was protected from eviction under clause (iii) of Section 30 of the Act, based on the rental value exceeding Rs. 400 per month, prior to its amendment in 1964?
Whether Section 3 of the Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Amendment Act, XI of 1964, which abates certain proceedings, applies to invalidate the landlord's eviction petition?
holdings: Section 10(2)(ii)(a) applies to sub-lettings done after 23rd October 1945, regardless of when the Act came into force, as established by precedent and the plain language of the provision.

The protection under Section 30(iii) was removed by the 1964 Amendment Act, and the landlord gained a new right to seek eviction; hence, the tenant could no longer claim exemption based on pre-amendment law.

Section 3 of the 1964 Amendment Act does not apply to this case because no proceeding was based on the exemption under Section 30(iii), nor did any rights accrue to the landlord by virtue of that clause.
provisions: Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(ii)(a)
Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 30(iii)
Madras Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Amendment Act, XI of 1964, Section 3
doctrines: Statutory displacement of contractual tenancy rights
Prospective application of amendments removing exemptions
Plain meaning rule in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Ex-servicemen co-operative tenant farming societies fought the State of Haryana over the Collector's order to evict them from 230 acres of land after allegedly expiring 20-year leases under the East Punjab Utilization of Lands Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to order eviction under the East Punjab Utilization of Lands Act, 1949 in the absence of produced leases or Pattas.
Whether the alleged lessees were granted land under the Act or under other resettlement or land utilization laws.
Whether the Collector could decide questions of title or ownership while ordering eviction.
Whether the land in dispute vested in Gram Sabhas or private owners.
holdings: The Collector cannot proceed with eviction under the Act unless it is clearly established that the occupants were lessees under Section 5 of the Act.
In the absence of any produced lease or Patta, the source of allotment must be determined before applying the Act.
The Collector lacks power to adjudicate title disputes, and conflicting claims must be resolved by appropriate legal forums.
Where land may vest in Gram Sabhas, the Collector cannot direct its handover to private individuals without proper inquiry.
provisions: East Punjab Utilization of Lands Act, 1949, Section 4
East Punjab Utilization of Lands Act, 1949, Section 5
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional facts
Principle against adjudication of title by revenue authorities
Rule of inquiry into source of possession

card.dispute: The landlords challenged the State Government's revisional order setting aside their eviction proceedings against a tenant, arguing that the tenant had waived the protection of the Rent Control Act under the lease agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the State Government's revisional order under Section 7F of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947.
Whether a tenant can waive the benefit of Section 3(1) of the Act, which requires prior permission from the District Magistrate to institute an eviction suit.
holdings: The High Court has the power under Article 226 of the Constitution to review the legality of a revisional order passed by the State Government under Section 7F of the U.P. Act, but should exercise it sparingly.

Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 is based on public policy aimed at protecting tenants as a weaker class, and its benefit cannot be waived by private agreement.
provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(1)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7F
doctrines: Public policy doctrine
Non-waivability of statutory protections based on public policy
Judicial interpretation of public policy in socio-economic legislation

card.dispute: Nawab Ali challenged his conviction under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC for the murder of Abdul Hamid Khan, arguing he was not liable for acts done after he left the scene.
issues_decided: Whether Nawab Ali could be held vicariously liable under Section 149 IPC for murder committed by an unlawful assembly after he had left the scene?
Whether the prosecution proved that Nawab Ali was a member of the unlawful assembly at the time the murder was committed?
holdings: A person cannot be held liable under Section 149 IPC for an offence committed by an unlawful assembly after they have ceased to be a member by leaving the scene.
Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC requires the accused to be a member of the unlawful assembly at the time the offence is committed; mere prior presence is insufficient.
doctrines: Vicarious liability under unlawful assembly
Common object of unlawful assembly

card.dispute: The appellants (Kuthalia) and respondents (Oberoi) disputed the enforcement and adjustment of a foreign decree for recovery of earnest money in a hotel sale contract, complicated by Partition-related impediments in execution.
issues_decided: Whether the deposit of money into court by a judgment debtor during appeal, which became unavailable due to external circumstances beyond his control, should result in double liability upon him.
Whether equitable principles justify adjusting the deposited sum toward the decree despite non-execution due to extralegal reasons like Partition.
Whether the decree-holder is entitled to full recovery when the judgment debtor had already deposited the amount in court for pro tanto satisfaction of the decree.
holdings: A judgment debtor who deposits money into court as security during an appeal cannot be held liable again if the decree-holder fails to withdraw the amount due to circumstances beyond the debtor’s control.
Equity requires that such a deposit be treated as pro tanto satisfaction of the decree, especially when execution was rendered impossible by extraordinary events like Partition.
The decree amount must be adjusted by the sum already deposited, with interest calculated on the balance from the date the decree-holder could have accessed the deposit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 2(1)
doctrines: Equitable adjustment of decrees
Doctrine of pro tanto satisfaction
Principle of justice, equity and good conscience
Enforcement of foreign decrees with equitable modification

card.dispute: The State of Bihar and a private respondent appealed the acquittal of nine accused in a murder case, leading to their conviction by the High Court, which the appellants challenged in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on re-appreciation of evidence
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that all nine appellants were involved in the murder of Palaknath Singh
Whether the injuries on the deceased were consistent with the prosecution's version of death by bladed weapons rather than an accidental gunshot
holdings: The High Court has full power to re-appreciate evidence in appeals against acquittal and can reverse acquittal if the trial court's reasons are found clearly unreasonable, provided it considers the presumption of innocence and credibility assessments.

The prosecution proved the guilt of seven appellants beyond reasonable doubt based on consistent eyewitness testimony and medical evidence, but the case against Dhuli Rai and Dhora Rai was not free from reasonable doubt and thus they were entitled to acquittal.

The injuries on the deceased, including multiple incised wounds and extrusion of brain matter, were caused by garasa and bhala blows followed by kicks, and were inconsistent with death by gunshot, thereby rejecting the defense's accidental shooting theory.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
doctrines: Re-appreciation of evidence in appeal against acquittal
Presumption of innocence and benefit of reasonable doubt
Consistency between medical and eyewitness evidence in homicide cases

card.dispute: The decree-holder (Prem Raj) sought to execute a foreclosure decree for possession of half the house, but the judgment-debtor (Ram Charan) resisted, claiming the execution application was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the fifth execution application was a 'step in aid of execution' under Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Whether the application was barred by limitation
Whether the prior litigation obstructing execution affected the timeliness of the execution application
holdings: Litigation undertaken by a decree-holder to defend the validity of a decree being executed is a 'step in aid of execution' under Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
An execution application filed within three years of the final order in obstructive litigation is not time-barred, even if more than three years have passed since the decree.
A decree that has been effectively suspended or impaired by a court order or adverse finding cannot be executed until such impediment is removed.
doctrines: Step in aid of execution
Impediment to execution
Liberal interpretation of limitation provisions in favour of decree-holders

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for murder and related offences committed in a factional dispute; they challenged the conviction, raising issues of alibi, self-defence, and reliability of eyewitness testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt the individual roles of all six accused in the murder and injuries?
Whether contradictions between earlier statements and trial testimony of eyewitnesses affect the credibility of the prosecution case?
Whether the medical evidence corroborated the eyewitness accounts regarding the weapons used and injuries inflicted?
Whether the conviction under Section 149 IPC can be sustained or should be altered to Section 34 IPC?
holdings: A-1, A-2, and A-3 were conclusively proven to have participated in the murder and injuries with common intention; their convictions were upheld.
The significant improvements in eyewitness testimony regarding A-4, A-5, and A-6, combined with lack of corroboration, left their participation subject to reasonable doubt; they were acquitted.
Medical evidence supported the use of a rice-pounder and spear as alleged against A-1, A-2, and A-3, but failed to confirm the involvement of A-4, A-5, and A-6.
Convictions of A-1, A-2, and A-3 were altered from Sections 302/326/324 with Section 149 IPC to the same offences with Section 34 IPC, as the case was one of common intention, not unlawful assembly.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Corroboration of interested witnesses
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Rejection of improved testimony
Requirement of consistency between medical and ocular evidence

card.dispute: The appellant (Rangnath) challenged the State Government's decision upholding the tenant's (Daulatrao's) right to occupancy after the abolition of his inam, claiming the tenancy had already ended and that he was entitled to a speaking order in his statutory appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government is bound to pass a speaking order and grant a personal hearing while deciding a statutory appeal under the Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act, 1954
Whether the tenancy of the respondent came to an end upon service of notice and filing of application for possession under the Tenancy Act
Whether the appellant could take a stand contrary to his earlier pleadings in previous proceedings
Whether the question of the respondent acquiring occupancy rights was barred by res judicata
holdings: While a speaking order is expected in statutory appeals under the Abolition Act, especially when subject to constitutional scrutiny, the failure to provide one does not automatically invalidate the decision if the matter involves only questions of law and no factual adjudication.

Mere service of notice and filing of an application for possession under the Tenancy Act does not terminate a tenancy; termination occurs only upon an order for possession by the competent authority, as per statutory provisions and rules.
A party cannot take a stand in appeal that is contrary to its earlier case in proceedings where it actively claimed the applicability of the Tenancy Act to evict the same tenant.
The issue of the tenant acquiring occupancy rights under the Abolition Act was directly and substantially decided in prior proceedings and is barred by res judicata, preventing re-litigation.
provisions: Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act, 1954, Section 2A(2)
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act, 1954, Section 6(1)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, Section 44(1)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, Section 32(2)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, Section 44(10)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Rules, Rule 28(5)
doctrines: Principle of speaking orders in administrative justice
Doctrine of res judicata
Prohibition against taking inconsistent pleas
Rule of statutory interpretation regarding termination of tenancy

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of six appellants in a criminal case involving the murder of Viswanath and related charges; the High Court convicted them, and the appellants challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Judge's order of acquittal based on appreciation of evidence
Whether the prosecution's evidence, including eyewitness testimony and medical opinion, was reliable and sufficient to sustain conviction
Whether discrepancies in the prosecution's evidence were material enough to discredit the entire case
Whether the convictions under Sections 147, 148, 302, and 323/149 IPC were legally sustainable
holdings: The High Court has full power to reverse an acquittal if the trial court's decision is perverse or based on erroneous appreciation of evidence, especially when it ignores credible eyewitness testimony.
Minor discrepancies in time, sequence, or investigation details do not fatally undermine reliable prosecution evidence if the core narrative remains consistent and credible.
The benefit of reasonable doubt and presumption of innocence apply, but appellate courts may uphold convictions if the trial court's acquittal is based on flimsy or irrational grounds.

Convictions under Section 302 read with 149 IPC for the main assailant and under Sections 147, 323/149 for others in an unlawful assembly are valid when the common object involved likely use of deadly force.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Benefit of reasonable doubt
Appreciation of evidence in appeals against acquittal
Common object under Section 149 IPC
Perverse findings doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Judicial Commissioner's decision to set aside the lease of a distillery granted to him in favor of the respondent, who had submitted the highest tender, on grounds of violation of Article 14 and procedural illegality.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's reservation of the right to accept any tender or reject all tenders without assigning reasons violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the Government is bound to accept the highest tender in a public bidding process
Whether the lease process was governed by the Portuguese-era Legislative Diploma No. 1761, Article 9, para 2, requiring an auction
Whether the Government's action in negotiating a higher amount with the appellant after rejecting the highest tender was illegal
holdings: The Government's right to accept or reject tenders without assigning reasons does not violate Article 14, as it is acting in its executive capacity to protect state revenue.
The Government is not legally bound to accept the highest tender in a tender process, as no contractual obligation arises until acceptance.
The process was an invitation to tender, not an auction, and therefore not governed by Article 9, para 2 of Legislative Diploma No. 1761.
The appellant's payment of Rs. 1,000 more than the highest tender was valid to safeguard state revenue and did not amount to mala fide or arbitrary action.
doctrines: Distinction between auction and invitation to tender
Government's executive discretion in contractual matters
No vested rights in bidders until acceptance of tender
Judicial non-interference in revenue protection decisions absent mala fides or arbitrariness

card.dispute: The partners of an unregistered electrical supply business fought over whether they could recover their contributions and share compensation money after the partnership was declared illegal under the Indian Electricity Act.
issues_decided: Whether the partnership was void ab initio due to non-compliance with the Indian Electricity Act, 1910
Whether the partners could claim a share in the compensation money despite the alleged illegality of the partnership
Whether money advanced by partners under an agreement later discovered to be void is recoverable
holdings: A partnership not formally licensed under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 is not automatically void if the partners acted in good faith and were unaware of illegality.
Even if the partnership was void, contributors are entitled to recover their shares from the partnership assets under Section 65 of the Indian Contract Act.
Section 65 applies when an agreement is discovered to be void, allowing recovery of money advanced, regardless of whether the agreement was void from the beginning.
doctrines: Restitution under void agreements
In pari delicto exception in cases of good faith
Discovery of voidness under Section 65

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction and life sentence for the murder of his brother, claiming insufficient evidence and improper identification.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was the assailant in the murder of his brother.
Whether the evidence of test identification parades was essential for conviction when there is corroborative circumstantial evidence.
Whether discrepancies in the testimonies of eyewitnesses warranted rejection of their evidence in toto.
holdings: The identity of the accused as the assailant can be established through reliable circumstantial evidence even if test identification is weak or valueless.
Test identification under Section 9 of the Evidence Act is only corroborative and not substantive; its absence does not collapse the prosecution case if other evidence is strong.

Minor discrepancies in eyewitness accounts regarding details like number of blows or victim's posture do not discredit their testimony if the core facts are consistent and supported by corroborative evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration through circumstantial evidence
Principle of reliability of eyewitness testimony despite minor inconsistencies
Requirement of reasoned orders in appellate decisions

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, former partners in a business, disputed whether an unregistered arbitration award allotting partnership assets, including immovable property, could be enforced by a court judgment.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award created rights in immovable property requiring registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the unregistered award could be enforced by pronouncing judgment under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the award could be partially enforced for parts not involving immovable property
holdings: An arbitration award that creates rights in immovable property worth more than Rs. 100 must be registered under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 to be admissible in court.
A court cannot pronounce judgment in terms of an unregistered award that creates rights in immovable property, as it cannot be legally examined or enforced.
An award that is an inseparable composite of clauses, some involving immovable property, cannot be partially enforced even for movable property components.
doctrines: Doctrine of inadmissibility of unregistered documents creating rights in immovable property
Doctrine of non-severability of interdependent award clauses

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Dayali Devi contested the Rama Krishna Mission's claim to exclusive possession of property bequeathed under Shamsher Singh's will, arguing the Mission was only entitled to joint possession as co-sharers.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could raise for the first time in the Supreme Court the plea that the plaintiff was entitled only to a decree for joint possession as a co-sharer, despite not raising it in the trial court or High Court.
Whether the observation in the High Court judgment that certain findings were not disputed could be challenged in the Supreme Court when not contested in the special leave petition.
holdings: A new legal plea not raised in the trial court or High Court cannot be allowed for the first time in the Supreme Court, especially after a long and protracted litigation, to prevent abuse of process and ensure finality.

A challenge to the High Court's statement that certain issues were conceded cannot be entertained in the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the special leave petition or certificate application, as it amounts to an afterthought.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 27
doctrines: Appellate Courts will not entertain new pleas not raised in lower courts
Principle of finality of litigation and judicial economy
Doctrine of approbation and reprobation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the grant of a Nazul plot lease to the third respondent, alleging it violated the Orissa State Urban Land Settlement Rules of 1959 and was arbitrary, while his own application was rejected.
issues_decided: Whether the Orissa State Urban Land Settlement Rules of 1959 confer justiciable rights or are merely administrative in nature.
Whether the Revenue Authorities' decision to grant the lease to the third respondent was arbitrary, capricious, or unfair.
holdings: Administrative rules may confer rights in certain cases, but the mere existence of such rules does not create a vested right to a government lease; only a right to fair and non-arbitrary treatment.

The Revenue Authorities' decision was not arbitrary or unfair, as they considered public benefit and housing needs, and their factual determination about eligibility under the rules is within their domain.
provisions: Orissa State Urban Land Settlement Rules, 1959, Rule 4(b)
doctrines: Administrative orders can confer rights in exceptional cases.
Judicial review of administrative action applies when the decision is arbitrary, capricious, or unfair.
Deference to administrative authorities on factual determinations within their expertise.

card.dispute: The appellant religious trust challenged the land acquisition notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, claiming it was not given an opportunity of being heard on its objection that the land was attached to a religious institution and thus exempted.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector is under a mandatory duty to afford an opportunity of being heard to an objector under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the appropriate Government can validly decide an objection under Section 5A without the Collector first hearing the objector and making a recommendation.
holdings: The duty of the Collector under Section 5A to afford an opportunity of being heard to an objector is mandatory, and the power to hear objections lies with the Collector, not the appropriate Government.
A decision by the Government on an objection without the Collector first hearing the objector and making a recommendation is invalid, as it violates the statutory procedure for land acquisition.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Mandatory nature of statutory procedure in deprivation of property
Rule of law in administrative action

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of tenants on grounds of non-payment of rent and personal requirement, but the Rent Controller and appellate authority dismissed the claim; the High Court reversed in revision, leading to a dispute over the scope of revisional power under the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reappreciate evidence in revision under section 26(c) of the Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Lease) Control Act, 1954, contrary to concurrent findings of fact by lower authorities.
Whether the revisional power under section 26 of the Act is wider than appellate power or akin to the limited revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code.
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or overturn concurrent findings of fact in revision; its power under section 26(c) is limited to correcting jurisdictional errors or material irregularities in procedure.

The revisional power under section 26 of the Act is not wider than appellate power and is substantially similar to the narrow scope of section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, confined to jurisdictional illegality or material procedural irregularity.
provisions: Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Lease) Control Act, 1954, Section 24
Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Lease) Control Act, 1954, Section 25
Hyderabad Houses (Rent, Eviction and Lease) Control Act, 1954, Section 26(c)
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction is narrower than appellate jurisdiction
Section 115 CPC limits revision to jurisdictional errors, illegal exercise of jurisdiction, or material procedural irregularities
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts cannot be overturned in revision unless there is a jurisdictional error

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of a provision in the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922 and the method used to determine compensation for land acquired for urban development.
issues_decided: Whether Section 59(a) of the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an unreasonable classification and denying appeal rights
Whether the Tribunal applied an incorrect and unreasonable principle in determining compensation by excluding sale deeds after the notification date
holdings: Section 59(a) does not violate Article 14 as acquisition under the Improvement Act is based on a reasonable classification linked to town improvement, and the denial of appeal is justified to prevent delays in development schemes.
The Tribunal did not adopt an unreasonable principle by excluding post-notification sale deeds, as such sales are speculative and not reliable indicators of market value on the material date.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Principle of non-speculative market value determination
Finality of administrative tribunal awards to prevent delay

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of tenants on grounds of bona fide personal necessity after serving notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act; tenants contested the claim and the applicability of rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs proved bona fide personal necessity for eviction under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 applied to the area where the suit premises were located
Whether the High Court erred in not allowing additional evidence under Section 151 of the CPC at the second appeal stage
holdings: The plaintiffs successfully proved bona fide personal necessity for the suit premises based on the evidence, and the courts below properly recorded findings on this issue.
The Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 was applicable to Chomu, but the High Court's initial error was corrected upon review and did not affect the final outcome.
The High Court did not commit error in refusing to admit additional evidence at the second appeal stage, especially when no such request was made in the first appeal.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950
doctrines: Bona fide personal necessity as a ground for eviction
Principle of judicial review correcting jurisdictional error
Discretion to admit additional evidence in second appeal under CPC

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and a private landholder disputed over whether the government had an express right to trees on Bane lands, affecting the landholder's ability to cut and sell timber.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 10 of the Rules for Classifiers contains an express order reserving the right to trees on Bane lands in favour of the State Government under Section 75(1) of the Mysore Land Revenue Act, 1964.
Whether the High Court's interpretation of Rule 10 as an express reservation was correct.
holdings: Rule 10 of the Rules for Classifiers does not constitute an express order reserving the State Government's right to trees on Bane lands under Section 75(1) of the Mysore Land Revenue Act, 1964.
The Rule is merely instructional for classifiers during survey settlement and does not create or declare a substantive right over trees in favour of the government.
provisions: Rules for Classifiers issued under Regulation 1 of 1899
doctrines: Express reservation doctrine
Interpretation of statutory rules in context

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed the High Court's acquittal of four accused persons charged with the murder of three individuals based on circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution established that the recovered bodies were those of the alleged victims and that their deaths were homicidal
Whether the extra-judicial confessions attributed to three accused were credible and sufficient to sustain conviction
Whether the evidence of association between the accused and the victims was reliable
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the High Court's acquittal based on reappraisal of evidence
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the identity of the dead bodies or that the deaths were homicidal, as medical evidence showed unrecognizable features and no ascertainable cause of death.
Extra-judicial confessions were inherently improbable and lacked credibility, especially given the lack of motive to confess to unconnected persons.
The evidence of one witness seeing an accused with a victim on a cycle was unreliable due to delayed reporting and lack of corroboration.
The Supreme Court will not overturn an acquittal by the High Court unless there is a glaring infirmity in its evaluation of evidence, which was absent here.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Suspicion cannot replace proof
Extra-judicial confession requires corroboration and scrutiny
Limited scope of appellate interference in acquittals

card.dispute: The state of Punjab (now Haryana) challenged the inclusion of certain lands in a landowner's surplus area after tenants abandoned them and the land was gifted and sold, while the purchasers claimed rights under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether a transfer of land under Section 18 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, constitutes a 'transfer or other disposition' under Section 10A(b) of the Act.
Whether the Collector could include lands previously under tenancy but later transferred via Section 18 in the landowner's surplus area.
Whether a change in tenancy after the commencement of the Act affects the determination of surplus area.
Whether lands held by tenants within their permissible area on April 15, 1953, can be included in the landowner's surplus area.
holdings: A transfer under Section 18 is not a 'transfer or other disposition' under Section 10A(b) because it is an involuntary transfer by operation of law, not a volitional act by the landowner.
Lands held by tenants within their permissible area on the commencement date of the Act cannot be included in the landowner's surplus area under Section 2(5a).
A mere change in tenancy does not amount to acquisition of land by the landowner or make the land part of the surplus area.
Section 10A does not apply to lands that were not part of the surplus area on April 15, 1953, even if later transferred under Section 18.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(5a)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 10A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19-A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19-B
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19-F
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes in light of object and context
Distinction between voluntary and involuntary transfers
Determination of surplus area as of the commencement date of the Act
Reconciliation of seemingly conflicting statutory provisions

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the acquittal of Harihar Bux Singh and Rudra Pratap Singh, convicted by the trial court for the murder of Hargovind Singh, a case based primarily on the testimony of a single eyewitness.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the appellants by disbelieving the eyewitness testimony of Rajeshwari Devi?
Whether the prosecution established a motive for the murder?
Whether the inconsistencies in the eyewitness account rendered the conviction unsafe?
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the acquittal in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution?
holdings: The High Court was justified in disbelieving the eyewitness testimony due to material contradictions and suspicious circumstances, including external influence.
No motive was proved regarding a property dispute, weakening the prosecution's case.
Material discrepancies between the first information report and court testimony undermined the reliability of the eyewitness.
The Supreme Court will not interfere with an acquittal unless there is a glaring infirmity in the evaluation of evidence by the High Court.
doctrines: Double jeopardy and finality of acquittal
Principle of appreciation of evidence in criminal appeals
Requirement of reliable and consistent eyewitness testimony
Judicial restraint in special leave appeals under Article 136

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's acquittal and reduced sentences of accused involved in five murders and destruction of evidence, arguing that all participants in the unlawful assembly should be vicariously liable for the murders under Section 149 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the assembly of accused became an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 IPC?
Whether the members of the assembly could be held vicariously liable under Section 149 IPC for murders committed in prosecution of the common object or which they knew were likely to be committed?
Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting certain accused due to insufficient evidence of their presence or participation?
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the High Court's order of acquittal in criminal appeals?
holdings: An assembly that starts lawfully may become unlawful if its members develop a common object involving the use of criminal force; the transformation is permissible under the Explanation to Section 141 IPC.

Under Section 149 IPC, every member of an unlawful assembly is liable not only for acts done in prosecution of the common object but also for acts they knew were likely to be committed in that prosecution, including murder.

The High Court erred in acquitting five accused of murder charges under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC while finding their participation in post-murder acts; their conviction for murder must be restored.
The Supreme Court will not interfere with an acquittal by the High Court unless the findings are perverse or against the weight of evidence; in doubtful cases, the benefit of doubt is maintained.
doctrines: Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC
Transformation of a lawful assembly into an unlawful assembly
