doctrines: Vesting of rights at the time of filing the action
Substantive rights under statute are not defeated by subsequent events
Agrarian reform laws must be interpreted to fulfill legislative purpose and social justice

card.dispute: S. Kalawati challenged the order of the Deputy Director of Consolidation before the High Court under Article 226, which was dismissed in limine, but a certificate under Article 133(1)(a) was granted; the respondent contested the validity of the certificate.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's order dismissing a writ petition in limine amounts to a judgment affirming the decision of the authority below for the purpose of Article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution?
Whether a certificate under Article 133(1)(a) is valid when the High Court does not decide the merits of the case but dismisses the petition in limine?
holdings: An order dismissing a petition under Article 226 or 227 in limine is not a judgment on appeal or an affirmation of the lower authority's decision, as the High Court does not adjudicate on the merits.
A certificate under Article 133(1)(a) is valid if the case involves a substantial question of law or valuation, even if the High Court dismisses the petition in limine without reasoning.
doctrines: Doctrine of affirmance
Doctrine of judicial affirmation requiring adjudication on merits
Principle of competent certification under Article 133

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of two deeds of sale executed by his father in 1934, claiming they were void due to his father's minority and lack of legal necessity or consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's father was a minor at the time of executing the deeds of sale in 1934.
Whether the deeds of sale were supported by legal necessity and valid consideration.
holdings: The appellant's father was not a minor when he executed the deeds; he was consistently described as a major in prior legal documents and proceedings, and the burden of proving minority was not discharged.
The deeds of sale were valid as they were executed for the purpose of discharging antecedent debts and domestic needs, constituting legal necessity and valid consideration.
doctrines: Doctrine of Legal Necessity
Doctrine of Family Settlement
Burden of Proof in Minority Claims

card.dispute: The landlords challenged the constitutional validity of the U.P. Cantonments (Rent Control & Eviction) Act, 1952, which required their permission from the District Magistrate to evict tenants, alleging violations of fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and (g) and excessive delegation violating Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14 of the U.P. Cantonments (Rent Control & Eviction) Act, 1952, violates Article 19(1)(f) and (g) by imposing unreasonable restrictions on property rights and freedom to carry on business?
Whether Section 14 involves excessive delegation of legislative power, thereby violating Article 14?
Whether the writ petition remains maintainable after the repeal of the impugned Act?
holdings: The petition was dismissed as infructuous because the challenged Act had been repealed, and no live controversy remained before the Court.
The Court held that with the repeal of the Act, the writ petition under Article 32 could not be entertained, as there was no ongoing violation of fundamental rights.
The Court noted that if new circumstances arose after the refusal of permission under the repealed Act, the petitioners could seek relief under the new applicable law.
provisions: U.P. Cantonments (Rent Control & Eviction) Act, 1952, Section 14
doctrines: Infructuousness of writ petitions due to supervening events
Doctrine of repeal rendering challenges to statutes moot
Principle of maintainability of constitutional challenges when statutory regime changes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of the respondent's application to set aside a property sale under Order 21 Rule 89 of the CPC, arguing it was not permissible without a formal court order recording withdrawal of a prior Rule 90 application.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order 21 Rule 89 CPC is maintainable without a formal court order recording withdrawal of a prior application under Rule 90.
Whether the word 'make' in Rule 89(2) includes both filing and prosecuting an application.
Whether steps taken to serve notice on the prior Rule 90 application nullified its withdrawal.
holdings: The words 'make or prosecute' in Rule 89(2) must both be given effect; a prior Rule 90 application must be withdrawn before a Rule 89 application can be made or pursued.
An applicant can unilaterally withdraw a Rule 90 application by communicating withdrawal to the court; a formal court order is not required for the withdrawal to be effective.
Steps taken to serve notice on a Rule 90 application after withdrawal do not nullify the withdrawal if the intent to discontinue is clearly communicated later.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 89(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
doctrines: Unilateral withdrawal of an application
Effective date of withdrawal without court order
Literal and purposive interpretation of procedural provisions

card.dispute: The petitioner sought contempt proceedings against municipal and state officials and a cinema licensee for allegedly disobeying a Supreme Court judgment that invalidated the conversion of a hall into a cinema theatre.
issues_decided: Whether respondents 1 and 2 committed contempt by recommending revocation of the Town Planning Scheme and not stopping film exhibitions.
Whether respondent 3 committed contempt by continuing to exhibit films after the Supreme Court invalidated the conversion of the hall.
Whether respondent 4 committed contempt by not revoking the cinema licence upon receipt of an uncertified copy of the Supreme Court judgment.
holdings: Merely recommending revocation of a town planning scheme and lacking authority to stop film exhibitions does not constitute contempt.

Continuing film exhibitions after the Court held the conversion invalid amounts to contempt, but a bona fide belief in the validity of the licence and a conditional apology warrant discharge of contempt proceedings.
A public official cannot be held in contempt for not acting on an uncertified copy of a Supreme Court judgment, especially when departmental practice requires certification.
doctrines: Bona fide belief as a defence in contempt
Requirement of certified copies for official action
Contempt requires wilful disobedience

card.dispute: The State of Haryana challenged the validity of transfers made by respondents who, after inheriting land exceeding the permissible ceiling, gifted or otherwise transferred the surplus land to relatives to avoid surrendering it to the state.
issues_decided: Whether transfers of surplus land made by a person who inherited land exceeding the ceiling area are valid under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
Whether Section 19B of the Act, read with Section 10A, permits such transfers to defeat the ceiling laws
Whether the period prescribed for filing returns under Section 19B allows time for making gifts to circumvent the law
holdings: Section 19B mandates that any person acquiring land by inheritance that exceeds the permissible area must declare and surrender the surplus to the state, regardless of subsequent transfers.

Transfers made to relatives of surplus land after inheritance do not defeat the operation of the ceiling laws and are invalid if they aim to circumvent the statutory obligation to surrender surplus land.
The time allowed for filing returns under Section 19B is procedural and not an opportunity to alienate surplus land; such alienations are void as they frustrate the agrarian reform policy.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 10A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19B
doctrines: Interpretation of agrarian reform laws to promote equitable ownership and redistributive justice
Statutory construction in favour of the general purpose of the Act, especially for economic legislation
Judicial refusal to allow procedural provisions to be used to subvert substantive legislative objectives

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and a company fought with landowners over the legality of land acquisition for industrial expansion, specifically whether proper procedures were followed before issuing notifications under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners were entitled to be heard during the enquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963
Whether the agreement between the State and the company under Section 41 of the Act was required to precede the notification under Section 4
Whether the enquiry under Section 40 of the Act was mandatory and whether the enquiry under Section 5-A could substitute it
Whether the acquisition proceedings were vitiated due to non-compliance with Section 39 of the Land Acquisition Act as amended
holdings: Landowners are entitled to be heard during the enquiry under Rule 4 because it involves determining whether the company made reasonable efforts to acquire the land by negotiation.
The agreement between the State and the company under Section 41 must precede the notification under Section 4; a prior agreement that was cancelled does not suffice.
An enquiry under Section 5-A cannot fulfill the requirement of Section 40, as the Gujarat Amendment Act deleted references to Section 5-A from Section 40, making them distinct.
The acquisition proceedings were invalid due to non-compliance with Section 39, as there was no valid prior agreement or proper enquiry before initiating acquisition.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Gujarat Unification and Amendment) Act, 1963
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Procedural fairness in administrative action
Strict compliance with statutory conditions precedent

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and others fought against landowners over the validity of land acquisition notifications for an Engineering College, specifically whether failure to notify the Education Department under Madras Land Acquisition Rules invalidated the process.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 3(b) of the Madras Land Acquisition Rules, requiring notice to the department acquiring land, is mandatory or directory
Whether the failure to give notice to the concerned department under the rule renders the acquisition proceedings invalid
Whether the delay in challenging the Section 4 notification renders it non-justiciable
holdings: Rule 3(b) of the Madras Land Acquisition Rules is mandatory, as it ensures the Collector receives all relevant inputs before making a recommendation, and does not conflict with Section 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
Proceedings under Section 5A and the subsequent Section 6 notification are invalid if the department concerned was not given notice and opportunity to respond, as required by the mandatory rule.

A challenge to a Section 4 notification after an unreasonable delay, especially when the objector participated in the process, is barred by inordinate lapse of time and cannot be quashed on procedural grounds.
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory distinction in statutory interpretation
Principle of quasi-judicial fairness in administrative proceedings
Inordinate delay in filing writ petitions affecting maintainability

card.dispute: The vendees (appellants) challenged the pre-emption decree granted to tenants (respondents) who failed to deposit the pre-emption price within the time fixed by the trial court.
issues_decided: Whether the pre-emptor's suit stands dismissed for failure to deposit the pre-emption amount within the time fixed by the trial court under Order 20 Rule 14 of the CPC
Whether the appellate court had the power to extend the time for depositing the pre-emption amount beyond the trial court's deadline
Whether the High Court was correct in upholding the decree in favor of one pre-emptor (Sohan Lal) while setting aside the decree for another (Nathi)
holdings: A pre-emptor's suit stands automatically dismissed if the pre-emption price is not deposited within the time fixed by the trial court, as mandated by Order 20 Rule 14 CPC.
An appellate court cannot extend the time for depositing the pre-emption amount unless the decree is modified; mere filing of appeal does not suspend compliance.
The High Court erred in distinguishing between the two pre-emptors; failure to deposit on time invalidated both decrees, and no extension could be granted retroactively.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20, Rule 14
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with decree conditions in pre-emption suits
No suspension of decree obligations by mere filing of appeal
Conditional performance in reciprocal obligations under CPC

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the restoration of her land to the respondent raiyat after he failed to pay the first instalment of compensation within the stipulated time, and later sought to pay the entire amount after more than five years.
issues_decided: Whether the order dated February 17, 1958, was final and binding, such that failure to pay the first instalment extinguished the right to restoration
Whether a second application under Section 3 of the Kosi Act, made after expiry of the payment period, was maintainable
Whether the principle 'court's action should not prejudice any party' justified extending the time for payment
Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, could be invoked to condone delay in such administrative proceedings
holdings: An order under the Kosi Act, though conditional, acquires finality if it specifies consequences of non-compliance; failure to pay the first instalment as per terms extinguishes the right to restoration.
Successive applications under Section 3 for the same land are not maintainable as they undermine the finality of orders under Section 13 of the Act.
The principle that 'court's action should not prejudice any party' does not justify extending time for compliance when remedies were pursued at the applicant’s own risk.
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, does not apply to applications before the Collector under the Kosi Act, as he is not a 'court' and no prescribed period exists for such applications.
provisions: Kosi Area (Restoration of Lands to Raiyats) Act, 1951, Section 3
Kosi Area (Restoration of Lands to Raiyats) Act, 1951, Section 7
Kosi Area (Restoration of Lands to Raiyats) Act, 1951, Section 13
Kosi Area (Restoration of Lands to Raiyats) Act, 1951, Section 16
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Res judicata and against multiplicity of proceedings
Strict compliance with conditional orders
Non-applicability of Section 5 of the Limitation Act to non-appeal administrative applications

card.dispute: The Municipal Council, Madurai increased licence fees on hoteliers under the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, and the hoteliers challenged the increase, arguing it was an invalid tax disguised as a fee.
issues_decided: Whether the licence fee imposed under Section 321(2) of the Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920 is a tax or a fee
Whether the fee can be treated as a tax on land and buildings under Entry 49, List II, Seventh Schedule of the Constitution
Whether the procedure under Section 78(3) of the Act, requiring prior invitation and consideration of objections, applies to such a levy
holdings: The levy under Section 321(2) is not a tax but a fee, as the provision expressly authorizes a 'fee' and is located in a non-taxation part of the Act.
The fee cannot be recharacterized as a tax on land and buildings because it lacks the necessary nexus and procedural safeguards required for taxation.
Resort to fee-like levies to circumvent mandatory tax procedures under Section 78(3) frustrates statutory protections and renders the levy invalid.
provisions: Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, Section 78(1A) and Section 78(3)
Constitution of India, Entry 49, List II, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Procedural fairness in fiscal measures

card.dispute: Tameshwar Sahi, Ram Naresh, and Harihar appealed their convictions for murder and attempted murder arising from a property dispute involving the fatal assault on Chandrabali and Ram Adhar.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of Tameshwar and Ram Naresh for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC was legally sustainable based on the evidence
Whether the reliance on the testimony of PW3 (Raj Ballabh), a partisan witness, without corroboration from other eyewitnesses, was justified
Whether the conviction of Harihar under Section 307 IPC for attempted murder was correct
holdings: The conviction of Tameshwar and Ram Naresh for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is upheld as their acts were proven through credible and consistent testimony of PW3, supported by medical evidence.

The testimony of a partisan witness like PW3 can form the basis of conviction if it is reliable, consistent with circumstances, and corroborated by medical evidence, even without independent eyewitness support.

Harihar's conviction is reduced from Section 307 to Section 324 IPC as the evidence only proves he caused a simple hurt, not an intent to commit murder, due to lack of specificity in injury attribution.
doctrines: Partisan witness doctrine
Corroboration through medical evidence
Principle of individual liability in common intention
Benefit of doubt in case of insufficient evidence for graver charges

card.dispute: The mortgagee-decree holder challenged the validity of a lease deed executed by the mortgagor during pending litigation, claiming it was void under the doctrine of lis pendens and other statutory provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff had sufficient legal interest to maintain a suit for declaratory relief under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877
Whether the lease deed of 1956 was void under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, due to lis pendens
Whether Section 65A(2)(e) of the Transfer of Property Act displaced the operation of Section 52 in this case
Whether the lease was invalid under Section 64 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to prior attachment
holdings: A party with a legal interest, such as a mortgagee or assignee of a decree-holder with attached property, can seek a declaratory decree under Section 42 even if not a formal party to prior litigation.
A lease executed during pending litigation that creates new rights in immovable property is void under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, as it violates the doctrine of lis pendens.
Section 65A(2)(e), which limits leases by mortgagors, does not override Section 52 where the doctrine of lis pendens applies to invalidate transactions during litigation.
A lease executed while property remains under attachment in execution proceedings is invalid under Section 64, CPC, which applies the doctrine of lis pendens in such circumstances.
doctrines: Doctrine of lis pendens
Declaratory relief under Section 42
Priority of special doctrines over general statutory provisions

card.dispute: The dispute was between a sugar manufacturing company and sugarcane growers' cooperative societies over whether the government was required to hear the growers before exempting the company from paying an additional price for sugarcane.
issues_decided: Whether the sugarcane growers must be given an opportunity of being heard before the government grants exemption to a sugar factory from paying additional price for sugarcane.
Whether the High Court was justified in directing the government to consider affording such an opportunity to the growers.
holdings: The government must afford sugarcane growers a hearing before granting exemption from payment of additional price, as such exemption affects their legitimate rights and interests under the Sugar Cane Control Order, 1966.

The power to grant exemption is not independent of the price fixation process and must be exercised judicially, in accordance with principles of natural justice, considering the interests of both growers and manufacturers.
provisions: Sugar Cane Control (Additional Powers) Act, 1962, Clause 3A
Sugar Cane Control Order, 1966, Clause 5(1), Clause 5(3), Clause 5(4), Clause 5(5), Clause 5(6)
doctrines: Principles of Natural Justice
Right to a Fair Hearing
Legitimate Expectation
Duty to Act Judicially in Administrative Action Affecting Rights

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal appealed against the High Court's decision to increase compensation for danga land cultivated with sabai grass and other danga land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation for danga land on which sabai grass was grown should be based on the annual income from the land rather than just the value of the standing crop.
Whether the compensation awarded by the High Court for the remaining danga land was justified.
holdings: Land used for growing sabai grass is productive over multiple years and compensation must reflect its annual income, justifying a multiplier of 20 times the annual income.
The High Court was justified in raising compensation for danga land to Rs. 100 per acre based on evidence of market value and comparable sales.
doctrines: Compensation based on annual income multiplier
Market value as a determinant of compensation

card.dispute: Licence holders of country liquor shops in Bihar fought with the Board of Revenue over claims for refund or reduction of licence fees, arguing lack of quid pro quo, inability to open shops, or incurring losses due to speculative bidding.
issues_decided: Whether licence holders under the Bihar & Orissa Excise Act, 1915 are entitled to refund of fees when unable to open liquor shops despite holding a licence?
Whether licence holders can claim reduction of licence fees on grounds of incurring losses due to speculative bidding?
Whether absence of quid pro quo entitles licence holders to refund of fees paid under the Act?
Whether instructions in the Excise Manual create enforceable rights for licence fee reduction?
holdings: Licence holders are not entitled to refund of fees merely because they could not open their outstill, as the fee is for the exclusive privilege granted, not for operational success.

Losses due to speculative bidding do not entitle licence holders to fee reduction, as the Board has discretionary power under Section 39 to reduce fees only during the unexpired term and not as a matter of right.
There is no requirement of quid pro quo for fees paid under Section 22, as the exclusive privilege itself constitutes valid consideration, as settled in prior decisions.
Instructions in the Excise Manual do not create legal rights; they are administrative guidelines and cannot override the discretionary authority of the Board under the Act.
doctrines: Exclusive privilege as valid consideration
Discretionary administrative power
Non-enforceability of executive instructions
No right to refund for business losses

card.dispute: The appellant landowner and the State of Bihar fought over the correct compensation rate for acquired land, after the State successfully reviewed a higher award but failed to appeal the original decree.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the cross-appeal challenging the maintainability of the review petition.
What is the legal effect of a review order on the original decree?
holdings: Allowing a review petition vacates the original decree, and the new decree on review supersedes it entirely.
When a reviewing court finds the review was wrongly allowed, the original decree revives and becomes final if no appeal was filed against it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 47, Rule 1
doctrines: Revival of original decree upon invalidation of review
Finality of decrees in absence of appeal

card.dispute: Ajmer Singh and others appealed their convictions and sentences for the murders of Dev Singh, Nikka Singh, and Gurdev Singh, claiming lack of evidence and errors in the application of common intention and sentencing.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of eyewitness Mehar Singh P.W. 4 was reliable enough to sustain the convictions of all appellants.
Whether the trial and High Court erred in relying on Section 149 IPC instead of Section 34 IPC for conviction.
Whether the sentence of death awarded to Ajmer Singh was justified compared to co-accused.
holdings: The court upheld the reliability of Mehar Singh’s testimony only for Ajmer Singh, Chanan Singh, and Ujagar Singh, but found insufficient evidence to sustain the convictions of Mehar Singh, Bachan Singh, Jarnail Singh, Sardara Singh, and Surjit Singh, who were acquitted due to benefit of doubt.

The convictions under Section 149 IPC were set aside; instead, the convictions of Ajmer Singh, Chanan Singh, and Ujagar Singh were altered to Section 34 IPC, as the offence was committed with common intention, not as an unlawful assembly.

The death sentence of Ajmer Singh for the murder of Dev Singh was commuted to life imprisonment, as there was no justification for distinguishing his sentence from that of his co-accused who were sentenced to life.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration and inconsistency in statements
Principle of parity in sentencing

card.dispute: The appellant, Vidya Sagar, claimed pre-emption rights over a share in land sold by co-sharers to respondents, but execution of his pre-emption decree was challenged after the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, came into force.
issues_decided: Whether a pre-emption decree based on proprietary co-sharer rights is executable after the vesting of land under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950?
Whether the absence of an express provision voiding a decree in the Act preserves its executability despite abolition of proprietary rights?
holdings: A pre-emption decree based on proprietary rights becomes inexecutable when those rights cease to exist and vest in the State under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, as the decree loses its underlying subject matter.
A decree cannot be executed if the property rights it depends on are extinguished by law, even without an express provision voiding the decree, because the decree lacks substance post-vesting.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of extinguishment of rights by operation of law
Doctrine of executability of decrees dependent on subsisting rights
Doctrine of substitution of rights under land reform statutes

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against a High Court decision that quashed the President's order dismissing a customs officer, arguing that the President's delegate (a Minister) could not legally hear the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the President's appellate function under Rule 23(2)(b) of the CCS (CCA) Rules, 1957 is a constitutional duty or an executive function.
Whether the President can validly entrust the hearing of an appeal to a Minister, or whether such a quasi-judicial act is non-delegable.
holdings: The President's power to decide appeals under Rule 23(2)(b) is an executive function, not a personal or constitutional duty, and is exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

The hearing of an appeal under statutory rules, even if quasi-judicial, can be performed by a Minister as the President's representative, because the decision is deemed to be that of the President under Articles 77(3) and 166(3) of the Constitution.
provisions: Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1957, Rule 23(2)(b)
Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1957, Rule 30(2)(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of Constitutional Head of State
Doctrine of Aid and Advice of Council of Ministers
Doctrine of Executive Function under the Constitution

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their convictions and sentences for murder and related offenses, arguing that the prosecution's case, particularly regarding the FIR and the alleged firing, was unreliable.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in delivering the special report to the Magistrate casts doubt on the authenticity of the FIR.
Whether the prosecution failed to prove the occurrence of firing beyond reasonable doubt, thereby undermining the entire case.
holdings: Delay in delivering the special report does not discredit the FIR if the witness who lodged it is credible and there is no evidence of tampering.
The absence of proof of firing beyond reasonable doubt does not collapse the entire prosecution case if other evidence independently supports the convictions.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Presumption of regularity in official acts

card.dispute: The appellants, who bid for toddy shops but failed to pay the balance amount, challenged the state's recovery of dues under Section 28 of the Kerala Abkari Act, claiming they were not 'grantees' without a formal contract under Article 299 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants became 'grantees' under the Kerala Abkari Act despite non-execution of formal agreements under Article 299 of the Constitution.
Whether the State could recover unpaid auction amounts under Section 28 of the Act without a formal contract.
holdings: A successful bidder becomes a 'grantee' under the Act upon fulfilling initial conditions and being permitted to operate, even before formal execution of agreements or issuance of licences.
Liability to pay rental dues arises under the statute itself and can be enforced under Section 28 without a formal contract compliant with Article 299 of the Constitution.
doctrines: Statutory liability independent of contractual formalities
Equitable obligation and restitution
Literal and purposive interpretation of 'grantee'

card.dispute: The dispute involved conflicting claims over seized timber and whether a Magistrate committed criminal contempt by ordering its release without notice to the opposing party while a revision petition was pending in the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate committed criminal contempt by passing an ex parte order for the release of seized timber without notice to the other party while a revision petition was pending.
Whether the Magistrate had a deliberate intention to obstruct justice or circumvent the High Court's authority.
Whether the High Court was justified in convicting the Magistrate for contempt based on alleged bias and improper motive.
holdings: A judicial officer does not commit criminal contempt unless there is a willful disobedience of court process or a deliberate intent to obstruct justice; mere erroneous exercise of jurisdiction does not amount to contempt.
The absence of mens rea and the presence of an honest, though mistaken, belief based on a court order negates the willfulness required for criminal contempt.
Contempt proceedings against a judicial officer must be based on clear evidence of deliberate defiance, not on vague allegations of bias or notoriety surrounding the case.
doctrines: Willful disobedience requirement in criminal contempt
Absence of mens rea as a defense in contempt of court
Judicial immunity from contempt for bona fide judicial acts
Doctrine of fair and objective adjudication free from public舆论 or rumor

card.dispute: The Visakhapatnam Municipality sought to levy property tax on residents of two newly included villages from the date of inclusion, but the residents challenged the levy for lack of compliance with statutory procedures.
issues_decided: Whether clause 12 of Schedule 9 of the Andhra Pradesh District Municipalities Act, 1965 allows continuation of property tax in newly included areas from the date of inclusion
Whether the municipality could impose property tax on newly included areas without following the procedure under Section 81(2) first proviso
Whether a notification under Section 3(3) automatically extends existing tax resolutions to newly included areas
Whether objections raised during the inclusion process under Section 3(1)(b) suffice for tax imposition under Section 81
holdings: Clause 12 of Schedule 9 applies only to taxes lawfully levied at the commencement of the Act; it does not permit levying tax in newly included areas where no tax was previously imposed.
Property tax imposed for the first time in newly included areas must follow the mandatory procedure under Section 81(2) first proviso, including notice and consideration of objections.
Section 3(4) brings the Act into force in newly included areas but does not automatically extend prior tax resolutions; fresh resolution under Section 81 is required.
Objections under Section 3(1)(b) relate only to inclusion of area, not tax imposition; separate opportunity to object to tax must be given under Section 81.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh District Municipalities Act, 1965, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh District Municipalities Act, 1965, Section 81
Andhra Pradesh District Municipalities Act, 1965, Section 83
Andhra Pradesh District Municipalities Act, 1965, Schedule 9, Clause 12
doctrines: Mandatory procedural compliance for tax imposition
Principle of fair opportunity to object
Statutory interpretation of 'continuance of taxes'
Non-retrogression in municipal taxation

card.dispute: The plaintiff and her mother disputed over the nature of the mother's interest in family properties under a settlement deed—whether it was an absolute ownership or a life interest—and the plaintiff's entitlement to mesne profits.
issues_decided: Whether the first defendant (mother) acquired an absolute interest or only a life interest in her share of the properties under the settlement deed
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to mesne profits from the properties during the mother's lifetime
holdings: The first defendant acquired an absolute interest in her 1/3 share under the settlement deed; the restriction in Clause 4 only limited her daughters' rights during her lifetime, not her own ownership.

The first defendant was entitled to enjoy the profits of the properties during her lifetime, and thus could not be held liable for mesne profits; the plaintiff had no right to claim them while the mother was alive.
doctrines: Doctrine of testamentary construction
Doctrine of life estate versus absolute interest

card.dispute: The Board of Revenue sought to impose stamp duty and sales tax on agreements resulting from annual auctions of forest produce, which the respondents challenged as not amounting to leases or business sales.
issues_decided: Whether the right to collect forest produce under auction agreements constitutes a lease of immovable property under Article 31(c) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Whether the Government of Andhra Pradesh was carrying on 'business' in forest produce, making the sales taxable under the Sales Tax Act
Whether the security deposits made by bidders amounted to mortgages under Article 35(c) of the Stamp Act
holdings: The right to collect forest produce is a mere licence to take fructus naturales and does not create an interest in immovable property, hence not a lease under Article 31(c).
The Government's annual auction of forest produce lacks frequency, continuity, and regularity, and thus does not constitute 'business' for sales tax liability.
Security deposits under the auction terms do not create a right over property in favor of the Government and hence are not mortgages under Article 35(c).
provisions: Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, including definitions of 'dealer', 'business', and 'sale'
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence based on creation of interest in immovable property
Test for 'business' based on volume, frequency, continuity, and regularity of transactions
Essential elements of a mortgage under the Stamp Act requiring creation of a right over specified property

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder under Section 302/34 IPC, challenged their conviction based on unreliable eyewitness testimony and uncorroborated dying declarations.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction could be sustained based on the testimony of interested or uncorroborated eyewitnesses?
Whether the dying declaration made by the deceased was reliable and sufficiently proved?
Whether the medical evidence contradicted the prosecution's version of the dying declaration and the nature of injuries?
holdings: Conviction cannot be based solely on interested or uncorroborated eyewitness testimony without reliable supporting evidence.
A dying declaration must be medically and factually plausible; if it contradicts post-mortem findings, it cannot be relied upon.
Where the medical evidence suggests the deceased could not have regained consciousness, a claimed dying declaration is inherently unreliable.
doctrines: Benefit of the doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of dying declarations
Corroboration of interested witnesses
Medical evidence overriding testimonial inconsistency

card.dispute: Beant Singh challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the cancellation of Smt. Rup Kaur's auction bid for a property, which allowed her to retain rights over the property despite non-payment of the balance sale price.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the factual findings of the departmental authorities in a writ petition under Article 226?
Whether the cancellation of Smt. Rup Kaur's bid and forfeiture of earnest money was valid under Rule 90 of the Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955?
Whether the appellate authority's dismissal of Rup Kaur's appeal without a proper hearing violated Rule 105 and principles of natural justice?
holdings: The High Court can interfere with departmental authorities' orders if there is an error apparent on the face of the record, even though it does not sit as a court of appeal; such an error need not require prolonged argument to be discerned.
The cancellation of Rup Kaur's bid was invalid because the mandatory notice requirements under Rule 90(13) were not complied with, rendering the order without jurisdiction.

The appellate authority's dismissal of Rup Kaur's appeal on the ground that extension of time was merely an administrative matter was void, as it violated Rule 105 and the principles of quasi-judicial fairness requiring a proper hearing.
provisions: Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955, Rule 90
Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955, Rule 92
Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Rules, 1955, Rule 105
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Jurisdictional error in administrative action
Principles of natural justice in quasi-judicial proceedings
Non-compliance with mandatory procedural rules vitiates administrative orders

card.dispute: The riparian landowner challenged the State's auction of sand and gravel deposits on his land, claiming ownership over them against the State's assertion of exclusive rights.
issues_decided: Whether riparian owners have superior rights over sand, gravel, and bajri deposited on their land by river action.
Whether the State, under the Mines and Minerals Act, can regulate and auction such surface mineral deposits.
Whether the right to mines and minerals vested in zamindars survived the abolition of zamindari.
holdings: Riparian owners do not have any title superior to the State over sand, gravel, or bajri deposited on their land by rivers; such deposits are 'minor minerals' owned by the State.
The Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and U.P. Rules, 1963, empower the State to regulate and auction minor minerals, even when deposited on private land by fluvial action.
The right to mines and minerals formerly held by zamindars was extinguished and vested in the State under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(e)
Uttar Pradesh Mines and Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 2(7)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Rule 6(a)(i) and 6(a)(ii)
doctrines: State ownership of river beds and alluvial minerals
Statutory definition prevails over common law riparian rights
Extinguishment of zamindari rights in favor of the State

card.dispute: The appellants claimed title and possession over 142 bighas of land in Bihar, asserting it was the same land purchased by Mina Kuer in Uttar Pradesh in 1935, while respondents denied this identity and contested the suit on grounds of limitation and lack of title.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants proved that the land in dispute was the same as that purchased by Mina Kuer in 1935 in U.P.
Whether the suit was barred by limitation.
Whether the case should be remanded for further determination of the identity of the land.
holdings: The appellants failed to discharge the onus of proving that the land in dispute in Bihar was the same as the land purchased by Mina Kuer in U.P. in 1935, especially given the change in river course and lack of cogent evidence.
The suit for possession was barred by limitation, and the appellants did not establish a valid cause of action within the prescribed period.

The case will not be remanded as there was no valid basis for the appellants' assumption that the identity of the land was not disputed, and prolonged litigation must end after more than 25 years with the original parties deceased.
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver and acquiescence
Onus of proof in establishing title and identity of property
Principle that long-drawn litigation must come to an end

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court after their acquittal by the trial court, based on conflicting evaluations of eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court's rejection of eyewitness testimony was reasonable
Whether discrepancies in the first information report and medical evidence warranted discarding the prosecution's case
Whether the failure to examine a witness mentioned in the FIR required rejection of the entire prosecution case
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal
holdings: The trial court's rejection of eyewitnesses based on assumed bias and speculative reasons was unreasonable and unjustified.
Minor omissions in the FIR and slight inconsistencies with medical evidence do not discredit reliable eyewitness testimony.
The prosecution is not obligated to examine every witness named in the FIR; failure to do so does not automatically invalidate the case.
The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal when the trial court's findings were based on an unreasonable assessment of evidence.
doctrines: Reasonable evaluation of evidence
Corroboration through medical and circumstantial evidence
Principle of reliability of eyewitness testimony
Doctrine of appellate review of acquittal

card.dispute: The appellant contested contempt proceedings for failing to vacate premises as per undertakings given to the High Court, claiming it was merely a consent order between parties.
issues_decided: Whether the order of the High Court was based on enforceable undertakings to the court or merely a consent order between parties.
Whether the appellant's failure to vacate the premises constituted contempt of court under Section 19(1)(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
holdings: An order based on express undertakings given to the court has the same force as an injunction, regardless of any agreement between the parties.
Deliberate breach of an undertaking given to the court amounts to misconduct constituting contempt, even if the order was passed with consent.
doctrines: Undertakings to the court have the force of an injunction
Deliberate flouting of court undertakings constitutes contempt

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax sought to revise an assessment allowing deductions for maintenance of immature rubber plantations, which the assessee's widow challenged as beyond the Commissioner's revisional powers under the Kerala Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner's exercise of revisional power under Section 34 was valid when the assessment involved under-assessment due to excessive deductions, not omission to assess disclosed income.
Whether the revisional order was barred by the time limits under Section 35 for reassessing escaped income.
holdings: Every under-assessment is not an escaped assessment; where the assessing officer considered and allowed deductions after applying mind, it is not a case of income escaping assessment under Section 35.
Section 34 revisional power is not restricted by Section 35 time limits when the case does not involve escaped income, as Section 35 procedures apply only where income was not assessed at all.
provisions: Kerala Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950, Section 34
Kerala Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1950, Section 35
doctrines: Distinction between under-assessment and escaped assessment
Revisional jurisdiction subject to statutory limitations

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth-Tax challenged the High Court's decision that certain land owned by the Court of Wards was 'agricultural land' and thus exempt from wealth tax.
issues_decided: Whether land capable of agricultural use but not actually used or intended for such use qualifies as 'agricultural land' under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether entries in revenue records classifying land as agricultural constitute conclusive evidence for exemption from wealth tax.
What test should be applied to determine if land is 'agricultural' for the purpose of exemption under the Wealth Tax Act?
holdings: Land must be actually used, ordinarily used, or set apart with clear intention for agricultural use to qualify as 'agricultural land' under the Wealth Tax Act; mere capability is insufficient.
Entries in revenue records are only a rebuttable presumption of agricultural use and not conclusive proof for claiming exemption from wealth tax.
The correct test for determining agricultural land involves examining the actual condition, use, and intention of the owner, not merely potential for agricultural use.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Section 50
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption
Statutory interpretation based on context and purpose
Factual determination of land use and intention

card.dispute: The Controller of Estate Duty, Kerala, appealed against the High Court's decision that forest land with wild and natural growth in Malabar District was agricultural land and thus not liable to estate duty.
issues_decided: Whether forest land with spontaneous or natural growth can be classified as 'agricultural land' under Section 5 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953
Whether the burden of proof lies on the assessee or the revenue to establish that land is non-agricultural for estate duty purposes
holdings: Forest land with wild and natural growth is prima facie non-agricultural and cannot be treated as agricultural land unless there is evidence that it was cleared, prepared, or earmarked for agricultural use.

The burden of proving that land qualifies for exemption as agricultural land lies on the assessee, and mere capability of future cultivation is insufficient without evidence of actual intent or preparation.
doctrines: Prima facie classification of land based on use and character
Burden of proof in tax exemption claims

card.dispute: The appellant, D. D. Suri, challenged the legality of his suspension order and the investigation against him, alleging mala fide action by state officials, while the respondents defended the suspension as valid under service rules.
issues_decided: Whether the suspension order under Rule 7(3) of the All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1955 was valid without prior compliance with executive instructions on preliminary inquiry
Whether the suspension order continued after the appellant's compulsory retirement
Whether the charges against the appellant were baseless and the action mala fide
holdings: The suspension order under Rule 7(3) was valid as an investigation was pending after the FIR was filed, even if executive instructions on preliminary inquiry were not fully followed.
The suspension order ended upon the appellant's compulsory retirement, as a retired government servant cannot remain under suspension.
The question of mala fide and falsity of charges cannot be decided without the criminal trial judgment; the issue is remitted for fresh consideration after trial conclusion.
provisions: All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1955, Rule 7(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of disciplinary and criminal proceedings
Doctrine of ripeness for adjudication
Principle of finality of administrative action upon retirement

card.dispute: The Controller of Estate Duty and Kantilal Trikamlal disputed whether a coparcener's unequal share in a partition of joint family property within two years of death constitutes a 'disposition' liable to estate duty.
issues_decided: Whether a partition of joint family property resulting in a coparcener receiving less than his legal share constitutes a 'disposition' under the Estate Duty Act, 1953
Whether the extinguishment of a right or benefit in property during partition falls within the scope of 'property' under Explanation 2 to Section 2(15) of the Act
Whether such a disposition within two years of death is deemed to pass on death and attract estate duty under Sections 9 and 27 of the Act
holdings: A partition where a coparcener receives a share less than his entitlement constitutes a 'disposition' under the Estate Duty Act due to the fictional extension provided by Explanation 2 to Section 2(15).

The benefit conferred by the extinguishment of a coparcener's right to a larger share is 'property' under the Act, as the deeming fiction treats it as a disposition in favour of the other coparceners.
Sections 9 and 27 together deem such dispositions in favour of relatives within two years of death as gifts, attracting estate duty, regardless of bona fides if within the two-year period.
doctrines: Deeming fiction in taxation statutes
Liberal interpretation of fiscal statutes to meet legislative intent
Constructive disposition through legal fiction
Supreme Court's role in resolving conflicting High Court opinions on questions of public importance

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and the assessee, Madho Pd. Jatia, disputed whether irrecoverable rent exceeding one year's rent could be deducted over multiple assessment years or only once.
issues_decided: Whether the exemption under Item 38 of Notification No. 878F can be claimed only in one assessment year for irrecoverable rent?
Whether the balance of irrecoverable rent exceeding one year's rent can be carried forward and claimed in subsequent years?
holdings: The exemption for irrecoverable rent under Item 38 can be claimed in successive years until the full amount is exhausted, as long as the annual deduction does not exceed one year's rent.
There is no bar in the language of Item 38 restricting the benefit to a single year; the assessee remains entitled to claim the exemption for the balance in subsequent years.
doctrines: Principle of beneficial interpretation in favour of the assessee where statutory language is ambiguous
Notional income taxation with subsequent adjustment for actual loss

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax assessed a family governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law as a Hindu Undivided Family; the respondents claimed separate individual assessment based on definite shares in inherited property.
issues_decided: Whether coparceners governed by the Dayabhaga School can be assessed as a Hindu Undivided Family under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957
Whether inherited property among Dayabhaga co-heirs constitutes joint ownership or fractional ownership for wealth tax purposes
holdings: Coparceners under the Dayabhaga School do not have unity of ownership but only unity of possession; each heir owns a definite, ascertainable share in inherited property.
Where shares are definite and ownership is fractional, wealth tax must be assessed individually on each coparcener’s share, not collectively as a Hindu Undivided Family.
doctrines: Fractional ownership under Dayabhaga School
Unity of possession vs. unity of ownership in Hindu joint family law

card.dispute: The Corporation of the City of Bangalore sued B.T. Kampanna for possession of land after the lease expired, while Kampanna claimed protection under tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether Section 107 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 applies to land held on lease from a local authority after lease expiry
Whether the civil court should stay the suit and refer the question of tenancy to a Tribunal under Section 133 of the Act
Whether the respondent could be considered a tenant after the lease ended by efflux of time
holdings: Section 107 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 limits applicability to such lands to only Section 8; no other provisions, including Section 133, apply.
Once a lease ends by efflux of time, the lessee becomes a trespasser; no tenancy continues, so the Tribunal has no jurisdiction under Section 133.
The civil court retains jurisdiction to decide possession suits when lease has expired and occupation is unauthorized, even if the defendant claims tenancy.
provisions: Mysore Tenants (Temporary Protection from Eviction) Act, 1961, Section 3
doctrines: Expiry of lease by efflux of time terminates tenancy
Exclusive jurisdiction of Tribunal under Section 133 does not apply where tenancy has lawfully ended
Statutory exclusion of land from tenancy laws when held from local authority

card.dispute: The dispute was between a cultivating tenant and the new landowners (remainder-men) who sought to evict him after the death of the life-estate holder who originally granted the tenancy, claiming the tenancy could not survive beyond her lifetime.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'landlord' under the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 includes successors in title who can evict a tenant, not just the original lessor
Whether statutory protection under Section 3(1) of the Act applies only to tenants in existence when the Act came into force in 1955
Whether a tenancy created by a life-estate holder can be protected under the Act beyond the life-estate holder's death
holdings: The term 'landlord' under the Act includes any person entitled at the time of suit to evict the tenant or realize rent, not merely the original creator of the tenancy.
Section 3(1) protection applies prospectively and is not limited to tenants who were in possession in 1955 when the Act came into force.
A tenancy created by a life-estate holder is protected under the Act if the lessee remains in possession and qualifies as a cultivating tenant, even after the life-estate ends.
provisions: Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 2(e)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 2(aa)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3(1)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, Section 3(4)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection (Amendment) Act, 1956, Section 4(A)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation in favor of tenant protection
Prospective operation of protective tenancy laws
Inclusiveness of the term 'landlord' in social welfare legislation

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of tenants for arrears of rent, while the tenants contested the standard rent, raising the issue of when such a dispute must be raised to avoid eviction under the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant must raise a dispute as to standard rent within one month from the receipt of notice of termination to avoid eviction under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rent Act.
Whether a dispute raised for the first time in the written statement, after the one-month period, is sufficient to invoke protection under Section 12(3)(b).
holdings: A tenant must raise a dispute regarding standard rent within one month from the service of notice terminating tenancy to avail protection under Section 12(3)(b) of the Act.
Raising a dispute for the first time in the written statement, beyond the one-month period, does not prevent the operation of Section 12(3)(a) and thus does not bar eviction for arrears.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Explanation I to Section 12
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tenant protections under rent control legislation
Temporal requirement for raising disputes to invoke statutory defenses

card.dispute: The Receiver of Nabu building sued the tenant for arrears of rent, and the tenant challenged the suit's validity on grounds including court fee, jurisdiction, and misjoinder of causes of action.
issues_decided: Whether the Receiver was competent to sue for arrears of rent?
Whether the suit was improperly framed due to misjoinder of causes of action?
Whether the agreed rent of Rs. 1250/- per month was legally sustainable?
Whether the transferee (Receiver) could claim arrears of rent accrued before the transfer under the Transfer of Property Act?
holdings: The Receiver, being a court-appointed officer authorized to realize arrears of rent, was competent to sue for rent arrears.
The suit was properly framed; reliefs for rent and rent fixation are legally connected and do not constitute misjoinder.
The admission of Rs. 1250/- as rent before the Custodian amounted to an agreed rent and could serve as the basic rent under Section 6(2) of the Rajasthan Premises Act.
A transferee can claim pre-transfer rent arrears if there is a contractual agreement to the contrary, such as a court-approved compromise decree.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 6
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20, Rule 21
doctrines: Court-appointed Receiver as officer of the court
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of implied admission in judicial proceedings
Enforceability of compromise decrees without registration

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act 1961, arguing that grouping family members' land holdings for ceiling limits violated Article 31A(1)’s second proviso and created unequal treatment.
issues_decided: Whether the second proviso to Article 31A(1) of the Constitution prohibits different ceiling limits for different individuals based on family status
Whether Section 6(2) of the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act 1961 violates the concept of 'person' under Article 31A(1)
Whether legislation protected under Article 31A(1) can also receive protection under Article 31B via inclusion in the 9th Schedule
Whether the grouping of land holdings of spouses and minor children amounts to acquisition without compensation in violation of constitutional rights
holdings: The second proviso to Article 31A(1) does not prohibit different ceiling limits for differently situated individuals, including based on family status.
Section 6(2) does not merge legal personalities but only groups holdings for ceiling computation, leaving individual rights intact.
A law can receive dual protection under both Article 31A(1) and Article 31B if it satisfies the conditions of both provisions.
Grouping separate holdings for ceiling determination does not constitute acquisition violating the second proviso, as separate ownership rights remain unaffected.
provisions: Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act 1961, Section 2(21)
Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act 1961, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of protective umbrella under Article 31B
Doctrine of classification under Article 14 (implied)

card.dispute: The appellant, a public servant, was accused of demanding and accepting illegal gratification in connection with expediting a property sale permission, leading to his conviction, which he challenged on appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved that the appellant demanded and accepted Rs. 20/- as illegal gratification on January 28, 1969
Whether the appellant was rightly convicted for accepting Rs. 70/- as illegal gratification on February 26, 1969
Whether the High Court could sustain the conviction based on a part of the prosecution story it otherwise disbelieved
holdings: The High Court could not safely rely on the bare testimony of the complainant to prove the initial payment of Rs. 20/- without corroboration.
The conviction for accepting Rs. 70/- could not stand independently as it was part of an integrated prosecution story whose foundation (demand of Rs. 100/- and initial payment) was disbelieved.
A conviction cannot be sustained on a fragment of an otherwise rejected prosecution case, especially when the accepted part depends on the credibility of the rejected part.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, Section 5(1)(d) read with Section 5(2)
doctrines: Corroboration in bribery cases
Integrated prosecution story doctrine
Principle of judicial caution in convicting on uncorroborated testimony

card.dispute: The tenant (Gyan Chand) fought against eviction by the landlord (K.B. Lal) on grounds of non-payment of rent, seeking protection under Section 13A of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, as amended.
issues_decided: Whether Section 13A of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 applies to proceedings pending in the Supreme Court?
Whether an application for special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution amounts to a 'memorandum of appeal' under Section 13A(c)?
Whether the term 'proceeding' in Section 13A includes appeals by special leave to the Supreme Court?
holdings: Section 13A applies only to suits, appeals, and revision applications under the Act pending before courts within Rajasthan’s hierarchy, not to proceedings in the Supreme Court.
An application for special leave under Article 136 is not equivalent to a 'memorandum of appeal' under Section 13A(c), as the procedures and requirements differ significantly.

The term 'proceeding' in Section 13A is limited by the Explanation to suits, appeals, or revision applications under the Act, and does not extend to constitutional remedies like special leave petitions.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13A
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 22
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 1(2)
Supreme Court Rules, 1966, Order 16 Rule 4 and Rule 11
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Distinction between statutory appeals and constitutional remedies
Legislative intent inferred from specific terminology and context

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers) and respondents (sellers) disputed whether their agreement for sale of agricultural land became void due to the Prant Officer's refusal of permission under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, and whether the suit by the sellers to declare the agreement void was maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether the refusal of permission by the Prant Officer rendered the contract impossible to perform under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (doctrine of frustration)
Whether the authority under Section 63(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 exercises administrative, judicial, or quasi-judicial power
Whether an order dismissing an application on a formal defect bars a subsequent application on the same relief under the doctrine of res judicata
holdings: A contract is not frustrated under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act unless a supervening event makes performance impossible or impracticable; a mere technical refusal of permission does not amount to frustration.

The authority under Section 63(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 acts in an administrative capacity, not judicial or quasi-judicial, when granting or refusing permission for sale of agricultural land.
An order dismissing an application on a procedural or formal ground does not operate as res judicata and does not bar a fresh application on the same relief when the defect is cured.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 63(1)
Civil Procedure Code, doctrine of res judicata
doctrines: Doctrine of frustration
Doctrine of res judicata
Administrative vs. quasi-judicial function

card.dispute: The appellant (mortgagee) and respondent (mortgagor's successor) fought over whether a mortgage clause that made the transfer of leasehold property absolute upon a notice of re-entry was a clog on the equity of redemption.
issues_decided: Whether Clause 9 of the mortgage deed, which made the transfer of leasehold rights absolute upon service of a notice of re-entry before the redemption period expired, was a clog on the equity of redemption.
holdings: A condition in a mortgage deed that extinguishes the mortgagor's right of redemption upon a third-party notice of re-entry, before the redemption period ends, is a clog on the equity of redemption and therefore void.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Clog on redemption

card.dispute: The appellants claimed possession of ancestral land after the presumed death of the last owner, Kishan Singh, while the respondents, former transferees of his rights, resisted on grounds of limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the right to sue for possession accrued only upon proof of the exact date of death of Kishan Singh or upon his presumption of death under Section 108 of the Evidence Act after seven years of absence
Whether the period of limitation under Article 2(b) of the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 began to run from the presumed date of death
Whether the time spent in earlier litigation could be excluded under Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908
holdings: A cause of action for reversioners accrues when the presumed death of the last owner is established under Section 108 of the Evidence Act, not upon proof of the exact date of death.

The period of limitation for a suit for possession of ancestral immovable property begins from the date the right to sue accrues, which in this case was within three years before the filing of the suits, making them within time.

Section 14(1) of the Limitation Act does not apply where the cause of action in the subsequent suit is different from the earlier litigation, but the suits were still not time-barred due to timely accrual of the cause of action.
provisions: Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920, Article 2(b) of the Schedule
doctrines: Accrual of cause of action based on presumption of death
Liberal interpretation of limitation statutes to prevent injustice
Identity of matter in issue for applicability of Section 14 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, members of a joint Hindu family, disputed over whether certain properties allotted to the respondent's father for discharging family debts were his separate property and whether the appellant was liable to render accounts from 1938.
issues_decided: Whether the properties allotted to V (respondent's father) in 1929 became his separate property free from partition claims
Whether there was a blending of the allotted properties with the joint family estate
Whether the appellant was liable to render accounts for management of joint family properties from 1938
holdings: Properties given to V for discharging family debts became his separate property from the date of the 1929 partition deed, as the allotment was in consideration of his personal obligation and exclusive liability, irrespective of sufficiency of the properties.

There was no blending of the separate properties with the joint family estate, as mere non-maintenance of separate accounts or use of joint funds for debt repayment does not negate separate ownership without clear intention to abandon rights.

A coparcener is not entitled to demand accounts from a manager for past dealings unless there is proof of misappropriation or fraudulent conduct; in absence of such proof, account rendering is limited to the state of property at partition.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family and Partition
doctrines: Family arrangement doctrine
Doctrine of separate property by allotment for debt discharge
Doctrine of no account without fraud or misappropriation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment and rent recovery, but the tenant argued the civil court lacked jurisdiction due to the applicability of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, based on whether the property was in a notified urban area.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by disturbing concurrent findings of fact on the applicability of the Delhi Rent Control Act?
Whether the property in Khasra No. 203, located in Chowkri Mubarakabad, fell within the notified urban area under the relevant notifications?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by interfering with concurrent factual findings without identifying a substantial question of law.

The notifications clearly extended the Delhi Rent Control Act to the entire Mauza of Chowkri Mubarakabad, including Onkar Nagar and Lekhupura, and a clerical omission in specifying Khasra numbers did not exclude any part of the notified area.
doctrines: Falsa Demonstratio non nocet
Concurrent finding of fact not to be disturbed in second appeal without substantial question of law
Interpretation of statutory notifications as a whole to avoid absurdity

card.dispute: The Kerala State Electricity Board cut trees on the respondents' land for laying electric lines and assessed compensation; the respondents filed a petition under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 for enhanced compensation, which the Board challenged as time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies only to applications under the Code of Civil Procedure or extends to petitions under special statutes like the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885.
Whether a petition filed before the District Judge under section 16(5) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 falls within the scope of 'application' under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
holdings: Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to any petition or application filed under any Act before a civil court, not merely those under the Code of Civil Procedure.

A petition under section 16(5) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 seeking enhanced compensation is an 'application' within Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, as the District Judge acts judicially as a civil court in such matters.
doctrines: ejusdem generis
judicial function of statutory authorities
implied conferment of civil court status

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence for the murder of Roor Singh, arguing insufficiency of evidence and procedural irregularities.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of eyewitnesses should be rejected due to non-naming of the accused in the first information report
Whether the recovery of fired cartridge cases was reliable despite procedural irregularities in packaging
Whether the ballistic evidence linking the accused to the firearms used in the crime was credible
Whether the sentence of death should be commuted to life imprisonment
holdings: The failure to name an accused in the first information report does not discredit eyewitness testimony if the witness was not acquainted with the accused.
Procedural irregularities in packaging cartridge cases do not render recovery evidence unreliable when the sealed parcel reached the lab intact and tampering was implausible.
Ballistic evidence showing fired cartridges matched to licensed guns of the accused is reliable and corroborates eyewitness accounts.
The sentence of death need not be reduced to life imprisonment in the absence of demonstrated mitigating circumstances.
doctrines: Corroboration of eyewitness testimony by forensic evidence
Presumption of regularity in official conduct
Reliability of ballistic fingerprinting in criminal cases

card.dispute: The tenant, K. Eapen Chacko, challenged his eviction and sought protection under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, as amended, while the landlord, Provident Investment Company, sought to enforce eviction and recovery of arrears of rent.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to the benefit of fixity of tenure under the proviso to Section 3(1)(vii) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, as amended in 1969?
Whether Sections 125(3) and 108(2) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, as amended, apply retrospectively to pending proceedings?
Whether the amendments introduced by the 1969 Amendment Act, including Sections 50A, 52, and 73, are applicable to the appellant's case?
holdings: A tenant is not entitled to fixity of tenure under the proviso to Section 3(1)(vii) if, under the prior law (Malabar Tenancy Act, 1929), he was liable to eviction for wilful waste and prolonged rent default.
Section 125(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act is prospective; it does not apply to proceedings pending before the 1969 Amendment Act's commencement, which are saved by the proviso to Section 125(1).
Amendments like Sections 50A, 52, and 73 are prospective and do not benefit tenants in leases with government companies or in cases where rights were already determined under prior law.
doctrines: Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutes
Statutory interpretation respecting vested rights
Procedural vs. substantive amendments
Doctrine of implied exclusion from amended jurisdiction

card.dispute: Kishori Lal sued Birdhi Lal for possession of land, claiming he was a trespasser or alternatively a tenant liable to be ejected under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of revenue authorities under Article 226 of the Constitution on an error of law apparent on the face of the record.
Whether the appellant could succeed on an alternative plea under Section 180 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, despite lack of specific averments and proof.
holdings: The High Court was justified in quashing the orders of the revenue authorities as there was an error of law apparent on the face of the record, since the essential conditions under Section 5(44) to classify Birdhi Lal as a trespasser were not satisfied.
The alternative plea under Section 180 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, could not be entertained due to absence of necessary pleadings and proof regarding the nature of tenancy.
doctrines: Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Concurrent findings of fact by lower authorities not immune from judicial review when legal error is evident
Plea in alternative must be supported by pleadings and evidence

card.dispute: Ishwar Singh and four others were convicted of murder and related charges for a village altercation; they appealed, challenging the reliability of prosecution evidence and the fairness of their convictions.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution case was proved beyond reasonable doubt given discrepancies in the F.I.R. and non-examination of material witnesses
Whether the conviction under Section 302 IPC for murder could be sustained without reliable corroboration of the weapon used
Whether convictions under Sections 302/149, 326/149, 324/149, and 323/149 IPC were valid in absence of proof of common object or individual participation
Whether failure to show the recovered weapon to the medical expert vitiated the prosecution's case
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt due to material discrepancies in the F.I.R., unexplained delay in reporting, and non-examination of key witnesses named in the F.I.R.
A conviction under Section 302 IPC cannot be sustained solely on eyewitness testimony when the medical evidence fails to reliably link the accused to the fatal weapon.
Convictions under Section 149 IPC require proof of active participation or shared common object; mere presence is insufficient, especially without evidence of individual acts.
The prosecution must show the alleged weapon of offence to the medical expert for opinion; failure to do so creates reasonable doubt about the cause of injury and identity of the assailant.
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Common object under Section 149 IPC
Duty to produce material witnesses
Requirement of medical corroboration for weapon identification

card.dispute: Jai Singh, a mining leaseholder, fought the Union of India and others over the rate of royalty charged for gypsum mined, claiming it should be lower based on the mineral's purity.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition involving disputed questions of fact?
Whether the appellant could invoke the High Court's extraordinary jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 when an alternative remedy was available?
holdings: The extent of purity of gypsum mined is a question of fact, and courts should not decide such factual disputes in writ proceedings.
The appellant cannot simultaneously pursue a writ petition and a civil suit for the same grievance, especially when an alternative remedy is available.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 9(2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Second Schedule
doctrines: Alternative remedy doctrine
Judicial restraint in writ jurisdiction
Bar against concurrent remedies

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict tenants from a slum-area property after already obtaining a prior eviction decree; the dispute centered on whether the suit was maintainable without prior permission under the Slum Areas Act and whether it was barred by res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for eviction of a tenant in a slum area is maintainable without prior permission from the competent authority under Section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956
Whether a person against whom an eviction decree has been passed is a 'tenant' within the meaning of Section 19(1)(a) of the Slum Areas Act
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to entertain such a suit in view of Section 37A of the Slum Areas Act
Whether the subsequent suit is barred by the principle of res judicata, even though the earlier proceeding was not a suit
holdings: A suit for eviction of a tenant in a slum area is not maintainable without prior permission from the competent authority under Section 19 of the Slum Areas Act.
The term 'tenant' under Section 19(1)(a) of the Slum Areas Act includes a person against whom an eviction decree has been passed, to advance the protective purpose of the statute.
Section 37A bars civil court jurisdiction over matters entrusted to the competent authority under the Slum Areas Act, including permission to evict tenants in slum areas.
The principle of res judicata applies to quasi-judicial determinations by the competent authority under the Slum Areas Act, and a subsequent suit seeking relief already denied is barred.
