provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19(1), Section 19(3), Section 19(4), Section 37A
doctrines: Res judicata (constructive and direct)
Statutory interpretation (purposive construction, advancing the remedy)
Bar of jurisdiction (exclusive authority of statutory body)
Pith and substance doctrine (substance over form)

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murdering two relatives during a family dispute over a temporary wedding structure (Marwa), and they challenged the convictions on grounds of unreliable evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants committed murder under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether the ocular evidence was reliable despite contradictions with medical evidence?
Whether the High Court properly analyzed the evidence before affirming the convictions?
Whether the accused were falsely implicated due to enmity and inherent improbabilities in the prosecution case?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of any appellant beyond reasonable doubt due to material contradictions between eyewitness accounts and medical evidence.
Ocular evidence cannot be relied upon when it is fundamentally inconsistent with medical findings, especially on crucial aspects like nature and number of injuries.
The High Court erred in law and fact by failing to consider serious infirmities in the prosecution case, including unexplained injuries on the accused and lack of motive.
When witnesses falsely implicate innocent persons, the entire prosecution case becomes suspect and cannot sustain any conviction.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Corroboration of ocular evidence by medical evidence
Inherent improbability of prosecution case
Principle of false implication due to enmity

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents filed cross-suits over whether the respondents had acquired an easement right over the appellant's land for the flow of water for agriculture and prawn fishing.
issues_decided: Whether the second appeal by the respondents was barred by res judicata due to the finality of the unchallenged appellate decision in their own suit.
Whether the remanding judgment of the High Court, not appealed against, could be challenged in an appeal against the final decision.
holdings: The High Court erred in deciding an issue already finally decided in a former suit; the unchallenged appellate decision in the respondents' suit operated as res judicata in the second appeal arising from the other suit.
A remanding interlocutory order not appealed against can still be challenged in an appeal from the final judgment, as per the principle in Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Explanation I to Section 11
doctrines: Res judicata
Challengeability of interlocutory orders in appeal from final decree

card.dispute: The tenant-appellants challenged the High Court's refusal to interfere with the eviction order in favor of the landlord, claiming the court did not assess comparative hardship.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in not independently examining the comparative hardship of the landlord and tenant in eviction proceedings under Article 226
Whether findings of fact by the Prescribed Authority and affirmed by the District Judge can be disturbed by the High Court in a writ petition
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or substitute its own findings on comparative hardship when factual findings have been made by the Prescribed Authority and confirmed by the appellate court.
A finding of fact, such as the landlord's greater need, cannot be disturbed in writ proceedings under Article 226 even if the High Court might have reached a different conclusion on the evidence.
doctrines: Principle of finality of findings of fact
Limited scope of judicial review under Article 226

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Indore challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the enhanced property tax assessment on Viram Lodge, a hotel property, arguing that the annual value could be determined independently of rent control laws due to a non-obstante clause.
issues_decided: Whether the annual value of a building for property tax purposes must be limited by the standard rent under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, when a non-obstante clause is present in the taxing statute.
Whether the Municipal Commissioner followed due process and proper principles in determining the annual value of the building.
holdings: The non-obstante clause in Section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 allows the annual value to be determined based on reasonable letting value without being constrained by rent control legislation, especially where no standard rent has been fixed.
The Municipal Commissioner acted fairly and considered all relevant factors, and the High Court erred in setting aside the assessment on grounds of inadequate hearing or lack of principle.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 138(b)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 7
doctrines: Non-obstante clause interpretation
Reasonable letting value as basis for property tax assessment
Principle of harmonious construction between tax and rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant (landlord) and respondent (paying guest) disputed whether the respondent was entitled to protection against eviction under the Bombay Rent Act as a deemed tenant or was merely a licensee whose tenancy had expired.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a Special Civil Application under Article 227 of the Constitution when an adequate alternative remedy by appeal was available.
Whether the City Civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit for eviction despite the pendency of a similar suit in the Small Causes Court.
Whether a direction by the High Court staying execution of a decree and declaring that the decision of the City Civil Court would not bind the parties in a pending suit was legally valid.
holdings: The High Court should not exercise its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution when an adequate alternative remedy by way of appeal is available, unless there are exceptional circumstances, which were absent here.

The City Civil Court had jurisdiction to try the eviction suit based on the allegations in the plaint, and the pendency of a similar issue in another court does not bar adjudication if jurisdictions differ.
A High Court cannot issue directions about the binding effect of a decree in a pending suit before that suit is decided; such a direction is premature and beyond the scope of Article 227.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15A
doctrines: Doctrine of alternative remedy
Doctrine of res judicata and issue estoppel
Principle of judicial hierarchy and limits on supervisory jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Indore revised the annual rental value of a building used as a hotel by its owners, who challenged the revision on the ground that it should not exceed the standard rent under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the annual rental value of a building under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 must be limited by the standard rent under the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 when the building is not let out but used by the owner.
Whether the non-obstante clause in Section 138(b) of the Municipal Corporation Act overrides the provisions of the Accommodation Control Act in determining reasonable rent.
holdings: When a building has never been let out and is used by the owner for business, such as a hotel, the question of fixing standard rent under the Accommodation Control Act does not arise, and the reasonable rent for property tax can be determined independently.

The non-obstante clause in Section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act allows the assessing authority to determine annual value based on reasonable letting value without being bound by the Accommodation Control Act, provided there is no fraud or collusion.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 138(b)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 7
doctrines: Non-obstante clause interpretation
Reasonable letting value as basis for property taxation
Distinction between rented and owner-occupied premises in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Hubli sought to levy property tax based on an assessment list authenticated after the official year ended, and the rate-payers challenged the validity of the tax demand.
issues_decided: Whether the authentication of an assessment list under the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act must occur before the expiry of the official year to be valid and effective.
Whether the suit filed by the rate-payers was barred by limitation under Section 206A of the Act.
holdings: The assessment list must be authenticated before the expiry of the official year to be valid and effective; otherwise, it is void and does not create a liability to pay tax.

The suit was not barred by limitation under Section 206A because the cause of action arose only when the corporation attempted to enforce the invalid assessment, and there was no evidence to show the suit was filed beyond the six-month period.
provisions: Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, Sections 78 to 84
doctrines: Stare decisis
Harmonious construction of statutes
Legislative acquiescence

card.dispute: The State and Gaon Sabha sued to eject a former zamindar from land after it was vested in the Gaon Sabha; the State appealed when the trial court dismissed the suit, raising the question of its locus standi.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had locus standi to appeal as a 'person aggrieved' after land was vested in the Gaon Sabha under Section 117(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the State's right to appeal survived vesting of land in the Gaon Sabha.
holdings: The State Government retains locus standi as a 'person aggrieved' to appeal against a decision affecting land even after vesting it in a Gaon Sabha under Section 117(1), as it retains residual control and responsibility.
Vesting under Section 117(1) does not divest the State of all interest; it may still be affected by the adjudication and thus is entitled to appeal.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 9
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 117(1)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 117(6)
doctrines: Locus standi of the State as 'person aggrieved'
Doctrine of continuing interest after vesting
Appurtenance and vesting of rights

card.dispute: The appellant (landlord) challenged whether tenants could purchase inam land under the Tenancy Act after the abolition of inams under the Abolition Act, claiming the landlord-tenant relationship had ended.
issues_decided: Whether the abolition of inams under the Abolition Act extinguished the landlord-tenant relationship between the ex-inamdar and tenants.
Whether tenants retained the right to purchase agricultural land under Section 32 of the Tenancy Act despite the Abolition Act.
Whether Section 32-O of the Tenancy Act applied to tenancies existing before the Abolition Act.
holdings: The abolition of inams under the Abolition Act did not extinguish the landlord-tenant relationship; tenants' rights continued under the Tenancy Act.
Tenants retained the right to purchase land under Section 32 of the Tenancy Act, as the Abolition Act did not override this right and Section 28 preserved mutual rights.
Section 32-O applies only to tenancies created after 'tillers' day' and does not affect pre-existing tenancies or require re-notice for purchase rights.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32G
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-O
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32G(6)
Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, Section 4
Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, Sections 6, 7, 8, 9
Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, Section 28
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of non-derogation from existing rights
Harmonious construction of statutes
Presumption against extinguishment of rights by implication
Priority of specific provisions over general ones

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the income tax assessments and attachment orders on the grounds that the Hindu Undivided Family had been partitioned in 1954, and that the tax authorities were bound by a later civil court decree confirming partition.
issues_decided: Whether the income tax authorities were bound by a subsequent civil court partition decree when they had earlier rejected the claim of partition under Section 25-A(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1922.
Whether a junior member of a Hindu Undivided Family can act as karta with the consent of other members after the senior member relinquishes management.
Whether tax proceedings conducted in the name of a deceased karta are nullities.
Whether the appellant, who did not participate in the tax proceedings, could be held liable for the family's tax dues.
holdings: The income tax authorities are not bound by a subsequent civil court partition decree; under Section 25-A(3), a family remains deemed undivided for tax purposes unless partition is recorded by the tax authorities.
A junior member may act as karta if the senior member relinquishes management and other members consent, as per Hindu law principles.
Proceedings in the name of a deceased karta are not void if notices were effectively served on the managing member and the family continued business under that name.
The appellant is liable for the family's tax dues as the family remained undivided in law, and he benefited from its properties.
doctrines: Deemed continuation of HUF under tax law
Karta's authority under Hindu Law
Collateral attack on assessment orders
Principle of constructive notice in tax proceedings

card.dispute: Natha Singh and others challenged the declaration of their land as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, and the rejection of their claims by revenue authorities, seeking relief through a writ petition dismissed in limine by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition in limine without reviewing the factual findings of the revenue authorities.
Whether the revenue authorities committed an error of law in computing the 'surplus area' and rejecting the appellants' claims regarding tenancy and banjar land.
Whether the appellants were denied a fair opportunity to present their case before the revenue authorities.
Whether additional documentary evidence should be admitted at the appellate stage before the Supreme Court.
holdings: The High Court cannot act as an appellate court under Article 226 and may not re-examine factual findings unless there is an error of law apparent on the record.

The concurrent findings of the revenue authorities that the revenue records were tampered with and that no tenancy or banjar land claim was substantiated do not suffer from any error of law warranting interference.
The appellants were afforded full opportunity to prove their claims before the revenue authorities, and there is no evidence of denial of natural justice.

The discretion to admit additional evidence under Order 41, Rule 27 CPC is judicial and limited; such evidence cannot be admitted if the court can decide the case on existing records, especially when the proffered documents are found to be spurious.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(8)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: High Court's limited writ jurisdiction under Article 226
No re-appreciation of facts in absence of error of law
Judicial discretion in admission of additional evidence
Principle of concurrent findings by administrative authorities

card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Committee sought to enhance the rateable value of a property for house tax based on the actual rent received in 1966, while the landlord (M.N. Sol) challenged this, arguing that the standard rent fixed under rent control law should govern the assessment.
issues_decided: Whether the rateable value of a property for house tax purposes should be based on the actual rent received or on the standard rent fixed under rent control legislation.
Whether the reasonable expectation of rent for rating purposes must take into account penal provisions of rent control laws that prohibit charging rent above the standard rent.
holdings: The reasonable rent at which a house is let, as determined by fair or standard rent under rent control laws, governs its valuation for house tax purposes.

Rating cannot be based on actual rent received if it exceeds the standard rent, because rent control laws make such excess rent irrecoverable and penal, thus limiting the reasonable expectation of landlords in the open market.
provisions: New Delhi House Rent Control Order, 1939, Clause 5
Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 5(1) and Section 48(1)(a)
doctrines: Reasonable expectation in an open market must conform to legal restrictions and penal consequences under rent control laws.
Judicial adherence to precedent (stare decisis) as the Court followed the ratio in Smt. Padma Debi v. Additional District Magistrate, Delhi (1962).

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification under the U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, arguing it was invalid due to vagueness, lack of compliance with statutory requirements, and misuse for non-refugees.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition notification could be invalidated for not explicitly stating that the State Government 'decided' to acquire the land under Section 7(1) of the Act.
Whether the notification was invalid because the beneficiaries were displaced persons rather than 'refugees' as defined under Section 2(7) of the Act.
Whether the notification was vague for failing to precisely specify the portion of land to be acquired from larger field areas.
holdings: A land acquisition notification satisfies Section 7(1) if its substance shows a clear decision to acquire, even if the word 'decided' is omitted; substantial compliance suffices over hypertechnical invalidation.

A party cannot challenge the refugee status of beneficiaries on factual grounds without pleading specific averments in the writ petition; the court will not entertain factual assumptions unsupported by pleadings.

A notification is not vague if it refers to a site-plan and specifies the area acquired, and any ambiguity due to incorrect field plans does not invalidate the notification if the intended area is clearly identifiable.
provisions: U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, Section 2(7)
U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, Section 6
U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act, 1948, Section 7(1)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Pleading requirement for factual challenges in writ petitions
Judicial reluctance to invalidate administrative actions on hypertechnical grounds

card.dispute: A family member appealed against the liability to render accounts in a partition suit, arguing that the preliminary decree limited accounting obligations to specific parties and could not be extended to others.
issues_decided: Whether the preliminary decree limited the accounting obligation only to certain parties and could not be extended to all parties including defendant No. 4.
Whether the final decree could go beyond the terms of the original preliminary decree in imposing accounting duties.
holdings: The preliminary decree, as modified by the High Court on appeal, validly extended the duty to render accounts to all parties, including those representing family branches.
A final decree in a partition suit can give effect to the modified preliminary decree and is not confined to the unamended version if the modification was properly made on appeal.
provisions: Article 133 of the Constitution of India (unamended)
doctrines: Final decree cannot go behind a preliminary decree unless the preliminary decree has been modified on appeal
Doctrine of lis pendens in partition suits
Principle of family representation in suits involving joint family property

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed whether an 'otti deed' was a mortgage or lease, determining who was entitled to compensation when the land was acquired by the government.
issues_decided: Whether the 'otti deed' was a mortgage or a lease deed based on its terms and the parties' intention
Whether the appellant, after purchasing janmam rights in 1967, was entitled to the entire compensation for the acquired land
holdings: When an instrument has mixed features of mortgage and lease, the court must determine the predominant intention based on the substance of the transaction.
A deed is a lease if the property is transferred for enjoyment with fixed rent, and lacks the essential feature of mortgage—security for debt—absent here.
The absence of a right to sell the property for debt recovery and the presence of annual 'purappad' as rent support the lease character of the deed.
The appellant’s purchase of janmam rights after the Kerala Land Reforms Act was enacted did not entitle him to compensation beyond his 1/4th share.
doctrines: Predominant intention doctrine
Substance over form in document interpretation
Ususfructuary lease vs. mortgage distinction

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming a right over a public road, forcibly entered land encroached upon by the complainant who had cultivated a paddy crop, leading to a violent clash in which one person died; the dispute centered on whether the appellants could claim private defence while dispossessing a trespasser.
issues_decided: Whether the true owner or public can use private defence to dispossess a trespasser who has established peaceful possession by cultivating crops on public land.
Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence of person or property.
Whether the prosecution case was vitiated due to unexplained injuries on the accused.
Whether the medical evidence contradicted the prosecution's version of the assault causing death.
holdings: A true owner cannot use force to dispossess a trespasser who has completed possession, especially by cultivating crops, and must instead use legal remedies.
The appellants, as aggressors entering cultivated land without legal recourse, could not claim private defence of person or property.
The prosecution need not explain injuries to the accused if evidence shows a mutual fight; the case cannot be discarded on that ground alone.
Minor discrepancies between eyewitness accounts and medical evidence about the manner of injury do not undermine the prosecution case if the core facts are consistent.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Aggressor cannot claim private defence
Peaceful possession by trespasser
Concurrent possession and cultivation as evidence of settled possession
Presumption of fact from medical and circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, being grandson and daughter respectively of two brothers, disputed over succession to land previously held by the respondent's mother, who had inherited it from her husband.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent's mother inherited an interest in the holding under the Oudh Rent Act, 1886, such that her succession is governed by Section 172 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the interest acquired by the widow was self-acquired or inherited, thereby determining applicability of Section 172 or Section 174 of the Act
Whether the origin of title, rather than subsequent statutory upgrades in tenancy status, determines the mode of devolution under the Abolition Act
holdings: A widow who retains occupation of a holding after her husband's death under Section 48 of the Oudh Rent Act, 1886, inherits a limited interest, making the succession governed by Section 172 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act.
The devolution of a bhumidar's interest depends on the origin of the title; if it originated in inheritance, Section 172 applies regardless of later statutory upgrades in tenancy status.
Section 174 applies only when a female tenant holds an independent, self-acquired interest, not when her interest stems from inheritance, even if limited or precarious.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 172
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 174
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 171
doctrines: Origin of title doctrine
Devolution based on nature of interest
Preferential succession under statutory schemes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent under the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, and the tenant challenged the validity of the eviction on grounds of non-compliance with notice requirements under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether compliance with Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is necessary for eviction under the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Whether a registered notice is deemed served when returned with an endorsement of refusal, in the absence of the postman's testimony
holdings: The Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 provides a self-contained procedure for eviction, making compliance with Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act unnecessary.

A registered notice returned with an endorsement of refusal may be deemed served without producing the postman, if the addressee’s conduct or admissions indicate knowledge and refusal; denial under oath may rebut the presumption but is not conclusive without supporting evidence.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10
doctrines: Self-contained statutory procedure
Rebuttable presumption of service
Distinction between civil suit and special summary proceedings

card.dispute: Ramdas Oil Mills fought the Union of India over the amount of compensation awarded for requisitioned property, including damages to buildings, GI water pipes, and interest.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the compensation awarded by the arbitrator for damages to the building and for GI water pipes?
Whether the appellant was entitled to interest on the compensation awarded?
holdings: The High Court correctly reduced compensation for damages to the building and GI water pipes where the appellant failed to produce relevant account books, warranting an adverse inference.
Interest is not a matter of right and cannot be awarded as damages; thus, the High Court rightly disallowed the claim for interest.
doctrines: Adverse inference from non-production of documents
No entitlement to interest as of right in compensation claims

card.dispute: Members of a cooperative society challenged the Lt. Governor's supersession of the elected managing committee and the extension of the nominated committee's term, along with rules for membership and plot allotment.
issues_decided: Whether the Lt. Governor's action in superseding the elected managing committee and extending the nominated committee's term was valid
Whether the procedures for membership application, affidavit submission, and payment of dues were mandatory
Whether plot allotments made under the impugned process were valid
Whether default in payment or documentation led to automatic disqualification
holdings: The court upheld the validity of the Lt. Governor’s power to supersede the elected committee and extend the nominated committee’s term under the applicable rules.
Compliance with procedural requirements such as timely application, affidavit submission, and payment within stipulated periods was mandatory for eligibility to membership and plot allotment.
Plot allotments were to follow the priority and draw-of-lots system specified in Mr. Mookerjee’s report, subject to full compliance with all conditions.
Failure to comply with any condition, including payment or documentation, resulted in automatic cancellation of allotment, with reallocation to the next eligible person.
provisions: Bombay Co-operative Societies Act 1925 (as applied to Delhi)
doctrines: Doctrine of mandatory and directory provisions
Principle of strict compliance with court-ordered procedures
Doctrine of lawful delegation of administrative functions
Principle against creating precedents for other societies

card.dispute: The State of Orissa prosecuted Rabindra Kumar Dey, an Additional District Magistrate, for criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, alleging he dishonestly retained Rs. 10,000 meant for land compensation, while Dey claimed he handed the money to the Nazir for disbursement.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant misappropriated government funds under Section 5(2) r/w Sections 5(1)(c) and 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947
Whether the explanation given by the accused that he delivered the money to the Nazir was reasonable and unrebutted
Whether an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution for not examining a material witness, Ghansham Das, the Accountant
Whether the evidence of a hostile witness (the Nazir) could be relied upon without corroboration
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove misappropriation beyond reasonable doubt where the accused offered a reasonable explanation supported by a prosecution witness.
A public servant's explanation that he transferred government funds to a subordinate for official purposes is credible if supported by circumstances and not disproved by the prosecution.
An adverse inference can be drawn against the prosecution for failing to examine a material witness whose statement supported the defense, especially when the defense explanation is plausible.
The uncorroborated testimony of a prosecution witness, especially one with a motive to deflect blame, cannot form the basis of conviction if contradicted by other credible evidence.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Benefit of reasonable doubt
Adverse inference against prosecution for non-examination of material witness
Standard of preponderance of probabilities in evaluating defense explanation

card.dispute: Ratna Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. contested liability to pay holding tax under the U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, claiming the land was held for industrial purposes and not agricultural use.
issues_decided: Whether the land held by the appellant qualifies as 'land' under Section 2(15) of the U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, despite being intended for industrial use.
Whether uncultivated land held by a sirdar is liable to holding tax under the Act.
holdings: Land held by a sirdar, even if uncultivated, falls within the definition of 'land' under Section 2(15) of the U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, if it is held for a purpose connected with agriculture, horticulture, or allied activities.
The appellant cannot escape liability to pay holding tax by keeping land uncultivated, especially when permission to use it for industrial purposes was not granted.
provisions: U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, Section 2(15)
U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, Section 2(16)
U.P. Large Land Holdings Act, 1957, Section 3
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 143
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 146
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory definition
Purpose of tax legislation to promote efficient land use

card.dispute: Nawn Estates (P) Ltd, a private family-owned company primarily earning income from house property, contested its classification as an 'investment company' under the Income Tax Act, 1922, which would subject it to super tax on undistributed profits.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant company was an 'investment company' within the meaning of section 23A(1) and Explanation 2(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, making it liable to super tax on undistributed profits.
Whether the term 'investment company' should be interpreted in a technical sense or in the ordinary commercial sense used by businessmen.
Whether legislative history and evolution of the term 'investment company' in subsequent amendments support a broad interpretation including companies earning mainly from property income.
holdings: A company whose income arises mainly from house property and investments is an 'investment company' under section 23A(1), even if not engaged in manufacturing or trading.
The term 'investment company' is not restricted to technical or statutory definitions but is to be understood in the ordinary commercial sense based on the nature of income.
Legislative history and amendments show a consistent intent to treat companies with mainly unearned income as investment companies for tax purposes.
provisions: Income Tax Act, 1922, Explanation 2(i) to Section 23A(1)
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes in ordinary commercial sense
Use of legislative history and evolution as an aid to interpretation
Distinction between earned and unearned income in tax law

card.dispute: The tenant, Prem Chand, fought against his eviction from two rooms in a residential building, arguing that the landlord's personal requirement was not bona fide and that the premises ceased to be residential due to his tailoring business.
issues_decided: Whether the building in question qualifies as a residential building despite the tenant using one room for a tailoring shop.
Whether Explanation (iv) to Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 applies when the landlord occupies part of the building for residence.
holdings: A building remains residential even if the tenant uses one room for a small tailoring business; the primary use determines the character of the building.

Explanation (iv) to Section 21(1) creates a conclusive presumption of bona fide requirement if the building is residential and the landlord occupies part of it for residence, requiring no further proof.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1) Explanation (iv)
doctrines: Conclusive presumption
Character of building based on primary use

card.dispute: The dispute was between a municipal president who obtained a lease of land from the municipality and a respondent who challenged his continued membership as a councillor on grounds of conflict of interest.
issues_decided: Whether a councillor is disqualified under Section 38(1)(b)(i) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963 for obtaining a lease of municipal land without actively participating in the decision-making process.
Whether the general supervisory powers of a municipal president amount to 'acting as a councillor' in the grant of a lease to himself.
Whether influence arising from the office of president, without formal action, triggers disqualification under Section 38(1)(b)(i).
holdings: A councillor is not disqualified merely for holding a lease from the municipality; disqualification under Section 38(1)(b)(i) arises only if he actively 'acts as a councillor' in the matter of allotment to himself.
The general power of supervision vested in the president does not equate to 'acting as a councillor' in securing a lease, and thus does not trigger disqualification.
Even if the chief officer was influenced by the applicant's position as president, such influence alone does not constitute the councillor 'acting' within the meaning of Section 38(1)(b)(i).
doctrines: Plain meaning rule
Doctrine of non-obstante and exceptions
Doctrine of functional separation in municipal governance

card.dispute: The landlords (Sarwan Singh & Anr) fought against the tenant (Kasturi Lal) over whether they could evict him under the Delhi Rent Control Act without prior permission from the competent authority under the Slum Areas Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14A and Chapter IIIA of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 override the provisions of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 requiring prior permission for eviction suits in slum areas.
Whether the non-obstante clauses in both statutes create a conflict, and if so, which statute prevails.
Whether the decision in Jyoti Prasad's case settles the issue of precedence between the two Acts.
holdings: The provisions of Section 14A and Chapter IIIA of the Delhi Rent Control Act override those of the Slum Areas Act, even though both contain non-obstante clauses, because they serve a special purpose and were enacted later.
When two statutes with non-obstante clauses conflict, the later enactment prevails, especially when it was passed with knowledge of the earlier law and addresses a specific situation.
The decision in Jyoti Prasad’s case does not resolve the present conflict because it predated the 1975 amendments introducing the overriding provisions in the Delhi Rent Act.
provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 39
doctrines: Doctrine of non-obstante clause
Doctrine of implied repeal
Doctrine of later enactment prevailing over earlier law
Doctrine of harmonious construction in case of conflicting statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a tenant who became a mortgagee in possession, claimed the right to retain possession after redemption of the mortgage; the respondent mortgagor claimed the right to recover actual possession upon redemption.
issues_decided: Whether the tenancy of the appellant continued or was surrendered upon execution of the possessory mortgage deed.
Whether the doctrine of merger applied to merge the tenancy and mortgage interests in the appellant.
Whether the tenancy could revive after redemption of the mortgage.
holdings: The tenancy was surrendered on 7 November 1953, as evidenced by the terms of the mortgage deed and conduct of the parties, making the relationship purely that of mortgagor and mortgagee.
The doctrine of merger does not apply because a lease and a mortgage are distinct interests and neither is a lesser estate in the other; their coexistence in one person does not extinguish either.
The tenancy could not revive after redemption because the surrender was clear and the mortgage deed did not contemplate restoration of tenancy rights.
provisions: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 62
The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 111(d), (e), (f)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15
doctrines: Doctrine of Surrender
Doctrine of Merger
Implied Surrender by Conduct

card.dispute: The widowed mother of Karuna and her brother-in-law fought over inheritance to Karuna's property, with the brother-in-law claiming the mother was barred due to her remarriage.
issues_decided: Whether a mother's remarriage bars her from inheriting her son's property under Hindu law
Whether the bar on a widow's inheritance upon remarriage applies equally to a mother
holdings: A mother's remarriage does not disqualify her from succeeding to her son's property under Hindu law.
The bar on inheritance due to remarriage applies only to widows, not to mothers, as the spiritual marital bond is unique to the wife-husband relationship.
doctrines: Distinction between widow and mother in Hindu succession
Remarriage as a bar to inheritance under Hindu law

card.dispute: The dispute was between Seth Loonkaran Sethiya and others, and Ivan E. John and others, over the enforcement of a financial agreement concerning John Mills, where the plaintiff sought recovery of dues based on an unregistered partnership and a materially altered contract.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, given that the plaintiff's firm was unregistered.
Whether the plaintiff could maintain the suit without impleading his co-partner, Seth Suganchand.
Whether material alterations made by the plaintiff to the agreement rendered it void.
Whether the trial court and High Court were justified in decreeing a specific sum without a proper accounting process.
holdings: A suit by a partner of an unregistered firm to enforce a right arising from a contract is barred under Section 69 of the Indian Partnership Act, rendering the suit non-maintainable.
A partner cannot maintain a suit for recovery of firm dues without impleading the other necessary partners, especially when the claim relates to the firm's assets.
Material alterations made to a deed without the consent of the party bound void the deed, preventing its enforcement by the party making the alteration.
Where no settled account exists, courts cannot pass a decree for a specific sum but must direct a preliminary inquiry and accounting with opportunity for the defendant to challenge the accounts.
doctrines: Bar of suit by unregistered firm under Section 69
Voidness of deed due to material alteration without consent
Necessity of impleading indispensable parties
Requirement of accounting in absence of settled account

card.dispute: The Special Land Acquisition Officer and the City Improvement Trust Board fought with landowner P. Govindan over the correct date for determining market value for compensation in a land acquisition under the City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903.
issues_decided: What is the relevant date for determining market value for compensation under the City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, in light of amendments to the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?

Whether the unamended version of Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (referring to notification under Section 6) applies to acquisitions under the Mysore Act after the 1927 amendment changed the relevant date to Section 4(1) notification?
Whether Section 23 of the City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903 incorporates the Land Acquisition Act as amended from time to time or only as it stood in 1903?
holdings: The relevant date for determining market value under the City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903 is the date of notification under Section 16 of that Act, which corresponds to Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 as amended in 1927.
Section 23 of the Mysore Act incorporates the Land Acquisition Act as amended from time to time, unless expressly deviated from, and not merely as it existed in 1903.

The unamended procedure under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act (linking value to Section 6 notification) ceased to apply after 1927 and cannot govern acquisitions initiated after that amendment.
provisions: City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, Section 23
City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, Section 16
City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, Section 18
doctrines: Doctrine of incorporation by reference
Doctrine of contemporaneous statutory interpretation
Doctrine of implied repeal and substitution
Principle that no vested right exists in procedural law

card.dispute: The landlord and sub-tenant disputed whether the sub-tenant could be declared a direct tenant under the superior landlord under the 1956 Act despite a pending ejectment suit.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-tenant can avail the benefit of Section 16(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, to become a direct tenant when an ejectment suit was pending against him at the time the Act came into force.
Whether the pendency of an ejectment suit bars the operation of Section 16(3) of the 1956 Act, which creates a new tenancy relationship.
holdings: A sub-tenant is entitled to the benefit of Section 16(3) of the 1956 Act even if an ejectment suit was pending when the Act came into force, as no decree for eviction had been passed.

The relationship of landlord and tenant between the original tenant and sub-tenant ceases upon a valid declaration under Section 16(3), and such declaration must be given effect in the ejectment suit.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 16(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 40
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, Section 14(4)
doctrines: Lis pendens
Statutory interpretation of repeal and savings clauses
Legislative intent to upgrade sub-tenants to direct tenants

card.dispute: The appellants claimed a hereditary right to permanently store and sell dry Mahaprasad in two rooms of the Jagannath Temple based on a Sanad granted to their ancestor, while the temple authorities contested the validity of the Sanad and sought to reclaim possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Sanad granted a lease or a licence to use the temple property
Whether a permanent lease of temple debutter property could be validly granted by the Raja of Puri
Whether the Sanad conferred a right to sell dry Mahaprasad in the temple premises
holdings: The Sanad did not create a lease because it did not confer exclusive possession or an interest in the property, but only a revocable licence to use the space.
A shebait or manager of a Hindu temple cannot grant a permanent lease of debutter property at a fixed rent without legal necessity or benefit to the estate.
The Sanad did not confer any right to sell dry Mahaprasad; it only permitted storage for temple-related purposes, and no such right can be inferred from the document.
provisions: Puri Shri Jagannath Temple (Administration) Act, 1952, Section 2(d)
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence based on intention and substance of the agreement
Rule against permanent alienation of religious endowment (debutter) property without legal necessity
Doctrine of lis pendens not applicable where no valid lease is established

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and others appealed against a High Court decision that quashed land acquisition notifications because the enquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, did not comply with principles of natural justice, depriving landowners of a fair hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the enquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, requires compliance with the principles of natural justice.
Whether landowners have a right to be heard during the Collector's enquiry under Rule 4 before land acquisition proceeds.
holdings: The enquiry under Rule 4 is not merely administrative but quasi-judicial, and the Collector must observe principles of natural justice by affording affected landowners a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to present evidence.

Landowners are entitled to participate in the Rule 4 enquiry to challenge the company's claim that it made reasonable efforts to acquire the land by negotiation, especially since the Section 5A enquiry may be dispensed with under Section 17 of the Act.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial function
Right to fair hearing
Implied procedural fairness in administrative action

card.dispute: The State of Kerala contested whether voluntary land transfers made by K.A. Gangadharan to his children after the notified date of 1 January 1970 were valid or should be ignored in determining his liability to surrender excess land under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964.
issues_decided: Whether voluntary transfers of land made after the notified date of 1 January 1970 are valid under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1964, even if they fall within exceptions in Section 84?
Whether the liability to surrender excess land is determined as of the notified date and unaffected by post-notified date transfers?
Whether Section 87 of the Act implies that valid gifts can be made after the notified date?
holdings: Voluntary transfers of land made after 1 January 1970, even if falling within exceptions in Section 84, do not affect the transferor's liability to surrender excess land held on the notified date.
The obligation to surrender excess land is fixed as of 1 January 1970; subsequent transfers cannot alter the extent of land deemed to be held by the owner on that date.
Section 87 does not permit valid post-notified date gifts to defeat ceiling limits; it only governs acquisition of land by others, not validation of transfers meant to evade surrender.
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative intent to prevent evasion of land ceiling laws
Doctrine of fixed liability on the notified date
Doctrine of deeming provisions to counteract fraudulent transfers

card.dispute: The State of Kerala challenged the validity of voluntary land transfers in Kuttanad's kayal areas between 1963 and 1970, and donees defended gifts made after 1970 claiming exemptions under love and affection.
issues_decided: Whether voluntary transfers of kayal padasakharams between September 15, 1963, and January 1, 1970, were valid despite Section 84 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963
Whether the 1969 amendment withdrawing exemption for kayal lands could be given retrospective effect from April 1, 1964
Whether gifts made between 1970 and 1972 were valid under the 'natural love and affection' exception in Section 84
holdings: Voluntary transfers of kayal padasakharams between September 15, 1963, and January 1, 1970, were valid because these lands were exempt from Chapter III restrictions until the amendment was enforced on January 1, 1970.
The 1969 amendment withdrawing exemption for kayal lands cannot be given retrospective effect; a statute must not be read retrospectively unless necessity demands, which is absent here.

Gifts made after January 1, 1970, were invalid as the 'natural love and affection' exception was omitted with deemed effect from August 16, 1968, and did not cover gifts to grandchildren through a living daughter.
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective operation of statutes
Doctrine against retrospective interpretation unless necessary
Deemed retrospectivity by statutory declaration

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and Orient Paper Mills Ltd disputed whether the lease of forest areas and the extraction of timber constituted a 'sale of goods' liable to sales tax under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the lease deed for forest areas involving the right to cut and remove bamboo and salai wood amounted to a 'sale of goods' under the MPGST Act, 1958.
Whether the royalty paid by the lessee constituted 'sale price' for the purpose of sales tax.
Whether the amendment to the MPGST Act validating such transactions as sales retrospectively affected the case.
Whether the quantum of tax demanded was legally correct and subject to challenge.
holdings: A lease deed granting the right to cut and remove specified timber results in a 'sale of goods' when the trees are severed, as property in the timber passes upon severance under the contract.
The royalty paid under the lease is not merely compensation for occupation but functions as the 'price' for the timber removed, thus constituting 'sale price' under the MPGST Act.
The legislative amendment clarifying that such transactions are taxable sales validates the State's claim, and the amendment supports the imposition of sales tax on such leases.
The respondent is entitled to challenge the quantum of tax assessed, including the applicable rate, and must be given an opportunity to prove that the demand exceeds the legally permissible amount.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, Section 2(g)
Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, Section 2(n)
Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, Section 2(o)
Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, Section 2(t)
Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, Section 8
doctrines: Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of severance under the Sale of Goods Act
Doctrine of legislative validation
Principle of fair opportunity to contest tax liability

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and jagirdars contested the quantum and components of compensation awarded for abolished jagirs, including entitlement to solatium, interest, and the meaning of 'three multiples' in the compensation formula.
issues_decided: Whether jagirdars are entitled to solatium of 15% on compensation under the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1954
Whether interest is payable on delayed instalments of compensation
What is the meaning of 'three multiples' in Section 11(2) of the Jagirs Abolition Act
Whether Bagayat kas should be included in the assessment for computing compensation
holdings: Solatium under Section 11(3) is not payable because the Act does not provide for it and the Land Acquisition Act's solatium provision does not apply by analogy.
Interest at 3% is payable on delayed instalments of principal compensation, calculated year-wise on each overdue instalment, but not on delayed interest amounts.
The term 'three multiples' in Section 11(2) means three times the assessment, not six times, and is used in common parlance, not in a mathematical sense.
Bagayat kas is a separate tax and not part of the land assessment; hence, it cannot be included in computing compensation under the Act.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1954, Sections 8, 11, 13, 14, 15, 22
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 22
doctrines: Principle of compensation for deprivation of property
Interest as compensation for delayed payment in land acquisition
Literal and contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Doctrine of legislative intent in compensation statutes

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and landholders ('Wargadars') of 'Bane lands' in Coorg disputed the right to redeem trees on such lands, specifically whether the landholders could remove timber by paying only 50% of its value or were entitled to do so without any payment under the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964.
issues_decided: Whether holders of Bane lands had a vested right to redeem trees on payment of 50% of the timber value under the Coorg Land and Revenue Regulations, 1899, after its repeal.
Whether Section 75 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 conferred an absolute right on Bane landholders to remove trees without payment to the State.
Whether the Division Bench of the High Court erred in making observations on the nature and tenure of Bane lands beyond what was necessary for deciding the case.
holdings: The right to redeem trees on Bane lands on payment of 50% of the value, under Rule 137 of the Karnataka Forest Rules, 1969, was valid and protected even after the repeal of the Coorg Land and Revenue Regulations, 1899, due to Section 202 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964.

The High Court did not need to decide whether Section 75 of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, 1964 granted an absolute right to remove trees without payment, and such a question was left open for future determination.

The observations by the High Court Division Bench on the nature and tenure of Bane lands were unnecessary and do not constitute res judicata; parties remain free to contest these issues in future disputes.
provisions: Coorg Land and Revenue Regulations, 1899, Section 97
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Doctrine of severability of operative from obiter dicta
Principle of res judicata not applying to unnecessary findings

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra contested whether Narayan Vyankatesh Deshpande was entitled to compensation under the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, for resumption of lands, depending on whether his watan was in respect of land revenue or the soil.
issues_decided: Whether the watan held by the respondent was a watan of land revenue only or of the soil.
Whether the respondent was entitled to compensation under Section 6(2) of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950.
holdings: The grant under the sanad was a grant of land revenue only, not of the soil, as the term 'land' in the sanad must be construed under the Exemption From Land Revenue (No. 1) Bombay Act 2 of 1863 to include a share of land revenue.

Since the watan was of land revenue, the respondent was entitled to compensation under Section 6(2) of the Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, amounting to ten times the land revenue.
provisions: Bombay Paragana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 6(2)
The Exemption From Land Revenue (No. 1) Bombay Act 2 of 1863
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of land grants
Contemporaneous construction by revenue authorities
Principle of public accountability in state litigation

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and the Registrar of Public Trusts fought with Shri Chander Kant over whether a suit challenging the declaration of a religious trust as a public trust required prior notice under Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to a suit filed under Section 8(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951.
Whether the Registrar of Public Trusts is a public officer within the meaning of Section 80 CPC when acting under the MP Public Trusts Act.
holdings: Section 80 CPC applies to suits under Section 8 of the MP Public Trusts Act because the suit is against a public officer in his official capacity.

The Registrar of Public Trusts is a public officer and his act of declaring a trust as public is an act done in official capacity, thus attracting the mandatory notice requirement under Section 80 CPC.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Public Trusts Act, 1951, Section 8
doctrines: Act done in official capacity
Mandatory notice requirement for suits against government or public officers

card.dispute: The State of Madras challenged the High Court's enhancement of compensation from Rs. 1800 to Rs. 3000 per acre for 18.34 acres of land acquired for a hydro-electric project, arguing it was speculative and not based on sound principles.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing compensation based on speculation or conjecture?
Whether awards and sale deeds of nearby lands could be used as reliable material for determining compensation?
Whether a flat rate of compensation without regard to land quality violated principles of fair compensation?
holdings: Awards by the Land Acquisition Collector are relevant and may constitute an admission of land value; if the land is comparable and proximate, such awards can reliably guide compensation determination.
Enhancing compensation based on evidence of price rise, location advantages, and comparable transactions is valid and not mere speculation when supported by material on record.
A flat rate of compensation may be justified if surrounding areas have similar value and facilities, and if the overall assessment adheres to recognized principles of market value.
doctrines: Admissibility of prior awards as evidence of market value
Compensation not based on speculation if supported by material evidence
Use of comparable sales in proximate areas to determine land value

card.dispute: The State of Mysore challenged the High Court's decision to quash only the illegal condition attached to the assignment of kumki land in favor of the respondent, while upholding the assignment itself.
issues_decided: Whether the condition limiting the kumkidar's right to trees in the assigned kumki land was validly imposed by an executive order
Whether the illegal condition in the assignment order could be severed from the rest of the order
holdings: An executive order cannot curtail statutory property rights of kumkidars; such rights can only be altered by law, making the impugned condition violating Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution.
The illegal condition in the assignment order is severable; the valid part of the order assigning kumki land remains effective after striking down the invalid condition.
provisions: Madras Forest Act Rules, Rule 5(a), Rule 7(A)
doctrines: Severability of illegal conditions from administrative orders
Property rights under statutory privileges
Rule of law in executive action

card.dispute: The Kerala State Electricity Board cut trees on the respondent's property for laying an electric line, leading to a dispute over compensation and whether the claim was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the petition under Section 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act 1885 is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act 1963
Whether the District Judge acts as a civil court when deciding compensation disputes under the Telegraph Act
Whether Article 137 of the Limitation Act 1963 applies only to applications under the Civil Procedure Code or extends to applications under special statutes
holdings: Article 137 of the Limitation Act 1963 applies to any application or petition made to a civil court under any statute, not just those under the Civil Procedure Code.
The District Judge, when adjudicating compensation claims under the Indian Telegraph Act, acts in a judicial capacity as a civil court.
The term 'application' in Article 137 includes petitions under special laws, and the provision is not confined to applications under the CPC.
doctrines: ejusdem generis
statutory interpretation
judicial function of statutory authorities
extension of limitation under Section 5 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The appellant's legal heirs challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for land acquired by the State of Bihar for an Irrigation Research Station.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reducing the compensation awarded by the Additional District Judge for the acquired land.
What factors are relevant in determining the market value of land under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether sale transactions by the claimant after notification under Section 4 could be considered for assessing market value.
holdings: The High Court correctly considered sale transactions that the Additional District Judge had wrongly excluded, and its overall assessment of market value at Rs. 475 per katha was based on relevant evidence.
Market value under Section 23 includes the property's existing condition, advantages, and potential possibilities when optimally developed, excluding benefits from the acquisition scheme itself.
Sale deeds executed by the claimant after notification for acquisition, especially of roadside plots for commercial use, are not reliable indicators of market value and may be excluded.
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Exclusion of post-notification sale transactions
Consideration of potential and locational advantages in valuation

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of respondents Het Ram and others, which was based on a judicial visit to a dark place unrelated to the crime scene to assess witness credibility.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's visit to a place with no artificial light at 7:30 p.m. on 11-1-1974 constituted a valid local inspection under Section 539B of the Cr.P.C.
Whether the High Court could base its acquittal on observations made during such a visit, unconnected to the time and place of the alleged offence.
holdings: Section 539B Cr.P.C. permits local inspection only of the place where the offence was alleged to have been committed or any other place necessary to appreciate evidence; the High Court’s visit to an unrelated location did not qualify.

The High Court erred in substituting its own observations from a non-representative site and time for the recorded evidence, rendering its decision illegal and contrary to proper appreciation of evidence.
doctrines: Proper appreciation of evidence
Judicial review of appellate court procedures
Limits of judicial notice and local inspection

card.dispute: Tata Engineering challenged the Gram Panchayat's levy of taxes on its factory buildings, arguing the Panchayat lacked authority under the 1952 resolution and that the 1964 resolution was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'house' in the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1933, as amended, includes factory buildings for taxation purposes prior to the 1954 substitution of the word 'building' for 'house'.
Whether the 1964 resolution replaced and invalidated the 1952 resolution, and whether the tax demands were lawful in the absence of a valid resolution.
holdings: The term 'house' in the Act encompasses all types of buildings, including factory structures, and is not limited to residential dwellings.
The 1964 resolution did not supersede the 1952 resolution, and tax demands under the 1952 resolution remain valid if not inconsistent with later law.
doctrines: Contemporanea expositio est optima et fortissima in lege
Interpretation of statutory terms based on context and purpose
Use of rules and legislative history as aids to construction

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought against villagers who claimed their customary right of pasturage over an acquired estate survived the state's acquisition under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the customary right of pasturage enjoyed by villagers constitutes an 'encumbrance' under Section 2(h) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953
Whether such a customary right survives the vesting of estates in the State free from all encumbrances under Sections 4 and 5 of the Act
Whether Section 3 of the Act, which gives overriding effect to its provisions, nullifies customary rights contrary to the acquisition
holdings: The right of pasturage, even if recognized as a customary or public right, falls within the definition of 'encumbrance' under Section 2(h) if it relates to land in the estate and affects the intermediary's rights.

Such customary rights do not survive acquisition because Sections 4 and 5 vest estates in the State free from all encumbrances, and Section 3 gives the Act overriding effect over customs and other laws.
The legislature's intent to abolish intermediary rights comprehensively cannot be limited by customary usage, and courts must apply the statute as written, regardless of socio-economic consequences.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 2(h)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 3
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 5
doctrines: Overriding effect of statute
Literal interpretation of statutory definitions
Vesting of property free from encumbrances
Legislative supremacy in land reform laws

card.dispute: The assessee company and the Commissioner of Income-Tax disputed whether distributions received from liquidated tea companies were taxable as dividends or exempt as agricultural income, and whether land used for tea cultivation qualified as a capital asset.
issues_decided: Whether 40% of the surplus from sale of tea estate land constituted taxable capital gain or was exempt as agricultural income
Whether distributions from liquidated companies attributable to accumulated profits were taxable as dividends in the hands of shareholders
Whether land from which 60% of income was agricultural income could be treated as a capital asset under Section 2(4A) of the Income Tax Act, 1922
holdings: Land used for tea cultivation yielding agricultural income does not qualify as a capital asset under Section 2(4A), and any gain from its transfer is not taxable as capital gain.

Distributions received by a shareholder from a liquidated company are taxable as dividends to the extent attributable to accumulated profits, regardless of the agricultural nature of underlying income.

The character of income as agricultural or non-agricultural is determined by the source, and manufacturing income (40%) is distinct from agricultural income (60%) derived from land, but the land itself remains agricultural in character.
doctrines: Integrated business activity doctrine in tea production
Doctrine of source of income
Doctrine of statutory interpretation: courts cannot read words into statutes
Doctrine of accumulated profits in liquidation

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi fought with property owner Suresh Chandra Jaipuria over whether an interim injunction should restrain the Corporation from collecting house tax pending a suit for permanent injunction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an interim injunction despite concurrent findings by lower courts that no prima facie case existed.
Whether the balance of convenience favoured the grant of an interim injunction in a tax recovery matter.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on a Full Bench decision concerning the Delhi Rent Control Act to justify the injunction in a property tax assessment case.
holdings: The High Court erred in granting an interim injunction when the lower courts had concurrently found no prima facie case for such relief.
The balance of convenience in tax matters favours the civic authority, as non-payment may impair public services, and financial injury can be remedied otherwise.
The High Court misapplied the law by relying on the Delhi Rent Control Act and a Full Bench decision irrelevant to property tax assessment under the Municipal Corporation Act.
doctrines: Prima facie case for interim injunction
Balance of convenience in equitable relief
Interference under Section 115 CPC only if there is a jurisdictional error

card.dispute: The State of Kerala and another appellant contested whether M.T. Joseph's children, under a 1957 settlement deed, held separate rights to reclaimed government land entitling them to individual compensation upon land surrender, or whether the land remained a single unit under M.T. Joseph’s ownership.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8 of the Kerala Govt. Land Assignment Act, 1960, rendered invalid the alienation of land by M.T. Joseph through a 1957 settlement deed during the subsistence of government conditions restricting alienation.
Whether the children of M.T. Joseph acquired separate legal rights in the reclaimed land entitling them to individual compensation upon land acquisition.
holdings: Section 8 of the Kerala Govt. Land Assignment Act, 1960, does not invalidate a transfer if the restraint on alienation had already ceased due to full payment of dues and subsequent government recognition.

The children of M.T. Joseph acquired separate rights in the land through a valid settlement deed, recognized by government mutations and issuance of pattas, making them entitled to individual compensation.
provisions: Kerala Government Land Assignment Act, 1960, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of restraint on alienation
Recognition of rights by government action
Constructive possession

card.dispute: The appellant company contested the exclusion of fertilisers and agricultural equipment from its certificate of registration, claiming they were intended for use in the manufacture or processing of tea for sale, which the tax authorities, tribunal, and high court had rejected.
issues_decided: Whether fertilisers, chemicals, weedicides, pesticides, and related goods used in tea cultivation are 'intended for use in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale' under Section 8(3)(b) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956.
Whether weighing and measuring equipment used in tea estates, but not in factories, qualify for inclusion in the registration certificate under the same provision.
holdings: Fertilisers and agricultural inputs used in growing tea plants are not goods intended for use in the manufacture or processing of tea, as cultivation is distinct from manufacturing, which begins after plucking the leaves.
Goods such as weighing machines used in tea fields, not in factories, do not qualify as materials used in the manufacturing or processing of goods for sale under the Central Sales Tax Act.
provisions: Central Sales Tax (Registration and Turnover) Rules, 1957, Rule 13
doctrines: Distinction between agricultural operations and manufacturing processes
Literal interpretation of 'intended for use in manufacture or processing'
Integration of cultivation and processing does not equate cultivation with manufacturing

card.dispute: The Mahant of a temple sued to recover possession of temple lands from respondents who claimed hereditary tenancy based on entries in revenue records, which the appellant alleged were fraudulent.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to set aside the District Court's finding on the genuineness of revenue record entries in second appeal.
Whether entries in revenue records, alleged to be fraudulent, can be relied upon to establish possessory rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951.
holdings: The High Court has no jurisdiction in second appeal to overturn a concurrent finding of fact by the trial and appellate courts that entries in revenue records were fraudulent.
Presumption of correctness attached to revenue record entries does not apply if the entries are shown to be fraudulent or fictitious; fraud vitiates all legal effect of such entries.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 20(b)(ii)
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of revenue records
Fraud vitiates all legal documents
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The appellant (Vidya Vati) and respondent (Devi Das) disputed whether the respondent could recover possession of premises without repaying a loan, given that the agreement made repayment and return of possession concurrent obligations.
issues_decided: Whether the obligation to repay the loan and to deliver possession were concurrent and required simultaneous performance
Whether a premature tender of repayment before the due date could entitle the respondent to claim possession
Whether the High Court was correct in rejecting the revision application on the ground that the review order was appealable
holdings: The obligation to repay the loan and to deliver possession were mutual and concurrent; possession could not be claimed without repayment or deposit of the loan amount.

A tender of repayment made before the due date (26th August 1969, before the two-year term ended on 27th September 1969) was invalid, and refusal to accept it did not absolve the respondent of the duty to repay.
The High Court erred in rejecting the revision application; the direction to deposit the loan amount in court was valid and should have been upheld.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII, Rule 1
doctrines: Concurrent obligations in contract law
Doctrine of valid tender of performance
Principle of conditional possession linked to repayment

card.dispute: The appellants (Y.B. Patil and others) challenged the restoration of watan lands to the respondent (Y.L. Patil) after being declared strangers to the watan, contesting the finality of concurrent factual findings and the applicability of res judicata in revision proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether concurrent findings of fact by revenue authorities can be reopened in a writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution?
Whether the principle of res judicata applies to a subsequent stage within the same proceeding?
holdings: Concurrent findings of fact by the Assistant Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner, and Revenue Appellate Tribunal cannot be disturbed in a writ petition as they are binding and not subject to re-examination in proceedings under Articles 226 and 227.

The doctrine of res judicata applies not only to separate proceedings but also to subsequent stages of the same proceeding; once an order becomes final, it binds the parties in later stages of the same case.
doctrines: Res judicata
Concurrent findings of fact not re-examinable in writ jurisdiction
Finality of judicial orders in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the restoration of a decree for specific performance of an agreement to sell a half-share in agricultural land, arguing that consolidation proceedings had altered the land's identity.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement to sell agricultural land could be specifically enforced despite prior consolidation proceedings that altered the land's demarcation.
Whether the land retained sufficient identity post-consolidation to allow specific performance of the contract.
Whether the court could impose modified terms, including additional payment, in the interest of minors and to resolve long-standing family litigation.
holdings: Specific performance of a contract for sale of agricultural land can be granted even after consolidation proceedings if substantially the same land is allotted.
The land's identity is not lost due to consolidation; minor changes in area do not prevent enforcement of the agreement.
Courts may modify relief, including ex gratia payments, in family disputes involving minors to promote fairness and avoid wasteful litigation.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
doctrines: Specific performance of contracts
Discretionary equitable relief
Benefit to minors doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioners (tenants in Delhi) sought transfer of a defamation suit filed against them by the respondent in the Calcutta High Court, arguing that it was inconvenient and improperly instituted, while the respondent opposed transfer.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to transfer a suit pending on the original side of a High Court under Section 25 of the Civil Procedure Code (C.P.C.)?
Whether the possibility of lack of territorial jurisdiction in the Calcutta High Court is a relevant factor for transfer?
Whether the ends of justice require transfer of the suit from Calcutta High Court to Delhi High Court?
holdings: The Supreme Court has the power under Section 25 C.P.C. to transfer any suit from one High Court to another, regardless of whether it is pending on the original side, as all High Courts stand on equal constitutional footing.

The apparent lack of territorial jurisdiction in the Calcutta High Court, based on pleadings showing publication of the alleged libel in Delhi, is a relevant factor to consider when determining transfer for the ends of justice.
It is expedient for the ends of justice to transfer the suit to the Delhi High Court due to hardship on the defendants, convenience of parties and witnesses, and the cause of action arising in Delhi.
doctrines: Ends of justice
Territorial jurisdiction
Convenience of parties and witnesses

card.dispute: The landlord-respondent sought eviction of the tenant-appellant on grounds of bona fide requirement to start a hardware business, which the tenant challenged.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord had a bona fide requirement to repossess the property for starting a business.
Whether the tenant's long occupation of the premises should affect the eviction order.
holdings: The court upheld the finding that the landlord had a bona fide requirement to use the property for his sons' hardware business.
Although eviction was justified, the tenant was granted time until 13th April, 1978 to vacate due to hardship from 27 years of continuous occupation.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Rent, Rent Control and Eviction) Act, 1350 Fasli
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for eviction
Equitable relief in eviction cases
