card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict tenants after issuing a notice to quit; tenants challenged the notice's validity for not conforming to statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the notice to quit complied with the requirements of Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act by expiring with the end of the month of tenancy?
Whether a notice requiring tenants to vacate 'within the month of October 1962' is invalid due to ambiguity or non-conformity with Section 106?
holdings: A notice to quit must be construed ut res magis valeat quam pereat and not in a hyper-critical or pedantic manner; it should be interpreted in a common-sense way.
The phrase 'within the month of October 1962' followed by 'treated as trespassers from 1st November' clearly indicates termination of tenancy at the end of October 1962, satisfying Section 106.
doctrines: Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
Common-sense interpretation of legal notices
Notice to quit validity under statutory tenancy laws

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and eight accused persons fought over whether the accused were guilty of murder and related offences arising from a violent clash between shepherds and crop watchmen in a village dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the accused were guilty of murder under Section 302/149 IPC based on common object of an unlawful assembly
Whether accused No. 13 was guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC
holdings: The accused could not be convicted under Section 302/149 IPC because the prosecution failed to establish the sequence of participation in the assault necessary to prove shared common object to cause death.

Accused No. 13 was guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC because the injuries inflicted were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, satisfying the third clause of Section 300 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Common object of unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Test for intention to cause death under Section 300 Clause 3 IPC

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant sought declaration of tenancy rights over land against the deity-landlord, leading to a dispute over his status as a khatedar tenant under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to the status of a khatedar tenant under the Rajasthan Tenancy Act
Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the lower authorities' findings in favor of the tenant
holdings: The appellant is entitled to the status of a khatedar tenant irrespective of conflicting factual versions, as the statutory framework supports such recognition.
The appeal is allowed, the High Court judgment is reversed, and the tenant must pay compensation under Section 19(4) of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tenancy rights
Binding effect of revenue authority decisions
Concession by party leading to equitable resolution

card.dispute: Four appellants challenged their convictions by the Allahabad High Court in a criminal case arising from a land dispute that led to the killing of Ram Lal during a confrontation over crop harvesting.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Trial Court's acquittal and convicting the appellants.
Whether the prosecution evidence was reliable and sufficient to sustain the convictions of the appellants.
Whether ballistic and medical evidence corroborated the prosecution's version of the incident.
Whether the application of Section 34 IPC was valid in the absence of clear evidence of common intention.
holdings: The High Court erred in overturning the Trial Court's acquittal of three appellants due to serious infirmities in the prosecution's evidence.
Conviction of Birpal Singh under Section 302 IPC is upheld based on consistent prosecution evidence and ballistic proof linking his gun to the fatal shot.
The prosecution case against Suraj Pal Singh and Kunendrapal Singh failed due to lack of corroborating evidence and contradictions in the injury pattern and witness accounts.
Section 34 IPC cannot be applied where the presence and participation of accused persons in the offence are not clearly established.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 229-B
Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Judicial restraint in overturning acquittals
Corroboration of prosecution evidence through forensic and medical testimony

card.dispute: The tenant deposited rent in court due to strained relations with the landlord, who sought eviction for arrears; the dispute was whether court deposit suffices as payment under the rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether deposit of rent in court amounts to 'payment to the landlord' under Section 3(1)(a) of the United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 when the landlord refuses to accept rent.
Whether strained relations between tenant and landlord justify court deposit of rent under Section 7-C(1) of the Act.
What constitutes 'payment' under Section 7-C(1) — must it be physical tender, or can it include other modes?
holdings: A liberal interpretation of 'paid to him by a tenant' in Section 7-C(1) is required; physical tender is not mandatory when relations make it impractical or dangerous.
Court deposit of rent is deemed payment to the landlord under Section 7-C(6) only if the conditions in Section 7-C(1) are met, including the landlord's refusal to accept lawful payment.
Payment under Section 7-C(1) may include money order, messenger, or notice to nominate a bank; if the landlord refuses such modes, court deposit becomes permissible.
The lower courts erred in not examining whether alternative modes of payment were attempted or feasible; the case is remanded for such determination.
provisions: United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3(1)(a)
United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-C(1)
United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-C(6)
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of rent control statutes
Deemed payment doctrine
Conditional applicability of statutory remedies based on party conduct
Judicial encouragement of amicable settlement in neighbor disputes

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed an acquittal order, leading to convictions by the High Court, which the appellants challenged in the Supreme Court over the sufficiency of evidence and investigation flaws.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on the prosecution's evidence.
Whether material contradictions and omissions in witness testimony undermined the prosecution's case.
Whether the failure to investigate licensed weapons and recover the murder weapon vitiated the prosecution's case.
Whether the absence of bloodstains and other physical evidence at the alleged crime scene discredited the prosecution's version.
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal as the trial court's view that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt was reasonably possible.
Material omissions, such as the belated mention of the injured witness falling on wood, and lack of corroboration, rendered key testimony unreliable.
The prosecution's failure to recover or test the weapon used, despite knowing of licensed arms with other individuals, created a fatal gap in the evidence.
The absence of bloodstains at the scene and unexplained movement of the deceased's body raised serious doubts about the prosecution's narrative.
provisions: Enlargement of Supreme Court Jurisdiction Act
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reasonable possibility test in appellate review of acquittals
Duty of prosecution to investigate alternative leads
Reliability of inimical witnesses

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling of Holdings) Act, arguing that the creation of an artificial family unit for ceiling purposes violated the second proviso to Article 31A(1) and was not saved by Article 31B.
issues_decided: Whether the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling of Holdings) Act, as amended, is void for violating the second proviso to Article 31A(1) of the Constitution?
Whether Article 31B provides immunity to the impugned provisions despite alleged violations of Part III rights?
Whether the second proviso to Article 31A(1) confers a fundamental right or merely limits legislative power?
holdings: The amendments to the Maharashtra Act creating a family unit for land ceiling purposes are valid agrarian reform measures and do not violate the Constitution.
Article 31B grants absolute immunity to laws in the Ninth Schedule from challenges based on Part III rights, including any alleged breach of the second proviso to Article 31A(1).

The second proviso to Article 31A(1) confers a fundamental right to compensation at market value for land within the ceiling limit under personal cultivation, but this right is overridden by the protection afforded by Article 31B.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling of Holdings) Act, 1961, as amended by Maharashtra Acts 21 of 1975, 47 of 1975, and 2 of 1976, Sections 2(11A), 2(22), 3, 4, 5(1) read with Schedule I and Section 6
doctrines: Immunity under Article 31B from Part III challenges
Liberal interpretation of agrarian reform laws
Fundamental rights as limitations on state power

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax and the assessee, P.N. Sikand, disputed whether 50% of the unearned increase in the value of a leasehold property, payable to the lessor upon assignment, should be deducted when valuing the asset for wealth tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether 50% of the unearned increase in the value of a leasehold interest, payable to the lessor under the lease deed, constitutes a deductible burden in determining the market value of the asset for wealth tax assessment.
Whether the amount payable to the lessor represents a diversion of income by paramount title or merely an application of income by the assessee.
holdings: When valuing a leasehold interest burdened by a clause requiring payment of 50% of the unearned increase to the lessor, that amount must be deducted from the market value as it represents a realisable limitation on the assessee's wealth.
The 50% payment is a diversion of value by paramount title under the lease terms and never becomes part of the assessee’s wealth, as it is held in substance for the lessor.
doctrines: Valuation of assets on hypothetical open market sale
Diversion of income by paramount title vs. application of income

card.dispute: The tenant (Charan Dass) fought against the landlord's (respondent No. 3) claim for eviction to use a shop for his son's carpentry business, arguing lack of bona fide need and greater hardship to him.
issues_decided: Whether the District Court was correct in not considering the comparative hardship between landlord and tenant while deciding the eviction under Section 21 of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972?
Whether the retrospective amendment to Section 21 of the Act affects the validity of the District Court and High Court orders that did not consider comparative hardship?
holdings: The District Court erred in not considering comparative hardship, as required by the amended law, and its order must be set aside.
The retrospective amendment to Section 21 mandates consideration of comparative hardship, rendering prior judicial orders that ignored it invalid.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, Rule 16(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed possession of a hotel on vacant land, with the respondent claiming forcible dispossession and seeking relief under Section 145 CrPC, while the appellants challenged the Magistrate's jurisdiction after the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975 came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8 of the Maharashtra Vacant Lands (Prohibition of Unauthorised Occupation and Summary Eviction) Act, 1975 bars a proceeding under Section 145 of the CrPC between private parties over possession of land?
Whether a proceeding under Section 145 CrPC amounts to a proceeding for eviction within the meaning of Section 8 of the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975?
holdings: Section 8 of the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975 does not bar proceedings under Section 145 CrPC between private parties over possession, as it only applies to evictions by the Competent Authority, not private disputes.

A proceeding under Section 145 CrPC is not for eviction but for maintaining public order by determining possession; hence, it does not fall within the scope of Section 8 of the Maharashtra Vacant Lands Act, 1975.
provisions: Maharashtra Vacant Lands (Prohibition of Unauthorised Occupation and Summary Eviction) Act, 1975, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional exclusivity
Legal fiction of deemed possession
Prevention of breach of peace as basis for Section 145 proceedings

card.dispute: Chet Singh challenged an order restoring Gurdev Singh's application under the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, after Gurdev Singh claimed illness prevented his appearance.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Director had jurisdiction under Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings Act to set aside an earlier order without affording notice and hearing to the affected party.
Whether the order passed under Section 42 without notice violated the proviso requiring a hearing, unless proceedings were vitiated by unlawful consideration.
holdings: The Additional Director could validly act under Section 42 without notice when non-compliance with the proviso was due to the applicant's inability to attend caused by illness, which vitiated the fairness of the original proceeding.

An order passed without affording a hearing may be set aside if the proceedings were vitiated by circumstances beyond the party's control, and such orders can be ignored as not being 'honest' orders under Section 42.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 42
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Doctrine of constructive review in administrative action
Invalidity of orders not based on 'honest' application of mind

card.dispute: The appellants, former hereditary village accountants, challenged the constitutional validity of recruitment rules and the appointment of new village accountants, seeking continuation in their posts.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had locus standi to challenge the constitutional validity of the 1970 Recruitment Rules under Article 226
Whether the appellants could claim a right to continue as village accountants after the abolition of hereditary offices
Whether Rules 4 and 5 of the 1970 Rules violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution
holdings: A person not aggrieved by a legal provision cannot maintain a writ petition under Article 226; the appellants lacked standing as they did not apply for reappointment and lacked prescribed qualifications.
The abolition of hereditary offices having been upheld, the appellants had no vested right to continue in service after fresh appointments under valid rules.
Rules 4 and 5 of the 1970 Rules do not violate Articles 14 and 16 as they prescribe reasonable classification and educational qualifications for recruitment.
provisions: Karnataka General Services (Revenue Subordinate Branch) Village Accountants (Recruitment) Rules, 1970, Rules 4 and 5
doctrines: Locus standi in writ petitions
Equality before law and reasonable classification
Prescriptive qualifications and state discretion in recruitment

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the municipal corporation's levy of house tax from April 1, 1954, arguing it should only be payable from April 1, 1965 after a fresh assessment notice, and that the High Court lacked jurisdiction to interfere with the District Judge's final order.
issues_decided: Whether house tax could be levied retrospectively from April 1, 1954 after a remand and fresh notice under the M.P. Municipal Corporation Act, 1956
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition against the District Judge's order under Section 149(2) of the M.P. Municipal Corporation Act, 1956
holdings: The tax could be levied from April 1, 1954 as the proceedings constituted a continuous process initiated under the earlier Act and the fresh notice was part of the same assessment, not a new one.

The High Court had jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC to entertain the revision petition, and the appellant could not raise the issue of lack of jurisdiction for the first time in the Supreme Court.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 3(3) and Section 3(4)
Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 146
Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 147(1)
Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 149
doctrines: Continuity of proceedings doctrine
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Finality of appellate orders subject to revisional jurisdiction

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of tenants on grounds of bona fide necessity and arrears of rent, and claimed damages from the date of termination of tenancy; tenants contested the eviction and liability for damages.
issues_decided: Whether a new plea regarding the landlord's occupation of another accommodation can be raised for the first time in second appeal?
Whether the phrase 'of his own in his occupation' in Section 12(1)(f) of the MP Accommodation Control Act, 1961 requires ownership and not mere possession?
From what date is a tenant liable to pay damages for continued possession after termination of contractual tenancy?
holdings: A new plea not raised in the written statement cannot be permitted for the first time in second appeal, especially when no issue was framed or evidence led on it.
Under Section 12(1)(f) of the MP Accommodation Control Act, 1961, the landlord must own and occupy another suitable non-residential accommodation; mere occupation is insufficient to bar eviction.
A tenant remains a statutory tenant after contractual tenancy ends and is not liable for damages until an eviction decree is passed; damages can only be awarded from the date of the decree.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 2(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Statutory tenant doctrine
Relation back theory rejected
Plea not taken in defence cannot be raised in appeal

card.dispute: Chetsingh challenged the Additional Director's order restoring Gurdev Singh's application under the East Punjab Holdings Act, claiming lack of jurisdiction to review a prior order without hearing all parties.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Director had jurisdiction under Section 42 of the East Punjab Holdings Act to set aside his earlier order without affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard.
Whether the order passed without complying with the proviso to Section 42 could be treated as 'non-est'.
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to interfere under Articles 226 and 227.
holdings: An order under Section 42 of the Act must comply with the proviso requiring notice and hearing to affected parties, unless proceedings were vitiated by unlawful consideration.
Where an interested party was deprived of a hearing due to circumstances beyond their control, such as illness, the prior order may be treated as 'non-est' and can be corrected without formal review.
The failure to comply with the conditions precedent under Section 42 does not automatically invalidate the action if the omission is justified by exceptional circumstances like illness.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act 1948, Section 42
doctrines: Non-est doctrine
Principle of audi alteram partem
Judicial review under Article 136

card.dispute: Three accused appealed their convictions for murder arising from a land dispute-related riot in which one person was killed.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302 IPC simpliciter is sustainable for each of the three appellants based on the medical evidence of fatal injuries?
Whether the injury caused by accused No. 6 alone was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death?
holdings: Conviction under Section 302 IPC simpliciter is sustainable for accused Nos. 1 and 9 as their respective injuries were independently fatal based on medical opinion.

Conviction under Section 302 IPC is not sustainable for accused No. 6 as the medical evidence did not establish that his injury alone was fatal; he is instead convicted under Section 326 IPC for causing grievous hurt.
doctrines: Simpliciter conviction in murder cases
Medical evidence determining sufficiency of injury to cause death
Principle of individual liability in absence of common intention or unlawful assembly

card.dispute: The Controller of Estate Duty Madras appealed against the High Court's decision exempting the widow's interest in joint family property from estate duty after her death, arguing it passed to coparceners and was taxable.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow, under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, is a member of the coparcenary and possesses a coparcenary interest liable to estate duty upon her death
Whether the interest of such a widow in joint family property 'passes' on her death within the meaning of Section 7(1) of the Estate Duty Act, 1953
Whether the value of the benefit accruing to the coparcenary on the cesser of the widow's interest is taxable under Section 39 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953
Whether the Estate Duty Act, being a fiscal statute, should be strictly construed to exclude such interest from taxation
holdings: A Hindu widow under the 1937 Act, though not a coparcener by birth, is a member of the coparcenary and holds a coparcenary interest with all its incidents except birth-based acquisition.
The widow's interest in joint family property 'passes' on her death as it lapses and merges into the coparcenary, attracting liability under Section 7(1) of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
The value of the benefit arising from the cesser of the widow's interest is taxable under Section 39 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, based on the share she would have received on partition.
Fiscal statutes must be construed strictly, but where legislative intent clearly brings a transaction within the tax net, courts must uphold the tax liability.
provisions: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Legislative intent in fiscal statutes
Incidents of coparcenary interest
Strict construction of fiscal statutes with due regard to statutory language and purpose
Merger of a widow's interest in coparcenary property upon death

card.dispute: The Everest Coal Company sued a court-appointed Receiver (representing the State of Bihar) for damages after the Receiver cancelled their coal mine contract, but did not obtain prior court leave to sue, leading to dismissal of the suit on procedural grounds.
issues_decided: Whether prior leave of the court that appointed a Receiver is a mandatory condition precedent to filing a suit against the Receiver.
Whether leave obtained after the institution of the suit but before its conclusion can cure the initial lack of permission.
Whether the failure to obtain prior leave affects the jurisdiction of the court or the cause of action.
holdings: Prior leave of the court that appointed a Receiver is not a jurisdictional requirement but a procedural safeguard to prevent contempt of court.
Leave obtained after the suit is filed but before its termination is sufficient to cure the initial defect and allows the suit to proceed.
The requirement of leave is peripheral and does not affect the cause of action or the jurisdiction of the court; it can be granted during the pendency of the suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XL
doctrines: Contempt of court
Inherent powers of the court
Procedural compliance as curable defect
Liberal interpretation of procedural rules to serve justice

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a building used for both residential and non-residential purposes, claiming bona fide need for both parts, which the tenant resisted.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can seek eviction for bona fide residential and non-residential requirements under Section 12(1)(e) and (f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, when the accommodation is let out for dual purposes.
Whether the court can consider separate residential and non-residential requirements in a composite lease without splitting the contract.
holdings: A landlord is entitled to eviction if he proves bona fide need for both residential and non-residential portions of a building, each being a distinct 'accommodation' under the Act.
The composite nature of a lease with dual purposes does not bar eviction under both Section 12(1)(e) and (f), provided the requirements are genuine and fit within the statutory grounds.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(e)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Statutory interpretation of 'accommodation'
Non-splitting of lease contracts in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord sought to evict the tenant on grounds of bona fide and reasonable requirement, but the tenant challenged the High Court's interference with concurrent factual findings of lower courts under Article 227 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could exercise its power under Article 227 to overturn concurrent factual findings of lower courts in a tenant eviction matter.
Whether the High Court's interference was justified on the ground of gross error or injustice warranting exercise of supervisory jurisdiction.
holdings: The High Court cannot use Article 227 to overturn factual conclusions of lower courts, even if they are erroneous, as its power is supervisory and not appellate.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by acting as a court of appeal when no such right existed, and there was no gross injustice or perversity to justify intervention under Article 227.
doctrines: Judicial superintendence under Article 227
No appellate function under Article 227
Concurrent findings of fact not liable to be disturbed

card.dispute: The heirs of Hassanand challenged the Additional Settlement Commissioner's order vacating a prior compensation award of 291 standard acres granted under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional Settlement Commissioner had the power to review and set aside an earlier order granting compensation under the 1954 Act?
Whether the order passed by the Additional Settlement Commissioner was valid in law?
holdings: The Additional Settlement Commissioner had no statutory power of review to set aside an order passed by a co-ordinate authority under the 1954 Act.
The impugned order, being one of review not contemplated by the statute, must fail, though the Chief Settlement Commissioner may initiate fresh revision proceedings under Section 24 if warranted.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of no implied power of review
Rule of fair hearing (audi alteram partem)

card.dispute: The trustees of the Varadaraj Venkataramana Temple fought against the Assistant Commissioner over whether the temple was a public temple or a denominational temple belonging exclusively to the Goud Saraswat Brahmin community.
issues_decided: Whether the temple in question is a 'public temple' within the meaning of Section 6(17) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951
Whether mere public use of a temple allows an inference of dedication to the general Hindu public
Whether endowments by non-community members and references to a 'general body' in a prior award indicate public character
holdings: A temple is not deemed public merely because the public is allowed to worship; there must be evidence of dedication or use as of right by the general Hindu community or a section thereof.
Public admission without more does not establish a legal right of worship; the inference of dedication requires supporting circumstances showing user as of right.
The term 'general body' in the award referred only to the Goud Saraswat Brahmin community, and there was no evidence of substantial endowments by outsiders to prove public character.
provisions: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 6(17)
Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, Section 57
doctrines: Doctrine of dedication by user
Presumption against inferring public dedication from mere public access
Interpretation of statutory definition of 'temple' in Section 6(17)

card.dispute: The receiver in insolvency proceedings challenged the validity of a gift deed executed by the insolvent over seven years before adjudication, claiming it was a sham transfer, while the donee argued the insolvency court lacked jurisdiction to decide the matter due to the two-year limit under Section 53.
issues_decided: Whether the insolvency court has jurisdiction to decide the validity of a property transfer made more than two years before insolvency adjudication when it is alleged to be a sham or fictitious transaction.
Whether Section 53 of the Provincial Insolvency Act bars the insolvency court from determining title in cases of void transfers.
holdings: The insolvency court has jurisdiction under Section 4 of the Provincial Insolvency Act to determine the validity of a transfer alleged to be sham or fictitious, even if made more than two years before insolvency, as such void transactions fall outside the scope of Section 53.
Section 53 of the Provincial Insolvency Act applies only to voidable transfers and does not restrict the court’s power to declare a transfer void ab initio if it is nominal, sham, or fictitious.
doctrines: Distinction between void and voidable transactions
Jurisdiction of insolvency courts to determine title in sham transactions
Interpretation of statutory provisions in pari materia

card.dispute: The receiver in insolvency proceedings challenged a gift deed executed by the insolvent to his wife seven years earlier, claiming it was a sham transaction, while the donee argued the insolvency court lacked jurisdiction due to the time elapsed.
issues_decided: Whether an insolvency court can examine the validity of a transfer made more than two years before insolvency proceedings if it is alleged to be void (sham or fictitious).
Whether Section 53 of the Provincial Insolvency Act bars insolvency courts from deciding title questions in respect of transfers made beyond two years.
holdings: An insolvency court has jurisdiction under Section 4 to decide questions of title regarding transfers alleged to be void (e.g., sham or fictitious), even if made more than two years before insolvency.
Section 53 applies only to voidable transfers; it does not strip the court of power to declare a transaction void ab initio if it was never intended to pass title.
doctrines: Distinction between void and voidable transfers
Jurisdiction of insolvency courts to determine title under general powers subject to statutory limitations

card.dispute: The appellant tenant refused to pay rent to the Assistant Controller under a garnishee notice issued to recover unpaid estate duty from the lessors, challenging the validity of the notice.
issues_decided: Whether the Assistant Controller could issue a garnishee notice under Section 73(5) of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 read with Section 46(5A) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 without first serving a notice of demand on the accountable persons under Section 73(1)?
Whether the garnishee notice was invalid for not naming the lessors as the persons to whom rent was payable?
Whether the appellant was legally bound to comply with the garnishee notice requiring payment of rent to recover estate duty?
holdings: A garnishee proceeding under Section 73(5) of the Estate Duty Act read with Section 46(5A) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 does not require prior service of a notice of demand on the accountable person under Section 73(1).
The garnishee notice was valid even though it did not name the lessors, as it sufficiently required payment of amounts due to the estate of the deceased.
The appellant was legally bound to comply with the garnishee notice and pay rent arrears and future rent to the Assistant Controller up to the amount of outstanding estate duty.
provisions: Estate Duty Act, 1953, Section 73(5) read with Section 46(5A), Income Tax Act, 1922
doctrines: Garnishee proceedings for tax recovery
Binding precedent from larger bench decisions
Substance over form in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The India Cable Company Ltd. sued to declare title and recover possession of two disputed land plots from the appellant, Korin alias Etwari Devi, heir of Rajdeo, who had occupied the land as a homestead, claiming protection under tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether the findings in an earlier suit (No. 116 of 1938) operated as res judicata in the subsequent eviction suit (No. 280 of 1954).

Whether the appellant, as heir of Rajdeo, was entitled to protection under Section 78 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, after Rajdeo was dispossessed of his agricultural holding under Section 50 of the same Act.
Whether the suit for recovery of possession by the plaintiff company was maintainable after the enactment of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, which vested intermediary interests in the State.
holdings: The rule of res judicata did not apply because the legal character of Rajdeo’s interest in the disputed land changed after dispossession under Section 50, making the earlier findings inapplicable.

Section 78 of the Chhota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, ceased to protect Rajdeo’s homestead once he lost his status as a raiyat by dispossession of his agricultural holding; thus, his tenancy became subject to the Transfer of Property Act.

The maintainability of the suit depended on whether the land vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950; the Supreme Court remanded the issue for a factual finding on vesting and subsistence of the plaintiff’s interest.
doctrines: Res judicata
Change of circumstances affecting res judicata
Cessation of tenancy protection upon loss of raiyat status
Vesting of intermediary interests under land reform laws

card.dispute: Allottees of industrial housing challenged the validity of an amendment to the Punjab Industrial Housing Rules, 1972, which disqualified them from retaining their houses due to their income exceeding Rs. 350 per month.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 4(3) of the Punjab Industrial Housing Rules, 1972, as amended, is ultra vires the Punjab Industrial Housing Act, 1956, for excluding industrial workers earning above Rs. 350 per month from the definition of 'industrial worker' under Section 2(e) of the Act.
Whether the amended Rule 4(3) operates retrospectively and is invalid on that ground.
Whether the amendment violates Article 14 of the Constitution by making arbitrary discrimination based on income.
holdings: The State Government has the power under Section 24 of the Punjab Industrial Housing Act, 1956, to impose and modify conditions for allotment, including income limits, and such conditions do not render the rule ultra vires the Act.
The amended Rule 4(3) does not operate retrospectively because cancellation of allotment takes effect only upon expiry of one month's written notice, not from the date income exceeded the limit.

The contention under Article 14 was not raised before the High Court and could not be entertained due to the Presidential Order of June 27, 1975, suspending enforcement of Article 14 during the Emergency.
doctrines: Deeming provision under statutory scheme
Power to make rules subject to conditions of occupation
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of rules
Doctrine of preclusion of constitutional challenges during Emergency under Article 359

card.dispute: The Life Insurance Corporation of India fought against agriculturists who claimed their pre-nationalisation debts should be scaled down under the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, despite the Corporation's argument that the debts were now due to a 'Corporation formed in pursuance of a Special Indian Law'.
issues_decided: Whether the debts owed to private insurance companies before nationalisation are protected from debt relief under Section 4(e) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, after being taken over by the Life Insurance Corporation of India.
Whether Section 9(1) of the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956 creates a legal fiction that contracts with insurers are deemed to have been entered into with the Corporation from the beginning.
holdings: The debts remained subject to the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938 because the liability to scale down arose before nationalisation and vested with the Corporation along with the debts.
Section 9(1) of the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956 does not create a legal fiction that contracts were originally with the Corporation; it only ensures continuity of enforceability.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of vesting of liabilities
Doctrine of legal fiction

card.dispute: The landlord, after attaining majority, sought possession of agricultural land from the tenant who refused to vacate after the lease expired, leading to a dispute over tenancy rights and entitlement to possession under tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's tenancy was lawfully terminated under Section 9A of the Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951
Whether the landlord was entitled to possession under Sections 36 and 38 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1958
Whether the tenant retained tenancy rights after the expiry of the protected period and beyond the termination order
holdings: The tenant's tenancy was lawfully terminated by the order of 8th August, 1955 under Section 9A of the Berar Act, and he ceased to be a tenant thereafter.
The landlord was entitled to possession under Section 36 read with Section 38 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, as the tenant had no continuing rights after 31st March, 1958.
Mere continued possession by the tenant without legal recognition from the landlord does not confer tenancy rights after the statutory protection period ended.
provisions: Berar Regulation of Agricultural Leases Act, 1951, Section 9A
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region and Kutch Area) Act, 1958, Sections 36, 38, 100(2), 132(3)
doctrines: Termination of tenancy by statutory order
No revival of tenancy by mere possession
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227

card.dispute: Krishna Kumar Mediratta and Phulchand Agarwala contested over a prospecting licence for overlapping mineral areas, with Mediratta claiming preferential right based on earlier application despite a minor fee deficiency.
issues_decided: Whether an application for a prospecting licence is invalid ab initio if accompanied by an incorrect or deficient fee?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Central Government's order under Article 226 for an error apparent on the face of the record?
Whether the appellant retained a preferential right under Section 11(2) of the Mines and Minerals Act despite the fee discrepancy?
holdings: An application for a prospecting licence accompanied by a deficient fee due to oversight is not void ab initio if the deficiency is later made good, as the rules distinguish between the application and the fee.

The High Court erred in exercising its writ jurisdiction under Article 226, as there was no error apparent on the face of the record in the Central Government's order; the error lay instead in the High Court's own interpretation.

A bona fide application with a minor technical defect, such as an underpaid fee later corrected, retains validity and confers preferential right under Section 11(2) over later applications for the same area.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 11(2)
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 19
doctrines: Substance over form
Distinction between mandatory and directory provisions
Error apparent on the face of the record
Preferential right in mineral concessions

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Financial Commissioner's decision in ejectment proceedings, and the High Court dismissed his writ petition; the dispute arose over whether his Letters Patent Appeal was barred by limitation due to non-filing of three document sets initially.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to file three sets of documents with a Letters Patent Appeal renders it time-barred?
Whether Rule 3 of Chapter 2-C of the Punjab High Court Rules, requiring three copies of documents, is mandatory or directory?
Whether the High Court erred in treating the appeal as time-barred and refusing condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act?
holdings: The requirement to file three sets of documents under Rule 3 is directory, not mandatory, and substantial compliance suffices.
Filing one complete set of documents with the memorandum of appeal constitutes substantial compliance, and the appeal is deemed filed within time.
Since the appeal was filed within the limitation period, Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply, and the High Court wrongly treated the delay as requiring condonation.
provisions: Punjab High Court Rules, Chapter 2-C, Rule 3
Punjab High Court Rules, Chapter I, Rule 5(1)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Directory vs mandatory rule distinction
Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The petitioners sought a review of the Supreme Court's earlier judgment concerning the validity and principles governing orders passed under Section 144 of the CrPC by magistrates, particularly in relation to property disputes between Shia and Sunni Muslim sects.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court should review its earlier decision for failing to lay down guiding principles for the exercise of power under Section 144 CrPC.
What are the legal principles governing the exercise of jurisdiction under Section 144 CrPC?
Whether questions of title to property can be decided in proceedings under Section 144 CrPC or in writ petitions under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution.
holdings: No rigid rules can govern the exercise of power under Section 144 CrPC; it must be based on the facts and circumstances of each case and the situation at a particular time and place.

Section 144 CrPC empowers a magistrate to direct a person to abstain from an act or manage property to prevent danger to public peace, health, safety, or tranquility, even on one's own property if the act poses such danger.

Questions of title cannot be decided for the first time in proceedings under Section 144 CrPC or in writ petitions; such disputes must be resolved through civil suits, though prior judicial decisions may inform the magistrate’s order.
Magistrates need not determine individual rights but must assess what is reasonably necessary to maintain public order, based on their perception of the local situation.
doctrines: Separation of powers between civil and criminal remedies
Principle of temporary administrative orders in aid of public order
Judicial restraint in writ petitions concerning ongoing or non-justiciable factual disputes
Magisterial discretion based on situational necessity

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the Division Bench's decision invalidating a notice to quit, seeking possession of a shop leased to the tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the notice to quit served by the landlord was valid under the applicable rent control law.
holdings: The notice to quit was valid and in full compliance with the law, and the landlord was entitled to possession, but equitable considerations warranted a temporary stay of eviction.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1950, Section 106
doctrines: Equitable relief in eviction matters
Compliance with statutory notice requirements
Doctrine of fair rent and tenant protection

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the state's acquisition of land for the Rourkela Steel Plant and allied industries, arguing it was beyond the statutory definition of 'development of industries'.
issues_decided: Whether the establishment of a steel plant falls within the statutory definition of 'development of industries' under the Orissa Act.
Whether using part of the acquired land for a civil township invalidates the acquisition.
Whether subsequent transfer of a portion of acquired land to a local body for railway-related infrastructure voids the original acquisition.
holdings: The State Government can include a steel plant project within 'development of industries' through notification, as the statute grants wide powers to specify such projects.
The creation of a civil township is a valid and necessary adjunct to a major industrial project like a steel plant and does not invalidate the acquisition.
A valid land acquisition is not rendered void if, at a later stage, part of the land is used for a related public purpose, even if different from the original stated purpose.
provisions: Orissa Development of Industries, Irrigation, Agriculture, Capital Construction and Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 2(c)
Orissa Development of Industries, Irrigation, Agriculture, Capital Construction and Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 3(1)
Orissa Development of Industries, Irrigation, Agriculture, Capital Construction and Resettlement of Displaced Persons (Land Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 5(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of ancillary and incidental use
Doctrine of permissible subsequent use of acquired land for public purposes

card.dispute: The landlord (Miran Devi) challenged the fixation of a low fair rent (Rs. 4.50/month) for her shop leased to tenant Birbal Dass, arguing that the rate prevailing in 1939 could not be applied due to changed circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the phrase 'in similar circumstances' in Section 4(2)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 applies to both 'the same' and 'similar accommodation'
Whether development of the locality or general increase in town prosperity constitutes a change of circumstances justifying departure from pre-1939 rent rates
Whether the District Judge's finding on prevailing rent in 1938 can be interfered with in appeal
holdings: The phrase 'in similar circumstances' qualifies both 'the same' and 'similar accommodation', so pre-1939 rent can only be used if the building existed under similar conditions then.
Development of the locality or substantial alterations to the building constitute a change of circumstances; general town prosperity alone does not.
The District Judge's factual finding that the prevailing rent in 1938 was Rs. 36/- per annum in similar circumstances is not legally infirm and cannot be overturned.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 4(2)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 4(5)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory language
Factual findings not interfered with in absence of legal error
Legislative intent to prevent exorbitant rent increases due to general urban growth

card.dispute: The appellants (vendees) challenged the respondent's (pre-emptor's) right to claim pre-emption of agricultural land, arguing that his tenancy had been extinguished due to non-filing of a possession recovery suit under the Punjab Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether the pre-emptor had a subsisting tenancy on the date of sale, institution of suit, and decree.
Whether tenancy can be deemed to continue despite dispossession without a formal decree of eviction.
holdings: A tenant remains entitled to pre-emption if they were in tenancy on the date of sale and their tenancy was not lawfully terminated under the Pepsu Tenancy Act.

Tenancy continues despite dispossession unless a decree for eviction is obtained under the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, and mere failure to file a possession suit does not extinguish tenancy rights.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 7
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 7A
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 4
doctrines: Overriding effect of special statutes
Continuity of tenancy without lawful termination
Necessity of court decree for eviction to end tenancy

card.dispute: The appellants sued the respondents for declaration of title, possession, and mesne profits over land in Matihani, which became vested in the government under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 3 of Schedule III of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885
Whether the appellants could claim mesne profits despite being unable to claim possession due to vesting of land in the government
holdings: Article 3 of Schedule III of the Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885 does not apply because the suit was not based on dispossession but on the defendants' possession becoming unlawful.
The appellants are entitled to recover mesne profits for the period from May 26, 1950 to January 26, 1955, when the land vested in the government, subject to the law of limitation.
provisions: Bihar Tenancy Act, 1885, Article 3 of Schedule III
doctrines: Vesting of land in the State extinguishes right to possession but not to mesne profits for prior period
Limitation under Article 3 applies only where there is actual dispossession

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, who were brothers, fought over whether the appeal in a partition suit was barred by res judicata due to failure to appeal a related money suit decided by the same court.
issues_decided: Whether the bar of res judicata under Section 11 CPC applies when a party does not appeal a decision in one suit but appeals in a related suit decided by the same court.
Whether the existence of a right of appeal in one suit but not in another affects the application of res judicata.
Whether the appellant, having litigated a common issue in a money suit, can be deemed to have represented other parties under Section 11 Explanation VI CPC.
holdings: The bar of res judicata applies if the same issue was finally decided in a former suit, regardless of whether a right of appeal existed in both suits.
A decision becomes final and binding under Section 11 CPC if it is not appealed, even if another related decision is appealed as a matter of right.
Parties litigating a common private right in good faith represent all others with identical interests under Explanation VI of Section 11 CPC, making the decision binding on them.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation II
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation VI
doctrines: Res judicata
Representative litigation
Finality of judicial decisions

card.dispute: Munshi Dass and Mal Dass fought over who was the rightful Mahant entitled to possession of a Dharamshala and its properties after the death of Mahant Sobha Ram.
issues_decided: Whether Munshi Dass proved he was a Chela of Mahant Sobha Ram.
Whether the custom of succession to the Mahantship was proved by sufficient evidence.
Whether Munshi Dass was duly installed as Mahant based on the alleged custom or other evidence.
holdings: Munshi Dass failed to prove he was a Chela of Sobha Ram, as the evidence did not satisfy Section 50 of the Evidence Act and was legally insufficient.
The alleged custom of succession was not proved by cogent or reliable evidence, and the denial in the written statement required the plaintiff to prove it, which he failed to do.
The entry in the Bahi and other oral evidence were insufficient to prove installation as Mahant, and the High Court rightly rejected the claim based on lack of possession and credibility.
doctrines: Requirement of cogent evidence to prove custom
Opinion evidence must satisfy legal standards under Section 50 of the Evidence Act
Possession and conduct after death of prior Mahant relevant to assess credibility of succession claim

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC, which the High Court had upheld after overturning his initial conviction under Section 326 IPC, based on a dying declaration and eyewitness testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the non-production of the operating surgeon vitiates the conviction when other medical and testimonial evidence is available?
Whether the dying declaration, corroborated by an eyewitness, is sufficient to sustain a conviction under Section 302 IPC?
Whether the accused had the intention to cause death, justifying a conviction for murder rather than culpable homicide not amounting to murder?
holdings: The non-production of the doctor who performed the operation does not invalidate the conviction if the prosecution has otherwise established that the injury was sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death.
A dying declaration, when found reliable and corroborated by credible eyewitness testimony, can form the basis of a conviction under Section 302 IPC.

An intentional stab wound to a vital organ with a dangerous weapon, inflicted in pursuance of a premeditated act, demonstrates the intention to cause death, satisfying the requirements of Section 300 IPC (clause thirdly), even if death occurs during surgery.
doctrines: Dying declaration as substantive evidence
Corroboration of dying declaration by eyewitness
Deemed causation of death under Explanation 2 to Section 299 IPC
Intention to cause death under Section 300 IPC thirdly

card.dispute: The appellant, Mohinder Singh, fought for allotment of urban agricultural land under rehabilitation rules, claiming continuous possession since 1954, despite absence of his name in revenue records.
issues_decided: Whether possession under Rule 34C of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955 requires an entry in revenue records like Jamabandi or Khasra Girdawari.
Whether oral evidence and subsequent court decrees correcting revenue entries can be considered for allotment under Rule 34C.
Whether the Chief Settlement Commissioner erred in disregarding the civil court's ex-parte decree and the Naib Tahsildar's correction of records.
holdings: Entry in revenue records is not a mandatory condition for allotment under Rule 34C; it is only one piece of evidence regarding possession.
A valid court decree or revenue authority's order directing correction of entries can be considered under Rule 34C, even if made after initial proceedings.
The authorities must reconsider the claim by taking into account the civil court decree and Naib Tahsildar's order, subject to legal objections on their validity.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 33
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 34C
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption of revenue records
Principle of reconsideration of administrative decisions in light of new evidence
Judicial deference to civil court decrees in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The landlords sought to evict tenants without obtaining prior permission from the Controller, raising the question of whether rent control laws applied to a municipality constituted after the initial notification.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Chapter II of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, automatically apply to a municipality constituted after the 1949 notification?

Whether a fresh notification under Section 2 of the C.P. and Berar Regulation of Letting of Accommodation Act, 1946, is required to extend rent control protections to a newly constituted municipality?
holdings: The phrase 'all the Municipalities' in the 1949 notification includes municipalities constituted after the notification date; no fresh notification is needed for applicability.
Chapter II of the Rent Control Order became applicable to Tiroda Municipality from June 12, 1956, the date it was constituted, without requiring a new notification.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Regulation of Letting of Accommodation Act, 1946, Section 2
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Chapter II, Clause 13
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Prospective application of statutory notifications

card.dispute: The National Textile Corporation challenged whether land acquisition notifications issued under the Land Acquisition Act became ineffective as 'incumbrances' upon the vesting of a sick textile undertaking in the Central Government under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974.
issues_decided: Whether notifications issued under sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act constitute 'incumbrances' within the meaning of section 4(2) of the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 1974.
holdings: Notifications under the Land Acquisition Act are not 'incumbrances' as they do not constitute a liability or burden attached to the property but are exercises of the State's sovereign power, and thus do not cease to operate upon vesting under the Sick Textile Act.
doctrines: Principle of ejusdem generis
Sovereign power of the State in land acquisition

card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Committee sought to revise property tax assessments for five past years on the ground that part of a building's rent had escaped assessment, but the Life Insurance Corporation challenged the retroactive application of these amendments.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Committee could amend assessment lists retrospectively under Section 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 for properties that had entirely escaped assessment
Whether amendments under Section 68A of the Act could have retrospective effect
Whether the expression 'at any time' in Section 67 limits only the timing of when an amendment can be made, or also restricts its operational effect
Whether previous judicial decisions on other municipal laws were applicable to the interpretation of the Punjab Municipal Act
holdings: Section 67 allows the Municipal Committee to amend assessment lists at any time to include properties that escaped assessment, and such amendments can apply to the year for which the original list was effective, even if the amendment is made later.

Section 68A applies only to cases of erroneous valuation of already-assessed properties and does not permit retroactive correction of entirely omitted properties; amendments under it operate prospectively from specified dates.

The phrase 'at any time' in Section 67 refers to the power to amend without time limitation and enables amendments to take effect for the year the original list covered, not just from the date of amendment.
Decisions under different municipal statutes, such as the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, are not binding when interpreting the Punjab Municipal Act, which must be read as a whole in its own context.
doctrines: Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutory amendments
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory provisions
Distinction between omission from assessment and erroneous assessment
Principle of statutory construction: reading provisions in context and as part of a scheme

card.dispute: Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd. and Prannath Vishwanath Rawlley disputed over whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction to allow an additional claim of Rs. 68,582 for transporting iron ore from a new quarry beyond the original claim specified in the plaint.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator exceeded his jurisdiction by entertaining a fresh claim not confined to the order of reference.
Whether the order of reference included claims relating to transportation from quarry No. 5 beyond the specified amount in the plaint.
Whether an error apparent on the face of the record exists due to the arbitrator's decision on an extra claim.
holdings: An arbitrator cannot entertain a fresh or additional claim beyond the scope of the order of reference derived from the plaint without a further court order.
When the claim amount is specifically mentioned in the plaint and the reference is based on it, the arbitrator must limit the award to that claim.
The arbitrator exceeded his jurisdiction by allowing an additional claim of Rs. 68,582 not contemplated in the original reference, constituting an error apparent on the face of the record.
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Limits of arbitral jurisdiction under court-referred arbitration

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be right-holders in village Tripari, challenged the state's reservation of land for a link road connecting their village to nearby villages and the tehsil town of Kharar, arguing it was not a 'common purpose' under the East Punjab Holdings Act.
issues_decided: Whether the reservation of land for a link road connecting Tripari with other villages and Kharar was for a 'common purpose' under Section 2(bb)(iii) of the East Punjab Holdings Act, 1948.
Whether the existence of a pre-existing link road negated the need for a new road and thus invalidated the land reservation.
holdings: Reservation of land for a village road that connects Tripari to other villages and the tehsil headquarters constitutes a 'common purpose' under Section 2(bb)(iii) of the Act, as it serves the common convenience and benefit of the villagers.
The argument that a new road is unnecessary due to an existing road was not raised in the writ petition and cannot be considered for the first time in appeal before the Supreme Court.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 2(bb)(iii)
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 18(c)
doctrines: Res judicata and curative of pleading: New arguments not raised in lower courts generally not entertained in appeal.
Statutory interpretation: 'Common purpose' includes village roads serving common needs, convenience, or benefit.

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Prithvi Raj Taneja fought the State of Madhya Pradesh over the quantum of compensation for land acquired for a police station and residential quarters.
issues_decided: What was the fair market value of the acquired land for determining compensation?
Could the sale price of small adjoining plots be used to determine compensation for a large area of land?
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing solatium and awarding compensation for loss of earnings?
holdings: The market value of land for compensation must reflect what a willing buyer would pay to a willing seller, excluding advantages from the acquisition scheme.
The price of small plots of land cannot reliably determine compensation for a large tract of land due to differences in market dynamics.
The High Court’s assessment of compensation at Re. 1 per square yard, along with enhanced solatium and loss of earnings, was reasonable and based on relevant factors.
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Rule against using small plot prices for large area valuation
Principle of solatium for compulsory acquisition

card.dispute: Piarey Lal refused to sell his land to Hori Lal after consolidation of holdings, claiming the agreement was void; Hori Lal sued for specific performance, arguing the liability under the agreement transferred to the new consolidated plot.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement for sale creates a liability 'in' the original holding within the meaning of section 30(b) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
Whether such liability, if any, is transferred to the new 'chak' allotted after consolidation
Whether the agreement for sale became void due to impossibility of performance under section 56 of the Indian Contract Act after consolidation
holdings: An agreement for sale does not create any interest or liability 'in' the property under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, and thus no liability exists in the original holding that can be transferred under section 30(b) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
Since no liability 'in' the original holding arose from the agreement for sale, there is no liability to be transferred to the new 'chak' under section 30(b) of the Act.

When the subject property ceases to exist due to consolidation and the tenure-holder's rights in it end, the agreement for sale becomes void under section 56 of the Indian Contract Act due to impossibility of performance.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 30(b)
doctrines: Doctrine of impossibility of performance
Doctrine of transfer of liabilities under land consolidation laws
Principle that a contract for sale does not create an interest in immovable property

card.dispute: The Income Tax Officer sought to reassess the income of Kastur Bhai Lalbhai (H.U.F.) based on an audit note pointing out a legal error in the original assessment, which the High Court quashed, leading to a dispute over whether such an audit note constitutes 'information' under section 147(b) of the Income Tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether an intimation from the Audit Department pointing out an erroneous application of law amounts to 'information' under section 147(b) of the Income Tax Act.
Whether the Income Tax Officer can reopen an assessment under section 147(b) if the information could have been discovered during the original assessment with due diligence.
holdings: The term 'information' under section 147(b) includes information as to the correct state of law, including opinions from competent authorities like the Audit Department, even if the officer was aware of the underlying facts.

Information that could have been discovered during the original assessment but was not actually obtained still qualifies as valid information for initiating reassessment proceedings under section 147(b).
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive knowledge does not bar reassessment if information was not actually known during original assessment.
Doctrine of competent authority: pronouncements on law by authorized bodies, including audit departments, constitute valid 'information' for reassessment purposes.

card.dispute: The landowner fought with the state over the compensation amount for land acquired for a police station, claiming higher compensation based on nearby small plot sale prices.
issues_decided: Whether the sale price of small adjoining plots can be used to determine compensation for a large acquired land area.
Whether the High Court's assessment of market value under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act was legally sound and should be upheld.
holdings: The price paid for small plots of land cannot serve as a reliable benchmark for compensating a large area, as larger tracts typically do not fetch the same per-unit price as smaller plots.
If the High Court has considered the relevant factors under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, its assessment of market value should not be disturbed by the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Market value determination in compulsory acquisition
Non-application of small plot sale prices to large area compensation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from the entire premises, but the courts below did not consider whether partial eviction would suffice under the Jammu and Kashmir rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the second proviso to the Explanation to Section 11(1)(h) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 requires the court to consider partial eviction even in the absence of a specific pleading?
Whether the failure of the courts below to consider and record a finding on partial eviction under the proviso constitutes an error?
holdings: The second proviso to the Explanation to Section 11(1)(h) mandates the court to consider whether partial eviction would satisfy the landlord's reasonable requirements, irrespective of specific pleadings.
Courts must actively examine the possibility of partial eviction and record findings based on evidence, even if not specifically pleaded, to comply with the statutory mandate.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, Section 11(1)(h), Second Proviso to Explanation
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Mandatory judicial duty to consider statutory requirements
Procedural fairness in rent control proceedings

card.dispute: The Karta of a Hindu undivided family challenged the validity of Rule 23 of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Rules, 1939, which deemed a family to remain undivided for tax purposes unless a partition order was passed, after claiming the family had been disrupted.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 23 can deem a Hindu undivided family to continue as such for tax assessment in the absence of a partition order apportioning tax liability
Whether the State Government had the legislative competence to make Rule 23 under the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act
holdings: Rule 23 validly deems a Hindu undivided family to remain undivided for tax purposes unless an order apportioning tax liability based on partition is passed, ensuring continuity in assessment.

The State Government had the authority under Section 50(1) of the Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act to make Rule 23 as it was necessary to carry out the purposes of the Act and was validly framed with prior publication.
doctrines: Deemed continuation of HUF for tax purposes
Delegated legislation in taxation
Validity of executive rule-making under taxing statutes

card.dispute: Saksena Brothers (P) Ltd. and Bhudhar Chandra Banerjee disputed over correction of a partition decree, and whether a subsequent lease to a third party bound them to the compromise.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to correct the final partition decree under Sections 151 and 152 of the CPC?
Whether the compromise between the appellant and the plaintiff-respondent binds a third party in possession as a lessee?
holdings: An application under Sections 151 and 152 of the CPC to correct a final decree on grounds of miscalculation in metes and bounds is maintainable.
A compromise between original parties to a suit does not bind a third party in possession under a lease, whose rights were not adjudicated in the appeal.
doctrines: Principle of finality of decrees
Doctrine of binding effect of compromise
Doctrine of lis pendens

card.dispute: Creditor and debtor coparceners fought over the right to receive shares of compensation money from acquired joint family property, specifically whether debtor coparceners could receive their share before settling their outstanding debt.
issues_decided: Whether the debtor coparceners are entitled to immediate payment of their share of the compensation amount without first satisfying the dues owed to the creditor coparceners under the compromise decree.
Whether Clause (8) of the compromise decree creates a priority in favor of creditor coparceners regarding the distribution of compensation proceeds.
holdings: The debtor coparceners are not entitled to immediate payment of their share of the compensation money until the dues owed to the creditor coparceners under the compromise decree are satisfied.
Clause (8) of the compromise decree gives priority to creditor coparceners, and any payment to debtor coparceners before satisfying those dues violates the terms of the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of Compromise Decree
Priority of Claims under Judicial Compromise
Principle of Equitable Distribution in Partition Suits

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of habitual default in rent payment, which the tenant contested, leading to a conflict over whether the High Court could interfere under Article 227 despite concurrent findings of fact by lower tribunals.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution in interfering with concurrent factual findings of the Rent Controller and the Collector?
Whether the tenant could be considered a habitual defaulter despite regular acceptance of rent by the landlord at 3-4 month intervals?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by overturning concurrent findings of fact by the Rent Controller and the Collector without showing any perversity or illegality.

A tenant cannot be deemed a habitual defaulter where the landlord has consistently accepted rent at regular intervals of 3-4 months without protest, indicating an implied contract modifying the monthly payment obligation.
doctrines: Limited scope of interference under Article 227
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed without strong cause
Implied contract from conduct of parties

card.dispute: The appellant (mortgagor) and respondent (mortgagee bank) disputed whether trees in a grove could be separately attached in execution of a mortgage decree after the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, extinguished the original proprietary rights and created new bhumidari rights vested in the State free from encumbrances.
issues_decided: Whether trees forming part of a grove are included in 'grove-land' that vests in the State free from encumbrances under Section 6(a)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether a distinction can be drawn between trees and grove-land for the purpose of execution of a mortgage decree after the abolition of zamindari
holdings: Trees that are part of a grove are inseparable from the grove-land and fall within the definition of 'intermediary's grove' under Section 3(13) of the Act, which vests in the State free from all encumbrances.

The mortgagee cannot execute the decree by attaching trees in a grove, as such rights were extinguished and replaced by bhumidari rights; enforcement is limited to compensation under Section 6(h) read with Section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(13)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(a)(i)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6(h)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18(1)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of inseparability of standing trees from land
Doctrine of extinguishment of prior rights under land reform statutes
Doctrine of limited enforcement of mortgage rights post-land reform

card.dispute: The appellant sued the respondent for possession of land or, alternatively, for a decree of Rs. 5,000 as the balance of the purchase price, after the respondent failed to pay the full amount under an alleged agreement to buy the land for Rs. 17,000.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was ready and willing to perform the agreement for sale under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Whether the respondent could challenge the finding that the sale price was Rs. 17,000 without filing a cross-objection
Whether the High Court was justified in granting relief based on part performance when it was not pleaded and no extension of time was established
Whether the certificate under Article 133 of the Constitution was validly challenged at the appellate stage
holdings: Under Section 53A, the transferee must be ready and willing to perform the contract; the respondent failed to meet this requirement as he refused to pay the balance of Rs. 5,000 and denied the higher sale price.
A respondent cannot challenge a finding in their favour on appeal without filing a cross-objection; the respondent could not dispute the Rs. 17,000 sale price determination without one.
The High Court erred in allowing relief based on part performance when no issue was framed on extension of time and the defence was not pleaded; such relief cannot be granted on unpleaded grounds.
An objection to the value of the suit for the purpose of a certificate under Article 133 must be raised at the earliest opportunity and cannot be raised for the first time in this Court.
doctrines: Doctrine of part performance under Section 53A
Requirement of cross-objection to challenge a decree in appeal
Principle of readiness and willingness under specific performance law
Procedural requirement of raising valuation objections at the appropriate stage

card.dispute: The appellant, a former lessee of Jairam Theatre, challenged the award of mesne profits from the date of lease expiry in 1960, claiming he became a statutory tenant under the 1961 Act and that damages should be limited to the lease rent.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 applies retroactively to a suit filed before its commencement under the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the appellant continued as a statutory tenant after lease expiry, thereby delaying liability for mesne profits until the eviction decree
Whether the rate of mesne profits awarded at Rs. 4,000 per month was justified despite a contractual rent of Rs. 1,600
holdings: The 1961 Act does not apply to suits pending under the Transfer of Property Act when the suit was filed before the Act's commencement and the property was exempt under the earlier 1955 Act.
The appellant’s possession became wrongful immediately upon lease expiry in 1960, not from the 1962 eviction decree, making him liable for mesne profits from May 22, 1960.
The courts below properly assessed evidence to fix mesne profits at Rs. 4,000 per month, and this Court found no reason to interfere with the concurrent factual finding.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 2(1)(d)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 51(1) and (2)
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospectivity in statutory interpretation
Doctrine of pending proceedings unaffected by repeal unless expressly provided
Principle of concurrent findings in factual assessment by lower courts

card.dispute: The appellant firm challenged the attachment and auction-sale of its properties by revenue authorities for recovery of unpaid sales tax, claiming improper service of notice.
issues_decided: Whether the service of notice by affixation, without personal service, was valid under the relevant rules.
Whether the failure to comply with the prescribed mode of service invalidated the attachment and sale of the properties.
holdings: Service by affixation is valid when a partner of the firm refused to accept the notice and there is evidence of actual awareness of the proceedings.
