Non-compliance with personal service rules does not invalidate the recovery proceedings if the party had actual knowledge and opportunity to be heard.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Sales Tax Act, Rules 11, 12, 13, and 14
doctrines: Actual notice doctrine
Doctrine of substantial compliance

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat fought forest contractors over whether unregistered documents transferring rights to cut trees were valid, after lower courts upheld the contractors' rights.
issues_decided: Whether the question of registration of documents could be raised for the first time in second appeal
Whether the documents creating rights to cut trees required compulsory registration under the Registration Act
holdings: A question about the registration of documents, which involves a factual determination of whether trees are standing timber, cannot be raised for the first time in second appeal.

The documents in question could not be declared void for lack of registration without a factual inquiry into the nature of the trees; such an inquiry was not conducted, so the issue could not be decided at that stage.
doctrines: Res judicata
Principle of constructive res judicata
Factual determination prerequisite to legal conclusion on registration

card.dispute: The appellant claimed tenancy rights over agricultural land sold by his wife to the respondent, while the respondent denied creating any tenancy and challenged the validity of entries in the record of rights and alleged admissions.
issues_decided: Whether the Revenue Tribunal had jurisdiction to interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower authorities under Section 76 of the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948?
Whether an unproven and uncontroverted admission can be used against a party under the Indian Evidence Act?
Whether entries in the record of rights create a presumption of tenancy when contradicted by oral evidence and contextual inconsistencies?
holdings: The Revenue Tribunal cannot interfere with findings of fact unless there is an error of law apparent on the record; concurrent factual findings by lower authorities cannot be overturned merely on grounds of differing appreciation of evidence.
An admission under the Indian Evidence Act must be proven and the party must be given an opportunity to explain it during cross-examination; otherwise, it cannot be used against them.

Entries in the record of rights do not create an irrebuttable presumption of tenancy; when they are inconsistent with other evidence or internal entries, and no notice was given in mutation proceedings, they cannot be relied upon to establish tenancy.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 76
doctrines: Principle of constructive notice in mutation proceedings
Doctrine of burden of proof and its irrelevance when entire evidence is considered
Rule of fair opportunity to explain admissions under Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act

card.dispute: The appellants sued for possession of land and mesne profits, but the properties had vested in the State Government under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, raising questions about their right to relief.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could obtain a decree for possession of the suit properties after vesting under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the appellants were entitled to mesne profits for the period prior to vesting of the properties in the State
holdings: The appellants cannot obtain a decree for possession as the properties vested in the State Government on January 1, 1956, under Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.

The appellants are entitled to mesne profits for the period from January 25, 1952, when the suit was filed, to January 1, 1956, the date of vesting, as the respondents were in wrongful possession during that time.
doctrines: Vesting of property in the State extinguishes private claims to possession
Right to mesne profits may survive for period of wrongful possession prior to vesting

card.dispute: The State of Mysore and others fought against Hutchappa and another over whether an Assistant Commissioner in charge of a Sub-Division could validly carry out land acquisition proceedings without a separate government notification, under the Mysore Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether an Assistant Commissioner in charge of a Sub-Division is included within the definition of 'Deputy Commissioner' under Section 3(c) of the Mysore Land Acquisition Act without requiring a separate notification.
Whether the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the Assistant Commissioner were valid in law.
holdings: The term 'Deputy Commissioner' under Section 3(c) of the Mysore Land Acquisition Act expressly includes an Assistant Commissioner in charge of a Sub-Division without requiring any separate government notification.
The High Court erred in quashing the acquisition proceedings; such proceedings initiated by the Assistant Commissioner are valid and do not require additional empowerment.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Inclusion by express definition

card.dispute: The State of Orissa and others contested whether the Collector could exercise revisional powers under Section 59 of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 over a final appellate order passed under Section 44(2) regarding ceiling surplus land.
issues_decided: Whether an order passed by an appellate authority under Section 44(2) of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, which has become final, is subject to revision by the Collector under Section 59?
Whether the finality of orders under Section 44(2) excludes revisional jurisdiction under Section 59?
holdings: The Collector has revisional jurisdiction under Section 59 to revise any order passed under the Orissa Land Reforms Act, including appellate orders under Section 44(2), despite their declared finality.
The finality clause in Section 44(2) does not bar revision under Section 59, as the revisionary powers are wide and intended to correct errors in proceedings of an expropriatory statute.
provisions: Orissa Land Reforms (Second Amendment) Act, 1976, Act 29 of 1976
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Revisional jurisdiction
Finality of orders
Presumption against nullification of statutory powers

card.dispute: The petitioner, son of a tenant who lost an eviction case, filed multiple suits and obtained injunctions to delay vacating the premises, which the landlord challenged as an abuse of court process.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner's successive lawsuits and injunction applications constituted an abuse of the legal process.
Whether the trial court should have dismissed the plaint at the outset for being vexatious and meritless.
Whether the advocate's participation in such litigation violates professional ethics.
holdings: Filing repetitive and meritless suits to delay execution of a final eviction order amounts to gross abuse of the judicial process.
A court must scrutinize the plaint meaningfully and dismiss it under Order VII Rule 11 CPC if it is manifestly vexatious and discloses no clear cause of action.
Advocates must refrain from aiding frivolous or fraudulent litigation, as they are officers of the court and owe a duty to justice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII, Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order X
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Judicial activism in dismissing frivolous litigation
Advocate's duty as officer of the court

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the validity of a Sub-Divisional Officer's order ejecting Smt. Sarjoo Devi, a hereditary tenant, from land claimed as customary pasture land by the Gaon Sabha.
issues_decided: Whether the Sub-Divisional Officer had jurisdiction to order ejectment under Section 212-A of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950, when the land was not recorded or used as customary common pasture land
Whether the order of ejectment under Section 212-A is final and bars a civil suit
Whether Smt. Sarjoo Devi qualified as a hereditary tenant entitled to sirdari rights under the Act, even if the land was not continuously cultivated
holdings: The Sub-Divisional Officer acted without jurisdiction because the land was not recorded or used as customary common pasture land as required under Section 212; hence, the ejectment order was null and void.
An order under Section 212-A is not final; the affected party has the right to file a civil suit to establish their claim, and the order only becomes conclusive if the suit fails.

The term 'land' under Section 3(14) includes land held or occupied for agricultural purposes; 'held' means possession by legal title, so cultivation is not mandatory. Respondent was a hereditary tenant entitled to sirdari rights.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(14)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 212
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 212-A
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 19
doctrines: Jurisdictional error rendering administrative orders null and void
Conclusiveness of administrative orders subject to judicial challenge
Interpretation of 'held' as legal possession, not physical occupation

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision to quash the compulsory retirement of IAS officer Chandra Mohan Nigam, who had been cleared by a prior review committee.
issues_decided: Whether a second review committee could recommend compulsory retirement of a civil servant after a prior review had recommended continuance in service, in absence of exceptional circumstances

Whether the compulsory retirement order passed under Rule 16(3) of the All India Services (DCRB) Rules, 1958, was valid when it contradicted the procedural instructions issued by the Central Government
Whether the High Court was justified in examining the government files to assess the validity of the retirement order
holdings: A second review committee cannot revisit a civil servant's case within a short period after a prior review has recommended continuance, unless exceptional circumstances such as new adverse material emerge.

The compulsory retirement order was invalid as it violated the binding procedural instructions issued under the All India Services (DCRB) Rules, 1958, which limit reviews to specific ages and prevent arbitrary re-evaluation.
The High Court was justified in examining the service records since the government did not claim privilege over the documents and had produced them without objection.
provisions: All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958, Rule 16(3)
doctrines: Pleasure doctrine under Article 310 subject to Article 311 safeguards
Procedural fairness in administrative action
Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Rule of law against arbitrariness in service matters

card.dispute: The appellants fought the Gram Sabha over whether inherited land was 'shamlat deh' (village common land) under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, claiming it was excluded due to prior private acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the suit land retained its character as 'shamlat deh' despite being recorded as under the possession of private owners in revenue records.
Whether the land was excluded from the definition of 'shamlat deh' under proviso (iv) to section 2(g) of the Act based on prior purchase or gift from a co-sharer.
holdings: The fact that land is recorded as 'shamlat deh' in jamabandi, even if also noted as being in possession of owners, does not negate its legal character as common village land.
Proviso (iv) to section 2(g) excludes land from 'shamlat deh' only if acquired by purchase or exchange from a co-sharer in the common land; acquisition from a non-co-sharer does not qualify.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 2(g) proviso (iv)
doctrines: Presumption of continuity of land character based on revenue records
Strict interpretation of statutory exceptions in land reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant, an auction-purchaser, challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the sale of properties in village Gudipadu, arguing that the sale was valid despite the decree being fully satisfied by the sale of properties in Devanoor.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court could continue the sale of properties in Gudipadu after the decree was fully satisfied by the sale of properties in Devanoor under Order XXI Rule 64 of the CPC
Whether non-compliance with Order XXI Rule 64 of the CPC amounts to a jurisdictional error vitiating the sale
Whether the auction-purchaser is entitled to compensation for improvements made on the property if the sale is set aside
holdings: The executing court must stop further sales once the decree is satisfied by the sale of part of the attached property, as continuing the sale exceeds its jurisdiction under Order XXI Rule 64 CPC.
Failure to comply with the mandate of Order XXI Rule 64 CPC, which limits sale to what is necessary to satisfy the decree, is a jurisdictional defect that vitiates the sale.
If a sale is set aside, the auction-purchaser is entitled to the return of the purchase amount and the value of any improvements made, but not interest on improvements if in possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 64
doctrines: Jurisdictional limits of executing court
Mandatory nature of procedural provisions in execution
Equitable adjustment upon setting aside of sale

card.dispute: Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd. challenged whether it was required to file a return under Section 9 of the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, despite owning exempted land as a company running a sugarcane factory.
issues_decided: Whether a company owning a sugarcane factory is bound to file a return under Section 9 of the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, even if the land held is exempted from ceiling limits.
Whether the requirement to file a return under Section 9 applies to all persons holding land, including those with exempted land.
holdings: Section 9 of the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, requires every person, including companies, to file a return of all lands held, including exempted lands, to ensure effective enforcement of land reform laws.

The purpose of Section 9 is to enable the State Government to have complete information about all agricultural holdings, regardless of exemption from ceiling limits, and thus the provision must be interpreted broadly.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 2(d)
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 7
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 9
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Literal interpretation with contextual reading

card.dispute: The Trustees for the Improvement of Calcutta imposed a betterment fee on property owners under a street scheme, and the owners challenged the constitutional validity of the fee and related rules.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 78A to 78G of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911, suffer from excessive delegation of legislative power
Whether Rules 11 to 21 made under the Act are ultra vires for being made under an incorrect statutory provision
holdings: Sections 78A to 78G do not involve excessive delegation as they provide sufficient guidance and safeguards against arbitrary inclusion of land in a scheme and tie betterment fees to actual increases in land value.
Rules 11 to 21 are valid as they were properly made under clause (3a) of Section 137 to regulate arbitrator proceedings, not under Section 86, which applies only to Chapter V of the Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Principle of constitutional validity of delegated legislation
Rule of statutory interpretation regarding scope of rule-making power

card.dispute: The appellants (Telang) challenged the recognition of respondents as independent tenants and the validity of a notice terminating tenancy, after sub-tenants were declared protected tenants under tenancy law.
issues_decided: Whether respondents Nos. 2 and 3 were independent tenants or sub-tenants of respondent No. 1 after being declared protected tenants under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
Whether the notice of termination of tenancy issued by the landlord to respondent No. 1 alone was valid
Whether the agreed rent of Rs. 320/- per year was the reasonable rent for the land in dispute
holdings: Respondents Nos. 1 to 3 were independent tenants of separate portions of the land, as evidenced by separate rent payments and official records recognizing them as protected tenants.
The notice of termination served only on respondent No. 1 was invalid because it did not address the tenancies of respondents Nos. 2 and 3 who were independent tenants.
The agreed rent of Rs. 320/- per year was upheld as the reasonable rent since it did not exceed the statutory limit and no party claimed it was excessive.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1939
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 12
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 5
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1918, Section 31
doctrines: Principle of protected tenancy under tenancy laws
Doctrine of independent tenancy based on conduct and recognition
Rule against interference under Article 227 unless there is manifest injustice or legal error

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be Indian nationals, sued for a declaration of Indian citizenship and an injunction against deportation, but the lower courts held they failed to prove their citizenship.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants proved their Indian citizenship by birth or residence.
Whether the unregistered mortgage deed and oral testimony were sufficient to establish the appellants' claim of Indian nationality.
holdings: The appellants failed to prove they were born in India or had any legal status as Indian citizens, as no official documents or credible evidence were produced.
An unregistered and unmarked mortgage deed, unsupported by ownership proof or witness testimony, cannot substantiate a claim to Indian citizenship.
doctrines: Burden of proof in citizenship cases
Requirement of documentary evidence to substantiate claims of nationality

card.dispute: A divorced wife sought maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 of the Cr.P.C., despite a prior consent decree involving mehar payment and a clause waiving future claims.
issues_decided: Whether a divorced woman is entitled to maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C. despite divorce and a prior settlement of mehar?
Whether Section 127(3)(b) Cr.P.C. bars maintenance if mehar has been paid under personal law?
Whether the husband proved that the wife was living separately by mutual consent under Section 125(4) Cr.P.C.?
Whether neglect to maintain must be proven for a claim under Section 125 Cr.P.C.?
holdings: A divorced woman who has not remarried is eligible for maintenance under Section 125 Cr.P.C., as the Explanation (b) to Section 125(1) explicitly includes divorcees.
Section 127(3)(b) does not cancel a maintenance order unless the mehar or customary payment is adequate to serve as a reasonable substitute for ongoing maintenance.
Divorce itself negates the presumption of mutual consent to live together; thus, Section 125(4) does not bar maintenance claims by divorcees.
Neglect to maintain is established when the husband fails to provide financial support, and the burden lies on him to prove otherwise, which he did not.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation in favor of destitute women
Purposeful and teleological interpretation of law
Social justice and economic protection under Article 39
Non-derogation from statutory rights by private contract

card.dispute: The co-owners of a small property disputed over partition, with the appellants seeking partition or buyout of the respondent's share, while the respondent opposed partition and sought to buy the appellants' share at an older valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint contained a request under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893, justifying a sale under Section 3(1) of the Act
Whether the court could order a partition by owelty in the absence of applicability of Sections 2 and 3 of the Partition Act, 1893
What method of valuation is equitable when property value has significantly appreciated after purchase
holdings: A request under Section 2 of the Partition Act, 1893 must clearly seek a public sale; a proposal to buy a co-owner's share at court-determined value does not satisfy this requirement.
When partition in specie is impracticable and Sections 2 and 3 of the Partition Act do not apply, courts may use equitable methods like owelty to effect partition.
Fixing the value of a co-owner’s share based on outdated purchase price is inequitable if the property value has substantially increased; valuation must reflect current market conditions.
doctrines: Owelty in partition
Equitable partition in absence of statutory mechanism
Concurrent finding of fact not interfered with

card.dispute: The landlords (B.N. Mutto & Anr) sought recovery of possession of rented premises from the tenant (T.K. Nandi) under Section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which grants a right to government employees to evict tenants if required to vacate government accommodation; the tenant resisted the eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can seek eviction under Section 14A without satisfying the conditions of Section 14(1)(e), particularly that the premises were let for residential purposes?
Whether the special procedure under Section 25B applies to applications under Section 14A and on what grounds a tenant may contest such an application?
Whether a retired government employee who was required to vacate government accommodation is entitled to the benefit of Section 14A?
holdings: Section 14A creates an independent and special right for certain government employees to recover possession; it does not require that the premises be let for residential purposes, unlike Section 14(1)(e).

Under Section 25B(5), a tenant can only contest an eviction application under Section 14A if the affidavit shows the landlord is not entitled to relief under Section 14A, such as not being in occupation of government accommodation or no order requiring vacation.
A landlord who retired before the government issued the notice to quit is still entitled to the benefit of Section 14A, as the right accrues based on the status at the relevant time.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of special provisions creating independent rights
Limited scope of tenant's right to contest under special eviction procedures
Deeming provisions and retrospective operation of amendment acts

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the eviction decree on grounds of the landlord's ineligibility to sue under a newly amended tenancy law and sought to adduce additional evidence in the second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether sub-section (3A) of Section 13 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, has retroactive effect and renders the eviction suit incompetent if filed within three years of the landlord's acquisition of interest
Whether the High Court, in a second appeal under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent, can permit amendment of pleadings and appreciate additional evidence without jurisdiction
Whether the remedy under Section 17E of the Act is alternative or additional to an appeal
Whether the Supreme Court can entertain grounds beyond those specified in the special leave granted under Article 136
holdings: Sub-section (3A) of Section 13 bars eviction suits by transferee landlords within three years of acquisition; if the suit is filed earlier, it is incompetent, and the court must assess requirement at the time the suit could lawfully be filed.

A High Court hearing a second appeal lacks inherent jurisdiction to allow amendment of pleadings or receive and appreciate additional evidence unless authorized; doing so causes prejudice and warrants remand.
Section 17E provides an additional, not exclusive, remedy for tenants against eviction decrees based on Section 13(1)(f); it does not bar an ongoing appeal challenging the suit's competence.

The scope of an appeal under Article 136 is confined to the grounds specified in the leave, but these must be broadly construed; in exceptional cases, the Court may expand the grounds under Article 137 to meet the ends of justice.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(3A)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17E
Letters Patent of the High Court, Clause 15
doctrines: Doctrine of retroactive operation of statutes
Doctrine of additional vs. exclusive remedies
Doctrine of limited scope of special leave appeals
Doctrine of jurisdictional limits of appellate courts in second appeals

card.dispute: The appellants, Bakhtawar and Satbir, challenged their conviction for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, after the High Court enhanced their sentence from ten years' rigorous imprisonment to life imprisonment.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the appellants guilty of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC?
Whether the injuries inflicted were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, satisfying the requirement of Section 300(3) IPC?
holdings: The court held that the appellants had the intention to cause the injuries which were actually inflicted, and those injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, thereby satisfying the ingredients of murder under Section 300(3) IPC.
The conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC was legally unsustainable, and the enhancement to life imprisonment under Section 302 IPC was justified based on the nature and effect of the injuries.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive intention under Section 300(3) IPC
Principle of corroboration of eyewitness testimony by medical and circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: Bhajya and Sonu (defendants) fought with Gopikabai (plaintiff) over possession of Bhumiswami rights in agricultural land after the death of the last female holder, Smt. Sarji, who inherited it from her husband.
issues_decided: Whether the inheritance to the estate of Smt. Sarji, who died in 1956, is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, or by the Mitakshara Law under Section 4(2) of the Hindu Succession Act?
Whether Section 151 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, incorporates personal law as amended up to the date of the devolution of interest?
Who are the heirs of the husband under Section 15(2)(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and as of which date are they to be determined?
Whether the plaintiff, being the sister's daughter of the last male holder, is a preferential heir over the sapindas (agnates) under the Act?
holdings: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 governs the devolution of interest in agricultural land where the female Hindu died after the Act came into force, despite Section 4(2), because personal law under Section 151 of the MP Land Revenue Code includes amendments up to the date of death.
Section 151 of the MP Land Revenue Code, 1954 adopts personal law as it exists at the time of devolution, not as it stood when the Code was enacted.

For determining 'heirs of the husband' under Section 15(2)(b), the law applicable is that in force at the time of the female's death, with the fiction that the husband died intestate immediately after her.
The sister's daughter, being a Class II heir under the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, is a preferential heir over agnates and thus entitled to inherit ahead of them.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 151
doctrines: Legislation by referential incorporation
Fiction of simultaneous death under Section 16(3)
Devolution of property inherited from husband under Section 15(2)(b)
Preferential heirship under Class I and Class II of the Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether brick-earth could be classified as a 'minor mineral' under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, after the Central Government notified it as such.
issues_decided: Whether brick-earth qualifies as a 'mineral' within the meaning of 'minor mineral' under Section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957.
Whether the Central Government had the authority to notify brick-earth as a minor mineral under Section 3(e).
holdings: The term 'mineral' is context-dependent and not confined to precious or subterranean substances; in the context of the Act, it includes materials like brick-earth.
Since 'ordinary clay' and 'ordinary sand' are explicitly included as minor minerals, brick-earth falls within the scope of 'any other mineral' that can be notified as a minor mineral.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 3(e)
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Deference to administrative notification within statutory framework
Rejection of rigid, scientific definitions in favor of functional and regulatory context

card.dispute: Baldev Singh appealed his conviction for the abduction and murder of Inder Singh, challenging the reliability of the approver's testimony and the sufficiency of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the testimony of the approver (Gurmel Singh) is reliable and sufficiently corroborated to sustain a conviction for murder and abduction.
Whether the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 and Section 364 IPC can be upheld based on the available evidence.
Whether the conviction under Section 201 IPC for causing disappearance of evidence is proved beyond reasonable doubt.
holdings: The approver's testimony is inherently improbable and untrustworthy due to material contradictions and late embellishments, and thus cannot form the basis of a conviction for murder or abduction.
The convictions under Section 302 read with Section 34 and Section 364 IPC are set aside due to insufficient and unreliable evidence.
The conviction under Section 201 IPC is upheld as the recovery of the dead body at the instance of the appellant is independently corroborated and proves concealment of evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration of approver's testimony
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of retracted or inconsistent statements

card.dispute: Baru and others versus Dalip Singh and others over the maintainability of revision applications before the Superintending Canal Officer for shifting the heads of water courses under the Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873.
issues_decided: Whether a revision lay before the Superintending Canal Officer under Section 30B(3) of the Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, in the absence of an approved scheme by the Divisional Canal Officer?
Whether the applications for shifting the heads of water courses could be treated as applications for preparation of a scheme under the Haryana Water Supply and Sewerage Act, 1974?
holdings: Section 30B(3) of the Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, allows revision only against an approved scheme by the Divisional Canal Officer; in the absence of such a scheme, no revision lies before the Superintending Canal Officer.

Applications for shifting water course heads, though not maintainable as revisions, should be treated as applications for scheme preparation under Sections 17, 18, 19 of the Haryana Act 29 of 1974, and decided accordingly.
provisions: Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 30B(3)
Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 30C
Northern India Canal and Drainage Act, 1873, Section 30A(1)
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory jurisdiction
Substantial justice over technicality
In pari materia (treatment of applications in light of new legislation)

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC, arguing he acted in private defence or in a sudden fight without premeditation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could claim the right of private defence under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC
Whether the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC due to sudden fight and heat of passion
holdings: The right of private defence did not accrue to the appellant as the deceased was unarmed and posed no threat justifying defensive force.
Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC does not apply because there was no bilateral fight, and the use of a lethal axe on an unarmed person with multiple fatal blows negates the claim of sudden passion.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304, Part I
doctrines: Right of private defence
Sudden fight doctrine
Heat of passion

card.dispute: The appellant, a refugee allottee of evacuee property, challenged the High Court's decision to allow respondents to restore their claim over a one-third share in composite property after the statutory period for appeal had expired.
issues_decided: Whether the Competent Officer had jurisdiction to review his own vesting order under the Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951.
Whether the respondents could file a 'restoration' application after the statutory period to appeal had expired, thereby invalidating the final vesting order.
Whether the High Court ought to have granted certiorari relief despite the respondents' delay and improper invocation of review jurisdiction.
holdings: The Evacuee Interest (Separation) Act, 1951 contains no provision for review by the Competent Officer; hence, any review order is without jurisdiction.
An order under Section 11 becomes final under Section 18 if no appeal or revision is filed within the prescribed period, and cannot be reopened via a 'restoration' application.
The High Court erred in granting certiorari when the respondents had themselves improperly invoked non-existent review jurisdiction to their advantage, making their conduct inequitable.
doctrines: Finality of statutory orders
Review as a creature of statute
Equitable conduct in writ petitions
Non-justiciability of orders without jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Chief Commissioner of Delhi imposed a registration fee under a notification, which the trustees of a debenture trust deed challenged as an illegal levy not constituting a valid fee under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the registration fee levied under the impugned notification qualifies as a 'fee' within the meaning of the Constitution.
Whether the fee, which formed part of the general revenues of the State, satisfied the essential conditions of a valid fee.
holdings: A valid fee must involve a quid pro quo, meaning the authority must render some service, however remote, in return for the fee.
A fee must be earmarked for the purpose of its imposition and not form part of the general revenues of the State; if it does, it fails to qualify as a constitutional fee.
doctrines: Quid pro quo for fees
Non-merger of fees with general revenue
Essential characteristics of a valid fee

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the High Court after their acquittal by the trial court, challenged their conviction in a case involving rioting, unlawful assembly, and the death of Pakhar Singh during a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of the appellants and convicting them under sections 302/149, 325/149, and 323/149 IPC?
Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence of property?

Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Section 2(a) of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, must consider the sufficiency of the High Court's reasons for reversing an acquittal?
What is the appropriate offence and sentence when an unlawful assembly causes injuries resulting in death, but the fatal injury was not necessarily inflicted in prosecution of the common object?
holdings: The Supreme Court has full appellate jurisdiction under Section 2(a) of the 1970 Act and must decide the case on its merits, independently of whether the High Court gave sufficient reasons for reversing the acquittal.
The plea of private defence of property fails when the defence does not produce evidence to rebut the prosecution's proof of lawful possession protected by a court order.
The appellants are not guilty under Section 302/149 IPC because the fatal injury was not shown to be inflicted in prosecution of the common object of the unlawful assembly.

The appellants are guilty under Section 326/149 IPC as the common object of the assembly was to cause grievous hurt with dangerous weapons, and their conviction under Section 325/149 IPC for injuring Pritam Kaur is upheld.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Appreciation of evidence in statutory appeals under Section 2(a) of the 1970 Act
Burden of proof in claiming right of private defence of property
Common object under Section 149 IPC
Principle of independent appellate review on merits

card.dispute: The appellants, sons of the testatrix's husband's brother, contested the validity of a will executed by Smt. Chandi Rani, which bequeathed all her property to the respondent, her grand-nephew, alleging suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
issues_decided: Whether the will was executed under suspicious circumstances due to the testatrix being under the control of the beneficiary.
Whether the testatrix was of sound mind and capable of executing the will despite her physical condition.
Whether the lack of registration on the day of execution and the general terms of the will invalidate it.
holdings: Mere allegations of confinement or control by the beneficiary do not invalidate a will if there is no clear evidence of coercion or undue influence, especially when the testatrix had shown prior affection and trust towards the beneficiary.

A testatrix may use a thumb impression instead of a signature due to physical incapacity, and this does not affect the validity of the will if she was of sound disposing mind at the time of execution.
Delay in registration and the general nature of the will’s language are not fatal to its validity if the execution is otherwise proved and no fraud or coercion is established.
doctrines: Sound disposing mind
Attestation of wills
Suspicious circumstances doctrine

card.dispute: The former Maharaja of Alwar sued the Union of India to enforce a 'decision' by the States Ministry regarding ownership of certain properties, which the government later reversed.
issues_decided: Whether the communication dated 14th September 1949 constituted a final and binding decision under the Matsya or Rajasthan Covenants
Whether the communication was an agreement covered by Article 363 of the Constitution, thereby barring judicial review
Whether the terms of the inventory attached to the 1949 communication attained finality and could not be altered
holdings: The 14th September 1949 communication was not a decision under the Covenants but a record of a tentative agreement between the parties.
Any agreement arising from negotiations under the Covenants, even if not the primary covenant, is covered by Article 363 and bars civil court jurisdiction.
The terms of the 1949 inventory were part of an ongoing process and did not attain finality until all disputes were resolved through an overall agreement.
doctrines: Bar on jurisdiction of courts under Article 363 for disputes arising out of pre-constitutional agreements with rulers
Principle of finality of settlement through overall agreement
Distinction between binding arbitral decisions and non-binding negotiated agreements

card.dispute: The dispute was between Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. and Shri Parmeshwar Kumar Agarwala over whether a coke oven was a 'coke oven plant' under the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, and whether the owner retained title to claim rent from the Central Government after nationalisation.
issues_decided: Whether the coke oven in question qualifies as a 'coke oven plant' under Section 3(b) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972
Whether the respondent retained ownership of the coke oven after transferring the coal mine
Whether the Central Government is liable to pay rent for the use of the coke oven despite nationalisation
holdings: A 'coke oven plant' is distinct from a 'mine' under the Act, and only facilities specifically used for manufacturing hard coke qualify as a coke oven plant.
The respondent retained ownership of the coke oven as it was not transferred or nationalised, based on the lease and sale documents.
The Central Government is liable to pay rent for the use of the coke oven, but equitably reduced to one-third of the original lease rent due to nationalisation.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to give effect to legislative dichotomy
Distinction between integral plant and subsidiary equipment
Equitable adjustment of contractual obligations under state acquisition

card.dispute: The dispute was between Bhajya and Gopikabai over the devolution of bhumidari rights in agricultural land after the death of the last female holder, Smt. Sarji, with Gopikabai claiming as heir under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and Bhajya claiming as an agnate under pre-1956 Hindu law.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'subject to his personal law' in Section 151 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954 refers to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 as amended up to the date of the holder's death
Whether the devolution of a female Hindu's tenancy rights inherited from her husband is governed by the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and in what order heirs succeed
Whether the heirs of the husband under Section 15(2)(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 are determined as of the date of the husband's death or the wife's death
holdings: Section 151 of the MP Land Revenue Code incorporates personal law as amended up to the date of the holder's death, including the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Property inherited by a female Hindu from her husband devolves on the husband's heirs if she dies intestate and without issue, under Section 15(2)(b) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
The heirs of the husband are determined as if the husband died immediately after the wife, so succession is governed by the law in force at the wife's death.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 151
doctrines: Legislation by referential incorporation
Fiction of simultaneous death under Section 16 Rule 3
Devolution of property under personal law as amended

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over possession of disputed land during proceedings under Section 145 of the CrPC, 1898, following a police report.
issues_decided: Whether the finding of the Civil Court on possession under Section 146(1B) of the CrPC, 1898 is final and immune from challenge in revision.
Whether the High Court can interfere with the Magistrate's order passed in conformity with the Civil Court's finding on possession.
Whether the High Court can exercise its power under Article 227 of the Constitution to review the finding of the Civil Court in such proceedings.
holdings: The finding of the Civil Court on possession under Section 146(1B) of the CrPC, 1898 is final and cannot be challenged by appeal, review, or revision due to the express bar in Section 146(1D).
The High Court cannot interfere under Sections 435 or 439 of the CrPC with a Magistrate’s order that conforms to the Civil Court’s finding on possession.
The High Court’s power under Article 227 is limited to ensuring subordinate courts stay within jurisdiction and cannot be used to correct factual errors or re-evaluate evidence in such cases.
doctrines: Finality of findings under statutory bar
Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Doctrine of judicial superintendence under Article 227

card.dispute: The assessee company fought with the State of U.P. over whether it could change its method of computing agricultural income for tax purposes when filing a fresh return under the U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether an assessee is entitled to change its option for computing agricultural income under Section 6(1) of the U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948 when filing a fresh return in response to a notice under Section 15(3)?
Whether a best judgment assessment under Section 16(4) must respect the assessee's earlier option under Section 6(1)?
holdings: An assessee is entitled to change its option for computing agricultural income under Section 6(1) when filing a fresh return in response to a notice under Section 15(3), as the option is not irrevocable if the return is filed within time and in compliance with statutory requirements.

In a best judgment assessment under Section 16(4), the assessing authority must make the assessment with due regard to the provisional estimate under Section 15(3-B), irrespective of any prior option exercised by the assessee under Section 6(1).
provisions: U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 6(1)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 6(2)(a)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 6(2)(b)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 15(3)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 15(3-B)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 16(2)
U.P. Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1948, Section 16(4)
doctrines: Best judgment assessment
Option under taxing statute
Non obstante clause interpretation
Revival of fresh return in tax proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants, J.S. Kalsi and J.S. Nanda, challenged their conviction and sentence for conspiracy and cheating involving forgery of cheques and opening fictitious bank accounts to defraud the government.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of J.S. Kalsi was supported by sufficient corroborative evidence, particularly regarding his role in facilitating the encashment of forged cheques?
Whether the testimony of the approver, Amarjit Singh, could be relied upon without proper corroboration?
Whether procedural irregularities in the investigation, including non-supply of Section 164 CrPC statements and improper pardon procedure, vitiated the trial?
holdings: J.S. Kalsi's participation in the crime was proved beyond reasonable doubt through independent evidence, including bank officials' testimony that he arranged for verification of forged signatures, even though the approver's statement about a cash payment to him lacked corroboration.

The testimony of the approver can be relied upon if corroborated in material particulars by independent evidence linking the accused to the crime, which was satisfied in part by documentary and witness evidence.

Alleged procedural irregularities, including non-supply of Section 164 statements and manner of approver's examination, were not substantiated and did not invalidate the trial, as the accused had access to the statements and the courts below properly evaluated the evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration of approver's testimony
Principle of constructive participation in criminal conspiracy
Presumption of regularity in investigation procedures

card.dispute: The landlord and his transferee fought with the original tenant's sons over whether the latter could reclaim possession of agricultural land after the landlord sold it within twelve years of regaining possession.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant disqualified under Section 88(1A) of the Bombay Tenancy Act still retains the right to regain possession under Section 37(1) if the landlord sells the land within twelve years.
Whether the landlord's sale of the land within twelve years of taking possession triggers the obligation to restore possession under Section 37(1).
Whether the status of a protected tenant is completely extinguished under Section 88(1A), including the right to apply under Section 37(1).
holdings: Section 88(1A) only removes the tenant's rights under Sections 32 and 34 but does not extinguish the tenancy status for the purpose of Section 37(1); the tenant or his legal heirs can still reclaim possession if the landlord fails to use the land as declared.
The landlord's obligation under Section 37(1) to restore possession arises if he ceases to use the land for the declared purpose within twelve years, including by selling it to a third party.
Possession transferred to a purchaser is not deemed the continued possession of the landlord for personal cultivation, thus triggering the tenant's right to regain possession.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 34
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 34(2A)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 37(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88(1A)
doctrines: Conditional restoration of possession
Statutory tenancy rights
Interpretation of tenant disqualification

card.dispute: The Dharmaposhanam Co. Kerala fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax, Kerala over whether income from its chit fund (kuries) and money-lending business was exempt from tax under Section 11(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as being used for charitable purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the business income of the company from kuries and money lending qualifies for exemption under Section 11(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as being applied to charitable purposes
Whether the objects clause of the company, including 'industries' and 'public good', falls within the definition of 'charitable purpose' under Section 2(15) of the Act
Whether amendments to the Memorandum and Articles of Association, replacing 'industries' with 'medical relief', made the income eligible for exemption from the assessment year 1966-67 onwards
holdings: Business can be 'property' under Section 11(1)(a), but exemption depends on whether the purpose is charitable and not involving profit-making activity.

Objects like 'industries' and 'public good' do not qualify as 'charitable purposes' under Section 2(15) if they involve profit-making activities, as they fail the 'not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit' test.

Even after amending its Memorandum to remove 'industries' and add 'medical relief', the company’s object of 'other matters of public good' still falls under a non-charitable, profit-linked residual head, disentitling it to exemption.

The mere application of income to charitable purposes is insufficient for exemption if the trust's objects include non-charitable, profit-oriented activities, and no finding exists that the business itself was held in trust for charity.
doctrines: Charitable purpose must not involve profit-making activity
Entire trust must be for charitable purposes; mixed objects defeat exemption
Exemption under Section 11 depends on the nature of objects in the trust deed, not just actual use of income
Judicial precedent limited to factual matrix of the case (Dharmodayam Co. distinguished)

card.dispute: The appellants, co-sharers in abadi land, appealed against the dismissal of their partition suit, claiming entitlement to partition despite a prior compromise between some parties in an earlier appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to the death of parties and whether delay in substituting legal representatives could be condoned.
Whether the High Court's order of 16th September 1954, based on a partial compromise, amounted to a valid preliminary decree against all defendants, including non-compromising parties.
Whether a final decree for partition could be validly executed against defendants who were not parties to the compromise.
holdings: An appeal does not abate if delay in substituting legal representatives is condoned under Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act, and this Court has power to enlarge time under Order XLV, Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 1950.

A compromise between only some parties cannot result in a decree binding on non-compromising defendants; no preliminary decree was passed against them, rendering the appeal undecided as to those parties.
Proceedings for a final decree based on a compromise not binding on all parties are invalid; no final decree can be passed against non-compromising defendants without a proper preliminary decree.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XVI, Rule 12
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XVI, Rule 13
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XVI, Rule 14
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XVI, Rule 14A
Supreme Court Rules, 1950, Order XLV, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of substitution of parties upon death
Doctrine of condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Principle of non-binding effect of compromise on non-consenting parties
Requirement of a valid preliminary decree before final decree in partition suits

card.dispute: The heirs of the First and Third Baronets fought over the distribution of trust properties after the repeal of the Sir Currimbhoy Ebrahim Baronetcy Act, 1913, and the migration of the Fourth Baronet to Pakistan.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislature had competence to declare trust properties as evacuee property under Section 7(4) of the Repealing Act, 1959
Whether the trust failed on the death of the Third Baronet in 1952, leading to devolution of properties to his heirs
Whether the trust properties falling to the Fourth Baronet became evacuee property and were liable to vest in the Custodian under the Repealing Act
holdings: The State Legislature had the power under Entry 41, List III of the Seventh Schedule to enact Section 7(4) of the Repealing Act, making trust properties evacuee property upon devolution to an evacuee.
The trust did not fail on the death of the Third Baronet; the benefit passed to the Fourth Baronet as the lawful successor.
Trust properties devolving to the Fourth Baronet, an evacuee, became evacuee property and were rightly vested in the Custodian under Section 7(4) of the Repealing Act.
provisions: Sir Currimbhoy Ebrahim Baronetcy (Repealing and Distribution of Trust Properties) Act, 1959, Section 7(4)
Constitution of India, Article 254(2), Entry 41 and Entry 27, List III, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254(2)
Doctrine of vesting of evacuee property

card.dispute: The dispute was between Durgi Devi and others, former landlords, and the State of U.P., over the computation of compensation for forests vested in the state under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation officer must consider the appraised annual yield of forests on the date of vesting while assessing average annual income under Section 39(1)(e)(i) of the Act
Whether a 15% deduction for management expenses under Section 44(c) is permissible from forest income assessed under Section 39(1)(e)
holdings: The compensation officer must consider both the average annual income from past sales and the appraised annual yield on the date of vesting under Section 39(1)(e) to avoid inflated or illusory compensation.
The 15% deduction for management expenses under Section 44(c) does not apply to forest income under Section 39(1)(e), as the deduction is limited to rental and khudkasht land income.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 39(1)(e)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 44
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 34
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutes
Rule of harmonious construction
Avoidance of absurdity in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, who was the son of the original tenant, over arrears of rent in a shop, and the dispute centered on whether the tenant qualified for protection under the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether a member of the family of a deceased tenant residing with him qualifies as a tenant under Section 5(11)(c) of the Bombay Rent Act in case of business premises
Whether the conditions under Section 12(3)(b) of the Act are mandatory or confer discretion on the court to protect a tenant
Whether the High Court can interfere under Articles 226 and 227 with findings of fact and exercise of discretion by a subordinate court
holdings: Section 5(11)(c) of the Bombay Rent Act applies only to residential premises; it does not extend protection to family members of a deceased tenant in respect of business premises.
Section 12(3)(b) does not confer judicial discretion; its conditions must be strictly complied with by the tenant to claim protection against eviction.
The High Court cannot interfere under Articles 226 or 227 with factual findings or discretionary decisions of a subordinate court unless they are perverse or beyond jurisdiction.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(c)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(a)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
doctrines: Strict construction of rent control statutes
No judicial discretion where statute prescribes mandatory conditions
Limits on High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227
Separation of powers: courts cannot legislate or relax statutory conditions

card.dispute: Gopal Singh appealed his conviction and death sentence for the quadruple murder of family members during a land dispute over ancestral property.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Gopal Singh committed the murders?
Whether the time of occurrence being nighttime undermines the prosecution's case?
Whether delays and irregularities in recording the FIR and inquest reports vitiate the conviction?
Whether the death sentence was justified in this case?
holdings: The prosecution established the appellant's guilt through credible eyewitness testimony and motive, despite the absence of direct forensic linkage.
Discrepancies in time of death estimates do not negate the evidence that the murders occurred in broad daylight, as corroborated by witnesses and circumstances.
Procedural delays in FIR registration and inquest reporting do not invalidate the conviction when the overall evidence is reliable and consistent.
The death sentence was justified due to the brutal, premeditated nature of quadruple murder with no mitigating factors.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, Sections 87 and 88
doctrines: Principle of ocular evidence reliability in presence of motive and consistency
Doctrine of benefit of doubt not applicable when evidence is overwhelming
Procedural irregularities not fatal if they do not affect the fairness of trial
Rarest of rare doctrine for awarding death penalty

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of a contract to sell agricultural land, and the defendant resisted, claiming the plaintiff was not an agriculturist and thus barred from purchasing the land under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to decide the question of whether a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance is an agriculturist under Section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the civil court can decide an issue that falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Mamlatdar under Section 70 read with Sections 85 and 85A of the Act.
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide whether a person is an agriculturist under Section 70 of the Act, as this issue falls exclusively within the domain of the Mamlatdar.

When a question arises in a civil suit that is required to be decided by a competent authority under the Act, the civil court must refer it to that authority under Section 85A and cannot decide it itself.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 63
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85A
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Reference to statutory authority as mandatory
Exclusive jurisdiction of revenue authorities

card.dispute: The heirs of a former intermediary (Harbans Kumari and others) challenged the High Court's computation of compensation for forests vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh under land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the average annual income for forest compensation under Section 39(1)(e) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 must be computed by considering both the historical income and the appraised yield on the date of vesting.
Whether the High Court erred in calculating the average annual income by giving weight to both clauses (i) and (ii) of Section 39(1)(e).
holdings: The word 'average' in Section 39(1)(e) requires consideration of both the historical income and the appraised annual yield on the date of vesting; neither factor can be ignored.

The compensation officer must compute average annual income by giving due weight to both clauses (i) and (ii) of Section 39(1)(e), as they together ensure a fair and realistic assessment linked to the forest’s actual value at vesting.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 39(1)(e)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction
Principle of fair compensation

card.dispute: The appellant sought restoration of possession of immovable property under Section 456(2) Cr.P.C. after the appellate court had disposed of the appeal, which the High Court set aside holding that the power to order restoration must be exercised only 'while disposing of' the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the Court of appeal, confirmation, or revision has the power to order restoration of possession under Section 456(2) Cr.P.C. after the appeal, reference, or revision has been disposed of?
What is the correct interpretation of the phrase 'while disposing of the appeal, reference or revision' in Section 456(2) Cr.P.C.?
holdings: The appellate or revisional court has the power under Section 456(2) Cr.P.C. to order restoration of possession at any time after the trial court's failure to do so, provided it is exercised within a reasonable time of disposing of the appeal, reference, or revision.

The phrase 'while disposing of the appeal, reference or revision' does not require the order for restoration to be passed simultaneously with the judgment; it allows the court to exercise its discretion to pass such an order in continuation of the disposal process.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to resolve ambiguity
Discretionary power of appellate/revisional courts
Legislative intent based on Law Commission recommendations

card.dispute: The appellant, Guruswamy, challenged his conviction and death sentence for the murder of his father and brother, claiming private defence, while the prosecution alleged premeditated murder during a family dispute over property.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution case, based on eyewitness testimony, was reliable despite alleged inconsistencies in the FIR and non-mention of a witness therein.
Whether the defence of private defence was credible and sufficient to absolve the appellant of murder charges.
Whether the death sentence was appropriate in the circumstances of the case.
holdings: The discrepancies in the time and place of FIR recording by an illiterate witness do not undermine its credibility if the report was otherwise prompt and consistent.
The defence of private defence was improbable and rightly rejected where the accused attacked two unarmed family members with a deadly weapon without provocation.
The death sentence may be commuted to life imprisonment in family murder cases, and the court may impose a compensatory fine payable to the victim's dependants if the accused has the capacity to pay.
doctrines: Private defence
Credibility of eyewitness testimony
Compensatory justice in criminal sentencing

card.dispute: The respondent trust sued the appellant for possession of two lands, alleging he was a trespasser, while the appellant claimed he was a tenant or deemed tenant of the lands.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was in possession of the suit lands as a tenant of the respondent trust.
Whether a sub-tenant can be deemed a tenant under Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 in interfering with the concurrent findings of revenue authorities.
holdings: The appellant was not a tenant of the respondent but a sub-tenant under Pandharinath Vale, and thus not entitled to protection as a tenant under the Act.
A sub-tenant cannot be deemed a tenant under Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy Act because sub-letting is prohibited under Section 27 and renders cultivation unlawful.
The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction under Article 227 in setting aside the revenue authorities' findings, which lacked evidentiary support.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14(1)(a)(iii)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 27
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 31
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-G
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85-A
doctrines: Limitation of High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Prohibition of sub-tenancy under tenancy laws
Requirement of lawful cultivation for deemed tenancy

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Jagdish Chander challenged the decree of specific performance granted to Brij Mohan and others, who claimed the right to repurchase land based on a prior agreement between the original seller and Jagdish Chander.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs (respondents) had a validly assigned right to repurchase the land, given a prior sale of the same right to another party.
Whether the transfer violated Section 154 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, due to landholding limits.
holdings: The right to repurchase vested in the plaintiffs, not in the earlier transferees, because the prior sale was found to be a sham and the transferees had relinquished their interest.
Section 154 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 did not apply because the plaintiffs did not hold land exceeding the statutory ceiling of 12½ or 30 acres.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 154
doctrines: Finality of findings of fact in appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution
Non-liquet on judicial discretion in specific performance where statutory bar does not apply

card.dispute: The appellant Keshoram Gora was prosecuted for murder, claiming he acted in private defence, while the State alleged he murdered the deceased during a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the Sessions Judge erred in relying on the evidence of hostile prosecution witnesses as representing the prosecution's case.
Whether the High Court was justified in convicting the appellant despite contradictions in the prosecution's evidence.
Whether the inculpatory part of the accused's statement can be accepted while rejecting the exculpatory part.
Whether the accused exceeded the right of private defence under Section 99 IPC.
holdings: A Sessions Judge cannot treat the evidence of declared hostile witnesses as the official version of the prosecution, as the prosecution has disavowed reliance on them.
The principle of 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' does not apply rigidly in criminal cases; courts must sift truthful evidence from false, even if parts of the prosecution case are unreliable.
Where an admission or confession is separable, the court may accept the inculpatory part and reject the exculpatory part if unsupported by evidence.
The accused exceeded the right of private defence as neither he nor his brother sustained injuries, indicating the use of disproportionate force.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus (with qualification for criminal trials)
Right of private defence under IPC
Separability of inculpatory and exculpatory statements
Evaluation of evidence of hostile witnesses

card.dispute: The worker Lalla Ram challenged the management's dismissal order and the Industrial Tribunal's refusal to approve it under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether the Industrial Tribunal acted within its jurisdiction in refusing approval to the dismissal order under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Whether the domestic enquiry was conducted fairly and in accordance with principles of natural justice.
Whether there was a prima facie case of misconduct justifying dismissal based on legal evidence.
Whether the punishment of dismissal amounted to victimisation or unfair labour practice.
holdings: The Industrial Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction by acting as an appellate authority and could not reject the domestic enquiry findings unless they were perverse or unsupported by legal evidence.
A domestic enquiry conducted in accordance with standing orders and natural justice, with no bias, satisfies procedural requirements for approval under Section 33(2)(b).
A prima facie case for dismissal exists if the misconduct is connected to employment duties and supported by legal evidence, even if punishment appears severe.
Mere severity of punishment does not imply victimisation; mala fides must be inferred from procedural unfairness or disproportionate penalty in absence of justification.
doctrines: Limited scope of judicial review under Section 33(2)(b)
Principles of natural justice in domestic enquiries
Perversity test for overturning domestic enquiry findings
Management's discretion in awarding punishment unless mala fide

card.dispute: The appellant, Lakshmi Ammal, sought partition and separate possession of her share in suit properties, while respondents challenged the adequacy of court fee paid.
issues_decided: Whether the correct court fee was paid under the applicable court fee legislation for a suit seeking partition?
Whether a court should prioritize adjudicating real disputes over technical objections like court fee?
holdings: The court fee payable in a partition suit is determined by Section 37(2) of the Madras Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, corresponding to Article 17-D of the Central Court Fees and Suit Valuation Act, where the plaintiff seeks separate possession of her share.
Courts must prioritize resolving substantive disputes and, where there is reasonable doubt, construe court fee requirements liberally to ensure access to justice.
provisions: Court Fees and Suit Valuation Act (Central Act), Article 17-D
Madras Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, Section 37(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rules 1(i) and 11(b)
doctrines: Liberal construction of court fee laws to ensure access to justice
Primacy of real issues over technical objections in litigation

card.dispute: The appellants, Kailash and Ram Sunder, challenged their conviction for the murder of Mahraji, an elderly woman, arguing that the evidence was insufficient and circumstantial.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt in a circumstantial evidence case.
Whether the appellants' escape from the scene despite villagers being present weakens the prosecution's case.
Whether the offence should be punished under Section 302 or Section 304 Part II of the Penal Code.
holdings: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence is valid if the chain of circumstances is complete and excludes the possibility of guilt of any other person.

The failure of unarmed villagers to prevent the appellants’ escape does not undermine the prosecution case, especially given the appellants were armed and the villagers had no personal stake in the victim’s safety.

The intentional and forceful strangulation of a 70-year-old woman, resulting in hyoid bone fracture and asphyxia, constitutes murder under Section 302, not the lesser offence under Section 304 Part II.
doctrines: Principle of complete chain of circumstantial evidence
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Distinction between murder and culpable homicide not amounting to murder

card.dispute: The Mahant of a Hindu religious trust challenged the constitutional validity of a provision in the Orissa Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1947, claiming it discriminated against non-Muslim public trusts by granting more favourable tax exemptions to Muslim wakfs.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8(1) of the Orissa Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1947, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by discriminating between Hindu and Muslim religious trusts?
Whether Section 9 of the Act grants broader tax exemption to all Muslim wakfs compared to non-Muslim public charitable trusts under Section 8(1)?
Whether the classification between types of wakfs under the Act is constitutionally valid?
holdings: Section 8(1) does not violate Article 14 as it applies equally to public charitable or religious trusts, and the exemption is limited to income actually spent for such purposes.
Section 9 applies only to wakf-alal-aulad (private Muslim family wakfs) and not to all Muslim wakfs, and its exemption is justified by the unique legal and historical context of such wakfs.

The distinction between public trusts under Section 8(1) and private wakfs under Section 9 is based on intelligible differentia and has a rational relation to the object of the Act, hence it does not amount to discrimination.
provisions: Orissa Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1947, Section 8(1)
Orissa Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1947, Section 9
Orissa Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1947, Section 16
doctrines: Equal protection under Article 14
Classification test for equality
Doctrine of intelligible differentia
Doctrine of harmonious construction

card.dispute: The appellant lessee claimed an easement of way and flow of water over his landlord's adjacent land, which the landlord contested.
issues_decided: Whether a lessee can acquire an easement by prescription over the lessor's other land during the lease period.
Whether a lessee can tack the period of possession as a tenant to the period after becoming the owner to claim prescriptive easement.
holdings: A lessee cannot acquire an easement by prescription over the lessor's land for his own benefit as he is not the owner and lacks the legal capacity under Section 12 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882.
A lessee cannot tack the period of enjoyment as a tenant to the period after acquiring ownership to claim a prescriptive easement over the former landlord's land.
doctrines: Easement by prescription
Tacking of possession
Lessee's incapacity to acquire easement against lessor

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu appealed the acquittal of 27 accused by the Sessions Court in a case involving murder, assault, and property damage; the High Court convicted them, and the accused appealed to the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution evidence, particularly eyewitness testimony, was reliable and consistent enough to sustain convictions under Sections 302/34 and 302/149 IPC.
Whether the accused could be convicted under Section 149 IPC for specific assaults committed by individuals during a large unlawful assembly.
Whether convictions for property damage under Section 427/34 IPC were supported by credible evidence.
Whether contradictions in witness statements and delayed identification affected the benefit of doubt entitlement.
holdings: Convictions under Section 302/34 IPC were confirmed for accused 1, 2, 4, and 5, but set aside for accused 3, 6, 7, and 19 due to inconsistent and improved evidence and lack of early corroboration.

Convictions under Section 149 IPC for individual assaults under various charges were set aside as the acts were not in furtherance of a common object and knowledge of such acts could not be imputed to all members of the assembly.
Conviction under Section 427/34 IPC was upheld for accused 2, 3, 8, and 9 based on credible eyewitness testimony and material evidence, but set aside for others due to lack of reliable evidence.

The benefit of doubt must be given where there are material contradictions in evidence, especially in delayed or improved identification, and the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Common object under Section 149 IPC
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Improvement in testimony as a factor for doubt
Principle of concurrent sentences

card.dispute: The appellants, sons of a displaced person, claimed ejectment of a tenant by asserting they were small landowners under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, but the respondents argued their landholding exceeded permissible limits.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, as heirs of a displaced person, are entitled to the enhanced permissible area under proviso (ii) of Section 2(3) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
Whether Banjar and Gair Mumkin land should be excluded in computing the permissible area under the Act
holdings: The enhanced permissible area under proviso (ii) of Section 2(3) is not available to heirs of a displaced person; it applies only to the displaced person themselves, not successors to whom land is allotted.

Banjar Qadim, Banjar Jadid, and Gair Mumkin lands, not being used for agriculture or allied purposes, fall outside the definition of 'land' and must be excluded when computing permissible area under the Act.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(3)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(8)
East Punjab Displaced Persons (Land Resettlement) Act, 1949
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Exclusion of non-agricultural uncultivated land from landholding calculations

card.dispute: The Mangalore Electric Supply Co. Ltd. contested whether compensation received for the compulsory acquisition of its undertaking constituted a 'transfer' of a capital asset liable to capital gains tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'transfer' in Section 12B(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 includes compulsory acquisition of a capital asset.
Whether part of the compensation received could be attributed to goodwill and thus excluded from capital gains.
holdings: The word 'transfer' in Section 12B(1) includes both voluntary and involuntary transfers, such as compulsory acquisition under law, and results in capital gains if there is extinguishment of an existing title and creation of a new one.

The claim that part of the compensation was attributable to goodwill could not be accepted as no evidence was presented before the authorities to establish the value of goodwill or its separate recognition in the acquisition.
doctrines: Ejusdem generis
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Mixed question of law and fact
