card.dispute: The landlords appealed against the dismissal of their eviction suit, arguing that the tenant's irregular rent payments during the appeal did not comply with the mandatory requirements of Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement in Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act to pay or tender rent 'regularly' during the pendency of a suit or appeal is mandatory or directory.
Whether irregular payments made at intervals of two to four months constitute 'regular' payment under Section 12(3)(b).
holdings: The provisions of Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act are mandatory and must be strictly complied with; the court has no discretion to treat irregular payments as substantial compliance.
The term 'regularly' requires payment at intervals reasonably close to when rent falls due; payments at 2–4 month intervals do not meet this standard, even if arrears are cleared by judgment.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)(b)
doctrines: Strict construction of tenant protection provisions when they limit landlord rights
No judicial discretion to relax mandatory statutory conditions for eviction protection

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether the appeal, filed after the liberation of Goa, Daman and Diu, was governed by the limitation period under the Portuguese Civil Procedure Code or the Indian Limitation Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal was filed in the proper forum under the applicable procedural law after the extension of the Indian Civil Procedure Code to Goa, Daman and Diu.
What law of limitation applied to an appeal filed in respect of a suit pending prior to the liberation of Goa, Daman and Diu—Portuguese Code or the Indian Limitation Act, 1963?
holdings: The right of appeal being substantive vests when the suit is filed, but the forum for appeal is procedural and governed by the repealing enactment; thus, the appeal lay to the Judicial Commissioner's Court under the Indian Civil Procedure Code as extended by Central Act XXX of 1965.

Where a complex and doubtful question of applicable limitation law exists, a party's bona fide belief in the applicability of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, and consequent delay in filing, constitutes sufficient cause for condonation of delay under Article 145 of the Portuguese Code.
provisions: Goa, Daman and Diu (Extension of CPC 1908 and Arbitration Act, 1940) Act, 1965 (Central Act XXX of 1965)
Goa, Daman & Diu Civil Court Act, 1965 (Goa Act XVI of 1965)
Portuguese Civil Procedure Code, Article 637 and Article 145
doctrines: Substantive vs. procedural law distinction
Savings of vested rights and remedies under repealing statutes
Condonation of delay for sufficient cause
Bona fide belief in applicable law as just impediment

card.dispute: The intermediary claimed entitlement to retain land with bamboo and banana plantations as 'orchards' under the West Bengal Estate Acquisition Act, 1954, which the state contested.
issues_decided: Whether a bamboo garden falls within the meaning of 'orchard' under Section 6(1)(f) of the West Bengal Estate Acquisition Act, 1954.
Whether a banana plantation qualifies as an 'orchard' under the same provision.
holdings: A bamboo garden, though agricultural land, does not constitute an 'orchard' under Section 6(1)(f) because it lacks fruit-bearing trees on a compact area as required by law.
A banana plant is not a 'tree' as it is not perennial and has a herbaceous, not woody, stem; thus, a banana plantation cannot be considered an 'orchard' under the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Estate Acquisition Act, 1954, Section 2(p), Section 6(1)(f)
West Bengal Land Reforms Act, Section 14K(e)
doctrines: Interpretation of undefined statutory terms by reference to related statutes and dictionaries
Botanical and legal distinction between trees and herbaceous plants in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The plaintiff claimed permanent tenancy rights over land and challenged the Official Receiver's possession after purchasing structures in an auction, arguing that only the structures, not the land or tenancy rights, were sold.
issues_decided: Whether the sale in execution of the decree included the permanent tenancy rights in the land or only the structures.
Whether the Official Receiver was entitled to possession of the land underlying the structures.
holdings: The sale in execution of the decree transferred only the materials of the structures, not the underlying land or permanent tenancy rights appurtenant to them.
The purchaser’s right is limited to what the court intended to sell, and mere attachment or purchase does not confer title to land where tenancy rights were disputed and not adjudicated.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 54
doctrines: Intention of the court in execution sales
Doctrine of lis pendens
Principle of limited sale in execution

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the rejection of his delayed application for reference to court to determine compensation, after the Collector had refused to forward his review request and he filed under Section 14 of the Hyderabad Land Acquisition Act over four months past the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether a court can examine the timeliness of an application for reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (or its equivalent) when the Collector has made a reference without determining limitation.
Whether the fulfilment of conditions under Section 18, including the limitation period, is a prerequisite to the Collector's power to make a reference.
holdings: A court must determine whether a reference under Section 18 is valid, including whether the application was made within the prescribed time, as jurisdiction depends on compliance with statutory conditions.

The conditions in Section 18, especially the limitation period, are mandatory and constitute a condition precedent to the Collector’s power to make a reference; non-compliance renders the reference invalid.
doctrines: Condition precedent to jurisdiction
Tribunal of limited jurisdiction
Statutory compliance for jurisdictional validity

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Poona and industrialists, including Bijlee Products (India) Ltd., disputed whether the government's repeal of an octroi exemption rule took away vested rights granted to industries that had set up operations based on assurances of tax exemption.
issues_decided: Whether the Government's resolution dated 30-7-1968, repealing Rule 5(8) of the octroi rules, impliedly retained the exemption already granted to industrialists.
Whether the Government, while sanctioning the repeal, could unilaterally withdraw vested rights without referring the matter back to the Corporation for reconsideration.
Whether the repeal of the rule without preserving existing exemptions would amount to retrospective withdrawal of a vested right.
holdings: The Government's resolution must be interpreted as including the proviso that existing exemptions continue, based on the context and materials before it, despite not stating so explicitly.

The Government cannot modify a municipal recommendation in a way that affects vested rights without referring it back to the Corporation, especially when such modification extends taxation to previously exempt areas.
A statutory amendment affecting individual rights is presumed to be prospective unless clearly made retrospective, and thus the repeal did not abrogate prior exemptions.
provisions: Bombay Provisional Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 127(1), (2), (3)
Bombay Provisional Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 149
Bombay Provisional Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, Section 455(1)
doctrines: Presumption against retrospective operation of statutes
Doctrine of reading down statutory provisions to preserve vested rights
Principle of harmonious construction with reference to government's intent and administrative materials

card.dispute: The appellants sought possession of land from the respondent, who claimed to be a protected tenant under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, raising questions about the jurisdiction of civil courts versus revenue tribunals.
issues_decided: Whether the jurisdiction of the civil court is barred by the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 when a defendant claims tenancy protection in a suit for possession.
Whether the provisions of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, particularly Sections 132, 133, and 142(IA), exclude civil court jurisdiction in pending proceedings.
Whether the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 applies to proceedings under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act.
holdings: The jurisdiction of the civil court is not automatically barred when a defendant claims to be a tenant; the court must first determine whether the claim falls within the exclusive purview of the Revenue Tribunal.

Sections 132 and 133 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act do not oust civil court jurisdiction entirely but require reference to the Tribunal only on specific tenancy issues, after which the civil court may proceed.

The doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act remains applicable unless there is an express or implied exclusion by statute, which is not present in the Karnataka Land Reforms Act.
provisions: Mysore Tenants (Temporary Protection from Eviction) Act, 1961, Section 4(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 54, Order XX Rule 18, Order XXI Rule 35
doctrines: Exclusion of civil jurisdiction only by express or necessary implication
Doctrine of lis pendens
Concurrent jurisdiction of civil courts and revenue tribunals in tenancy matters

card.dispute: Agriculturist debtors challenged the constitutional validity of the Kerala Agriculturists' Debt Relief Act, 1970, particularly Section 20, which allowed them to reclaim properties sold in execution of debt decrees, while purchasers and decree-holders claimed it violated their fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20 of the Kerala Agriculturists' Debt Relief Act, 1970 violates Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution by restricting the right to hold property acquired in court auctions
Whether Section 20 is void for being unreasonable under Article 19(5)
Whether Section 20 violates Article 14 by creating arbitrary classifications between decree-holder purchasers, other purchasers, and bona fide alienees
holdings: The restriction under Section 20 on the right to property is saved by Article 19(5) as it imposes reasonable restrictions in the interest of the general public, particularly indebted agriculturists.

The differential treatment under Section 20 is reasonable and justified, as decree-holders purchasing at auction are a distinct class often viewed with suspicion, warranting stricter conditions for property retention.

The classification between auction purchasers and bona fide alienees who acquired property before the Bill's publication is valid, as the latter could not have anticipated the law and thus deserve protection.
provisions: Kerala Agriculturists' Debt Relief Act, 1970, Section 20
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 72
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5)
Classification test under Article 14
Liberal construction of constitutional and legislative provisions
Protection of bona fide purchasers

card.dispute: The appellant Ram Adhar challenged his conviction and death sentence for the murder of his uncle Phool Chand, claiming false implication due to a property dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was falsely implicated in the murder case due to enmity arising from property disputes?
Whether the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, alleged to be interested, could be relied upon?
Whether the delay of six years in deciding the appeal warranted commutation of the death sentence?
holdings: The motive for the murder arose from the appellant's objection to the victim's gift deed and mutation proceedings, making the appellant more likely to commit the crime rather than being falsely implicated.
The testimony of the four eyewitnesses, including family members and independent witnesses, was consistent and credible, and could not be discarded merely on grounds of alleged interest.
Due to the unexplained delay of six years in the disposal of the appeal, the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment, though the conviction was upheld.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of delay in capital punishment
Reliability of interested witnesses if testimony is consistent and unshaken
Appreciation of motive in murder cases

card.dispute: The appellant (Raghunath Pradhani) challenged the validity of a court auction sale of Scheduled Tribe property, claiming his prior private purchase of the property was valid and that the auction sale violated statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the attachment and auction sale of Scheduled Tribe property without prior permission under Orissa Regulation 2 of 1956 is void
Whether the doctrine of res judicata bars the appellant from challenging the auction sale
Whether the auction sale could convey title when the judgment-debtor had already sold the property privately with required permission
holdings: Attachment or sale of immovable property belonging to a member of a Scheduled Tribe is void unless made with prior permission of the competent authority under Orissa Regulation 2 of 1956.
The failure to raise a contention in earlier proceedings does not operate as res judicata, constructively or otherwise, when the party was not bound to raise it at that stage.
A judgment-debtor’s private sale of property with valid permission vests title in the purchaser, leaving no saleable interest for a subsequent court auction.
provisions: Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property by Scheduled Tribes Regulation 2 of 1956, Clause 6
Rule 4 of the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property by Scheduled Tribes Regulation 2 of 1956
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 89 and 90
doctrines: Res judicata (constructive and actual)
Void attachment for non-compliance with statutory conditions
Priority of title based on valid private sale with statutory permission

card.dispute: The appellants, directors of a quarry company, challenged the maintainability of criminal proceedings for failing to employ a qualified geologist, arguing that the 'Shahabad Stones' they extracted were minor minerals exempt from the applicable rules.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court should have quashed the criminal proceedings at the interlocutory stage under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on the ground that 'Shahabad Stones' are minor minerals excluded from the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1958.
Whether the Supreme Court should intervene under Article 136 of the Constitution at the threshold of the case without evidence on the nature and use of the extracted minerals.
holdings: The High Court rightly declined to interfere under Section 482 CrPC at an interlocutory stage, as the question of whether 'Shahabad Stones' are minor or major minerals requires factual determination based on evidence of their use.

The Supreme Court should not exercise its discretionary power under Article 136 at the initial stage of proceedings where complex factual issues, such as the classification of minerals, remain unresolved and require evidentiary assessment.
provisions: Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 1958, Rule 21(1)(ii) and Rule 27
Andhra Pradesh Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1966, Rule 10, Schedule I, Item 15
doctrines: Non-interference at interlocutory stages by higher courts
Exercise of extraordinary jurisdiction only in exceptional circumstances
Requirement of evidence for classification of minerals

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Ram Rattan (deceased) sued to declare his right to a rotational worship (Osra) in a temple based on a will, which the defendants challenged as inadmissible due to lack of registration and proper stamping.
issues_decided: Whether the Trial Court was obligated to decide the preliminary objection regarding the admissibility of the document for want of registration and proper stamping at the time of evidence recording.
Whether the hereditary office of Shebait, including a rotational right of worship (Osra), constitutes immovable property under Hindu law.
Whether a deed gifting a right to rotational worship requires compulsory registration under the Registration Act.
holdings: The Trial Court is obligated to decide promptly any preliminary objection to the admissibility of a document on grounds of stamping or registration, rather than deferring the decision.
The hereditary office of Shebait, including rights to rotational worship such as 'Osra', is immovable property under Hindu law, as recognized by ancient texts and consistent judicial precedent.
A deed transferring a right to rotational worship, being a gift of immovable property, must be registered to be admissible in evidence; unregistered documents are inadmissible.
doctrines: Hindu law recognition of hereditary offices as immovable property
Doctrine of admissibility of documents under stamp and registration laws
Judicial duty to rule on preliminary objections promptly

card.dispute: An advocate was convicted of criminal contempt for publishing a pamphlet criticizing a magistrate's judgment, and he appealed the conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the pamphlet constituted fair comment under Section 5 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Whether the publication substantially interfered with the administration of justice under Section 13
Whether the sentence imposed was appropriate in the circumstances
holdings: Criticism that imputes improper motives or a pre-judged mind to a judge does not qualify as fair comment under Section 5, as it undermines public confidence in the judiciary.
In rural, illiterate settings, such criticism is more likely to substantially interfere with the administration of justice, satisfying the threshold under Section 13.
While the conviction for contempt was justified, the sentence was excessive; a token fine of Re. 1/- was appropriate to uphold judicial authority without stifling legitimate critique.
doctrines: Fair comment in judicial criticism
Substantial interference with administration of justice
Balancing freedom of speech and judicial dignity

card.dispute: The appellants claimed a refund of Rs. 35,000 paid to the State for removing timber under a forest contract, arguing that their title to the trees was complete before the estate vested in the State under the Abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the forest contract dated 15th March 1951 transferred ownership of the trees to the contractor before the estate vested in the State on 31st March 1951
Whether the payment of Rs. 35,000 to the proprietor (second respondent) before vesting was proved and could bar the State's claim
Whether the State's permission to remove timber on payment of Rs. 35,000 constituted ratification of the prior contract or created a new obligation
holdings: Ownership of trees under a forest contract does not pass until they are felled and ascertained in compliance with contract terms; since this was not done before vesting, the property remained part of the estate and vested in the State.
The claim that Rs. 35,000 was paid to the proprietor before vesting was not credible due to lack of evidence, non-examination of the appellant, and improbability given the circumstances.
The State’s conditional permission to remove timber after vesting was not ratification but a new administrative act; payment made under it is not refundable as it discharged a lawful obligation.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 6
doctrines: Vesting of proprietary rights in the State extinguishes prior unperfected claims
Title to goods under a sale contract does not pass without ascertained goods and delivery
Estoppel by conduct does not apply where there is no valid prior right

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murdering four persons in a land dispute, challenged the death sentence awarded to them, seeking commutation on grounds of private defence of property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to the benefit of private defence of property under Exception II to Section 300 IPC?
Whether the death sentence should be commuted to life imprisonment given the circumstances of the case?
holdings: The appellants had a right to private defence of property, but the force used was recklessly excessive, so they were not entitled to the exception under Section 300 IPC.
Considering the circumstances, including the appellants' possession of the land and the aggressive, armed approach of the deceased, the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Proportionality of force in self-defence
Commutation of death sentence in light of mitigating circumstances

card.dispute: The dispute was between displaced persons over the allotment of land previously given to one party, where the government re-allotted part of the land to others without cancelling the original allotment.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent had an enforceable right in the land allotted to him under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954
Whether the land could be re-allotted to others without cancelling the original allotment and without affording the original allottee a hearing
holdings: The respondent had an enforceable proprietary right in the land due to a valid permanent allotment made in his favour, which could not be disregarded.

Re-allotment of land already allotted to a displaced person without cancelling the original allotment and without giving the allottee a reasonable opportunity of being heard is illegal and violates statutory safeguards.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 19
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 102
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 67A
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 72(2)
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Enforceability of statutory allotment rights
Illegality of administrative action violating statutory procedure

card.dispute: Sadhu Singh appealed his conviction and death sentence for the murders of Shyama Devi and Randhir Singh, challenging the reliability of the prosecution's evidence, particularly the First Information Report and child witness testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the First Information Report (FIR) was credible despite being lodged 2.5 hours after the incident and allegedly drafted by an adult on behalf of a 13-year-old girl.
Whether the testimony of Deomani, a 13-year-old eyewitness, was reliable and free from tutoring or fabrication.
Whether the appellant Sadhu Singh was rightly convicted under Section 302 IPC for the murders.
Whether the death sentence imposed on the appellant was appropriate.
holdings: An FIR lodged 2.5 hours after the incident is credible if there is no opportunity for confabulation, especially when supported by contemporaneous police diary entries.

The testimony of a child witness, even if detailed and articulate, can be reliable if it demonstrates naturalness, consistency, and a capacity for observation, and withstands rigorous cross-examination.
The appellant was rightly convicted under Section 302 IPC as the evidence, particularly the eyewitness account, conclusively established his guilt in the murders.
The death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment considering the appellant's prolonged time under sentence and possible instigation by his father.
doctrines: Credibility of First Information Report
Reliability of child witness testimony
Benefit of doubt in criminal conviction
Principle of commutation of death sentence

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of both the structures and the land beneath them after purchasing them in a court-ordered sale, while Kumud Bala Dasi, the original owner, contested that only the structures were sold, not the land or her permanent tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the sale in execution of the decree included the permanent tenancy rights in the land or only the structures standing on it.
What was the true nature of the right, title, and interest intended to be sold in the execution proceedings.
holdings: The sale in execution of a decree must be determined by what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser understood they were buying; any misapprehension does not alter the legal effect of the sale.

In this case, only the materials of the structures were intended to be sold, not the underlying land or the permanent tenancy rights, as evidenced by the schedule of property, the decree holder's application, and the low sale price.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 94
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 54
doctrines: Intention of the court and purchaser governs the scope of execution sale
Principle of factual and mixed law determination in execution proceedings
Doctrine of lis pendens implied by pending litigation affecting property rights

card.dispute: The appellant, Rani Ratnesh Kumari, claimed a continuing right to 'malikana' payments from 133 biswadari villages after the abolition of zamindari, while the State denied it, asserting her interest had been extinguished under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the taluqdar was an 'intermediary' under Section 3(12) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, in respect of the 133 biswadari villages
Whether the taluqdar's interest in the biswadari villages was extinguished by the 'malikana' arrangement
Whether the 'malikana' was a pensionary benefit or a revenue-based right connected to land
holdings: A taluqdar receiving 'malikana' from biswadari villages, tied to land revenue and recorded as proprietor in revenue records, is an 'intermediary' under the Act.
The 'malikana' arrangement did not extinguish the taluqdar's proprietary interest; it was a share in revenue, not a pension.
Payments linked to land revenue and varying with it constitute a right in land, not a pension, and thus fall within the Act's abolition scheme.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(12)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(8)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 27
doctrines: Definition of intermediary based on proprietary interest and revenue connection
Continuity of proprietary status despite limited management rights
Distinction between pension and revenue-based allowances

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the dismissal of his Letters Patent Appeal as barred by limitation, after the Calcutta High Court quashed the allotment of requisitioned premises in his favour.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to exclude the period between his application for a certified copy of the judgment and its receipt while computing the limitation for filing the Letters Patent Appeal.
Whether the appellant was guilty of laches or undue delay in filing the appeal.
holdings: A party is entitled to exclusion of time taken to obtain a certified copy if the delay is reasonable and due to administrative processes, especially when the party is in personam.
A rule of practice regarding certified copies cannot be treated as a rule of limitation; courts must independently assess whether there was laches or undue delay.
provisions: Letters Patent of the High Court of Calcutta
doctrines: Laches and delay
Rule of practice vs. rule of limitation

card.dispute: The appellants, who were close relatives of the deceased, were convicted of murder under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC for killing the deceased during a family dispute over water rights, and they challenged the conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the injuries caused were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, thereby attracting Section 300 IPC?
Whether the common object of the unlawful assembly was to cause death, justifying conviction under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC?
Whether compensation can be awarded to the dependants of the deceased under Section 357(3) CrPC even when fine is not part of the sentence?
holdings: If an injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the offence falls under Section 300 IPC, clause (iii), punishable under Section 302 IPC.

To convict under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC, the prosecution must prove that the offence was committed in prosecution of the common object to cause death; mere presence in an unlawful assembly is not sufficient.
Under Section 357(3) CrPC, a court may direct the accused to pay compensation to the victim's dependants even when a fine is not part of the sentence, provided the accused has the capacity to pay.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 300 read with Section 149
doctrines: Common object of unlawful assembly
Presumption of intention to cause death under Section 300 IPC
Compensation to victims' families as part of criminal sentencing

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed the acquittal of Salim Zia, who was accused of murdering Habib by firing upon him during a dispute over paddy harvesting, with Zia claiming self-defence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reversing the Sessions Judge's order of acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 302 IPC and Section 27 of the Arms Act
Whether the appellant successfully established the right of private defence of person or property
Whether the burden of proof for private defence was discharged by a preponderance of probabilities
holdings: The High Court did not act with material irregularity in reversing the acquittal, as it properly considered the entire evidence and was justified in rejecting the appellant's uncorroborated defence.
The appellant failed to prove the right of private defence of person or property, as there was no credible evidence that the deceased had fired first or committed theft.

The burden on an accused to prove private defence requires only a preponderance of probabilities, but this burden must be met through credible evidence or cross-examination, which the appellant failed to do.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Right of private defence under IPC
Standard of preponderance of probabilities for accused in criminal cases
Principles for appellate review of acquittal

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the municipal tax levied on huts built by tenants on leased land, arguing he could not recover the tax from tenants due to rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951 allows recovery of municipal rates from tenants for huts they own on leased land.
Whether the Thika Tenancy Act bars such recovery by landlords.
Whether Section 202 violates Article 14 by treating basti owners differently.
holdings: Section 202 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951 is a self-contained code allowing the owner to recover rates attributable to tenant-owned huts.
The Thika Tenancy Act, which governs rent, does not bar recovery of municipal rates under Section 202, as rates and rent are distinct.
Section 202 does not violate Article 14, as basti dwellers form a distinct class and the provision addresses a real social condition without arbitrary discrimination.
doctrines: Self-contained statutory provision
Special law prevails over general law
Classification under Article 14

card.dispute: The dispute was between an intermediary who became a bhumidar and tenants of sir over whether the tenants were adhivas or asamis under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and thus whether the plaintiff could recover possession.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant of sir recorded as an occupant in the khasra or khatauni of 1356 F. becomes an adhivasi under Section 20(b)(i) or an asami under Section 21(h) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether a tenant of sir not in actual possession but recorded as such is entitled to adhivasi status over an actual occupant recorded in the revenue records.
holdings: A tenant of sir who is recorded as an occupant in the khasra or khatauni of 1356 F. becomes an adhivasi under Section 20(b)(i), and if the conditions of Section 21(h) are met, may be deemed an asami, not entitled to adhivasi rights.

The statute prefers actual possessors (tillers of the soil) over intermediaries; thus, an occupant in actual possession is given adhivasi status in preference to a tenant of sir not in possession, to fulfill the Act’s object of eliminating intermediaries.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 21
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 157
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative intent to eliminate intermediaries
Doctrine of preferring actual possession in land reform statutes
Rule of harmonious construction in statutory interpretation
Preference for constructions that advance the object of social welfare legislation

card.dispute: The municipality sued the property owner for unpaid holding and latrine taxes, claiming the old assessment remained valid despite a quinquennial revision under the Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, from which the property was excluded.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement under Section 106 of the Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, to revise valuation and assessment lists every five years is mandatory or directory.
Whether the exclusion of a holding from quinquennial revision causes the previous assessment to lapse.
holdings: The word 'ordinarily' in Section 106(1) makes the requirement to revise assessments every five years directory, not mandatory, allowing exceptions for good reasons.
Where a holding is excluded from quinquennial revision, the previous valuation and assessment do not lapse but remain in force until a new list is completed and takes effect.
provisions: Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, Section 106
Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, Section 102
Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, Section 107
Bihar and Orissa Municipality Act, 1922, Section 115
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation
Continuity of assessment in absence of valid revision
Res judicata and waiver of new legal pleas in appeal

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Sher Singh fought against the Joint Director of Consolidation and others over whether Sher Singh validly acquired bhumidhari rights in certain land under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether Sher Singh, as a hereditary tenant, was entitled to become a sirdar and subsequently acquire bhumidhari rights under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide suits for ejectment and cancellation of lease prior to the vesting of land under the Act
Whether the lease in favour of Sher Singh was fictitious and executed to defeat pre-emption rights
holdings: A hereditary tenant in possession immediately before vesting became a sirdar and could acquire bhumidhari rights by depositing ten times the land revenue under Section 134 of the Act.
Civil courts lacked jurisdiction to decide ejectment and lease validity disputes concerning tenancy rights; such matters were reserved for revenue courts.
The lease in favour of Sher Singh was valid and not fictitious, as no evidence proved it was fraudulent or that revenue records were incorrect.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 19
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 131
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 134
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 135
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 136
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 137
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 139
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 209
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Jurisdictional exclusivity of revenue courts in tenancy matters
Presumption of validity of revenue records
Doctrine of statutory acquisition of bhumidhari rights

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra sought to levy water charges on ex-proprietors and occupants for using water from the Navegaon Bandh reservoir for irrigation, while the respondents claimed a customary right to free water use as recorded in the Wazib-ul-Arz.
issues_decided: Whether the customary right to free irrigation water was extinguished by the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950
Whether the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954 abolished the customary right to free irrigation
Whether the State could levy water charges under the Central Provinces Irrigation Act, 1931
holdings: The Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950 preserved the customary irrigation rights of occupancy tenants and malik-makbuza under sections 45 and 46, ensuring continuity of such rights after vesting of land in the State.
The Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954 did not extinguish customary water rights; section 239 saved all rights acquired under prior laws, including free irrigation rights.

The State could not levy water charges under the Central Provinces Irrigation Act, 1931 as the Navegaon Bandh is an artificial tank, not a natural water body, and customary rights to water use were protected.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals and Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Sections 45, 46, 47
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 238, Section 239
doctrines: Preservation of customary rights under revenue statutes
Continuity of tenancy rights post-vesting under abolition laws
Doctrine of survival of rights under repealed enactments via saving clauses
Recognition of customary water rights as enforceable against the State

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and the respondent, Maharaj Shri Amarshinhji Himatsinhji, disputed whether a second inquiry under Section 37(2) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code into the respondent's rights over mines and minerals was valid after his jagir had already been determined as proprietary and certain mineral rights recognized.
issues_decided: Whether a determination that a jagir is proprietary under Section 2(4)(i) of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 necessarily implies the jagirdar's right to mines and minerals.
Whether an inquiry under Section 37(2) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code can be initiated without a claim being made by either the State or the individual over a property or right.
holdings: A finding that a jagir is proprietary does not automatically confer rights over mines and minerals; such rights depend on the terms of the grant and any reservations.

An inquiry under Section 37(2) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code can only be initiated if there is a claim by or against the Crown over a property or right; mere requests for record entries do not constitute a claim.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, Section 2(4)(i), 2(vi), 2(vii), 2(xv), 2(xviii), Section 10, Section 16
Bombay Land Revenue Code, Section 37(1), Section 37(2), Section 37(3)
doctrines: Condition precedent to administrative inquiry
Separability of proprietary rights from mineral rights
Finality of civil court adjudication on property rights

card.dispute: The landlady and tenants disputed over the apportionment of enhanced compensation awarded in a land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the enhanced compensation determined under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act should be paid entirely to the landlady or apportioned between the landlady and tenants.
Whether the direction of the District Judge to pay the entire enhanced amount to the landlady was legally valid.
holdings: Enhanced compensation under Section 18 does not automatically belong entirely to the landowner; tenants with recognized rights are entitled to their lawful share.
The direction to pay the entire enhanced amount to the landlady, ignoring tenants' claims, is legally incorrect and must be set aside.
doctrines: Principle of just and equitable apportionment of compensation
Doctrine of binding effect of recognition of tenant rights in acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and others fought against Man Singh Surat Singh Padvi and others over the constitutional validity of a regulation and notification that abolished proprietary rights in Mehwassi estates and affected land ownership and tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the West Khandesh Mehwassi Estate (Proprietary Rights Abolition etc.) Regulation, 1961 is constitutionally valid despite allegedly infringing Article 19(1)(f)?
Whether the Notification dated 24th February, 1962 is valid and severable from the impugned Regulation?
holdings: The inclusion of the 1961 Regulation in the Ninth Schedule via the 40th Constitutional Amendment immunised it from challenges based on fundamental rights under Part III, including Article 19(1)(f), with retrospective effect.

The Notification of 24th February, 1962, which restored pre-existing rights to the estate holder, cannot be challenged as it was beneficial, not detrimental, to him and is valid if the Regulation stands.
provisions: West Khandesh Mehwassi Estate (Proprietary Rights Abolition etc.) Regulation, 1961
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
Government of India Act, 1935, Section 91 and Section 92
Fifth Schedule to the Constitution of India, Para 5
doctrines: Doctrine of curative validation through the Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of retrospective validation of legislation
Principle of beneficial legislation not being subject to challenge by the beneficiary

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction under Section 302 and 307 IPC, arguing he acted in self-defence during a land dispute-related altercation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's act fell under Section 302 IPC or the first part of Section 304 IPC
Whether the appellant acted in private defence and, if so, whether he exceeded it
Whether the sentence under Section 307 IPC should be reduced
holdings: The appellant's act did not constitute murder under Section 302 IPC but fell under the first part of Section 304 IPC as he exceeded the right of private defence.
The appellant acted in self-defence when attacked with a stick, but the fatal knife blow to the heart was disproportionate to the threat.
The sentence under Section 307 IPC is reduced from seven to five years rigorous imprisonment, to run concurrently with the other sentence.
doctrines: Right of private defence
Excess in private defence
Proportionality in self-defence

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan sought to recover alleged revenue dues from Rao Raja Sardar Singh, a jagirdar, after the Jagir Commissioner and the Board of Revenue had rejected the claim under the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the civil or revenue courts had jurisdiction to entertain the State's claim for recovery of dues after the Jagir Commissioner and Board of Revenue had finally decided the matter under the 1952 Act?
Whether the State could bypass the finality of the Jagir Commissioner's order by initiating recovery proceedings under the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1956?
Whether the resolution of the Jaipur State Council dated 1936 constituted a decree immune from review by the Jagir Commissioner under the 1952 Act?
holdings: The Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, ousts the jurisdiction of civil and revenue courts in matters settled by the Jagir Commissioner or Board of Revenue under the Act.

Once the Jagir Commissioner and the Board of Revenue have finally decided on the recoverability of dues under the 1952 Act, the State cannot initiate alternative recovery proceedings under another statute.

The Jagir Commissioner has the authority under the 1952 Act to examine and determine the validity of any claim, including those based on prior state resolutions, and such determination is final and binding.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 46
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 47
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 32
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 22
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Finality of administrative orders
Exhaustion of statutory remedies

card.dispute: The State of Haryana appealed against the High Court's acquittal of three accused—Harpal Singh, Ram Swarup, and Bahadur—in a murder and abetment case arising from a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in acquitting Ram Swarup and Bahadur based on the reliability of the dying declaration and eyewitness testimony.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Harpal Singh abetted the commission of the murder.
holdings: The dying declaration and eyewitness testimony were reliable and sufficient to prove the guilt of Ram Swarup and Bahadur beyond reasonable doubt; their acquittal by the High Court was set aside and conviction restored, though the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

The circumstantial evidence against Harpal Singh, though suspicious, did not unerringly point to his guilt; the prosecution failed to prove abetment beyond reasonable doubt, and his acquittal was upheld.
doctrines: Dying declaration can be relied upon if made under sound state of mind and in fit condition, even if the declarant is critically injured.
Circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain that unerringly leads to the guilt of the accused; mere suspicion, however strong, is insufficient to convict.

card.dispute: The State of Kerala appealed against the High Court's enhancement of compensation awarded to the landowner in a compulsory land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing the compensation for the land without committing a legal error or principle of valuation.
Whether depreciation should have been mandatorily deducted from the value of a five-year-old residential building at the time of acquisition.
holdings: The Supreme Court will not re-evaluate evidence or interfere with compensation unless there is a violation of legal principle or manifest injustice; the High Court's land valuation based on local comparables was valid.
Depreciation of a building cannot be presumed mechanically; for a well-maintained residential property of five years, no deduction is warranted unless actual deterioration is proven.
doctrines: Limited appellate review in factual findings
Realistic assessment over theoretical depreciation

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and life sentences for the murder of two individuals and abduction of a third, claiming false implication due to prior enmity, while the State relied on eyewitness and forensic evidence to prove guilt.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's eyewitness testimony was reliable despite the lighting conditions at the scene.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Court's acquittal based on reappraisal of evidence.
Whether the medical evidence corroborated the nature of injuries caused by the weapons used by the accused.
Whether the accused could be linked to the crime through recovery of a firearm and ballistic evidence.
holdings: Eyewitness identification was reliable as sufficient light from lanterns and torches enabled clear visibility of the assailants.
The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal because the Sessions Judge's decision was based on perverse and speculative reasoning contrary to the weight of evidence.
Medical evidence of incised and punctured wounds corroborated the use of sharp-edged weapons like banka and ballam, consistent with the prosecution's version of the assault.
The recovery of the accused's licensed firearm and ballistic match of cartridge cases provided strong circumstantial evidence linking the accused to the crime scene.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Jurisdiction) Act
doctrines: Perversity in judicial reasoning justifies appellate reversal
Corroboration of ocular and medical evidence strengthens conviction
Presumption against accused in case of unexplained possession and use of weapon
Common object under Section 149 IPC for unlawful assembly

card.dispute: Co-owner landlords appealed against the dismissal of their petition for eviction of a thika tenant on grounds of improper notice service.
issues_decided: Whether the notice to quit was validly served on behalf of all co-owner landlords including minors.
Whether the appeal should be decided under the amended Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act after legislative changes.
holdings: A notice to quit is valid if signed by co-owners or their lawful representatives, even if not explicitly stated that a minor co-owner is represented, provided the minor is named in the notice.
Pending eviction appeals must be decided afresh under the amended Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1919, as per Section 13 of the 1969 Amendment Act.
provisions: Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Second Amendment) Act, 1969 (West Bengal Act 29 of 1969), Section 7A
Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Second Amendment) Act, 1969, Section 13
doctrines: Notice validity in tenancy eviction
Prospective application of amended law to pending cases

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the discharge of two respondents accused of conspiring to illegally obtain compensation for government land during a land acquisition process.
issues_decided: Whether there was sufficient evidence to frame charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act and IPC for conspiracy and illegal gain in a land acquisition case.
Whether the land acquisition officer and the lessee acted in collusion to fraudulently obtain compensation for government-owned land.
Whether the compensation awarded represented the lessee's interest and was legally justified.
Whether the rapid completion of land acquisition proceedings indicated criminal conspiracy.
holdings: No charge should be framed as there was no sufficient evidence of conspiracy or illegal conduct by the respondents.
The compensation was lawfully paid for the lessee's interest in the land, not for ownership, and the government did not need to acquire its own proprietary interest.
The amount of compensation was reasonable and reflected the market value of the lessee's interest, with no overvaluation established.
The speed of the acquisition process was due to administrative urgency and not proof of criminal collusion between the parties.
doctrines: Doctrine of discharge under Section 227 CrPC
Principle of conspiracy requiring meeting of minds
Rule against self-acquisition in land acquisition law
Standard of sufficiency of evidence for framing charges

card.dispute: The Baranagore Municipality, through its Law Assistant, fought against Kumar P.N. Tagore over whether a prosecution for failing to remove an unauthorized culvert was barred by limitation under the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932.
issues_decided: Whether the offence under Section 500(1)(b) of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 is committed at the time of erecting the obstruction or upon failure to comply with a notice to remove it within the stipulated time
From which date the limitation period under Section 533 of the Act begins to run for such an offence
Whether 'six months' under Section 533 means six calendar months or 180 days
holdings: The offence under Section 500(1)(b) consists not in erecting an obstruction but in failing to comply with a lawful direction to remove it after the permitted time expires.

The limitation period under Section 533 begins to run from the date of default, i.e., the expiry of the time allowed to comply with the notice, not from the date of the notice or the erection of the obstruction.
The term 'six months' in Section 533 means six calendar months, not 180 days, as per the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899.
doctrines: Limitation period commences from the date of commission of offence, interpreted as the date of default
Literal interpretation of statutory terms based on general clauses acts
Distinction between continuing offence and initial act in municipal law

card.dispute: The defendant appealed against the cancellation of an assignment deed and the condition requiring the plaintiff to pay Rs. 13,000 to regain possession of land; the plaintiff cross-objected seeking mesne profits.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could modify the trial court's decree under Order 41, Rule 33 CPC regarding the payment condition without a valid cross-objection?
Whether the High Court was justified in awarding mesne profits from the date of the suit?
holdings: The High Court erred in modifying the decree under Order 41, Rule 33 CPC because the plaintiff did not challenge the payment condition in the cross-objection and no court fee was paid for such relief.
The defendant cannot be held liable for mesne profits before the plaintiff paid Rs. 13,000, as possession was contingent on that payment; mesne profits can only accrue from the date of such payment.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
doctrines: Principle of constructive res judicata
Limitation on appellate court's power under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC

card.dispute: The Union of India, as owner of the Southern Railway, contested the Bellary Municipal Council's suit for arrears of municipal taxes on railway property, claiming immunity under Article 285 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Union of India is liable to pay municipal taxes on railway property under Article 285(1) of the Constitution.

Whether the Bellary Municipal Council can continue to levy taxes on Union property under Article 285(2) despite the transfer of Bellary from Madras State to Mysore State after the Constitution's commencement.
Whether a change in the governing municipal law from the Madras District Municipalities Act to the Mysore Municipalities Act affects the continuity of 'that tax' under Article 285(2).
holdings: Property of the Union of India is exempt from all taxes imposed by a State or local authority under Article 285(1), unless Parliament provides otherwise by law.

A local authority can only continue levying a tax on Union property under Article 285(2) if it is located in the same State as it was before the Constitution’s commencement; transfer of territory breaks this continuity.

A change in the applicable municipal legislation due to territorial reorganization does not make the tax a different one if its nature and subject remain the same, but this does not help if the State identity condition under Article 285(2) is not met.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional immunity of Union property from state taxation
Doctrine of continuity of pre-constitutional laws under Article 372 subject to the Constitution
Doctrine of territorial continuity in application of saving clauses in constitutional provisions

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the Bellary Municipal Council's claim to levy municipal taxes on railway property owned by the Union after the area was transferred from Madras State to Mysore State.
issues_decided: Whether the Bellary Municipal Council could continue to levy tax on Union-owned railway property under Article 285(2) of the Constitution after the territory was transferred from Madras to Mysore.
Whether the Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, saved the Council's right to tax Union property despite Article 285(1).
Whether a change in the applicable municipal law (from Madras Act to Mysore Act) affected the continuity of 'that tax' under Article 285(2).
holdings: A local authority can only continue levying tax on Union property under Article 285(2) if it remains in the same State as before the Constitution's commencement; transfer to another State breaks this continuity.
The Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, is repugnant to Article 285(1) and does not save the tax liability because it was not enacted by Parliament after the Constitution.
A change in the governing municipal legislation due to territorial reorganization does not make the tax different from 'that tax' if the nature and subject of taxation remain the same.
doctrines: Repugnancy doctrine
Doctrine of constitutional continuity under Article 372
Literal interpretation of constitutional provisions

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the discharge of a Land Acquisition Officer and an IAS officer who were accused of conspiring to fraudulently obtain compensation for government-owned land.
issues_decided: Whether there was sufficient ground for framing a charge under Section 227 of the Cr.P.C. against the respondents in a corruption case?
Whether the Special Judge was justified in discharging the accused based on the charge-sheet and materials on record?
Whether the High Court was correct in upholding the discharge order?
holdings: At the stage of Section 227 Cr.P.C., the judge must only determine if there is sufficient ground to proceed, based on the existence of suspicious circumstances on the face of the evidence.
The Special Judge correctly discharged the accused as the materials did not disclose any legally sustainable evidence of conspiracy or illegal gain.
The High Court rightly upheld the discharge, and the Supreme Court will not interfere with concurrent findings of lower courts in the absence of special circumstances.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, Section 5(1)(d) and Section 5(2)
Land Acquisition Act, Section 9(1) and Section 10(1)
doctrines: Sufficiency of grounds for framing charge under Section 227 Cr.P.C.
Principle of concurrent findings of fact by two courts
Doctrine of separation of proprietary and lessee interest in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder by the High Court, appealed against their conviction, challenging the reliability of eyewitness and dying declaration evidence used to overturn their acquittal by the Sessions Judge.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Judge's order of acquittal based on the evaluation of eyewitness testimony and dying declarations.
Whether the oral and written dying declarations made by the deceased were reliable and admissible to sustain a conviction for murder.
Whether the Sessions Judge committed an error in disregarding key pieces of evidence, including the dying declaration recorded by Dr. Doshi and the Honorary Magistrate.
holdings: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal as the Sessions Judge erred in rejecting credible eyewitness testimony without valid grounds.
A dying declaration, if found truthful and made under sound consciousness, can alone be sufficient to base a conviction for murder.
The Sessions Judge committed a serious error of law by failing to consider the dying declaration recorded by Dr. Doshi, which was reliable and free from infirmity.
provisions: Supreme Court Enlargement of Appellate Jurisdiction Act
doctrines: Dying declaration as substantive evidence
Principle of reversal of acquittal on substantial grounds
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony through dying declarations

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land at a revenue auction, fought against the respondents, who claimed the sale was void because the land had been allotted to them in a prior partition and could not be sold for their father's personal debt.
issues_decided: Whether the father's Tagai loan was a joint family debt for which joint family property could be made liable.
Whether the Karta of a joint Hindu family can be a 'borrower' under the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883 in a representative capacity.
Whether the sale of joint family property in auction for recovery of the father's loan was valid despite a prior partition allotting the property to the sons.
Whether the doctrine of pious obligation applies to statutory improvement loans under the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883.
holdings: A loan taken by the Karta for improving joint family land constitutes a joint family debt, making the entire joint family property liable for recovery.
The term 'borrower' under Section 7 of the Land Improvement Loans Act, 1883 includes the Karta of a joint Hindu family acting in a representative capacity.
Joint family property remains liable for sale in recovery proceedings for the father's antecedent debt, even if partitioned, due to the sons' pious obligation to repay such debts.
The pious obligation of sons to repay their father's legitimate debts is a legal principle applicable even to statutory loans for family benefit, unless the debt is immoral or illegal.
doctrines: Pious obligation of Hindu sons to repay father's legitimate debts
Karta's capacity to bind joint family property for legal necessity or family benefit
Joint family property liable for debts incurred for its benefit
Statutory interpretation: 'borrower' includes representative capacity

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued his former power of attorney agent for rendition of accounts of transactions and amounts received; the dispute centered on whether the suit was properly valued for court fee purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for accounts was properly valued based on the plaintiff's estimate in the plaint.
Whether the High Court erred in holding that the plaintiff had quantified the amount due, thereby requiring higher court fee.
Whether the plaintiff's valuation of the relief sought was a deliberate undervaluation warranting rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
holdings: A suit for accounts requires only a reasonable estimate of the relief sought, not an exact amount, especially when the plaintiff lacks knowledge of the agent's management.
The plaintiff’s valuation was adequate and not a deliberate undervaluation, as the suit sought comprehensive accounting beyond a specific sum mentioned in earlier paragraphs.
The High Court misread the plaint in concluding that the plaintiff had quantified a fixed amount; the suit was primarily for accounting of all transactions under the power of attorney.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, Section 35
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
doctrines: Proper valuation of relief in suits for accounts
Duty to pay reasonable court fee based on fair estimate
Rejection of plaint for undervaluation under CPC

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether a prior decision on the civil court's lack of jurisdiction in a suit operated as res judicata to bar a subsequent suit on the same matter.
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the civil court on the preliminary issue of its own jurisdiction operates as res judicata in a subsequent suit.
Whether the revenue court could re-examine the question of jurisdiction already decided by the civil court.
holdings: If a defendant appears in a suit, and an issue on the civil court's jurisdiction is raised and decided, that decision operates as res judicata in a subsequent suit, even though the reasoning may not be binding.
A revenue court has no jurisdiction to go behind a civil court's decision on its own jurisdiction when that decision was made after contest and adjudication.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Section (implied on res judicata, particularly Order 14, Rule 1 and Section 11)
doctrines: Res judicata
Jurisdictional bar and its finality
Doctrine of constructive res judicata (implied)

card.dispute: The ex-Zamindars and ex-Thekadars disputed whether the latter became Sirdars (tenants) or the former became Bhumidars (landowners) of certain Sir and Khudkasht lands after vesting under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Thekadars became hereditary tenants under Section 12(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, 1950
Whether the Thekadars became Asamis under Section 13(2)(a) of the Act instead
Whether the Arbitrator's award in favour of the Thekadars was legally sustainable
holdings: A Thekedar cultivating land personally as of 1st May 1950 with the purpose of cultivation becomes a hereditary tenant under Section 12(1), overriding other provisions.
If a Thekedar was merely managing the estate and incidentally cultivating the lessor’s Sir or Khudkasht land, he becomes only an Asami under Section 13(2)(a), not a hereditary tenant.
The Arbitrator correctly interpreted the Theka deed and found personal cultivation for agricultural purposes; thus, the award was legally sound and not subject to interference.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 12(1)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 13(1)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 13(2)(a)
doctrines: Deemed tenancy under statutory fiction
Error of law apparent on the face of the record
Principle of non obstante clause

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether the respondent, a woman who married outside her sub-caste, could inherit her father's share in temple offerings under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, despite a custom restricting such rights to members of four specified sub-castes.
issues_decided: Whether the right to receive a share in temple offerings is heritable property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, or merely an office like that of a shebait.
Whether the right to share offerings is transferable despite being coupled with non-priestly duties.
Whether a custom restricting the right to offerings to certain sub-castes can prevail over the statutory scheme of succession under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
holdings: The right to a share in temple offerings, though coupled with secular duties, is heritable property and not a mere office, as the duties do not require personal or priestly qualifications and can be performed by agents.
A right to offerings coupled with non-personal, secular duties is transferable and falls within the ambit of property under Hindu law.
Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, supersedes customs that restrict succession to certain sub-castes, and inheritance must follow the statutory order of succession.
doctrines: Supremacy of statutory succession over customary law
Property vs. office distinction in Hindu religious rights
Heritability of rights coupled with secular duties

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for murder based on unreliable eyewitness testimony, a possibly involuntary judicial confession, and the recovery of a weapon.
issues_decided: Whether the eyewitness testimony of P.Ws. 1 to 7 could be relied upon to sustain a conviction for murder.
Whether the judicial confession made by the appellant before a Magistrate was voluntary and admissible.
Whether the recovery of the blood-stained tangia (axe) from the appellant's house was sufficient to sustain the conviction under Section 8 or Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
holdings: The eyewitnesses' testimony was unreliable because they claimed to witness the incident from a low-lying area that was not visible from the scene, and their statements before police contradicted their court testimony.
The judicial confession was inadmissible because the Magistrate failed to ensure it was made voluntarily, particularly by not verifying the duration of police custody or allowing time for reflection.

The mere production of the axe from under the appellant’s cot was insufficient for conviction as there was no statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Act linking it to the crime, and the place of recovery was not known exclusively to the accused.
doctrines: Voluntariness of judicial confession
Corroboration requirement for recovery evidence under Section 27
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The appellant was found guilty of contempt for failing to hand over property to a court-appointed receiver under a consent order, which he appealed.
issues_decided: Whether non-compliance with a consent order amounts to contempt of court under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Whether a party can be held guilty of contempt for breach of an implied undertaking not expressly recorded in a court order
holdings: Non-compliance with a consent order does not amount to contempt unless there is a clear and express undertaking given to the court that is wilfully breached.
An implied undertaking cannot form the basis of contempt; only a written or expressly recorded undertaking before the court can lead to contempt proceedings upon breach.
doctrines: Wilful disobedience of court order
Express undertaking doctrine
Distinction between breach of contract and contempt of court

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for forgery of a will based on disputed thumb impression evidence, which they appealed, challenging the reliability of expert testimony and circumstantial suspicion.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the thumb impression on the will (Exh. PD) was forged?
Whether suspicious circumstances alone are sufficient to sustain a criminal conviction for forgery in the absence of conclusive evidence?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court’s acquittal based on re-examination of a single expert witness?
holdings: Circumstantial suspicion and conflicting expert opinion cannot substitute for proof beyond reasonable doubt in a criminal prosecution for forgery.
A conviction under Sections 467 and 471 IPC cannot be based solely on suspicious circumstances when the evidence of forgery is not conclusive.
The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal where the trial court had rightly found the prosecution's evidence unreliable and no cogent reason was given to reject that finding.
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases
Benefit of doubt in case of conflicting expert evidence
Presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the settlement of part of a public road to respondents 1 to 4, which blocked his access to the road from his adjoining land, and later contested the judicial review that overturned the initial writ ruling in his favor.
issues_decided: Whether the Judicial Commissioner had jurisdiction to review and set aside an earlier order of his predecessor allowing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
Whether the grounds cited for review—overlooking documents and alleged procedural defect in joining multiple settlements in one petition—were valid grounds for review.
holdings: A Judicial Commissioner cannot exercise appellate powers under the guise of review; review jurisdiction does not permit re-examination of merits or errors of law apparent on the record unless there is a patent error or new evidence.
Failure to consider documents already in the record and a procedural objection to the joinder of parties do not constitute valid grounds for review under Article 226.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 47, Rule 1
Manipur Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, 1958
Manipur Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, 1960
doctrines: Review jurisdiction limited to correcting patent errors or miscarriage of justice
Distinction between review and appellate jurisdiction
Principle that review cannot be used to re-litigate merits of a case

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, arguing that the market value was underestimated by the Land Acquisition Officer and wrongly revised downward by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether sale transactions of the acquired land itself (Exhibits B-11 and B-12) are reliable indicators of market value.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on sale deeds of nearby lands occupied by squatters or near a public latrine to determine compensation.
Whether the claimants' failure to object to certain sale deeds before the Land Acquisition Officer barred their challenge in court.
holdings: Sale transactions of the acquired land are the best evidence of market value if genuine, and Exhibits B-11 and B-12 were found to be authentic and indicative of fair market price.
Sales of lands occupied by squatters or located near a public latrine do not reflect true market value and cannot reliably guide compensation assessment.
The claimants' lack of opportunity to object to evidence before the Land Acquisition Officer does not preclude them from challenging its relevance in court.
doctrines: Best evidence rule in valuation disputes
Principle of comparable sales for market value determination
Judicial review of administrative compensation awards

card.dispute: The plaintiff challenged the adoption of defendant No. 1 and the validity of wills bequeathing property to him, while defendant No. 1 claimed ownership over all properties including those inherited by his adoptive father's widow from her husband.
issues_decided: Whether a recital in a will that a person is an adopted son is sufficient to prove adoption under Hindu law
Whether the wills executed by Govind Ram and Smt. Chhoti were valid and operative despite the unproven adoption
Whether Smt. Chhoti could validly bequeath properties inherited from her husband to defendant No. 1
holdings: A statement in a will that someone is an adopted son is admissible evidence but not conclusive proof of adoption; the burden to prove adoption remains heavy and must be satisfied by clear evidence.

A will can be valid and operative even if the relationship described (e.g., adoption) is not legally established, provided the testator was motivated by affection and service rather than legal relationship.

A Hindu widow has only a limited interest in her husband's property and cannot bequeath it to someone outside the line of succession; such a bequest is invalid and the property devolves on reversioners.
doctrines: Burden of proof in adoption cases
Limited estate of a Hindu widow
Testamentary disposition based on affection rather than legal relationship

card.dispute: The appellants were prosecuted for criminal breach of trust and cheating after allegedly collecting money from third parties for issuing discharge certificates but not depositing it with the society, leading to a conviction by the High Court which reversed the Magistrate's acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether there was reliable evidence that the appellants received money from PWs 6 and 11 for the society's dues.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Magistrate's order of acquittal based on the same evidence.
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove entrustment of money to the appellants due to lack of credible evidence and proven interpolations in the discharge certificates.
The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal without displacing the Magistrate's findings, as the conviction was based on a view not sufficiently supported by reliable evidence.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Principle against reversal of acquittal unless evidence clearly supports conviction

card.dispute: The Revenue challenged whether acquiring a co-owned property through release deeds from brothers for monetary consideration qualifies as 'purchase' under Section 54(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, to claim exemption from capital gains tax.
issues_decided: Whether a transfer of co-owners' shares in a property to one of them via release deeds for monetary consideration constitutes 'purchase' within the meaning of Section 54(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
holdings: A transfer of co-owners' shares through release deeds for monetary consideration amounts to a 'purchase' under Section 54(1), as the term 'purchase' includes acquisition for money paid or adjusted, consistent with its ordinary meaning.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule
Literal interpretation of statutory terms

card.dispute: Two brothers disputed over the partition of their father's residuary estate, with one seeking amendment of the plaint to include correct property details and the other opposing it, relying on a prior compromise alleged to be binding.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in allowing the amendment of the plaint after a preliminary decree was passed.
Whether a preliminary decree for partition could be passed without a written statement, trial, or framing of issues.
holdings: The High Court was justified in allowing the amendment of the plaint to include fuller and correct particulars of properties, as the earlier order did not bar such amendments and the suit had not been properly tried.

A preliminary decree for partition cannot be passed without a written statement, framing of issues, and trial, especially when the document relied upon does not specify property details and was not formally marked in the suit.
doctrines: Principle of fair trial and proper adjudication
Liberal amendment of pleadings to serve justice

card.dispute: The appellant, Chanan Singh, challenged his conviction for individual assault under Section 304 Part-I IPC arising from an irrigation dispute where injuries were sustained by members of both parties.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt in light of the High Court's rejection of the prosecution's version of events.
Whether the appellant could have acted in self-defence given the injuries sustained by both sides and the absence of a free fight.
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt as the High Court had rejected the prosecution's version of the incident and found the eyewitness accounts unreliable.

Where there is a probability of the accused having acted in self-defence, especially when the prosecution version is unproven and the accused bears injuries, the benefit of the doubt must go to the accused, warranting acquittal.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Presumption of innocence
Self-defence as a ground for acquittal when prosecution version is unproven

card.dispute: Landowners challenged orders of the Taluk Land Board requiring them to surrender land under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, on grounds including exemption claims, validity of purchase certificates, and factual findings about land use and family status.
issues_decided: Whether lands converted into plantations between April 1, 1964, and January 1, 1970, qualified for exemption under Section 81(1)(e) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963
Whether a certificate of purchase issued under Section 72K of the Act was binding on the Land Tribunal or Land Board
Whether transfers of land by gift after January 1, 1970, could be excluded from ceiling calculations under Section 84 of the Act
