holdings: The amended proviso to Section 28(1), requiring the landholder to give notice of default within six months, applies where the termination notice and ejectment proceedings were initiated after the amendment came into force.
A mere right to institute ejectment proceedings is not an accrued right and can be modified by subsequent legislation that does not expressly or impliedly operate retrospectively.
provisions: Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 28(1)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 19(2)
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1960, Section 7
doctrines: Accrued rights doctrine
Prospective operation of amendments
Statutory interpretation of provisos

card.dispute: The Union of India and others challenged the Andhra Pradesh High Court's decision invalidating the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 in Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, arguing over its constitutional validity and applicability.
issues_decided: Whether the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is ultra vires Parliament in relation to the State of Andhra Pradesh.
Whether the Act applies to Warangal in the absence of a master plan under Section 244(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) District Municipalities Act, 1956.
Whether Parliament had legislative competence to include Rajasthan in the Schedule and categorize its urban areas under the Act.
holdings: The Act is validly enacted under Article 252(1) of the Constitution based on resolutions passed by multiple state legislatures, including Andhra Pradesh, and thus applies to those states.
The absence of a master plan under Section 244(1)(c) does not bar the application of the Act to Warangal, as the Act operates independently of municipal planning requirements.

Parliament had the power to structure the Act so it could be adopted by other states, including Rajasthan, and the inclusion of Rajasthan and classification of its cities is within legislative competence.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) District Municipalities Act, 1956, Section 244(1)(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of legislative competence under Article 252(1)
Doctrine of severability
Doctrine of implied powers in federal legislation

card.dispute: The assessee company and the tax authorities disputed whether salami, premia, and compensation received from sub-leasing zamindari land were taxable as business income or were non-taxable capital receipts.
issues_decided: Whether the receipts from salami and premia on sub-leasing coal-bearing land were of a revenue or capital nature.
Whether compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was a capital or revenue receipt.
Whether the company was carrying on business as a trader in land or merely managing a family estate.
holdings: Receipts from salami and premia were capital in nature because the company acted as a landowner managing family estate, not as a trader dealing in land as stock-in-trade.
Compensation for compulsory acquisition of land was a capital receipt, being a substitute for a capital asset lost, not income from business.
The company's incorporation and operations were primarily for preservation and management of family zamindari property, not for carrying on trade in land.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue receipts
Doctrine of substance over form in determining business purpose
Relevance of memorandum and articles of association, but not decisive
Test of real nature and object of transactions in determining trading activity

card.dispute: The Union of India and Jardine Henderson Ltd. disputed whether tax recovery proceedings could continue without a fresh notice of demand after the assessed tax amount was reduced or enhanced in appeal.
issues_decided: Whether recovery proceedings under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 can continue without a fresh notice of demand when the tax liability is reduced or enhanced on appeal?
Whether Section 3(1) of the Taxation Laws (Continuation and Validation of Recovery Proceedings) Act, 1964 mandates a fresh notice of demand in cases of enhancement or reduction of tax dues?
Whether the requirement of intimation under Section 3(1)(b)(ii) of the Validation Act is mandatory for continuing recovery proceedings after a reduction in tax demand?
holdings: Recovery proceedings can continue from the stage prior to appeal disposal without a fresh notice of demand, even if the tax amount is enhanced or reduced, provided procedural requirements are met.
Under Section 3(1)(a) of the Validation Act, a fresh notice of demand is required only for the enhanced portion of the tax, not for the original amount.

The requirement to give intimation of reduction under Section 3(1)(b)(ii) is not strictly mandatory where the assessee and recovery officer are otherwise aware of the reduction, and proceedings may continue.
provisions: Taxation Laws (Continuation and Validation of Recovery Proceedings) Act, 1964, Section 3(1)
Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, Section 7
Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, Section 8(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of substantial compliance
Validation of retrospective legislation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the original vendees and the appellants (subsequent purchasers from a pre-emptor) over whether the latter could execute a decree for pre-emption and possession of land despite not being the original decree-holders.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for pre-emption is a personal right and thus non-assignable, barring execution by a subsequent purchaser.
Whether a purchaser from a pre-emptor who has perfected title can execute the pre-emption decree under Section 146 of the CPC.
Whether Order XXI Rule 16 of the CPC is the only mode for assignment of a decree, excluding application under Section 146.
holdings: The nature of the right of pre-emption as creating an interest in property, not merely a personal right, was already decided between the parties and cannot be re-agitated.

A person claiming under a decree-holder, such as a purchaser from a pre-emptor who has perfected title, can maintain an execution application under Section 146 CPC, even if not covered by Order XXI Rule 16.

Section 146 CPC allows execution by a person claiming under the decree-holder unless a specific provision of the CPC to the contrary applies; Order XXI Rule 16 does not bar such execution when the decree itself is not assigned but the subject matter is transferred.
The appellants, having purchased the land from the pre-emptor after title was perfected, are entitled to execute the decree as persons claiming under the decree-holder.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 14(1)(b)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 16
doctrines: Res judicata
Assignment of decree
Beneficial interpretation of procedural law
Representation and succession in interest under CPC

card.dispute: The granddaughter of a non-redeeming co-mortgagor sued to redeem her share of mortgaged property after the other co-mortgagor's line had fully redeemed the mortgage decades earlier, raising issues of limitation and equitable rights.
issues_decided: Whether the suit by the non-redeeming co-mortgagor's successor for redemption of her share was barred by limitation under the Travancore Limitation Regulation
What is the nature and extent of the equitable right of a non-redeeming co-mortgagor to redeem his share from the redeeming co-mortgagor
Which limitation period applies to a claim by a non-redeeming co-mortgagor to recover possession of his share after the mortgage has been fully redeemed by the other co-mortgagor
holdings: A non-redeeming co-mortgagor has a correlated equitable right to redeem his share by paying his proportionate liability as long as the redeeming co-mortgagor’s right to contribution subsists.

The right of a non-redeeming co-mortgagor to recover possession is governed by the limitation period for redemption under Article 136 of the Travancore Limitation Regulation, which is fifty years from the accrual of the right to redeem.

The suit was time-barred because it was filed in 1946, more than fifty years after the mortgages were created (1881–1884) and long after the redemption (1913–1918), regardless of which limitation article applied.
doctrines: Equitable subrogation
Principles of justice, equity and good conscience
Right of contribution among co-mortgagors
Correlative rights in co-mortgage redemption

card.dispute: The landowner appealed against the quantum of compensation awarded by the Andhra Pradesh High Court for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act for railway gauge conversion.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in rejecting comparable compensation awards and the capitalization method for determining market value?
What is the appropriate compensation for agricultural land acquired near developed areas with potential for higher use?
holdings: The High Court should have considered comparable compensation awards and the capitalization of rent method as relevant factors in assessing market value.
Compensation must reflect not only current use but also the nature, location, and potential of the land; Rs. 20,000 per acre is just in this case.
doctrines: Principle of market value based on comparable sales and capitalization of rent
Consideration of potential use and location in compensation assessment

card.dispute: Bhagwan Dass & Co. Pvt. Ltd. fought the State of Uttar Pradesh over whether land it held was exempt from the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, on the grounds that it was meant for a housing scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the land in question was held for a housing scheme as of the relevant date (7th July 1949), thereby exempting it from the operation of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
holdings: The land did not qualify for exemption under the Act because there was no evidence of a housing scheme, even in embryo, on or before 7th July 1949, as found by the High Court.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 2(c) read with explanation to Section 2(2)
doctrines: Factual findings of the High Court are binding when not perverse or unsupported by evidence
Exemption under a statute must be strictly proved by material facts existing on the relevant date

card.dispute: Minor brothers challenged the validity of a sale of joint family property by their elder brother, claiming it was not for legal necessity or benefit to the estate.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of joint family property by the managing brother was for legal necessity or benefit of the estate
Whether the purchaser-mortgagee was required to make an independent enquiry into the existence of legal necessity
Whether inadequacy of consideration invalidated the sale when most of the amount discharged family debts
holdings: A sale of ancestral property that discharges pre-existing family debts constitutes legal necessity and benefits the estate, even if only part of the consideration is unaccounted for.
When a mortgagee purchases mortgaged property and applies most of the sale proceeds to discharge the mortgage debt, they are not required to make an independent enquiry into legal necessity.
A sale for Rs. 3050 is not grossly inadequate for property worth Rs. 4000, especially in light of ongoing family transactions, and does not invalidate the sale.
provisions: Hindu Law of Joint Family Property
doctrines: Legal necessity in alienation of joint family property
Benefit to the estate doctrine
Good faith purchase from a family manager

card.dispute: The landlord, Bishan Chand, sought ejectment of the tenant, leading to a dispute over whether the appellate court properly considered comparative hardship under rent control rules.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court properly evaluated the question of comparative hardship in the ejectment suit.
Whether Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972 was correctly applied.
holdings: A finding that hardship to both landlord and tenant is equal cannot justify an ejectment order in favour of the landlord without additional circumstances favouring the landlord.

The appellate court must consider Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Rules, 1972, which mandates a proper assessment of comparative hardship, and may allow additional evidence for a just decision.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 16(2)
doctrines: Comparative hardship doctrine
Remand for proper application of rent control rules

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of Angad, who was accused of murdering Mathurbai, leading to a dispute over the reliability of eyewitness testimony and the sufficiency of evidence to secure a conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court erred in disbelieving the eyewitness testimony, particularly of Mahananda, the injured witness?
Whether the discrepancies in the timing of events undermined the credibility of the prosecution's witnesses?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal based on corroboration and credibility of witnesses?
holdings: An injured eyewitness's testimony is credible even with minor inconsistencies, especially when supported by medical evidence of injuries sustained during the incident.
Minor discrepancies in time estimates by rustic, uneducated witnesses do not fatally undermine their testimony, particularly under emotional distress.
The High Court correctly reappraised the evidence and upheld the conviction where multiple independent witnesses corroborated the prosecution's case without motive to fabricate.
doctrines: Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Credibility assessment of injured witnesses
Reappraisal of evidence by appellate courts

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the declaration of 25.93 acres of his land as surplus under the U.P. Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, arguing that prior sales of land should be recognized to reduce his holding.
issues_decided: Whether the sales of land by the appellant were valid and could be considered under Section 5(6) of the U.P. Ceiling on Land Holdings Act despite lack of 'compelling necessity'
Whether the land in question was correctly classified as irrigated or unirrigated
holdings: Once a transfer is shown to be genuine, for adequate consideration, and made in the ordinary course of management without collusion or intent to evade the Ceiling Act, the burden of proving good faith is satisfied without requiring proof of compelling necessity.
The entire land held by the appellant on the crucial date was unirrigated, and this finding is binding as res judicata on the authorities.
provisions: U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5(6) Proviso (b) with Explanation II
U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10(2)
doctrines: Res judicata
Good faith transfer in ordinary course of management
Burden of proof under ceiling laws

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, who claimed he needed the premises for his business, but evidence showed he had already shifted operations elsewhere.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was still using the suit premises for his business as claimed in the appeal.
Whether the appeal should be dismissed for abuse of the judicial process due to false statements.
holdings: The tenant had vacated and abandoned the suit premises, as evidenced by disconnection of electricity, absence of signage, and non-use.
The appeal was dismissed as an abuse of the process of the Court where the tenant made false claims about continuing business in the suit premises.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 13
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Judicial notice of facts through judicial inquiry

card.dispute: The Assistant Custodian-General sought to recover mesne profits from Lila Devi under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, while she claimed the property was hers and not part of the evacuee estate.
issues_decided: Whether the decree for mesne profits could be enforced under Section 48 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act despite non-payment of court fee?
Whether the Assistant Custodian-General was entitled to recover the decreed amount without fulfillment of the condition precedent regarding court fee payment?
holdings: A decree for mesne profits is conditional upon payment of the full court fee and does not become operative until that condition is fulfilled.
Non-payment of court fee renders the decree unenforceable, and recovery cannot be effected even under Section 48 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, Section 48
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21 Rule 63
doctrines: Conditional decree
Execution barred by non-compliance with decree conditions

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the decision denying Badami Kaur absolute ownership of disputed land, which the consolidation authorities and High Court held was only a life interest, in favor of collaterals.
issues_decided: Whether Badami Kaur acquired absolute proprietary rights in the land under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act and the Hindu Succession Act
Whether the collaterals (respondents) had locus standi to challenge her ownership
Whether the mutation recording her as widow in 1931, prior to the enactment of relevant laws, entitled her to full ownership retrospectively
holdings: The Hindu Succession Act and U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act conferred absolute proprietary rights on Badami Kaur as the widow, extinguishing any rights of collaterals.
Once Badami Kaur became absolute owner, the reversionary interest of the collaterals ceased, and they lacked locus standi to challenge her status.
The earlier mutation as a widow, though initially for consolation, became the basis for full ownership upon the enactment of the relevant statutes.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
doctrines: Retrospective application of beneficial legislation
Extinction of reversionary interests upon vesting of absolute ownership in widow
Locus standi dependent on subsisting legal interest

card.dispute: The appellant, Brijendra Singh, challenged the declaration of his 25 acres of land as surplus under the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, after selling the land before the cut-off date, claiming the transfers were in good faith and thus exempt from being ignored under Section 5(6) proviso (b).
issues_decided: Whether a transfer of land made between January 24, 1971, and June 8, 1973, is exempt from being ignored under Section 5(6) of the U.P. Ceiling Act if made in good faith, for adequate consideration, and under an irrevocable instrument not being a benami transaction or for family benefit?
Whether proof of 'pressing necessity' is a legal requirement to establish 'good faith' under proviso (b) to Section 5(6) of the Act?
Whether the Appellate Authority erred in disallowing the exemption under proviso (b) solely on the ground that constructing a residential house in New Delhi was not an 'impelling necessity'?
holdings: A transfer made after January 24, 1971, is not to be ignored under Section 5(6) if it is in good faith, for adequate consideration, under an irrevocable instrument, not benami, and not for the benefit of the transferor or his family.
Good faith does not legally require proof of pressing or legal necessity; such necessity may support but is not essential to establish a bona fide transfer.

The Appellate Authority erred in denying good faith solely because constructing a house in New Delhi was not an 'impelling necessity'; the need must be judged from the transferor's perspective, especially considering his impending retirement and lack of alternative residence.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5(6) proviso (b)
doctrines: Good faith in property transfers
Bona fide alienation of property
Statutory fiction in land ceiling laws
Res judicata

card.dispute: Two auction purchasers, one under a prior mortgage and another under subsequent mortgages, contested over who had the preferential right to redeem the mortgaged property.
issues_decided: Whether the prior mortgagee who purchased the property at auction could redeem the subsequent mortgages as assignee of the equity of redemption.
Whether the right of the prior mortgagee to redeem subsequent mortgages takes precedence over the right of the subsequent mortgagee to redeem the prior mortgage.
holdings: A prior mortgagee who purchases the mortgaged property at auction acquires the equity of redemption and can redeem subsequent mortgages.
The right of the prior mortgagee, as assignee of the equity of redemption, to redeem subsequent mortgages takes priority over the right of the subsequent mortgagee to redeem the prior mortgage.
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Priority of redemption rights
Doctrine of lis pendens not applicable due to lack of impleadment

card.dispute: The Director of Industries, U.P. and others challenged the High Court's decision that Section 3 of the Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1965 violated Article 14 by allowing recovery of state loans as arrears of land revenue.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1965 offends Article 14 of the Constitution by enabling recovery of state dues as arrears of land revenue.
Whether the absence of express guidelines in the Act for initiating recovery proceedings results in arbitrary power and discriminatory application.
holdings: Section 3 of the Act does not violate Article 14 as the classification between state dues and private debts bears a reasonable relation to the object of ensuring expeditious recovery of public moneys.
The Act provides sufficient guidance by its purpose, and the expectation that officers use the speedier remedy for recovering public dues prevents arbitrary or discriminatory action.
provisions: Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1965, Section 3
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Sections 279 and 281
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Presumption against arbitrariness in administrative action
Doctrine of expeditious recovery of public dues

card.dispute: The appellant sought to revise a previously sanctioned layout plan to include a cinema, and claimed deemed sanction under Section 313 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, after the Standing Committee failed to decide within 60 days.
issues_decided: Whether failure by the Standing Committee to decide on a layout plan application within 60 days under Section 313(3) results in deemed sanction.
Whether an application for revision of a previously sanctioned layout plan falls under Section 313 and can be made after initial development has begun.
holdings: Non-compliance by the Standing Committee with the 60-day time limit under Section 313(3) does not result in deemed sanction; such a legal fiction requires express statutory language, which is absent here.

An owner may apply for sanction of a revised layout plan under Section 313 even after initial development under the original plan, as it constitutes a fresh application for a differently constituted plan.
doctrines: Deemed sanction
Legal fiction by express statutory provision
Statutory interpretation based on context and comparison with analogous provisions

card.dispute: D.L.F. United Private Ltd. appealed against the Delhi High Court's decision allowing Prem Raj to amend his plaint to seek allotment of 22 plots of land despite earlier being barred from seeking specific performance of a contract he claimed was void.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff could amend his plaint to seek relief equivalent to specific performance after being barred from doing so by a prior Supreme Court decision.
Whether the relief sought in the proposed amendment could be granted as a consequence of the contract being declared void.
holdings: A plaintiff cannot circumvent a prior judicial determination by rephrasing the same relief through an amendment that effectively seeks specific performance of a contract while disaffirming it.
Relief based on restitution due to a void contract must be genuinely rooted in the consequences of invalidity, not used as a device to obtain the same result as specific performance.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rule 17
doctrines: Res judicata and abuse of process
Doctrine of restitution upon avoidance of contract
Amendment of pleadings not permitted to achieve impermissible relief

card.dispute: The appellant claimed title to a property he purchased at auction under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, while the respondents contested the sale, arguing the property was never validly declared evacuee property under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide if the property was validly declared evacuee property under the 1950 Act, despite Section 46 of that Act barring civil court jurisdiction.
Whether the property in question was validly declared evacuee property under Section 7 of the 1950 Act, making it eligible for acquisition and sale under the 1954 Act.
Whether the finality clause in Section 27 of the 1954 Act barred the respondents from challenging the sale in a civil court.
holdings: Section 46 of the 1950 Act bars civil court jurisdiction only over matters within the Act’s scope; it does not bar challenges to actions taken without jurisdiction or legal authority.
The property was not validly declared evacuee property under Section 7 of the 1950 Act, and thus could not be acquired under Section 12 or sold under Section 20 of the 1954 Act.
Section 27 of the 1954 Act makes orders final only if made under the Act; a sale of non-evacuee property is a nullity and can be challenged in civil court.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(d)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7A
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 28
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 46
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 2(c)
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 22
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 23
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 24
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 27
doctrines: Condition precedent doctrine
Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Finality of administrative orders
Civil court jurisdiction in presence of special statutes

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assessee disputed whether expenditure incurred to resume operations of a derequisitioned colliery was capital or revenue in nature and thus deductible under the Income Tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to re-appreciate facts regarding the nature of expenditure.
Whether the expenditure should be assessed under Section 10(2)(v) or Section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the expenditure of Rs. 1.61 lakhs was of a capital or revenue nature.
holdings: The High Court had jurisdiction to evaluate the nature of expenditure based on admitted or established facts.
Even if the expenditure does not qualify as 'current repairs' under Section 10(2)(v), it may be considered under the residuary clause Section 10(2)(xv).
The expenditure was revenue in nature as it was incurred to reinstate an existing business unit, not to create a new asset or secure enduring benefit.
doctrines: Residuary clause interpretation
Capital vs revenue expenditure test
Business as a whole principle

card.dispute: The appellants, who had been provisionally allotted plots and were in possession, challenged the state's derequisition of the plots in favour of a third party after the state had requisitioned the plots from them under the Defence of India Act, 1962.
issues_decided: Whether the property derequisitioned under Section 35(1) of the Defence of India Act, 1962 must be restored to the person from whom possession was taken at the time of requisition
Whether the government can specify a third party as the recipient of possession upon derequisition without adjudicating prior title
Whether the appellants had locus standi to claim possession upon derequisition despite provisional allotment being cancelled
holdings: The property derequisitioned under Section 35(1) should generally be restored to the person from whom possession was taken at the time of requisition, as the inquiry under the section does not require adjudication of prior title.

The government's power under Section 35(1) does not extend to determining antecedent title; it may only specify the person entitled to possession at the time of derequisition based on factual possession during requisition.
Despite lack of final allotment, the appellants had a sufficient interest to claim possession upon derequisition since they were in actual possession when the requisition order was executed.
doctrines: Doctrine of possession under requisition
Principle of limited inquiry under Section 35(1)
Doctrine of conditional relief in public law remedies

card.dispute: The appellants, who were provisionally allotted industrial plots by the Uttar Pradesh government but later had their allotments cancelled, challenged the state's refusal to return possession of the plots after they were de-requisitioned under the Defence of India Act, 1962.
issues_decided: Whether a person from whom possession of requisitioned property was taken is entitled to have it returned upon de-requisition, despite lack of final allotment or legal title.
Whether the government can lawfully direct release of de-requisitioned property to a department or third party instead of the person in possession at the time of requisition.
Whether the inquiry under Section 35(1) of the Defence of India Act requires determination of prior title or merely identifies the person entitled to possession at the time of release.
holdings: Upon de-requisition, possession of property should prima facie be restored to the person from whom it was taken, as Section 35(1) of the Defence of India Act mandates return to the person appearing entitled at the time of release.
The government’s power under Section 35(1) does not extend to adjudicating prior title; inquiry is limited to identifying the person in possession unless post-requisition events create disputes.
Despite the general rule, equitable considerations may justify conditional or denied relief where third-party interests have crystallized or formalities of possession recovery were pending.
doctrines: Principle of restitution of possession upon de-requisition
Limited scope of administrative inquiry under statutory requisition laws
Equitable discretion in enforcement of rights under special factual circumstances

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for subletting the premises without consent, while the tenant argued that he had a right to sublet under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can sublet premises without the landlord's permission under section 108(j) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, if the lease does not expressly prohibit it.

Whether section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, allows eviction for unauthorized subletting despite the general right to sublease under the Transfer of Property Act.
holdings: Section 108(j) of the Transfer of Property Act does not confer an absolute right to sublet; such a right must be conferred by the lease or subsequent consent of the landlord.
Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Act permits eviction for subletting without landlord’s consent, and overrides any implied right to sublet under the Transfer of Property Act.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(4)(i)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory displacement
Doctrine of implied terms in lease agreements

card.dispute: The judgment-debtors challenged their imprisonment for non-payment of a debt, arguing it violated constitutional and human rights principles.
issues_decided: Whether a judgment-debtor can be imprisoned for non-payment of a decree debt without proof of current ability to pay or mala fide refusal to pay
How Section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure should be interpreted in light of Article 21 of the Constitution and Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
holdings: Imprisonment for civil debt is impermissible if the debtor is currently unable to pay and has not acted in bad faith or deliberately evaded payment.

Section 51, CPC must be interpreted to require proof of either current means to pay or wilful refusal to pay despite past means, in order to comply with Article 21 and the spirit of Article 11 of the ICCPR.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 37
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 11
doctrines: Rule of law
Fair procedure under Article 21
Incorporation of international covenants into domestic interpretation
Presumption of liberty and strict interpretation of laws restricting personal freedom

card.dispute: The Jain Ink Manufacturing Company, a tenant, fought against the Life Insurance Corporation of India's attempt to evict it from premises after LIC purchased the building at auction.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was an 'unauthorised occupant' under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, despite being inducted before LIC's ownership
Whether the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 overrides the Public Premises Act, 1971
Whether the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 overrides the Public Premises Act, 1971
holdings: A tenant in possession before the premises became public property can still be an 'unauthorised occupant' under the Public Premises Act if not authorised by the current public authority.
The Public Premises Act, 1971 prevails over the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 as it is a subsequent and special law dealing specifically with public premises.
The Public Premises Act, 1971 overrides the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 due to being both subsequent in time and a special law with a distinct field of operation.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 2(2)(g)
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 4(1)
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
doctrines: Doctrine of specialia generalibus derogant
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of non-obstante clause interpretation by object and purpose

card.dispute: Landlords sought to enforce a 1967 compromise decree for possession against tenants, after earlier execution was rejected on grounds that the Bombay Rent Act did not apply to cantonment areas.
issues_decided: Whether the 1967 compromise decree, passed before the 1972 amendment, was saved by the retrospective validation under the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957 as amended by Act 22 of 1972
Whether the executing court's earlier declaration that the decree was a nullity operated as res judicata barring a fresh execution
holdings: The 1972 amendment validates all decrees, including compromise decrees, made by the erroneous application of state rent laws to cantonment areas, provided they were passed before the extension of such laws and meet the conditions in Section 3(4).

A decision that a decree is a nullity due to lack of jurisdiction under a statute does not operate as res judicata when the law is later amended to validate such decrees, as res judicata cannot override legislative validation.
provisions: The Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 3
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Res judicata
Validation by retrospective legislation
Legislative competence over cantonment areas

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the state's decision to award a resin tapping contract to another party without public auction, alleging violation of equality and fair procedure under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the State is constitutionally obligated to advertise or invite tenders before awarding a tapping contract linked to industrial development.
Whether the impugned contract violated Article 14 and Article 19 of the Constitution due to lack of transparency or arbitrariness.
Whether the State's selection of the second respondent for the contract was mala fide or unreasonable.
holdings: The State is not required to advertise or invite tenders when allocating natural resources as part of a package deal to encourage industrialization, provided the action is bona fide, reasonable, and in public interest.
A contract for resource allocation tied to industrial development does not violate Articles 14 and 19 merely because it was not awarded through public auction.

The State's decision to award the contract to the second respondent was reasonable and not mala fide, given their superior experience and prior successful performance, and served public interest in industrial growth.
doctrines: Doctrine of reasonableness in state action
Public interest as a basis for executive discretion
Non-arbitrariness under Article 14

card.dispute: The complainant sought prosecution of Suraj Bhan for attempted murder and killing Banta Singh, but the Magistrate dismissed the complaint; the dispute was whether this dismissal was legally valid.
issues_decided: Whether the Magistrate erred in dismissing the complaint against Suraj Bhan under Section 203 CrPC in a case exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the lower court's order under Article 136 of the Constitution.
holdings: At the stage of Sections 203/204 CrPC, the Magistrate must only determine if there is prima facie evidence to proceed; detailed evaluation of evidence is not warranted.
The Magistrate overstepped by minutely assessing evidence, but the error did not cause a gross miscarriage of justice, so the Supreme Court declined to interfere under Article 136.
doctrines: Prima facie evidence standard at pre-trial stage
Double jeopardy and risk of conflicting findings in connected cases
Limited scope of Supreme Court's discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of land acquisition notifications under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming mala fide, non-application of mind, excess acquisition, and lack of specification of the instrumentality for public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act were mala fide and in excess of requirement?
Whether a notification under Section 6 is invalid if it does not specify the instrumentality through which the public purpose is to be carried out?
holdings: The acquisition was not in excess of requirement, as the entire plot was needed for a 60 ft. road, 60 ft. walking platform, and 30 ft. service platform under a town planning scheme, making the challenge to mala fide and excess acquisition untenable.
Failure to specify the instrumentality for carrying out the public purpose in a Section 6 notification does not invalidate the notification, as affirmed by precedent.
doctrines: Mala fide and colourable exercise of power
Non-application of mind
Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)

card.dispute: The appellants, decree-holders who purchased property in execution of a decree transferred from a Small Causes Court to a Munsif's Court, challenged a suit declaring that sale null and void due to lack of jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the decree-holder had a substantive right to get the decree transferred from the Small Causes Court to the Munsif's Court for execution before the 1954 amendment took effect.
Whether the transferee court (Munsif's Court) had jurisdiction to execute the decree by attachment and sale of immovable property after the 1954 amendment to Section 42 of the CPC.
holdings: The right to apply for transfer of a decree under Section 39(1)(d) is procedural, not substantive; the decree-holder has no indefeasible right to such transfer, which lies in the discretion of the court passing the decree.

After the 1954 amendment, the transferee court has only the same powers as the court which passed the decree; since the Small Causes Court lacked power to sell immovable property in execution, the Munsif's Court also lacked such jurisdiction, rendering the sale a nullity.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 82
U.P. Civil Laws (Reform and Amendment) Act, 1954, Section 3
doctrines: Jurisdictional nullity doctrine
Substantive vs. procedural rights distinction
Doctrine of non est factum in execution proceedings
Prospective operation of amendments

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction for murder based on a dying declaration, arguing it was unreliable due to the deceased's state of shock, incompleteness, and mention of other unchallenged persons.
issues_decided: Whether a dying declaration can be relied upon if the deceased was in a state of shock.
Whether a dying declaration is invalid if it is incomplete because the deceased became semi-unconscious at the end.
Whether a dying declaration loses credibility if it names persons not prosecuted.
holdings: A dying declaration can be relied upon even if the deceased was in shock, provided the court is satisfied that the declarant was conscious and coherent when making the statement.
A dying declaration is not rendered invalid merely because the deceased could not answer the last formal question due to becoming semi-unconscious, if the essential facts had already been conveyed.
The fact that a dying declaration names persons not prosecuted does not invalidate it, as omissions in prosecution may stem from ulterior motives and do not affect the declaration’s truthfulness.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Dying declaration as an exception to hearsay rule
No mandatory corroboration required for a reliable dying declaration
Special sanctity accorded to dying declarations under Indian evidence law

card.dispute: The appellants, minors represented by their mother as guardian, sued for specific performance of a contract to purchase property, which the High Court denied on grounds of lack of mutuality.
issues_decided: Whether a contract for the purchase of immovable property entered into by a guardian on behalf of a minor is enforceable under Hindu law and the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956.
Whether such a contract lacks mutuality and thus cannot be specifically enforced.
Whether a guardian's act of entering into a purchase agreement binds the minor by a personal covenant, which is prohibited under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act.
holdings: A guardian can validly enter into a contract for the purchase of immovable property on behalf of a minor if it is for the minor's benefit, and such contract is enforceable under Hindu law.
The doctrine of want of mutuality does not bar specific performance of a contract entered into by a guardian for a minor’s benefit.

A contract for purchase of property by a guardian does not amount to a personal covenant binding the minor, as the liability arises under the Transfer of Property Act and is within the guardian’s powers under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
doctrines: Doctrine of mutuality in specific performance
Guardian's power under Hindu law to bind minor for beneficial acts
Distinction between personal covenant and statutory liability under transfer of property

card.dispute: Meharban Singh (plaintiff) fought Bhagwant Singh and others over possession of mortgaged land after redemption, following abolition of zamindari.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to possession of the suit land under Section 4(2) of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, despite having lost possession to the mortgagee.
Whether tenants inducted by the mortgagee could retain possession after redemption of the mortgage.
holdings: Proprietors who mortgaged their khud-kasht land with possession are entitled to decree for possession under Section 4(2) of the Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, if the land was recorded as their khud-kasht before vesting.
Tenants inducted by a mortgagee cannot claim statutory protection against the mortgagor’s right to possession upon redemption, unless a specific law grants them such rights.
provisions: Madhya Bharat Zamindari Abolition Act, 1951, Section 4(1)(f) and Section 4(2)
Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 76(a) and (e)
doctrines: Right to possession under zamindari abolition laws
Rule that a mortgagee cannot create interests beyond his own tenure
Exception where statute confers rights on tenants during mortgage period

card.dispute: The lessors' successors (plaintiffs) sued to eject the defendant who claimed ownership of leasehold land transferred through a bank in liquidation, after the original lessee company was dissolved.
issues_decided: Whether the voluntary liquidator had the authority to execute a deed of sale after the company was dissolved.
What was the effect of the company's dissolution on its leasehold interest in the land.
Whether the plaintiffs were estopped from denying the defendant's right to the leasehold interest.
holdings: A liquidator has no authority under the Companies Act, 1913 to execute a deed of sale after the company is dissolved, as the company ceases to exist and no statutory power permits such an act.
The leasehold interest of a dissolved company vests in the Government by escheat or as bona vacantia, unless a specific statutory provision or trust directs otherwise.
The plaintiffs were estopped from denying the defendant's interest in the land due to their conduct in accepting rent and failing to object to the sale or construction on the land.
doctrines: Doctrine of Escheat or Bona Vacantia
Doctrine of Estoppel by Conduct
Statutory Authority of Liquidators

card.dispute: Nasir Ahemed challenged the validity of a notice and declaration declaring him an evacuee under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, on grounds of procedural irregularity and lack of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the notice issued under section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 was valid when it only cited clause (iii) of section 2(d) but the declaration was made under clauses (i), (ii), and (iii)?
Whether the notice complied with rule 6 requiring a statement of factual grounds enabling the petitioner to answer the case?
Whether the authority applied its mind and had sufficient material before initiating proceedings under section 7?
holdings: A declaration under section 7 cannot be based on grounds beyond those specified in the notice; proceeding on clauses (i) and (ii) when only clause (iii) was mentioned violates principles of fair hearing.
A notice under rule 6 must contain specific factual grounds to enable the affected person to respond; a mere reproduction of the prescribed form without particulars is invalid.
The authority must apply its mind and possess credible material before issuing a notice under section 7; initiation of proceedings without such basis renders the action unlawful.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 2(d)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 7
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 19
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 24
Administration of Evacuee Property Rules, Rule 6
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Jurisdictional error doctrine
Procedural fairness in administrative action

card.dispute: Moola, claiming ancestral occupancy rights over land, fought against the Financial Commissioner and a displaced person allottee over whether his lease was validly terminated under resettlement laws.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing Moola's writ petition without considering Section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Whether a lease existing prior to August 14, 1947, can be automatically terminated under Section 9 of the Displaced Persons (Land Resettlement) Act, 1947
Whether Moola or his ancestors were in possession of the land as lessees prior to August 14, 1947
holdings: The High Court failed to consider Section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, which protects pre-August 14, 1947 leases from arbitrary cancellation by the Custodian.
Section 9 of the Displaced Persons (Land Resettlement) Act, 1947 does not automatically terminate pre-August 14, 1947 leases if not exempted; the Custodian must act under Section 12.
The question of whether Moola or his ancestors were lessees prior to August 14, 1947, and the legal effect of Section 12 and Section 9 on his rights, must be examined by the High Court on remand.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 12
doctrines: Protection of pre-partition tenancy rights
Statutory interpretation of custodial powers over evacuee property
Judicial review of administrative land allotment decisions

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against his eviction, arguing the landlord's application for possession was filed within three years of purchasing the property, making it barred by the proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act.
issues_decided: Whether the application for eviction on the ground of landlord's personal need is barred if made within three years of purchase of the property under the proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act?
Whether the date of purchase for the purpose of the three-year bar is the date of execution or registration of the sale deed?
holdings: The proviso to Section 21(1)(a) bars courts from entertaining eviction applications on the ground of personal need within three years from the date of purchase of the property.
The date of purchase for the three-year period is the date of execution of the sale deed, not the date of registration, as per Section 47 of the Indian Registration Act.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
doctrines: Date of execution prevails over date of registration for determining vesting of rights
Proviso as a condition precedent to maintainability of eviction application

card.dispute: New India Steel Industries fought V.D. Steel Industries over the revocation of special leave to appeal, based on misrepresentation and misconduct.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant made a misstatement of material fact in the special leave petition.
Whether the appellant's conduct in publishing a false court notice warranted revocation of the special leave.
holdings: The appellant misrepresented a material fact by omitting that the sale proclamation noted the property was subject to a mortgage charge.
Publishing a 'Court Notice' implying judicial authority without orders from the Court constitutes misconduct justifying revocation of special leave.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 9
Supreme Court Rules, 1966, Order V Rule 1
doctrines: Judicial propriety
Misrepresentation and abuse of process

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the validity of an arbitration award in land acquisition proceedings, claiming for the first time before the High Court that the arbitration agreement violated Article 299 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether a point not raised in pleadings or before lower courts can be raised for the first time in an application for a certificate of fitness to appeal to the Supreme Court.
Whether the arbitration agreement in question complied with Article 299 of the Constitution of India.
holdings: A party cannot raise a new legal point for the first time in an application for a certificate of fitness to appeal to the Supreme Court if it was not raised in the pleadings or before the lower courts.
The question of compliance with Article 299 involves factual investigation and cannot be raised for the first time at a belated stage, as it prejudices the other party's ability to present evidence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 8
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII Rule 2
doctrines: Plea must be raised in pleadings to be considered by courts
No evidence can be considered without a foundation in pleadings
Doctrine of waiver by conduct in arbitration proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant landowner fought the Collector of Darrang over compensation for land requisitioned and later derequisitioned, claiming damages for erosion, land covered by roads and canals, and inadequate solatium.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to compensation for land erosion caused allegedly due to government construction.
Whether the appellant was entitled to full acquisition compensation for land covered by roads and canals.
Whether the compensation rate awarded per bigha was justified based on comparable sales.
Whether the appellant was entitled to solatium at 15% under the Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948.
holdings: The erosion was due to natural causes, and no liability was established against the government for damage caused.
Compensation for land covered by roads and canals is limited to the cost of restoration, not full acquisition value.
The compensation rate of Rs. 300 per bigha was justified, as higher sales relied upon were not comparable or fictitious.

The appellant is entitled to 15% solatium, as there should be no discrimination in solatium between acquisitions under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Assam Act where its provisions are applicable.
provisions: Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 7(3)(b)
Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact by lower courts not disturbed by Supreme Court
Principle of comparable sales in land acquisition compensation
Equal treatment in payment of solatium across acquisition statutes
Restoration cost as measure of compensation where land use is impaired but not acquired

card.dispute: The appellant, a litigant, issued a notice accusing a judicial officer of mala fides and misconduct in a decided case, leading to contempt proceedings initiated by the Advocate-General.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's notice imputing mala fides to a judicial officer amounts to criminal contempt under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Whether the exemption under Section 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act applies when judicial proceedings have been decided but execution is pending
Whether the contempt, if established, substantially interferes with the due course of justice under Section 13 of the Act
holdings: Imputing mala fides, bias, or dishonesty to a judge in relation to judicial functions constitutes criminal contempt under Section 2(c)(i), as it scandalizes the court and lowers its authority, regardless of the pendency of proceedings.

Section 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act does not protect criticism of concluded judicial proceedings, as it only applies to interference with pending proceedings; it does not extend to contempt under Section 2(c)(i).
Contempt that scandalizes the judiciary substantially interferes with the due course of justice under Section 13, even if no active proceeding is prejudiced, justifying punishment.
doctrines: Scandalizing the court
Substantial interference with the due course of justice
Exception for pending proceedings under Section 3

card.dispute: Zamindars (appellants) fought with lease-holders (respondents) over whether the latter qualified as hereditary tenants under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents, as thekedars, fulfilled the conditions to be deemed hereditary tenants under Section 12 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
Whether the Theka granted to the respondents was primarily for personal cultivation, as required by Section 12 of the Act.
holdings: To qualify as a hereditary tenant under Section 12, a thekedar must (1) be in possession of the land on 1 May 1950, (2) hold under a Theka, and (3) the Theka must be for personal cultivation, not for other purposes like subletting.
The respondents did not qualify as hereditary tenants because the terms of the Theka permitted subletting and appointing temporary tenants, indicating purposes beyond personal cultivation.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 12
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 13
doctrines: Land reform doctrine: securing land for the tiller of the soil
Strict interpretation of statutory conditions for acquiring hereditary tenancy rights

card.dispute: The landowner, Raj Kanta, fought against tenants and the Financial Commissioner over whether a single default in rent payment entitled her to eject the tenants under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'regularly' in Section 9(1)(ii) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 requires consistent and punctual rent payment without any default.
Whether a single default in rent payment, without sufficient cause, attracts the ejectment provision under Section 9(1)(ii).
Whether the words 'without sufficient cause' in Section 9(1)(ii) render a single default sufficient for ejectment if no cause is shown.
holdings: The word 'regularly' in Section 9(1)(ii) means consistent, punctual, and uninterrupted payment of rent; even a single default breaks regularity.
A single default in rent payment without sufficient cause is sufficient to invoke ejectment under Section 9(1)(ii) of the Act.
The phrase 'without sufficient cause' requires the tenant to justify any default; its presence confirms that even one default can lead to ejectment if unexplained.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)(ii)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
doctrines: Strict construction of confiscatory statutes in favor of landlords where rights are limited
Interpretation of statutes to avoid rendering words or phrases redundant
Principle that courts must interpret law as enacted, not legislate through interpretation (jus dicere, not jus dare)

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against the Calcutta High Court's decree for his ejectment on grounds of rent default under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was in default under Section 13(1)(i) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955 for failing to pay rent for two months within twelve months.
Whether deposits of rent with the Rent Controller under Section 21(4A) are valid in the absence of a prior valid tender to the landlord.
Whether the tenant's deposits of rent with the Rent Controller were within the time limits prescribed by Section 22(1) of the Act.
holdings: The tenant was not in default under Section 13(1)(i) because he made a timely tender of rent for July 1965 by money order on August 11, 1965, and subsequent deposits were within time.
A valid tender to the landlord before depositing rent with the Rent Controller is not required after the landlord has refused a valid tender, as per Section 21(4A).
Rent deposits with the Rent Controller are governed by Section 22(1), which allows deposit by the last day of the month following the rent month, not Section 4’s fifteenth-day rule.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 13(1)(i)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 21(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 21(4A)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 22(1)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 4(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of valid tender and deposit of rent
Statutory interpretation of rent deposit provisions
Protection of tenant against eviction for non-payment of rent upon timely deposit

card.dispute: R. R. Engineering Co. challenged the constitutional validity of the 'Circumstances and Property Tax' imposed by Zila Parishad, Bareilly, arguing it was a tax on income or profession beyond state legislative competence.
issues_decided: Whether the 'Circumstances and Property Tax' is a composite tax referable to entries in the State List or a distinct tax falling under the Union's residuary powers
Whether the tax can be sustained under Article 277 of the Constitution
Whether the tax is ultra vires the State Legislature as being a tax on income in disguise
holdings: The 'Circumstances and Property Tax' is a composite tax primarily referable to Entries 49 and 60 of List II, covering taxes on lands and buildings and on professions, trades, and employments.
The tax does not fall under the residuary powers of Parliament (Entry 97, List I), and Article 277 is not required to validate it, as it is within the State Legislature's competence.

Though income may be a measure for assessing 'circumstances', the tax remains distinct from an income tax so long as it does not become disproportionately excessive and transform income into the subject matter.
provisions: U.P. Kshetra Samitis and Zila Parishads Act, 1961
Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49: Taxes on lands and buildings
Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 58: Taxes on animals and boats
Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 60: Taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments
Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 97: Residuary powers
doctrines: Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Doctrine of Colourable Legislation
Rule against excessive delegation
Principle of constitutional limitation on local taxation

card.dispute: The dispute arose over whether a vacation judge of the High Court could grant an ex parte stay to halt a re-auction mandated by the Supreme Court, despite no prior involvement of the petitioners in the original challenge.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could grant an ex parte stay against a re-auction directed by the Supreme Court under Article 136
Whether the petitioners before the High Court had locus standi to challenge the re-auction notification
Whether the State Government acted appropriately in not challenging the stay before the High Court
holdings: The High Court should not have granted an ex parte stay that effectively nullified a mandatory direction of the Supreme Court.
Petitioners who were not parties to the original challenge and had no prior interest lacked locus standi to obstruct the re-auction.
The State Government failed in its duty by not promptly challenging the stay in the High Court, raising suspicions of collusion.
doctrines: Principle of judicial discipline and respect for superior court orders
Locus standi in writ petitions under Article 226
Abuse of process of court

card.dispute: Padman Meher and his son Bhagabat Meher appealed against their conviction by the High Court in a murder case where they were acquitted by the Sessions Judge but later convicted on appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the Sessions Judge's acquittal based on reappreciation of evidence.
Whether the dying declarations made by the deceased were reliable given the nature of his injuries.
Whether the prosecution's alteration of the accused in the FIR (from Indra Meher to Bidhu Meher) without explanation affected the credibility of the case.
Whether PW 4, a 13-year-old, could be considered a credible eyewitness given his relationship with the accused and inconsistencies in his testimony.
holdings: The High Court was not justified in overturning the Sessions Judge's acquittal as the view taken was reasonable and based on probable interpretation of evidence.
The nature of the injury to the deceased, particularly the spinal cord damage, made it medically improbable that he could have made the alleged dying declarations.
The unexplained substitution of one accused with another in the FIR without justification casts serious doubt on the prosecution's case.
The testimony of PW 4, a 13-year-old farm servant with no clear employment terms and not named in the FIR, was unreliable and likely influenced to support the prosecution.
doctrines: Principle of reappreciation of evidence by High Court in appeal against acquittal
Reliability of dying declarations
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Credibility assessment of eyewitnesses

card.dispute: The Member of the Board of Revenue challenged the High Court's jurisdiction to initiate contempt proceedings suo motu based on a private petition, without a reference from the subordinate court or a motion by the Advocate-General.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can take suo motu cognizance of criminal contempt of a subordinate court under Section 15(2) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, in the absence of a reference from the subordinate court or a motion by the Advocate-General.
Whether Section 15(2) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, restricts the High Court's power to act only on a reference or motion, thereby excluding suo motu action.
holdings: The High Court has the power to take suo motu cognizance of criminal contempt of a subordinate court, as Section 15(2) must be harmoniously construed with Section 10 to preserve co-extensive powers over contempt of itself and subordinate courts.

While the High Court may act on its own motion based on information from a private party, it should do so sparingly and only when the contempt alleged is serious, to preserve procedural safeguards and avoid frivolous complaints.
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Suo motu jurisdiction
Power of superintendence under Article 227
Contempt of court (criminal contempt)

card.dispute: Sada Kaur, a widow, married her deceased husband's brother and claimed a right to retain her life interest in his estate, while the respondents claimed she forfeited it under customary law.
issues_decided: Whether a special custom among Dhaliwal Jats of Muktsar Tehsil permits a widow remarrying her deceased husband's brother to retain her life interest in his estate.
Whether entries in the riwaj-i-am or Rattigan's Digest should prevail in case of conflict on customary law.
Whether the appellant had forfeited her interest in her deceased husband's estate by remarrying his brother.
holdings: There was no special custom among Dhaliwal Jats of Muktsar Tehsil allowing a widow who remarries her deceased husband's brother to retain her life interest in his estate.
Entries in the riwaj-i-am, being based on local inquiry and expert compilation, should prevail over general statements in Rattigan's Digest when there is a conflict.
A widow who remarries, even her deceased husband's brother, forfeits her right to his estate under the prevailing custom of the Dhaliwal Jats of Muktsar.
doctrines: Customary law prevails over general legal principles if proved and local.
Presumption of correctness of riwaj-i-am entries in matters of Punjab customary law.
Special custom must be clearly established and cannot be inferred from general or erroneous secondary sources.

card.dispute: The appellants challenged a decree for preemption on the ground that it was barred by the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973, which came into force during the pendency of the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973 bars the passing of a decree for preemption even in an appeal decided after the Act's commencement?
Whether a decree passed by a trial court and affirmed by an appellate court after the Repeal Act came into force falls within the prohibition of Section 3?
holdings: Section 3 of the Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973 prohibits the passing of any decree for preemption on or after its commencement, including in appellate proceedings.
An appellate decree affirming a preemption claim after the Repeal Act came into force is invalid, as the appellate decree supersedes the trial court decree and is subject to the statutory bar.
doctrines: Merger of decrees
Prospective operation of repeal legislation
Statutory bar to judicial relief

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 4(c) of the Consolidation of Holdings & Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, which divested civil courts of jurisdiction over land disputes pending before consolidation authorities.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4(c) of the Consolidation of Holdings & Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956 violates Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution of India?
Whether the High Court was justified in nullifying a civil court decree due to the operation of Section 4(c)?
holdings: Section 4(c) does not violate Articles 14 and 19 as the exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in favour of consolidation authorities is a valid legislative policy and has been upheld in prior decisions.

The High Court erred in 'nullifying' the decree but was correct in holding the proceeding abated; however, the effect is that the civil court proceeding becomes infructuous due to the exclusive jurisdiction under the Act.
provisions: Consolidation of Holdings & Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 4(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by statute
Reasonable classification under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed possession of land, leading to proceedings under Section 145 Cr.P.C., where the Magistrate awarded possession to the appellant, later set aside by the High Court for lack of a finding on breach of peace in the final order.
issues_decided: Whether a finding of breach of peace is required in the final order under Section 145 Cr.P.C. when it was already recorded in the preliminary order
Whether the omission to record a finding on breach of peace in the final order vitiates the order
Whether the High Court could exercise its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the Magistrate's order on this ground
holdings: A finding of breach of peace in the final order under Section 145 Cr.P.C. is not necessary if it was already recorded in the preliminary order, as jurisdiction is established at that stage.
The continuation of breach of peace at every stage is not required unless the dispute has clearly ended, as per Section 145(5) Cr.P.C.

Omission to record a finding on breach of peace in the final order is a curable procedural irregularity, not vitiating the order, especially where no prejudice occurred and parties had full opportunity to present evidence.
doctrines: Curable irregularity doctrine
Finality of magisterial satisfaction in preliminary orders
Limitation on revisional jurisdiction over sufficiency of material

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of provisions in the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, alleging violations of Article 14 and illusory compensation.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 4(1), 4(3), 7, 8, 9, 11(1), and 11(2) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, violate Article 14 by creating an artificial definition of family unit
Whether Rule 5(2)(a) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1973, unreasonably reduces permissible landholding area
Whether Section 18(7), requiring a deposit of 30 times the land revenue tax for filing an appeal or revision, unconstitutionally restricts the right to appeal
Whether the compensation provided under Section 16 is illusory
holdings: The provisions defining family unit and permissible landholding do not violate Article 14 as they are based on reasonable classification and serve the purpose of land reform.
Rule 5(2)(a) does not reduce permissible land arbitrarily; it scientifically converts land categories and ensures equitable application of ceiling limits.
Section 18(7)'s deposit requirement is not unconstitutionally onerous as it prevents frivolous appeals and is tied to a reasonable multiple of nominal land tax.
Compensation under Section 16 is not illusory as it is based on soil quality and yield, and no evidence was presented to show it results in inadequate payment.
provisions: Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Sections 4(1), 4(3), 7, 8, 9, 11(1), 11(2), 16, 18(7)
Constitution of India, Article 14, Article 31A, Article 31B, Article 39(b) and (c)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1973, Rule 5(1), Rule 5(2)(a)
doctrines: Right to appeal is statutory and subject to reasonable conditions
Presumption of constitutionality for laws in the Ninth Schedule under Article 31B
Classification under Article 14 must be based on intelligible differentia and rational nexus
Compensation need not be market value to be constitutional

card.dispute: The landlady sought to evict the tenant by claiming exemption from rent control laws on the ground that the building was newly constructed within ten years, while the tenant argued it was an old building.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord bears the burden of proving that the building was completed within ten years to claim exemption from rent control laws.
Whether the trial court erred in granting eviction without properly determining the date and nature of construction based on municipal records.
Whether a building with additions or remodelling qualifies as 'new construction' under the U.P. Rent Control Act.
holdings: The burden of proving that a building was completed within ten years lies on the landlord claiming exemption from rent control laws.
A finding of new construction cannot be based on speculation; municipal records must be examined to determine the date and nature of completion.
Substantial additions that render the original building a minor part may constitute new construction, but this must be established through objective evidence, not oral testimony alone.
provisions: U.P. Rent Control Act, 1972, Section 2(2) with Explanation 1
doctrines: Burden of proof in statutory exemptions
Primacy of documentary and municipal records over oral evidence
Statutory interpretation of 'new construction' in rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the death sentence imposed for the murder of a young boy, arguing it was not a rarest of rare case.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence was justified in this case of murder arising from a land dispute?
Whether the normal sentence for murder should be life imprisonment, with death penalty reserved for extreme cases?
Whether the government should be restrained from reducing the life sentence to less than fourteen years?
holdings: The death sentence was set aside as the crime, though serious, arose from a land dispute, was not for personal gain, and the appellant was not a habitual offender; life imprisonment sufficed.
The normal sentence for murder is life imprisonment; the death penalty should be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases with special reasons.
The government should not reduce or commute the life sentence to less than fourteen years save for weighty reasons, given the gravity of the crime.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Normality principle in sentencing for murder
Special reasons requirement for death sentence

card.dispute: The wife of the detenu challenged the legality of her husband's detention under COFEPOSA, claiming lack of material connecting him to smuggling activities.
issues_decided: Whether the grounds of detention under COFEPOSA disclosed sufficient material to justify the detenu's detention?
Whether the detaining authority applied its mind to the material before passing the detention order?
Whether mere ownership of premises, without control or possession, is sufficient to justify preventive detention for smuggling?
holdings: The grounds of detention must disclose tangible material linking the detenu to smuggling; mere allegations or remote connections are insufficient.
The detaining authority must apply its mind to the material and form an independent satisfaction regarding the necessity of detention.
Mere joint ownership of premises where smuggled goods are found, without proof of possession, control, or active involvement, does not justify preventive detention.
provisions: Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of effective application of mind by detaining authority
Principle of sufficiency and relevance of material in preventive detention
Rule against detention based on vague or remote allegations

card.dispute: The respondent tenant sought eviction of the appellant sub-tenant on grounds including bona fide requirement for setting up a dyeing factory, which was denied by lower tribunals but allowed by the High Court in revision; the appellant challenged the High Court's interference with concurrent factual findings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 25 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, could interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority on the landlord’s bona fide requirement?
Whether the jurisdiction under Section 25 is wide enough to permit the High Court to act as a second court of appeal on factual matters?
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with concurrent findings of fact in revision under Section 25 unless there is a manifest error, illegality, or miscarriage of justice; mere disagreement with the finding is insufficient.
Section 25 confers supervisory jurisdiction, not appellate power; it is not wide enough to make the High Court a second court of first appeal, even though the language is broad.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 23
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 25
doctrines: Distinction between appellate and revisional jurisdiction
Supervisory power under revisional jurisdiction
Concurrent findings of fact not lightly disturbed in revision

card.dispute: The widow of Kedar Nath fought with other family members over her entitlement to a one-third share in joint family property, contested by a claim that she had adopted her husband's nephew with his prior authority.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant widow was validly authorised by her deceased husband to adopt a son under the Banaras School of Hindu Law
Whether the adoption of the third respondent was valid in the absence of clear authorisation from the deceased husband
Whether the subsequent conduct of the appellant, such as performing adoption ceremonies and executing a deed, could prove prior authorisation
holdings: A Hindu widow governed by the Banaras School of Hindu Law cannot make a valid adoption without express or implied authorisation from her deceased husband.
The mere performance of adoption ceremonies and execution of a deed of adoption do not, by themselves, prove that the widow had lawful authority to adopt.
