The tenant is entitled to compensation equivalent to two years' rent as per the proviso to Section 21(1) when ejected under the Act.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1) proviso
doctrines: Mandatory consideration of statutory provisos
Conditional stay of eviction with compensation

card.dispute: Displaced persons challenged the classification and valuation of their sailab land as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, arguing it was arbitrary and not based on soil quality or yield.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of land under Annexure 'A' of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Rules, 1953 violates Section 2(5) of the Act for not considering yield and soil quality.
Whether the revenue authorities erred in classifying the appellants' sailab land as unirrigated and valuing it at nine annas per standard acre.
holdings: The classification under Annexure 'A' is valid as it adheres to Section 2(5) of the Act, having been made based on assessment circles that inherently consider soil quality and yield.
The revenue authorities correctly classified the land as unirrigated since sailab land was not listed for Karnal District in Annexure 'A', and the valuation at nine annas per acre was lawful.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(5)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Rules, 1953, Rule 2
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 27
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Deference to administrative classification based on expert settlement practices
Presumption of validity of statutory rules

card.dispute: The appellants (successors of a disabled landholder and her heir) challenged the respondents' (tenants') claim to be recognized as Sirdars under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition Act, arguing they should remain Asamis.
issues_decided: Whether the benefit of section 21(1)(h) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act extends to a landholder who was a disabled person or whose predecessor was a disabled person on the relevant dates, even if the landholder's status changed before vesting.
Whether tenants under a disabled landholder become Sirdars under section 240B if the landholder or predecessor was disabled on the material dates.
holdings: Section 21(1)(h) benefits a landholder on the vesting date if either the landholder or their predecessor was a disabled person on the material dates; continuity of identity is not required.
Tenants do not become Sirdars under section 240B if the landholder or predecessor was a disabled person entitled to protection under section 21(1)(h); they remain Asamis.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 21(1)(h)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 157(1)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 240B
doctrines: Deeming fiction of succession in landholding
Literal vs. purposive interpretation of statutory provisions
Continuity of disability status for statutory protection

card.dispute: The assessee, Shiela Kaushish, challenged the assessment of income tax on her warehouse based on actual rent received, arguing that the annual value should be determined by the standard rent under the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the annual value of a let-out property for income tax purposes should be based on the actual rent received or the standard rent determinable under the Rent Control Act.
How to compute the standard rent of non-residential premises under the Delhi Rent Control Act when it was not formally fixed by the Controller.
holdings: The annual value of a property under Section 23(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 is not necessarily the actual rent received, but the sum for which the property might reasonably be expected to be let, which in rent-controlled areas is the standard rent determinable under the Rent Act.

For non-residential premises first let after June 19, 1955, the agreed rent at first letting is deemed the standard rent for five years; thereafter, it is calculated based on a percentage of construction cost and land value as per the Rent Act.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 2(k), Section 6
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Use of hypothetical annual value over actual rent in rent-controlled areas
Legislative approval of judicial interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the dismissal of his appeal before the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court, which had held that the single Judge's order refusing interim relief was not a 'judgment' appealable under the Letters Patent.
issues_decided: Whether an order refusing appointment of a receiver or ad-interim injunction on the original side of the Bombay High Court is appealable under Section 104 read with Order 43 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Whether such an order constitutes a 'judgment' under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court
Whether the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure apply to appeals from orders of a single Judge on the original side of the High Court
holdings: Section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, read with Order 43 Rule 1, applies to the original side of the High Court and makes orders refusing interim reliefs like appointment of a receiver or injunction appealable.

An order refusing interim relief that finally determines a substantial right in the context of the suit qualifies as a 'judgment' under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent, even if not finally disposing of the suit.
The Code of Civil Procedure governs internal appeals on the original side of the High Court, and there is no subordination of a single Judge to the Division Bench in such appeals.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1
Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court, Clause 15
doctrines: Finality of orders determining substantial rights
Statutory right of appeal as a creature of law
Interpretation of 'judgment' under Letters Patent

card.dispute: Smt. (Dr.) D. Kaur fought with Smt. Kanti Khare and others over the allotment of accommodation under the U.P. Rent Control Act, 1972, specifically regarding deemed vacancy and the residential nature of the property.
issues_decided: Whether an applicant for allotment of accommodation on the ground of deemed vacancy must be given notice and hearing before the Rent Control and Eviction Officer decides on the vacancy and allotment
What is the test to determine whether accommodation is residential or non-residential under the U.P. Rent Control Act, 1972
holdings: An applicant for allotment on the ground of deemed vacancy is entitled to a hearing before the Rent Control and Eviction Officer makes an order, though this issue required resolution of conflicting High Court views.
The High Court should have decided the residential or non-residential character of the accommodation based on existing evidence, rather than remanding it to the Rent Control and Eviction Officer.
provisions: U.P. Rent Control and Eviction Act, 1972, Section 16
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem (right to hearing)
Appellate court's duty to decide factual questions when evidence is complete

card.dispute: Smt. Kamlesh Kumari challenged the determination of surplus land, arguing that transferred land should have been excluded from the surplus area calculation.
issues_decided: Whether the Prescribed Authority erred in failing to exclude transferred land from the surplus area despite finding the transfer non-bona fide?
Whether the surplus land should be recalculated under Section 12A(d) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act?
holdings: The Prescribed Authority was incorrect in not excluding the transferred land from the surplus area even if the transfer was found non-bona fide.
The case must be remitted to the Prescribed Authority to recalculate surplus land under Section 12A(d) of the Act, excluding the transferred area as far as possible.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, Section 12A(d)
doctrines: Principle of exclusion of transferred land from surplus area under ceiling laws
Remand for proper application of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant, a life estate holder, contested whether tenants she leased agricultural land to could become deemed tenants and purchasers under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, given her limited ownership rights.
issues_decided: Whether a life estate holder under a settlement deed could lawfully lease agricultural land despite restrictions on encumbrance.
Whether tenants inducted by such a life estate holder could be deemed tenants under Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the life estate holder had a vested or contingent interest in the property during her lifetime.
Whether a lease by a life estate holder would be invalid as an impermissible encumbrance under the settlement deed.
holdings: A life estate holder with a right to manage property has the inherent right to lease agricultural land unless there is a clear contrary intention in the settlement deed.
Tenants lawfully inducted by a life estate holder are cultivating the land 'lawfully' and can acquire deemed tenant status under Section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
A life estate holder has a vested interest in the property during her lifetime, while remaindermen have contingent interests that vest only upon her death.
A lease by a life estate holder does not necessarily constitute an encumbrance prohibited by a settlement deed, especially when management rights are conferred.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(18)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32F
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32G
doctrines: Vested vs contingent interest under transfer law
Rule against perpetuities and prior interest in favor of life tenant
Lease as an incident of management by a limited owner
Statutory betterment of tenant rights despite limited title of lessor

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and landowners cross-appealed against the High Court's determination of compensation at Rs. 12 per square yard for land acquired in 1958, with claimants seeking higher compensation and the State seeking a reduction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in fixing the market value of the acquired land at Rs. 12 per square yard without considering adverse features like marshy land and poor access.
Whether the sale transactions at Rs. 20 per square yard should be the basis for determining compensation.
Whether the rate of interest on compensation should be uniform across similar cases.
holdings: The High Court properly considered relevant factors in fixing compensation at Rs. 12 per square yard, and its valuation falls within a reasonable range, warranting no interference by the Supreme Court.
Sale transactions at Rs. 20 per square yard, even involving the government, cannot be solely relied upon for valuation if other relevant factors justify a lower rate.
Interest rate on compensation must be uniform in similar cases; thus, the interest rate was increased from 5% to 6% to ensure parity.
doctrines: Principle of uniformity in award of interest in land acquisition cases
Rejection of mechanical reliance on comparable sale deeds in land valuation
Sustained deference to appellate valuation if within reasonable limits

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat appealed against a High Court decision that struck down Section 233 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act and Section 193-A of the Gujarat Village Panchayats Act as unconstitutional, which were used to evict occupants from municipal premises.
issues_decided: Whether Section 233 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act and Section 193-A of the Gujarat Village Panchayats Act violate Article 14 of the Constitution by allowing arbitrary discretion in eviction proceedings
Whether the said provisions impose unreasonable restrictions on the fundamental right to property under Article 19(1)(f)
holdings: The provisions do not violate Article 14 as the discretion conferred is not unguided and is subject to procedural safeguards, including notice and opportunity to be heard.
The summary eviction mechanism under the provisions is reasonable and does not violate Article 19(1)(f), as the right to property is subject to reasonable restrictions for public purposes.
doctrines: Equal protection of laws under Article 14
Reasonable restrictions on fundamental rights
Summary eviction as a valid exercise of state power for recovery of public property

card.dispute: The appellant, Sooraj Devi, challenged the High Court's refusal to clarify its earlier criminal order directing restoration of property possession to Pyare Lal, claiming it did not affect her rights in the property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can alter or review its final judgment under Section 362 of the CrPC by invoking inherent powers under Section 482?
Whether the appellant's request for clarification of the judgment amounted to correction of a clerical or arithmetical error under Section 362?
Whether the inherent powers under Section 482 can override the bar imposed by Section 362 of the CrPC?
holdings: Section 362 prohibits a court from altering or reviewing its final judgment except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error, and no other power can circumvent this restriction.
The appellant's request for a declaration that the order did not affect her possession rights is not a correction of a clerical or arithmetical error but a substantive legal determination.
The inherent powers under Section 482 cannot be used to do what is expressly prohibited by the CrPC, including altering a final order under Section 362.
doctrines: Inherent powers doctrine
Clerical or arithmetical error doctrine
Statutory prohibition override limitation

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant after the lease expired, and the tenant argued the suit was not maintainable without a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is necessary to maintain an ejectment suit when the lease is for a definite term and has expired by efflux of time.
Whether the tenant became a statutory tenant after the lease expired.
holdings: A notice under Section 106 is not required when a lease for a definite term expires by efflux of time under Section 111(a) of the Transfer of Property Act.
The tenant did not become a statutory tenant as the premises were in a Notified Area, not a Municipality, and thus outside the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
doctrines: Lease by efflux of time
Statutory tenancy
Holding over

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka prosecuted two individuals for forgery and perjury related to a fabricated sale deed in a mortgage redemption suit, but the High Court acquitted one respondent due to lack of a court complaint under Section 195 CrPC; the State appealed.
issues_decided: Whether prosecution under Section 193 IPC requires a written complaint from the court when the forged document was not used in court proceedings?
Whether Section 195(1)(b)(i) CrPC bars private prosecution for offences under Section 467 IPC read with Section 114 IPC if the forgery preceded and was not used in court proceedings?
holdings: Section 195(1)(b)(i) CrPC does not apply if the forged document was not produced or used in any stage of court proceedings; thus, no court complaint is needed for prosecution.

A private person can initiate prosecution for forgery under Section 467 IPC read with Section 114 IPC when the offence was committed prior to and independent of any court proceeding, as it lacks a close nexus with the proceeding.
doctrines: Strict construction of Section 195 CrPC
Close nexus doctrine
Private right to initiate prosecution under Section 190 CrPC

card.dispute: The State of Haryana appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Sher Singh and others convicted of murdering two half-brothers in a family property dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution must prove motive in a murder case
Whether the burden of proving alibi lies on the accused
Whether the First Information Report (F.I.R.) must contain all details of the occurrence
Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving prosecution evidence and accepting the defence version based on conjecture
holdings: Motive is not an essential ingredient of murder; the prosecution need not prove motive to secure conviction.
When an accused pleads alibi, the burden of proof lies on the accused under Section 103 of the Indian Evidence Act.
An F.I.R. need not contain every detail of the occurrence; omissions in it do not render the report unreliable or contradictory.
The High Court erred in acquitting the accused based on conjectures and unsupported hypotheses, while rejecting credible prosecution evidence without valid reason.
doctrines: Burden of proof in alibi defence
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Reliability of extra-judicial confession
Principle of judicial review of acquittals based on conjecture

card.dispute: The appellants (accused) challenged their conviction for murder and related charges, claiming they acted in private defence during a land dispute with the deceased's family.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution failed to explain how the appellants sustained injuries, thereby casting doubt on its case.
Whether the courts below properly evaluated the question of who was the aggressor in the incident.
Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence.
Whether the conviction under Sections 302, 307, 323 read with Section 149 IPC was legally sustainable.
holdings: The prosecution case was reliable and supported by evidence; the failure to explain the appellants' injuries did not undermine the conviction where the defence was inconsistent and false.
The appellants were the aggressors, as found by both trial and appellate courts, and the incident occurred on the victim's land.
Aggressors who sustain injuries during their own unlawful attack cannot claim the right of private defence.
The conviction under Sections 302, 307, 323 read with Section 149 IPC was valid as the appellants were part of an unlawful assembly acting with common object.
doctrines: Right of private defence is not available to aggressors
Principle of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Inconsistency in defence pleas weakens credibility
Burden of proof in criminal cases and evaluation of prosecution evidence

card.dispute: The State of Assam and landowners disputed whether an agreement to accept a fixed sum for acquired land barred a later claim for interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to accept a specified amount 'with no further claim in regard to compensation' excluded the right to claim interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the term 'compensation' in the agreement was used in the technical sense of the Land Acquisition Act or in a broader sense encompassing interest.
holdings: The phrase 'no further claim in regard to compensation' in the agreement was used in a comprehensive sense, meaning full and final settlement of all claims, including interest, and not limited to the statutory definition of compensation.
By accepting the agreed amount subject to timely payment, the landowners condoned the delay in payment and waived their right to claim interest under Section 34 unless they had expressly reserved it.
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Waiver of statutory claims by agreement
Interpretation of settlement agreements in administrative law

card.dispute: The State of Assam and others contested whether the government's decision to auction leasehold rights of land, instead of renewing the respondent's lease, was mala fide and for a collateral purpose after initially claiming the land was needed for defence.
issues_decided: Whether the government's refusal to renew the lease and decision to auction the land was mala fide or for a collateral purpose
Whether the delegation of power under the Defence of India Act to requisition land was valid
Whether the government's claim that the land was required for defence purposes was bonafide
holdings: The government's decision to auction the leasehold rights was not mala fide, as defence needs could change and the condition allowing resumption for defence purposes was consistently maintained.
The delegation of power under Section 29 of the Defence of India Act to district authorities via notification was valid and unrestricted.
The government's assertion of defence necessity was bonafide, especially given the 1965 war with Pakistan, and the failure to plead it in early title suits did not invalidate the claim.
doctrines: Mala fide actions and abuse of power
Collateral purpose doctrine
Judicial review under Article 226
Delegation of statutory power

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the Allahabad High Court's acquittal of four respondents accused of murdering four people during a land dispute, seeking to reinstate their conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the respondents by rejecting the prosecution's evidence without proper reasoning
Whether the prosecution case under Section 302/149 IPC was proven beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the respondents could claim right of private defence
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the acquittal order passed by the High Court
holdings: The High Court committed a serious error by rejecting credible eyewitness testimony on general grounds without analyzing intrinsic merits, especially in a case involving four murders.
The prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused acted with a common object to encroach on land and used deadly force, establishing guilt under Section 302/149 IPC.
The right of private defence was not available to the accused as they were the aggressors who initiated the violence to further an illegal common object.
The Supreme Court can interfere with an acquittal if it results in a grave miscarriage of justice due to perverse or erroneous evaluation of evidence.
doctrines: Perverse reasoning
Extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 136
Common object under Section 149 IPC
Right of private defence not available to aggressors

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged a High Court order that set aside an eviction order on the ground that the U.P. Public Lands Act was unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether the U.P. Public Lands (Eviction and Recovery of Rent and Damages) Act, 1959 is ultra vires the Constitution?
Whether the eviction order passed under the Act should be set aside on grounds of the Act's alleged unconstitutionality?
holdings: The U.P. Public Lands (Eviction and Recovery of Rent and Damages) Act, 1959 is not ultra vires the Constitution and is valid.
The High Court erred in setting aside the eviction order solely on the ground of the Act's unconstitutionality; the case is remanded for consideration of other grounds in revision.
provisions: U.P. Public Lands (Eviction and Recovery of Rent and Damages) Act, 1959
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the acquittal of Smt. Kalki and her husband Amara, convicted by the trial court for the murder of Poona, arguing that the High Court erred in disbelieving the testimony of the sole eyewitness, the deceased's wife.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the testimony of P.W. 1, the deceased's wife, on the ground that she was an 'interested' witness.
Whether the discrepancies in the testimony of P.W. 1 were material enough to reject her evidence entirely.
Whether the Supreme Court can interfere with the High Court's factual findings in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
holdings: A witness being related to the deceased does not automatically make her 'interested'; interest implies a personal benefit from the outcome, which was absent here.
Discrepancies in a witness's testimony regarding minor details under traumatic circumstances are normal and not material if they do not affect the core of the testimony.
The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 when factual findings are perverse and result in a miscarriage of justice, even if the appeal involves appreciation of evidence.
doctrines: Miscarriage of justice doctrine
Perversity in factual findings
Credibility of interested witnesses
Material versus minor discrepancies in witness testimony

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against the acquittal of six accused by the High Court in a double murder case, seeking conviction based on eyewitness and circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt in the murders of Hazara Singh and Resham Singh.
Whether the failure of the investigating officer to involve local respectable persons in the recovery of the weapon rendered the evidence inadmissible.
Whether the ballistic evidence could be relied upon despite procedural lapses in sending materials to the forensic lab.
Whether the eyewitness testimony was reliable and sufficiently corroborated to base conviction upon.
holdings: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of Wasson Singh and Mukhtar Singh for the murder of Hazara Singh based on corroborated eyewitness testimony and circumstantial evidence, including recovery of the weapon and ballistic match.
Failure of the investigating officer to involve local respectable persons in the recovery of evidence does not render the evidence inadmissible, though it may reduce its weight.
The ballistic evidence linking the recovered rifle to the crime was valid and could be relied upon despite initial procedural errors in dispatching evidence to the forensic lab.
The prosecution failed to prove the involvement of the other four accused due to lack of motive and insufficient corroboration of eyewitness accounts, warranting their acquittal.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Evaluation of circumstantial evidence
Principle of adverse inference from investigation bias
Test of reliability of discovery evidence

card.dispute: The tenant, Syed Asadullah Kazmi, fought against the partition and release of a portion of a bungalow to the landlord's son after the landlord's death, seeking to halt proceedings following a final order for partial eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the prescribed authority could reopen final ejectment proceedings after the death of the landlord.
Whether the appellate authority or the Supreme Court could revisit a final order for partial release of tenanted premises based on subsequent events.
holdings: A final order by the appellate authority for partial release of tenanted premises cannot be reopened due to a subsequent event like the landlord's death.
Even the Supreme Court cannot reopen final ejectment proceedings once they have been concluded and all appeals, including special leave, have been dismissed.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 24
doctrines: Finality of judicial orders
Doctrine of res judicata
Principle of non-reopening of concluded litigation

card.dispute: The forest contractor sued the State of Madhya Pradesh for refund of the first instalment paid for forest produce, claiming that the quantity and quality of timber available after auction were substantially less than what was announced, due to subsequent reservation of a marked area.
issues_decided: Whether the contractor could repudiate the contract and claim refund due to substantial variance in quantity and quality of forest produce after auction?
Whether Condition No. 3 of the sale notice, disclaiming accuracy of announced quantities, barred the contractor from repudiating the contract?
Whether the suppression of the inspection report and subsequent reservation of a marked area vitiated the contract?
holdings: A contractor can repudiate a contract and claim refund if there is a substantial variance between the announced and actual availability of forest produce, even if the quantity was not guaranteed.
Condition No. 3 of the sale notice does not bar repudiation of the contract for fundamental change in the subject matter; it only bars claims for compensation.

Non-production of the inspection report and subsequent reservation of a marked area, which formed part of the auctioned produce, amounted to suppression of material facts and justified repudiation of the contract.
provisions: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 56 (Impossibility of performance)
doctrines: Suppressio veri
Fundamental change in the foundation of contract
Repudiation of contract for variation in subject matter

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the adequacy of compensation awarded for land acquired by the state in Jalna, claiming it was undervalued compared to market rates in the developing locality.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation of Rs. 2 per square yard awarded for the acquired land was legally adequate given the locality's development and market value.
Whether the unchallenged evidence of the Municipal President regarding land value at Rs. 15 per square yard could serve as a reliable basis for determining compensation.
holdings: Compensation must reflect the true market value of land, considering its location, building potential, and nearby development; Rs. 2 per sq. yard was grossly inadequate.
Unchallenged evidence of a credible witness on land value, such as a Municipal President, provides a valid basis for compensation, and courts must consider it seriously.
doctrines: Principle of just equivalent compensation
Deduction for undeveloped areas (1/3rd rule for development costs)

card.dispute: The landlord (Rajkumari Jain) and tenant (Babu Singh Chauhan) disputed the validity of an allotment of tenancy in favor of the appellant without the landlord's nomination as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies when the landlord is not in physical occupation of the premises but retains legal possession.
Whether the rent control authority could allot vacant premises to a person not nominated by the landlord under Section 17(2) without affording the landlord an opportunity to nominate.
holdings: Section 17(2) applies even if the landlord is not physically residing in the premises, as legal possession through locked storage of belongings or occasional use constitutes sufficient occupation.
An allotment made without affording the landlord an opportunity to nominate a tenant under Section 17(2) is without jurisdiction and violates the statutory protection granted to landlords.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 16(1)(b)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 17(2)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to give effect to legislative intent
Jurisdictional error in administrative action
Legal possession distinct from physical occupation

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased tenant challenged the continuation of land ceiling proceedings after his death, arguing that such proceedings should be dropped if the holder dies before a surplus declaration under section 21.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, for determining surplus land, lapse upon the death of the holder before a declaration under section 21 is published?
Whether the liability to surrender surplus land is determined as of the appointed day, irrespective of the holder's death before formal declaration?
Whether the amendment to section 3(2) of the Act, which explicitly ignores death for surplus determination, altered the pre-existing legal position?
holdings: Proceedings under the Act do not abate upon the death of a landholder before a section 21 declaration; the liability to surrender surplus land is fixed as of the appointed day and survives death.
The liability to surrender surplus land is attached to the holding as of the appointed day and continues against the estate, irrespective of the holder’s death before formal declaration.
The amendment to section 3(2) merely clarifies the pre-existing law and does not change the legal position; the doctrine of ignoring death for surplus determination applied even before the amendment.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 3(2)
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 21
doctrines: Stare decisis
Continuation of statutory liability post mortem
Declaratory nature of amendments
Determination of liability as of the appointed day

card.dispute: The Controller of Estate Duty assessed the Madra Math properties as part of the deceased Mahant's estate, and the successor Mahant challenged the assessment, claiming the properties were trust properties not liable to estate duty.
issues_decided: Whether the Madra Math properties were personal properties of the deceased Mahant liable to estate duty or trust properties not liable to such duty.
Whether, assuming the properties were trust properties, the deceased Mahant had a beneficial interest that passed on death under Section 7 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
holdings: The Madra Math properties were trust properties, not the personal estate of the deceased Mahant, as determined by the proper interpretation of the Firman and the District Judge's judgment in the Title Suit.

The deceased Mahant had no beneficial interest in the properties that could pass on death; his interest was limited to common enjoyment with disciples, which ceased on death and did not pass to any successor, so no property passed under Sections 6 and 7 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
doctrines: Mixed question of law and fact
Deemed transfer of property on death
Beneficial interest under trust law
Cesser of interest upon death

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired in 1959, disputing the market value, interest rate, and denial of solatium.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded at Rs. 80 per sq. yd. reflects the fair market value on the relevant date?
Whether the claimants are entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the entire compensation amount?
Whether solatium at 15% was wrongly denied to the claimants?
holdings: The High Court correctly upheld the market value of Rs. 80 per sq. yd. as fair and based on proper appreciation of evidence.
Claimants are entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the entire compensation from the date of possession, not just on the enhanced amount.
Solatium was wrongly denied; compensation at Rs. 80 per sq. yd. could not be presumed inclusive of solatium without clear basis, warranting additional compensation of Rs. 3 per sq. yd.
doctrines: Principle of fair market value in land acquisition
Entitlement to solatium under land acquisition law
Award of interest on compensation to ensure just equivalent

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land during the pendency of a partition suit, challenged the Collector's partition under Section 54 CPC, claiming they had a right to be considered for equitable allotment despite not being named in the decree.
issues_decided: Whether transferees pendente lite have locus standi to seek equitable partition before revenue authorities under Section 54 CPC
Whether the Collector can consider the claims of transferees pendente lite in partition proceedings even if their names do not appear in the decree
holdings: Transferees pendente lite have locus standi to seek equitable partition before the Collector under Section 54 CPC if their title is undisputed and they apply to be heard.

The Collector may equitably allot shares to transferees pendente lite without referring back to the civil court, provided there is no dispute about the transfer, to advance justice and avoid unnecessary delay.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
doctrines: Pendente Lite Doctrine under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act
Locus Standi of Transferees in Execution Proceedings
Equitable Partition in Revenue Proceedings

card.dispute: The Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and the Income Tax Department disputed whether an oral partial partition of 18 immovable properties in 1963 was valid under the Income Tax Act, 1961, affecting the inclusion of income from those properties in the HUF's assessment.
issues_decided: Whether a partial partition of immovable properties under Hindu law, without physical division or monetary equalisation, qualifies as a valid partition under Section 171 of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Whether income from properties claimed to be partitioned can be included in the HUF's total income if no valid partition is recorded under Section 171.
holdings: A partial partition under Section 171 requires either physical division of properties or apportionment with monetary equalisation; mere severance of status or oral agreement without such steps does not suffice.
Until a valid partition is recorded under Section 171, the HUF remains the deemed owner of the property and its income must be included in the HUF's total income for assessment purposes.
doctrines: Deemed ownership under tax law
Physical division or apportionment as essential for valid partition under tax law
Continuity of HUF assessment until formal partition is established

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation from Rs. 10 to Rs. 7 per square yard for land acquired under the same notification as other lands compensated at Rs. 9 per square yard.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the compensation rate to Rs. 7 per square yard when similar lands under the same acquisition notification were awarded Rs. 9 per square yard?
Whether awarding differential compensation for adjoining lands under the same acquisition scheme violates principles of equity and non-discrimination?
holdings: When lands are acquired under the same notification for the same housing scheme and are comparable in location and size, they should be treated uniformly for compensation.
It is inequitable and discriminatory to award lower compensation to claimants for lands adjoining those awarded higher compensation under identical circumstances, warranting equalization of rates.
doctrines: Principle of equal treatment in acquisition compensation
Doctrine against arbitrariness in compensation awards

card.dispute: The decree-holder in a pre-emption suit deposited 25 paise less than the required amount by the deadline, later making up the shortfall; the vendee objected to execution, claiming the suit stood dismissed due to non-compliance.
issues_decided: Whether the execution of the decree was barred due to a short deposit of 25 paise beyond the court-ordered deadline
Whether the default in depositing the full amount could be condoned under the Civil Procedure Code
Whether the appeal to the High Court was barred by limitation due to delayed filing of the certified copy
holdings: A minor shortfall of 25 paise, due to bona fide mistake and subsequently made up, does not result in automatic dismissal of the suit under Order XX Rule 14(1)(b) CPC.
Courts have discretionary power under Section 148 CPC to condone delay and enlarge time to meet the ends of justice, especially where default is trivial and not deliberate.

An appeal filed without a certified copy but with court permission to file it later, and where the copy is filed promptly, is not barred by limitation if delay is condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 14(1)(b)
doctrines: Condonation of trivial default
Discretionary power of courts to prevent miscarriage of justice
Liberal interpretation of procedural requirements to serve substantive justice

card.dispute: The Government of Andhra Pradesh sought to summarily evict Thummala Krishna Rao and another from three plots of land under the Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, despite a prior suit having dismissed the University's claim to the land, raising a bona fide dispute over title.
issues_decided: Whether the Government can resort to summary eviction under Section 6 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, when there is a bona fide dispute over title to the land?
Whether the summary procedure under the Act is maintainable in cases involving long-standing occupation and complex questions of title?
Whether the Government can unilaterally decide its own title to land and evict occupants without due process of law?
holdings: The summary eviction remedy under Section 6 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, is not available when there is a genuine dispute over title between the Government and the occupant.
Long and open possession by the occupant raises a bona fide claim requiring adjudication by civil courts, not summary proceedings.
The Government cannot unilaterally assert title and evict occupants through summary action; due process of law requires a judicial determination of title in such cases.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 2
Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 5
Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 6
Andhra Pradesh Land Encroachment Act, 1905, Section 7
doctrines: Due process of law
Summary remedy not applicable to title disputes
Bona fide dispute doctrine
Adverse possession

card.dispute: The assessee Hindu undivided family and the Commissioner of Income Tax disputed whether a partial partition of family properties was validly effected under Section 171 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and whether income from such properties should be included in the family's taxable income.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in dispute were capable of physical division among coparceners as required by Explanation (a)(i) to Section 171 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and whether severance of status alone entitled the assessee to claim partial partition.
Whether income from properties claimed to be partitioned but without a valid finding under Section 171 should be included in the assessee's total income.
holdings: Properties capable of equitable physical division among coparceners, with monetary adjustments if needed, must be actually divided to qualify for partial partition under Section 171; mere severance of status is insufficient.
Where no valid partial partition is established under Section 171, the HUF remains the deemed owner of the property and its income must be included in the HUF's total income for taxation purposes.
doctrines: Physical division requirement for partial partition under Hindu law and income tax law
Deemed ownership doctrine under Section 171 of the Income-tax Act, 1961

card.dispute: The dispute was between Mool Chand Yadav and Raza Buland Sugar Company over whether Hari Bhawan, including a room occupied by Yadav, vested in the Corporation and whether he could continue occupying it.
issues_decided: Whether the operation of a court order directing vacation of a disputed room should be suspended during the pendency of an appeal.
Whether the continuation of possession during appeal would amount to flouting a court order.
holdings: During the pendency of an appeal, especially when admitted, the operation of an order with serious civil consequences should be suspended to prevent a swinging pendulum of possession.
While court orders must be respected, judicial prudence requires interim relief to maintain status quo when an appeal is pending against such an order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1
doctrines: Doctrine of status quo during appeal
Principle against multiplicity of proceedings and judicial economy

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's suit for eviction, claiming the U.P. Rent Act applied as ten years had passed since the building's construction, while the landlord argued the Act was inapplicable due to the building being less than ten years old.
issues_decided: Whether the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies to buildings constructed before its enforcement
What is the 'date of completion of construction' under Section 2(2) and Explanation I of the Act when both assessment and occupation dates exist
Whether Section 39 of the Act applies to a suit filed after the Act's commencement
holdings: The Act applies to all buildings regardless of whether construction was completed before or after the Act came into force; the language of Section 2(2) is clear and unambiguous.
For a building subject to assessment, the date of first assessment is deemed the date of completion of construction, not the date of first occupation.

Section 39 applies only if a suit was pending on the date of the Act’s commencement; it does not apply to suits filed later, especially when the Act itself is inapplicable due to the building being under ten years old.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(2) and Explanation I
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent derived from unambiguous statutory language
Doctrine of non-derogation from statutory conditions for retrospective application

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a joint Hindu family over whether the Kundgol Deshgat Estate, a watan property, was impartible and governed by lineal primogeniture or was partible as joint family property.
issues_decided: Whether the watan estate was impartible and governed by the rule of lineal primogeniture

Whether the provisions of the Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950 and the Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955 extinguished the right to partition under personal law
Whether the regrant of watan lands to the watandar under the Acts changed the character of the property from joint family property to individual impartible property
holdings: The watan property belonged to the joint Hindu family, and the right to partition such property under personal law was not affected by the abolition of watan under the statutes.

The extinguishment of watan rights under the Acts did not destroy the underlying character of the property as joint family property; the regrant of land to the watandar enured to the benefit of the entire family.

The restrictions on transfer or partition under the Acts are regulatory and require Collector's sanction, but do not create a statutory bar to partition; the property remains capable of partition subject to conditions.
provisions: Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950, Section 4(1)
Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955, Section 7
Bombay Inferior Village Watans Abolition Act, 1959, Section 4
doctrines: Canon of construction of non-obstante clauses
Continuity of property interests under personal law despite statutory abolition of tenures
Regulatory vs. substantive restrictions on property rights

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against the High Court's interference in a factual finding that a sub-tenant was protected under a rent control ordinance due to sub-letting occurring before May 21, 1959.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could reappreciate evidence and reverse concurrent factual findings of lower courts under Article 227 of the Constitution.
Whether the date of sub-letting was a pure question of fact or a mixed question of law and fact justifying High Court interference.
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence and reverse concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in exercise of its Article 227 jurisdiction; such action exceeds its scope.
The determination of the date of sub-letting is a pure question of fact, not a mixed question of law and fact, and thus not subject to interference under Article 227.
provisions: Bombay Rent, Rate and Tenancy Act, 1947
doctrines: Limited scope of interference under Article 227
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed
Distinction between questions of fact and mixed questions of law and fact

card.dispute: Mohammad Arif challenged the High Court's order declaring his appeal abated after the death of co-appellant Mohammad Ahmad, asserting his right to continue the appeal as a legal representative and property transferee.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated upon the death of a co-appellant when another appellant, who is a transferee of the deceased's interest, remains on record.
Whether Mohammad Arif, as a transferee of the deceased appellant's property, could be recognized as a legal representative without a formal application.
holdings: An appeal does not abate if a co-appellant, who is a transferee of the deceased appellant's interest in the disputed property, remains on record and can represent the deceased's estate.

A transferee of the deceased appellant's property is entitled to be treated as a legal representative in the appeal, at least as an intermeddler, without requiring a formal application to bring legal representatives on record.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 9
doctrines: Doctrine of abatement of appeal
Doctrine of legal representation in appeals
Intermeddler doctrine in succession

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, both displaced persons, applied for plots of nazul land; the State Government initially rejected all applications, then reversed its decision and allotted plots to the appellants without reconsidering others' claims, leading to a challenge over the fairness and legality of the allotment.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government could legally grant nazul land without auction without recording reasons in writing.
Whether the State Government could allot plots to the appellants without reconsidering or inviting fresh applications from other claimants after reversing its earlier policy of non-allotment.
Whether the power to dispose of nazul plots lies with the State Government or the Collector based on the land's value.
holdings: Granting leasehold rights in nazul land without auction is permissible only if the State Government records in writing good reasons for doing so; failure to do so renders the grant invalid.

When the State Government reversed its policy of not allotting land, it was obligated to reconsider all pending claims or invite fresh applications; allotting land solely to appellants without such process was arbitrary and unfair.
The question of whether the State Government or Collector has authority to dispose of plots need not be decided as the entire allotment process was vitiated at inception.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 149(2)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1954, Section 164(3)
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code Rules, 1956, Rules 2 to 26
doctrines: Principle of reasoned decision-making
Doctrine of equal opportunity in public allotment
Rule of fair procedure in administrative action
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness in state action

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the constitutional validity of two Gujarat amending acts that modified tenancy and agricultural land laws, alleging violations of Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Gujarat Act No. 16 of 1960 violates Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution?
Whether Gujarat Act No. 36 of 1965 violates Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution?
holdings: Gujarat Act No. 16 of 1960 is valid as it is included in the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution, which grants protection from challenges based on fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31.
Gujarat Act No. 36 of 1965 is valid as it forms part of agrarian reform, falls under Article 31A(1)(a), and is clarificatory in nature, thus protected from fundamental rights challenges.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (Bombay Act No. 67 of 1948)
doctrines: Doctrine of Protection under the Ninth Schedule
Doctrine of Agrarian Reform under Article 31A
Doctrine of Clarificatory Legislation

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murder and attempt to murder in connection with a violent altercation arising from a land dispute, and challenged the conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants Sunil Kumar and Ved Prakash committed murder under Section 302/34 IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304(1)/34 IPC
Whether appellant Ram Karan instigated and participated in the attack, warranting conviction under Section 302/34 and 307/34 IPC
Whether the prosecution proved premeditation or whether the incident occurred in a sudden fight in the heat of passion
holdings: Sunil Kumar and Ved Prakash were guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304(1)/34 IPC, not murder under Section 302/34 IPC, as the incident arose from a sudden quarrel without premeditation.

Ram Karan was entitled to benefit of doubt due to age and lack of reliable evidence linking him to active participation or instigation; his convictions under Sections 302/34 and 307/34 IPC were set aside and he was acquitted.

The attack was not in self-defence or under Exception 2 or 4 to Section 300 IPC, but the absence of premeditation and presence of sudden provocation reduced the offence from murder to culpable homicide.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Sudden fight in the heat of passion under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Grading of culpable homicide based on presence or absence of premeditation

card.dispute: The appellants, descendants of a family granted land and titles by the Peshwa and later rulers, claimed entitlement to money or pension as descendants of a 'Ruling Chief' under a 1948 Act, which the State denied.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were descendants of a 'Ruling Chief' within the meaning of Section 5(3)(ii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948.
Whether the historical status of the appellants' ancestors as jagirdars with certain privileges amounted to sovereign or semi-sovereign authority.
holdings: The appellants were not entitled to money or pension under Section 5(3)(ii) of the 1948 Act because they were not descendants of a 'Ruling Chief' as required by the provision.

The ancestors of the appellants, though holding jagirs and described as 'chieftains' in some records, were classified by the British Government as ordinary subjects, not feudatory or ruling chiefs with sovereign powers.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948, Section 5(3)(ii)
doctrines: Doctrine of classification by the Crown: The actual status conferred by the sovereign authority after investigation determines legal rights, not historical descriptions or titles.

Doctrine of sovereign status: Mere use of terms like 'chief' or 'ruling' does not confer sovereign or quasi-sovereign status without evidence of independent authority and recognition by the paramount power.

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Kanwal Sood, was prosecuted for criminal trespass after continuing to reside in a house gifted to a religious trust, following the death of the donor, who had originally permitted her to live there.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's continued occupation of the property after the donor's death amounted to criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC as amended by U.P. Act 31 of 1961
Whether the appeal to the Sessions Court was maintainable despite the imposition of only a fine
Whether criminal proceedings were an abuse of process in a primarily civil dispute over possession
holdings: Mere unauthorized possession after the termination of a lawful license does not constitute criminal trespass unless there is intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor.
An order imposing a fine and directing eviction under Section 456 CrPC is appealable, making the appellant's appeal to the Sessions Court maintainable.

When the right to possession is disputed and involves interpretation of a gift deed, initiating criminal proceedings amounts to an abuse of process; such disputes are civil in nature and must be resolved in civil court.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 441 (as amended by U.P. Act 31 of 1961)
doctrines: Criminal trespass requires mens rea
Distinction between civil and criminal proceedings in possession disputes
Doctrine of abuse of process

card.dispute: The appellant, a decree-holder in a pre-emption suit, sought possession of agricultural land but faced resistance over a 25 paise shortfall in deposit, leading to dismissal of execution proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the second execution appeal as barred by limitation due to delayed filing of certified copy
Whether the executing appellate court was correct in holding that a 25 paise shortfall in deposit led to automatic dismissal of the suit under Order 20, Rule 14 CPC
holdings: The High Court erred in dismissing the appeal on limitation grounds without considering its power under Section 148 CPC to condone delay, especially since it had permitted filing of the certified copy when available.

A 25 paise shortfall in deposit, made good later and arising from a bona fide mistake, does not warrant dismissal of a pre-emption decree; courts should exercise discretion under Section 148 CPC to prevent injustice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 14
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 1(2)
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Mandatory vs. directory interpretation of procedural rules
Discretionary power of courts to secure ends of justice

card.dispute: Sourindra Mohan Hazra fought against the State of West Bengal and others over the ex-parte dismissal of his case in the Calcutta High Court due to non-appearance allegedly caused by lack of notice.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had sufficient cause for not appearing at the hearing of the second appeal in the Calcutta High Court?
Whether the ex-parte order of the High Court allowing the second appeal should be set aside?
holdings: An appellant must be given a fair opportunity of being heard, and non-receipt of notice constitutes sufficient cause for non-appearance.
An ex-parte order passed without proper service of notice is unjust and must be set aside, and the appeal should be remitted for fresh disposal according to law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 27
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem
Natural justice

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh challenged the High Court's enhancement of compensation for land acquired for a housing society in Meerut.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing the compensation rate for acquired land based on a subsequent sale deed.
Whether the High Court wrongly relied on a sale deed from three years after the acquisition notification.
holdings: A sale deed executed three years after the acquisition notification can be relied upon to determine compensation if there is no evidence of market rate fluctuations.
The High Court did not commit an error in preferring a sale deed involving the acquiring body itself, especially when other comparable sales were unreliable due to financial distress of the seller.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in land compensation
Judicial deference to High Court's appreciation of evidence in absence of legal error

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision excluding land transferred by Mohd Ashrafuddin under unregistered sale deeds from his agricultural holding for ceiling purposes.
issues_decided: Whether land transferred under unregistered sale deeds but not formally conveyed can be included in the transferor's 'holding' under the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act?
Whether possession under part performance of a contract for sale vests the land in the transferee's holding to the exclusion of the transferor?
Whether the same piece of land can form part of the holdings of both the transferor and transferee under the Act?
holdings: The transferor remains the holder of land even if possession is transferred under an unregistered sale deed, as ownership continues despite defective title transfer.
The term 'held' in the definition of 'holding' includes both ownership and possession, and cannot be restricted to mere physical possession.
The same land may form part of the holdings of different persons in different capacities, as contemplated by the Act and its explanation, without causing legal inconsistency.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 3(i)
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 10
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 12
doctrines: Part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of constructive holding

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and the Forest Corporation challenged the High Court's order directing the government to accept the highest bids from a forest auction and allow contractors to work the forest lots, instead of allotting them to the Forest Corporation.
issues_decided: Whether the government was legally bound to accept the highest bids in the auction of forest lots
Whether the government's decision to cancel the auction and allot forest lots to the Forest Corporation was arbitrary or without reason
Whether the government's change of policy after the auction but before ratification was a valid ground for rejecting the highest bids
holdings: The government was not bound to accept the highest bid as the auction conditions made acceptance provisional and subject to ratification.
The government's decision to cancel the auction and allot forest lots to the Forest Corporation was valid and based on a legitimate policy reversion, not arbitrary.
A change in government policy after provisional acceptance but before final ratification is a sufficient reason to reject the highest bid.
doctrines: Principle of governmental policy change as a valid administrative reason
Non-acceptance of highest bid in public auction based on public interest and suspicion of mala fides
Doctrine of implied policy decision based on legislative and executive action

card.dispute: The appellant company sought to execute decrees for enhanced compensation against the State of Bihar, which objected that the State of West Bengal, not Bihar, was liable after the transfer of territories.
issues_decided: Whether the Patna High Court had jurisdiction to decide appeals pending after the transferred territories came under West Bengal
Whether the State of West Bengal was legally substituted for the State of Bihar in pending legal proceedings under Section 47 of the West Bengal (Transfer of Territories) Act, 1956
Whether the executing court could refuse execution on the ground that the State of West Bengal was the proper judgment-debtor
holdings: The Patna High Court retained jurisdiction to dispose of appeals pending before it if the Chief Justice did not certify transfer to the Calcutta High Court under Section 17(2) of the Act.
Under Section 47 of the Act, the State of West Bengal is deemed to be substituted for the State of Bihar in legal proceedings relating to transferred properties, even without a formal order.
A legal fiction in statute must be carried to its logical end; thus, decrees passed against Bihar are binding on West Bengal and execution must proceed against it after substitution.
provisions: West Bengal (Transfer of Territories) Act, 1956, Section 17
West Bengal (Transfer of Territories) Act, 1956, Section 47
doctrines: Legal fiction
Deemed substitution
Jurisdiction under territorial transfer statutes

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the method of compensation determination for his father's resumed jagir, arguing it should be based on actual income from rents as the jagir was unsettled, not on retrospectively applied rent rates.
issues_decided: Whether the jagir was 'settled' within the meaning of section 2(n) of the Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, after the 1953 rent rates were quashed by the High Court.
Whether compensation could be determined based on rent rates assessed in 1955 and applied retrospectively to 1953, despite the invalidation of prior settlement.
holdings: A jagir cannot be deemed settled if the earlier rent determination was quashed for procedural violations, as it creates a clean slate, rendering the village unsettled on the date of resumption.

Retrospective application of new rent rates after the date of resumption cannot alter the legal status of the jagir on that date; compensation must reflect the actual settled or unsettled status as of resumption.
provisions: Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 2(n)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 6(3)(a)(i)
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 7
Rajasthan Land Reforms and Resumption of Jagirs Act, 1952, Section 26
Jaipur State Grants Land Tenures Act, 1947, Section 82
Jaipur State Grants Land Tenures Act, 1947, Section 86
doctrines: Vested right doctrine
Tabula rasa doctrine
Prospective vs retrospective operation of administrative orders

card.dispute: Abu Khan and other non-evacuees fought against the Union of India and Maljimal over the possession and ownership of two properties in Jodhpur, specifically challenging the government's order allowing Maljimal, a displaced person, to retain one of the houses under Section 20-B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20-B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 was constitutional and could be used to justify the government's order in 1964?
Whether the order passed by the Central Government under Section 20-B, without hearing the non-evacuee claimants, was valid?
holdings: Section 20-B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 was declared ultra vires and struck down by this Court in 1968 for violating Article 31(2) of the Constitution, and since it was not re-enacted after the repeal of Article 31(2), it could not be used to pass a valid order in 1964.

An order made under an unconstitutional provision is illegal, invalid, and of no effect, regardless of whether the affected parties were heard, and thus the government's action under Section 20-B could not stand.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 20-B
doctrines: Ultra vires doctrine
Doctrine of invalidity of actions under struck-down statutes

card.dispute: The Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Tribes Cooperative Corporation and private traders, including tribals and non-tribals, fought over whether the Corporation had a monopoly on the trade of minor forest produce in the Rampa Agency or whether individuals could freely sell such produce to anyone.
issues_decided: Whether the Government of Andhra Pradesh could grant a monopoly over minor forest produce trade to the Corporation under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution.
Whether the High Court's declaration and injunction allowing tribals to sell minor forest produce freely to any buyer could stand after the enactment of Andhra Pradesh Regulation 1 of 1979.
holdings: The Government of Andhra Pradesh, under the Fifth Schedule, has the power to create a state monopoly in the trade of minor forest produce through a designated agency like the Corporation.

Andhra Pradesh Regulation 1 of 1979 nullifies any prior judicial declaration allowing free sale of minor forest produce; only the Corporation can buy such produce, and no individual may sell or trade it independently.
provisions: The Constitution of India, Article 133, Fifth Schedule, paragraph 5(2)
Andhra Pradesh Regulation 1 of 1979, Sections 2(d), 3, and 4
doctrines: State monopoly doctrine
Doctrine of legislative override by statutory regulation
Doctrine of tribal protection and economic welfare

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal heirs of a tenant who became a deemed purchaser under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, and subsequent purchasers claiming title through a will of the original landlord, over ownership and possession of agricultural land.
issues_decided: Whether a will executed by a landlord after the tenant became a deemed purchaser under Section 32 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, could validly transfer ownership of the land
Whether revenue authorities had jurisdiction to postpone the date of compulsory purchase under Sections 32-F and 32-G when the tenant had already become the deemed purchaser on April 1, 1957
Whether a statement by the deemed purchaser agreeing to deliver possession could create an estoppel against his claim of ownership
holdings: A will executed by a landlord after April 1, 1957, has no legal effect on land already transferred by operation of law to the tenant as a deemed purchaser under Section 32.
Proceedings under Sections 32-F and 32-G to postpone the date of purchase are void if initiated after the tenant has already become the deemed purchaser, as the tribunal lacks jurisdiction.

A statement by a deemed purchaser agreeing to deliver possession does not create estoppel, especially when made under ignorance of rights and where the landlord had no legal title to reclaim possession.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-F
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-G
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 14
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 15
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 84
doctrines: Estoppel by conduct
Jurisdictional fact doctrine
Nullity of orders passed without jurisdiction
Operation of law under statutory deemed purchase

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the inclusion of lands transferred by separated minor sons and the constitutional validity of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973, arguing violations of Articles 14 and 21.
issues_decided: Whether a 'separated minor son' is part of the family unit under Section 3(f) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973
Whether lands transferred by such separated sons before the Act's enforcement can be included in the family's holding
Whether the Act's definition of 'family unit' and ceiling limits violate Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the deprivation of surplus land under the Act violates the right to life under Article 21
holdings: A separated minor son does not form part of the family unit for determining ceiling limits under the Act.
Lands transferred before the cut-off date but not protected under Section 7 may still be included in the holding if the transferor is deemed to 'hold' the land under Section 3(i).
The classification under the Act is reasonable and does not violate Article 14, as it serves agrarian reform and reduces inequality.
Deprivation of surplus land for redistribution does not violate Article 21, as the right to livelihood is not included within the right to life.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 3(f)
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 3(i)
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 7
doctrines: Presumption of constitutionality
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Literal interpretation of 'holding' and 'held'
Right to life under Article 21 does not include right to livelihood

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a deceased appellant in a ceiling appeal fought over whether their delayed application for substitution, filed beyond 150 days of death, should be allowed despite abatement of the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, including Order XXII, applies to appeals under the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960?
Whether Articles 120 and 121 of the Limitation Act, 1963, apply to applications for substitution in ceiling appeals?
Whether the delay in filing the substitution application beyond 90 days could be condoned?
holdings: Section 38(1) of the U.P. Ceiling Act incorporates the entire procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure relevant to appeals, including Order XXII on death of a party.

If Order XXII of the Code applies, Articles 120 and 121 of the Limitation Act automatically apply, requiring substitution within 90 days of death and application to set aside abatement within 60 days of abatement.
The application filed after 150 days was barred by limitation, and the appellate court rightly dismissed it; no error in refusing condonation of delay.
provisions: U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 38(1)
U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 42
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rules 3, 9, 11
doctrines: Statutory incorporation of procedural law
Implied application of limitation periods when procedure is adopted
Abatement of appeal for non-substitution within prescribed time

card.dispute: Thekedars claimed possession of land against lessees, asserting they became hereditary tenants under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, while lessees claimed adhivasi rights under the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952.
issues_decided: Whether the Thekedars acquired the status of hereditary tenants under Section 12(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the lessees were in lawful cultivatory possession during 1359 Fasli to claim adhivasi rights under Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952
holdings: A Thekedar becomes a hereditary tenant under Section 12(1) only if the theka was granted exclusively for personal cultivation of the land and such cultivation was ongoing on 1st May 1950.
Cultivatory possession under Section 3 of the 1952 Act must be lawful; possession obtained by displacing a hereditary tenant is unlawful and does not confer adhivasi status.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 12(1)
doctrines: Lawful possession requirement for statutory rights
Strict interpretation of hereditary tenancy under land reform laws

card.dispute: The legal heirs of appellants sought to continue an appeal in a partition suit after the death of a respondent, but the appeal was held to have abated due to failure to timely substitute the deceased respondent's legal representatives.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to non-substitution of the deceased respondent's legal representatives within the prescribed time?
Whether the abatement should be set aside to allow the appeal to be heard on merits?
holdings: An appeal abates if legal representatives of a deceased party are not brought on record in time, and such abatement results in a valuable right accruing to the other party.
Despite negligence in delay, the abatement may be set aside in rare cases, especially in partition suits, to serve substantial justice, even if it prolongs proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10
doctrines: Substantial justice over technical compliance
Abatement of suit or appeal due to non-substitution
Laches and negligence in procedural matters

card.dispute: The state appealed the acquittal of Babu Ram and others by the Sessions Court in a murder case, leading to a conflict over whether the High Court could overturn the acquittal based on circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Court's acquittal based on two possible views of the evidence
Whether the prosecution's circumstantial evidence, including witness testimony and motive, was sufficient to sustain a conviction
Whether the witnesses were independent or biased due to caste and proximity to the victim's family
Whether the place and time of occurrence were correctly established by the prosecution
holdings: If two views on the evidence are possible, the appellate court must not interfere with the trial court's acquittal unless the view taken was not reasonably possible.
The prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt, especially given unreliable witness testimony and lack of corroborative evidence like serology reports.
Witnesses from the same caste and locality as the victim's family, with no independent motive to testify, may be considered biased and not credible.
The High Court erred in shifting the burden to the accused to disprove alternate facts; the prosecution must conclusively establish the scene and timing of the crime.
provisions: Powers of the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, Section 2
doctrines: Presumption of innocence in appeals against acquittal
Benefit of doubt in favour of the accused
Appreciation of circumstantial evidence requiring full satisfaction of all links in the chain
Deference to trial court's assessment of witness credibility and demeanour

card.dispute: Hereditary tenants (Thekadars) claimed possession of land against lessees who had been inducting into possession by Zamindars after 1950, asserting superior rights under land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Thekadars became hereditary tenants under Section 12 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the lessees acquired adhivasi rights under Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952
holdings: A Thekedar becomes a hereditary tenant if the Theka was granted exclusively for personal cultivation and such cultivation existed on 1st May, 1950.
A lessee cannot acquire adhivasi status under the 1952 Act if their possession is unlawful, i.e., they were inducted after depriving a hereditary tenant of lawful possession.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 12
doctrines: Lawful possession required for statutory rights
Strict interpretation of conditions for acquisition of hereditary tenancy

card.dispute: The appellant tenant sought to set aside an ex parte rent decree but was denied relief due to a technical defect in the stamping of a security bond, leading to a conflict over whether the bond was governed by the Court-fee Act or the Indian Stamp Act.
issues_decided: Whether a surety bond furnished under the proviso to Section 17(1) of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 must be stamped under the Indian Stamp Act or the Court-fee Act.
Whether non-compliance with stamping requirements, later cured, warrants dismissal of an application to set aside an ex parte decree on technical grounds.
