holdings: The Supreme Court declined to resolve the conflict between the Madras and Calcutta High Courts on whether the Indian Stamp Act or Court-fee Act applies to surety bonds under Section 17(1) proviso, leaving it open for future determination.

A litigant should not be denied justice on a technical defect in stamping a security bond if the defect is subsequently cured and the delay was due to conflicting judicial opinions; the application to set aside an ex parte decree cannot be dismissed solely on such grounds.
provisions: Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, Section 17(1) proviso
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Justice over technicality
Cure of procedural defect
Conflict of judicial precedent

card.dispute: Two rival pairs of claimants fought over the grant of a liquor licence, with the High Court initially quashing the Board of Revenue's decision in favour of the appellants and directing a fresh decision, leading to a conflict between judicial and administrative authorities.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 226 by reappraising evidence and directing the grant of a liquor licence to respondents No. 1 and 2.
Whether respondent No. 2, a student pursuing a B.Sc., qualifies as an 'educated unemployed youth' under Rule 223 of the Assam Excise Rules, 1945.
Whether the Board of Revenue was bound by the High Court's observations when it remanded the matter.
Whether the High Court's procedure of deciding one writ petition while keeping another pending was fair and lawful.
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 226 by reappraising evidence and substituting its own findings on suitability, which is beyond the scope of certiorari or mandamus.
A student still pursuing education cannot be considered an 'educated unemployed youth' as the term implies completion of education and subsequent unemployment.
The Board of Revenue was not bound by the High Court's observations unless they were clear directions, and it was entitled to rely on confidential reports without disclosing them to the parties.
The High Court's decision to adjudicate one writ petition while leaving another pending in the same matter violated principles of fair play and proper judicial procedure.
doctrines: Limitations on writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Rule of preference for 'educated unemployed youth'
Principle of fair play in judicial procedure
Confidentiality in administrative decision-making and natural justice

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the cancellation of his land allotment due to a 50% premium cut imposed on semi-urban evacuee land, arguing that the managing officer lacked authority under the Displaced Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the Managing Officer under the Displaced Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 could cancel an allotment originally made under the East Punjab Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1947.
Whether the action taken to impose a 50% premium cut prior to the amendment of Rule 14(6) of the Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 was valid.
Whether the appellant was entitled to be treated differently from other allottees who accepted the premium cut.
holdings: The Managing Officer had the authority to implement the premium cut and adjust allotments under the 1954 Act, as the land had become part of the compensation pool after the 1954 Act came into force.

The action to impose the 50% cut was valid because it was taken before Rule 14(6) of the Evacuee Property (Central) Rules, 1950 was amended; thus, the prior action did not need to comply with the amended rule.
No differential treatment could be allowed to the appellant as all 117 allottees in the semi-urban area were subject to the same policy decision, and 97 had already paid the extra premium.
provisions: East Punjab Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1947
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective operation of rules
Principle against undue enrichment in rehabilitation schemes
Doctrine of equal treatment among similarly situated allottees

card.dispute: The appellants sought interim injunction to prevent respondents from interfering with their possession of a disputed portion of land and from using FSI for the entire land, claiming title over 8006.04 sq. metres out of 17,000 sq. metres.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants had a prima facie case for grant of interim injunction regarding possession of the disputed land?
Whether the balance of convenience favoured granting interim injunction restraining use of FSI over the entire land?
holdings: The appellants established a prima facie case for interim injunction as they claimed lawful possession and risked irreversible loss if construction proceeded on disputed land.
The balance of convenience favoured the appellants because allowing construction on the entire land would make the dispute moot, while respondents could still use the undisputed 9,000 sq. metres.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX
doctrines: Prima facie case in injunction suits
Balance of convenience
Irreversible injury doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of provisions allowing their arrest and detention for recovery of dues owed to the U.P. State Electricity Board under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether Section 279(1)(b) read with Section 281 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, permitting arrest and detention for recovery of dues, is constitutionally valid?
holdings: The provisions allowing arrest and detention for recovery of dues under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, are constitutionally valid, as upheld in Ram Narayan Agarwal v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
provisions: U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 279(1)(b)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 281
doctrines: Constitutional validity of civil imprisonment for recovery of dues
Res judicata or binding precedent from a co-equal bench

card.dispute: Landowners and a sub-tenant (Sewa Ram) fought over entitlement to compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, with the sub-tenant claiming Bhumidhar status under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners became Bhumidhars under Section 15(2) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954 after redeeming the mortgage.
Whether the sub-tenant Sewa Ram acquired Bhumidhar rights under Section 13(1) of the Act despite being a sub-lessee.
Whether delay or absence of a formal declaration under the Act affects acquisition of Bhumidhar rights.
holdings: Mortgagor landowners are entitled to be declared Bhumidhars only for land under the mortgagee’s personal cultivation; not for land let out to tenants or sub-tenants.
A sub-tenant in possession on the commencement of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954 acquires Bhumidhar rights if he falls under a recognized tenant category under Section 13(1).
A tenant entitled to Bhumidhar rights acquires them from the date of the Act’s commencement, regardless of delay or absence of formal declaration.
doctrines: Acquisition of rights by operation of law
Mandatory declaration of Bhumidhars
Continuity of tenancy rights despite mortgage

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued the State and a Block Development Officer for injunction to protect their possession of two parcels of land, one based on purchase and the other on long possession with plantations, against interference.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was maintainable against the State and the Block Development Officer without notice under Section 80 of the CPC being served on the latter?
Whether the plaintiffs' long possession of government land entitled them to protection from forcible dispossession, especially regarding plantations raised by them?
holdings: Service of notice under Section 80 CPC on the State suffices for a suit against its officers acting as its agents; lack of separate notice to the officer does not bar the suit.
Mere long possession of government land without title does not confer ownership, but a trespasser may remove improvements like plantations made during possession before vacating the land.
doctrines: Notice requirement for suits against the government
Protection of improvements by possessors without title

card.dispute: The Shia and Sunni communities in Varanasi fought over the use of a plot of land containing graves, particularly regarding religious practices and the shifting of two graves allegedly encroaching on Shia religious space.
issues_decided: Whether the shifting of two graves from the northern to the southern side of an existing grave violates the fundamental rights of Sunnis under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution
Whether the suggestion to shift the graves is irreligious or destructive of religious rights under Islamic law
Whether the court has the jurisdiction and power to direct the implementation of the committee's suggestion to shift the graves
holdings: The exercise of religious rights under Articles 25 and 26 is subject to public order, and measures to maintain peace, including shifting graves, do not violate fundamental rights when necessary.
Shifting graves for maintaining public order does not amount to an irreligious act, as religious obligations are not absolute and must yield to societal interests.
The court has inherent power to implement its orders and remove obstacles, and directing the shifting of graves falls within the scope of ongoing proceedings to ensure peace.
doctrines: Public order as a limitation on fundamental rights
Balancing of religious rights with societal harmony
Inherent powers of the court to ensure implementation of its orders

card.dispute: The heirs of Haji Umar Kasam challenged the taking over of his properties as evacuee property by the Custodian under the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, after he left for Haj in 1947 and did not return.
issues_decided: Whether sub-section (2A) of section 8 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 validates vesting of property as evacuee property even if there was no defect in the prior law or court order?
Whether civil courts have jurisdiction to question the declaration or custody of evacuee property under the Act?
Whether the vesting of the suit properties under the Junagadh Act was valid and continued under the 1950 Act?
Whether the subsequent notification under the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extinguished the owners' rights in the property?
holdings: Section 8(2A) validates vesting of property as evacuee property regardless of any defect or invalidity in the prior law, and gives retrospective effect to such vesting.
Civil courts are barred from entertaining suits challenging the status of property as evacuee property or the legality of actions taken by the Custodian under the Act.
Properties taken over under a repealed law like the Junagadh Act are deemed to have validly vested under the 1950 Act if they purport to be evacuee property.

Publication of a notification under section 12 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, extinguishes all rights of the original owner in the property, which then vests absolutely in the Central Government.
provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 8(2A)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 28
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 46
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of deeming fiction
Doctrine of retrospective validation
Doctrine of ouster of jurisdiction
Doctrine of constructive vesting

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's acquittal of respondents convicted of murder, which was based on a compromise between village panchayats rather than evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could acquit accused in a murder case without evaluating the evidence, based solely on a compromise between caste panchayats.
Whether a criminal appeal against conviction for a non-compoundable offence like murder can be disposed of by treating it as a civil dispute settled by compromise.
holdings: A High Court cannot acquit an accused in a criminal case without considering the evidence on record, especially in a non-compoundable offence like murder.
Justice in criminal cases must be administered according to legal norms and not through informal panchayat-style compromises that bypass evidentiary scrutiny.
doctrines: Justice according to law
Non-compoundability of murder
Proper judicial procedure in criminal appeals

card.dispute: The Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) and the HUF's partnership firm challenged the Wealth Tax Officer's valuation of the HUF's interest in the firm based on market value rather than book value of properties.
issues_decided: Whether the interest of a HUF, through its Karta, in a partnership firm is includible in the HUF's net wealth for wealth tax purposes.
Whether the Wealth Tax Officer can depart from book value and refer assets to a Valuation Officer when market value significantly exceeds book value.
Whether Rule 2B(2) of the Wealth Tax Rules mandates use of market value when it exceeds book value by more than 20%.
holdings: A partner's interest in a firm, whether as an individual or as Karta of a HUF, is property liable to inclusion in the net wealth of the assessee under the Wealth Tax Act.

The Wealth Tax Officer has discretion under Section 7(2)(a) to determine the net value of a business as a whole having regard to the balance sheet, but is not bound by it and may make prescribed adjustments.
Where the market value of an asset exceeds its book value or written down value by more than 20%, Rule 2B(2) requires the use of market value for valuation under the Wealth Tax Rules.
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Discretionary power of assessing officer
Market value override doctrine under Rule 2B(2)

card.dispute: A simple mortgagee challenged the attachment of mortgaged property by a subsequent decree-holder, claiming entitlement to raise the attachment despite not being in possession.
issues_decided: Whether a simple mortgagee not in possession can file a claim petition under Order 21 Rule 58 CPC to raise an attachment before judgment?
Whether the attachment before judgment on 24-9-1964 attached the entire property or only the equity of redemption?
Whether a simple mortgagee has a legal standing to object to the attachment of the mortgagor's equity of redemption?
holdings: A simple mortgagee who is not in actual or constructive possession of the property cannot maintain a claim petition under Order 21 Rule 58 CPC to raise an attachment.
The attachment before judgment attached only the equity of redemption, not the entire interest in the property, as the mortgage predated the attachment.
A simple mortgagee has no legal right to object to the attachment of the mortgagor's equity of redemption, as the mortgagee’s interest is secured and unaffected by such attachment.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 58
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 38, Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 38, Rule 8
doctrines: Equity of redemption
Priority of security interest over unsecured decree
Constructive possession in mortgage law

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the validity and retrospective application of notifications exempting certain buildings from rent control laws in Chandigarh under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether Section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 is valid.
Whether the notifications issued on January 31, 1973, and later dates, operate retrospectively.
Whether buildings that satisfied exemption conditions before January 31, 1973, are entitled to exemption.
holdings: Section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 is valid as it empowers the government to exempt buildings from the Act.
The notifications issued under Section 3 do not have retrospective effect and apply only to buildings meeting conditions on or after January 31, 1973.
Exemption does not extend to buildings that were granted sewerage, electric connection, or occupied before January 31, 1973.
provisions: The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 3
The East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act (Extension to Chandigarh) Act, 1974, Section 3
doctrines: Presumption against retrospectivity of statutes affecting vested rights
Interpretation of statutory notifications based on language and surrounding circumstances
Distinction between legislative exemptions and delegated notifications in applying retrospectivity

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Madan Naik challenged the dismissal of a first appeal that had abated due to failure to substitute the deceased respondent in time, contesting the validity of the appellate court's decree and subsequent High Court rulings.
issues_decided: Whether the first appellate court could pass a decree dismissing the appeal on merits after holding that the appeal had abated.
Whether a second appeal under Section 100 CPC lies against an order refusing to set aside abatement of an appeal.
Whether the High Court was correct in allowing a Letters Patent Appeal after dismissing the second appeal as incompetent.
Whether the appeal from an order refusing to set aside abatement remains valid despite dismissal of an incompetent second appeal.
holdings: An appeal that abates due to non-substitution of a deceased party does not result in a decree on merits, and any such decree is null and void.
An order refusing to set aside abatement under Order 22 Rule 9 CPC is appealable under Order 43 Rule 1(k), but it is not a 'decree' and thus no second appeal under Section 100 CPC lies against it.
The dismissal of an incompetent second appeal does not render an appeal from an order refusing to set aside abatement infructuous; the latter remains valid and unaffected.
A Letters Patent Appeal against an order in an appeal under Order 43 Rule 1(k) does not lie, and the High Court erred in entertaining it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1(k)
doctrines: Abatement of appeal for non-substitution
No second appeal unless against a decree
Survival of appeal from non-merits order despite dismissal of second appeal
Nullity of decree where no adjudication on merits

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the certificated landlord's right to obtain possession of exempted land under Section 33-B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, alleging lack of bona fide requirement and disputing the validity of the partition that granted the landlord ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants could challenge the bona fides of the partition in proceedings under Section 33-B after the exemption certificate under Section 88-C had become final.
Whether the Revenue Tribunal was justified in remanding the case for admission of additional evidence relating to the partition's bona fides.
Whether the landlord bona fide required the land for personal cultivation under Section 33-B.
holdings: Once a certificate under Section 88-C is granted and confirmed, the validity and bona fides of the partition are conclusively determined, and tenants cannot re-agitate the issue in subsequent Section 33-B proceedings.
The Revenue Tribunal erred in remanding the case to admit evidence on the partition's bona fides, as that issue was already concluded between the parties.
The concurrent findings of fact by revenue authorities that the landlord bona fide required the land for personal cultivation are binding and cannot be re-examined by higher courts at a late stage.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 33-B
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88-C
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
doctrines: Res judicata in revenue proceedings
Conclusive effect of final orders under special statutes
Principle of finality of findings in fact-based revenue inquiries

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, which reduced land ceilings and strengthened tenants' rights, arguing violations of fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 14M, 17(c), 17(6), and 21B of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, as amended in 1972 and 1977, violate fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution
Whether the amendments have a reasonable nexus with the Directive Principle in Article 39(b)
Whether the amendments amount to confiscatory taking without compensation
Whether the requirement of raiyats residing in villages for a greater part of the year is arbitrary
holdings: The amendments are protected under Article 31C as they directly aim to secure the objectives of Article 39(b) by distributing agricultural land to tillers.
There is a sufficient nexus between the law and Article 39(b); 'distribution' includes apportionment and allocation of land to landless cultivators.
The amendments do not amount to confiscation as landlords retain land within ceiling limits and non-agricultural properties.
The residence requirement is reasonable and essential to ensure effective cultivation and prevent absentee landlordism.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, Sections 14M, 17(c), 17(6), 21B
Constitution of India, Article 39(b), Article 31C, Articles 14, 19, 31
doctrines: Doctrine of Nexus under Article 31C
Protection of laws implementing Directive Principles under Article 31C
Broad interpretation of 'distribution' in Article 39(b)
Unamendability of fundamental rights when overridden by valid social legislation under Article 31C

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the constitutional validity of West Bengal land reform amendments that redistributed surplus agricultural land to tillers, claiming violation of fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned land reform amendments violate fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 of the Constitution.
Whether there is a sufficient nexus between the amendments and the Directive Principle in Article 39(b).
Whether the requirement of residence for allottees is arbitrary or unreasonable.
holdings: Legislation aimed at securing Article 39(b) objectives is protected under Article 31C and cannot be challenged on grounds of violating Articles 14, 19, or 31.
There is a valid and close nexus between the land reform amendments and Article 39(b) as they facilitate equitable distribution of agricultural resources.
The residence requirement for land allottees is reasonable and essential to ensure effective cultivation and prevent absentee landlordism.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955 (as amended by the 1972 and 1977 Amendment Acts)
doctrines: Doctrine of Nexus
Protective scope of Article 31C
Pragmatic interpretation of Directive Principles

card.dispute: Munshi Ram sued Narsi Ram and another for possession of land based on his right of pre-emption, but the suit was dismissed due to non-joinder of a necessary party, Munni Devi, leading to an appeal on whether the amendment to include her was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the omission to implead Munni Devi as a defendant was due to a bona fide mistake under the proviso to Section 21(1) of the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the suit against Munni Devi could be deemed to have been instituted on the original date of filing despite her subsequent addition
Whether the bar of limitation applied to the application for amendment of the plaint to include a necessary party
holdings: Where a necessary party is omitted due to a bona fide mistake evident from official documents, and promptly added upon discovery, the suit against that party can be deemed to have been instituted on the original filing date.

A plaintiff who relies on a certified copy of a sale deed showing only some vendees acts with due care and attention, satisfying the requirement of 'good faith' under Section 2(h) of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The proviso to Section 21(1) of the Limitation Act allows the court to treat the suit as instituted on an earlier date if the omission was in good faith, thereby overcoming the bar of limitation.
Amendment to add a necessary party under Order I, Rule 10 CPC does not require a separate amendment of pleadings under Order VI, Rule 17 when the cause title is corrected to reflect all parties.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order I, Rules 9 and 10
Code of Civil Procedure, Order VI, Rule 17
doctrines: Bona fide mistake in non-joinder
Relation back of amendment under good faith
Deemed institution of suit
Necessary party under Order I Rule 10 CPC

card.dispute: The petitioner, claiming to be the successor of a surety, fought against the decree-holder and auction-purchaser over the validity of an execution sale and whether the decree was satisfied before the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner could move a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution after alternative remedies were available.
Whether the High Court could interfere with the Subordinate Judge's order refusing to set aside the execution sale.
Whether the decree could be deemed satisfied after the execution sale had taken place, affecting the rights of the auction-purchaser.
holdings: A petition under Article 227 is not maintainable when alternative remedies like appeal or revision under the CPC are available.
The High Court cannot use its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 to correct mere errors of law or re-appreciate evidence.
Once an execution sale is held and a third party's interest intervenes, the decree cannot be adjusted under Order XXI, Rule 2; only remedies under Order XXI, Rules 89 or 92 apply.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 92
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Inherent powers of court under Section 151 CPC
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Principles of natural justice
Fraud vitiating execution proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant advocate was accused of professional misconduct involving forgery and manipulation in a civil suit, leading to disciplinary proceedings initiated by complainants before the Bar Council of Uttar Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India had the jurisdiction to remand the matter to the State Bar Council for assigning reasons?
Whether the principle of 'autrefois acquit' applies to disciplinary proceedings against advocates?
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the remand order in the interest of justice and the appellant's pending job interview?
holdings: The disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India has wide discretion under Section 37(2) of the Advocates Act, 1961 to decide an appeal 'as it deems fit', including remanding the case for reasons, provided the order is germane to the Act and its objectives.

Disciplinary proceedings against advocates are not governed by the criminal law principles of 'autrefois acquit' or 'autrefois convict' as they are quasi-judicial and concern the integrity of the legal profession as a whole.

The Supreme Court declined to interfere with the remand order as the appellant had not participated in the proceedings before the State Bar Council and could still present his defense there, preserving the statutory scheme of peer adjudication under the Advocates Act.
doctrines: Wide discretionary power 'as it deems fit' must be exercised within the confines of the statute's purpose
Non-applicability of double jeopardy principles in professional disciplinary proceedings
Judicial restraint in disciplinary matters to uphold the autonomy of the legal profession

card.dispute: The appellant Mansaram, a retired government servant, fought against eviction from leased premises by respondent S.P. Pathak, who claimed Mansaram's occupation was unauthorized under the Rent Control Order.
issues_decided: Whether Mansaram's occupation of the premises was in contravention of clause 22(2) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
Whether Mansaram was liable to be evicted under clause 25 for ceasing to hold an office of profit
Whether the House Allotment Officer had jurisdiction to order eviction 22 years after Mansaram's entry
Whether the delay in challenging the occupation barred eviction on equitable grounds
holdings: Mansaram could not be evicted solely on the ground of contravention of clause 22(2) if he had entered on the landlord's assurance under clause 23(2), as such assurance validated his occupation.
Clause 25 applies only if the occupant received an allotment order due to holding an office of profit; in absence of such order, eviction on cessation of service is not permissible.
The House Allotment Officer lacked jurisdiction to evict Mansaram on the ground of ceased government service without proof of an initial allotment order.
Even if entry was initially unauthorized, eviction after 22 years is unreasonable and violates principles of fair exercise of power due to inordinate delay and acquiescence by landlords.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 22
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 23
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 25
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 28
doctrines: Reasonable exercise of statutory power within reasonable time
Acquiescence and delay vitiating enforcement of technical violations
Sine qua non of allotment order for application of eviction clause
Equitable discretion in enforcement of public policy provisions

card.dispute: The appellants (ryots) and respondents (landlords) fought over whether the land in question was 'ryoti land' in an 'Estate' under the Madras Estates Land Act, which would determine whether civil or revenue courts had jurisdiction to hear rent recovery suits.
issues_decided: Whether Uruturu village was an 'Estate' within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
Whether the land in dispute was 'ryoti land' within an Estate, thereby ousting the jurisdiction of the Civil Court.
Whether the burden of proof was correctly placed and discharged regarding the status of the land as part of an Estate.
holdings: A grant expressed to be of a named village is deemed to be an Estate under Section 3(2)(d), raising a statutory presumption that the entire area forms an Estate.
The burden of proving that a grant does not fall within the definition of an Estate lies on the party asserting it, and that burden was not discharged here.
The High Court erred in reversing the Lower Appellate Court’s finding, misinterpreted evidence, and wrongly shifted the burden of proof to the defendants.
provisions: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
doctrines: Statutory presumption
Burden of proof
Jurisdiction of Civil Court vs Revenue Court

card.dispute: The appellant, as reversioner of the last male owner, claimed a share in compensation for acquired property, challenging the binding nature of an alienation by the widow, a limited owner.
issues_decided: Whether a reversioner can claim apportionment of compensation during the lifetime of a widow who holds a limited interest in the property.
Whether an alienation by a widow with a limited interest binds the reversioner.
holdings: A reversioner cannot claim any present title or compensation in respect of property during the lifetime of a widow holding a limited interest.
The right of a reversioner to claim compensation does not arise until after the death of the limited owner, regardless of the validity of the alienation.
doctrines: Doctrine of limited interest of a Hindu widow
Doctrine of reversionary rights under Hindu law

card.dispute: The landlord challenged the tenant's application under Section 32PP of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, seeking determination of purchase price after the statutory sale was earlier declared ineffective due to the tenant's non-appearance.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord is precluded from challenging the tenant's status in proceedings under Section 32PP after the sale was declared ineffective under Section 32G(3) due to non-appearance?
Whether the status of the applicant as a tenant is conclusively determined by the issuance of notice under Section 32G and the declaration of ineffective sale?
holdings: A landlord is not precluded from challenging the tenant's status in a Section 32PP proceeding merely because notice was issued under Section 32G and the sale was declared ineffective; the tenant's status must be independently proved.

The mere issuance of notice under Section 32G and non-appearance does not conclusively establish tenancy; the Tribunal must determine jurisdictional facts, including actual tenancy on April 1, 1957, unless estoppel applies by landlord's admission.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32G
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32PP
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Estoppel
Jurisdictional facts doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's reversal of their acquittal and conviction in a murder case arising from a land dispute, arguing that they acted in private defence.
issues_decided: Whether the Sessions Judge erred in acquitting the accused by misreading and improperly evaluating the prosecution evidence.
Whether the plea of right of private defence was sustainable given the nature and extent of injuries inflicted.
Whether non-production of an alleged earlier FIR report undermines the prosecution case.
holdings: The Sessions Judge erred in rejecting credible prosecution evidence based on trivial discrepancies and artificial reasoning, warranting reversal of acquittal.
The nature and number of injuries, and the fact that the attack continued after victims were incapacitated, negated any claim of private defence under Exception (ii) to Section 300 IPC.
The non-production of an alleged earlier FIR does not discredit the prosecution case when the substance of the complaint was timely conveyed and corroborated.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Exception (ii) to Section 300
Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, Section 2
doctrines: Right of private defence cannot justify excessive force causing death when the threat has ceased.
Principles for reversing acquittal: only when no other view is reasonably possible.
Corroboration of FIR through independent witnesses removes suspicion of concealment.

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976, arguing it violated Articles 14, 19, and 31 by not being a genuine agrarian reform measure.
issues_decided: Whether the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976 is a measure of agrarian reform within the meaning of Article 31A of the Constitution.
Whether the application of the Act to agricultural lands in urban areas affects its character as agrarian reform.
Whether the payment of higher compensation to landholders undermines the agrarian reform objective of the Act.
holdings: The Act is a measure of agrarian reform as its dominant purpose is the equitable redistribution of land by making tillers the owners and imposing land ceilings.
The inclusion of agricultural lands within urban limits does not alter the agrarian character of the Act if such lands are predominantly used for agriculture.
The amount of compensation paid to landholders is a legislative choice and does not negate the agrarian reform purpose of the law.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976, Sections 2(12), 7(2)(b), 13, 14, 17
doctrines: Dominant purpose test for determining agrarian reform legislation
Liberal interpretation of Article 31A expressions like 'estate' and 'rights in an estate'
Legislative competence to determine compensation and scope of agrarian laws

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the procedure for recovering sales tax arrears through arrest and detention under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, claiming it violated Articles 14, 19(1)(d), and 21 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure of arrest and detention for recovery of tax arrears under the U.P. ZALR Act violates Articles 14, 19(1)(d), and 21 of the Constitution
Whether Section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to the process of arrest under the U.P. ZALR Act
Whether Rule 251 of the U.P. ZALR Rules mandating an inquiry before detention was complied with
holdings: The procedure of arrest and detention for recovering tax arrears is not punitive but a coercive measure for recovery and does not violate Articles 14, 19(1)(d), or 21 if applied lawfully.
Section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply as the U.P. ZALR Act and its rules provide a complete code for arrest and detention.
The failure to conduct a mandatory inquiry under Rule 251 before detention renders the arrest warrants invalid and requires them to be quashed.
provisions: U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, Section 8(3) and (8), Section 33
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 279(1)(b), Section 281, Section 341
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rule 247, Rule 247A, Rule 247B, Rule 251
Constitution of India, Article 14, Article 19(1)(d), Article 21
doctrines: Coercive recovery not violative of fundamental rights if not punitive
Complete code doctrine
Mandatory procedural compliance for deprivation of liberty

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of the tenant from the entire shop, but the court had to decide whether partial eviction was justified and from which portion of the shop.
issues_decided: Whether the landlady was entitled to complete eviction of the tenant from the shop.
Whether partial eviction was justified and, if so, from which portion of the shop—front or back.
holdings: The landlady failed to prove necessity for full eviction; partial eviction was justified due to her need to accommodate her son's business.
Partial eviction from the back portion of the shop was equitable, as it minimized hardship to the tenant and did not prejudice the landlady's legitimate needs.
doctrines: Doctrine of proportionality in eviction
Balancing of hardships between landlord and tenant

card.dispute: The landlords challenged the liquidator's caretaker agreement for office premises, arguing it violated rent control laws and exceeded the liquidator's powers under the Companies Act.
issues_decided: Whether the liquidator could legally enter into a caretaker agreement for the company's premises without court sanction under Section 457(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1956.
Whether the caretaker agreement was a permissible arrangement or a disguised lease/sub-lease in violation of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
Whether the liquidator could part with possession of premises not required for winding up the company.
holdings: The liquidator cannot carry on any business, including leasing premises, without court sanction and only if necessary for the beneficial winding up of the company.
A caretaker agreement that effectively grants exclusive possession and compensation is impermissible if it circumvents rent control laws and does not serve the winding-up purpose.
Where the liquidator does not need the premises for winding-up activities, the court must direct surrender of possession to the landlord to avoid unlawful occupation.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Sections 13 and 15
doctrines: Beneficial winding-up doctrine
Prohibition against colourable exercise of power
Statutory tenancy protection under rent control laws

card.dispute: The assessee (Seth Gopaldas HUF) fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over the validity of a partial partition of joint family properties for tax assessment purposes.
issues_decided: Whether a partial partition of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) is valid under the Income-tax Act, 1961
Whether the Income-tax Officer is obligated to recognize a valid partial partition for assessment purposes
holdings: A partial partition of a Hindu Undivided Family is valid if there is a clear separation of interests in specific properties among coparceners.
The Income-tax Officer must recognize a valid partial partition and assess the resulting smaller HUFs or individual shares accordingly.
doctrines: Partial partition of HUF
Recognition of family arrangements in tax law

card.dispute: The sub-tenant, Shyam Babu, challenged the eviction order passed under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, arguing that the authorities failed to consider his hardship as required by the fourth proviso to Section 21.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-tenant is entitled to the protection of the fourth proviso to Section 21 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972?
Whether the prescribed authority must consider the comparative hardship of a sub-tenant when deciding a release application under Section 21?
holdings: A sub-tenant, whose sub-tenancy was created with the landlord's consent, is entitled to the protection of the fourth proviso to Section 21 of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972.
The prescribed authority must consider the comparative hardship of both the sub-tenant and the landlord before ordering release of premises under Section 21.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21 (fourth proviso)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(j) and Section 3(a)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation in favor of beneficial legislation
Constructive tenancy relationship between sub-tenant and tenant-in-chief
Binding effect of factual findings in prior proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over the demarcation of property boundaries and the removal of eaves protruding onto the appellant's land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in allowing a review petition and setting aside its own judgment as well as those of the lower courts.
Whether the High Court could remand the case to the trial court without framing additional issues and calling for fresh findings.
holdings: A High Court is not fully justified in setting aside its own judgment and those of the lower courts solely on account of an alleged error in measurement noticed in a review petition.
The proper course is for the High Court to frame additional issues arising from the pleadings and call for findings from the trial court, rather than remanding the entire case.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
doctrines: Review of judgment
Concurrent findings of fact
Principle of finality of decrees
Proper procedure in second appeals

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent entered into a court-approved compromise requiring the appellants to deposit Rs. 60,000 by a fixed date to set aside a property sale; when they failed to deposit on time, they sought an extension of time, which the High Court denied, leading to a dispute over whether the court had power to grant such an extension.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the power to extend time for depositing money under a court-approved compromise when time was stipulated as the essence of the agreement?
Whether Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to extend time in cases where a compromise has been made an order of the court?
holdings: When a compromise is made an order of the court, the time stipulated in the compromise becomes time allowed by the court, and the court retains jurisdiction to extend time under Section 148 CPC in appropriate cases to prevent manifest injustice.

The court's power to extend time is not ousted merely because parties agreed that time was of the essence; the court may relieve against forfeiture when the compromise has merged into a judicial order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV, Rule 5
doctrines: Merger of compromise into court decree
Power of court to extend time under Section 148 CPC
Relief against forfeiture
Consensual postponement of statutory mandates

card.dispute: The sister of a deceased man fought with his paternal uncle's sons over inheritance of his ancestral and non-ancestral property.
issues_decided: Whether property inherited from paternal ancestors is ancestral property in the hands of a male holder as regards collaterals and female heirs when there is no surviving male issue.
Whether procedural defects in filing an appeal and second appeal should lead to dismissal of the appeals on technical grounds.
holdings: Property inherited from paternal ancestors is ancestral only as regards the male lineal descendants of the holder; for collaterals and female heirs, it is the holder’s absolute property and devolves by succession.

Procedural rules must serve justice; appeals should not be dismissed on technical grounds like non-personal presentation or delayed filing of a trial court copy if substantial justice demands consideration on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 33, Rule 3
doctrines: Ancestral property under Hindu law
Rule of absolute ownership in absence of coparceners
Liberal interpretation of procedural rules to secure justice on merits

card.dispute: The appellants, including Surjit Singh, were convicted of murder; the dispute centered on whether Surjit Singh should be sentenced to death under Section 303 IPC or have his conviction altered to Section 302 IPC with a lesser sentence, and whether the other appellants should be convicted under a lesser offense.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 303 IPC is valid after it was declared unconstitutional?
What sentence should be imposed on Surjit Singh under Section 302 IPC?
Whether the other appellants should be convicted under Section 323 IPC instead of Section 302/34 IPC?
holdings: Conviction under Section 303 IPC cannot stand as it was struck down for violating Articles 14 and 21; it must be altered to a conviction under Section 302 IPC.
The death sentence is not warranted under Section 302 IPC given the circumstances, including the use of the blunt side of the weapon and the underlying land dispute.
Section 34 IPC applies to the other appellants as they shared a common intention to kill, evidenced by their presence and participation at midnight; conviction under Section 302/34 IPC is upheld.
doctrines: Unconstitutionality of Section 303 IPC for violating equality and right to life
Doctrine of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Proportionality principle in sentencing

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and a liquor vendor, Dina Nath, fought over whether his residential property could be attached and sold in recovery proceedings for unpaid licence fees under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887, despite an exemption under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
issues_decided: Whether Section 60(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applies to attachment and sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887.
Whether a residential house is exempt from attachment and sale in revenue recovery proceedings under clause (ccc) of the proviso to Section 60(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
holdings: Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies only to execution of civil court decrees and does not govern attachment or sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887.

The exemption under clause (ccc) of the proviso to Section 60(1) of the Code does not apply to revenue recovery proceedings, as the Punjab Land Revenue Act contains its own complete scheme and does not incorporate such exemptions.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of execution provisions
Exemption from attachment in execution
Self-contained code doctrine

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra fought against Vyasendra over whether land held by his wife as her separate or stridhan property could be included in the family unit's total holding for computing agricultural land ceiling limits.
issues_decided: Whether land held by a wife as her separate or stridhan property can be clubbed with the family unit's holdings for determining ceiling limits under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961.
Whether the High Court erred in directing the tribunal to inquire into the nature of the wife's property interest when assessing the family's ceiling area.
holdings: All land held by any member of a family unit, whether jointly or separately, including a wife's separate or stridhan property, must be deemed held by the family unit for ceiling calculation.
The nature or character of a member's interest in land, including claims of separate ownership, is irrelevant for determining the ceiling area permissible to the family unit.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 4(1)
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 3
doctrines: Pooling of family holdings for ceiling purposes
Irrelevance of individual property character in ceiling legislation

card.dispute: The landlord sued to eject the tenant, who claimed a right to extend the lease and purchase the property under the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act; the dispute centered on whether the amended version of Section 9 applied to the pending proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the amended Section 9 of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1960 applies to pending ejectment suits.
Whether the tenant's right to purchase the property is governed by the original or amended provisions of Section 9.
Whether the landlord could seek relief under the amended Section 9 after the Supreme Court disposed of the appeal concerning the unamended Act.
holdings: If a suit is pending when an amendment comes into force, the amended provisions govern the disposal of the suit.
An incomplete proceeding under the original Section 9 must yield to the amended provisions, and the earlier order under the unamended law stands aborted.
It was open for the landlord to seek relief under the amended Section 9 in the lower court after the Supreme Court decided the appeal limited to the validity of the unamended provisions.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
Madras City Tenants' Protection (Amendment) Act, 1960, Section 9
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 10
doctrines: Prospective vs retrospective operation of amendments
Incomplete proceedings yield to amended statutes
Doctrine of implied repeal and statutory substitution

card.dispute: Ved Gupta, the individual licensee of a cinema theatre, versus the partnership firm and its partners who claimed the licence was a firm asset and sought to operate the theatre after expelling him.
issues_decided: Whether the cinema exhibition licence held by Ved Gupta in his personal name was an asset of the partnership firm?
Whether the District Magistrate had the authority to suspend film exhibitions by persons other than the licensee?
Whether the impugned order violated the principles of natural justice?
Whether the District Magistrate had jurisdiction to pass the order under the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1933?
holdings: A cinema exhibition licence granted to an individual is personal to the licensee and does not become a partnership asset merely because the firm claims ownership or uses the premises.
The District Magistrate has the implied power to suspend film exhibitions by unauthorized persons to enforce compliance with the Cinematograph Act and its rules.
Principles of natural justice do not apply when restricting unauthorized operation of a cinema, as no legal right or legitimate expectation exists to violate statutory licensing requirements.
The impugned order did not suspend the licence but only unauthorized exhibitions, and thus fell within the District Magistrate’s administrative and enforcement powers under the Act.
doctrines: Principle of statutory licensing as personal to the licensee
Implied powers of administrative authorities to enforce regulatory statutes
No application of natural justice where no legal right is infringed
Distinction between suspension of licence and suspension of unauthorized activity

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of provisions allowing their arrest and detention for non-payment of dues recoverable under the U.P. Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972 and the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether Section 279(1)(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, which authorises arrest and detention for recovery of arrears, is constitutionally valid?
Whether Section 281 of the same Act, enabling imprisonment for non-payment of dues, violates constitutional rights?
holdings: Section 279(1)(b) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 is constitutionally valid as it serves a public purpose and does not violate Article 21.
Section 281 of the Act, allowing imprisonment for recovery of dues, is valid and does not amount to punitive detention without due process.
provisions: U.P. Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 279
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 281
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional validity
Doctrine of due process under Article 21

card.dispute: Sunni Muslims of Varanasi challenged the Supreme Court's direction to shift two graves, arguing it violated their religious rights, while the state and Shia Muslims supported the order to maintain public order.
issues_decided: Whether the direction to shift the graves violated the Sunni Muslims' fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution?
Whether the shifting of graves constitutes desecration or is prohibited under Islamic law?
Whether the Court's interference was proportionate to the need for maintaining public order?
holdings: The fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26 are not absolute and must yield to public order; the direction to shift graves was justified to prevent recurring violence.
Shifting graves is not prohibited under the Holy Koran or Islamic law, especially when required for public order, and does not amount to desecration.
The interference was proportionate, as less drastic measures were previously rejected, and the direction aimed at a permanent solution to sectarian violence.
doctrines: Proportionality doctrine
Public order limitation on religious rights
Judicial review of religious practices

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict tenants, claiming need for personal occupation and unauthorized sub-letting; tenants contested both grounds.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for eviction on the ground of personal occupation was maintainable within three years of the landlord's acquisition of the property
Whether the tenant was liable for eviction on the ground of sub-letting without consent after the enforcement of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act
holdings: A suit for eviction on the ground of personal occupation is not maintainable if filed within three years of the landlord's acquisition of the property, as prohibited under Section 13(3A) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act.

Eviction on the ground of sub-letting is not sustainable if the sub-tenancy was created before the Act's enforcement with the landlord's consent, and the issue was already decided against the landlord's predecessor-in-title.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(3A)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(i)(f)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 16(2)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 16(3)
doctrines: Res judicata
Prohibition on eviction suits within three years of property acquisition
Validity of sub-tenancy with prior landlord consent

card.dispute: The appellants (surety) challenged the validity of a fresh execution application filed by the decree-holder (respondent No. 1), arguing it was barred by limitation due to delay beyond the 12-year period under Section 48 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a partial stay of execution (e.g., stay of sale of attached property) qualifies as a 'stay of execution' under Section 15(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908, thereby excluding the period of stay from limitation.
Whether the decree-holder is entitled to the benefit of Section 15(1) when only a part of the decree or execution against a particular property is stayed.
holdings: A partial stay of execution, such as a stay on the sale of attached property while attachment continues, constitutes a 'stay of execution' under Section 15(1) of the Limitation Act, 1908.
The benefit of Section 15(1) is available to the decree-holder even if the stay is not absolute, provided the injunction or order prevented execution in any form during the period.
doctrines: Beneficent construction of limitation laws
Stay of execution extends the limitation period for decree enforcement

card.dispute: The appellants (sub-tenants cultivating land) and respondents (transferees from the Rani of Tuni) fought over whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide who was the lawful ryot under the Andhra Pradesh Estates Abolition Act, 1948, in suits for possession.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the question of who is the lawful ryot under Section 56 of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1948?
Whether the jurisdiction of the civil court is ousted in favour of the Settlement Officer for deciding disputes regarding lawful ryot status?
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide the question of who is the lawful ryot under Section 56(1)(iii) of the 1948 Act, as this issue is exclusively within the purview of the Settlement Officer.
The decision of the Settlement Officer under Section 56 is final and cannot be questioned in any civil court, thereby ousting civil court jurisdiction over such disputes.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1948, Section 56(1)(iii)
Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari Act, 1948, Section 56(2)
doctrines: Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Finality of administrative determination

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the imposition of octroi duty by Jharsuguda Municipality after its factory area was included within municipal limits.
issues_decided: Whether the octroi duty imposed under Section 131(1)(kk) of the Orissa Municipal Act, 1950 was valid after the area was included in the municipality?
Whether the bye-laws imposing octroi duty were legally applicable to the newly included area?
Whether the levy of octroi duty violated Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as being unreasonable or excessive?
holdings: The inclusion of an area into a municipality under Section 4(3) of the Orissa Municipal Act, 1950 makes all existing provisions of the Act, including bye-laws and notifications, automatically applicable to that area under Section 5, unless the State Government directs otherwise.

A statutory presumption under Section 3 of the Orissa Municipal Act upholds the validity of bye-laws published in the Gazette, and no separate publication or notice is required for their application in newly included areas.

The octroi duty imposed at 1% ad valorem is reasonable and does not violate Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, as the municipality provides essential civic amenities necessitated by the entry of goods.
doctrines: Statutory presumption of validity of Gazette notifications
Automatic extension of municipal laws to newly included areas
Reasonableness test under Article 19(1)(g)

card.dispute: Co-owners disputed whether one party could use a common channel on jointly owned land to irrigate their property using water from their exclusive well.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner can use common property for irrigation from an exclusive well without consent of other co-owners
Whether the use of a common channel by one co-owner imposes an impermissible burden on the common property
Whether the High Court could rely on prejudice not pleaded or proved by the defendants
holdings: A co-owner has the right to use common property in a beneficial manner as long as it does not prejudice other co-owners.
Use of a common channel to carry water from an exclusive well does not create an unlawful burden if it causes no damage or detriment.
A court cannot base its decision on prejudice to co-owners unless it is specifically pleaded and proved.
doctrines: Right of co-ownership
Stare decisis
Judicial propriety

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction and arrears of rent, but the tenant challenged the validity of the notice for not correctly describing the tenanted premises.
issues_decided: Whether the notice under section 12(1)(a) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 must relate to the entire accommodation actually let to the tenant.
Whether a defective notice under section 12(1)(a) can be cured by subsequent amendment of the plaint.
holdings: A notice under section 12(1)(a) must demand arrears of rent in respect of the accommodation actually let to the tenant; a notice relating to a different or lesser portion invalidates the suit.
An amendment of the plaint cannot cure a defective or invalid notice under section 12(1)(a), as the notice is a prior condition for maintainability of the suit and is independent of the pleadings.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(3)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Notice as a condition precedent to suit
Relation back of amendments does not validate prior procedural defects

card.dispute: The government companies challenged the High Court's decision to include the value of stock of coking coal on April 30, 1972, in determining the amount payable to the mine owner for the management period.
issues_decided: Whether the value of the stock of coking coal on April 30, 1972, should be included in the accounts for determining the amount payable to the owner under Section 21(2) of the Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1971.
holdings: The stock of coking coal on April 30, 1972, must be accounted for in the statement of accounts under Section 22 to determine the net amount due to or from the owner under Section 21(2), as per commercial accounting principles.
provisions: Coking Coal Mines (Statement of Account) Rules, 1972
doctrines: Principle of commercial accounting
Statutory interpretation in light of legislative purpose
Balancing of accounts for management period under nationalisation

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued the State of Bihar for declaration of title and possession of immovable property, but filed the suit before the two-month notice period under Section 80 CPC expired, leading to a dispute over the suit's maintainability.
issues_decided: Whether a suit against the government is maintainable if instituted before the expiry of the two-month notice period under Section 80 CPC?
Whether Section 80 CPC is a mandatory provision that bars the institution of a suit during the notice period?
holdings: A suit against the government or a public officer cannot be validly instituted until two months after notice is delivered under Section 80 CPC; filing before expiry renders the suit not maintainable.
Section 80 CPC is mandatory and creates a statutory bar to suit institution, not merely a procedural requirement, and admits no exceptions even for urgent relief.
doctrines: Mandatory statutory notice
Public policy underlying procedural requirements
Plain meaning rule in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord filed an eviction application against a partnership firm without naming its partners, and the firm challenged the maintainability of the application.
issues_decided: Whether an eviction application under the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, can be maintained against a partnership firm in the firm's name without impleading the partners.
Whether non-joinder of partners amounts to a fatal defect or can be treated as a mere misdescription correctable during proceedings.
holdings: Since the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to proceedings under the HRC Order, a firm cannot be sued in its name alone without the partners being impleaded.
An eviction application against a firm without naming partners is a case of misdescription, which can be corrected at any stage by amending the application to include the partners.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(vi) and (vii)
doctrines: Misdescription of parties
Suing and being sued in the name of a firm

card.dispute: The partnership firm of Chhotelal Pyarelal challenged the maintainability of an eviction application filed against it by the landlord, Shikarchand, under the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether an eviction application under the HRC Order can be maintained against a partnership firm without impleading its individual partners?
Whether misnaming the firm as the sole respondent in an eviction proceeding amounts to a fatal defect?
holdings: An eviction application under the HRC Order can be maintained against a partnership firm even if individual partners are not impleaded, as the firm represents its partners.
The omission to name individual partners is a mere misdescription that can be corrected by amendment at any stage of the proceedings without dismissing the application.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(vi) and (vii)
doctrines: Misdescription of parties
Amendment of pleadings to reflect proper parties

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Dalhousie Properties Ltd fought over whether municipal taxes could be deducted from annual value for income tax purposes even if not actually paid by the assessee.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'borne by the owner' in the proviso to section 23(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 refers to the municipal tax liability the owner is legally liable to pay or only to the amount actually paid.
Whether an assessee can claim deduction of municipal taxes under section 23(1) without having actually paid them, especially when the liability is disputed.
holdings: The term 'borne by the owner' in the proviso to section 23(1) refers to the tax liability the owner is legally obligated to pay, not the amount actually paid.

An assessee is entitled to deduct municipal taxes from annual value under section 23(1) even if the taxes have not been paid, provided the liability exists and is enforceable, regardless of a pending dispute over the levy.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'borne' in fiscal legislation
Annual value as a notional, not actual, income concept
Consistency and stability in computation of annual value

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax and the assessee, Raghubir Narain Singh, disputed over the correct valuation of 'net wealth' under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, particularly regarding compensation receivable, decrees not yet executed, and set-offs for agricultural income tax and garnishee orders.
issues_decided: Whether unexecuted monetary decrees should be valued at their full face value or at a discounted market value considering realisation hazards under Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
Whether the value of compensation receivable under the Bihar Land Reforms Act should be reduced by the debt of agricultural income tax before inclusion in net wealth.
Whether amounts due under decrees, already attached by garnishee orders, should be included in the assessee's net wealth.
Whether the valuation of an asset must account for liabilities or set-offs that directly affect its realisable value in the open market.
holdings: Unexecuted decrees must be valued at their market value on the valuation date, considering the hazards of realisation, not at their full decretal amount.
The market value of an asset must be determined after accounting for any statutory or enforceable deductions, such as agricultural income tax, that reduce its realisable value.
A decree attached by a garnishee order remains an asset but must be valued at its net realisable value, considering the likelihood of recovery after attachment.
When an asset is subject to a liability that diminishes its value, such as a set-off, that factor must be considered in valuing the asset under Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act.
doctrines: Market value assessment considering realisation hazards
Net realisable value principle for encumbered assets
Separate valuation of assets and liabilities with interplay in market estimation
Principle of open market willing buyer-willing seller

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Wealth Tax and the assessee, Maharaja Kumar Kamal Singh, disputed whether arrears of agricultural income tax could reduce the value of the assessee's right to compensation under the Bihar Land Reforms Act for wealth tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the possibility of deduction of arrears of agricultural income tax under Section 4(c) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act affects the valuation of the right to compensation under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.

Whether such arrears, though non-deductible as a debt under Section 2(m) of the Wealth Tax Act if outstanding for more than twelve months, can still be considered in estimating the market value of the asset.
holdings: The possibility of deduction of agricultural income tax arrears under Section 4(c) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act is a relevant factor in estimating the market value of the right to compensation, as it affects what a willing buyer would pay.

Section 7(1) of the Wealth Tax Act requires valuation based on open market price, and any legal obligation or hazard affecting value must be considered, even if the debt cannot be directly deducted under Section 2(m).
doctrines: Open market value principle
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Distinction between asset valuation and debt deduction

card.dispute: The appellant, a former licensee, fought against the respondents (licensors) over possession of rooms, claiming title by adverse possession after the license was terminated.
issues_decided: Whether mere continuation of possession after termination of a license can lead to acquisition of title by adverse possession?
Whether an overt act asserting hostile title is necessary for a licensee to claim adverse possession?
holdings: Mere unauthorized possession after license termination, even for over 12 years, does not by itself result in adverse possession.
A licensee must perform an overt act demonstrating assertion of title hostile to the licensor to claim adverse possession.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Hostile title assertion
Overt act requirement in adverse possession by licensee

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition notification on grounds of delayed public notice and unjustified invocation of urgency provisions.
issues_decided: Whether a 29-day delay between publication in the Official Gazette and public notice in the locality invalidates a notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether pre-notification administrative delays negate the validity of invoking urgency provisions under Section 17(4) to bypass the enquiry under Section 5-A.
holdings: Section 4(1) requires contemporaneous but not necessarily simultaneous publication in the Gazette and public notice; a reasonable gap does not invalidate the notification if both are completed before further action.
Pre-acquisition administrative delays do not invalidate the invocation of Section 17(4) if urgency existed at the time of notification; the focus is on the urgency at that moment, not prior delays.
doctrines: Contemporaneity doctrine in statutory compliance
Strict compliance with mandatory procedural requirements
Doctrine of urgency in land acquisition

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the execution of an eviction decree, arguing it was inexecutable under the 1972 Rent Act and could not be revived by the 1976 Amendment Act.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for eviction, rendered inexecutable by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, could be revived and made executable by the 1976 Amendment Act with retrospective effect.
Whether the doctrine of eclipse applies to a post-enactment statutory amendment that removes a legal bar to execution of a decree.
holdings: A decree that becomes inexecutable due to a statutory provision is not nullified but remains dormant; it revives when the legal bar is removed by a subsequent validating amendment.
The doctrine of eclipse applies to statutory laws: a law rendered inoperative by a prior enactment regains validity when the conflicting provision is amended or removed, without needing re-enactment.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 9
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) (Amendment) Act, 1976, Section 26
doctrines: Doctrine of Eclipse
Retrospective Operation of Amending Statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a nephew of a deceased tenant, claimed tenancy rights over a shop by virtue of a will and continuous possession, while the landlord sought eviction under the U.P. Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be deemed a tenant under Section 3(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, as an 'heir' by virtue of a will
Whether tenancy rights in a non-residential building can be devised by a will under the Act
Whether the appellant was entitled to protection under Section 14 of the Act, as amended or unamended
holdings: A nephew is not an heir under Section 3(a) of the Act merely by being named in a will, as 'heir' in this context refers to those entitled by law of succession, not by testamentary disposition.
Tenancy rights under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 are not heritable by will; they devolve only as per the statutory scheme and personal law, and cannot be transferred via testament.
The appellant did not satisfy the conditions for protection under Section 14 of the Act, as he was neither a tenant nor an heir at the relevant time, and eviction proceedings were pending.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(g)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 11
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 13
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 14
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 15
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'heir' in rent control laws
Non-transferability of tenancy rights by will
Scheme of rent control legislation restricting devolution of tenancy

card.dispute: The appellant, H. D. Vora, challenged the eviction from a requisitioned flat after the state failed to derequisition it, while the third respondent, the new owner, sought to end the 30-year-old requisition order.
issues_decided: Whether a requisition order for a residential flat can remain valid indefinitely without being quashed or revoked
Whether the High Court could entertain a writ petition challenging a requisition order after thirty years
Whether the appellant became a direct tenant of the landlord by paying rent, thereby nullifying the requisition order
holdings: A requisition order is inherently temporary and cannot continue indefinitely; it ceases to be valid after a reasonable period, such as thirty years, as it would otherwise amount to a fraud on the power of requisition.

The long delay in challenging the requisition does not bar judicial review when the continuing validity of the order is in question, especially where the requisition has lost its transitory character.
Payment of rent by the allottee to the landlord with state assent does not convert the allottee into a direct tenant or nullify the requisition order; possession remains governed by the requisition.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950, Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 42
doctrines: Distinction between acquisition and requisition of property
Fraud on power doctrine
Temporary nature of requisition for public purpose

card.dispute: The appellants claimed to be members of the larger joint Hindu family of Pannalal Girdharlal and sought a declaration of their entitlement to a share in the family business and properties, which the respondents contested on grounds of res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by the appellants was barred by res judicata due to earlier judicial findings.
Whether the larger joint Hindu family of Pannalal Girdharlal continued to exist after 1940–41 or had undergone disruption.
holdings: The earlier suit (No. 338 of 1957) conclusively determined that the larger joint Hindu family was disrupted in 1940–41 and the business thereafter became a partnership of five brothers, which operates as res judicata against the current claim.
The finding of disruption and conversion into a partnership, having been specifically contested and decided by all three courts, bars the relitigation of the same issue in the present suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11 (Res Judicata)
doctrines: Res judicata
Disruption of joint Hindu family
Partition by metes and bounds

card.dispute: The tenant, Ishar Singh, fought the landlords and revenue authorities over whether his application for possession of agricultural land was barred by limitation under the Pepsu Tenancy Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 50 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, applies to proceedings under Section 43 of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, in the absence of a prescribed limitation period.
Whether the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955.
holdings: Section 50 of the Punjab Tenancy Act does not apply to proceedings under the Pepsu Tenancy Act unless expressly incorporated; no external limitation period can be imported in the absence of such a provision.
The Limitation Act does not apply to proceedings under the Pepsu Tenancy Act, and where no limitation is prescribed by the Act itself, the application cannot be dismissed as time-barred.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 43
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory incorporation by reference
Principle of exclusion of limitation in special statutes
