provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 1(3)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 26
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Prospective vs retrospective operation of law
Validation of legislative provisions

card.dispute: The adopted son of a deceased man sued to recover possession of land from a tenant of the deceased's widow, who resisted eviction claiming protection under tenancy law.
issues_decided: Whether a widow is deemed to cultivate land personally when it is cultivated through a tenant under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the successor-in-title of a widow can evict a tenant without following the procedure under Section 31 of the Act.
holdings: A widow is deemed to cultivate land personally even if the land is cultivated through a tenant, as per Explanation 1 to Section 2(6) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.

The successor-in-title of a widow must follow the procedure under Section 31 of the Act, including giving notice and applying to the Mamlatdar within one year of the widow's death, to evict a tenant and claim personal cultivation.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(6)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(18)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 4
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 31
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32F
doctrines: Deemed personal cultivation
Successor-in-title obligations under tenancy law
Statutory protection of tenants

card.dispute: The petitioner claimed ownership of a one-third share in agricultural land after the death of a widow who held it under a compromise decree for maintenance, but the widow had bequeathed it by will; the dispute centered on whether her interest became absolute under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the interest of a Hindu widow in property allotted to her in lieu of maintenance becomes an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is vague, discriminatory, and violative of Articles 14 and 15(1) of the Constitution
holdings: A Hindu widow's limited interest in property allotted for maintenance becomes an absolute estate upon the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, under Section 14(1), even if the source of the interest is a compromise decree.
Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act is not vague or unconstitutional; it is saved by Article 15(3) of the Constitution as a special provision for women.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional validity presumption
Benign interpretation of statutes benefiting women
Enlargement of limited estate into absolute ownership under Section 14(1)

card.dispute: The petitioner, an adopted son, fought to claim ownership of land previously allotted to his adoptive father's widow for maintenance, after her death, challenging the constitutional validity of Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, which granted her an absolute estate.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is void for vagueness and uncertainty?
Whether Section 14(1) of the Act violates Article 14 and Article 15(1) of the Constitution by discriminating on the basis of sex in favour of Hindu women?
holdings: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is not void for vagueness; though judicially criticized for poor drafting, it is capable of consistent interpretation and application as demonstrated in prior rulings.

Section 14(1) does not violate Article 14 or 15(1) because it constitutes a valid special provision for women protected under Article 15(3), aimed at remedying historical disabilities faced by Hindu women in property rights.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional validity presumption
Benign interpretation of remedial statutes
Classification under Article 14
Protective discrimination under Article 15(3)

card.dispute: The plaintiffs claimed an easement right to light and air through doors and windows opened into a gali (passage) adjacent to their land, which the defendant had enclosed after acquiring ownership of the gali.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff acquired an easementary right by implication from the deed of gift to open doors and windows into the gali for light and air.
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts in second appeal.
holdings: The deed of gift did not confer any easementary right to the plaintiff; it only mentioned that the gali was left for the defendant’s enjoyment of architectural features, with no implication of rights in favor of the plaintiff.
The High Court erred in interfering with concurrent factual findings of the lower courts in second appeal, especially based on a misinterpretation of the deed.
doctrines: Easement by implication
Concurrent finding rule in second appeal

card.dispute: Reversioners claimed possession of home-farm land under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950, despite not being in physical possession on the vesting date.
issues_decided: Whether a reversioner can claim possession of home-farm land under Section 4(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act, 1950 without being in physical possession on the vesting date.
holdings: To retain possession of home-farm land under Section 4(2), the proprietor must have been in physical possession on the vesting date; mere entitlement to possession is insufficient.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 2(g)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 3
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(1)
Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, Section 4(2)
doctrines: Physical possession as a prerequisite for retention rights
Vesting of proprietary rights in the State extinguishes private rights unless specifically preserved
Principle of continuation of possession, not recovery of possession

card.dispute: The petitioner NGO fought the State of U.P. and others over the environmental damage caused by limestone quarrying in the Dehradun-Mussoorie region.
issues_decided: Whether limestone quarrying in certain categories should be allowed to continue given environmental and ecological concerns.
Whether a balance can be struck between industrial development and environmental conservation in mining activities.
Whether the recommendations of the Bhargava Committee and the Working Group on quarry classification should be accepted.
holdings: Quarries classified as Category C by the Bhargava Committee and those in the Sahsatdhara Block must be permanently closed due to environmental risks.
Quarries in Category B (Bhargava) or Category 2 (Working Group) must not operate until a high-powered committee evaluates submitted schemes and recommends conditions for operation.
Quarries in Category A (Bhargava) or Category 1 (Working Group) outside Mussoorie city limits may continue, subject to compliance with mining and environmental laws.
Industrial development must not come at the cost of ecological imbalance; a balance must be struck between growth and environmental protection.
doctrines: Sustainable development
Precautionary principle
Public trust doctrine
Balance between development and environmental protection

card.dispute: Environmental activists fought the State of U.P. and limestone quarry lessees over the environmental damage caused by unregulated quarrying in the Dehradun-Mussoorie region.
issues_decided: Whether limestone quarrying in ecologically sensitive areas should be permanently or temporarily stopped due to environmental degradation.
Whether the court can direct closure of quarries and creation of afforestation programs despite economic and employment consequences.
Whether displaced lessees are entitled to priority in new mining leases.
Whether lessees can remove minerals already mined but lying at the site after closure orders.
holdings: Quarries in ecologically critical categories (C and some B) must be permanently closed to prevent irreversible environmental harm, regardless of existing leases.
The state must initiate reclamation, afforestation, and soil conservation using the Eco-Task Force and provide displaced workers employment in these programs.
Displaced lessees must be given priority in new mining leases in other areas, subject to eligibility, to balance ecological and economic interests.
Lessees may remove minerals already mined and lying at the site within four weeks under strict supervision, provided such minerals fall within their lease terms.
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Sustainable Development
Precautionary Principle
Polluter Pays Principle

card.dispute: The appellant lessee refused to pay rent for fishery rights, claiming the lessors' interest had vested in the State under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, while the respondents sought recovery of rent for two years.
issues_decided: Whether the fishery rights in question vested in the State under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, thereby ending the lessors' interest
Whether khas (direct) possession is required for an intermediary to retain tank fishery rights under Section 6 of the Act
holdings: Tank fisheries do not vest in the State under Section 6 of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, and are retained by intermediaries, so the lessors' rights continued despite the Act.
Khas possession is not a necessary condition for an intermediary to retain tank fisheries under Section 6; the provision does not require direct possession for retention.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 5
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6
doctrines: Frustration of contract
Vesting of intermediary interests free from encumbrances
Retention of specific properties by intermediaries despite vesting

card.dispute: The landholder (Sakuru) challenged the declaration of the tenant (Tanaji) as owner of agricultural land, seeking to appeal after delay and condone it under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is applicable to appeals filed before the Collector under Section 90 of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950?
Whether the Collector had jurisdiction to condone delay in filing an appeal under Section 5 of the Limitation Act prior to the 1979 amendment?
holdings: The provisions of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 do not apply to proceedings before the Collector under the Tenancy Act unless expressly made applicable, as the Collector is not a 'Court'.
Section 93 of the Tenancy Act, as originally enacted, only incorporated provisions for computing limitation (Sections 12–24 of the Limitation Act), not for condonation of delay under Section 5.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 90
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 91
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 93
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of limitation provisions in special enactments
Distinction between courts and quasi-judicial/executive authorities for applicability of Limitation Act
Prospective operation of amendments to statutory law

card.dispute: The appellant, Sardar Tota Singh, claimed to be a lawful sub-tenant of premises sub-sublet to him, while the respondent, Gold Field Leather Works, argued that the sub-sub-tenancy was invalid due to unauthorized subletting.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-sub-tenancy created by a lawful sub-tenant falls within the protection of Section 15(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the appellant's continued possession since before May 21, 1959, entitles him to protection under Section 15(2)
Whether a concession by the respondent that an intermediate sub-tenant was lawful binds the parties in determining the validity of further sub-tenancies
holdings: Section 15(2) of the Bombay Rent Act validates sub-tenancies created before May 21, 1959, if the sub-tenant was in possession on that date, even if the sub-tenancy was created by a lawful sub-tenant.
The appellant’s sub-sub-tenancy is valid because he was in continuous possession before and on May 21, 1959, and the intermediate sub-tenant was lawfully entitled to sublet.
A concession by a party in court that an intermediate sub-tenant was lawful binds that party and supports the validity of subsequent sub-tenancies dependent on it.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15(2)
Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(a)
doctrines: Validation of illegal sub-tenancies by statutory fiction
Binding effect of judicial admissions
Statutory interpretation of rent control provisions in favor of tenants in possession

card.dispute: The appellant claimed management rights over a religious endowment based on a will by the founder's widow, while the respondents, including an adopted son, claimed succession to the shebaiti rights.
issues_decided: Whether the founder's widow succeeded to the shebaiti rights after the founder's death.
Whether the widow's shebaiti right, as a Hindu female, was a limited or absolute right under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Whether the widow could validly transfer her shebaiti rights by will to another person.
holdings: The shebaiti right devolves as heritable property on the founder's heirs in absence of a contrary provision in the endowment deed or custom.
Under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the widow's limited shebaiti right became an absolute right, which she could dispose of by will.
A widow holding absolute shebaiti rights can transfer them by will to a qualified Hindu who can perform or arrange for the religious duties.
doctrines: Hereditary devolution of shebaitship
Enlargement of female Hindu's limited interest to absolute ownership under Section 14(1)
Blending of office and property in the concept of shebaitship

card.dispute: The appellant, a minor, sued for partition of joint family property, claiming a share in land later declared as surplus under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, which the state sought to acquire.
issues_decided: Whether a court decree for partition constitutes a 'disposition' under Section 21(2) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, and is invalid if it involves surplus land.
Whether the vesting of surplus land in the State Government under Section 21(4) depends on actual possession being taken by the Collector.
holdings: A partition decree that allocates surplus land is a 'disposition' within the meaning of Section 21(2) of the Act and is invalid and of no effect, as the term includes transfers under court decrees.
The prohibition under Section 21(2) on any disposition of surplus land applies immediately upon notification in the Official Gazette, regardless of when the State takes physical possession.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 8
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 9
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 10
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 12
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 14
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 16
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 18
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 21
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 18(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation (literal and purposive)
Doctrine of forfeiture of surplus land under ceiling laws
Collusive litigation

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the High Court's decision allowing a lessee to mine felspar and quartz in a reserved forest area without prior approval from the Central Government under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
issues_decided: Whether the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 applies to mining leases granted before its commencement when new minerals are discovered within already disturbed forest land.

Whether prior approval of the Central Government under Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 is required for extracting additional minerals from forest land already broken up for mining before the Act came into force.
holdings: The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 does not require prior approval from the Central Government for extracting new minerals from forest land already used and disturbed for mining before the Act's commencement.

Section 2 of the Act only prohibits fresh breaking up or clearing of forest land; it does not apply to continued or expanded mineral extraction within areas already converted to non-forest use prior to October 25, 1980.
doctrines: Strict construction of environmental statutes to prevent deforestation
Non-application of statutory restrictions to pre-existing rights or uses

card.dispute: The State of Bihar fought with the heirs of Prithwi Chand Lall Choudhary over liability for damages due to alleged mismanagement during the state's temporary control of the Raj Nazarganj estate.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Bihar and its officers were protected from tortious liability under Section 31 of the Bihar State Management of Estates and Tenures Act, 1949, for actions done in good faith during the management of the estate.
Whether the officers of the State acted with wilful default or gross negligence in managing the estate or in filing certificate cases for rent recovery.
Whether the State was liable to reimburse a penalty of Rs. 2,000 paid by the plaintiff for non-payment of Agricultural Income Tax.
Whether the cost of management exceeding 25% of gross collections had to be refunded by the State.
holdings: Section 31 of the Bihar State Management of Estates and Tenures Act, 1949, read with Section 4(22) of the Bihar and Orissa General Clauses Act, 1917, bars claims against the State or its officers for acts done in good faith, unless wilful default or gross negligence is proven.

The filing of a large number of certificate cases based on the plaintiff’s own arrears list does not amount to wilful default or gross negligence on the part of the State’s officer, especially given the short time available and lack of specific proof.

The penalty of Rs. 2,000 for non-payment of Agricultural Income Tax was too remote from the management act and could not be attributed to the State’s actions, particularly after the initial notification was found lawful.
The State must refund Rs. 8,000 as management costs exceeded the statutory limit of 25% of gross collections, and the officer had offered to return such excess.
provisions: Bihar State Management of Estates and Tenures Act, 1949, Section 31
Bihar and Orissa General Clauses Act, 1917, Section 4(22)
doctrines: Good faith under statutory immunity
Wilful default and gross negligence as exceptions to state immunity
State liability in tort for unauthorized acts or excessive costs
Burden of proof in claims against the State

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra fought with the heirs of Abhimanji over whether surplus agricultural land should be determined based on the original holder's holding on the appointed day or recalculated in favor of heirs as independent tenure holders after his death.
issues_decided: Whether the death of a landholder before declaration of surplus land extinguishes the liability to surrender surplus land under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961.
Whether the heirs of a deceased landholder can claim to be treated as independent tenure holders entitled to individual ceiling limits.
holdings: The liability to surrender surplus land is determined as of the appointed day and continues despite the death of the landholder before formal declaration.
Heirs cannot claim to be independent tenure holders entitled to separate ceiling limits; the surplus is determined based on the original holder's holding on the appointed day.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 12
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 16
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 21
doctrines: Relation back doctrine
Res judicata
Continuity of liability despite death

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Lalloo and others, who had been convicted and sentenced to death for the murder of Babu Jaleshwar Singh based on eyewitness testimony and circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the First Information Report (FIR) was recorded at the spot on the night of the incident or at the police station the next morning, and whether its delayed registration affected its credibility.
Whether discrepancies in the testimonies of eyewitnesses regarding their presence in Ballia on the day of the murder were material enough to discredit their account of witnessing the crime.

Whether the prosecution's case, based on the evidence of three eyewitnesses, was strong enough to sustain a conviction under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC when the High Court had acquitted the accused.
Whether the death sentence should be upheld given the long delay in the disposal of the appeal.
holdings: The FIR was recorded at the spot on the night of the incident and handed over to the police station the same evening; minor procedural irregularities do not undermine its reliability.
Minor discrepancies in eyewitness accounts about travel to Ballia were not material and did not affect their credibility as witnesses to the murder.
The evidence of the three eyewitnesses was consistent and credible, and the High Court erred in acquitting the accused when only one reasonable conclusion—guilt—was possible from the evidence.

Although the murder was brutal and death sentence initially justified, the inordinate delay in hearing the appeal warranted commutation of the sentence to life imprisonment under Article 142(1) of the Constitution.
doctrines: Appreciation of eyewitness testimony in criminal cases
FIR as a contemporaneous document and test of its reliability
Principle of constructive res gestae
Doctrine of inordinate delay in criminal appeals affecting sentence severity
Power of Supreme Court under Article 142 to do complete justice

card.dispute: The State of Punjab fought Labh Singh over whether he was liable to surrender surplus agricultural land after redeeming a mortgage, which increased his holding beyond the statutory ceiling.
issues_decided: Whether redemption of a mortgaged land constitutes a 'transfer' under Section 32-L of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955
Whether Section 32-A of the Act applies only at the time of its commencement or continues to apply subsequently
Whether a landowner who exceeds the permissible landholding limit after redemption of mortgage is liable to surrender surplus land
holdings: Redemption of a mortgage does not amount to a 'transfer' under Section 32-L, as it merely restores the mortgagor’s possession and does not constitute a new transfer.
Section 32-A operates continuously and not merely at the time of the Act’s commencement; it prohibits holding land beyond the ceiling at any time.
A landowner who acquires excess land through redemption of mortgage is liable to surrender the surplus under Section 32-A.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 2(f)
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-A
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-L
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 32-M
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Purpose and object of land ceiling legislation
Equity of redemption in mortgage law

card.dispute: The State of Punjab sought to recover a housing loan from members of a cooperative society by arresting and detaining them, but the society argued that the State must first proceed against the mortgaged property as per the loan agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the State can recover a housing loan as arrears of land revenue by arresting and detaining borrowers without first proceeding against the mortgaged property.
Whether the contractual terms of the loan agreement restrict the State's power under the Punjab Land Revenue Act to resort to personal arrest for recovery.
holdings: The State must first proceed against the mortgaged property to recover the loan amount before resorting to personal recovery measures like arrest and detention.
The government is bound by the terms of the loan agreement and cannot bypass the agreed recovery mechanism by directly invoking powers under the Punjab Land Revenue Act.
doctrines: Contractual obligation prevails over statutory recovery mechanisms when parties have agreed to a specific mode of recovery.
Doctrine of pacta sunt servanda – agreements must be honored by all parties, including the State.

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and Dhrangadhra Chemical Works Ltd fought over whether the company was liable to pay minimum guaranteed royalty for failing to manufacture 50,000 tons of salt annually, despite selling less than that amount.
issues_decided: Whether clauses 3 and 5 of the 1950 agreement impose a binding obligation to pay minimum royalty for shortfall in salt production
Whether royalty under clause 2 is chargeable only on salt sold and delivered, not on total manufactured quantity
holdings: Clauses 3 and 5 of the agreement create a separate liability to pay minimum guaranteed royalty when production falls below 50,000 tons, even if less salt is sold; clause 5 is not rendered otiose by clause 2.
Royalty under clause 2 is chargeable only on the quantity of salt actually sold and delivered, not on total manufactured, as per the clear terms of the clause.
doctrines: Interpretation of contractual clauses to avoid rendering any clause otiose
Principle of harmonious construction of contract terms

card.dispute: The State of Orissa fought against residents of Ganjam and Damodarpur villages over the validity of a notification constituting their area as a notified area under the Orissa Municipal Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the proclamation issued under Section 417-A(1-a) of the Orissa Municipal Act, 1950 was sufficiently clear regarding the purposes of the Act for which administrative provision was intended.
Whether the publication of the proclamation in English in a local newspaper, where the local population primarily understood Oriya, satisfied the statutory requirement of public notice.
holdings: A proclamation under Section 417-A(1-a) must clearly specify whether administrative provisions are proposed for all or only some purposes of the Act, and if only some, which ones, to enable residents to make informed objections.

Publication of a proclamation in a local newspaper must be in the local language (Oriya) to effectively inform and enable participation by residents, as the purpose is to elicit genuine public response.
doctrines: Principle of fair notice in administrative action
Substantial compliance with statutory public consultation requirements
Effective public participation in local governance

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's decision to allow a writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of eviction proceedings under the U.P. Act on grounds of arbitrariness and discrimination.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned U.P. legislation permitting eviction of unauthorized occupants of government premises violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating arbitrary or discriminatory classification
Whether the Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in Raja Ram Verma v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which struck down the Act as ultra vires, remains good law
holdings: Legislation enabling speedy eviction of unauthorized occupants from government and municipal premises does not violate Article 14 if it provides a reasonable purpose and procedure, and does not entail harsh or onerous discrimination.

The decision of this Court in Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay impliedly overrules Raja Ram Verma's case, and thus the impugned Act cannot be struck down on grounds of constitutional invalidity under Article 14.
doctrines: Doctrine of equality before law (Article 14)
Doctrine of implied overruling
Doctrine of classification under Article 14

card.dispute: The State of U.P. and authorities challenged the High Court's mandamus directing the grant of a cinema licence to Raja Ram Jaiswal, arguing that licensing decisions should not be dictated by courts.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could issue a writ of mandamus directing the licensing authority to grant a cinema licence.
Whether the District Magistrate validly refused the licence on grounds of public interest.
Whether the refusal of the licence was based on relevant considerations under the U.P. Cinema (Regulation) Act and Rules.
holdings: A writ of mandamus cannot compel a statutory licensing authority to grant a licence; courts can quash illegal orders but cannot supplant the authority’s discretion.
The District Magistrate’s refusal of the licence was based on extraneous and irrelevant considerations, particularly the objections of the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan, and thus vitiated the decision.
Public interest cannot be equated with the preferences of a private institution; licensing decisions must be grounded in legally relevant and valid considerations.
doctrines: Prohibition of arbitrariness in administrative action
Relevance of considerations in licensing decisions
Separation of powers in judicial review of administrative discretion
Doctrine of extraneous considerations in administrative law

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the quantum of compensation awarded to Mohinder Singh and another for acquired land.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents are entitled to enhanced solatium and interest under Act 68 of 1984.
Whether the appeal has merit concerning the quantum of compensation.
holdings: Respondents are entitled to 30% solatium from the date of publication to the date of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, as amended by Act 68 of 1984.
Respondents are entitled to interest at 9% from the date of possession, with credit for 6% already paid, due to the amendment under Act 68 of 1984.
doctrines: Prospective application of amendments benefiting claimants
Entitlement to enhanced compensation under amended law if decision is after one year

card.dispute: The landlord sought to evict the tenant on grounds of unlawful subletting allegedly done by the tenant's father, not the tenant himself.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can be evicted under Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for unlawful subletting done by his predecessor in interest?
Whether the contravention of the Rent Act by a former tenant can be imputed to the successor in tenancy?
holdings: A tenant cannot be evicted under Section 10(2)(ii)(a) for subletting done by his predecessor; the tenant himself must have committed the unlawful act.
The penal nature of eviction requires strict construction; liability cannot be imposed for acts of a predecessor in which the current tenant had no role.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(ii)(a)
doctrines: Strict construction of penal provisions
Personal liability for statutory contraventions

card.dispute: The ryots challenged the Tribunal's order confirming that Lingamguntla Agraharam was not an Inam Estate, claiming violation of procedural fairness due to non-receipt of notice in the appeal filed by the State.
issues_decided: Whether the delay of 4.5 years in filing the writ petition under Article 226 rendered the petition inadmissible.
Whether non-service of notice on the ryots in the appeal before the Tribunal amounted to a violation of mandatory procedure entitling them to relief.
holdings: A delay of 4.5 years in filing a writ petition under Article 226, without sufficient explanation, justifies dismissal of the petition, especially when alternative remedies were available.
Non-service of notice on the ryots in an appeal does not vitiate the proceedings if they suffered no prejudice and had opportunity to appeal themselves but failed to do so.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Estates (Abolition And Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, Section 9(1)
Madras Estate Land (Third Amendment) Act, 1936, Section 3(2)(d)
doctrines: Alternative remedy doctrine
Doctrine of laches
Principle of no prejudice from procedural irregularity

card.dispute: The appellants, holders of pre-existing mining leases in reserved forests, fought against the State's rejection of their lease renewals on the grounds that the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 required central approval for non-forest use of forest land.
issues_decided: Whether renewal of a mining lease in a reserved forest, granted before the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, can be claimed as a matter of right despite the Act's restrictions.
Whether the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 applies to renewals of pre-existing leases in forest areas.
Whether the decision in State of Bihar v. Banshi Ram Modi applies to lease renewals in forest areas.
holdings: Renewal of a mining lease in forest land governed by the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 cannot be claimed as a right if it results in continued non-forest use without prior approval of the Central Government.
The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 applies to renewals of leases in forest areas, as renewal would perpetuate non-forest use and defeat the Act’s purpose of preventing deforestation.
The ratio in State of Bihar v. Banshi Ram Modi is limited to its facts and does not extend to lease renewals; it does not permit bypassing central approval for renewed non-forest use in forest areas.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation must advance the purpose of the legislation
The principle that 'may' does not always mean 'shall'
Ratio decidendi is confined to the facts of the case
Prospective overruling and binding force of precedent under Article 141

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the right of pre-emption based on consanguinity under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 as applied in Haryana, alleging it violated Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of kinsfolk entitled to pre-emption under Section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 is reasonable and non-discriminatory under Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution.
Whether the right of pre-emption based on consanguinity serves a public interest and is consistent with modern constitutional values.
Whether certain clauses of Section 15(1) and Section 15(2) of the Act can be sustained as constitutionally valid.
holdings: The classification of kinsfolk under Section 15 based on consanguinity lacks reasonable basis and violates Article 14 due to arbitrary exclusion of female relatives and those related through females.
The right of pre-emption based on consanguinity is a feudal relic, inconsistent with modern constitutional values and the principles of equality under Articles 14 and 15.

Clauses of Section 15(1)(a), (b), (c) labeled 'Firstly', 'Secondly', and 'Thirdly', and the entire Section 15(2) are unconstitutional; however, clauses granting pre-emption to co-sharers and tenants are valid as they serve public interest.
The declaration of unconstitutionality will not affect final decrees that have become binding inter partes.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Equality before law
Public interest justification for property restrictions
Doctrine of severability

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide personal need, and after rejection by lower courts, challenged the order in the High Court via revision under CPC Section 115, raising the issue of whether such revision was maintainable given the finality clause in the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent) Control Act, 1965.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court has revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to interfere with an order passed under Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent) Control Act, 1965?

Whether the phrase 'shall be final and shall not be liable to be called in question in any court of law' in Section 18(5) of the Act excludes further revision by the High Court after a revision under Section 20?
holdings: The High Court does not have jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC to revise an order already subject to revision under Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent) Control Act, 1965, as such jurisdiction is excluded by the scheme and language of Sections 18(5) and 20.

The phrase 'shall be final and shall not be liable to be called in question in any court of law' in Section 18(5) implies an exclusion of further revision, including under Section 115 CPC, to ensure finality and prevent multiplicity of proceedings.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent) Control Act, 1965, Section 18(5)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent) Control Act, 1965, Section 20
doctrines: Exclusion of jurisdiction by statutory finality clauses
Implication of ouster of revisional jurisdiction
Principle of finality in special statutes
Scheme of the Act as a self-contained code

card.dispute: The auction-purchaser challenged the setting aside of a property sale in execution of a decree, arguing the judgment-debtor's deposit was made beyond the 30-day limit under CPC Rule 92(2).
issues_decided: Whether an application to set aside an auction sale is maintainable if the deposit is made after 30 days but within 60 days from the date of sale?
Whether Rule 92(2) of Order XXI of the CPC is consistent with Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963 as amended?
Whether the provisions of the CPC and the Limitation Act should be harmoniously construed?
holdings: Both the application and deposit under Order XXI Rule 89 CPC must be made within the limitation period, now sixty days under Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Rule 92(2) of Order XXI CPC, requiring deposit within thirty days, is inconsistent with Article 127 of the Limitation Act as amended to sixty days and requires parliamentary amendment.

The provisions of Order XXI Rules 89 and 92(2) CPC and Article 127 of the Limitation Act should be given harmonious construction, allowing setting aside of sale if deposit and application are made within sixty days.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 92(2)
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Limitation period for statutory applications
Judicial recognition of legislative inconsistency

card.dispute: The landowner fought with the State of Uttar Pradesh over whether statutory solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was payable on compensation awarded for temporary occupation of land under Section 35.
issues_decided: Whether statutory solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applies to compensation awarded under Section 35 for temporary occupation of land.
Whether temporary occupation under Part VI of the Act is equivalent to acquisition under Part II for the purpose of claiming solatium.
holdings: Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which provides for statutory solatium, does not apply to compensation awarded under Section 35 for temporary occupation of land.
Temporary occupation under Part VI of the Act is distinct from acquisition under Part II, as ownership remains with the landowner, and thus solatium based on market value is not payable.
doctrines: Distinction between temporary possession and permanent acquisition
Statutory interpretation of compensation provisions
Solatium linked to market value and permanent acquisition

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's requirement to pay ad valorem court fees on their appeal against an arbitrator's compensation award under the Requisitioning Act, arguing for a fixed fee under the residuary provision of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees Act.
issues_decided: Whether the memorandum of appeal under Section 11 of the Requisitioning Act is subject to ad valorem court fee under Section 51 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955
Whether the term 'order' in Section 51 includes an arbitrator's award under the Requisitioning Act
Whether the residuary provision in Article 3(iii)(A)(1)(a) of Schedule II applies to such an appeal
holdings: An appeal under Section 11 of the Requisitioning Act falls under Section 51 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees Act, requiring ad valorem court fee based on the disputed compensation amount.
The term 'order' in Section 51 includes an arbitrator's award relating to compensation under a property acquisition law, even if not issued by a civil court.
The residuary provision in Article 3(iii)(A)(1)(a) of Schedule II does not apply where a specific provision like Section 51 governs the court fee.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, Section 51
Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, Article 3(iii)(A)(1)(a) of Schedule II
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8
Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 11
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Specific provision prevails over general/residuary provision

card.dispute: The Revenue authorities fought with Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation over whether compensation received from the Burmese Government for the nationalisation of forest leases and assets was a taxable revenue receipt or a non-taxable capital receipt.
issues_decided: Whether compensation received in the form of teak logs for the cancellation of forest leases and depreciable assets was a capital or revenue receipt
Whether a balancing charge could be levied under section 10(2)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 in the absence of a sale transaction
Whether proceeds from logs received in exchange for assets were taxable as revenue receipts
holdings: Compensation received for the cancellation of long-term forest leases, which formed the profit-making apparatus of the business, is a capital receipt and not taxable as revenue.
A balancing charge under section 10(2)(vii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 is not applicable where there is no sale but a barter or exchange of assets due to nationalisation.
Logs received in exchange for depreciable assets and rights under forest leases are capital receipts and not part of circulating capital, hence not taxable as revenue.
doctrines: Capital vs revenue receipt distinction
Profit-making apparatus doctrine
Fixed capital and circulating capital distinction
Balancing charge applicability only on sale

card.dispute: The appellants were prosecuted for dacoity, robbery, and house-trespass in connection with the alleged forcible taking of articles from a sweet-meat shop; they claimed rightful ownership and possession of the property and articles, leading to a dispute over whether the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution established the ingredients of offences under Sections 395, 397, 436, and 380 IPC beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal by the Trial Court without adequately considering the Trial Court's reasoning and the benefit of witness demeanor?
Whether the defence claim of ownership and possession of the shop and articles was supported by the evidence on record?
Whether the identification of the recovered articles and the testimony of prosecution witnesses were reliable?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the charges under Sections 395, 397, 436, and 380 IPC beyond reasonable doubt, as the evidence did not establish use of force, assault, or unlawful taking.
The High Court erred in overturning the acquittal without sufficient reasoning and without due regard to the Trial Court's assessment of witness credibility and demeanor.
The defence version that the appellants lawfully owned and possessed the shop and articles was supported by prosecution witnesses and documentary evidence, including a lease deed.
The identification of the allegedly stolen articles lacked evidentiary foundation, and the prosecution failed to prove ownership or unlawful removal.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence in appeals against acquittal
Appellate court must consider reasons of trial court before reversing acquittal
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Demeanor of witnesses as a factor in credibility assessment

card.dispute: The Chief Settlement Commissioner cancelled an excess land allotment made to displaced persons and refused to sell them the excess land; the allottees claimed a legal right to purchase it under Rule 73(2)(ii) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 73(2)(ii) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955 imposes a legal obligation on the Settlement Commissioner to sell excess land to allottees who are willing to pay for it.
Whether the High Court erred in directing the sale of excess land to the original allottees despite the discretionary language of the rule.
holdings: The use of the word 'may' in Rule 73(2)(ii) confers discretion on the Settlement Commissioner and does not create a legal right in favour of allottees to claim sale of excess land.
An interpretation that would allow persons with excess allotments to purchase the land would defeat the rehabilitation purpose of the Rules by depriving rightful claimants of available land.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 73(2)(ii)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Precedent based on parimateria rule interpretation
Judicial discretion in administrative action

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assessee disputed whether additional compensation received for land acquisition could be taxed as income in the assessment year when the amount was provisionally received, or only when the right to such compensation was finally determined.
issues_decided: Whether the additional compensation for land acquisition accrued as income during the relevant assessment year when it was provisionally received subject to appeal.
Whether income is deemed to accrue when the right to receive it is still in dispute or only upon final determination.
holdings: Income from enhanced compensation does not accrue until the right to it is finally determined by the court; mere provisional receipt does not make it taxable income.
There is no liability in praesenti for additional compensation until the dispute over the right to payment is conclusively resolved, distinguishing cases where only quantification remains.
doctrines: Accrual of income doctrine
Distinction between disputed right to payment and mere quantification of admitted liability
Final determination rule for contingent claims

card.dispute: The appellant (Dr. Keshav Devi) and the landlord (Shri Girdhari Lal Pahwa) disputed the validity of an allotment order granting her tenancy of the first floor of a building, after the landlord had purchased the property and was residing on the ground floor.
issues_decided: Whether the Additional District Magistrate had jurisdiction to allot the premises to the appellant without notifying the new landlord under Section 17(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972?
Whether the landlord had the right to nominate a tenant of his choice under Section 17(2) even after the previous landlord's release application was rejected?
Whether the Additional District Magistrate could legally recall the allotment order in review on grounds of non-compliance with mandatory statutory requirements?
holdings: An allotment under Section 16(1)(a) is invalid if the landlord occupying part of the building is not given notice and opportunity to nominate a tenant under Section 17(2).
The right of a landlord to nominate a tenant under Section 17(2) is independent of any prior release application and remains enforceable even after a change in ownership.
An allotment order violating a mandatory provision like Section 17(2) is a nullity and may be recalled in review, even if procedural irregularities exist, to prevent injustice.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 16(1)(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 17(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 19
doctrines: Statutory compliance with mandatory provisions
Protection of landlord's right to peaceful enjoyment
Jurisdictional error vitiating administrative orders

card.dispute: The District Council of Jowai levied royalty on timber from private forests, and landowners challenged its constitutional validity, arguing the Council lacked power to impose such a tax.
issues_decided: Whether the royalty imposed on timber from private forests is a tax and within the legislative competence of the District Council under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution
Whether the District Council can levy fees for services rendered under Paragraph 3 of the Sixth Schedule
Whether the forests in question are private forests
holdings: The royalty on timber from private forests is in the nature of a tax on forest produce, which the District Council has no power to levy under Paragraph 8 of the Sixth Schedule.

Although the District Council can levy fees as quid pro quo for services under Paragraph 3 of the Sixth Schedule, the impugned levy cannot be upheld as a fee due to lack of evidence linking it to services rendered.
The forests from which timber was removed are private forests, and the Council's notification presupposes their existence.
provisions: United Khasi and Jaintia Hills Autonomous District (Management and Control of Forests) Act, 1958, Sections 3, 4, 8, 11, 13
Constitution of India, Article 244(2), Sixth Schedule, Paragraphs 3 and 8
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Fee vs. tax distinction
Doctrine of colourable legislation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of Dudh Nath Pandey and Suresh Chandra Bhattasali over ownership and possession of a piece of land measuring 3 Kathas and 8 Dhurs, claimed by the plaintiff based on a 1949 settlement from Dhalbhum Raj, while the defendant claimed prior possession and adverse title.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred by limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act
Whether the High Court erred in reversing the Appellate Court's finding on limitation while exercising jurisdiction under Section 100 of the CPC
Whether the plaintiff had established title over the disputed land based on the 1949 settlement
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation as the plaintiff failed to establish possession within 12 years prior to filing the suit.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 of the CPC by making a fresh appraisal of evidence and reversing a concurrent finding of fact on limitation.
The finding on the plaintiff's title based on the 1949 settlement had attained finality and was not open for re-evaluation in this appeal.
doctrines: Res judicata
Adverse possession
Principle of finality of findings in second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: Co-owners of a property fought over whether it should be sold by public auction or one co-owner should be allowed to buy out the others' shares at a valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the property should be sold by public auction to determine its market value or one co-owner should be allowed to purchase the others' shares at a court-determined valuation.
Whether the method of valuation adopted by the court-appointed valuer was legally valid.
Whether a party who sought to buy out other co-owners could later demand a public auction.
holdings: A co-owner seeking to buy out other co-owners cannot later demand a public auction, as such conduct amounts to blowing hot and cold.
The valuation method used—separately assessing land and depreciated building value—was valid and fact-based, even though land and building could be treated as a unit in some contexts.
When a co-owner is willing and able to buy out others at a court-approved valuation, the property need not be auctioned, to ensure expeditious disposal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 18
doctrines: Doctrine of election
Principle against blowing hot and cold

card.dispute: The appellant, a legatee under a joint will, contested the Controller of Estate Duty's claim that estate duty was payable on the full property after the second death, arguing exemption under Section 29 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether estate duty was payable on the entire property after the death of the second executant of a joint will?
Whether the joint will created a mutual and irrevocable obligation after the death of one executant?
Whether the surviving executant had disposing power over the property after receiving benefits under the will?
Whether the provisions of Section 29 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 applied to exempt duty on the second death?
holdings: Estate duty under Section 29 is not payable on the full property if the will is mutual and irrevocable after the first death, as the survivor lacks disposing power over the inherited share.
A joint will becomes irrevocable after the death of one executant if there is a clear mutual agreement, express or implied, not to revoke it after receiving benefits.
The survivor of a mutual will who accepts benefits under it cannot dispose of the property contrary to the ultimate bequest to the legatees.
Section 29 exemption applies when property passes on the second death and duty was already paid on the first death, provided the will is mutual and binding.
doctrines: Mutual will doctrine
Doctrine of irrevocability after acceptance of benefit
Contemporaneous exposition of wills
Interpretation of testamentary intent

card.dispute: Ganpat Giri (judgment-debtor) challenged a court sale in which a decree-holder purchased the property without court permission, arguing the sale was invalid under the amended Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment made by the Allahabad High Court to Order 21 Rule 72, deleting sub-rules (1) and (3), continued in force after the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976 came into effect.
Whether the decree-holder's purchase of property without court permission was voidable under Order 21 Rule 72(3) after the 1976 Amendment Act.
Whether the application to set aside the sale was barred by limitation.
holdings: Section 97(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976 repealed all inconsistent local amendments, including the Allahabad High Court's deletion of Order 21 Rule 72(1) and (3), regardless of whether Rule 72 was amended by the central Act.
The original provisions of Order 21 Rule 72(1) and (3) were revived and applicable after the 1976 Amendment, so a decree-holder purchasing without court permission could have the sale set aside.

The plea of limitation was not considered just to raise at that stage, especially since lower courts did not reject the application on that ground and there was genuine doubt about the rule's applicability.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976, Section 97
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 72
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 89
doctrines: Doctrine of implied repeal
Doctrine of revival of central provisions upon repeal of inconsistent local amendments
Principle of prospective application of procedural amendments

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of the takeover of their Ginning and Pressing Factory under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act, arguing it was a separate establishment from the textile undertaking.
issues_decided: Whether the Ginning and Pressing Factory was part of the Textile Undertaking and thus validly taken over under the Act.
Whether separate accounting and provident fund schemes indicate that the Ginning and Pressing Factory was a distinct establishment.
holdings: The Ginning and Pressing Factory was part and parcel of the textile undertaking because it supplied ginned cotton to the mill and shared supervision, administration, and finances.
Separate valuation in balance sheets and distinct provident fund schemes do not establish a separate legal or operational entity if control and integration with the main unit are present.
provisions: Sick Textile Undertakings (Taking Over of Management) Act, Section 4(3)
doctrines: Integration of units doctrine
Substance over form doctrine

card.dispute: The Government of Tamil Nadu fought with Ahobila Matam over whether certain inam lands held by the religious institution were exempt from full land assessment under the Madras Inams (Assessment) Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 3(1) of the Madras Inams (Assessment) Act, 1956 exempts lands held by religious institutions on 'service tenure' from full assessment
Whether the imposition of land assessment on religious institutions violates their fundamental right under Article 26 of the Constitution
holdings: The expression 'service tenure' in the proviso to Section 3(1) refers only to grants burdened with personal service obligations, not to lands granted to religious institutions for their support; thus, such lands are liable to full assessment.

The imposition of land revenue assessment on religious institutions does not violate Article 26 of the Constitution, as it is a general fiscal burden applicable to all landowners and does not interfere with the right to administer religious property.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
General tax burden not infringing fundamental rights

card.dispute: Hindustan Tea Co. and K. Sashikant Co. disputed over the management of two tea estates, leading to an arbitration award that the appellant sought to set aside.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award could be challenged under Sections 30 and 33 of the Arbitration Act on the grounds that the arbitrator reached a wrong conclusion or failed to appreciate facts.
Whether the arbitrator acted contrary to Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, thereby rendering the award invalid.
holdings: An arbitration award cannot be challenged merely because the arbitrator reached a wrong conclusion or misappreciated facts, as the arbitrator is the final arbiter under the Arbitration Act.
The award cannot be set aside on the ground that the arbitrator acted contrary to Section 70 of the Contract Act, as such a challenge falls outside the limited scope permitted by the Arbitration Act.
doctrines: Finality of arbitration award
Limited judicial review of arbitral awards

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of a sub-tenant firm after obtaining a decree against the principal tenant, while the sub-tenant claimed protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether a sub-tenant is entitled to protection against eviction under Sections 17 and 18 of the Delhi Rent Control Act without formal written consent and notice if the landlord attested the sub-tenancy letter?
Whether attestation by the landlord of a letter concerning the sub-tenancy constitutes sufficient written consent and notice under the Act?
holdings: A sub-tenant is entitled to protection under Sections 17 and 18 of the Delhi Rent Control Act if the landlord's consent and notice of sub-tenancy are evidenced in writing, which may be satisfied by the landlord attesting the sub-tenancy letter.

The attestation of the sub-tenancy letter by the landlord constitutes sufficient documentary evidence of both prior consent and notice, satisfying the requirements of Sections 17 and 18, even in the absence of a formal agreement.
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes to advance legislative purpose
Protection of sub-tenants with documentary evidence of landlord’s consent
Strict compliance with statutory conditions as a general rule, with rare exceptions based on conduct

card.dispute: The landlord sought execution of a pre-existing decree for possession against a tenant, after the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 became applicable to the area, which restricted grounds for eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for possession, passed before the applicability of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 to the area, could be executed after the Act became applicable?
Whether the tenant retained protection under Section 21(1) of the Act despite a prior decree for possession?
holdings: A decree for possession passed before the Rent Control Act became applicable to an area can be executed even after the Act's applicability, as Section 21(1) only bars new eviction orders, not execution of prior decrees.

The protection under Section 21(1) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 does not revive tenancy or nullify a final decree for possession passed earlier; the tenant’s status is extinguished post-decree.
provisions: Karnataka Municipal Corporation Act, Section 4(1) read with Section 501(A)
doctrines: Beneficial legislation interpretation in favour of tenants
Prospective operation of rent control laws
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutes

card.dispute: Jagdish Sugar Mills Ltd fought the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether the excess amount from a compulsory auction sale of its properties for unpaid cane cess should be taxed as business income.
issues_decided: Whether a compulsory auction sale of property for recovery of arrears of cane cess, treated as arrears of land revenue, constitutes a 'sale' under clause (vii) of section 10(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
Whether the sale was deemed to occur on the date of auction (November 10, 1955) or on the date the sale certificate was issued (July 4, 1956) for tax purposes.
holdings: A compulsory auction sale of an assessee's property for arrears of land revenue falls within the meaning of 'sale' under clause (vii) of section 10(2) of the 1922 Act, as the statutory framework implies consent to such a sale when engaging in the activity attracting the cess.
The sale is deemed to take place only when the sale certificate is issued under Rule 285-M, as it is this certificate that operates as a valid transfer of property, not the date of auction.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Sections 279, 286, 341
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules, 1952, Rules 281, 285-M
doctrines: Statutory sale includes compulsory auction under revenue recovery laws
Deemed transfer doctrine under special statutes overrides general law
Consent inferred from voluntary engagement in regulated activity

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant based on damage caused by the sub-tenant, despite compromise allowing sub-letting and no direct relationship between landlord and sub-tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant can be held responsible for damage caused by a sub-tenant in the absence of privity between the landlord and sub-tenant.
Whether damage caused by a sub-tenant constitutes a valid ground for eviction under Section 11(b) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947.
holdings: A tenant remains legally and contractually obligated to maintain the premises in good condition and return them undamaged, regardless of sub-letting.
The tenant is liable for wrongful acts of a sub-tenant, and such damage can be a ground for eviction under Section 11(b) of the Act.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(b)
doctrines: Privity of contract
Lessee's duty to preserve leased property
Vicarious liability of tenant for sub-tenant's actions

card.dispute: The tenant fought against eviction by landlords who refused to accept rent, claiming he had lawfully deposited arrears in court under the U.P. Rent Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could deposit rent in court under Section 30 of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act when landlords refused to accept it.
Whether such deposit deems rent as paid, protecting the tenant from eviction for arrears.
Whether the tenant failed to comply with the notice of demand within one month under Section 13(6).
holdings: A tenant may deposit rent in court under Section 30 if there is a bona fide dispute or unjustified refusal by the landlord to accept rent.
Deposit of rent under Section 30(1) is deemed payment under Section 30(6), preventing eviction for arrears.
The tenant was not in default as he was ready to pay and the landlords did not respond to his conditional offer to pay upon written acceptance.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 13(6)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 40
doctrines: Deeming fiction of payment
Legislative intent to protect tenants from eviction
Bona fide dispute exception to rent payment obligation

card.dispute: The appellant (brother of a widow) claimed ownership of properties under a will executed by the widow, while the respondent (son of the original settlor) claimed the properties based on a reversionary interest under a settlement deed that created a life estate in the widow.
issues_decided: Whether the life estate granted to the widow under a 1937 settlement deed was transformed into full ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the exception in Section 14(2) of the Act applies to bar such transformation
holdings: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not apply where a restricted estate is created by an instrument such as a settlement deed that contemplates limited interest.

Section 14(2) is an exception to Section 14(1), and when a restricted estate is created by a deed of settlement, the widow does not acquire full ownership or an alienable interest that can be bequeathed by will.
doctrines: Doctrine of restricted estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act
Doctrine of statutory exception overriding beneficial construction

card.dispute: The assessee-company fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether a loss from selling land used for a railway contract was a deductible revenue loss or a non-deductible capital loss.
issues_decided: Whether the loss of Rs.30,045 claimed by the assessee is a capital loss or a revenue loss under the Income Tax Act, 1961
holdings: The loss arose from the sale of land that was a capital asset, not stock-in-trade, and thus constitutes a capital loss not deductible under revenue expenditure.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Capital asset doctrine
Wasting asset doctrine (rejected in this context)

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Mewa Ram and others sought special leave to appeal for enhancement of land compensation, claiming entitlement due to higher compensation awarded in similar cases, despite inordinate delay in filing.
issues_decided: Whether inordinate delay in filing special leave petitions can be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 based on subsequent enhancement of compensation in similar cases?
Whether Sections 25 and 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permit reopening of a final award for redetermination of compensation in this case?
holdings: Mere enhancement of compensation in similar cases does not constitute sufficient cause for condoning inordinate delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.

Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not apply to landowners who had already exercised their right to reference under Section 18, and there is no other provision to reopen a final award.
doctrines: Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act requires sufficient cause
Finality of awards under the Land Acquisition Act
Interpretation of remedial provisions in favor of intended beneficiaries only

card.dispute: Mary Roy and others challenged the applicability of the discriminatory Travancore Christian Succession Act, 1092, seeking equal rights in intestate succession for Indian Christians in former Travancore under the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the Travancore Christian Succession Act, 1092 was repealed by the Part States (Laws) Act, 1951 upon the extension of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 to Travancore-Cochin
Whether Chapter II of Part V of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 governs intestate succession for Indian Christians in the former State of Travancore from 1951
Whether Section 29(2) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 saves the Travancore Christian Succession Act, 1092 from repeal
holdings: The Travancore Christian Succession Act, 1092 stood expressly repealed by Section 6 of the Part States (Laws) Act, 1951 as it was a corresponding law to Chapter II of Part V of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
Intestate succession for Indian Christians in the former Travancore has been governed by Chapter II of Part V of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 since the extension in 1951.
Section 29(2) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 does not incorporate or save the Travancore Christian Succession Act, 1092; it is not a provision for incorporation by reference.
doctrines: Express repeal by statute
Legislative incorporation by reference
Doctrine of repeal of corresponding laws

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad sought to levy general tax on the Hyderabad Race Club's property, which the Club claimed was exempt as being used for a 'charitable purpose'.
issues_decided: Whether the use of property for running a race course and training horses qualifies as 'charitable purpose' under Section 202(1)(b) of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation Act, 1955.
Whether the manner in which the Club's income is utilized affects eligibility for tax exemption.
Whether the tax assessment for the year 1966-67 was validly levied.
Whether the valuation of the property by the lower courts was correct.
holdings: Exemption under Section 202(1)(b) depends on the actual use of the property, not the use of income; conducting horse races is not a charitable purpose.
The term 'charitable' requires a benevolent activity benefiting the poor or deprived; horse racing does not meet this standard.
The High Court correctly found no valid tax assessment for 1966-67 based on evidence, and that finding is upheld.
The property valuation by the Small Causes Court and confirmed by the High Court is not disturbed.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory exemption clauses
Distinction between use of property and use of income for charitable purposes
Principle that tax exemptions must be strictly construed

card.dispute: The tenant advanced a loan to the landlord to secure tenancy, and when sued for rent arrears, claimed adjustment of the loan; the landlord argued the loan was illegal under rent control law and thus not adjustable.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could claim adjustment of an illegally advanced loan against accrued rent under the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1947
Whether the doctrine of pari delicto bars the tenant from seeking relief when the illegal transaction was compelled by the landlord's exploitative position
holdings: A tenant who advances a loan in violation of rent control law to secure tenancy is not in pari delicto with the landlord, especially when the law is designed to protect tenants from exploitation.
The doctrine of pari delicto does not apply where the tenant is compelled by necessity to comply with the landlord's illegal demand due to housing shortage and unequal bargaining power.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of pari delicto
Exception to pari delicto in cases of statutory protection for vulnerable parties

card.dispute: The tenant claimed he was not in arrears because he deposited rent in court under s. 7C after the landlord refused payment, while the landlord sued for eviction and arrears, denying any refusal to accept rent.
issues_decided: Whether permission granted by the Munsif under s. 7C to deposit rent is binding in an eviction suit
Whether the tenant must independently prove the landlord's refusal to accept rent in an eviction suit
Whether the first appellate court's finding on the landlord's refusal was legally sustainable
holdings: An order permitting deposit of rent under s. 7C is not conclusive; the eviction court can examine whether the landlord actually refused rent.
The tenant bears the burden to prove in the eviction suit that the landlord refused to accept lawfully tendered rent.
A finding based on conjecture or surmise about the landlord’s refusal, without reliable evidence, cannot stand in an eviction proceeding.
provisions: United Provinces (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7C
doctrines: Burden of proof in eviction cases
Limited finality of administrative or interim orders in civil suits
Requirement of evidentiary proof over presumptions in civil liability

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's determination of market value and compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, and raised a new point regarding the applicability of the Amending Act No. 20 of 1984 to pending cases.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court committed an error in determining the market value and compensation for the acquired land?
Whether the Amending Act No. 20 of 1984 applies retrospectively to pending land acquisition cases?
holdings: The High Court correctly determined the market value by correcting the trial court's reliance on non-comparable small plots, and no error of principle was found.
The question of retrospective applicability of Amending Act No. 20 of 1984 is pending before a Constitution Bench; if it is held applicable, appellants may seek review of this order.
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in market value assessment
Doctrine of prospective vs. retrospective operation of amending statutes

card.dispute: The landlord, Om Prakash, sought eviction of tenant Bhagwan Das on grounds of bona fide need, which the High Court reversed, leading to an appeal before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the lower authorities' decision allowing eviction under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972?
Whether the landlord fulfilled the requirement of the 4th proviso to Section 21(1)(a) by showing bona fide need and offering reasonable alternative accommodation?
holdings: The High Court erred in interfering with the Prescribed Authority and Additional District Judge’s order; their findings of bona fide need and comparative hardship favoring the landlord were valid and free from infirmity.

Where refusal to grant eviction would deprive the landlord of beneficial enjoyment of his own property, it cannot be said that he failed to meet the 4th proviso to Section 21(1)(a), especially when he offered reasonably suitable alternative accommodation.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a) 4th Proviso
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 16(1)(f)
doctrines: Bona fide need of landlord
Balancing of hardship between landlord and tenant
Liberal consideration of eviction claim when alternative accommodation is offered

card.dispute: The appellants, Palanisamy and Raju, challenged their conviction and death sentence for murder and house-trespass with intent to commit arson, arguing that the prosecution's evidence was unreliable.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of eyewitnesses P.Ws. 5 and 6 was reliable enough to sustain the conviction
Whether the retracted confessional statements of the appellants could be acted upon without independent corroboration
Whether the investigation and arrest procedures were credible and free from suspicion
holdings: The evidence of P.Ws. 5 and 6 was not free from reasonable doubt and could not form the basis of a conviction, especially since no suggestion was raised during cross-examination to test their credibility.
Retracted confessions require independent corroboration; in this case, the confessions were rendered unreliable due to the doubtful presence of the witnesses mentioned in them.
The investigation was deficient and delayed, raising suspicion about the authenticity of the arrests and the overall prosecution case, warranting the benefit of doubt to the accused.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of retracted confessions
Fair investigation and presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The landlords challenged the tenants' entitlement to protection from eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, after having previously benefited from similar protection under the earlier 1952 Act.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant who had earlier obtained protection from eviction under section 13(2) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, could claim protection again under section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, despite a second default in rent payment.
Whether the proviso to section 14(2) of the 1958 Act, which bars a second benefit, applies when the first benefit was granted under the 1952 Act.
holdings: A tenant is entitled to the protection of non-eviction under section 14(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, even if they previously obtained similar relief under section 13(2) of the 1952 Act, because the two provisions are not in pari materia.
The proviso to section 14(2), which bars a second benefit, applies only if the prior benefit was granted under the same provision—section 14(2) of the 1958 Act—and not under the earlier 1952 Act.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(2)
doctrines: In pari materia
Proviso interpretation
Statutory construction (golden rule)
Saving clause under repeal

card.dispute: The defendant sought to set aside an ex-parte decree passed against him, claiming he was unaware of the final judgment until the plaintiff attempted to take possession.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court correctly disposed of the suit under Order 17 Rule 3 CPC when the defendant was absent and had not led any evidence
Whether the application under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC to set aside the ex-parte decree was maintainable
