holdings: When a defendant is absent and has not recorded any evidence, the court must proceed under Order 17 Rule 2 CPC and cannot decide the suit on merits under Order 17 Rule 3.
An application under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC is maintainable to set aside an ex-parte decree if the decree was passed in violation of procedural safeguards under Order 17 Rules 2 and 3.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 17 Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 17 Rule 3
doctrines: Procedural fairness in ex-parte decrees
Strict compliance with CPC procedural rules for disposal of suits

card.dispute: The Peoples' Union for Democratic Rights sought compensation for victims of police firing at Arwal, Bihar, where 21 people were killed and several injured during a peaceful gathering, alleging unjustified use of force and a false police case.
issues_decided: Whether compensation should be awarded to the families of those killed and the injured due to police firing
Whether the report of the Member, Board of Revenue, should be disclosed to the public
Whether the ongoing police investigation should be expedited
holdings: The state must pay compensation of Rs. 20,000 for each death and Rs. 5,000 for each injury caused by police firing, as a measure of rehabilitation, regardless of criminal liability.
The High Court may examine whether the inquiry report by the Member, Board of Revenue, should be made public if privilege is claimed, and decide on disclosure accordingly.
The investigation into the pending police case must be completed within three months, and aggrieved parties retain the right to challenge the charges legally.
doctrines: Public Interest Litigation
State liability for compensation in violation of fundamental rights
Judicial review of executive privilege

card.dispute: Punjab National Bank challenged an eviction order for using a residential tenanted premises for commercial purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant can be evicted under Section 14(1)(k) of the Delhi Rent Control Act for changing the residential premises to non-residential use.
Whether the court can impose a penalty in lieu of eviction for unauthorized change of user.
holdings: A tenant’s change of user from residential to commercial does not automatically justify eviction if the landlord's real motive is to obtain higher rent.
The court may allow continued occupation by enhancing rent and directing payment of penalty for unauthorized use, leaving quantification of penalty to the Controller.
doctrines: Doctrine of proportionality in eviction remedies
Penalty as an alternative to eviction for breach of tenancy conditions

card.dispute: The appellants, heirs of a tenant, challenged the respondent trustee's suit for recovery of rent, claiming protection under tenancy laws, while the respondent argued that tenancy rights ceased due to a government notification reserving the land for non-agricultural use.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 apply to lands within the municipal limits of Baroda after a notification under Section 88(1)(b) was issued in 1958.
Whether tenancy rights accrued before the 1948 Act or under the repealed 1939 Act survived the 1958 notification.
Whether Section 89(2)(b) of the 1948 Act preserves tenancy rights despite the exclusion under Section 88(1)(b).
holdings: A notification under Section 88(1)(b) of the 1948 Act excludes the application of the Act to specified lands, rendering tenancy protections inapplicable from the date of notification.
Tenancy rights under the 1948 Act, including those accrued before its commencement, cease to exist in areas notified under Section 88(1)(b), unless expressly preserved.

Section 89(2)(b) does not preserve tenancy rights in notified areas because Section 88(1)(b) contains an express exclusion, and only rights under Sections 3, 3A, and 4 of the 1939 Act are preserved via Section 89A.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88(1)(b)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89(2)(b)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89A
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Schedule I
doctrines: Doctrine of express exclusion overriding implied rights
Doctrine of statutory notification overriding tenancy protections
Doctrine of prospective and retrospective operation of tenancy law amendments

card.dispute: The petitioners (Ram Singh & Ors.) sued the Gram Panchayat seeking declaration of ownership and possession over land shown as shamlat deh in revenue records, while the Panchayat claimed the land was vested in it under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to try a suit involving a claim over land alleged to be shamlat deh vested in a Gram Panchayat?
Whether the correctness of entries in revenue records showing land as shamlat deh can be challenged in a civil suit despite statutory bars?
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide questions regarding title or interest in land claimed to be shamlat deh vested in a Panchayat, as such matters are exclusively adjudicated by the Collector under Section 11 of the Act.

A suit cannot be maintained in civil court merely because the plaintiffs avoided pleading that the land is not shamlat deh, when the real dispute involves the vesting of such land in the Panchayat under the Act.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 11
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 12
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, Order I, Rule 8
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by statute
Finality of administrative orders
Pith and substance doctrine (to determine true nature of the dispute)

card.dispute: Ramveer Jatav challenged the validity of his detention under the National Security Act, 1980, claiming it was based on an irrelevant ground and without proper application of mind by the detaining authority.
issues_decided: Whether the order of detention was based on an irrelevant ground and disclosed non-application of mind by the detaining authority.
Whether a single ground of detention, without supporting circumstances, can justify preventive detention under the National Security Act, 1980.
holdings: A solitary ground of detention, such as involvement in a murder case without any additional circumstances indicating a threat to public order, is insufficient to justify preventive detention.
The detaining authority cannot rely on material outside the grounds of detention, such as statements in a counter-affidavit, to justify the detention.
doctrines: Doctrine of relevancy of grounds in preventive detention
Prohibition against post-facto justification in administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant, who became statutory occupant of land after the original owner failed to sell it to him, refused to execute a sale deed to the respondents based on an earlier agreement to sell, claiming the agreement was contingent and unenforceable; the respondents sued for specific performance.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to sell was contingent on the appellant first obtaining the property from the Girasdar and thus unenforceable when that failed
Whether the vendor had an implied covenant to obtain necessary permissions for transfer, including conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural use
Whether the suit for specific performance was barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963
holdings: An agreement to sell creates an implied covenant on the vendor to do all things necessary to give effect to the contract, including obtaining required permissions, even if the vendor later acquires title independently.
The failure of an initial agreement does not render a subsequent agreement unenforceable if the vendor later acquires title and the subject matter becomes transferable.
The suit for specific performance was filed within the three-year limitation period, which began only when the vendor obtained permission to convert the land and could legally execute the sale deed.
doctrines: Implied covenant in contracts to do all things necessary for performance
Doctrine of feeding the estoppel
Contingent contract under Section 32 of the Contract Act

card.dispute: The landlord sued the tenant for eviction on grounds of subletting and non-residential use; the tenant claimed the occupants were paying guests, not sub-tenants.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant unlawfully sub-let part of the premises by taking in paying guests without the landlord's consent under Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act
Whether the tenant used the premises for a non-residential purpose by hosting paying guests, warranting eviction under Section 13(1)(h) of the Act
Whether the High Court could allow a new ground of eviction for the first time in second appeal
holdings: Taking persons as paying guests without creating any interest in the property does not amount to sub-letting under Section 13(1)(a) if the tenant retains possession and control.
Using a residential premises to host paying guests, while continuing to reside there with family, does not constitute a change of purpose under Section 13(1)(h).
A new ground for eviction not raised in the plaint or lower courts cannot be permitted for the first time in second appeal.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 13(1)(a)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, Section 13(1)(h)
doctrines: Principle of res judicata and finality of findings of fact in first appeal
Prohibition against raising new grounds for the first time in second appeal
Distinction between sub-tenancy and paying guest arrangement

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for default in rent payment, and the dispute centered on whether the tenant had paid arrears by the 'first day of hearing' as required under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
issues_decided: What is the meaning of 'first day of hearing of the application' under Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949?
Whether the tenant's payment of arrears after the returnable date of summons but before framing of issues was made in time to avoid eviction.
holdings: The 'first day of hearing' under Section 13(2)(i) means the date when the court begins to apply its mind to the case, typically after the filing of the written statement and framing of issues, not the returnable date of summons.

A tenant satisfies the condition to avoid eviction for rent default if arrears are paid or tendered on the date when the court first hears the case after issues are framed, not on the initial appearance date.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 10 Rule 1, Order 14 Rule 1(5), Order 15 Rule 1
doctrines: Beneficial interpretation of tenant protection laws
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory terms
Consensus on meaning of 'first hearing' across rent control legislations

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 30(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, which excluded residential buildings fetching rent over Rs. 400 per month from the Act's protection, alleging it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Section 30(ii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, which excludes residential buildings with rent exceeding Rs. 400 per month from the Act’s protection, creates an arbitrary classification violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
Whether the distinction between tenants of residential and non-residential buildings based on rent bears a rational nexus with the object of the Act.
Whether the continued application of a rent ceiling fixed in 1973 remains constitutionally valid in light of changed economic conditions.
holdings: Section 30(ii) violates Article 14 as the classification based on rent for residential buildings lacks rational nexus with the object of protecting weaker sections.
The distinction between residential and non-residential buildings is arbitrary, as tenants of both types need equal protection, and higher rent does not imply lesser need for protection.
A rent ceiling of Rs. 400 set in 1973 has become constitutionally invalid due to inflation and changed economic realities, rendering the provision discriminatory over time.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 30(ii)
doctrines: Equal protection under law (Article 14)
Reasonable classification doctrine
Doctrine of change in circumstances affecting constitutional validity

card.dispute: Landowners and the Central Warehousing Corporation contested the compensation awarded by the Collector for acquired land, with the Corporation seeking reduction of the award through a writ petition.
issues_decided: Whether a company or local authority at whose instance land is acquired can seek a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to reduce compensation awarded by the Collector.
Whether a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is maintainable by the acquiring authority to challenge the Collector's award as excessive.
holdings: The proviso to Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 bars any company or local authority from demanding a reference under Section 18 to reduce compensation, and Section 25 prohibits courts from awarding less than the Collector’s amount.

A writ petition under Article 226 cannot be used by the acquiring authority to circumvent statutory bars and challenge the compensation awarded by the Collector as excessive, absent allegations of fraud, corruption, or collusion.
doctrines: Statutory bar doctrine
Offer and acceptance in land acquisition
Prohibition of circumvention of statutory remedies through writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: Sonik Industries, Rajkot, challenged the validity of tax rules imposed by the Rajkot Municipal Corporation, arguing that the rules were not properly published under Section 77 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925.
issues_decided: Whether the publication of tax rules under Section 77 of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, requires the full text of the rules to be published in a newspaper, or if notice of availability for inspection and purchase at the municipal office suffices.
Whether the mode of publication adopted by the Municipality satisfied the mandatory requirements of Section 77 for imposing a tax.
holdings: Publication under Section 77 is satisfied if affected persons can reasonably access the rules through notice informing them of the sanction and availability for inspection or purchase at the municipal office.
The mode of publication is not strictly prescribed by the Act; substantial compliance is sufficient if it enables affected persons, with reasonable diligence, to become acquainted with the rules.
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Doctrine of reasonable accessibility in statutory publication
Strict construction of tax statutes

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the Civil Judge's decision that surplus land should be determined based on the heirs' holdings after the death of the original tenure-holder, rather than on the date the ceiling was imposed.
issues_decided: Whether the liability to surrender surplus land under the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, ends upon the death of the tenure-holder before notice under Section 10(2) is issued.
What is the relevant date for determining surplus land: the date the ceiling was imposed or the date of computation by authorities?
Whether the heirs of a tenure-holder are entitled to treat their individual shares as separate units for ceiling purposes.
holdings: The liability to surrender surplus land is determined as of the date the ceiling is imposed and does not cease upon the death of the tenure-holder.
The relevant date for determining surplus land is the appointed date when the ceiling became effective, not the date of notice or disposal.
The estate of the deceased tenure-holder, not the individual shares of heirs, is the unit for determining surplus land; heirs collectively retain only what the original holder could have retained.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 9
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1961, Rule 19
doctrines: Res judicata
Continuity of liability in land ceiling laws post-death of tenure-holder
Fixed point-in-time determination of ceiling area

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged the High Court's exercise of power under Article 227 to set aside factual findings of a Surplus Land Determination Tribunal after the landowner had accepted a remand order without objection.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can use Article 227 powers to set aside factual findings of a tribunal when the party later challenged an order issued after accepting the remand.
Whether the order of remand by the Revenue Tribunal was invalid due to lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
holdings: The High Court cannot invoke Article 227 to overturn factual findings after a party has waived objections by submitting to a remand order.
The Revenue Tribunal had jurisdiction to remand the case, and its order was valid, especially since no party challenged it at the time.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 12
Hyderabad Tenants and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 38-E
doctrines: Waiver of right by conduct
Limits on supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Doctrine of acquiescence

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the Allahabad High Court's acquittal of 19 accused persons convicted by the Sessions Court for the brutal murder and dismemberment of two individuals, arguing that the High Court erred in rejecting reliable evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the eyewitness testimony of P.Ws. 1, 6, and 7 and the early FIR (Ex. Ka-7) based on alleged inconsistencies and lack of 'implicit reliance'.
Whether the convictions of Accused 12 to 15 could be sustained in the absence of their names in the initial complaint and lack of attributed overt acts by eyewitnesses.
Whether the death sentences awarded to Accused 1, 2, and 16 should be confirmed or commuted given the delay in appeal.
holdings: The High Court erred in demanding 'implicit reliance' on evidence instead of applying the standard of 'proof beyond reasonable doubt'; the testimony of P.Ws. 1, 6, and 7 and the FIR (Ex. Ka-7) were reliable and consistent enough to sustain conviction.
The convictions of Accused 12 to 15 cannot be sustained as their names were absent in the initial report and no overt acts were attributed to them by eyewitnesses; their acquittal is upheld.
The death sentences for Accused 1, 2, and 16 are commuted to life imprisonment due to the inordinate delay in the disposal of the appeals, though their convictions are restored.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 201 read with Section 149
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Reliability of child witness
Requirement of overt act in abetment under common object (Section 149 IPC)
Appreciation of eyewitness testimony in murder cases
Commutation of death sentence due to delay in appeal

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the maintainability of eviction proceedings filed by the University of Delhi, claiming that using a bequeathed building for employee housing did not fall within the 'furtherance of its activities' under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether the University of Delhi qualifies as a 'public institution' under Section 22 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether providing residential accommodation to university employees falls within the expression 'for the furtherance of its activities' under Section 22(d).
Whether the eviction applications filed by the University were maintainable despite the terms of the will bequeathing the property.
holdings: The University of Delhi is a 'public institution' within the meaning of Section 22, Explanation, as it is an educational institution.
Providing residential accommodation to employees is essential for the smooth functioning of a university and thus falls within 'for the furtherance of its activities' under Section 22(d).
The will only restricted the sale or disposal of the property, not its use for institutional purposes, so the eviction applications were maintainable.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Explanation to Section 22
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Purposive interpretation of 'furtherance of activities'
Judicial deference to institutional needs in rent control matters

card.dispute: The Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee sued the Union of India and others for damages and an apology over military action at the Golden Temple during Operation Blue Star, while the Union of India sought to transfer the suit out of Punjab due to security and fairness concerns.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed in Punjab alleging massive damage to Gurdwara properties during Operation Blue Star should be transferred to another state for the ends of justice
Whether there was a reasonable apprehension that a fair trial could not be conducted in Punjab due to communal tensions and sensitivities surrounding the Golden Temple
holdings: The Supreme Court held that due to the extraordinary and sensitive nature of the allegations, and the potential for communal passions to interfere with justice, the ends of justice required the suit to be transferred out of Punjab.

The Court held that even if the judiciary in Punjab is independent, a reasonable apprehension exists that justice may not be perceived as being done, and thus transfer to a calmer jurisdiction is necessary to uphold public confidence in the judicial process.
doctrines: Justice must not only be done but must also be seen to be done
Power to transfer cases for ends of justice under exceptional circumstances
Act of State doctrine (not applied, but raised as a defence)

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the validity of a transfer of assets by a loss-making company to Rajeswari & Co., alleging it was done to fraudulently defeat tax liabilities.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer of assets by the company was voidable under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 due to fraudulent intent to defeat creditors
Whether the transfer in favour of a non-creditor (Rajeswari & Co.) rendered the transaction invalid
Whether inadequate consideration or undervaluation of assets invalidated the transfer
Whether the directors' personal benefit from the sale proceeds affected the validity of the transfer
holdings: A transfer is not voidable under Section 53 if it is made for adequate consideration, satisfies genuine debts, and the debtor retains no benefit, even if it prejudices some creditors.
It is permissible for a debtor to prefer one creditor over others; transferring assets to a non-creditor does not invalidate the transaction if proceeds are used to pay genuine debts.
Allegations of undervaluation or inadequate consideration require concrete findings; in absence of such findings, the court will not interfere with concurrent findings of lower courts.
Mere relationship between directors and transferee does not prove fraud unless there is a finding that the debtor retained a benefit, which was not established here.
doctrines: Fraudulent transfer doctrine under Section 53
Preference of creditors not fraudulent per se
Principle of adequate consideration and no retention of benefit
Finality of findings of fact in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellants (Suraj Mal and another) challenged the arbitration award in favor of the respondents (Ram Singh and others), claiming rights over disputed land based on a sale deed and subsequent possession, while the respondents claimed the sale was invalid and they were rightful owners as heirs of Sona Devi.
issues_decided: Whether the consolidation proceedings barred the appeals and affected their maintainability
Whether the arbitration proceedings were invalid due to non-joinder of parties
Whether the arbitrator committed legal misconduct by failing to consider Section 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the appellants were entitled to the benefit of Section 3 of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952 based on cultivatory possession
holdings: The notification under Section 4(2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 does not bar appeals arising from proceedings prior to consolidation; thus, the appeals were maintainable.
Objections to the maintainability of arbitration proceedings must be raised at the time of reference under Section 12, not later; the delay in raising the objection rendered it inadmissible.

The arbitrator did not commit legal misconduct; the appellants had no valid intermediary interest under Section 18 of the Zamindari Abolition Act as the sale deed was invalid and did not confer any title.

A person in illegal possession of land cannot claim cultivatory possession under Section 3(1) of the U.P. Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952; thus, the appellants were not entitled to its benefits.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 4
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 4A
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 5
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 52
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 18
Uttar Pradesh Land Reforms (Supplementary) Act, 1952, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of legal necessity in transfers by limited owners
Doctrine of adverse possession
Doctrine of res judicata in arbitration proceedings
Principle that illegal possession cannot form the basis of statutory benefits

card.dispute: The appellant Surinder Singh challenged the High Court's quashing of a government order allowing him to deposit the balance purchase price for an evacuee property, after earlier defaults, while respondents Sohan Lal and Sunder Lal opposed the restoration of his bid.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could quash an order under Article 226 without the impugned order being produced before it.

Whether the Central Government, under Section 33 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, could set aside an earlier cancellation of an auction sale and allow the appellant to deposit the balance amount.
Whether the exercise of power under Section 33 without affording a hearing to the respondents, who were subsequent highest bidders, violated the principles of natural justice.
holdings: It is improper for a High Court to quash an order under Article 226 of the Constitution without the impugned order being produced, as the court cannot assess the reasoning behind the order in its absence.

The Central Government has wide residuary powers under Section 33 of the Act to set aside prior orders and extend time for compliance, and such extensions do not amount to a review of the original order.

Although the subsequent highest bidders have no legal right to the property until sale confirmation, they have a sufficient interest in the matter and must be given a hearing before an order under Section 33 affects their position, failing which the order violates natural justice.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 33
doctrines: Principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Residuary powers of administrative authorities
In terrorem nature of peremptory procedural orders

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the maintainability of an intra-court appeal against a single judge's order under Article 227 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court against an order of a single judge exercising jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.
Whether a petition filed under both Articles 226 and 227 allows a right of appeal under Clause 15 if the substantial part relates to Article 226.
holdings: No appeal lies under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent against an order passed by a single judge in exercise of powers under Article 227 of the Constitution, as such appeals are expressly barred.
Where a petition is filed under both Articles 226 and 227, and the substantial part of the relief sought is under Article 226, the right of appeal under Clause 15 should not be denied.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 36(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 39
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958, Section 52
doctrines: Intra-court appeal bar under Letters Patent
Doctrine of finality of orders under Article 227
Principle of preserving valuable rights of appeal where substantial relief is under Article 226

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a joint Hindu family over whether adopted sons of widows of deceased coparceners were entitled to a share in the joint family property, and whether a prior partition in 1956 barred their claims.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 applied to the parties, who were residents of the erstwhile Hyderabad State.
Whether Section 12 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 barred the adopted sons from claiming a share in the joint family property.
Whether a partition of the joint family property in 1956 had taken place, which would have vested separate estates in the defendants.
holdings: The Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937 did not apply to the parties as it was extended to the Hyderabad State after the deaths of the coparceners in question.

Section 12 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 does not bar an adopted child from claiming a share in joint family property, as adoption does not 'divest' any person of a vested estate under proviso (c) of the section.
The claim of a partition in 1956 was not proved, as no partition deed was produced, no issue was framed on it, and the evidence was insufficient to establish its occurrence.
provisions: Hindu Women's Right to Property Act, 1937
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of survivorship in Hindu joint family law
Doctrine of vested estate under Section 12 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956
Burden of proof in establishing a partition of joint family property

card.dispute: The appellants (owners of requisitioned premises) fought with the Ministry of Communication over their entitlement to interest on compensation awarded for the requisition of their property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are entitled to interest on the amount awarded by the Arbitrator for the requisition of premises under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952.
If so, from which date and at what rate the interest should be payable.
holdings: The appellants are entitled to interest on the compensation amount from the date possession was taken (March 1975) until the amount was paid or the premises were derequisitioned (up to July 31, 1987).
Interest is payable at 6% per annum from March 7, 1975, to February 28, 1985, and at 12% per annum from August 8, 1985, to July 31, 1987, only on the unpaid balance of the award.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
doctrines: Entitlement to interest as compensation for loss of possession
Presumption of interest in statutory expropriation unless statute shows contrary intention
Equitable principle that purchaser in possession owes interest on unpaid purchase price

card.dispute: The dispute was between Bal Niketan Nursery School and its tenants, including Kesari Prasad, over the school's right to file eviction suits and whether the suit was filed by the proper plaintiff.
issues_decided: Whether the Bal Niketan Nursery School, as a recognised institution, was exempt from the U.P. Urban Building Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction Act, 1972, and thus entitled to file eviction suits.
Whether the suit was maintainable when filed in the name of the school instead of the registered society managing it.
Whether the High Court erred in not allowing substitution of the proper plaintiff under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code.
holdings: A recognised educational institution under the U.P. Basic Education Act, 1972 is exempt from the U.P. Rent Act and may file eviction suits through its manager.
A suit filed by a school managed by a registered society is not invalid if the society is the real party in interest, even if not formally named as plaintiff.
Where a suit is filed due to a bona fide mistake in naming the wrong plaintiff, the court must allow substitution or addition of the proper party under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to serve justice.

The High Court should have exercised its power under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to add the registered society as a plaintiff instead of remitting the case, to prevent failure of justice on technical grounds.
provisions: U.P. Urban Building Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction Act, 1972 -- Section 2(1)(b)
doctrines: Bona fide mistake in litigation
Substitution of proper party under CPC
Exemption of recognised institutions from rent control laws
Liberal interpretation of procedural rules to meet ends of justice

card.dispute: The appellants, Asharfi Lal & Sons, challenged their conviction and death sentence for the brutal murders of two nieces, committed out of personal vengeance over a property dispute with their mother, Smt. Bulakan.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence awarded to Asharfi Lal and Babu was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case?
Whether the case falls within the 'rarest of the rare' category warranting capital punishment?
holdings: The court held that the murders were cold-blooded, extremely brutal, and shocked the judicial conscience, thus justifying the death penalty.
The death sentence was upheld as a measure of social necessity and deterrence, confirming it fits the 'rarest of the rare' category under Indian sentencing jurisprudence.
doctrines: Rarest of the rare doctrine
Judicial conscience test
Proportionality principle in sentencing
Deterrence as a basis for punishment

card.dispute: Residents of four villages challenged the state's notification constituting part of their villages as a notified area under the Himachal Pradesh Municipal Act, 1968, arguing it violated natural justice and statutory conditions.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government can constitute a notified area without affording residents an opportunity of being heard, despite civil consequences.
Whether the requirements of Section 256 of the Himachal Pradesh Municipal Act, 1968 were satisfied in declaring the area as a notified area.
holdings: Where administrative action under a statute results in civil consequences, the principles of natural justice require that affected persons must be given an opportunity of being heard, unless the law explicitly excludes it.
The State Government’s decision to constitute a notified area without considering statutory conditions or inviting objections from residents is invalid and contrary to the rule of law.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Rule of law
Administrative action and civil consequences

card.dispute: The Bank of India sued Vijay Transport and others for recovery of a loan, while the respondents claimed the debt should be scaled down under the Andhra Pradesh Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as the bank was a corporation formed under a special Indian law.
issues_decided: Whether the Banking Companies Act, 1970 is a 'special Indian law' within the meaning of Section 4(e) of the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938
Whether debts due to the Bank of India are liable to be scaled down under Section 4(e) of the Act
Whether the latter part of Section 4(e) of the Act violates Article 14 of the Constitution
holdings: The Banking Companies Act, 1970 is a special Indian law, and the Bank of India is a corporation formed under it, thus falling within the exception in Section 4(e) of the Andhra Pradesh Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938.
Debts due to the Bank of India are not liable to be scaled down under Section 4(e) of the Act as the bank is covered by the exception for corporations formed under a special Indian law.
The exception in Section 4(e) for corporations formed under a special Indian law does not violate Article 14, as it does not create invidious discrimination in favour of British corporations.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, Section 4(e)
Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and context
Doctrine of equality under Article 14
Deeming provisions and retrospective operation of statutes

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the release order passed by the Prescribed Authority in favor of the respondents who sought possession of leased premises, alleging lack of jurisdiction and breach of undertaking.
issues_decided: Whether the Prescribed Authority was legally competent to pass the release order under Section 3(e) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972
Whether the order of the Prescribed Authority could be challenged on the ground of lack of jurisdiction in a collateral proceeding
Whether the rule of merger applies when the tribunal lacks jurisdiction
Whether the respondents breached their undertaking to the court by recovering possession
holdings: An officer appointed as Prescribed Authority with colour of lawful authority can validly pass orders even if there is a defect in qualification, due to the de-facto doctrine.
The validity of an appointment to a judicial or quasi-judicial office cannot be challenged collaterally in a private dispute between litigants.
It is unnecessary to decide if the rule of merger applies to jurisdictional defects because the de-facto doctrine already validates the order.
The respondents did not breach their undertaking as it was time-bound and expired, and possession was taken in good faith after its lapse.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(e)
doctrines: De-facto doctrine
Rule against collateral attack on judicial appointments
Rule of merger of orders
Rule of finality of judgments

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of tenants on grounds including material alteration of the premises by constructing a wooden balcony without permission; the tenants challenged the eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of a wooden balcony (Dochhatti) amounted to a material alteration under Section 13(1)(c) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950
Whether minor or temporary constructions by a tenant can constitute grounds for eviction on the basis of material alteration
holdings: A material alteration requires a substantial change in the form, front, or structure of the building without destroying its identity, and must be of essential or important nature.
Construction of a temporary wooden balcony that can be removed without damage does not constitute a material alteration justifying eviction.
The permanence or temporariness of a structure is a relevant factor in determining whether an alteration is material.
Minor alterations made for convenient use of premises, which do not affect the building’s structure or front, do not amount to material alterations.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(c)
doctrines: Material alteration doctrine
Substantial change test
Temporary vs permanent construction distinction

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased appellant sought to condone delay in applying to be brought on record in a pending appeal after the suit abated due to the appellant's death.
issues_decided: Whether sufficient cause was shown under Section 5 of the Limitation Act to condone the delay in applying to bring the legal representatives on record after abatement of the appeal?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the application for condonation of delay on grounds of lack of knowledge and procedural default?
holdings: Delay in filing an application to bring legal representatives on record can be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act if sufficient cause is shown, especially when the applicants are agriculturists with little legal knowledge.

The court must adopt a liberal approach to condonation of delay to advance justice, and the mere fact that co-appellants had knowledge does not bar relief when the applicant himself had no knowledge and acted promptly upon learning of the appeal.
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Liberal interpretation for ends of justice
Abatement of suit due to non-substitution of legal representatives

card.dispute: The dispute was between land allottees and the heirs of a deceased landholder over whether the allottees could be dispossessed after the landholder's death due to alleged re-determination of surplus land.
issues_decided: Whether the surplus area from the holding of Abdul Latif Khan could be re-determined after his death under the Punjab Land Reforms Act, 1972.
Whether the Commissioner had jurisdiction to entertain an appeal by the heirs challenging the allotment of surplus land made before the landholder's death.
Whether the allottees' rights to the land, allotted between 1967 and 1973, could be disturbed after they had paid for and possessed the land for over a decade.
holdings: The determination of surplus area from a landholder's estate becomes final during their lifetime and cannot be re-opened after death for re-determination.
The Commissioner lacked jurisdiction to entertain an appeal by heirs against an order that did not adversely affect them or their predecessor.
Allottees who lawfully purchased and possessed surplus land for resettlement cannot be dispossessed due to a subsequent re-determination that has no legal basis.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act
doctrines: Finality of administrative determination of surplus land during a landholder's lifetime
Doctrine of lawful acquisition and protection of vested rights
Lack of jurisdiction over non-justiciable or non-adverse proceedings

card.dispute: The tenant-appellants challenged their eviction on grounds of rent default and landlord's bona fide requirement, claiming adjustment of excess rent paid over 30 years and contesting the landlord's need for the shop.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of 'in pari delicto' bars tenants from claiming adjustment of excess rent paid in violation of rent control laws
Whether the High Court could interfere with the appellate court's finding on the landlord's bona fide requirement in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Whether the tenant could be evicted based on the landlord's bona fide need for the premises for family business
holdings: The doctrine of 'in pari delicto' may not apply where one party is exploited, but it can apply when both parties voluntarily violate rent control laws for mutual benefit.
A High Court can interfere in a second appeal if the lower appellate court's finding is based on erroneous assumptions, misreading of evidence, or incorrect legal tests.
The landlord's bona fide need for the shop to employ family members was established, justifying eviction, and the High Court rightly restored the trial court's decree.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act
doctrines: In pari delicto
Bona fide requirement
Second appeal on questions of law

card.dispute: Bharat Coking Coal Limited alleged that Ram Nath Singh and his son committed contempt by suppressing a Supreme Court status quo order and obtaining a fresh order from the High Court permitting slurry extraction.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed contempt by obtaining a High Court order while concealing the Supreme Court's status quo direction?
What is the meaning and scope of the phrase 'status quo as in the High Court' in the Supreme Court's order?
Whether the respondents were entitled to continue extracting slurry under a prior High Court order?
holdings: The phrase 'status quo as in the High Court' refers to the state of affairs existing while the matter was pending before the High Court, before its final judgment, and not thereafter.
Since the status quo order did not explicitly prohibit actions under prior High Court orders, the respondents' conduct, though deplorable, did not amount to criminal contempt.
The respondents had no legal right to extract slurry from the land, as it was acquired under Section 9(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, along with mineral rights.
provisions: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, Section 2
doctrines: Doctrine of status quo in interim orders
Doctrine of wilful disobedience in contempt proceedings
Doctrine of implied limitation on interim orders

card.dispute: The State of Jammu & Kashmir fought with landowners over whether a four-day delay in filing an appeal against a compensation enhancement in a land acquisition case should be condoned.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to condone a four-day delay in filing an appeal by the State under Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963?
Whether the State, as a litigant, should be held to a different standard when seeking condonation of delay?
holdings: The expression 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act is elastic and must be interpreted liberally to ensure substantial justice, especially when the delay is non-deliberate and the case raises important legal questions.

The State, as a representative of public interest, should not be denied equitable treatment in condonation of delay; it is entitled to the same liberal approach as private litigants to ensure justice on merits.
doctrines: Substantial justice over technicalities
Equality before law
Liberal interpretation of limitation for condonation of delay

card.dispute: The tenant sought to evict the sub-tenant for non-payment of rent and denial of title, while the sub-tenant had attorned to the landlord due to a threat of eviction by a paramount title holder.
issues_decided: Whether the sub-tenant could be evicted under s. 10(2)(i) and (vi) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 for non-payment of rent and denial of title
Whether the rule of estoppel under s. 116 of the Evidence Act, 1872 barred the sub-tenant from denying the tenant-landlord's title
Whether attornment under threat of eviction by a paramount title holder breaks the estoppel under s. 116
holdings: No order of eviction under s. 10(2)(i) or (vi) can be made unless the dispute over title is found to be not bona fide, which was not established here.
A sub-tenant under threat of eviction by a paramount title holder is not estopped under s. 116 of the Evidence Act from denying the intermediate tenant's title.
When a tenant attorns to a paramount title holder due to threat of eviction, a new tenancy is created and the estoppel under s. 116 no longer applies.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(vi)
doctrines: Estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act
Eviction by paramount title
Attornment under threat of eviction

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of personal need, which the tenant challenged after subsequent events, including an attempted property sale and changes in circumstances.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide need for personal occupation remained valid despite subsequent events, including an agreement to sell part of the property.
Whether the finality of an eviction order under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 could be disturbed due to events occurring after the order became final.
Whether an agreement to sell the property to the tenant's wife negated the landlord's claim of personal need.
holdings: A landlord's bona fide need for personal occupation, once established, continues unless clearly satisfied or negated by material changes, which were absent here.
Final orders under rent control legislation must be respected and not reopened due to subsequent events, especially when statute prohibits such re-examination.
An unexecuted and lapsed agreement to sell part of the property does not invalidate the landlord's original need, particularly when permission was denied and the agreement was forfeited.
provisions: U.P. Temporary Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 43(2)(rr)
doctrines: Finality of judicial orders
Bona fide requirement for personal need in landlord-tenant law
Doctrine of res judicata in rent control proceedings
Subsequent events not altering final eviction orders

card.dispute: The landlord, Dr. Saroj Kumar Das, sought eviction of tenant Arjun Prasad Jogani on grounds of personal requirement, but the tenant argued the landlord's need was satisfied by acquiring another flat in South Calcutta.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's genuine requirement for personal occupation was established despite acquiring alternative accommodation?
Whether the alternative accommodation in South Calcutta was reasonably suitable to meet the landlord's requirement?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact in second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC?
holdings: A landlord's genuine need for personal use must be assessed based on actual circumstances, and prior findings of fact by lower courts should not be overturned without strong justification.
An alternative accommodation is not reasonably suitable if it does not align with the landlord’s professional and personal needs, especially when relocating would hinder established medical practice.

The High Court erred in relying on isolated facts like a residence agreement and intention to start a laboratory, while ignoring unchallenged evidence that the new flat was unsuitable for the landlord’s purpose.
doctrines: Genuine requirement of landlord
Reasonable suitability of alternative accommodation
Limited scope of interference in second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to demarcate the boundary of a property he purchased and to obtain an injunction against the defendant for trespass, after a dispute arose over the boundary between their adjacent lands.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for demarcation of the boundary of a property is maintainable when the plaintiff is uncertain about the precise boundary.
Whether Indian courts can rely on English precedents distinguishing legal and equitable estates to deny boundary demarcation suits.
holdings: A suit for demarcation of boundaries between adjacent properties is maintainable if it is of a civil nature and not expressly or impliedly barred, regardless of the plaintiff's uncertainty about the boundary.

Indian courts need not follow English technical distinctions between legal and equitable estates; the maintainability of a suit depends on Section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code, not English precedents.
doctrines: Jurisdiction under Section 9 CPC
Rejection of English common law technicalities in Indian civil jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the applicability of Section 34 of the CPC to proceedings under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, specifically whether interest could be awarded at the contractual rate after the decree date when the order was silent on future interest.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings under Section 31 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 are in the nature of a suit and whether an order under Section 32 thereof amounts to a decree?
Whether Section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies to such proceedings for awarding interest from the date of decree to the date of payment?
Whether interest on the principal amount is payable at the contractual rate in the absence of an express order under Section 34 CPC?
holdings: Proceedings under Section 31 of the State Financial Corporations Act are not suits but akin to execution proceedings for attachment or sale of property, and orders under Section 32 are not decrees in the traditional sense.

Section 34 of the CPC does not apply to proceedings under Section 31 of the Act because such proceedings are not suits and do not culminate in a decree to which interest provisions under Section 34 attach.

Interest is payable on the principal amount at the contractual rate as per the agreement between the parties until full payment, even if the order is silent on future interest, because the Act allows recovery as per contract.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rules 6 and 11
doctrines: Nature of statutory proceedings versus civil suits
Applicability of interest under Section 34 CPC to non-suit proceedings
Contractual liability for interest in execution-like proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether specific performance of a contract for the sale of land should be granted despite structures built on the land by the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in decreeing specific performance in favour of the plaintiffs
Whether granting specific performance would cause special hardship to the defendants
holdings: The High Court correctly found the plaintiffs ready and willing to perform and the defendant in breach of contract.

Specific performance should not be granted where it would cause special hardship due to costly structures already built; instead, compensation may be awarded under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
doctrines: Doctrine of specific performance
Doctrine of special hardship
Equitable relief under Section 20

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of a deceased auction-purchaser and the judgment-debtor over whether an application for delivery of possession filed beyond one year of confirmation of sale was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order XXI Rule 95 CPC for delivery of possession is governed by Article 134 or Article 136 of the Limitation Act
Whether the period of limitation for filing an application for possession starts from the date of confirmation of sale or from the dismissal of a subsequent application to set aside the sale
Whether Explanation II to Section 47 CPC, inserted by the 1976 Amendment, alters the limitation period applicable to possession applications
holdings: An application under Order XXI Rule 95 CPC for delivery of possession is governed by Article 134 of the Limitation Act, which prescribes a one-year limitation period from the date of confirmation of sale.

The limitation period cannot be extended by subsequent objections to the sale; once a sale is confirmed and becomes absolute, later applications to set aside the sale do not restart the limitation clock.
Explanation II to Section 47 CPC does not equate an application for possession with execution of a decree, and thus Article 136 (12-year limitation) does not apply.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 95
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 47 (Explanation II)
doctrines: Res judicata
Limitation period computation from finality of sale
Distinction between execution of decree and application for possession

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, which abolished their right to resume tenanted land for personal cultivation and restricted advocates from appearing before land tribunals.
issues_decided: Whether the Karnataka Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1974, which removed landlords' right to resume land for personal cultivation, is constitutionally valid under the basic structure doctrine?
Whether the Land Tribunals constituted under Section 48(8) of the Act must be manned by judicial personnel?
Whether Section 48(8) of the Act, which barred legal practitioners from appearing before tribunals, is repugnant to the Advocates Act, 1961?
holdings: The 1974 Amendment Act is a valid agrarian reform law aimed at securing Directive Principles under Articles 39(b) and (c), and does not violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
Land Tribunals under Section 48(8) do not require judicial personnel, as the disputes involved do not necessarily demand a trained judicial mind.
Section 48(8) cannot be enforced to prevent advocates from appearing before tribunals, as it is repugnant to Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and must yield to central legislation.
provisions: Constitution of India, Articles 31-A, 31-B, 31-C, 39(b), 39(c), Ninth Schedule
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Repugnancy between state and central laws
Agrarian reform as part of Directive Principles enforcement
Non-requirement of judicial mind for certain administrative tribunals

card.dispute: The legatees of a Hindu widow contested the reversioners' claim to half the gifted land, arguing the widow had absolute ownership via the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and could validly bequeath it by will.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree declaring the gift ineffective affected the widow's ownership status
Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, converted the widow's limited interest into absolute ownership despite the prior invalid gift
Whether the widow was competent to bequeath the property by will after 1956
holdings: The compromise decree rendered the gift ineffective, so the widow retained her limited ownership until 1956.
By operation of Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the widow's limited interest became absolute, giving her full power to dispose of the property by will.
Since the will was genuine and executed after the Act came into force, the legatees' claim under the will prevails over reversioners' claims.
doctrines: Conversion of limited estate into absolute estate under Section 14(1)
Doctrine of testamentary competence of Hindu female after 1956 Act

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed whether an oral compromise in court, not reduced to writing and signed, could be enforced under the Civil Procedure Code.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise made orally during court proceedings but not reduced to writing and signed by the parties can be enforced under Order XXIII Rule 3 of the CPC
Whether the two parts of Order XXIII Rule 3 are disjunctive and apply to different types of compromises
holdings: A compromise under Order XXIII Rule 3 must be in writing and signed by the parties, even if made in court, to be enforceable.
The first part of Order XXIII Rule 3 applies to all lawful compromises, whether in or out of court, and the requirement of writing and signature is mandatory to prevent fraudulent claims.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with procedural requirements
Interpretation of statutory provisions based on object and reason

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant, alleging subletting of the premises to a partnership firm, while the tenant claimed he was part of the partnership using the premises for business, not subletting.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant committed subletting by allowing a partnership to use the leased premises.
Whether the High Court could reappraise evidence and overturn findings of fact in revision under Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents Act.
Whether the existence of a partnership is a mixed question of law and fact.
holdings: Mere use of leased premises by a partnership, without parting with legal possession, does not constitute subletting under the Rent Act.
The High Court cannot, in revision, substitute its view of evidence for that of the trial court if the lower court's finding is plausible and based on proper legal principles.
Whether a partnership exists is a mixed question of law and fact, depending on agreement, profit-sharing, and agency, and must be determined on a case-by-case basis.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 29
doctrines: Subletting requires parting with legal possession
Revisional jurisdiction does not allow reappreciation of evidence to substitute a possible finding
Partnership determination is a mixed question of law and fact

card.dispute: The landlord, Dr. Jeetsingh, sued to evict tenant Govind on grounds of bona fide need for the premises; the tenant claimed the landlord already had sufficient accommodation and the suit was for higher rent.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord had a bona fide need for the suit premises justifying eviction under Section 12(1)(e) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the first appellate court's finding that the landlord's need was not bona fide in second appeal.
holdings: The landlord's need for eviction must be both reasonable and bona fide, judged objectively from evidence, not merely by parties' assertions.
The High Court exceeded its limited scope in second appeal by overturning factual findings of the first appellate court without showing legal error or perversity.
Subsequent death of the landlord's first wife and vacancy of her three rooms negated any ongoing bona fide need, warranting setting aside of the eviction order.
doctrines: Bona fide requirement test for landlord eviction
Objective assessment of factual claims in rent control cases
Limited scope of second appeal under civil procedure

card.dispute: Members of a Scheduled Caste community from villages within the Nasirpur Panchayat in Delhi fought for the implementation of a Gaon Sabha resolution allotting them land for residential use, against authorities who resisted the allotment and initiated land acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Gaon Sabha resolution of 25.2.1984 allotting land to Scheduled Caste members for residential purposes should be implemented despite objections and acquisition proceedings.
Whether non-residents of the specific village where the land is located but residents within the broader Panchayat area could be eligible for allotment.
Whether the land acquisition notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act should be quashed to allow the allotment.
holdings: The resolution passed by the Gaon Sabha for allotting land to economically backward Scheduled Caste members for housing is valid and must be implemented.
Residence within the Panchayat area, not limited to the specific revenue village, satisfies the residence requirement for allotment, allowing flexibility for socially beneficial purposes.
The land acquisition notification is quashed as it undermines the welfare objective of providing housing to underprivileged sections who have long resided in the area.
doctrines: Principle of social justice
Welfare state doctrine
Judicial review of administrative action
Beneficial interpretation for marginalized communities

card.dispute: The tenant of a mortgaged shop, let out by the mortgagee, resisted the mortgagor's claim for possession after redemption of the mortgage, claiming protection under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether a lease created by a mortgagee during the subsistence of a mortgage survives after redemption of the mortgage
Whether the tenant of a mortgagee is entitled to protection under the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 after the mortgage is redeemed
Whether the lease granted by the mortgagee was an act of prudent management under Section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act
holdings: A lease created by a mortgagee during the subsistence of a mortgage terminates upon redemption of the mortgage, as the mortgagee cannot confer a better title than he himself possesses.
A tenant of a mortgagee is not entitled to protection under rent control laws against the mortgagor after redemption, as the landlord-tenant relationship ends with the mortgage.
A lease by a mortgagee binds the mortgagor only if it is an act of prudent management; otherwise, it does not survive redemption, especially if prohibited by mortgage terms or found imprudent.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950
doctrines: Doctrine of privity of estate and limited title of mortgagee
Doctrine of prudent management under Section 76 of the Transfer of Property Act
General rule that one cannot transfer better title than one possesses

card.dispute: The landholder Hari Shanker sued to eject his tenant Habib and sub-tenant Ida for violating the five-year limit on sub-tenancy under the United Provinces Tenancy Act, 1939, while the tenant's right to retain possession under stay orders was contested.
issues_decided: Whether the continuation of a sub-tenancy beyond five years entitled the landholder to eject both the tenant and sub-tenant under Section 171 of the United Provinces Tenancy Act, 1939
Whether the question of termination of sub-tenancy is distinct from the question of recovery of possession
Whether pending applications for ejectment and execution were affected by prior stay orders under the Uttar Pradesh Agricultural Tenants (Acquisition of Privileges) Act, 1950
holdings: A sub-tenancy continuing beyond five years in violation of Section 40 of the United Provinces Tenancy Act, 1939, entitles the landholder to a decree for ejectment of both tenant and sub-tenant under Section 171.
The question of whether a sub-tenancy was validly terminated is separate from whether possession can be recovered; the latter must be decided in separate proceedings.
The entitlement to a decree under Section 171 is not defeated by the tenant’s inability to recover possession from the sub-tenant or by pending stay orders on related proceedings.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Agricultural Tenants (Acquisition of Privileges) (Amendment) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1950, Section 10
doctrines: Separability of ejectment decree from possession recovery
Strict compliance with statutory limits on sub-tenancy
Distinction between validity of tenancy and executability of decree

card.dispute: The mortgagors sought possession of their property after redemption, while the tenant, inducted by the mortgagee, claimed tenancy rights under rent control laws.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagee had authority to create a tenancy binding on the mortgagors beyond the term of the mortgage
Whether the tenant could claim protection under the Saurashtra Rent Control Act, 1951 or the Bombay Rent Act
Whether the tenant was a necessary party to the execution proceedings for possession after redemption
holdings: The mortgagee did not have unconditional authority to create a tenancy that would bind the mortgagors after redemption, as the mortgage deed did not contemplate such long-term obligations.

The tenant’s rights were not protected under rent control legislation because the lease was created without the mortgagors’ express concurrence and the tenancy could not survive the mortgagee’s interest.
The tenant, having no independent right to possession, was bound by the execution proceedings between the mortgagors and mortgagee, even though not formally impleaded.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Doctrine of limited authority of mortgagee in possessory mortgages
Doctrine of privity of contract in tenancy relations
Doctrine of binding effect of execution proceedings on those in privity

card.dispute: The dispute was between a cooperative housing society and the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority over the refusal to permit development of the society's land and the potential acquisition of that land for industrial and urban development.
issues_decided: Whether the Government Order (G.O.) dated 9.4.1980, stating that lands of cooperative house building societies should not be acquired 'as far as may be', is mandatory or directory.
Whether the refusal of permission by NOIDA to develop the land was based on relevant and cogent reasons.
Whether the modification of the development plan by NOIDA, changing the land use from residential to regional park, was arbitrary or discriminatory.
Whether NOIDA had taken sufficient steps towards land acquisition, and whether allotment of alternative sites was required at the stage of refusal of development permission.
holdings: The G.O. dated 9.4.1980 is directory and not mandatory, as it lacks statutory force and does not create a legal bar to acquisition of land belonging to cooperative housing societies.
NOIDA validly refused permission for development because allowing haphazard construction would frustrate the planned development objectives under the U.P. Industrial Development Act, 1976.
The Authority has implied power to modify the development plan, and the change in land use was not arbitrary or violative of Article 14, as it was done to ensure planned development.
NOIDA had taken concrete steps towards acquisition, including financial arrangements and notification processing, and alternative site allotment was not required before acquisition.
doctrines: Directory vs Mandatory interpretation of government orders
Implied powers of statutory authorities to modify development plans
Principle of planned development as a public purpose
Non-arbitrariness under Article 14 in administrative decision-making

card.dispute: The appellant, Kansa Behera, challenged his conviction for the murder of Bhatal Majhi based on circumstantial evidence, including his presence with the deceased and recovery of blood-stained clothes.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's presence with the deceased on the evening before the murder, by itself, is sufficient to sustain a conviction?
Whether the recovery of blood-stained clothes from the appellant can conclusively link him to the murder in the absence of blood grouping evidence?
Whether an extra-judicial confession, partly retracted and made after a long delay, can form the basis of conviction?
holdings: Mere presence of the accused with the deceased before the murder is not sufficient to prove guilt unless it is part of a chain of circumstances leading exclusively to guilt.
Recovery of blood-stained clothes without evidence of blood group matching the victim does not conclusively establish the accused's guilt.
An extra-judicial confession, especially when one of two witnesses retracts and the statement is made after a long delay under suspicious circumstances, cannot be relied upon for conviction.
doctrines: Principle of circumstantial evidence requiring all circumstances to be proven beyond doubt and forming a complete chain pointing exclusively to guilt
Doubtful or weak circumstantial evidence cannot sustain a conviction
Extra-judicial confession must be reliable, consistent, and corroborated to be actionable

card.dispute: The dispute was between Smt. Ram Lubhai, a daughter claiming pre-emption rights, and three vendees (Kewal Ram, Chet Ram, and Kuldip Ram) over ownership of land sold by her father, specifically concerning the validity of an ex parte decree and the setting aside of that decree in part.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order IX Rule 13 of the CPC was maintainable before the trial court after the appellate court had confirmed the ex parte decree, where the defendants were not served in either court.
Whether a joint decree in a pre-emption suit could be partially set aside against unserved defendants while being upheld against the served defendant.
holdings: An application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC is maintainable before the trial court even after an appellate decree, if the defendants were not served in either the trial or appellate proceedings, as no valid decree exists against them.

A joint pre-emption decree can be partially set aside against unserved defendants without affecting the decree against the served defendant, as the rights of the plaintiff against each vendee can be separately enforced.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Merger of decree doctrine
Principle of valid service as prerequisite to a binding decree
Partial setting aside of joint decree in equitable proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Hindu widow's claim to full ownership of property that was reconveyed to her after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, arguing she held only a limited interest.
issues_decided: Whether a Hindu widow who regains possession of her husband's property through reconveyance after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 becomes a full owner under Section 14(1)
Whether the reconveyance of alienated property to a widow amounts to a fresh acquisition under Section 14(1) of the Act
Whether the widow's original limited interest is revived and enlarged into an absolute interest upon lawful retransfer after the Act's commencement
holdings: A Hindu widow who regains possession of property by lawful reconveyance after the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 becomes the full owner under Section 14(1), as she acquires possession of the property subsequent to the Act.
Section 14(1) applies to any property possessed by a female Hindu after the Act's commencement, regardless of when the interest originated, and converts a limited interest into an absolute one.

Reconveyance to the widow nullifies the prior alienation and restores her original interest, which then ripens into full ownership under Section 14(1); she is not treated as a stranger acquiring property anew.
The purpose of Section 14(1) is to benefit the widow, and the focus must be on her acquisition of possession, not on the status or intent of the alienee who retransfers the property.
doctrines: Doctrine of complete nullification of alienation by mutual reconveyance
Doctrine of ripening of limited interest into absolute interest under Section 14(1)
Beneficial construction of statutes in favour of Hindu women's property rights

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's eviction petition, arguing that the premises were needed not for the landlord or his family directly, but for a partnership business involving his sons and strangers.
issues_decided: Whether an eviction petition under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 is maintainable when the landlord seeks possession for a partnership firm in which his sons are active partners along with strangers.

Whether the requirement of the demised premises for a business carried on by the landlord's sons in partnership with others qualifies as 'requirement for the business of a member of the family' under the Act.
holdings: A landlord can seek eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) if the premises are bona fide required for the business of his sons who are active partners in a partnership firm, even if strangers are co-partners.
Where sons are actively involved in the business and not merely sleeping partners, the requirement of the premises for the partnership amounts to a requirement for the sons' business under the Act.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
doctrines: Active participation in partnership business distinguishes it from sleeping partnership
Interpretation of 'business of a member of the family' in rent control statutes

card.dispute: The tenant (Kashi Ram) challenged the landlord's (Rakesh Arora) belated attempt to execute an eviction order from 1960, arguing it was barred by limitation and res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the application for execution of the eviction order was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether permission under Section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 was required to execute the eviction decree
Whether a second application for such permission after a lapse of over 15 years could revive a time-barred decree
holdings: A decree for eviction becomes executable from the date it is passed, and the 12-year limitation period under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 runs from that date, not from when permission under the Slum Act is obtained.
No permission under the Slum Areas Act was required to execute an eviction order based on bona fide requirement under the Delhi Rent Control Act, as such provisions had overriding effect.

The right to execute a decree accrues immediately upon its passing; delay due to non-compliance with procedural requirements does not suspend limitation, and a decree barred under the 1908 Act remained barred even after the 1963 Act.
provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19
doctrines: Accrual of right to execute decree
Overriding effect of special statutes
Limitation as a bar to stale claims
No suspension of limitation for procedural delays

card.dispute: Lachman Singh, Amarjit Singh, and Gurbax Kaur contested Kirpa Singh's claim to the entire property of Khem Kaur, arguing that they were entitled to shares as co-heirs alongside Kirpa Singh, who claimed to be the sole son of Khem Kaur.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'son' in Section 15(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 includes a 'step-son' for the purpose of inheriting the property of a Hindu female dying intestate.
Whether a step-son can inherit simultaneously with a natural son under Section 15(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
holdings: The word 'son' in Section 15(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not include a 'step-son'; it refers only to children born of the deceased woman's body.
Step-sons fall under the category of heirs of the husband in Section 15(1)(b) and cannot inherit simultaneously with natural sons under Section 15(1)(a) unless no such children exist.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Principle of propinquity in succession law
Precedence of natural children over step-children in inheritance

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad fought with allottees of low-income housing over whether it could levy property tax on houses still owned by it but occupied by allottees under a hire-purchase scheme.
issues_decided: Whether the exemption under Section 202(1)(c) of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation Act, 1955 applies to properties owned by the Corporation but occupied by others under hire-purchase agreements
Whether the term 'vesting' in Section 202(1)(c) requires both ownership and possession by the Corporation to claim tax exemption
holdings: Section 202(1)(c) exempts only properties that are both owned and actually occupied by the Corporation; mere ownership is insufficient for exemption.
The term 'vesting' must be construed as vesting in both title and possession, and thus the Corporation can levy property tax on allottees occupying the properties under hire-purchase agreements.
