doctrines: Purposeful interpretation of statutes
Vesting in both title and possession
Futility principle in taxation

card.dispute: The Math, led by its Mahant, challenged the validity of property alienations by a former Mahant and sought possession from Madan Mohan and others, while Madan Mohan appealed against the declaration of invalidity of the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the Math could file a cross-objection against Madan Mohan, a co-respondent, under Order 41 Rule 22 of the CPC?
Whether the appellate court could entertain the cross-objection under Order 41 Rule 33 of the CPC despite it not being maintainable under Rule 22?
holdings: A cross-objection under Order 41 Rule 22 CPC is generally maintainable only against the appellant, and not against a co-respondent, except in exceptional cases where the relief sought requires reopening issues between respondents.

Even if a cross-objection is not maintainable under Rule 22, the appellate court may consider it under Rule 33, which empowers it to pass any decree necessary for justice, including between co-respondents, provided the parties are before the court and the issue arises from the lower court’s judgment.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 22
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 33
doctrines: Maintainability of cross-objections
Appellate powers under Rule 33 for ends of justice
Exceptional circumstances for cross-objection against co-respondent

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested ownership of a treasure found during renovation, and whether a counter-claim filed after the written statement was maintainable under the Civil Procedure Code.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Section 14 of the Indian Treasure Trove Act, 1878 can be filed when a suit has already been initiated under Section 8 of the Act
Whether a counter-claim can be filed after the submission of a written statement under Order VIII, Rule 6A(1) of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908
holdings: A suit under Section 14 of the Indian Treasure Trove Act is not maintainable if the Collector has not declared the treasure ownerless under Section 9, as Section 14 applies only after such a declaration and an order under Section 13.

A counter-claim is maintainable under Order VIII, Rule 6A(1) of the CPC if the cause of action arose before or during the time for filing the written statement, even if filed after the statement was submitted.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII, Rule 6A(1)
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Maintainability of counter-claims under CPC

card.dispute: Landlords fought with tenants and the judiciary over whether an eviction application under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 was maintainable after a prior suit based on the same permission was dismissed on technical grounds.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 43(2)(rr) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 is maintainable when a prior suit based on permission under Section 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 was dismissed on technical grounds?
Whether the permission under Section 3 of the 1947 Act is exhausted after a failed suit decided on technical grounds?
Whether the District Judge had jurisdiction to set aside the order of the Prescribed Authority when no appeal lay before him?
holdings: An application under Section 43(2)(rr) of the 1972 Act is maintainable even if a prior suit on the same permission was dismissed on technical grounds, as the permission is not exhausted until the eviction purpose is fulfilled.

Permission under Section 3 of the 1947 Act does not get exhausted by a failed suit decided on technical grounds, especially when the legislature intended to allow subsequent proceedings under the 1972 Act.

Though no appeal lay before the District Judge, the High Court could uphold the result using its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to set aside an erroneous and invalid order of the Prescribed Authority.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 43(2)(rr)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 3
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, Section 7-F
doctrines: Finality of judicial orders
Purposeful interpretation of statutory permissions
Writ jurisdiction to correct jurisdictional errors despite absence of appeal

card.dispute: The decree-holder (Nancy John Lyndon) sought to execute a money decree with attachment of property, which was dismissed for default but later restored; the respondents, who purchased portions of the attached property during the pendency of the execution, claimed the attachment had ceased and their titles were valid.
issues_decided: Whether the dismissal of an execution petition for default automatically terminates the attachment of property under Order 21 Rule 57 of CPC
Whether restoration of an execution petition revives the prior attachment and its legal consequences
Whether alienations of attached property during the subsistence of attachment are void despite subsequent dismissal and restoration of the execution petition
holdings: An attachment ceases upon dismissal of an execution petition for default unless the court orders otherwise under Order 21 Rule 57.
Restoration of an execution petition revives the attachment for the period it was originally in force, i.e., prior to dismissal.
Alienations made during the subsistence of attachment are void against the decree-holder, even if the execution was later dismissed and restored.
The revival of execution proceedings restores all ancillary orders, including attachment, without the need for a fresh order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 57
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 63
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 66
doctrines: Revival of proceedings doctrine
Attachment during execution
Voidness of alienation during subsisting attachment
Relation back of restoration orders

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of tenants who argued they were protected under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972; the tenants claimed benefit of the Act during pending litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 applies to newly constructed buildings within ten years of completion
Whether Sections 39 and 40 of the Act protect tenants when the eviction suit was filed after the Act came into force
Whether a tenant can claim protection under the Act if ten years elapsed during litigation
holdings: Newly constructed buildings are exempt from the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 for ten years, computed from the date of first house-tax assessment.
Sections 39 and 40 of the Act do not apply to eviction suits filed after the Act's commencement on July 15, 1972.
Tenants cannot claim protection under the Act during litigation if the suit was instituted within the ten-year exemption period.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 40
doctrines: Prospective application of rent control laws
Literal interpretation of statutory commencement clauses
Binding precedent from larger benches

card.dispute: The appellant, a returned candidate elected to the Deolali Cantonment Board, challenged the setting aside of his election on grounds of disqualification under Section 28(2)(h) of the Cantonments Act, 1924, due to unpaid arrears despite no formal notice being served.
issues_decided: Whether the disqualification under Section 28(2)(h) of the Cantonments Act, 1924, can be invoked without service of a statutory notice demanding payment of arrears.
Whether awareness of liability by the candidate is sufficient to satisfy the 'notice' requirement under Section 28(2)(h).
holdings: The disqualification under Section 28(2)(h) of the Cantonments Act, 1924, cannot be invoked unless a statutory notice demanding payment of arrears has been formally served on the candidate.
Mere knowledge or awareness of dues by the candidate does not constitute 'notice' as required by Section 28(2)(h); the statutory requirement of notice must be strictly complied with.
doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory requirements in election disputes
Election proceedings are purely statutory and not governed by common law
Presumption in favor of validity of election of returned candidate

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, claiming the tenant made material alterations to the tenanted premises without consent, which the tenant denied.
issues_decided: Whether the partition wall in the hall constituted a material alteration under Section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952.
Whether the construction of the tin shed on open land adjacent to the premises amounted to a material alteration.
Whether the nature of construction (permanent or temporary) is relevant in determining 'material alteration'.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of the lower courts on factual issues.
holdings: A temporary partition wall of 6 feet height that does not touch the ceiling or foundation and can be removed without damage does not materially alter the accommodation.
A tin shed constructed on open land adjacent to the premises, made of kuchha materials and extendable without structural change, does not constitute material alteration.
The temporary or permanent nature of a construction is a relevant factor in determining whether an alteration is 'material'.
The High Court erred in overturning concurrent factual findings of lower courts on mixed questions of fact and law without sufficient justification.
provisions: U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 14(c)
doctrines: Material alteration doctrine in tenancy law
Mixed question of fact and law
Principle of non-interference with concurrent findings of fact

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether an arbitral award affecting immovable property, filed for registration after a delay of nearly six years, was validly registered within the period of limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the period during which judicial proceedings were pending, including when the award was in court custody, should be excluded from the limitation period for registration of an arbitral award under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the Sub-Judge had the authority to retain the award and whether such retention affected the arbitrators' ability to register the award in time
Whether an unregistered award affecting immovable property can have legal effect
holdings: The period during which the award was in the custody of the court and could not be presented for registration due to judicial orders must be excluded from the limitation period under Section 15 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
The act of the court in retaining the award and the injunction order prevented the arbitrators from registering the award, and such circumstances excuse the delay under equitable maxims.
An award affecting immovable property must be registered to be effective, but failure to register within time is excusable if prevented by court orders or impossibility.
doctrines: Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Lex non cogit ad impossibilia
Equitable exclusion of time during judicial proceedings under Section 15 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether the appellants, who occupied private forest land, were entitled to tenant protection under Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, despite having initially entered the land by trespass.
issues_decided: Whether Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 grants tenant status to occupants whose possession originated unlawfully through trespass or forcible entry.
Whether the expression 'in occupation' under Section 7D includes only lawful occupation or also unlawful possession.
holdings: Section 7D does not extend protection to persons whose occupation of private forests or unsurveyed lands began through wilful trespass or unlawful entry.
The term 'in occupation' under Section 7D must be construed as 'lawful occupation', consistent with the legislative intent evident in Sections 7A to 7C and Sections 8 and 9 of the Act.
doctrines: Lawful origin of possession
Statutory interpretation in context
Protection of bona fide occupants

card.dispute: The dispute was between printing press owners and the Chandigarh Administration over the allotment of industrial sites, where the owners challenged the cancellation of a prior allotment and the introduction of a revised policy for smaller sites in a different area.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel applies to compel the government to allot sites based on an initial promise or action?
Whether the revised policy of allotting smaller sites in Phase I instead of larger sites in Phase II violated Article 14 of the Constitution?
holdings: The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked against the government when the promise or action is contrary to statutory rules or legal procedure, especially where no clear assurance was given and the process lacked statutory sanction.

The revised policy of allotting smaller sites in Phase I did not violate Article 14 as it was based on a rational classification and bona fide administrative necessity, and did not amount to arbitrariness or discrimination.
provisions: Chandigarh Lease Hold of Sites and Building Rules, 1973
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Prohibition of arbitrariness in State action

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the eviction order on grounds that the landlord had agreed to withdraw the petition and accepted rent, leading the tenant to believe the case was dropped.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's non-appearance in court due to the landlord's alleged promise to withdraw the eviction petition was a valid ground to set aside the ex parte decree.
Whether the finding that the landlord agreed to withdraw the petition and accepted rent binds the landlord in later stages of the same proceedings.
holdings: A tenant’s non-appearance in court due to the landlord’s misrepresentation that the eviction petition would be withdrawn constitutes a valid ground to set aside an ex parte decree.
A finding recorded in proceedings to set aside an ex parte order that the landlord agreed to withdraw the petition and accepted rent is binding in later stages of the same litigation unless appealed.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, Section 13
doctrines: res judicata in interlocutory proceedings
binding effect of judicial findings at different stages of the same litigation
equitable estoppel by conduct

card.dispute: The successors of an ex-landlord claimed compensation for unexploited coal reserves in mineral-bearing land vested in the State, which the State refused on grounds no compensation was due for untapped minerals.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 provides for compensation for unexploited minerals in an estate vested in the State?
Whether the exclusion of compensation for unexploited minerals renders the Act unconstitutional as expropriatory legislation?
Whether statutory provisions for compensation under Section 25 of the Act extend to potential sources of income not actively exploited at the time of vesting?
holdings: The Act only provides compensation for existing, actively exploited sources of income, not for unexploited mineral reserves which were not generating income at the time of vesting.
The absence of compensation for untapped minerals does not violate constitutional rights because no property right in those minerals existed independently at the time of vesting.
Statutory compensation schemes must be interpreted as limited to existing rights; they do not create new liabilities unless clearly stated by the legislature.
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Interpretation of statutes as a whole
Presumption against expropriation without compensation
Statute creating liability only with clear language

card.dispute: Ramchandra Goverdhan Pandit challenged the Charity Commissioner's order declaring his properties as public trust property, and contested the maintainability of a Letters Patent Appeal from a District Court decision under Section 72 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings under Section 72 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 are in the nature of an appeal or a special application?
Whether the District Court exercises appellate jurisdiction under Section 72, making a Letters Patent Appeal to the High Court subject to the requirement of prior leave?
holdings: Proceedings under Section 72 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 are in substance appellate in nature, despite the use of the word 'application' instead of 'appeal', because the District Court has plenary power to confirm, modify, or set aside the Charity Commissioner’s order on both law and fact.

The District Court exercises appellate jurisdiction under Section 72, and therefore, a Letters Patent Appeal to the High Court is subject to the requirement of obtaining prior leave under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court.
provisions: Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court, Clause 15
doctrines: Substance over form in determining jurisdiction
Appellate jurisdiction test based on powers exercised rather than nomenclature
Requirement of leave for Letters Patent Appeals under Clause 15

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide requirement under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the dispute centered on whether additional permission under the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 was required.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 14(1)(e) and 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 are special provisions overriding other laws including the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956
Whether there is any legal or principled difference between Sections 14(1)(e) and 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act
Whether permission under Section 19(1)(a) of the Slum Areas Act is required before filing an eviction suit under Sections 14(1)(e) or 14A of the Rent Act
holdings: Sections 14A, 14(1)(e), 25A, 25B, and 25C of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 are special provisions with a non-obstante clause, overriding inconsistent laws including the Slum Areas Act.
There is no difference in principle or law between Section 14(1)(e) and Section 14A of the Delhi Rent Control Act, despite their application in different factual contexts.

Due to the special procedure in Chapter III-A of the Rent Act, the Slum Areas Act does not apply to the extent of inconsistency, and no prior permission under Section 19(1)(a) of that Act is needed for eviction under Sections 14(1)(e) or 14A.
provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, Section 19(1)(a)
doctrines: Non-obstante clause overrides general laws
Specialia generalibus derogant
Statutory interpretation of special provisions

card.dispute: The appellant, a property owner, challenged the constitutional validity of Section 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, which used 1938 rent levels as the basis for determining fair rent, claiming it violated Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) due to unreasonableness and discrimination compared to rent laws in other states.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of a statute can be maintained without specifying the facts or particulars of the petitioner's property?
Whether Section 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, which bases fair rent on 1938 rent levels, is arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether a law can be struck down on the ground that other states have different or more favorable rent control provisions?
holdings: A petition challenging the constitutional validity of a statute must be grounded in specific facts and cannot be decided in the abstract; absence of such facts warrants dismissal.
Section 4 is not per se unreasonable or arbitrary under Article 14, as it allows for increases over the 1938-based rent and was enacted with the legitimate object of restricting rent increases.
Article 14 does not permit invalidating a state law by comparing it with laws of other states, as each state legislature has the authority to enact laws suited to local conditions.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949: Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of locus standi in public interest litigation
Principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Separate legislative competence of states under federal structure
Presumption of constitutionality of statutes

card.dispute: The judgment debtors (Shalimar Cinema proprietors) challenged the validity of a court-ordered auction sale of their 28/48 share in the cinema hall, claiming lack of proper notice and inadequate sale price.
issues_decided: Whether the auction sale held on September 1, 1977, was valid despite no proper announcement of adjournment from August 29, 1977?
Whether the sale could be set aside due to inadequate consideration?
holdings: The sale on September 1, 1977, was invalid because no proper announcement was made on August 29, 1977, about its continuation, depriving bidders of fair opportunity to participate.
A sale in execution of a decree can be set aside if the price is so inadequate as to shock the conscience of the court, especially when combined with procedural irregularities.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 66
doctrines: Principle of fair procedure in court-conducted sales
Doctrine of inadequate consideration vitiating execution sale
Duty of auction purchaser to produce best evidence when contesting sale

card.dispute: The assessee challenged the denial of depreciation benefits on a 1/6th share in a sugar mill and the taxability of receipts from lease surrenders and compromise agreements, as well as the set-off of carried forward business losses.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee was entitled to claim depreciation under Section 10(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 on a fractional 1/6th share in a sugar mill without being the full owner of the property
Whether the amounts received by the assessee under compromise or mutual arrangement for surrendering leasehold interests constituted taxable income
Whether the unabsorbed business loss from the previous year could be set off against lease receipts under Section 24 of the Income-tax Act, 1922
holdings: Depreciation benefit under Section 10(2)(vi) is available only to the full owner of the property; a fractional share in machinery or plant does not entitle the assessee to claim depreciation.
Receipts from surrender of leasehold interest in a business, even by compromise, are in the nature of profits from the business interest and constitute taxable income.

Carried forward business losses can be set off only against income from the same business; lease receipts received through a court-appointed receiver do not constitute business income for this purpose.
doctrines: Ownership requirement for depreciation allowance
Taxability of profits from surrender of business interests
Conditions for set-off of carried forward business losses

card.dispute: The appellants obtained a decree for ejectment of the respondent-tenant under the Punjab Tenancy Act; the respondent later filed a civil suit claiming to be a mortgagee in possession, not a tenant, and sought restoration of possession, challenging the ejectment decree as a nullity.
issues_decided: Whether the decree passed by the Revenue Court under Section 77(3) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, operates as res judicata in a subsequent civil suit challenging the tenant-landlord relationship?
Whether the Civil Court has jurisdiction to decide a dispute over the title and nature of possession (tenant vs. mortgagee) even after an ejectment decree by the Revenue Court?
holdings: A decree for ejectment by a Revenue Court under the Punjab Tenancy Act does not operate as res judicata in a subsequent civil suit where the defendant challenges the very existence of the landlord-tenant relationship and asserts a claim of title or mortgagee possession.

The Civil Court retains jurisdiction to determine questions of title and the true nature of possession when such issues were not within the competence of the Revenue Court, which can only decide specified disputes assuming the landlord-tenant relationship.
doctrines: Res judicata
Ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Jurisdiction of revenue courts vs. civil courts
Fundamental principles of judicial procedure

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent for two months, while the tenant claimed the arrears should be set off against an advance rent payment made at the start of the tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could claim set-off of advance rent paid in violation of Section 3 of the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 against arrears of rent?
Whether the tenant was a defaulter under Section 11(1)(d) of the Act despite the advance payment?
Whether the doctrine of in pari delicto barred the tenant from claiming such set-off?
holdings: A tenant can claim set-off of advance rent against arrears even if the advance exceeded one month’s rent and was accepted in violation of Section 3 of the Act, in the absence of an agreement requiring formal request for adjustment.
The tenant was not in default under Section 11(1)(d) where the advance payment was sufficient to cover the arrears and could be adjusted without a formal request.
The doctrine of in pari delicto does not bar a tenant from claiming such set-off when the landlord accepted prohibited advance rent, as the court may still grant relief to prevent injustice.
provisions: Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 3
Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(d)
doctrines: in pari delicto
set-off of advance rent

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of two accused, including Seriyal Udayar, who were charged with murder and other offences arising from a land dispute; the High Court convicted them, and the appellant challenged that reversal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Sessions Court's acquittal based on re-appreciation of evidence
Whether the prosecution proved the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the possibility of the accused acting in private defence could be excluded
holdings: The High Court erred in overturning the Sessions Judge's acquittal as the trial court's assessment of witness credibility and evidence deserves greater weight.
The prosecution failed to prove the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, especially given inconsistencies in witness accounts and suppression of injuries on the accused.
The possibility that the incident occurred in exercise of the right of private defence could not be ruled out based on the evidence.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Right of private defence under exceptional circumstances
Limited scope of appellate interference in acquittal

card.dispute: The appellant, a revenue patwari, was convicted of accepting a bribe of Rs. 200 for providing a copy of Jamabandi, and challenged the conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved that the appellant accepted illegal gratification.
Whether the prosecution witnesses were credible despite alleged bias and contradictions.
Whether the conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act and IPC was legally sustainable.
holdings: A public servant who accepts money in exchange for official action is guilty of corruption, even if the demand is small and the official document is eventually provided.
The evidence of prosecution witnesses, including those from the same village, can be relied upon if corroborated and not inherently improbable.
Recovery of marked currency with forensic confirmation and absence of explanation from the accused supports conviction for bribery.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, Section 5(1)(d) read with Section 5(2)
doctrines: Corroboration of prosecution testimony through independent evidence
Presumption of guilt from unexplained possession of marked currency in bribery cases

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of the appellant (Rashpal Malhotra) and Haryana Milk Food Corporation from rented premises, claiming non-payment of rent, subletting, and bona fide personal need, while the appellant contested the suit's maintainability on the ground that Haryana Milk Food Corporation was not a legal entity.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for eviction can be maintained against an entity like 'Haryana Milk Food Corporation' which is not a juristic person but an assumed name of a company?
Whether the appellant, Rashpal Malhotra, was the tenant or merely a signatory to the lease on behalf of a corporate entity?
Whether the High Court and lower courts were correct in upholding the eviction order despite procedural irregularities in naming the lessee?
holdings: A suit for eviction can be maintained against an entity operating under an assumed name if it is owned by a legal person, such as a company, and all parties are aware of the true identity of the lessee.
The appellant was not the tenant; he signed the lease as an agent for Haryana Milk Food Corporation, which was effectively owned by Kailash Chemical and Textile Mills Ltd., a legal entity.

The Supreme Court, exercising discretion under Article 136, declined to interfere with the eviction order as there was no manifest injustice, especially given the landlord’s bona fide need and the awareness of all parties regarding the real lessee.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 2(i)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 30, Rule 10
doctrines: Court of equity jurisdiction under Article 136
Doctrine of corporate personality and capacity to sue/be sued
Doctrine of substantial justice over technicalities
Principle of bona fide personal requirement in eviction law

card.dispute: The appellants, heirs of Balwant Singh, challenged the finality of a pre-reorganisation order declaring part of his land as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, seeking to claim permissible land holdings in both Punjab and Haryana after the 1966 reorganisation.
issues_decided: Whether an order declaring land as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, which became final before the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, came into force, continues to be effective even if the surplus land has not been utilised for tenant resettlement?

Whether a landowner can claim separate permissible holdings of 50 standard acres each in both Punjab and Haryana after the territorial reorganisation, despite a prior final order declaring surplus land?
holdings: A final order declaring land as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, remains binding and effective even if the government has not utilised the land for resettling tenants; non-utilisation does not restore ownership rights.

The Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, does not allow landowners to claim separate permissible areas in both Punjab and Haryana; the final pre-reorganisation surplus declaration binds the owner across both states.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, Section 9(1)(i)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, Section 10A(a)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, Section 10A(b)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1930, Section 10B
Haryana Adaptation of Laws (States and Concurrent Subjects) Order, 1968, Clause 10
Haryana Adaptation of Laws (States and Concurrent Subjects) Order, 1968, Clause 11
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Continuity of rights and liabilities post-state reorganisation
Doctrine of indefeasible government rights in surplus land
Statutory continuity under adaptation orders

card.dispute: The landlord's heirs sought eviction of the tenant from the ground floor used as a godown, claiming bona fide need for additional residential accommodation, despite the tenant's non-residential use of the premises.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can seek eviction under Section 10(3)(c) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for additional accommodation even if the tenant's use of the leased portion (non-residential) does not match the landlord's need (residential)?
Whether the non obstante clause in Section 10(3)(c) overrides the restrictions in Section 10(3)(a)(i) and (iii) regarding the nature of the building and user?
Whether the Rent Controller must consider comparative hardship between landlord and tenant before granting eviction under Section 10(3)(c)?
holdings: Section 10(3)(c) allows a landlord to seek eviction of any tenant, regardless of whether the tenant uses the premises for residential or non-residential purposes, to meet bona fide additional accommodation needs.

The non obstante clause in Section 10(3)(c) overrides the restrictions in Section 10(3)(a)(i) and (iii), including the requirement that the landlord not occupy a similar building and that the use types match.
The Rent Controller must balance comparative hardship between the parties and may deny eviction if hardship to the tenant outweighs the landlord's benefit, even if the need is bona fide.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(2)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(c)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation to avoid rendering provisions otiose
Use of non obstante clause to give overriding effect
Principle of comparative hardship in eviction cases

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the High Court could exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against a revisional order passed by the District Judge under Section 50(2) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, which declared such orders 'final'.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure over a final order of the District Judge passed under Section 50(2) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.

Whether the Full Bench decision of the Karnataka High Court in Krishnaji Venkatesh Shriodkar v. Gurupad Shivaram Kavalekar, upholding such jurisdiction, was still binding law after subsequent decisions of the Supreme Court.
holdings: The High Court retains jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC to revise orders of the District Judge under Section 50(2) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act unless the statute expressly excludes such jurisdiction.
A Full Bench decision of a High Court, based on a binding Supreme Court precedent, cannot be overruled by a coordinate bench without an express or implied overruling by the Supreme Court.
provisions: Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, Section 50(1) and (2)
doctrines: Binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution
Principle of judicial hierarchy and stare decisis
Presumption against ousting of High Court's revisional jurisdiction unless clear statutory language exists

card.dispute: The landlord sued to recover possession of premises from the tenant alleging breach of tenancy conditions and structural alterations; the tenant argued the suit was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for recovery of possession under section 13 of the Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 is governed by a 12-year limitation under Article 66 or 67 of the Limitation Act, 1963, or a 3-year limitation under Article 113
Whether sections 12 and 13 of the Bombay Rent Act operate independently and how they affect the landlord's right to sue for possession
Whether breach of a condition of tenancy under section 13(1) gives rise to an immediate right to file suit for possession
holdings: A suit for possession under section 13 of the Bombay Rent Act is governed by a 12-year limitation period under Article 66 or 67 of the Limitation Act, not the 3-year period under Article 113.

Sections 12 and 13 of the Bombay Rent Act must be harmoniously construed: section 12 protects tenants who perform conditions, while section 13 allows eviction on specified grounds despite such protection.
The right to sue for possession under section 13 arises only upon court satisfaction of a ground for eviction, not immediately upon breach of a tenancy condition.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Bombay Rents, Hotels and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Statutory protection of tenants
Limitation period for recovery of possession

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Malkani, challenged the genuineness of a will executed by her mother in favor of her paternal cousins, alleging it was procured by fraud after her mother's abduction.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated August 24, 1972, was executed voluntarily and without fraud or undue influence
Whether the propounders of the will created suspicious circumstances by actively participating in its execution
holdings: The will was genuine and executed freely by the testatrix, as there were no suspicious circumstances affecting her testamentary capacity or free will.
Mere active participation by beneficiaries in the execution of a will does not, without more, create suspicion requiring the propounders to adduce clear and unimpeachable evidence.
doctrines: Suspicious circumstances doctrine in will contests
Principle of testamentary freedom
Burden of proof in cases alleging fraud in will execution

card.dispute: The dispute was between a Hindu undivided family (lessor) and the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether the lessor could claim deductions for repair expenses when the tenant had undertaken to bear the cost of repairs under the lease agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's covenant to carry out repairs attracted the application of Section 24(1)(i)(b) of the Income Tax Act, 1961
Whether the assessee was entitled to claim actual repair expenses under Section 24(1)(i)(a) despite the tenant's obligation to bear repair costs
holdings: Where a tenant has undertaken to bear the cost of repairs, including routine and structural maintenance, Section 24(1)(i)(b) applies, limiting the owner's deduction to the lesser of one-sixth of the annual value or the excess of annual value over rent received.

A covenant by the tenant to maintain and execute all repairs, even if major structural repairs are to be borne by the landlord, constitutes an undertaking to bear the cost of repairs within the meaning of Section 24(1)(i)(b), thereby excluding the owner from claiming actual repair expenditures under Section 24(1)(i)(a).
doctrines: Doctrine of repair in landlord-tenant law
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on commercial and legal understanding of 'repair'

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Arati Dutta, challenged the High Court's computation of liabilities under a compromise in a petition filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, and whether an appeal lay against the Single Judge's order in the absence of Letters Patent.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies to the Division Bench of the High Court against an order of a Single Judge passed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, in the absence of applicable Letters Patent or procedural rules for such appeal.
Whether the absence of procedural rules for filing an appeal before the Division Bench bars the right to appeal when the statute confers such a right.
holdings: An appeal lies to the Division Bench from an order of a Single Judge under Sections 397 and 398 read with Section 483 of the Companies Act, 1956, as the statute provides for appeal to the same court in the same manner, irrespective of the absence of Letters Patent.

The absence of procedural rules for filing an appeal does not extinguish the substantive right to appeal conferred by statute, and the High Court must frame rules under its rule-making power to give effect to such rights.
doctrines: Substantive right to appeal under statute prevails over procedural gaps
Principle of statutory interpretation in pari materia
High Court's rule-making power to ensure access to justice

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat and landowners disputed whether lands notified for acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, but also exceeding urban land ceiling limits, qualified as 'vacant land' under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976.
issues_decided: Whether land notified for acquisition under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, ceases to be 'vacant land' under Section 2(q)(i) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976.
Whether the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, applies to land reserved for public purposes under a town planning scheme.
holdings: Land notified for acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, remains 'vacant land' under the 1976 Act if construction is not absolutely prohibited under local building regulations.

The definition of 'vacant land' includes land on which construction is permissible by any person or authority, even if not by the owner, such as land reserved for public buildings under a town planning scheme.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(q)(i)
doctrines: Definition of 'vacant land' based on legal permissibility of construction, not practical or economic feasibility
Overriding effect of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, over other laws

card.dispute: The landlady filed a suit in the High Court for possession, arrears of rent, and mesne profits, but the tenant argued the suit was improperly valued and should be filed in a lower court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could return the plaint at a preliminary stage on the ground that the suit was over-valued due to an allegedly invalid claim for mesne profits/damages?
Whether the claim for mesne profits/damages at Rs.7,800 per month was so untenable as to constitute a dishonest attempt to invoke the High Court's jurisdiction?
holdings: A court cannot return a plaint at a preliminary stage by deciding the merits of a claim for mesne profits; such issues must be determined after trial.
A claim for mesne profits is not inherently frivolous if it raises a debatable legal question, and cannot be dismissed without trial merely because the defendant disputes its validity.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 10
doctrines: Pecuniary jurisdiction determined by plaintiff's valuation unless mala fide
Principle against premature adjudication of merits in jurisdictional disputes

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh challenged the discharge of ten accused persons, including public officials, in a criminal case involving illegal felling of government trees and corruption, after the Special Judge discharged them without recording evidence and the High Court summarily dismissed the revision.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Judge was justified in discharging the accused without recording evidence and by reviewing the predecessor's order?
Whether the Special Judge erred in his understanding of the offence of criminal conspiracy?
Whether the Special Judge based his order on surmises and assumptions not supported by evidence?
Whether the High Court's summary dismissal of the revision warranted interference by the Supreme Court?
holdings: A Special Judge cannot review a predecessor's order at the charge-framing stage; discharge under Section 239 Cr.P.C. is impermissible if a prima facie case exists.
The offence of criminal conspiracy does not require each conspirator to participate in every act; liability extends to all for acts done in furtherance of the agreement.
Discharge based on conjectures, such as assumptions about motives of officials or proportion of trees cut, without evidence, is legally unsustainable.
The High Court's cryptic dismissal of revision without addressing legal infirmities in the discharge order justified Supreme Court intervention under Article 136.
doctrines: Principle of prima facie case at charge-framing stage
Doctrine of criminal conspiracy (meeting of minds)
Prohibition of review by successor judicial officer
Supreme Court's discretionary power under Article 136

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka sought to recover damages for breach of contract from private parties, assessing the damages itself and attempting to recover them as arrears of land revenue, which the parties challenged as unconstitutional and beyond statutory authority.
issues_decided: Whether the State, as a party to the contract, can unilaterally adjudicate the question of breach of contract and assess damages under Clause 12 of the agreement.
Whether damages for breach of contract, even if provided in the agreement, can be recovered as arrears of land revenue under the Revenue Recovery Act.
holdings: The State cannot act as an adjudicator in its own cause; the power to assess damages under the contract is only valid when the breach is admitted or not disputed, as the authority to assess does not include the power to adjudicate on disputed breaches.

Damages for breach of contract, when provided under a contractual clause, constitute amounts 'payable under the contract' and can be recovered as arrears of land revenue if the agreement so provides, as they fall within the contractual liability.
doctrines: Nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in their own cause)
Literal rule of interpretation
Distinction between primary and subsidiary contractual powers

card.dispute: The State of Kerala and another contested whether eucalyptus plantations in a tea estate constituted 'private forests' under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, thereby vesting in the government.
issues_decided: Whether eucalyptus plantations raised in a tea estate for fuel purposes qualify as 'private forest' under Section 2(f) of the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971.
Whether land used for cultivating eucalyptus with human skill and labour for industrial use falls within the vesting provisions of the Act.
holdings: Eucalyptus plantations in a tea estate, raised not for forest but for fuel necessary for tea manufacturing, do not constitute a 'private forest' under Section 2(f) of the Kerala Private Forests Act, 1971.

Lands where human skill, labour, and resources are applied for agricultural or industrial purposes, such as fuel production for tea processing, are excluded from the definition of 'private forest' under the Act.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 2(f)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms in context
Exclusion of agriculturally cultivated lands from forest definitions
Purpose-based classification of land use

card.dispute: The appellant, a patwari, was convicted of demanding and accepting money as a bribe for supplying copies from revenue records, which he claimed was for a government small savings scheme, leading to a challenge against his conviction and sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's explanation that the money recovered was for deposit in a small savings scheme was credible
Whether the conviction under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Section 161 of the Indian Penal Code was legally sustainable
Whether the sentence imposed required modification given the delay in disposal of the case
holdings: The explanation that the money was collected for a small savings scheme was an afterthought, as the appellant did not disclose it at the time of recovery or in his initial statement, undermining its credibility.

The conviction under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and Section 161 IPC is valid as the prosecution proved demand and acceptance of money by a public servant for official action.
The sentence of imprisonment is reduced to the period already undergone, considering the 14-year pendency of the case, but the fine is upheld to meet the ends of justice.
doctrines: Benefit of delayed trial
Credibility of defence explanation as afterthought
Presumption against public servant in corruption cases

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh, as tenant, contested a landlord's suit for eviction after termination of lease, claiming protection under the Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings Rent Control Act, while the landlord argued the premises were outside the Act's scope.
issues_decided: Whether the building leased by the State Government falls under the definition of 'public building' under Section 2(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, as amended?
Whether the State Government, as a tenant, is entitled to protection under the Rent Act or can be evicted by a simple suit after notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act?
Whether Section 3(0) of the Act should be interpreted narrowly to exclude Government tenancies from the definition of 'public building' in order to avoid absurd or unjust consequences?
holdings: A building taken on lease by the State Government falls within the definition of 'public building' under Section 2(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings Act, as amended in 1976, and is covered by the Act.

The State Government, as a tenant, does not automatically get protection under the Rent Act; if the building is a 'public building', the landlord's remedy is restricted to the provisions of the Act and not a civil suit, unless the Act allows eviction.

Courts should not read down the plain language of a statutory provision unless it leads to absurdity or unconstitutionality; the wider interpretation of 'public building' is consistent with legislative intent and history.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(1)(a)
Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(0)
Uttar Pradesh Public Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21
doctrines: Statutory construction
Plain meaning rule
Reading down of statutes
Legislative intent

card.dispute: The appellants were charged with forgery for using a forged partnership deed in a civil suit, but challenged the magistrate's power to frame charges under Sections 471 and 474 IPC without a complaint from the civil court.
issues_decided: Whether the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. applies when a forged document is not produced in court but only a copy is used in civil proceedings.
Whether a magistrate can take cognizance of offences under Sections 471 and 474 IPC without a prior complaint from a civil court in such a case.
holdings: The bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. does not apply if the original forged document was not produced or given in evidence in court.
A magistrate can take cognizance of offences under Sections 471 and 474 IPC without a civil court's complaint when the allegedly forged document was not produced in court.
doctrines: Cognizance of offences in relation to forged documents used in court proceedings
Plain grammatical meaning and practical common sense in statutory interpretation
Doctrine of precedent as applied to Privy Council and Supreme Court judgments

card.dispute: The widow of a coparcener challenged the validity of a gift deed executed by her husband, conveying his undivided interest in coparcenary property to his brother, claiming it was void without consent of other coparceners.
issues_decided: Whether a gift by a coparcener of his undivided interest in coparcenary property to another coparcener without consent of other coparceners is valid or void.
Whether the deed in question should be construed as a gift or as a renunciation/relinquishment under Hindu law.
holdings: A gift by a coparcener to another coparcener, if genuinely intended to benefit the family, may be construed as a valid renunciation of interest in favour of all other coparceners, making consent of other coparceners immaterial.

A coparcener cannot generally make a valid gift of undivided interest in coparcenary property without consent of others, but such an act may be upheld if it is in substance a genuine relinquishment or renunciation.
doctrines: Mitakshara coparcenary law
Doctrine of renunciation or relinquishment of coparcenary interest
Alienation of coparcenary interest by gift
Legislative intent and continuity in personal law

card.dispute: The Union of India deducted an amount from a retired Wing Commander's commuted pension for unauthorized occupation of government accommodation, and he challenged this deduction as illegal.
issues_decided: Whether the amount recovered from the commuted pension was contrary to Section 11 of the Pensions Act, 1871
Whether the government could unilaterally deduct dues from a commuted pension without violating statutory protection
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel or relaxation applied to the unauthorized occupation of government housing
holdings: Money due on account of a pension, including the commuted portion, is protected under Section 11 of the Pensions Act, 1871, and cannot be unilaterally seized by the government.
A commuted pension retains its character as pensionary benefit 'on account of' the pension and thus falls within the statutory protection against attachment or recovery.
The government cannot bypass statutory safeguards by recovering dues from commuted pensions; alternative remedies like suit or proceedings under the Public Premises Act must be used.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 7(2) and Section 14
Allotment of Government Residences (General Pool in Delhi) Rules, 1963
doctrines: Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Doctrine of promissory estoppel
Principle of statutory protection of pensionary benefits

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's award of compensation to landowners whose property was requisitioned during World War II, arguing they were not entitled to compensation beyond 1955 when the land vested with the state under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the claimants were entitled to recurring compensation for mooram and coloured clay deposits on the requisitioned land
Whether the claimants could claim recurring compensation beyond April 15, 1955, after the land vested with the state
Whether the claimants were entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the compensation awarded
holdings: Recurring compensation cannot be awarded for mineral deposits like mooram and coloured clay in the absence of evidence showing their availability, quality, quantity, or actual loss suffered by the claimants.

Claimants are entitled to recurring compensation only up to April 15, 1955, the date the land vested with the state under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, as they ceased to have any right or interest thereafter.
The claimants are entitled to interest at 6% per annum on the compensation amount from the date of requisition (October 1, 1942) until payment, as the lower rate awarded was inadequate.
provisions: Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 28
doctrines: No compensation without proven loss
Vesting of property extinguishes private rights
Interest as compensation for delayed payment

card.dispute: The petitioners, holders of long-term licenses to collect sal seeds from government forests, challenged the validity of a notification and subsequent ordinance that rescinded their contracts and established a state monopoly over sal seeds, arguing it violated their rights and encroached on judicial authority.
issues_decided: Whether the State can create a monopoly over trade in forest produce under Article 19(6)(ii) of the Constitution
Whether the legislature can retrospectively validate an ordinance that nullifies a judicial decision
Whether the Statement of Objects and Reasons of an Act can control the interpretation of its provisions
Whether the amendment and validation of a notification rescinding private contracts amounts to an encroachment on judicial power
holdings: The State is empowered to create partial or complete monopolies in trade or business, and such laws are presumed reasonable and in the public interest under Article 19(6)(ii).
The legislature can validly render a judicial decision ineffective by enacting a retrospective law, provided it does so by changing the legal basis and not by directly overruling the court.
The Statement of Objects and Reasons of a bill cannot control or override the plain meaning of statutory provisions and is only admissible to understand the background of legislation.
An ordinance that amends a law to remove the cause of judicial invalidity and validates prior actions is constitutional and does not encroach on judicial power.
provisions: Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 1(3)
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Amendment and Validation Ordinance, Sections 1 to 5
doctrines: Presumption of reasonableness of state monopoly laws
Legislative competence to enact retrospective laws
Non-utility of Statement of Objects and Reasons in statutory interpretation
Validation of void acts through curative legislation

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for dissolution of a partnership firm and rendition of accounts, valuing the suit at Rs.150, which defendants challenged as grossly undervalued given the substantial financial stakes involved.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff has an absolute right to assign any valuation to a suit for accounts under Section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, irrespective of the actual financial implications?
Whether the court can examine and reject a valuation in a suit for accounts if it appears arbitrary or manifestly inadequate?
holdings: A plaintiff in a suit for accounts may assign a tentative valuation but does not have an absolute right to choose an arbitrary or unreasonably low figure.
The court has the authority and duty to reject a valuation that is patently arbitrary or manifestly inadequate, even in suits for accounts, to prevent misuse of jurisdictional limits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII
doctrines: Plaintiff's right to valuation is not absolute
Judicial scrutiny of arbitrary undervaluation
Pecuniary jurisdiction based on realistic valuation

card.dispute: A private company occupying bank premises challenged the constitutional validity of applying the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 to premises of public sector corporations, arguing Parliament lacked legislative competence.
issues_decided: Whether the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 is ultra vires Parliament to the extent it applies to premises owned or controlled by public sector corporations established under Central Acts?
Whether the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 prevails over the Central Act under Article 254(2) of the Constitution due to Presidential assent?
Whether the appointment of a bank officer as Estate Officer under the 1971 Act violates Article 14?
holdings: Parliament has legislative competence to extend the 1971 Act to public premises of corporations owned or controlled by the Central Government, as the subject falls under Entry 64 of List I and Entry 18 of List III of the Seventh Schedule.

A Central law on a Concurrent List subject prevails over a State law under Article 254(1), and Presidential assent to a State law does not make it immune if a subsequent Central law covers the same matter.
The appointment of a bank officer as Estate Officer does not violate Article 14, as the Act provides for appeal to an independent judicial authority, ensuring fairness.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
doctrines: Doctrine of Repugnancy
Implied Repeal
Separation of Powers in Administrative Action
Principle of Constitutional Supremacy of Parliamentary Legislation in Concurrent Field

card.dispute: The dispute was between a private contractor and the State of Orissa over whether a government notification under the Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981 rescinded existing contracts for the collection and sale of sal seeds from government forests.
issues_decided: Whether the Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981 applies to forest produce grown on government lands.
Whether the notification issued under the Act rescinded existing contracts between the State and private parties for the collection and sale of sal seeds from government forests.
holdings: The Act applies only to forest produce grown on private holdings, not on government lands, as its scheme and object are to create a government monopoly in purchasing such produce from private growers.
Section 5(1)(a) of the Act does not rescind contracts relating to forest produce from government lands, as such a construction would contradict the Act's overall purpose and design.
provisions: Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 5(1)(a)
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 5(1)(b)
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 1(3)
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 4
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 5(3)
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 7
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 8
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 9
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 10
Orissa Forest Produce (Control of Trade) Act, 1981, Section 12
doctrines: Statutory interpretation requiring contextual and purposive construction
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Avoidance of literal interpretation when it defeats legislative purpose

card.dispute: The Bihar State Housing Board and the State of Bihar fought with landowners over the legality of land acquisitions for public development.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's findings on the legality of the land acquisition should be upheld.
What relief is appropriate in light of the public interest and peculiar facts of the case.
holdings: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's findings without ruling on the legality of the acquisition, based on the unique facts and public interest.
The acquisitions are upheld subject to payment of compensation determined as of 1-3-1988, to be assessed within six months and paid within three months thereafter.
doctrines: Public interest doctrine
Conditional affirmation of acquisition

card.dispute: The appellants (beneficiaries under the will of the life estate holder) fought with the daughters of the original Bhumidhar over who should be recognised as Bhumidhars after the life estate holder's death.
issues_decided: Whether a Bhumidhar with transferable rights can bequeath a life estate in favour of one beneficiary and the remainder to others.
Whether the interest of a life estate holder under a will gets enlarged into absolute ownership, defeating the remainder interest.
holdings: A Bhumidhar with transferable rights can validly bequeath a life estate in favour of one person and the remainder to others under Section 169(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951.
The interest of a life estate holder created by will remains a life estate and does not enlarge into absolute ownership, preserving the remainder interest in favour of the daughters.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 169(1)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 155
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 156
U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1951, Section 171
doctrines: Exhaustive statutory succession scheme
Nature of Hindu widow's estate
Life estate under English law distinguished from Hindu limited ownership

card.dispute: An advocate challenged his three-year suspension for withdrawing a suit without client instructions, arguing lack of fair procedure and absence of dishonesty or mens rea.
issues_decided: Whether a specific charge detailing the nature of professional misconduct must be framed against an advocate
Whether professional misconduct can be established without proof of dishonesty or mens rea
Whether allegations of professional misconduct must be proven beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the doctrine of benefit of doubt applies in disciplinary proceedings against advocates
holdings: An advocate must be clearly informed of the precise charge of professional misconduct to have a fair opportunity to defend himself.
A finding of professional misconduct and severe punishment require proof of mala fides, dishonesty, or mens rea; mere negligence may not suffice without showing culpability.
In disciplinary proceedings, facts leading to professional misconduct must be proven beyond reasonable doubt.
The doctrine of benefit of doubt applies in professional misconduct cases, especially where the advocate acted in good faith.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Benefit of doubt in disciplinary proceedings
Requirement of mens rea in professional misconduct
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in professional misconduct cases

card.dispute: The appellants (Babu Ram & Ors) sued to declare their ownership of disputed land by adverse possession, while the respondent Gram Sabha claimed it as shamilat deh (village common land).
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to try a suit involving shamilat deh land after amendments to the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961.
Whether the question of title by adverse possession over shamilat deh land falls within the bar of jurisdiction under Section 13(a) of the Act.
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to try the suit because it involves the question of whether the land is shamilat deh, which is barred under Section 13(a)(i) of the Act.

Even if the issue is adverse possession, the civil court cannot decide whether the land vests in the Gram Sabha, as such questions are excluded from its jurisdiction under Section 13(a)(ii) of the Act.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 13(a)(i)
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 13(a)(ii)
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 2(g)
doctrines: Bar of jurisdiction
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in revenue matters

card.dispute: The petitioners sought contempt action against the Union of India and its officers for failing to comply with Supreme Court orders directing reinstatement and provision of residential accommodation to petitioner No. 9.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed contempt of court by disobeying the Supreme Court's orders regarding reinstatement and accommodation of petitioner No. 9.
Whether the delay and non-compliance were willful or due to administrative and communication challenges.
Whether the unconditional apologies tendered by the respondents warranted discharge of the contempt notice.
holdings: Public officers must render due obedience to court orders, and failure to do so undermines the rule of law and invites judicial punishment.
Non-compliance with court orders, even if attributed to administrative delays, attracts serious judicial concern, especially when it affects individual rights.
Contempt proceedings may be closed if there is subsequent compliance and unconditional apology, but costs may be imposed to uphold the dignity of the court.
doctrines: Rule of Law
Judicial Supremacy
Contempt for disobedience of court orders

card.dispute: The landlord filed a suit for possession of a shop, claiming rent arrears and termination of tenancy, while the tenant argued that the exemption from rent control expired during litigation, bringing the property under the Rent Act and barring civil court jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the expiration of a 10-year exemption period under the Rent Control Act during the pendency of an eviction suit brings the property under the Act's protection
Whether the civil court retains jurisdiction to decide the eviction suit if the exemption period lapses during litigation
Whether the cause of action for eviction must be determined as of the date of filing the suit or as of the date of decision
holdings: The rights of the parties crystallize on the date of institution of the suit; subsequent events, including the lapse of the 10-year exemption, do not affect the maintainability of the suit.
The exemption under the Rent Control Act continues until the suit is finally adjudicated, provided it was instituted within the 10-year period.
A purposive interpretation of social welfare legislation requires that court delays or procedural timelines should not nullify statutory rights, applying the maxim 'actus curiam neminem gravabit'.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 1(3)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(1)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(1)
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Crystallization of rights on date of suit
Actus curiam neminem gravabit
Substantial justice over technicalities

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the applicability of the Uttar Pradesh Rent Control Act to cantonment areas, arguing that eviction orders passed before the Act's formal extension were invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applies to cantonment areas in Uttar Pradesh.
Whether orders passed by authorities before the formal extension of the Rent Control Act to cantonments are valid under Section 3(4) of the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957.
holdings: The provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Rent Control Act, 1972, as amended, apply to cantonment areas in Uttar Pradesh by virtue of central notifications issued under the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957.

Orders passed before the formal extension of the Act to cantonments are deemed valid under Section 3(4) of the 1957 Act, as if the law were in force at the time, provided they were made under the state law then prevailing.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, Section 3
Uttar Pradesh Temporary Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1957
doctrines: Legislation by incorporation
Deemed validity of orders under retrospective application doctrine
Separability and independent operation of statutory sub-sections

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, arguing that the High Court wrongly reduced the valuation determined by the Trial Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reducing the market value of the land from Rs.8,692 to Rs.4,845.87 per acre.
Whether the High Court correctly applied deductions for the interior location and time lag for development.
Whether the High Court wrongly applied a further discount on the already depreciated value of Rs.7,000 per acre by using Miram's Tables for present value.
holdings: The High Court did not err in valuing the interior land at Rs.7,000 per acre, considering the delay in development and inferior accessibility.
A 25% deduction for land required for roads and infrastructure is appropriate, replacing the earlier 20% deduction.

The High Court erred in applying present value calculations to Rs.7,000; instead, present value should have been calculated on Rs.20,000 (the future value of developed land) after 12 years, resulting in a just compensation of Rs.5,250 per acre.
doctrines: Principle of market value assessment based on location and development potential
Use of hypothetical purchaser test in land valuation
Prohibition against double discounting in compensation calculation

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the confiscation of 565 foreign wristwatches and a penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs imposed under the Customs Act, 1962, on grounds of invalid extension of time for issuing a show-cause notice and arbitrary penalty determination.
issues_decided: Whether the extension of the six-month period for issuing a show-cause notice under Section 110(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, without notice to the petitioner, violates principles of natural justice?
Whether the value of the seized goods was properly determined for imposing a penalty?
Whether the penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs was arbitrary or excessive?
holdings: An extension of time under Section 110(2) of the Customs Act must be preceded by notice to the affected party, as it involves a valuable civil right and requires a quasi-judicial approach adhering to natural justice.

The value of the seized watches was validly determined based on the show-cause notice, and the petitioner’s failure to refute it, coupled with the burden of proof under Section 123, supported the assessment.
The penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs was not arbitrary or excessive given the value of goods (Rs. 87,455), the permissible fivefold limit, and the petitioner's long non-payment, indicating financial benefit.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Quasi-judicial action requiring fair procedure
Burden of proof in smuggling cases
Proportionality in penalty imposition

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assessee company fought over whether expenditure incurred by the company for providing water, electricity, and road infrastructure to a municipality was deductible as revenue expenditure under the Income-tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the expenditure incurred by the assessee for laying pipelines and infrastructure under a tripartite agreement was of a revenue or capital nature.
Whether the benefit derived by the assessee—immunity from municipal taxes for 15 years—was of an enduring nature bringing the expenditure into the capital field.
holdings: Expenditure incurred by the assessee did not result in acquisition of any capital asset by the company, as the assets created belonged to the municipality, and thus the expenditure was revenue in nature and deductible.
The benefit of tax immunity for 15 years was not a capital advantage but merely facilitated the conduct of business; hence, the enduring nature of the benefit did not make the expenditure capital.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Enduring benefit test from Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd.
Revenue nature of expenditure even for long-term benefits if it does not alter capital structure

card.dispute: The legal representatives of deceased plaintiff Dammu Lal, including minors represented by their guardian, fought with tenants over the validity of a compromise decree that set aside a prior eviction and money decree.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree was validly entered into with proper court permission under Order XXXII Rule 7 of the CPC when minors were involved?
Whether the guardian of the minors acted in their best interests and whether the compromise was one-sided?
Whether the court applied its mind independently in approving the compromise?
holdings: A compromise involving minors requires court permission under Order XXXII Rule 7 CPC only after evaluating all relevant circumstances to ensure it serves the minors' interests.
The compromise was one-sided and amounted to gross negligence as the minors gave up substantial rights to eviction, rent arrears, and damages without adequate consideration.
The court’s approval was based solely on the advocate’s opinion and failure to independently assess the compromise, warranting setting aside of the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXII, Rule 7
doctrines: Best interests of the minor
Gross negligence in compromise
Court's duty to independently scrutinize compromises involving minors

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's eviction petition under Section 13A of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985, arguing the landlord was not a 'specified landlord' at the time of retirement.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-landlord qualifies as a 'specified landlord' under Section 2(hh) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985
Whether the landlord is entitled to file an eviction petition under Section 13A after letting out the premises post-retirement
holdings: A 'specified landlord' under Section 2(hh) must be a landlord in respect of the premises and tenant at the time of retirement from public service.
A landlord who lets out premises after retirement does not qualify as a 'specified landlord' and cannot maintain an eviction petition under Section 13A.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985, Section 2(hh)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985, Section 13A
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985, Section 18A
doctrines: Strict interpretation of statutory exceptions
Temporal requirement for statutory benefits

card.dispute: Two appellants convicted of murder by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court challenged their death sentences, arguing lack of motive and unreliability of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction based on eyewitness testimony and FIR is reliable despite absence of independent witnesses and alleged police bias
Whether the sentence of death is justified in the absence of motive for one of the appellants
Whether the manner of recording the FIR affects its credibility
Whether the brutality of the crime justifies the death penalty for both appellants
holdings: The eyewitness testimony and FIR were reliable as they were consistent, corroborated by medical evidence, and recorded promptly without material contradiction.
The death sentence cannot be sustained for an accused who lacked motive and was only peripherally involved, even if present during the crime.
The timing and mode of travel to file the FIR do not undermine its credibility in the absence of specific contradictory evidence or cross-examination on those points.
The extreme brutality of the crime, especially the targeted killing of family members to eliminate inheritance claims, justifies the death penalty for the principal offender.
doctrines: Principle of corroboration through medical and testimonial evidence
Doctrine of collective liability under Section 34 IPC
Proportionality principle in sentencing
Rarest of rare doctrine for death penalty

card.dispute: The tenant, Dr. M. K. Salpekar, challenged the eviction orders passed by lower courts on the grounds that the rent control provision relied upon did not apply to non-residential premises where he ran a clinic.
issues_decided: Whether clause 13(3)(v) of the C.P. & Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 applies to non-residential buildings.
