The state lacked legislative competence to impose such a levy on tea despatches, as the subject falls under Union control under the Tea Act, 1953, and is not covered by any Entry in List II or List III.
provisions: West Bengal Rural Employment and Production Act, 1976, Sections 4(2)(aa) and 4(4)
Constitution of India, Article 301, Article 304(b), Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 49
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of repugnancy
Nexus test for determining the true nature of a tax

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the occupant, claiming he was a licensee, while the occupant claimed to be a protected tenant under the Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the document (Ext. 20) created a lease or a licence
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the eviction suit under Section 56 of the Goa, Daman and Diu Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1968
Whether the concurrent findings of fact by lower courts were binding in second appeal under Section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code
holdings: The document, despite being titled as a leave and licence agreement, created a lease because it granted exclusive possession and included terms like rent payment, prohibition on subletting, and right of renewal.
The suit was not maintainable in civil court as the appellant was a protected month-to-month tenant under the Rent Control Act, which barred jurisdiction under Section 56.
The nature of the document is a question of law, not pure fact, so the High Court could interfere under Section 100 CPC despite concurrent findings.
provisions: Goa, Daman and Diu Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1968, Section 56
doctrines: Substance over form in determining lease vs licence
Intention of parties as the real test for lease or licence
Exclusive possession as a prima facie test for tenancy
Binding effect of concurrent findings of fact under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The tenants, inducted by a mortgagee, fought against eviction by the original owner who redeemed the mortgage, claiming protection under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether tenants inducted by a mortgagee are protected under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 after redemption of the mortgage by the original owner.
Whether the non obstante clause in Section 11(a) of the Act prevents eviction in execution of a decree for redemption.
Whether the relationship of landlord and tenant exists between the original owner and tenants inducted by the mortgagee.
holdings: Tenants inducted by a mortgagee do not have a landlord-tenant relationship with the original owner, who regains independent title upon redemption.
Section 11(a) of the Kerala Act does not protect tenants from eviction when the original owner redeems the mortgage, as no tenancy exists between them.
Rights created by a mortgagee cease upon redemption, and the mortgagor is not bound by leases entered into by the mortgagee unless authorized by the mortgage deed.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 2(3)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 2(6)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of redemption under mortgage law
Doctrine of privity of contract in landlord-tenant relationships
Non obstante clause interpretation in rent control statutes

card.dispute: The Revenue and the assessee disputed whether assets transferred by gift before April 1, 1964, but chargeable to gift-tax, were exempt from inclusion in the donor's net wealth for assessment years commencing after March 31, 1964, under the proviso to Section 4(1)(a) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 4(1)(a) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957 applies to gifts made before April 1, 1964, if they were chargeable to gift-tax?
Whether the phrase 'for any assessment year commencing after the 31st day of March, 1964' refers to the timing of gift-tax assessment or the applicability of wealth-tax exemption?
Whether a construction that avoids constitutional invalidity on grounds of arbitrariness should be preferred if the statutory language is plain?
holdings: The phrase 'for any assessment year commencing after the 31st day of March, 1964' in the proviso to Section 4(1)(a) refers to the timing of gift-tax assessments, not the exemption from wealth-tax.

Gifts made before April 1, 1964, even if chargeable to gift-tax, do not qualify for exemption under the proviso, as the proviso applies only to gifts assessed to gift-tax for assessment years beginning after March 31, 1964.

Where statutory language is clear, courts must apply it literally, even if the result appears arbitrary or raises constitutional concerns; the rule favoring constitutional validity applies only when there is genuine ambiguity.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Principle of constitutional avoidance
Presumption of legislative validity in taxing statutes

card.dispute: The Controller of Estate Duty sought to reopen an assessment under Section 59 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, after the amendment of 1958, but the accountable persons challenged the reopening on the ground that the provision was not retrospective.
issues_decided: Whether Section 59 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, as amended in 1958, has retrospective operation?
Whether an assessment completed before the commencement of the amended Section 59 can be reopened under that section?
holdings: Section 59 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, as amended in 1958, does not have retrospective effect because it lacks express or implied language to that effect and creates a substantially different power than the earlier Section 62.
An assessment already completed before the commencement of Section 59 cannot be reopened under that provision, as it would infringe vested rights without legislative authority.
doctrines: Principle against retrospectivity in fiscal statutes
Reopening of assessment under reassessment provisions
Distinction between rectification of mistakes and reassessment for escaped assessment

card.dispute: The Corporation of the City of Bangalore fought with M. Papaiah and another over possession and title to five acres of land in Bangalore, claimed by the plaintiffs as privately owned after cancellation of an earlier acquisition for a burial ground.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for perpetual injunction was maintainable without a specific prayer for declaration of title?
Whether the High Court committed errors in reversing the first appellate court's findings on title and possession?
Whether revenue records can be treated as documents of title in determining ownership?
holdings: A suit for permanent injunction is maintainable even without a specific prayer for declaration of title if the plaint, read as a whole, seeks to establish title.
The High Court committed serious errors by making inconsistent observations on the issue of title and by wrongly treating findings on revenue records as questions of law.
Revenue records are not documents of title, and their interpretation does not amount to a question of law warranting interference in second appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 8
doctrines: Maintainability of suit based on the plaint as a whole
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Revenue records not constituting title documents

card.dispute: The bank sued a man for loan recovery; after his death, it sought to substitute his widow and children as legal representatives, but the widow contested on grounds of delay and her status as only a 'Meeira' holder under Portuguese law.
issues_decided: Whether the widow, holding 'Meeira' rights under Portuguese law, qualifies as a 'legal representative' under Order XXII Rule 4 of CPC
Whether the suit abates if not all legal heirs are brought on record within the time limit
Whether a party can be added later as a legal representative upon discovery of their existence
holdings: A person with 'Meeira' rights under Portuguese law is a 'legal representative' under CPC if they represent the deceased's estate, even if not the sole heir.
If some legal heirs are brought on record within time after diligent inquiry, the suit does not abate; they represent the entire estate in the absence of fraud or collusion.
Additional legal representatives may be added later if the plaintiff was unaware of their existence and acted in good faith.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 9
doctrines: Legal representative under CPC includes those who represent the estate, not necessarily legal heirs
Doctrine of bona fide representation of estate by some heirs
Principle of binding effect of decree on entire estate when some heirs represent it without fraud

card.dispute: Major married sons challenged the clubbing of their land with their father's under the Orissa Land Reforms Act, claiming they were entitled to separate ceiling units despite not having separated by partition before September 26, 1970.
issues_decided: Whether Section 37(b) of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the term 'family' in Section 37(b) should be interpreted to exclude major sons who separated by partition before September 26, 1970, even if not married
Whether the words 'as such' in Section 37(b) qualify 'son' or 'major married son'
Whether land of a son not falling under the exception can be clubbed with that of the father without double jeopardy under ceiling laws
holdings: Section 37(b) has a rational nexus with agrarian reform and is protected under Article 31(C), thus not violating Article 14.

The definition of 'family' excludes only a 'major married son' who separated by partition before September 26, 1970, as a major married son; insertion of 'or' between 'major' and 'married' is impermissible.
The phrase 'as such' qualifies 'major married son', meaning the separation must have occurred in that status.
Clubbing of land of a son not falling under the exception with his father's does not amount to double declaration of surplus, as the son is not treated as a separate individual for ceiling purposes.
doctrines: Doctrine of ejusdem generis
Principle of literal interpretation
Doctrine of rational nexus
Rule against judicial legislation

card.dispute: The appellants sued for possession and injunction based on a sale deed from a widow, while the respondents claimed the widow had no title to transfer the property after executing an unregistered adoption deed that allegedly divested her of rights in favor of the adopted son.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered adoption deed could divest the widow of her property rights and confer immediate rights on the adopted son.
Whether the part of the adoption deed conferring rights on the adopted son and restricting the widow's power to alienate required registration under the Registration Act.
Whether the widow retained the right to transfer the property after adoption, despite the covenant in the unregistered deed.
holdings: An adopted child does not divest the adoptive mother of her vested estate; she retains all rights in her property during her lifetime under Section 12(c) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.
A document that creates an immediate right in immovable property or extinguishes the transferor's right must be registered under Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908.

An unregistered document containing a covenant that divests the mother of her rights and confers them on the adopted son is inadmissible in evidence to prove such divestment under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908.
The widow remained the absolute owner of the property and had the right to transfer it by sale, as the unregistered adoption deed could not legally strip her of ownership.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12(c)
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 13
doctrines: Vesting of property rights under Hindu law
Requirement of registration for documents affecting immovable property
Inadmissibility of unregistered documents creating rights in immovable property

card.dispute: Dr. Subramaniam Swamy sought to transfer a defamation suit filed against him by Ramakrishna Hegde in the Bombay High Court to a civil court in Bangalore on grounds of convenience and access to evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court should transfer a civil suit from one high court to another under Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure on grounds of forum non-conveniens and ends of justice.
Whether the convenience of the parties and availability of evidence outweigh the plaintiff's right to choose the forum.
Whether transfer would cause substantial prejudice to the respondent.
holdings: The Supreme Court can transfer a civil suit to another court if it is expedient for the ends of justice, even if the plaintiff has a right to choose the forum.
When the bulk of evidence and witnesses are located in a different jurisdiction, transfer is justified to ensure a fair trial and prevent hardship to the defendant.
No substantial prejudice will occur to the plaintiff if the suit is transferred to a place where the events occurred and evidence is readily available.
doctrines: Forum non-conveniens
Ends of justice
Dominus litis

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay's decision to evict it and allot the entire plot to another tenant holding a major portion, alleging arbitrariness and violation of constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay is a 'State' under Article 12 and its actions are subject to judicial review under Articles 14 and 32/226
Whether the eviction and re-allotment of the plot by the Port Trust was arbitrary, unreasonable, or contrary to public purpose
Whether the Port Trust's action in favoring a major holder for development under the Town Planning Scheme was a valid exercise of discretion
holdings: The Port Trust, though a statutory authority, must act in pursuance of a public purpose, and its actions are subject to judicial review to ensure reasonableness and non-arbitrariness.
The decision to evict the appellant and allot the plot to the major holder was not improper, as it was based on a policy aimed at development under the Town Planning Scheme.
The Port Trust's policy of allotting plots to major holders to facilitate development is a feasible and justifiable means, and courts should not substitute their opinion for that of the authority.
provisions: Constitution of India, 1950: Article 12, Article 14, Article 32, Article 226, Article 227
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947
doctrines: Doctrine of Public Purpose
Doctrine of Reasonableness in Administrative Action
Judicial Review of Statutory Authorities
Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness under Article 14

card.dispute: The Gram Panchayat of Kanonda challenged the consolidation and allotment of its land under a consolidation scheme, seeking revocation of the scheme and fresh repartition, after the Director initially allowed its delayed application under Section 42 of the Act, which the High Court later quashed.
issues_decided: Whether the confirmation of a consolidation scheme under Section 20 of the East Punjab Holdings Act is an 'order' within the meaning of Rule 18 of the Rules, thereby attracting a limitation period?
Whether the Director could condone the delay in filing the application under Section 42 of the Act when no express limitation applied to challenges against confirmation of a scheme?
Whether the Director's order amounted to an impermissible review of his own earlier decision, rendering it ultra vires?
holdings: Confirmation of a consolidation scheme under Section 20 does not amount to an 'order' under the Act; thus, Rule 18's six-month limitation applies only when an 'order' is passed, not to the scheme's preparation or confirmation.

In the absence of a prescribed limitation period for challenging the confirmation of a scheme under Section 42, the Director has discretion to condone delay, especially where practical hardships and lack of awareness justify the belated application.
The Director’s action did not constitute a review of a prior order, as no earlier decision on the same matter existed; hence, the order was not ultra vires or without jurisdiction.
The High Court erred in interfering with the Director’s order, which was legally valid and based on equitable considerations; the appeal was allowed and the Director’s order restored.
provisions: East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 19
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 20
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 21
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 42
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Rules, 1949, Rule 18
doctrines: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Ex praecedentibus et consequentibus optima fit interpretatio
Condonation of delay in absence of statutory limitation
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant sought to amend his plaint to include an averment of readiness and willingness to perform a contract for sale of property, which was initially omitted, while the respondent opposed the amendment on grounds of delay and prejudice.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court erred in rejecting the application to amend the plaint to include an averment of readiness and willingness to perform the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Whether the amendment would cause injustice to the respondent or affect a vested right.
holdings: An amendment to include an averment of readiness and willingness to perform a contract in a suit for specific performance is permissible if it does not introduce a new cause of action and is necessary to determine the real controversy.
Amendments should be allowed unless they cause irreparable injustice; since no fresh cause of action was introduced here, the amendment did not prejudice the respondent.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, 1908: Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings to meet the ends of justice
Principle of avoiding technical dismissal of claims for specific performance due to curable omissions

card.dispute: The dispute was between a firm and decree-holders over whether the firm and related parties frustrated an eviction order by obtaining an injunction through third parties after the Supreme Court had dismissed their appeal and granted conditional time to vacate.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to file an undertaking as required by the Supreme Court amounted to contempt under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Whether the sons and grandsons of the firm's partners could be bound by or held accountable for complying with the Supreme Court's order
Whether the application for contempt was barred by limitation under Section 20 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
holdings: No formal contempt was established under Section 2(b) because no express undertaking was filed, and implied undertakings cannot form the basis of contempt.
The parties who obtained the injunction were not bound by the order directly but were complicit in frustrating it, and thus must ensure compliance in the interest of justice.
The application was not barred by limitation under Section 20 as the failure to vacate constituted a continuing contempt.
doctrines: No implied undertaking can found contempt
Continuing contempt doctrine
Frustration of judicial orders

card.dispute: The landlord sued for ejectment after serving a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act only on one of the co-tenants, the respondent, who inherited the tenancy along with other family members.
issues_decided: Whether a notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act served on one co-tenant is sufficient to terminate the tenancy of all co-tenants who inherited the tenancy?
Whether the heirs of a deceased tenant hold the tenancy as joint tenants or as tenants-in-common?
holdings: On the death of the original tenant, the tenancy devolves as a single tenancy on the heirs, who hold it as joint tenants, not as tenants-in-common, absent any contrary provision.
Where one co-tenant acts on behalf of all—paying rent and receiving notices—service of notice under Section 106 on that co-tenant is sufficient to determine the entire tenancy.
doctrines: Joint tenancy in inherited tenancies
Notice under Section 106 effective when served on agent or representative co-tenant

card.dispute: The appellants claimed ownership of leasehold land used for mining activities, while the respondent argued the land vested in the Central Government under the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973.
issues_decided: Whether the suit land is a 'mine' within the meaning of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973
Whether parties can retract from evidence they led during trial
holdings: Land adjacent to a coal mine and used for mining purposes, such as stacking coal and local sales, falls within the statutory definition of 'mine' under Section 2(h)(vi) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, and thus vests in the Central Government free from encumbrances.

Parties cannot retract from evidence they have voluntarily led during trial, especially when both sides understood the issues and adduced evidence accordingly; absence of a formal issue does not vitiate the decision if the subject was substantially in issue.
doctrines: Vesting of property free from encumbrances
Voluntary election to lead evidence binds parties to its consideration

card.dispute: The landlords (Kamala Devi Budhia & Ors) fought to evict tenants (Ram Prabha Ganguli & Ors) after the expiry of a 20-year lease, claiming the tenants had no right to continue possession.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947 is maintainable after the expiry of a fixed-term lease when the tenant claims a month-to-month tenancy?
Whether a proceeding filed as an application under Section 12 can be treated as a suit for eviction if it was conducted like a suit?
Whether the Supreme Court can restore a decree of eviction when the lower appellate court declined to pass one and directed a fresh application under Section 12(3)?
holdings: Even if an application under Section 12 is not maintainable, the proceeding can be treated as a suit if both parties led evidence and the case was tried as an eviction suit.
A civil court's proceedings should be judged by their substance, not by form; a petition filed as an application under Section 12 can be treated as a plaint if tried as a suit.

Under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court can pass a decree for eviction to do complete justice, even in the absence of a formal appeal by the landlords, when the facts support eviction.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 2(b)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 12
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 58
doctrines: Substance over form in judicial proceedings
Doctrine of effective remedy and complete justice under Article 142
Jurisdictional validation: exercise of power under a valid provision despite mislabeling

card.dispute: The appellant's legal heirs claimed that she had complied with the Supreme Court's order to deposit money for specific performance of a contract to sell property, while the respondent contested whether payment by cheque on the last day met the deposit requirement.
issues_decided: Whether payment by cheque tendered on the last date of compliance, but encashed later, constitutes due deposit under the Supreme Court's order.
Whether compliance with the deposit condition must strictly follow the Madras High Court's Original Side Rules requiring deposit into the Reserve Bank of India by the deadline.
holdings: Payment by cheque, if duly honoured, relates back to the date of delivery and constitutes compliance with a court-ordered deposit deadline, absent a specific requirement for cash.
Substantial compliance with court orders is sufficient when the intent and purpose of the order are met, even if procedural rules are not strictly followed.
provisions: Original Side Rules of the Madras High Court, Order XXXI Rules 1-6
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Relation back of payment by cheque

card.dispute: The Darjee community and its representatives fought against Gangaram and others over ownership of a garden with temples in Jaipur, with Gangaram claiming title based on a sale deed and a will, while the community asserted collective ownership and administration rights.
issues_decided: Whether the will dated 1916 in favour of Gangaram was genuine and validly executed
Whether the sale deed dated 1875 could be proved through an unverified ordinary copy (Ex. 3) in the absence of the original or a certified copy
Whether the court could consider surrounding circumstances to assess the credibility of a will
holdings: A will, being a solemn document, must be proved with trustworthy evidence; if suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must fully explain them, and the court may consider surrounding circumstances and inherent improbabilities to determine its genuineness.

Secondary evidence of a document under the Indian Evidence Act must strictly comply with Section 63; an unverified ordinary copy of a registered sale deed, without certification or authentication, does not constitute valid secondary evidence under Sections 63 or 66.

The court is entitled to examine surrounding circumstances, including the conduct of parties and the unnatural nature of dispositions, in evaluating the authenticity of a will, especially when the testator disinherits close family members.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order I Rule 8
doctrines: Propounder's burden to dispel suspicious circumstances surrounding a will
Strict compliance with mode of proving documents under the Indian Evidence Act
Court's power to consider intrinsic and extrinsic improbabilities in will disputes

card.dispute: The appellant claimed partition and possession of Watan (Inam) land held by ancestors, which the High Court dismissed, holding that the right to partition ceased upon abolition of Watan rights.
issues_decided: Whether the right to partition of Watan (Inam) land survives the abolition of Watan under the Bombay Inferior Village Watans Abolition Act, 1958
Whether the Watan land became partible and available for partition among joint family members after abolition
holdings: The abolition of Watan rights does not extinguish the right to partition; instead, the property becomes partible and enures for the benefit of the joint family.
The extinction of Watan tenure converts the land into Rayatwari land, making it subject to partition under personal law as joint family property.
provisions: Bombay Inferior Village Watans Abolition Act, 1958 (Bom. Act 1 of 1959)
Bombay Pargana and Kulkarni Watans (Abolition) Act, 1950
doctrines: Survival of partition rights post-abolition of tenure
Conversion of impartible Watan property into partible joint family property upon state abolition

card.dispute: The appellant, Johri Singh, sought to enforce a pre-emption decree but failed to deposit the full purchase money within the stipulated time due to an alleged arithmetical error; the respondents challenged the condonation of this delay.
issues_decided: Whether the Senior Subordinate Judge had jurisdiction under Section 148 CPC to extend time for depositing a small deficit amount after the deadline had passed.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the lower court's order under Section 115 CPC in revision.
holdings: A court has inherent discretion under Section 148 CPC to extend time for depositing decretal amounts even after expiry of the fixed period if sufficient cause, such as a bona fide inadvertent mistake, is shown.

The High Court cannot interfere in revision under Section 115 CPC unless there is a jurisdictional error or material procedural illegality; mere disagreement with the lower court’s factual or legal conclusion is insufficient.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 14
doctrines: Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Revisional jurisdiction limited to jurisdictional errors
Discretionary power of court under Section 148 CPC

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the method of determining 'irrigated land' under the U.P. Ceiling Act, arguing that two crops must be grown on the entire landholding and that independent proof of assured irrigation is required.
issues_decided: Whether 'irrigated land' under Section 4A of the U.P. Ceiling Act requires independent evidence of assured irrigation beyond official records
Whether two crops must have been actually grown on the entire extent of the land to classify it as irrigated
holdings: The Prescribed Authority can determine assured irrigation based on statutory records like khasras and village maps without requiring additional independent evidence.
Land can be classified as irrigated if two crops were grown on any portion of it, as the soil's capacity is presumed uniform unless proven otherwise.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 4A
doctrines: Presumption of uniformity of soil quality
Statutory interpretation of social legislation
Administrative determination based on official records

card.dispute: The contractor (K.V. George) and the Government (Water and Power Department) fought over whether a second arbitration claim was maintainable after the first arbitration award ignored counterclaims.
issues_decided: Whether the first arbitration award, which did not consider counterclaims, was legally valid
Whether the trial court's review order setting aside its earlier remand order was sustainable
Whether the second arbitration claim was barred by res judicata or constructive res judicata
holdings: An arbitrator must consider both claims and counterclaims; failing to do so constitutes misconduct, rendering the award illegal.
A review order is not maintainable without a mistake apparent on the face of the record; the trial court's review was invalid.
The principle of res judicata applies to arbitration; a party cannot split a cause of action and file a second reference after the first award.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order 2, Rule 2
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Arbitrator misconduct
Cause of action splitting

card.dispute: Tenants challenged the validity of a notification exempting new buildings in Chandigarh from rent control laws, arguing that civil courts lost jurisdiction to pass eviction decrees after the exemption period ended.
issues_decided: Whether the notification under Section 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, granting a five-year exemption to new buildings in Chandigarh, is constitutionally valid
Whether the civil court retains jurisdiction to pass or execute an eviction decree after the expiry of the exemption period if the suit was filed during the exemption period
Whether the exemption notification creates invidious discrimination between tenants of old and new buildings in violation of Article 14
holdings: The notification granting temporary exemption to new buildings is valid as it advances the object of rent control legislation and does not violate the Act or the Constitution.
The civil court retains jurisdiction to pass and execute an eviction decree if the suit was instituted within the exemption period, even if the period expires during litigation.
The classification between tenants of old and new buildings based on construction date is reasonable, has a rational nexus with the Act's purpose, and does not violate Article 14.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949: Section 3
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949: Section 13
doctrines: Doctrine of harmonious construction
Doctrine of prospective overruling
Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Binding precedent under Article 141

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant on grounds of rent default and denial of title; the tenant challenged a municipal notice and claimed possession as a tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's pleadings in a civil suit amounted to a denial of the landlord's title under Section 13(1)(f) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950.
Whether a tenant can be evicted for denying the landlord's title based on statements made in a suit against a third party?
holdings: A denial of the landlord's title under Section 13(1)(f) must be clear and unequivocal; mere ambiguous or contextual statements do not amount to a valid disclaimer.

Statements made in a plaint against a municipal authority, where no relief is sought against the landlord and the tenant acknowledges his own status as a tenant, do not constitute a denial of title sufficient for eviction.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(f)
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Strict construction of eviction clauses
Denial of title requiring clear and unambiguous language

card.dispute: Lachhman Dass and Ram Lal disputed over an arbitration award that transferred ownership of a plot of land, with the key issue being whether an unregistered award affecting immovable property could be enforced.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitration award affecting immovable property valued over Rs. 100 requires registration to be enforceable under Section 14 of the Arbitration Act, 1940
Whether the failure to raise the issue of non-registration within 30 days under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act bars a party from later challenging the award on that ground
Whether subsequent registration of an initially unregistered award cures the defect when enforcement is sought
holdings: An arbitration award that affects immovable property valued over Rs. 100 must be registered to be acted upon by a court under Section 14 of the Arbitration Act, 1940; otherwise, the court cannot pronounce judgment on it.

The objection to an unregistered award can be raised in proceedings under Section 14 even if not raised within 30 days under Section 30, because the court must have jurisdiction to consider the award at the enforcement stage.

Subsequent registration of an award does not cure the defect of non-registration at the time enforcement is sought; the award must be registered when presented to the court for making it a rule of the court.
doctrines: Strict construction of disabling statutes
Constructive res judicata
Jurisdictional requirement of registration for enforcement of documents affecting immovable property

card.dispute: A social worker challenged the prolonged delay in deciding a death row convict's mercy petition, arguing it violated his fundamental rights.
issues_decided: Whether undue delay in deciding a mercy petition entitles a death row convict to relief under Article 21
Whether prolonged mental agony from delay in execution can lead to commutation of death sentence
Whether a fixed time period can be set for deciding mercy petitions
holdings: Undue long delay in deciding a mercy petition violates Article 21 and entitles the convict to approach the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Prolonged mental agony caused by inordinate delay in execution can justify commutation of death sentence to life imprisonment.
No fixed period of delay can automatically entitle a convict to commutation; each case must be examined on its circumstances.
doctrines: Right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 includes protection against inordinate delay in execution
Mental torture from prolonged death row incarceration is a relevant factor for commutation
Principle of fair and speedy disposal of mercy petitions as part of executive fairness

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the decree declaring the respondent as the real owner of a property held benami, while the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 came into force during the pendency of the appeal.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 applies retrospectively to pending appeals?
Whether the appellate court can consider subsequent legislative changes while deciding an appeal?
Whether the right of a real owner to enforce rights in benami property is extinguished by the Act even if the suit was filed before its commencement?
holdings: Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 applies to pending suits and appeals as it bars any action to enforce rights in benami property, regardless of when the transaction occurred.
An appellate court is competent to consider legislative changes occurring after the decree and apply them in moulding relief, as an appeal amounts to a re-hearing of the case.
The prohibition on filing suits or claims under Section 4 extinguishes the right of the real owner to recover benami property, rendering such rights unenforceable even if they existed before the Act.
doctrines: Ubi jus ibi remedium
Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Presumption against retrospective operation of statutes
Declaratory and disqualifying nature of statutes

card.dispute: The tenant disputed the landlord's title to the property during eviction proceedings initiated by the landlord on grounds of bona fide personal requirement and denial of title.
issues_decided: Whether denial of the landlord's title by the tenant during eviction proceedings can constitute a valid ground for eviction under the A.P. Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Whether such denial must be anterior to the filing of the eviction petition to be actionable
Whether the landlord was required to amend the eviction petition to include the ground of denial of title after it emerged in the tenant's written statement
holdings: A tenant's denial of the landlord's title during eviction proceedings is a valid ground for eviction under Section 10(2)(vi) of the A.P. Rent Act if the denial is clear and not bona fide.
The denial of title need not be anterior to the filing of the eviction petition; subsequent denial in the course of proceedings can support eviction.
Amendment of the eviction petition is not mandatory if the Rent Controller frames an issue on denial of title and the tenant fully contests it, thereby having notice of the claim.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 12
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 13
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Subsequent events rule in judicial proceedings
Amendment of pleadings where issues are tried with consent

card.dispute: Co-heirs fought over the right to manage a Dargah and share in its offerings, with male defendants claiming the plaintiffs' predecessor was ousted by adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the female co-sharer Fathima Bee was ousted from her right to manage the Dargah and share in its offerings
Whether the judgment in a prior suit (1909) operated as res judicata or evidence of ouster
Whether adverse possession was established among co-heirs without open assertion of hostile title
holdings: A co-heir cannot be deemed ousted without open and hostile assertion of title coupled with exclusive possession known to the excluded party.
A prior judgment not involving the co-sharer and not deciding her rights cannot constitute res judicata or proof of ouster.
Mere non-receipt of income or non-possession by a co-heir does not prove adverse possession if family relations remain cordial and benefits are shared.
doctrines: Adverse possession among co-heirs
Res judicata
Hostile title requirement in co-ownership

card.dispute: Mortgagor (Maganlal) challenged the validity of a property sale conducted by a State Financial Corporation under the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, and sought redemption under Order 34 Rule 5 of the CPC, while two purchasers contested the setting aside of successive auction sales.
issues_decided: Whether Order 34 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to a sale of mortgaged property under Section 32 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951
Whether the mortgagor retains a right of redemption after the sale but before confirmation of sale under the Act
Whether the provisions of the CPC relating to execution of decrees apply to orders under Section 32 of the Act
holdings: Order 34 Rule 5 CPC is applicable to sales under Section 32 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, as the legal fiction in the Act treats such orders as decrees for execution purposes.
The mortgagor retains the right to redeem the property after sale but before confirmation, as the right of redemption is not extinguished until confirmation.
Provisions of the CPC relating to execution of decrees for sale of mortgaged property apply to orders under Section 32 of the Act, as directed by Section 32(8) and established legal principles.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: Order 34 Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: Order 21 Rule 90
doctrines: Legal fiction in statutory interpretation
Right of redemption in mortgage law
Application of civil procedure to special statutes by implication

card.dispute: The landlord sought contempt action against the tenant and another person for failing to hand over vacant possession of the premises as per an undertaking given to the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the first respondent committed contempt by breaching the undertaking to vacate the premises by 31.3.1989?
Whether the second respondent could be restrained from possession by a temporary injunction despite the Supreme Court's order for eviction?
What relief and punishment should be granted for breach of the undertaking?
holdings: The first respondent was guilty of contempt for willfully breaching the undertaking to vacate the premises, as he had falsely represented possession and misled the Court.
The injunction granted by the Thane Civil Court in favor of the second respondent was unjustified and not operative, as it interfered with the Supreme Court's eviction decree.

The first respondent must purge contempt by immediately delivering vacant possession, pay a fine of Rs. 500 within four weeks (or face one month’s imprisonment), and the District Magistrate must enforce eviction.
doctrines: Breach of undertaking given to court amounts to contempt
Undertaking treated as court order for enforcement purposes
Contempt requires wilful disobedience, and remedy includes fine, imprisonment, and purging of contempt

card.dispute: The landlords filed a civil suit for possession of land after their application before the Mamlatdar was dismissed; the tenants contested, claiming the civil court lacked jurisdiction and that they were rightful tenants under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act.
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the Mamlatdar rejecting the landlords' application operates as res judicata in the subsequent civil suit.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit despite prior proceedings before the Mamlatdar.
Whether the ex parte order of the Mamlatdar could conclusively determine the tenancy status under the Act.
holdings: The Mamlatdar's ex parte rejection of the possession application does not operate as res judicata on the issue of tenancy, as the matter was not directly and substantially in issue in that proceeding.
The civil court retains jurisdiction to decide questions of tenancy and title even after a prior administrative decision by the Mamlatdar, especially when the Mamlatdar declined jurisdiction.
A decision by a court or authority lacking jurisdiction, or one that did not finally and substantially hear an issue, cannot constitute res judicata in a subsequent civil suit.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(5)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(8)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(17)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(18)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 25(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 70(b)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85A
doctrines: Res judicata
Exclusive jurisdiction
Summary proceedings vs. civil suits
Finality of ex parte decrees
Jurisdictional competence and res judicata

card.dispute: The appellants (lessees) fought the respondents (lessors) over whether they were protected thika tenants under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, or were liable to be evicted after failing to exercise an option for extension of their lease.
issues_decided: Whether the lease dated 26th September 1946 was for a period of less than 12 years, thereby excluding the lessees from protection as thika tenants under Section 2(5)(b) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949
Whether the respondents waived their right to eject the appellants or were estopped from denying thika tenancy status due to prior proceedings before the Controller
holdings: A lease with an initial term of 10 years and options for further extensions totaling up to 20 years is deemed to be for a period not less than 12 years; thus, the appellants did not qualify as thika tenants under Section 2(5)(b) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949.

Mere initiation of proceedings before the Controller under the Thika Tenancy Act does not confer thika tenant status; there was no voluntary relinquishment of rights or conduct warranting estoppel or waiver by the respondents.
doctrines: Distinction between 'extension' and 'renewal' in lease agreements
Doctrine of waiver requiring voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right
Doctrine of estoppel under Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act
Interpretation of contracts based on ex antecedentibus et consequentibus

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the sale of trust properties permitted under a scheme-decree, claiming they had locus standi as beneficiaries despite not being original plaintiffs in the representative suit.
issues_decided: Whether a suit under Section 92 of the CPC is a representative suit binding all persons interested in the trust.
Whether non-plaintiffs who are beneficiaries of a public trust have locus standi to apply under clauses of a scheme-decree arising from a Section 92 suit.
Whether the sale of trust property through private negotiation at a price below market value is permissible.
holdings: A suit under Section 92 CPC is representative in nature, and all persons interested in the trust are deemed parties to it, bound by the decree under constructive res judicata.
Beneficiaries of a public trust, even if not named plaintiffs, have locus standi to move applications under a scheme-decree from a Section 92 suit.
Sale of trust property by private negotiation at significantly undervalued price violates the duty to protect charitable assets; public auction is required to ensure fair value.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation VI
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Representative suit
Constructive res judicata
Locus standi in public interest litigation
Protection of charitable and religious endowments

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent, while the tenant claimed he had a prior oral agreement to purchase the property and thus was not obligated to pay rent.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's failure to pay rent constituted wilful default under Section 10(2) of the A.P. Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960.
Whether the tenant's bona fide belief in a right to purchase the property negates wilfulness in non-payment of rent.
holdings: A tenant's default in paying rent is not wilful if it arises from a bona fide belief in a right to purchase the property, even if that belief is later found incorrect.
The Controller must grant the tenant an opportunity to pay arrears if the default was not wilful, as per the proviso to Section 10(2) of the Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(2)
doctrines: Wilful default requires intentional, deliberate, and conscious non-compliance with full knowledge of consequences.
Proviso to Section 10(2) acts as a mitigating provision to prevent harsh outcomes in eviction cases.

card.dispute: The landlord, Excelsior Needle Industries, sought to evict the tenant, Rubber House, for arrears of rent, but the tenant challenged the eviction on grounds including non-compliance with procedural rules regarding disclosure of the quantum of arrears.
issues_decided: Whether non-mentioning of the quantum of arrears of rent in an eviction petition renders the petition invalid under the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1976
Whether Rules 4(c), 5(1), and 6 of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1976 are mandatory or directory
holdings: Non-mentioning of the quantum of arrears in an eviction petition does not invalidate the proceedings if the tenant is aware of the amount due and suffers no prejudice.

Rules 4(c), 5(1), and 6 of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1976 are directory, not mandatory, and non-compliance does not nullify the eviction petition in the absence of prejudice.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(2)(i)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1976, Rules 4(c), 5(1), and 6
doctrines: Distinction between mandatory and directory provisions in statutory interpretation
Requirement of prejudice for invalidation of proceedings due to procedural non-compliance

card.dispute: The State appealed the acquittal of 15 accused in a murder case; the High Court convicted them on constructive liability, which they challenged in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants can be held constructively liable under Section 34 IPC for the murder committed by Dinesh Singh?
Whether the appellants can be held liable under Section 149 IPC for being part of an unlawful assembly with common object to commit murder?
Whether the prosecution established a common intention or common object among the accused to murder Kumar Gopal Singh?
holdings: Mere presence at the scene of crime is not sufficient to establish common intention under Section 34 IPC; there must be evidence that the act was done in furtherance of a shared intention.
To invoke Section 149 IPC, there must be proof that the accused were members of an unlawful assembly with a common object to commit murder, which was not established here.
The embellishments in witness testimony, absent from the first information report, create doubt about the prosecution's claim of common intention or common object.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 34 IPC
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Fardbeyan as a reliable initial statement

card.dispute: The appellant brother refused to execute a sale deed in favour of the respondent sister as per an agreement after she redeemed a mortgaged property, leading to a suit for specific performance which was challenged as time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether a date was 'fixed' for performance under Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963 when performance was contingent on redemption of a mortgage?
From which date does the limitation period begin to run for a contingent contract of sale?
holdings: A date is 'fixed' under Article 54 of the Limitation Act if the basis for determining it is ascertainable from the contract, even if not specified by calendar date.
The limitation period for specific performance of a contingent contract begins when the contingency (here, redemption of mortgage) occurs, not from the contract date or notice of refusal.
doctrines: certum est quod certum reddi potest
specific performance of contingent contracts

card.dispute: Landlords challenged the constitutional validity of a central government notification extending the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985 to Chandigarh, arguing it violated principles of legislative delegation and conflicted with existing laws.
issues_decided: Whether Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 permits the extension of future state laws and amendments to the Union Territory of Chandigarh without violating constitutional limits on delegation.
Whether the Central Government's notification extending the 1985 Amendment Act to Chandigarh is invalid due to inconsistency with the existing rent control regime under the 1974 Act.
Whether the power under Section 87 results in impermissible delegation of legislative authority or abdication of parliamentary function.
holdings: Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 validly empowers the Central Government to extend state laws to Chandigarh with sufficient guidelines, and does not constitute abdication of legislative power.
The extension of the 1985 Amendment Act to Chandigarh is valid as it does not conflict with or repugn the scheme of the 1974 Act, and both can operate together.

The power under Section 87 allows extension of laws as they exist on the date of notification, with only minor modifications, and does not permit substantial changes, thus avoiding unconstitutional delegation.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985
doctrines: Doctrine of permissible delegation
Doctrine of non-merger of powers under separation of functions
Doctrine of repugnancy
Principle of ancillary and incidental modification in delegated legislation

card.dispute: The landlord sued the tenant for eviction, alleging that the tenant had unlawfully parted with possession of the leased premises by allowing a social club to operate there, violating the lease terms and the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's allowing a social club to use the leased premises amounts to 'parting with possession' under Section 13(1)(e) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, even without subletting for rent.
Whether the respondent could be permitted to file additional documents (auditor and committee reports of the club) as evidence at the appellate stage before the Supreme Court.
holdings: Allowing a social club to use the leased premises, especially with a registered office there and continuous exclusive access, constitutes parting with possession under Section 13(1)(e), even without subletting or receiving rent.
Additional documents that were available during earlier proceedings cannot be admitted at the Supreme Court stage without a satisfactory explanation for their non-production before lower courts.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(e)
Indian Companies Act, Section 146, Section 163, Section 303, Section 20, Section 143, Section 144
doctrines: Parting with possession
Admissibility of additional evidence in appeal

card.dispute: The appellant, as successor to a mortgagor, sued to redeem mortgaged property, but the respondents resisted on grounds of limitation, arguing the suit was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the recital in a 1913 sale deed constituted an acknowledgment of a subsisting right of redemption under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
Whether the suit for redemption was within the limitation period under Section 30 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
holdings: A recital in a sale deed acknowledging the continued existence of mortgage debt and the mortgagor's right to redeem constitutes a valid acknowledgment under Section 19, restarting the limitation period.
The suit was instituted within the seven-year grace period under Section 30 of the Limitation Act, 1963, as it was filed on 28.12.1968, and thus was not barred by limitation.
doctrines: Acknowledgment under Section 19 of the Limitation Act
Savings clause under Section 30 of the Limitation Act, 1963

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for wilful default in rent payment and bona fide requirement, while the tenant argued that rent was paid with landlord's acceptance and no default occurred.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was a habitual defaulter in rent payment justifying eviction under Clause 13(3)(ii) of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
Whether the landlord proved bona fide requirement of the premises under Clause 13(3)(vi) of the Rent Control Order
holdings: A tenant is not a habitual defaulter if rent is paid in lump sums over several months and consistently accepted by the landlord without objection, as this conduct implies an agreement modifying the payment terms.
The landlord failed to prove bona fide requirement of the premises, and concurrent findings of lower courts on this factual issue cannot be overturned without compelling reason.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(ii)
C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(vi)
doctrines: Implied agreement by conduct
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed
Doctrine of estoppel by conduct in rent payment

card.dispute: The appellant claimed exemption from tenant purchase rights under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 for compensation land received for a pre-1950 gallantry award, while the respondent tenant sought to enforce his right to purchase the land.
issues_decided: Whether land allotted in India as compensation for a pre-1950 gallantry award land lost due to partition is exempt from the operation of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 under Section 19DD
Whether a tenant's right to purchase land under Section 18 of the Act survives when the landlord claims exemption under Section 19DD
Whether the Displaced Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 extends the exemption available under Section 19DD of the Punjab Act
holdings: Section 19DD of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 applies only to land originally granted for gallantry before January 26, 1950, not to compensation land allotted later in India.
The right of a tenant to purchase land under Section 18 of the Act is not barred if the land does not qualify for exemption under Section 19DD.
The Displaced Persons (Compensation & Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 does not extend the statutory exemption under Section 19DD to compensation land.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 14A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 19DD
doctrines: In aequali jure, melior est conditio possidentis
Statutory interpretation based on plain language
Non-extension of exemptions by implication

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenant-firm for unlawful subletting to another firm, and the tenant challenged the maintainability of the eviction petition for non-joinder of partners of the sub-tenant firm.
issues_decided: Whether the eviction petition was not maintainable for failure to join partners of the sub-tenant firm as parties?
Whether there was sufficient evidence to support the finding of unlawful subletting under Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960?
holdings: An objection to the maintainability of an eviction petition on the ground of non-joinder of partners of a firm is not available at the special leave stage if not raised earlier in trial or appellate proceedings, as it can be corrected as misdescription.

A finding of unlawful subletting can be inferred from the sub-tenant firm's occupation of the premises and non-production of account books when notice was issued, as such conduct permits adverse inference of rent payment.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960: Section 10(2)(ii)(a)
doctrines: Principle of maintainability of suits by or against a firm
Adverse inference from non-production of documents
Doctrine of waiver of procedural objections not raised at appropriate stages

card.dispute: Southern Roadways Ltd. sued its former agent S.M. Krishnan for interfering with its business and possession of a godown after termination of his agency, seeking a temporary injunction to restrain him.
issues_decided: Whether the agent could retain possession of the premises after termination of agency
Whether the principal could enforce its right to possession without filing a separate suit for recovery of possession
Whether the agent could deny the principal's title to property held by him as agent
holdings: An agent's possession of property on behalf of the principal is not his own; it is deemed to be the possession of the principal, and he cannot retain it after termination of agency.
A principal need not file a separate suit for recovery of possession to seek an injunction against a former agent; the fiduciary nature of agency allows for equitable relief.
An agent cannot deny the principal's title to property or set up adverse possession, as his possession is always on behalf of the principal and does not vest him with any proprietary interest.
doctrines: Fiduciary relationship in agency
Constructive possession of principal through agent
Agent cannot acquire title by adverse possession

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on the ground that she had acquired alternative accommodation by obtaining vacant possession of her own house.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant acquired 'vacant possession of a residence' under Section 14(1)(h) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 when she briefly possessed her own house before selling it.
Whether the existence of an oral agreement to sell the house before possession was obtained negates the availability of alternative accommodation.
holdings: A tenant acquires 'vacant possession of a residence' under Section 14(1)(h) if she obtains possession of her own house at any time before the eviction petition, even if she later sells it.
The mere existence of a legal obligation to sell a house does not prevent it from being alternative accommodation if the owner actually took possession and could occupy it.
doctrines: Interpretation of 'acquired vacant possession'
Alternative accommodation doctrine in rent control law

card.dispute: The appellant society contested the validity of the withdrawal of its suit by a person claiming to be its Secretary, arguing he was not duly elected and thus not authorized to withdraw the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court has inherent jurisdiction under Section 151 CPC to recall an order permitting withdrawal of a suit if it was misled by a party.
Whether the High Court could intervene under Section 115 CPC when the trial court failed to exercise its inherent jurisdiction.
Whether the finding that Hari Narain Swami was the duly elected Secretary entitled to withdraw the suit was legally sustainable.
holdings: A court has inherent power under Section 151 CPC to correct its own proceedings if it was misled by a party, especially where the purported authorization to withdraw a suit is fraudulent or non-existent.
The High Court ought to have intervened under Section 115 CPC because the trial court failed to exercise a jurisdiction it legally possessed, amounting to a failure of justice.
The finding that Hari Narain Swami was the authorized Secretary is tainted by serious errors and must be reconsidered by the trial court with an opportunity to adduce further evidence.
doctrines: Inherent powers of civil courts to prevent abuse of process and to do justice
Fraud on the court doctrine: distinction between fraud on a party and fraud on the court
Revisional jurisdiction to correct jurisdictional errors

card.dispute: The legal representative of a deceased proprietor challenged the inclusion of disputed property in the Gaon Sabha's land records under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, claiming it was not 'land' and that she was entitled to bhumidhari rights.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed property constituted 'land' under Section 3(13) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954
Whether a civil suit for declaration of bhumidhari rights under Section 11 of the Act is maintainable
holdings: The property on which fuel wood was grown falls within the inclusive definition of 'land' under Section 3(13), particularly as 'groveland', and thus became liable to vest in the Gaon Sabha.
A civil suit for declaration of bhumidhari rights is not maintainable as Section 185 of the Act vests exclusive jurisdiction in revenue courts.
provisions: Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, Schedule I
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of revenue courts under statutory ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Inclusive statutory definition of 'land'
Prohibition on relying on definitions from other statutes when a clear definition exists in the statute in question

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent, claiming arrears extended beyond the notice period, while the tenant argued he had tendered the rent due at the time of notice.
issues_decided: Whether arrears of rent under Section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 include rent that falls due after service of the notice of demand
Whether the tenant's tender of two months' rent via bank drafts within two months of the notice satisfied the requirement under Section 14(1)(a)
holdings: Arrears of rent under Section 14(1)(a) are limited to those due on the date of service of the notice and do not include rent that becomes due afterward.
Tender of the full amount of arrears specified in the notice within two months satisfies the requirement, even if not accepted by the landlord.
doctrines: Interpretation of statutory notice requirements
Tender of payment as compliance with rent demand

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, both displaced persons, claimed rights over land allotted post-partition, where the appellant received a permanent Sanad, and the respondent sought reallocation during consolidation proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Consolidation authorities could modify or cancel proprietary rights granted via Sanad under Section 10 of the Displaced Persons Act, 1954
Whether Section 30 of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, bars the transfer of rights through a Sanad during consolidation
Whether the dismissal of the appellant's writ petition in limine operates as res judicata against her civil suit
holdings: Authorities under the Consolidation Act cannot modify or cancel proprietary rights granted by a Sanad under Section 10 of the Displaced Persons Act, as such grants confer absolute title.
Section 30 of the East Punjab Holdings Act does not apply to transfers via Sanad under the Displaced Persons Act, as they are compensatory and statutorily distinct.
A writ petition dismissed in limine on grounds of laches or alternative remedy does not constitute res judicata and does not bar a subsequent civil suit.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 10
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1954, Rule 68
East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, Section 30
doctrines: Res judicata
Statutory interpretation
Principle of finality in writ proceedings

card.dispute: The State of Assam appealed against the Gauhati High Court's acquittal of respondents convicted of murdering Majibur Rahman and Dhansa Sheikh, claiming the High Court erred in rejecting the prosecution's evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the respondents despite their conviction by the Sessions Judge.
Whether the prosecution evidence, including the dying declaration and eyewitness accounts, was sufficient to sustain the convictions.
Whether the failure to record the dying declaration before a Magistrate affected its reliability.
Whether the injuries on the accused could be reconciled with the prosecution's version of events.
holdings: The High Court did not err in acquitting the respondents as the prosecution evidence was infirm, doubtful, and lacked corroboration from independent witnesses.
The eyewitness accounts of family members were unreliable due to contradictions, late disclosure, and physical implausibility of witnessing the attack.
A dying declaration, though admissible, loses significant weight if not recorded by a Magistrate, especially when it fails to mention key details like the presence of eyewitnesses.
The unexplained injuries on the accused raise a reasonable doubt about the prosecution's claim of a one-sided attack, supporting the benefit of the doubt to the accused.
doctrines: Benefit of the doubt to the accused in criminal cases
Dying declaration must be reliable and consistent to be acted upon
Corroboration required for interested witnesses
Reasonable doubt arising from unexplained injuries on accused

card.dispute: The State of Jammu & Kashmir challenged the High Court's direction to cease entertaining applications under Section 8 of the Evacuee Property Act, arguing that the provision was still valid and necessary.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in declaring that Section 8 of the Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 had outlived its utility
Whether Section 8 should continue to be operative in light of ongoing relevance of Section 6 of the Act
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing directions against entertaining future applications under Section 8
holdings: The High Court erred in declaring Section 8 obsolete as it had no occasion to rule on the continued relevance of the provision when the appeal was limited to factual findings.
Section 8 remains relevant because it is closely linked to Section 6, which still authorizes the notification of evacuee properties in active cases.
Given that part of Jammu & Kashmir remains under alien control, the possibility of new evacuee properties arising justifies the continued operation of Section 8.
provisions: Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 of Jammu & Kashmir: Section 6
Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 of Jammu & Kashmir: Section 8
Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 of Jammu & Kashmir: Section 9
Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 of Jammu & Kashmir: Section 14
Evacuee (Administration of Property) Act, 2006 of Jammu & Kashmir: Section 25
doctrines: Separability of statutory provisions
Principle of judicial restraint
Continuing relevance of legislation based on factual necessity

card.dispute: The appellant, Surinder Kumar, was convicted of murder for killing Nitya Nand during a quarrel over kitchen possession, and challenged whether the killing fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, reducing it to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's act fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, i.e., whether the killing occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation and in the heat of passion?
Whether the appellant acted in a cruel or unusual manner, thereby disentitling him from the benefit of Exception 4?
Whether the number of injuries inflicted is determinative of cruelty under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC?
holdings: A killing during a sudden quarrel, without premeditation, and in the heat of passion, qualifies for Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC even if a weapon is picked up during the altercation.
The mere fact that multiple injuries were inflicted does not per se establish cruel or unusual conduct if the act occurred in the heat of a sudden fight.
An accused is entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 if the provocation was sudden, the response immediate, and the act not involving undue advantage, regardless of who initiated the quarrel.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Heat of passion
Sudden quarrel doctrine
Cruel or unusual manner test under Exception 4

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Chet Ram, Buddhi, and Puttu, who were convicted by the Sessions Judge for the murder and robbery of Kishori, a widow whose land they coveted.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the respondents by disregarding reliable prosecution evidence, including the dying declaration and medical evidence?
Whether the conduct of the respondents after the incident supports their guilt?
Whether the prosecution's case, including the recovery of the lantern and presence of a yoke for scaling the wall, was wrongly disbelieved by the High Court?
Whether the motive of land grabbing is inconsistent with the act of robbing the victim of her ornaments?
holdings: The dying declaration made by Kishori was reliable and consistent with medical evidence, and the High Court erred in doubting her capacity to make it due to injuries.
The respondents' flight after the incident and absence from their house indicated consciousness of guilt and supported the prosecution's case.
The prosecution evidence regarding the burning lantern and the yoke fixed in the wall was credible and should not have been disregarded by the High Court.
The act of snatching ornaments was a deliberate attempt to divert suspicion towards robbery, and does not negate the primary motive of land grabbing.
doctrines: Dying declaration requires no corroboration if found reliable
Principle of appreciation of evidence in appeals against acquittal
Conduct subsequent to offence as evidence of guilt
Judicial duty to interfere in cases of miscarriage of justice despite presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The appellants, Suryamoorthi and his mother, challenged the acquittal of seven police constables and others accused of robbing them of Rs. 40,000 while in police custody at a bus stand.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused committed robbery under Section 395 IPC?
Whether the recovery of money from accused Nos. 1, 4, and 7 corroborated the prosecution's case?
Whether the courts below erred in requiring the victims to prove the source of their money?
Whether accused No. 1 was guilty of misconduct in office under Section 220 IPC?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the involvement of accused Nos. 2, 3, 5, and 6 due to lack of reliable identification and corroboration; hence, their acquittal was upheld.

The recovery of Rs. 39,170 from accused Nos. 1, 4, and 7, combined with their statements during investigation, sufficiently corroborated the victims' testimony, warranting conviction for robbery under Section 392 IPC.
Courts should not require victims to prove the source of their money when the recovery of a substantial part of the claimed amount supports their credibility.
Section 220 IPC does not apply where there is no evidence of actual confinement; mere wrongful restraint does not constitute the offence.
doctrines: Corroboration of victim testimony through recovery of property
Benefit of doubt in absence of reliable identification
Judicial review of concurrent findings under Article 136 in cases of miscarriage of justice
Requirement of actual confinement for Section 220 IPC

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu fought with Shakti Estates over whether the sale of trees felled during forest clearance for a coffee and cardamom plantation constituted taxable turnover under the sales tax law.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of trees felled from a leased reserve forest for plantation purposes amounts to a 'business' under the Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959.
Whether the disposal of natural forest growth incidental to land development constitutes an 'adventure in the nature of trade'.
Whether the definition of 'business' includes transactions incidental to the main business activity.
holdings: The felling and sale of trees as part of land development for a plantation constituted an adventure in the nature of trade, given the systematic and commercial manner of disposal.
The activities of clearing forest and selling timber, firewood, sleepers, and charcoal were part of an integrated business venture, not mere realisation of capital assets.
Under Section 2(d) of the Act, 'business' includes transactions incidental or ancillary to the main business, making such sales taxable even without a profit motive.
provisions: Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959, Section 2(d)
Tamil Nadu General Sales Tax Act, 1959, Section 2(g)
doctrines: Adventure in the nature of trade
Incidental or ancillary transactions doctrine
Integrated business venture doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Collector's order to impound an arbitration award and realize unpaid stamp duty, arguing lack of jurisdiction, limitation, and procedural defects, while the respondent sought enforcement of stamp duty on the award.
issues_decided: Whether the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority had jurisdiction to interfere with the Collector's order under Section 56 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
Whether respondent No. 1 had locus standi to initiate proceedings for impounding the award and whether the Collector’s action was barred by limitation.
Whether the Collector had the power to examine the valuation of the property in the arbitration award for stamp duty purposes under Uttar Pradesh law.
holdings: The Chief Controlling Revenue Authority has the power to review and set aside a Collector's order if it is passed without jurisdiction, as such orders are challengeable in the same manner as those passed within jurisdiction.
The Collector’s action was not barred by limitation as it was a follow-up to the civil court’s 1976 order impounding the award; the delay did not invalidate the proceedings.
In Uttar Pradesh, the Collector has authority under Section 47-A of the Indian Stamp Act to examine the correctness of valuation in an arbitration award for stamp duty assessment.
doctrines: Jurisdictional error renders an order challengeable through revision or appeal
Follow-up action to a court order is not time-barred merely due to delay
Statutory interpretation based on state-specific amendments to central acts

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision to grant enhanced solatium and additional compensation to a landowner whose land was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent is entitled to enhanced solatium at 30% under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, despite the award being made after 24 September 1984?

Whether the respondent is entitled to an additional amount at 12% per annum under Section 23(1A) for delayed compensation, even though acquisition proceedings began before 30 April 1982 and the award was made prior to that date?
holdings: Benefit of higher solatium under Section 23(2) applies even if the award was made after 24 September 1984, to avoid arbitrary and unconstitutional distinctions under Article 14.
