The additional amount under Section 23(1A) is not payable where acquisition proceedings commenced before 30 April 1982 and no proceedings were pending before the Collector on that date, as Section 30(1)(a) and (b) do not apply.
doctrines: Literal interpretation vs. purposive interpretation of statutes
Avoidance of unconstitutional arbitrariness under Article 14
Prospective operation of amendments with transitional provisions
Overruling of precedent (Bhag Singh overruled by Raghubir Singh)

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Vimla Bai fought Hiralal Gupta and others over possession of a house, claiming rightful succession under the Bombay School of Hindu Law, while respondents argued governance under the Banaras School where female heirs have no claim.
issues_decided: Whether the parties are governed by the Bombay School or Banaras School of Hindu Law for succession purposes.
Whether a female bandhu (cognate relative) is an heir under the applicable Hindu law.
Whether the gift deed by Sonubai, a widow with limited interest, could validly transfer the property.
Whether the mortgagee is entitled to a decree for refund of mortgage money from the plaintiff.
holdings: The parties are governed by the Bombay School of Hindu Law, which recognizes female bandhus as heirs to the estate of the last male holder.
A female bandhu within five degrees of the last male holder is an heir under the Bombay School, and the enumeration of bandhus in Mitakshara is illustrative, not exhaustive.
Sonubai, as a widow with a limited interest, could not validly gift the property; the gift deed is void and does not bind the rightful heir.
The mortgagee cannot claim refund from the plaintiff as the money was not paid to her; he may pursue remedies against the mortgagor.
doctrines: Presumption against migration in personal law
Illustrative enumeration of bandhus in Mitakshara
Limited interest of a Hindu widow
Admissibility of statements in Government Gazetteer as evidence

card.dispute: The heirs of Wali Mohammad fought against Ram Surat and others over possession of two plots of land, claiming redemption of a mortgage, while respondents claimed Adhivasi status based on revenue entries.
issues_decided: Whether an entry in the Khasra or Khatauni of Fasli Year 1356 is sufficient to confer Adhivasi rights under Section 20(b)(i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, despite incorrectness.
Whether a mere incorrect entry in revenue records can be treated as fictitious or non-est for denying Adhivasi rights.
Whether the Board of Revenue erred in law by relying solely on the revenue entry without inquiring into its factual accuracy.
holdings: An entry in the Khasra or Khatauni of Fasli Year 1356 under Section 20(b)(i) of the Act determines Adhivasi status, regardless of factual correctness, unless it is fictitious, fraudulent, or made with ill-will.
An incorrect entry in revenue records does not become void unless it is made fraudulently or surreptitiously; mere inaccuracy does not nullify its legal effect.
Courts should not re-examine the correctness of revenue entries in Adhivasi claims; the presumption of genuineness applies unless fraud or forgery is proven.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 20(b)(i)
U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, Sections 28 and 33
doctrines: Presumption of correctness of revenue records
Distinction between incorrect and fictitious entries
Fraud vitiates all legal documents

card.dispute: The contractor (Vishwanath Sood) and the Union of India disputed whether compensation for delay, determined by the Superintending Engineer under a contract clause, could be challenged before an arbitrator.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction to decide on the quantum of delay compensation under Clause 2 of the contract, which vested final decision-making power in the Superintending Engineer.
Whether the exclusion of certain disputes from arbitration under Clause 25 of the contract applied to disputes over delay compensation under Clause 2.
holdings: The determination of compensation for delay under Clause 2 is exclusively within the authority of the Superintending Engineer and cannot be questioned before an arbitrator.
Clause 25's arbitration clause excludes disputes already provided for elsewhere in the contract, such as the administrative determination of delay compensation under Clause 2.
doctrines: Non-arbitrability of disputes where contractually assigned to administrative authorities
Interpretation of 'final' decisions in contractual clauses
Exclusion of matters from arbitration when alternative dispute resolution mechanisms are provided in the contract

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged whether the enhanced solatium of 30% under the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applied to awards made before April 30, 1982, when appeals against those awards were decided after the amendment came into force.
issues_decided: Whether Section 30(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies to awards made by the Collector or court before April 30, 1982, but where appeals were decided between April 30, 1982 and September 24, 1984.
Whether the phrase 'any such award' in Section 30(2) refers only to awards made between April 30, 1982 and September 24, 1984.
holdings: Section 30(2) of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies only to awards made by the Collector or court between April 30, 1982 and September 24, 1984, and not to earlier awards, even if appeals were decided during that period.

The phrase 'any such award' in Section 30(2) refers restrictively to awards made during the specified period, and the benefit of enhanced solatium does not extend to appeals arising from earlier awards.
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation emphasizing the significance of the word 'such' in limiting legislative intent
Doctrine that general principles like 'appeal as re-hearing' must yield to specific statutory language
Rule against unintended retrospectivity unless clearly expressed by Parliament

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of non-occupation of the shop for over four months; the tenant argued that the non-occupation had ceased before the eviction petition was filed.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can be evicted under Section 13(2)(v) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, if the non-occupation of the premises did not continue until the date of filing the eviction application.
Whether the cessation of occupation under Section 13(2)(v) must be ongoing at the time of filing the eviction petition.
holdings: A tenant who stops business and closes a shop continuously for four months without reasonable cause is liable for eviction under Section 13(2)(v).
The non-occupation of the premises by the tenant must continue until the date of filing the eviction application for the ground under Section 13(2)(v) to be made out.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(v)
doctrines: Interpretation of statutes
Use of external aids in statutory interpretation
Present perfect tense in legislative language

card.dispute: The tenant, Bhagwan Das, challenged the eviction order passed in favor of the landlord, Smt. Jiley Kaur, who sought possession of a shop for her unemployed sons to start a business.
issues_decided: Whether the District Judge erred in finding the landlord's need to be bona fide under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972?
Whether the District Judge properly considered the provisions of Rule 16(2) of the Rules regarding comparative hardship?
Whether the benefit of equal hardship should have been given to the tenant, warranting dismissal of the eviction application?
holdings: The finding of bona fide need by the landlord, based on her sons' unemployment and desire for self-employment, is a factual determination supported by evidence and not interfered with in writ jurisdiction.
The District Judge did not ignore Rule 16(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Rules; he considered all relevant factors, including the tenant’s long occupation and lack of alternative accommodation.
Even if hardships were balanced, the presence of an outweighing circumstance—unemployed educated sons needing the shop for self-employment—justified granting possession to the landlord.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, Rule 16(2)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement of landlord
Comparative hardship in eviction cases
Burden of proof on both parties to establish relative hardship
Judicial notice not permissible on availability of alternative accommodation

card.dispute: The dispute was between coal companies and the State of Bihar over whether the state could legally lease out rights to collect coal slurry deposited on riverbeds and land, which the companies claimed as their waste product from mining operations.
issues_decided: Whether coal slurry escaping from coal mine washeries constitutes a 'mineral' under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Whether the State Government has legislative or executive power to grant leases for collection of such slurry in the absence of central rules
Whether the State's action in leasing slurry collection rights is valid under Section 18 of the Act
Whether the appellants have ownership rights over the land where slurry was deposited
holdings: Coal slurry, as waste from coal washing operations in a mine, falls within the regulatory domain of the Mines and Minerals Act, 1957, and qualifies as a mineral by connection to mining activity.

The State Government lacks legislative competence to regulate or lease slurry where the subject falls under the Union List and Parliament has enacted a regulatory framework, even without framed rules.
Section 18 of the Act empowers the Central Government to regulate disposal of mine waste, including slurry, thereby excluding state authority to grant collection leases.

The appellants are the rightful owners of Plot No. 370 in Sudamdih, having acquired it through statutory notifications and transfers, and the State had no authority to lease slurry collection rights over that land.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Sections 2, 3, 5, 13, 18
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, Sections 4, 7, 9
Constitution of India, Article 245, Article 246, Schedule VII, List I Entry 54, List II Entry 23
doctrines: Legislative competence based on the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution
Doctrine of occupation of the field by Parliament
Estoppel by conduct in pleadings
Executive power co-extensive with legislative power

card.dispute: The tenant and sub-tenant challenged their eviction on grounds of unauthorized subletting and landlord’s bona fide need under the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether subletting done after the expiry of contractual tenancy without fresh written consent of the landlord constitutes a valid ground for eviction under Section 21(1)(f) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
Whether the written consent for subletting given during the contractual tenancy continues to be valid after its expiry.
holdings: Subletting requires fresh written consent of the landlord under the applicable rent law at the time of subletting, even if prior consent was given during the contractual tenancy.

A subletting carried out after the expiry of the contractual tenancy without written consent of the landlord is unlawful and constitutes a valid ground for eviction under Section 21(1)(f) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
provisions: Bangalore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1946, Section 9(2)(iii)
doctrines: Statutory tenancy
Requirement of written consent for subletting
Continuity of landlord consent

card.dispute: The appellant contested the execution of a preemption decree by the respondent, who had acquired the decree through assignment, claiming it was non-transferable and that the original decree-holder had failed to deposit the sale price in time.
issues_decided: Whether a preemption decree is transferable under the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the original decree-holder's delay in depositing the sale price invalidated the decree
Whether the assignee of a preemption decree can maintain execution proceedings
holdings: A right of preemption is personal and generally non-transferable because it defeats the purpose of excluding strangers from co-ownership or neighbourhood.
Despite the technical delay, the deposit made by the decree-holder was valid due to administrative difficulties, and the decree remained enforceable.
An assignee of a preemption decree who is substituted as decree-holder is entitled to execute the decree if the assignment effectively transfers interest in the property.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20 Rule 14
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21 Rule 16
doctrines: Personal nature of preemption rights
Substitution of decree-holder in execution proceedings
Validity of assignment of preemption decrees when coupled with transfer of interest

card.dispute: The assessee company, Bikaner Gypsums Ltd., fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether a payment of Rs. 3 lakhs to shift railway infrastructure within its mining lease area was a deductible revenue expenditure or a non-deductible capital expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the payment of Rs. 3 lakhs made by the assessee for shifting railway structures within its leased mining area was a revenue or capital expenditure.
Whether the benefit derived from the payment was of an enduring nature, amounting to acquisition of a capital asset.
Whether the removal of a restriction on mining operations constitutes acquisition of an advantage of enduring benefit or merely facilitates existing business operations.
holdings: A payment made to remove an obstruction or disability that hampers the profitable operation of an existing business is a revenue expenditure, even if the benefit lasts for several years.
No capital asset is acquired if the expenditure only enables the assessee to exercise pre-existing rights under a mining lease without creating new or additional rights.
The shifting of railway infrastructure, which removed a restriction on mining, did not result in an enduring benefit of a capital nature but merely facilitated ongoing business operations.
doctrines: Distinction between capital and revenue expenditure
Doctrine of enduring benefit
Removal of disability doctrine
Commercial expediency test

card.dispute: The revenue challenged the cancellation of a penalty for concealment of income under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, after the Tribunal and High Court held the assessee had not concealed income despite a significant under-reporting.
issues_decided: Whether the Appellate Tribunal was correct in canceling the penalty under Section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961?
Whether the rebuttable presumption of concealment under the Explanation to Section 271(1)(c) was properly applied when the returned income was less than 80% of the assessed income?
Whether the assessee discharged the burden of proving that the under-reporting did not result from fraud or gross/wilful neglect?
holdings: When the returned income is less than 80% of the assessed income, a rebuttable presumption arises that the assessee concealed income due to fraud or gross/wilful neglect.
The presumption under the Explanation to Section 271(1)(c) can be rebutted only by cogent, relevant, and reliable evidence showing the under-reporting was not due to fraud or neglect.

The Tribunal erred in canceling the penalty without identifying any cogent material to rebut the presumption, and the High Court failed to apply the correct legal principles from CIT v. Mussadilal Ram Bharose.
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption
Burden of proof shifting
Falsity of explanation in tax proceedings
Judicial review of factual findings in tax appeals

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a judgment debtor challenged the validity of a court auction sale conducted during the pendency of their appeal, seeking restitution after the decree was reversed.
issues_decided: Whether a stranger-auction purchaser can retain property bought in court sale after the decree is reversed on appeal.
Whether knowledge of pending appeal affects the bona fide status of an auction purchaser.
Whether restitution under Section 144 CPC applies against a non-party auction purchaser who colluded with the decree holder.
holdings: A stranger-auction purchaser who is aware of the pending appeal against the decree cannot be considered a bona fide purchaser and must return the property if the decree is reversed.
Knowledge of litigation makes a purchaser speculative, not innocent, and removes protection from restitution even if they are not a party to the decree.
Where collusion exists between decree holder and auction purchaser, or where the purchaser lacks independent funds and is a relative, restitution must be granted if the decree is set aside.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 89-91
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution under Section 144 CPC
Bona fide purchaser doctrine
Principle that courts must not cause injury to suitors through their acts

card.dispute: A social organisation alleged environmental pollution by an oil mill and refinery, endangering public health and ecology, and sought judicial intervention under Article 32, while the respondents denied violations and accused the petitioner of ulterior motives.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations of environmental pollution warranted judicial intervention under Article 32?
Whether the petitioner had genuine public interest standing or was misusing the process of law?
Whether there was any violation of the Air and Water Pollution Control Acts by the industrial unit?
holdings: The court found no credible evidence of environmental pollution or statutory violations, as the Pollution Control Board confirmed compliance and no other complaints existed.
Article 32 cannot be invoked without genuine public interest; it must not be misused to settle personal rivalries or for ulterior motives like extortion.
Courts must exercise caution in epistolary petitions to prevent abuse of process and ensure only bona fide fundamental rights violations are entertained.
provisions: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
doctrines: Epistolary jurisdiction
Public interest litigation standing
Judicial circumspection against misuse of constitutional remedies
Balancing environmental protection with economic development

card.dispute: The Chairman of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board challenged the maintainability and merits of a representative suit filed by T.N. Ganapathy, who sought to restrain the Board from enforcing belated supplementary demands for development charges and land compensation from low-income allottees of Ashok Nagar.
issues_decided: Whether a representative suit under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable when the persons represented have different causes of action?
Whether the Housing Board could lawfully make fresh demands after more than a decade for development charges and enhanced land compensation?
holdings: A representative suit under Order 1 Rule 8 CPC is maintainable even if the represented persons have different causes of action, provided they share a common interest or grievance.

The Housing Board could determine and recover enhanced compensation for acquired land, but could not enforce belated demands for development charges beyond the three-year period stipulated in the lease deed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 8
doctrines: Representative suit doctrine
Doctrine of common interest in representative litigation
Doctrine of limitation by stipulated contractual period

card.dispute: The appellants, reversioners under Hindu law, challenged alienations of immovable property on the ground of being contrary to custom, but their right to contest was barred by the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973, which came into force during their pending appeals.
issues_decided: Whether the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973 has retrospective effect and applies to pending proceedings.
Whether the right to contest alienations on the ground of custom survived the 1973 Amendment Act.
Whether a custom confirmed by statute but later abolished revives pre-existing rights under personal law.
holdings: The Amendment Act of 1973 applies to all pending proceedings as it removes a procedural right, not a vested one, and operates as a retroactive rule of decision.
The right to contest alienations on the ground of custom was completely abolished from January 23, 1973, and does not survive in pending cases.
The abolition of the customary right to contest does not affect underlying rights under Hindu law, which remain available as an independent basis for challenge.
provisions: Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, Section 7
Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973
doctrines: Retrospectivity of statutes
Custom as part of law
Statutory abolition of customary rights
Appeal as continuation of suit

card.dispute: Private parties challenged the Jalgaon Municipal Council's decision to partner with a private developer to construct a commercial complex on municipal land, alleging illegality, ultra vires action, and violation of constitutional principles.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Council could legally enter into a contract with a private developer for financing and executing a commercial project under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965.
Whether the agreement involved impermissible delegation of statutory powers under Section 272 of the Act.
Whether the project violated Section 92 of the Act by amounting to an unauthorized disposal of municipal property.
Whether the project was arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution.
holdings: A municipal authority may lawfully enter into an agreement with a private developer for financing and executing a project, provided it does not exceed statutory powers; unconventional methods are permissible if not legally prohibited.

The Municipal Council did not impermissibly delegate its statutory functions under Section 272(1) by authorizing the developer to induct occupiers, as such action was done with council consent and within its powers.

The project did not violate Section 92 of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, as the disposal of occupancy rights by the developer, with council approval, did not constitute an unauthorized lease or disposal of municipal property.
The project was not arbitrary or violative of Article 14, as it was based on a valid policy choice, adopted transparently, and did not demonstrate abuse of power or lack of public accountability.
doctrines: Judicial Review of administrative action requiring a public law element
Reasonableness as a standard in administrative law distinct from tort or constitutional contexts
Deference to policy decisions by governmental instrumentalities within legal bounds
No impermissible delegation of statutory power when done with express statutory authority and consent

card.dispute: The Gram Panchayat sought to recover property tax and other dues from Shree Vallabh Glass Works, a declared sick industrial company, through coercive proceedings, which the company challenged under Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.
issues_decided: Whether recovery proceedings by a local authority for unpaid taxes can proceed against a sick industrial company without the Board's consent under Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985?
Whether the suspension of legal proceedings under Section 22(1) is mandatory during the pendency of revival proceedings?
Whether the limitation period for recovery of dues is extended during the suspension period under Section 22(5)?
holdings: Recovery proceedings against the properties of a sick industrial company, including execution or distress, are automatically suspended under Section 22(1) and cannot proceed without the Board's consent.
The suspension under Section 22(1) applies regardless of the nature of the creditor, including government and local bodies like Gram Panchayats.
The period during which proceedings are suspended under Section 22 is excluded from the limitation period for enforcing recovery rights under Section 22(5).
provisions: The Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 16
The Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 17
The Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22
The Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 25
doctrines: Automatic suspension of legal proceedings during revival process
Discretionary power of the Board to permit recovery
Tolling of limitation during statutory suspension

card.dispute: The appellant company contested the vesting of its eucalyptus plantations in the Kerala government under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, claiming they were not 'private forests' but agricultural crops.
issues_decided: Whether eucalyptus plantations fall within the definition of 'private forest' under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971
Whether the term 'any other agricultural crop' in the Vesting Act includes all tree species, including eucalyptus
Whether judicial interpretation of 'private forest' under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 can be applied to the Vesting Act, 1971
holdings: Eucalyptus plantations are 'private forests' under the Vesting Act and do not qualify as 'any other agricultural crop' because the term excludes non-fruit-bearing trees.
The phrase 'any other agricultural crop' in the Vesting Act does not encompass all tree species; it is limited to crops other than fruit-bearing trees, which are separately mentioned.
Judicial interpretations of 'private forest' under the Kerala Land Reforms Act do not apply to the Vesting Act, as the two statutes are not pari materia and have different objects and scopes.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 2(f)(1)(i)(C)
Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 3(1) and (2)
Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (as amended by Amendment Act 35 of 1969), Section 2(47)(iv)
Madras Preservation of Private Forests Act, 1949
doctrines: Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent
Principle of pari materia in statutory construction
Use of context, preamble, and legislative scheme to interpret definitions
Distinction between agricultural crops and tree plantations in land reform laws

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of a deceased taxpayer and the Commissioner of Wealth Tax over whether leasehold properties, whose leases had expired and were continuing on a month-to-month basis, were taxable assets under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in respect of which the leases had expired and tenancy continued on a month-to-month basis constituted 'assets' under Section 2(e)(v) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957
Whether the interest of the assessee in the properties was available for a period exceeding six years, making it liable to be included in net wealth
holdings: An interest that is precarious and can be terminated at any time under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act does not constitute an interest available for a period exceeding six years, and thus falls outside the definition of 'asset' under Section 2(e)(2)(iii) of the Wealth Tax Act.

The amendment to Section 2(e)(v) in 1964 changed the reference date to 'when the interest vests' but did not alter the requirement that the interest must remain available for more than six years from that date to be taxable.
doctrines: Principle of prospective availability of interest for over six years to constitute a taxable asset
Judicial interpretation of 'is available' as referring to future availability from the relevant vesting date
Doctrine of parliamentary acceptance of judicial interpretation through re-enactment

card.dispute: The petitioner, Elizabeth Antony, opposed the grant of letters of administration to the respondent, Michel Charles John Chown Lengera, claiming a caveatable interest in the estate of Mary Aline Browne based on a will and gift-deed from her daughter Zoe, while the respondent challenged the validity of that interest.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner had a caveatable interest in the estate to justify opposing the grant of letters of administration.
Whether the subsequent probate of Zoe Enid Browne’s will could validate the petitioner’s interest retrospectively.
Whether the findings of the lower courts on caveatable interest would bar the petitioner from later seeking revocation of the probate.
holdings: A person must show a real and substantiated interest in the estate to oppose probate; mere assertions without documentary support do not establish caveatable interest.

A subsequent probate of a will cannot be used to retroactively establish caveatable interest at the time of filing the caveat, especially when the probate was granted without notice to affected parties.
Findings on caveatable interest in probate proceedings are limited to the grant stage and do not bar a party from later seeking revocation of probate under Section 263 if just cause exists.
doctrines: Caveatable interest doctrine
Probate estoppel and its limits
Revocability of probate for just cause
Principle of limited effect of probate findings on title

card.dispute: A displaced person who bought land at a public auction clashed with another displaced person claiming allotment of the same land as a continuous cultivator under rehabilitation rules.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, a bona fide purchaser at auction, was entitled to possession of the entire land despite pending claims by another displaced person.
Whether the second respondent, claiming continuous cultivation since 1956, was entitled to allotment under Rule 34C despite gaps in official records.
Whether the Financial Commissioner could lawfully allot the land to the second respondent after earlier rejections of his claim.
holdings: A bona fide purchaser for value at a public auction should be protected and placed in the position he would have been had the sale been effective from the date of purchase.
Continuous possession for allotment under Rule 34C may be presumed despite missing or mutilated Girdawari records if possession is proven before and after the gap.
Equity permits the division of disputed land between competing claimants where both have legitimate claims and the state’s delay created an unjust situation.
provisions: Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 14
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, Section 34C
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 34C
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 34H
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955, Rule 92
doctrines: Equity
Commutative and distributive justice
Presumption of continuity of possession
Protection of bona fide purchasers

card.dispute: The appellant Hamda Ammal claimed ownership of a property based on a sale deed executed before, but registered after, the respondent Avadiappa obtained an attachment of the property in a money suit against the vendors.
issues_decided: Whether the attachment before judgment of the property, following execution of the sale deed but prior to its registration, affected the rights of the vendee.
Whether the rights of the purchaser under an unregistered sale deed relate back to the date of execution upon registration under the Registration Act.
holdings: A sale transaction completed before the institution of a suit cannot be considered as intended to obstruct or delay decree execution.

Under Section 47 of the Registration Act, the rights of the vendee relate back to the date of execution of the sale deed upon registration, and such rights are protected under Order 38 Rule 10 of the CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 38 Rules 5 and 10
doctrines: Relation back of rights upon registration
Protection of bona fide purchasers under procedural law

card.dispute: The landlords filed an eviction suit against the tenants for shop premises under a tin shade on land owned by the landlords, raising the question of whether the structure constituted a 'building' under the U.P. Rent Act and which court had jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the tin shade structure constitutes a 'building' within the meaning of Section 3(i) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
Whether the lease was of the structure or the open land, depending on who constructed the tin shade
holdings: The question of whether a tin shade supported by wooden pillars constitutes a 'building' under the U.P. Rent Act requires careful consideration and cannot be decided solely based on precedent involving open land leases.

The determination of whether the tenant or landlord constructed the tin shade is essential, as a tenant-constructed shed would mean the lease is of open land, not a building, and thus outside the Rent Act's ambit.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(i)
doctrines: Jurisdictional competence under rent control legislation
Construction of statutory definitions in rent control acts
Importance of factual determination in landlord-tenant disputes

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Board of Revenue's jurisdiction to refer a dispute arising from a suit under Section 229-B of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, to arbitration during a second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Revenue had jurisdiction to refer a dispute in a second appeal under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, to arbitration under Section 203 of the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901.
Whether Section 293 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act limits the applicability of Chapter IX of the Land Revenue Act only to proceedings under Chapter X of the Act.
Whether the difference in terminology between Sections 293 and 339(c) of the Act indicates a legislative intent to restrict the application of the Land Revenue Act's procedural provisions.
holdings: Arbitration is a valid method for resolving disputes under the Zamindari Abolition Act, and the rationale for referring disputes to arbitration applies equally beyond Chapter X proceedings.

Section 293 must be read with Section 339(c), which broadly applies all provisions of the Land Revenue Act to areas covered by the Zamindari Abolition Act, making Chapter IX procedures generally available.

The Board of Revenue had jurisdiction under Section 203 of the Land Revenue Act to refer the second appeal arising from a Section 229-B suit to arbitration, as the procedural provisions of the Land Revenue Act are not limited to Chapter X proceedings.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 229-B
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 293
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 339(c)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 341
U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901, Chapter IX
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Legislative intent
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Arbitration as a mode of dispute resolution

card.dispute: The tenant, Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd., challenged the constitutional validity of a provision in the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966 that denied rent control protection to tenants with annual net income exceeding Rs. 40,000.
issues_decided: Whether Section 1(3)(iii) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, which denies protection to tenants earning more than Rs. 40,000 annually, violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the classification based on annual net income is arbitrary and lacks rational relation to the object of the Act?
holdings: The classification of tenants based on annual net income exceeding or not exceeding Rs. 40,000 is based on an intelligible differentia and satisfies the test of Article 14.
The distinction based on income has a rational nexus with the Act’s objective of protecting economically weaker tenants while encouraging construction by excluding affluent tenants from rent control.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966: Section 1(3)(iii)
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Intelligible differentia and rational nexus test
Presumption of constitutionality of social and economic legislation

card.dispute: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd challenged the High Court's decision to invalidate the appointment of an employee as competent authority for determining land compensation, alleging no bias.
issues_decided: Whether the corporation could file a special leave petition against the High Court's order removing the competent authority
Whether appointing an employee of the corporation as competent authority violates natural justice due to bias
Whether the determination of compensation by the competent authority is administrative or quasi-judicial
Whether the High Court's direction to exclude corporate employees from such appointments is legally justified
holdings: The corporation had an independent cause of grievance and could file a special leave petition despite not being the primary party in the appointment process.
A person is not disqualified from acting as a judge merely due to employment with a party; personal interest in the outcome, not institutional affiliation, determines bias.
The Act does not prohibit appointing a corporation employee as competent authority, and such persons may be better qualified due to experience.
Bias can be alleged only with sufficient material showing a reasonable apprehension of bias, not merely from employment; here, the authority’s personal litigation created such apprehension.
provisions: Petroleum and Minerals Pipeline (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 1962, Sections 2(a), 7, 8, 9, 10
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua)
Reasonable apprehension of bias test
Distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial functions

card.dispute: The appellant (Indira Bai) purchased property and constructed buildings with the respondent's (Nand Kishore's) knowledge; after construction, the respondent claimed pre-emption rights, leading to a legal dispute over whether he was estopped from doing so.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of estoppel can be applied to bar a claim of pre-emption under the Rajasthan Pre-emption Act, 1966, in the absence of notice by the vendor under Section 8?
Whether the conduct of the pre-emptor, who remained silent and assisted the purchaser, amounts to waiver of the right to pre-empt?
Whether the right of pre-emption is a public right such that estoppel cannot operate against it?
holdings: Estoppel can be invoked against a claim of pre-emption when the pre-emptor, with full knowledge of the sale, remains silent and encourages the purchaser to act to their detriment.
The right of pre-emption is a private, statutory right that may be waived by conduct, including acquiescence or failure to act promptly.
The right of pre-emption is not a public or inalienable right; thus, estoppel may apply unless the statute renders the transaction void, which it does not in this case.
doctrines: Doctrine of Estoppel
Doctrine of Waiver by Conduct
Equity, Justice and Good Conscience
Public Policy Exception to Estoppel

card.dispute: The Hissar Improvement Trust appealed against the Punjab and Haryana High Court's decision holding it jointly and severally liable with the State to pay interest on delayed compensation to landowner Smt. Rukmani Devi.
issues_decided: Whether the Hissar Improvement Trust is liable to pay interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for delayed payment of compensation when the amount was deposited with the Collector before possession was taken.
Whether the High Court was justified in impleading the Trust as a respondent and directing it to appear before the Executing Court for determination of interest liability.
holdings: Interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is payable if compensation is not paid or deposited in court before possession, and such liability rests with the Collector and the State, not necessarily with the acquiring authority like the Trust.

The High Court was justified in directing the Executing Court to determine the liability for interest, but the Supreme Court expressed no view on the Trust’s independent liability arising from its agreement with the Government.
doctrines: State liability for compensation under eminent domain
Conditional liability based on timely deposit of compensation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the rejection of his application under Order 21, Rule 90 of the CPC, claiming irregularities in a court auction conducted during insolvency proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had locus standi to file an application under Order 21, Rule 90 after an insolvency petition was filed and adjudication order passed retroactively.
Whether the executing court’s permission to decree-holders to bid at 80% of the upset price without notice to the judgment debtor constituted a material irregularity under Order 21, Rule 72.
Whether the irregularity, if any, caused substantial injury to the appellant warranting setting aside the sale under Order 21, Rule 90.
holdings: It is unnecessary to decide if the appellant lacked locus standi due to insolvency, as the courts below rejected the application on merits.
While notice to the judgment debtor is necessary under Order 21, Rule 72 when reducing the upset price, the provision of such notice is not mandatory in all cases.
An irregularity in auction procedure does not vitiate the sale unless it causes substantial injury to the judgment debtor, which was not proven here.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 72
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 20
doctrines: Substantial injury doctrine in auction irregularities
Relation back of adjudication in insolvency
Locus standi of insolvent judgment debtor in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The Income Tax Officer assessed Smt. N.K. Sarada Thampatty as head of a Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) for three assessment years, but she claimed the HUF had been partitioned and thus could not be taxed as such.
issues_decided: Whether a partition of an HUF effected by a court decree but without physical division of property disrupts the HUF status for income tax assessment purposes?
Whether the Explanation to Section 171 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which requires physical division of property, overrides a partition recognized under Hindu law?
Whether the HUF can be assessed to tax if no income was received by it during the accounting period due to prior partition?
holdings: For tax purposes, a partition of an HUF requires actual physical division of the property by metes and bounds; a mere decree or severance of status does not suffice.

The Explanation to Section 171 of the Income Tax Act assigns a special meaning to 'partition' that prevails over general Hindu law principles, requiring physical division to recognize partition for taxation.
An HUF continues to be assessable even if members have severed status or agreed to divide income, unless there is proof of actual physical partition in accordance with Section 171.
doctrines: Legal fiction in taxation
Special meaning of statutory terms
Revenue protection doctrine

card.dispute: The petitioner sought contempt action against the respondent for failing to hand over possession of requisitioned premises as ordered by the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent committed wilful or deliberate disobedience of the Supreme Court's order dated January 16, 1990, by not handing over possession of the premises?
Whether the ongoing land acquisition proceedings and the status quo order from the Calcutta High Court justified non-compliance with the Supreme Court's direction?
holdings: No contempt was committed because the respondent's failure to hand over possession was not wilful or deliberate, but due to pending acquisition proceedings and a status quo order from the High Court.

Although no contempt was found, the respondent must deposit Rs. 10,000 per month from October 1, 1990, in addition to existing compensation, to account for prolonged possession if the acquisition is later invalidated.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Requisition and Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1947
Land Acquisition (West Bengal Amendment) Act, 1986, Section 49A
doctrines: Wilful disobedience required for contempt
Status quo orders as legal justification for non-compliance
Compensation as equitable remedy in absence of contempt

card.dispute: The appellants claimed title and possession of suit properties in T.S. No. 666/2 based on sale deeds and inheritance, while the respondents contested this, asserting the appellants lacked valid title and that their possession was not adverse.
issues_decided: Whether the interpretation of documents of title raises a substantial question of law warranting interference under Article 136 of the Constitution
Whether the concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and High Court can be disturbed in a special leave petition
Whether the appellants established title to the suit properties through valid sale deeds and delivery
Whether the respondents' possession could be considered adverse possession against the appellants
holdings: Interpretation of a document of title is a question of law, but concurrent factual findings by lower courts are not disturbed unless there is a miscarriage of justice or violation of legal principles.
Concurrent findings of fact based on evidence and documents are binding in appeals by special leave unless they are perverse, based on inadmissible evidence, or suffer from a legal error.
The appellants failed to prove title to T.S. No. 666/2 as the sale deeds and decree did not include the property, and there was no delivery of possession to their father.
Adverse possession requires hostile intent and knowledge by the true owner; since the appellants had no proven title, no adverse possession could arise against them.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 1
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Adverse possession
Delivery of possession under the Transfer of Property Act
Interpretation of documents of title as a question of law

card.dispute: Karnani Properties Ltd. contested whether its real estate and service activities constituted an 'industry' under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and whether a prior settlement could be validly terminated, leading to a fresh adjudication on wages and allowances.
issues_decided: Whether the activities of a real estate company providing various services to tenants constitute 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
Whether a prior settlement under the Act was validly terminated without formal notice
Whether fresh evidence could be admitted before the High Court under Article 226 to challenge an industrial award
Whether the Industrial Tribunal erred in awarding dearness allowance without assessing the employer's capacity to pay
holdings: A real estate company providing systematic services like water, electricity, cleaning, repairs, and lift services to tenants through hired workmen engages in an 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as per the functional test laid down in the Bangalore Water Supply case.

A settlement under Section 2(p) can be terminated without formal notice if the intention to terminate is clearly communicated and inferred from the parties' correspondence, satisfying Section 19(2) requirements.

The High Court, while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226, must generally rely on materials before the Tribunal; fresh evidence should not be admitted unless exceptional circumstances justify it.
The Tribunal's award on dearness allowance does not require remand merely because of non-consideration of post-award financial documents not produced before it.
doctrines: Functional test for 'industry' under Section 2(j) as per Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board v. A. Rajendra Prasad
Notice by conduct or correspondence can imply termination of settlement
Principle of finality of industrial adjudication and limited scope of judicial review under Article 226
No remand for fresh evidence not produced before the Tribunal without justification

card.dispute: The Krishna Kishore Firm, a cinema licensee, fought with the Government of Andhra Pradesh and others over whether its possession of the cinema site was 'lawful' for the purpose of renewing its license under the A.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1955, after the lease expired and a co-owner sold his share to the licensee.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's possession of the cinema site was 'lawful' within the meaning of Rule 11 of the A.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1970, despite not being the legal owner or lessee.
Whether an agreement of sale conferring a future interest in property can render possession 'lawful' for license renewal purposes.
Whether 'lawful possession' requires formal legal title or includes possession supported by a valid, unchallenged agreement.
holdings: A person in physical control of property who acquires an interest through an unchallenged agreement of sale has lawful possession, even if not yet a legal owner or lessee.
Lawful possession under Rule 11 does not require strict legal title; it includes possession that is not forbidden by law and is supported by a valid contractual interest.
The terms 'lawful' and 'legal' are not synonymous; 'lawful' is broader and includes possession that is excusable or authorized, even if not formally legal.
doctrines: Distinction between 'lawful' and 'legal' possession
Possession supported by agreement of sale as lawful
Doctrine of excusable or rightful possession

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) and the respondent-Corporation fought over whether the civil court could determine compensation for acquired land without serving notice to the Corporation, which was to bear the cost of compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-Corporation was entitled to notice under Section 20(c) of the Land Acquisition Act before the reference court determined compensation.
Whether the civil court's award of compensation in the absence of notice to the Corporation was valid and binding.
holdings: Under Section 20(c) of the Land Acquisition Act, when land is acquired for a non-government authority, that authority must be served with notice before the reference court determines compensation.
Failure to serve notice to the Corporation deprived it of a fair opportunity to present its case, rendering the court's judgment illegal and not binding on the Corporation.
doctrines: Principle of audi alteram partem (right to be heard)
Mandatory compliance with statutory notice requirements

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Pramod Kumar Gupta disputed whether a certificate of sale issued by a civil court in an auction sale is subject to duty under Section 147 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether a certificate of sale issued under Order XXI, Rule 94 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 constitutes an 'instrument of sale of immovable property' within the meaning of Section 147 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.
Whether the term 'instrument' in Section 147 has the same meaning as under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899.
holdings: The term 'instrument of sale of immovable property' under Section 147 refers to a document that effects transfer of title, not one that merely records a completed transfer.

A certificate of sale issued under Order XXI, Rule 94, CPC does not create or transfer title; it only declares the effect of a transfer already completed by operation of law, and thus is not an 'instrument of sale' chargeable under Section 147.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rules 92-94
Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Section 2, Clauses (10) and (14)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Transfer of property by operation of law
Distinction between documents effecting transfer and those evidencing transfer

card.dispute: The appellants, former tenants, fought to regain possession of land sold in a court auction for arrears of rent, against purchasers who claimed protection as bona fide buyers under the Kerala Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, as tenants, were entitled to restoration of possession under Section 13(B) of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 despite an intervening suit for possession filed by the auction purchaser.
Whether the deposit made under the earlier Act (9 of 1967) could be treated as valid under Section 13(B) of the later Act (35 of 1969).
Whether Respondents 1 and 2 were bona fide purchasers for value entitled to protection under the Act.
holdings: Tenants dispossessed in execution of a decree for arrears of rent are entitled to restoration of possession under Section 13(B), even if the purchaser later obtained possession via a separate suit for trespass.
An application pending under Section 6 of Act 9 of 1967 continues under Act 35 of 1969, and prior deposit of purchase money with interest suffices for restoration.
Purchasers who acquired property from a court auction purchaser via sale deeds without real consideration are not bona fide purchasers entitled to protection under the Act.
doctrines: Continuity of rights under repealed legislation
Literal interpretation of tenant protection statutes
Burden of proving bona fide purchase

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over tenancy rights in land plots, with the appellants challenging the respondents' claim based on a 1945 deed and asserting their own rights under earlier documents.
issues_decided: Whether the appeals were barred by limitation and if the delay could be condoned under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the respondents had valid tenancy rights under the deed dated 30.7.1945
Whether the appellants could claim tenancy rights under Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act based on the deed of 23.11.1943
holdings: The appeals were time-barred as the delay could not be condoned under Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 because the subsequent proceedings were not pursued in good faith and were legally invalid.

The respondents acquired valid tenancy rights under the deed of 30.7.1945, as confirmed by the Consolidation Officer and upheld by the High Court due to apparent error in the lower authorities' decisions.

Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply because the initial transfer under the 1943 deed was invalid due to a subsisting tenancy, not fraudulent representation, and no estoppel could arise.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, Section 9
doctrines: Estoppel by deed
Good faith in legal proceedings
Apparent error on the face of the record

card.dispute: The tenant challenged whether the legal representatives of a deceased landlord could continue proceedings for recovery of possession under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, after the landlord's death before the tenancy expired.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'landlord' in Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act includes legal representatives of a deceased landlord for the purpose of filing and continuing possession proceedings.
Whether the cause of action for recovery of possession under Section 21 abates upon the death of the landlord who obtained permission for short-term tenancy.
holdings: The term 'landlord' under Section 21 includes legal representatives, as the definition in Section 2(e) refers to the person entitled to receive rent at the time of enforcement, not only the original grantee of permission.
The cause of action for recovery of possession arises from the tenant's failure to vacate after the fixed term, not the landlord's personal need; thus, it survives the landlord's death.
doctrines: Actio personalis moritur cum persona
Strict construction of statutory exceptions
Survival of cause of action

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant under the Tamil Nadu Rent Act for demolition and reconstruction, claiming bona fide need, while the tenant argued the building was structurally sound and the claim was not genuine.
issues_decided: Whether the condition of the building is a decisive factor in determining bona fide requirement under Section 14(1)(b) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Whether a landlord's requirement for demolition and reconstruction can be considered 'immediate purpose' if the building is structurally safe.
Whether the findings of the Rent Controller and appellate authorities could be interfered with in judicial review.
holdings: The condition of the building is a basic and essential requirement under Section 14(1)(b); a structurally sound building does not qualify for demolition under this provision.
The expression 'immediate purpose' denotes a direct and timely connection to demolition, not instant action, but the requirement must be genuine and not remote or secondary.
Findings of fact by a statutory authority are final unless there is a failure to consider relevant evidence, misapplication of law, or perversity, which allows judicial review.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14(1)(b)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Judicial review of administrative findings
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutes
Principle of perversity in factual findings

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership over 1720 acres of forest land granted by his father, the former Raja of Bushahr, and challenged the State's notification declaring the land as government forest under the Himachal Pradesh Private Forest Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government was entitled to issue notifications under Section 4 of the Himachal Pradesh Private Forest Act, 1954, declaring private land as forest land.
Whether the Indian Forest Act, 1927, particularly Section 29, applied to private forests where the government had only managerial control but no proprietary rights.
Whether oral evidence could be admitted under Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act to prove the intention behind a lost document (patta) granting land.
holdings: The State Government was competent to issue notifications under Section 4 of the Himachal Pradesh Private Forest Act, 1954, but erred in annulling them on the incorrect assumption that the land belonged to the State.

Section 29 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, does not apply to private forests where the government has only managerial control and is obligated to account for forest produce, as it lacks independent proprietary entitlement.
Oral evidence is admissible under Section 92 of the Indian Evidence Act to prove the existence and terms of a lost document when its existence is not disputed and secondary evidence is permitted.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Private Forest Act, 1954, Section 2(b), 4, 11
doctrines: Doctrine of proprietary rights vs. managerial control
Doctrine of lapse of treaties and agreements post-independence
Rule against using oral evidence to contradict written documents (with exception for proof of lost documents)

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Ram Chandra Sinoh challenged the inclusion of land gifted by his father before his death in the calculation of his ceiling area under the U.P. Ceiling Act.
issues_decided: Whether the amendments introduced by the U.P. Act 18 of 1973 are retrospective in operation
Whether a gift of land made by a predecessor-in-interest after January 24, 1971, can be ignored in determining the ceiling area of the successor
Whether Section 5(6) of the U.P. Ceiling Act applies to transfers made by someone other than the tenure-holder
holdings: The amendments to the U.P. Ceiling Act apply from June 8, 1973, but the determination of surplus land considers transactions from January 24, 1971.
A transfer of land made after January 24, 1971, which would have been surplus but for the transfer, must be ignored even if made by a predecessor-in-interest.
Section 5(6) applies to any transfer after January 24, 1971, regardless of whether the transferor was the tenure-holder, to prevent evasion of ceiling laws.
provisions: U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 3(9), Section 3(11), Section 5(1), Section 5(6), Section 10(2)
U.P. Act 2 of 1975 (inserting Explanation I and II to Section 5)
doctrines: Doctrine of evasion of fiscal laws
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Presumption against benami or sham transfers

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for unauthorized use of the premises for a printing press and non-payment of rent, while the tenant claimed the premises were let out for running the press and contested the eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the findings of fact by the Appellate Authority in revision under Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949
Whether the tenant changed the user of the premises from residential to commercial by operating a printing press
Whether the landlord established a bona fide requirement of the premises
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction under Section 15(5) to reverse findings of fact if they are improper or illegal, even in revisional jurisdiction.
The lease was granted to the tenant personally for residential use, and using the premises for a printing press constituted a change of user, justifying eviction.
The High Court validly found that the landlord required the premises for her bona fide use, supporting the eviction order.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 11
East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 15
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction in factual findings
Change of user doctrine in tenancy law
Bona fide requirement for personal occupation

card.dispute: The appellant and petitioner challenged the admissibility of their confessional statements made to DRI officials, arguing that such officials are not 'police officers' under Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
issues_decided: Whether officers of the Department of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) invested with powers under Section 53 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 are 'police officers' within the meaning of Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
Whether confessional statements made to DRI officials are admissible in evidence if such officials lack the powers of a police officer under Chapter XII of the CrPC.
holdings: Officers empowered under Section 53 of the NDPS Act, including those from the DRI, are not 'police officers' within the meaning of Section 25 of the Evidence Act because they lack the power to file a charge-sheet under Section 173 of the CrPC.

The investigation by non-police officers under the NDPS Act concludes with a complaint under Section 190 of the CrPC, not a police report under Section 173, and thus such officers do not exercise full investigative powers of a police officer.
provisions: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 25
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 36A(d)
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 52
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 52A
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 53
doctrines: Badku Joti Savant doctrine
Literal interpretation of 'police officer' based on functional powers
Non obstante clause in special statutes

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) sought possession from tenants (respondents) after a fixed-term tenancy ended, but the tenants resisted, claiming the tenancy was invalid due to prior tenancy and fraud on the statute.
issues_decided: Whether a stipulation for rent, even if unpaid, creates a tenancy under the Indian Contract Act and Transfer of Property Act
Whether a permission granted under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act can be challenged collaterally in execution proceedings
Whether the High Court could interfere under Section 39 of the Act on a substantial question of law
Whether suppression of a prior tenancy vitiates permission under Section 21 as a fraud on the statute
holdings: A stipulation for rent, even if not paid due to a returned cheque, is sufficient to create a tenancy if exclusivity of possession is established.
A permission granted under Section 21 is valid until set aside and cannot be challenged collaterally in execution; only a nullity from lack of jurisdiction can be so challenged.
A substantial question of law must not be a settled issue and must have wider legal significance beyond the parties.
Suppression of facts does not render a Section 21 permission void ab initio unless there is lack of inherent jurisdiction; mere factual disputes do not justify collateral attack.
doctrines: Collateral challenge
Substantial question of law
Fraud on the statute
Presumption of validity of administrative orders
Jurisdictional facts and inherent jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellants sought leave to institute a representative suit concerning a public charitable trust without notice to the respondents, who challenged the validity of the ex parte leave granted under Section 92 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether leave to institute a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure must be preceded by notice to the proposed defendants
Whether an order granting leave without notice is void or legally invalid
Whether the grant of leave under Section 92 is an administrative or judicial act
holdings: While it is advisable as a rule of caution to give notice to proposed defendants before granting leave under Section 92, such notice is not a mandatory statutory requirement.
An order granting leave without notice does not render the suit invalid or non-maintainable; the suit remains legally sustainable.
The grant of leave under Section 92 is not a purely administrative act, but the court retains discretion to act without notice to prevent delay and protect public interest.
doctrines: Rule of caution in judicial discretion
Maintainability of suit despite procedural irregularity
Judicial versus administrative function distinction

card.dispute: The auction-purchaser challenged the High Court's decision allowing a judgment-debtor to make a deposit beyond 30 days to set aside a sale of immovable property in execution of a decree.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation for making a deposit under Order XXI Rule 89 of the CPC is 30 days under Rule 92(2) or 60 days under Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Whether Article 127 of the Limitation Act overrides Rule 92(2) of Order XXI regarding the time for deposit.
holdings: The time for making a deposit under Order XXI Rule 89 is strictly 30 days from the date of sale as per Rule 92(2), and this is not affected by Article 127 of the Limitation Act.
Article 127 governs only the period for filing the application (60 days), not the deposit, and does not override Rule 92(2); the two provisions operate independently.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 92(2)
doctrines: Generalia specialibus non derogant
Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent from Statement of Objects and Reasons
Courts cannot add words to statutes or correct perceived omissions

card.dispute: Revenue authorities versus Prafulla Kumar Pati and others over the validity of land sales by Scheduled Caste individuals to non-Scheduled Caste persons without prior permission under the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the caste 'Rajaka' mentioned in the sale deeds is synonymous with 'Dhoba', a notified Scheduled Caste under the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950

Whether the transfer of land by Scheduled Caste individuals to non-Scheduled Caste persons without the Revenue Officer's permission is invalid under Sections 22 and 23 of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960
Whether the High Court erred in quashing the orders of the Revenue Authorities that upheld the inclusion of 'Rajaka' within 'Dhoba'
holdings: The caste 'Rajaka' is a literal synonym for 'Dhoba', which is a notified Scheduled Caste; thus, individuals described as 'Rajaka' in sale deeds but certified as 'Dhoba' belong to a Scheduled Caste.

Land transfers by Scheduled Caste raiyats to non-Scheduled Caste persons without prior written permission of the Revenue Officer are invalid under Section 22, read with Section 23, of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960.
Courts must examine all relevant evidence, including caste certificates and revenue records, to determine Scheduled Caste status when there is a discrepancy in nomenclature.
doctrines: Literal synonymy in caste nomenclature
Burden of proof on transferee to establish validity of transfer under Section 23-B
Judicial duty to interpret Scheduled Caste identity in light of evidence despite nomenclature differences

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the dismissal of his election petition, which was filed after the 45-day limitation period expired during a court vacation, on the grounds that the High Court was closed and filing was justified under the General Clauses Act.
issues_decided: Whether an election petition filed after the 45-day limitation period, which expired during a court vacation, could be filed on the reopening day under Section 10 of the General Clauses Act.
Whether the High Court remained closed during the Sankranthi vacation such that the filing of election petitions was not permissible.
holdings: If a court is closed for vacation and the limitation period expires during that closure, an election petition may be filed on the first reopening day under Section 10 of the General Clauses Act.

The High Court’s vacation notification stating it would remain closed for Sankranthi vacation meant both the court and its registry were closed, and no filing, including election petitions, was permitted during that period.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 81
Representation of the People Act, 1951, Section 86
doctrines: Doctrine of condonation of delay under Section 10 of the General Clauses Act
Strict interpretation of court vacation notifications regarding filing of legal documents

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Sardara Singh (plaintiff) sued to restrain the Punjab State and auction-purchasers from taking possession of his land, arguing the auction sale was void due to non-compliance with payment deadlines.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to deposit the balance of the auction purchase price within the prescribed time rendered the sale void ab initio
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit despite statutory bars under Section 158(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act
holdings: Failure to pay the balance auction amount within the mandatory period under Section 88 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act renders the sale null and void in the eye of law, and no right, title, or interest passes to the defaulting purchaser.

The civil court has jurisdiction to decide a suit challenging possession based on a void sale, as such a claim does not amount to setting aside a sale under the statute and thus falls outside the exclusion under Section 158(2).
provisions: Punjab Land Revenue Act, Section 158(2)(xiv) and (xv)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXI, Rules 84, 85, 86
doctrines: mandatory statutory compliance
jurisdictional exclusion of civil courts
void ab initio for non-compliance with mandatory conditions

card.dispute: Smt. Dularia Devi sued to cancel a sale deed executed through fraud, while the respondents argued the suit was barred by consolidation proceedings under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether a suit to cancel a sale deed is maintainable when consolidation proceedings are pending under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
Whether a transaction induced by fraudulent misrepresentation as to the character of the document is void or merely voidable
holdings: A suit to set aside a voidable document is maintainable in civil court, but a claim that a transaction is void falls within the jurisdiction of consolidation authorities and is barred by Section 49 of the Act.

A transaction where consent is obtained by fraudulent misrepresentation as to the character of the document is void ab initio, as the signer’s mind did not accompany the signature, and such a claim must be adjudicated by consolidation authorities.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 49
doctrines: Distinction between void and voidable transactions
Fraud as to the character of a document renders the transaction void
Doctrine of jurisdictional bar under consolidation statutes

card.dispute: The de facto complainant challenged the High Court's reduction of the conviction from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder and the inadequate sentence awarded to the accused.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the conviction under Section 302 IPC and convicting the accused under Section 304 Part-I IPC?
Whether the sentence of imprisonment already undergone, as awarded by the High Court, was adequate in the circumstances of the case?
holdings: The accused caused injuries intentionally sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, but acted in the exercise of private defence, though they exceeded such right; hence, conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC is correct.
The sentence of imprisonment already undergone was grossly inadequate; to meet the ends of justice, the sentence is enhanced to five years of rigorous imprisonment.
doctrines: Right of private defence and its excess
Proportionality of punishment to the gravity of the offence
Supreme Court's power under Article 136 to interfere with findings of fact in cases of grave injustice

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Gitarani Paul, sued for declaration of title and possession of land purchased from under-raiyats, after defendants disturbed her possession; the dispute centered on whether the suit was maintainable and whether the sale by under-raiyats was valid.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in allowing the second appeal by setting aside concurrent findings of fact not challenged on a new issue not raised in lower courts
Whether the suit for possession was maintainable in the absence of a specific plea regarding the date of dispossession
Whether the sale of rights by under-raiyats under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 requires approval of higher authorities
holdings: The High Court erred in accepting a new issue not raised or argued below and in overturning concurrent findings of fact, which cannot be disturbed in second appeal without a substantial question of law.
The suit for possession was maintainable despite lack of specific date of dispossession, as the plaintiff proved title and wrongful dispossession, which suffices for relief.
There was no pleading or evidence to show that under-raiyats required prior approval to sell their rights; hence, the sale was valid in absence of statutory restriction being pleaded or proved.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact not to be disturbed in second appeal
Substantial question of law under Section 100, CPC
Maintainability of suit for possession based on title and wrongful dispossession

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession of premises, and the tenant challenged the court's jurisdiction, having previously taken an inconsistent stance on jurisdiction in earlier proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res judicata applies to a question of jurisdiction in eviction suits.
Whether a party can be estopped from taking an inconsistent plea regarding the jurisdiction of courts.
holdings: A decision on the jurisdiction of a court, being a pure question of law, does not operate as res judicata in subsequent proceedings between the same parties.
Estoppel cannot apply to confer jurisdiction on a court that lacks it under law, as jurisdiction is a pure question of law and cannot be created by inconsistent pleadings.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Rent Control Act, 1960, Section 3
doctrines: Res judicata
Estoppel
Approbation and reprobation

card.dispute: The appellant, Smt. Mayawanti, sued for specific performance of an alleged contract to purchase property from the respondent, Smt. Kaushalya Devi, who denied the existence of a valid agreement.
issues_decided: Whether there was a valid and enforceable contract between the parties evidenced by Exhibit PW-11/A.
Whether the terms of the alleged agreement were certain and clear enough to warrant specific performance.
Whether the document Exhibit PW-11/A was admissible in evidence or could be relied upon for specific performance.
Whether an oral agreement preceding Exhibit PW-11/A could form the basis for specific performance.
holdings: There was no valid and enforceable contract as the parties were not ad idem and the terms of the agreement were uncertain.
Specific performance cannot be granted unless the contract's stipulations are clear and certain, and the burden to prove this lies on the plaintiff.
The court assumed without deciding that Exhibit PW-11/A could be treated as an agreement, but it was too ambiguous to be specifically enforceable.
An oral agreement not clearly established in evidence cannot support a decree for specific performance.
doctrines: Consensus ad idem
Specific performance as equitable remedy
Judicial discretion in granting specific performance
Burden of proof in contract disputes

card.dispute: The tenant fought the landlord's eviction suit, arguing that non-payment of electricity charges did not constitute default in rent payment under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the additional amount charged for electricity formed part of 'rent' under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
Whether failure to pay electricity charges amounted to default in payment of rent justifying eviction.
holdings: The term 'rent' under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 includes charges for amenities like electricity provided by the landlord as part of the tenancy agreement.
Failure to deposit charges for essential services like electricity constitutes default in rent payment, warranting eviction under the Act.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 8(3)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 34
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 35
doctrines: Interpretation of 'rent' to include service charges to prevent circumvention of tenancy law
Inclusion of amenity charges within statutory rent to uphold legislative intent
