card.dispute: Ratanlal sued the legal representatives of Motilal to set aside a 1959 consent decree dissolving a partnership and regain possession of Goyal Talkies, claiming the decree was a nullity; the defendants argued the suit was barred by res judicata and Order 23 Rule 3A CPC, and that the plaint disclosed no cause of action.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed by Ratanlal was maintainable despite the finality of the 1959 consent decree?
Whether the plaint disclosed a cause of action or raised any triable issue warranting rejection under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC?
Whether the mere issuance of summons bars the court from rejecting a plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC?
holdings: A suit challenging a final consent decree on grounds already adjudicated or based on procedural lapses, without alleging fraud, coercion, or misrepresentation, does not disclose a cause of action and is not maintainable.
The plaint did not disclose any triable issue or cause of action as the grounds of nullity—such as decree against a non-existent party or lack of consideration—were factually and legally untenable.

The issuance of summons does not prevent the court from rejecting a plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC if it manifestly lacks a cause of action; failure to reject earlier does not mandate continuation of frivolous litigation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3A
doctrines: Res judicata
Cause of action
Triable issue
Finality of consent decree

card.dispute: The appellants, purchasers of property in tax recovery auctions, fought with tax and registration authorities over whether they were required to pay stamp duty and registration fees to perfect their title via the sale certificate.
issues_decided: Whether a certificate of sale issued by a Tax Recovery Officer in an income tax recovery auction is liable to stamp duty under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Whether the purchaser of property in a tax recovery sale must get the certificate of sale registered under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the Sub-Registrar is obligated to file a copy of the sale certificate in Book No. 1 upon receipt from the Tax Recovery Officer
holdings: The question of stamp duty liability on a certificate of sale is not decided at this stage and must be adjudicated under Section 31 or 33 of the Stamp Act when the document is presented for registration or relied upon in evidence.
A certificate of sale from a tax recovery auction is not compulsorily registrable under Section 17(2)(xii) of the Registration Act, and registration is not necessary to perfect title.

The Sub-Registrar is statutorily bound under Section 89(4) of the Registration Act read with Rule 21 of the Income Tax (Certificate Proceedings) Rules, 1962, to file the copy of the sale certificate received from the Tax Recovery Officer in Book No. 1.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Schedule I, Article 18
doctrines: Doctrine of lis mota
Principle of statutory interpretation distinguishing registration from filing
Adjudication of stamp duty under the Stamp Act

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh appealed against the High Court's quashing of an FIR filed against P.V. Pavithran, an IPS officer, for alleged corruption, citing inordinate delay in investigation.
issues_decided: Whether inordinate delay in investigation ipso facto warrants quashing of an FIR?
Whether delay in investigation caused grave prejudice to the accused, justifying quashing of proceedings?
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR based on delay, despite the complexity of the case and conduct of the accused?
holdings: Inordinate delay in investigation does not automatically justify quashing of an FIR; each case must be examined on its facts and whether the delay caused grave prejudice to the accused.
Courts must consider factors like the nature of the offence, reasons for delay, and whether it was deliberate or due to the accused's own conduct before quashing proceedings.
The High Court's general proposition that any inordinate delay merits quashing of an FIR is too wide and incorrect in law; the appeal was dismissed on factual grounds, not legal principle.
doctrines: Right to speedy investigation and trial under Article 21
Case-by-case assessment of prejudice due to delay
Judicial restraint in quashing FIRs without showing actual prejudice

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and the Municipal Council contested whether a prior judgment entitled the respondent to construction permission on land reserved for a town planning scheme, or if the scheme could be modified for public purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the earlier High Court judgment operated as constructive res judicata in favour of the respondent.
Whether the Municipal Council was bound by its 1967 resolution permitting construction.
Whether the town planning scheme under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act could be modified for public purposes.
holdings: The earlier High Court judgment did not finally decide the controversy and thus could not operate as res judicata; it merely directed the Municipal Council to decide the application according to law.
The 1967 resolution was not a binding compromise and did not prevent the Municipal Council from later rescinding permission due to changed public needs.
A town planning scheme framed under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act may be modified or substituted to meet evolving public needs, as public purposes are not static.
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Public purpose doctrine
Principle of changing public needs

card.dispute: The State of Haryana sought to evict Khalsa Motors Ltd. from a piece of land it claimed was public property, while Khalsa Motors challenged the eviction order and the applicability of the relevant land recovery law.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could declare the Collector's 1970 eviction order illegal under the 1972 Act after remedies under that Act had been exhausted.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit given the bar under Section 15 of the Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972.
Whether the disputed land qualified as 'public premises' under the 1972 Act.
holdings: The High Court erred in declaring the 1970 eviction order illegal and void, as the validity of such orders must be determined under the 1972 Act through prescribed appellate and writ remedies, not through a civil suit.

Section 15 of the 1972 Act bars civil courts from entertaining suits challenging eviction orders under the Act, and this bar applies even if the order is alleged to be a nullity due to lack of jurisdiction.

The disputed land was rightly determined to be public premises belonging to the State Government under the 1972 Act, and the High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact by lower courts without sufficient basis.
provisions: Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972, Section 15
Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972, Section 5
Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972, Section 9
Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972, Section 18
Haryana Public Premises and Land (Eviction & Land Recovery) Act, 1972, Section 19
doctrines: Bar of jurisdiction of civil courts by special statutes
Finality of administrative findings under special eviction laws
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts not to be lightly overturned in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellants, who submitted the highest bids in a public tender for plots, challenged the rejection of their offers without reasons by a government development authority, alleging arbitrariness and unconstitutionality.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, a government company, qualifies as 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution.
Whether the power to reject the highest tender without assigning reasons is arbitrary and violative of Article 14.
Whether public authorities are required to record and communicate reasons for rejecting the highest bids in public tenders.
holdings: The respondent is an instrumentality of the State under Article 12 and must act within the rule of law, subject to judicial review.
Unfettered power to reject tenders without guidelines or reasons violates Article 14 if it leads to arbitrary action, even in commercial dealings.
Public authorities should record and, unless justified otherwise, communicate reasons for rejecting the highest bids to ensure transparency and accountability.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 113(3)
Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 159
doctrines: Rule of Law
Principle of Judicial Review
Doctrine of Arbitrariness (Article 14)
Right to Know (derived from Freedom of Speech)
State Action under Article 12 (Instrumentality Doctrine)

card.dispute: The landlady sought possession of premises after a limited tenancy expired, but the tenant objected to the validity of the tenancy on grounds of fraud and collusion, which the lower authorities accepted.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant can challenge the validity of a limited tenancy under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act after its expiration?
Whether the Rent Controller can entertain objections to the validity of a limited tenancy at the time of eviction proceedings?
holdings: A tenant must raise objections to the validity of a limited tenancy under Section 21 during the currency of the tenancy; such objections cannot be raised as a defence in eviction proceedings after the tenancy has ended.

The special procedure under Section 21 requires the tenant to approach the Rent Controller promptly upon discovering facts that vitiate the tenancy; belated objections are not maintainable unless the tenant proves he had no prior opportunity to raise them.
doctrines: Doctrine of timely objection under special statutory tenancy
Presumption of regularity in statutory proceedings
Fraud and collusion as limited grounds for challenging tenancy

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed the High Court's acquittal of Moti Ram and others accused in a mass murder case, challenging the reliability of prosecution evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's evidence was reliable enough to sustain convictions in the absence of credible eyewitness testimony.
Whether suspicion against the accused, based on their conduct, was sufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the eyewitness accounts and acquitting the accused.
holdings: The prosecution's evidence was ambulatory, vacillating, and tainted with falsehood, making it unworthy of credence.
Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute for legal proof required to convict an accused.
The High Court rightly acquitted the accused due to the inextricable mix of truth and falsehood in the evidence, which made conviction unsafe.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Separation of grain from chaff in evidence evaluation
Requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged the appellate tribunal's decision that allowed intermediaries to retain land classified as 'tank fisheries' excluded from vesting under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed land was used for pisciculture at the time of vesting (1955–56) so as to qualify for exclusion under Section 6(1)(e) of the Act
Whether the appellate tribunal committed an error in reversing the findings of the primary authority without assigning valid reasons
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition without judicial review
holdings: The crucial date to determine use of land for pisciculture is the vesting period (1955–56); post-vesting use is irrelevant for claiming exclusion under Section 6(1)(e).
An appellate authority must provide independent and cogent reasons for disagreeing with the primary authority; reversal based on conjectures and surmises constitutes a patent error of law.
The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition without reviewing the tribunal’s order, which was based on no evidence and suffered from a manifest legal error.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 2(i)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4(1)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6(1)(e)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 44(2a)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 44(3)
doctrines: Duty to give reasons in quasi-judicial proceedings
Appellate authority must independently justify reversal of findings
Judicial review on grounds of error apparent on the face of record
Presumption against non-production of documentary evidence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a public notice issued under the Delhi Development Act, 1957, which proposed changing land use from residential to recreational, arguing that the notice was not published as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the public notice under Section 44 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 was validly published.
Whether the requirements of Section 44 are mandatory or directory.
holdings: Section 44 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 mandates that notice of proposed modifications to the Master Plan must be published through at least two of the three prescribed methods: affixing in conspicuous places, beat of drum, or advertisement in a local newspaper.

The notice issued was invalid because it relied solely on newspaper publication, failing to comply with the mandatory requirement of using at least two methods, thereby rendering subsequent actions invalid.
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with statutory notice requirements
Literal and contextual interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the bank's right to recover the amount of dishonored cheques from it, claiming the bank was not a 'holder in due course' as it credited the proceeds before collection and had reason to doubt the title of the drawer.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent bank qualifies as a 'holder in due course' under Section 9 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, when it credited the cheque amount to the customer's account before realization of proceeds.
Whether the bank had sufficient cause to believe that there was a defect in the title of the person from whom it derived title to the cheques.
Whether crediting a cheque to a customer's account before clearance converts the bank into a holder for value and affects its status as a holder in due course.
holdings: A banker who credits a cheque to a customer's account before realization can still be a holder in due course if there is an express or implied contract allowing the customer to draw against the amount before clearance.
The bank acted in good faith and without sufficient cause to believe in a defective title, satisfying the requirements for being a holder in due course under Section 9.
Crediting a cheque to an account does not automatically make the bank a holder for value; the true relationship depends on the contract and conduct between the banker and customer.
doctrines: Holder in due course
Good faith and reasonable caution in negotiable instruments
Implied contract in banker-customer relationship
Presumption under Section 118(g) and its rebuttal

card.dispute: The heirs of Tek Chand fought the Union of India over the compensation amount for land acquired in 1959, claiming it should be based on higher development-driven sale prices.
issues_decided: Whether the ability of a landowner to develop land is a relevant factor in determining compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on the developer's potential to enhance land value when fixing compensation.
holdings: Compensation in land acquisition must be based on a hypothetical sale between a willing buyer and willing seller at the time of notification, excluding the specific capacity of a party to develop the land.
The High Court wrongly relied on the developer’s ability to realize higher value; such potential is not a relevant factor in assessing compensation for other landowners in the same area.
doctrines: Willing buyer-willing seller rule
Hypothetical market value principle

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant over non-payment of rent, and the dispute centered on whether the tenant could claim protection under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, by depositing arrears after the ten-year moratorium period ended in 1977.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could avail the benefit of Section 39 of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972, by depositing arrears of rent after the expiry of the ten-year moratorium period in 1977, despite the Act commencing in 1972.
Whether the suit was pending on the date of commencement of the Act, and whether the deposit was made within one month from that date as required by Section 39.
holdings: To claim protection under Section 39 or 40, the suit must have been pending on the date the Act commenced (15th July, 1972), and the tenant must deposit all arrears, interest, and costs within one month from that date.

The benefit of Section 39 is not available if the deposit is made after the expiry of the ten-year moratorium; the legislature intended immediate application of the Act to pending cases, not delayed applicability.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 40
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Consistent interpretation of the same statutory expression
Legislative intent to exclude new buildings from rent control for ten years

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants, but one son (respondent) was not impleaded in the original eviction suit; he later challenged the ex parte decree claiming it was not binding on him.
issues_decided: Whether the ex parte eviction decree passed against some joint tenants is binding on a co-tenant not impleaded in the suit
Whether a co-tenant can be granted exclusive possession when others have equal rights
holdings: An ex parte decree for eviction against some joint tenants is not binding on a co-tenant who was not impleaded in the suit and had an independent tenancy.
Exclusive possession cannot be granted to one tenant when other co-tenants have equal rights; the decree must be set aside and the omitted tenant impleaded.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Principle of constructive res judicata
Joint tenancy and impleadment of necessary parties

card.dispute: The Union of India and others fought against Sukumar Sengupta and others over whether implementing the 1974 and 1982 agreements granting Bangladesh access to the Teen Bigha corridor required constitutional amendment due to cession of Indian territory.
issues_decided: Whether the implementation of the 1974 and 1982 agreements involved cession of Indian territory to Bangladesh requiring constitutional amendment under Article 368
Whether the Ninth Amendment Act, 1960, which was never brought into force, necessitated constitutional changes for the agreements
Whether the Indian courts could direct the legislature or executive to amend laws or the Constitution to implement the agreements
holdings: Granting perpetual right of passage and limited rights over Teen Bigha to Bangladesh does not amount to cession of territory or loss of sovereignty, hence no constitutional amendment was required.
The Ninth Amendment Act, 1960, did not come into force as no appointed day was notified, and thus could not be a basis for requiring further constitutional changes.
Courts cannot direct the legislature or executive to amend laws or the Constitution; such directions violate the separation of powers.
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers
Doctrine of effective occupation in international law
Doctrine of restricted sovereignty through servitudes
Principle of peaceful settlement of boundary disputes

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of 80 cents of land under a sale agreement executed before attachment, while the respondents, as attaching creditors, argued the sale was subject to the attachment.
issues_decided: Whether a sale deed executed after attachment but in pursuance of an agreement for sale entered into before attachment prevails over the attachment.
Whether the attaching creditor gets a better title than the judgment debtor had at the time of attachment.
holdings: An agreement for sale creates a binding obligation on the property, and the attaching creditor takes the property subject to that obligation.
A conveyance in pursuance of a pre-attachment agreement for sale passes good title, and the attaching creditor cannot ignore the contractual obligation to claim absolute rights.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 38, Rule 10
doctrines: Equitable obligation under contract of sale
Priority of prior contractual obligations over attachment
Title subject to existing encumbrances

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over whether a suit challenging an order under the Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953 was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit challenging the Compensation Officer's order under Section 27(4) of the Act is governed by Article 65, 100, or 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Whether an order passed without jurisdiction under a special statute must be formally set aside before a civil court can grant relief.
holdings: If an order under a special statute is passed without jurisdiction, it is a nullity and need not be formally set aside; the suit can proceed under Article 65 of the Limitation Act.
Where the impugned order stands in the plaintiff's way but is void ab initio due to lack of jurisdiction, the suit is not one to set aside the order and thus Articles 100 or 113 do not apply.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, 1953, Section 27(4)
doctrines: Nullity of orders passed without jurisdiction
Applicability of residuary and special limitation periods based on nature of relief sought

card.dispute: The landlord (Mrs.) Roshan Sam fought against B.R. Cotton Mills Ltd. and others over the eviction decree execution being thwarted by a sub-tenancy suit and breach of undertaking.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed civil contempt by giving a false undertaking and obtaining a stay to delay execution of the eviction decree?
Whether the Supreme Court can intervene to ensure justice in a contempt proceeding despite technical deficiencies?
Whether the appellant-landlord should be put in possession of the premises pending final disposal of the sub-tenancy suit?
holdings: Giving an undertaking to the court implying possession, while knowing that possession cannot be handed over, amounts to civil contempt when done with intent to mislead.
The Supreme Court under Article 142(1) can pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, even if technical contempt is not fully established.
The appellant-landlord must be put in possession of the premises during the pendency of the declaratory suit, subject to payment terms, to prevent abuse of process.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947
doctrines: Civil contempt for breach of undertaking given to court
Use of inherent powers under Article 142 for complete justice
Prevention of abuse of legal process to delay execution

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the reduction of compensation and denial of interest from the date of land takeover, claiming entitlement to higher compensation and interest from 1949 instead of 1955.
issues_decided: Whether interest on compensation can be awarded from the date of possession rather than the notification date under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether higher courts can award interest and costs not granted by lower courts under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
holdings: Interest under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act is automatic and mandatory once conditions are met, and does not depend on a claim by the landowner or the existence of a dispute.

Higher courts can award interest and costs under Sections 28 and 27 even if not awarded by lower courts, as these are part of the consolidated compensation deemed to be a decree under Section 23 read with Section 26.
doctrines: Automatic entitlement to interest under fiscal statutes
Power of appellate courts to enhance compensation by including costs and interest
Composite notification doctrine

card.dispute: Property owners challenged the validity of a government order directing the Vijayawada Municipal Council to levy property tax under the old repealed Act, after a new Act had come into force.
issues_decided: Whether the Government Order (G.O. Ms. No. 255 dated 15.6.73) directing levy of property tax under the old Act was valid after the repeal of that Act?
Whether the legislature could retrospectively validate tax assessments made under an allegedly invalid procedure?
Whether Section 4(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975, which validated past tax actions, was constitutionally valid?
holdings: A government order can lawfully direct a municipal council to follow the assessment procedure of a repealed Act as a transitional measure without reviving the repealed law.
The legislature has the power to retrospectively validate tax assessments and collections that were made under procedural irregularities, provided constitutional limits are respected.
Section 4(1) of the Fourth Amendment Act validly amended the new Act to validate past actions taken under government orders, and such validation does not amount to overruling a judicial decision.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, Schedule IX, Rule 12
Andhra Pradesh Municipalities (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975, Section 4(1)
Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Areas) District Municipalities Act, 1920
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective validation
Doctrine of legislative competence in taxation
Doctrine of non-revival of repealed laws
Principle of legal fiction in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Three coparceners contested the denial of their pro-rata share in enhanced compensation after one coparcener alone filed a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act filed by one coparcener entitles other coparceners to enhanced compensation pro-rata even if they did not join the reference.
Whether the absence of an express averment in the reference application that the applicant was acting on behalf of all coparceners bars the others from claiming their share.
holdings: A reference under Section 18 by one coparcener for enhanced compensation benefits all coparceners, who are entitled to receive their pro-rata share in the enhanced award.
An express statement in the reference application that the applicant is acting on behalf of others is not mandatory; necessary implication of joint interest suffices to bind all co-owners.
doctrines: Right of coparceners in joint Hindu family property
Implied representation in litigation by one co-owner
Pro-rata entitlement to compensation in case of joint ownership

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the deduction of development costs from the market value of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing for higher compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in upholding a 20% deduction for development costs in determining compensation?
What was the appropriate market value of the land at the time of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
holdings: The High Court correctly determined compensation based on the market value at the time of notification, not merely by applying a percentage deduction for development costs.
The finding that land prices in the area rose after 1980 and that valuations post-1980 could not be used as a benchmark for 1978–79 acquisitions was valid and supported by evidence.
doctrines: Market value determination at the time of notification
Judicial review of compensation awards based on factual appreciation

card.dispute: The assessee tenant challenged the assessment of capital gains tax on a sum received for relinquishing tenancy rights in favor of a new lessee.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's right of tenancy constituted a capital asset under Section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Whether there was a 'transfer' of the tenancy rights under Section 2(47) of the Act.
Whether the sum of Rs. 1,83,201/- represented taxable capital gains under Section 45(1) for the assessment year 1967-68.
holdings: The Court did not decide this issue as it was not open to reconsider findings already accepted by the Tribunal and not challenged in appeal.
The Court did not decide this issue due to procedural bar; it assumed the transfer without ruling on it.

The Court did not rule on the merits of capital gains computation, as the assessee failed to raise the key argument on actual cost before the High Court or secure its reference, creating a procedural bar.
doctrines: Procedural bar to raising new questions in Supreme Court
Advisory jurisdiction of High Court in tax references
Principle from Commr of Income-tax v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty (no capital gains if cost of acquisition is not ascertainable)

card.dispute: The contractor and the Government of Andhra Pradesh disputed whether the arbitrator had exceeded his jurisdiction by awarding claims not supported by the contract for work on the Nagarjunasagar Dam project.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator exceeded his jurisdiction by deciding claims not within the scope of the contract
Whether a non-speaking award prevents judicial review of jurisdictional errors
Whether extrinsic evidence can be admitted to determine if an arbitrator acted beyond his jurisdiction
Whether manifest disregard of the contract by an arbitrator vitiates the award
holdings: An arbitrator exceeds his jurisdiction if he decides matters outside the contract, and such an award can be set aside even if it is non-speaking.
A dispute about an arbitrator's jurisdiction is external to the award and can be examined using extrinsic evidence, including pleadings and the contract.
An arbitrator derives authority solely from the contract and cannot widen his jurisdiction; acting contrary to the contract amounts to a jurisdictional error.
A deliberate or conscious disregard of the contract by an arbitrator constitutes misconduct and may amount to mala fide action, rendering the award void.
doctrines: Ultra vires arbitration
Manifest disregard of the contract
Jurisdictional error in arbitration
Admissibility of extrinsic evidence to determine jurisdiction

card.dispute: The Bhatinda Improvement Trust challenged the High Court's decision that its 1980 notification sanctioning a development scheme was invalid due to being issued beyond the three-year time limit from the initial 1977 notice.
issues_decided: Whether the three-year time limit in the first proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended in 1984, applies to development schemes under the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922.
Whether provisions of the Land Acquisition Act were incorporated by reference into the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, as they existed in 1922 or as they may be amended later.
holdings: The first proviso to Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including its three-year time limit, applies to notifications under the Punjab Town Improvement Act, 1922, when such notifications are treated as equivalent to those under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act.
Provisions of the Land Acquisition Act are not frozen as of 1922; they apply as amended, unless the incorporating statute shows a contrary intention, which is absent here.
doctrines: Incorporation by reference
Statutory interpretation
Prospective application of amended law

card.dispute: The Cantonment Board and Union of India appealed against the Patna High Court's decision requiring the Officer Commanding-in-Chief to grant a hearing to landowners, lessees, or occupiers before making absolute an order suspending building construction permissions in cantonments.
issues_decided: Whether the Officer Commanding-in-Chief must provide a hearing to the owner, lessee, or occupier of land before making an interim suspension order under Section 52(1)(b) of the Cantonments Act, 1924 absolute
Whether the denial of a hearing to the affected individual violates the principles of natural justice and Article 14 of the Constitution
holdings: The principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem, require that the owner, lessee, or occupier be given a hearing before an order affecting their rights is made absolute, as they are the real aggrieved parties.

The scheme of the Cantonments Act, 1924, read with Article 14, mandates that the right to be heard cannot be limited only to the Cantonment Board, as excluding affected individuals would result in discrimination and civil injustice.
doctrines: Audi alteram partem
Rule of law under Article 14
Principles of natural justice
Reading down of statutory provisions to conform with constitutional rights

card.dispute: The appellant, a father's brother's son of the vendors, claimed the right of pre-emption as an 'other co-sharer' under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, which was denied by lower courts relying on a previous decision.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, being a co-sharer and falling within the erstwhile first three clauses of Section 15(1)(b) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, can claim pre-emption under the 'fourthly' clause after those clauses were struck down as unconstitutional?
Whether the term 'other co-sharers' in Section 15(1)(b), Fourthly, excludes co-sharers who would have fallen under the earlier clauses of the provision?
holdings: The term 'other co-sharers' in Section 15(1)(b), Fourthly, is a residuary provision meant to include all co-sharers not covered by the earlier clauses, and does not exclude those who would have been covered by the now-invalid clauses based on consanguinity.

The interpretation in Jagdish v. Nathi Mal Kejriwal, which excluded such co-sharers, is incorrect and is overruled; co-sharers cannot be denied pre-emption merely because they are related to the vendor in a manner previously classified under struck-down clauses.
doctrines: Doctrine of constitutional validity and severability
Doctrine of ejusdem generis (in interpreting residuary clauses)
Rule against discrimination under Article 14
Pre-emption rights based on co-ownership

card.dispute: The company challenged the vesting of certain land parcels in its estate to the State of Kerala under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting & Assignment) Act, 1971, claiming they were part of its plantations and thus exempt.
issues_decided: Whether abandoned or poorly maintained plantation areas within a company's estate are deemed 'private forests' vested in the State under the 1971 Act?
Whether areas with sparse or scattered plantation crops (like cardamom, coffee, tea) and natural forest growth qualify as exempted plantations under the Act?
Whether the peripheral or enclave location of disputed plots within a larger plantation estate affects their vesting status?

Whether the provisions of the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting & Assignment) Act, 1971, were correctly applied in light of the Madras Preservation of Private Forests Act and the objects of the legislation?
holdings: Abandoned or poorly maintained plantation areas that were originally part of a working plantation and located within the estate enclave do not automatically become 'private forests' vested in the State.

Areas with scattered or sparse plantation crops, even if not fully maintained, may still be considered part of the plantation if evidence shows prior cultivation and intent to replant, and thus are exempt from vesting.

Plots located deep within a plantation estate, even if not currently cultivated, may be treated as enclaves and not subject to vesting if they are surrounded by cultivated areas and part of the operational estate.

The Vesting Act must be interpreted in light of its purpose and in conjunction with prior laws like the Madras Preservation of Private Forests Act; mere presence of forest growth does not override plantation status.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting & Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 2(f)
Kerala Private Forests (Vesting & Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 3
Kerala Private Forests (Vesting & Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 8
Madras Preservation of Private Forests Act
doctrines: Doctrine of purposive interpretation
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Enclave principle in land classification
Presumption against automatic reversion to forest

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of wilful default in rent payment and unauthorized change of user from residential to commercial; the tenant contested both grounds.
issues_decided: Whether non-payment of three months' rent constituted wilful default given the landlord's practice of collecting rent every two to three months
Whether the landlord could raise the issue of change of user after seven years of inaction
holdings: Non-payment of rent for three months does not amount to wilful default when the landlord has consistently accepted rent in two- to three-month instalments.
A landlord who acquiesces to a change of user for seven years cannot later use it as a ground for eviction.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10
doctrines: Wilful default as a distinct ground for eviction
Acquiescence and estoppel in landlord-tenant relations

card.dispute: The dispute was between the appellant (sub-lessee) and the original lessee, along with the Government, over liability for misuse charges and eviction due to non-residential use of premises reserved for residential purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was liable to be evicted for misusing the premises for non-residential purposes.
Whether the High Court could determine misuse charges without a determination by the Controller under Section 14(11) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
holdings: A sub-lessee is liable to eviction for misusing premises contrary to lease conditions, but can avoid eviction by stopping the misuser and paying compensation as directed by the Controller.
Misuse charges must be determined by the Controller under Section 14(11); the High Court cannot unilaterally endorse government claims without such determination.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of eviction provisions
Principle of adjudication by competent authority

card.dispute: The outgoing licensee (Doongaji & Co) challenged the state's takeover of the distillery and the valuation of plant and machinery, claiming it was entitled to restitution until payment was made.
issues_decided: Whether valuation and payment for plant, machinery, and stock before handing over possession to the incoming licensee is mandatory under the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act and licence conditions.
Whether the state's takeover of the distillery without prior payment to the outgoing licensee was illegal.
Whether the outgoing licensee is entitled to restitution of the distillery and warehouses.
holdings: Valuation and payment to the outgoing licensee before handing over possession are not mandatory or a condition precedent under the licence or the Act.
The state's takeover of the distillery on August 28, 1981, and subsequent handover to the incoming licensee was not illegal, even without prior payment.
The outgoing licensee is not entitled to restitution of the distillery or warehouses, as the licence conditions do not require prior payment as a precondition for transfer.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915, Sections 13 and 14
doctrines: Pragmatic interpretation of contractual and statutory provisions
Condition precedent
Finality of government decision in valuation disputes

card.dispute: The landlord sued for possession of a building on grounds of rent default, while the tenant denied the landlord-tenant relationship, claiming co-ownership, and the case raised the issue of civil court jurisdiction after a relevant rent control provision was struck down.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decree eviction when the premises became subject to the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 after the suit was filed due to the invalidation of Section 30(ii)?
Whether the decree passed by the civil court became null and void after the exclusionary clause (Section 30(ii)) was declared unconstitutional?
Whether the procedural conditions under Section 10(1), second proviso, of the Act were mandatory for civil court jurisdiction over eviction?
holdings: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to pass an eviction decree because the statutory conditions under Section 10(1), second proviso, of the Tamil Nadu Act were not met, and the Controller had not determined the tenant’s denial of title as bona fide.

Once Section 30(ii) was struck down, the premises fell under the Act, and the civil court’s continued exercise of jurisdiction without compliance with Section 10 rendered its proceedings coram non judice and the decree a nullity.

The jurisdiction of civil courts in eviction matters is impliedly barred under the Act except in the limited case where the Controller certifies a tenant’s denial of title or claim of permanent tenancy as bona fide.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 14
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 15
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 16
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 30(ii)
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, Section 9
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Order, 1948, Section 16
doctrines: Implied bar on civil court jurisdiction
Coram non judice
Finality of tribunal decisions under special statutes
Doctrine from Dhulabhai v. State of Madhya Pradesh
Effect of declaration of unconstitutionality under Article 14

card.dispute: The company sued its retired employees for failing to vacate company quarters, arguing the offence was continuing and not time-barred, while the employees claimed the complaints were filed beyond the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the offence under Section 630(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 is a continuing offence for the purpose of limitation.
Whether the criminal complaints filed by the company were barred by limitation.
holdings: The offence under Section 630(1)(b) of the Companies Act is a continuing offence as long as the employee wrongfully withholds company property, including quarters, after retirement.
A fresh period of limitation under Section 472 of the CrPC begins each day the offence continues, so the complaints were not time-barred when filed within six months of the continuing possession.
doctrines: Continuing offence doctrine
Legislative intent in penal provisions for company property protection
Interpretation of limitation in relation to ongoing wrongful possession

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the re-opening of their ceiling cases under the Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973, after final orders had been passed, arguing that the state government's power to do so violated constitutional principles.
issues_decided: Whether Section 15 of the Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973, which allows the state government to re-open final ceiling cases, is constitutionally valid?
Whether the power under Section 15 amounts to an encroachment on judicial functions and violates the basic structure of the Constitution?
Whether a final order by a ceiling authority can be re-opened by executive action under the Act?
holdings: Section 15 does not confer arbitrary power; it allows re-opening of cases only when there is a contravention of the Act, new evidence, or prejudice to state interest, and is subject to judicial review.
The power under Section 15 does not violate the basic structure of the Constitution or encroach upon judicial powers, as it operates within statutory limits and safeguards agrarian reform objectives.
Finality of a ceiling order is not absolute; it may be re-opened under Section 15 if justified by specified conditions, without infringing constitutional rights.
provisions: Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973, Section 15
Constitution of India, Entry 18, State List, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Judicial review of executive action
Finality of administrative orders subject to statutory exceptions

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction for the murder of Harnam Singh, arguing that the prosecution's case relied on interested witnesses and lacked reliable corroboration.
issues_decided: Whether the testimony of close relatives of the deceased can be relied upon for conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
Whether non-examination of one of the eyewitnesses (Narain Singh) affects the reliability of the prosecution case.
Whether contradictions in statements under Section 161 CrPC, allegedly fabricated by police, undermine the credibility of eyewitnesses.
Whether the motive in the case was sufficiently established to sustain a conviction.
holdings: The testimony of close relatives of the deceased can be accepted if found credible and corroborated, and being interested witnesses does not automatically render their evidence unreliable.
The non-examination of one eyewitness does not fatally weaken the prosecution case if the remaining witnesses provide consistent and credible testimony.
Contradictions based on fabricated Section 161 statements, created to cover up illegal detentions, have no evidentiary value and do not discredit the eyewitnesses.
The motive, arising from prior enmity over elections and a dispute over sullage water, was sufficient to support the prosecution's case despite being an old grievance.
doctrines: Corroboration of interested witnesses
Falsity of official fabrication as a ground to reject contradictory statements
Sufficiency of motive in circumstantial cases
Reliability of eyewitness identification under adequate lighting

card.dispute: Emc Steel Limited challenged the widow-landlady's right to evict a tenant for her own residence under Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, arguing the benefit should only apply if she became a widow after the premises were let out.
issues_decided: Whether a widow can claim eviction of a tenant under Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, even if she became a widow before the premises were let out.
Whether allowing widows to claim eviction under Section 14-D would lead to abuse of the provision.
holdings: A widow-landlord can claim eviction under Section 14-D regardless of whether she became a widow before or after the premises were let out, as the law grants her a special privilege based on her vulnerable status.
The right under Section 14-D can be exercised only once, requires proof of bona fide need for residence, and is subject to Section 19 of the Act, which prevents abuse of the provision.
doctrines: Special protection for women under Article 15(3)
Statutory interpretation favoring vulnerable groups
Safeguards against abuse of statutory privileges

card.dispute: The appellants were accused of causing the death of the deceased during a land dispute, with the prosecution alleging murder under Section 302 read with 34 IPC, and the defence claiming private defence of person and property.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants participated in the offence and to what extent?
Whether the appellants acted in private defence of person and property?
Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of all appellants beyond reasonable doubt?
holdings: Appellants A2 and A4 participated in the assault using axes and exceeded the right of private defence, thereby committing an offence under Section 304 Part I IPC.
The medical evidence did not support the use of sickles, casting doubt on the involvement of appellants A1 and A3, whose conviction was set aside due to insufficient evidence.
The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of appellants A1 and A3 beyond reasonable doubt, warranting their acquittal.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 34
doctrines: Right of private defence of body and property
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Principle of common intention

card.dispute: The appellant resisted the respondent's suit for specific performance of an agreement to share property purchased at an auction of evacuee land, claiming the agreement was void as opposed to public policy.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties to jointly participate in a public auction and share the purchased property is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 for being opposed to public policy?
Whether the agreement amounted to a fraudulent bid-rigging arrangement that defeats the purpose of public auctions?
holdings: An agreement between bidders to jointly participate in a public auction and share the acquired property is not void under Section 23 if it does not intend to suppress bidding or defraud the public exchequer.

The agreement in question did not aim to peg down the price or prevent fair competition, as multiple bidders participated and the final price was significantly higher than the upset price, so it was not opposed to public policy.
doctrines: Public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Voidness of agreements injurious to public interest or involving fraud
Judicial recognition of variable nature of public policy with changing societal needs

card.dispute: The petitioners, landowners, challenged the acquisition of their land by the Karnataka government, arguing that the acquisition lapsed due to delay in making the award beyond the statutory period under the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the special leave petitions should be dismissed due to non-disclosure of material facts regarding interim stay orders?
Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act due to delay in making the award?
holdings: A petitioner seeking special leave under Article 136 must make full and frank disclosure of material facts; suppression of such facts, especially court-issued stay orders affecting the case, warrants dismissal of the petition.

The existence of interim stay orders issued by courts in prior proceedings was highly material under Section 11-A of the Land Acquisition Act, and their non-disclosure amounted to suppression, justifying rejection of the special leave petitions.
doctrines: Doctrine of suppression of material facts
Discretionary nature of special leave under Article 136
Effect of court stay orders on statutory time limits

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) fought against certain family members of the original tenant (respondents 1–5) over whether they could be evicted under an existing eviction decree, with the respondents claiming independent tenancy rights as part of a joint Hindu family.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a writ petition under Article 226 when an alternative remedy under the Civil Procedure Code was available.
Whether respondents 1 to 5, not being parties to the original eviction suit, could challenge their eviction through a writ petition without first raising their claim in execution proceedings.
holdings: The High Court should not have exercised its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 when an effective alternative remedy was available under Order XXI, Rules 97–106 of the Civil Procedure Code.

A writ petition is not maintainable to determine disputed questions of fact, such as the nature of possession or tenancy rights, which require evidence and are properly adjudicated in civil proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: Order XXI, Rules 97-106
doctrines: Supervisory nature of writ jurisdiction
Availability of an alternative remedy as a bar to invoking Article 226
Prohibition on using writs to bypass civil adjudication of factual disputes

card.dispute: The appellants (mortgagees) and respondents (successors of the mortgagor) disputed whether the respondents' suits for redemption of agricultural land mortgages were barred by limitation and whether civil courts had jurisdiction despite prior dismissal of a redemption application under the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgagor's right of redemption was barred by the dismissal of the application under Section 11 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 and the operation of Section 12 thereof
Whether a suit for redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 is maintainable in civil court despite the provisions of the Punjab-specific Act
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain the redemption suits after the expiry of one year from the dismissal of the application under the 1913 Act
Whether the principles of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 apply in Punjab where the Act is not directly applicable
holdings: The dismissal of a redemption application under Section 11 of the Redemption of Mortgages (Punjab) Act, 1913 does not bar the right to redeem; the bar under Section 12 only prevents re-litigation of matters conclusively decided, not a fresh suit for redemption.

A suit for redemption under Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 is maintainable in civil court, and the civil court retains jurisdiction to grant a decree of redemption despite the 1913 Act.
The one-year limitation in Section 12 of the 1913 Act does not oust civil court jurisdiction; suits filed beyond that period are not automatically barred if within the general limitation period.
Though the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 does not apply directly in Punjab, its principles apply under the doctrine of justice, equity, and good conscience where no contrary statutory law exists.
doctrines: Justice, Equity and Good Conscience
Doctrine of Clogging of Equity of Redemption
Principle of Conclusive Findings in Summary Proceedings
Maintainability of Civil Suits Despite Administrative Remedies

card.dispute: The Goa, Daman and Diu Housing Board challenged arbitration awards favoring Ramakant Darvotkar, claiming the arbitrator failed to record reasons as required by the agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitrator committed misconduct by not recording reasons for the awards as required under clause 25 of the arbitration agreement.
Whether the High Court was justified in remitting the awards to the arbitrator for recording reasons under Section 16(1)(c) of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
Whether the awards could be upheld despite the absence of explicit reasoning in the arbitral awards.
holdings: Failure to record detailed reasons does not amount to misconduct if the arbitrator has considered all issues and reached reasoned conclusions evident from the award.
Remission under Section 16(1)(c) is not justified when there is no apparent illegality affecting the award’s validity and the arbitrator has fairly dealt with the parties’ submissions.
Arbitration awards can be upheld if the reasoning is discernible from the record, even if not formally elaborated, especially where no bias or procedural unfairness is shown.
doctrines: Apparent illegality doctrine under Section 16(1)(c)
Arbitral misconduct requiring proof of procedural unfairness or bias
Reasoned award requirement not absolute if reasoning is inferable from context

card.dispute: Nine accused were tried for murder and attempt to murder; four were acquitted and five convicted, leading to a challenge on the credibility of the prosecution case due to selective acquittals.
issues_decided: Whether the acquittal of four co-accused persons undermines the credibility of the prosecution case against the remaining five accused.
Whether the principle of 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' applies when some accused are acquitted in a multi-accused trial based on witness testimony.
Whether the prosecution failed to explain injuries on members of the complainant party, suggesting concealment of their own wrongdoing.
holdings: The acquittal of some accused does not automatically discredit the prosecution case against others, especially when the trial court applied a cautious approach and reasonable doubt to specific roles.
The maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not applicable merely because some accused were acquitted; the prosecution case as a whole can still be reliable.
The injuries sustained by members of the complainant party were accidental and consistent with the prosecution's version, and there is no evidence of concealment or guilt on their part.
doctrines: falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
benefit of doubt
credibility of prosecution witnesses in multi-accused trials
evaluation of circumstantial evidence and witness consistency

card.dispute: The appellants, tenants in possession of a plot, challenged the validity of a Town Planning Scheme that reconstituted their plot without giving them notice or opportunity as required under Rule 21(3) and (4) of the Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether compliance with Rule 21(3) and (4) of the Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955 is mandatory or directory
Whether a tenant or sub-tenant is a 'person interested' entitled to notice and opportunity under Rule 21(3) and (4)
Whether non-compliance with Rule 21(3) and (4) vitiates the validity of a Town Planning Scheme
Whether the principle of waiver applies to non-receipt of statutory notice under the Rules
holdings: Compliance with Rule 21(3) and (4) is mandatory, as these provisions uphold the principles of natural justice and protect property rights under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
A tenant or sub-tenant in possession of a plot within a Town Planning Scheme is a 'person interested' and entitled to special notice and opportunity to be heard under Rule 21(3) and (4).
Non-compliance with Rule 21(3) and (4) renders the Town Planning Scheme invalid, as it violates fair procedure and affects property rights.
Waiver of the right to notice and hearing only applies if notice was actually issued and the person chose not to respond; non-issuance of notice cannot be waived.
provisions: Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955, Rule 21(3) and (4)
doctrines: Principles of Natural Justice
Mandatory vs. Directory Interpretation of Statutory Provisions
Waiver of Statutory Rights
Fair and Just Procedure under Article 21

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Lakhan Sao (defendant) challenged the decree in favour of Dharamu Chaudhary (plaintiff) who claimed title and possession based on a 1964 sale deed, while the defendant relied on an earlier 1959 deed from the same vendor, alleging the 1959 deed was sham and without consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the burden of proof to show that the 1959 deed was sham and without consideration lay solely on the plaintiff and whether failure to adduce fresh evidence on remand vitiated the appellate finding.
Whether the appellate court erred in considering and relying on the defendant's evidence when the burden was on the plaintiff.
Whether the findings of the appellate court gave rise to a substantial question of law warranting interference under Section 100 CPC.
holdings: In a suit for declaration of title, the burden is initially on the plaintiff to prove that an earlier deed in favour of the defendant is sham and unsupported by consideration.
When both parties adduce evidence, the court may consider the entire record and the rigid rule of burden of proof becomes less significant in reaching a just conclusion.
The appellate court did not commit a legal error by evaluating the defendant's evidence and rejecting it; such an approach does not shift the burden but is part of holistic evidence appreciation.
Findings based on factual appreciation, even if touching on burden, do not amount to a substantial question of law unless there is a wrong conception of law in evaluating evidence.
doctrines: Burden of proof in title suits
Appreciation of evidence when both parties lead proof
Substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC
Farzi Kebala (sham transaction) doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant (mortgagor) challenged the validity of an auction sale of mortgaged property, arguing that a substituted preliminary decree by the High Court rendered the earlier final decree and subsequent auction sale invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the substituted preliminary decree passed by the High Court in appeal overrides the original preliminary and final decrees, thereby invalidating an auction sale conducted under the original final decree.
Whether auction purchasers in execution of a final decree are deemed parties to the suit at the stage of the preliminary decree and have rights to object to a substituted preliminary decree.
Whether the executing court's failure to evaluate the property or incorporate conflicting evaluations in the proclamation of sale invalidates the auction sale.
holdings: The only valid preliminary decree is the one substituted by the High Court; the final decree must conform to it, and any auction sale under a superseded decree is non-est.
Auction purchasers in execution of a final decree are not deemed parties to the suit prior to the passing of the preliminary decree and cannot object to its modification in appeal.
It is unnecessary to decide on alleged procedural violations in the proclamation of sale, as the auction sale is already rendered invalid due to the substituted preliminary decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34, Rules 1-5
doctrines: Doctrine of deemed parties under Section 47 CPC
Doctrine of preliminary and final decrees under Order 34 CPC
Inherent powers of the court under Section 151 CPC and Article 142 Constitution
Principle of complete justice

card.dispute: Two daughters of a Hindu widow disputed over the validity of a gift deed executed by the widow in 1954 in favor of one daughter, and whether the donee could claim absolute ownership or adverse possession against reversioners.
issues_decided: Whether a gift by a Hindu widow of her entire estate prior to 1956 could confer absolute ownership on the donee under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether a female alienee from a Hindu widow could become a limited owner entitled to benefit under Section 14 of the Act
Whether adverse possession by the alienee during the widow's lifetime could defeat reversioners' rights
Whether Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act (estoppel) applies against reversioners in case of a gift by a widow to a reversioner
holdings: A gift by a Hindu widow of her entire estate prior to 1956, made without legal necessity, does not confer absolute ownership on the donee under Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
A female alienee receiving property from a Hindu widow prior to 1956 does not become a limited owner and thus cannot benefit from the enlargement of estate under Section 14(1) of the Act.
Adverse possession by the alienee during the lifetime of the widow cannot extinguish the reversioners' right to claim the property after the widow's death.
Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act does not create estoppel against reversioners where a widow makes a gift of her estate to a reversioner without legal necessity.
doctrines: Limited ownership under Hindu law
Reversionary rights of heirs
Alienation by Hindu widow without legal necessity
Adverse possession against reversioners
Statutory estoppel under Section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a public auction sale of his coffee estate under the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894, on grounds of non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements regarding publication of the place of sale and timely deposit of the balance sale consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the omission to specify the place of sale in the Gazette notification under Section 36 of the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894, renders the sale invalid
Whether the failure to deposit the balance 85% of the sale amount within 30 days from the date of auction, as required under Section 36, invalidates the sale
holdings: The specification of both date and place of sale in the Gazette under Section 36 is mandatory, and omission to publish the place of sale invalidates the sale, as it undermines fair competition and transparency.
The deposit of the balance 85% of the sale consideration within 30 days from the date of auction is mandatory; failure to do so renders the confirmation of sale illegal and void.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894, Section 36
Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894, Forms 7 and 7A
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutory language
Principle of fair and transparent public auction
Forfeiture for non-compliance with mandatory conditions
Statutory form must conform to the law and cannot override substantive provisions

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed over the specific performance of a reconveyance agreement for two plots, which became impossible due to acquisition of the land during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to compensation in lieu of specific performance when the contract becomes impossible to perform due to acquisition of the property during the pendency of the appeal, without fault of the plaintiff?
Whether the High Court could reappreciate evidence and reverse concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC?
Whether a notice returned unserved should be presumed as served under the General Clauses Act, 1897?
holdings: Where a contract becomes impossible of performance without fault of the plaintiff, the court may award compensation in lieu of specific performance under Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, even if not specifically claimed, by amending the plaint.
The High Court in a second appeal can interfere with concurrent findings of fact if they are based on non-consideration of material evidence.
A notice returned as undelivered shall be presumed to have been served under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and its contents can be treated as part of the plaint.
provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 21(2), (4), (5) and Proviso
doctrines: Compensation in lieu of specific performance
Lord Cairn's Act principle and its divergence in Indian law
Re-appreciation of evidence in second appeal
Presumption of service of notice

card.dispute: The Wakf Board appealed a trial court's dismissal of its suit for declaration of right to a passage, but the appeal was dismissed for insufficient court fee, leading to a dispute over whether the appellate court should have allowed correction of the deficiency.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court was justified in dismissing the memorandum of appeal without giving an opportunity to cure the deficiency in court fee.
Whether the Wakf Board was entitled to the same court fee exemption in appeal as in the trial court.
holdings: When an appellate court finds a memorandum of appeal insufficiently stamped, it must first give the appellant an opportunity to pay the deficient court fee within a specified time; only upon failure to comply may the appeal be dismissed.
The court fee exemption available to the Wakf Board at the trial stage did not extend to the appellate stage, as the exemption was specifically limited to the trial.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII
doctrines: Principle of fair procedure in appellate adjudication
Doctrine of statutory interpretation regarding limited application of exemptions

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal heirs of a deceased taxpayer and the Income-Tax Officer over whether reassessment proceedings under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, could be initiated beyond the limitation period to include income after a partial partition was recognized in appeals decided under the earlier 1922 Act.
issues_decided: Whether reassessment proceedings under Section 148 of the 1961 Act could be initiated after the repeal of the 1922 Act to give effect to appellate orders passed under the 1922 Act?
Whether the bar of limitation under Section 149 of the 1961 Act applies to such reassessment proceedings?
Whether Section 150(1) of the 1961 Act applies to lift the limitation bar when reassessment is based on orders passed under the repealed 1922 Act?
holdings: Reassessment proceedings under Section 148 of the 1961 Act can be initiated to give effect to appellate orders passed under the 1922 Act, despite the repeal of the earlier Act.
The limitation period under Section 149 does not apply to such reassessments when they are initiated pursuant to Section 297(2)(d)(ii) of the 1961 Act, read with necessary modifications.

Section 150(1) applies to remove the limitation bar if the reassessment is to give effect to an order on appeal, revision, or reference, even if that order was passed under the 1922 Act, when interpreted with necessary adaptations.
doctrines: Continuity of proceedings under transitory provisions
Liberal and purposive interpretation of statutory provisions
Deeming fiction under statutory interpretation
Avoidance of anomalous or absurd results in interpretation

card.dispute: The assessee Hindu undivided family contested whether part of rental income paid directly to a college by a lessee was taxable to it, and whether income from properties held under a family-created charitable trust was exempt from tax.
issues_decided: Whether the amount of Rs.10,000, which the lessee was required to pay directly to a college under the lease deed, is includible in the assessee's taxable income?

Whether the income from properties purportedly transferred to a charitable trust is exempt under Section 4(3)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, in the absence of a registered conveyance of the properties to trustees?
holdings: The entire rental income, including the Rs.10,000 paid directly to the college, is taxable to the assessee because the obligation was self-imposed and did not constitute a diversion of income at source.

Where the settlor of a trust is also the sole trustee, a registered conveyance is not necessary; a valid trust is created by a declaration showing clear intent to divest beneficial interest, making the income exempt from the assessee's taxation.
doctrines: Diversion of income at source vs. application of income
Self-imposed obligation does not constitute diversion of income
Declaration of trust by settlor as sole trustee without conveyance

card.dispute: The landlord of Masjid Kacha Tank, Nahan, sought to evict tenant Tuffail Mohammed on grounds of dilapidation requiring reconstruction, which the High Court reversed, leading to a dispute over the validity of that revisional order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could re-appreciate evidence and reverse concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in revision under Section 115 of the CPC.
Whether the building was in a dilapidated condition warranting eviction for reconstruction.
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or substitute its view for concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless those findings are perverse or based on non-appreciation of material evidence.

The order of the High Court setting aside the eviction is invalid; the landlord must reconstruct the building within six months of the tenant vacating, and offer the premises back at market rent upon completion.
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Limits of revisional jurisdiction

card.dispute: Landholders challenged the validity of a gift transfer of land made after the appointed date under the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, seeking exemption from ceiling restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether a gift of land made after the appointed date but before the Act came into force is protected under the proviso to Section 5(6) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960?
Whether a gift, being without consideration, can qualify as a transfer for 'adequate consideration' under the proviso?
holdings: A transfer by way of gift does not qualify for protection under the proviso to Section 5(6) of the Act because it lacks adequate consideration.
The term 'adequate consideration' excludes transfers based on love and affection, such as gifts, and requires tangible or monetary consideration to be valid under the proviso.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5(6)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory terms
Exclusion of benami and gratuitous transfers from ceiling law exceptions

card.dispute: Whether legal heirs of a deceased tenant not impleaded in eviction proceedings can contest execution of a decree for eviction on the ground that they were not bound by the decree.
issues_decided: Whether a person not impleaded in eviction proceedings is bound by the decree if their interest was represented by a named party?
Whether an objection to execution under Section 47 CPC can be dismissed without trial of disputed questions of fact?
Whether heirs of a deceased tenant succeed as joint tenants or tenants-in-common in relation to the landlord?
holdings: A person not formally impleaded may still be bound by a decree if their interest was bona fide represented by a party to the litigation, as per Explanation VI to Section 11 CPC.
Where there are disputed questions of fact regarding representation or collusion, the executing court must allow evidence to be led and cannot summarily dismiss the objection.

The nature of succession under the Hindu Succession Act as tenants-in-common governs rights among heirs, but does not determine their collective relationship with the landlord, which depends on factual representation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation VI
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 8
doctrines: Constructive res judicata (Section 11 CPC, Explanation VI)
Principle of representation in litigation
Bona fide representation and mala fide neglect
Tenancy devolution upon death of tenant

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for the murder of Bali and assault on his wife, but challenged the convictions on grounds of unreliable prosecution evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's evidence, including eyewitness accounts, was reliable and sufficient to sustain the conviction?
Whether the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court could be interfered with under Article 136 of the Constitution?
holdings: The evidence of the prosecution witnesses, including the eyewitnesses, was found to be inconsistent, interested, and unworthy of credence, making it unsafe to base a conviction upon.
The Supreme Court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts when the evidence is inherently unreliable and the conviction is based on perversely evaluated testimony.
provisions: Indian Penal Code - Section 302 read with Section 34
Indian Penal Code - Section 304 Part II read with Section 34
Indian Penal Code - Section 323 read with Section 34
doctrines: Danger of relying on interested and inconsistent eyewitness testimony
Principle of perversity in judicial evaluation of evidence
Scope of special leave petition under Article 136 in criminal cases involving factual errors

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Narain Das Jain fought with Agra Nagar Mahapalika over the denial of solatium on compensation awarded for land acquired under the U.P. Town Improvement Act, 1919.
issues_decided: Whether solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory in cases of land acquisition even if not claimed in appeal?
Whether the High Court was obligated to award solatium on the entire compensation, including the amount awarded by the Tribunal, despite no specific claim in grounds of appeal?
Whether the striking down of discriminatory provisions in the U.P. Town Improvement Act entitles landowners to solatium under the Land Acquisition Act?
holdings: Solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act is a statutory right arising automatically upon compulsory acquisition and must be awarded in every case, regardless of claim or demand.
The High Court erred in denying solatium on the Tribunal-awarded amount; once solatium was granted on enhanced compensation, it must apply uniformly to the entire market value determined.

The omission of solatium in acquisitions under the U.P. Town Improvement Act was unconstitutional after Om Prakash v. State of U.P., and claimants are entitled to solatium as per Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 33
doctrines: Mandatory nature of solatium in land acquisition
Automatic application of statutory benefits post-declaration of law
Equality under Article 14 as a basis for extending solatium
Rectification of judicial error under statutory duty

card.dispute: The heirs of a judgment-debtor challenged the validity of an auction sale of agricultural land to a decree-holder firm on the ground that the firm, being non-agriculturist, could not purchase the land under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether a firm can be considered an agriculturist under Section 2(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether the auction sale of agricultural land to the firm was void under Section 63 of the Act due to ceiling limits.
holdings: A firm, though legally inanimate, can be considered an agriculturist if its partners personally cultivate the land, as the term 'agriculturist' depends on the activities of the partners.

The auction sale was void under Section 63 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, as it resulted in the firm's partners—members of a joint family—exceeding the statutory ceiling limit on landholding.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 2(2)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 63
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85-A
doctrines: Doctrine of vicarious cultivation by partners of a firm
Ceiling limit restriction under land reform laws

card.dispute: The appellant, Pancham Dass, claimed hereditary office-holder status to challenge the management of a religious institution under the Sikh Gurdwara Act, 1925, while the SGPC contested his locus standi.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had locus standi to file the petition under Sections 8 and 10 of the Sikh Gurdwara Act, 1925
Whether the Tribunal was justified in allowing amendment to the petition to include the plea of hereditary office-holder status
holdings: A party's concession during arguments that the petitioner is a hereditary office-holder settles the issue of locus standi in his favour.
