An amendment to plead hereditary status, allowed by the Tribunal and accepted by the respondent with costs, cannot be overturned merely on appeal if not challenged at the time.
doctrines: Concession by counsel binding on the party
Principle of acquiescence and waiver
Amendment of pleadings under procedural fairness

card.dispute: The appellant, a member of a Scheduled Tribe, challenged the respondent's possession of land, claiming it was obtained through fraudulent means, while the respondent claimed title via resumption and long possession.
issues_decided: Whether the transfer in this case falls within the ambit of Section 71A of the Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act, particularly under the category of transfer by fraudulent method
Whether the term 'transfer' under Section 71A should be interpreted narrowly as per the Transfer of Property Act or more broadly to include de facto changes in possession
holdings: Section 71A applies to cases where possession has passed from a Scheduled Tribe member to a non-member by fraudulent means, even without a formal legal transfer.
The term 'transfer' under Section 71A must be given a broad and liberal interpretation to fulfill the protective purpose of the Act, covering de facto transfers of possession.
doctrines: Liberal construction of beneficial legislation
Protective legislation for Scheduled Tribes
Fraud vitiates legal transactions

card.dispute: The appellant, a former president of a cooperative housing society, challenged an ex-parte arbitration award directing him to pay damages for alleged irregularities in the purchase of building materials during his tenure.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute regarding financial irregularities by a past managing committee falls under Section 60 (arbitration) or Section 59 (surchage) of the Delhi Co-operative Societies Act, 1972.
Whether Section 60(2) of the Act is exhaustive or merely illustrative in defining disputes relating to the management of a cooperative society.
holdings: Section 60(1), not Section 59, applies to disputes concerning the management of a cooperative society, including financial misconduct by past office-bearers.
Section 60(2) is illustrative and not exhaustive; disputes between a society and its past committee or officers are covered under Section 60(1)(c) even if not specifically listed in sub-section (2).
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)
Principle of statutory interpretation (illustrative vs. exhaustive provisions)

card.dispute: The dispute was between a legatee and the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether the legatee was liable to be taxed on half the income from a deceased grandfather's estate during 1963–1968, or whether the executor should remain liable until full administration was complete.
issues_decided: Whether the estate of the deceased vested in the legatees immediately upon the testator's death, making them liable to income tax on their shares.
Whether the administration of the estate was complete enough for the legatees to be considered owners of the property for tax purposes.
Whether the Income Tax Officer was correct in assessing half the estate's income in the hands of the legatee.
holdings: The estate does not vest in legatees merely upon the death of the testator; vesting occurs only after the executor has completed administration and ascertained the residue.
Until the executor has disposed of all debts, legacies, and assets—including partnership shares—and acknowledged the residue, the legatees do not acquire a vested interest in the estate.
Section 168(3) of the Income Tax Act continues the executor’s liability for taxation until the estate is distributed according to the beneficiaries’ interests.
doctrines: Doctrine of vesting of property in legatees upon completion of administration
Executor's assent implied by conduct under the Succession Act
Residuary estate must be ascertained before vesting in beneficiaries
Continuation of executor's tax liability under Section 168(3) until distribution

card.dispute: The Radhasoami Satsang, Saomi Bagh, Agra, fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether its income from offerings, property, and sales was exempt from taxation under Sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the income of Radhasoami Satsang is entitled to exemption under Sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as charitable or religious trust income
Whether the Revenue could reassess the trust's exempt status after years of non-assessment and accepted refund claims
Whether the principle of finality or quasi-res judicata applies to prevent the Revenue from re-opening a settled question of trust status
holdings: Income of Radhasoami Satsang is exempt under Sections 11 and 12 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 as it is used for religious purposes and the property is held in trust for the community, not for personal benefit of the Satguru.
The Revenue cannot reopen the question of trust status after long-standing acceptance of exemption without a material change in facts or law.
Where a fundamental issue like trust character is settled and not challenged over years, the principle of finality bars re-agitation, even if strict res judicata does not apply to tax assessments.
doctrines: Principle of finality in quasi-judicial proceedings
Exemption for religious and charitable trusts under income tax law
Constructive trust based on usage and dedication to public religious purpose

card.dispute: Rattan Chand Hira Chand sued the legal representatives of Askar Nawaz Jung (Sajjid Yar Jung) to recover Rs.75,000 advanced under an agreement to help secure recognition as heir to Nawab Salar Jung's estate in exchange for a one anna share of the proceeds, but the defendant contested enforcement on grounds of public policy.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement between the parties was void for being opposed to public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Whether the amount advanced under such an agreement is recoverable under Sections 65 or 69 of the Indian Contract Act
holdings: An agreement where one party advances money to help another secure property by using influence with public officials is void as opposed to public policy, as it undermines rule of law and democratic governance.

Money advanced under a void agreement with an unlawful object cannot be recovered under Section 65 or 69 of the Indian Contract Act when the advancement was part of an illegal bargain involving influence over public authorities.
doctrines: Public policy doctrine
Void agreements with unlawful object or consideration
Non-recovery of benefits under void contracts
Judicial development of public policy

card.dispute: Classified landlords (retired armed forces and government employees) sought eviction of tenants for bona fide residence, while tenants resisted, claiming procedural defects and broader defences under general rent control provisions.
issues_decided: Whether tenants can raise defences under Section 14(1)(e) against eviction applications filed under Sections 14B to 14D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the absence of corresponding amendments to Section 25B(4), (5), and the Third Schedule invalidates the summary procedure under Sections 14B to 14D
Whether Section 14(6) or Section 25C(2) applies to eviction applications under Sections 14B to 14D
Whether the requirement of 'bona fide need' must be proved by landlords under Sections 14B to 14D despite its omission in the text
holdings: Tenants cannot raise defences under Section 14(1)(e) when evicted under Sections 14B to 14D; defences must be confined to the specific grounds in those sections.

The summary procedure under Sections 14B to 14D is valid; Section 25B(5) is self-contained and must be interpreted purposively to give effect to legislative intent despite lack of formal amendments to related provisions.
Sections 14(6) and 25C(2) do not apply to evictions under Sections 14B to 14D, which are distinct and exclude transferred landlords or protections meant for Section 14A tenants.
Landlords under Sections 14B to 14D must still prove 'bona fide requirement'; its omission does not negate this essential condition for eviction.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 37 Rule 3
doctrines: Purposive interpretation of statutes
Harmonious construction
Implied reading of words into statutes to avoid nullity
Summary trial in rent control proceedings

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the High Court's decision to grant the landlord possession based on unproven subsequent events without a proper evidentiary hearing.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could grant possession solely on the basis of pleaded subsequent events without proof.
Whether the distinction between pleading and proof of subsequent events must always be maintained in revision proceedings.
Whether the tenant must be given an opportunity to contest or present counter subsequent events.
holdings: A court may consider subsequent events in revision or appeal if they materially affect the relief, but their proof depends on the nature of the allegations and whether they are traversed.
Pleading and proof of subsequent events need not always be in separate stages; unchallenged allegations may be treated as admitted, especially when counsel fails to appear.
Where new subsequent events are raised, the court must ensure a fair opportunity to contest them, and may remit the matter for fresh consideration including evidence if necessary.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 19, Rule 1
doctrines: Cautious cognizance of subsequent events
Admission by non-traverse
Equity and substantial justice over technicalities

card.dispute: Four appellants were convicted for murder and assault under common intention; they appealed, challenging the evidence and applicability of Section 34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution witnesses PWs 10 and 11 could reliably testify about the incident despite not being expected to accompany the deceased.
Whether all four appellants shared a common intention to commit murder under Section 34 IPC.
holdings: The presence of PW-10 at the scene is corroborated by a contemporaneous telegram, making his testimony reliable.

Only the second appellant, Shetan Singh, who inflicted the injuries, is guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC; the others lacked common intention under Section 34 IPC due to absence of prior concert, participation, or incitement.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires prior meeting of minds and active participation or shared intent.
Conviction under Section 34 IPC cannot be based solely on presence; there must be evidence of shared criminal intent.

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a mortgagor challenged the validity of a court-confirmed property sale and the issuance of a sale certificate to an educational institution, claiming they were the true owners and the institution was a trespasser.
issues_decided: Whether the sale certificate issued to Mahila Vidyalaya was void for lack of jurisdiction
Whether the sale in execution proceedings was void and could be ignored by the judgment-debtor without filing a timely challenge
Whether Mahila Vidyalaya was a trespasser despite possession and prior execution of the decree
holdings: A sale certificate issued under Order XXI Rule 94 CPC is a ministerial act, and the executing court had jurisdiction to issue it to Mahila Vidyalaya based on Gopal Rao Mutatkar's bid on its behalf.

Once a sale is confirmed under Order XXI Rule 92 CPC, the auction purchaser's title relates back to the date of sale under Section 65 CPC, and the sale is not void even if the certificate is issued in error.
Mahila Vidyalaya was not a trespasser as it lawfully obtained possession through execution proceedings and had been in possession under a validly issued sale certificate.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 92
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 94
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 95
doctrines: Relation back of title upon confirmation of sale
Ministerial nature of issuing sale certificate
Principle of constructive res judicata and limitation for challenging execution orders
Doctrine of lawful possession defeating claim of true owner

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's interpretation of a will, arguing that the testator's daughter acquired an absolute estate in the property, not merely a life estate.
issues_decided: Whether the daughter under the will acquired an absolute estate or only a life estate in the property.
Whether a contention not raised in the lower courts or in the special leave petition can be raised for the first time during arguments before the Supreme Court.
holdings: The daughter did not acquire an absolute estate because the will's direction that the property pass to her male children after her death negated any intention to confer absolute ownership.
A contention not raised in the lower courts, before the High Court, or in the special leave petition cannot be raised for the first time during arguments in the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Principle of construction of wills: effect should be given to all dispositions if legally possible
Rule against raising new contentions for the first time in appeal

card.dispute: An association of slum dwellers and a resident challenged the state government's re-declaration of a smaller slum area without hearing, alleging violation of natural justice and equality.
issues_decided: Whether the slum dwellers and their representative association have locus standi to challenge the notification redeclaring a smaller slum area.
Whether the government's rescission of the earlier slum area notification and declaration of a smaller area without hearing the affected parties violates the principles of natural justice.
Whether the power to rescind a notification under the Karnataka Slum Areas Act can be exercised using Section 21 of the General Clauses Act.
holdings: The association representing slum dwellers and a resident of the area have locus standi to challenge the notification as they are directly affected.
The government must afford an opportunity of hearing to affected slum dwellers before altering a declared slum clearance area, as denial violates the principle of natural justice.

The power to rescind a notification under the Act can be exercised under Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, but only if done in a manner consistent with the parent statute and principles of natural justice.
provisions: Karnataka Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1973, Sections 3(1) and 11(1)
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Locus standi of affected persons and representative associations
Rule of construction under Section 21 of the General Clauses Act
Implied power to rescind subject to statutory conditions and fairness

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the State of Haryana for a residential-cum-commercial complex, seeking uniform higher compensation based on a comparable sale and prior judicial determination.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded by the High Court for the acquired land was adequate or required enhancement.
Whether belting of land into different compensation zones was justified in this case.
Whether a prior judgment awarding Rs. 42 per sq. yd. in a similar case could be relied upon to enhance compensation.
holdings: The High Court's compensation rates of Rs. 23 and Rs. 16 per sq. yd. for belts A and B were adequate, and no enhancement was warranted.
Belting of land based on quality and location is permissible and need not be discarded merely because it appears haphazard.
A judgment allegedly awarding Rs. 42 per sq. yd. in a similar case cannot be relied upon when it is not placed on record or admitted as evidence.
doctrines: Principle of adequate compensation under the Land Acquisition Act
Requirement of evidence on record to support claims for enhancement
Non-reliance on judicial precedents not formally brought on record

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) fought with the Union of India over whether the Collector should include the entire land acquired in the reference to court for enhanced compensation, despite only part being specified in the application.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector is obligated to include all acquired land in the reference under Section 19 of the Land Acquisition Act, even if the claimant's application under Section 18 specifies only part of it.
Whether the High Court erred in restricting the claim for enhanced compensation to only those lands specified by khasra number in the application.
holdings: The Collector must provide full information about the entire land acquired to the court under Section 19, regardless of whether the claimant specified all khasra numbers, as the state cannot benefit from the claimant's ignorance.

An application under Section 18 seeking enhanced compensation for the whole land acquired cannot be restricted to only specified khasra numbers, especially when the claimant clearly expressed dissatisfaction with the compensation rate for the entire holding.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order X Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIV Rule 3
doctrines: Duty of fair play in administrative action
Protection against technical denial of justice
Implied authority of counsel to make binding statements

card.dispute: The State of Kerala and the Kanan Devan Hills Produce Co. Ltd fought over ownership of timber and the right to levy 'Kuttikanam' (government share) on trees felled in the Concession Area.
issues_decided: Whether the Government had the right to levy Kuttikanam on trees felled in the Concession Area.
Whether the ownership of tree growth and timber in the Concession Area vested with the Government.
Whether a 1932 government letter exempted the company from paying Kuttikanam on non-Royal Trees.
holdings: The Government has the right to levy Kuttikanam as it represents its share of the value of trees, not a tax or fee, and ownership of reserved tree growth vests with the Government.
Rules under the Travancore-Cochin Forest Act, 1951, read with Clause 7 of Exhibit P-64, empower the Government to demand Kuttikanam on timber removed from the Concession Area.
A 1932 letter stating no seigniorage was due on non-Royal Trees applied only to internal use, not removal outside the area, and cannot override the clear terms of the agreement.
doctrines: Doctrine of Governmental proprietary rights over forest growth
Interpretation of contractual clauses in light of statutory rules
Principle that administrative letters cannot override clear statutory or contractual language

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the determination that her predecessor-in-interest held excess vacant land under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, arguing that built-up property constructed before the appointed day should not be included in the calculation.
issues_decided: Whether built-up property existing before the appointed day falls within the definition of 'vacant land' under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, 1976
How 'vacant land' and 'any other land' are to be distinguished for computing ceiling limits
Whether the gap period between the appointed day and the commencement of the Act has legal significance in determining land holdings
holdings: Built-up property constructed or under construction before the appointed day is excluded from the definition of 'vacant land' and cannot be counted toward ceiling limits.
The term 'vacant land' excludes land with buildings commenced before the appointed day, while 'any other land' includes only land with buildings started after that date.
The gap period between the appointed day and the Act's commencement is legally significant, and actions during this time must not defeat the Act's objectives.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(g)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(q)(ii) and (iii)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2A
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(9)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(11)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Schedule 1, Item 15
doctrines: Literal and purposive interpretation of statutes
Distinction between 'vacant land' and 'any other land' based on timing of construction
Presumption against futility in legislative drafting
Protection of rights based on status as of the appointed day

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant's legal representatives over alleged rent arrears and personal requirement; the dispute centered on whether rent sent by money order after non-payment for one month justified eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was in arrears of rent for two months under Section 11(1)(d) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947
Whether remittance of rent by postal money order without prior personal tender is valid under Section 13(1) of the Act
holdings: A tenant is not in arrears for two months if rent for one month is unpaid but rent for another overdue month is remitted by money order before the statutory deadline.
Section 13(1) permits remittance of rent by money order without prior personal tender if the landlord is uncooperative, and such remittance before the due date constitutes valid payment.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 11(1)(d)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)
doctrines: Liberal construction of rent control laws to protect tenants
Substantial compliance over technical defaults

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the execution of a High Court decree that included certain payments in land acquisition compensation, specifically regarding the inclusion of amounts under Section 23(1A) in solatium and interest calculations.
issues_decided: Whether the amount awarded under Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act can be included in the calculation of solatium under Section 23(2)
Whether the interest payable under Section 34 of the Act should be calculated by including the interest component from Section 23(1A)
holdings: The amount under Section 23(1A) is not part of the market value and therefore should not be included in calculating solatium under Section 23(2).
Interest under Section 34 must be calculated on the compensation amount excluding the interest component under Section 23(1A), preventing compounding.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule
Non-compounding of interest in statutory compensation

card.dispute: The mother of a detainee challenged the legality of her son's preventive detention under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, on grounds that his representation against detention was not independently considered by the Central Government as required by Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government must independently consider a detenu's representation against detention even if it is addressed only to the Advisory Board and not directly to the Government.
Whether the mode of addressing the representation affects the constitutional obligation under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
holdings: The detenu's right to have their representation considered by the detaining authority under Article 22(5) is independent of the Advisory Board's consideration and must be fulfilled regardless of whether the representation was addressed to the Government or only to the Board.
The mode of addressing the representation is a matter of form and cannot undermine the constitutional mandate under Article 22(5); the detaining authority must still consider it independently.
provisions: Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988: Section 3, Section 8(c)
doctrines: Dual obligation doctrine in preventive detention
Substance over form in constitutional safeguards
Independent consideration of representation under Article 22(5)

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and defendants contested a suit by Balwant Singh, the grandson of the deceased's brother, claiming inheritance to agricultural land left by a Hindu woman who died intestate, with the State asserting escheat due to no qualified heirs.
issues_decided: Whether property inherited by a Hindu female from her husband devolves under Section 15(1) or Section 15(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the absence of heirs under Section 15(2) results in escheat to the State under Section 29 in the presence of heirs under Section 15(1)
Whether Section 15(2) eliminates other heirs under Section 15(1) or merely alters the order of succession
holdings: Property inherited by a Hindu female from her husband is governed by Section 15(2), which alters the order of succession but does not eliminate heirs under Section 15(1).
Escheat under Section 29 applies only when there is a total absence of heirs under both Section 15(1) and Section 15(2); existence of any heir precludes escheat.
Section 15(2) is not intended to exclude heirs under Section 15(1) entirely but to prioritize heirs of the husband in the absence of issue, ensuring property reverts to its source.
doctrines: Doctrine of escheat
Fiction of devolution under Section 16 Rule 3
Parliamentary intent in succession law
Presumption against total exclusion of heirs

card.dispute: The landlord, Sri Chand Gupta, fought to evict tenants Gulzar Singh and another, claiming sub-letting based on an affidavit by Gulzar Singh's brother claiming tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether an admission made by a tenant's brother in an affidavit before Income Tax authorities is binding on the tenant under Section 18 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact by the Rent Controller and Tribunal.
holdings: An admission made by a tenant's brother in an affidavit is not binding on the tenant under Section 18 of the Evidence Act if the brother has no proprietary, pecuniary, or derivative interest in the property and is not the tenant's authorized agent.
The High Court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact when those findings are based on inadmissible evidence, and it is entitled to reappreciate the evidence on record.
doctrines: Admission under Section 18 of the Indian Evidence Act
Principle of reappreciation of evidence when findings are based on inadmissible evidence
Rule against binding a party by statements of another without legal authority or interest

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu and others sought interim relief from the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal to restrain Karnataka from impounding Cauvery river waters and to secure water releases, which the Tribunal refused on grounds of lack of jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain applications for interim relief without an explicit reference by the Central Government.
Whether the disputes over annual water releases and unilateral impoundment by Karnataka were covered under the original reference to the Tribunal.
holdings: The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide applications for interim relief if such disputes emerge from the original complaint referred by the Central Government under Section 5 of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956.

The reliefs sought by Tamil Nadu in its interim applications fell within the scope of the dispute referred by the Central Government, as the complaint highlighted ongoing injury due to Karnataka's annual water impoundment and delay in resolution.
doctrines: Incidental and ancillary powers of tribunals
Statutory interpretation of tribunal jurisdiction
Exclusion of Supreme Court jurisdiction in inter-State water disputes under Article 262

card.dispute: The appellants, a family under the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms Act, challenged the denial of deductions for a claimed land sale and the invalidation of a partition deed made during a statutory transfer holiday.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of land in 1962 was genuine and excludible from the family holding for ceiling purposes as of 6-4-1960
Whether the partition of family land by registered deed on 29-4-1970 fell within the transfer holiday under Section 21A and thus valid despite Section 23
holdings: The appellants were not given a fair opportunity to prove the genuineness of the 1962 sale; the matter must be remitted for fresh consideration.
Section 21A, with its non obstante clause, may override Section 23 if the partition was by registered instrument within the 15 February 1970 to 2 October 1970 window; the tribunal must examine this.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 3(14)
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 21A
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 23
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 83
doctrines: Non obstante clause supremacy
Remand for fresh consideration due to material irregularity
Prospective application of amended ceiling limits

card.dispute: The landlord, an allottee of a flat under a 99-year sub-lease from a housing cooperative, sought to evict the tenant on grounds of reasonable requirement, but the appellate courts denied relief on the ground that he was not an 'owner' under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant, as a sub-lessee holding a 99-year heritable and transferable sub-lease from a housing cooperative, qualifies as an 'owner' under Section 13(1)(ff) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.
Whether the appellate courts erred in examining the appellant's title when the tenant did not challenge it in the trial court.
holdings: A person holding a heritable and transferable 99-year sub-lease from a housing cooperative society has a superior right in relation to the tenant and qualifies as an 'owner' for the purpose of seeking eviction under Section 13(1)(ff) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.

Where the tenant does not challenge the landlord's title in the trial court, no issue on ownership arises, and appellate courts cannot set aside a decree solely on that ground without remanding for a proper trial on merits.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 2
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(ff)
West Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1983, Sections 87 and 89
doctrines: Definition of ownership as a bundle of rights in rem, not necessarily absolute
Principle that a plaintiff need only prove better title than the defendant
Rule that appellate courts cannot introduce new issues not raised or framed in trial

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued to evict the defendants, who claimed protection under the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, leading to disputes over the applicability of the Act and compliance with its procedural requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants were entitled to the protection of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act based on the timing of the Act's extension to Salem and the commencement of their tenancy.

Whether the defendants' application under Section 9 of the Act, dismissed by the trial court, could be considered pending during the pendency of the appeal despite no separate appeal being filed against its dismissal.
Whether the plaintiffs' failure to issue a notice under Section 11 of the Act rendered the eviction suit non-maintainable.
holdings: The court did not finally decide the applicability of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act due to unclear record on the dates and effects of its extensions and rescission; this issue was remitted to the High Court for clarification.

An application under Section 9 of the Act is an interlocutory application in an eviction suit, and its dismissal can be challenged in an appeal against the final decree without filing a separate appeal, under Section 105 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The High Court erred in holding that the suit failed for lack of a Section 11 notice; the correctness of interlocutory orders, including dismissal of a Section 9 application, can be reviewed in second appeal.
provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, Section 9
Tamil Nadu City Tenants Protection Act, Section 9A
doctrines: Interlocutory order challenge in appeal
Doctrine of deemed pending application during appeal
Remittal for clarification of statutory applicability

card.dispute: The landlord (Surinder Singh Sibia) sought eviction of the tenant (Vijay Kumar Sood) for personal occupation, but the lower courts rejected the application, holding that the landlord had vacated his premises without sufficient cause within five years due to a requisition order.
issues_decided: Whether vacating a building pursuant to a requisition order constitutes 'vacation without sufficient cause' under the second proviso to Section 14(3) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987.
Whether the validity or invalidity of a requisition order affects the determination of 'sufficient cause' under the Rent Control Act.
Whether the landlord's failure to object to the requisition order bars him from claiming sufficient cause for vacation.
holdings: Vacating a building under a requisition order by a competent authority cannot be considered 'without sufficient cause' as the landlord has no choice but to comply with the legal compulsion.
The Rent Control authorities cannot examine the validity or merits of a requisition order; thus, even an erroneous requisition order constitutes sufficient cause for vacation.
The failure to file an objection in requisition proceedings, whether due to legal advice or ignorance, does not negate the existence of sufficient cause for vacation under the Rent Control Act.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Section 14(3), second proviso
Himachal Pradesh Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1972, Section 3(2)
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of 'sufficient cause'
Separation of legal proceedings under different statutes
Non-justiciability of requisition order merits in eviction disputes

card.dispute: The appellant, a deemed purchaser of agricultural land under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, fought against the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal and others over whether a sale of the land by the son of the insane Karta of a Hindu joint family was valid and whether the appellant's statutory right to purchase the land was divested by a notification under Section 88(1)(b) of the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the son of the Karta of a Hindu joint family could validly sell joint family property during the lifetime and insanity of the Karta without court appointment as manager.

Whether a notification under Section 88(1)(b) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, exempting land from Sections 1 to 87 of the Act, divests a tenant's statutory right as a deemed purchaser acquired under Section 32(1).
Whether the second proviso to Section 88(1)(b) applies to a sale made during the subsistence of the landlord's disability when such sale is invalid.
holdings: A son cannot alienate joint family property as manager while the Karta is alive and competent to manage, and if the Karta is incapacitated, a court order under the Indian Lunacy Act is required to appoint a manager; absence of such order renders the sale invalid.

A statutory right of a tenant as a deemed purchaser under Section 32(1) is not divested by a subsequent notification under Section 88(1)(b) if the transfer during the exemption period is invalid, fraudulent, or not bona fide.
The second proviso to Section 88(1)(b) applies only to valid and bona fide transfers; an invalid sale by a person without authority does not trigger the proviso’s protective effect.
provisions: The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32(1)
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-F
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88(1)(b)
The Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 89(2)(b)
doctrines: Statutory protection of deemed purchaser rights
Managerial authority in Hindu Joint Family under Mitakshara law
Bona fide transfer doctrine under statutory exemption
Retrospective operation of exemption notifications with exceptions

card.dispute: The appellant and another contractor disputed the forfeiture of their deposits and demands for further payment under mining contracts, claiming they were unable to commence quarrying due to lack of possession and no-objection clearance from the Flood Control Department.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was at fault for not commencing mining operations under the contract?
Whether the State was justified in forfeiting the security deposit and demanding further payments?
Whether the contractor could be held liable to pay contract money when prevented from performing due to governmental inaction?
holdings: The contractor was not at fault as he was ready and willing to perform but was prevented by the State's failure to provide necessary clearance and possession.
The State was not entitled to forfeit the deposit or demand further payment since the contract became inexecutable due to governmental obstacles beyond the contractor's control.
Where a contract cannot be performed due to the State's failure to coordinate between departments, the contractor cannot be penalized for non-performance.
provisions: Haryana Minerals (Vesting of Rights) Act, 1973, Section 3(1)
Punjab Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964, Rule 28, Rule 33, Rule 61
doctrines: Doctrine of State accountability
Doctrine of contractual fairness
Doctrine of impossibility of performance

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the entitlement of landowners, including Zora Singh, to benefits under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing the provision did not apply because the Collector's award was made before April 30, 1982.
issues_decided: Whether landowners are entitled to the benefit of Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 when the Collector made the award before April 30, 1982 but the Reference Court made its award after September 24, 1984
Whether the applicability of Section 23(1-A) depends on the Collector's award or the Court's award
holdings: Section 23(1-A) applies to cases where the Reference Court makes its award after September 1, 1984, regardless of when the Collector made the award.

The benefit under Section 23(1-A) is available if the Court's award is pending on September 1, 1984, and the use of 'also' in Section 30(1) does not restrict the benefit based solely on the Collector's award date.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Beneficial construction of provisions conferring benefits on claimants

card.dispute: The Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority challenged the High Court's decision invalidating the levy of development fees under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, which the respondents argued lacked statutory authority.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 119(1) and 119(2)(c) of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, authorise the levy and recovery of development fees by the Development Authority.
Whether the power to impose development fees can be implied in the absence of an express statutory provision.
Whether the regulations framing the development fee are ultra vires and unconstitutional under Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
holdings: The power to levy a fee or tax must be expressly conferred by statute and cannot be implied, especially when exercised by a delegated authority.
A delegated body like the Development Authority cannot impose fiscal exactions without clear legislative authorisation, as fiscal powers do not admit of implied or ancillary powers.
The absence of an express provision for levying development fees renders the regulations and demands for such fees unauthorised and illegal, even if the funds are used for development purposes.
provisions: Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 119(1)
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 119(2)(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of strict interpretation of fiscal statutes
Doctrine of no implied powers in fiscal matters
Doctrine of express statutory authorisation for compulsory exaction

card.dispute: The Gram Panchayat and descendants of an inam grantee fought over possession of land and a tank, where the Panchayat claimed vesting of property under the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, and the descendants claimed rights under a ryotwari patta granted under the A.P. Inams Act.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to retry issues already decided under the A.P. Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, particularly regarding the grant of ryotwari patta.
Whether the property in question, including the tank and surrounding land, vests in the Gram Panchayat under the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964.
Whether the descendants of the inam grantee can maintain a suit for possession and mesne profits despite the grant of ryotwari patta for public purpose.
holdings: The Inams Act, 1956 is a complete code that excludes civil court jurisdiction over matters decided by revenue authorities, except on grounds of fraud, misrepresentation, or collusion.

Land and tanks used for public purposes, including those granted as inam for maintaining a tank, vest in the Gram Panchayat under Section 85 of the A.P. Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, overriding individual rights under ryotwari patta.
A suit by descendants of the inam grantee for possession is not maintainable when the ryotwari patta was granted for a public purpose, and the property has vested in the Gram Panchayat.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 64
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 65
Andhra Pradesh Gram Panchayat Act, 1964, Section 85
Andhra Pradesh Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, Section 8
Andhra Pradesh Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1956, Section 7
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in favour of statutory tribunals
Vesting of public property in local self-government bodies
Finality of revenue court decisions under special statutes
Doctrine of res judicata and constructive res judicata in revenue matters
Prescriptive rights of villagers in common property resources

card.dispute: Arvind Mills Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether betterment charges paid under a town planning scheme were deductible as revenue expenditure.
issues_decided: Whether the betterment charges paid by the assessee under the Bombay Town Planning Scheme qualify as revenue expenditure deductible under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Whether the nature of payment (voluntary or compulsory) is relevant in determining if an expenditure is revenue or capital in nature.
Whether an improvement benefiting the business indirectly can render a capital expenditure deductible as revenue expenditure.
holdings: Expenditure is capital if it results in enduring benefit or enhancement of asset value, even if it indirectly aids business operations.
The character of expenditure depends on its nature and effect, not whether it was voluntary or compulsory.
An expenditure lacks direct nexus with day-to-day business if it primarily enhances the value of a capital asset, and thus cannot be treated as revenue expenditure.
doctrines: Direct nexus test for revenue expenditure
Capital vs. revenue expenditure distinction
Enduring benefit doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant, Ashwani Kumar Dhingra, challenged the maintainability of a writ petition to quash a land acquisition notification after having accepted compensation under protest, while his father and brother had earlier successfully challenged the same notification in a separate proceeding.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner can maintain a writ petition to quash a land acquisition notification after accepting compensation under protest, despite not being a party to earlier litigation involving other co-owners?
Whether a writ petition is maintainable on the ground that a previous appellate decision wrongly restricted the quashing of a notification to only some co-owners?
Whether acceptance of compensation under protest preserves the right to challenge the acquisition itself?
holdings: A co-owner who accepts compensation under protest solely to seek enhancement under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act does not preserve the right to later challenge the validity of the acquisition if no such challenge was timely made.
A writ petition cannot be maintained merely on the ground that a previous appellate decision was erroneous or based on a concession between parties, especially after a significant delay.

Acceptance of compensation under protest safeguards the right to seek reference for enhancement under Section 18, but not the right to challenge the acquisition proceedings themselves if not done promptly.
doctrines: Maintainability of writ petitions
Doctrine of co-ownership in land acquisition
Acceptance of compensation under protest
Effect of concession in appellate proceedings
Limitation and laches in writ petitions

card.dispute: The appellant sought a succession certificate for his deceased father's estate, but was denied due to non-production of an estate duty clearance certificate; he argued that assessment proceedings were time-barred under Section 73A of the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings for estate duty assessment are barred after five years from the date of death under Section 73A of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, even if initiated voluntarily by the accountable person.
Whether the requirement to produce a certificate under Section 56(2) of the Act survives when assessment proceedings are time-barred under Section 73A.
Whether 'proceedings for the levy of estate duty' under Section 73A include proceedings under Section 56 and Section 59 of the Act.
holdings: Section 73A bars all proceedings for the levy of estate duty after five years from the date of death, including those initiated by a voluntary return by the accountable person.
The obligation to produce a certificate under Section 56(2) cannot be enforced when the underlying assessment proceedings are time-barred under Section 73A.

The phrase 'proceedings for the levy of any duty' in Section 73A includes proceedings under Sections 56 and 59, as the language is comprehensive and the purpose of the provision is to impose a complete bar after five years.
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutes should not override the clear intent and purpose of the law.
Quia Haeret in Litera Haeret in Cortice: adherence to the strict letter of a statute should not defeat its spirit or object.
Statutory limitation under Section 73A is mandatory and applies uniformly to all assessment proceedings, regardless of initiation method.

card.dispute: The Revenue (C.I.T., Bombay) challenged the allowance of depreciation on roads and drains within the factory premises claimed by Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd.
issues_decided: Whether roads and drains within factory premises qualify as 'buildings' under Section 32 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for claiming depreciation.
Whether the Income Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 1983, which included roads as buildings for depreciation, can retrospectively validate such claims.
holdings: Roads and drains within factory premises are necessary adjuncts to factory buildings and qualify as 'buildings' under Section 32 for depreciation allowance.
Rules validly made under the Act, such as the Income Tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 1983, have the same force as the Act and can clarify existing law without requiring an amendment to the parent Act.
doctrines: Purposive interpretation of tax statutes in favour of the assessee
Principle of consistent administrative interpretation
Validity and binding force of subordinate legislation
Prospective application of statutory amendments unless otherwise indicated

card.dispute: Bhagwan Swaroop was prosecuted for murder and other charges after firing a gun during a land dispute, claiming he acted in private defence to save his father from lathi blows.
issues_decided: Whether Bhagwan Swaroop could claim the right of private defence of his father's person when he fired the gun.
Whether the conviction under Section 307 IPC for attempt to murder was justified based on the evidence.
Whether using his father's licensed firearm in an emergency situation amounted to an offence under Section 25-A of the Arms Act.
holdings: A son can reasonably apprehend danger to his father's life when the father is being beaten with a lathi, even if injuries are later found to be simple, justifying use of lethal force in private defence.
Only one shot was fired and the injury to Shahid was accidental due to pellet spread; hence, conviction under Section 307 IPC was not justified.
Using a licensed firearm belonging to one's father in an urgent situation to prevent grievous harm does not constitute an offence under Section 25-A of the Arms Act.
doctrines: Right of private defence of person
Reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt
Proportionality in self-defence

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed over whether the limitation period for rectifying a symbolic possession beyond the decree terms began in 1963 or only in 1973 when the decree-holder filed a partition suit claiming the excess land.
issues_decided: Whether the limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for filing an application to correct symbolic possession beyond the decree terms commenced on the date of such possession (1963) or later?
Whether the right to apply for restitution accrues only when there is an actual threat of dispossession?
holdings: The right to apply for correction of erroneous symbolic possession accrues when there is an actual threat of dispossession, not from the date the symbolic possession was recorded.
Limitation under Article 137 begins when the decree-holder's action, such as filing a partition suit, threatens the judgment-debtor's possession, not from the date of the erroneous execution act.
doctrines: Accrual of right to sue
Restitution in execution proceedings
Rectification of clerical or arithmetical mistakes under Section 152
Constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The Belgaum Gardeners Cooperative Society sued the State of Karnataka for specific performance of a contract of sale, which was denied by lower courts on the ground that the right to specific performance was not transferred to the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the right to specific performance of the contract of sale (Ext.1) was transferred to the appellants under the sale deed (Ext.2).
Whether the recitals and operative part of the sale deed (Ext.2) effectively conveyed all rights, including future rights, in the suit property.
holdings: The right to specific performance of the contract of sale was transferred to the appellants under the sale deed, as it conveyed all present and future rights in the property.
The operative portion of the sale deed clearly indicated that all rights and privileges were transferred, and the vendor retained no right, thus including the right to re-conveyance.
doctrines: Doctrine of assignment of rights
Doctrine of effective conveyance of future rights

card.dispute: Central Coal Fields Ltd challenged the imposition of motor vehicle tax on dumpers and rockers used in mining, arguing they were not adapted for use on public roads and that the amending tax legislation was invalid.
issues_decided: Whether dumpers and rockers are 'motor vehicles' adapted for use on public roads under the Orissa Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1975
Whether the retrospective amendment to the definition of 'motor vehicle' was valid
holdings: Dumpers and rockers are motor vehicles adapted for use on public roads because they are suitable for road use, as evidenced by their rubber tyres and ability to move on roads at regulated speeds, even if primarily used within mining premises.

The amendment retrospectively expanding the definition of 'motor vehicle' to include such vehicles is valid, as the state legislature has competence to tax vehicles suitable for public road use, including for regulatory and compensatory purposes.
provisions: Bihar and Orissa Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1930, Section 2(c) and Section 6
Orissa Motor Vehicles Tax Act, 1975, Section 2(b) and Section 3(1)
Constitution of India, Entry 57, List II
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Doctrine of legislative competence
Interpretation of 'adapted for use upon roads' as 'suitable for use on roads'

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a civil court had jurisdiction to decide a suit for possession of land claimed as 'abadi land' or whether the issue required referral to a revenue authority under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the nature of the land (agricultural or abadi) without following the procedure under Section 331-A of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950?
Whether the existence of a building and appurtenant land automatically excludes the land from the definition of 'land' under the Act?
Whether the civil court could independently decide the use of land for agricultural purposes without a declaration under Section 143 or 144 of the Act?
holdings: When a suit involves land held by a bhumidhar and the question of its use for agriculture, horticulture, or animal husbandry arises, and no declaration exists under Section 143 or 144, the court must refer the issue to the Assistant Collector under Section 331-A before deciding the suit.
The mere presence of a building and surrounding land does not automatically make it 'abadi land'; the extent and use of the land must be determined under the statutory procedure under the Act.

A civil court cannot independently decide the nature of land use if it falls under the ambit of Section 331-A; doing so amounts to exercising jurisdiction not vested by law, which the High Court must correct in revision.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 2(14)
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 143
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 144
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 331-A
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional error
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (ejusdem generis and harmonious construction)
Presumption of correctness of revenue records

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax appealed against the reduction of penalty for concealment of income by Onkar Saran and Sons, disputing whether the penalty should be determined by the law in force at the time of the original return or the return filed in response to a notice under section 148.
issues_decided: Which law applies to penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961: the law at the time of the original return or the law at the time of the return filed in response to a notice under section 148?
Whether concealment in the original return can form the basis for imposing a penalty even during re-assessment proceedings.
holdings: The law applicable to penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) is the law in force on the date of the original return filed for the assessment year, not the return filed in response to a notice under section 148.
Concealment of income in the original return justifies imposition of penalty during re-assessment, even if the subsequent return discloses the income or no return is filed in response to the notice.
doctrines: Principle of continuity of original return for penalty determination
Re-assessment reopens entire assessment year for correction of escaped income
Penalty based on concealment at earliest point of return filing

card.dispute: The Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Company challenged the legality of cess demands made by the District Board Bhojpur, claiming they were based on the entire net profits of the railway business rather than only the net profits from immovable property as required by law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to quash the demand for arrears of cess for the years 1953-54 to 1966-67 on the ground of illegality, despite delay in filing the writ petition.
Whether the levy of cess based on the net profits of the entire railway undertaking, rather than only on net profits from immovable property, is valid under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880.
Whether the appellant is barred from relief due to laches and delay, having previously litigated the matter on the basis of an unregistered agreement rather than statutory illegality.
holdings: The appellant is entitled to relief despite delay, as the demand for cess was illegal ab initio and based on a mistaken interpretation of the law, and the delay was reasonably explained by pending litigation.
Cess under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880 can only be levied on the net profits derived from immovable property used for the railway, not on the total net profits of the business.

The rule against delay in filing writ petitions is discretionary; where a fundamental right is infringed and the illegality is manifest, relief cannot be denied solely on grounds of laches if there is a reasonable explanation for the delay.
doctrines: Illegality of tax demand based on incorrect interpretation of statutory charging provision
Discretionary nature of laches in writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Principle that tax cannot be levied beyond the authority conferred by statute (Article 265)

card.dispute: The landholders challenged the revisionary order of the Commissioner that increased their landholding extent and directed surrender of surplus land under the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether an order determining a holding below the ceiling limit under Sections 14–20 of the Act is appealable?
Whether the State Government can exercise suo motu revision under Section 45(2) of the Act despite a non-appealable order?
Whether a prior determination of holding operates as res judicata in subsequent proceedings for surplus land?
Whether land acquired by alleged exchange, when disbelieved, must be excluded from the holding if no other basis of acquisition is claimed?
holdings: An order under Sections 14–20 determining that a person's holding is below the ceiling limit is not a 'declaration' under Section 21 and is not appealable.
The State Government can exercise suo motu revision under Section 45(2) even after an appeal, if the order is not appealable in law, as no bar arises from an incompetent appeal.
A prior order determining the extent of holding does not operate as res judicata in later proceedings for surplus land, though it remains relevant.
If the theory of land acquisition by exchange is disbelieved and no other basis of ownership is alleged, the land in question must be excluded from the holding.
provisions: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 3
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 5
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 9
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Sections 14 to 20
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 21
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 33
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling and Holdings) Act, 1961, Section 45
doctrines: Res judicata
Suo motu revisionary power
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Legislative intent in ceiling laws

card.dispute: The dispute was between Jeet Singh and his first wife, who sought to exclude certain land transferred to his second wife from his landholding under the Ceiling Act, claiming it was part of a judicial separation settlement via a Nyaya Panchayat.
issues_decided: Whether a wife can be considered 'judicially separated' under Section 2(7) of the U.P. Land Reforms and Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1973 based on a compromise recorded by a Nyaya Panchayat?
Whether the Nyaya Panchayat has jurisdiction to effect a judicial separation between spouses?
holdings: A wife is 'judicially separated' only if the separation results from an order of a competent court; a compromise before a Nyaya Panchayat does not qualify as judicial separation.

The Nyaya Panchayat lacks jurisdiction under the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 to decide matrimonial disputes or grant judicial separation, and thus its consent order cannot confer benefits under the Ceiling Act.
provisions: U.P. Land Reforms and Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1973, Section 2(7)
doctrines: Judicial separation requires intervention of a court of law
Statutory interpretation of 'judicially' as requiring a formal judicial order

card.dispute: The landlords sued for possession of the premises on grounds of alleged non-receipt of termination notice and default in rent payment, which the tenants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the termination notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was properly served when sent by registered post and one acknowledgment receipt was available.
Whether the tenants committed persistent default in rent payment justifying a decree for possession under Section 13(1)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act.
holdings: Service of notice sent by registered post to a company tenant creates a presumption of service, which is not rebutted merely by a director denying receipt; the burden shifts to the tenant to disprove service, which was not done here.

Persistent default in rent payment during the pendency of the suit and appeal, including non-deposit of arrears on the first hearing date, justifies a decree for possession under the Bombay Rents Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(b)
doctrines: Presumption of service of registered post notices
Rebuttal of presumption requiring credible evidence beyond mere denial
Persistent default in rent as grounds for eviction

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant from a shop and verandah, claiming bona fide need to use the premises for his son's business, leading to a dispute over whether partial eviction could satisfy the need.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below erred in ordering full eviction without considering partial eviction under the proviso to Section 11(1)(c) of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982?
Whether a presumption that single-room premises cannot be partially evicted is legally valid?
holdings: When a landlord's bona fide need is proved, the court must consider whether partial eviction would substantially satisfy that need before ordering full eviction.
No legal presumption exists that a single-room premises is indivisible; divisibility depends on facts, including size and practicality of division.
provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1982, Section 11(1)(c) proviso
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Presumption against impracticability rebutted by factual inquiry

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the conferment of occupancy rights to tenants under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, arguing that the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, rendered the state law inoperative in urban agglomeration areas.
issues_decided: Whether the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, particularly Chapter III, is ultra vires due to legislative incompetence after the state's resolution under Article 252 of the Constitution empowered Parliament to legislate on urban land ceiling.
Whether there is a conflict between the Karnataka Land Reforms Act and the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, such that the state law is rendered inoperative.
holdings: The resolution under Article 252 transferred only the power to impose a ceiling on urban immovable property to Parliament, not other aspects of land regulation like landlord-tenant relations or conferment of occupancy rights, which remain within the State's legislative competence.

There is no conflict between the two laws as they deal with distinct subjects: the Central Act on urban land ceiling and the State Act on agrarian reforms and tenancy rights; hence, the Karnataka Land Reforms Act remains valid and operative.
provisions: Constitution of India, Schedule VII, List II, Entry 18
Karnataka Land Reforms Act, as amended in 1974
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of harmonious construction
Welfare legislation interpretation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants on grounds of habitual default in rent payment and bona fide need, which the tenants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants were 'habitually in arrears' with rent under Clause 13(3)(ii) of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
Whether the landlord established a bona fide need for the premises for residence and clinic under Clause 13(3)(vi)
Whether the High Court's remand for determining extent of landlord's need was justified
Whether the Letters Patent Appeal was maintainable against a writ order under Articles 226 and 227
holdings: A tenant is not 'habitually in arrears' if rent is regularly accepted by the landlord despite delayed payments, especially when an established practice of lump-sum or delayed payment exists over years.
A landlord must prove ownership and genuine need for eviction on bona fide grounds, and failure by lower courts to recognize such evidence is erroneous.
Remanding the case to the Rent Controller to determine the extent of the landlord’s need and to allow amendment of pleadings and evidence is a valid exercise of judicial discretion.
An order by a Single Judge under Article 226 is appealable via Letters Patent Appeal, and the Division Bench has jurisdiction to hear it.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(ii)
C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13(3)(vi)
doctrines: Doctrine of habitual default in rent payment
Doctrine of bona fide need in landlord-tenant law
Doctrine of implied agreement by conduct
Doctrine of estoppel by practice in rent collection

card.dispute: The appellants (Mohan Pandey and another) challenged the High Court's exercise of writ jurisdiction to enforce a private property right claimed by the respondent (Usha Rani Rajgaria) against them, including a direction to remove grills blocking access to a backyard.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can exercise its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to enforce a private right over immovable property between private individuals.
Whether the remedy of a civil suit is primary and writ jurisdiction inappropriate where disputes involve property rights and pending litigation.
holdings: The High Court should not exercise its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to settle private disputes over immovable property; such matters must be resolved through civil suits.
Writ jurisdiction is extraordinary and not meant to replace ordinary remedies like civil suits or criminal procedure, especially when statutory duties are not violated.
doctrines: Extraordinary nature of writ jurisdiction
Primacy of ordinary legal remedies over constitutional remedies in private disputes

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their acquired land, seeking higher compensation and enhanced interest rates under the amended Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the claimants are entitled to enhanced solatium at 15% on the enhanced compensation awarded by the appellate court.
Whether the claimants are entitled to interest at 9% per annum from 24.9.1984, or only at the original 6%, under the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984.
Whether the provisions of the 1984 Amendment Act apply to awards made prior to its enactment, particularly for interest and solatium.
holdings: Claimants are entitled to solatium at 15% on the enhanced compensation, as the awards by the Collector and Reference Court predated 30.4.1982, and thus do not qualify for higher solatium under the 1984 Amendment.
Both judges agreed that interest at 6% per annum is payable from the date of possession up to 23.9.1984; however, they disagreed on the rate thereafter, leading to a reference to a larger bench.
The applicability of the enhanced interest rate of 9% (and 15% after delay) under the 1984 Amendment Act to cases with awards prior to its enactment is unresolved and referred to a larger bench.
doctrines: Prospective application of amendments
Harmonious construction of statutes
Appellate correction of awards
Binding effect of Constitution Bench decisions

card.dispute: Nagendra Pal Singh appealed his conviction for murder and causing injuries, claiming he acted in self-defence when he fired at an attacking mob that had injured him and his brothers.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to complete acquittal on the ground of right of private defence of person and property
Whether the appellant exceeded the right of private defence
holdings: The appellant was entitled to complete acquittal as he acted in lawful private defence of himself and his brother, given the imminent threat to life from an armed mob.
The appellant did not exceed the right of private defence, as firing was a last resort in the face of persistent and deadly attack.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 96 to 106 (right of private defence)
doctrines: Right of private defence of person
Proportionality in self-defence
Last resort doctrine in self-defence

card.dispute: The dispute involved a sub-tenant (appellant) seeking protection of tenancy rights in a flat previously held by a company in liquidation, against the official liquidator and the landlord-trust, over possession and validity of a sub-tenancy agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the directions by the High Court allowing the liquidator to dispossess the appellant were justified at the interlocutory stage
Whether the landlord's oral consent to sub-tenancy affects the appellant's claim for protection under the Bombay Rent Control Act
Whether the official liquidator must surrender possession of the flat to the landlord-trust pending final disposal of the matter
holdings: The High Court's directions dispossessing the appellant and altering her possession to that of an agent of the liquidator were not warranted at the interlocutory stage, as her tenancy rights were yet to be adjudicated.

Prima facie, the sub-tenancy agreement is valid, especially given the board resolution and the landlord-trust’s counsel confirming oral consent, entitling the appellant to interim protection under tenancy law.
The liquidator may retain possession of the flat for legitimate purposes like storing company records or pending revival proposals, and the landlord cannot claim immediate surrender of possession.
doctrines: Prima facie protection of tenancy rights during insolvency proceedings
Interim orders should not prejudice final adjudication of rights
Continuity of contractual and tenancy rights despite corporate liquidation

card.dispute: The owners of tea, rubber, and cardamom estates fought with the State of Kerala over whether land used for growing firewood for estate workers or for use in smokehouses was exempt from being classified as 'private forests' under the Kerala Private Forests Act, 1971.
issues_decided: Whether land set apart for growing firewood for use by estate employees or in smokehouses for processing rubber or tea qualifies as used for a purpose ancillary to cultivation or preparation of crops for market under Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B) of the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971.
Whether the supply of firewood to estate workers or for use in processing crops falls within the statutory exclusion from the definition of 'private forests'.
holdings: Land used for growing firewood for estate workers or for use in smokehouses does not constitute a purpose ancillary to the cultivation of plantation crops or their preparation for market under Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B) of the Kerala Private Forests Act, 1971.

The supply of firewood, whether for employee use or industrial processing, is not an ancillary agricultural purpose and therefore such land is included in the definition of 'private forests' and vests in the State.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Legislative intent as an aid to interpretation
Ancillary purpose doctrine

card.dispute: The brothers disputed whether the plaintiff was the real owner of land held in the defendants' names as benamidars, and whether the suit was barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
issues_decided: Whether a suit based on a benami transaction, filed before the Benami Act came into force, is barred if an appeal is pending when the Act becomes law
Whether the defendants could raise a new plea under Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, for the first time in appeal
holdings: Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 applies to pending appeals, and bars any suit or claim to enforce rights in benami property, even if the suit was filed before the Act came into force.
A plea under Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act cannot be raised for the first time in appeal if no foundation was laid in the pleadings or written statement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6, Rules 1, 2, 7
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, Section 49
doctrines: Prospective operation of statutes
Pleading estoppel
Continuity of appeal with suit

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a mortgagee and mortgagor disputed over the recovery of possession of mortgaged land, limitation of the claim, adverse possession, and entitlement to mesne profits after the debt was discharged.
issues_decided: Whether the application for recovery of possession under the Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1947 is barred by limitation
Whether the mortgagee acquired title by adverse possession
Whether the executing court has the power to award mesne profits
holdings: Section 27 of the Limitation Act does not apply to proceedings under the Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1947, as the legislature intentionally did not prescribe a limitation period for recovery of possession under the Act, making such applications not time-barred.
The appellants did not acquire title by adverse possession because the possession was not hostile or adverse to the mortgagor’s rights, especially after the debt was discharged under the compromise.

The civil court has the inherent power to award mesne profits as a consequence of unlawful retention of possession after the charge under the award ended, and such award is integral to the order for delivery of possession.
provisions: Bombay Agricultural Debtors Relief Act, 1947, Sections 32(2)(v), 38(3), 51-A
doctrines: Doctrine of adverse possession
Doctrine of extinguishment of right by limitation under Section 27 of the Limitation Act
Doctrine of beneficial legislation interpretation
Doctrine of implied exclusion of limitation in special statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a public servant, challenged his conviction for possessing disproportionate assets under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, arguing he had satisfactorily accounted for his income.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's finding of disproportionate assets was supported by legal evidence
Whether the appellant had satisfactorily explained the sources of his assets
Whether the alleged benami transactions were proven beyond reasonable doubt
Whether the prosecution established the offence under Section 5(1)(e) read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947
holdings: The High Court's finding of disproportionate assets was not sustainable due to incorrect inclusion of Rs. 29,000 as benami and erroneous expense calculations.
The appellant satisfactorily accounted for his income, including from leasehold land and sale of pulses, warranting inclusion in legitimate sources.
The prosecution failed to discharge the burden of proving benami transactions, as required by law, especially without conclusive evidence.
The prosecution did not prove the charge under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, beyond reasonable doubt, entitling the appellant to acquittal.
doctrines: Burden of proof in benami transactions
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Strict proof required for disproportionate assets

card.dispute: The mortgagor (appellant) fought against the mortgagee (respondent) over whether the mortgagee could claim additional compensation for improvements after the decretal amount was deposited, and whether the mortgagee qualified as a deemed tenant under the Kerala Land Reforms Act to prevent eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgagee's right to remain in possession after redemption is affected by the Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958
Whether a mortgagee can be deemed a tenant under Section 4A of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 without 50 years of continuous possession preceding the 1969 Amendment
Whether land held by a mortgagee vests in the State under Section 72 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act
holdings: Deposit of the decretal amount, including mortgage and improvement costs, extinguishes the mortgagee’s right to possession; continued possession thereafter is unlawful.

A mortgagee cannot be deemed a tenant under Section 4A of the Kerala Land Reforms Act unless they had 50 years of continuous possession immediately before the 1969 Amendment; statutory possession under the Improvements Act does not count toward this period.
Land does not vest in the State under Section 72 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act unless held by a cultivating tenant under fixity of tenure; mortgagees do not qualify.
provisions: Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958, Section 2(d)
Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958, Section 4
Kerala Compensation for Tenants Improvements Act, 1958, Section 5
doctrines: Cessation of mortgagee's possession upon redemption
Statutory fiction of tenancy for compensation purposes only
Condition precedent for eviction: payment of improvement compensation
Vesting of land in the State only for cultivating tenants under fixity of tenure

card.dispute: The tenant (petitioner) fought against eviction by the landlord (respondent) who claimed to be a 'specified landlord' under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, after the High Court allowed eviction but gave the tenant one month to vacate upon filing an undertaking.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could invoke the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 136 after accepting protection from eviction by filing an undertaking in the High Court?
Whether the tenant's conditional undertaking, reserving the right to file a special leave petition, permitted him to challenge the High Court's eviction order?
