holdings: A party cannot both accept the benefit of a court order and later challenge its validity; by filing an undertaking to avail temporary protection from eviction, the tenant elected to accept the order and cannot subsequently assail it under Article 136.
The reservation of rights in the undertaking to file a special leave petition does not override the legal bar against approbating and reprobating the same judicial order.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 - Section 2(hh)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 - Section 13A
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 - Section 18-A(8)
doctrines: Doctrine of election
Prohibition against approbation and reprobation

card.dispute: The appellant (vendor) fought for relief after being unable to receive payment for her property due to a government order under the Income-tax Act and a court stay, which blocked both compulsory acquisition and private sale.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to interest on the unpaid purchase price due to the delay caused by the government's purchase order and court stay?
Whether the appellant, who did not oppose the government's acquisition or the private sale, should be compensated for being deprived of the sale proceeds?
holdings: A seller who does not obstruct either the government's purchase under Section 269UD or the private sale but is deprived of the sale price due to such proceedings may be awarded interest if equity so requires.

The Government must pay the agreed sale price with 15% annual interest if its acquisition order is upheld; if the order is set aside and the private sale completes, the buyer must pay 20% annual interest on the balance from the date of the interim order.
doctrines: Equity, justice and good conscience
Judicial notice of rising property prices

card.dispute: Eight appellants convicted under Section 302 read with 149 IPC for murder as part of an unlawful assembly appealed, challenging the sufficiency of evidence and the application of common object doctrine.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC was justified based on the nature of injuries and common object of the unlawful assembly
Whether the evidence of interested witnesses could solely sustain the conviction for murder
Whether the injuries caused were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death under Section 300 IPC
holdings: The common object of the unlawful assembly could not be inferred to be murder where injuries were mostly simple and on non-vital parts, and no injury was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
Conviction under Section 302 read with 149 IPC was unsafe; substituted with conviction under Section 304 Part II read with Section 149 IPC due to lack of intention to cause death.
Mere presence of injuries leading to death by shock and haemorrhage, without objective proof of grievous or fatal injuries, does not attract Clause III of Section 300 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 307 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 324 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II read with Section 149
doctrines: Common object of unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Requirement of objective evidence to prove injuries sufficient to cause death under Section 300 IPC
Principle of cautious reliance on interested witnesses in criminal cases

card.dispute: The tea company fought with the land revenue authorities over whether surcharge on land revenue and local rates should be included in 'annual land revenue' for computing compensation for excess land acquired under the Assam Ceiling Act.
issues_decided: Whether the surcharge on land revenue under the Assam Land Revenue and Land (Surcharge) Act, 1970 forms part of 'annual land revenue' for compensation under Section 12 of the Assam Ceiling Act, 1956.
Whether the local rate payable under the Local Rates Regulation, 1879 constitutes 'annual land revenue' for the purpose of compensation under Section 12 of the Ceiling Act.
holdings: Surcharge on land revenue under the 1970 Act is an enhancement of land revenue and forms part of 'annual land revenue' for computing compensation under Section 12 of the Ceiling Act.
Local rate under the Local Rates Regulation, 1879 is a distinct levy for local purposes and does not form part of 'annual land revenue' for compensation under Section 12 of the Ceiling Act.
provisions: Assam Fixation of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1956, Section 12
Assam Land Revenue and Land (Surcharge) Act, 1970, Sections 3 and 7
doctrines: Principle of statutory interpretation: nature of tax levy determines inclusion in compensation base
Doctrine of characterisation: distinguishing between land revenue and special-purpose cesses or rates

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant in 1977, claiming the U.P. Rent Control Act, 1972 did not apply as the building was constructed in 1968; the tenant argued the Act applied and barred eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 applied to a building constructed in 1968 when the suit was filed in 1977, before the expiry of the 10-year exemption period.
Whether the Act became applicable during the pendency of the suit upon expiry of the 10-year period from completion of construction.
Whether Section 39 of the 1972 Act applied to protect the tenant despite non-compliance with its conditions.
holdings: The 1972 Act does not apply to any building for ten years from the completion of its construction, regardless of whether construction was before or after the Act's commencement.
The law applicable on the date of filing the suit governs the proceedings; expiry of the 10-year exemption period during pendency does not bring the Act into force.
Section 39 of the Act does not benefit a tenant who fails to comply with its deposit requirements, making its applicability academic.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 2(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 39
doctrines: Prospective operation of statutes
Law applicable at the time of suit institution governs
Strict compliance with conditional statutory protections

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction based solely on an oral dying declaration, arguing it was unreliable and uncorroborated.
issues_decided: Whether the oral dying declaration, as testified by P.W. 18 and P.W. 20, could be relied upon for conviction despite delays and inconsistencies?
Whether the medical evidence supported the possibility of the deceased making a coherent oral dying declaration?
Whether the conviction could be sustained in the absence of corroboration and with serious infirmities in witness conduct?
holdings: An oral dying declaration cannot form the basis of conviction if it suffers from material contradictions, delays in disclosure, and lack of corroboration.
The court cannot rely on an oral dying declaration when the medical evidence suggests the deceased was physically incapable of making a coherent statement.
Serious infirmities in the conduct of witnesses, such as failing to report the declaration for three days without explanation, render the evidence unreliable.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 323 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 324 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 449 read with Section 149
doctrines: Dying declaration must be reliable and free from infirmities to be the basis of conviction
Benefit of doubt must be given when conviction rests solely on uncorroborated and suspect testimony
Courts must scrutinize the physical and mental capacity of the deceased to make a dying declaration

card.dispute: The appellant, a dealer operating a service station, challenged a municipal notice to demolish structures, while the lessee of the land sought to be impleaded as a necessary party in the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the lessee (Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd.) is a necessary or proper party in a suit challenging a municipal demolition notice issued to the dealer.

Whether the court can direct the plaintiff to implead a party as a defendant under Order I Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, when that party lacks a direct legal interest in the subject-matter of the suit.
holdings: A person is a necessary party only if the court cannot effectively and completely adjudicate the issues without them, and their legal rights would be directly affected by the judgment.

The lessee had no direct legal interest in the chattels targeted by the demolition notice and thus was neither a necessary nor a proper party; impleading them would introduce unrelated issues and prejudice the plaintiff.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 10
doctrines: Necessary and proper party doctrine
Rule of present interest in joinder of parties
Test of direct legal effect on intervenor's rights

card.dispute: The appellants, tenants of a property acquired by the Central Government under Chapter XX-A of the Income-tax Act, 1961, challenged the constitutional validity of the provisions and claimed their right to continue in possession as statutory tenants.
issues_decided: Whether immovable property acquired under Chapter XX-A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 vests in the Central Government free from all encumbrances after a final order under section 269F(6)
Whether a tenant, including a statutory tenant under the Bombay Rents Act, can continue in possession of such acquired property
holdings: Property acquired under section 269F(6) vests absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances upon taking possession, extinguishing all prior rights including tenancy.
A tenant, whether contractual or statutory, cannot retain possession after acquisition; their only remedy is a share in compensation or a damages suit against the transferee, not the government.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
doctrines: Vesting of property free from encumbrances
Statutory tenancy rights extinguished by compulsory acquisition
Compensation as sole remedy for affected occupants
Doctrine of implied exclusion of rent control laws for government-owned properties

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds that the building was unsafe and unfit for habitation, but the tenant had since repaired the damaged roof, leading to a legal dispute over whether the eviction was still justified.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement for eviction under Section 13(3)(a)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, continues if the tenant repairs the building making it fit for habitation?
Whether a tenant's unilateral repair of a fallen roof without invoking Section 12 of the Act negates the landlord's right to eviction?
Whether subsequent events, such as repairs by the tenant, can render an eviction order unnecessary?
holdings: If a tenant repairs a building and makes it safe and fit for habitation, the landlord's requirement to evict for repairs no longer subsists, and eviction cannot be ordered.
A tenant's act of repairing a fallen roof at their own cost without invoking Section 12 does not invalidate the repair or preserve the landlord's right to eviction under Section 13(3)(a)(iii).
Subsequent events, including repairs by the tenant, must be considered, and if they eliminate the need for eviction, the eviction order must be set aside.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)(a)(iii)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(4)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 12
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Subsequent events affecting relief
Necessity of eviction for extensive repairs

card.dispute: The appellant (Smt. Guro) and respondent no. 1 (Atma Singh) disputed the genuineness of a will by which Ganga Singh bequeathed his one-third share in property to Atma Singh, with Guro claiming rightful inheritance as the nearest heir.
issues_decided: Whether the will was executed genuinely by the testator under free will and sound mind.
Whether the propounder of the will discharged the burden of proving its validity in the face of suspicious circumstances.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the appellate court's finding that the will was not proved to be genuine.
holdings: When suspicious circumstances surround a will’s execution, the propounder must fully explain them to the court’s satisfaction before the will can be accepted as genuine.

The presence of multiple suspicious circumstances—such as incorrect statements in the will, the testator’s serious illness, use of thumb impression despite literacy, and the sole legatee’s involvement—requires strict proof of due execution and testamentary capacity.

The High Court erred in reversing the appellate court’s finding; it failed to properly appreciate the suspicious circumstances and the burden on the propounder, and thus its restoration of the trial court’s decree was unjustified.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder in case of suspicious circumstances
Due execution and testamentary capacity in will disputes
Principle of judicial review in second appeals under Article 136

card.dispute: The dispute was between a sick industrial company (tenant) and its landlord (Church) over whether eviction proceedings could continue despite the company's reference to the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.
issues_decided: Whether eviction proceedings against a sick industrial company are suspended under Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985.
Whether the leasehold interest of a sick industrial company, which is a statutory tenant under the Karnataka Rent Control Act, constitutes 'property' under Section 22(1) of the SIC Act.
holdings: Section 22(1) of the SIC Act does not suspend eviction proceedings initiated by a landlord against a sick industrial company that has defaulted on rent and lost contractual tenancy protection.

The leasehold interest of a company occupying premises as a statutory tenant under the Karnataka Rent Control Act is not 'property' under Section 22(1) of the SIC Act because it is non-transferable and non-assignable.
provisions: Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 22(1)
Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, Sections 3(r), 21(1)(f), and 23
doctrines: Statutory tenancy doctrine
Legislative intent interpretation
Property rights under insolvency and rent control laws

card.dispute: The landlord (Smt. Pushpa Talwar) sought eviction of the tenant (Smt. A.N. Kapoor) on grounds of bonafide personal requirement, while the tenant argued the premises were used commercially as a boarding house with the landlord's implied consent, thus excluding eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the premises let for residential purposes were used incidentally for commercial purposes without the landlord's consent, thereby still qualifying for eviction under Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the landlord's knowledge and implied consent to the tenant running a boarding house negated the residential character of the tenancy.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of the statutory authorities on factual grounds.
holdings: Premises let for residential purposes but used incidentally for commercial purposes without landlord’s consent still fall under Section 14(1)(e) if the three conditions in the Explanation are met.

Where the landlord has knowledge of and does not object to regular and open commercial use of the premises, implied consent is presumed, altering the character of the premises and excluding applicability of Section 14(1)(e).
The High Court erred in reversing concurrent factual findings of the Rent Controller and Tribunal that were supported by evidence; no substantial question of law justified interference.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 14(1)(e) with Explanation
doctrines: Implied consent to change in use of premises
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed in second appeal
Residential character of premises determined by actual use and landlord's knowledge

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the initiation of proceedings to sell his 22 acres of agricultural land to recover a bank loan, arguing that the bank should first realize dues from the already attached tractor pledged as security.
issues_decided: Whether recovery proceedings under Section 11-A of the U.P. Agricultural Credit Act, 1973 can proceed for sale of mortgaged agricultural land when a tractor, already attached under Section 10-B of the same Act, had an estimated value exceeding the outstanding dues?
Whether the creditor (State Bank of India) can simultaneously pursue recovery through both movable and immovable property without accounting for realization from the movable asset first?
Whether the court can exercise discretion to prevent simultaneous execution proceedings against multiple properties for the same debt?
holdings: The recovery proceedings against immovable property must be held in abeyance until the amount realized or deemed to be realized from the attached movable property (tractor) is ascertained.
A creditor cannot proceed with the sale of multiple properties under different statutory provisions without verifying whether the debt has already been satisfied from prior attachments.
Courts have judicial discretion under Order 21, Rule 21 of the CPC to restrict simultaneous execution against both person and property, especially when recovery from one source suffices.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 279(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 21
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 30
doctrines: Judicial discretion in execution proceedings
Principle against double recovery
Simultaneous execution under CPC
Statutory recovery mechanisms override equitable estoppel in creditor-debtor relations

card.dispute: The appellant claimed a 'thika tenancy' right under the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1981 based on long possession, while the respondent contested this claim, leading to litigation over the validity of the tenancy and possession rights.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the first appellate court's findings of fact without remanding the case or properly reappraising the evidence?

Whether the High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC, can dismiss the suit solely on the ground that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his case and not on the weakness of the defence?
holdings: The High Court cannot set aside findings of fact in a second appeal without either remanding the case for rehearing or deciding the factual issue itself under Section 103(b) CPC after considering the entire evidence.
A finding of fact vitiated by legal error does not automatically justify a contrary finding; the High Court must reassess all relevant evidence before reaching a final conclusion in a second appeal.
provisions: Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Acquisition and Regulation) Act, 1981
doctrines: Finality of findings of fact by the first appellate court
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Proper procedure for factual determination in second appeal under Section 103(b) CPC

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh contested whether the term 'building' under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act includes the land underneath it for rent enhancement purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'building' in Section 3(i) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 includes the land underneath the super-structure.
Whether the valuation for rent enhancement under Section 21(8) of the Act can include the value of the land on which the building stands.
holdings: The term 'building' under Section 3(i) of the Act includes the land underneath the super-structure, as the land is intrinsically inseparable from the building.
Valuation for rent enhancement under Section 21(8) may lawfully include both the value of the structure and the land, as together they form a single composite unit.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(i)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(8)
doctrines: Intrinsic unity of land and building for valuation
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory definitions

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Sundra Naicka Vadiyar and Ramaswami Ayyar disputed over possession of agricultural land, each seeking permanent injunction against the other based on claims of possession.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could disturb the finding on possession recorded by the lower courts in second appeal.
Whether the High Court erred in re-appreciating evidence regarding possession.
holdings: The High Court was justified in disturbing the finding on possession as the lower courts ignored vital documents affecting the question of possession.
Re-appreciation of evidence by the High Court was valid where findings were based on incomplete consideration of material documents.
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Interference with concurrent findings of fact

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell land after the seller transferred the property to others instead of executing the sale deed.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract despite deficit in court-fee?
Whether the High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact by lower courts?
Whether specific performance should be granted despite delay and change in property value?
holdings: Deficiency in court-fee does not negate readiness and willingness to perform; deposit of balance consideration shows capacity and intent to perform.
High Court committed error by reversing concurrent findings of fact on readiness and willingness without valid reason.
Specific performance granted with additional payment of Rs. 12,000 due to long delay and appreciation in urban property value.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform contract
Concurrent finding of fact rule
Discretionary nature of specific performance
Equitable adjustment for delay and inflation

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted of murder by the High Court after being acquitted by the trial court; they challenged the conviction, while the State had cross-appealed for harsher punishment.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in convicting both appellants under Section 302/34 IPC instead of Section 304 Part II IPC?
Whether the injury inflicted by the first appellant falls under Clause III of Section 300 IPC, making it murder?
Whether the second appellant shared the common intention to commit murder under Section 34 IPC?
holdings: The first appellant intended to cause an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, attracting Clause III of Section 300 IPC, hence his conviction under Section 302 IPC is upheld.
The use of a deadly weapon like a knife on a vital part of the body without provocation shows intention to commit murder, even in a sudden quarrel.

The second appellant inflicted only a simple injury and there was no evidence of shared common intention to commit murder; thus, conviction under Section 302/34 IPC is unsafe and set aside in favor of Section 326 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 300 Clause III
Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires active participation or shared intent
Intention to cause death can be inferred from the nature, location, and force of the injury
Sudden quarrel is not a complete defense if the act shows premeditated use of deadly weapon on a vital part

card.dispute: Aruby Sales And Services (P) Ltd fought the State of Maharashtra over whether a consent decree transferring title to immovable property is liable to stamp duty under the Bombay Stamps Act, 1958.
issues_decided: Whether a consent decree that expressly conveys title to immovable property falls within the definition of 'conveyance' under Section 2(g) of the Bombay Stamps Act, 1958.
Whether such a consent decree qualifies as an 'instrument' under Section 2(1) of the Act.
holdings: A consent decree that operates to transfer title to immovable property is a 'conveyance' under Section 2(g) of the Bombay Stamps Act, 1958, as it effectively transfers property inter vivos.
A consent decree that creates or records a transfer of property rights is an 'instrument' under Section 2(1) of the Act and is liable to stamp duty.
provisions: Bombay Stamps Act, 1958, Schedule I, Entry 25
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutory definitions
Consent decree as a creature of the underlying agreement
Substance over form in determining legal character of documents

card.dispute: Three appellants challenged their conviction in a murder case where they were held constructively liable under Sections 34 and 149 IPC, arguing that the same evidence could not sustain their conviction after six co-accused were acquitted.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of the three appellants can be sustained under Sections 34 and 149 IPC based on the same eyewitness testimony that failed to convict six other accused?
Whether there was inordinate delay in lodging the FIR that would render the prosecution case suspect?
Whether the appellants can be held liable for murder when specific fatal injuries were not directly attributed to them and the only inside witness turned hostile?
holdings: The conviction of the three appellants is sustainable under Sections 34 and 149 IPC if specific overt acts were consistently attributed to them and the evidence was reliable, even if other accused were acquitted due to lack of such attribution.
A delay of about five hours in filing the FIR is not inordinate when the priority was to transport the injured to the police station or hospital, and does not discredit the prosecution case.

Constructive liability under Sections 34 and 149 IPC can be invoked if the appellants were members of an unlawful assembly with common object, actively participated in the attack, and the fatal injuries resulted from the collective action, even without direct proof of who caused the fatal blow.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Evaluation of interested eyewitness testimony
Benefit of doubt in cases of inconsistent attribution of overt acts

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the High Court for murder and related offences, challenged their convictions, arguing that the eyewitness testimony was unreliable and there was no immediate motive.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution established a sufficient motive for the offence.
Whether the evidence of the injured eyewitnesses could be rejected on grounds of interest, delay in FIR, or minor inconsistencies.
Whether the accused could be convicted under Section 149 IPC without specific overt acts being attributed to them.
holdings: Evidence of past hostility and recent disputes over land and crop damage established an immediate motive, making the Sessions Judge's finding to the contrary incorrect.
The evidence of injured eyewitnesses, though interested, cannot be rejected outright due to interest or minor discrepancies, especially when corroborated by medical evidence and presence of injuries.

In cases relying on interested witnesses, it is unsafe to convict accused under Section 149 IPC without proof of specific overt acts; mere presence or instigation is insufficient when evidence requires strict scrutiny.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in cases with interested witnesses
Corroboration through medical evidence
Requirement of overt act for conviction under constructive liability (Section 149 IPC)
Caution in appreciating evidence of interested witnesses

card.dispute: Legal representatives of a deceased person disputed over who should represent the estate, particularly regarding the validity and execution of the deceased's will, with one party seeking arbitration while probate proceedings were pending.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitrator can decide the validity and execution of a will when probate proceedings are pending.
Whether the probate court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine the genuineness of a will.
holdings: An arbitrator lacks jurisdiction to decide the execution or genuineness of a will, as such matters fall exclusively within the domain of the probate court under the Indian Succession Act.
The probate court has exclusive jurisdiction to grant or refuse probate, and this jurisdiction cannot be ousted by consent of parties or by arbitration.
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of probate court
Lack of inherent jurisdiction of arbitrator in matters of will validity
Nullity of decrees or awards passed without jurisdiction
Non-derogability of statutory jurisdiction by party consent

card.dispute: The wife appealed against the High Court's grant of a divorce decree on grounds of cruelty under the Hindu Marriage Act, challenging both the finding of cruelty and the standard of proof applied.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in treating matrimonial proceedings as quasi-criminal and requiring the wife to prove adultery beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the findings of fact by the lower courts justified the grant of divorce on grounds of cruelty?
Whether the marriage could be said to be irretrievably broken down?
holdings: The Court expressed concern over the application of a quasi-criminal standard in matrimonial cases, noting that such a high burden of proof may not be appropriate, but did not formally rule on the issue.
The factual findings of misconduct by both parties were not overturned, but the Court observed that the findings against the wife were shaky and directed their deletion from all judgments.
The marriage was deemed irretrievably broken down, and in the interest of justice and to prevent further agony, the Court upheld the divorce decree despite not interfering with findings of fact.
doctrines: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage
Equity and judicial discretion in family law
Standard of proof in matrimonial disputes

card.dispute: The Committee of Management of Pachaiyappa's Trust challenged the grant of a long-term lease by the Official Trustee of Madras to a private firm, arguing it was against the trust's interests and that the High Court overstepped its supervisory role.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, under Section 25 of the Official Trustees Act, 1913, could modify lease terms contrary to the Official Trustee's recommendations and without regard to the trust's interests?
Whether the appellant trust had locus standi to object to the lease granted by the Official Trustee?
Whether the High Court could allow substantial modifications to a final lease order under the guise of 'modification'?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by altering lease terms in a manner prejudicial to the trust estate without justifying the changes.
The appellant, as a residuary legatee and tenant adjacent to the property, had locus standi to object to the lease on grounds of trust interest.
Substantial changes to lease terms after the order became final under the pretext of modification amounted to an impermissible review of a final order.
doctrines: Principle of judicial restraint in supervisory jurisdiction
Locus standi of a beneficiary in trust matters
Prohibition against substantive modification of final orders under procedural guise

card.dispute: Members of the public sued landowners for a declaration of customary right to bury the dead in two parcels of land; after one defendant died during appeal, the High Court set aside the decree only against the surviving defendant, leading to inconsistent outcomes.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal abated due to the death of defendant No. 2 during the pendency of the appeal without bringing his legal heirs on record
Whether the High Court could extend relief to the entire suit property under Order 41, Rule 33 of the CPC
Whether the non-exercise of power under Order 41, Rule 34 led to a miscarriage of justice
holdings: The appeal did not abate as the plaintiffs proceeded on the basis that the customary right was against the entire suit property, which was sufficiently represented by the surviving defendants.
The High Court failed to exercise its power under Order 41, Rule 33 CPC to pass a decree that would do complete justice, especially where a common right was claimed over the entire property.
The non-exercise of discretionary power under Order 41, Rule 34 CPC resulted in contradictory decrees and miscarriage of justice, warranting appellate intervention.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 34
doctrines: Survival of cause of action despite death of a party where right is against property as a whole
Doctrine of complete justice under appellate powers
Avoidance of inconsistent or contradictory decrees in the same suit

card.dispute: Dev Raj and Des Raj appealed their convictions for murder and attempted murder, claiming they acted in self-defence during a violent altercation at a sawmill.
issues_decided: Whether Dev Raj and Des Raj were entitled to the right of private defence under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC
Whether the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on the accused affects the credibility of their version of events
Whether the accused exceeded the right of private defence in causing fatal injuries
holdings: The accused are entitled to the benefit of Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC if the evidence shows they acted in self-defence, even if the prosecution does not explain their injuries.
In cases where two views are possible, the accused must be given the benefit of doubt regarding the plea of self-defence.

While Dev Raj had a right to private defence, he exceeded it by inflicting fatal injuries, reducing his liability from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Right of private defence under Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC
Exceeding the right of private defence

card.dispute: The tenant (appellant) fought the landlord and mortgagee (respondents) over whether he had surrendered tenancy and was dispossessed, thus losing protection under the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant-tenant had surrendered tenancy rights before or after the 1952 transaction, thereby losing protection under Section 32(1-B) of the Act.
Whether the High Court could interfere with the Revenue Tribunal's factual finding that the appellant remained a tenant despite entries in revenue records.
holdings: A tenant does not cease to have tenancy rights merely due to an entry in revenue records; actual surrender of possession must be proved by positive evidence.
The High Court erred in overturning the Revenue Tribunal’s finding that the tenant continued in possession; such factual determinations cannot be disturbed under Article 227 without legal error.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32(1-B)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 29(2)
doctrines: Presumption against dispossession without proof
Limited scope of interference under Article 227 against concurrent factual findings

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed possession of a house, leading to criminal attachment proceedings under Section 146 CrPC and subsequent civil injunction proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a second revision application under Section 482 CrPC after the first revision was dismissed by the Sessions Court.
Whether the Magistrate had the power to withdraw an attachment order under Section 146 CrPC before the civil court finally decided the rights of the parties.
holdings: The High Court cannot entertain a second revision application by the same party when Section 397(3) CrPC bars such revision, even under its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC.

A Magistrate may withdraw an attachment order under Section 146(1) CrPC when a civil court has assumed jurisdiction, even by an interim order like injunction or appointment of a receiver, as the likelihood of breach of peace ceases.
doctrines: Inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC cannot override express statutory bars.
Doctrine of repugnancy between magisterial and civil court orders.

card.dispute: Squatters and hawkers challenged the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's scheme for granting tehbazari permissions, alleging unfair subclassification and denial of covered stalls.
issues_decided: Whether the MCD's subclassification of squatters based on possession of a survey report receipt was valid?
Whether the MCD could deny covered tehbazari/kiosks to those previously granted such facilities?
Whether requiring clearance of past dues as a condition for tehbazari permission was reasonable?
Whether late claims should be entertained for those who had pending litigation before the Saudan Singh judgment?
holdings: The subclassification of squatters into those with and without survey receipts is unwarranted; all who squatted between 1970–1982 must be treated as one category and considered based on seniority.
The MCD cannot alter the nature of tehbazari for those previously granted covered stalls; only uncovered spaces are to be given to others not earlier permitted such facilities.
Requiring proof of past dues causes hardship; squatters unable to produce receipts may pay a lump sum of Rs. 3,000 in four instalments instead.
Claimants with pending court cases before March 13, 1992, may file applications within one month, provided they submit verified copies of their petitions or suits.
doctrines: Principle of equal treatment under Article 14
Right to livelihood as part of personal liberty under Article 21
Balancing of public interest and individual rights in regularization schemes

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from a residential building used partly for professional purposes, claiming personal need, while the tenant argued that 'scheduled buildings' were exempt from eviction on personal need grounds.
issues_decided: Whether a 'scheduled building' under Section 2(h) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1948 is excluded from the ground of eviction on personal need under Section 13(3)(a)(i)(a) after the 1956 Amendment?
Whether the omission of the words 'or a scheduled' in Section 13(3) by the 1956 Amendment implied exclusion of scheduled buildings from personal need eviction?
Whether the insertion of Section 13A in 1985 indicates that personal need eviction remained available under Section 13 for residential buildings including scheduled ones?
holdings: A 'scheduled building' is a subset of 'residential building' and remains eligible for eviction on personal need under Section 13(3)(a)(i)(a); the 1956 Amendment did not remove this ground for such buildings.
The omission of 'or a scheduled' in Section 13(3) in 1956 was superfluous because a scheduled building is already a residential building; the deletion aimed only to exclude non-residential buildings.

The 1985 insertion of Section 13A providing expedited eviction for certain landlords confirms that personal need eviction under Section 13 remained generally available for residential (including scheduled) buildings.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1948, Section 2(a), (d), (g), (h)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1948, Section 13(3)(a)(i)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1948, Section 13A
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1948, Section 4
doctrines: Principle of harmonious construction
Statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and context
Definition clauses interpreted to avoid redundancy and maintain classification consistency

card.dispute: The appellant, Harendra Nath Mandal, challenged his conviction under Section 304 Part 1 IPC after the High Court reduced his conviction from Section 307 IPC in a case involving an assault during a dispute over paddy harvesting.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be convicted under Section 304 Part 1 IPC when no death occurred.
Whether the right to private defence of person and property was available to the appellant given the circumstances of the incident.
holdings: Conviction under Section 304 Part 1 IPC is not sustainable in the absence of death, as the provision applies only to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

When the prosecution fails to disclose the true version of events and evidence shows the accused was injured while fending off an attack, the right to private defence cannot be ruled out, warranting acquittal.
doctrines: Right of private defence of person and property
Burden of proof in establishing private defence
Requirement of death for culpable homicide under Section 304 IPC

card.dispute: The heirs of a deceased plaintiff sued to restore possession of a coconut grove from defendants, alleging trespass, while the defendants claimed tenancy rights under a changed law.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide tenancy issues after a statutory amendment excluded such jurisdiction?
Whether a suit for restoration of possession from a trespasser is maintainable in civil court when the defendant raises a tenancy plea?
What procedure should a civil court follow when a pending suit is affected by a subsequent change in law excluding its jurisdiction?
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to decide tenancy disputes once the law vests such questions in a special authority like the Mamlatdar under the Tenancy Act.
A suit for possession against a trespasser is maintainable in civil court, but if tenancy is disputed, the issue must be referred to the Mamlatdar for determination.
When a pending suit is rendered non-maintainable due to a change in law, the court should not dismiss it outright but may stay proceedings and refer the tenancy issue to the competent authority.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 2, Rule 2(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rules 10 and 10A
The Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, Sections 2, 2(7A), 2(7B), 7, 8, 9, 58
doctrines: Res judicata
Jurisdictional bar to civil courts in tenancy matters
Doctrine of lis pendens with legislative change
Reference to quasi-judicial authority for preliminary determination

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of Jodha Ram, challenged the declaration of certain lands as surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, and sought eviction of tenants to regain possession, which the authorities and courts denied.
issues_decided: Whether a landowner can evict tenants and resume possession under Section 9(1)(i) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 after the land has been declared surplus?
Whether a transfer of surplus land prior to 30.7.1958 is protected under Section 8(1)(a) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972?
Whether the rights of a landowner in surplus land vest in the State Government under Section 12 of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972?
holdings: Once land is declared surplus under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, the landowner loses the right to resume possession under Section 9(1)(i); only the State Government may utilize such land.

Transfers of surplus land made before 30.7.1958 are exempt from vesting under Section 12(3) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, per Section 8(1)(a), but this does not restore possession rights.

All rights, title, and interest in surplus land declared under the Land Tenures Act vest in the State Government free from encumbrances upon declaration, under Section 12 of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)(i)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 10-A
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 8
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 12
doctrines: Vesting of surplus land in the State Government
Non-derogation from statutory limitations on landowner rights post-surplus declaration
Cut-off date doctrine for protected land transfers

card.dispute: Kikar Singh fought with the state of Rajasthan over whether his act of causing fatal injuries during an altercation amounted to murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the accused's act fell within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, reducing the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder?
Whether the injuries caused were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death under clause 'thirdly' of Section 300 IPC?
Whether the accused took undue advantage or acted in a cruel manner during the altercation?
holdings: The act does not fall within Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC because the accused, being armed with a spade, attacked an unarmed man and inflicted multiple blows, including a fatal neck injury, after the victim fell, thus taking undue advantage and acting cruelly.

Culpable homicide amounts to murder under clause 'thirdly' of Section 300 IPC if the injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, regardless of absence of intention to kill, provided the intention to cause that specific injury is proven.

The use of a deadly weapon against an unarmed person in a one-sided attack, especially after the victim is incapacitated, negates the protection of Exception 4, making the offence murder under Section 302 IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Exception 4 to Section 300
doctrines: Doctrine of undue advantage in sudden fight
Objective test for sufficiency of injury to cause death under clause 'thirdly' of Section 300 IPC
Heat of passion and sudden quarrel as a defence under Exception 4

card.dispute: Lohia Properties (P) Ltd. sued Atmaram Kumar for eviction of a tenant's son, claiming valid notice of ejectment was served; the tenant's son contested the suit, arguing the notice was invalid and not properly served.
issues_decided: Whether the notice of ejectment was validly served on the tenant under the Assam Urban Areas Rent Control Act
Whether the defendant's failure to specifically deny service of notice in the written statement amounts to an admission under Order 8 Rule 5 of the CPC
holdings: A notice of ejectment sent by registered post to the tenant's home address, with postal and acknowledgment receipts, and not specifically denied in the written statement, constitutes valid service.

Under Order 8 Rule 5 of the CPC, where a defendant does not specifically deny or imply denial of a fact in the plaint, such fact is deemed admitted, and courts below were justified in relying on this implied admission.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8 Rule 5
Assam Non-Agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act, 1955, Section 11
doctrines: Implied admission under Order 8 Rule 5 CPC
Judicial admission and its effect on trial
Validity of service of notice under tenancy law

card.dispute: The appellant claimed perpetual injunction to restrain his uncles from interfering with his possession of certain agricultural lands, asserting individual tenancy rights, while the respondents claimed the tenancy belonged to the joint family.
issues_decided: Whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction to decide the question of tenancy in view of the exclusive jurisdiction conferred on the Land Tribunal under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, as amended in 1974.
Whether the tenancy rights over the disputed lands vested in the appellant individually or in the joint family.
holdings: The Land Tribunal established under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act has exclusive jurisdiction to decide questions of tenancy and rival claims to occupancy rights, and the Civil Court’s jurisdiction under Section 9 of the CPC is excluded by necessary implication.

When land is cultivated by a member of a joint family, the tenancy vests in the joint family as a whole, not in the individual cultivator, and such determination must be made by the Tribunal under Section 48A(5) of the Act.
doctrines: Exclusion of Civil Court jurisdiction by statutory ouster
Res judicata
Deemed cultivation by joint family
Finality of tribunal decisions under special statutes

card.dispute: Landlords appealed against the High Court's decision upholding the tenant's delayed deposit of rent arrears, challenging the executing court's power to extend time for deposit under the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court had jurisdiction to extend the statutory 30-day period for depositing rent arrears under Section 14(2)(i), third proviso, of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987?
Whether the tenant's partial and delayed deposit of rent, followed by court-extended time, invalidated the eviction order?
holdings: The executing court lacks jurisdiction to extend the 30-day deposit period specified in the third proviso to Section 14(2)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, as the period is statutorily fixed and not subject to judicial discretion.

An eviction order becomes inexecutable only if the tenant deposits the full amount due within the statutory 30 days; any extension granted by the executing court is a nullity and does not save the tenant from eviction.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Section 14(2)(i) with third proviso
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of mandatory time periods
No inherent power to extend time where statute specifies a fixed period
Execution court's lack of discretion to modify statutory timelines

card.dispute: The petitioners alleged that the respondents allotted flats in violation of a Supreme Court order dated 1.8.1991, thereby committing contempt of court.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed contempt by allotting flats after the Supreme Court's order prohibiting further allotments.
Whether the word 'allotment' in the court order includes acts such as handing over possession and registering sale deeds.
Whether the respondents acted under a bona fide belief that they were complying with the court order.
Whether the apology tendered by the respondent was unconditional and sufficient to purge contempt.
holdings: The respondents committed contempt by violating the court's order prohibiting further allotments, regardless of prior agreements.
The term 'allotment' must be interpreted broadly to prevent nullification of court orders; subsequent acts like possession and registration breach the order.
A claim of bona fide belief cannot excuse deliberate actions that contravene a clear court order, especially without seeking clarification.
An apology is not valid if qualified by justifications; the respondent's apology was conditional and thus rejected.
doctrines: Contempt by disobedience of court orders
Liberal interpretation of court orders to give effect to their purpose
No condonation of contempt without a true and unconditional apology
Duty to seek clarification rather than adopt a restrictive interpretation of court orders

card.dispute: Morvi Municipality challenged the High Court's decision invalidating its property tax rules and assessment lists for 1967-68 to 1969-70, arguing they were legally valid under the Gujarat Municipalities Act.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 5 of the Gujarat Municipalities Rules, allowing property tax based on actual rent, is ultra vires the Gujarat Municipalities Act where rent control laws apply
Whether the assessment list for 1967-68 was invalid due to late authentication by the municipality after 31st July
Whether Sections 105 to 112 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act prescribe mandatory or directory procedures for preparing and authenticating assessment lists
holdings: Rule 5 is not ultra vires if read down to apply only to properties not governed by rent control laws; for rent-controlled properties, annual letting value must be based on standard rent under the Rent Control Act

Section 112's requirement to authenticate the assessment list by 31st July is directory, not mandatory; late authentication by the municipality is valid, especially when the state government permits it
The failure to follow procedural timelines under Sections 105 to 112 does not invalidate the assessment list if substantial compliance is shown and the state does not intervene
doctrines: Doctrine of reading down
Doctrine of directory vs. mandatory provisions
Doctrine of substantial compliance

card.dispute: The appellant, Mani Ram, challenged his conviction by the High Court for murder and illegal possession of arms, which had overturned his acquittal by the Trial Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the Trial Court's acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 302 IPC and Section 27 of the Arms Act?
Whether the prosecution's evidence, including eyewitness testimony and ballistic reports, was reliable and sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the medical evidence regarding the time of death contradicted the prosecution's timeline of the incident?
Whether there was a possibility of tampering or substitution of cartridges sent for ballistic examination?
holdings: The High Court correctly reversed the acquittal as the Trial Court erred in relying on inconclusive medical opinion about digestion time to discredit eyewitness accounts.
The testimony of eyewitnesses PW1 and PW2 was credible, consistent, and sufficiently corroborated by medical and ballistic evidence to sustain the conviction.
Medical evidence indicating semi-digested food in the stomach did not contradict the timeline of the incident, as digestion varies individually and depends on food type and quantity.
The possibility of substitution of cartridges was ruled out due to unbroken chain of custody and consistent testimony of multiple custodians confirming the integrity of sealed evidence.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Appreciation of evidence in criminal cases
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Presumption of reliability of official custody of evidence
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's conviction in a murder case, arguing that the prosecution's evidence, including the timing of the FIR and injury patterns, was unreliable and that the trial court's acquittal should not have been overturned.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on its own appreciation of evidence.
Whether discrepancies in the prosecution's evidence, such as the timing of the FIR and nature of injuries, rendered the conviction unsafe.
Whether the testimony of alleged partisan eye-witnesses could form the basis of a conviction.
holdings: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal if the trial court's reasons are against the weight of evidence and lack proper appreciation of material on record.
Discrepancies in the timing of the FIR and the nature of injuries do not automatically invalidate the prosecution case if reasonably explained by the appellate court.
Testimony of eye-witnesses, even if allegedly partisan, can support a conviction if it is reliable, consistent, and corroborated by other evidence.
doctrines: Appellate review of acquittal
Evaluation of eyewitness testimony
Principle of corroboration in criminal cases
Reasoned reversal of trial court findings

card.dispute: The New Redbank Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the Calcutta High Court's decision to allow Terai Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. to be impleaded as a defendant in a suit concerning the Dharanipur Tea Estate.
issues_decided: Whether Terai Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. should be impleaded as a defendant in E.O. Suit No. 1 of 1985 for effectual and complete adjudication of the dispute
Whether Terai Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. has a direct legal interest in the subject-matter of E.O. Suit No. 1 of 1985
holdings: A person may be added as a party only if they have a direct legal interest in the subject-matter of the suit, not merely a commercial or indirect interest.

Terai Tea Co. Pvt. Ltd. cannot be impleaded as a defendant because it lacks a direct legal interest in the validity of the 1981 share transfer agreement, which is the core issue in E.O. Suit No. 1 of 1985.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10(2)
doctrines: Direct interest test for party impleadment
Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of the premises under a consent decree after the tenant failed to pay arrears of rent by the stipulated date, while the tenant argued the decree's enforcement was penal and unenforceable.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree's clause allowing eviction upon non-payment of arrears by a specified date is penal in nature and unenforceable
Whether the executing court can grant relief against forfeiture under Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in a case governed by Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act
holdings: A compromise term that allows a landlord to execute a decree for possession if arrears are not paid by a stipulated date is not penal but a concession, and is fully executable if the condition is not met.

Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents Act is a special provision that supersedes Section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act, and relief against forfeiture must be granted only as per the Rent Act, not independently under the T.P. Act.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 35
doctrines: Relief against forfeiture
Special statute prevails over general law
Concession in compromise vs. penal clause

card.dispute: Two individuals detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985 challenged the legality of their detention, arguing violations of constitutional safeguards under Articles 21 and 22(5) of the Constitution of India.
issues_decided: Whether the detention order remained valid when not approved by the State Government within 12 days as required under Section 3(3) of the Gujarat PASA?
Whether the detaining authority or the State Government had the power to revoke or rescind the detention order after approval by the State Government?
Whether the delay in considering and disposing of the detenue's representation under Article 22(5) rendered the detention illegal?
What is the meaning and implication of the term 'forthwith' in the context of considering a detenue's representation?
holdings: A detention order that is not approved by the State Government within 12 days of its execution becomes non est and cannot be revived by subsequent confirmation.
Once the State Government approves a detention order, only it—not the original detaining authority—can revoke or rescind the order under Section 15 of the Gujarat PASA or Article 22(5).
Failure to consider and dispose of a detenue’s representation without delay, especially without satisfactory explanation, violates Article 22(5) and renders detention illegal.
The word 'forthwith' means action must be taken as soon as possible, with reasonable speed and urgency; unexplained delay in considering representation breaches constitutional obligations.
provisions: Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985, Section 3
Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985, Section 15
Gujarat Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 1985, Section 11
doctrines: Doctrine of legality of preventive detention
Doctrine of effective enforcement of fundamental rights under Article 21
Doctrine of mandatory compliance with procedural safeguards in detention cases
Doctrine of contemporaneous construction of 'forthwith' as requiring prompt action

card.dispute: The appellant, Rameshwar Dayal, sought to enforce an eviction decree against the respondent Banda (a sub-tenant), who in turn filed a suit claiming ownership of the property and challenging the validity of the eviction decree on grounds of res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether the eviction decree passed by the Small Causes Court operated as res judicata on the issue of title in a subsequent suit?
Whether the order of the Small Causes Court amounted to a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure?
holdings: A finding on title by a Small Causes Court does not operate as res judicata unless the issue was directly and substantially in issue; mere incidental determination is insufficient.
An order that does not address points for determination or contain a formal adjudication on contested issues does not constitute a decree under Section 2(2) of the CPC and is not binding.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 2(2), Section 2(9), Section 2(14), Order XIV Rules 1 and 3, Order XX Rules 4(1) and 5
Provincial Small Causes Court Act, Section 17(1), Section 23
doctrines: Res judicata
Direct and substantial issue vs. incidental determination
Formal expression of adjudication as a decree

card.dispute: The State appealed against the acquittal of two appellants in a murder case arising from a land dispute, leading to conflicting findings between the trial court and the High Court on the credibility of eyewitnesses and common intention.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of eyewitnesses PWs 2-4 was reliable and sufficient to convict the appellants?
Whether the conviction of A-2 under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC was legally sustainable?
Whether A-1 and A-2 shared a common intention to commit murder within the meaning of Section 34 IPC?
holdings: The evidence of eyewitnesses PWs 2-4 is reliable and consistent, and minor discrepancies or unexplained injuries on the accused do not discredit their testimony.
A-2’s conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is unsustainable as he did not share the common intention to kill and only caused simple injuries.
Only A-1 inflicted fatal injuries; hence, a clear case of murder under Section 302 IPC is made out against him, but not against A-2 under common intention.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, Section 2(a)
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires active participation or shared criminal purpose
Reliability of eyewitness testimony is not vitiated by minor inconsistencies or failure to explain non-essential circumstances
Corroboration through medical and circumstantial evidence strengthens eyewitness accounts

card.dispute: The appellants, including Ram Phal, were convicted for the death of Sant Ram and injuries to others during a violent altercation, and they appealed, claiming the right of private defence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants did not act in private defence?
Whether the appellants exceeded the right of private defence under Section 100, IPC?
holdings: The prosecution failed to explain the numerous injuries on the accused, raising a reasonable doubt about the completeness of its version, thus entitling the accused to benefit of doubt.

Since only one blow was attributed to the appellant Ram Phal and the accused suffered multiple injuries, including on vital parts, they did not exceed the right of private defence under Section 100, IPC.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Right of private defence
Reasonable doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The appellant landowner fought the state over whether her vacant land should be excluded from 'urban land' under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, based on its agricultural use and absence of a master plan at the Act's commencement.
issues_decided: Whether land can be excluded from 'urban land' under Explanation (C) to Section 2(o) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, if it was recorded for agricultural use before the Act's commencement and no master plan existed then.
Whether a master plan prepared after the commencement of the Act can affect the determination of 'urban land' under Explanation (C).
holdings: Land recorded for agricultural use before the Act's commencement cannot be excluded from agricultural use status based on a later master plan; the master plan under Explanation (C) must exist at the time of the Act's commencement.
The rights and liabilities under the Act, including ceiling limits, crystallize at the Act's commencement; subsequent actions, including new master plans, cannot alter the extent of excess land.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(o) with Explanation (C)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(h)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5
doctrines: Crystallization of rights at commencement of statute
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Prospective vs. retrospective application of master plan

card.dispute: The appellant sued to eject the respondent company from the premises, and the respondent sought to set aside the ex-parte decree passed due to its non-appearance, blaming its advocate's advice.
issues_decided: Whether the non-appearance of the defendant due to alleged advice of the advocate constitutes sufficient cause under Order 9 Rule 13 of the CPC to set aside an ex-parte decree?
Whether the principle in Rafiq v. Munshilal applies to allow setting aside a decree based on advocate's negligence?
holdings: Mere non-appearance due to alleged advice of an advocate does not constitute sufficient cause under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC, especially when the party is a knowledgeable corporate entity.
The principle in Rafiq v. Munshilal is fact-specific and does not grant an absolute right to set aside a decree; parties cannot disown their advocate's conduct at will.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9, Rule 13
doctrines: Principle of agency in legal representation
Sufficient cause for non-appearance
Judicial discretion in setting aside ex-parte decrees
Limited applicability of precedent (Rafiq v. Munshilal)

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the High Court for the murder of their mother under Sections 302/34 IPC, challenged the reversal of their acquittal by the Sessions Court, primarily contesting the reliability of eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal based on the credibility of three eyewitnesses despite discrepancies in their testimony and medical evidence on time of occurrence.
Whether the presence of semi-digested food in the stomach of the deceased could reliably contradict eyewitness accounts of the time of the incident.
Whether material contradictions in the eyewitness accounts regarding location, lighting, and sequence of events rendered their testimony unreliable.
holdings: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal as the eyewitnesses' presence and testimony were credible and consistent with the prosecution's case, and minor discrepancies did not undermine their overall reliability.

The medical evidence of semi-digested food cannot precisely determine the time of death and cannot be the sole basis to discredit eyewitness testimony, especially when witnesses are illiterate and describe events in general terms.

Alleged contradictions in the eyewitness accounts regarding location and lighting were insignificant and did not go to the root of the case, particularly when the accused were known to the witnesses and the injuries corroborated the narrative.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, Section 2
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration through medical and circumstantial evidence
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the Karnataka government's exemption allowing a partnership firm to sell excess vacant land to builders to overcome financial hardship, arguing it violated the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976 and Article 14 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 20(1)(b) of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976 permits the State Government to grant exemption for transfer of excess vacant land on grounds of undue hardship
Whether the classification of landowners under Section 20(1)(b) into debtors and non-debtors is reasonable and non-discriminatory under Article 14
Whether the State Government's power under Section 20(1)(b) includes permission to sell excess land to third parties
holdings: Section 20(1)(b) does not authorize the State Government to grant exemption for the purpose of transferring excess vacant land; exemption is only for use, not for sale.
The classification between debtors and non-debtors under Section 20(1)(b) is arbitrary and creates irrational discrimination, violating Article 14.
The State Government lacks jurisdiction to permit sale of excess vacant land under Section 20(1)(b), rendering such permissions void ab initio.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 20(1)(a)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 20(1)(b)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 21
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 23(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of unconstitutional classification under Article 14
Doctrine of void ab initio for acts beyond jurisdiction
Principle of statutory interpretation based on legislative intent and object of social welfare legislation

card.dispute: The assessees, wives of two brothers in a bullion firm, fought the Revenue over whether their profit from selling subdivided land was an adventure in the nature of trade and assessable as income.
issues_decided: Whether the profit of Rs. 41,667 derived by the assessees was from an adventure in the nature of trade
Whether, if so, the assessment could be made in the status of an association of persons
holdings: A transaction undertaken soon after purchase, involving subdivision and quick sale of land, indicates an intention to trade, making the profit taxable as business income.
The question of assessment as an association of persons was not decided by the Supreme Court, as the appeal was dismissed on the first issue.
doctrines: Adventure in the nature of trade
Intention at the time of acquisition

card.dispute: Six brothers in a partnership disputed the distribution of firm assets upon dissolution, specifically whether the arbitration award allocating immovable properties required registration under the Registration Act.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitration award distributing partnership assets, including immovable properties, required registration under Section 17(1) of the Registration Act, 1908
Whether the award amounted to a partition or transfer of immovable property, thereby attracting compulsory registration
Whether the nature of the award was an assignment of partnership shares or an allotment creating new rights in specific immovable properties
holdings: An arbitration award that distributes the residue of partnership assets upon dissolution does not require registration under Section 17(1) of the Registration Act if it merely allocates properties in proportion to partners' shares without creating new rights or effecting partition.
The share of a partner in partnership assets, including immovable property, is movable property; its distribution does not amount to transfer of immovable property requiring registration.

Where an award merely reflects the allocation of surplus assets after settlement of accounts under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, it does not effect a partition, transfer, or extinction of rights in immovable property, and thus falls outside Section 17(1) of the Registration Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of movable nature of partnership share in immovable assets
Doctrine of non-registration for awards distributing partnership residue
Principle of interpretation of arbitration awards as a whole

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and Brigadier Sukhjit Singh disputed over ownership of the Jallowkhana Complex, specifically a double-storeyed building, with the State in possession and the plaintiff claiming title under a Farman issued by the erstwhile Ruler of Kapurthala.
issues_decided: Whether the Jallowkhana Complex was personal property of the Ruler or State property after merger of the princely state.
Whether the Farman issued by Maharaja Jagatjit Singh created a binding legal right in favour of succeeding heirs apparent.
Whether permissive possession by the State for a long period could ripen into adverse possession.
Whether non-payment of licence fee invalidated the licensee's continued possession or the right to seek eviction.
holdings: The Jallowkhana Complex was not personal property of the Ruler nor State property, but a unique, impersonal estate vested in each succeeding heir apparent by primogeniture to preserve the Ahluwalia dynasty’s legacy.

The Farman issued by the sovereign Ruler had the force of law and effectively created a perpetual, hereditary right in the property for the heirs apparent, independent of formal property listings at merger.
Permissive possession, no matter how long, does not become adverse possession unless there is a clear assertion of hostile title, which was absent here.
The absence of a licence fee does not invalidate a licence or prevent the grantor from revoking it and seeking eviction; payment is not essential to the existence of a licence.
doctrines: Sovereign will of princely rulers as law under Article 13
Doctrine of impersonal estate
Doctrine of permissive possession not ripening into adverse possession
Revocability of licence under the Easements Act

card.dispute: The State of Haryana enacted a law allowing authorities to ignore prior civil court decrees recognizing private rights in village common lands ('shamilat deh'), which the Karnal Co-Op Farmers' Society challenged as unconstitutional.
issues_decided: Whether the Haryana Legislature could constitutionally enact a law that nullifies prior judicial decrees recognizing private rights in village common lands.
Whether a legislative provision that directs executive authorities to disregard final civil court orders encroaches upon judicial power.
holdings: A legislature cannot render judicial decrees ineffective by a mere declaration that they are not binding; it can only do so by altering the legal basis on which those decrees were founded.
Provisions that require executive authorities to ignore final civil court decrees are unconstitutional as they encroach upon judicial power under the Constitution.
provisions: The Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Sections 2, 4, 5, 7, 13
The Punjab Village Lands (Regulation) Haryana Amendment Act, 1980, Sections 13-A, 13-B
doctrines: Separation of powers
Legislative competence to alter legal basis of judicial decisions
Unconstitutionality of laws attempting to override judicial decisions by declaration

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and the respondents (landowners) disputed whether a company's continued possession of leased agricultural land after the lease expired could trigger vesting of the land in the State under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, as amended in 1974.
issues_decided: Whether the company was a 'holder' of the land under Section 79-B of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, after the lease expired but possession continued.
Whether the company's declaration under Section 79-B was valid despite being mistakenly filed under Section 66.
Whether the continued possession of the company was lawful or unlawful for the purpose of vesting under the Act.
holdings: A company that continues in possession after the expiry of a lease retains juridical possession under Section 6 of the Act, making it a 'holder' subject to the prohibition on corporate landholding under Section 79-B.
A declaration filed under the wrong section (Section 66 instead of Section 79-B) does not invalidate the proceedings if the substance and purpose of Section 79-B are fulfilled.
The continued possession of a lessee company after lease expiry is lawful under the Act due to statutory protection under Section 6, which prevents termination of tenancy by efflux of time.
doctrines: Juridical possession
Statutory tenancy
Doctrine of substance over form
Legislative intent in agrarian reform

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's order removing the named arbitrator (Chief Engineer) and appointing an advocate as arbitrator in a construction dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the power to remove the named arbitrator and appoint a new one under the Arbitration Act
Whether the conduct of the party seeking removal of the arbitrator warranted such removal
Whether the arbitration agreement intended to restrict arbitration to the named technical expert only
holdings: The High Court erred in removing the named arbitrator as there was no sufficient lack of dispatch to justify removal under the Arbitration Act.
The delay by the arbitrator was not unjustified given the prolonged inaction by the party seeking removal, who failed to pursue arbitration diligently.
The parties intended the Chief Engineer, a technical expert, to be the sole arbitrator due to the technical nature of the dispute, and thus appointment of an advocate arbitrator is invalid.
doctrines: Doctrine of party autonomy in arbitration
Doctrine of reasonable dispatch in arbitral proceedings
Presumption of intent to fill vacancy in arbitration unless otherwise agreed

card.dispute: Tarun Bharat Sangh, a voluntary organization, sued the Union of India and others to stop illegal mining in the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan, alleging violations of environmental and forest protection laws.
issues_decided: Whether mining activities in the protected forest and tiger reserve areas of Alwar are illegal under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
Whether the mining leases granted within the protected forest were valid without prior central government approval
Whether the Central Government's notification under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, applies to the Sariska Tiger Reserve
Whether mining can continue in areas within the tiger reserve but outside the protected forest
holdings: Mining in areas declared as protected forest under the Rajasthan Forest Act, 1953, without prior central government approval under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, is illegal and must cease.
The Central Government's notification under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, validly prohibits mining in tiger reserves, including Sariska, without its prior permission.
