Mining leases granted after 1980 within protected forests without central approval are inherently illegal, regardless of state government action.
Mining outside protected forests but within the tiger reserve may continue for four months, subject to obtaining central government permission under the Environment (Protection) Act.
provisions: Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1986: Rule 4(6)
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Precautionary Principle
Sustainable Development
Doctrine of Illegality in Environmental Governance

card.dispute: Surendra Pal Singh challenged the Board of Revenue's power to set aside a final order in ceiling proceedings that had benefited his father, arguing the Board could not act suo motu against the State's interest.
issues_decided: Whether the Board of Revenue's power under Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 includes judicial superintendence over subordinate revenue courts.
Whether the Board could set aside an order in ceiling proceedings despite the State not appealing or revising it.
holdings: Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 vests the Board of Revenue with both administrative and judicial powers of superintendence over all revenue courts.
The Board can exercise its power under Section 221 to set aside an order with gross illegality even if the State did not appeal, provided it is in the interest of justice.
provisions: Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973
doctrines: General superintendence and control doctrine
Suo motu exercise of power in interest of justice
Illegality as ground for judicial intervention

card.dispute: The appellant claimed specific performance of agreements of reconveyance after purchasing the right of repurchase from the original vendees, but the respondents refused to execute the reconveyance deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a 'representative in interest' under Section 15(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, entitled to enforce the right of repurchase.
Whether the right of repurchase under the agreements (Exhibits A.3 and A.4) was assignable.
Whether the appellant could maintain a suit for specific performance of the agreement of sale against the original vendees.
holdings: A person who acquires the right of repurchase by assignment falls within the definition of 'representative in interest' under Section 15(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and can enforce the right against the original vendees.
A right of repurchase is assignable unless the agreement expressly or impliedly shows it to be personal to the original party; absence of such restriction allows assignment.

The assignee of a right of repurchase, who is ready and willing to perform, can sue for specific performance of the reconveyance even if the original period for repurchase differs from the enforcement period under the assignment.
doctrines: Assignment of contractual benefits
Representative in interest
Specific performance of assignable rights

card.dispute: The Union of India sought to be impleaded as a respondent in land acquisition compensation proceedings, which the landowners opposed.
issues_decided: Whether the Union of India is a 'person interested' under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and thus entitled to be impleaded in compensation reference proceedings.

Whether the decision in Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad v. Chandulal Shamaldas Patel conflicts with Himalayan Tiles & Marbles (P) Ltd. v. State of Himachal Pradesh and requires resolution by a larger bench.
holdings: The Union of India is a 'person interested' under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 when land is acquired for its use and it is liable to pay compensation, and thus has the right to be impleaded in proceedings affecting compensation.

The definition of 'person interested' under Section 18 must be liberally construed to include entities for whose benefit land is acquired and who are bound to pay compensation; Himalayan Tiles & Marbles case correctly states the law and overrules contrary views.
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'person interested'
Locus standi in land acquisition proceedings
Principles of equity, justice and good conscience

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for constructing a wall and door in the varandah without permission, impairing the building's value and utility.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's unauthorized construction materially impaired the value or utility of the building under Section 13(2)(iii) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether the Rent Controller failed to exercise discretion in granting eviction despite having discretion under Section 13(2).
Whether concurrent findings of fact by lower courts can be interfered with by the Supreme Court in a special leave petition.
holdings: A tenant is liable to eviction if their acts materially impair the building's value or utility from the landlord's perspective, and such impairment can be inferred from proven unauthorized constructions affecting light, air, and fixtures.
The Rent Controller properly exercised discretion under Section 13(2) since the tenant did not plead or prove mitigating circumstances warranting refusal of eviction.
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts, especially on inferential conclusions like material impairment, are not lightly overturned by the Supreme Court.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(3)
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact doctrine
Inferential fact doctrine
Discretionary relief under rent control statutes

card.dispute: The widows of Bachan Singh fought over whether his estate should pass under a registered will to his brother's son or devolve upon the widows as legal heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the registered will dated 30-3-1977 was duly executed in compliance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925
Whether the evidence of attesting witnesses was sufficient to prove the due execution of the will under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the concurrent findings of the lower courts on the credibility of the will
holdings: A will's due execution requires strict compliance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, including attestation by two witnesses in the presence of the testator.
Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, if attesting witnesses are available, one must be called to prove execution, and their inconsistent testimony cannot suffice.
The mere registration of a will does not dispense with the need for proof of due execution when the attesting witnesses contradict themselves and suspicious circumstances exist.
doctrines: Due execution of wills
Proof of attested documents
Concurrent findings rule

card.dispute: The petitioner sought to implead a person who acquired co-ownership of the disputed land through a separate decree as a necessary party in a pending suit for specific performance of a sale agreement to which she was not originally a party.
issues_decided: Whether a person who acquires interest in suit property through a court decree during the pendency of a suit for specific performance is a necessary or proper party under Order 1 Rule 10(2) CPC?
Whether Order 22 Rule 10 CPC applies when a person acquires interest by a decree rather than by devolution, assignment, or creation?
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to implead the respondent as a party defendant in the suit for specific performance?
holdings: A person who acquires co-ownership of property through a court decree during the pendency of a specific performance suit is not a necessary party under Order 22 Rule 10 CPC, as such acquisition does not amount to interest by devolution, assignment, or creation.
The respondent, not being a party to the sale agreement, cannot be considered a necessary party under Order 1 Rule 3 CPC, as no relief arises against her from the same transaction.

A person may be added as a proper party under Order 1 Rule 10(2) CPC only if their presence is necessary for complete adjudication; however, in a specific performance suit, such presence is not required if the agreement does not involve them.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1 Rule 10(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22 Rule 10
doctrines: Necessary and proper party doctrine under CPC
Doctrine of effective and complete adjudication
Doctrine of constructive res judicata under Section 43 of the Specific Relief Act

card.dispute: The appellant, Bhanwari Lal, sought execution of a decree for possession of immovable property, but faced obstruction from Satyanarain, a third party not bound by the decree, leading to disputes over the proper legal remedy and applicability of limitation and res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether an application for police assistance under Order 21, Rule 35(3) CPC can be treated as a valid application under Order 21, Rule 97 CPC when filed against a person not bound by the decree.
Whether the application filed on 25-5-1979 was barred by limitation under Article 129 of the Limitation Act.
Whether the subsequent applications were barred by res judicata after dismissal of the first application.
holdings: An application filed against a person not bound by the decree must be treated as one under Order 21, Rule 97 CPC, not Rule 35(3), and the court must consider its substance over form.
The application dated 25-5-1979 was maintainable and not barred by limitation, as it constituted a valid cause of action under Rule 97 at the time of filing.
The principles of res judicata do not apply to successive applications under Rule 97 when each obstruction creates a fresh cause of action.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 35(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 97
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 98 to 103
doctrines: Substance over form in legal pleadings
Fresh cause of action for each obstruction in execution proceedings
Limitation does not bar applications under Order 21, Rule 97 when timely resistance occurs
Res judicata does not apply to successive applications for removal of obstruction by third parties

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed the appellants' entitlement to a 1/4th share in compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, with the appellants seeking to produce delayed revenue records to prove title.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court was justified in rejecting the appellants' application to produce delayed documentary evidence under Order 13 Rule 1 of the CPC?
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the revision petition without properly considering the relevance of the delayed documents?
holdings: The trial court must receive relevant documents if produced before arguments conclude, especially public documents, and may condone delay under Order 13 Rule 1 CPC when justice so requires.
An appellate or revisional court must consider the relevance and importance of documents; failure to do so warrants setting aside the order and allowing admission of the documents.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 13 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Interest of justice
Condonation of delay
Relevance of documentary evidence

card.dispute: The Bombay Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA) and Gokak Patel Volkart Ltd. disputed whether the BMRDA could lawfully pass a fresh development permission order after a prior order was quashed by the High Court, and whether the statutory 60-day time limit under Section 13(3) of the BMRDA Act applied to such a fresh order.
issues_decided: Whether the deeming provision under Section 13(3) of the BMRDA Act applies when an order is passed within 60 days but later quashed by a court
Whether a fresh order passed on remand after quashing of the original order must comply with the 60-day time limit under Section 13(3)
Whether the fresh order passed by BMRDA is maintainable in law and subject to appeal rights under Section 13(3)
holdings: The deeming clause under Section 13(3) of the BMRDA Act applies only when no order is passed within 60 days; it does not apply if an order was passed and later quashed.

Once an order is passed within the statutory period and subsequently quashed, the requirement of time limitation is satisfied; a fresh order on remand need not be passed within the original 60-day period.
A fresh order passed pursuant to a court's direction is valid and appealable under Section 13(3), with limitation for appeal running from the date of the fresh order.
provisions: Bombay Metropolitan Region Development Act, 1974, Section 13(3)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, Section 13(bb)
doctrines: Deeming provision
Mandamus and certiorari in administrative law
Doctrine of laches
Jurisdiction to pass consequential orders after appellate intervention

card.dispute: The Revenue challenged whether Rule 1BB of the Wealth Tax Rules, 1957, which prescribes a method for valuing residential house property, is substantive or procedural and whether it applies to pending proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 1BB of the Wealth Tax Rules, 1957 is a substantive or procedural provision
Whether Rule 1BB applies to pending proceedings at the time of its enactment
holdings: Rule 1BB is procedural and not substantive, as it provides a method of valuation to ensure uniformity and does not alter vested rights.
Procedural rules apply to pending proceedings unless expressly excluded, so Rule 1BB applies retrospectively to pending cases.
doctrines: Distinction between substantive and procedural law
Presumption in favor of retrospective application of procedural laws
Rule of evidence and statutory presumptions in valuation

card.dispute: The landowner and tenant disputed over entitlement to compensation for land acquired by the state, depending on whether acquisition occurred before or after the tenant became deemed owner under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the landowner was entitled to compensation when the land was acquired after the tenant had become its deemed owner under Section 18(4) of the Tenures Act.
How the purchase price under Section 18 of the Tenures Act should be determined—by market value or statutory formula?
Whether the landowner, who received compensation for acquired land after losing interest in it, was liable to return the amount to the tenant.
holdings: If land is acquired after the tenant becomes deemed owner under Section 18(4), the landowner has no claim to compensation as their interest in the land has already ceased.

The purchase price under Section 18 of the Tenures Act must be calculated based on three-fourths of the average price of similar land in the neighborhood over the preceding ten years, not the market value at the time of acquisition.

A landowner who receives compensation for land in which they no longer hold an interest must repay the amount to the tenant, with interest, and such liability constitutes a debt enforceable against the landowner's estate.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 18
doctrines: Deemed ownership
Statutory interpretation of compensation entitlement
Apportionment of compensation based on prior rights

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority and a flat allottee disputed whether the allottee was liable to pay revised land rates notified after the draw of lots but before formal allotment.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in issuing the allotment-cum-demand letter was due to the inefficiency of the Delhi Development Authority.
Whether the respondent acquired a vested right to allotment at the land rates prevailing on the date of the draw of lots.
holdings: The three-month delay between the draw of lots and issuance of the allotment letter did not amount to inefficiency or inordinate delay, especially given the large number of flats involved and absence of a prescribed timeline in the scheme.

The draw of lots is merely a method of selecting allottees and does not create a vested right; the right to allotment arises only upon communication of the allotment letter, making the rates prevailing then applicable.
provisions: Registration Scheme of New Pattern, 1979, Clause (11) and Clause (14)
doctrines: Vested right doctrine
Principle of reasonable delay in administrative action

card.dispute: Petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993, and the maintainability of the President's reference to the Supreme Court under Article 143(1) regarding the Ayodhya dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993, is constitutionally valid?
Whether the Presidential Reference made under Article 143(1) of the Constitution is maintainable?
Whether the Supreme Court should answer the reference given the nature and purpose of the questions posed?
holdings: The Act was unconstitutional as it favored one religious community over another, violating the principle of secularism enshrined in the Constitution.

The Presidential Reference under Article 143(1) is maintainable in form, but the Court has the discretion to decline to answer if the reference undermines constitutional values or judicial credibility.

The Court refused to answer the reference because it was intended to be used as a tool for negotiation rather than genuine adjudication, and answering it without full adversarial hearing would compromise judicial integrity.
provisions: Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993 (Act No. 33 of 1993)
doctrines: Secularism as a basic feature of the Constitution
Judicial discretion under advisory jurisdiction
Principle of impartiality and adversarial hearing in judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The Corporation Bank challenged the High Court's decision restricting its right to charge compound interest with six-monthly rests on agricultural loans, arguing it was entitled to do so under banking regulations.
issues_decided: Whether a bank can charge compound interest with periodical rests on agricultural advances.
Whether banks must follow Reserve Bank of India (RBI) directives on interest structures issued under Section 21 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
Whether Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act bars courts from scrutinizing bank interest rates even if they contravene RBI directives.
Whether RBI directives can be considered 'special circumstances' under the Mysore Usurious Loans Act, 1923.
holdings: Banks cannot charge compound interest with quarterly or half-yearly rests on agricultural advances, as it is unfeasible given farmers' annual income cycle and contrary to RBI directives.
Banks are bound to follow RBI directives issued under Section 21 of the Banking Regulation Act, and charging interest contrary to such directives renders the excess interest illegal and void.

Section 21-A does not bar court intervention when interest charged exceeds rates prescribed by RBI; courts can disallow such excess interest despite the bar on challenging 'excessive' rates generally.

RBI directives issued under Section 21 have statutory force and may constitute 'special circumstances' under Explanation 1 to Section 3 of the Mysore Usurious Loans Act, 1923, though this point was not conclusively decided.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of banking regulations
Judicial non-interference in bank-customer transactions absent statutory violation
Primacy of regulatory directives in determining lawful interest structures
Distinction between excessive interest and interest contrary to regulatory directives

card.dispute: An association of cooperative societies and allottees of requisitioned commercial and residential premises in Maharashtra fought against the state's decision to derequisition and evict them from long-held properties.
issues_decided: Whether the continuance of requisition orders for several decades is legally permissible under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948
Whether the state can be directed to provide alternate accommodation to allottees of derequisitioned premises
Whether the eviction of cooperative societies running fair price shops and residential allottees would cause undue hardship warranting relief
holdings: Requisition orders under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 cannot continue indefinitely; their continuation for 30 years or more is unreasonable and unconstitutional.
The state is not legally obligated to provide alternate accommodation, but may do so based on administrative feasibility and public interest.

To mitigate hardship, eviction of cooperative societies and economically weaker residential allottees must be stayed until suitable alternative arrangements are made, with a deadline of 31 May 1996 for such measures.
doctrines: Unreasonableness in continued executive action
Mitigation of hardship in enforcement of legal rights
Judicial discretion to grant interim relief in public interest

card.dispute: The daughter (Jaibai) challenged the validity of a will by which her stepmother (a widow with a life interest) bequeathed property to a stranger (Gumpha), claiming the stepmother had only a life estate and could not transfer absolute ownership.
issues_decided: Whether a widow's life estate created under a will executed in 1941 gets enlarged into an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, when the succession opened after the Act came into force.
Whether property acquired by a female Hindu under a will falls within the purview of Section 14(1) or is excluded by Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
holdings: A life estate created under a will does not automatically become an absolute estate under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, if the property was acquired under a will that prescribed a restricted interest.

Section 14(2) excludes from the operation of Section 14(1) any property acquired under a will where the terms of the will create a restricted estate, and such exclusion prevails even if the female is in possession of the property.
doctrines: Doctrine of restricted estate under Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act
Legislative intent to not confer greater rights on females than males under testamentary dispositions
Interpretation of 'property' under Section 14 with reference to mode of acquisition

card.dispute: The original tenant, Gurjoginder Singh, fought to regain possession of rented premises after being evicted, following a subsequent tenant's claim of being a bona fide transferee from the landlord.
issues_decided: Whether a person inducted as a tenant by a decree-holder landlord after an ex parte eviction order can claim protection as a bona fide transferee against restitution of possession under Section 144 of the CPC.
Whether the principle protecting bona fide auction purchasers applies equally to a tenant granted possession by a decree-holder.
holdings: A tenant who takes possession from a decree-holder landlord does not have an independent title and can be dispossessed upon setting aside of the eviction decree, as his possession derives from the decree-holder.
The protection afforded to bona fide auction purchasers who are strangers to the litigation does not extend to tenants inducted by decree-holders, as their possession is dependent on the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Doctrine of restitution under Section 144 CPC
Distinction between bona fide purchaser in auction and transferee under decree-holder

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, arguing that the market value should be based on the Basic Valuation Register used for stamp duty, which valued the land at Rs 300 per sq. yard.
issues_decided: Whether the Basic Valuation Register maintained under the Indian Stamp Act can be used to determine the market value of land under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act
Whether the fixation of compensation at Rs 75 per sq. yard was arbitrary and unjust
Whether the landowner is entitled to interest at 6% under the Land Acquisition Act
holdings: The Basic Valuation Register has no statutory foundation and cannot be used as a basis to determine market value under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act.
Market value must be determined based on actual sale transactions between willing buyers and sellers, or other reliable evidence, not on administrative valuations for stamp duty.
The interest rate for compensation is governed by the applicable State rules, and no discrimination is established in paying 4% instead of 6%.
provisions: Constitution of India, List III (Concurrent List), Entry 44
doctrines: Market value determination in land acquisition
Statutory basis for administrative valuation
Principle of just compensation
Burden of proof in land acquisition claims

card.dispute: Jay Laxmi Salt Works (P) Ltd. sued the State of Gujarat for damages due to negligence in constructing a reclamation bundh, leading to flooding of its factory, and the dispute centered on whether the claim was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether Article 36 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applies exclusively to all tort claims including those based on negligence or strict liability
Whether the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher is governed by Article 36 or another provision of the Limitation Act
From which point the period of limitation begins to run in tort claims involving delayed discovery of damage
holdings: Article 36 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is not exhaustive of all torts and does not exclusively govern claims based on negligence, strict liability, or breach of public duty; Article 120 applies to broader tortious liability.
The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher has not been modified in Indian law and remains distinct, but the applicable limitation period depends on the nature of the wrong and the duty violated.
In tort cases involving latent damage, the limitation period under Article 36 begins to run not from the act of negligence but from the date the damage occurs or the claim is rejected by authorities.
doctrines: Rule in Rylands v. Fletcher
Strict liability
Public duty doctrine
Residuary nature of limitation provisions
Cause of action accrual in tort

card.dispute: The dispute was between earlier and subsequent purchasers of property, where the earlier purchasers sued for specific performance of a sale agreement, and the subsequent purchasers challenged the suit on grounds of the plaintiffs' readiness and willingness to perform.
issues_decided: Whether the subsequent purchasers (petitioners) could raise the plea that the plaintiff was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Whether the trial court and High Court were correct in rejecting the petitioners' contention on the readiness and willingness of the plaintiff.
holdings: The plea of plaintiff's readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is personal to the vendor/defendant and cannot be raised by subsequent purchasers.
Subsequent purchasers, even if necessary parties, can only defend their title on the basis of being bona fide purchasers without notice, not on the plaintiff’s alleged lack of readiness to perform.
doctrines: Personal equity in specific performance
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Necessary party in a suit for specific performance

card.dispute: The landlord (Kamla Devi) sought eviction of the tenant (Vasdev) for non-payment of rent arrears, and challenged the Rent Controller's discretion in handling the default.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has mandatory or discretionary power to strike out a tenant's defence under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 upon failure to pay rent arrears.
Whether the Rent Controller can condone a tenant's delay in payment or extend the time for compliance with a deposit order.
holdings: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 grants the Rent Controller discretionary, not mandatory, power to strike out a tenant's defence for non-payment of rent arrears.
The Rent Controller has the implied power to condone a tenant's delay in payment or extend the time for compliance, based on the facts and circumstances of the case.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13
doctrines: Discretionary power of quasi-judicial authorities
Directory vs. mandatory provisions
Condonation of delay by statutory authorities

card.dispute: The Kerala State Housing Board and the State challenged the High Court's decision regarding the validity of a compensation agreement and the Collector's power to make an award under it after a delay in land acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector retained the power to make an award under Section 16(1) of the Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961 after a significant delay following the agreement on compensation.
What is the correct interpretation of 'such date' in the proviso to Section 16(1) — whether it refers to the date of the agreement or the date of the notification under Section 3(1).
Whether the agreement on compensation remains enforceable after the statutory period for making an award has expired.
holdings: The Collector's power under Section 16(1) to make an award in terms of the agreement ceases after four years from the date of the agreement, as per the proviso, to prevent arbitrariness and injustice.

'Such date' in the proviso to Section 16(1) must be interpreted as referring to the date of the agreement, not the notification under Section 3(1), to avoid unconstitutional delay and ensure fairness.
An agreement under Section 16(1) remains valid but becomes unenforceable after the statutory period; it can still be used as evidence of market value, though not binding on the civil court.
provisions: Kerala Land Acquisition Act, 1961, Section 16(1) and proviso
doctrines: Principle of constitutional avoidance
Harmonious construction of statutes
Reasonable time for administrative action
Evidentiary value of lapsed agreements

card.dispute: The appellant claimed title by prescription over land transferred in violation of grant conditions, while the respondent sought restoration of the land under the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could acquire title by adverse possession over land transferred in contravention of statutory restrictions?
Whether the proceedings under Section 42 of the Karnataka Act were valid in the absence of notice to tenants in possession?
holdings: A person cannot acquire title by adverse possession over land transferred in violation of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978, as such transfers are null and void and do not confer valid title for prescription.

Proceedings under Section 42 of the Act are invalid if conducted without notice to tenants or other 'interested parties' whose rights may be affected, as the proviso to Section 42 mandates compliance with principles of natural justice.
provisions: Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978, Section 42
Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Doctrine of nullity of transactions contrary to statutory prohibitions
Interpretation of 'interested parties' in administrative proceedings

card.dispute: The dispute was between Neyvely Lignite Corporation Ltd. and the Special Tahsildar (Land Acquisition) over whether the corporation, as a beneficiary of land acquisition, was an 'interested person' entitled to participate in compensation proceedings and appeal against enhanced awards.
issues_decided: Whether the beneficiary of land acquisition (a company) is an 'interested person' under Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether such a beneficiary has the right to adduce evidence, be heard, and file an appeal under Section 54 of the Act.
Whether the beneficiary can challenge an award of enhanced compensation through a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
holdings: A beneficiary company is an 'interested person' under Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and has the right to be heard and participate in compensation proceedings.
The right to be heard includes the right to adduce evidence before the Collector and the reference court, and to file an appeal under Section 54 if the State fails to do so.
Denial of such rights violates principles of natural justice and Article 14 of the Constitution, as the beneficiary bears the financial burden of compensation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Right to fair procedure
Doctrine of necessary and proper parties
Doctrine of effective remedy under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over whether the High Court could review its earlier decision allowing partition of a jointly claimed plot (C.S. Plot No. 74) based on alleged errors apparent on the record.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in exercise of its review jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC, could re-appreciate evidence and reverse findings of a prior Division Bench decision in a second appeal?
Whether an error in the earlier Division Bench's reasoning regarding title and possession of C.S. Plot No. 74 amounted to an error apparent on the face of the record justifying review?
holdings: The High Court cannot, under review jurisdiction, re-appreciate evidence or sit as an appellate court; review is limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of the record, not re-evaluating findings.
A mere difference of opinion or alleged erroneous conclusion does not constitute an error apparent on the face of the record; the earlier Division Bench’s decision could not be overturned in review.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47, Rule 1
doctrines: Limited scope of review
Error apparent on the face of the record
Finality of judicial decisions

card.dispute: Petitioners alleged that the State of Uttar Pradesh and its Chief Minister, Kalyan Singh, willfully disobeyed court orders regarding the acquisition of land in Ayodhya.
issues_decided: Whether the State and its Ministers can be held liable for contempt of court for failing to comply with judicial orders.
Whether the Chief Minister of a State can be held personally liable for contempt in his official and personal capacity.
Whether an undertaking given by a Chief Minister to the court binds the State and is enforceable through contempt proceedings.
holdings: The State and its executive, including Ministers, are amenable to contempt proceedings for willful disobedience of court orders, as the judiciary enforces the law against the executive to uphold the rule of law.
A Minister can be held liable in contempt in both official and personal capacity; if the violation involves a personal element or a flagrant breach of an undertaking, personal liability may arise.
An undertaking given by a Chief Minister to the court is binding on both the individual and the government, and its breach constitutes willful disobedience warranting contempt action.
doctrines: Rule of law
Contempt of court
Separation of powers
Executive accountability to judiciary

card.dispute: The legal heirs and family members of Naraindas Lilaram Adnani fought over the ownership and possession of three properties, including whether certain properties were personal or partnership assets and entitlement to possession following an arbitration award.
issues_decided: Whether the Arbitrator's award regarding the Narain Niwas property was defective for not granting possession and could be corrected by the court
Whether the tenancy rights in Room No. 13, Vasantwadi, were a partnership asset and how the dispute over shared ownership should be resolved
Whether possession of the Ganeshpuri property should be handed over to respondents 1 and 2 despite the appellant's ownership interest
holdings: The Arbitrator's failure to grant possession of Narain Niwas was due to a mistaken belief that the Bombay Rent Act applied; this error could be corrected under Section 15(b) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, without affecting the substance of the award.

The tenancy rights in Room No. 13 are jointly owned, and the parties must follow a valuation and buyout mechanism: the appellant shall value the property, and respondents 1 and 2 may either pay his share or receive monetary compensation for their shares.
The appellant has no objection to handing over possession of the Ganeshpuri property to respondents 1 and 2, who are co-owners with equal shares, and must do so within four weeks.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22, Rule 3
doctrines: Correction of obvious errors in arbitral awards
Finality of arbitral awards
Substitution of legal representatives in pending proceedings

card.dispute: The judgment-debtor sought to set aside a court-ordered sale after the limitation period had expired, which the auction purchaser challenged.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order 21 Rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside a sale is maintainable after the expiry of the limitation period under Article 127 of the Limitation Act?
Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act applies to an application under Order 21 Rule 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
Whether Section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure can extend the time for filing an application under Order 21 Rule 89?
holdings: An application under Order 21 Rule 89 of the CPC to set aside a sale must be filed within the 60-day limitation period from the date of sale as prescribed by Article 127 of the Limitation Act; after expiry, the court lacks jurisdiction to entertain it.

Section 5 of the Limitation Act, which allows condonation of delay, does not apply to applications under Order 21 of the CPC, including Rule 89, as it is expressly excluded by the provision's language.
Section 148 of the CPC, which allows extension of court-granted time, does not apply because the time for filing an application under Order 21 Rule 89 is fixed by statute, not by court order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90
doctrines: Statutory limitation bars jurisdiction
Exclusion of Section 5 of the Limitation Act for specified applications under Order 21 CPC
Distinction between statutory time and court-extended time under Section 148 CPC

card.dispute: The petitioner, an agent and power of attorney holder, purchased property in his own name at a court auction meant for his principal, the respondent, who claimed the purchase was made fraudulently without her consent and sought declaration of title and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the title to the property purchased at court auction vests in the agent or the principal when the agent acted in a fiduciary capacity
Whether a suit for declaration of title is maintainable despite Section 66(1) of the CPC
Whether the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 bars a claim by the principal where the agent holds property in a fiduciary capacity
holdings: The property purchased by an agent in his own name at court auction, using the principal's funds and without consent, vests in the principal as the agent holds it in fiduciary capacity under Section 88 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882.

A suit for declaration of title is maintainable under Section 66(2) of CPC when the name of the purchaser was inserted fraudulently or without the real purchaser's consent, despite the bar in Section 66(1).

Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not apply where the property is held by a person in a fiduciary capacity for another, as carved out by exception under Section 3(3)(b) of the Act.
provisions: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, Section 3(3)(b), Section 4, Section 7
doctrines: Fiduciary agency
Constructive trust
Fraud exception to statutory bar
Benami transaction exception for fiduciary holders

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant fought against eviction by landlords, claiming protection under Section 106 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act due to a commercial lease and prior construction, while landlords argued res judicata and estoppel based on earlier proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the eviction suit or was required to refer the tenant's claim under Section 106 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act to the Land Tribunal under Section 125(3)

Whether the tenant was barred by constructive res judicata from raising the plea under Section 106 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act in the civil suit after not raising it in earlier rent control proceedings
Whether the tenant was estopped from raising a plea under Section 106 after having unsuccessfully pursued relief under Section 72-B of the same Act
holdings: The civil court was not barred from deciding the eviction suit; it could proceed without referring the issue to the Land Tribunal because the plea under Section 106 was not raised in prior proceedings where it ought to have been.
A plea that could and should have been raised in earlier proceedings is deemed constructively res judicata, and the tenant cannot raise it for the first time in a later stage to avoid eviction.
By choosing to pursue relief under Section 72-B and failing to raise the Section 106 claim, the tenant waived the right to raise inconsistent pleas later, amounting to estoppel by conduct.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11, Explanation IV
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Estoppel by conduct
Waiver of legal pleas
Jurisdictional bar under special statutes

card.dispute: The landlords sued for ejectment of tenants on grounds of bona fide requirement, which the High Court reversed due to lack of specific pleadings; the landlords appealed.
issues_decided: Whether specific pleading regarding the nature of business is necessary to establish bona fide requirement for ejectment?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's decree for ejectment?
holdings: It is not necessary for landlords to plead the precise nature of the business they intend to start to prove bona fide requirement.
The High Court erred in reversing the trial court's decision solely for lack of details about the business; the trial court's decree is restored.
provisions: Bihar and Orissa Tenancy Act, 1920, Section 13(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 1
doctrines: Liberal construction of pleadings
Substantial justice over technicalities

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of the tenant, who denied their title and claimed the documents were executed under undue influence, leading to a dispute over whether ad valorem court fees based on the property's market value were required.
issues_decided: Whether the suit should be valued for court fees based on the rent or on the market value of the property when the tenant disputes the landlord's title.
Whether the requirement to pay ad valorem court fees arises when the title is contested in a landlord-tenant eviction suit.
holdings: For determining court fees, the plaint alone governs; the suit must be valued based on the relief sought and averments made, not on the defendant's denial of title.
A suit for eviction remains one for recovery of possession, and court fees under Section 7 of the Court Fees Act, 1870, are based on rent, not market value, even if title is disputed.
doctrines: Plaint governs valuation for court fees
Incidental determination of title does not require ad valorem court fees

card.dispute: The husband and wife sought mutual divorce after living separately for over three years, with disputes over property settlement and maintenance.
issues_decided: Whether the court can grant a divorce decree based on mutual consent despite the marriage having irretrievably broken down without formal petition by both parties.
Whether property and maintenance can be settled by agreed terms in a divorce decree.
holdings: The Supreme Court can grant a divorce decree in cases of irretrievable breakdown of marriage when both parties jointly request it, even if only one party filed the original petition.
The court may approve a divorce decree on agreed terms including property division and waiver of maintenance, provided it ensures complete justice between the parties.
doctrines: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage
Mutual consent divorce
Complete justice doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant judgment-debtor sought to rescind a contract for sale of immovable property on the ground that the respondent failed to deposit the balance consideration within the time fixed by the appellate decree, leading to a dispute over whether such a remedy is available on the execution side.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is maintainable on the execution side when the decree for specific performance was passed by an appellate court.
Whether the court in which the original suit was filed can entertain an application for rescission under Section 28 of the Act even during execution proceedings.
holdings: An application under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is maintainable in the same court where the original suit was filed, even during execution, but must be treated as an interlocutory application on the original side, not on the execution side.

The court retains jurisdiction to grant relief under Section 28(1) of the Act, including extension of time or rescission, after decree, and such application should not be dismissed merely because it is filed on the execution side if the court has the power to transfer or treat it appropriately.
doctrines: Continuation of suit doctrine
Substantial justice over technicalities
Court's retained jurisdiction post-decree

card.dispute: The appellant Ram Kumar challenged his conviction for murder and attempt to murder, claiming wrongful reversal of his acquittal by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of the appellant by the Sessions Court?
Whether the testimony of eyewitnesses Kamla (PW 3) and Rajinder (PW 4) is reliable despite non-reporting to village authorities on the night of the incident?
Whether the prosecution failed to prove the involvement of the appellant in the offences under Section 302/34 and 307/34 IPC?
holdings: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal as the trial court's rejection of eyewitness testimony was based on unreasonable and trivial grounds.

The failure of eyewitnesses to inform village authorities immediately after the incident does not discredit their testimony, especially given the fear and circumstances of a winter night murder in a familial dispute.
The consistent and corroborated testimony of eyewitnesses, supported by medical evidence, proves the appellant's guilt under Sections 302/34 and 307/34 IPC beyond reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Perverse finding
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration through medical evidence
Presumption of guilt when evidence overwhelmingly supports conviction

card.dispute: The appellants, successors of Barkhalidars and Girasdars, challenged the constitutional validity of the Gujarat Amendment Act that abolished their land tenure rights and provided for compensation based on pre-1960 income, claiming violations of Articles 14, 21, and 300A of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 69A(4) of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as amended, violates Article 14 by providing allegedly illusory and arbitrary compensation for expropriated mineral rights?
Whether the fixation of compensation based on the average net annual income from three years preceding May 1, 1960, violates the right to property under Article 300A?
Whether the differential compensation mechanisms across statutes result in discriminatory treatment under Article 14?
Whether the procedure for deprivation of property under the Amendment Act offends Article 21?
holdings: The principle of determining compensation based on the average net annual income from the three years preceding vesting in 1960 is not arbitrary or illusory and bears a reasonable relation to the object of the law, thus not violating Article 14.

After the 44th Amendment, the right to property is no longer a fundamental right; therefore, the deprivation of property under Article 300A does not require payment of full market value or just equivalent, and the compensation scheme is valid.

Different compensation mechanisms in different statutes do not amount to discrimination under Article 14 if each bears a rational relation to the object of the legislation; comparative analysis cannot invalidate a validly enacted scheme.

Article 21 does not apply to the determination of compensation in property acquisition cases under Article 300A, as the procedure for deprivation of property is governed by statute and not personal rights under life and liberty.
provisions: The Bombay Land Revenue Code and Land Tenure Abolition Laws (Gujarat Amendment) Act, 8 of 1982
doctrines: Doctrine of Reasonable Classification
Doctrine of Eclipse
Doctrine of Harmonious Construction
Principle of Non-Retrospective Devaluation in Compensation
Integrated Scheme Doctrine in Nationalisation

card.dispute: The appellants, former owners of surplus land declared under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, challenged the vesting of that land in the State of Haryana under the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, claiming entitlement to retain it due to family changes and continued possession.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could retain possession of surplus land declared under the 1953 Punjab Act after the Haryana Ceiling Act, 1972 came into force
Whether the vesting of surplus land under Section 12(3) of the Haryana Act was affected by prior exemption under Rule 8 of the 1953 Act
Whether the ceiling authority could reopen final surplus land determinations under the 1953 Act due to changes in family composition
holdings: Surplus land declared under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, stood vested in the State of Haryana under Section 12(3) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, irrespective of continued possession by the appellants.
Exemption under Rule 8 allowing continued use of surplus land was nullified by Section 32 of the Haryana Act, making possession unlawful from the appointed date.
Final surplus land determinations under the 1953 Act could not be reopened under the 1972 Act, even if minors became majors or family units changed.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 2(5)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 7
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 9
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 12(3)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 32
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 33(2)(ii)
doctrines: Vesting of property by operation of law
Finality of administrative orders
Non-reopening of concluded proceedings
Statutory exemption withdrawal

card.dispute: House-owners challenged the revision of property tax by the Belgaum Municipal Corporation in 1984, claiming it was arbitrary and illegal, while the Corporation argued the civil court lacked jurisdiction due to an alternative statutory remedy.
issues_decided: Whether the civil suit challenging the revision of property tax is barred by Rule 25 of Part I of Schedule III of the Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976?
Whether the remedy of appeal under the Act is inadequate, thereby making a civil suit maintainable?
Whether allegations of excessive, arbitrary, or unreasonable tax enhancement are sufficient to bypass the statutory bar on civil court jurisdiction?
holdings: A civil suit is not maintainable if a statute provides an adequate alternative remedy and finality to orders of a statutory authority, unless there is non-compliance with fundamental statutory provisions or violation of principles of natural justice.

The onerous requirement of depositing full tax before appeal does not render the statutory remedy inadequate for the purpose of maintaining a civil suit, though it may justify a writ petition under Article 226.

Mere allegations of excessive, arbitrary, or unreasonable tax enhancement, without pleading non-compliance with statutory provisions or mala fides, are insufficient to override the statutory bar on civil court jurisdiction.
provisions: Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976, Rule 25, Part I, Schedule III
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction when adequate statutory remedies exist
Dhulabhai v. State of M.P. principles on civil court jurisdiction in tax matters
Distinction between writ jurisdiction under Article 226 and civil suit jurisdiction
Requirement of fundamental non-compliance with statute to bypass finality clauses

card.dispute: Government employees in categories (iii) and (vi) challenged their exclusion from priority allotment of government housing under a hire purchase scheme.
issues_decided: Whether employees who voluntarily vacated government quarters at Pahari, Ahmedabad, to move to better accommodation in Gandhinagar (category iii) are entitled to priority in hire purchase allotment.
Whether employees transferred permanently outside Ahmedabad (category vi) are eligible for allotment under the hire purchase scheme.
Whether the exclusion of these categories violates Article 14 or Article 21 of the Constitution.
holdings: Employees who voluntarily vacated their allotted quarters for better accommodation cannot claim priority in the hire purchase scheme as they no longer have a continuing residential link with the premises.

Employees transferred permanently outside Ahmedabad lost their entitlement to allotment at Pahari, as the June 22, 1972 resolution fixed eligibility based on residence at the time of conversion to hire purchase.

The exclusion of categories (iii) and (vi) does not violate Article 14 or 21, as the classification is based on rational criteria and the right to housing under Article 21 does not override scheme-specific eligibility conditions.
doctrines: Right to life under Article 21 includes right to livelihood and shelter
Principle of reasonable classification under Article 14
Harmonious construction of fundamental rights and directive principles
Rational nexus test for equality claims

card.dispute: The landlord, Smt. Kamla Devi, sought eviction of tenant Shri Vasdev for non-payment of rent arrears, after the Rent Controller ordered eviction following the tenant's failure to comply with a payment direction.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has mandatory or discretionary power under Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 to strike out a tenant's defence for non-payment of rent arrears?
Whether the Rent Controller can condone a tenant's delay or extend time for payment of arrears under Section 15(1) of the Act?
holdings: Section 15(7) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 confers discretionary, not mandatory, power on the Rent Controller to strike out a tenant's defence for failure to pay arrears; the power must be exercised judiciously, not mechanically.

The Rent Controller has implied power to condone a tenant's default and extend time for payment under Section 15(1), as the discretion to not strike out defence includes the power to grant relief from strict compliance.
doctrines: Discretionary power under penal provisions
Implied power to condone delay
Directory vs mandatory interpretation
Judicial discretion in eviction proceedings

card.dispute: Smt. Ramti Devi fought the Union of India over ownership of a property in Delhi, claiming she was the absolute owner and challenging the validity of a 1947 sale deed executed by Shri Ratti Ram.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaration of ownership and invalidity of the 1947 sale deed was within the period of limitation
Whether the 1947 sale deed could be treated as void ab initio for being executed to stifle prosecution
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation under Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963, as the cause of action arose when the plaintiff became aware of the sale deed in 1947, and the suit was filed in 1966, well beyond the three-year period.

A registered sale deed, even if allegedly executed to stifle prosecution, cannot be ignored without a formal declaration of cancellation; oral evidence or mere pleading cannot render it void under Section 23 of the Contract Act without a judicial finding.
doctrines: Doctrine of limitation for cancellation of instruments
Doctrine of inadmissibility of oral evidence to contradict written documents under Section 92 of the Evidence Act
Requirement of formal declaration to set aside registered documents

card.dispute: The State Bank of Bikaner & Jaipur and the Commercial Taxes Officer, Bharatpur, disputed over priority in recovering dues from the sale proceeds of mortgaged property, with the bank claiming precedence due to an earlier mortgage and the officer asserting priority under a statutory first charge for sales tax.
issues_decided: Whether Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 gives a statutory first charge that prevails over an earlier mortgage on the same property.
Whether the statutory charge under Section 11-AAAA operates only on the equity of redemption or on the entire property, including the mortgagee's interest.
holdings: A statutory first charge created under Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 operates on the entire property of the dealer, not merely on the equity of redemption, and thus takes precedence over an earlier mortgage.
The phrase 'first charge' in Section 11-AAAA means the charge is prior to all other interests, including those of a mortgagee, even if the mortgage was created before the tax liability arose.
doctrines: Statutory charge prevails over prior equitable or legal interests
First charge doctrine
Priority of tax dues over private creditors

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka and Shankara Textiles Mills Ltd disputed over when agricultural land held by the company vested in the State Government under the Karnataka Land Revenue Act.
issues_decided: Whether the date of vesting of agricultural land in the State Government under Section 79-B(3) of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act is the date the provision came into force or the date of the Deputy Commissioner's notification?
Whether the High Court's interpretation of Section 79-B(3), relying on Mysore Feeds Ltd., was correct?
holdings: The date of vesting of agricultural land in the State Government under Section 79-B(3) is 1-3-1974, the date the provision came into force, not the date of the Deputy Commissioner's notification.
The High Court's decision relying on Mysore Feeds Ltd. was incorrect and is overruled; the language of Section 79-B(3) clearly fixes vesting from the commencement date.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Legislative intent
Scheme of the Act as a guide to interpretation

card.dispute: The State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur and the Commercial Taxes Officer, Bharatpur, disputed over priority in recovering dues from the sale proceeds of mortgaged property belonging to National Iron and Steel Rolling Corporation.
issues_decided: Whether Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 gives a statutory first charge that prevails over an earlier mortgage on the same property.
Whether the statutory charge under Section 11-AAAA operates only on the equity of redemption or on the entire property, including the mortgagee's interest.
holdings: A statutory first charge created under Section 11-AAAA of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 has priority over an earlier mortgage, even if the mortgage was created prior to the liability for sales tax.
The statutory charge under Section 11-AAAA applies to the entire property of the dealer, including all interests and estates, and is not limited to the mortgagor's equity of redemption.
doctrines: Statutory charge prevails over prior equitable or legal interests
First charge by operation of law
Priority of tax dues over private creditors

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh fought against S.B.P.V. Chalapathi Rao over whether 220.25 acres of land sold before the enactment of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act should be included in computing his ceiling area.
issues_decided: Whether the land transfers made by the respondent were in anticipation of and intended to defeat the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973
Whether the Appellate Tribunal was justified in reversing the Land Reforms Tribunal's finding that the sales were made to evade the Act
Whether the bona fide nature of the sale and existence of consideration are sufficient to exclude the transferred land from ceiling area under the Act
holdings: Under Section 7(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973, a transfer of land made between January 24, 1971 and May 2, 1972 is disregarded for ceiling purposes if it was made in anticipation of or to defeat the Act, regardless of its genuineness or good faith.
The burden lies on the transferor to prove a compelling reason or necessity for the sale; absence of such necessity leads to the inference that the sale was intended to circumvent the Act.

The Appellate Tribunal erred in law by reversing the Tribunal's finding, as the timing and scale of the sale—over 220 acres in December 1971, before any licence for industrial expansion was granted—supports the conclusion that the sale was made to avoid the Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 7(1)
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 21
doctrines: Presumption against transactions made in anticipation of legislation
Burden of proof on transferor to show necessity under Section 7(1)
Non-applicability of 'good faith' and 'adequate consideration' as standalone defenses under the Act

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Special Land Acquisition Officer and landowners over the adequacy of compensation awarded for 60 acres of land acquired for industrial development.
issues_decided: Whether the Civil Court erred in relying solely on a single small land sale deed to determine market value of acquired land?
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing compensation without considering voluntary settlements for similar lands?
Whether the compensation determined by the Land Acquisition Officer was adequate based on prevailing market conditions and comparable transactions?
holdings: The Civil Court erred in basing market value on a single uncorroborated sale deed of 3 guntas without examining the parties or considering larger comparable sales.
The High Court wrongly enhanced compensation while ignoring that owners of 240 acres (four-fifths) of similar land accepted Rs. 4,000 per acre under a voluntary settlement.
The award of Rs. 4,000–4,500 per acre by the Land Acquisition Officer was valid and supported by evidence of actual settlements and average sale prices in the area.
provisions: Karnataka Industrial Area Development Act, 1966, Section 28(1)
Karnataka Industrial Area Development Act, 1966, Section 29(2)
doctrines: Principle of comparable sales in land valuation
Doctrine of judicial review of compensation awards
Relevance of voluntary settlements in determining market value

card.dispute: The State of Haryana challenged the High Court's decision invalidating land acquisition due to non-publication of the substance of Section 6 declaration in the locality, while the landowner argued that such publication was mandatory.
issues_decided: Whether publication of the substance of the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act in the locality is mandatory and whether delay in such publication invalidates the notification.
Whether publication of the substance of the declaration under Section 6(2) in the locality is mandatory and whether its omission invalidates the acquisition.
holdings: Publication of the substance of the Section 4(1) notification in the locality is mandatory to ensure landowners receive notice, but delay in such publication does not invalidate the notification if substantial compliance is shown.

The requirement under Section 6(2) to publish the declaration's substance in the locality is directory, not mandatory; non-compliance does not invalidate the acquisition unless prejudice is proven, especially when the landowner participated in later proceedings.
doctrines: Mandatory vs. directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Substantial compliance doctrine
Presumption of regularity in administrative action
Prejudice test in procedural non-compliance

card.dispute: The State of Mizoram challenged the jurisdiction of the civil court to entertain a suit for enhanced compensation after the respondent received compensation under protest but no reference was made under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to decide a claim for enhanced compensation without a valid reference by the Collector under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the filing of a civil suit is maintainable in place of a statutory reference under Section 18 when compensation is accepted under protest?
holdings: A valid reference by the Collector under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act is a mandatory precondition for the civil court to acquire jurisdiction to determine a dispute over compensation.
The civil court cannot entertain a regular suit for enhanced compensation when the remedy lies under the special procedure of the Land Acquisition Act; such a suit is not maintainable.
doctrines: Statutory ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Mandatory compliance with procedural prerequisites
Substance over form in statutory interpretation (rejected in this context)

card.dispute: The State of Orissa appealed against the Orissa High Court's order granting bail to Rajendra Prasad Bharadia and Purakh Chand Chandak, who were charged with murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the respondents in a case involving serious charges under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC
Whether the prosecution had established a strong prima facie case against the respondents to oppose bail
holdings: The appeal was allowed and the High Court's order granting bail was set aside, as the case involved serious charges of murder with a possible common intention, warranting custodial investigation and trial.
The respondents were not entitled to bail at that stage because the prosecution had made out a prima facie case against them based on the available evidence, including dying declarations.
doctrines: Principle of prima facie case in bail matters
Test of gravity of offence and likelihood of tampering with evidence

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's direction to take possession of acquired land and pay compensation based on an award allegedly made on 20-12-1992, which the State contended was only a 'proposed award' lacking mandatory prior approval and thus invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Officer made a valid award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 by 20-12-1992?
Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 11-A due to non-making of an award within two years from the declaration under Section 6?
Whether prior approval from the appropriate government or authorised officer is a condition precedent for the validity of an award under Section 11?
holdings: An award under Section 11 is not valid unless made with prior approval of the appropriate government or authorised officer where required by the proviso to Section 11.
A 'proposed award' sent for approval but not approved before the two-year deadline under Section 11-A does not constitute a valid award, and the acquisition proceedings lapse.
Section 11-A imposes a mandatory time limit; failure to make a valid award within two years from the date of the Section 6 declaration causes the entire acquisition process to lapse.
doctrines: Condition precedent
Mandatory statutory time limit
Lapse of acquisition proceedings
Jurisdictional validity of administrative action

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the enhanced compensation awarded for land acquired for a Panchayat Office building, disputing the method used to determine market value.
issues_decided: Whether the method of averaging sale prices from different transactions and times was valid for determining market value under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
What was the just and reasonable market value of the acquired land as of the date of acquisition?
holdings: The court held that averaging sale prices from different lands, at different times, and under different conditions is not a legally sound method to determine market value in land acquisition cases.

The court held that the market value of the acquired land should be fixed at Rs 100 per marla, considering the agreed benchmark transaction and subsequent development, with 15% solatium and 6% interest from possession to payment.
doctrines: Principle of bona fide sale transactions for market value determination
Rule against averaging disparate sale transactions
Compensation based on willing buyer-willing seller in normal market conditions

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the Allahabad High Court's decision setting aside the conviction of respondents for disobeying a magisterial order, on the ground that the complaint was filed by a successor magistrate, not the 'public servant concerned'.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'the public servant concerned' in Section 195(1)(a)(i) of the Code of Criminal Procedure includes a successor in office of the public servant who passed the order?
Whether a complaint under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC is maintainable if filed by a successor magistrate rather than the original magistrate who passed the order?
holdings: The expression 'public servant concerned' in Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC includes the successor in office of the public servant who passed the order, as the successor steps into the same legal position.

A complaint under Section 195(1)(a)(i) CrPC for disobedience of a magisterial order is maintainable when filed by a successor magistrate, especially when the original magistrate is no longer in office.
doctrines: Successor in office doctrine
Mandatory nature of Section 195 CrPC
Judicial continuity in magisterial proceedings

card.dispute: The dispute was between Styabrata Biswas and Kalyan Kumar Kisku over whether a sub-tenancy created after a status quo order was valid and whether the lower courts exceeded their jurisdiction in allowing possession to the sub-tenant.
issues_decided: Whether the creation of a sub-tenancy after a status quo order dated September 15, 1988 was valid?
Whether the lower courts acted within their contempt jurisdiction in directing possession to Somani Builders?
Whether the status quo order applied to the state of affairs as of September 15, 1988, and not to a later date?
holdings: A sub-tenancy created after a status quo order is illegal and cannot be recognized, as it violates the court's directive to maintain the existing state of affairs.
Lower courts exceed their contempt jurisdiction when they adjudicate rights of third parties or confer possession without proper legal basis in contempt proceedings.
The status quo to be preserved is the state of affairs as of the date of the order—September 15, 1988—and not any subsequent condition.
provisions: Supreme Court of India Act, 1957, Article 136
doctrines: Status quo ante
Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Contempt jurisdiction limits

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu challenged the Madras High Court's declaration that Section 52-A of the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864 was ultra vires, arguing it had legislative competence to authorize recovery of loans given by state-owned corporations as arrears of land revenue.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Legislature had the legislative competence to enact Section 52-A of the Revenue Recovery Act, 1864?
Whether the Collector acting under the Act qualifies as a 'revenue court' for the purpose of recovering dues?
Whether Section 52-A falls within the legislative domain of the State under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution?
holdings: The State Legislature has the power to confer jurisdiction on revenue courts to recover public dues as arrears of land revenue under Entry 11-A, List III of the Seventh Schedule.
The Collector under the Act exercises judicial powers of the State in resolving disputes between the government and defaulters, and thus functions as a revenue court.

Section 52-A pertains to 'moneylending and moneylenders' under Entry 30, List II, and is a valid exercise of State legislative power aimed at expeditious recovery of public funds advanced by state corporations.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864, Section 52-A
Constitution of India, Entry 11-A, List III (Seventh Schedule)
Constitution of India, Entry 30, List II (Seventh Schedule)
doctrines: Judicial power of the State
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Recovery as arrears of land revenue

card.dispute: The tenant, Super Forgings & Steels (Sales) Pvt. Ltd, challenged the eviction order granted to the landlord, Thyabally Rasuljee (deceased), under the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, on the ground that the landlord no longer met the statutory requirement for eviction after his death and the co-ownership of another building by his legal heirs.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner of a non-residential building can be considered as occupying 'his own building' under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960?

Whether the legal heirs of a landlord who died during the pendency of an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution can retain the benefit of an eviction order passed under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Act, despite subsequent disentitling developments?
Whether this Court can consider events occurring during the pendency of an appeal under Article 136 to mould or set aside an eviction order?
holdings: A co-owner of a non-residential building is entitled to be treated as an owner occupying 'his own building' under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Act, and thus cannot claim eviction on the ground of non-occupation of any building owned by him.

The right to eviction under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) is not an accrued or indefeasible vested right; it can be denied if subsequent developments disentitle the claimant, even during the pendency of an appeal under Article 136.

This Court has the power in an appeal under Article 136 to consider factual developments occurring after the institution of proceedings, especially when they fundamentally affect the right to relief, to do substantial justice.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(iii)
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Equitable doctrine of taking notice of subsequent events
Co-ownership as ownership for statutory purposes

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their convictions under IPC and TADA for the abduction and murder of Varun Kumar, with the prosecution relying on circumstantial evidence and disclosure statements.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Sukhdev Paul authored the ransom letters?
Whether the specimen handwriting of Sukhdev Paul was lawfully obtained under Section 73 of the Evidence Act?
Whether the disclosure statement and recovery of the dead body were sufficient to sustain Sukhvinder Singh's conviction?
Whether the chain of circumstances against Sukhvinder Singh conclusively established his guilt?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove that Sukhdev Paul authored the ransom letters, as the evidence was unreliable and the handwriting specimens were improperly obtained.
Handwriting specimens obtained by an unauthorized officer cannot be used under Section 73 of the Evidence Act to establish authorship.
The voluntary disclosure statement and recovery of the body from Sukhvinder Singh’s house were credible and incriminating, forming strong evidence of guilt.
The cumulative circumstantial evidence against Sukhvinder Singh formed a complete chain pointing exclusively to his guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
provisions: Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987, Section 3
doctrines: Chain of circumstances
Voluntary disclosure and recovery
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Improper admission of handwriting evidence

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu fought against Ananthi Ammal and others over the constitutional validity of a law allowing land acquisition for Harijan welfare, which the High Court had struck down.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the provisions for payment of compensation in instalments under Section 11(1) of the Act are reasonable?
Whether the Act is protected under Article 31-C of the Constitution?
Whether Chapter VI of the Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, is also invalid in light of the impugned Act's fate?
holdings: The Act is constitutionally valid except for the provision allowing compensation to be paid in instalments, which violates Article 14 due to unreasonableness.
Section 11(1) of the Act, insofar as it mandates instalment payments, is ultra vires Article 14 and must be struck down; only lump-sum payment is permissible.
It is unnecessary to decide on Article 31-C protection since the Act is valid under Article 14 except for the severable instalment clause.
Chapter VI of the Slum Areas Act is intra vires as it does not provide for instalment payments and non-payment of solatium is not unreasonable in public interest.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 2
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 11
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 20
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 22
Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, Chapter VI
doctrines: Doctrine of Severability
Reasonableness under Article 14
Public Purpose in Land Acquisition
Doctrine of Eclipse (implied)

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside a magistrate's order taking cognizance of a criminal case against Aruna Devi and others for allegedly transferring land through a forged power of attorney.
issues_decided: Whether the magistrate had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence after accepting a final report under Section 173(2) of the CrPC.
Whether a second investigation and subsequent challan amount to impermissible entertainment of a second complaint.
