holdings: A magistrate retains jurisdiction to take cognizance of an offence after a final report if further investigation under Section 173(8) of the CrPC uncovers new evidence pointing to the commission of an offence.

The filing of a challan after further investigation does not constitute an impermissible second complaint when fresh evidence emerges, as allowed under the principles in Pramatha Nath Taluqdar v. Saro Ranjan Sarkar.
doctrines: Further investigation under Section 173(8) CrPC
Permissibility of second complaint on fresh evidence

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's order directing payment of additional compensation, solatium, and interest to landowners under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act after the statutory period had expired.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 28-A(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is maintainable when the earliest reference award was made before the 1984 Amendment Act came into force?
Whether a subsequent award or Supreme Court judgment enhancing compensation can provide a fresh cause of action under Section 28-A(1)?

Whether the Collector or High Court could legally award additional compensation, solatium, and interest under Section 23(1-A) and Section 28 when the enhancement was not made in a valid proceeding under Section 28-A?
holdings: Section 28-A applies only prospectively from September 24, 1984, and does not revive time-barred claims; the earliest award date determines the limitation period.
A later award or Supreme Court judgment does not create a fresh cause of action under Section 28-A(1) if the initial award predated the 1984 Amendment Act.

The Collector lacked jurisdiction to grant enhanced compensation under Section 28-A(2) based on later awards, and statutory benefits under Sections 23(1-A) and 28 cannot be awarded independently or substituted by the High Court.
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Cause of action accrual under limitation law
Jurisdictional limits of administrative authorities
Doctrine of merger of decrees
Principle of parity in compensation rejected under Article 14

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Additional Special Land Acquisition Officer and landowners over whether the landowners' application to the Civil Court for directing a reference was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the application to the Civil Court under Section 18(3)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is governed by the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the application filed after five years was barred by time under Article 137 of the Limitation Act
holdings: Applications under Section 18(3)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act are governed by the residuary limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, where no specific period is prescribed.

The cause of action arose when the Deputy Commissioner failed to make a reference within 90 days; thus, the application to the Civil Court must be filed within three years from that date, or it is time-barred.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Mysore Extension and Amendment Act, XVII of 1961), Section 4
doctrines: ejusdem generis
residuary limitation under Article 137
cause of action accrual

card.dispute: The appellant, Tarseem Kumar, challenged his conviction and life sentence for the murder of Gulshan Rai, claiming that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was in exclusive possession of the house where the murder took place and had the opportunity to commit the crime.
Whether the circumstantial evidence, including the presence of the appellant with the deceased and alleged extra-judicial confessions, was reliable and sufficient to sustain the conviction.
Whether the recovery of blood-stained clothes at the instance of the appellant could be relied upon under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, given the credibility issues with the prosecution witnesses.
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove that the appellant was in exclusive possession of the rooms or that he had committed the murder, as the chain of circumstantial evidence was not complete.
The evidence of key prosecution witnesses was unreliable due to their status as 'stock witnesses' and inherent improbabilities, and thus could not support a conviction.
Even if some incriminating material was recovered, it could not sustain the conviction without credible supporting evidence linking the appellant to the murder beyond reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of circumstantial evidence
Credibility assessment of 'stock witnesses'
Use of discovery evidence under Section 27 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu fought with landowners over the constitutional validity of a law that acquired land for Harijan welfare, challenging whether it violated fundamental rights and if it was protected under constitutional provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, violates Article 14, 19, or 300A of the Constitution?
Whether the Act is protected under Article 31-A or Article 31-C of the Constitution?
Whether the provision for payment of compensation in instalments under Section 11(1) is reasonable and non-discriminatory?
Whether Chapter VI of the Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Act, with similar provisions, is also constitutionally valid?
holdings: The Act does not violate Articles 14, 19, or 300A except insofar as Section 11(1) mandates payment of compensation in instalments, which is arbitrary and violates Article 14.
The Act is not entitled to protection under Article 31-C, but it is unnecessary to decide on Article 31-A since the Act is largely valid apart from the offending instalment clause.
The requirement to pay compensation in instalments under Section 11(1) is unreasonable and severs from the Act; only lump-sum payment is constitutionally permissible.
Chapter VI of the Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Act is intra vires the Constitution, as non-payment of solatium and absence of instalment-based compensation do not violate Article 14.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 2
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 11
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 20
Tamil Nadu Acquisition of Land for Harijan Welfare Schemes Act, 1978, Section 22
Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Act, Chapter VI
doctrines: Doctrine of Severability
Principle of Reasonableness under Article 14
Protection of laws under Article 31-C (partial application)
Doctrine of Equal Protection of Laws

card.dispute: The appellant restaurant sued to restrain the respondents from interfering with its possession of land based on an alleged agreement of sale, while the respondents sought to amend their pleading to deny it was a sale agreement and claim it was instead for mutual development.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents could amend their written statement to retract their admission of an agreement of sale.
Whether the High Court erred in allowing the amendment under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC.
holdings: An admission in pleadings can be explained or modified, and inconsistent pleas are permissible if they clarify the true nature of the transaction.
The High Court did not commit material irregularity in allowing the amendment to the written statement under its powers under Section 115 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Admissions can be explained but not contradicted by subsequent pleadings
Liberal amendment of pleadings to serve justice

card.dispute: The heirs of Abubakar Abdul Inamdar contested against his brothers and sisters over the devolution of erstwhile Inam lands and a dwelling unit after abolition of the Inam system, claiming shares as co-heirs.
issues_decided: Whether the re-granted Inam lands became partible among the heirs after abolition of the Inam system, despite earlier impartibility and primogeniture
Whether Abubakar could claim ownership of the house through adverse possession
holdings: The re-granted Inam properties ceased to be impartible after abolition and became partible among the heirs according to Muslim personal law, as the rule of primogeniture no longer applied.
The plea of adverse possession over the house failed due to absence of pleaded overt acts showing hostile, open, and continuous possession excluding other heirs.
provisions: Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act, 1955
doctrines: Rule of primogeniture
Adverse possession
Partibility of property upon abolition of impartible estates

card.dispute: The legal representatives of V. Gopal Reddiar and another appellant contested the exclusion of land transferred to an educational institution from ceiling area calculations under the Tamil Nadu land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether Section 21-A of the Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, as amended by the Reduction Act, applies to pending proceedings initiated under the Principal Act?

Whether land voluntarily transferred to an educational institution between 15.2.1970 and 2.10.1970 can be excluded from a person's holding for ceiling purposes despite ongoing proceedings under the Principal Act?
holdings: Section 21-A, with its non-obstante clause, overrides all other provisions of the Principal Act, including Section 3(1) of the Reduction Act, and applies to pending proceedings.

Land transferred voluntarily to a public educational institution between 15.2.1970 and 2.10.1970 is excluded from ceiling area calculations, even if proceedings were initiated earlier under the Principal Act.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, Section 3(1), Section 5, Section 7, Section 8, Section 10(1), Section 12, Section 14, Section 21-A, Section 22, Section 23
Tamil Nadu Land Reforms (Reduction of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1970, Section 3(1), Section 3(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of non-obstante clause
Doctrine of prospective operation of amendments
Doctrine of continuation of pending proceedings

card.dispute: Ajit Singh and Babulal Gupta disputed over the grant of a mining lease for marble in Rajasthan, after a prior lease was revoked due to non-execution of a formal agreement.
issues_decided: Whether Rule 56 of the Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1977 applies to determine the availability of a mining area after revocation of a lease under Rule 19(1)
Whether an area becomes immediately available for regrant upon deemed revocation of a mining lease under Rule 19(1)
Whether the application filed by respondent No. 5 on January 19, 1983 was premature
holdings: Rule 56 of the Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1977 does not apply to areas where a mining lease has been revoked under Rule 19(1); hence, it cannot render an application premature on that basis.
An area does not become available for regrant immediately upon deemed revocation under Rule 19(1); a public notice or administrative order is required to make the area available to third parties.
An application for a mining lease filed before the expiry of 15 days from the publication of an administrative order declaring the area available for re-allotment is premature and invalid.
provisions: Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1977, Rule 19(1)
Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1977, Rule 56
doctrines: Deemed revocation
Principle of equal opportunity in grant of state privileges
Requirement of public notice for transparency in administrative action

card.dispute: The appellant buyer sued for refund of Rs. 50,000 paid as advance to the respondents (sellers) under a land sale agreement, which failed due to non-registration of sale deed and disputes over minor's share; sellers contended the amount was forfeitable due to buyer's default.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to refund of Rs. 50,000 paid as advance, given his failure to perform the contract?
Whether the presence of a minor co-owner made the agreement void and excused performance?
Whether the respondents were entitled to forfeit the entire advance amount without proving actual damages?
holdings: The appellant, having defaulted in performing the contract by failing to register the sale deed and develop the land as agreed, is not entitled to refund of the advance amount.
The agreement was not void due to the minor's involvement; once the minor attained majority and adopted the contract, it became binding, and court permission for alienation was no longer required.

The respondents were entitled to forfeit the entire Rs. 50,000 as per the contract's forfeiture clause, especially since the appellant’s actions caused demonstrable loss, including destruction of crops and inability to sell at agreed price.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
Specific Relief Act, 1963 (implied by forfeiture and decree principles)
doctrines: Doctrine of clean hands
Doctrine of forfeiture in contracts where time is of the essence
Doctrine of election by a minor upon attaining majority

card.dispute: The appellants (coparceners in a Hindu joint family) sued for partition of watan lands previously held under a rule of primogeniture, after the abolition of the Patel office and re-grant of the land to the eldest member, who claimed exclusive ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the watan properties, after abolition and re-grant under the Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962, became partible among coparceners or remained the exclusive property of the re-grantee.
Whether the eldest member acquired title by adverse possession over the watan properties after re-grant.
Whether the suit for partition was barred by limitation.
holdings: After the abolition of the Patel watan and re-grant under Section 5 of the Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962, the properties ceased to be impartible and became partible among the coparceners.

Mere possession by the eldest member under re-grant does not amount to adverse possession; there must be clear and unequivocal evidence of hostile assertion of exclusive title known to the coparceners and their acquiescence for 12 years.
The cause of action for partition arose only after the re-grant under the Act, and thus the suit was not barred by limitation.
provisions: Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962, Section 3
Maharashtra Revenue Patels (Abolition of Office) Act, 1962, Section 5
doctrines: Adverse possession
Unity of possession in Hindu joint family
Change in character of impartible property to partible upon statutory abolition

card.dispute: The appellant claimed eviction of the respondent from tenanted premises based on a will bequeathing tenancy rights, while the respondent argued that such bequest was impermissible under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947.
issues_decided: Whether tenancy rights under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 can be devised by a will.
Whether the words 'assign' and 'transfer' in Section 15 of the Act include 'bequest'.
Whether a legatee under a will can succeed to statutory tenancy rights under Section 5(11)(c)(i) of the Act.
holdings: The right to succeed to a statutory tenancy under the Act is restricted to family members or heirs by succession, not by testamentary disposition; a bequest of tenancy rights is not permitted.
The terms 'assign' and 'transfer' in Section 15 of the Act are used in a broad sense and include transfer by will, thereby rendering such bequests invalid under the Act.
The word 'heir' in Section 5(11)(c)(i) refers to legal heirs by succession, not legatees, to prevent strangers from becoming tenants and to uphold the personal nature of statutory tenancy.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(11)(c)(i)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 15
doctrines: Statutory tenancy is personal and not heritable by will
Interpretation of statutory terms in light of legislative object and scheme
Noscitur a sociis and ejusdem generis in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The judgment-debtor (B. Gangadhar) fought against the decree-holder (B.G. Rajalingam) over the execution of a decree for possession, specifically challenging the demolition of shops constructed by him and the eviction of tenants during the pendency of the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court has the power to order demolition of structures built by the judgment-debtor during the pendency of the suit in absence of a mandatory injunction in the decree?

Whether tenants inducted by the judgment-debtor during the pendency of the suit, without court permission, are bound by the decree and can be evicted in execution proceedings without being party to the suit?
holdings: The executing court has inherent and ancillary power under Order 21, Rules 35(3) and 101 of CPC to remove obstructions, including demolition of unauthorized constructions made pendente lite, to effectively enforce a decree for possession, even without a mandatory injunction.

Tenants inducted by the judgment-debtor during the pendency of the suit without court permission are bound by the decree and can be evicted in execution proceedings; their non-joinder as parties does not bar enforcement of the decree against them.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 35(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 98
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 101
doctrines: Ancillary and incidental powers of executing court
Constructive possession
Binding effect of decree on persons claiming under judgment-debtor
Avoidance of multiplicity of litigation

card.dispute: Baldev Singh and Roor Singh appealed their conviction and sentence for the murders of Balbir Singh and Amrik Singh, arguing the offence was culpable homicide not amounting to murder and seeking sentence mitigation through compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' actions amounted to murder under Section 300 IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 299 IPC?
Whether the sentence of imprisonment should be substituted with compensation under Section 357 Cr.P.C. given the familial relationship and property dispute?
Whether the conviction under the Arms Act should be upheld?
holdings: The appellants' act caused death but lacked intention or knowledge to cause death, thus constituting culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 299 IPC read with Section 304 Part-I IPC, not murder under Section 302 IPC.

Considering the familial relationship, nature of the dispute, and time served, the sentence of imprisonment is commuted to the period already undergone, and compensation of Rs.35,000 each is directed to be paid to the victim's family under Section 357(3) Cr.P.C.
The conviction under Section 25 of the Arms Act is set aside due to lack of evidence on the fatal use of the weapon or its licensing status affecting the outcome.
doctrines: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 299 IPC
Three-stage test for distinguishing murder from culpable homicide as laid down in State of Andhra Pradesh v. Rayavarapu Punnayya
Compensation as a restorative justice measure under Section 357 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the municipal assessment of their property's annual value based on actual rent received, arguing it should be limited by the standard rent under rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether the actual rent received by a landlord can be the basis for determining the annual ratable value of a property under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911.
Whether a landlord's admission to pay tax based on actual rent creates an estoppel against claiming the benefit of standard rent under rent control legislation.
holdings: The annual ratable value of a property must be determined by the standard rent reasonably expected under the Rent Act, not the actual rent received, which cannot exceed the legally permissible standard rent.
An admission by a property owner to pay tax based on actual rent does not create estoppel against statutory provisions that mandate assessment based on standard rent under rent control law.
doctrines: Estoppel against statute
Reasonable expectation in open market
Standard rent as upper limit for ratable value

card.dispute: The dispute was between landowners and the Union of India over whether the landowners could pay deficit court fees after the High Court enhanced compensation in land acquisition appeals.
issues_decided: Whether claimants can pay deficit court fee after the High Court enhances compensation in land acquisition appeals.
Whether the claimants acted in good faith by delaying payment of deficit court fee until after the judgment was reserved.
Whether Section 149 of the CPC allows courts to permit payment of deficit court fee when the appeal has already been heard and decided.
holdings: Claimants must pay the proper court fee at the time of filing the appeal based on the claimed compensation; they cannot delay payment until after a favorable judgment.
The power under Section 149 CPC is discretionary and not a right; it should not be exercised if the delay results from strategic choice rather than bona fide mistake or hardship.
Allowing deficit court fee after judgment encourages an unhealthy litigation practice and undermines fairness, as respondents are deprived of notice on the true claim value.
provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 4(1), Section 18, Section 54
doctrines: Judicial discretion under Section 149 CPC
Bona fide mistake doctrine
Principle of fair notice in appellate claims

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority fought with a cooperative housing society over whether it could forfeit the society's Rs. 5 lakh earnest money after the society refused to accept a land allotment at an enhanced premium rate.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the refund of earnest money deposited by the respondent society.
Whether the appellant was legally entitled to forfeit the earnest money due to the respondent's failure to pay the enhanced premium.
holdings: The respondent society had accepted the allotment offer, including the enhanced premium, through its prior conduct and deposit of earnest money, making it bound to pay the revised amount.
The Delhi Development Authority was entitled to forfeit the earnest money for default, but only the fixed Rs. 5 lakh deposited, not 10% of the enhanced premium, as per the original terms.
provisions: Delhi Development Authority (Disposal of Developed Nazul Land) Amendment Rules, 1981, Rule 24(2)
doctrines: Forfeiture of earnest money upon buyer's default
Continuity of contractual obligations across successive communications

card.dispute: The tenant's legal heirs challenged the High Court's order for eviction on grounds of subletting, claiming the landlady failed to prove transfer of exclusive possession.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to reappreciate findings of fact in revision under Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949?
Whether the tenant incurred liability of eviction under Section 13(2)(ii)(a) by sub-letting the premises?
holdings: The High Court can examine the legality and propriety of findings in revision, including factual conclusions, but cannot act as a second appellate court; interference is only justified if findings are perverse or no reasonable person could have reached them.
Mere presence of another party conducting business in the tenant’s premises under a different name does not prove subletting; exclusive possession must be established, which was not done here.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(ii)(a)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Doctrine of perversity in revisional jurisdiction
Doctrine of exclusive possession in subletting
Presumption against clandestine subletting without direct evidence

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the respondent tenant's right to purchase tenanted land, claiming the respondent exceeded the statutory ceiling limit on landholding.
issues_decided: Whether the land held by a minor son and cultivated by the father as guardian should be included in the father's landholding for ceiling limits under the Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands Act, 1948.
Whether land allegedly partitioned in favor of the tenant's brother should be excluded from the tenant's holding based on oral evidence and entries in the Record of Rights.
Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower tribunals while exercising revisional jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution.
holdings: Land cultivated by a tenant as guardian of his minor son is not part of his own holding under Section 32B of the Act and should not be counted toward ceiling limits.
A partition between coparceners can be valid without a registered deed; entries in the Record of Rights, coupled with oral evidence, suffice to prove partition and exclude land from the holding.
The High Court, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, can interfere with findings of fact if they are based on ignoring relevant evidence or misapplying statutory provisions.
provisions: Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32B
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32G
doctrines: Doctrine of deemed tenancy
Doctrine of partition under Hindu Law
Revisional jurisdiction under Article 227

card.dispute: The appellants sued for specific performance of a reconveyance agreement, seeking to amend their plaint to include alternative relief for mortgage redemption, which the trial court and High Court had disallowed.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment of the plaint to include alternative reliefs would change the nature of the suit or cause of action
Whether the appellants could plead inconsistent but alternative reliefs in the same suit
holdings: Amendment of the plaint to include alternative reliefs does not change the cause of action or nature of the suit if the core transaction remains the same.
A plaintiff is entitled to plead inconsistent alternative pleas, and allowing such amendments does not prejudice the defendant if they are given opportunity to respond.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 16 Rule 17
doctrines: Alternative relief doctrine
Liberal amendment of pleadings

card.dispute: Dr. Ranbir Singh (appellant) sued Asharfi Lal (respondent) for eviction on the grounds of tenancy, claiming ownership of the property through purchase from Shri Hemant Singh, the adopted son of the late Maharaja of Dholpur; the respondent denied the plaintiff's title and the existence of a valid tenancy.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was the rightful landlord and the respondent was a tenant under the Rent Control Act.
Whether the denial of the appellant's title by the respondent was bona fide and sufficient to resist eviction.
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with concurrent findings of fact by the trial and first appellate courts in a second appeal.
holdings: The appellant proved ownership through a valid sale from Shri Hemant Singh, who was lawfully adopted and succeeded to the private properties of the late Maharaja; attornment established a valid landlord-tenant relationship.
The respondent’s denial of the appellant’s title was not bona fide, and such denial, in absence of legal justification, constitutes a valid ground for eviction under tenancy law.

The High Court erred in reappreciating evidence in second appeal; concurrent findings of fact by lower courts on landlord’s genuine need and comparative hardship cannot be overturned without a substantial question of law.
doctrines: Privity of contract and attornment in landlord-tenant relationships
Substantial question of law in second appeals under Section 100 CPC
Concurrent findings of fact not interferable in second appeal
Bona fides of denial of title as ground for eviction

card.dispute: The appellants, Gurnam Singh and Pala Singh, challenged their conviction for murder under Section 302/34 IPC, arguing that the killing occurred during a sudden quarrel and warranted conviction under the lesser offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC was justified or whether it should be reduced to Section 304 Part I/34 IPC based on the circumstances of a sudden quarrel.
Whether the prosecution failed to explain the injuries on the accused, thereby rendering the eyewitness testimony unreliable.
Whether the plea of private defence raised by the appellants was substantiated by the evidence.
holdings: The appellants' act fell under Section 304 Part I IPC, not Section 302 IPC, as the killing occurred in the heat of a sudden quarrel over water rights, without premeditation.
The absence of an explanation for the accused's injuries in the FIR does not undermine the prosecution's case, as such explanation is required only during trial, not at the FIR stage.
The appellants were the aggressors, and the deceased and eyewitness acted in private defence; thus, the plea of private defence by the accused fails.
provisions: Terrorist Affected Area (Special Courts) Act, 1984, Section 14
doctrines: Right of private defence
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Sudden fight exception to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC
Reliability of dying declaration
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony

card.dispute: The appellant, Gian Chand, sued for refund of earnest money paid to the respondents for purchasing a share of land, after learning that the land was under notification for acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which had been concealed.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement for sale of land became void due to the pendency of land acquisition proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the appellant was entitled to refund of earnest money despite not being ready and willing to perform the contract on the stipulated date.
Whether the courts below erred in reversing the trial court's decree for refund of earnest money.
holdings: An agreement to sell land is frustrated when the land is under notification under Section 4(1) and subsequent declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, making any private transaction void and unenforceable against the government.

The vendee is entitled to refund of earnest money under Section 33 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when performance becomes impossible due to a contingent event, even if the vendee was not ready and willing to perform on the stipulated date.

The appellate courts committed a manifest error in law by ignoring the effect of acquisition proceedings and the contractual term for refund of earnest money upon acquisition, warranting restoration of the trial court's decree.
doctrines: Frustration of contract
Contingent contract
Effect of government acquisition on private contracts

card.dispute: Residents of Sarita Vihar challenged the Delhi Development Authority's (DDA) allotment of park land for a nursery school, alleging violation of statutory planning provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the allotment of park land for a nursery school violated the Delhi Development Act, 1957 and its rules
Whether the DDA had the authority to carve out space from a park for a nursery school without prior reservation in the development plan
holdings: The DDA cannot allot land meant for a park for any other purpose, including a nursery school, unless such use was reserved in the zonal or master plan as required by law.
The allotment of park land to a private institution for a nursery school, in absence of prior reservation, constitutes a misuse of power and must be cancelled.
provisions: Delhi Development (Master Plan and Zonal Development Plan) Rules, 1959, Rule 4(3)(g)
doctrines: Misuse of power
Statutory planning compliance
Public trust doctrine (implied in protection of park land)

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for the murder of Deokaran Singh under Section 304 Part II read with Section 149 IPC, and they challenged the conviction, claiming false implication and absence from the scene of the crime.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal and convicting the appellants based on the prosecution's evidence?
Whether the testimony of Jethabhai (CW-1) and other prosecution witnesses was reliable enough to establish the identity of the assailants?
Whether the conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC read with Section 149 IPC was legally sustainable?
holdings: The High Court correctly reversed the trial court's acquittal as it was perverse, given the overwhelming and consistent evidence identifying the appellants as participants in the assault.

The testimony of Jethabhai (CW-1), though partially corroborated by circumstances, along with the prompt FIR and consistent accounts of other eyewitnesses, sufficiently established the identity of the appellants as assailants.

The conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC read with Section 149 IPC was justified, as the nature of injuries and absence of premeditation supported culpability for culpable homicide not amounting to murder by members of an unlawful assembly.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Perverse acquittal
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Principle of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Appreciation of evidence in appeals against acquittal

card.dispute: The Income Tax Officer sought to reassess Ch. Atchaiah individually on capital gains from land acquisition compensation, which had already been taxed in his hands, while also potentially taxing an association of persons, leading to a dispute over double taxation and the proper interpretation of 'person' under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the same income can be taxed both in the hands of an individual and in the hands of an Association of Persons (AOP) or must the tax liability lie exclusively with one entity?
Whether the Income Tax Officer has the discretion under the Income Tax Act, 1961, to choose between taxing an AOP or its members individually, as was permissible under the earlier 1922 Act?
holdings: The same income cannot be taxed both in the hands of an Association of Persons and its individual members; if the income is legally taxable in the hands of the AOP, only the AOP can be taxed.

The Income Tax Act, 1961, does not confer discretion on the Income Tax Officer to choose between taxing an AOP or its members individually, unlike the 1922 Act, and such a choice is no longer permissible in law.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Principle against double taxation
Legislative intent doctrine

card.dispute: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. challenged the Municipal Corporation's assessment of annual value of its property for tax purposes, contesting the interpretation of Section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the decision of the Supreme Court in Municipal Corporation, Indore v. Ratna Prabha (1977) is binding on the Madhya Pradesh High Court regarding the construction of Section 138(b) of the M.P. Municipal Corporation Act?
Whether Section 138(b) of the M.P. Act, due to its non-obstante clause, permits the assessment of annual value without regard to rent control legislation when no standard rent is fixed?
Whether the Supreme Court should reconsider its decision in Ratna Prabha (1977) in light of subsequent judgments?
holdings: The Supreme Court's decision in Ratna Prabha (1977) is binding on all lower courts and co-equal benches, as it directly interprets Section 138(b) of the M.P. Act and cannot be overruled by a coordinate bench.
Section 138(b)'s non-obstante clause allows the annual value to be determined independently of rent control laws when no standard rent is fixed and there is no fraud or collusion.
The decision in Ratna Prabha (1977) should not be reconsidered, as it remains a permissible interpretation and no compelling reason exists to depart from it under the principle of stare decisis.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, Section 138(b)
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)
Non-obstante clause interpretation
Principle of bindingness of larger bench decisions
Judicial discipline and hierarchy of courts

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the maintainability of a civil suit seeking declaration that land acquisition proceedings were invalid after the Land Acquisition Officer had temporarily halted the process due to the Gram Panchayat's lack of funds.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition Officer had jurisdiction to resume and complete acquisition proceedings after temporarily halting them due to lack of funds.
Whether a civil court has jurisdiction to declare land acquisition proceedings invalid when an alternative statutory remedy exists under the Land Acquisition Act.
holdings: The Land Acquisition Officer retained jurisdiction to proceed with the award under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, as the government never formally withdrew the acquisition under Section 48, and mere suspension of proceedings did not extinguish statutory authority.

The civil court lacks jurisdiction to entertain suits challenging the validity of land acquisition proceedings when the Act provides an exclusive remedy through reference under Section 18 and appeal under Section 54, barring such suits by necessary implication.
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by necessary implication
Statutory exclusivity of remedies under special enactments
Doctrine of conclusive presumption of public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the High Court's deduction of 40% from the market value of acquired land for developmental charges and reliance on small plot sale deeds to fix compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in deducting 40% of the market value for developmental charges and for considering small plot sales in determining compensation for a large extent of land?
Whether the principle of uniform deduction (e.g., 1/3rd) for developmental charges applies when market value is based on small-sized sale deeds?
holdings: When market value is determined based on sale deeds of small plots, a substantial deduction must be made to arrive at the fair market value of a large tract of land, even if part of it is termed as developmental charges.

The High Court’s 40% deduction was reasonable as it considered both developmental needs and the non-comparability of small plot sales to large land acquisitions, and thus did not warrant interference.
doctrines: Twin test for valuation based on small sale deeds
Principle of reasonable deduction for developmental charges and non-comparability of small plots

card.dispute: The tenant, Kuldeep Singh, fought against his eviction by landlords Ganpat Lal & Anr over alleged default in rent payment for six months under the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could claim protection from eviction under Section 13(6) of the Act after depositing rent in court under Section 19-A despite not fulfilling the conditions for such deposit.

Whether the deposit of rent in court by the tenant before the filing of the eviction suit, but without fulfilling the conditions under Section 19-A(3)(c), amounted to valid payment or tender of rent under the Act.
holdings: A tenant cannot claim protection from eviction under Section 13(6) if they have previously availed such protection and later defaulted again in rent payment for six months.

A deposit of rent in court is valid under Section 19-A(4) only if the conditions in Section 19-A(3)(c) are met; failure to meet these conditions means the deposit does not constitute deemed payment or tender of rent.
Legal fictions, such as deemed payment under Section 19-A(4), must be confined to their intended scope and cannot be extended beyond statutory conditions.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(a)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(6)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 19-A(3)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 19-A(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of strict construction of legal fictions
Doctrine of compliance with statutory conditions for deemed payment

card.dispute: The landlord, Lachhman Dass, fought to evict his tenant, Santokh Singh, on grounds of non-payment of rent, misuse of premises, and non-occupation, which the High Court reversed despite concurrent findings by lower courts.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in re-appreciating evidence and overturning concurrent factual findings in revision under Section 15(6) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973?
Whether the tenant had ceased to occupy the tenanted premises without reasonable cause?
Whether the tenant had a reasonably sufficient alternative residence to justify eviction?
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or overturn concurrent findings of fact in revision unless those findings are perverse, based on no evidence, or result from a superficial analysis.
The tenant had ceased to occupy the tenanted premises for over a year without reasonable cause, as found by the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority based on reliable evidence.
The house acquired by the tenant in his wife’s name was reasonably sufficient for his family of six, and the High Court erred in relying on the presence of occasional visitors to conclude otherwise.
provisions: Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(2)(i)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(2)(iii)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(2)(v)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 13(3)(a)(iv)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 15(2)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, Section 15(6)
doctrines: Distinction between appeal and revision
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed in revision
Revisional jurisdiction limited to legality and propriety, not re-appreciation of evidence

card.dispute: The Karnal Improvement Trust challenged the validity of compensation awards granted by the sole President of a Tribunal under the Punjab Improvement Trust Act, 1922, arguing that such awards require a multi-member bench.
issues_decided: Whether the President of the Tribunal alone can pass a valid award under the Punjab Improvement Trust Act, 1922
Whether the doctrine of stare decisis applies to uphold the single-member Tribunal's award
Whether the award passed by the single President of the Tribunal is void for lack of jurisdiction
Whether the decision should be given only prospective operation to avoid disturbing past awards
holdings: The Tribunal must function as a multi-member body; an award by the President alone is invalid as it violates the statutory scheme requiring plural adjudication.
The doctrine of stare decisis does not apply where a decision is plainly erroneous, defeats statutory purpose, or involves lack of jurisdiction.
An award passed by a Tribunal President without a bench is void ab initio and cannot be enforced.
The declaration of invalidity applies prospectively from the date of judgment; past single-member awards that have become final are not reopened.
doctrines: stare decisis
void for lack of jurisdiction
prospective overruling
statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of a deceased testator and a respondent over the interpretation of a will, specifically whether an earlier bequest in favor of Kannan was overridden by a later recital creating a 'Tavazhi' interest in the same property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in interpreting the will by giving effect to a subsequent recital over an earlier bequest?
Whether the principle that the last inconsistent clause in a will prevails applies to the construction of the will in question?
holdings: The court held that in case of inconsistency between clauses in a will, the later clause prevails as it reflects the testator's last intention.
The High Court correctly applied the principle under Section 88 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and relevant precedents, and thus its interpretation of the will was upheld.
doctrines: Last inconsistent clause rule in will interpretation
Testator's last intention prevails
Principle of 'cum duo inter se pugnantia reperiuntur in testamento ultimum ratum est'

card.dispute: The landlords sought possession of the premises from the tenants on grounds of arrears of rent and bona fide requirement, leading to a dispute over the applicability of eviction provisions under the Bombay Rents Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants neglected to make rent payment within the period specified under Section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents Act, 1947, thereby warranting eviction

Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its revisional jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution to interfere with the appellate court's decision in a landlord-tenant dispute governed by a special statute
holdings: Sending a money order within the statutory period constitutes due attempt to pay, and refusal by the landlord does not amount to 'neglect' under Section 12(3)(a); thus, eviction is not justified.

The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by reappreciating evidence in a case governed by a special statute where legislature intended finality of appellate decisions, and interference is limited to cases of grave injustice or legal error.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation of 'neglect to make payment'
Doctrine of limited scope of Article 227 in special statutory proceedings

card.dispute: Two public officials, a Tehsildar and a village assistant, were convicted for accepting a bribe in connection with the issuance of a land patta, and they appealed their convictions and sentences.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction can be based solely on the uncorroborated testimony of a trap witness or a complainant in a bribery case
Whether the evidence of a complainant who sets up a trap with the police requires corroboration in material particulars
Whether the sentence imposed should be reduced in light of the time already served and the circumstances of the case
holdings: A conviction in a bribery case can be based on the uncorroborated testimony of a complainant or trap witness if the court, after careful scrutiny, finds the evidence trustworthy and reliable.
There is no rigid rule requiring corroboration of a trap witness’s evidence in material particulars; the need and extent of corroboration depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

While the convictions were upheld, the sentence of imprisonment was reduced to the period already undergone, considering the time spent in legal proceedings and incarceration, though the fine with default clause was upheld.
doctrines: Rule of prudence in appreciating accomplice evidence
No hard and fast rule for corroboration of trap witnesses
Conviction based on sole testimony if found reliable after scrutiny

card.dispute: The dispute was between auction purchasers of industrial units and the Bihar State Electricity Board over whether the purchasers were liable to pay the electricity arrears of the previous owners as a condition for reconnection of power supply.
issues_decided: Whether an auction purchaser is liable to pay the electricity dues of the previous consumer as a precondition for obtaining a new electricity connection.
Whether the Bihar State Electricity Board can enforce the contractual liability of the previous owner against a third-party auction purchaser.
Whether the change in ownership through auction sale affects the Board's right to recover past electricity dues.
holdings: An auction purchaser is not liable for the electricity arrears of the previous owner unless they are the same entity or a continuation of the former consumer.
The liability for electricity dues is personal to the consumer who entered into the contract; it cannot be enforced against a third-party purchaser who was not a party to the agreement.
Reconnection of electricity cannot be denied to an auction purchaser on the ground of unpaid dues of the former owner, provided the purchaser is willing to enter into a fresh contract.
Where the auction purchaser is found to be the same entity or a continuation in management and ownership, they may be held liable for past dues.
provisions: Bihar State Financial Corporation Act, 1951, Section 29(1)
Bihar and Orissa Public Demands and Recovery Act, 1914 (Act 46 of 1982), Rule 15 of Schedule I
doctrines: Privity of contract
Personal liability for statutory dues
Successor liability exception for sham transactions
Public property protection vs. legal enforceability

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the High Court's deduction of 60% from the determined market value of their land acquired for an orphanage, arguing it resulted in inadequate compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in deducting 60% from the market value of the acquired land in determining compensation.
Whether sales of small plots in nearby areas could be used as comparable evidence for valuing a large tract of land.
holdings: A court determining compensation must act actively to assess just market value by considering all relevant factors, including location, size of land, and potential development restrictions.
Sales of small developed plots are not reliable comparables for large land acquisitions; deductions for development costs and lack of infrastructure are permissible when valuing large tracts.
doctrines: Prudent purchaser principle
Hypothetical layout method
Active role of court in valuation

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India, claiming they were entitled to higher compensation due to the lapse of time compared to a previous similar case.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are entitled to higher compensation than the uniform rate awarded by the High Court due to the delay between the acquisition notification and final award.
Whether the decision in Sanwalia & Ors. vs. Union of India warranted enhanced compensation for the present appellants.
holdings: The court held that there was no sufficient justification to grant enhanced compensation to the appellants despite the lapse of time, as the High Court had awarded a uniform rate to all landowners.
The court found no basis to distinguish the present case from Sanwalia's case in a manner that would justify higher compensation for the appellants.
doctrines: Principle of uniform compensation in land acquisition
Precedent reliance on earlier compensation decisions

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested whether a preliminary decree in a partition suit abates when a consolidation notification is issued under Section 4 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, where the suit was pending at the revisional stage.
issues_decided: Whether a preliminary decree abates under Section 5(2) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act when a notification under Section 4 is issued during pendency of proceedings for final decree or revision.
Whether the pendency of an appeal or revision against a preliminary decree affects its abatement upon issuance of a consolidation notification.
holdings: A preliminary decree does not abate if no appeal is filed against it and it becomes final under Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure, even if a consolidation notification is issued under Section 4 of the Act.
Only when an appeal or revision against the preliminary decree is pending at the time of the notification does the entire suit, including the preliminary decree, abate under Section 5(2) of the Act.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, Section 4
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, Section 5(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20 Rule 18
doctrines: Finality of preliminary decree under Section 97 CPC
Abatement of proceedings under consolidation laws
Distinction between preliminary and final decrees in partition suits

card.dispute: The Market Committee, Hodal challenged the High Court's decision invalidating the government's decision to dispense with an enquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, in a case where land was acquired and an award was made, but the respondents had constructed an oil mill on the land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the government's power under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to dispense with an enquiry under Section 5A after the award and possession had been taken?
Whether the delay of 3240 days in filing the Special Leave Petition should be condoned?
Whether the respondents are entitled to compensation for the construction of an oil mill on the acquired land?
holdings: The High Court erred in interfering with the government's valid exercise of power under Section 17(4) to dispense with a Section 5A enquiry after the award and possession, as the land had already vested absolutely in the government under Section 16.
The inordinate delay of 3240 days in filing the SLP is condonable due to a just and rational explanation involving administrative failure by the Central Agency.

If the oil mill was constructed after the High Court's judgment allowing the writ petition, the appellants must pay ex-gratia compensation for the value of the construction; otherwise, no compensation is due.
doctrines: Vesting of property in the government upon award and possession under Section 16
Judicial restraint in interfering with executive powers under Section 17(4)
Condonation of delay with sufficient cause
Equitable compensation for post-acquisition constructions

card.dispute: Landowners appealed for higher compensation and additional benefits after their land was acquired for municipal expansion, challenging the adequacy of compensation awarded by the tribunal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are entitled to higher compensation based on subsequent awards or unproven sale transactions.
Whether the High Court or Supreme Court can reappreciate evidence in a land acquisition reference under Article 226 or Article 136.
Whether the appellants are entitled to additional benefits under the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, including enhanced solatium and interest.
holdings: The appellants failed to prove inadequacy of compensation as no evidence was adduced before the tribunal; reliance on unproven sale instances or mutation entries is impermissible.
Courts under Article 226 or 136 cannot reappreciate evidence or substitute their own findings on market value if the tribunal's award is based on legal principles and evidence.
Appellants are entitled to solatium at 30% and interest at 9% for one year and 15% thereafter on enhanced compensation, but not to additional amount under Section 23(1-A) due to pre-1984 award date.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: No reappreciation of evidence in writ or special leave jurisdiction
Burden of proof on claimant to establish higher market value
Principle of just and fair compensation based on reliable evidence
Limitation on applying retrospective benefits of amendment

card.dispute: The dispute was between Mathunni Mathai (decreet-holder) and Hindustan Organic Chemicals Ltd. (judgment-debtor) over whether the deposited decretal amount should be adjusted first towards interest or principal.
issues_decided: Whether the decretal amount deposited by the judgment-debtor should be adjusted first towards principal or interest and other charges.
Whether the principle in Meghraj & Ors. v. Mst. Bayabal & Ors. applies after the 1976 amendment to Order XXI Rule 1 of the CPC.
Whether a court-ordered deposit without specific direction implies appropriation towards principal.
holdings: Where a judgment-debtor deposits decretal amount without notice to the decree-holder as required under Order XXI Rule 1(2) CPC, the decree-holder is entitled to appropriate the payment towards interest and costs first.
The amendment to Order XXI Rule 1 CPC in 1976 reinforces the requirement of notice for cessation of interest and does not alter the rule allowing creditor’s discretion in appropriation.

A deposit made pursuant to a court order does not automatically amount to payment of principal unless notice is given and appropriation specified; the decree-holder retains discretion in absence of such notice.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order XXI Rule 1
doctrines: Creditor's right to appropriation of payments
Principle of cessation of interest upon notice under amended CPC
Rule of payment towards interest before principal in absence of appropriation

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming to be licensees in possession of shop premises, sued the respondent-licensor in the City Civil Court for injunction against threatened eviction; the dispute was whether such a suit falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court under Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882.
issues_decided: Whether a suit by a licensee against a licensor for injunction against threatened dispossession is cognizable by the City Civil Court or the Small Causes Court under Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882.
Whether such a suit relates to 'recovery of possession' within the meaning of the Small Causes Courts Act and the Bombay Rent Act.
holdings: A suit by a licensee against a licensor seeking injunction against threatened dispossession is a suit relating to recovery of possession and falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Small Causes Court under Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882.

The substance of the relief sought, not its form, determines jurisdiction; where possession is at issue between licensor and licensee, the Small Causes Court has exclusive jurisdiction even if no declaration of status is sought.
provisions: Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, Section 41(1)
doctrines: Substance over form in determining jurisdiction
Exclusive jurisdiction of Small Causes Court in possession disputes between licensor and licensee
Possessory remedies distinguished from title-based claims

card.dispute: The heirs of the Maharaja of Nabha sued the State of Punjab to recover possession of 'Bir Bhadson', a property they claimed was granted to them by the Maharaja, but which had become state forest land after the merger of Nabha into PEPSU and later Punjab.
issues_decided: Whether the property 'Bir' vested in PEPSU upon the merger of Nabha under the 1948 Covenant.
Whether private individuals can challenge the vesting of state property in PEPSU through a civil suit.
Whether courts have jurisdiction to entertain disputes arising from covenants entered into by rulers of princely states before the Constitution's commencement.
holdings: All state properties of Nabha, including 'Bir', vested in PEPSU upon the formation of the Union on August 20, 1948, under the terms of the Covenant.
A private claim to property that became part of a princely state’s assets merged into PEPSU cannot be enforced in civil court as it involves an act of state.
Courts lack jurisdiction over disputes arising from pre-constitutional treaties or covenants under Article 363(1) of the Constitution.
doctrines: Act of State doctrine
Bar on judicial review of pre-constitutional treaties (Article 363)
Doctrine of merger of princely states and vesting of state property

card.dispute: The dispute was between former tenants and the Pune Municipal Corporation over the grant of an ad interim injunction preventing eviction after the land they occupied was acquired for road widening.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to set aside an appellate order granting ad interim injunction under Article 227 of the Constitution despite the existence of an alternate remedy under CPC
Whether the appellate court was justified in granting ad interim injunction in a suit for perpetual injunction
Whether public interest and delay in public projects are relevant factors in granting or refusing injunctions
Whether the court can award damages beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction when an injunction is wrongly granted
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction under Article 227 to interfere even if an alternate remedy exists, provided there is a failure of justice.
An ad interim injunction should not be granted if it causes serious prejudice to public interest, especially in cases involving public utility projects.
Courts must consider the balance of convenience, prima facie case, and potential irreparable harm to both parties, including the public, when granting injunctions.
A court may award damages for loss caused by an injunction, even beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, as part of equitable relief to prevent abuse of process.
doctrines: Balance of convenience
Prima facie case
Irreparable injury
Public interest doctrine
Inherent powers of court to award damages for wrongful injunction

card.dispute: The appellant claimed rights over land allotted to a tribal respondent by arguing for permission to purchase it, while the authorities refused alienation and the High Court dismissed his writ petition.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector and Commissioner were justified in refusing permission for alienation of land allotted to a tribal under land reform policies?
Whether the appellant could claim protection under Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act despite lack of permission for alienation?
Whether the agreement to sell tribal-allotted land without prior sanction violated public policy and was void under the Contract Act?
holdings: The refusal to grant permission for alienation of land allotted to a tribal was valid as it aligned with constitutional goals of economic empowerment under Articles 38, 39, and 46.
Section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply where possession is based on an agreement that violates statutory restrictions and public policy.
An agreement to transfer land allotted to a tribal without prior sanction is void under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act as it is opposed to public policy.
doctrines: Public policy doctrine
Constitutional mandate for socio-economic justice
Doctrine of proportionality in distributive justice
Protection of tribal land under Directive Principles of State Policy

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Gurdial Singh (plaintiffs) sued to recover 7/8th share of land from Harmel Kaur and subsequent purchasers, claiming she only had a life interest, while defendants argued she acquired absolute ownership under the Hindu Succession Act.
issues_decided: Whether Harmel Kaur acquired an absolute or restricted estate in the suit land given to her in lieu of maintenance under a compromise decree.
Whether Section 14(1) or Section 14(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to property given in lieu of maintenance under a compromise.
holdings: Property given to a female Hindu in lieu of maintenance, even with restrictive covenants, becomes her absolute property under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act if she is in possession.
Section 14(2) does not apply where property is transferred in lieu of maintenance under a compromise, as it arises from a pre-existing right and not a mere gift or will.
doctrines: Transformation of limited estate into absolute ownership under Section 14(1)
Distinction between pre-existing rights and gratuitous transfers under Section 14(2)

card.dispute: The Municipal Committee, Jind, appealed against the decree of the Additional District Judge granting injunction to Jagat Singh, who claimed ownership and possession of 5 kanals of land, which the Committee claimed was public land ('gair-mumkin johar') where it had constructed a park.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was entitled to a decree of injunction based on ownership and possession of the disputed land?
Whether the Court of Appeal erred in decreeing the suit without deciding the question of title?
Whether the suit could be treated as one for possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, despite being filed on the basis of title?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the second appeal in limine?
holdings: The respondent failed to prove title and settled possession over the disputed land, and thus was not entitled to a decree for injunction.
The Court of Appeal committed a substantial error of law by decreeing the suit without first adjudicating the issue of title, which was actively disputed.

A suit filed on the basis of ownership and possession cannot be treated as a claim under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, unless it specifically alleges dispossession without consent and outside due process of law.
The High Court ought not to have dismissed the second appeal in limine, as a substantial question of law was involved in the impugned judgment.
doctrines: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 protects possession irrespective of title, but only if dispossession is alleged and proven.
Revenue entries are not conclusive proof of title and can be rebutted by evidence.
A civil court must decide the issue of title in a suit based on ownership before granting relief based on possession.
Substantial question of law in second appeal requires adjudication, not summary dismissal.

card.dispute: The appellant, Nani Gopal Paul, challenged the impleadment of respondents and the legality of a court-confirmed property sale in a foreclosure suit, after he was declared the highest bidder but had paid only part of the bid amount.
issues_decided: Whether the court sale in the foreclosure suit was vitiated by illegality in procedure
Whether the confirmation of sale to the appellant was valid despite non-payment of the full bid amount
Whether the appellate court could intervene in the sale process without a formal application under CPC
holdings: A court sale confirmed without proper judicial scrutiny and while ignoring higher bids is vitiated by illegality and can be set aside.
Confirmation of a sale is illegal if the purchaser has not paid the required amount or provided lawful assurance for payment.
An appellate court may intervene suo motu to correct manifest illegality in a court-ordered sale, even without a formal application under Order 21 Rules 89 or 90 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90
doctrines: Suo motu judicial notice of illegality
Manifest illegality in court-conducted sales
Principle of open and fair auction in court sales

card.dispute: The husband filed a suit claiming properties purchased in his wife's name as benami, which the wife contested, leading to a legal question on whether such suits are barred by the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 bars a suit or defence in respect of a property purchased by a person in the name of his wife or unmarried daughter?
Whether the statutory presumption under Section 3(2) of the Act affects the husband's right to prove that the property was not purchased for the benefit of the wife?
holdings: Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not prohibit a suit or defence in respect of a benami transaction where property is purchased by a person in the name of his wife or unmarried daughter under Section 3(2) of the Act.

A husband can file a suit to enforce rights over property purchased in his wife's name, but must prove that the purchase was not for her benefit, as a statutory presumption under Section 3(2) favours such a benefit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 11
doctrines: Statutory interpretation
Presumption of law
Reconciliation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff challenged the validity of a judgment dismissing a suit for specific performance of a property sale agreement, claiming it was a nullity due to the plaintiff's death before judgment was pronounced.
issues_decided: Whether the judgment and decree passed after the death of the plaintiff is a nullity under the CPC.
Whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, entitling him to specific performance.
holdings: A judgment pronounced after the conclusion of hearing but after the death of a party does not abate and remains valid under Order 22 Rule 6 of the CPC.
The plaintiff failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his contractual obligations, a necessary condition for granting specific performance under the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 6
doctrines: No abatement of proceedings due to death after hearing
Readiness and willingness as a condition precedent for specific performance
Equitable discretion in granting specific performance

card.dispute: The housing society and a flat owner challenged the acquisition of their land by the State, arguing it violated Article 21 by depriving them of shelter and dignity, and sought protection from eviction pending compensation determination.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of land under the Land Acquisition Act violates Article 21 of the Constitution by depriving a person of shelter and dignity?
Whether delay in making the award under Section 11 renders the acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 11-A?
Whether the court can direct that the appellants not be evicted until the reference for enhanced compensation is decided?
Whether the acquisition was vitiated by mala fide intentions?
holdings: Acquisition of property for public purpose under the Land Acquisition Act does not violate Article 21, even if it results in loss of shelter, as long as it is done according to law and with payment of compensation.

A delay in making the award does not automatically render the acquisition lapsed under Section 11-A if the issue was not argued before the High Court; the Supreme Court will not entertain fresh legal arguments not raised below.
Once compensation is deposited under Section 31, the State can take possession under Section 16, and courts cannot restrain eviction merely because a reference for higher compensation is pending.
Mere existence of a prior dispute over title or earlier requisitioning of flats does not prove mala fide in the current acquisition for public purpose.
doctrines: Right to life under Article 21 includes right to shelter but does not bar lawful acquisition for public purpose
Principle of eminent domain
Rule against raising new legal grounds for the first time in Supreme Court
Doctrine of restitution not applicable in determining compensation under Section 23(1)
Mala fide in acquisition must be proven by clear evidence, not inferred from prior disputes

card.dispute: The dispute was between the heirs of a landlord and tenants over whether a decree for ejectment became inexecutable and the suit liable to be dismissed under Section 4(4) of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, due to non-payment of compensation for superstructure within the stipulated time.
issues_decided: Whether the orders directing payment of compensation for superstructure were passed under Section 4(1) of the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921
Whether the suit became inexecutable and was liable to be dismissed under Section 4(4) of the Act due to non-payment within three months
Whether the executing court could direct payment of value of superstructure despite dismissal of the application as time-barred
holdings: Orders directing payment of compensation for superstructure were not passed under Section 4(1) of the Act, as the underlying applications were dismissed as barred by limitation and no valid application under Section 10(2) remained pending.
Section 4(4) of the Act is not attracted where directions for payment are made dehors the Act; hence, non-payment does not render the ejectment decree inexecutable or lead to dismissal of the suit.

A court may direct payment of value of superstructure on equitable grounds even if statutory applications are time-barred, but such directions do not invoke the provisions or consequences of Section 4(4) of the Act.
provisions: Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 3
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 4(1)
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 4(4)
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 10(1)
Madras City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 10(2)
Madras City Tenants' Protection (Amendment) Act, 1955, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of equitable compensation
Doctrine of finality of orders
Statutory limitation and its effect on applicability of tenant protection laws
Interpretation of procedural provisions in rent control legislation

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of government-allocated land originally granted to a Scheduled Caste beneficiary, challenging the cancellation of his purchase on grounds that the sale violated prohibitions on alienation of such land.
issues_decided: Whether the prohibition on alienation of land granted to Scheduled Castes under Rule 43(5) of the Karnataka Revenue Code is absolute and continues beyond an initial 10-year period
Whether the alienation of such land is void as being against public policy under Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act
Whether the purchaser can acquire title by adverse possession despite deriving title from an invalid sale
holdings: The prohibition on alienation under Rule 43(5) of the Karnataka Revenue Code is absolute and perpetual, not limited to ten years, to ensure economic empowerment and prevent dispossession of Scheduled Caste beneficiaries.

Alienation of land granted to Scheduled Castes in violation of statutory rules is void under Section 23 of the Contract Act as it contravenes public policy rooted in constitutional goals of social and economic justice.

A purchaser who takes possession under a void sale cannot claim adverse possession against the State without disclaiming the title under which he entered and asserting a hostile claim, which was not done here.
doctrines: Public policy under Section 23 of the Contract Act
Economic empowerment as part of the right to life and dignity under Article 21
Harmonious construction of fundamental rights and directive principles
Requirement of hostile possession for adverse possession claims

card.dispute: Landlords sued tenants for rent arrears and possession; tenants challenged the validity of a Uttar Pradesh rule allowing courts to strike off defences for non-payment of admitted rent, claiming it was inconsistent with central law and violated constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether Order 15 Rule 5 of the CPC, as amended by Uttar Pradesh legislation, is repugnant to the Central CPC (Amendment) Act, 1976, and thus void under Article 254(1) of the Constitution
Whether Order 15 Rule 5 violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating arbitrary or discriminatory classifications among tenants
Whether the Central CPC (Amendment) Act, 1976, has retrospective operation and applies to pending proceedings
holdings: Order 15 Rule 5, introduced by Uttar Pradesh law and not amended by the Central Act, does not occupy the same field as the Central Act and thus there is no repugnancy; it remains valid under Article 254(1) with presidential assent.

The classification under Order 15 Rule 5 between tenants who default on admitted rent and those who dispute liability is based on intelligible differentia and has a rational nexus with the objective of protecting landlords, so it does not violate Article 14.
Section 97(3) of the Central CPC (Amendment) Act, 1976, clearly provides for retrospective application to pending suits, appeals, and proceedings, regardless of when the cause of action arose.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 15 Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 16
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 11 Rule 21
U.P. Civil Laws (Reforms and Amendment) Act, 1976
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of Repugnancy under Article 254(1)
Doctrine of Prospective and Retrospective Operation of Statutes
Doctrine of Classification under Article 14
Presidential Assent to State Laws under Article 254(2)

card.dispute: The appellant-tenant and respondent-landlord disputed ownership and possession of land after the abolition of minor inams, specifically whether the tenant's patta for a building entitled him to the site and barred eviction for non-payment of rent.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of a joint ryotwari patta under the Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963 vested ownership of the site in the appellant-tenant who owned the building
Whether the Civil Court's jurisdiction to decide the suit for possession was ousted by the said Act or the patta granted by revenue authorities
Whether the decree for possession in favor of the respondent-landlord became unenforceable due to the patta granted during the pendency of the suit
holdings: The patta granted only gave the appellant a right to the building under Section 13(1), not the site, which remained with the respondent; thus, the appellant did not acquire ownership of the land.
The Civil Court retains jurisdiction to decide title and eviction matters not covered by the Act; the revenue authorities' decisions do not oust civil jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes.
The decree for possession was valid and executable despite the patta, as the patta did not transfer ownership of the site to the appellant.
provisions: Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 13(1)
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 13(2)
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 43
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, Section 46
doctrines: Ouster of civil jurisdiction requires clear statutory language
Finality of revenue orders is limited to matters within the scope of the statute
Statutory vesting under land reform laws does not automatically transfer site ownership to building owners

card.dispute: The petitioner, claiming benami ownership of land through a benamidar, challenged the validity of a partition decree in favor of Bibi Raifunnisa, arguing it was collusive and did not bind him, but the respondent contended the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner's suit to set aside a decree was governed by Article 59 or the residuary Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the petitioner had constructive notice of the preliminary and final decrees in the partition suit
Whether the suit filed in 1981 was within the period of limitation
