holdings: Article 59 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to suits seeking to set aside a decree, even by a person claiming through a party to the decree, if they had knowledge of it.
A person deriving title from a party to litigation is deemed to have constructive notice of the proceedings and decrees, especially when the benamidar participated in the suit.
The suit was barred by limitation as it was filed beyond three years from the date the petitioner was deemed to have knowledge of the decrees.
doctrines: Constructive notice
Benami transaction and derivative title
Residuary provision versus specific limitation period
Fraud and collusive decree as grounds for setting aside a decree

card.dispute: The auction purchaser challenged the High Court's decision to remit the matter for a local inspection to determine whether an 'upstair building' within the property boundaries was included in the auction sale.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Subordinate Judge's finding that the entire property within the boundaries mentioned in the sale certificate was sold to the auction purchaser.
Whether the expression 'terraced house' in the sale certificate limited the sale to only a portion of the property within the described boundaries.
holdings: The sale certificate, which clearly described the boundaries and property details, conclusively determined the extent of the property sold, and the entire area within those boundaries was transferred to the auction purchaser.

The High Court erred in exercising revisional jurisdiction to re-evaluate a factual finding by the Subordinate Judge that the property description in the sale certificate included all structures within the stated boundaries.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rules 90 and 91
doctrines: Finality of sale certificates as documents of title
Principle of finality of findings of fact in execution proceedings
Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) fought with the National Fertilizers Corporation over the appropriation of deposited compensation amounts, specifically whether they could claim priority in adjusting payments towards costs, interest, and solatium before compensation, and entitlement to interest on solatium and additional amounts under amended provisions.
issues_decided: Whether the claimant can appropriate payments received towards costs, interest, and solatium before the principal compensation under the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether interest is payable on solatium and additional amounts under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to award additional benefits under Amendment Act 68 of 1984 in revision when the enhancement was made prior to the amendment?
holdings: The right to appropriate payment lies with the debtor only if expressly stated or implied; under the Land Acquisition Act, the award specifies components, and claimants cannot unilaterally appropriate payments towards interest or costs before compensation.
No interest is payable on solatium under Section 23(2) or on additional amounts under Section 23(1-A), as these are distinct and excluded from interest liability under Sections 28 and 34.

The High Court lacked jurisdiction to apply Amendment Act 68 of 1984 to grant additional benefits retrospectively, as the amendment could not be applied to cases where compensation was enhanced prior to its enactment.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 1
doctrines: Appropriation of payment under statutory framework
Retrospective application of amendments
Distinction between compensation, solatium, and interest under land acquisition law
Exclusion of CPC provisions where inconsistent with special statutes

card.dispute: Whether Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 applies to suits pending before its enforcement, where a person claims to be the real owner of benami property.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 has retrospective application to pending suits filed before its commencement.
Whether Section 4(2) bars defences based on benami ownership in suits already ongoing when the Act came into force.
Whether the Act is declaratory or substantive in nature.
Whether the Act affects vested rights and thus requires explicit language for retrospective operation.
holdings: Section 4(1) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not apply to suits filed before its commencement, as it lacks retrospective effect.
Section 4(2) does not bar defences based on benami ownership in pending suits unless such defences were raised after the Act came into force.
The Act is not declaratory but prohibitory in nature, as it creates new rights and obligations and destroys existing rights of real owners.
A statute affecting vested rights cannot be given retrospective effect unless the language clearly mandates it, which is absent here.
doctrines: Presumption against retrospective operation of statutes
Distinction between declaratory and substantive legislation
Rule of statutory interpretation: statutes affecting vested rights require clear language for retroactivity

card.dispute: The appellants, executors named in a will, challenged the refusal of probate by lower courts which found suspicious circumstances surrounding the will and codicils executed by Saroj Bala.
issues_decided: Whether the will and codicils were surrounded by suspicious circumstances requiring the propounder to discharge a higher burden of proof.
Whether the natural heirs' disinheritance raised suspicion invalidating the will.
Whether interested witnesses and the involvement of a relative in executing the will vitiated its validity.
Whether the testatrix had the requisite testamentary capacity and the will was voluntarily executed.
holdings: A will is not automatically suspect merely because natural heirs are disinherited, as the essence of testamentary freedom is to alter normal succession.
Identification of the testatrix by an advocate connected to an executor does not raise suspicion if the identity was correctly verified and no fraud is alleged.
Interested witnesses do not invalidate a registered will if the Sub-registrar confirmed the testatrix understood and voluntarily executed the document.

Execution of codicils years later, financial transactions, and property dealings by the testatrix support her testamentary capacity and voluntary execution, outweighing alleged suspicious circumstances.
doctrines: Testamentary capacity
Suspicious circumstances doctrine
Propounder's burden of proof
Voluntariness in execution of will

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted for murder and other offences during a land dispute, challenged their conviction, claiming right of private defence against alleged criminal trespass by the complainant party.
issues_decided: Whether the complainant party's entry onto the disputed land constituted criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC, thereby entitling the accused to private defence of property?
Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence of person, justifying the use of lethal force?
Whether the trial court could rely on the same prosecution witnesses to convict some accused while acquitting others?
holdings: The unauthorised entry by the complainant party onto the disputed land did not amount to criminal trespass under Section 441 IPC, as there was no intention to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult, or annoy the accused.

The right of private defence does not extend to causing death in response to mere civil trespass; even if criminal trespass were made out, the appellants' premeditated and disproportionate attack disentitled them to claim private defence under Section 104 and Exception 2 to Section 300 IPC.

The trial court was justified in relying on the prosecution evidence to convict some accused while acquitting others, as the principle 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' does not apply in criminal trials, and courts must sift truth from falsehood.
provisions: Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1985, Section 6
doctrines: Right of private defence of property
Right of private defence of person
Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
Principle of proportionality in self-defence
Doctrine of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC

card.dispute: The husband sought dissolution of a marriage that had emotionally and practically ended after 25 years, citing cruelty, while the wife opposed it despite long separation.
issues_decided: Whether the marriage, though not legally dissolved, could be terminated due to emotional and practical death of the relationship
Whether cruelty could be inferred from the continued existence of a defunct marriage
Whether the court could dissolve the marriage under its equitable powers despite lack of proof of statutory cruelty
holdings: A marriage that is emotionally and practically dead, with no possibility of reconciliation, may be dissolved to prevent further agony.
Continuance of a defunct marital relationship amounts to cruelty when there is no hope of revival and the spouses have lived apart for decades.
The Supreme Court, under Article 142, can dissolve a marriage equitably, even if statutory grounds are not fully met, to do complete justice.
doctrines: Equitable dissolution of marriage
Constructive cruelty
Dead marriage doctrine
Plenary powers under Article 142

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India for planned development, arguing that the method used to calculate market value was legally flawed.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of acquired land in an undeveloped area adjacent to a developed locality should be based on the price of small developed plots.
Whether the principle of averaging prices of developed and undeveloped land is legally sound when determining compensation.
Whether deductions for development costs and non-saleable land require further reduction in market value.
holdings: Market value of large tracts of undeveloped land cannot be equated with prices from small plot sales in developed areas, even if nearby, due to differences in realization potential.
Averaging the price of developed and undeveloped land without accounting for development potential and time for realization leads to incorrect compensation.
After deducting land meant for development and accounting for layout constraints, a 50% reduction on the resalable price is appropriate to determine fair market value.
doctrines: Principle of resalable future price in land acquisition compensation
Wholesale price deduction doctrine for large land acquisitions
Non-equivalence of small plot sale prices with bulk land valuation

card.dispute: Shabi Construction Company sued the City and Industrial Development Corporation for failing to grant a higher FSI as allegedly promised in a lease agreement, seeking enforcement of contractual rights despite lack of statutory approval.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent could be estopped from denying a higher FSI based on its representation and contract with the appellant?
Whether the fixation of FSI under the Regulations is ultra vires the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966?
Whether the agreement granting higher FSI could create a legally enforceable right without prior state government sanction?
holdings: The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked against a public authority when the promise is contrary to statutory provisions or beyond its legal authority.

Fixation of FSI under the Regulations is not ultra vires, as it falls within the regulatory power under section 159 of the Act, provided it conforms to the Development Plan and receives state approval.
A contractual right to higher FSI does not become legally enforceable unless the modification is sanctioned by the State Government under sections 31 and 37 of the Act.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 22(m)
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 31
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 37
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 159
doctrines: Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel
Ultra Vires Doctrine
Statutory Sanction Requirement for Development Plan Modifications

card.dispute: The appellants challenged whether their right to catch fish in a tank was a lease or licence, and thus whether it was subject to compulsory registration and stamp duty.
issues_decided: Whether the right to catch fish in a tank constitutes immovable property under the law
Whether the instrument granting the right to catch fish is a lease or licence
Whether such a lease is compulsorily registerable under the Indian Registration Act
Whether the instrument is liable to stamp duty under the Indian Stamp Act
holdings: The right to catch fish in a tank is a benefit arising out of land and thus constitutes immovable property under the M.P. General Clause Act.
The instrument is a lease, not a licence, as the parties proceeded on that basis and no contrary contention or document was presented.
A lease for more than one year or reserving yearly rent is compulsorily registerable under Section 17(1)(c) of the Registration Act; a nine-month lease is not.
The right to catch fish, being a profit a prendre and immovable property, is an instrument liable to stamp duty regardless of duration.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, Section 2(16), Article 35(a) of Schedule 1-A
doctrines: Profit a prendre as immovable property
Doctrine of constructive res judicata (implied acceptance of lease premise)
Compulsory registration of leases exceeding one year
Stamp duty applicability to instruments involving immovable property benefits

card.dispute: The husband sought dissolution of a long-broken marriage on grounds of cruelty, while the wife opposed it, leading to a dispute over whether a dead marriage should be legally ended despite lack of proven statutory cruelty.
issues_decided: Whether the marriage, though emotionally and practically dead, could be dissolved without proven statutory cruelty?
Whether the court could dissolve the marriage in the interest of justice despite failure to prove grounds under the Hindu Marriage Act?
holdings: A marriage that is irretrievably broken and dead emotionally and practically causes continued suffering, and its continuation amounts to cruelty.
The Supreme Court, under Article 142, can dissolve a marriage to do complete justice, even if statutory grounds for divorce are not fully established.
doctrines: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage
Equitable powers under Article 142
Constructive cruelty

card.dispute: The appellants, decree-holders who purchased land in an auction-sale from Jagdish Chander, challenged the validity of the ceiling authorities' decision to ignore the sale and treat the land as part of the surplus holding under the Uttar Pradesh Ceiling Act.
issues_decided: Whether an involuntary transfer of land through court auction during pending ceiling proceedings is valid under Section 5(6) and Section 5(8) of the Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
Whether such a transfer can be excluded from the tenure-holder's holding while determining surplus land
Whether the auction-sale was bona fide and for adequate consideration within the meaning of the proviso to Section 5(6)
holdings: Involuntary transfers such as court-ordered auction sales are subject to the same restrictions as voluntary transfers under Section 5(6) and Section 5(8) of the Ceiling Act and must meet the conditions of being in good faith and for adequate consideration to be recognized.
Any transfer of land during the pendency of surplus land proceedings, whether voluntary or involuntary, is void under Section 5(8) of the Ceiling Act.

The burden lies on the claimant to prove that a transfer falls within the exception in Section 5(6) proviso (b), and failure to demonstrate bona fides and adequate consideration results in the transfer being disregarded for ceiling purposes.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5(6)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 5(8)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10(2)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 9(2)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 11(1)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 12(1)
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, Section 13
doctrines: Strict construction of agrarian reform legislation to prevent evasion of land ceiling limits
Presumption against transfers during pendency of ceiling proceedings
Voidness of transactions violating mandatory statutory prohibitions (Section 5(8))
Burden of proof on party claiming exception to deemed invalid transfers

card.dispute: The appellant, S.P. Goel, challenged the dismissal of his consumer complaint against the Collector of Stamps, Delhi, for alleged deficiency of service in failing to register a will or issue a certified copy despite payment of registration charges.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant qualifies as a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, in relation to the registration of a document and payment of stamp duty.
Whether the functions performed by the Collector of Stamps and registering officers amount to 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act.
Whether the Collector of Stamps can be held liable for deficiency in service given the statutory and quasi-judicial nature of his functions.
holdings: A person presenting a document for registration and paying stamp or registration fees does not become a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, as the transaction is revenue-oriented, not commercial.
The acts of registration and stamp duty assessment are statutory, sovereign functions, some being quasi-judicial, and do not constitute 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act.

The Collector of Stamps is protected from civil liability under Section 1 of the Judicial Officers (Protection) Act, 1850, and Section 86 of the Registration Act, 1908, for bona fide official actions, and no mala fide was alleged or proven.
doctrines: Sovereign immunity
Quasi-judicial functions
Bona fide official action
Statutory duty vs. service under consumer law

card.dispute: The appellants sought to execute a preliminary decree for partition after a final decree had not been fully passed, while the respondent argued the execution application was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether limitation for executing a decree begins to run from the date of the preliminary decree or only after a final decree is passed and engrossed on stamped paper?
Whether a partial final decree in favour of one party crystallizes the rights of all parties for execution purposes?
Whether the failure to supply non-judicial stamps for a final decree renders the decree unexecutable and affects the limitation period?
holdings: Limitation for execution of a decree begins only after a final decree is passed and duly engrossed on stamped paper, not from the date of the preliminary decree.
A final decree that is only partial and not demarcating the entire property does not crystallize the rights of all parties; hence, no executable decree exists until full adjudication.
The requirement to engross a final decree on stamped paper is a condition precedent; until fulfilled, no executable decree exists under Order 20 Rule 18(2) of CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 20 Rule 18(2)
Bombay Stamp Act, 1958, Section 2(a) and Section 34
doctrines: Condition precedent to execution
Crystallization of rights doctrine
Doctrine of executable decree

card.dispute: The State of Haryana challenged the High Court's enhancement of compensation for fruit-bearing trees in a land acquisition case, arguing it violated legal principles on valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing compensation for fruit-bearing trees separately from the land value.
Whether the multiplier used for determining market value of land with fruit-bearing trees was legally correct.
holdings: Compensation for land and fruit-bearing trees must not be determined separately; the value of trees must be included in the land's market value based on yield and an appropriate multiplier.
When land value is based on yield from trees, an 8-year multiplier is the maximum allowable; using a higher multiplier or enhancing compensation further is illegal.
doctrines: Principle of single market valuation
Multiplier rule for agricultural and tree-yielding land

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the maintainability of a civil suit and ad-interim injunction granted to respondents who were in possession of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether a civil suit is maintainable in respect of land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 after issuance of notification under Section 4 and declaration under Section 6?
Whether a civil court can grant ad-interim injunction against the state from taking possession of land acquired under the Act?
holdings: A civil suit is not maintainable as the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is a complete code, and civil courts lack jurisdiction to question the validity of notifications under Section 4 or declarations under Section 6.

An injunction cannot be granted by a civil court once possession has been taken under the Act, as such matters are outside the jurisdiction of civil courts except in proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39 Rule 1
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction in statutory acquisition proceedings
Doctrine of eminent domain
Finality of public purpose declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act

card.dispute: The State of Kerala fought against M.K. Kunhikannan Nambiar and others over whether two sisters could be impleaded as cultivating tenants in ceiling proceedings after a prior order had rejected their tenancy claim.
issues_decided: Whether the order of the Taluk Land Board dated 28.6.1977 rejecting the impleadment application of respondents No. 3 and 4 became final and binding between the parties.
Whether the subsequent observation in another revision petition (C.R.P. 3696 of 1977) that the Board's proceedings were 'void' affected the validity of the earlier final order.
Whether the High Court erred in treating the earlier final order as non-est and allowing impleadment in later proceedings.
holdings: An order, even if later declared void in a separate proceeding, remains effective between the parties until set aside by a competent court.
The affirmation of the Board's order in C.R.P. 3440 of 1977 made it final and binding between the State and respondents No. 3 and 4, despite any infirmity noted in another case.
A court's decision confirming an order, even on an incorrect legal ground, is not a nullity and cannot be treated as non-est if it was within jurisdiction.
doctrines: Inter partes finality of orders
Distinction between void and voidable orders
Presumption of validity of administrative decisions
Jurisdiction of appellate courts to affirm decisions even with errors of law

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh challenged the High Court's direction to pay 12% interest on equitable grounds in addition to statutory interest under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, in a land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could award 12% interest on equitable grounds in addition to statutory interest under Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the court has power to grant interest at a higher rate than prescribed by statute based on equitable considerations?
holdings: The High Court cannot award interest at 12% on equitable grounds in addition to statutory interest where the Land Acquisition Act prescribes specific rates and methods for interest payment.
Equitable jurisdiction does not empower courts to alter the rate or mode of interest payment when the statute provides a complete code on the subject.
doctrines: Statutory exclusivity doctrine
Equity cannot override statutory provisions
Complete code doctrine

card.dispute: The State of Gujarat challenged whether landowners could seek a reference to a civil court for higher compensation under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act after having accepted compensation and waived their right to reference in a written, unregistered agreement.
issues_decided: Whether landowners who entered into a written agreement under Section 11(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, accepting compensation and waiving their right to a Section 18 reference, could later seek such a reference.
Whether an unregistered agreement under Section 11(2) is valid and enforceable despite the Registration Act, 1908.
Whether acceptance of compensation without protest bars a claim under Section 18 of the Act.
holdings: Landowners who voluntarily entered into a written agreement under Section 11(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, accepting compensation and waiving their right to a reference, are estopped from later seeking a reference under Section 18.
An agreement under Section 11(2) of the Land Acquisition Act does not require registration under the Registration Act, 1908, as Section 11(4) expressly overrides such requirement.

Acceptance of compensation without protest, especially under a consensual award, extinguishes the right to seek a reference under Section 18, as the statutory condition for such a reference is non-acceptance of the award.
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver
Doctrine of estoppel
Non obstante clause interpretation
Statutory bar on reference upon acceptance of compensation

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision that Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 is unconstitutional for violating Articles 14 and 21 by denying anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether Section 18 of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 violates Article 14 by creating an unreasonable classification in denying anticipatory bail?
Whether Section 18 violates Article 21 by depriving a person of the right to seek anticipatory bail?
holdings: Section 18 does not violate Article 14 as offences under the SC/ST Act constitute a distinct class due to their social and historical context, justifying differential treatment.
The right to anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC is a statutory, not constitutional, right; its exclusion under the SC/ST Act does not infringe Article 21.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 18
doctrines: Classification test under Article 14
Essential procedural fairness under Article 21
Statutory vs. constitutional rights

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra and others fought against landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, particularly regarding delays in issuing declarations and awards.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to publish a declaration under Section 126(2) within three years of the notification under Section 125 renders the acquisition proceedings invalid
Whether Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, applies to acquisitions under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
Whether the amendment introduced by Section 126(4) applies to both pending and future proceedings
holdings: Failure to issue a declaration within three years under Section 126(2) does not invalidate the notification under Section 125; a fresh declaration under Section 126(4) is valid and revives the acquisition process.

Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, does not apply to acquisitions under the Maharashtra Act because the state legislature only incorporated specific provisions of the Central Act, not all procedural amendments.
The amendment under Section 126(4) applies to both pending and subsequent proceedings, as the legislative intent supports its retrospective and prospective application.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 125
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 127
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 128
doctrines: Legislative incorporation vs. adoption by reference
Presumption against implied application of amended central laws to state statutes
Savings clause for procedural lapses in land acquisition
Legislative intent in revival of lapsed acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The state of Punjab and others fought against Mohabir Singh and others over whether government-issued property valuation guidelines could override the quasi-judicial discretion of a Sub-Registrar under Section 47A of the Indian Stamp Act, 1982, in determining stamp duty.
issues_decided: Whether the Sub-Registrar can rely solely on government-prescribed valuation guidelines to demand higher stamp duty without independent quasi-judicial satisfaction under Section 47A(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1982.
Whether the government's guidelines, which set minimum property values, are consistent with the statutory discretion conferred by Section 47A of the Indian Stamp Act, 1982.
holdings: The Sub-Registrar must independently form a quasi-judicial belief that the value stated in a property instrument is understated; reliance solely on government guidelines violates Section 47A(1).
Government guidelines prescribing minimum property values cannot override the Sub-Registrar’s statutory discretion under Section 47A(1); such guidelines must remain advisory and not binding.
doctrines: Quasi-judicial discretion
Statutory interpretation
Administrative guidelines vs. statutory authority

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the High Court's decision to allow a delayed application for reference to court under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming the application was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the notice under Section 12(2) of the Land Acquisition Act must contain detailed reasons for the determination of compensation to start the limitation period under Section 18(2).
Whether the High Court was correct in holding that the limitation period for filing a reference application did not begin due to an allegedly defective notice.
holdings: The notice under Section 12(2) only needs to inform the interested person of the award and does not require detailed reasons for the compensation determination to trigger the limitation period.

The limitation period under Section 18(2) begins upon receipt of the Section 12(2) notice, regardless of whether the notice contains detailed valuation particulars, provided the award is accessible for inspection or copy.
doctrines: Conclusive evidence doctrine under Section 12(1)
Limitation bar under statutory time limits
Notice sufficiency under statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The state of Orissa challenged the enhancement of land compensation by 25% for future potential value after market value had already been determined based on existing potentialities.
issues_decided: Whether compensation can be further enhanced by 25% for future potential value after market value has already accounted for existing potentialities of the land.
Whether the courts below erred in considering future potential development of the locality while determining compensation under the Land Acquisition Act.
holdings: When market value is determined under Section 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, it must reflect the land's potentialities as they existed on the date of the Section 4(1) notification, including its possible future use.

A further enhancement of 25% for future potentiality is impermissible under Section 24 of the Act, which prohibits considering increases in value due to the intended use of the acquired land or its effect on neighboring lands.
doctrines: Prohibition on consideration of future use under Section 24
Market value includes existing potentialities as of notification date
Judicial adherence to statutory limits in compensation determination

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged the Civil Judge's order granting additional compensation, solatium, and interest under the 1984 Amendment Act to landowners after the original compensation award had already been made.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to award benefits under the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 68 of 1984 after the compensation decree has been passed.
Whether the civil court can invoke inherent powers under Section 151 of the CPC to grant additional compensation and interest post-decree.
holdings: A civil court lacks jurisdiction to award additional compensation, solatium, or interest under the 1984 Amendment Act after the decree under Section 26(2) of the Land Acquisition Act has been passed, as such powers are not conferred by the Act.

The inherent powers under Section 151 of the CPC cannot be invoked to grant additional benefits under the Amendment Act, as the express provisions of the Land Acquisition Act exclude such application by necessary implication.
doctrines: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Jurisdictional limitation of civil courts
Doctrine of necessary implication
Finality of decree under Section 26(2)

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra appealed against the Bombay High Court's decision to direct it to pay compensation to Digambar for land allegedly used for a scarcity relief road project in 1971–72 without consent or payment.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in granting compensation under Article 226 despite a 20-year delay by the respondent in filing the writ petition?
Whether the doctrine of laches applies to claims for compensation under Article 226 of the Constitution?
holdings: A delay of 20 years in seeking relief under Article 226, without adequate explanation, constitutes laches and disentitles the petitioner to equitable relief.
The High Court must consider the petitioner’s conduct, including undue delay, before granting discretionary relief under Article 226; failure to do so renders the order arbitrary and unsustainable.
doctrines: Doctrine of laches
Clean hands doctrine
Discretionary nature of writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: The dispute was between family members over the partition of property and the validity of an assignment of a share in the suit property by one co-sharer despite a court order restraining alienation.
issues_decided: Whether the assignment of a decree for a share in immovable property, made during the pendency of a suit and in violation of a court's restraint order, is valid under Order 22 Rule 10 of the CPC.
Whether the assignees of a party's share in a suit can be impleaded as parties when the assignment violates a court order prohibiting alienation of the property in dispute.
holdings: An assignment of a decree relating to immovable property constitutes a transfer of property and falls within the scope of a court order restraining alienation of the suit property.
A transfer or assignment made in defiance of a court's injunction during the pendency of a suit is invalid and cannot be recognized for the purpose of impleading assignees as parties to the suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
doctrines: Lis pendens
Court's inherent power to maintain status quo during pendency of proceedings

card.dispute: The Assistant Commissioner challenged whether landowners were entitled to additional compensation at 12% per annum under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act from the date possession was taken, even though the notification under Section 4(1) was published later.
issues_decided: Whether landowners are entitled to additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act from the date of taking possession when possession was taken before the publication of the notification under Section 4(1)?
How should the phrase 'whichever is earlier' in Section 23(1-A) be interpreted when possession precedes notification?
holdings: Landowners are entitled to additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) from the date of taking possession, even if the notification under Section 4(1) was published later, provided the possession was not legally challenged.

The phrase 'whichever is earlier' in Section 23(1-A) must be interpreted to give effect to the legislative intent of compensating owners for loss of enjoyment, especially when possession is taken prior to notification.
doctrines: Literal vs. purposive interpretation of statutes
Mitigation of hardship to landowners
Strict construction leading to unjust results

card.dispute: The Cantonment Board revoked construction permission granted to S.N. Awasthi and others, who challenged the cancellation; the Board appealed the High Court's decision restoring the permission.
issues_decided: Whether cancellation of construction permission without hearing the licensee violates natural justice
Whether the Defence Estates Officer had the authority to cancel the permission under the amended law
Whether equity justifies non-compliance with mandatory statutory conditions for construction in a cantonment area
holdings: Non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of prior consultation with the Defence Estates Officer renders the sanction illegal, and such illegality cannot be cured by equitable considerations.
The cancellation of permission without a hearing does not invalidate the action where the original sanction was void due to non-fulfilment of a statutory condition precedent.
Equity cannot override statutory mandates; construction without lawful sanction cannot be validated merely because work has commenced.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Mandatory statutory compliance
Equity cannot prevail over law

card.dispute: The Bihar State Housing Board challenged the High Court's decision to quash a show-cause notice and eviction proceedings against Ramesh Kumar Singh, who allegedly occupied a quarter allotted to another person on a hire-purchase basis.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash a show-cause notice issued under the Bihar State Housing Board Act, 1982, without the petitioner first challenging it before the competent authority.
Whether the show-cause notice issued under Section 59 of the Bihar State Housing Board Act was without jurisdiction or a nullity.
holdings: The High Court erred in entertaining the writ petition against a show-cause notice where no fundamental rights were violated and the jurisdiction of the competent authority was not manifestly absent; the petitioner should have first raised objections before the statutory authority.

A show-cause notice under Section 59 of the Bihar State Housing Board Act is not a nullity merely because ownership is disputed; such factual disputes must be adjudicated by the competent authority, not the High Court in writ proceedings.
provisions: Bihar State Housing Board Act, 1982, Section 59
Bihar State Housing Board Act, 1982, Section 58
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act
doctrines: Proper invocation of Article 226
Alternate remedy doctrine
Doctrine of non-interference with pending statutory proceedings

card.dispute: The dispute was between a sugar mill officers' association and the State of Uttar Pradesh over whether the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court had jurisdiction to hear a writ petition concerning a government order issued in Lucknow.
issues_decided: Whether the Lucknow Bench of the Allahabad High Court had territorial jurisdiction to entertain writ petitions arising from government orders issued in Lucknow, even if the original action occurred outside the Oudh region.
Whether the Explanation added to Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure in 1977 affected the interpretation of 'cases arising in such areas Oudh' under Clause 14 of the Amalgamation Order.
holdings: The Lucknow Bench has jurisdiction if part of the cause of action, including a government order or notification, arises within the Oudh area, as 'cause of action' is understood in Article 226 proceedings.

The interpretation of Clause 14 of the Amalgamation Order by this Court in Nasiruddin's case remains valid and binding, unaffected by the 1977 Explanation to Section 141 CPC, as it was based on the special law and not general civil procedure.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 141 (with Explanation added w.e.f. 1.2.1977)
doctrines: Cause of action doctrine in writ jurisdiction
Special law prevails over general law
Binding precedent of a larger bench
Forum conveniens in territorial jurisdiction

card.dispute: The government of Madras fought with landowners over the validity of ad-valorem court fees without an upper limit under the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, in appeals for enhanced compensation in land acquisition cases.
issues_decided: Whether the ad-valorem court fee of 7.5% without an upper limit under the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, is unconstitutional as being arbitrary and excessive?
Whether the levy of court fees must exactly match the administrative cost of civil justice?
Whether expenses on criminal justice and government law officers can be included in the cost of civil justice for fee justification?
holdings: A broad and general correlation, not exact equivalence, between court fee collections and administrative costs is sufficient; excess collections do not invalidate the fee if the primary purpose is service delivery.
The ad-valorem court fee without an upper limit is not unconstitutional, as it serves the purpose of funding civil justice, even if it causes financial burden.
Expenses on judicial officers handling both civil and criminal cases, and government law officers, are part of civil justice administration and may be included in cost calculations.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, Article (1) in Schedule (1)
High Court Fees Rules, 1956, Order II, Sub-rule (1), Rule (1)
doctrines: Broad correlation test for fee and expenditure
Administrative feasibility in cost estimation
State's obligation to fund justice without enrichment

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh fought Keshav Prasad Singh over the legality of acquiring land it had encroached upon after a civil court ordered demolition of the encroachment.
issues_decided: Whether the State's invocation of eminent domain under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was a colourable exercise of power after a civil court had declared the respondent the owner and ordered demolition of the encroachment.
Whether the State could validly invoke Section 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to dispense with the Section 5A inquiry given the urgency and public purpose.
holdings: The State's issuance of a notification under Section 4(1) was a valid exercise of eminent domain, not colourable, as the land was needed for a public purpose despite prior encroachment and pending appeal.
The State was justified in invoking Section 17(4) to dispense with the Section 5A inquiry due to urgency arising from the need to retain the compound wall for the safety of a public office.
doctrines: Colourable legislation doctrine
Eminent domain
Public purpose
Urgency in land acquisition

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the order allowing Pradeep Kumari to claim enhanced compensation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 based on a later court award, not the first one after the amendment's enactment.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be based on any award made after the amendment, or only the first such award.
Whether the Collector can award interest on additional compensation determined under Section 28-A.
holdings: Section 28-A allows re-determination of compensation based on any award made after its commencement, not just the first one, provided the application is filed within three months of that award.

The Collector can award interest on additional compensation under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act when determining compensation under Section 28-A, as the process is governed by Sections 18 to 28 upon reference.
doctrines: Beneficial construction of statutes
Literal rule of interpretation
Limitation period begins from cause of action

card.dispute: The dispute was between the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad and a cooperative housing society over whether a housing scheme could be implemented without prior government approval under exception (iii) to Section 59(1)(a) of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965.
issues_decided: Whether prior approval of the State Government is mandatory under exception (iii) to Section 59(1)(a) of the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 for a housing scheme to be valid after declaration of a development area.
Whether subsequent approval by the State Government can validate actions taken under the scheme, including notifications under Sections 28 and 32 of the Adhiniyam.
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere under Article 136 in light of conflicting High Court decisions and the facts of the case.
holdings: The term 'approval' in exception (iii) to Section 59(1)(a) does not require prior approval; subsequent approval by the State Government is sufficient to validate the scheme.
Once government approval is granted, all prior actions taken in anticipation of such approval, including notifications under Sections 28 and 32, are validated and become legally effective.

Despite clarifying the law, the Court declined to interfere under Article 136, as the appellant had compromised with others but not the respondents, and the respondents' right to shelter under Article 21 warranted relief.
provisions: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 59(1)(a) exception (iii)
U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 3
U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 28
U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, Section 32
doctrines: Doctrine of Subsequent Validation
Literal Rule of Statutory Interpretation
Fundamental Right to Shelter as part of Article 21

card.dispute: The petitioner Vidyawati, as legal representative of her deceased husband, sought to file an additional written statement asserting her own title to the suit property based on a will, which the plaintiffs and her husband were also claiming under.
issues_decided: Whether a legal representative of a deceased defendant can assert an independent title to the suit property in the same suit?
Whether the trial court and High Court were justified in disallowing the filing of an additional written statement asserting a hostile title by the legal representative?
holdings: A legal representative can raise any defence available to the deceased, including those the deceased could have raised, but cannot assert an independent or hostile title unless impleaded in their personal capacity.

If a legal representative wishes to assert an independent title, they must either seek impleadment in their personal capacity under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC or file a separate suit; otherwise, such a plea is not maintainable in the existing suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 4(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10
doctrines: Legal representative's capacity to defend under Order 22 Rule 4(2) CPC
Separate impleadment required for asserting independent title

card.dispute: The appellant, a former employee, was convicted under Section 630 of the Companies Act for wrongful occupation of a company residential flat after resignation; the dispute centered on whether this conviction could stand given a civil court's finding that he was a direct tenant of the landlords, not the company.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 630 of the Companies Act is sustainable in light of a civil court's finding that the appellant was not in possession as a licensee of the company but as a direct tenant of the landlords.
Whether criminal proceedings under Section 630 can proceed independently despite a conflicting finding in a civil eviction suit.
holdings: A conviction under Section 630 of the Companies Act cannot be sustained if the civil court has found that the accused was not in possession by virtue of employment but held independent tenancy rights, and that finding remains binding until overturned on appeal.

While criminal proceedings are generally not stayed due to pendency of civil suits, where a civil court has recorded a final finding on possession, it supersedes the criminal court's conclusion in a summary trial under Section 630.
doctrines: Continuing offence doctrine
Primacy of civil court findings on title or possession when finally determined
Independence of criminal and civil proceedings, with preference to criminal justice in case of pendency but not when civil findings are conclusive

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Raghunath, including Vidya Devi and Prem Prakash, disputed over partition of jointly held land, with some claiming adverse possession to resist partition.
issues_decided: Whether a co-bhumidhar can acquire title by adverse possession against other co-bhumidhars under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954
Whether a plea of adverse possession, if not specifically pleaded with all necessary ingredients, can be considered to raise a question of title under Section 186 of the Delhi Land Reforms Act
Whether the Revenue Court was required to refer the question of title to the Civil Court under Section 186
holdings: A co-owner can acquire title by adverse possession against other co-owners only if there is ouster or something equivalent, with open, continuous, and hostile possession denying the co-owner's title.
A plea of adverse possession must be specifically pleaded with all essential ingredients; otherwise, it does not constitute a valid question of title under Section 186 of the Delhi Land Reforms Act.
The Revenue Court need not refer a title issue to the Civil Court if the plea is not bona fide or is insufficiently pleaded, as per the Explanation to Section 186.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, Section 332
doctrines: Adverse possession
Ouster by co-owner
Pleading requirements for title disputes
Constructive trust of co-possessor

card.dispute: The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation challenged the High Court's enhancement of compensation to Rs. 190 per square meter for land acquired for a Ring Road, while landowners cross-appealed seeking further enhancement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing compensation based on an average of comparable sale instances without specific evidence linking them to the acquired plots?
Whether the compensation awarded was just and adequate under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, given the nature of the acquisition of small, non-contiguous strips of land?
holdings: The High Court's reliance on general evidence of comparable sales was permissible due to the fragmented nature of the acquisition, making exact comparables difficult to obtain.

The enhancement to Rs. 190 per square meter was not unreasonable in the peculiar facts, and the principle against averaging compensation does not strictly apply to acquisitions of small, scattered land strips.
doctrines: Prudent and willing buyer test
Just and adequate compensation
Relaxation of strict comparability in fragmented acquisitions

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed the distribution of compensation for acquired land, with the appellants claiming entitlement under a probated will granting them 2/3 share, while the respondents claimed equal 50% shares as determined by the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the reference court or the High Court can determine the share of parties in compensation under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, despite a valid probate of a will specifying shares?
Whether a probate granted under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is binding in proceedings for distribution of land acquisition compensation?
holdings: A probate granted by a competent civil court under the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is conclusive and binding on all parties until lawfully revoked, and cannot be disregarded in compensation distribution proceedings.

Courts dealing with land acquisition compensation must respect the shares specified in a valid probate and cannot redistribute shares contrary to the probated will without first setting aside the probate.
doctrines: Conclusiveness of probate
Binding nature of court grants under the Indian Succession Act
Separation of property rights from land acquisition compensation distribution

card.dispute: The dispute was between a temple and individuals over title, possession, and mesne profits of 29 acres of agricultural land granted to a temple archaka—whether the grant was personal to the archaka or in favour of the temple.
issues_decided: Whether the Letters Patent Bench of the High Court could overturn a finding of fact based on document interpretation by a Single Judge.
Whether the grant of land was made personally to the archaka or to the temple through the archaka.
holdings: The Letters Patent Bench, acting as a Court of Correction, has the jurisdiction to re-examine findings of fact and law from a Single Judge’s decision when it involves a mixed question of law and fact.
The grant of land was intended for the temple, not personally to the archaka, as determined by reconciling the two key documents and surrounding circumstances.
provisions: Letters Patent of the High Court
doctrines: Court of Error doctrine
Mixed question of law and fact
Intra-court appeal under Letters Patent

card.dispute: The appellant tenant sought allotment of a building under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, but the landlord argued the structure was no longer a 'building' due to being roofless at the time of allotment.
issues_decided: Whether a roofless structure can be considered a 'building' under Section 3(i) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 for the purpose of an allotment order under Section 16(1).
Whether the District Magistrate retains jurisdiction to pass an allotment order in respect of a structure that became roofless after vacancy but before the allotment order.
holdings: A structure that was a building at the time of vacancy retains its character as a 'building' for allotment purposes even if it becomes roofless thereafter, provided the roof was removed by the landlord.

The District Magistrate retains jurisdiction under Section 16(1) to pass an allotment order if the structure was a building when it fell vacant, and does not lose jurisdiction due to subsequent removal of the roof by the landlord.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 3(i)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 16(1)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 11
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 15
doctrines: Nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria (No one can profit from their own wrong)
Contextual interpretation of statutory definitions
Liberal interpretation to prevent injustice

card.dispute: The appellant trust challenged the validity of land acquisition by the State of Punjab, arguing that the urgency clause used to dispense with the Section 5-A enquiry was unjustified and that possession was not legally taken.
issues_decided: Whether the use of the urgency clause under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Punjab, to dispense with the Section 5-A enquiry was legally justified for providing house sites to the poor.
Whether the acquisition became final upon taking of possession, despite the appellant's continued physical possession of the land.
Whether the failure to produce complete records before the High Court vitiated the acquisition proceedings.
holdings: The State's use of the urgency clause under Section 17(4) to dispense with the Section 5-A enquiry is valid when acquiring land to provide house sites to the poor, as such a purpose constitutes an urgent public necessity.

Acquisition becomes final upon legal taking of possession, which can be effected by Panchnama and delivery to beneficiaries; continued physical possession by the owner does not invalidate the acquisition.

The omission to produce complete records before the court does not invalidate the acquisition where the process was otherwise complete, though the responsible officer may face administrative consequences.
provisions: Punjab Amendment Acts II/1954, XVII/1956, and XLVIII/1956
doctrines: Finality of land acquisition upon completion of possession
Judicial deference to executive opinion on urgency in land acquisition
Legal possession vs. physical possession in acquisition cases

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired for an explosive magazine, seeking enhancement after having already received compensation under an agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners could file a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act after accepting compensation without protest?
Whether the acceptance of compensation under a written agreement barred the right to object under Section 18?
holdings: A person who receives compensation without protest is barred from making an application under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1890.
Acceptance of compensation under a written agreement stating it is 'fully acceptable' constitutes a waiver of the right to object, rendering the reference under Section 18 non-maintainable.
doctrines: Waiver of statutory rights
Condition precedent to statutory remedy
Protest as prerequisite for objection

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, seeking parity with higher compensation awarded in similar cases from the same village.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are entitled to the same compensation as determined in other cases (Raghuvir Singh and Chet Ram) arising from the same notification?
Whether a Letters Patent Appeal (LPA) lies against the judgment of a single judge in a land acquisition reference?
What is the reasonable market value of the acquired land as on the date of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act?
holdings: Compensation must be determined based on individual land characteristics and market value, not by applying a uniform rate to all lands in the same village; parity is only valid if lands have identical advantages and features.
A Letters Patent Appeal lies against a single judge’s decision in a land acquisition matter, and the Division Bench erred in holding otherwise.

The market value of the acquired agricultural land, not developed at the time of notification, is Rs. 3,250 per bigha, based on contemporaneous sale evidence, with 6% interest and 15% solatium on enhanced compensation.
doctrines: Willing buyer-willing seller test for market value determination
Principle of equality in compensation only applicable to lands with similar advantages
No ad hoc uniform compensation for all lands in a village
Solatium and interest on delayed compensation

card.dispute: The appellant, Bhaiya Bahadur Singh, was convicted of murder and challenged the conviction by claiming he acted in self-defence while protecting his person and property during a dispute over alleged crop damage by his tractor.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant successfully established the right of private defence of person and property
Whether, if the right of private defence existed, it was exceeded by the appellant
holdings: The appellant failed to prove that he acted in self-defence, as the injuries on him were superficial and possibly self-inflicted, and the prosecution version was more probable.

Even if the right of private defence initially existed, it was exceeded when the appellant fired two shots at close range, especially after re-loading, which showed premeditated use of excessive force.

The right of private defence ceased once the appellant jumped off the tractor and was at a safe distance, as the attackers were not armed with lethal weapons and posed no imminent threat justifying lethal retaliation.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 96 to 106 (Right of Private Defence)
Indian Arms Act, relevant provisions on unlicensed possession of firearms
doctrines: Right of private defence must be proportionate and necessary
Burden of proving self-defence lies on the accused to make it probable, not beyond reasonable doubt
Self-defence cannot be claimed if the force used is disproportionate or after the threat has ceased

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder and related charges in connection with the killing of Lal Babu during a property dispute, challenged their convictions and sentences, arguing lack of evidence and procedural irregularities.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding common intention and participation in the murder.
Whether the non-examination of the Investigating Officer vitiated the trial.
Whether the conviction of Sheoji Prasad under Section 302/34 and 302/149 IPC was legally sustainable based on his role.
holdings: The prosecution established the guilt of accused Nos. 2, 3, and 4 beyond reasonable doubt through credible eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and consistency with the FIR, proving common intention under Section 34 IPC and liability under Section 149 IPC.
The non-examination of the Investigating Officer does not automatically vitiate a trial; prejudice must be shown, and in this case, no such prejudice was established.

Sheoji Prasad’s conviction under Section 302/34 and 302/149 IPC is unsustainable as there was no evidence that he shared the common intention to commit murder or exhorted the killing, though his conviction for rioting and causing hurt stands.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Unlawful assembly and constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Test of reliability of eyewitness testimony in murder cases
Principle of prejudice in criminal trial procedure

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the taxability of interest received on delayed compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing it was not 'income' under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether interest paid under Section 34 or Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 constitutes 'income' under the Income Tax Act, 1961
Whether such interest is exempt from tax as agricultural income under Section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act
Whether the definition of 'interest' in Section 2(28A) of the Income Tax Act limits taxability only to interest from borrowed money
holdings: Interest paid for delayed compensation under the Land Acquisition Act is a revenue receipt and constitutes taxable income under Section 4 of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Such interest is not agricultural income and does not fall under the exemption in Section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act.
The definition of 'interest' in Section 2(28A) is inclusive and does not exclude statutory interest under the Land Acquisition Act from taxability.
doctrines: Revenue receipt doctrine
Literal construction of statutory terms
Settled law by judicial precedent

card.dispute: The appellants (C. Padma & Ors) fought the government and its agencies over the restitution of land acquired in 1962, claiming the public purpose for acquisition had ceased to exist.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could challenge the land acquisition after 32 years on the ground that the public purpose had ceased.
Whether cessation of the original public purpose entitled the former owners to restitution of the acquired land.
holdings: Once land is acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and compensation is paid, the land vests in the state, and former owners cannot challenge the acquisition after decades have passed.
When a public purpose for which land was acquired ceases, and the land is reassigned to another public purpose, the acquisition does not become void, and no restitution is due to former owners.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon acquisition and payment of compensation
Doctrine of finality of acquisition proceedings
Substitution of public purpose

card.dispute: The dispute was between a company and the State of Rajasthan over the validity of a municipal boundary extension and the legality of octroi tax collected from the company in areas not properly included in the municipality.
issues_decided: Whether the Kota Municipal Limits (Continued Existence) Validating Act, 1975, could legally validate the inclusion of villages Raipura and Ummedganj within the Kota municipal limits despite non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements under the Rajasthan Town Municipalities Act, 1951 and 1959.
Whether a deeming provision in a validating statute can override mandatory legal requirements that were not followed during the initial municipal extension.
holdings: A validating statute cannot cure defects arising from non-compliance with mandatory procedural requirements unless it amends the law to retrospectively address the defect; mere deeming of legal status without curing the procedural flaw is invalid.

Facts may be deemed by legislation, but legal consequences dependent on mandatory procedures cannot be created by deeming fiction if those procedures were not followed and not retrospectively validated by substantive amendment.
provisions: Rajasthan Town Municipalities Act, 1951, Sections 4 to 7
Rajasthan Town Municipalities Act, 1959, Sections 4 to 7
Kota Municipal Limits (Continued Existence) Validating Act, 1975
doctrines: Deeming fiction
Validity of retrospective legislation
Mandatory procedural compliance
Doctrine of curative amendment in validating statutes

card.dispute: The tenants challenged the High Court's decision that their second application for ownership rights under the Pepsu Tenancy Agricultural Lands Act, 1955 was barred by res judicata after an earlier rejection.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of res judicata applies to proceedings under Section 22 of the Pepsu Tenancy Agricultural Lands Act, 1955
Whether the tenants were entitled to claim ownership rights under Section 22 despite a prior rejected application
Whether the tenants were protected from ejectment under Section 7A of the Act
holdings: The doctrine of res judicata does not apply to summary proceedings under the Pepsu Tenancy Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, as the statute does not prescribe it and the proceedings are administrative in nature.

Tenants who were in continuous possession for 12 years prior to the commencement of the President's Act, 1953, and were in possession as of December 3, 1953, are entitled to claim ownership under Section 22 of the Act.

A tenant in possession of land under personal cultivation not exceeding 15 standard acres, and who had held the land for 12 years before the President's Act, cannot be evicted under Section 7A unless alternative land is provided.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 22
Pepsu Tenancy Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 7A
doctrines: Res judicata
Beneficial construction of tenancy laws
Summary proceedings exception to res judicata

card.dispute: The decree-holder challenged the substitution of a third party as transferee of her interest in a decree, claiming the third party's acquisition through a municipal tax sale was invalid due to non-compliance with payment deadlines.
issues_decided: Whether a dispute over the status of a transferee by operation of law can be decided in execution proceedings under Section 47 of the CPC

Whether non-payment of the balance sale amount within 15 days under Rule 8(2) of the Maharashtra Municipalities (Sale of Distrained or Attached Movable and Immovable Property) Rules, 1967 renders the sale void
Whether the first respondent became a transferee by operation of law entitled to be substituted under Order 21 Rule 16 of the CPC
holdings: A dispute regarding whether a person is a representative of a decree-holder, including a transferee by operation of law, is determinable by the executing court under Section 47 CPC and does not require a separate suit.

Failure to pay the balance sale amount within the mandatory 15-day period under Rule 8(2) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Rules, 1967 renders the sale void ab initio, and no legal rights vest in the purchaser.

A person who fails to comply with mandatory payment conditions in a municipal tax sale does not become a transferee by operation of law and cannot be substituted in execution proceedings under Order 21 Rule 16 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 16
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rules 84 and 85
Maharashtra Municipalities (Sale of Distrained or Attached Movable and Immovable Property) Rules, 1967, Rule 8(2), Rule 8(3), and Rule 13
doctrines: Doctrine of mandatory compliance with procedural rules in public sales
Doctrine of representation under Section 47 CPC
Doctrine of voidness for non-compliance with statutory conditions

card.dispute: Harish Kumar and Ram Sharan appealed their conviction for murder and attempt to murder, claiming self-defence after a violent clash between rival village factions.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Harish Kumar and Ram Sharan committed murder under Section 302/34 IPC and attempt to murder under Section 307/34 IPC?
Whether the dying declaration of the deceased was sufficient to sustain the conviction of Harish Kumar?
Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence of person and property?
holdings: The evidence against Ram Sharan was unreliable and insufficient; his conviction for murder and attempt to murder was set aside due to lack of credible eyewitness testimony and his absence of overt act in the murder.
The dying declaration, though admissible, cannot override a plea of self-defence when the prosecution fails to disprove the accused’s claim of apprehension of danger.

Harish Kumar’s single act of firing in the face of an armed and advancing hostile group, without further aggression, was a reasonable exercise of private defence of person, entitling him to acquittal.
doctrines: Right of private defence of person
Appreciation of dying declaration
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony

card.dispute: The petitioner sought specific performance of a contract to purchase 500 sq. yds. of land in Delhi, but the respondent refused, alleging the petitioner failed to perform his obligations within the stipulated time.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract within the stipulated time?
Whether time was the essence of the contract?
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing the discretionary relief of specific performance?
holdings: The petitioner failed to prove readiness and willingness to perform his contractual obligations, particularly in terms of financial capacity and conduct.
Time was the essence of the contract, and the petitioner's delay in executing the sale deed invalidated his claim for specific performance.
The High Court properly exercised its judicial discretion in refusing specific performance due to the petitioner's non-performance and dilatory conduct.
doctrines: Readiness and willingness to perform under specific performance
Time as essence of contract
Discretionary nature of specific performance relief

card.dispute: The dispute was between licensees of Palika Bazar shops and the New Delhi Municipal Committee over unequal allotment of shops, trade zoning violations, and payment of licence fees at concessional versus agreed rates.
issues_decided: Whether the preferential allotment of 98 shops at concessional rates without trade zoning restrictions to Panchkuian Road stall-holders violated Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether other licensees could claim the same concessions on the basis of equality before law when those concessions were granted illegally or irregularly
Whether licensees who violated trade zoning must revert to permitted trades and pay arrears with interest
Whether the court could impose a structured payment plan for arrears arising from interim orders
holdings: Preferential allotment of shops to displaced stall-holders was justified and did not violate Article 14 if there was a rational basis for the classification.
Article 14 does not entitle a person to demand illegal or irregular benefits merely because others have received them; equality cannot be used to perpetuate illegality.
Licensees who deviated from trade zoning must revert to permitted trades and pay arrears with higher interest; those who complied pay lower interest and reasonable instalments.
Courts may direct payment of arrears in instalments with reasonable interest under the principle 'actus curiae neminem gravabit' to prevent injustice caused by interim orders.
doctrines: Equality before law (Article 14)
Prohibition against perpetuation of illegality under equality doctrine
Act of court shall not prejudice any person (actus curiae neminem gravabit)

card.dispute: The Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation fought with landowners over the amount of compensation payable for land acquired for industrial development.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in enhancing compensation based on a sale deed of a small nearby plot
What is the proper method to determine market value for compulsory land acquisition
What compensation rate is just and adequate for the acquired land
holdings: Reliance on a small nearby sale deed to determine compensation for a large acquired tract is unjustified in law.
The market value in land acquisition must be determined by imagining what a prudent willing buyer would pay, avoiding speculative or imaginative valuations.
The fair compensation for the acquired land is Rs. 22 per sq. meter, considering potential value and deducting one-third for development charges.
doctrines: Prudent purchaser rule
Potential value doctrine
Just and adequate compensation

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the High Court's order directing the suit for possession to proceed in the District Court from the stage at which it was transferred, after the plaint was returned due to pecuniary jurisdiction issues, while also seeking to raise a counter-claim for improvements without having paid court fees.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be permitted to raise a counter-claim for improvements without having paid court fees within the prescribed time?
Whether the High Court's direction to proceed from the stage at which the suit stood transferred was legally valid?
holdings: A counter-claim cannot be entertained if court fees have not been paid within the prescribed time, and such a claim cannot be allowed at a later stage as it is barred by limitation.
The High Court did not commit any illegality in directing the District Court to proceed from the stage at which the suit was transferred, especially since evidence had already been adduced.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 21 (pecuniary jurisdiction)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 7 (pleading of set-off and counter-claim)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 14 (limitation for suits)
doctrines: bar of limitation
pecuniary jurisdiction
framing of issues based on court fee payment

card.dispute: The State of Kerala appealed the acquittal of two accused, Krishnan and Vijay Kumar, who were alleged to have murdered Madavan with a common intention arising from a property dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting Vijay Kumar under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC despite no direct evidence of him causing fatal injuries?
Whether an overt act by an accused is a mandatory requirement to invoke Section 34 IPC for common intention?
Whether identification of the accused in low light conditions and discrepancies in medical evidence about time of death vitiate the prosecution case?
holdings: The High Court correctly convicted Vijay Kumar under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC based on clear evidence of shared common intention, even if he did not cause fatal injuries.
Section 34 IPC does not mandate proof of an overt act by each accused; it suffices to show that the criminal act was done in furtherance of a common intention.
Identification of accused was reliable despite low light, and presence of undigested food in the stomach does not discredit the time of incident or witness testimony.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Res ipsa loquitur in inferring common intention
Reliability of eyewitness identification in criminal cases

card.dispute: The assessee's legal heirs challenged the Calcutta High Court's decision against them on questions of revised return validity, assessment time-bar, and applicability of penalty provisions under the Income-Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether a revised return under Section 139(5) can be filed if the original return was filed under Section 139(4)?
Whether the assessments for 1964-65 and 1965-66 were time-barred under Section 153(1)(b)?
Whether the cases fell within Section 271(1)(c), justifying extended assessment period?
holdings: A revised return under Section 139(5) can only be filed if the original return was filed under Section 139(1) or (2); returns filed under Section 139(4) do not permit revision under Section 139(5).
Assessments under Section 153(1)(b) are time-barred unless the Income Tax Officer records a finding or initiates proceedings under Section 271(1)(c) within the original limitation period.
Since no finding or notice under Section 271(1)(c) was made within four years, the extended eight-year assessment period was not triggered, and the assessments are invalid.
doctrines: Strict construction of limitation periods in tax assessment
Presumption against retrospective extension of assessment powers
Requirement of recorded finding for invoking extended limitation under Section 153(1)(b)

card.dispute: The petitioners sought specific performance of a 1976 sale agreement, but the respondents resisted, claiming the petitioners lacked clean hands and that a third party was a bona fide purchaser.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to specific performance despite making false allegations in the plaint?
Whether the third respondent was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the prior agreement?
Whether the courts below properly exercised their discretion in refusing specific performance?
holdings: A party seeking specific performance must come to court with clean hands; making false allegations bars equitable relief.
The third respondent was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the prior agreement, protected under law.
Discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act must be exercised on sound legal principles, and its refusal is upheld when supported by findings of fact and equity.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Equitable discretion in specific performance
