card.dispute: The lessee challenged the impleadment of landlords as parties in a suit for injunction against the Municipal Corporation's demolition of an allegedly unauthorized structure on leased property.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords are necessary or proper parties under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC in a suit for injunction against the Municipal Corporation's demolition action?
Whether a party with a direct interest in the property, though not sought to be reliefs against, can be added as a proper party?
holdings: A landlord is a proper party in a suit for injunction against municipal demolition of a leased building, even if no relief is sought against them, because their rights in the property are directly affected by the demolition.

A person is a proper party under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC if their presence is necessary for complete and effective adjudication, particularly where their legal interest, not merely commercial interest, is substantially affected.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10
doctrines: Necessary and proper party doctrine under CPC
Direct legal interest versus commercial interest distinction

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the dismissal of their applications for redetermination of compensation, claiming the three-month limitation period under Section 28-A should start from the appellate court's decision, not the initial reference court's award.
issues_decided: Whether the three-month period for filing an application under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 begins from the date of the award by the reference court under Section 18 or from the date of the appellate court's decision.
Whether successive awards or appellate decrees can trigger a fresh period for filing applications under Section 28-A.
holdings: The three-month limitation period under Section 28-A starts from the date of the award by the reference court under Section 18, not from the date of any appellate court's decision.
Successive appellate awards do not give rise to a fresh cause of action under Section 28-A; the right to apply must be exercised within three months of the relevant reference court's award.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule
Limitation period computation
Reference to precedent and overruling

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of amendments to the Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax Act, arguing that the tax was beyond the state legislature's competence and that the law was 'still-born' due to initial constitutional defects.
issues_decided: Whether the 1973 amendment to the Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax Act imposed a tax under Entry 86 of List I (Union) or Entry 49 of List II (State).
Whether the invalid portion of Section 3(1) was severable from the rest of the Act.
Whether the 1973 Ordinance and subsequent Amending Act could retrospectively cure the constitutional defect and revive the legislation.
holdings: The tax, as amended and cured, falls within Entry 49 of List II, as it is a tax on lands and buildings as separate units, not on the totality of a person's assets.
The invalid proviso in Section 3(1) was severable because the remaining provisions formed a complete and workable code independent of the invalid part.
The Ordinance and Amending Act 18 of 1973 validly and retrospectively corrected the defect, reviving the legislation without rendering it 'still-born'.
provisions: Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax Act, 1964, Section 3
Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax (Amendment) Act, 1973 (Act 15 of 1973)
Rajasthan Urban Lands Tax (Amendment) Act, 1973 (Act 18 of 1973)
doctrines: Severability of unconstitutional provisions
Pith and substance doctrine
Retrospective validation by amendment
Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a promissory note (Ex.A1) for Rs.1.5 lakhs, arguing it lacked valid consideration after an underlying land sale agreement (Ex.B1) failed, while the respondents claimed the note was supported by delivery of additional land and a building.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption of consideration under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies when the plaintiff pleads a consideration different from the one recited in the promissory note
Whether the promissory note in question was supported by valid and enforceable consideration despite the failure of the main sale agreement
Whether the courts below were justified in relying on documentary and oral evidence to conclude that consideration had passed for the promissory note
holdings: When a plaintiff pleads a consideration different from what is recited in the promissory note, the statutory presumption of consideration under Section 118(a) of the Negotiable Instruments Act does not arise.
A promissory note can be supported by valid consideration even if the underlying transaction fails, provided there is evidence of actual transfer of property or benefit in exchange for the note.

Courts may rely on surrounding documents, correspondence, and conduct of parties to prove that a promissory note was supported by legally enforceable consideration, independent of the statutory presumption.
doctrines: Presumption of consideration in negotiable instruments
Burden of proof in cases involving promissory notes
Enforceability of consideration independent of statutory presumptions

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the landlord's eviction petition on the ground that her foster son did not qualify as a 'member of the family' under the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether a foster son can be considered a 'member of the family' within the meaning of Section 2(6A) of the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Whether the landlord can seek eviction for personal need, including the need of a foster son.
holdings: A foster son, though not a biological descendant, can be considered a member of the family if he is brought up with parental care, love, and is treated as a son in all respects.
The term 'family' under the Act is flexible and context-dependent, and includes persons bound by emotional and caregiving relationships, not just blood or marriage.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(6A)
doctrines: Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Flexible meaning of 'family' in rent control laws

card.dispute: The appellants (Laxmikant & Ors) challenged the High Court's order directing the Nagpur Improvement Trust to transfer a plot to the respondent (Satyawan & Ors), the highest bidder at an auction, after the Trust had reinstated the plot in favor of the original allottees.
issues_decided: Whether the Nagpur Improvement Trust was legally bound to transfer the land to the highest bidder despite the auction not being fully concluded and no confirmation letter being issued.
Whether the conditions of the auction, which required Board approval for accepting the highest bid, were valid and binding.
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the Trust's resolution reinstating the plot in favor of the original allottees.
holdings: The Trust was not obligated to transfer the land to the highest bidder because the auction was not completed and no formal acceptance or confirmation letter was issued.
The auction conditions, which reserved the Trust's right to accept or reject the highest bid, were valid and binding on the bidder.
The High Court erred in quashing the Trust's resolution as no legal right had accrued to the respondent, and the Trust retained discretion under its rules and auction terms.
provisions: Nagpur Improvement Trust Land Disposal Rules, 1955, Rule 4(3)
doctrines: Principle of auction law: no binding contract until formal acceptance
Statutory discretion of public authorities in land disposal
Conditions of tender override general statutory provisions when explicitly notified

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over whether specific performance of an agreement to sell immovable property should be granted or if alternative relief in the form of damages should be awarded.
issues_decided: Whether the courts below were justified in granting a decree for specific performance of the agreement for sale of immovable property after a long delay.
Whether it is equitable to grant specific performance when the plaintiff has alternatively claimed damages and property values have significantly appreciated.
holdings: Specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property is not a matter of right but a discretionary remedy to be granted based on justice, equity, and fairness.
Where the rise in property value makes specific performance inequitable and the plaintiff has claimed alternative relief, courts may justifiably award damages instead.
doctrines: Discretionary nature of specific performance
Equity and good conscience in granting specific relief
Alternative relief in lieu of specific performance

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the male-only succession provisions of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 as discriminatory against women and violative of constitutional equality.
issues_decided: Whether the male-line succession under Sections 7 and 8 of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether the exclusion of female heirs from inheritance under the Act infringes the right to life under Article 21
Whether the Court should strike down the impugned provisions or interpret them in light of fundamental rights
holdings: The male-only succession under the Act does not violate Article 14 when viewed in the context of tribal customs, but must be read subject to the right to livelihood under Article 21.

The right to livelihood is an integral part of the right to life under Article 21, and female dependents of the deceased tenant have a constitutional right to continue holding land as long as they depend on it for survival.
The Court refrained from striking down the provisions but read them down to suspend male succession until female dependents cease to rely on the land for livelihood.
doctrines: Right to livelihood as part of right to life
Harmonious construction of statutes with fundamental rights
Reading down of statutory provisions to avoid unconstitutionality
Primacy of constitutional values over customary law

card.dispute: The appellant Mahesh was convicted of murder under Section 302 IPC by the High Court, while the trial court had convicted him under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC; the dispute was over the correct classification of the offence and appropriate sentence.
issues_decided: Whether the offence committed by the appellant falls under Section 302 IPC or Section 304 (Part-I) IPC?
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the trial court's conviction under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC?
Whether the sentence awarded by the trial court was adequate?
holdings: The appellant's act was committed in the heat of a sudden quarrel without premeditation, and thus falls under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, attracting liability under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC, not Section 302 IPC.
The High Court erred in reversing the trial court’s conviction under Section 304 (Part-I) IPC without rebutting its reasoning, especially given the reliable eyewitness and corroborative evidence.
The sentence of two years RI and a fine of Rs. 500 imposed by the trial court was inadequate; a just sentence is six years RI and a fine of Rs. 1,000, with default imprisonment of four months.
doctrines: Sudden fight exception under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC
Appreciation of eyewitness testimony
Principle of proportionate sentencing
Standard of appellate interference with concurrent findings

card.dispute: The dispute was between landowners and the State of Bihar over whether certain markets (bazars) in urban areas vested in the State under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, or remained private property as 'homesteads'.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'bazar' in Section 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 includes urban markets held by intermediaries?
Whether urban bazars constructed on estate land are excluded from vesting if they qualify as 'homestead' under Section 2(j) of the Act?
Whether the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 distinguishes between rural and urban properties for vesting purposes?
holdings: The term 'bazar' under Section 4(a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act includes markets in both rural and urban areas if held by intermediaries as part of the estate.

Urban bazars, including 'Patna Market', do not qualify as 'homesteads' under Section 2(j) when used commercially and constructed for business purposes, even if residential structures previously existed.
The Act does not distinguish between rural and urban properties; all rights, title, and interest in an estate, including bazars, vest in the State upon notification under Sections 3, 3A, and 3B.
doctrines: Proprio vigore
Vesting of estate rights in the State free from encumbrances
Statutory interpretation without implied rural-urban distinction
Acquisition for revenue augmentation as valid public purpose

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition process after the government dispensed with a mandatory inquiry under Section 5A, and later reinitiated proceedings following a court order.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act is valid if published more than one year after the original Section 4(1) notification but within one year of a court-ordered fresh inquiry?
Whether the date for computing market value under Section 23(1) shifts to a second declaration under Section 6(1) when the first declaration is quashed and a fresh one issued?
holdings: When a court quashes a declaration under Section 6 and directs a fresh inquiry under Section 5A, the one-year limitation for publishing a new declaration under Section 6(1) runs from the date of the court's order, not the original notification.

The date of the original notification under Section 4(1) remains the relevant date for determining market value under Section 23(1), even if a fresh declaration under Section 6(1) is issued after court intervention.
doctrines: Relation back of judicial orders
Validity of administrative action post-court direction
Interpretation of limitation periods in statutory contexts
Efficacy of judicial review under Article 226

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to allow a second appeal based on a will, claiming no substantial question of law existed under Section 100 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Section 100 CPC in a second appeal when the lower courts dismissed a will due to suspicious circumstances?
Whether the rejection of the attesting witnesses' evidence by the lower courts was based on sustainable legal grounds?
holdings: The High Court can interfere in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC if the reasons for rejecting a will are based on flimsy or unsustainable grounds, raising a substantial question of law.
The mere delay in producing a will and adverse relations of an attesting witness in unrelated litigation are insufficient to reject the will; such reasons must be tested for legal sustainability.
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Propounder's duty to remove suspicious circumstances in will execution
Reliability of attesting witnesses

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the Patna High Court for the murder of Sona Devi and Ram Janam Rai, challenged their conviction and sentence, which had been upheld on appeal after the trial court's acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the identification of the appellants as the assailants by eyewitnesses was reliable despite the dim lighting conditions at the time of the incident.
Whether the statements made by injured witnesses immediately after the incident could be used to corroborate their later testimony under Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act.
Whether the prosecution's failure to establish a strong motive for the crime undermined the conviction.
holdings: Eyewitness identification under dim light is credible if the witnesses were familiar with the assailants and the lighting was sufficient for recognition, as the same conditions that enabled the assailants to identify victims also allowed victims to identify attackers.

Statements made by witnesses immediately after the incident, identifying the accused, are admissible under Section 157 of the Evidence Act for corroboration if made without delay and without opportunity for fabrication.

Absence of a strong or clear motive does not invalidate a conviction if there is reliable evidence of guilt, as motive is a psychological factor and many serious crimes are committed over seemingly trivial reasons.
provisions: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, Section 2A
doctrines: Corroboration through contemporaneous statements
Presumption of guilt in absence of strong motive if evidence is reliable
Liberal interpretation of 'at or about the time' in Section 157 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Committee challenged whether state governments are exempt from paying property taxes on their properties situated in Union Territories under Article 289(1) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether properties owned by State Governments in Union Territories are exempt from property taxes under Article 289(1) of the Constitution.
Whether the definition of 'State' in the General Clauses Act includes Union Territories for the purpose of Article 246(4).
Whether municipal property taxes in Union Territories fall within the scope of 'Union Taxation' under Article 289(1).
Whether Parliament must legislate under Article 289(2) to tax commercial activities of State Governments in Union Territories.
holdings: Properties owned by State Governments and situated in Union Territories are exempt from property taxes under Article 289(1), as affirmed in the Sea Customs case and reaffirmed in APSRTC.
The definition of 'State' in Section 3(58) of the General Clauses Act does not extend to Union Territories for interpreting Article 246(4) of the Constitution.
The term 'Union Taxation' in Article 289(1) includes property taxes levied by municipalities in Union Territories, making such taxes subject to the exemption.
The power to tax commercial activities of State Governments in Union Territories cannot be delegated to municipal authorities; only Parliament can make such a law under Article 289(2).
doctrines: Doctrine of Presumption of Constitutionality
Doctrine of Non-Delegation of Essential Legislative Functions
Ratio decidendi
Interpretation of Constitutional Exemptions

card.dispute: The appellant, a retired Income Tax Officer, challenged the continuation of criminal prosecution against him under the Prevention of Corruption Act after he was exonerated in departmental proceedings based on a Central Vigilance Commission report.
issues_decided: Whether criminal prosecution under Section 5(2) read with Section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act can proceed despite exoneration in departmental proceedings based on CVC and UPSC findings.
Whether the criminal proceedings amounted to an abuse of process given the lack of credible evidence and the prior exoneration.
holdings: Criminal proceedings under the Prevention of Corruption Act cannot be pursued when the accused has been exonerated in departmental proceedings on the same charge, especially where the Central Vigilance Commission and UPSC have found no disproportionate assets.
The continuation of prosecution in such circumstances amounts to an abuse of process and falls within the categories justifying quashing under Section 482 CrPC or Article 226 of the Constitution.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Quashing of criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC
Principles laid down in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992)

card.dispute: Radhika Devi sought to amend her plaint in a partition suit to challenge the validity of a gift deed in favour of Bajrangi Singh and others, which the respondents claimed was time-barred and prejudicial to their accrued rights.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to amend the plaint to include a declaration that the gift deed was obtained illegally and fraudulently after a long delay?
Whether the amendment of the plaint would take away the accrued legal rights of the respondents protected by limitation?
holdings: The court held that the amendment sought after a significant delay of about four years, after the gift deed was registered and after the respondents had pleaded their title, would defeat their accrued legal rights and is not permissible.

An amendment that seeks to introduce a claim already barred by limitation and which prejudices the opposing party’s vested rights cannot be allowed, even if such amendments are generally permitted under Order 6 Rule 17 of the CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Accrual of rights by limitation
Amendment of pleadings as clarificatory vs. substantive change
Notice by registration of documents

card.dispute: Mineral owners challenged the validity of a parliamentary Act that validated past mineral taxes and cesses, arguing it was unconstitutional and temporary in nature.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament had the competence to enact the Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992 to validate past levies declared void by courts.
Whether the Act was a temporary statute that ceased to operate after April 4, 1991, making recovery of unpaid taxes invalid.
Whether the absence of a saving clause under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act barred recovery proceedings after the deemed expiry of the levy.
Whether the validation would result in double taxation under two different state laws for the same mineral extraction.
holdings: Parliament has the power to validate past taxes or cesses that were struck down, provided the validation does not violate constitutional limitations.
An Act is not temporary merely because the levy it validates is time-bound; the Act continues in force until repealed by Parliament.
The machinery for recovery and refund of taxes remains operative even after the cessation of the levy, as expressly preserved by the Act.
Validation of two separate state laws does not permit double taxation; the state must ensure only one cess is collected for the same mineral extraction.
provisions: The Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992, Section 2
doctrines: Doctrine of validation by subsequent legislation
Distinction between temporary and permanent statutes
Doctrine of continuity of enforcement machinery post-levy
Principle against double taxation

card.dispute: The New Delhi Municipal Corporation (NDMC) levied property tax on state government properties in Delhi, and the states challenged this on the ground of constitutional immunity under Article 289(1).
issues_decided: Whether the property tax levied by NDMC on state government properties in Delhi is exempt under Article 289(1) of the Constitution?
Whether the exemption under Article 289(1) applies to properties used by states for trade or business?
Whether the impugned tax levies constitute 'Union taxation' within the meaning of Article 289(1)?
Whether the decision should be applied retrospectively?
holdings: Property taxes levied under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, NDMC Act, 1994, and Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 constitute 'Union taxation' under Article 289(1).
State government properties are exempt from property tax under Article 289(1) only if not used for trade or business; such exemption does not extend to properties used for commercial purposes.
The assessing authorities have jurisdiction to determine whether a property is used for government or commercial purposes, with appeal to civil courts available.
The judgment operates prospectively from the financial year 1996–97 onwards, in exercise of the Court’s power under Article 142, to avoid retrospective hardship.
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective overruling
Presumption of constitutionality of statutes
Principle of inter-governmental tax immunity
Rule of constitutional interpretation: courts interpret legislative intent based on statutory language and context

card.dispute: The appellants (leaseholders) challenged the High Court's apportionment of compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, claiming entitlement to full compensation, while the State contested the valuation and apportionment of compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to full compensation for the leased land acquired before the lease expiry, despite having only a limited leasehold interest.
Whether the High Court was justified in apportioning compensation between the State and the leaseholders in a 50:50 ratio for land within the ceiling limit.
Whether the State could seek reference under Section 18(3) of the Land Acquisition Act to challenge excess compensation awarded by the Collector.
holdings: Leaseholders with a determinable lease ending in 1992 are not entitled to full compensation as their interest is limited to the unexpired lease period (about 7 years), and the State retains reversionary interest.
The High Court correctly apportioned compensation in a 50:50 ratio between the State and the leaseholders for land within the ceiling limit, considering the limited leasehold interest.
Section 18(3) allows the Land Reforms Commissioner to seek reference only when compensation is excessive; it does not apply to disputes over apportionment under land ceiling laws.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Land Reforms Act, Section 11(6)
doctrines: Reversionary interest of the State in leasehold land
Apportionment of compensation based on extent of interest in land
Limited scope of reference under Section 18(3) for excessive compensation
Distinction between lease and licence under property law

card.dispute: The appellant, S. Gopal Reddy, challenged his conviction for demanding dowry under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, arguing that the evidence, particularly handwriting analysis and witness testimony, was insufficient to prove his involvement.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of a handwriting expert, without substantial corroboration, is sufficient to prove authorship of incriminating letters?
Whether a witness who did not receive the letters and had no prior familiarity with the accused's handwriting can reliably identify the handwriting?
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant demanded dowry under Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961?
holdings: Expert opinion on handwriting is not conclusive and cannot form the sole basis of conviction without substantial independent corroboration by direct or circumstantial evidence.
A witness must demonstrate actual familiarity with the accused's handwriting to be competent to identify it; mere assertion of familiarity without basis is insufficient.
The prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant demanded dowry; conviction cannot rest on assumptions or emotional considerations but requires legally reliable evidence.
doctrines: Unsafe to convict based solely on expert handwriting opinion
Requirement of corroboration for opinion evidence
Proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases
Benefit of doubt to the accused

card.dispute: Rehmat fought against the State of Haryana over his conviction for attempted murder, robbery, and illegal possession of arms under TADA.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond doubt that the appellant committed offences under Sections 307 and 393 IPC?
Whether the recovery of the weapon and cartridges was credible to sustain conviction under Section 25 of the Arms Act read with Section 6 of TADA?
Whether the appellant's injuries support his plea of self-defence and false implication?
holdings: The prosecution failed to explain 13 injuries on the appellant, making the defence version of assault and self-defence more probable; conviction under Sections 307 and 393 IPC cannot be sustained on doubtful evidence.
The evidence regarding recovery of the pistol and cartridges lacks credibility and consistency; conviction under Section 25 of the Arms Act read with Section 6 of TADA is unsustainable.
Non-disclosure of the assailant's name in medical records and delayed FIR indicate possible false implication; prosecution failed to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
provisions: Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1985, Section 6
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Credibility of prosecution evidence
Right of private defence
Presumption of innocence

card.dispute: The petitioner sought contempt action against the respondent for failing to vacate rented premises by the court-ordered deadline and for filing false affidavits claiming compliance.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was guilty of civil contempt for breaching the Supreme Court's order extending time to vacate the premises without filing an undertaking.
Whether the respondent committed criminal contempt by filing false affidavits stating he had vacated the premises.
Whether the respondent's unconditional apology warranted discharge instead of punishment.
holdings: No civil contempt was committed because the order extending time was based on an agreement between the parties, not a unilateral representation or undertaking by the respondent.
The respondent was guilty of criminal contempt for filing false affidavits, as such conduct obstructs justice and undermines judicial proceedings.
The apology was not genuine due to repetition of false claims; however, considering partial compliance and custody, a fine of Rs. 2,000 with default imprisonment was imposed instead of jail.
doctrines: Criminal contempt for filing false affidavits
Civil contempt requires breach of an undertaking or order induced by party's representation
Apology in contempt must be bona fide and unconditional to warrant leniency

card.dispute: The appellants sued to restrain the respondents from interfering with their possession of a property, while the respondents filed a counter-claim seeking injunction over a different property, leading to a dispute over the maintainability of such a counter-claim in an injunction suit.
issues_decided: Whether a counter-claim for injunction over a different property is maintainable in a suit for injunction?
Whether a counter-claim can be based on a cause of action independent of the plaintiff's claim?
holdings: A counter-claim for injunction, even in respect of a different property, is maintainable in a suit for injunction if it arises from a cause of action accruing to the defendant before the deadline for filing the written statement.

A counter-claim under Order 8, Rule 6A CPC can be based on an independent cause of action, not necessarily connected to the plaintiff's claim, and must be treated as a cross-suit within the same proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8, Rule 6A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 8, Rule 6C
doctrines: Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings
Counter-claim as a cross-suit

card.dispute: The landowners challenged whether the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies to acquisitions made under the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, and claimed compensation based on the market rate at the time of declaration.
issues_decided: Whether the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 applies to acquisitions under the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965
Whether the notifications and declarations under the Adhiniyam lapse after two years from the commencement of the 1984 Amendment Act
What compensation is due to landowners when there is a delay in awarding compensation
holdings: The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 does not apply to acquisitions under the U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965, as certain provisions of the 1894 Act are already incorporated by reference.
Notifications and declarations under the Adhiniyam, analogous to Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, do not lapse after two years from the commencement of the 1984 Amendment.

Compensation shall be determined at the market rate prevalent at the time of the declaration; if the award is delayed beyond six weeks, interest at 18% shall apply, and acquisition may be withdrawn if compensation is not deposited within three months thereafter.
provisions: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965
doctrines: Incorporation by reference
Settled law doctrine
Compensation based on market value at declaration date

card.dispute: Shangrila Food Products Ltd. fought with the Life Insurance Corporation of India over whether it was a lawful sub-tenant entitled to protection from eviction and not liable for damages for unauthorised occupation of public premises.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could remand the case to reassess the appellant's status as an authorised or unauthorised occupant while also allowing the respondent to claim damages.
Whether the appellant had acquired a vested right to be free from a damages claim after the appellate court had previously rejected it.
holdings: The High Court, exercising jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, can remand a case to reassess both the nature of occupation and the claim for damages to ensure complete justice.
No vested right to escape liability for damages accrues to an occupant until their lawful status is finally determined; equitable considerations allow the court to balance both claims.
provisions: Life Insurance Corporation of India Act, 1956
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses (Rate Control) Act, Section 2(f), Section 4, Section 5, Section 7
doctrines: Principles of equity in writ jurisdiction
Doctrine of authorised vs unauthorised occupation
Conditional liability for damages based on tenancy status

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the legality of land acquisition for the Indira Gandhi International Airport, arguing that the government took possession before publishing the required notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the publication of notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory before taking possession under Section 17(4)
Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) must be published and whether its quashing required fresh publication
Whether the manner of publication of statutory notifications is directory or mandatory
holdings: When the government exercises urgent possession powers under Section 17(4), it is not mandatory to publish the Section 4(1) notification in newspapers or locally before taking possession, as such procedural compliance is directory to serve public purpose.

Publication of the declaration under Section 6(1) is mandatory to give conclusiveness to the public purpose, but once quashed and later found to be legally invalid, the original declaration stands restored by operation of law upon reversal of the quashing order.
The word 'shall' in statutory provisions is not always mandatory; the nature, object, and consequences of non-compliance must be considered to determine if a provision is mandatory or directory.
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutes
Doctrine of relation back of judicial decisions
Public purpose and urgency in eminent domain

card.dispute: Co-owners disputed over the maintainability of a civil suit for declaration of title and injunction, after mutation entries and a dismissed revenue appeal.
issues_decided: Whether Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act bars a civil suit between private parties over property title?
Whether a civil court can entertain a suit challenging a revenue officer's order without exhausting appeal remedies under Section 11?
Whether mutation entries confer title to land?
holdings: Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act does not bar civil suits between private parties; it only applies to suits against the government for acts of revenue officers.
A private party can maintain a civil suit under the CPC without first exhausting remedies under Section 11, as it does not override the jurisdiction of civil courts in inter se disputes.
Mutation entries do not create or confer title; they are only for revenue collection and serve as evidence of possession, not ownership.
doctrines: Exhaustion of remedies
Jurisdiction of civil courts
Lis pendens
Mutation entries do not confer title

card.dispute: Six appellants challenged the High Court's decision to set aside their acquittal and convict them for murder and related offences under the Indian Penal Code.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's order of acquittal based on re-appreciation of evidence.
Whether the testimony of close relatives of the deceased could be relied upon as substantive evidence.
Whether discrepancies in the prosecution's evidence, including medical reports, rendered the conviction unsafe.
holdings: The High Court can interfere with an acquittal if there are compelling reasons and the trial court's reasoning is found to be unsustainable upon re-appreciation of evidence.
The evidence of close relatives of the deceased is not automatically unreliable and can be accepted if it is consistent and corroborated in material particulars.
Minor contradictions in witness testimony and alleged discrepancies with medical evidence do not invalidate the prosecution case if the overall evidence supports the conviction.
doctrines: Re-appreciation of evidence by High Court in criminal appeals
Principle of corroboration in eyewitness testimony
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation from Rs.74,953 to Rs.56,000 per acre for land acquired for industrial development near Dharwad.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court committed an error in law by reducing the compensation to Rs.56,000 per acre after a 65% deduction for developmental charges?
Whether the market value determined by the High Court, based on comparable sales and deductions, was legally sustainable?
holdings: The High Court did not commit an error in law by deducting 65% for developmental charges, as the deduction was justified by the lack of actual development and the long waiting period for development.

The compensation of Rs.56,000 per acre was legally valid, as the High Court properly considered comparable sales, location differences, and developmental potential in determining just and fair market value.
doctrines: Principle of just and fair market value for large tracts of land
Deduction for developmental charges based on factual matrix
Relevance of time lag and waiting period in compensation determination

card.dispute: The appellants, members of a Joint Hindu Family, challenged the validity of a sale of joint family property by the Karta, alleging it was vitiated by fraud and that the sale required court permission under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, due to the involvement of minors' undivided interests.
issues_decided: Whether Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 applies to the sale of joint Hindu family property by the Karta involving the undivided interest of a minor?
Whether the sale of joint family property by the Karta without court permission is voidable under Section 8 when minors' interests are affected?
holdings: Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 does not apply to the sale of joint Hindu family property by the Karta, as it excludes the undivided interest of a minor in such property from the scope of 'minor's property' under the section.

No court permission under Section 8 is required for the disposal of a minor's undivided interest in joint family property, as such interest is managed by the Karta or adult family members, and no separate natural guardian is needed under the Act.
provisions: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 6
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 8
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 12
doctrines: Legislative intent in beneficial legislation
Exclusion of undivided joint family property from guardianship under natural guardianship
Karta's authority to manage joint family property including minors' undivided interests

card.dispute: The ex-mother-in-law of the respondent challenged the High Court's order setting aside an ex parte divorce decree after the husband's death, arguing that the application to set it aside abated upon his death.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC to set aside an ex parte divorce decree survives the death of the husband who obtained the decree.
Whether the divorce proceedings can continue after the death of the husband who filed the petition.
holdings: An application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC to set aside an ex parte divorce decree does not abate upon the death of the husband; the wife can proceed against his legal heirs due to the decree's impact on status and property rights.
Once a divorce decree is set aside and the husband is dead, the original divorce petition abates because the marriage is automatically dissolved by death, leaving no subsisting marriage to dissolve.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Survival of legal proceedings after death where rights in status or property are affected
Abatement of personal causes of action upon death when no enforceable right survives

card.dispute: The appellant, Sri Samir Sobhan Sanyal, fought against Tracks Trade Private Ltd. and others over unlawful dispossession from a tenanted property without due process of law.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be dispossessed in execution of a decree in a title suit without a personal decree of eviction or due process of law.
Whether the appellant is entitled to remain in possession pending adjudication of his rights under Order 21, Rules 98 and 99 of the CPC.
Whether the respondents' actions in dispossessing the appellant amounted to high-handed and unlawful conduct violating due process.
holdings: A person in lawful possession cannot be dispossessed in execution of a decree in a title suit without a personal decree of eviction or an order under due process of law.
The status quo must be maintained, and the appellant is entitled to be restored to possession pending final disposal of his application under Order 21, Rules 98 and 99, CPC.
High-handed dispossession without legal authority undermines the rule of law and cannot be condoned by the court.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rules 98 and 99
doctrines: Due process of law
Rule of law
Status quo in execution proceedings
Protection against unauthorized dispossession

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the compensation awarded for acquiring 20.40 acres of land for the Getalsud Dam, disputing the quantum of compensation and additional amounts granted by lower courts.
issues_decided: What is the appropriate market value per acre of the acquired Class I wet crop land?
Whether separate compensation can be awarded for a tank and well used for irrigation?
Whether additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act is legal when the award is delayed?
What interest and solatium are payable on delayed payment of compensation?
holdings: The appropriate market value of the acquired land is Rs. 6,000 per acre, considering all land as Class I in absence of reliable evidence on land quality.
No separate compensation is admissible for tanks and wells if their water is used for cultivating the acquired land, as their value is included in the land's market value.
Additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) is illegal when the Collector's award is made after the possession date, as it applies only when the award is delayed beyond two years from possession.

Claimants are entitled to interest at 9% for one year from the date of possession (1.1.1966), then 15% thereafter, solatium at 30%, and an additional 12% on market value from notification to award or possession, whichever is earlier.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination based on comparable sales and quality of land
Doctrine of amalgamation of value of irrigation structures with agricultural land when used integrally
Rule against double compensation for the same asset in land acquisition
Doctrine of enhanced compensation and interest for delayed payment under the Land Acquisition Act

card.dispute: The children from the second marriage of P.K.K. Raman Nair contested their right to inherit his property after being declared illegitimate by the children from his first marriage.
issues_decided: Whether children born from a void marriage are legitimate under the Hindu Marriage Act after the amendment of Section 16
Whether the amended Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act removes the constitutional infirmity of discriminatory treatment between illegitimate children
Whether the legal fiction of legitimacy under Section 16 applies retrospectively to children born before the amendment
holdings: Children born of a void marriage are deemed legitimate for all purposes, including inheritance from their parents, under Section 16(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act as amended.
The amendment to Section 16 removes the classification between illegitimate children and is constitutionally valid, as it confers legitimacy uniformly on children of void marriages.
The legal fiction of legitimacy under Section 16 applies retrospectively, so children born before the amendment are also entitled to inherit their father's property.
doctrines: Heydon's Rule of statutory interpretation
Legal fiction (fictio juris)
Prospective and retrospective operation of amendments

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the High Court's decision to reinstate a government servant, Nand Kiskore Shukla, who was removed from service following a disciplinary enquiry.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the disciplinary authority's order of removal based on proven misconduct?
Whether oral permission suffices under Rule 24 of the U.P. Government Servant Conduct Rules, 1956 for disposal of immovable property?
Whether the disciplinary authority could impose removal from service based solely on charge 2, given that other charges were not fully adjudicated due to the respondent's non-cooperation?
holdings: Even if only one charge is proved and considered sufficient by the disciplinary authority, the court should not interfere with the penalty unless the order is perverse or arbitrary.
Oral permission does not satisfy the requirement of 'previous knowledge or sanction' under Rule 24 of the U.P. Government Servant Conduct Rules, 1956, which mandates formal approval.
The disciplinary authority is entitled to pass an order of removal based on a single proven charge, especially when the employee failed to cooperate in the enquiry process.
provisions: U.P. Government Servant Conduct Rules, 1956, Rule 24
doctrines: Principle of non-interference with departmental punishment if supported by some evidence
Requirement of formal sanction under service conduct rules for property transactions
Consequence of non-cooperation in departmental enquiry

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu appealed against the Administrative Tribunal's order reinstating S. Subramaniam, a Deputy Tehsildar, after his removal for allegedly accepting illegal gratification.
issues_decided: Whether the Administrative Tribunal had the authority to re-appreciate evidence and arrive at its own conclusion on the proof of charges in a service matter?
Whether the Tribunal acted beyond its jurisdiction by substituting its view on the credibility of evidence in a disciplinary proceeding?
holdings: The Administrative Tribunal does not have the power to re-appreciate evidence or substitute its own findings on the proof of charges; its role is limited to judicial review of the procedure and legality of the disciplinary authority's decision.

The Tribunal erred in law by trenching upon the domain of the disciplinary authority; judicial review does not permit a tribunal to reassess witness credibility or reach independent conclusions on the merits of the charge if supported by evidence.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Civil Services (Control & Appeal) Rules, Rule 23(i)
doctrines: Judicial review vs. appellate jurisdiction
Principle of limited scope of judicial review in service matters
Finality of disciplinary authority's findings based on evidence

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan challenged the High Court's decision to quash land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, which the respondents opposed on grounds of non-compliance with statutory requirements.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the notification under Section 4(1) and declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, due to non-compliance with procedural requirements?
Whether inordinate delay in filing the writ petition affects the maintainability of the challenge to land acquisition?
Whether the vesting of title in the State after possession renders the acquisition immune from being quashed despite procedural defects?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the acquisition proceedings as the land had already vested in the State upon possession, and subsequent procedural defects do not divest the State's title.

When possession is taken and compensation proceedings are concluded, the court should not exercise its discretion under Article 226 to quash acquisition on grounds of delay or technical non-compliance.
Once the award is made and accepted, and the acquisition process is complete, the proceedings attain finality and cannot be invalidated even if there were earlier procedural irregularities.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon possession
Finality of acquisition proceedings
Discretionary nature of writ jurisdiction under Article 226
Effect of laches in land acquisition challenges
Void vs. voidable administrative action

card.dispute: The State of U.P. and others appealed against the High Court's enhancement of compensation awarded to Rajendra Singh for the acquisition of his agricultural land.
issues_decided: Whether the reference court and High Court properly evaluated the market value of the acquired land while determining compensation?
Whether the reliance on unexamined sale transactions without proof of their authenticity was legally valid?
holdings: Courts must base compensation on reliable evidence and comparable sales proven to be between willing buyers and sellers; unexamined sale deeds cannot form the basis of valuation.
When courts fail to properly assess evidence or compare land characteristics, their awards are legally unsustainable and must be set aside.
doctrines: Burden of proof in land acquisition compensation
Prudent purchaser rule
Requirement of comparable sales for market value determination

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh and others appealed against the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for the acquisition of 13.75 acres of land, while the landowner cross-appealed for further enhancement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court and District Judge applied the correct legal principle in determining compensation based on per square foot rates derived from small land sales and stamp duty rates.
What is the reasonable market value of the acquired land for determining just compensation.
holdings: The High Court and District Judge erred in law by relying on small land sale transactions and stamp duty rates to fix compensation per square foot, as a prudent purchaser would not buy 13.75 acres on such a basis.
The market value of the acquired land is fixed at Rs. 30,000 per acre, based on the State's own admission in the case synopsis.
doctrines: Prudent purchaser rule
Compulsory acquisition compensation principle
Market value determination avoiding inflated transactions

card.dispute: The landlady, Sultana Begum, sought eviction of tenant Prem Chand Jain under a compromise decree, but Jain resisted execution, claiming he had been granted a licence by her attorney, thereby satisfying the decree.
issues_decided: Whether possession handed over to the landlady's attorney discharged the eviction decree
Whether a licence granted by the attorney after the decree extinguished the right to execute the decree
Whether a compromise or adjustment of a decree must be recorded under Order XXI Rule 2 CPC to be effective
holdings: Delivery of possession to an attorney does not automatically satisfy a decree unless the decree-holder confirms acceptance.
A licence granted post-decree does not extinguish the decree for eviction, as it does not confer exclusive possession or create a fresh tenancy.
Any adjustment of a decree must be judicially recorded under Order XXI Rule 2 CPC; otherwise, execution can proceed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 2
doctrines: Intention of the parties determines creation of tenancy or licence
Doctrine of judicial recording of decree adjustments

card.dispute: The appellant claimed sole ownership of a 25.12-acre property purchased in 1961, while the respondents claimed it was joint family property and they were entitled to a share in the compensation awarded upon its acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the non-inclusion of the disputed property in an earlier partition suit barred the current claim under Order II Rule 2 CPC.
Whether the property in question was joint family property or self-acquired property of the appellant.
holdings: Non-inclusion of the property in the earlier partition suit did not bar the current claim because the property was acquired after the suit was filed, and thus Order II Rule 2 CPC does not apply.
The property is joint family property as it was purchased by the family manager from joint funds, and the appellant failed to prove that the purchase was made from his separate or personal funds.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order II Rule 2
doctrines: Presumption of joint family property in Hindu law
Burden of proof in establishing self-acquisition of property by a coparcener

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the criminal court's jurisdiction to proceed with a private complaint alleging forgery and conspiracy, claiming a bar under Section 195 of the CrPC since the forged document was later used in civil proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the criminal court was barred under Section 195(1)(c) of the CrPC from taking cognizance of a private complaint for forgery when only a copy of the forged document was initially before the civil court?
Whether the subsequent production of the original forged document in civil court after cognizance in the criminal case invalidates the criminal proceedings?
holdings: Section 195 CrPC does not bar a private criminal complaint if the original forged document was not produced before the civil court at the time cognizance was taken by the criminal court.
Once cognizance is validly taken by a criminal court, subsequent use of the forged document in civil proceedings does not nullify the criminal trial.
doctrines: Bar on private prosecution under Section 195 CrPC
Cognizance and its irrevocability once validly taken
Nexus between forged documents and judicial proceedings for applicability of Section 195

card.dispute: The dispute was between the Land Acquisition Officer and landowners over whether the delay in filing a reference application under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector (LAO) is a 'court' within the meaning of Section 5 of the Limitation Act when dealing with applications under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the proviso to Section 18(2) of the Land Acquisition Act is a special law that excludes the application of Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
holdings: The Collector or LAO is not a 'court' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act when performing statutory functions under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, and thus cannot condone delays beyond the prescribed period.
The specific limitation period in the proviso to Section 18(2) of the Act is a special law that excludes the operation of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, and no extension of time is permissible.
doctrines: Doctrine of exclusion of Section 5 of the Limitation Act by special statutes
Distinction between 'court' and 'statutory authority' for purposes of limitation

card.dispute: The U.P. Jal Nigam and the landowner fought over whether the purchaser of acquired land could claim compensation at the market value prevailing in 1992, after the land was acquired in 1973 for a pumping station.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, having purchased the land after the notification under Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, could claim compensation.
Whether the market value for compensation should be determined based on the basic valuation register for stamp duty purposes.
From what date and at what rate the compensation should be determined under the Land Acquisition Act.
holdings: A purchaser of land after a Section 4(1) notification cannot acquire title but may step into the shoes of the original owner to claim compensation under the Act.
Market value for compensation must be determined based on evidence of prevailing rates at the time of notification, not on stamp duty valuation registers.

Compensation is to be fixed as of the date of the Section 4(1) notification; subsequent development is irrelevant under Section 24, and compensation here is set at Rs. 25,000 with 15% solatium and 6% interest from date of possession.
doctrines: Vesting of land in the State free from encumbrances upon taking possession under Section 17(2)
Compensation based on market value at the time of notification under Section 4(1)
Subsequent development irrelevant for compensation under Section 24
Principle of stepping into the shoes of the original owner for claiming compensation

card.dispute: TISCO and IDCOL challenged the reduction of TISCO's mining lease area and the Central Government's decision to prioritize equitable distribution and captive mining needs of other industries over TISCO's renewal claim.
issues_decided: Whether the concept of 'mineral development' under Section 8(3) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 includes captive mining and equitable distribution of mining leases.
Whether the Central Government's order reducing TISCO's lease area to 406 hectares was valid.
Whether the Committee constituted by the Central Government properly considered TISCO's technical objections and legal rights.
holdings: The concept of 'mineral development' under Section 8(3) encompasses both captive mining needs and equitable distribution of leases among deserving industries.
The Central Government acted within its discretion in renewing TISCO's lease over a reduced area of 406 hectares based on expert assessment.
Courts must show deference to expert committees on technical and policy matters unless there is a constitutional or legal inconsistency.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 8
doctrines: Deference to expert administrative bodies in technical and policy matters
Equitable distribution of natural resources
Captive mining as a relevant factor in mineral development

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's dismissal of its appeal against the quashing of a land acquisition declaration, arguing urgency justified bypassing inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the appeal could be condoned.
Whether the urgency clause under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act was validly invoked to dispense with the Section 5A inquiry.
Whether the land acquisition served a public purpose and remained justified under the revised Master Plan.
holdings: The delay in filing the appeal was substantial but excusable due to administrative inaction, and the appeal deserved to be heard on merits.
The invocation of Section 17(4) to dispense with the Section 5A inquiry was valid as the acquisition for shifting timber depots to decongest Old Delhi constituted an urgent public purpose.
The continued need for the land under the MPD-2001 and the legitimacy of the public purpose upheld the acquisition, despite the notification using 'likely to be needed'.
doctrines: Subjective satisfaction in urgency decisions under Section 17(4)
Public purpose in planned urban development
Condonation of delay in appeals due to government inaction

card.dispute: The Union of India appealed against the award of solatium and interest to landowners whose property was acquired under the Jammu & Kashmir Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1968.
issues_decided: Whether landowners are entitled to solatium and interest under the Jammu & Kashmir Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1968?
Whether the omission to pay solatium and interest violates Article 14 or Article 31 of the Constitution?
Whether non-payment of solatium and interest results in unjust enrichment of the State?
holdings: The Jammu & Kashmir Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1968 does not provide for solatium or interest, and the arbitrator or court cannot award them in the absence of statutory provision.
The omission to provide for solatium and interest in the Act is a deliberate legislative policy and does not violate Article 14 or Article 31 of the Constitution.
Non-payment of solatium and interest does not amount to unjust enrichment of the State, as public funds are used for public purposes in accordance with constitutional provisions.
provisions: Jammu & Kashmir Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1968
Section 8 of the Jammu & Kashmir Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1968
Article 14 of the Constitution of India
Article 31 of the Constitution of India
doctrines: Legislative policy in compensation laws
Principle of unjust enrichment
Equity in award of interest
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (expressio unius est exclusio alterius)

card.dispute: The Urban Improvement Trust, Jodhpur, challenged the award of additional compensation benefits (solatium, interest, and additional amount) to landowner Gokul Narain in a land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984, apply to land acquired under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959?
Whether the award of additional benefits under the 1984 Amendment Act was beyond the jurisdiction of the District Judge?
Whether objections to the jurisdictional validity of a decree can be raised in execution proceedings under Section 47 of the CPC?
holdings: The Central Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 68 of 1984, applies prospectively from August 1, 1987, and only to pending cases under the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, as per Section 60A of the Rajasthan Amendment Act, 29 of 1987.

The award of additional benefits under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and 28 of the Central LA Act was without jurisdiction because the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, does not provide for such benefits and the amendment was not retroactively applicable.

A decree passed without jurisdiction is a nullity and can be challenged at any stage, including in execution proceedings under Section 47 of the CPC, as it strikes at the root of the court’s authority.
doctrines: Nullity of decree for lack of jurisdiction
Prospective application of amendment laws
Separability of compensation components in land acquisition

card.dispute: An environmental group challenged the granting of 305 fishing permits to displaced tribals in the Pench National Park, arguing it harmed wildlife and violated forest laws.
issues_decided: Whether the tribals had traditional fishing rights in the Pench National Park area despite its status as a reserved forest and tiger reserve
Whether the Chief Wildlife Warden had the authority to issue fishing permits in a national park
Whether the ecological concerns outweighed the livelihood rights of displaced tribals
holdings: Tribals displaced from within the national park have traditional livelihood rights, including fishing, which must be recognized even after relocation.
Fishing permits can be granted to displaced tribals as settlement of traditional rights before final notification of a national park, not under Section 33 of the Wildlife Act.
Permits must be strictly regulated to prevent ecological damage, with monitoring, restricted access, and adherence to environmental safeguards.
doctrines: Doctrine of Sustainable Development
Precautionary Principle
Public Trust Doctrine
Principle of Environmental Protection under Fundamental Duties

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murdering Bagicha Singh as an act of revenge for the earlier murder of Karnail Singh, challenged their conviction and sentence, arguing witness bias and incredibility of detailed testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution witnesses were so ill-disposed towards the appellants as to render their testimony unreliable
Whether the conviction in the earlier murder case of Karnail Singh's killers negated the motive for revenge
Whether the precise and detailed testimony of eyewitnesses about each assailant's role was inherently incredible, especially given the nighttime occurrence
holdings: The fact that witnesses were convicted based on the appellants' prior testimony does not automatically make their current testimony biased, especially since one of them was also injured in the attack.
The conviction of the earlier murderers did not eliminate the motive for revenge, as they were released on bail during appeal, leaving the appellants' desire for vengeance unquenched.

Detailed eyewitness testimony, even if precise, cannot be rejected outright as 'tutored'; its credibility depends on the witness's capacity, the traumatic nature of the event, and the trial court's assessment.
doctrines: Testimony evaluation: Eyewitness accounts should not be judged by hyper-technical standards or 'golden scales'
Hostility of witnesses must be assessed in context, not presumed to vitiate testimony
Motive in criminal cases may persist despite legal resolution of prior incidents if practical grievances remain

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, which transferred management of the shrine from private trustees (Baridars) to a state-appointed Board, alleging violation of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.
issues_decided: Whether the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board constitutes a 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution.
Whether the Act results in acquisition of property under Article 31(2) without compensation, violating fundamental rights.
Whether the rights of the Baridars to collect offerings were extinguished in a manner contrary to Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31(2).
Whether the provisions for compensation under Section 19(1) with its proviso are constitutionally valid.
holdings: The Shrine Board is not a 'State' or a corporation controlled by the State within Article 12, as the State does not exercise control over its management or property.
The vesting of shrine properties and collection rights in the Board does not amount to acquisition by the State under Article 31(2), hence no compensation is mandated under that provision.
The extinction of Baridars' rights to offerings does not violate Article 19(1)(f) because the Act provides a mechanism for compensation through a Tribunal, satisfying procedural fairness.

Section 19(1) with its proviso is constitutionally valid as it allows for just compensation determined by a Tribunal and reviewed by the Board with reasoned decisions, complying with post-4th Amendment jurisprudence on compensation.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, Section 1(2)
Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, Section 2
Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, Section 3
Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, Section 19
Jammu and Kashmir Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Act, 1988, Section 24
doctrines: Doctrine of State under Article 12
Doctrine of acquisition of property under Article 31
Principle of just compensation post-4th Amendment
Doctrine of procedural fairness in property rights extinction

card.dispute: The appellant, a stranger to the decree, claimed independent possession of decretal property and resisted execution, seeking adjudication of his claim without first surrendering possession.
issues_decided: Whether a stranger resisting execution of a decree for possession can seek adjudication of his claim under Order XXI Rule 97 CPC without first vacating the property.
Whether the executing court was obligated to adjudicate the appellant's resistance as an application under Order XXI Rule 97 CPC.
holdings: A stranger resisting execution of a decree for possession of immovable property can raise his claim under Order XXI Rule 97 CPC, and the executing court must adjudicate it without requiring prior surrender of possession.

The executing court and the High Court erred in law by refusing to adjudicate the appellant's objection, as the application under Order XXI Rule 97 must be considered on its merits when resistance is alleged by any person, including a stranger.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 35(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 97
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 98
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 99
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 105
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of effective enforcement of decree
Adjudication of third-party claims in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The company disputed the validity of re-assessments and claimed credit for excess royalty paid to the state government as payment towards its income-tax and super-tax liability.
issues_decided: Whether re-assessments for 1950-51 to 1956-57 were valid under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922?
Whether an appeal lies against an order levying penal interest under section 18A of the Act?
Whether the company is entitled to credit for excess royalty paid to the State Government in lieu of income-tax and super-tax?
Whether excess royalty beyond Rs. 1,50,000 is a permissible deduction under the lease deed?
holdings: The Supreme Court did not decide on the validity of re-assessments under section 34(1)(a), as the appeal was remitted to the High Court for reconsideration.
No independent appeal lies against an order levying penal interest under section 18A, but the issue can be raised in an appeal against the assessment order if interest is part of that order.

The High Court failed to consider judicial orders and factual material showing that excess royalty was paid to the State on behalf of the Union; remitted for fresh consideration of credit entitlement.

The High Court’s finding that only the portion of excess royalty beyond tax liability is deductible was not upheld; matter remitted for reconsideration in light of the District Court decree and agency relationship.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive payment
Principle of permissible deduction under tax law
Judicial estoppel and effect of court decrees
Right to appeal against composite assessment orders

card.dispute: The reversioners of Khushal Singh challenged the widow Durga Devi's alienations of property, claiming she lost title and possession after a 1954 mutation in favor of adopted sons, while the appellants argued she retained title and became absolute owner under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the 1954 mutation in favor of Balwant Singh and Kartar Singh divested the widow Durga Devi of her title and possession in the suit property
Whether the subsequent re-mutation in favor of Durga Devi (Mutation No. 1348) restored her title
Whether Durga Devi, as a limited owner, became the absolute owner of the property upon the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Whether the alienations made by Durga Devi were valid and binding on the reversioners
holdings: Mutation in revenue records does not convey or extinguish title; it only enables payment of land revenue. Thus, Mutation No. 1311 did not divest Durga Devi of title or possession.
A re-mutation allowed to remain unchallenged, even if based on misunderstanding, cannot be ignored and has legal effect for revenue purposes, though not conclusive on title.
As Durga Devi remained in possession and her limited interest was not extinguished, it ripened into absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Alienations by Durga Devi were valid as she became absolute owner; however, the gift to Makan Singh remained invalid and in favor of reversioners.
provisions: Punjab Land Revenue Act, relevant provisions on mutation
doctrines: Mutation does not confer title
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Enlargement of limited estate into absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income-Tax and Podar Cement Pvt. Ltd. disputed whether rental income from flats should be taxed as 'income from house property' under Section 22 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, when the assessee was not the legal owner due to incomplete conveyance of title.
issues_decided: Whether rental income from flats can be assessed as 'income from house property' under Section 22 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 when the assessee is not the legal owner of the property?
Whether the amendment to Section 27 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, introduced by the Finance Act, 1988, is declaratory and retrospective in nature?
Whether the assessee, despite not having formal title, could be deemed the 'owner' for tax purposes based on control and entitlement to income?
holdings: For the purpose of Section 22, 'owner' includes a person who is entitled to receive income from the property in their own right, even without formal legal title.
The amendment to Section 27(iii), (iiia), and (iiib) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, is declaratory and clarificatory, and therefore retrospective in operation.
The rental income from the flats is taxable as 'income from house property' under Section 22, not as 'income from other sources' under Section 56.
doctrines: Declaratory statute doctrine
Retrospective operation of clarificatory amendments
Substance over form in statutory interpretation
Deemed ownership for tax purposes

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder under Section 302/34 IPC by the Bombay High Court, challenged their conviction, while the State had earlier appealed the trial court's acquittal of two of them.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of a 10-year-old child witness (Sarubai) can be the basis for conviction without corroboration?
Whether the child witness's testimony was reliable and sufficiently corroborated by other evidence?
Whether the prosecution case against all three appellants was strong enough to overturn the trial court's acquittal of two accused?
holdings: The evidence of a child witness is admissible and can form the basis of conviction if the child is competent to understand questions and give rational answers under Section 118 of the Evidence Act.
The testimony of the child witness was reliable, unblemished, and sufficiently corroborated by independent witnesses and the First Information Report.
The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of two appellants and upholding the conviction of all three under Section 302/34 IPC based on credible and corroborated evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration of child witness
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Use of circumstantial evidence including forensic analysis

card.dispute: The appellants, accused in a mass violence case, challenged their convictions for murder under Sections 302/34 and 302/149 IPC, arguing lack of common intention to commit murder.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants shared a common intention to commit murder under Section 34 IPC in the killing of Ahmed Shah?
Whether the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC for the murder of Razaullah was legally sustainable based on the evidence of common intention?
Whether the conviction under Section 147 IPC in the second appeal was valid?
holdings: Conviction under Section 302/34 IPC for the murder of Ahmed Shah was not sustainable for six appellants due to insufficient evidence of common intention; they were instead convicted under Section 325/34 IPC for causing grievous hurt.
The conviction under Section 302/34 IPC for the murder of Razaullah was upheld as the nature of injuries and use of deadly weapons established a common intention to kill.
The conviction under Section 147 IPC was upheld based on credible eyewitness testimony and evidence of participation in unlawful assembly.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires a meeting of minds and shared purpose to commit the offence.
Common object of an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC may not suffice for murder unless intention to cause death is clearly established.
Sustained and brutal assault with deadly weapons on vital body parts supports inference of common intention to kill.

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a land acquisition declaration, arguing it was barred by limitation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was barred by limitation
Whether the date of publication of the declaration for limitation purposes includes all modes of publication under Section 6(2)
holdings: The declaration under Section 6 is deemed published for limitation purposes when first published in the Official Gazette, not on the last date of all publications.
The proviso to Section 6(1) requires the declaration to be published within one year of the Section 4(1) notification, and this was satisfied by the Official Gazette publication on 5.8.93.
doctrines: Conclusiveness of declaration under Section 6
Literal and mischief rule of statutory interpretation
Requirement of official publication for completion of declaration

card.dispute: The appellant (Heeralal) and respondents (Kalyan Mal & Ors) fought over whether the respondents could amend their written statement to withdraw earlier admissions that certain properties were joint family assets, thereby affecting the claim for partition.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants could be permitted to amend their written statement to withdraw admissions regarding ownership of seven properties in Schedule-A?
Whether such amendment would cause irretrievable prejudice to the plaintiff's case?
Whether the amendment sought in relation to Schedule-B properties could be allowed?
holdings: A defendant cannot be allowed to amend a written statement to withdraw clear admissions that would displace the plaintiff's case and cause irretrievable prejudice.
Where an admission in the written statement confers a legal right on the plaintiff, allowing an inconsistent plea through amendment is impermissible.
