An amendment seeking to alter the nature of possession regarding Schedule-B properties, as no admission was previously made, does not prejudice the plaintiff and may be allowed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI, Rule 17
doctrines: Principle of irretrievable prejudice
Binding precedent of larger bench (per incuriam)
Amendment of pleadings under CPC

card.dispute: The Jaipur Development Authority appealed against the Rajasthan High Court's rejection of its application to produce additional evidence in appeal, on the ground that it had not led any evidence in the trial court.
issues_decided: Whether a party not having led any evidence in the trial court can be permitted to produce additional evidence in the appellate court under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC?
Whether the word 'additional' in Order 41 Rule 27 CPC requires a party to have already adduced evidence in the trial court?
holdings: A party who did not lead any evidence in the trial court is not barred from producing additional evidence in the appellate court if it satisfies the conditions under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC.

The term 'additional' in Order 41 Rule 27 CPC does not imply that the party must have already produced some evidence in the trial court; the rule only requires that the evidence could not have been produced despite due diligence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Due diligence
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant challenged the eviction order passed in favor of the landlord, who died during the pendency of the writ petition, arguing that the bona fide requirement for eviction no longer existed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can consider the death of the landlord during the pendency of a writ petition as a ground to quash a final eviction order passed on the basis of bona fide requirement?
Whether the bona fide requirement for eviction under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Tenancy Act ceases to exist upon the death of the landlord?
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere with a final eviction decree under Article 226 by considering subsequent events like the landlord's death, as the decree becomes final and is not subject to revision on such grounds.

The bona fide requirement for eviction is determined as of the date of the application; its validity does not lapse due to the landlord's death, especially when the business can be continued by legal heirs.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
doctrines: Finality of decree
Bona fide requirement doctrine
Supervisory jurisdiction of High Court under Article 226/227
Doctrine of lis mota

card.dispute: The heirs of a defendant contested a High Court decision that declared certain gift deeds void and allowed a partition suit based on prior adjudication of the deeds' invalidity.
issues_decided: Whether the family settlement and gift deeds could be upheld despite a prior court declaration that the deeds were invalid under Hindu law.
Whether the principle of estoppel could prevent the parties from challenging the validity of the gift deeds after having benefited from them.
holdings: A prior judicial declaration that gift deeds are invalid under Hindu law binds the parties, and subsequent claims based on those deeds cannot be maintained.
The principle of estoppel does not override a binding prior adjudication on the legal invalidity of transactions, even if parties previously benefited from them.
provisions: Hindu Law, as applicable to family arrangements and gifts
doctrines: Estoppel
Binding effect of prior adjudication
Family settlement

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the quantum of compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India for planned development of Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether post-notification sale transactions can be relied upon to determine the market value of acquired land under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether a court judgment or award dated after the notification under Section 4 is admissible as evidence for determining market value.
Whether the claimants discharged the burden of proving stable land prices to justify reliance on post-notification transactions.
holdings: Post-notification sale transactions may be considered to determine market value if reliable evidence shows no appreciation in land prices after the Section 4 notification.
Only previous judgments or awards—those predating the Section 4 notification—can be used as evidence for assessing market value in land acquisition cases.
The claimants failed to prove that land prices remained stable after the notification; thus, reliance on later transactions was unjustified.
doctrines: Market value determination in compulsory acquisition
Admissibility of subsequent sale transactions as evidence
Principle of previous judgment as benchmark for valuation

card.dispute: The appellant sued to declare his title and recover possession of 1.80 acres of land from respondents who had trespassed and got themselves recorded as tenants, challenging the maintainability of the suit and the High Court's reversal of a factual finding in second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a new legal plea in a second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC as amended in 1976?
Whether the High Court acted in excess of jurisdiction by deciding the second appeal on a new point not raised in the lower courts?
holdings: The High Court must formulate a substantial question of law before entertaining a second appeal; mere questions of law are insufficient.

Entertaining a new legal plea in second appeal without formulating a substantial question of law and without affording opportunity to the opposite party violates Section 100 CPC and amounts to acting in excess of jurisdiction.
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Jurisdictional limitation in second appeals
Natural justice in appellate procedure

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's exercise of revisional and inherent powers in a criminal case where the complainant alleged fraud in the execution of an agreement to sell her land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 397(1) read with Section 401 CrPC despite the bar under Section 397(3) CrPC?
Whether the High Court could exercise inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to correct a miscarriage of justice in the face of an express bar on revision?
Whether the High Court's interference in the criminal proceedings was justified on the grounds of abuse of process or failure of justice?
holdings: The bar under Section 397(3) CrPC does not affect the High Court's inherent power under Section 482 CrPC, which is preserved to prevent abuse of process and ensure justice.
The High Court can exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC even when revision is barred, provided there is a grave miscarriage of justice or failure of justice.

The High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Section 483 CrPC and inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC allow it to intervene to correct orders that undermine justice, especially when statutory remedies are inadequate.
doctrines: Inherent powers of the High Court
Prevention of abuse of process
Miscarriage of justice
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court

card.dispute: The appellant contractor sued the Government of Tamil Nadu for damages after the government unilaterally terminated an agreement granting rights to collect chank shells, claiming the termination clause was invalid and violated natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether a clause allowing the government to unilaterally terminate a contract without reason is valid and enforceable despite being contrary to general contract principles
Whether the Government Grants Act, 1895 protects such termination clauses in government agreements
Whether the agreement in question constituted a lease or a licence, and whether it qualifies as a 'grant' under the Grants Act
holdings: A clause enabling the government to terminate a contract unilaterally is valid and enforceable if protected by the Government Grants Act, 1895, even if it contradicts general contract law.
Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act, 1895 insulate government grants from the Transfer of Property Act and other laws, allowing full effect to be given to the terms of the grant.
A licence coupled with interest granted by the government falls within the meaning of 'grant' under the Grants Act and is subject to its protective provisions.
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory insulation of government grants
Literal interpretation of 'grant' to include licences coupled with interest
Non-application of general contract law and principles of natural justice where statutes confer unfettered discretion on government

card.dispute: The appellants (sellers) challenged the High Court's decree for specific performance of a sale agreement in favor of the respondent (buyer), after the Trial Court had refused specific performance but ordered refund of earnest money.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to specific performance of the sale agreement despite a delay of over 2.5 years in seeking performance?
Whether the court can refuse specific performance on grounds of inequity arising from long delay and substantial rise in property value?
Whether the purchaser in appeal (defendant 4) had sufficient equities in his favor to resist specific performance?
holdings: A plaintiff must perform his part of the contract within a reasonable time, and unreasonable delay in acting under the agreement may make specific performance inequitable.
Even if time is not of the essence, prolonged inaction by the plaintiff coupled with a significant rise in property value can justify denial of specific performance on equitable grounds.
The fact that a subsequent purchaser bought the property after litigation began does not automatically negate his equities, especially when the original plaintiff delayed unreasonably.
doctrines: Discretion in granting specific performance
Equity and good conscience
Reasonable time for performance despite time not being of the essence

card.dispute: The hotel company appealed against the High Court's decision to vacate a status quo order, arguing that a Letters Patent Appeal lay against the single Judge's appellate order, while the Finance Corporation contended no such appeal was maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether a Letters Patent Appeal lies against an order of a single Judge of the High Court in appellate jurisdiction under Order XXXIX Rule 1 of the CPC?
Whether an order granting or vacating status quo in an interim injunction application is a 'judgment' allowing a second appeal under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent?
Whether Section 104(2) of the CPC bars a Letters Patent Appeal against an appellate order on interim relief?
holdings: No Letters Patent Appeal lies against an order passed by a single Judge in appellate jurisdiction under Order XXXIX Rule 1, as such appeals are barred by Section 104(2) of the CPC.
An appellate order on interim injunction, though termed a 'judgment' in certain contexts, does not permit a second appeal under Clause 10 of the Letters Patent when barred by statute.
The prohibition under Section 104(2) of the CPC on appeals from orders passed in appeal under Section 104(1) is absolute and overrides any contrary interpretation of the Letters Patent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 104(1) and (2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII Rule 1(r)
doctrines: Right of appeal is a statutory creature
Statutory bar under Section 104(2) CPC overrides Letters Patent provisions
Finality of appellate orders in interim matters

card.dispute: Homebuyers (appellants) sued the builder and New Delhi Municipal Council after four unauthorized floors of their building were demolished, seeking compensation for financial loss.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants are entitled to compensation for the loss suffered due to the demolition of unauthorized floors constructed by the builder?
Whether the builder is liable to refund the amount paid by flat purchasers along with escalation in value due to delay?
holdings: The builder is liable to compensate the flat purchasers for the loss caused by illegal construction and subsequent demolition, as the buyers were not informed of the illegality.
The builder must pay Rs. 60 lakhs per flat, including the amount paid by allottees, within six months, with interest at 21% per annum if payment is delayed beyond that period.
doctrines: Concurrent liability in contract and tort
Equitable relief against unjust enrichment
Breach of duty independent of contract giving rise to tortious liability

card.dispute: The landlady appealed against the High Court's reversal of an eviction order in favour of the tenant, claiming eviction under a special provision for ex-servicemen or their families.
issues_decided: Whether the certificate issued under Section 13A(1) of the Bombay Rent Act is conclusive proof of the landlord's eligibility for eviction on grounds of no other suitable residence?
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the Competent Authority's finding on bona fide requirement and ownership?
Whether minor inaccuracies in the certificate could render it invalid or indicate malafide?
holdings: A certificate under Section 13A(1) is conclusive proof that the landlord does not possess any other suitable residence in the local area, and courts cannot re-examine its correctness unless mala fides are proven.
The High Court, exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 31F, cannot substitute its view of evidence for that of the Competent Authority unless the findings are perverse or unreasonable.
Minor discrepancies in the certificate, such as incomplete address details, do not invalidate it, especially when the premises and parties are not in dispute and no mala fide is established.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13A(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Part IIA
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 31F
doctrines: Conclusiveness of statutory certificates
Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Presumption of legitimacy in co-ownership arrangements approved by housing societies

card.dispute: Sawmill licensees challenged the validity of the Madhya Pradesh Kashtha Chiram (Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1984 and transit rules, claiming they unreasonably restricted their freedom to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) by imposing excessive record-keeping and enabling confiscation of wood.
issues_decided: Whether the Madhya Pradesh Kashtha Chiram (Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1984 and Rule 27 of the M.P. (Transit (Forest Produce) Rules, 1961 violate Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution by imposing unreasonable restrictions on trade.
Whether the presumption of unlawful possession and risk of confiscation under the Act and Rules are arbitrary and violative of Article 14.
Whether the High Court erred in upholding the validity of the impugned provisions.
holdings: The record-keeping and reporting requirements under the Act and Rules are reasonable and serve the legitimate state interest of ensuring lawful possession and preventing illicit felling of forest wood.
The presumption that unaccounted wood is unlawfully obtained does not violate Article 14 or 19(1)(g) as it is a valid regulatory measure consistent with the Act's objective.
The High Court did not commit any manifest error in law in upholding the validity of the provisions, and the appeal for interference fails.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Kashtha Chiram (Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1984, Section 7
Madhya Pradesh Kashtha Chiram (Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1984, Section 8
Madhya Pradesh Kashtha Chiram (Viniyaman) Adhiniyam, 1984, Section 9
doctrines: Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(g)
Presumption of constitutionality of statutes
Regulatory measures for environmental and forest conservation
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellants claimed khas possession of a plot of land from the respondent who was allowed permissive use for two years but refused to vacate after expiry, while the respondent claimed to be a prospective purchaser under an oral agreement to sell.
issues_decided: Whether the second appeal was maintainable when a new plea of irrevocability of licence under Section 60(b) of the Easements Act was raised for the first time in the High Court
Whether Section 60(b) of the Easements Act could apply in Assam where the Act was not extended by the legislature
Whether the principles of 'justice, equity and good conscience' could grant relief to the respondent despite his denial of being a licensee and assertion of title
holdings: A new plea of irrevocability of licence under Section 60(b) of the Easements Act cannot be allowed for the first time in second appeal if not raised in pleadings or lower courts, but the Court proceeded to decide on merits.
Section 60(b) of the Easements Act does not operate in Assam as the Act is not applicable there; courts cannot extend its provisions by judicial interpretation.
Relief based on 'justice, equity and good conscience' is not available to a party who denies being a licensee and sets up a false claim of title, as he does not come with clean hands.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Justice, equity and good conscience
Irrevocability of licence upon permanent construction in good faith

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted by the High Court for the murder of their maternal uncle under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, after the trial court had acquitted them; they challenged the reversal of their acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on disbelief of prosecution witnesses?
Whether minor discrepancies and improvements in witness statements vitiate their credibility?
Whether the time discrepancy in the charge and witness accounts undermines the prosecution case?
Whether unexplained minor injuries on the accused cast doubt on the prosecution's version?
holdings: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal as the trial court's disbelief of prosecution witnesses was perverse and based on insignificant discrepancies.
Minor improvements and contradictions in witness testimony, especially from village residents, do not discredit otherwise consistent and credible evidence.
A minor variance in the time of the incident between the charge and witness accounts does not materially affect the prosecution case, particularly when witnesses estimate time by natural events.
Superficial injuries on the accused do not outweigh overwhelming evidence of guilt in a brutal, premeditated murder involving multiple attackers and weapons.
doctrines: Perversity in evaluation of evidence
Benefit of doubt in cases of minor contradictions
Continuous transaction doctrine
Re-appreciation of evidence by appellate court

card.dispute: The assessee (R. M. Arunachalam) fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether estate duty paid on inherited property could be treated as 'cost of acquisition' or 'cost of improvement' for computing capital gains under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether estate duty paid under the Estate Duty Act, 1953, can be treated as 'cost of acquisition' of property inherited through a will for the purpose of computing capital gains under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Whether payment of estate duty can be regarded as 'cost of improvement' of the inherited property under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Whether the creation of a charge under Section 74(1) of the Estate Duty Act results in an incomplete or imperfect title in the hands of the assessee.
holdings: Estate duty paid on inherited property does not constitute 'cost of acquisition' under Section 48 read with Section 55(2) of the Income Tax Act, as no new right is acquired by the payment.
Payment of estate duty does not amount to 'cost of improvement' under Section 48 read with Section 55(1)(b), as it does not result in any tangible enhancement or alteration to the property.

A charge created under Section 74(1) of the Estate Duty Act does not create an interest in the property; it only gives priority in recovery and does not affect the completeness of the assessee’s title.
doctrines: Doctrine of cost of acquisition under capital gains taxation
Doctrine of cost of improvement in capital assets
Principle of priority of charge versus creation of interest in property

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the state's requisition of their land under the Defence and Internal Security of India Act, 1971, arguing it was invalid due to prolonged and indefinite continuation long after the emergency ended.
issues_decided: Whether the requisition order under Section 23 of the Defence and Internal Security of India Act, 1971, could be continued indefinitely after the parent Act ceased to operate and the emergency ended.
Whether prolonged requisition of property for over two decades amounts to an abuse of power and effective acquisition without compensation.
Whether the state could retain possession of requisitioned property when it did not exercise the option to acquire it permanently under Section 30 of the Act during its currency.
holdings: An emergency requisition order under Section 23 cannot continue indefinitely; it must be limited to a reasonable period based on the facts, and prolonged requisition becomes unconstitutional.
Requisitioning property for over two decades, especially after the emergency and the Act's expiry, amounts to a colourable exercise of power and virtual acquisition without compensation.
Failure to exercise the power of permanent acquisition under Section 30 during the Act’s operation indicates the state did not need the land permanently, negating continued possession.
provisions: Defence and Internal Security of India Act, 1971, Section 23
Defence and Internal Security of India Act, 1971, Section 30
doctrines: Doctrine of temporary requisition
Doctrine of colourable exercise of power
Doctrine of reasonable duration in executive action

card.dispute: Reliance Industries Ltd challenged the Gujarat High Court's order directing polluting industries, including itself, to contribute towards the cost of laying effluent pipelines, while the respondents, agriculturists, sought enforcement of environmental safeguards.
issues_decided: Whether a review petition before a Division Bench of the High Court, where judges differ, must be referred to a third judge or dismissed under CPC Order XLVII Rule 6
Whether the appellant's special leave petition challenging the main judgment can proceed on the issue of pro rata cost contribution if the review petition is dismissed
holdings: When two judges of a Division Bench differ in a review petition arising from original writ proceedings, the matter must be referred to a third judge as per Clause 36 of the Letters Patent, not dismissed under CPC Order XLVII Rule 6.

It is premature to decide the SLP challenging the main judgment on the issue of cost contribution until the remanded review petition is finally decided by the High Court with the third judge’s participation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLVII Rule 6
Letters Patent of the High Court of Gujarat, Clause 36
doctrines: Doctrine of judicial consistency in review proceedings
Doctrine of reference to a larger bench on disagreement in review

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide need for own occupation due to threatened acquisition of his other property, which the tenant challenged as mala fide and unsubstantiated.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord established a bona fide need for eviction under Section 11(3) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965?
Whether the High Court erred in interfering with the statutory Revisional Authority's findings while exercising jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution?
Whether the acquisition proceedings relied upon by the landlord were still valid and sufficient to justify eviction?
holdings: A landlord's claim for eviction on grounds of bona fide need must be objectively tested, and mere assertion of desire is insufficient; the burden lies on the landlord to prove genuine necessity.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by substituting its factual appreciation for that of the statutory Revisional Authority, which is impermissible.
The acquisition proceedings initiated in 1987 were deemed lapsed due to inaction, removing the foundational basis for the landlord’s claim of urgent need for the premises.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(3)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement test in rent control cases
Limited scope of interference under Article 227
Lapse of acquisition proceedings due to efflux of time

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India near Delhi airports, claiming it was undervalued.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in rejecting certain sale deeds (Ex.A.W.1/7 to Ex.A.W.1/10) as unreliable for determining market value of acquired land?
Whether the market value of the land determined by the High Court was legally sustainable?
holdings: The High Court was justified in rejecting sale deeds showing a sudden, unexplained price jump of over 100% within a short period as unreliable for market value assessment.
The High Court's determination of market value based on realistic sale transactions and proper application of law did not call for interference by the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Principle of reliable comparable sales for market value determination
Appreciation of evidence and factual findings by lower courts not to be disturbed without perversity

card.dispute: Convicted persons sentenced to death for brutal mass murder challenged the severity of their sentence, while the state sought to uphold or enhance sentences.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence awarded to six accused was justified in light of the 'rarest of rare' doctrine
Whether mitigating circumstances warranted commutation of death sentence to life imprisonment
Whether the High Court erred in enhancing sentences or confirming convictions
holdings: Death sentence is justified in cases of extreme brutality, dehumanizing conduct, and societal shock, especially when the crime falls within the 'rarest of rare' category.
Mitigating circumstances such as family loss or age do not outweigh aggravating factors like pre-planning, barbaric methods, and total disregard for human dignity.
High Court did not err in confirming or enhancing death sentences; however, one convict's sentence was commuted to life imprisonment based on individual circumstances.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Doctrine of aggravating and mitigating circumstances in sentencing
Principle of proportionality in capital punishment

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Gopichand fought with the State of U.P. over whether land occupied by a factory should be included in computing 'vacant land' under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976.
issues_decided: Whether Section 4(9) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 applies to land with a factory building in the computation of vacant land.
Whether the interpretation of Section 4(9) in Johnson's Case and Meera Gupta's Case are conflicting and which prevails.
holdings: Section 4(9) requires that land occupied by a building and appurtenant land be included in computing vacant land, even if the building is a factory and not a dwelling unit.
The larger bench decision in Meera Gupta's case casts doubt on Johnson's Case, and the conflict in interpretation requires resolution by a larger bench of the Supreme Court.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(q)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(9)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 6(1)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 8(3)
doctrines: Literal interpretation of statutes
Harmonious construction
Binding precedent and stare decisis
Resolution of conflicting judgments by a larger bench

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether a counter claim application filed under Order VIII Rule 6A of the CPC after the written statement was barred by procedural rules.
issues_decided: Whether an application for counter claim under Order VIII Rule 6A of the CPC is barred if filed after the written statement.
Whether the cause of action for the counter claim was time-barred under the Limitation Act.
holdings: A counter claim under Order VIII Rule 6A of the CPC can be filed even after the written statement if the cause of action arose before or after the suit and continued until the date of filing the written statement.
The question of limitation was not decided as it was not raised before the lower court; the court refrained from expressing an opinion on it.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order VIII Rule 6A
doctrines: Accrual of cause of action doctrine
Principle of judicial discipline against deciding issues not raised below

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased tenant challenged the High Court's order for eviction, claiming the landlady did not genuinely require the premises for her cloth business.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the lower appellate court's finding on the landlady's bona fide requirement of the premises under Section 100, CPC.
Whether the lower appellate court properly appreciated the evidence and documents relevant to the issue of bona fide requirement.
holdings: The High Court was justified in interfering under Section 100, CPC, as the lower appellate court failed to consider all relevant documents and evidence, leading to a substantial question of law.
A finding based on incomplete appreciation of evidence and reliance on earlier irrelevant notices, while ignoring the notice preceding the suit, is vitiated and open to challenge in second appeal.
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Appreciation of evidence and findings of fact
Bona fide requirement in eviction cases

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Rebti Devi and Ram Dutt Gupta disputed over ownership of property, with claims based on a benami transaction and a contested will.
issues_decided: Whether a plea of benami can be raised in a suit filed after 19.5.1988 under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988
Whether the exceptions under Section 3(2) and Section 4(3) of the Act allow benami defences even after the cut-off date
Whether the decision in Nand Kishore Mehra's case conflicts with R. Rajagopala Reddy's case
holdings: A plea of benami is barred in suits filed after 19.5.1988 unless the case falls under an exception in the Act.
Section 3(2) permits a benami plea after 19.5.1988 if the property is in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter, subject to a rebuttable statutory presumption.
Section 4(3) allows benami defences after 19.5.1988 if the property is held by a coparcener or a trustee for the benefit of others, unaffected by the general bar.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11
doctrines: Statutory presumption
Rebuttable presumption
Prospective vs retrospective operation of statute
Exceptions to statutory bars

card.dispute: The petitioner sought specific performance of a contract for sale of agricultural land, and challenged the High Court's decision to extend time for the respondent to comply with the decree and to award additional compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the court has jurisdiction to extend time for compliance with a decree for specific performance after the stipulated period has expired.
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the amount to be deposited by the judgment-debtor for loss of enjoyment of money.
holdings: The court retains jurisdiction to extend time for compliance with a decree for specific performance until the sale deed is executed, and is not functus officio upon passing the decree.
The High Court had the discretion to enhance the amount payable to compensate for loss of enjoyment of money, in line with the contractual terms and principles of justice.
doctrines: Functus officio
Discretionary power of court in execution proceedings
Compensation for loss of enjoyment of money

card.dispute: The State of Haryana and Satbir challenged the High Court's acquittal of certain accused in a 1984 village massacre, while appealing against the conviction of others involved in the murders of four persons during a riot.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the ocular testimony of three eyewitnesses.
Whether the delay in lodging the FIR rendered the prosecution case unreliable.
Whether the prosecution was required to prove motive in the face of reliable eyewitness and medical evidence.
Whether the individual roles of the accused in the murders were sufficiently established to sustain convictions under Sections 302/149 IPC.
holdings: The evidence of chance witnesses, even if related to the deceased, cannot be rejected solely on that basis if their testimony is consistent and corroborated.
A delay of four and a half hours in lodging the FIR was reasonable given the distance to the police station and does not undermine the prosecution's case.
Motive is not a fundamental ingredient of murder; when ocular and medical evidence establish the offence, absence of proven motive is immaterial.
Five accused—Surat Singh, Balwant Singh, Dola Ram, Subh Ram, and Chhajju—were proven to have participated in the offence with common object; the rest were entitled to benefit of reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Benefit of reasonable doubt
Reliability of ocular evidence
Corroboration through prompt FIR
Common object under Section 149 IPC

card.dispute: The Special Land Acquisition Officer challenged the enhancement of compensation from Rs. 250 to Rs. 2,500 per Are for land acquired for the Ahmedabad-Baroda Express Highway, arguing the reference court erred in principle.
issues_decided: Whether the reference court committed an error of law in enhancing compensation based on a prior award for similar land in the same village?
Whether the compensation awarded was vitiated by a wrong principle of law given the similarity of the lands and finality of a prior award?
holdings: The reference court correctly used a prior final award for similar land in the same village as a comparable base for determining compensation.
In the absence of tangible evidence showing material differences in land quality, the court cannot interfere with the reference court's assessment based on comparable awards.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Finality of prior compensation awards as a benchmark for subsequent awards

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the Patna High Court's decision invalidating the Bihar Forest Restoration and Improvement of Degraded Forest Land Taxation Act, 1992, which imposed a tax on mining and non-forest use of forest land, against companies holding mining leases.
issues_decided: Whether the Bihar Forest Restoration and Improvement of Degraded Forest Land Taxation Act, 1992, is within the legislative competence of the State under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule?
Whether the tax imposed by the impugned Act is a tax on land or on the activity of excavation and non-forest use of forest land?
holdings: The tax under the impugned Act is not a tax on land as required by Entry 49 of List II, but is in substance a tax on the activity of excavation and removal of land, and thus falls outside the State's legislative competence.

A tax levied based on the extent of void created by mining, and contingent on non-rehabilitation, is a tax on the absence of land and not on land itself, and therefore cannot be sustained under Entry 49 of List II.
doctrines: Pith and substance doctrine
Doctrine of legislative competence

card.dispute: The State of Haryana challenged the High Court's decision to award solatium and higher interest rates to landowners in a land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent is entitled to solatium at 30% under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act despite the award being made before the amendment's applicability
Whether the respondent is entitled to interest at 9% for one year and 5% thereafter, or limited to 6% per annum
holdings: Solatium under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act cannot be granted if the award was made before the amendment's applicability, as per K.S. Paripoornan's precedent.
Interest is limited to 6% per annum when the award and reference were decided prior to the applicability of higher interest rate provisions.
doctrines: Prospective application of amendments
Binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged a compromise decree that set aside a valid forest land acquisition award, alleging fraud and collusion by a forest officer without government sanction.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court and High Court erred in refusing to grant an injunction to prevent execution of a decree obtained by fraud and collusion?
Whether a forest officer could lawfully enter into a compromise decree without the State Government's sanction?
holdings: The State was entitled to an interim injunction to prevent execution of a decree obtained by fraud and collusion, especially when the decree was passed without lawful authority.
A forest officer cannot enter into a compromise decree binding the State without the sanction of the State Government; such a decree is liable to be set aside.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2
doctrines: Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Acting without authority binds no one
Injunction in cases of fraudulent decrees

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's acquittal of a revenue inspector, Zakaullah, who was convicted for accepting a bribe of Rs. 400 under the Prevention of Corruption Act and IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the respondent by rejecting the prosecution's evidence on grounds of lack of corroboration and alleged improbabilities?
Whether the evidence of the complainant and the Anti-Corruption officials, including the use of phenolphthalein test, was reliable enough to sustain a conviction?
Whether the panch witnesses could be considered independent despite their prior contact with the police?
Whether minor contradictions in the prosecution's evidence warranted acquittal?
holdings: The High Court erred in acquitting the accused based on speculative and flimsy grounds; the prosecution made out a complete and reliable case.
The phenolphthalein test, though not sent to the Chemical Examiner, is a valid corroborative method and its non-forensic verification does not invalidate the trap.
Mere acquaintance with police does not disqualify a witness as independent; panch witnesses retain credibility unless shown to be dependent on police.
Minor discrepancies in testimony, such as pocket of recovery or uncorroborated oral demand, do not undermine the overall reliability of credible prosecution evidence.
doctrines: Corroboration requirement in corruption cases
Presumption of independence of panch witnesses
Reliability of trap cases and scientific tests in graft prosecutions
Principle of judicial review of acquittals based on perverse reasoning

card.dispute: The landlord sued to restrain the tenant from constructing on fire-destroyed premises, obtained an interim injunction, but later it was found the civil court lacked jurisdiction; the issue was whether the tenant could still be punished for violating the injunction.
issues_decided: Whether a person can be punished under Order 39 Rule 2-A of the CPC for violating an interim injunction when the civil court is later found to lack jurisdiction to try the suit
Whether interim orders passed before a jurisdictional defect is determined are void ab initio
holdings: A party can be punished for violating an interim injunction even if the court is later found to lack jurisdiction, provided the violation occurred before the jurisdictional defect was decided.
Interim orders passed by a civil court pending determination of jurisdiction are not void ab initio and must be obeyed until set aside.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39 Rule 2-A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 9-A (Maharashtra Amendment)
doctrines: Orders passed pending jurisdictional determination are valid until jurisdiction is negated
Violation of interim orders before jurisdictional dismissal constitutes contempt under CPC

card.dispute: The appellants sought specific performance of a land sale agreement, but the respondent repudiated the contract, leading to a dispute over whether the suit was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether time was the essence of the contract for the sale of land.
Whether the amendment of the plaint to seek specific performance was barred by limitation.
From which date the limitation period for seeking specific performance begins to run.
holdings: Time was the essence of the contract as the parties had fixed a specific performance date, and repudiation before that date made the right to sue accrue immediately.
The application to amend the plaint to claim specific performance was barred by limitation as it was filed more than three years after the date fixed for performance.
Limitation for specific performance begins to run from the date stipulated for performance in the contract, not from the date of amendment of the plaint.
provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Article 54 of the Limitation Act
doctrines: Time as essence of contract
Doctrine of id certum est quod certum reddi potest
Accrual of cause of action in specific performance

card.dispute: The appellants, acquitted by the trial court, were convicted by the High Court for rioting, murder, and attempted murder; they challenged the conviction in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of the injured eyewitness (P.W.1) was reliable despite discrepancies noted by the trial court
Whether the non-examination of material witnesses warranted an adverse presumption under Section 114(q) of the Evidence Act
Whether the telephonic message to the police constituted the F.I.R. of the case
Whether the dying declaration, though not used as such due to the victim's survival, could be relied upon for corroboration
holdings: The testimony of the injured eyewitness (P.W.1) was reliable as minor contradictions did not undermine the core of his account, especially given medical and corroborative support.
No adverse presumption under Section 114(q) of the Evidence Act can be drawn unless the defense proves other witnesses were present and deliberately not examined.
The telephonic message to the police, recorded in the daily diary, amounted to the F.I.R. as it disclosed a cognizable offence, even without naming the accused.
A statement recorded under Section 164 Cr.P.C., though not a dying declaration due to survival, can be used for corroboration if made voluntarily and in a critical condition.
doctrines: Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Presumption under Section 114(q) of the Evidence Act
F.I.R. based on telephonic information
Use of statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C. for corroboration

card.dispute: The Commonwealth Trust Ltd. fought the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether it could substitute the fair market value as on January 1, 1954, for the cost of acquisition of a depreciable asset when computing capital gains under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee could substitute the fair market value as on January 1, 1954, for the cost of acquisition of a depreciable asset under Section 55(2) when depreciation had already been claimed.
Whether Section 50 of the Income Tax Act applies to depreciable assets acquired by purchase where depreciation has been allowed.
holdings: Section 55(2) allows substitution of fair market value as on January 1, 1954, for cost of acquisition only under Sections 48 and 49, not under Section 50, which governs depreciable assets.

Where depreciation has been claimed on a depreciable asset, the cost of acquisition must be determined under Section 50, which uses written down value, not fair market value, and excludes the option under Section 55(2).
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tax provisions
Specific provision prevails over general provision
Avoidance of double taxation in capital gains computation

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer appealed against the High Court's confirmation of enhanced compensation awarded to landowners, challenging the validity of the reference made beyond the statutory limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the reference application under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was filed within the prescribed limitation period?
Whether claimants who received compensation without protest are eligible to seek reference under Section 18?
Whether third parties impleaded after the original reference can claim enhanced compensation?
holdings: When claimants were present at the time of the award and received compensation without protest, the limitation period for filing a reference is six weeks from the date of the award under Section 18(2)(a).
Receipt of compensation without protest bars a claimant from seeking reference under Section 18 due to the operation of the second proviso to Section 31(2).
Third parties impleaded after the limitation period cannot circumvent the statutory requirement and claim enhanced compensation through an otherwise time-barred reference.
doctrines: Limitation bar under statutory provisions
Constructive notice and presumption of presence at award
Jurisdictional bar due to delay and lack of statutory compliance

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer appealed against the High Court's confirmation of compensation awarded to Smt. Sreelatha Bhoopal for land acquired for a bus depot in Gadwal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in relying on a sale deed of a small piece of land to determine market value for compensation?
What is the just and reasonable market value of the acquired agricultural land adjacent to Gadwal town?
holdings: Reliance on sale deeds of small plots is impermissible when determining compensation for large tracts of land, as such plots do not reflect true market value in an open market transaction.
The appropriate market value for the acquired agricultural land adjacent to a town is Rs.20,000 per acre, with 30% solatium and interest at 9% during possession and 15% thereafter until deposit.
doctrines: Prudent purchaser principle
Substantial justice in compensation determination
Inadmissibility of small plot sale comparisons for large land acquisitions

card.dispute: The Secretary, Taliparamba Education Society fought against Moothedath Mallisseri Illath M.N. and others over whether the respondents could terminate the lease of an educational institution's property.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents were entitled to terminate the lease based on alleged misuse of the property and trespass
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts
holdings: The respondents are not entitled to terminate the lease as there was no proven misuse of the property for non-educational purposes or acquiescence to trespass.
The High Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact by the trial and appellate courts, which is impermissible under Section 100 CPC.
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Proper construction of lease covenants
Prohibition on reappreciation of evidence in second appeal

card.dispute: Thiru Arooran Sugars Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Income-Tax over whether the price paid by the company for sugarcane from its own region could be considered 'market price' for computing taxable non-agricultural income under Rule 7 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962.
issues_decided: Whether the existence of an actual open market with a concourse of buyers and sellers is necessary to determine 'market price' under Rule 7(2)(a) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962?
Whether the price paid by a single buyer (the assessee) in a region can be treated as 'market price' for valuation purposes?
Whether the High Court could remand the case to the Tribunal for consideration of new facts not raised during the original proceedings?
holdings: The term 'market price' does not require an actual open market with multiple buyers and sellers; it refers to the hypothetical price a willing buyer and willing seller would transact at.
Where sugarcane purchases are made regularly in commercial transactions, even by a single buyer, the price paid reflects market value, especially if governed by statutory control orders.
The High Court cannot direct the Tribunal to consider new factual issues not raised during the original appeal; the Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority.
doctrines: Hypothetical market value doctrine
Finality of findings by tribunal
Commercial reality in valuation

card.dispute: The Union of India and others fought with tenant A. Ajit Singh over the apportionment of compensation, applicability of the 1984 Amendment Act, and entitlement to solatium and interest in a land acquisition case.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent tenant is entitled to the benefit of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 68 of 1984?
What is the proper apportionment of compensation between the landlord and the tenant?
Whether the market value determined by the High Court is legally sound?
holdings: Since the reference court's award was made in 1973 and the acquisition process continued, the Amendment Act 68 of 1984 applies, and the claimants are entitled to 15% solatium and 6% interest on enhanced compensation from the date of possession to deposit.
Considering the 99-year lease, duration of possession, and tenant's improvements, apportionment of compensation at 60% to the tenant and 40% to the landlord is just and reasonable.
The High Court's determination of market value at Rs. 28,387 per bigha based on the land's location in a developed area with potential for building use is not vitiated by any error of principle.
doctrines: Apportionment of compensation between landlord and tenant in land acquisition
Retrospective application of amendment in land acquisition law
Principle of just equivalent compensation based on market value and potential use

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision to grant uniform compensation to all landowners without classification, while some landowners sought further enhancement or re-determination of compensation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in granting uniform compensation without classifying lands based on proximity to the main road?
Whether landowners who did not file a reference under Section 18 are entitled to re-determination of compensation under Section 28-A if they apply within three months of the reference court's award?
Whether applications under Section 28-A filed beyond three months from the reference court's award are barred by limitation?
holdings: Classification of land into 'A' and 'B' classes based on proximity to the main road is justified; uniform compensation violates the principle of market value and is legally unsustainable.

Landowners not seeking reference under Section 18 are entitled to apply under Section 28-A for re-determination of compensation within three months of the reference court's award, excluding time to obtain a certified copy.
Applications under Section 28-A filed beyond the statutory three-month period are time-barred, and any compensation awarded on such basis is illegal and without jurisdiction.
doctrines: Principle of market value in land acquisition compensation
Classification of land based on locational advantage
Limitation under special statutes is mandatory
Article 14 does not mandate equal compensation for unequal lands

card.dispute: The appellant tenant challenged the execution of an eviction order after 12 years, claiming it was barred by delay and lack of limitation period under the Mamlatdar's Court Act.
issues_decided: Whether the execution of an eviction order under the Mamlatdar's Court Act, 1906 is barred by limitation after 12 years in the absence of a prescribed time limit?
Whether the general law of limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to the execution of orders under the Mamlatdar's Court Act, 1906?
holdings: The absence of a limitation period under Section 21 of the Mamlatdar's Court Act, 1906 implies that the Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply, and execution can proceed at any time.
Where a statute provides a specific procedure without prescribing limitation, the general principle of reasonable time does not override the statutory power to execute the order.
doctrines: Exclusion of general limitation law by specific statutory regime
Statutory power exercisable in absence of time limit

card.dispute: The appellant (Baby) fought with the Travancore Devaswom Board over whether she was a cultivating tenant under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, and whether the High Court had jurisdiction to interfere with the tribunals' decision in revision.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction under Section 103 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act to set aside the tribunals' order on the ground of non-consideration of material documents?
Whether the High Court could interfere under Article 227 of the Constitution if the findings of fact were based on non-consideration of relevant and material documents?
holdings: The High Court could not interfere under Section 103 of the Kerala Land Reforms Act merely because tribunals failed to consider material documents, as this does not amount to erroneous or non-decision of a question of law.

The High Court retains power under Article 227 of the Constitution to quash orders if factual findings were reached without considering material documents that could have led to a different conclusion.
doctrines: Limited scope of revision under special statutes
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Distinction between questions of law and questions of fact

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder and related charges in a land dispute, claimed they acted in self-defence when a violent clash resulted in four deaths.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to the defence of self-defence under the circumstances of the case.
Whether the presumption of possession under revenue records was sufficient to establish the appellants' right to use force.
Whether the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellants were not acting in self-defence.
holdings: The right of self-defence cannot extend to using lethal force merely to prevent trespass, especially when the attackers were not armed with firearms.
A revenue record entry creates only a rebuttable presumption of possession, which was successfully rebutted by evidence showing the opposing party's possession.
The absence of injuries on the accused party and lack of credible evidence that the deceased fired first negates the claim of self-defence.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1939, Section 117
doctrines: Right of private defence under exceptional circumstances
Rebuttable presumption of possession from revenue records
Appreciation of evidence in criminal appeals

card.dispute: Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. challenged the High Court's order directing absorption of contract labour employed by a contractor for cleaning staff quarters and sports complex, claiming they were not covered under the central government's 1976 notification abolishing contract labour under the Contract Labour Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government has the power under Section 10(1) of the Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970 to abolish contract labour engaged in non-industrial areas like staff housing colonies and sports complexes?

Whether the 1976 notification abolishing contract labour applies to workers employed at the residential and recreational facilities of the corporation, even if these are not part of the main industrial establishment?
holdings: The Supreme Court did not decide the issue definitively, but expressed doubt about the correctness of the earlier Constitution Bench observation in Gammon India Ltd. v. Union of India regarding the limited scope of Section 10, noting it was not strictly necessary to that decision.

The Court held that the question of whether Section 10 of the Contract Labour Act extends to contract labour in staff quarters and sports complexes requires authoritative interpretation by a Constitution Bench and referred the matter accordingly.
provisions: Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, Section 2(f)
doctrines: Doctrine of ejusdem generis in interpreting statutory phrases like 'in connection with the work of an establishment'
Doctrine of precedent and per incuriam
Doctrine of constitutional bench referral for substantial questions of law
Principle of wide interpretation of welfare legislation

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of tenants on grounds of rent default and bona fide requirement, but the tenants challenged the landlords' review petition filed after dismissal of their SLP by the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could review its order after the Supreme Court dismissed SLPs challenging the same order?
Whether the review petitions filed after dismissal of SLPs were maintainable?
holdings: The High Court cannot review an order that was the subject of a dismissed special leave petition in the Supreme Court after a contested hearing.
Entertaining review petitions after dismissal of SLPs amounts to abuse of process and is contrary to judicial discipline.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, 1966 (implied under SLP jurisdiction)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLVII (Review)
doctrines: Judicial discipline
Finality of Supreme Court orders
Abuse of process

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of an appeal before the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court against a Single Judge's order in a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether an appeal lies before a Division Bench of the High Court against an order passed by a Single Judge in proceedings under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1960, despite Section 6(3) barring appeals or revisions.
Whether Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court preserves the right of appeal even when a statutory provision like Section 6(3) seeks to bar it.
holdings: Section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1960 bars appeals or revisions against orders passed under Section 6, but this statutory bar does not override the Letters Patent of the High Court.

Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court allows an appeal from a judgment of a Single Judge exercising original jurisdiction, and such a right is not extinguished by Section 6(3) unless the statute expressly excludes Letters Patent appeals.
provisions: Letters Patent of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Clause 15
doctrines: Primacy of Letters Patent in conferring appellate jurisdiction
Statutory bar on appeal does not override constitutional or charter-based powers unless expressly excluded

card.dispute: The first purchasers' legal heirs challenged the validity of a cancellation deed and a subsequent sale deed, claiming they had already acquired absolute title to the suit property under an earlier sale deed.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deed dated April 30, 1963 (Exhibit-C) conveyed absolute title to the first purchasers despite part of the consideration allegedly remaining unpaid and the registration receipt not being delivered.
Whether the vendors could unilaterally cancel the sale deed (Exhibit-C) by executing a cancellation deed (Exhibit-H) and subsequently sell the property to second purchasers (Exhibit-C/1).
Whether non-payment of the 'sudhbharna' mortgage amount or retention of the registration receipt affected the transfer of title under Exhibit-C.
holdings: The sale deed dated April 30, 1963 (Exhibit-C) conveyed absolute title to the first purchasers upon execution and registration, as the recitals unambiguously indicated an intention to transfer title for the stated consideration.
The vendors had no right to unilaterally cancel Exhibit-C by executing Exhibit-H; such cancellation was invalid and did not affect the rights of the first purchasers.

Non-payment of the 'sudhbharna' amount or retention of the registration receipt did not prevent title from passing, as there was no express condition in the deed linking title transfer to these events.
doctrines: Doctrine of absolute sale
Doctrine of intention of parties in conveyance
Doctrine of constructive delivery of title

card.dispute: The appellants, including Biharilal Soni, Murarilal, and Leelabai, were convicted of murdering Sarita, their daughter-in-law, by causing burn injuries; they appealed, challenging the evidence and their convictions.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that all three appellants were involved in the murder of Sarita under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC?
Whether the defence of accidental or suicidal burn injuries due to mental illness (schizophrenia) was credible?
Whether the evidence of cruelty by all three appellants, particularly Biharilal, was sufficient to sustain a conviction?
holdings: The prosecution proved that Sarita was murdered due to burn injuries and that Murarilal and Leelabai were involved in the offence under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
The defence of accidental or suicidal death due to schizophrenia was rightly rejected by the courts below, as unsupported by credible evidence.
Biharilal’s conviction was set aside as there was no specific or credible evidence that he participated in the cruelty or murder; his acquittal was warranted due to lack of evidence.
doctrines: Principle of constructive liability under Section 34 IPC requires active participation or common intention.
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases when evidence against an accused is insufficient or uncorroborated.

card.dispute: The Revenue authorities challenged the maintainability of a suit for partition filed by Parmeshwari Devi Sultania, claiming it was barred by Section 293 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, as it sought to indirectly set aside an order related to seized assets.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for partition filed by the respondent was barred by Section 293 of the Income Tax Act, 1961
Whether a civil court can entertain a suit that indirectly seeks to modify or set aside an order passed under the Income Tax Act
holdings: Section 293 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 bars any civil suit that seeks to directly or indirectly set aside or modify any proceeding or order under the Act, even if the suit is framed as one for partition.

The substance of the suit, not its form, determines whether it falls within the bar of Section 293; if the effect is to challenge an assessment or seizure, the suit is not maintainable in civil court.
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by statutory bar
Substance over form doctrine
Doctrine of adequate alternative remedy

card.dispute: The appellant, Jagdish Chandra Nijhawan, was accused by S.K. Saraf, representing ABC Products Ltd., of criminal breach of trust and wrongful withholding of a company-leased flat after his employment ended, leading to criminal charges and a dispute over whether the matter was civil or criminal in nature.
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the parties is of a civil or criminal nature
Whether a prima facie case under Section 630 of the Companies Act and Sections 406, 408, and 409 IPC was made out
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the discharge order passed by the Magistrate
holdings: The dispute between the parties is essentially civil in nature, arising from the interpretation of contractual terms regarding continued occupancy of a flat post-employment.

No prima facie criminal case under Sections 406, 408, and 409 IPC or Section 630 of the Companies Act is made out, as the appellant's possession of the flat was under a contractual agreement and not wrongful.
The High Court erred in interfering with the discharge order, as the Magistrate correctly determined the matter to be civil and not requiring criminal prosecution.
doctrines: Principle of distinction between civil and criminal disputes
Prima facie case requirement for framing criminal charges
Doctrine of contractual rights overriding criminal allegations in employment-related possession disputes

card.dispute: The appellants (legatees) challenged the dismissal of their claim to a valid will executed by Harnam Singh in their favor, which the lower courts rejected due to suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution.
issues_decided: Whether the registered will of Harnam Singh was validly executed and attested under the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
Whether the propounders of the will discharged the burden of dispelling suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution?
holdings: A registered will, even with Sub-Registrar's endorsement, does not automatically prove its valid execution if suspicious circumstances exist.
The propounder of a will must positively dispel all suspicious circumstances regarding its due execution and attestation; failure to do so leads to rejection of the will.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder of will in case of suspicious circumstances
Registration of will not conclusive proof of due execution

card.dispute: The plaintiff-appellant filed a suit under Order 21 Rule 103 CPC to establish his right to possession of property after a revision petition against an execution order was dismissed; the defendant-respondent contested the suit as barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the benefit of Section 14 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 can be extended to a suit filed under Order 21 Rule 103 CPC after dismissal of a revision petition against an order under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC
Whether the plaintiff-appellant prosecuted the earlier revision petition in good faith despite it being filed instead of a fresh suit
holdings: Section 14 of the Limitation Act applies to a suit under Order 21 Rule 103 CPC if the plaintiff was pursuing a remedy in good faith and with due care, even if the prior revision was not maintainable.

An illiterate litigant who files a revision petition on the advice of counsel, which is entertained by the High Court, acts in good faith, and the time taken for the revision can be excluded under Section 14.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rules 97, 98, 103
doctrines: Good faith in prosecution of legal remedies
Exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act for proceedings pursued in good faith
Finality of execution court orders under Order 21 Rule 98 unless challenged under Rule 103

card.dispute: The Indian Bank and the Official Liquidator of Chemmeens Exports (P) Ltd. disputed whether an unregistered charge in favour of the bank was void under Section 125 of the Companies Act, 1956, and whether the preliminary decree creating a charge was enforceable against the liquidator.
issues_decided: Whether the Company Court has jurisdiction to declare a decree passed by a competent civil court as void under Section 125 of the Companies Act, 1956.
Whether an unregistered charge, which was the subject of a preliminary decree, remains void under Section 125 of the Companies Act after the decree attains finality.
Whether the rights of a secured creditor are governed by the original charge or by the terms of the decree after the passing of a preliminary decree.
holdings: The Company Court does not have the power to declare a decree of a competent civil court void merely on the ground that the underlying charge was unregistered under Section 125 of the Companies Act.

Once a preliminary decree is passed and becomes final, the rights of the parties are governed by the decree, not by the original contract or unregistered charge, and the decree is not void under Section 125.

After the passing of a preliminary decree, the matter passes from the domain of contract to that of judgment, and the creditor's rights depend on the decree, not on the validity of the original unregistered charge.
doctrines: Doctrine of merger of contract into decree
Doctrine of finality of decree
Doctrine of jurisdiction of Company Court

card.dispute: Hope Plantations Ltd. challenged the Taluk Land Board's refusal to exempt 'fuel area' and 'rested tea area' from ceiling limits under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, after a prior judicial decision on similar issues.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of issue estoppel or res judicata bars the re-litigation of claims regarding exemption of fuel and rested tea areas in a subsequent proceeding.
Whether new legal interpretations or material can justify re-opening an issue already decided between the same parties.
holdings: The doctrine of res judicata and issue estoppel applies strictly under Indian law, and a party cannot re-agitate issues already decided, even if new legal arguments or materials emerge, unless there is a change in law or judicial interpretation by a higher court.

The appellant is not permitted to re-litigate the extent of exemption for fuel and rested tea areas as those issues were conclusively decided in earlier proceedings, but they may seek relief under Section 81(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act based on subsequent judicial pronouncements.
doctrines: Res judicata
Issue estoppel
Constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for rioting, assault on public servants, and attempted murder during a land dispute, but challenged the fairness of the investigation and trial.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution witnesses were reliable and their testimony trustworthy
Whether the investigation and trial were conducted fairly
Whether the conviction based on the evidence, including the FIR and ballistic reports, was legally sustainable
holdings: The testimony of prosecution witnesses, including police officers, was found to be partisan and inconsistent with material evidence, thus unreliable.
The investigation was biased and the trial unfair, particularly due to the non-examination of key defense witnesses and failure to conduct ballistic tests.
The conviction under sections 147, 353, 447, and 307 read with 149 IPC could not be sustained due to serious doubts about the prosecution's version and evidence.
doctrines: Fair trial
Benefit of doubt
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Right to impartial investigation

card.dispute: Two court auction purchasers disputed over superior rights to the same property, based on competing claims of hypothecation and charge arising from prior litigation and security deeds.
issues_decided: Whether the document Exhibit A6 created a charge over the property in favor of the appellant's predecessor-in-interest.
Whether the appellant, as a purchaser in execution of a decree, acquired rights as a puisne mortgagee under Exhibit A6.
Whether the High Court could set aside the decree in favor of the appellant despite no appeal being filed by the respondent.
holdings: A document executed to vacate an attachment before judgment does not create a charge unless it clearly imposes an obligation to pay the decree amount out of the property.
The appellant did not acquire any rights as a puisne mortgagee because the decree was a simple money decree and not one based on a charge or mortgage.
The High Court could exercise its discretion under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to set aside a decree in favor of a non-appealing party if it was necessary to correct a legal anomaly.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 33
doctrines: Charge under Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act
Puisne mortgagee rights
Appellate jurisdiction under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC
Res judicata inapplicability during pendency of appeal

card.dispute: Chetak Construction Ltd. and Om Prakash & Ors. disputed over land possession and the validity of a sale agreement, with the appellant seeking injunction and the respondent resisting it in court.
issues_decided: Whether a single judge of the High Court has the jurisdiction to refer an appeal pending before them to the Supreme Court for final decision?
Whether the judge should have recused themselves due to a reasonable apprehension of bias?
Whether contempt proceedings could be initiated against the appellant and their lawyers for requesting recusal?
holdings: A single judge of the High Court lacks jurisdiction to refer an appeal to the Supreme Court for final disposal; such a direction is without legal authority and subversive of judicial discipline.
Where facts create a reasonable apprehension of bias, a judge should recuse themselves to uphold the principle that justice must not only be done but also be seen to be done.

Contempt proceedings cannot be initiated merely for requesting recusal; such jurisdiction must be exercised sparingly and only when there is substantial and malafide interference with judicial functioning.
doctrines: Principle of judicial recusal on grounds of apprehension of bias
Doctrine of proper judicial discipline and hierarchy
Doctrine of cautious use of contempt jurisdiction

card.dispute: The landlord, Life Insurance Corporation of India, sought eviction of tenant M/s Bharat Sales Ltd for subletting the premises, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether subletting under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act requires proof of payment of monetary consideration as a mandatory condition?
Whether a finding of subletting can be based on inference from exclusive possession without direct evidence of agreement or payment?
holdings: Proof of payment of consideration is not mandatory to establish subletting; courts may infer it from the fact of exclusive possession granted to another person.

A finding of subletting can be sustained based on inference from clandestine possession, even without direct evidence of agreement or rent payment, especially given the secretive nature of such transactions.
doctrines: Inference from conduct in absence of direct evidence
Exclusive possession as indicator of subletting
Clandestine nature of subletting arrangements

card.dispute: Existing food-grain dealers in Punjab fought against the state's decision to require them to compete in open auctions for space in newly created market townships, claiming it violated their right to trade under Article 19(1)(g) and disregarded their prior presence in old market areas.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government has an obligation to provide sufficient accommodation to existing licensed dealers in a newly created market area under the Punjab New Mandi Township Act, 1960.
Whether allowing existing traders to compete with new entrants in open auctions satisfies the State's obligation to ensure continuity of trade under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Whether the State can prioritize revenue generation over protecting the legitimate interests of established traders displaced by new market townships.
holdings: The State has an inherent obligation to ensure that existing licensed dealers are provided sufficient accommodation in new market areas to continue their trade when old markets are effectively rendered non-functional.

Merely allowing existing traders to compete in open auctions does not fulfill the State’s obligation, as it fails to account for the disadvantage they face due to displacement and regulatory compulsion to move.

The State must give preference to existing dealers in allotting plots or buildings in new market townships, though not necessarily at concessional rates, to protect their right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g).
provisions: Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, Section 3
Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, Section 4
Punjab New Mandi Township (Development and Regulation) Act, 1960, Rule 3
doctrines: Right to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g) of the Indian Constitution
Principle of legitimate expectation
State's duty to mitigate adverse impact of regulatory changes on established businesses
Precedent hierarchy: three-judge bench decision binding over two-judge bench

card.dispute: The appellants (heirs of Banarsi Das) challenged the allotment of surplus land to Mangat Ram, claiming it was not properly utilized before Banarsi Das's death and thus should not have been excluded from their inheritance.
issues_decided: Whether the surplus land was validly utilized prior to the death of the original owner, Banarsi Das, despite non-production of the Kabuliyat document.
Whether non-execution of Kabuliyat renders the allotment and possession of surplus land invalid under the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.
holdings: The land was validly utilized prior to the owner's death as possession was delivered to Mangat Ram in 1964, and all mandatory formalities, including execution of Kabuliyat, are presumed to have been completed.
Non-production of Kabuliyat does not invalidate the allotment, as it is a technicality and the continued possession of the tenant implies compliance with legal requirements.
provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 10A
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, Section 9(1)(vi)
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Rules, 1953, Rule 20-B
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Rules, 1953, Rule 20-C
doctrines: Presumption of regularity in official acts
Substantial compliance over technical non-compliance
Conditional admission and its limited evidentiary value

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the quantum of compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Union of India in village Rangpuri, Delhi, claiming it was below market value.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for the acquired land reflected its true market value as of the date of notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the market value of land in village Rangpuri could be determined by reference to compensation awarded in adjoining villages like Masoodpur and Mahipalpur.
Whether the sale transactions relied upon by the claimants were genuine and could be used to assess market value.
holdings: Market value for land acquisition compensation must be determined based on genuine sale transactions of similar land at or near the time of the Section 4 notification.
Compensation rates from different villages cannot be applied mechanically to another village unless the land's situation and potentiality are proven to be identical.
The High Court correctly relied on contemporaneous sale instances from the same village and rejected non-genuine transactions, justifying its assessment of Rs. 3,000 per bigha.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination based on comparable sales
Requirement of proof of genuine transactions for valuation
