Whether the prohibition on alienation of orchards under Section 3 of the 1975 Act rendered the decree for specific performance unenforceable
holdings: The High Court correctly held that the land was purchased by the father with his own funds and held in the name of the minor son, justifying specific performance for that share.
The Agrarian Reforms Acts of 1972 and 1976 do not apply to orchard land as defined, and thus do not bar the suit for specific performance.
The father, as the real owner who purchased the land, could validly enter into the agreement for the minor's share, especially in absence of any contrary evidence or challenge after majority.
Section 3 of the 1975 Act does not prohibit specific performance suits; permission for alienation can be obtained post-decree, and the decree may be moulded accordingly.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1972, Section 2(4) and Section 2(5)
Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976, Section 2(9) and Section 2(10)
Jammu and Kashmir Prohibition on Conservation of Land and Alienation of Orchards Act, 1975, Section 3
doctrines: Specific performance of part of a contract
Benami transaction and real ownership
Maturity of plea raised for the first time in appeal
Moulding of decree to comply with statutory restrictions

card.dispute: An HPCL petrol pump dealer contested the re-allotment of a plot at San Martin Marg to Bharat Petroleum, alleging violation of natural justice as HPCL was not heard before the transfer.
issues_decided: Whether the re-allotment of the San Martin Marg plot to Bharat Petroleum without hearing HPCL violated principles of natural justice
Whether the court should grant relief for breach of natural justice when restoring the prior order would lead to an illegal outcome
holdings: Violation of natural justice is a serious matter, but the court may refuse relief if the facts admit only one lawful outcome and issuing a writ would be futile.
Where restitution of the status quo is mandatory after recall of a prior order, and only one legal result is possible, the court need not issue a writ despite procedural unfairness.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Futility of writ doctrine
Restitution and status quo ante
Discretionary nature of public law remedies

card.dispute: The appellants and the Revenue fought over whether Circular No. 455 issued by the C.B.D.T. applied to pending acquisition proceedings under Chapter XX-A of the Income Tax Act, including those at the appellate stage, when the apparent consideration was below Rs. 5 lakhs.
issues_decided: Whether Circular No. 455 dated 16.9.1986 applies to acquisition proceedings pending at the appellate stage under Chapter XX-A of the Income Tax Act?
Whether the term 'proceedings' in the Circular includes appeals before the Tribunal and High Court?
holdings: Circular No. 455 applies to all pending acquisition proceedings under Chapter XX-A that have not attained finality, including those at the appellate stage, if the apparent consideration is below Rs. 5 lakhs.
The term 'proceedings' includes all stages of legal action—initial, appellate, and further appeal—as a unified legal process under the Act.
doctrines: Intrinsic unity of legal proceedings
Binding nature of CBDT circulars under Section 119
Prospective application of administrative circulars in pending cases
Beneficial interpretation of administrative circulars

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of the proviso to clause (b) of sub-section (2) of Section 127-A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, which aggregated the annual letting value of multiple properties for tax purposes, leading to taxation of otherwise exempt properties.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to clause (b) of sub-section (2) of Section 127-A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 is ultra vires for violating the charging mechanism of the Act
Whether the aggregation of annual letting values of multiple properties for determining tax liability is permissible under the Act
Whether a property with annual letting value below Rs. 1,800 becomes taxable merely because the owner owns other properties in the same municipality
holdings: The proviso to Section 127-A(2)(b) is ultra vires as it contradicts the charging section by making exempt properties taxable without specifying the rate of tax.
A taxing statute must clearly specify the subject, liability, and rate of tax; ambiguity or omission in any component renders the tax invalid.
Aggregating the annual letting values of all properties owned by a person to tax a previously exempt property violates the plain language and structure of the Act.
doctrines: Strict construction of taxing statutes
Rule of literal interpretation in fiscal laws
Principle that tax cannot be imposed by analogy or inference
Doctrine of non-derogation from charging provisions

card.dispute: The appellant, a former estate proprietor, challenged the State's revision of a compensation award for land and mineral rights acquired under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, after having accepted the initial payment.
issues_decided: Whether the 1974 Amending Act, which revised the compensation rate, had retrospective operation
Whether the appellant's acceptance of compensation constituted an agreement under Section 25(4)(a) of the Act, barring a claim for higher compensation under Section 25(4)(b)
Whether the Compensation Officer had jurisdiction to revise the final assessment roll under Sections 30 or 30-A of the Act after payment was accepted
holdings: An amending statute that affects substantive rights operates prospectively unless expressly or by necessary implication made retrospective; the 1974 Amending Act had no retrospective effect.
Acceptance of compensation without objection constitutes a deemed agreement under Section 25(4)(a), waiving the right to refer the matter to a tribunal for higher compensation under Section 25(4)(b).
Sections 30 and 30-A do not empower revision of a final assessment roll after payment is accepted; the reopening of the case and order of refund were invalid due to lack of jurisdiction.
doctrines: Lex prospicit non respicit (law looks forward, not backward)
Prospective vs. retrospective operation of statutes
Deemed agreement by conduct
Distinction between procedural and substantive law

card.dispute: The dispute was between Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. and the Andhra Pradesh Revenue Department over whether the company, as a lessee of government land used for industrial purposes, was liable to pay non-agricultural land tax under the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether a company registered under the Companies Act, wholly owned by the Central Government, is liable to pay non-agricultural assessment on leased government land used for industrial purposes after amendments to the Act in 1974.
Whether the principle of promissory estoppel applies to exempt such a company from tax based on a government letter promising exemption.
Whether the amendments to the Act have retrospective effect, making the company liable for tax prior to 1974.
holdings: A company incorporated under the Companies Act is a distinct legal entity from the Government, even if wholly owned by it, and is liable to pay non-agricultural assessment as a lessee of government land used for industrial purposes under the amended Act.
The principle of promissory estoppel cannot be applied against a statute, and the government's letter did not promise tax exemption to corporate entities separate from the Government.
The 1974 amendments to the Act do not have retrospective effect; thus, no tax can be levied for periods before the amendments came into force.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 2(j)
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 12
doctrines: Corporate personality separate from shareholders
No estoppel against statute
Prospective operation of amendments unless expressly retrospective

card.dispute: Two brothers, Mohan Singh and Kailash Singh, appealed their conviction for the murder of Bhagat Singh, with the dispute centering on whether both shared a common intention to kill under Section 34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that Mohan Singh committed murder under Section 302 IPC?
Whether Kailash Singh shared the common intention to commit murder under Section 34 IPC based on his exhortation?
Whether the evidence regarding the seizure of weapons was reliable and admissible?
Whether the lack of detail in the FIR regarding individual roles affected the credibility of the prosecution case?
holdings: Mohan Singh was rightly convicted for murder as eyewitnesses clearly identified him as the shooter, and ballistic evidence corroborated the use of his gun.
Kailash Singh’s mere exhortation ‘Mar Sale Ko’ without prior involvement or additional conduct did not prove common intention to kill beyond reasonable doubt; conviction set aside.
The seizure of cartridges from Mohan Singh’s house was validly proved through his own disclosure and witness testimony, making the evidence reliable.
The FIR’s lack of detail about individual roles was immaterial since it was lodged by a non-eyewitness chowkidar acting on behalf of a grieving father.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires active participation or prior meeting of minds, not mere presence or isolated words.
Benefit of doubt must be given when prosecution fails to prove common intention beyond reasonable doubt.
Disclosure leading to recovery of evidence is admissible under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act.
FIR need not contain detailed roles of accused, especially when lodged by a non-eyewitness in exigent circumstances.

card.dispute: Mysore Minerals Ltd. fought with the Commissioner of Income Tax over whether it could claim depreciation under Section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for seven houses it possessed but did not hold a formal deed of conveyance for.
issues_decided: Whether the assessee can claim depreciation under Section 32(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 without a formal deed of conveyance?
What is the meaning of 'owned' in Section 32(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the context of possession and use of a building for business purposes?
holdings: A person in possession of a building in their own right, using it for business and exercising dominion over it, is the 'owner' for claiming depreciation under Section 32(1), even without a registered deed of conveyance.

The term 'owned' in Section 32(1) must be interpreted contextually and purposively to include possessory owners who have paid part consideration, taken possession, and are using the property in their own right for business.
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Contextual interpretation
Possessory ownership
Substance over form

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the respondent's suit for permanent injunction, claiming the respondent had no right to seek relief based solely on possession without asserting title to the property.
issues_decided: Whether the Letters Patent Appeal was maintainable against the judgment of the Single Judge of the High Court?
Whether a suit for injunction based solely on possession, without claiming title, is maintainable?
Whether the Single Judge was justified in permitting additional evidence and deciding the issue of title when it was not in controversy?
holdings: The Letters Patent Appeal was maintainable as the judgment of the Single Judge fell within Clause 15 of the Letters Patent, and Section 100 CPC did not apply to High Court appellate decrees.
A suit for injunction based on possessory rights is maintainable even without asserting title, as possession itself confers a right to protection from dispossession except by due process of law.
The Single Judge acted beyond jurisdiction by permitting additional evidence and deciding title when no issue of title was framed and the remand was limited to possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 27
doctrines: Possession follows title
Equity and good conscience
Due process of law in dispossession
Maintainability of possessory suits

card.dispute: The Punjab Wakf Board and the Gram Panchayat disputed over ownership of a piece of land, with the Wakf Board claiming it as a Muslim graveyard and the Panchayat asserting it as community land.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to hear the suit filed by the Punjab Wakf Board, given the bar under Section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961
Whether the land in question qualified as 'shamilat deh' under Section 2(g) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, thereby excluding it from civil court jurisdiction
holdings: The dispute between the Wakf Board and a third party (Gram Panchayat) is not barred by the one-year limitation in Section 6(1) of the Wakf Act, 1954, and revenue authorities have jurisdiction to decide such disputes, making the civil suit barred under Section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands Act.

The land, being recorded in revenue records as used for community purposes, falls within the definition of 'shamilat deh' under Section 2(g), and thus the civil court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, Section 13
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, Section 2(g)
Wakf Act, 1954, Explanation to Section 6(1) (as amended by Act 69 of 1984)
doctrines: Jurisdictional bar of civil courts under special statutes
Doctrine of constructive res judicata in revenue proceedings
Statutory interpretation of 'person interested therein' in trust legislation

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's decision to reject his petition for eviction of a tenant who was transferred from his place of posting but claimed protection under the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960, as an employee in an essential service.
issues_decided: Whether a tenant employed in a government department declared as an essential service continues to enjoy protection from eviction under Section 10(4)(i) of the A.P. Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960 after being transferred to another town?

Whether the High Court, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, could re-assess evidence and overturn concurrent findings of fact by the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority on the landlord's bona fide need for eviction?
holdings: A tenant employed in an essential service loses protection under Section 10(4)(i) of the A.P. Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1960 upon being transferred to another town, as the object of the provision is to prevent hardship in serving essential duties at the place of posting.

The High Court cannot, in revision, re-assess evidence or overturn concurrent findings of fact by lower courts unless there is a jurisdictional error or legal infirmity, especially when no such infirmity was found.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(4)(i)
Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 10(3)
doctrines: Literal interpretation versus purposive interpretation of statutes
Principle of finality of concurrent findings of fact
Limits of revisional jurisdiction under civil procedure

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their convictions for murder, arguing lack of reliable evidence and inconsistencies in dying declarations regarding common intention.
issues_decided: Whether the oral dying declarations made by the deceased to witnesses and recorded in the FIR (farbdeyan) by the police officer are reliable despite not being formally recorded as dying declarations?
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that accused nos. 2 and 3 shared common intention under Section 34 IPC?
holdings: Oral dying declarations made by a deceased to multiple witnesses at the scene, and recorded in the FIR by a police officer shortly after the incident, can be relied upon if consistent and corroborated, even if not formally recorded as dying declarations.

Conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC cannot be sustained if there are material inconsistencies in the evidence regarding the role of the accused and no direct proof of common intention.
doctrines: Reliability of dying declarations
Requirement of proof of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Appreciation of evidence de hors official omissions

card.dispute: The appellants, transferees of the suit property during the pendency of an appeal, challenged the High Court's order dismissing the suit as not pressed by the original plaintiff, which effectively nullified a decree in his favour and prejudiced their acquired rights.
issues_decided: Whether a plaintiff can unilaterally withdraw a suit at the appellate stage after a decree has been in his favour and the property has been transferred to third-party transferees pendente lite?
Whether the rights of transferees pendente lite are protected against the withdrawal of a suit by the original plaintiff?
Whether the High Court erred in not considering the impact of Order 23 Rule 1-A CPC while allowing withdrawal of the suit?
holdings: A plaintiff cannot withdraw a suit as a matter of right at the appellate stage if such withdrawal would destroy vested rights of defendants or transferees under a decree passed by the trial court.

Transferees pendente lite, who have acquired property after a decree in favour of the plaintiff and have been impleaded in appeal, possess a substantial interest and cannot be deprived of the benefit of the decree by unilateral withdrawal.

The High Court must consider the applicability of Order 23 Rule 1-A CPC, which requires due regard to whether a defendant (or impleaded transferee) has a substantial question to decide, before permitting withdrawal of a suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 1(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 1-A
doctrines: Vested rights doctrine
Transferee pendente lite doctrine
Res judicata
Conditional right to withdraw suit

card.dispute: Om Prakash appealed against the death sentence imposed for the murder of seven people, arguing that the sentence was excessive given the circumstances of prolonged harassment and police inaction.
issues_decided: Whether the case qualifies as one of the 'rarest of the rare' justifying the death penalty.
Whether the sentence of life imprisonment would be inadequate in the facts of the case.
holdings: The murders, though gruesome, were the result of extreme mental disturbance caused by persistent harassment, family assaults, and police inaction, and thus do not fall within the 'rarest of the rare' category.

The appellant, a BSF constable with no criminal history, was driven to crime by a sense of injustice and lack of state protection, and remains capable of reform; hence, life imprisonment is an adequate and appropriate sentence.
doctrines: Rarest of the rare doctrine
Proportionality principle in sentencing
Reformative theory of punishment

card.dispute: Seven convicted accused appealed their convictions for murder and related offences arising from a land dispute where two persons were killed during a violent altercation.
issues_decided: Whether the accused formed an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC based on the evidence.
Whether the conviction under Section 302/34 IPC for murder by common intention was sustainable against all accused involved in the attack on Tapeshwar Yadav.
Whether the evidence supported individual roles in the offences to justify joint liability under Sections 149 or 34 IPC.
holdings: Conviction under Section 302/149 IPC cannot be sustained without proof of a common object under Section 141 IPC; mere presence with weapons does not make an assembly unlawful.
Section 34 IPC requires proof of prior concert or common intention; mere participation in part of an incident without shared intent does not attract joint liability.
Only those who directly caused fatal injuries with common intention or committed overt acts in furtherance of a common object can be convicted under Sections 302/34 or 302/149 IPC.
doctrines: Doctrine of Unlawful Assembly under Section 149 IPC
Doctrine of Common Intention under Section 34 IPC
Principle of Joint Liability in Criminal Law
Requirement of Prior Concert for Application of Section 34 IPC

card.dispute: The mortgagor-appellants claimed redemption of an oral mortgage from 1893, arguing that a fresh limitation period began in 1960 when the mortgagee rights were sold and acknowledged, while the mortgagee-respondents contended the suit was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for redemption of an oral mortgage executed in 1893 was barred by limitation
Whether a fresh period of limitation for redemption revived on 11 January 1960 due to acknowledgment in a registered sale deed of mortgagee rights
holdings: The right to redeem a mortgage accrues from the date of the mortgage, and the 60-year limitation period begins to run immediately unless restricted by the mortgage deed or law.
Section 18 of the Limitation Act does not revive a limitation period that has already expired; acknowledgment after expiry does not restart the limitation period.
provisions: Punjab Alienation of Land Act, Section 7(5)
doctrines: Doctrine of election (approbation and reprobation)
Revival of limitation under Section 18
Accrual of right to redemption

card.dispute: The landlord Resham Singh appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside eviction orders on grounds of sub-letting and rent arrears involving tenants Raghbir Singh and his brother Kuldeep Singh.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with findings of fact under sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Whether the tenant Raghbir Singh sub-let the premises to his brother Kuldeep Singh
holdings: The High Court can examine the legality and propriety of orders under Section 15(5), including questions of law arising from factual findings, but cannot re-appreciate evidence to reverse concurrent findings of fact.

Mere permission to a brother to manage a shop during the tenant's absence due to criminal proceedings does not constitute sub-letting without proof of transfer of exclusive possession, lease relationship, or consideration.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Sub-letting requires proof of transfer of exclusive possession, lease relationship, and consideration
High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Section 15(5) is limited to questions of legality and propriety, not re-evaluation of facts

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a circular that automatically increased circle rates for stamp duty by 20% after one year, arguing the Collector lacked authority to do so under the U.P. Stamp Rules, 1942.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector had the competence under Rule 340-A of the U.P. Stamp Rules, 1942 to enhance circle rates by 20% for the following year while fixing rates biennially.
Whether the automatic enhancement of circle rates by 20% violated the provisions of the Indian Stamp Act or the principles of fair valuation.
holdings: The Collector has the authority to indicate future rate enhancements in the biennially submitted circle rate statement if supported by material showing a trend of rising land prices, as the circle rate is only prima facie and not final.

The circle rate serves as a guideline for the registering authority and does not bind the final determination of market value, which remains subject to adjudication by the Collector after hearing the parties.
doctrines: Prima facie valuation
Guideline value doctrine
Division of powers between Registering Authority and Collector

card.dispute: Savita Devi, a mother, sued her four sons for maintenance and a charge on ancestral property, and opposed the impleadment of three purchasers who bought shares of the suit property from one of her sons during the pendency of the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the purchasers (respondents 3 to 5) were entitled to be impleaded as parties in the suit despite the trial court's injunction against alienation of the suit property?
Whether the sales to the purchasers were valid in light of the court's interim order restraining transfer of the property?
Whether judicial officers who decided civil matters can be impleaded as respondents in writ petitions or special leave petitions?
holdings: Transferees pendente lite who acquire an interest in suit property have a right to be impleaded if their presence is necessary for complete adjudication and to avoid multiplicity of proceedings.

The validity of the sales and the bona fide nature of the transferees must be adjudicated upon in the suit or in the impleadment application; mere violation of an injunction does not automatically bar impleadment.
Judicial officers deciding civil cases should not be impleaded as respondents in writ petitions or SLPs, as this practice disrupts judicial independence and is unjustified.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1, Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII, Rule 10
doctrines: Lis pendens
Necessary and proper parties
Judicial independence
Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings

card.dispute: The State Bank of India challenged the High Court's declaration that Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act was ultra vires, which had allowed a borrower to contest excessive interest rates.
issues_decided: Whether Parliament had the legislative competence to enact Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act?
Whether courts can interfere with the rate of interest, including compound interest, agreed upon in a mortgage transaction?
holdings: Parliament had the authority to enact Section 21-A under Entry 45 of List I (Banking) of the Seventh Schedule, and the provision is valid despite encroaching on state matters related to debt relief.
Courts cannot interfere with the agreed rate of interest, including compound interest, in a banking transaction secured by mortgage, as it is a matter of contract between the parties.
provisions: Seventh Schedule, Entry 45 of List I (Union List)
doctrines: Legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Doctrine of repugnancy
Freedom of contract in banking transactions

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh challenged a High Court decision that equated a former royal ruler with the state government and allowed him to claim monetary benefits, including forest royalties and related charges, from the State Forest Corporation.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, a former royal ruler and later a Forest Superintendent, could be equated with the State Government for claiming monetary benefits from forest produce.
Whether the term 'royalty' as used in the Pricing Committee's decision included extension fees, interest, damages, and other recoveries claimed by the respondent.
Whether the High Court was justified in issuing a writ of mandamus directing the State Forest Corporation to pay the claimed amounts to the respondent.
holdings: A former royal ruler who accepted a government appointment as Forest Superintendent could not be equated with the State Government and had no ownership rights over forest produce.
The term 'royalty' does not include extension fees, interest, damages, or other sovereign recoveries, which can only be claimed by the state under its statutory and sovereign powers.
No enforceable statutory right existed in favor of the respondent; hence, the writ of mandamus was improperly issued and the High Court’s judgment was set aside.
doctrines: Doctrine of Sovereign Immunity
Literal and Contextual Interpretation of Statutory Terms
Principle of Ejusdem Generis (in interpreting 'royalty' and related claims)
Separation of Powers and Judicial Restraint in Writ Jurisdiction

card.dispute: The State of Haryana appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Bhagirath, who was accused of participating in the murder of his blind son along with his two nephews.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting Bhagirath on the basis of 'abundant caution' despite accepting the reliability of eyewitness testimony.
Whether the medical evidence regarding the nature of the victim's neck injury created a reasonable doubt about Bhagirath's complicity.
holdings: The benefit of doubt can only be granted when there is a reasonable doubt arising from the evidence, not as a measure of judicial caution; the High Court erred in acquitting Bhagirath without identifying any specific doubt.
The medical opinion that a single blow caused the injury did not conclusively contradict the prosecution's case, and the court is not bound by expert opinion if it lacks logical reasoning.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal trials
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
Judicial evaluation of expert medical evidence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a 1966 land settlement order in favor of a deity, claiming procedural irregularities in service of notice and other grounds, leading to a review and eventual appeal before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the Estate Abolition Collector had the power to review or recall the 1966 settlement order under Section 151 CPC or inherent jurisdiction
Whether procedural irregularities in publication of notice rendered the settlement order a nullity
Whether delay in filing the claim application or its misclassification as a claim instead of lease affected the jurisdiction of the authority
holdings: The power to recall an order lies only in cases of lack of jurisdiction, fraud, collusion, or procedural defects that render the order void; mere procedural irregularities do not justify recall.
Failure to publish notice in the prescribed manner is an irregularity, not a jurisdictional defect, and cannot invalidate an otherwise valid order.
An order passed on a time-barred application or on misclassification of the nature of application does not lack jurisdiction; it may be illegal but not a nullity.
doctrines: Lack of jurisdiction vs. error in exercise of jurisdiction
Doctrine of nullity
Principle of estoppel and acquiescence
Fraud vitiates judicial orders

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the order declaring part of their inherited land as excess under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, and its constitutional validity, claiming their sister's share was not considered.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 are violative of Article 31-A(1) of the Constitution?
Whether the order of the Competent Authority declaring land as excess is valid despite non-consideration of a sister's share in joint family property?
Whether the delay of ten years in challenging the order renders the writ petition non-maintainable?
holdings: The constitutional validity of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is upheld, as previously confirmed by this Court, and does not violate Article 31-A(1).

The order declaring land as excess is final and binding when no appeal or revision was filed, and non-consideration of a sister's share does not invalidate it, especially as she did not object before vesting.
A writ petition filed ten years after the order and vesting of land is barred by delay and laches, justifying the High Court's summary dismissal.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(1)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(3)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(5)
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders in absence of appeal
Doctrine of laches
Binding nature of co-sharer's inaction in property disputes

card.dispute: The State of Kerala sought to recover time-barred debts through the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act, 1968, while the respondents argued that such recovery was impermissible under the Limitation Act.
issues_decided: Whether a debt barred by limitation can be recovered under the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act, 1968
Whether the expression 'amounts due' in Section 71 of the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act includes time-barred debts
Whether the recovery mechanism under the Act overrides the bar of limitation
holdings: A debt barred by limitation cannot be recovered under the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act, 1968, as the Act does not create a substantive right to recover time-barred dues.
The term 'amounts due' in Section 71 refers only to amounts legally recoverable, i.e., those not barred by limitation at the time of initiating recovery proceedings.
The summary recovery procedure under the Act does not enlarge the creditor's rights; it merely provides an alternative mode of recovery for valid, enforceable claims.
doctrines: Statute of limitation bars remedy but not the right
Principle of statutory interpretation based on context and scheme
Doctrine of separation between substantive and procedural law
Principle of legality in coercive recovery mechanisms

card.dispute: The appellant Sukhar challenged his conviction under Section 307 IPC for allegedly shooting his uncle Nakkal, based on the admissibility and reliability of hearsay evidence given by a witness who heard the injured identify the assailant.
issues_decided: Whether the statement of the injured person to PW 2, that his nephew Sukhar shot him, is admissible under Section 6 of the Indian Evidence Act as part of res gestae?
Whether the conviction under Section 307 IPC can be sustained solely on the basis of such hearsay evidence without corroboration, especially when the witness is found to be inimical to the accused?
holdings: A statement made by the injured to a witness immediately after the incident, while still under the influence of the event, is admissible under Section 6 of the Evidence Act as part of the same transaction, even if not made at the exact moment of the occurrence.

A conviction under Section 307 IPC cannot be based solely on uncorroborated hearsay evidence from a witness shown to be inimical to the accused, as such evidence lacks reliability and requires independent corroboration to be legally sufficient.
doctrines: Res gestae
Hearsay evidence exception
Requirement of corroboration for interested or inimical witnesses

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's acquittal of seven accused, including Teja Ram and Ram Lai, convicted by the Sessions Court for the double murder of Ram Lai and his mother using axes, based on circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the recovery of blood-stained axes without conclusive serological proof of human blood could be relied upon as incriminating evidence
Whether the signature of the accused on seizure memos under Section 27 of the Evidence Act vitiated the recovery process
Whether the inconsistency in a witness's statement regarding disclosure of assailants' names affected the prosecution's case
holdings: Failure to prove the blood on the recovered axes as human due to disintegration does not render the recovery evidence valueless if other circumstances strongly connect the accused to the crime.
Obtaining the accused's signature on seizure memos during recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act does not violate Section 162 CrPC and does not vitiate the evidence.

A witness's initial denial of disclosing assailants' names, later contradicted by evidence of prior disclosure, does not fatally undermine the prosecution case if the inconsistency is properly examined and explained.
doctrines: Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus not applied mechanically
Benefit of doubt only when doubt is reasonable and not speculative
Curative approach to evaluation of circumstantial evidence
Doctrine of constructive possession under Section 27, Evidence Act

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside eviction orders, claiming they needed the premises to live separately from the landlord's father, while tenants argued the need was not bona fide.
issues_decided: Whether a mere desire to live separately from one's father constitutes a bona fide need for eviction under the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Whether the High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction under Section 25 of the Act by interfering with concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts.
holdings: Mere desire to live separately from a family member does not amount to a bona fide need for eviction; the landlord must plead and prove a genuine, objective need for the premises.
The High Court can interfere in revision if findings are based on no evidence; since the landlord failed to plead or prove bona fide need, the High Court rightly set aside the eviction orders.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(a)(i)
Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(3)(e)
Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 25
doctrines: Bona fide requirement doctrine in rent control cases
Distinction between subjective desire and objective need
Limits of revisional jurisdiction under Section 25
Principle that findings based on no evidence can be corrected in revision

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's commutation of the death sentence of Dharmendra Singh and Narendra to life imprisonment for the brutal murder of five family members.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in commuting the death sentence to life imprisonment despite the trial court's imposition of the death penalty?
Whether the case qualifies as a 'rarest of the rare' case warranting the death penalty?
Whether the absence of clear attribution of individual overt acts in a joint offence precludes the confirmation of the death sentence?
holdings: The High Court erred in commuting the death sentence as the case falls within the 'rarest of the rare' category due to the premeditated, brutal, and diabolic nature of the crime.

The totality of circumstances—including the motive, vulnerability of victims, and extreme brutality—justifies the death penalty even if individual roles are not distinctly proven, provided the courts below have distinguished the accused's roles.
The principle from Ronny's case does not create an absolute bar to the death penalty in joint offence cases; sentencing must depend on the specific facts and evidence of each case.
doctrines: rarest of the rare doctrine
joint liability under Section 149 IPC
principle of proportionality in sentencing
obligation to impose death sentence in furtherance of public interest

card.dispute: The landlord filed a premature eviction petition under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, within one year of a gift deed transferring ownership, and contested whether the petition was maintainable despite a new lease agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's right to recover possession arose under an instrument of transfer inter vivos, triggering the one-year bar under Section 11(3) of the Act.
Whether a new lease agreement between the transferee-landlord and tenant impliedly terminated the old lease and circumvented the one-year prohibition.
Whether the Rent Control Court could validly decide the merits of an eviction petition filed during the prohibited period.
holdings: The landlord's right to seek possession arose from the gift deed (an inter vivos transfer), so the one-year bar under Section 11(3), proviso 3, applied, making the petition premature.
A new lease with increased rent and change of lessor does not imply surrender of the original lease unless the new relationship is inconsistent with the old; no such inconsistency was found.
Courts cannot adjudicate merits of an eviction petition filed during the prohibited period; such findings are without jurisdiction and must be disregarded.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(3)
doctrines: Implied surrender of lease
Maintainability of eviction petitions post-transfer inter vivos
Jurisdictional bar on deciding merits of premature petitions

card.dispute: The appellant (mortgagee) and respondent (mortgagor, now dead) disputed whether the mortgage could be discharged by deposit of the outstanding amount after auction sale, and whether the sale confirmation was valid.
issues_decided: Whether the mortgage stood discharged upon deposit of the balance amount under Order 34 Rule 5 CPC after the auction sale was held?
Whether the High Court could allow a revision petition challenging an order refusing return of title deeds when connected appeals were dismissed?
Whether the trial court’s order discharging the mortgage and returning documents was valid despite pending challenges to sale confirmation?
holdings: A mortgage can be discharged if the mortgagor deposits the decretal amount under Order 34 Rule 5 CPC even after auction, provided the sale is not yet confirmed.
The High Court’s judgment allowing return of documents while dismissing appeals against sale confirmation was inconsistent, but the outcome was justified as the mortgage stood discharged.
Once the mortgage is discharged by deposit, the mortgagor is entitled to return of title deeds under Order 34 Rule 5A CPC, irrespective of procedural inconsistencies.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34 Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34 Rule 5A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 33
doctrines: Doctrine of discharge of mortgage by deposit of amount due
Principle of harmonious construction to resolve inconsistent orders
Doctrine of doing complete justice under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued to recover possession of land from the defendant, who claimed to be a tenant since 1971, while the plaintiff argued the defendant was merely a caretaker and that no valid tenancy could exist due to statutory prohibitions.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court was obligated to refer the question of tenancy to the Land Tribunal under Section 125(3) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act when the claim was legally untenable?
Whether a tenancy created after the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms Act could be valid under Section 74 of the Act?
Whether the trial court had jurisdiction to reject the defendant's tenancy claim without referring it to the Land Tribunal?
holdings: A civil court is not bound to refer a tenancy claim to the Land Tribunal if the claim is legally unsustainable or raised merely to delay proceedings.
No tenancy can be created in any land after the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, and any such tenancy is invalid under Section 74.
The trial court had jurisdiction to decide the tenancy issue itself when the claim was clearly barred by statute, and the appellate court could independently review the finding.
doctrines: Statutory bar on creation of future tenancies
Reference to tribunal only when question genuinely arises
Judicial discretion to prevent abuse of process

card.dispute: The Gujarat Agro Industries Co. Ltd. challenged the constitutional validity of Section 406(2)(e) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, which required deposit of disputed tax before filing an appeal, claiming it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Section 406(2)(e) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, which mandates deposit of disputed tax as a condition for appeal, is constitutionally valid under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution.
Whether the condition of depositing tax before appeal renders the right of appeal illusory or violates principles of natural justice.
holdings: A statutory right to appeal is not a fundamental right and may be subject to conditions imposed by the legislature, including deposit of disputed tax, without violating Article 14.
Conditions on appeal, such as partial tax deposit, are valid if they prevent abuse of process and do not entirely bar access to justice, especially when alternative remedies exist.
provisions: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 406(2)(e)
Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, Section 408
doctrines: Statutory right to appeal
Reasonable classification under Article 14
Conditions on statutory remedies

card.dispute: The appellant, a public servant, challenged criminal proceedings initiated against him for firing during the removal of encroachments, arguing that prior sanction under Section 197 CrPC was required but not obtained.
issues_decided: Whether the provisions of Section 197(1) of the CrPC apply to the appellant's actions during the removal of encroachments?
At what stage can the objection regarding lack of sanction under Section 197 CrPC be raised?
holdings: The acts committed by the appellant, including ordering police to open fire, were in discharge of his official duty and had a reasonable nexus with such duty, thus attracting protection under Section 197(1) CrPC.
The question of sanction under Section 197 CrPC can be raised at any stage of the criminal proceedings, as it goes to the jurisdiction of the court to take cognizance.
doctrines: Jurisdictional bar without sanction under Section 197 CrPC
Reasonable connection between official duty and alleged act
Sanction as a condition precedent to prosecution of public servants

card.dispute: Ambika Prasad and others appealed their conviction for murder, attempt to murder, and unlawful assembly in a land dispute where they were accused of killing Virender Singh during a violent clash.
issues_decided: Whether the evidence of injured eyewitnesses could be relied upon despite minor inconsistencies
Whether the non-mention of accused Ram Chander in the FIR fatally affected the prosecution case
Whether the alibi and defence version of self-defence during a protest against demolition of a Gurudwara wall could be accepted
Whether the prosecution's failure to examine the Patwari required acquittal
holdings: Minor inconsistencies in eyewitness testimony, such as becoming unconscious yet reporting accused fleeing, do not undermine credible and consistent evidence.
Non-inclusion in the FIR does not discredit identification by eyewitnesses, especially when the accused was known and described by distinguishing features.
The defence of self-defence and alibi was rejected as baseless due to lack of supporting evidence and implausibility given the accused were armed with deadly weapons and inflicted serious injuries.
The prosecution is not obligated to examine every possible witness, including a Patwari, if the core facts are sufficiently proved by other reliable evidence.
doctrines: Reliability of eyewitness testimony
FIR not a substantive piece of evidence
Benefit of doubt not warranted in face of consistent prosecution evidence
Prosecution's discretion in selecting witnesses

card.dispute: The petitioners, Almitra H. Patel and another, fought against the Union of India and others over the failure of authorities to manage solid waste, control pollution, and maintain public health and sanitation in Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the authorities responsible for sanitation in Delhi have failed to comply with their statutory duties under relevant municipal laws.
Whether landfill and compost plant sites have been adequately identified and provided for scientific waste disposal in Delhi.
Whether measures are needed to enforce public discipline against littering and ensure accountability in sanitation management.
Whether inter-agency coordination among governmental bodies is necessary for effective waste management and environmental protection in Delhi.
holdings: The Municipal Corporation of Delhi, NDMC, and other statutory authorities must strictly enforce provisions of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, and Cantonments Act, 1924 to prevent accumulation and dumping of waste in public areas.

Landfill sites sufficient for twenty years and eight compost plant sites must be identified within four weeks and handed over free of cost and encumbrances within two weeks, with compliance monitored by the Central Pollution Control Board.
Authorities may levy and recover on-the-spot charges (initially Rs. 50) from litterers and must appoint magistrates under CrPC to prosecute violations, ensuring deterrence and public accountability.

All concerned governmental agencies must cooperate in preventing encroachments, improving slum sanitation, and filing compliance reports within eight weeks, failing which the Court will take serious view of violations.
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Precautionary Principle
Polluter Pays Principle
Sustainable Development

card.dispute: The plaintiff (Vidhyadhar) sued to redeem a property mortgaged by conditional sale or, alternatively, to enforce a repurchase agreement, after the defendant refused to reconvey the property upon repayment.
issues_decided: Whether the document dated 24th March 1971 was a mortgage by conditional sale or an outright sale
Whether the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff was valid despite non-payment of the full purchase price
Whether the right to redeem the mortgage was available when the mortgage money was tendered but refused
holdings: A document styled as a mortgage by conditional sale, with a stipulation for reconveyance upon repayment, is a mortgage under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, if the condition is in the deed.
Ownership passes under a sale deed even if part of the purchase money remains unpaid; the seller has only a statutory charge under Section 55(4)(b) for the unpaid amount.
Where a mortgagor tenders the mortgage money within the stipulated time and the mortgagee refuses it, there is no default, and the right to redeem remains intact.
doctrines: English Doctrine of Equitable Lien
Intention of the parties as the true test for determining the nature of a transaction
Statutory charge for unpaid purchase money upon transfer of ownership

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought an ex parte injunction to prevent defendants from dispossessing him from a property in Chennai, which the trial court granted; the defendants challenged the injunction's validity, leading to a High Court revision and a Supreme Court appeal on procedural compliance.
issues_decided: Whether an ex parte injunction order is void if the court fails to record reasons for granting it without notice under Order 39 Rule 3 of CPC
Whether non-compliance with Order 39 Rule 3-A (requiring final disposal within 30 days) invalidates the injunction
Whether the High Court should have entertained a revision under Article 227 when alternative remedies were available
holdings: An ex parte injunction is not void merely because the court failed to record reasons or comply with Rule 3 duties, but the beneficiary cannot enforce it if they fail to comply with statutory obligations like serving documents.

Failure to decide the injunction application within 30 days under Rule 3-A does not automatically invalidate the order, but the aggrieved party gains a right to appeal, and the order is deemed final for appeal purposes after 30 days.
The High Court should generally require parties to pursue alternative remedies before invoking Article 227, though it retains discretion to entertain revision petitions.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39 Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39 Rule 3-A
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 43 Rule 1
doctrines: Procedural fairness in ex parte injunctions
Remedy for judicial inaction in interim relief
Principle of alternative remedy barring Article 227

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the levy of stamp duty on an agreement for sale of a flat, arguing it was not a 'conveyance' and that duty could not be levied on the transaction rather than the instrument.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement for sale of a flat, with possession to be transferred before or at the time of execution, amounts to a 'conveyance' under the Bombay Stamp Act, 1958.
Whether Explanation I to Article 25 of Schedule I of the Bombay Stamp Act is ultra vires the Constitution for levying duty on a transaction rather than an instrument.
holdings: An agreement for sale of immovable property is deemed a 'conveyance' under Explanation I to Article 25 if possession is transferred before, at, or after execution of the agreement without a conveyance deed, attracting conveyance-level stamp duty.

The Explanation does not levy duty on a transaction but on the instrument itself, and it is within the legislative competence of the State to impose such duty based on the substance of the agreement and transfer of possession.
provisions: Bombay Stamp Act, 1958, Article 25 of Schedule I with Explanation I
Maharashtra Ownership Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963, Section 4 and Section 11
Constitution of India, Entry 44, List III (Concurrent List), Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Deeming fiction in fiscal statutes
Substance over form in stamp duty assessment
Legislative competence to levy stamp duty on instruments based on economic reality

card.dispute: An advocate challenged the enhancement of his suspension from legal practice from five to ten years by the Bar Council of India, arguing violation of natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the advocate was guilty of professional misconduct for resisting the court's order to produce his client personally despite a claimed compromise in a civil suit.
Whether the Bar Council of India could enhance the punishment without affording the advocate a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
holdings: An advocate commits professional misconduct by obstructing a court's lawful direction to verify a compromise through personal appearance of the party, especially when such conduct undermines judicial scrutiny.

The Bar Council of India cannot enhance punishment prejudicially affecting an advocate without issuing a specific show-cause notice and providing a reasonable opportunity to be heard, as mandated by Section 37(2) proviso of the Advocates Act, 1961.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 3 Rule 1
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Inherent power of court to require personal appearance of parties
Rule of fair hearing under statutory proviso

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants on grounds of wilful default in rent payment and denial of his title, which the tenants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants committed wilful default in payment of rent under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether the tenants denied the landlord's title within the meaning of Section 10(2)(vii) of the Act
holdings: Acceptance of rent by the landlord after deposit by tenants negates a claim of wilful default; no cause of action for eviction on that ground existed.
A tenant's assertion that the landlord is a co-owner, without renouncing tenancy or asserting adverse title, does not amount to denial of title, especially without knowledge of transfer.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(vii)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 8(5)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 25
doctrines: Wilful default in rent payment requires continued non-payment after notice
Approbation and reprobation: a party cannot both accept and reject a legal relationship
Burden of proving non-bona fide denial of title under rent control law
Constructive knowledge and attornment in landlord-tenant relationship

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant, claiming the premises was an open plot not covered by rent control, while the tenant argued it was part of a residential house and protected under the Rent Control Order.
issues_decided: Whether clause 13-A of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 applies to an appeal pending when the amendment was introduced
Whether the amendment introducing clause 13-A has retrospective effect
Whether the term 'premises' includes land associated with a residential house
holdings: Clause 13-A applies to pending appeals because an appeal is a continuation of the suit and constitutes a proceeding 'filed and pending' under the provision.
The amendment has prospective operation with retroactive effect but is not retrospective, as it regulates future enforcement of decrees without affecting past rights.
The term 'premises' includes land appurtenant to a residential house, especially when used in connection with the house, such as for access or utilities like a well.
provisions: C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13-A
C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 2(4-A)
C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Clause 13
doctrines: Appeal as continuation of suit
Prospective vs. retrospective legislation
Re-hearing theory of appeal

card.dispute: Dena Bank fought the State of Karnataka and others over priority of its mortgage claim versus the State's claim for sales tax arrears on the same property.
issues_decided: Whether the State of Karnataka had priority over Dena Bank's mortgage claim for recovery of sales tax arrears from the mortgaged property.
Whether Section 15(2A) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, could be applied to hold partners personally liable for the firm's tax dues.
Whether the amendment to Section 15(2A) had retrospective operation and could affect existing rights.
holdings: The State of Karnataka has priority over the bank's mortgage claim due to Section 158(1) of the Karnataka Land Revenue Act, which gives precedence to state recoveries under Chapter XVI, including sales tax.
Partners are personally liable for the firm's sales tax dues under Section 15(2A) of the Karnataka Sales Tax Act, 1957, which explicitly imposes joint and several liability on partners.
The amendment to Section 15(2A) is prospective, not retrospective, as it operates from its date of enactment and only applies to liabilities arising thereafter.
doctrines: Doctrine of State priority in recovery of public dues
Doctrine of joint and several liability of partners
Principle of prospective versus retrospective legislation

card.dispute: The Food Corporation of India challenged the validity of a municipal order amending the property tax assessment of its godown in Sangrur, Punjab, on grounds of vagueness and lack of material basis.
issues_decided: Whether the notice issued under Section 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 for amending the assessment list was valid and compliant with statutory requirements?
Whether the revision of the property tax assessment was based on sufficient material and proper application of mind?
Whether the principles of natural justice were followed in amending the assessment list?
holdings: A notice under Section 67 must specify the grounds and reasons for proposed amendment; a vague and non-specific notice does not satisfy statutory requirements.
An amendment to the assessment list must be based on material and proper application of mind; absence of such material renders the order unsustainable.
The principles of natural justice require that the affected party be given a meaningful opportunity to respond, which is defeated by a vague notice lacking particulars.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Requirement of reasoned decision-making
Doctrine of valid notice in administrative action

card.dispute: The tenant, G.P. Srivastava, fought against the landlord, R.K. Raizada, over an ex-parte decree for ejectment and recovery of rent arrears.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the trial court on the date of hearing?
Whether the ex-parte decree should be set aside under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure?
holdings: Sufficient cause under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC must be liberally construed, and illness and counsel's personal tragedy can constitute sufficient cause if not intentional.
An ex-parte decree should be set aside when the defendant approaches the court within the statutory period and shows non-malafide absence, even if there was prior negligence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'sufficient cause'
Condonation of delay for genuine and non-malafide reasons
Preference for adjudication on merits over technical dismissal

card.dispute: The successors of Sheetal Prasad (respondents) and Bala Prasad and Sadhau (appellants) disputed whether certain landholdings were joint Hindu family property, with respondents claiming co-ownership and appellants asserting individual ownership.
issues_decided: Whether the khatas in dispute were joint Hindu family property and whether the parties were members of a joint Hindu family.

Whether the Deputy Director of Consolidation had the power under Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 to overturn concurrent findings of fact by the Consolidation Officer and Settlement Officer.
Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the Deputy Director's order on the ground of error apparent on the face of the record.
holdings: The family was joint and the khatas were held as joint Hindu family property, with the khatedars holding the lands for the benefit of all family members.
The Deputy Director of Consolidation cannot overturn concurrent factual findings unless they are perverse, unsupported by evidence, or suffer from procedural illegality.
The High Court rightly quashed the Deputy Director’s order as it ignored relevant evidence and misapplied the presumption of jointness in Hindu families.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Presumption of jointness in a Hindu undivided family
Principle that a joint Hindu family, though not a juristic person, collectively owns coparcenary property through its members
Doctrine of limited revisional jurisdiction under Section 48 where findings are not perverse or legally flawed

card.dispute: The appellant, Gura Singh, challenged his conviction for the murder of his father, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove the origin of bloodstains on recovered items due to degradation over time.
issues_decided: Whether the failure to determine the origin of bloodstains due to disintegration over time renders the prosecution's case unreliable?
Whether the recovery of blood-stained articles based on the accused's disclosure statement can sustain a conviction in the absence of blood group analysis?
Whether non-mention of dimensions of bloodstains in seizure memos creates a fatal gap in the chain of circumstantial evidence?
holdings: Failure to determine the origin of blood due to disintegration does not negate that it was human blood; the circumstance retains evidentiary value when supported by other evidence.
Recovery of blood-stained chadar and weapon based on the accused’s disclosure, along with confessional statements, sufficiently connects him to the crime even without blood group matching.
Non-recording of bloodstain dimensions in seizure memos is not fatal unless it affects the reliability of evidence or points to malafide; it does not automatically create a reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Chain of circumstantial evidence
Benefit of reasonable doubt
Evidentiary value of disclosure statements under Section 27 of the Evidence Act
Context-specific application of judicial observations

card.dispute: The appellant, a Sub-Divisional Officer, challenged the High Court's decision that criminal proceedings could proceed against him without prior sanction under Section 197 Cr.P.C. for actions taken during an encroachment removal drive.
issues_decided: Whether Section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to the appellant's actions during the removal of encroachments on government land.
Whether the acts alleged against the public servant were committed while acting or purporting to act in discharge of official duty.
holdings: Section 197 Cr.P.C. applies when a public servant is accused of an offence alleged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in official duty, provided there is a reasonable nexus between the act and the duty.
The appellant, as a Sub-Divisional Officer, was acting in purported discharge of official duty during the encroachment removal, thus requiring prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197 Cr.P.C.
doctrines: Reasonable and rational nexus test for official duty under Section 197 Cr.P.C.
Mandatory requirement of prior sanction for prosecution of public servants acting in official capacity

card.dispute: The appellant, Jai Mangal Oraon, claimed rights over land originally belonging to a tribal tenant, challenging the validity of a 1942 surrender of tenancy and subsequent transfers to non-tribal purchasers, including the first respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the surrender of tenancy rights in 1942 required prior permission of the Deputy Commissioner under the CNT Act
Whether subsequent criminal conduct of the appellant affects his locus standi to pursue civil claims
Whether Section 71A of the CNT Act applies retrospectively to a surrender made in 1942
Whether non-tribals can legally hold land transferred after a valid surrender under the CNT Act
holdings: The surrender in 1942 did not require prior sanction of the Deputy Commissioner as Section 46(4)(a) and Section 71A were not in force at that time, making the surrender valid.
The appellant’s absconding in criminal proceedings and abuse of legal process disentitles him from claiming relief, affecting his locus standi.
Section 71A, introduced in 1969, cannot be applied retroactively to invalidate a 1942 surrender, especially after decades of changed circumstances.
The Deputy Commissioner is not obligated to re-allot land to a tribal if the original transfer was valid, and non-tribals may retain such land.
doctrines: Doctrine of Locus Standi
Doctrine of Retrospective Operation of Statutes
Principle of Abuse of Process of Court
Principle of Acquired Rights under Limitation

card.dispute: The Gram Panchayat challenged a prior injunction decree obtained by private respondents, alleging it was collusive and should not bind the Panchayat in proceedings under the Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether a plea of collusion against a prior decree can be raised in a subsequent proceeding without first filing a separate suit to set aside the decree
Whether the statutory authorities under the Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961 can examine the collusive nature of a prior decree
Whether a decree in a suit for injunction operates as res judicata on the question of title
holdings: A party can challenge a prior decree on the ground of collusion in a subsequent proceeding without first filing an independent suit to set it aside, as per Section 44 of the Indian Evidence Act.
Statutory authorities have the jurisdiction to examine whether a prior decree was obtained by collusion in proceedings under the Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961.

A decree in an injunction suit does not operate as res judicata on the question of title unless the finding on title was necessary for granting the injunction and the relief was based on that finding.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 7
doctrines: Res judicata
Collateral challenge to a decree
Fraud or collusion as an exception to res judicata
No requirement of prior rescission suit to challenge a collusive decree

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against a High Court decision that invalidated their eviction suit, arguing whether a decree for eviction under Section 12(1)(a) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, could be passed without first determining provisional rent under Section 13(2) when the tenant admitted the rent rate but failed to prove payment of arrears.
issues_decided: Whether a court can pass an eviction decree under Section 12(1)(a) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961 without first determining provisional rent under Section 13(2) when the tenant admits the rent rate but disputes payment of arrears.
Whether the operation of Section 13(1) of the Act is automatically suspended when a tenant raises a dispute under Section 13(2), even if the rate of rent is not in dispute.
holdings: A decree for eviction under Section 12(1)(a) can be passed without determining provisional rent under Section 13(2) when the tenant admits the rent rate but fails to prove payment of arrears.

The operation of Section 13(1) is not automatically suspended merely because a dispute is raised; only the disputed portion of rent obligations may be affected, and compliance with undisputed portions remains mandatory.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(2)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(5)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(3)
doctrines: Suspension of statutory obligation pending provisional determination
Burden of proof in tenant's compliance with rent deposit requirements
Limited scope of rent dispute under Section 13(2) when rate is admitted

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide personal requirement, while the tenant challenged the refusal of leave to defend the eviction petition.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant made out a triable issue to warrant grant of leave to defend an eviction petition under Section 25B(5) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
Whether the Additional Rent Controller exceeded jurisdiction by deciding merits at the stage of granting leave to defend?
Whether the High Court erred in affirming the refusal of leave to defend without considering the legal standard for triable issues?
holdings: A tenant is entitled to leave to defend if they raise a triable issue, even if the defence may ultimately fail; the test is not final success but prima facie entitlement to contest.
The Additional Rent Controller acted beyond jurisdiction by adjudicating the merits of disputed facts at the leave stage, which violates the summary procedure under Section 25B(5).
Refusing leave to defend without allowing cross-examination or proper proof violates principles of natural justice, especially when serious disputes about bona fide requirement exist.
doctrines: Principle of triable issue
Burden of proof on landlord in eviction for bona fide requirement
Principles of natural justice in summary eviction proceedings
Judicial restraint at the stage of granting leave to defend

card.dispute: The appellant, Gobind Ram, challenged the decree of specific performance of a property sale agreement in favor of the respondent, Gian Chand, seeking instead to cancel the contract by paying compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in decreeing specific performance of the sale agreement?
Whether the appellant can avoid specific performance by offering monetary compensation instead?
holdings: A decree for specific performance of a sale agreement is valid when the plaintiff has performed or is ready to perform their part and the defendant has failed to perform.
Specific performance cannot be denied merely because the defendant offers to compensate the plaintiff; the plaintiff has a right to enforce the contract as agreed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 58
doctrines: Doctrine of Specific Performance
Doctrine of Equitable Relief

card.dispute: The defendants appealed against the Madras High Court's order allowing the plaintiffs to withdraw their suit with permission to file a fresh one, after the appellate court had partly decided the case on merits.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court properly exercised its discretion under Order XXIII Rule 1(3) CPC in permitting withdrawal of the suit with liberty to file a fresh suit at the appellate stage.
Whether the plaintiffs had sufficient grounds for withdrawal of the suit under Order XXIII Rule 1(3) CPC, particularly in light of findings already made against them on merits.
holdings: The High Court must apply its mind strictly to the conditions in Order XXIII Rule 1(3) CPC and cannot grant permission to withdraw a suit with leave to file afresh merely by stating that the defendant will not be prejudiced.

Permission to withdraw a suit with liberty to file a fresh suit at the appellate stage should not be granted if it nullifies findings or a decree in favour of the defendant on merits, as it causes prejudice and wastes judicial time.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 1(3)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 1
doctrines: Judicial discretion must be exercised judiciously and in compliance with statutory conditions.
Prevention of abuse of process of court by allowing withdrawal to circumvent adverse findings.

card.dispute: The landlords sought eviction of tenants on grounds of bonafide requirement, while tenants contested the landlord's title, claiming the property was vested in the Custodian of Enemy Properties and thus could not be sold.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller was justified in rejecting the tenants' application for leave to defend without a proper enquiry into their pleaded grounds.
Whether the property in question was validly alienated by persons who had become Pakistani nationals and whether it stood vested in the Custodian of Enemy Properties for India.
Whether the Rent Controller had jurisdiction to entertain the eviction petition if the property was vested under the Enemy Properties Act, 1968.
holdings: The Rent Controller must grant leave to defend if the tenant discloses facts that prima facie disentitle the landlord from eviction, without requiring proof at that stage.
Pleas regarding title, vesting of property under the Enemy Properties Act, and lack of jurisdiction are not frivolous and must be examined during trial, not rejected at the threshold.
The Rent Controller erred in conflating the Evacuee Property Act with the Enemy Property Act, and failed to consider the legal consequences of vesting, necessitating a full adjudication.
doctrines: Principle of liberal interpretation of rent control laws in favour of tenants
Prima facie enquiry standard for granting leave to defend under rent control legislation
Doctrine of vested property under the Enemy Properties Act overriding private alienation

card.dispute: The State of Kerala challenged the High Court's dismissal of its appeal against a Forest Tribunal order, and later sought review of that same order after the Supreme Court rejected its special leave petition.
issues_decided: Whether an order rejecting a special leave petition under Article 136 of the Constitution leads to the merger of the impugned order into the Supreme Court's order
Whether the doctrine of merger applies when special leave to appeal is refused
Whether a speaking or non-speaking order rejecting a special leave petition binds lower courts on questions of law or fact
Whether the High Court retains jurisdiction to review its own order if the Supreme Court refuses special leave to appeal
holdings: The doctrine of merger does not apply when the Supreme Court refuses special leave to appeal, as no appellate jurisdiction is exercised at that stage.
An order rejecting a special leave petition, whether speaking or not, does not merge the lower court’s order; the original order remains enforceable and subject to review.
A speaking order rejecting special leave may declare law under Article 141 and contain binding findings, but it does not affirm or replace the impugned order.
The High Court retains jurisdiction to review its own order if the Supreme Court merely refuses special leave, especially where statute permits such review.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 8C(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of Merger
Judicial Discipline
Binding Nature of Supreme Court's Declaration of Law (Article 141)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of a rule imposing a transfer restriction on land subservient to tea estates, arguing it exceeded the state government's rule-making power under the Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had the authority under the Act to impose a prohibition on the transfer of land subservient to tea estates through delegated rules.
Whether the proviso added to Rule 3(1) of the Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1973 is intra vires the parent Act.
Whether the restriction on transfer of land within tea estates serves any purpose of the Ceiling Act.
holdings: The State Government cannot, through delegated rule-making power, impose restrictions on land that the parent Act has explicitly excluded from its operation.
The proviso prohibiting transfer of subservient land without government permission is ultra vires the Act, as it creates a substantive restriction not contemplated by the legislature.
A rule restricting transfer of land within tea estates does not advance the purposes of the Ceiling Act and cannot be sustained as a valid exercise of rule-making power.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 5(g)
Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 26
Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Rules, 1973, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of Delegated Legislation
Doctrine of Ultra Vires
Principle of Subordinate Legislation conforming to Parent Act
Right to dispose of property as part of fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f)

card.dispute: M.C. Mehta filed a public interest litigation against Kamal Nath and others for environmental degradation caused by the Span Motel's construction activities on the riverbed and banks of the River Beas in Himachal Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether a pollution fine can be imposed on Span Motel without a criminal trial under environmental statutes?
Whether the Supreme Court can use its powers under Article 142 to impose a fine bypassing statutory procedures?
Whether exemplary damages can be awarded for environmental harm in addition to restitutionary damages?
holdings: A pollution fine punishable by imprisonment or fine under environmental laws cannot be imposed without a trial and a finding of guilt under the relevant statutes.
The Supreme Court cannot use its power under Article 142 to bypass substantive statutory procedures for imposing penal fines, as this would supplant statutory law.
While penal fines require prosecution, the Court can award compensatory and exemplary damages for environmental harm under Article 32 to restore ecology and deter future violations.
provisions: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, Sections 43, 44, 45, 45A, 47, 48
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, Sections 37, 38, 39, 40, 41
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Polluter Pays Principle
Sustainable Development
