Inherent powers under Article 142 are complementary, not a substitute for statutory law

card.dispute: Lakhan Sao and Baldeo Chauhan appealed their conviction and sentence for the murder of Parmeshwar Sao, claiming false implication and lack of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved common intention under Section 34 IPC between the appellants in committing the murder.
Whether the eyewitness account of PW 6 was reliable and sufficiently corroborated.
Whether the non-recovery of the weapon and cartridge weakened the prosecution's case.
Whether the motive of the two accused being different negated the possibility of a common intention.
holdings: Common intention under Section 34 IPC can exist even if the motives of the accused differ, as long as they shared the objective to commit the murder.
The eyewitness testimony of PW 6 was credible, consistent, and corroborated by other witnesses and evidence, making it sufficient for conviction.
Non-recovery of the weapon or cartridge does not vitiate the prosecution's case if the eyewitness evidence is reliable and unshaken.
The act of Lakhan Sao holding the victim while Baldeo Chauhan shot him demonstrated active participation, establishing liability under Section 302/34 IPC.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Corroboration of eyewitness testimony
Presumption of reliability of prompt and consistent first information report (FIR)
Conviction based on substantive evidence despite non-recovery of weapon

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's review of its own judgment in a case under the Kerala Private Forests Act, questioning whether the High Court had the power to review its decision without fulfilling the conditions under Section 8C(2) of the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can exercise power to review its own decision under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971 in the absence of conditions specified under Section 8C(2).
Whether the High Court has inherent power to review its own judgment de hors the provisions of Section 8C(2) of the Act.
holdings: The High Court, as a Court of Record under Article 215 of the Constitution, possesses inherent and plenary power to correct errors apparent on the face of the record, independent of statutory provisions like Section 8C(2).

The power of review by the High Court is not limited to the grounds specified in Section 8C(2) of the Act, as its inherent jurisdiction to correct its own orders flows from its status as a superior court of record.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 8C
doctrines: Inherent powers of a Court of Record
Error apparent on the face of the record
Plenary jurisdiction of High Courts

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the validity of a land acquisition award passed after two years from the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, claiming the proceedings lapsed, while the state argued the time during which dispossession was stayed should be excluded.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed due to delay in passing the award beyond two years from the Section 6 declaration
Whether the period of court-ordered stay on dispossession is excluded in computing the two-year period under Section 11A of the Land Acquisition Act
holdings: The acquisition proceedings do not lapse if the delay in passing the award is due to a court-ordered stay on any action pursuant to the Section 6 declaration, even if only dispossession was stayed.

The period during which a court stay operates on any action following the declaration under Section 6, including dispossession, must be excluded when computing the two-year limit for passing an award under Section 11A.
doctrines: Self-operating lapse of acquisition proceedings
Exclusion of judicial stay period from statutory time limits
Purpose-based interpretation of statutory exceptions

card.dispute: The tenant, M/S Chordia Automobiles, fought against eviction for alleged wilful default in rent payment after a dispute arose over rent enhancement and failure by the landlord to provide agreed facilities.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's failure to pay rent constituted a wilful default under Section 10(2)(i) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Whether the landlord could initiate eviction proceedings before the expiry of the two-month period provided under the Explanation to the proviso of Section 10(2)(i)
holdings: A default in rent payment is not wilful if it arises from a genuine dispute over the amount or the landlord's failure to perform obligations, and the tenant has a history of regular payments.
Eviction for wilful default cannot be sustained if the landlord files the petition before the two-month period for curing the default expires, especially when part of the arrears is in dispute.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 10(2)(i)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 11
doctrines: Wilful default requires intentional and deliberate non-payment with knowledge of consequences
Explanation to proviso of Section 10(2)(i) as a substantive safeguard against premature eviction

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside the eviction of tenants who allegedly changed the use of the premises, caused nuisance, and used the property imprudently.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts under Article 227 of the Constitution
Whether the tenant committed a change of user of the leased premises
Whether the tenant caused nuisance and annoyance to the landlord
Whether the tenant used the premises imprudently, causing damage and waste
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or reverse concurrent factual findings unless they are perverse or without evidence.
Mere use of leased commercial premises for additional purposes, without structural changes or excessive burden, does not amount to change of user.
Absence of evidence from a nearby landlord-witness about nuisance creates doubt, and without supporting evidence, the finding of nuisance cannot stand.

Imprudent use causing damage is established if the tenant stores heavy materials on a tin roof leading to breakage, and failure by the High Court to consider pleadings and evidence renders its reversal erroneous.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(a)
doctrines: Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution
Doctrine of perversity in factual findings
Doctrine of imprudent use and waste under lease law

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's order allowing the respondents to adduce additional evidence in an appeal concerning a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Section 115 CPC with an order of the first appellate court refusing to allow additional evidence under Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC?
Whether the conditions under Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC were satisfied to permit the adduction of additional evidence in the appeal?
Whether the availability of advanced forensic facilities for the first time in 1999 constitutes a 'substantial cause' for admitting additional evidence?
holdings: The High Court cannot interfere under Section 115 CPC with an interlocutory order passed by the first appellate court under Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC unless there is a clear jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

Additional evidence under Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC can only be admitted if the appellate court requires it to pronounce judgment or for any other substantial cause, not merely because better scientific facilities have become available.

The mere emergence of new forensic technology after trial does not constitute a sufficient cause to admit additional evidence if the first appellate court found the existing record adequate to decide the appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI, Rule 27
doctrines: Limited scope of appellate review under Order XLI, Rule 27 CPC
Judicial discretion in admitting additional evidence must be exercised sparingly
Principle of finality of trial court record absent exceptional circumstances
Non-interference by revisional court under Section 115 CPC with discretionary orders in appeal unless jurisdictional error is shown

card.dispute: The Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd. challenged the Commissioner of Income-Tax's revision of a nil assessment order, arguing that the receipt of Rs.3,66,649 as compensation for delayed payment in a land sale was not taxable and that the revision was not justified under Section 263 of the Income Tax Act.
issues_decided: Whether the Commissioner of Income-Tax was justified in invoking jurisdiction under Section 263(1) of the Income Tax Act to revise the Assessing Officer's nil assessment order on the ground that it was erroneous and prejudicial to revenue.
Whether the amount of Rs.3,66,649 received by the appellant as compensation for delayed payment in a land sale agreement constituted a taxable receipt under the head 'income from other sources'.
holdings: The Commissioner can invoke Section 263(1) only if the Assessing Officer's order is both erroneous and prejudicial to revenue; mere disagreement with the assessment is insufficient.
An order is prejudicial to revenue if it results in loss of tax due to an erroneous application of law or fact, including failure to apply mind, even if not subversive of revenue administration.

The receipt of Rs.3,66,649 was not agricultural income as it was not linked to ongoing agricultural operations, which had ceased before the receipt, and thus was taxable under 'income from other sources'.
The High Court rightly upheld the Commissioner’s revision as the Assessing Officer failed to apply mind and acted without sufficient material in accepting the claim of agricultural income.
doctrines: Erroneous order prejudicial to revenue
Failure to apply mind by Assessing Officer
Natural justice in tax assessment
Taxability of compensation under 'income from other sources'

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents contested whether a succession certificate granted under the Indian Succession Act could operate as res judicata in a subsequent partition suit between the same parties.
issues_decided: Whether an order granting a succession certificate under Section 373 of the Indian Succession Act operates as res judicata in a later civil suit for partition?
Whether the findings in a succession certificate proceeding can finally determine the rights of heirs in a family property dispute?
holdings: A succession certificate granted under Section 373 of the Indian Succession Act is based on prima facie title and does not constitute a final adjudication of heirship or ownership rights.

Proceedings under Part X of the Indian Succession Act are summary in nature, and any decision therein does not bar a subsequent suit on the same issue between the same parties under Section 387 of the Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11 (Explanation VIII)
doctrines: Res judicata
Prima facie determination
Summary proceedings
Indemnity under succession certificate

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Mushir Mohammed Khan (defendant) fought against the legal heirs of Habibur Rehman (plaintiff) over whether the 1955 property transfer was a mortgage or an outright sale, and if redemption was permissible.
issues_decided: Whether the transaction involving the sale deed and a separate agreement for reconveyance constituted a mortgage under the Transfer of Property Act
Whether the High Court was correct in treating the transaction as a usufructuary mortgage
Whether the appellant could be allowed to redeem the property despite not filing for redemption under Order 34 Rule 5 CPC
holdings: A transaction involving a sale at a price significantly below market value, followed by a contemporaneous agreement to reconvey upon repayment, may indicate a mortgage despite the absence of an explicit mortgage deed.
The High Court erred in treating the transaction as a usufructuary mortgage without considering the agreement of reconveyance as part of the composite transaction.
Equity permits redemption where financial exploitation is evident, and the Court may intervene to prevent unjust enrichment, even if technical requirements for redemption are not met.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 34 Rule 5
doctrines: Substance over form in determining the nature of a transaction
Equitable intervention to prevent exploitation in distressed property transactions
Composite reading of contemporaneous documents to ascertain true intention of parties

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's dismissal of his second appeal on the ground that it was filed out of time without an accompanying application to condone delay.
issues_decided: Whether a second appeal filed beyond the limitation period without an accompanying application to condone delay is liable to be dismissed at the threshold.
Whether an application to condone delay filed after the memorandum of appeal can be considered valid under Order 41 Rule 3-A of the CPC.
holdings: Non-compliance with Order 41 Rule 3-A(1) of the CPC, by not filing an application to condone delay along with the appeal, does not make the appeal inherently invalid or incurably defective.
The defect of not filing a delay condonation application at the time of filing the appeal is curable, and the court may consider a belated application if filed before the appeal is rejected.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 3-A
doctrines: Curable procedural defect
Liberal interpretation of procedural rules to advance justice
Mandatory vs. directory interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The appellant, Om Prakash Jaiswal, challenged the High Court's order dropping contempt proceedings against the respondents for allegedly violating a court undertaking not to demolish his construction.
issues_decided: Whether the proceedings under Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 were initiated within the one-year limitation period prescribed under Section 20 of the Act
Whether the issuance of a show-cause notice to explain why contempt proceedings should not be initiated amounts to initiation of proceedings for contempt
holdings: Proceedings for contempt are initiated only when the court, after applying its mind, forms a prima facie opinion that a case for contempt exists and issues a show-cause notice for punishment; mere issuance of a notice to show cause why proceedings should not be initiated does not amount to initiation.

The limitation under Section 20 of the Contempt of Courts Act begins from the date of initiation of proceedings, which occurred on 6.1.1988 in this case, and was within one year of the alleged contempt, hence the proceedings were not barred.
doctrines: Initiation of contempt proceedings requires a conscious application of judicial mind
Section 20 of the Contempt of Courts Act is jurisdictional and not subject to the Limitation Act

card.dispute: Murray and Co. accused Ashok Kr. Newatia and another of committing contempt of court by filing a false affidavit in proceedings before the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed contempt of court by making a false statement in an affidavit filed before the Supreme Court.
Whether an unconditional apology can absolve a contemnor from punishment for contempt.
Whether the false statement substantially interfered with the due course of justice, warranting punishment under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
holdings: A deliberate false statement in an affidavit filed before the court constitutes criminal contempt, regardless of whether any advantage was gained.
An unconditional apology does not automatically exonerate a contemnor, though it may be considered in mitigation of punishment.
Punishment for contempt requires that the act substantially interferes with the due course of justice, and mere technical contempt is insufficient for punishment.
doctrines: Substantial interference with the due course of justice
Technical contempt
Judicial discretion in contempt punishment

card.dispute: The dispute involved whether the punishments awarded to certain DDA officers for misconduct in the Skipper Construction land allotment case were arbitrary and required upward revision.
issues_decided: Whether the punishment of 'censure' awarded to Om Kumar was arbitrary under Article 14
Whether the major punishment awarded to Virendra Nath required upward revision on grounds of arbitrariness
holdings: When administrative action in service matters is challenged as arbitrary under Article 14, courts apply Wednesbury principles of review, not proportionality, and will not interfere unless the decision is shockingly disproportionate or violates reasonableness.

The punishment of 'censure' awarded to Om Kumar did not violate Wednesbury standards, as the authority considered relevant factors and there was no illegality or perversity, making judicial non-interference appropriate.
doctrines: Wednesbury unreasonableness
Proportionality in administrative action
Secondary review in service disciplinary matters

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the declaration of 4314.60 sq. mtrs. of land as surplus under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, which was upheld in appeal and by the High Court, leading to appeals in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the proceedings under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 abate after the enactment of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999?
Whether the exception under Section 4 of the Repeal Act applies to the present case?
holdings: All pending proceedings under the principal Act abate upon the commencement of the Repeal Act, unless they relate to Sections 11–14 and involve land in the possession of the State Government or authorized authority.
Since the State failed to show it had taken possession of the surplus land, the exception under Section 4 does not apply, and the proceedings stand abated.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, Section 4
doctrines: Abatement of proceedings upon repeal of statute
Strict construction of exceptions to statutory abatement

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for specific performance of a contract to purchase property, while defendants 2 to 5, who later purchased the same property, claimed to be bona fide purchasers without notice of the prior agreement.
issues_decided: Whether defendants 2 to 5 were bona fide purchasers for value without notice of the prior agreement for sale in favour of the plaintiff?
Whether the subsequent purchasers were under a duty to inquire into the nature of the plaintiff’s possession at the time of their purchase?
Whether the defendants had constructive notice of the plaintiff’s equitable interest under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, Explanation II?
holdings: A subsequent purchaser of immovable property is deemed to have notice of the title of a person in actual possession, and must make inquiry into the nature of that possession at the time of purchase.
Mere knowledge that a person is a tenant does not absolve a purchaser from inquiring whether that tenant has any further interest, such as an agreement to purchase.

Defendants 2 to 5 failed to make necessary inquiries and acted negligently, thus they were not bona fide purchasers without notice and could not claim protection under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act.
provisions: Transfer of Property Act, Section 3 (with Explanation II)
doctrines: Constructive notice of possession
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice
Equity of the agreement to sell binding on subsequent purchasers
Duty to inquire into possessory rights

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a subsequent purchaser contested a suit for specific performance, arguing that the original plaintiff and her legal representatives were not ready and willing to perform their part of the agreement to sell the property.
issues_decided: Whether subsequent purchasers can raise the defence that the plaintiff in a suit for specific performance was not ready and willing to perform her part of the contract under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act
Whether the judgment in Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh, which restricted this defence to the original vendor, is correct
holdings: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act creates a personal bar to relief that can be invoked by any defendant, including subsequent purchasers, to challenge the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform the contract.

The decision in Jugraj Singh v. Labh Singh is erroneous to the extent it holds that only the original vendor or their legal representatives can raise the plea under Section 16(c); the plea is available to all defendants in the suit.
doctrines: Personal bar to relief under specific performance
Readiness and willingness as a condition for specific performance

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide requirement for business, which the High Court reversed, leading the tenant to appeal the restoration of eviction by the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in setting aside concurrent findings of fact by re-appreciating evidence in a second appeal?
Whether the burden of proof was wrongly placed on the tenant to show unsuitability of alternative accommodation?
Whether the landlord's admission of owning other properties negated his claim of bona fide requirement?
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence and set aside concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is involved.
The burden of proving bona fide need lies with the landlord, but once established, the tenant cannot be required to prove unsuitability of alternative premises as a defense.
Ownership of other properties does not disqualify a landlord from claiming bona fide need if those properties are occupied or unsuitable for the intended business purpose.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Burden of proof in eviction cases
Bona fide requirement doctrine

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal and its officers appealed against the High Court's order initiating contempt proceedings for non-payment of land acquisition compensation, claiming the land had already vested in the government and the decree was obtained by fraud.
issues_decided: Whether the initiation of contempt proceedings was justified against state officers for non-payment of disputed compensation in a land acquisition case.
Whether an appeal is maintainable against an order issuing a rule in contempt proceedings when the matter is pending and an unconditional apology has been accepted.
holdings: Contempt proceedings cannot be used as a substitute for execution of a decree when alternative legal remedies exist, especially where there is no willful disobedience and the compensation claim is disputed on substantial grounds.
An order issuing a rule in contempt proceedings is appealable if it involves adjudication on preliminary objections raised by the contemnor, even if the proceedings are not finally decided.
doctrines: Contempt jurisdiction should not be used for execution of money decrees when alternate remedies exist
Principle of conditional maintainability of appeals under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act

card.dispute: The heirs of Rosammal Issetheenammal Fernandez challenged the validity of a gift deed and settlement deed executed by Jossa Mariyan Fernandez, claiming they were forged and executed during his illness, while the respondents claimed the documents were valid and barred the plaintiffs' claim to a 2/5th share in the property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in admitting the registered gift deed (Exhibit B-1) in evidence under the proviso to Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act despite non-examination of attesting witnesses.
Whether the execution of the gift deed was specifically denied by the plaintiffs so as to attract the requirement of examining an attesting witness under Section 68.
holdings: The proviso to Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act does not apply if there is a specific denial of execution of a registered document; in such cases, at least one attesting witness must be examined.

The plaintiffs clearly and specifically denied the execution of the gift deed by alleging forgery and lack of capacity of the executant, which amounts to a specific denial, thus requiring proof through an attesting witness.
doctrines: Specific denial under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act
Proof of execution of attested documents

card.dispute: Rohini Prasad (defendant) and Kasturchand (plaintiff) fought over possession of agricultural land, with Rohini Prasad claiming Bhumiswami rights due to lease renewal, and Kasturchand asserting ownership after purchase.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit for possession when remedies under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code were available
Whether the High Court could interfere with the finding of fact in second appeal regarding continuation of lease
Whether Rohini Prasad had acquired Bhumiswami rights under Section 168 of the Code
holdings: Civil courts have jurisdiction to try suits for possession based on title unless there is an express statutory bar; Section 257 of the Code does not oust such jurisdiction when title is in question.
The High Court can interfere in second appeal if the lower appellate court's finding is based on a misreading of evidence leading to a miscarriage of justice.
Rohini Prasad did not acquire Bhumiswami rights under Section 168 as there was no evidence that the lease was renewed or continued beyond 1975-76.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 168
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 250
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 257
doctrines: Jurisdiction of civil courts is not ousted by revenue statutes in matters of title unless expressly excluded
Perverse finding doctrine: appellate courts may interfere if a finding is based on a misreading of evidence
Possession following title: civil courts can adjudicate possession when rooted in title

card.dispute: The decree-holder sought to execute a decree for possession after 12 years, relying on a High Court order dismissing a second appeal as time-barred, but the District Court held the execution was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the dismissal of a second appeal as time-barred affects the enforceability of the appellate decree for the purpose of limitation under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
From which date the 12-year limitation period for execution of a decree begins when an appeal is dismissed without modifying the decree.
holdings: The dismissal of a second appeal as time-barred does not constitute a decree and does not restart or affect the enforceability of the original appellate decree.
The 12-year limitation period for executing a decree begins from the date the appellate decree becomes enforceable, which is the date of the final appellate decision confirming the decree.
doctrines: Definition of 'decree' under Section 2(2) of CPC
Enforceability of decree from date of final appellate order
Limitation period commences from enforceable date of decree
Non-decree status of orders dismissing appeals as time-barred

card.dispute: Two appellants, Rajendra Singh and Triloki Singh, challenged their conviction and sentence for the murder of Kameshwar Singh, claiming the incident was a sudden fight and that common intention under Section 34 IPC was not established.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution complied with Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act while seeking to contradict a witness with a previous statement?
Whether the case falls under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, reducing the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder?
Whether Triloki Singh shared a common intention with the other accused under Section 34 IPC to attract liability for murder?
holdings: The prosecution failed to comply with Section 145 of the Evidence Act as the witness was not specifically confronted with the part of his prior statement sought to be used for contradiction, and the document was not properly authenticated.
Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC does not apply because the attack was not sudden or unpremeditated; the accused went to fetch weapons and launched a coordinated assault, indicating pre-planning.

Triloki Singh did not share the common intention to commit murder; his act of striking a non-fatal blow on the leg does not establish participation in the fatal assault, so conviction under Section 302/34 IPC is unsustainable.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Exception 4 to Section 300
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires active participation and shared purpose, not merely similar intention.
Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies only to sudden, unpremeditated fights without undue advantage or cruelty.
Section 145 of the Evidence Act mandates that a witness must be specifically shown the part of a prior statement intended to contradict him before it can be used.

card.dispute: Rajendra Kumar (appellant) claimed possession of property as the adopted son of Mahadeo, whose own adoption by Mohanlal had been previously contested, against Kalyan's legal heirs who relied on prior judicial findings negating Mahadeo's adoption.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of res judicata or constructive res judicata under Section 11 CPC applies to bar the present suit?
Whether the appellant could claim rights in Mohanlal's property independently as an adopted son of Mahadeo, despite Mahadeo's adoption having been previously negated?
Whether procedural changes by the 1976 Amendment Act apply retrospectively to pending actions?
holdings: The second suit is barred by res judicata under Section 11 CPC read with Explanation VIII, as the appellant's claim arose out of the same title and was directly related to issues already decided against Radhabai, his adoptive mother, in a prior suit.

The appellant cannot claim co-parcenary rights in Mohanlal’s property independently through legal fiction of being deemed born at the time of Mahadeo’s adoption, since Mahadeo’s adoption was conclusively negated in earlier proceedings.
Procedural laws, including the 1976 Amendment to CPC, apply retrospectively to pending cases unless expressly excluded, as no vested rights exist in procedural matters.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12(c)
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Legal fiction of deemed birth in adoption
Retrospective application of procedural law

card.dispute: The Sajjadanashin of three Rozas contested whether proceedings to declare them as public trusts under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 were barred by res judicata due to earlier rulings.
issues_decided: Whether the findings in earlier proceedings operated as res judicata against the present inquiry into the public trust status of the Rozas at Broach and Surat.
Whether a change in the legal definition of 'wakf' under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 affected the applicability of res judicata based on pre-1950 findings.
Whether a 1967 order declaring the wakf as private created res judicata when later overruled by a contrary High Court judgment.
holdings: A finding in a prior suit is not res judicata if it was merely incidental, collateral, or auxiliary to the main issue and not necessary for the decision.

The 1931 determination that a wakf was private does not bar a new inquiry because the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 expanded the definition of public wakf to include family maintenance if ultimate benefit goes to charity.
An earlier administrative decision on the nature of a wakf is not binding if superseded by a subsequent contrary judgment between the same parties.
doctrines: Res judicata
Incidental or collateral findings not binding
Prospective overruling of administrative decisions by judicial precedent

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the High Court's interference with the Appellate Authority's decision that had overturned the Rent Controller's order permitting termination of tenancy on grounds of habitual default, subletting, and bona fide need.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 by re-appreciating evidence and interfering with findings of fact by the Appellate Authority under the Rent Control Order.
Whether the tenant was a habitual defaulter in rent payment within the meaning of Section 13(3)(ii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949.
Whether the tenant sub-let the premises in violation of Section 13(3)(iii) of the Rent Control Order.
holdings: The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 when it interfered with the Appellate Authority’s findings, as the interference was justified due to manifest error, misconstruction of documents, and failure to consider relevant material.

A tenant who consistently delays rent payment beyond the due date, even if paid within a grace period, can be considered a habitual defaulter under Section 13(3)(ii) if the pattern shows continuity of default.

Subletting was established where the tenant allowed another party to conduct business in the premises for a monthly payment, satisfying both parting with possession and consideration, even if not formally leased.
provisions: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Section 13(3)(ii)
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Section 13(3)(iii)
Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, Section 21
doctrines: Supervisory jurisdiction of High Court under Articles 226 and 227
Manifest error doctrine
Mixed question of law and fact
Principle of re-appreciation of evidence by High Court

card.dispute: The appellants claimed Sirdari rights by adverse possession over land previously held by Jethu, while the Deputy Director awarded the land to the Gram Sabha after finding revenue entries forged; the appellants challenged this decision.
issues_decided: Whether the Gaon Sabha could be awarded the property in the absence of a valid claimant when the tenure-holder was declared dead and no legal heir was proven.

Whether the Deputy Director exceeded his jurisdiction under Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 by reviewing claims across all three villages despite a revision being filed for only one.
holdings: The Deputy Director was justified in vesting the property in the Gram Sabha when the tenure-holder was found to have died a civil death and no legitimate heir or valid adverse possession claim was established.

The Deputy Director had wide powers under Section 48 to review the entire record and adjudicate on all claims if revenue entries were found forged or made contrary to law, even if the revision was limited to one village.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Escheat and bona vacantia
Adverse possession
Revisional jurisdiction

card.dispute: The taxpayer challenged the constitutional validity of provisions taxing capital gains from the sale of agricultural land within municipal limits, arguing such income is exempt as agricultural income under the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Explanation to sub-section (1A) and clause (iii) of sub-section (14) of Section 2 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 are unconstitutional
Whether capital gains from the sale of agricultural land within municipal limits constitute agricultural income exempt from Union taxation
holdings: The definition of agricultural income in Article 366(1) of the Constitution refers to the definition in current income tax enactments, which Parliament may amend.
Income from the transfer of agricultural land within specified municipal limits is excluded from agricultural income and is liable to capital gains tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 46, List II, Seventh Schedule
Constitution of India, Entry 82, List I, Seventh Schedule
doctrines: Referential incorporation
Division of legislative powers between Union and States
Amendment by reference to evolving statutory definitions

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh and others fought with private landowners over whether a property was subject to a public or charitable trust under the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966.
issues_decided: Whether the order under Section 77 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, declaring the property not to be an endowment, operates as a bar to the civil suit?
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit after the Act came into force?
Whether the order under Section 77 of the Act could be challenged by a civil suit not filed under Section 78 of the Act?
holdings: An order under Section 77 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, if not challenged under Section 78, is final and conclusive, and bars a civil court from re-examining the question of whether a property is an endowment.
The civil court's jurisdiction is excluded when a statute provides an adequate alternative remedy, as long as the statutory authority acts within its powers and follows due procedure.
A suit not filed under Section 78 of the Act cannot challenge an order under Section 77, even if the same issue of endowment is raised in civil proceedings.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 77
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1966, Section 78
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction by statutory alternative remedy
Finality and conclusiveness of quasi-judicial orders under special statutes
Res judicata and binding effect of administrative orders in specialized domains

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh and a Sales Tax Officer challenged the admissibility of a delayed second appeal filed without an accompanying application to condone delay, which the High Court dismissed on that ground alone.
issues_decided: Whether a second appeal filed beyond the prescribed period without an accompanying application to condone delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is liable to be dismissed at the threshold
Whether non-compliance with Order 41 Rule 3-A(1) of the CPC, requiring a delay condonation application to accompany a time-barred appeal, is a curable defect
holdings: A second appeal filed out of time without an accompanying application to condone delay is not automatically invalid; the defect is curable if the application is filed later before the appeal is rejected.

Order 41 Rule 3-A(1) of the CPC, though mandatory in requiring a delay condonation application to accompany a time-barred appeal, does not make non-compliance fatal if the defect is subsequently cured.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 3-A
doctrines: Curable defect doctrine
Mandatory vs. directory interpretation
Liberal construction of procedural rules to secure justice

card.dispute: The villagers challenged the Gram Panchayat's leasing out of 'charand' land, claiming it violated their grazing rights and constitutional protections.
issues_decided: Whether 'charand' land is included within the definition of 'shamilat-deh' under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961
Whether the Gram Panchayat can legally lease out shamilat-deh land for cultivation under the Rules
Whether the leasing of the land violated Article 31A of the Constitution or the rights of the villagers
Whether the appellants' delay and prior conduct barred their legal challenge
holdings: Charand land in Haryana is legally part of shamilat-deh and vests in the Gram Panchayat under Section 2(g) of the Act.
The Gram Panchayat may use shamilat-deh land for any purpose specified in Rule 3(2), including leasing for cultivation or forestry.
The leasing does not violate Article 31A or villagers' rights, as the land's use may change post-vesting and no compensation is required.
The appellants' delay in challenging the leasing, coupled with their prior acceptance of leases, renders their suit non-bona fide and barred by laches.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, Section 2(g)
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Rules, 1964, Rule 3(2)
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Statutory Interpretation of 'shamilat-deh'
Bona fide litigation doctrine

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's acquittal of seven accused, including Teja Ram and Ram Lal, convicted by the trial court for the double murder of Ram Lal and his mother under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the accused based on the insufficiency of circumstantial evidence, particularly regarding the recovery of blood-stained axes?
Whether the signature of the accused on seizure memos under Section 27 of the Evidence Act vitiates the recovery evidence?
Whether the inconsistency in a witness's statement regarding disclosure of assailants' names affects the prosecution's case?
holdings: The High Court erred in discarding the recovery of blood-stained axes as unreliable; failure to determine blood origin does not negate that the blood was human or that the weapons were used in the crime.
Obtaining the accused's signature on seizure memos under Section 27 of the Evidence Act does not violate Section 162 CrPC and does not vitiate the recovery evidence.

A witness’s initial failure to name assailants, followed by disclosure during investigation, can be used to impeach credibility under Sections 14 and 155(3) of the Evidence Act, and does not fatally undermine the prosecution case.
doctrines: Principle of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Standard of proof in circumstantial evidence cases
Doctrine of benefit of doubt in criminal trials
Use of prior inconsistent statements to impeach witness credibility

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the initiation of disciplinary proceedings against two senior bureaucrats, alleging mala fide and bias by the new state government after a change in political regime.
issues_decided: Whether the initiation of disciplinary proceedings against the respondents was mala fide and biased.
Whether the courts could interfere at the stage of initiation of inquiry due to alleged bias and pre-determination.
Whether the Chief Secretary's actions in forwarding vigilance complaints and initiating inquiries were justified and free from personal vendetta.
holdings: The court held that the initiation of disciplinary proceedings showed signs of bias and pre-determination, particularly due to the Chief Minister's public announcement of an inquiry irrespective of the reply, undermining fair process.
Courts can intervene at the initial stage of disciplinary proceedings if there is clear evidence of mala fide, bias, or a predetermined mind, to prevent harassment of public officials.

The Chief Secretary's actions in forwarding complaints and initiating CBI inquiries were justified given the serious irregularities and lack of cabinet approval, and could not be attributed to personal vendetta.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (implied by CBI investigation context)
doctrines: Principle of fairness in administrative action
Doctrine of mala fide in service jurisprudence
Rule against bias and pre-determination in inquiry proceedings
Judicial review at pre-inquiry stage in cases of alleged bias

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra fought with the legal heirs of Pravin Jethalal Kamdar over whether the state's acquisition of property under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 was valid and whether the suit for possession was barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaration and possession was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the order under Section 27(1) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 and the subsequent sale deed were void ab initio
Whether equitable considerations barred the plaintiff from seeking relief of possession despite receiving sale consideration
holdings: When a document is void ab initio and without jurisdiction, it can be ignored as a nullity, and a suit for possession based on title is governed by Article 65 of the Limitation Act, making it within time if filed within 12 years of adverse possession.

An order under Section 27(1) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, which restricts transfer of land within the ceiling limit, is without jurisdiction and void, rendering any sale deed executed pursuant to it also a nullity.

Equitable relief cannot be denied solely because consideration was accepted when the sale was compelled by an illegal order; the plaintiff is entitled to possession upon refund of the amount received.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 27(1)
doctrines: Void ab initio
Adverse possession
Equitable relief
Without jurisdiction nullity

card.dispute: The assessee company and the tax department disputed whether forfeited amounts from an abortive sale of rubber trees were capital or revenue receipts for income tax purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the amounts forfeited from an uncompleted sale of rubber trees constitute capital or revenue receipts.
Whether the nature of a receipt can change due to subsequent events after the initial receipt.
holdings: Amounts received and retained as advance or earnest money in negotiations for the transfer of a capital asset are capital receipts, even if the sale does not materialize.
The character of a receipt is determined at the time of receipt and does not change merely because the sale transaction is later aborted.
doctrines: Rule in Morley v. Tattersall
Compensation under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act treated as capital if linked to capital asset
Principle from London and Thames Haven Oil Wharves Ltd. v. Attwooll

card.dispute: The revenue and the assessee fought over whether compensation received for the compulsory purchase of electricity undertakings was taxable under Section 41(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in the assessment year 1965-66, before the final price was determined.
issues_decided: Whether the addition of Rs.1,29,35,557/- under Section 41(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 was justified in the assessment year 1965-66 when the final compensation for the compulsory purchase of the assessee's undertakings had not been determined.
Whether income under Section 41(2) accrues only when compensation is finally ascertained or when it is received or becomes due.
holdings: The balancing charge under Section 41(2) of the Income-tax Act is taxable in the year the compensation is received or becomes due, even if the final amount is subject to dispute or later determination.

Pendency of litigation or arbitration over the compensation amount does not prevent the accrual of taxable income; the taxable event is the receipt or accrual of compensation, not its final judicial or arbitral determination.
doctrines: Accrual of income doctrine
Balancing charge under Section 41(2)
Taxability on receipt or due date, not final determination

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the Central Administrative Tribunal's decision that Dudh Nath Prasad, born in Bihar but raised in West Bengal, belonged to the 'Nuniya' Scheduled Caste of West Bengal and was thus validly appointed against a reserved vacancy.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was 'ordinarily residing' in West Bengal for the purpose of being classified as a member of the 'Nuniya' Scheduled Caste notified in that state.
Whether the concept of 'domicile' under private international law applies to the interpretation of 'ordinarily residing' in the context of caste certification and reservation benefits.
Whether the respondent's birth and ancestral property in Bihar affected his status as a member of a Scheduled Caste in West Bengal.
holdings: A person is 'ordinarily residing' in a place if they have a settled intention to live there for a considerable time, which does not require formal domicile or ownership of property.
The legal concept of 'domicile' from private international law does not apply to the interpretation of 'ordinarily residing' in statutes related to electoral rights or reservation policies.

The long-term residence of the respondent's parents in West Bengal for over 30 years established their ordinary residence there, entitling the respondent to be classified under the 'Nuniya' Scheduled Caste of that state.
provisions: Representation of the People Act, 1950, Section 20
doctrines: Ordinary residence
Domicile in private international law
Contextual interpretation of statutory terms

card.dispute: Quarry owners challenged Bihar's notifications enhancing royalty rates for minor minerals, arguing the delegation of power to fix rates was unguided and ultra vires.
issues_decided: Whether the delegation of power to the State Government under Section 15 of the Mines and Minerals Act, 1957 is unbridled and without sufficient guidelines
Whether the State Government must confine royalty fixation within the 12% benchmark laid down in D.K. Trivedi v. State of Gujarat
Whether the requirement to place notifications before the State Legislature under Section 28(3) acts as a valid check on delegated power
Whether the royalty enhancement in the impugned notifications was arbitrary or excessive
holdings: The delegation of power under Section 15 is not unbridled, as the Act provides sufficient guidelines through its Preamble, object, and provisions.
The State Government is not bound by the 12% royalty benchmark from D.K. Trivedi; it may fix rates beyond that if justified by the Act’s framework.
Placing rules or notifications before the State Legislature under Section 28(3) serves as a valid procedural check on the exercise of delegated power.
Non-compliance with the requirement to place the 1994 notification before the Legislature is a procedural lapse, but the requirement is directory, not mandatory, so the notification remains valid.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 15
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 28(3)
Constitution of India, Entry 54 List I, Entry 23 List II, Article 151, Article 338
doctrines: Doctrine of delegated legislation with sufficient guidelines
Doctrine of harmonious construction in federal structure
Directory vs mandatory provision
Principle of legislative control over subordinate legislation

card.dispute: Industries in Andhra Pradesh challenged the state's interpretation of 'used' in the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, arguing that only land actually used for industrial purposes, not land meant to be used, should be taxed.
issues_decided: Whether the word 'used' in Section 3 of the Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, includes land meant to be used or set apart for industrial or commercial purposes, or only land actually in use.
Whether a wider interpretation of 'used' is permissible in a fiscal statute when the language is not explicit.
holdings: The word 'used' in a taxing statute must be given its plain, literal meaning; it refers only to land actually in use for industrial, commercial, or other non-agricultural purposes, not land merely intended for such use.
Courts cannot impute unexpressed legislative intent in fiscal statutes; when language is clear, no addition or implication is permitted, and any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of the taxpayer.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 2(d)
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 2(g)
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, 1963, Section 3
doctrines: Strict construction of taxing statutes
Rule of literal interpretation in fiscal laws
Benefit of doubt in favor of the assessee

card.dispute: U.P. State Sugar Corporation Ltd. and Dewa Ram (respondents 2 to 5) fought over sirdari rights to Plot Nos. 1366, 1367, and 1368 in Village Maliyana, Meerut, based on competing claims of ownership and lease by the Gaon Sabha.
issues_decided: Whether the land in dispute vested in the State under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, thereby enabling its vesting in the Gaon Sabha under Section 117.
Whether the Gaon Sabha had the legal authority to grant a lease of the disputed land to Dewa Ram.
Whether the Consolidation Authorities had jurisdiction to examine the validity of the lease granted by the Gaon Sabha.
holdings: The land, being appurtenant to the staff quarter and used for mill purposes, did not vest in the State under Section 6 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and hence could not vest in the Gaon Sabha under Section 117.
Since the Gaon Sabha had no title to the land, its lease to Dewa Ram was void ab initio and conferred no legal rights.
Consolidation Authorities have jurisdiction to examine and reject void documents, including leases, when adjudicating rights under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 6
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 117
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 195
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 197
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 198
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 9
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Void acts and documents do not deprive quasi-judicial authorities of jurisdiction to examine their validity.
Concurrent findings of fact by lower authorities are binding unless overturned.
Jurisdiction of consolidation authorities includes determining title where rights under land reform laws are claimed.

card.dispute: Residents challenged the State's notification proposing to include their area within the Tarikere Town Panchayat, claiming their objections were not considered.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petition challenging the preliminary notification under Section 349 of the Karnataka Municipalities Act was maintainable?
Whether the rights of the petitioners were substantially affected by the preliminary notification?
holdings: A writ petition challenging a preliminary notification under Section 349 of the Karnataka Municipalities Act is not maintainable if no final notification has been issued.
The rights of the petitioners are not affected merely by the issuance of a preliminary notification; hence, judicial intervention at that stage is premature.
doctrines: Prematurity of writ jurisdiction
Doctrine of ripeness

card.dispute: The landlord sued to recover possession of land after the tenant rebuilt a shop on the site without permission following the original shop's destruction by fire; the tenant claimed tenancy continued under the Transfer of Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether tenancy under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act survives the total destruction of the leased premises by natural calamity
Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit for recovery of possession of land when the superstructure has been destroyed and no tenancy under the Rent Act can be enforced
holdings: Tenancy under the Kerala Rent Act is extinguished upon total destruction of the leased superstructure, as the Act protects occupation of the building, not vacant land.
The civil court has jurisdiction to hear a suit for possession of land when the tenancy ends due to destruction of the building, as the Rent Act does not provide remedies in such cases.
provisions: The Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, Section 2(1)
The Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, Section 4
The Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, Section 11
The Transfer of Property Act, Section 108(B)(e)
doctrines: Extinguishment of tenancy by destruction of subject matter
Jurisdiction of civil court in absence of specific statutory remedy

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a decree-holder sought to execute a decree for specific performance, while the legal heirs of the deceased judgment-debtor resisted, claiming the appellate decree was a nullity as it was passed after the death of the appellant.
issues_decided: Whether a judgment passed by a High Court in a second appeal after the death of the appellant, without impleading legal heirs, is a nullity?
Whether the doctrine of merger applies when a second appeal abates due to the death of the appellant?
Whether the decree of the first appellate court becomes final upon abatement of the second appeal?
holdings: A judgment passed against a deceased party in an appeal, without impleading legal representatives, is a nullity.
The doctrine of merger does not apply when a second appeal abates due to the death of the appellant and no legal heirs are brought on record.
Upon abatement of an appeal, the decree of the lower appellate court becomes final and executable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 4
doctrines: Doctrine of merger
Abatement of proceedings due to death of a party

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the limitation period for executing a partition decree begins only after the decree is engrossed on stamp paper, or from the date of its pronouncement.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation for execution of a partition decree starts from the date of its pronouncement or from the date it is engrossed on stamp paper.
Whether an unstamped or insufficiently stamped partition decree affects the running of limitation under the Limitation Act.
holdings: The limitation period for execution of a partition decree begins from the date of its pronouncement, not from when it is engrossed on stamp paper.
Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act does not suspend the limitation period; non-compliance with stamping requirements does not render the decree unenforceable for limitation purposes.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Section 2(15) and Section 35
doctrines: Strict construction of fiscal statutes
Later legislation prevails in case of conflict
Judicial avoidance of absurdity in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property qualifies as a 'suit for land' under clause 12 of the Bombay High Court's Letters Patent, affecting the court's jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether a suit simpliciter for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property is a 'suit for land' within clause 12 of the Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court?
Whether the relief of possession, when not specifically claimed, makes a suit for specific performance a 'suit for land'?
holdings: A suit simpliciter for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property is not a 'suit for land' under clause 12 of the Letters Patent if the relief of possession is not specifically claimed.

A suit for specific performance is primarily for enforcement of a contract; it does not directly adjudicate title or seek possession, and thus does not amount to a 'suit for land' unless such reliefs are expressly claimed.
provisions: Letters Patent of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Clause 12
doctrines: Interpretation of 'suit for land'
Relief must be specifically claimed to be granted (under Section 22, Specific Relief Act)
Distinction between enforcement of contract and adjudication of title

card.dispute: The tenant challenged the eviction order on the grounds that the landlord failed to serve a six-month notice as required under the first proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972.
issues_decided: Whether the first proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the Act requires a six-month notice for eviction applications filed more than three years after the landlord's purchase of the property.
Whether the failure to serve a six-month notice invalidates eviction proceedings when the application is filed after the three-year period from purchase.
holdings: The six-month notice requirement under the first proviso to Section 21(1)(a) of the Act is not mandatory if the landlord files the eviction application more than three years after purchasing the property.
The proviso's purpose is to prevent fraudulent transfers for eviction; it does not create a permanent restriction, and no notice is needed after the three-year period has elapsed.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a) and its first proviso
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutes
Interpretation of welfare legislation to protect tenants

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the order imposing stamp duty and penalty for an insufficiently stamped sale agreement, and the maintainability of his appeal against that order.
issues_decided: Whether the procedure under Section 47A of the Indian Stamp Act applies when an insufficiently stamped document is produced before a civil court, not for registration but as evidence?
Whether an appeal under Section 47A is maintainable without depositing the differential stamp duty as mandated by the proviso to Section 47A(2)?
What is the correct procedure to be followed by a civil court when an insufficiently stamped document is produced before it?
holdings: Section 47A of the Indian Stamp Act does not apply when a document is presented before a civil court for use as evidence and not for registration; the correct procedure is under Section 40 of the Stamp Act.
The appeal under Section 47A is not maintainable unless the appellant deposits the differential stamp duty as required by the proviso to Section 47A(2), which is a condition precedent.

A civil court must first determine if a document is insufficiently stamped, then give the party an option to pay the deficient stamp duty with penalty; if paid, the document may be admitted in evidence and a copy sent to the Collector; if not, the original must be forwarded to the Collector for adjudication.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Amendment to the Indian Stamp Act
doctrines: Condition precedent
Proper legal procedure under fiscal statutes
Impounding of insufficiently stamped instruments
Adjudication of stamp duty by Collector

card.dispute: Indian Christians challenged Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 as discriminatory for requiring them to obtain probate, unlike Hindus and Muslims who are exempt in certain cases.
issues_decided: Whether Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is unconstitutional for being discriminatory against Indian Christians?
Whether the requirement of probate under Section 213 applies exclusively to Christians?
Whether differential treatment in testamentary succession based on historical and territorial grounds violates the right to equality?
holdings: Section 213 does not exclusively apply to Christians but also to Hindus, Parsis, and others in specified territories, hence no religious discrimination exists.
The requirement of probate under Section 213 is a procedural rule of evidence and not a condition for vesting of property, and its applicability varies by region for historical reasons.
Differential treatment in testamentary succession based on geographical and historical factors does not violate equality if it has a rational basis and is not solely religion-based.
doctrines: Doctrine of Equality under Article 14
Procedural vs. Substantive Law Distinction
Doctrine of Rational Classification

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for dishonour of a post-dated cheque, arguing that the six-month period for presentation should be calculated from the date of delivery, not the date on the cheque.
issues_decided: Whether a post-dated cheque is a 'cheque' under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act before the date mentioned on it.
From which date the six-month period for presenting a post-dated cheque under Section 138 should be reckoned.
holdings: A post-dated cheque is not a cheque under Section 138 until the date mentioned on it arrives; until then, it is a bill of exchange.
The six-month period for presenting a cheque under Section 138 of the Act must be calculated from the date on the cheque, not the date of delivery.
doctrines: Cheque becomes payable on demand only on the date mentioned on it
Distinction between bill of exchange and cheque under the Negotiable Instruments Act

card.dispute: Christ the King Cathedral challenged the validity of government notifications exempting religious buildings from rent control laws, which tenants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the government exercised proper discretion in issuing notifications exempting religious and charitable institutions from the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 under Section 25
Whether the exemption notifications were arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether material was required to be placed on record to justify the exemption in public interest
holdings: The government can exempt religious and charitable institutions from rent control if the exemption serves public interest, even without recorded reasons, provided the class is distinct and purpose is legitimate.
Exemption of religious buildings like churches, mosques, and trusts from rent control does not violate Article 14 if they form a distinct class serving public purposes.
Prior judicial recognition of religious and charitable institutions as a valid class supports exemption; absence of detailed material does not invalidate the decision if public interest is evident.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 25
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 29
doctrines: Classification under Article 14
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness in administrative action
Public interest as a ground for statutory exemption
Judicial precedent as justification for executive action

card.dispute: The plaintiffs appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside the trial court's order restoring their suit, which had been dismissed for default, on grounds of limitation in the restoration application.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court failed to consider the issue of limitation while restoring the suit under Order 9 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court's order in revision on the ground of non-consideration of delay condonation
holdings: The trial court implicitly considered and condoned the delay in filing the restoration application by accepting the grounds stated in the application, even without an explicit reference to the Section 5 petition.

The High Court erred in setting aside the trial court's order as there was no jurisdictional error or material irregularity, and the trial court's decision to restore the suit was validly based on sufficient cause.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 9 Rule 9
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Revisional jurisdiction
Sufficient cause for non-appearance
Deemed consideration of delay

card.dispute: The landlord sued to evict the tenant from a shop for rent default, while the tenant claimed protection from eviction by depositing rent in court under Section 19A of the Rajasthan Premises Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's deposit of rent in court under Section 19A was valid in the absence of proof of service of notice to the landlord under Section 19A(3)(b)?
Whether the tenant fulfilled the conditions for deemed payment of rent under Section 19A to avoid being a defaulter?
holdings: A tenant's right to deposit rent in court under Section 19A arises only if they first attempt payment via one of the two methods in clauses (a) or (b) of sub-section (3), which include sending a written notice to the landlord requesting bank details.

The tenant failed to prove service of the written notice to the landlord as required under Section 19A(3)(b), and the certificate of posting was insufficient to raise a presumption of service under Section 114(f) of the Evidence Act.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 19A
doctrines: Deemed payment under statutory fiction
Rule of harmonious construction
Permissive presumption under Section 114 of the Evidence Act
Contextual interpretation of 'and' as 'or' in statutes

card.dispute: The landlord, G. C. Kapoor, fought to evict tenant Nand Kumar Bhasin from commercial premises, claiming bonafide need to start a computer consultancy centre for his son who had completed technical education.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord established a bonafide requirement of the premises for self-employment of a family member under Section 21(1)(a) of the UP Urban Buildings Act, 1972?
Whether the landlord's financial capacity to start the proposed business is a necessary condition for granting eviction?
Whether the son's lack of affidavit or prior business activity negates the claim of bonafide need?
Whether the tenant would suffer disproportionate hardship upon eviction?
holdings: A landlord can seek eviction if the premises are bonafide required for self-employment of a family member with technical education, provided all conditions under Rule 16(2)(d) are met.
Financial capacity to fund the proposed business is not a legal prerequisite for eviction; ownership of property and ability to raise funds suffice.
The absence of an affidavit from the son or delay in starting the business does not disprove bonafide need if the crucial date of application shows genuine intent.
Eviction may be granted if the landlord suffers greater hardship than the tenant, especially when the tenant has alternative business space and the landlord has none.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Rules, 1972, Rule 16(2)(d)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 41
doctrines: Bonafide requirement doctrine
Rule of constructive consideration for self-employment under tenancy law
Hardship balancing test in eviction cases
Crucial date rule for determining bonafide need

card.dispute: The auction purchaser challenged the setting aside of a property sale, arguing the judgment-debtor's deposit was made beyond the 30-day period under CPC Order XXI Rule 92(2), while the judgment-debtor claimed the 60-day limitation under Article 127 of the Limitation Act applied.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation for depositing money under Order XXI Rule 89 CPC is 30 days under Rule 92(2) CPC or 60 days under Article 127 of the Limitation Act.
Whether Order XXI Rule 92(2) CPC prescribes a mandatory time limit for deposit or merely removes judicial discretion if deposit is made within 30 days.
holdings: Order XXI Rule 92(2) CPC does not prescribe a period of limitation for deposit but only mandates setting aside the sale if deposit is made within 30 days.
The deposit for setting aside a sale can be made within 60 days under Article 127 of the Limitation Act, and beyond 30 days it is within the court's discretion to allow the application.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXI Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXI Rule 92(2)
doctrines: Harmonious construction of statutes
Legislative intent in statutory interpretation
Judicial restraint in amending statutory language

card.dispute: The landlord, Deena Nath, sought eviction of tenant Pooran Lal on grounds of default and bonafide requirement for his son's business, which the tenant contested as non-genuine and motivated by rent enhancement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of the lower courts on the landlord’s bonafide requirement under Section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961?
Whether the landlord had a bonafide need for the suit premises for starting his son's business despite having other reasonably suitable non-residential accommodations available?
holdings: The High Court can interfere with concurrent findings if they are manifestly erroneous or fail to apply statutory requirements under Section 12(1)(f), especially when the landlord has other suitable accommodations available.

A bonafide requirement under Section 12(1)(f) must be genuine and pressing, not a mere desire; it cannot be upheld if the landlord possesses other reasonably suitable non-residential premises in the same town.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Manifest error doctrine
Limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for personal use to start a medical clinic for his son and a radio repair business for himself, but the tenant resisted eviction citing changes in circumstances during the 23-year litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide need for eviction under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act remains valid despite subsequent events during prolonged litigation.
Whether the passage of time and changes in circumstances during litigation extinguish the landlord's right to eviction based on personal need.
holdings: The crucial date to assess the landlord's bona fide need for eviction is the date of filing the petition, and such need does not automatically lapse due to delays in litigation.

Subsequent events during litigation will not defeat the claim for eviction unless they completely satisfy the landlord's original need; mere passage of time or personal changes do not erase established bona fides.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for personal use in eviction cases
Continuing nature of cause of action in rent control litigation
Cautious consideration of subsequent events affecting relief
Adjudication based on lis mota principle (rights as on date of suit)

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the limitation period for executing a partition decree begins only after the decree is engrossed on stamp paper, or from the date of its pronouncement.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation for execution of a partition decree starts from the date of its pronouncement or from the date it is engrossed on stamp paper?
Whether Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 bars the enforceability of a partition decree and suspends the limitation period until it is properly stamped?
holdings: The limitation period for executing a partition decree begins from the date of its pronouncement, not from when it is engrossed on stamp paper.

Section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act does not suspend the limitation period; it only bars unstamped documents from being admitted in evidence or acted upon, but does not affect the running of limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963.
doctrines: Strict construction of fiscal statutes
Presumption that legislature is aware of existing laws
Separate legal conceptions of 'executability' and 'enforceability'

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the allotment of 15 biswas of pond land to respondents, arguing it was public land meant for community use and not eligible for private allotment under land reform laws.
issues_decided: Whether the disputed land, being part of a pond, could be allotted as an abadi site under Section 122-C(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Whether the High Court was correct in partially confirming the allotment of 10 biswas of the pond land
holdings: Land that forms part of a pond, even if partially dried, cannot be allotted as an abadi site because it vests in the Gaon Sabha under Section 117(vi) and does not fall under the categories of land eligible for allotment under Section 122-C(1).
No portion of a pond, regardless of its current use or condition, can be lawfully allotted for private construction, as such land is meant for public utility and ecological preservation.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 117
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 122-C
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 3(14)
doctrines: Ecological balance and environmental protection as integral to the right to life under Article 21
Strict interpretation of statutory eligibility for land allotment under land reform laws
Concurrent findings of fact by revenue authorities given due weight unless perverse

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent, a married couple, disputed the validity of a mutual consent divorce agreement and related property and custody arrangements.
issues_decided: Whether the Family Court had the jurisdiction to modify its own decree in a mutual consent divorce proceeding under the Special Marriage Act, 1954
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition challenging the modification of the divorce decree
Whether the agreement for dissolution of marriage by mutual consent was valid and enforceable
holdings: The Family Court has the inherent power to modify its decree in a mutual consent divorce case before the statutory period for appeal expires.
The High Court was correct in upholding the Family Court's modified order as it was passed within its jurisdiction.
The mutual consent divorce agreement, including terms on property and child custody, was valid and binding on both parties.
doctrines: Principle of finality in mutual consent divorce
Inherent powers of civil courts
Judicial review of family court orders

card.dispute: M.C. Mehta, a social activist, fought against the Union of India and others over the non-compliance of Supreme Court orders directing hazardous (H category) industries in Delhi to relocate and surrender their land for public green space.
issues_decided: Whether the order directing surrender of land by H category industries applies universally despite a contrary decision in a specific case (vegetable oil industry)
Whether land must be surrendered with an approach road and free from encumbrances
Whether industries entitled to retain up to 100 sq. meters of land must still surrender it
Whether industries that have relocated or obtained fresh clearances need to surrender land
Whether industries not appearing before the Court can later claim they were closed before the 1996 order
Whether the obligation to surrender land applies to landowners even if the hazardous industry was run by a tenant
