holdings: The 1996 order mandating surrender of land by H category industries remains binding and was not diluted by a later decision in a fact-specific case.

Land must be surrendered with an approach road if the owner controls it; otherwise, surrender is on an 'as is where is' basis, but the owner cannot benefit from retained land unless encumbrances are removed within five years.
Industries entitled to retain up to 100 sq. meters of land need not surrender it, as such small plots are of no use to the public.
Industries that have obtained fresh clearances and started operations in compliance with the Master Plan need not surrender land; others must comply with the surrender order.
Industries listed in court orders but not objecting at the time cannot later claim exemption by asserting closure before the 1996 order.
Landowners are bound to surrender land if a hazardous industry operated on it, regardless of tenancy, as the closure and surrender orders apply to the land itself.
doctrines: Sustainable development
Public trust doctrine
Principle of environmental protection in public interest litigation

card.dispute: The tenant, Lekh Raj, challenged the High Court's decision in revision to evict him on grounds that the shop was unfit for human habitation, based on a local commissioner's report.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in exercise of revisional jurisdiction, could reverse the appellate court's finding on the fitness of the shop for human habitation based on evidence on record.
Whether the High Court could appoint a local commissioner and rely on the commissioner's report in revision to determine the condition of the property.
holdings: The High Court, while exercising revisional jurisdiction, can consider subsequent facts such as the deteriorated condition of a property and reverse findings if such facts are legally brought on record.

The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction in appointing a local commissioner to assess the current condition of the property and relying on the report to determine unfitness for human habitation.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 15(5)
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction allows consideration of subsequent events affecting the subject matter of litigation.
A local commissioner may be appointed in revision to ascertain current factual conditions, though not to determine questions of fault or title.

card.dispute: The appellant sought to set aside an ex-parte decree passed against him in a suit for possession of agricultural land and mesne profits, claiming he was unaware of the proceedings due to his counsel's withdrawal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had sufficient cause for not appearing in the trial court and for filing a delayed application to set aside the ex-parte decree?
Whether the delay in filing the application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the CPC could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act?
holdings: A party seeking to set aside an ex-parte decree must show sufficient cause for non-appearance, and the court may condone delay if the explanation is acceptable and there is no malafide or deliberate inaction.

Section 5 of the Limitation Act allows condonation of delay in filing an application to set aside an ex-parte decree if the court is satisfied with the explanation, and length of delay is not decisive if the cause is sufficient.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Substantial justice over technicalities
Discretion to condone delay to prevent failure of justice

card.dispute: The appellant (A-One Granites) and respondent no. 4 fought over the grant of a mining lease for 10 acres of land in Baghwa, Mahoba, after the state government sanctioned the lease in favor of the appellant without following prescribed procedures.
issues_decided: Whether rule 72 of the Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963 applies to an area previously leased under Chapter IV (auction) but withdrawn and made subject to Chapter II procedures?
Whether the state government's sanction of mining lease in favor of the appellant without following rule 72 is valid?
Whether the High Court was justified in directing the District Magistrate to consider an old application (dated 4.7.1995) filed by respondent no. 4?
holdings: Rule 72 applies even when an area was previously leased under Chapter IV, because withdrawal under rule 24 brings Chapter II into force and necessitates transparency in re-granting leases.
The state government's order sanctioning the lease in favor of the appellant without following rule 72 is invalid as it defeats the purpose of public notice and fair competition.
The High Court erred in directing consideration of the 1995 application; a fresh public notice under rule 72 must be issued and all applications, including new ones, must be considered afresh.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 23
Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 24
Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 72
Uttar Pradesh Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963, Rule 27
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 17A
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Transparency in administrative action
Suppression of mischief rule (Heydon's rule)

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased tenant fought the successors of a deceased landlord over eviction from a rented premises on grounds of rent default and unauthorized occupation of additional land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC when the lower appellate court misapplied the law?
Whether the tenant could be evicted under Section 12(1)(o) of the MP Accommodation Control Act, 1961 for unauthorized occupation of non-let portion without proof of detriment to the landlord?
Whether the tenant's defense should have been struck out under Section 13(6) of the MP Accommodation Control Act for failure to deposit rent during appeal?
holdings: The High Court can determine issues of fact in a second appeal if the lower court's error arose from a misinterpretation of law, provided the evidence is on record under Section 103 CPC.

Eviction under Section 12(1)(o) does not require proof of detriment to the landlord; unauthorized occupation of non-let portion without permission, and non-compliance with court direction to vacate, suffices.
Failure to deposit rent during appeal as required under Section 13(5) allows the court to strike out the tenant's defense under Section 13(6), if the default is unrebutted.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(m)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(o)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(11)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(5)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(6)
doctrines: Substantial question of law in second appeal
Strict compliance with statutory conditions for eviction
Burden of proof in rent deposit cases
Distinction between unauthorized construction and unauthorized occupation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for using a residential building for non-residential purposes by using one room for office work, while the tenant argued this minor use did not constitute a change of user under the rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether using one room of a residentially leased building for handling office files constitutes a change of user under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
Whether a minor deviation in the use of leased premises, without specific prohibition in the lease, amounts to a ground for eviction.
holdings: Using one room in a residential building for personal office work does not change the character of the building into a 'scheduled building' under the Act, especially when there is no specific lease clause prohibiting such use.
A small change in the user of the premises that does not prejudice the landlord or alter the essential residential character of the building does not attract eviction under Section 13(2)(ii)(b).
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 2(d), 2(g), 2(h), 4, 13(2)(ii)(b)
doctrines: Change of user doctrine
Strict construction of eviction grounds in rent control legislation
Principle of reasonable and purposive interpretation of lease terms

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the eviction order passed by the Special Court under the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, claiming ownership and possession of the disputed government land through an agreement for sale.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court ought to have expressed an opinion on the merits of the case when alternative remedies like review under Section 17-A of the Act were available?
Whether a civil suit for declaration of title is maintainable in respect of land alleged to be grabbed under the Act?
holdings: The High Court should not have expressed an opinion on the merits of the case after observing that alternative remedies like review under Section 17-A were available, as such an opinion would prejudge the outcome of those remedies.

No civil suit for declaration of title is maintainable in respect of land alleged to be grabbed under the Act, as jurisdiction lies exclusively with the Special Court under Section 8(2) read with Section 15.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 8
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 15
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 17-A
doctrines: Exhaustion of alternative remedies
Exclusive jurisdiction of special courts
Principle against pre-judgment of pending remedies

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought eviction of the defendant from the suit property on grounds of reasonable requirement and rent default, while the defendant sought to amend its written statement to challenge the landlord-tenant relationship, which the High Court disallowed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution in setting aside the District Judge's order allowing amendment of the written statement?
Whether the proposed amendment to the defendant's written statement should have been permitted under Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by acting as a revisional or appellate court rather than exercising supervisory powers, as it did not identify any flagrant illegality or violation of fundamental principles of justice.

The amendment to the written statement should be allowed if it aids in the proper adjudication of the dispute and does not cause serious prejudice to the plaintiff, especially when alternate defences are involved and the plaintiff can file a reply.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 17(2) and 17(2A)
doctrines: Judicial superintendence under Article 227
Liberal amendment of pleadings
Avoidance of multiplicity of proceedings
Alternate and additional defences in pleadings

card.dispute: The appellants, a company and its executive director, fought with the State of Karnataka and others over the legality of acquiring land for a clay processing industry in violation of land reform and environmental laws.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of agricultural land by the second appellant violated the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, particularly Sections 79A, 79B, and 80?
Whether the exemption granted under Section 109 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, after the sale deed, could validate the land acquisition?
Whether the clearances granted for establishing the industrial unit were valid in light of environmental and forest protection laws?
holdings: The Karnataka Land Reforms Act provisions do not automatically invalidate a land transaction; vesting of land in the State requires formal proceedings under Sections 79(4), 79B, or 80.
An exemption under Section 109 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act can be granted after land acquisition and renders the restrictions under Sections 79A, 79B, and 80 inapplicable to the exempted land.
Prior clearances for the industrial unit lose validity if withdrawn; fresh environmental and regulatory clearances must be obtained in accordance with law before commencing operations.
doctrines: Doctrine of prospective validation through statutory exemption
Doctrine of conditional legality of administrative clearances
Principle of sustainable development in environmental regulation

card.dispute: The respondents sued to declare their joint ownership of the suit property and the ineffectiveness of certain gift and sale deeds, which the appellants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court properly adjudicated the first appeal by considering all issues and evidence?
Whether the impugned judgment of the High Court suffers from failure to address findings on limitation and res judicata?
holdings: A first appellate court must consciously apply its mind to all issues of fact and law, and its judgment must record reasoned findings on all contentions.
The High Court failed in its duty by not discussing evidence or addressing the trial court's grounds of dismissal, rendering its judgment cryptic and unsatisfactory.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI
doctrines: First appeal as a valuable right
Conscious application of mind by appellate court
Res judicata
Principle of reasoned judgment

card.dispute: The petitioners alleged that the respondents committed contempt of court by initiating land vesting proceedings in violation of a Supreme Court order maintaining status quo.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents committed contempt by initiating land vesting proceedings against members not specifically covered by the status quo order?
Whether the ambiguity in the scope of the status quo order permits a finding of contempt beyond reasonable doubt?
holdings: An order maintaining status quo applies only to those clearly within its terms; ambiguity in its scope prevents a finding of contempt.
In contempt proceedings, the alleged contemnor is entitled to the benefit of doubt, especially when the order's interpretation is reasonably disputed.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in quasi-criminal proceedings
Strict proof beyond reasonable doubt in contempt cases
Judicial restraint in contempt jurisdiction

card.dispute: The dispute was between two sets of transferees of a property, with the appellants claiming title through pattas issued by the Pygah Committee, and the respondents claiming through transfers by decree-holders in a partition suit.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, claiming independent title to the property, could file objections under Order 21 Rules 97 and 99 CPC during execution proceedings?
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellants' objections as non-maintainable without adjudicating their claim?
Whether a person in possession of property claiming an independent title can resist execution of a decree for possession?
holdings: A person in possession of immovable property claiming an independent right can file objections under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC and is entitled to have their claim adjudicated in execution proceedings.
The executing court must decide disputes regarding title or possession raised by such persons; dismissal of objections as non-maintainable without considering merits is legally unsustainable.
A decree-holder cannot take possession of property until the rights of a person obstructing execution on grounds of independent title are finally adjudicated in appropriate proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rules 35, 36, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101, 103
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Jagirdar Regulation Act, 1958
doctrines: Adjudication of third-party rights in execution proceedings
Protection of possession pending legal determination
Doctrine of constructive res judicata not applicable to independent title claims by non-parties

card.dispute: Agricultural universities and the state contested whether daily wage labourers were entitled to permanent status, enhanced wages, and benefits awarded by an industrial tribunal, and whether non-implementation constituted unfair labour practices.
issues_decided: Whether the Award dated 20th February 1985 in (IT) No. 48 of 1981 required ongoing payment of daily wages calculated as 1/30 of the basic starting wage and dearness allowance
Whether non-implementation of the Award amounted to an unfair labour practice under the Industrial Disputes Act
Whether the principle of equal pay for equal work entitled non-award-covered daily wage labourers to the same benefits as those covered by the Award
Whether the State Government could be compelled to fund the payment of dues arising from the Award
holdings: The Award's wage enhancement was not a one-time payment but a continuing entitlement tied to the prevailing basic wage and dearness allowance, requiring universities to pay 1/30 of the current basic wage.
Failure to implement the Award constitutes an unfair labour practice under Item 9 of Schedule IV of the Industrial Disputes Act, as it undermines workers' legitimate entitlements.
The principle of equal pay for equal work applies among daily wage workers; uncovered workers are entitled to the same wages and benefits as those awarded, except those covered by a separate award.

The State Government cannot avoid funding workers' dues on grounds of financial burden, as it is responsible for ensuring proper functioning and fair treatment in educational institutions it controls.
provisions: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Schedule IV, Item 9
doctrines: Equal pay for equal work
Unfair labour practice
Continuing obligation under arbitral awards

card.dispute: Madanlal appealed against the High Court's dismissal of his revision petition seeking to produce documents in a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, which the trial court had rejected as belatedly filed.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court committed a material irregularity in rejecting the appellant's application under Order 13 Rule 2 CPC for production of documents after the plaintiff had closed evidence?
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to interfere under Section 115 CPC with the trial court's order rejecting the production of documents?
holdings: The trial court did not commit a material irregularity in rejecting the application for production of documents under Order 13 Rule 2 CPC, as no good cause was shown for the delay and the documents were not part of the written statement.

The High Court correctly refused to interfere under Section 115 CPC because an error of law or fact does not amount to a material irregularity in jurisdiction, and the appellant could raise the issue in appeal if a decree was passed against him.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 13 Rule 2
doctrines: Material irregularity in jurisdiction
Liberal construction of 'good cause' under Order 13 Rule 2 CPC

card.dispute: The appellants and the State of West Bengal disputed whether the appellants were entitled to compensation for land already vested in the State under the Land Acquisition Act, when the State later attempted to re-vest the same land under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether land already taken possession of and vested under the Land Acquisition Act can be re-vested under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act.
Whether the appellants are entitled to compensation for their land despite the subsequent notification under the Estates Act.
holdings: Land that has already vested in the State under the Land Acquisition Act cannot be re-vested under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act through a later notification.
The appellants are entitled to compensation as their land had already vested under the Land Acquisition process prior to the Estates Act notification.
provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of vested rights
Priority of statutory vesting based on timing
Rule against double vesting under different statutes

card.dispute: The landlords appealed against the High Court's exercise of Article 227 powers to allow tenants to deposit arrears of rent after the statutory period, thereby setting aside an eviction order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can extend the time for depositing arrears of rent under Section 11(2)(c) of the Kerala Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965 while exercising powers under Article 227 of the Constitution?
Whether the High Court's revisional jurisdiction under Article 227 can be treated as an extension of statutory appellate or revisional proceedings under the Act?
Whether the tenants were entitled to deposit arrears of rent after the statutory period based on a stay order or a petition under Article 227?
holdings: The High Court’s power under Article 227 is extraordinary and discretionary, but cannot be used to extend statutory time limits unless there is a showing of grave injustice and a fit case for equitable relief.
Proceedings under Article 227 are not an extension of statutory appeals or revisions under the Act, and thus do not automatically entitle a party to the benefits of statutory time extensions.
A stay order does not confer a substantive right or extend statutory time limits; tenants must deposit arrears within the period prescribed by law, irrespective of interim relief.
provisions: Kerala Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(2)(c)
Kerala Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 12
Kerala Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 18
Kerala Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 20
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of orders under special statutes
Doctrine of limited scope of Article 227 jurisdiction
Doctrine of no extension of statutory time limits in absence of exceptional circumstances
Doctrine that stay orders do not confer substantive rights

card.dispute: The appellant, who purchased property in a court auction, challenged the appellate court's decision setting aside an ex parte decree and attachment in a loan recovery suit, alleging fraud and collusion.
issues_decided: Whether the auction purchaser was a stranger to the suit and could be considered a bona fide purchaser for value.
Whether the first Appellate Court erred in holding that the promissory note (Ex.A-39) was sham and fraudulent despite no such pleading in the plaint.
holdings: The auction purchaser was not a stranger to the suit as evidence showed his close relationship with one of the defendants, and the finding by the first Appellate Court was based on permissible inference from evidence.

The first Appellate Court could infer that the promissory note was antedated and fraudulent based on the counter affidavit (Ex.A-49), even without an explicit pleading, as the document was admitted with consent and supported the finding.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 53
doctrines: Constructive res judicata
Inference from documentary evidence
Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Limited scope of interference under second appeal

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against the High Court's decision to restore the trial court's decree for his eviction on grounds of rent arrears and the landlord's bona fide need for the premises.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant was entitled to protection under Section 13(5) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, by depositing arrears of rent during the first appeal.
Whether the landlord established a bona fide requirement for the suit premises for residential purposes.
Whether the High Court was justified in making adverse remarks against the first appellate judge.
holdings: A tenant can avail protection under Section 13(5) only if arrears are deposited within one month of notice or within such extended time as the court permits; deposit during appeal without application for extension does not absolve default.
The landlord's bona fide need for personal residence must be respected; courts should not impose alternative accommodations or question her choice of living arrangement.

High Courts must exercise judicial restraint and avoid making adverse remarks against subordinate judicial officers, as such remarks undermine institutional confidence and lack corrective recourse for the judge concerned.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 13(5)
doctrines: Judicial restraint in superior courts
Bona fide requirement of landlord
Protection against eviction for rent arrears under conditional deposit

card.dispute: The landlord-tenant relationship was disputed between the plaintiffs (Basudeo Prasad & Anr) and defendant (Rajendra Tiwary), with the former seeking eviction on grounds of rent default, personal need, and damage, while the latter claimed ownership via an agreement for sale.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties under the Bihar Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982.
Whether the High Court could remand the case for determination of title and decree under Order VII Rule 7 of the CPC.
Whether a Rent Controller or appellate court under the Act can grant relief beyond the grounds specified in the Act.
holdings: No landlord-tenant relationship was established between the parties, which is a prerequisite for eviction under the Act.
The High Court erred in remanding the case for a finding on title, as title is irrelevant in eviction suits under the Act and courts under the Act lack jurisdiction to decide title.
Courts under the special rent law cannot grant relief under Order VII Rule 7 CPC beyond the grounds and reliefs permitted by the Act.
provisions: The Bihar Building (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982, Section 2(clauses f and h), Section 11(1)(b), (c), (d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 7
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation of special courts
Relief must conform to pleadings and statute
No decree on alternate grounds outside statutory framework

card.dispute: The appellant sued to restrain the respondents from demolishing his compound wall and later sought to amend the plaint to claim damages for the demolition, which the trial court and High Court denied.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment of the plaint to include a claim for damages was permissible under Order 6 Rule 17 of the CPC?
Whether the amendment would introduce a new cause of action or change the nature of the suit?
Whether the amendment was barred by limitation?
holdings: Amendment of pleadings is permissible under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC if it promotes justice and does not cause unfair prejudice, provided costs can compensate the other side.
The amendment did not introduce a new cause of action but arose from the same facts and circumstances as the original suit.
The plea of limitation was arguable and could be decided as an issue at trial after the amendment was allowed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Liberal approach to amendment of pleadings
Avoidance of multiplicity of litigation
Amendment not to be refused on technical grounds when justice so requires

card.dispute: The decree-holder sought to enforce a money decree through attachment and auction of the judgment debtor's property, while the respondents claimed prior purchase of the property under agreements to sell and challenged the validity of the attachment and sale.
issues_decided: Whether an attachment before judgment is invalid if the order was not sent to the District Court under Section 136 of the CPC when the property is outside the jurisdiction of the issuing court
Whether mere inadequacy of the auction price is a ground to set aside a court sale
Whether prior agreements to sell (Baibeyana) can prevail over an attachment in execution
holdings: An attachment order passed by a court without sending it to the District Court under Section 136 CPC is not automatically void; non-compliance with Section 136 is procedural and does not invalidate the attachment if no timely objection was raised.
Mere inadequacy of the price in a court auction is not sufficient to set aside the sale in the absence of fraud or material irregularity.

An agreement to sell creates an obligation tied to the ownership of the property, and an attaching creditor takes the property subject to such prior contractual obligations; the issue must be examined based on the nature of the agreements.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXVIII Rule 5
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXVIII Rule 7
doctrines: Attachment before judgment under Order XXXVIII Rule 5 CPC
Procedural compliance vs. jurisdictional validity
Priority of contractual obligations over attachment in execution

card.dispute: The appellant, a beneficiary of enhanced compensation in a land acquisition case, challenged the initiation of criminal proceedings against him based on alleged forged documents, arguing that he should have been heard before the court ordered prosecution under Section 340 of the CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether a person against whom a complaint is proposed under Section 340 of the CrPC has a right to be heard during the preliminary inquiry by the court?
Whether principles of natural justice require the court to issue a show-cause notice before ordering prosecution for offences affecting the administration of justice?
holdings: There is no statutory or constitutional requirement to afford an opportunity of hearing to a person before a court decides to make a complaint under Section 340 of the CrPC.

The court's role under Section 340 is limited to determining whether it is expedient in the interest of justice to initiate an inquiry, not to decide guilt, and thus principles of natural justice do not mandate a prior hearing.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of expediency in the interest of justice
Separation between inquiry and trial

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the validity of a land acquisition declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, arguing it was time-barred as it was not published within one year of the Section 4(1) notification.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 must be published within one year of the Section 4(1) notification as per the proviso to Section 6(1).
Whether the time limit under the proviso to Section 6(1) applies to the publication requirements under Section 6(2).
holdings: The requirement to make a declaration under Section 6(1) within one year of the Section 4(1) notification is mandatory, but this time limit does not extend to the publication of the declaration under Section 6(2).

The publication steps under Section 6(2), including in the Gazette and newspapers, need not be completed within the one-year period, as the legislature intentionally did not impose a time limit for publication.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 4(2)
doctrines: Conclusive declaration doctrine under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act
Distinction between making and publication of a declaration
Binding precedent by larger bench
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for their land acquired by Indian Oil Corporation for a bottling plant, arguing that the compensation should be based on comparable sales at market value.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could lawfully award compensation lower than the value in a comparable sale deed (Ex. A-4) when determining market value under the Land Acquisition Act.
Whether the High Court improperly relied on the capitalisation of net income method despite the parties agreeing to use the comparable sales method.
holdings: A court may award compensation below the price in a comparable sale if there are material differences in locality, access, land type, or size, even if the sale is genuine and proximate in time.
The High Court did not err in referring to capitalisation of net income as illustrative, as it primarily relied on the comparable sales method for valuation.
doctrines: Comparable Sales Method of valuation
Market value determination in land acquisition
Capitalisation of Net Income Method as illustrative

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant, claiming a monthly tenancy with 15 days' notice, while the tenant argued it was a permanent manufacturing lease deemed yearly under Section 106, requiring six months' notice.
issues_decided: Whether an oral lease for manufacturing purposes can be deemed a year-to-year tenancy under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act in absence of a registered instrument?
Whether Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act can override the mandatory requirement of Section 107 for a registered instrument to create a year-to-year lease?
holdings: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act applies only when a valid lease exists; an oral agreement for a year-to-year lease for manufacturing purposes cannot satisfy Section 107 and thus cannot invoke Section 106.
A lease from year to year or for more than one year must be by registered instrument under Section 107; absence of such instrument renders the lease invalid, making Section 106 inapplicable.
doctrines: Rule of construction in tenancy duration
Mandatory registration for long-term leases

card.dispute: Ramji Singh and his sons were convicted of murdering his brother Indradeo Singh over a property dispute, and they appealed on grounds including lack of charge under Section 34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is valid in the absence of a formal charge under Section 34?
Whether the prosecution failed to prove common intention among the accused due to lack of prior meeting of minds?
Whether the testimony of interested witnesses like the deceased's wife can be relied upon?
holdings: A conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC can be sustained even without a formal charge under Section 34 if there is no prejudice and evidence supports common intention.
Common intention can be inferred from the conduct and circumstances of the assault, even without prior concert or direct evidence of pre-planning.
The testimony of an interested witness, such as the deceased's wife, can be relied upon if it is credible, natural, and corroborated by other evidence.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 34 IPC
Common intention from conduct and circumstances
Reliability of interested witnesses

card.dispute: The heirs of a deceased landlord fought with tenants over whether they could evict the tenants under Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, after initially seeking eviction under Section 14(1)(e), claiming bona fide need as a widow for self-occupation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to allow conversion of the eviction petition from Section 14(1)(e) to Section 14-D of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the landlord's widow had a bona fide need for the premises for her own residence under Section 14-D
holdings: Courts may allow modification of an eviction claim from Section 14(1)(e) to Section 14-D if the claim can be decided on existing evidence without requiring fresh proof, especially when the statutory purpose is to grant relief based on changed circumstances.

A widow's claim under Section 14-D is valid if she proves she is a widow and requires the premises for her own residence; the claim is bona fide if not feigned or pretextual, and courts must not impose technical or hyper-technical interpretations to deny such relief.
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Judicial discretion in modifying reliefs
Liberal interpretation of tenant eviction statutes in favour of statutory beneficiaries
Avoidance of hyper-technical adjudication

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought a declaration that the disputed property was a valid Wakf and for recovery of possession from the defendant, who claimed ownership based on a partition decree.
issues_decided: Whether the property in dispute was validly dedicated as a Wakf under Muslim law
Whether the courts below erred in holding that the property was acquired from tainted earnings of a prostitute
Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC
holdings: A valid Wakf was created when Zohra Bibi gifted the property to her husband, who then executed a Wakf deed; the dedication fulfilled all legal requirements.
The stigma of tainted income does not attach to property once validly gifted and dedicated; courts below erred in presuming illegality without evidence.
The High Court was justified in interfering with findings of fact due to perversity, misreading of evidence, and errors of law, which warranted review under Section 100 CPC.
doctrines: Doctrine of pious obligation in Wakf
Principle of non-attachment of stigma to lawfully transferred property
Doctrine of interference with concurrent findings on substantial questions of law

card.dispute: The plaintiff-appellant sued the defendant's legal heirs for declaration of title, recovery of possession, and permanent injunction over a piece of land, claiming illegal dispossession, while the defendant contested on grounds of adverse possession and limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the first appellate court properly reversed the trial court's findings on possession and adverse possession without adequate reasoning?
Whether a substantial question of law was involved in the second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC?
holdings: An appellate court must provide reasoned findings when reversing trial court's factual conclusions, especially on credibility of witnesses and adverse possession, and cannot reverse without closely engaging with the trial court's reasoning.

A substantial question of law arises if it is debatable, not settled by precedent, and materially affects the rights of the parties; the High Court must decide such questions in second appeal when properly framed or capable of being framed.
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Adverse possession
Appellate review of findings of fact
Principle of judicial discipline in appellate courts

card.dispute: Co-sharers claimed the right to pre-empt a sale during the pendency of an appeal after a 1995 amendment removed that right in Haryana.
issues_decided: Whether the substituted Section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended by the Haryana Amendment Act, 1995, has retrospective effect?
Whether the right to pre-empt survives during the pendency of an appeal if the amendment extinguishing that right came into force during the appeal?
holdings: The Haryana Amendment Act, 1995, which substituted Section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, is not a declaratory or explanatory statute and therefore has no retrospective operation.
The right to pre-empt is determined as of the date of the trial court’s decree; subsequent amendments during appeal do not affect the pre-emptor’s right if it existed at the time of adjudication.
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Declaratory statute doctrine
Retrospective effect of beneficial legislation

card.dispute: Co-sharers contested whether the 1995 amendment removing pre-emption rights during appeal applies retrospectively to pending pre-emption suits.
issues_decided: Whether the substituted Section 15 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended by the Haryana Amendment Act, 1995, has retrospective effect?
Whether the right to pre-empt survives during the pendency of an appeal if the amendment extinguishing such right came into force during the appeal?
holdings: A statutory amendment that removes a right of pre-emption is prospective unless expressly or by necessary implication declaratory or retrospective.
The substituted Section 15 is not declaratory or explanatory, as the original provision was clear and unambiguous; hence, it does not operate retrospectively.
doctrines: Prospective operation of statutes
Declaratory and explanatory legislation
Retrospective effect of amending laws

card.dispute: The landlady sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide requirement for her own occupation due to health and family needs, which the High Court reversed, prompting the landlady to appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the landlady had a bona fide requirement of the premises for her own occupation under Section 21(1)(h) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961.
Whether the amendment to the eviction petition to include changed circumstances (death of husband and landlady's health) was legally permissible.
Whether the High Court erred in reversing the Trial Court's decree for possession without addressing comparative hardship.
holdings: A bona fide requirement for eviction must be real, sincere, and based on actual need, not a mere pretext; the landlady's need due to health and family circumstances was genuine.
An amendment to pleadings permitted by the Trial Court relates back to the original filing date, and the evidence must be assessed on the amended pleadings.
The High Court should have applied a realistic approach; denying eviction while allowing a fresh petition undermines justice when bona fide need is established.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 6, Rule 17
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Doctrine of relation back of amendments
Comparative hardship in eviction cases

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) fought with the Special Land Acquisition Officer over the period for which additional compensation under Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 should be awarded—whether from the date possession was taken (1977) or from the date of the Section 4(1) notification (1991).
issues_decided: Whether additional compensation under Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is payable from the date of taking of possession or from the date of publication of the Section 4(1) notification when possession was taken prior to the notification.
Which of the two conflicting decisions—M.A. Jabbar or Mathapathi Basavannewwa—correctly interprets Section 23(1A)?
holdings: Additional compensation under Section 23(1A) is payable from the date of publication of the Section 4(1) notification, not from the earlier date of possession.
The correct interpretation of Section 23(1A) is given in Special Tahsildar (LA), P.W.D. Schemes v. M.A. Jabbar; the decision in Asstt. Commr. v. Mathapathi Basavannewwa is overruled.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Overruling of precedent
Exclusion of unjust results when statutory language is clear

card.dispute: The landlord, Sri Kempaiah, fought to evict tenants Lingaiah and others on grounds of bonafide personal requirement and rent arrears under the Karnataka Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the Trial Court's finding on bonafide requirement in revision under Section 50 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act.
Whether the landlord proved a reasonable and bonafide requirement of the premises under Section 21(1)(h) of the Act.
Whether the tenants were liable for eviction due to arrears of rent.
holdings: The High Court has wide revisional powers under Section 50 of the Karnataka Rent Control Act to examine the legality and correctness of findings, including appreciation of evidence on bonafide requirement.

A landlord's 'requirement' under Section 21(1)(h) must be genuine and necessary, not merely a desire; the court must independently assess its reasonableness and bonafides even if the tenant does not contest.
Eviction for rent arrears cannot be granted if the landlord fails to prove the rate of rent or quantify the arrears clearly, especially when relying solely on uncorroborated testimony.
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction
Bonafide requirement
Independent judicial scrutiny in eviction cases

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged the constitutional validity of Section 82 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious Institutions & Endowments Act, 1987, which terminated tenancy rights on lands held by religious institutions, arguing it violated Articles 14, 21, and 31A of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether Section 82(1) of the Act violates Article 14 by arbitrarily discriminating against tenants of religious institutions
Whether Section 82(2) of the Act violates Article 21 by depriving tenants of livelihood without compensation
Whether tenants under different tenancy laws (Andhra vs Telangana) can be treated as a single class
Whether the Act requires payment of compensation under Article 31A
holdings: Tenants of religious institutions form a distinct class and can be treated differently; the classification under Section 82(1) is reasonable and does not violate Article 14.
The termination of tenancy under Section 82 does not violate Article 21 as the Act's purpose is better management of religious properties, not deprivation of livelihood.
Differences in tenancy rights under Andhra and Telangana Acts do not prevent grouping tenants of religious institutions into one class for legislative purposes.
Article 31A does not apply here as the State has not enacted a law acquiring property, and no compensation is required for cancellation of leases under this Act.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious Institutions & Endowments Act, 1987, Section 82
Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious Institutions & Endowments Act, 1987, Section 80
Andhra Pradesh Charitable & Hindu Religious Institutions & Endowments Act, 1987, Section 38-E (Telangana Act)
doctrines: Classification test under Article 14
Presumption of constitutionality
Separate class doctrine for religious institutions
Legislative policy and social objectives justification

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh fought with residents of Majra Dughe over whether their traditional grazing rights on shamilat land survived the vesting of all land rights in the State under the Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act, 1974.
issues_decided: Whether easementary rights such as grazing rights over village common land survived the vesting of all rights, title, and interests in the State free from encumbrances under Section 3 of the Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act, 1974.
Whether the expression 'free from all encumbrances' in Section 3 of the Act includes extinguishment of customary or community rights over the land.
holdings: Easementary rights, including the right to graze cattle, are encumbrances on land, and when land vests in the State free from all encumbrances under Section 3 of the Act, such rights stand extinguished and vest in the State.

The phrase 'free from all encumbrances' means the State acquires absolute and unburdened title, which necessarily includes the extinguishment of all customary, communal, or easementary rights over the land.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act, 1974, Section 3
Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act, 1974, Section 8
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulations) Act, 1961, Section 4
doctrines: Doctrine of extinguishment of easements upon vesting of property free from encumbrances
Doctrine of legislative competence over land and rights in land under Entry 18, List II, Seventh Schedule, Constitution of India

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the High Court's decision to quash a criminal investigation against eight accused, including six revenue officers and two private individuals, accused of forgery, fraud, and conspiracy in connection with land compensation under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the investigation based on the absence of specific allegations against the private respondents in the FIR?
Whether the allegations in the FIR, if taken at face value, disclosed cognizable offences warranting investigation?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the investigation as the FIR contained specific allegations of forgery, fraud, and conspiracy, which, if accepted as true, disclosed cognizable offences.
The power to quash criminal proceedings is extraordinary and should be exercised only in rarest of rare cases, which this was not; hence, the High Court's interference was unwarranted.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 156(1) and Section 155(2)
doctrines: Bhajan Lal doctrine on quashing of criminal proceedings
Principle of privity of allegations in FIR for determining maintainability of investigation
Doctrine of limited judicial interference in ongoing criminal investigations

card.dispute: The appellants (accused) challenged their conviction and sentence in a criminal case where they were found guilty of assaulting and causing the death of Daya Nand, based primarily on the testimony of a single eyewitness, PW-7.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction based solely on the testimony of PW-7, an interested witness, without corroboration, was legally sustainable?
Whether the non-examination of material witnesses, including Sumer, Dani Ram, and Tara Chand, vitiated the prosecution's case?
Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt?
holdings: A conviction cannot be based solely on the testimony of an interested and potentially biased eyewitness without independent corroboration, especially when contradictions and falsehoods are evident in the witness's statements.

The non-examination of material eyewitnesses mentioned in the prosecution's own case, such as Sumer, Dani Ram, and Tara Chand, creates a serious lacuna and casts doubt on the reliability of the prosecution's version.

The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, and the concurrent findings of the Sessions and High Courts were perverse and unsafe, warranting interference by the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Benefit of doubt
Corroboration of interested witness
Unsafe conviction based on solitary testimony

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged the Calcutta High Court's decision to set aside the confiscation of a band saw and other implements used in a forest offence involving illegally felled timber belonging to the state.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta High Court erred in setting aside the confiscation of tools and implements under Section 59-A(3) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927 as amended by West Bengal in 1988?
Whether tools and implements used in a forest offence can be confiscated independently of the status of prosecution for the offence?
holdings: The confiscation of tools, including a band saw, used in committing a forest offence is valid under Section 59-A(3) of the Indian Forest Act if the seized timber is state property and the officer is satisfied that an offence was committed in relation to it.
The power to confiscate tools used in a forest offence is independent of any criminal prosecution and constitutes a separate administrative proceeding under the Act.
doctrines: Separate and distinct proceeding doctrine
Administrative confiscation independent of prosecution

card.dispute: The Tamil Nadu Wakf Board sued the respondents to recover possession of properties claimed as wakf, but the respondents contested the validity of the wakf and the Board's right to sue, arguing the properties were not properly notified as wakf and had been acquired through revenue sale and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the suit properties were validly notified as wakf properties under Section 5(2) of the Wakf Act, 1954
Whether the Wakf Board could file a suit for recovery of possession without following the mandatory procedures under the Wakf Act, 1954
Whether the character of wakf property persists indefinitely despite alienation or adverse possession
holdings: The suit properties were not included in the notification under Section 5(2) of the Wakf Act, 1954, and thus the Board could not rely on such notification to claim possession.
The Wakf Board must follow the procedure under Sections 4, 5, 6, or 27 of the Wakf Act, 1954 before instituting a suit; failure to do so bars the suit for declaration and possession.
Even if a property was once a wakf, the Board cannot recover possession without complying with the statutory procedure, regardless of the permanence of wakf dedication.
doctrines: Statutory compliance doctrine
Doctrine of mandatory procedural requirements
Finality of administrative decisions subject to judicial review

card.dispute: The landowner and the Union of India disputed whether solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 should be included in the amount on which interest is payable under Section 34 of the Act.
issues_decided: Whether the solatium under Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 forms part of the compensation for the purpose of computing interest under Section 34 of the Act.
Whether there is a conflict between the decision in Union of India v. Shri Ram Mehar and subsequent co-equal bench decisions on the inclusion of solatium in interest calculations.
holdings: The solatium under Section 23(2) is an integral part of the compensation and must be included in the amount on which interest is payable under Section 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The term 'awarded amount' in Section 34 includes all components of compensation under Section 23, and the legislature did not intend to exclude solatium from interest accrual.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction
Principle of inclusive compensation in land acquisition

card.dispute: The claimants and the State challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation for acquired land, disputing the quantum of compensation based on market value comparisons with a prior acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the compensation by Rs. 10 per sq. mtr. based on distance and size of the acquired land.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on Ex. 16 instead of Ex. 46 for determining market value.
holdings: The High Court erred in reducing compensation by 25% based on the size of the total acquired area, as individual holdings were small and the comparison with Ex. 16 was valid.
Distance alone, without evidence of inferior quality or potential, cannot justify reducing compensation when lands are similarly situated with respect to town connectivity and development potential.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Rejection of yield method in favor of market-based evidence when sale transactions or expert opinions exist

card.dispute: The state and landowners disputed whether a later master plan, not in existence when the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulations) Act, 1976 came into force, could be used to classify land as vacant for determining ceiling limits.
issues_decided: Whether the master plan in existence at the time of the Act's enforcement (17th February 1976) or a subsequent master plan should be used to determine if land is vacant under the Act.
Whether authorities can classify land as vacant under the Act based on a master plan created after the Act's commencement.
holdings: The master plan prepared after the Act's enforcement can be used to determine if land is vacant, as the Act contemplates changes in land status over time.
The date of commencement of the Act for a piece of land that becomes vacant later is the date it becomes vacant, not necessarily 17th February 1976.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(h)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(o)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 6
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 15
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 16
doctrines: Dynamic interpretation of statutory provisions
Ongoing nature of town planning and development

card.dispute: Private sub-lessees challenged the Andhra Pradesh government's withdrawal of permission for sub-leasing mining areas, seeking extension of leases and damages for breach of contract.
issues_decided: Whether the sub-leases were void ab initio for lack of prior central government permission under Section 4-A of the Mines and Minerals Act and Rule 37 of the Mineral Concession Rules
Whether the High Court could intervene under Article 226 in a matter arising from a contractual dispute involving a statutory authority
Whether the High Court could extend the period of expired mining sub-leases as a remedy
Whether the appellants were entitled to damages for breach of contract
holdings: Sub-leases granted before the 1991 amendment to Rule 37 did not require central government permission and are not void ab initio; the Full Bench was correct in upholding their validity.
Even if a dispute arises from a contract, judicial review under Article 226 is available when statutory powers are exercised unfairly, irrationally, or in violation of public law principles.
Extension of expired sub-leases was impermissible due to lapse of time, government policy against private leasing, and public interest concerns, especially after mine operations had ceased.
The question of damages for breach of contract is left open for determination in a civil suit, with cause of action accruing from the date of this judgment.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Section 4-A
doctrines: Doctrine of void ab initio
Public law exception to purely contractual disputes
Judicial review of administrative contracts
Discretionary equitable relief in lease extension

card.dispute: The appellant (Veerayee Ammal) sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, which the respondent (Seeni Ammal) refused to execute; the High Court reversed the lower courts’ decree in favour of the appellant, leading to this appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disturbing concurrent findings of fact by the Trial and First Appellate Courts on the appellant's readiness and willingness to perform the contract.
Whether the question of law raised in the second appeal was a 'substantial question of law' under Section 100 of the CPC.
Whether the appellant filed the suit for specific performance within a reasonable time despite time not being of the essence of the contract.
holdings: The High Court erred in overturning concurrent factual findings on readiness and willingness to perform, as such findings cannot be disturbed in second appeal absent a substantial question of law.
A mere difference in appreciation of evidence or possible alternative view does not constitute a substantial question of law justifying second appeal jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC.

The appellant filed the suit within a reasonable time, as determined by the nature of the property, contract terms, and surrounding circumstances, including steps taken to remove a telegraph pole and issuance of notice.
doctrines: Concurrent finding of fact rule
Substantial question of law doctrine
Equitable relief in specific performance
Reasonable time doctrine in contracts where time is not of the essence

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the remand of compensation proceedings to the Civil Court, arguing that the Kerala Water Authority was bound by prior proceedings and had no right to be impleaded after a Constitution Bench decision clarified its rights.
issues_decided: Whether the Kerala Water Authority was entitled to be impleaded in compensation proceedings before the Civil Court despite not being a party originally.
Whether the Constitution Bench decision in U.P. Awas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Gyan Devi applies retrospectively to pending appeals.
Whether the claimants should be protected from procedural disadvantages due to the remand.
holdings: A local authority for whose benefit land is acquired has a right to be impleaded in reference court proceedings and to challenge compensation enhancement under Section 50(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
The Constitution Bench decision applies to cases pending appeal, as finality had not been achieved, warranting remand for compliance with the new legal position.
While remand is necessary, claimants are protected: prior witness statements need not be re-recorded, and unavailable witnesses’ evidence remains admissible.
doctrines: Prospective overruling
Impleadment of necessary parties in compensation proceedings
Continuity of appeal as part of original proceedings

card.dispute: The defendants challenged the validity of an ex-parte decree, claiming improper service of summons in a landlord-tenant suit.
issues_decided: Whether service of summons by registered post with acknowledgment due constitutes sufficient notice under Order 5 Rule 19A, second proviso, CPC read with Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897
Whether substituted service via newspaper publication in 'Aacharan' instead of 'Dainik Bhaskar' invalidates the service
Whether the trial court rightly refused to set aside the ex-parte decree under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC
holdings: Service of summons by registered post with acknowledgment due, properly addressed and prepaid, raises a rebuttable presumption of due service under Order 5 Rule 19A CPC and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
Substituted service through a widely circulated local newspaper other than the one specified by court is a mere irregularity and does not invalidate service if actual notice is probable.
An ex-parte decree cannot be set aside merely on grounds of procedural irregularity in service if the defendant fails to rebut the statutory presumption or show sufficient cause for non-appearance.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 5 Rule 19A
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 5 Rule 20
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption of service
Substituted service
Irregularity vs. invalidity in procedural law

card.dispute: The appellants, Bachhitar Singh and Amarjit Singh, were convicted of murdering eight members of two families over a land dispute, and challenged the death sentence awarded by lower courts.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the case falls within the 'rarest of rare' category warranting the death penalty?
holdings: The court upheld the conviction, holding that the prosecution proved the appellants' guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on eyewitness testimony, recovery evidence, and forensic corroboration.

The death sentence was set aside as the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare' category; life imprisonment was deemed sufficient considering the absence of past criminal conduct and potential for rehabilitation.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Principle of proportionality in sentencing
Reformation and rehabilitation in criminal justice

card.dispute: The appellant, Beg Raj Singh, fought the State of U.P. and a private respondent over the renewal of a sand mining lease, claiming entitlement to a three-year lease period under state policy, after the State cancelled the renewal and opted for an auction.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government was justified in setting aside the Collector's order granting a two-year lease extension to the appellant?
Whether the High Court erred in denying relief to the appellant on the ground of public interest through auction despite finding the State's interference unjustified?
Whether the appellant is entitled to operate the mine for the remaining period to complete three years of operation as per policy?
holdings: The State Government was not justified in interfering with the Collector’s order granting lease extension, as the original lease should have been for three years per policy, and the extension was lawful.
The High Court erred in denying relief solely on the basis of potential higher revenue from auction, as no third-party rights were created and no auction had taken place.

The appellant is entitled to operate the mine for the balance period required to complete three years of operation, subject to adjustment for time already operated, as the delay was not his fault and no equities weighed against him.
provisions: Rules or regulations governing mining leases in Uttar Pradesh (implied under state mining policy)
doctrines: Legitimate expectation
Crystallization of rights at the commencement of litigation
Equitable relief despite delay when no fault of the party and no prejudice to others

card.dispute: The appellants were acquitted by the trial court for murder and related charges but were convicted by the High Court; they challenged the conviction, arguing lack of evidence and common object under Section 149 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on witness testimony?
Whether the prosecution proved the existence of a common object under Section 149 IPC?
Whether the appellants could be convicted even if some witnesses were related to the deceased?
holdings: The High Court correctly reversed the acquittal as the trial court ignored reliable and legally admissible evidence from key witnesses.
Common object under Section 149 IPC can be inferred from conduct and circumstances, even without prior meeting of minds, especially in a violent group attack.
Family members of victims can be natural and credible witnesses; their relationship does not automatically discredit their testimony.
doctrines: Common object under Section 149 IPC
Benefit of right of self-defence
Credibility of eyewitnesses and family witnesses
Reversal of acquittal on basis of legal error

card.dispute: Balu Sonba Shinde was convicted for murdering his brother Shankar during a property dispute, and he appealed the conviction based on unreliable circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt through circumstantial evidence?
Whether the testimony of a hostile witness can be relied upon to sustain a conviction?
Whether the non-examination of a material witness (Gorakh) vitiated the prosecution's case?
holdings: In cases relying solely on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be complete and point exclusively to the accused’s guilt; any gap entitles the accused to benefit of doubt.
A hostile witness’s evidence can be partially relied upon if consistent with the prosecution’s case, but must be scrutinized carefully and cannot form the sole basis of conviction.
The failure to examine Gorakh, a vital witness who allegedly helped carry the victim, created a serious lacuna in the prosecution’s case, undermining its reliability.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in circumstantial evidence cases
Principle of complete chain of circumstances
Partial reliance on hostile witness

card.dispute: The Airports Authority of India challenged the High Court's determination of compensation for cutting trees, arguing that the 18-year multiplier used was excessive under established precedent.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in applying an 18-year multiplier for determining compensation for trees cut on private land?
Whether the decision in State of Haryana v. Gurcharan Singh, which capped the multiplier at 8 years for tree yield-based compensation, should be followed?
holdings: The High Court erred in applying an 18-year multiplier as it contradicted the binding precedent in Gurcharan Singh, which limits the multiplier to 8 years when compensation is based on yield from trees or plantations.
Despite the legal error, the appeal was not interfered with due to the small amount of compensation involved and the principle of judicial restraint in cases involving limited impact.
doctrines: Principle of capitalization of income for compensation
Precedent of 8-year multiplier for fruit-bearing trees
Judicial restraint in non-substantial compensation cases

card.dispute: The sons of a village office holder challenged the alienation of service inam lands after the office was abolished, while alienees claimed protection under estoppel and waiver.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were estopped from challenging the alienation of service inam lands despite their prior conduct implying acceptance?
Whether there was a waiver of the right to object to the alienation of the property?
Whether the doctrine of election or ratification applied to preclude the plaintiffs from challenging the transactions?
holdings: A person who by conduct or representation induces another to alter their position detrimentally cannot later challenge the transaction; estoppel applies even without intent to relinquish a right.
Waiver requires intentional relinquishment of a known right, and mere delay or inaction without benefit-taking does not amount to waiver.
Where a presumptive reversioner accepts benefits under a transaction, especially after attaining majority, they may be estopped from challenging it based on election or ratification.
provisions: Mysore Village Offices Abolition Act, 1961, Section 4
doctrines: Estoppel by representation
Waiver as a rule of conduct
Election and ratification in property transactions
Equitable doctrines: clean hands, vigilance, and doing equity

card.dispute: Bhavnagar University challenged the Gujarat High Court's decision on whether land reservations under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 lapsed after 10 years if the state failed to acquire the land, despite a revised development plan being published.
issues_decided: Whether the reservation of land under Section 20 of the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976 lapses after 10 years if the state does not acquire the land.
Whether the 10-year period for acquisition under Section 20(2) is interrupted or reset by the publication of a revised development plan.
Whether the decisions in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority and Murari Lal's case are applicable to the present facts.
holdings: The reservation under Section 20 does not automatically lapse after 10 years if acquisition proceedings have not been completed, especially when a revised development plan has been published within that period.

The 10-year period for acquisition under Section 20(2) is to be calculated from the date the final development plan comes into force, which may be the date of a revised and legally sanctioned plan, not an earlier invalid one.
The precedent in Ahmedabad Urban Development Authority’s case does not apply where the facts differ, particularly regarding the validity and timing of development plan sanctions.
provisions: Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 20
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 21
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis with factual distinction)
Doctrine of statutory interpretation (contextual and purposive interpretation of town planning laws)
Principle that judicial records are conclusive on what transpired in court

card.dispute: Bhaiji, a tribal landholder, challenged the Sub-Divisional Officer's show-cause notice seeking reversion of agricultural land under Section 170-B of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, arguing the provision did not apply to transfers between tribal members.
issues_decided: Whether Section 170-B of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1980 applies to land transfers between members of aboriginal tribes?
Whether the failure to file a notice under Section 170-B(1) automatically results in reversion of land without an enquiry under Section 170-B(3)?
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the writ petition challenging the show-cause notice?
holdings: Section 170-B, as originally enacted in 1980, applies to all transfers of tribal agricultural land, including those between members of aboriginal tribes, as the language is clear and unambiguous.

The presumption under Section 170-B(2) of unlawful possession is rebuttable, and an enquiry under Section 170-B(3) must be conducted before reversion; automatic divestment without enquiry violates Article 21.
The writ petition was premature; the petitioner should have participated in the statutory enquiry instead of seeking immediate judicial intervention.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 170-B
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 165
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Rebuttable presumption in administrative law
Principle of audi alteram partem
Doctrine of constitutional avoidance

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority and flat allottees disputed whether the Authority could legally revise the price of flats under its 1979 scheme, and whether the High Court could intervene in the pricing under Article 226 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere under Article 226 in the pricing or cost escalation of flats by the Delhi Development Authority under a registration scheme.
Whether the revision of flat prices by the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in 1990 was illegal or arbitrary.
holdings: The court held that judicial review under Article 226 does not extend to pricing or cost escalation in a contractual scheme where clauses explicitly state that prices are illustrative and subject to revision.
The court upheld the Lieutenant Governor's revision of flat prices, finding it neither illegal nor arbitrary, especially after the Authority provided material justifying the cost revision.
doctrines: Limited scope of judicial review in contractual administrative actions
Principle of consistency in judicial pronouncements to avoid conflicting orders on the same issue

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh challenged a High Court order directing it to pay interim compensation to landholders under the Estates Abolition Act, despite the Supreme Court having upheld the constitutional validity of an amendment affecting such payments.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents acquired an indefeasible right to interim payments under Section 39 of the Andhra Pradesh Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, based on a prior High Court judgment that was rendered contrary to a subsequent Supreme Court ruling on the constitutional validity of an amendment.
Whether the High Court could issue a writ of mandamus to enforce such a right after the Supreme Court had declared the amendment constitutionally valid in Venkatagiri's case.
Whether the principle of res judicata preserves a right established by a final judgment even when the legal basis of that judgment is later overruled by the Supreme Court.
Whether the decision in Shenoy's case requires reconsideration by a larger bench in light of the principles of res judicata and Article 141 of the Constitution.
holdings: No indefeasible right accrued to the respondents under the earlier High Court judgment once the Supreme Court in Venkatagiri's case upheld the constitutional validity of the amendment, as that decision became the binding law of the land under Article 141.

The High Court erred in issuing mandamus to enforce interim payments because the legal basis for the claimed right—invalidity of the amendment—no longer existed after the Supreme Court’s declaration in Venkatagiri's case.

A final judgment based on a legal interpretation that is later overruled by the Supreme Court cannot sustain a subsisting legal right, as the law declared by this Court binds all courts and parties under Article 141, overriding res judicata in such contexts.

The decision in Shenoy's case does not require reconsideration by a larger bench, as it correctly applied Article 141 and the principle that a law declared by the Supreme Court governs all pending and future cases, regardless of res judicata.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, Section 39
doctrines: Doctrine of binding precedent (Article 141)
Doctrine of mandamus
Principle of res judicata
Supremacy of Supreme Court's interpretation of law

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be a deemed tenant under the Bombay Rents Act, while the respondents argued he was a 'paying guest' and not entitled to tenancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a 'paying guest' or a deemed tenant under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Whether the definition of 'paying guest' under Section 5(6A) of the Act is exhaustive and excludes other common law criteria
holdings: A person is a 'paying guest' if the licensor resides in the premises of which a part is occupied by the licensee, even if they reside in separate parts of the same building.
The definition of 'paying guest' under Section 5(6A) is restrictive and exhaustive; no additional conditions from common law or other statutes can be imported.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 5(6A)
doctrines: Exhaustive statutory definition
Literal rule of interpretation
Legislative competence to define terms restrictively

card.dispute: The appellants (grandsons of Rulia Singh) and respondents (collaterals of Jagjit Singh) fought over whether the appellants had acquired title by adverse possession to Jagjit Singh's share of land, or whether Gujjar Singh, a collateral, was entitled to inherit it.
issues_decided: Whether Gujjar Singh, a sixth-degree collateral, could succeed to the estate of Jagjit Singh in the absence of proof of Jagjit Singh's date of death.
Whether the appellants perfected title by adverse possession over Jagjit Singh's share of the property.
holdings: Succession to Jagjit Singh's estate could not open without proof of his death; since the plaintiff failed to plead or prove the date of death, he could not establish a right to inherit.

The appellants' mutation in revenue records after rejecting claims of collaterals, along with exclusive, continuous, and open possession, amounted to clear ouster and established adverse possession over Jagjit Singh's share.
doctrines: Burden of proof in cases of presumed death
Adverse possession among co-sharers requiring clear ouster
Effect of mutation in revenue records as evidence of adverse possession

card.dispute: Dhruv Green Field Ltd (defendant) fought against Hukam Singh and others (plaintiffs) over whether a civil court had jurisdiction to declare a lease of village common land illegal and void, or whether such disputes fell exclusively under revenue authorities under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging the legality of a lease of village common land granted by a Gram Panchayat under the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961.
Whether the provisions of Section 13 read with Section 10-A of the Act bar the jurisdiction of civil courts in such matters.
holdings: The civil court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes concerning the legality of leases of land vested in a Panchayat when such matters are entrusted to the Assistant Collector of the First Grade under Section 10-A of the Act.
