Section 13 of the Act bars civil court jurisdiction over matters that revenue authorities are empowered to decide, including challenges to leases based on fraud or violation of rules, unless the impugned action is a nullity, which this lease was not.
provisions: Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 13
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, Section 10-A
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction
Doctrine of ouster of jurisdiction by statute
Nullity exception to ouster of jurisdiction

card.dispute: The tenant challenged his eviction on grounds of rent default, claiming he had substantially complied with deposit procedures under the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's deposit of rent in court without following prior procedural steps under Section 8 of the Act constitutes compliance?
Whether the tenant can be evicted for default in rent payment despite depositing arrears in court?
holdings: A tenant must strictly follow the sequential procedure under Section 8 of the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1960; depositing rent in court without first issuing a notice to the landlord and attempting payment via bank or money order is not valid compliance.

Mere deposit of rent in court does not absolve a tenant of default if statutory procedures are not followed; refusal by the landlord to accept rent does not justify bypassing mandatory steps under Section 8.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 8
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 19-A
doctrines: Strict compliance with rent control statutes
Legal fiction limited to its statutory purpose
Procedural prerequisites as conditions precedent

card.dispute: The Government of Orissa challenged the execution of an ex parte decree passed against a company division it had taken over, arguing it was not a party to the suit and the decree should not bind it.
issues_decided: Whether an ex parte decree passed against a company division after the State Government took over its assets can be executed against the State Government without impleading it as a party?
Whether the State Government, as successor-in-interest, is automatically bound by a decree passed against the original defendant without being brought on record?
Whether the plaintiff's failure to implead the State Government under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC bars execution of the decree against the State?
holdings: A decree passed against a company division after the State Government has taken over its assets is not binding on the State unless the State is impleaded as a party in accordance with Order XXII Rule 10 CPC.
The State Government, as a successor-in-interest, is not automatically liable to be bound by a decree; the plaintiff must apply for leave to continue the suit against the transferee.
Failure of the plaintiff to bring the State on record as a successor-in-interest renders the decree inexecutable against the State, even if the State did not challenge the decree earlier.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
Orissa Ordinance No. 8 of 1991, Section 3 and Section 6(5)
doctrines: Successor-in-interest doctrine
Doctrine of necessary parties
Principle of binding effect of decrees only on parties or those properly impleaded

card.dispute: The Housing Board, Haryana and contractor Inder Sain Mittal disputed the validity of arbitration awards after the arbitrator continued proceedings post-transfer, leading to challenges under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
issues_decided: Whether a party can object to an arbitration award on the ground that the arbitrator continued proceedings after transfer, having participated without protest.
Whether acquiescence in arbitration proceedings bars a party from raising jurisdictional objections under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
Whether the continuation of arbitration by a transferred arbitrator violates a mandatory provision of law or merely breaches the agreement between parties.
holdings: A party who participates in arbitration proceedings without protest, despite knowing of a defect such as an arbitrator's transfer, is estopped from later challenging the award on that ground.
Acquiescence through conduct defeats the right to object under Section 30 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, where the issue arises from agreement, not mandatory law.

Continuation of arbitration by a transferred arbitrator does not violate any mandatory statutory provision, and thus parties cannot claim jurisdictional invalidity after participating without objection.
doctrines: Estoppel by conduct
Waiver by acquiescence
No estoppel against statute
Mandatory vs. directory provisions

card.dispute: The state and three convicted accused appealed conflicting judgments on convictions and acquittals arising from a violent incident involving an unlawful assembly, murder, and assault in a village in Punjab.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting three accused (Ajaib Singh, Inderjit Singh, Satinderpal Singh) due to insufficient evidence?
Whether the remaining three accused could be convicted under Sections 148 and 149 IPC in the absence of a common object with the acquitted co-accused?
Whether the conviction of the three appellants under Sections 302 and 307 IPC read with Section 34 IPC was legally sustainable based on the evidence?
holdings: The acquittal of Ajaib Singh, Inderjit Singh, and Satinderpal Singh is upheld due to lack of reliable and clinching evidence, including inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts and absence of independent corroboration.

Conviction under Sections 148 and 149 IPC cannot be sustained against the remaining accused as the unlawful assembly could not be established with at least five members, and the acquitted accused were not proven participants.

Harjit Singh's conviction under Section 302 IPC is maintained, but he is acquitted of Section 307; Varinderjit Singh and Gursharan Singh are convicted only for causing hurt under Sections 323, 324, and 326 IPC with common intention under Section 34, not for murder or attempt to murder.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal appeals
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Unlawful assembly and common object under Sections 148/149 IPC
Reliability of disclosure statements and recovery evidence without independent witnesses

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's reversal of their acquittal, seeking to restore the trial court's decision that acquitted them of murder charges.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's order of acquittal based on the prosecution's evidence.
Whether the High Court properly applied Section 34 IPC to convict the appellants despite no evidence of common intention.
Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt.
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal without adequately addressing or dispelling the trial court's reasoned doubts about the prosecution's evidence.
Conviction under Section 302 IPC with aid of Section 34 IPC is unsustainable when there is no evidence of pre-meditation or common intention among the accused.
In cases of conflicting evidence, the benefit of reasonable doubt must be given to the accused, especially when the prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond doubt.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Principle against interference with acquittal unless perverse or manifestly unjust
Requirement of proof of common intention under Section 34 IPC

card.dispute: The Industrial Finance Corporation of India Ltd. appealed against the Thletdc.An&Naonrosr.E Spinning & Weaving Mills regarding the liability of a surety after the creditor lost security due to nationalisation of the debtor's assets.
issues_decided: Whether the surety is discharged from liability under Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act when the creditor loses security due to a statutory event like nationalisation?
Whether the doctrine of frustration under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act applies to a contract of guarantee in such circumstances?
Whether a creditor can simultaneously proceed before a Commissioner under a nationalisation statute and file a civil suit for recovery?
holdings: A surety is not automatically discharged from liability under Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act merely because the creditor loses security due to a statutory vesting of assets, as the surety retains an independent obligation under the guarantee.

The doctrine of frustration under Section 56 does not apply to a contract of guarantee when performance becomes difficult due to a supervening event like nationalisation, as the guarantee is an independent obligation.

A creditor is not barred from pursuing a civil suit for recovery even after partially receiving dues from a Commissioner appointed under a nationalisation statute; the amounts recovered are to be adjusted accordingly.
provisions: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1974
doctrines: Doctrine of Frustration
Surety's Right to Securities
Independent Obligation under Guarantee

card.dispute: Jai Singh, claiming to be the adopted son of Sunda Ram, fought with Shakuntala, Sunda Ram's daughter, over inheritance of property.
issues_decided: Whether a registered adoption deed under Section 16 of the Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956 raises an irrebuttable presumption of valid adoption
Whether the presumption under Section 16 can be rebutted by evidence showing lack of valid adoption ceremonies and suspicious conduct
Whether the courts below were justified in rejecting the adoption based on documentary and conduct evidence
holdings: Section 16 creates a rebuttable presumption of valid adoption from a registered deed; it is not conclusive or irrebuttable.
The presumption can be displaced by evidence showing absence of essential adoption ceremonies, inconsistent conduct, or fraudulent intent.
Courts may examine the credibility of adoption if evidence contradicts the deed, especially when wills and records show suspicious circumstances.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 16
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 11(vi)
doctrines: rebuttable presumption
perversity of findings
essential ceremonies in Hindu adoption
fraud vitiates legal documents

card.dispute: The Jalandhar Improvement Trust challenged the order granting enhanced compensation to a co-owner whose initial claim was time-barred, after her children successfully obtained enhancement in a land acquisition reference.
issues_decided: Whether a co-owner whose claim for reference under Section 18 was rejected due to delay can still benefit from enhanced compensation awarded to other co-owners in the same reference?
Whether Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applies to allow redetermination of compensation in such circumstances?
holdings: A co-owner is entitled to the benefit of enhanced compensation awarded to other co-owners in a joint holding, even if their individual claim was rejected on grounds of limitation.
It is unnecessary to decide on the applicability of Section 28A where substantial justice has been achieved by extending the benefit of enhancement to all co-owners.
doctrines: Principle of equal benefit among co-owners in joint property
Substantial justice over technical objections

card.dispute: The dispute was between the children of a second, void marriage and other family members over entitlement to a share in ancestral coparcenary property.
issues_decided: Whether children born from a void second marriage are entitled to inherit ancestral coparcenary property under Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
Whether Section 16(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 restricts the inheritance rights of children from void marriages to only the parents' property
holdings: Children born from a void marriage are legitimized under Section 16(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, but this legitimacy does not extend to inheritance rights in ancestral coparcenary property.
Section 16(3) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 explicitly limits the inheritance rights of children from void marriages to the property of their parents only, and not to any other person’s property.
doctrines: Legitimization by statute
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Prohibition of polygamy under Hindu law

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against the eviction order passed by the Revisional Court and upheld by the High Court, primarily over whether rent arrears were lawfully cleared through court deposit.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's deposit of rent under Section 30(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act could be considered as payment in discharge of arrears under Section 20(4) of the Act.
Whether the Revisional Court and High Court erred in holding that the deposit under Section 30(2) was not bona fide and could not be set off against rent arrears.
holdings: A deposit made under Section 30(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings Act has the statutory effect of payment to the landlord and must be considered in determining whether arrears are cleared under Section 20(4).

Section 20(4) must be read harmoniously with Section 30(6) to avoid rendering Section 30(2) and (6) otiose, ensuring deposits under Section 30(2) are treated as effective payment unless challenged on valid grounds.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(4)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30(6)
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Statutory interpretation to avoid otioseness
No isolated reading of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The dispute was between private companies and the National Textile Corporation over whether the Maharashtra State eviction law could override central laws governing tenancy in government-owned premises.
issues_decided: Whether the President's assent under Article 254(2) of the Constitution, when granted generally, extends to all repugnant central laws or only to those specifically mentioned in the proposal.

Whether the Bombay Rent Act, as an extension of a pre-constitutional 'existing law', could prevail over the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, in the absence of specific presidential assent for that central law.
holdings: The President’s assent under Article 254(2) can be granted in a general manner by referring to entries in the Concurrent List and illustrative central laws, and such assent extends to all repugnant central laws on the same subject.

A declaration in the preamble of a state law that it has received presidential assent under Article 254(2) is conclusive and not subject to judicial review; courts cannot probe into the President’s application of mind.
doctrines: Presidential assent as a substantive legislative act
Finality of presidential assent under Article 254(2)
Non-justiciability of the President's application of mind in granting assent
Doctrine of legislative competence in Concurrent List matters

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Khazan Singh fought against the Union of India over the dismissal of a land acquisition reference for default due to non-appearance.
issues_decided: Whether a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be dismissed for default by the claimant or his counsel.
Whether a Civil Court can restore a dismissed reference under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure despite non-appearance.
holdings: A reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act cannot be dismissed for default; the Civil Court must proceed to determine the objection and pass an award.
The Civil Court has inherent power under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to restore a reference, even if the application cites Order 9 Rule 9, to do justice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 9
doctrines: Inherent powers of civil courts
Statutory duty to adjudicate under special enactments
Finality and executability of awards as decrees

card.dispute: The defendant appealed against the High Court's decision to uphold a will that granted the plaintiff ownership of agricultural land and a house, challenging the will's validity due to insufficient attestation.
issues_decided: Whether the will was validly attested by two witnesses as required under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925
Whether the execution of the will could be proved under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 with only one attesting witness who failed to prove the attestation by the second witness
Whether Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 can be invoked to dispense with the evidence of an available attesting witness
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the first appellate court's decree based on a factual finding without identifying a substantial question of law
holdings: A will must be attested by at least two witnesses as per Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, and mere signing by the testator is insufficient without proof of attestation.

Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, if the sole attesting witness examined fails to prove the attestation by the second witness, the will is not proved, even if the second witness is available.
Section 71 of the Indian Evidence Act applies only when attesting witnesses deny execution or have no recollection, not when a party chooses not to examine an available witness.
The High Court erred in reversing the first appellate court’s decree on factual appreciation without identifying a substantial question of law, and such reversal is impermissible.
doctrines: Best evidence rule
Mandatory proof of attestation for wills
Limited applicability of Section 71 as an exception to Section 68
Prohibition on drawing adverse inference under Section 114(g) if evidence is deliberately withheld

card.dispute: The appellant, Km Sharma, challenged the Income Tax Officer's attempt to reopen his tax assessments for past years based on a court award in a land acquisition case, arguing that the assessments had become time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 150(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, effective from 1.4.1989, can be applied retrospectively to reopen assessments that had already attained finality due to the expiry of the limitation period under Section 149 prior to the amendment?
Whether Section 150(2) of the Income Tax Act operates to bar reassessment proceedings based on court orders under any law when the original assessment had become time-barred?
holdings: The amendment to Section 150(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, has only prospective operation and cannot be used to reopen assessments that had already become final due to the expiry of the limitation period under Section 149 before 1.4.1989.

Section 150(2) bars the reopening of assessments that have attained finality due to limitation, regardless of whether the basis for reassessment is an order under the Income Tax Act or a court order under any other law.
doctrines: Prospective operation of amendments
Presumption against retrospectivity in tax statutes
Finality of time-barred assessments
Principle of non-discrimination in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The parents of a deceased woman fought against her husband and in-laws over whether he abetted her suicide through dowry-related cruelty.
issues_decided: Whether the husband abetted the suicide of his wife under Section 306 IPC based on proven cruelty.
Whether an accused can be convicted under Section 306 IPC despite the absence of a formal charge under that section.
holdings: Cruelty by a husband, including pressuring his wife to surrender her stridhana property and isolating her from family, can constitute abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC when it drives her to self-harm.
A conviction under Section 306 IPC is valid even without a specific charge if the facts were included in the charges under other sections and the accused had a fair opportunity to defend.
doctrines: Presumption of abetment in cases of suicide by married women under Section 113A
Doctrine of constructive charge under Section 221 Cr.P.C.
Doctrine of substantial justice over technical defects under Section 215 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The landlord filed a suit for rent arrears and eviction; the tenant sought to set aside the ex-parte decree after decree-holder obtained possession, without depositing the decretal amount or seeking security in compliance with the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 17(1) of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 is mandatory or directory?
Whether the application to set aside an ex-parte decree is maintainable without depositing the decretal amount or obtaining prior court permission to furnish security?
holdings: The proviso to Section 17(1) of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 is mandatory, and non-compliance renders the application to set aside an ex-parte decree non-entertainable.

An application to set aside an ex-parte decree must be accompanied by deposit of the decretal amount or a prior court order permitting security in lieu; failure to do so makes the application incompetent.
provisions: Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, Section 17(1) proviso
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 20(2)(a)
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Summary procedure and finality of decrees in small causes courts
Principle of non-entertainability for non-compliance with mandatory conditions

card.dispute: The accused, Lehna, was convicted of murdering his mother, brother, and sister-in-law, and the dispute centered on whether the death sentence imposed should be upheld or commuted to life imprisonment.
issues_decided: Whether the case falls within the 'rarest of rare' category warranting a death sentence?
Whether the mitigating circumstances, including the accused's mental condition and family dispute over land, justify commutation of the death sentence?
Whether the balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances supports life imprisonment instead of death?
holdings: Death sentence should be awarded only in the rarest of rare cases where life imprisonment is inadequate and the collective conscience of society is shocked.
A balance must be struck between aggravating and mitigating circumstances, with full weight given to factors like mental condition, family conflict, and absence of premeditation.
The crime, though brutal, appeared to be an impulsive act arising from familial dispute over land, not a premeditated or diabolical act, thus life imprisonment is more appropriate than death.
The sentence of death is modified to life imprisonment, while the conviction under Section 302 IPC is upheld.
doctrines: Rarest of rare doctrine
Principle of proportionality between crime and punishment
Balance-sheet of aggravating and mitigating circumstances
Sentencing discretion guided by judicial conscience and societal norms

card.dispute: The judgment-debtors challenged the High Court's order directing the Trial Court to prepare a decree after the second appeal, due to ambiguity in the reliefs granted.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's appellate judgment sufficiently specified the reliefs granted to enable a decree to be drawn up in conformity with it?
Whether the Trial Court could lawfully be directed to draw up the decree when the High Court reversed the dismissal of the suit?
Whether an omission to specify reliefs in the appellate judgment could be rectified under Section 152 of the CPC?
holdings: An appellate judgment must clearly specify the reliefs granted so that the decree conforms to the judgment; a mere statement that the appeal is allowed is insufficient.
The High Court, not the Trial Court, should ordinarily draw up the decree when reversing a dismissal, unless its rules provide otherwise.
An omission in specifying reliefs due to an accidental slip or omission can be corrected under Section 152 CPC to reflect the court's true intention.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 31
doctrines: Decree must conform to judgment
Clerical or arithmetical error correction under Section 152 CPC
Appellate court's duty to specify relief on reversal

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal representatives of two brothers from the Lachiah Setty family over the partition and valuation of joint family properties, including coffee estates and securities, following a long-pending arbitration and litigation initiated in 1938.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to a 2/19th share in the joint family properties despite non-availability of certain movable assets?
What is the correct date for valuation of shares in a partition suit — the date of the preliminary decree or the final decree?
Whether non-availability of shares, bonds, and securities can deprive a coparcener of their rightful share in joint family property?
Whether parties in possession of joint family property are liable to account for rents, income, profits, and dividends from the date of severance?
holdings: A coparcener is entitled to their declared share in joint family property regardless of the non-availability of specific movable assets, provided the value is accounted for at the time of final partition.
The valuation of joint family property for partition must be as of the date of the final decree, to ensure equitable distribution based on current values.
The mere non-availability of movable properties like securities does not disentitle a coparcener from receiving their share if they are otherwise entitled by valuation at the time of final decree.
Parties in possession of joint family property are liable to render accounts of rents, profits, income, and dividends from the date of severance (11th July 1940) up to the date of the final decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 18
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 26 Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 26 Rule 14
doctrines: Character of joint family property remains unchanged until actual partition, even after severance of status
Equitable partition requires valuation as of the date of final decree to balance equities
Principle of accounting for income and profits during possession in partition suits

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the maintainability of recovery proceedings initiated by the U.P. Financial Corporation under the U.P. Public Monies (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972, after the enactment of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993.
issues_decided: Whether recovery proceedings under the U.P. Public Monies (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972 are maintainable after the enactment of the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993?
Whether Section 34(2) of the Recovery of Debts Act saves the mode of recovery under the U.P. Act?
Whether the jurisdiction of the Debt Recovery Tribunal under the 1993 Act is exclusive for recovery of debts due to financial institutions?
holdings: The Debt Recovery Tribunal established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 has exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate and recover debts due to financial institutions.

Proceedings under the U.P. Public Monies (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972 are not maintainable as they are not saved by Section 34(2) of the 1993 Act and conflict with its overriding effect under Section 34(1).
The U.P. Act does not provide an alternative mode of recovery parallel to the 1993 Act, and its proceedings cannot proceed once the 1993 Act has occupied the field.
provisions: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 17
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 18
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 31
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 34
Uttar Pradesh Public Monies (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1972
doctrines: Doctrine of exclusive jurisdiction
Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Casus omissus
Doctrine of legislative intent
Doctrine of ouster of jurisdiction

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted by the trial and high courts for murder and other offences, challenged their convictions and sentences, arguing lack of evidence for murder and unlawful assembly.
issues_decided: Whether the accused were guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC or culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-I IPC
Whether the accused formed an unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Whether the conviction under Section 225 IPC for resisting lawful apprehension was valid
Whether the convictions under Sections 323 and 324 IPC were legally sustainable
holdings: The accused committed culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-I IPC, as the act occurred in sudden heat of passion without premeditation, and common intention was formed during the incident.
The conviction under Section 149 IPC cannot be sustained as there was no evidence of an unlawful assembly with a common object as required under Section 141 IPC.
The conviction under Section 225 IPC is invalid because detaining the accused for a village panchayat does not constitute lawful apprehension, and no force was used to resist it.
Convictions under Sections 323 and 324 IPC are upheld as the injuries and assaults were proven, and the sentences are proportionate and legally sound.
doctrines: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC: sudden fight and heat of passion
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Unlawful assembly under Section 141 IPC
Requirement of lawful apprehension under Section 225 IPC

card.dispute: The complainant and the State of Punjab appealed the acquittal of two accused, Prem Singh and Deepinder Singh, in a murder case, challenging the High Court's decision to overturn their conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution made out a case for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC based on reliable evidence?
Whether the inculpatory part of the accused's statement under Section 313 CrPC can be the sole basis for conviction?
Whether Deepinder Singh was rightly acquitted due to lack of evidence of common intention?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the charges due to unreliable eyewitness testimony, delayed FIR, and fabricated evidence, justifying the acquittal.
The inculpatory part of an accused's statement under Section 313 CrPC cannot form the sole basis of conviction if the prosecution's evidence is untrustworthy.
Deepinder Singh was falsely implicated with no motive or credible evidence linking him to the crime, warranting his acquittal.
doctrines: Prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt
Partially inculpatory statements under Section 313 CrPC require corroboration by reliable prosecution evidence
Acquittal upheld when evidence is fabricated or inherently improbable

card.dispute: The landlord-appellants sought ejectment of a tenant who had stopped paying rent, but the High Court dismissed the writ petition relying on a Full Bench decision holding that lease agreements violating the U.P. Urban Buildings Act were unenforceable.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement of lease in contravention of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 is void.
Whether such an agreement is enforceable for the purpose of seeking ejectment of the tenant.
holdings: An agreement of lease that contravenes the U.P. Urban Buildings Act, 1972 is not automatically void unless the statute expressly declares it so.
Such an agreement remains enforceable between the parties for ejectment if it does not violate a specific prohibition in the statute rendering it void.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 13
doctrines: Binding precedent of larger bench (Nanakram v. State)
Enforceability of contracts contrary to statutory provisions unless expressly void
Public policy exception to contract enforcement

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction of the tenant due to rent arrears, but the tenant resisted by citing a subsequent eviction by a paramount title (HUDA/Trust).
issues_decided: Whether the tenant could resist eviction by relying on a subsequent event of eviction by paramount title after the suit was filed?
Whether the court could take cognizance of a subsequent factual event to alter the relief granted in a landlord-tenant dispute?
Whether the tenant's attornment to a third party (Trust) extinguished the landlord's right to seek eviction?
holdings: A tenant cannot resist eviction by invoking a subsequent eviction by paramount title unless the landlord's title has legally and finally ended and the tenant has no defence against such eviction.

Courts may consider subsequent events only in exceptional circumstances, provided they are pleaded properly, do not violate fair procedure, and substantially affect the relief; otherwise, rights are crystallized at the time of suit institution.
Voluntary attornment to a third party without a final order ending the landlord's title does not extinguish the landlord's right to evict the tenant or defeat a pending eviction decree.
provisions: Haryana Urban Development Authority Act, 1977, Section 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Crystallization of rights at the time of institution of suit
Doctrine of eviction by paramount title
Power of court to consider subsequent events 'inter partes' in exceptional cases
Requirement of amendment of pleadings to introduce new factual events

card.dispute: Family members disputed the validity of an arbitration award passed by two arbitrators, claiming it violated the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, which prohibits an even number of arbitrators.
issues_decided: Whether an arbitration agreement with two arbitrators is invalid under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, despite Section 10 prohibiting an even number of arbitrators
Whether a party can challenge the composition of the arbitral tribunal after participating in the proceedings without raising a timely objection
Whether the composition of the arbitral tribunal can be challenged under Section 34 of the Act if it conforms to the parties' agreement
holdings: An agreement for two arbitrators is not automatically invalid; parties may derogate from Section 10 of the Act by mutual consent, making the provision derogable.
A party that participates in arbitration without timely objection under Section 16(2) is deemed to have waived the right to later challenge the tribunal’s composition.

Under Section 34(2)(a)(v), an award cannot be set aside if the tribunal's composition follows the parties' agreement, even if it conflicts with a statutory provision, provided the agreement is not against a non-derogable rule.
doctrines: Derogability of statutory provisions in arbitration by party agreement
Deemed waiver of objections under the doctrine of delay and acquiescence
Party autonomy in arbitration

card.dispute: Petitioners challenged the Union Government's 2002 order cancelling all petroleum product dealership allotments made since 2000, alleging arbitrary cancellation without distinguishing between tainted and merit-based selections.
issues_decided: Whether the government's blanket cancellation of dealership allotments was valid and lawful.
Whether allotments recommended by Dealer Selection Boards were made on merits or due to political connections.
Whether an independent inquiry was necessary to examine the fairness of the allotments.
Whether the cancellation order violated principles of fair play and good governance.
holdings: The blanket cancellation of all allotments, including those possibly made on merit, was arbitrary and violated principles of non-arbitrariness and fair play.
An independent committee must examine whether specific allotments were made on merits or due to political or extraneous considerations.
The government should have ordered a probe into allegedly tainted allotments instead of cancelling all, which scuttled transparency and due process.
The impugned order was quashed except for cases referred to the independent committee for further examination.
provisions: Guidelines dated 9th October, 2000 (Government of India, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas)
doctrines: Principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14 of the Constitution
Doctrine of fair play and reasoned decision-making
Principle of good governance and transparency in public appointments
Doctrine of proportionality in administrative action

card.dispute: The dispute was between the appellants (Ombalika Das and another), who were major daughters of a retired military engineer, and the respondent tenant, over whether the appellants could use a special eviction procedure under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, based on their father's military status after his retirement.
issues_decided: Whether major daughters of a retired member of the General Reserve Engineering Force, who were dependent and residing with him, could invoke Section 29B of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act for eviction of a tenant under Section 13(1)(ff) after the father's retirement?
Whether the term 'a member of the naval, military or air force' in Section 29B includes a retired member when referring to relations who are landlords?
holdings: Section 29B of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act does not extend the benefit of summary eviction to major relations of a retired military member unless the member died while in service or within five years of retirement.

The phrase 'a member' in the context of relations (category iv) is distinct from 'such member' used for active or recently retired members, and does not include a retired person who is still alive beyond the one-year post-retirement window implied in other clauses.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 13(1)(ff)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, Section 29B
doctrines: Principle of ejusdem generis and use of 'such' to refer back to previously defined terms
Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The tenant-appellant and sub-tenant-turned-landlord disputed whether the sub-tenancy merged into ownership upon the latter's purchase of the entire property, affecting the right to evict.
issues_decided: Whether the sub-tenancy of the respondent merged into the ownership upon purchase of the entire property by him from the original landlords.
Whether the respondent, after purchasing the property, could maintain an eviction petition against the appellant-tenant under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965.
Whether Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act allows severance of reversion and statutory attornment, enabling a transferee of part of leased property to evict the tenant.
holdings: When a sub-tenant purchases full ownership of leased premises, including the reversion, his sub-tenancy merges into the larger estate of ownership and cannot coexist.
A transferee of a part of leased property acquires all rights of the landlord over that part by operation of law under Section 109 of the Transfer of Property Act, without needing tenant's consent.
The doctrine of merger applies even if a tenant's estate intervenes, as statutory attornment occurs upon transfer, enabling the new owner to seek eviction.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(2)(b), 11(3), 11(8)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 111(d)
doctrines: Doctrine of Merger
Statutory Attornment
Severance of Reversion under Section 109

card.dispute: The Nagpur Improvement Trust challenged orders granting landowners additional compensation and interest in land acquisition cases, arguing entitlement under amended provisions of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the acquiring authority under state-specific improvement trust acts is the Government or the Trust.
Whether landowners are entitled to additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) of the Land Acquisition Act when acquisition awards were made before 30th April, 1982.
Whether subsequent amendments to the Land Acquisition Act, such as the proviso to Section 6 inserted in 1967, apply to state acquisition laws that incorporate the original Act.
Whether landowners are entitled to interest on enhanced solatium and additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) and Section 23(2) of the Land Acquisition Act.
holdings: The acquiring authority under the state improvement acts is the Government, not the Improvement Trust, as Section 17-A of the Land Acquisition Act applies uniformly.
Landowners are not entitled to additional compensation under Section 23(1-A) if the Collector’s award was made before 30th April, 1982, as per the ruling in K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala.
State acquisition laws incorporate the original Land Acquisition Act as modified by state amendments; thus, later central amendments (e.g., 1967, 1984) do not apply to such state laws.
Landowners are entitled to interest on both enhanced solatium under Section 23(2) and additional compensation under Section 23(1-A), in line with Sunder v. Union of India.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967, Section 6
doctrines: Doctrine of Incorporation by Reference
Prospective vs. Retrospective Application of Amendments
Principle of Equal Protection under Article 14 (discussed but not applied)
Right to Interest on Delayed Compensation

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the land acquisition proceedings after 17 years, seeking quashing of notifications and restoration of land, while the company and state defended the acquisition as final and barred by delay and laches.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a writ petition after 17 years of delay and without sufficient explanation for laches.
Whether the land could be restored to the original owners on the ground that it was not used for the public purpose for which it was acquired.
Whether non-payment of enhanced compensation justified quashing of acquisition proceedings.
holdings: A writ petition challenging land acquisition notifications under Sections 4 and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act is barred by delay and laches if filed after a reasonable time, especially when the petitioner has participated in compensation proceedings without timely challenge.
Once possession is taken and compensation paid, the land vests absolutely with the state; non-utilization for the stated public purpose does not entitle former owners to restoration of possession.
Failure to pay enhanced compensation does not invalidate acquisition or justify quashing of proceedings, nor does it amount to unjust enrichment of the beneficiary.
doctrines: Delay and laches
Vesting of title upon acquisition
Finality of acquisition proceedings
No restitution for non-utilization of acquired land
Prohibition of sitting on the fence in acquisition challenges

card.dispute: The appellants, Nandu Rastogi and Bal Mukund Rastogi, challenged their conviction and sentence for the murder of Shankar Rastogi, alleging that the evidence did not support their involvement or a common intention under Section 34 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 302/34 IPC and Section 27 of the Arms Act was legally sustainable based on the evidence on record?
Whether Bal Mukund Rastogi could be held guilty under Section 34 IPC despite not directly participating in the act of shooting?
Whether the failure to examine the informant's grandchild affected the prosecution's case?
Whether the principles laid down in Parshuram Singh and Suresh regarding common intention under Section 34 IPC apply to exonerate the appellants?
holdings: The conviction of both appellants under Section 302/34 IPC and Section 27 of the Arms Act is upheld as the evidence, including eyewitness testimony, is reliable and consistent with guilt.
Bal Mukund Rastogi is liable under Section 34 IPC as his act of preventing others from intervening was part of a common intention to commit murder, even though he did not fire the fatal shot.
The non-examination of the informant’s grandchild does not materially weaken the prosecution case when multiple credible witnesses support the occurrence.

Section 34 IPC applies where there is a pre-arranged plan or common intention, which may develop on the spot; mere presence is not enough, but active participation in furtherance of the common goal suffices.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Vicarious liability in criminal law
Principle of pre-arranged plan or prior concert
Inference of common intention from conduct and circumstances

card.dispute: Tenants appealed against the High Court's decision denying them protection from eviction, claiming ownership of the superstructure and that the property was in a notified slum area under the Tamil Nadu Slum Areas Act, while the landlady contested these claims.
issues_decided: Whether the burden of proof lay on the tenants to establish that the suit property was situated in a notified slum area under Section 3 of the Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971?
Whether the tenants were entitled to injunction against eviction under Section 29 of the Act without proving the property was in a declared slum area?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the factual findings of the lower courts regarding the location of the property?
holdings: The burden of proof to establish that the property was in a notified slum area under Section 3 of the Act lay on the tenants, as they were claiming protection under Section 29.
Tenants are not entitled to injunction under Section 29 of the Act unless they prove the property is in a declared slum area with legal and cogent evidence.

The High Court was justified in interfering with the lower courts' findings when those findings were based on no legal evidence or misreading of evidence, especially where the burden of proof was wrongly placed on the landlady.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, Section 3
Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, Section 29
doctrines: Burden of proof
Interference with findings of fact in second appeal
Perverse findings doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction by the Bombay High Court in a murder case, arguing against the admissibility of evidence and the correctness of the legal principles applied.
issues_decided: Whether the ratio in Pulikuri Kottaya v. Emperor, regarding the interpretation of Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, remains binding on High Courts.
Whether the recovery of a gun pursuant to information given by an accused leads to the discovery of a fact within the meaning of Section 27.
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal of two accused (A4 and A6) and convicting them under Section 326 read with Section 149 IPC.
Whether A2 could be convicted under Section 302 IPC based on common intention or under Section 149 IPC.
holdings: The decision of the Privy Council in Pulikuri Kottaya remains binding on High Courts until overruled by the Supreme Court, and its ratio interpreting Section 27 of the Evidence Act is still valid.
Information leading to the recovery of a weapon leads to the discovery of the fact that the accused concealed it, not the discovery of the object itself, satisfying Section 27 of the Evidence Act.

The High Court erred in convicting A4 and A6 as there was no evidence they shared common intention or knowledge of the attack; their acquittal by the trial court was legally sound and should not have been reversed.

A2 was rightly convicted for murder under Section 302 IPC with aid of Section 34 (common intention), not Section 149 (unlawful assembly), as the acts were part of a shared plan despite only injuring a bystander.
doctrines: Binding precedent from Privy Council decisions until overruled by the Supreme Court
Doctrine of discovery of fact under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act
Principle of common intention under Section 34 IPC
Doctrine of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings and the failure to issue fresh notifications or awards after the Supreme Court's deemed date order, seeking enhanced compensation and claiming the acquisition lapsed.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings lapsed due to non-issuance of a fresh declaration under Section 6 or award under Section 11 within statutory timeframes after the Supreme Court's deemed date order.
Whether the Supreme Court's earlier order creating a deemed date for notification under Section 4(1) was invalid for contravening statutory provisions or Article 142 of the Constitution.
Whether the claimants were entitled to compensation despite the delay in redetermination and possession.
holdings: The deemed date of notification under Section 4(1) was a legal fiction created solely for enhanced compensation and did not require fresh proceedings under Sections 6 or 11; thus, the acquisition did not lapse.
The Supreme Court's exercise of power under Article 142 to grant a deemed date for compensation is valid and not contrary to statutory provisions, especially when beneficial to claimants.
The development authority must pay compensation within one month of this order if not already paid, and any reference petition under Section 18 must be decided per the 1991 directions.
doctrines: Legal fiction
Doctrine of merger
Principle of beneficial interpretation
Limitation of Article 142 powers to statutory framework

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent Nos. 2 to 5 fought against respondent No. 1 over joint ownership of mortgaged land and sought to amend their plaint to include new facts, which the High Court disallowed on grounds of limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could exercise revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC to set aside an interlocutory order allowing amendment of a plaint.
Whether the trial court's order allowing amendment of the plaint would finally dispose of the suit or lead to failure of justice or irreparable injury.
holdings: An interlocutory order allowing amendment of pleadings is revisable under Section 115 CPC only if it finally disposes of the suit or causes failure of justice or irreparable injury.
Amendment of pleadings does not cause failure of justice or irreparable injury, as the affected party retains full opportunity to defend and appeal, so the High Court erred in interfering.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC
Principle of failure of justice in revision
Amendment of pleadings under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC

card.dispute: The landlord's legal heirs sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent, while the tenant contested the arrears claimed and the procedure followed by the Rent Controller.
issues_decided: Whether the proviso to Section 13(2)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949 requires the Rent Controller to pass a provisional order assessing arrears, interest, and costs before eviction proceedings can proceed
Whether the tenant must comply with a provisional assessment order to avoid eviction for non-payment of rent
What remedies are available to the tenant if the final adjudication of arrears differs from the provisional order
holdings: The proviso to Section 13(2)(i) requires the Rent Controller to pass a provisional order assessing arrears, interest, and costs, which the tenant must pay or tender on the first date of hearing after the order.
If the tenant complies with the provisional order, the eviction proceeding must continue to a final adjudication on the arrears; non-compliance leads to automatic eviction.

If the final arrears are less than the amount deposited, the tenant is entitled to a refund; if more, the tenant must be given a reasonable time to pay the deficit before eviction, provided they have regularly paid ongoing rent.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restrictions Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(i) proviso
doctrines: Inherent powers of the court to ensure justice
Principle of equity and fair play
Procedural innovation to effectuate legislative purpose

card.dispute: The heirs of deceased appellants in a partition suit appeal against the dismissal of their appeal due to abatement for failure to substitute the deceased parties in time.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing an application for substitution of legal representatives after the death of parties during appeal could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act?
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to set aside the abatement of the appeal?
holdings: Delay in filing an application for substitution can be condoned if sufficient cause is shown, especially when the party is illiterate and not negligent, and courts must interpret 'sufficient cause' liberally to advance substantial justice.
The High Court erred in refusing to set aside the abatement; the trial court's discretion to condone delay should not be disturbed unless arbitrary, and the appeal must be decided on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 9
doctrines: Liberal construction of 'sufficient cause'
Substantial justice over technicalities
Principle of condonation of delay
Balance between litigant's rights and procedural compliance

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a fresh notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, issued after a previous declaration was quashed, arguing that the one-year time limit to issue such a declaration must be reckoned from the original Section 4(1) notification date.
issues_decided: Whether a fresh notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be issued within one year from the date of a court order quashing a prior Section 6 notification, or whether the one-year period is strictly computed from the original Section 4(1) notification date.
Whether judicial precedents allowing the limitation period under Section 6 to restart after a quashing order are consistent with the statutory language.
holdings: The one-year period for issuing a declaration under Section 6 must be computed from the date of the original notification under Section 4(1), and a fresh declaration after quashing of a prior one does not restart the limitation period.

Judicial attempts to extend the limitation period from the date of a court order quashing a Section 6 notification are impermissible, as they contradict the plain and unambiguous language of Section 6(1) of the Act.
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Casus omissus
Separation of powers in judicial interpretation
Prospective overruling
Stare decisis with legislative amendment context

card.dispute: The parties disputed over the execution of a decree for specific performance of an agreement to sell 8 kathas of land, primarily due to inadequate property description in the plaint and mishandling of a security deposit during appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the defect in the plaint due to lack of proper description of the immovable property can be cured during execution.
Whether the Executing Court can determine the correct boundaries of the decretal property.
Whether the decree-holders are entitled to retain the Rs. 5,000 security deposit made during the stay of execution.
holdings: A defect in the plaint regarding inadequate property description can be cured during execution by invoking Section 47 CPC, as it relates to the execution and satisfaction of the decree.

The Executing Court has the power to ascertain and rectify the correct boundaries of the decretal property by examining maps, revenue records, or through a survey, to ensure the decree is properly implemented.
The Rs. 5,000 security deposit made during the stay of execution must be returned to the judgment-debtors as there was no final judicial order appropriating it to the decree-holders.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 32
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 34
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of decree
Doctrine of curative process under Section 47 CPC
Principle of complete justice under Article 142 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a fresh notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 after a previous Section 6 notification was quashed, arguing that the fresh notification was time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether a fresh notification under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 can be issued after the quashing of a previous Section 6 notification, beyond the one-year period from the original Section 4(1) notification.
Whether the period of limitation under Section 6(1) can be extended based on court orders or quashing of prior declarations.
holdings: After quashing of a Section 6 notification, a fresh declaration under Section 6 must still comply with the one-year time limit from the date of the original Section 4(1) notification; no fresh period begins upon quashing.
The courts cannot read exceptions into Section 6(1) of the Act; the time limit is peremptory and cannot be extended even if the earlier declaration was quashed by court order.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Casus omissus
Stare decisis
Separation of powers (judicial non-legislation)

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction in a case involving the abduction and alleged murder of Sukhchain Singh and assault on Nishan Singh, arguing that the evidence was unreliable and inconsistent.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could be held guilty of abduction and murder of Sukhchain Singh based on the prosecution's evidence, particularly under Section 34 IPC?
Whether the appellants could be convicted for causing injuries to PW-4 (Nishan Singh) based on the evidence of the injured witness?
holdings: The conviction of the appellants for abduction and murder of Sukhchain Singh cannot be sustained due to lack of reliable evidence, especially since the key witness (PW-7) was disbelieved by the courts and the identification of the body was uncorroborated.

The appellants are guilty of voluntarily causing hurt to PW-4 under Section 324 read with Section 34 IPC, as the injured witness's testimony about the assault was credible and uncontradicted in material particulars.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Corroboration in cases of identification of dead bodies
Partial reliance on prosecution evidence

card.dispute: Rattan Dev (appellant) sued Pasam Devi (respondent) for a permanent injunction, which was dismissed by the First Appellate Court primarily due to the appellant's non-examination as a witness; the High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine.
issues_decided: Whether the First Appellate Court failed to properly appreciate all the evidence on record, including documentary and oral evidence, while reversing the Trial Court's decree?
Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the second appeal in limine on the ground that no substantial question of law arose under Section 100 CPC?
holdings: The First Appellate Court must consider all evidence on record, including oral and documentary, and cannot solely rely on the non-examination of the plaintiff to reverse a decree.
Failure to apply judicial mind to material evidence raises a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC, warranting hearing of the second appeal on merits.
doctrines: Adverse inference from non-examination of plaintiff
Substantial question of law
Appellate court's duty to consider entire evidence

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Madras City Tenants Protection (Amendment) Act, 1994, and whether the Supreme Court's earlier dismissal of appeals in a similar case had binding effect on the High Court's ability to reconsider the law.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court's dismissal of appeals in 1986 without reasoning amounted to a declaration of law under Article 141 of the Constitution affirming the High Court's decision in M. Vardaraja Pillai's case.
Whether the Full Bench of the High Court was precluded from re-examining the legal correctness of its earlier Division Bench judgment after the Supreme Court dismissed appeals on technical grounds.
holdings: A dismissal of an appeal by the Supreme Court without reasoned orders does not constitute a declaration of law under Article 141 and does not bind courts on the legal reasoning of the lower court.

The Full Bench of the High Court retains the authority to review or reconsider a Division Bench’s legal opinion even if appeals against it were dismissed by the Supreme Court on technical grounds like non-joinder of a necessary party.
doctrines: Doctrine of precedent under Article 141
Binding nature of Supreme Court decisions only when law is declared
Distinction between operative and obiter parts of a judgment
Principle that summary dismissal does not amount to affirmation of law

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants) challenged the trial court's refusal to reject the plaintiffs' plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, which sought declaration that prior judicial orders were null and void, while the plaintiffs argued those orders did not bar their suit.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC should be decided solely on the averments in the plaint without requiring the defendant to file a written statement.
Whether the trial court committed a procedural irregularity by directing the filing of a written statement without first deciding the rejection application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
holdings: An application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC must be decided based only on the plaint's averments; the defendant's written statement is irrelevant at that stage.

Directing a defendant to file a written statement without first deciding a rejection application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC constitutes procedural irregularity and amounts to non-exercise of jurisdiction.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII Rule 10
doctrines: Res judicata
Lis pendens
Procedural jurisdiction and judicial duty to decide preliminary applications

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought to amend his suit from one for permanent injunction to include declaration of title and recovery of possession after being allegedly dispossessed during the pendency of the suit, which the defendant opposed.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for permanent prohibitory injunction can be amended to include claims for declaration of title and recovery of possession when the cause of action arose during the pendency of the suit.
Whether permitting such an amendment would prejudice the defendant, especially regarding adverse possession.
holdings: A plaintiff may amend a pending suit to include new reliefs like declaration of title and recovery of possession if the cause of action arises during the suit, without altering the basic structure of the case.

Such amendment should be allowed to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, provided the defendant is protected by directing that the amended claims do not relate back to the original suit date, but to the amendment application date to safeguard rights under limitation or adverse possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings
Relation back of amendments
Avoidance of multiplicity of suits
Protection of accrued rights during litigation

card.dispute: The accused-appellant was convicted of murder for killing his younger brother based on dying declarations, but challenged the conviction arguing lack of intent and insufficient evidence for murder under Section 300 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the accused had the intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death under Section 300 IPC
Whether the injuries inflicted were sufficient to bring the case within Clause Thirdly of Section 300 IPC
Whether the conviction should be under Section 302 or a lesser offence under Section 304 Part I IPC
holdings: The accused did not have the intention to cause death, as the attack arose from a sudden quarrel over a petty issue and he ceased aggression when intervened.
The injuries, though serious, were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, given the medical evidence that death resulted from septicemia, not immediate trauma.
The appellant is guilty of culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC due to intention to cause severe bodily injury, but not death.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Doctrine of intention in murder under Section 300 IPC
Objective test for sufficiency of injury to cause death in the ordinary course of nature
Principle of reasonable doubt in criminal conviction

card.dispute: The railway administration sought to evict a retired employee from official accommodation, but the High Court ruled it could not invoke Section 138 of the Railways Act without proving ownership; the appeal challenged that ruling.
issues_decided: Whether Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890 can be invoked to recover possession from a retired railway employee without the railway proving ownership of the premises.
Whether a retired employee, who was inducted into official accommodation, can deny the railway administration's title to the property.
holdings: Section 138 of the Indian Railways Act, 1890 applies to employees who retire, as 'discharge' includes retirement, and the provision can be invoked to recover possession without the railway proving ownership.

A retired employee inducted into railway accommodation is estopped under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, 1872 from denying the railway's title to the premises during the continuance of the license or tenancy.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act
Liberal construction of public interest statutes
Mutatis mutandis application of landlord-tenant estoppel to licensee and sub-tenant

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against eviction from a shop, challenging the landlord's claim of ownership and the need to re-build the property.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's plea questioning the landlord's ownership amounted to a denial of title under Section 12(1)(c) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961
Whether the tenant was liable to be evicted under Section 12(1)(h) of the Act for bona fide requirement of the premises for re-building
holdings: A tenant's request for proof of ownership to defend against eviction does not amount to a denial of the landlord's title if the tenant continues to recognize the landlord-tenant relationship and does not disown tenancy.
Eviction is justified under Section 12(1)(h) if the landlord bona fide requires the premises for re-building and such work cannot be done without vacancy.
doctrines: Doctrine of estoppel under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act
Doctrine of approbate and reprobate
Requirement of clear and unequivocal disclaimer for forfeiture of tenancy

card.dispute: The State of Haryana sued the State of Punjab and the Union of India to enforce the completion of the Sutlej-Yamuna Link (SYL) Canal for sharing Ravi and Beas waters, based on prior agreements and orders.
issues_decided: Whether the 1976 notification, 1981 agreement, and 1985 Punjab Accord are legally binding on Punjab?
Whether Haryana has a enforceable right to the completion of the SYL Canal?
Whether a mandatory injunction can be issued against Punjab to complete the canal?
Whether the Union of India has a constitutional obligation to ensure the canal's completion if Punjab fails?
holdings: The 1976 notification, 1981 agreement, and 1985 Punjab Accord are binding and enforceable, and Punjab cannot renege on commitments made under them.
Haryana has a legitimate right to the completion of the SYL Canal to access its allocated share of Ravi and Beas waters.
A mandatory injunction lies against Punjab to complete the unfinished portion of the SYL Canal within one year.
If Punjab fails, the Union of India must complete the canal through its agencies to prevent waste of public funds and ensure Haryana’s water rights.
doctrines: Federal dispute resolution under Article 131
Enforceability of inter-state agreements
Mandatory injunction in public interest
Doctrine of legitimate expectation

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh fought with trainees under the Dairy Scheme over whether they could be denied additional training as veterinary pharmacists, a facility granted exclusively to trainees under the Veterinary Scheme (Gopal Sahayaks).
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions concerning training schemes.
Whether the State's policy to provide additional training only to Gopal Sahayaks was arbitrary or discriminatory.
Whether the classification between Dairy Scheme trainees and Gopal Sahayaks was constitutionally valid.
holdings: The High Court had jurisdiction to examine the policy decision since the matter involved training, not direct employment.
The State's decision to grant additional training only to Gopal Sahayaks was a valid policy choice and not arbitrary, as it was based on intelligible differentia and rational objectives.
The classification between Dairy Scheme trainees and Gopal Sahayaks was constitutionally valid, as it was based on distinct eligibility, training objectives, and post-training roles.
doctrines: Separation of powers
Reasonable classification
Non-interference with executive policy unless arbitrary or discriminatory

card.dispute: The State of Punjab challenged the High Court's invalidation of government notifications that created a new Gram Sabha for Khanpur, which Tehal Singh and others opposed on grounds of procedural fairness and territorial contiguity.
issues_decided: Whether the power under Sections 3 and 4 of the Punjab Panchayati Raj Act, 1994 to declare the territorial area and establish a Gram Sabha is legislative, administrative, or quasi-judicial in nature
Whether the rule of natural justice, particularly the right to a hearing, applies to such declarations
Whether Harijan Colony's inclusion in Gram Sabha, Khanpur violated the requirement of territorial contiguity
holdings: The power under Sections 3 and 4 of the Punjab Panchayati Raj Act, 1994 to declare and establish a Gram Sabha is legislative in character as it affects a geographical area generally and not individuals specifically.

The rule of natural justice, including the right to a hearing, does not apply to legislative acts unless the statute expressly mandates it; the Act does not require a hearing before such declarations.
The inclusion of Harijan Colony in Gram Sabha, Khanpur is valid as it is partially contiguous to Khanpur, satisfying the statutory requirement of contiguity.
doctrines: Legislative vs. administrative/quasi-judicial function distinction
Rule of natural justice not applicable to legislative actions unless statute provides
Doctrine of substantial compliance

card.dispute: The State of U.P. appealed against the High Court's acquittal of eight accused persons convicted by the trial court for the murder of Ram Lachhan and Rajendra in furtherance of an unlawful assembly.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the accused solely on the ground of alleged faulty investigation and minor discrepancies in the evidence?
Whether the testimony of interested eye-witnesses, including family members of the victims, can be entirely rejected?
Whether the prosecution case, supported by consistent eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, was sufficient to sustain the convictions?
holdings: A conviction can be sustained despite minor procedural lapses in investigation if the substantive evidence, especially eyewitness testimony, is reliable and consistent.
The fact that an eyewitness is a family member or interested party does not automatically discredit their testimony; courts must apply caution but not disregard it entirely.
The High Court erred in acquitting the accused without properly evaluating the totality of evidence, especially when the trial court's findings were well-reasoned and supported by credible evidence.
doctrines: Principle of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Reliability of interested eyewitnesses
Appreciation of evidence in criminal trials
No miscarriage of justice due to investigative lapses if prosecution case is otherwise strong

card.dispute: The appellants, who had been in possession of land for over 50 years, fought with a group attempting to take over the land, leading to criminal charges after the High Court convicted them of exceeding the right of private defence.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants exceeded their right of private defence of property and person under the IPC
Whether the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on the appellants undermines its case
Whether the High Court's conviction under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 IPC is sustainable without individual findings on who exceeded self-defence
holdings: The appellants were entitled to exercise private defence of property and person as the prosecution party were aggressors and not in settled possession, and the force used was justified given the attack on vital body parts.
The prosecution's omission to explain injuries on the appellants supports an inference that it suppressed the true origin of the incident, casting serious doubt on its reliability.
In absence of specific findings on which appellants exceeded self-defence, and given the need to liberally construe the right, all appellants are entitled to the benefit of acquittal.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Right of private defence of property and person
Liberal construction of private defence
Settled possession doctrine
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The landlord sought recovery of rent arrears and eviction, while the tenant challenged the ex-parte decree on grounds of improper service of summons.
issues_decided: Whether the defendant-tenant was properly served with summons as required under the Code of Civil Procedure?
Whether the ex-parte decree could be sustained despite alleged irregularities in service?
Whether the defendant’s knowledge of the pendency of the suit suffices to deny relief under Order 9, Rule 13 CPC?
holdings: Service of summons was not properly effected as the process server failed to comply with Order 5, Rules 17 and 18 CPC, and his testimony was inconsistent and uncorroborated.
An ex-parte decree cannot be upheld where there was no due service of summons, and the court must satisfy itself that service was duly made under Order 9, Rule 6 CPC.

Knowledge of the pendency of the suit is not equivalent to knowledge of the date of hearing; only the latter satisfies the proviso to Order 9, Rule 13 CPC for refusing to set aside an ex-parte decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 5, Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 5, Rule 18
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9, Rule 6
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9, Rule 13
doctrines: Proper service of summons is a prerequisite for a valid ex-parte decree
Judicial conscience must be applied before proceeding ex-parte
Oath against oath: credibility determination based on consistency and corroboration

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged the High Court's decision restoring the rights of intermediaries to retain land appurtenant to leased buildings under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the intermediary is entitled to retain land appurtenant to a building or structure under Section 6(1)(b) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, without being in khas possession.
Whether the land in question vested in the State free from encumbrances under Section 4 and Section 5 of the Act.
Whether the State could revise the record of rights after 38 years under Section 44(1) of the Act.
holdings: Section 6(1)(b) of the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953 allows an intermediary to retain land appurtenant to a building or structure even if not in khas possession, provided the building is owned by the intermediary.
The land did not vest in the State because the intermediary retained rights under Section 6(1)(b), and thus the State could not take possession under Section 5 of the Act.
The State cannot revise the record of rights under Section 44(1) after a long lapse without following proper procedures, and such revision was not the basis of the impugned order.
provisions: The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 4
The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 5
The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 6(1)(b)
The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 44(1)
The West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 57A
doctrines: Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Doctrine of expressio unius est exclusio alterius
Principle of legislative intent in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: Tanzeem-E-Sufia, a third party in possession of property, fought against Bibi Haliman's attempt to obtain possession through execution of a decree, claiming independent title and seeking to object under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a third party in possession can file objections under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC when a decree holder seeks possession?
Whether the executing court must adjudicate objections under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC before ordering delivery of possession?
Whether a third party must first be dispossessed and then file under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC, or can object prior to dispossession under Rule 97?
holdings: A third party in possession, not bound by the decree, is entitled to file objections under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC if resistance to possession is alleged.
The executing court must adjudicate objections under Order 21 Rule 97 CPC on merits before ordering delivery of possession.
It is erroneous to insist that a third party must first be dispossessed and then file under Order 21 Rule 99 CPC; Rule 97 allows pre-dispossession objection.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 97
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 99
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 101
doctrines: Summary adjudication of third-party rights in execution proceedings
Preference for adjudicating title questions at execution stage under Rule 101 to avoid multiplicity of suits

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted under Section 304 Part II IPC for causing the death of two persons during a land dispute-related assault, challenged the conviction and sentence, arguing for a lesser offence and reduced punishment.
issues_decided: Whether the offence committed by the appellants falls under Section 304 Part II IPC or the lesser offence under Section 325 IPC
