Whether the sentence of 5 years' rigorous imprisonment awarded by the High Court should be further reduced
holdings: The injuries, particularly a severe incised wound causing skull fractures, were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature, and the appellants must have known this, justifying conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC.
The sentence of 5 years' rigorous imprisonment is reasonable given the gravity of the offence, and further reduction is not warranted despite the appellants' age and time elapsed since the incident.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Knowledge of likelihood of death from injuries
Proportionality in sentencing
Re-appreciation of evidence by appellate courts

card.dispute: The Land Acquisition Officer and the claimant company, M/S. B.V. Reddy & Sons, fought over whether compensation for acquired land could exceed the amount claimed by the claimant before the Land Acquisition Officer under Section 9 of the Land Acquisition Act.
issues_decided: Whether the unamended Section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, which restricted compensation to the amount claimed by the claimant, was substantive or procedural in nature.
Whether the amended Section 25 of the Act, which removed the restriction on awarding higher compensation, applied retrospectively to cases pending during the amendment.
Whether the High Court could award compensation exceeding the claimant's original claim when the unamended Section 25 was still applicable.
holdings: Section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, in its unamended form, is a substantive provision that restricts courts from awarding compensation exceeding the claimant's initial claim.
The amended Section 25 does not have retrospective effect and applies only to acquisitions after September 24, 1984; it does not apply to pending appeals arising from earlier acquisitions.

The reference court lacked jurisdiction to award more than Rs. 30,000 per acre, as claimed by the claimant, because the unamended Section 25 was in force at the time of notification and created a statutory bar.
doctrines: Substantive vs. procedural law distinction
Prospective application of amendments
Statutory interpretation of retrospective effect
Jurisdictional limits of reference courts in land acquisition

card.dispute: The Corporation of Calicut fought with K. Sreenivasan over whether he could be evicted as a licensee from a public building under the Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968 after defaulting on licence fees.
issues_decided: Whether a licensee falls within the scope of 'unauthorised occupant' under Section 2(f) of the Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968 after termination of licence?
Whether the special eviction procedure under the Act applies to licensees or only to lessees?
holdings: A licensee whose licence has been terminated becomes an 'unauthorised occupant' under Section 2(f) of the Act, as the occupation ceases to be permissive and continues without lawful authority.
The expression 'any other mode of transfer' in Section 2(f) includes licence, and the Act's special eviction procedure applies to licensees to prevent incongruous results compared to lessees.
provisions: Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968, Section 2(f)
Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968, Section 4
Kerala Public Buildings (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1968, Section 5
doctrines: Distinction between lease and licence
Doctrine of unauthorised occupation
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: The Urban Improvement Trust, Udaipur, challenged the High Court's decision quashing land acquisition proceedings initiated for the Udaipur Bhuwana Extension Scheme, arguing that the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was timely.
issues_decided: Whether the declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 must be published in the Official Gazette within one year of the publication of the notification under Section 4(1)?
Whether the prior publication of the Section 4 notification in newspapers in 1990, without official gazette publication, could trigger the one-year limitation for the Section 6 declaration?
Whether delay in filing the writ petitions challenging the land acquisition vitiated the proceedings due to laches?
holdings: The one-year time limit under Section 6(1) applies only to the making of the declaration, not its publication in the Official Gazette; publication can occur after one year.

The date of publication of the Section 4(1) notification in the Official Gazette is the relevant date for computing the one-year period; prior newspaper publication without gazette notification is ineffective.
Writ petitions filed after a delay of over two years from the Section 6 declaration, in a public purpose acquisition for urban development, are barred by laches and should not be entertained.
doctrines: Condition precedent in statutory interpretation
Doctrine of laches
Mandatory vs. directory provisions

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) sued the respondents (tenants) for rent arrears and ejectment, and challenged the trial court's conditional order setting aside an ex-parte decree, which required the tenants to deposit monthly lease amounts as a term for contesting the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the condition imposed by the trial court under Order 9 Rule 7 of the CPC—requiring the tenant to deposit monthly lease rent as a term for setting aside the ex-parte decree—was too onerous and beyond the court's powers?
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the trial court's conditional order while allowing the defendant to contest the suit?
holdings: A court may impose terms under Order 9 Rule 7 of the CPC while setting aside an ex-parte decree, but such terms must not be so onerous as to pre-judge the suit or place the defendant in a worse position than if they had not applied.
The condition requiring deposit of lease rent was too onerous, vague, and uncertain, and thus invalid; the High Court was justified in setting it aside to serve the ends of justice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 7
doctrines: Orderly conduct of proceedings
Conditional relief under Order 9 Rule 7
Prohibition against pre-judging the suit through procedural terms

card.dispute: The Union of India and others fought with the legal representatives of Shakuntala Gupta over the validity of a land acquisition notification affecting her property, following a prior judicial decision that invalidated a similar acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the impugned notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was legally valid after being quashed in a previous case (Banwari Lal) involving the same notification and grounds.
Whether the High Court erred in quashing the acquisition proceedings in respect of the respondent's property by following the Banwari Lal judgment.
Whether the review petition was maintainable on the ground of error apparent on the face of the record.
holdings: The notification under Section 4 was composite and the grounds for its invalidity in Banwari Lal’s case applied uniformly to all 14 properties, including the respondent's, making the acquisition unsustainable.
The expression of urgency under Section 17(1) of the Act, having been held invalid in Banwari Lal, could not be selectively upheld for other properties covered by the same notification.
The order dismissing the appeal was correct, and no error apparent on the face of the record was found to justify recall of the order or grant of review.
doctrines: Doctrine of binding precedent (stare decisis)
Doctrine of merger of notification in judicial order
Doctrine of error apparent on the face of the record (for review petitions)

card.dispute: The Union of India and others contested whether landowners whose Section 18 reference applications were dismissed due to delay, or who accepted compensation without protest, could still file applications under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether dismissal of a Section 18 application on grounds of delay amounts to 'not filing an application' under Section 28-A.
Whether a person whose Section 18 application was dismissed on technical grounds is entitled to file under Section 28-A.
Whether a person who accepted compensation without protest is a 'person aggrieved' under Section 28-A if they did not file a Section 18 application.
holdings: Dismissal of a Section 18 application due to delay does not constitute an effective application and thus amounts to 'not filing' under Section 28-A, allowing the applicant to seek relief under that provision.
A landowner whose Section 18 application was dismissed on grounds of delay or other technicalities remains entitled to file an application under Section 28-A, provided other conditions are met.

Acceptance of compensation with or without protest does not bar a person from being a 'person aggrieved' under Section 28-A if they did not file a Section 18 application, as the statute does not impose such a restriction.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Beneficial construction of remedial statutes
Rule against surplusage in statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The Union of India contested whether landowners whose Section 18 applications were dismissed due to delay or who accepted compensation without protest could still file applications under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether dismissal of a Section 18 application on grounds of delay amounts to 'not filing an application' under Section 28-A.
Whether a person whose Section 18 application was dismissed on technical grounds is entitled to file under Section 28-A.
Whether a person who received compensation without protest is a 'person aggrieved' under Section 28-A.
holdings: Dismissal of a Section 18 application due to delay does not constitute an effective application and thus amounts to 'not filing' under Section 28-A, allowing the applicant to seek relief under that provision.
A landowner whose Section 18 application was dismissed on grounds of delay or other technicalities remains eligible to file under Section 28-A if other conditions are met.
Acceptance of compensation with or without protest does not bar a person from being a 'person aggrieved' under Section 28-A if they did not file a Section 18 application.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Beneficial construction of remedial statutes
Doctrine of judicial discipline and hierarchy of benches

card.dispute: The complainant Amar Singh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of the accused, who had been convicted by the trial court for murder and attempted murder based on eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution case should be discarded due to alleged defects in investigation, including failure to seize physical evidence and omissions in the Daily Diary Report (DDR).
Whether the non-examination of some eyewitnesses, including injured persons, renders the prosecution case unreliable.
holdings: Defects in investigation, such as not seizing the wire gauze or sending firearms for forensic analysis, do not vitiate the prosecution case if it is fully supported by credible eyewitness testimony and medical evidence.

The prosecution is not required to examine all possible eyewitnesses; the testimony of a few reliable injured eyewitnesses is sufficient, and the accused can call unexamined witnesses as defense witnesses if needed.
doctrines: Evidence must be weighed, not counted
Principle of defective investigation not leading to acquittal if evidence is reliable
Prosecution not bound to examine all eyewitnesses

card.dispute: The plaintiff-appellant, Amrendra Pratap Singh, sued to recover possession of agricultural land purchased from a non-tribal who had bought it from a tribal, claiming encroachment by the defendant-respondent, Tej Bahadur Prajapati, who asserted title by adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether a non-tribal can acquire title by adverse possession over immovable property belonging to a tribal in a scheduled area?
Whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act?
What relief, including demolition or compensation, is appropriate for encroachment on tribal-origin land after invalid adverse possession?
holdings: A non-tribal cannot acquire title by adverse possession over immovable property belonging to a tribal in a scheduled area, as such transfer is prohibited under special protective laws like the Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property (By Scheduled Tribes) Regulation, 1956.
The suit was not barred by limitation because the period during which the land was under tribal ownership is excluded, and only six years of hostile possession had elapsed before the suit was filed.

The trial court must determine the exact extent of encroachment and decide whether demolition and restoration of possession or compensation is the appropriate relief, with compensation conditional on payment and assessed as of the date of this judgment.
provisions: Orissa Scheduled Areas Transfer of Immovable Property (By Scheduled Tribes) Regulation, 1956, Para 3A, Para 7-D
doctrines: Adverse possession
Doctrine of tribal property protection
Special law prevails over general law
State as trustee of tribal property

card.dispute: The landlord, Waryam Singh, sought eviction of tenant Baldev Singh for material alteration of the shop by enclosing the verandah without consent, claiming it impaired the shop's value and utility.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant made unauthorized alterations to the demised premises
Whether the alterations materially impaired the value or utility of the premises
Whether the landlord discharged the burden of proving material impairment
holdings: Unauthorized enclosure of a verandah by a tenant does not automatically amount to material alteration warranting eviction.
Material impairment of value or utility must be proven by evidence and cannot be presumed from the mere fact of alteration.
The landlord bears the burden to prove that the tenant’s alterations have substantially and permanently diminished the value or utility of the premises from the landlord’s perspective.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13(2)(iii)
doctrines: Burden of proof on landlord in eviction cases based on material alteration
Cumulative conditions for eviction under Section 13(2)(iii): unauthorized construction, by tenant, causing material impairment
Material alteration requires substantial and permanent changes affecting value or utility

card.dispute: Badam Singh appealed his conviction for the murder of Bhamra Singh, challenging the reliability of eyewitness testimony and the prosecution's case.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt based on the eyewitness accounts?
Whether the conduct of the eyewitnesses was natural and credible?
Whether the medical evidence corroborated the version of the eyewitnesses regarding the manner of shooting?
Whether the absence of motive and delay in filing the special report affected the credibility of the prosecution case?
holdings: The Court held that the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to inconsistencies and improbabilities in the eyewitness testimony.

The conduct of the eyewitnesses was found to be highly unnatural, undermining their credibility, especially their failure to report the crime en route and the implausible time taken to cover a short distance.
The medical evidence, which showed no blackening or charring on the body, contradicted the eyewitness claim that the gun was fired from point-blank range, casting doubt on their account.
The absence of a motive, coupled with the appellant’s peaceful prior relationship with the deceased and the unexplained delay in the special report, further weakened the prosecution’s case.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, Section 173 (filing of charge sheet/report)
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Requirement of reliable and credible eyewitness testimony
Corroboration of medical evidence with ocular testimony
Critical scrutiny of prosecution evidence by appellate courts

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against a decree denying eviction despite proving bona fide need under the Bombay Rents Act, arguing that the courts failed to properly assess comparative hardship and the possibility of partial eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant proved greater hardship under Section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents Act to defeat the landlord's claim for eviction under Section 13(1)(g)?
Whether partial eviction could meet the ends of justice in light of the comparative hardship suffered by both parties?
holdings: The burden of proving greater hardship under Section 13(2) lies on the tenant, and failure to adduce evidence of attempts to find alternative accommodation or financial disadvantage may result in eviction.

Courts may order partial eviction if it satisfies the landlord's bona fide need while minimizing hardship to the tenant, especially where parts of the premises are not essential for the tenant's business.
provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 13(1)(g)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 13(2)
doctrines: Comparative hardship doctrine
Partial eviction doctrine
Burden of proof on tenant to show hardship

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the incorporation of respondent No. 7's name in the municipal lease register for a plot of land, alleging that no valid title arose from an incomplete auction and that the decision violated public interest and statutory procedures.
issues_decided: Whether the auction purchaser acquired a valid title in the absence of payment of the full premium and compliance with statutory formalities?
Whether possession of the land was effectively delivered to the auction purchaser?
Whether the municipal corporation's decision to include respondent No. 7 in the lease register was lawful and in public interest?
Whether the impugned order passed in haste and under external influence was legally sustainable?
holdings: No valid title arose from the auction as full payment was not made and mandatory conditions under Section 79 of the Gujarat Provincial Municipal Corporations Act and Section 17 of the Indian Registration Act were not fulfilled.
There was no credible evidence of delivery of possession; mere oral assertion or file noting cannot establish possession without documentary or physical proof.
The decision to include respondent No. 7 in the lease register violated public interest and statutory authority, especially since it followed a ministerial direction and lacked procedural fairness.
An order passed hastily and at the behest of a non-statutory authority is ultra vires and mala fide, warranting judicial intervention even in public interest litigation.
provisions: Gujarat Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, Section 79
doctrines: Mandatory compliance with Article 299 of the Constitution for enforceable state contracts
No estoppel against the State in matters of public property
Presumption of mala fides in post-haste administrative actions
Ultra vires doctrine for decisions influenced by non-statutory authorities

card.dispute: Fifteen accused persons, including appellants, were tried for the murder of Sarjug Rai, with the prosecution alleging a common unlawful object under Section 149 IPC, while the defense raised alibi and challenged the reliability of evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were guilty of murder under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC?
Whether the common object of the unlawful assembly was established despite absence of direct motive?
Whether the plea of alibi raised by accused Mahendra Rai was credible?
Whether the concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court based on eyewitness testimony could be interfered with in appeal?
holdings: Members of an unlawful assembly can be held liable for murder under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC if the offence was committed in prosecution of the common object or was a likely consequence known to the members.
Motive, though stale or trivial, is not essential when there is credible direct evidence establishing the commission of the offence and participation of the accused.

A plea of alibi must be supported by reliable and cogent evidence; mere certificates without corroboration or appointment letters, especially for implausible short-term 'regular' appointments, are insufficient to displace eyewitness testimony.

The Supreme Court will not re-appreciate evidence or reassess witness credibility unless findings are perverse or there is a serious legal error resulting in miscarriage of justice; concurrent findings of fact by lower courts are binding in appeal.
doctrines: Common object under Section 149 IPC
Perversity in findings as ground for appellate interference
Credibility of eyewitnesses and familial relationship
Burden and standard for proving alibi

card.dispute: The State, through the Collector, sought to cancel land assignments made decades earlier on grounds of illegality, while the assignees resisted, claiming inordinate delay and inapplicability of the relevant law.
issues_decided: Whether the Andhra Pradesh Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977 applies to assignments made under the Special Loani Rules by the Nizam government?
Whether cancellation proceedings initiated after about 30 years can be maintained as being within a reasonable time?
Whether the Division Bench erred in setting aside the Single Judge’s direction for a fresh adjudication on merits?
holdings: The applicability of the Prohibition Act to pre-existing assignments, including those by the Nizam, must be determined based on statutory interpretation and factual findings, which were not adequately considered.
The reasonableness of the time for initiating cancellation proceedings depends on the facts and circumstances of each case; no rigid rule can disqualify action solely due to a 30-year delay.
The Division Bench erred by focusing only on delay without considering other jurisdictional and statutory issues; the matter must be remitted for a comprehensive reconsideration.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act, 1977, Section 3
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act, 1950, Section 166(B)
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act, 1950, Sections 47 and 48
doctrines: Reasonableness of time in absence of limitation period
Deemed continuation of statutory prohibitions
Remittal for fresh consideration of jurisdictional issues

card.dispute: The heirs of Rana, as perpetual lessees, fought with the State of Uttar Pradesh over the apportionment of compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, where the State claimed a larger share despite long-standing leasehold rights.
issues_decided: Whether the State could deny the claimants' rights to compensation for acquired land held under perpetual lease.
What respective interests the claimants and the State had in the acquired land.
Whether the apportionment of compensation by the Land Acquisition Officer and confirmed by the High Court was correct.
holdings: The claimants, as perpetual lessees under Nazul land, had a valid and enforceable interest entitling them to a substantial share of the compensation.
The State could not deny the claimants' rights despite not formally renewing the lease, due to estoppel by conduct over long possession.
The apportionment of compensation at 75% to the claimants and 25% to the State was just and reasonable, based on the nature of leasehold rights and settled law.
doctrines: Estoppel by conduct
Apportionment of compensation between lessee and landlord
Perpetual lease under Nazul land system

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the validity of a codicil to a will, claiming it was not properly executed or attested, while the respondents relied on the codicil to support their title derived from the will's beneficiary.
issues_decided: Whether the registration of a will dispenses with the requirement of proving its execution and attestation under Section 68 of the Evidence Act
Whether a Registrar of Deeds can be considered an attesting witness to a will solely by virtue of registering it
Whether the codicil dated 21.5.1973 was validly executed and attested as required by law
holdings: Registration of a will does not obviate the need to prove its execution and attestation as mandated by Section 68 of the Evidence Act.

A Registrar of Deeds is not an attesting witness merely by performing statutory duties; to be an attesting witness, the Registrar must sign with the intention of attesting and in the presence of the testator.
The codicil was not proved as required under Section 68 of the Evidence Act because no attesting witness was examined to confirm its execution.
doctrines: Requirement of attestation under Section 63 of the Succession Act
Rule of proof of wills under Section 68 of the Evidence Act
Presumption under Section 114 illustration (e) of the Evidence Act
Statutory duty vs. attesting intention of a registering officer

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh appealed the acquittal of Bhagwan Singh and two others for murder and dacoity, leading the High Court to convict them; the appellants challenged this reversal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on the child witness's testimony and a retracted judicial confession
Whether the judicial confession of co-accused Pooran Singh was voluntary and reliable
Whether the prosecution's evidence, including recoveries and motive, was sufficient to sustain conviction
holdings: The High Court erred in relying on the child witness's testimony and overturning the trial court's credibility assessment, as the child's identification was unreliable.
A judicial confession made while in police custody and later retracted cannot be considered voluntary or reliable, especially without compliance with Section 164 CrPC safeguards.
Mere recovery of ordinary articles and a civil dispute as motive are insufficient to sustain conviction without reliable corroborative evidence.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh (Dacoity Vihavaran Kshetra) Adhiniyam, 1981, Section 11/13
doctrines: Retracted confession doctrine
Voluntariness of confession under Section 164 CrPC
Standard of proof in appeal against acquittal
Reliability of child witness testimony

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent disputed whether an agreement to sell land was a genuine sale or a disguised loan, and whether the appellate court could grant relief not sought in a cross-appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the appellate court could modify the trial court's decree in favour of the respondent without a cross-appeal or cross-objection by the respondent?
Whether the transaction between the parties was a sale or a loan?
Whether the appellants could be relieved from specific performance of the agreement upon repayment of money with compensation?
holdings: The appellate court cannot grant additional relief to a respondent who has not filed a cross-appeal or cross-objection, especially when the reliefs are separable and no inconsistency arises from non-interference.
The nature of the transaction was determined to be a loan, not a genuine sale, based on the conduct of the parties and the terms of the agreement.
The appellants are entitled to be relieved from specific performance upon repayment of the amount received plus additional compensation, where equity and hardship so require.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 33
doctrines: No relief without cross-appeal
Doctrine of comparative hardship
Equitable relief in conditional decrees

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired by the State of Haryana in 1990, seeking higher amounts based on sale instances and prior judicial rates.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in relying on earlier judgments rather than sale instances to determine compensation.
Whether the High Court was correct in taking a mean of three prior compensation rates to fix the current rate.
Whether a deduction of 20% from the computed rate was justified despite prior deductions in earlier awards.
Whether auction prices of developed plots in 1989 could be used to determine compensation for agricultural land acquired in 1990.
holdings: The High Court rightly relied on prior judicially determined compensation rates instead of unexamined sale deeds, especially where this Court had approved earlier rates for the same area and purpose.

Taking a mean of prior compensation rates was a fair and claimant-friendly method, particularly since the current lands were not abutting a highway and were comparable to lower-rate belts in prior acquisitions.
A 20% deduction was justified as the appellants failed to prove that prior awards already included such deductions, despite having access to those records.
Auction prices of developed plots cannot be the basis for compensating agricultural land, as development significantly enhances value separate from raw land worth.
doctrines: Principle of consistent compensation for similar lands in same area and purpose
Use of prior judicially determined rates over unverified sale instances
Belting system in land valuation near highways
Burden of proof in establishing prior deductions in compensation

card.dispute: The Bank of Baroda sought to initiate contempt proceedings against Sadruddin Hasan Daya and Shohin S. Daya for failing to comply with the terms of a consent decree, including payment instalments and a prohibition on alienating attached properties.
issues_decided: Whether the respondents' breach of the consent decree and undertaking to the Court amounts to civil contempt
Whether the petitioner's remedy was limited to execution of the decree, or could include contempt proceedings
Whether the limitation period for initiating contempt proceedings had expired
What appropriate punishment should be imposed for the contempt
holdings: A willful breach of an undertaking given to the Court in a consent decree constitutes civil contempt under Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
The availability of an execution remedy does not bar contempt proceedings, as contempt involves the Court's authority, not just private rights between parties.
The limitation period for contempt begins when the aggrieved party gains knowledge of the breach, not from the date of the decree.
The respondents are sentenced to four months' imprisonment, with a conditional release on bail for three months to deposit the full amount, failing which the full sentence will be served.
doctrines: Contempt by breach of court undertaking
Consent decree as a rule of court
Limitation period from date of knowledge
Judicial authority and dignity in contempt

card.dispute: A husband and wife and their son disputed over whether two properties were joint Hindu family property or self-acquired by the husband, seeking declaration, partition, and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs proved that Item No.1 property was joint Hindu family property based on a nucleus of joint family assets
Whether the burden of proof shifted to the defendant to show that the property was self-acquired
Whether the husband blended the self-acquired property with the joint family property by clear intention
holdings: A presumption that a property is joint family property arises only if there is proof of a sufficient nucleus of joint family property from which the acquisition could have been made.
The burden of proving the existence of such a nucleus lies on the party claiming joint family status; without it, the burden does not shift to the defendant to prove self-acquisition.

Blending of self-acquired property into joint family property requires clear and positive evidence of intention to abandon separate ownership; mere use by family members or generosity does not suffice.
provisions: Hindu Law (unwritten personal law principles regarding joint family and coparcenary)
doctrines: Presumption of joint family property from nucleus
Burden of proof in establishing joint family property
Doctrine of blending (impression of joint character on self-acquired property)

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the exclusion of interest and solatium in compensation for land acquired under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, seeking re-opening of settlement agreements based on a later arbitral award.
issues_decided: Whether Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applies to acquisitions under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
Whether the landowners had a legal right to re-open their compensation agreements based on a subsequent arbitral award
Whether the Union of India could maintain a writ petition challenging the Collector's supplementary award
holdings: Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not apply to acquisitions under the 1952 Act, as the statutory scheme excludes interest and solatium unless expressly provided.
A concluded compensation agreement under the 1952 Act cannot be re-opened merely because a later award granted higher compensation; such a right must be expressly conferred by statute.
The Union of India was a 'person aggrieved' by the Collector's illegal invocation of Section 28A and thus entitled to file a writ petition, despite delay, as the order was a jurisdictional nullity.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, Section 8(1)(a)
doctrines: What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly
Plain meaning rule of statutory interpretation
Jurisdictional error renders an administrative order a nullity
Principle of finality of contracts in statutory compensation schemes

card.dispute: The Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee challenged the Kerala High Court's intervention in temple administration following a corruption inquiry, questioning the scope of public interest litigation in matters governed by a statutory framework.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a public interest litigation concerning the management of a temple governed by a statutory enactment.
Whether the findings and directions of the High Court based on a commission of inquiry could be challenged in appeal when no effective objection was raised during the proceedings.
Whether the conduct of the Managing Committee in not consistently opposing the inquiry barred subsequent challenge to the High Court's orders.
holdings: Public interest litigation can be entertained in matters of temple administration if there are allegations of mismanagement or corruption, even when governed by a statute.
Findings of fact and judicial observations regarding conduct in court, as recorded in a judgment, are conclusive and cannot be contradicted by affidavits or oral claims in appeal.
A party that fails to raise objections before a commission or court, especially after having an opportunity, cannot later challenge the outcome on grounds of lack of hearing or procedural defect.
doctrines: Conclusive nature of judicial records
Public Interest Litigation jurisdiction under Article 226
Doctrine of preclusion by conduct

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence for murder under Section 302 IPC read with Section 149 IPC, arguing that the killing occurred in a sudden fight and fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, warranting conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder instead.
issues_decided: Whether the act of the accused fell within the exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, reducing liability from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder?
Whether the accused took undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner during the incident?
Whether the conditions for 'sudden fight' under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC were satisfied?
holdings: The accused caused injuries in a sudden fight arising from a verbal quarrel without premeditation, and thus Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applied, reducing the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC.
The accused did not take undue advantage or act in a cruel or unusual manner, as the injuries were inflicted at random and not when the deceased was helpless.
A sudden fight under Exception 4 requires mutual provocation and absence of premeditation, and the facts showed both parties contributed to the escalation.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC: Sudden fight without premeditation
Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
Principle of mutual provocation in sudden fights

card.dispute: A society of agricultural labourers challenged the cancellation of validation certificates for land sales, arguing the Collector's suo-motu power under Section 50-B(4) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1950 was exercised after an unreasonable delay.
issues_decided: Whether the Collector can exercise suo-motu power under Section 50-B(4) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1950 after a long delay
Whether the validation certificates issued by the Tahsildar can be cancelled under Section 50-B(4) if the action is taken 13–15 years later
holdings: The suo-motu power under Section 50-B(4) must be exercised within a reasonable time; a delay of 13–15 years without explanation renders the action invalid.
Cancellation of validation certificates after a long delay undermines settled legal positions and legitimate expectations, and cannot be sustained in law.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Land Act, 1950, Section 50-B(4)
doctrines: Principle of reasonable time for administrative action
Legitimate expectation
Suo-motu power subject to reasonableness

card.dispute: Jandel Singh and others convicted in a murder case challenged their conviction, arguing that the prosecution's evidence was unreliable and the investigation flawed.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether the testimony of the two eyewitnesses could be relied upon despite contradictions and improvements?
Whether the investigation was conducted properly, particularly regarding the recording and dispatch of the FIR?
Whether the conviction under Section 304 Part-I read with Section 149 IPC was legally sustainable in absence of attribution of specific fatal injury?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt due to improbability of the story and lack of reliable evidence.
The testimony of the eyewitnesses was untrustworthy due to material contradictions between their police statements and court depositions.
The investigation was defective, including failure to send FIR to magistrate and lack of immediate search, raising doubts about the prosecution's version.
Conviction under Section 304 Part-I read with Section 149 IPC cannot stand where no specific injury causing death is attributed to any accused and main accused were acquitted.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Reliability of eyewitness testimony
Proper investigation under CrPC
Requirement of attribution of fatal injury in absence of direct evidence

card.dispute: The dispute was between K. Vinod Kumar and S. Palanisamy over the validity of Kumar's selection as an LPG distributor by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited, challenged on grounds of non-compliance with land-furnishing requirements and lack of transparency in the selection process.
issues_decided: Whether the requirement to furnish land details at the time of application was mandatory or directory
Whether the selection process conducted by the Dealer Selection Board was fair and transparent
holdings: The requirement to furnish land details at the time of application is directory, not mandatory; failure to provide such details initially does not invalidate selection, but non-availability of land within two months of selection may lead to cancellation.
The selection process was valid and fair; in the absence of prescribed procedure, the Board could adopt its own method, and no mala fides or arbitrariness was shown.
doctrines: Doctrine of Fair Procedure
Doctrine of Reasonableness in Administrative Action
Distinction between Mandatory and Directory Requirements

card.dispute: The appellants challenged whether the Assistant Charity Commissioner is a 'court' under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, arguing that contempt proceedings initiated by him were invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the Assistant Charity Commissioner appointed under Section 5 of the Bombay Public Trust Act, 1950 (as applicable to Karnataka) is a 'court' within the meaning of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
Whether contempt proceedings initiated by the Assistant Charity Commissioner are maintainable.
holdings: The Assistant Charity Commissioner is a 'court' under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 because he possesses all essential attributes of a court, including adjudicatory powers, ability to record evidence, and render binding decisions.
The Commissioner's authority to conduct judicial proceedings, hear parties, and issue final orders subject to appeal establishes his status as a court, making contempt proceedings maintainable.
doctrines: Test for determining whether a statutory authority is a 'court' based on adjudicatory powers and attributes of a court
Finality and conclusiveness of orders as indicators of judicial function
Bar on civil court jurisdiction indicating exclusive adjudicatory role
Incorporation of civil court powers under CPC as evidence of judicial character

card.dispute: The divorced husband challenged the Family Court's jurisdiction to decide a property dispute initiated by the wife after divorce.
issues_decided: Whether the Family Court has jurisdiction to adjudicate property disputes between parties to a marriage after divorce.
Whether a proceeding before the Family Court is maintainable when a claim under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 has already been decided.
holdings: The Family Court has jurisdiction to decide property disputes between parties to a marriage even after divorce, as 'disputes relating to marriage and family affairs' must be broadly construed.
A proceeding before the Family Court for property settlement is maintainable independently of a claim under Section 3 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986.
provisions: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, Section 3
doctrines: Liberal construction of special court jurisdiction
Res judicata
Broad interpretation of 'family affairs'

card.dispute: Christian petitioners challenged the constitutionality of Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which imposed special restrictions on their ability to make religious and charitable bequests, arguing it discriminated against them compared to other religious communities.
issues_decided: Whether Section 118 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 violates Article 14 by arbitrarily discriminating against Christians in making religious and charitable bequests
Whether Section 118 infringes the fundamental rights under Articles 25 and 26 by restricting religious freedom to make charitable donations through wills
Whether the procedural and substantive restrictions under Section 118 have a rational nexus with the object of the law
holdings: Section 118 violates Article 14 as it imposes an arbitrary and discriminatory burden on Christian testators alone, without reasonable classification or nexus to the law's objective.
Restrictions on religious and charitable bequests under Section 118 infringe the fundamental right to freedom of religion under Articles 25 and 26, as such acts are integral to Christian faith.
The classification created by Section 118 lacks intelligible differentia and rational nexus, making it unconstitutional as it applies only to Christians while exempting other religious communities.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Equal protection of laws
Freedom of religion under Articles 25 and 26
Judicial review of discriminatory legislation

card.dispute: The parties, members of a joint Hindu family, disputed the validity of an arbitral award on partition, with the respondents challenging it on multiple grounds including improper composition of the tribunal and lack of stamping and registration.
issues_decided: Whether the issue of stamping and registration of an arbitral award can be raised at the stage of setting aside the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether the High Court erred in invalidating the arbitral award on the ground of non-stamping and non-registration
holdings: The question of stamping and registration of an arbitral award is not a ground for setting aside the award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as it pertains to enforcement under Section 36.

The issue of stamping and registration is to be decided under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure during enforcement, not at the challenge stage under Section 34; thus, the High Court's decision on this ground was premature and invalid.
doctrines: Preclusion of additional grounds for setting aside an award beyond those in Section 34
Separation of challenge and enforcement stages in arbitration proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants, ten accused tribal persons, were tried for murder and unlawful assembly over a land dispute, leading to conviction by the Trial Court, which was challenged on grounds of unreliable evidence and defective investigation.
issues_decided: Whether the testimony of a single eyewitness (Mannu) could be relied upon to convict the accused without corroboration?
Whether the prosecution proved the charges under Sections 302/149 IPC beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the investigation was conducted properly and whether material evidence was collected?
Whether the Trial Court properly complied with Section 313 Cr.P.C. by giving the accused a fair opportunity to explain incriminating circumstances?
holdings: The testimony of a single eyewitness, especially when improved in court and inconsistent with earlier statements, cannot be relied upon without corroboration in material particulars.
The prosecution failed to prove the charges under Sections 302/149 IPC due to lack of reliable evidence, medical corroboration, and contradictions in the eyewitness account.
Defective investigation, including failure to prepare a site plan, recover weapons, or examine material witnesses, undermines the reliability of the prosecution case.
Non-compliance with Section 313 Cr.P.C. renders the trial unfair, and incriminating evidence cannot be used against the accused if they were not properly questioned.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
doctrines: Corroboration of single eyewitness testimony
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Presumption of innocence
Fair trial under Section 313 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: Krishna Mohan Pvt. Ltd. challenged the inclusion of plant and machinery costs in the rateable value of its cinema property for municipal taxation, and the constitutional validity of Section 116(3) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.
issues_decided: Whether the cost of plant and machinery installed in a building can be included in the rateable value of the building for property tax purposes?

Whether Section 116(3) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, which empowers the Commissioner to include plant and machinery in the rateable value, constitutes excessive delegation of legislative power?
holdings: The cost of plant and machinery, lifts, and air conditioners fixed on land or building cannot be included in the rateable value for property tax as they are not part of the building itself.

Section 116(3) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, is unconstitutional for excessive delegation because it grants unguided and uncanalised legislative power to the Commissioner without laying down any policy or standards.
doctrines: Doctrine of excessive delegation
Doctrine of non-delegation of essential legislative functions
Principle of guided discretion in delegated legislation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the quashing of an FIR alleging forgery and fraud by respondents in connection with property documents, while the respondents argued that the police lacked jurisdiction to investigate due to Section 195 CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether the police can investigate a cognizable offence under the CrPC despite the applicability of Section 195 CrPC, which restricts courts from taking cognizance of certain offences without prior judicial sanction.
Whether an FIR can be quashed on the ground that the complaint was false, frivolous, or vexatious based on allegations of mala fides at a preliminary stage.
Whether the High Court ought to have considered the applicability of Section 195 CrPC before quashing the FIR.
holdings: The police have the statutory power to investigate cognizable offences under Chapter XII of the CrPC even if the alleged offence involves documents used in court proceedings; Section 195 does not restrict investigation but only the court's power to take cognizance.

An FIR cannot be quashed at the threshold merely on allegations of mala fides or personal vendetta; the investigation must proceed to determine the truth, as a prosecution is not vitiated solely by the complainant's ill motive if it is otherwise supported by evidence.

The High Court was not required to decide the applicability of Section 195 CrPC at the investigation stage, as that issue arises only when the court considers taking cognizance, not during the investigation phase.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Chapter XII
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Chapter XXVI
doctrines: Separation between police investigation and judicial cognizance under CrPC
Mala fides of a complainant does not vitiate prosecution if allegations are serious and supported by evidence
Judicial restraint in quashing FIRs at preliminary stages

card.dispute: Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation challenged the applicability of enhanced compensation benefits under amended Sections 23 and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to land acquired under the Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966.
issues_decided: Whether amendments to Sections 23 and 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (by Act 68 of 1984), apply to acquisitions under the MRTP Act, 1966?
Whether excluding such amendments would result in unconstitutional discrimination under Article 14?
holdings: The amendments to Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as introduced by Act 68 of 1984, apply to land acquisitions under Chapter VII of the MRTP Act, 1966, where the Act incorporates the Land Acquisition Act.
To exclude enhanced compensation benefits based on the acquiring authority or purpose would result in arbitrary and invidious discrimination, violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126(3)
doctrines: Doctrine of Equal Protection under Article 14
Doctrine of Incorporation by Reference
Principle against Arbitrary and Invidious Discrimination

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased co-plaintiff sought to be brought on record in a suit for specific performance, but the High Court's Division Bench held the suit had abated entirely due to delay; the appeal challenged that decision.
issues_decided: Whether the suit abated in its entirety due to the death of one of the three co-plaintiffs and failure to promptly substitute his legal representatives.
Whether the trial court's order allowing substitution of the legal representatives and setting aside abatement was a 'judgment' appealable under the Letters Patent.
holdings: The suit does not abate in its entirety merely due to the death of one co-plaintiff; substitution of legal representatives within the statutory period revives the suit, and the failure of surviving plaintiffs to act does not bar revival when the legal representatives apply in time.

An order setting aside abatement or allowing substitution of legal representatives is procedural, does not decide valuable rights or merits of the case, and is not a 'judgment' appealable under the Letters Patent.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 9(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1
doctrines: Sufficient cause for condonation of delay
Abatement and revival of suits
Maintainability of Letters Patent appeals
Procedural orders vs. substantive judgments

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai sought to assess the rateable value of vacant land after demolition of buildings, while Kamla Mills Ltd. contested the basis of valuation based on market value of land.
issues_decided: Whether the Municipal Corporation can assess the rateable value of land alone, after demolition of a building, by relying on the market value of the land?
Whether the standard rent under the Bombay Rent Act, 1947 limits the rateable value for municipal taxation?
Whether the burden of proving the correct rateable value lies with the assessee when challenging a municipal assessment?
holdings: The rateable value for municipal tax cannot be determined solely by the market value of land when the land was previously part of a composite assessment with buildings.
The standard rent under the Bombay Rent Act, 1947 sets the upper limit for rateable value, even after demolition of a building.
The burden of proving the correct rateable value lies on the assessee when disputing a municipal assessment, and failure to produce evidence weakens their case.
doctrines: Burden of proof on assessee in tax disputes
Composite assessment of land and building
Standard rent as cap on rateable value

card.dispute: The landlord appealed against the High Court's decision to condone the tenant's delay in depositing rent arrears under the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950.
issues_decided: Whether the court has power to condone delay in depositing rent under Section 13(4) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950 in the absence of an express provision permitting such condonation.
Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to condone delay in depositing rent under Section 13(4) of the Act.
holdings: Where a special statute does not expressly empower the court to extend time or condone default in depositing rent, the court lacks inherent power to do so.

Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 does not apply to defaults in depositing rent under Section 13(4) of the Rajasthan Act, as such deposit is not an 'application' and the statute prescribes a strict time limit.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent & Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(3), (4), (5)
doctrines: Strict construction of special statutes
No extension of time without express statutory authority
Distinction between 'application' and statutory compliance

card.dispute: The petitioner challenged the acquisition of land adjacent to the disputed Ram Janma Bhumi-Babri Masjid site under the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993, arguing it was unnecessary and violated constitutional rights.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of adjacent undisputed land under the Act is constitutionally valid?
Whether the extent of land acquired adjacent to the disputed site can be judicially reviewed?
Whether the status quo should be maintained until final disposal of the title suits in the High Court?
holdings: Acquisition of adjacent land is valid as it is incidental to ensuring effective enjoyment of the disputed site by the successful party and serves the larger purpose of communal harmony.
The extent of adjacent land acquired is a matter of policy and not subject to judicial scrutiny at this stage, though superfluous land must be returned after final adjudication.
Status quo must be maintained until final disposal of the title suits to preserve the property and ensure appropriate relief to the parties.
provisions: Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993, Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 11
doctrines: Doctrine of Severability
Principle of Status Quo in Pending Litigation
Doctrine of Harmonious Construction
Principle of Communal Harmony and Secularism

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's order reversing the Competent Authority's decision to allow him to defend an eviction proceeding under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, after delay was condoned.
issues_decided: Whether the Competent Authority had jurisdiction to condone delay and permit the appellant to defend the eviction petition?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the order of the Competent Authority allowing the defence to be filed after delay?
holdings: The Competent Authority has the power under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 to condone delay in filing a defence in eviction proceedings if sufficient cause is shown.

The High Court erred in reversing the order of the Competent Authority which had validly condoned the delay and permitted the appellant to contest the eviction, especially in the absence of any legal infirmity.
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Judicial review of administrative orders

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for the murder of Pyara Singh and related offences; they challenged their conviction and sentence, while the informant separately appealed the acquittal of some accused and rejection of constructive liability under Section 149 IPC.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants could be held guilty of murder under Section 302/34 IPC based on common intention?
Whether the conviction under Section 149 IPC was sustainable in the absence of shared unlawful object to cause death or grievous hurt?
Whether Nihal Singh (Appellant No. 4) was rightly convicted under Section 326 IPC for causing grievous hurt to Satpal Singh?
Whether the appellants could claim self-defence in the context of a violent confrontation?
holdings: The appellants did not share a common intention to murder Pyara Singh, but developed a common intention on the spot to cause injuries likely to cause death; hence, conviction under Section 302 IPC was unsafe and they were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 IPC.

Section 149 IPC was not attracted as there was no prior common object to commit murder or grievous hurt, but the appellants were members of an unlawful assembly under Section 148 IPC due to shared object of rioting.

Nihal Singh was rightly convicted under Section 326 IPC as the evidence established his active participation in causing grievous injury to Satpal Singh, and self-defence was not available due to the nature of the attack.

The plea of self-defence was rejected for all appellants as the use of deadly force was disproportionate and not in response to imminent threat, given the collective and pre-escalated nature of the violence.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Development of common intention on the spot
Principle of prior concert in joint liability
Self-defence in the context of unlawful assembly

card.dispute: The appellant cooperative society claimed enhancement of compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, but the dispute centered on whether a valid reference under Section 18 was made to confer jurisdiction on the civil court.
issues_decided: Whether a valid reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 was made by the Special Land Acquisition Officer (SLAO) in favor of the appellant society?
Whether the Additional District Judge had jurisdiction to decide on the claim for enhancement of compensation in the absence of a proper reference under Section 18?
Whether a subsequent clarification by the SLAO could be treated as a valid reference under Section 18 of the Act?
holdings: A reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act must be explicitly and formally made by the Land Acquisition Officer; mere mention of an application in a later letter does not constitute a valid reference.

The reference court has no jurisdiction to decide objections not specifically referred to it under Section 18 or Section 30 of the Act; jurisdiction cannot be assumed or extended based on subsequent impleadment.

A subsequent clarification by the SLAO, issued after the reference was sent, cannot cure the absence of a formal reference under Section 18, as jurisdiction depends on strict compliance with statutory conditions.
doctrines: Jurisdiction by statute
Strict compliance with conditions precedent
No jurisdiction without valid reference
Non-waiver of lack of inherent jurisdiction

card.dispute: The dispute involved whether a consent order passed by the High Court in a mortgage recovery case could set aside the rights of an auction purchaser who had acquired property in execution of a decree, where the consent order was allegedly obtained by suppressing material facts including the auction sale.
issues_decided: Whether a court has inherent jurisdiction to set aside a decree obtained by fraud even if specific provisions of CPC do not explicitly allow it?
Whether a consent decree can override the vested rights of a third-party auction purchaser not impleaded in the proceedings?
Whether the High Court committed an error in not considering subsequent events affecting third-party rights while deciding a review application?
holdings: Courts possess inherent jurisdiction under Section 151 CPC to set aside a decree obtained by fraud, as fraud vitiates judicial proceedings and renders them nullities, irrespective of absence of specific procedural provisions.
A consent decree cannot extinguish the vested rights of a third-party auction purchaser who was not a party to the compromise, especially when material facts like the auction sale were suppressed.
The High Court must consider subsequent events and third-party rights in a review petition, and failure to do so amounts to a misdirection in law and denial of justice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX, Rule 18
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXVI, Rules 13 and 14(2)
doctrines: Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Actus curiae neminem gravabit
Inherent powers of civil courts
Res judicata does not apply to judgments obtained by fraud

card.dispute: The tenants' legal heirs challenged the executability of a 1986 eviction decree, claiming the court failed to afford them an opportunity to deposit arrears under the Rajasthan Rent Act after the jurisdictional change in 1956.
issues_decided: Whether the executing court can declare a decree non-est or inexecutable on the ground of lack of jurisdiction due to failure to allow deposit of rent under the Rajasthan Rent Act.
Whether a procedural lapse in not allowing the tenant to deposit rent arrears during pendency of suit renders the decree a nullity.
holdings: A decree passed by a court of competent jurisdiction is not a nullity merely due to procedural irregularity; it can only be challenged in a direct appeal, not in execution proceedings.
Failure to allow deposit of rent arrears under the Rajasthan Act, even if erroneous, does not deprive the court of jurisdiction and cannot be raised collaterally in execution.
provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, Section 13(1)(a)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13(1)(a)
doctrines: Doctrine of jurisdictional nullity
Principle of finality of decrees
Prohibition on collateral attack on decrees
Distinction between lack of jurisdiction and mere procedural illegality

card.dispute: The appellant Ramakant Rai and the state challenged the High Court's acquittal of accused persons in a murder and mischief case arising from a property dispute involving a fatal shooting.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting Madan Rai of murder under Section 302 IPC?
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the acquittal of Sachidanand, Rasbehari, and Janardan Rai under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC?
Whether the High Court wrongly set aside the conviction of the accused under Section 440 IPC?
holdings: The conviction of Madan Rai under Section 302 IPC is restored as the High Court failed to properly appreciate credible eyewitness testimony and erroneously relied on speculative reasoning.
The acquittal of Sachidanand, Rasbehari, and Janardan Rai under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC stands, as no fault was found in the Trial Court's benefit of doubt.
The High Court's reversal of conviction under Section 440 IPC is set aside; the Trial Court's conviction and sentence of two years' rigorous imprisonment and fine are reinstated as legally sound.
doctrines: Proof beyond reasonable doubt
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Primacy of eyewitness testimony over medical or circumstantial doubt
Requirement of reasoned judgment when reversing trial court findings

card.dispute: The landlord (Ravinder Kaur) fought to enforce an eviction decree and regain possession of a shop from tenants (Ashok Kumar & another) who resisted execution by disputing the property's identity despite prior admissions and final orders.
issues_decided: Whether the tenants could re-agitate the issue of property identity and site plan correctness during execution after having failed to challenge it in earlier proceedings including appeal and revision.
Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the delivery of possession based on a disputed property description without considering prior admissions and finality of the decree.
Whether the execution court could be directed to reconsider an issue already decided and concluded in the original ejectment proceedings.
holdings: A party cannot re-open an issue of property identity or site plan correctness in execution when it was already decided against them in the original proceedings and not challenged in appeal or revision.

The High Court erred in interfering with the execution process by accepting a belated objection to property description, especially when the tenant had previously admitted the correctness of the site plan.
Courts must not allow judgment debtors to abuse the legal process by raising frivolous disputes during execution to delay compliance with a final decree.
doctrines: Finality of decree
Res judicata in execution
Abuse of process of court
Binding effect of admissions in judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The wife sought transfer of a property injunction suit from Delhi to Mumbai, alleging it was part of matrimonial harassment by her husband.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for permanent injunction over a flat in Delhi should be transferred to Mumbai for the sake of justice
Whether the petitioner, as the alleged owner of the flat, is a necessary party in the suit
holdings: The suit should be transferred to Mumbai to ensure the petitioner can fairly defend herself, given its connection to ongoing matrimonial disputes.
The petitioner is a necessary party to the suit, as evidenced by the trial court’s order to implead her, which was upheld by the High Court.
provisions: Supreme Court Rules, Order XVII, Rule 1
doctrines: Transfer of suits for the ends of justice
Necessary and proper parties in civil litigation

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners) fought with the Union of India over the compensation amount for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, claiming higher market value based on comparable sales.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of acquired land should be based on sale prices of small residential or shop plots.
Whether the High Court correctly adjusted the market value by considering only plotted areas and deducting development and administrative costs.
Whether comparable sales used for valuation were contemporaneous and similar in character to the acquired land.
holdings: Rates from sales of small plots can be considered for valuing large acquired land only if proper adjustments are made, and they are not a safe criterion otherwise.
The market value must reflect what a willing buyer would pay to a willing seller, disregarding compulsion, with consideration of location, development potential, and plotted area.
Comparable sales must be contemporaneous, bona fide, and from similar or adjacent land with like advantages to be reliable for valuation.
doctrines: Willing buyer-willing seller rule
Principle of comparable sales
No unjust enrichment or undue deprivation
Adjustment for plotted vs. plotable area
Exclusion of speculative potential value

card.dispute: The widow of a detained smuggler challenged the forfeiture of three properties held in her name under SAFEMA, arguing lack of nexus between the properties and her husband's illegal income.
issues_decided: Whether the competent authority must establish a nexus between the detenu's illegal income and the property held by a relative for forfeiture under SAFEMA
Whether the notice under Section 6(1) of SAFEMA was validly issued without explicitly proving a link between the property and smuggled wealth
Whether the burden of proof lies on the relative of the detenu to show that the property is not illegally acquired
holdings: No nexus need be established by the authorities between the property and the detenu’s illegal income if the property is held by a close relative like a spouse, as such a link may be inferred.
A notice under Section 6(1) of SAFEMA is valid if it records reasons for belief that the property is illegally acquired, even without direct evidence linking it to smuggling proceeds.
The burden lies on the relative or associate of the detenu to prove that the property was not acquired from the detenu’s illegal income or assets.
provisions: Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976, Section 2(2)(c)
Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976, Section 3(1)(c)
Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976, Section 6(1)
Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, Section 3(1)
doctrines: Presumption of illegal origin in case of unexplained wealth
Burden of proof on accused relatives in forfeiture proceedings
Liberal interpretation of preventive and forfeiture statutes to meet legislative purpose

card.dispute: The landlords sought to execute a decree for ejectment of commercial tenants, who objected on the ground that civil courts lacked jurisdiction over tenancies governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether a decree for ejectment passed by a civil court in respect of a commercial tenancy governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act is executable when the civil court lacked inherent jurisdiction?
Whether the judgment-debtors can challenge the executability of such a decree on the ground of lack of jurisdiction even after the decree has been executed?
holdings: A decree passed by a civil court for ejectment of a tenant from premises governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act is a nullity because the civil court inherently lacks jurisdiction, which vests exclusively in the Rent Controller.
An objection to the execution of a decree on the ground of lack of inherent jurisdiction can be raised at any stage, including execution, and such a decree does not operate as res judicata.
doctrines: Doctrine of inherent jurisdiction
Doctrine of res judicata
Doctrine of nullity (coram non judice)
Doctrine of retrospective effect of judicial interpretation

card.dispute: Shanti Kumar Panda and Shakutala Devi disputed possession of a shop, following police-initiated proceedings under Section 145/146 CrPC that excluded Shakutala Devi despite her being the actual owner and possessor.
issues_decided: Whether an order under Section 145/146 CrPC binds a civil court in subsequent proceedings on the question of possession
Whether a civil court can grant an interim injunction inconsistent with an order of an Executive Magistrate under Section 145 CrPC
Whether a suit for declaration of entitlement to possession without claiming recovery of possession is maintainable when property is under attachment under Section 146 CrPC
holdings: An order under Section 145/146 CrPC is based on summary enquiry and not binding on a civil court; it is only one piece of evidence at trial, though entitled to weight at the interim stage.

A civil court has jurisdiction to grant an injunction inconsistent with a Section 145 CrPC order, but only in exceptional cases where the magistrate's order is without jurisdiction, palpably wrong, or leads to injustice.
A suit seeking only a declaration of entitlement to possession is maintainable without claiming recovery of possession when the property is under attachment under Section 146 CrPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 39, Rule 1 and 2
doctrines: Summary nature of CrPC proceedings does not bind civil courts on questions of title or possession
Doctrine of comity and restraint in judicial interference with executive magisterial orders
Principles governing ad interim injunctions: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence for assaulting Jhanguram and others with intent to cause death, claiming they acted in private defence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the appellants were entitled to the benefit of the right of private defence under the IPC?
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the conviction and sentence?
holdings: The prosecution case was supported by consistent and credible evidence, and the conviction under Sections 307, 147, 148, 34, and 323 IPC was upheld.
The plea of private defence was not available to the appellants as there was no evidence of reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt, and no injuries on the accused to support such a claim.
The sentences imposed were not excessive and the appeal was dismissed as without merit.
doctrines: Right of private defence under IPC
Burden of proof in self-defence cases
Preponderance of probabilities standard for defence
Reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt

card.dispute: The widow of a deceased partner claimed her share in the partnership assets, including goodwill and profits, following the death of her husband and the administration of his estate.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the goodwill of the partnership firm upon the death of her husband.
Whether the plaintiff could claim profits and assets, including closing stock and loans, for the period after her husband's death.
Whether the debt owed by Darjeeling Tea Plantations Company to the partnership was still recoverable.
Whether the plaintiff's husband was liable to pay 13% interest to the defendants.
holdings: Goodwill is an intangible asset of a partnership and forms part of the estate upon dissolution or death of a partner, provided it is not excluded by agreement.
The plaintiff is entitled to a share in the profits and assets of the firm up to the date of her husband's death, including properly accounted closing stock.
The debt from Darjeeling Tea Plantations Company was adjusted in 1972 and no longer subsisted; thus, it could not be claimed as an outstanding asset.
The claim for 13% interest was not maintainable as it was not pleaded in the written statement or supported by a counterclaim.
doctrines: Goodwill as an intangible asset in partnership dissolution
Principle of proper accounting of partnership assets upon death of a partner
Doctrine of pleadings and issue estoppel

card.dispute: The state of Andhra Pradesh challenged the respondents' application for enhanced compensation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, claiming it was barred by limitation, as it was filed five years after the court's award.
issues_decided: Whether the period of limitation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 begins from the date of the court's award or from the date the applicant acquires knowledge of the award.
Whether the High Court's interpretation of Section 28-A as allowing limitation to run from the date of knowledge is legally sustainable.
holdings: The limitation period under Section 28-A begins from the date of the court's award, excluding only the day of pronouncement and time to obtain a certified copy; knowledge by the applicant is irrelevant.
Beneficial interpretation of Section 28-A does not justify extending the limitation period based on delayed knowledge, as finality of awards and administrative certainty must be preserved.
doctrines: Express language of statute
Beneficial legislation
Constructive knowledge
Finality of administrative and judicial awards

card.dispute: The State of Bihar challenged the Patna High Court's declaration that Sections 15(1) and 15(2) of the Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956 were unconstitutional and that civil courts could entertain certain disputes despite statutory bars.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 15(1) and 15(2) of the Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956 are ultra vires Articles 13 and 14 of the Constitution
Whether the Patna High Court was justified in holding a previous Full Bench decision (Ramkrit Singh) to be per incuriam
Whether civil courts are barred from entertaining disputes covered by notifications under Sections 3, 4(b), 4(c), and 37 of the Act
holdings: Sections 15(1) and 15(2) of the Act are not ultra vires Articles 13 and 14 of the Constitution and are valid.
A coordinate bench cannot declare a previous Full Bench decision per incuriam merely because it did not consider all legal aspects; such a decision must be followed or referred to a larger bench.
The bar of civil court jurisdiction under Sections 4(b), 4(c), and 37 of the Act applies to matters covered by notification under Section 3, and civil courts cannot entertain such disputes.
provisions: Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 3
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 4(b)
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 4(c)
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 15(1)
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 15(2)
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act, 1956, Section 37
doctrines: Doctrine of Stare Decisis
Per Incuriam
Binding Nature of Precedent under Article 141
Judicial Discipline and Reference to Larger Bench

card.dispute: The State of Haryana and Haryana Roadways challenged the award of Rs.6.5 lakhs compensation to the widow and minor son of a man who died in a road accident, arguing that the income assessment of the deceased was without evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal and High Court erred in estimating the deceased's monthly income at Rs.4,500 without sufficient evidence?
