Whether the compensation awarded was just and reasonable under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988?
holdings: The Tribunal and High Court erred in fixing the deceased's income at Rs.4,500 per month without any material evidence; such estimation must be based on rational and equitable principles, not guesswork.

Just compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act must be fair, reasonable, and non-arbitrary, considering all relevant factors; in this case, the deceased's monthly income is assessed at Rs.3,000 with a personal expense deduction of Rs.1,000, leading to a revised compensation of Rs.4,32,000.
doctrines: Principle of just and reasonable compensation
Doctrine of rational basis for income estimation in motor accident claims
Non-arbitrariness in assessment of damages

card.dispute: The State of Maharashtra challenged whether two strangers jointly owning land in Pune could exclude it from 'vacant land' under the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulations) Act, 1976, and whether their flats in Bombay should count toward ceiling limits.
issues_decided: Whether two strangers acquiring property jointly qualify as 'person' under Section 2(i) of the Act
Whether land where construction is permissible but no building exists on the appointed date can be excluded from 'vacant land' under Section 2(q)(i)
Whether land appurtenant to dwelling units in Bombay must be included in determining ceiling area under Section 4(9)
holdings: Joint ownership by strangers does not disqualify them from being treated as separate 'persons' entitled to individual ceiling rights under the Act.
Land where construction is permissible under building regulations is excluded from 'vacant land' under Section 2(q)(i), even if no building exists on the appointed date.
For ceiling calculation under Section 4(9), only land held with a dwelling unit is considered; where no land is appurtenant to a flat, it does not count toward the ceiling limit.
The definition of 'vacant land' in Section 2(q) is exhaustive and must be strictly construed, with exclusions interpreted liberally in favor of the landholder.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(i)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(q)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 4(9)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 3
doctrines: Strict construction of expropriatory legislation
Liberal interpretation of exclusionary clauses in beneficial statutes
Plain meaning rule in statutory interpretation
Harmonious construction to give effect to all statutory provisions

card.dispute: The State of Andhra Pradesh and its authorities fought with property owner Goverdhanlal Pitti over the validity of the acquisition of a school building and land, which the High Court had quashed as 'malicious in law'.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition of the school building and land by the State was mala fide or malice in law due to pending eviction orders.
Whether there was a genuine public purpose for the acquisition of the property.
Whether the State's delay in acquisition, after being ordered to vacate, rendered the acquisition proceedings invalid.
holdings: The State's decision to acquire the property after court-ordered eviction does not imply mala fide intent, especially when public purpose continues to exist.
A genuine public purpose existed for the acquisition, as the State needed control over the property to reconstruct or repair the dilapidated school building for continued public education.
The exercise of eminent domain is valid even if initiated after adverse court orders, provided the purpose is public and not a mere pretext.
doctrines: Eminent domain
Malice in law
Colourable legislation
Public purpose in land acquisition

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Bhawani and others, who had been convicted for murder, rioting, and illegal possession of arms based on an incident involving firing in a village Nohara.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the accused without properly evaluating the testimony of eye-witnesses?
Whether the High Court wrongly relied on the testimony of hostile witnesses to conclude there was cross-firing?
Whether the High Court illegally based its decision on inadmissible evidence from a site plan prepared by the investigating officer?
Whether the recovery of 303 bore cartridges could reasonably doubt the prosecution's version of the weapons used?
holdings: The High Court violated Section 386 Cr.P.C. by reversing the conviction without properly examining the eye-witness testimony, warranting interference by the Supreme Court.
The testimony of hostile witnesses who did not identify the accused or either party cannot support a finding of cross-firing, and such reliance is legally unsustainable.
Findings based on a site plan incorporating statements recorded during investigation are inadmissible under Section 162 Cr.P.C. and cannot form the basis of an acquittal.
The recovery of 303 bore cartridges does not discredit the prosecution case, as country-made pistols may use such cartridges and minor discrepancies do not create reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Principle of judicial review under Article 136 of the Constitution for gross miscarriage of justice
Requirement of corroboration for hostile witness testimony
Inadmissibility of police-recorded statements under Section 162 Cr.P.C. for substantive evidence
Primacy of eye-witness testimony in direct evidence cases

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's decision to reduce the conviction of Dhool Singh from murder (Section 302 IPC) to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 Part II IPC) in a case involving the fatal use of a sharp-edged weapon during a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the injury caused by the respondent was sufficient to attract Section 302 IPC rather than Section 304 Part II IPC
Whether the absence of recovery or production of the alleged weapon (sword) undermines the prosecution's case
Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the sentence to the period already undergone without proper reasoning
holdings: An injury caused by a sharp-edged weapon that the offender knows is likely to cause death, and which results in death, constitutes murder under Section 302 IPC, even if medical complications contributed to death.

The non-production of the alleged weapon does not negate the fact that a sharp-edged weapon was used, where medical evidence confirms the nature of the injury as an incised wound caused by such a weapon.

Courts must apply judicial discretion and provide reasoned orders when sentencing; reducing sentence to time already served without considering the nature of the offence or period served is impermissible.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive knowledge under Section 300 IPC
Principle of judicial review of concurrent findings when contrary to evidence
Requirement of reasoned sentencing discretion

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the Calcutta High Court's acquittal of the respondent accused in a murder and attempted murder case arising from a family dispute over property and a fence erection.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's evidence, including ocular testimony and a dying declaration, was reliable despite contradictions with medical evidence?
Whether the trial court could base conviction on a revised prosecution version inconsistent with the initial case?
Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting the accused based on the improbability of the prosecution's case?
holdings: A conviction cannot be sustained on a prosecution version that materially departs from the original case to reconcile with medical evidence; the prosecution must stand on its own evidence.
A dying declaration is inadmissible if the deceased merely repeated answers given by another person, as it lacks voluntariness and authenticity.
When medical evidence fundamentally contradicts the prosecution's oral testimony, the appellate court may accept the accused's acquittal if the prosecution's case becomes inherently improbable.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence in appeals against acquittal
Prosecution must prove its case on its own legs
Dying declaration must be voluntary and direct
Reconciliation of evidence cannot alter the foundation of the prosecution's case

card.dispute: The State of U.P. challenged the renewal of a lease for a property originally leased in 1887, arguing that the right to renewal had been exhausted after one renewal and could not be exercised again.
issues_decided: Whether the lessee had a right to successive renewals of the lease under the original lease covenant?
Whether the State could deny renewal on the ground of having 'acquired' its own land?
Whether breach of lease terms by the lessee barred the right to renewal?
holdings: A covenant for renewal that is incorporated by reference in a renewed lease without reservation allows for another renewal, but only once, unless the language clearly permits perpetual renewals.
The Land Acquisition Act, 1894 does not apply to land already owned by the State; thus, the State cannot use acquisition proceedings to avoid lease renewal obligations.
The right to renewal cannot be denied due to alleged breach of lease terms if the lessor did not exercise the right of re-entry before the renewal option was exercised.
doctrines: Doctrine of incorporation by reference
Doctrine against perpetual renewals
Equitable doctrine of lessee's position upon specific enforceability of renewal covenant

card.dispute: Surinder Singh appealed his conviction for murder under Section 302/34 IPC, arguing that merely holding the deceased's arms without common intention to kill did not justify conviction, especially after the main accused was acquitted.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC based on his role in holding the deceased's arms during the assault.
Whether the acquittal of the principal accused, Darshan Singh, in a subsequent trial affects the appellant's liability under Section 34 IPC.
Whether there was sufficient evidence of common intention to attract Section 34 IPC.
holdings: Mere presence or minimal physical assistance, such as holding the arms of a victim, without active participation in the fatal act or shared intention to kill, is insufficient to sustain a conviction under Section 302/34 IPC.

The acquittal of a co-accused in the same incident, especially the principal offender, is highly relevant and undermines the prosecution’s case for inferring common intention against the remaining accused.
Section 34 IPC cannot be invoked mechanically due to a group assault; there must be clear evidence of pre-existing or developed common intention to commit murder, which was absent here.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Principle of vicarious criminal liability
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Requirement of active participation and shared intention for group liability

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the respondent's eligibility to contest from a reserved constituency on the grounds that he did not belong to the Scheduled Caste despite holding a caste certificate.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent, born to a Kurmi father and a Pasi mother, could be considered a member of the Scheduled Caste for the purpose of contesting elections from a reserved constituency.
Whether a circular issued by the Bihar government allowing children of non-Scheduled Caste fathers and Scheduled Caste mothers to be classified as Scheduled Caste is legally valid.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on the said circular without requiring proper legal or evidentiary basis for the caste determination.
holdings: A person's caste for constitutional purposes is determined by customary law, primarily patrilineal descent, and cannot be altered by administrative circulars.
A circular issued by a state government without legislative backing cannot override the constitutional scheme under Article 341 or modify the list of Scheduled Castes.

The High Court erred in accepting the respondent’s claim of Scheduled Caste status based on an unverified caste certificate and a legally non-binding circular, especially when no proper inquiry was conducted.
doctrines: Doctrine of Patrilineal Descent in Caste Determination
Doctrine of Constitutional Supremacy over Administrative Circulars
Fraud on the Constitution
Burden of Proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The Thirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) and the descendants of saint Annamacharya disputed over ownership and control of 28.58 acres of land on Tirumala Hills, originally granted as inam, concerning whether TTD could file a civil suit challenging the grant of Ryotwari patta to the descendants despite prior revenue proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the civil suit filed by TTD is barred under Section 14 of the Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987
Whether the principles of res judicata or estoppel bar the civil suit after prior revenue proceedings resulted in a patta being granted to the respondents
Whether the High Court was justified in issuing a writ of prohibition preventing the civil court from adjudicating the suit
holdings: The civil suit's maintainability under Section 14 of the 1987 Act must be decided by the civil court through preliminary issues, not precluded by revenue proceedings.
The question of res judicata or estoppel arising from prior patta grant must be determined by the civil court as a preliminary issue.
The High Court erred in prohibiting the civil court from proceeding; the prohibition shall remain stayed pending decision on preliminary issues.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 14
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 2A
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 4(1)
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 7
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 97
Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, Section 153
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Estoppel
Separation of jurisdiction between revenue and civil courts

card.dispute: Surya Dev Rai sought a permanent and interim injunction over agricultural land in a civil suit, but after courts denied relief, he approached the High Court under Article 226; the High Court dismissed the petition, holding it not maintainable as it involved private parties.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment to Section 115 of the CPC by Act 46 of 1999 affects the High Court's jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution?

Whether an order refusing interim injunction by a subordinate court can be challenged via writ of certiorari or under supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227, even if the dispute is between private parties?
What are the limits and guiding principles for exercising writ and supervisory jurisdiction in cases involving interlocutory orders?
holdings: The amendment to Section 115 of the CPC does not curtail or affect the High Court’s constitutional powers under Articles 226 and 227.

Interlocutory orders, even if not revisable under Section 115 as amended, remain subject to challenge through certiorari or supervisory jurisdiction when there is a gross error of jurisdiction or failure of justice.

Writ and supervisory jurisdiction cannot be used to correct mere errors of fact or law but are available only for patent errors causing grave injustice, and must be exercised sparingly to avoid turning the High Court into a court of appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2
doctrines: Doctrine of separation between certiorari and supervisory jurisdiction
Doctrine of gross or patent error
Doctrine of judicial restraint in writ jurisdiction
Principle of finality of interlocutory orders unless grave injustice occurs

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the constitutional validity of the Defence of India Act, 1971, specifically its denial of solatium and interest in land acquisition, claiming it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether Section 31 of the Defence of India Act, 1971, which excludes payment of solatium and interest in land acquisition, violates Article 14 of the Constitution?
Whether the classification between land acquired under the Defence of India Act and the Land Acquisition Act is reasonable and non-arbitrary?
Whether the respondents are entitled to solatium and interest on compensation for requisitioned land?
Whether the amounts already paid as solatium and interest should be refunded to the Union of India?
holdings: The exclusion of solatium and interest under the Defence of India Act, 1971, does not violate Article 14 as the classification is based on intelligible differentia and rational purpose.
Owners of requisitioned land under the Defence of India Act are not similarly situated with those under the Land Acquisition Act due to differences in possession and use during requisition.
The criteria for compensation under Section 31 of the Defence of India Act are reasonable, considering prior compensation during requisition, and do not require solatium or interest.
The Union of India shall not recover solatium and interest already paid to respondents, though this is a one-time equitable direction and not a precedent.
doctrines: Reasonable classification under Article 14
Principle of non-arbitrariness in state action
Doctrine of precedent (ratio decidendi vs. obiter dicta)
Equitable relief in exceptional factual circumstances

card.dispute: A public-spirited citizen challenged the NOIDA commercial hub scheme for allegedly selling prime land at an arbitrary low price, causing loss to the state exchequer, while the state defended the scheme as fair and in public interest.
issues_decided: Whether the fixation of the reserve price at Rs.27,500 per sq. mtr. was arbitrary and violative of Article 14
Whether the concessions in ground rent and transfer charges under the scheme were arbitrarily granted to benefit the developer
Whether the tender process and final award of the commercial plot violated principles of fairness and transparency
holdings: The reserve price was not arbitrary as it was determined based on past failed tenders, comparative sales, and cost factors like mandatory ECS construction, and courts cannot substitute administrative expertise.

Concessions in ground rent for initial years and waiver of transfer charges for two years were reasonable incentives under the scheme, not arbitrary largesse, and part of a broader development package.
The tender process was validly conducted with adequate publicity, and absence of competing bids does not invalidate the process if the administrative procedure was followed fairly.
provisions: Board Resolution dated 10.7.2003, Clause 4(c) and Clause 2(e)
doctrines: Principle of judicial review in administrative action
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness under Article 14
Standard of reasonableness in government contracts
Non-interference with administrative discretion in absence of mala fides

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Patel Chikkahanumaiah challenged the restoration of an ex-parte decree in favor of Boraiah, claiming it was obtained by fraud due to improper service of summons.
issues_decided: Whether the ex-parte decree could be set aside on the ground of fraud and misrepresentation in the service of summons
Whether a suit under Section 9 CPC is maintainable to set aside a decree solely on the basis of non-service of summons alleged as fraud
Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the trial court's decision that had cancelled the ex-parte decree
holdings: A decree cannot be set aside on the ground of fraud unless it is proven that the party made a false representation knowing it to be false or without belief in its truth.
Non-service of summons, without more, does not constitute fraud or misrepresentation sufficient to set aside a decree under Section 9 CPC.

A suit alleging fraud to set aside a decree is not maintainable if the allegation is bare and not supported by evidence, especially when no such plea was raised in earlier proceedings under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
doctrines: Fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved with high standard of evidence
Non-service of summons per se does not amount to fraud
Principle of consistency in grounds taken across remedies

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) fought the sub-tenants (respondents) over whether a decree for possession against the original tenant's heirs could be executed against them despite not being formally impleaded in the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the decree passed against the heirs of the original tenant is void ab initio for non-joinder of sub-tenants as parties
Whether sub-tenants can challenge a decree in execution proceedings when they were not impleaded in the original suit
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the decree under Article 227 on the ground of non-joinder of 'necessary parties'
holdings: A decree passed by a competent court against the heirs of a tenant is not a nullity merely because sub-tenants were not joined as parties to the suit.
Sub-tenants, not being necessary parties, are bound by a decree in a landlord-tenant suit and must challenge it through appeal or review, not execution proceedings.
Non-joinder of sub-tenants does not render a decree inexecutable or void, and the High Court erred in interfering under Article 227 on this ground alone.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX, Rule 13
doctrines: Distinction between necessary and proper parties
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of binding effect of decree on privies

card.dispute: The Cement Corporation of India Ltd. challenged the enhancement of land acquisition compensation based on certified sale deeds, arguing against the High Court's reliance on them without considering other relevant evidence.
issues_decided: Whether Section 51A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 mandates courts to accept certified copies of sale deeds as conclusive proof of transaction value
Whether the contents of certified sale deeds under Section 51A can be relied upon without examining the vendor or vendee
Whether the High Court erred in enhancing compensation solely based on two sale deeds without considering other relevant evidence
holdings: Section 51A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is an enabling provision that allows courts to accept certified copies of sale deeds as evidence, but does not make their contents conclusive or binding.
A certified copy under Section 51A may raise a rebuttable presumption of genuineness, but the court must evaluate its weight in light of other evidence and is not bound to rely on it.

The High Court erred in fixing compensation based solely on two sale deeds without considering comparative factors like location, market potential, and other relevant evidence; remand ordered for proper assessment.
provisions: Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, Section 13(5)
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption
Appreciation of evidence
Standard of judicial review in land acquisition compensation
Principle of comparative market value in land valuation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's dismissal of a first appeal against an ex-parte decree in a partition suit, raising questions about the availability and limits of remedies under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC.
issues_decided: Whether a defendant can simultaneously pursue relief under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC and also challenge the ex-parte decree on grounds of lack of opportunity to be heard in a first appeal under Section 96 CPC.
Whether dismissal of an application under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC bars the defendant from raising the same grounds in a first appeal.
Whether a defendant can challenge the merits of an ex-parte decree in a first appeal even after failing under Order 9 Rule 13 CPC.
holdings: A defendant cannot raise the same contention regarding the correctness of the ex-parte order both under Order 9 Rule 13 and in a first appeal, as it may lead to conflicting decisions.
Once an application under Order 9 Rule 13 is dismissed, the defendant is barred from re-agitating the issue of non-appearance or procedural fairness in the first appeal.
However, the defendant retains the statutory right to challenge the merits of the decree in a first appeal, including the sufficiency of evidence or maintainability of the suit, based on the record.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 17 Rule 2
doctrines: Res judicata
Issue estoppel
Cause of action estoppel
Strict construction of statutory provisions
Statutory right of appeal

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. as tenant after lease expiry, while the tenant claimed protection and right to purchase the leased land under the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant had a statutory right to purchase the leased premises under Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921 upon filing of eviction suit
Whether the right under Section 9 of the Tenants Act creates a property interest or is merely an equitable privilege
Whether the court must determine the extent of land necessary for the tenant's convenient enjoyment before deciding an eviction suit
holdings: Section 9 of the Tenants Act grants a statutory right to a tenant facing eviction to apply for purchase of land necessary for convenient enjoyment, but this right is not absolute and depends on factual determination by the court.
The right under Section 9 is a statutory privilege of an equitable nature and does not create any property interest or vested right in the tenant.
The court has a mandatory duty to conduct an enquiry to determine the minimum extent of land required by the tenant for convenient enjoyment before deciding on eviction or sale.
provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, Section 9
Burmah Shell (Acquisition of Undertakings in India) Act, 1976
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of tenant rights
Equitable nature of statutory privileges
Principle of convenient enjoyment
Precedent and factual specificity in judicial decisions

card.dispute: Bharat Hydro Power Corp. Ltd. challenged the constitutional validity of an Assam Act that acquired its hydro power project, arguing it conflicted with central electricity laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Assam Acquisition Act is repugnant to the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 and the Electricity Supply Act, 1948
Whether the appellants qualify as 'licensees' under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910
Whether the provisions of the 1910 and 1948 Acts bar the State from acquiring the undertaking
holdings: The Assam Acquisition Act does not conflict with central electricity laws as it operates in a distinct field—acquisition with compensation—while the central laws regulate supply and use of electricity.
The appellants are not 'licensees' under the 1910 Act, as they are a generating company specifically excluded from the definition of licensee under Section 2(6) of the 1948 Act.
Sections 3 to 11 of the 1910 Act, including those on purchase of undertakings, do not apply to generating companies, so the State's acquisition power remains unimpeded.
doctrines: Doctrine of Repugnancy
Doctrine of Exclusion from Statutory Definition
Doctrine of Field Classification in Federal Legislation

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents disputed whether the application for execution of a decree was barred by limitation, specifically the date from which the limitation period for execution begins when a second appeal is dismissed and a formal decree is drawn later.
issues_decided: From which date does the limitation period for execution of a decree begin when a second appeal is dismissed and a formal decree is drawn up later?
Whether the doctrine of merger applies when a second appeal is dismissed and a formal decree is subsequently drawn?
Whether the dismissal of an appeal on grounds of delay without a speaking order results in a decree that can be executed?
holdings: The limitation period for execution of a decree begins from the date the decree becomes enforceable, which is when the appellate court disposes of the appeal and a formal decree is drawn, not from the date of the appellate order alone.
The doctrine of merger applies when a second appeal is dismissed and a formal decree is drawn, as the appellate decree supersedes the lower court’s decree and becomes the operative decree.

A formal decree drawn after dismissal of a second appeal, even if the dismissal was on merits, constitutes an enforceable decree under the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 136 of the Limitation Act.
doctrines: Doctrine of Merger
Enforceability of Decree
Limitation for Execution of Decree

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax challenged the exemption of Malaysian business income and capital gains from taxation in India for a firm owned by a resident of India with properties in Malaysia, under the India-Malaysia Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.
issues_decided: Whether income from rubber estates in Malaysia can be taxed in India under the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Malaysia?
Whether capital gains from the sale of immovable property situated in Malaysia can be taxed in India?
holdings: Business income from rubber estates in Malaysia cannot be taxed in India when the assessee has no permanent establishment in India and closer economic ties with Malaysia, as the treaty determines fiscal residence based on personal and economic relations.

Capital gains from the sale of immovable property located in Malaysia constitute income under the treaty and are taxable only in Malaysia, as Article 6 of the agreement allocates taxing rights to the country where the property is situated.
provisions: Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Malaysia, Article IV
Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Malaysia, Article 6
Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement between India and Malaysia, Article II
doctrines: Fiscal domicile doctrine
Source-based taxation of immovable property
Treaty override doctrine
Principle of double taxation avoidance

card.dispute: Dashrath Singh and Raja Ram challenged their convictions for murder and related offences arising from a 1977 incident in which Pratap Singh died after being injured during a clash over a disputed land.
issues_decided: Whether Raja Ram caused the death of Pratap Singh with the intention to kill, thereby committing murder under Section 302 IPC
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the injury inflicted by Raja Ram was the cause of death
Whether the injury on Hari Lal, allegedly caused by a sharp-edged weapon, undermined the prosecution's case
Whether Dashrath Singh was rightly convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC
holdings: The act of Raja Ram in causing a grievous head injury with a dangerous weapon was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, but there was no intention to kill, so the offence is not murder under Section 300 IPC.

The prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the injury caused by Raja Ram was the sole cause of death due to lack of post-operative medical records and absence of a post-mortem, warranting conviction under Section 326 IPC instead of Section 302 or 304.
An injury resembling an incised wound on Hari Lal could have been caused by a blunt object like a lathi due to the anatomical nature of the scalp, and thus does not discredit the prosecution's case.

Dashrath Singh's conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC is upheld as the prosecution proved his active participation in the unlawful assembly and use of firearms, justifying common intention.
doctrines: Presumption as to causation of death in absence of post-mortem
Distinction between lacerated and incised wounds in medical jurisprudence
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Cyril Lasrado challenged the Karnataka High Court's decision to remit a land occupancy matter to the Land Tribunal without issuing notice to them, despite Cyril's death and a 19-year delay in filing the writ petition.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court committed an error by disposing of a writ petition without issuing notice to the legal representatives of a deceased party.
Whether the delay of about 19 years in filing the writ petition required explanation and consideration by the High Court.
Whether the absence of reasoned orders by the Single Judge and Division Bench amounts to non-application of mind and violates principles of natural justice.
holdings: A writ petition filed against a deceased person without impleading legal representatives and without notice violates principles of natural justice.
Unexplained delay of nearly 19 years in filing a writ petition must be considered by the court before entertaining it.
An order lacking reasons, especially in judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings, constitutes non-application of mind and undermines the validity of the decision.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Right to reasoned order
Non-application of mind
Merits of writ petition after death of party

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority and Union of India challenged the High Court's enhancement of land acquisition compensation from Rs. 76,550 per bigha to Rs. 3,45,000 per bigha, arguing that the earlier Supreme Court decision in Karan Singh's case should apply uniformly.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in enhancing compensation by relying on post-Notification transactions and government schedule of rates not considered in prior identical cases?
Whether the principle of consistent compensation applies to lands acquired under the same Notification when evidence is identical?
Whether a differential escalation in compensation is justified for lands notified later under the same acquisition scheme?
holdings: Compensation for land acquired under the same Notification must be consistent when evidence and material are identical, and cannot be enhanced based on post-Notification transactions or schedule of rates contrary to a binding Supreme Court precedent.
The High Court's enhancement of compensation to Rs. 3,45,000 per bigha was unjustified and set aside, with the market value restored to Rs. 76,550 per bigha as decided in Karan Singh’s case.

For lands notified under subsequent notifications, a reasonable escalation of 5% and 10% respectively was allowed to account for time-based price increases, ensuring fairness while maintaining consistency.
doctrines: Principle of consistent compensation in same acquisition proceedings
Binding effect of precedent in co-ordinate cases with identical facts
Consideration of temporal escalation in market value for delayed notifications

card.dispute: The tea estate owner challenged the adequacy of compensation awarded for land acquired for an oil refinery, seeking review of the High Court's dismissal of its review application.
issues_decided: Whether the special leave petition was barred by res judicata or similar principles.
Whether the High Court committed an error apparent on the face of the record in dismissing the review petition.
Whether the compensation awarded for the acquired tea estate land was manifestly inadequate given government's own valuation norms.
holdings: The appeal is maintainable as the special leave petition was not barred by res judicata, especially since the review petition preceded the appeal.
The High Court erred in dismissing the review petition without considering material on record showing inconsistency in compensation valuation.
The compensation fixed at Rs. 22,000 per bigha was inadequate when the State itself had accepted Rs. 55,000 per bigha for similar tea estate land.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47, Rule 1
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Review jurisdiction under CPC
Principle of fair compensation in land acquisition
Judicial approach to justice and rectification of mistaken orders

card.dispute: Gopal Sardar and Karuna Sardar fought over whether Karuna could claim a right of pre-emption under the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, for land purchased by Gopal, after a significant delay in filing her application.
issues_decided: Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to an application under Section 8 of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, for condonation of delay?
Whether the respondent's application for pre-emption was barred by limitation?
holdings: Section 5 of the Limitation Act does not apply to proceedings under Section 8 of the West Bengal Land Reforms Act, as the Act is a self-contained code with an express exclusion of Section 5, inferred from its scheme and provisions.
An application under Section 8 must be filed within the prescribed period; delay cannot be condoned, and such applications filed beyond time are liable to be dismissed outright.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, Section 8
doctrines: Express exclusion doctrine under Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act
Self-contained statutory scheme
Strict enforcement of statutory limitation
Condonation of delay not permitted in absence of enabling provision

card.dispute: Street vendors and hawkers in Delhi fought with municipal authorities over their right to vend on public streets and the regulation of such activities.
issues_decided: Whether street vending constitutes a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
How to balance the fundamental rights of hawkers to carry on livelihood with the public's right to free movement under Article 19(1)(d)
Whether a judicially monitored scheme for regulating street vending can substitute for a legislative framework
Whether hawkers must first exhaust a dispute redressal mechanism before approaching the Court
holdings: The right to carry on street vending is a fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) as it constitutes a means of livelihood for the poor.
The rights of hawkers and the public to unimpeded movement must be harmonized through reasonable restrictions under law.
A permanent legislative framework is necessary to define the rights and regulation of street vendors, rather than relying on court-monitored schemes.
Hawkers must first use the established dispute redressal mechanism and cannot bypass it by directly approaching the Court.
provisions: New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, Section 226
doctrines: Harmonious construction of fundamental rights
Judicial direction to enact legislation
Exhaustion of alternative remedies

card.dispute: Gaon Sabha and Union of India fought with private landholders over who was entitled to compensation for acquired land—Gaon Sabha as the vestee of waste land or the private respondents as claimed owners.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging the vesting of land in Gaon Sabha under the relevant land reform Act?
Whether the High Court’s reliance on its earlier judgment in Sher Singh v. Ors. was legally valid, given contrary binding precedents?
Whether the disputed land qualified as 'waste land' under the Act, making it eligible for vesting in the Gaon Sabha?
Whether the private respondents, claiming proprietorship, were entitled to compensation after the abolition of proprietary rights under the Act?
holdings: A civil suit challenging the vesting of land in Gaon Sabha is barred by statute; civil courts lack jurisdiction as such matters fall under the exclusive domain of revenue authorities.
A decree passed by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity and can be challenged at any stage; the High Court’s reliance on an earlier incorrect judgment does not validate its decision.
Land not part of a proprietor’s holding qualifies as 'waste land' under the Act, and a notification under Section 7(2) for vesting such land in Gaon Sabha is valid.

With the abolition of proprietary rights under the land reform Act, former proprietors cannot claim compensation; only bhumidhars or asamis are entitled, and the Gaon Sabha receives compensation for vested waste land.
provisions: U.P. Land Reforms Act, Explanation (i) to Section 7
doctrines: Jurisdictional bar on civil courts in land reform matters
Nullity of decrees passed without jurisdiction
Doctrine of precedent (stare decisis)
Abolition of proprietary rights under land reform laws
Exclusive jurisdiction of revenue authorities

card.dispute: Essar Oil Ltd. and other companies fought with environmental groups over permission to lay crude oil pipelines through the Jamnagar Marine National Park and Sanctuary in Gujarat.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had validly granted permission under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 for laying pipelines in the Marine National Park and Sanctuary.
Whether the High Court erred in denying Essar Oil Ltd. permission to lay pipelines while allowing Bharat Oman Refineries Ltd. to do so.
Whether the inclusion of corals in Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 after the initial clearances required fresh environmental approvals.
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting Essar Oil Ltd.'s review application without addressing the factual controversy.
holdings: The State Government had, in substance, granted permission under Sections 29 and 35 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 through a letter, and the absence of a formal order was only an irregularity that did not invalidate the permission.

The High Court erred in denying Essar Oil Ltd. permission while allowing BORL, especially since both had similar expert recommendations and conditions; the decision lacked equal treatment and proper reasoning.
The amendment including corals in Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act did not invalidate prior clearances, but required a coral survey and management plan, which Essar agreed to comply with.
The High Court wrongly rejected the review application by treating a substantial factual dispute as beyond review; it should have corrected its earlier decision made without hearing Essar.
doctrines: Principle of equal treatment in environmental clearances
Substantial compliance with statutory requirements
Doctrine of judicial review to correct factual errors
Sustainable development with expert-based environmental safeguards

card.dispute: The lessees of the Port of Mumbai challenged the rent revision rates imposed by the Board of Trustees, seeking fair and uniform rent determination for leasehold properties.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-Board could file cross-objections in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution after the limitation period had expired?
Whether the 'Compromise Proposals' for rent revision, as modified, should be binding on all lessees including non-parties?
Whether a mechanism should be created to allow lessees to seek individual relief based on special circumstances?
holdings: A respondent cannot file cross-objections in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution as a substitute for a delayed special leave petition; such cross-objections are not maintainable.

The 'Compromise Proposals' for rent revision, with modifications setting return rates at 10% (non-residential) and 8% (residential) based on the Kirloskar report, are fair and binding on all lessees, including those not directly involved in the litigation.

A mechanism through a Sole Adjudicator is established for lessees to file representations seeking exceptions based on material distinguishing features, with final and binding decisions to be made summarily.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1 Rule 8
doctrines: Maintainability of cross-objections under special leave jurisdiction
Binding effect of compromise decrees on similarly situated parties
Principle of summary adjudication for equitable relief

card.dispute: The State appealed against the High Court's acquittal of two accused, while other convicted accused appealed against their conviction, in a case involving murder during an unlawful assembly.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in acquitting A-5 Daddan Yadav and A-6 Ram Pratap Yadav despite finding them present as members of the unlawful assembly?
Whether mere presence in an unlawful assembly with common object is sufficient for conviction under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC, even without participation in the actual assault?
Whether the delay in sending dead bodies for post-mortem casts doubt on the authenticity of the FIR?
Whether contradictions between medical and oral evidence undermine the prosecution's case?
holdings: Presence in an unlawful assembly with knowledge of its common object makes a member liable for offences committed in furtherance of that object, even without overt participation.
Acquittal cannot be based solely on absence of direct participation if membership of unlawful assembly and shared common object are established.
Delay in post-mortem due to logistical issues does not invalidate the FIR or suggest it was ante-dated.
Corroborated medical and eyewitness evidence establishing cause of death and nature of injuries upholds the prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
doctrines: Constructive liability under Section 149 IPC
Common object of unlawful assembly
Principle of joint liability in criminal acts

card.dispute: The appellants, who had their granite quarry leases quashed for being granted in violation of mining rules, challenged the state's demand for payment of the price of minerals they had extracted under interim Supreme Court orders.
issues_decided: Whether the demand for the price of minerals extracted without lawful authority under Section 21(5) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 is penal in nature?
Whether the appellants could retain the benefit of mineral extraction under interim orders after the final dismissal of their appeals?
Whether the Supreme Court or High Court could have granted equitable relief from the consequences of the vacated interim orders?
holdings: The demand for the price of minerals under Section 21(5) is compensatory, not penal, as it recovers the value of state-owned minerals unlawfully extracted.
The appellants cannot retain the benefit of extraction under interim orders once those orders were vacated by the final dismissal of their appeals.
The Court may, in appropriate cases, grant equitable relief under Article 142 to mitigate hardship, but no such relief was sought or granted here.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 21(5)
doctrines: Compensatory recovery doctrine
Equitable relief under Article 142
Distinction between penal and compensatory liability

card.dispute: The tenant appealed against an eviction order sought by landlords who claimed a bona fide need for the shop for business, but both landlords died during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the death of the landlords during the pendency of eviction proceedings affects the continuation of the eviction petition.
Whether the legal representatives of deceased landlords can pursue eviction on the basis of their own need under Section 21(7) of the UP Urban Buildings Act.
holdings: The bona fide requirement for eviction must continue until final determination; the death of the applicants renders their personal need defunct unless legal representatives assert independent need.
Under Section 21(7) of the UP Urban Buildings Act, legal representatives may continue the eviction application based on their own bona fide need, replacing that of the deceased landlord.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(7)
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for personal use must subsist till final order in eviction cases.
Subsequent events during litigation, especially death of parties, must be considered where they affect the basis of eviction.

card.dispute: The appellants were convicted for murder and other offences under the IPC, and they challenged the conviction by claiming they acted in private defence during a land and irrigation dispute with the deceased's family.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence under Sections 96 to 100 of the Indian Penal Code?
Whether the prosecution case, including the dying declaration and eyewitness accounts, was reliable and sufficient to convict the appellants?
Whether the initiation of the assault was by the appellants or the deceased party?
holdings: The right of private defence under Sections 96–100 IPC is not available when the accused are the aggressors or have trespassed with deadly weapons.
The prosecution's case, supported by eyewitness testimony, medical evidence, and a corroborated dying declaration, was reliable and sufficient for conviction.
The burden of proving private defence lies on the accused, and it was not discharged here due to lack of credible evidence and suspicious delay in seeking medical help.
doctrines: Right of private defence
Burden of proof in criminal cases
Corroboration of dying declaration
Presumption against aggressors in self-defence claims

card.dispute: The appellant sought to be brought on record as a legal representative in an appeal filed by his deceased father, which was rejected by the lower courts on technical grounds.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant's application to be brought on record as a legal representative was liable to be rejected on technical grounds for not praying to set aside abatement or for condonation of delay?
Whether the High Court ought to have exercised its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to prevent failure of justice?
holdings: An application under Order 22, Rule 3 CPC read with Section 151 CPC should not be rejected on hyper-technical grounds if the applicant acted promptly upon learning of the pendency of an appeal after the death of the original litigant.
Courts must ensure full and complete justice; failure to allow substitution of legal representatives in such circumstances amounts to a failure of justice, warranting interference in revision.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22, Rule 3
doctrines: Doctrine of substantial justice
Judicial discretion under Section 151 CPC
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The plaintiff, Bernadette B. Pereira, claimed an easementary right of motorable access over the defendants' property, which the defendants contested.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff acquired an easementary right of way by prescription under Section 15 of the Easements Act, 1882?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a permanent injunction to prevent obstruction of the claimed access?
Whether the plaintiff could claim a prescriptive right despite having alternative access to her property?
holdings: To claim an easement by prescription, the use must be peaceful, open, continuous, and as of right for at least 20 years, with specific pleadings and evidence to that effect.
The plaintiff failed to plead or prove uninterrupted use of the defendants' land as of right for 20 years, and thus could not establish a prescriptive easement.
The existence of an alternative accessible route to the plaintiff’s property negates the claim for a prescriptive right over another’s land, especially in absence of necessity.
doctrines: Easement by prescription
Necessity for specific pleadings in property claims
Alternative access negating easement claims

card.dispute: The Karnataka Board of Wakf and the Government of India disputed ownership of three properties in Bijapur, with the Government claiming ownership under the Ancient Monuments Act and the Wakf Board declaring them as Wakf properties.
issues_decided: Whether the suit properties are rightfully owned by the Government of India under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904 and the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958
Whether the Wakf Board's notification declaring the properties as Wakf properties is valid
Whether the Government of India could claim ownership through adverse possession
holdings: The Government of India is the rightful owner of the suit properties based on entries in the Register of Ancient Protected Monuments and continuous, lawful possession for about a century.
The Wakf Board's notification declaring the properties as Wakf is null and void because the properties were not existing wakf properties at the time of the survey under the Wakf Act, 1954.

The plea of adverse possession by the Government of India is unsustainable as it is inconsistent with its claim of lawful title under the Ancient Monuments Act and was not specifically pleaded or proved.
provisions: Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958
doctrines: nec vi, nec clam, nec precario
adverse possession
mutual exclusivity of title and adverse possession claims
principle of lawful possession under statutory acquisition

card.dispute: The plaintiffs, legal heirs of Narayanan Nair, sued to recover possession of property from the appellant, Kunjan Nair Sivaraman Nair, who claimed co-ownership and improvements made in good faith.
issues_decided: Whether the second suit for recovery of possession was barred by Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure due to a previous suit on the same cause of action.
Whether the appellant was entitled to compensation for improvements made on the property under Section 2(d) of the Kerala Land Reforms (Fixation of Compensation for Tenants) Act, 1965.
holdings: A subsequent suit for recovery of possession is not barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC if it is based on a distinct cause of action, such as actual dispossession, even if a prior suit involved a claim for declaration of title.

A person in possession of another's land may claim compensation for improvements under Section 2(d)(iii) of the Kerala Land Reforms Act if made in bona fide belief of entitlement, a question requiring factual determination by the trial court.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
Kerala Land Reforms (Fixation of Compensation for Tenants) Act, 1965, Section 2(d)
doctrines: Cause of action estoppel
Bona fide belief in right to make improvements

card.dispute: M/s Anand Buttons Ltd. and others challenged the acquisition of their land for Phase-IV of Kundli Industrial Estate, claiming discrimination under Article 14 as some similarly situated industrial units were exempted from acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the acquisition proceedings violated Article 14 due to alleged discriminatory exemption of certain industrial units from acquisition.
Whether the failure of the State Government to file a return in the writ petition rendered the acquisition proceedings illegal.
Whether the satisfaction of the authorities in not exempting the appellants' land from acquisition was justiciable.
holdings: The exemption of some units from acquisition, even if erroneous, does not entitle others to the same relief, as Article 14 does not permit 'negative equality' or claiming a right based on another's wrong.
The acquisition proceedings were not vitiated by the State Government’s failure to file a return, as the nodal agency filed affidavits and was competent to represent the facts.
The decision to exclude certain lands from exemption to ensure planned industrial development is within the policy domain and not subject to judicial review unless mala fide or arbitrary.
provisions: Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas (Restriction of Unregulated Development) Act, 1963
doctrines: Article 14 - Equal Protection of Laws
Principle of Negative Equality
Justiciability of Administrative Satisfaction
Planned Development as a Valid Ground for Acquisition

card.dispute: Co-owners of a property sued tenants for eviction; one co-owner sold her share to partners of a tenant during litigation, leading to disputes over tenancy rights and eviction.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for eviction by one co-owner is maintainable without consent of all co-owners?
Whether tenancy stands extinguished by partial merger when a tenant acquires the share of one co-owner?
Whether the decree for eviction can be executed against tenants when part of the landlord's interest has been transferred pendente lite?
holdings: A co-owner can maintain an eviction suit as an agent for other co-owners; consent is presumed unless dissent is proven.
Partial merger of tenancy with ownership—where only one co-owner’s share vests in the tenant—does not extinguish the tenancy under Section 111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act.
The decree for eviction remains enforceable against the tenant in respect of the continuing landlord’s share, even if another co-owner transferred her interest during litigation.
doctrines: Doctrine of agency among co-owners
Doctrine of merger under Section 111(d)
Principle of lis pendens
Finality of decree in absence of appeal

card.dispute: The appellant Narayanan and respondents, including Kumaran, fought over ownership and possession of a disputed property (D Schedule) that was allegedly fraudulently included in a transfer deed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the suit and reappreciating evidence after the lower appellate court set aside the trial court's decree?
Whether the disputed property (D Schedule) was intended to be transferred to Kumaran under the Ext.A1 deed?
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in a second appeal by re-examining findings of fact?
holdings: The High Court erred in remanding the case and reappreciating evidence when the lower appellate court had already decided the suit on merits; remand was unjustified as identity of the property was clear.

The D Schedule property was not intended to be transferred to Kumaran; the recitals in Ext.A1 show only C Schedule property was conveyed, and inconsistencies in the schedule do not override the document’s clear intention.
The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by reappreciating evidence in a second appeal where no substantial question of law arose, as the first appellate court was the final fact-finding authority.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43, Rule 1(u)
doctrines: Recitals in a deed prevail over inconsistent schedules
Second appeal limited to substantial questions of law
Appellate court should not remand when facts are clear and no preliminary point exists

card.dispute: The appellants (Metro Marins) challenged the High Court's interim order directing them to hand over possession of a property to the respondents (Bonus Watch Co.) in a pending suit for possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Appellate Bench of the High Court was justified in granting an interim mandatory injunction directing the appellants to hand over possession of the suit property during the pendency of the suit?
Whether the appointment of a receiver to oversee the property and facilitate possession to the plaintiff was warranted in the facts of the case?
holdings: An interim mandatory injunction directing possession to be handed over cannot be granted unless exceptional circumstances exist, and mere non-use of property or alleged luxury litigation does not justify disturbing the status quo.
The appointment of a receiver to supervise possession in such circumstances is unnecessary and impermissible when the trial court has rightly refused interim relief to avoid pre-judging the suit.
doctrines: Status quo doctrine in interim injunctions
Last non-contested status doctrine
Exceptional circumstances requirement for mandatory injunctions

card.dispute: The Maharwal Khewaji Trust sought possession of a property and an injunction to prevent Baldev Dass from alienating or constructing on it during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the lower courts were justified in permitting the respondent to construct on and alienate the suit property during pendency of the suit?
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the revision without examining the legal grounds, relying solely on counsel's oral undertaking?
holdings: Courts should not permit changes to the nature of property, including construction or alienation, during litigation unless a party demonstrates irreparable loss; no such exceptional circumstances existed here.
The High Court erred in dismissing the revision based solely on counsel's oral undertaking without addressing the legal merits, and thus failed to properly exercise its revisional jurisdiction.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39 Rules 1 and 2
doctrines: Lis pendens
Status quo during litigation
Judicial discretion in granting interim injunctions

card.dispute: The Madhya Pradesh Special Police Establishment challenged the High Court's decision quashing the Governor's sanction to prosecute two former ministers, after the Council of Ministers had refused sanction, over allegations of illegal land release and criminal conspiracy.
issues_decided: Whether the Governor can grant sanction to prosecute ministers in his discretion, contrary to the advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 163 of the Constitution?
Whether the Council of Ministers' refusal to grant sanction was legally valid given the material indicating a prima facie case of conspiracy?
Whether the doctrine of bias or necessity applies to collective decisions of the Council of Ministers in sanctioning prosecution?
holdings: The Governor can act in his discretion under Article 163 where the Council of Ministers' decision is irrational, based on non-consideration of relevant material, or violates the rule of law.

The Council of Ministers' refusal to grant sanction was vitiated by manifest error and non-application of mind, as it ignored substantial material from the Lokayukta report indicating a prima facie case.
The doctrine of bias or necessity does not automatically apply to collective ministerial decisions; bias or malice must be specifically proven against individuals and cannot be presumed.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(d) and Section 13(2)
Madhya Pradesh Special Police Establishment Act, Section 4(1)
doctrines: Doctrine of separation of powers
Doctrine of aid and advice
Doctrine of apparent bias
Doctrine of necessity
Doctrine of rule of law
Doctrine of non-application of mind
Doctrine of manifest arbitrariness

card.dispute: Pramod Mandal challenged his conviction under Section 396 IPC for dacoity with murder, arguing that the delay in conducting the test identification parade undermined the reliability of the identification.
issues_decided: Whether the delay of about one month in conducting the test identification parade rendered the identification unreliable?
Whether the conviction can be sustained solely on the basis of in-court identification without corroboration from a test identification parade?
Whether the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's presence and participation in the dacoity?
holdings: A delay of one month in holding a test identification parade is not fatal if there is no allegation of irregularity or motive to manipulate, and the witness had sufficient opportunity to observe the accused during the offence.

In-court identification can be reliable and sufficient to sustain conviction even without a test identification parade, especially when the witness is credible and the identification is based on a clear view during a traumatic event.

The testimony of an eyewitness who suffered injuries during the incident and identified the accused both in court and in a test identification parade is trustworthy and sufficient to uphold the conviction.
doctrines: Test identification parade as corroboration, not substantive evidence
Substantive value of in-court identification
Principle of traumatic imprint on memory affecting witness reliability

card.dispute: The appellant, a landlord, challenged the Bar Council of India's refusal to investigate alleged misconduct by the respondent tenant, an advocate, who was accused of physical assaults and threats during a rent control proceeding.
issues_decided: Whether the acts attributed to the respondent advocate amounted to professional or other misconduct under the Advocates Act, 1961
Whether the Bar Council of India erred in refusing to initiate disciplinary proceedings based on the alleged incidents
Whether the inaction of the appellant in not promptly reporting the incidents to the Bar Council or court affected the validity of the complaint
holdings: Alleged physical assaults and threats by an advocate outside professional duties do not automatically constitute professional misconduct unless linked to legal practice or affecting professional integrity.
The Bar Council of India's decision not to proceed with disciplinary action is sustainable if the complaint lacks promptness, corroboration, or judicial notice, and is not perverse or irrational.
Failure to report incidents to judicial authorities or file timely complaints before the Bar Council weakens the credibility of the allegations and justifies non-initiation of proceedings.
doctrines: Professional misconduct under the Advocates Act requires a connection to the legal profession or its standards
Principle of proportionality in disciplinary action
Judicial deference to Bar Council's factual findings in misconduct cases

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased appellant challenged the maintainability of a Letters Patent Appeal before the Madras High Court against an order dismissing an appeal in an execution matter, in light of Section 104 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues_decided: Whether a Letters Patent Appeal lies against an order passed by a Single Judge of the High Court in an appeal under Section 104(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure?
Whether Section 104(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure bars a further appeal under the Letters Patent of the High Court?
Whether the Letters Patent of the High Court can override a statutory bar on appeal created by an Act of Parliament?
holdings: A Letters Patent Appeal does not lie against an order passed in appeal under Section 104(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure when Section 104(2) expressly bars any further appeal from such orders.
Section 104(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure prohibits second appeals from orders passed in appeals under Section 104(1), thereby rendering Letters Patent Appeals in such cases non-maintainable.
The Letters Patent of a High Court, being subordinate to parliamentary legislation, cannot override the statutory bar on appeals created by Section 104(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.
provisions: Letters Patent of the High Court of Madras, Clause 15
doctrines: Right of appeal is a creature of statute
Harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Subordination of Letters Patent to parliamentary legislation
Finality of appellate orders under statutory bar

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted for murder and related offences, challenged their convictions and sentences, arguing lack of evidence on intention and improper recording of their statements under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants Parshuram, Bishram, and Somaru Pandey had the intention to commit murder under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC?
Whether the appellants Parshuram and Bishram were guilty of attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC?
Whether the improper recording of the accused's statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. warrants setting aside the conviction?
holdings: Mere presence and indiscriminate firing without specific targeting does not establish common intention to commit murder; conviction under Section 302/149 IPC set aside.
Absence of evidence showing intention to kill or knowledge that injuries could cause death negates offence under Section 307 IPC; conviction under this section set aside.
Though the recording of statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. was unsatisfactory, no prejudice was shown, and no benefit can be granted in absence of objection at lower courts.
doctrines: Common intention under Section 34 IPC requires active participation and shared purpose.
For attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC, intention or knowledge to commit murder is essential, regardless of the result.
Improper compliance with Section 313 Cr.P.C. does not automatically vitiate trial unless prejudice is demonstrated.

card.dispute: The landlords sued for eviction of tenants on grounds of rent default, subletting, and bona fide personal need; tenants challenged the eviction, citing changed circumstances during litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the landlords had a continuing bona fide need for the premises as of the date of final judgment
Whether subsequent events during litigation (tenant's son settling abroad) nullified the landlords' need
Whether the court could consider events occurring after the filing of the suit while deciding eviction on grounds of personal need
holdings: The bona fide need of a landlord must exist at the time of filing and continue until the final order; courts must assess whether such need has been wholly satisfied by subsequent events.
Mere possibility or probability that a family member may not return to India does not extinguish the landlord’s bona fide need for self-occupation.
Courts may cautiously consider subsequent factual developments that materially affect the landlord’s need, but judicial delays do not justify denying relief based solely on pendente lite changes.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(a)(b)(f)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41, Rule 27
doctrines: Bona fide requirement for self-occupation
Cautious cognizance of subsequent events
Continuing requirement doctrine in eviction cases

card.dispute: The heirs of Pohla Singh (allottees of surplus land) fought against the State of Punjab and Gurcharan Singh (son of the original landholder Dhanna Singh) over whether they could be dispossessed from land allotted to them in 1962 after a 1980 High Court judgment set aside the surplus declaration in proceedings from which they were excluded.
issues_decided: Whether the allottees could challenge a 1980 High Court judgment that set aside the surplus declaration when they were not parties to those proceedings
Whether the second writ petition filed by the allottees was maintainable under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution
Whether the Full Bench of the High Court was correct in setting aside the Single Judge’s decision that favored the allottees
holdings: A person whose rights are adversely affected by a court order in proceedings from which they were excluded can file a writ petition to seek recall of the judgment and rehearing.
The second writ petition filed by the allottees was maintainable as they were deprived of an opportunity to be heard, violating principles of natural justice.
The Full Bench erred in overturning the Single Judge’s decision; the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgments are set aside to prevent miscarriage of justice.
provisions: Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 3
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955, Section 51A
doctrines: Principle of natural justice (audi alteram partem)
Maintainability of writ petitions by affected non-parties
Inherent power of courts to review orders to prevent miscarriage of justice

card.dispute: The Pune Municipal Corporation and the State Government fought with builders over whether the State could unilaterally add conditions, like restricting additional FSI to the 'very said plot', when sanctioning amendments to the Development Control Rules.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government can make its own changes or additions to the Development Control Rules while sanctioning modifications proposed by the Planning Authority under Section 37(2) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966.
Whether the State Government is required to conduct a public hearing or follow principles of natural justice before sanctioning modifications under Section 37(2).
Whether the principle of promissory estoppel can be applied to bind a municipal corporation in granting additional Floor Space Index (FSI) benefits.
holdings: The State Government has the statutory power under Section 37(2) to sanction modifications to the Development Control Rules with changes or conditions of its own, even if not proposed by the Planning Authority.

The State Government is not required to provide a hearing or follow principles of natural justice when exercising legislative powers under Section 37(2), as no such requirement is mandated by the statute.
Promissory estoppel cannot be invoked against a statutory body to enforce a benefit that contradicts statutory provisions, as such estoppel does not apply against statutes.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 37(1)
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 37(2)
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 158
doctrines: Delegated legislation
Principles of natural justice
Promissory estoppel
Statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The government appealed against the annulment of disciplinary proceedings that led to the dismissal of a Deputy Director for possessing disproportionate assets and violating conduct rules.
issues_decided: Whether the Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal had jurisdiction to examine charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Whether the respondent committed misconduct by acquiring assets without prior intimation as required under Rule 9 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Conduct) Rules
Whether the Administrative Tribunal was justified in overturning the findings of the Disciplinary Tribunal
holdings: A disciplinary tribunal is competent to examine charges involving disproportionate assets under the Prevention of Corruption Act, as such conduct constitutes grave misconduct under service rules.
Failure to provide prior intimation before acquiring immovable property violates Rule 9 of the Conduct Rules and amounts to misconduct under the disciplinary framework.
An administrative tribunal cannot act as a court of appeal; it may not re-evaluate evidence or overturn factual findings of a disciplinary tribunal if they are based on legally permissible material.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(e) and Section 13(2)
Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964, Rule 9
Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Conduct and Appeal) Rules, 1991, Rule 9(IX)
Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, Rule 3(1) as amended by G.O.Ms. No. 514 dated 15.10.1994
doctrines: Doctrine of judicial review limited to procedural fairness, not re-appreciation of evidence
Principle that disciplinary tribunals have competence over service misconduct, including corruption-related charges
Rule of finality of findings of fact by quasi-judicial bodies when supported by evidence

card.dispute: A minor, Prithvi, and the State of Rajasthan challenged the acquittal of four accused persons by the Rajasthan High Court in a murder case involving the deaths of three family members.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the eyewitness testimony of the minor Prithvi due to alleged inconsistencies and investigative delays
Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the evidence of other prosecution witnesses on technical grounds
Whether the motive for the crime was sufficiently established
Whether the case warranted the death penalty for the ringleader
holdings: The High Court's reasons for disbelieving the child eyewitness Prithvi were perverse; his testimony, consistent and credible, could not be rejected merely due to investigative shortcomings or lack of mathematical precision in injury count.
Defective investigation or delay in recording statements does not automatically vitiate reliable eyewitness testimony, especially when the witness is credible and the story rings true.
The motive—resentment over property inheritance and prior threats—was strongly supported by evidence and could not be ignored as the High Court did.
While the ringleader deserved life imprisonment for the planned triple murder, the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare' category warranting the death penalty.
doctrines: Perverse reasoning in appellate appreciation of evidence
Doctrine of 'rarest of rare' in death penalty jurisprudence
Credibility of child eyewitnesses in criminal trials
Principle that defective investigation does not nullify reliable prosecution evidence

card.dispute: The appellants sought to amend their plaint to include a prayer for declaration of title over a property in a pending suit for injunction and possession, which the trial and appellate courts rejected on grounds of delay and limitation; the respondents resisted the amendment claiming it was barred by time and created a vested right in their favour.
issues_decided: Whether a belated application for amendment of plaint to include a declaration of title is maintainable when the original suit was for injunction and possession?
Whether the amendment seeking a declaratory relief is barred by limitation under Entry 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
Whether courts below erred in rejecting the amendment without considering the arguable nature of the limitation issue and the existing averments on title in the plaint?
holdings: An amendment to include a declaration of title is permissible if the factual basis for title is already in the plaint, even if sought after long delay, provided it does not cause serious prejudice.

The limitation period for a declaration of title depends on the nature of the right; if arguable that Entries 64 or 65 (12-year limitation) apply instead of Entry 58 (3-year limitation), the amendment should not be rejected outright.
Courts must exercise discretion in allowing amendments in the interest of justice; a disputed limitation plea should be decided at trial, not used to reject amendment at threshold.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings to prevent multiplicity of litigation
Discretionary power of court to allow amendments despite delay if justice so requires
Plea of limitation must be decided on merits if arguable, not used as a technical bar to amendment

card.dispute: The Punjab State Electricity Board appealed against a High Court order directing it to appoint Malkiat Singh, a landowner whose land was acquired, to the post of Homeopathic Physician under a rehabilitation policy.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent acquired a vested right to appointment upon being recommended under the 1994 rehabilitation policy
Whether the revised policy of May-June 1998 could be applied to deny the respondent appointment
