Whether the respondent was eligible for the post of Homeopathic Physician under the original or revised policy
Whether the High Court was justified in directing appointment on grounds of discrimination
holdings: Mere inclusion in a list of recommended candidates does not create a vested right to appointment; such rights arise only upon actual appointment.
The Board had the authority to revise its rehabilitation policy and apply it prospectively; no vested right was violated.
The respondent was ineligible for the Class-II post of Homeopathic Physician as it was created after the original policy and he did not meet revised eligibility criteria.
No discrimination occurred, as the Board acted bona fide and the respondent failed to meet eligibility conditions under the revised policy.
doctrines: No vested right arises from mere recommendation in recruitment processes
State may revise administrative policies unless legally bound by statutory rules
Principle of non-arbitrariness in public employment decisions
Rehabilitation schemes are concessions, not enforceable rights

card.dispute: The landlords sought possession of two rented premises for demolition and reconstruction, and later refused to re-let the rebuilt premises to the original tenants at the old rent, leading to a dispute over the tenants' right to re-entry and rent revision.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant has a right to re-enter the premises after reconstruction if the landlord fails to re-let it as per undertaking?
Whether the revision of rent is permissible after reconstruction under the A.P. Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960?
What is the applicable limitation period for a tenant's application for re-possession after reconstruction?
holdings: A tenant has a right to re-enter the premises upon completion of reconstruction if the landlord had given an undertaking to that effect, enforceable even if not recorded in the order.

Rent can be revised after reconstruction under Section 5(1) of the Act, as reconstruction amounts to 'alteration or improvement', but the revision must follow the formula in the proviso and be decided by the Rent Controller.

A tenant's application for re-possession is not an execution petition and is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, allowing three years from the date the right accrues, not Rule 23's six-month limit.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 12(1)(b)
Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, Section 5(1)
doctrines: One-time fixation of fair rent with exception for improvements
Enforceability of landlord's undertaking as condition precedent
Distinction between execution petition and enforcement of statutory right

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the right of a transferee pendente lite (respondent No. 4) to file an application to set aside an ex parte decree passed against the original defendants in a suit over immovable property.
issues_decided: Whether a transferee pendente lite, not brought on record, can file an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the CPC to set aside an ex parte decree passed against the transferor-defendant.
Whether such a transferee has locus standi to seek relief under Order 9 Rule 13 despite not being a formal party to the suit.
holdings: A transferee pendente lite, though not formally brought on record, is a person claiming under the defendant and can file an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the CPC to set aside an ex parte decree, by virtue of Section 146 of the CPC.

The term 'he' in Order 9 Rule 13 includes a person who has stepped into the shoes of the defendant, and Section 146 allows such a representative-in-interest to maintain proceedings as if they were the original party.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 9 Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 16
doctrines: Lis pendens
Representative-in-interest under Section 146 CPC
Liberal interpretation of procedural provisions to advance justice
Locus standi of a transferee pendente lite

card.dispute: Sachchey Lal Tiwari and Bachchey Lal Tiwari were tried for murder; the former challenged his life sentence, while the state appealed the acquittal of the latter.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of Sachchey Lal Tiwari under Section 302 IPC, read with Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, was sustainable
Whether the High Court was justified in acquitting Bachchey Lal Tiwari based on the reliability of prosecution witnesses
holdings: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC does not apply if the killing involved premeditation, undue advantage, or cruel conduct; the evidence showed the act was not part of a sudden fight in the heat of passion.

An appellate court may interfere with an acquittal only if the judgment is unreasonable or ignores compelling evidence; the High Court's view on witness reliability was a possible view and thus not interfered with.
doctrines: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC (sudden fight exception)
Presumption of innocence in appeals against acquittal
Standard of 'two reasonable views' in criminal appeals

card.dispute: The landlord, Ranjeet Singh, fought to evict tenant Ravi Prakash from shop premises on grounds of bona fide personal requirement and dilapidated condition, which the High Court reversed after the Appellate Court had allowed eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution in setting aside the Appellate Court's eviction order?
Whether the Appellate Court's findings on the landlord's bona fide need and the shop's dilapidated condition were sustainable?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by re-appreciating evidence and correcting inferential errors, which is impermissible under Articles 226 and 227 when a patent error is not evident.

The Appellate Court's findings that the landlord required the premises bona fide for his business and that the shop was dilapidated and needed reconstruction were validly based on evidence and local commissioner reports.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a) and (b)
doctrines: Limits on High Court's certiorari jurisdiction under Article 226
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 not to be used as an appellate function
Re-appreciation of evidence not permissible in writ jurisdiction if two views are possible

card.dispute: The descendants of original tribal tenants challenged the appellants' possession of land, claiming it was fraudulently acquired after a surrender and settlement in 1938, leading to a dispute over restoration under the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Officer could exercise power under Section 71A of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 after a lapse of 40 years to restore land based on alleged fraud?
Whether the surrender and settlement of tenancy in 1938 violated any provisions of the Act?
Whether the phrase 'at any time' in Section 71A excludes the application of limitation principles?
holdings: The power under Section 71A of the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, though not bound by the Limitation Act, must be exercised within a reasonable time; a 40-year delay is unreasonable even in cases of alleged fraud.

The 1938 surrender and settlement did not violate any applicable provisions of the Act, as Section 46, requiring prior sanction for transfer, came into force only in 1948 and had no retrospective effect.

The phrase 'at any time' in Section 71A grants flexibility but does not allow indefinite delay; it must be interpreted contextually to mean within a reasonable time depending on facts, especially to protect third-party rights.
doctrines: Reasonable time doctrine for statutory powers
Prospective operation of statutes
Socio-economic justice in tenancy laws

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the admissibility of certified copies of a sale deed and gift deed used by the respondent to prove title over a property, after having not objected to their admission during trial.
issues_decided: Whether the lower appellate court erred in rejecting the admissibility of certified copies of registered documents (Ex.P1 and Ex.P2) due to lack of primary evidence?
Whether an objection to the mode of proof of a document, as opposed to its substantive admissibility, can be raised for the first time in the second appeal?
holdings: Certified copies of registered documents over 30 years old are admissible under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, and the trial court rightly relied on them.
An objection regarding the mode of proof of a document, if not raised at the trial stage when the document is marked as an exhibit, is waived and cannot be raised for the first time in appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XIII Rule 3
doctrines: Waiver of procedural objections
Admissibility of secondary evidence under Section 90 of the Evidence Act
Distinction between admissibility of a document and mode of proof

card.dispute: The dispute was between a mosque management committee (plaintiff) and an individual (defendant) over title and possession of property containing a mosque and graveyard, where the plaintiff claimed title via an agreement or alternatively as de facto mutawalli.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff was entitled to declaration of title and possession based on an agreement dated 13.2.1973?
Whether the plaintiff could succeed on the basis of being a mutawalli under Section 3(f) of the Wakf Act, 1954, despite lack of pleading and evidence?
Whether the High Court could base its decision on a substantial question of law not framed under Section 100 of the CPC and without notice to parties?
holdings: A plaintiff in a suit for declaration of title and possession must succeed on the strength of its own title, not on the weakness of the defendant's case.
A finding that a party is a mutawalli under the Wakf Act, 1954 requires specific pleading and evidence, which were absent here.
The High Court erred in deciding a substantial question of law not framed under Section 100 CPC without giving parties notice, rendering the judgment infirm.
doctrines: Decision on strength of one's own case, not on weakness of opponent's
Necessity of pleading and proof for legal claims
Compliance with Section 100 CPC in second appeals

card.dispute: The appellant contested the maintainability of a petition under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure after having filed an appeal against an ex parte decree that was dismissed as time-barred.
issues_decided: Whether a petition under Order IX Rule 13 CPC is maintainable when an appeal against the ex parte decree has been dismissed on the ground of limitation?
Whether the explanation to Order IX Rule 13 CPC applies even if the appeal was dismissed for default or due to rejection of condonation of delay?
holdings: A petition under Order IX Rule 13 CPC is not maintainable if an appeal against the ex parte decree has been disposed of on any ground, including dismissal on limitation, and not withdrawn.

The explanation to Order IX Rule 13 CPC bars such a petition even when the appeal was dismissed for default or due to rejection of a condonation application, as it constitutes a disposal of the appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Doctrine of merger
Explanation to Order IX Rule 13 CPC as a bar to successive remedies
Finality of disposal of appeal on any ground

card.dispute: The vendors appealed against the decree of specific performance granted to the purchaser in a land sale agreement, arguing breach of payment terms and lack of readiness to perform.
issues_decided: Whether time was of the essence for the payment of Rs.75,000 by 30.9.1981 under the sale agreement
Whether the purchaser failed to prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform his obligations under the contract
holdings: Time was not of the essence for payment of Rs.75,000 by 30.9.1981, as there was no express stipulation or intention to that effect, and the vendors had extended the completion date to 31.12.1981.
The purchaser was continuously ready and willing to perform his obligations, as evidenced by his conduct, attempts to pay, and absence of abandonment of the contract.
doctrines: Time is not presumed to be of the essence in contracts for sale of immovable property
Burden of proving that time is of the essence lies on the party alleging it
Test of continuous readiness and willingness in specific performance suits

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction under Section 306 read with Section 34 IPC for abetment of suicide of the deceased, alleging dowry harassment, while the prosecution argued that sustained dowry demands led to the suicide.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC read with Section 34 IPC due to dowry-related harassment
Whether the evidence of dowry demand 'soon before death' was sufficiently established
Whether the absence of complaints by the deceased to friends or relatives about harassment negates the charge of abetment
holdings: To convict under Section 306 IPC, there must be clear evidence of abetment, including instigation or intentional aid in committing suicide, and a close temporal link between dowry demand and suicide.
Evidence of dowry demand by family members, even without direct disclosure by the victim to friends, can be reliable and sufficient to uphold conviction if supported by credible witnesses.

Courts must carefully assess whether the alleged cruelty was severe enough to drive an ordinary person in similar circumstances to commit suicide, and not merely based on hypersensitivity to domestic discord.
doctrines: Proximity rule in abetment of suicide
Principle of collective liability under Section 34 IPC
Requirement of corroborative evidence in dowry death and abetment cases

card.dispute: The landlord's heirs sought eviction of a tenant for bona fide business need, but the High Court dismissed the suit after the landlord's death during appeal, prompting the heirs to challenge that decision in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the bona fide requirement of a landlord for eviction must exist until the final decree, or only at the time of filing the suit.
Whether the death of a landlord during the pendency of an eviction appeal renders the suit non-maintainable.
Whether the High Court could dismiss the eviction suit on grounds not based on the amended pleadings tried by the lower courts.
holdings: The bona fide need of the landlord must be assessed only on the date of filing the eviction suit, not at later stages of litigation.
The death of a landlord during appeal does not extinguish the cause of action; the heirs can continue the eviction proceedings.
The High Court erred in dismissing the suit based on the original landlord's death when the case was tried on amended pleadings asserting the heirs' own bona fide need.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)
doctrines: Crucial date doctrine for eviction based on bona fide need
Survival of cause of action after death of a party
Binding effect of amended pleadings on adjudication

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh and the heirs of Raja Lakshman Singh fought over whether the Financial Commissioner could declare additional land as surplus under the Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, after the State had withdrawn its appeal and 15 years after the original order.
issues_decided: Whether the Financial Commissioner could exercise suo moto power under Section 20(3) of the Act after the State withdrew its appeal against the Collector's order.
Whether the Financial Commissioner’s exercise of suo moto power after a delay of 15 years was valid.
holdings: The Financial Commissioner has statutory authority under Section 20(3) to act suo moto regardless of the State’s decision to withdraw an appeal, as the power is independent of the State’s litigation stance.
The suo moto power under Section 20(3) must be exercised within a reasonable time; a 15-year delay in this case rendered the order invalid as it undermined finality.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, Section 20
doctrines: Suo moto power of revisionary authorities
Principle of finality of orders
Reasonable delay in administrative action

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision declaring a notification fixing registration fees under the Registration Act as ultra vires and ordering refund of fees paid by industrialists for mortgage registration.
issues_decided: Whether the registration fee fixed by the State Government under Section 78 of the Registration Act is a valid fee or an impermissible tax?
Whether there must be a direct quid pro quo between the fee paid by an individual and the service received by them for the levy to qualify as a fee?
Whether the notification fixing registration fees is ultra vires for lack of correlation between the fee and cost of services rendered?
holdings: A levy qualifies as a fee if there is a broad and general correlation between the total fees collected and the total expenses incurred for the service, not requiring exact proportionality for each individual payer.

The true test for determining a fee is at the aggregate level—whether the overall receipts match the overall costs of providing the service—regardless of disproportionate incidence on individual payers.

The State Government's notification fixing registration fees under Section 78 is valid as long as the total revenue from registration does not substantially exceed the administrative costs, even if no separate fund is maintained.
doctrines: Doctrine of fee versus tax
Doctrine of quid pro quo in fiscal levies
Aggregate correlation test for validity of fees

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Mast Ram, who was convicted by the trial court for the murder of Uttam Chand.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disbelieving the eyewitness testimony of PW-1 and PW-3 due to their relationship with the deceased and alleged bias?
Whether the failure to send recovered pellets for ballistic examination undermines the prosecution's case?
Whether the absence of injuries on accompanying witnesses casts doubt on their presence at the scene?
Whether the High Court erred in discarding the testimony of independent witness PW-4?
holdings: The mere fact that witnesses are relatives of the deceased does not render their testimony unreliable; such testimony must be scrutinized carefully but can be accepted if credible and consistent.
It is not mandatory to send recovered pellets for ballistic examination to establish the cause of death; the presence of gunshot injuries corroborates the prosecution's version.
The absence of injuries on accompanying witnesses does not disprove their presence at the scene, especially when the accused specifically targeted the deceased.
The High Court committed an error in ignoring the consistent and credible testimony of the independent eyewitness PW-4, which supported the prosecution's case.
doctrines: Principle of appreciation of witness testimony
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Natural human behavior in reaction to threat
Corroboration of ocular and medical evidence

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan and the complainant challenged the High Court's acquittal of Bhanwar Singh and Dharma Ram, who were convicted by the trial court for the murder of Arjun Singh and other charges.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court's acquittal of the respondents was perverse or unjustified?
Whether the prosecution's evidence, particularly the testimony of PW1, was sufficient to sustain the conviction despite contradictions and omissions?
Whether the defence version of accidental firing was probable and reasonable enough to create doubt in the prosecution's case?
holdings: The High Court was justified in doubting the prosecution's case due to material contradictions, omissions, and lack of corroboration, and its acquittal cannot be termed perverse.
The sole testimony of PW1 was insufficient to sustain conviction as it was inconsistent with other evidence and raised serious doubts about reliability.
The defence version of accidental firing was probable, supported by medical and site evidence, and where two views are possible, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Perversity test in appellate review of acquittals
Reliability of sole eyewitness testimony
Reasonable possibility of defence version

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh challenged the High Court's dismissal of its revision petition against the acquittal of a truck owner from confiscation of his vehicle for illegal transport of forest produce.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could exercise its powers under Section 482 CrPC or Article 227 of the Constitution despite finality of the appellate order under Section 59(3) of the Indian Forest Act, as amended.
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to examine the applicability of the statutory presumption of State ownership under Section 69 of the Indian Forest Act.
holdings: Statutory finality under Section 59(3) of the Indian Forest Act does not bar the High Court from exercising its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The High Court must examine substantial questions of law, including the applicability of the presumption under Section 69 of the Indian Forest Act, even if revision is not maintainable.
doctrines: Finality of statutory orders does not oust constitutional jurisdiction
Inherent powers under Article 227 are not barred by statutory exclusivity
Statutory presumption of State ownership of forest produce

card.dispute: The State of Orissa challenged the High Court's non-speaking order refusing leave to appeal against the acquittal of Dhaniram Luhar in a forest encroachment case.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court is required to record reasons while refusing leave to appeal under Section 378(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Whether a non-speaking order refusing leave to appeal in a criminal case involving substantial questions of law is sustainable.
holdings: The High Court must record at least brief reasons while refusing leave to appeal under Section 378(3) CrPC to demonstrate an application of judicial mind.
A non-speaking order refusing leave to appeal in a case involving public importance and substantial questions of law is unsustainable and violates principles of natural justice.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Section 378(1) and Section 378(3)
Orissa Forest Act, 1972, Section 21 and Section 22
doctrines: Principle of speaking orders
Judicial review and application of mind
Natural justice – right to reasons

card.dispute: The State and complainant challenged the High Court's acquittal of accused persons convicted for voluntarily causing hurt and house trespass with common intention, seeking restoration of the conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction in acquitting the accused by re-appreciating evidence?
Whether the prosecution proved the offence under Sections 324, 452, and 34 IPC?
Whether the accused were entitled to the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by re-evaluating evidence and overturning concurrent findings of fact without showing perversity.
The medical certificate and testimony of prosecution witnesses, including a defence witness admitting the incident, sufficiently proved the occurrence of assault and common intention.
Given the trivial nature of the dispute, long delay, and conduct of the parties, the accused deserved release on probation instead of imprisonment.
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Benefit of probation in minor offences

card.dispute: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against the High Court's acquittal of Devendra Singh, who was convicted by the Trial Court for the rape, murder, and destruction of evidence of a 10-year-old girl.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in discarding the testimony of PW-4, the alleged eyewitness to the murder?
Whether the circumstantial evidence, including the 'last seen' theory and discovery of the body in the accused's field, was sufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the High Court erred in appreciating the conduct of the witness as 'unnatural' for not disclosing the incident immediately?
holdings: A witness's delayed disclosure of a crime due to fear, especially when the accused is perceived as violent, cannot render the testimony inherently unreliable or 'unnatural'.
The 'last seen' theory, combined with the discovery of the victim's body in the accused's field and his initial refusal to allow access, constitutes strong circumstantial evidence of guilt.
The High Court erred in fact and law by relying on an unrecorded admission that PW-4 did not witness the crime and by incorrectly stating the witness refused cross-examination.
doctrines: Last seen doctrine
Appreciation of eyewitness testimony in sexual assault and murder cases
Principle of circumstantial evidence and reasonable doubt

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal challenged a High Court judgment that struck down parts of the West Bengal Land Reforms and Tenancy Tribunal Act, 1997, as unconstitutional, with advocates arguing the tribunal did not qualify under Article 323B for excluding judicial review.
issues_decided: Whether the West Bengal Land Reforms and Tenancy Tribunal falls within the scope of Article 323B(2)(d) of the Constitution
Whether the tribunal's creation and exclusion of civil court jurisdiction violate the basic structure of the Constitution
holdings: A tribunal constituted under Article 323B(2)(d) need not exclusively deal with agrarian reform laws; it suffices that it handles matters related to land reforms as defined under the entry in List II, including tenancy and land rights.

The phrase 'or in any other way' in Article 323B(2)(d) is broad enough to include various forms of land reform legislation, and such tribunals can validly exclude civil court jurisdiction, subject to Supreme Court's power under Article 136.
provisions: West Bengal Land Reforms and Tenancy Tribunal Act, 1997, Section 9
doctrines: Basic structure doctrine
Doctrine of constitutional interpretation (substance over form)
Doctrine of exclusion of jurisdiction by validly constituted tribunals

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal imposed cesses on coal, tea, and brick earth, and the affected parties challenged the constitutional validity of these levies, arguing that Parliament had occupied the legislative field, thereby excluding state power.
issues_decided: Whether the State of West Bengal has legislative competence to levy cess on coal-bearing land, tea plantations, and brick earth under Entries 52, 54, and 97 of List I and Entries 23, 49, 50, and 66 of List II of the Seventh Schedule
Whether Parliamentary legislation (Mines and Minerals Act, 1957 and Tea Act, 1953) has occupied the field of mineral and tea taxation, thereby denuding the State of its power to levy taxes or cesses
Whether the impugned cesses are ultra vires due to lack of clarity in identifying the liable party and the taxable unit, especially concerning underground mining rights and surface ownership
Whether the levy of cess on tea estates, including processing units and standing crops, is valid under Entry 49 of List II given the definition of 'land' and 'immovable property'
holdings: The State lacks legislative competence to levy cess on minerals including coal, as Parliament has occupied the field through the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, supported by Entries 52 and 54 of List I and residuary power under Entry 97.

The Tea Act, 1953, enacted under Entries 10 and 14 of List I and Article 253, fully occupies the field of tea regulation and taxation, thereby excluding State power to impose cess on tea plantations or related activities.

Cesses on mineral-bearing lands are unconstitutional because the statutes fail to distinguish between surface and subsurface rights and do not specify the liable party, making the levy arbitrary and ultra vires.

No cess can be levied on tea estates under the Bengal Cess Act, 1880, on structures, factories, or standing crops, as 'land' under Entry 49 of List II must be taxed as a unit and cannot include processing units or agricultural produce.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I, Entries 52, 54, 97
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entries 23, 49, 50, 66
Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, Sections 2, 9, 9A, 13, 18, 25
doctrines: Doctrine of occupied field
Doctrine of pith and substance
Federalism and legislative supremacy of Parliament
Principle of legislative competence
Ultra vires doctrine

card.dispute: The Tamil Nadu Kalyana Mandapam Association challenged the constitutional validity of service tax imposed on mandap-keepers and outdoor caterers under the Finance Act, 1994, arguing it infringed state taxing powers and did not constitute a 'service'.
issues_decided: Whether the levy of service tax on mandap-keepers and outdoor caterers is constitutionally valid under the residuary powers of Parliament?
Whether the activity of mandap-keepers amounts to 'service' under the Finance Act, 1994?
Whether the service tax on such services infringes the State List Entry 62 (tax on luxuries)?
holdings: Parliament has the constitutional authority under Entry 97 of List I to impose service tax on mandap-keepers and caterers as a valid exercise of residuary legislative power.

The activities of mandap-keepers, including providing premises and ancillary services, constitute 'taxable service' under the Finance Act, 1994, as the service element is dominant over any transfer of goods.
The service tax does not violate the State's power to tax luxuries under Entry 62 of the State List, as incidental overlap does not invalidate a law enacted under valid legislative competence.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, Entry 97 (Union List)
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 62 (State List)
doctrines: Doctrine of Pith and Substance
Doctrine of Incidental Encroachment
Residuary powers under Entry 97 of List I
Judicial deference to legislative discretion in taxation matters

card.dispute: Suman Verma and another candidate disputed the appointment to the post of Extra Departmental Branch Post Master, with the rival claimant challenging Verma's appointment on grounds of eligibility and merit.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent No. 6 was eligible for the post despite the mutation entry for her agricultural land being recorded after the last date of application submission?
Whether the selection based on higher marks in Matriculation was valid when both candidates met the minimum educational qualification?
Whether the continued service of the appellant for nearly eight years should prevent setting aside her allegedly illegal appointment?
holdings: A candidate is eligible if she owns agricultural land before the last date of application, even if mutation entry occurs later, as mutation does not confer title.
When educational qualifications are equal, the candidate with higher marks in the qualifying examination must be preferred, as per the Executive Order emphasizing merit.
Long continuation in service does not protect an illegal appointment if the aggrieved party promptly challenged it through proper legal channels.
provisions: Executive Order dated May 10, 1991, issued by the Director General of Posts, New Delhi
doctrines: Rekha Chaturvedi doctrine: eligibility must be determined as of the last date for application submission
Mutation entry does not create or extinguish title to land
Principle of merit in public appointments where minimum eligibility is met

card.dispute: The dispute arose between Tirupati Balaji Developers and the State of Bihar over the High Court's non-compliance with Supreme Court directions regarding urban development and public interest litigation, leading to contentious remarks by the High Court against the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was obligated to comply with the Supreme Court's directions issued under Article 136 of the Constitution.
Whether the High Court's observations criticizing the Supreme Court's orders were permissible and appropriate.
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the High Court, as a subordinate forum in the appellate hierarchy, must comply with directions issued by the Supreme Court under Article 136 to maintain judicial discipline and hierarchy.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court's observations derogatory of the Supreme Court were uncalled for, disparaging, and inconsistent with the dignity of the judiciary, and must be expunged from the record.
doctrines: Hierarchy of courts and appellate jurisdiction
Judicial discipline and comity between courts
Principle of self-restraint in Supreme Court's exercise of special leave jurisdiction

card.dispute: The State of West Bengal fought with Kesoram Industries Ltd. and others over the constitutional validity of cesses levied on coal-bearing land, tea estates, and brick earth under state legislation.
issues_decided: Whether the State of West Bengal had legislative competence to levy cesses on coal-bearing land, tea plantations, and brick earth under Entries 23, 49, 50, and 66 of List II of the Seventh Schedule?
Whether the Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992, validly cured the legislative incompetence of the state laws struck down in earlier judgments?
Whether the classification of land into coal-bearing, mineral-bearing, and other land for differential cess rates violated the principle of equality under Article 14?
holdings: States have no independent legislative power to levy cesses on minerals, including coal, as the field is occupied by Union legislation under Entries 52 and 54 of List I; however, such state cesses are validated if adopted by Parliament through a valid central law.

The Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992, constitutionally validated both past collections and future enforcement of cess liabilities under state laws by incorporating them into Union legislation with retrospective effect.

The classification of land based on productivity and resource yield for differential cess imposition is reasonable and satisfies Article 14, as it is grounded in intelligible differentia and serves a legitimate public purpose.
provisions: Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List I (Entries 52, 54, 97)
Constitution of India, Seventh Schedule, List II (Entries 23, 49, 50, 66)
Cess and Other Taxes on Minerals (Validation) Act, 1992
West Bengal Rural Employment and Production Act, 1976
doctrines: Doctrine of legislative competence
Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of colourable legislation
Doctrine of classification under Article 14
Doctrine of validation by retrospective legislation
Doctrine of incorporation by reference

card.dispute: The dispute was between sugarcane growers' unions and sugar mills over whether state governments could legally fix a sugarcane price higher than the minimum price set by the central government.
issues_decided: Whether a state government has the competence to fix a sugarcane price higher than the statutory minimum price fixed by the Central Government under the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966.
Whether the procedure adopted by state governments to ensure payment of the state-advised price to sugarcane growers is valid.
Whether the High Courts erred in quashing state-advised prices without examining the respective state sugarcane legislation.
holdings: State governments have the power to fix a sugarcane price higher than the central minimum if empowered by valid state legislation.
The validity of the state-advised price depends on the existence of statutory authority under state laws to regulate sugarcane purchase and supply.
High Courts must examine the relevant state legislation before invalidating state-advised prices; reliance solely on the central control order is insufficient.
provisions: Bihar Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1981
Punjab Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1953
Andhra Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1961
doctrines: Federalism in legislative competence
Doctrine of pith and substance
Principle of statutory interpretation

card.dispute: The appellants (Thiagarajan & Ors) fought against the respondents (Sri Venugopalaswamy B. Koil & Ors) over title, possession, and injunction in respect of certain suit properties, following conflicting decisions by lower courts.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in admitting a new legal plea in the second appeal without satisfying the requirement of a 'substantial question of law' under Section 100 CPC
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by reappreciating evidence and making fresh factual findings in a second appeal
Whether the findings of the first appellate court based on evidence could be overturned by the High Court in a second appeal
Whether the High Court properly considered the finality of a prior decision in a land reference proceeding (Exhibit A1) binding on the parties
holdings: A second appeal under Section 100 CPC is maintainable only if a substantial question of law is involved, and the High Court must record reasons for admitting such a question.
The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or make a roving enquiry into facts in a second appeal, as it is not the final court of fact.
Findings of fact by the first appellate court, if supported by evidence, cannot be overturned merely because another view is possible.
A final decision in a prior proceeding binding on the parties (e.g., under Section 30 of the Land Acquisition Act) must be respected and cannot be re-examined in a second appeal.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 100(1) and Section 100(5)
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Limited scope of second appeal
Finality of findings by the court of fact
Binding effect of prior adjudication (res judicata in rem)

card.dispute: The Union of India and others appealed against the High Court's decision that the Lt. Governor of Delhi failed to apply his mind while dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, in land acquisition for a religious festival.
issues_decided: Whether the appropriate Government must independently apply its mind before dispensing with the inquiry under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, even if urgency exists under Section 17(1) or unforeseen emergency under Section 17(2)?
Whether a composite order under Section 17(1) and Section 17(4) automatically dispenses with the Section 5A inquiry without a separate application of mind?
Whether the Lt. Governor had sufficient material before him to justify dispensing with the Section 5A inquiry?
holdings: The appropriate Government must independently apply its mind to justify dispensing with the Section 5A inquiry, even if urgency or emergency exists under Section 17(1) or (2); such dispensation is not automatic.
A composite order under Section 17(1) and Section 17(4) does not eliminate the need for a separate application of mind regarding the dispensation of the Section 5A inquiry.
The Lt. Governor did not have adequate material before him and failed to apply his mind to the relevant facts, rendering the decision to bypass Section 5A inquiry invalid.
doctrines: Doctrine of reasoned decision-making
Doctrine of application of mind
Principle of audi alteram partem
Doctrine of strict interpretation of provisions depriving property rights

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide requirement, and the tenant sought to produce additional documents in appeal to challenge the genuineness of that requirement.
issues_decided: Whether the first appellate court erred in allowing the tenant to produce additional evidence under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the appellate court's order permitting additional evidence?
holdings: An appellate court may allow additional evidence if it is necessary for a just decision and was not available despite due diligence.

Documents showing post-trial negotiations, revised construction plans, and fundraising efforts are material to assess bona fide requirement and can be admitted in appeal if they emerged after trial or were outside the tenant’s knowledge.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, Section 13
doctrines: Bona fide requirement
Additional evidence in appeal
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115

card.dispute: The heirs of Aanaimuthu Thevar (purchaser) challenged the dismissal of their suit for declaration of title to a house, which was dismissed by the High Court on the ground of res judicata arising from a prior suit between the predecessor-in-title (Muthuswami Naidu) and the respondents (his wife and children).
issues_decided: Whether the prior suit between Muthuswami Naidu and his wife operated as res judicata in the subsequent suit by the purchaser from Muthuswami?
Whether the issue of title to the suit property was directly and substantially in issue in the former suit?
Whether the doctrine of constructive res judicata under Explanation IV to Section 11 applies to the present case?
holdings: A subsequent suit by a purchaser from a party to a former suit is barred by res judicata if the predecessor had a title or interest and litigated under the same title.
The issue of ownership and title was directly and substantially in issue in the former suit, as the relief of permanent injunction was based on the plaintiff's claim of ownership.
Constructive res judicata applies where a party could and ought to have raised a title-based defence or claim in the former suit but failed to do so, binding their successors-in-title.
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Privity of title

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision to award compensation at the market value of Rs. 47,224 per bigha for land acquired in Shahbad Mohamadpur, arguing that contiguity alone should not determine compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in awarding compensation based on the market value of lands in contiguous villages acquired for the same purpose?
Whether similarity in nature and quality of land, rather than mere contiguity, justifies uniform compensation across different villages?
holdings: Compensation for acquired land may be based on comparable market values of similar lands in different villages if the nature and quality of the land are substantially alike, even if villages are not contiguous.
Uniform compensation is justified when lands are identical and acquired for the same purpose, and discrimination between landowners should be avoided.
doctrines: Principle of non-discrimination in land acquisition compensation
Use of comparable market value for determining compensation

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed whether an interim injunction order automatically revives upon restoration of a suit dismissed for default.
issues_decided: Whether an order of injunction automatically revives upon restoration of a suit dismissed for default.
Whether the power to grant injunction is an ancillary or supplemental proceeding under the Code of Civil Procedure.
holdings: An interim injunction does not automatically revive upon restoration of a suit unless the court expressly orders its revival.
Orders of injunction are supplemental proceedings, not ancillary, and thus require express judicial revival after restoration of the suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 39, Rules 1 and 2
doctrines: Ancillary jurisdiction doctrine
Supplemental proceedings doctrine
Strict construction of jurisdictional statutes

card.dispute: The legal heirs of deceased defendants sought substitution in pending appeals after purchasing the suit property, but the High Court rejected their application, leading to a dispute over their right to be impleaded.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, as transferees pendente lite, could be substituted as parties in pending second appeals under Order XXII Rule 10 of the CPC
Whether the High Court erred in treating the application as one for addition of a party rather than substitution
Whether the interest of the appellants in the suit property entitled them to be impleaded to protect their rights
holdings: A transferee pendente lite is a representative-in-interest and may be substituted under Order XXII Rule 10 if they have a substantial interest in the suit property.
The High Court wrongly treated the application as for addition of a party; since the original parties had no further interest, substitution was warranted.
The presence of the appellants was necessary to completely decide the appeals, as their rights would be vitally affected by the outcome.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
doctrines: Lis pendens
Representative-in-interest
Necessary and proper parties in litigation

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder and related offences, challenged their convictions and sentences, arguing the applicability of private defence and seeking lesser punishment.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence under the IPC
Whether the High Court's application of common intention (Section 34 IPC) and abetment (Section 109 IPC) was consistent and justified
Whether the conviction for murder (Section 302 IPC) should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 IPC)
holdings: The right of private defence was not available to the appellants as the force used was disproportionate and not in response to a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt.
The High Court's inconsistent application of Sections 34 and 149 IPC without explanation vitiated the conviction, warranting reconsideration.
Given the peculiar facts, the appellants may have acted without intention to cause death; hence, conviction under Section 302 IPC was reduced to Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 IPC.
doctrines: Right of private defence of body and property
Proportionality in self-defence
Common intention under Section 34 IPC
Reasonable apprehension of danger

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent no.1 (Kamal Abrol) competed for an LPG dealership in Kangra district, with the dispute centering on whether Abrol satisfied the eligibility criterion of being a 'resident of Kangra district'.
issues_decided: Whether the term 'resident of Kangra district' in the eligibility criteria for an LPG dealership requires de facto (actual) residence or includes de jure (legal/constructive) residence.
Whether the High Court erred in holding that a casual or ancestral connection to Kangra district suffices for fulfilling the residence criterion.
holdings: The term 'resident' in the eligibility criteria must be interpreted as de facto residence, i.e., actual and physical habitation in Kangra district with an intention to stay for a considerable time, not mere legal or ancestral connection.
The dealership requires full-time personal operation, so the dealer must actually reside in the district; a temporary or casual presence does not meet the mandatory eligibility condition.
doctrines: De facto vs de jure residence
Contextual interpretation of statutory terms
Intention of the legislature in eligibility conditions

card.dispute: The tenant, Atma Ram, fought against eviction by his landlord, Shakuntala Rani, over alleged default in rent payment from 1992 to 1995, claiming he had made valid deposits under the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's deposit of rent under the Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, 1934, instead of under Section 27 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1951, constituted a valid payment of rent?
Whether the tenant could claim protection under beneficial provisions of the Rent Act without strictly complying with its procedural requirements?
Whether the High Court was justified in exercising revisional jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution to set aside concurrent findings of lower courts?
holdings: A deposit of rent under a different statute (Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act) does not satisfy the requirements of the Delhi Rent Control Act, and thus does not absolve the tenant of default.
Tenants must strictly comply with the procedural conditions in rent control laws to claim benefits; equitable considerations do not override statutory mandates.
The High Court rightly exercised revisional jurisdiction where lower courts committed an error of law by ignoring statutory procedures, even if their findings were concurrent.
doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory procedure
No equitable override of rent control procedures
Revisional jurisdiction for error of law

card.dispute: Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. challenged the reinstatement of an employee, M. Chandrasekhar Reddy, who was dismissed for misconduct involving theft, fraud, and forgery related to mortgaged property documents.
issues_decided: Whether the Labour Court had unlimited jurisdiction under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 to modify the punishment of dismissal?
Whether the misconduct of the employee was so serious as to justify loss of employer's confidence and warrant dismissal?
Whether the Labour Court could reduce the punishment based on extenuating circumstances like no prior misconduct and participation in cultural activities?
holdings: The Labour Court does not have unlimited or unfettered jurisdiction under Section 11-A; its power must be exercised judicially and reasonably, not arbitrarily.
Once an employer's bona fide loss of confidence is established, especially in cases involving breach of trust, the court should not interfere with the punishment of dismissal.
Extenuating factors such as no prior misconduct or employee participation in cultural activities cannot outweigh proven acts of theft, fraud, and forgery justifying dismissal.
doctrines: Doctrine of proportionality in punishment
Doctrine of employer's loss of confidence
Judicial restraint in interference with disciplinary actions
Reasoned decision-making in quasi-judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The Commissioner of Income Tax and D.P. Sandu Bros. Chembur (P) Ltd disputed whether the Rs. 35 lakhs received by the assessee on surrender of tenancy rights was taxable as capital gains or as income from other sources.
issues_decided: Whether the amount received on surrender of tenancy rights is taxable as capital gains under Section 45 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 when the cost of acquisition cannot be determined?
Whether, in the absence of a determinable cost of acquisition, the receipt can be taxed under the residuary head 'income from other sources' under Section 56?
holdings: A tenancy right is a capital asset and its surrender constitutes a 'transfer' under Section 45, making the consideration a capital receipt, but only if the cost of acquisition can be determined for computing capital gains under Section 48.

If capital gains cannot be computed due to indeterminable cost of acquisition, the receipt cannot be taxed under Section 45, and nor can it be taxed under Section 56 as 'income from other sources' because the heads of income are mutually exclusive.
doctrines: Mutual exclusivity of heads of income
Principle from Commissioner of Income Tax v. Srinivasa Setty
Residuary charging clause cannot override specific exclusions

card.dispute: The Competent Authority and NHAI challenged the High Court's decision to award additional compensation to landowners whose land was compulsorily acquired for a national highway project, while the landowners challenged the validity of the acquisition itself.
issues_decided: Whether the initial notification under Section 3A of the National Highways Act, 1956, was validly issued and compliant with statutory requirements.
Whether the possession taken by the authorities of the acquired land was in accordance with the law.
What relief, if any, should be granted to the landowners when the acquisition process is flawed but the project has been completed.
holdings: An invalid notification under Section 3A of the National Highways Act renders all subsequent steps in the acquisition process, including vesting and possession, legally void.
Possession of the land was taken in violation of statutory requirements under Section 3E and 3H of the Act, as compensation was not properly deposited and required procedures were not followed.

Though the acquisition notification was invalid, quashing it would not serve public interest due to project completion; instead, compensation must be determined as of the date of possession (19th February 2003) to fairly compensate the landowners.
doctrines: Foundation fallacy doctrine: if the initial step in a statutory process is invalid, all subsequent actions based on it are also invalid.
Doctrine of equitable compensation: when quashing an acquisition would cause public hardship, courts may award enhanced compensation instead.
Doctrine of strict compliance with procedural safeguards in land acquisition.

card.dispute: The Calcutta Municipal Corporation imposed a mutation fee for changing ownership details in its assessment records, and the developers challenged whether this charge was a 'fee' or a 'tax', and if it violated Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the mutation charge imposed by the Calcutta Municipal Corporation is in the nature of a fee or a tax.
Whether the mutation charge is arbitrary, discriminatory, and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
holdings: The mutation charge is a tax, not a fee, because it lacks quid pro quo and is primarily intended to augment municipal revenue rather than provide a specific service to the payer.
The mutation charge is arbitrary and violative of Article 14 as it is levied on an ad valorem basis without reasonable classification, resulting in unequal burden on similarly situated persons.
doctrines: Quid pro quo test for distinguishing fee from tax
Doctrine of arbitrariness under Article 14
Principle of reasonable classification

card.dispute: The parties disputed whether the limitation period for executing a partition decree begins from the date the decree is passed or from the date it is engrossed on stamp paper.
issues_decided: When does the limitation period under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 begin for execution of a partition decree?
Whether a partition decree becomes enforceable only after it is engrossed on stamp paper?
holdings: The limitation period for executing a partition decree begins from the date the decree is passed, not from the date it is engrossed on stamp paper.
Engrossment of a decree on stamp paper relates back to the date of the decree, and non-engrossment cannot suspend limitation as it is within a party's control.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Section 2(14), Section 2(15), Section 3, Article 45, Section 33, Section 35, Section 40(b), Section 42(1) and (2)
doctrines: Relation back of validatory acts
No one can take advantage of their own wrong
Fiscal purpose of stamp laws

card.dispute: A father and his daughter disputed ownership of a house purchased in the daughter's name when she was a minor, with the father claiming it was a benami transaction.
issues_decided: Whether the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 applies retrospectively to pending suits filed before its enforcement.
Whether the presumption under Section 3(2) of the Act that property purchased in the name of an unmarried daughter is for her benefit can be rebutted.
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts in second appeal.
holdings: Section 4 of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 does not have retrospective operation and cannot affect pending suits where the benami defence was already raised before the Act came into force.
The presumption under Section 3(2) of the Act that property purchased in the name of an unmarried daughter is for her benefit is rebuttable by evidence showing the real owner's interest.

The High Court cannot interfere with concurrent findings of fact in second appeal unless they are perverse, based on no evidence, or ignore material evidence; doing so on mere arguments is impermissible.
doctrines: Doctrine of Retrospectivity
Rebuttable Presumption
Concurrent Findings of Fact
Perverse Findings Doctrine

card.dispute: ONGC Ltd. challenged the enhanced compensation awarded by the Reference Court and upheld by the High Court for land acquired in Gujarat, arguing that the award was based on insufficient evidence and legal error.
issues_decided: Whether the Reference Court erred in enhancing compensation solely based on witness testimony while ignoring registered sale deeds?
Whether the High Court misdirected itself in law by upholding the Reference Court's award without proper application of Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act?
Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the compensation award under Article 136 in light of the principles of equity and judicial discretion?
holdings: The Reference Court committed a serious error by relying solely on witness testimony and ignoring registered sale deeds; it was obligated to consider such sales and provide cogent reasons for departing from the Collector's award.

The High Court misdirected itself by failing to apply the settled principles under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, including comparison with similar sales and adjustment for positive and negative factors affecting market value.

The Supreme Court declined to interfere under Article 136, holding that the small financial stakes and prior deposit of compensation made it inappropriate to exercise discretionary jurisdiction, despite legal errors.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination based on comparable sales and adjustments for locational and physical factors
Doctrine of judicial discretion under Article 136
Doctrine of social justice and equitable relief under Article 142
Requirement of reasoned decision-making in land acquisition compensation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant for non-payment of rent and for making structural alterations to the rented room, which the tenant contested.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant's structural alterations to the rented premises amounted to material and permanent impairment of the building's value or utility under Section 11(4)(ii) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
Whether the tenant's failure to pay rent entitled the landlord to eviction under Section 11(2) of the Act, despite a substantial security deposit held by the landlord
holdings: Structural changes like lowering the floor, cutting rafters, and erecting pillars do not justify eviction unless the landlord proves material and permanent impairment of the building's value or utility, which was not established here.

A tenant's default in rent payment may not warrant eviction if a substantial refundable security deposit is held by the landlord, and the tenant deposits arrears within a specified time to avail relief under Section 11(2)(c).
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(2)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(4)(ii)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 8(1)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 8(2)
doctrines: Material and permanent impairment test for structural alterations
Relief against forfeiture for rent arrears under statutory discretion
Judicial discretion in eviction cases based on proportionality and equity

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought to have the suit transferred to the Gurgaon Court with proceedings continuing from the stage reached in the Delhi Court, while the defendants opposed this, arguing the suit must restart afresh due to lack of jurisdiction in Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the suit, after being returned for want of jurisdiction, can be continued from the stage at which it was left in the court lacking jurisdiction?
Whether the provisions of Section 24, Section 25, or Rule 15 of Order 18 CPC apply to a case where the original court lacked jurisdiction?
Whether the inherent powers under Section 151 CPC or Article 142 of the Constitution can be invoked to allow continuation of proceedings in the proper court?
holdings: A suit filed after the plaint is returned for want of jurisdiction is deemed to be instituted only when presented in the proper court and is not a continuation of the earlier proceedings.
Sections 24 and 25 CPC and Rule 15 of Order 18 do not apply where the original court lacked jurisdiction, as this is not a case of transfer but of invalid institution.
The inherent powers under Section 151 CPC and Article 142 of the Constitution cannot override the statutory bar on continuation of proceedings when the original court lacked jurisdiction.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7, Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 18, Rule 15
doctrines: Lack of jurisdiction vitiates proceedings ab initio
Doctrine of constructive res judicata does not apply to jurisdictional defects
Principle of continuity of proceedings not applicable where court lacked inherent jurisdiction

card.dispute: The dispute was between original grantees of government land (belonging to Scheduled Castes/Tribes) and third-party purchasers over whether transfers of such land in violation of a 15-year alienation restriction were void under Karnataka law.
issues_decided: Whether the authorities could impose a condition prohibiting alienation of granted land for 15 years under the Mysore Land Revenue (Amendment Rules), 1960

Whether transfers of such land in violation of the terms of grant are null and void under Section 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands), Act, 1978
Whether third-party transferees can challenge the validity of conditions imposed between the government and the original grantees
holdings: The government, as paramount title-holder, can impose conditions like non-alienation for 15 years when granting land at concessional rates or free of cost, even if not explicitly stated in Rule 43-J.
Any transfer of granted land in contravention of the terms of grant is null and void under Section 4 of Act 2 of 1979, regardless of when the transfer occurred.
Third-party purchasers cannot challenge the validity of conditions imposed between the government and the original grantee, especially when aware of such conditions at the time of purchase.
provisions: Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978, Section 4
Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978, Section 5
doctrines: Restrictive covenant in land grants
Paramount title of the State
Voidness of transactions contrary to statutory restrictions
Doctrine of privity of contract

card.dispute: Harwindra Kumar and others, employees of Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam, challenged the denial of enhanced superannuation age from 58 to 60 years granted to state government servants.
issues_decided: Whether the amendment in Rule 56(a) of Uttar Pradesh Fundamental Rules enhancing superannuation age to 60 years applies to employees of Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam.
Whether the Nigam can override the application of state government service rules through administrative directions without amending its own regulations.
holdings: The enhanced superannuation age of 60 years applies to Jal Nigam employees as Regulation 31 makes state government service rules applicable unless specifically amended.
The Nigam cannot bypass Regulation 31 by administrative decisions; only a formal amendment to Regulation 31 with state approval can alter service conditions.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 3
Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 31
Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 37
Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 15(1)
Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 89
Uttar Pradesh Water Supply & Sewerage Act, 1975, Section 97
Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam Regulations, Regulation 31
doctrines: Statutory corporation must act within powers conferred by enabling statute
Administrative action cannot override statutory regulations
Doctrine of implied continuity of service conditions unless lawfully altered

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, being relatives of the deceased Mukhtar Singh Marwah, fought over whether a will allegedly executed by him was forged, and whether criminal prosecution for forgery could proceed without prior court sanction under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Cr.P.C. bars private prosecution for forgery of a document that was forged before being produced in court?
Whether the bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) applies when the alleged forgery occurred prior to the document's production in judicial proceedings?
Which interpretation of Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. correctly balances procedural fairness and access to justice in forgery cases?
holdings: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) Cr.P.C. applies only when an offence is committed in relation to a document while it is in custodia legis, i.e., after it has been produced or given in evidence in court.
The bar on cognizance without court complaint under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) does not apply to forgeries committed prior to the document’s production in court.
Courts must interpret procedural statutes like the Cr.P.C. to advance legislative purpose, not strictly as penal laws, especially to ensure victims of forgery can seek justice.
doctrines: Custodia legis
Strict construction of penal statutes
Harmonious construction
Suppression of mischief and advancement of object

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent claimed ownership of the same property through rival lineages, leading to a title suit where the High Court granted relief to the respondent, overturning lower court decisions.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC, can re-appreciate evidence and reverse findings of fact without identifying a substantial question of law.
Whether the questions of law framed by the High Court were substantial and involved in the case as required by Section 100 of the CPC.
Whether the High Court's reversal of factual findings without holding them to be perverse was legally sustainable.
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence in a second appeal unless a substantial question of law is properly framed and decided.
A substantial question of law must be debatable, not settled by precedent, and must materially affect the rights of the parties.
Findings of fact by courts below cannot be overturned in second appeal unless they are perverse, i.e., based on no evidence or misreading of evidence.
The High Court failed to decide the substantial questions of law it framed, rendering its judgment legally infirm.
doctrines: Substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC
Perverse findings doctrine
Limited scope of second appeal
Re-appreciation of evidence in second appeal

card.dispute: The appellant sued for specific performance of a plot purchase agreement and possession of a residential plot in Gurgaon, but the defendants challenged the jurisdiction of the Delhi court where the suit was filed.
issues_decided: Whether the Delhi court had territorial jurisdiction to try a suit for specific performance and possession of immovable property situated in Gurgaon, Haryana.
Whether an objection to territorial jurisdiction, not raised at the earliest stage or in the written statement, can be permitted to be raised later by way of amendment.
Whether consent or waiver by parties can confer jurisdiction on a court otherwise lacking jurisdiction over immovable property situated outside its territorial limits.
holdings: A suit for specific performance of a contract and for possession of immovable property must be instituted where the property is situated, as per Section 16(c) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
Objection to territorial jurisdiction must be raised at the earliest possible opportunity and in any case before settlement of issues; delay bars the plea unless jurisdiction is entirely absent.
Consent or waiver cannot confer jurisdiction on a court lacking territorial jurisdiction over immovable property, as such jurisdiction is conferred by statute and cannot be created by agreement.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI, Rule 32
doctrines: Jurisdiction as to subject matter and territorial jurisdiction are distinct; lack of the latter can be waived if not timely raised, but subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent.
A decree passed by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity and can be challenged even in collateral proceedings.
Waiver and acquiescence cannot cure lack of jurisdiction when the court has no statutory authority to entertain the suit.

card.dispute: The H.P. State Electricity Board challenged a High Court decision upholding the right of landowners to access their property through land acquired by the government and used by the Board.
issues_decided: Whether the right of passage by way of necessity over acquired land is extinguished under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
Whether the findings of fact by the lower courts regarding the existence of a right of way can be interfered with in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC?
holdings: An easement of necessity, such as a right of passage, is not extinguished by land acquisition under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, if it could not have been compensated under Section 11.
The High Court was correct in not interfering with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts on the existence of a right of way, as no substantial question of law was involved.
doctrines: Easement of necessity
Doctrine of extinguishment of encumbrances upon land acquisition
Concurrent findings of fact not interfered with in second appeal
Principle of binding precedent by larger bench

card.dispute: The Shankaracharya of Kanchi Mutt appealed against the Madras High Court's rejection of his bail in a murder conspiracy case.
issues_decided: Whether the confessions of co-accused under Section 10 of the Evidence Act can be used to establish the petitioner's involvement in the conspiracy for bail purposes.
Whether the telephonic statement of the deceased qualifies as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act.
Whether the restrictions under Section 437(1)(i) Cr.P.C. apply to bail applications under Section 439 Cr.P.C.
holdings: Confessions of co-accused recorded after the conspiracy ended are not admissible under Section 10 of the Evidence Act to prove the petitioner's involvement.
A telephonic statement not relating to the cause or circumstances of death does not qualify as a dying declaration under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act.
Section 437(1)(i) Cr.P.C. restrictions do not categorically bar courts from granting bail under Section 439 Cr.P.C.; bail must be decided on facts and circumstances.
doctrines: Common intention in conspiracy
Admissibility of dying declarations
Prima facie case for bail
Judicial restraint in pre-trial orders

card.dispute: The appellants (owners) sued the respondents (licensees) for mandatory and prohibitory injunction to recover possession of property after the licence expired; the dispute centered on whether such a suit was maintainable or if a separate suit for possession was required.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for mandatory injunction to recover possession from a licensee after expiry of licence is maintainable without a separate suit for recovery of possession.
Whether the High Court erred in holding the suit for injunction not maintainable on the ground that possession could only be recovered through a possessory suit.
Whether the delay in filing the suit affected the right to seek mandatory injunction after the licence ended.
holdings: A suit for mandatory injunction to recover possession from a licensee after termination of licence is maintainable, especially when the licensee continues in possession without title.
The High Court erred in requiring a separate suit for possession; courts should avoid multiplicity of suits where the relief sought is effectively recovery of possession.
The question of whether time taken to file suit was reasonable is a factual issue that cannot be raised for the first time in second appeal without supporting evidence or plea in lower courts.
doctrines: Avoidance of multiplicity of suits
Plea of reasonable time must be raised at the earliest and supported by evidence
Relief can be granted on a case admitted by the defendant even if not specifically pleaded, if no prejudice is caused

card.dispute: Jagjit Singh @ Jagga appealed his conviction and death sentence for murder, arguing that the sole eyewitness identification was unreliable and insufficient to sustain the conviction.
issues_decided: Whether the testimony of a seven-year-old eyewitness, recorded days after the incident, can be relied upon to convict the accused without corroboration.
Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant was known to the eyewitness and could be identified by her.
Whether the conviction based solely on the testimony of a child witness, allegedly influenced by her father, is safe in law.
Whether the absence of motive and corroborative evidence undermines the prosecution's case.
holdings: The testimony of a seven-year-old eyewitness, recorded with delay and lacking independent corroboration, cannot be relied upon if there is no evidence she had prior knowledge of the accused.
A conviction cannot rest solely on the testimony of a child witness who likely named the accused based on suggestion by an adult, especially when no prior acquaintance is established.
Delay in recording the statement of a sole eyewitness raises suspicion of tutoring, particularly when no explanation is offered by the prosecution.
In the absence of motive, corroborative evidence, or reliable identification, the benefit of doubt must be given to the accused.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Reliability of child witness
Corroboration in cases of sole eyewitness
Test of safe conviction

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the reassessment of building tax on his shopping complex, arguing that the authorities could not rectify the original assessment order under the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975.
issues_decided: Whether the assessing authority had jurisdiction to assess the building tax based on rental value when the local authority had not yet determined the capital value under Section 6(1) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975.
Whether the subsequent rectification of the assessment under Section 15(1) of the Act amounted to an illegal reassessment or was a valid correction of a mistake apparent on the record.
holdings: The original assessment based on rental value was without jurisdiction because for newly constructed buildings, the capital value must be determined by the local authority under Section 6(1), which had not been done.
The rectification under Section 15(1) was valid as it corrected a jurisdictional error apparent on the record and did not amount to a prohibited reassessment.
doctrines: Mistake apparent on the face of the record
Functus officio
Distinction between rectification and reassessment

card.dispute: The dispute was between the children of Mottaya Poosali over the partition of properties, specifically whether certain properties were self-acquired or joint family assets, and the validity of a settlement deed and will executed by Mottaya Poosali in favor of one son.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could re-appreciate evidence and reverse concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC.
Whether the High Court could decide on the validity of a settlement deed and will without a substantial question of law being framed on those issues.
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or reverse concurrent findings of fact in a second appeal unless the findings are perverse, based on no evidence or misreading of evidence.

The High Court lacks jurisdiction to decide on the validity or genuineness of a settlement deed or will unless a substantial question of law on those issues is specifically framed at admission or later with recorded reasons.
doctrines: Perverse findings doctrine
Substantial question of law requirement under Section 100 CPC
Limited scope of second appeal

card.dispute: NGEF Ltd. and its creditors challenged the Karnataka High Court's approval of a private sale of company land to Chandra Developers, arguing the court lacked jurisdiction and the sale undermined creditor interests.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to sanction a private sale of assets of a sick company under SICA when no winding-up order had been passed.
Whether the Company Court could validly approve a sale transaction without considering the interests of creditors and adequacy of price.
Whether BIFR could delegate its power to the High Court to approve asset sales by private negotiation.
holdings: The High Court lacks jurisdiction under the Companies Act to sanction private sale of a company's assets unless a winding-up order has been made; such power rests with BIFR during the moratorium period under SICA.

A Company Court must ensure that any transaction benefits unsecured creditors and that the sale price is adequate, exercising its discretion judicially and equitably, especially in cases affecting creditor priorities.
BIFR cannot delegate its statutory powers to the High Court; the principle of 'delegatus non potest delegare' applies, and no authority can confer jurisdiction where none exists by law.
provisions: Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, Section 20(4)
doctrines: Delegatus non potest delegare
Pari passu distribution of debts
Judicial discretion in Company Court proceedings
Protection of creditor interests during insolvency

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Mangal Prasad Tamoli challenged the validity of proceedings in a mortgage redemption suit, arguing that a premature suit could not be continued even if the plaintiff agreed not to take possession before the mortgage period ended.
issues_decided: Whether a mortgage redemption suit filed before the expiry of the mortgage term is maintainable if the plaintiff agrees not to seek possession until the term ends.
Whether an interlocutory order of remand by a High Court can be challenged in appeal after final judgment.
holdings: A premature suit for redemption of a mortgage cannot be sustained merely because the plaintiff agrees not to take possession before the mortgage period expires; such a suit must be dismissed.
