Whether the landowners' application for reference was filed in time given their lack of notice of the award?
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the writ petition on grounds of alternative remedy?
holdings: The six-month period under Section 18(2) starts from the date of knowledge of the award's contents, not the date of the award, to prevent unjust deprivation of rights.
When a landowner neither receives notice under Section 12(2) nor is present at the award, the time to apply begins only upon actual or constructive knowledge of the award.
The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition on grounds of alternative remedy, as the Collector failed to serve notice and the landowners acted promptly upon learning of the award.
doctrines: Doctrine of effective notice
Principle of fair procedure under Article 14
Constructive knowledge in land acquisition
Literal vs. purposive interpretation to avoid absurdity

card.dispute: The Board of Wakf, West Bengal, challenged the Calcutta High Court's decision on the demarcation of a Wakf property and the applicability of the Wakf Act, 1995 to a family Wakf (Wakf-al-al-aulad), which was originally the subject of a suit in the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the Calcutta High Court had jurisdiction to decide disputes regarding the demarcation and classification of a Wakf property?
Whether the Wakf Act, 1995 applies to the portion of the property designated as Wakf-al-al-aulad?
holdings: All disputes relating to a Wakf or Wakf property must first be adjudicated by the Wakf Tribunal under the Wakf Act, 1995, and civil courts or high courts cannot entertain such matters directly under Article 226 of the Constitution.

The Wakf Tribunal has wide jurisdiction under Sections 83 and 84 of the Wakf Act, 1995 to decide any dispute relating to Wakf property, even in the absence of a prior order under the Act, and parties must approach it first before any higher court.
doctrines: Special forum doctrine: when a special law creates a special tribunal, ordinary civil courts are barred from jurisdiction.
Doctrine of primary jurisdiction: disputes under a specialized statute must first be addressed by the designated tribunal.

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Kallu (appellants) challenged a High Court decision that set aside an appellate court's restoration of an ex-parte decree in a property suit, claiming they were unaware of the proceedings due to a prior compromise.
issues_decided: Whether the application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC to set aside an ex-parte decree was barred by limitation when filed after 30 days from the decree but within 30 days of knowledge of the decree.
Whether a separate application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act was required to condone delay in filing the Order IX Rule 13 application.
Whether the appellate court had jurisdiction to decide the application on merits without a formal condonation plea.
holdings: Limitation for filing an application under Order IX Rule 13 CPC begins from the date of knowledge of the decree when the party had no notice due to a compromise, not from the date of the decree.
A separate application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is not mandatory if the delay is adequately explained in the body of the Order IX Rule 13 application itself.
Courts may decide applications under Order IX Rule 13 on merits if the delay is justified by bona fide reasons, and procedural technicalities must not defeat justice.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Justice over procedural technicality
Bona fide belief as valid explanation for delay
Merits-based adjudication of Order IX Rule 13 applications

card.dispute: Chirra Shivraj appealed against his conviction under Section 304 Part II IPC for allegedly causing the death of his sister-in-law by setting her on fire, challenging the reliance on a dying declaration and the registration of a second FIR after her death.
issues_decided: Whether a dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction?
Whether the registration of a second FIR after the death of the victim in the same incident renders the investigation defective?
holdings: A dying declaration, if found to be voluntary, truthful, and made in a conscious state without external influence, can be the sole basis for conviction even without corroboration.

The registration of a second FIR to record the death resulting from injuries in the same incident does not vitiate the investigation, especially when no prejudice is caused and no fresh investigation is conducted.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Dying declaration as sole basis for conviction
FIR as first information and subsequent information under CrPC
Principle of prejudice in criminal procedure

card.dispute: Darshan Singh, accused of shooting during a family dispute over agricultural land, fought against his conviction by the High Court which had overturned his acquittal by the Sessions Court.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on its assessment of witness credibility and rejection of the defence of private defence?
Whether the appellant's act of firing in the course of a physical confrontation was covered by the right of private defence under the IPC?
Whether the absence of recovered pellets from non-fatal injuries negates the possibility of firearm use, and whether the High Court erred in rejecting the trial court's inference on this point?
holdings: The High Court cannot reverse a trial court's acquittal unless the acquittal is utterly perverse and no other plausible view can be taken from the evidence.

The right of private defence is available if there is a reasonable apprehension of death or grievous harm, and the force used need not be precisely proportionate but must not be wholly disproportionate.

The absence of recovered pellets does not necessarily mean a firearm was not used; the trial court’s factual inference that injuries were not caused by a firearm was plausible and should not have been overturned without cogent reasoning.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 96 to 106 (Right of Private Defence)
doctrines: Presumption of innocence strengthened by acquittal
Right of private defence based on reasonable apprehension
Appellate court's limited scope of review in acquittal cases

card.dispute: The appellant claimed reconveyance of land sold to the respondent, alleging the sale was conditional, while the respondent argued it was an absolute sale.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deed dated 24th April 1986 was an absolute or conditional sale deed.
Whether unattested interlineations in the sale deed could be given legal effect.
Whether the appellant was entitled to specific performance for reconveyance of the property.
holdings: A sale deed with unattested interlineations made after execution cannot be treated as a conditional sale deed binding on the purchaser.
Interlineations, erasures, or alterations in a registered document must be attested and noted at the foot of the document to be valid under Karnataka Registration Rules.
The appellant failed to prove a conditional sale; the additions in the deed were made unilaterally and are void, not binding the respondent.
doctrines: Principle of attestation and execution as distinct acts
Severability of contracts
Probative value of documents with suspicious alterations

card.dispute: Dinesh Chandra Pandey, a civil judge, challenged the dismissal of his departmental appeal over charges of possessing disproportionate assets, claiming denial of natural justice and perversity in the inquiry.
issues_decided: Whether the refusal to allow the appellant to engage a lawyer during the departmental inquiry violated principles of natural justice?
Whether the findings of the inquiry officer and the High Court on the appellant's disproportionate assets were perverse or based on no evidence?
holdings: The refusal to allow legal representation did not violate natural justice because the appellant was legally trained and could competently defend himself, and he had not sought assistance from a colleague despite parity with the presenting officer.

The findings on disproportionate assets were not perverse; the appellant failed to produce evidence of agricultural income or witnesses, and his inconsistent statements and property returns undermined his defence.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Proportionate assets and burden of proof in departmental inquiries
Perversity in factual findings
Clean hands doctrine

card.dispute: Hawkers and vendors fought with municipal authorities over their right to carry on street vending in Delhi and the regulation of hawking spaces.
issues_decided: Whether street vendors have a fundamental right to carry on hawking under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
How to balance the fundamental rights of hawkers with the public's right to unimpeded movement under Article 19(1)(d)
Whether a judicially monitored scheme can regulate hawking in the absence of a law
holdings: Street vending is a livelihood activity protected under Article 19(1)(g), and hawkers have a fundamental right to carry on such business.
The rights of hawkers must be harmonized with the public’s right to free movement under Article 19(1)(d) through reasonable restrictions under law.
Regulation of hawking cannot permanently rely on court-monitored schemes; the appropriate government must enact a law to define vendors' rights.
provisions: New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, Section 226
doctrines: Harmonious construction of fundamental rights
Judicial direction to enact legislation
Right to livelihood as part of right to life

card.dispute: The appellants sued for declaration and injunction to enforce their 4/9th share in land based on a 1972 compromise, but the respondents argued the suit was barred by limitation due to an 18-year delay.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaration and injunction was barred by limitation under Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963
When the cause of action accrued for filing a declaratory suit under Article 58
holdings: The cause of action for a declaratory suit under Article 58 arises only when the right is infringed or there is a clear and unequivocal threat to infringe that right, not merely from an adverse entry in revenue records.

The suit filed in 1990 was within time as the cause of action accrued only when the plaintiffs came to know of the wrong entries and the defendants refused to correct them, shortly before filing the suit.
doctrines: Accrual of cause of action
Infringement or threat to right as basis for cause of action
Declaratory relief limitation

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the quantum of compensation, solatium, and interest awarded for land acquired under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, while the government contested the award of solatium and interest.
issues_decided: Whether solatium and interest can be awarded under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
Whether landowners are entitled to enhanced compensation beyond Rs. 200 per marla
holdings: Solatium and interest are permissible under the 1952 Act in cases of inordinate delay in appointing an arbitrator, based on equitable principles and precedent.
Landowners are entitled to enhanced compensation of Rs. 350 per marla where similar claims for the same acquisition and purpose were previously awarded that amount, ensuring equal treatment.
provisions: Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
doctrines: Equitable compensation
Principle of equal treatment in acquisition cases
Interest on delayed compensation

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant on grounds of bona fide personal need, which the tenant opposed, claiming the need was a pretext to increase rent.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in allowing the second appeal on a substantial question of law regarding the landlord's bona fide need?
Whether the finding of the First Appellate Court that the landlord's need was not bona fide was perverse?
Whether partial eviction could serve the ends of justice in balancing the interests of both parties?
holdings: A second appeal under Section 100 CPC is maintainable only on a substantial question of law, but courts may re-appreciate evidence if findings are perverse or based on no evidence.
The First Appellate Court's finding that the landlord's need was not bona fide was perverse, given the unhygienic and inadequate conditions of his current business place.
The landlord is entitled to partial possession of the premises—half the area—to meet his bona fide need, while allowing the tenant to retain the other half.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, Section 12(1)(f)
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Perverse finding
Bona fide requirement of landlord
Partial eviction for balancing equities

card.dispute: The appellants (Gopal Singh and others) challenged the High Court's reversal of their acquittal in a double murder case, where the prosecution relied on dying declarations and eyewitness testimony.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal based on the prosecution's evidence.
Whether the oral dying declarations made by the deceased were reliable given their medical condition.
Whether the conduct of the solitary eyewitness was credible and consistent with normal human behaviour.
Whether the prosecution's failure to produce evidence about the timing and transmission of the first information report (FIR) undermined the case.
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal as the trial court's findings were based on a plausible evaluation of evidence, which must be respected unless there are compelling reasons to overturn.
The oral dying declarations were unreliable because medical evidence indicated the deceased would have lost consciousness within 10–15 minutes of injury, making statements two hours later improbable.
The eyewitness's account was not credible as his failure to inform family members immediately after the incident contradicted normal human behaviour.
The prosecution's suppression of the initial report and lack of proof regarding the FIR's timing cast serious doubt on the authenticity of the official version of events.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Requirement of reliable and credible evidence for reversing acquittal
Dying declaration must be scrutinized for medical and factual feasibility
Courts must consider normal human conduct in evaluating witness testimony

card.dispute: The Haryana State Electricity Board sought to recover unpaid electricity dues from a previous owner by demanding payment from a new purchaser of the premises, who refused to pay.
issues_decided: Whether a new purchaser of premises can be held liable for electricity arrears of the previous owner in the absence of a statutory or contractual provision?
Whether the electricity supplier can enforce recovery of arrears from a transferee without privity of contract?
Whether the terms and conditions of supply, lacking an express clause for recovery from transferees, permit such recovery?
holdings: Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge on the property, and a transferee cannot be held liable for the previous owner's dues in the absence of statutory or contractual authorization.
An electricity supplier may condition a new or reconnection of supply on clearance of prior arrears only if such condition is provided in statutory rules or valid terms and conditions of supply.
In the absence of an enabling provision in the terms or rules at the relevant time, the Board could not lawfully demand arrears from the new purchaser.
provisions: Haryana Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1970
doctrines: Privity of contract
Statutory terms and conditions of supply
No charge on property for electricity dues
Reasonableness of conditions for service provision

card.dispute: The appellant, Kalabharati Advertising, challenged the removal of its hoarding by the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, done pursuant to orders from the Bombay High Court in a writ petition that was later withdrawn by the respondents.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to allow the Municipal Corporation to recall its earlier permission and pass a fresh order without hearing the affected parties?
Whether the withdrawal of the writ petition by the respondents rendered the interim and consequential orders ineffective?
Whether the Municipal Corporation's action in removing the hoarding violated principles of natural justice and amounted to legal malice?
holdings: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to enable the Municipal Corporation to recall its prior order and issue a fresh one without statutory authority for review and without affording a hearing to the affected parties.
The withdrawal of the writ petition with liberty to file a similar petition in the future nullified all interim and consequential orders, as the foundation of the relief was voluntarily abandoned.
The Corporation’s order recalling its earlier permission without recording reasons and without a hearing violated natural justice and demonstrated legal malice, rendering the order a nullity.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Legal malice
Nullity of orders without jurisdiction
Withdrawal of litigation extinguishing ancillary reliefs

card.dispute: Bajaj Hindustan Ltd. challenged the High Court's decision to quash a central government notification de-licensing the sugar industry, which affected its and other companies' investments in new sugar mills.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the Central Government's Press Note and Notification de-licensing the sugar industry under Section 29B of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951.
Whether de-licensing under Section 29B is limited only to small industries or extends to large industries as well.
Whether judicial review is applicable to executive policy decisions in economic and fiscal matters.
holdings: The Central Government validly issued the Press Note and Notification under Section 29B of the Act, and the High Court erred in quashing them.
Section 29B allows de-licensing of industries based on the stage of development, which includes large industries, not just small ones.
Courts must exercise judicial restraint in economic policy matters and should not interfere unless there is clear illegality, unconstitutionality, or arbitrariness.
doctrines: Judicial restraint in economic policy
De-licensing as a valid executive policy
Non-application of legitimate expectation doctrine to policy changes
Wide discretion to government in social and economic experimentation

card.dispute: The landlord sought possession of a leased flat from the tenant, claiming the lease had expired and tenancy was determined, while the tenant contested the validity of termination and denied admitting it.
issues_decided: Whether the tenant made a clear and unequivocal admission of the landlord's case in its pleadings to justify a judgment on admission under Order 12 Rule 6 of the CPC.
Whether the lower courts were justified in passing a judgment of ejectment based on alleged admissions in the tenant's written statement.
holdings: A judgment under Order 12 Rule 6 CPC can only be passed if there is a clear, unambiguous, and unequivocal admission of the plaintiff's case by the defendant in the pleadings.
The tenant did not make a clear admission of tenancy termination in its written statement or reply, and thus the lower courts erred in granting ejectment on admission.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 12 Rule 6
doctrines: Judgment on admission
Clear and unequivocal admission
Pleading estoppel

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Manohar Lal and Ugrasen contested the allotment of acquired land, with Ugrasen seeking allotment over Manohar Lal, whose allotment was initially made on the Chief Minister's direction.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government, as a revisional authority, could directly entertain applications and bypass the statutory authority (GDA).
Whether an allotment made in violation of court directions or land policy is enforceable.
Whether a party approaching the court under Article 226 must make full and true disclosure of material facts.
holdings: The State Government cannot assume the role of a subordinate statutory authority; doing so constitutes a colourable exercise of power and is arbitrary.
An allotment made in a commercial area contrary to the Land Policy, especially on the direction of a non-statutory authority like the Chief Minister, is illegal and unenforceable.

A party seeking relief under Article 226 must approach the court with clean hands; suppression of material facts, such as the commercial nature of the allotted land, amounts to abuse of the judicial process.
doctrines: Colourable exercise of power
Doctrine of clean hands
Abuse of process of court
Principle of legitimate expectation
Public interest vs. private interest in judicial discretion

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the land acquisition award on the ground that she was not served with a notice under Section 9(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, claiming violation of her rights.
issues_decided: Whether non-service of notice under Section 9(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 renders the acquisition proceedings and award invalid
Whether the irregularity in service of notice is curable and does not affect the vesting of land in the state
Whether the appellant was entitled to challenge the acquisition proceedings after a delay of ten years and after the land had vested in the state
holdings: Non-service of notice under Section 9(3) is a curable irregularity and does not invalidate the award or vesting of land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The failure to serve notice does not defeat the acquisition process as the statute provides remedies for aggrieved persons to claim compensation under Sections 18 and 30 of the Act.
The appellant’s delay of ten years in challenging the acquisition, after vesting of land in the state and her prior knowledge of the proceedings, renders her challenge inadmissible.
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation of statutory provisions
Curable irregularity in procedural compliance
Vesting of title in the state free from encumbrances upon possession
Principle of inordinate delay and laches in challenging administrative action

card.dispute: Malayalam Plantations Ltd. and the State of Kerala contested the vesting of 2588 hectares of land under the Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, with the company claiming exemption for land used for fuel and employee purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in failing to decide an application under Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC for additional evidence?
Whether the Forest Tribunal correctly exempted 2588 hectares from vesting under Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B) of the Kerala Private Forests Act, 1971?
holdings: The High Court was obligated to decide the application for additional evidence under Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC and its failure to do so was an error; the matter must be remanded for proper adjudication.

The determination of the reasonable area required for fuel in factories and for employees under Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B) of the Act is a factual question to be decided by the Forest Tribunal, not assumed in toto.
provisions: Kerala Private Forests (Vesting and Assignment) Act, 1971, Section 2(f)(1)(i)(B)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: Doctrine of procedural fairness
Principle of remand for factual determination

card.dispute: The legal representatives of a deceased partner in a partnership firm fought over the ownership and distribution of partnership assets, including land, buildings, and movables, after the firm's dissolution.
issues_decided: Whether the land, buildings, and movables used in the partnership became partnership property under the deed
Whether the automatic vesting of property in the original plaintiff after 42 years under Clause 24 overrides general partnership property rights
Whether the respondents are entitled to remove movables and claim value for structures embedded in the land
holdings: Property brought into or acquired during a partnership becomes partnership property only if there is an express or implied agreement; mere use for business does not make it partnership property.

Clause 24 of the partnership deed, which provides for automatic vesting of property in the original plaintiff after 42 years, indicates no intention to treat the land and buildings as partnership property.

Upon dissolution, the appellants are entitled to exclusive possession of the land, while respondents may remove movables and claim the value of buildings and structures after technical assessment and adjustment of dues.
doctrines: Partnership property doctrine
Doctrine of business efficacy in contract interpretation
Implied agreement for property to become partnership asset

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, claiming to be legal heirs of Chandra Deo Singh, fought over whether the respondents were his legitimate sons and entitled to inclusion in land records under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether the documents produced by the appellants to disprove the respondents' parentage were reliable and sufficient to rebut the presumption of legitimacy arising from long-term cohabitation.
Whether the findings of the statutory authorities and lower courts recording the respondents as legal heirs could be disturbed based on the appellants' documentary evidence.
What probative value should be assigned to official documents like school certificates and medical practice certificates when they lead to factual impossibilities.
holdings: Documents may be admissible under the Evidence Act but lack probative value if they lead to absurd or impossible conclusions, such as a person giving birth before being born.

A long-term live-in relationship between a man and woman gives rise to a presumption of marriage under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, and children born during such a relationship are presumed legitimate.
The burden lies on the party disputing parentage to rebut the presumption of legitimacy with unimpeachable evidence, which the appellants failed to do.
Courts must critically assess the authenticity and consistency of documents relied upon, especially when they conflict with established facts or natural possibilities.
provisions: U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 9-A(2)
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Presumption of marriage from prolonged cohabitation
Distinction between admissibility and probative value of documents
Rebuttable presumption of legitimacy of children born during cohabitation
Standard of proof in civil cases regarding parentage and age

card.dispute: Mumbai International Airport Pvt. Ltd. challenged its exclusion as a party in a suit for specific performance between Regency Convention Centre & Hotels and the Airport Authority of India over land within the airport premises.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was a necessary or proper party in the suit for specific performance between the respondent and AAI?
Whether the appellant had a semblance of title or sufficient interest in the suit property to warrant impleadment?
Whether the provisions of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 enabled the appellant to step into the shoes of AAI over non-leased land?
holdings: A party is necessary only if adjudication cannot proceed effectively without them; the appellant, having no title, interest, or relief sought against it, was neither a necessary nor proper party.
A person expecting to gain a lease upon dismissal of a suit does not have a semblance of title sufficient to justify impleadment as a proper party.
Under Section 12A of the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994, a lessee only acquires powers of AAI over demised premises; it does not extend to land not leased or subject to litigation.
provisions: Airports Authority of India Act, 1994, Section 12
Airports Authority of India Act, 1994, Section 12A
doctrines: Necessary and proper party doctrine under Order I, Rules 9 and 10 of CPC
Discretionary impleadment of parties in suits for specific performance
Statutory interpretation of delegated powers under special acts

card.dispute: Mumbai International Airport and Airport Authority of India challenged the High Court's decision favoring Golden Chariot Airport, which claimed an irrevocable licence to operate a restaurant at Mumbai Airport beyond the original term.
issues_decided: Whether the licence granted to Golden Chariot Airport was irrevocable and could be extended orally beyond its fixed term
Whether the Estate Officer acted fairly and within his authority in rejecting the claim of oral extension and refusing to summon AAI officers
Whether the contesting respondent could raise a plea of discrimination under Article 14 for not extending its licence when others' were extended
Whether Mr. K.K. Gupta had valid authority to act as Estate Officer under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
holdings: A licence granted for a fixed term cannot be rendered irrevocable by oral assurance, and written terms prevail over alleged oral extensions.
The Estate Officer acted fairly and within his powers by relying on written documents and refusing to consider unprovable oral extensions.
A plea of discrimination under Article 14 is not maintainable when the claimant has no legal right to licence renewal.
An Estate Officer appointed by designation under a valid government notification holds lawful authority to decide eviction proceedings.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 3
doctrines: Doctrine of Approbation and Reprobation
Doctrine of Election
Principles of Natural Justice
Plea of Discrimination under Article 14 (Negative Equality)

card.dispute: Landowners appealed against the denial of enhanced compensation and interest benefits under the amended Land Acquisition Act, 1894, despite not filing a formal appeal in the High Court, seeking relief through an application under Order 41, Rule 33 of the CPC.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners were entitled to the benefit of the amended Section 23(1A) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, given the timing of the acquisition proceedings?
Whether the landowners could claim additional compensation and interest under Order 41, Rule 33 of the CPC without filing a formal appeal in the High Court?
holdings: Landowners whose acquisition proceedings commenced after 30-4-1982 and award was made after that date are entitled to the benefit of Section 23(1A) as per the transitional provisions of Section 30(1) of the 1984 Amendment Act.

An appellate court can grant relief under Order 41, Rule 33 of the CPC to ensure complete justice, even if no appeal is filed, provided the law so entitles the party and no legal prohibition is violated.
provisions: Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, Section 15(b) and Section 18
doctrines: Doctrine of binding precedent (Article 141)
Principle of statutory interpretation (harmonious reading of Section 23(1A) with Section 30(1))
Doctrine of complete justice under Order 41, Rule 33 CPC

card.dispute: The appellant, Paramjeet Singh, challenged his conviction for murder and attempted murder, arguing that the trial was unfair due to non-consideration of key circumstances during his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court's failure to question the accused on certain incriminating circumstances under Section 313 Cr.P.C. vitiated the conviction
Whether the pardon granted by a village panchayat absolves the accused of criminal liability for a heinous crime
Whether the prosecution case can be sustained despite hostile witnesses when supported by other evidence
holdings: Failure to question the accused on some circumstances under Section 313 Cr.P.C. does not vitiate the conviction if it did not cause prejudice or miscarriage of justice.
A pardon by a family or panchayat in a heinous crime like murder has no legal sanctity and does not absolve the accused of criminal liability.
The prosecution case can be upheld despite hostile witnesses if the initial statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C., FIR, and medical evidence consistently point to the accused's guilt.
doctrines: Hostile witness doctrine
Panchayat pardon irrelevance in criminal prosecution
Cumulative effect of circumstantial evidence
No miscarriage of justice without prejudice

card.dispute: The tenant, Om Prakash, fought against eviction by landlord Ashwani Kumar Bassi after failing to file his application for leave to contest the eviction within the 15-day statutory period under the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949.
issues_decided: Whether the Rent Controller has the power to condone a one-day delay in filing an application for leave to contest an eviction petition under Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949?
Whether Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is applicable to proceedings before the Rent Controller under the 1949 Act?
holdings: The Rent Controller has no power to condone delay in filing an application for leave to contest under Section 13-B of the 1949 Act, as the statute does not confer such authority and the procedure is strictly time-bound.
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is not applicable to proceedings before the Rent Controller under the 1949 Act when the statute does not expressly permit condonation of delay.
provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 13-B
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, Section 18-A
Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, 1882, Section 17
doctrines: Strict construction of special statutes
Statutory authority bound by conferred powers
Exhaustive code doctrine

card.dispute: The appellant challenged water charges imposed by the respondent corporation, obtained an ex parte decree, and the respondent later sought to appeal after a delay of over four years, which the High Court condoned.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in condoning a delay of over four years in filing an appeal by the respondent corporation.
Whether the respondent corporation approached the court with clean hands while seeking condonation of delay.
holdings: The High Court erred in condoning a delay of over four years without considering the appellant's reply and based on incorrect facts, especially since the delay was misrepresented as 1067 days.

The respondent corporation did not approach the court with clean hands, as its officers were aware of the litigation but failed to appear or instruct advocates, and made false averments in the condonation application.
doctrines: Condonation of delay
Clean hands doctrine
Liberal approach to delay for State entities with justification
Judicial discretion under Section 5 of the Limitation Act

card.dispute: The Wakf Board filed eviction suits against tenants occupying Wakf properties; the tenants challenged the Wakf Tribunal's jurisdiction to hear such eviction disputes.
issues_decided: Whether the Wakf Tribunal under Section 83 of the Wakf Act, 1995 is competent to adjudicate disputes regarding eviction of tenants from Wakf property.
Whether the jurisdiction of civil courts is excluded in matters of tenant eviction from Wakf properties.
holdings: The Wakf Tribunal does not have inherent jurisdiction to decide eviction disputes unless the Act specifically requires such matters to be determined by the Tribunal.
The jurisdiction of civil courts is not excluded for eviction suits concerning Wakf property, as the Wakf Act, 1995 does not mandate the Tribunal to decide such disputes.
doctrines: Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction must be clearly and expressly provided by statute.
Special tribunals have limited jurisdiction confined to matters specifically assigned by statute.

card.dispute: The landlords (appellants) challenged the maintainability of a suit by the tenant's landlord for possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act after the tenant was forcibly dispossessed by third parties.
issues_decided: Whether a landlord can maintain a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 for immediate possession when a tenant in exclusive possession is forcibly dispossessed by a third party.
Whether the tenant is a necessary party in such a suit for possession filed by the landlord.
holdings: A landlord retains legal or constructive possession of the property even after letting it out and is entitled to file a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 against a third-party trespasser who forcibly dispossessed the tenant.
The tenant is not a necessary party to such a suit; while it is desirable to implead the tenant, non-joinder does not render the suit under Section 6 non-maintainable.
doctrines: Constructive possession
Legal possession vs. physical possession
Maintainability of possessory suits by landlords
Necessary and proper parties in possessory suits

card.dispute: Safiya Bee and Mohd. Vajahath Hussain disputed ownership and possession of a property, with Safiya claiming purchase via a 1969 sale deed and the respondent denying its validity and asserting independent possession.
issues_decided: Whether the Special Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the possession claim under the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982?
Whether the decision in an earlier writ petition operated as res judicata in the later writ petition?
Whether a coordinate bench of the High Court could overrule a prior decision of equal strength on the interpretation of Section 2(c) of the Act?
holdings: The Special Tribunal had jurisdiction to adjudicate the possession claim under Section 7-A of the Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982.
The dismissal of an earlier writ petition did not operate as res judicata on the maintainability of a subsequent writ petition challenging the same order.
A coordinate bench of the High Court cannot overrule a decision of equal strength; judicial discipline requires reference to a larger bench in case of disagreement.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 2(c)
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Section 7-A
doctrines: Res judicata
Binding nature of judicial precedent
Principle of judicial discipline and hierarchy of benches

card.dispute: The landowners challenged the compensation awarded for the acquisition of 196 acres of land for expanding a state-owned company, arguing that the land had potential for use as house sites and deserved higher compensation.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of the acquired land was correctly determined by treating it as agricultural land or should have accounted for its potential as house sites.
Whether the High Court erred in rejecting relevant sale deeds and failing to consider the purpose of acquisition in determining compensation.
Whether interest under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act includes solatium.
holdings: The market value of land must consider its potential use as house sites if supported by evidence of surrounding development and proximity to residential areas.
The purpose of acquisition and available amenities are relevant factors in assessing compensation, and reliable sale deeds indicating potential use can support higher valuation.
Interest under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act is payable on the entire compensation, including solatium, as it forms an integral part of the award.
doctrines: Market value includes potential use and advantages of land excluding benefits from the acquisition scheme.
Purpose of acquisition is a relevant factor in determining just compensation.
Interest on compensation includes statutory solatium under Section 28.

card.dispute: The dispute was between members of a co-operative housing society and the society itself over the validity of the expulsion of the members, which the High Court had set aside but the Supreme Court reinstated.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the orders of the Registrar and Financial Commissioner rejecting the expulsion of members.
Whether the delay by the Registrar in deciding the matter rendered him functus officio.
Whether the High Court applied the correct legal standard in issuing a writ of certiorari.
holdings: The High Court erred in interfering with the orders of the statutory authorities as it failed to appreciate the reasons recorded and did not find any jurisdictional error.
Delay in disposal by a statutory authority does not make it functus officio, especially when the delay was attributable to the society's failure to submit records.
A writ of certiorari under Article 226 requires a jurisdictional error or breach of natural justice, which was absent here, and the High Court failed to record any such error.
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Functus officio
Error apparent on the face of the record
Judicial review under writ jurisdiction

card.dispute: A widow fought her brother-in-law and his sons over the fraudulent transfer of her inherited property through a collusive court decree.
issues_decided: Whether the decree in Civil Suit No. 253 of 1985 was obtained by fraud?
Whether the appellant's suit was barred by limitation?
Whether the caveat proceedings under Section 148-A CPC were legally valid and could support issuance of summons?
holdings: A decree obtained through collusion, fabricated pleadings, and manipulation of an illiterate widow is a nullity and can be set aside as it amounts to fraud on the court.
The cause of action arose when the respondents interfered with the appellant’s possession, making her suit filed in 1990 within limitation.
Caveat proceedings under Section 148-A CPC do not authorize the issuance of summons or create independent proceedings; using them as such is legally invalid.
doctrines: Fraud vitiates all judicial proceedings
Decree obtained by fraud is a nullity
Courts must look into material irregularities suggesting collusion

card.dispute: The appellants, whose land was acquired in 1974, sought enhanced solatium and interest under a 1984 amendment to the Land Acquisition Act, after the original compensation award had become final.
issues_decided: Whether a final judgment in a land acquisition reference case can be reopened under Sections 151 and 152 of the CPC to grant enhanced solatium and interest under a subsequent amendment?
Whether a court can modify a final decree to incorporate benefits introduced by a later amendment to the Land Acquisition Act?
holdings: A final judgment and decree in a land acquisition case cannot be altered under Sections 151 and 152 of the CPC, as those provisions do not empower courts to revise decrees on merits after they become final.
Enhanced solatium and interest under the 1984 amendment (Act 68 of 1984) cannot be granted retrospectively in a case where the compensation award had already attained finality before the amendment.
doctrines: Functus officio
Finality of judgment
Prospective application of amendments
No perpetuation of illegality under Article 14

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the direction to pay court fee based on the market value of the property in a suit for cancellation of a sale deed executed by her attorney, arguing that court fee should be based on the value mentioned in the document.
issues_decided: Whether court fee in a suit for cancellation of a document must be computed on the market value of the property or on the value stated in the document sought to be cancelled under Section 40 of the Kerala Court-Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959.
Whether the term 'value of the property' in Section 40(1) of the Act means market value or the value for which the document was executed.
holdings: In a suit for cancellation of a document, court fee must be computed on the value stated in the document sought to be cancelled, not on the market value of the property.

The expression 'value of the property for which the document was executed' in Section 40(1) refers to the value mentioned in the document, as the legislature deliberately used 'value' instead of 'market value'.
provisions: Kerala Court-Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959, Section 40
Kerala Court-Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959, Section 7(1)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Specialia generalibus derogant

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants) and respondents (plaintiff's legal representatives) fought over whether the respondent had an easement right by implied grant over 'B' Schedule property as a pathway to access the 'A' Schedule property.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent acquired an easement right by implied grant over the 'B' Schedule property for access to the 'A' Schedule property.
Whether the courts below could base their decision on implied grant even if not specifically pleaded in the plaint.
Whether the doctrine of easement by necessity applied to the facts of the case.
holdings: An easement by implied grant can be inferred when the use of a pathway is necessary and continuous, and no alternative access is provided, especially where the common owner intended such use.
Courts may uphold a finding of implied grant even if not specifically pleaded, provided evidence was led on the issue and the parties had a fair opportunity to contest it.
Easement by necessity requires absolute necessity; since the claim was based on implied grant and not necessity, the doctrine of easement by necessity did not apply.
doctrines: Easement by implied grant
Implied grant from common ownership and prior use
Doctrine of easement by necessity

card.dispute: Sandur Manganese & Iron Ores Ltd. and others challenged the Karnataka government's decision to grant mining leases to Kalyani Steels and Jindal Vijayanagar Steels without following proper procedures under the MMDR Act and Rules.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in upholding the grant of mining leases without compliance with Rule 59(1) and Rule 60 of the Mineral Concession Rules.
Whether applications made prior to the Notification under Rule 59(1) could be entertained after the 30-day period.
Whether the Central Government's approval based on an invalid state recommendation could sustain the grant of mining leases.
Whether the matter should be remitted to the Central Government for fresh consideration.
holdings: The High Court erred in upholding the mining lease grants because the State Government failed to follow mandatory procedures under Rule 59(1) and Rule 60 of the Mineral Concession Rules.
Applications made before the Rule 59(1) Notification are premature and do not revive after the 30-day period; only applications made during or after that period are valid.
Central Government approval under Section 5(1) of the MMDR Act is invalid if based on a legally flawed state recommendation, as it merely endorses, not independently evaluates, the proposal.
The matter should not be remitted to the Central Government because it lacks independent adjudicative capacity and would be influenced by prior invalid decisions.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 5(1)
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 11(2), 11(4)
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation to avoid rendering provisions otiose
Doctrine of legality in administrative action
Post-decisional hearing impermissibility
Conditional approval under delegated legislation

card.dispute: The tenant and her legal representatives fought against the landlord's suit for eviction over alleged breach of tenancy terms, damage to property, and unauthorized occupation of a common area.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition under Article 226 is maintainable in a private landlord-tenant dispute?
Whether the High Court was justified in entertaining a writ petition against a private landlord?
Whether property disputes between private parties can be adjudicated through writ jurisdiction?
holdings: A writ petition under Article 226 is not maintainable in a purely private dispute between landlord and tenant absent any statutory violation or public function.
The High Court erred in entertaining the writ petition as the respondent was a private individual not discharging public duty.
Courts should not entertain property disputes between private parties via writ jurisdiction; civil suits are the appropriate remedy.
doctrines: Writ jurisdiction is extraordinary and not for adjudicating private rights
Doctrine of separation between civil and writ remedies in property disputes
Principle that private individuals are not amenable to writs unless discharging public function

card.dispute: Skyline Education Institute (Pvt) Ltd fought against S.L. Vaswani and another over the use of the name 'Skyline' in educational services and alleged passing off.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to a temporary injunction to restrain the respondents from using the name 'Skyline' in their educational institute.
Whether the High Court was justified in partially upholding the injunction restricting the respondents from starting similar courses and requiring a disclaimer in advertisements.
holdings: The appellant failed to establish a prima facie case for injunction as 'Skyline' is a generic term and the appellant's own use of the name lacked transparency regarding recognition by statutory bodies.
The High Court's partial injunction was erroneous; since it found no justification for restricting course offerings or requiring disclaimers, the injunction should have been vacated entirely.
doctrines: Passing off
Discretion in granting temporary injunctions
Generic terms in trademark law

card.dispute: The appellants, convicted of murder and related offences, challenged their conviction by arguing they acted in private defence during a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to the right of private defence of body and property under the IPC
Whether the appellants were the aggressors in the incident
What is the evidentiary value of the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on one of the appellants
holdings: The right of private defence is not available where there is no reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt or danger, especially against an unarmed person not committing any overt act.
The appellants were the aggressors and could not claim self-defence as the right does not extend to offensive or retaliatory violence.
Non-explanation of injuries by the prosecution does not discredit its case unless the injuries are serious and sustained during the occurrence.
doctrines: Right of private defence
Burden of proof in self-defence cases
Proportionality in use of force
Aggressor cannot claim self-defence

card.dispute: The State of Haryana challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the recovery of deficit stamp duty from Manoj Kumar, who had registered a sale deed at a value lower than the notified circle rate.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the concurrent findings of fact under Article 227 of the Constitution in a stamp duty recovery matter?
Whether the sale consideration in a registered deed can be presumed genuine solely because it stems from a court decree?
Whether the Collector's assessment of undervaluation under Section 47-A of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 was justified?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by reappreciating evidence and overturning concurrent factual findings without showing any perversity or illegality.
A sale price reflected in a court-decreed sale deed cannot be presumed genuine if it is significantly below the notified circle rate and suggests stamp duty evasion.

The Collector's determination under Section 47-A is valid if based on objective satisfaction that the declared value does not truly reflect the transaction value, with circle rates being a relevant but not conclusive factor.
doctrines: Limited scope of interference under Article 227
Objective satisfaction in stamp valuation
Circle rate as a factor, not conclusive proof, of market value

card.dispute: The appellant, a coparcener, sued to declare certain sale deeds void against the coparcenary and sought joint possession and injunction, leading to a dispute over the correct court fee payable for such reliefs.
issues_decided: Whether the suit, seeking declaration that sale deeds were void qua coparcenary and consequential reliefs of possession and injunction, required ad valorem court fee on the sale consideration.
Whether a non-executant coparcener seeking declaration against sale deeds and consequential relief must pay court fee under Section 7(iv)(c) of the Court Fees Act, 1870.
holdings: A non-executant coparcener seeking a declaration that sale deeds are not binding on the coparcenary, along with consequential relief of possession and injunction, must pay ad valorem court fee under Section 7(iv)(c) of the Court Fees Act, 1870.

The court fee is not based on the sale consideration but must be computed according to the value of the property as determined under Section 7(v) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, with a minimum fee prescribed.
provisions: Court Fees Act, 1870, Second Schedule, Entry 17(iii)
doctrines: Distinction between cancellation of deed by executant and declaration of invalidity by non-executant
Principle of valuation of relief for court fee in declaratory suits with consequential reliefs

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the acquisition of her land under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, claiming it was not within urban limits when the Act commenced, while the respondents argued the land became part of the urban area later and was validly acquired.
issues_decided: Whether the land could be acquired under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, if it was included in the urban area after the Act's commencement date.
Whether the judgment in Atia Mohammadi Begum v. State of U.P., which held that only the master plan existing at the time of the Act’s commencement is relevant, remains good law.
Whether delay and laches bar the appellant's revision petition filed decades after acquisition and possession.
holdings: Land that becomes part of an urban area after the Act's commencement on 17.2.1976 can still be subject to the Act if it is later classified as vacant urban land under a validly prepared master plan.

The judgment in Atia Mohammadi Begum is no longer good law; it has been overruled by N. Audikesava Reddy, which holds that subsequent master plans can determine urban status for the purposes of the Act.
A long delay in challenging land acquisition, especially when possession was taken decades earlier and no appeal was filed, constitutes laches and bars judicial relief.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 2(h)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 6(1)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 34
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999
doctrines: Doctrine of Laches
Prospective Overruling
Finality of Acquisition Proceedings
Subsequent Master Plan Validity

card.dispute: Sunder Singh appealed against his conviction and death sentence for the murder of five family members and attempted murder of a sixth by setting them on fire.
issues_decided: Whether the death sentence awarded to Sunder Singh was justified under the 'rarest of the rare' doctrine.
Whether there were any mitigating circumstances that warranted commutation of the death sentence.
holdings: The death sentence was justified as the crime was premeditated, extremely brutal, and fell within the 'rarest of the rare' category due to its cruelty and scale.
There were no mitigating circumstances sufficient to commute the sentence, as the accused acted with cold-blooded intent and showed no remorse, despite prolonged absconding.
doctrines: Rarest of the rare doctrine
Focus on both crime and criminal in death penalty sentencing
Aggravating and mitigating circumstances in capital punishment

card.dispute: The appellant's mother sought to eject tenant Ramesh Chand Girdhar and recover arrears of rent, leading to a dispute over whether the tenant could be evicted for non-payment of rent given his claim to occupancy rights.
issues_decided: Whether the proceedings initiated by the appellant's mother were under Section 77(3) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887 or under the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975
Whether the tenant was liable to be ejected under Section 9(1)(ii) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975 for non-payment of rent
holdings: The application for ejectment and recovery of rent was governed by Section 14-A read with Section 10(2) of the Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975, not by Section 77(3) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887.
The tenant had sufficient cause for non-payment of rent as he was legally pursuing a claim to occupancy rights, and thus could not be ejected under Section 9(1)(ii) of the 1975 Act.
provisions: Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975, Section 9(1)(ii)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975, Section 10(2)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1975, Section 14-A
doctrines: Summary adjudication under revenue law
Burden of proving sufficient cause for non-payment of rent lies on the tenant
Protection of tenant rights during legal disputes over occupancy

card.dispute: The Tamil Nadu Housing Board appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside the land acquisition notification for the Ellis Nagar Development Scheme, which was challenged by landowners 16 years after the award was passed.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court ought to have entertained the writ petition filed by the landowners after a delay of 16 years without any explanation?
Whether inordinate delay and laches should disentitle the petitioners from relief under Article 226 of the Constitution in land acquisition cases?
holdings: The High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition after 16 years of unexplained delay, especially when the petitioners had participated in the acquisition proceedings and were aware of the award.
Courts should be cautious in exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226 where there is inordinate delay in challenging land acquisition, as it may prejudice public interest and settled rights.
doctrines: Delay and laches in writ petitions
Discretionary nature of writ jurisdiction
Public interest in land acquisition for development projects
Non-entertainment of stale claims in land acquisition matters

card.dispute: The landowners and the Union of India disputed the market value of acquired land in Karol Bagh, Delhi, with the owners seeking higher compensation and the government challenging the High Court's enhancement.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of acquired land can be determined solely based on government circle rates?
What is the just and reasonable market value of the land in question as of the notification date?
Whether the High Court was justified in enhancing compensation based on commercial potential and locality development?
holdings: Circle rates issued by the government cannot solely determine market value but may be used as corroborative evidence when supported by other material.
The High Court's determination of Rs.3,000 per sq. yd. as compensation is just and reasonable, considering the land's commercial potential and development in the area.
Evidence of nearby commercial activity, actual use of the land for a hospital, and post-acquisition developments support a higher valuation than awarded by the Collector.
doctrines: Principle of just equivalent compensation
Use of corroborative evidence in valuation
Rejection of sole reliance on circle rates for market value

card.dispute: The appellant landowner challenged the High Court's quashing of his application under Section 28A(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, seeking reference to court for enhanced compensation after other landowners secured higher compensation under the same acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether an application under Section 28A(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is maintainable after the applicant has received enhanced compensation under Section 28A(1) and (2)?
Whether the right to seek reference under Section 28A(3) is barred if the determination under Section 28A(2) has already granted compensation at par with other landowners?
Whether the pendency of appeals by other landowners in the High Court affects the maintainability of a Section 28A(3) application?
holdings: A person who has received enhanced compensation under Section 28A(1) and (2) can still file an application under Section 28A(3) if dissatisfied with the award, as the right to seek court reference remains intact.
Section 28A(3) allows a reference to court for determination of fair market value, provided the compensation claimed does not exceed what is payable to those who sought reference under Section 18.
The pendency of appeals by other landowners does not render a Section 28A(3) application infructuous; the court must await the final decision in those appeals before determining compensation.
doctrines: Doctrine of equality in compensation for land acquisition
Beneficent interpretation of statutory provisions in favor of disadvantaged landowners
Finality of compensation determination pending appellate decisions

card.dispute: The appellant corporation challenged the High Court's decision that invalidated land acquisition proceedings, while landowners argued the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was delayed and thus invalid.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners' challenge to the declaration under Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act was barred by delay and laches
Whether the High Court erred in quashing the acquisition proceedings despite possession being taken and an award being made
holdings: A challenge to a land acquisition declaration must be made promptly; delay in filing after possession and award renders the writ petition inadmissible due to laches.
Courts should not interfere with acquisition proceedings after award and possession, as such steps render the process final and protect public interest.
doctrines: Laches in land acquisition challenges
Finality of acquisition after award and possession
Judicial restraint in quashing completed acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Ambya Kalya Mhatre fought the State of Maharashtra over the adequacy of compensation awarded for land, trees, and a well acquired for the New Bombay project, and whether they could claim enhanced compensation for trees before the reference court despite initially seeking enhancement only for land.
issues_decided: Whether the reference court can consider claims for enhanced compensation for trees and other appurtenances even if the landowner initially sought enhancement only for land in the section 18 application
Whether the requirement to pay ad valorem court fee under the Bombay Court Fees Act restricts the claimant's right to seek higher compensation in the reference court
Whether separate compensation can be awarded for fruit-bearing trees when the market value of the land was determined based on vacant agricultural land
holdings: The reference court has full jurisdiction to decide compensation for land, trees, buildings, and other appurtenances, regardless of whether the initial section 18 application mentioned only land; the claimant can seek enhancement under any head during the reference proceedings.

The requirement to pay ad valorem court fee under the Bombay Court Fees Act does not restrict the claimant's right under the Land Acquisition Act to seek higher compensation; non-payment of additional court fee does not bar amendment of claim if the statute does not mandate specifying the amount in the reference application.

When the market value of acquired land is determined based on vacant agricultural land and not on orchard value or capitalized yield, the value of fruit-bearing trees must be added separately to the land compensation.
provisions: Bombay Court Fees Act, 1959, Schedule I, Entry 15
doctrines: Liberal construction of land acquisition laws in favor of landowners
Compensation must reflect true market value without technical impediments
Principle of complete jurisdiction of reference court in determining just compensation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to quash an order by a Special Judge that allegedly directed prosecution in a corruption case, arguing that the direction was merely an obiter dictum.
issues_decided: Whether the portion of the Special Judge's order directing challan proceedings was a binding direction or a mere obiter dictum
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Special Judge's order based on that direction
holdings: The portion of the Special Judge's order referring to challan proceedings was not a binding judicial direction but a mere obiter dictum, as it was neither specific nor essential to the decision.
The High Court erred in treating the obiter dictum as a binding direction and thus wrongly interfered with the Special Judge's order.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(d) and 13(2)
doctrines: Ratio decidendi vs. obiter dictum
Stare decisis
Binding nature of judicial orders

card.dispute: APM Terminals B.V. challenged its exclusion from bidding for the Fourth Container Terminal at Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, while PSA Sical Terminals Ltd. sought transfer of petitions concerning its exclusion from bidding at Tuticorin Port.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Government could validly change its policy to exclude existing licensees from bidding for subsequent container terminals in major ports.
Whether the exclusion of APM Terminals B.V. from the tender process violated its contractual or legitimate expectations.
Whether the doctrine of legitimate expectation applies when a policy change is made in public interest.
holdings: The Central Government can change its policy to prevent monopolisation of port facilities, even if it affects existing contractual rights, provided the change is non-arbitrary and in public interest.
APM Terminals B.V. must be allowed to participate in the Fourth Container Terminal bid as the policy change permitting alternate bidding should not be applied retroactively to disqualify it unfairly.
The doctrine of legitimate expectation does not override a bona fide policy change made in public interest, especially to promote competition and prevent cartelisation in port operations.
doctrines: Wednesbury reasonableness
Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Public interest overriding private contractual rights

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's dismissal of their second appeal and review petition in a property dispute over land ownership and injunction claimed by the respondent.
issues_decided: Whether the doctrine of merger applies to an order dismissing a Special Leave Petition (SLP) in the Supreme Court.
Whether a review petition is maintainable after dismissal of an SLP by the Supreme Court.
Whether the appellants were entitled to relief on grounds of counsel's conduct and alleged loss due to concession made during proceedings.
holdings: The doctrine of merger does not apply to an order dismissing a Special Leave Petition; it only applies when leave is granted and appellate jurisdiction is invoked.
An aggrieved party remains entitled to file a review petition in the concerned court even after dismissal of an SLP, as dismissal of SLP does not bar the remedy of review.
The appellants could not claim relief merely because their counsel made a concession; absence of objection to counsel’s conduct and failure to raise it earlier barred relief.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 3 Rule 1 and Rule 4
doctrines: Doctrine of merger
Principle of res judicata
Judicial discipline and binding nature of Supreme Court's observations in speaking orders
Public policy against bench-hunting in litigation

card.dispute: The appellant, a retired IAS officer and State Information Commissioner, fought with the Chandigarh Administration over her right to retain government accommodation beyond the prescribed period and the validity of rules allowing extended retention and multiple allotments.
issues_decided: Whether the authorities can extend the retention period of government accommodation beyond the period specified in Rule 13(2) under Rule 13(5) of the Allotment Rules?
Whether a government servant can be allotted two government houses simultaneously—one at the place of posting and another in Chandigarh?
Whether the list of allottees must be published online with an invitation for objections?
holdings: Rule 13(5) of the Allotment Rules, which allows extension of retention period beyond the specified time on payment of higher licence fee, is arbitrary and unguided, and hence unsustainable; no extension beyond the periods in Rule 13(2) shall be permitted.

A government servant shall not be allotted two government houses simultaneously unless under exceptional circumstances, and Rule 11(1)(b) must be invoked sparingly and only with the House Allotment Committee’s recommendation.
There is no requirement under the Allotment Rules to invite public objections to allotments; however, the final list of allotments must be published on the government website for transparency.
provisions: Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration General Pool) Allotment Rules, 1996, Rule 8
Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration General Pool) Allotment Rules, 1996, Rule 9
Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration General Pool) Allotment Rules, 1996, Rule 11(1)(b)
Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration General Pool) Allotment Rules, 1996, Rule 13
doctrines: Doctrine of Certainty
Principle of Legitimate Expectation
Administrative Jurisprudence on Excessive Discretion

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the quantum of compensation awarded for their land acquired by the Gulbarga Development Authority, arguing that deductions applied by the High Court were excessive and unjustified.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in applying a 55% deduction for lack of development on the acquired land?
Whether the 10% deduction for de-escalation was arbitrary and unsustainable?
Whether the 5% deduction for waiting period was valid?
Whether the total cumulative deduction of 70% was within permissible legal limits?
holdings: A 55% deduction for development was justified because the acquired land was totally undeveloped while the comparable sale deed was for a fully developed site, and such deduction falls within judicially accepted parameters.

A 10% deduction for de-escalation was valid given the rise in land prices and the 1 year 7-month gap between the preliminary notification and the exemplar sale deed, consistent with precedents allowing 7.5–10% escalation.
The 5% deduction for waiting period is legally permissible as this Court has recognized it as a relevant factor in valuation, and the appellants did not challenge it.
Cumulative deductions of 70% (55% + 10% + 5%) are within the 75% outer limit set by this Court and hence legally sustainable.
provisions: City Improvement Trust Board Act, 1976, Section 15(1)
doctrines: Principle of uniformity in compensation for land acquired under the same notification
Judicial notice of rising land prices
Cumulative deduction cap of 75% from Lal Chand and Andhra Pradesh Housing Board cases
Use of comparable sale deeds with adjustments for development, de-escalation, and waiting period

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the acquisition of their land by the Moradabad Development Authority, arguing that the urgency clause was wrongly invoked and that they were not heard during appellate proceedings in the High Court.
issues_decided: Whether the invocation of the urgency clause under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, was valid in these cases.
Whether the decisions in earlier cases (specifically Gafar's case) on the same notification and urgency grounds are binding precedents.
Whether the appellants were denied a fair hearing by the High Court due to non-listing or absence of counsel.
Whether the appeals abated due to the death of appellants and non-substitution of legal heirs.
holdings: The urgency clause under Section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, could not be validly invoked in these cases, following the precedent set in Gafar's case.
The decision in Gafar's case is binding on the same question of law and facts, and applies to all cases involving the same notification and circumstances.
The appellants were not denied a fair hearing; the High Court’s orders indicate that some counsel were heard, and courts are bound by their recorded orders.
The appeals did not abate due to non-substitution, as no valid order rejecting substitution was produced, and the matter remains governed by the binding precedent.
doctrines: Binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution
Res judicata and ratio decidendi distinction
Principle of judicial discipline among co-equal benches
Rule of natural justice – audi alteram partem

card.dispute: The appellants (daughters) fought with their brothers (respondents) over whether they were entitled to a share in the coparcenary property under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, despite a preliminary decree having been passed before the amendment.
issues_decided: Whether the benefits of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 are available to daughters in a partition suit where a preliminary decree had been passed but not the final decree.
Whether a preliminary decree in a partition suit can be modified to account for changes in law during the pendency of the suit.
holdings: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 applies to pending partition suits even after a preliminary decree, as long as the final decree has not been passed, because partition is not complete until then.
A preliminary decree determining shares is not final and can be modified due to supervening events, including legislative changes that confer rights on daughters as coparceners.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 18
doctrines: Beneficial construction of laws meant to empower women
Partition not complete until final decree
Power of court to pass second preliminary decree in changed circumstances

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's quashing of criminal proceedings against the respondents, who were initially charged but later exonerated in a police report after further investigation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. when the Magistrate had not yet applied judicial mind to the police reports under Section 173 Cr.P.C.?
Whether a further investigation report under Section 173(8) Cr.P.C. absolving an accused can be the basis for quashing proceedings without the Magistrate's evaluation?
holdings: The High Court cannot exercise inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash proceedings at an interlocutory stage if the Magistrate has not yet applied judicial mind to the police reports under Section 173 Cr.P.C.
The Magistrate must evaluate both the initial and further investigation reports under Section 173 Cr.P.C. before deciding whether to take cognizance, even if the police recommend closure.
doctrines: Judicial discretion in cognizance under Section 190 Cr.P.C.
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. not to override specific statutory procedures
Principle of non-interference at interlocutory stage to prevent abuse of process

card.dispute: The Goa Housing Board and a landowner disputed the compensation amount for acquired agricultural land, with the Board challenging the high valuation and the landowner seeking an increase.
issues_decided: Whether the land in question ceased to be agricultural land prior to the enforcement of the Goa Land Use (Regulations) Act, 1991 due to its notification for industrial use under the Town & Country Planning Act, 1974.
Whether the land was subject to restrictions under the Land Use Act at the time of acquisition, affecting its market value.
What is the correct market value of the acquired agricultural land for compensation purposes under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894?
holdings: Notification of land for industrial use under the Town & Country Planning Act does not automatically convert it from agricultural to non-agricultural use; conversion requires compliance with the Land Revenue Code.
Land vested in a tenant under the Agricultural Tenancy Act remains agricultural and subject to Land Use Act restrictions, even if earmarked for industrial use, unless formally converted under law.
Market value of agricultural land restricted by the Land Use Act must be assessed based on agricultural potential only, warranting a 50% deduction from the value of developable land.
provisions: Goa, Daman and Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, Sections 18A, 18C, 18D, 18E, 18H, 18J, 18K
Goa, Daman and Diu Town & Country Planning Act, 1974, Sections 13, 15, 17, 18, 29, 31, 37, 41, 42
Goa, Daman and Diu Land Revenue Code, 1968, Sections 30, 32
doctrines: Doctrine of statutory interpretation
Principle of restricted land use affecting market value
Doctrine of effective vesting under tenancy laws

card.dispute: The appellant Gurdeep Singh challenged his conviction for dowry death and cruelty under Sections 304B and 498A IPC, arguing lack of evidence on unnatural death and dowry demands soon before death.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the ingredients of Section 304B IPC, particularly unnatural death and cruelty soon before death?
Whether the presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act applies in the absence of proof of dowry demand soon before death?
Whether the unexplained cremation of the deceased's body raises a presumption against the accused?
Whether the contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' statements affect their credibility?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove that the death was unnatural, as no poison was detected in the forensic analysis, and thus the first ingredient of Section 304B IPC was not satisfied.

The demand for dowry made one year before death does not meet the 'proximity test' and cannot be considered 'soon before death' under Section 304B IPC, so the presumption under Section 113B of the Evidence Act does not apply.
The mere fact of unexplained or hurried cremation cannot, without corroborative evidence, sustain a conviction under Section 304B IPC.
Material contradictions between the statements under Section 161 Cr.P.C. and court testimony of close relatives of the deceased severely undermine their credibility and weaken the prosecution case.
doctrines: Proximity test for dowry demand under Section 304B IPC
Presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act
Credibility of prosecution witnesses and effect of contradictions
Requirement of corroborative evidence in dowry death cases
