holdings: The State may invoke Section 17(1) to take early possession even after allowing Section 5A objections, without invalidating the process, as Sections 17(1) and 17(4) operate in different contexts.
Dispensing with Section 5A under Section 17(4) is not mandatory upon invoking urgency; the State may later allow objections without undermining prior possession under Section 17(1).
Payment of compensation under Section 17(3A) after taking possession does not invalidate the acquisition if statutory requirements are otherwise met.
A notification issued in the Governor’s name pursuant to a file decision by a competent authority (e.g., Departmental Secretary) complies with Article 166(1) of the Constitution.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
doctrines: Strict construction of expropriatory legislation
Doctrine of harmonious construction of statutory provisions
Doctrine of competent authority under executive rules
Doctrine of separation between urgency and procedural dispensation in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents, brothers and sons of the deceased Narayana, fought over the partition of three items of suit property, with claims over joint family versus self-acquired status of the lands.
issues_decided: Whether items No. 1 and 2 were joint family properties and subject to partition
Whether item No. 3 was self-acquired property of the appellant or joint family property
Whether there was a prior division of status between the brothers before the grant of patta for item No. 3
Whether the patta granted in respect of item No. 3 inured to the benefit of the joint family
holdings: Items No. 1 and 2 were not subject to partition as there was a prior division of status among the brothers, affirmed by panchayat resolution and conduct, and the courts below erred in ignoring this evidence.

Item No. 3, though granted patta in the appellant's name after the suit was filed, was held to be joint family property as the application was made during the period of undivided status and development occurred from joint family efforts.
The grant of patta in the name of the appellant for item No. 3 did not convert the property into self-acquired property, as it was granted for the benefit of the entire joint family.

All five coparceners, including the appellant and four respondents, are entitled to equal 1/5th shares in item No. 3, with liberty to plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 to relinquish their shares at final decree.
provisions: Karnataka Land Revenue (Amended) Rules of 1991, Rule 108
doctrines: Doctrine of family arrangement
Doctrine of patta not altering coparcenary rights in joint family property
Principle of benefit of family in grant of land tenure
Concurrent findings can be overturned for perversity or misappreciation of evidence

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the exclusion of residents of illegally constructed buildings from electoral rolls in a Cantonment area, arguing for their right to vote.
issues_decided: Whether persons residing in illegally constructed buildings in a Cantonment area are entitled to be included in electoral rolls under Rule 10(3) of the Cantonment Electoral Rules, 2007
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition challenging the preparation of electoral rolls despite alternative remedies under the Rules
Whether the direction to prepare electoral rolls strictly in accordance with Rule 10(3) permits inclusion of encroachers with a notation of unauthorized construction
holdings: Persons living in illegally constructed buildings not assigned house numbers are not entitled to inclusion in electoral rolls, as Rule 10(3) requires arrangement by house number and only those in numbered houses can be enrolled.

Writ petitions are maintainable to challenge the preparation of electoral rolls even if alternative remedies exist, especially when no election petition can be filed for inclusion or exclusion under Rule 55.
The Division Bench’s modified order does not permit inclusion of encroachers in the electoral roll; marking structures as unauthorized does not entitle such residents to vote.
doctrines: Substantial compliance with statutory rules
Finality of judicial orders
Deeming fiction in electoral law
Legislative policy against encroachment on defence land

card.dispute: The Energy and Resources Institute and heirs of Akhilesh Kala challenged the High Court's cancellation of their long-term orchard leases granted by the State of Uttarakhand, arguing that they were not properly heard despite opposing the public interest litigation that led to the cancellation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in cancelling the lease grants in favour of the appellants without considering their specific submissions and affidavits?
Whether the High Court could proceed against a deceased person (Akhilesh Kala) without proof of service of notice on legal heirs?
Whether the High Court failed to comply with the Supreme Court’s earlier remand direction to hear all affected nominees before deciding on the validity of the State's policy of leasing orchards?
holdings: The High Court failed to consider the specific affidavits and contentions of The Energy and Resources Institute, making its decision against them cryptic and legally unsustainable.
The High Court could not proceed to decide the writ petition against Akhilesh Kala, a deceased person, without verifying service of notice on his legal heirs, violating principles of natural justice.

The impugned judgment did not examine whether the State’s policy of leasing orchards was in public interest or lawful, as directed by the Supreme Court earlier, warranting remand for fresh consideration.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of speaking orders
Compliance with remand directions
Protection of legitimate expectations

card.dispute: Uco Bank and the respondents, members of Scheduled Tribes in Tripura, fought over whether a bank's sale of mortgaged tribal land to non-tribals under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, was invalid due to conflict with Section 187 of the Tripura Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, 1960.
issues_decided: Whether Section 187 of the Tripura Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, 1960, which restricts sale of tribal mortgaged land to non-tribals, prevails over the SARFAESI Act, 2002, given its inclusion in the Ninth Schedule and protection under Article 31-B of the Constitution.

Whether the bank's sale notification and auction were invalid for non-compliance with Rule 5 and Rule 8(5) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, particularly regarding valuation of the property.
holdings: The SARFAESI Act, 2002, being a Parliamentary legislation on banking (Entry 45, List I), is the dominant legislation and prevails over Section 187 of the Tripura Act, 1960, which incidentally encroaches on banking; thus, the State law is pro tanto invalid.
The bank complied with Rule 5 and Rule 8(5) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, as a valuation report was obtained and a reserve price was set; hence, the sale is valid.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
Tripura Land Revenue and Land Reforms Act, 1960, Section 187
doctrines: Doctrine of federal supremacy
Doctrine of pith and substance
Dominant legislation doctrine in federal conflicts

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents, two families, fought over ownership and possession of a portion of government burial land in Kurnool, with the respondents claiming title through adverse possession against the State.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in admitting second appeals under Section 100 of the CPC by framing non-substantial questions of law?
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to remand the cases for de novo trial without any party pleading for remand or a substantial question of law on remand being framed?
Whether the respondents proved their title over the suit land based on adverse possession against the State?
holdings: The High Court erred in admitting second appeals because the questions framed were essentially factual and did not constitute substantial questions of law under Section 100 CPC.
The High Court had no jurisdiction to remand the cases for de novo trial as no party requested remand and no substantial question of law on remand was framed under Section 100 CPC.
The respondents failed to prove title by adverse possession against the State due to lack of satisfactory evidence, and the concurrent findings of lower courts were binding on the High Court.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 23-A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 25
doctrines: Concurrent finding rule
Substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC
Burden of proof in adverse possession claims
Appellate jurisdiction and remand principles

card.dispute: The Union of India and private respondents fought over ownership and title to a plot of land near Krishnarajapuram Railway Station, with the Union claiming ownership and the respondents asserting ancestral occupancy rights under tenancy laws.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court failed to properly discharge its duties as a first appellate court by delivering a cryptic judgment without addressing all issues and evidence?
Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the Union of India's application under Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC to adduce additional evidence in appeal?
holdings: The High Court failed to meet the requirements of a first appellate court by not recording reasoned findings on all issues and evidence; its judgment was cryptic and inadequate, warranting remand.

The application under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC should have been allowed as the Union of India provided justifiable reasons, the evidence was relevant public documents, and no party opposed; thus, opportunity to file additional evidence must be granted.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 31
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
doctrines: First appeal as a valuable right requiring full rehearing on facts and law
Principle of substantial justice in admission of additional evidence on appeal
Conscious application of mind by appellate courts

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the land acquisition proceedings initiated by the State of Haryana, claiming that the acquisition had lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act due to non-payment of compensation and non-taking of physical possession.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 due to non-payment of compensation?
Whether the requirement of physical possession was satisfied by the State taking over the land 'as is where is'?
Whether the landowners' failure to claim compensation bars them from relief under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act?
holdings: Where an award has been made under the 1894 Act but compensation has not been paid or deposited in court, the acquisition proceedings lapse under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act.
The question of whether 'as is where is' possession satisfies the requirement of physical possession is left open.
The obligation to pay compensation lies with the acquiring authority; the landowner's failure to claim it does not absolve the state of its duty or prevent lapse of proceedings.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
doctrines: Lapse of acquisition proceedings for non-compliance with statutory conditions
State's duty to proactively pay compensation in compulsory acquisition

card.dispute: The appellants, landowners in Gujarat, fought against the state's claim to surplus land under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, arguing they were entitled to retain possession under the Repeal Act, 1999.
issues_decided: Whether the state had taken de facto possession of the land before the Repeal Act, 1999 came into force
Whether a corrigendum could be used to correct notified plot numbers from 1-16 to 36-43 after repeal
Whether the writ petition was barred by res judicata
holdings: Deemed vesting under Section 10(3) of the 1976 Act does not amount to de facto possession; actual possession must be established for the state to claim rights pre-repeal.
A corrigendum cannot substitute entirely different plot numbers in statutory notifications after repeal; such changes require compliance with mandatory procedural provisions.
The earlier writ petition did not decide the issue of dispossession or the effect of the Repeal Act, so the current petition is not barred by res judicata.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(1), (3), (5), (6)
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, Section 4
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 45
doctrines: Deemed vesting does not imply de facto possession
Mandatory notice requirement in dispossession proceedings
Saving clause under repeal legislation preserves rights if no final dispossession occurred

card.dispute: The appellants (landowners in Chandapora) challenged the lower compensation awarded for their land compared to owners of similar lands in adjacent villages acquired for the same public purpose.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded to landowners in Chandapora should be at par with that awarded to landowners in adjacent villages for similar lands acquired at the same time and for the same purpose?
Whether discrimination in compensation is justified when lands are similar, adjacent, and acquired for the same public purpose?
holdings: When lands are similar, adjacent, and acquired at the same time for the same public purpose, landowners must receive equal compensation to avoid unjust discrimination.
The Reference Court erred in awarding lower compensation to the appellants; they are entitled to the same rate of Rs.4,00,000 per Kanal as awarded to others in Bhagichandpora and Pazwalpora.
provisions: Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act, Section 4(1)
Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act, Section 6
doctrines: Principle of non-discrimination in land acquisition compensation
Use of comparable market value in determining fair compensation

card.dispute: The appellants, landowners near the Mazum dam, sued the State of Gujarat for damages after their plantation was destroyed due to water release from the dam, alleging negligence, while the State claimed the release was due to an 'Act of God' and in public interest.
issues_decided: Whether the State's release of water from the dam, causing damage to the appellants' land, constitutes an 'Act of God' absolving it of liability.
Whether the State failed to discharge the burden of proving that it exercised due care in maintaining water levels before the monsoon.
Whether the appellants are entitled to compensation despite lack of exact proof of damages.
holdings: A natural event like heavy rain does not automatically qualify as an 'Act of God' if damage results from prior negligence in failing to take preventive measures.

The State failed to prove it maintained safe water levels or that the rainfall was unforeseeable, thus failing to discharge the burden of showing no negligence under the Rylands v. Fletcher principle.

Even without precise proof of loss, claimants are entitled to reasonable compensation when fact of damage is proved, and damages can be apportioned where both natural causes and negligence contribute to harm.
doctrines: Act of God (vis major)
Rylands v. Fletcher rule
Apportionment of damages in cases of concurrent causes
Standard of reasonable care in state liability for negligence

card.dispute: The dispute was between two brothers, Vijay Prakash Jarath and Tej Prakash Jarath, over whether a counter-claim filed by the defendants (including Vijay) after the framing of issues but before the conclusion of evidence was maintainable.
issues_decided: Whether a counter-claim can be filed after the framing of issues in a suit?
Whether the High Court was justified in rejecting the counter-claim on the ground that it was filed belatedly?
Whether the cause of action for the counter-claim accrued before the defendant filed his written statement?
holdings: A counter-claim is maintainable if the cause of action accrued before the defendant filed his written statement, even if filed after framing of issues.
The High Court erred in disallowing the counter-claim solely on grounds of delay when no prejudice was shown and evidence was still ongoing.
The provisions of Order VIII Rule 6A CPC allow a counter-claim if the cause of action arose before the defence was filed, and such claim must be permitted to serve justice.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VIII Rule 6A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Subservience of procedural rules to the ends of justice
Counter-claim as an additional right under CPC
Discretionary power of court to allow amendments to pleadings

card.dispute: The appellant sued to restrain respondents from interfering with his possession of agricultural land, which had been declared surplus under the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973, after he sold it to them.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had lawful possession of the suit land at the time of filing the suit?
Whether the civil court could grant injunction between private parties over land declared surplus under ceiling laws without impleading the State?
Whether the sale of surplus land in excess of ceiling limits is valid under the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973?
Whether proceedings under the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973 override those under the earlier Land Encroachment Act, 1971?
holdings: The appellant was not in lawful possession of the suit land as his ownership stood extinguished by the final tribunal order declaring the land surplus under the ceiling Act.
A civil suit for injunction between private parties concerning ceiling-surplus land must implead the State, as any decree would affect State rights.
A sale of land in excess of ceiling limits after the Act came into force is invalid, as the seller cannot transfer rights already vested in the State.
Section 28 of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1973 gives overriding effect to its provisions, rendering inconsistent proceedings under the Land Encroachment Act, 1971 ineffective.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 3(o)
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 7
Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973, Section 28
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10 (as amended by M.P. Act No. 29 of 1984)
doctrines: Doctrine of lawful possession for grant of injunction
Doctrine of clean hands
Principle of finality of tribunal orders under ceiling laws
Doctrine of overriding effect of special statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, an informant, challenged the High Court's decision setting aside the trial court's order allowing further police investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. after cognizance had been taken and the accused had appeared.
issues_decided: Whether a Magistrate can direct further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. after cognizance has been taken and the accused has appeared in court?
Whether the power to order further investigation under Section 173(8) lies with the Magistrate or only with the investigating agency?
Whether the trial court's order permitting further investigation at a post-cognizance stage was legally valid?
holdings: A Magistrate cannot direct further investigation under Section 173(8) of the Cr.P.C. after cognizance has been taken and the accused has appeared; only the investigating agency can initiate such investigation with court approval.
The power under Section 173(8) is exclusively vested in the investigating agency, not the Magistrate, and applies at any stage of the proceedings but must be exercised by the police, not the court.
The trial court’s order allowing further investigation at a post-cognizance stage, especially on an application by the informant, is not maintainable and violates the statutory scheme of the Cr.P.C.
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of procedural law
Separation of investigative and judicial functions
Doctrine of legislative intent
Principle of harmonious construction

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence for murder, arguing that the evidence did not support a charge under Section 302 IPC and that the incident occurred during a sudden fight without premeditation.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC is sustainable given the nature of the incident?
Whether the appellants are entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC?
Whether the evidence of hostile witnesses can be relied upon to sustain the conviction?
What is the appropriate sentence if the conviction is altered from Section 302 to Section 304 IPC?
holdings: The conviction under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC is not sustainable as the incident occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation, attracting Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
The appellants are entitled to the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC because the fight was sudden, there was no undue advantage or cruelty, and the act was done in the heat of passion.
The evidence of a hostile witness can be relied upon to the extent it supports the prosecution case, especially when corroborated by other evidence.
The sentence is reduced to the period already undergone, considering the modified conviction under Section 304 Part I IPC and the time served by the appellants.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 304 Part I
doctrines: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC: Sudden fight without premeditation
Reliance on partial testimony of hostile witnesses
Heat of passion in sudden quarrel doctrine
Modification of sentence based on reclassification of offence

card.dispute: The defendants appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside the trial court's rejection of a suit, which had been compromised in Lok Adalat, and instead allowed the suit to proceed on grounds of alleged fraud in the compromise.
issues_decided: Whether the expression 'law' in Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC includes judicial precedents, particularly those laid down by the Supreme Court.
Whether a suit barred by a binding judicial precedent, such as one requiring a writ remedy to challenge a Lok Adalat award, should be rejected at the threshold.
holdings: The term 'law' in Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC includes judicial precedents, especially those declared by the Supreme Court under Article 141 of the Constitution.

A suit that is barred by a binding judicial precedent must be rejected at the threshold under Order 7 Rule 11(d), and cannot proceed even if fraud is alleged; the proper remedy is a writ petition under Articles 226/227.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11(d)
doctrines: Binding nature of Supreme Court precedents under Article 141
Doctrine of rejection of plaint at threshold when barred by law
Proper remedy rule: availability of an alternative and exclusive remedy bars civil suit

card.dispute: The plaintiff-appellant challenged the High Court's dismissal of his appeal against a trial court decision that dismissed his suit for declaration of title and injunction while decreeing the defendant's cross-suit, alleging the High Court failed to properly adjudicate the first appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, as a first appellate court, discharged its duty under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure by adequately addressing all issues and evidence?
Whether the impugned judgment of the High Court was so cryptic and inadequate as to require remand?
holdings: The first appellate court must independently appreciate all evidence, address all issues of fact and law, and record reasoned findings; failure to do so vitiates the appellate process.
A cryptic appellate judgment that does not reflect conscious application of mind must be set aside and remanded for fresh disposal in accordance with law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 31
doctrines: First appeal as a valuable right
Conscious application of mind by appellate court
Duty of first appellate court to reappreciate evidence

card.dispute: The appellants sought enhancement of land acquisition compensation under Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, based on a later appellate award, after their initial application was decided while the underlying award was still under appeal.
issues_decided: Whether a second application under Section 28A is maintainable when the first application was decided during pendency of appeal against the relied-upon award.
What course should the Land Acquisition Collector adopt under Section 28A when the award on which enhancement is sought is pending in appeal.
holdings: Only one application under Section 28A is permissible, and successive applications are not allowed.

When an award relied upon under Section 28A is pending in appeal, the Collector must keep the application pending and decide it only after the final appellate decision to ensure compensation is based on the final adjudicated amount.
doctrines: Beneficial construction of statutory provisions
Finality of appellate decisions in determining compensation
Judicial discipline in administrative action during pendency of appeals

card.dispute: A brother and sister from a Muslim family disputed over the partition of landed and house properties, with the sister claiming inheritance under Mohammedan Law and the brother asserting the property as his self-acquired asset.
issues_decided: Whether the second appeal involved a substantial question of law warranting admission under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908?
Whether the High Court committed a jurisdictional error by dismissing the second appeal at the admission stage without framing substantial questions of law?
holdings: A second appeal must be admitted if it raises substantial questions of law, especially involving document interpretation and title disputes, even if factual findings are not challenged.

The High Court committed a jurisdictional error by dismissing the second appeal in limine without framing substantial questions of law as required under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
doctrines: Substantial question of law
Jurisdictional error
Interpretation of documents as a question of law

card.dispute: The workers' union and others contested whether the company's management violated a court order by using tax refunds from compensation money meant to be protected under court supervision.
issues_decided: Whether the utilization of the tax refund by the company violated the court's order dated 23.02.2011 directing deposit of the entire compensation with the High Court
Whether the tax refund, though processed through the Income-Tax Department, formed part of the protected compensation amount
Whether the Division Bench was correct in setting aside contempt proceedings for alleged violation of the 2011 order
holdings: The refund received from the Income-Tax Department was part of the compensation and thus fell within the scope of the court's order to protect the entire amount.
Utilizing the refund without court permission violated the 23.02.2011 order, as the court intended to safeguard all parts of the compensation, including TDS amounts.
The Division Bench erred in dismissing the contempt proceedings; the Single Judge’s order to secure the amount and issue a rule was justified.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 32
doctrines: Plainly self-evident directions doctrine
Restitutive powers of the court
Contempt for wilful disobedience of court orders

card.dispute: Baliraj Singh appealed against his conviction for murder under Section 302/34 IPC, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on unreliable eyewitness testimony and inconsistent medical evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the guilt of the appellant beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the ocular testimony of closely related witnesses can be relied upon without corroboration?
Whether the medical evidence corroborated the prosecution's version of the incident?
Whether the non-examination of the police officer who conducted the seizure of the alleged weapon affects the reliability of the prosecution case?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt due to contradictions in eyewitness accounts and lack of independent corroboration.
Ocular testimony of close relatives of the deceased must be scrutinized with great care and cannot form the sole basis of conviction without reliable corroboration.
The medical evidence indicating a sharp piercing injury contradicts the prosecution's claim that a lathi coated with iron caused the death, creating reasonable doubt.
The non-examination of the police officer who conducted the seizure of the alleged weapon renders the recovery evidence unreliable and weakens the prosecution's case.
doctrines: Principle of benefit of doubt
Requirement of corroboration for interested witnesses
Primacy of reliable medical evidence over interested ocular testimony
Strict scrutiny of evidence in cases relying solely on eyewitness accounts

card.dispute: The landlord sought to evict the tenant for default in paying municipal property tax, arguing it formed part of rent under the NDMC Act, while the tenant claimed protection under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
issues_decided: Whether property tax recoverable under Section 67(3) of the NDMC Act can be treated as part of rent for eviction purposes under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
Whether the NDMC Act overrides the Delhi Rent Control Act in matters of tenant eviction when tax arrears are involved.
holdings: Property tax recoverable under Section 67(3) of the NDMC Act cannot be considered part of rent for eviction under the Delhi Rent Control Act.
The Delhi Rent Control Act, being a special law with a non-obstante clause, prevails over the NDMC Act in landlord-tenant matters, including recovery of taxes.
provisions: New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, Section 67(3)
New Delhi Municipal Council Act, 1994, Section 411
doctrines: Specialia generalibus derogant
Harmonious construction
Non-obstante clause precedence
Implied repeal

card.dispute: The auction purchaser challenged the High Court's decision to set aside an auction sale of a judgment debtor's property on grounds of alleged irregularities in the sale process.
issues_decided: Whether the auction sale could be set aside under Order 21 Rule 90 of the CPC due to material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale.
Whether the judgment debtor suffered substantial injury due to alleged procedural defects in the auction process.
Whether the requirements of notice, valuation disclosure, and publicity under Order 21 Rules 54, 64, 67, and 68 were complied with.
Whether bald allegations of irregularity without supporting evidence are sufficient to set aside an auction sale.
holdings: An auction sale cannot be set aside merely on the basis of material irregularity or fraud; the applicant must prove that such irregularity or fraud caused substantial injury.
The judgment debtor failed to prove substantial injury or provide evidence that the property was undervalued or that inadequate publicity affected the sale outcome.
Compliance with Order 21 Rules 54, 64, 67, and 68 was sufficient, including proper notice, valuation details, and publicity through beat of drum and posting at relevant locations.
Mere allegations of procedural defects without specific particulars or evidence do not justify setting aside an auction sale under Order 21 Rule 90(2) of the CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 54(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 64
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 67
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 68
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 90(2)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 Rule 151
doctrines: Substantial injury doctrine in auction sales
Requirement of specific particulars for allegations of fraud or irregularity
Strict compliance with procedural rules in execution sales
Presumption of regularity in judicial proceedings

card.dispute: The petitioners, who were in occupation of commercial premises under a conducting agreement, fought against eviction after the High Court upheld a decree for possession in favor of the respondents.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioners' filing of an unconditional undertaking to vacate the premises barred them from later challenging the eviction order before the Supreme Court?
Whether the petitioners' conduct amounted to an abuse of the judicial process by seeking repeated adjournments and extensions while not pursuing substantive legal remedies?
Whether the plea of the petitioners that their licensee status had fructified into tenancy was maintainable in law?
holdings: Filing an unconditional undertaking to vacate premises with the High Court, while obtaining time to do so, constitutes a waiver of further legal challenges and renders any subsequent appeal an abuse of process.
A litigant who obtains time to vacate and then files frivolous applications or review petitions without pursuing genuine legal remedies abuses the judicial process and is liable to exemplary costs.
The petitioners could not claim tenancy rights as there was no license in their favour, and the conducting agreement did not create a landlord-tenant relationship.
provisions: Presidency Small Causes Courts Act, Section 41
doctrines: Abuse of process
Undertaking estoppel
Frivolous litigation and imposition of exemplary costs

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Dagadabai, the sole heir of Rustum, sued Abbas @ Gulab Rustum Pinjari, who claimed ownership of agricultural land either by adoption or adverse possession, seeking possession of the land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in admitting and allowing the second appeal under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure by reversing concurrent findings of fact?
Whether the defendant could succeed on the plea of adverse possession without admitting the plaintiff's title?
Whether the plea of adoption under Muslim law is legally valid to claim inheritance?
holdings: The High Court erred in admitting the second appeal as no substantial question of law arose from the concurrent factual findings of the lower courts.
A plea of adverse possession cannot succeed unless the defendant admits the plaintiff's title and proves hostile, continuous possession for over 12 years; mere mutation entries are insufficient.
Under Mohammadan Law, adoption is not recognized, and thus the defendant could not inherit the property through adoption.
provisions: Mulla Principles of Mahomedan Law, 20th Edition, Section 347
doctrines: Concurrent findings of fact by two courts below are binding on the High Court in second appeal
Adverse possession requires admission of true owner's title and proof of hostile, continuous possession
Non-recognition of adoption under Muslim personal law

card.dispute: The petitioner NGO Common Cause and other parties fought against the Union of India and state authorities over rampant illegal mining in Odisha's mineral-rich districts, seeking accountability, environmental restoration, and tribal welfare measures.
issues_decided: Whether illegal mining in Keonjhar, Sundergarh, and Mayurbhanj districts warranted investigation and remedial action
Whether a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) should be established and funded for tribal welfare and area development
Whether mining lease holders should be allowed to resume operations after payment of dues
Whether the National Mineral Policy, 2008 required revision to address conservation and sustainable development
holdings: The court approved the Odisha government's scheme for a Special Purpose Vehicle to use 50% of additional net present value (NPV) funds for tribal welfare and area development in mining-affected regions.
The ad hoc CAMPA must transfer 50% of the additional NPV recovered from mining lease holders to the SPV within a month for welfare works.
Mining lease holders may restart operations only after full compliance with statutory clearances and payment of all compensation and dues by 31 December 2017.
The Union of India must review the National Mineral Policy, 2008 with focus on conservation and sustainable mineral development by 31 December 2017.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
doctrines: Sustainable development
Precautionary principle
Polluter pays principle
Public trust doctrine

card.dispute: The Federation of Indian Mineral Industries challenged the requirement to pay contributions to the District Mineral Foundation under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, arguing against retrospective liability.
issues_decided: Whether the obligation to pay contributions to the District Mineral Foundation (DMF) arose retrospectively from 12th January, 2015, when the MMDR Ordinance was promulgated.
Whether the notification dated 31st August, 2016, making DMF contributions effective from 12th January, 2015, was valid.
Whether the establishment of DMFs from 12th January, 2015, by state notifications could justify retroactive collection of contributions.
From what date the liability to pay DMF contributions arose for mining leaseholders of different categories of minerals.
holdings: The liability to pay DMF contributions does not arise retrospectively merely because DMFs were established with effect from 12th January, 2015; the rate of contribution must be notified for liability to arise.

The notification dated 31st August, 2016, which sought to make DMF contributions effective from 12th January, 2015, is ultra vires and invalid as subordinate legislation cannot have retrospective effect.
Section 9B of the MMDR Act is not conditional legislation; however, the obligation to pay arises only after the rate is prescribed and the DMF is established.

For minerals other than coal, lignite, and sand for stowing, contributions are due from 17th September, 2015; for coal, lignite, and sand for stowing, from 20th October, 2015 or the date of DMF establishment, whichever is later.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 9B
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Rule-making powers of Central and State Governments
doctrines: Doctrine of retrospectivity of subordinate legislation
Doctrine of conditional legislation
Principle of non-retrogression in fiscal obligations
Doctrine of delegated legislation and its limits

card.dispute: The landlord, Gandhe Vijay Kumar, sought possession of the rented premises from tenant Mulji @ Mulchand on grounds of bonafide requirement, which the High Court reversed despite concurrent findings by the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in revisional jurisdiction, can re-appreciate evidence and overturn concurrent factual findings of the Rent Controller and Appellate Authority?
Whether the High Court can act as a second court of first appeal in revision proceedings under rent control statutes?
holdings: The High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence or overturn concurrent factual findings merely because it might have reached a different conclusion; its role is limited to checking legality, perversity, or procedural irregularity.

Revisional jurisdiction under rent control laws does not empower the High Court to function as a second court of first appeal; it cannot substitute its view of facts for that of the lower authorities.
provisions: Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 (or relevant Rent Control Act under which revision was sought)
doctrines: Limits of revisional jurisdiction
Concurrent findings rule
Perversity test in factual findings
No second court of first appeal doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the admission of a demarcation report, created during conciliation proceedings, as evidence in judicial proceedings, arguing it violated confidentiality under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
issues_decided: Whether a demarcation report prepared during conciliation proceedings can be admitted as evidence in judicial proceedings despite confidentiality obligations under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

Whether Section 81 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 exhaustively covers all exclusions to admissibility of evidence from conciliation, or whether broader confidentiality under Section 75 applies independently.
holdings: The demarcation report cannot be admitted as evidence because it originated in conciliation proceedings and is protected by the broad confidentiality mandate of Section 75 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

Section 75 operates independently of Section 81; even if a piece of evidence does not fall within the four categories of Section 81, it may still be inadmissible if it relates to conciliation proceedings and would undermine the confidentiality essential to effective conciliation.
doctrines: Confidentiality in conciliation proceedings
Judicial non-admissibility of conciliation-related materials
Literal and purposive interpretation of statutory provisions

card.dispute: Haryana Urban Development Authority and others fought against Orchid Infrastructure Developers over the rejection of the latter's highest bid in a public auction for a commercial property.
issues_decided: Whether the Authority could reject the highest bid in a public auction without assigning valid reasons
Whether the rejection of the bid was arbitrary or violated principles of fair treatment
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a mandatory injunction for allotment without paying ad valorem court fee
holdings: A public authority has the right to reject the highest bid in a public auction if there are rational, tangible, and non-arbitrary reasons, especially when large public stakes are involved.
The rejection of a bid must be based on recorded reasons and cannot be validated by subsequent justifications; the decision must stand on the grounds originally stated.
A plaintiff seeking relief based on a bid valuation must pay ad valorem court fees corresponding to the bid amount, and failure to do so renders the suit improperly valued.
doctrines: Principle of fair treatment in public tenders
Doctrine of non-arbitrariness in administrative action
Requirement of recorded reasons for rejection of bids
Objective construction of public orders

card.dispute: H.P. Financial Corporation challenged the High Court's decision to set aside an auction notice for recovering loans from Anil Garg, who defaulted on two loans for a truck and a steel trunk manufacturing unit.
issues_decided: Whether the withdrawal of a civil suit barred subsequent recovery proceedings under the Himachal Pradesh Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1973
Whether the recovery proceedings were time-barred due to inaction between 1996 and 2002
Whether the principle of public policy or doctrine of election prevented the Corporation from initiating fresh recovery proceedings
holdings: Withdrawal of a civil suit does not bar recovery under the HP Public Moneys Act, as the proceedings are before an executive authority and not a court, and the Act provides an independent remedy.
The recovery claim was not time-barred as a recovery certificate was issued in 1994, and subsequent delays were due to the respondent's own writ petitions.
Public policy supports recovery of public funds and does not allow a borrower to escape liability; the doctrine of election does not apply where the statute allows multiple remedies.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1973, Section 3(1)(d)(iv)
Himachal Pradesh Public Moneys (Recovery of Dues) Act, 1973, Section 85
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 1
doctrines: Doctrine of Public Policy
Doctrine of Election
Principle of Abandonment of Claim

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the execution of a decree for possession, claiming the civil court lacked jurisdiction as the land was agricultural and disputes over such land are barred under the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court had inherent jurisdiction to pass a decree for possession under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act when the land in question was agricultural and thus potentially outside the civil court's jurisdiction under Section 185(1) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954?
Whether the executing court could set aside the decree on the ground that it was a nullity due to lack of jurisdiction?
holdings: A decree can be challenged in execution only on grounds of inherent lack of jurisdiction, such as when the subject matter is entirely outside the court's jurisdiction or the defendant was dead at the time of suit.

The civil court had jurisdiction because the land had ceased to be agricultural in character by the time the suit was filed, and thus Section 185(1) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act did not bar its jurisdiction; the decree was not a nullity.
doctrines: Inherent lack of jurisdiction doctrine
Doctrine of nullity of decree
Conversion of agricultural land to non-agricultural use

card.dispute: The appellant owner challenged the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's reassessment of its property's annual value for tax purposes, disputing whether land and building should be assessed together or separately.
issues_decided: Whether land and building appurtenant to each other should be assessed as a single unit under the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980
Whether the High Court was correct in directing the tribunal to separately assess the land and building for determining annual rental value
holdings: Land and building that are appurtenant must be assessed as a single unit under Section 174(1) of the Calcutta Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, and cannot be separated for valuation.
The High Court erred in directing separate assessment under Sections 174(1) and (2); these provisions apply to distinct categories and must not be combined.
doctrines: Liberal construction of taxing statutes in favor of the assessee
Rule of statutory interpretation that distinct provisions must not be conflated

card.dispute: Indian Oil Corporation challenged the High Court's order directing it to convert Shashi Prabha Shukla's petrol pump dealership under a new policy and restrain interference with her possession.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the conversion of the respondent's dealership under IOC's 2004 policy despite its earlier cancellation on grounds of arbitrariness and favouritism.
Whether the respondent was entitled to a fresh dealership at the same location after the original allotment was declared illegal.
Whether the Corporation's failure to conduct a fresh auction after cancellation vitiated the continuation and conversion of the dealership.
holdings: The direction to convert the cancelled dealership into a new one under the 2004 policy perpetuated an illegal benefit and undermined the purpose of cancellation.
A dealership cancelled for arbitrariness and favouritism cannot be revived or converted into a fresh allotment without a transparent and fair process.
The Corporation must initiate a fresh dealership allotment process in public interest, adhering to constitutional norms of fairness, transparency, and non-arbitrariness.
doctrines: Rule of law
Administrative fairness and transparency
Non-arbitrariness under Article 14
State largesse doctrine
Public interest in allocation of resources

card.dispute: The appellant, Hari Shankar Shukla, challenged his conviction by the High Court for culpable homicide not amounting to murder, while the State defended the conviction based on eyewitness testimony of a fatal shooting.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the trial court's acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 304 Part-I IPC?
Whether the prosecution's eyewitness accounts were reliable despite discrepancies in their testimonies?
Whether the sentence imposed by the High Court was appropriate given the nature of the offence and the time already served?
holdings: The High Court correctly reversed the trial court's acquittal because all three eyewitnesses consistently stated that the appellant alone fired the fatal shot, which caused the death.
Discrepancies in the eyewitness accounts regarding the scuffle did not undermine the reliability of their unanimous testimony about the shooting, which was the crucial fact.
The conviction is upheld but the sentence is reduced from 10 years to 6 years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 7,000, considering the appellant’s conduct and time served.
doctrines: Principle of consistency in eyewitness testimony
Appellate court's power to interfere with acquittal if evidence supports conviction
Doctrine of proportionality in sentencing
Common intention under Section 34 IPC

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Harjas Rai Makhija fought against Pushparani Jain and another over whether a decree in her favor was obtained by fraud, thereby invalidating it.
issues_decided: Whether the decree obtained by Pushparani Jain on 4th October, 1999 was vitiated by fraud due to non-disclosure of a Power of Attorney dated 30th April, 1983?
Whether a collateral attack on a final decree is permissible on the ground of alleged fraud based on a certified copy of a photocopied document?
Whether the appellant had sufficient opportunity to prove fraud during earlier proceedings but failed to do so?
holdings: A decree obtained by fraud is a nullity, but fraud must be specifically alleged and proven with evidence of intent to deceive, not merely inferred from non-disclosure.
A collateral attack on a final decree cannot succeed based on unproven allegations and inadmissible evidence, such as a certified copy of a photocopied Power of Attorney.
The appellant had the opportunity to present evidence of fraud during earlier appellate proceedings under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC but failed to do so, and cannot now raise it anew.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 27
doctrines: Fraud vitiates judicial proceedings
Principle of finality of judgments
Collateral attack on decrees
Requirement of due diligence in adducing evidence

card.dispute: The appellant (plaintiff) fought against the respondents (defendants) over the title and possession of a suit property, seeking declaration of title and permanent injunction.
issues_decided: Whether the first Appellate Court was justified in remanding the case to the Trial Court under Order 41 Rule 23-A of the CPC?
Whether the High Court had jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits when it was only hearing a challenge to the remand order under Order 43 Rule 1(u) of the CPC?
Whether the first Appellate Court was right in allowing additional evidence under Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC?
holdings: The first Appellate Court was justified in remanding the case under Order 41 Rule 23-A when a re-trial was necessary after admitting additional evidence.
The High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits in an appeal against a remand order under Order 43 Rule 1(u); it could only examine the legality of the remand.
The first Appellate Court rightly allowed additional documents under Order 41 Rule 27 where they were material and the delay in filing was satisfactorily explained.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 23
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 23-A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 25
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 27
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1(u)
doctrines: Limited jurisdiction of High Court in appeals against remand orders
Principle of fair trial and substantial justice
Proper use of appellate powers under CPC for remand and evidence admission

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the supplementary chargesheet that added charges under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, alleging it was added at the behest of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes to harass them, not based on investigation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash the supplementary chargesheet filed under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act on directions from the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.
Whether external direction to add charges in a criminal case amounts to abuse of process.
Whether a chargesheet can be quashed in part under Section 482 CrPC.
holdings: Directions from an external agency like the National Commission for Scheduled Castes to add charges under the SC/ST Act, without independent police decision, constitute an abuse of process.
The High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash the supplementary chargesheet to the extent it was added under external pressure.
A chargesheet can be quashed in part if only certain charges are vitiated by illegality or abuse of process.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(x)
doctrines: Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 CrPC to prevent abuse of process
Prohibition on external interference in criminal investigation
Principle of quashing charges in part when only some charges are illegal

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the dismissal of their suit for inadequate court fee, arguing that the trial court and High Court wrongly applied a provision of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suit Valuation Act, 1955.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was liable to be dismissed for inadequate court fee due to misapplication of a provision of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suit Valuation Act, 1955
Whether the defendant can challenge the valuation of the suit for court fee purposes as a mixed question of fact and law
Whether a special provision in a state's court fee law overrides general provisions of the Court Fees Act
holdings: A suit cannot be dismissed for inadequate court fee if a special state provision governs the fee and is misapplied; the plaintiff must be given an opportunity to pay the correct fee.
The question of court fee valuation under a specific statutory provision is not a mixed question of fact and law that the defendant can contest to block the suit.
Where a state amendment specifically prescribes court fee for a category of suits, it overrides general provisions of the Court Fees Act.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suit Valuation Act, 1955
Section 7(iv-A) of the U.P. Court Fees Act, as amended
Article 17(iii) of Schedule II of the Court Fees Act, 1870
doctrines: Special provision overrides general provision (lex specialis derogat legi generali)
Court fee is primarily a revenue matter between plaintiff and state, not a weapon for defendant to delay trial
Principle of fair opportunity to cure procedural defects

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction by the High Court, which had reversed the Trial Court's acquittal in a criminal case involving alleged assault and murder on a public road.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's evidence, including ocular and medical testimony, was reliable and sufficient to sustain the conviction?
Whether contradictions and discrepancies in witness statements and investigation lapses vitiated the prosecution's case?
Whether the failure to seal and produce weapons of offence (MOs) and non-explanation of injuries on accused affected the fairness of the trial?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Trial Court's order of acquittal?
holdings: The evidence of prosecution witnesses was inconsistent, filled with contradictions, and lacked credibility, making it insufficient to base a conviction upon.
Serious discrepancies in the investigation, including non-mention of accused names in FIR and unexplained delays, went to the root of the case and warranted acquittal.
Failure to produce and seal weapons of offence, and non-explanation of injuries on accused, created doubt about the prosecution's version and required benefit of doubt to accused.
The High Court erred in convicting the accused without properly addressing material contradictions; the Trial Court's acquittal was restored.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Corroboration of interested witnesses
Reliability of ocular and medical evidence
Adverse inference from unexplained investigation lapses

card.dispute: The appellant company fought with the State of Gujarat and Savarkundla Municipality over its right to automatic renewal of a lease on municipal land for running an oil mill, after constructing a commercial complex and continuing to occupy the land beyond the lease term.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had a right to automatic renewal of the lease deed as a matter of right based on the original lease and arbitration award?
Whether the Municipality could lawfully grant a lease exceeding 10 years without prior State Government permission?
Whether the appellant could use the leased land for commercial purposes unrelated to the original purpose of running an oil mill?
holdings: The appellant has no inherent right to claim automatic renewal of the lease; renewal is not a matter of right but depends on the lessor's discretion and compliance with statutory conditions.
A municipality cannot grant a lease exceeding 10 years without prior permission of the State Government under Section 65(2) of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963.
The leased land must be used for the purpose for which it was originally leased; deviation to commercial use unrelated to the oil mill violates the lease terms and public interest.
doctrines: Lease renewal as a matter of right
Statutory limitation on municipal leasing power
Doctrine of permissible use of leased property

card.dispute: Life Insurance Corporation of India (appellant) fought against Sanjeev Builders Pvt Ltd and others over the impleadment of Kedia Construction Company as a plaintiff in a decades-old suit for specific performance of an agreement of sale.
issues_decided: Whether the order allowing impleadment of a party after 27 years in a suit for specific performance is a 'judgment' under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent enabling a Letters Patent Appeal
Whether the High Court was justified in allowing the impleadment of respondent No.3 as a party under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC after an inordinate delay of 27 years
Whether the application for impleadment was maintainable when filed as a Chamber Summons seeking amendment without first seeking leave to continue the suit under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC
holdings: An order allowing impleadment after 27 years in a suit for specific performance, which affects the valuable rights of the defendant, is a 'judgment' under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent and thus appealable.

The impleadment of a party under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC after 27 years without explanation for delay causes serious prejudice to the defendant and should not be allowed, especially in commercial litigation.

An application for impleadment under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC must be filed in the correct manner seeking leave to continue the suit; a Chamber Summons seeking amendment without such leave is not maintainable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
Letters Patent of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Clause 15
doctrines: Prejudice to substantial rights of defence
Liberal approach to amendment with exceptions for inordinate delay and commercial litigation
Necessary and proper party doctrine in impleadment

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the decree of specific performance granted to the respondent for the sale of a residential property, claiming the agreement to sell was actually a security for a loan.
issues_decided: Whether the agreement to sell was a genuine agreement for sale or a security for a loan transaction.
Whether specific performance of the agreement should be granted in light of equitable considerations under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Whether compensation in lieu of specific performance should be awarded and, if so, the appropriate amount.
holdings: An agreement to sell may be set aside from specific performance if it was entered into under circumstances giving one party an unfair advantage, particularly in a lender-borrower relationship.

Courts must consider equitable factors such as the conduct of parties, nature of the contract, and potential hardship before decreeing specific performance under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
Where specific performance is inequitable, compensation in lieu may be awarded; here, Rs. 15 lakhs was held just compensation for the respondent in place of the property.
doctrines: Equitable discretion in granting specific performance
Unfair advantage in contractual relations
Compensation in lieu of specific performance

card.dispute: The appellant, one of three daughters, challenged the probate granted to her mother under her father's will, seeking its revocation after 36 years on grounds of fraud and undue influence.
issues_decided: Whether the application for revocation of probate under Section 263 of the Indian Succession Act is barred by limitation?
Whether the appellant established just cause for revocation of probate on grounds of fraud or undue influence?
Whether the distinction between probate granted in common form versus solemn form affects the right to challenge it?
holdings: An application for revocation of probate is governed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and must be filed within three years from when the right to apply accrues, which in this case began when the appellant attained majority.
The appellant failed to provide specific particulars or evidence of fraud or undue influence, and general allegations without proof are insufficient to justify revocation of probate.
The form in which probate was granted (common or solemn) does not bar a subsequent challenge; however, the issue is academic when the application is time-barred and lacks merit.
doctrines: Fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved
Limitation begins to run when the right to apply accrues, especially upon attaining majority
Probate operates as judgment in rem

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the validity of land acquisition proceedings for a railway line, claiming the award was invalid and seeking compensation at current market rates.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings were liable to be set aside due to an invalid award under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the writ petition challenging the acquisition was barred by laches.
Whether the appellants could raise a fresh challenge to the acquisition under the Right, Title and Interest provisions of the 2013 Act.
holdings: The award was validly made and acted upon, as compensation was paid, possession taken, and reference proceedings concluded, rendering the challenge to its validity untenable.
The writ petition was barred by laches, as the appellants delayed unreasonably in challenging the acquisition despite having availed remedies under the Act.
Permission to file proceedings under the 2013 Act does not override the legal bar of laches; appellants must still overcome this hurdle to succeed.
doctrines: Laches in land acquisition challenges
Finality of acquisition proceedings after compensation and possession
Limited scope of judicial review after statutory remedies exhausted

card.dispute: The dispute was between M/s Kaushik Coop. Building Society and others over whether the Special Court had jurisdiction to entertain a land grabbing case concerning Survey No.129/68 Paiki, which had already been finally decided in prior litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the principle of res judicata applies to bar the Land Grabbing Case No.44/2000?
Whether the Special Court under the A.P. Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982 had jurisdiction to re-examine title and identity of the suit land already adjudicated?
Whether the High Court was justified in upholding the Special Court's decision without recognizing finality of prior decrees?
holdings: The question of identity and title of the suit property in Survey No.129/68 Paiki was directly and substantially decided in earlier proceedings, particularly in CCCA No.14/1972, and thus operates as res judicata.

The Special Court lacked jurisdiction to re-adjudicate title and property identity once these were finally determined in prior litigation, as the Land Grabbing Act does not override the doctrine of res judicata.
The High Court erred in not recognizing the finality of prior judgments and failed to intervene despite a manifest error by the Special Court in ignoring binding precedents on res judicata.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act, 1982, Sections 2(d) and 2(e)
doctrines: Res judicata
Constructive res judicata
Jurisdictional facts
Finality of judicial decisions

card.dispute: The appellants, a private medical college and its affiliated university, challenged amendments to the Himachal Pradesh Private Medical Educational Institutions Act, 2006, which required their constituent college to obtain affiliation from Himachal Pradesh University, thereby infringing on the autonomy of their own university established under a separate state law.
issues_decided: Whether Sections 3(6), 3(6a), and 3(6b) of the 2006 Act, as amended, violate the autonomy of a private university established under the 2010 Act?
Whether the requirement for a constituent college of a private university to obtain affiliation from another university is constitutionally valid?
Whether the amended definition of 'Private Medical Educational Institution' in Section 2(j) of the 2006 Act can be read down to save the constitutionality of Section 3(6a)?
holdings: A private university established under a special state legislation has the autonomy to affiliate its constituent colleges, and this power cannot be overridden by a general law regulating admissions and fees in private medical institutions.

The requirement under Section 3(6a) of the 2006 Act that private medical institutions must affiliate with Himachal Pradesh University violates the autonomy of a private university created under a separate statute and is therefore unconstitutional.

Section 3(6a) cannot be saved by reading down because striking out 'Himachal Pradesh' would create ambiguity and conflict with the statutory limitations on the private university’s power to affiliate other institutions.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Private Medical Educational Institutions (Regulation of Admission and Fixation of Fee) Act, 2006, Section 2(j), Section 3(6), Section 3(6a), Section 3(6b)
The Maharishi Markandeshwar University (Establishment and Regulation) Act, 2010, Section 7
doctrines: Autonomy of universities
Doctrine of repugnancy
Principle of constitutional validity and reasonableness
Doctrine of reading down

card.dispute: The appellants challenged their conviction and sentence in a criminal case arising from a fatal assault during a family feud over a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction of the appellants was legally sustainable based on the evidence?
Whether the sentence awarded to the appellants was excessive and required modification?
holdings: The conviction of the appellants was upheld as it was supported by prosecution evidence and concurrent findings of the lower courts.

The sentence was found to be excessive; it was modified to five years for appellants 1, 3, and 5, and reduced to time already served for appellants 2 and 4, applying the principle of proportionality in sentencing.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 324 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 355 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 506(ii) read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 302 read with Section 149
Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II read with Section 149
doctrines: Principle of proportionality in sentencing
Doctrine of reformation of offenders
Collective conscience of society
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts

card.dispute: An 84-year-old man appealed against a court order allowing his 62-year-old former companion, who claimed to be his wife, to reside in his property under the Domestic Violence Act.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent had a right to reside in the appellant's property under the Domestic Violence Act despite never having lived with him in that household.
Whether the High Court was justified in withdrawing an appeal from the appellate court and transferring it to itself.
holdings: The right to reside in a shared household under the Domestic Violence Act requires actual past cohabitation in that household, which was absent here; thus, the respondent could not claim protection under Section 17.

The High Court erred in withdrawing the appeal to itself without reason, depriving the appellant of an effective appellate remedy, and the matter must be heard by an Additional Sessions Judge in Bangalore.
provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 2(f)
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 2(s)
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 17
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 19
doctrines: Right to residence in shared household under DV Act requires factual cohabitation
Principle of effective remedy and access to justice

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the Wakf Tribunal's order, which had dismissed a suit seeking cancellation of a sale deed on the grounds that the property in question was Wakf property.
issues_decided: Whether the property in question was validly notified as Wakf property under the Wakf Act, 1954 or 1995.
Whether the civil court or Wakf Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging the non-inclusion of a property in the Wakf list after a long delay.
Whether the plaintiff had a valid cause of action to file the suit for cancellation of the sale deed.
holdings: A property becomes Wakf only upon formal notification in the Official Gazette following a survey and due inquiry; mere claim or belief does not suffice.
Jurisdiction to decide Wakf-related disputes lies exclusively with the Wakf Tribunal, and civil courts are barred from entertaining such suits under Section 85 of the Waqf Act, 1995.
A challenge to the non-inclusion of property in the Wakf list must be made within one year of the Gazette notification; a delay of 50 years renders the suit meritless and barred by law.
doctrines: Finality of Gazette notification under the Wakf Act
Exclusive jurisdiction of the Wakf Tribunal
Doctrine of delay and laches in statutory disputes
Merger of Survey Commissioner's report with Gazette notification

card.dispute: The company (Unichem Laboratories Ltd) filed eviction suits against former employees and their families occupying industrial housing quarters after retirement, which the High Court dismissed, holding the company lacked locus standi; the company appealed.
issues_decided: Whether the civil court has jurisdiction to try the eviction suit under the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act, 1955, despite Section 13 of the Act?
Whether the company had the right to file an eviction suit against the workers or their successors in occupation?
Whether a tenancy relationship existed between the company and the employee in respect of the allotted quarter?
What is the status of the employee's occupation of the quarter after retirement from service?
holdings: Section 13 of the Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act does not oust the jurisdiction of civil courts; exclusion of jurisdiction must be explicit or clearly implied and is to be strictly construed.
The company had locus standi to file the eviction suit as it was the allottee of the quarters from the State and had granted them to employees under a contractual arrangement.
A tenancy-like relationship arose between the employer and employee regarding the quarter, making the employer entitled to seek eviction for breach of terms.
The tenancy terminates upon cessation of employment; continued occupation after retirement is unauthorized, and the employer can seek eviction.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Industrial Housing Act, 1955, Section 13
doctrines: Strict construction of jurisdiction ouster clauses
Privity of contract in employer-employee tenancy
Termination of service tenancy upon employment cessation

card.dispute: The appellant (Mohan Kumar) fought against the State of Madhya Pradesh and others over ownership and possession of land (Survey No. 899) allegedly encroached upon by public authorities for construction of temples, Darghas, latrines, and sewer lines.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appellant's appeal and the suit without affording an opportunity to prove ownership due to non-examination of the vendor?
Whether the High Court erred in overturning the Trial Court's finding on ownership without remanding the case for additional evidence?
holdings: The High Court should not have dismissed the suit solely because the appellant did not examine the vendor; instead, it should have remanded the case for the appellant to adduce further evidence to prove title.

Where a party's title is challenged on procedural grounds and no cross-objection is filed by the respondents, the appellate court must not dismiss the suit entirely but may remand it for retrial on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 41 Rule 23A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 27 Rule 5B
Madhya Pradesh Public Premises and Devasthanam (Regulation) Act, Section 4(2)
doctrines: Remand for fair trial
Appellate court's duty to allow opportunity to prove title
Judicial encouragement of settlement in suits against the government

card.dispute: The appellant sought to amend his plaint to include a claim for a share in the sale proceeds of a property sold in 2000, which the trial court and High Court rejected on grounds of limitation and post-trial amendment, leading to an appeal in the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether an application for amendment of pleadings under Order VI Rule 17 CPC can be allowed after the commencement of trial when evidence has already been led on the amended issues?
Whether the claim for a share in the sale proceeds of a partitioned joint family property is governed by Article 110 of the Limitation Act, with a 12-year limitation, or by a shorter period?
holdings: An amendment application under Order VI Rule 17 CPC may be allowed even after trial has commenced if no prejudice is caused to the opposing party and evidence has already been led on the amended pleadings.

At the stage of considering an amendment, it is premature to dismiss the application on limitation grounds when the nature and existence of the plaintiff’s share in the property requires determination based on evidence.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Amendment of pleadings to serve ends of justice
No dismissal on technical grounds in absence of prejudice
Limitation to be determined based on cause of action and nature of right

card.dispute: The landlord (Nidhi) sought possession of a non-residential rented premises for bona fide personal requirement, which the tenant (Ram Kripal Sharma) resisted; the tenant challenged the release order before the High Court, which set it aside on grounds that the landlord's requirement ceased after her marriage.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord's bona fide requirement for possession of the rented premises continued despite her marriage and relocation during the pendency of the appeal?
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the release order based on subsequent events without considering comparative hardship?
Whether the court can take note of subsequent events in landlord-tenant proceedings under the U.P. Urban Buildings Act?
holdings: A landlord's bona fide requirement for possession does not automatically cease upon marriage and relocation, especially when the need is for accommodating family members like parents and grandparents.

The High Court erred in denying possession without considering the comparative hardship to the landlord’s family, who lacked alternative accommodation, while the tenant could shift business without significant loss.
Courts may consider subsequent events during litigation to mould relief, provided it promotes substantial justice, does not violate fair procedure, and fundamentally affects the rights or relief.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
doctrines: Bona fide personal requirement of landlord
Comparative hardship in eviction cases
Crystallisation of rights and judicial consideration of subsequent events

card.dispute: The appellant sued to set aside a sale deed but filed the suit against a defendant who had already died; the dispute was whether the legal representatives of the deceased could be brought on record under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC after the application under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC was dismissed.
issues_decided: Whether an application to bring legal representatives on record is maintainable under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC when the defendant was already dead at the time of filing the suit?
Whether a court can treat an application filed under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC as one under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to prevent failure of justice?
Whether the rejection of an application under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC bars the subsequent invocation of Order 1 Rule 10 CPC for impleading legal representatives?
holdings: Order 1 Rule 10 CPC applies to add necessary parties at any stage of the suit, including legal representatives of a deceased person who was already dead before the suit, as the suit against a dead person is a nullity.
Courts may treat an application filed under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC as one under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to prevent injustice due to technicalities, provided the party acted in good faith.
Dismissal of an application under Order 22 Rule 4 CPC does not bar a subsequent application under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC, especially when the legal heirs are necessary parties to the litigation.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 1 Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 22 Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 6
doctrines: Substantial justice over technicalities
Liberal interpretation of procedural rules
Courts' inherent powers to prevent failure of justice

card.dispute: The dispute was between the appellant, a managing partner of a firm, and the respondent, a power of attorney holder, over whether prosecution could be initiated against a company beyond the limitation period under the Negotiable Instruments Act based on a dishonoured cheque.
issues_decided: Whether a prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act can be initiated against a company after the statutory limitation period by invoking Section 319 of the CrPC?
Whether cognizance of an offence under Section 138 can be taken without identifying the accused at the time of filing the complaint?
