Whether the Collector can be directed to determine damages for pre-acquisition possession loss due to submergence?
holdings: Interest under Section 34 cannot be awarded for any period prior to the Section 4 notification; it can only be granted from the date of such notification if possession was effectively lost by then.

Landowners whose land was submerged before acquisition proceedings began are entitled to claim damages or rent for the period prior to Section 4 notification, to be determined by the Collector under Section 48.
The Collector must examine whether the land was submerged from 1991 onward and determine the quantum of damages, if any, within six months after hearing the parties.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon issuance of Section 4 notification and award
Entitlement to damages for pre-acquisition possession loss
Limitation on interest under Section 34 to post-notification period
Capitalization method for determining market value

card.dispute: The appellant, Dr. Nallapareddy Sridhar Reddy, challenged the High Court's order directing the framing of additional charges under Sections 406 and 420 IPC in a dowry harassment case initiated by his father-in-law.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in directing the framing of additional charges under Sections 406 and 420 IPC after the initial charge-sheet was filed?
Whether the material on record was sufficient to prima facie attract the offences under Sections 406 and 420 IPC at the stage of framing of charges?
holdings: The High Court has the power under Section 216 CrPC to add or alter charges at any time before judgment, provided the accused is not prejudiced and a fair trial is ensured.

At the stage of framing charges, the court need not evaluate the full probative value of evidence; it is sufficient if there is a prima facie link between the material and the ingredients of the alleged offence under Sections 406 and 420 IPC.
doctrines: Prima facie satisfaction in framing of charges
Power of court to alter or add charges under Section 216 CrPC
Test of prejudice in alteration of charges
Distinction between framing of charge and conviction

card.dispute: Chunthuram appealed against his conviction for the murder of Laxman, claiming lack of reliable evidence despite the prosecution alleging a land dispute and prior animosity as motive.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution evidence, including eyewitness testimony and Test Identification Parade (TIP), was reliable enough to sustain the conviction?
Whether the recovery of weapons and forensic evidence could be used to link the appellant to the crime?
Whether the motive of land dispute and prior family enmity was sufficiently established?
Whether the conduct of the eyewitness was consistent with human nature and credible?
holdings: The eyewitness testimony was unreliable due to poor eyesight, inconsistent hearing claims, and failure to report the incident, making it unsafe to base conviction on it.

The recovered weapons and forensic evidence could not be linked to the crime due to absence of bloodstain reports and non-production of chemical analysis, warranting adverse inference against prosecution.
The Test Identification Parade was vitiated by police presence and procedural flaws, rendering it inadmissible as substantive evidence.
The alleged motive of land dispute and prior murder charge was speculative and insufficient to support conviction, especially without proximate connection to the incident.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases when two views are possible
Test Identification Parade not substantive evidence
Adverse inference from non-production of forensic evidence
Conduct contrary to human nature affecting witness credibility

card.dispute: Mining leaseholders challenged the denial of lease extension for periods when mining was obstructed due to judicial orders, seeking relief from the State of Uttar Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether mining leases can be extended for periods when operations were obstructed by judicial interdicts.
Whether the State is obligated to refund security deposits and advance royalties paid during obstructed periods.
Whether interest can be awarded on such refunded amounts in the absence of statutory or contractual obligation.
holdings: Lease extension for obstructed periods cannot be granted if it violates statutory provisions or subsequent transparent auction policies, especially when leases do not contractually provide for such extension.
The State must refund security deposits and advance royalties paid during periods when mining was obstructed and could not be carried out.
Under Article 142, the Court can direct refund with simple interest at 9% per annum on blocked funds to do complete justice, even in absence of statutory obligation.
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Principle of complete justice under Article 142
Legislative intent in mining lease policy

card.dispute: Seven accused appealed their conviction for murder and related offences arising from a mob assault that caused the death of Govind Singh and injuries to Dhanwaram in Chhattisgarh in 1998.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt the involvement of the appellants in the unlawful assembly and the murder of Govind Singh under Section 302/149 IPC?
Whether the appellants Khemuram (A-8) and Lakhan (A-13) were entitled to the benefit of doubt based on lack of corroborative evidence?
Whether the conviction should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part I IPC?
holdings: The prosecution proved the involvement of Bharosaram, Duleshwar, Bhanjan Singh, Keshav Prasad, and Nand Kumar in the unlawful assembly that caused the death, justifying their conviction under Section 302/149 IPC.
Khemuram and Lakhan were entitled to the benefit of doubt due to lack of reliable and corroborated evidence linking them to the scene and the assault, warranting their acquittal.
The brutality of the attack, including dragging the deceased and multiple blunt force injuries, demonstrated intent to cause death, making Section 304 IPC inapplicable.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Common object of unlawful assembly under Section 149 IPC
Corroboration of witness testimony
Hostile witness evaluation

card.dispute: The Food Corporation of India challenged the Bombay High Court's decision upholding the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation's demand for property tax on FCI's godowns built on land owned by the Central Government.
issues_decided: Whether the Food Corporation of India is liable to pay property tax on land owned by the Central Government under the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, 1888
Whether the exemption under Article 285 of the Constitution applies to property of the Union used by a statutory corporation like FCI
Whether service charges for utilities like water and sewerage can be levied on FCI despite tax immunity under Article 285
holdings: The property being owned by the Central Government, FCI is exempt from payment of property tax under Article 285 of the Constitution, which prohibits state taxation on Union property.
The exemption under Article 285 applies even when the property is occupied and used by a statutory body like FCI, as it remains property of the Union.
While FCI is immune from property tax, it remains liable to pay service charges for utilities like water and sewerage, which are fees for services rendered and not taxes on property.
doctrines: Tax immunity of Union property under Article 285
Distinction between tax and fee for services rendered
Doctrine of occupation not overriding constitutional tax exemption

card.dispute: The appellant challenged his conviction for possession of cannabis under the NDPS Act, arguing that ownership of the house where drugs were found was not properly established and investigation was flawed.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved conscious possession of the contraband by the appellant beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the conviction based solely on voter list entries, without investigating the sale deed and panchayat records, was legally sustainable?
Whether the failure to investigate exculpatory evidence violated the right to a fair trial under Article 21?
holdings: Conviction under the NDPS Act cannot be based on presumptions of ownership alone; the prosecution must prove conscious possession beyond reasonable doubt.
Reliance on outdated voter list entries without verifying subsequent sale deeds or panchayat records renders the conviction based on conjecture and insufficient evidence.
A flawed and incomplete investigation that ignores available exculpatory evidence violates the right to a fair trial under Article 21, warranting acquittal.
provisions: Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 8C
Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 20(b)(ii)(c)
Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 35
Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, Section 54
doctrines: Presumption under NDPS Act is rebuttable and does not replace prosecution's burden to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
Right to fair trial includes right to fair investigation under Article 21
Gross misappreciation of evidence by lower courts justifies interference under Article 136

card.dispute: The appellant, Jugut Ram, challenged his conviction under Section 302 IPC and life sentence for murdering the deceased during a land dispute, claiming lack of premeditation and intent to kill.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had the intention to cause death under Section 302 IPC when he assaulted the deceased with a lathi on the head?
Whether the conviction should be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC given the circumstances of the assault?
Whether the evidence of witnesses related to the deceased could sustain a conviction under Section 302 IPC?
holdings: An assault on the head with a lathi does not automatically imply intention to cause death; the nature, manner, and context must be considered to determine intent.

When death results from a sudden assault in the heat of passion without premeditation, and the accused also suffers injuries, the offence may amount to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC.
The fact that witnesses are related to the deceased does not render their testimony inadmissible, but such evidence must be scrutinized carefully and supported by corroborative evidence.
provisions: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
doctrines: Doctrine of intention vs. knowledge in homicide cases
Principle of sudden fight in the heat of passion
Credibility of interested witnesses

card.dispute: The appellants (Iqbal Basith and others) sued the respondents (N. Subbalakshmi and others) for permanent injunction to prevent encroachment on their property; the dispute centered on whether the appellants had lawful possession despite the lower courts dismissing the suit.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants proved lawful possession of the suit property
Whether the appellants proved interference by the respondents with their possession
Whether the courts below erred in rejecting documentary evidence due to non-production of originals
Whether the identity of the suit property was established
holdings: Lawful possession can be established through long-standing tax payments, official records, and possession confirmed by commissioners, even without formal title adjudication.
An adverse inference may be drawn against a party who fails to appear as a witness and submit to cross-examination, especially when possession is disputed.
Old documents (over 30 years) produced from proper custody are entitled to presumption of genuineness under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, and rejection without valid reason is perverse.
Courts should not decide title issues in injunction suits when possession and identity are established through municipal records and other reliable evidence.
doctrines: Presumption of regularity of official acts
Adverse inference under Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act
Relevance of Section 90 of the Evidence Act for ancient documents
Separation of title and possession in suits for injunction

card.dispute: The appellants sought to prove a copy of a will by secondary evidence after the original was lost, while the respondents opposed this, leading to a dispute over the admissibility of the secondary evidence and the validity of mutations based on a rival will.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants established the foundational facts necessary to admit secondary evidence of a lost will under Sections 65 and 66 of the Indian Evidence Act?
Whether the High Court erred in holding that the existence of the original will was not proved?
holdings: Secondary evidence of a document may be admitted if the party shows that the original is lost or in the possession of an adverse party and that foundational facts for non-production are established.
The High Court erred in rejecting secondary evidence without properly evaluating evidence that established the will's existence, including witness testimony and admissions by revenue officials.
doctrines: Secondary evidence as an exception to primary evidence
Foundational facts requirement for admissibility of secondary evidence

card.dispute: The appellant Gurcharan Singh challenged his conviction for abetting his wife's suicide under Section 306 IPC, arguing lack of evidence of mens rea or active abetment.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction under Section 306 IPC can be sustained based on conjecture in absence of direct evidence of abetment?
Whether mens rea for abetment of suicide was established in this case?
Whether there was sufficient evidence of cruelty or harassment proximate to the suicide?
holdings: A conviction under Section 306 IPC requires clear evidence of active abetment and mens rea, not mere conjecture about circumstances.
Mens rea for abetment must be visibly established; it cannot be presumed from the fact of suicide alone.
Absence of evidence showing persistent cruelty or harassment proximate to the suicide renders the conviction unsustainable.
doctrines: Mens rea in abetment
Requirement of active act in abetment of suicide
Prohibition of conviction based on conjecture
Scrutiny of evidence in dowry death and abetment cases

card.dispute: The Hari Krishna Mandir Trust challenged the Maharashtra government's refusal to modify a town planning scheme to reflect its ownership of a private road, which the state claimed had vested in it under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition on the ground of disputed questions of fact.
Whether the private road in question had vested in the State under Section 88 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966.
Whether the proposed modification of the town planning scheme was permissible under Section 91 of the Act.
holdings: The High Court has jurisdiction to decide writ petitions involving disputed questions of fact and should not automatically relegate parties to a civil suit.
Land does not vest in the State under Section 88 of the Act unless acquisition proceedings are initiated; mere inclusion in a scheme does not result in vesting.
Modification of a town planning scheme to correct ownership records of a private road, not acquired by the State, is permissible under Section 91 and does not amount to a substantial alteration.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 88
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 91
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 125
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 126
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 65
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Section 66
doctrines: Vesting of land under town planning schemes requires compliance with acquisition procedures
Writ jurisdiction is not barred by disputed questions of fact
Principle of complete justice under Article 142

card.dispute: Hukum Chand Deswal accused Satish Raj Deswal of contempt for failing to file an undertaking, pay outstanding dues, and allegedly damaging property before vacating the premises as directed by the Supreme Court.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent committed wilful disobedience of the Supreme Court's order dated 22.2.2019 by not filing an undertaking and not paying alleged outstanding dues?
Whether the respondent caused damage to the suit property while vacating, amounting to contempt?
Whether the petitioner is entitled to initiate contempt proceedings for disputes that could be resolved in execution proceedings?
holdings: The failure to file an undertaking or pay disputed dues does not constitute wilful disobedience when the obligation was ambiguous and subject to determination by the executing court.

Alleged damage to the property, such as leaving debris, does not amount to defacement or wilful disobedience, especially when the property resumed operations shortly after, and the issue involves complex factual disputes.
Contempt jurisdiction cannot be used to decide substantive disputes not finally adjudicated in the original order; such matters must be resolved in execution proceedings.
provisions: Rules to Regulate Proceedings for Contempt of the Supreme Court, 1975, Rule 3
doctrines: Contempt must be based on clear and specific directions; ambiguity precludes contempt liability
Contempt jurisdiction is not a substitute for adjudication of disputed factual or legal claims
Principle of finality and clarity in orders for contempt to lie

card.dispute: Hitesh Verma challenged the High Court's dismissal of his petition to quash a criminal charge-sheet filed against him under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, alleging that the case arose from a property dispute and not caste-based harassment.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations in the FIR disclose an offence under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, particularly Section 3(1)(r), when the dispute is primarily over land possession?
Whether a charge-sheet can be quashed in part under Section 482 CrPC if certain charges do not make out an offence under the Atrocities Act?
Whether the mere fact that the complainant belongs to a Scheduled Caste is sufficient to attract offences under the Atrocities Act without proof of caste-based animus?
holdings: An offence under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act is not made out merely because the complainant belongs to a Scheduled Caste; there must be specific allegations that the accused targeted the victim on caste grounds.
The High Court can quash a charge-sheet in part under Section 482 CrPC if certain charges constitute an abuse of process or do not disclose a cognizable offence.
In property disputes, caste-based abuse must be central to the allegations; otherwise, invoking the Atrocities Act is not justified, and the court may intervene to prevent misuse of the law.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(r)
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(e)
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(2)(v)
doctrines: Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 CrPC to prevent abuse of process
Requirement of caste-based animus for invoking the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
Principle of proportionality in quashing criminal proceedings
Judicial restraint in interfering with investigations, except in cases of clear abuse

card.dispute: The Hospitality Association of Mudumalai challenged the state government's notification of an elephant corridor on their private forest land, arguing it infringed on their property rights and was based on flawed data.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government had the authority to notify an elephant corridor on private forest land.
Whether commercial activities like resorts in ecologically sensitive areas can be restricted to protect wildlife.
Whether the Expert Committee's identification of the elephant corridor was scientifically valid and legally sound.
Whether the variance in acreage between the Expert Committee's recommendation and the government order was arbitrary.
holdings: The State Government has the power to notify elephant corridors on private forest land to protect wildlife habitats under environmental laws and constitutional mandates.
Commercial activities, including resorts, may be restricted in ecologically sensitive zones to uphold the precautionary principle and protect wildlife.
The State Government's adoption of the Expert Committee’s recommendations is valid, especially where human-elephant conflict and elephant presence are documented.
Alleged discrepancies in the notified acreage require factual inquiry; hence, an independent committee must investigate the claims of arbitrariness.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Preservation of Private Forests Act, 1949
doctrines: Precautionary Principle
Sustainable Development
Public Trust Doctrine

card.dispute: The appellants (landlords) fought the respondents (tenants' legal heirs) over eviction from three shop rooms, seeking eviction on grounds including subletting of one portion without consent.
issues_decided: Whether subletting of a part of a single tenanted premises entitles the landlord to eviction from the entire premises under the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
Whether a new legal plea regarding eviction based on partial subletting can be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court
holdings: Subletting of any portion of a single tenanted premises entitles the landlord to seek eviction from the entire premises if the lease prohibits subletting, as per Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Act.

A pure question of law, such as the legal consequence of partial subletting in a single tenancy, can be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court if the factual foundation is established on record.
provisions: Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965, Section 11(2)(b), Section 11(2)(c), Section 11(4)(i)
doctrines: Pure question of law doctrine
Single tenancy doctrine
Legal consequences of subletting under rent control legislation

card.dispute: The appellants, bank officials, challenged the initiation of criminal proceedings based on a complaint by a borrower alleging fraud in the disbursement of a loan and subsequent sale of mortgaged property under the SARFAESI Act.
issues_decided: Whether criminal proceedings can be initiated against bank officials for actions taken in the course of sanctioning and disbursing a loan governed by the SARFAESI Act?
Whether the police investigation and FIR in this case amount to an abuse of process given the existence of an alternative remedy under the SARFAESI Act?
Whether the dispute between the borrower and the bank is essentially contractual and not suited for criminal prosecution?
holdings: Criminal proceedings cannot be invoked for disputes arising from loan disbursement and recovery actions under the SARFAESI Act when the matter is essentially contractual and alternative remedies before DRT/DRAT are available.
Allowing police investigation in such cases would amount to permitting a review of SARFAESI proceedings, which is impermissible and undermines the statutory framework.
The borrower’s delay in raising grievances and resorting to criminal complaint after dismissal of remedies under SARFAESI constitutes an abuse of process of law.
provisions: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Securities Interest Act, 2002, Section 32
doctrines: Alternative remedy doctrine
Abuse of process of law
Statutory exclusivity of remedies under SARFAESI Act
Immunity for actions taken in good faith under Section 32 of SARFAESI Act

card.dispute: The appellant, an IAS officer in Bihar, challenged the CBI's investigation into corruption allegations without prior consent from the Bihar government, claiming territorial jurisdiction and procedural invalidity.
issues_decided: Whether the CBI can investigate an offence allegedly committed in Delhi without the prior consent of the State of Bihar under Section 6 of the DSPE Act, 1946, when one of the accused is a public servant employed by the State of Bihar.
Whether a proviso in the Bihar government's general consent notification requiring prior state consent for investigation of its public servants applies to offences committed outside Bihar.
Whether differential treatment of public servants based on state employment violates Article 14 of the Constitution when it impedes CBI investigations into corruption.
holdings: The CBI has jurisdiction to investigate offences committed in Delhi under the DSPE Act, 1946, without requiring consent from the State of Bihar, even if a state public servant is involved.

The proviso in Bihar's 1996 notification requiring prior state consent for investigating its officials does not apply to offences committed outside Bihar, as state police lack jurisdiction over such offences.

Executive conditions that classify public servants based on state versus central employment for investigation purposes violate Article 14 if they create arbitrary distinctions and impede anti-corruption investigations.
provisions: Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, Section 2
Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, Section 3
Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, Section 6
doctrines: Territorial jurisdiction of investigation
Doctrine of equal protection under Article 14
Doctrine of repugnance between executive instructions and statutory powers
Principle against approbation and reprobation

card.dispute: The heirs of Ambalal Patel challenged the state's possession of their land based on a 1986 Panchnama, claiming it was illegal, while the state argued the challenge was barred by delay and laches.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petition filed in 2001 was barred by delay and laches given the 1986 possession action?
Whether the legal heirs were entitled to challenge the validity of the possession Panchnama after a lapse of 14 years?
Whether the notice under Section 10(5) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1976 was invalid due to service on a deceased person?
holdings: A writ petition challenging possession taken in 1986 cannot be entertained after 14 years without sufficient explanation, and is barred by laches.
Mere ignorance of legal intricacies or reliance on a deceased power of attorney does not excuse inordinate delay in challenging acquisition proceedings.
Service of notice on a deceased owner does not invalidate the process if prior valid service occurred and other legal heirs were part of subsequent proceedings.
doctrines: Laches in writ petitions
Constructive and physical possession in land acquisition
Service of notice on legal heirs in acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants, a charitable trust and its trustees, challenged the appointment of an arbitrator based on an insufficiently stamped lease deed containing an arbitration clause, which the respondents sought to enforce for dispute resolution.
issues_decided: Whether a court can act upon an arbitration agreement contained in an instrument that is not duly stamped under the Stamp Act?

Whether the High Court erred in appointing an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, when the underlying lease deed was insufficiently stamped and the deficit stamp duty and penalty had not been paid?
Whether the respondents' conduct and inconsistent pleadings disentitled them to seek relief in arbitration?
holdings: A court cannot act upon an arbitration agreement contained in an instrument that is not duly stamped; the court must examine stamping at the outset, even if no objection is raised.

An unstamped or insufficiently stamped instrument cannot be acted upon or used to refer parties to arbitration until the deficit stamp duty and penalty are paid under Section 35 or Section 40 of the Stamp Act.
The respondents’ failure to pay the deficit stamp duty and their contradictory legal stands before different courts rendered them ineligible for relief under the Arbitration Act.
doctrines: Impounding of insufficiently stamped documents
Non-justiciability of unstamped instruments
Court's duty to examine stamping suo motu
Arbitrability dependent on validity of underlying contract

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Kirpa Ram (defendant No. 4) appealed against the dismissal of their second appeal in a suit for permanent injunction filed by Surender Deo Gaur and others, who claimed ownership and possession of land in Khasra No. 238, Village Basai Darapur, Delhi.
issues_decided: Whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction to decide the suit for permanent injunction despite the bar under Section 85 of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954?
Whether the High Court was obligated to frame a substantial question of law under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure while dismissing a second appeal?
holdings: The Civil Court had plenary jurisdiction to decide the injunction suit as no express or implied bar under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure was established, and the dispute over possession could not be resolved under the Land Revenue Act machinery.

The High Court is not required to frame a substantial question of law under Section 100 CPC if it finds no error in the first appellate decree and concludes that no substantial question of law arises.
doctrines: ubi jus ibi remedium
implied bar of jurisdiction
plenary jurisdiction of civil courts

card.dispute: The tenant company was accused of fabricating evidence by altering a balance sheet to falsely claim reduced share capital in a rent control dispute over jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner company committed perjury by fabricating evidence before the Supreme Court.
Whether the affidavit filed by the company's representative contained false statements based on altered documents.
holdings: The court found prima facie evidence that the company altered the balance sheet by replacing 'Weighted Average number of Equity Shares' with 'number of Equity Shares as on 1/4/07' to misrepresent share capital, constituting fabrication of evidence.
A prima facie case of perjury was also established against the company’s representative who affirmed the veracity of the altered documents in an affidavit.
provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Section 340 read with Section 195(1)(b)
doctrines: Prima facie case of perjury
Fabrication of evidence before judicial forums
Judicial reliance on authentic documentary evidence

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents fought over whether the plaintiff's relinquishment of her share in the coparcenary property through a release deed executed by her mother during her minority was valid, and whether the property of the deceased coparcener devolved by survivorship or under the Hindu Succession Act.
issues_decided: Whether the interest of a deceased male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary devolves by survivorship or under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act when there are Class I female heirs
Whether a mother can validly execute a release deed on behalf of her minor daughter relinquishing her share in coparcenary property
Whether the Karta of a joint family can act as guardian for a minor member when the minor's share is being relinquished in his favour
holdings: The interest of a deceased male Hindu in coparcenary property devolves under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, not by survivorship, if there are Class I female heirs.

A mother, as natural guardian, can execute a release deed on behalf of her minor child, but such a deed is voidable, not void, and must be challenged within three years of the minor attaining majority.
The Karta of a Hindu Undivided Family cannot act as guardian of a minor when there is a conflict of interest, such as when the minor's share is being relinquished in favour of the Karta.
doctrines: Devolution of interest in coparcenary by succession, not survivorship, in presence of female Class I heirs
Tenancy in common among heirs under Section 19
Voidability of transactions by natural guardians affecting minor's property without court sanction

card.dispute: The appellant, M. Vanaja, claimed to be the adopted daughter of the respondent and her husband, seeking a declaration of adoption and a partition of their property, which the respondent denied.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant proved that she was validly adopted by the respondent and her husband under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956
Whether the appellant is entitled to a declaration as the adopted daughter of the deceased couple
Whether the appellant has a right to claim partition of the properties owned by the adoptive father
holdings: Adoption under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 must strictly comply with statutory conditions, including proof of the ceremony of giving and taking in adoption.
Mere treatment as a child in school, service, or other records does not prove valid adoption without evidence of the required ceremonial act and intent.
The consent of the wife and the performance of the act of giving and taking are mandatory conditions for a valid adoption under Sections 7 and 11 of the Act.
The judgment in L. Debi Prasad is inapplicable to adoptions occurring after the 1956 Act, as post-Act adoptions require strict compliance with statutory formalities.
provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 6
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 7
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 9
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 11
doctrines: Strict compliance with statutory adoption formalities
Doctrine of mandatory conditions for valid adoption
Rejection of adoption by conduct in absence of statutory compliance

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the rejection of their application to impound power of attorney documents in a partition suit on grounds of insufficient stamp duty under the Orissa Stamp Act.
issues_decided: Whether the power of attorney in question amounts to a conveyance under the Orissa Stamp Act requiring higher stamp duty upon transfer of possession.
Whether a document objected to for insufficient stamp duty must be decided immediately or can be deferred until final judgment.
Whether the trial court erred in admitting the power of attorney without determining its stamp duty liability based on possession transfer.
holdings: A power of attorney transferring possession of immovable property is deemed a conveyance under Article 23 of the Orissa Stamp Act and attracts higher stamp duty.

An objection regarding insufficient stamp duty must generally be decided before proceeding further, but if the nature of the document depends on factual findings, the decision may be deferred until final adjudication.
The trial court must determine the admissibility of a power of attorney for insufficient stamp duty after evaluating evidence on whether possession was transferred.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Article 23 (as amended by Orissa Act No. 1 of 2003)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIII Rule 8
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIII Rule 4
doctrines: Deemed conveyance doctrine under stamp law
Principle of deferred adjudication of admissibility based on factual determination
Judicial duty to impound insufficiently stamped instruments

card.dispute: The Madhya Pradesh Housing Board appealed against a High Court judgment that quashed its modification of a layout plan, changing land use from commercial to residential, and declared lease deeds to third-party purchasers void.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in applying the doctrine of promissory estoppel to prevent modification of a layout plan?
Whether the modification of land use from commercial to residential, in accordance with statutory provisions, could be invalidated?
Whether the High Court should have entertained a writ petition after a delay of seven years, during which third-party rights were created?
Whether the authorities can change land use in a layout plan without violating development and zonal plans?
holdings: The doctrine of promissory estoppel does not bar statutory authorities from modifying land use if the change complies with the law and development plans.
A layout plan can be modified if the change adheres to the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973 and conforms to development and zonal plans.
Unexplained delay of seven years in filing the writ petition, coupled with creation of third-party rights, warrants refusal of relief in writ jurisdiction.
Courts should not interfere with administrative decisions on land use that follow statutory norms, especially when public interest and third-party rights are involved.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, Section 31
Madhya Pradesh Housing and Infrastructure Development Board Act, 1972
Madhya Pradesh Bhumi Vikas Rules, 1984, Rule 49
Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, Sections 17, 21, 49
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Laches and delay in judicial remedies
Separation of powers in land use planning
Protection of third-party rights

card.dispute: The appellant (plaintiff's legal heirs) challenged the dismissal of a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell, claiming the High Court failed to properly adjudicate the issues of limitation and the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, as the first appellate court, is required to record reasoned findings on all issues of fact and law?
Whether the High Court's cryptic order dismissing the appeal without re-appreciating evidence or giving reasons amounts to a failure to exercise its appellate jurisdiction properly?
holdings: The first appellate court must address all issues of fact and law, record its own findings, and give reasons in support of its decision, as mandated by Order XLI Rule 31 of the CPC.

A cryptic order by the High Court that merely affirms the trial court's decision without independent reasoning or re-appreciation of evidence fails to meet the requirements of appellate jurisdiction and renders the judgment infirm.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 31
doctrines: First appeal as a continuation of the trial court proceedings
Conscious application of mind by the appellate court
Re-hearing on facts and law in first appeal

card.dispute: The landlord (Mohd. Asif Naseer) fought to evict the tenant (West Watch Company) from a shop in Lucknow for personal use, but the High Court had set aside earlier orders allowing eviction.
issues_decided: Whether the notice under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Rent Control Act, sent by certificate of posting and supported by affidavit, constituted valid service?
Whether the concurrent findings of fact by the Prescribed Authority and Appellate Authority could be overturned by the High Court in a writ petition?
Whether the landlord's hardship justified release of the shop under the Rent Control Act?
holdings: Notice sent by certificate of posting, supported by affidavit and corroborated by surrounding circumstances, constitutes valid service under the U.P. Rent Control Act.
Concurrent findings of fact by quasi-judicial authorities, based on valid evidence, should not be disturbed by the High Court in writ jurisdiction unless perverse or without evidence.
Where the landlord faces greater hardship than the tenant and seeks possession for personal use, release of the premises may be granted under Section 21(1)(a) of the Act.
provisions: U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 21(1)(a)
U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 34(1)
U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 30(1)
doctrines: Presumption of service of notice based on certificate of posting, when supported by affidavit and surrounding circumstances
Concurrent findings of fact by lower authorities are binding unless clearly erroneous
Balancing of hardship between landlord and tenant in eviction matters under rent control laws

card.dispute: The landlords sought to declare the tenanted premises vacant on grounds of subletting by the tenant's family members, which the tenant's son challenged.
issues_decided: Whether the occupation of the premises by family members of the tenant and his brother attracted deemed vacancy under Section 12(1)(b) of the U.P. Act, 1972
Whether the High Court erred in exercising its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution to overturn the District Judge's order
holdings: Deemed vacancy under Section 12(1)(b) of the U.P. Act, 1972 arises only when a non-family member is allowed to occupy the premises in their own right; mere residence alongside family does not attract the provision.
The High Court cannot use Article 227 jurisdiction to act as a court of appeal; it must only intervene when there is illegality or material irregularity, not to correct mere errors of fact or law.
provisions: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 12(1)(b)
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, Section 18
doctrines: Deemed vacancy doctrine under rent control laws
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 must not be exercised in the manner of an appellate court

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the rejection of a 1985 compromise decree in evidence for non-registration, which they relied upon to establish title over land in a subsequent suit for injunction and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the compromise decree dated 04.10.1985 required registration under the Registration Act, 1908
Whether a decree based on adverse possession can be used offensively to claim title
Whether the trial court and High Court erred in rejecting the decree as inadmissible due to non-registration
holdings: A decree or order of a court, including a compromise decree, does not require registration if it pertains only to the subject matter of the suit, as exempted under Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act.
A person who has perfected title by adverse possession can use such title as a 'sword' to file a suit for restoration of possession, not merely as a 'shield' in defence.

The rejection of the 1985 compromise decree as inadmissible due to non-registration was erroneous, as court decrees are exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(vi), and the decree was not collusive.
doctrines: Exemption of court decrees from registration
Adverse possession as a basis for declaratory relief
Use of adverse possession as a sword and not merely a shield

card.dispute: The appellant challenged whether the moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, applies to prevent MHADA from taking possession of property occupied under a joint development agreement during insolvency proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether Section 14(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, creates a moratorium that extends to occupation of property under a joint development agreement.
Whether the MHADA Act provisions relating to housing and redevelopment override the Insolvency Code's moratorium.
holdings: Section 14(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code only applies to physical occupation of property and does not freeze rights created under development agreements; the moratorium does not protect occupation granted under such agreements.
Section 238 of the Insolvency Code gives it overriding effect over inconsistent laws, including the MHADA Act, during the insolvency resolution period.
provisions: Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Act, Sections 76 and 79
doctrines: Statutory moratorium
Lex specialis
Overriding effect of insolvency law

card.dispute: The landlord (Om Prakash) sought eviction of the tenant (Suresh Kumar) for reconstruction, but later refused to re-induct him in the new building despite prior assurances to the court.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord is bound by his undertaking before the High Court to re-induct the tenant in the reconstructed premises?
Whether the tenant is entitled to a portion of equivalent area and suitable for non-residential use after reconstruction?
What compensation is due if the re-inducted area is less than the original?
holdings: A party is bound by solemn assurances given before a court, and cannot later renege on them; the landlord must re-induct the tenant as promised.
The tenant is entitled to a commercially viable portion of the reconstructed ground floor with frontage access, even if less than original area.
The landlord must compensate the tenant for the shortfall in area based on prevailing circle rates, and cannot use upper floors until compensation is paid.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, Section 14(3)(c)
doctrines: Doctrine of binding nature of undertaking given to court
Principle of equitable compensation for loss of tenancy rights
Doctrine of complete justice under Article 142 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The legal representatives of Raghunath appealed against the decision allowing Radha Mohan's legal representatives to enforce a right of pre-emption over a property sold in 1974, claiming the right was barred by limitation due to prior unchallenged sales after the Rajasthan Pre-Emption Act, 1966 came into force.
issues_decided: Whether the right of pre-emption under the Rajasthan Pre-Emption Act, 1966 is a recurring right exercisable in every subsequent sale or only once when the cause of action first arises.
Whether the right of pre-emption is barred by limitation if not exercised within one year of a registered sale, especially after prior unchallenged transactions.
holdings: The right of pre-emption under the Rajasthan Pre-Emption Act, 1966 is not a recurring right; it is exercisable only once when the cause of action first arises, and failure to exercise it then extinguishes the right for all future transactions.

The right of pre-emption is barred by limitation if not enforced within one year of the registered sale deed, and non-exercise in an earlier transaction amounts to a waiver, preventing its revival in later sales.
doctrines: Doctrine of waiver of pre-emption rights
Doctrine of one-time enforceability of weak rights
Doctrine of limitation under Article 97 of the Limitation Act, 1963

card.dispute: The appellant landowner contested the taxability of capital gains from land acquisition, arguing the gains should be assessed on the notification date, while the revenue claimed taxation on the award date.
issues_decided: Whether capital gains arising from land acquisition are taxable with reference to the date of notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, or the date of award under Section 11(1) of the same Act?

Whether the Revenue is precluded from challenging the date of accrual of capital gains in this case due to its acceptance of a contrary decision in a prior assessment year (1975-76) involving the same assessee?
holdings: For capital gains taxation under Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the transfer of a capital asset in an ordinary acquisition is complete only on the date of the award, not the notification date, when the compensation is finally determined.

The Revenue is not estopped from taking a contrary position in one assessment year based on a prior unchallenged decision in another year, especially where the facts and legal provisions (ordinary vs. urgency acquisition) differ materially.
doctrines: Doctrine of accrual of capital gains
Principle of estoppel against Revenue
Distinction between ordinary and urgency land acquisition
Finality of transfer under award in land acquisition

card.dispute: The appellant, Prem Chand Singh, challenged his prosecution in a second criminal case for allegedly forging a power of attorney, after having been acquitted in a prior case involving the same document.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant could be tried again for offences arising from the same general power of attorney after being acquitted in a previous trial.
Whether the second FIR, though containing additional charges, constituted an abuse of process due to identity of facts and subject matter with the first.
holdings: A second prosecution based on the same general power of attorney and related transactions is barred by Section 300 Cr.P.C. after an earlier acquittal on the same facts.
The addition of different penal sections in the second FIR does not alter the identity of the substratum of facts, and thus cannot justify a fresh prosecution.
doctrines: Autrefois acquit
Abuse of process of law
Identity of facts doctrine

card.dispute: Ratnagiri Nagar Parishad (municipal body) fought against residents of nearby villages who sought to block the setting up of a Solid Waste Disposal Project on allotted land, alleging potential health and environmental hazards.
issues_decided: Whether a civil suit for permanent injunction to prevent a proposed solid waste disposal project is maintainable on the basis of apprehended nuisance?
Whether the plaintiffs made out a case for a quia timet injunction based on imminent and irreparable harm?
Whether the civil court was justified in granting an injunction when equally efficacious remedies were available under environmental statutes and before specialized tribunals?
holdings: A civil suit seeking injunction against a proposed project must show a strong probability of imminent and irreparable harm; mere apprehension or possibility of nuisance is insufficient to grant relief.
No case for quia timet injunction was made out where the project was at a nascent stage, permissions were pending, and no concrete evidence showed inevitable harm.
Civil courts should not grant injunctions when equally effective remedies exist under statutory frameworks, such as making representations to environmental authorities or appealing to the NGT.
doctrines: quia timet injunction
precautionary principle
alternative efficacious remedy
imminent and irreparable harm

card.dispute: The daughter-in-law (appellant) fought against her in-laws' application for her eviction from a residential property under the Senior Citizens Act 2007, asserting her right to reside there as a 'shared household' under the PWDV Act 2005.
issues_decided: Whether the Senior Citizens Act 2007 can be used to evict an aggrieved woman from a 'shared household' without regard to her rights under the PWDV Act 2005.
Whether the summary procedure under the Senior Citizens Act 2007 can override competing remedies under the PWDV Act 2005.
Whether the appellant is entitled to interim protection and reliefs while pursuing her remedies under the PWDV Act 2005.
holdings: The Senior Citizens Act 2007 cannot be used to nullify a woman's right to reside in a 'shared household' under Section 17 of the PWDV Act 2005.
Tribunals under the Senior Citizens Act must consider competing claims under special statutes like the PWDV Act and cannot issue eviction orders that defeat such rights.
The appellant is entitled to interim protection from dispossession and reliefs under Article 142 to pursue her statutory remedies under the PWDV Act 2005.
provisions: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, Section 3
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, Section 23(2)
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, Section 17
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005, Section 26
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, Section 10
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007, Section 27
doctrines: Harmonious construction of special statutes
Remedial interpretation of protective legislation
Equitable enforcement of rights under Article 142
Non-derogation from statutory protections for vulnerable groups

card.dispute: Sadhna Chaudhary, a judge in the Uttar Pradesh Higher Judicial Services, challenged her dismissal based on allegations of misconduct arising from two land acquisition judgments she delivered.
issues_decided: Whether the enhancement of compensation in land acquisition cases by a judicial officer, without evidence of extraneous considerations, can constitute misconduct warranting dismissal?
Whether the dismissal of a judicial officer based solely on the outcome of judicial orders, without proof of corrupt gratification or procedural impropriety, is legally sustainable?
holdings: A judge cannot be penalized solely for the result of a judicial order; misconduct must be supported by evidence of illegal gratification or extraneous influence, not mere suspicion arising from generous compensation awards.
When superior courts uphold or enhance the compensation awarded by a judge, the inference of dishonesty based solely on the quantum of award collapses, and dismissal on such grounds is unjustified.
doctrines: Standard of conduct for judges higher than ordinary public servants
Misconduct in judicial office requires proof beyond mere suspicion
Principle that judicial outcomes alone cannot imply corruption

card.dispute: The appellants, who ran restaurants and guesthouses on Virupapura Gaddi island in Karnataka, challenged the state's action to demolish their structures, arguing that the authorities lacked power under the Hampi Act to enforce prior heritage protection notifications.
issues_decided: Whether the Hampi Act overrides or continues the enforcement of prior restrictions under the Mysore Ancient Monuments Act, 1961
Whether the HWHAMA could lawfully demolish structures without issuing a fresh notification under Section 14(1) of the Hampi Act
Whether the Master Plan 2021 and its Zonal Regulations satisfy the requirements of Section 14(1) of the Hampi Act
holdings: The Hampi Act and the 1961 Act are not mutually exclusive but form a continuous legislative scheme to protect Hampi’s heritage, so prior illegality under the 1961 Act persists under the Hampi Act.
The HWHAMA can enforce demolition under Section 14(6) even without a fresh notification under Section 14(1), as existing notifications and regulations continue to apply.

The Master Plan 2021 and its Zonal Regulations, which prohibit development in ecologically sensitive areas like river islands, fulfill the requirement of Section 14(1) by specifying restricted development types.
provisions: Mysore Ancient and Historical Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1961, Section 19(1), Section 19(3), Section 20(1)
Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority Act, 2010, Section 11, Section 14(1), Section 14(6)
Hampi World Heritage Area (Regulation of Development) Rules, 2007, Regulation 2(f)
doctrines: Continuity of legislative purpose
Harmonious construction of statutes
Enforcement of prior illegality under successor legislation

card.dispute: The appellant, Santosh Prasad, challenged his conviction for rape and house-trespass based on the prosecution's reliance solely on the testimony of the prosecutrix, which he claimed was uncorroborated and unreliable.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction can be sustained solely on the testimony of the prosecutrix without corroboration?
Whether the evidence of the prosecutrix was trustworthy, consistent, and of 'sterling quality'?
Whether contradictions and delays in the prosecution version, along with lack of medical and forensic support, warrant acquittal?
holdings: The conviction cannot be based solely on the testimony of the prosecutrix if it is inconsistent, uncorroborated, and fails to inspire confidence.
The evidence of the prosecutrix must be of 'sterling quality'—consistent, natural, and corroborated by material or other credible evidence—to be accepted without corroboration.
Material contradictions, delay in FIR, absence of forensic support, and enmity between parties create reasonable doubt, entitling the accused to benefit of doubt.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Sterling witness doctrine
Presumption under Section 114-A of the Evidence Act is restricted
Need for corroboration in rape cases with inconsistent testimony

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's reduction of compensation awarded for land acquired for the Hiwra Dam project, particularly contesting the 40% deduction for development costs and reductions in compensation for civil and electrical works.
issues_decided: Whether the 40% deduction for development cost was justified in determining the market value of the acquired land?
Whether the High Court was justified in reducing the compensation for electrical installation based on depreciated market value?
Whether the compensation awarded for loss of business was supported by evidence?
holdings: A deduction of 40% for development cost was excessive; 20% is reasonable when land is acquired for a dam project with minimal layout development needs.
The High Court erred in reducing electrical installation compensation to depreciated value; the full amount for dismantling and reinstallation must be paid.
The compensation for loss of business was justified based on concurrent findings despite lack of profit documentation due to prolonged idling of the sugar mill.
doctrines: Principle of reasonable deduction for development cost in land valuation
Concurrent finding rule in factual assessment by lower courts
Compensation for dismantling and reinstallation as part of market value

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Sri Uttam Chand (plaintiff) sued the legal heirs of Nathu Ram (defendants) for possession of a property, claiming ownership through a government auction, while the defendants claimed ownership through long-standing possession and adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether the defendants acquired title by adverse possession?
Whether the plaintiff established a valid title based on purchase from the government?
Whether the defendants' possession was hostile, open, and continuous for the statutory period?
Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the plaintiff's suit for possession?
holdings: To claim adverse possession, a defendant must plead and prove open, continuous, and hostile possession with animus possidendi, which the defendants failed to do.
Mere long possession without acknowledgment of the true owner’s title and a hostile claim does not ripen into a possessory title.
The defendants did not admit the plaintiff’s or the government’s title, nor did they assert their possession as adverse, thus failing to meet the legal requirements for adverse possession.
The High Court erred in holding that the defendants perfected title by adverse possession; the plaintiff’s suit based on valid purchase and title is restored.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Animus possidendi
Nec vi nec clam nec precario
Pleading and proof requirement in civil suits

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Shri Partap Singh sued the legal heirs of Shiv Ram, claiming ownership of land and seeking injunction and accounts, while the defendant claimed tenancy rights based on oral evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the revenue records create a rebuttable presumption of truth regarding land ownership and tenancy.
Whether oral evidence alone can rebut the statutory presumption arising from official revenue records.
Whether the burden of proving the existence of a landlord-tenant relationship lies on the party asserting it.
holdings: Entries in revenue records under the Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1954 are presumed truthful and form a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof.
Oral evidence alone is insufficient to rebut the statutory presumption of truth in revenue records; credible and reliable documentary evidence is required for rebuttal.
Under Section 109 of the Indian Evidence Act, the burden of proving that a landlord-tenant relationship exists or has ceased lies on the party asserting it.
provisions: Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1954, Section 32(2)(a)
Himachal Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1954, Section 44
doctrines: Rebuttable presumption of truth in revenue records
Burden of proof in landlord-tenant relationships
Primacy of documentary evidence over oral testimony
Fraud or procedural irregularity as grounds to challenge revenue entries

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Shri Ram Sahu fought against Vinod Kumar Rawat and others over the validity of a sale deed and possession of a disputed house.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in reviewing its judgment under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC by deleting observations on possession made in para 20?
Whether non-framing of an issue on possession barred the court from making findings on possession when evidence was led on it?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its review jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC by deleting observations on possession based on appreciation of evidence, as no error apparent on the face of the record was shown.
Findings on possession can be made even if no formal issue was framed, provided pleadings and evidence addressed the question and no prejudice was caused to either party.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 6 Rule 17
doctrines: Error apparent on the face of the record
Substantial justice over technicalities
Review jurisdiction limitations

card.dispute: The father challenged the High Court's order on visitation rights, seeking access to both children, while the mother opposed visitation, especially for the daughter, and sought to withdraw a prior consent order.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent-wife can unilaterally withdraw from a trilateral consent order on custody and visitation dated 1st March 2013
Whether visitation rights for the father should continue for both children under interim arrangements
Whether the High Court's observations and contempt proceedings influenced the ongoing custody and divorce matters unfairly
holdings: A trilateral consent order cannot be unilaterally withdrawn by one party; it remains binding until jointly revoked or set aside by a competent court.
The interim custody and visitation arrangement ordered by this Court on 7th September 2017 shall continue until further orders, ensuring the father's visitation rights.
Either parent may file a custody or guardianship petition independently, which must be decided on the child's best interest without being influenced by this Court's observations.
doctrines: Best interest of the child
Finality of consent orders
Judicial non-interference in ongoing matrimonial disputes unless necessary

card.dispute: The State of Karnataka challenged the classification of land held by the respondents as plantation land under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961, which would exempt it from land ceiling restrictions.
issues_decided: Whether the land declared as plantation under Section 66(4) of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961 qualifies for exemption under Section 104 from restrictions under Section 79-B
Whether the Tribunal and High Court adequately examined the transformation of forest land into plantation land
Whether the property of a registered partnership firm could be validly declared as individual holding without legal devolution
holdings: If land qualifies as 'plantation' under Section 104, the restrictions under Section 79-B do not apply, but the burden is on the declarants to prove such status.
The authorities failed to conduct a proper factual inquiry into whether the forest land claimed as plantation was genuinely under plantation cultivation.
The devolution of firm property to individual partners without legal instrument raises legal concerns under Section 79-B's prohibition on non-family associations holding land.
doctrines: Presumption against holding by associations under Section 79-B
Exemption of plantations from land ceiling laws
Requirement of factual scrutiny in land classification proceedings
Procedural fairness in administrative land reform determinations

card.dispute: The petitioner sought appointment of a sole arbitrator to resolve disputes arising from a sub-lease deed, which the respondent did not oppose despite notice.
issues_decided: Whether disputes arising from a lease governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are arbitrable when an arbitration clause exists
Whether statutory protections under Sections 114 and 114A of the Transfer of Property Act render lease disputes non-arbitrable
Whether the special statutes like Rent Acts affect the arbitrability of tenancy disputes
holdings: Disputes arising from private lease agreements governed by the Transfer of Property Act are arbitrable if there is an arbitration clause, as they do not involve public interest or statutory tenancy protections.

Sections 114 and 114A of the Transfer of Property Act confer discretionary equitable relief against forfeiture, but do not make such disputes non-arbitrable; arbitrators can consider these provisions when deciding on eviction.

Disputes under special rent control statutes are non-arbitrable due to statutory protections and the need for court adjudication on issues like bona fide requirement and hardship, but this does not apply to ordinary lease disputes outside such statutes.
doctrines: Arbitrability of disputes
Equitable discretion in forfeiture cases
Public policy and statutory exclusivity in rent control laws

card.dispute: The Project Director and NHAI challenged the Madras High Court's decision invalidating land acquisition notifications for the Chennai-Krishnagiri-Salem National Highway project, while landowners opposed the acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the notifications issued under Section 3A(1) of the National Highways Act, 1956 for land acquisition were illegal due to deemed lapsing under Section 3D(3)
Whether continuing the same consultant for a revised highway alignment without fresh appointment process invalidated the acquisition
Whether mutation entries in favour of NHAI based solely on Section 3A notification were legally valid
holdings: Notifications under Section 3A(1) do not lapse automatically under Section 3D(3) if the acquisition process is ongoing with due diligence.

Continuation of the same consultant for a revised project stretch does not invalidate the acquisition, especially when no challenge was raised against the consultant’s appointment in the writ petitions.

Mutation entries made in favour of NHAI solely on the basis of a Section 3A notification are invalid and must be restored, as possession and vesting occur only after completion of the acquisition process.
doctrines: Deemed lapsing of notifications under statutory provisions
Principle of maintainability of writ petitions
Doctrine of separation of administrative irregularities from substantive acquisition validity

card.dispute: The dispute was between a power distribution company and an auction-purchaser over whether the purchaser was liable to pay the previous owner's unpaid electricity dues.
issues_decided: Whether an auction-purchaser is liable to pay the electricity dues of the previous owner under the SARFAESI Act auction conducted on 'as is where is' basis.
Whether electricity dues are statutory in nature and can be enforced against a subsequent purchaser.
Whether a specific clause in the auction notice absolving or including liability for electricity dues affects the purchaser's liability.
holdings: An auction-purchaser is liable to pay the previous owner's electricity dues if the auction notice explicitly mentions such liability and the sale is on 'as is where is, without recourse' basis.
Electricity dues under the Electricity Act, 2003 and General Terms & Conditions of Supply are statutory, not merely contractual, and cannot be waived.
A purchaser who bids in an auction with knowledge of existing dues, especially when quantified in the notice, cannot avoid liability even if no formal transfer application is made.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Rules 8 & 9
doctrines: Statutory dues doctrine
As is where is and without recourse doctrine
Successor liability in auction purchases

card.dispute: The State of Punjab appealed against the High Court's decision to quash an FIR alleging that Jasbir Singh forged documents in revenue proceedings, raising the question of whether a preliminary inquiry and hearing must precede a court's complaint under Section 340 CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether a preliminary inquiry and opportunity of hearing must be afforded to the alleged offender before a court makes a complaint under Section 340 CrPC?
What is the scope and necessity of a preliminary inquiry under Section 340 CrPC in the interest of justice?
holdings: There is no statutory requirement to afford a hearing to the person against whom a complaint may be made under Section 340 CrPC before initiating proceedings; the decision to hold an inquiry lies in the court's discretion based on expediency in the interest of justice.

A preliminary inquiry under Section 340 CrPC is not mandatory; the court may form an opinion to file a complaint based on existing material, weighing the impact of the alleged forgery on the administration of justice rather than private injury.
doctrines: Expediency in the interest of justice
Preliminary inquiry under Section 340 CrPC
Judicial discretion in initiating prosecution for contempt of court

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan appealed against the High Court's order reinstating police constable Heem Singh, who was dismissed for alleged involvement in a murder and later acquitted in criminal court.
issues_decided: Whether an acquittal in a criminal trial mandates reinstatement of a public servant in disciplinary proceedings?
Whether the disciplinary enquiry's finding of misconduct was supported by evidence on a preponderance of probabilities?
Whether the High Court erred in ordering reinstatement without considering the impact on public confidence in the police force?
holdings: An acquittal in a criminal trial, especially due to hostile witnesses or benefit of doubt, does not automatically entitle a public servant to reinstatement in disciplinary proceedings.
Disciplinary authorities may dismiss a public servant if misconduct is proven on a preponderance of probabilities, even if not proven beyond reasonable doubt in a criminal trial.
Reinstatement of a police constable accused of murder may undermine public confidence in the police force, justifying dismissal despite criminal acquittal.
doctrines: Preponderance of probabilities
Perversity in findings
Proportionality in punishment
Honourable acquittal

card.dispute: The Trustees of H.C. Dhanda Trust challenged the imposition of a tenfold penalty on deficient stamp duty for a property transfer executed as a 'Deed of Assent' instead of a sale deed, which the state claimed was an attempt to evade stamp duty.
issues_decided: Whether the imposition of a tenfold penalty under Section 40(1)(b) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 is justified based on mere intention to evade stamp duty?
Whether the Collector has discretion to reduce the penalty below ten times the deficient stamp duty?
Whether the High Court was correct in upholding the tenfold penalty without considering mitigating factors?
holdings: The imposition of a tenfold penalty under Section 40(1)(b) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 is not automatic and must be reserved for extreme cases involving fraud or undue enrichment.
The Collector has statutory discretion under Section 40(1)(b), guided by 'if he thinks fit', to impose a penalty less than ten times based on facts, intent, and conduct.
A mere intention to evade stamp duty does not justify the maximum penalty; absence of dishonesty or contumacious conduct warrants a reduced penalty, here halved to five times.
doctrines: Penalty as deterrence, not retribution
Statutory discretion to be exercised reasonably
Principle of proportionality in penalty imposition

card.dispute: The Union Bank of India challenged the Bombay High Court's direction that no pre-deposit was required for Rajat Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. to appeal before the DRAT against a property auction conducted under the SARFAESI Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in holding that pre-deposit under Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act is not required for entertaining an appeal before the DRAT.
Whether a guarantor or mortgagor, though not a borrower, is required to comply with the pre-deposit condition under Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act.
holdings: The High Court erred in holding that no pre-deposit is required; Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act mandates 50% pre-deposit by the borrower, reducible to 25% by the DRAT, and creates an absolute bar otherwise.
A guarantor or mortgagor seeking to challenge an order under Section 17 stands on the same footing as a borrower and must comply with the pre-deposit requirement under Section 18.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 18
doctrines: Condition precedent to appeal
Literal interpretation of statutory provisions
Doctrine of efficacious alternative remedy

card.dispute: The appellant, Triloki Nath Singh, challenged the validity of a compromise decree in a partition suit to which he was not a party, claiming it was obtained by fraud and sought to protect his rights under a sale deed from one of the parties to the suit.
issues_decided: Whether a stranger to a suit can challenge a compromise decree in a separate civil suit?
Whether a decree passed on the basis of a compromise can be declared illegal and void on grounds of fraud by a person not party to the original proceedings?
Whether Order 23 Rule 3A of the CPC bars a suit by a non-party to challenge the legality of a compromise decree?
holdings: A person who is not a party to a suit cannot file a separate suit to challenge the validity of a compromise decree passed in that suit.
Order 23 Rule 3A of the CPC creates a complete bar to any suit seeking to set aside a decree on the ground that the compromise was not lawful, even on grounds of fraud.
A person claiming under a party to a compromise may assert their rights independently, but cannot challenge the compromise decree itself in a separate suit.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 43 Rule 1A
doctrines: Finality of compromise decrees
Bar on suits challenging compromise decrees under Order 23 Rule 3A CPC
Relational back of compromise decrees to the date of institution of suit
Remedy of non-parties limited to independent suits on their own title, not challenging decrees

card.dispute: The appellants, who purchased land via sale deeds executed by power of attorney holders, challenged the High Court's refusal to grant them leave to appeal against a trial court decree that declared certain agreements to sell as time-barred and cancelled them.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants, not being parties to the original suit, had locus standi to file an appeal against the trial court's decree?
Whether the appellants were 'persons aggrieved' by the decree cancelling the agreements to sell, so as to be entitled to seek leave to appeal?
holdings: The appellants were not parties to the suit and were not bound by the decree, which only affected the rights under the agreement to sell between the original parties.

The appellants failed to demonstrate that their legal rights were prejudicially affected by the decree, as their title arose from sale deeds based on power of attorney, independent of the cancelled agreements to sell.
doctrines: Person aggrieved
Locus standi to appeal by non-party
Prejudicial effect on legal rights

card.dispute: Vidya Devi, an illiterate widow, fought the State of Himachal Pradesh for compensation after her land was taken over in 1967–68 for road construction without legal acquisition proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the State could deprive the appellant of her property without legal authority or due process of law?
Whether the State could claim adverse possession over land taken without acquisition proceedings?
Whether the appellant's delay in filing the claim barred her right to compensation?
Whether the appellant was entitled to compensation on the same terms as similarly situated landowners?
holdings: The State cannot deprive a person of property without authority of law; any such deprivation violates Article 300-A of the Constitution.
The State, as a welfare entity, cannot acquire title by adverse possession, which is impermissible against citizens' property rights.
Delay and laches do not bar relief in cases of continuing violation of fundamental rights, especially when the claimant is disadvantaged and unaware of legal remedies.
The appellant is entitled to compensation on the same terms as awarded in a comparable case, treated as a deemed acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
doctrines: Rule of law
Deemed acquisition
Continuing cause of action
State cannot claim adverse possession

card.dispute: The appellant, as the alleged legatee under a will, sought to execute a partition decree as the legal representative of the deceased Umadevi, while the respondents challenged his status and the validity of the will.
issues_decided: Whether the determination of legal representation under Order XXII Rule 5 CPC operates as res judicata on the question of succession or title to property?
Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the Executing Court's order allowing the appellant to act as legal representative under Section 115 CPC?
holdings: A determination under Order XXII Rule 5 CPC regarding legal representation is for limited purposes only—to continue proceedings—and does not confer final title or operate as res judicata against rival claimants.

The High Court erred in exercising revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC by substituting its view without any jurisdictional error, illegality, or material irregularity in the Executing Court's order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 5
doctrines: Res judicata
Summary nature of legal representative determination
Limits of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the constitutional validity of certain provisions of a Gujarat land reform law, arguing that they encroached upon the Union List and conflicted with central laws like the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the State Legislature had the competence to enact provisions that incidentally encroach upon subjects in the Union List.
Whether there was repugnancy between the state legislation and central laws such as the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the doctrine of pith and substance applies to uphold the validity of the state law despite overlapping with central legislation.
Whether testamentary dispositions fall within the prohibition on assignment of land under the state law.
holdings: A state law remains valid if its pith and substance falls within the State List, even if it incidentally encroaches upon the Union List.
No repugnancy arises where state and central laws operate in distinct spheres and can coexist harmoniously.
