The doctrine of incidental encroachment saves overlapping provisions when the dominant purpose of the state law is within its legislative competence.
The prohibition on 'assignment' in the state law may include testamentary dispositions, but such inclusion does not invalidate the law due to incidental encroachment.
provisions: Constitution of India, Entry 5, List II, Seventh Schedule
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, Sections 126 and 127
doctrines: pith and substance
incidental encroachment
legislative competence
harmonious construction

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's decision upholding the respondents' claim to compensation as lessees of acquired land, alleging the lease was fraudulently created.
issues_decided: Whether the judgment and decree in proceedings under Sections 30 and 31 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, awarding compensation to the respondents as lessees, could be set aside on grounds of fraud.
Whether the respondents were entitled to protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, despite the absence of a registered lease deed.
holdings: A decree obtained in proceedings under the Land Acquisition Act cannot be challenged in a separate suit on grounds of fraud unless the fraud is specifically pleaded with particulars and proved by cogent evidence, which was not done here.

The respondents were entitled to protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, as they acted in reliance on an unregistered lease agreement by taking possession and cultivating the land.
doctrines: Fraud must be specifically pleaded and proved with particularity, especially when challenging a final decree.
Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act protects possession where there is part performance of an unregistered lease agreement.

card.dispute: The plaintiff sought permanent injunction against the defendants for disturbing his possession of a property, which the defendants claimed to own but had previously lost in litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for permanent injunction without a prayer for declaration of title was maintainable?
Whether the plaintiff had established possessory rights sufficient to grant injunction despite no formal title?
Whether the defendants could challenge possession after having lost a prior suit for declaration and recovery of the same property?
holdings: A suit for permanent injunction is maintainable without seeking declaration of title if the plaintiff establishes lawful possession.
Possession, even without formal title, is sufficient to grant injunction against others except the true owner.
Defendants cannot deny plaintiff's possession when they previously failed to establish their own title and possession in earlier litigation over the same property.
doctrines: Possession good against all but the true owner
Principle of res judicata
Maintainability of injunction suit without declaration of title

card.dispute: The appellant claimed to be the son of deceased parents and sought a declaration of ownership in their property, while the respondents (the deceased's daughters) denied his claim and sought a DNA test to disprove his biological relationship.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court should have ordered a DNA test to determine the paternity of the appellant in a property dispute?
Whether the right to privacy outweighs the need for DNA testing in civil disputes over family relationships?
Whether an adverse inference can be drawn under Section 114 of the Evidence Act if a party refuses to undergo a DNA test?
holdings: Courts should refrain from ordering DNA tests in civil disputes when other reliable evidence exists, as such tests infringe upon the right to privacy and may have serious social consequences.

The right to privacy, protected under Article 21, must be balanced against the quest for truth; DNA testing should only be ordered if there is an 'eminent need' and not merely at the instance of the opposing party.

While refusal to undergo a DNA test may allow an adverse inference under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, it cannot be compelled if the party has already produced credible documentary evidence in support of their claim.
doctrines: Right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21
Presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Evidence Act
Doctrine of adverse inference under Section 114 of the Evidence Act
Proportionality test in fundamental rights adjudication

card.dispute: Original landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired in 1976 by the state for NOIDA's industrial development, seeking higher compensation based on parity with later awards.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners are entitled to compensation of Rs.297 per square yard based on the High Court's decision in Mangu and Ors. (relating to 1991 acquisition)?
Whether the landowners can claim Rs.297 per square yard based on the judgment in Jagmal v. State of U.P., later reviewed to Rs.28.12 per square yard?
Whether compensation can be calculated by applying a 10% annual depreciation to the Khazan case award (1983 acquisition) to determine 1976 compensation?
holdings: The High Court's decision in Mangu and Ors. awarding Rs.297 per square yard is not applicable due to a 15-year time gap and was based on a factual mistake in tagging 1977 acquisition appeals with 1991 cases.
The Jagmal judgment initially awarding Rs.297 was corrected by review to Rs.28.12 per square yard for 1976 acquisitions, which is the correct benchmark.
Compensation for earlier acquisitions cannot be derived by depreciating later awards, especially when later acquisitions benefited from post-1980 development not present in 1976.
provisions: Civil Procedure Code, Order XLI Rule 27
doctrines: Principle of parity in land acquisition compensation
Non-comparability of compensation awards separated by significant time and development changes
Prohibition on benefiting from judicial or procedural mistakes

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent fought over ownership of a property in India, where the respondent claimed title through gift deeds from a foreigner who did not obtain prior RBI permission under Section 31 of FERA, 1973, while the appellant claimed prior rights under an agreement of sale.
issues_decided: Whether a transaction in contravention of Section 31 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 is void or merely voidable.
Whether prior permission from the Reserve Bank of India is mandatory for a foreign national to transfer immovable property in India.
Whether courts can enforce a property transaction by a foreigner without RBI permission under Section 31 of FERA, 1973.
holdings: A transaction violating Section 31 of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973 is unenforceable in law and cannot be legally recognized.

The requirement of obtaining prior general or special permission from the Reserve Bank of India under Section 31 of FERA, 1973 is mandatory for any transfer of immovable property in India by a foreign national.
Courts cannot enforce a property transfer by a foreigner without RBI permission, as such enforcement would violate statutory mandate and public policy.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 20 Rule 12
doctrines: Mandatory statutory compliance
Public policy under contract law
Prospective overruling
Stare decisis with exception for conflicting precedents
Unenforceability of illegal transactions

card.dispute: The accused and the deceased were involved in a dispute over a pathway, which escalated into a violent confrontation leading to criminal charges and appeals over conviction and acquittal.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the charges beyond reasonable doubt, particularly in light of the plea of private defence?
Whether the FIR and complaint were properly recorded and whether suppression of material facts affected the credibility of the prosecution case?
Whether the convictions in the second trial were sustainable given contradictions in evidence and findings of over-implication?
Whether the benefit of doubt and the plea of private defence should be extended to the appellants based on the evidence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt due to material contradictions, suppression of facts, and lack of reliable eyewitness testimony.
The genesis of the FIR and complaint was suspect, with evidence of suppression and involvement of unknown persons in drafting, undermining the prosecution's case.
The convictions in the second trial cannot stand as the evidence revealed over-implication, delayed FIR, and inconsistencies, rendering the case unreliable.
The appellants are entitled to the benefit of doubt and the plea of private defence is plausible, given the injuries on both sides and the civil origin of the dispute.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt
Right of private defence
Prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt
Concurrent findings of fact can be overturned if based on perversity or suppression

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Bajranga challenged the state's acquisition of surplus agricultural land, claiming the proceedings were invalid due to non-compliance with statutory requirements regarding a pending title suit.
issues_decided: Whether the competent authority violated the Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960 by proceeding with surplus land acquisition despite a pending civil suit affecting title.
Whether non-issuance of notice to a party with a pending title claim violated principles of natural justice.
Whether the civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit challenging the order declaring land as surplus.
holdings: The competent authority must await the decision of a civil court on a title dispute if such a suit is pending, as mandated by the proviso to Section 11(4) of the Act.
Failure to issue notice to a person with a pending title claim violates natural justice and renders the acquisition proceedings invalid.
The civil court has jurisdiction to entertain a suit to set aside an order under Section 11(5) of the Act, which is expressly permitted by the statute.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 7(b)
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 9(iv)
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 10
Madhya Pradesh Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1960, Section 11
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, Section 248
doctrines: Principle of natural justice
Statutory compliance in land acquisition
Jurisdiction of civil courts in ceiling Act matters
Procedural fairness in administrative action

card.dispute: The Assam Industrial Development Corporation challenged the High Court's dismissal of its appeal, which had confirmed the rejection of land acquisition approval for a plastic park on Gillapukri Tea Company's land.
issues_decided: Whether the State Government approved the land acquisition award on 05.03.2010 or only on 06.01.2014
Whether the land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Whether the State could initiate fresh acquisition proceedings over land already acquired
holdings: The letter dated 05.03.2010 constituted approval of the award, as evidenced by subsequent actions like fund release and compensation payment.
Acquisition does not lapse under Section 24 when award is approved, compensation paid, and possession taken before the 2013 Act's commencement.
The State cannot re-acquire land already vested in it; a second notification under Section 4 is invalid for already acquired land.
doctrines: Vesting of title upon possession
Finality of acquisition proceedings after approval and payment
Prohibition on re-acquisition of government-owned land

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's reversal of a trial court decision enforcing an agreement to sell joint Hindu family agricultural land, executed by the Karta without consent of other coparceners.
issues_decided: Whether the Karta had legal authority to execute the agreement to sell joint Hindu family property without the son's signature
Whether the sale was supported by legal necessity
Whether the agreement to sell could be enforced despite subsequent sale to a third party
holdings: A Karta has the authority to alienate joint Hindu family property for legal necessity or benefit of the estate, and such alienation binds all coparceners, including minors.
The existence of legal necessity depends on facts of each case; need for funds for domestic purposes and clearing mortgage debts constitutes legal necessity.
An alienation during pendency of suit is subject to doctrine of lis pendens and does not defeat the rights of a purchaser under a valid prior agreement.
provisions: Hindu Law (as per Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XIV Rule 1
doctrines: Legal necessity under Hindu law
Doctrine of lis pendens
Karta's power of alienation in joint Hindu family

card.dispute: The builder, Brigade Enterprises Limited, challenged the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's order allowing 91 apartment buyers to file a class action complaint on behalf of over 1,000 purchasers in the same residential complex.
issues_decided: Whether a group of 91 apartment buyers can file a consumer complaint in a representative capacity under Section 35(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for numerous consumers having the same interest.
Whether the definition of 'complainant' under Section 2(5) of the Act allows multiple consumers to jointly file a complaint even if not representing others.
Whether a joint complaint by a few consumers is permissible under the Act without invoking representative capacity.
holdings: Section 35(1)(c) applies only when a complaint is filed on behalf of numerous consumers; a mere joint complaint by a few consumers does not require such permission.
The term 'consumer' in the singular includes multiple consumers under the General Clauses Act, 1897, allowing joint complaints by a few consumers under Section 35(1)(a).
A complaint by a small group of consumers with the same grievance can be maintained as a joint complaint even if not filed in a representative capacity for all affected consumers.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 8
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Inclusion of plural in singular under General Clauses Act
Distinction between joint and representative complaints

card.dispute: Dena Bank (now Bank of Baroda) appealed against the NCLAT's decision to set aside the admission of its insolvency petition under Section 7 of the IBC against the corporate debtor, on grounds of limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the Section 7 insolvency petition was barred by limitation
Whether a decree or recovery certificate from the DRT provides a fresh cause of action under the IBC
Whether acknowledgment of debt through financial statements or a one-time settlement proposal extends the limitation period
Whether the Adjudicating Authority could allow additional documents to be filed during the pendency of a Section 7 petition
holdings: A petition under Section 7 of the IBC is not barred by limitation if filed within three years from the date of a recovery certificate or final decree, as it provides a fresh cause of action.
A final judgment, decree, or recovery certificate in favour of a financial creditor for unpaid dues creates a new right to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC.
Acknowledgment of debt through financial statements or a one-time settlement offer during the limitation period extends the limitation by three years under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
The Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to allow amendment of pleadings and filing of additional documents in a Section 7 petition before final order, in the absence of inordinate delay.
doctrines: Fresh cause of action doctrine
Acknowledgment extending limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act
Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act
Liberal amendment of pleadings in insolvency proceedings

card.dispute: Delhi Airport Metro Express Pvt. Ltd. (DAMEPL) and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Ltd. (DMRC) fought over the computation of termination payment, specifically whether Rs.611.95 crore advanced by DAMEPL's promoter and later converted to subordinated debt could be included as 'Adjusted Equity' in the termination payout.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the arbitral tribunal's interpretation of 'Adjusted Equity' under the Concession Agreement to include Rs.611.95 crore despite its conversion to subordinated debt.
Whether DAMEPL waived its right to terminate the Concession Agreement by participating in reconciliation and operating the metro line post-termination notice.
Whether the arbitral award granting interest on termination payment should be set aside on grounds of unjust enrichment.
holdings: An arbitral tribunal's reasonable interpretation of contractual terms, such as 'Adjusted Equity', cannot be overturned by courts merely because an alternative view is possible, especially under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act.
Participation in reconciliation and continued operation of the project after a termination notice does not constitute waiver if done without prejudice to rights under the contract.
Interest awarded under the Concession Agreement on termination payment is enforceable and does not result in unjust enrichment if contractually stipulated.
doctrines: Limited judicial interference in arbitral awards
Doctrine of waiver
Doctrine of unjust enrichment
Contractual interpretation over statutory definitions

card.dispute: Financial creditors appealed against the NCLT's refusal to admit their Section 7 insolvency petition against a real estate developer, challenging the tribunal's direction to settle claims outside the IBC framework.
issues_decided: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 7 petition by directing settlement without adjudicating on its merits under the IBC.
Whether the Appellate Authority was correct in holding the appeal against the NCLT's order as not maintainable.
holdings: The Adjudicating Authority cannot abdicate its statutory duty under Section 7 of the IBC by merely directing settlement; it must decide the petition on its merits within the IBC framework.
The Appellate Authority erred in dismissing the appeal as not maintainable, as the NCLT's order amounted to a refusal to admit the petition, which is appealable.
doctrines: Statutory jurisdiction of Adjudicating Authorities under IBC
No uncharted equity jurisdiction for NCLT/NCLAT
IBC as a complete code

card.dispute: DLF Home Developers Limited sought appointment of a sole arbitrator to resolve disputes with Rajapura Homes Private Limited and Begur OMR Homes Private Limited arising from Construction Management Agreements, while the respondents argued that disputes should be referred under Share Purchase Agreements with arbitration in Singapore.
issues_decided: Whether the disputes fall within the scope of the arbitration clause in the Construction Management Agreements or the Share Purchase Agreements
Whether the disputes are arbitrable under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether the two arbitration petitions should be referred to a single arbitrator or separate tribunals
holdings: The disputes primarily concern construction management obligations and payment of fees, which fall under the arbitration clause of the Construction Management Agreements, not the Share Purchase Agreements.
The petitioner satisfied the twin requirements under Section 11(6) of the Act, making the petitions maintainable for appointment of an arbitrator.
Despite being separate agreements, the interconnected nature of the disputes and the need to compute fees from both projects warrant appointment of a sole arbitrator to avoid conflicting awards.
provisions: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Fourth Schedule
doctrines: Competence-competence
Separability of arbitration agreements
Harmonious construction of arbitration clauses

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the West Bengal Housing Industry Regulation Act, 2017, arguing it was repugnant to the central Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, and lacked Presidential assent under Article 254(2) of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether WB-HIRA is repugnant to RERA under Article 254(1) of the Constitution?
Whether WB-HIRA required Presidential assent under Article 254(2) despite being enacted by a state legislature?
Whether the provisions of the earlier West Bengal Act of 1993 would revive upon the invalidation of WB-HIRA?
holdings: WB-HIRA is repugnant to RERA because both laws substantially deal with the same subject matter under the Concurrent List, and WB-HIRA contains provisions inconsistent with RERA.

A state law that occupies the same field as a central law on a Concurrent List subject must receive Presidential assent under Article 254(2) if it is to prevail; WB-HIRA lacked such assent and is therefore unconstitutional.
The West Bengal Housing Industry Regulation Act, 1993, stands impliedly repealed by RERA and does not revive upon the invalidation of WB-HIRA.
provisions: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Sections 88 and 89
Seventh Schedule, List III, Entries 6 and 7
doctrines: Doctrine of Repugnancy under Article 254
Implied Repeal
Presidential Assent under Article 254(2) as a condition for state law to prevail

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Tamil Nadu's 2019 Act that retrospectively revived three state land acquisition laws previously rendered inoperative due to repugnancy with the central Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
issues_decided: Whether the Tamil Nadu legislature could validly revive three state land acquisition enactments through a retrospective law despite their prior repugnancy with a central law under Article 254 of the Constitution.
Whether the President’s assent to the 2019 Act was constitutionally valid when sought without specifically identifying the repugnant central law.
Whether the retrospective operation of the 2019 Act from 26.09.2013 rendered it constitutionally invalid, especially since the central 2013 Act came into force on 27.09.2013.
holdings: A State legislature may validly enact a law to revive and validate earlier state laws rendered inoperative due to repugnancy with a central law, provided it obtains Presidential assent under Article 254(2), and such action does not encroach upon judicial functions.

The President’s assent under Article 254(2) is valid only if the State government specifically identifies the repugnant central law in its communication, enabling a deliberate and informed decision, as required by the constitutional scheme.

For determining repugnancy under Article 254, the relevant date is the date of making of the law (i.e., Presidential assent), not the date of commencement; thus, a retrospective commencement does not invalidate a law if repugnancy is resolved at the time of assent.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
doctrines: Separation of powers
Doctrine of repugnancy
Doctrine of retrospective legislation
Presidential assent under Article 254(2)

card.dispute: The complainant challenged the High Court's decision to grant protection from prosecution to a lower division clerk under Section 197 of the CrPC in a land fraud case involving forged municipal documents.
issues_decided: Whether the lower division clerk was acting in discharge of official duty, thereby requiring prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197 of the CrPC?
Whether the trial court erred in denying protection under Section 197 of the CrPC to the clerk when similar protection was granted to superior officers in the same transaction?
holdings: A public servant is entitled to protection under Section 197 of the CrPC if the alleged act has a reasonable connection with official duties, even if the act amounts to an offence.

When superior officers involved in the same transaction were granted protection under Section 197, the lower division clerk performing related paperwork cannot be denied such protection without a showing of mala fide or personal gain.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, Section 3(1)(4)/3(15)/3(5)
doctrines: Protection of public servants from vexatious prosecution
Principle of consistency in granting sanction under Section 197 CrPC
Acting 'in discharge of official duty' as a threshold for Section 197 applicability

card.dispute: The Estate Officer appealed against orders directing conversion of a leasehold plot to freehold, payment of compensation, and costs in favor of Charanjit Kaur, who sought conversion upon payment of the requisite fee.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent is a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act for seeking plot conversion by paying a fee?
Whether the Estate Officer's refusal to convert leasehold to freehold property was arbitrary and non-citizen-friendly?
Whether systemic inefficiencies and ad-hocism in the Chandigarh Administration's estate management require judicial intervention?
holdings: A person paying a conversion fee to the Chandigarh Administration for changing leasehold to freehold status qualifies as a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, as held in Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta.

The Estate Office's refusal to process conversion applications and its arbitrary procedures, including demands for no-objection certificates not statutorily mandated, are not bona fide and cause undue harassment to citizens.

The Chandigarh Administration must constitute a high-powered committee to review and streamline mutation, occupancy, no-objection certificate processes, and recommend statutory reforms to modernize the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 and the Chandigarh Estate Rules.
doctrines: Doctrine of Consumer Jurisdiction in Public Utility Services
Principle of Bona Fide Administrative Action
Judicial Direction for Executive Accountability and Statutory Reform
Prohibition of Judicial Legislation with Recognition of Casus Omissus

card.dispute: The Government of Kerala fought with religious and charitable institutions over whether buildings used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes are exempt from building tax under the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975.
issues_decided: Whether buildings used principally for religious, charitable, or educational purposes are exempt from building tax under Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975.
Whether beneficial exemptions in fiscal statutes should be interpreted strictly or liberally.
Whether the High Court's interpretation of a local tax statute deserves deference.
holdings: Buildings used principally for religious, charitable, or educational purposes are exempt from building tax under Section 3(1)(b) of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975, given the beneficial purpose of the provision.
Beneficial and promotional exemptions in tax laws must be interpreted liberally to advance their objective, even if general exemptions are to be strictly construed.
High Courts' interpretations of local tax statutes, especially those long-standing, deserve judicial deference due to reliance by the public in arranging their affairs.
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of beneficial exemptions
Deference to High Court interpretation of local statutes
Purpose-based statutory construction

card.dispute: The original plaintiff and auction purchaser challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a consent decree and court auction on grounds of fraud, arguing the decree and sale were valid.
issues_decided: Whether the appeal against a consent decree was maintainable in the High Court despite Section 96(3) CPC barring appeals against consent decrees.
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the consent decree on the ground that it was obtained by fraud.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the court auction sale on the ground that the auction purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser.
Whether the High Court could set aside the executing court's order confirming the sale when no timely challenge was filed and the sale had become absolute.
holdings: An appeal against a consent decree is maintainable if it challenges the legality of the compromise, under Order XLIII Rule 1A CPC, even if Section 96(3) CPC generally bars such appeals.
The High Court erred in holding the decree was obtained by fraud, as the judgment debtors had signed the consent terms and no evidence of fraud in the compromise was adduced.
The High Court wrongly set aside the auction sale on grounds not raised in the application; the purchaser was bona fide, especially since the firm was dissolved and the plaintiff inherited the claim.
Once a sale is confirmed and becomes absolute under Order XXI Rules 92 and 94 CPC, and no timely challenge is made, the High Court cannot set aside the sale retrospectively.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII Rule 1(m)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLIII Rule 1A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 89
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 90
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 91
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 92
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 94
doctrines: Doctrine of finality of consent decrees
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of bona fide purchaser for value
Doctrine of approbate and reprobate

card.dispute: The dispute was between a real estate developer and apartment buyers over refund of amounts paid due to inordinate delay in project completion and non-issuance of an Occupation Certificate.
issues_decided: Whether the developer committed deficiency of service by delaying project completion and failing to obtain an Occupation Certificate?
Whether apartment buyers are entitled to a full refund of amounts paid?
What rate of interest should be awarded on the refund amount for delayed possession?
Whether the developer can forfeit the earnest money deposit due to its own defaults?
holdings: Delay in obtaining the Occupation Certificate and completing construction constitutes deficiency of service under consumer law.
Buyers who faced prolonged delays and no progress in construction are entitled to a full refund of amounts paid.
Refund shall carry simple interest at 9% per annum from 27.11.2018, with default interest at 12% if not paid within stipulated time.
The developer cannot forfeit 20% earnest money or any other amount due to its own defaults, including delay in obtaining statutory clearances.
doctrines: Deficiency in service
Balancing of interests in awarding compensation
Forfeiture not allowed for developer's own defaults

card.dispute: The decree-holders challenged the High Court's decision to set aside an ex parte decree for specific performance on the ground that it was passed against a minor without appointing a proper guardian.
issues_decided: Whether the ex parte decree passed against a minor without appointment of a guardian under Order XXXII, Rule 3 of the CPC is a nullity
Whether the High Court could invoke its powers under Article 227 of the Constitution to set aside the ex parte decree in a revision petition under Section 115 CPC
Whether the minor was prejudiced by the failure to appoint a guardian
Whether the decree could be set aside only against the minor or against all defendants
holdings: A decree passed against a minor without compliance with Order XXXII, Rule 3 of the CPC is a nullity, as the procedural safeguard is mandatory to protect the minor's interests.

The High Court can exercise its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 to set aside a nullity, even in a revision petition under Section 115 CPC, as the powers under Article 227 are wider and additional.
The minor was prejudiced due to lack of representation, and the failure to appoint a guardian adversely affected the minor's ability to defend the suit.
A decree that is a nullity due to non-compliance with mandatory procedure binds no one and can be set aside in its entirety, not just against the minor.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXII, Rule 3
doctrines: Nullity for non-compliance with mandatory procedural safeguards for minors
Parens patriae jurisdiction of the High Court
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227
Prejudice in cases involving minors under disability

card.dispute: The appellants and respondent fought over ownership and possession of certain lands, with the respondent claiming title under a registered sale deed and the appellants alleging it was nominal and that an agreement to sell existed instead.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with the first appellate court's finding on the genuineness of document Ex.D-3 in second appeal under Section 100 CPC?
Whether the findings of fact by the first appellate court were perverse or based on an erroneous appreciation of evidence?
Whether the High Court could determine a factual issue under Section 103 CPC in a second appeal?
holdings: The High Court can interfere in a second appeal if the findings of fact are palpably perverse or outrage logic, even though concurrent findings are generally final.
A finding of fact can be set aside under Section 103 CPC if it is based on no evidence, ignores relevant material, or is arrived at through an erroneous approach.
The High Court may determine a factual issue in second appeal if the lower courts failed to decide it or decided it wrongly due to an error in law under Section 100 CPC.
doctrines: Perversity in findings of fact
Limited factual review in second appeal
Concurrent findings of fact are not immune to interference if vitiated by legal error or irrationality

card.dispute: The appellant, Kaptan Singh, challenged the High Court's decision to quash criminal proceedings against private respondents accused of offences related to cheating and criminal breach of trust in a property transaction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. after a chargesheet was filed?
Whether the High Court wrongly entered into the merits of the case and appreciated evidence at the quashing stage?
Whether the complainant had locus standi to file the complaint?
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by quashing the proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. after a chargesheet was filed and evidence collected, as triable issues existed.
The High Court must not appreciate evidence or draw inferences at the quashing stage; such an exercise is reserved for trial, especially when material is disputed.
The complainant's locus standi cannot be rejected merely for not producing the power of attorney at the quashing stage; it is a matter to be decided during trial.
doctrines: Inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. are exceptional and must be exercised sparingly
Appreciation of evidence is impermissible at the stage of quashing criminal proceedings
Triable issues of fact and law must be left for determination at trial

card.dispute: The Himachal Pradesh Bus Stand Management Authority and the Central Empowered Committee disputed over the legality of a bus stand complex constructed on forest land, specifically whether unauthorized commercial construction required demolition.
issues_decided: Whether the construction of a hotel-cum-restaurant within the bus stand complex on forest land violated the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
Whether the National Green Tribunal had jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter despite the involvement of the Town and Country Planning Act
Whether prior approval from the Central Government was necessary for non-forest use of forest land
holdings: Any construction on forest land for non-forest purposes without prior approval from the Central Government is illegal under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.

The National Green Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide cases involving substantial environmental questions arising from enactments in Schedule I of the NGT Act, even if other statutes are also involved.
The unauthorized hotel-cum-restaurant structure must be demolished as its continued existence would legitimize illegal construction on forest land.
provisions: Town and Country Planning Act, 1977 (Himachal Pradesh)
doctrines: Precautionary Principle
Environmental rule of law
Illegality of non-forest use of forest land without central approval

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to quash an FIR against several respondents accused of forgery, criminal conspiracy, and extortion in connection with a property dispute, except for two accused against whom investigation was allowed to continue.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the FIR under Section 482 CrPC without examining the allegations of criminal conspiracy against all accused.
Whether the High Court abused its process by entertaining quashing petitions from persons not named in the FIR but only in a draft charge-sheet.
Whether the High Court's interference at a premature stage of investigation was justified.
holdings: The High Court cannot quash an FIR under Section 482 CrPC when specific allegations of criminal conspiracy and extortion are made against accused, unless the allegations are manifestly frivolous or mala fide.
Entertaining quashing petitions under Section 482 CrPC by persons not named in the FIR but only in a draft charge-sheet amounts to an abuse of the judicial process.
Judicial interference in ongoing investigations under Section 482 CrPC is impermissible at a premature stage, especially when the charge-sheet has not been formally filed.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Principle of premature judicial interference in criminal investigations
Limited scope of Section 482 CrPC in quashing FIRs

card.dispute: The appellant (defendant) challenged the High Court's decision to allow specific performance of a property sale agreement, which had been denied by the Trial Court due to the plaintiff's lack of willingness to perform the contract as pleaded.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in allowing the appeal for specific performance based on an affidavit that altered the plaintiff's case without amending the plaint?
Whether the plaintiff proved readiness and willingness to perform the contract as required under the Specific Relief Act?
Whether the High Court failed to comply with Order XLI Rule 31 of the CPC in re-appreciating evidence?
holdings: A first appellate court cannot rely on an affidavit that changes the plaintiff's case without a formal amendment of the plaint under Order VI Rule 17 CPC.
For specific performance, readiness and willingness must be established as per the pleadings; a new case raised for the first time in appeal cannot be the basis for decreeing the suit.
The High Court must independently evaluate all evidence and frame issues under Order XLI Rule 31 CPC; failure to do so renders the judgment non-compliant and unsustainable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 31
doctrines: Doctrine of Pleadings
Readiness and Willingness in Specific Performance
First Appellate Court's Duty to Re-appreciate Evidence

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a property based on a registered assignment deed and sought injunction against the respondent for trespassing, while the respondent claimed ownership of part of the property based on inheritance and a purchase certificate under the Kerala Land Reforms Act.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court could decide the question of title in a suit for injunction?
Whether the plaintiff's title was clear enough to grant an injunction without a full trial on title?
Whether the dispute involved complicated questions of fact and law requiring a separate declaratory suit?
holdings: A court may decide title in a suit for injunction only if the plaintiff's title is clear and the matter is simple; otherwise, parties must resort to a declaratory suit.
Where there is a serious dispute over title and property identification, the issue cannot be resolved in an injunction suit without a full trial.
When the defendant raises a genuine dispute over title, a suit for bare injunction is not maintainable unless the plaintiff's title is undisputed.
doctrines: Title not ordinarily decided in injunction suits
Exception for clear title and simple cases
Maintainability of injunction suit depends on clarity of possession and title

card.dispute: Homebuyers and other stakeholders of Jaypee Infratech Limited (JIL) challenged the approved resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, raising objections over its fairness, treatment of various creditors, and impact on homebuyers and related entities.
issues_decided: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to modify a resolution plan beyond the scope of Section 31 of the IBC?
Whether two resolution plans can be voted upon simultaneously by the Committee of Creditors?
Whether the resolution plan adequately addressed the interests of homebuyers, dissenting financial creditors, land providing agencies, and minority shareholders?
Whether the accounting and financial arrangements between JIL and its holding company Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL), including a sum of INR 750 crores, were properly reconciled?
holdings: The Adjudicating Authority cannot modify a resolution plan but may only approve or reject it as submitted by the Committee of Creditors, ensuring compliance with the IBC.
Simultaneous voting on multiple resolution plans is not permissible; the Committee of Creditors must evaluate and vote on one plan at a time.
The resolution plan must fairly consider the interests of all stakeholders, including homebuyers and dissenting creditors, and any significant adverse impact requires justification and safeguards.
Reconciliation of accounts between JIL and JAL, including the INR 750 crore issue, must be completed separately and should not delay the final decision on the resolution plan by the CoC.
doctrines: Doctrine of Stakeholder Interest in Insolvency
Principle of Creditor-Led Resolution
Doctrine of Limited Judicial Interference in CIRP
Doctrine of Finality and Time-Bound Resolution under IBC

card.dispute: Kewal Krishan sued his brother Sudarshan Kumar and family members over the validity of sale deeds executed by Sudarshan, using a power of attorney, transferring jointly owned properties to his wife and minor sons without adequate consideration.
issues_decided: Whether the sale deeds executed by Sudarshan Kumar in favor of his wife and minor sons were valid in law despite absence of proof of consideration?
Whether the appellant's claim was barred by limitation after amending the plaint to include a declaration of nullity of the sale deeds?
Whether a declaration is necessary to challenge a void document, or can its invalidity be asserted collaterally?
holdings: A sale of immovable property under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act requires payment or promise of price; absence of consideration renders the sale void and ineffective in transferring title.
The sale deeds were void as no evidence was adduced to prove that the wife or minor sons had independent income or paid the stated consideration, making the transactions sham and legally ineffective.
A void document does not require a formal declaration of invalidity; its nullity can be pleaded and established in any proceeding, including as a defence or in a suit for possession.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive notice
Sham transaction doctrine
Void ab initio principle

card.dispute: Real estate developers challenged the constitutional validity of certain provisions of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, the Uttar Pradesh Rules, and the functioning of the Uttar Pradesh Real Estate Regulatory Authority, particularly concerning pre-deposit requirements and recovery mechanisms.
issues_decided: Whether Section 43(5) of RERA, requiring a 30% pre-deposit to file an appeal, violates Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution?
Whether the Authority can issue recovery certificates for the principal amount under Section 40(1) of RERA?
holdings: The pre-deposit requirement under Section 43(5) of RERA is a valid legislative condition to prevent frivolous appeals and does not violate Articles 14 or 19(1)(g), as the right to appeal is statutory and subject to conditions.

Section 40(1) of RERA allows recovery of the principal amount, along with interest and penalty, as arrears of land revenue, as a harmonious reading of Sections 18 and 40 ensures effective enforcement of allottees' rights.
provisions: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Section 18
The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Section 40(1)
The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Section 43(5)
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, Section 19
Punjab Value Added Tax Act, 2005, Section 62(5)
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Statutory right to appeal
Principle of avoiding redundancy in statutory interpretation
Legislative wisdom in imposing pre-deposit conditions

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the High Court's interim order granting protection from coercive action to accused persons during the pendency of a petition to quash an FIR alleging forgery and fraudulent sale of property.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can pass an interim order of 'no coercive steps' during the pendency of a quashing petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. or Article 226 of the Constitution?
Under what circumstances can a court restrict investigation or arrest while deciding a quashing petition?
Whether the High Court's interim order directing 'no coercive measures' against the accused in a cognizable offence is justified?
holdings: Courts should not interfere with police investigation into cognizable offences unless no offence is disclosed; interim orders of 'no coercive action' should not be passed routinely.
The power to quash FIRs is to be used sparingly and only in rare cases; courts must not assess the merits of allegations at the investigation stage.
An interim order of 'no coercive steps' can only be passed in exceptional circumstances with clear reasons, and the term must be clearly defined to avoid misuse.
Accused persons should generally seek anticipatory bail under Section 438 Cr.P.C. rather than seek blanket protection through quashing petitions.
doctrines: Separation of powers between judiciary and police
Judicial restraint in criminal investigations
Principle of complementary functions of police and courts
Doctrine of restraint in exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

card.dispute: The appellant and others sought bail or anticipatory bail in connection with two FIRs involving a violent clash with firearms, resulting in death and injuries, while the State opposed the release on grounds of the seriousness of the charges and ongoing investigation.
issues_decided: Whether the grant of regular bail to accused in FIR No. 406 of 2020 was justified given the gravity of charges under Section 302 IPC and Arms Act?
Whether anticipatory bail should be granted to the accused in FIR No. 407 of 2020 based on the allegations of attempted murder and use of illegal weapons?
Whether the High Court applied incorrect legal principles in granting bail by relying on disapproved reasoning from a previous judgment?
holdings: The bail granted to the accused in FIR No. 406 of 2020 was unjustified due to the seriousness of charges including murder and use of firearms, and the need for a fair investigation.
Anticipatory bail should not be granted in FIR No. 407 of 2020 as the allegations are grave, investigation is incomplete, and the role of each accused is not yet clear.
The High Court erred in applying sweeping observations similar to those disapproved in Mahipal's case, without recording specific reasons for granting bail to each accused.
doctrines: Principle of parity in bail decisions
Grave nature of offence as a factor against bail
Need for fair investigation and non-interference by accused during probe
Proper application of precedent and avoidance of mechanical reasoning

card.dispute: Kotak Mahindra Bank challenged the Delhi High Court's order allowing personal guarantors to appeal before the DRAT without pre-deposit of a portion of the debt under the RDB Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in permitting the respondents to prosecute an appeal before the DRAT without pre-deposit of a portion of the debt as mandated under Section 21 of the RDBA Act?
Whether the requirement of pre-deposit under Section 21 of the RDBA Act is mandatory or directory?
Whether the DRAT has the power to reduce the pre-deposit amount, and to what extent in the facts of this case?
holdings: The requirement of pre-deposit under Section 21 of the RDBA Act is mandatory and a condition precedent to maintain an appeal before the DRAT.
A complete waiver of pre-deposit by the High Court is impermissible and contrary to statutory provisions.
In the peculiar facts, the pre-deposit is reduced to 25% of the decretal amount of Rs.68.18 crores, to be deposited within 8 weeks, failing which the appeal will not subsist.
provisions: Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, Section 21
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 18
doctrines: Condition precedent
Mandatory statutory requirement
Judicial restraint in modifying pre-deposit under special statutes

card.dispute: The appellant, a director of a builder company, was accused by the respondent of cheating and criminal breach of trust in a property development agreement, leading to criminal proceedings which the appellant sought to quash.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations against the appellant disclose criminal offences under Sections 406, 419, and 420 IPC read with Section 34 IPC?
Whether the dispute is essentially civil in nature and thus liable to be quashed to prevent abuse of process?
Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash the FIR and criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC?
holdings: The ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust were not made out, as there was no dishonest or fraudulent intention at the inception of the transaction.
A dispute arising from a breach of contractual obligations, without evidence of fraud at the outset, is essentially civil and should not be given a criminal complexion.

The High Court failed to prevent abuse of process; the FIR and criminal proceedings were quashed as they fell within the categories permitting exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to secure justice.
doctrines: Distinction between civil breach and criminal cheating
Inherent powers to prevent abuse of process
Requirement of fraudulent intent at the time of promise for cheating
Judicial caution against converting civil disputes into criminal cases

card.dispute: The National Company sued Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. and its licensee for possession of leased land after the lease expired, seeking eviction and unpaid rent.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 2(4)(i) and Section 2(4)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960?
Whether the lessee (BPCL) is entitled to protection under the Act despite sub-letting the premises to a third-party licensee?
Whether the High Court erred in not deciding the appellant's entitlement to statutory protection under the Act?
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the High Court must first determine whether the appellant qualifies for protection under Section 2(4)(i) and Section 2(4)(ii)(a) of the Act, as this was not adequately considered.
A lessee who has sub-let or given possession to a third party, including a licensee, is not entitled to protection under Section 2(4)(ii)(b) of the Act unless in actual physical possession.
The decision in R. Chandramouleeswaran v. BPCL, which requires actual physical possession for tenancy protection, is binding under Article 141 and applies to identical factual situations.
provisions: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 2(4)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, Section 9(1)
doctrines: Res judicata
Binding precedent under Article 141
Actual physical possession as a condition for tenancy protection

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether a will was validly executed and whether Letters of Administration should be granted based on that will.
issues_decided: Whether the will (Ex-P1) was validly executed and proved in accordance with law
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the Trial Court's dismissal of the suit for Letters of Administration
Whether the High Court's judgment reversing the Trial Court was reasoned and in compliance with appellate standards
holdings: The respondents failed to prove the validity of the will as suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution were not adequately explained, and the will appeared to be a concocted document.
The High Court erred in reversing the Trial Court's decision without proper reappreciation of evidence or assigning sufficient reasons, especially on findings based on oral testimony.
An appellate court must consciously apply its mind and provide detailed reasoning when reversing a trial court’s judgment, particularly in a first appeal which is a valuable statutory right.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 31
doctrines: First appeal as a valuable right requiring reasoned judgment
Conscious application of mind by appellate courts
Presumption against wills executed under suspicious circumstances

card.dispute: The appellant (original plaintiff) challenged the High Court's decision to condone a 1011-day delay in filing a second appeal by the respondents (original defendants) in a property dispute involving a decree for permanent injunction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in condoning a delay of 1011 days in filing the second appeal under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963?
Whether the respondents showed sufficient cause for the delay in filing the second appeal?
Whether the High Court exercised its discretion judiciously in condoning the delay?
holdings: The High Court erred in condoning a delay of 1011 days without finding any sufficient cause, as no explanation was provided for the majority of the delay period.
A party seeking condonation of delay must show sufficient cause, and mere absence of wilful negligence is not enough if there is gross negligence or want of due diligence.
Courts must exercise discretion judiciously in condoning delay, and failure to do so violates statutory principles and undermines public policy behind limitation laws.
doctrines: Interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium
Delay defeats equity
Vigilant not the sleepy

card.dispute: Complainants challenged the High Court's order granting 90-day protection from arrest to accused after rejecting their anticipatory bail applications.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can grant protection from arrest after rejecting an anticipatory bail application under Section 438, Cr.P.C.
Whether the High Court's grant of 90 days' protection without reasoned order is legally valid.
holdings: The High Court has inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to grant limited protection from arrest even after rejecting anticipatory bail, to secure the ends of justice.
Such protection must be narrowly tailored, reasoned, and of the shortest duration necessary; a 90-day unreasoned protection order exceeds judicial discretion and is invalid.
doctrines: Liberal interpretation of personal liberty under Article 21
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
Judicial restraint and reasoned orders in exercise of discretion

card.dispute: NBCC (India) Limited appealed against the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's order directing it to pay compensation for delayed possession of a flat allotted to Shri Ram Trivedi.
issues_decided: Whether the consumer forum can award compensation for delayed possession beyond the rate specified in the allotment agreement?
Whether the delay in handing over possession amounted to a deficiency in service under the Consumer Protection Act?
Whether the force majeure defence raised by the developer was valid?
Whether the respondent was entitled to both interest and separate compensation for loss of rent?
holdings: Consumer forums have the jurisdiction to award just and reasonable compensation for delayed possession, even if the agreement specifies a lower rate, especially when the clause is one-sided and unfair.
A delay in handing over possession beyond the stipulated period constitutes a deficiency in service under Section 14(1)(e) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
Force majeure defence cannot be claimed for routine business risks or delays that an experienced developer should anticipate, such as contractor disputes or regulatory delays.
Once compensation in the form of interest is awarded for delayed possession, an additional amount for loss of rent is not justified and amounts to double compensation.
doctrines: Deficiency in service
Unfair trade practice
Force majeure
Compensation for delay

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the transfer of their consumer complaint, filed before the 2019 Act came into force, to a different forum based on the new pecuniary jurisdiction limits under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
issues_decided: Whether pending consumer cases filed under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 should be transferred to different fora based on the pecuniary limits introduced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?
Whether Section 107 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 implies a legislative intention to transfer pending cases to fora with revised pecuniary jurisdiction?
holdings: Proceedings initiated under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 must continue before the same fora and are not to be transferred based on the revised pecuniary limits under the 2019 Act.
The legislature's omission to include a provision for transfer of pending cases indicates an intention to protect ongoing proceedings and ensure consumer welfare.
doctrines: Prospective application of jurisdictional amendments
Legislative intendment and statutory interpretation
Continuity of pending proceedings
Protection of consumer welfare as a legislative object

card.dispute: PSA SICAL Terminals Pvt. Ltd. challenged the setting aside of an arbitral award that had ruled in its favor against the Board of Trustees of V.O. Chidambranar Port Trust regarding tariff adjustments under a BOT agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the arbitral award was liable to be set aside on the ground of patent illegality under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether the Arbitral Tribunal acted beyond its jurisdiction by applying a unilateral circular not agreed to by the parties
Whether the award violated the public policy of India by altering the contract without mutual consent
holdings: An arbitral award that creates a new contract by unilaterally altering agreed terms breaches fundamental principles of justice and amounts to patent illegality.
An Arbitral Tribunal cannot apply a circular or formula not consented to by both parties, as its jurisdiction is confined to the four corners of the agreement.
Rewriting a contract without mutual agreement shocks the conscience of the court and falls within the exceptional category of awards that violate public policy under Section 34.
doctrines: Public policy of India
Patent illegality
Confinement of arbitral jurisdiction to the terms of the contract
Principle that a party cannot be forced to perform a bargain not agreed upon

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to allow lessees to claim rights over forest land that had been notified as reserved forest, arguing that such rights were extinguished by statutory notifications.
issues_decided: Whether the lessees could claim proprietary or tenurial rights over land declared as reserved forest under the Forest Act.

Whether the consolidation authorities could alter revenue records contrary to a notification under Section 4 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 and Section 20 of the Indian Forest Act, 1927.
Whether entries in revenue records can confer title or presumptive ownership over forest land once it is notified as reserved forest.
Whether the failure to publish a final notification under Section 20 of the Forest Act nullifies the regulatory effect of an earlier notification under Section 4 of the same Act.
holdings: Lessees do not acquire any right, title, or interest over land once it is notified as reserved forest under the Forest Act, especially without a written contract with the government.
Consolidation authorities are bound by statutory notifications under the Forest Act and cannot alter revenue records to recognize claims extinguished by such notifications.
Revenue records do not confer title or presumptive ownership; they merely record liability to pay land revenue and cannot override statutory vesting of land in the state or Gaon Samaj.

The regulatory power of the state under the Forest Act begins with the notification under Section 4, and the absence of a final notification under Section 20 does not negate the bar on acquiring rights over the land.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 4
U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 117
U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, Section 49
doctrines: Statutory vesting of land in Gaon Samaj
Finality of forest notifications
Revenue records do not confer title
Forest Act as a complete code

card.dispute: The legal representatives of the elder brother sued the younger brother for possession and accounts, claiming the younger brother had sold him the southern portion of ancestral property via a registered sale deed, which the younger brother later disputed.
issues_decided: Whether oral evidence can be admitted to contradict the terms of a registered sale deed?
Whether the sale deed dated 14.9.1970 could be challenged as a sham transaction in the absence of a plea or proof of fraud, illegality, or lack of consideration?
holdings: Oral evidence is inadmissible to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from the terms of a registered document like a sale deed under Section 92 of the Evidence Act, unless the party alleges and proves the document is a sham or is vitiated by fraud, intimidation, illegality, or failure of consideration.

A party cannot rely on feigned ignorance or mere denial of the nature of a document to escape its terms; without a specific plea and proof of fraud or other vitiating factors, the registered sale deed binds the parties and their representatives.
doctrines: Best evidence rule
Parol evidence rule
Sham transaction exception to Section 92

card.dispute: The appellant Parubai challenged her conviction for murder and house-trespass by fire, arguing that the circumstantial evidence did not conclusively prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution established the guilt of the appellant through a complete chain of circumstantial evidence?
Whether the appellant's failure to explain the cause of fire under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act could sustain her conviction?
Whether suspicion, however strong, can substitute for legal proof in a criminal trial based on circumstantial evidence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to establish a complete and unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence pointing exclusively to the appellant's guilt, and the conviction cannot be based on mere suspicion.

The failure of the accused to explain circumstances under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act is only an additional link and cannot sustain conviction if the other links in the chain of evidence are missing.

In cases relying on circumstantial evidence, the court must ensure that the circumstances lead only to the conclusion that the accused is guilty and not merely that it may be true; where two views are possible, the benefit of doubt must go to the accused.
doctrines: Chain of circumstantial evidence
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Principle of 'must be true' not 'may be true'

card.dispute: Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. and others fought with Emta Coal Limited over whether EMTA had a first right of refusal in the allotment of a mining lease under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015.
issues_decided: Whether Section 11 of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 grants EMTA Coal Limited a first right of refusal in the re-allotment of a mining lease.
Whether the administrative decision of PSPCL to reject EMTA's claim and opt for competitive bidding was subject to judicial review on grounds of illegality, irrationality, or procedural impropriety.
holdings: Section 11 of the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 does not confer any first right of refusal to prior allottees or their successors; the re-allotment must be through a competitive bidding process.

The decision of PSPCL to reject EMTA’s representation and proceed with competitive bidding was not irrational or arbitrary, as it aimed to secure the best operator and was in line with statutory objectives and Wednesbury reasonableness.
doctrines: Wednesbury unreasonableness
Principle of competitive bidding in public resource allocation
Judicial review of administrative action on grounds of illegality, irrationality, and procedural impropriety

card.dispute: The appellants, who were buyers in a property deal, challenged the High Court's quashing of criminal proceedings against the seller for alleged cheating and criminal breach of trust.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC based on the existence of a civil dispute and pending arbitration?
Whether the allegations in the FIR disclose the commission of offences under Sections 420, 406, and 34 IPC?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the criminal proceedings merely because the dispute arose from a commercial transaction and arbitral proceedings were initiated; civil remedies do not preclude criminal prosecution.
Allegations in the FIR, if proven, disclose ingredients of offences under Sections 420 and 406 IPC, and thus a criminal trial must proceed to determine the truth.
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Separate domain of civil and criminal remedies
Inherent powers of High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Principle of not short-circuiting criminal trial at threshold

card.dispute: The legal heirs of former partners in a dissolved partnership firm sued to declare co-ownership of firm assets and to dissolve the firm, which the other heirs opposed.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs, as legal heirs of deceased partners, could claim co-ownership of the partnership firm's assets?
Whether the plaintiffs could seek dissolution of the partnership firm and accounts for winding up?
Whether the plaint disclosed a cause of action warranting trial?
holdings: Legal heirs of deceased partners cannot claim co-ownership of partnership assets during the subsistence of the firm, as ownership vests in the firm, not individual partners.
Only active partners, not legal heirs, can seek dissolution of a partnership firm or accounts for winding up under the Partnership Act.
The plaint disclosed no cause of action and was liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC as the reliefs sought were not maintainable in law.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
doctrines: No cause of action
Maintainability of suit
Rejection of plaint at threshold
Partnership firm as a separate entity

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to grant anticipatory bail to two accused, Jogendra Singh and Suryabhan Singh, in a murder and assault case arising from a sand mining rivalry.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court applied the correct legal principles in granting anticipatory bail to the accused?
Whether the nature and gravity of the offence and the specific role of the accused were adequately considered?
Whether material aspects of the investigation were ignored in granting anticipatory bail?
holdings: The High Court failed to apply the correct principles governing anticipatory bail as laid down in Sushila Aggarwal, particularly regarding the nature of the offence and role of the accused.
Anticipatory bail should not be granted when there is a serious offence with specific allegations supported by consistent statements and evidence on record.
The order granting bail ignored material discrepancies and deficiencies in the investigation, justifying its cancellation by the Supreme Court.
doctrines: Sushila Aggarwal principle for anticipatory bail
Judicial review of bail orders based on material omissions
Distinction between anticipatory bail and regular bail

card.dispute: The appellant Ramawatar was convicted under the SC/ST Act for allegedly insulting and threatening his neighbour Prembai, a member of a Scheduled Caste, during a property dispute; he challenged the conviction, seeking quashing of proceedings after a compromise.
issues_decided: Whether the criminal proceedings under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act can be quashed in light of a compromise between the parties despite the special nature of the statute?
Whether the offence in this case was primarily civil in nature and not motivated by caste-based animosity?
Whether the exercise of power under Article 142 of the Constitution is permissible to quash proceedings even when statutory provisions mandate strict enforcement of the SC/ST Act?
holdings: Criminal proceedings under the SC/ST Act may be quashed under Article 142 if the dispute is essentially private or civil, the caste element is incidental, and the compromise is voluntary, without undermining the Act’s protective purpose.
An offence under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act may be treated as private in nature if it arises from a property dispute and lacks evidence of caste-based humiliation as the primary motive.

The Supreme Court can exercise its power under Article 142 to quash proceedings under special statutes like the SC/ST Act to do complete justice, provided statutory objectives are not defeated and no coercion is involved in the compromise.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(x)
doctrines: Doctrine of complete justice under Article 142
Voluntary compromise in criminal cases
Balancing statutory mandates with equitable powers
Protection against abuse of process of law

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Haji Ali Mohammed Agboatwala sued to declare void a deemed purchase order and certificate issued in favor of the respondents under tenancy law, claiming fraud and lack of notice due to the estate being under court receivership.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint was liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the CPC on the ground of lack of jurisdiction due to Section 85 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
Whether the bar of jurisdiction under Section 85 is absolute when Section 85-A provides a mechanism for civil courts to refer issues to revenue authorities
Whether the plaintiffs' claim of fraud and collusion in the deemed purchase proceedings could be examined by a civil court despite alternative remedies under the Act
Whether lands under court receivership are exempt from the operation of the Act under Section 88-B(1)(d)
holdings: The civil court cannot reject a plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d) merely because revenue authorities have passed orders; it must first consider whether exceptions like fraud or court receivership apply.
Section 85-A modifies the absolute bar of jurisdiction under Section 85 by allowing civil courts to stay suits and refer issues to competent authorities under the Act.
Allegations of fraud and collusion in revenue proceedings cannot be addressed by appellate or revisional authorities under the Act and must be adjudicated by a civil court.
The exemption under Section 88-B(1)(d) of the Act may apply to lands under court receivership, raising a substantial legal question that must be decided on merits.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(d)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 3
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-G
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 32-M
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 74
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 76-A
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 79
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 85-A
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, Section 88-B(1)(d)
doctrines: Constructive notice under Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act
Fraud as an exception to statutory bars of jurisdiction
Doctrine of ouster of civil court jurisdiction
Interpretation of jurisdictional bars in light of saving clauses and alternative remedies

card.dispute: The appellant, who filed the FIR, challenged the High Court's grant of bail to six accused persons implicated in five homicidal deaths arising from a land dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in granting bail to the accused in a case involving multiple murders?
Whether the grant of bail was based on a non-application of mind or irrelevant considerations?
Whether the seriousness of the charges and risk of tampering with evidence were adequately considered?
Whether the principle of parity in bail decisions was correctly applied?
holdings: Bail may be granted in serious offences, but the gravity of the charge, prima facie evidence, and risk of witness tampering must be considered.
An order granting bail can be set aside if it suffers from perversity, non-application of mind, or failure to consider relevant factors.
Seriousness of the offence is a relevant but not sole factor; courts must balance constitutional rights and the need for pre-trial liberty.
Granting bail on grounds of parity without examining individual culpability and evidence is impermissible.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence
Bail as a rule, jail as an exception
Perversity in judicial orders
Non-application of mind
Parity in bail jurisprudence

card.dispute: A father, Rama Narang, was accused of contempt by his son, Ramesh Narang, for allegedly violating court orders related to share transfers and proceedings before the Company Law Board.
issues_decided: Whether the petitioner committed contempt by violating interim orders passed by the Court despite challenging the jurisdiction of the forum?
Whether interim orders passed by a court or tribunal are binding until the jurisdictional issue is finally decided?
Whether the petitioner could challenge the maintainability of proceedings before the Company Law Board (CLB) without first appealing the interim orders?
holdings: An objection to jurisdiction does not nullify interim orders; such orders remain binding and enforceable until the jurisdictional issue is finally decided.
Violation of interim orders can constitute contempt even if the court later decides it lacked jurisdiction, provided the violation occurred before the jurisdictional ruling.
By not challenging the CLB's order on maintainability and jurisdiction, the petitioner was estopped from later claiming the orders were without jurisdiction.
doctrines: Interim orders remain operative until jurisdiction is finally determined
Contempt for disobedience of court orders despite pending jurisdictional challenges
Doctrine of finality and estoppel by failure to appeal

card.dispute: The appellant sued to protect his possession of property without claiming a declaration of title, and the respondents moved to reject the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d) CPC, leading to a dispute over the maintainability of the suit and the validity of the rejection.
issues_decided: Whether the suit was barred under Order 7 Rule 11(d) of the CPC for being barred by any law, specifically Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act
Whether the Trial Court could grant liberty to amend the plaint after rejecting it under Order 7 Rule 11(d)
Whether the writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution was maintainable against the order rejecting the plaint
holdings: A suit seeking only protection of possession without a declaration of title is not automatically barred by Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, but the absence of a claim for declaration may affect maintainability if further relief is available.
The Trial Court cannot grant liberty to amend the plaint after rejecting it under Order 7 Rule 11(d), as such an order conclusively determines the rights and operates as a decree.
A writ petition under Article 227 is not maintainable when the order rejecting the plaint operates as a decree, and the proper remedy is a first appeal under Section 96 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order 7 Rule 11
doctrines: Order 7 Rule 11(d) bar
Decree under Section 2(2) CPC
Alternative remedy doctrine
Liberty to amend not permissible after rejection under Order 7 Rule 11(d)

card.dispute: The appellant, a property owner, filed a criminal complaint against company officials for trespass and property damage, but the courts dismissed proceedings for lack of specific allegations linking the individuals to the alleged offences.
issues_decided: Whether directors and officers of a company can be prosecuted vicariously for offences allegedly committed by the company without specific allegations of personal involvement?
Whether the Magistrate applied the correct legal standard in issuing process against company officials under Sections 427, 447, 506, and 120B read with Section 34 IPC?
Whether a prima facie case was made against the company officials to justify the issuance of summons?
holdings: Directors or officers of a company cannot be prosecuted merely by virtue of their position; there must be specific allegations of active role and criminal intent.
Vicarious liability in criminal law does not apply unless a statute explicitly provides for it, and the complaint must allege facts attracting such statutory liability.
The Magistrate must record satisfaction of a prima facie case against each accused, especially company officials, based on specific roles and evidence before issuing summons.
doctrines: No vicarious criminal liability without statutory basis
Principle of individual culpability in criminal law
Alter ego doctrine applied only in one direction (from individuals to company, not vice versa)
Requirement of prima facie case for issuance of process

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision allowing a civil suit for permanent and mandatory injunction over waqf property, arguing that such disputes must be adjudicated by the Waqf Tribunal under the Waqf Act, 1995.
