issues_decided: Whether a suit for permanent and mandatory injunction concerning waqf property is maintainable in a civil court when the property is admitted to be a waqf property?
Whether the Waqf Tribunal has jurisdiction under Section 83 of the Waqf Act, 1995 to decide disputes relating to waqf property even if the waqf status is not disputed?
Whether the decision in Ramesh Gobindram v. Sugra Humayun Mirza Waqf correctly limits the jurisdiction of the Waqf Tribunal only to cases where the existence of a waqf is disputed?
holdings: The Waqf Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction over disputes relating to waqf or waqf property under Section 83 of the Waqf Act, 1995, regardless of whether the waqf status is admitted or disputed.

A civil court cannot entertain a suit for permanent or mandatory injunction concerning waqf property when the subject matter falls within the ambit of Section 83, as such matters must first be adjudicated by the Waqf Tribunal.

The decision in Ramesh Gobindram was misapplied to restrict the Tribunal’s jurisdiction only to cases where waqf status is disputed; the correct position is that Section 83 confers broad jurisdiction covering all disputes relating to waqf or waqf property.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order XXXIX, Rule 1
doctrines: Exclusive jurisdiction of statutory tribunals
Statutory interpretation based on express language of the statute
Finality of transfer orders to tribunal

card.dispute: The landlord (Shubhas Jain) appealed against a Bombay High Court order allowing a tenant (Rajeshwari Shivam) to remove an adjoining wall for structural repairs, despite the building being declared unsafe.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in allowing the tenant to remove a wall without ensuring the building's structural stability?
Whether the High Court overlooked official reports classifying the building as 'C-1' (requiring immediate evacuation and demolition)?
Whether the proposed repair by architects Shetgiri and Associates amounted to a valid certificate of stability?
Whether the landlord's redevelopment proposal offering alternative accommodation and rent was sufficient to justify eviction of the tenant?
holdings: The High Court erred in permitting wall removal as the building was in C-1 category and required demolition, not repair.
The order was legally unsustainable because it ignored the Municipal Corporation’s report and structural audit declaring the building dangerous.
The report by Shetgiri and Associates did not constitute a certificate of stability, as explicitly stated in Note 1 of the report.
The landlord’s redevelopment proposal, including ownership of equivalent area post-redevelopment and interim rent, was reasonable and justified eviction for demolition.
provisions: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (MCGM) Building Bye-Laws
doctrines: Principle of judicial review of administrative orders
Doctrine of adherence to expert structural audit reports
Public interest in safety of dilapidated buildings

card.dispute: The Telangana State Waqf Board and the Mutawalli of a graveyard wakf fought with a tenant, Mohamed Muzafar, over whether the properties he occupied were part of the wakf and whether the Waqf Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the dispute.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed before the Waqf Tribunal was maintainable given the dispute over the wakf status of the property?
Whether the Waqf Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the question of wakf property extent when the tenant denied its wakf character?
Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the Waqf Tribunal's decision on grounds of maintainability and jurisdiction?
holdings: A suit before the Waqf Tribunal is maintainable when the tenant disputes the wakf nature or extent of the property, as such disputes fall within the Tribunal’s jurisdiction under the Waqf Act.

The Waqf Tribunal has jurisdiction to determine the extent and wakf status of property, especially when the tenant challenges the gazette notification, which invokes rights under Sections 6 and 7 of the Waqf Act.
The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by overturning the Tribunal’s decision on maintainability without recognizing the factual and legal basis for the Tribunal’s jurisdiction.
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Jurisdiction of Waqf Tribunal over disputes concerning wakf property status and extent
Principle of maintainability of suits before special tribunals under statutory framework

card.dispute: The appellants, sons of M. Krishna Reddy, challenged the allotment of land by the Bangalore Development Authority, claiming ownership over part of the acquired land and suppression of facts regarding prior litigation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants suppressed material facts by not disclosing prior civil proceedings concerning the same land?
Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to review its earlier order due to abuse of process?
Whether the writ petition was maintainable given the finality of prior civil court decisions on the acquisition?
holdings: Suppression of material facts, especially pending or past litigation on the same subject, vitiates a writ petition as it amounts to abuse of the court's process.
A party seeking equitable relief under Article 226 must approach the court with clean hands; failure to disclose adverse litigation disentitles them to relief.
Findings of a civil court on land acquisition and maintainability of suit, when final, bind the parties and cannot be re-agitated in writ proceedings.
provisions: Mysore (Personal & Miscellaneous) Inam Abolition Act, 1954, Section 5
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Abuse of process
Finality of judgment
Constructive res judicata

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership and possession of a property and sought a permanent injunction against the respondents, who disputed his title and claimed ownership themselves.
issues_decided: Whether a suit for permanent injunction can be decided on the question of title when the plaintiff's title is disputed?
Whether the plaintiff's title was clear and free from dispute so as to grant an injunction without a full trial?
Whether revenue entries like 'khata' can establish title in a civil suit for injunction?
holdings: A court may decide title in a suit for injunction only if pleadings and issues on title exist and the matter is simple; otherwise, parties must seek a declaration suit.
When the plaintiff's title is genuinely disputed and involves complex questions of fact and law, a suit for injunction cannot be used to determine title.
A 'khata' entry is a fiscal record for tax purposes and does not confer or extinguish title; only a civil court can determine ownership.
doctrines: Title not decided in injunction suits unless exceptional circumstances exist
Fiscal entries do not confer title
Principle of maintaining possession in injunction suits when title is undisputed

card.dispute: The Bijnor Urban Cooperative Bank challenged a High Court order directing it to grant Meenal Agarwal the benefit of a One Time Settlement (OTS) for her non-performing loan account.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could issue a writ of mandamus directing the Bank to grant OTS benefits to the borrower.
Whether a borrower can claim the benefit of OTS as a matter of right.
Whether the Bank's refusal to grant OTS was justified based on its commercial wisdom and recovery prospects.
holdings: The High Court erred in issuing a writ of mandamus directing the Bank to grant OTS, as such relief cannot be enforced as a matter of right.
The benefit of OTS is not a statutory or enforceable right; it is discretionary and subject to eligibility criteria and bank guidelines.
A bank may refuse OTS if it believes full recovery is possible through SARFAESI proceedings or asset auction, and such decision falls within its commercial wisdom.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
doctrines: Principle of commercial wisdom of financial institutions
Doctrine of non-justiciability of discretionary administrative decisions
Principle of natural justice

card.dispute: The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) appealed against the Madras High Court's order halting the expansion of National Highway 45-A for requiring environmental clearance, which NHAI claimed was not necessary due to project segmentation below 100 km.
issues_decided: Whether the segmentation of a highway project exceeding 100 km into packages under 100 km to avoid environmental clearance is permissible under environmental notifications?
Whether the 'right of way' under the 2013 Notification includes toll plazas and other amenities?
Whether the NHAI is required to obtain environmental clearance for the expansion of NH 45-A from Villuppuram to Nagapattinam?
holdings: Segmentation of a highway project exceeding 100 km into smaller packages to avoid environmental clearance is not permissible as a strategy, as it would render environmental notifications ineffective.

The 'right of way' includes toll plazas, rest areas, and other associated infrastructure, and must conform to the 40-meter (existing alignment) or 60-meter (realignments) limit under the 2013 Notification.
Environmental clearance is not required for the NH 45-A project as the land acquisition does not exceed the 40/60-meter threshold, provided the project adheres to the Notification limits.
doctrines: Sustainable development
Precautionary principle
Polluter pays principle
Doctrine against circumvention of statutory requirements

card.dispute: The appellants (purchasers) and respondents (protected tenants) disputed over ownership and occupancy rights to agricultural land in Village Jeedimetla, with the tenants claiming rights under a certificate issued under Section 38-E of the Tenancy Act and the purchasers relying on a 1982 occupancy rights grant under the Inams Act.
issues_decided: Whether the occupancy rights granted to the purchasers under the Inams Act override the ownership rights of the protected tenant under Section 38-E of the Tenancy Act
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the occupancy rights granted to the purchasers
Whether the certificate issued under Section 38-E of the Tenancy Act confers complete ownership on the protected tenant
Whether the Inams Act or the Tenancy Act prevails in case of conflict
holdings: The ownership certificate issued under Section 38-E of the Tenancy Act overrides any occupancy rights granted under the Inams Act, as Section 38-E has a non-obstante clause giving it precedence.
The occupancy rights granted in 1982 are void in respect of Survey Nos. 53, 54, 55, and 56, as those lands were covered by the protected tenant’s certificate under Section 38-E.
The protected tenant is entitled to restoration of possession under Section 32 of the Tenancy Act, as the dispossession was not in accordance with law.
The occupancy rights certificate remains valid only for Survey Nos. 61 and 62, which were not part of the protected tenant’s tenancy.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 38-E
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, Section 32
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955, Section 33
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955, Section 7
Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Abolition of Inams Act, 1955, Section 3(2)(b)
doctrines: Doctrine of non-obstante clause
Doctrine of statutory precedence
Protection of tiller’s rights
Summary enquiry and restoration of possession for protected tenants

card.dispute: CIDCO challenged the allotment of land to Shishir Realty and its partners for hotel development, seeking to cancel the lease on technical grounds, while the lessees claimed protection under promissory estoppel.
issues_decided: Whether the cancellation of land allotment by CIDCO was arbitrary and contrary to the principles of fairness and good faith?
Whether the doctrine of promissory estoppel applies against a public authority in the context of government contracts?
Whether public interest justifies resiling from a contractual promise made by a government agency?
holdings: The cancellation of allotment by CIDCO on technical grounds was arbitrary and disproportionate, violating principles of fairness and good faith in government contracts.
The doctrine of promissory estoppel applies to public authorities, who must fulfill legitimate expectations created by their representations unless overriding public interest is proven.
Mere invocation of public interest or loss to treasury without concrete evidence cannot justify withdrawing from a contractual obligation; such action undermines investor confidence.
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Arbitrariness under Article 14
Good faith in government contracts
Proportionality in administrative action

card.dispute: The Union of India challenged the High Court's order allowing a retired Kashmiri migrant government employee, Onkar Nath Dhar, to retain government accommodation indefinitely after retirement.
issues_decided: Whether a retired government employee has a right to continue occupying government accommodation on a nominal licence fee after retirement due to displacement from Jammu & Kashmir.
Whether the High Court could direct retention of government accommodation based on the right to shelter under Article 21.
Whether the decision in J.L. Koul v. State of J&K laid down a binding precedent for indefinite retention of government housing by displaced retirees.
holdings: There is no indefeasible right to government accommodation after retirement, even for displaced persons; such accommodation is meant for serving employees.
The right to shelter under Article 21 does not entitle a retired government servant to indefinite possession of government housing at a nominal fee.
Directions issued under Article 142 in J.L. Koul were specific to that case and do not constitute a binding precedent or create a legal right for others to claim similar relief.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
doctrines: Ratio decidendi vs. obiter dicta
Principle of binding precedent under Article 141
Limited scope of Article 142 directions as non-precedential on special facts
Non-justiciability of policy decisions regarding distribution of state resources

card.dispute: The State of Rajasthan challenged the decision to allow Love Kush Meena, acquitted on benefit of doubt in a serious criminal case, to join as a constable in the Rajasthan Police.
issues_decided: Whether an acquittal based on benefit of doubt in a serious criminal case disqualifies a candidate from police recruitment.
Whether a government circular allowing appointment of candidates acquitted on benefit of doubt overrides judicial precedents to the contrary.
Whether the employer can consider the nature of the offence and the circumstances of acquittal while assessing suitability for police service.
holdings: An acquittal based on benefit of doubt in a serious criminal case, especially involving violence, does not entitle a candidate to appointment in the police force.
A government circular permitting appointment of those acquitted on benefit of doubt must be read in light of binding judicial precedents and cannot override them.
The employer has the right to consider the nature of the charges, the role attributed to the accused, and whether the acquittal was honourable when assessing suitability for a police post.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt acquittal
Honourable acquittal
Employer's right to assess suitability
Judicial precedent over administrative circulars

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's decision to set aside the respondent's conviction for dishonour of a cheque issued as partial repayment of an advance payment for a property sale that could not proceed.
issues_decided: Whether the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, in favour of the holder of a cheque was rebutted by the respondent.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the conviction based on new contentions raised for the first time in revision.
holdings: The presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, that the holder of a cheque received it for discharge of a liability, stands unrebutted where the accused fails to raise a credible explanation before the trial court.

The High Court erred in accepting a belated contention about undue influence by a relative of the complainant, not raised during trial or appeal, to overturn a conviction based on documentary evidence and statutory presumption.
doctrines: Presumption of validity of cheque under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
Rebuttal of statutory presumption must be based on credible evidence and not mere assertion
Principle of constructive res judicata and estoppel by record
Limited scope of revision jurisdiction under CrPC

card.dispute: Unitech Limited sought compensatory payment from Telangana State Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (TSIIC) after a land allotment deal fell through, while TSIIC and the State of Telangana contested liability, raising issues of stamp duty and inter-state apportionment of liabilities post-bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petition under Article 226 was maintainable given the existence of an alternative remedy under contract law
Whether Unitech was entitled to compensatory payment under the Development Agreement despite non-payment of stamp duty and non-registration of the agreement
How liabilities between APIIC (Andhra Pradesh) and TSIIC (Telangana) should be apportioned under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014
holdings: The writ petition was maintainable as the dispute involved a public law element concerning an instrumentality of the state, despite the existence of a contractual remedy.

Unitech is entitled to refund and interest under the Development Agreement; non-payment of stamp duty does not invalidate the claim, as the Stamp Act is fiscal, not punitive, and the agreement must be impounded for assessment.

TSIIC is liable to refund Unitech, but may pursue apportionment of liability against APIIC under Section 53 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014; the Court expressed no final opinion on the inter-state claim.
doctrines: Fiscal nature of stamp duty laws
Maintainability of writ under Article 226 in public law disputes despite alternative contractual remedies
Doctrine of apportionment of liabilities between successor states

card.dispute: The State of Madhya Pradesh challenged the High Court's decision to quash government circulars directing the deletion of priests' names from revenue records and inserting the Collector as temple manager.
issues_decided: Whether the circulars dated 21.03.1994 and 07.06.2008 directing deletion of Pujari names from revenue records are illegal
Whether the name of a priest or manager must be recorded in revenue records under the land revenue code
Whether the State Government can issue executive instructions to record the Collector as manager of temple properties
holdings: The circulars dated 21.03.1994 and 07.06.2008 are not illegal, as the State Government has authority to issue executive instructions consistent with law.
The name of a priest or manager is not required to be entered in ownership or occupancy columns of revenue records; it may be noted only in the remarks column.
The Collector cannot be recorded as manager of all temples, especially private ones, unless the temple is vested in the State.
provisions: Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, Samvat 1959, Sections 108, 109, 110
Rules under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code (Form I, Khasra entries)
doctrines: Distinction between public and private religious endowments
Executive instructions valid if not contrary to statute
Idol as juristic person; ownership of temple property vests in deity

card.dispute: The appellants (V. Anantha Raju and son) challenged the lower courts' decision that they were entitled to only 10% share in the profits and losses of the partnership firm and were validly expelled from the firm.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to 50% share in the profits and losses of the partnership firm until their expulsion in 2004?
Whether the expulsion of the appellants from the partnership firm was valid under the partnership deed?
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the 1995 Deed, being a written document, had higher evidentiary value under Section 91 of the Evidence Act, and the appellants were entitled to 50% combined share in profits and losses until 2004, despite the conditional clause in the 1992 Deed.

The Court upheld the expulsion of the appellants from the partnership firm as valid, relying on clause 17 of the 1992 Deed, which permitted expulsion of an erring partner with reasonable opportunity of being heard, and no contrary provision existed in the 1995 Deed.
doctrines: Best evidence rule
Continued operation of unaltered partnership deed clauses

card.dispute: The State of Tamil Nadu and another appealed against a High Court decision that struck down a loan waiver scheme limited to small and marginal farmers, directing that it be extended to all farmers.
issues_decided: Whether the classification of beneficiaries under the loan waiver scheme based on landholding size violates Article 14 of the Constitution
Whether a law that is under-inclusive in economic welfare legislation is automatically unconstitutional
Whether a scheme introduced pursuant to an electoral promise is constitutionally suspect
holdings: Classification based on landholding size in a welfare scheme for farmers does not violate Article 14 if it has a rational nexus with the object of the policy.
Under-inclusiveness in economic legislation does not invalidate a scheme if there are fair reasons for the classification, and courts must show deference to legislative policy choices.
A welfare scheme introduced to fulfill an electoral promise is not constitutionally invalid merely because of its political origin.
doctrines: Rational nexus test
Principle of judicial deference in economic legislation
Proportionality test (distinguished from rational nexus in classificatory schemes)

card.dispute: The appellant claimed ownership of a property under a registered will, while the respondents contested it with an unregistered will, leading to a dispute over testamentary validity and possession.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in disregarding the trial court's findings on oral evidence and credibility of witnesses?
Whether the registered Will (Exhibit P4) was validly executed and free from suspicious circumstances?
Whether the unregistered Will (Exhibit D1) could supersede the registered Will (Exhibit P4)?
Whether the appellate court erred in creating suspicion around the registered Will without legal basis?
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the trial court's findings on witness credibility without addressing the reasons recorded by the trial court, violating settled principles of appellate review.
The registered Will (Exhibit P4) was validly executed under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, with no suspicious circumstances warranting scrutiny.
An unregistered Will (Exhibit D1), alleged to replace a registered Will, cannot prevail when found forged and unsupported by pleadings, issues, or evidence.
A testamentary court must not create suspicion where none exists, especially when beneficiaries’ close relatives participated in and supported the will’s execution.
doctrines: Appellate court must respect trial court's assessment of witness credibility unless there is material irregularity or misreading of evidence.
Principle of suspicious circumstances in testamentary cases requires concrete surrounding factors, not mere exclusion of heirs.
Presumption of validity of registered will under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act.
Doctrine of constructive res judicata and issue estoppel in appellate proceedings.

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's rejection of his plea against the sanction granted under MCOCA for his prosecution in a kidnapping and extortion case.
issues_decided: Whether the sanction order under Section 23(2) of MCOCA was validly passed based on relevant material and without relying solely on confessional statements?
Whether the acquittal in a prior criminal case and the appellant being declared an absconder are relevant to the invocation of MCOCA?
Whether the use of confessional statements by the sanctioning authority violates the principles of fair trial or admissibility under the Evidence Act?
holdings: The sanction order under MCOCA is valid if based on an overall assessment of evidence, including but not limited to confessional statements, and the authority applied its mind to relevant factors.
Acquittal due to witnesses turning hostile or not appearing does not bar invocation of MCOCA, as witness protection is one of its core objectives.
Confessional statements made to police officers are admissible under Section 18 of MCOCA, which overrides Sections 25 and 26 of the Evidence Act, for the purpose of trial of co-accused.
provisions: Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999, Section 2(1)(d), (e), (f)
Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999, Section 18
Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999, Section 19
Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act, 1999, Section 23(2)
doctrines: Non obstante clause under special statutes
Strict interpretation of exceptions to evidence rules
Witness intimidation as justification for invoking special laws
Absconsion affecting entitlement to judicial relief

card.dispute: The Asset Reconstruction Company challenged the High Court's reversal of a Single Judge's order that declared the registration of a sale deed by the Registering Authority to be null and void, based on the authority of the power agent to execute and register the document.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court can exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to challenge the registration of a document on grounds of the Registering Authority's failure to perform statutory duties.
Whether a challenge to the registration of a document, as opposed to its execution, can be entertained in writ proceedings.
Whether the Registering Authority has a duty to verify the power of attorney holder's authority to present a document for registration.
holdings: The High Court can exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to examine whether the Registering Authority failed to perform statutory duties during registration, without encroaching on civil court's domain over title and execution.

A challenge limited to the procedural act of registration by the Registering Authority is maintainable in writ proceedings, especially where there is a clear statutory duty to verify the agent's authority.
The Registering Authority must verify whether a power agent has the legal authority to present a document for registration, particularly when the power of attorney explicitly restricts such power.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13
doctrines: Separation between challenge to execution of document and challenge to registration process
Writ jurisdiction under Article 226 for enforcement of statutory duties by public authorities
Judicial review of administrative and quasi-judicial acts of registering officers

card.dispute: The appellant landlord sought eviction of the respondent tenant on grounds of bona fide need, while the tenant challenged the landlord's title and claimed protection under the Enemy Property Act.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction in exercising revisional power under the proviso to Section 25B(8) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
Whether the tenant could challenge the landlord's title in an eviction petition?
Whether the existence of alternative accommodation negates the landlord's bona fide need for eviction?
Whether the properties in question fall under the purview of the Enemy Property Act, 1968?
holdings: The High Court cannot exercise appellate jurisdiction while hearing a revision; it may only interfere if the Rent Controller's findings are wholly unreasonable or based on a wrong legal premise.
A tenant cannot challenge the landlord's title in a proceeding under Section 14(1)(e) when the tenant has previously acknowledged such title.
The mere allegation of alternative accommodation, without pleadings or evidence of suitability, does not rebut the landlord's bona fide need for eviction.
Properties owned by non-evacuees whose predecessors were not enemies under the Enemy Property Act do not fall under its ambit, especially when confirmed by the Assistant Custodian's report.
provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, Section 25B(8) proviso
doctrines: Limited scope of revisional jurisdiction
Bona fide need of landlord in eviction proceedings
Res judicata and estoppel against raising collateral issues
Presumption of validity of title in eviction petitions

card.dispute: Asian Hotels (North) Ltd. fought against licensees, including Alok Kumar Lodha, over the revocation of shop licenses and the licensees' attempt to amend their suits to declare mortgages on the property void and implead banks as parties.
issues_decided: Whether the licensees can amend their plaints to declare mortgages on the hotel premises void ab initio?
Whether the mortgagee banks are necessary or proper parties in a suit challenging revocation of irrevocable licenses?
Whether the High Court erred in allowing amendments that change the nature of the suit?
holdings: Licensees cannot amend their plaints to declare mortgages void ab initio as the mortgages predate most licenses and were created with the licensor’s right reserved under the license agreement.
Mortgagee banks are not necessary or proper parties in a suit solely about license revocation, as the mortgages are unrelated to the licensees’ rights until those rights are adjudicated.
Amendments that alter the nature of the suit or result in misjoinder of causes of action should not be allowed, even if the plaintiff is dominus litus.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order 6 Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 1 Rule 10
doctrines: Dominus litus
Amendment of pleadings
Necessary and proper parties
Change in nature of suit

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Azgar Barid (defendant No. 1) challenged the Karnataka High Court's decision restoring a trial court decree that granted shares in ancestral properties to the descendants of Mohiyuddin Pasha, including Mazambi @ Pyaremabi and her children, and recognized the claims of Rahaman Barid’s widow and daughter despite his predecease.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the First Appellate Court's reversal of the trial court's findings on the marriage of Mohiyuddin Pasha to Mazambi @ Pyaremabi and the legitimacy of their children?
Whether the Mehar Deed executed in favor of Noorbi, the first wife of Mohiyuddin Pasha, effectively divested him of ownership of the suit properties?
Whether the findings of fact recorded by the trial court, based on oral and documentary evidence, could be overturned by the First Appellate Court without sufficient reason?
holdings: The High Court was justified in reversing the First Appellate Court’s findings, as the trial court’s conclusions about the marriage and parentage were based on credible oral and documentary evidence, including birth certificates and testimony from independent witnesses.

The Mehar Deed in favor of Noorbi was nominal and not acted upon, as established by admissions in a prior suit (O.S. No. 514/1961), and thus did not transfer ownership of the properties away from Mohiyuddin Pasha.

The First Appellate Court erred in reversing concurrent findings of fact without valid grounds, especially when those findings were supported by substantial evidence, making the reversal perverse and warranting High Court intervention under Section 100, CPC.
doctrines: Perverse findings doctrine
Concurrent finding of fact rule
Constructive res judicata
Appreciation of evidence

card.dispute: The appellants, who had entered into sale agreements with the respondent and filed civil suits for specific performance, challenged the criminal proceedings initiated by the respondent under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., alleging those were malicious and abusive.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the appellants' petitions under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIRs?
Whether the criminal proceedings were initiated with mala fide intent and constitute an abuse of process?
Whether the Magistrate failed to follow the legal requirements while ordering investigation under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.?
holdings: The court held that the criminal proceedings were initiated with an ulterior motive to harass the appellants and fit within the category of cases warranting quashing under the precedent in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal.

The court held that applications under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. must be supported by a sworn affidavit, and the Magistrate should verify the veracity of allegations, especially in cases prone to misuse.

The court held that the Magistrate failed to ensure compliance with prior requirements under Sections 154(1) and 154(3) Cr.P.C. and ignored the need for an affidavit, rendering the initiation of investigation legally flawed.
doctrines: Abuse of process of law
Inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
Mala fide prosecution
Requirement of affidavit in Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. applications

card.dispute: The appellant and respondents disputed whether Clause 18 of their Development Agreement constituted a valid arbitration agreement under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
issues_decided: Whether Clause 18 of the Development Agreement qualifies as a valid arbitration agreement under Section 7 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?
Whether the absence of the words 'final and binding' in the arbitration clause renders it invalid?
Whether the court can cure deficiencies in the appointment mechanism of arbitrators to give effect to party autonomy?
holdings: Clause 18 constitutes a valid arbitration agreement as it clearly mandates reference to arbitration and evinces an unambiguous intention by the parties to resolve disputes through arbitration.
The omission of the words 'final and binding' does not invalidate the arbitration clause if the overall intent and substance of the clause indicate a binding arbitration process.

Courts may read in missing elements, such as the method for appointing a third arbitrator, to make an arbitration clause workable, provided it aligns with the parties' intention and stays within legal boundaries.
provisions: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Fourth Schedule
doctrines: Party autonomy in arbitration
Substance over form in interpreting arbitration agreements
Minimal judicial intervention in arbitration
Binding nature of arbitration agreements despite technical omissions

card.dispute: The appellant (original defendant) challenged the decree of permanent injunction granted to the respondent (original plaintiff) based on an unregistered agreement to sell, after the High Court dismissed his second appeal.
issues_decided: Whether an unregistered agreement to sell can be the basis for granting a decree of permanent injunction without seeking specific performance?
Whether the plaintiff can indirectly obtain the benefit of an unregistered agreement to sell by claiming only injunction while avoiding a claim for specific performance?
holdings: An unregistered agreement to sell, being inadmissible in evidence, cannot serve as the foundation for a decree of permanent injunction when the plaintiff avoids seeking specific performance due to the document's inadmissibility.
A plaintiff cannot use clever drafting to obtain indirect relief through injunction that would not be available through specific performance of an unregistered agreement to sell.
doctrines: Collateral use of unregistered documents
Prohibition against indirect enforcement of inadmissible agreements

card.dispute: The appellant, convicted of rape and murder of a 6-year-old girl based on circumstantial evidence, challenged the conviction and death sentence on grounds of unreliable evidence and failure to conduct a medical examination under Section 53A CrPC.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution's failure to conduct a medical examination of the accused under Section 53A CrPC, despite reasonable grounds, undermines the case in a circumstantial evidence scenario?
Whether the ocular evidence in the case was reliable and sufficient to sustain a conviction for rape and murder?
Whether the absence of DNA evidence and forensic analysis of stains on the victim's clothing creates a fatal gap in the prosecution's case?
Whether the lower courts properly evaluated the quality and consistency of the prosecution's evidence, particularly the testimonies of key witnesses?
holdings: The failure to medically examine the accused under Section 53A CrPC, when there were reasonable grounds, is fatal to the prosecution’s case, especially when relying solely on circumstantial evidence.
Ocular evidence, particularly from PWs 1 to 3, was inherently contradictory and unreliable, and thus insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The prosecution’s failure to obtain forensic analysis of blood/semen stains on the victim’s clothing compounded the evidentiary deficiencies and raised serious doubts.
Lower courts failed to apply rigorous scrutiny to the prosecution’s evidence in a capital case, leading to an unsafe conviction that must be set aside.
doctrines: Last seen doctrine
Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Adverse inference from non-production of available evidence
Principle of rigorous scrutiny in cases based on circumstantial evidence

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation of Rs.4 lakhs per acre awarded for their land acquired by the Union in Village Sohana, claiming higher compensation based on awards in nearby villages and subsequent acquisitions.
issues_decided: Whether the market value of land in Village Kambali could be used as a benchmark for determining compensation for land in Village Sohana.
Whether compensation awarded in subsequent land acquisitions could be used to determine market value for earlier acquisitions by applying deductions.
Whether the Reference Court and High Court erred in upholding Rs.4 lakhs per acre as just compensation for land in Village Sohana.
holdings: The market value of land in Village Kambali cannot be used to determine compensation for land in Village Sohana as the villages are not in close proximity and are over 2 km apart.
Market value for earlier land acquisition cannot be determined by deducting appreciation from later acquisitions, as intervening development inflates prices and distorts comparability.
The award of Rs.4 lakhs per acre was valid as it was based on a final award for land in Village Lakhnaur under the same notification and no comparable sale instances were available.
doctrines: Principle of comparable market value in land acquisition compensation
Prohibition against using subsequent acquisition values to retroactively determine earlier market value
Finality of unchallenged compensation awards as binding precedent in same notification cases

card.dispute: The dispute was between the legal heirs of Bhadar Ram, a Scheduled Caste person from Punjab, and Jassa Ram, the son of Chunilal (a Scheduled Caste allottee in Rajasthan), over the validity of a sale deed concerning Scheduled Caste allotted land in Rajasthan.
issues_decided: Whether a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste in one State can claim the same status and rights in another State for the purpose of purchasing Scheduled Caste allotted land?
Whether the sale of Scheduled Caste allotted land to a person from outside the State violated Section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and Section 13 of the Rajasthan Colonization Act, 1954?
Whether the Board of Revenue could legally compound the illegal transfer under Section 13A of the Rajasthan Colonization Act, 1954 after an order of ejectment had already been executed?
holdings: A person belonging to a Scheduled Caste in one State does not automatically qualify as a Scheduled Caste in another State for availing benefits, including land ownership rights, under the Constitution and relevant laws.

The sale of land allotted to a Scheduled Caste person in Rajasthan to a Scheduled Caste person from Punjab violated Section 42 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and Section 13 of the Rajasthan Colonization Act, 1954, rendering the transaction void.

The Board of Revenue could not legally compound the transfer under Section 13A(2) of the Rajasthan Colonization Act, 1954 after the possession had already been restored to the original allottee pursuant to an ejectment order.
doctrines: State-specific applicability of Scheduled Caste status
Strict interpretation of protective land laws for Scheduled Castes
Doctrine of judicial precedent (stare decisis) as applied to Constitution Bench rulings in Marri Chandra Shekar Rao and Action Committee cases

card.dispute: The Delhi Development Authority challenged the High Court's order declaring land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, which was claimed by Godfrey Phillips (I) Ltd., a purchaser of the acquired land.
issues_decided: Whether the land acquisition proceedings lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
Whether a purchaser of acquired land after vesting can claim lapsing of acquisition proceedings
Whether physical possession and deposit of compensation satisfy the twin conditions for non-lapsing under Section 24(2)
holdings: Acquisition proceedings do not lapse under Section 24(2) if either physical possession was taken or compensation was deposited before the 2013 Act came into force.
A purchaser who acquires land after vesting under the 1894 Act cannot claim lapsing of acquisition as such transactions are void and against public policy.
The larger Bench decision in Shiv Kumar v. Union of India overrules Manav Dharam Trust, holding that a purchaser has no right to challenge acquisition or seek declaration of lapse.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 11(4)
doctrines: Lapsing of land acquisition under Section 24(2) requires failure to take possession and pay compensation
Doctrine of per incuriam applied to overrule Manav Dharam Trust
Binding precedent from larger Bench prevails over smaller Bench decisions

card.dispute: The plaintiff sued for mandatory and prohibitory injunction and damages over a property, and the defendant challenged the trial court's pecuniary jurisdiction based on the suit's valuation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in rejecting the plaint for want of pecuniary jurisdiction based on the market value of the property?
Whether a suit for mandatory and prohibitory injunction must be valued at the market value of the property under the Court Fees Act?
holdings: A suit for mandatory and prohibitory injunction is not required to be valued at the market value of the property; the plaintiff's valuation based on the reliefs claimed, including nominal and damage claims, is valid.

The High Court erred in relying solely on the market value of the property to deem the valuation arbitrary, without considering the applicable legal principles under Section 7(iv)(d) of the Court Fees Act.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
doctrines: Pecuniary jurisdiction based on proper valuation of suit
Plaintiff's discretion in valuation of injunction suits under Section 7(iv)(d)
Judicial review of arbitrary valuation only where objective standards exist

card.dispute: Essar House Private Limited and Essar Services India Private Limited fought against Arcellor Mittal Nippon Steel India Limited over the enforcement of interim relief requiring them to deposit significant sums or provide bank guarantees during ongoing arbitration proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could direct the deposit of Rs.35.5 crores by Essar House Private and Rs.47.41 crores by Essar Services under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, despite their claims of limited or encumbered assets.
Whether the principles of Order 38 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure apply to applications under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act.
Whether a strong prima facie case and balance of convenience are sufficient for granting interim relief under Section 9, even in the absence of proof of asset dissipation.
holdings: The Court can grant interim relief under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act even if the respondent has no unencumbered assets, to secure the efficacy of arbitration and prevent injustice.
The principles of Order 38 Rule 5 CPC guide but do not strictly bind the Court in Section 9 applications; procedural rigors must not defeat the ends of justice.
A strong prima facie case and balance of convenience suffice for interim relief under Section 9; actual proof of asset disposal is not mandatory if there is a real risk of asset diminution.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 38 Rule 5
doctrines: Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury test for interim relief
Efficacy of arbitration as a dispute resolution mechanism
Equitable powers of the court under Section 9 to secure claims despite technical limitations

card.dispute: The original landowners challenged the High Court's decision to allow Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Limited (MRPL), a lessee, to participate in compensation proceedings for land acquired under the KIAD Act, 1966.
issues_decided: Whether MRPL, as a lessee of the acquired land, is a 'person interested' or beneficiary entitled to participate in compensation determination proceedings under the KIAD Act, 1966.
Whether the High Court erred in relying on precedents under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when interpreting the KIAD Act, 1966.
Whether the High Court was bound to follow the Supreme Court’s earlier decision in Peerappa Hanmantha Harijan regarding the rights of allottees under the KIAD Act.
holdings: A lessee like MRPL, who acquires possession after acquisition by KIADB, is neither a 'person interested' nor a beneficiary entitled to be heard during compensation determination under the KIAD Act, 1966.
The provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, particularly Section 50, are not applicable to acquisitions under the KIAD Act, 1966, which has its own distinct procedure and framework.

The High Court was bound by the binding precedent of Peerappa Hanmantha Harijan, where this Court distinguished earlier decisions and held that allottees under KIAD Act cannot claim rights in compensation proceedings.
provisions: Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, Section 28(4)
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, Section 32(2)
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, Section 41(2)(b)
doctrines: Doctrine of binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution of India
Distinction between acquisition statutes and their exclusive applicability
Principle of 'person interested' in land acquisition proceedings limited to those with legal interest at the time of acquisition

card.dispute: The homebuyer sued the developer for failing to deliver possession of the apartment within the stipulated time, seeking refund of payments with interest.
issues_decided: Whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has the power to direct refund of amounts under Section 14 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986
Whether a consumer can seek refund under the Consumer Protection Act despite remedies available under RERA
From which date interest should be calculated on the refund amount
What rate of interest is appropriate in cases of delayed possession
holdings: The Commission has the jurisdiction under Section 14 of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 to direct refund of amounts paid by a consumer for deficiency in service.
The remedies under the Consumer Protection Act and the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 are not mutually exclusive and must be read harmoniously.
Interest on refunded amounts should be calculated from the date of each deposit to ensure restitution and compensation.
An interest rate of 9% per annum is fair and just in cases of delayed possession, balancing consumer protection and developer liability.
provisions: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Section 18
doctrines: Harmonious construction
Restitution and compensatory interest
Consumer's right to choose remedy

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution against an order of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission passed in appeal under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
issues_decided: Whether a writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India is maintainable against an order passed by the National Commission in an appeal under Section 58(1)(a)(iii) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?
Whether the High Court committed an error in staying the order of the National Commission while exercising jurisdiction under Article 227?
holdings: A writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution is maintainable against an order of the National Commission passed in appeal under Section 58(1)(a)(iii) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, as it preserves the High Court's supervisory jurisdiction and ensures access to justice.

While exercising jurisdiction under Article 227, the High Court must act within the limited scope of superintendence and not interfere with the merits of the National Commission's order, especially when granting interim relief.
doctrines: Judicial review under Article 227
Principle of access to justice
Doctrine of limited supervisory jurisdiction
Doctrine of constitutional safeguards in statutory tribunals

card.dispute: The husband of the deceased challenged the discharge of accused persons from a murder charge, arguing that the trial court prematurely downgraded the charge to culpable homicide without evaluating full evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court can discharge accused from a murder charge under Section 302 IPC based solely on the post-mortem report without evaluating oral and expert evidence?
Whether the High Court erred in affirming the discharge without recognizing the procedural illegality in prematurely discarding the possibility of murder?
Whether a charge under Section 302 IPC can be dropped at the initial stage without allowing the prosecution to present all relevant evidence?
holdings: A trial court cannot discharge accused from a murder charge under Section 302 IPC solely based on the post-mortem report; oral and expert evidence must first be evaluated.
The post-mortem report is not substantive evidence but can only corroborate, refresh memory, or contradict a medical witness’s testimony in court.
At the charge-framing stage, the prosecution must be allowed to present its full case; downgrading the charge prematurely restricts the prosecution and undermines fair trial principles.
doctrines: Presumption under criminal law
Principle of fair trial
Evaluation of evidence at charge stage
Role of expert medical testimony

card.dispute: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. and M/s Shree Ganesh Petroleum disputed over an arbitral award that modified the lease rent and lease period of a land lease agreement, which the former challenged as beyond the arbitrator's jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the Arbitrator had the jurisdiction to modify the lease rent and lease period under the lease agreement?
Whether the arbitral award altering the contractual terms violated the principles of public policy and fundamental justice?
holdings: An Arbitrator cannot alter the terms of a valid contract, such as lease rent and duration, as this exceeds their jurisdiction and violates the parties' agreed bargain.

Rewriting contractual terms by an Arbitrator shocks the conscience of the court and breaches fundamental principles of justice, falling within the exceptional grounds for setting aside an award under public policy.
doctrines: Separation of powers in arbitration: Arbitrators must operate within the scope of the contract
Public policy exception under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Principle that a party cannot be forced into a contract not agreed upon
Non-interference with merits of arbitral award unless fundamental justice is violated

card.dispute: The auction purchaser challenged the High Court's order directing a re-auction of temple land, claiming his 1998 purchase at a price higher than the base value should be upheld.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in ordering a re-auction of the property after 23 years despite a fair public auction in 1998?
Whether a non-participant in the auction could maintain a public interest litigation to challenge the sale?
Whether the temple trust could challenge its own conducted auction after a long delay without alleging fraud or irregularity?
holdings: A public auction that is free from fraud, collusion, or irregularity and results in a bid significantly above the base price must be respected, and re-auction should not be ordered after 23 years.
A person who did not participate in the auction lacks locus standi to challenge the sale under the guise of public interest litigation, especially when the petition serves private interests.
A temple trust cannot challenge its own lawful auction conducted by its executive officer long after the fact, particularly when no irregularities were alleged at the time.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987
doctrines: Locus standi in public interest litigation
Finality of public auctions
Mala fide litigation and abuse of process
Principles governing bona fide public interest litigation

card.dispute: Family members fought over the validity of a compromise decree in a partition suit, with some parties alleging fraud in the Lok Adalat settlement.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the Lok Adalat's compromise decree without adequate reasoning.
Whether the compromise decree could be invalidated on grounds of fraud without strict proof.
Whether the recipients of settlement amounts could rescind the compromise without returning the money.
holdings: The High Court erred in setting aside the Lok Adalat's compromise decree without considering the findings recorded in its favor, violating principles of finality and sanctity of consent decrees.
A compromise decree cannot be set aside on mere allegations of fraud; strict and conclusive proof of fraud inducing consent is required.
Parties who accepted monetary benefits under a compromise cannot later challenge it without returning the amounts received, absent proof of fraud.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXIII Rule 3
doctrines: Sanctity of consent decrees
Finality of compromise settlements
Strict proof of fraud to invalidate agreements
Doctrine of clean hands

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the compensation awarded for their land acquired for the Jhajjar Thermal Power Plant, seeking higher compensation comparable to that awarded in a similar nearby acquisition.
issues_decided: Whether the landowners are entitled to higher compensation than the Rs. 16,00,000 per acre awarded by the High Court for land acquired for the Jhajjar Thermal Power Plant.
Whether the compensation awarded in the Arawali Power Company case (Rs. 25,00,000 per acre) could be a relevant benchmark despite being labeled as 'peculiar to the facts' and not a precedent.
Whether landowners in certain appeals are entitled to interest on enhanced compensation given the delay in filing appeals before the High Court.
holdings: Landowners whose land was acquired for the Jhajjar Thermal Power Plant are entitled to just and reasonable compensation, and given the proximity and similarity of the land to that in the Arawali Power case, compensation should be enhanced to Rs. 22,00,000 per acre.

The observation in the Arawali Power case that it was 'in the peculiar facts and not to be treated as precedent' applies only to the use of post-Section 4 sale deeds by agreement, not to the principle of comparable compensation for similarly situated lands.

Landowners in appeals arising from RFA Nos. 4322/2016, 4682/2016, 804/2017, and 805/2017 are not entitled to interest on enhanced compensation due to the condition imposed by the High Court while condoning delay in filing appeals.
doctrines: Principle of just and reasonable compensation
Doctrine of comparable market value in land acquisition
Precedent value of prior compensation awards in similarly situated lands
Conditional waiver of interest due to delay in filing appeals

card.dispute: Indian Overseas Bank challenged the setting aside of a SARFAESI Act sale of assets of RCM Infrastructure Ltd. after insolvency proceedings were initiated.
issues_decided: Whether the sale of secured assets under SARFAESI Act was complete before the commencement of CIRP and thus outside the moratorium under Section 14 of IBC
Whether the provisions of IBC override those of SARFAESI Act in case of conflict
Whether the bank could continue enforcement proceedings under SARFAESI Act after initiation of CIRP
holdings: The sale under SARFAESI Act is complete only upon full payment and issuance of sale certificate; since both occurred after CIRP commencement, the sale was invalid.
Section 14(1)(c) of IBC imposes a moratorium on enforcement of security interests, including under SARFAESI Act, and overrides inconsistent laws under Section 238.
Once CIRP is initiated, no action to enforce security interest can continue, even if part payment was made before the moratorium.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 13(4)
Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, Rule 8 and Rule 9
doctrines: Doctrine of priority of IBC over other laws
Doctrine of moratorium under IBC
Doctrine of statutory sale completion under SARFAESI

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction and recovery of arrears of rent from the tenant, who claimed to have become a purchaser of the property through agreements to sell, thereby extinguishing the landlord-tenant relationship.
issues_decided: Whether the Trial Court could pass a decree under Order XII Rule 6 of the CPC based on admissions without considering the tenant's defense of having become a purchaser.
Whether the admissions made by the tenant were clear and categorical enough to warrant a decree under Order XII Rule 6 of the CPC.
Whether the tenant is liable to pay arrears of rent and future rent during the pendency of the suit.
holdings: The Trial Court erred in passing a decree under Order XII Rule 6 of the CPC without considering the tenant's defense based on agreements to sell, as the defense required a full trial to determine its justiciability.

Admissions regarding tenancy do not amount to clear and categorical admissions justifying a decree under Order XII Rule 6 when a plausible defense is raised that changes the jural relationship between the parties.

The tenant is liable to pay arrears of rent and future monthly rent as per the extended lease agreement, with annual increases, pending final disposal of the suit, subject to the outcome of the dispute.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XII Rule 6
doctrines: Doctrine of categorical admission under Order XII Rule 6 CPC
Doctrine of part performance under Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of change in jural relationship by agreement

card.dispute: The appellants claimed a half share in ancestral property as descendants of one of the coparceners, while the respondents denied their legitimacy and right to inherit.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were legitimate descendants entitled to a share in the ancestral property
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the trial court's decree for partition
What is the proper procedure for passing a final decree in partition suits after a preliminary decree?
holdings: The plaintiffs were held to be legitimate sons of Damodaran through a valid marriage with Chiruthakutty, and thus entitled to a share in the ancestral property.
The High Court erred in setting aside the trial court’s partition decree without sufficient grounds, and the trial court’s findings on legitimacy and entitlement were upheld.
After a preliminary decree in a partition suit, the trial court must proceed suo motu to finalize the decree under Order XX Rule 18 CPC without adjourning sine die or requiring separate proceedings.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 18
doctrines: Suo motu continuation of proceedings after preliminary decree
Distinction between preliminary and final decree in partition suits
Need for a continuous and seamless civil justice process to ensure effective relief

card.dispute: Frost International Ltd. sued Milan Developers and Builders to declare that a cheque it issued was only a security and not liable for enforcement under the Negotiable Instruments Act, and to prevent its use in criminal proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the plaint seeking declaratory reliefs against enforcement of a cheque could be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC?
Whether a civil court can grant an injunction or declaration to restrain a party from initiating or prosecuting proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act?
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the revisional court's order rejecting the plaint?
holdings: The plaint seeking declarations that the cheque was handed over as security and that the plaintiff is not liable to deliver iron ore or pay the cheque amount is barred by law and liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.

A civil court cannot grant declaratory or injunctive relief that effectively restrains a party from prosecuting a proceeding under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, as it violates Section 41(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
The High Court erred in remanding the case for reconsideration; the revisional court had jurisdiction to reject the plaint under Section 115 CPC, and its order was legally sound.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11
doctrines: Access to justice under Section 41(b) of the Specific Relief Act
Bar on civil courts interfering with criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act
Declaratory relief cannot be used to pre-empt statutory remedies

card.dispute: The borrower challenged the High Court's interpretation of Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, which allowed Additional District Magistrates and Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrates to assist in taking possession of secured assets, instead of only the District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate personally.
issues_decided: Whether the District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate is a persona designata under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act.
Whether the expression 'District Magistrate' and 'Chief Metropolitan Magistrate' in Section 14 includes Additional District Magistrate and Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate.
holdings: The District Magistrate and Chief Metropolitan Magistrate are not persona designata under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, as the functions under this section are ministerial and do not require personal performance by the designated officer.

The terms 'District Magistrate' and 'Chief Metropolitan Magistrate' in Section 14 include Additional District Magistrates and Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrates, as they exercise equivalent powers under the CrPC and such inclusion ensures expeditious disposal of applications.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 14
doctrines: Purposive interpretation
Ministerial vs. adjudicatory function
Successor-in-office doctrine

card.dispute: Emaar India Ltd. and Tarun Aggarwal Projects LLP disputed whether their conflict over a collaboration agreement fell under a non-arbitrable clause (Clause 36) or an arbitration clause (Clause 37).
issues_decided: Whether the dispute between the parties falls under Clause 36 or Clause 37 of the Addendum Agreement.
Whether the High Court erred in appointing arbitrators without conducting a preliminary inquiry into the arbitrability of the dispute.
Whether disputes relating to enforcement of Clauses 3, 6, and 9 of the agreement are non-arbitrable.
holdings: The High Court must conduct a prima facie inquiry into whether a dispute falls under a non-arbitrable clause before appointing arbitrators under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration Act.
Disputes concerning enforcement of specific contractual clauses (3, 6, 9) under Clause 36 may be non-arbitrable if they involve rights enforceable only by courts.
Courts may intervene at the reference stage under Section 11 only when it is manifestly clear that disputes are non-arbitrable, but such intervention requires a preliminary judicial assessment.
doctrines: Competence-competence
Separability of arbitration agreement
Judicial review at referral stage
Non-arbitrability doctrine

card.dispute: The landlord, M/s Puri Investments, sought eviction of tenants M/s Young Friends & Co. and others from a shop in Connaught Place, Delhi, alleging unauthorized sub-letting of part of the premises to medical practitioners.
issues_decided: Whether the occupation of part of the premises by medical practitioners constituted sub-letting or mere licensing under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Whether the Appellate Tribunal's finding of sub-letting was perverse and liable to be set aside by the High Court under Article 227
Whether the respondents were entitled to continue in possession and at what terms
holdings: Allowing medical practitioners to occupy exclusive portions of the premises with separate telephone connections and fixed timings amounts to sub-letting, not mere licensing, under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act.
The High Court erred in interfering with the Appellate Tribunal's factual findings by acting as an appellate authority rather than a supervisory body under Article 227 of the Constitution.

The respondents must vacate the premises within 53 weeks and pay occupation charges of ₹30,000 per month from November 14, 2018, until vacation, with interim payments and an affidavit of undertaking to be filed.
doctrines: Distinction between lease and license
Standard of perversity in factual findings
Limits of High Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227

card.dispute: Kotak Mahindra Bank challenged the NCLAT's decision that its insolvency application under Section 7 of the IBC was time-barred, arguing that a Recovery Certificate issued under the Debt Recovery Act could serve as the basis for initiating CIRP within three years.
issues_decided: Whether a Recovery Certificate issued under Section 19(22) of the Debt Recovery Act constitutes a financial debt under the IBC.
Whether the issuance of a Recovery Certificate triggers the limitation period for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC.
Whether the NCLAT was correct in holding that the application was time-barred.
holdings: A liability arising from a Recovery Certificate is a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and the certificate holder is a 'financial creditor'.
The holder of a Recovery Certificate can initiate CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC within three years from the date of issuance of the certificate.
The application filed by Kotak Mahindra Bank was within the limitation period, and the NCLAT erred in holding it time-barred.
The legislative intent behind Section 19(22A) of the Debt Recovery Act does not restrict the use of a Recovery Certificate solely for winding-up proceedings.
provisions: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, Section 5(7) and Section 5(8)
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 19(22) and Section 19(22A)
doctrines: Literal rule of statutory interpretation
Presumption against superfluity in legislation
Res judicata
Legal fiction

card.dispute: The landlord sued for eviction, possession, rent recovery, and mesne profits from tenants who continued occupying the commercial property after a decree of eviction, while the tenants challenged the quantum of mesne profits and applicability of the new rent control law.
issues_decided: Whether proceedings initiated under the repealed Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, are governed by the old law even after the enactment of the new Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2019?
Whether the High Court could lawfully direct payment of mesne profits during the pendency of a second appeal with a stay on eviction?
Whether the quantum of mesne profits set at Rs. 2,50,000 per month was reasonable and justified?
Whether the tenant could dispute the area of tenancy already admitted in prior proceedings?
holdings: Pending proceedings under the repealed Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, continue to be governed by the old law, and the new Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2019, does not apply to such cases.
The High Court has jurisdiction to order payment of mesne profits during a stay on eviction to compensate the landlord for delayed possession, in line with settled principles.
The amount of Rs. 2,50,000 per month as mesne profits is just and reasonable, considering the property's commercial location, market rent, and prolonged delay in execution.
A party is estopped from disputing factual admissions, such as the area of tenancy, made in earlier proceedings before the same court.
provisions: Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, Section 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 5
doctrines: Doctrine of merger in eviction decrees
Doctrine of estoppel by admission
Principle of reasonable mesne profits equivalent to market rent
Savings clause under repeal legislation (Section 32 of the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 2019)

card.dispute: The appellant developers challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by the respondent seeking declaration of title, recovery of possession, and cancellation of deeds, which implicitly sought to invalidate a prior compromise decree.
issues_decided: Whether a suit challenging a compromise decree indirectly through alternative reliefs is maintainable under the CPC?
Whether the Trial Court was justified in rejecting the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d) CPC on the ground of non-maintainability?
Whether a separate suit can be filed to challenge the validity of a compromise decree when an application under Order 23 Rule 3A CPC is already pending?
holdings: A suit that seeks reliefs which can only be granted by effectively setting aside a compromise decree is not maintainable, even if the plaintiff avoids explicitly praying for its cancellation.
The Trial Court correctly rejected the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11(d) CPC as the suit was barred by Order 23 Rule 3A CPC, which prohibits separate suits to challenge compromise decrees.
A party must challenge the validity of a compromise decree only before the court that passed it under Order 23 Rule 3A CPC; a separate civil suit for the same purpose is not maintainable.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 7 Rule 11(d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23 Rule 3A
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 32 Rule 7
doctrines: Bar on suits challenging compromise decrees under Order 23 Rule 3A CPC
Clever drafting doctrine to prevent circumvention of legal bars
Finality of compromise decrees
Maintainability of suits based on cause of action and reliefs sought

card.dispute: The Life Insurance Corporation of India (defendant) appealed against the Bombay High Court's order allowing Sanjeev Builders Private Limited (plaintiff) to amend their plaint to enhance the claim for damages in a suit for specific performance of a 1979 agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff can amend the plaint to enhance the claim for damages in a suit for specific performance after the initial pleading.
Whether the provisions of Order II Rule 2 and Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC, along with Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, permit such an amendment.
Whether the amendment would cause prejudice or injustice to the defendant or change the nature of the suit.
holdings: A plaintiff in a suit for specific performance can amend the plaint to enhance a claim for damages if the facts supporting the claim are already pleaded, and such amendment is necessary for effective adjudication.

Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC mandates that amendments should be allowed to determine the real question in controversy, provided they do not cause injustice, change the nature of the suit, or introduce a time-barred claim.
The provisos to Section 21(5) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 do not bar an amendment seeking enhanced damages when compensation was already claimed in the original plaint.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
doctrines: Liberal approach to amendment of pleadings
Amendment to prevent multiplicity of proceedings
Principle of avoiding technicalities in the interest of justice
Doctrine of real controversy between parties

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the maintainability of a single appeal filed against a common judgment and two separate decrees in consolidated suits, raising procedural issues about court fees and res judicata.
issues_decided: Whether a single appeal can be maintained against a common judgment and two separate decrees passed in consolidated suits?
Whether the High Court committed an error by dismissing the appeal on a preliminary objection without deciding the application (CLMA) seeking permission to file a single appeal?
Whether non-decision of the CLMA application caused prejudice to the appellant's right to be heard on merits?
holdings: A single appeal against a common judgment and two separate decrees in consolidated suits may be maintainable if the suits were consolidated for all purposes and tried as one.
The High Court erred in dismissing the appeal on a preliminary objection without first deciding the CLMA application seeking permission to file a single appeal.
Non-adjudication of the CLMA application caused serious prejudice to the appellant, depriving it of the opportunity to rectify procedural defects and be heard on merits.
doctrines: Res judicata
Principle of fair procedure and opportunity to be heard
Consolidation of suits for trial and appeal

card.dispute: M.P. Power Management Company Limited challenged the High Court's decision to quash its termination of a Power Purchase Agreement with Sky Power Southeast Solar India Private Limited over alleged delays and fraud in project commissioning.
issues_decided: Whether the termination of the Power Purchase Agreement was valid without issuing a prior default notice as mandated by the agreement.
Whether the appellant's allegations of fraud regarding duplicate inverter serial numbers justified unilateral termination of the PPA.
Whether the High Court was correct in quashing the termination order and upholding the respondent's readiness to commission the project.
holdings: The termination of the PPA was invalid because the appellant failed to issue a default notice under Article 9.1, which required an opportunity to cure the defect before termination.
Allegations of duplicate inverter serial numbers did not prove fraud or non-readiness, especially since the CEIG had certified the project and no physical inspection revealed discrepancies.
The appellant's attempt to negotiate a lower tariff during litigation indicated the project was ready, undermining its claim of default, and rendered the termination arbitrary.
doctrines: Doctrine of contractual compliance
Doctrine of opportunity to cure
Arbitrariness in administrative action

card.dispute: The wife of a murder victim challenged the bail granted to one of the accused, arguing that the High Court failed to properly consider his criminal antecedents and the seriousness of the offence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court applied its judicial mind while granting bail to the accused?
Whether the gravity of the offence and the accused's criminal antecedents were adequately considered before granting bail?
Whether the order granting bail must contain reasoned analysis, especially in serious non-bailable offences?
holdings: A bail order in serious offences must record prima facie reasons for granting bail and cannot be based on a mechanical reproduction of submissions.
The High Court failed to apply its judicial mind by not considering the accused's extensive criminal antecedents and the societal impact of the offence.
Courts must balance individual liberty with societal concern, especially in grave offences, and give reasons that reflect a conscious evaluation of relevant factors.
doctrines: Reasoned judicial orders
Balancing individual liberty and societal interest
Non-application of mind in bail decisions
Judicial discretion in bail matters

card.dispute: The appellant (plaintiff) challenged the High Court's decision to set aside an ex parte decree for specific performance of an agreement to sell, which the defendants sought to vacate after significant delays.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a revision petition under Article 227 of the Constitution to set aside an ex parte decree when an alternative remedy under the CPC was available?
Whether the High Court erred in setting aside the ex parte decree without first considering the trial court's refusal to condone delay in filing applications under Order IX Rule 13 of CPC?
holdings: Where a specific statutory remedy of appeal is available under the CPC, the High Court should not exercise its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227, as it amounts to an abuse of process and undermines the discipline of civil procedure.

The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by directly setting aside an ex parte decree on merits without first addressing whether the trial court was justified in refusing to condone the long delays in filing applications to set aside the decree.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 104(1)(i) read with Order 43 Rule 1(r)
doctrines: Availability of alternative remedy under CPC as a bar to Article 227 jurisdiction
Discipline and prudence in exercise of High Court's supervisory powers
Proper hierarchical use of civil remedies to prevent circumvention of appellate process
