The auctioning authority has the right to reject the highest bid and reissue a tender if there are valid and cogent reasons, such as correcting an erroneous reserve price.
The High Court cannot assume the powers of the auctioning authority by directing allotment or confirming a sale in the absence of a concluded contract.
doctrines: No vested right in bidding process
Authority's discretion to reject highest bid
Judicial restraint in contractual tender matters
Principle of fair treatment in public auctions

card.dispute: The Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority challenged the approval of a resolution plan in insolvency proceedings, claiming it was not treated as a secured operational creditor and was excluded from key processes.
issues_decided: Whether the NCLT has inherent power to recall an order under Section 60(5) of the IBC even when an appeal lies to the NCLAT
Whether the applications for recall were barred by limitation
Whether the resolution plan complied with Section 30(2) of the IBC read with Regulations 37 and 38 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016
Whether the appellant was entitled to notice and participation in COC meetings as an operational creditor with dues exceeding ten percent of the debt
holdings: The NCLT has inherent power to recall its orders under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC, supported by Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, to prevent abuse of process or secure justice, even if an appeal is available.
The recall applications were not barred by limitation as they were filed promptly after the lifting of the suspension of limitation due to the pandemic.

The resolution plan did not meet statutory requirements because it ignored the appellant's claim, misclassified its creditor status, and failed to secure necessary approvals for using third-party land, affecting feasibility.
The appellant, as a secured operational creditor with dues over ten percent, had a right to notice of COC meetings and to have its claim properly considered, which was violated.
provisions: U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, Section 3
doctrines: Inherent powers of the tribunal
Feasibility and viability of resolution plans
Protection against abuse of process
Commercial wisdom of Committee of Creditors subject to statutory compliance
Fair and equitable treatment of creditor classes

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Joginder Singh and Dr. Virinderjit Singh Gill disputed over the execution of a partition decree, specifically regarding possession of a portion of land (Khasra No. 2259) already decreed in a prior suit.
issues_decided: Whether procedural defects in filing objections under Section 47 and Order XXI Rules 58 and 97 of the CPC can lead to denial of substantive rights in execution proceedings.
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the revision petition on purely procedural grounds without considering the merits of the objection.
Whether the first partition decree's finality affects the scope of a subsequent partition suit involving overlapping land.
holdings: Procedural irregularities in execution objections cannot defeat substantive rights, especially when a party seeks to protect a previously decreed entitlement.
The High Court's dismissal of the revision on the ground of misinvoking procedural provisions is unsustainable, as procedural rules are meant to serve justice, not obstruct it.
The second partition suit must respect the finality of the first partition decree, and any decision affecting land already allotted therein must safeguard the earlier decree holder’s possession.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 58
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 97
doctrines: Procedure is the handmaiden of justice
Substantive rights prevail over procedural defects
Finality of decree doctrine
Principle of res judicata in execution proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, Jalaluddin Khan, challenged the rejection of his bail application in a prosecution under the UAPA and IPC, arguing no prima facie case was made against him.
issues_decided: Whether there are reasonable grounds to believe that the accusations against the appellant under the UAPA are prima facie true.
Whether the appellant is entitled to bail given the absence of incriminating material in the charge sheet.
holdings: The court held that the charge sheet lacked material to establish a prima facie case under Sections 13, 18, 18A, and 20 of the UAPA against the appellant.
The court held that the appellant is entitled to bail as the stringent conditions under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA were not met due to absence of connecting evidence.
doctrines: Bail is the rule, jail is the exception
Prima facie satisfaction test under Section 43D(5) of UAPA
No presumption of guilt at bail stage
Objective evaluation of charge sheet material without mini-trial

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the decree of pre-emption granted to the respondents, tenants who sought to purchase a property in Jagadhri on the basis of their preferential right under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, after it was sold to the appellants.
issues_decided: Whether the notification dated 08.10.1985 under Section 8(2) of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, excluding the right of pre-emption for land in municipal areas of Haryana, applied to the sale of urban immovable property in dispute.
Whether the respondents, as tenants, had a valid right of pre-emption under Section 16 of the 1913 Act in respect of the disputed property.
holdings: The notification dated 08.10.1985 applies only to 'land' and not to 'urban immovable property', which includes constructed sites; hence, it does not bar the right of pre-emption in this case.
The respondents, being tenants in occupation of the urban immovable property since 1949, had a valid right of pre-emption under Section 16 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913.
provisions: The Punjab Alienation of Land Act, 1900, Section 2(3)
doctrines: Statutory interpretation of 'land' and 'immovable property' as distinct terms
Doctrine of ejusdem generis applied to interpret scope of notification under Section 8(2)
Pre-emption rights of tenants in urban immovable property under Section 16

card.dispute: The complainant challenged the High Court's order granting bail to three convicted accused in a murder case, arguing they were dangerous and involved in another murder of a police constable.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in granting bail to the accused based on prolonged incarceration and parity with co-accused?
Whether the subsequent criminal conduct of two accused in murdering a police constable affects their bail eligibility?
Whether the bail granted to Arvind Kumar should be interfered with despite the conduct of his co-accused and sons?
holdings: Bail granted solely on grounds of prolonged incarceration and parity is unsustainable when material facts about serious subsequent crimes were not considered.
Accused involved in the murder of a police constable during trial and who absconded after the act are not entitled to bail despite long incarceration.
No interference with bail is warranted for an accused not charged in the subsequent murder, even if co-accused were involved in it.
doctrines: Bail based on parity must consider qualitative differences in accused's conduct
Subsequent criminal conduct during trial affects bail eligibility
Principle of judicial discretion in bail cancellation based on public safety

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the compensation awarded for his land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, while the state cross-appealed seeking refund of excess compensation withdrawn.
issues_decided: Whether the Reference Court was correct in awarding compensation at Rs. 100 per sq. ft. based on a sale deed between unrelated parties?
Whether sale deeds between family members could be relied upon for determining market value?
Whether the proximity of the land to developed areas justified higher compensation?
Whether development charges could be factored into compensation for acquired land?
holdings: Compensation can be based on a sale deed between unrelated parties at arm's length, even if other deeds involve relatives, provided the transaction is genuine and proximate in time.
Sale deeds between family members are unreliable for determining market value and may be disregarded in favor of arm's-length transactions.
The close proximity of acquired land to prominent institutions and developed areas is a relevant factor in assessing higher market value.
Development charges and the potential for future development may be considered when determining compensation for land acquisition.
doctrines: Arm's length transaction principle
Proximity and development potential as valuation factors
Preference for independent sale evidence over related-party transactions

card.dispute: The Kolkata Municipal Corporation claimed to have acquired Bimal Kumar Shah's property under Section 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, which the landowner challenged as illegal and without statutory authority.
issues_decided: Whether Section 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 empowers compulsory acquisition of immovable property?
Whether the Corporation could validly acquire land and take possession without following due procedure and paying compensation?
Whether the absence of procedural safeguards in Section 352 violates the principles of fair compensation and lawful acquisition under Article 300A of the Constitution?
holdings: Section 352 does not confer power of compulsory acquisition; it only enables the Municipal Commissioner to recommend acquisition for public purpose.
The power to acquire land lies with the State under Section 537 of the Act, not the Corporation under Section 352, and no valid acquisition can occur without statutory procedure.
A valid acquisition requires not only a legal provision but also adherence to principles of fair compensation, notice, hearing, and reasoned decision, which were absent here.
doctrines: Principle of lawful authority for compulsory acquisition
Procedural fairness in deprivation of property
Integration of fair compensation and due process under Article 300A
Doctrine of statutory interpretation based on text and context

card.dispute: Kukreja Construction Company and other landowners fought the State of Maharashtra and the Mumbai Municipal Corporation over the grant of 100% additional TDR (Transferable Development Rights) for land handed over for development of DP Roads, after delays in making claims.
issues_decided: Whether the writ petitions seeking additional TDR were liable to be dismissed on grounds of delay and laches
Whether the claim for additional TDR was abandoned due to inaction over several years
Whether the State has a constitutional duty to grant TDR as compensation under Article 300-A
Whether the Bombay High Court erred in rejecting the petitions based on delay without finding prejudice to the Corporation or third-party rights
holdings: Delay and laches cannot be a ground to deny additional TDR when the claim is for statutory compensation for land surrendered, especially in the absence of demonstrated prejudice to the State or third parties.
The doctrine of abandonment or waiver does not apply to claims for TDR compensation under the regulatory framework, particularly after binding precedents like Godrej & Boyce I.
The State has a constitutional obligation under Article 300-A to compensate land losers through TDR, which arises automatically and does not depend on timely representation.
The Bombay High Court erred in dismissing the petitions on grounds of delay; the claims must be considered afresh in light of Supreme Court precedents on TDR entitlement.
provisions: Development Control Regulations, Mumbai Municipal Corporation (Regulation granting TDR for amenity land)
doctrines: Doctrine of delay and laches
Doctrine of abandonment of claim
Principle of waiver
Constitutional right to property (Article 300-A)

card.dispute: The petitioner sought institutional reform and reconstitution of the Central Empowered Committee (CEC), which had been functioning in an ad hoc manner for nearly two decades, raising concerns about its composition and effectiveness in monitoring compliance with environmental orders.
issues_decided: Whether the Central Empowered Committee should be institutionalised as a permanent body with clear structural and functional norms?
What are the essential institutional features required for effective functioning of environmental regulatory bodies?
Whether the Supreme Court should continue to monitor the functioning of environmental bodies?
holdings: The Central Empowered Committee must be reconstituted as a permanent body under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, with clear norms for composition, tenure, and functioning, and subject to ongoing judicial oversight.

Environmental regulatory bodies must have clear mandates, adequate funding, technical expertise, transparency, accountability mechanisms, and public participation to ensure effective environmental governance.
Constitutional courts have a continuing role in monitoring the institutional integrity and performance of environmental bodies to uphold the environmental rule of law.
doctrines: Environmental rule of law
Judicial review in environmental matters
Institutional integrity and accountability
Sustainable environmental governance

card.dispute: The Lucknow Nagar Nigam and the Kohli Brothers Colour Lab Pvt Ltd disputed whether the respondent, a lessee of a property formerly declared as enemy property, was exempt from paying property tax under the UP Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1959, on the grounds that the property was vested in the Custodian for Enemy Property and allegedly belonged to the Union of India.
issues_decided: Whether statutory vesting of enemy property in the Custodian under the Enemy Property Act, 1968 amounts to transfer of ownership to the Union of India
Whether such property is exempt from local taxation under Article 285 of the Constitution
Whether the lessee of enemy property is liable to pay property tax when the Union does not hold ownership
holdings: The Custodian under the Enemy Property Act, 1968 does not acquire ownership of enemy property; vesting is only for management and administrative purposes, and title remains with the original owner.

The Union of India does not become the owner of enemy property merely because it is vested in the Custodian; hence, such property is not 'property of the Union' under Article 285(1) of the Constitution.
Since enemy property is not Union property, Article 285 does not grant tax exemption, and municipal authorities can levy property and local taxes on such properties from the lessee or occupier.
The High Court's order exempting the respondent from tax liability is set aside; the Nagar Nigam may levy taxes from the fiscal year 2024–2025 onward, though past payments are not refundable.
provisions: Enemy Property Act, 1968, Section 2(b), Section 2(c), Section 13
Enemy Property (Management and Disposal) Rules, Rule 15
doctrines: Statutory vesting without transfer of ownership
Trustee theory of custodianship under the Enemy Property Act
Principle of tax exemption under Article 285 limited to Union-owned property
Lessee liability for local taxes in absence of Union ownership

card.dispute: The Goa Foundation challenged the criteria used by the State of Goa to identify private forests, seeking modification of the canopy density and minimum area requirements for classification as forest land.
issues_decided: Whether the criteria adopted by the State of Goa for identifying private forests are valid and adequate.
Whether the appellant can challenge the criteria for identifying private forests while previously relying on them in other proceedings.
Whether a uniform national criterion for identifying forests can be applied across all states.
holdings: The criteria set by the State of Goa—75% forest species composition, minimum 5-hectare area, and 0.40 canopy density—are valid and adequate, and do not require modification.
The appellant cannot take contradictory positions by challenging the same criteria it previously relied upon, amounting to approbation and reprobation.
There is no uniform national standard for identifying forests; states may adopt criteria suited to their geographical conditions, as recognized by this Court in 1996.
provisions: Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006
doctrines: Approbation and reprobation
Principle of non-uniformity in environmental regulation based on regional geography
Delegation of administrative authority to expert committees

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Lehna Singh and Gurnam Singh fought over the validity of a will concerning land, with the plaintiff challenging the will's authenticity and claiming rightful possession.
issues_decided: Whether the First Appellate Court erred in setting aside the trial court's decree without properly addressing its findings on the will's validity.
Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by reappreciating evidence and substituting its own factual conclusions.
Whether the will was validly executed or arose from suspicious circumstances undermining its authenticity.
holdings: The First Appellate Court must address and rebut the trial court's reasoning when overturning its judgment, especially in cases involving credibility of witnesses and findings on wills.
The High Court cannot, in second appeal, reappreciate the entire evidence or substitute its view of facts for that of the First Appellate Court unless a substantial question of law is involved.

A will executed under suspicious circumstances, especially when propounders were accused in the testator's murder and no special affection is proved, may be invalidated even if attested by disinterested witnesses.
doctrines: Principle of limited scope of second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Appellate court's duty to provide cogent reasons for reversing findings based on witness credibility
Requirement of addressing trial court's findings in first appeal under Section 96 CPC

card.dispute: Al-Can Export Pvt. Ltd. (purchaser in a revenue auction) vs Prestige H.M. Polycontainers Ltd. and ARCIL over the validity of a land auction and possession of industrial property.
issues_decided: Whether Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to writ proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution in revenue auction matters?
Whether the Additional Commissioner had jurisdiction to hear appeals under Section 247 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966?
holdings: The provisions of Order XXI Rule 90 CPC do not apply to revenue auction proceedings conducted under the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, as they are governed by special statutory provisions.

The Additional Commissioner had jurisdiction under Section 247 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code to hear appeals, and the High Court rightly declined to interfere where quashing the order would revive an illegal order.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXI Rule 90
doctrines: Doctrine of revival of illegal order: Writ courts may refrain from quashing an impugned order if it results in the revival of a more pernicious or illegal order.
Special statutes override general laws: Revenue proceedings are governed by the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, not by the general provisions of the CPC.

card.dispute: Ultra Tech Cement Limited challenged the High Court's order directing it to pay compensation to landowners whose land was acquired for a cement project, arguing liability fell on Jaiprakash Associates Limited (JAL).
issues_decided: Whether the State could transfer possession of acquired land without passing a supplementary award for additional compensation?
Whether the State had a constitutional and statutory duty to ensure timely payment of compensation?
Whether JAL was liable to bear the cost of acquisition under the 1894 and 2013 Acts?
holdings: Possession of land cannot be taken without full payment of compensation and passing of a supplementary award, as mandated by Section 38(1) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
The State, as a welfare State, has a constitutional obligation under Article 300-A to ensure prompt payment of compensation and cannot abdicate this duty to private companies.
Under Section 41 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the company benefiting from acquisition must pay the cost of acquisition to the State before transfer of land, making JAL ultimately liable.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 38
doctrines: Right to property as a human right under Article 300-A
Welfare State obligation to protect citizens' rights during land acquisition
Statutory compliance in sequence of land acquisition proceedings

card.dispute: The appellants (original defendants) challenged the decree of declaration of title and possession in favor of the respondents (original plaintiffs) over suit property, claiming the suit was barred by limitation and that adverse possession could not be claimed alongside a lawful title.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff proved ownership and possession of the suit property?
Whether the defendants proved lawful possession or adverse title over the suit property?
Whether the plaintiff's suit was barred by limitation given the nature of reliefs claimed?
Whether a claim of adverse possession can be maintained when possession arises from a lawful title?
holdings: The plaintiff established her title and possession, and the burden then shifted to the defendants to prove adverse possession, which they failed to do.
A licensee or permissive possessor cannot acquire title by adverse possession without an overt act asserting hostile title, and mere continued possession is insufficient.

When a suit seeks both cancellation of a sale deed and recovery of possession, limitation is determined by the substantive relief (cancellation), which is governed by a three-year period under the Limitation Act, 1963.
Claiming both a lawful title and adverse possession is contradictory; one cannot simultaneously assert permissive possession and hostile, adverse possession.
doctrines: Adverse possession
Burden of proof in title disputes
Pleas of inconsistent claims
Substantive vs. consequential reliefs in limitation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's invalidation of the acceptance of Change Reports regarding the appointment of a new Vahiwatdar and Trustees of a public trust, which the High Court had remanded for reconsideration due to delayed filing.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing a Change Report under Section 22 of the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, 1950, without a separate order condoning delay, renders the acceptance of the report invalid
Whether the High Court erred in remanding the matter for fresh consideration without examining whether the delay was effectively condoned
Whether delay in filing a Change Report automatically invalidates the assumption of office by a Vahiwatdar of a public trust
holdings: Delay in filing a Change Report does not automatically invalidate the appointment; the defect is curable under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, even in the absence of a formal application for condonation.

The High Court erred in invalidating the Change Reports solely on procedural delay when the Joint Charity Commissioner had already acted on the basis of condoned delay, and the issue was not raised earlier in proceedings.

Failure to file a Change Report within 90 days does not nullify the assumption of office as Vahiwatdar; penal consequences under Section 66 are separate and do not affect the validity of the change in administration.
doctrines: Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Liberal and justice-oriented interpretation of procedural requirements
Non-pedantic approach to technical defects in administrative compliance

card.dispute: The appellants, who are depositors in a credit cooperative society, challenged the bail granted to respondent no.1, accused in a financial fraud case involving misappropriation of deposits, on grounds that the bail order was legally flawed and prejudicial to victims' interests.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in granting bail to the respondent accused in a serious economic offence affecting numerous depositors?
Whether the bail order failed to consider material indicating the respondent's active involvement in the alleged financial irregularities?
Whether the bail conditions imposed were inadequate given the nature and gravity of the offence?
holdings: The High Court erred in granting bail without proper application of judicial mind, as the order relied on mere allegations and ignored material from the charge-sheet and forensic audit indicating the accused's involvement in fund siphoning.

The bail order was illegal and perverse because it downplayed the accused's role despite evidence of large withdrawals and property investments made through society funds, warranting stricter conditions or denial of bail.
In serious economic offences affecting vulnerable depositors, courts must impose stringent bail conditions to prevent tampering and dissipation of assets, which the High Court failed to do.
provisions: Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999, Section 3
doctrines: Judicial discretion in bail matters must be grounded in established legal principles and material record.
Bail orders in economic offences must balance individual liberty with societal interest and victim protection.
Principle of cautious approach in granting bail when there is prima facie evidence of active involvement in large-scale financial fraud.

card.dispute: The appellants, family members of the complainant's husband, challenged the dismissal of their petition to quash an FIR and chargesheet alleging dowry harassment and domestic violence, claiming the proceedings were mala fide and abusive.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash the FIR and chargesheet under Section 482 CrPC despite identical allegations being dismissed in a domestic violence proceeding?
Whether the continuation of criminal proceedings amounts to abuse of process of court?
Whether the allegations in the FIR and chargesheet disclose cognizable offences under Sections 498A, 323, 504, 506 read with Section 34 IPC?
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the criminal proceedings were initiated with mala fide intent and constituted an abuse of process, especially since identical allegations were rejected after trial in a domestic violence case.
The Court ruled that quashing of criminal proceedings is permissible under Section 482 CrPC even after a chargesheet is filed if the case amounts to abuse of process or miscarriage of justice.
The Court concluded that the allegations, even if taken as true, did not make out any offence under Sections 498A, 323, 504, 506 read with Section 34 IPC, warranting quashing of the proceedings.
doctrines: Abuse of process of law
Inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC
Quashing of criminal proceedings to secure ends of justice
Corroboration of sole testimony in domestic violence cases

card.dispute: The plaintiffs sued for specific performance of an agreement to sell agricultural land, after the first defendant sold the land to others, and the defendants challenged the maintainability and scope of the decree.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for specific performance of the agreement to sell the suit property.
Whether the second plaintiff's non-participation affected the maintainability and scope of the suit.
Whether the court could direct the defendants to apply for government permission required under the Zamindari Abolition Act for the sale of the property.
What relief is admissible if the required government permission is not granted.
holdings: A decree for specific performance can be granted even if the sale requires government sanction, provided the vendor is directed to apply for such permission as part of their implied obligation under the contract.
Where one co-plaintiff is not interested in specific performance, the decree must be limited to the share of the willing plaintiff, here one-half undivided share in favour of the first plaintiff.
The court may direct the parties to jointly apply for necessary government permission and empower the executing court to appoint a commissioner if they fail to do so.
If permission is denied, the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for refund of the advance amount with interest, limited to the estate of the deceased defendant.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21, Rule 35
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 154-B(2)(h)
doctrines: Implied covenant to perform necessary acts for execution of contract
Readiness and willingness to perform as a condition for specific performance
Contingent decree for specific performance subject to government sanction
Equal shares in co-purchasers in absence of defined shares under Section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act

card.dispute: The appellants claimed compensation or alternative land allotment due to the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation's failure to deliver a plot of land after a town planning scheme variation.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were entitled to compensation or land allotment for the shortfall in plot area after variation of the town planning scheme.
Whether the Corporation's failure to deliver possession of a plot entitled the appellants to damages.
Whether the appellants could challenge the reduced plot area after accepting the allotment and depositing compensation.
holdings: A landowner surrendering property under a town planning scheme has no guaranteed right to re-allotment of land; compensation is the only assured remedy.
The appellants failed to provide evidence of market value to support their claim for compensation, which must be based on material proof.
By accepting the allotment and depositing the compensation amount, the appellants waived any right to challenge the reduced plot area or claim additional compensation.
provisions: Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 45
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 52
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 54
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 70
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 71
Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act, 1976, Section 82
doctrines: No vested right in land re-allotment under town planning schemes
Estoppel by conduct
Requirement of evidence to prove damages

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the classification of a BOT concession agreement as a lease for stamp duty purposes and the validity of amendments to the stamp law, while the state defended the levy of stamp duty on the entire project cost.
issues_decided: Whether a BOT concession agreement granting the right to collect tolls in return for construction expenditure constitutes a 'lease' under the Transfer of Property Act and the Indian Stamp Act
Whether the amendment to the Indian Stamp (M.P.) Act, 2002 inserting proviso (c) to Clause (C) of Article 33 of Schedule 1-A is ultra vires
Whether the principles of promissory estoppel or legitimate expectation bar the state from amending the stamp law despite prior executive assurances
On what amount is stamp duty chargeable under proviso (c) — the total project cost or only the amount spent by the lessee?
holdings: A BOT concession agreement granting toll collection rights in exchange for construction expenditure satisfies the definition of a lease under Section 2(16) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, which has an expanded meaning compared to Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

The amendment via M.P. Act No.12 of 2002 inserting proviso (c) is valid and not ultra vires, as the legislature can modify fiscal policies in public interest without being bound by prior executive actions.

The doctrine of promissory estoppel or legitimate expectation does not apply against the legislature when exercising its sovereign legislative power, especially in matters of fiscal policy and public interest.

Stamp duty under proviso (c) is chargeable at 2% only on the amount likely to be spent by the lessee, not on the total project cost; any excess collected must be refunded after proper determination by the Revenue Officer.
provisions: Indian Stamp (M.P.) Act, 2002, proviso (c) to Clause (C) of Article 33 of Schedule 1-A
doctrines: Promissory estoppel
Legitimate expectation
No estoppel against legislature in exercise of sovereign functions
Fictional expansion of 'lease' under fiscal statutes

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed whether the appeal could be restored after a compromise was not complied with, despite the High Court not granting explicit liberty to restore.
issues_decided: Whether an application for restoration of appeal is maintainable when the court recording the compromise did not grant liberty to restore
Whether non-compliance with compromise terms allows the aggrieved party to seek recall of the compromise decree
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the recall application solely on the ground of absence of liberty to restore
holdings: Restoration of appeal is a statutory right under Order 23, Rule 3 CPC and does not require prior judicial grant of liberty.
A party aggrieved by non-compliance with a compromise may file a recall application to challenge its validity, as the court must examine whether the compromise was lawful.
The absence of liberty to restore in the compromise order does not bar a party from seeking restoration, as statutory remedies cannot be curtailed by court orders.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 23, Rule 3A
doctrines: Consent decree as a contract with judicial seal
Statutory right to restoration upon compromise failure
Public policy against ousting legal remedies
Judicial duty to examine legality of compromise

card.dispute: NOIDA fought with landowners over the validity of land acquisition proceedings challenged on grounds of non-compliance with Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
issues_decided: Whether the consolidation of objections under Section 5A of the 1894 Act into groups vitiated the acquisition process
Whether exclusion of some objections from grouped disposal rendered the acquisition proceedings illegal
Whether issuance of a corrigendum to the Collector's order affected the fairness of the process
Whether acquisition could be annulled despite substantial compliance and development post-acquisition
holdings: Grouping similar objections under Section 5A does not violate principles of natural justice if each objection is fairly considered.
Exclusion of some objections from grouped orders does not invalidate acquisition if their substance was addressed in the reasoning.
A corrigendum clarifying procedural history without altering merits does not undermine the fairness of acquisition proceedings.
Acquisition proceedings cannot be annulled at a late stage where substantial compliance occurred, compensation accepted by majority, and significant public investment made.
provisions: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(1)
doctrines: Substantial compliance doctrine
Principles of natural justice
Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Public interest doctrine

card.dispute: Navin Kumar Rai challenged the quashing of an FIR against Surendra Singh and others for allegedly forging a power of attorney and sale deed to illegally transfer his land.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in quashing the FIR for offences under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 IPC on the ground that the dispute was merely a civil wrong and an abuse of process?
Whether the initiation of criminal proceedings by the Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act, 1908, without prior permission from the Inspector-General, invalidates the FIR?
Whether the High Court correctly applied the test for quashing criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C.?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR merely because a civil suit was pending; criminal proceedings can proceed independently if there is a prima facie case of criminality.

The Sub-Registrar has the authority under Section 83 of the Registration Act, 1908, to initiate or permit prosecution without prior approval from the Inspector-General, so the FIR was validly registered.

The High Court failed to apply the correct legal standard under Section 482 Cr.P.C.; absence of 'criminality' must be determined at trial, not at the quashing stage, based on a mere possibility of civil dispute.
doctrines: Prima facie case for criminal prosecution
Independence of criminal and civil proceedings
Inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
Abuse of process of court

card.dispute: The appellants, officers of the Special Armed Forces, were accused by the respondent of trespassing, damaging property, and threatening him on land the respondent claimed as Bhumiswami, leading to criminal proceedings which the appellants challenged as an abuse of process.
issues_decided: Whether the criminal complaint against SAF officers required sanction under Section 197 CrPC
Whether the prosecution constituted an abuse of the process of law given the prior dismissal of a contempt petition over the same dispute
Whether the magistrate properly evaluated the evidence before taking cognizance
holdings: Acts alleged were part of an official boundary dispute and required sanction under Section 197 CrPC, which was not obtained.
The criminal complaint amounted to an abuse of process as it arose from the same facts as the previously dismissed contempt petition.
The magistrate failed to consider material omissions, including lack of specific dates and non-mention of the pending contempt case, rendering cognizance legally unsustainable.
doctrines: abuse of process of law
sanction for prosecution of public servants
res judicata in contempt and criminal proceedings

card.dispute: The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai challenged a Bombay High Court order that framed issues for determination by an Inquiry Officer in eviction proceedings against unauthorized occupants, arguing that the High Court overstepped its jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by framing points of determination for the Inquiry Officer in summary eviction proceedings under the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, 1888
Whether the Inquiry Officer, being a municipal officer, suffers from bias or lack of independence under the principle of 'nemo judex in causa sua'
Whether the absence of regulations framed under Section 105H of the Act bars the Inquiry Officer from proceeding with eviction inquiries
holdings: The High Court acted in excess of jurisdiction by framing issues for the Inquiry Officer, as the proceedings are summary and quasi-judicial, and the Inquiry Officer must independently determine issues based on evidence and defence.

The Inquiry Officer does not suffer from bias merely by being a municipal officer, as he acts in a quasi-judicial capacity and the law ensures impartiality through procedural safeguards and appeal to a judicial officer.
Proceedings under the Act can continue even in the absence of regulations under Section 105H, provided the Inquiry Officer adheres to the principles of natural justice.
provisions: Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, Chapter V-A
doctrines: nemo judex in causa sua
principles of natural justice
summary adjudication
quasi-judicial authority

card.dispute: The appellant Mukesh challenged the High Court's order upholding the demand for stamp duty on a compromise decree for mutation of land he claimed through adverse possession.
issues_decided: Whether a compromise decree asserting pre-existing rights over land is exempt from registration under Section 17(2)(vi) of the Registration Act, 1908?
Whether a consent decree declaring title based on pre-existing rights is chargeable with stamp duty under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899?
holdings: A compromise decree is exempt from registration if it affirms pre-existing rights and does not create new title, provided there is no collusion and the suit pertains to the same property.

A court decree, including a consent decree, is not an instrument chargeable with stamp duty under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, when it merely recognizes pre-existing rights and does not operate as a conveyance.
provisions: Indian Stamp Act, 1899, Schedule I and Schedule I-A
doctrines: Adverse possession can confer a pre-existing right that may be recognized through a compromise decree
Revenue records do not confer title; possession and declaration of ownership are relevant to establish rights
Consent decrees not creating new rights are not instruments of conveyance and hence not liable to stamp duty

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Zahoor Ahmed and the legal heirs of Abdul Ghafoor disputed over shares in certain khatas and plots of land in village Bhati Jarouli, claiming rights under the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953.
issues_decided: Whether Zahoor Ahmed and his legal heirs were entitled to a half share in Khata Nos. 99 and 100 under the consolidation proceedings
Whether the consolidation authorities erred in applying Hindu joint family principles to determine shares among Muslim parties
Whether the relinquishment deeds in favor of the respondents were valid and binding
holdings: The High Court correctly dismissed the appellants' writ petition as Zahoor Ahmed had validly relinquished claims to specific plots in favor of the respondents through registered deeds.
Consolidation authorities erred in applying Hindu joint family principles to Muslim parties; such principles are not recognized under Muslim personal law.
The appellants were entitled only to a 1/12 joint share in the disputed land, not a 1/2 share, as the property was acquired under a lease by specific individuals, not as joint family property.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 4
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 5(2)
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 9
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 11
Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, Section 48
doctrines: Doctrine of tenancy by estoppel
Doctrine of finality of consolidation proceedings
Principle against application of Hindu joint family law to Muslim parties

card.dispute: The dispute was between NOIDA and landowners over the quantum of compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, with landowners seeking higher compensation based on market value and parity with prior awards.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for acquired land should be enhanced based on appreciation in land value and principle of guesstimation.
Whether miscellaneous applications seeking parity in compensation based on a subsequent change in law are maintainable.
Whether Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 applies to grant uniform compensation to all landowners under the same notification.
holdings: The court held that compensation should be enhanced to INR 403 per sq. yd. based on a 15% annual appreciation and the principle of guesstimation, supported by urban land value trends.
Miscellaneous applications for parity in compensation are maintainable in exceptional circumstances to prevent miscarriage of justice, even if earlier remedies were dismissed.
Section 28A of the 1894 Act need not be invoked where uniform compensation is granted independently under Article 142 to ensure equality and complete justice.
doctrines: Principle of guesstimation in land valuation
Doctrine of parity in compensation under Section 28A
Equitable application of Article 142 for complete justice
Maintainability of miscellaneous applications based on change of law in exceptional circumstances

card.dispute: Nusrat Parween and Ahmad Khan challenged their conviction for the murder of Hamida Parween, claiming the prosecution failed to prove their presence at the crime scene and the evidence was insufficient.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the presence of the appellants at the scene of the incident contemporaneous with the murder?
Whether the prosecution established a complete chain of incriminating circumstances to warrant conviction beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the failure to examine material witnesses like Md. Javed Khan and Kahkasan Anujam affects the credibility of the prosecution case?
Whether the prosecution's reliance on the 'last seen together' theory was legally sustainable in light of the evidence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the presence of the appellants at the crime scene, and no evidence showed they were last seen with the deceased, undermining the prosecution's case.
The chain of incriminating circumstances was not established by credible and convincing evidence, and the conviction could not be sustained beyond reasonable doubt.
The failure to examine Md. Javed Khan and Kahkasan Anujam, who were material witnesses, warrants an adverse inference against the prosecution.
The 'last seen together' theory cannot be invoked without solid evidence of presence, and Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not relieve the prosecution of its burden to prove guilt.
doctrines: Benefit of doubt in criminal cases
Last seen together doctrine
Adverse inference from non-examination of material witnesses
Prosecution's burden of proof under Section 106 of the Evidence Act

card.dispute: The heirs of Sultan Saheb fought over whether he had validly transferred property to his sons during his lifetime by way of partition or gift.
issues_decided: Whether an owner can transfer property to his heirs by way of partition during his lifetime under Mohammedan law
Whether the requisites of a valid gift were satisfied in this case
Whether the mutation entry can indicate intention to gift or partition
holdings: A partition among heirs during the lifetime of the owner is not recognized under Mohammedan law as heirs do not become co-owners until after the owner's death.
A valid gift requires a clear and unequivocal declaration of intention, which must be evident from the document or act; oral statements without such clarity do not constitute a valid gift.
Mutation entries in revenue records do not confer title or indicate intention to create a gift or partition; they are relevant only for revenue collection purposes.
provisions: Revenue Records and Mutation Rules (State-specific, Karnataka)
doctrines: Doctrine of clear and unequivocal intention for gift
Substance over form in determining nature of transaction
No recognition of pre-death partition under Mohammedan law

card.dispute: The legal heirs of a deceased claimant in a land acquisition reference sought to file an appeal after a delay of over 15 years, challenging the dismissal of the reference and seeking condonation of delay.
issues_decided: Whether the inordinate delay of 5,659 days in filing the appeal under Section 54 of the Land Acquisition Act could be condoned?
Whether the heirs of a deceased claimant who were not substituted in the original reference proceeding could still maintain an appeal?
Whether the conduct of the claimants showed sufficient cause and due diligence to justify condonation of delay?
holdings: Courts must strictly apply the law of limitation; delay can only be condoned if sufficient cause is shown, and mere hardship does not justify relaxing statutory time limits.
An inordinate delay of 5,659 days without explanation of sufficient cause cannot be condoned, especially when the claimants showed negligence and lack of due diligence.
The fact that some similarly situated claimants had their delays condoned in other cases does not entitle others to the same relief if they fail to establish sufficient cause.
doctrines: dura lex sed lex
sufficient cause for condonation of delay
public policy against endless litigation
judicial discretion in condoning delay

card.dispute: The appellant, Perumal Raja, challenged his conviction for the murder of Rajini @ Rajinikanth and destruction of evidence, arguing insufficiency of evidence and reliance on the acquittal in a related murder case.
issues_decided: Whether the conviction based on circumstantial evidence satisfies the 'five golden principles' for proving guilt?
Whether the appellant's false or absent explanation under Section 313 CrPC can form an additional link in the chain of circumstantial evidence?
Whether the acquittal of the appellant in a separate murder case (of Rajaram) affects the validity of his conviction in this case?
Whether the acquittal of co-accused and a juvenile impacts the appellant's conviction?
holdings: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete and unbroken chain that conclusively points to the accused's guilt and excludes all other hypotheses of innocence.
A false or absent explanation by the accused, especially when proximate to the crime and after a strong prosecution case, can serve as an additional link under Section 106 of the Evidence Act.
Acquittal in a separate criminal case based on different evidence does not invalidate a conviction in another case where the evidence is independently sufficient.

Acquittal of co-accused due to lack of evidence or inapplicability of Section 27 of the Evidence Act does not undermine the conviction of the main accused if evidence against them is independently established.
doctrines: Five golden principles for circumstantial evidence
Adverse inference from failure to explain under Section 106 of the Evidence Act
Doctrine of constructive use of disclosure statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Act
Principle of independent evidentiary basis for separate charges

card.dispute: The appellant (Parswanath Saha) sued for specific performance of an agreement to buy land from the respondents, who resisted on grounds of hardship after the original seller's death.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the Trial Court's decree for specific performance on grounds of hardship to the defendants?
Whether the defendants established unforeseeable hardship under Section 20(2)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963?
Whether the plaintiff was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract?
holdings: The High Court erred in reversing the Trial Court’s decree for specific performance solely on grounds of hardship without framing a proper issue or finding that the hardship was unforeseeable at the time of contract.

Hardship under Section 20(2)(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 must be unforeseeable at the time of contract and not caused by the plaintiff’s subsequent acts; mere post-contract personal hardship is insufficient without such factors.
The plaintiff was found to be consistently ready and willing to perform his obligations, and the Trial Court’s finding on this was not disturbed by the High Court.
provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Explanation 2 to Section 20
doctrines: Doctrine of comparative hardship
Discretionary nature of specific performance
Requirement of readiness and willingness in specific performance

card.dispute: The appellant, Prem Prakash, challenged the denial of bail in a money laundering case investigated by the Enforcement Directorate.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant had committed the offence of money laundering under Sections 3 and 4 of the PMLA
Whether the twin conditions under Section 45 of the PMLA for granting bail were satisfied
holdings: The court found no reasonable grounds to believe that the appellant was guilty of money laundering, as there was no evidence linking him to the creation of forged documents or knowledge thereof.
The appellant satisfied the twin conditions of Section 45 of the PMLA, as there were reasonable grounds to believe in his innocence and that he would not commit any offence if released on bail.
provisions: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Section 3
Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Section 4
Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Section 45
doctrines: Twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of PMLA
Presumption of innocence in bail decisions
Finality of bail orders in co-accused cases as relevant consideration

card.dispute: The borrower, Dr. M.V. Ramana Rao, sought to restore a previously withdrawn Securitization Application under SARFAESI after the bank sold his mortgaged properties; the bank and appellant challenged the High Court's interference in allowing the restoration despite confirmation and registration of the sale.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could entertain a writ petition under Article 226 despite the availability of an alternative remedy under the SARFAESI Act.
Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the DRT's dismissal of the application for restoration of a withdrawn Securitization Application.
Whether a confirmed and registered auction sale under SARFAESI can be reopened in the absence of fraud or collusion.
holdings: The High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition under Article 226 when an effective alternative remedy was available under the SARFAESI Act, and no exception to the rule of alternative remedy applied.
The High Court erred in setting aside the DRT’s order dismissing the application for restoration, as the DRT had the discretion to reject the revival of a withdrawn application.

Once an auction sale under SARFAESI is confirmed and registered, the right of redemption stands extinguished and the sale cannot be reopened without proof of fraud or collusion, which was absent here.
provisions: Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Section 17
doctrines: Rule of alternative remedy under Article 226
Extinguishment of right of redemption upon confirmation and registration of sale
Principle that confirmed auction sales can only be set aside on grounds of fraud or collusion

card.dispute: The appellants, who constructed buildings on a residential plot in Meerut, challenged the High Court's order directing demolition of their unauthorized commercial constructions and affirming action against erring officials.
issues_decided: Whether unauthorized commercial construction on a residential plot can be demolished despite delay and investment by the builder?
Whether public interest justifies strict enforcement of building regulations and accountability of officials?
Whether regularization of unauthorized constructions should be permitted as a matter of course?
holdings: Unauthorized constructions, even if longstanding, must be demolished if they violate zoning and building laws, and cannot be protected by delay, cost, or administrative inaction.
Public interest demands strict compliance with development plans and accountability of officials; failure to act encourages illegality and harms urban order and the environment.
Regularization schemes should be exceptional, one-time measures for residential structures only, after considering environmental impact and public interest, not applied to commercial violations.
provisions: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Act, 1975
U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1972
doctrines: Public Trust Doctrine
Sustainable Development
Principle of Non-Regression in Environmental Law
Doctrine of Strict Compliance with Statutory Planning Regulations

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of tenants who inherited tenancy rights, claiming their right to stay ended five years after the 1997 Act came into force, while tenants argued the Act did not retrospectively extinguish their inherited rights.
issues_decided: Whether Section 2(g) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 operates retrospectively to terminate inherited tenancy rights from the date of the original tenant's death prior to 1997?
Whether the Calcutta High Court was correct in decreeing eviction based on an 'admission' in another case without a full trial?
holdings: Section 2(g) of the 1997 Act does not have retrospective effect to extinguish tenancy rights inherited under the old law, unless there is a clear and unambiguous legislative intent for retrospectivity.
The High Court erred in granting judgment on admission based on a statement from another case, as it did not constitute a binding admission in the present suit.
provisions: West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997, Section 2(g)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XII Rule 6
doctrines: Lex prospicit non respicit (law looks forward, not backward)
Principle of fairness in statutory interpretation
Judgment on admission under CPC requires clear and binding admission in the same proceeding

card.dispute: The contractor challenged the High Court's confirmation of a lower court order modifying an arbitral award that reduced the amount awarded to him due to alleged delays and cost escalations in a construction project.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in confirming the modification of the arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Whether the courts below acted within the limited scope of review under Sections 34 and 37 of the Act
Whether the reduction of interest from 18% to 9% by the courts below was legally justified
holdings: Courts under Section 34 and Section 37 have a narrow scope of review and cannot re-appreciate evidence or modify awards on merits; interference is only permissible on limited grounds such as patent illegality or public policy.
The High Court erred in modifying the award by acting like a first appellate court, which is beyond the statutory limits set by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

The reduction of interest from 18% to 9% lacked legal basis; the arbitral tribunal has the power under Section 31(7) to award interest for the pre-award period, and such award must be respected unless it violates public policy.
doctrines: Limited judicial interference in arbitral awards
Public policy exception to enforcement of awards
Principle of finality of arbitral awards

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's recall of its earlier order and dismissal of contempt and review petitions concerning mutation of land, alleging abuse of process and limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court had the jurisdiction to review its earlier order dismissing the contempt petition?
Whether the contempt petition was barred by limitation?
holdings: The High Court lacked jurisdiction to review its original order as no reviewable error was demonstrated, and the review was impermissibly used to overturn a time-barred contempt decision.
The contempt was not a continuing wrong; the limitation period ended by May 2010, so the 2014 contempt petition was time-barred and rightly dismissed.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLVII Rule 9
doctrines: Contempt not a continuing wrong unless the breach is ongoing
Fraud on the court vitiates judicial orders and affects maintainability of writ petitions
Principle of finality of litigation cannot be used to perpetrate fraud

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the refusal of a refund of court fees paid in a civil suit that was settled via mediation under Section 89 CPC, seeking parity with refunds available for Lok Adalat settlements.
issues_decided: Whether the refund of court fees under the Court Fees Act, 1870, granted for Lok Adalat settlements, applies by analogy to disputes settled through mediation under Section 89 CPC.
Whether the State of Maharashtra lacked legal authority to issue a notification denying such refunds, contrary to the Court Fees Act, 1870, read with the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
Whether the appellant is entitled to a full refund of court fees in the interest of justice, despite the lack of statutory entitlement at the time of settlement.
holdings: The refund provision under the Court Fees Act, 1870, for Lok Adalat settlements does not extend to mediation under Section 89 CPC, as Lok Adalat and mediation are distinct processes and cannot be equated.
The State of Maharashtra had the legislative competence under Entry 3, List II of the Seventh Schedule to regulate court fees, and its notification was not ultra vires the Court Fees Act, 1870.

Though the appellant had no statutory right to a refund at the time, the Court exercised its powers under Article 142 to grant a full refund of approximately Rs. 5 lakhs in the interest of justice, given the amicable settlement and subsequent legislative amendment.
provisions: Seventh Schedule, Entry 3, List II; Entry 11A, List III
doctrines: Principle of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule
Distinction between adjudicatory and non-adjudicatory dispute resolution mechanisms
Doctrine of equivalence not applicable to statutory benefits in different ADR mechanisms
Equitable powers under Article 142 of the Constitution

card.dispute: The appellants, Puneet Sabharwal and R.C. Sabharwal, challenged the framing of charges against them in a corruption case, arguing that prior exoneration in income tax proceedings warranted discharge.
issues_decided: Whether exoneration in income tax proceedings bars prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Whether findings from income tax proceedings can be relied upon to quash criminal charges at the stage of discharge
Whether the decision in Radheyshyam v. State of Maharashtra applies to proceedings under different statutes and authorities
Whether the minority of one accused during part of the check period affects the validity of the charge
holdings: Exoneration in income tax proceedings does not automatically bar prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, as the scope and authority differ.
Findings from income tax proceedings cannot conclusively determine discharge in criminal cases, as they are not binding in corruption trials.
The decision in Radheyshyam applies only when both proceedings arise under the same statute and authority, which is not the case here.
Partial minority during the check period does not invalidate charges, especially when the accused was major for a significant portion.
provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(e) and 13(2)
doctrines: Abuse of process of court
Double jeopardy (implied distinction)
Principles of discharge at pre-trial stage
Separate proceedings under different statutes

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's bail conditions requiring them to demolish a wall and hand over possession of disputed property to the complainant, arguing that these conditions exceeded the court's jurisdiction.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 439 CrPC by imposing bail conditions unrelated to the purpose of bail, such as demolition of a wall and delivery of possession of disputed property.
Whether the police had lawful authority to take possession of immovable property in connection with the criminal case.
holdings: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by imposing bail conditions that deprived the appellants of civil rights, as such conditions are not related to ensuring the accused's presence during trial or preventing abuse of liberty.
The police have no legal authority to take possession of immovable property in a criminal case, and such action amounts to lawlessness in the absence of statutory sanction.
doctrines: Bail conditions must be reasonable and directly related to securing the presence of the accused and ensuring the administration of justice.
Criminal courts cannot adjudicate civil disputes or enforce civil obligations while granting bail.
Police cannot assume custody of immovable property in criminal proceedings without statutory authority.

card.dispute: The heirs of Ramachandra Reddy and Ramulu Ammal disputed the validity and effect of a 1963 settlement deed transferring a 2/3rd share in joint family property to Govindammal, claiming she was not entitled to it.
issues_decided: Whether the 1963 settlement deed in favour of Govindammal was valid and supported by sufficient consideration?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts regarding the settlement and possession?
holdings: A settlement deed can be supported by valid consideration even if non-monetary, such as familial care and commitment to charitable acts, especially among family members.
The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in a second appeal, as no substantial question of law was involved, violating the limits of Section 100 CPC.
doctrines: Doctrine of consideration
Principle of constructive consideration in family settlements
Limitation on second appeal under Section 100 CPC
Concurrent findings of fact not to be disturbed

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over the devolution and ownership of certain properties governed by Marumakkathayam law, specifically whether the properties belonged to the tharwad of the mother or were inherited from the father under the Travancore Act.
issues_decided: Whether the properties in question devolved under Marumakkathayam law through the female line or were inherited from the father under Section 22(1) of the Travancore Hindu Family Property Act, 1916
Whether the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court on ownership and possession of the properties can be interfered with
Which view in Mary Cheriyan v. Abraham (minority or majority) correctly interprets the devolution of property under Marumakkathayam law
holdings: Properties governed by Marumakkathayam law devolve through the female line, and membership in the tharwad is acquired by birth; inheritance does not pass through the male line to his descendants.
Concurrent findings of fact by the Trial Court and High Court are not to be disturbed unless exceptional circumstances exist, which are absent here.
The minority view in Mary Cheriyan v. Abraham correctly interprets Marumakkathayam law, but this ruling applies prospectively only, without disturbing past or ongoing transactions.
provisions: Travancore Hindu Family Property Act, 1916, Section 22(1)
doctrines: Marumakkathayam law of succession
Doctrine of concurrent findings
Prospective overruling

card.dispute: The petitioners challenged the validity of the Explanation to Rule 38 of the MCR, 2016 and Rule 45 of the MCDR, 2017 concerning the computation of royalty on mined ores, alleging unfair and arbitrary State action violating Article 14.
issues_decided: Whether the Explanation to Rule 38 of the MCR, 2016 and Rule 45(8)(a) of the MCDR, 2017, which include royalty in the 'average sale price' for further royalty calculation, are constitutionally valid?
Whether the State's delay in deciding on proposed amendments to address the royalty computation anomaly amounts to arbitrary administrative action?
Whether the petitioners can be denied relief due to ongoing public consultation on the issue?
holdings: The Court did not strike down the impugned Explanations but observed that they raise serious concerns about fairness and proportionality, and may face constitutional challenge if not reviewed.
The State cannot indefinitely delay policy decisions affecting private rights; prolonged inaction renders administrative discretion arbitrary under Article 14.
The petitioners are not precluded from challenging the final policy decision after the consultation process concludes.
provisions: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Section 9
Mineral (Other than Atomic and Hydrocarbons Energy Minerals) Concession Rules, 2016, Rule 38
Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 2017, Rule 45(8)(a)
doctrines: Principle of legitimate expectation
Doctrine of arbitrariness under Article 14
Proportionality in State action
State duty to act fairly and transparently

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent disputed whether an insufficiently stamped sale agreement could be admitted in evidence, and whether the trial court wrongly imposed a tenfold penalty under the Karnataka Stamp Act.
issues_decided: Whether the trial court could impose a tenfold penalty under Section 34 of the Karnataka Stamp Act when the instrument was referred to the District Registrar under Section 39?
Whether an insufficiently stamped document can be admitted in evidence after payment of deficit stamp duty and penalty as per the procedure under Sections 34 or 39?
holdings: The trial court cannot impose a tenfold penalty under Section 34 when the document has been referred to the District Registrar under Section 39; the quantum of penalty is to be determined by the District Registrar, not the court.
An insufficiently stamped instrument becomes admissible in evidence once the deficit stamp duty and penalty are paid in compliance with Sections 34 or 39 of the Karnataka Stamp Act.
doctrines: Admissibility of unstamped or insufficiently stamped instruments
Separation of powers between judicial authorities and stamp authorities
Remedial nature of stamp legislation

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's order quashing a criminal complaint and chargesheet against a village accountant and others for allegedly fabricating property documents, arguing that prosecution required prior sanction under Section 197 Cr.PC.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in quashing the FIR and chargesheet without requiring sanction under Section 197 of the Cr.PC for prosecution of a public servant?
Whether the acts attributed to the public servant fell within the scope of official duty so as to attract protection under Section 197 Cr.PC?
holdings: The High Court erred in quashing the complaint and chargesheet in their entirety without determining whether the acts alleged against the public servant were done in discharge of official duty warranting sanction under Section 197 Cr.PC.

Section 197 Cr.PC does not protect a public servant when the alleged acts, such as fabrication of records, are not part of official duty but misuse of official position, even if connected to official role.
doctrines: Section 197 Cr.PC protection applies only if the act is in discharge of official duty, not merely because it was done by a public servant
Fabrication of records or misuse of official position for illegal gain does not constitute discharge of official duty

card.dispute: The wife sought transfer of a divorce petition and alimony, while the husband sought dissolution of marriage on grounds of irretrievable breakdown under Article 142 of the Constitution.
issues_decided: Whether the Supreme Court can dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown under Article 142(1) of the Constitution?
Whether the wife is entitled to permanent alimony and, if so, the appropriate quantum?
Whether the wife is entitled to reside in the matrimonial home owned by the husband's father?
Whether criminal proceedings between the parties should be quashed in light of the settlement and dissolution of marriage?
holdings: The Supreme Court can exercise its powers under Article 142(1) to dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown, even if not a statutory ground, to meet the ends of justice.
The wife is entitled to permanent alimony of Rs.12 crores as a full and final settlement, considering the husband's financial status, the failed mutual consent attempt, and her economic position.
The wife is not entitled to reside in the flats owned by the husband's father and must vacate them upon receiving alimony.
Criminal proceedings initiated by the wife against the husband and a third party are quashed in the interest of justice and finality of the settlement.
doctrines: Irretrievable breakdown of marriage
Equitable dissolution of marriage under Article 142
Full and final settlement of marital claims
Quia timet relief in family disputes

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the impounding of six agreements for sale that transferred possession of property but were not duly stamped, arguing they should not be treated as conveyances for stamp duty purposes.
issues_decided: Whether an agreement for sale that transfers possession of immovable property is deemed a conveyance under the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, attracting higher stamp duty?
Whether the subsequent execution of a sale deed absolves the liability to pay stamp duty on the earlier agreement for sale?
Whether the trial court was justified in impounding the agreements and directing adjudication of stamp duty and penalty?
holdings: An agreement for sale transferring possession of immovable property is deemed a conveyance under Explanation I to Article 25 of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, and must be stamped accordingly.
The subsequent execution of a sale deed does not negate the obligation to pay stamp duty on the agreement for sale if it already fulfilled conditions of a conveyance, such as transfer of possession.

The trial court correctly impounded the documents and directed adjudication, as unstamped or insufficiently stamped instruments cannot be used in evidence under Section 34 of the Maharashtra Stamp Act.
provisions: Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, Article 25 (Schedule-I) with Explanation I
doctrines: Deemed conveyance doctrine under stamp law
Principle of principal instrument for stamp duty
Impounding of insufficiently stamped documents
Adjustment of stamp duty under second proviso to Article 25

card.dispute: The bank appealed against the High Court's decision to set aside the forfeiture of the earnest money deposit made by a successful auction bidder who failed to pay the balance amount for a secured asset under SARFAESI proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the forfeiture of the entire earnest money deposit amounts to unjust enrichment when the bank has already recovered its dues from a subsequent sale?
Whether exceptional circumstances exist to justify judicial interference with the forfeiture of the earnest money deposit?
holdings: Forfeiture of earnest money under SARFAESI Rules does not amount to unjust enrichment even if the bank recovers its dues from a later sale, as the statutory framework permits such forfeiture to ensure timely payment.

Judicial interference with forfeiture is warranted only in rare and exceptional circumstances, such as those arising from the COVID-19 pandemic; demonetization and delayed document requests do not qualify as such.
provisions: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, Rule 9(5) of the SARFAESI Rules
doctrines: Principle of unjust enrichment
Doctrine of exceptional circumstances for judicial review
Reading down of statutory provisions
Strict adherence to limitation and statutory timelines

card.dispute: The State of Himachal Pradesh and others fought against Yogendra Mohan Sengupta and another over the validity of a development plan and whether environmental concerns required its complete suspension.
issues_decided: Whether the National Green Tribunal (NGT) could direct a legislative body to exercise its legislative functions in a particular manner?
Whether observations in a previous judgment would operate as res judicata in the present case?
Whether the NGT was justified in passing an order on 14th October 2022 while the High Court was already seized of the matter?
Whether the development plan adequately balanced environmental and developmental concerns?
holdings: The NGT cannot issue directions to a legislative body to perform its legislative functions in a specific manner, as this would violate the separation of powers.
Observations in a previous judgment, particularly those not directly adjudicated, do not constitute res judicata and cannot bind the court in subsequent proceedings.
The NGT ought not to have proceeded with the case when the High Court was already hearing the same issue, as this leads to forum shopping and duplication of judicial effort.
The development plan, having undergone statutory processes and expert consultations, sufficiently balances development and environmental protection and cannot be stalled in entirety.
provisions: Tribunals Reforms (Rationalisation and Conditions of Service) Ordinance, 2021
Town and Country Planning Act, Himachal Pradesh, 1977
doctrines: Sustainable Development
Intergenerational Equity
Precautionary Principle
Polluter Pays Principle
Separation of Powers

card.dispute: The State of Telangana challenged a High Court order that, in review, set aside concurrent findings that the suit property was forest land, and instead granted relief to the respondent based on post-decree evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court, in exercise of review jurisdiction, could re-appreciate evidence and effectively act as an appellate court?
Whether the suit for declaration of title and injunction was maintainable without challenging the final proceedings under the A.P. Forest Act?
Whether the District Collector had jurisdiction to deal with forest land already declared under the A.P. Forest Act?
holdings: A High Court cannot, in review, re-appreciate evidence or act as an appellate court; doing so exceeds its jurisdiction.

A suit for declaration of title is not maintainable if it does not challenge final and conclusive proceedings under the A.P. Forest Act, especially when the Forest Settlement Officer was not impleaded.
The District Collector lacks jurisdiction to deal with land already declared as forest land under the A.P. Forest Act, and any action in that regard is without legal authority.
provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Section 87
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XLI Rule 22
doctrines: Jurisdictional limitation of review
Finality of proceedings under forest laws
Maintainability of declaratory suits
Error apparent on the face of record

card.dispute: The State of Punjab and the deceased respondent's legal heirs fought over possession of a piece of land allegedly donated in 1958 for a veterinary hospital, with the respondent claiming possession after 43 years.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for possession was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the State could claim ownership based on donation and long possession despite absence of registered deed
Whether the revenue records in the plaintiff's name were sufficient to establish title in a suit for possession
Whether the burden of proof was correctly placed on the State or should have been on the plaintiff
holdings: A suit for possession of immovable property is barred if filed beyond 12 years from when possession became adverse, and in this case, the delay of 43 years rendered the suit time-barred under Article 65 of the Limitation Act.

The State's long, uninterrupted possession since 1958-59 for a public purpose, supported by documentary evidence of donation and construction, established lawful possession even without a registered deed.
Entries in revenue records (Jama Bandi) do not confer title and cannot override evidence of donation and continuous possession; such records are only for tax assessment.

The burden of proving lack of ownership lies on the plaintiff when the defendant is in possession, as per Section 110 of the Evidence Act, and the courts below wrongly shifted this burden to the State.
doctrines: Adverse possession
