Title follows possession
Presumption against delay in filing suits
Revenue records not conclusive on title

card.dispute: The dispute was between two branches of a family, both descended from a common ancestor, over the ownership of ancestral land, specifically whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to the tribal members in question.
issues_decided: Whether the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 applies to members of Scheduled Tribes in the absence of a governing custom?
Whether the principle of justice, equity and good conscience can govern succession when personal law is inapplicable or silent?
Whether the appellants, as members of a tribal community, had sufficiently adopted Hindu customs to be governed by Hindu law?
holdings: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 does not automatically apply to Scheduled Tribes, but its general principles may inform decisions when applied through justice, equity and good conscience.

In the absence of a specific personal law or custom, courts may apply the principles of justice, equity and good conscience to ensure fair devolution of property, especially in matters of intestate succession.
The appellants were found to have adopted Hindu customs and were 'sufficiently hinduised', thus governed by Hindu law, excluding the respondents from claiming rights in the property.
doctrines: Justice, equity and good conscience
Intestate succession
Application of personal law to tribal communities

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Vasantha and Rajalakshmi disputed over ownership and possession of property originally settled by Thayammal in 1947 and later re-settled in 1952, following a suit filed in 1993 by Rajalakshmi's husband for declaration of title.
issues_decided: Whether the suit filed in 1993 was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act, 1963
Whether the suit for declaration of title without seeking recovery of possession was maintainable under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
holdings: The suit was barred by limitation as no cause of action arose after 1993, and the plaintiff failed to file within the three-year period from the accrual of the cause of action.

A suit seeking only a declaration of title is not maintainable under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 when the plaintiff is not in possession and could have sought consequential relief like recovery of possession.
doctrines: Doctrine of maintainability of declaratory suits
Doctrine against multiplicity of proceedings
Rule that limitation bars remedy but not title

card.dispute: The appellant and six others were convicted by the trial court for the abduction and murder of Neelam, but challenged the conviction, claiming the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved the abduction and murder of the deceased beyond reasonable doubt?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of two accused (A-6 and A-7) without finding perversity in the trial court's judgment?
Whether the circumstantial evidence established a complete chain pointing to the guilt of the accused?
Whether the post-mortem report regarding time of death could be relied upon in the absence of credible eyewitness testimony?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove abduction or murder beyond reasonable doubt, as the circumstantial evidence was inconsistent and did not form a complete chain of guilt.

The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal of A-6 and A-7 without finding the trial court's view to be perverse or impossible, violating the principle that acquittals are entitled to strong presumption of innocence.
In a case based solely on circumstantial evidence, the chain must be unbroken and point exclusively to guilt; here, it was broken and insufficient to sustain conviction.
The post-mortem report indicating time of death around 5:00 PM on 30.08.1985 was reliable in the absence of credible eyewitness accounts contradicting it.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence strengthened by acquittal
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases
Test of complete chain of circumstantial evidence
Principle against reversal of acquittal without strong grounds of perversity or illegality

card.dispute: The CBI challenged the discharge of two appellants accused of cheating and criminal conspiracy in connection with undisclosed mortgages on land used for an educational institution, after the High Court set aside the discharge order.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could invoke its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to set aside a discharge order when an alternative remedy under Section 397 Cr.P.C. was available but time-barred.
Whether the appellants had committed cheating under Section 420 IPC by allegedly concealing the mortgage of land in applications to AICTE.
Whether there was sufficient evidence to sustain a charge of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC.
holdings: The High Court could not invoke Section 482 Cr.P.C. to bypass the limitation period for revision under Section 397 Cr.P.C. when a specific statutory remedy was available.

Mere non-disclosure in subsequent applications, after full disclosure in the first, does not establish fraudulent intent under Section 420 IPC, especially when the recipient authority did not claim to be misled.
Absence of evidence showing a conscious agreement to deceive negates the charge of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC.
doctrines: Inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. cannot be used when a specific statutory remedy is available.
Dishonest or fraudulent intent is essential to constitute cheating under Section 420 IPC.
Conspiracy requires a meeting of minds and conscious agreement to commit an illegal act.

card.dispute: The State of Bihar prosecuted seven accused for the abduction and murder of Neelam, leading to appeals against conviction and acquittal, culminating in a challenge to the reliability of evidence and the reversal of acquittals.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the deceased was abducted and murdered by the accused?
Whether the High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal of two accused (A-6 and A-7) without finding perversity or illegality in the Trial Court's reasoning?
Whether the circumstantial evidence, including eyewitness testimony and post-mortem findings, established a complete chain pointing to the guilt of the accused?
Whether the prosecution sufficiently proved the residence of the deceased and the informant at the place of occurrence?
holdings: The prosecution failed to prove the abduction and murder beyond reasonable doubt due to unreliable eyewitness accounts and lack of corroborative evidence.
The High Court erred in reversing the acquittal of A-6 and A-7 without finding the Trial Court's view to be perverse, illegal, or impossible, violating settled principles on appeal against acquittal.
In a circumstantial evidence case, the chain must be complete and point exclusively to guilt; here, it was broken, making conviction unsustainable.
The prosecution did not prove the deceased’s or informant’s residence at the crime scene, undermining the credibility of the entire case.
doctrines: Presumption of innocence strengthened by acquittal
Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases
Principle of complete chain of circumstantial evidence
High threshold for reversal of acquittal on appeal

card.dispute: Ajay Singh and Khacheru disputed over the classification and ownership of Khasra No.103, whether it was a 'Johad (Pond)' or 'Oosar' land, and the validity of the respondent's claim based on revenue records.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could interfere with concurrent factual findings of revenue authorities under Article 226 of the Constitution.
Whether the disputed land was correctly classified as 'Johad (Pond)' in revenue records and excluded from consolidation.
Whether the permanent injunction granted by the Civil Judge could be invalidated solely due to the setting aside of the Collector's order.
holdings: The High Court cannot reappreciate evidence or reverse concurrent factual findings of revenue authorities under Article 226 unless there is perversity, illegality, or lack of jurisdiction.
The disputed land was rightly classified as 'Johad (Pond)' based on revenue records and usage, and no valid patta was issued in favor of the respondent.
A permanent injunction, based on independent judicial consideration, cannot be rendered ineffective merely because a prior administrative order was set aside in writ proceedings.
provisions: U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, Section 198(4)
doctrines: Principle of non-reappreciation of evidence by High Court under Article 226
Supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 not equivalent to appellate jurisdiction
Doctrine of perversity in factual findings

card.dispute: The appellant, a former Tehsildar, challenged the revival of disciplinary proceedings against him for a land settlement order passed in 1997, arguing that the 14-year delay in issuing the chargesheet and the nature of the allegations as mere errors in quasi-judicial functioning warranted quashing of the proceedings.
issues_decided: Whether the chargesheet against the appellant falls within the exceptions allowing disciplinary action against a quasi-judicial officer for passing an erroneous order
Whether unexplained inordinate delay of 14 years in issuing the chargesheet warrants quashing of the disciplinary proceedings
holdings: Disciplinary proceedings cannot be initiated against a quasi-judicial officer solely for passing an erroneous order unless there are allegations of misconduct, extraneous influence, corruption, or negligence; mere legal error does not amount to misconduct.

An unexplained inordinate delay of 14 years in initiating departmental proceedings, especially when the alleged misconduct was known earlier, renders the proceedings unjust and liable to be quashed to protect the employee from undue mental distress and reputational harm.
provisions: Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules
doctrines: Doctrine of proportionality in disciplinary proceedings
Protection of quasi-judicial officers from departmental action for judicial errors
Principle of promptness in initiating disciplinary proceedings
Doctrine of fairness in administrative action

card.dispute: A shareholder and former Managing Director of a company challenged the validity of an e-auction conducted by the liquidator during insolvency, seeking to set it aside due to non-payment of balance sale consideration and procedural issues.
issues_decided: Whether the e-auction sale should be set aside due to the successful bidder's delay in paying the balance sale consideration beyond 90 days under Rule 12 of the IBBI (Liquidation) Regulations, 2016
Whether Rule 13 of the IBBI (Liquidation) Regulations, 2016 is mandatory or directory
Whether the liquidator could complete the sale despite an income tax attachment on the property
Whether the court should cancel the auction and declare the sale void given the delay and subsequent development on the property
holdings: Rule 12 of the IBBI (Liquidation) Regulations, 2016 is mandatory; failure to pay within 90 days renders the sale liable to be cancelled, but equitable considerations may prevent cancellation.
Rule 13 is directory, not mandatory, as it prescribes procedural steps for completing the sale and does not specify adverse consequences for non-compliance.
The liquidator lawfully took steps to lift the income tax attachment, and the bidder’s awareness of the issue and failure to act negated its claim of impossibility.

The auction and sale will not be set aside due to equitable considerations, including the bidder’s significant investment and operational hospital, but the bidder must pay 50% of the auction value differential with interest.
doctrines: Mandatory vs directory interpretation of procedural rules
Equitable relief in insolvency proceedings
Principle of sanctity of public auctions
Doctrine of balancing of equities

card.dispute: Landowners challenged the delay in receiving compensation for their land acquired for the Bengaluru-Mysuru Infrastructure Corridor Project, seeking updated market value assessment due to inflation and administrative delay.
issues_decided: Whether the State's delay in determining compensation entitles landowners to a revised market value date for compensation under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Whether the appellate court could have exercised powers under Article 226 or Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice despite lack of jurisdiction in the lower authority.
Whether quashing the acquisition would be appropriate due to violation of Article 300-A from non-payment of timely compensation.
holdings: Prolonged delay in compensation due to State inaction warrants shifting the valuation date to ensure just compensation under Article 300-A.
The High Court should have used Article 226 powers to do complete justice instead of dismissing the claim on technical grounds.
This Court, under Article 142, directed compensation to be calculated based on the market value as of 2019 to prevent a travesty of justice.
provisions: Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, Section 28
doctrines: Doctrine of Delay and Laches
Doctrine of Just Compensation
Doctrine of Constitutional Morality
Power under Article 142 to do complete justice

card.dispute: The appellants (judgment debtors) challenged the High Court's affirmation of the executing court's decision allowing the plaintiff to deposit the balance sale consideration despite delay, and rejecting their application for rescission of contract under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.
issues_decided: Whether the direction to deposit the balance sale consideration within 20 days, originally given by the trial court, continued to be binding after the High Court affirmed the decree in second appeal without specifying any time limit?

Whether the executing court could permit deposit of the balance sale consideration after the stipulated time had expired, in the absence of an extension of time under Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963?

Whether the failure to deposit the balance sale consideration within the stipulated time rendered the decree inexecutable, especially when the judgment debtor did not seek rescission under Section 28?
holdings: When a superior court affirms a decree without modifying or specifying a time limit for deposit, the original time stipulation does not survive; the appellate decision merges and supersedes the trial court's order.

The time stipulated in a decree for specific performance is for the benefit of both parties, but if the judgment debtor does not seek rescission under Section 28 and has refused to accept payment, the decree remains executable even after the stipulated period.

Section 28 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 does not automatically render a decree inexecutable upon delay; rescission must be sought by the judgment debtor, and the court may consider extension or rescission only upon application.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XX Rule 12-A
doctrines: Merger of decree doctrine
Strict compliance with conditions precedent to enforcement
Beneficial interpretation of decrees to sustain accrued rights

card.dispute: The appellant tenants sought to modify a 2013 court order via an oral mention in 2016 to correct survey numbers in a land occupancy dispute, which the respondents challenged as violating natural justice.
issues_decided: Whether the learned Single Judge erred in allowing modification of a final order via an oral 'for being spoken to' application after three years without notice to the other side?
Whether the Division Bench's clarification of the modified order was legally sustainable?
holdings: A court order cannot be unilaterally modified through an oral mention without notice to the opposite party, as it violates principles of natural justice and judicial propriety.
The impugned modification and subsequent clarifications are set aside; the original writ petition is restored for fresh adjudication on merits.
doctrines: Principles of natural justice
Finality of judicial orders
Procedural propriety in judicial corrections

card.dispute: The Central Bank of India challenged the maintainability of a suit filed by borrower Smt. Prabha Jain seeking declaration that certain sale and mortgage deeds were nullities, after the bank had initiated debt recovery proceedings against her before the DRT.
issues_decided: Whether the jurisdiction of a civil court to try a suit filed by a borrower against a bank is ousted by the RDB Act when recovery proceedings are pending before the DRT.
Whether a civil court can transfer an independent suit filed by a borrower to be tried along with recovery proceedings before the DRT.
Whether such a transfer can be ordered with the consent of the plaintiff.
holdings: The jurisdiction of a civil court is not ousted by the RDB Act merely because debt recovery proceedings are pending before the DRT; civil courts retain jurisdiction over independent suits by borrowers.
A civil court has no power to transfer an independent suit filed by a borrower to the DRT for joint trial, as the RDB Act does not confer such a power and Section 151 CPC cannot be used to imply it.
Since there is no power to transfer a suit to the DRT, the question of doing so with or without consent does not arise.
provisions: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 19(7)
Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, Section 25
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 10
doctrines: Strict interpretation of jurisdictional bar clauses
Presumption in favour of civil court jurisdiction
Statutory tribunals have no inherent powers beyond those conferred by statute

card.dispute: Cuddalore Powergen Corporation Ltd (appellant) fought against M/S Chemplast Cuddalore Vinyls Limited (respondent) over whether a second suit for specific performance and cancellation of a sale deed was barred by Order II Rule 2 of the CPC due to a prior suit involving the same property.
issues_decided: Whether the second suit was barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC due to identity of cause of action with the first suit
Whether new developments, namely court orders lifting a government ban, gave rise to a distinct cause of action for the second suit
Whether the plaints must be read as a whole to determine the applicability of the bar under Order II Rule 2 CPC
Whether failure to specifically plead dates of court decisions in the cause of action paragraph defeats a new cause of action
holdings: A second suit is not barred under Order II Rule 2 CPC if it is based on a cause of action that is distinct from the first suit, even if the subject matter and parties are the same.
The lifting of a government-imposed ban by court orders constituted a new and distinct cause of action, enabling the plaintiff to file a second suit for specific performance.
Plaints must be read as a whole rather than in a piecemeal manner to determine whether a cause of action is truly different under Order II Rule 2 CPC.
Technical omissions such as not specifying exact dates of judicial orders in the cause of action paragraph do not negate a new cause of action if the facts are otherwise pleaded in the plaint.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order II Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(d)
doctrines: Cause of action estoppel under Order II Rule 2 CPC
Holistic reading of pleadings doctrine
New cause of action arising from supervening events

card.dispute: Delhi Development Authority challenged the validity of an auction sale of a plot it leased to M/s Mehta Constructions, which was later sold to S.G.G. Towers (P) Ltd. in liquidation proceedings, over rights to the property and recovery of unearned income.
issues_decided: Whether the auction sale in liquidation proceedings conferred leasehold or ownership rights on the first respondent (S.G.G. Towers)?
Whether the Delhi Development Authority could claim unearned income from the amount deposited in liquidation proceedings?
Whether the first respondent could be recognized as a lawful lessee under the original lease agreement?
holdings: The first respondent acquired only such lease rights as were held by M/s Mehta Constructions, but no ownership or valid leasehold interest, since the original lease was void and no rights were ever validly created.
The court cannot direct payment of unearned income from funds in liquidation as multiple creditors have claims, and the High Court overseeing liquidation must determine distribution.
The appellant retains the right to recover possession or unearned income from the first respondent separately, and the first respondent may apply for regularization of the transaction by paying dues.
doctrines: Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Doctrine of limited transmission of rights in insolvency auctions
Principle of unearned income recovery in lease defaults

card.dispute: The Delhi Agricultural Marketing Board appealed against the enforcement of an arbitration award that upheld an agreement to return part of acquired land to Bhagwan Devi, challenging its legality and validity under land acquisition and public policy laws.
issues_decided: Whether the Board could validly enter into an agreement to return part of land already acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 after possession had been taken.
Whether the agreement dated 30.09.1988 was contrary to public policy and the fundamental policy of Indian law.
Whether the arbitral award upholding the agreement should be set aside under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
holdings: After possession is taken under Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the land vests absolutely in the Government, and neither the Government nor the beneficiary Board can unilaterally withdraw or reverse the acquisition.
The agreement to return part of the acquired land was contrary to the fundamental policy of Indian law, as it undermined the sovereign power of eminent domain and amounted to a fraud on public power.
The arbitral award upholding the agreement was in conflict with public policy under Section 34(2)(b) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and ought to have been set aside.
provisions: Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1998, Section 6
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1998, Section 24(1) and (2)
doctrines: Eminent domain
Public policy of India
Fundamental policy of Indian law
Fraud on power doctrine
Vesting of title upon possession under land acquisition law

card.dispute: The appellants (plaintiffs) obtained an ex-parte decree for specific performance of a sale agreement, which the respondents (defendants) sought to set aside after delay; the dispute centers on whether the High Court could set aside the ex-parte decree when only the delay condonation order was challenged in revision.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could set aside an ex-parte decree in revision when no challenge was filed against the order dismissing the application to set it aside?
Whether the High Court was justified in condoning the delay in filing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree?
holdings: The High Court cannot set aside an ex-parte decree in revision when no revision was filed against the order dismissing the application to set it aside, as the remedy for delay condonation is independent of the remedy to set aside the decree.

The High Court was justified in condoning the delay in filing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree, given the explanation of inadvertent non-filing and the substantial rights involved in the property.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Independence of remedies under CPC
Revisional jurisdiction limited to challenged orders
Substantial justice over technicalities

card.dispute: A former Gujarat Minister challenged criminal proceedings under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, alleging he was wrongly accused of illegal fishing contract allocations without tender, causing loss to the state.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations against the appellant Minister disclose ingredients of an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Whether mere misuse of authority without demand or acceptance of illegal gratification amounts to an offence under the Act
Whether the criminal proceedings against the appellant should be quashed for lack of material
holdings: Mere allegation of misuse of authority, without any evidence of demand or acceptance of bribe or illegal gratification, does not constitute an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
The prosecution failed to produce any material indicating that the appellant received or agreed to receive illegal gratification, which is essential to invoke the Act.
The criminal proceedings against the appellant are liable to be dropped due to absence of prima facie evidence supporting corruption charges.
provisions: Gujarat Government Rules of Business, Schedule-2 (1990), Rule 9
doctrines: Requirement of mens rea in corruption offences
Presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act applies only after proof of demand or acceptance of gratification
Absence of material evidence leading to no prosecution in corruption cases

card.dispute: Godrej Projects Development Limited appealed against the NCDRC's order directing it to refund most of the amount paid by homebuyers Anil Karlekar and others, minus only 10% of the Basic Sale Price, with interest, after they cancelled their apartment booking due to falling property prices.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to forfeit more than 10% of the Basic Sale Price upon cancellation of the apartment booking by the complainants?
Whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission was justified in awarding interest on the amount to be refunded to the complainants?
holdings: A forfeiture clause in a real estate agreement that allows the developer to retain more than 10% of the Basic Sale Price as cancellation charges is unfair and contrary to consumer protection laws, as it constitutes an unfair trade practice or unfair contract under the Consumer Protection Act.

The NCDRC was not justified in awarding interest on the refund amount where the complainants cancelled the booking due to falling market prices and likely used the funds elsewhere, making compensation through interest unwarranted.
doctrines: Unfair trade practice
Unfair contract
Penalty versus liquidated damages under Section 74

card.dispute: The appellants fought with the State of Maharashtra over the rejection of their claim for refund of stamp duty paid on a cancelled property purchase agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants' claim for refund of stamp duty is barred by limitation under the amended provisions of Section 48(1) of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958?
Whether the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority (CCRA) had the power to review and recall its earlier order sanctioning the refund of stamp duty?
Whether the appellants are entitled to interest on the wrongfully retained stamp duty amount?
holdings: The appellants' refund claim is governed by the unamended proviso to Section 48(1) of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, as their right crystallized upon execution of the cancellation deed, and thus the claim is not time-barred.
The CCRA lacked statutory authority to review or recall its final order granting refund; such powers cannot be created by consent or participation in proceedings.
The appellants are entitled to simple interest at 6% per annum from the date of the original refund order (08.01.2018) until payment, with default interest at 12% if delayed beyond four weeks.
doctrines: Limitation bars remedy but not the right
State must act as an honest person and not rely on technicalities against citizens
Jurisdiction cannot be created by consent or acquiescence
Principle of equitable fairness in fiscal determinations

card.dispute: The original plaintiffs (appellants) challenged the High Court's decision to allow subsequent purchasers (respondents) to file an appeal against a decree of specific performance despite their delay and non-impleadment in the suit.
issues_decided: Whether a transferee pendente lite who was not impleaded in the suit can be granted leave to appeal against a decree passed in the suit?
Whether the High Court was justified in condoning a delay of 586 days in filing the appeal by the subsequent purchasers?
Whether a transferee pendente lite is entitled to be impleaded as a matter of right under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC?
holdings: A transferee pendente lite, even if not impleaded in the suit, may seek leave to appeal against a decree affecting the property, but such leave is discretionary and must be exercised judiciously based on the facts.

The High Court erred in granting leave to appeal and condoning the 586-day delay without considering that the subsequent purchasers bought the property during pendency of the suit and under an injunction, thus failing to make out a good case for leave.

A transferee pendente lite is not entitled to be impleaded as a matter of right; the court must consider the nature of the suit and circumstances before allowing impleadment under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I Rule 10
doctrines: Lis pendens
Transferee pendente lite as representative-in-interest
Discretionary leave to appeal for non-party transferees
Liberal construction of procedural provisions to advance justice

card.dispute: The appellants and respondents fought over whether the will of Sanjhi Ram was validly executed under Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, particularly concerning the requirement of 'direction of the testator' when a will is signed by another person.
issues_decided: What is the meaning of the phrase 'by the direction of the testator' in Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
Whether the will was validly proved in light of the attesting witness's deposition?
Whether the High Court was correct in holding that the will was not proved due to absence of evidence on 'direction of the testator'?
holdings: The phrase 'by the direction of the testator' in Section 63(c) applies only when someone other than the testator signs the will; it does not impose an additional requirement when the testator himself affixes his mark.

The word 'or' in Section 63(c) is disjunctive and must be interpreted as such; the requirements of seeing the testator sign, seeing another sign by direction, or receiving acknowledgment are alternative, not cumulative.
The will was validly proved because the attesting witness saw the testator affix his thumb impression, which satisfies Section 63(c); evidence of 'direction' was not necessary in these circumstances.
doctrines: Principle of disjunctive interpretation of statutory language
Rule of literal construction of statutes
Judicial conscience test in will disputes
Burden of proof on propounder in cases of suspicious circumstances

card.dispute: Independent Sugar Corporation Limited challenged the Competition Commission of India's approval of a combination involving AGI during a corporate insolvency resolution process, arguing procedural irregularities and incorrect market assessment.
issues_decided: Whether the CCI must issue notice to both the acquirer and the corporate debtor (target) in a combination arising out of CIRP under the IBC
Whether the CCI's decision not to call for a Director General's report under Section 29(1A) of the Competition Act was legally permissible
Whether the CCI's assessment of market share and AAEC based on proposed capacity rather than actual usage was sustainable
holdings: The CCI must issue show-cause notice to both the acquirer and the target (corporate debtor represented by the resolution professional) in a combination arising from CIRP, as 'parties' in Section 29(1) implies plural entities.
The word 'may' in Section 29(1A) of the Competition Act confers discretion on the CCI; it is not mandatory to call for a Director General’s report if the CCI is satisfied with the parties’ reply.

The CCI’s determination of AAEC based on actual or consented capacity, not theoretical maximum output, is entitled to deference as an expert body, and courts should not re-evaluate such economic findings absent strong grounds.
doctrines: Principle of literal interpretation
Deference to expert regulatory bodies
Purposive interpretation distinguished from plain meaning
Doctrine of judicial restraint in economic matters

card.dispute: The appellant (Inder Singh) and the State of Madhya Pradesh disputed over title and possession of land, with the State challenging the condonation of delay in filing a second appeal after the land was allotted to the appellant but later occupied by the State for public purposes.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing the second appeal under Section 100 of the CPC could be condoned under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Whether the High Court was justified in allowing the application for condonation of delay in filing the second appeal.
holdings: Delay in filing an appeal may be condoned if there is sufficient cause, particularly when the dispute involves the State and requires adjudication on merits to prevent injustice.
The High Court's decision to condone delay in the second appeal is sustainable where the case involves public interest, possession by the State, and the need for a decision on the merits.
doctrines: Liberal approach to condonation of delay
Substantial justice over technicalities
State as a party and its impact on delay

card.dispute: The appellant, Gangubai Raghunath Ayare, challenged the High Court's reversal of a trial court decision that had set aside a sale deed concerning a property in which she claimed a share, against the legal heirs of the purchaser, Gangaram Sakharam Dhuri.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was correct in reversing the Trial Court's decision to set aside the sale deed dated 10.01.1969 executed by Vishnu in favor of the second defendant?
Whether the plaintiff was entitled to seek partition or separate possession of the suit property in a suit for administration of the deceased's estate?
Whether the suit was maintainable without impleading all necessary parties, including the legal heirs of Vishnu?
holdings: The sale deed dated 10.01.1969 is valid only to the extent of Vishnu's 1/5th undivided share in the property, and the High Court rightly upheld its validity in part.
A plaintiff cannot obtain a decree for partition or separate possession in a suit for administration of an estate unless it is properly framed and all necessary parties are impleaded.

Non-joinder of necessary parties, such as Vishnu's legal heirs, renders the suit incapable of granting effective relief, even though non-joinder does not automatically defeat a suit under CPC Order I Rule 9.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order I, Rule 10
doctrines: Non-joinder of necessary parties
Maintainability of suits for administration versus partition
Relief must conform to pleadings and prayers

card.dispute: The appellant, Gambhir Singh, challenged his conviction and death sentence in a murder case involving six victims, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on flawed circumstantial evidence.
issues_decided: Whether the prosecution established a complete chain of circumstantial evidence linking the appellant to the murders?
Whether the recoveries of weapons and stolen articles were legally and properly proved?
Whether the investigation was conducted with due diligence and in compliance with procedural safeguards?
holdings: In a circumstantial evidence case, the prosecution must prove each circumstance beyond reasonable doubt, and the chain of circumstances must be complete and point exclusively to the guilt of the accused.

Recoveries of weapons and articles cannot be relied upon if disclosure statements are not proved, accused did not sign recovery memos, and investigating officer failed to identify who led to which recovery.

A flawed and negligent investigation, including failure to establish motive, last seen theory, or proper custody of evidence, renders the prosecution case unreliable and insufficient to sustain conviction.
doctrines: Chain of circumstantial evidence must be unbroken and exclude all other hypotheses of innocence
Principle of benefit of doubt in criminal cases when prosecution fails to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt

card.dispute: The Indian Evangelical Lutheran Church Trust Association (appellant) and Sri Bala & Co. (respondent) fought over whether a second suit for specific performance of a 1991 sale agreement, filed after rejection of the plaint in an earlier suit, was within the limitation period.
issues_decided: Whether the second suit for specific performance is governed by Article 54 or Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963
When the cause of action or right to sue accrues for a second suit filed under Order VII Rule 13 of the CPC after rejection of a plaint in a prior suit
Whether the second suit was barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act
holdings: Article 54 of the Limitation Act does not apply to a second suit for specific performance filed after rejection of a plaint; instead, Article 113 applies.
The right to sue for a second suit accrues from the date of rejection of the plaint in the earlier suit, not from the original cause of action.
The second suit was barred by limitation as it was filed beyond three years from the date the right to sue accrued under Article 113, i.e., after 12.01.1998.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 11(d)
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VII Rule 13
doctrines: Accrual of cause of action
Continuous running of limitation period
Revival of right to sue
Limitation as a bar to relief

card.dispute: Jagwant Kaur challenged the allotment of an L.P.G. distributorship to the 4th respondent, alleging disqualification due to duplicate land offering and lack of valid lease at the time of application.
issues_decided: Whether the 4th respondent was disqualified for offering the same land as another applicant for L.P.G. distributorship.
Whether the 4th respondent could offer alternate land not in her possession at the time of application.
Whether consent from co-owners or co-sharers was required when the leased land was under sole ownership of the lessor.
holdings: The 4th respondent did not violate guidelines as the lands offered by her and the other applicant were distinct parcels from the same lessor, verified by revenue records.
An alternate land could be accepted post-application if the initial land became disputed, provided it met all eligibility criteria, under the flexible guidelines of 2015.
No consent or NOC was required from co-sharers when the leased property was solely owned by the lessor and leased exclusively to the applicant.
provisions: Indian Oil Corporation L.P.G. Distributorship Guidelines (2013, 2015, 2016)
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas Guidelines dated 18.12.2015 and 25.02.2016
doctrines: Doctrine of legitimate expectation
Principle of non-discrimination in public allotment processes
Judicial deference to administrative flexibility in implementation of guidelines

card.dispute: The appellants (Defendant Nos. 3 to 6) challenged the lower courts' decision to mould relief in favour of the executors of a will, setting aside a sale deed concerning a property originally bequeathed under the will, instead of decreeing the suit in favour of the trust.
issues_decided: Whether the court could legally mould the relief in favour of the executors of the will despite the suit being filed in the name of the trust?
Whether the moulding of relief by the lower courts caused prejudice or took the parties by surprise?
Whether the findings of title and ownership in favour of the testatrix entitled the court to mould relief to avoid multiplicity of litigation?
holdings: A court may mould relief to meet the ends of justice if the facts established during trial justify it, even if the original prayer is not granted, provided no party is prejudiced.
Moulding of relief is permissible when it prevents unnecessary litigation, especially where executors are aged and some have died, making fresh litigation impractical.
The court can grant relief to a party in a capacity different from that in which the suit was filed, if the findings support such a course and the relief aligns with the evidence and justice.
doctrines: Moulding of relief
Equitable jurisdiction
Judicial discretion to prevent multiplicity of suits

card.dispute: The appellant (Jai Ram) and respondent (Som Prakash) disputed over the validity of competing wills and the revocation of Letters of Administration granted to Som Prakash for the estate of Satwanti Devi.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the District Court's order revoking Letters of Administration on the ground of limitation, despite no such plea being raised before the District Court?
Whether an appellate court can dismiss an appeal on a ground of limitation not raised or contested in the trial court, where no evidence was led on that issue?
holdings: The High Court erred in setting aside the District Court's order on limitation grounds when the plea was not raised before the trial court and no evidence was adduced on the issue.
Where a limitation defense is not pleaded or contested in the trial court, the appellate court must decide the appeal on merits and cannot rely on limitation to overturn the decision.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order IX Rule 13
doctrines: Principle of issue estoppel and constructive res judicata
Appellate review on unpleaded grounds
Merits-based adjudication in the absence of a pleaded limitation defense

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the registration of an FIR under the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters & Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986, seeking to quash it on grounds of vagueness and mala fide initiation due to personal vendetta.
issues_decided: Whether the allegations in the FIR disclose sufficient material to invoke the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh Gangsters & Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986?
Whether the High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition seeking quashing of the FIR based solely on its averments without considering the context and pattern of multiple complaints?
Whether the invocation of a stringent penal law like the Gangsters Act is justified at the pre-trial stage based on unproven allegations?
holdings: The allegations in the FIR are vague and lack concrete material showing 'violence, threat, intimidation or coercion' necessary under Section 2(b) of the Gangsters Act, and thus do not meet the threshold for invoking the Act.

Courts can look beyond the FIR to surrounding circumstances, including patterns of multiple complaints and private disputes, when considering quashing under Section 482 CrPC or Article 226, especially to prevent misuse of stringent laws.

Invoking the Gangsters Act based on pending criminal cases with unproven allegations is premature; the seriousness required must go beyond ordinary criminal cases and demonstrate a pattern of anti-social activity involving fear or terror.
provisions: Uttar Pradesh Gangsters & Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986, Section 2(b)
doctrines: Strict construction of penal statutes
Look into the substance over form
Judicial review to prevent abuse of process
Presumption of innocence and protection of liberty under Article 21

card.dispute: The appellant, Jit Vinayak Arolkar, challenged the FIR alleging cheating under Section 420 IPC in connection with the sale of a property where the complainant claimed co-ownership, while the appellant acted as attorney for vendors who sold their claimed share.
issues_decided: Whether the ingredients of cheating under Section 415 IPC are made out against the appellant in relation to the sale of the disputed property.
Whether the FIR amounts to an abuse of process given the pendency of civil suits over the same property.
holdings: The act of executing sale deeds by the appellant as attorney for the vendors did not constitute cheating under Section 415 IPC, as there was no deception of the complainant nor any inducement to part with property or suffer harm.
The initiation of criminal proceedings two years after filing civil suits, without disclosing the pendency of those suits, constitutes an abuse of the process of law.
doctrines: Abuse of process of law
Ingredients of cheating under Section 415 IPC
Distinction between civil disputes and criminal prosecution

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the imposition of a 10% penalty under Section 271AAA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on undisclosed income detected during a search, arguing that the conditions for penalty exemption were met.
issues_decided: Whether penalty under Section 271AAA(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is leviable when the assessee admits and substantiates undisclosed income during search and pays tax with interest, albeit belatedly?

Whether income discovered as a result of actions taken during the search but not physically found at the assessee's premises qualifies as 'undisclosed income found in the course of search' under Section 271AAA?
Which previous year is the 'specified previous year' under Section 271AAA when a search is conducted after the return filing deadline for the prior year?
holdings: Penalty under Section 271AAA(1) is not leviable if the assessee admits the undisclosed income, substantiates its source during the search, and pays tax with interest, even if payment is delayed.
Income derived from documents collected from a third party as a direct consequence of the search falls within the scope of 'found in the course of search' under Section 271AAA.
The 'specified previous year' under Section 271AAA is the year in which the search is conducted if the return filing deadline for the earlier year had expired before the search date.
doctrines: Strict construction of penalty provisions
Conditional exemption from penalty based on voluntary disclosure and compliance
Causal connection test for 'found in the course of search'
Sound discretion guided by law

card.dispute: The appellant challenged the High Court's dismissal of his petition to quash criminal proceedings under the SC-ST Act, arguing that the alleged offence did not occur in a 'place within public view'.
issues_decided: Whether the alleged offence under Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the SC-ST Act occurred in a 'place within public view' as required by law.
Whether the High Court erred in not considering the argument that the allegations in the FIR do not prima facie constitute an offence under the SC-ST Act.
holdings: An offence under Sections 3(1)(r) or 3(1)(s) of the SC-ST Act must occur in a place within public view, which requires members of the public to be able to witness or hear the act; a private office not open to public view does not qualify.
The allegations in the FIR, even if accepted as true, do not make out a prima facie case under the SC-ST Act, warranting exercise of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash the proceedings.
provisions: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(r)
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Section 3(1)(s)
doctrines: Bhajan Lal guidelines for quashing criminal proceedings
Principle of 'place within public view' distinct from 'public place'

card.dispute: Citicorp Finance (India) Limited appealed against a National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission order directing it to refund money with interest and pay litigation costs in a housing loan dispute involving a flat sale between the consumer and a borrower.
issues_decided: Whether a consumer dispute governed by the Consumer Protection Act can be referred to arbitration when there is an arbitration clause in the agreement?
Whether the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had jurisdiction to decide the matter despite the alleged tripartite agreement containing an arbitration clause?
holdings: Consumer disputes under the Consumer Protection Act are non-arbitrable by nature, as the Act is a special welfare legislation providing consumers an exclusive choice to seek redressal in public fora.
The consumer has the sole right to choose between arbitration and a consumer forum; the presence of an arbitration clause does not bar access to consumer courts if the consumer opts for them.
doctrines: Non-arbitrability of consumer disputes
Primacy of consumer choice in dispute resolution forum
Public policy underlying welfare legislation

card.dispute: The landowner challenged the rejection of his request to release his land from acquisition, claiming entitlement under state policies and discrimination, while the state opposed on grounds of lack of valid CLU, delay, and public interest.
issues_decided: Whether the appellant was entitled to release of land from acquisition under prevailing state policies?
Whether the appellant's plea of discrimination against other released landowners was valid?
Whether the appellant's claim was barred by res judicata or laches?
Whether compensation could be granted under the 2013 Act despite rejection of release?
holdings: The appellant was not entitled to release of land as he lacked a valid Change of Land Use (CLU) certificate, a mandatory requirement under state policy and law.
The plea of discrimination failed because other landowners had obtained CLU or were situated outside the acquisition notification, placing them in a distinguishable position.
The petition was not barred by res judicata or laches as prior writ petitions did not decide the release claim on merits and the request was timely pursued.
In exercise of Article 142, compensation shall be calculated under the 2013 Act due to continuous possession and operational factory, based on the unique facts of the case.
provisions: Punjab Scheduled Roads & Controlled Areas (Restrictions of Unregulated Development) Act, 1963, Section 4(1)(a)
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
doctrines: Res judicata
Principle of non-discrimination/equal treatment
Doctrine of laches
Equitable relief under Article 142

card.dispute: The appellants (defendants in the trial court) challenged the High Court's finding of contempt for allegedly violating an undertaking not to alienate property during the pendency of a suit over a Joint Development Agreement.
issues_decided: Whether the appellants were bound by the undertaking given by their counsel not to alienate the property during the pendency of the suit?
Whether the appellants were guilty of contempt of court for alienating the property despite court orders based on the undertaking?
Whether the High Court was justified in imposing civil contempt penalties including imprisonment, attachment of property, and compensation?
holdings: An advocate has no implied or apparent authority to make an undertaking that affects the client's substantial rights without express instructions from the client.

However, where an undertaking is given by counsel and adopted by the court as an order, and the client remains silent for years without seeking discharge, the undertaking binds the client and violation amounts to contempt.

Civil contempt may be punished with attachment of property and compensation; imprisonment may be modified considering age and circumstances, but the deterrent purpose of contempt jurisdiction must be upheld.
doctrines: Fiduciary relationship between lawyer and client
Implied vs. express authority of counsel
Contempt by disobedience of court order
Judicial discretion in sentencing for civil contempt

card.dispute: Faime Makers Pvt. Ltd. challenged the District Deputy Registrar's order granting a cooperative society a unilateral deed of assignment of land and building, claiming lack of jurisdiction and prior binding orders.
issues_decided: Whether the Competent Authority had jurisdiction to entertain a second application for unilateral assignment after dismissing the first with conditions?
Whether the principle of res judicata applies to quasi-judicial authorities in this context?
Whether the High Court erred in interpreting the first order as granting unconditional liberty to re-apply?
holdings: A quasi-judicial authority cannot entertain a second application contrary to its prior order requiring pre-resolution of legal complications.
The principle of res judicata binds quasi-judicial authorities; their final orders cannot be circumvented by fresh applications.
The first order did not grant unconditional liberty to re-apply; the High Court erred in interpreting it as such.
provisions: Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963, Section 5/11
doctrines: res judicata
principles of quasi-judicial jurisdiction
finality of administrative orders

card.dispute: M/s Maxim India Integrated Circuit Design (P) Ltd. fought with Andappa (by his legal representatives) and others over ownership and possession of land in Survey No. 1/3, formerly 49/43-A, after the Karnataka High Court allowed Andappa's delayed writ appeal challenging earlier revenue orders in favor of the appellant.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court was justified in condoning a delay of 1378 days in filing the writ appeal by Andappa?
Whether non-disclosure of final adverse revenue orders against Andappa amounted to suppression of material facts?
Whether the High Court erred in allowing the writ appeal after the issues had attained finality?
holdings: The High Court erred in condoning the inordinate delay of 1378 days without considering that the issues had already been finally decided against the appellant.
Non-disclosure of final adverse orders passed in revenue proceedings amounts to suppression of material facts, disentitling a party from equitable relief.
A litigant who fails to approach the court with clean hands is not entitled to judicial relief, especially when there is an attempt to manipulate proceedings.
doctrines: Clean hands doctrine
Principle of suppression of material facts
Finality of orders in revenue proceedings

card.dispute: The landlord sought eviction of the tenant from municipal premises in Jharkhand on grounds of bona fide need to establish an ultrasound business for his unemployed sons, which lower courts denied, prompting a Supreme Court appeal.
issues_decided: Whether the landlord established a bona fide need for eviction to set up an ultrasound machine for his unemployed sons.
Whether the earlier compromise decree granting perpetual tenancy in part barred the present eviction suit.
Whether the landlord’s prior partial eviction for a different family member affected the current claim of bona fide need.
holdings: A landlord's bona fide need for eviction is established if he proves real necessity, capacity to invest, and suitability of premises, even if his sons lack technical expertise to operate the machine.
A compromise allowing perpetual tenancy in part of a property does not bar future eviction if the landlord retains the legal right to seek eviction for bona fide needs.
A prior eviction for another family member’s need does not negate a subsequent claim of bona fide need for different beneficiaries, assessed as of the suit’s filing date.
provisions: Rent Control Act, applicable provisions regarding eviction on grounds of bona fide need (though specific section not cited, principles applied)
doctrines: Bona fide need doctrine in landlord-tenant law
Principle of maintainability of successive eviction suits for different familial needs
Judicial recognition of landlord’s autonomy in choosing premises for personal use

card.dispute: The appellant company challenged the High Court's decision to set aside a Single Judge's order allowing its writ petition, which sought to quash proceedings under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, over the alleged illegal takeover of its land by the Tahsildar.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court could decline to entertain a writ petition on the ground of disputed questions of fact.
Whether the issue of physical possession of land under Section 10(5) and (6) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is a pure question of fact or a mixed question of law and fact.
Whether the Division Bench was justified in setting aside the Single Judge's order allowing the writ petition.
holdings: The High Court may decline to entertain a writ petition if there is a serious dispute of fact requiring oral evidence or where materials on record are insufficient to reach a definite conclusion.

The question of whether physical possession was taken under Section 10(5) and (6) of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 is a mixed question of law and fact, which a writ court can decide based on available evidence.
The Division Bench erred in setting aside the well-reasoned judgment of the Single Judge without sufficient grounds, and the Single Judge's order allowing the writ petition was restored.
provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(5) and (6)
doctrines: Mixed question of law and fact
Judicial review in writ jurisdiction
Principle against arbitrary deprivation of property

card.dispute: The appellant (landlord) and respondent (tenant) disputed whether the landlord was liable to refund the full security deposit after the tenant remained in possession of the flat for years without paying rent.
issues_decided: Whether the respondent was entitled to the entire security deposit despite not vacating the flat or paying rent for nearly five years after the lease ended?
Whether the post-dated cheques issued by the respondent represented a legally enforceable debt for the full security amount?
Whether the courts below were justified in enhancing compensation to the full security deposit and imposing imprisonment in default?
holdings: A landlord is entitled to deduct unpaid rent and maintenance from the security deposit when a tenant continues occupation without payment beyond the lease term.
The respondent failed to prove that the entire amount under the post-dated cheques was a legally enforceable debt, given his continued unauthorized occupation.
The enhancement of compensation to Rs. 9,00,000 and imprisonment in default was unjustified; compensation is limited to Rs. 3,00,000, with the remainder to be reimbursed to the landlord.
provisions: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 21 (relating to execution of decrees)
doctrines: Deduction of dues from security deposit
Burden of proof in cheque bounce cases
Principle of unjust enrichment

card.dispute: The widow of a murder victim challenged the bail granted to two accused in a case involving offences under MCOCA and other laws, arguing that the High Court wrongly assessed the evidence and role of the accused at the bail stage.
issues_decided: Whether the High Court erred in evaluating the sufficiency of evidence and the role of the accused while granting bail in a case involving MCOCA offences.
Whether the High Court's observations on the accused's non-involvement prejudiced the prosecution's case and violated the principles of fair trial.
Whether the High Court failed to apply the stringent bail conditions mandated under Section 21(4) of MCOCA.
holdings: The High Court erred in making findings about the accused's role and the sufficiency of evidence at the bail stage, which is impermissible as it prejudices the trial and invades the domain of the trial court.
Appreciation of evidence to determine the guilt or innocence of the accused is not allowed when deciding bail, especially in serious cases like those under MCOCA and murder.
The impugned bail order must be set aside and the bail application remanded for fresh consideration in accordance with law, strictly adhering to Section 21(4) of MCOCA.
provisions: Maharashtra Police Act, 1951, Section 37(1)(3) read with Section 135
Maharashtra Control of Organized Crime Act, 1999, Sections 3(1)(ii), 3(2), 3(4), and Section 21(4)
Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, Section 45(1)
doctrines: Principle of fair trial
Presumption of innocence
Limited scope of evidence evaluation at bail stage
Stringent bail conditions under special statutes like MCOCA

card.dispute: The petitioner, M/s Shri Sendhur Agro & Oil Industries, sought to transfer a criminal case under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act from Chandigarh to Coimbatore, arguing that the cause of action arose entirely in Tamil Nadu.
issues_decided: Whether the court in Chandigarh has territorial jurisdiction to try the complaint under Section 138 of the N.I. Act?
Whether the proceedings should be transferred to Coimbatore or Delhi for the ends of justice under Section 406 Cr.P.C.?
holdings: The court in Chandigarh has jurisdiction if the payee's bank branch for cheque collection is located there, as clarified by Section 142(2)(a) and Explanation thereof, read with Section 142-A of the N.I. Act.
Transfer under Section 406 Cr.P.C. is not warranted merely due to inconvenience or language barriers; the petitioner can seek exemption from personal appearance or request virtual hearing.
doctrines: Territorial jurisdiction under Section 138 N.I. Act as amended
Doctrine of legislative validation
Principle of ends of justice in transfer of criminal proceedings

card.dispute: The appellant, a purchaser of disputed land, fought against former students and citizens who sued to declare that the appellant's earlier decree of injunction did not bind the state and that the state was the rightful owner of the land.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiffs in the present suit had locus standi to file a representative suit challenging a decree in which they were not parties?
Whether the decree passed in a prior suit between the appellant and the State was binding on the State and those claiming through it?
Whether the present suit was maintainable despite the finality of the earlier decree in O.S. No. 80/1978?
holdings: The plaintiffs lacked locus standi to file a representative suit to enforce rights on behalf of the State, especially when the State had already litigated the matter and failed to challenge the decree.
A decree in a prior suit between the appellant and the State, decided on merits and upheld in appeal, is binding on the State and cannot be collaterally attacked by third parties.
The present suit was not maintainable as it sought to challenge a final decree in proceedings to which the plaintiffs were not parties and in which they did not participate.
provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order VI Rule 17
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 11 (Res Judicata)
doctrines: Res judicata
Locus standi
Representative suit
Finality of decree

card.dispute: The appellant and respondent contested the grant of Letters of Administration based on the validity of a Will, with the appellant challenging the High Court's reversal of a lower court decision that had denied the grant due to suspicious circumstances surrounding the Will's execution.
issues_decided: Whether the findings of the Single Judge on due execution, testamentary capacity, and absence of forgery or undue influence amounted to a conclusive finding on the genuineness of the Will?
Whether the Division Bench was justified in treating the Single Judge’s findings as determinative of the Will’s genuineness and thereby declining to consider suspicious circumstances?
holdings: Findings on due execution, attestation, testamentary capacity, and failure to prove forgery or undue influence do not automatically constitute a finding on the overall genuineness of a Will.

A court must independently assess whether a Will is surrounded by suspicious circumstances even if certain issues are decided in favour of the propounder, and the Division Bench erred in not conducting this assessment.
doctrines: Requirement to prove Will under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act
Duty of court to examine suspicious circumstances despite proof of due execution and testamentary capacity

card.dispute: Tomorrowland Limited sued HUDCO for refund of a forfeited payment after HUDCO cancelled a 99-year lease for a 5-star hotel project; HUDCO refused refund citing non-performance, leading to litigation over maintainability, breach, and entitlement to interest.
issues_decided: Whether the suit for declaratory relief and refund was maintainable despite prior litigation and withdrawal of earlier suits?
Whether HUDCO was entitled to forfeit the amount paid by the appellant under the allotment letter?
Whether the appellant was entitled to interest on the refund of the principal amount under Section 34 of the CPC?
holdings: The suit was maintainable in part, as the withdrawal of earlier suits did not bar subsequent litigation on merits, especially where justice required adjudication.
HUDCO was in breach of its reciprocal contractual obligations and therefore not entitled to forfeit the amount paid by the appellant under Clause 5(iii) of the allotment letter.

The appellant, having engaged in forum shopping and failed to approach the court with clean hands, was not entitled to discretionary interest under Section 34 of the CPC, though interest at 6% would accrue if refund was delayed beyond three months.
provisions: Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 5 (implied condition of reciprocal performance)
doctrines: Clean Hands Doctrine
Forum Shopping
Equitable Discretion in Award of Interest

card.dispute: The appellants, claiming under an unregistered will, fought against the respondents who sought partition of ancestral property, disputing the will's validity.
issues_decided: Whether the unregistered Will dated 06.04.1990 was validly executed in accordance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and Section 68 of the Evidence Act.
Whether the propounder of the Will discharged the burden of proving the testator's sound disposing mind and free will.
Whether the circumstances surrounding the execution of the Will were suspicious enough to reject it.
holdings: A registered Will is not automatically valid; execution must still be proved under Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act and Section 68 of the Evidence Act.
The propounder of a Will must prove by satisfactory evidence that the testator signed it voluntarily, with sound mind, and understood its contents.
Suspicious circumstances, such as the Will being executed far from the testator’s residence, attesting witness being a relative, and lack of proof of reading to the testator, undermine its validity.
Non-examination of the scribe and inconsistencies in witness testimony may support rejection of a Will when viewed collectively.
doctrines: Burden of proof on propounder of a Will
Suspicious circumstances doctrine in Will execution
Concurrent findings of fact by lower courts not lightly interfered with

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Manilal Shamalbhai Patel fought with the Officer on Special Duty (Land Acquisition) over the adequacy of compensation for agricultural land acquired for industrial development in Vadodara, Gujarat.
issues_decided: Whether the compensation awarded for the acquired agricultural land should be enhanced based on the price at which nearby industrial plots were allotted by GIDC.
Whether additional compensation should be awarded for fruit-bearing trees on the land based on income generated.
holdings: The Supreme Court held that the market value of the acquired agricultural land should be determined by using the GIDC's allotment price of Rs.180 per sq. mt. for a nearby industrial plot as a benchmark, adjusted upwards for inflation to Rs.190, then reduced by 50% (40% for development costs and 10% for bulk area discount), resulting in a fair compensation rate of Rs.95 per sq. mt.

The Court held that no additional compensation for fruit-bearing trees can be granted in the absence of documentary evidence proving annual income from the sale of fruits, and upheld the Special Land Acquisition Officer’s lump sum award of Rs.1,06,300 for the trees.
doctrines: Principle of market value determination using comparable sales with adjustments for development potential and area size
Requirement of cogent evidence to claim compensation for standing crops or trees based on income

card.dispute: The appellants challenged the High Court's decision affirming the trial court's dismissal of their suit for injunction, which arose from a property dispute involving a General Power of Attorney and an unregistered agreement to sell.
issues_decided: Whether a finding on title can be recorded in a suit for injunction simpliciter?
Whether the holder of a General Power of Attorney can maintain a suit for injunction without a registered agreement to sell?
Whether the trial and appellate courts were justified in dismissing the injunction suit based on lack of title adjudication?
holdings: A suit for injunction simpliciter ordinarily does not require adjudication of title, but title may be examined if it is necessary to determine possession, especially in cases involving vacant land.
A finding on title can only be recorded in an injunction suit if there are proper pleadings, issues, and evidence on title; otherwise, the court should not decide title questions.
The failure to register an agreement to sell, which is required under Section 17 of the Registration Act, renders it inadmissible to establish title or affect immovable property.
doctrines: Res judicata in relation to findings on possession and title
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Rule against deciding title in injunction suits unless necessary
Doctrine of public notice and constructive notice under the Registration Act

card.dispute: The appellants, former transit camp tenants, challenged the Slum Rehabilitation Authority's notice directing them to vacate their premises for redevelopment, arguing the land was a MHADA layout and not a slum area eligible for redevelopment under the Slum Act.
issues_decided: Whether the land in question is a 'censused slum' eligible for redevelopment under the Maharashtra Slum Areas Act and DCR Regulation 33(10), or a MHADA layout requiring redevelopment under DCR Regulation 33(5)?
Whether the appellants, as transit camp tenants, are eligible slum dwellers entitled to object to the redevelopment scheme?
Whether the failure to challenge the AGRC's 2019 order dismissing their objections bars the appellants from challenging the 2022 eviction notice?
Whether a separate notification under Section 4 of the Slum Act is required for a 'censused slum' already recognized under DCR Regulation 33(10)?
holdings: Land classified as a 'censused slum' under DCR Regulation 33(10), even if owned by MHADA, is eligible for redevelopment by SRA without being a formal MHADA layout.
Transit camp tenants who are not recognized as MHADA tenants and were found ineligible as slum dwellers cannot obstruct redevelopment after accepting benefits under the scheme.
The appellants' failure to challenge the final AGRC order of 2019 bars them from relitigating the same issues in 2022; their delay and lack of diligence disentitle them to relief.
No separate notification under Section 4 of the Slum Act is required for a 'censused slum' already included in redevelopment plans under DCR Regulation 33(10).
provisions: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 4
Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 33
Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 35(1A)
Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Section 38
doctrines: Finality of administrative orders
Doctrine of constructive res judicata
Principle of diligence and clean hands in equitable relief
Statutory interpretation of 'censused slum' under DCR

card.dispute: The appellant Mahesh challenged the High Court's decision that upheld a gift deed transferring properties to respondents 4 and 5, claiming he was the sole legal heir of the donor and entitled to the properties.
issues_decided: Whether the gift deed dated 27.08.2008 in favour of respondents 4 and 5 was validly executed and accepted?
Whether the appellant, as the adopted son and sole legal heir of the donor, was entitled to the suit properties B and C?
Whether the High Court was justified in overturning the trial court's finding that the gift deed was null and void?
holdings: A registered gift deed is invalid if there is no delivery of possession and no acceptance by the donee; mere registration does not validate a gift lacking these essentials.

The appellant, being the legally adopted son of the donor, is her sole legal heir and entitled to properties B and C under the doctrine of relation back, especially where the gift deed failed for lack of acceptance.
The High Court erred in setting aside the trial court's well-reasoned finding on the invalidity of the gift deed without providing sustainable grounds, particularly when supported by evidence.
provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12
doctrines: Doctrine of Relation Back
Essential elements of a valid gift: delivery of possession and acceptance

card.dispute: The appellants challenged an arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, after the limitation period, seeking condonation of delay, which the High Court rejected as barred by limitation.
issues_decided: Whether the delay in filing a Section 34 petition beyond 120 days (90 days + 30 days condonable period) can be condoned?
Whether Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies when the limitation period expires on a working day?
Whether Section 10 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 applies to extend the filing date to the next court day if the last day falls on a closed court day?
holdings: The period of limitation for filing a Section 34 petition is 90 days, extendable by 30 days for sufficient cause; no further condonation is permitted beyond 120 days.
Section 4 of the Limitation Act applies only if the limitation period expires on a day when the court is closed; it does not apply if the last day is a working day.
Section 10 of the General Clauses Act does not apply to proceedings governed by the Limitation Act, as excluded by its proviso, including arbitration challenges under the A&C Act.
doctrines: Strict adherence to statutory limitation periods
Exclusion of General Clauses Act benefits where Limitation Act applies
Non-application of Section 4 of the Limitation Act when limitation expires on a working day

card.dispute: The appellant (son) and respondent (daughter) disputed whether a registered deed was a valid gift/settlement in favor of the daughter or a conditional gift/will that the father could later cancel.
issues_decided: Whether the registered deed dated 26.06.1985 was a valid gift or settlement deed or a conditional gift/will?
Whether the gift was complete under Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
Whether the father could unilaterally cancel the deed and subsequently sell the property?
Whether the High Court was correct in setting aside the concurrent findings of the lower courts?
holdings: A registered deed executed as a gift is complete if acceptance is proved by conduct, such as taking possession of the title deed and registration, even without physical delivery of possession.
A gift of immovable property can be valid without immediate physical possession if title deeds are delivered or other acts demonstrate acceptance during the donor's lifetime.
A donor cannot unilaterally cancel a completed gift; cancellation must be judicially proven on grounds recognized by law.
The High Court correctly held that the deed was a valid settlement and not a will, and that the cancellation and subsequent sale were invalid.
doctrines: Doctrine of completed gift under the Transfer of Property Act
Doctrine of acceptance by conduct
Unilateral cancellation of a completed gift is invalid
Distinction between gift, will, and settlement

card.dispute: The legal heirs of Naganna (plaintiff) sued to establish ownership and possession of a vacant site and house, seeking cancellation of a sale deed and permanent injunction, against the legal heirs of Siddaramegowda (defendant) who were in possession.
issues_decided: Whether the plaintiff established ownership and possession of the suit property to justify the decree for injunction and cancellation of sale deed?
Whether revenue records alone are sufficient to prove title and ownership over immovable property?
Whether the trial and appellate courts were justified in holding that Khata Nos. 71 and 111 referred to the same property and in decreeing the suit in absence of clear evidence?
holdings: The plaintiff failed to prove ownership or possession of the suit property with cogent oral or documentary evidence, and thus was not entitled to decree for injunction or cancellation of sale deed.
Revenue records, including khata entries, do not confer title and cannot alone establish ownership; the plaintiff must prove title independently with reliable evidence.
Courts below erred in equating Khata Nos. 71 and 111 without certainty or evidence, and in relying on weak documentary records to decree the suit in favour of the plaintiff.
doctrines: Title cannot be based solely on revenue records
Plaintiff must succeed on the strength of their own case, not the weakness of the opponent's
Presumption of ownership from possession requires clear and consistent proof

card.dispute: New Mangalore Port Trust challenged the High Court's dismissal of its writ petition seeking recovery of arrears of licence fees from licensees who contested the retrospective revision of fees and raised limitation as a defence.
issues_decided: Whether the proceedings under Section 7 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 are barred by limitation
Whether the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to proceedings under the PP Act
Whether an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act extends the period of limitation in this case
Whether the High Court ought to have awaited the outcome of pending intra-court appeals before deciding the writ petition
holdings: The Limitation Act, 1963 applies to proceedings under the PP Act, including Section 7, even though the PP Act does not specify a limitation period.
An acknowledgment of liability, even with a plea that payment is premature due to pending appeals, triggers a fresh period of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
The respondents' communication acknowledging liability but deferring payment due to pending appeals constitutes sufficient acknowledgment in writing under Section 18.

The High Court should have stayed the writ petition until disposal of the pending intra-court appeals challenging the retrospective revision of licence fees, as the outcome would directly affect the claim.
provisions: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, Section 7
